- PrivateLink: Validate ENI creation in the customer subnet and that security groups allow traffic to the service endpoint.

Test vectors and verification steps (execute with SE)

1) DNS validation
   - From a host in-customer-VPC: nslookup redwood-control.example.com <customer-dns-ip>
   - Expected: resolves to Redwood-provided control-plane IPs (or private endpoint IPs)

2) TCP handshake and TLS validation
   - curl -v --resolve 'redwood-control.example.com:443:<ip>' https://redwood-control.example.com/health
   - Expected: HTTP 200 and a valid TLS certificate matching the hostname. If certificate is customer-mTLS, provide client certs.

3) Peering route test (ICMP/TCP)
   - ping <data-plane-ip> (if ICMP allowed) or 
   - nc -vz <data-plane-ip> 443
   - Expected: connection establishes within 50ms for same-region peering or within agreed latency SLO.

4) End-to-end inference call test
   - curl -X POST https://<inference-host>/v1/generate -d '{"prompt":"ping"}' -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' -H 'Content-Type: application/json'
   - Expected: 200 with model response; token auth validated. Record request latency and token usage.

5) Telemetry and metrics egress
   - Confirm outbound connectivity to telemetry endpoints (if using SaaS telemetry) or ensure logs are forwarded to provided collector address.

Acceptance criteria (must be green to proceed to provisioning)

- Control-plane API resolves and TLS handshake succeeds from a customer-hosted instance.
- Data-plane CIDRs are routable across peering attachment and security groups allow TCP/443.
- End-to-end inference call completes successfully from a customer test VM.
- Time synchronization is within tolerance (+/- 2s).
- Agreed monitoring/probe IPs are whitelisted if customer requires inbound probes.

Common failure modes and quick mitigations

1) DNS resolves to public IP but customer expected private endpoint
   - Cause: split-horizon DNS not configured or DNS forwarding missing.
   - Mitigation: Update private DNS zone with records provided by Redwood or configure conditional forwarding to Redwood DNS resolver.

2) Connection times out to data plane IP
   - Cause: Route table missing peering route or security group denying egress.
   - Mitigation: Validate route table entries and security group/ACLs; run traceroute to identify hop where packets drop.

3) TLS handshake fails with certificate name mismatch
   - Cause: using IP address instead of hostname or incorrect SNI through proxy.
   - Mitigation: Use hostname in SNI; update proxy to forward Host header and SNI.

4) Intermittent failures under load
   - Cause: asymmetric routing, stateful firewall timeouts, or SNAT port exhaustion.
   - Mitigation: Use connection tracking tuning, increase ephemeral port range, or enable NAT gateway autoscaling patterns.

Diagnostic commands matrix (copy/paste friendly)

- DNS: dig +short redwood-control.example.com @<customer-dns>
- TLS: openssl s_client -connect <ip>:443 -servername redwood-control.example.com
- TCP: nc -vz <ip> 443
- Traceroute: traceroute <ip> (Linux) / tracert <ip> (Windows)
- BGP: (on-customer-router) show ip bgp summary

Escalation path (when checklist verification fails)

1) Network owner coordinates immediate troubleshooting with Redwood SE during the validation call.
2) If unresolved within 60 minutes, SE opens a Customer Incident with level: "network-blocking" and notifies Redwood Private Ops.
3) Private Ops will collect packet capture (pcap) from both sides where possible and run a 1:1 session diagnostic. (Provide pcap, timestamps, and test vectors.)
4) If vendor appliance or carrier issue suspected (Transit GW, Direct Connect), escalate to cloud provider support with session history and BGP details.

On-call and SLAs

- Redwood will aim to respond to network-blocking incidents within 30 minutes during business hours and 60 minutes outside business hours per the Enterprise onboarding commitment.
- Target resolution time depends on root cause: misconfiguration (<= 8 hours), provider/carrier (<72 hours with provider support).

Customer checklist sign-off (to be completed by customer network owner)

1) I confirm the fields in the provisioning manifest are accurate.
2) I confirm the firewall and route table entries listed above are applied and verified.
3) I confirm the end-to-end inference test succeeded and recorded latency is within acceptable bounds.

Signed: _______________________  Name: _______________________  Date: _______________________

Appendix: Example iptables rules (customer Linux NAT host)

# Allow outbound TLS to Redwood control plane
iptables -A OUTPUT -p tcp -d <redwood-control-ip> --dport 443 -m conntrack --ctstate NEW,ESTABLISHED -j ACCEPT
# Allow established/related inbound for return traffic
iptables -A INPUT -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT

Appendix: When using an egress proxy (common enterprise pattern)

- Ensure SNI passthrough (not SNI rewrite) for redwood-control.example.com or configure explicit proxy bypass for the Redwood control/data-plane domains.
- If mTLS is used, ensure the proxy allows client certificate forwarding or use a sidecar that terminates mTLS locally and forwards plaintext to the proxy only within the VPC.

References and related artifacts

- Deployment manifest template (provided during provisioning): includes IP/CIDR map, hostnames, and required probe IPs.
- Troubleshooting playbook: /confluence/customer-success-and-support/support-process/enterprise-ratelimit-quota-adjustment-and-cost-protection-playbook-2026 (for non-network related failures).
- Eng private deployments reference: /confluence/eng-private-deployments/reference-architectures/vpc-peering-patterns

Document change log

- 2026-02-10: Created by Ava Martinez (initial checklist and tests).
- 2026-03-02: Reviewed and expanded failure modes and diagnostic commands (reviewers Marcus Chen, Priya Nair).

title: Migration cutover stability playbook
content:
Overview

This playbook describes the operational steps, monitoring, and escalation paths to ensure a stable migration/cutover for enterprise customers moving traffic to Redwood (Hosted / Dedicated / Private). It is intended for Customer Success, SRE, and the customer's technical owners. The document covers pre-cutover validation, immediate cutover actions (0–2 hours), degradation thresholds and automated mitigations, rollback criteria, and the 72-hour stabilization window.

When to use

- Planned migrations from another provider or self-hosted inference to Redwood Dedicated or Private.
- Large traffic shifts (>= 50% traffic change) or model variant swaps for production customers.
- Post-contract go-lives where SLAs and cost constraints are in effect.

Key goals

- Maintain SLOs: p95 latency < 500 ms (generation endpoints), error rate < 0.5% (5xx + client failures), embedding throughput within agreed baseline.
- Detect and contain regressions within 5–15 minutes.
- Provide deterministic rollback when criteria are exceeded.

Stakeholders and primary contacts

- Customer Success (primary owner): Aisha Patel (lead) — oncall: +1-415-555-0172, pager: @cs-oncall
- SRE/Platform: Carlos Rivera — slack: #sre-redwood, pager: @sre-oncall
- Serving Runtime Lead: Sophie Nguyen — slack: @sophie-nguyen
- Customer Technical Contact: (populate from onboarding worksheet) — recommended escalation cadence included below

Pre-cutover checklist (complete 72–1 hours before cutover)

1. Configuration & access
   - Confirm API keys and IP allowlists are provisioned. Example allowed CIDR list for customer egress: 10.2.0.0/16, 198.51.100.0/24.
   - If Private: validate VPC peering and firewall rules; test TCP handshake to inference endpoints (TLS 443).

2. Capacity & model readiness
   - Ensure dedicated capacity pool size matches forecasted TPS + 30% buffer. Documented in order: gpu-pool-size and expected token/sec.
   - Model variant pinned for cutover (model-id, quantization profile, kernel tag).

3. Test plan and synthetic traffic
   - Prepare a synthetic traffic generator with representative prompt mixes (short/long sequences, embeddings, chat). Sample CLI:

   rcli simulate traffic --target https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate --concurrency 50 --profile enterprise-cutover.json

   - Validate KV cache priming: run warmup scripts that exercise common prefixes and expected session lengths.

4. Observability preps
   - Create a cutover dashboard (p90/p95/p99 latency, error rate, request rate, GPU util, queue depth per pool).
   - Ensure tracing is enabled for customer requests; add sample span tag customer_id and route.

Immediate cutover steps (0–2 hours)

1. Communicate T-0 to stakeholders (status channel, customer contact).
2. Switch routing: update traffic router (or DNS) to send 10% of traffic to Redwood for 10 minutes, then 50% for 15 minutes, then 100% if green (recommended gradual ramp).
3. During each ramp phase execute checklist:
   - Verify p95 latency remains < 500 ms.
   - Verify error rate < 0.5%.
   - Confirm no queue depth exceeding threshold (see Alert thresholds table below).

Monitoring and health indicators

Primary metrics (track in dashboard):
- request.rate (rps) — baseline and delta
- request.p95_latency_ms — target < 500 ms
- request.error_rate_percent — target < 0.5%
- gpu.utilization_percent — avoid sustained > 90% for more than 5 minutes
- serving.queue_depth — alert when > 250 requests in queue per pool
- kv_cache.hit_rate_percent — expected > 70% after warmup for session-heavy apps

Alert thresholds (recommended)

| Alert name | Trigger | Severity | Notes |
|---|---:|---|---|
| High error rate | error_rate_percent > 1.5% for 2m | P1 | Consider immediate rollback if sustained |
| Latency spike | p95_latency_ms > 1200 for 3m | P1 | Investigate model or kernel bottleneck |
| Queue saturation | queue_depth > 500 for 5m | P1 | Autoscale/limit ingestion; see mitigations |
| GPU saturation | gpu.utilization_percent > 95% for 10m | P2 | Trigger capacity expansion/eviction policies |
| KV cache missstorm | kv_cache.hit_rate_percent < 30% for 10m | P2 | May indicate warmup needed or routing mix issue |

Degradation behavior and automated mitigations

- For minor degradation (error_rate 0.5%–1.5% or p95 500–1200 ms): automatically throttle non-critical requests, reduce batch size, and enable fallback model variant with smaller footprint.
- For severe degradation (error_rate > 1.5% or sustained queue_depth > 500): engage rollback to previous provider routing or previous model version.
- Built-in automated actions (what Redwood platform can perform):
  - route.rebalance --move 50% traffic to fallback pool
  - model.variant_switch --to model-id:golden-small-quant

Rollback criteria and procedure

Rollback should be considered when ANY of the following are true for 10 minutes:
- request.error_rate_percent > 2.0% AND increasing
- p95_latency_ms > 1500 ms AND user impact confirmed
- queue_depth > 800 or sustained GPU OOM errors

Rollback steps (execute in order)
1. Notify stakeholders: open a migration incident and ping P1 channels.
2. Execute route rollback: revert routing to previous provider or traffic mirror. Command example:

   rcli traffic update --route customer-123 --percent 0 --target previous-provider

3. If rollback is to a previous model version in Redwood:

   rcli model promote --customer customer-123 --model-id "model-v1-stable"

4. Scale down any warm pool to reduce cost and surface residual errors for investigation.

Escalation matrix and communication

- Phase 0 (informal): Customer Success lead + customer tech contact (first 5 minutes).
- Phase 1 (operational): Add SRE and Serving Runtime lead (10–30 minutes).
- Phase 2 (critical): Engage Engineering on-call, Platform PM, SOC if security incident suspected (>30 minutes).

Contact table (primary means)
- Customer Success lead: Aisha Patel — slack: @aisha-patel, cell: +1-415-555-0172
- SRE oncall: Carlos Rivera — pager: @sre-oncall, slack: #sre-redwood
- Runtime lead: Sophie Nguyen — slack DM or escalation channel #runtime-oncall

Post-cutover stabilization (2–72 hours)

- Hours 2–6: Keep traffic at production level while running heavy monitoring. Run daily regression checks against representative prompt set (n=5000).
- 6–24 hours: Execute sample customer transactions end-to-end with logging enabled. Pay special attention to stateful chat sessions and embedding index builds.
- 24–72 hours: Prepare a stabilization report with metrics and anomalies; schedule a review with the customer to confirm SLA satisfaction and plan any follow-up mitigations.

Operational runbook snippets

- Check p95 for the last 10 minutes:

   rcli metrics query --service inference --customer customer-123 --metric request.p95_latency_ms --range 10m

- Promote fallback model (example JSON payload):

   {
     "customer_id": "customer-123",
     "action": "promote_model",
     "model_id": "model-v1-stable"
   }

- Quick health summary (one-liner for status channel):

   cutover-status: green | p95=320ms | errs=0.12% | gpu=48% | qd=42

Postmortem and RCA guidance

- If an incident occurs that required rollback or manual mitigation, create a postmortem within 72 hours. The postmortem should include: timeline, contributing factors, detection method, impact, remediation, and follow-up actions owners with SLAs (30 days for code fixes, 90 days for capacity changes).

Appendices

Appendix A — Example warmup script (bash):

#!/usr/bin/env bash
for i in {1..200}; do
  curl -s -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_KEY" -d '{"prompt":"Summary of user event ${i}","max_tokens":64}' >/dev/null &
 done
wait

Appendix B — Useful links

- Hosting status page: https://status.redwood.ai
- Cutover dashboard template: /dashboards/cutover/migration-template
- Incident runbook: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/incident-process/postmortem-template

- Owner: Customer Success (Aisha Patel). SRE and Runtime teams own automated mitigations.

title: Billing dispute and chargeback resolution playbook
content:
Summary:
This playbook defines the operational process, SLAs, communications templates, and ownership for resolving enterprise billing disputes and chargeback requests during onboarding and the first 90 days post-go-live. It is intended for CSMs, BillingOps, Finance, Support Engineering, and Legal.

Purpose and scope:
- Purpose: Reduce mean time to resolution (MTTR) for billing disputes, ensure consistent customer communications, protect revenue recognition, and capture audit evidence for chargebacks or credits.
- Scope: Applies to all enterprise tenants (Dedicated and Private) with contract value >= $50k ARR during onboarding and the first 90 days after go-live. Does not replace Finance-led invoicing corrections for legacy invoices; it coordinates with Finance for those cases.

Definitions:
- Dispute: A customer-initiated claim that an invoice, usage charge, or billing calculation is incorrect.
- Chargeback: A request to reverse or offset billed amount against a future invoice or issue a formal credit.
- Priority levels:
  1) P0 — Billing outage affecting all invoices or system-side errors that systematically overcharge customers; target acknowledgement < 1 business hour; remediation plan in 4 hours.
  2) P1 — Material dispute where customer-facing usage appears incorrect (>10% deviation or > $5k discrepancy); target acknowledgement < 4 business hours; resolution in 3 business days.
  3) P2 — Minor disagreement or clarification (<10% and < $5k); target acknowledgement within 1 business day; resolution in 10 business days.

Ownership and contacts:
- First responder: Customer Success Manager (CSM) — initial intake, triage, and customer comms.
- Technical validation: Support Engineering (SE) — investigates telemetry, request logs, KV/cache behavior, and model fallback records.
- Billing operations: BillingOps — recalculates usage, verifies aggregation + quota logic, prepares credits.
- Finance: Signs off on formal credits and updates AR records.
- Legal: Engaged when contractual dispute or potential revenue recognition impact.

Escalation matrix:
1) CSM escalates to SE (channel: #billing-ops-escalations, tag @oncall-se) after initial intake if P0/P1.
2) SE triages, produces technical findings and a short timeline (within 8 hours for P1).
3) If disagreement remains after technical validation, CSM opens BillingOps ticket (billing-api) and informs Finance.
4) If resolution crosses 5 business days or exceeds $50k, escalate to Director of Customer Success + Head of Billing for approval and external comms.

Operational procedure (step-by-step):
1) Intake (CSM)
   - Capture: customer contact, invoice ID, invoice date, disputed amount, business impact, and preferred remedy (credit, refund, or adjustment).
   - Assign priority (P0/P1/P2) and open the internal incident in the Customer Success ticketing queue (prefix: BILL-). Attach customer-provided artifacts (screenshots, billing CSVs).
2) Triage (CSM, within SLA for priority)
   - Verify customer identity and contract tier. Confirm invoice numbers and timeframe.
   - If P0, immediately declare incident and notify #ops-all and on-call SRE.
3) Technical investigation (SE)
   - Confirm request routing and model selection logs: check `billing-api` request logs, `ingress-gateway` traces, and `telemetry-gatekeeper` aggregation.
   - Query usage records: run query against `usage-aggregation` table (example SQL):
     SELECT tenant_id, sum(tokens) as total_tokens, model_name, date
     FROM usage_aggregation
     WHERE tenant_id = 'TENANT_X' AND date BETWEEN '2026-10-01' AND '2026-10-31'
     GROUP BY tenant_id, model_name, date;
   - Verify any cache-busting events, canary rollouts, or model-fanout that could double-count tokens.
   - Produce a short findings doc (one-page) that lists root-cause candidates and evidence links.
4) BillingOps reconciliation
   - Recompute the invoice using the canonical aggregation export (CSV/JSON) and the rate-card in effect for the invoice period. Maintain a checksumed export and attach to the case.
   - If code/aggregation bug found, create a paging ticket in engineering backlog with severity and request a hotfix/retroactive adjustment.
5) Proposal and customer communication (CSM + BillingOps)
   - Draft proposed remedy (credit/refund/adjustment) and the timeline for application.
   - Use the communication templates below.
6) Finance sign-off and execution
   - Finance validates credit amount, posts credit memo or refund, updates AR, and records reason codes.
   - BillingOps updates invoice metadata and attaches evidence to the ticket.
7) Closure and retrospective
   - Confirm customer acceptance, update ticket with resolution artifacts, and schedule a 1-week postmortem for P0/P1 cases.
   - Capture follow-up actions in the customer QBR if systemic.

Evidence and artifacts to collect (minimum):
- Customer-submitted dispute form or email (archive).
- Relevant invoice PDF and raw aggregation export (CSV/JSON).
- Query IDs and trace IDs from `ingress-gateway` and `billing-api` (trace links).
- Findings doc from SE and final recalculation spreadsheet with checksum.
- Finance credit memo number or refund transaction ID.

Communication templates (examples)
1) Acknowledgement (send within SLA)
Subject: Acknowledged — Billing enquiry for invoice INV-12345
Body: Hi [Customer Name],
Thank you — we have received your billing enquiry for invoice INV-12345 (amount: $X). We have opened case BILL-6789 and assigned it priority [P1]. Our technical and billing teams will investigate and we will update you inside the SLA timelines. If you have additional artifacts, please attach them to this thread.
2) Interim status (P1/P0)
Subject: Interim update — Billing enquiry INV-12345 (case BILL-6789)
Body: Hi [Customer Name],
We are actively investigating. Current findings: [short summary]. Target resolution: [date/time]. If the issue is high-impact we will provide hourly updates.
3) Resolution and credit confirmation
Subject: Resolved — Billing enquiry INV-12345 (case BILL-6789)
Body: Hi [Customer Name],
We have completed our investigation and applied the following remedy: [credit/refund/adjustment details with reference #]. The credit will appear on your next invoice (or refund dispatched on [date]). Summary of cause: [one-paragraph root cause]. Preventative steps taken: [bullet list].

Customer-facing acceptance criteria (must be documented in ticket):
- The refunded or credited amount equals the agreed remedy.
- Finance has produced a credit memo or refund transaction ID and AR is updated.
- Customer confirms acceptance in writing.

Automation and tooling recommendations:
- Automate evidence collection: attach aggregated usage export and trace IDs at intake using the `billing-intake` Lambda hook.
- Add a billing dispute webhook to notify `#billing-ops-escalations` with structured payload: {"case_id":"BILL-XXXXX","tenant_id":"T-123","priority":"P1","invoice_id":"INV-..."} (engineering backlog item: BILLING-2381).
- Maintain a shared Google Sheet (read-only for customers) for long-running reconciliations; link in the ticket.

Reporting and KPIs:
- SLA compliance: percent of disputes acknowledged within target SLA (goal >= 98%).
- MTTR by priority: target P1 <= 3 business days (rolling 90-day median).
- Error rate: percent of invoices requiring adjustment after go-live (target <= 0.5%).
- Fiscal impact: mean credit amount and top contributing root causes.

Playbook examples and edge cases:
- Duplicate charge due to canary rollback: If SE confirms double-counting tied to canary rollback, proceed with immediate credit and create an engineering incident.
- Customer claims lost feature credits (promo/discount not applied): verify contract-level entitlements and reconcile with rate card; escalate to Finance/Legal for contract amendment if needed.
- Suspected fraud / abuse: pause account billing (billing-api flag: billing_hold = true), notify Legal and follow fraud handling SOP.

Postmortem and continuous improvement:
- For P0/P1 incidents, schedule a 1-week postmortem with CSM, SE, BillingOps, and Finance. Capture root cause, corrective action, and preventive measures.
- Feed recurring root causes into the onboarding playbook and update rate-card validations in the billing pipeline.

Appendix A — Quick triage checklist (for CSMs)
1) Confirm invoice ID, disputed amount, and date range.
2) Confirm tenant tier and active contract adjustments.
3) Attach customer artifacts and create BILL- ticket.
4) Ping #billing-ops-escalations with case link for P0/P1.
5) Confirm SE assigned and expected update time.

Appendix B — Example internal Slack alert (to #billing-ops-escalations)
Payload (one-line): BILL-6789 | TENANT_T-123 | P1 | INV-12345 | $8,900 | @priya.nambiar — investigation assigned to @oncall-se. Link: <ticket_url>

Appendix C — Minimal JSON export schema for reconciliation artifacts
- ticket_id: string
- tenant_id: string
- invoice_id: string
- period_start: YYYY-MM-DD
- period_end: YYYY-MM-DD
- raw_usage_export_url: https://...
- recalculated_amount: string (decimal)
- evidence_links: [comma-separated links]

Notes and links:
- Service names referenced: billing-api, ingestion-gateway, usage-aggregation, telemetry-gatekeeper, billing-intake lambda.
- See related playbooks: tenant-finops-cutover-governance-playbook (onboarding), enterprise-cost-anomaly-detection-and-action-playbook (health & QBR).

Owner and maintenance cadence:
- Document owner: Priya Nambiar (Customer Success).
- Review cadence: quarterly or after any P0/P1 incident.

title: tenant-chaos-gaming-and-resilience-onboarding-playbook-2026
content:
Overview:

This playbook defines the tenant-level chaos gaming and synthetic-resilience program used during enterprise onboarding and the first 90 days post-cutover. It standardizes simulated failure scenarios, telemetry assertions, success criteria, and escalation steps to validate that a new tenant meets Redwood Inference stability, performance, and cost-safety requirements prior to and immediately after canary-to-100% rollouts.

Purpose and scope:

- Purpose: Reduce production surprises by exercising realistic failure modes against a customer’s dedicated or private deployment in a controlled, observable way.
- Scope: Applies to Dedicated and Private tenants (VPC/on-prem) being onboarded or undergoing major model/capacity cutovers. Does not replace load testing performed by SRE for platform-wide capacity.

Service-level targets (tenant SLOs):

- Availability SLO: 99.95% for API success rate (5xx and client-facing errors excluded per contract).
- Median latency target: <120ms for small-gen calls (<128 tokens) during canary windows.
- Cost safety guardrail: 2x expected cost spike tolerance during orchestrated synthetic tests; anything beyond triggers immediate throttling.

Owners and contacts:

- Playbook owner: Customer Success (Aisha Patel)
- Runtime escalation owner: Eng SRE (Miguel Ramos)
- Dedicated/private deployment owner: Eng Private Deployments (Jordan Lee)
- Customer POC: (fill per customer onboarding sheet)

Prerequisites (before running a game day):

1. Tenant must be deployed to a non-prod or canary tenant slice with identical routing, or to a production tenant with explicit consent and an agreed blast radius.
2. Observability contract validated: metrics, traces, and logs forwarded to Redwood telemetry cluster and customer-observability link.
3. Canary token/key configured and QA test suite green.
4. Rollback and safe-failover plans approved by customer and SRE.

Game day checklist (pre-execution):

- Schedule and obtain approvals from customer, SRE, and account team (minimum 72 hours notice).
- Configure synthetic load generator (see examples below) and ensure isolation of test traffic via label/filter.
- Snapshot current tenant config and telemetry baseline (last 24h).
- Confirm cost cap and automatic throttles are active.
- Run a brief smoke test of observability dashboards and alerting rules.

Synthetic scenarios (recommended list):

1) KV-cache corruption simulation
   - Intent: Ensure graceful detection and refetch behavior for prefix cache invalidation.
   - Method: Inject cache-miss pattern by toggling a feature flag in the canary runtime to disable cached lookup for 60s.
   - Success criteria: Error budget unaffected; latency increase <50% for affected requests; automated PK cache warm-up completes within 120s.

2) Model-variant fallback under load
   - Intent: Validate model fallback routing if primary quantized model fails or is cyclically unavailable.
   - Method: Simulate model-worker OOM by marking worker pool unhealthy via the orchestration API.
   - Success criteria: Requests routed to fallback variant within 10s; tail latency spike limited to 2x baseline for under 5 minutes.

3) Sudden traffic surge from one tenant (ingress storm)
   - Intent: Confirm tenant fairshare and quota protector sidecar behavior.
   - Method: Generate a 10x RPS spike for 5 minutes using synthetic generator.
   - Success criteria: No cross-tenant degradation; affected tenant receives throttling with appropriate 429s and customer-notification webhook triggers.

4) Telemetry pipeline delay and partial loss
   - Intent: Ensure offline buffering and alerting are robust when telemetry forwarding lags.
   - Method: Introduce deliberate forwarding latency in the staging observability forwarder for 3 minutes.
   - Success criteria: Alerts that depend on telemetry use alternative guard signals (health check pings); post-mortem shows no blind spots longer than 5 minutes.

Execution play (numbered runbook):

1. Kickoff: Confirm attendees and intent. Document start time in the incident timeline channel.
2. Baseline sampling: Start 5m metric sampling to baseline key telemetry (request_rate, error_rate, p50/p95 latency, cost_per_minute).
3. Scenario run: Execute scenario steps as defined. One scenario per 15–30 minute window.
4. Observability watch: SRE and CS watch dashboards for SLO violations. Assign a single comms owner.
5. Containment: If a hard threshold is crossed (see thresholds table), immediately stop the synthetic generator and trigger rollback if needed.
6. Cooldown: 15–30 minutes post-scenario for caches and queues to settle. Collect logs and traces.
7. Post-checks: Run validation tests (sanity generations, embedding consistency checks).

Thresholds and automated actions (table represented in plain text):

- If 5xx rate > 0.5% for >2 minutes -> Automated throttle and page SRE (Pager).
- If median latency > 3x baseline for >5 minutes -> Pause canary rollouts and create severity-3 incident.
- If cost rate > 3x baseline sustained >10 minutes -> Trigger cost-protector webhook and notify finance-safety.

Telemetry assertions (examples to add to the telemetry contract):

- request.success_rate >= 99.5% (rolling 10m)
- model.fallback.count <= 5 per 10m window during synthetic tests
- cache.hit_ratio >= 70% post-warmup (rolling 5m)
- ingress.rps <= documented expectation for the tenant + 10% burst allowance

Observability queries (examples):

- Error rate: sum(rate(http_requests_total{tenant=\"<TENANT>\",status=~\"5..\"}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{tenant=\"<TENANT>\"}[5m]))
- Median latency: histogram_quantile(0.5, sum(rate(request_latency_bucket{tenant=\"<TENANT>\"}[5m])) by (le))

Synthetic load generator examples:

- k6 (simple RPS spike)
  - Command: k6 run --vus 0 --iteration-duration 5m --rps 200 spike-script.js
  - Note: Use request headers to tag traffic: {\"X-Tenant-Test\":\"chaos-game-2026\"}

- locust (ramp test):
  - Command: locust -f locustfile.py --headless -u 500 -r 50 --run-time 10m --host=https://tenant.example

Rollback and safe-failover steps:

1. Stop synthetic generators immediately.
2. If degradation is tenant-isolated and within cost guardrails, hold and let cooldown complete.
3. If cross-tenant impact or severity thresholds exceeded, perform automatic fairshare enforcement and execute configured rollback (model pin to previous stable version).

Post-game day analysis (deliverables):

- Short RCAs for any threshold breach (published within 3 business days).
- Telemetry snapshot and comparison to baseline (attach to the onboarding ticket).
- Action items with owners and target completion dates (tracked in JIRA).

QBR & onboarding handoff checklist:

- Add game day results to the QBR packet: include pass/fail per scenario, regression deltas for p95, and cost delta.
- Recommend final tenant readiness vote (Accept / Accept with mitigations / Reject) during the commercial go/no-go.

Appendix A — Example alerting rule YAML (snippet):

alert: TenantHigh5xx
expr: sum(rate(http_requests_total{tenant=\"<TENANT>\",status=~\"5..\"}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{tenant=\"<TENANT>\"}[5m])) > 0.005
for: 2m
labels:
  severity: page
annotations:
  summary: "High 5xx rate for tenant <TENANT>"
  runbook: "/confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/incident-process"

Appendix B — Tracing play snippet:

- When a scenario runs, add a trace tag: chaos.game=tenant-onboard-<ID> so Perf and Trace teams can filter.

Appendix C — Postmortem template fields to include:

- Timeline of actions (UTC)
- What failed vs expected
- Root cause and contributing factors
- Immediate mitigations and permanent fixes
- Customer impact and communications

Frequently asked questions:

Q: Can we run game days against production?
A: Only with explicit customer written consent and a pre-negotiated blast radius. Use a dedicated canary slice where possible.

Q: Who authorizes rollbacks?
A: SRE owns urgent rollbacks; CS must be informed within 15 minutes for customer-facing incidents.

Document history and maintenance:

- Version 1.0: Created 2026-10-12 by Aisha Patel
- Review update: 2026-11-02 - clarified thresholds and added telemetry assertions

Related reading and links:

- Onboarding runbook: /confluence/customer-success-and-support/enterprise-onboarding/onboarding-handback-and-first-90-days-ops-guide-2026
- Incident process: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/incident-process

title: Security review escalation and handoff (CS/Support playbook)
content:
## Purpose
This playbook defines how Customer Success (CS) and Support partner with Sales, Solutions Engineering (SE), and Security/GRC during late-stage security reviews. It standardizes:
- When and how to loop in Security/GRC
- How to handle urgent deadlines and incomplete questionnaires
- Escalation tiers, response SLAs, and handoff points
- How we avoid unapproved claims and keep a clear audit trail

This is an internal operating document. It references restricted evidence processes (e.g., SOC 2 report) but does not include restricted artifacts.

---

## When to use this playbook
Use this playbook when any of the following occur:
- A prospect/customer requests SOC 2 report, pen test summary, subprocessor list, or other formal evidence.
- A prospect/customer sends a security questionnaire, RFP security section, or needs a security addendum.
- Procurement/security introduces a hard deadline (\<= 5 business days) or threatens deal delay without answers.
- The customer requires deployment-specific assurances (Dedicated vs Private vs Hosted) around data flows, retention, encryption, KMS, logging, SSO/RBAC, or incident notification.

Not in scope:
- Product roadmap commitments or “custom features” to satisfy a questionnaire. Use the Exceptions Policy for non-supported controls.

---

## Roles and responsibilities (who does what)
### Primary owners
- Sales / AE: owns customer timeline, coordinates meetings, maintains CRM notes, ensures customer has correct links.
- Solutions Engineering (SE): owns technical narrative (deployment mode, architecture diagrams, controls explanations).
- Security Engineering: validates technical claims, clarifies implementation details, reviews non-standard security language.
- GRC (Governance, Risk, Compliance): owns audit/compliance language and evidence distribution process (SOC 2 under NDA, artifact lists, timelines).
- Legal: owns contractual language (DPA, security addendum, breach notification terms).
- CS / Support: owns the escalation workflow, ensures correct process is followed, prevents churn/relationship damage, and creates a clean handoff to post-close operations.

### CS/Support “single-threaded owner” (STO)
For any security review that is time-bound or involves evidence requests, CS/Support assigns a single-threaded owner who:
- Creates/updates the tracking ticket(s)
- Confirms next steps and internal owners
- Drives SLA compliance and escalations
- Ensures final approved language is used

---

## Golden rules (do / don’t)
### Do
- Use the published Security FAQ and standard answer blocks as the starting point.
- Confirm the customer’s deployment mode (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private) before answering.
- Route formal evidence requests through the Evidence Request Playbook (NDA checks, controlled distribution).
- Track all customer asks, versions, and approvals in a ticket and in CRM.

### Don’t
- Don’t claim certifications we do not have (e.g., “ISO 27001 certified”) or imply “compliant with X” unless approved.
- Don’t promise data residency beyond what is available in the customer’s selected region/deployment mode.
- Don’t share restricted evidence (SOC 2 report, pen test summary) over email or Slack without following the controlled process.
- Don’t edit standard RFP/security language “just to make it fit.” Use the approval workflow.

---

## Intake checklist (required information before escalating)
CS/Support STO should collect the following before pulling in Security/GRC:
1) Account + deal context
- Customer/prospect name, segment, region
- Stage (evaluation, procurement, renewal, expansion)
- Business impact and date the deal will stall without response

2) Deployment mode and architecture
- Hosted API / Dedicated / Private (VPC or on-prem)
- Target cloud/region(s) and any data residency constraints
- Any special requirements (HIPAA/BAA request, financial services controls, air-gapped constraints)

3) Customer asks (exact wording)
- Questionnaire/RFP sections pasted verbatim or attached
- Specific artifacts requested (SOC 2, policies, subprocessor list, pen test summary)
- Required response format and due date/time zone

4) Constraints
- NDA status (executed? pending? required?)
- Customer’s requested response channel (portal, email, GRC tool)
- Any customer “red lines” (e.g., retention must be configurable to X days)

5) Internal context
- Existing approved snippets used (link to FAQ section or RFP library block)
- Any planned deviations from standard language (must be explicitly flagged)

If any of the above is missing, proceed with escalation but mark as “incomplete intake” and request missing items in parallel.

---

## Escalation tiers and SLAs
CS/Support uses the following tiers to set expectations and drive responsiveness.

### P0 — Imminent deadline / deal-stopping within 24 hours
Criteria:
- Customer deadline in \<= 1 business day OR live procurement call requiring answers
- Customer requires evidence distribution (SOC 2) to proceed immediately

SLA targets:
- Acknowledge internally within 30 minutes (business hours)
- First response plan within 2 hours

Approvals:
- Any non-standard claim requires Security + GRC approval (and Legal if contractual)

### P1 — Time-bound security review (2–5 business days)
Criteria:
- RFP/questionnaire due in 2–5 business days
- Customer is blocked pending “security sign-off” meeting

SLA targets:
- Acknowledge internally within 4 business hours
- Draft response/plan within 1 business day

### P2 — Standard review (\>= 6 business days)
Criteria:
- No imminent risk; customer requests information for internal review

SLA targets:
- Acknowledge within 1 business day
- Provide materials/plan within 3 business days

Business hours assumption: Mon–Fri, local team coverage. If customer is in EMEA/APAC and timing is critical, treat as one tier higher to account for time zone compression.

---

## Step-by-step workflow (CS/Support STO)
### Step 1 — Create a tracking ticket and identify the STO
Create a ticket in the internal system of record (Support/Jira or the designated GTM intake queue) with:
- Tier (P0/P1/P2)
- Due date/time zone
- Links/attachments to the questionnaire/RFP portal
- Requested artifacts list
- Deployment mode and region

Add watchers:
- AE + SE lead on the account
- GRC on-call analyst (or team alias)
- Security Engineering reviewer (if technical claims are involved)
- Legal reviewer (if contract language requested)

### Step 2 — Send the internal “first plan” message
Within the SLA window, post a clear plan (in the ticket and in the designated internal channel):
- What we will answer with standard language
- What requires review/approval
- What evidence requires NDA + controlled process
- Who owns each workstream and deadlines

### Step 3 — Separate “language” work from “evidence” work
Run two tracks in parallel:
A) Response language
- Use the Security FAQ and Standard Answers as the baseline.
- If the questionnaire asks for non-supported controls, use the Exceptions Policy to propose alternative language.
- If the customer requires a custom architecture/security narrative, SE drafts and Security validates.

B) Evidence requests
- Follow the SOC 2 Customer Evidence Request Playbook.
- Confirm NDA status before any restricted artifact is shared.
- Log exactly which artifacts were shared, when, and via what method.

### Step 4 — Run a time-boxed review cycle
For P0/P1, use a single redline pass with explicit approvers:
- Security Engineering: technical controls, logging, encryption, runtime behavior
- GRC: compliance posture wording, audit periods, “report under NDA” phrasing
- Legal: DPA/addendum terms, breach notification, liability language

If edits exceed one pass or the customer changes scope, re-baseline and reset expectations with Sales.

### Step 5 — Customer-facing delivery
CS/Support STO ensures:
- Final answers use approved language and correct deployment mode caveats
- Restricted artifacts are delivered only via the approved method
- The customer receives a concise “what we sent + how to follow up” summary

Recommended customer email structure:
- One-paragraph overview
- Bullets of attached/linked documents
- Evidence request steps (if applicable)
- Offer a 30-minute security review call with Security/GRC if needed

### Step 6 — Close the loop and create post-close handoff notes
Once the security review is complete (or “good enough” for procurement), capture:
- Final list of commitments made (e.g., log retention option selected, region selection)
- Any exceptions granted and their approvers
- Any open items that must be implemented/configured during onboarding

Add the notes to CRM and to the account’s implementation plan.

---

## Common scenarios and how to handle them
### Scenario A: “Send us your SOC 2 report today”
1) Confirm whether NDA is executed.
2) If NDA is not executed, coordinate with Legal/Sales immediately; do not share the report.
3) Use the approved wording: “SOC 2 Type II report available under NDA upon request.”
4) Open an evidence request per the playbook and track distribution.

### Scenario B: Customer asks “Do you train on our data?”
- Use the exact FAQ language and definitions (training vs transient processing; prompts/logs vs model weights).
- Do not introduce new qualifiers. If customer asks for contract language, route to Legal.

### Scenario C: EU data residency objection (must stay in EU)
- Confirm which regions are available for the chosen deployment mode.
- Use the approved residency language (no blanket promises). If constraints can only be met with Private, have SE present options.
- Escalate to GRC/Security if the customer requests written guarantees beyond standard documentation.

### Scenario D: Questionnaire asks for a control we do not support (e.g., specific IdP feature, custom audit event)
- Do not answer “Yes” with future intent.
- Use the Exceptions Policy to provide alternative language and document compensating controls.
- If customer insists on a “must-have,” flag to Product Security PM for capability alignment (without committing roadmap).

---

## Communication channels and meeting guidance
### Internal channels (recommended)
- Use the designated security review intake channel and link the tracking ticket.
- Keep decisions in the ticket. Slack is for coordination, not for the authoritative record.

### Customer call structure (30–45 minutes)
1) Confirm deployment mode + region + data flow expectations
2) Walk through top 5 controls customer cares about (usually: data use, encryption, access controls, logging, retention)
3) Evidence requests: explain NDA gating and timelines
4) Capture remaining blockers and assign owners

Avoid:
- Live “off the cuff” answers to compliance/certification questions. Offer to follow up with approved language.

---

## Handback to CS/Support after close (operationalization)
If any of the following were discussed, CS must validate configuration during onboarding:
- Audit log export destination (SIEM/S3) and retention window
- SSO/SAML and SCIM provisioning requirements
- RBAC roles and least-privilege model for admins
- Data retention/deletion configuration for the chosen deployment mode
- Private deployment network boundaries (VPC peering, egress controls) and key management (KMS/HSM)

Create an onboarding checklist item for each requirement and confirm acceptance criteria with the customer security contact.

---

## Templates
### Internal escalation summary (paste into ticket)
Account:
Deployment mode:
Region(s):
Tier (P0/P1/P2):
Customer deadline (date/time zone):
Top asks (verbatim):
Artifacts requested:
NDA status:
Draft response plan (what we can answer with standard language vs needs review):
Owners:

### Customer follow-up email (minimal)
Subject: Redwood security review materials + next steps

Hi <Name>,

Sharing the requested security materials for your review:
- <Doc link 1>
- <Doc link 2>
- <Audit logging / retention overview>

For the SOC 2 Type II report (restricted), we can provide it under NDA via our controlled evidence request process. If you confirm NDA status, we will initiate distribution.

Happy to schedule a 30-minute security review call to walk through data handling, encryption, access controls, and audit logging.

Best,
<Name>

---

## Metrics and continuous improvement
CS/Support STO should log the following for quarterly review:
- Time-to-acknowledge and time-to-first-draft by tier
- # of evidence requests and average turnaround time
- Top repeated questionnaire questions and where our standard language was insufficient
- Any instances of “unapproved language” caught in review (and required remediation)

Feedback loop:
- If a question repeats \>= 3 times in a month, open a request to update the Security FAQ or RFP library rather than rewriting per deal.

---

## Ownership and review cadence
Owner: Customer Success (CS sponsor), in partnership with Security/GRC.
Review cadence: Quarterly, or immediately after any material change to security posture, evidence availability, or product behavior affecting common questionnaire answers.

Last review highlights (2026-02-21):
- Tightened P0/P1 SLA expectations and clarified NDA gating for evidence.
- Standardized separation of “language” vs “evidence” workstreams.
- Added explicit post-close operationalization checklist items (SSO/SCIM, audit logs, retention).

title: Onboarding Handback and First-90-Days Operational Guide
content:
Summary

This document defines the technical handback process and the operational expectations for the first 90 days after an enterprise customer goes live on Redwood Inference (hosted or Dedicated). It is intended for CSMs, Solutions Engineering (SE), Onboarding Engineers, and the L2 oncall team.

Scope

- Applies to enterprise customers with Dedicated or Private deployments and enterprise-level Hosted integrations that require an SE handover.
- Covers: handoff checklist, SLA matrix, runbook entries for common post-go-live issues, escalation steps, monitoring baseline, and QBR readiness checklist for the first 90 days.

Goals and success metrics (first 90 days)

- Availability SLO: 99.95% per calendar month for production inference endpoints.
- Latency SLO: P95 request-to-first-token < 300 ms for short-text generation workloads (<= 256 tokens) on Dedicated pools.
- Error budget: < 0.05% failed requests (5xx) attributable to Redwood services. Customer-side errors (4xx) excluded.
- Onboarding health: 80% of customer-defined success criteria met by day 30, 95% by day 90.
- QBR readiness: onboarding artifacts, traffic profile, cost trends, and open action items delivered two weeks before the 90-day review.

Handback checklist (must be completed before formal handoff)

1) Contractual & access items (owner: CSM)
   1. Confirm customer account and billing profile in Finance (billing contact verified).
   2. Verify list of whitelisted IPs, VPC peering, or VPN endpoints (for Dedicated/Private).
   3. Confirm KMS/HSM key rotation schedule and access for logs/audit.

2) Technical verification (owner: SE / Onboarding Engineer)
   1. Baseline performance test completed: runbench report attached and passing acceptance criteria (attach: runbench-<customer>-v1.json).
   2. Model versions pinned and documented (model-id, quantization profile if any).
   3. Ingress/egress networking validated: HTTPS termination, MTU checks, and route tables.
   4. Observability hooks installed: metrics, ingest for traces, and token-level cost tagging enabled.

3) Operational readiness (owner: Oncall + CSM)
   1. Oncall runbooks created for the customer under team wiki (link to runbook entry).
   2. Alerting thresholds verified (see SLA matrix below).
   3. Access matrix for customer ops and Redwood SRE/SE is finalized (least privilege).

Operational SLA matrix (reference thresholds and owners)

| Area | SLO / Threshold | Primary owner | Escalation target |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| Endpoint availability | 99.95% monthly | Customer Success (CSM) / SE | SRE oncall within 30m |
| P95 latency (<=256 tokens) | < 300 ms (Dedicated) | SE / Runtime team | Runtime oncall within 60m |
| Error rate (5xx) | < 0.05% | Runtime team | SRE within 30m |
| Cold-start median | < 1200 ms | Runtime team | Engineering within 2h |
| Cost anomaly | < 25% deviation vs forecast | Finance + CSM | Growth/RevOps notified 1 business day |

Note: thresholds above are targets agreed during onboarding and may be tuned per-contract. All alerts should map to the customer-specific alerting policy in PagerDuty and Slack channel.

Escalation & handoff timeline (high level)

- Day 0 (Go-live): SE oncall and CSM present. Monitor first 24 hours for errors and latency regressions.
- Day 1–7: Daily sync between CSM, SE, and SRE for the first-week incidents and visibility.
- Day 8–30: Bi-weekly operational check-ins, performance tuning (batching/KV cache config), and cost review.
- Day 31–90: Weekly check-ins until SLA stability and customer success criteria are met; prepare QBR artifacts by day 75.

Handoff procedure (detailed, numbered)

1. Pre-handoff readiness demo (SE + customer): run the baseline load test (recommended: k6 or locust harness) and demonstrate acceptance criteria.
2. Fill the Onboarding Runbook template: include endpoints, model pins, route policies, alerting, and contact matrix.
3. Create customer-specific monitoring dashboard: tokens-per-minute, p95 latency, 5xx rate, cost-by-route. Share read-only link with customer.
4. Add the customer to the SRE PagerDuty rotation as a secondary for the first 30 days.
5. Formal handoff meeting: CSM presents business context, SE presents technical state, SRE presents monitoring/alerts. Capture action items in Jira and assign owners.

Post-handoff runbook excerpts (copy these into the customer runbook)

- Immediate checks when an alert fires:
  - Step 1: Verify if alert is customer-generated (4xx) vs platform (5xx) by checking trace id and edge logs.
  - Step 2: If platform (5xx), run diagnostic command: curl -v -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' https://api.redwood.example/v1/engines/<engine-id>/health || cat /var/log/runtime/errors.log (SE only).
  - Step 3: Check KV cache hit rate and batching stats from /metrics endpoint (prometheus name: redwood_runtime_kv_cache_hit_ratio). Thresholds: < 60% indicates mis-priming.
  - Step 4: Escalate per matrix (see table above) and create a postmortem if the incident causes > 30m downtime affecting > 10% of requests.

Common post-go-live issues and mitigations

- High P95 latency after deployment:
  - Likely causes: non-optimal batching, model quantization fallback, and warmup not run.
  - Mitigation steps: confirm batching policy in route config, enable prefix/KV cache for repeated prompts, trigger a lightweight warmup job: POST /internal/warmup {"engine":"<engine-id>","samples":10}.

- Increased token spend vs forecast:
  - Likely causes: prompt inflation, unexpected retries, or high token-per-request usage.
  - Mitigation steps: enable token-limit policy on the route, add request logging with sampling to capture outlier prompts, review SDK integration to verify retries/backoff.

- Frequent 429s (rate limit) during ramp:
  - Likely causes: client-side concurrency and missing client-side rate limiting.
  - Mitigation: apply client-side leaky-bucket throttling; coordinate with SE to provision burst capacity for first 48 hours.

Monitoring & instrumentation checklist (must be visible in the first 24 hours)

- Dashboards: Tokens/minute, per-route cost, p95 latency, 5xx rate, KV cache hit ratio.
- Traces: sample 1% of requests with full request/response payload for the first 7 days. Ensure PII redaction enabled.
- Logs: structured JSON logs with request_id, trace_id, route, model_id. Retention: 90 days by default for enterprise customers.

CLI and example snippets

- Fetch engine health:
  - Example: curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_API_KEY" https://api.redwood.example/v1/engines/my-prod-engine/health

- Warmup job (cURL example):
  - curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"engine":"my-prod-engine","samples":["Hello","Summarize: short text"],"concurrency":2}' https://api.redwood.example/internal/warmup

- Sample route config (JSON fragment to include in onboarding runbook):
  - {
      "route_name": "customer-a-default",
      "engine": "my-prod-engine",
      "batching": { "max_batch_tokens": 1024, "max_batch_size": 32 },
      "cache": { "prefix_cache": true, "kv_profile": "high-hit" },
      "slo_tags": ["enterprise-2026"],
      "rate_limits": { "requests_per_minute": 1200 }
    }

QBR readiness checklist (to deliver by day 75)

- Usage trends and cost breakdown (token-level) for day 0–75.
- Performance baseline vs current (p50/p95/p99).
- Open incidents and remediation items.
- Proposed optimization roadmap (batching/cache/quantizaton) with estimated cost impact.

Owner & contacts

- Onboarding SE: name & email (populate in runbook).
- Customer Success Manager: name & email (populate in runbook).
- Runtime Oncall: rotas listed in Ops PagerDuty.

Appendix: Acceptance test checklist (sample commands)

1. Latency smoke test (10 concurrent requests): run k6 script; expected p95 < configured threshold.
2. Fault injection: simulate a dropped node and verify automatic fallback to other capacity pools within 60s.
3. Cost smoke test: replay representative traffic for 1 hour and measure tokens-per-minute vs forecast.

Notes and links

- Attach: baseline runbench JSON, onboarding runbook template, SLA addendum (if different from platform defaults).
- For security-sensitive customers, coordinate with Security & Compliance for audit logging and evidence packages.

If you have questions about any step, ping #cs-onboarding or open a ticket in the Onboarding queue.

title: Regional compliance and localized onboarding playbook - 2026
content:
Overview:

This playbook defines the end-to-end onboarding process for enterprise customers whose accounts require region-specific compliance and localized operational controls. It codifies pre-provisioning checks, region matrices, telemetry gating, localized SLA expectations, and safe rollback procedures. Use this document when the customer requests any of the following:

- Data residency guarantees for a jurisdiction (EU, UK, CA, APAC jurisdictions).
- Private networking (VPC peering, on-prem deployments, or air-gapped installs).
- Localized legal or regulatory controls (data classification, DPA/GDPR addenda, sector-specific controls such as HIPAA or FINRA).

Scope:

This playbook applies to:
- Hosted accounts with region pinning in AWS/EU/GC/East-APAC regions.
- Redwood Dedicated tenants that must be physically located in a defined region.
- Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem) with KMS/HSM and audit log routing requirements.

Not in scope: model-level tuning or evaluation procedures (see applied-ml-and-evals), or deep security architecture decisions (see security-and-compliance).

High-level objectives:
- Ensure legal/regulatory boxes are validated before data ingress.
- Minimize go-live disruption with region-aware smoke tests and telemetry gating.
- Provide a repeatable rollback path for failures during cutover.

Region requirements matrix (summary):

| Region | Residency guarantee | Default storage location | Default KMS boundary | Common customer asks | Recommended provisioning tier |
|--------|---------------------|--------------------------|----------------------|----------------------|-------------------------------|
| EU (Frankfurt/Amsterdam) | EU-only data at rest + transit | S3 eu-central-1 / eu-west-1 | Customer-managed KMS in same region | DPA, SCCs, EU-only audit logs | Hosted pinned or Dedicated EU |
| UK (London) | UK-residency option | S3 eu-west-2 | Optional CMK in London | UK Addendum, export controls | Hosted pinned (UK) or Dedicated |
| Canada (Montreal) | Canadian residency | S3 ca-central-1 | Customer CMK recommended | PIPEDA questions, province-level data requests | Dedicated recommended |
| APAC (Singapore, Tokyo) | Region-specific residency on request | S3 ap-southeast-1 / ap-northeast-1 | Customer CMK recommended | Local security questionnaires, latency-sensitive | Hosted pinned or Dedicated APAC |

Pre-provisioning checklist (owner: Customer Success + Solutions Eng):

1. Contract gating
   - Confirm signed DPA/region addenda.
   - Verify export control and sector clauses (e.g., HIPAA, FINRA) if applicable.
2. Identity & Access
   - Confirm customer SSO/SAML attributes and expected admin list.
   - Collect service account thumbprints / SSH keys for on-prem agents.
3. Networking
   - Determine VPC peering, firewall rules, proxy requirements.
   - Confirm public egress constraints and NAT/whitelisting needs.
4. Key management
   - Confirm KMS/HSM provider, CMK ARNs, and key rotation cadence.
5. Telemetry & Logging
   - Determine what telemetry can leave the region (metrics only, no event payloads).
   - Configure telemetry gating policy (see Telemetry Gating section).
6. Cutover windows and stakeholders
   - Agree on blackout windows, contact matrix, and rollback thresholds.

Network & connectivity requirements (quick-reference table):

| Component | Direction | Ports | Notes |
|-----------|-----------|-------|-------|
| redwood-provisioner (control plane) | Outbound | 443 | TLS 1.2+, destination must be reachable from provisioning host; allow only to redwood-managed IP ranges for restricted setups. |
| tenant-data-plane | Inbound (customer) | 443/8443 | For Dedicated: customers may request private endpoints; require mutual TLS in sensitive deployments. |
| telemetry-gatekeeper | Outbound | 443 | Supports proxy (HTTP CONNECT) and syslog forwarding. |

Data residency and encryption – configuration template (use when provisioning Dedicated or Private):

| Setting | Recommended value | Rationale | Verification step |
|--------|-------------------|-----------|-------------------|
| object_store.region | eu-central-1 | Ensures data writes remain in EU | S3 bucket location check post-provisioning |
| kms.key_arn | arn:aws:kms:eu-central-1:123456:key/abcd | Customer CMK ensures separation of key control | Perform test envelope encryption/decryption with customer's key |
| audit_log_sink | s3://redwood-audit-eu-logs | Centralized but region-anchored logs | Verify last 24h log arrival and object ACLs |

Telemetry gating and SLO signoffs (owner: Customer Success + Observability):

Principles:
- Customers may require that request/response payloads never leave the region until a compliance gate is satisfied. Telemetry (metrics and non-sensitive traces) can be forwarded under an agreed policy.
- Gate states:
  - BLOCKED: No customer payload or PII leaves region. Provisioning proceeds using metadata-only validation steps.
  - PENDING_VERIFICATION: Non-sensitive telemetry (metrics, anonymized traces) allowed for 48 hours.
  - RELEASED: Full telemetry (payloads, logs) forwarded to central Redwood observability.

Typical gating workflow:
1. Initial provision with BLOCKED gate. Validate network, KMS, and control-plane reachability using metadata-only smoke checks.
2. Customer completes legal checklist and confirms retention policy. Move gate to PENDING_VERIFICATION.
3. Run 48h telemetry-only soak with synthetic traffic. Observability team validates no policy violations.
4. If clear, customer signs release confirmation and gate moves to RELEASED.

SLOs for onboarding validation tests:
- Control plane reachability: 99.9% within provisioning window (5 minute probe cadence).
- KV cache warm-up: 95% of synthetic requests served from cache within 15 minutes of steady traffic.
- API latency (p50): <= 120ms for host-region tests in Dedicated deployments.

Localized support model and SLA adjustments:

- For region-residency accounts, provide an on-call roster that includes regional support engineers during customer business hours.
- SLA ramp for first 90 days: 24x7 response within 60 minutes for Sev1, 4 hours for Sev2, 1 business day for Sev3. After QBR sign-off, revert to standard SLA in the contract.
- Translate key onboarding docs (summary, validation checklist, rollback steps) to customer's preferred language for accounts > $250k ARR.

Onboarding timeline (example for Dedicated EU tenant) – recommended milestones:

| Week | Activity | Owner | Exit criteria |
|------|----------|-------|---------------|
| -2 | Contract & legal gating complete | Legal / Sales | DPA signed, region addendum attached |
| -1 | Network & KMS details supplied | Customer + Solutions Eng | VPC CIDRs, allowed egress, CMK ARNs submitted |
| Day 0 | Provision Dedicated tenant (EU) | Infra Provisioning | Tenant active, control plane reachable (BLOCKED gate) |
| Day 1-2 | Basic smoke tests + KMS verification | Customer Success + Observability | Encryption roundtrip successful; basic API responses validated |
| Day 3-4 | Telemetry PENDING soak (48h) | Observability | No policy violations; synthetic workload passes SLOs |
| Day 5 | Go/no-go meeting & release | Customer + CS + Infra | Customer signs release; gate set to RELEASED |
| Day 6-30 | Monitoring, stabilization, QBR prep | CS + Product | Performance baseline established; handback to customer ops |

Runbook: failed provisioning and rollback (immediate steps):

1. Detect: Provisioning failed alarms sent to #cs-provisioning and on-call.
2. Triage: Owner on-call confirms failure type (network/KMS/legal/infra).
3. If network or KMS misconfiguration: attempt non-invasive reconfiguration (update security groups, correct CMK ARN).
4. If stateful corruption or data residency risk: execute tenant quiesce and rollback to snapshot. Commands (examples):

- Quiesce tenant traffic: curl -X POST https://internal-api.redwood/api/v1/tenants/{tenant_id}/quiesce -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'
- Create daily snapshot: redwoodctl snapshot create --tenant {tenant_id} --label pre-rollout-2026-11-02
- Rollback: redwoodctl tenant rollback --tenant {tenant_id} --snapshot pre-rollout-2026-11-02 --confirm

5. Communicate: CS Lead posts incident update to customer within 30 minutes of decision. Include ETA, remediation steps, and next update window.

Escalation matrix (contacts and responsibilities):

| Priority | Who to escalate to | Contact method | Responsibility |
|----------|--------------------|----------------|----------------|
| Tier 1 (Network/KMS) | Solutions Engineering on-call | Pager + Slack #se-oncall | Validate VPC/KMS and apply config fixes |
| Tier 2 (Provisioning infra) | Infra SRE lead (Elena Park) | Pager + PagerDuty | Investigate control-plane issues, re-run provisioner |
| Tier 3 (Legal/Compliance) | Security & Compliance (Aisha Patel) | Email + legal channel | Review legal gating items and exceptions |

Validation test-suite (run post-provisioning):

- Test 1: Control-plane API health
  curl -fsS -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' https://tenant-eu.redwood/api/v1/health && echo OK
- Test 2: KMS envelope encrypt/decrypt sample (script)
- Test 3: Data residency verification (list and verify bucket locations)
- Test 4: Telemetry gate enforcement (simulate payload with PII and ensure it is blocked)

Sample CLI/automation snippets (use with redwoodctl v2.1+):

# Provision EU tenant (automation pipeline example)
redwoodctl tenant create --name "acme-eu" --region eu-central-1 --kms-arn arn:aws:kms:eu-central-1:123456:key/abcd --storage-class regional --telemetry-gate BLOCKED

# Toggle telemetry gate (observability only)
redwoodctl telemetry gate update --tenant acme-eu --state PENDING_VERIFICATION --note "Customer signed retention addendum"

Handback and QBR preparation checklist (owner: Customer Success):

- Baseline metrics compiled: p50/p95 latency, token cost per request, uptime.
- Incident log for first 90 days summarized.
- Security posture & audit log shipping validated.
- Recommend deferred items list (integration work, additional tooling).

Appendix A — Regional doc templates and required artifacts:

- Data processing addendum (EU template) — attach to contract.
- Network diagram template (customer to Redwood data-plane).
- KMS attestation checklist and sample CMK policy.

Appendix B — Troubleshooting tips (common failure modes):

- Failure: CMK permission denied — check key policy allows redwood-provisioner principal and kms:Encrypt/kms:Decrypt.
- Failure: Telemetry blocked after RELEASED — verify proxy ACL and allowlist for telemetry-gatekeeper certificate.
- Failure: Provisioner times out at 15 minutes — check control plane IP reachability and DNS SRV records for tenant endpoints.

Glossary and ownership:

- redwood-provisioner: internal control-plane service that orchestrates tenant creation (owner: Infra).
- telemetry-gatekeeper: regional agent that enforces telemetry gates and forwards observability events (owner: Observability).
- CS Lead: primary customer success contact for the account (owner: Customer Success).

Document change log:
- 2025-07-15: Created by Miguel Torres (initial draft).
- 2026-03-10: Added telemetry gating states and SLOs (reviewers: Aisha Patel).
- 2026-11-02: Finalized rollback commands and on-call escalation contacts (publisher: Miguel Torres).

title: Compact first-responder playbook and light postmortem scaffold
content:
Summary:
This compact playbook is designed for first responders who need focused, action-oriented guidance for common Redwood-serving incidents and a lightweight postmortem template to accelerate learning. It favors short, repeatable actions (micro-runbooks), clear decision points, and prewritten comms to reduce cognitive load during high-severity events. Use this as the primary on-call cheat-sheet; link to deeper runbooks when needed.

Scope:
- Audience: first responders (on-call engineers), bridge operators, support leads.
- Coverage: performance SLO regressions, KV-cache/embedding cache failures, request throttling/backpressure, model quality regressions, regional connectivity blips, and noisy neighbor incidents.
- Not for: security incidents (use security incident runbook), full forensic investigations.

How to use this doc (quick):
1) Identify the incident class using the "Incident quick classifier" below.
2) Run the micro-runbook for that class (1–3 remediation steps).
3) If unresolved in 20 minutes or customer-impacting, escalate to the appropriate on-call (pager escalation ladder).
4) Publish a short customer-facing status update using the template.
5) After stabilization, fill the light postmortem scaffold within 72 hours and schedule a 30–60 minute blameless review.

Incident quick classifier (decision tree):
- Is the symptom increased latency or elevated error rate across many customers? -> Check p50/p95/p99 latency and error rate. If p99 > 2x baseline or errors > 1% traffic, classify as P1/P2.
- Is the symptom isolated to a single customer or tenant? -> Treat as customer-impacting P2; open dedicated bridge with solutions/CS.
- Are model-quality signals (eval infra or user reports) showing semantic regressions? -> Model quality incident.
- Is there a rapid rise in throttled requests or 429s? -> Throttle/backpressure incident.
- Is KV/embedding cache miss rate > 25% and latency spiking? -> Cache degradation.

Micro-runbooks (one-page actionable steps):
1) Throttle/backpressure (common cause: bursty traffic, downstream saturation, autoscaler lag)
- Owner: inference-gateway on-call.
- Immediate check (COMMANDS):
  - curl -s https://metrics.internal/api/series?query=inference.gateway.throttled_count | jq .
  - kubectl -n platform get hpa inference-gateway -o yaml
- Mitigation steps (in order):
  1. Scale a fallback pool: runbook-ops-cli scale-pool --pool reserved-burst --replicas +2 (if dedicated pools exist).
  2. Activate traffic shaping policy: platformctl set-routing --policy degrade-to-fast-variant (falls back to cheaper/fast variant).
  3. Temporarily increase client-level quotas for critical tenants via admin-api update-quota --tenant X --burst 2000.
- Timebox: each change 5–10 minutes, observe metrics for 2 minutes.
- Escalate if no improvement within 20 minutes.

2) KV / embedding cache degradation (misses, cold cache, or eviction storms)
- Owner: serving-runtime on-call.
- Immediate check:
  - grafana dashboard: Cache Overview -> miss_rate, hit_latency, eviction_rate
  - redis-cli -h cache.internal INFO stats | egrep "keyspace_hits|keyspace_misses|evicted_keys"
- Mitigation steps:
  1. Increase cache memory for affected cluster: infra-ops change-mem --cluster kv-cache-primary --delta +8GB (requires infra approval path if >16GB).
  2. Toggle read-through to passive mode to avoid stampeding: configctl set kv.read_through false
  3. Warm prefix caches for top tenants: cache-warm --tenant-list top-10 --prefixes recent
- Note: If warm-up would spike CPU, prefer toggle (2) and reduce client TTLs.

3) Model quality regression (nonsensical outputs, hallucination ramp)
- Owner: model-onboarding / applied-ml on-call.
- Immediate check:
  - eval-signal: compare latest evaluation job to baseline across prompt-sets (failure delta > 5% on guardrail prompts).
  - Customer reports: search 'quality regression' tag in support queue.
- Mitigation steps:
  1. Roll traffic to previous verified model revision: rolloutctl rollback --service model-serving --version v2025-12-18
  2. Enable inference-sanitizer: modelctl set-sanitizer --level conservative (adds n-gram heuristics and response filters).
  3. Open dedicated incident channel with model and product owners; capture failing prompts to eval harness.
- Escalation: product owner if rollout fails or regression persists > 60 minutes.

4) Regional connectivity blip / cloud region incident
- Owner: eng-sre on-call.
- Immediate check:
  - platform status map (internal): see region availability and circuit breaker metrics
  - curl -I https://inference.us-west2.internal/healthz
- Mitigation steps:
  1. Reroute traffic to healthy region: routingctl set-region-priority --service inference-gateway --from us-west2 --to us-east1
  2. Enable degraded-mode policies for stateful features (turn off long-polling, increase short timeouts)
  3. If cross-region failover will cause data residency issues, open legal/compliance advisory before broad reroute.

5) Noisy neighbor (GPU OOMs, preemption, or model eviction causing SLO spikes)
- Owner: gpu-fleet on-call.
- Immediate check:
  - ML node logs: elk query "OOM|preempted" | tail -n 200
  - scheduler events: kubectl get events -n gpu-run | grep eviction
- Mitigation steps:
  1. Drain offending node: kubectl drain node/<node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
  2. Pin high-priority pools to reserved hardware: fleetctl migrate --pool high-priority --node-type reserved
  3. Adjust eviction thresholds if autoscaler misconfigured; notify capacity planning.

Incident evidence collection (minimum required):
- Attach to incident: relevant Grafana dashboards, last 30 minutes of gateway logs, sampling of 10 failed requests with IDs, stack traces if present, affected tenant list.
- Use incident-evidence-cli collect --incident-id <INC> --type all --since 00:30:00

Escalation ladder (when to escalate and to whom):
- T+0–20 min: on-call responder attempts mitigation. If consumer-visible impact or <80% SLO compliance -> escalate to service owner.
- T+20–40 min: bring in eng-sre lead and product owner.
- T+40+ min or unresolved P1: exec-notification (VP eng, support director), consider declaring customer incident and external status page entry.

Communication templates (copy/paste and edit):
- Internal Pager note (first 10 minutes):
  "[INCIDENT] <short-summary> | Impact: <customers/regions> | Owner: <team> | Initial action: <action taken> | Next update: <T+10m>"
- Customer-facing status (initial):
  Subject: "Service disruption affecting {feature} — {region/tenants}"
  Body: "We are investigating an issue causing {latency/errors} for {feature} impacting {scope}. Our on-call team has identified {high-level-cause-or-symptom} and is executing mitigations (e.g., traffic reroute, model rollback). We will provide an update by {time}. Contact your CS rep for urgent questions."
- Engineering bridge opener message:
  "Bridge open: {INC-ID} — symptom: {latency/error/quality} — first responder: {name} — runbook: compact-first-responder-playbook — mitigation in progress: {actions}. Artifacts: <grafana link> <logs link>"

Game-day scenarios and success criteria (15–60 minute drills):
- Scenario A: KV cache eviction storm for top-5 tenants. Objective: recover hit rate to >90% within 20 minutes while keeping p95 latency <2x baseline. Steps: follow KV micro-runbook, collect evidence, run postmortem scaffold within 48 hours.
- Scenario B: Model rollback under load. Objective: verify rollback process without request loss, rollback time <15 minutes, monitor model-quality sanity checks.
- Scenario C: Multi-region failover test (planned). Objective: routing cutover <10 minutes, no data residency violation, customer status template executed.

On-call rotation guidance (compact rules):
- Shift length: 12 hours (primary), 24 hours (backup) recommended cadence for SRE; rotate weekly for fairness.
- Handover checklist (to run at shift start/end):
  1. Review active incidents and bridges.
  2. Check on-call dashboard for alerts > 6h unresolved.
  3. Confirm contact info and escalation points.
- Shadowing: new on-call engineers must complete two monitored shifts and one game-day within the first 30 days.

Light postmortem scaffold (fill within 72 hours):
- Title: single-line summary of incident and impact.
- Incident ID: {INC-YYYYMMDD-###}
- Severity: P1 | P2 | P3
- Timeline (UTC, short bullets): immediate sequence of key events (discovery, mitigation steps with timestamps).
- Impact summary (customers, duration, SLO deviation): bullet list.
- Root cause (1–2 sentences): brief technical root cause statement.
- Contributing factors: short list with one-sentence explanations.
- Immediate remediation (what we changed): bullets.
- Long-term actions (owners + ETA): table-like bullets with owner and target date.
- Follow-up: status of verification, who will close the action, and acceptance criteria.

Light postmortem example (abridged):
- Title: KV cache eviction storm caused p95 latency spikes for embeddings API (INC-20260111-007)
- Severity: P2
- Timeline:
  - 08:03 UTC — alerts: cache_miss_rate > 30%
  - 08:08 UTC — on-call toggled read_through -> false (mitigation)
  - 08:23 UTC — hit_rate returned to 88%, p95 improved to baseline
- Impact: ~12% of API requests saw increased latency for 20 minutes affecting three large tenants.
- Root cause: misconfigured TTL and a surprise migration that increased memory pressure leading to eviction storms.
- Contributing factors: lack of pre-migration cache warm, missing autoscaler headroom, no migration checklist.
- Immediate remediation: toggled read-through, increased cache memory by 8GB.
- Long-term actions: add migration checklist (owner: infra-ops, ETA: 2026-02-20), implement cache warm-run in deploy pipeline (owner: serving-runtime, ETA: 2026-03-01).

Governance and runbook hygiene:
- Maintain micro-runbooks as <= 1 page. If a runbook requires > 6 steps or multiple teams, convert it into a full runbook and link it from this doc.
- Quarterly review: each micro-runbook owner must confirm validity or mark for rewrite.
- Runbook retirement: deprecate and archive runbooks with no updates for 18 months and no incidents referencing them.

Appendix: useful commands and links
- Incident CLI: incident-cli open --title "<title>" --sev P2 --assignee "on-call"
- Evidence collector: incident-evidence-cli collect --incident-id {INC} --targets grafana,logs,request-samples
- Grafana dashboards: Cache Overview | Gateway Latency | Model Quality Signals | Region Health
- Playbook owners: Maya Patel (eng-sre, playbook steward), Liam Chen (serving-runtime owner), Aria Gomez (oncall program manager)

If you discover gaps during an event: log them immediately under the incident as "runbook-gap" and add to the postmortem actions list. This document is intentionally compact — expand to a full runbook for repeat incidents or when a single mitigation requires >1 hour of coordinated work.

title: Tenant FinOps Cutover & Governance Playbook
content:
Summary

This playbook defines the operational and governance steps Customer Success, SRE, and FinOps must follow when performing a tenant-level cutover that changes billing or capacity controls (examples: moving a customer from trial to committed Dedicated, enabling quota-protector webhooks, or toggling per-tenant burst limits). The goal is to ensure cost predictability, tenant safety, and clear rollback paths while minimizing customer-visible disruption.

Scope and When to Use this Playbook

- Applies to any tenant cutover that will alter: billing plan, reserved capacity assignment, per-tenant rate/quotas, or cost-protecting automations.
- Not for routine model version upgrades or small config tweaks that are covered by our standard canary rollout playbooks.

Definitions

- Cutover: The event during which a tenant transitions from one financial/operational state to another (e.g., trial -> paid committed, hosted -> dedicated, or quota cap changes).
- FinOps Gate: A pre-approved financial control threshold that requires Finance + CS sign-off before enabling.
- Safety Net: Automated quota/fallback rules that prevent unbounded spend or dangerous latency regressions.

Stakeholders and Responsibilities

- Customer Success (CS): primary contact for customer comms, scheduling, and acceptance.
- FinOps: validate contract terms, commit levels, and billing triggers; approve FinOps Gates.
- Eng SRE / Platform: implement routing changes, capacity reservations, and alerting.
- Oncall (runtime): 72-hour monitoring and first-responder for incidents.
- Account Executive (AE): commercial ownership, billing follow-up.

Prerequisites (pre-cutover checklist)

1) Contract & Billing
   - Verified signed MSA and SOW in Salesforce with committed throughput and billing start date.
   - Billing metadata (billing_contact_email, billing_entity_id, billing_region) present in tenant metadata.
   - FinOps has generated the pro-forma invoice and validated charge schedule.

2) Technical Readiness
   - Tenant tags: "tier=dedicated|hosted", "finops_commit_id=<id>", and "slo_profile=<profile>" set in tenant record.
   - Capacity reserved: GPU pool assignment and reservation confirmed in capacity inventory.
   - Quotas: quota config (requests/min, tokens/day, embedding-ops/day) created in quota service. Example JSON stored in deployment ticket.

3) Observability and Alerts
   - Dashboards prepared: Tenant Overview, Cost Burn Rate, Token Distribution by Route, Cache Hit Rate, p99 Latency.
   - Alerts provisioned (see Alert matrix section).
   - Billing report configured to deliver daily usage CSV to FinOps and CS (S3 or internal bucket).

4) Communication
   - Cutover schedule agreed with customer and internal teams (UTC timezone).
   - Customer-facing FAQ and rollback expectations drafted.

Cutover Phases

Phase A — Pre-cutover (T-minus 72 to 2 hours)
1. Confirm tickets and approvals: ticket in triage board links to contract and capacity reservation.
2. Run validation script locally or via CI to verify tenant config:

   $ ./tools/validate-tenant-config --tenant-id T-12345 --assert-quotas --assert-tags

   Expected output: PASS for quotas, tags, billing metadata.

3. Snapshot current state: export tenant routing, quota, and billing metadata to the ticket.

4. Create safety net override set: temporary conservative quotas one tier below target for first 24 hours unless FinOps approves full limits.

Phase B — Cutover execution (T0)
