6) Communication artifacts ready: customer email template, incident-communication template, and support-runbook snippets.
7) Rollback playbooks validated in a dry-run: scripted rollback and clear state reconciliation steps.
8) Approval gate signoffs: Product, CS, Serving Runtime, and Security as required.

Scheduling & Tenant Notification:
- Maintenance window: prefer low-traffic windows in tenant region (e.g., 0100–0400 local). For multi-region tenants, coordinate a single targeted rollout with time-zone-aware notices.
- Notification cadence (enterprise tenants):
  * 14 days before: high-level notice with expected impact, upgrade window, and opt-out instructions (if available).
  * 3 days before: detailed technical notice including canary percentage, API version pin instructions, and rollback SLAs.
  * 24 hours before: reminder and pre-upgrade checklist for tenant (recommended testing plan).
  * 1 hour before: imminent reminder via Slack/email to named contacts.
- Communication templates: include standard subject lines, summary sections, and a clear “what to do if you see issues” section. See template snippets below.

Canary Rollout Strategy (recommended default):
1) Stage 0 — Internal smoke (0% tenant traffic): run all internal synthetic scenarios and trace logs for 60–120 minutes.
2) Stage 1 — Very small external canary (1–2% of traffic or single volunteer tenant): monitor for 30–60 minutes.
3) Stage 2 — Expanded canary (5–10% of traffic or a small cohort of non-critical tenants): monitor for 60–120 minutes.
4) Stage 3 — Progressive ramp (25% then 50%): if metrics stable, increase to these bands with 2× monitoring intervals.
5) Stage 4 — Full rollout (100%): gated final decision after passing Stage 3 checks.

For Dedicated/Private customers where per-tenant pinning is supported: use tenant selector labels to apply the model only to specified tenants; prefer volunteer tenants for initial stages. If tenant declines participation, do not include them in the canary.

Automated Metrics & Acceptance Criteria (must be continuously evaluated during canary):
- Latency: p50 and p95 should not regress by more than +20% (absolute threshold: p95 <= 800ms for text-generation default profile).
- Error rate: total 5xx and request-failures must remain <= existing baseline + 0.1 percentage points and absolute <= 0.5%.
- Token cost: average tokens-per-request should not increase more than +10% without documented cause.
- Quality regression: automated eval on canonical prompt set must show no >3% drop in primary metric (BLEU/ROUGE/embedding-similarity or custom eval).
- Fuzzy anomaly detection: anomaly score on model outputs (semantic drift detector) must remain below configured threshold for the canary cohort.

If any single critical threshold is violated, the system will:
- Immediately pause canary ramping.
- Notify the on-call Serving Runtime engineer and Customer Success Lead.
- Trigger a fast rollback if the issue materially impacts customer SLAs (see Rollback Criteria).

Rollback Criteria & Procedure:
Decision matrix (examples):
- Severity 1 (service-impacting, persistent): automatic rollback within 15 minutes. Examples: sustained p95 > 1200ms, error rate > 1.5% sustained over 5 minutes, or loss of model responses for a tenant.
- Severity 2 (quality-impacting but non-blocking): pause and evaluate; manual rollback within 60 minutes if no mitigation. Examples: quality metric drop > 6% on canonical eval or customer-reported misbehavior on production prompts.
- Severity 3 (transient anomalies): continue monitoring; remediation via config patch or retry logic. Examples: short-lived spike in latencies or intermittent downstream infra error.

Rollback steps (serving runtime owner executes):
1) Re-route affected traffic back to prior pinned model version using the canary control plane API. Example CLI: redwoodctl rollout --tenant <tenant-id> --from-version <new> --to-version <previous> --reason "automatic-rollback: latency regressed"
2) Validate traffic routing and confirm that pre-upgrade model is serving for the affected tenant(s).
3) Re-run smoke generation tests against the restored model and confirm baseline metrics.
4) Notify Customer Success and the customer POC immediately with the rollback summary and next steps.
5) Open a post-incident triage ticket and schedule a cross-team RCA within 72 hours.

Post-Upgrade Verification (after full rollout):
- 24-hour and 7-day checks: confirm sustained SLO adherence and no regression in quality metrics.
- Customer validation: deliver a short validation checklist to the customer POC to confirm expected behavior.
- Billing/Cost reconciliation: capture token-cost delta and alert finance if variance > 8% month-to-date.

Observability Playbook (quick commands and dashboards):
- Dashboards to monitor: Model Serving Overview, Canary Cohort Health, Latency Heatmap (by tenant), Error Distribution, Model Quality Snapshot.
- Quick checks (CLI / API):
  * Get canary assignment: curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://api.redwood.ai/v1/tenants/<tenant-id>/model-assignment
  * Fetch model metrics: redwood-metrics query "model.latency.p95{model=\"<model-name>\"}" --last 15m
  * Trigger synthetic test: curl -X POST https://ops.redwood.ai/synthetics/run -d '{"test_suite":"upgrade-smoke","model":"<model-name>"}'

Customer-Facing Messaging (templates):
- Subject: "Planned model upgrade for <Tenant Name> — maintenance window <date/time>"
- Body: include short summary, expected impact (likely none), canary approach, opt-out link (if applicable), contact info, and guidance for quick verification.
- Incident messaging (if rollback occurs): short description of customer exposure, actions taken (rollback executed), expected follow-up timeline, and link to RCA.

Support Triage Flow (if customers report issues during or after upgrade):
1) First-line support: run the tenant validation checklist and capture examples (request_id, timestamps, prompt text, returned output).
2) If reproducible, escalate to Serving Runtime on-call with logs, metrics, and customer-observed sample.
3) If issue is quality-related, hand off to Applied ML & Evals team for evaluation against canonical prompt sets.
4) Engage Product & CS to determine whether to pause rollout for additional testing or to rollback.

Runbook Attachments (snippets):
- Example canary API payload: {\"canary_percent\":5,\"cohort_selector\":\"label:volunteer\",\"max_duration_min\":120}
- Example rollback CLI snippet: redwoodctl rollback --scope tenant --id <tenant-id> --target-version <sha-or-tag> --reason "fast-rollback: automatic-threshold"

Postmortem & RCA expectations:
- For any automatic rollback or Severity 1 outage: publish a written RCA within 72 hours, with timeline, root cause, corrective actions, and responsible owners for fixes.
- For Severity 2 escalations: summary RCA within 7 days and a follow-up plan for model tuning or augmenting synthetic tests.

Customer Success Playbook Actions (for CSMs):
- Pre-upgrade: confirm POC has a test plan and knows how to pin model versions if they want a freeze.
- During canary: maintain an open channel with the customer POC and provide live updates at milestone gates.
- After rollback: coordinate follow-up postmortem call and share remediation timelines.

Appendix: Example Email Template (short)
Subject: Planned model upgrade for <TenantName> — <Date/Window>
Hi <POC>,
We will be performing a scheduled model upgrade that may affect inference quality for a small subset of requests. We are using a conservative canary rollout and expect no disruption for most customers. If you prefer to be excluded from the canary, reply to this message before <X>.
Planned window: <Date/Time>
What we will do: staged canary, monitoring, and rapid rollback if thresholds are violated.
How you can test: run the quick verification checklist attached.
Who to contact: <CS POC contact> (phone/slack)
Thanks,
Customer Success (Redwood)

Appendix: Quick Verification Checklist for Tenants
- Run 5 representative prompts and compare responses to baseline.
- Verify latency for 10 requests does not exceed usual p95 by >40%.
- Report any unexpected formatting, hallucination, or API errors with timestamps and request IDs.

Change Log:
- 2025-11-03: Initial draft (Ravi Patel).
- 2025-12-10: Added canary percentage guidance and automated metrics (Maya Chen).
- 2026-02-14: Clarified rollback thresholds and added observability CLI snippets (Sofia Alvarez).

Related pages and references:
- Upgrade coordination checklist for Dedicated tenants (see related_pages).
- Runtime rollback API reference: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/rollback-api-reference
- Canary cohort selection guide: /confluence/eng-platform/how-tos/canary-selection-guidelines

Contacts (primary):
- Customer Success Lead: rpatel@redwood.ai
- Serving Runtime On-call: oncall-serving@redwood.ai (pager duty link)
- Observability Slack channel: #observability-upgrades

title: Enterprise Metric Ownership and Alert Routing Cookbook
content:
Overview

Purpose: This cookbook defines a pragmatic, repeatable approach for mapping customer-visible telemetry to clear owners, creating routing rules in our alerting stack, and operationalizing those alerts inside Customer Success (CS) and Engineering workflows. It is intended for CS onboarding leads, SREs, and product owners who need consistent, auditable alerts that drive fast, customer-facing outcomes.

Scope: applies to all enterprise tenants (hosted, dedicated, private) and the following telemetry sources: telemetry-gateway, redwood-proxy, model-router, kvcache-service, embeddings-indexer. This doc focuses on customer-impacting metrics (latency, error-rate, cost-anomaly, model-quality regression) rather than internal infra-only metrics.

Owner and Contact

- Primary owner: Customer Success Observability (team-ops-cs-observability)
- Secondary owner: Eng SRE (team-sre-platform)
- Oncall escalation: Eng SRE PagerDuty (PD: team-sre-platform)

Definitions and Goal Metrics

- Customer-visible metric: any metric or log pattern that maps to a customer SLA, feature, or billing impact (examples below).
- Severity tiers and target time-to-ack (TTA):
  - Sev P0 (Critical): customer-facing outage, >5% of tenant traffic impacted or entire tenant unreachable — TTA: 15 minutes
  - Sev P1 (High): degraded experience (latency or increased error rate) for a production route — TTA: 60 minutes
  - Sev P2 (Medium): cost anomaly or single-model quality regression flagged by evaluations — TTA: 8 hours
  - Sev P3 (Low): informational alerts, trend warnings for QBR — TTA: 72 hours

Metric-to-Owner Matrix (examples)

| Metric name | Observable source | Owner team | Default severity | Notes |
|-------------|-------------------|------------|------------------|-------|
| request.p50.latency| telemetry-gateway | team-sre-platform | P1 | If tenant p50 increases > 2x baseline for >10m |
| request.error_rate | redwood-proxy | team-sre-platform | P0 | If error_rate > 5% for a tenant and sustained |
| embed.indexing.lag | embeddings-indexer | team-data-ops | P1 | Backpressure on indexer affecting search freshness |
| kvcache.kv_miss_rate | kvcache-service | team-serving-runtime | P1 | Rapid rise correlates with token spend increase |
| model.quality.regression.alpha | model-router/evals | team-applied-ml | P2 | Triggered by evaluation harness comparing model vN to baseline |
| tenant.cost.per_hour | billing-collector | customer-success | P2 | Sudden cost > 3x expected forecast |

Alert Routing and Naming Conventions

- Alert name format: cs.<tenant>.<service>.<metric>.<severity>. Example: cs.acme-corp.redis-proxy.request-error-rate.P0
- Tags/labels to include: tenant_id, customer_tier (enterprise/dedicated/private), region, route, last_deployed_model, runbook_id
- Recommended Slack channels: #cs-alerts (triage), #sre-ops (escalation), #cust-<tenant_short> (customer-specific comms if enabled)

Routing Rules (examples)

1) Immediate P0 routing
   - Condition: alert severity == P0 AND tenant.tier == enterprise
   - Action: page Eng SRE PD (team-sre-platform) AND notify #cs-alerts Slack channel. Create CS incident in Zendesk with priority urgent.
2) P1 automated triage
   - Condition: severity == P1 AND first_alert_count >= 3 in 30m
   - Action: create short-lived support ticket assigned to CS Observability, attach grafana dashboard and recent traces. If no ack in 60m, escalate to Eng SRE PD.
3) Cost/Quality P2 handling
   - Condition: metric in {tenant.cost.per_hour, model.quality.regression.alpha}
   - Action: assign to CS FinOps or Applied ML respectively; auto-generate customer notification draft for review.

Alert Payload Example (YAML for routing system)

---
alert_name: "cs.{{tenant}}.telemetry-gateway.p50.latency.P1"
tenant: "{{tenant}}"
threshold: "p50 > baseline*2 for >10m"
owner: "team-sre-platform"
pagerduty: "team-sre-platform"
slack_channels: ["#cs-alerts", "#sre-ops"]
runbook_id: "rr-metric-p50-latency-v1"

Runbook: p50 latency spike (rr-metric-p50-latency-v1)

1) Verify the scope
   - Query: Grafana dashboard: Dashboard ID: cs-onboarding/latency-summary. Apply tenant filter = <tenant_id> and route filter = <route>.
   - Confirm whether spike is single region or cross-region and whether multiple tenants are affected.
2) Quick mitigations (first 30 min)
   - If proxy CPU > 85%: scale proxy pool (kubectl scale deploy proxy --replicas=+2 for dedicated pools).
   - If model hot-sharding: switch route to fallback model variant (use model-router override API: POST /v1/admin/overrides).
   - If KV cache miss storm: temporarily enable cache-skim mode (feature flag: kvcache.skim=true) for tenant.
3) Deeper triage (30m–4h)
   - Collect flamegraphs (perf profiler), recent traces (x-trace-id), and last 6 hours of redeploy events.
   - Correlate with release tags: last_deployed_model and infra-deploy-id.
4) Communication
   - Customer comms template (initial):
     Subject: "[Redwood] Brief outage affecting <feature> for <tenant>"
     Body: "We are investigating elevated latency impacting <route>. Initial mitigation steps are in progress. We will update within 60 minutes with next steps. Owner: <owner_name> (CS). Escalation: Eng SRE oncall."

Onboarding Checklist for New Enterprise Tenants (observability handoff)

- Before prod cutover:
  1. Ensure tenant metadata is registered in the telemetry-gateway (tenant_id, billing_code, support_contacts).
  2. Validate tenant-specific dashboards exist (latency, error-rate, cost, model-quality) and are shared with CS and SRE.
  3. Add tenant to alert routing rules with correct owner and Slack channels.
  4. Confirm PagerDuty escalation path is present and tested (test page with PD test key).
  5. Run a synthetic journey (see synthetic-journey-sla-calibration-playbook) and confirm alerts are not noisy.

Operational Playflows

- Normal triage (P1/P2): CS Observability owns first-touch. Use the CS triage checklist inside the Zendesk ticket: attach dashboards, record mitigation actions, propose next steps (mitigate, rollback, model-swap, capacity increase).
- Immediate escalation (P0): Eng SRE paged immediately. CS takes ownership of customer communication cadence and QBR action items.
- Post-incident: create an RCA within 48 hours if incident severity >= P1 and affected revenue or >10 customers. Assign action owners with due dates and track in the QBR.

Noise Reduction and Alert Health

- Weekly review: CS Observability runs an alert hygiene sweep every Monday: remove stale alerts, update thresholds based on tenant baselines, and collapse duplicate alerts across services.
- Signal-to-noise metric: track alerts_per_week_per_tenant and target < 3 actionable alerts/week for enterprise. If exceeded, assign an action to reduce.

Integration snippets and examples

1) Grafana dashboard sharing (CLI snippet)
   - grafana-cli dashboard export 12345 > acme-latency-dash.json
   - grafana-cli dashboard import --folder "Tenants/Acme" acme-latency-dash.json
2) Routing rule (example JSON for alert manager):
   {
     "match": {"tenant":"acme-corp","severity":"P1"},
     "route_to": ["team-sre-platform","channel:#cs-alerts"],
     "suppress_if": {"maintenance_mode":true}
   }

Customer Communication Templates

- 60-minute update (short)
  - Subject: "Update: ongoing issue affecting <feature> — <tenant>"
  - Body: "Summary: elevated latency persisted affecting <route>. Mitigation: scaled proxy and switched to fallback model. Next update in 2 hours or sooner. Contact: <cs_owner>@redwood.ai"

- Post-incident summary (example)
  - Subject: "Incident report: <short-id> — impact summary and remediation"
  - Body: "What happened, Customer impact, Timeline of mitigations, Root cause (investigating/identified), Actions taken, Preventative actions and expected timeline for completion."

SLO and Escalation thresholds (customer-facing)

- Availability: 99.95% per month for hosted Tier 1 routes. Escalate to P0 when availability drops below 99.5% in a rolling 1h window.
- Latency: p95 < 450ms. Escalate to P1 when p95 > 900ms for >10 minutes.
- Error rate: <1% across tenant traffic. Escalate to P0 when error rate >5% for >5 minutes.

Governance, Reporting, and QBR Inputs

- Each month CS Observability exports the following artifacts for QBRs: top 3 incidents for the tenant, alert burn rate, cost anomalies detected, model quality deltas.
- Action ownership: every alert that results in an RCA must have an owner and a completion date recorded in the quarter backlog.

Appendices

A. Common mitigations quick list
- Scale dedicated pools, swap to model-variant, enable cache-skim, temporary rate-limiting per-tenant, rollback last infra deploy.

B. Useful links
- Dashboards: https://grafana.redwood.internal/d/cs-onboarding/latency-summary
- PagerDuty: https://pd.redwood.internal/services/team-sre-platform
- Runbook repo: docs/runbooks/rr-metric-p50-latency-v1

C. Change log
- 2025-09-12: Document created by Maya Chen (CS Observability).
- 2026-02-10: Updated severity TTA targets and added cost anomaly routing (reviewers: Julian Park, Lena Novak).

If you have questions or need a tenant added to routing rules, open a ticket to #cs-ops-requests with payload: tenant_id, owner_email, desired_channels.

title: Reducing Alert Fatigue and Clear Oncall Ownership: A Customer-Facing Incident Playbook
content:
Overview

Purpose: This playbook defines how Redwood’s Customer Success, Support, and Platform teams should coordinate to reduce alert noise, establish unambiguous oncall ownership, and manage customer-visible incidents with minimal customer disruption. It is focused on enterprise tenants (Dedicated/Private) but also applies to hosted API incidents where customer impact is suspected.

Goals
- Reduce actionable pager noise by >=50% for customer-impacting alerts within three months of adoption.
- Ensure every alert has a single owning team and a documented remediation runbook or a suppression policy.
- Provide clear steps for customer-safe remediation and communications to minimize churn and SLA exposure.

Scope
- Included: alerts generated by Redwood control plane, tenant routing/proxy, model serving (inference failures), quota and billing anomalies, and integration connectors that impact request processing.
- Excluded: internal CI/CD job failures (owned by eng-infra) and local developer tooling alerts.

Definitions
- Noise: alerts that repeatedly fire without leading to a meaningful action within the past 30 days.
- Actionable Alert: an alert with a documented owner, severity, and a runbook that is executed at least once when it fires.
- Customer-facing Incident: an event where customer SLOs (availability/latency) are materially impacted, or billing/data integrity is at risk.

Roles & Ownership
- First Responder (Support/Platform): The oncall person who owns initial triage within 15 minutes. Responsibilities: validate, gather impact, open incident if needed, begin mitigation.
- Engineering Owner (Runtime/Infra/Product): Team responsible for full remediation and post-incident follow-up. Must be staffed for major incidents.
- Customer Success Lead (CS): Primary communicator to customer stakeholders and coordinates internal communications for ERs/SEVs.
- Incident Commander (IC): Assigned for Sev2+/Sev1 incidents. Coordinates cross-team tasks and manages escalation.

Alert Classification Matrix
(Use this table to assign ownership and expected response time)

| Category | Example alert | Owner | Response SLA | Customer impact | Auto-suppress allowed? | Severity |
|---|---:|---|---:|---|---:|---:|
| Platform Availability | control-plane-400-errors > 5% over 5m | eng-platform | 5m | High | No | Sev1 |
| Model Degradation | p95_token_latency_increase > 2x baseline | eng-serving-runtime | 15m | Moderate/High | No | Sev2 |
| Tenant Quota Hit | tenant_x_rate_limit_429s > 10/min | support | 15m | Moderate | Yes (1m suppression) | Sev2 |
| Telemetry Drop | metrics-forwarder_lag > 120s | eng-infra | 30m | Low/Moderate | Yes (grouped) | Sev3 |
| Billing Anomaly | invoice_delta > $5k unexpected | finance-legal & support | 60m | High (customer) | No | Sev1 |

Triage & Escalation Procedure (first 30 minutes)
1. First Responder acknowledges alert within Response SLA.
2. Determine if alert is symptomatic or root: check runbook tags: symptomatic -> follow immediate mitigations; root -> route to Engineering Owner.
3. If multiple alerts correlate (same tenant or upstream), mark incident and assign IC.
4. IC coordinates: set incident priority, notify CS Lead, open incident bridge, document initial timeline.
5. If customer-visible, CS Lead drafts initial comms template (internal + external) and posts a holding message to the customer’s designated channel within 30 minutes of incident start.

Runbook Patterns (examples)
- Symptomatic mitigation (fast path):
  - Example: tenant_x_rate_limit_429s
    - Action: enable short suppression (1m) for duplicate alerts; find offending tenant key; apply temporary burst-limit increase for that tenant via admin API:
      - curl -X POST https://admin.redwood/api/v1/tenants/{tenant}/burst-adjust 
        -H 'Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN' 
        -d '{"burst_window": 60, "max_burst": 500}'
    - Verify: run `curl https://telemetry.redwood/api/tenant/{tenant}/metrics | jq .rates` and ensure 429s drop below threshold for 5 consecutive minutes.

- Root cause engagement (slow path):
  - Example: p95_token_latency_increase > 2x baseline
    - Action: collect traces (tracer query examples below), review recent deployments, check GPU health and KV cache hit rate.
    - PromQL snippet to attach with incident: `increase(request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="runtime",quantile="0.95"}[5m])`
    - Escalate to eng-serving-runtime and provide packet of: tenant list, timestamps, top traces, and pre/post deploy diffs.

Alert Reduction Playbook (how to reduce noise)
1. Ownership mapping: every alert must have the `owner_team` label and a single Slack/Pager contact. No alert without owner is considered noise.
2. Suppress identical alerts for the same tenant for a configurable debounce window (default 1 minute) unless it evidences growing error rates.
3. Dedup & group by root cause: implement correlation rules in the alert router (grouping-key: tenant|service|error-code).
4. Use adaptive thresholds based on rolling windows and baseline seasonality instead of static fixed thresholds.
5. Implement an alert lifecycle: open -> acknowledged -> resolved -> closed. Alerts that bounce back without remediation are automatically escalated to IC.
6. Maintain a suppression whitelist for noisy 3rd-party integrations with documented mitigation steps.

Key Metrics to Track
- Pager burn rate: number of paged alerts per oncall shift (target < 8 actionable pages/shift).
- Alert to incident conversion: percent of alerts that become incidents (target < 10%).
- Mean time to acknowledge (MTTA) and mean time to remediate (MTTR) by alert class.
- Noise ratio: alerts suppressed / total alerts (target > 30% but balanced).
- Customer-impacting incidents per quarter (trend must be non-increasing).

Customer Communication Templates
- Holding message (30m):
  - Subject: We’re investigating a service disruption affecting {tenant-name}
  - Body: We are aware of increased errors for your requests and our teams are investigating. We will provide an update within 1 hour. Reference: {incident-link}
- Update cadence: 30m until root cause identified, 60m after that while in mitigation, then hourly as needed.
- Post-incident summary: include timeline, root cause, customer impact (tokens/requests affected), remediation steps taken, and scheduled follow-ups.

Escalation Matrix (customer-impacting)
- Sev1 (platform down for tenant or billing integrity risk): escalate to IC, eng-platform lead, CS Director, and Legal/Finance on call. Pager -> immediate bridge.
- Sev2 (degraded inference quality/latency impacting SLAs): Support first responder -> eng-serving-runtime -> CS Lead -> scheduled customer update.
- Sev3 (telemetry or low-impact errors): owner team handles within standard SLAs; escalate on repeated bounce.

Implementation Checklist (for Support & Platform)
- [ ] Annotate all alerts with owner_team, severity, and runbook link.
- [ ] Configure the alert router: suppression windows, grouping keys, and dedupe rules.
- [ ] Add Slack channel / PagerDuty escalation bindings per team.
- [ ] Create customer comms templates and CS contact list per enterprise tenant.
- [ ] Create dashboards: Alert noise panel, top firing rules, MTTA/MTTR trends, per-tenant alert volume.

Sample Alert Definitions (examples for runtime engineers)
- p95 latency spike (Prometheus):
  - ALERT RuntimeHighP95Latency
  - IF histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, instance)) > 2.0
  - FOR 3m
  - LABELS { severity="page", owner_team="eng-serving-runtime" }

- Tenant error rate (example rule):
  - ALERT TenantHighErrorRate
  - IF increase(http_requests_total{status=~"5..",tenant=~".+"}[5m]) / increase(http_requests_total[5m]) > 0.05
  - LABELS { severity="page", owner_team="support" }

Oncall Handover & Fatigue Reduction Practices
- Handover notes: outgoing oncall must leave the top 3 active alerts, any muted rules, and follow-ups in the team Handoff doc.
- Scheduled quiet windows: non-urgent noisy alerts may be auto-muted during scheduled low-traffic maintenance windows if documented and approved by CS.
- Rotation length: prefer 7-day rotations for platform teams and 3-4 day rotations for support to balance knowledge and burnout. Review quarterly.
- Pager triage cap: any engineer receiving >12 pages in a day must have their load reviewed by manager; consider temporary rotation pause.

Post-Incident & Continuous Improvement
- Post-Incident Tasks (within 72 hours):
  1. Full RCA and timeline (eng owner).
  2. Action items assigned with owner and due date.
  3. Alert audit: any alert that fired and did not lead to remediation must be suppressed or reclassified.
  4. Customer-facing summary drafted and approved by CS Lead and Legal (if PII/financial impact).
- Quarterly Alert Review: each team publishes an alert inventory and noise metrics; operations council reviews and approves suppression/threshold changes.

Playbook for Customer-Facing Degraded Performance (quick checklist)
1. Validate incident and measure customer impact (requests, latency, error rate).
2. If impact confirmed, IC open and CS Lead notified.
3. Apply symptomatic mitigations (traffic shaping, fallback models, tenant routing to warm capacity).
4. If mitigation succeeds, prepare customer rollback and update comms.
5. If mitigation fails, escalate to engineering and determine rollback or multi-tenant fallback.

Appendices
A. Useful Queries and Tools
- Traces: `trace-search --tenant {tenant} --from {iso-ts} --to {iso-ts}`
- Top error sample: `curl https://telemetry.redwood/api/errors?tenant={t}&window=10m | jq .top`
- Alert router health check: `kubectl -n observability exec router-0 -- /bin/healthcheck`

B. Contacts
- Support Pager: #support-pager (Slack) and PagerDuty escalation policy: Redwood-Support-Escalation
- Eng Platform oncall: eng-platform-oncall@redwood.internal
- CS Director: cs-director@redwood.internal

C. Change History
- 2026-03-01: Created by Asha Murthy (published).
- 2026-06-10: Added sample PromQL and tenant mitigation API examples (reviewer: Benji Park).
- 2026-10-12: Expanded metrics section and added rotation guidance (reviewer: Lena Hoffmann).

If you are implementing these changes, coordinate with Observability (eng-platform) and Support for a staged rollout. For assistance, tag @cs-ops in #ops-requests.

title: Tenant data redaction and privacy verification runbook
content:
Summary:
This runbook defines the operational process for verifying tenant data privacy and performing content redaction for Redwood Dedicated and Private deployments. It is intended for customer success engineers (CSEs), on-call support (Tier 2/3), and SREs responsible for tenant onboarding or remediation after a data exposure event. The goal is to provide repeatable, auditable steps to detect, redact, verify redaction, and produce evidence for customers and internal compliance teams.

Scope and applicability:
- Applies to: Dedicated tenants, Private (VPC/on-prem) deployments, and customer-supplied S3/FTP data sources connected to Redwood ingestion pipelines.
- Does NOT replace: Legal escalation, incident response (see security incident runbook), or full data-erasure certification for decommissioning.
- When to use: suspected exposure of PII, customer request for emergency redaction, detection from telemetry indicating sensitive token leakage, or audit-triggered verification.

Primary owners and escalation path:
- Primary owner: Customer Success (Tenant Safety) — Maya Patel (owner)
- Secondary: Security & Compliance — Priya Ramanathan
- SRE on-call: paged for remediation steps that require infra changes
- Legal: contacted for confirmed data breaches or regulatory exposures
- Escalation matrix (hours): 0–2h (CSE triage); 2–6h (security review + redaction plan); >6h (exec brief + customer notification)

Pre-remediation checklist (perform before any destructive redaction):
1) Confirm scope: tenant_id, dataset(s), date ranges, ingestion paths.
2) Snapshot evidence: collect sample hits, query results, and save logs to secure bucket (retain per compliance).
3) Create a remediation ticket in Zendesk and link to internal incident channel.
4) Schedule a maintenance window if live customer traffic might be impacted.

Required information table (for ticket creation):
| Field | Expected value | Example |
|-------|----------------|---------|
| Tenant ID | Redwood tenant GUID | tenant-3f2a1c |
| Source type | ingestion / webhook / s3 / manual | s3 |
| Affected datasets | index name / table / bucket path | embeddings-prod/2026-07/* |
| Time range | ISO timestamps | 2026-07-30T00:00:00Z–2026-07-31T23:59:59Z |
| PII types suspected | email / ssn / card / key | email, aws_access_key |

Detection and triage steps (ordered):
1. Run targeted queries on the ingestion index using the tenant_id and time range. Example CLI:
   redwoodctl search --index embeddings-prod --tenant tenant-3f2a1c --query "contains_email:true" --from 2026-07-30 --to 2026-07-31
2. If matches found, capture a hashed sample (SHA256 of the content) and save to secure evidence bucket with access restricted to "tenant-safety" and "security-compliance" roles.
3. Cross-reference model-call traces and request payloads to identify whether the PII was used in embeddings generation, prompt storage, or persisted logs.
4. Classify exposure severity (low/medium/high) using the table below:
   - Low: single non-sensitive email, non-identifiable metadata.
   - Medium: multiple emails, names tied to identifiers, partial SSN.
   - High: full SSN, card numbers, keys, or any confirmed exfiltration to external endpoints.

Redaction strategy (choose one, document chosen option in ticket):
- In-place redaction (preferred when index supports field-level deletion): redact fields and reindex sanitized records.
- Backfill & reindex (preferred for embedding indexes): remove affected documents and trigger a reingest from source after sanitization.
- Token replacement (emergency mask): replace sensitive tokens with stable pseudonyms (e.g., <REDACTED_EMAIL_1>) when immediate availability must be maintained.

Redaction commands and examples:
- Field-level delete (Elasticsearch example):
  curl -X POST "https://es.prod/redwood-index/_delete_by_query" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"query": {"bool": {"must": [{"term": {"tenant_id": "tenant-3f2a1c"}}, {"term": {"contains_email": true}}, {"range": {"@timestamp": {"gte": "2026-07-30","lte": "2026-07-31"}}}]}}}'

- Embeddings index removal + reingest pattern (S3 source):
  1) Mark objects in S3 with metadata tag redaction-pending=true using aws cli
  aws s3api put-object-tagging --bucket customer-bucket --key path/to/object --tagging 'TagSet=[{Key=redaction-pending,Value=true}]'
  2) Run redwoodctl reingest --source s3://customer-bucket/path --tenant tenant-3f2a1c --filter-tag redaction-pending=true

Verification and proof generation:
1) After redaction, rerun the original detection queries and save zero-match screenshots/CLI output into the ticket.
2) Produce an evidence bundle (zip) that includes: query outputs, redaction commands run (with timestamps), reingest job IDs, and access-control audit logs.
3) Create an audit note in the tenant record: who performed redaction, justification, and links to evidence.

Automated verification jobs (recommended):
- Nightly PII sweep for high-risk tenants (cron job): runs yara-like patterns against ingested text and flags matches.
- Weekly sample rehydrate and diff: rehydrate a 1% random sample of embeddings and check for PII via NER model.
- Alerts: create PagerDuty for >3 distinct PII matches in 24h from same tenant.

SLOs and thresholds:
- Triage SLA: acknowledge within 60 minutes for suspected PII exposures (business hours), 4 hours outside business hours.
- Containment SLA: implement initial redaction plan within 8 hours for medium, 4 hours for high.
- Verification SLA: provide evidence packet to customer within 48 hours for medium, 24 hours for high.

Customer communication templates (summary):
- Initial notification: brief description, mitigation steps in progress, expected time-to-update.
- Post-verification: summary of actions taken, evidence bundle link, recommended follow-ups, security contact.
(Templates stored in: /confluence/customer-success-and-support/templates/privacy-notifications)

Audit logging, retention, and compliance notes:
- Store redaction evidence in the encrypted evidence bucket (retention 365 days by default) and add a retention override only with Security approval.
- Record all redaction commands and job IDs in the tenant audit trail.
- For regulated customers (PCI/PHI), require Security & Legal sign-off before communicating externally.

Rollback and accidental-redaction recovery:
1) If accidental over-redaction occurs, restore from index snapshot created before redaction.
2) Steps: request SRE snapshot-restore, validate restored documents in a staging tenant, then reapply correct redaction script.
3) Document root cause and add a prevention checklist to the ticket.

Post-incident review (within 7 days):
- Participants: CSE owner, Security, SRE, Product (if needed).
- Deliverables: RCA, updated detection rules, change to onboarding checklists, communication lessons learned.

Appendix: Useful commands and helpers
- redwoodctl evidence bundle create --ticket TICKET-1234 --out /tmp/TICKET-1234-evidence.zip
- redwoodctl reindex --index embeddings-prod --tenant tenant-3f2a1c --job-name reindex-20260802
- NER quick-check (Python snippet):
  from transformers import pipeline
  ner = pipeline('ner', model='dbmdz/bert-large-cased-finetuned-conll03-english')
  ner('Contact me at m.patel@example.com')

Related pages and references:
- Tenant onboarding acceptance tests (telemetry & privacy checks)
- Security incident response runbook
- Templates: privacy-notification and executive-brief

Revision history:
- 2026-03-12: Created by Maya Patel
- 2026-06-18: Added automated verification recommendations (Diego Alvarez)
- 2026-08-02: Clarified SLA targets and added S3 reingest pattern (Priya Ramanathan)

title: Enterprise Support Lifecycle — Dedicated & Private Customers Playbook
content:
Overview

This playbook defines the end-to-end support lifecycle for Dedicated and Private customers (Reserved capacity, VPC/on-prem installs). It covers onboarding milestones, operational handoff criteria, support tiers and SLAs, escalation pathways, routine health checks, QBR agenda items, and common workarounds. Use this document during pre-sale handoffs, SOW signings, and the first 90 days of customer go‑live.

Scope

- Applies to Redwood customers with Dedicated capacity contracts or Private deployments (VPC or on‑prem).
- Excludes Hosted self‑serve customers; see hosted support guidelines for that flow.
- Covers technical onboarding, first‑line support (CSE/Customer Success), and engineering escalations.

Definitions

1. CSE: Customer Success Engineer (Redwood) — primary technical point of contact during onboarding and post‑go‑live.
2. TAM: Technical Account Manager — commercial/relationship owner for enterprise contracts.
3. Severity levels: P0 (service down / data loss), P1 (major degradation), P2 (partial impact), P3 (questions / minor issues).

Owner & Operating Model

- Primary owner: Customer Success team (owner_team).
- Support partners: Eng‑SRE (incidents), Eng‑Serving‑Runtime (performance/regressions), Security (sensitive incidents), Professional Services (deployment customization).
- Communication channels: Slack private channels, PagerDuty for P0/P1, Zendesk ticketing for ongoing work, JIRA for engineering bugs.

Support Tiers & SLAs

| Tier | Target response (business) | Target initial response (after hours) | Availability SLO | Typical use cases |
|------|--------------------------:|-------------------------------------:|---------------:|------------------|
| Platinum | 1 hour (P0/P1) | 2 hours | 99.95% | Global products, revenue critical |
| Enterprise (Dedicated) | 2 hours (P0/P1) | 4 hours | 99.9% | High throughput, single‑tenant pools |
| Private (on‑prem) | 4 hours (P0/P1) | 8 hours | N/A (customer infra) | Regulated / air‑gapped environments |

Notes: SLAs above reflect support response targets and availability guarantees in contracts. For Private deployments, Redwood provides support for the Redwood stack; infrastructure SLOs remain customer responsibility unless otherwise contracted.

Onboarding checklist (90‑day timeline)

1. Pre‑kickoff (sales → CS handoff)
   - Deliverables: signed SOW, network requirements, account and org IDs, requested models and capacity targets.
   - Owner: TAM + CSE
2. Week 0: Technical kickoff (within 5 business days)
   - Agenda: architecture review, network/firewall requirements, key contacts, success criteria, go‑live date.
   - Output: shared onboarding RFC and project plan.
3. Week 1–2: Environment provisioning and connectivity test
   - Tasks: allocate GPU pools (Dedicated) or validate on‑prem package install, verify routing, test TLS and KMS integration, run sample inference load test (10k tokens/min baseline).
   - Acceptance: successful end‑to‑end request/response and logs streaming to observability.
4. Week 3–4: Performance tuning & baselining
   - Tasks: collect p50/p95 latencies, throughput targets, KV cache hit rate, token cost estimates; tune batching and quantization profiles.
   - Output: Performance baseline doc and recommended runtime config (attached to ticket).
5. Week 5–8: Integration and validation
   - Tasks: implement SDK usage, validate streaming and function calling features, run privacy/security checklist (audit logging), complete sample evaluation prompts.
6. Week 9–12: Staged rollout and runbook handoff
   - Tasks: canary traffic ramp, failure injection test (see runbook steps), finalize runbooks and oncall rotation, schedule first monthly QBR.

Onboarding Handoff Criteria (must be met to declare ‘Ready for Business’)

- Successful canary serving at 10% traffic for 72 hours with no P1 regressions.
- Performance within 15% of baseline p95 targets.
- Runbook and escalation matrix published and acknowledged by customer.
- Backup and restore (model weights/kv) verified (if applicable).

Integration & Handoff Artifacts (table)

| Artifact | Owner | Where to store | Required by |
|---------|------|----------------|------------|
| Network diagram + ACL list | Customer & CSE | Confluence + secure S3 | Week 0 kickoff |
| Performance baseline report | CSE + Runtime Eng | Confluence | Week 4 |
| Runbooks (operational + failover) | CSE | Confluence | Week 9 |
| Oncall rotation & PagerDuty play | SRE | Internal oncall repo | Week 9 |

Escalation matrix & Procedures

1. P0 (Service down / data integrity risk)
   - Triage: Immediate page to SRE + CSE + TAM (use PagerDuty P0 routing).
   - First 15 minutes: Confirm scope, gather logs (request ID, node IDs, GPU pool status).
   - 15–60 minutes: Eng‑Serving‑Runtime lead and oncall SRE coordinate mitigation (rollback to previous model version / failover region).
   - Communication: Customer Slack channel + status page entry every 15 minutes.
2. P1 (Major degradation)
   - Triage: Page CSE and SRE P1 oncall.
   - Initial response within SLA target.
   - Mitigation actions: adjust batching policies, scale GPU pool, apply temporary rate limits.
3. P2/P3 (Partial impact / questions)
   - Tracked in Zendesk; CSE handles initial remediation; engineering bug filed if needed.

Contact roles and escalation contacts (example)

- Customer Success (primary): Nora Patel — CS Slack / zendesk handle @nora.p
- Technical Account Manager: Mateo Alvarez — tam@redwood.ai
- SRE oncall (P0/P1): use PagerDuty rotations (see internal rota).
- Eng‑Serving‑Runtime escalation: eng-runtime-oncall@redwood.ai

Incident Communication Templates

- Initial P0 template (post to Slack & email):
  Subject: [P0] Region X — Inference service degraded for <customer-name>
  Body: Short summary, impact (requests/sec affected), start time, immediate mitigation steps taken, next update ETA (15m).

- Postmortem structure (published within 72 hours for P0):
  1) Summary and impact numbers (duration, error count)
 2) Root cause analysis
  3) Timeline of key events
  4) Remediation & preventative actions with owners and due dates

Health Check cadence & QBR agenda

- Weekly operational health check (15–30 mins): CSE + customer SRE/TAM. Topics: error rate, p95 latency, cache hit ratio, model drift alerts, open high‑priority tickets.
- Monthly operational review: deeper metrics, billing & usage anomalies, any upcoming rollouts.
- Quarterly Business Review (QBR) template (high level):
  1) Executive summary & usage trends
  2) Reliability review (SLOs, incidents since last QBR)
  3) Performance and cost optimization recommendations (batching/quantization changes)
  4) Roadmap & model roadmap alignment
  5) Action items & owners (tracked in Confluence)

Example monitoring checks (recommended)

- p95 latency (api.generate) — warn at 200ms, critical at 300ms.
- 5m error rate (5xx) — warn at 0.5%, critical at 2%
- GPU utilization per pool — warn at 70%, critical at 85%
- KV cache hit rate — warn below 40%

YAML alert example to share with customer (for on‑prem Prometheus):

alert: HighP95Latency
expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) > 0.3
for: 5m
labels:
  severity: critical
annotations:
  summary: "p95 latency > 300ms for 5m"

Known limitations & pragmatic workarounds

- Model cold start cost: Large models may show elevated first‑token latency. Workaround: warm pools by scheduled synthetic warmup jobs.
- File‑system performance on certain on‑prem appliances: If model load times exceed 30s, stage weights onto tmpfs or use preloaded snapshot.
- Audit log gaps for early releases: If audit-log retention is shorter than required, enable S3‑forwarding and verify lifecycle policies.

Support ticket template (Zendesk)

- Subject: [P#] <short description> — <customer-org>
- Fields: severity, customer impact, request-id(s), affected model/version, region/pool, recent deploy id, attachments (logs).

Operational runbook excerpt — failover (simplified)

1) Detect: Confirm p95 latency > critical threshold + error rate spike.
2) Reduce load: Apply temporary rate limit to non‑critical routes.
3) Failover: Route traffic to standby Dedicated pool or fallback model variant.
4) Rollback: If deploy suspected, rollback to previous model in 30 minutes and monitor for stabilization.
5) Post‑incident: Start RCA and schedule fixes.

Metrics & success criteria for CSE handoff

- 99% of onboarding tasks closed in 90 days.
- No more than 1 P1 incident in first 30 days post‑go‑live.
- Performance within 15% of baseline for 95% of traffic.

Appendices

A. Reference links
- Internal PagerDuty rota: <internal-link/pagerduty/rota>
- Oncall runbook repo: <internal-link/runbooks/oncall>
- Perf baseline template: <internal-link/templates/perf-baseline>

B. Example checklist (copyable)
- [ ] Kickoff completed
- [ ] Network tests passed
- [ ] TLS & KMS verified
- [ ] E2E sample requests successful
- [ ] Performance baseline recorded
- [ ] Runbooks published
- [ ] QBR scheduled

If you have questions about applying any checklist item to a specific customer configuration, contact the CSE lead or open a Zendesk ticket with tag `dedicated-onboarding`.

title: Billing & Quota Discrepancy Triage and Customer Communication Playbook
content:
Summary:
This playbook describes the end-to-end triage, technical investigation, remediation, and customer communications process for billing and quota discrepancies reported by enterprise, dedicated, and private tenants. It covers initial intake, data collection, technical verification, remediation options (including safe-mode and temporary caps), crediting thresholds, and the escalation matrix when there is suspected metering, aggregation, or accounting system error.

Purpose and scope:
- Purpose: Resolve customer-reported billing or quota issues quickly while preserving trust and avoiding unnecessary credits.
- Scope: Applies to all enterprise and Dedicated/Private tenants. Does not replace formal legal billing dispute processes if requested by finance; instead this playbook prepares evidence for finance handoff.
- Out-of-scope: One-off developer test accounts on self-serve plans (handled by Growth Support).

Owner and Roles:
- Primary owner: Customer Success (owner_team).
- Technical lead: Oncall Observability Engineer (eng-platform / eng-sre on rotation).
- Billing coordinator: Revenue Ops / Billing team (finance-legal).
- Communications owner: Customer Success AM or Technical Account Manager (TAM).
- Escalation contacts: SRE Pager (pager duty), Billing Ops Slack channel (#billing-ops), Legal counsel (only invoked for formal disputes).

SLA expectations (customer-facing):
1) Acknowledgement: 1 business hour during business hours (M-F 08:00–18:00 local).
2) Triage update: within 6 hours with next steps and ETA for investigation.
3) Technical findings: within 24 hours for straightforward cases; up to 72 hours for cross-system investigations.
4) Temporary mitigation or credit decision: within 3 business days for high-impact outages; 7 business days for complex disputes requiring finance/legal review.

Intake checklist (what the support engineer/TAM must capture at first contact):
- Customer report summary (short): how the discrepancy was discovered and customer impact.
- Tenant identifier (tenant_id), account id, contract #, billing cycle, affected date/time window.
- Examples: Request IDs, timestamps, sample requests/responses, and any exported telemetry the customer has.
- Quota measure: type of quota (concurrent requests, daily token budget, embedding units, dedicated GPU-hours) and expected vs observed values.
- Billing issue type: overcharge, missing charge, incorrect tier, double-billing, credit not applied, invoice mismatch.
- Permission to pull account-level logs and invoices (confirm customer consent where required).

Initial technical verification steps (engineer):
1) Reproduce the reported symptom on internal dashboards where possible. Check tenant-level metrics: ingress token count, egress, request count, peak concurrency.
2) Compare telemetry across three sources: API gateway logs, serving runtime metering, and billing aggregation pipeline (ETL).
3) Verify timezones and billable windows; many disputes come from timezone misalignment and daylight savings.
4) Check for recent model rollouts, canaries, or bulk ingest jobs that could spike usage.
5) If rate-limited or throttled: verify whether client retries inflated apparent request counts (see retry amplification section below).

Important commands and paths (internal):
- Fetch tenant metrics (CLI): redwood-metrics query --tenant <tenant_id> --from <ISO> --to <ISO> --metrics tokens,requests,embeddings
- Pull serving logs (K8s): kubectl -n tenant-<id> logs deployment/ingress-proxy --since=72h | grep <tenant_id>
- Billing pipeline debug: billing-tools fetch-aggregate --tenant <tenant_id> --cycle <YYYY-MM> --output json
- Correlate request -> invoice: correlate-requests --requests-file requests.json --billing-file billing_aggregate.json --out correlation_report.json

Common root causes and detection heuristics:
- Retry amplification: large client retries (short client backoff) cause repeated billable requests; detection: identical payloads with short (<5s) spacing from same source IP and client_id.
- Dual-ingress misconfiguration: tenant traffic routed via two ingress endpoints (e.g., edge+proxy) resulting in double-counting. Detect via mismatched request IDs across gateways.
- Billing ETL lag or late-arriving events: billing aggregate missing streaming events until next window. Detect via delta between real-time runtime counters and billing aggregate for same window.
- Timezone/window mismatch: Customer expecting UTC but invoice uses customer local timezone.
- Quota assignment errors: customer migrated between SKUs and quota assignment did not update. Detect by comparing tenant record in Account DB vs Quota Service.

Mitigations and remediation paths:
- Immediate safe-mode: apply temporary quota cap or soft throttle to prevent further spend while investigating. Steps: Customer Success -> Confirm with customer -> Apply cap using admin console -> Notify SRE and Billing.
- Temporary credit provisional: For high-impact customers where a suspected metering bug exists, provision a provisional credit (up to $X or N% of disputed amount) pending final reconciliation. Finance must be notified for credits > $5k.
- Recompute and replay billing window: Re-run ETL with corrected inputs or use the reconciliation tool to regenerate invoice for the affected period.
- Rollback configuration changes: If a recently deployed routing or metering change caused double-counting, rollback the change via standard deploy rollback runbook and re-process billing events.

Escalation matrix (when to escalate):
- Level 1 (Support Engineer): handles routine mismatches and data collection.
- Level 2 (SRE / Observability): escalate if root cause requires log-level correlation or cluster-level replay.
- Level 3 (Billing Ops): escalate for invoice regeneration, formal credits, legal notices.
- Level 4 (Executive / Legal): escalate when customer demands formal dispute, regulatory implication, or credit > $50k.

Severity mapping and action table:
| Severity | Customer impact | Priority | Target action | Owner |
| P0 | Service offline or runaway spend causing major business impact | Urgent | Acknowledge 1h; safe-mode; exec notify; provisional credit | Support + SRE + Finance |
| P1 | Significant unexpected spend or quota exhaustion impacting core flows | High | Acknowledge 1h; mitigate with cap; technical investigation 24h | Support + SRE |
| P2 | Moderate discrepancy or invoice mismatch with low immediate impact | Medium | Investigate 72h; prepare evidence for billing ops | Support |
| P3 | Cosmetic or minor invoice rounding differences | Low | Document and correct on next invoice cycle | Support/Billing Ops |

Customer communication templates (short examples):
- Initial acknowledgement (1 hour):
  "Hi <Customer>, thank you for reporting this. We have opened ticket RED-<id> and will investigate. We will provide an update within 6 hours. Could you please confirm the tenant_id and attach any example request IDs or invoice line items? -- <TAM>"

- Update after initial verification (6 hours):
  "Update: We verified that X tokens were recorded in runtime vs Y in billing aggregate for window <time>. We are re-running the billing reconcile and have applied a temporary cap to prevent further unexpected spend. Next update by <ETA>. -- <TAM>"

- Resolution and credit summary: 
  "Resolution: Root cause was <cause>. We have regenerated the invoice for <period> and applied a credit of $<amount> to your account. The corrected invoice is attached. If you prefer, we can arrange a follow-up call to review details. -- <Billing Ops>"

Audit evidence required for Finance handoff:
- Correlation report (request -> billing line).
- Raw logs for sampled requests (timestamps, request_ids, tenant_id).
- ETL run IDs and commit hashes if a code change is suspected.
- Internal incident timeline and mitigation actions.

Retry amplification guidance (preventative):
- Recommend that customers use exponential backoff with capped retries and idempotency tokens for non-idempotent operations.
- For high-volume ingest jobs, encourage batch APIs that are cheaper and reduce per-request accounting.

Operational runbook snippets (step-by-step):
1) Intake: Create ticket, record all intake checklist items, assign P0/P1/P2/P3.
2) Triage: Run quick reconciliation scripts and capture delta.
3) Mitigate: If runaway spend, apply safe-mode cap and notify account.
4) Investigate: Pull logs, run correlation, reproduce if possible.
5) Remediate: Recompute invoice or rollback offending release.
6) Communicate: Use templates. Confirm final credit and close ticket after finance sign-off.

Post-incident actions and telemetry improvements (retrospective):
- If root cause is internal: open engineering ticket to fix meter or ETL bug, include test cases and synthetic workload to reproduce.
- If caused by customer behavior: create guidance for the customer and update onboarding docs to include recommended retry/backoff and suggested quotas.
- Add or refine synthetic monitors that compare runtime live counters with billing aggregates and auto-alert on >5% drift for any tenant for a 12-hour sliding window.

Metrics to track for this playbook's effectiveness:
- Mean time to acknowledgement (target < 1 hour).
- Mean time to provisional mitigation (target < 6 hours for P0/P1).
- % disputes resolved without finance credit (target 60% where correction is internal).
- False positives in synthetic monitor (target < 2% per month).

Appendix A: Example correlation command usage
- Example: redwood-metrics query --tenant 98765 --from 2026-05-01T00:00:00Z --to 2026-05-02T00:00:00Z --metrics tokens,requests > /tmp/98765_runtime.json
- Example reconciliation: correlate-requests --requests-file /tmp/98765_runtime.json --billing-file /tmp/98765_billing.json --out /tmp/correlation_98765.json

Appendix B: Sample temporary customer-facing email for P0
"""
Subject: Immediate action taken on your account — temporary cap applied and investigation underway

Hi <Customer Name>,

We have applied a temporary spend cap to your account to stop any further unexpected charges and begun a full investigation. Our support ticket is RED-<id>. We will update you within one hour with the current findings and next steps. We apologize for the disruption and appreciate your patience.

If you would like immediate contact, reply to this email and we will arrange a call.

Best,
<Your TAM>
"""

Document maintenance:
- Review cadence: quarterly.
- Last review: 2026-06-10. Next review target: 2026-09-10.
- Suggested reviewers: Billing Ops, SRE, Observability, Legal for credit policy updates.

Related reading and links:
- Billing dispute & chargeback resolution playbook (finance).
- Tenant observability onboarding kit.
- Synthetic health and billing reconciliation monitors design doc.

End of document.

title: Enterprise Rate Limit & Quota Adjustment — Operational Playbook
content:
Summary
-------
This playbook defines the operational procedures for investigating, mitigating, and permanently resolving customer-impacting rate limit and quota incidents for enterprise accounts. It also documents short-term cost-protection actions we can take on behalf of customers (or for platform health) and the escalation paths for cross-team involvement.

Scope
-----
- Applies to enterprise, dedicated, and private customers where quota/rate-limit events affect availability, throughput, or unexpected billing spikes.
- Excludes self-service free-tier rate-limit automation unless the event escalates to an enterprise impact.
- Covers: token/per-minute throttles, concurrent connection limits, embedding unit quotas, burst policies, and billing protection requests.

Definitions
-----------
- Rate limit: per-customer throughput constraints (requests/minute, tokens/minute, connections).
- Quota: monthly or annual allocation associated with billing commitments (tokens, embedding units, inference-hours).
- Cost protection: temporary measures (throttling, capped billing, emergency credit) to prevent unexpected financial exposure.
- Mitigation owner: CS engineer or SRE assigned to runbook execution.

Monitoring & Alerts
-------------------
Primary signals and alert sources:
- Redwood Console / Alerts: "customer.rate_limit.error_rate > 5% over 5m" and "customer.quota_usage >= 90%".
- Billing pipeline: anomalous daily spend > 3x baseline or > configured alert thresholds.
- Support tickets tagged: "rate-limit" or "quota-spike".
- Customer-provided telemetry via partner integrations (when available).

Dashboards and links (examples):
| Dashboard | Purpose | Owner |
| / | / | / |
| Customer Quota Overview | Live quota consumption by customer and model | Eng SRE |
| Per-tenant Rate Limit Heatmap | Active throttles and 429 spike sources | Serving Runtime |
| Billing Anomaly Feed | Real-time billing spikes > configured thresholds | Finance Ops |

SLOs and Thresholds Table
-------------------------
| Signal | Warning Threshold | Critical Threshold | Initial Action |
| Tokens/min usage | 75% of quota | 90% of quota OR sudden rise > 3x baseline | Notify CS + generate invoice hold? |
| 429 error rate | 1% over 5m | 5% over 5m | Start triage, apply temporary throttles |
| Concurrent connections | 70% of allowed | 95% of allowed | Autoscale/migrate to dedicated pool |

Immediate Triage Steps (0–15 minutes)
-------------------------------------
1. Acknowledge: CS on-call acknowledges ticket/alert in Slack #cs-oncall and sets incident status.
2. Identify customer and tier: confirm customer_id, deployment type (hosted/dedicated/private), active models and pinned versions.
3. Gather telemetry: attach links to the customer quota dashboard, recent API logs (last 30 minutes), and billing spike report.
4. Assign Mitigation Owner: CS engineer if customer-facing actions required; escalate to SRE if platform-wide.

Triage Checklist (copy into ticket):
- Customer ID: 
- Region: 
- Deployment type: hosted/dedicated/private
- Models in use: 
- First observed: timestamp
- 429 % (5m avg): 
- Tokens/min trend (last 1h): 
- Billing delta (24h): 

Mitigation Playbook (ordered)
----------------------------
A. Short-term customer-protective actions (CS-led)
1. Soft-throttle: apply a short-lived per-key throttle via the Console: set requests/min to 60% of current peak for 15 minutes. Use only with customer consent for non-critical workloads.
2. Temporary quota top-up: for committed enterprise customers, request a one-time quota add via billing ops. Use emergency path (see Appendix). Document with a CHANGE request.
3. Cost cap: enable temporary billing cap for the tenant (blocks further consumption and prevents surprise charges). Requires Finance Ops approval for enterprise with contractual implications.
4. Response template: send initial customer message acknowledging the event, actions taken, and ETA for permanent fix (template in Customer Communications Templates section).

B. Platform/Service mitigations (SRE-led)
1. Autoscale: if the customer is in Dedicated and available GPU pool has spare capacity, trigger migration to a bigger pool using the dedicated migration runbook.
2. Bypass routing: for latency-critical traffic, route to an alternative region or compatible model variant with lower resource usage.
3. Rollback recent model rollouts or configuration changes if the issue correlates with a recent change (check below for rollout correlation queries).

Sequence example (fast path):
1) CS acknowledges and applies soft-throttle (step A1).
2) SRE examines logs; if platform-constrained, SRE scales or migrates (B1).
3) Finance Ops authorizes temporary quota top-up (A2) if customer revenue risk is high.

Escalation Matrix
-----------------
- CS Engineer (level 1): initial mitigation, customer comms. Slack: @cs-oncall. Pager: CS-Pager-1.
- SRE Lead (level 2): platforms mitigations, autoscaling, migrations. Pager: SRE-Pager-1.
- Product / Legal (level 3): contract interpretation for cost protection, emergency credits. Email: enterprise-legal@redwood.ai.
- Executive Escalation: required for outages > 4 hours affecting revenue-critical customers. Contact: Head of CS, Head of SRE.

Customer Communications Templates
--------------------------------
Initial acknowledgement (short):
Hi <Customer Contact>,

We detected elevated rate-limit errors on your account beginning at <time>. We've applied a temporary throttle and started a deeper investigation. We'll update you within 60 minutes with next steps.

- CS team

Initial acknowledgement (detailed):
Hi <Customer Contact>,

Summary: Elevated 429s and unexpected quota usage observed starting <time>.
What we did: applied a short throttle to protect your spend and avoid downstream failures; opened an internal mitigation ticket and requested SRE support.
Next steps: full triage, temporary quota top-up or migration if appropriate, and a post-incident report within 72 hours.

If you prefer us to pause traffic to avoid charges, reply with "PAUSE" and we'll block new requests until you confirm.

Regards,
Redwood Customer Success

Permanent Remediation and Change Requests
-----------------------------------------
- Root cause analysis: collect logs, compare traffic patterns, and test with reproducer prompts.
- Engineering change request (ECR): if the incident was caused by misconfigured default quotas or a model rollout, file ECR with the serving-runtime team. Include reproducible steps and expected rollout backout plan.
- Policy updates: for recurring quota spikes caused by customer integrations, propose updated onboarding checks in Integration Guides (see Related Pages).

Requesting a permanent quota increase (process)
1. CS prepares the quota increase request: justification, expected new quota, billing implications, timeline for change.
2. Submit request to Finance Ops with tagging: "quota-increase: enterprise". Attach usage dashboards and customer PO if available.
3. Finance Ops approves and creates change in billing system. Engineering applies config change and verifies in console.

Rollback and Recovery Steps
-------------------------
1. If a mitigation (throttle/top-up) causes regression, immediately revert the change and notify the customer.
2. Use the serving-runtime rollout dashboard to rollback to the prior model version if a recent rollout correlates with the event.
3. After rollback, run smoke tests with representative prompts and monitor metrics for 30 minutes before marking resolved.

Post-Incident Review and QBR Metrics
-----------------------------------
Required items in the PIR (post-incident review):
- Timeline of detection, mitigation, and resolution with timestamps.
- Root cause and contributing factors.
- Customer impact (minutes of degraded service, error rate, billing exposure in $).
- Action items with owners and deadlines.

Suggested QBR / health-check metrics to include for enterprise customers:
- Monthly quota utilization rate (avg and 95th percentile).
- Number of quota-related incidents in last 90 days.
- Cost-protection actions invoked (count + $ amount protected).
- Average time-to-mitigate for rate-limit events.

Ownership and Contacts
----------------------
- Primary owner: Customer Success (Enterprise CS Team).
- Secondary owner: Eng SRE (platform-scale incidents).
- Finance ops contact: finance-ops@redwood.ai.
- Emergency legal: enterprise-legal@redwood.ai.

Appendix: sample CLI/API commands and config snippets
----------------------------------------------------
1) Example: apply soft throttle via admin API (pseudo-CLI)

curl -X POST https://admin.redwood.ai/internal/quota-adjust \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"customer_id":"cust_12345","action":"throttle","requests_per_min":300,"duration_minutes":15,"reason":"temporary-mitigation"}'

2) Example: check recent 429s in logs (query language):

select count(*) from api_logs where customer_id='cust_12345' and status=429 and ts > now() - interval '15 minutes'

3) Billing emergency quota top-up request (email subject template):
Subject: [Quota Top-up Request] cust_12345 — +2M tokens — urgent
Body: customer, justification, expected new monthly quota, PO/contract reference, CS owner, requested effective time.

Change record template (for engineering):
- Change: apply_quota_increase_cust_12345
- Owner: eng-runtime-oncall
- Rollback: revert_quota_cust_12345
- Validation: verify quota reflected in console and ingestion metrics

Postmortem checklist (before closing ticket)
-------------------------------------------
- [ ] Timeline and evidence attached
- [ ] Customer notified of resolution and root cause summary
- [ ] Engineering action item created for permanent fix
- [ ] Review scheduled with customer (if they request) within 7 business days
- [ ] Lessons added to Integration Guide for relevant SDKs if applicable

Last updated by Rosa Kim on 2026-02-14.

title: Enterprise failure injection and resilience runbook
content:
Summary
-------
This runbook describes a safe, repeatable program for conducting failure-injection and resilience validation exercises for enterprise tenants that use Redwood Inference (hosted, Dedicated, or Private). The goal is to validate customer-facing behaviours (failover, throttling, model fallback, and data isolation) and ensure Customer Success (CS) and Support teams have playbooks for communication, rollback, and remediation.

Scope
-----
- Applies to enterprise onboarding, stability game-days, and periodic resilience testing for dedicated/private tenants.
- Exercises include network partitioning, ingress throttling, model variant fallback, KV cache eviction, GPU preemption simulation, and telemetry loss scenarios.
- Not intended for experiments that modify persistent customer data or escalate to legal/regulatory gates without prior approvals.

Goals and acceptance criteria
----------------------------
- Assert that customer SLOs degrade gracefully with automated fallback policies engaged (latency SLO: p95 < 750ms under nominal; during controlled degradation, p95 may increase to 2s but requests must not return internal server error > 1% for 1h).
- Validate canary rollback path: 100% automated switchback to last-known-good model or region within 5 minutes of abort.
- Telemetry completeness: 99% of experiment events are recorded and grouped under experiment_id tag within Redwood tracing/metrics.
- Customer-facing incidents are handled within the escalation SLA documented in the Customer Incident Communications Matrix.

Owners and roles
----------------
- Experiment owner: Customer Success (CS) Solutions Engineer (primary contact for customer).
- Run executor: Platform Reliability (or customer SRE for Private installs).
- Observability lead: Observability engineer assigned to the tenant.
- Escalation liaison: Support Tier 2 lead.
- Approval authority: Customer Success manager + Security reviewer for Private/Dedicated customers.

When to use this runbook
------------------------
1. During enterprise onboarding (week 2–6) to validate cutover safety nets.
2. Prior to production model changes where rollback risk must be validated.
3. As part of quarterly resilience game-days or after major infra updates.
4. Whenever a customer requests a proof-of-resilience report for compliance.

Prerequisites
-------------
- Experiment plan approved (signed by CS manager and customer SRE if Private).
- Maintenance window scheduled and customer opt-in obtained when required.
- Backup/abort hooks verified (model pinning, routing policy override, traffic split control).
- Observability asserts configured: synthetic journey, per-route p50/p95/p99, error-rate alerts, and experiment_id tagging.
- Safety guardrails enabled: automatic circuit-breaker with threshold and manual abort endpoint.

Experiment catalogue (examples)
-------------------------------
Each experiment below includes intent, expected customer impact, telemetry assertions, and safe abort steps.

1) Ingress throttling (controlled egress saturation)
- Intent: validate adaptive rate limiter and quota-protector webhook under client surge.
- Customer impact: elevated latency, some client 429s expected within quota design.
- Telemetry asserts: 95th-percentile latency and 429-rate should match modelled profile.
- Abort: revert rate limiter to baseline policy, clear client token bucket; traffic should normalize within 60s.

2) Regional failover simulation (control-plane switch)
- Intent: ensure request routing falls back to alternate region or model variant without exposing token leakage.
- Customer impact: ~100–300ms added latency for routed requests, no data exposure.
- Telemetry asserts: requests routed via fallback path include header X-Redwood-Fallback: true and trace link.
- Abort: revert routing policy, trigger warm cache rebuild for primary region.

3) Model variant fallback under degraded GPU throughput
- Intent: validate automatic model switchover to quantized/fast variant when latency SLO is violated.
- Customer impact: small semantic variance in outputs; provide notice to customers during test.
- Telemetry asserts: model_variant metric should flip to fallback model id and tokenization stats logged.
- Abort: force-publish pinned model version for tenant and drain fallback nodes.

4) KV cache eviction and cold-start behavior
- Intent: emulate cache purge and validate KV cold-warm startup times and cost spike characteristics.
- Customer impact: transient cost spike and higher token latency for first requests.
- Telemetry asserts: cache-miss-rate, kv-lookup-latency, and per-token cost tags.
- Abort: warm caches using synthetic seeds and verify hit-rate > 90% within window.

5) Telemetry ingestion throttling / partial metrics loss
- Intent: test how downstream alerting and QBR metrics behave when observability sampling rate is reduced.
- Customer impact: none to user-facing systems, but internal dashboards may report degraded fidelity.
- Telemetry asserts: sampling tags and synthetic route alerts must surface to incident channel; missing spans must be flagged.
- Abort: restore sampling rate and reindex experiment traces.

Safe experiment design pattern
-----------------------------
- Start small: run experiments in a narrow tenant subset or sandboxed tenant.
- Canary stages: 1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% traffic, with explicit automated hold/pause gates between stages.
- Timebox: every stage should have a maximum duration and an automatic rollback trigger on threshold breach.
- Communication: annotate customer slack channel and incident bridge before starting.

Scheduling, communications and customer consent
---------------------------------------------
- For hosted customers: experiments requiring visible degradation must include email + console notification 72 hours before, and a maintenance window with opt-out link.
- For Dedicated/Private customers: follow the private deployment change control and require SRE signoff; schedule during agreed maintenance windows.
- Template customer notification: (1) summary of intent, (2) expected customer impact, (3) start/end time, (4) roll back criteria, (5) contact matrix.

Execution checklist (pre-flight)
-------------------------------
1. Verify feature-flag toggles and model pins are set.
2. Confirm observability asserts and experiment_id tagging in tracing.
3. Snapshot current routing and scaling policies.
4. Notify stakeholders and create incident bridge.
5. Run low-risk dry-run in sandbox.
6. Have abort playbook open and test abort endpoint.

Numbered procedure: running an ingress throttling experiment
---------------------------------------------------------
1. Create experiment run: POST /internal/experiments with body {\n   "experiment_id": "exp-<tenant>-20260610",\n   "type": "ingress-throttle",\n   "stage": "canary-1"\n}
2. Apply rate limit via adaptive-rate-limiter API:
   redwood-cli rate-limit apply --tenant <ID> --policy ex-throttle-1 --limit 100req/s
3. Verify traces: run query tracer.query("service:ingress AND experiment_id:<id>")
4. Wait 10 minutes monitoring p95 and error rate.
5. If thresholds exceeded (error-rate > 1% or p95 > 2s), call abort.
6. Abort: redwood-cli rate-limit revert --tenant <ID> --policy ex-throttle-1
7. Confirm traffic normalized and post metrics to experiment dashboard.

Telemetry assertions and SLO checks
----------------------------------
- Mandatory dashboards for every experiment: synthetic-journey, per-tenant error-rate, per-model latency, token-cost per-minute, and experiment_event_log.
- SLO guardrails to configure before start: p95 latency thresholds, error-rate ceilings, and model-fidelity signal (eval set pass-rate).
- Example PromQL checks:
  - latency_p95_tenant{tenant="<id>"} > 2.0 (trigger),
  - http_error_rate{tenant="<id>"} > 0.01 (trigger)

Abort/rollback paths and verification
------------------------------------
- Automated abort: circuit-breaker triggers will stop canary progression and run abort-hooks.
- Manual abort: support-runbook command documented below can be executed by Support Tier 2.
- Verification: confirm post-abort metrics return to baseline within the timewindow defined in the run plan.

Customer communications and incident templates
--------------------------------------------
- Short blurb for console banner: "Redwood is running a resilience validation for tenant <org>. Expected transient latency increases; contact <CS> for concerns."
- Incident postmortem summary template for customer: summary, timeline, root cause, impact, corrective actions, and compensation if SLA breached.

Post-experiment analysis and QBR deliverables
--------------------------------------------
- Deliverables: resilience report (one-pager), experiment artifacts (traces, config diffs, logs), customer-facing summary, and action items.
- QBR signals to include: mean-time-to-rollback, percentage of experiments passing acceptance, number of customer-visible degradations, and suggested mitigations (e.g., increase warm-start capacity, adjust model fallback thresholds).

Risk matrix and mitigations
--------------------------
- High risk: experiments that touch customer data pipelines or long-lived storage (require legal review). Mitigation: use synthetic data or isolated sandbox.
- Medium risk: full-tenant failover tests during business hours. Mitigation: timebox and use staged canaries.
- Low risk: observability sampling reductions. Mitigation: test in non-production first.

Appendix: CLI snippets and Kubernetes plays
-----------------------------------------
- Sample abort command (Support Tier 2):
  curl -X POST \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $SUPPORT_TOKEN" \
    https://internal-api.redwood.local/v1/experiments/exp-<tenant>-20260610/abort

- Force model pin via API:
  redwood-cli models pin --tenant <ID> --model-id rwd-fast-quant-1 --reason "abort experiment"

- Simulate GPU preemption (dev-only):
  kubectl cordon <node> && kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data

Postmortem and RCA template
---------------------------
1. Executive summary (3 bullets)
2. Timeline of events (with timestamps in UTC)
3. Impact analysis (customers affected, duration, business impact)
4. Root cause hypothesis and evidence (traces, logs, recordings)
5. Remediation steps and owners (who will fix, timeframe)
6. Follow-up experiments and regression checks

Change log
----------
- 2026-02-12: Initial published runbook by Maya Chen.
- 2026-04-21: Added telemetry asserts and PromQL examples (reviewer: Evan Hart).
- 2026-06-10: Expanded experiment catalogue with KV cache eviction case and regional failover scenario.

Related pages
-------------
- See also: enterprise-onboarding/private-deployment-acceptance (link internal), incident-response-security runbooks, and observability-fallback-circuit guide.

Contact and escalation list
--------------------------
- CS Solutions (primary): maya.chen@redwood.ai
- Platform Reliability: platform-sre@redwood.ai
- Support Tier 2: support-t2@redwood.ai
- Observability: obs-team@redwood.ai

title: Enterprise Avalanche Surge: Preparation and Stabilization Playbook
content:
Summary:
This playbook describes the end-to-end procedures for preparing for, detecting, and stabilizing a sudden high-volume traffic event we call an "avalanche surge" for enterprise tenants (e.g., large customer marketing campaigns, viral product hooks, or third-party spikes). It covers pre-cutover preparation, detection thresholds, immediate actions (first 15–60 minutes), escalation behavior, automated mitigations, safe-failback, customer communications templates, and post-incident QBR artifacts.

When to use this playbook:
- Any customer-facing production spike where observed request volume, token throughput, or request concurrency increases by >= 5x baseline within a 5 minute window.
- Alerts triggered by the Avalanche Detector rule (see Telemetry) or when a customer reports widespread latency / 5xxs tied to a single tenant.

Goals and acceptance criteria:
- Preserve customer-visible availability (success rate >= 99.5%) during surge where possible.
- Maintain 95th percentile token latency <= 2x baseline SLO for dedicated tenants; notify if this cannot be met.
- Ensure cost containment and fairness across multi-tenant pools (automatic throttles engaged when thresholds are hit).
- Provide clear, timely communications to stakeholders and customers within 15 minutes of detection.

Key services and components referenced:
- ingress-proxy (tenant routing / ingress rate shaping)
- model-router (routes to model variants: full, quantized, low-cost-fallback)
- kvcache (KV cache for prefix reuse)
- rate-limiter (per-tenant quotas and adaptive throttling)
- telemetry-gatekeeper (synthetic checks, avalanche detector)
- batch-gateway (batched inference for asynchronous workloads)
- billing-telemetry (cost-attribution and anomaly flags)

Pre-runbook: preparation checklist (owner: customer-success + eng-sre)
1) Tenant profiling: ensure each enterprise customer has a current surge profile in the tenant registry. Profile fields: typical QPS, peak QPS observed historically, critical endpoints, consumer-facing SLAs.
