2) Canary thresholds: add tenant to synthetic canary with 30s and 10s latency checks; ensure synthetic runner frequency is 1m during high-risk windows.
3) Capacity reservations: for Dedicated customers verify reserved GPU capacity is provisioned and autoscale policy is set (min, target, max).
4) Communication plan: assign primary CSM, escalation engineer (oncall SRE), and product contact. Document these contacts on the tenant row in the Customer Ops spreadsheet.
5) Automated fallback policy: ensure the tenant has an allowed fallback model-variant list and an explicit fallback policy (e.g., prefer quantized-7b then low-cost-llama if full model unavailable).
6) Cost protections: optional quota-protector enabled for tenant with threshold 2x baseline QPS by default.

Telemetry and detection (owner: eng-sre / telemetry):
- Avalanche Detector rule: 
  - Trigger when tenant QPS >= 5x baseline over 5 consecutive minutes OR 95th-token-latency >= 3x baseline for 6+ minutes.
  - Secondary triggers: sudden KV cache miss ratio > 50%, rate-limiter saturation, or sustained 5xx > 0.5% for 10 minutes.
- Dashboards to monitor: Tenant Surge Overview, Pool Utilization, Model Router Latency by variant, Rate-limiter saturation heatmap, KVC cache hit/miss.
- Automatic Pager: if Avalanche Detector triggers, send page to SRE oncall with priority P1 and notify CSM and account owner via email/SMS bridge.

Immediate response (first 0–15 minutes):
1) Triage owner acknowledges alert within 2 minutes.
2) Run a quick impact sweep: check error rates, 95th latency, queue depth on ingress-proxy, and which model-variant is receiving traffic.
3) Communication out: send initial customer-facing note (template below) within 15 minutes.
4) If available capacity exists in dedicated pool: issue temporary horizontal scale:
   - CLI: rcap scale --tenant <TENANT_ID> --pool dedicated --delta +2 --reason "avalanche temporary"
5) If autoscale cannot provision fast enough, initiate controlled throttling:
   - Increase per-tenant rate-limiter token cost for non-critical routes by 50% (see routing rule list).
   - Enable adaptive batching for synchronous endpoints where latency impact is acceptable.
6) Activate model-router fallback: shift a percentage of traffic to lower-cost quantized variants. Example policy: 30% -> 60% -> 100% over 10-minute windows if success rate stabilizes.

Stabilization checklist (minutes 15–60):
- Observe error rate and latency trends every 60s.
- If 5xxs remain high after fallback and throttles, escalate to multi-tier mitigations:
  - Enable per-endpoint backpressure headers to clients (Retry-After).
  - Move non-critical tenants on same pool to spillover routing.
  - Offload heavy batch workloads to batch-gateway with relaxed latency SLA.
- If costs are rising quickly, flip on the quota-protector to enforce hard cap; notify customer immediately.

Escalation and ownership matrix:
- CSM: primary customer comms, coordinates commercial/cost decisions.
- SRE oncall: technical triage and execution of scaling/route changes.
- Serving runtime lead (if >30 minutes): coordinates kernel/quantization swap or emergency model-reload.
- Product PM (optional): decides on temporary feature gating if surge is caused by a new product hook.

Automated mitigations (what we rely on):
- Adaptive batching toggle (runtime flag): toggles between low-latency and high-throughput batch profiles.
- KV cache aggressive TTL fallback: short-circuit cache rehydration for high churning prefixes.
- Prefill cold KV for high-frequency prefixes using synthetic runner.
- Traffic-splitting policy: automated progressive traffic shifting to fallback variants with health checks.

Safety and rollback (safe-failback):
1) If degradation persists or customer explicitly requests rollback, revert traffic split to primary model and drain fallback nodes gracefully.
   - CLI: model-router set-split --tenant <TENANT_ID> --primary 100 --fallback 0 --drain 300s
2) If scaling caused noisy neighbor effects, revert temporary scale and open a capacity incident to procure additional GPUs.
3) Record all changes with runbook tags and timestamps. Use audit CLI: runbook log --incident <INC_ID> --changes "..."

Customer communications (templates):
- Initial (within 15m):
  Subject: [Redwood] We detected elevated traffic for your account — initial update
  Body: Hello <CustomerName>,

  We detected a sudden increase in traffic for your account beginning at <time>. Our automated systems flagged an "avalanche" event and our operations team is actively stabilizing traffic. Expected impacts: transient increased latency and limited throttling on non-critical routes. We will follow up in 15 minutes with more detail.

  Owner: <CSM name> | support@redwood.ai | Escalation: +1-555-0123

- Follow-up (30–60m):
  Subject: [Redwood] Update on traffic surge for your account — actions taken
  Body: Hello <CustomerName>,

  Summary of actions taken: enabled adaptive batching, progressive model fallback (quantized variants), and temporary rate shaping on non-critical endpoints. Current status: success rate: 99.3% (target 99.5%), 95th-token-latency: 1.8x baseline. Next steps: monitoring and preparing safe-failback.

  If you need to pause traffic from your side we recommend returning HTTP 429 with Retry-After.

Post-incident actions and QBR artifacts (owner: CSM + SRE):
- Incident timeline with all runbook logs and CLI commands.
- Cost delta report: compute minutes used vs baseline and estimated bill impact.
- Root-cause hypothesis and mitigation grooming ticket for product/serving teams.
- Customer-facing RCA draft and final RCA with timeline and preventative actions.
- Add a segment to the next QBR titled "Surge events and capacity readiness" including:
  - What happened, customer impact, timeline of mitigations, residual risk, recommended capacity reservations, and any commercial remedies.

Operational playbook snippets (CLI examples):
- Scale dedicated pool: rcap scale --tenant TEN-42 --pool dedicated --delta 3 --tag "avalanche-temp"
- Set progressive fallback: model-router split --tenant TEN-42 --primary 70 --fallback 30 --policy progressive-10m
- Lock quota-protector: quota-protector lock --tenant TEN-42 --limit 2x-baseline --reason "avalanche"

Postmortem checklist (owner: SRE lead):
1) Collect telemetry (raw traces, ingress logs, model router metrics, KV cache traces).
2) Annotate timeline with all automated interventions and human actions.
3) Complete RCA within 7 business days and share with customer and internal stakeholders.
4) Propose concrete changes: autoscale tweak, pre-warming policy, fallback variants list update, cost-guard thresholds.

Appendices:
A. Quick triage matrix (one-page):
- Symptom: High 95th latency; Likely cause: KV cache miss spike or model hot path saturation; Immediate action: enable quantized fallback, prefill KV, scale.
- Symptom: Rising 5xx; Likely cause: ingress-proxy queue overflow; Immediate action: enable backpressure headers, spill to batch gateway, scale ingress.

B. Dashboard IDs and links: Tenant Surge Overview: dash-ops-tn-surge-17; Model Router Health: dash-model-router-04; KV Cache Monitor: dash-kvcache-02.

C. Recommended QBR slides (bullets):
- Event summary, mitigation timeline, compute delta, recommended SLA/commit changes, open action items with owners and target dates.

Document ownership and review cadence:
- Owner: Customer Success (playbook steward)
- Technical reviewer: Eng SRE (runtime stability)
- Review cadence: annual or after any enterprise-scale surge incident.

Revision history:
- 2026-11-10: Initial draft (Marcus Lee).
- 2026-12-18: Added automated mitigation CLI and telemetry thresholds (Aisha Patel).
- 2027-01-15: Formal review and publication; added customer comms templates and QBR artifacts (Sofia Ramirez).

title: Enterprise Self-Heal Automation Playbook
content:
Summary

This playbook describes the standardized approach Redwood Customer Success (CS) and Support teams use to implement, validate, and operate enterprise self-heal automation for customer production incidents. Self-heal automation refers to fully automated remediation actions that are safe to run without human approval when a monitored condition maps to a validated remediation recipe. The goal is to reduce mean time to recovery (MTTR), lower toil for on-call engineers, and preserve customer SLAs while maintaining auditability and revertibility.

When to use this playbook

- Enterprise customers with a Dedicated or Private deployment where the customer has agreed to automated remediation in their onboarding contract.
- Routine, well-understood failure classes where automated remediation has been tested end-to-end and has a clear rollback path.
- Situations where automation improves availability and cost predictability (e.g., autoscaling policies, model switchover, cache invalidation, connector restarts).

Scope and non-goals

- Scope: networking reconnections, connector/ingest restarts, GK (gateway) route fallback, model variant switchovers, KV-cache warmup, automated quota adjustments with throttled rollback.
- Non-goal: Automated changes to customer data schema, irreversible data migrations, or actions that materially change billing without human sign-off.

Roles and ownership

- Customer Success (CS): negotiates automation consent, documents high-level workflows in the customer onboarding packet, approves business-level safety constraints.
- Support (Tier 1/2): triage alerts, confirm automation mapping, escalate when automation does not resolve incident.
- Platform Reliability (Eng-SRE): implements and maintains automation recipes and ensures telemetry coverage and safety gates.
- Customer Oncall: receives notices of automatic remediation and can request immediate pause/rollback.

Alerting and detection (signals)

Primary signals that may trigger self-heal automation:

1) Service health metrics exceeding thresholds
   - API error rate > 5% over 3 minutes AND p95 latency > 1.2s on critical routes
   - Model inference tail latency > 2x baseline for 5 minutes
2) Capacity saturation
   - GPU pool utilization > 92% sustained for 10 minutes
   - Pod eviction rate > 1/min for 3 minutes
3) External integrations failing
   - Upstream telemetry forwarding HTTP 5xx > 2% for 5 minutes
4) Data pipeline stalls
   - Connector lag > 30 minutes and backlog growth > 10% over 15 minutes

Every trigger must map to a single canonical alert ID (format: cs/selfheal/{customer}/{alert-type}) and include the following context: customer_id, tenant_type (hosted/dedicated/private), service, region, recent_error_snippet, and current_runbook_version.

Safety gates and preconditions

Automation must not run unless all the following are true:

- Customer has opted-in in the onboarding contract and the opt-in record exists in the CS portal.
- The active SLOs for the customer are known and automation allowed for the SLO class.
- At least one recent successful telemetry heartbeat from the effected service in the last 5 minutes.
- No active incident labeled "major-outage" for the same customer.
- Automation run quota for the customer has not been exhausted (default 6 runs / 24 hours).

Automation recipes and examples

Each automation recipe is a small documented unit with: trigger definition, preconditions, exact steps, rollback procedure, runbook link, required RBAC role, and audit metadata. Examples below are canonical recipes we use as templates.

Recipe: connector-restart-with-backoff
- Trigger: connector HTTP 5xx > 3% for 5 minutes OR connector crashlooping > 3 restarts / 10 minutes
- Preconditions: opt-in, recent heartbeat, automation quota available
- Steps (automated):
  1. Create incident stub and link to customer's CS record.
  2. Annotate monitoring event with automation_run_id and start timestamp.
  3. Graceful restart of connector (POST /customer/{id}/connectors/{id}/actions/restart?mode=graceful) with timeout 45s.
  4. Wait for successful healthcheck: GET /health/connectors/{id} (retry 3x @ 10s).
  5. If healthcheck passes, warm cache prefetch job (async).
  6. Close incident stub with resolution code AUTOMATED_RESTART_SUCCESS.
- Rollback: If healthcheck fails after step 3, perform a forced restart and escalate to Support Tier 2.
- Audit: All steps produce structured events to /events/selfheal with policy_id and automation_run_id.

Recipe: model-variant-failover
- Trigger: model container OOM or degraded token throughput > 40% for 10 minutes
- Preconditions: compatible fallback model available for customer's deployment, model cost tier alignment checked
- Steps:
  1. Mark route read-only for new non-essential low-priority requests for 60s.
  2. Gradually shift 10% traffic to fallback variant and monitor quality/regression metrics over 5 minutes.
  3. If quality regression <= 3% on customer eval prompts and latency improves, continue rollout to 100% with incremental steps (10% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100%).
  4. Notify customer and CS with rollout timeline and telemetry links.
- Rollback: Immediate rollback to pinned model if regression > 3% at any step.

Implementation patterns and safe primitives

- Idempotent actions: All APIs called by automations must be idempotent or have safe detect-and-noop semantics.
- Circuit breaker: Automations include a local circuit that prevents repeated runs against the same target if failure rate does not drop after 3 attempts.
- Scoped throttling: Rate-limit automation actions per customer and per resource to prevent cascading failures.
- Audit trail: Structured JSON logs for every automation run (fields: automation_run_id, policy_id, initiator=automation, preconditions, steps, outcomes, timestamps, owner_contact).

Change control and deployment process for recipes

1. Author drafts recipe as a PR in infra-selfheal repo. PR must include unit tests, integration tests that run in the staging harness, and a safety checklist.
2. Reviewer from Eng-SRE + CS reviews. At least one security review if the recipe touches credentials or billing APIs.
3. Merge to canary namespace. Run automated canary for 72h against internal staging tenants.
4. After canary, run a small customer pilot (customer consented) for 7 days. Collect metrics.
5. Publish recipe and enable policy with default disabled. CS will opt-in customers per onboarding workflows.

Testing and validation

- Unit tests: validate precondition checks and idempotency.
- Integration tests: run simulated alert flows in the staging harness with injected failures.
- Chaos tests: periodically run chaos scenarios (connector failures, model OOMs) in a controlled environment.
- Observability: every test run writes to a test-results index and dashboard with pass/fail and measured MTTR impact.

Runbook: manual handoff if automation fails

1. Alert hits Support Tier 1 with automation_run_id. Tier 1 examines automation logs and outcome.
2. If automation indicates escalation, escalate to Tier 2 with all artifacts and recent logs.
3. Tier 2 can trigger manual remediation steps defined in recipe replaced with the suffix "-manual" (e.g., connector-restart-with-backoff-manual).
4. If remediation is not possible, initiate incident bridge and follow incident process in oncall-and-incident-response/runbooks.

Customer onboarding checklist for self-heal

- Confirm opt-in consent documented in contract and entered in CS portal.
- Capture customer SLOs and forbidden actions (e.g., no automated model changes).
- Define allowed automation classes (networking, connectors, autoscaling, model failover) and list explicit exclusions.
- Validate telemetry coverage: API, model, and infra metrics mapped and test alerts fired in staging.
- Schedule pilot window and agree on rollback SLA.

KPIs and QBR evidence

- Primary KPIs: automated MTTR reduction (target: 35% lower MTTR vs manual), automation success rate (target >= 85%), false positive initiations (target <= 5% of runs).
- QBR artifacts: automation run summary (CSV), incident reduction chart, example case studies, telemetry dashboards links, and an agreed action list for tuning policies.

Safety checklist before enabling automation for a customer

- [ ] Contract opt-in present and timestamped
- [ ] Telemetry heartbeat validated in prod -> last 5 minutes
- [ ] Run quota and circuit settings reviewed with CS
- [ ] Emergency pause playbook shared with customer oncall
- [ ] Customer acceptance test (CAT) executed in canary environment

Example webhook payload (automation start event)

{\n  "automation_run_id": "arun-20260112-9b7f",\n  "policy_id": "policy-connector-restart-v2",\n  "customer_id": "cust-4512",\n  "trigger": "connector_http_5xx_threshold",\n  "preconditions": ["opt_in", "heartbeat_ok"],\n  "initiator": "automation",\n  "timestamp": "2026-01-12T18:22:11Z"\n}

CLI example: pause automation for a customer

# Pause automation for cust-4512 for 1 hour
redwoodctl customers automation pause --customer cust-4512 --duration 60m --reason "customer requested pause for maintenance"

Operational play: emergency pause and rollback

- CS or oncall may invoke redwoodctl to pause automation immediately; this action must generate a notification to CS leads and the customer oncall.
- To rollback a model switchover: redwoodctl routeset rollback --customer cust-4512 --from variant-b --to variant-a --force \\n  (Allowed only if manual approval present or regression threshold exceeded.)

Appendix: related pages and templates

- Template: automation-recipe-template.md (infra-selfheal repo)
- Incident path: sources/confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/incident-process/major-incident-playbook-2025.json
- Example: onboarding opt-in UX: sources/confluence/customer-success-and-support/enterprise-onboarding/onboarding-optin-policy-2025.json (internal reference)

Change log

- 2026-01-12: Initial published draft (Leah Kim)
- 2026-02-10: Added model-variant-failover recipe and safety gates; updated KPIs (Leah Kim)

Contact and escalation matrix

- CS Lead (auto programs): leah.kim@redwood.ai
- Eng-SRE oncall: +1-555-0102 (PagerDuty: eng-sre-oncall)
- Support Tier 2 inbox: support-tier2@redwood.ai

title: tenant-snapshot-and-safe-replay-runbook-2026
content:
Summary:

This runbook describes the approved, auditable process for capturing production-like snapshots of a tenant (configuration + sanitized telemetry + optional minimal payloads) and safely replaying traffic in a controlled sandbox for debugging hard-to-reproduce issues. The goal is to enable Customer Success and Support to reproduce customer-facing failures while minimizing data exposure and preserving customer SLAs and compliance commitments.

Scope:
- Applies to Dedicated and Private tenants and to hosted tenants where customer consent and legal approvals are present.
- Intended for escalations where live debugging is not possible (non-deterministic model regressions, KV-cache corruption, routing anomalies, telemetry sampling gaps, prefix-caching defects).
- Excludes full PII exports; any snapshot containing sensitive data must be redacted per the Data Handling section below.

Owner & Roles:
- Requestor: Customer Success or Support engineer who opened the escalation (owner of the ticket).
- Data Guardian: Security & Compliance engineer responsible for approving redaction and retention policy for the snapshot.
- Sandbox Operator: Platform engineer who performs the capture and replay steps.
- Observability Lead: Owner of tenant telemetry dashboards who validates that replay data surfaced expected signals.

SLO / Safety Requirements:
- Snapshot requests must be approved within 4 business hours for Sev2 and within 24 business hours for Sev3 after ticket triage.
- Replays must not be performed against production model endpoints. Replays occur in an isolated sandbox (no egress to customer endpoints).
- All artifacts stored in snapshot buckets expire automatically within 30 days; retention extensions require Data Guardian sign-off.
- Audit records (who requested, who approved, who executed) must be recorded in the ticket and the snapshot metadata.

Prerequisites & Approvals:
1. Customer consent recorded in the ticket (link to signed form or email).
2. Data Guardian approval if snapshot includes any of the following fields: email, ssn, phone, or free-text fields longer than 2k characters.
3. Sandbox namespace and replay cluster provisioned (see Commands section).
4. Dry-run of redaction script must pass local test vectors before execution.

Data Handling & Privacy Controls:
- Redaction-first policy: before any storage or transfer, run the redaction pipeline. Redaction steps: mask_email, pseudonymize_ids, remove_attachments, truncate_large_text.
- Redaction tool: redwood-data-sanitize v1.3 (see example below).
- Pseudonymization: replace tenant_user_id with deterministic salt keyed by tenant-id to allow joinability within the replay but not to reidentify the user set.
- Access control: snapshot buckets use encryption (KMS) and are only accessible by the Data Guardian and Sandbox Operator principals for the duration of the retention window.

Runbook: Capture a tenant snapshot (step-by-step)
1) Open a ticket and collect approvals (see Prerequisites).
2) Create snapshot job:
```bash
# create job metadata in support-api
support-cli snapshots create --tenant-id=tenant-123 --reason="Investigate intermittent truncation" --duration-days=30 --notify="#cust-success-ops"
```
- This registers the snapshot request and assigns an id (SNAP-<id>).

3) Run redaction pipeline against a streaming export (managed by telemetry exporter):
```bash
telemetry-exporter stream --tenant tenant-123 --from="2026-06-20T00:00:00Z" --to="2026-06-20T01:00:00Z" | \ 
  redwood-data-sanitize --policy minimal --salt="tenant-123-salt" > /tmp/SNAP-SNAPID.jsonl
```
- The policy flags available: minimal, default, strict (strict removes nearly all free-text fields). Default should be avoided without Data Guardian approval.

4) Validate sanitization: run the snapshot validator which checks for residual PII markers and for field size anomalies.
```bash
snapshot-validator /tmp/SNAP-SNAPID.jsonl --check-pii --check-length
```
- Validator returns non-zero on issues; resolve them before proceeding.

5) Upload to secure bucket:
```bash
aws s3 cp /tmp/SNAP-SNAPID.jsonl s3://redwood-snapshots/tenant-123/SNAP-SNAPID.jsonl --sse aws:kms --tagging "retention=30d,requestor=alice"
```
- File metadata in support-api: link to S3 object, retention expiry, approvers.

Runbook: Safe replay (isolated sandbox)
1) Provision sandbox replay cluster (if not already available for tenant): request via infra-ops-runbook. Typical cluster name pattern: replay-tenant-123-<shortid>.
2) Load snapshot into replay environment:
```bash
replayctl create --name=replay-tenant-123-01 --snapshot=s3://redwood-snapshots/tenant-123/SNAP-SNAPID.jsonl --model-variant=redwood/ggml-13b-q4_0 --no-external-io
```
- --no-external-io enforces that any external callbacks are disabled in the runtime layer.

3) Execute replay scenario sets (start with conservative traffic profile):
```bash
replayctl run --name=replay-tenant-123-01 --traffic-profile=conservative --duration=15m --trace=on
```
- Traffic profiles defined: conservative (10% of peak QPS), nominal (30%), aggressive (70%); aggressive requires Observability Lead sign-off.

4) Observe telemetry and capture diffs: validate tokenization traces, latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99), KV-cache hit ratios, model logits diffs exported to /tmp/replay-diffs.json.

Decision matrix: When to escalate after replay
- If replay reproduces incident: open RCA path and schedule a model/serve fix with engineering. Attach replay artifacts, diffs, and sanitized logs.
- If replay does not reproduce: increase traffic conservatively (one step) and re-run once. If still not reproducible, capture a second, longer snapshot (no more than 2x duration) with approver consent.
- If redaction fails to meet compliance checks: stop and escalate to Security & Compliance; do not store or forward the artifact.

Rollback & Clean-up
- After troubleshooting completes, the Sandbox Operator must delete the replay cluster and all ephemeral compute and then mark the snapshot as archived.
- Archival: snapshot objects remain in S3 until retention expiry. To remove early: Data Guardian must sign removal request.
- Deletion steps (example):
```bash
replayctl destroy --name=replay-tenant-123-01 || true
aws s3 rm s3://redwood-snapshots/tenant-123/SNAP-SNAPID.jsonl
```
- Record deletion confirmation in the ticket with timestamps and operator identity.

Audit & Logging
- All snapshot actions produce an audit entry in the support-api: create, approve, sanitize, upload, replay-start, replay-end, destroy.
- Tickets must include the snapshot id and KMS key id used for encryption.

Common failure modes & mitigations
- Sanitizer rejects edge-case attachments: convert attachments to metadata-only and reference a stub file; escalate to Data Guardian if attachments are required for repro.
- Model variant mismatch: use the model-variant-matrix to choose a closest compatible variant; note differences in result artifacts.
- Replays diverge due to random seeds: run with seed fixed when available (replayctl --seed=42).

Checklist (pre-playback)
- [ ] Ticket has customer consent link.
- [ ] Data Guardian approval recorded.
- [ ] Redaction pipeline run and validator OK.
- [ ] Snapshot uploaded to KMS-encrypted bucket.
- [ ] Replay cluster provisioned and network-isolated.
- [ ] Observability dashboard configured for replay traces.

Commands & Example Configs
- Redaction config snippet (YAML):
```yaml
policy: minimal
fields:
  - mask_email
  - pseudonymize: [tenant_user_id]
  - truncate: {field: user_input, max_chars: 2000}
```
- Replay traffic profile JSON (example):
```json
{
  "name": "conservative",
  "qps_multiplier": 0.1,
  "arrival_process": "poisson"
}
```

Ownership & Escalation Contacts
- Customer Success: Aisha Ramirez (aisha@redwood.com)
- Platform / Sandbox Ops: Jonas Park (jonas@redwood.com)
- Security & Compliance (Data Guardian): Meera Gupta (meera@redwood.com)
- Observability Lead: Lars Hoffman (lars@redwood.com)

References & Related Docs
- See tenant-observability-contract-lifecycle-and-versioning-playbook for telemetry contract requirements.
- See tenant-data-classification-and-onboarding-privacy-scan-playbook for data classification thresholds.

Appendix: Quick play example (minimal reproduction)
1) request snapshot: support-cli snapshots create ... -> SNAP-42
2) export + sanitize -> /tmp/SNAP-42.jsonl
3) upload -> s3://redwood-snapshots/tenant-foo/SNAP-42.jsonl
4) create replay -> replayctl create --name=tmp-replay --snapshot=... --no-external-io
5) run conservative profile and collect diffs

This runbook is intended to be used verbatim when possible. Where local or customer-specific policies diverge, follow the stricter control. If any step is unclear, contact the Security & Compliance Data Guardian before proceeding.

title: Model Change Approval & Customer Governance Runbook
content:
Summary
-------
This runbook defines the governance, approval paths, operational checks, and customer communication templates for any model or model-configuration change that impacts enterprise customers (Hosted, Dedicated, or Private deployments). It is intended for Customer Success, Product, SRE, Serving Runtime, and Security teams. The goal is to reduce surprise regressions, keep customers informed, and make rollbacks predictable.

Scope
-----
- Applies to model version swaps, quantization profile changes, prompt-template migrations, model serving config changes (e.g., max_tokens, sampling defaults), and runtime kernel changes that may alter output semantics or latency by >5%.
- Includes both Redwood-initiated and customer-requested changes for enterprise tenants.
- Excludes purely infra-only upgrades that do not alter model observable behavior (see Appendix A for classification rules).

Why we need this
-----------------
Enterprise customers require predictable output quality and clear change windows. Uncoordinated changes generate escalations, churn risk, and operational burden. This runbook balances speed with customer safety using a two-track approval model (minor vs major) and objective telemetry gates.

Primary stakeholders and ownership
---------------------------------
- Customer Success (CS): final customer communications, risk assessment for accounts, QBR notes.
- Product: change justification, rollout strategy, canary criteria.
- Eng - Serving Runtime: technical rollout, canary execution, rollback hooks.
- Eng - SRE: capacity and latency SLO guardrails, escalation path.
- Security/Compliance: signoff for private deployments or regulated customers.
- Owner: Customer Success (contact: marcos.rivera@redwood.com).

Decision categories (classification)
-----------------------------------
1) Minor change (fast-track):
   - Non-production-facing prompt-template tweaks, minor sampling seed updates, telemetry-only instrumentation.
   - Expected impact: negligible change to model outputs; latency delta <5%.
   - Approval: Product + CS peer review.
2) Major change (full review):
   - Model family change (e.g., v1->v2), quantization profile change altering float->int path, new architecture variant, or changes that affect factuality/behavior.
   - Expected impact: potential behavioral regressions or latency change >=5%.
   - Approval: Product + CS + Serving Runtime + SRE + Security (if Private) + Exec sponsor.

Approval matrix (summary)
-------------------------
- Minor: Product (owner) -> CS notify -> rollout during maintenance window or low-traffic canary.
- Major: Model Change Request (MCR) RFC -> Cross-functional review meeting -> Signed approval via ticket (Jira PRD) -> Scheduled canary -> Customer opt-in for early testing or staged opt-out.

Pre-change checklist (must be completed before any scheduled rollout)
-------------------------------------------------------------------
- Define classification (minor/major) and document justification.
- Owner assigns cross-functional reviewers (list in ticket).
- Identify impacted customers (list enterprise tenants) and their SLA tier.
- Create a rollback plan with RTO goals and quick rollback triggers.
- Create automated telemetry assertions (see Telemetry & validations).
- Schedule rollout window and reserve SRE on-call for the change window + 2 hours.
- Draft customer-facing communication (CS drafts, Product approves).

Change execution procedure (canary & rollout)
-------------------------------------------
1) Pre-canary steps (T-48 to T-2 hours):
   - Deploy change to internal staging and run the predefined prompt-suite (see Appendix B).
   - Run synthetic traffic at production-like token distribution for 30m.
   - Verify cost delta and latency distribution vs baseline.
2) Canary (T):
   - Route 0.5-2% steady-state traffic from canary tenants or synthetic tenancy to the new variant for 1 hour.
   - Run automated evals: output-delta metric, hallucination score, top-k token distribution, and latency P95.
   - Monitor errors and backend resource consumption.
3) Scale canary (T+1h):
   - If all assertions pass, increase to 10% for 2 hours.
   - If still green, schedule a rolling increase with checkpoints at 25%, 50%, 100% each with 2-hour observation windows.
4) Abort/rollback:
   - Any assertion failure or customer-reported regression escalates to the Runbook Owner who initiates rollback. See Rollback criteria.

Telemetry & validations (objective gates)
---------------------------------------
Create assertions that are executed automatically during rollout. Example set: 
- Functional quality: output-delta rate < 2% across canonical prompt-set (per tenant).
- Hallucination signal: composite hallucination score delta <= 0.5 points (normalized).
- Latency: P95 latency delta <= 15% absolute or <= 200ms (whichever is smaller).
- Error budget: 5xx rate not to exceed 0.1% above baseline.
- Cost: per-token compute cost delta <= 10% for Dedicated customers without prior consent.
- Tokenization/regression checks: no >0.2% increase in truncation/invalid-token counts.

Incident/escalation flow for regressions during rollout
-----------------------------------------------------
1) Tier 1 detection: automated assertion breach -> Alert on Slack #canary-alerts and PagerDuty to Serving Runtime on-call.
2) Triage (10–30 minutes): Owner and runtime on-call validate and reproduce.
3) Customer notification (30–60 minutes): If customer MCR was not pre-signed, CS sends a status update using the "Short Incident Notice" template below.
4) Decision window (60–120 minutes): Either quick rollback or targeted mitigation (e.g., revert sampling param).
5) Postmortem and RCA: If rollback occurred or customer impact exceeded 15 minutes, open a postmortem ticket and schedule a cross-team review in 3 business days.

Rollback criteria (explicit triggers)
-----------------------------------
- Any assertion breach listed above for >15 minutes sustained.
- More than one enterprise tenant reports a reproducible semantic regression within 60 minutes.
- P95 latency increase >250ms causing SLA violation risk.
- Unexpected 5xx spike >0.5% absolute.
- Cost surge alarm for Dedicated customer where budget controls exist.

Customer communication templates (use and adapt per account)
-----------------------------------------------------------
1) Short Incident Notice (for initial outreach):
Subject: Service update: model rollout observation - [CustomerName]
Body:
Hi [CustomerName] team,
We are observing an unexpected behavior during a model update that may impact a subset of requests. We have paused the rollout for your tenant and our engineering team is investigating. We will share an update within 60 minutes and provide mitigation steps if needed.
Best,
[CS Rep]

2) Post-Rollback Summary (within 24 hours):
Subject: Post-rollback summary & next steps - [CustomerName]
Body:
Hi [CustomerName],
We reverted the recent model change for your tenant at [time]. Summary of what happened, impact window, and next steps (including optional test schedule and QBR notes). Attach the synthetic test-report PDF and link to the RCA when available.

Post-change QA and QBR integration
----------------------------------
- Add the change event to the next customer QBR agenda under "Operational Changes & Risk" with: description, canary metrics, customer impact (if any), and recommended next steps.
- Maintain a change log for each enterprise tenant with: change id, date, owner, pre/post metric snapshots, and artifacts (test reports, canary dashboards).

Edge cases and private deployments
---------------------------------
- For Private deployments, Security must confirm that the new model binary/quantization artifacts meet the customer FIPS/HSM constraints before approval.
- For heavily regulated customers (marked in account metadata as "regulated: true"), require an explicit customer opt-in unless the change is security-critical.

Operational tooling and runbook automation
----------------------------------------
- Use the MCR (Model Change Request) ticket template in Jira and attach: rationale, canary plan, telemetry assertions, rollback plan, impacted tenant list, and customer comms draft.
- Canary dashboards: link to Grafana panels: model_canary_{change_id}_quality and model_canary_{change_id}_latency.
- Automate assertion evaluation via the canary-orchestrator job (CLI example below).

CLI examples and request payloads
--------------------------------
- Start a canary run (internal):
  redwood-canaryctl start --change-id MCR-1234 --duration 60m --traffic 2% --prompt-suite default-sanity

- Example MCR JSON payload (attach to Jira):
  {
    "change_id": "MCR-1234",
    "author": "marcos.rivera@redwood.com",
    "classification": "major",
    "description": "Upgrade from model-x-1.3 to model-x-2.0 (chiefly factuality and perf improvements)",
    "impact_scope": ["tenant-abc", "tenant-xyz"],
    "telemetry_assertions": ["output-delta<2%","p95-latency-delta<15%"],
    "rollback_plan": "automated switch to model-x-1.3 and invalidate kvcache for canary tenants",
    "scheduled_window": "2026-07-29T02:00:00Z/2026-07-29T06:00:00Z"
  }

Note: The JSON above should be pasted into the Jira change artifact.

Postmortem and RCA expectations
-------------------------------
- If the change causes customer-visible regression, open a postmortem within 24 hours. Include: timeline, root causes, detection signals, and action items with owners and due dates.
- If regression is prevented by telemetry, capture the assertion data and mark the MCR as "near-miss". Add to monthly governance review for trending.

Appendix A — classification decision rules (quick)
------------------------------------------------
- If the change modifies model weights or tokenizer, classify as Major.
- If change only tweaks hyperparameters that do not cross a rational threshold (e.g., temperature 0.7->0.72), classify as Minor.
- If ambiguity remains, default to Major and follow full signoff.

Appendix B — recommended canonical prompt-suite (summary)
---------------------------------------------------------
- Customer-canonical: 30 representative prompts derived from top-ten customer intents.
- Safety-canonical: 40 prompts designed to surface hallucinations, instruction following, and refusal behavior.
- Latency-canonical: 20 long-sequence prompts (avg 1024 tokens).

Appendix C — escalation contacts
-------------------------------
- CS Runbook Owner: marcos.rivera@redwood.com (Pager: paged via #cs-runbook)
- Serving Runtime on-call: runtime-oncall@redwood.com (PagerDuty)
- SRE: sre-oncall@redwood.com
- Security: security-escalation@redwood.com

Revision history
----------------
- 2026-03-11: Created by Marcos Rivera.
- 2026-07-20: Added explicit telemetry assertions and Private deployment signoff requirement.

This document should be used as a normative checklist for all enterprise-impacting model changes. Questions or suggested updates should be submitted to the runbook owner or opened as a Confluence comment against this page.

title: Support playbook: help customers rotate/revoke Hosted API keys
content:
# When to use
Use this playbook when a customer asks how to rotate/regenerate a key, requests emergency revocation, or reports suspected compromise.

# Guardrails
- Never ask a customer to paste an API key value into email/Jira/Slack.
- If the customer is unable to access Console due to RBAC, escalate to Security for an approved admin-assisted revoke.

# Quick decision tree
1) **Suspected compromise?**  Revoke first, then rotate.
2) **Planned rotation?** Create new key, deploy, validate, then revoke old key.

# Customer instructions (canonical)
Send the customer the link/steps from: "Hosted API key rotation & revocation (customer guide)".

# Emergency revoke procedure (internal)
1. Create/locate the support ticket (SUP-*).
2. Confirm authorization in writing (email from authorized admin or known customer security contact).
3. In Console (admin view), go to Settings  API Keys  select key  Disable.
4. Document: key name, key id, timestamp, who authorized.
5. Ask customer to deploy replacement key.

# Post-actions
- If compromise is likely: tag ticket with `security-incident` and page Security on-call.
- Recommend customer updates any leaked build logs, CI variables, or screenshots.

# Common pitfalls
- Customer confuses **key id** with **key value**  results in 401 after update.
- Customer rotates key but keeps old key in a background job  intermittent 401s.
- Customer uses one key for multiple services  rotation requires coordinated deploy.

# Templates
## Email snippet
"You can rotate a Redwood Hosted API key by regenerating it in Console (Settings  API Keys) or via API. After you deploy the new key and validate traffic, disable the old key. If you suspect exposure, disable first and we can help you recover quickly."

title: Support Process: Customer Communications Requirements for Model Rollouts
content:
h1. Purpose
This page defines the minimum customer-facing communication requirements for production model version rollouts. Rollout plans MUST include a Customer communications section that follows these rules.

h1. Who must be notified

h2. Always notify
* Any Dedicated customer receiving the new version as default
* Any Private customer (VPC/on-prem) impacted by the change

h2. Notify when material behavior changes
For Hosted API customers, notify when any of the following change materially for a commonly used alias:
* output format or tool-calling behavior
* maximum context/output token limits
* latency or reliability expectations
* safety behaviors (refusals, content filtering)

h1. Timing
* Dedicated: at least 5 business days before the change window, unless the customer agrees otherwise.
* Private: per customer contract; default to 10 business days prior to the maintenance window.
* Hosted: at least 72 hours prior for material behavior changes; otherwise release notes are sufficient.

h1. Required message content
All customer communications MUST include:
* What is changing (model alias and new version id if customer pins versions)
* Why we are changing (benefit statement)
* When (date/time + timezone + duration)
* Impact assessment (best-case and worst-case)
* How to opt out or pin a version
* How to get help (support channel and escalation path)
* Rollback posture (we can roll back during window if thresholds violated)

h1. Channels
* Dedicated/Private: email to customer technical contacts + a support ticket for tracking
* Hosted: release notes; optionally email to top impacted orgs
* If the change triggers an incident or wide impact, use the status page rules

h1. Approvals
Customer communications MUST be reviewed by:
* Customer Success owner for the account
* Product Manager for inference

For Private customers in regulated environments, also require Security review.

h1. Templates (snippets)

h2. Subject line options
* Upcoming update to <model alias> (new version rollout)
* Maintenance window: model version upgrade for Redwood Inference

h2. Opt-out language (required)
If you need to remain on the previous model version, we can pin your deployment to <old version> for at least 30 days. Reply to this email or comment on the support ticket to request pinning.

h1. Tracking and record
The rollout plan MUST link to the customer ticket(s) and note when the communication was sent.

title: Deferred Request Routing and SLA Eligibility Playbook
content:
Summary

This playbook defines the operational procedure for deferred request routing and SLA eligibility determination for enterprise tenants during transient capacity or model degradations. It prescribes the routing policies, telemetry signals, customer communication templates, and post-event reconciliation needed to ensure predictable behavior and fair SLA handling.

Scope

- Applies to Redwood-hosted and Dedicated tenants using the Redwood API or customer SDKs.
- Covers transient degradations: capacity surges, model fallback, regional congestion, and circuit-breaker-driven deferrals.
- Does not replace tenant cutover or long-term migrations; see Enterprise Cutover playbooks for those flows.

Objectives

1. Route requests in a way that preserves availability and latency SLOs where possible.
2. Provide deterministic rules for when a tenant is eligible for SLA credits following deferrals.
3. Maintain transparent, auditable telemetry to support QBR and billing reconciliation.
4. Minimize noisy alerts and unnecessary escalations through automated remediation.

Definitions

- Deferred request: a user request intentionally delayed, queued, or routed to a lower-capacity lane to protect system SLOs.
- Eligible deferral window: contiguous period where >= 90% of a tenant's requests were auto-deferred.
- SLA-qualifying deferral: a deferral that meets thresholds for credit according to the customer contract.

Ownership and Contacts

- Primary owner: Customer Success Engineering (CSE) — Lena Patel (author).
- Secondary support: Platform Reliability — Jordan Kim.
- Escalation (S3+): Oncall SRE rotation, contact via PagerDuty schedule ‘platform-sre’.

Preconditions (what must be in place before using this playbook)

- Tenant has telemetry forwarding enabled (OpenTelemetry or Redwood-agent) and per-tenant request IDs.
- Route policies configured in the routing service (see Routing config snippet below).
- SLA configuration recorded in billing system and accessible via tenant metadata.
- Customer accepted notification channel (email + webhook) on file.

Routing policy principles

- Prefer graceful degradation over hard failures. If latency budgets are exhausted, requests may be:
  1) deferred to a short-lived queue with a configurable TTL,
  2) routed to a lower-cost model variant (quantized or smaller), or
  3) served from the customer’s best-effort cached response (for embeddings/long-running ops).
- Deferrals must be rate-limited per-tenant to avoid unbounded queues.
- Any routing decision that alters output semantics (model variant or cache) must tag the response with X-Redwood-Fallback and include the reason code.

SLA eligibility rules (summary)

A tenant is eligible for SLA credit for a calendar day if ALL of the following are true: 
- The tenant experienced an SLA-impacting deferral window of >= 15 consecutive minutes;
- During the window, >= 95% of production (non-test) requests were either deferred or had a fallback tag;
- The tenant’s contract does not list the event as an excluded cause (maintenance, customer-provided network outage, blacklisted traffic, or scheduled capacity maintenance previously communicated).

Signal thresholds (operational table)

| Signal | Threshold | Action owner | Notes |
|--------|-----------|--------------|-------|
| Deferred rate (1m) | > 20% and rising | CSE (first triage) | Alerts when trend sustained 3 consecutive 1m buckets |
| Deferred rate (15m) | > 80% | CSE + SRE | Consider SLA eligibility evaluation |
| Latency p95 (prod) | > 2x baseline | SRE | May trigger routing policy change |
| Error rate (5m) | > 1% | CSE | Investigate model or request source |

Routing configuration snippet (example)

JSON routing rule example for a tenant-level policy: 

{
  "tenant_id": "tenant-abc-123",
  "rules": [
    { "priority": 100, "match": { "model_tags": ["prod"] }, "action": { "type": "serve", "variant": "primary" } },
    { "priority": 200, "match": { "system_load": ">=0.85" }, "action": { "type": "defer", "queue_ttl_s": 20, "fallback_variant": "lite-quant" } }
  ]
}

(When a rule fires, routing service emits routing.event.* with fields: tenant_id, rule_id, action.type, reason_code.)

Operational runbook (step-by-step)

1. Detection and initial triage (Automated)
   - Alert fires when deferred rate (15m) > 80% or p95 latency > 2x baseline.
   - Automated playbooks attempt a local policy rollback (if recently rolled), temporarily increase queue_ttl to 30s, and enable short-lived fallback variant.

2. First responder (CSE) — 0–10 minutes
   - Confirm tenant and scope (are requests all from one region or route?).
   - Verify routing.event.* and request IDs in traces.
   - If deferral is due to a burst, notify customer via pre-approved template and mark the incident as informational.

3. SRE engagement (10–30 minutes)
   - Correlate host-level metrics, GPU queue depths, and model-specific errors.
   - If a capacity issue persists, trigger capacity-burst allocation for Dedicated tenants per Capacity Surge Playbook.

4. SLA eligibility check and customer notification (30–90 minutes)
   - If the deferral window meets SLA thresholds, begin internal SLA credit calculation: aggregate per-tenant deferred_time, total_requests, and fallback_tagged_requests.
   - Notify customer with a templated message: reason, observed impact, remediation steps, and expected credit timeline.

5. Post-event reconciliation (1–7 days)
   - Produce a reconciliation report with raw traces, aggregated metrics, and routing.rule history.
   - If SLA credit applies, route to Billing with computed credit and documentation.
   - Schedule a QBR item if event degrades customer trust or recurs.

Customer communication templates

- Initial (informational): "We observed elevated request deferrals for your tenant {tenant_id} in region {region} between {start} and {end}. We have applied temporary fallbacks and are monitoring. No action required from your side unless you observe functional regressions. — Redwood Support"

- SLA-eligibility notice: "We have completed an initial review of the deferral event on {date}. Based on contract terms and observed telemetry, your tenant is eligible for a credit. The credit amount will be communicated within 5 business days after reconciliation. A detailed report is attached."

- Rollback / action-required: "We have routed your traffic back to the primary variant as of {time}. If you continue to see degraded outputs, please provide a sample request ID and our SRE team will investigate. — Redwood Support"

Templates live in: /confluence/customer-success-and-support/support-process/communication-templates

Telemetry and evidentiary artifacts (what to collect)

- Per-request trace (trace_id) and routing.event.* logs for the window.
- Aggregated metrics: deferred_rate (1m, 15m), p95 latency, error rate, model_fallback_count.
- Routing rule versions and any policy changes applied during the window.
- Customer notification history and acceptance of credits (email/webhook receipts).

Automations to reduce toil

- Automated eligibility pre-check: nightly job that flags windows meeting SLA thresholds and pre-populates reconciliation tickets.
- Auto-tagging: any response served via fallback must include X-Redwood-Fallback in headers and the routing.reason_code in logs.
- Billing integration: a microservice that consumes reconciliation outputs and creates draft credits for review.

Testing and verification

- Simulated burst testcases are available in the CSE test harness. Run these before enabling new routing rules:
  1) 10x request burst for 5 minutes to a single tenant,
  2) Regional cross-traffic spikes with model-variant throttles,
  3) Gradual ramp to verify queue_ttl behavior.

- Verification checklist after policy changes:
  - Routing event emission validated in tracing (sample 10 requests).
  - Fallback-tag header present for fallback responses.
  - Automated reconciler does not mark test tenants as eligible.

Postmortem and QBR recommendations

- For any event that results in SLA credit or multiple customer complaints, produce a postmortem within 7 days that includes root cause, action items, and timelines.
- Add a QBR slide with: event summary, impact metrics, mitigations executed, and proposed systemic fixes (e.g., more burst capacity, improved routing rules, or tenant-specific rate limit adjustments).

Appendix: quick CLI snippets

- Fetch routing events for a tenant (example):
  curl -H \"Authorization: Bearer ${REDWOOD_API_KEY}\" \"https://ops.redwood.internal/api/v1/routing-events?tenant=tenant-abc-123&since=2025-10-01T00:00:00Z\"

- Example query to compute deferred percentage (PromQL-style):
  sum(increase(redwood_requests_deferred_total{tenant=\"tenant-abc-123\"}[15m])) / sum(increase(redwood_requests_total{tenant=\"tenant-abc-123\"}[15m]))

Related pages and references

- Capacity surge playbook (eng-sre/capacity-planning)
- Tenant cutover and safety net (customer-success-and-support/enterprise-onboarding)
- SLA credits billing runbook (finance-and-legal/billing)

Change history

- 2025-03-12: Initial draft (Lena Patel).
- 2025-06-18: Added automation integration and PromQL examples (Jordan Kim).
- 2025-10-04: Finalized SLA thresholds and customer templates; published (Priya Raman).

End of document

title: Enterprise Severity Matrix and Customer Communication Playbook
content:
Overview

Purpose
This playbook defines a standardized severity matrix for enterprise customers during onboarding and production, and prescribes customer-facing communication workflows for each severity. The goal is to ensure consistent, transparent, and timely communications while aligning engineering, SRE, and customer success actions with contractual SLAs and business expectations.

Scope
- Applies to Redwood-hosted API, Dedicated, and Private deployments for enterprise customers.
- Covers incidents affecting availability, correctness of outputs, performance regressions, and billing/quotas that materially impact customer business outcomes.
- Does NOT replace product-specific runbooks or legal escalation paths for data breaches (see security-and-compliance incident playbooks).

Definitions and Severity Matrix
Use the following table and criteria to classify customer-impact incidents. Classify on customer-visible impact; escalate by highest impacted customer tier when multiple tenants are affected.

Severity Levels (quick reference)
- P0 (Critical): Customer-facing outage or corrupted responses that prevent core business flows, repeated for >5 minutes, affects 25%+ of requests or one or more high-value tenants.
- P1 (High): Significant degradation in throughput/latency or consistent quality regressions affecting >10% of requests for a specific tenant or features used in production.
- P2 (Medium): Partial feature outage, degraded quality with mitigations available, or single-tenant rate limiting causing customer-visible errors but with fallback.
- P3 (Low): Minor functional issues, intermittent errors, non-urgent quality differences, or documentation gaps.
- P4 (Informational): Non-customer-impacting background issues, upcoming maintenance notices, or low-risk changes.

Severity Scoring Criteria (short form)
1. Impact: % of requests affected or number of customers/tenants impacted.
2. Business Criticality: Revenue at risk, compliance implications, or go-live status.
3. Duration: Time since onset without effective mitigation.
4. Reproducibility: Deterministic vs intermittent.

SLA and Target Responses
- P0: Acknowledge to customer within 5 minutes. Formation of incident bridge with engineering and SRE within 10 minutes. Initial public-facing or customer-facing update within 15 minutes. Target time-to-recover (TTR) depends on root cause; communicate ETA if >30 minutes.
- P1: Acknowledge within 15 minutes. Bridge within 30 minutes. Customer-facing update within 60 minutes and then every 2 hours until resolved.
- P2: Acknowledge within 1 business hour. Customer update within 4 hours and daily status until resolved.
- P3/P4: Acknowledge within 24 business hours. Weekly or as-needed updates.

Owner and Escalation Roster
The following ownership matrix is used when classifying and communicating incidents. Replace names with on-call rotation contact where appropriate.
- First responder: Support Tier 1 (CS Operations)
- Technical owner: SRE / Runtime on-call
- Product owner: Product Manager assigned to the affected feature
- Account lead: Customer Success Manager (CSM) for the tenant
- Executive notify: VP Customer Success (for P0 and repeated P1 on production customers)

Contact escalation paths (order)
1. Support Tier 1 -> 2. SRE on-call -> 3. Runtime engineering -> 4. Product -> 5. VP Customer Success / Head of Eng (as needed)

Operational Checklist by Severity (numbered steps for responders)
P0 (Critical)
1. Classify severity and escalate to SRE immediately.
2. Launch incident bridge (Zoom/Slack/Bridge) and add: Support lead, SRE on-call, runtime eng, product PM, account CSM, and communications.
3. Stabilize traffic: enable fallback model, route to standby region, or activate quota protections. Document actions in the bridge.
4. Craft initial customer-facing update (see templates). Post to customer’s preferred channel (email + support portal ticket + CSM slack).
5. Track metrics and logs: error rate, 95/99th percentile latency, tail drop %, model output error metrics. Attach graphs to updates.
6. Confirm mitigation, run customer verification steps, and coordinate rollback if change-induced.
7. After resolution, run RCA and share timeline within 48 hours and a corrective action plan in the QBR cadence.

P1 (High)
1. Acknowledge and open incident ticket. Notify SRE and product.
2. Attempt quick mitigations (scaling, model fallback, rolling to previous model checkpoint).
3. Provide updates every 2 hours until stable.
4. If unresolved after 6 hours, escalate to executive notify list.

Customer Communication Templates
Use the templates below and customize per tenant (replace tokens in {{braces}}). Always coordinate final messages with the CSM and legal when regulatory language or credits are discussed.

P0 Initial Notification (email/portal)
Subject: URGENT: Incident affecting Redwood Inference API for {{customer_name}} ({{incident_id}})
Body:
Hello {{customer_name}} team,

We are aware of a critical incident affecting {{feature_or_api}} that is impacting production traffic for your account (incident ID: {{incident_id}}). Our on-call engineering and SRE teams have launched a bridge and are actively investigating.

What we know now:
- Time detected: {{iso_timestamp}}
- Observed impact: {{brief-impact-summary}}
- Immediate mitigation actions: {{mitigations}}

Next update: We will provide an update within 15 minutes or sooner. Your Customer Success Manager {{csm_name}} is available at {{csm_contact}} for direct coordination.

We understand the urgency and appreciate your patience.

— Redwood Inference Support

P1 Update Example
Subject: Update: Ongoing service degradation for {{customer_name}} ({{incident_id}})
Body:
Hello {{customer_name}} team,

Status update ({{iso_timestamp}}):
- Current impact: {{current-impact}}
- Actions taken: {{actions}}
- Next steps / ETA: {{eta}}

Assignee: {{technical_owner}}

Regards,
Redwood Inference Support

P2 Customer Guidance (short)
Subject: Notice: partial functionality impacted for {{customer_name}}
Body:
We identified an issue affecting {{feature}}. A workaround is available: {{workaround_steps}}. We will update you by {{next_update_time}}.

Incident Posture and Tone Guidance
- Tone: factual, empathetic, and action-oriented. Avoid speculative technical claims.
- Transparency: If unknowns remain, state what is unknown and planned investigative steps.
- Credits/Compensation: Route any compensation requests to Billing and legal. Do not promise credits in customer message; escalate to finance for approval.

Onboarding-specific Escalations and Go-Live Safeguards
During enterprise onboarding and initial cutover, apply a lower tolerance for regressions and ensure the following:
- Pre-cutover: confirm runbook and contact list, stomping on-call handoff validation.
- Canary phase: require minimum 24-hour monitoring with dedicated telemetry dashboards and synthetic checks for edge-cases.
- Cutover hold gate: no model or config changes that impact the tenant for 72 hours post go-live unless approved by the CSM + SRE.
- Onboarding rapid response team: Onboarding PM, CSM, SRE representative, and runtime eng must be on-call during cutover windows.

Telemetry and Dashboard Recommendations (examples)
- Ingress: request/sec, 50/95/99 latency, HTTP error 5xx/4xx by route.
- Model: token generation rate, kv-cache hit ratio, GPU utilization, OOM events, and per-tenant queue length.
- Quality: perplexity drift, top-1 response divergence from baseline evaluation set, and customer feedback rate.

Example monitoring queries (PromQL-like pseudocode)
- api_errors_total{tenant="{{tenant_id}}"} / api_requests_total{tenant="{{tenant_id}}"} > 0.05
- histogram_quantile(0.95, api_request_duration_seconds_bucket{route="/v1/generate"}) > 1.2

Escalation Communication Channels
- Primary: Customer ticketing portal + dedicated support email.
- Real-time: Slack DM to CSM and customer production channel (if provisioned).
- Bridge: Zoom + pinned Slack incident channel.
- Public status: status.redwood.ai for multi-tenant incidents.

Post-Incident Activities and QBR Integration
1. Within 48 hours: publish timeline, mitigation steps, and next actions to the customer and internal ticket.
2. Within 7 days: share a draft RCA and proposed corrective actions.
3. In next QBR: include incident summary, SLA impact table, and long-term remediations (owners and milestones).
4. For repeated issues: propose permanent routing or quantization changes via Redwood Optimize recommendations and include cost/latency tradeoffs.

Runbook Snippets (copyable checklist for responders)
- Confirm impact and severity.
- Validate customer's on-call and preferred communication channel.
- Collect: logs, trace IDs, example request payloads and model outputs.
- If code/config change suspected: capture deployment IDs and roll back marker.
- For Private deployments: verify network connectivity and customer firewall rules before code rollback.

Templates and Forms
- Incident ticket tags: severity:P0|P1|P2|P3, tenant_id, impacted_feature, psa_required:true|false.
- Customer update subject prefix: [Incident][P{n}] or [Maintenance][Info] for scheduled events.

Related pages
- /confluence/customer-success-and-support/enterprise-onboarding/onboarding-handback-and-first-90-days-ops-guide-2026
- /confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/incident-bridge-template
- /confluence/security-and-compliance/incident-response-security/major-incident-classification

Change log
- 2026-02-15: Created by Samantha Lee.
- 2026-04-02: Revised response SLAs and added onboarding cutover gates (reviewers: Jordan Kim, Priya Nair).
- 2026-07-12: Added telemetry query examples and post-incident QBR integration guidance.

Ownership and Review
- Document owner: Samantha Lee (Customer Success Operations)
- Review cadence: Quarterly or after any P0/P1 incident affecting enterprise customers.

Appendix: Example short-form verification checklist for customers to run after mitigation
1. Send 5 canonical requests used in production and compare outputs to baseline.
2. Verify 95th percentile latency improvement.
3. Confirm no new 5xx errors for 30 minutes.
4. Confirm billing/quotas unchanged (if relevant).

End of document

title: Regression Cascade Escalation and Customer Guardrails
content:
Summary:
This playbook defines the observable triggers, triage steps, mitigation actions, and customer communications for simultaneous model-quality regressions and inference cost or token-spend spikes (a "regression cascade"). It is intended for Customer Success, First-Line Support (L1), SRE, and Runtime Engineering to rapidly protect customer SLAs while preserving throughput and minimizing rollback scope.

When to use this playbook:
- Any time a customer, tenant, or cohort exhibits a quality drop (synthetic-eval delta or customer complaint) that co-occurs with a >30% increase in per-request cost or per-token compute time for the same time window.
- Automated detection fires when both a quality metric and a cost/latency metric cross configured thresholds (see Detection and triggers).

Goals and guardrails:
- Protect customer-facing applications within 15–60 minutes for critical customers.
- Maintain availability SLO: 99.9% request success for dedicated tenants; 99.5% for hosted API customers.
- Limit blast radius: prefer per-tenant or per-route mitigations before global rollbacks.
- Preserve telemetry for postmortem and for QBR discussion.

Roles and responsibilities:
- Customer Success (owner): primary comms to customer, coordinate QBR follow-up and mitigations with engineering.
- L1 Support: initial alert acknowledgment, surface customer impact, apply documented mitigations (circuit-breakers, throttles, short-term rate-limits).
- Runtime/SRE (on-call): containment actions (fallback routing, model variant switch, capacity throttles).
- Runtime Engineering/Model Onboarding: root-cause investigation for model artifact or quantization regressions.
- Trust & Safety / Security (if sensitive data exposure suspected): immediate involvement.

Detection and triggers (signals):
- Quality signals (any of):
  - "quality_score_delta" (synthetic eval score) <= -4.0 points over baseline in last 30m.
  - Increase in customer-reported output variance or repeat-content ratio >2x.
  - Automated eval alert: personalisation-eval-failure rate >5% on golden prompts.
- Cost / performance signals (any of):
  - per-request GPU ms p95 increases by >40% vs baseline over 30m.
  - per-token compute cost (GPU-time tokens) > 1.3x baseline for the same model/sequence distribution.
  - Unexpected spike in per-tenant charges or throttling events.
- Composite trigger (requires 1 quality + 1 cost signal):
  - Composite_Regression_Cascade = true when both cross thresholds within same 30-minute window.

Immediate triage (0–15 minutes):
1) Acknowledge the alert and tag in incident channel: #cust-alerts/regression-cascade, post short summary and links to dashboards.
2) L1: confirm customer impact and severity using:
   - Query: SELECT count(*) FROM requests WHERE tenant_id = <T> AND last_30m AND (quality_score < baseline - 4 OR error IS TRUE);
   - Dashboard panels to check: "Tenant: Quality Heatmap", "Tenant: Per-request CPU/GPU ms", "Model: Canary eval pass rate".
3) If critical customer affected (enterprise plan, SLA-bound), escalate immediately to Runtime/SRE on-call and Customer Success (use the on-call rota).

Containment steps (15–60 minutes):
1) Apply per-tenant defensive throttling: reduce burst allowance to 30% for the tenant for 30 minutes. CLI example:
   - curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/admin/tenants/<T>/throttle -H 'Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN' -d '{"burst":0.3, "duration_minutes":30}'
2) Route affected traffic to fallback model variant (lower-latency or previously-known-good model):
   - Preferred order: model.fallback.stable -> model.fallback.quantized -> model.fallback-smaller.
   - API example to pin model:
     PATCH /v1/tenants/<T>/routes/<route_id>
     {"pinned_model": "gpt-open-4-fallback-v2"}
3) If regression accompanied by tokenization anomalies, enable prefix-caching bypass and drop aggressive auto-batching for the tenant to isolate KV-cache behavior.
4) Open a short-lived incident channel and attach traces, request ids, and representative failing outputs. Preserve at least 72 hours of request bodies for postmortem (encrypted at rest).

Mitigation and customer protection (60–240 minutes):
1) Apply model-level rollback if artifact/weight corruption is suspected. Rollback checklist:
   - Confirm candidate model SHA and compare checksums: sha256sum model-vX.tar.gz
   - Verify that the previous model variant (vX-1) had stable synthetic-eval metrics for the affected prompts.
   - Initiate canary rollback with 5% traffic for 30 minutes, monitor quality/cost deltas.
2) If cost spike is due to a serving configuration (batching/sequence-length kernel changes): revert to previous kernel selection policy via runtime config flags. Example flag toggles:
   - runtime.feature_flags.kernel_selector = "legacy"
   - runtime.batch.window_ms = 10
3) For customer-facing protection, offer temporary quota relief or a safety-mode model with guaranteed latency and cost caps (coordinate with Finance for credits).
4) Customer Comms: Customer Success drafts an initial status note (see templates below) and schedules an incident-specific sync if the customer requests.

Longer-term analysis and QBR integration (>24 hours):
- Collect and store: request traces, model SHAs, quantization config, kernel selections, and the sequence-length distribution during the incident window.
- Postmortem: standard 5-part RCA (timeline, impact, root cause hypothesis, mitigation, preventive actions). Owner: Runtime Engineering. Deliverable within 72 hours.
- QBR inclusion: define actions and metrics to present to the customer (quality regression delta, unblock timeline, and planned mitigations).

Escalation matrix (summary):
- L1 Support (first 15m) -> Runtime/SRE on-call (15–60m) -> Runtime Engineering & Model Onboarding (60–240m) -> Engineering leadership + Customer Success + Finance (if credits needed).

Service-level thresholds and decision points table:
- If composite trigger active AND tenant is SLA-bound -> immediate route + pin fallback + notify exec on-call.
- If rollback candidate fails to recover quality for canary -> escalate to full rollback approval within 3 hours.

Runbook configs and alert rules (examples):
- Alert: tenant_quality_drop_30m
  - expr: delta(quality_score_sum[30m]) / avg(quality_score_sum[7d]) < -0.05
  - for: 10m
  - labels: severity=high, domain=quality
- Alert: tenant_cost_spike_p95
  - expr: increase(per_request_gpu_ms_p95[30m]) / avg(per_request_gpu_ms_p95[7d]) > 0.4
  - for: 10m
- Composite alert rule (pseudo):
  - if tenant_quality_drop_30m && tenant_cost_spike_p95 then fire Composite_Regression_Cascade (route to #cust-alerts/regression-cascade).

Customer communication templates (use Customer Success to tailor):
- Initial short status (sent within 30–60m):
  - Subject: Brief update on observed model quality and cost impact
  - Body: We detected an unexpected drop in output quality coincident with elevated inference latency/cost affecting your tenant. We have applied short-term mitigations (pinned fallback model + throttles) and are actively investigating root cause. We will share a follow-up within 3 hours with next steps. Owner: Customer Success (contact: cs-lead@redwood.ai).
- Follow-up (post-containment):
  - Body: Containment measures and observed effect (metrics), planned rollback or mitigation, expected timeline for full resolution, and next QBR-level artifacts.

Post-incident checklist (deliverables):
1) 72-hr initial RCA draft with timeline and telemetry (Runtime Eng).
2) Customer-facing incident summary and compensation proposal where applicable (Customer Success + Finance).
3) Config and automation changes to prevent recurrence (Infrastructure PRs, Model onboarding checks).
4) Update onboarding docs and QBR materials to include new detection rules and sample prompts for customers to exercise.

Appendix: handy commands and queries
- Fetch recent failing requests for tenant <T> (example):
  - curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $READONLY" "https://telemetry.redwood.ai/api/v1/requests?tenant=<T>&since=30m&filter=quality_score<{{baseline-4}}"
- Pin a route to a fallback model (example):
  - curl -X PATCH 
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN" 
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" 
    https://api.redwood.ai/v1/tenants/<T>/routes/<route_id> 
    -d '{"pinned_model":"gpt-open-4-fallback-v2","reason":"regression-cascade containment"}'
- Example Prometheus alert fragment (YAML-like):
  - alert: Composite_Regression_Cascade
    expr: (tenant_quality_drop_30m == 1) and (tenant_cost_spike_p95 == 1)
    for: 10m
    labels: {severity: critical}

title: Enterprise Offline Diagnostic Bundle and Customer Handback Protocol
content:
Summary:
Provide a standardized, privacy-conscious process for producing an "offline diagnostic bundle" (ODB) that support engineers assemble and hand back to enterprise customers for offline analysis. This document codifies when and how to generate an ODB, required artifacts, redaction and sampling rules, packaging format, delivery SLA, and verification steps. The ODB is intended only for allowed support/legal/engineering stakeholders and must follow the redaction rules and retention constraints below.

Audience:
- Customer Success Engineers (CSEs)
- Solutions Engineers (SEs)
- Support oncall and L2/L3 engineers
- Customer security/compliance reviewers

When to use this runbook:
1) Customer requests an offline bundle for root-cause analysis after an escalated incident (SEV1/SEV2) or quality investigation that cannot be resolved with live telemetry.
2) Legal or compliance requires an extract for audit that cannot be satisfied by live telemetry exports.
3) Customer asks for a reproducible data slice for model-eval or labeling that must be processed offline.

Primary objectives:
- Provide engineers with a deterministic, reproducible bundle sufficient for debugging (trace IDs, request payloads, timestamps, small model artifacts) while minimizing PII/exposure.
- Meet customer compliance requirements (data minimization, pseudonymization) and Redwood's internal confidentiality controls.
- Deliver within a clear SLA and with traceable ownership.

Ownership and approvals:
- Requesting party: CSE assigned to the account (owns request, notifications, customer signoff).
- Producer: Support engineer (L2+).
- Approver: Security reviewer (required when bundle contains <confidential> data fields or when customer is in regulated industry).
- Delivery: Secure transfer by CSE (S3 pre-signed URL with expiration, or SFTP endpoint approved by customer).

Delivery SLA (target):
- High (SEV1 / legal): 24 hours initial package + 48 hours full package.
- Medium (SEV2 / QBR request): 72 hours.
- Low (non-urgent request): 10 business days.

Required artifacts (minimum):
- manifest.yaml (see spec below)
- request-sample.jsonl (sampled inference requests, max 10k rows by default)
- response-sample.jsonl (associated model responses)
- traces/ (zipped set of trace files matching sample request IDs)
- ingress-metadata.csv (tenant id, route, model name, client-ip-hash)
- runtime-metrics.csv (CPU/GPU utilization and latency histograms for the window)
- config-snapshot.json (model routing, quantization profile, batch config at time-of-incident)
- optional: small model checkpoint diff (<=100MB) OR model-profiles.txt (performance/kv cache stats)

Manifest spec (manifest.yaml) - example fields:
- bundle_id: string (UUID)
- tenant_id: string (pseudonymized)
- time_window_start: RFC3339 timestamp
- time_window_end: RFC3339 timestamp
- request_count: integer
- sample_strategy: deterministic | random | criteria-filtered
- redaction_profile_version: v1.3
- produced_by: <engineer name/email>
- verification_hash: sha256 hex of the top-level tarball

Packaging format and file layout (tar.gz):
- bundle-<bundle_id>.tar.gz
  - manifest.yaml
  - samples/request-sample.jsonl
  - samples/response-sample.jsonl
  - traces/traces-<bundle_id>.zip
  - metadata/ingress-metadata.csv
  - metadata/runtime-metrics.csv
  - config/config-snapshot.json
  - redaction-log.txt
  - verification/sha256.txt

Sanitization and redaction rules (MUST follow):
1) PII removal: Remove or pseudonymize any fields defined in Redwoods PII catalog. Common examples: user_email, user_name, phone_number, ssn, credit_card_number. Replace with deterministic pseudonym hash: sha256(<tenant_salt>+<original_value>) truncated to 16 chars.
2) IP handling: Replace client_ip with hashed_ip = sha256(client_ip + tenant_salt) and remove last-octet for IPv4 if hashing is not permitted.
3) Sensitive customer tokens/keys: redact entirely (REDACTED) and record the key name in redaction-log.txt.
4) Full-text heuristics: For response payloads, scan with the redaction regex list (Appendix A). If heuristics match >3 tokens resembling PII, remove full utterance and record in redaction-log.txt.
5) Audit trail: Every automated redaction must append a single-line entry to redaction-log.txt with fields: file,path,redaction_type,rule_id,timestamp,operator.

Sampling policy (defaults and overrides):
- Default sampling: stratified by route and latency bucket — choose up to 1% of total requests or 10k rows (whichever smaller), with deterministic seeding (tenant_id + time_window_start).
- For model-quality investigations: allow up to 50k rows if customer approves and security reviewer signs off.
- For legal/audit: follow the exact custody instructions from legal; do not exceed requested scope.

Step-by-step production procedure (numbered):
1) Intake and verify authorization
   a) CSE confirms written customer authorization including allowed data categories and transfer mechanism.
   b) If customer is in regulated sector (finance/health/government), require security approval before extraction.
2) Create an incident branch and set bundle_id: uuidgen
3) Reserve temporary storage: create ephemeral S3 prefix named s3://redwood-sandbox/odb/<bundle_id>/ with 7-day lifecycle.
4) Run extraction script (example CLI below) with redaction_profile=v1.3 and deterministic seed.
5) Validate manifest.yaml and run redaction audit tool (must produce zero high-severity violations).
6) Compute verification hash and sign with producer's GPG key (optional internal requirement).
7) Move tar.gz to secure delivery area and populate pre-signed URL with 72-hour expiry (unless customer requires shorter).
8) Notify customer and internal stakeholders with delivery checklist and access instructions.
9) After handback confirmation, schedule automated deletion per retention policy.

Example CLI and commands (reference):
# create bundle (internal tool: odb-create)
# requires: --start, --end, --tenant, --profile, --seed
$ odb-create --tenant tenant-1234 --start 2026-02-01T08:00:00Z --end 2026-02-01T12:00:00Z --profile v1.3 --seed 20260201T08 --out /tmp/odb-<bundle_id>.tar.gz

# validate redaction audit (internal tool: odb-verify)
$ odb-verify /tmp/odb-<bundle_id>.tar.gz --policy redaction-v1.3 --report /tmp/verify-report-<bundle_id>.json

# compute sha256 (verify)
$ sha256sum /tmp/odb-<bundle_id>.tar.gz > verification/sha256.txt

Delivery checklist (must include):
- Customer authorization record attached to support ticket (ticket ID)
- Security approval if required
- manifest.yaml verified and signed by producer
- redaction-log.txt present and non-empty
- verification/sha256.txt matches transmitted archive
- Delivery mechanism documented (S3 pre-signed URL expiry, recipient email, audit entries)

Retention and deletion policy:
- Default retention: 7 days from bundle creation.
- Extended retention: up to 90 days only with documented customer approval and security signoff.
- After retention window, support automation will run secure-delete (s3 rm + immutable-delete for external storage) and append deletion record to ticket.

Verification and customer acceptance:
- After delivery, CSE requests customer confirmation that the bundle meets their needs and whether additional slices are required.
- If customer requests further slices, repeat intake and follow the sampling/approval steps.

Troubleshooting common failure modes:
- "Extraction exceeded storage quota": switch to filtered extraction (shorter window) and request quota bump from eng-infra with priority label.
- "Redaction audit failed": escalate to security reviewer, provide failure report, and hold delivery until reviewed.
- "Customer rejects bundle for missing context": work with the customer to identify missing IDs or specific trace ranges, re-run extraction with narrow time window.

Appendix A: Example redaction regex list (non-exhaustive)
- email: [A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}
- ssn (US): \\b\d{3}-\d{2}-\d{4}\\b
- credit card: (?:4[0-9]{12}(?:[0-9]{3})?|5[1-5][0-9]{14}|3[47][0-9]{13})

Appendix B: Example manifest.yaml (minimal)
bundle_id: "123e4567-e89b-12d3-a456-426614174000"
tenant_id: "tenant-xxxx"
time_window_start: "2026-02-01T08:00:00Z"
time_window_end: "2026-02-01T12:00:00Z"
sample_strategy: "deterministic"
redaction_profile_version: "v1.3"
request_count: "87432"
produced_by: "mchen@redwood.ai"

Appendix C: FAQ (short)
Q: Customer wants the raw client IPs for forensic analysis.
A: Do NOT provide raw IPs unless customer signs a justified exceptional data access form and security approves. Prefer hashed_ip with tenant_salt.

Q: Can we provide full model checkpoints?
A: Only provide model artifacts under an approved data transfer agreement and never include customer data embedded in the checkpoint. Prefer model diffs and profiling text files.

Related resources:
- /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/temporary-s3-prefix-management
- /confluence/security-and-compliance/data-protection-redaction-rules-v1.3
- /confluence/customer-success-and-support/support-process/tenant-snapshot-safe-replay-runbook-2026
