- A security questionnaire requires audit log delivery details and customer wants automated export.

# Request intake checklist (CS/Support)
Collect the following in the internal-support Jira ticket:
- Customer company
- Deployment mode: Hosted | Dedicated | Private
- Regions in use
- Desired sink: S3 | GCS | Azure Blob
- Destination details:
  - bucket/container name
  - prefix
  - destination region
- Identity method:
  - AWS assume-role / IRSA
  - GCP workload identity
  - Azure workload identity
- Retention intent (customer-owned)
- Operational contact + escalation contact
- Target date (if tied to an audit)

# Handoff and approvals
## 1) Create the internal-support Jira ticket
- Project: internal-support
- Issue type: Support Request
- Priority guidance:
  - P2 for standard requests
  - P1 if tied to a customer audit deadline within 14 days
  - P0 only if this blocks a live incident response obligation

## 2) Security approval
- Assign Security reviewer and request approval per the Security controls page.
- Attach destination policy snippets and encryption confirmation.

## 3) Legal/Privacy approval (conditional)
Escalate to Legal/Privacy if:
- cross-region export is requested
- customer requests additional PII fields beyond standard audit schema
- contract includes bespoke data residency clauses

# Execution routing
After approvals:
- Hosted: route to Eng Platform oncall / platform ops
- Dedicated: route to Eng Infra
- Private: route to Private Deployments engineering (and the customer’s operator)

# Customer communication template (email)
Subject: Audit log export enablement – next steps

Body:
- Thanks for the request. We can enable automated export of Redwood platform audit logs to your [S3/GCS/Azure] destination.
- Please confirm you have created the destination bucket/container and enabled encryption at rest.
- Please provide the workload identity / role configuration using the attached template.
- Once received and approved, we will enable export and ask you to confirm objects are landing under the agreed prefix.
- Typical initial enablement time: 3–5 business days (may vary by deployment mode and approvals).

# Validation responsibilities
- Redwood: verifies connector health metrics and initial delivery to the destination.
- Customer: verifies ingestion into their SIEM and configures their own retention/alerts.

# Post-enablement notes
- CS should confirm the customer understands delivery semantics (at-least-once, possible duplicates).
- CS should remind the customer that the destination is customer-owned (storage cost, lifecycle policies).

# Related pages
- Security controls and approval gates
- Hosted runbook
- Dedicated runbook
- Private configuration guide

title: Tenant SLA reconciliation and automated crediting playbook
content:
Overview:

This playbook describes the end-to-end process for reconciling tenant SLAs against observed service behavior and issuing automated (or semi-automated) service credits when contractual SLOs are not met. It is intended for Customer Success, Support, Billing, and SRE teams working with enterprise customers on Dedicated and Private deployments. The document covers detection triggers, verification steps, credit calculation, communication templates, ownership, audit trails, and QBR reporting hooks.

Goals and scope:
- Ensure consistent, auditable reconciliation between observed SLA breaches and customer-facing credit outcomes.
- Reduce manual effort for routine reconciliations while retaining human review for complex cases.
- Provide clear timelines and owners for each stage of the reconciliation lifecycle.
- Integrate reconciliation outcomes into QBRs and renewal conversations.

Applicability:
- Applies to enterprise customers with explicit SLA language in contract attachments (latency SLOs, availability SLOs, throughput guarantees).
- Covers both Hosted/Dedicated and Private (VPC/on-prem) deployments where Redwood has monitoring/telemetry access or agreed telemetry exports.

Key definitions (SLO/SLA brief):
- Availability SLO: percentage of successful 2xx responses for production tenant routes measured per calendar month (default baseline: 99.9% for Dedicated customers unless contract differs).
- P95 latency SLO: 95th percentile end-to-end request latency as measured by Redwood telemetry for the tenant's production route(s).
- Incident window: contiguous time range where an SLI drops below the configured threshold for more than the configured degradation-duration (default: 5 minutes).

Detection and alerting (automatic triggers):
1) Telemetry-based alerts (SRE):
   - Alert when tenant-monthly availability falls below SLA threshold OR when P95 exceeds threshold for more than 3 consecutive sampling periods (5m).
   - Alert names/IDs: tenant.slo.availability.breach, tenant.slo.latency.breach.
   - Alert payload must include tenant_id, tenant_org_name, observed_metric, threshold, time_window, and primary SRE runbook link.
2) Customer reports (CS/Support):
   - Support ticket containing reproducible examples, timestamps, and expected vs observed behavior escalates to SLA triage.

Triage and verification workflow (24–72 hour window):
1. Initial Triage (within 4 hours of alert): owner: oncall-sre / support-rotating-operator
   - Confirm alert validity (noise filter): correlate with platform-wide incidents, config changes, and known deploy windows.
   - If global or third-party provider outage: tag as "external" and route to Incident Coordination.
2. Data Collection (within 24 hours): owner: SRE metrics engineer
   - Pull raw request logs, ingress/egress times, model variant IDs, region, pod/node ids, and KV cache hit rates for the incident window.
   - Export telemetry snapshot to archive (S3 path: s3://redwood-slo-audits/{tenant_id}/{year}/{month}/{incident_id}/).
   - Record any service fallback events (model fallback, regional fallback, queued requests).
3. Attribution analysis (24–48 hours): owner: SRE + CS
   - Determine attribution: platform-controlled degradation vs tenant misconfiguration vs customer-origin traffic anomaly.
   - Use checklist:
     - Are there recent tenant config changes? (yes/no)
     - Do request traces show consistent 5xx from Redwood stack? (yes/no)
     - Is KV cache miss spike correlated with latency? (yes/no)
   - Outcome tags: platform, customer, third_party, inconclusive.
4. Resolution and remediation note (48–72 hours): owner: SRE + CS + Support
   - Document remediation steps taken, time windows, and ETA for permanent fix if applicable.

Credit calculation rules and examples:
- Contractual baseline: most contracts define a credit band tied to percent-of-month downtime or latency breach severity. This playbook provides a formula for automated preliminary calculation (subject to legal review if >$X).
- Automated credit formula (preliminary):
  credit_amount = min(max_credit_cap, monthly_commit_amount * breach_fraction * severity_multiplier)
  where breach_fraction = impacted_time_seconds / seconds_in_month
  severity_multiplier (examples):
    - minor: 0.25 (P95 > threshold by < 25%)
    - moderate: 0.5 (P95 > threshold by 25–100%)
    - severe: 1.0 (availability drop > 1% or sustained P95 > 3x threshold)
  max_credit_cap defaults to 50% of monthly commit for automated paths (contracts may override).

- Example 1: Tenant A monthly commit $10,000, 3 hours (10,800 seconds) of availability impact in a 30-day month (2,592,000 seconds): breach_fraction = 0.00417; severity_multiplier = 0.5; preliminary_credit = 10000 * 0.00417 * 0.5 = $20.8 -> round to $21 and flag for review.

Manual review thresholds (escalation to Finance/Legal):
- Any preliminary credit > $5,000 -> manual approval required from Billing Manager and Legal (auto path aborts).
- Attribution tag = third_party or inconclusive -> require SRE and Legal signoff before issuing credit.
- If remediation is partial or customer opted for alternative remediation (e.g., free private support), crediting may be adjusted per contract terms.

Automation pattern (systems involved):
- Triggering system: SLO-alerts -> Ticketing (Zendesk/Jira) -> Reconciliation service (internal microservice: sla-reconciler) -> Billing system (Stripe/Financial ERP)
- Reconciliation service responsibilities:
  - Fetch telemetry archive for incident window
  - Run credit formula with configured contract parameters
  - Generate reconciliation record with audit fields (computed_by, computed_at, telemetry_snapshot_uri, preliminary_amount, attribution_tag)
  - Create Jira ticket with reconciliation details and attach telemetry archive link
  - Post Slack notification to #cs-sla-reconciliations for manual review if thresholds crossed

Audit record schema (stored as JSON blob in Reconciliation DB) - required fields:
| field | description | example |
|------|-------------|---------|
| tenant_id | Redwood tenant UUID | t-123e4567 |
| incident_id | auto-generated ID | inc-20260810-001 |
| computed_by | service/user id | sla-reconciler-v1 |
| computed_at | ISO timestamp | 2026-08-10T14:12:00Z |
| telemetry_snapshot_uri | s3 path | s3://redwood-slo-audits/t-123e4567/2026/08/inc-20260810-001/ |
| preliminary_amount | USD cents | 2100 |
| attribution_tag | platform/customer/third_party/inconclusive | platform |
| approval_status | auto_pending/manual_approved/rejected | auto_pending |

Approval & issuing credits (process):
1. Auto-path (preliminary_amount <= $5,000 and attribution_tag == platform):
   - sla-reconciler auto-creates a billing credit draft and notifies Billing team via Slack and Jira. A 48-hour human review window is opened. If no objection is raised, the credit is applied automatically at 48 hours.
2. Manual-path (preliminary_amount > $5,000 OR attribution_tag != platform):
   - Reconciliation ticket assigned to Billing Manager. Billing Manager reviews audit artifacts and either approves or escalates to Legal. Billing issues customer-facing credit memo and records reason in the tenant ledger.

Communication templates (to customers):
- Initial acknowledgement (sent when SLO incident confirmed and under review):
```
Subject: Redwood — SLA review initiated for {tenant_org_name}
Hi {customer_contact},
We’ve detected a potential SLA deviation for your environment between {start_time} and {end_time}. Our team is collecting telemetry and will provide a recommended remediation and credit estimate within 72 hours. We’ll share the audit artifacts and next steps in the follow-up.
Regards,
Customer Success — Redwood
```
- Credit confirmation (after approval):
```
Subject: Redwood — SLA credit issued for {tenant_org_name}
Hi {customer_contact},
Following our review of the incident on {start_date}, Redwood has issued a service credit of ${credit_amount} in accordance with section {contract_section} of your agreement. Attached: audit-report-{incident_id}.zip
If you prefer an alternate remediation, please reply and we’ll coordinate.
Best,
Billing Operations — Redwood
```

Ownership matrix and SLAs for reconciliation process:
| Step | Primary owner | SLA | Secondary owner |
|------|---------------|-----|-----------------|
| Detection alert | SRE | 5m from breach detection | Support |
| Initial triage | Oncall-SRE / Support | 4 hours | CS |
| Data collection | SRE metrics engineer | 24 hours | Support |
| Attribution analysis | SRE + CS | 48 hours | Legal (if needed) |
| Preliminary credit computed | sla-reconciler | 1 hour after analysis | Billing |
| Final credit applied | Billing | 48 hours after approval | Finance |

QBR integration and metrics for Customer Success:
- Each reconciled SLA incident is recorded as part of the monthly QBR package. The following fields are surfaced in QBR dashboards: incident_count, total_credits_issued, percent_monthly_revenue_credited, mean_time_to_reconcile, attribution_breakdown.
- Talk track recommendation for CS during renewal conversations: present incident context, remediation roadmap, credit outcome, and improvements (e.g., routing changes, KV cache tuning, batching adjustments).

Operational playbook for common scenarios (quick reference):
- Platform-wide outage affecting many tenants: flag as P0, suspend automatic credit application until Incident Command posts final timeline (manual coordination required).
- Tenant misconfiguration discovered (e.g., mistaken rate-limiter policy): confirm customer impact window; crediting allowed only if contract permits. Tag attribution=customer; escalate to CS for remediation and customer advisory.
- Inconclusive telemetry (e.g., private deployment with limited telemetry exports): open forensic request to customer, pause auto-credit path, route to Legal for contract interpretation.

Monitoring and telemetry requirements (minimum):
- Per-tenant SLIs for availability (1m resolution) and P95 latency (5m resolution).
- Request trace id propagation across ingress -> runtime -> model runtime -> response.
- Daily snapshots of tenant traffic distribution and model variant percentages.

Operational checklist for first 90 days of enterprise onboarding (tie-in):
1. Confirm contract SLA fields are encoded in contract parameters in the reconciliation service.
2. Confirm telemetry export for tenant is configured and archived to S3 with retention 13 months.
3. Configure Slack and Jira routing for automatic reconciliations.
4. Run a dry-run (no credit) simulation during the onboarding acceptance window to validate end-to-end audit trail.

Appendices:
A. Example alert rule (Prometheus alert expression):
```
- alert: TenantAvailabilityBreach
  expr: sum(rate(tenant_request_success_count{tenant_id="${tenant_id}"}[5m])) / sum(rate(tenant_request_total_count{tenant_id="${tenant_id}"}[5m])) < 0.999
  for: 10m
  labels:
    severity: critical
  annotations:
    summary: "Tenant ${tenant_id} availability below SLA"
```
B. Sample reconciliation Jira workflow states: draft -> under_review -> approved -> applied -> closed
C. Contacts and escalation list: CS Lead (Aisha Patel, cs-lead@redwood.com), Billing Manager (Diego Morales, billing@redwood.com), SRE Oncall roster (see internal roster page).

Related pages and artifacts:
- Onboarding acceptance telemetry checklist (link in related_pages)
- Cost anomaly detection and linked playbook (link in related_pages)
- Billing and credit legal template (internal Legal doc ID: LEG-CC-2025-04)

Revision history:
- 2026-02-15: Draft authored by Aisha Patel
- 2026-04-02: Added automated reconciliation flow and audit schema (reviewers: Diego Morales)
- 2026-08-10: Updated manual review thresholds and example formulas after pilot (reviewers: Priya Nair, Samir Gupta)

If you have questions or discover gaps in the automation path, contact the CS tooling owner (cs-tooling@redwood.com) for follow-up.

title: QBR telemetry storyboard and action plan
content:
Summary

This document defines a repeatable "telemetry storyboard" and actionable runbook for Quarterly Business Reviews (QBRs) with enterprise customers. The intent is to provide a concise narrative that links telemetry signals to customer outcomes, surface prioritized actions, and assign owners with deadlines. The storyboard helps Customer Success Managers (CSMs), Solutions Engineers (SEs), and Product leads present a coherent operational story to executive and engineering stakeholders.

Audience

- CSMs and SEs preparing QBRs for enterprise accounts
- Customer engineering and platform teams that consume telemetry
- Product and Engineering stakeholders responsible for post-QBR follow-up

Goals

1. Convert raw telemetry into a 5–7 minute operational narrative for executives.
2. Produce a prioritized action plan with owners, deadlines, and acceptance criteria.
3. Reduce time-to-resolution for top customer risks by 40% quarter-over-quarter.

Required data sources

Collect the following telemetry ahead of every QBR:

- Ingress/egress request volume (per-tenant, per-route)
- Per-request latency percentiles (P50/P90/P99) by model and sequence length
- Token-level cost and token usage by model variant
- Error rates and error class distribution (4xx vs 5xx, model fallbacks)
- Model-quality regressions from evaluation harness (monthly prompt set scores)
- Cache hit ratio (prefix / KV cache) and cache utilization trends
- Capacity allocation and reservations for Dedicated tenants
- Recent incidents and customer-impacting config changes

Data contract table (example):

| Data source | Owner | Required fields | Freshness | Retention | Query template |
|-------------|-------|-----------------|-----------|----------|----------------|
| Request logs | ingress-team | tenant_id, route, timestamp, latency_ms, model | 5m | 90d | SELECT ... WHERE tenant_id=... |
| Error stream | platform-observability | tenant_id, error_code, request_id, stack | 1m | 180d | SELECT count(*) ... |
| Cost ledger | billing | tenant_id, model, tokens_in, tokens_out, cost_usd | 1d | 365d | SELECT SUM(cost_usd) ... |

Storyboard format

Use this short template to craft the QBR narrative. The final narrative should fit in a single slide or the first 5 minutes of the review.

1) Executive one-liner (30s):
- Current state in one sentence (health + trend + top ask). Example: "Tenant X had steady throughput in Q1 with a 12% P99 latency increase driven by larger context workloads; proposed action is to enable adaptive batching and a canary of the quantized v2 model."

2) One visual (60s):
- A single chart that ties user-visible latency or error spikes to a root cause signal (e.g., sudden increase in long-sequence requests, cache degradation, or a model rollout). Prefer overlays: request size distribution + P99 latency + cache-hit ratio.

3) Risk & impact (60s):
- Top 3 customer risks (e.g., sustained P99 > 2s on interactive routes, >10% traffic fallback to slower variants, monthly cost delta > 20% budget).
- For each risk: expected business impact and estimated cost/time to remediate.

4) Proposed actions (90s):
- Short-term (<= 2 weeks): tactical mitigations with owners and acceptance criteria.
- Medium-term (<= 3 months): config or model changes with canary plan.
- Long-term (>= 3 months): architecture or product requests (e.g., dedicated capacity increase, region expansion).

Pre-QBR checklist (to be completed 7 business days before meeting)

1. Validate data freshness from all required sources and confirm queries run without errors.
2. Create the single-chart visual and attach raw query results.
3. Run the evaluation harness on the customer prompt sample and note any regressions.
4. Confirm assigned owners and preliminary remediation estimates.
5. Send an executive summary (one-pager) to customer 3 business days before QBR.

During-QBR playbook (facilitator: CSM)

1. Opening (3 minutes): executive one-liner and agenda.
2. Data narrative (6–8 minutes): present the storyboard visual and explain causal links. Keep technical detail for the appendix.
3. Action negotiation (7–10 minutes): propose short- and medium-term actions, capture customer preferences and constraints.
4. Commitment & next steps (2–3 minutes): confirm owners, deadlines, and success criteria; schedule follow-up checkpoint within 2 weeks.

Action runbook (post-QBR)

Every action is tracked as a ticket in the customer success tracker (preferred backends: Jira project REDWOOD-CUST or internal tracker). For each action, fill in the ticket template below:

- Title: short description (e.g., "Enable adaptive batching for tenant X on route /chat")
- Owner: person/team
- Priority: P0/P1/P2
- Acceptance criteria: precise metric change and timeframe (e.g., "P99 latency reduction from 2.1s -> <=1.2s within 7 days")
- Test plan / Canary: route traffic fraction, monitoring queries, rollback trigger conditions
- ETA and dependency list

Action ticket example: priority P1, owner: infra-performance, acceptance criteria: 20% token cost reduction on inference-heavy routes measured over 72h, canary 5% of production traffic, automatic rollback if error rate > 0.5% above baseline.

Alert-to-action mapping (quick lookup)

- P99 latency spike & correlated increase in long-context requests -> Action: enable batching with max batch latency 40ms + increase KV cache TTL by 30% (Owner: serving-runtime).
- Sudden fallback to smaller model variant -> Action: investigate model-serving capacity and rollback recent deploys; if capacity constrained, route traffic to regional spare pool (Owner: infra-sre).
- Regressions in eval harness score (->3 points on customer prompt set) -> Action: open model-quality incident, pause canary rollout, and schedule rollback (Owner: applied-ml).

Example queries and dashboard snippets

- Example Prometheus/SQL pseudo query for P99 by route:
  SELECT route, percentile_cont(0.99) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY latency_ms) as p99_latency
  FROM request_logs
  WHERE tenant_id = 'TENANT_X' AND timestamp > now() - interval '7 days'
  GROUP BY route

- Cache hit ratio:
  SELECT SUM(cache_hits) / NULLIF(SUM(cache_hits + cache_misses),0) AS hit_ratio FROM kvcache_metrics WHERE tenant_id='TENANT_X' AND timestamp > now() - interval '14 days'

Post-QBR cadence and SLA for action closure

- Short-term actions (<=2 weeks): SLA = 14 calendar days from QBR date to implement or to produce a mitigation plan.
- Medium-term actions (<=3 months): Progressive checkpoints at 2 weeks, 6 weeks, and 12 weeks.
- If any action exceeds SLA without customer-agreed extension, escalate to Customer Success Manager Director and Product PM.

Ownership and escalation path

- CSM: primary facilitator and owner of customer comms and ticket backlog.
- SE (solutions engineer): technical owner for on-calls to implement canaries and run tests.
- Infra/SRE: owner for capacity, routing, and network fixes.
- Applied ML/Product: owner for model-quality actions and rollbacks.

Escalation ladder:
1) Owner -> CSM
2) CSM -> SE Lead or Infra SRE on-call (if technical unblock needed)
3) CSM -> Customer Success Manager Director -> Product PM -> Head of Engineering (if cross-team commitments required)

Templates and attachments (appendix)

- Executive one-pager template (copy/paste):
  Title: QBR Executive Brief – Tenant X
  One-liner (30s): <fill>
  Visual: attach chart file
  Top 3 risks: list
  Top 3 actions: owner, ETA, acceptance criteria

- Ticket template (copy/paste):
  Summary: <short text>
  Description: <context + query links + raw results>
  Acceptance criteria: <quantified metric>
  Canary plan: <traffic % and rollback triggers>
  Attachments: <links to dashboard + raw CSVs>

Appendix: common pitfalls and mitigations

- Pitfall: Telemetry freshness mismatch. Mitigation: Run sanity queries and include raw CSVs in QBR packet; push a data contract alert to platform-observability.
- Pitfall: Overfitting to noisy P99 spikes. Mitigation: Require correlated signal (request size, cache drop, or deployment event) before actioning high-cost remediations.
- Pitfall: Customer acceptance criteria too vague. Mitigation: Convert criteria to measured SLO deltas and require a 72h verification window.

Related pages and templates

- Use the QBR operational checklist as the pre-QBR timeline: /confluence/customer-success-and-support/health-and-qbr/qbr-template-and-operational-checklist-2026
- For telemetry contract examples see: /confluence/eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/tenant-telemetry-contracts

Change history

- 2026-02-15: Created by Priya Menon.
- 2026-03-10: Clarified SLA table and added alert-to-action mapping (reviewers: Diego Alvarez, Maya Chen).

Contact

For questions about the storyboard or to request a custom template for a specific customer, contact the Customer Success Enablement team at cs-enablement@redwood.ai.

title: Tenant Capacity Profiling, Cost Prediction, and QBR Template
content:
Overview

This document describes the standardized approach Redwood Customer Success (CS) and SRE use to: 1) profile an enterprise tenant’s capacity and request shape, 2) produce a 3–12 month cost and capacity prediction for QBRs, and 3) include a reusable QBR template that surfaces risk, recommended actions, and contractual implications for Dedicated/Private customers. The goal is to make capacity conversations data-driven and reproducible across accounts.

Goals
- Provide a canonical set of metrics and queries for tenant-level capacity profiling.
- Define a lightweight forecasting methodology (short, medium, long horizon) that balances observed telemetry with business signals.
- Produce a QBR-ready one-pager and supporting appendix for technical stakeholders and commercial owners.
- Define ownership, cadence, and escalation steps when capacity risk exceeds thresholds.

Scope
- Applies to: Dedicated and Private tenants, customers with committed capacity contracts, and any Hosted customer requesting formal capacity planning.
- Not covered: model training costs, third-party model hosting (unless integrated through Redwood routing), or non-inference infrastructure (storage-only pipelines).

Definitions and Key Metrics
- 95th/99th P90/P99 Latency: token-level generation latency at the configured model route.
- Token-throughput (tokens/s): measured per model pool.
- Requests per second (RPS): API request rate.
- Concurrency: number of simultaneous in-flight requests per tenant.
- Tail utilization: percent of time a tenant consumes >80% of its reserved GPU pool.
- Cost-per-1k-tokens: unit-cost metric normalized for forecasting.

Primary Data Sources (examples)\- Metrics: telemetry ingestion (Prometheus) -> metric names: redwood.request.count, redwood.request.latency_ms, redwood.kv_cache.hit_rate, redwood.tokens.generated
- Billing: per-tenant billing records (BigQuery table: billing.tenant_usage)
- Traces: sampled request traces in X-Ray/Jaeger for degradation analysis
- Config: tenant_config table for reserved pool sizes, routing policies, model pins

Profiling Methodology (step-by-step)
1) Baseline window: collect a 14-day rolling window and a 90-day window to surface seasonality.
2) Slice by route/model: generate per-route metrics (latency, tokens/s, RPS).
3) Identify burst patterns: compute 5-min and 1-hour rolling percentiles to detect short vs sustained peaks.
4) Compute cost-normalized utilization: join billing.tenant_usage with tokens generated -> compute cost-per-1k-tokens and effective spend distribution.

Example queries (BigQuery / SQL)
- 14-day per-route RPS and P95 latency:

SELECT route,
  COUNT(1)/1400.0 AS rps_avg_per_min,
  APPROX_QUANTILES(latency_ms, 100)[OFFSET(95)] AS p95_latency_ms
FROM telemetry.requests
WHERE tenant_id = "${TENANT_ID}"
  AND ts BETWEEN TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 14 DAY) AND CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()
GROUP BY route;

- Cost normalization (simplified):

SELECT tenant_id, SUM(tokens_generated) AS tokens, SUM(billed_amount_usd) AS billed
FROM billing.tenant_usage
WHERE tenant_id = "${TENANT_ID}"
  AND billing_period BETWEEN "2024-01" AND "2024-12"
GROUP BY tenant_id;

Forecasting approach
- Short horizon (0–30 days): exponential smoothing on the 14-day window + incorporate scheduled events (product launches) provided by the customer. Use conservative uplift of observed peaks (x1.25) when unknown.
- Medium horizon (1–3 months): ARIMA-lite with seasonality (weekday vs weekend) applied to daily RPS and tokens. Use contractual ramp if provided.
- Long horizon (3–12 months): scenario-based forecast: low/expected/high using business-reported growth rates and 3x stress overlay for capacity planning.

Quantitative thresholds (operational triggers)
- Yellow: tail utilization > 50% for 6+ hours/day for 3 consecutive days -> CS notified, schedule review.
- Orange: tail utilization > 70% for 12+ hours/day for 2 consecutive days or sudden 2x increase in sustained RPS -> Initiate capacity burst plan and FinOps review.
- Red: tail utilization > 90% for 4+ hours or sustained P99 latency > 2x SLO -> Incident escalation to Eng-SRE and commercial lead; consider immediate autoscale/burst and compensation discussion.

Runbook: When forecast crosses threshold
1) Validate telemetry: confirm data integrity (check missing metrics, agent restarts). Typical checks: Prometheus scrape errors, gap detection in request.count.
2) Verify tenant config: confirm reserved pool size, route pins, and any routing policies that could be diverting load.
3) Short mitigation: enable burst for 72 hours (Dedicated burst policy), temporarily increase concurrency caps, apply model switchover to compatible smaller model.
4) Medium mitigation: schedule capacity re-provisioning request with Eng-SRE; propose revised commit/renewal sizes to customer.
5) Post-event analysis: generate postmortem and update tenant forecast model with new observed parameters.

Communications and Ownership
- CS Owner: primary point for customer comms (owns QBR delivery, business context).
- Eng-SRE Owner: responsible for capacity changes, autoscale parameters, and burst provisioning.
- FinOps Owner: validates cost assumptions and prepares commercial options.
- Escalation path: CS -> Eng-SRE on-call -> Platform Engineering escalations manager -> VP Customer Success for contract-level interventions.

QBR one-pager template (use during quarterly reviews)
1) Executive summary (1–2 sentences): current capacity health, forecast band, and recommended commercial action.
2) Key metrics (table): 30/90/365 day RPS, tokens/month, P95/P99 latency, tail utilization, cost-per-1k-tokens.
3) Forecast snapshot (graph placeholder): expected low/med/high for next 12 months and recommended committed capacity.
4) Risk & mitigation (bulleted): scheduled events, model upgrades, potential multi-region cutover risk.
5) Action items (owner + due date): clear next steps and decision points.

Sample QBR table (text representation)
| Metric | Last 30 days | Last 90 days | Forecast next 90d (median) | Action |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Avg RPS | 12.5 | 9.8 | 15 (median) | Consider +1 reserved GPU 
| Tokens / month | 85M | 72M | 110M | Approve 20% uplift commit
| P95 latency (ms) | 320 | 290 | 340 | Monitor; possible model swap to v2-compact

Operational appendix (artifacts to produce)
- Export: 14 & 90-day CSVs (per-route RPS, tokens, latency).
- Cost model: one-line spreadsheet with unit costs and forecasted monthly spend by scenario.
- Synthetic test runs: 3 synthetic journeys (typical, burst, adversarial) with expected latency targets and pass/fail.

Synthetic test example (k6 CLI pseudo)
- Command: k6 run --vus 200 --duration 5m synthetic-journey.js --tenant ${TENANT_ID}
- Pass criteria: median latency < 500ms, 95th < 1.5x SLO for the route.

Commercial guidance and decision matrix
- If forecasted median spend exceed committed spend by <15% -> recommend short-term burst + FinOps review.
- If forecasted median spend exceed committed spend by 15–35% -> propose contract amendment or tiered burst schedule.
- If forecasted median spend exceed committed spend by >35% or sustained tail utilization in Orange/Red -> escalate to Sales/Legal for SLA amendment and potential credits.

Template delivery checklist (before QBR)
1) Generate profiling CSVs and forecast scenarios.
2) Run synthetic journeys and attach results.
3) Prepare one-pager QBR and internal appendix.
4) CS reviews with customer 7 days prior; collect product launch dates or known events.
5) Present QBR; capture decisions and convert to action items in the customer Jira board.

Appendix: Quick diagnostic checklist (for CS on-call)
- Are Prometheus scrapes healthy for tenant metrics? (yes/no)
- Is there a sudden change in request.size distribution? (investigate payload changes)
- Is KV cache hit rate degraded? (if < 25% for model routes, consider cache warm-up)
- Any model switch or deployment in the last 48 hours? (check release-notes)

References and links
- Telemetry metric catalog: /confluence/eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/metric-catalog
- Dedicated capacity playbook: /confluence/eng-sre/capacity-planning/dedicated-provisioning-playbook
- Billing model reference: /confluence/finance-and-legal/billing/per-tenant-billing-model

Change log
- 2024-11-15 (Asha Patel) created initial draft.
- 2024-12-20 (Evan Brooks) added SQL examples and forecasting thresholds.
- 2025-02-03 (Priya Nair) finalized thresholds and QBR template language.

Contacts
- CS lead: Asha Patel (asha@redwood.example.com)
- Eng-SRE on-call: see internal rota /confluence/eng-sre/oncall-rotations
- FinOps: Miguel Gonzalez (miguel@redwood.example.com)

title: Post-Go-Live Performance & Cost Ops Playbook
content:
summary:
Operational playbook for the first 90 days after enterprise customer go-live focused on latency, throughput, and cost optimization. Includes baselining steps, tuning levers, triage matrix, escalation contacts, and QBR-ready metrics.

content:
Overview:

This playbook helps Customer Success (CS), Site Reliability (SRE), and the customer engineering teams stabilize performance and unit economics after an enterprise go-live on Redwood Inference. It is intended for the first 90 days but is reusable for periodic performance reviews.

Goals:
- Ensure production P95 latency and error rate meet contractual targets.
- Reduce per-token compute cost where possible without degrading quality.
- Establish reliable escalation paths and observable dashboards for stakeholder reporting.

When to use this document:
- Post-go-live in the first 90 days (high-priority).
- Before QBRs to prepare performance and cost slides.
- During performance regressions or unexpected cost spikes.

Key metrics & SLOs (example targets):
- P95 latency (in-region, 512 token context): target <= 300 ms; alert >= 450 ms.
- Request error rate: target <= 0.1%; alert >= 0.5% over 5m.
- KV cache hit ratio: target >= 60%; action < 40%.
- Tokens/sec per GPU (steady-state throughput): baseline target 120k tokens/s for dedicated gpus (varies by model).
- Cost per 1k tokens (hosted): target depends on committed tier; track delta vs baseline.

Baseline measurement (Day 0–7):
1) Collect workload samples: 5–10 representative request traces covering short, medium, and long contexts (example: 32, 512, 2048 tokens).
2) Run synthetic load with production prompt mixes (use small blast tests then ramp):
   - Script: curl -X POST 'https://api.redwood.example/v1/generate' -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' -d '{"model":"rwd-4b","input":"<sample>"}'
3) Capture metrics: P50/P95/P99 latencies, CPU/GPU utilization, batching distribution, KV cache hit ratio, tail queue length, and cost estimate.
4) Record baseline table (example layout):

| Context | P50 (ms) | P95 (ms) | KV hit % | tokens/s | cost/1k tokens | Notes |
|---------|----------|----------|---------:|---------:|---------------:|-------|
| 32      | 45       | 120      | 78%      | 140k     | $0.38          | fast RPS paths |
| 512     | 120      | 280      | 62%      | 120k     | $0.60          | typical convo |
| 2048    | 320      | 670      | 35%      | 80k      | $1.10          | long-context heavy |

Tuning levers (ordered by recommended risk profile):
- Caching: implement/review prefix and KV cache settings first. Small prompts benefit most; aim to improve KV hit ratio via client-side prefixing or shared conversation keys.
- Batching: increase batch sizes for non-latency-critical routes. Target average tokens per batch > 256 where possible.
- Model variant routing: use a lower-cost quantized variant for background tasks; keep high-fidelity model for critical routes.
- Quantization profiles: enable 4-bit quantization on compatible models after validation on a small eval prompt set.
- Sequence length caps: enforce sensible max_input_tokens and max_completion_tokens per route.
- Rate-limiting & prioritization: route user-facing low-latency requests to low-latency pools; batch background jobs.
- Autoscaling and reservation: adjust Dedicated pool size and burst policy to match steady-state traffic and predictable peaks.

Operational runbook: triage matrix (fast path):
1) Symptom: increased P95 latency (> alert threshold)
   - Check 0–5m: Query Redwood Console dashboard for model-specific P95, queue length, and GPU utilization.
     - If queue length high & GPU utilization < 90% -> likely batching inefficiency (increase batch window or batchable traffic).
     - If GPU utilization > 95% and sustained -> request capacity (auto-scale or open Dedicated change) or enable model variant fallback.
     - If KV hit ratio dropped > 20% -> investigate prompt prefixing change or new user behavior.
   - Remediation steps: temporarily enable cheaper model variant for non-critical traffic, increase autoscaler target, or throttle background jobs.

2) Symptom: sharp cost spike (daily cost > 30% of baseline)
   - Check: per-route token consumption, embeddings vs generation mix, continuous vs batch jobs.
   - Remediation: disable noisy background routes, enable caching for embeddings, review quantization profile.

3) Symptom: elevated error rate (>= 0.5%)
   - Check: 5xx vs 4xx breakdown, auth failures, malformed payloads, model health.
   - Remediation: rollback recent client or server changes, restart serving pool, open bug with engineering if model runtime errors are recurring.

Escalation path (contact chain):
- Tier 1 CS (oncall): assigned CSM (customer success manager) — contact via Slack #cs-oncall and PagerDuty.
- Tier 2 SRE: eng-sre oncall rotation — page via PagerDuty with subject 'Post-Go-Live Performance Incident: <customer>'.
- Tier 3 Runtime Eng: runtime-owner@example.redwood.com — escalate when GPU-level faults, kernel OOMs, or profiling indicates runtime bug.
- Enterprise escalation: VP Customer Success and CTO if SLA breach is imminent.

Provide these fields in the PagerDuty page: incident_type, customer_name, cluster_id, model, observed_p95, baseline_p95, KV_hit, cost_delta, recent_deploy_commit.

Pre-approved mitigation actions (CS can execute):
- Apply route config override to reduce max_context_tokens to a safe cap.
- Switch traffic on a route to 'variant-low-cost' for X% of requests (canary 10% -> 50% -> 100%).
- Increase autoscaler min_replicas for the dedicated pool by N (N=1–3 depending on pool size).

Canary rollback and rollout checklist:
1) Validate change in staging with production-weighted traces.
2) Start 10% traffic for 15 minutes, monitor P95 and error rate.
3) If metrics stable, move to 50% for 15 minutes.
4) Full rollout if stable; otherwise rollback immediately and notify stakeholders.

Automated scripts & queries (examples):
- Query recent P95 by route (example with Console API):
  curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' 'https://console.redwood.example/api/v1/metrics?route_id=<route>&window=5m&metric=p95'
- KV cache diagnostic extractor (pseudo):
  rwd-kv-inspect --cluster cluster-a --route <route> --last 1h --output csv
- Cost delta report (daily cron):
  /bin/bash generate-cost-delta.sh --customer <customer> --since 2026-02-01

QBR & reporting templates (what to include):
- Executive summary: availability, response times vs SLA, cost trend, top actions taken.
- Technical appendix: baseline vs current tables for P50/P95/P99, KV hit ratio, tokens/s, autoscaler events.
- Action items & owners: e.g., enable quantization profile by 2026-03-01 (owner: customer eng), validate prompts for cacheability (owner: CSM).

Checklist for first 90 days (owner assignments):
- Day 0–7: Baseline collection and dashboard creation (owner: CSM + CS eng).
- Day 8–30: Implement low-risk levers (caching, batching config) and measure impact (owner: CS eng).
- Day 31–60: Trial quantization on a small test set and review quality metrics (owner: CS eng + Applied ML).
- Day 61–90: Finalize model routing policy and submit recommendations for Dedicated sizing adjustments (owner: SRE + CS).

Postmortem and continuous improvement:
- For any incident causing SLA degradation, complete postmortem within 7 days and include: timeline, root cause, mitigations, customer impact, and follow-up actions.
- Store postmortems at /confluence/customer-success-and-support/postmortems/ and link to related QBR slides.

Appendix A — Example route configuration snippet (YAML-style):

route_id: convo-fast
model: rwd-4b
max_input_tokens: 1024
max_completion_tokens: 256
batching:
  enabled: true
  max_wait_ms: 25
  target_tokens_per_batch: 512
cache:
  prefix_cache: true
  kv_cache_policy: LRU
  ttl_seconds: 3600
variant_fallbacks:
  - variant: rwd-4b-quantized
    weight: 0.1

Appendix B — Quick sanity checklist before a QBR slide: 
- Are P95 and cost delta updated for the reporting window?
- Have all mitigations been applied and documented?
- Is there a clear ask from the customer (capacity, product changes, pricing)?

Appendix C — Ownership table (example):
| Role | Responsibility | Contact |
|------|----------------|---------|
| CSM | Customer liaison and first responder | priya.nambiar@redwood.ai |
| CS Engineer | Baseline, configs, run actions | ethan.brooks@redwood.ai |
| SRE | Autoscaling, infra capacity | maya.chen@redwood.ai |
| Runtime Eng | Kernel and model runtime issues | runtime-owner@redwood.ai |

Notes and references:
- See eng-serving-runtime/release-notes for recent runtime changes before major triage.
- Use the dedicated 'cs-go-live' Slack channel for realtime coordination.

Change log:
- 2025-11-03: Created by Priya Nambiar.
- 2026-01-20: Added KV cache diagnostic steps and canary rollout checklist (reviewer: Ethan Brooks).
- 2026-02-15: Clarified escalation chain and added example Console API queries (reviewer: Maya Chen).

title: Onboarding Stability Sprint: Post-Go-Live Retro & Repair Sprint
content:
Summary
-------
This document defines the "Onboarding Stability Sprint": a focused 7–10 day cross-functional activity that runs immediately after an enterprise customer’s first live traffic cutover. The goal is to close early reliability gaps, stabilize cost/latency profiles, and deliver a structured retro that feeds QBR metrics and long-term remediation tickets.

Why this exists
----------------
Many go-lives appear successful on day-0 but surface repeated, low-severity reliability and cost issues over weeks (burst throttles, KV cache misses, cold-starts for rare routes). The Stability Sprint is a bounded, repeatable process to:
- Reduce mean time to remediation for non-critical but high-frequency issues
- Align engineering, SRE, product, and customer success on priority fixes
- Produce measurable outcomes for the customer’s first QBR and SLA review

Audience
--------
- Customer Success (primary owner)
- SRE and Runtime Engineering (operational remediation)
- Integrations and Solutions Engineering
- Product Manager for the customer
- Customer engineering contacts (participation as required)

Scope and success criteria
-------------------------
Inbound scope (what we cover during the sprint):
1) Stability: Reduce 95th/99th latency and error spikes for tenant routes observed in the first 72 hours
2) Cost alignment: Identify top 3 per-token cost drivers and produce short-term mitigations (batching changes, latency/cost routing)
3) Observability gaps: Add or refine telemetry assertions used for QBRs
4) Process: Triage and convert urgent fixes into tracked engineering work with owners and ETA

Success criteria (pass/fail):
- Pass: 3 of the 4 inbound scope goals completed and customer signs off on readiness for QBR metrics collection
- Partial: 1–2 goals completed with clear remediation plan and committed ship dates
- Fail: fewer than 1 goal completed and no committed remediation plan

Sprint cadence and timeline (example 7-day sprint)
-------------------------------------------------
Day 0 (cutover evening)
- Customer Success runs the cutover acceptance checklist and starts the sprint document
- SRE enables increased short-term telemetry retention for the tenant (72h high-fidelity window)

Day 1: Triage & quick wins
- Morning: 60–90 minute cross-functional triage meeting (see Meeting agenda below)
- Identify top 5 signals (errors, 99p latency routes, token-cost anomalies) and assign owners
- Implement 1–2 quick fixes (e.g., route pinning, temporary rate caps, client-side batching guidance)

Day 2–4: Focused repair work
- Parallel squads work queued tickets: instrumentation gaps, caching adjustments, configuration tuning
- Daily 30-minute sync for blockers and status updates

Day 5: Validation and hardening
- Run synthetic journeys (customer-specific) against fixed routes for 24–48h validation window
- Confirm telemetry assertions and cost telemetry alignment

Day 6–7: Retro and QBR prep
- Draft the sprint retro artifacts, remediation backlog, ownership matrix, and QBR-ready dashboard snapshots
- Customer Success coordinates a 60-minute stakeholder retro and produces a 1-page QBR summary

Roles and responsibilities
--------------------------
- Customer Success (CS): sprint owner; coordinates meetings, customer comms, and sign-off
- SRE Lead: owns incident-style triage and operational changes (routing, SLAs, infra tweaks)
- Runtime Eng: implements kernel/runtime/quantization configuration changes that affect latency/cost
- Integrations/SE: assists with client-side SDK guidance and validates contract changes
- Product: prioritizes cross-cutting product changes into roadmap if necessary

Triage meeting agenda (60–90 minutes)
------------------------------------
1) Quick status & customer impact summary (CS) — 5m
2) Top signals review (observability owner) — 10m
3) Action items and owners for quick fixes — 20m
4) Risk heatmap and decide if escalation to priority path required — 10m
5) Communication plan for customer (who says what and when) — 10m
6) Schedule re-checks and define success criteria — remaining time

Telemetry and synthetic checks (examples)
--------------------------------------
Key signals to monitor (minimum):
- 99th latency per route (ms)
- Error rate by tenant and route (5m/1h windows)
- KV cache miss ratio and effective hit amplification
- Per-request token cost variance (7d baseline comparison)
- Streaming connection resets & gRPC idle stream resets

Example telemetry assertion (JSON snippet used by the synthetic runner):
{
  "assertion_name": "tenant-99p-latency-under-400ms",
  "metric": "route.latency.99p",
  "tenant_id": "TENANT-1234",
  "threshold_ms": "400",
  "window_mins": "60"
}

Observability checklist (table)
------------------------------
| Item | Owner | Minimum requirement | Why it matters |
|------|-------|---------------------|----------------|
| 99p latency per-route | SRE | 5m resolution | Detect tail latency spikes |
| Token cost breakdown | Finance/CS | per-route / per-model | Surface cost drivers |
| KV cache hit rate | Runtime Eng | 1m resolution | Affects downstream latency & cost |
| Streaming resets | Integrations | 5m resolution | Client compatibility and stability |

Quick remediation patterns (common fixes)
-----------------------------------------
- Route-level pinning to a stable model variant for 24–72 hours
- Apply temporary soft rate-limits to bursty tenant endpoints (CS+SRE approved)
- Enable aggressive prefix caching for high-reuse prompt families
- Adjust batching window for low-latency interactive routes to reduce token churn
- Short-term increase in dedicated capacity (if contract allows) for traffic hot-paths

Escalation ladder for issues discovered during the sprint
------------------------------------------------------
1) Sprint triage owners (first responders) — 30m SLA for acknowledgement
2) SRE lead + Runtime Eng — 2h SLA to propose temporary mitigations
3) On-call manager / Eng Director — 4h SLA to approve emergency capacity or cross-region failover
4) Exec stakeholder & customer leadership — notify if >8h unresolved customer-impacting degradation

Communication templates (customer-facing)
----------------------------------------
Subject: Post-go-live stability sprint: initial findings
Hi <Customer Name> team,

Thank you again for your cutover last night. We’ve initiated a 7-day stability sprint to ensure the experience meets your SLAs. Initial observations: increased 99p latency on conversational route ‘chat/v1-consumer’, and an elevated token cost variance on the re-ranking route. We will: (1) pin the route to a stable model variant within 2 hours, (2) deploy a temporary rate cap on low-impact endpoints, and (3) share a daily 09:30 PST update for the next 72 hours.

If you prefer a different cadence or immediate technical deep-dive, please let us know.

Best,
Customer Success (Aisha Patel)

Retro template (to capture outcomes)
----------------------------------
- What went well (bullet list)
- What surprised us
- Highest impact fixes delivered (with ticket IDs)
- Outstanding risks and owners
- Recommended product/roadmap changes
- QBR metrics to include for next meeting

QBR integration and artifacts to produce
-------------------------------------
- 1-page sprint summary with: top-5 signals, fixes delivered, outstanding items, and customer sign-off
- QBR dashboard snapshot with: 99p latency trend, per-route cost, error-rate trend, synthetic journey pass-rate
- Remediation backlog grouped by priority and owner with ETA

Post-sprint handoff checklist
----------------------------
1) Ensure all temporary mitigations have explicit TTLs and owners (no open temporary configs)
2) Create corresponding tickets in the product/engineering backlog with linked JIRA IDs
3) Schedule follow-up check at 30 and 90 days post-cutover to validate long-term stability
4) Attach synthetic run artifacts and telemetry snapshots to the account record

Runbook snippets and commands
----------------------------
Example: temporarily pin a route to a model variant via the admin CLI:

bash
redwoodctl route update --tenant TENANT-1234 --route chat/v1-consumer --pin model:openlite-v2-quant --ttl 72h

Example: query 99p latency via metrics CLI (Prometheus-compatible):

bash
redwoodctl metrics query "histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(route_request_duration_seconds_bucket{tenant=\"TENANT-1234\"}[5m])) by (le, route))"

Appendix: typical remediation effort sizing
------------------------------------------
- Quick fixes: 1–4 engineer-hours (routing, config changes)
- Instrumentation gaps: 1–3 engineer-days (add metrics/assertions)
- Runtime changes requiring deploys: 3–10 engineer-days (may span releases)
- Product/roadmap work: tracked as epics (multi-sprint)

Appendix: decision log (example entries)
--------------------------------------
- 2026-11-05: Sprint framework ratified by CS and SRE leadership — A. Patel
- 2026-12-10: Added per-route cost telemetry requirement — M. Chen
- 2027-02-12: Expanded communication templates and telemetry assertions (Ravi Kumar)

Related documents and where to store artifacts
--------------------------------------------
- Store sprint artifacts (telemetry snapshots, synthetic runs) in the customer record folder: s3://redwood-enterprise-artifacts/<tenant-id>/stability-sprints/<date>/
- Link JIRA epics to the customer account in the CRM and include sprint summary PDF.

Notes and caveats
-----------------
- The Stability Sprint is not a replacement for emergency incident response. If a P0 occurs, follow the standard incident process and pause the sprint cadence in favor of incident postmortem flows.
- Customer opt-in: this sprint is part of our enterprise onboarding offering and should be presented as recommended but may be opted out by customers under special circumstances.

Document history
----------------
- 2026-11-05: Created (Aisha Patel)
- 2026-12-10: Added cost telemetry requirements (Michael Chen)
- 2027-02-12: Expanded communication templates and telemetry assertions (Ravi Kumar)

title: Client Observability Playground: Templates & Experiment Catalog
content:
Summary:

This page describes the "Client Observability Playground": a set of lightweight templates, runnable quickstarts, and an experiment catalog designed to help SDK and integration teams iterate on telemetry coverage and dashboards before landing changes in the production telemetry pipeline. The playground is intended for feature teams, SDK maintainers, and developer-experience engineers who want to prototype, validate, and compare instrumentation strategies with minimal ops overhead.

Goals:
- Make safe, repeatable experiments for SDK telemetry and ingestion changes.
- Provide reusable templates (telemetry config, ingestion helpers, dashboard JSON, alert rules).
- Catalog reproducible experiments with hypotheses and measurable success criteria.
- Capture canonical fixes for the top support issues uncovered during experiments.

When to use the playground:
- You're rolling out a new SDK metric, event, or tracing span and want to validate signal quality before production ingestion.
- You need to compare two sampling strategies (e.g., 0.1% vs 10%) and quantify tradeoffs on cost vs. coverage.
- You want to prototype a dashboard or alert and verify it maps to useful behavior for oncall.

Quickstarts (runnable templates)

1) Local sandbox: instrument + forward to test ingestion
- Purpose: Validate SDK events, tags, and JSON schema locally without touching prod pipelines.
- Artifact: telemetry-config.yaml (template below), docker-compose sandbox, example ingestion lambda.
- Run steps:
  1. git clone git@redwood:dx/observability-playground.git
  2. cd observability-playground/local-sandbox
  3. cp telemetry-config.yaml.example telemetry-config.yaml && edit sampling/sink settings
  4. docker-compose up --build
  5. run the sample client: 
     - Python: python samples/simple_client.py --config telemetry-config.yaml
     - Node: node samples/simple_client.js --config telemetry-config.yaml
  6. Open Kibana/Tempo/Dashboard at http://localhost:5601 (see README for port mapping)

2) Canary telemetry for SDK releases
- Purpose: Send new metric/span names to a canary ingestion path for 1% of traffic and validate cardinality and latency impact.
- Key pieces: canary-ingest rule, canary-dashboard, automated comparison job that calculates percent-change in cardinality.
- Acceptance: cardinality growth < 3x and p95 ingestion latency < 300ms for canary path.

3) Sampling strategy A/B
- Purpose: Compare full-span capture vs. sampled spans for heavy customers to find cost/coverage sweet spot.
- Experiment harness: load generator + telemetry-forwarder that can toggle sampling at runtime via feature-flag.
- Success metric: % of user-facing errors correlated with spans captured; cost delta per million requests.

Template: telemetry-config.yaml (example)

# telemetry-config.yaml (example for local-sandbox and canary)
service_name: "redwood-client-sample"
output_sink: "http://localhost:4318/v1/traces"   # OTLP collector in sandbox
sampling:
  mode: "fractional"        # options: always, none, fractional, adaptive
  fraction: 0.01             # for canary tests set 0.01
metrics:
  enable: true
  export_interval_ms: 10000
  groups:
    - name: "client_requests"
      labels: ["endpoint", "model", "region"]
events_schema_version: "v2"
json_schema_validation: true

Prometheus alert (example)

# Alert: High telemetry event loss in canary pipeline\groups:
- name: telemetry-canary.rules
  rules:
  - alert: CanaryTelemetryEventLossHigh
    expr: (sum(rate(canary_telemetry_events_dropped_total[5m])) / sum(rate(canary_telemetry_events_total[5m]))) > 0.01
    for: 10m
    labels:
      severity: critical
    annotations:
      summary: "Canary telemetry event loss > 1% for 10m"
      runbook: "/confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/canary-telemetry-loss"

Instrumentation checklist (SDK authors)
- Use the telemetry-config.yaml template as the single source of sampling/label configs.
- Limit cardinality on event tags (avoid user_id/email at top-level). Use hashed identifiers if needed.
- Record model name, token_count, and prompt_length for each request.
- Emit a compact span for latency-critical code paths with attributes: {service, route, model, seq_len}.
- Expose a runtime toggle (ENV var or feature flag) to switch sampling fraction.
- Ensure each telemetry event includes a stable "experiment_id" tag when running an experiment.

Experiment catalog (summary table)

| id | experiment_name | hypothesis | instrumentation | success_metric | owner |
|----|-----------------|------------|-----------------|----------------|-------|
| EXP-001 | sampling-fraction-sensitivity | Reducing sampling to 0.5% preserves error-detection power while cutting costs by >6x | client sampled metrics + canary pipeline | relative error-detection rate >= 90% and cost/M requests reduced >= 6x | Aisha K. |
| EXP-002 | span-lightweight-vs-full | Lightweight spans (reduced attributes) reduce ingestion latency without losing the ability to triage common errors | span schema variants v1/v2 | triage coverage delta < 5% and p95 ingest < 200ms | Tom M. |
| EXP-003 | model-tag-normalization | Normalizing model tag values reduces cardinality noise and makes dashboards stable | normalization library + cardinality check job | unique tag cardinality reduced by >= 70% | Sofia L. |

(Full catalog lives in the repository: observability-playground/experiments/catalog.md)

Top support issues observed during playground runs (canonical fixes)

1) Symptom: Dashboard shows frequent spikes labeled "unknown_model"
   - Root cause: SDK allowed arbitrary model identifiers; missing normalization step in client.
   - Canonical fix: Add model_tag_normalizer utility (see templates/model_normalizer.py) and add unit test mapping unknown values to "model:unknown".

2) Symptom: Canary path shows high event drop rate after traffic bursts
   - Root cause: OTLP collector queue sizing too small for bursty canary traffic; default collector config used.
   - Canonical fix: Increase receiver memory_buffer_limit to 256Mi and tune exporter retry_on_failure with backoff policy. Apply change in telemetry-config.yaml for canary.

3) Symptom: New metric created high-cardinality label causing billing spikes
   - Root cause: Instrumentation used raw customer email as label.
   - Canonical fix: Remove email label; replace with hashed_customer_id and add a label_policy linter rule in CI.

How to run an experiment (standard operating procedure)

1. Create a fork of observability-playground and add a new experiment directory under experiments/EXP-###.
2. Populate: hypothesis.md, telemetry-config.yaml, sample_client_changes/, dashboard.json, and runbook.md.
3. Request a canary key by filing a small PR to dx/configs/canary-keys with the experiment_id and owner.
4. Run the local-sandbox and smoke-test your events. For canary runs, submit a kiss-off via Slack channel #dx-canary with the experiment_id.
5. Collect data for 48h (or according to the experiment run-length), run the automated analysis job: scripts/analyze_experiment.py --id EXP-### --baseline last-7d
6. Publish results: update experiments/catalog.md with results and attach the dashboard snapshot.
7. If successful, follow the rollout checklist in runbook.md to merge changes into sdk/main and schedule a gradual rollout.

Analysis guidelines (what to look for)
- Signal quality: check completeness (% of requests that emit required tags) and schema validity errors. Target: >99.5% completeness.
- Cardinality: track 7-day unique counts for each label; target is no more than 5x growth from baseline unless justified.
- Cost: estimate ingestion cost per million events for both old and new instrumentation.
- Mean time to triage (MTTT): measure whether new signals reduce MTTT for the bug class targeted by the experiment.

Example instrumentation snippets

Python (middleware style):
```python
# simple telemetry middleware for requests
from telemetry import TelemetryClient
client = TelemetryClient.from_config('telemetry-config.yaml')

def instrumented_request(route, model_name, payload):
    with client.span('request', attributes={'route': route, 'model': model_name}):
        res = call_model_api(payload)
        client.metric('client.requests', 1, labels={'route': route, 'model': normalize_model(model_name)})
        return res
```

Node (express middleware example):
```javascript
const Telemetry = require('@redwood/telemetry');
const client = Telemetry.fromConfig(process.env.TELEMETRY_CONFIG || './telemetry-config.yaml');

app.use((req, res, next) => {
  const start = Date.now();
  res.on('finish', () => {
    const latency = Date.now() - start;
    client.emitMetric('client.requests', 1, { route: req.path, model: req.headers['x-model'] || 'unknown' });
    client.emitSpan('client.request', { route: req.path, duration_ms: latency });
  });
  next();
});
```

Rollout and rollback guidance
- Always run canary for at least 24-48h or until you have 10k canary events, whichever is later.
- If cardinality growth > 5x or event_loss > 1%, rollback immediately and open an incident in #platform-incidents.
- Use experiment_id and replay logs to reproduce for postmortem.

Ownership and contact points
- Playground owner: eng-devex (Aisha Kapoor) — primary contact in #dx-playground.
- Canary key approvals: eng-sre reviewers on the PR.
- Template changes: submit PRs to observability-playground repo; reviewers: Tom Myers, Sofia Lind.

References and related artifacts
- observability-playground repository (internal): git@redwood:dx/observability-playground.git
- Common dashboards: dashboards/client-overview.json (in repo)
- Runbooks: /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/canary-telemetry-loss

Appendix: useful metrics and SLOs to track during experiments
- telemetry_event_loss_target: 0.001  # 0.1% acceptable loss
- ingestion_p95_target_ms: 250
- tag_completeness_target: 0.995
- max_cardinality_multiplier: 5.0

If you have questions or want a walkthrough, schedule a 30m pairing with eng-devex via the #dx-playground channel or request a session in the devx calendar.

title: Customer Health Audit & Risk Mitigation Playbook
content:
Summary

This playbook describes the Customer Health Audit process used by Redwood Customer Success to surface operational, cost, and quality risks for enterprise accounts running Redwood Hosted, Dedicated, or Private deployments. The goal is to provide a repeatable audit cadence, a quantitative risk score, concrete remediation actions, and an executive-ready summary for QBRs and escalations.

Scope

- Applies to enterprise and dedicated customers with production traffic > 10k API calls/day or with a Dedicated/Private contract.
- Covers three domains: Service Reliability (latency/errors), Model Quality (regression & hallucination signals), and Economics (cost per 1k tokens / spend trending).
- Audit cadence: monthly for at-risk customers, quarterly for healthy customers, and ad-hoc after major incidents or rollouts.

Roles & Ownership

- Customer Success Manager (CSM): overall owner of the audit, primary contact for the customer, coordinates remediation work.
- Solutions Engineer (SE): operational lead; runs diagnostics, implements configuration changes (batching, cache), and validates fixes.
- Product/Applied ML: consulted when pattern suggests model/quality regression or recommended model changes.
- SRE/Support: handles low-level runtime issues, capacity, or infra incidents.

Audit Preparation (2–3 business days before assessment)

1. Trigger: CSM schedules audit in calendar and notifies SE and customer with scope and data window (last 30 days by default).
2. Data collection checklist (attach to audit ticket):
   - Logs: request/response traces, latency histograms (p50/p90/p99), error logs (last 30 days).
   - Billing: per-route token breakdown, monthly spend, top 10 routes by cost.
   - Model settings: pinned model versions, quantization profile, batch/timeout configs.
   - Prompts and evals: recent prompt sets, failing prompts flagged by QA.
   - Customer config: routing policies, region preferences, cache settings.

Audit Checklist (executed by SE + CSM)

- Service Reliability
  - Median latency per route (p50): check against SLO. Thresholds: p50 > 250ms (warning), p50 > 500ms (critical).
  - Tail latency (p99): p99 > 1.5s (warning), p99 > 3s (critical).
  - Error rate: total 5xx > 0.5% (warning), > 2% (critical).
  - Throttling/rate-limit events: frequency and root cause (customer spikes vs infra).

- Model Quality
  - Regression alerts: responses failing customer gold prompts increased by >10% vs baseline.
  - Hallucination signals: manual QA or automated semantic checks flagged >3% of sampled responses.
  - Token truncation/early-eos events: >1% of responses truncated unexpectedly.

- Economics
  - Cost-per-1k tokens: compare current month vs prior 3-month average. Delta > +20% => warning; > +50% => critical.
  - Inefficient routes: top 5 routes by cost and token-per-call ratios.
  - Batching utilization: low utilization on high-throughput routes indicates missed savings.

Risk Scoring Rubric

Assign numeric points per observed item then compute a weighted score (0–100). Categories and weights: Reliability 40, Quality 35, Economics 25.

- Example point assignments (single audit window):
  - Reliability: critical p99 events (+30), repeated 5xx spikes (+20), throttling blocking production (+25).
  - Quality: regression alert cluster (+20), hallucination >5% (+25), degradation on Canary vs Prod (+15).
  - Economics: sudden spend delta +50% (+20), misconfigured batching (+10), cache disabled (+15).

Total Score Interpretation:
- 0–29: Healthy. Routine follow-up.
- 30–59: At-risk. Action items required within 14 days.
- 60–100: High risk. Escalation recommended; consider canary rollback or temporary throttling.

Example Audit Table (for insertion into ticket)

| Domain | Metric | Observed | Threshold | Severity |
|-------|--------|----------|-----------|----------|
| Reliability | p99 latency (route /generate) | 2.8s | 1.5s (warn) / 3s (crit) | warning |
| Quality | Gold prompt pass rate | 78% (down from 92%) | 90% baseline | critical |
| Economics | Cost / 1k tokens (monthly) | $18.20 | +20% warning | warning |

Immediate Remediations (actions to perform in the first 72 hours)

1. If Quality critical: rollback model variant or pin prior working model; open applied-ml ticket for evaluation. Steps:
   a. Identify offending model deployment and associated rollout ID.
   b. Execute canary rollback: follow internal runbook (link: /eng-developer-experience/api-examples/canary-rollback).
   c. Notify customer and schedule investigation call.
2. If Reliability critical: apply temporary rate-limiter or route traffic to fallback region/model. Steps:
   a. Enable emergency throttles on affected routes (SE + SRE).
   b. Re-route high-cost/latency traffic to a cheaper lower-latency region or a smaller model variant with comparable quality.
3. If Economics critical: enable batching and prefix/KV caching where safe; review quantization profile. Steps:
   a. Suggest config changes: increase batch_size cap, set adaptive batching to true, enable KV prefix cache for repeated prompts.
   b. Validate token accounting and project expected cost delta.

Escalation Flow & Triage Matrix

- At-risk (score 30–59): CSM + SE action within 14 days, weekly check-ins. If unresolved after 2 cycles escalate to Customer Success Lead.
- High risk (score 60+): Immediate cross-functional war room: CSM, SE, SRE, Product, Applied ML; timeline goals: initial mitigation within 24 hours, full remediation plan within 72 hours.
- Executive escalation: prepare a 1-page exec summary; notify account executive and VP Customer Success for renewal-impacting accounts.

Communication Templates

- Customer initial notice (CSM to customer):
  Subject: Customer Health Audit — Findings & Immediate Actions
  Body: Short summary (2–3 bullets), impact statement, immediate mitigations applied, next steps and timeline,war-room contact.

- Internal war-room kickoff (CSM to cross-functional list):
  Subject: WAR ROOM — [Account] — High Risk Audit (score: XX)
  Body: One-line TL;DR, key metrics, links to dashboards, owner assignments, meeting link.

Quarterly Executive Summary Template (for QBR slide deck)

- Page title: Operational Health & Trends — [Customer Name] — Last 90 days
- TL;DR: one-sentence health band (Healthy / At-risk / High risk) and recommended executive ask (e.g., budget approval, architecture change).
- Key metrics: uptime %, p99 latency, monthly spend trend, model pass-rate on gold prompts.
- Top incidents and mitigations: list 3–5 items with dates and impact.
- Action plan & commitments: items, owners, due dates.
- Ask of the customer: engineering time, dataset for evals, or approval to change model variant.

Audit Ticketing & Tracking

- Create a case in Zendesk (or internal tracker) with prefix CHA-[account]-YYYYMM. Include: audit score, checklist, remediation tasks (as subtasks), and due dates.
- Use label: health-audit and priority tags (P2 for at-risk, P1 for high risk).
- Link ticket to the customer’s support backlog and to the QBR board for follow-up.

Post-Audit Follow-ups (14–90 days)

- 14-day: verify mitigations are effective, update customer and close immediate fixes.
- 30-day: confirm metric regressions reversed and any config rollouts stabilized.
- 90-day: re-run audit cadence, update QBR materials, and assess if SLA amendments are needed.

Instrumentation & Dashboards

- Required dashboards and saved queries (examples):
  - Per-route latency: p50/p90/p99 and traffic volume.
  - Model pass-rate on gold prompt set (rolling 7d/30d).
  - Cost rollup by route and model variant (daily).
  - Batching/caching utilization by service.

Example SQL snippet (monthly cost by route)

SELECT route, SUM(tokens_in + tokens_out) AS total_tokens, SUM(cost) AS total_cost
FROM billing.events
WHERE account_id = '<<ACCOUNT_ID>>' AND event_date >= DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE, INTERVAL 30 DAY)
GROUP BY route
ORDER BY total_cost DESC
LIMIT 20;

Appendix: Common Findings & Recommended Fixes

- Large spikes in p99 tied to specific third-party integrations: recommend isolating those flows and adding retry/backoff.
- Quality dip after model refresh: recommend immediate canary rollback + larger regression evaluation on labelled prompts.
- Unexpected token spend: typically caused by template expansion loops or verbose system prompts — recommend prompt audit and token budget caps per route.

References & Links

- Support runbooks: ../support-process/enterprise-support-lifecycle-dedicated-private-playbook-2025
- Canary rollback runbook: ../eng-developer-experience/docs/canary-rollback-guide
- Model evaluation harness: ../applied-ml-and-evals/eval-harness/overview

Change log

- 2025-02-10: Created by Lina Park (initial framework).
- 2025-10-05: Added scoring rubric and immediate remediation templates (review: Marcus Liu).
- 2026-01-18: Updated thresholds and SQL sample; clarified escalation timelines (review: Priya Natarajan).

title: QBR Transition: Technical and Commercial Handoff Playbook
content:
Summary:
This playbook defines a standardized cross-functional process for transitioning an enterprise customer from post-provisioning operations into a regular QBR (Quarterly Business Review) cadence. It focuses on a two-track handoff: (1) Technical handoff into steady-state SRE/Customer Success operations, and (2) Commercial handoff into Customer Success/Account teams for QBRs and renewed commercial commitments. The goal is to reduce post-go-live friction, ensure telemetry and SLO alignment, and provide a repeatable checklist for both technical and commercial stakeholders.

Scope and Intent:
- Applies to enterprise customers after successful go-live and the first 14 days of stability verification.
- Intended for customers using Hosted API, Dedicated, or Private deployments.
- Covers telemetry gating, runbook ownership transfer, QBR readiness criteria, and obligations for escalation.

When to use this playbook:
1. After the 72-hour and 14-day stability sweeps complete and the customer is marked "operational" in the cutover checklist.
2. When the customer is expected to enter the first revenue-bearing QBR cycle or when an SLA/commercial review is requested.

Pre-handoff (Technical) Checklist - must be completed before commercial handoff:
1) Telemetry and Dashboards
   - Confirm tenant-specific dashboards exist in Grafana/Looker: "Tenant Overview", "Token Economics", "Model Quality Trends", "Latency & Errors".
   - Confirm synthetic journeys (happy path + edge cases) are running and passing for 14 consecutive days.
2) SLO and Alerting
   - SLOs validated: availability P99 >= 99.5% (for Dedicated) or SLA baseline met per contract.
   - Alert definitions and on-call rotation ownership documented and tested.
3) Security & Compliance Gates
   - Network controls (VPC peering, firewall rules) verified and recorded.
   - Logs retention and access review completed with security contact.
4) Operational Runbooks and Playbooks
   - Tenant runbook created: include common triage steps, known quirks, and rollback criteria.
   - Escalation contacts confirmed and smoke-test call executed.
5) Cost and Quota Protections
   - Billing alerts and quota caps configured; cost-protection webhook validated.

Roles and Responsibilities:
- Customer Success (CS): drive commercial handoff, coordinate QBR agenda, own account-level risks.
- SRE/Platform: own technical stabilization, SLO validation, and on-call readiness.
- Solutions Engineering (SE): provide architecture decisions, post-cutover optimizations, and model migration notes.
- Customer: confirm business objectives, authorized stakeholders for QBRs, and acceptance of operational telemetry.

Telemetry Gating Criteria (hard gates):
- Synthetic success rate >= 99% over 14d for primary flows.
- Observed token throughput within 20% of projected ramp for 7d or documented variance with mitigating plan.
- No P1 incidents in last 7d and P2 incidents trend stable or decreasing.

Technical Handoff Steps (numbered):
1. Finalize and publish tenant runbook to internal wiki; tag SRE on the page and mark as "owned".
2. Export tenant dashboards to the account folder and assign CS read-only links.
3. Run a joint smoke test between SRE, CS, and the customer that simulates these failure modes: model fallback, region failover, quota limit triggered.
4. Confirm on-call rotation contains a named owner for the tenant and verify escalation path to engineering.
5. Record the handoff meeting minutes with action items and owners in the ticketing system.

Commercial Handoff Checklist (concurrent with or after technical handoff):
- Confirm QBR cadence (quarterly by default) and primary agenda items: availability, cost/perf, model quality, roadmap alignment, risk and escalations.
- Prepare the Customer Health one-pager: activation metrics, synthetic pass rate, spend vs. forecast, open action items.
- Deliver a short technical appendix for the QBR: current model hosted, quantization profile, recent rollouts, and performance baselines.
- Agree on success metrics for the next quarter and an escalation SLA (response targets and review triggers).

Abort and Rollback Criteria (explicit stop conditions):
- Abort a commercial handoff if any hard telemetry gate fails (synthetic < 99% over 7d) or a P1 incident was recorded in the last 72h.
- Rollback model/route changes if model quality regression is above the agreed threshold: labeled false-positive rate increase > 4% or a decrease in mean quality score > 6 points on the evaluation harness.

Post-handoff Verification and QBR Triggers:
- Daily health digest for the first 14 days following handoff (email + Slack) summarizing synthetic pass rate, error budget burn, and cost delta.
- Trigger a Technical QBR (mini-review) if cost delta exceeds 25% of forecast or if SLO burn is > 30% in a 7d window.
- Add an item to the next QBR if any major action item remains open at handoff.

Standard QBR Agenda Template (recommended):
1) Executive summary (5m) - health and key asks
2) Operational review (15m) - availability, latency, incidents, SLO burn
3) Cost and capacity (10m) - spend trends, quota requests, committed units
4) Model quality (15m) - eval results, prompt regressions, A/B experiments
5) Roadmap and asks (10m) - upcoming migrations, dedicated capacity requests
6) Action items and owners (5m)

Sample alert thresholds and recommended dashboards (appendix table):
| Area | Metric | Threshold | Owner |
| Tenant Availability | P99 request latency | > 800 ms for 5m | SRE |
| Synthetic Journeys | Failure rate | > 1% over 15m | CS + SRE |
| Cost | Daily spend delta | > 25% above forecast | FinOps/CS |
| Model Quality | Eval pass delta | Drop > 4 points | SE/Research |

Operations examples and CLI snippets:
- Export synthetic test logs for a tenant (example):
  curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_API_KEY" \ 
    "https://api.redwood.ai/v1/tenants/{tenant_id}/synthetic-tests?from=2027-01-01&to=2027-01-15" 
    -o tenant-synthetics.json

- Example alert query (PromQL-like pseudo):
  rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{tenant_id="TENANT_123",le="0.8"}[5m]) < 0.95

Handoff meeting template (items to capture):
- Date/time, participants (roles), final telemetry snapshot, known risks, outstanding action items with owners and due dates, next QBR date.

Escalation alignment (who to call first):
1) Customer Success (primary commercial contact)
2) SRE on-call (technical P1/P2)
3) Solutions Engineering (architectural guidance)
4) Research/Model Onboarding (model regressions or quality escalations)

Reference materials and links:
- Tenant runbook template: /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/tenant-runbook-template
- QBR slide template: /confluence/customer-success-and-support/health-and-qbr/qbr-template-and-operational-checklist-2026
- Escalation matrix: /confluence/customer-success-and-support/escalation-playbook/urgent-escalation-handoff-and-sla-triage-2026

Appendix: common failure-mode playbooks to attach at handoff:
- Model fallback fanout and mitigation playbook (for heavy tail prompts)
- Quota surge and fair-share isolation playbook
- Observability mismatch triage checklist

Notes and best practices (guidance for teams):
- Keep the technical handoff independent of commercial readiness: do not finalize a QBR cadence until telemetry gates pass.
- Err on the side of shorter QBRs for the first two cycles: operational detail should be minimized in favor of clear action items.
- Keep dashboards minimal and focused: 4–6 widgets per dashboard for executives, 8–12 for technical owners.

title: Synthetic Acceptance Gates and Cost Stability Playbook
content:
Overview

Purpose: This playbook defines a structured set of synthetic acceptance gates and cost-stability checks used during enterprise onboarding and model cutovers. The goal is to provide deterministic, repeatable validation steps that prove functional correctness, SLO alignment, and cost predictability before a tenant moves to full production traffic.

Scope: Applies to Dedicated and Private tenants and to hosted customers undergoing canary or full cutovers for new model versions, runtime changes (kernel/quantization), or routing policy updates.

When to use this playbook
- New tenant go-lives (first 14 days).
- Model version upgrades that alter tokenization, sampling, or decoding paths.
- Runtime upgrades (quantization profile change, kernel swap, scheduler update).
- Observability or billing pipeline changes that could impact telemetry fidelity.

Key outcomes
- Clear pass/fail criteria for synthetic tests covering correctness, latency, and per-token cost.
- Ownerable rollback/mitigation actions and automated cutover safety nets.
- Actionable signals for QBRs and post-go-live remediation.

Acceptance gates (summary table)
| Gate | Objective | Minimum pass criteria | Primary metric | Tolerance | Owner |
|---|---|---:|---|---:|---|
| Functional correctness | Ensure prompts produce expected structured outputs | >= 95% of golden prompts match structure / key fields present | Golden-match-rate | - | CS-Integration + Model-Onboard |
