| Latency SLO | Verify p50/p95 token latency within contract SLO | p50 <= 80ms, p95 <= 350ms (tenant baseline) | Latency (ms) | p50:+10ms / p95:+50ms | Eng-SRE + Runtime |
| Cost stability | Confirm per-token cost not exceeding baseline by more than threshold | per-token cost delta <= +12% vs baseline (7d) | Per-token-cost (cents) | +12% | FinOps + CS |
| Error & Rate | No increase in request failures or 429s beyond baseline | error-rate delta <= +0.1% absolute, 429s <= baseline*1.5 | error-rate, 429-rate | see tolerance | Support |
| Observability fidelity | Logs, traces, and token-level cost attribution present | 100% telemetry coverage for synthetic requests | telemetry-coverage | 0% tolerance | Telemetry Team |

Detailed procedure (step-by-step)
1) Pre-cutover: prepare tenant baseline (owner: Customer Success engineer)
   a) Capture 7-day baseline: median token cost, latency percentiles, error rates, and golden prompt pass rates. Use the telemetry snapshot tool:

   $ curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $API_KEY" \n     "https://telemetry.redwood.internal/api/v1/tenants/{tenant_id}/baseline?window=7d"

   b) Store baseline as a stable artifact in the tenant onboarding folder and tag it with: baseline:YYYYMMDD.

2) Canary injection: run synthetic suite at increasing traffic levels (owner: Onboarding automation)
   - Phase A: 0.5% of production traffic OR up to 20 rps (whichever is lower) for 30 minutes.
   - Phase B: 2% for 60 minutes.
   - Phase C: 10% for 2 hours (only if A and B pass).

   Synthetic runner configuration (example YAML snippet)

   runner:
     suite_name: "onboard-synthetic-v1"
     concurrency: 4
     ramp: [30, 120, 600] # seconds for phases A,B,C
     sample_set: "tenant-golden-v1.json"
     telemetry_tags: ["onboarding", "tenant:{tenant_id}"]

   Note: YAML above is illustrative — runner accepts JSON or CLI flags. Ensure telemetry_tags include the tenant id for attribution.

3) Synthetic checks (automation)
   - Functional correctness: run golden prompts against the candidate model variant and compute structured field extraction F1 and golden-match-rate. Accept if >= 95%.
   - Latency: compute p50/p95 token latency across synthetic requests. Map percentile anomalies using the runtime profiler.
   - Cost: measure token consumption and billing attribution per synthetic request (includes prefix caching). Compare against baseline.
   - Telemetry: assert logs/traces exist for each synthetic request and that token-level cost tags are present.

4) Automated gate evaluation and alerting
   - The synthetic runner posts results to the onboarding-orchestrator webhook: /onboarding/v1/{tenant_id}/gate-results.
   - If any gate fails, an automated rollback is triggered (see section Rollback & mitigation) and an incident is created in PagerDuty with playbook tag: tenant-onboard-gate-failure.

Rollback & mitigation actions
- Soft rollback: automatically route new requests to previous model variant for 15 minutes while alerting owners. This is fast-fail and requires no manual approval.
- Full rollback: if the soft rollback does not restore metrics within 10 minutes, an auto-change to the previous routing policy is executed and a Severity 2 incident is opened.
- Compensating actions: disable kernel-level optimizations or quantization profile used in the candidate build and re-run Phase A.

Ownership and escalation matrix
- Customer Success (Onboarding): primary owner for test scheduling, baseline capture, and stakeholder comms.
- Eng-SRE: owns latency and runtime performance investigations.
- Runtime Team: owns kernel/quantization mitigations.
- FinOps: validates cost anomalies and approves temporary cost shields.
- PagerDuty escalation: use support-onboard rota; if unresolved for 30 minutes escalate to oncall-lead.

Checklist: pre-cutover (owner: Customer Success)
- [ ] Baseline artifact saved and verified.
- [ ] Synthetic golden set validated and reviewed with customer.
- [ ] Telemetry ingestion confirmed for tenanted tags.
- [ ] Cost attribution hooks enabled (token-level tags).
- [ ] Contact list with 24/7 pager IDs added to onboarding ticket.

Checklist: canary phases (owner: Onboarding automation + SRE)
- [ ] Phase A run complete and gates green.
- [ ] Phase B run complete and gates green.
- [ ] Phase C run complete and gates green (optional).
- [ ] Final go/no-go decision recorded in the onboarding ticket.

Telemetry assertions and sampling guidance
- Required traces: request_id, model_variant, tenant_id, token_count, cache_hit, cost_cents.
- Minimum trace sample rate: 100% for synthetic runner, 1% for production traffic during initial 72 hours after go-live.
- Billing telemetry: ensure per-request cost_cents is emitted and matches billing pipeline within 5% for synthetic traffic.

Integrating with QBRs and health reviews
- Store synthetic-run artifacts as evidence for the first QBR. Include the following in QBR materials:
  - Baseline vs go-live comparison for p50/p95 latency and per-token cost.
  - Golden-match-rate trends for the first 30 days.
  - Any mitigations performed and residual action items.

Common failure modes and workarounds
- Symptom: sudden p95 latency jump during Phase B.
  - Likely causes: kernel swap with unoptimized attention kernel, unexpected batching change.
  - Quick actions: revert kernel flag, increase per-node concurrency limit, re-run Phase A.
- Symptom: per-token cost spike > +12%.
  - Likely causes: cache bypass (prefix mismatch), tokenization change leading to longer sequences.
  - Quick actions: validate tokenization diff tool, enable prefix cache warm-up, engage FinOps to apply temporary cost cap.
- Symptom: missing telemetry or incomplete traces.
  - Workaround: run synthetic runner with telemetry_tags=["onboarding","tenant:{tenant_id}"] and use the telemetry replay tool to re-ingest payloads.

Troubleshooting commands (examples)
- Fetch recent synthetic run results:
  $ rwdctl onboarding runs list --tenant {tenant_id} --limit 10

- Re-run a single golden prompt locally:
  $ rwdctl synth run --tenant {tenant_id} --prompt-file golden/001.json --model variant-a

- Compare tokenization diff:
  $ rwdctl utils token-diff --model-a v1 --model-b v2 --prompt-file golden/001.json

Appendix A: Example golden prompt structure (JSON)
{
  "id": "golden-001",
  "input": "Summarize the following support ticket into category and severity:
> The user's invoice shows incorrect token charges.",
  "expected_fields": {
    "category": "billing",
    "severity": "high"
  }
}

Appendix B: Run frequency and cost guardrails
- Synthetic runner default cadence: run full suite every 6 hours during onboarding.
- Cost budget for synthetic runs: cap at $0.03 per tenant per hour by default. Increase requires FinOps approval.

Appendix C: Contact matrix
- Onboarding CS: asha.patel@redwood.ai
- Eng-SRE lead: diego.ramirez@redwood.ai
- Runtime oncall: runtime-oncall@redwood.ai
- FinOps: finops@redwood.ai

Related artifacts and templates
- Tenant baseline artifact template: /templates/onboarding/tenant-baseline-template.md
- Synthetic runner config template: /templates/onboarding/synthetic-runner-template.yaml

Revision history
- 2025-09-15: Created by Asha Patel.
- 2025-11-02: Added cost guardrail guidance (reviewer: Meera Singh).
- 2026-02-10: Clarified rollback timing and added automated webhook contract.

title: SLO Safeguard & Canary Governance Playbook
content:
Overview:
This playbook defines governance, operational controls, and tooling patterns for running SLO-focused experiments and model canaries on Redwood's inference fleet. It establishes a safety-first approach so teams can iterate model rollouts and runtime tuning while protecting customer-facing SLOs and error budgets.

Scope:
- Applies to any production-facing model rollout, quantization change, kernel-switch, or runtime configuration that can alter latency, tail latency, or correctness metrics.
- Intended audience: SREs, Service Stewards, Model Owners, Capacity Engineers, Release Engineers.

Definitions:
- SLO (Service Level Objective): the target level of reliability (example: p99 latency & availability).
- Error Budget: allowable SLO violation over a window (30d default).
- Canary: a staged rollout (traffic percentage + time) used to validate changes.
- Safety Net: automated and manual mitigations triggered when canary threatens SLOs or budget.

Principles:
1) Safety before speed — experiments must not consume more than 10% of a service's remaining short-term error budget without SRE sign-off.
2) Observable experiments — all canaries must ship with an experiment dashboard, trace sampling, and dedicated alert rules.
3) Capacity-aware rollouts — canaries must include headroom checks and a reversible capacity reservation.
4) Evidence-driven rollback — rollback decisions must be based on pre-defined metrics and documented hypotheses.

Roles & Responsibilities:
- Service Steward (Model Owner): defines acceptance criteria, test prompts, and production evaluation prompts; owns the rollout plan.
- Release Engineer: coordinates deployment artifacts, feature flags, and traffic routing.
- Oncall SRE: monitors canary, authorizes emergency rollbacks, and triggers escalation.
- Capacity Team: approves temporary capacity reservations and verifies headroom.
- SRE Review Board: reviews experiments that exceed thresholds in this playbook.

Pre-flight Checklist (required before canary):
1) SLO & acceptance criteria documented in the rollout PR. Example: "latency_p99 <= 240ms, availability >= 99.95%, semantic-quality-regression <= 0.5%".
2) Baseline capture: 72h baseline of key metrics (latency quantiles, error rate, token cost, GPU utilization, KV hit-rate).
3) Dedicated canary dashboard created with at least: p50/p90/p99, error rate, burn rate, GPU mem, input size distribution.
4) Alert rules defined and validated in staging (see alert snippets below).
5) Capacity pre-approval if expected additional peak usage > 5% of cluster capacity.
6) Traffic routing plan: percentages and scheduled ramp steps.

Governance thresholds (auto vs manual):
- Auto-abort (immediate): breach of critical safety thresholds for 3 consecutive 1m windows:
  - Error rate spike > 5x baseline absolute and > 0.1%
  - p99 latency increase > 2x baseline and > 500ms absolute
  - GPU OOM, host OOM, or model load failures > 1
  If any auto-abort triggers, the rollout system must revert traffic within 2 minutes and create an incident ticket.
- Soft-fail (notify + pause ramp): sustained metric degradation for 10m:
  - error budget burn rate > 5 (5x expected burn) over 10m
  - p95 latency increase > 30% for 10m
  For soft-fail, ramp is paused and SRE oncall is paged with the experiment dashboard link.
- SRE Review (board approval): experiments expected to consume > 15% of 30d error budget or increase cluster utilization > 10% for >1h.

Canary Execution Template (recommended):
1) Start: 1% traffic for 15 minutes (validation window).
2) Ramp: 1% -> 5% (30 min) -> 25% (1h) -> full or target share after 24h if no issues.
3) Metrics sampling: increase trace sampling for canary traffic to 10x baseline to collect quality signals.
4) Preserve prefix caches: ensure canary instances share cache layer to avoid cold-start skew unless validating cache behavior.
5) Shadow traffic: mirror 5% of production to non-critical replicas to compare outputs without affecting users.

Capacity & Headroom Negotiation:
- Every canary must submit a "headroom manifest" with expected memory/GPU cycles and tail latency profile. The Capacity Team uses the manifest to run a quick simulated pressure test in a shadow pool.
- Minimum required headroom: 25% free CPU/GPUs and 30% free memory on impacted nodes for the duration of the experiment.
- If headroom cannot be met, the rollout must use lower traffic or extended ramp with SRE-approved acceptance criteria.

Alert rule examples (Prometheus-style pseudo-yaml):
- name: canary-critical-error-rate
  expr: |
    increase(inference_errors_total{job="inference",canary="true"}[1m]) / increase(inference_requests_total{job="inference",canary="true"}[1m]) > 0.001 && increase(inference_errors_total{job="inference",canary="true"}[1m]) > 10
  for: 1m
  labels:
    severity: critical
  annotations:
    summary: "Canary error rate spike on {{ $labels.model }}"

- name: canary-p99-latency-regression
  expr: |
    (histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(inference_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="inference",instance=~"canary.*"}[5m])) by (le)) ) > (baseline_p99_seconds * 2)
  for: 3m
  labels: { severity: critical }

Runbook: immediate actions on auto-abort
1) System reverts traffic to previous stable rollout within 2 minutes (automated).
2) Oncall SRE pages: summary, canary id, revert timestamp, immediate evidence (errors, last 20 traces).
3) Release Engineer opens rollback PR that documents suspected cause and next steps.
4) Capacity Team runs node health checks (oom, gpu-reset, driver errors).
5) If issue persists after automatic revert, follow incident escalation (see Incident Response Playbook).

Rollback decision matrix (condensed):
- If auto-abort triggered: mandatory rollback + postmortem.
- If soft-fail and root cause is configuration (e.g., kernel selection): pause + SRE triage (may patch and resume).
- If soft-fail and root cause is data/semantic drift: stop rollout and run offline eval; SRE Review Board required.

Post-experiment review (required artifacts):
- Canary run summary: duration, traffic curve, metric deltas vs baseline, traces sampled, top 5 failure modes.
- Evidence pack: links to dashboards, raw traces (safely redacted), capacity logs, pod events.
- Decision log: resume/rollback decision with rationale and owner sign-off.
- Action items and owner list with due dates.

Quality & Semantic Checks:
- For model changes, include a prompt set (min 200 examples) representing high-risk customer flows. Define acceptance as: semantic-quality-regression <= 0.5% (measured by automatic eval harness) or a narrower tolerance for high-SLA tenants.
- Monitor non-functional regressions: hallucination rate proxies, truncation rate, and function-call failures.

Tooling integrations and automation suggestions:
- Canary controller (release-engineering) should integrate with:
  - Telemetry: Prometheus, Tempo/Jaeger, Loki
  - Feature flags: LaunchDarkly or internal toggle service
  - Capacity orchestrator: capacity-orchestrator service for temporary reservations
  - Incident system: PagerDuty with experiment runbook links
- Automation: implement a canary-run summary webhook that posts to the experiment ticket when run completes or aborts.

Example quick commands (for runbook operators):
- Fetch canary pods: kubectl get pods -l canary=true,model=mymodel -n inference\-Describe failing pod events: kubectl describe pod <pod> -n inference\-Fetch recent traces (tempo): curl "https://telemetry.prod.internal/api/traces?canary_id=<id>&limit=50"

Audit & Evidence retention:
- Keep canary artifacts for 180 days (dashboards, traces, raw metrics) tied to the experiment ticket id.
- For any canary that triggers an auto-abort, extend retention to 2 years for forensic needs.

Postmortem & Continuous Improvement:
- All non-trivial rollbacks (>5% traffic or >1h run) require a lightweight postmortem within 3 business days.
- Maintain an experiment registry indexed by model, canary id, owner, and verdict to avoid re-running failing experiments without addressing root cause.

Appendix A — Example acceptance table (copy into PR):
| Metric | Baseline | Acceptance | Monitoring window | Reaction |
|-------|---------:|-----------:|------------------:|--------|
| availability | 99.98% | >= 99.95% | 30d | SRE review if breach |
| p99 latency | 220ms | <= 250ms | 1h rolling | auto-abort if >500ms |
| error rate | 0.02% | <= 0.1% | 10m | auto-abort if >0.5% |
| error budget burn rate | 1 | <= 5 (for ramp) | 10m | pause ramp if >5 |

Appendix B — Triage contact tree:
- Primary oncall SRE: oncall-sre@redwood.ai (page via PagerDuty)
- Capacity lead: capacity-oncall@redwood.ai
- Release engineer: releases@redwood.ai
- Model owner: listed on rollout PR

Notes & rationale:
This playbook intentionally separates automated abort conditions (fast, conservative) from reviewable soft failures to balance developer velocity with platform stability. By combining capacity pre-approvals, conservative ramping, and trace-forward evidence collection we can reduce false positives while keeping rollouts reversible and auditable.

Related policies and references:
- /confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/multi-model-rollout-hedge-and-escrow-runbook-2026
- /confluence/eng-sre/operational-tooling/capacity-orchestrator-and-slo-reconciliation-cookbook-2026
- Incident Response Playbook: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/incident-process/runbook

Document history:
- 2024-09-12: created by Ava Chen
- 2025-06-03: added capacity manifest requirements (Rafael Ortega review)
- 2026-03-01: finalized alert thresholds and auto-abort behavior

title: PRD: Retention Controls (Enterprise Security & Compliance Foundation)
content:
## 1. Summary
Retention Controls productize customer-configurable data retention across core Redwood Inference data classes (request/response logs, prompts/completions where stored, audit logs, traces/metrics, and limited artifacts) with safe defaults per deployment tier. The feature set includes:
- A consistent retention policy model, evaluated centrally, with tier-aware validation.
- Enforcement mechanisms (TTL + purge jobs) for supported stores with verification metrics.
- Change history and exportability for customer security reviews and internal audits.

This PRD covers the Retention Controls component of the broader “Retention controls + compliance reporting pack” initiative.

## 2. Problem statement
Enterprise and regulated customers increasingly require:
- Explicit retention periods per data class (and sometimes per region).
- Clear deletion semantics (TTL vs. purge, time-to-delete, idempotency).
- Legal hold / incident hold capabilities with an auditable trail.
- Evidence that policies are enforced (monitoring + verification signals).

Today, retention behavior is inconsistent across stores and hard to describe during security reviews. This increases sales/CS overhead, creates compliance risk (over-retention), and increases operational risk (unbounded storage growth).

## 3. Goals / non-goals
### 3.1 Goals
1) Ship customer-configurable retention controls with safe defaults by tier (Hosted/Dedicated/Private) and clear behavior:
- TTL configuration and enforcement
- Purge semantics and verification
- Legal hold and exceptions workflow (policy surface + auditability)

2) Provide auditable visibility:
- Retention policy change history
- Exportable configuration (machine-readable)

3) Reduce security-review overhead:
- Standardized terminology and predictable answers (ties into Security FAQ + compliance report pack work).

### 3.2 Non-goals (initial release)
- Full custom report builder or “bring your own GRC” integrations beyond export formats.
- Arbitrary per-field redaction policies (handled separately under logging standards).
- “Instant delete” guarantees across all systems (we will provide bounded purge SLAs, not synchronous deletion).

## 4. Personas and user stories
### 4.1 Personas
**Security Admin (Customer)**
- Owns compliance posture; needs proof of retention configuration and enforcement.
- Wants safe defaults and guardrails to avoid accidental over-retention.

**SRE / Platform Admin (Customer + Redwood)**
- Needs retention changes to be safe, reversible, and operationally observable.
- Needs break-glass and incident exceptions to preserve debuggability with approvals.

**Auditor / GRC (Customer + Redwood Internal)**
- Needs an exported view of retention settings and a change trail (who changed what, when, why).
- Needs clear mapping of data classes to storage systems and deletion mechanisms.

### 4.2 Core user stories
1) As a Security Admin, I can set retention for request/response logs and traces to 7 days and keep audit logs for 400 days.
2) As a Security Admin, I can enforce “no storage of prompts/completions” (where supported) or set a short TTL.
3) As an SRE, I can see purge backlog and TTL lag to ensure deletions are keeping up and not impacting production.
4) As an Auditor, I can download an export of the current retention policy and the last 90 days of retention policy changes.
5) As a Security Admin, I can place a legal hold on audit logs for a defined case, with approvals and an audit trail.

## 5. Definitions and data classes (v1)
Retention Controls applies to the following logical data classes (each maps to one or more backing stores):
- **Request/Response Logs**: API gateway/service request metadata + response metadata. May include prompts/completions only if logging is enabled to capture them.
- **Prompts/Completions (where stored)**: content captured for debugging/analytics when a tenant enables content logging.
- **Audit Logs**: immutable event trail of control-plane and security-relevant actions (e.g., policy changes, access changes, key events).
- **Traces/Metrics**: telemetry emitted by the platform (service traces, performance metrics, error aggregates).
- **Artifacts (limited, where applicable)**: evaluation datasets or artifacts stored within Redwood-managed systems (not customer-owned buckets).

Out of scope for v1 (explicitly): customer-managed exports stored in customer-controlled locations, and data stored entirely in customer-managed infrastructure in Private deployments where Redwood is not the data processor.

## 6. Product requirements
### 6.1 Functional requirements
**R1: Retention policy model (tenant-scoped)**
- A tenant-scoped policy defines retention per data class.
- Policy supports: TTL duration, enabled/disabled state (where applicable), and legal hold overlays.
- Policies must be versioned for forwards compatibility (schema version field).

**R2: Tier-aware defaults**
- Every tenant has explicit defaults applied at provisioning.
- Defaults differ by product tier: Hosted, Dedicated, Private.
- Defaults are visible in Console and retrievable via API.

**R3: Validation + guardrails**
- Enforce minimum/maximum TTL bounds per tier and per data class.
- Prevent invalid combinations (e.g., setting prompts/completions TTL when content logging is disabled).
- Require explicit acknowledgement for settings that materially reduce debuggability (e.g., request logs < 24 hours), with warnings and an audit event.

**R4: Enforcement mechanisms**
- For each supported backing store:
  - TTL is enforced via a purge job framework and/or native TTL where available.
  - Purge jobs must be idempotent and safe to retry.
  - Deletion must be observable with metrics (rows deleted, failures, lag).
- Retention enforcement must not cause material production regressions (see NFRs).

**R5: Purge semantics and SLAs (behavioral contract)**
- Define “retention TTL” as the maximum age at which data becomes eligible for deletion.
- Define “purge lag” as time from eligibility to actual deletion.
- Provide a documented purge lag target and alert thresholds per store (details in verification dashboards/runbooks).

**R6: Legal hold and exceptions**
- Support legal hold overlays for specified data classes (v1: audit logs; optional in later phases: request logs).
- Holds must be:
  - time-bounded or explicitly “until released”
  - tied to a case ID
  - approval-gated (role-based)
  - fully audited (who created/extended/released)
- Support incident-related “break-glass retention extension” with approvals and automatic expiry.

**R7: Auditability and change history**
- Every retention policy create/update must emit an audit event.
- Provide change history view (UI) and export endpoint (API) including:
  - previous value → new value
  - actor, timestamp, source (UI/API/Terraform)
  - reason (optional but recommended) and ticket/case link

**R8: Access control (RBAC)**
- Only appropriate roles may read/write retention settings:
  - Read: Security Admin, Org Admin, Auditor (read-only), Redwood Support (as scoped)
  - Write: Security Admin, Org Admin (or equivalent), with optional two-person approval for hold actions (configurable by enterprise contract)

**R9: Console experience (baseline)**
- Retention Settings page must:
  - display effective policy + defaults
  - show warnings for risky configurations
  - show last updated / actor
  - link to change history
  - support “Download policy export”

**R10: API surface (baseline)**
- Retention policy CRUD endpoints (tenant-scoped) with:
  - validation errors that are actionable
  - ETag / optimistic concurrency to prevent accidental overwrite
  - export endpoint for the effective policy and bounds

**R11: Private deployment support**
- Where Redwood provides Private deployment packaging:
  - include secure defaults and documentation for required backing services and purge jobs
  - support configuration via Terraform/module where applicable
  - clearly document customer responsibilities (e.g., if customer swaps the telemetry store)

### 6.2 Default retention by tier (proposed v1 defaults)
Note: Final defaults require Security sign-off. Defaults are “effective retention” assuming the tenant has not explicitly overridden.

| Data class | Hosted default | Dedicated default | Private default |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Request/Response logs (metadata) | 7 days | 14 days | 7 days |
| Prompts/Completions (where stored) | Disabled by default; if enabled: 7 days | Disabled by default; if enabled: 14 days | Disabled by default; if enabled: 7 days |
| Audit logs | 365 days | 400 days (≈13 months) | 400 days |
| Traces/Metrics | 14 days | 30 days | 14 days |
| Artifacts (limited, where applicable) | 30 days | 90 days | 30 days |

### 6.3 Validation bounds (proposed v1)
| Data class | Min TTL | Max TTL | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Request/Response logs | 24 hours | 90 days | <72h triggers “reduced debuggability” warning/ack |
| Prompts/Completions | 24 hours | 30 days | Only applicable when content logging enabled |
| Audit logs | 180 days | 7 years | Legal hold supported for audit logs v1 |
| Traces/Metrics | 24 hours | 90 days | Cardinality and cost constraints apply |
| Artifacts | 7 days | 365 days | Limited scope; not all artifact types supported |

## 7. Non-functional requirements (NFRs)
**NFR1: Performance and safety**
- Purge jobs must be rate-limited and batch deletes to avoid production DB pressure.
- Retention enforcement must not measurably increase request latency for inference paths.

**NFR2: Reliability and observability**
- Emit standardized metrics for:
  - ttl_lag_seconds (by store + region)
  - purge_rows_deleted
  - purge_failures
  - purge_backlog (where applicable)
- Provide dashboards and alerts with clear runbook links.

**NFR3: Idempotency and correctness**
- Purge jobs must be safe to re-run and resilient to partial failures.
- Where stores have eventual consistency, document expected delay windows.

**NFR4: Security**
- Retention policy changes must be audited.
- Exports must be access-controlled and recorded.
- No sensitive content should be exposed via error messages or logs.

## 8. Success metrics
### 8.1 Customer/Business outcomes
- Reduce time-to-complete enterprise security reviews where retention is a blocker:
  - Target: 30% reduction in “retention-related back-and-forth” measured via Sales Engineering/CS tagged threads and ticket counts.
- Increase enterprise win rate in deals blocked on retention/audit evidence (qualitative + pipeline tracking in HubSpot).

### 8.2 Product adoption and usability
- % of enterprise tenants with an explicit retention override configured (indicates control is discoverable): target 40% within 90 days of GA.
- Support ticket volume for “what is your retention?” questions decreases after GA (baseline from prior quarter).

### 8.3 Operational SLIs/SLOs (enforcement)
- Purge job error rate: < 0.5% of runs failing per day (per store), with auto-retry.
- Purge lag (p95):
  - Request/response logs: < 24 hours
  - Audit logs: < 72 hours
  - Traces/metrics: < 24 hours
- Backlog recovery: after a 24-hour maintenance window, return to steady-state purge lag within 48 hours.

## 9. Rollout plan (phased)
### Phase 0 (1–2 weeks): Requirements + inventory
- Finalize data inventory per data class and map to backing stores.
- Confirm terminology for customer-facing docs.
- Draft policy schema + validation rules.

### Phase 1 (3–5 weeks): Policy service + core enforcement
- Implement retention policy CRUD + validation + change history.
- Implement purge framework and enforce TTL for:
  - request/response logs store
  - audit logs store
- Ship verification metrics and initial dashboards.
- Internal-only rollout (Redwood tenants) + load testing.

### Phase 2 (2–4 weeks): Console surface + enablement hooks
- Console retention settings page + download/export.
- Harden alerts/runbooks and add operational guardrails.
- Enable design partners (Dedicated + Private) with feature flag.

### Phase 3 (2 weeks): GA hardening and broad release
- GA criteria met (see Section 12).
- Publish internal docs + external-facing docs stubs.
- Sales/CS enablement (FAQ + standard evidence artifacts).

## 10. Dependencies
- Control plane retention policy service and evaluator (tier-aware caching/invalidation).
- Purge job framework and store-specific enforcement implementations.
- Observability pack: dashboards/alerts, metrics naming conventions.
- RBAC permissions model for Console and API.
- Legal hold approval workflow and audit events (policy + process alignment).

## 11. Risks and mitigations
**Risk 1: Purge jobs cause DB pressure or telemetry ingestion regressions**
- Mitigation: batching, throttling, safety limits per run, canary rollout, SRE sign-off on thresholds.

**Risk 2: Conflicts with incident response / on-call debugging**
- Mitigation: documented break-glass exception, minimum TTL bounds, “reduced debuggability” warnings, and audit trail.

**Risk 3: Terminology mismatch with legal/compliance expectations**
- Mitigation: Security + Legal review of customer-facing wording; keep “audit logs” strictly scoped to security-relevant events.

**Risk 4: Partial enforcement across stores leads to false confidence**
- Mitigation: explicitly label supported stores per data class; ship verification dashboards; block GA until core stores are enforced.

## 12. GA criteria / acceptance checklist
- Retention policy CRUD available (API + Console) with tier-aware validation.
- Enforcement shipped and verified for request/response logs + audit logs in at least one production region.
- Verification dashboards live with on-call alerts and runbooks.
- Change history and export endpoint available and tested.
- Legal hold workflow available for audit logs with approvals and audit events.
- Security review complete (CISO delegate sign-off) and docs ready for customer-facing enablement.

## 13. Open questions
1) Should audit log minimum TTL be 365 days or 400 days across all tiers for consistency with “13 months” expectation?
2) Do we allow per-region retention overrides in v1, or only global per-tenant settings (with region summary handled separately)?
3) Do we support legal hold for request logs in v1, or only audit logs?
4) Private deployments: how do we document responsibility splits when customers replace telemetry backends?
5) What is the default behavior for prompts/completions capture in Hosted (fully disabled vs “metadata-only” logging)?

## 14. Appendix: Customer-facing commitments (draft)
- Redwood provides configurable retention periods for supported data classes with documented bounds.
- Data becomes eligible for deletion at TTL expiration; Redwood performs asynchronous purges within documented purge lag targets.
- Retention policy changes and holds are audited and exportable.
- Customers can request evidence (policy exports + enforcement verification) as part of standard security reviews (delivered via the compliance reporting pack workstream).

title: QBR Playbook: Inference Economics & Availability for Enterprise Accounts
content:
Summary:

This playbook defines a reproducible QBR (Quarterly Business Review) format focused on two topics that consistently drive value decisions for enterprise customers: inference economics (cost per call / cost per 1k tokens / embedding unit economics) and availability (SLOs, incidents, throttling/fallback). It is designed for Customer Success (CS) leads running QBRs with engineering stakeholders, finance owners, and product managers on the customer side.

When to use this playbook:
- Quarterly Business Reviews for enterprise and Dedicated/Private customers with non-trivial inference spend.
- Ad-hoc cost/availability deep-dives triggered by a cost spike, capacity incident, or contract renewal.
- Pre-renewal negotiating sessions where unit economics and reliability metrics inform pricing/commitments.

Audience:
- Customer Success Managers (owner)
- Solutions Engineers / Oncall Engineers (data/technical escorts)
- Account Finance / Procurement contacts (customer)
- Customer Platform/ML Engineers and Product Managers (customer)

QBR Objectives (measurable):
1. Verify that monthly inference unit cost trends match commitments and identify 2–3 concrete optimization actions.
2. Validate SLO adherence for the review period and document mitigation/rollout plans for any SLO misses.
3. Align on capacity requirements and recommended Dedicated/Private sizing changes (if required).
4. Agree on 3 follow-up action items with owners, deadlines, and acceptance criteria.

Standard QBR Agenda (60–90 minutes):
1) Welcome & goals (5 min)
2) Usage and unit economics snapshot (15 min)
   - Total tokens, embeddings units, average request size, and cost per 1k tokens
   - Cost drivers (model mix, quantization, caching hit-rate)
3) Availability and reliability review (15 min)
   - SLO metrics (p50/p95/p99 latency, error rate, availability %)
   - Incidents since last QBR and RCA/high-level remediation status
4) Optimization opportunities and proposals (15 min)
   - Batching, caching rules, model switchover suggestions, routing policies
5) Roadmap & upcoming platform changes (10 min)
6) Action items, ownership, and close (5–10 min)

Pre-QBR Checklist (owner: Customer Success with Solutions Engineering support) – do these at least 10 business days before meeting:
- Data pulls: usage CSVs, token-level cost breakdown, model routing logs (last 90 days).
- Dashboards: ensure the customer-facing cost dashboard and availability dashboard are refreshed and have annotations for major incidents.
- Internal sync: Solutions Engineer and oncall review to identify technical risks and proposed recommendations.
- Customer pre-read: send a two-page summary (Key metrics + proposed agenda + 3 suggested actions).

Required Data Sources & Canonical Queries:
- Metric store: Prometheus / Cortex (latency, error-rate, availability per model/version)
- Billing: internal billing export (per-customer, per-model, per-day)
- Logs: request routing and model selection logs (to assess fallback frequency)

Example Prometheus queries (examples to run in dashboards):
- 95th percentile latency (tokens endpoint):
  histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(inference_request_duration_seconds_bucket{route=~"/v1/generate.*",customer_id=\"<ID>\"}[7d])) by (le))

- Error rate (5m rolling):
  sum(rate(inference_requests_total{customer_id=\"<ID>\",status=~\"5..|4..\"}[5m])) / sum(rate(inference_requests_total{customer_id=\"<ID>\"}[5m]))

Sample billing CSV columns (expected):
- date, customer_id, model_name, model_variant, request_count, tokens_in, tokens_out, embedding_units, total_cost_usd

SLOs & KPI Table (Use these as baseline; adjust per-customer SLA):
- SLO name: Availability (per-route) | Target: 99.95% | Measurement: uptime excluding scheduled maintenance | Rollback threshold: <99.90%
- SLO name: P99 latency (text-generation) | Target: <= 1.2s per token at typical batch size | Measurement: p99 of token emission latency | Rollback threshold: >1.6s
- KPI: Cost per 1k tokens | Target: agreed contract baseline (e.g., $X / 1k tokens) | Measurement: billing export aggregated monthly

Action Playbook: Common Findings and Recommended Responses
1) Finding: Sudden 30% cost spike month-over-month with no obvious traffic increase.
   Steps:
   a) Verify billing export: group by model_variant and time-of-day to see concentrated increases.
   b) Check routing logs for increased fallback to larger models or degraded quantization usage.
   c) If fallback is the cause, enact short-term mitigation: route traffic to fallback limits, enable per-customer cost caps, and schedule canary switchover to a cheaper variant.
   d) Owner: Solutions Engineer (SE) to provide triage within 24 hours; CS to schedule cost remediation call within 3 business days.

2) Finding: P99 latency breach during daily peak windows.
   Steps:
   a) Confirm whether breach correlates with increased batch sizes or KV cache misses (run cache hit-rate query).
   b) If cache misses increased, review prefix caching rules and customer prompt patterns.
   c) Short-term: increase burst capacity or enable regional routing to lower latency.
   d) Long-term: propose model quantization or a smaller model for cheap paths.
   e) Owner: Oncall Engineer to propose mitigation within 48 hours; SE to test proposed fix in staging within 7 days.

3) Finding: Repeated transient 503s with no persistent service degradation.
   Steps:
   a) Cross-check ingress/load-balancer throttling metrics; validate whether request throttles align with customer quota thresholds.
   b) If quota throttles are the cause, recommend quota increase or implement client-side retry/backoff guidance.
   c) Owner: Customer Success to negotiate quota changes; Engineering to implement conservative quota bump and monitor.

Escalation Matrix (severity and contacts):
- Sev 1 (Critical production outage impacting >=1% of customer traffic or >30 minutes):
  - Primary oncall: eng-sre-oncall@redwood.ai (pager)
  - SE: solutions-oncall@redwood.ai
  - CS lead: <CS manager email>
  - Response SLA: 30 minutes initial response, incident channel created, daily exec updates.

- Sev 2 (High-impact but partial):
  - Eng oncall: eng-platform-oncall@redwood.ai
  - SE: assigned per-account
  - CS: assigned CSM
  - Response SLA: 2 hours initial response.

- Sev 3 (Low-impact / cost questions / non-urgent reliability trends):
  - Handle in the next business-day operating cadence; owner is CSM and Solutions Engineer.

Meeting artifacts & templates (copy for reuse)
- Two-page pre-read template (send 3 business days before):
  1) Executive summary (1 paragraph): top-line cost delta, availability summary, 1 recommended action.
  2) Key metrics: last 3 months trend charts (tokens, cost, p95/p99).
  3) Incidents & status: list of incidents since last QBR with RCA links.
  4) Proposed actions and impact estimate (e.g., expected cost reduction %).

- Action item tracker rows (example):
  - \"Reduce model X usage on low-cost paths\" | Owner: SE-Jordan | ETA: 2026-03-15 | Acceptance: 10% cost reduction in low-cost path within 30 days

Follow-up & tracking:
- All action items must be captured in the CS ticketing system (Zendesk/Jira) with a label qbr-<customer-id>-YYYYQn.
- CS to run a 30-day follow-up email with progress and updated metrics visualization.
- If cost or availability objectives are not met within 60 days, schedule a remediation game-day with engineering (2 hours) to drive higher-priority fixes.

Appendix A — Sample queries and scripts
- Cost breakdown extraction (example CSV extractor):
  curl -s -H \"Authorization: Bearer <API_KEY>\" 
    \"https://billing.internal.redwood.ai/v1/exports?customer_id=<ID>&start=2026-01-01&end=2026-02-28\" > billing-<ID>-jan-feb.csv

- KV cache hit rate example (PromQL):
  sum(rate(kv_cache_hits_total{customer_id=\"<ID>\"}[7d])) / sum(rate(kv_cache_requests_total{customer_id=\"<ID>\"}[7d]))

Appendix B — Suggested optimization playbacks (examples to present)
- Batching policy change: expected savings 8–18% for chat-heavy workloads; risk: increases p99 latency for tail callers.
- Prefix caching rules: expected savings 12–30% when customers use repeated system prompts.
- Quantized model recommendation: move 20% of low-sensitivity traffic to a 4-bit quantized variant to reduce cost 25–40% (requires QA for accuracy regression).

Ownership & touchpoints:
- Document owner: Customer Success (Aisha Patel)
- Engineering SME: Liam Chen (Runtime Performance)
- Billing SME: Marco Rossi (Revenue Operations)

Related documents and dashboards:
- Customer-facing \"Cost & Usage\" dashboard (link provided in pre-read)
- Incident RCA links (attach in related_pages)

Revision history:
- 2025-11-12: Initial draft (Aisha Patel)
- 2026-01-06: Added sample PromQL queries and escalation matrix (Liam Chen)
- 2026-02-18: Revised pre-QBR checklist and action templates; publish (Aisha Patel)

End of document.

title: Degradation → QBR: RCA & Escalation Matrix (Operational Playbook)
content:
Overview:
This playbook defines the operational path from an observed service degradation to coordinated RCA (root cause analysis) and structured QBR (quarterly business review) follow-up with enterprise customers. It standardizes detection signals, triage windows, escalation matrix, customer communication templates, and handoff into QBR action items. The goal is to reduce time-to-resolution, maintain consistent customer comms, and ensure learnings feed back into product/infra roadmaps.

Scope:
- Applies to enterprise customers on Hosted API, Dedicated, and Private deployments.
- Covers degradations that affect availability, response latency (generation or embedding), cost-per-token anomalies, or model-quality regressions tied to a deployed model version.
- Excludes planned maintenance (use go-live/maintenance communications).

Key definitions:
- Degradation: measurable negative change in service behavior relative to SLOs (availability, latency, quality, cost).
- Severity Levels: S1 (critical outage affecting >10% of requests or single-customer availability loss), S2 (degraded latency or increased error rates for targeted routes/customers), S3 (minor quality deviations or cost anomalies for small cohort).
- Triage Window: time budget to perform initial diagnosis before customer communication; varies by severity (see Matrix).

Escalation & Triage Matrix (quick reference):
| Signal | Detection Query (examples) | Threshold | Initial Owner | Triage Window | Escalation Action |
|---|---|---:|---|---:|---|
| API 5xx spike (multi-customer) | rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.*"}[5m]) > 0.02 | >2% 5xx rate over 5m | Platform SRE | 15m | Open incident, notify CS Ops, page infra on-call |
| Per-customer availability drop | sum(rate(requests_failed{customer_id="$CID"}[5m])) / sum(rate(requests_total{customer_id="$CID"}[5m])) > 0.05 | >5% | Customer Success (CS) + Tenant Ops | 30m | Initiate customer-specific status, add to incident if cross-tenant |
| Latency p95 increase (generation) | histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le)(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[10m]))) | p95 > 350ms | Serving Runtime Team | 30m | Run perf profile, check KV-cache hitrate, notify CS |
| Model quality regression (eval failures) | failed_prompts_total{model=~"v.*"}[1h] > baseline + 20% | +20% vs baseline evaluation set | Applied ML | 1h | Revert model variant or enable fallback, inform CS + Product |
| Cost-per-token anomaly | cost_per_token_daily{customer_id="$CID"} > expected * 3 | >3x | Billing / Cost Ops | 24h | Block suspicious routes, notify account owner |

Note: The Prometheus/Query examples are implementation patterns. Teams must keep authoritative queries in the shared dashboard library (see Related pages).

Detailed Playbook: Detection → RCA → QBR Handoff
1) Detection (0–15 minutes for S1, 0–30 minutes S2):
  - Automated alert fires into PagerDuty / Opsgenie and creates an incident in Incident Manager.
  - CS Ops watches customer-specific alerts via the Customer Health Sentinel and flag impacted accounts.
  - First responder confirms whether degradation is internal, external (cloud provider), or customer-side (network/VPC misconfig).

2) Initial Triage (15–60 minutes depending on severity):
  - Gather: recent deploys/rollouts, model versions, routing fallback events, kernel/quantization changes, config changes.
  - Key telemetry to collect: per-tenant request rates, p50/p95/p99 latency, 5xx/error class breakdown, KV cache hit rate, model variant IDs, GPU-queue lengths, and cost burn rate.
  - Use these canonical queries (examples):
    - Per-customer 5xx rate: sum(rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.*",customer_id="$CID"}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{customer_id="$CID"}[5m]))
    - KV cache hit rate: sum(rate(kv_cache_hit_total[5m])) / sum(rate(kv_cache_lookup_total[5m]))
    - Model variant rollouts: SELECT deploy_id, model_version, started_at FROM model_rollouts WHERE started_at > now() - interval '90 minutes';

3) Communication (within triage window):
  - If S1/S2: CS Ops posts an initial templated update to the customer within 60 minutes (see templates below) and provides hourly updates until mitigated.
  - If S3: CS Ops prepares a targeted message for affected customers and aims for communication within 24 hours.
  - All outbound communications must include: what we know, what we're doing, ETA for next update, and contact for escalation.

4) Mitigation & Short-term Fix (1–6 hours):
  - Mitigation options: route to fallback model variant, increase pod count in Dedicated pool, enable prefix-KV cache warming, fail open to cheaper model for non-critical routes, or rollback last deploy.
  - Ownership: infra/runtime teams execute mitigation; CS tracks customer-facing changes and confirms impact.

5) Root Cause Analysis (24–72 hours):
  - Post-incident, the owning engineering team produces an RCA document with: timeline, contributing factors, corrective actions, risk assessment, and detection gaps.
  - CS consolidates customer impact summary (who, when, duration, measurable customer effects) into a one-page incident summary.

6) QBR Handoff & Action Itemization (1–2 weeks):
  - Any customer impacted by an S1 or repeated S2 for >2 incidents in a quarter is flagged for QBR agenda.
  - Handoff packet to QBR owner (CS lead) must include: incident summary, RCA link, proposed triage & product mitigations, ETA for fixes, and customer-facing remediation (credits, SLAs).
  - The QBR agenda item template: context → timeline → business impact metrics → remediation plan → prevention roadmap → open decisions.

Ownership Matrix (who does what):
- CS Ops: customer notifications, ticket routing, QBR agenda coordination, executive summaries.
- Platform SRE: multi-tenant infra issues, cloud provider escalations, incident commander for S1s.
- Serving Runtime: profiling, kernel/quantization rollback, scaling actions.
- Applied ML: model evaluation, rollback of model variants, quality investigation.
- Billing/Cost Ops: cost anomalies, credits, billing adjustments.

Customer Communication Templates (examples)
- Initial S1 update (subject): "[Redwood] Incident: Service degradation affecting requests — investigating"
  Body (first update):
  "We’re investigating increased error rates impacting API requests. What we know: Affected endpoints: /v1/generate, /v1/chat; Scope: ~12% of production traffic; Started: 2026-02-15 09:12 UTC. What we’re doing: paging infra and runtime teams, running targeted rollbacks for the most recent model rollout, and applying read-through cache warming. Next update: in 60 minutes. Contact: cs-ops@redwood.ai"

- RCA summary template (one page):
  - Incident ID, Start/End, Customers impacted (list), Root cause (summary), Contributing factors (bullet list), Actions taken, Long-term mitigations, Estimated customer impact (hours, failed requests, revenue exposure).

Acceptance & Escalation Criteria (examples)
- Move incident to QBR: any single customer experiencing >2 hours of degraded availability in a 30-day window, or any S1 affecting enterprise revenue.
- Automatic escalation to senior leadership: when an incident triggers cross-region failover or when SLA credits > $50k are projected.

Postmortem and QBR Integration:
- For flagged incidents, CS includes incident summaries in the next QBR as a discrete item with a clear set of owner-assigned actions and timelines. The QBR should always close actions or re-prioritize into the product roadmap with a named owner and ETA.
- Template QBR action tracking columns: Action, Owner, Due Date, Status, Customer Impact Metric, Link to PR/Issue.

Operational tooling & dashboards to maintain:
- Customer Health Sentinel: per-tenant SLO heatmap and active incident list.
- Degradation Triager dashboard: top N errors by route, per-model quality drift graphs, KV cache hit rate, GPU queue depth.
- Cost anomaly tracker: rolling 24h cost-per-token by customer and model variant.

Runbook snippets (one-line commands):
- Re-route traffic to fallback variant (CLI): redwoodctl traffic reroute --from model:v2.3 --to model:v2.2 --percent 100 --tenant $CID
- Inspect model rollout history (SQL): SELECT * FROM model_rollouts WHERE model_version = 'v2.3' ORDER BY started_at DESC LIMIT 20;

Governance & SLOs referenced:
- Platform availability SLO: 99.95% global per month (excl. maintenance windows).
- p95 latency target (generation): 350ms for hosted API default route; per-customer contracts may differ.
- Quality SLOs: baseline eval pass-rate > 92% for curated prompt-sets.

Appendix: Example queries and alerts to copy into the shared alerts library:
- Alert: CUSTOMER_AVAILABILITY_DROP
  Query: (sum(rate(http_requests_total{customer_id="$CID",status=~"5.*"}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{customer_id="$CID"}[5m]))) > 0.05
  Severity: S2
  Notify: cs-ops, tenant-ops, serving-runtime

- Alert: MODEL_QUALITY_REGRESSION
  Query: increase(failed_prompts_total{model=~"production-.*"}[1h]) > 0.2 * baseline_failed_prompts
  Severity: S2
  Notify: applied-ml, cs-ops

Related documents & references:
- QBR template and operational checklist (linked in Related pages).
- Incident manager runbooks and postmortem templates in eng-sre.

Change log:
- 2026-01-12: Created by Priya Nair (initial draft).
- 2026-02-18: Published — added mitigation options for Dedicated pool and expanded ownership matrix (reviewers: Liam O'Connor, Sara Velasquez, Rajat Malhotra).

Contacts (for escalation):
- CS Ops lead: priya.nair@redwood.ai
- Platform SRE on-call: pagerduty (platform-sre)

title: Quarterly Business Review (QBR) Template & Operational Health Checklist for Enterprise Accounts
content:
Summary:

This document provides a reusable QBR template and an operational health-check runbook tailored for Redwood Inference enterprise customers. The goal is to standardize pre-QBR data collection, meeting agenda, and follow-up actions so Customer Success (CS) and Product/Engineering stakeholders can run consistent, impact-oriented reviews. This is intended for CS Managers, Solutions Engineers, and account owners.

Scope:

- Applies to all enterprise accounts on Dedicated or Private deployments and self-serve hosted accounts that have reached 100k monthly tokens or have an assigned account team.
- Covers technical health metrics, usage economics, feature adoption, incidents and mitigations, and roadmap alignment.
- Does NOT replace security reviews, compliance audits, or billing dispute processes (see related pages).

Before the QBR — Pre-meeting checklist (Owners & timeline):

1. Two weeks prior: CS Manager (owner) creates QBR doc and shares calendar hold.
2. Ten business days prior: Solutions Engineer assembles technical pack (dashboards + raw queries).
3. Five business days prior: Finance/Account Ops confirms invoicing/committed usage data.
4. Two business days prior: Run automated health checks and upload results to the QBR doc.

Automated health checks (what to run and why):

- Latency distribution: p50/p95/p99 for generate and embed APIs (why: detect tail spikes affecting UX).
- Error rates: 4xx vs 5xx split, token-based vs request-based errors (why: surface integration bugs vs runtime failures).
- Token efficiency: avg tokens in vs tokens billed, cache hit ratio (why: cost optimization opportunities).
- Model fallback events: count of automatic fallbacks and fallback latency delta (why: reliability and SLA implications).
- Throughput & saturation: concurrent streams vs GPU pool capacity and queue depth (why: capacity planning).
- Recent incidents: all Sev>=3 incidents in period with MTTD/MTTR metrics.

Required data artifacts (attach to QBR):

- CSV export: token usage by route for the period (columns: date, route, model_version, tokens_in, tokens_out, cost_estimate).
- Dashboard snapshots: daily p95 latency and error-rate chart images.
- Incident timeline: chronological list with brief RCA links.
- Change log: model version pinning and rollout notes in the period.

Example quick queries (source: internal metrics DB) — paste into SE notebook:

-- Top 10 routes by token consumption in period
SELECT route, SUM(tokens_in + tokens_out) as tokens_used
FROM inference_usage
WHERE account_id = 'ACCOUNT_XYZ' AND date >= '2026-01-01'
GROUP BY route
ORDER BY tokens_used DESC
LIMIT 10;

-- p95 latency by model
SELECT model_version, percentile_cont(0.95) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY latency_ms) as p95_latency_ms
FROM request_latencies
WHERE account_id = 'ACCOUNT_XYZ' AND date >= '2026-01-01'
GROUP BY model_version;

Operational health thresholds (SLOs & alert thresholds):

| Metric | SLO target | Alert threshold (page) | Owner |
| --- | ---: | --- | --- |
| API availability (hosted) | 99.95% monthly | < 99.9% sustained 10m | eng-sre |
| p95 generation latency | < 400ms | p95 > 750ms for 30m | eng-serving-runtime |
| Error rate (5xx) | < 0.05% | > 0.25% for 15m | eng-sre |
| Model fallback rate | < 0.1% of requests | > 1% in a day | eng-platform |
| Token billing consistency | 100% accurate | any discrepancy > $500/day | finance-legal |

Health-check runbook (step-by-step):

1. Run the automated dashboard exports and save artifacts to the QBR folder.
2. Verify token billing export against internal cost calc: reconcile top 10 routes.
3. Inspect p95/p99 latency heatmap and flag sequences that show growth (>20% week-over-week).
4. Check prefix/KV cache hit rate — if < 60% for chat routes, add caching config recommendation.
5. Review recent deploys and model changes; correlate deploy timestamps to metric deviations.
6. If error rate spike found, triage: replicable test case -> capture request_id -> escalate to oncall per escalation guide.

QBR meeting agenda (60–90 minutes):

1. Introductions and objectives (5 min) — CS Manager
2. One-slide exec summary (top 3 wins, top 3 risks) (5 min) — CS Manager
3. Usage & economics deep dive (15 min) — Finance/SE: top routes, cost by model, seasonality
4. Reliability & incidents (15 min) — Eng SRE/SE: MTTD/MTTR, recent mitigations, outstanding risks
5. Feature adoption & product feedback (10 min) — Product/CS: experiments, quality regressions
6. Roadmap alignment and ask list (10 min) — Customer success & Product: timelines & impact
7. Action items, owners, and timing (5–10 min) — CS Manager closes

Post-QBR deliverables and follow-up (owners & SLAs):

- Action tracker created within 48 hours (owner: CS Manager).
- Engineering commit for high-priority reliability fixes defined within 7 days or logged in product backlog with priority tag.
- Monthly checkpoints for long-running items, status updates posted to QBR doc.

Template for QBR exec summary (one paragraph):

[Customer] continues to grow usage across routes X and Y (+22% MoM) with 84% of tokens consumed by model m-v1. Performance remained within SLOs for the period (p95=320ms), but two incidents in January increased MTTD and require a deployment policy change to improve fallback behavior. Action items: (1) enable prefix caching on chat routes (owner: SE, due in 14 days), (2) prioritize model rollback testing (owner: eng-platform).

Common integration checklists (for SEs during QBR prep):

- Verify SDK versions in customer code (JS/Python) and recommend upgrades for known bugfixes.
- Confirm retry/backoff strategies and idempotency for client requests.
- Confirm that customers use model pinning where deterministic output is required.

Known caveats & workarounds (short list for QBR discussion):

- Large batch inference on Dedicated pools can exhibit higher p99 latency under autoscaling transitions. Workaround: pre-warm additional nodes for predictable high-throughput windows.
- Quantized model outputs may exhibit minor tokenization differences vs FP32; advise regression tests on golden prompt sets before rolling to prod.
- Third-party CDN misconfigurations can cause 4xx errors that mimic client SDK bugs — validate request_id and raw request headers before escalating.

Risk levels and escalation path (summary):

- Risk tier 1 (Critical business impact): finance-impacting billing errors, data leakage, or sustained outages -> escalate to Eng SRE Lead and CS Director within 30 minutes.
- Risk tier 2 (High): frequent fallbacks or model quality regressions that materially affect UX -> notify Eng Platform and Product; schedule hotfix/rollback within 48 hours.
- Risk tier 3 (Medium): feature adoption gaps and non-urgent performance tuning -> track in backlog and review quarterly.

Appendix: sample slide list and artifacts to attach

- Slide 1: Executive summary + 3 bullets (wins/risks)
- Slide 2: Top routes & cost-by-model chart
- Slide 3: Latency curves (p50/p95/p99) and anomaly annotations
- Slide 4: Incident timeline + RCA links
- Slide 5: Roadmap & open asks with owners
- Attachments: CSV exports, dashboard images, relevant incident postmortems

Owner and contact info:

- Document owner: Aisha Patel (CS Manager) — aisha.patel@redwood.ai
- Engineering escalation contact: Miguel Torres (eng-sre lead) — miguel.torres@redwood.ai
- Solutions Engineering: Priya Desai — priya.desai@redwood.ai

How to reuse this template:

1. Copy this file into the customer's QBR folder and replace placeholders (ACCOUNT_XYZ, dates).
2. Attach generated artifacts from dashboards and the metrics SQL exports.
3. Tag the QBR doc with the customer-wide label and assign reviewers two weeks before the meeting.

Version history:

- 2024-11-02: Initial draft by Aisha Patel
- 2025-07-10: Added token-efficiency checks and billing reconciliation steps (reviewers: Miguel Torres)
- 2026-02-15: Clarified escalation SLAs and added SQL examples (reviewers: Priya Desai, Liam O'Connell)

Notes & links:

- See related: [Incident Escalation Playbook](/confluence/customer-success-and-support/escalation-playbook)
- See related: [Dashboards & Alerts index](/confluence/eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts)

End of document.

title: Customer Adoption Segmentation and Action Playbook
content:
Overview:

This playbook defines a repeatable approach to segmenting enterprise tenants after go-live and driving measurable adoption actions. It is intended for Customer Success Managers (CSMs), Technical Account Managers (TAMs), Customer Support Engineers (CSEs), and partner Solutions Engineers. The goal is to create prioritized, automated, and measurable interventions that improve stability, product value realization, and renewal velocity.

Scope:
- Applies to Dedicated and Private tenants in early to mid-post-go-live (day 7 -> month 6).
- Excludes pilot/proof-of-concept tenants still under active engineering feature trials.
- Intended to complement the first-90-days operational checklist; this document focuses on segmentation, signals, and playbook actions.

Key definitions:
- Tenant: customer-owned instance registered in Redwood control plane.
- Active Call: successful API request to generation/embedding endpoints in the last 30 days.
- Primary SLA: the latency and availability commitment for a tenant (e.g., 95th pct latency < 350ms, availability 99.9%).
- Adoption Index: composite score (0-100) combining usage, success rate, cost efficiency, and eval pass rate.

Segmentation framework (high level):
1) Business priority (tier)
   - Strategic: enterprise logo accounts with reserved capacity or contract value > $300k/year.
   - Growth: customers with sustained usage committing to expand in 90 days.
   - Self-serve: small tenants using hosted API only.
2) Technical posture
   - Green: stable requests, low error rate, KV-cache hit rate > 60%.
   - Yellow: intermittent errors, increased latency, or model quality regressions detected.
   - Red: sustained errors, rollout failures, or repeated customer escalations.
3) Adoption maturity (using Adoption Index)
   - Explorer (0-29): low integration, few API calls, limited telemetry.
   - Integrator (30-69): integrations live, moderate traffic, early caching/batching patterns.
   - Optimizer (70-100): mature telemetry, cost controls, good latency and quality metrics.

Operational signals and thresholds (examples):
- Traffic signal: < 50 unique user sessions or < 1k API calls / week -> exploration alert.
- Stability signal: 5xx rate > 1% for 30m or 0.5% sustained for 24h -> stability alert.
- Latency signal: P95 generation latency > 750ms for 15m -> investigate kernel/runtime or route fallback.
- Quality signal: Regression eval failure on core prompt set (accuracy drop >= 5%) -> model quality alert.
- Cost signal: Cost per 1k tokens exceeds baseline by 40% for billing period -> cost anomaly.

Adoption actions by segment (playbook table):
- Explorer -> Step actions:
  1) Automated email + usage tips (day 7) including quickstart snippets for prefix caching and batching.
  2) Invite to a 30-minute onboarding clinic (TAM) if calls remain low at day 14.
  3) Provide pre-configured prompt set and eval harness for basic quality checks.
- Integrator -> Step actions:
  1) Schedule 60-minute technical review within 7 business days of reaching Integrator threshold.
  2) Provide recommended batching/quantization profiles and cost-saving suggestions via Redwood Optimize.
  3) Configure synthetic journey monitors and run weekly synthetic QBR checks.
- Optimizer -> Step actions:
  1) Quarterly QBR focusing on model economics and feature/add-on expansion.
  2) Offer joint runbook and SLO tuning session with Eng-SRE.
  3) Propose Dedicated reservation sizing review for cost savings.

Example SLA mapping matrix (table):
| Tenant Tier | Minimum monitoring | SLOs tracked | Standard intervention | Escalation owner |
|-------------|---------------------|--------------|----------------------|------------------|
| Strategic   | 1m metrics; traces   | Availability 99.9%; P95 < 350ms | TAM-led weekly sync | Escalation: Eng-SRE on-call |
| Growth      | 5m metrics; traces   | Availability 99.5%; P95 < 500ms | CSM technical review | CSE + TAM |
| Self-serve  | 1h metrics           | Availability 99.0%; P95 < 800ms | Auto-notifications + docs | Support Tier 1 |

Runbook: Stability incident (example trigger: 5xx spike > 1% sustained 30m)
1) Triage (0-15m):
   - On-call CSE checks tenant dashboard: error rates, recent deploys, model variants in use.
   - Run quick query: SELECT count(*) as errors, time_bucket('1m', ts) FROM tenant_logs WHERE tenant_id = '<TENANT>' AND status >= 500 GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY ts DESC LIMIT 60;
   - If spike aligns with deploy, tag incident as "deploy-regression" and notify Eng-Serving-Runtime.
2) Mitigation (15-45m):
   - If model fallback configured, execute route-switch to warm-compatible-variant: POST /admin/tenants/<TENANT>/route-fallback {"variant":"stable-v1"} (use admin API).
   - If KV cache invalidation suspected, issue cache-warm: POST /admin/tenants/<TENANT>/kvcache/warm?prefix=default
3) Customer comms (15-60m):
   - CSM/TAM sends templated status update to customer with RCA-in-progress tag and ETA for next update.
4) Remediation (60m+):
   - Coordinate rollback or patch with eng. Produce post-incident checklist and RCA in the ticket.
   - If SLA credit condition met, notify Finance SLA team per contract matrix.

Synthetic telemetry and QBR metrics (recommended):
- Weekly: Adoption Index, Active Calls, KV-cache hit rate, P95 latency, Error rate (5xx), Cost per 1k tokens.
- Monthly: Evals pass rate on canonical prompt set, model variance usage, reserved capacity utilization.
- Queries (example):
  - Prometheus P95 latency: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(redwood_api_request_duration_seconds_bucket{tenant_id="<TENANT>",route="generate"}[5m])) by (le))
  - SQL cost anomaly: SELECT tenant_id, sum(billing_tokens) / NULLIF(sum(successful_requests),0) as tokens_per_call FROM billing_usage WHERE month = '2026-01' GROUP BY tenant_id HAVING tokens_per_call > 1.4 * (SELECT avg(tokens_per_call) FROM ... ) ;

Customer engagement templates (concise):
- Low-usage nudge (automated): Subject: "Quick wins with Redwood: caching & batching tips" Body: short tips + link to one-click sample repo.
- Quality regression alert (CSM template): includes ETA, impact, temporary mitigations (model fallback) and link to eval results.

Escalation ladder (when to involve who):
1) CSM/TAM -> handles adoption nudges and scheduling.
2) CSE (Tier 2) -> owns tenant-level technical triage and routing fixes.
3) Eng-Serving-Runtime on-call -> required for regressions linked to model runtime or kernel failures.
4) Eng-SRE -> required for infra-level outages, capacity exhaustion, or long-running performance regressions.
5) Legal/Support-Contract -> engaged if SLA credit calculation or contract breach is likely.

Playbook automation recipes (examples):
- Auto-classify tenants weekly using Adoption Index with a scheduled job: POST /internal/jobs/classify-tenants {"window_days":30} -> outputs CSV to S3 and triggers CSM notifications for Explorers.
- Create synthetic tests per tenant and failover rules via terraform templates; sample variable file excerpt: 

terraform vars:
```
tenant_id = "<TENANT>"
synthetic_check_cron = "0 6 * * MON"
failover_variant = "stable-v1"
```

Operational checklist for first 30 days (concise):
- Day 1: Verify control-plane registration, API keys, and firewall peering.
- Day 3: Confirm telemetry ingestion and synthetic journey baseline.
- Day 7: Validate prefix/KV cache configuration and run initial evals.
- Day 14: Reach out with technical review if Integrator thresholds not met.
- Day 30: CSM conducts adoption health review and proposes next quarter roadmap.

QBR agenda template (30–45 minutes):
1) Executive summary (5m): Adoption Index trend and business impact highlights.
2) Stability & SLO review (10m): Availability, latency, recent incidents, and mitigations.
3) Quality & Evals (8m): Results from canonical prompt sets and any model swaps.
4) Cost & Efficiency (7m): Token economics, batching/quantization savings, reserved capacity recommendations.
5) Roadmap & Actions (5–10m): Proposed improvements, feature requests, and ownership.

Ownership and SLAs for the playbook: 
- Playbook owner: Customer Success Operations (owner: Jordan Kim).
- Monitoring & alerts: Eng-Platform (onboarded to all tenant dashboards).
- Escalation owners: CSE (Tier 2), Eng-Serving-Runtime (runtime regressions).
- Review cadence: Quarterly review of thresholds and Adoption Index formula.

Appendix: Useful links and snippets
- Admin API examples: https://internal-api.redwood.ai/docs/admin
- Adoption Index calculation (pseudo): AdoptionIndex = 0.4*normalized_usage + 0.25*stability_score + 0.2*efficiency_score + 0.15*eval_pass_rate
- Contact list: TAM rotation roster (internal link), Eng-SRE on-call (pager link), Support Slack channel #support-tenant-triage.

Change log:
- 2026-01-15: Created initial playbook (Jordan Kim).
- 2026-02-20: Added SLA mapping matrix and runbook templates; updated signal thresholds (reviewers: Priya Menon, Liam O'Connor, Sofia Alvarez).

title: Activation SLA Exception & Timebox Playbook
content:
Overview

Purpose:
This playbook defines a deterministic process for handling activation-window SLA exceptions during enterprise customer onboarding. It provides timeboxed steps for containment, investigation, mitigation, escalation, and customer communications to minimize time-to-stability while protecting cost and product quality.

When to use this playbook:
- Customer experiences degraded latency, elevated error rates, or cost-velocity exceeding onboarding projections within the first 30 days of activation.
- Automated health checks or customer-reported incidents indicate sustained SLA breach during activation that may impact go-live commitments.
- Normal runbooks (standard incident or SRE playbooks) have been attempted and the issue persists beyond the defined timebox thresholds.

Goals:
- Contain impact within defined timeboxes (Investigation: 60m, Mitigation candidate deploy: 120m, Customer stabilization: 8h).
- Preserve telemetry needed for RCA while limiting downstream cost exposure.
- Provide standardized customer-facing messaging and governance for SLA exceptions and credits.

Ownership and roles
- Customer Success (CS) — Primary communications owner. Owning the customer relationship and timely updates.
- Oncall SRE — Technical triage lead for production incidents; responsible for topology, routing, and infra mitigations.
- Serving Runtime Team — Deep model-serving investigations, KV-cache, batching, and model variant rollout.
- Solutions/Integration Engineer — Tenant configuration, API contract verification, quota/rate-limit checks.
- Product Ops / Finance — Engage if cost-velocity or billing exceptions are likely.

Timeboxes and Expected Actions
1) T0 — Alert/Report (0 minutes):
- Trigger: automated health check or CS report.
- CS sends initial acknowledgement to customer (template below) within 15 minutes.
- Triage owner assigned (SRE oncall or Solutions eng).

2) Investigation Window — T+60 minutes:
- Goal: determine impact domain (serving, networking, model variant, tenant misconfig).
- Primary checks (execute in parallel):
  - Ingress gateway metrics: 5xx rate, connection errors, TLS handshake failures.
  - Per-tenant rate and quota counters (requests/min, tokens/min).
  - Model-level latency P95/P99 and token-emit rates.
  - KV cache hit-rate and cache TTL evictions.
  - Autoscaler events and pod/gpu scheduling failures.
- Outcome: classify as one of: Infrastructure, Serving Runtime, Model Quality/Variant, Client Misuse (unexpected traffic), or Billing/Quota.

3) Mitigation Window — T+120 minutes from alert start (if unresolved):
- Apply the fastest safe mitigation depending on classification:
  - Infrastructure: shift traffic to warm fallback region or enable burst pool.
  - Serving Runtime: switch to lower-memory model variant, disable aggressive batching, or clear stale KV cache for tenant.
  - Model issue: pin previous model version and enable canary rollback.
  - Client misuse: apply temporary throttling or temporary API key suspension and coordinate with customer.
- All mitigations require a short preflight checklist and a rollback plan; prefer configuration changes over code deploys.

4) Stabilize & Monitor — T+8 hours (target):
- Stabilization defined as 95% of requests within SLO for 1 hour and no sign of cost-velocity growth.
- If stabilizing, produce a stabilization note (CS + SRE) and schedule RCA.
- If not stabilized after 8 hours, escalate to incident review and cross-functional war room (see escalation matrix).

Escalation Matrix
- Level 1: Oncall SRE, CS owner, Solutions Eng (T0–T+2h).
- Level 2: Serving Runtime Lead, Platform Engineering Manager (T+2–8h) if mitigations incomplete.
- Level 3: Head of Customer Success, Head of Engineering, Product Lead (T>8h or major SLA breach with contractual impact).

Telemetry checklist (ordered)
1) Correlate alert ID to tenant ID and request examples (x-request-id) for replay.
2) Capture production traces (retain for 72h beyond default retention for this tenant).
3) Snapshot relevant dashboards (ingress, model latency, gpu telemetry, cost per-tenant).
4) Export KV cache stats, batching histograms, and model-variant routing logs.

Quick containment commands (examples)
- Throttle tenant to safe rate (k8s/ingress example):
  kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
  apiVersion: networking.example.com/v1
  kind: RateLimit
  metadata:
    name: throttle-tenant-1234
  spec:
    tenant: tenant-1234
    requestsPerMinute: 600
  EOF

- Pin model rollout (runtime CLI):
  runtimectl set-tenant-model --tenant tenant-1234 --model redwood-model-v2 --force-pin

- Clear tenant KV cache (runtime RPC):
  curl -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN' https://runtime-api.internal/tenants/tenant-1234/cache/clear

Decision table: mitigation selection
| Classification       | Fast mitigation (<=120m)                      | Rollback safety notes |
|----------------------|-----------------------------------------------|-----------------------|
| Infrastructure       | Route to warm fallback region                 | Ensure data residency allowed for fallback |
| Serving Runtime      | Switch to smaller quantized variant; disable batching | May increase token-cost; monitor latency |
| Model Quality        | Roll model to prior pinned version            | Validate sample prompts prior to switch |
| Client Misuse        | Apply temporary throttle or API key freeze    | Confirm with CS before permanent block |

Customer communication templates
- Initial acknowledgement (within 15m):
  Subject: "[Redwood] We received your report — investigating"
  Body: "Hi <CustomerName>,\n\nThank you for reporting this. Our team has acknowledged the issue and started triage. We will provide an initial update within 60 minutes. If you have any immediate logs or examples (request IDs) please share them in reply. — Riya (Customer Success)"

- Update at Investigation completion (T+60m):
  Subject: "[Redwood] Update: preliminary cause identified for activation disruption"
  Body: "Hi <CustomerName>,\n\nWe’ve completed an initial investigation and identified the likely cause: <short-classification>. We are applying a temporary mitigation and will follow up with stabilization status within 2 hours. Current impact: <summary>. — CS & SRE"

- Stabilization summary (T+8h):
  Subject: "[Redwood] Stabilized: activation window incident summary"
  Body: "Hi <CustomerName>,\n\nThe issue has been stabilized as of <timestamp>. Next steps: full RCA and timeline for permanent fix within 3 business days. If you'd like a joint review session, we can schedule one. — CS"

Governance and SLA crediting rules (summary)
- If the customer experiences >2 hours of degraded throughput or >4 hours of elevated error rates during the agreed activation window and the root cause is provider-side, triggering of credit review is automatic.
- Finance/Product Ops approves credit estimates. CS files a credit request ticket referencing the incident ID and attaches stabilization snapshot and mitigation timeline.

RCA & Follow-up (post-stabilization)
- Required artifacts: timeline.csv, traces.zip, snapshot-dashboards.png, mitigation-decisions.md.
- RCA author: Serving Runtime or SRE (depending on root cause) with CS contribution for impact timeline.
- RCA timeline: draft within 48 hours; final RCA and action-items in 7 business days.

Preventive measures and playbook improvements
- For each activation exception, the owning team must propose at least one preventive control: autoscaler tuning, pre-warmed capacity pool, tiered rate limits, model quantization guidance, or preflight telemetry assertions.
- Add any identified new telemetry assertions to the onboarding synthetic suite and QBR telemetry storyboard.

Appendices
A) Sample incident tagging conventions
- tag:activation-window, tag:tenant-<id>, tag:sla-exception, tag:playbook-v1
\B) Example alert payload (JSON) — use for debugging and replaying the event:
{
  "alert_id": "alert-20260112-9243",
  "tenant_id": "tenant-1234",
  "metric": "p99_latency_ms",
  "value": "3120",
  "threshold": "2000",
  "timestamp": "2026-01-12T10:22:00Z"
}

C) Postmortem checklist (for RCA owner)
- Confirm timeline and attach trace samples (x-request-id list)
- Validate mitigation and document rollback path taken
- Identify owner and ETA for permanent fix(s)
- Confirm crediting decision or rejection with Finance
- Schedule QBR slot to review trends if similar incidents repeat across customers

Related resources
- Onboarding telemetry storyboard (link above)
- Runtime rollback playbook (internal link to runtime runbooks)

Revision history
- 2026-01-12: Created by Riya Kapoor (initial draft)
- 2026-02-03: Reviewed by Ethan Park and Sofia Martinez; clarified timeboxes and added customer communication templates

Contact points
- CS Pager: cs-pager@redwood.internal
- SRE Oncall Channel: #sre-oncall
- Runtime Lead: runtime-lead@redwood.internal

title: Canary Simulation and Auto-Alert Playbook for Enterprise Cutovers
content:
Overview

This playbook describes a reproducible simulation and automated alert strategy for canary rollouts during enterprise customer cutovers (dedicated and private). It pairs realistic traffic simulation, telemetry checks, and an escalation ladder so Customer Success (CS), SRE, and Platform teams can validate stability before broad traffic migration and capture actionable signals for QBRs.

Goals

- Validate end-to-end request/response correctness for the customer’s integration paths (API, streaming, embedding)
- Detect regressions in inference quality, latency, and cost within the canary window
- Automate high-confidence alerts with clear ownership and rollback criteria
- Produce artifacts for post-cutover QBR and health audits

Scope

Applies to: Hosted -> Dedicated migrations, Dedicated capacity model swaps, Private environment cutovers where Redwood controls the control plane. Excludes large data-only backfills and purely offline batch ingestion.

Key Services and Metrics

- Services referenced in this playbook: redwood-inference-api, routing-proxy, tenant-gateway, telemetry-collector, cost-attribution-worker
- Telemetry surfaces used: request_latency_ms, token_error_rate, model_confidence_degradation (by prompt-set), p99_kvcache_hit_rate, tokens_per_request_avg, infra_gpu_util_pct

Pre-Canary Checklist (owners in parentheses)

1. Configuration and isolation
   - Create a dedicated canary tenant or sub-tenant and pin model_version (Platform).
   - Ensure KV cache warmers are seeded with canonical prefixes for the customer workload (SRE/Platform).
   - Confirm no shared-tenant quotas will throttle canary traffic (Customer Success / Billing).
2. Observability setup
   - Enable the canary dashboard and add the canary tenant filter (SRE).
   - Confirm Prometheus/OTEL queries for p99 latency, error rate, and KV hit rate are returning historical baselines (SRE).
3. Communication
   - Announce window to the customer and internal stakeholders; publish PagerDuty escalation policy (Customer Success).
   - Ensure on-call SRE and Platform engineers are present for the duration (SRE Manager).

Simulation Scenarios

A. Baseline synthetic workload
- Objective: validate steady-state latency and token economics.
- Traffic profile: 200 rps sustained for 10 minutes, steady distribution across short (<=64 tokens), medium (65-512 tokens), and long (>512 tokens) sequences.
- Expected: p95 <= 150ms for short/medium requests; p99 <= 400ms; tokens_per_request_avg within +/-20% of historical baseline.

B. Quality regression injection
- Objective: catch regressions in model outputs (hallucinations or structured output drift).
- Method: run the customer’s canonical prompt-set (50 prompts) and compute similarity/metric (BLEU/ROUGE embed-sim) vs. golden responses.
- Expected: model_confidence_degradation < 3% absolute drop.

C. KV cache pressure scenario
