title: Synthetic Health Suite Implementation and SLO Migration Guide
content:
Overview

This runbook describes how Customer Success (CS) and Support teams implement a standardized Synthetic Health Suite for enterprise tenants, and how to migrate existing per-tenant SLOs to a multi-dimensional SLO model used in QBRs. The goal is to compress detection-to-remediation time, improve fidelity of incident escalation for inference regressions, and centralize metrics used in Customer QBRs.

Audience

- Customer Success, Support, and Oncall engineers
- Platform/Monitoring owners (dashboards/alerting)
- Solutions Engineers who implement tenant instrumentation during onboarding

When to use this document

- During enterprise onboarding (week 1–4) to provision synthetic checks
- When customers request production-grade SLOs or ask to migrate from simple latency-only SLOs
- Prior to a QBR where synthetic coverage and SLO changes will be reviewed

Key definitions

- Synthetic Health Suite: a set of automated, scheduled requests that exercise a customer’s production inference path with representative prompts and assertions (latency, correctness, token-cost).
- Multi-dimensional SLO: an SLO composed of multiple metrics (latency, availability/error rate, and quality/regression) with weighted objectives.
- Check: a single synthetic job (e.g., streaming completion for chat route)

High-level rollout summary

1. Capture tenant profile (input distribution, typical sequence length, model variant).
2. Create synthetic checks (happy path, edge-case correctness, high-throughput pressure) and store config in tenant synthetic repo.
3. Wire checks into the Synthetic Runner (scheduled job service) and monitoring pipeline (Prometheus -> Cortex -> Grafana).
4. Define multi-dimensional SLO and thresholds; create dashboard panels and alert rules.
5. Validate for 72 hours, tune thresholds, and add to tenant QBR artifacts.

Tenant profile checklist

- Primary route(s): e.g., /v1/generate-chat, /v1/embeddings
- Representative prompt templates (3–5) and expected tokens-per-response
- Typical concurrency and burst patterns (RPS / minute)
- Accepted latency distribution (p50/p90/p99 targets)
- Quality acceptance criteria (sample eval prompts and golden answers)

Synthetic check types and examples

- Latency check (happy path): ensure p95 < configured target for route.
- Correctness assertion: run evaluation prompts and fuzzy-match responses against golden set (BLEU/ROUGE or embedding-similarity > 0.88).
- Cost sanity check: detect token inflation (per-response tokens suddenly increase > 2x baseline).
- KV-cache smoke: repeated prefix requests should have reduced tail latency by >= 20% vs cold runs.
- Throughput pressure: short burst to validate autoscale & queueing behavior.

Sample synthetic configuration (YAML)

# example synthetic job config for tenant-123
name: tenant-123-chat-happy
route: /v1/generate-chat
schedule: "*/5 * * * *"   # every 5 minutes
payload_templates:
  - id: welcome-1
    prompt: "User: Summarize the following product note in 2 bullets: {text}"
    expected_token_range: "20-80"
assertions:
  - type: latency_p95
    threshold_ms: 600
  - type: embedding_similarity
    prompt_id: welcome-1
    threshold: 0.88
notifications: ["pagerduty:CS-Tenant-Alerts", "slack:#cs-tenant-123"]
owner: se-team@example.com

Implementation steps (detailed)

1) Gather inputs (SE + CS)
   - Owner: Solutions Engineering (SE)
   - Inputs: prompt templates, golden answers, tenant concurrency profile
   - Deliverable: tenant-synthetic.yaml in repo /synthetics/tenant-123.yaml

2) Author synthetic job and test locally
   - Locally run runner: ./synthetic-runner --config tenant-123.yaml --test
   - Validate assertions pass for a minimum of 3 successive runs before scheduling

3) Deploy to Synthetic Runner and enable telemetry pipeline
   - CI step creates job in synthetic scheduler (k8s CronJob or managed scheduler)
   - Metrics emitted: synthetic.latency_ms{tenant,route,check}, synthetic.error_count{...}, synthetic.tokens_per_response{...}

4) Create dashboards and alert rules
   - Grafana panels: p50/p90/p95 latency, error rate (5m), tokens per response, similarity score distribution
   - Prometheus alert examples (rule language):
     - ALERT SyntheticLatencyDegraded
       IF histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(synthetic_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le, tenant, route)) > 0.6
       FOR 10m
       LABELS {severity=\"page\"}
       ANNOTATIONS {summary=\"Synthetic p95 > 600ms for {{ $labels.tenant }} {{ $labels.route }}\"}

     - ALERT SyntheticQualityRegression
       IF sum(rate(synthetic_similarity_below_threshold[1h])) by (tenant) > 0
       FOR 5m
       LABELS {severity=\"ticket\"}
       ANNOTATIONS {summary=\"Quality regression detected for {{ $labels.tenant }}\"}

5) Map alerts to escalation and ownership
   - PagerDuty: Severity=page -> oncall SRE -> if >30min -> Escalate to CS escalation engineer
   - Slack: Severity=ticket -> CS team queue -> SE to triage within 8 business hours

Multi-dimensional SLO model (recommendation)

- SLO composition (example monthly window):
  - Latency objective (weight 0.5): p95 latency <= 600ms for critical routes (target 99.5% success)
  - Availability/objective (weight 0.3): successful responses (HTTP 200 + no model errors) >= 99.9%
  - Quality/regression objective (weight 0.2): similarity to golden responses >= 0.88 for 98% of checks

SLO calculation notes

- Use error budget burn rate dashboards for each tenant. For quality regressions, count the check as failed if similarity < threshold or token inflation > 2x.
- When migrating from a single metric SLO (e.g., p95 latency only): run both SLOs in parallel (shadow mode) for 30 days and compare burn rates before full cutover.

Migration playbook (step-by-step)

1. Baseline (day 0–7): enable synthetic checks and run both old SLO and new multi-dim SLO in shadow.
2. Evaluate (day 8–21): collect burn rate deltas, false positives, and customer impact notes.
3. Tune thresholds (day 22–28): adjust similarity thresholds and latency targets where synthetic coverage is insufficient.
4. Stakeholder sign-off (day 29–33): SE, CS, Oncall, and customer rep sign migration ticket.
5. Cutover (day 34): flip multi-dimensional SLO into production as the authoritative SLO; keep old SLO as read-only archive for 90 days.

Validation and QA checklist

- Synthetic checks run without false positives for 72 hours (<= 1 FP per week acceptable)
- Metrics pipeline latency < 2 minutes end-to-end
- Dashboard panels display tenant-specific metrics and links to sample failing traces
- Playbook entry in customer’s onboarding checklist complete and linked in their QBR artifact bundle

Operator runbook for common failures

- Alert: SyntheticLatencyDegraded
  - Step 1: Confirm scope (tenant and route) and if burst or baseline shift using query: rate(synthetic_requests_total{tenant=\"...\"}[5m])
  - Step 2: Check model variant swaps in last 24h (audit logs: /infra/change-log?tenant=...)
  - Step 3: If KV cache coldness suspected, run warmup: replay 10 recent prefixes to the model and monitor latency; if latency reduces by >= 20% mark incident as KV-cache-related
  - Step 4: If traffic spike, validate autoscaler metrics (gpu_utilization, queue_length); escalate to infra if autoscaler not scaling within 2 minutes

- Alert: SyntheticQualityRegression
  - Step 1: Retrieve last 20 failing synthetic outputs and compute embedding similarity vs golden answers locally
  - Step 2: If regression correlates with a model version rollout, initiate immediate rollback policy per the tenant’s rollout config
  - Step 3: If no rollout correlation, file a quality incident and assign to Applied-ML for triage with example IDs and golden sets

QBR artifacts and reporting

- For each QBR include: synthetic coverage matrix (routes x check types), SLO burn rate trend (90/30/7 days), top 5 failing prompts/examples, remediation actions taken, and action plan for next quarter.
- Slide template: 1) Executive summary, 2) SLO heatmap, 3) Incident highlights (customer impact), 4) Action items and owners

Ownership and contacts

- Synthetic runner & scheduler: eng-platform / owner: Maya Chen (maya@redwood.com)
- Monitoring & alerts: eng-sre / owner: Omar Reyes (omar@redwood.com)
- Applied ML triage (quality): applied-ml / owner: Dr. Nina Kapoor (nina@redwood.com)
- Customer-facing CS lead: assigned per-customer in customer CRM.

Appendix: Useful queries and CLI snippets

- Quick similarity investigation (local python snippet):
  python -c \"from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer, util; m=SentenceTransformer('all-MiniLM-L6-v2'); a=m.encode('golden'); b=m.encode('candidate'); print(util.cos_sim(a,b))\"

- Prometheus query: p95 latency for tenant-123 over last 1h
  histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(synthetic_latency_bucket{tenant=\"tenant-123\"}[1h])) by (le))

- Create synthetic job via API (curl):
  curl -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    https://internal-synthetics.redwood/api/v1/jobs \
    -d '{"name":"tenant-123-chat-happy","schedule":"*/5 * * * *","route":"/v1/generate-chat","payload_template_id":"welcome-1"}'

Notes and best practices

- Keep golden answer sets short (5–20 examples) and refresh quarterly as product prompts evolve.
- Avoid including customer PII in synthetic inputs; use pseudonymized data from onboarding export.
- For latency objectives, synthetic runs should mimic real latency distribution (e.g., realistic token-lengths and system prompt context).

Revision history

- 2026-01-05: Created by Priya Shah (initial implementation playbook).
- 2026-02-12: Added migration timeline, Prometheus alert examples, and escalation mapping (reviewers: Ethan Moreno, Sofia Alvarez).

End of document

title: Enterprise Synthetic SLA Validation Framework
content:
Overview

This playbook defines a repeatable, instrumented framework for validating enterprise SLAs using synthetic traffic prior to and during customer cutover. It is intended for Customer Success (CS), Onboarding Engineers, and SREs to ensure predictable availability, latency, and inference economics for Dedicated and Private tenants.

Goals

- Give a single, opinionated validation sequence that maps synthetic test outcomes to go/no-go decisions.
- Provide concrete Prometheus queries, synthetic payloads, and run steps that can be executed by CS within 2 hours.
- Surface regressions that materially affect customer SLAs or cost-per-token before cutover.

Scope

- Applies to Dedicated and Private deployments and to hosted accounts with enterprise SLAs.
- Does NOT replace long-term load tests performed by Platform performance team; this is a deterministic functional+SLO check suite.

SLA and Synthetic Metric Definitions

Primary SLOs to validate (examples; match the customer's contract and tenant profile):

| SLO name | Target | Measurement window | Notes |
|---|---:|---|---|
| P99 inference latency (inference.request.duration_seconds) | <= 700ms (hosted), <= 1200ms (dedicated) | 30m rolling | Measured at ingress e2e, including queue and KV cache access |
| Availability (http 2xx ratio) | >= 99.95% | 1h | Counts 2xx / total requests to model endpoint |
| Error budget burn (failed requests) | < 0.05% of tokens | 24h | Flag if synthetic increases failure rate |
| Median tokens-per-request cost delta | <= +15% vs baseline | 2h | Detects model fallback or quantization mismatch |

Test harness and tooling

- Recommended runner: synthetic-runner v1.3 (internal binary) or fallback: python harness + requests.
- Telemetry sources required: Prometheus metrics (ingress and runtime), Distributed traces (Zipkin/Jaeger), and token accounting from billing sidecar.
- Test user: create a shared service account for on-call that triggers synthetic tests and writes annotations to the tenant timeline.

Prometheus queries (examples)

- P99 e2e latency (last 30m):
  - histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(inference_request_duration_seconds_bucket[30m])) by (le))
- Availability (last 1h):
  - (sum(rate(inference_requests_total{code=~"2.."}[1h])) / sum(rate(inference_requests_total[1h]))) * 100
- Error rate (last 30m):
  - sum(rate(inference_requests_total{code!~"2.."}[30m])) / sum(rate(inference_requests_total[30m]))
- Token cost delta (30m compare to baseline stored in metric token_cost_baseline):
  - (avg_over_time(token_cost_per_request[30m]) - token_cost_baseline) / token_cost_baseline * 100

Synthetic payload examples

- Representative customer short-turn prompt (JSON):
  {
    "messages": [{"role":"system","content":"You are a helpful assistant."},{"role":"user","content":"Summarize the key points from this 150-word policy text."}],
    "max_tokens": 256
  }

- Long-turn conversational sequence (helps expose KV cache and attention scaling): run 10 turns with average 200 tokens per turn.

CLI run examples

1) Quick single-tenant check (curl):

curl -s -X POST https://ingress.redwood.example/v1/tenants/TENANT_ID/contexts/generate \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer $SYNTH_KEY' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '@short_prompt.json' | jq .

2) Runner bulk test (using synthetic-runner):

synthetic-runner --tenant TENANT_ID --profile short-turn --concurrency 20 --duration 15m --annotations "pre-cutover:synthetic-sla-check"

Pre-cutover validation sequence (ordered steps)

1. Prepare tenant and telemetry
   - Confirm billing sidecar is enabled and token accounting metrics exist: token_cost_per_request, token_count_total.
   - Ensure Prometheus scrape targets include ingress and runtime pods for tenant.
   - Create run annotation in tenant timeline: "synthetic-sla-validation:YYYY-MM-DD".

2. Baseline collection (10m)
   - Run low-concurrency (c=3) short-turn profile for 10 minutes to collect a baseline.
   - Record baseline metrics and store them as a short-lived baseline with a tag (baseline_id).

3. Stress & stability pass (30m)
   - Ramp to target concurrency (based on customer profile, default 20) over 5 minutes. Maintain for 20 minutes.
   - Observe P50/P95/P99 and availability; annotate anomalies.
   - Run two long-turn sessions (10-turn dialogs) to exercise KV cache and memory growth paths.

4. Failure injection (optional, with SRE permission)
   - Brief 60s network egress loss to storage or slow KV lookup simulation. Validate graceful fallback and error rate thresholds.

5. Post-run analysis (15m)
   - Execute PromQL queries above to compute SLOs.
   - Produce a one-page test report (see Reporting below).

Go / No-Go criteria (example thresholds)

- FAIL if any of the following occur during the Stress pass:
  1. P99 > contract threshold for two consecutive 5-minute windows.
  2. Availability < 99.90% during the 30m stress window.
  3. Token cost delta > +25% compared to baseline.
  4. Unhandled errors (5xx or segfaults) seen in runtime logs more than 5 occurrences.

- WARN if:
  - P95 is within 15% of threshold or token cost delta is between +15% and +25%.

Runbook checklists (pre-cutover)

- CS Engineer: tenant config validated, timeline annotation created, customer notified of test window.
- SRE/Platform: Prometheus scrapes verified, alert suppression for synthetic run times configured.
- On-call: escalation contacts listed and reachable.

Failure modes and mitigation

- Symptom: P99 spikes with no corresponding increase in token count.
  - Likely cause: KV cache misses or increased queueing on runtime.
  - Mitigation: Roll back to smaller batch profile, enable prefix cache warm-up, open a high-priority ticket with Runtime team.

- Symptom: Token cost increases by >25% with similar latency profile.
  - Likely cause: Model switched to fallback variant or higher-precision quantization was selected.
  - Mitigation: Pin model variant to baseline, revert quantization change, and notify Model Onboarding team.

- Symptom: Availability drop to <99% during test.
  - Likely cause: Ingress throttling or misconfigured rate limiter.
  - Mitigation: Increase per-tenant rate limit temporarily, capture traces, and coordinate with Ingress infra.

Escalation path (concise)

1. CS Engineer -> On-call SRE (15m SLA)
2. On-call SRE -> Runtime Pager (30m SLA)
3. Runtime Pager -> Platform Eng & Model Onboarding (60m coordination)

Mapping to alerts

- Create ephemeral alerts active only for the run window:
  - SLO: p99_latency > threshold for 2 consecutive 5m -> pager to Runtime Pager.
  - Error rate > 0.5% -> page On-call SRE.
  - Token cost delta > +25% -> page CS Owner.

Reporting and QBR artifacts

- One-page test report (template below) to be attached to onboarding ticket and QBR:
  - Tenant ID, test window, profile used, concurrency patterns, baseline_id.
  - Key metrics: p50/p95/p99, availability, error rate, token cost delta.
  - Fail/Warn flags and root cause hypothesis.
  - Action items and owners with target dates.

Template (plain text):

---
Tenant: TENANT_ID
Window: 2028-01-08T10:00Z - 2028-01-08T11:00Z
Profile: short-turn + long-turn mix
Baseline ID: baseline-2028-01-08T09:40Z
Metrics:
  P50: 120ms  P95: 250ms  P99: 680ms
  Availability: 99.98%
  Error rate: 0.02%
  Token cost delta: +5%
Result: PASS
Action items:
  - Owner: Runtime Team -> Investigate transient GC spikes (ETA 48h)
  - Owner: CS -> Schedule follow-up synthetic after model pin deployment
---

Operational notes and best practices

- Always run synthetic checks outside of the customer SLA business hours unless explicitly agreed.
- Annotate every synthetic run; these become part of the tenant audit trail.
- Prefer representative prompts over random text — they catch semantic model fallbacks.
- Keep synthetic concurrency conservative on first pass; escalate to higher concurrency if stable.

Ownership and contacts

- Playbook owner: Priya Raman (Customer Success)
- Runtime contact: oncall-runtime@redwood.example (pager duty)
- Platform contact: infra-platform@redwood.example
- Escalation manager: Ethan Blake

Appendix: quick troubleshooting commands

- Tail runtime logs for tenant: kubectl -n runtime logs -l tenant=TENANT_ID --since=30m | grep -i error
- Quick PromQL check for P99: curl -G 'https://prometheus.redwood.example/api/v1/query' --data-urlencode 'query=histogram_quantile(0.99,sum(rate(inference_request_duration_seconds_bucket[30m])) by (le))' | jq .

End of document

title: SLO-driven telemetry orchestration for enterprise cutover
content:
Overview
--------
This playbook defines the SLO-driven telemetry and automated-orchestration patterns used during enterprise cutovers (provisioned Dedicated or Private tenants) and the post-cutover stabilization window. It is intended for Customer Success (CS), Site Reliability Engineering (SRE), and the onboarding customer engineering teams. The goal is to detect regressions quickly, drive automated mitigations where safe, and provide clean inputs into QBRs and post-incident reviews.

Scope
-----
- Applies to: Dedicated tenants, Private deployments (VPC/on-prem), and any high-commit enterprise account cutover.
- Excludes: Small self-serve accounts and non-production sandbox cutovers.
- Timebox: Primary playbook focuses on the first 72 hours after cutover (Day 0 -> Day 3).

Goals and Acceptance Criteria
-----------------------------
- Detect customer-impacting regressions within 5 minutes of onset for critical SLOs (latency, availability, error rate).
- Automatically reduce non-critical throughput (traffic shaping) within 10 minutes when token cost or latency SLOs are violated.
- Maintain p95 inference latency <= 250 ms for low-latency tiers; error rate < 0.5% (HTTP 5xx & model errors) during cutover.
- Produce a QBR-ready cutover report (SLO timeline + remediation actions) within 48 hours of cutover completion.

Roles and Responsibilities
--------------------------
- Customer Success (owner): coordinate cutover cadence, communications, stakeholder alignment, runbook execution.
- SRE (owner): author and own alerts, automation playbooks, capacity throttles, and rollback primitives.
- Solutions/Onboarding Engineer: performs tenant-specific validations, smoke tests, and acceptance gating.
- Customer Engineering (customer): participates in acceptance tests and approves go/no-go.

Key SLOs and Signals to Monitor
-------------------------------
- Availability SLO: requests with 2xx/3xx >= 99.95% over rolling 1h. Alert: drop below 99.9% for 10m.
- Latency SLOs: p50/p95/p99 for token generation RPCs. Example targets: p50 <= 70ms, p95 <= 250ms, p99 <= 600ms. Alert: p95 > 350ms for 5m.
- Error Rate: API-level 5xx + model-internal errors <= 0.5% over 15m. Alert: >= 1% sustained for 5m.
- Cost per 1k tokens (telemetry): track to detect runaway unit-costs; alert when > 2x expected baseline for 30m.
- KV/Cache Hit Ratio: goal >= 85% for workloads using prefix caching. Alert: drop below 70%.
- Queueing Depth / Backpressure: queue length per instance > 100 for 3m -> trigger autoscaler or shed traffic.

Instrumentation and Data Sources
--------------------------------
- Metrics: Prometheus-style metrics for request_latency_ms (histogram), request_success_total, request_failure_total, token_cost_total, kv_cache_hit_total.
- Traces: Distributed traces forwarded to the central tracing cluster (Jaeger/Tempo). Ensure 1:100 sampling at minimum during cutover window.
- Logs: Structured JSON request logs (request_id, tenant_id, model_id, seq_len, latency_ms, error_code). Indexed and searchable for at least 7 days.
- Telemetry Gateway: tenant-specific forwarder that tags data with tenant_id and cutover_phase.

Example Prometheus alert rules (copy into SRE alerting repo)
------------------------------------------------------------
- name: CutoverSLOs
  rules:
  - alert: TenantHighLatencyCutover
    expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_latency_ms_bucket{tenant_id=~"TENANT_REPLACE"}[5m])) by (le)) > 350
    for: 5m
    labels:
      severity: page
    annotations:
      summary: "p95 latency > 350ms for {{ $labels.tenant_id }}"

  - alert: TenantAvailabilityDrop
    expr: (sum(rate(request_success_total{tenant_id=~"TENANT_REPLACE"}[10m])) / sum(rate(request_success_total{tenant_id=~"TENANT_REPLACE"}[10m]) + rate(request_failure_total{tenant_id=~"TENANT_REPLACE"}[10m]))) < 0.999
    for: 10m
    labels:
      severity: page
    annotations:
      summary: "Availability below 99.9% for {{ $labels.tenant_id }}"

Automated Orchestration Patterns
--------------------------------
We support three levels of automated actions. All automation must be gated by safe-guards and require an owner to sign-off for rollbacks.
1) Non-blocking mitigation (automated, no human approval)
   - Examples: switch on aggressive batching for affected model variant, increase KV cache TTL, temporary token-rate shaping for non-critical routes.
   - Trigger conditions: p95 latency breach for 5 minutes AND queue_depth > threshold.
   - Safety checks: only allowed for tenants with 'auto-mitigate' flag enabled; actions are reversible and logged.

2) Assisted remediation (automated runbook + human confirm)
   - Examples: scale dedicated GPU pool by adding burst nodes, switch to lower-cost quantized model variant and notify CS + SRE.
   - Trigger conditions: cost per 1k tokens > 2x baseline OR error rate spike > 1%.
   - Human step: on-call SRE must acknowledge within 15 minutes or system reverts to conservative traffic shaping.

3) Rollback (manual, highest impact)
   - Examples: rollback to previous model version, failover to hosted pool, or revert tenant network configuration.
   - Preconditions: requires product owner + CS + SRE approval.
   - Trigger conditions: sustained violation of Availability SLO for 30m or safety checks indicating data corruption.

Runbook: Pre-Cutover Checklist (Day -7 to Day 0)
------------------------------------------------
1) Confirm business stakeholders and cutover window.
2) Verify SRE alerting templates cloned and tenant_id variables configured.
3) Validate telemetry forwarding for tenant (Prometheus relabels, trace sampling, log pipeline).
4) Smoke test with synthetic traffic: 10k tokens/min for 30 minutes; confirm p95 latency and success-rate.
5) Baseline cost measurement: record expected token cost and model selection.
6) Confirm automated-mitigation flags with customer.
7) Preload KV cache with canonical prefixes where applicable.

Runbook: Day 0 (Cutover) Steps
------------------------------
1) Coordinate go/no-go with customer and CS lead.
2) Start cutover marker: set cutover_phase=active on telemetry gateway.
3) Run smoke tests for each critical route (synchronous generation, streaming, embeddings) and confirm success.
4) Observe SLO dashboards for first 30m with 1m refresh cadence.
5) If p95 > 350ms or availability < 99.9%, trigger Non-blocking Mitigation sequence (see automation).
6) If mitigations do not normalize SLOs in 15m, escalate to Assisted remediation.

Runbook: Day 1-3 (Post-cutover Stabilization)
-------------------------------------------
- Maintain elevated sampling and dashboard refresh intervals.
- Run periodic synthetic tests every 2 hours.
- Capture representative traces and attach to cutover incident.
- Produce interim cutover report at 24h with the following sections: traffic profile, SLO timeline, interventions applied, customer impact estimate, and recommended next steps.

Escalation Matrix and Contacts
-----------------------------
- Page (P0): SRE on-call (pager duty) -> primary on-call + backup.
- CS escalation: CS lead (Aisha Benitez) -> solutions engineer -> account executive (if customer-visible outage).
- Product / Model owner: for model-behavior regressions.
- Security: security-oncall for data-exposure concerns.
Contact formatting example: role: name (channel) / pager.

Rollback Criteria and Safe-Rollback Procedure
--------------------------------------------
Rollback is a last-resort action. Criteria for rollback include:
- Availability < 99% for 30m and no recoverable cause found.
- Data integrity concerns (new model producing unsafe labels or PII leakage).
- Unacceptable cost surge causing billing exposure >= 3x baseline.

Safe-rollback steps (high-level):
1) Freeze auto-mitigation changes and document current state.
2) Notify stakeholders and schedule immediate rollback conference.
3) Execute rollback in maintenance window: revert model version or failover to hosted pool.
4) Validate smoke tests (same as pre-cutover).
5) Re-open cutover review and plan root-cause analysis.

QBR integration: Cutover Report Template (deliver within 48h)
---------------------------------------------------------
- Executive summary (1 paragraph): success state and any customer-visible impact.
- Key metrics: Availability, p95 latency, error rate, cost per 1k tokens, KV cache hit ratio.
- Timeline: annotated SLO graph (timestamps of mitigations & escalations).
- Actions taken: automated and manual.
- Open items & follow-ups: model tuning, capacity commitment, telemetry gaps.

Testing and Validation Guidance
------------------------------
- Synthetic traffic generator (recommended CLI):
  rcli cutover-test --tenant TENANT_REPLACE --duration 30m --tokens-per-sec 167 --routes "generation,streaming,embedding"
- Acceptance criteria for tests: all core routes meet p95 targets and success-rate >= 99.9%.
- Include chaos testing (network latency injection) during staging cutover to validate failover logic.

Auditability and Post-Incident Attachment Requirements
----------------------------------------------------
- All automated actions must write a reversible change record to the cutover incident log with: timestamp, actor, action-id, and revert procedure.
- Attach 3 representative traces for every automated mitigation and 10 for every rollback.
- Retain cutover incident artifacts for 90 days.

Maintenance and Runbook Ownership
--------------------------------
- This document is owned by Customer Success. SRE maintains the alerting rules and automation repository.
- Review cadence: every cutover OR quarterly, whichever is sooner.
- Change process: propose change in the CS runbook PR board; SRE must approve changes to alerts/automation.

References and Links
-------------------
- SRE alerting repo: git+ssh://git.internal.redwood/sre/alerts (replace TENANT_REPLACE variables as required).
- Cutover incident template: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/postmortems/cutover-incident-template
- QBR dashboard template: /confluence/eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/qbr-cutover-template

Appendix: Example Grafana Panel queries
-------------------------------------
- p95 latency (PromQL): histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_latency_ms_bucket{tenant_id=~"TENANT_REPLACE"}[5m])) by (le))
- Availability ratio: sum(rate(request_success_total{tenant_id=~"TENANT_REPLACE"}[5m])) / (sum(rate(request_success_total{tenant_id=~"TENANT_REPLACE"}[5m])) + sum(rate(request_failure_total{tenant_id=~"TENANT_REPLACE"}[5m])))

End of document.

title: Tenant Resilience Synthetic Suite: Onboarding & Readiness Playbook
content:
Overview

This playbook describes the Tenant Resilience Synthetic Suite used during enterprise onboarding and the first-90-days readiness checks. The suite simulates realistic tenant workloads, cost-sensitive load patterns, and failure modes to verify SLO alignment, throttling behavior, and safe failback paths before and after go-live.

Goals

- Validate tenant-specific SLOs (p99 latency, error rate, and cost-per-1k-tokens) under realistic mixes.
- Confirm automatic fallback behavior (model variants, region/failover routing).
- Surface tenant-side cost sensitivity and quota protection thresholds.
- Produce artifacts for QBR: synthetic run report, drift signals, and remediation checklist.

When to run

1. Pre-cutover: complete nightly run for 3 consecutive days before scheduled cutover.
2. Post-cutover: hourly smoke runs during first 72 hours, then daily for first 30 days.
3. On-demand: after model upgrades, routing policy changes, or infra capacity events.

Prerequisites

- Customer tenant onboarded to test environment with production-like routing and telemetry keys.
- telemetry-gatekeeper integration completed and metrics forwarded to obs-dashboard.
- Access to synthetic-orchestrator project and API keys.

Suite Components

- Synthetic Orchestrator: coordinate workload scenarios, scale, and schedule.
- Traffic Templates: templates for text-gen streaming, embeddings bulk-index, and reranking bursts.
- Cost Sensitivity Harness: measures token spend vs latency and throttling.
- KV Cache Emulation: toggles warm/cold cache conditions to exercise cache hit behavior.
- Failure Injectors: network latency, dropped packets, model-serving errors, and GPU OOM triggers.
- Reporting Generator: produces PDF/JSON artifact for QBR and attaches to customer record.

Test Scenarios (recommended canonical set)

1) Baseline throughput profile
- Objective: establish stable p50/p95/p99 latency at nominal traffic for tenant commit.
- Load: 100 RPS steady (for small tenants) or tenant-specific baseline (derived from ingress estimate).
- Checks: p99 < SLO threshold, token cost within expected range (+/- 10%), 0 uncaught 5xx.

2) Spike + Quota Protection
- Objective: validate adaptive rate limiting and quota-protector webhook behavior.
- Load: ramp 10x for 60s, hold 5m, then decay.
- Expected: graceful 429s with quota header, no downstream cascades, telemetry annotation on rate-limit events.

3) Cold KV Cache Recovery
- Objective: ensure prefix/KV cache warming strategy keeps latency recovery under 2x baseline.
- Procedure: purge tenant cache, send burst of prefix-heavy requests, measure token-per-response and latency tail.

4) Model Fallback Simulation
- Objective: trigger primary model failure and verify fallback to compatible variant and alerting.
- Failure: synthetic-orchestrator flips a readiness flag on primary model instance.
- Expected: requests seamlessly routed to fallback, quality-safety gates log warnings, customer-facing latency within fallback SLO.

5) Cost Sensitivity Staircase
- Objective: quantify cost vs latency tradeoffs when changing batching and quantization profiles.
- Steps: run constant workload under three profiles: high-throughput (bigger batches), latency-first (smaller batches), quantized (int8).
- Report: delta cost per 1k tokens and quality regression notes.

Metrics & SLOs (example thresholds)

| Metric | SLO / Threshold | Operational Action |
|--------|-----------------|--------------------|
| p99 latency (token stream) | <= 800ms (Tier B) | If breached 3x in 10m, run canary rollback or throttle non-critical routes |
| 5xx rate | < 0.5% | Alert P1 if sustained > 1% for 5m |
| 429 rate (adaptive RL) | <= 2% | Verify quota-protector webhooks and notify CS if > 5% |
| Cost / 1k tokens | within +/- 15% of estimate | Trigger FinOps review if > +20% |
| KV cache hit rate | >= 65% after warmup | If < 40%, run cache-warm strategy and investigate prefix skews |

Runbook: executing a full suite run

1. Preparation (10–30 min):
   - Confirm tenant staging mapping and that ingress-gateway points at synthetic-orchestrator.
   - Check obs-dashboard baseline dash for last 24h.
   - Notify stakeholders (CS lead, customer-eng, infra-owner) via the go-live Slack channel.

2. Kickoff:
   - Start baseline scenario and verify health checks pass.
   - Start cost-sensitivity harness sequentially; do not run quantized profile concurrently with other heavy tests.

3. Monitoring during run:
   - Watch p99/p95/p50 in obs-dashboard.
   - Watch synthetic orchestrator logs for dropped requests and failures.
   - Confirm telemetry events include tags: tenant_id, synthetic_run_id, scenario_name.

4. Post-run artifact generation (automated):
   - Reporting generator emits report to /customer-records/<tenant>/synthetic-reports/<run-id>.pdf and JSON.

Automated checks & alert mapping

- If p99 > threshold for > 5m -> alert ops-sre channel and create Incident stub with "synthetic-resilience" template.
- If cost / 1k tokens deviates by > 20% -> notify FinOps and CS; attach cost-sensitivity CSV.
- If fallback triggered -> send structured webhook to customer and open a follow-up ticket in Jira (label: synthetic-fallback).

Triage & Remediation Playbook (priority ladder)

1) Latency tail increases (p99 breach)
   - Check KV cache warmup metrics. If cold, execute cache-warm run using prefix-replay tool.
   - If cache healthy, throttle non-essential routes and escalate to eng-serving-runtime.

2) Elevated 5xx errors
   - Look for OOMs on GPU hosts; if present, mark node and trigger node-drain.
   - If errors originate from tenant proxy, roll forward to next stable tenant-proxy commit or apply immediate rollback.

3) Unexpected cost spike
   - Pause quantized/large-batch scenarios. Re-run small-sample to confirm.
   - Attach run trace to FinOps review and propose batch-sizing or model-variant changes.

4) Fallback quality concerns
   - Compare prompt-set evals captured during run. If regression > configured threshold, add to model-onboarding backlog and schedule immediate rollback to pre-upgrade pin.

Post-onboarding artifacts to produce

- Synthetic Run report (PDF + JSON) with: scenario definitions, raw telemetry links, SLO compliance badges, and remediation tasks.
- Tenant Resilience Checklist (signed-off by CS and infra).
- QBR short brief (1 page) highlighting: stability score, cost variance, and known open remediation items.

Ownership & escalation

- Primary owner: customer-success (Aisha Khan).
- Secondary owners: eng-serving-runtime (on-call rotation), eng-sre (capacity and infra remediation).
- Escalation path: CS -> Infra Pager -> Eng SRE lead -> Oncall Eng Serving Runtime -> Product PM (for model/variant decisions).

Frequently asked questions

Q: What if synthetic runs pass but production diverges?
A: Confirm traffic parity (routing weights), client prompt differences, and dataset split. Schedule a focused production-sampling run with lower-fidelity sampling to identify prompt drift.

Q: Can the suite run against Dedicated / Private tenants?
A: Yes. For Private deployments, use local synthetic-orchestrator deployment and ensure you run within customer's air-gapped testing window. Coordinate with Private deployment owner for network allowances.

Appendix: Example synthetic-orchestrator scenario config

{
  "scenario_id": "resilience-staircase-2026-01",
  "tenant_id": "tenant-xyz-123",
  "steps": [
    {"name": "baseline", "rps": 100, "duration_s": 600},
    {"name": "spike", "rps": 1000, "duration_s": 300},
    {"name": "decay", "rps": 200, "duration_s": 300}
  ],
  "tags": ["onboarding", "resilience"],
  "notify": {"channels": ["#cs-go-live", "#ops-sre"]}
}

CLI quick checks

- Start a run: curl -X POST "https://synthetic-orchestrator.internal/api/v1/runs" -H "Authorization: Bearer $SYNTH_KEY" -d '@scenario.json'
- Fetch run status: curl "https://synthetic-orchestrator.internal/api/v1/runs/<run-id>/status"

Revision history

- 2025-11-04: Created by Aisha Khan (initial structure and baseline scenarios).
- 2026-02-15: Updated thresholds and added cost-sensitivity staircase (reviewers: Miguel Ortega, Priya Subramanian).

Related resources

- obs-dashboard tenant template: /confluence/eng-platform/dashboards/tenant-resilience-template
- Synthetic orchestrator runbook: /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/synthetic-orchestrator-runbook

End of document

title: Synthetic Journey & SLA Calibration Playbook
content:
Overview:

This playbook defines a standard, repeatable approach for creating, validating, and operating synthetic customer journeys used to calibrate SLAs/SLOs and drive data into QBRs. Synthetic journeys are deterministic, automated requests that emulate customer behavior across the Redwood Inference product surface (API calls, streaming, embeddings, and model switchover flows). The goal is twofold: (1) provide stable, reproducible signals for SLI measurement and drift detection, and (2) offer a lightweight smoke harness for onboarding and post-cutover verification.

Intended audience:
- Customer Success Engineers (CSEs)
- Onboarding Engineers
- SRE and Observability owners
- Product Managers running QBRs

Purpose and success criteria:
- Produce at least 6 stable synthetic journeys per enterprise tenant within the first 30 days of onboarding.
- SLIs derived from synthetic runs (latency P95, request success rate, model-consistency pass rate) should correlate with 0.8+ Pearson correlation against real-traffic SLIs across three sampled customers before being used for SLA enforcement.
- Synthetic-driven alerts should reduce false-positive operational tickets by 25% within 90 days when used as preflight checks for deployments.

Scope:
- Applies to Hosted and Dedicated deployments. Private (on-prem/VPC) deployments should adopt the same tests but may need network-specific configuration documented in the tenant's runbook.

Owners and contacts:
- Playbook owner: Maya Chen (Customer Success)
- Observability owner: Arjun Patel (Eng SRE)
- Runtime/Model owner: Dr. Priya Singh (Eng - Serving Runtime)
- Escalation contact: Support oncall (pager duty)

Prerequisites (before running a tenant's synthetic suite):
1. Tenant telemetry forwarding is enabled and validated (traces -> APM, metrics -> Prometheus/TSDB, logs -> ELK).
2. Tenant has a test API key (scoped to synthetic traffic) and a dedicated telemetry_id label for grouping.
3. Baseline artifacts checked in: canonical prompts, seed tokens for deterministic model outputs, and expected top-k outputs for consistency checks.
4. Canary traffic window scheduled (if running during a production rollout).

Synthetic journey inventory (recommended canonical suite):
1) Basic Text Generation - single-shot
   - Purpose: measure cold-start latency and first-token P95 across model variants.
   - Inputs: 3 canonical prompts (short/medium/long).
   - SLI: P95 generation latency, tokens/sec, success_rate.

2) Streaming Chat Session - streaming/long-lived connection
   - Purpose: validate chunked streaming, connection stability and knobged backpressure.
   - Inputs: 1 multi-turn conversation script (7 turns).
   - SLI: median chunk latency, connection drop rate, stream completeness.

3) Embedding Batch - high-throughput micro-batch
   - Purpose: verify batch sizing, throughput, and embedding vector stability.
   - Inputs: 128 short texts per batch.
   - SLI: throughput (vectors/sec), P99 latency per batch, cosine similarity against baseline.

4) Model Switchover & Fallback Path
   - Purpose: exercise smart routing and automatic fallback to variant models during simulated capacity constraints.
   - Inputs: request stream flagged to prefer low-cost variant.
   - SLI: success_rate_on_fallback, failover_time_ms.

5) Prefix/KV Cache Reuse Simulation
   - Purpose: validate prefix caching behavior for conversational workloads (KV-hit ratio).
   - Inputs: repeated conversation sequences to create cacheable prefixes.
   - SLI: KV_cache_hit_rate, median response delta vs uncached.

Defining SLIs -> SLOs mapping (reference):

| Synthetic test name                    | Primary SLI                        | SLO (90d lookback)                      | Alert threshold (per-tenant)             | Notes |
|----------------------------------------|------------------------------------|------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------|-------|
| Basic Text Generation                  | P95 latency (ms)                   | <= 650 ms                                | P95 > 900 ms (sustained 10m)             | Short prompts only |
| Streaming Chat Session                 | Chunk latency (ms)                 | median chunk <= 120 ms                   | median > 200 ms (5m)                     | failover to non-stream if degraded |
| Embedding Batch                        | Batch throughput (vectors/sec)     | >= 1000 vec/s                            | throughput < 500 vec/s (sustained 10m)  | tune batch size |
| Model Switchover & Fallback Path       | failover_time_ms                   | <= 300 ms                                | failover_time > 700 ms (3 tries)        | measure end-to-end |
| Prefix/KV Cache Reuse Simulation       | KV cache hit rate                  | >= 78%                                   | hit_rate < 60% (1h sustained)            | important for cost savings |
\nNote: The SLOs above are suggestions. For enterprise customers we recommend negotiating tenant-specific SLOs during the onboarding contract and recording them in the tenant runbook.

Test implementation patterns and sample commands:
- Execution harness: the recommended runner is the Redwood-synth-runner (python) located in the onboarding repo. It tags telemetry with tenant_id and synthetic=true.

Example CLI (run all canonical tests against tenant):

rdr-synth run --tenant-id tenant-abc --api-key synthetic:tenant-abc --suite canonical --interval 60s --telemetry-id tenant-abc-synth

Example minimal YAML test config (use in tenant repo):

suite: canonical
interval: 60s
tests:
  - name: basic-text-short
    type: generation
    model: rdx-base-1.2
    prompts:
      - "Summarize the following policy in one sentence: [text]"
    assertions:
      - p95_latency_ms: 650
      - success_rate: 0.995

Operational cadence and run schedules:
- Stable customers: run canonical suite every 60s, rollup hourly for dashboarding.
- Newly onboarded customers (<30 days): run extended suite every 30s and capture raw traces for the first 72 hours.
- During deploy/stability windows: increase frequency to 10s for targeted tests that validate the change (e.g., model switchover).

Alerting and routing (playbook for alerts triggered by synthetic failures):
1. Alert triage should start in the Synthetic Alert channel in Slack and create a P0/P1 incident only if real traffic SLIs also degrade or the synthetic failure is accompanied by infra-level alerts (GPU errors, network egress drops).
2. If alert is synthetic-only, follow these steps:
   a. Verify telemetry_id and that the synthetic runner tag is applied.
   b. Compare to control customers (3 control tenants with identical model profile). If only this tenant fails, escalate to CSE to validate tenant-specific configs.
   c. For repeat failures across many tenants, escalate to Eng-SRE and Mark incident as 'possible regression'.
3. Required incident fields: earliest synthetic failure timestamp, test name, recent commit hashes for runtime/model, telemetry_id, runbook link.

Triage playbook (step-by-step):
1) Confirm reproducibility:
   - Re-run the failing test from the quick-run CLI with verbose tracing: rdr-synth run --test <test-name> --tenant-id <tenant> --verbose --limit 5
   - Capture trace IDs and include in the incident.
2) Check model/variant health:
   - Inspect model-serving dashboard for kernel errors, OOMs, and recent restarts.
   - If GPU errors present, coordinate with GPU-fleet team.
3) Isolate networking/failure domain:
   - Validate that telemetry signals (request/response counts) are reaching the central TSDB.
   - For Private deployments, validate peering and NAT gateway metrics.
4) Validate configuration drift:
   - Compare tenant's pinned model version and routing policy to the onboarding baseline.
   - Check for accidental changes to caching TTLs or batch sizing.
5) Rollback/fallback decisions:
   - If a model update is the likely cause and reproduces in control tenants, execute immediate rollback to previous model version (follow model rollback runbook).
   - If the issue is degraded hardware performance, apply routing to alternate region or dedicated pool.

Reporting into QBRs and customer communications:
- Weekly digest: automated weekly summary delivered to the customer report folder (S3) showing synthetic pass/fail, trends for primary SLIs, and notable anomalies.
- QBR artifact: include a 3-month synthetic vs real-traffic correlation chart, top 3 synthetic incidents and remediation notes, and action items for improving telemetry or test fidelity.
- Post-mortem: all synthetic incidents that resulted in customer-impacting outages must have a linked postmortem in the incident tracker and an update in the tenant's onboarding playbook.

Best practices for onboarding teams (checklist):
1. Create tenant-scoped synthetic API key and label telemetry_id before provisioning.
2. Check in 3 canonical prompts and expected outputs under the tenant's repo.
3. Run extended suite for 72 hours after go-live and record baseline SLI values to the tenant runbook.
4. Publish tenant-specific SLOs in the runbook and share them during the first QBR.
5. Re-run the entire canonical suite after any runtime or model change and compare to baseline using the 'synth-delta' tool (part of rdr-synth).

Example synthetic delta command and output snippet:

rdr-synth delta --baseline tenant-abc/baseline-2024-09-12 --current tenant-abc/latest --metrics p95_latency,p99_latency,kv_hit_rate

Output (human readable):
- p95_latency: baseline 540 ms -> current 610 ms (+13%)
- kv_hit_rate: baseline 82% -> current 63% (-23%) -> ACTION: review cache TTLs

Retention and data governance:
- Synthetic logs/traces are retained for 90 days by default.
- Aggregated synthetic SLI rollups are retained for 13 months for QBR trend analysis.
- For customers with restricted data policies, mark synthetic payloads as PII-free and avoid using customer data in test prompts. Use synthetic placeholders.

Known pitfalls and mitigations:
- Pitfall: Synthetic tests are too similar and overfit the cache behavior.
  Mitigation: Rotate prompt corpus weekly and include non-cacheable prompts in 20% of runs.
- Pitfall: Synthetic-only alert fatigue.
  Mitigation: Tie synthetic alerts to a short list of high-fidelity checks (e.g., failover_time, P95 latency) and suppress noisy metrics at the alerting layer.
- Pitfall: Misaligned SLOs between commercial contract and telemetry.
  Mitigation: Always derive tenant SLOs from a calibrated 30-day synthetic baseline and get legal/finance signoff if contract-linked.

Appendix A — YAML schema (reference) for a canonical test definition:

# test definition schema (YAML)
name: basic-text-short
type: generation
model: rdx-base-1.2
prompts:
  - text: "Summarize policy: [placeholder]"
    seed: 42
assertions:
  - metric: p95_latency_ms
    max: 650
  - metric: success_rate
    min: 0.995

Appendix B — Quick escalation matrix:
- Synthetic-only failure, tenant-local: CSE -> customer success manager (CSM) -> eng-sre (if persists 30m).
- System-wide synthetic regressions: eng-sre (P0) -> runtime team -> CTO on-call if outage persists >2 hours.

Appendix C — Example dashboard widgets to include in customer QBR page:
1. Synthetic pass rate (24h / 7d / 30d)
2. P95 latency trend (synthetic vs production)
3. KV cache hit rate trend with histogram of prefix lengths
4. Top synthetic incidents and root cause tags

Document change log:
- 2024-09-12: Created by Maya Chen.
- 2024-10-28: Added model switchover test and fallback SLI (Arjun Patel review).
- 2025-03-18: Clarified alert thresholds and added retention policy (Sofia Ramos review).

End of document.

title: Activation Signals & Churn-Mitigation Runway: Early-Warning Playbook
content:
summary:
Operational playbook for detecting customer activation failures and near-term churn risk, automating alerts, running deterministic remediation steps, and standardizing outreach and QBR metrics for the first 90 days and ongoing retention efforts.

body:
Purpose
-------
This page codifies a repeatable, measurable process to catch customers who are failing to activate or are showing early signs of churn. It combines instrumentation, automated runbook actions, human escalation, and customer-facing outreach templates so CSMs and support can react within the first 72 hours and through the 90-day handback.

Scope
-----
Applies to: all trial and self-serve customers and newly onboarded enterprise accounts (first 90 days after initial sign-up or first production API call). Excludes legacy customers with custom contracts on >6 months cadence; those follow enterprise playbooks in enterprise-onboarding.

Definitions and Key Terms
-------------------------
- Activation window: first 30 days after account creation (primary), observed through 90 days for retention patterns.
- Active API session: any authenticated request that results in a generation/embedding response (excluding health-check-only pings).
- Primary signals: a prioritized set of telemetry used to infer activation and churn risk (see Signals table).
- CSM: Customer Success Manager assigned to the account.
- MTL: Mean time to live (internal shorthand used only for SLA windows in runbooks).

Signals and Thresholds (early-warning map)
-----------------------------------------
The platform emits signal categories that are mapped to severity levels. Severity determines automated actions and human involvement. Thresholds are conservative; adjust per-customer segment (ARR bucket): SMB / Mid-Market / Enterprise.

| Signal category | Concrete metric | Severity 1 (action) | Owner | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| Activation activity | < 5 API calls in first 7 days | True | CSM + Growth | Indicates likely non-starter for PLG trials |
| Feature usage | No embedding calls after enabling embeddings feature | True | CSM | Could be integration incomplete |
| Latency regressions | 95th percentile latency > 2s above baseline for 12 hours | True | Eng oncall + Support | Potential runtime regression or region capacity issue |
| Error rate | 5xx rate > 1% sustained > 30min | True | Support + Eng oncall | Triage for infra or model variant fallback |
| Cost surprises | Daily token spend > 5x projected run-rate | True | CSM + Finance | Potential misconfiguration or abuse |
| Quality regressions | Regression alerts from eval-suite on customer prompt set | True | Applied ML + CSM | May require model rollback or prompt adjustments |

Instrumentation and Example Queries
----------------------------------
We maintain shared dashboards and alerts in Grafana/Datadog + BigQuery for retrospective signals. Below are canonical queries (adapt to dataset names).

Sample BigQuery: 7-day activation check
```
SELECT customer_id,
  COUNTIF(event_type='api_request') AS api_calls_7d,
  COUNT(DISTINCT DATE(event_ts)) AS active_days_7d
FROM `redwood-prod.telemetry.events`
WHERE customer_id = @customer_id
  AND event_ts >= TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 7 DAY)
GROUP BY customer_id;
```

PromQL: 95p latency spike (Grafana alert)
```
max_over_time(histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, route))[12h:5m]) > (baseline_p95 + 2)
```

Slack alert example (format)
- channel: #cs-alerts
- message: "[ALERT] customer={{customer_id}} 95p latency spike: {{value}}ms; baseline={{baseline}}ms — CSM={{csm}}; runbook: <link>"

Automated Playbook (0–72 hour automation)
-----------------------------------------
1) Trigger: any Severity 1 signal.
2) Automated actions (system) — run within 5 minutes of alert:
   - Create a ticket in Zendesk: autotag = ew-<signal>-<customer_id>.
   - Post structured alert to #cs-alerts with runbook link and owners.
   - If signal = error-rate OR latency: automatically route traffic to fallback model variant (if available) and enable short-term caching TTL to mitigate volume.
3) System waits 30 minutes to observe whether automated mitigation reduces signal. If signal resolves, ticket annotated with automated-mitigated=true and CSM receives a summary email.
4) If signal persists after 30 minutes, escalate to human steps below.

Human Response Steps (escalation ladder)
--------------------------------------
1) First responder: CSM (primary) initiates customer outreach and opens a triage call if customer is impacted. Use the "Initial check-in" email template below. Within 60 minutes: confirm receipt in Zendesk and update Slack thread.
2) If impact = platform (latency/error): Support (Tier 2) owns technical triage; engage Eng oncall if degradation continues > 30 minutes.
3) If impact = integration or misconfiguration: CSM/Solutions Eng run guided troubleshooting (see Integration checklist).
4) If customer financial exposure > $5k/day or SLA breach likely: Immediately escalate to Customer Success Lead and Sales Engineering for executive comms.

Escalation Matrix (contact window and timeout)
---------------------------------------------
| Escalation step | Role | Contact method | Timeout |
|---|---|---|---:|
| 1 | CSM | Slack + email | 60 min |
| 2 | Support Tier 2 | Pager/Slack | 30 min |
| 3 | Eng oncall | Pager + call bridge | 15 min |
| 4 | CS Lead / Sales Eng | Phone + executive email | 60 min |
| 5 | Legal / Finance (if billing risk) | Email + Ops channel | 4 hours |

Customer Outreach Templates (use and track)
------------------------------------------
Initial check-in (short—sent after automated mitigation or first responder acknowledges):
Subject: Quick check — we saw low activity / a problem on your Redwood account
Hi {{first_name}},

Wanted to check in: our systems detected low activity / an alert for your account ({{customer_id}}) that may affect your initial setup. We ran an automated mitigation and wanted to confirm whether you see degraded responses or errors. Can you reply with: (1) whether you attempted to run a request in the last hour, and (2) any error messages you see?

If you prefer, we can jump on a 15-minute troubleshooting call — here is a link to book: {{calendar_link}}

Thanks,
{{csm_name}}

Post-resolution (explain what happened + next steps):
Subject: Incident summary and next steps — {{incident_id}}\Hi {{first_name}},

Thanks for your patience. We identified {{root_cause}} and took {{actions}} to remediate. To prevent recurrence we will: 
- Action 1: {{permanent_fix}} (owner: ENG)
- Action 2: {{guidance}} (owner: CSM)

We recommend the following product changes for your integration: {{recommendations}}.

If you’d like, we can include this item on your QBR agenda so your team has visibility.

Guided troubleshooting checklist (for CSMs / Solutions Eng)
1) Confirm API key scopes and region configuration.
2) Check ingestion of customer config flags and feature toggles.
3) Reproduce the failure with a minimal request (include request/response examples).
4) If errors are 5xx, capture request_id and escalate to Support with logs and timing.
5) For perceived low-quality outputs, run the customer prompt set through the eval harness and attach results.

30/60/90-Day Activation & Retention Playbook (CSM cadence)
---------------------------------------------------------
- Day 0–7: Activate
  - Tasks: Welcome call, verify API keys, run reference sample requests, ensure first successful generation in sandbox.
  - KPI guardrails: >= 5 successful API calls and >= 3 active days in first 7 days.
- Day 8–30: Adopt
  - Tasks: Assist with embedding/indexing flow or fine-tune integration; ship 1 internal example that uses production tokens.
  - KPI guardrails: token usage >= projected onboarding plan; at least one quality check using eval harness.
- Day 31–90: Expand
  - Tasks: QBR prep, map success metrics, recommend Dedicated/Private options if predictable throughput needed.
  - KPI guardrails: 30-day retention > 60% for target segment; expansion activity (feature upsell or reserved capacity ask) reviewed by Sales.

QBR Metrics & Dashboard (standardized deck)
------------------------------------------
Include these sections in every QBR slide set for churn-risk customers and for accounts at renewal:
- Executive summary: status (Green/Amber/Red), ARR, product usage trends.
- Adoption metrics: DAU/WAU, avg tokens/day, top API routes used.
- Reliability metrics: uptime, error rate, p95 latency, incidents since last QBR.
- Cost & efficiency: cost per 1k tokens, unusual spend patterns.
- Quality: eval harness results on customer prompt set, customer-reported quality issues.
- Action plan: next 90-day objectives, owners, and measurable targets.

Retention Experiments & Hypotheses (R&D adjacent)
------------------------------------------------
We recommend small, measurable experiments to reduce early churn. Example hypotheses and experiment designs: 
- Hypothesis: A 15-minute onboarding call within the first 48 hours increases 30-day activation by 25%. Experiment: randomized control group on new signups for 8 weeks.
- Hypothesis: Automated onboarding nudges (sample code snippets tailored to detected SDK language) reduce time-to-first-success by 40%. Experiment: A/B test within trial bucket.

Postmortem & Continuous Improvement
----------------------------------
- After any Severity 1 event affecting an active customer, complete a 1-pager postmortem: timeline, root cause, fixes, preventative actions, and owner for each action. Attach to the Zendesk ticket and QA during the weekly CS Ops review.
- Quarterly: review activation thresholds by segment; update detection logic if false positive rate > 10% for a given signal.

Ownership and Review Cadence
---------------------------
- Playbook owner: Head of Customer Success (Priya Natarajan).
- Reviewers (operational): Support Lead (Lucas Chen), Applied ML (Maya Patel), Platform SRE (Elena Rodriguez).
- Review cadence: monthly for the first 6 months after rollout, then quarterly.

Appendix A — Known integration gotchas (quick references)
-------------------------------------------------------
- Region mismatch: customer keys scoped to eu-west but calls hitting us-east leading to silent failures. Check key region claim in token metadata.
- Unbounded streaming: customers who forget to set max_tokens or streaming chunk size can incur runaway spend; recommend SDK defaults in customer onboarding templates.
- Cache TTL pitfalls: setting prefix cache TTL too long may mask upstream model regressions; prefer short TTLs during active troubleshooting.

Appendix B — Links and runbook artifacts
----------------------------------------
- Shared dashboards: Grafana:LinkToActivationDashboards (internal)
- Runbooks: /confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/incident-triage-latency.json
- Ticket template: Support Ticket Template (Zendesk) link

Change log
----------
- 2024-10-03: Created by Priya Natarajan (initial draft).
- 2024-12-14: Added automated mitigation steps and Slack templates (reviewer: Lucas Chen).
- 2025-02-12: Updated thresholds for latency and error-rate; added QBR metric standardization (reviewer: Maya Patel).

title: Meadowgate Customer Intelligence — Account Health (Q3 2026)
content:
h1. Q3 2026 Account Health — Meadowgate Customer Intelligence (meadowgate-ci.com)

h2. Executive summary
Meadowgate Customer Intelligence is *re-engaging after a prolonged budget and hiring freeze* that paused the original doc-search + support-agent program. The initial POC (Nov–Dec 2025) was technically successful (latency/throughput within targets for mid-sized traffic) and the primary gaps remain *commercial timing* and *internal sponsorship continuity*. 

As of Q3 2026, Procurement has indicated that limited new vendor spend can be approved for *time-bound pilots* if tied to measurable support deflection and cost controls. We have a credible path to restart via a short “POC refresh” focused on *cost model validation (caching/batching)*, *data residency confirmation*, and *security evidence completeness*.

*Health (Q3):* Amber (improving)

h2. Account snapshot
|| Field || Current (Q3 2026) || Notes / history ||
| Company ID | mhci-00472 | From CRM record | 
| Segment | Mid-market (201–1000 employees) | Unchanged | 
| Region | North America | Unchanged | 
| Primary use cases | Doc-search; Support-agent; Summarization | Unchanged | 
| Products in scope | Dedicated; Private; Optimize | Unchanged | 
| Deployment requirement | VPC | Still a hard requirement | 
| Security requirements (baseline) | SSO (SAML); SOC 2; Audit logging; Data residency; KMS | Additional asks added in Q3 (see Security) | 
| Key stakeholders | Data org + Support Ops + Procurement | Champion gap is narrowing (see Stakeholders) | 
| Competitive set | Anthropic; OpenAI; Cohere | Still active, but discount pressure has softened | 

h2. What changed since the last documented status (Mar 2026)
*Budget / procurement*
- The earlier CFO guidance (“no new vendor commitments until Q3 2026”) has shifted to: *pilot-only approvals allowed*, with strict spend caps and clear ROI gates.
- Procurement’s prior near-term preference for a competitor discount remains a reference point, but the evaluation has reopened due to renewed focus on *support cost reduction* and *knowledge base quality*.

*Internal champion situation*
- Original internal champion (Head of AI) remains departed (left Jan 2026).
- A new interim sponsor has emerged in the Data org (Director-level) to restart evaluation contingent on pilot scope discipline and measurable outcomes.

*Technical stance*
- Technical fit remains positive based on the original 4-week POC (Nov–Dec 2025).
- Meadowgate requested an updated cost model and performance notes tailored to their current ticket volume and KB growth rate (their volumes have increased since late 2025).

h2. Current status and forecast
*CRM stage (operational view):* Re-engaged / Pilot Planning (internal)

*Best-case close window:* 2026-10
- This replaces the prior target of 2026-06, which was invalidated by the freeze.

*Commercial shape (unchanged range, higher scrutiny):* 100k–250k ARR
- Finance remains cost-sensitive and expects a 12-month model with explicit assumptions and savings levers.

h2. Recent activity (key events)
- 2026-08-01 — Re-engagement call: Procurement confirmed pilot exception process; requested updated security packet and a not-to-exceed pilot SOW.
- 2026-07-22 — Solution review with Data + Support Ops: aligned on doc-search + support-agent as Phase 1; agreed to include caching/batching cost test plan.
- 2026-02-12 — Final POC review call: engineering confirmed latency & throughput within targets for mid-sized traffic.
- 2026-01-28 — Security SIG: requested SOC2 attestation + KMS integration details.

h2. POC recap (Nov–Dec 2025) — what still matters
*Scope*
- Doc-search + Support-agent workflows with VPC deployment requirement.

*Performance result (reference)*
- Median latency: ~120ms for 512-token generation on Dedicated profile during test load.

*Key takeaway*
- Engineering was satisfied; the blocking issues were organizational (freeze + champion loss) and commercial (cost model scrutiny + competitor discount comparisons).

h2. Q3 2026 risks and blockers
*1) ROI / cost model skepticism (High)*
- Meadowgate’s finance team is highly sensitive to inference spend and expects clear savings mechanisms.
- Mitigation: deliver a short-form model with explicit assumptions + show caching/batching impact and “Optimize” levers in a controlled pilot.

*2) Champion durability (Medium)*
- New sponsor is interim and needs quick wins.
- Mitigation: anchor on Support Ops outcomes (deflection, handle time reduction) with weekly readouts.

*3) Security packet completeness (Medium)*
- Baseline requirements remain: SOC2, SAML SSO, audit logging, data residency, KMS.
- New Q3 asks: a) most recent penetration test attestation/executive summary, b) DPA template review, c) audit log example events aligned to their incident response workflow.
- Mitigation: provide updated evidence bundle and a one-page “data residency statement (US-only)” consistent with our deployment option.

h2. Security and compliance status (Q3 2026)
*Confirmed required controls*
- SOC 2: required
