title: QBR KPI inference-to-business-metrics mapping playbook
content:
summary:
How to translate Redwood inference telemetry and model signals into customer business KPIs for QBRs. Includes a repeatable mapping matrix, telemetry queries, slide checklist, and escalation points to keep QBR conversations actionable.

body:
Overview

This playbook describes a repeatable process for mapping low-level inference telemetry (latency, p50/p95/p99, token usage, model variant switches, error rates, and cost-per-1000-tokens) to customer-facing business KPIs (conversion, time-to-answer, cost per active user, SLA adherence). The goal is to produce concise, business-oriented QBR slides that clearly identify risks, opportunities, and recommended actions.

When to use

- Quarterly Business Reviews (QBRs) with product/ops stakeholders.
- Post-cutover stabilization reviews (weeks 1–6).
- Any time a model rollout or pricing change materially affects customer costs or latency.

Audience

- Customer success leads (owner)
- Customer engineering / integration contacts
- Internal product and platform stakeholders

Roles and responsibilities

1. Customer Success (CS) owner: assemble data, narrative, and slides; own action items.
2. Observability engineer: provide verified telemetry queries and raw data extracts.
3. Solutions engineer: validate mapping assumptions with customer integration details.
4. Finance/RevOps (if cost material): validate cost-per-unit computations.

Mapping matrix (example)

Use this matrix to convert telemetry signals into one-line business impacts. Replace values with customer-specific thresholds during prep.

| Inference telemetry signal | Typical threshold | Business KPI impacted | One-line interpretation for customer |
|---------------------------|-------------------|----------------------|------------------------------------|
| p95 latency (in ms) | > 1200 ms | Time-to-answer / conversion | Increased answer time — potential drop in conversions for interactive flows |
| Token churn per session | +20% vs baseline | Cost per active user | Higher token usage → higher monthly bill per seat |
| Model fallback rate (%) | > 3% | Feature availability / SLA | Frequent fallbacks to cheaper variant → degraded feature fidelity |
| Streaming disconnects per 10k sessions | > 5 | User experience (dropouts) | Session truncation risk; affects retention during long sessions |
| Error rate (5xx) | > 0.5% | SLA and incident risk | Elevated errors → SLA may be breached; remediation required |
| Embedding latency (p99) | > 300 ms | Search relevance and UX | Indexing/search slowdown → query throughput/latency regressions |

Step-by-step prep for the QBR (2-week cadence before meeting)

1. Week -2: CS owner requests telemetry dumps from observability team for the past 90 days and a delta window of last 14 days. Define baseline period (customer’s historical median).
2. Week -2: Solutions engineer confirms model variants and expected tokenization differences for known flows. Document any recent prompt or prompt-template changes.
3. Week -10 days: Observability engineer runs production queries (examples below) and validates sampling. Attach raw CSVs to the QBR folder.
4. Week -7 days: CS owner drafts 6-slide narrative: headline, current-state metrics (business KPI), top 3 technical signals, root cause hypotheses, proposed actions, and ask.
5. Week -4 days: Circulate draft to reviewers (product, finance, customer-eng).
6. Week -1 day: Finalize slides and run internal dry-run with internal stakeholders.

Queries and telemetry snippets (examples)

Note: adapt to your telemetry stack (Prometheus, ClickHouse, BigQuery, Datadog). Below are pseudocode/SQL patterns.

- P95 latency (per route):
  SELECT route, PERCENTILE(latency_ms, 95) as p95_latency, date
  FROM inference_latency
  WHERE tenant_id = 'T_<CUSTOMER_ID>' AND date >= DATE_SUB(current_date, INTERVAL 90 DAY)
  GROUP BY route, date

- Token churn per session (session-level token delta):
  SELECT session_id, SUM(output_tokens + input_tokens) as tokens, date
  FROM token_events
  WHERE tenant_id = 'T_<CUSTOMER_ID>'
  GROUP BY session_id, date

- Model fallback rate:
  SELECT date, SUM(fallbacks)/SUM(requests) as fallback_rate
  FROM request_events
  WHERE tenant_id = 'T_<CUSTOMER_ID>'
  GROUP BY date

Sample business narratives (write these as slide headlines)

- Headline (Good): "Stable inference latency; conversion unchanged; opportunities to reduce token churn by 12% via prompt templates."
- Headline (Risk): "p95 latency increased 45% in last 14 days — predicted 2–4% drop in trial-to-conversion for interactive chat flows."
- Headline (Cost): "Token churn up 30% after model upgrade: estimated $12k/mo incremental spend; recommended stop-gap: roll back or enable aggressive prefix caching."

Slide checklist for QBR

- One-line executive summary (impact + ask)
- Top-level business KPI(s) with trend lines (90d and 14d)
- Top 3 technical signals mapped to KPIs (with thresholds annotated)
- Root-cause hypotheses with confidence levels and data references
- Action plan with owners, ETA, and expected KPI delta (e.g., reduce p95 by 200 ms → recover 1.5% conversions)
- Financial impact estimate (if > $5k / month)
- Risk and rollback criteria for any recommended changes

Post-QBR follow-up and measurement

1. Create a triage ticket in CS board with: summary, telemetry links, owners, and success criteria.
2. Tag the ticket with labels: qbr-action, telemetry, cost-impact.
3. Observability engineer adds a synthetic test to the customer’s synthetic suite to verify the remediation.
4. Re-check the mapped KPIs at 7 and 30 days; report back as a short one-slide update.

Escalation thresholds (customer-facing)

- Immediate (page): p95 latency > 2x target and > 2 seconds for core interactive route.
- High (email & Slack CC): fallback rate > 10% sustained for 1 hour and impacting top route.
- Medium (ticket + weekly sync): token cost delta > 25% month-over-month and projected spend > $5k.

Operational tips and guardrails

- Use model variant tags in telemetry to attribute cost/quality to each variant.
- Normalize token cost calculations by customer-specific pricing tiers and reserved commit adjustments.
- Avoid attributing conversion regressions to model performance unless you can show temporal alignment and user cohort parity.

Appendix: sample mapping CSV (columns to include)

- timestamp, route, model_variant, requests, p50_latency_ms, p95_latency_ms, errors_5xx, tokens_in, tokens_out, fallbacks, synthetic_check_pass, notes

Related resources and links

- QBR template and operational checklist (link to internal page)
- Telemetry cost attribution connector guide (link to internal page)

Ownership and review cadence

- Document owner: Customer Success (Nina Park) — review quarterly.
- Observability owner: Eng Platform (Arjun Mehta) — provide telemetry within 10 business days of request.

Change log

- 2026-02-12 — Draft and initial internal review.
- 2026-04-01 — Added fallback rate thresholds and sample SQL patterns.
- 2026-05-10 — Finalized slide checklist and added escalation thresholds.

title: PLG Signal Handoff: Sales ↔ Customer Success (CS) Process
content:
## Purpose
This page defines how Redwood routes and follows up on PLG-to-sales signals without creating conflicting outreach or a poor customer experience. It clarifies:
- When Customer Success (CS) is notified vs. when Sales owns first outreach
- How to avoid duplicate touches (Sales vs. CS vs. Marketing) and manage suppression windows
- How to use PLG signal history in QBRs and expansion planning

This process applies to the NA pilot and is the default operating model unless overridden by a named account plan.

## Background / What is a “PLG Signal”?
A PLG Signal is a scored, deduped account-level event created from product telemetry and intent behavior (e.g., sustained spend velocity, repeated 429s, Dedicated/Private docs interest, security FAQ views, multi-workspace expansion). Qualified signals are routed into HubSpot as:
- Company properties (latest signal type, score, timestamps)
- Timeline note (signal context)
- A follow-up task (assigned to an owner based on routing rules)

Signals are designed to surface "sales-worthy" moments while minimizing noise and false positives.

## Guiding principles
1) **One throat to choke:** Every signal has a clear primary owner for first action.
2) **No surprise outreach:** If CS already has a relationship, we coordinate before Sales contacts (unless SLO/production risk requires immediate response).
3) **Customer experience > speed:** We prefer a slightly slower, coordinated touch over duplicated outreach.
4) **Context travels with the signal:** Signal notes must be useful in a QBR and in an opportunity.
5) **Privacy-aware:** We use account-level signals and aggregate metrics; we do not share raw end-user PII in HubSpot.

## Roles and responsibilities
**Sales (AE/SDR)**
- Owns follow-up for new self-serve accounts and net-new conversions triggered by signals
- Logs outcome fields in HubSpot for attribution
- Pulls in SE for technical evaluation triggers

**Customer Success (CSM/Enterprise CS)**
- Owns follow-up for existing paying customers where the signal indicates expansion, risk, or multi-team rollout
- Ensures outreach aligns with ongoing success plan and renewal timing
- Uses signal history in QBRs to propose Dedicated/Private/Optimize where relevant

**Solutions Engineering (SE)**
- Engages when signals indicate performance/SLO issues, Dedicated/Private intent, or regulated/compliance requirements

**Sales Ops / BizOps (HubSpot Admin)**
- Maintains routing rules, suppression logic, and HubSpot workflow configuration

**Marketing (Lifecycle/Nurture)**
- Coordinates nurture streams to avoid overlap with active Sales/CS motion; respects suppression and “active owner touch” windows

## Definitions
**Existing customer:** Company has an active paid contract or a named CSM assignment in HubSpot.

**Active touch window:** A period during which automated nurture or additional routed tasks should be suppressed to prevent spamming.

**Signal categories (high level):**
- Scale: sustained token volume, spend velocity, multi-workspace/team expansion
- Reliability: repeated 429s, latency regressions, error spikes
- Compliance/Security: security/SOC2 doc views, VPC/Private docs interest, retention/audit log interest

## Ownership & handoff rules (who acts first)
Ownership is determined by HubSpot routing plus CS guardrails.

### Default ownership decision table
| Condition | Primary owner | CS notified? | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Net-new self-serve company (no CSM, no open opp) | AE/SDR per routing | Optional (only if escalated / high score) | Sales-first motion; CS not required at first touch. |
| Existing paying customer with an assigned CSM | CSM | Yes (CS owns) | Sales should not outreach without CSM coordination. |
| Existing customer with open expansion opp already | AE + CSM jointly (AE owns opp) | Yes (CS + AE) | Use existing opp; do not create parallel opp. |
| Reliability signal that looks like production risk (e.g., repeated 429s + high throughput) | CSM if assigned; otherwise AE | Yes | Prefer “help-first” framing; may route to Support/SE quickly. |
| Compliance/Private intent (VPC/Private docs, security FAQ burst) | AE (or Enterprise AE) + SE | Yes (if customer has CSM) | If CSM exists, coordinate before outreach; if none, Sales/SE first. |
| Multi-workspace / org expansion (team invites, multiple projects) in existing account | CSM | Yes | Treat as expansion within success plan; align to rollout/QBR timing. |

### Hard guardrails
- **If a company has an assigned CSM in HubSpot, CS must be notified on any qualified PLG signal.**
- **Sales should not send an outbound email to an existing customer without a CSM heads-up** unless one of the "Immediate action" triggers applies (below).

### Immediate action triggers (allow Sales/SE outreach within 24 hours)
Sales/SE may act immediately (with same-day CSM notification) when:
- Signal indicates **sustained 429s / rate limiting** affecting production behavior and account is high usage
- Signal indicates **critical latency regression** (where available) and customer has time-sensitive launch
- Customer explicitly requested **Dedicated/Private/VPC** via contact form or direct reply (not just doc views)

## Notification rules (when CS gets notified)
CS notification happens via HubSpot and Slack (pilot) depending on the account type.

### HubSpot-based notification (source of truth)
CS is notified when:
1) **Company has a CSM owner** AND a new qualified signal is routed
2) **Company is tagged as “Customer”** (lifecycle stage) and signal score ≥ threshold
3) **Company has an active renewal window** (within 120 days) and signal indicates expansion potential

Minimum expected artifacts in HubSpot:
- Timeline note: “PLG Signal Routed: <type>” with plain-language summary
- Task assigned: to primary owner (CSM or AE)
- Properties updated: latest signal type, score, date, and suppression state

### Slack notification (pilot convenience)
For NA pilot only, a lightweight Slack ping may be used for high-impact signals:
- Existing customer + compliance/private intent
- Existing customer + repeated reliability signal in 7 days

Slack is not the system of record; the HubSpot task and note are required.

## Conflict avoidance: suppression and “single-thread” rules
Conflicting outreach is the most common failure mode for PLG signals. Use the following rules.

### Touch coordination rules
- If **a task is already open** for the company from a PLG signal, do not create a second task for the same signal category within the suppression window.
- If the company is in an **active evaluation/POC** (Dedicated/Private), avoid marketing nurture sends that conflict with Sales/SE motion.
- If Support has an **active Sev2+** or escalated ticket, do not run an “upgrade” outreach until the customer confirms stability (help-first stance).

### Recommended suppression windows (operational defaults)
| Scenario | Suppression window | Rationale |
|---|---:|---|
| Same signal type repeats (e.g., 429s again) | 7 days | Prevent spam; keep one active thread. |
| Different signal types but same theme (Scale + Reliability) | 5 days | Use one combined outreach. |
| Marketing nurture after Sales/CS outreach | 10 business days | Avoid double-touch; preserve reply channel. |
| False positive marked | 30 days (or until override) | Prevent re-triggering on vanity behavior. |

**Exceptions:** If a signal crosses a materially higher threshold (e.g., spend velocity doubles or reliability worsens), owners may override suppression with a note explaining why.

## The handoff workflow (step-by-step)
### A) When Sales owns first action (net-new / no CSM)
1. AE/SDR reviews the HubSpot task and the timeline note.
2. AE checks for:
   - Existing open deals or prior disqualification reason
   - Recent marketing touches (to avoid duplicating messaging)
   - Basic product usage context (volume, errors)
3. AE performs first touch per the playbook.
4. If the prospect responds with implementation/security questions, AE pulls in SE.
5. If the prospect converts to paid and gets a CSM assigned, Sales ensures signal notes remain visible for onboarding/QBR.
6. AE logs outcome fields (see “Outcome logging”).

### B) When CS owns first action (existing customer / has CSM)
1. CSM reviews the signal note and recent account plan.
2. CSM decides the intent classification:
   - Expansion opportunity (Dedicated/Private/Optimize)
   - Adoption coaching (multi-workspace growth)
   - Risk/Support escalation (reliability pain)
3. CSM posts a short internal note in HubSpot:
   - Proposed next step
   - Whether Sales/SE should be pulled in now vs. at QBR
4. If expansion is likely, CSM coordinates with AE (or requests assignment if none) before any customer-facing outreach about upgrades.
5. CSM performs the customer touch (or schedules it for a QBR) using “help-first” framing.

## What goes into the HubSpot timeline note (required format)
Signal notes should be readable by CS during a QBR and by Sales during a deal cycle.

Required fields (in plain language):
- Signal category and name (e.g., Reliability: Repeated 429s)
- Time window (e.g., last 7 days)
- Why it matters (customer impact + Redwood recommendation)
- Suggested next step (e.g., “Offer Dedicated throughput sizing call; loop in SE”)
- Suppression state (e.g., “Suppressed until 2025-06-17 unless threshold materially increases”)

Example note template:
"PLG Signal Routed — Reliability: Repeated 429s (7d). Account has sustained high request volume with rate-limit errors. Recommended: offer Dedicated sizing / capacity planning call; SE can help benchmark + propose autoscaling policy. Next step: owner to reach out within 2 business days."

## Outcome logging (for attribution and learning)
Owners must log outcomes so the team can tune thresholds and measure impact.

Minimum outcome fields to log (as HubSpot properties or task completion notes):
- First contact attempted (Y/N) + date
- Connected conversation (Y/N)
- Meeting booked (Y/N)
- Evaluation started (Y/N) (Dedicated/Private)
- Opportunity created (Y/N) + opp link/name
- Disposition if no: Not now / Already solved / Price / Wrong persona / False positive / Other

If the signal was a false positive:
- Mark “False positive” and add a one-line reason (e.g., “Student project; doc browsing only; no active usage”).

## Using signal history in QBRs and expansion planning
Signal history should be treated as a factual “behavior timeline” that complements the success plan.

### QBR preparation checklist (CSM)
1. Review last 90 days of PLG signals in HubSpot (timeline + signal properties).
2. Bucket signals into:
   - Growth drivers (team expansion, new workspaces)
   - Friction points (429s, errors, latency)
   - Enterprise readiness (security/compliance intent)
3. Map each bucket to:
   - Current deployment mode (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private)
   - Operational needs (SLOs, capacity planning, residency)
   - Enablement actions (best practices, batching/caching guidance)
4. Decide whether to propose:
   - Dedicated for predictable throughput / lower unit cost / isolation
   - Private for residency / compliance / customer-managed networking
   - Optimize as cost/perf initiative when usage is growing but budgets are constrained

### Recommended QBR slide inputs (optional)
- “Usage & reliability highlights” (top 1–2 signals, translated into customer outcomes)
- “What changed since last QBR” (new workspaces, growth rate)
- “Risks & mitigations” (e.g., 429s → capacity plan)
- “Expansion hypothesis” and “mutual action plan” (MAP) steps

## Communication templates (internal)
### Internal note from CSM to AE (existing customer expansion)
Subject: PLG signal suggests expansion path for <Company>
Message: “New PLG signal indicates <type>. This aligns with <success plan / upcoming launch / renewal timeline>. I recommend we position <Dedicated/Private> as <benefit>. I can lead first touch (relationship) and loop you in for pricing + next steps. SE involvement: <yes/no>.”

### Customer framing guidance (CS-led)
- Lead with help: “We noticed you may be hitting scaling limits; want to make sure you stay reliable.”
- Avoid: “We saw you looking at pricing/security docs” (do not cite intent browsing directly).
- If asked “How did you know?”: “We monitor aggregate service usage patterns to help customers scale and to route you to the right deployment options.”

## Escalations and exceptions
### When this process is not followed
If a customer complains about unwanted outreach:
1. CSM acknowledges and apologizes; confirm preferences.
2. Mark the signal as “False positive” or “Do not contact” as appropriate.
3. Notify Sales Ops (Isabelle Laurent) and BizOps/HubSpot Admin (David Kim) to adjust suppression/routing if needed.

### Exception handling
- Named strategic accounts may have account-plan-specific rules. Document exceptions in the account plan and reference it in HubSpot.

## Common pitfalls (and how to avoid them)
- **Pitfall:** Sales emails an existing customer the same day CS is working an adoption issue.
  - **Fix:** Always check CSM assignment and open tickets; coordinate first.

- **Pitfall:** Treating reliability pain as an upgrade hook.
  - **Fix:** Help-first stance; solve pain, then discuss Dedicated/Private as the structural solution.

- **Pitfall:** QBRs ignore signal history.
  - **Fix:** Add a standard “Signals since last QBR” section to prep.

## Owners, cadence, and change management
- Process owner: Jasmine Liu (CS)
- Routing/HubSpot workflow owner: David Kim (BizOps)
- Sales pilot owner: Stephanie Nguyen (VP Sales NA)
- Review cadence during pilot: weekly 30-min quality review with Sales/CS/Growth
- Change control: updates to suppression windows or ownership rules require Sales Ops + CS approval and must be documented in the routing ADR.

## FAQ
**Q: Should we tell customers we saw them viewing security docs?**
A: No. Use neutral wording: “We often see teams at your scale ask about …” and respond if they raise security needs.

**Q: Who owns if a company is both an existing customer and shows Private intent?**
A: CS leads first coordination and customer touch; Sales/SE supports the Private evaluation motion. Do not run parallel outreach.

**Q: What if the signal is clearly wrong?**
A: Mark false positive with reason, suppress for 30 days, and flag in the weekly review so thresholds can be tuned.

title: Automated QBRs and Tenant Synthetic Healthchecks Playbook
content:
summary:
Runbook and implementation guide for automating quarterly business reviews (QBRs) with tenant-level synthetic healthchecks and escalation triggers. Covers probe design, onboarding checklist, alert thresholds, automated report generation, and customer communication templates.

body:
Overview:
This playbook defines a production-ready approach to combine tenant-scoped synthetic healthchecks with automated QBR generation for enterprise customers. The goal is to surface service regressions early, quantify inference economics for customer stakeholders, and reduce manual effort for Customer Success (CS) and Support teams during QBR cadence or incident follow-ups.

Use cases:
- Ongoing tenant stability monitoring with SLA-aligned synthetic probes.
- Auto-generated QBR starter packs (latency/cost/quality metrics) for CS to curate.
- Early drift detection for model outputs and routing fallbacks.
- Customer-facing incident summaries synthesized from probe history.

Ownership and responsibilities:
- Customer Success: owns QBR cadence, stakeholder invites, and narrative.
- Observability/Platform: maintains probe templates, probe scheduling service, and data exports.
- Support: triages alerts that cross severity thresholds and coordinates remediation.

High-level architecture:
1) Probe engine (service: telemetry-probes) runs tenant-scoped synthetic requests at configured frequencies.
2) Telemetry ingestion stores probe results in metrics DB (prometheus long-term + clickhouse for traces).
3) QBR generator (service: qbr-orchestrator) pulls aggregated metrics, runs evaluation suites (sample prompts/evals), and renders a QBR bundle (PDF + CSV + slide deck).
4) CS UI integration surfaces the latest QBR bundle in the account dashboard and creates a draft calendar invite.

Design principles for probes:
- Lightweight and deterministic: synthetic payloads should be small and reproducible across runs.
- Representative workload: each probe should map to a customer workload archetype (e.g., short-chat, long-context-generation, embedding-query).
- Isolated side-effects: probes must use a read-only instrumented model version or a dedicated probe model variant to avoid affecting production KV caches and billing.
- Per-tenant scoping: include tenant_id, routing tag, and pinned model version in probe metadata.

Probe catalog (recommended minimal set):
- latency-short: 100ms target P95, frequency: 1m, description: 16-token prompt generation.
- latency-long: 500ms target P95, frequency: 5m, description: 2048-token continuation sampling.
- embedding-query: frequency: 10m, description: 512-dim embedding for a canonical phrase.
- correctness-check: frequency: 30m, description: run eval on 10 curated prompts, compute pass-rate.
- kvcache-hit-rate: frequency: 5m, description: run prefix queries to estimate cache warmness.

Configuration table (example):
| probe_name | frequency | target_slo | sample_payload | model_variant | probe_account_role |
| latency-short | 1m | P95 < 120 ms | {"prompt": "Hello"} | pinned-v1 | probe-only-key |
| correctness-check | 30m | pass_rate >= 95% | 10-prompts.json | eval-pinned | probe-only-key |

Onboarding checklist (step-by-step):
1. CS Owner creates the tenant probe profile in the Onboarding Hub with: tenant_id, contact list, pinned_model, preferred-region, business-hours window.
2. Platform provisions a probe-only API key scoped to tenant probe profile (TTL: 365d, rotation: automated quarterly).
3. Platform maps the tenant profile to the probe execution schedule and deploys probes into the tenant's routing group.
4. Run a 48-hour smoke window: validate probes produce results, check for false positives, and confirm cost estimate.
5. CS reviews the initial auto-QBR draft produced after 48 hours and adjusts which metrics are surfaced to stakeholders.
6. Mark onboarding complete once stabilization (no critical alerts) for 7 days is met.

Alerting and escalation matrix:
- Severity P0 (Immediate action): any probe indicating total unavailability for > 5 minutes across multiple model variants or region failover.
  - Trigger: probe engine stops receiving responses (HTTP 5xx or timeouts) across >=3 consecutive probes.
  - Notification: PagerDuty P0 to oncall SRE + CS lead + account executive.
  - Customer comms: immediate incident banner and dedicated Slack/phone bridge.

- Severity P1 (High): probe correctness-check pass_rate drops >= 10 percentage points below baseline OR P95 latency exceeds SLO for 30 minutes.
  - Trigger: rolling 30-minute window breach.
  - Notification: Support oncall, CS Owner, Platform engineer assigned.
  - Customer comms: templated email within 60 minutes and QBR note.

- Severity P2 (Medium): intermittent latency spikes or embedding variance above threshold affecting < 5% of probes.
  - Trigger: sporadic single-probe anomalies.
  - Notification: Support ticket auto-created, CS Owner notified next business day if unresolved.

Alert thresholds (recommended):
- Availability: <= 99.9% -> Severity P0 if outage confirmed.
- Latency: tenant P95 > configured_slo * 1.25 -> Severity P1 after 30m sustained.
- Correctness: pass_rate drop >= 10% absolute or sliding window drop >= 3% per 24h -> Severity P1.

Automated QBR generation templates and fields:
- QBR bundle includes: executive summary, availability & latency trends, inference economics, embedding stability, probed eval pass rates, incident timeline (last quarter), recommended actions, and appendix (raw CSVs, probe configs).
- Example CLI to generate a one-off bundle on demand:
  - curl -X POST "https://internal-api.redwood.local/qbr/generate" -H "Authorization: Bearer PROBE_KEY" -d '{"tenant_id":"acct-123", "range":"90d", "include_evals": true}'
- Output: a zip with files: qbr-summary.pdf, metrics.csv, top-alerts.json, slide-deck.pptx.

Customer communication templates (short):
- Incident banner (templates/incident-banner.md):
  - Title: Service Degradation – [Short description]
  - Body: We are investigating increased latency affecting some requests for your account. Our engineers are working on a fix. We will post updates on this page and via your designated Slack channel.

- Post-incident summary (templates/post-incident-summary.md):
  - Title: Incident summary: [date] – [short title]
  - Sections: timeline, root cause, customer impact, mitigation steps taken, follow-up actions with ETA and owners.

False positives and calibration guidance:
- Initial two-week period: set probe sensitivity to conservative (wider thresholds) to avoid alert fatigue.
- Keep a rolling baseline window of 28 days for latency and correctness baselines.
- Label probes as diagnostic vs. business-critical; only business-critical probes trigger P1/P0 paths.

QBR cadence and automation schedule:
- Weekly: automated micro-report (1-page) emailed to CS Owner with rolling 7-day highlights.
- Monthly: draft QBR bundle auto-created and placed in CS draft folder for review.
- Quarterly: finalized QBR generated 7 days prior to customer meeting and attached to the calendar invite.

Sample metrics to include in QBR (minimum):
- Tenant availability (90d), error rate (4xx/5xx), P50/P95/P99 latency by route, per-token cost trends, embedding cosine drift, eval pass rates (trend), top 5 incidents with MTTR.

Operational playbook for escalations (numbered runbook):
1. Triage: Support receives alert -> create ticket with tags: tenant_id, probe_name, severity, link to recent probe traces.
2. Initial Diagnosis (15 min): Support verifies probe metadata and reproduces using probe-only-key. If reproduced, escalate to Platform engineer.
3. Mitigation (30-90 min): If mitigation is available (fallback to alternate model variant, restart worker pool, clear KV cache for that tenant), perform action and document steps.
4. Customer Communication (within 60 min for P1/P0): CS drafts and sends templated update; update incident banner.
5. Postmortem: For any P1/P0, create a postmortem within 72 hours and include probe history snippets and QBR implications.

Instrumentation and data retention:
- Probe raw payloads: retained 14 days.
- Aggregated metrics & rollups: retained 540 days for QBR trend analysis.
- Eval sample outputs (for correctness-check): stored in encrypted blob store with tenant access controls, retained 90 days by default.

Privacy and compliance notes:
- Probes must avoid sending any customer-sensitive real data. Use synthetic canonical text or pseudonymized samples.
- For regulated tenants requiring Private deployment, probes must run inside the tenant's VPC or with on-prem probe runner.

FAQ (short):
Q: Will synthetic probes increase my bill?
A: Probes are billed at a minimal rate and can be scoped to a probe-only billing key. We include an estimated monthly cost in the onboarding smoke window.

Q: Can a probe cause false cache warming?
A: Probes use probe-only model variants when possible. If probes must exercise the same model path as production, include metadata so KV cache metrics can be filtered out of customer billing.

Related pages and templates:
- Onboarding Hub -> Probe Profiles (internal link: /confluence/xxxxx)
- templates/post-incident-summary.md (internal templates repo)
- qbr-orchestrator README (github: internal/qbr-orchestrator)

Appendix: Example probe JSON (for latency-short)
{
  "probe_name": "latency-short",

title: Service Degradation Credit Calculator and Approval Flow
content:
Overview
========

Purpose
-------
This playbook defines the operational calculator, approval workflow, and customer communication templates used when Redwood Inference determines an eligible service credit after a verified service degradation. It is intended for Customer Success (CS), Billing, SRE, and Legal to coordinate consistent, auditable credit actions for enterprise customers.

Scope
-----
- Applies to hosted and dedicated customers covered by an SLA or SLO agreement.
- Covers degradations affecting availability, tail latency SLO breaches, and sustained quality regressions that meet the credit policy thresholds in the customer contract.
- Does not cover discounts for product/feature requests, account disputes unrelated to service degradation, or third-party billed items.

Definitions
-----------
- Incident period: window of time for which SLO behavior is measured.
- Eligible degradation: measurable breach where verified telemetry and RCA show platform responsibility.
- Credit cap: maximum credit allowed per billing period, defined by contract (commonly 100% of monthly usage for the impacted service or the contract-specified cap).

When to use this calculator
---------------------------
1. Incident has a postmortem and owner-confirmed root cause assigning primary responsibility to Redwood.
2. Telemetry artifacts (traces, metrics, request logs) are available for the incident window.
3. Customer has requested compensation or CS/SRE recommends offering a credit based on SLA terms.

Credit calculation methodology
============================
Principles
- Calculation must be deterministic and reproducible from telemetry.
- Prefer simple, contract-aligned formulas over ad hoc amounts.
- Include throttling to enforce contract credit caps and avoid double-counting across related incidents.

Base formula (availability SLO example)
- Let SLO_target = contractual availability percentage (e.g., 99.9).
- Let Actual = measured availability during the incident window as a percentage.
- Degradation = max(0, SLO_target - Actual).
- RawCreditPercent = (Degradation / (100 - SLO_target)) * 100.
- AppliedCreditPercent = min(RawCreditPercent, ContractCreditCapPercent).

Example: 99.9 SLO, Actual 99.6 over billing month
- Degradation = 99.9 - 99.6 = 0.3
- RawCreditPercent = (0.3 / 0.1) * 100 = 300% -> capped to ContractCreditCapPercent (e.g., 100%)

Latency SLO (p99 example)
- Define SLO_target_p99 in ms (e.g., 150ms).
- Compute p99_actual for incident window.
- If p99_actual <= SLO_target_p99 -> no credit.
- If p99_actual > SLO_target_p99: LatencyDelta = p99_actual - SLO_target_p99.
- RawCreditPercent = clamp((LatencyDelta / SLO_target_p99) * LatencyWeight, 0, ContractCreditCapPercent)
- LatencyWeight is a policy constant (default 50) to avoid overcompensating short bursts.

Quality regressions (model outputs)
- Credits for quality regressions are only eligible when a regression is (a) caused by a platform rollout or model swap and (b) leads to measurable downstream failure (e.g., >X% increase in downstream error rates or customer-reported failure rate).
- Use a metric-based threshold with an evaluative audit (example: >15% increase in failed QA checks for a validated evaluation prompt set).

Composite incidents and aggregation
- Multiple adjacent incidents that share root cause within the same billing period should be aggregated and calculated once to avoid double-crediting. Aggregation window defaults to 72 hours.

Operational calculator (CLI example)
=================================
Use the builtin credit-calc tool (internal) to produce a reproducible proposal. Example invocation:

$ rwi credit-calc --customer-id=C12345 --start=2026-11-02T10:00:00Z --end=2026-11-02T18:00:00Z --slo-type=availability --slo-target=99.9 --contract-cap=100

Sample output (human readable):

{
  "customer_id": "C12345",
  "slo_type": "availability",
  "slo_target": "99.9",
  "actual": "99.63",
  "raw_credit_percent": "240",
  "applied_credit_percent": "100",
  "billing_month": "2026-11"
}

Approval workflow (concrete steps)
================================
1. Proposal generation (SRE/CS): run credit-calc and attach telemetry artifacts + incident postmortem.
2. CS initial review: verify customer contract terms, check for overlapping third-party exclusions, prepare draft customer communication. (Owner: CS Lead).
3. Finance validation: validate usage baseline, compute monetary amount from AppliedCreditPercent * billable_amount_for_impacted_products. (Owner: Billing Analyst).
4. Legal review (if > ContractLargeCreditThreshold or customer is flagged): confirm wording and check contractual implications. (Owner: Legal Counsel).
5. Executive approval: required when AppliedCreditPercent > ExecutiveApprovalThreshold (default 50%). (Owner: Head of Customer Success).
6. Final sign-off and scheduling: Billing issues credit memo; CS sends customer communication. Record in CRM ticket and update postmortem.

Approval matrix (quick reference)
--------------------------------
| AppliedCreditPercent | Finance OK? | Legal Needed? | Exec Approval? | Notes |
|----------------------|-------------|---------------|----------------|-------|
| <= 10%               | automatic   | no            | no             | Standard low-impact credit |
| >10% and <=50%       | required    | no            | no             | Manager sign-off in Finance |
| >50% and <=75%       | required    | yes (if flagged) | yes          | Escalate to Head CS + CFO |
| >75%                 | required    | yes           | yes            | Full Exec + Legal review |

Roles and responsibilities
==========================
- SRE (incident owner): produce telemetry, run credit-calc, and record the incident RCA link.
- CS (customer owner): craft customer-facing message and confirm customer billing details.
- Billing/Finance: compute monetary impact and apply credit memo to next invoice or issue refund per contract.
- Legal: advise on contract language and approval when necessary.
- Audit (internal ops): record all steps in the Credit Ledger (internal DB) for future QBR reconciliation.

Customer communication templates
===============================
Use the templates below as a starting point; tailor tone to customer relationship. Attach: incident summary, RCA link, and proposed credit amount or percentage.

Short notification (for small credits):

Subject: Service Update and Account Credit

Hi <CustomerName>,

Thank you for working with us during the incident on <date>. Our investigation shows that your service experienced reduced availability between <start> and <end>. Per your contract SLO (99.9% availability), you are eligible for a credit of <X%> against the impacted service for billing period <YYYY-MM>. We will apply this credit to your next invoice; no action is needed on your side.

We sincerely regret the disruption and have summarized fixes in the attached RCA. If you would like a walkthrough, we can schedule a 30-minute technical review.

Regards,
<Customer Success Rep>

Extended notification (for significant credits or enterprise customers):
- Include detailed timeline, customer-impact table, mitigation steps taken, and a proposed remediation plan (e.g., configuration changes, compensating controls).
- Offer an optional executive briefing and credits processed as either invoice credit or refund per customer preference.

Accounting and bookkeeping steps
===============================
1. Billing computes monetary amount: MonetaryCredit = AppliedCreditPercent * BillableAmountForImpactedService.
2. Create credit memo in ERP referencing incident ID and credit_calc output.
3. Update CRM contract notes and attach postmortem + credit memo ID.
4. Notify customer via CS with copy to billing@redwood.ai and update the billing ticket.

Audit table example (append to ledger)
------------------------------------
| incident_id | customer_id | billing_period | credit_percent | credit_amount | approver | memo_id | timestamp |
|-------------|-------------|----------------|----------------|---------------|----------|---------|-----------|
| INC-20261102-3 | C12345 | 2026-11 | 100% | $12,300 | S. Rodriguez | MEMO-8812 | 2026-11-10T14:22Z |

Operational safeguards and anti-abuse controls
============================================
- Credits must be tied to verified telemetry and an incident that names Redwood as primary root cause.
- CS cannot unilaterally issue monetary credits without following approval workflow above.
- Any credit that exceeds the customer's contractual cap must be escalated to Finance and Legal for exception handling.
- Keep a rolling 12-month credit summary per customer to detect potential abuse patterns (e.g., repeated large credits).

Monitoring and QBR integration
============================
- Aggregate credits by customer and include as a regular QBR line item: "Credits issued (6mo)".
- Use the credit ledger to identify customers with recurring degradations and propose long-term remedies (capacity reservations, Dedicated plan offers, or contractual SLO adjustments).

Appendix: sample credit-calc YAML config
======================================
# credit policy applied by the CLI tool
policy_version: v1
default_latency_weight: 50
aggregation_window_hours: 72
contract_large_credit_threshold_percent: 50
executive_approval_threshold_percent: 50

Appendix: quick checklist for CS before sending credit notice
============================================================
1. Confirm incident RCA link and that Redwood is primary owner.
2. Verify the billing entity and impacted products.
3. Obtain Finance memo_id or draft if immediate application requested.
4. Ensure Legal review if > contract_large_credit_threshold_percent or flagged.
5. Send notification and update CRM ticket and ledger.

Related documents and links
=========================
- QBR inference economics and availability playbook (linked)
- Multi-tenant SLO escalation and SLA credit playbook (linked)
- Incident postmortem template (internal link)

Document change log
==================
- 2025-09-18: Created by Maya Chen (initial draft).
- 2026-02-10: Added latency weighting and sample CLI invocation (reviewers: Arjun Patel).
- 2026-12-05: Updated approval matrix, added audit table and anti-abuse controls (reviewers: Lena Martinez, Diego Alvarez).

title: Kernel Priority Calibration Lab Notebook
content:
Summary
-------
This lab notebook documents a sequence of controlled experiments to calibrate kernel-level priorities and credit assignments in the Redwood serving runtime. The objective is to produce a repeatable mapping from request traffic characteristics to scheduler priority/weight settings that meet our latency SLOs while minimizing cost and token-level variance.

Purpose and scope
------------------
- Purpose: Establish a defensible, observable calibration process for kernel priority settings used by kernel-manager and scheduler-coordinator.
- Scope: Experiments span the dedicated GPU pool (gpool-rt-prod-sim), the local experiment cluster (lab-gpu-01..04), and the shadow-routing infrastructure used by the performance lab. This notebook does NOT change production configuration; it defines candidate settings for canary rollout.

Background and motivation
-------------------------
Over the last 18 months we've observed recurring p95 tail spikes for small interactive chat workloads when mixed with long-running batch generations. Investigation shows credit starvation and kernel handoff delays in the dispatcher + kernel pipeline. This calibration aims to:
1) Quantify how per-request weight, kernel quantum size, and preemption granularity affect latency distribution.
2) Generate recommended rule sets for the priority expression language used by kernel-manager.
3) Provide an audit trail and artifacts (traces, kernel-profiles, sample payloads) for sign-off prior to rollout.

Key concepts and definitions
---------------------------
- Kernel: GPU execution unit as exposed by kernel-agent (e.g., attn-kernel-v2).
- Priority weight: numeric weight applied by scheduler-coordinator when allocating slot quantum.
- Quantum: minimal GPU time-slice unit in microseconds (default 2000us in lab).
- Preemption point: safe boundary (KV cache alignment) where kernels can be interrupted.

Testbed and baseline configuration
----------------------------------
- Hardware: 4 x A100-80GB (lab-gpu-01..04), NVLink disabled for determinism in early runs.
- Software: runtime v3.14.2 (branch: experiment/kernel-calibration), kernel-agent v2.7.0, dispatch-service v1.22.
- Telemetry: traces via trace-proxy -> jaeger-lab, metrics to prometheus-lab, payload capture persisted to s3://redwood-lab-artifacts/kernel-calib/2026-04.
- Baseline SLOs used in lab: p50 < 30ms, p95 < 120ms for short-chat profile; throughput target 400 reqs/s for medium packing.

Experiment matrix (summary)
---------------------------
| Run | Priority profile | Quantum (us) | Preempt? | Workload mix | Note |
|-----|------------------|--------------:|:--------:|---------------|------|
| A   | default (1,1,1)  | 2000         | no       | 80% short /20% long | baseline
| B   | favor-short (3,1,0.5) | 2000  | yes      | 80% short /20% long | test preemptive handoff
| C   | weight-linear (2,1,1) | 1000   | yes      | 50/50 mixed        | smaller quantum
| D   | conservative (1,1,0.25) | 4000 | no      | 20% short /80% long | test long-run impact
| E   | dynamic-adaptive* (see rule) | 2000 | yes | synthetic burst traces | adaptive weight function

(See "Experiment logs" below for raw outputs and links to traces.)

Calibration procedure (step-by-step)
-----------------------------------
1. Prepare lab cluster: reboot lab-gpu nodes, disable NVLink, ensure kernel-agent v2.7.0 running.
2. Load baseline model: llama-compat-13b-int8 (tag: lab-2026-02) to isolate kernel behavior from model variance.
3. Deploy traffic generator (tg-runner) with recorded production short-chat and long-burst corpora. Command: 

   ./tg-runner --target lab-gateway:8443 --corpus corpora/short-chat.json --rps 320 --duration 900 --tag run-A

4. Apply priority profile via kernel-manager CLI (example):

   rwd-kernelctl set-profile --profile-name favor-short --rules "priority(expression='request.shape == \"short\" ? 3 : 1', preempt=true, quantum_us=2000)"

5. Collect telemetry: Ensure sampling via experiment-telemetry job. Key artifacts:
   - jaeger traces: trace-id prefix "calib-2026-04-A"
   - prometheus metrics: histogram rwd_kernel_latency_{quantile}
   - captured payloads: s3://redwood-lab-artifacts/kernel-calib/2026-04/run-A/

6. Run 1-hour trial, then a 6-hour steady-state for stability measurement.
7. Post-process: run analysis notebook /notebooks/kernel-calib-analysis.ipynb to compute p50/p95, fairness index, and variance.

Telemetry and measurement definitions
-----------------------------------
- Latency decomposition: request_total = frontend_queue + dispatch_delay + kernel_wait + kernel_exec + post_process. Each is traced and tagged.
- Fairness Index (FI): normalized Jain's index on per-cohort latency at p95 (goal >= 0.85).
- Kernel Utilization: GPU active seconds / wall-time (target 0.6-0.85 depending on workload).
- SLO thresholds: alert if burst p95 > 2x target or FI < 0.7.

Example priority rule table (recommended canonical format)
--------------------------------------------------------
| name | expression | weight | preempt | quantum_us | notes |
|------|------------|-------:|:-------:|-----------:|-------|
| favor-short | request.shape == "short" AND model.family == "llama-compat" | 3 | true | 2000 | Good for interactive agents
| default | true | 1 | true | 2000 | Fallback
| background-batch | request.type == "batch" | 0.5 | false | 4000 | Allow large runs but deprioritize

Sample kernel-manager JSON profile (apply via rwd-kernelctl)
-----------------------------------------------------------
{
  "profile_name": "favor-short",
  "rules": [
    {
      "id": "short-interactive",
      "expr": "request.shape == \"short\" and request.max_tokens < 512",
      "weight": 3.0,
      "preempt": true,
      "quantum_us": 2000
    },
    {
      "id": "batch-low",
      "expr": "request.type == \"batch\"",
      "weight": 0.5,
      "preempt": false,
      "quantum_us": 4000
    }
  ]
}

(When saving this document into kernel-manager, remember to redact any sensitive model keys.)

Experiment logs (high level)
---------------------------
- Run A (2026-04-20): baseline run, observed p95=138ms (exceeded target). Notes: dispatcher queueing prominent. Trace set: calib-2026-04-A.*
- Run B (2026-04-22): favor-short, preemption enabled, p95=86ms, FI=0.82. Short requests improved; tails reduced but long jobs saw increased runtime by 6%.
- Run C (2026-05-03): smaller quantum (1000us) reduced tail by 12% but increased kernel dispatch overhead (extra context switches). Kernel exec variance up 8%.
- Run D (2026-05-18): conservative quantum for long jobs reduced throughput by 14% with negligible improvements to short p95.
- Run E (2026-09-07): dynamic-adaptive rule using recent-ten-second-load reduced peak p95 by 20% in burst scenarios; needs further stability testing.

Decision rules and acceptance criteria
------------------------------------
Use the following rule to accept a candidate profile into canary:
1. Candidate must achieve p95 <= 1.1 * lab SLO for three independent 6-hour runs under synthetic production-mix.
2. FI >= 0.8 across cohorts for the same runs.
3. GPU utilization not below baseline by more than 10% (to avoid wasteful idle capacity).
4. No increase in observed model inference errors (model failure rate <= baseline + 0.1%).

Rollout checklist (pre-canary)
----------------------------
- [ ] Create canary plan: targeted to dedicated pool canary-nodes (2 nodes).
- [ ] Prepare automatic rollback policy in control-plane: revert-to-profile=default if p95 > threshold for 15m.
- [ ] Create dashboard: /dashboards/kernel-calibration-canary with alert rules (p95, FI, top-kernel-waits).
- [ ] Run security review for config file storage (CI secrets redaction).
- [ ] Schedule 48h passive monitoring window with oncall coverage.

Troubleshooting checklist
-------------------------
- If p95 regresses after profile apply:
  1) Re-run short deterministic microbenchmarks (script: tools/microbench/kernel_probe.sh).
  2) Collect full jaeger traces with full payload sampling for 30m.
  3) If kernel wait dominates >60% of tail, revert profile and open ticket on #sre-runtime.

Observed side-effects and mitigation notes
----------------------------------------
- Smaller quantum increases context-switch overhead. Mitigation: only use quantum <= 1000us for sub-100ms expected executions.
- Aggressive preemption can increase cache thrash for models with large KV caches; avoid preemption for models with >60M KV footprint.

Open experiments (next steps)
---------------------------
- Evaluate adaptive-weight learning that uses online p95 feedback loop with conservative damping.
- Test hardware-tiered profiles (fast-gpu vs econ-gpu) for cross-pool routing decisions.
- Validate interaction with quantization-profiles: int8 kernels show different preemption sensitivity.

Ownership and contacts
----------------------
- Document owner: Maya Chen (serving-runtime / kernel-experiments).
- Primary contacts: Arjun Kapoor (scheduler), Lena Ortiz (telemetry), Diego Morales (SRE).
- Escalation: oncall-runtime -> #oncall-runtime -> PagerDuty escalation as per runbook.

Artifacts and storage locations
-----------------------------
- Traces: jaeger-lab (query tag calib-2026-04-*)
- Metrics: prometheus-lab (job=rwd-runtime-lab)
- Artifacts: s3://redwood-lab-artifacts/kernel-calib/2026-04/
- Analysis notebooks: /notebooks/kernel-calib-analysis.ipynb (gitlab: infra/perf-lab)

Change log (notable entries)
---------------------------
- 2026-04-15 (Maya Chen): created notebook and executed Runs A-B.
- 2026-05-03 (Maya Chen): added Run C results and small-quantum guidance.
- 2026-09-07 (Maya Chen): added adaptive profile (Run E) summary and acceptance criteria.
- 2026-11-02 (Maya Chen): consolidated logs, added rollout checklist and decision rules for canary sign-off.

Appendix: useful commands and snippets
-------------------------------------
- Apply JSON profile: rwd-kernelctl apply --file favor-short.json --target lab-kman-01
- Query p95 from prometheus-lab (example):
  curl -s "http://prom-lab:9090/api/v1/query?query=histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(rwd_kernel_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le))" | jq

- Microbenchmark script: tools/microbench/kernel_probe.sh
  #!/bin/bash
  for i in $(seq 1 100); do 
    rwd-client --model llama-compat-13b-int8 --prompt "hello" --max-tokens 64 >/dev/null; 
  done

Related reading
--------------
- Scheduler observability contract and simulated injector (see related pages).
- Telemetry feedback & kernel autotune playbook.

Notes on document conventions
----------------------------
- This notebook is intentionally structured as a lab-first artifact: preserves time-stamped experiment runs, raw artifact locations, and decision rationale.
- When moving candidate profiles into production, create a dedicated ADR referencing this notebook and link to the canonical profile artifacts in /infra/configs/kernel-profiles/ with immutable tags.

End of notebook.

title: SLO Governance and Customer Ops QBR Playbook
content:
Purpose
-------
This playbook defines a repeatable SLO governance-centered QBR (Quarterly Business Review) and associated operational procedures for enterprise customers. It is intended to align Customer Success, SRE, and Account Engineering on what to measure, how to act on regressions, and the cadence for communication during onboarding and steady-state.

Scope and audience
------------------
- Scope: enterprise accounts using Redwood Hosted, Dedicated, or Private deployments that require SLO-driven operational reviews.
- Audience: Customer Success Managers (CSMs), SREs, Account Engineers, Solutions Architects, and Customer stakeholders (technical leads).

High-level principles
---------------------
1. Make QBRs evidence-driven: every recommendation must reference metric trends or incident artifacts.
2. Tie remediation to economic impact (latency/cost/error-rate).
3. Default to short, repeatable actions: small policy changes + measurement cycles.
4. Use the same SLO definitions and dashboards across Hosted/Dedicated/Private to avoid measurement drift.

SLO catalog (recommended defaults)
--------------------------------
| SLO name | Target | Measurement window | Alert threshold | Owner | Rationale |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| API p95 latency (generation) | < 350ms | 30d rolling | p95 > 450ms for 12h | eng-sre | User latency impacts product UX and token throughput |
| Request success rate (4xx/5xx) | >= 99.6% | 30d rolling | error rate < 99.0% for 6h | customer-success / eng-sre | Core availability for customer integrations |
| Token e2e cost per 1k tokens | <= baseline + 15% | 30d rolling | cost delta > +25% for 7d | customer-success/finance | Prevent billing shocks and ROI regressions |
| Embeddings recall on canonical dataset | >= 92% | 14d rolling | recall < 88% for 3d | applied-ml | Data quality regressions detected early |

Note: For Private deployments, measurement window may be locally configured — ensure telemetry export to centralized metrics when possible.

QBR cadence, agenda, and templates
----------------------------------
Cadence: Quarterly (standard), with accelerated QBRs triggered by:
- Repeated SLO breaches (three alerts in a 30d window)
- Post-migration or major model swap within 30 days
- Customer request following business-impacting event

Standard QBR agenda (60–90 minutes)
1) Welcome, participants, and outcomes (5 mins)
2) Health snapshot: SLOs and trend lines (10 mins)
3) Incident summary and root cause highlights since last QBR (10 mins)
4) Cost & utilization review (10 mins)
5) Model/feature changes and A/B results (10 mins)
6) Action items and owners (15 mins)
7) Open discussion / roadmap alignment (10–20 mins)

QBR slide checklist (deliverables to attach)
- Single-page SLO dashboard (p50/p95/p99, error rate, throughput)
- Top 3 incidents with timelines and mitigations
- Cost-per-1000 token trend with annotation of config changes
- SLA/SLO compliance table for the quarter
- Action item register with owner+ETA

Operational playbook: SLO breach -> action path
------------------------------------------------
1. Detection and Triage (0–30 minutes)
   - Auto-alert on relevant channel (PagerDuty or shared Slack #customer-{id}-alerts).
   - Triage lead (SRE on-call) acknowledges within 15 minutes.
   - Quick snapshot: deployment hash, model name, route, region, recent deploys.

2. Short-term mitigation (30–240 minutes)
   - If latency spike: shift traffic to a lower-latency model variant or region (policy: canary fallback).
   - If error-rate spike: enable degraded-response mode (reduce max_tokens, disable streaming) or rollback last deploy.
   - Document mitigations in incident ticket and notify CSM.

3. Root Cause Analysis and Remediation (24–72 hours)
   - Post-incident RCA meeting within 72 hours.
   - Assign engineering/ML owners for code/runtime/model changes.
   - For cost regressions: run per-route costing job and propose batching/quantization changes.

4. QBR escalation and follow-up (quarterly/triggered)
   - If regression persists across measurement windows, schedule an accelerated QBR and include product leadership.

First-90-days operational checklist (onboarding)
------------------------------------------------
- Day 0–7: Account setup, API keys, basic integration test, confirm telemetry ingestion to customer dashboards.
- Day 7–30: Baseline SLO measurement; identify high-frequency routes and token distributions.
- Day 30–60: Apply initial performance optimizations (batching, KV cache hints, model variant routing).
- Day 60–90: Run a QBR-lite with customer stakeholders: show baseline, changes, and next 90-day plan.

Ownership matrix
----------------
| Activity | Primary owner | Secondary owner | Escalation contact |
| On-call triage | eng-sre | account-engineering | Pager duty SRE lead |
| SLO reporting | eng-platform | customer-success | Head of Analytics |
| Cost review | finance | customer-success | Billing ops |
| Model performance | applied-ml | account-engineering | Model onboarding lead |

Required dashboards and reports
------------------------------
- Live SLO dashboard (Grafana): p50/p95/p99 latency, error-rate, throughput per route/model/region.
- Cost report (daily): cost per route and per 1k tokens (CSV export).
- Embeddings quality (weekly): recall/precision on canonical prompt set.
- Onboarding audit (one-time): integration checklist with timestamps.

Example queries and snippets
---------------------------
Prometheus example (p95 latency over 30d):
- query: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_bucket[30d])) by (le, route))

SQL example (cost per route):
- SELECT route, SUM(cost_usd) / (SUM(tokens) / 1000) AS cost_per_1k_tokens
  FROM billing.events
  WHERE account_id = 'ACCOUNT_ID' AND ts >= now() - interval '30 days'
  GROUP BY route;

Slack/PD routing conventions
---------------------------
- Channel naming: #cust-{account_short}-alerts, #cust-{account_short}-ops (for runbook comms).
- PagerDuty: use service per product tier; escalate to on-call SRE for Sev>=2.

Customer comms templates
------------------------
- Immediate notification (post-detection)
  Subject: [Action required] {Account} SLO breach - {metric} - {short summary}
  Body: one-paragraph summary + link to incident ticket + expected ETA for mitigation.

- QBR invite template: include SLO snapshot and pre-read (2 slides). Request 30 minutes pre-brief with CSM + SRE.

Change policy for QBR recommendations
------------------------------------
- All QBR recommendations must include: technical owner, expected impact (metric delta), risk classification (low/medium/high), rollout plan, and rollback plan.
- Low-risk changes (config tweaks) can be executed by Account Engineering after CSM approval.
- Medium/high risk changes require a documented canary and SRE sign-off.

Post-QBR follow-up and tracking
-------------------------------
- Action items auto-created in Jira with labels: qbr/{account}/{quarter}. Owners update status weekly.
- CSM sends a 10-day check-in email summarizing progress on action items.
- Persistent items roll into the next QBR with additional monitoring.

Appendix: Example action register (CSV-friendly)
------------------------------------------------
- columns: action_id, account_id, short_description, owner, due_date, status, notes
- sample row: QBR-2024-07-001, ACCOUNT_123, "Reduce p95 by 40ms with KV cache hinting", account-eng-jane, 2024-08-10, in-progress, "Canary rolling now"

Appendix: Common recovery patterns and estimated times
------------------------------------------------------
- Traffic reroute to fall-back model variant: 5–20 minutes (automation + validation).
- Rollback to previous deployment: 10–30 minutes (depends on stateful caches).
- Apply batching/kv-cache tuning: 1–3 days (measure then iterate).

Contacts and escalation roster
-----------------------------
- Customer Success lead: Asha Mehta (asha@redwood.ai)
- SRE on-call: see PagerDuty schedule (link)
- Account Engineering: ae-oncall@redwood.ai

Change log
----------
- 2024-05-10: Created playbook (Asha Mehta).
- 2024-11-14: Added cost-per-1k token guidance and SQL example (Liam Chen).
- 2025-02-03: Clarified QBR cadence and added accelerated-QBR triggers (Sofia Patel).

title: Escalation Paths & Contacts (2026) — Hosted, Dedicated, Private
content:
## Purpose
This page is the single source of truth for **who Support/CS should page, when, and how** for customer-impacting issues across **Hosted**, **Dedicated**, and **Private** tiers.

Goals:
- Reduce time-to-triage and time-to-mitigation by routing issues to the correct on-call quickly.
- Keep Support processes aligned with Engineering incident response (no ad-hoc bypassing).
- Standardize handoffs, coverage expectations, and backup contacts.

> For priority/severity definitions and escalation triggers, use: **Severity Matrix & Escalation Triggers**.

---

## How to use this directory (Support/CS)
1. **Classify the ticket** using the severity matrix (P0–P4 and Sev mapping).
2. **Confirm scope** (tier + region + model + symptom) and gather minimum diagnostics (see the Support Intake Checklist).
3. Choose the correct escalation path:
   - **Customer-specific** issue with unclear blast radius → escalate in **#support** with a short bridge if needed.
   - **Multi-customer / suspected platform issue** → move into **#incidents** per the bridge conventions.
4. **Page only the owning on-call** (SRE vs Platform vs Runtime) using the routing rules below.
5. If the issue meets Sev0/Sev1 criteria, start a **Slack bridge** immediately and link the SUP ticket.

Minimum context required for any page/bridge:
- SUP ticket link
- Customer tier (Hosted / Dedicated / Private / Enterprise)
- Region(s)
- Model + version (or “pinned version” policy, if relevant)
- Request IDs / trace IDs (at least 3 examples)
- Start time + whether ongoing
- Current impact statement (e.g., “~40% streaming disconnects in us-east; retries succeed ~60%”)
- Any recent changes known (customer-side deploy, SDK version, runtime release if mentioned)

---

## Coverage & expectations
### Support coverage (triage + comms)
- **Primary coverage:** Mon–Fri, 07:00–19:00 PT (business hours coverage across NA/EU).
- **After-hours:** For P0/P1 impacting Enterprise, Dedicated, or Private, Support will initiate a bridge and page the relevant on-call per the rules below.

### Engineering on-call coverage
- **SRE On-Call:** 24x7 for Sev0/Sev1 platform incidents; best-effort for lower severity.
- **Platform On-Call:** 24x5 with after-hours escalation for Sev0/Sev1 (pager enabled).
- **Serving Runtime / Gateway On-Call:** 24x5 with after-hours escalation for Sev0/Sev1 (pager enabled).
- **Private Deployments On-Call:** 24x5 with after-hours escalation for Sev0/Sev1 (pager enabled).

> If you are unsure whether paging is appropriate, ask in **#eng-oncall** with the minimum context above. Do not “broadcast page” multiple rotations.

---

## Primary routing by product area
Use the table below to determine who owns initial investigation.

| Symptom / Area | Examples | Primary on-call | Secondary / consult | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Hosted API availability / elevated 5xx** | /v1/chat 5xx, gateway errors, region degradation | **SRE On-Call** | Runtime/Gateway On-Call | If multi-customer or metrics show elevated error rate → treat as incident (Sev0/Sev1). |
| **Hosted latency regression** | p95 latency jump, slow streaming tokens | **SRE On-Call** | Runtime On-Call, Observability | SRE owns incident coordination; Runtime owns runtime-specific fixes. |
| **Streaming disconnects / truncated streams** | stream reset mid-generation, client sees EOF | **Runtime/Gateway On-Call** (if isolated) OR **SRE On-Call** (if multi-customer) | Platform (if auth/quota involved) | If >1 customer or region-wide signal, route to SRE and open incident bridge. |
| **Auth / SSO / Console login** | SAML loop, auth failures, console access issues | **Platform On-Call (Control Plane)** | SRE (if widespread outage) | If affects Console broadly across tenants, escalate to SRE after Platform confirms. |
| **Quota / rate limits / headers** | unexpected 429s, header mismatch, quota confusion | **Platform On-Call** | Runtime/Gateway (classification), SRE (if systemic) | Support should include example response headers + request IDs. |
| **Dedicated capacity / autoscaling / GPU pool stability** | autoscaling oscillation, burst not activating, latency spikes tied to scaling | **SRE On-Call (Capacity)** | Platform (control plane), Runtime (perf) | Dedicated customer impact is usually Sev1 if sustained and no workaround. |
| **Private deployment installer / upgrades** | migrations stuck, install failures, rollback guidance | **Private Deployments On-Call (Platform)** | SRE (if platform bug impacts multiple customers) | Collect diagnostics bundle/logs per the Private installer KB and avoid customer-sensitive data in Slack. |
| **Audit logs / compliance exports** | delivery lag, missing records, retention export delays | **Platform On-Call (Audit/Events)** | SRE (pipeline backlog), Security (policy) | Confirm expected delivery SLO and whether backlog is known. |
| **Billing / usage anomalies** | suspected double count, usage spike | **Support Ops** (triage) then **Platform (Billing hooks)** | SRE (if metering pipeline incident) | Keep customer comms factual; avoid claiming “billing bug” until confirmed. |

---

## PagerDuty / paging endpoints (internal)
Use these PD services (or the equivalent entry in PagerDuty). If any service name changes, file an internal request to update this page and the Support macro library.

- **SRE Platform Incidents:** `pd-redwood-sre-primary`  
  Backup/escalation: `pd-redwood-sre-secondary`
- **Platform (Control Plane: Auth/SSO/Console):** `pd-redwood-platform-control-plane`  
  Backup: `pd-redwood-platform-secondary`
- **Platform (Quota & Rate Limits):** `pd-redwood-platform-quotas`
- **Platform (Audit Logs / Events Pipeline):** `pd-redwood-platform-audit-events`
- **Serving Runtime / Gateway:** `pd-redwood-runtime-gateway`
- **Dedicated Capacity / Autoscaling:** `pd-redwood-sre-capacity`
- **Private Deployments (Installer/Upgrades):** `pd-redwood-private-deployments`

If PagerDuty is unavailable:
- Post in **#eng-oncall** with full context and tag **@sre-oncall**.
- If Sev0 and comms needed, move to **#incidents** and follow the bridge conventions.

---

## Slack channels & bridge rules (quick reference)
### Primary channels
- Support triage: `#support`
- CS coordination: `#customer-success`
- Engineering on-call coordination: `#eng-oncall`
- Incident coordination: `#incidents`
- Docs/KB coordination: `#docs`

### When to start a bridge
Start a bridge when ANY are true:
- P0/P1 (or Sev0/Sev1 equivalent)
- Multiple customers affected or likely platform-level issue
- High-risk enterprise account with escalating comms cadence needs
- You need live coordination across Support + Engineering

### Bridge naming standard
`#bridge-<yyyymmdd>-<customer-or-scope>-<symptom>-<region>`

Examples:
- `#bridge-20260214-acme-streaming-resets-us-east`
- `#bridge-20260208-eu-west-embeddings-timeouts`

### Required pins in the bridge
- SUP ticket link(s)
- Current impact + scope
- Owner on-call + timestamp of page
- Customer comms owner (Support/CS) and next update time

(See: Slack Bridge & Incident Channel Conventions)

---

## Escalation triggers: when to involve SRE vs Platform vs Runtime
### Involve SRE (incident ownership) when
- **Broad impact** is suspected (multiple customers, multiple tenants, or region-level signals).
- There is **availability or latency SLO risk** (e.g., sustained elevated 5xx, sharp p95/p99 increase).
- You need **capacity intervention** (Dedicated GPU pool instability, burst capacity not activating).
- You need coordinated **status page / incident comms** decisions.

### Involve Platform when
- The issue is about **control plane** or customer configuration enforcement:
  - Auth/SSO/Console access
  - Quota enforcement and rate-limit header correctness
  - Audit logs delivery and export pipelines
  - Org/project settings, keys, entitlements

### Involve Runtime/Gateway when
- The issue is likely in **request handling / streaming / tokenization / runtime release behavior**:
  - Streaming disconnects/truncation
  - Runtime version regressions
  - Model-serving behavior issues strongly correlated with runtime/gateway signals

### If ambiguous
- Start with the **closest owning team** and include SRE if any cross-customer impact is plausible.
- Do not ask multiple teams to investigate independently; request **one clear DRI**.

---

## Backup contacts (non-paging) and ownership boundaries
Use these contacts for clarification, handoff, and coverage gaps. Do not use as the first step for time-sensitive paging.

### Support/CS escalation SMEs
- **Owen Phillips** — Support incidents SME (bridge operations, incident hygiene)
- **Rachel Kim** — Enterprise CS lead (SLA alignment, enterprise comms expectations)
- **Jasmine Liu** — CS/Support exec sponsor (exec escalation DRI)

### Engineering sponsors (ownership clarification)
- **Sean Gallagher** — SRE partner (incident process, paging thresholds)
- **Rafael Mendes** — SRE (on-call/escalations owner)
- **Priya Natarajan** — Platform engineering sponsor (Control Plane, enterprise features)
- **Ethan Park** — Control plane + workflow integration lead (Jira/incident-bot workflow dependencies)
- **Mina Haddad** — Tier-aware routing/escalation input (fallback behavior, customer expectations)

### Observability / dashboards
- **Allison Grant** — Observability + SLO dashboard advisor

### Automation / tooling
- **Benji Okafor** — Platform automation implementer (Slack workflows)
- **Dylan Brooks** — Jira automation owner (SLA timers/required fields)

---

## Handoff rules (Support ↔ Engineering)
### Support → Engineering handoff (required)
Before handing off an active escalation, Support must provide:
- A single-sentence **impact statement** (who, what, where, since when)
- **Scope** (customers count if known, tiers, regions, models)
- **Evidence** (request IDs, sample errors, dashboards if available)
- **What has been tried** (customer-side retries, timeouts, SDK downgrade, workaround steps)
- **Customer comms plan** (next update time; whether status page is being considered)

### Engineering → Support handoff (required)
Engineering must provide:
- Current **DRI** and plan (investigating / mitigating / monitoring)
- A customer-safe **mitigation statement** (what changed, expected timeline, what customers should do)
- Any **temporary workaround** and the criteria for when it’s safe to stop using it
- Whether a **status page** update is recommended (and who will author/approve)

### “Waiting on Customer” state
If additional customer data is needed:
- Put the SUP ticket into “Waiting on Customer” only after sending a clear ask.
- The SLA clock behavior must remain consistent with the SLA policy (do not use “Waiting on Customer” to hide active outages).
- If the incident is platform-wide, continue incident handling regardless of a single customer’s response.

---

## Escalation path by tier (summary)
### Hosted (Self-serve + standard)
- Route by symptom (Runtime/Gateway vs Platform).
- Involve SRE when multi-customer impact is suspected.

### Dedicated
- Default to **SRE Capacity** for scaling/capacity symptoms.
- Platform consulted for control-plane or policy configuration issues.

### Private (VPC / on-prem)
- Default to **Private Deployments On-Call**.
- Escalate to SRE only when there is evidence of a shared service bug or multi-customer pattern.

---

## Change management for this page
- Owner: **Dev Patel (Support Ops)**
- Review cadence: monthly, and after any major on-call rotation changes.
- To request updates (contacts, PD services, ownership boundaries):
  1) Comment on this page with the change request and rationale
  2) File internal helpdesk ticket if tooling changes are required (PagerDuty, Slack workflows, Jira automations)

Last review cycle: 2026-02 (Escalation Playbook Refresh / Known-Issues Sprint)

---

## Appendix: quick “who do I page?” decision tree
1) Is it clearly **control plane** (SSO/auth/quota/audit logs/console)? → **Platform On-Call**
2) Is it **capacity/autoscaling** for Dedicated? → **SRE Capacity**
3) Is it **streaming/runtime behavior** and isolated to a single customer? → **Runtime/Gateway On-Call**
4) Is it **multi-customer** or you can’t rule out a platform incident? → **SRE On-Call** + start bridge
5) Is it **Private installer/upgrade**? → **Private Deployments On-Call**

If still unsure: post in **#eng-oncall** with minimum context and request a DRI assignment.

title: Urgent Escalation Handoff and SLA Triage Playbook
content:
Overview

Purpose: This playbook defines the operational steps, artifact requirements, and communication templates for urgent escalations affecting enterprise customers (Hosted, Dedicated, Private). It standardizes handoff from Support -> Customer Success -> Engineering/SRE/On‑Prem teams and ensures SLA alignment, rapid mitigation, and consistent post‑mortem follow-through.

Scope: Applies to incidents triggered by customer-facing outages, severe quality regressions, billing anomalies tied to inference, or security-sensitive events that impact an enterprise account. Not intended for routine tickets or feature requests.

Audience: Support L2/L3, Customer Success Managers (CSM), Solutions Engineers (SE), SRE/Runtime Engineers, Dedicated/Private deployment owners.

Problem statement: Enterprise customers expect predictable SLAs and clear escalation paths. During multiteam incidents we observe delays due to missing telemetry, unclear ownership for Dedicated/Private handoffs, and inconsistent customer comms. This playbook remedies those gaps.

---

Severity definitions and SLA targets

1) Severity taxonomy (enterprise standard)
   - Sev1 (Critical): Complete or near-complete service unavailability for production traffic (e.g., 100% request failures, model serve crash, data exfiltration).
   - Sev2 (High): Severe degradation impacting a large subset of traffic or major feature (e.g., P95 latency > 5x SLO, repeat hallucination producing sensitive output).
   - Sev3 (Medium): Partial loss of functionality or reduced performance affecting a minority of users; workaround exists.
   - Sev4 (Low): Minor issues, documentation questions, enhancement requests.

2) SLA targets (enterprise response/acknowledge + mitigation expectations)
   - Sev1: Acknowledge within 15 minutes. Initial mitigation plan within 60 minutes. Customer update every 30 minutes until mitigation. Target full resolution or acceptable workaround in 6 hours (unless constrained by on‑prem factors).
   - Sev2: Acknowledge within 60 minutes. Plan within 4 business hours. Updates every 2–4 hours. Target resolution in 2 business days.
   - Sev3: Acknowledge within 1 business day. Resolution in the next scheduled release or 10 business days depending on root cause.
   - Sev4: Acknowledge in 3 business days. Standard backlog handling.

Note: SLA windows for Dedicated/Private include an additional coordination layer (customer network access/maintenance windows) — see Handoff constraints.

---

Initial triage checklist (Support L2) — required within first 15 minutes for Sev1 or 60 minutes for Sev2

1) Collect required artifacts (attach to ticket and PagerDuty incident):
   - Customer account ID and Org name.
   - Endpoint / route / deployment ID.
   - Model name + pinned version + quantization profile.
   - Timestamped example request and response (redact PII if present).
   - Correlation ID / request_id(s) and approximate client-side timestamps.
   - Error messages, stack traces, HTTP status codes, and any gateway logs.
   - Last successful invocation timestamp and recent deployment/rollout history.
   - Telemetry: P95/P99 latency, error rate, tokens per request, GPU utilization, queue depth for the affected pool, KV-cache hit rate.
   - Billing anomaly snapshot if cost-related (token counts, cost per token, sudden spike windows).

2) Quick checks (yes/no, mark in ticket):
   - Has customer performed any recent config changes, model pin/rollback, or prompt changes?
   - Is the problem reproducible from a Redwood test account? (If yes, include test case.)
   - Are all upstream dependencies healthy (KMS, networking, storage)?

3) Escalate to CSM and SE immediately for enterprise accounts. If Sev1, trigger PagerDuty on the on-call SRE and schedule an ad‑hoc war room Slack channel using the naming convention: #incident-<org>-<YYYYMMDD>-sevx

---

Handoff rules: Support -> Customer Success -> Engineering/SRE/Private Deployment Owners

Required before handing to engineering (pre-handoff gate):
   - Ticket contains the artifact checklist above. Tickets missing artifacts should be blocked and returned to Support for completion.
   - Customer impact statement: exact percentage of traffic affected and business impact (e.g., checkout failures, revenue impact).
   - Existing mitigations attempted (rolling restart, retry config changes, temporary routing).

Handoff steps (numbered):
   1. Support creates or updates the PagerDuty incident and attaches the artifact checklist.
   2. Support posts the initial summary to the incident Slack channel using the template below and @mentions on‑call SRE and the SE.
   3. CSM joins and validates customer impact and expectations (maintenance windows, acceptable rollback).
   4. SE/Engineer reviews artifacts within SLA windows and responds with assigned owner, triage hypothesis, and next steps.
   5. If Dedicated/Private deployment is involved, contact the dedicated deployment owner and confirm remote access, scheduled maintenance windows, and KMS/HSM availability.

Access & permissions check (for Private/Dedicated):
   - Confirm support SSH bastion or SSM access exists to the customer appliance or private control plane.
   - Confirm service account roles and KMS key access are present for debug actions.
   - Confirm network ACLs allow control-plane callbacks or metrics scraping.

---

Mitigation patterns and temporary fixes (SRE/Runtime):

Common quick mitigations (ordered by risk):
   - Route traffic to a fallback model variant with compatible API surface (example: model-v2 -> model-v1-fallback).
   - Increase autoscale pool size for Dedicated temporarily (documented approval required for > 2x baseline).
   - Apply rate limiting at the customer route to protect shared capacity while retaining critical flows.
   - Disable affected feature flags or re-enable previous rollout hold.
   - Perform targeted rollback to last-known-good model version or quantization profile.

Commands and steps (examples)
   - Check running pods: kubectl -n inference get pods -l deployment=<deployment-id> --context=<cluster>
   - Restart gateway: systemctl restart redwood-gateway or restart deployment via orchestration console
   - Roll back model: redact CLI example to ensure correct cadence: rwctl deploy rollback --deployment <id> --to-version <sha>

Safety notes: Always capture hashes and export model artifacts before any destructive change. For Private deployments, coordinate snapshot creation with the customer's ops lead.

---

Communication templates (copy-and-send)

Slack initial incident post (paste into #incident-...):

"<INCIDENT SUMMARY>
Severity: <Sev1|Sev2>
Customer: <Org name> (Account ID: <id>)
