Impact: <short statement e.g., 80% of production calls failing; checkout flow blocked>
First seen: <ISO timestamp>
Affected endpoints: <route ids>
Artifacts attached: example request/response, logs, metrics snapshot, deployment history
Assigned: @oncall-sre @se-owner @csm-<org>
Next step: <hypothesis or action>"

Email update subject line (to customer):
   [ACTION REQUIRED] Incident <INCIDENT-ID> — <Short impact> — Redwood Inference status and next steps

Email body (initial):
   Short summary, what we know, what we're doing, expected next update cadence, and a single POC contact (CSM). Attach the incident link and support ticket.

Customer update cadence examples:
   - Sev1: 30-minute cadence until mitigated.
   - Sev2: 2–4 hour cadence until stabilised.

---

PagerDuty and on-call routing guidance

Suggested policy:
   - PagerDuty escalation: Support L2 -> SRE on-call -> Runtime engineer -> Platform lead.
   - For Dedicated/Private critical incidents, add the Dedicated Deployment on-call rotation as an escalation step.
   - If incident remains unresolved after 3 hours with customer impact, escalation to Director-level (CS and Engineering Directors) required.

On-call runbook excerpt (short):
   - Step 0: Acknowledge incident.
   - Step 1: Verify artifacts present.
   - Step 2: Assign pairing engineer and open console/war room.
   - Step 3: Identify whether mitigation is routing/scale/rollback.
   - Step 4: Execute mitigation with a single operator performing change and another observing / capturing logs.

---

Dedicated & Private deployment-specific considerations

Constraints often encountered:
   - Customer network maintenance windows prevent immediate access.
   - KMS/HSM approval gating prevents key rotation or model loads.
   - On‑prem hardware nodes may require physical intervention or vendor escalation.

Handoff checklist additions for Private/Dedicated:
   - Network topology diagram and bastion credentials (or ticket to request access).
   - Onsite maintenance window preferences and escalation phone numbers.
   - Location of on‑prem runbooks and vendor SLAs.
   - Customer technical contact and on‑call schedule.

Recommended temporary fallback prioritization: Hosted fallbacks first (if allowed by contract), then Dedicated pool scaling, then Private local mitigations.

---

Required telemetry & dashboards (for incident and postmortem)

Minimum charts to capture at the start of incident:
   - P95 and P99 request latency for affected route and global.
   - Error rate (5-minute and 1-hour windows) and error breakdown by HTTP status / internal error class.
   - GPU utilization per node, queue depth, and model KV cache hit rate.
   - Token throughput (tokens/sec), average tokens per invocation.
   - Autoscaler actions (recent scale events) and pod restart counts.
   - Billing token spikes correlated to timestamps.

Retention: snapshot of 72 hours around incident saved to incident artifacts storage.

---

Post-incident process & QBR inclusion

1) Immediate post-incident (within 24 hours):
   - Incident timeline and responsible owners posted to ticket.
   - Customer-facing summary drafted by CSM and approved by engineering for accuracy.
   - Short-term mitigations documented and follow-up tickets created for permanent fixes.

2) Root cause analysis (within 5 business days):
   - Full timeline, contributing factors, and a 3-point corrective action plan (short, medium, long term).
   - Identify whether regression was caused by model change, infra, config, or customer behavior.
   - Assign owners and target dates for remediation.

3) QBR / Health Check inclusion (next scheduled QBR):
   - Include incident summary, customer impact metrics, remediation status, and CSAT follow-up.
   - Present changes to SLOs or operational controls if required (e.g., new routing policies, additional observability).

4) Severity reclassification and SLA reconciliation:
   - Confirm final severity (may be downgraded after RCA).
   - Reconcile any SLA credits or contractual obligations with Finance and Legal.

---

RACI cheat sheet (flat table)

| Activity | Support L2 | CSM | SE/Dev | SRE/Runtime | Dedicated/Private Owner | Director/Leadership |
|---------|-----------:|-----:|-------:|-----------:|------------------------:|-------------------:|
| Initial triage and artifact collection | R | A | C | C | C | I |
| PagerDuty incident creation | R | I | C | A | C | I |
| Customer communications | C | R | I | I | I | I |
| Temporary mitigation (rollback/route) | I | I | C | A | R | I |
| Postmortem and RCA | I | R | C | A | C | I |

Legend: R = Responsible, A = Accountable, C = Consulted, I = Informed

---

Checklist for handoff artifacts (consolidated)

- [ ] Customer account ID & contact list
- [ ] Sample request/response with correlation IDs
- [ ] Exact error messages and deployment change history
- [ ] Live metrics snapshot (P95/P99 latency, error rate)
- [ ] Billing/cost spike evidence (if applicable)
- [ ] Access checklist for Dedicated/Private (bastion, KMS access)
- [ ] Customer impact statement and allowable mitigation window

---

Training & run frequency

- Run an enterprise escalation tabletop at least quarterly with SRE, Support, and CSM teams.
- Maintain a living incident playbook with retrospective updates post each Sev1/Sev2.
- Update dedicated/private access lists quarterly or after every major customer onboarding.

---

Appendix: Useful snippets and links

- PagerDuty runbook: /confluence/eng-sre/oncall/pagerduty-escalation-policy
- Incident template (Jira): /confluence/eng-platform/templates/incident-template
- Dedicated deployment owner roster: internal roster (CSM shared drive)
- Example rollback command (CLI): rwctl deploy rollback --deployment <id> --to-version <sha>

If you are missing any required artifact, do not proceed with engineering handoff — return the ticket to Support L2 with the missing fields explicitly listed.

Contact matrix for urgent escalation (primary):
   - Support lead on-call: @support-oncall (PagerDuty)
   - SRE on-call: @sre-oncall (PagerDuty)
   - CSM for enterprise accounts: see account roster (CS shared drive)
   - SE owner: per-customer mapping in account record

End of playbook.

title: Customer Comms Templates (Support + CS)
content:
## Purpose
Use these templates for consistent, customer-safe communication during escalations across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private tiers. These templates are designed for:
- Initial acknowledgement
- Mitigation / investigation updates
- Workaround guidance (known issues)
- Resolution + follow-up (including next steps and optional RCA workflow)

These templates are written to reduce back-and-forth, align to Support SLAs, and avoid overpromising.

## Tone + content guidance (read before using)
**Be clear, calm, and specific.** Customers mostly want: confirmation we see the issue, what they should do now, what we’re doing, and when they’ll hear from us next.

### Do
- Acknowledge impact in the customer’s terms (errors, timeouts, latency, blocked workflow).
- Ask for the minimum viable diagnostics: request IDs, timestamps, region, model, SDK version, and whether streaming/non-streaming.
- Provide a concrete next update time (“Next update by 14:30 PT”).
- If a workaround exists, provide it as copy/paste steps and clearly label it as **temporary**.
- Use “We believe / We’re investigating / Our current hypothesis” when not confirmed.
- If relevant, state what is safe to share (e.g., “No action needed” vs “Please retry with…”).

### Don’t (what not to promise)
- **Do not promise ETAs** unless SRE/Eng has provided an externally shareable estimate and you have confirmed it is appropriate for the customer tier.
- Do not speculate on root cause (“kernel bug”, “bad deploy”, “GPU failures”) unless confirmed and approved for external sharing.
- Do not imply contractual outcomes (credits, SLA breach confirmation) in-line. Route to the credits process and exec escalation protocol when needed.
- Do not ask for sensitive data (full prompts, customer datasets, secrets). Prefer request IDs and sanitized logs. If logs are needed: provide explicit redaction instructions and use approved secure channels.
- Do not imply that pinned model versions or routing policies are “guaranteed” in all failure modes—use the documented policy language.

### Consistency rules
- **Use the same severity language across channels.** If you use P0/P1 internally, translate externally to “high impact / degraded / intermittent” unless the customer already uses P-levels.
- **Status page vs email:** Follow the Status Page + Comms Alignment doc for when something qualifies as a status event.
- **Update cadence:** Follow the customer’s tier SLA table. If you’re unsure, default to the stricter cadence for the tier and confirm with Support lead/on-call.

---

## Variables (replace placeholders)
Use these placeholders to keep comms consistent:
- {customer_name}
- {account_tier} (self_serve | dedicated | private | enterprise)
- {case_id} (SUP-####)
- {region} (us-east, eu-west, etc.)
- {model} (e.g., redwood/llama-3-70b-instruct)
- {endpoint} (/v1/chat/completions, /v1/embeddings, streaming)
- {time_window} (e.g., “since 09:10–09:35 PT”)
- {request_ids} (a few representative IDs)
- {current_status} (investigating | identified | monitoring | mitigated | resolved)
- {next_update_time}
- {workaround_steps}
- {kb_link} (internal-to-customer-safe link)
- {mitigation_applied} (what we changed, in customer-safe language)
- {customer_actions}
- {support_signature} (name, role, timezone)

---

## Template 1 — Initial acknowledgement (incident / high impact)
**Channel:** Email (primary), optional ticket comment in customer portal

**Subject options (pick one):**
- Update: We’re investigating {symptom} impacting {endpoint} in {region}
- Acknowledged: {symptom} — {region} — Next update by {next_update_time}

**Body:**
Hi {customer_name},

Thanks for flagging this. We’re seeing and actively investigating **{symptom}** affecting **{endpoint}** in **{region}** {time_window}.

**What we know so far**
- Impact: {impact_summary} (e.g., increased timeouts / stream disconnects / elevated 5xx)
- Scope: {scope_summary} (e.g., intermittent; specific model; subset of requests)

**What we need from you (if available)**
If you can share any of the below, it will help us pinpoint the issue quickly:
- 3–5 request IDs: {request_ids}
- Approx. timestamps + timezone: {time_window}
- SDK + version (or raw HTTP): {sdk_version}
- Whether retries are enabled (and retry policy): {retry_details}

**What you can do now**
{customer_actions}

We’ll send the next update **by {next_update_time}** (or sooner if we identify a mitigation).

Regards,
{support_signature}

**Notes for Support (internal):**
- Link SUP ticket to the Slack bridge if created.
- If threshold meets escalation triggers, page the appropriate on-call per escalation paths doc.

---

## Template 2 — Initial acknowledgement (non-incident / investigation)
**Channel:** Email + ticket comment

**Subject:** Re: {symptom} on {endpoint} ({region}) — investigating

Hi {customer_name},

Acknowledged—thank you for the details. We’re investigating **{symptom}** for **{endpoint}** in **{region}**.

To help us narrow this down, could you confirm:
1) {model} and any model version pinning (if applicable)
2) Your approximate request rate (RPS) and whether requests are batched
3) 2–3 request IDs from the last hour: {request_ids}

We’ll follow up with an update by **{next_update_time}**.

Regards,
{support_signature}

---

## Template 3 — Mitigation / investigation update (no workaround yet)
**Channel:** Email; use for recurring cadence

**Subject options:**
- Update {#}: {symptom} on {endpoint} ({region}) — {current_status}
- Update: Continuing investigation — next update by {next_update_time}

Hi {customer_name},

Update on **{symptom}** impacting **{endpoint}** in **{region}**.

**Current status:** {current_status}

**What we’ve done since the last update**
- {action_1} (customer-safe wording)
- {action_2}

**What we’re seeing now**
- Impact level: {impact_level_now} (improving / stable degradation / worsening)
- Scope: {scope_now}

**Next steps**
- {next_step_1}
- {next_step_2}

Next update **by {next_update_time}**.

Regards,
{support_signature}

---

## Template 4 — Mitigation update (mitigation applied / monitoring)
**Channel:** Email

**Subject:** Update: Mitigation applied for {symptom} in {region} — monitoring

Hi {customer_name},

We’ve applied a mitigation for **{symptom}** affecting **{endpoint}** in **{region}**.

**What changed (customer-safe):**
- {mitigation_applied}

**What you should see:**
- {expected_outcome} (e.g., reduced timeout rate; fewer stream resets)

**What we’re monitoring:**
- {monitoring_summary}

**If you’re still seeing issues:**
Please reply with 2–3 recent request IDs and timestamps after {mitigation_time}.

Next update **by {next_update_time}** (or sooner if we confirm full resolution).

Regards,
{support_signature}

---

## Template 5 — Workaround guidance (Known Issue / temporary mitigation)
**Channel:** Email; link to KB article when customer-safe

**Subject options:**
- Suggested workaround: {symptom} on {endpoint} ({region})
- Temporary mitigation available: {symptom} — steps inside

Hi {customer_name},

Based on your symptoms and the request IDs shared, this aligns with a known issue we’re tracking: **{known_issue_name}**.

**Impact**
- {impact_summary}

**Recommended workaround (temporary)**
Please try the following:
{workaround_steps}

**What to expect**
- {expected_behavior}

**Reference**
- {kb_link}

**When to escalate back to us immediately**
Reply and reference {case_id} if:
- {escalation_condition_1} (e.g., error rate remains >X% after workaround)
- {escalation_condition_2} (e.g., streaming still disconnects within <N seconds)
- {escalation_condition_3} (e.g., issue expands to additional regions/models)

We’re continuing to work on a permanent fix; we’ll keep you updated on progress.

Regards,
{support_signature}

**Internal checklist (don’t include externally):**
- Confirm workaround validated by SRE/Eng for the customer’s tier.
- Mark as “temporary” and avoid implying the workaround is risk-free (call out tradeoffs if any).

---

## Template 6 — Rate limits / 429 clarification (quota vs headers)
**Channel:** Email

**Subject:** Clarification on 429s and rate-limit headers ({region})

Hi {customer_name},

Thanks for the examples. A 429 can be returned for a few distinct reasons (rate limiting, quota enforcement, or request bursts that exceed configured limits). We want to make sure we’re addressing the correct one.

**Please share**
- 2–3 request IDs that returned 429
- The full set of response headers for those requests (redact tokens/credentials)
- Your approximate RPS and whether you use concurrent streaming connections

**In the meantime, try**
- Reduce concurrency for {endpoint} temporarily (especially streaming)
- Use exponential backoff with jitter on retries
- Ensure you’re not re-sending identical requests due to timeouts (idempotency)

If helpful, here is the troubleshooting reference: {kb_link}

Next update by {next_update_time}.

Regards,
{support_signature}

---

## Template 7 — Private deployment comms (upgrade stuck / migrations)
**Channel:** Email; be explicit about safe diagnostics and rollback safety

**Subject:** Private deployment upgrade issue — diagnostics requested ({cluster_name})

Hi {customer_name},

Acknowledged. For Private upgrades that appear stuck at migrations, we typically need a small diagnostics bundle to confirm the failure mode and the safest recovery path.

**Please collect (safe + minimal) and share via the approved support channel**
- Installer logs from {path_or_command}
- Kubernetes events from the installer namespace
- Current installer version + target version
- Timestamp when the upgrade started

**Do not include** secrets, private keys, or application data. If any output contains sensitive values, please redact them before sharing.

**Immediate safety note**
Please avoid repeated re-runs of the upgrade until we confirm the state—this can complicate rollback in some scenarios.

We’ll review the artifacts and respond with next steps by {next_update_time}.

Regards,
{support_signature}

---

## Template 8 — Resolution note (issue resolved)
**Channel:** Email + ticket resolution comment

**Subject options:**
- Resolved: {symptom} on {endpoint} in {region}
- Update: Issue resolved — {case_id}

Hi {customer_name},

Confirming this issue is now **resolved**.

**Summary**
- Symptom: {symptom}
- Impact window: {impact_start} to {impact_end} ({timezone})
- Affected: {endpoint} in {region} (and {model} if applicable)

**What we changed (customer-safe):**
- {mitigation_applied_or_fix}

**What you should do**
- {customer_actions_post_resolution} (often “no action needed”)

If you continue to see symptoms, please reply with new request IDs and we’ll re-open the investigation.

Regards,
{support_signature}

---

## Template 9 — Resolution follow-up (offer RCA / post-incident review)
**Channel:** Email (enterprise/dedicated/private)

**Subject:** Follow-up: {case_id} resolution + next steps

Hi {customer_name},

Following up now that {case_id} is resolved. If helpful, we can provide either:
- A short written summary of contributing factors and mitigations (customer-safe), and/or
- A brief call to review what happened and prevention measures

**Proposed agenda (30 minutes)**
1) What you observed and business impact
2) Our findings at a high level (customer-safe)
3) Mitigations applied + prevention work in progress
4) Any configuration recommendations for your workload

If you’d like to schedule, please share a few times that work for your team.

Regards,
{support_signature}

---

## Template 10 — Waiting on customer (keep SLA expectations clear)
**Channel:** Email

**Subject:** Action needed: {case_id} — requesting details to proceed

Hi {customer_name},

To continue investigating {symptom}, we’ll need one of the following:
- 3–5 request IDs + timestamps from the last {N} hours, or
- A minimal reproduction (sanitized) and the response/error message

Once we have that, we’ll resume updates on the standard cadence for your tier. If you’re blocked and can’t provide request IDs, tell us what constraints you’re under and we’ll propose alternative options.

Regards,
{support_signature}

---

## Quick “blessed phrasing” (copy/paste)
- “We’re actively investigating and will provide the next update by {time}.”
- “We’ve applied a mitigation and are monitoring service health.”
- “This is a temporary workaround; we’re working on a permanent fix.”
- “We don’t have a confirmed ETA yet; next update by {time}.”
- “Please share request IDs (preferred) rather than payload content.”

## Approval / escalation reminders (internal)
- If the customer asks for credits or alleges an SLA breach: follow the exec escalation protocol and tier SLA guidance. Do not confirm breach in writing without approvals.
- If comms includes root cause details, scope beyond the customer, or planned release dates: confirm with on-call/SRE and use customer-safe language.
- If you think we should post a status event: follow the status page approval flow and keep email/status copy consistent.

title: SLA threshold to customer communications automation playbook
content:
Summary
This playbook describes the automated flow that translates tenant-level SLA/SLO threshold crossings into standardized customer communications and escalations. It covers detection rules, decision logic, message templates, required signals and telemetry, automation wiring (PagerDuty, Slack, SES, webhook), and manual intervention checkpoints. The goal is to deliver timely, consistent, and context-rich notifications while minimizing noise and protecting customer trust.

When to use this playbook
- Any tenant or customer whose availability, latency, or quality SLOs cross pre-defined warning or critical thresholds.
- During prolonged degraded throughput, persistent model-quality regressions for a tenant, or when downstream rate limits impede production traffic.
- As the canonical source for automated customer-facing comms; do not create ad-hoc messages outside this flow unless authorized.

Ownership and stakeholders
- Owner: Customer Success - Tenant Reliability (customer-success)
- On-call liaison: Platform SRE (eng-sre)
- Automation owner: Integrations team (eng-platform)
- Legal & Privacy reviewer: Security & Compliance (security-and-compliance)
- Communications lead: Customer Success Comms (customer-success)

Required signals and telemetry
- SLO evaluations (per-tenant): 1m and 5m rolling windows from the SLO engine.
- Latency p95/p99 and error rate per route (from Redwood Console metrics API).
- Throughput and queue length (serving-runtime metrics).
- Model quality regressions: evaluation harness alerts tied to customer prompt-sets.
- Active incident state from Incident Manager / PagerDuty.

Threshold definitions (table described)
- Warning: 3 consecutive 1m windows where SLO_missing_rate >= 5% OR p99 latency degraded > 50% vs baseline for 10m.
- Actionable: sustained degradation for 30m (SLO_missing_rate >= 10% OR p95 latency > 2x baseline).
- Critical: 60m sustained OR customer-visible errors affecting >=5% of requests in last 5m.

Decision matrix (high-level)
1) Warning -> internal ticket + scripted silent notification to customer (low-urgency email) after verification window.
2) Actionable -> escalate to on-call, open customer-facing incident channel (dedicated Slack channel + email) and run mitigations.
3) Critical -> Incident declared, trigger high-priority PagerDuty, send immediate customer SMS/email if configured, and route to senior CS + engineering leadership.

Automation flow (end-to-end)
1. Detection: SLO engine emits event -> Telemetry Gatekeeper evaluates thresholds.
2. Dedup & enrichment: Gatekeeper enriches event with tenant metadata (contract tier, contact preferences, active rate limits, pinned model versions) via Customer Metadata Service.
3. Policy decision: Rules engine selects message template and channel per tenant policy. Logic considers: tier, private/dedicated deployment, contractual notification SLAs, and regulatory constraints.
4. Communication: Message dispatched via Communication Orchestrator which supports: email (SES), transactional SMS (Twilio), webhook to customer webhook endpoint, and creating a private Slack channel for the incident.
5. Escalation: If no acknowledgement within configured window, escalate via PagerDuty to on-call and then to manager chain per escalation ladder.
6. Close loop: When SLO returns above threshold and stays stable for configured cool-down window, send recovery notification and update customer incident record and QBR metrics.

Message templates (examples)
- Warning (email subject): [Redwood] Service performance advisory for tenant {{tenant_name}}
  Body: "We detected a temporary degradation in response times for your tenant between {{start}} and {{end}}. Our systems are monitoring and you may experience intermittent latency. This is informational; no action is required unless you observe functional impact. If you would like faster updates, reply with 'subscribe'."

- Actionable (email + Slack): [Redwood] Degraded availability for tenant {{tenant_name}} - engineers engaged
  Body: "We have observed sustained elevation in error rate affecting approximately {{percent}} of requests. Our on-call engineers are investigating. Temporary mitigation steps: fallback to lower-cost model variant, reduce request concurrency, or enable autoscale burst for Dedicated. Estimated next update: {{eta}}.
  Action items: (1) Confirm whether in-progress traffic is OK to route to fallback variant (yes/no). (2) Provide any recent schema or prompt-set changes that may impact behavior."

- Critical (SMS + Email + Slack): [Redwood] Immediate action: Production impact for tenant {{tenant_name}}
  Body: "We are experiencing production-level impact for your tenant. Our senior engineers are engaged and we will provide continuous updates in the private channel. If you have a hotfix or immediate traffic control you want us to apply, reply with the instruction and contract-signed operator will execute after verification."

Notification policy and cadence
- Warning: single informational mail, 60-minute follow-up if persists.
- Actionable: initial notice immediately, follow-ups every 30 minutes until mitigated, then hourly for the first 6 hours.
- Critical: immediate notice + follow-ups every 15 minutes for first 2 hours, then every 30 minutes.
- All messages must include: root cause hypothesis (if available), mitigation steps taken, ETA for next update, who is the point of contact, and a link to the private incident channel and ticket number.

Escalation ladder (ordered)
1. Customer Success On-call (first responder)
2. Platform SRE on-call (operational mitigations)
3. Serving Runtime Owner (model execution mitigations)
4. Integrations/Network (if related to private networking/DNS/firewall)
5. Customer Success Manager / Account Owner
6. Director, Customer Success / Head of Platform (executive notification)

Manual overrides and sensitive customers
- For restricted/high-profile customers (confidentiality: restricted), all automated messages must be routed through the CS Manager for approval before external dispatch. This is enforced by a flag in Customer Metadata Service.
- Manual override steps: Authorized CS manager may pause automation via the Communications Orchestrator UI. After a pause, manual messages must reference the incident ID and be logged in the incident record.

Operational runbook (step-by-step)
1. Verify: Confirm the telemetry event in Redwood Console and the SLO engine. Run the query: SELECT tenant_id, window_start, p99_latency, error_rate FROM slo_evals WHERE tenant_id='{{tenant_id}}' AND window_start >= now() - interval '60 minutes';
2. Triage: Determine whether degradation is model, infra, or customer input related. Check: recent model rollouts, quantization profile changes, and recent customer prompt-set uploads.
3. Mitigate: Apply one of the following (ordered by least user-visible):  a) Activate KV cache warmup for hot prefixes. b) Route to dedicated lower-latency pool if available. c) Enable autoscale burst for Dedicated tenant. d) Fallback to a verified older model variant.
4. Communicate: Use the Communication Orchestrator to dispatch the appropriate template and open the private channel. Attach logs, key metrics, and the mitigation steps.
5. Track: Update the incident ticket with every customer-facing message and record time to acknowledgement.
6. Recovery: When SLOs are restored for the cool-down window, send recovery and summary, and schedule a post-incident review.

Automation wiring examples
- Sample webhook payload (Communication Orchestrator -> Customer Webhook):
  {
    "incident_id": "INC-20260203-1234",
    "tenant_id": "tenant_987",
    "severity": "actionable",
    "summary": "Elevated error rate: 12%",
    "start_time": "2026-02-03T14:12:00Z",
    "links": ["https://console.redwood.ai/incidents/INC-20260203-1234"]
  }

- PagerDuty trigger example (curl):
  curl -X POST https://events.pagerduty.com/v2/enqueue \\
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \\
    -d '{"routing_key":"<pd_integration_key>","event_action":"trigger","payload":{"summary":"Tenant tenant_987 critical latency","severity":"critical","source":"redwood-slo-engine"}}'

Testing and verification
- Test scenarios must include: transient spike (warning), sustained degradation (actionable), and catastrophic outage (critical).
- Create synthetic tenants in staging and configure varying contact preferences (email-only, webhook-only, email+SMS).
- Verify the deduplication logic works when repeated SLO events are emitted in a short window.
- Unit tests: rules engine policy selection and channel mapping. Integration tests: Communications Orchestrator to SES/Twilio/webhook and PagerDuty.

Audit and compliance
- All outgoing communications are logged to the Incident Archive (retention default: 365 days).
- For restricted customers, messages routed through CS Manager must include the approval id and timestamp.
- Attach transcripts of private Slack channels and webhook delivery responses to the incident record for legal audits.

Post-incident actions and QBR inputs
- Owner must complete an incident summary within 72 hours and tag the incident with cause, mitigations applied, time-to-detect, time-to-ack, time-to-recover.
- Include incident metrics in the next QBR: token-level cost delta during incident, SLO impact window, customer-reported impact.
- If the incident crosses contractual SLA thresholds (credits owed), route to Finance + Legal with the incident packet.

Appendix: quick-check checklist (for responders)
- [ ] Confirm telemetry and tenant metadata
- [ ] Verify escalation ladder and contact availability
- [ ] Choose mitigation (cache/route/fallback) and apply
- [ ] Dispatch initial customer message via Orchestrator
- [ ] Open private channel and pin logs + metrics
- [ ] Document all messages and trigger post-incident summary

Contact directory (roles with sample contacts)
- Customer Success On-call: cs-oncall@redwood.ai
- Platform SRE: platform-oncall@redwood.ai
- Integrations owner: integrations@redwood.ai
- Legal: legal@redwood.ai

Revision history
- 2026-01-15: Created by Maya Lin (initial draft)
- 2026-01-22: Added PagerDuty and webhook examples (review feedback)
- 2026-02-03: Finalized cadence and restrictive-customer overrides (published)

Related resources
- SLO engine architecture: /confluence/eng-platform/slo-engine/overview-2025
- Incident communication templates: /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/incident-communication-templates-2025
- Customer Metadata Service API: /confluence/eng-infra/cloud-accounts-and-networking/customer-metadata-api

title: Using Incident Taxonomy for Customer Communications (CS/Support Playbook)
content:
## Purpose
This playbook explains how Customer Success (CS) and Support should use the **Incident Taxonomy (v1)** in customer communications.

Goals:
- Communicate clearly and consistently without speculating on root cause.
- Set correct expectations for mitigations and next updates.
- Trigger the right escalation path based on incident type, severity, and customer tier (Hosted / Dedicated / Private).
- Ensure comms align with remediation SLA expectations (time-to-mitigate/time-to-fix) and contractual commitments.

## Audience
- Support engineers and CS managers handling active incidents and escalations
- Incident Comms Owners (ICOs) for Dedicated/Private accounts
- Support leadership coordinating status-page updates and executive escalations

## Ground rules (what we say / don’t say)
### Use the taxonomy as *classification*, not a root-cause claim
Allowed:
- “This is classified as a **Routing/Fallback** incident”
- “We are seeing **elevated 5xx** due to **capacity constraints in region X**” (only if confirmed by on-call)
- “Mitigation in progress: traffic shifting / scaling / rollback”

Avoid:
- Unverified causes (“GPU driver bug”, “kernel issue”, “bad deploy”) unless the incident owner explicitly confirms.
- Internal-only system names that confuse customers (e.g., “router v3”, “cp-write-path”) unless the customer already uses those terms and the owner approves.
- Over-specific ETAs (“fixed in 10 minutes”). Provide update cadence instead.

### Separate customer-facing language from internal classification
Internal incident_type/subtype should be captured in incident tooling and can be used verbatim **only** when the term is customer-safe. When in doubt, translate into plain language (examples below).

### Update cadence beats speculative detail
If we cannot share a cause, provide:
- Current impact and scope
- What mitigation is being attempted
- Next update time
- Workaround (if any)

## When CS/Support should reference incident type
Use incident taxonomy language in:
- Dedicated/Private customer emails and Slack channels
- Support ticket updates when the incident is active and customer-impacting
- Post-incident review (PIR) summaries

Do not proactively mention taxonomy to Hosted/self-serve customers unless it improves clarity. For Hosted, prefer plain-language “service degradation” wording plus a status page link.

## Quick decision guide: what’s the right comms posture?
1) **Is the customer actively impacted (errors/latency/disconnects/config failures)?**
- If yes: send an initial acknowledgement and link to status page (or state “status page update pending” for Dedicated/Private).

2) **Is there an open incident channel and an Incident Commander (IC)?**
- If yes: follow comms cadence set by IC/ICO.
- If no but impact is likely Sev0/Sev1: page/engage on-call via Support escalation immediately.

3) **Is the incident type one that requires proactive outreach?**
- See “Proactive outreach triggers” below.

4) **Does this involve Dedicated or Private?**
- If yes: use the Dedicated/Private templates and ensure the account owner (CSM) is looped.

## Proactive outreach triggers by incident type
Proactive outreach means: CS/Support initiates customer messaging even if the customer has not yet opened a ticket, because impact is likely and customer expectations are higher.

Trigger table (v1):

| Taxonomy type (customer-safe label) | Examples of customer symptoms | Proactive outreach for Hosted | Proactive outreach for Dedicated | Proactive outreach for Private |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Availability: 5xx / request failures | 5xx spike, failed completions/embeddings | Status page + only if widespread | Yes (within comms SLA) | Yes (within comms SLA) |
| Latency regression | p95/p99 latency elevated, timeouts | If widespread + material | Yes | Yes |
| Streaming disconnects | SSE/WebSocket resets, partial outputs | If widespread | Yes | Yes |
| Routing/fallback misbehavior | Wrong region/model, unexpected fallback, higher cost/quality change | If widespread | Yes (esp. committed capacity) | Yes |
| Capacity/fleet shortage | 429/overload, throughput drop, queueing | If widespread | Yes (capacity commitments) | Yes (if customer-managed fleet impacted) |
| Control plane outage | Cannot change policies, deploy model, update keys/config | Rare | Yes (if blocks ops) | Yes (often critical) |
| Auth/RBAC failures | 401/403, token rejected, permission issues | If widespread | Yes | Yes |
| Telemetry/metrics blind spot | “No data” dashboards, missing audit logs | No (unless blocks customer ops/compliance) | Sometimes (if affects reporting/audits) | Sometimes (esp. audit/compliance) |
| Private connectivity/config issue | DNS/TLS failures, VPC routing, firewall blocks after upgrade | N/A | N/A | Yes (direct outreach) |

Notes:
- “Proactive outreach” is triggered by **confirmed impact** OR **high confidence** that impact is imminent (e.g., region capacity incident where customer is pinned to that region).
- For Dedicated/Private, assume higher expectations; err on the side of earlier outreach.

## Handoff points and escalation workflow
### Who owns what during an incident
- **Incident Commander (IC)** (SRE or owning engineering team) controls internal timeline, mitigations, and severity.
- **Incident Comms Owner (ICO)** is responsible for customer-facing updates. For Dedicated/Private, this is usually CS (Account CSM) with Support as drafter; for broad outages, SRE may publish status updates and provide approved language.
- **Support** owns ticket hygiene: linking customer tickets to the incident, capturing customer-specific impact, and ensuring follow-ups are scheduled.

### Standard handoff rules
1) Support detects probable incident (multiple customers, clear outage signals)
- Open/confirm incident channel and tag on-call.
- Ask IC (or on-call) to confirm **incident_type/subtype** and **current mitigation plan**.

2) During active incident
- Support/CS publishes updates using approved content from IC/ICO.
- If the incident type changes (e.g., from “Capacity” to “Routing/Fallback”), update the customer summary without rewriting history (“Earlier we observed… We now believe primary driver is…”).

3) Resolution and post-incident
- Provide final update + next steps.
- For Sev0/Sev1, schedule PIR and ensure taxonomy is included.

### Escalation paths (when to pull in SRE vs service owner)
Escalate to SRE immediately when:
- Severity is Sev0/Sev1 (customer-impacting) OR the scope is unclear and potentially broad.
- You need approval for customer commitments (credits, contract language, bespoke mitigation plans).
- The incident type is unclear and paging/routing is disputed.

Escalate to Security Ops immediately when:
- Auth failures appear suspicious (credential stuffing, unusual geo/IP patterns).
- There is potential data exposure or integrity concerns.
- You are asked by a customer about “breach” implications.
Reference: Security incident alignment page.

## Customer-safe translations of common incident types
Use these translations by default unless IC approves more specific language.

- Availability: 5xx / overload
  - Customer-safe: “elevated error rates” / “requests failing”
- Latency regression
  - Customer-safe: “elevated response times” / “time-outs for some requests”
- Streaming disconnects
  - Customer-safe: “streaming responses intermittently disconnecting” / “partial responses”
- Routing/fallback misbehavior
  - Customer-safe: “traffic routing behavior not matching expected policy” / “unexpected failover/fallback behavior”
- Capacity/fleet shortage
  - Customer-safe: “insufficient capacity in the affected region/pool” / “throughput constrained; requests may be throttled”
- Control plane outage
  - Customer-safe: “management/API operations degraded (configuration updates failing)”
- Auth/RBAC failures
  - Customer-safe: “authentication/authorization failures affecting access”
- Telemetry/metrics blind spot
  - Customer-safe: “monitoring/visibility degraded; service may be healthy but reporting is delayed”
- Private connectivity/config issue
  - Customer-safe: “connectivity issues between your environment and the private deployment endpoint”

## Communication templates
Templates are intentionally generic. Fill in the bracketed fields with confirmed details.

### Template A — Initial acknowledgement (Dedicated)
Subject: [Dedicated] Service degradation — [short symptom] — [region/pool]

Hi [Name/Team],

We’re investigating an active service issue affecting your dedicated deployment.

- **What we’re seeing:** [elevated 5xx / elevated latency / streaming disconnects / throttling]
- **Scope:** [region/pool], starting at approximately [time + timezone]
- **Classification:** [taxonomy type in customer-safe terms]
- **Current mitigation:** [traffic shifting / scaling / rollback / config change in progress]

We will send the next update by **[time]** (or sooner if status changes).

If you can share request IDs, timestamps, and affected routes/models, we can validate impact faster.

Thanks,
[Your name]

### Template B — Initial acknowledgement (Private)
Subject: [Private] Connectivity/configuration issue — [customer env] — [symptom]

Hi [Name/Team],

We’re investigating an issue affecting your private deployment connectivity/configuration.

- **What we’re seeing:** [DNS/TLS failures / connection resets / config update failures]
- **Classification:** Private connectivity/config issue (taxonomy)
- **Current mitigation:** [workaround steps if available]
- **What we need from you:** [recent changes, firewall rules, certificate updates, upgrade version]

Next update by **[time]**.

Regards,
[Your name]

### Template C — Update during mitigation (Dedicated/Private)
Subject: Update — [Dedicated/Private] [symptom] — [region/pool/env]

Hi [Name/Team],

Update on the ongoing issue:

- **Current impact:** [still elevated / improving / intermittent]
- **What changed since last update:** [mitigation step attempted, rollback started, capacity added]
- **What we’re doing next:** [next mitigation step]
- **Next update:** [time]

We’ll continue to share confirmed information as it becomes available.

Thanks,
[Your name]

### Template D — Resolution notice + next steps
Subject: Resolved — [Dedicated/Private] [symptom] — [region/pool/env]

Hi [Name/Team],

The issue appears resolved as of **[time]**.

- **Summary:** [one paragraph, customer-safe]
- **Classification:** [taxonomy type]
- **Customer impact window:** [start–end]
- **What we did:** [rollback/scale/traffic shift]

Next steps:
- We will complete a post-incident review and share a summary / schedule a PIR if appropriate.
- If you are still seeing issues, please send [request IDs/timestamps] and we will investigate.

Regards,
[Your name]

## Status page guidance
- For broad Hosted incidents, rely on the public status page as the source of truth.
- For Dedicated/Private, coordinate with IC/ICO on whether to:
  - post a public status note (rare; only for multi-customer impact), or
  - keep comms direct to affected accounts.

If a customer asks “Why doesn’t this show on the status page?” use:
- “The status page covers broad platform impact. This incident is isolated to a specific dedicated/private deployment; we are providing direct updates here.”

## Handling “Unknown / Unclassified” incident type
During the first ~10–20 minutes, internal classification may still be **Unknown**. Customer comms should still go out.

Use:
- “We are investigating elevated [errors/latency] affecting [scope]. We will share additional details as soon as confirmed.”

Do not:
- Guess at whether it’s capacity vs routing vs runtime.

Once IC confirms the incident type, update the customer summary in the next message.

## SLA and expectation setting (customer-facing)
CS/Support should not quote internal remediation SLA numbers unless:
- it is part of the customer contract/commitment, AND
- the Account CSM + Support lead agrees, AND
- the IC (or SRE delegate) confirms it’s appropriate for the specific incident.

Instead, communicate:
- Update cadence
- Current mitigation plan
- Any available workaround

If a customer explicitly requests SLA adherence:
- Acknowledge and route to the CSM + SRE program lead for aligned response.

## Special cases
### Multi-cause incidents
If engineering identifies multiple contributing factors (e.g., “capacity shortage + routing fallback misbehavior”):
- Customer comms should describe the **primary symptom** and the **mitigation path**.
- Avoid listing multiple speculative causes.
- If asked, you can say: “We’re investigating multiple contributing factors; we’ll share confirmed findings in the post-incident summary.”

### Cloud provider/regional events
If the incident is driven by a cloud provider or regional disruption:
- Use: “an upstream cloud provider issue in [region]” only after IC confirmation.
- Do not blame a provider without confirmation.

### Security-adjacent incidents
If Security Ops is engaged:
- Do not discuss details of suspicious activity.
- Use: “We are investigating authentication failures; we’ll provide updates on service restoration.”
- Any mention of compromise, breach, or data exposure must be handled by Security + Legal/Comms.

## What to capture in the ticket / CRM notes
For every customer escalation linked to an incident:
- Incident channel/link (Slack) or incident ID
- Confirmed incident_type/subtype (once available)
- Customer-specific impact (routes/models/regions)
- Customer constraints (pinned region, strict latency, compliance requirements)
- Update timestamps and next update commitment
- Whether proactive outreach occurred and who approved messaging

## FAQs
**Q: Can I tell customers the incident_type/subtype verbatim?**
A: Only if it’s customer-safe and confirmed by IC. Prefer plain-language translations.

**Q: The customer is seeing 429s. Is that always capacity?**
A: No. It can be quota enforcement or true overload. Ask IC to confirm whether it’s “Quota/Policy” vs “Capacity/Fleet shortage” before stating cause.

**Q: Customer is Dedicated and wants a PIR. When do we schedule?**
A: For Sev0/Sev1 or high-impact Sev2, schedule within 3–5 business days after resolution, once the postmortem draft is available.

## Changelog
- 2026-02-12: Added “Unknown/Unclassified” guidance and security-adjacent language guardrails.
- 2026-01-18: Initial published version aligned to Incident Taxonomy v1 rollout.

title: Slack Bridge and Incident Channel Conventions (Support Escalations)
content:
## Purpose
This page standardizes **how Support starts and runs a Slack bridge** for customer-impacting escalations, and how/when we transition the conversation into **#incidents**.

Goals:
- Reduce time-to-triage by ensuring every bridge starts with complete context.
- Ensure Engineering/SRE can take action quickly without back-and-forth.
- Keep Jira (SUP tickets) and Slack synchronized so escalations are discoverable after the bridge ends.
- Ensure **one owner** is accountable for customer-facing updates (email / ticket / status page).

Non-goals:
- Replace the company incident process. If an issue meets incident criteria, we transition to #incidents and follow the incident playbook.

---

## Definitions
- **Support bridge:** A short-lived Slack channel created by Support to coordinate triage/mitigation for a customer escalation.
- **Incident channel:** A channel created/owned under **#incidents** conventions for cross-functional incident response.
- **SUP ticket:** Jira ticket in the Customer Support project (e.g., SUP-1842).

---

## When to start a Support bridge
Start a Support bridge when **any** of the following are true:
1) Potential **P0/P1** (see severity matrix) or escalating customer pressure.
2) Multiple reports suggest broader impact (same endpoint/model/region).
3) You need synchronous collaboration with SRE/Platform/Runtime to unblock mitigation.
4) A workaround requires coordinated comms and verification.

Do **not** start a bridge for routine troubleshooting if async triage in the SUP ticket is sufficient.

---

## Channel naming conventions
Use consistent, searchable names.

### Support bridge channel
Format:
- `#sup-bridge-<sup_id>-<short-topic>-<region>`

Examples:
- `#sup-bridge-sup-1842-streaming-resets-us-east`
- `#sup-bridge-sup-1850-embeddings-timeouts-eu-west`

Guidelines:
- Use the **primary SUP ticket** as the anchor.
- Keep `<short-topic>` under ~20 characters (abbreviate if needed).
- Include region when relevant (`us-east`, `eu-west`, `ap-sg`).

### If it becomes an incident
Transition to an incident channel with the incident naming standard (managed by incident tooling / SRE). The Support bridge can remain open for customer-specific comms, but decision-making and technical coordination should move to the incident channel.

---

## Required context (must be posted in the first message)
Immediately after creating the channel, post the **Bridge Kickoff Template** below. This is required for paging/on-call engagement.

### Bridge Kickoff Template (copy/paste)
**Summary (1–2 sentences):**
- 

**Customer impact:**
- Tier: (self_serve / dedicated / private / enterprise)
- Deployment: (Hosted / Dedicated / Private)
- Region(s):
- Endpoint(s): (chat/completions, embeddings, rerank, etc.)
- Affected model(s) + version pinning (if any):
- Blast radius: (single customer / multiple customers suspected)

**Severity (Support P0–P4):**
- Proposed priority:
- Why (symptoms + business impact):

**Timing:**
- Start time (approx):
- Still ongoing? (Y/N)

**Symptoms / errors:**
- Error codes/messages:
- % failure / latency impact (if known):

**Artifacts (do not paste sensitive payloads):**
- Request IDs (3–10 examples):
- Correlation IDs / Trace IDs (if available):
- SDK + version (and language):
- Client environment: (cloud/provider, VPC?, proxy?)

**What we’ve tried (and results):**
- 

**Links:**
- Jira: SUP-____ (primary) + related SUPs
- Dashboard(s):
- Known issue / workaround link (if applicable):

**Ask:**
- What do you need from Eng/SRE right now? (e.g., confirm degradation, enable mitigation, validate workaround)

### Notes on safe sharing
- Do **not** paste customer secrets, tokens, full prompts, or production payloads.
- Prefer request IDs and sanitized error snippets.
- If logs are needed, follow the Support intake checklist for customer-safe collection.

---

## Required participants (who to invite)
Invite only what you need, but ensure the minimum set is present.

### Minimum set
- **Support owner (Bridge Lead):** the person who created the bridge (default).
- **On-call Eng/SRE (as applicable):** based on product area and symptoms.
- **CSM (for Enterprise/Dedicated/Private):** to manage customer expectations and align comms.

### Add based on issue type
- **SRE**: suspected regional degradation, elevated errors/latency, capacity/routing/fallback behavior, multi-customer impact.
- **Platform**: auth/SSO, quota/rate limit enforcement, audit logs, control plane workflows, console access.
- **Serving Runtime**: streaming disconnects, runtime regressions, model-specific failures.
- **Dedicated/Capacity**: autoscaling oscillation, burst capacity issues, GPU pool saturation.
- **Docs/DevEx**: if we are validating or publishing a workaround/KB article during the incident.

### Escalation expectation (paging hygiene)
When you page or request on-call help, include:
- SUP ticket link
- Channel link
- 3–10 request IDs
- Region + endpoint + model
- “What’s the ask” (confirm issue? mitigation? rollback? routing policy?)

---

## Jira linking requirements (SUP tickets)
Slack bridges must be anchored in Jira to preserve context and support SLA tracking.

### 1) Choose a primary SUP ticket
- Pick the earliest/highest severity ticket that best represents the issue.
- If multiple customers are affected, keep separate SUP tickets per customer, but designate a single “primary” for the bridge.

### 2) Add Slack channel link to Jira
In the primary SUP ticket:
- Add the Slack channel URL in the designated field (per Jira field guidelines).
- Add it to the ticket description under **“Links”** if a dedicated field isn’t available.

### 3) Pin the primary SUP ticket in Slack
In the bridge channel:
- Pin the primary SUP ticket link.
- Also pin dashboards and any approved workaround/KB link.

### 4) Keep Jira updated with decision-quality notes
During the bridge, the Bridge Lead is responsible for:
- Adding a short timestamped summary of major decisions (mitigation enabled, rollback, routing change, customer workaround provided).
- Capturing next update time and owner.

### Tooling note
Incident tooling and automations are expected to prompt/pin SUP links during bridge creation (see internal automation work: Slack workflow updates and Jira reminders).

---

## When to move from a Support bridge to #incidents
A Support bridge is appropriate for **customer-specific escalations** or early triage. Move to #incidents when the situation is broader or requires formal incident management.

### Move to #incidents if any are true
- Suspected **multi-customer** or multi-region impact.
- Error rate or latency suggests a **service degradation/outage**.
- You need coordinated rollback/mitigation that affects production systems.
- You anticipate needing a status page update.
- You need a structured incident commander (IC) + comms lead roles.

### Transition process (do this fast; don’t debate in the moment)
1) Bridge Lead posts: “Escalating to #incidents due to <reason>.”
2) Create/join the incident channel (per incident process).
3) Post a short context handoff message in the incident channel (reuse the kickoff template; keep it tight).
4) Update the primary SUP ticket:
   - Link the incident channel.
   - Note that technical coordination has moved to the incident.
5) Keep the Support bridge open only if needed for customer-specific coordination; otherwise archive after resolution.

---

## Roles and ownership during a bridge
Clarity on “who does what” prevents dropped comms and duplicated work.

### Bridge Lead (Support)
Responsibilities:
- Post kickoff template and keep pins updated.
- Ensure Jira is linked and updated with key decisions.
- Drive the “next action / next update time” cadence.
- Decide when to escalate to #incidents (in partnership with on-call).

### Technical Lead (Eng/SRE)
Responsibilities:
- Own investigation plan and technical mitigation.
- Confirm whether symptoms match known issues.
- Provide customer-safe explanation of root cause hypothesis and mitigation status.

### Customer Comms Owner (single-threaded)
Default owner:
- **Support** owns customer updates in the SUP ticket for Hosted/self-serve.
- **CSM** owns customer updates for Dedicated/Private/Enterprise accounts, with Support support.

Rules:
- There must be exactly **one** named comms owner per escalation.
- The comms owner drafts and sends updates; Eng/SRE provides approved technical language.
- Status page updates follow the comms alignment guidance and required approvals.

### Executive escalation
If exec escalation triggers are met, follow the executive escalation protocol. Do not ad-hoc loop executives into a bridge without using the defined summary template.

---

## Update cadence inside the bridge
- **P0/P1:** Post an internal bridge update at least every **30 minutes** until stable mitigation is in place (even if the update is “still investigating”).
- **P2+:** At least every **60–120 minutes** during active investigation.

Each update should include:
- What changed since last update
- Current hypothesis
- Next action + owner
- Next internal update time
- Customer update plan (if applicable)

---

## Closing the bridge (resolution + follow-ups)
Before archiving the channel:
1) Ensure the primary SUP ticket has:
   - Final resolution summary
   - Mitigation steps taken
   - Customer-facing explanation (approved)
   - Links to incident review (if any)
   - Follow-up engineering tasks (Linear links) and owners
2) If a workaround was used:
   - Link the KB article (or create a doc task if missing)
   - Mark whether workaround is temporary and what “done” looks like
3) Post a final Slack message:
   - “Resolved at <time>”
   - What customers should do (if anything)
   - Where ongoing tracking lives (SUP/incident/Linear)

---

## FAQ
**Q: Can we keep everything in #support instead of creating a bridge channel?**
A: No for P0/P1 or when paging is involved. The dedicated bridge channel + template reduces time-to-triage and keeps escalation artifacts organized.

**Q: Who decides if this becomes a formal incident?**
A: The Support Bridge Lead should propose escalation; on-call SRE/Eng confirms and helps initiate the incident process. When in doubt, escalate.

**Q: Can Support post on the status page?**
A: Follow the customer incident comms alignment guidance. Status updates require the defined approval flow; Support/CS should not unilaterally post.

title: Customer incident chat-ops and stakeholder templates
content:
Summary:
This playbook provides ready-to-use chat-ops patterns, channel ownership mappings, incident severity communication templates, and stakeholder briefing message drafts for customer-facing incidents that affect inference quality, availability, or cost. It is intended for Customer Success Engineers (CSEs), Support on-call, Solutions Engineering, and the Incident Commander when coordinating public and private enterprise customers during a live event.

Goals:
- Ensure consistent, fast, and transparent customer communications.
- Reduce cognitive load on responders with pre-approved message templates.
- Clarify channel responsibilities and escalation points.
- Provide a safe rollback/mitigation checklist to surface with customers.

Scope:
- Multi-tenant and Dedicated deployments (hosted, dedicated, private).
- Incident severities Sev1 (customer-visible outage or quality regression) and Sev2 (significant degradation impacting SLAs).
- Not intended for security incident communications (see "incident-response-security" pages).

Owner and primary contacts:
- Owner: Customer Success (Marisol Vega)
- Primary escalation: CSE Oncall rota (cse-oncall@redwood.ai)
- Engineering escalation: Runtime SRE (eng-sre@redwood.ai)
- Exec escalation: Head of CS (head-cs@redwood.ai)

Channel map and responsibilities (table):
- Primary customer channel: Private Slack DM or sanctioned customer Slack workspace (CSE owns initial comms).
- Incident-wide coordination: #incident-redwood (IC owns timeline & action items).
- Engineering triage: #runtime-triage (SRE/Runtime engineer owns technical diagnosis).
- Billing/FinOps: #billing-escalations (Finance owns cost explanations and credits).
- External status visibility: Status Dashboard & optional customer-facing email (Comms PM owns public post).

Immediate steps for a customer-visible incident (0–10 minutes):
1) Acknowledge: CSE sends initial acknowledgment to customer within SLA window (default 15 minutes for enterprise).
2) Create incident in tracker (Jira/INC-##) and post summary to #incident-redwood with tags: [SEV, AFFECTED_CUSTOMERS, REGION, ROOT_SERVICE].
3) Assign roles: Incident Commander (IC), Communications Lead (CSE), Tech Lead (SRE), Customer Liaison (CSE).
4) Gather quick telemetry: top 3 graphs (requests/sec, error rate, p99 latency) + affected tenant IDs and model variants.

Template library (use the appropriate severity and update cadence). Replace bracketed tokens before sending.

Initial customer acknowledgment (fast template):
"Hi [Customer Name],
Thanks — we see the issue you're reporting for [tenant id / app]. We're investigating now. Our on-call engineering team has been engaged. Expected first update within [15 / 30] minutes. We're treating this as [SEV1/SEV2]. We'll share a short summary and next steps shortly. — [CSE name]"

First technical status update (15–30 mins):
"Status update for [Customer Name] (INC-[id]):
- Impact: [e.g., elevated error rate on generation requests causing 50% failures]
- Scope: [e.g., All US-hosted Dedicated tenants using model X v1.2.3; example tenant ids: T-1234, T-9876]
- What we're doing: [e.g., isolating degraded pool, shifting traffic to compatible variant quantized to q4_0, collecting traces, rolling temporary bypass] 
- Next update: [time + 30 mins]
If you have active customer requests, please forward them to this thread and we'll prioritise. — [CSE name]"

Customer-facing resolution message (post-fix):
"Root cause: [short cause statement].
Mitigation applied: [what we changed to restore service].
Current status: [Service restored/Degraded but mitigated].
Customer impact: [duration and scope].
Actions next: [follow-up items, timeline for permanent fix].
Credits: [if applicable, summary and next steps to apply credits].
If you want a post-incident call, we can schedule a run-through; tell us preferred times. — [CSE name]"

Escalation cadence and when to involve execs:
- Within 60 minutes: If the incident affects >3 enterprise customers or causes sustained SLA violations (error rate >5% and p95 latency >2x target), notify Head of CS and Head of Eng.
- Within 180 minutes: If no short-term mitigation is available or customer business is materially impacted, escalate to Exec Comms and Sales leadership.

Suggested internal Slack snippets (for #incident-redwood). Use code block format for clarity.
"INC-[id] | SEV1 | Impact: [brief]. Affected tenants: [list]. IC: [name]. CSE: [name]. Tech Lead: [name]. Primary mitigation in progress: [action]."

Contact templates for cross-functional owners (email/Slack):
- To Runtime team: "INC-[id] — request: reproduce high-rt error locally with sample request (tenant T-1234). Attached traces/RT: [link]. Priority: P0. Please ack in <10m. — [IC name]"
- To Billing: "INC-[id] — potential bill impact for tenants [T-1234]. Please prepare options for credits and spike analysis. — [CSE name]"

Checklist: safe mitigations to propose to customers (decision tree):
- Is the issue isolated to a single model variant? -> Propose a compatible variant fallback with identical API semantics.
- Is KV cache affecting prefixes? -> Suggest tenant-level cache clear and short rehydrate window.
- Is it network-related in a region? -> Offer regional failover (if configured) or temporary routing to alternative region (note data residency implications).
- If mitigation requires tenant restart: schedule within maintenance window and propose traffic drain procedure.

Communication frequency guidelines:
- SEV1: updates every 15–30 minutes until mitigation, then hourly until RCAs complete.
- SEV2: updates every 30–60 minutes.
- Post-mortem: delivered within 72 hours as a draft; final RCA and action items within 10 business days.

Post-incident follow-up meeting checklist (Customer + Internal):
1) Timeline review and customer impact summary.
2) Walkthrough of telemetry and root cause evidence.
3) Action items and owners with due dates (link to Jira).
4) Compensation/credit decision and approval path.
5) Preventative actions and SLA guardrails to add to QBR.

Short sample Q&A for customer calls (prep sheet):
- Q: Why did this happen? A: We identified a component X regression that, under [workload pattern], caused degraded scheduler decisions. We rolled back and applied a mitigant.
- Q: How can we avoid this? A: We recommend pinning to model variant X.y until the permanent fix and enabling supervised canary for major model upgrades.

Document retention and approvals:
- All outgoing customer messages related to SEV1 incidents must be reviewed by Communications Lead or Head of CS when possible.
- Save all conversations in the incident timeline and link to the customer's record in CRM with tags: incident, outage, credit_pending.

Appendix: Quick copy-paste snippets (use verbatim and fill tokens)
- Short public status page blurb: "Investigating: We are aware of increased errors for text-generation requests in US region. Engineers are actively investigating. No ETA yet. — Redwood Engineering"
- Customer opt-in for call: "We can schedule a 30-minute technical call to review impact and mitigation. Are you available [date/time options]?"

References and related pages:
- Incident comms standards (internal)
- Postmortem template and RCA tracker
- Dedicated tenant cutover safety net (see related pages)

Revision notes:
- 2027-08-18: Initial draft and CSE oncall validated rapid-ack template.
- 2027-11-05: Added KV-cache mitigation decision tree after two incidents.
- 2028-01-12: Finalized exec escalation thresholds and added billing coordination templates.

End of document.

title: Autoscaling Bounds (Dedicated) — Customer Escalation Playbook (CS/Support)
content:
## Purpose
This playbook helps Customer Success (CS) and Support respond to Dedicated customer escalations involving autoscaling **min/max bounds** and optional **predictive mode**. It provides:
- Intake questions to quickly identify root cause
- How to interpret bounded-scaling metrics and dashboards
- Common misconfigurations and how to correct them safely
- Guidance for recommending min/max settings aligned with SLA and cost controls
- Escalation criteria and internal routing (SRE vs Infra vs Platform)

## Scope
Applies to **Redwood Dedicated** deployments using the scaling policy feature:
- Hard bounds: `min_replicas` and `max_replicas` (and/or GPU quota equivalents)
- Optional predictive mode (forecast-biased scaling) with reactive override

Out of scope: Hosted API scaling behavior, cross-region capacity placement, contract renegotiation.

## Quick definitions (use consistent language with customers)
- **Requested desired**: what the autoscaler *wanted* to set based on signals (reactive and/or predictive).
- **Bounded desired**: requested desired after applying customer bounds (clamped to min/max).
- **Bound hit**:
  - **Max-bound hit**: autoscaler wanted more capacity, but max prevented scale-up.
  - **Min-bound hit**: autoscaler wanted less capacity, but min prevented scale-down.
- **Predictive mode**: autoscaler incorporates a forecast to scale ahead of demand ramps; reactive signals (queue depth/saturation) still take precedence for safety.
- **Unmet min**: platform attempted to provision at least min, but **could not** due to region/fleet capacity shortage (degraded state).

## First 5 minutes: intake checklist
Collect these before asking Engineering/SRE to engage.

### 1) Identify the deployment
Ask for:
- Account name and `deployment_id` (or Console URL)
- Region(s)
- Model(s) served (important for throughput characteristics)
- Dedicated tier (SLA tier if applicable)

### 2) Clarify the symptom (choose one primary)
- A) “Costs spiked / spend exceeded expectations”
- B) “Latency/queueing during known traffic ramp”
- C) “We hit max and started timing out / requests queued”
- D) “Capacity oscillates (up/down) and performance is jittery”
- E) “Min baseline isn’t being met / we see fewer replicas than configured”
- F) “Config changes aren’t taking effect / UI shows errors”

### 3) Capture the timeline
- When did it start (timestamp + timezone)?
- Is it periodic (daily ramp) or a one-off event?
- Any recent changes?
  - Scaling policy updated (min/max, cooldowns)
  - Predictive mode toggled
  - Model version change
  - Traffic pattern change (batch size, max_tokens, streaming)

### 4) Gather objective evidence
Request:
- Screenshot or export of Console scaling view: desired vs bounded, queue depth, and scale events
- Approximate RPS or token rate during the event
- p95 latency and error rate during the event

If the customer cannot share screenshots, ask for these numeric summaries:
- Current replicas and configured min/max
- Peak queue depth (or “queue time”)
- Frequency of scale events (e.g., “every 2–3 minutes”)

## Where to look (internal)
Use the autoscaling dashboard and event timeline first:
- **Autoscaling Bounds Dashboard** (Grafana): desired vs bounded replicas, bound-hit rate, queue depth, saturation signals, prediction vs actual.
- **Scale Events Timeline**: reasons for scale actions (reactive spike, forecast ramp, cooldown/dampening, bounds clamp).
- **Audit log**: who changed scaling policy, when, and what fields.

If you do not have dashboard access, route to CS on-call or SRE per escalation rules below.

## Interpreting bounded scaling metrics (what they mean and what to say)

### A) Max-bound hit + queue builds
**What you’ll see (typical):**
- Requested desired > max
- Bounded desired = max for a sustained period
- Bound-hit counter rising (max)
- Queue depth rising, p95 latency increases; saturation may remain high

**What it means:**
The platform is trying to add capacity but is contractually prevented by the customer’s `max`. The correct action is either:
- Increase max (customer decision), or
- Reduce demand per replica (prompt/token settings, batching configuration), or
- Implement application-level shedding/fallback (smart routing), or
- Move to higher reserved capacity

**Customer-safe wording:**
“Your deployment is operating at the configured maximum capacity. The autoscaler is requesting additional replicas, but the max bound is preventing scale-up. To eliminate queueing during peaks, we’ll need to either raise the max bound or reduce load per replica.”


### B) Min-bound hit (scale-down prevented)
**What you’ll see:**
- Requested desired < min
- Bounded desired = min
- Bound-hit counter rising (min)
- Latency stable; costs remain higher than a purely reactive policy

**What it means:**
This is expected when customers set a baseline. If they are unhappy with cost, recommend reducing min after confirming baseline SLO requirements.

**Customer-safe wording:**
“Your minimum baseline is being enforced as configured. The system would otherwise scale down, but it’s honoring the minimum to preserve your baseline performance.”


### C) Unmet min (degraded) due to region capacity shortage
**What you’ll see:**
- Configured min = N, but current replicas < N
- Autoscaler attempts to provision, but provisioning fails/retries
- “unmet_min” or “capacity_shortage” indicators; alerts may be firing internally

**What it means:**
This is a platform-side capacity issue, not a customer misconfiguration. Engage SRE/Infra immediately.

**Customer-safe wording:**
“We’re seeing a capacity shortage in the region preventing us from meeting the minimum baseline. We’re treating this as a service degradation and are actively working to restore your baseline.”


### D) Predictive mode enabled: forecast overshoot/undershoot
**What you’ll see:**
- Scale-up begins *before* traffic ramp when forecast available
- Prediction error metrics may show:
  - Overshoot: capacity grows, but demand does not
  - Undershoot: demand ramps faster than predicted; reactive signals should catch up

**What it means:**
Predictive mode biases early scale-up, but should not violate bounds. If the forecast is stale or wrong, reactive override should take over. Oscillation may indicate dampening/cooldown tuning or forecast noise.

**Customer-safe wording:**
“Predictive scaling is intended to reduce ramp latency by scaling ahead of demand. If the forecast is off, reactive signals still drive safety behavior, but we may need to tune cooldowns or adjust predictive settings.”

## Common customer issues and recommended actions

### 1) “We exceeded our budget cap”
**Most common cause:** max bound not set (or set too high), or customer assumed ‘soft cap’.

**Do:**
- Confirm whether bounds feature is enabled for the deployment (feature flag / policy present).
- Verify current `max_replicas` and recent scale events.
- If max is unset, recommend setting a max immediately.

**Suggest:**
- Set `max_replicas` to a value aligned with their monthly cap and peak-day expectations.
- Add alerting for max-bound saturation (so they get notified *before* queueing becomes severe).

**Escalate if:**
- Customer claims max was set but platform exceeded it (treat as potential bug; page Infra autoscaling).


### 2) “Queueing during our daily 9am ramp”
**Most common causes:**
- Min too low (cold start/insufficient baseline)
- Predictive mode disabled or forecast stale
- Cooldowns too conservative; scale-up step sizing too small

**Do:**
- Ask for ramp schedule (time + timezone) and typical lead time required (e.g., “need capacity 10 minutes before 9am”).
- Check whether predictive mode is enabled and whether forecasts are present and fresh.
- Check time-to-recover after queue begins (reactive catch-up time).

**Suggest:**
- Increase `min_replicas` to cover the first part of the ramp.
- Enable predictive mode if eligible, with a conservative ramp-up policy.
- If they cannot raise min (cost), consider an app-side mitigation plan (rate limiting, graceful degradation, fallback routing if configured).

**Escalate if:**
- Predictive mode is enabled but not acting ahead of ramp AND forecasts show as fresh (possible integration bug).


### 3) “We’re hitting max and latency is bad—should we raise max?”
**Do:**
- Confirm they are max-bound hit for the entire incident window.
- Estimate required headroom:
  - Compare queue depth growth vs stabilization at max.
  - Identify if max is hit only during brief spikes or sustained peaks.

**Suggest decision framework:**
- If max-bound hits are brief and latency impact is minimal: keep max, add alerting.
- If max-bound hits are sustained and queue grows: raise max or reduce load per replica.

**Important:**
- Never promise that raising max alone will fix latency if there is a region shortage risk or model throughput regression.


### 4) “Capacity oscillates up/down (thrashing)”
**Most common causes:**
- Cooldown too short (reacting to noise)
- Predictive mode noisy or misaligned with timezone
- Frequent config changes (churn)

**Do:**
- Check scale event frequency: if actions are happening every few minutes, it’s likely oscillation.
- Confirm whether predictive mode recently enabled or modified.

**Suggest:**
- Increase scale-down cooldown; add dampening.
- Ensure customer’s ramp schedule timezone aligns with deployment region settings.
- Avoid repeated manual edits; let the system stabilize.

**Escalate if:**
- Oscillation persists with reasonable cooldowns OR corresponds to known predictive-mode issues (see Known Issues page).


### 5) “We set min=10 but only see 6 replicas”
Treat as **P0** if customer is production impacted.

**Do:**
- Confirm whether they are in an unmet-min state (capacity shortage).
- Confirm region and time window; check if other accounts are affected.

**Escalate immediately to:**
- SRE on-call (Dedicated) + Infra fleet on-call

**What to tell the customer:**
- Acknowledge degraded baseline, provide ETA only if SRE supplies one.
- Offer temporary mitigations if available (traffic shaping, shifting to another region if contractually allowed, lowering min only if customer agrees and it aligns with available capacity—do not unilaterally change policy).

## Guidance: how to choose min/max (recommendation playbook)
Use this section for tickets like “How should we set bounds to meet our SLA?”

### Step 1: Determine objective constraints
Ask:
- What is the target p95 latency and error rate during peak?
- What is the peak window duration and how fast does it ramp?
- What is the maximum monthly spend or peak-day cap?
- Is the application allowed to degrade gracefully at peak (fallback model, rate limiting, shedding)?

### Step 2: Recommend a starting min
Principle: **Min should cover the first 5–15 minutes of the expected ramp** (or the time it takes reactive scaling to catch up), not the entire peak.

Heuristics (starting points):
- If they have a predictable daily ramp and strict SLOs: set min to the “pre-ramp steady-state need” + buffer.
- If they have sporadic spikes and cost sensitivity: keep min low, use predictive only if spikes are somewhat forecastable.

Anti-patterns:
- Setting min equal to full peak capacity (expensive; often unnecessary).
- Setting min=0 for production Dedicated workloads (can cause cold-start/queueing; some environments may block scale-to-zero).

### Step 3: Recommend a max
Principle: **Max is the contractual safety guardrail**. Set it to the highest acceptable cost exposure.

Heuristics:
- If the customer wants “never exceed $X”: translate to an approximate max replica/GPU count and set max accordingly.
- If they need “never queue during peak” and can pay: max should exceed historically observed peak requirement plus buffer.

Important caveat:
- A max that is too low will convert load spikes into queueing/timeouts. Ensure customer explicitly accepts that tradeoff.

### Step 4: Predictive mode guidance
Recommend enabling predictive mode when:
- Traffic ramps are regular (time-of-day/week), and
- The customer’s pain is “latency during ramp,” and
- They can tolerate minor overshoot in exchange for fewer queueing events.

Recommend leaving predictive mode off when:
- Workload is highly irregular with low historical signal, or
- Customer is extremely cost sensitive and will treat overshoot as unacceptable.

## Common misconfigurations (and what to do)
- **min > max**: invalid. Ask customer what they intended; correct to min <= max.
- **max set below current baseline need**: results in chronic max-bound hit; recommend raising max or reducing demand.
- **Cooldowns too short**: causes thrash; recommend longer scale-down cooldown.
- **Timezone mismatch for scheduled/ramp expectations**: clarify customer local time vs deployment region time.
- **Rapid repeated edits**: can make behavior appear “random.” Ask them to pause changes for one stabilization window.

## Escalation routing (internal)

### Severity guide
- **P0 (page SRE now):** unmet min affecting production, widespread elevated queueing with max-bound hit across multiple customers, suspected platform ignoring max.
- **P1:** single-customer sustained queueing with max-bound hit and strict SLA impact; predictive mode causing repeated oscillation; audit log discrepancies.
- **P2:** configuration guidance, cost questions, minor overshoot concerns.

### Who to loop in
- **SRE (Dedicated)**: unmet-min states, suspected fleet shortage, customer-visible degradation.
- **Infra/Fleet autoscaling** (Vanessa Ortiz / Keiko Yamamoto team): bound enforcement behavior, oscillation, scale-event reason correctness.
- **Platform Control Plane** (Ethan Park / Benji Okafor / Jordan Lee): policy schema, validation, RBAC, audit log issues.
- **Observability** (Allison Grant / Sergio Costa): missing metrics, dashboard gaps, alert tuning.
- **Product (Dedicated)** (Lauren Bishop): customer commitments, pilot/GA semantics questions, feature eligibility.

## Customer communications templates (Support macros)

### Macro: Max-bound hit explanation
Subject: Dedicated autoscaling at configured maximum

Message:
“We reviewed your Dedicated deployment scaling telemetry. During the incident window, the autoscaler requested additional replicas, but the deployment was clamped at your configured **max bound**. This means the platform is honoring your cost/ceiling setting, but it can lead to queueing during peak demand.

Next steps:
1) If you want to reduce queueing during peaks, we can increase the max bound (you choose the ceiling).
2) If you want to keep the ceiling fixed, we can discuss demand-reduction options (token limits, batching, or graceful degradation patterns).

If you share your target p95 latency and budget ceiling, we can propose a recommended min/max starting point.”

### Macro: Unmet min / capacity shortage
Subject: Dedicated minimum baseline temporarily unmet (service degradation)

Message:
“We’re currently seeing conditions in the region that prevent us from meeting the configured **minimum baseline capacity** for your deployment. We’ve engaged our on-call team and are actively working to restore capacity. We will provide updates as soon as we have confirmed progress or an ETA.

In the meantime, please let us know if you can temporarily reduce traffic, enable application rate limiting, or (if contractually acceptable) shift traffic to an alternate region.”

### Macro: Predictive mode expectations
Subject: Predictive autoscaling behavior and next steps

Message:
“Predictive autoscaling scales ahead of expected demand ramps using forecasts, while reactive signals still take over if demand differs from the forecast. If you’re seeing oscillation or overshoot, we can tune cooldown/dampening settings and validate forecast freshness/timezone alignment.

Please share:
- The time window(s) of the ramp (with timezone)
- Any scheduled events
- A screenshot of desired vs bounded replicas and queue depth during the event”

## Internal notes / do-not-do list
- Do not promise specific capacity availability during region shortages.
- Do not change customer scaling policy (min/max, predictive toggle) without explicit customer confirmation and a recorded ticket note.
- Do not frame max-bound hit as a “platform failure”—it is usually expected behavior.
- Avoid diagnosing solely from anecdotes; always anchor to desired vs bounded, bound-hit, and queue/saturation signals.

## Attachments and references
- Dedicated autoscaler troubleshooting runbook (SRE/On-call)
- Autoscaling bounds observability dashboard spec
- Predictive autoscaling known issues & workarounds
- ADR: bounds precedence and safety invariants

## Change log
- 2025-07-16: Initial version for pilot support readiness.
- 2025-08-01: Added predictive-mode oscillation triage and customer macros.
- 2025-09-04: Updated unmet-min routing and clarified min/max guidance for SLA vs cost-capped customers.

title: Multi-tenant SLO escalation and SLA credit playbook
content:
Summary:
This playbook defines the escalation paths, operational actions, and SLA credit calculation methodology for multi-tenant SLO degradations affecting Redwood Inference hosted customers.
