  - GPU utilization dips while queue length for inference requests stays high

- Example PromQL queries:
  - Pod eviction spikes (5m):
    increase(kube_pod_status_phase{phase="Failed"}[5m]) by (node)

title: Known-Issues Sprint Plan (2026-02) — Publish High-Impact Workarounds
content:
## Overview
This sprint is a focused Customer Success & Support initiative to reduce repeat tickets and speed customer mitigation by publishing validated, copy/paste-ready workaround articles for our most common, highest-impact issues across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private tiers.

This plan defines:
- Selection criteria for sprint issues (what qualifies and what does not).
- Owners/reviewers and the publication workflow.
- A publication checklist to ensure articles are safe, accurate, and consistent with Support escalation workflows.
- Target metrics and how we will measure impact.

**Sprint window:** 2 weeks (Planning week + Execution week) with a follow-up week for adoption/cleanup.

---

## Goals
1. **Reduce time-to-triage** for high-frequency issues by making troubleshooting steps and required diagnostics consistent.
2. **Reduce time-to-mitigation** for customer-impacting incidents via validated temporary workarounds (and clear “when to escalate” guidance).
3. **Decrease repeat tickets** by improving self-serve and Support-agent deflection (KB and macros linking).
4. **Standardize language** across Support (Jira priorities) and Engineering (incident severity and on-call thresholds).
5. **Ensure discoverability**: known-issues index as the landing page, consistently linked from Support workflows and relevant SDK docs.

## Non-goals (explicitly out of scope)
- Broad product roadmap or feature work not tied to top escalations.
- Long-form training programs (we will ship quick reference + templates only).
- Publishing customer-sensitive details (exact account names, unique payloads, internal-only dashboards) into broadly visible docs.

---

## Scope: What we will publish
Each known-issue article must include:
- **Symptoms** (what the customer sees) and quick confirmation checks.
- **Impact** (expected degradation, functional breakage, affected endpoints).
- **Affected scope**: tiers (Hosted/Dedicated/Private), models, regions, SDK versions.
- **Workarounds / mitigations** (validated by SRE/Engineering; clearly marked temporary when applicable).
- **Support steps** (what to ask for: request IDs, region, model, SDK version; safe log collection).
- **When to escalate**: explicit triggers mapped to the severity matrix.
- **Last updated** and ownership (who maintains it).

---

## Selection criteria (how issues are chosen)
Issues are selected using a weighted score across **impact**, **frequency**, and **workaround readiness**.

### Must-have criteria
- Appears in the top recurring Support themes (ticket volume, escalations, or time sink).
- Has a **repeatable symptom pattern** (not a one-off customer misconfiguration only).
- Has a **validated workaround or mitigation** that Support can safely recommend.
- Can be documented without exposing restricted customer details.

### Strongly preferred
- Impacts multiple customers or a material enterprise account.
- Frequently causes bridge/escalation churn due to missing context or inconsistent diagnostics.
- Has an Engineering follow-up ticket to permanently fix or improve observability/errors.

### Exclusions
- Issues requiring bespoke customer configuration that does not generalize.
- Items where “workaround” is effectively “we need Engineering to investigate from scratch.”
- Purely contractual/commercial topics (handled by CS/Sales enablement, not KB).

### Severity threshold guidance
Prioritize issues that commonly present as **Support P0/P1** and/or routinely trigger **Sev0/Sev1** escalation.

---

## Candidate shortlist for 2026-02 (initial set)
This sprint’s initial known-issues set (subject to final validation during planning):
1. **Streaming timeouts / connection resets / truncated streams** (Hosted, multi-region)
2. **429 quota mismatch + rate-limit header confusion** (Hosted; SDK upgrade correlation)
3. **Dedicated autoscaling oscillation causing latency spikes** (Dedicated)
4. **Private installer upgrade stuck at migrations** (Private)
5. **Audit log delivery latency (lag > expected)** (Enterprise/Private control plane)

Note: Additional issues may be added only if we can complete validation + publication without jeopardizing the above.

---

## Owners and review model
### RACI (high-level)
| Workstream | Responsible (R) | Accountable (A) | Consulted (C) | Informed (I) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sprint execution + coordination | Dev Patel | Jasmine Liu | Rachel Kim, Talia Benson | Support, CS |
| Article drafting (Hosted) | Wei Chen | Elliot Price | Owen Phillips, SRE on-call | Support |
| Article drafting (Dedicated/Private) | Kira Thompson | Elliot Price | Platform owners, SRE | Support, CS |
| Workaround validation | SRE partner (Sean Gallagher / Rafael Mendes) | Priya Natarajan (Eng sponsor) | Platform/Runtime owners | Support |
| Publication + IA (index/links) | Elliot Price | Dev Patel | DevEx/Docs, Design | Company |
| Macro/snippet alignment | Priya Shah | Dev Patel | Owen Phillips | Support |

### Required reviewers by category
- **Streaming / runtime / gateway behaviors:** SRE + Runtime/Serving representative
- **Dedicated autoscaling:** SRE + Capacity/Dedicated owner
- **Private installer:** Private Deployments/Platform + SRE
- **Audit logs / compliance-adjacent:** Platform Control Plane + Security/Compliance guidance (Naomi Feldman as needed)

---

## Timeline and milestones
### Week 0 (Prep: 1–2 days)
- Confirm shortlist from Support trends and current escalations.
- Assign doc owners + reviewers.
- Create tracking rows in the sprint spreadsheet (internal working doc).

### Week 1 (Planning week)
**Deliverables by end of week:**
- Final shortlist and score justification.
- Draft outlines for each article (headings, symptoms, workaround steps, escalation triggers).
- Confirm where each article will live and the tags to apply in the index.

**Key meetings:**
- 30 min kickoff (Support + Docs + SRE + Platform)
- 30 min midweek validation sync (confirm workaround safety)

### Week 2 (Execution week)
**Deliverables by end of week:**
- All articles published with consistent formatting and “when to escalate” sections.
- Known-issues index updated with tags and recency.
- Support macros updated to link to relevant known-issue articles.
- Cross-links from SDK troubleshooting pages where applicable.

### Week 3 (Adoption + cleanup)
**Deliverables:**
- Jira automation tweaks and field validation updates (if applicable).
- Backlog triage: convert repeat tickets into known-issue references.
- Metrics check-in: early deflection + time-to-mitigation signals.
- Ownership handoff: who maintains each article and update cadence.

---

## Publication checklist (definition of done)
Every article must pass the checklist below before being marked **Published**.

### Content quality
- [ ] Clear title that matches customer language (“timeouts”, “429”, “upgrade stuck”).
- [ ] “Symptoms” section includes 2–5 concrete examples (errors, behaviors) without customer identifiers.
- [ ] “Quick checks” include what Support should ask for (region, model, SDK version, request IDs).
- [ ] “Workaround” steps are numbered, copy/paste-ready, and include safe defaults.
- [ ] “When to escalate” includes thresholds/conditions and references the severity matrix.
- [ ] “Resolution / long-term fix” notes whether a permanent fix is planned and where to track it (internal ticket reference is okay; avoid sensitive details).

### Accuracy and validation
- [ ] Workaround validated by SRE/Engineering reviewer (explicit sign-off in comments or Jira).
- [ ] Any config change includes rollback guidance.
- [ ] Any client retry guidance includes idempotency and rate-limit considerations.

### Safety, confidentiality, and compliance
- [ ] No customer names, contract terms, or account-specific details.
- [ ] No internal-only dashboards/URLs unless the page is restricted (default: avoid).
- [ ] Log collection instructions are customer-safe (no secrets; explain redaction expectations).

### Discoverability and workflow integration
- [ ] Article linked from the **Known Issues Index** with appropriate tags (tier/region/model).
- [ ] Support macro/snippet updated to reference the article.
- [ ] If applicable, SDK troubleshooting docs cross-link to the article.
- [ ] Jira triage guidance updated (auto-suggest known issues where feasible).

---

## Metrics (targets + measurement plan)
We will track the following for the 2 weeks prior (baseline) and 2–4 weeks after publication.

### Primary success metrics
1. **Ticket deflection (repeat-ticket reduction)**
   - Definition: reduction in new tickets that match the known-issue categories (by tags/keywords + Support classification).
   - Target: **15–25% reduction** in weekly repeat tickets for the published issue set.

2. **Time-to-mitigation (TTM) for escalations in scope**
   - Definition: time from Support intake to first validated mitigation/workaround communicated to customer.
   - Target: **30% reduction** for P0/P1 tickets matching the published issue set.

3. **Time-to-triage (TTT)**
   - Definition: time from ticket creation to “root cause category identified” (or confirmed known-issue match) and next-step plan.
   - Target: **25% reduction** for tickets in scope.

### Secondary metrics
- **Fewer back-and-forth loops**: median number of Support replies before “actionable next step” is provided.
- **Macro adoption**: % of in-scope tickets where the updated macro is used.
- **Escalation quality**: % of pages/bridges that include required context (request IDs, region, model, recent deploys).

### Data sources
- Jira: ticket timestamps, priorities, labels, resolution notes.
- Slack: bridge creation timestamps and context completeness (spot-check).
- Docs analytics (if available): pageviews for known-issues index + articles.
- SRE incident tooling: references to mitigations and related SUP tickets.

---

## Workflow: How Support should use known-issues content
1. During intake, check the **Known Issues Index** for matching symptoms/tags.
2. If a match is found, apply the linked macro and request the exact diagnostics listed.
3. Provide the workaround steps exactly as written (avoid ad-hoc edits that change meaning).
4. If the issue meets “when to escalate” criteria, open/attach the escalation bridge and link the SUP ticket.
5. Add a resolution note referencing the known-issue article and whether the workaround resolved the customer impact.

---

## Risks and mitigations
- **Risk: Publishing incorrect or unsafe mitigations.**
  - Mitigation: required SRE/Eng sign-off + rollback guidance for any config change.

- **Risk: Customer-sensitive details leak into broadly visible docs.**
  - Mitigation: explicit confidentiality checklist; Docs review focused on redaction.

- **Risk: Articles become stale quickly.**
  - Mitigation: ownership field per article + quarterly review reminder (or on fix release).

- **Risk: Low discoverability / inconsistent linking.**
  - Mitigation: index as canonical landing page; macros and triage checklist updated; cross-links from SDK docs.

---

## Communication plan
- Internal announcement in #announcements once the index + first batch of articles are published.
- 10-minute Support standup walkthrough: where to find the index, what changed in macros, and escalation trigger reminders.
- Post-sprint update to CS leadership: metrics baseline + early impact and remaining gaps.

---

## Appendices
### A. Standard article template (copy/paste)
**Summary**
**Symptoms**
**Impact**
**Affected scope** (tier/region/model/SDK)
**Quick checks** (what to ask for)
**Workaround / mitigation** (numbered)
**Escalate when** (explicit triggers)
**Notes / long-term fix**
**Last updated / owner**

### B. Required escalation context (minimum viable page)
- Customer + tier (Hosted/Dedicated/Private)
- Region + model + endpoint
- Request IDs (3–5 examples)
- Start time + current status
- Error rates / symptoms summary
- Recent changes (SDK upgrade, deploy, config)
- What has already been attempted (and result)

title: Known Issues & Workarounds Index (Support + CS Landing)
content:
## Purpose
This page is the landing index for **Known Issues & Workarounds** used by **Support** and **Customer Success**. It is optimized for:
- Faster triage (copy/paste symptoms + quick checks)
- Lower repeat ticket volume (consistent workaround guidance)
- Clear escalation decisions (when to page SRE/Eng vs continue troubleshooting)

This index only includes issues that meet the **Known Issue publication criteria**: reproducible symptoms, validated workaround (or clear mitigation limits), and named owner + review cadence.

> Customer-sensitive details (account identifiers, internal hostnames, customer-specific configs) must not be added to KB pages or this index.

---

## How to use this index (Support/CS)
1) Identify the best matching issue by **symptom** and **tags** (tier/region/model).
2) Follow the linked **workaround article** and use the relevant **Support macro/snippet**.
3) If escalation criteria are met, escalate using:
   - **Severity Matrix + Escalation Triggers** (P0–P4 ↔ Sev mapping)
   - **SLA policy by customer tier** (response + update cadence)
   - **Slack bridge conventions** (when to move to #incidents)
4) Add the KB link to the ticket and include what was tried.

**Support workflow expectation:** When a ticket matches an entry below, link the KB article in the Jira ticket (SUP) and record:
- Which workaround steps were attempted
- Result (resolved / partial / no change)
- Whether escalation criteria were met

---

## Tags and terminology
**Tier tags**
- Hosted = Redwood API (self-serve + enterprise Hosted)
- Dedicated = Dedicated GPU pools
- Private = VPC / on-prem

**Region tags (examples)**
- us-east, us-west, eu-west

**Model tags (examples)**
- Any = model-agnostic (gateway/SDK/network/control plane)
- Embeddings = embeddings endpoints
- Chat/Completion = streaming/non-streaming generation

**Status tags**
- Active = currently observed recently and still possible
- Mitigated = mitigation in place; may recur under certain conditions
- Fixed pending rollout = fix merged/released but not fully rolled out
- Resolved = no longer expected; keep for 30–60 days as reference

---

## Escalation guidance (applies to all known issues)
Escalate using the standard escalation playbook; do not bypass incident processes.

**Escalate immediately (page on-call / start bridge) if any are true:**
- Customer impact meets **P0/P1** criteria (see Severity Matrix)
- Error rate spike / hard outage is suspected (auth failures, widespread 5xx, widespread timeouts)
- Multi-customer/regional impact or credible revenue/SLA risk
- Customer reports security/compliance risk (audit logs, access control) and is enterprise/private

**Escalate after initial checks if:**
- Workaround steps were applied correctly and **no improvement**
- We cannot confirm telemetry signals (missing request IDs/region/model, or inconsistent metrics)
- Symptoms deviate materially from the known issue description

**Before escalating, include (minimum context):**
- Request IDs (or sample request IDs), timestamps (with timezone), region, model, endpoint
- SDK + version, streaming vs non-streaming, retries/timeouts config
- Customer tier (Hosted/Dedicated/Private) and support coverage window
- Any recent change noted by customer (SDK upgrade, deploy, routing policy changes)

---

## Index of Known Issues (curated)
> Tip: When opening a Slack bridge, paste the relevant workaround link and the “Escalate when” line.

| Known issue | Symptoms (customer-visible) | Affected tags | Workaround / KB | Status | Last updated | Primary owner | When to escalate |
|---|---|---|---|---|---:|---|---|
| Streaming timeouts / disconnects (reset or truncated stream) | Stream resets mid-generation, truncated output, client sees ECONNRESET / incomplete chunks | Tier: Hosted, Dedicated · Region: us-east (most reports), Any · Model: Chat/Completion (streaming) | /customer-success-and-support/known-issues-and-workarounds/workaround-streaming-timeouts-and-reconnect | Active | 2026-02-14 | Owen Phillips (Support Incidents) | Escalate if reproducible on Redwood sample clients, >1 customer affected in 60 min, or any enterprise account blocked; escalate immediately if error rate spike/regional pattern suspected. |
| 429 quota mismatch / confusing rate-limit headers | Customer sees 429s after SDK upgrade; headers inconsistent vs Console quota; perceived “unexpected throttling” | Tier: Hosted · Region: Any · Model: Any | /customer-success-and-support/known-issues-and-workarounds/workaround-429-quota-mismatch-and-rate-limit-headers | Fixed pending rollout | 2026-02-13 | Ethan Park (Platform) | Escalate if headers are inconsistent across endpoints in same time window, or if customer is hard-blocked despite low observed usage; attach header samples + request IDs. |
| Dedicated autoscaling oscillation causing latency spikes | Latency spikes + throughput drops correlated with scale up/down churn; uneven tail lat | Tier: Dedicated · Region: Any · Model: Any | /customer-success-and-support/known-issues-and-workarounds/workaround-dedicated-autoscaling-oscillation | Mitigated | 2026-02-14 | Sean Gallagher (SRE) | Escalate if p95 latency breaches customer SLO for >15 min, replicas flap repeatedly despite cooldown changes, or if capacity/burst not activating as configured. |
| Private installer upgrade stuck at migrations | Upgrade hangs or fails during migration step; rollback uncertainty; repeated retries worsen | Tier: Private · Region: Customer VPC/on-prem · Model: N/A | /customer-success-and-support/known-issues-and-workarounds/workaround-private-installer-upgrade-stuck-migrations | Active | 2026-02-12 | Priya Natarajan (Platform) | Escalate immediately if production Private deployment is blocked, rollback is required, or customer is in a regulated window; collect diagnostics bundle/logs per article before paging. |
| Audit log delivery latency (lag > expected) | Audit logs delayed (e.g., 15–60+ min), customer compliance concerns, SIEM pipeline appears stale | Tier: Hosted Enterprise, Private · Region: Any · Model: N/A | /customer-success-and-support/known-issues-and-workarounds/workaround-audit-log-delivery-latency | Active | 2026-02-14 | Allison Grant (Observability) | Escalate if lag exceeds enterprise expectation threshold (per SLA policy), if multiple accounts show lag, or if customer states compliance breach risk; include timestamps + tenant/org ID via secure internal channel only. |

---

## Additional high-frequency issues (candidate / watchlist)
These are **not** fully published as Known Issues unless linked to a KB article with validated workaround. Keep an eye on trend changes and file tickets with consistent repro info.

| Issue (watchlist) | Symptoms | Tags | Current guidance | Owner | Last reviewed |
|---|---|---|---|---|---:|
| Model version pin perceived “ignored” during fallback | Customer expects pinned version but sees different behavior during degradation | Tier: Hosted/Dedicated · Region: Any · Model: Any | Use routing metrics + policy review; confirm fallback configuration and whether pinned version allows compatible variants. Escalate if metrics show fallback contradicts policy. | Mina Haddad | 2026-02-15 |
| Console latency dashboard missing region breakdown | eu-west (or other region) missing from Console filters; customers ask for interim reporting | Tier: Hosted/Dedicated · Region: Console · Model: N/A | Provide interim metrics export guidance; open Platform telemetry ticket if confirmed. | Ethan Park | 2026-02-15 |
| Embeddings endpoint timeouts (eu-west) | Increased timeout rate; customer sees retries and degraded throughput | Tier: Hosted · Region: eu-west · Model: Embeddings | Follow triage checklist; if multiple customers affected, move to #incidents and consider status-page criteria. | Sean Gallagher | 2026-02-15 |
| SAML SSO login loop in Console | Redirect loop after IdP login, cannot access Console | Tier: Enterprise Hosted/Private · Region: Any · Model: N/A | Collect IdP metadata + Console auth logs request; escalate to Control Plane if reproducible. | Ethan Park | 2026-02-15 |

---

## Maintenance policy (ownership + freshness)
- Each Known Issue must have a **Primary owner** and at least one **reviewer**.
- Owners review entries **weekly during the sprint window** and **biweekly** afterwards.
- If an issue is marked **Fixed pending rollout**, update this index once rollout is complete and record the date.
- If an issue becomes **Resolved**, keep it listed for **30–60 days** with a note pointing to the fix/release, then remove from the index.

**Change control:**
- Edits that change escalation thresholds or SLA language require review from **Support Ops (Dev Patel)** and **SRE (Sean Gallagher or Rafael Mendes)**.

---

## Where to link this from
- Jira SUP ticket templates/macros (auto-suggest this index for new tickets)
- Support triage intake checklist
- Slack bridge workflow pinned message
- CS QBR prep checklist (link relevant known issues for top accounts)

---

## Changelog (recent)
- 2026-02-15: Added watchlist section; clarified escalation minimum context; refreshed owners/reviewers. (Elliot Price)
- 2026-02-14: Published initial set of sprint-known issues (streaming, 429/quota, Dedicated autoscaling, Private upgrade, audit log lag). (Docs/Support/Eng reviewers)

title: Enterprise priority: 429 / quota / overload behavior (Support guide)
content:
## Purpose
This page is a Support/CS reference for explaining **429** responses after the **Hot-route capacity protection** rollout. It covers:
- What customers may see (payload + headers)
- How to distinguish **quota** vs **rate-limit** vs **overload shedding/admission control**
- Recommended customer-side retry/backoff behavior
- When and how to escalate (and what data to collect)

This doc is written for Support and TAMs. For implementation details, see the Platform design/ADR pages linked in Related pages.

---

## What changed (customer-visible)
Beginning with the enterprise priority rollout, Redwood enforces **tier-aware capacity protection** on a set of “protected routes” (commonly: `/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/embeddings`, `/v1/rerank`).

Customers may observe:
- **More predictable 429s** for best-effort/self-serve traffic during regional pressure.
- **Enterprise traffic preserved** longer (priority routing + per-tier budgets), but enterprise requests can still receive 429s when:
  - the account’s own limits are reached, or
  - the route is in sustained overload and the enterprise budget is exhausted.
- **New reason codes** and additional headers to explain why the request was rejected.

Important framing for customers:
- 429 is **not** a “generic outage” signal. It is a deliberate backpressure mechanism to protect overall fleet health and enterprise SLOs.
- 429 responses are **safe to retry** when the reason indicates transient pressure, using the guidance below.

---

## 429 response format (what Support should look for)

### Common JSON fields (all 429s)
Most clients will receive an error payload shaped like:
- `error.type`: `rate_limit_exceeded` or `quota_exceeded` or `overloaded`
- `error.code`: a stable machine-readable reason code (see table below)
- `error.message`: human-readable summary
- `error.request_id`: request identifier (also returned in response headers)

If a customer claims the payload is missing or inconsistent, ask for:
- raw response body
- full response headers
- SDK version / client library

### Standard headers (may vary by route)
Support should request and record these headers when present:
- `x-redwood-request-id`: request ID used for internal tracing
- `retry-after`: seconds to wait before retry (only set for some transient reasons)
- `x-redwood-retry-after-ms`: millisecond retry hint (preferred when present)
- `x-redwood-limit-scope`: `account` | `api_key` | `route` (where enforcement applies)
- `x-redwood-limit-policy`: policy identifier (internal-friendly string; customer can share as opaque)
- `x-redwood-429-reason`: short reason token (maps to reason codes below)
- `x-redwood-rate-limit-limit`: numeric limit (requests per window) when applicable
- `x-redwood-rate-limit-remaining`: remaining requests in current window (when applicable)
- `x-redwood-rate-limit-reset`: epoch time or seconds-until-reset (when applicable)

Notes:
- Some enterprise customers will only see a subset of limit headers depending on contract configuration and route group settings.
- Absence of headers is not automatically a bug; it can indicate a rejection occurred upstream of quota evaluation (e.g., admission control).

---

## Reason codes (how to interpret 429s)
Use the following table to classify the issue and advise the customer.

### A) Quota- and rate-limit-driven 429s (customer-specific)
These are expected when a customer exceeds their configured limits.

| Category | error.type | x-redwood-429-reason (typical) | Meaning | Customer guidance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hard quota exceeded | quota_exceeded | quota_window_exhausted | Customer has consumed their quota for the current window. | Do not retry immediately. Wait until reset. Consider limit increase request. |
| Rate limit exceeded | rate_limit_exceeded | rate_limit_account | Customer exceeded account-level request rate. | Retry with exponential backoff + jitter. Reduce concurrency / smooth bursts. |
| Route-group rate limit | rate_limit_exceeded | rate_limit_route_group | Customer exceeded a per-route or route-group cap. | Same as above; ask them to spread load or request a higher burst allowance. |
| Token / compute guardrail | rate_limit_exceeded | token_budget_exceeded | Customer exceeded a token/compute budget (if enabled for contract). | Reduce max_tokens / request size; smooth traffic; discuss contract sizing. |

### B) Overload protection / admission control 429s (fleet pressure)
These indicate transient capacity protection behavior.

| Category | error.type | x-redwood-429-reason (typical) | Meaning | Customer guidance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Admission control (best-effort shed) | overloaded | shed_best_effort | Fleet/route is under pressure; best-effort traffic is being throttled first. | Retry with exponential backoff + jitter. Prefer queueing client-side. |
| Admission control (enterprise budget exhausted) | overloaded | shed_enterprise_budget | Protected route is overloaded and enterprise budget is fully utilized. | Retry using Retry-After if present; reduce concurrency; contact Support if sustained. |
| Regional capacity constraint | overloaded | region_capacity | Selected region is capacity constrained; request rejected to prevent tail latency cascade. | Retry with backoff; if multi-region is enabled, allow client failover. |
| Policy evaluation deny | overloaded | policy_deny_overload | Policy engine denied admission due to active overload rule (e.g., queue depth trigger). | Treat as transient. Retry with backoff. Provide request IDs for investigation if frequent. |

Support positioning:
- For enterprise accounts: “This is protective backpressure to preserve latency/availability for protected routes. It can occur during unusual bursts or regional pressure.”
- For self-serve/best-effort: “During peak pressure, the platform prioritizes higher-SLA traffic; your requests may be throttled earlier.”

---

## Recommended customer retry & backoff guidance
Provide the following general guidance (tailor to the customer’s stack):

### When to retry
- Retry 429s when:
  - `error.type = overloaded` (most cases)
  - `error.type = rate_limit_exceeded`
- Do NOT aggressively retry when:
  - `error.type = quota_exceeded` and the response includes a reset hint (wait until reset)

### How to retry (recommended algorithm)
- Use **exponential backoff with full jitter**.
- Start with 250–500ms base delay.
- Cap max delay at 10–30s.
- Add client-side request queueing to avoid stampedes.
- Respect `retry-after` and/or `x-redwood-retry-after-ms` when present (prefer the ms header).

Suggested pseudocode guidance to share (language-agnostic):
1) if `retry-after` present → sleep for that duration (+ small jitter) then retry
2) else backoff = random(0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt))
3) stop after a reasonable max attempts (typically 5–8) and surface a retriable error to the application

### Concurrency guidance
Customers with high parallelism should:
- Implement a per-route concurrency limiter (token bucket / semaphore)
- Smooth bursty workloads (batching where possible)
- Avoid synchronized retries across many workers (jitter)

### Idempotency guidance
- For non-streaming requests, retries are generally safe.
- For streaming requests, see “Streaming semantics” below.

---

## Streaming semantics during shedding (common ticket driver)
Some customers report “inconsistent termination” on streaming responses during load shedding.

Support guidance:
- If a request is rejected **before** streaming begins, they should receive a normal 429 with reason + headers.
- If a request is accepted and then terminated due to downstream pressure, behavior depends on the transport:
  - Customers should treat early stream termination as retriable if they did not receive a completed response.
  - Advise customers to log the `x-redwood-request-id` and last event received.

Escalate if:
- customers see a successful HTTP status but the stream ends without an explicit termination signal and without consistent client-visible error handling, or
- the customer provides multiple request IDs showing premature termination correlated with new overload reasons.

---

## What Support should ask for (intake checklist)
Request the following in the initial reply to reduce ping-pong:
1) Affected route(s): e.g., `/v1/chat/completions`
2) Region/endpoint base URL (if multi-region)
3) Time window (with timezone) and approximate request rate
4) Sample `x-redwood-request-id` values (3–10 IDs)
5) Full 429 response headers + body (raw)
6) Whether they are using streaming
7) Their current retry policy (backoff, max attempts, concurrency)
8) Whether it’s isolated to a single API key or all keys in the account

Internal-only (if available to TAM/CS): contract tier (Hosted API vs Dedicated), priority class, and any approved exceptions.

---

## Escalation criteria (when to page/loop in Engineering)
Escalate to SRE/Platform when ANY of the following are true:

### Enterprise impact thresholds
- Enterprise customer reports sustained 429s on a protected route for **>10 minutes** AND:
  - reason indicates overload protection (`overloaded/*`), OR
  - they claim traffic is within contracted limits but still seeing 429s
- Enterprise customer reports p95/p99 latency degradation plus 429 spikes (possible mis-tuned thresholds)

### Suspected misconfiguration
- `x-redwood-limit-policy` changes unexpectedly after rollout / config migration
- A single tenant is denied while peers are not, and headers indicate route-group limits that don’t match the contract

### Possible platform bug
- Missing/incorrect reason codes across multiple requests
- `retry-after` values that are clearly wrong (e.g., negative, extremely large, inconsistent with window)
- Streaming termination inconsistencies correlated with overload events

### Security / access concerns
- Customer requests details about other tenants, fleet state, or priority policy internals beyond what we disclose. Route via TAM/CS + Security as needed.

---

## Escalation process (internal)
1) Create/attach a ticket in the Support queue and tag: `overload-protection` + `enterprise`.
2) Post in `#incidents` (if active event suspected) or `#eng-sre` with:
   - customer/account
   - affected routes/regions
   - timeframe
   - reason codes + sample request IDs
   - whether Retry-After was present and followed
3) Link the relevant dashboards (SRE on-call will pull). If you have access, include:
   - enterprise route SLO dashboard
   - overload protection shed-rate panel
   - admission control trigger annotations

If immediate paging is warranted, follow the runbook: “Overload protection and admission control” (Related pages).

---

## Approved external explanation (copy/paste)
Use this when responding to customers (edit for their tier/route):

“HTTP 429 indicates the request was throttled or temporarily rejected to protect latency and availability. For protected enterprise routes, Redwood prioritizes higher-SLA traffic under peak load to prevent fleet-wide degradation. Please implement exponential backoff with jitter and respect any Retry-After headers. If you share a few request IDs and the full response headers/body, we can confirm whether the 429s are due to your configured limits (quota/rate) or transient overload protection.”

---

## FAQ (Support)

**Q: Is a 429 an outage?**
A: Not necessarily. For many overload cases, it’s intentional backpressure to avoid tail latency/5xx cascading failures.

**Q: Can enterprise customers still get 429s?**
A: Yes—if they exceed their contracted limits, or in rare cases when a protected route’s enterprise budget is fully consumed during sustained overload.

**Q: Should customers increase retry aggressiveness to “push through”?**
A: No. Aggressive retries worsen overload. Encourage backoff + jitter + client-side queueing.

**Q: Customer says they stayed under their “RPM” but still got 429.**
A: Ask for headers and request IDs. They may be hitting a route-group limit, a token/compute guardrail, or experiencing transient admission control without Retry-After being honored.

---

## Change log
- 2026-02-06: Added streaming termination guidance + escalation triggers for inconsistent SSE termination.
- 2026-01-23: Updated reason-code table to include `shed_enterprise_budget` and `region_capacity`.
- 2026-01-09: Initial publication for Support enablement ahead of GA rollout.

title: Known issues: API key rotation/revocation edge cases
content:
# Summary
This page documents recurring customer issues encountered during Hosted API key rotation/revocation.

# Issue 1: intermittent 401s after rotation
**Symptoms**
- Some requests succeed, some fail with 401.

**Likely cause**
- Customer updated one service but not all workloads (cron jobs, background workers, edge functions).

**Recommended fix**
- Search customer repos/infra for the old key name/secret reference.
- Deploy new secret everywhere.
- After validating all components, revoke the old key.

# Issue 2: propagation delays (rare)
**Symptoms**
- Immediately after disabling a key, a small number of requests still authenticate for a short window.

**Notes**
- The system is designed for immediate revocation, but a limited edge-cache inconsistency has been observed in rare cases.

**Workaround**
- Advise customer to allow up to 60 seconds.
- If it persists > 5 minutes, open a support ticket and capture request ids.

# Issue 3: customer pasted key id, not key value
**Symptoms**
- All requests fail with 401 immediately after update.

**Fix**
- Clarify difference between the key record identifier vs the secret key value shown once at creation/regeneration.

# Issue 4: SDK env var mismatch
**Symptoms**
- Customer rotates key but still sees 401 in production.

**Likely cause**
- Different variable name between environments (e.g., `REDWOOD_API_KEY` vs `REDWOOD_HOSTED_API_KEY`).

**Fix**
- Confirm config in the runtime environment and redeploy.

# Related
- Support playbook: help customers rotate/revoke Hosted API keys
- Customer guide: Hosted API key rotation & revocation

title: Hosted API: Intermittent streaming disconnects (March 2026) - known issue + tracking
content:
## Overview
Some customers have reported intermittent disconnections during streaming responses on the Hosted API (OpenAI-compatible streaming/SSE). The symptoms often present as truncated completions, missing final chunk/[DONE], or client-side errors such as "unexpected EOF" or "socket hang up".

This page documents the known issue pattern observed in March 2026, affected environments, and where to track active customer cases.

## Customer-visible symptoms
- Streaming ends mid-generation (partial text returned)
- Client receives "connection closed" / "unexpected EOF"
- Missing final "done" signal
- Retries usually succeed

## Affected surfaces
- Hosted API OpenAI-compatible endpoints (chat.completions streaming=true)
- Regions observed: us-east, eu-west

## Workarounds (customer guidance)
1. Implement retries when a stream terminates unexpectedly (treat as retryable error).
2. Increase client read timeout for long generations.
3. Ensure SSE parser tolerates missing final chunk and does not deadlock UI state.

## Root cause (current understanding)
Edge/proxy configuration on streaming routes can prematurely close connections under certain backpressure/idle patterns, especially during/after edge rollouts. Model layer errors are typically not present.

## Active case tracking (MUST keep complete)
The following customer escalation cases are currently associated with this known issue pattern in March 2026:
- SUP-4821 (Acme Analytics, us-east)
- SUP-4877 (BetaAI, eu-west)
- SUP-4899 (CloudCart, eu-west)

If you see a new customer report that matches the symptoms, add the SUP key here and link to any Slack incident threads.

## Related incident threads
- Slack #incidents thread_ts=1773815400 (eu-west streaming disconnect ratio alert)

## Ownership
- Support triage: Customer Support
- Investigation: Platform + SRE
- Customer comms: CSM/Support

title: Enterprise Telemetry & Cost Attribution Connector Playbook
content:
Overview

This playbook describes recommended configurations and operational steps for integrating Redwood Inference usage telemetry and cost-attribution with an enterprise customer's billing/observability stack. The goal is to provide consistent, auditable usage exports, per-route/customer attribution, and near-real-time alerts for cost anomalies. Target audiences: customer success engineers, solutions engineers, platform engineers at customers, and finance contacts.

Scope

- Inbound integrations supported: Redwood Usage Webhook, Billing Export (S3/BigQuery), Prometheus metrics pull via our telemetry bridge.
- Downstream systems: Customer billing system (ERP), data warehouse (BigQuery/Redshift), observability tools (Grafana/Datadog), cost controllers (FinOps).
- Not in scope: Per-model weights for internal cost modeling (handled by internal finance team).

Goals

1. Deliver line-item granularity by API key / project / route (where available).
2. Ensure exports are delivered within 5 minutes for webhooks and within 1 hour for batch billing exports.
3. Provide a mapping template for customers to reconcile Redwood usage with their invoices.

Ownership & Contacts

- CS Lead: Sofia Martinez (author) - primary contact for playbook and cutover coordination.
- Integration Owner (Redwood): Evan Clarke - handles API keys, webhook signing, and support escalations.
- Customer Success Engineer: assigned per account (add name during onboarding).
- Customer FinOps contact: required; must approve mapping and reconciliation rules.

Prerequisites (Customer)

1. Stable endpoint for webhook receiver (HTTPS) or read-access service account for cloud export (GCS/BQ/Redshift).
2. Firewall rules allowing Redwood egress IPs (see appendix) or mutual TLS where required.
3. FinOps/finance stakeholder to validate mapping table.

Architecture & Data Flow

(Plain-text diagram)
[Client apps] -> Redwood API -> Inference Runtime -> Usage Aggregator -> (a) Usage Webhook -> Customer Receiver
                                                         
                                                          -> (b) Billing Export (S3/GCS/BQ) -> Customer Data Warehouse
                                                          
                                                          -> (c) Telemetry Bridge -> Prometheus/Grafana/Datadog

Connector Options (choose one or combine)

- Usage Webhook (recommended for near-real-time): pushes event-level or aggregated records. Supports HMAC signing and retry semantics.
- Billing Export (batch; canonical): daily/hourly files in parquet/CSV to S3/GCS or native BigQuery export. Best for invoice reconciliation.
- Telemetry Bridge (metrics): Prometheus scrape or pushgateway bridge for operational metrics (latency, qps, token counts).

Schema & Mapping Guidance

Use the following canonical fields when reconciling with customer systems. The table below is a suggested mapping; customers may add columns as needed.

| Redwood Field | Type | Description | Recommended target field name |
|---------------|------|-------------|------------------------------|
| timestamp | ISO8601 string | Event time | event_time |
| customer_id | string | Redwood customer id | customer_external_id |
| project_id | string | Customer project / org identifier | project_id |
| api_key_hash | string | 8-char hashed key for PII minimization | api_key_fingerprint |
| route | string | API route/operation name (text/generate/embed) | product_route |
| model | string | Model id or variant | model_id |
| tokens_consumed | integer | Total tokens billed in event | tokens |
| prompt_tokens | integer | Prompt tokens | prompt_tokens |
| completion_tokens | integer | Completion tokens | completion_tokens |
| cost_usd | decimal | Calculated cost USD | cost_usd |
| invoice_id | string | Optional invoice reference | invoice_reference |

Implementation Steps (detailed)

1) Design workshop (1–2 hours)
   - Participants: Redwood CSE, customer FinOps, customer platform engineer, relevant product owner.
   - Deliverable: mapping spreadsheet (CSV) with sample records and reconciliation rules.

2) Choose connector and provide credentials
   - Webhook: customer provides HTTPS endpoint and signing public key (or Redwood will sign requests with HMAC).
   - Batch export: customer provides S3/GCS bucket ARN with write permissions or a BQ dataset with write access.
   - Telemetry: customer shares Prometheus scrape endpoint or sets up a remote_write receiver.

3) Test harness setup (staging)
   - Redwood will enable test mode for the specific customer and send a fixed dataset for validation.
   - Run 3 reconciliation cycles: immediate webhook, hourly batch, and daily invoice-style export.

4) Validation checklist (must pass before production)
   - All fields in mapping table present and parsable.
   - Timestamps within 2 minutes for webhook flows.
   - No more than 0.5% dropped events over a 24-hour test.
   - Cost totals within ±0.5% compared to Redwood internal billing for test window.

Example: Usage Webhook payload (trimmed)

POST /customer/usage HTTP/1.1
Host: example-customer.com
Content-Type: application/json
X-Redwood-Signature: sha256=abcdef...

{
  "timestamp": "2026-01-17T15:12:03Z",
  "customer_id": "cust_8XY12",
  "project_id": "marketing-website",
  "api_key_hash": "a1b2c3d4",
  "route": "generate.text",
  "model": "redwood-rwkv-3-small-v1",
  "prompt_tokens": 72,
  "completion_tokens": 128,
  "tokens_consumed": 200,
  "cost_usd": 0.0142
}

CLI & IAM examples

- Granting Redwood write access to a GCS bucket (customer side - example):
  gcloud storage buckets add-iam-policy-binding gs://example-billing-export \\n    --member=serviceAccount:redwood-exporter@redwood-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com \\n    --role=roles/storage.objectCreator

- Minimal IAM for BigQuery export:
  roles/bigquery.dataEditor + dataset-level grant for redwood-exporter SA.

Validation & QA tests (automated)

- End-to-end smoke test: generate 10 synthetic requests from staging and confirm they appear in the warehouse and webhook receiver within expected windows.
- Reconciliation test: run a SQL aggregation to total tokens and cost; compare against Redwood expected totals. Example query (BigQuery):
  SELECT project_id, SUM(tokens_consumed) AS tokens, SUM(cost_usd) AS cost
  FROM `redwood_customer_billing.events_20260117`
  GROUP BY project_id

Monitoring, Alerts & SLOs

- Delivery latency: median webhook delivery <= 30s, 95th <= 120s.
- Delivery success: webhook retry success rate >= 99.5% over rolling 24h.
- Export availability: daily billing export available by 03:00 UTC daily.
- Alerts to configure in customer observability:
  - Missing export file for the day (trigger at 03:30 UTC)
  - Webhook status 4xx/5xx spike > 1% over 15m
  - Cost spike: rolling 6-hour cost increases > 200% vs trailing 7-day average (auto-mute rules recommended for releases).

Rollout & Cutover Checklist

- Week -2: Mapping workshop completed and signed by customer FinOps.
- Week -1: Staging export validated (3 cycles).
- Day -1: Final configuration exported; notify stakeholders and schedule cutover window (1 hour).
- Cutover: switch production export to customer endpoint; monitor first 2 hours closely.
- Day +1: Post-cutover reconciliation and sign-off by FinOps.

Common Troubleshooting & Known Gotchas

- Duplicate events in webhook receiver: usually caused by client-side retry without idempotency keys. Solution: use api_key_hash + timestamp + event_id dedupe window (configurable).
- Timezone mismatches: ensure all systems store timestamps in UTC.
- Partial fields in batch export: older export versions may omit prompt_tokens; mapping spreadsheet must include fallback rules (e.g., set prompt_tokens=NULL and flag record).
- Large payload rejections: customers behind strict WAFs may block long POST bodies; enable chunking or increase WAF body size to >= 512KB.

Maintenance & Upgrades

- Redwood will provide a deprecation notice for schema changes at least 90 days in advance.
- Backwards compatibility policy: we guarantee 6 months of support for deprecated fields.

Security & Compliance

- PII minimization: Redwood will redact API keys and provide api_key_hash only.
- Webhook signing: HMAC-SHA256 signing available; customers must verify signature.
- Data residency: batch exports will respect customer region settings (EU/US).
- Retention: exported files are customer property; Redwood retains temporary copies for up to 7 days in case of delivery failures.

Appendix: Network & IPs

- Redwood egress ranges (for firewall allowlist): 3.34.12.0/24, 52.14.200.0/22, 34.75.100.0/23 (note: customers should reference the canonical list in /confluence/eng-infra/cloud-accounts-and-networking/egress-ip-list).

Appendix: Sample reconciliation SQL (Postgres)

-- Aggregate daily cost per project
SELECT project_id, date_trunc('day', timestamp) AS day, SUM(cost_usd) AS total_cost 
FROM redwood_billing.events 
WHERE timestamp >= current_date - interval '7 days' 
GROUP BY project_id, day
ORDER BY day DESC;

Related pages

- /confluence/customer-success-and-support/health-and-qbr/enterprise-cost-anomaly-detection-and-action-playbook-2026
- /confluence/eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/usage-metrics-standardization

Change log

- 2025-11-10 (Sofia Martinez): Created initial draft.
- 2025-12-05 (Evan Clarke): Added webhook signing section and IP ranges.
- 2026-01-18 (Maya Patel): Finalized SLAs and added troubleshooting items.

title: Telemetry budget-aware sampling and onboarding guide
content:
Summary
-------
This playbook describes Redwood's recommended approach for onboarding enterprise customers to a budget-aware telemetry sampling strategy. It focuses on balancing fidelity and observability cost by combining adaptive sampling, reservoir sampling for high-cardinality tenants, and cost-feedback loops driven by billing/ingestion signals. The guide contains architecture patterns, configuration examples, rollout steps, acceptance criteria, and an operational runbook for support teams.

Goals
-----
- Ensure observable signal quality for SLOs and QBR metrics while controlling telemetry ingestion cost at tenant and org levels.
- Provide a reproducible onboarding checklist that Customer Success, Solutions Engineering, and Platform teams can follow.
- Reduce noise and storage costs without losing critical anomaly and regression signals.

When to use this guide
----------------------
Use this playbook for new enterprise tenants where expected telemetry volume or cost could exceed baseline thresholds, or for existing customers whose telemetry spend triggers a cost-protection review. Typical triggers:
- Projected ingestion > $2k/month for logs/metrics/traces (estimate)
- Hosting dedicated or high-throughput agents behind heavy API traffic
- Customers requesting strict cost caps or billing alerts

High-level architecture
-----------------------
1) Data sources: SDKs, agent-side sampling, edge sidecars, ingress proxies.
2) Adaptive sampling service: centralized orchestration that issues per-tenant sampling policies and receives cost/traffic telemetry.
3) Store & query: short-term hot store + long-term cold store; sampling tags preserved for deterministic rehydration.
4) Cost telemetry & feedback: ingestion meter emits cost estimates back to the adaptive sampling service for policy updates.

Core concepts and patterns
--------------------------
- Budget-aware sampling: set a target ingestion budget and tune sampling to meet it while prioritizing high-value traces/events.
- Priority buckets: classify events/traces into priority tiers (critical, high, normal, debug) using rules derived from tenant-provided signal sets.
- Reservoir sampling for high-cardinality keys: maintain a fixed reservoir per key (user_id/session_id) to avoid missing rare but important patterns.
- Deterministic retention tags: attach deterministic tags so downstream ingestion can rehydrate or re-evaluate samples if needed.
- Grace windows: when a model rollout or canary is active, temporarily raise fidelity for affected traffic slices.

Sampling algorithms we recommend
------------------------------
- Static-rate sampling: simple global rate for low-risk tenants. Good as a baseline.
- Adaptive latency-aware sampling: increase sampling for requests with latency > p95 to keep tail behavior visible.
- Budget-driven proportional sampling: compute per-minute budget deficit and multiply base sampling by budget_factor = target_spend/current_spend.
- Hybrid reservoir+probabilistic: reservoir for cardinality keys + probabilistic sampling for generic events.

Configuration examples
----------------------
Below is a representative YAML policy that the adaptive sampling service consumes. Replace variables as appropriate for the tenant.

# Example: tenant sampling policy
tenant_id: tenant-1234
budget_monthly_usd: 1200
priority_buckets:
  critical:
    selectors:
      - event.type == \"deployment_error\"
    sample_rate: 1.0
  high:
    selectors:
      - request.latency_ms > 500
    sample_rate: 0.75
  normal:
    selectors: []
    sample_rate: 0.2
  debug:
    selectors: []
    sample_rate: 0.02
reservoir_keys:
  - user_id
  - session_id
reservoir_target_per_minute: 1000
budget_mode: proportional
budget_evaluation_window_minutes: 60

CLI and API snippets
--------------------
- Inspect current policy: redwoodctl sampling get --tenant tenant-1234
- Apply policy: redwoodctl sampling apply --file tenant-1234-sampling.yaml
- Force snapshot of reservoir state: redwoodctl sampling snapshot --tenant tenant-1234 --out /tmp/snap.json

Rollout and onboarding steps (owner assignments)
------------------------------------------------
1) Pre-onboard (Solutions Eng)
   - Collect expected QPS, user cardinality, peak window and cost constraints from customer. (Owner: Solutions Eng)
   - Baseline: deploy instrumentation agent on staging and collect 72 hours of data. (Owner: Customer Success + SE)
2) Policy design (Customer Success + Eng Platform)
   - Create initial policy YAML using templates above. (Owner: Eng Platform)
   - Decide priority buckets and reservoir keys with customer. (Owner: Customer Success)
3) Staging validation (Customer Success + Customer)
   - Apply policy to staging, run synthetic traffic for 24-48 hours. Validate that SLO telemetry remains visible (p50/p95/p99). (Owner: Customer Success)\   - Generate cost estimate report for the month given observed ingest rates. (Owner: Finance-legal telemetry)
4) Canary (Eng SRE + Customer)
   - Canary to 5–10% production traffic slice or to a small service subset. Monitor signal fidelity and missed-anomaly rate. (Owner: Eng SRE)
5) Full rollout and tune (Customer Success + Eng SRE)
   - Gradually increase to 100% over 24–72 hours with close monitoring. Tune bucket rates and reservoir targets. (Owner: Customer Success)

Acceptance criteria and QBR signals
----------------------------------
- Telemetry cost at or below target budget ±10% after first full calendar month.
- No more than 2 missed P0 anomalies during the first 30 days attributable to sampling.
- SLO visibility: key SLI time-series (error rate, p95 latency, tokens-per-request) retain >= 95% of pre-sampling alert fidelity for critical services.
- QBR metrics to track: ingestion_cost_by_tenant, sampling_rate_by_bucket, missed_anomaly_count, reservoir_fill_ratio

Monitoring dashboards and alerts
------------------------------
Create the following dashboards before canary:
- Tenant overview: total ingestion per hour, cost estimate rolling 30d, sampling rate heatmap.
- Bucket fidelity: per-bucket event counts, anomaly detection hit-rate, representative examples.
- Reservoir health: fill ratio, eviction rate, top keys by cardinality.

Suggested alerts (examples)
- ingestion_cost_estimate > budget_monthly_usd * 1.15 (SEV-3)
- missed_anomaly_count > 1 in 24 hours (SEV-2)
- reservoir_fill_ratio < 0.5 for 30 minutes (SEV-2)

Operational runbook (support process)
------------------------------------
1) Customer reports increased cost or missing signals.
2) Triage owner (Customer Success) opens a joint incident channel and collects: tenant_id, sampling policy version, example event IDs, and timeframe.
3) Quick checks (Eng SRE)
   - Verify policy is applied: redwoodctl sampling get --tenant <id>
   - Check ingestion spike sources: ingress proxy logs and SDK agent versions.
   - Correlate ingest rate vs. billing meter for last 24h.
4) If fidelity issue confirmed, options: temporarily raise sampling for affected selectors, deploy a grace window, or snapshot and backfill high-priority traces to cold store for targeted windows.
5) Post-incident: adjust policy and add guardrail alerts to prevent recurrence.

Troubleshooting matrix
----------------------
- Symptom: sudden drop in p95 visibility
  - Likely cause: overly aggressive global rate; stale reservoir keys
  - Action: roll back to previous policy, increase normal bucket to 0.5, start a canary.
- Symptom: ingestion cost unexpectedly high
  - Likely cause: misconfigured selectors or policy not applied (agent mismatch)
  - Action: confirm agent version and policy hash; revert to earlier policy; throttle agent sidecar.
- Symptom: reservoir starvation for a key
  - Likely cause: incorrect key selection or hot-key anomaly
  - Action: temporarily promote key to high priority and increase reservoir_target_per_minute

Customer-facing communication templates
--------------------------------------
- Initial onboarding note: a one-paragraph summary of the expected behavior, staging dates, and cost guardrails.
- Incident advisory: brief description, immediate mitigation steps, timeline for root cause analysis, and next steps.

Appendix: checklist (quick)
--------------------------
- [ ] Collect traffic profile (QPS, peak QPS, cardinality)
- [ ] Baseline 72h staging data collected
- [ ] Initial policy created and reviewed
- [ ] Dashboards provisioned and alerts created
- [ ] Canary executed and acceptance criteria met
- [ ] Full rollout and cost validation completed

Appendix: useful links
----------------------
- Sampling policy templates: /confluence/eng-platform/how-tos/sampling-templates
- redwoodctl reference: https://internal.redwood.dev/tools/redwoodctl#sampling
- Cost attribution docs: /confluence/finance-and-legal/billing/ingest-cost-attribution

Ownership and escalation
------------------------
- Primary contact: Customer Success Manager (owner per tenant)
- Platform steward: Eng Platform (sampling service)
- SRE on-call: first responder for canary and production incidents
- Escalation path: Customer Success -> Eng Platform -> Security (if data integrity concerns) -> VP Customer Success

Change log
----------
- 2026-03-15: Draft created (Aisha Kapoor)
- 2026-04-20: Added reservoir recommendations and YAML examples (Miguel Ortega)
- 2026-06-02: Finalized alerts and acceptance criteria; published (Aisha Kapoor)

title: Batched Webhook Contracts for Large Payloads and Backpressure Handling
content:
Summary:

This integration guide defines the contract, operational controls, and recommended implementation patterns for integrating customer endpoints that receive batched webhooks containing large payloads. It is intended for platform engineers, integration engineers on customer teams, and Customer Success engineers who coordinate go-lives. The goal is to minimize dropped traffic, bound memory/CPU cost at the receiver, and ensure predictable retry/backpressure behavior across Redwood hosted and Dedicated/Private environments.

Audience:
- Customer Success (CS) and Solutions Engineers
- Integration/Platform Engineers at customer organizations
- Redwood SREs responsible for ingress proxies and client libraries

Why this exists:
- Customers frequently need batched delivery to reduce per-request overhead for high-throughput use cases (e.g., embedding sync, event batches, document uploads).
- Large payloads (>256 KB) amplify failure modes: slow receivers, head-of-line blocking, and unexpected client memory spikes.
- Without an explicit contract, different clients interpret retries/backoff differently leading to cascading load and downtime.

Scope and applicability:
- Applies to: webhook-style delivery (HTTP/HTTPS) from Redwood integration proxies to customer-owned endpoints used during onboarding and production flows.
- Not covered: pure streaming (gRPC) integrations or in-band synchronous inference responses. See streaming-webhook guide for streaming semantics.

Key definitions (used in this guide):
- Batch: a single HTTP POST containing an array of records/events/documents.
- Payload size: total bytes of the request body, after compression if compression negotiation is used.
- Delivery window: time period within which Redwood will attempt retries before handing the message to dead-letter or escalation flows.
- Backpressure token: short-lived header (X-RWBP-Token) issued by the receiver to indicate temporary capacity constraints.

Contract: request and response expectations

Required request headers:
- Content-Type: application/json
- X-RW-Tenant: <tenant-id> (mandatory for Dedicated/Private routing)
- X-RW-Batch-Count: <integer> (number of items in this batch)
- X-RW-Batch-Bytes: <integer> (uncompressed size in bytes)
- X-RW-Id: <uuid> (idempotency key for the batch)
- Accept-Encoding: gzip (supported, optional)

Recommended (optional) headers:
- X-RW-Prefetch: <estimated-items-ahead> (used by receivers to tune prefetch/buffers)

Response codes and semantics:
- 200 OK: Full acceptance. Redwood considers batch delivered; no retries. Body may contain a JSON acknowledgment mapping ids to per-item statuses (see per-item ack format below).
- 202 Accepted: Receiver accepted batch for asynchronous processing. Redwood treats as success (no retry).
- 429 Too Many Requests: Receiver is asking the sender to slow down. Must include Retry-After (seconds) header or X-RW-Backoff (ms). Redwood will respect Retry-After and fall back to exponential backoff.
- 503 Service Unavailable: Temporary capacity problem. Must include Retry-After or X-RW-Backoff. Redwood will attempt retry according to configured retry window and failover policies.
- 4xx (other): Permanent client errors (e.g., malformed payload). Redwood will surface to customer and not retry.
- 5xx: Transient server error. Redwood will perform retries and escalate per escalation policy if persistent.

Per-item acknowledgment format (optional body on 200):
- If receiver wants to indicate partial acceptance, return 200 with JSON: { "id_statuses": [{"id": "<item-id>", "status": "accepted|rejected|retry", "reason": "optional human text" } ] }
- Redwood will retry only items marked "retry" or missing from id_statuses when configured for fine-grained retries. Coarse-grained integrations should return full 200/202 and avoid partial acceptance.

Payload sizing and batching constraints (default recommended):
| Threshold | Value | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| Recommended max batch items | 200 | Prevent large CPU/JSON parse spikes on receivers |
| Recommended max batch bytes (uncompressed) | 8,388,608 (8 MB) | Soft recommendation; verify with customer during onboarding |
| Hard max batch bytes (policy) | 16,777,216 (16 MB) | Redwood will reject >16MB with 413 Payload Too Large unless negotiated |
| Preferred per-item size for stability | < 512 KB | Items larger than this should be split or uploaded separately

Negotiating larger payloads: multipart upload handshake
- For sustained use-cases requiring items >512KB or batches >8MB, customers should implement a two-phase handshake:
  1) Receiver responds with 202 and X-RW-Upload-Url: pre-signed URL for multipart upload (S3 or Azure blob allowed).
  2) Redwood will upload large blobs to the provided URL and then POST a trimmed batch with references (blob ids/URLs) instead of inlining payloads.
- Handshake failures should be returned as 4xx/5xx accordingly; Redwood will retry the batch flow but not the individual large-blob uploads unless the receiver accepts them.

Backpressure and flow control mechanism
- Short-term backpressure: receiver returns 429 or 503 with Retry-After in seconds or X-RW-Backoff in milliseconds. Redwood will:
  - Respect Retry-After and pause pushes to that endpoint for the duration plus jitter.
  - Gradually ramp down parallel connections (min connection limit = 1, not 0) then attempt slow probe requests.
- Token-based capacity signaling (recommended):
  - Receiver may issue an X-RWBP-Token header in responses (value valid for 30s). When set, Redwood reduces concurrency to the level encoded in the token metadata (opaque to Redwood). Tokens are advisory and used to coordinate multi-proxy setups.
- Long-term flow control: If an endpoint repeatedly signals backpressure (more than N times within M minutes), Redwood will move the tenant to an adaptive-fanout queue and notify the CS owner for remediation.

Retry policy (default, overridable by customer contract)
1) Immediate retries: on 5xx up to 2 immediate attempts, 200ms apart.
2) Exponential backoff: initial 1s, multiplier 2, max interval 60s. Total retry window default 15 minutes for individual batches.
3) For TTL-sensitive messages (configurable flag in integration manifest), total retry window reduced to 90 seconds.
4) After exhausting retry window, Redwood will:
  - Move batch to tenant-specific dead-letter queue (DLQ) for inspection, AND
  - Trigger CS escalation per the escalation matrix below.

Observability contract: metrics and traces the receiver must expose/emit during onboarding
- Required telemetry for onboarding:
  - DeliverySuccessRate (per tenant, per endpoint)
  - AvgProcessingLatency (p50/p95) measured from initial receipt to 202/200 response
  - CurrentQueueDepth or PendingJobs (if asynchronous processing)
- Redwood will correlate traces using the X-RW-Id and a trace header X-RW-Trace-Id (if present). Customers should log/emit the trace id in request processing logs.

Integration test checklist (onboarding preflight)
1) Basic handshake: Redwood POSTs a batch of 10 small items, endpoint returns 200.
2) Partial acceptance: return per-item ack and verify Redwood retries only expected items.
3) Backpressure simulation: return 429 with Retry-After=30 and confirm Redwood respects the pause.
4) Large payload: send a single 1.5 MB item and verify multipart handshake path completes.
5) Rate flood: simulate burst of 500 batches in 60s and confirm receiver CPU/heap remains within expected bounds.
6) Observability: confirm DeliverySuccessRate and AvgProcessingLatency are visible in both Redwood console and customer dashboards.

Operational runbook and escalation matrix
- Owners:
  - Redwood CS Integration Lead: Maya Chen (primary)
  - Redwood SRE Oncall: eng-sre team (pager)
  - Customer Engineering POC: named during onboarding
- Escalation steps (automated and manual):
  1) Automated: If DeliverySuccessRate < 95% for 5 consecutive minutes, send automated alert and open a P1 incident in Redwood PagerDuty.
  2) CS outreach: CS Integration Lead pages customer POC and opens joint debugging session.
  3) Platform mitigation: SRE may route affected tenant to a buffered DLQ/fanout layer, temporarily reducing direct push traffic.
  4) Executive: If outage extends beyond 2 hours and impacts SLA, CS and Sales notify customer execs and prepare credit/mitigation plan.

Rollout/canary guidance for customers
- Start with a small tenant sample of 1–5% of traffic.
- Enforce a hard peek-limit: max 1 connection and 1 batch/second during initial 24h.
- Gradually increase by doubling traffic every 24 hours while monitoring AvgProcessingLatency and server heap usage.

Examples and code snippets
- Example POST body (compact):
{
  "batch_id": "4c2b8a56-...",
  "items": [ {"id": "i1", "payload": "..."}, {"id": "i2", "payload": "..."} ]
}

- Example 429 response (recommended headers):
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 30
X-RW-Backoff: 30000
Content-Type: application/json
{ "message": "temporarily overloaded, try after 30s" }

- Example partial ack 200 body:
{ "id_statuses": [{"id": "i1", "status": "accepted"}, {"id": "i2", "status": "retry", "reason": "transient db lock"}] }

FAQ (short)
- Q: What if my endpoint cannot handle batches but can handle many small requests?
  A: Negotiate smaller batch sizes (items <= 20, bytes <= 256KB) and increase concurrency at the receiver side. We can configure Redwood to send more parallel requests instead of large batches.
- Q: Do you support mutual TLS?
  A: Yes. During Dedicated/Private onboarding, mutual TLS and pinned certificates are supported. See onboarding checklist to exchange certs.
- Q: What happens to items lost after retries?
  A: Items that exhaust retries land in a tenant DLQ and are available to the customer for inspection and re-ingestion. The CS team will coordinate DLQ access.

Appendix: configuration knobs (examples to share with customer)
- inbound.max_batch_bytes = 8388608
- inbound.max_items_per_batch = 200
- delivery.retry_window_seconds = 900
- delivery.immediate_retries = 2
- delivery.initial_backoff_ms = 1000

Related reading:
- Streaming webhook retry and deduplication guide (streaming-webhook-retry-and-deduplication-guide-2026)
- Tenant onboarding acceptance testing checklist (enterprise-onboarding/tenant-onboarding-acceptance-testing-and-telemetry-assertions-2027)

Ownership & contacts:
- Document author: Maya Chen (Customer Success Integration Lead)
- CS reviewer: Jonas Meyer
- SRE reviewer: Priya Rao

Change log:
- 2027-09-12: Initial draft and internal review.
- 2027-11-03: Added multipart upload handshake section after customer pilot.
- 2028-01-10: Finalized backpressure token recommendation and rollout guidance.

This guide should be applied during Dedicated and Private tenant onboarding by default and offered as an integration option for Hosted customers with high-throughput ingestion patterns. For implementation help, contact the CS Integration Lead or open a ticket routed to the integration squad.

title: Edge Telemetry Validation and Onboarding Playbook for Enterprise Tenants
content:
Overview:
This playbook defines the recommended validation, onboarding workflow, and operational handoff for enterprise customers connecting edge or client-side telemetry (web SDKs, mobile SDKs, edge ingestion proxies) into Redwood’s telemetry pipeline. It focuses on minimizing false positives in alerts, ensuring SLO alignment, and providing clear escalation and rollback steps for integration engineers and customer success teams.

Scope:
- Applies to enterprise tenants connecting production telemetry for: request traces, sampling events, client-side metrics (latency, token counts), and structured request metadata (tenant_id, route, model_version).
- Covers both SaaS-hosted customers and Dedicated/Private tenants where telemetry is proxied through a sidecar.
- Excludes proprietary third-party observability adapters (see related pages for adapter guides).

Owner and contact information:
- Playbook owner: Maya Chen (Customer Reliability Lead) — maya@redwood.com
- Primary oncall for telemetry ingestion: telemetry-oncall@redwood.com
- Engineering consult: eng-observability@redwood.com
- Customer Success (CS) handoff alias: cs-ops@redwood.com

Goals and acceptance criteria (must be green before handback):
1) Events accepted and parsed without >1% schema failures over 10,000 test events.
2) Ingress latency for validated events <200ms p95 to telemetry-gatekeeper in the customer region.
3) No more than 0.05% increase in global alert noise attributable to new tenant in the first 72 hours.
4) SLOs for tenant-specific dashboards created and reviewed with customer stakeholders.

Key services and components (names used in commands below):
- ingress-gateway (edge ingress HTTP/2 endpoints)
- telemetry-gatekeeper (validation and rate-limiting service)
- tenant-metrics-proxy (tenant-aware proxy that scrubs PII)
- observability-collector (aggregator -> timeseries/long-term storage)

Prerequisites from customer before starting:
- A test API key generated with telemetry:write scope and tenant_id provided.
- Network allowlist for Redwood ingress IPs (list provided by CS).
- A short test dataset (500–2,000 synthetic events) mapped to expected client SDK shapes.
- Designated technical contact and test window (2 hours).

Validation checklist (pre-cutover):
- 1) Schema validation tests
  - Use the test harness to run the sample suite against telemetry-gatekeeper. Expected result: schema_failures = 0 (or <= 1% of events).
  - Example curl payload (JSON):
    curl -X POST https://ingress-gateway.redwood.example/v1/events \n      -H "Authorization: Bearer <TEST_KEY>" \n      -H "Content-Type: application/json" \n      -d '{"tenant_id":"acme-corp","event_type":"generation_request","timestamp":"2026-03-04T15:23:10Z","request":{"model":"redwood-llm-v1","prompt_len":312,"tokens":138},"client":{"sdk":"js", "sdk_version":"2.1.0","session_id":"s-123"}}'

- 2) Ingress & validation latency
  - Run 500 events at 5 rps from customer side during test window. Measure time-to-ack from ingress-gateway to telemetry-gatekeeper.
  - Acceptable: p95 < 200ms; if p95 between 200–400ms tag for follow-up optimization.

- 3) Rate-limit and quota checks
  - Confirm tenant quotas in telemetry-gatekeeper: default_quota limits and burst settings.
  - Example admin check (internal CLI):
    rwdctl telemetry quotas get --tenant acme-corp --env prod
    Expected sample output: "daily_quota: 5,000,000; burst_rate: 2000r/s; overage_action: throttle"

- 4) PII scrubbing and allowed fields
  - Confirm tenant-metrics-proxy scrubbing rules. Provide sample event with PII fields and verify removal.

- 5) Dashboard and SLI creation
  - Create tenant-level dashboard: latency_by_route, schema_failure_rate, event_ingest_rate, error_rate.
  - Define SLIs and target thresholds with customer: 
    - Event delivery success = 99.9% over 7d
    - Schema-failure-rate <= 0.5% (initial target)

Step-by-step onboarding procedure:
1. Preparation (CS + Eng alignment, 2–5 business days)
   a) CS collects prerequisites and creates an onboarding ticket in JIRA: ONB-<TENANT>-<YYYYMMDD>.
   b) Assign owners: CS lead, Observability Eng reviewer, Network Engineer for allowlist.
   c) Schedule 2-hour integration window and share IP allowlist and test key.

2. Dry-run validation (1–2 hours, non-production)
   a) Customer pushes 500 synthetic events.
   b) Run schema validation harness: 
      telemetry-harness run --target https://ingress-gateway.redwood.example --key <TEST_KEY> --events sample-set.json
   c) CS and Eng review harness report. If schema_failures >1%: iterate on mapping and retry.

3. Canary (low-volume production-like, 3–24 hours)
   a) Allow 1–5% of production traffic (or 10 rps, whichever is lower) routed to telemetry-gatekeeper.
   b) Monitor dashboards and alert noise for 24 hours.
   c) If alert noise increases >0.05% attributable to tenant, reduce canary volume and troubleshoot.

4. Full cutover (after canary and SLA signoff)
   a) CS issues a go/no-go and schedules final cutover with customer.
   b) Switch traffic and monitor p95 latency, success rate, schema failures at 1, 6, 24, 72 hour marks.

5. Handback and documentation (post-cutover, within 5 business days)
   a) Compile onboarding report and attach to JIRA ticket.
   b) Create tenant-specific dashboard folder and grant read access to customer stakeholders.
   c) Update runbook snippets and signal any config changes to infra as a change request.

Quick verification queries (Grafana/PromQL examples):
- Schema failure rate (last 24h):
  sum(rate(telemetry_schema_failures_total{tenant="acme-corp"}[24h])) / sum(rate(telemetry_events_received_total{tenant="acme-corp"}[24h]))

- Ingest latency p95 (last 1h):
  histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(telemetry_ingest_latency_bucket{tenant="acme-corp"}[1h])) by (le))

Common failure modes and remediations:
- High schema_failure_rate (>1%)
  - Likely cause: SDK version mismatch or missing required fields.
  - Action: Ask customer to upgrade SDK or apply a mapping shim. Use telemetry-harness to generate failing samples and share stack traces.

- Sudden alert noise spike after cutover
  - Likely cause: low-cardinality fields or missing tenant scoping in metric labels.
  - Action: Re-scope metrics, add tenant label, and apply cardinality limits. Open change request to tenant-metrics-proxy.

- p95 ingest latency elevated
  - Likely cause: network peering or region mismatch.
  - Action: Check egress/ingress peering stats, validate region header, and consider routing via closer edge node.

Escalation matrix (when to page whom):
- Severity P0 (ingest down for tenant or >5% request failures for 15m):
  - Page: telemetry-oncall -> engage Observability Eng -> CS Lead -> Exec oncall if >60m.
- Severity P1 (schema failures >5% sustained for 30m or major alert noise increase):
  - Notify: eng-observability, cs-ops; Schedule 30-minute war room.
- Severity P2 (latency p95 >1s for 1 hour):
  - Triage with Network Eng and Observability Eng; schedule 2-hour fix window.

Rollback and safety net steps:
- Immediate rollback: update ingress routing to drop or re-route tenant traffic to a staging collector:
  rwdctl routing set --tenant acme-corp --target staging-collector --reason "emergency-rollback"
- Quarantine mode: enable quota throttle and scrubbers at telemetry-gatekeeper:
  rwdctl telemetry quarantine --tenant acme-corp --duration 30m --action throttle

Post-onboarding checklist (within 7 days):
- Confirm SLI/SLA targets in contract are instrumented and visible in QBR dashboards.
- Conduct a short post-mortem if any P1/P0 events occurred during onboarding.
- Move ticket to "Completed" and ensure knowledge transfer session recorded and stored in onboarding folder.

Operational guidance and best practices:
- Prefer SDK version parity: require customers to run a supported SDK (listed in SDK compatibility matrix).
- Low-cardinality labels only: advise customers to avoid user_id/session_id as primary metric labels; send as trace attribute instead.
- Use sampling for high-volume client events and send full traces for problematic sessions only.

Appendix A — Example minimal event schema (required fields):
{
  "tenant_id": "string",
  "event_type": "string",
  "timestamp": "ISO8601",
  "request": { "model": "string", "tokens": "int" },
  "client": { "sdk": "string", "sdk_version": "string" }
}

Appendix B — Helpful CLI tools and contacts:
- telemetry-harness: repo internal at git@redwood:observability/telemetry-harness.git
- rwdctl (internal CLI) for telemetry and routing changes
- For compliance-sensitive telemetry (PII concerns), involve privacy@redwood.com before canary

Revision history:
- 2026-01-12: Created by Maya Chen
- 2026-02-10: Added canary acceptance thresholds and quarantine CLI commands (reviewer: Diego Alvarez)
- 2026-03-04: Updated SLI targets and added Grafana queries (reviewer: Priya Nambiar)

End of playbook.

title: Tenant failover, observability & cost-safeguard contract
content:
Summary:
This document defines the tenant-level contract between Redwood and enterprise customers for automated failover, observability telemetry, and cost-safeguard behavior. It is intended for customer success, platform engineers, SREs, and partner integration teams.

Goals:
- Keep customer-facing inference traffic available during service/resource degradation with predictable, auditable behavior.
- Ensure minimal false-positive escalation by defining telemetry thresholds and synthetic checks.
- Provide clear economic safeguards to prevent runaway billing while preserving critical availability.

Scope:
- Applies to Dedicated and Private tenants only (hosted tier has separate defaults).
- Covers ingress failover, model fallback, burst throttling, billing-protection limits, and telemetry signals used for QBRs.
- Excludes cross-region DR for air-gapped on-prem installs unless explicitly contracted.

Ownership and Contacts:
- Primary owner: Customer Success (Priya Natarajan)
- Platform/Egress owner: Eng-Platform (oncall: platform-ops@redwood.com)
- SRE escalation: eng-sre-oncall@redwood.com
- Billing guard owner: Finance-legal (billing-ops@redwood.com)

Contracted SLOs and Thresholds (tenant-level):
| Metric | Target | Alert threshold | Pager | Notes |
|--------|--------|-----------------|-------|-------|
| 95th percentile token latency (p95-token-latency-ms) | < 220ms | > 350ms for 5m | SRE | measured at tenant egress gateway
| Request success rate (http 2xx) | > 99.9% | < 99.5% for 10m | Customer Success | Includes model-fallback responses as success unless response is 5xx
| Embedding index sync lag (sec) | < 30s | > 300s | Platform | Applies to enterprise embedding sync jobs
| Tenant cost rate (USD/hr) | N/A (billing) | > committed_rate * 1.5 for 1h | Billing Ops | triggers cost-safeguard (see below)

Telemetry contract (required signals and query examples):
- Required signals to be forwarded by the tenant to Redwood telemetry pipeline: tenant_id, route, model_variant, request_id, request_size_tokens, response_size_tokens, duration_ms, upstream_error_code, billing_cost_cents.
- Example PromQL queries used by Redwood and the customer in QBRs and alerting: 
  - Failed request rate (10m): sum(rate(http_requests_total{tenant="$TENANT",status=~"5.."}[10m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{tenant="$TENANT"}[10m]))
  - Synthetic journey latency (p95, 15m): histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(synthetic_request_latency_bucket{tenant="$TENANT"}[15m])) by (le))
  - Cost rate (1h): increase(billing_cost_cents_total{tenant="$TENANT"}[1h])

Failover behavior (automated, ordered):
1) Prefix and KV cache reuse: if a model node becomes unavailable, the router attempts local cache reuse and replays using warm KV where possible (no tenant-visible change).
2) Model variant fallback: route to preconfigured lower-cost or quantized model variant when latency SLOs risk breach. Configuration: model_fallback_policy in tenant config.
