3) Cross-pool fanout: for Dedicated tenants with reserved capacity, span requests across standby pool in same region.
4) Tenant ingress backpressure: when request queue exceeds 1000 concurrent requests or p95-token-latency > 400ms, adaptive rate-limiter returns 429 with Retry-After.
5) Graceful degradation: streaming/partial responses permitted if application has opted in.

Cost-safeguard policies (tenant-configurable):
- Billing guard level (enum): warn | throttle | hard-stop
- Default guard: warn at 125% of committed_rate for 30m; throttle at 150% for 1h; hard-stop only if explicitly requested in contract.
- Throttle behavior: dynamically downgrade non-critical model variants and apply token rate limit per-tenant to reduce cost growth while preserving low-volume interactive calls.
- Audit trail: all cost-safeguard actions emit audit events with fields: tenant_id, action, reason, previous_rate, new_rate, timestamp.

Example tenant config snippet (YAML):
---
tenant_id: "acme-corp-42"
model_fallback_policy:
  - prefer: [redwood-quant-3b, redwood-8k-quant]
  - max_latency_ms: 350
cost_safeguard:
  guard_level: throttle
  thresholds:
    warn_pct: 125
    throttle_pct: 150
    hard_stop_pct: 300
synthetic_checks:
  - name: login-journey
    frequency: 1m
    max_p95_ms: 300
---

Required integration steps (for customer success / integration teams):
1) Confirm tenant contract level (Dedicated vs Private) and committed_rate.
2) Exchange telemetry schema and sampling decision with the customer; ensure required signals are instrumented.
3) Configure tenant config (example above) in provisioning template and apply via provisioning API.
   - CLI example: curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -d @tenant-config.yaml https://controlplane.redwood/api/v1/tenants
4) Enable synthetic checks and verify p95 and success-rate metrics for 24h before go-live.
5) Run a failover dry-run game-day to validate fallback policies. Document results in the tenant runbook.

Failover dry-run checklist (run by Customer Success + Platform):
- Simulate node failure and confirm: prefix cache reuse occurs; model fallback engaged within 30s; no silent data loss; all audit events are recorded.
- Validate synthetic journey failure handling and Retry-After semantics.
- Confirm cost-safeguard warning is emitted and stakeholder emails are sent.

Escalation matrix (tenant-impacting):
- Severity P1 (tenant offline / >30% error rate for 15m): page SRE (pager), notify CS Lead, open bridge.
- Severity P2 (degraded latency / increased cost risk): notify CS and Platform via Slack; create ticket and runbook entry.
- Severity P3 (informational / billing warning): email to Finance-ops and CS, no page.

Runbooks and automation hooks (examples):
- runbook:tctl tenant-failover --tenant $TENANT --simulate (dry-run)
- Automation play: on alert "tenant_high_cost_rate" -> run lambda reduce-tenant-model-variants($TENANT) -> create ticket in JIRA and send notification to billing-ops.

Observability checklist (minimum dashboards and alerts required before go-live):
- Per-tenant p95/p99 latency heatmap
- Per-tenant success rate and 5xx breakdown by upstream component
- Synthetic journey health panel with per-step timings
- Cost burn rate panel (USD/hr) with committed vs actual overlay
- Audit events stream filtered by tenant_id

QBR artifacts and expected deliverables (monthly/quarterly):
- Monthly: cost burn analysis, top-5 requests by token volume, synthetic pass rate summary.
- Quarterly (QBR): incident RCA summary, model quality regressions, proposed adjustments to committed_rate or guard levels. Include dashboard links and agreed follow-up action items.

Acceptance criteria for go-live (all must pass):
1) Telemetry contract verified and flowing to Redwood pipeline for 72h.
2) Synthetic suite passes 95% of journeys at p95 < committed threshold for 24h.
3) Failover dry-run shows model fallback < 30s and no data loss.
4) Cost-safeguard test triggers warning and throttle behavior in a controlled test.

Post-go-live monitoring cadence:
- First 72 hours: 30-minute ops checks and daily customer sync.
- First 30 days: weekly QBR-lite with executive summary and any proposed parameter tuning.
- Ongoing: monthly cost and telemetry checkpoint.

FAQ:
Q: What happens to streaming connections during a model fallback?
A: If the client has opted into streaming fallback, partial stream frames will be returned with a final frame indicating a fallback model was used. Transparent field `x-redwood-fallback` is set to true.

Q: Can a customer opt out of throttling?
A: Customers can opt out (hard-stop disabled) only if contract explicitly allows and Finance signs off on overage liability. Otherwise the default is warn -> throttle.

Change log:
- 2026-01-11: Initial version (Priya Natarajan)
- 2026-02-12: Added synthetic-checks section and clarified throttle thresholds (Marco Alvarez)

Related references:
- Provisioning API docs: https://docs.redwood.ai/provisioning-api#tenant-config
- Observability playbook: /confluence/eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/tenant-observability-standards-2025
- Billing guard design: /confluence/finance-and-legal/billing-and-guardrails/tenant-billing-guards-2025

Appendix: sample alert definitions (Prometheus alert rules YAML snippet):
- alert: TenantHighCostRate
  expr: increase(billing_cost_cents_total{tenant="$TENANT"}[1h]) > (committed_rate_cents{tenant="$TENANT"} * 1.5)
  for: 1h
  labels:
    severity: warning
  annotations:
    summary: "Tenant {{ $labels.tenant }} cost exceeded 150% of committed rate"

title: Prescriptive Telemetry Handoff & Operational Roles for Enterprise Onboarding
content:
Overview

This playbook defines a prescriptive, role-based telemetry handoff used during enterprise onboarding at Redwood Inference. It focuses on what signals must be collected, minimal quality requirements for those signals, ownership of dashboards and alerts, and an operational escalation ladder that meshes Customer Success (CSM), Integration Engineering, and SRE responsibilities. Use this document as the canonical handoff checklist before signoff on the production acceptance gate.

Scope
- Applies to Dedicated and Private customers during the final 2 weeks of onboarding and first 30 days of production.
- Covers: request/response traces, per-tenant cost telemetry, model inference metrics, ingress/egress latency, error-classification, and synthetic health checks.
- Does not replace security/compliance artifacts (use the enterprise-deployment-compliance-evidence playbook for that).

Goals
1. Ensure telemetry provides sufficient context for rapid incident TTR (time-to-repair).
2. Prevent noisy alerts while surfacing customer-impacting anomalies.
3. Establish clear owner for each telemetry artifact to be handed to the customer operations contact.

Required Roles & Responsibilities
- Customer Success Manager (CSM): primary contact for business-level escalations, coordinates QBR artifacts.
- Integration Engineer (IE): owns onboarding of telemetry exporters, verifies schema conformance, and performs initial dashboard walk-through.
- SRE / Site Reliability: owns alert rules, runbooks, and escalation endpoints; responsible for uptime SLO enforcement.
- Customer Ops/Platform Engineer: recipient of the handoff; validates telemetry ingestion and runbook mapping on their side.

Ownership Matrix (text-table)
| Artifact | Primary Owner | Secondary Owner | Acceptance Criteria |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Ingress latency (p50/p95/p99) per-tenant | SRE | IE | p95 < 200ms for interactive tenants; dashboard populated for 30d of test traffic |
| Token cost by model & tenant (hourly) | Finance-ops (CS) | SRE | Hourly granularity, cost-tagging matches billing account |
| Model output quality (evals/feature-set) | IE | Customer Success | Prompt set coverage >= 80% of critical flows |
| Error classification (4xx vs 5xx vs model-misbehavior) | SRE | IE | Errors grouped and sampled with 1:100 sampling for traces |
| Synthetic journey (end-to-end) | IE | Customer Ops | Synthetic every 1m, depl. region coverage, alerts on 3 consecutive failures |

Telemetry Contract (required fields)
- Required metric labels: tenant_id, model_name, route, region, request_id, sampling_rate.
- Required trace context: trace_id, parent_span_id, request_id, backend_node.
- Metric retention for onboarding: 90 days at 1m granularity, 13 months at 1h for billing alignment.

Onboarding Handoff Checklist (step-by-step)
1. Integration Engineer deploys telemetry exporter and shares example payloads in JSON. Example payload snippet: 
```json
{
  "tenant_id": "acme-123",
  "model_name": "gptx-14b-q4",
  "latency_ms": 134,
  "p99_estimate": 210,
  "request_id": "r-7d6c4",
  "region": "us-west-2"
}
```
2. SRE verifies metrics in Redwood internal metrics cluster and confirms retention policy.
3. IE and Customer Ops complete dashboard walk-through: top-tokens trend, cost burn, and failure heatmap.
4. Runbooks attached and smoke-tested (see "Runbook Tests" section).
5. Final signoff: CSM confirms business acceptance and schedules the first QBR cadence.

Alert Thresholds & SLO Mapping
- Production SLOs (enterprise tier): Availability 99.95% (per-tenant), P99 inference latency < 350ms for up to 64-token responses.
- Initial onboarding alert thresholds (conservative to reduce noise):
  - Synthetic journey failure: 3 failures in 5 minutes -> Pager to IE oncall.
  - P95 latency deviation > 2x baseline for 10m -> Pager to SRE.
  - Hourly cost anomaly > +60% vs rolling 7-day median -> Alert to CSM & Finance-ops.

Runbook Tests (acceptance scenarios)
- Test A: Simulate KV cache miss storm and verify KV cache miss-rate metric rises and a specific runbook step (scale read replicas) succeeds.
- Test B: Induce model swap (canary -> full) and validate fallback policy triggers and customer route fails over to compatibility model.
- Test C: Inject 5xx error rate and validate triage classification and alert routing (CSM notified, IE paged if persistent).

Escalation Ladder (operational flow)
1. Detect: Oncall receives alert, triages using dashboard + recent traces.
2. Contain: If customer-facing, enable temporary traffic shaping/fairshare and notify CSM.
3. Remediate: Execute runbook steps; if unknown, escalate to Engineering on-call with labeled artifact (trace + minimal repro).
4. Postmortem: If P1 outage or persistent regression, SRE owns RCA within 72 hours and CSM prepares customer-facing summary for QBR.

Integration Checklist for Customer (action items)
- Provide service account with read-only access to exported metrics and traces.
- Validate tenant_id mapping and confirm billing_account tag.
- Run synthetic suite provided by IE for 48h and report anomalies.
- Confirm on-call contact list and escalation phone numbers.

QBR & Ongoing Health Handover
- After 30 days of production, handoff artifacts for the QBR should include: cost delta by model, top 5 failure modes, synthetic pass rate, and any closed RCA actions.
- CSM schedules QBR and invites IE + SRE for the technical deep-dive.

Templates & Attachments (inlined)
- Dashboard template IDs: dashboard.enterprise-onboard.tokens (ID: db-4421), dashboard.enterprise-onboard.errors (ID: db-4422).
- Runbook snippet: "Scale GPU pool -> verify KV cache warmup -> validate p95 latency <= baseline".

Acceptance & Signoff
- Acceptance signoff requires: telemetry checks green (all required artifacts present), 48h synthetic stability, and runbook smoke tests passed. Signoff by IE, SRE, and CSM.

Related pages and references
- See also: enterprise-onboarding/post-provisioning-stability-checklist-2026 for provisioning steps; model-migration-cutover-governance-telemetry-sla-carveouts-2027 for model upgrade notes.

Notes & Rationale
- This playbook biases for explicit telemetry contracts to reduce time-to-diagnosis across organizational boundaries. We prefer short, testable acceptance criteria rather than vague assurances.

Revision history
- 2026-02-10: Initial draft by Avery Chen.
- 2026-02-18: Added synthetic acceptance guidance (reviewer: Priya Nair).
- 2026-03-04: Finalized thresholds and signoff criteria (reviewer: Luis Martinez).

For questions or to schedule a handoff walkthrough, contact the author or the Customer Success tooling mailbox: customer-success-tooling@redwood.ai.

title: ClearData Stitch Adapter Integration Guide (SDK setup, endpoint migration, retries, rate limits)
content:
source_context:
This page supersedes earlier email-based guidance shared with ClearData AI (thread: th_20260729_grace_stitch_sdk_001). It consolidates the recommended production client defaults, retry/idempotency guidance, endpoint migration steps, and canary metrics used by CS for Stitch adapter rollouts.

integration_prereqs:
Prerequisites:
- Redwood account + environment-specific API key(s): staging and prod.
- Confirm target region (us/eu) and data handling constraints.
- Decide on traffic management approach: gateway/routing layer (recommended) vs direct application integration.
- Observability access: ability to log request_id, latency, status code, model_id, token usage headers.

Request to CS:
- Provision staging key tied to the customer account.
- Enable tracing tag for rapid rollbacks if using 24-hour ramp steps.
- Provide plan quota targets (sustained RPS + burst guidance) for customer-side token-bucket settings.

endpoint_migration_overview:
Migration objective:
Move from the customer’s legacy endpoint (e.g., https://api.cleardata.ai/v1/llm) to Redwood API endpoints while preserving reliability and enabling safe rollback.

Current Redwood endpoint (recommended):
- Non-streaming: POST /v1/responses
- Streaming: POST /v1/responses (stream=true)

Note: Older references may mention /v1/generate. That endpoint is supported for backward compatibility in some environments, but /v1/responses is the default for new integrations and has the most consistent behavior across SDKs.

implementation_checklist:
h2. Implementation checklist (high level)
1) Acquire API key
- CS provisions a staging key tied to the customer account.
- Confirm environment separation: do not reuse staging keys in production.

2) Sandbox test
- Make a single non-streaming call and validate:
  - HTTP 2xx
  - request_id present
  - model_id matches expectation
  - token counts are returned/observable

3) Dual-write gateway (recommended where feasible)
- Route traffic to both:
  - Redwood (new) and
  - Existing LLM endpoint (old)
- Log-only for the secondary path (do not return to user) to compare latency, errors, and output characteristics.

4) Canary traffic split
- Start at 5–10% for at least 48 hours.
- Increase in steps: 10% → 25% → 50% → 100%.
- If customer insists on a faster cadence, 24-hour steps are allowed only if tracing-based rollback hooks are enabled.

5) Telemetry
- Capture per request:
  - request_id
  - latency (client + server, if available)
  - token usage
  - model_id
  - customer correlation id (if available)

6) Rollback plan
- Immediate fallback to old endpoint on:
  - error rate spike, or
  - sustained latency regression vs agreed thresholds, or
  - unexpected model_id mismatches.
- Rollback should be executable without redeploy (gateway flag preferred).

sdk_setup_recommended_defaults:
h2. SDK setup (recommended defaults)
Use these as starting points; tune after benchmarking with representative prompts.

h3. Timeouts
- Connect timeout: 2s
- Read timeout:
  - Streaming: 45s (updated from older 30s guidance to reduce false timeouts for long generations)
  - Non-streaming: 20s (updated from older 15s guidance to accommodate longer outputs)

h3. Concurrency
- Max in-flight requests per process: start at 8
- Typical safe range after validation: 8–16 depending on prompt length and average max_tokens

h3. Client batching
- If using the Redwood SDK batching layer, keep the default batch window of ~25ms unless you have strict latency SLOs.

h3. Idempotency
- For retryable non-streaming POST requests, include an idempotency_key.
- For streaming requests:
  - Prefer stream resumption when supported (stream_id / cursor semantics).
  - Avoid blind “restart from scratch” retries unless the operation is explicitly idempotent and the customer experience tolerates duplication.

h3. Headers and tags
- Always log request_id.
- Tag requests with a stable integration identifier (e.g., "cleardata-stitch-adapter") to isolate traffic during canaries and incident triage.

retry_and_backoff_guidance:
h2. Retry and backoff guidance
h3. What to retry
Retry on:
- Network timeouts / connection resets
- HTTP 429
- HTTP 502 / 503 / 504

Do not retry on:
- HTTP 400 / 401 / 403 (except 429)
- Validation errors (treat as integration bugs)

h3. Backoff parameters (recommended)
- Strategy: exponential backoff with jitter
- initial_delay: 250ms (updated from older 200ms guidance)
- max_delay: 5s
- max_retries: 6 (updated from older 5 retries to reduce customer-visible failures on brief throttling events)

h3. Streaming retry guidance
- Streaming requests should not be aggressively retried from the beginning.
- Preferred approach:
  - reconnect and resume when stream resumption is supported (stream_id/cursor)
  - otherwise surface an ergonomic error to the caller and allow the application to decide whether to retry.

h3. Idempotency note
- If the application cannot guarantee idempotency_key uniqueness per logical request, it should disable automatic retries for non-streaming calls to prevent duplicate outputs and confusing UX.

rate_limiting_patterns:
h2. Rate limiting patterns
h3. Client-side limiter (recommended)
- Implement a local token-bucket limiter per process keyed by API key.
- Configure:
  - capacity = burst allowance (example starting point: 20)
  - refill rate = sustained RPS target (CS supplies plan-specific quota targets)

h3. Behavior on 429
- Back off client-side for a randomized window (2s–8s) in addition to exponential backoff.
- This reduces thundering-herd behavior during shared throttling windows.

h3. Route-level protections
- Apply per-route concurrency limits for heavy generation calls (long max_tokens / long contexts).
- Consider separate pools for streaming vs non-streaming to prevent long streams from starving short requests.

operational_checks_for_migration:
h2. Operational checks for endpoint migration
Before routing >50% traffic to Redwood:
- Verify metrics parity vs old endpoint
  - latency (p50/p95/p99)
  - error rates
  - token counts for a representative prompt set
- Validate output quality
  - run a fixed prompt set through both systems
  - review deltas with the customer
- Confirm cost and throughput expectations
  - validate sustained QPS and peak burst behavior against plan targets

Automated health checks CS can run (if enabled):
- 2xx ratio and 5xx/4xx trends
- token usage delta per request type
- model mismatch alerts (returned model_id differs from expected)

network_and_allowlisting:
h2. Network allowlisting / IPs
- By default, customers do not need to allowlist specific Redwood ingress IPs for outbound calls to the Redwood API.
- If the customer environment requires strict egress allowlisting, follow the Security page: confluence://security-and-compliance/network/egress-and-allowlisting-guidance.
- Important nuance: static IP ranges may differ by region and can change as infrastructure evolves; prefer domain-based allowlisting when possible and follow the current Security guidance rather than copying IPs into customer runbooks.

code_samples:
h2. Minimal code samples
These snippets are intentionally minimal; wrap them with your organization’s retry + rate limiting utilities.

h3. Node.js (minimal)
const { RedwoodClient } = require('@redwood-inference/sdk');

const client = new RedwoodClient({
  apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY,
  timeout: 20000,
  connectTimeout: 2000
});

async function generate(prompt, idempotencyKey) {
  return await client.responses.create({
    model: 'redwood-large-v2',
    input: prompt,
    idempotency_key: idempotencyKey
  });
}

h3. Python (minimal)
import os
from redwood import RedwoodClient

client = RedwoodClient(
  api_key=os.environ['REDWOOD_API_KEY'],
  connect_timeout=2,
  read_timeout=20
)

def generate(prompt, idempotency_key=None):
  return client.responses.create(
    model='redwood-large-v2',
    input=prompt,
    idempotency_key=idempotency_key
  )

rollout_tempo_and_thresholds:
h2. Rollout tempo and thresholds
Default canary windows:
- 48 hours minimum per ramp step
- Target thresholds during canary:
  - error rate < 0.5% (aggregate)
  - stable p95 latency vs baseline

Optional faster cadence:
- 24-hour steps permitted if tracing tag + rapid rollback hook is enabled.
- Use stricter on-call readiness (customer + CS) during the first 24 hours of each step.

ownership_and_support:
h2. Ownership and support
Customer Success (CS):
- Owns canary planning, ramp schedule, and success criteria.
- Coordinates staging/prod key provisioning and integration readiness.

Engineering Support (as needed):
- Assists with SDK-level issues, retries, streaming resumption, and performance tuning.

Escalation trigger examples:
- sustained 5xx rate increase
- repeated 429 spikes after client limiter deployed
- unexplained model_id mismatch alerts

changelog:
h2. Changelog
2026-09-12
- Updated default endpoint guidance to /v1/responses (non-streaming and streaming).
- Updated recommended read timeouts (streaming 45s, non-streaming 20s).
- Increased recommended max_retries from 5 to 6; initial backoff from 200ms to 250ms.
- Updated sample model from redwood-large-v1 to redwood-large-v2.
- Added explicit note on allowlisting guidance and avoiding hard-coded IPs.

2026-08-04
- Initial publication consolidating SDK setup, migration steps, retries, rate limiting, and canary metrics used for ClearData Stitch adapter rollout.

title: Secure telemetry sampling and unblinding playbook for enterprise onboarding
content:
Overview

Purpose
This playbook defines the recommended configuration and the operational steps for secure, privacy-preserving telemetry sampling and the tightly controlled unblinding process during enterprise onboarding and subsequent QBR investigations. It is intended for Customer Success Engineers (CSEs), Security Engineers, and Observability Onboarding Owners.

Scope
- Applies to all enterprise tenants using Dedicated or Private deployments and hosted customers requiring selective telemetry sharing.
- Covers sampling rules, storage retention for sampled records, pseudonymization and re-identification (unblinding) request flow, audit logging, and QBR data export patterns.
- Does NOT replace legal data-subpoena processes; follow Legal for formal data disclosures.

Key goals
- Minimize telemetry volume while preserving signal for SLOs and QBR metrics.
- Protect tenant PII with deterministic pseudonymization by default.
- Provide a short, auditable emergency unblinding path governed by least privilege.

Important services and topics referenced
- telemetry-gateway (edge ingestion service)
- ingest-proxy (tenant routing and token mapping)
- qbr-telemetry-pipeline (aggregation + retention)
- redwood-observability (internal dashboards)
- telemetry-audit-log (WORM log for unblinding approvals)
- kafka topic: telemetry-sampled-events
- tenant-mapper (maps tenant IDs to anonymized IDs)

Baseline sampling policy (recommended defaults)
- Latency slices: 100% for errors, 10% for tail requests (>= 95th percentile), 0.5% for p50–p90 generation tokens.
- Security/PII signals: drop or mask PII fields at ingest unless explicitly allowed by customer agreement.
- Session-based sampling: consistent per-session sampling using deterministic hash of session-id + tenant-salt to avoid double-sampling.
- Max global sample budget: 5 requests/sec per 10k active users for hosted plans; dedicated plans may negotiate higher budgets.

Example sampling config (YAML snippet)
sampling_policy: |
  version: 1
  default: "p0"
  policies:
    - name: errors
      match: "response.status >= 500 or response.error == true"
      rate: 1.0
    - name: tail-latency
      match: "response.latency_ms >= 300"
      rate: 0.10
    - name: regular-requests
      match: "response.latency_ms < 300"
      rate: 0.005
  session_consistent: true
  pseudonymize: true

Onboard step-by-step checklist (CSE)
1) Pre-provisioning (before ingress enabled)
   - Confirm customer telemetry policy in contract (retention, allowed fields, residency).
   - Assign tenant-salt and enter into tenant-mapper.
   - Create onboarding ticket in JIRA: project CS-ONBOARD and attach telemetry contract clause.

2) Initial configuration (first 48 hours)
   - Apply baseline sampling_policy to the tenant in the telemetry-gateway. CLI example:
     $ rwctl telemetry apply --tenant TENANT_ID --file sampling_policy.yaml
   - Verify ingest-proxy tag rules: ensure token scope contains telemetry:read:sampled and telemetry:admin false for non-admin tokens.
   - Deploy tenant dashboard in redwood-observability with p50/p90/p99 and sampled-events stream.

3) Validation (days 2–7)
   - Run a synthetic workload (see Synthetic probes below) to validate sampling match-rate within +/- 15% of expected.
   - Confirm pseudonymization fields are not reversible without unblinding protocol (see Audit requirements).

4) QBR and steady state
   - Present sampled-data summaries in the customer QBR. For deep investigations, escalate to the unblinding request flow with legal and security approval.

Synthetic probes (validation harness)
- Use the onboarding synthetic runner: onboarding-sim v2.1
- Run with tenant-salt attached and assert: sampled_count / total_requests ≈ configured_rate +/- 15% over 10k requests.
- Command example:
  $ onboarding-sim --tenant TENANT_ID --requests 10000 --check-sampling --expected-rate 0.005

Unblinding request flow (for investigative use)
Purpose: enable re-identification of pseudonymized telemetry for a narrowly scoped investigation (security incident or contractual investigation).
Prerequisites:
- Formal request ticket in Jira CS-UNBLIND-REQ with: tenant ID, scope, time window, justification, and approved approvers (cust success lead + security reviewer + legal reviewer).
- Customer written consent if contract requires (attach to ticket).

Steps:
1) Create Jira request and tag approvers. Template fields must include exact query and minimal time window.
2) Security reviewer validates scope and confirms logs required.
3) Legal confirms whether customer consent or subpoena is needed.
4) If approved, Security triggers the unblinding job via rwctl: 
   $ rwctl telemetry unblind --ticket CS-UNBLIND-REQ-1234 --tenant TENANT_ID --query "SELECT * FROM telemetry_sam WHERE session_hash = 'abc'" --audit true
5) telemetry-audit-log records the operator, approvers, timestamp, and HSM-signature.
6) Unblinded data is exported to a secure S3 bucket (customer-specific, access-expiring 24 hours) and an access event is recorded in the telemetry-audit-log.
7) Post-unblinding: CSE and Security perform a 3-day review to confirm no overexposure; results attached to the Jira ticket.

Access controls and technical guarantees
- Pseudonymization method: HMAC-SHA256(session_id + tenant_salt) truncated to 16 bytes stored as session_hash. Keys rotated quarterly.
- Unblinding keys stored in KMS/HSM with require-multi-party-approval (2 of 3 approvers).
- telemetry-audit-log is WORM and retained for at least 7 years for compliance customers.
- Only named roles: telemetry-admin, security-investigator, legal-auditor can initiate unblinding; role grants must be requested via IAM-REQ.

SLOs and telemetry health metrics we report to customers
- Sampling accuracy: sample-rate drift < 20% week-over-week.
- Sample ingestion latency: sampled events available in qbr-telemetry-pipeline within 30s of ingestion (95% of events).
- Unblinding turnaround for approved requests: target 4 business hours for emergency requests, 48 business hours for standard requests.

Common troubleshooting and known issues
- Symptom: sample rate appears at 0% for a tenant
  - Check ingest-proxy token scope and tenant-salt presence.
  - Verify that sampling_policy was applied: rwctl telemetry get --tenant TENANT_ID
- Symptom: unblinding job fails with KMS permission error
  - Ensure 2-of-3 approver signature present in telemetry-audit-log. Check KMS access policy for telemetry-service-account.
- Symptom: sampled events missing PII fields (expected) but QBR requires redacted user email for correlation
  - Use the unblinding flow with explicit customer consent; do not modify sampling policy to include PII unless contractually allowed.

Audit and reporting for QBRs
- For each QBR, provide an attachable PDF containing:
  - Sampling policy used during the quarter (YAML).
  - Aggregated sample counts (by latency slice, error vs success).
  - List of any unblinding requests and their Jira ticket IDs (redacted when required by customer).
- Maintain a quarterly internal memo summarizing sample-rate stability and any incidents related to telemetry exposure.

Rollbacks and emergency safeties
- If a sampling policy change causes unintended exposure, immediately:
  1) Revert to previous policy: rwctl telemetry revert --tenant TENANT_ID --to-revision REV_ID
  2) Open incident channel #telemetry-emergency and add Security and CSE owner.
  3) Notify legal if exposure involves PII.

Ownership and contacts
- Customer Success (primary): Maya Chen (author) — escalation contact: cs-oncall@redwood.ai
- Security (approval & investigation): Aisha Patel — security-oncall@redwood.ai
- Observability (dashboards & pipeline): Luca Romano — observability@redwood.ai
- Platform (ops): Diego Alvarez — infra-oncall@redwood.ai

Appendix: example audit log entry (text)
{timestamp: 2026-03-09T14:20:12Z, ticket: CS-UNBLIND-REQ-1234, operator: "diego.alvarez", approvers: ["aisha.patel","priya.nambiar"], hsm_sig: "SIG_BASE64", scope: "2026-03-01T00:00:00Z..2026-03-01T02:00:00Z", export_location: "s3://redwood-secure/tenants/TENANT_ID/unblind-CS-UNBLIND-REQ-1234.csv"}

title: Observability fallback circuit and customer escalation protocol
content:
Overview

Purpose:
This guide documents recommended integration patterns for Redwood customers to implement resilient telemetry and observability in the face of partial outages, plus the customer-facing escalation protocol that Support and Customer Success teams should follow when telemetry degrades or misreports. It covers: fallback circuit design, safe-mode telemetry striping, alert thresholds mapped to customer-facing severity levels, example Prometheus rules, sample incident payloads for downstream systems (PagerDuty / Zendesk), and a step-by-step escalation playbook for on-call and CSMs.

Scope:
- Applies to Dedicated and Private customers and to hosted customers with custom telemetry forwarding.
- Focuses on metrics, traces, and request/response sampling paths handled by the telemetry-gatekeeper and ingress-gateway.
- Does NOT replace per-tenant security or compliance checklists; see the private deployment acceptance playbook for those gates.

Key concepts and terminology:
- telemetry-gatekeeper: our sidecar/proxy component that validates and forwards telemetry from tenant workloads to Redwood collectors.
- circuit: a set of fallback rules that switch telemetry routing when an upstream path fails (e.g., forward to local buffer, sample down, or switch to light-weight health pings).
- striping: sending a subset of telemetry (e.g., 10% of spans + aggregated metrics) to reduce load while preserving signal.
- safe-mode: temporary mode where we reduce cardinality, increase sampling, and rely on synthetic checks for customer-facing health.

Executive summary (1 paragraph):
When telemetry ingestion becomes unavailable or unstable, customers should automatically enter a controlled fallback that maintains core SLO observability: request success rates, latency p50/p95, and token rate. Implement telemetry circuits in the telemetry-gatekeeper: primary path -> durable buffer -> reduced-sample forwarders -> synthetic pings. Support and CSMs must run the escalation protocol below when customer-facing SLAs are impacted or telemetry misreports greater than 2x for 15 minutes.

Design patterns and recommended configurations

1) Fallback circuit topology (recommended ordering)
- Normal: telemetry-gatekeeper forwards to primary-hosted-collector (TLS, compressed).
- Failover 1 (transient): telemetry-gatekeeper switches to local-durable-buffer (disk-backed) and also mirrors a sampled stream (10% metrics, 1% traces) to secondary-collector.
- Failover 2 (sustained): telemetry-gatekeeper flips to safe-mode: metrics aggregated at 60s resolution, traces disabled, synthetic pings every 30s to tenant-monitoring-probe.
- Recovery: gated rollout back to Normal after sustained 30m of stable forwarding and synthetic success.

Implementation checklist (config snippets and thresholds)
- telemetry-gatekeeper config (yaml) example:

  apiVersion: telemetry.redwood/v1
  kind: GatekeeperConfig
  metadata:
    name: customer-telemetry-policy
  spec:
    primaryForwarder: https://collector.redwood.example/v1/ingest
    buffer: {"type":"disk","max_size_mb":512}
    safeMode:
      metric_resolution_seconds: 60
      trace_sampling_rate: 0.01
      synthetic_probe_interval_seconds: 30
    fallbackRules:
      - trigger: [["upstream_connect_errors", ">", 5, "1m"]]
        action: "mirror_to_secondary_and_buffer"

- Prometheus alert rules (critical examples):

  - alert: TelemetryPrimaryUnavailable
    expr: rate(upstream_connect_errors[1m]) > 5
    for: 1m
    labels:
      severity: critical
    annotations:
      summary: "Primary telemetry collector connection error spike"

  - alert: TelemetrySampleRateDrop
    expr: telemetry_forwarded_samples_total / telemetry_received_samples_total < 0.5
    for: 10m
    labels:
      severity: major
    annotations:
      summary: "Effective telemetry sampling has dropped below 50%"

- SLO mapping table (example):
  | Customer SLA tier | Observability SLO maintained in fallback | Allowed data loss window | CSM notification level |
  | standard | request success rate p99 / 99% | 30m | Level 2 (notify) |
  | enterprise | request success rate p99 / 99.9% + latency p95 targets | 15m | Level 1 (paged) |

2) Telemetry striping recipes (to keep cardinality manageable)
- Metric cardinality cap: apply label whitelisting per tenant. Example policy: allow labels [route, status_code, model_family], drop others.
- Trace striping: use hash-based sampling: sample = hash(request_id) % 100 < N; recommended N=1-5 for safe-mode.
- Embedding/large-payload exclusion: do not forward raw embeddings; forward aggregated counts instead.

Operational thresholds and alerting matrix (customer-facing)
- Severity definitions for customer communications:
  - Sev 1 (P1) - Customer core inference is degraded or unavailable and no automatic fallback is possible. Action: page oncall SRE and CSM.
  - Sev 2 (P2) - Telemetry indicates degraded performance or misreporting that may materially affect incident response (e.g., sampling drop, metric staleness > 10m). Action: notify CSM and open a high-priority ticket.
  - Sev 3 (P3) - Non-urgent telemetry inconsistencies (dashboard gaps, minor metric divergence). Action: track in ticket queue; no page.

- Threshold examples (use as defaults; calibrate per customer):
  - Metric ingestion error rate > 2% sustained for 10m -> P2
  - Effective sample rate < 25% for 15m -> P2
  - Synthetic probe failure rate > 3 fails in 10m -> P1 if customer SLA is enterprise else P2

Escalation and customer communication protocol (step-by-step)

1) Detection and automatic mode switch (automated systems)
- Prometheus rule fires TelemetryPrimaryUnavailable -> alert routed to telemetry-team Slack channel and PagerDuty escalation policy "telemetry-forwarding".
- telemetry-gatekeeper automatically engages Failover 1 (buffer + mirror). An event is emitted to /events/telemetry/fallback with JSON payload (example below).

2) Triage by on-call SRE (within 10 minutes for P1 / 30 minutes for P2)
- Confirm the alert by checking collector health, network egress, and gatekeeper logs:
  - kubectl -n observability logs deploy/telemetry-gatekeeper --since=30m | grep "fallback"
  - curl -sS https://collector.redwood.example/health | jq .status
- Determine whether telemetry forwarding or customer traffic is impacted.
- If failover is successful and core customer traffic is unaffected, mark as "monitored" and notify CSM with templated status.

3) CSM outreach and customer notification templates (when to contact)
- Contact for P1 immediately after confirmation. P2 contact within 60 minutes.
- Use the following message template for CSMs (Slack/email/Zendesk):

  Subject: Redwood telemetry disruption for <tenant-name> — interim measures in place

  Hello <CustomerTeam>,

  We detected a transient issue impacting telemetry reporting for your deployment. We have automatically switched to a reduced telemetry mode to preserve application availability and are continuing to collect core metrics (request success rate, latency p50/p95). Our engineering team is investigating.

  Impact: reduced trace sampling and delayed metrics (up to 60s resolution)
  Expected next update: within 30 minutes
  Interim mitigations: safe-mode aggregation, synthetic probes enabled, buffering to durable storage

  If your team sees application-level errors or missing responses, please escalate to our oncall via PagerDuty (link) and include request IDs.

  Regards,
  Redwood Customer Success

4) Root cause analysis and recovery steps
- If the collector was the root cause: restore the collector, ensure TLS certs valid, and validate back-pressure counters are zero. Use these commands: 
  - kubectl -n observability rollout restart deploy/collector-primary
  - ssh collector-host && sudo journalctl -u collector -n 200
- If the gatekeeper buffer saturated: increase buffer size temporarily and force a replay from buffer once target collector reachable. 
- Recovery checklist (mark items in ticket):
  1. Confirm primary forwarder healthy for 30 consecutive minutes (no alert).
  2. Gradually reduce safe-mode sampling: 1% -> 5% -> 10% -> normal over 40 minutes.
  3. Rehydrate traces/metrics from buffer if required; check cardinality.
  4. Notify customer with final incident summary and link to RCAs.

Example event payload (emitted by telemetry-gatekeeper)

  {
    "event_type": "telemetry.fallback.engaged",
    "tenant_id": "tenant-1234",
    "timestamp": "2027-01-12T14:05:22Z",
    "fallback_stage": "mirror_to_secondary_and_buffer",
    "reason": "collector_connect_errors",
    "metrics_impact": "sample_rate_reduced_to_10%"
  }

Integration points with downstream systems
- PagerDuty: map Prometheus alerts: TelemetryPrimaryUnavailable -> PD escalation policy "infrastructure/telemetry". Include runbook link and event payload in PD notification.
- Zendesk: create ticket type "Telemetry Incident" and tag with tenant_id. Use send-to-customer template for P1/P2.
- QBR telemetry: automatically append incidents where a tenant entered safe-mode to the QBR summary feed; long-lived or repeated entries should trigger a stability review.

QBR & health-check signals to track
- Synthetic availability (30s probe pass rate) — target 99.9% enterprise, 99% standard.
- Number of safe-mode entries per quarter per tenant — target <=1 for enterprise.
- Mean time in safe-mode — target < 45 minutes.
- Percent of incidents where buffer replay caused data duplication — target 0%.

Testing and customer onboarding steps
- During onboarding, run the following simulation:
  1) Enable a controlled network block to the primary collector for 10 minutes.
  2) Verify gatekeeper enters Failover 1 and mirrors to secondary.
  3) Confirm telemetry sampling and synthetic probes continue to report.
  4) Restore network path and validate recovery checklist.
- Document results in the customer onboarding artifact and include telemetry circuit behavior in the cutover signoff.

Support playbook checklist (quick runbook for first responder)
1. Acknowledge alert and classify severity (P1/P2/P3).
2. Check collector health and gatekeeper logs.
3. Confirm fallback stage and whether core customer traffic is impacted.
4. Notify CSM with templated message.
5. If P1, page oncall SRE and open an incident ticket in the tracker.
6. Follow recovery checklist and update customer every 30 minutes until resolved.
7. After resolution, attach gatekeeper event payload and metrics to the incident and schedule RCA.

Ownership & contacts
- telemetry-runbook-owner: eng-platform-observability (pager: @telemetry-oncall)
- Customer Success escalation: cs-ops (email: cs-ops@redwood.example / pager: @cs-oncall)
- Escalation threshold arbiter: product-sre (for SLA disputes)

Appendix: useful commands and queries
- Check gatekeeper buffer stats (kubectl):
  kubectl -n observability exec deploy/telemetry-gatekeeper -- curl -s localhost:8080/metrics | grep buffer

- Prometheus query for sample-rate:
  rate(telemetry_forwarded_samples_total[5m]) / rate(telemetry_received_samples_total[5m])

- Example curl to replay buffer (operator-only):
  curl -X POST https://gatekeeper-admin.local/replay?tenant=tenant-1234 -H 'Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>'

- Incident postmortem template link: /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/incident-postmortem-template

Revision history
- 2026-11-04: Initial draft by Mariana Liu.
- 2026-12-10: Added synthetic probe guidance and sampling recipes (reviewer: Jonah Reed).
- 2027-01-12: Published and calibrated alert thresholds after playbook exercise (reviewers: Priya Patel, Evan Cho).

Related artifacts
- telemetry-gatekeeper config reference (internal repo): git@repo:redwood/telemetry-gatekeeper/configs.git
- Onboarding acceptance checklist: /confluence/customer-success-and-support/enterprise-onboarding/onboarding-data-sovereignty-verification-and-localization-test-plan-2026

If you find gaps or want a tenant-specific variant, open an edit request on this page and tag @cs-ops and @telemetry-oncall."

title: Observability contract and emergency backstop for real-time LLM deployments
content:
Summary:
This guide defines the minimal telemetry contract and emergency backstop (safety fallback) that Customer Success and Integrations teams should negotiate and validate with enterprise customers before enabling real-time LLM routes (streaming generation, chat, or low-latency embedding lookups). It is intended for customers using Dedicated or Private deployments and for any Hosted customers with strict availability or regulatory constraints.

Why this matters:
- Real-time LLM workloads are bursty and dependent on model sizing, KV cache behavior, and GPU scheduling.
- Clear telemetry enables fast root cause identification and automated failover decisions without expensive manual triage.
- A pre-agreed backstop ensures customer-facing apps remain available while we remediate model-serving or network incidents.

When to use this guide:
1) Prior to go-live for any enterprise cutover that relies on streaming / sub-200ms tail latencies.
2) When onboarding customers with internal SLAs that require deterministic error-handling and audit trails.

Definitions and scope:
- Observability contract: a minimal list of events, metrics, and traces the customer must forward or allow Redwood to collect via the agreed telemetry connector.
- Emergency backstop: pre-approved fallthrough behavior (e.g., degraded model variant, cached response, throttled-preset response, or traffic diversion) executed automatically when thresholds are hit.
- Tenant: the customer-specific logical instance (dedicated or tenant on a shared runtime).
- SLO: service level objective for latency, availability, and quality.

Telemetry contract (mandatory fields):
Provide or enable forward of the following keys at 1–10s granularity for real-time routes. If the customer cannot forward, integrate the Redwood telemetry sidecar described in the onboarding checklist.
- request.id (string): unique per-request identifier (UUID v4 preferred).
- tenant.id (string): tenant identifier assigned by Redwood.
- route.name (string): API route or logical endpoint, e.g., /v1/generate/chat.
- model.name (string): canonical model id used for the request.
- model.variant (string): quantized or fallback variant if applicable.
- request.start_ts, request.end_ts (ISO 8601): timestamps.
- request.tokens.input (int), request.tokens.output (int): token counts.
- latency.p50, latency.p95, latency.p99 (ms): per-minute aggregations.
- error.code (string) and error.class (string): categorization (e.g., retryable, quota, capacity, network).
- kvcache.hit_rate (float 0..1): prefix cache hit rate (per-model or per-tenant).
- gpu.util_pct (float 0..100): per-host or per-cluster.
- queue.depth (int): pending requests queue length.
- fallback.invocations (int): count of automatic fallbacks triggered.

Optional enrichments (recommended):
- request.prompt_hash (string): deterministic hash for prompt family grouping.
- quality.eval_score (float): if customer sends sample eval scores for production prompts.
- upstream.region, upstream.zone (string): hosting region tags.

Representation examples (JSON telemetry envelope):
{
  "request.id": "b2d9f9a8-2c34-4f6c-8a2b-c3a9a5f0e41f",
  "tenant.id": "acme-corp-42",
  "route.name": "/v1/generate/chat",
  "model.name": "redwood-7b-quant",
  "request.start_ts": "2026-03-01T15:04:05Z",
  "request.end_ts": "2026-03-01T15:04:05.180Z",
  "latency.p95": "180",
  "error.class": "none"
}

SLOs and thresholds (example customer baseline):
- Availability: 99.9% (client-consumable successful responses per rolling 30d).
- Tail latency: p95 < 250ms for streaming-start; p99 < 1.2s.
- Failure budget burn: >5% sustained over 6 hours triggers escalation.

Automated detection rules (implement these prior to cutover):
1) Latency surge: p95 increases by 2x vs baseline for 5 consecutive 1-minute buckets -> alert to oncall, reduce accepted concurrency by 25% and start backstop handshake.
2) KV cache collapse: kvcache.hit_rate drops below 0.25 for 2 minutes -> throttle low-priority tenants first, begin passive warming and notify customer.
3) Queue depth grow: queue.depth > 500 for a tenant for 30s -> reject new streaming requests with HTTP 429 and return backstop token.
4) Quality regression: quality.eval_score drop > 0.1 for a set of production prompts -> pause auto-quantized rollouts and route to a higher-fidelity variant.

Emergency backstop options (ordered by preference):
A) Serve from warm KV cache snapshot (fastest, preserves freshest user context).
B) Switch to a pinned, higher-latency but more reliable variant in same region (e.g., redwood-13b -> redwood-7b-high-qa).
C) Return a degraded but deterministic response (pre-approved template) for low-risk routes (e.g., confirmation flows).
D) Reroute to a customer-managed model endpoint (for Private deployments with mirror endpoints).
E) Soft-throttle: reject with HTTP 429 + Retry-After header and a short JSON body explaining the backstop.

Backstop handshake protocol (6-step automated flow):
1) Detection: Redwood autoscalers or SLO monitor fires detection alert (rule above).
2) Pre-check: orchestration checks model compatibility and pre-warms target variant for 30s.
3) Soft switch: route 10% of traffic to backstop variant for 60s, compare latency and quality heuristics.
4) Validation: if soft switch metrics are acceptable for 60s, increase to 100% and mark fallthrough_active=true.
5) Notification: send immediate notification to customer via configured channel (webhook/email/snowflake). Include request samples and telemetry digest.
6) Recovery: when baseline metrics recover for 10 minutes, orchestrator gradually switches back and logs change.

Onboarding checklist (customer + Redwood pre-cutover):
- Customer: agree telemetry fields and retention window (minimum 7d), provide endpoint for webhook or enable sidecar.
- Customer: designate 1 primary and 1 secondary operator with contact info and oncall windows.
- Redwood: pre-provision pinned fallback variant and capacity reservations for first 72 hours of go-live.
- Redwood: deploy tenant-specific alert rules into customer’s alerting workspace or coordinate forwarding.
- Joint: run canary with synthetic journey at 50 RPS for 30 minutes and validate contract keys are arriving.
- Joint: run failure injection (latency + 5% error spike) to verify backstop activation and notification plumbing.

Escalation matrix (who to call when):
- Triage (0–15 min): Customer Ops oncall (customer-success) + Redwood Integration Engineer.
- Incident (15–90 min): Redwood SRE lead + Customer engineering escalation contact.
- Major outage (>90 min): Eng SRE Director, Customer VP Engineering, and Account Executive.
- Post-incident (24–72h): Joint RCA and action items tracked in QBR deck.

Operational runbook (step-by-step for oncall):
1) Acknowledge alert. Post initial note to incident channel with request.id examples and affected tenants.
2) Pull last 15 minutes of the telemetry contract keys (use the telemetry query snippet below).
3) If backstop is not active, trigger soft-switch via admin CLI and monitor p95/p99 for 5 minutes.
4) If soft-switch fails, escalate to SRE and enable HTTP 429 policy with sanitized messaging.
5) Collect 10 representative request payloads and forward to customer-ops for quality review.
6) Schedule a hot patch or rollback of recent rollout (model/quantization) if identified as root cause.

Telemetry query snippet (prometheus / clickhouse style pseudo-queries):
- p95 latency per tenant (PromQL):
  histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_latency_seconds_bucket{tenant=~"acme.*"}[1m])) by (le))
- kvcache hit rate (ClickHouse):
  SELECT tenant_id, sum(hit) / sum(hit + miss) as hit_rate FROM telemetry.kvcache WHERE event_ts > now() - interval 5 minute GROUP BY tenant_id

Example admin CLI (safe mode):
# soft-switch 10% traffic for tenant
redwood admin route-split --tenant acme-corp-42 --route /v1/generate/chat --weight 10 --variant redwood-7b-high-qa --dry-run

Customer messaging templates (to be used by CS during incident):
- Short status update: "We observed an elevated latency event impacting your streaming route. We have activated an automated backstop and are monitoring performance. No additional action required at this time. ETA for full restore: 30–90 minutes."
- Technical summary for engineers: include request IDs, telemetry digest, fallback.invocations and patch/rollback actions.

QBR metrics and post-incident items to include:
- Number of backstop activations (30/60/90 day).
- Mean time to backstop and mean time to recover.
- Top 5 prompt families causing highest cost during backstop windows.
- Action items tracked and closure dates.

Frequently observed edge cases and workarounds:
- Symptom: intermittent HTTP 502 with p95 stable but p99 spikes.
  Workaround: increase model.variant pool size, enable KV cache pre-warm, and temporarily reduce accepted concurrency.
- Symptom: customer cannot forward request.id (legacy proxy).
  Workaround: Redwood sidecar will inject a stamped request_id and mark origin=sidecar for traceability.
- Symptom: Private deployment with no outbound telemetry.
  Workaround: enable batched secure pull (SFTP or S3) with 30s max delay and use a separate compensating alert for delayed telemetry.

Ownership and SLAs:
- Customer Success: primary owner for communication and QBR follow-up.
- Integrations team: responsible for onboarding the telemetry connector and running the initial failure injection.
- Eng SRE: owns alert rules, backstop orchestration, and CLI tooling.
- SLAs are contractual; this document defines operational defaults but customer contracts may override thresholds.

Appendix A — Telemetry retention and privacy:
- Minimum retention for high-fidelity telemetry: 7d. Aggregated metrics must be stored for 90d for QBRs.
- PII: telemetry must not include customer PII. Use prompt_hash for grouping rather than raw prompt text unless explicitly consented and encrypted at rest.

Appendix B — Sample canary script (bash):
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# simple canary runner to exercise route and verify telemetry arrival
for i in {1..300}; do
  REQUEST_ID=$(uuidgen)
  curl -s -X POST https://api.redwood.example/v1/generate/chat \n    -H "Authorization: Bearer ${REDWOOD_KEY}" \n    -H "X-Request-ID: ${REQUEST_ID}" \n    -d '{"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Hello"}]}' >/dev/null &
  sleep 0.2
done

Related resources:
- See also: observability-fallback-circuit-and-customer-escalation-protocol-2027 (for long-term escalation workflows).
- Runtime runbooks: eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/kvcache-warmup-and-eviction-playbook.

Contact
- Primary contact: Sofia Ramirez (Customer Success) — sofia@redwood.ai
- Oncall: integrations-oncall@redwood.ai

Change log:
- 2026-01-12: Initial draft and reviewer feedback.
- 2026-03-01: Added telemetry envelope examples, updated backstop automation steps and sample CLI.

title: GPU Fragmentation, Compaction, and Admission Control Playbook
content:
Summary

This playbook describes detection, triage, automated mitigation, and long-term controls for GPU-side memory fragmentation and allocation inefficiencies that lead to sudden request admission failures or unexpected latency spikes. It defines a compact, production-safe compaction daemon design, integration points with the scheduler admission controller, telemetry and SLOs to monitor, and an incident response runbook for on-call engineers.

Problem statement

- Symptom: bursts of OOM/admission-rejects for otherwise-capable GPUs, high allocation retry counts, or elevated tail latency for model requests despite available aggregate free memory.
- Root cause class: fragmentation of device memory and inefficient allocation patterns (many short-lived small allocations, large pinned KV caches, transient CUDA allocations by third-party kernels) that leave free memory fragmented into non-contiguous regions. On some GPUs this prevents large contiguous allocations required by kernels or model KV caches and forces the runtime to fall back to slower execution paths or reject requests.

Why this matters

- Impact on SLOs: admission failures and long alloc-retry loops can increase p95/p99 latency and reduce throughput. Customers experience degraded responsiveness while dashboards report available_free_bytes but high allocation failures.
- Cost: noisy retries and degraded kernels increase per-token GPU time and therefore cost.

Key concepts and terminology

- fragmentation_score: heuristic ratio of unusable free regions over total free memory (0..1). Higher means worse fragmentation.
- compaction: coordinated evacuation of low-priority allocations and re-creation of large contiguous free blocks (software-level: free & reallocate or runtime-level: memory defragmentation APIs where available).
- admission control threshold: configured fragmentation_score and free_pct thresholds that gate new request acceptance.
- compactor_daemon: lightweight service bound to each node/GPU that performs safe compaction cycles and exposes a handshake with the scheduler.

Telemetry and signals to monitor (recommended PromQL / queries)

- metrics to emit from runtime and compactor:
  - runtime_gpu_free_bytes_total (gauge)
  - runtime_gpu_largest_free_block_bytes (gauge)
  - runtime_gpu_allocation_retries_total (counter)
  - runtime_gpu_fragmentation_score (gauge: 0..1)
  - compactor_cycles_total (counter)
  - compactor_last_duration_seconds (gauge)
  - admission_rejects_by_reason{reason} (counter)

- Example PromQLs:
  - fragmentation score (per-gpu): avg(runtime_gpu_fragmentation_score) by (gpu_id)
  - allocation-failure rate: increase(runtime_gpu_allocation_retries_total[5m]) / increase(runtime_requests_total[5m])
  - usable-free-pct: runtime_gpu_largest_free_block_bytes / total_gpu_memory_bytes

Acceptable thresholds (guidelines — tune per fleet)

| Metric | Warning | Critical | Rationale |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| runtime_gpu_fragmentation_score | >= 0.35 | >= 0.60 | Above 0.35 we see elevated allocation retries; 0.6+ correlates with admission rejects in historical traces |
| runtime_gpu_largest_free_block_bytes | <= 0.25 * total_gpu_memory | <= 0.15 * total_gpu_memory | When largest contiguous block < 25% of device, large KV caches or batching fails |
| allocation retries per 10k requests | > 50 | > 250 | Empirical thresholds from production baselines |

Detection rules and alerting recommendations

1. Fire a P1 if: average(runtime_gpu_fragmentation_score) >= 0.60 on >= 3 GPUs in a rack for > 10m and admission_rejects_by_reason{reason="fragmentation"} increases by > 50/min.
2. Fire a P2 if: per-GPU runtime_gpu_fragmentation_score between 0.35 and 0.60 sustained for > 30m or allocation retry rate > threshold.
3. Add a transient ticketed warning when usable-free-pct < 0.30 for any GPU host.

Runbook: immediate triage (on-call steps)

1. Confirm incident context
   - Check dashboards: fragmentation_score, largest_free_block, allocation_retries, admission_rejects.
   - Identify impacted models, GPU IDs, node names, and recent deploys.
2. Quarantine and redirect traffic
   - If admission_rejects are affecting production paths, update the routing policy to divert traffic off affected GPUs to a fallback pool (use priority fallback model variants).
   - Apply fast chroots: mark GPUs as DRAINING via scheduler API to prevent new requests while preserving in-flight ones.
3. Trigger a controlled compaction cycle
   - Use the compactor control endpoint (see CLI below) to request an immediate compaction on specific GPUs.
   - If compaction does not reduce fragmentation_score by > 30% within timeout, escalate to manual eviction sequence.
4. Eviction sequence (if compaction fails)
   - Evict low-priority sessions and persistent KV caches according to eviction policy: first global LRU small sessions, then candidate long-lived KV caches tagged as "evictable".
   - Re-check fragmentation metrics. If still degraded, schedule node restart as last resort.
5. Post-incident analysis
   - Correlate with recent kernel rollouts, third-party library changes, and model variants.
   - Create a regression/bug entry if compactor failed or if specific model access patterns consistently cause fragmentation.

Automated compaction design (summary)

- Goals: minimize user-visible impact, preserve in-flight sessions, avoid full node restarts, and provide deterministic improvements for fragmentation_score.
- Phases:
  1. negotiate: compactor queries scheduler for safe eviction candidates; marks epochs for short allocation quiesce.
  2. drain-small-allocs: pause/serialize new small non-critical allocations and attempt to free short-lived buffers.
  3. move-and-realloc: for evictable objects (large KV caches with copy-on-restore semantics), copy to host memory or alternate GPU then free and reallocate to coalesce free regions.
  4. resume: restore paused allocations and release scheduler drain marks.

Compactor safety knobs and config example (YAML)

```yaml
compactor:
  enabled: true
  run_interval_seconds: 300
  max_duration_seconds: 120
  safe_eviction_percentage: 0.20 # will not evict more than 20% of active sessions without manual approval
  min_fragmentation_delta: 0.25 # required improvement for auto-marking success
  telemetry_window_seconds: 60
  backoff_multiplier: 2.0
  per_gpu_parallelism: 1
  eviction_tags_priority: ["background-lru","low-priority-kv","test-sandbox"]
  admission_thresholds:
    fragmentation_score_warning: 0.35
    fragmentation_score_critical: 0.60
    largest_free_block_pct_warning: 0.25
    largest_free_block_pct_critical: 0.15
```

Scheduler admission control contract (API sketch)

- Input: request metadata (model_id, expected_peak_alloc_bytes, priority) and current GPU stats (free_bytes, largest_free_block_bytes, fragmentation_score).
- Decision logic (high level):
  - If fragmentation_score >= critical and expected_peak_alloc_bytes > largest_free_block_bytes * 0.9 => REJECT with reason=fragmentation.
  - If fragmentation_score >= warning and priority == low => DELAY / QUEUE with backoff token.
  - Otherwise ACCEPT.

CLI and control endpoints (examples)

- Trigger compaction for gpu-4 on node-22 with 10m timeout:

```bash
redwoodctl compactor run --node node-22 --gpu 4 --timeout 600
```

- Query per-GPU fragmentation scores over the last 15m:

```bash
redwoodctl metrics query 'avg_over_time(runtime_gpu_fragmentation_score[15m])' --gpu all
```

Integration testing and benchmarking guidance

- Synthetic benchmark: the benchmark must exercise mixed allocation patterns (many small allocations + occasional large KV loads). Use the synthetic mix generator in the perf-suite:
  - small_alloc_rate: 400/s, size_distribution: lognormal(mu=8, sigma=1.1)
  - large_kv_loads: every 30s load 8GB KV block
  - concurrency: 128 sessions per GPU
- Measure before/after compactor: fragmentation_score, p99 latency, allocation_retries, throughput.
- Expected improvements: successful compaction should reduce fragmentation_score by >= 0.3 and reduce allocation_retries by >= 60% in controlled benchmarks.

Long-term mitigations and engineering actions

- Kernel hygiene: minimize transient device allocations in commonly used kernels; reuse buffers; prefer pooled allocators. Instrument third-party libraries used by model runtimes.
- KV cache reshaping: provide API for proactively chunked KV cache placement that avoids huge single contiguous allocations when model variant supports sharded KV.
- Scheduler heuristics: gradually prefer GPUs with low fragmentation_score for large-batch or high-memory requests; prefer dense placement for small-session workloads to increase contiguous free spans elsewhere.

Rollout and canary checklist

1. Unit and integration tests for compactor logic with synthetic fragmentation scenarios.
2. Canary compactor enabled on 5% of nodes with telemetry reporting and auto-rollback. Monitor fragmentation_score and allocation_retries for 72 hours.
3. Enable admission control in passive mode (log-only) for two weeks. Verify alert signal fidelity.
4. Switch to active mode with conservative thresholds for an additional two weeks, verify customer SLOs.
5. Incrementally increase compactor aggressiveness and tune safe_eviction_percentage.

Ownership and contacts

- Primary owner: eng/serving-runtime (Maya Chen)
- Secondary: eng/scheduler (Diego Alvarez)
- On-call rotation: serving-runtime pager team (see ops roster)

Post-incident review and RCA template

- Summary: one-paragraph incident description
- Timeline: 5–10 minute granularity events from detection to mitigation
- Detection root cause: instrumentation and signals that first indicated fragmentation
- Technical root cause: codepaths/kernels or workloads responsible for fragmentation
- Mitigation steps executed and effectiveness metrics
- Action items: short, medium, long-term (owners and deadlines)

Appendix: troubleshooting snippets and sample PromQL

- Find top 10 models contributing to allocation retries in the last 30m:

```
topk(10, sum by (model_id) (increase(runtime_model_allocation_retries_total[30m])))
```

- Compute per-node largest_free_block_pct:

```
runtime_gpu_largest_free_block_bytes / node_total_gpu_memory_bytes
```

- Example incident note to attach to postmortem:
  - "Compactor successfully reduced runtime_gpu_fragmentation_score from 0.68 -> 0.28 on node-42; admission rejects fell from 120/min to 2/min following controlled eviction of background caches. Root cause was a third-party kernel change that introduced ephemeral cudaMallocs without pooling."

Revision history

- 2025-11-03: Created by Maya Chen (initial draft).
- 2025-12-12: Added PromQL examples and safe_eviction knobs (review: Priya Nair).
- 2026-02-10: Expanded compactor design phase and added rollout checklist (review: Diego Alvarez).

Related reading

- See predictive-warmstart-and-cache-hinting-architecture for proactive KV shaping guidance.
- See numa-aware-shard-placement-eviction-playbook for host-level eviction interplay.

title: Edge observability resilience and offline onboarding playbook
content:
Summary:
This playbook describes Redwood’s recommended onboarding, verification, and escalation procedures for customers deploying edge or offline-capable telemetry collection with Redwood Private or Dedicated deployments. It focuses on ensuring telemetry continuity (metrics, traces, and request-level logs) when the customer’s network path to Redwood telemetry endpoints is interrupted, degraded, or intentionally air-gapped.

Audience:
- Customer Success Engineers, Solutions Engineers, Platform/Infra SRE, Customer Integrations teams.

Goals:
- Define telemetry delivery SLOs and verification tests for offline-capable collectors.
- Provide configuration templates for local buffering, encrypted disk persistence, and batched delivery.
- Standardize rollout verification and failure-mode drills.
- Provide an escalation matrix and runbook actions for delivery degradation and data-loss risk.

1) Non-goals:
- Replacing customer-specific compliance architectures; this playbook complements them.
- Prescribing exact collector projects (customers may use Fluentd, Vector, custom sidecars, or our Gateway agent).

2) Key definitions and SLOs:
- Telemetry Continuity SLO (customer-facing): 99.9% of telemetry events generated are successfully ingested within 72 hours.
- Real-time Telemetry SLO (platform-facing): 99.5% of events delivered within 30s under normal network conditions.
- Persistence Safety Threshold: local buffer must retain 48 hours of peak-event traffic with headroom >= 1.5x.
- Retry Backoff Policy: exponential backoff with jitter, max retry window 72 hours.

3) Roles and ownership:
- Customer Success (owner): onboarding coordination, acceptance criteria signoff, QBR reporting template.
- Integration/SE (owner): configuration guidance, test plan execution, verification artifacts.
- Customer Platform Team (owner): deploy collector agents, manage local storage and network policies.
- Eng-SRE (support): platform-side troubleshooting, ingestion backlog reconciliation, SLA adjustments.

4) Required customer-side capabilities (minimum):
- Persistent storage accessible to the collector agent with encryption-at-rest enabled.
- Outbound egress port allowances to Redwood telemetry endpoints OR a scheduled batch upload path (SFTP/HTTPS) approved in advance.
- A low-privilege service identity for the collector with scoped credentials and key rotation process.
- Synthetic traffic generator (simple script or load test) to produce deterministic test events.

5) Recommended configuration snippets (example YAML for Redwood Gateway agent):

# gateway-agent.yaml
collector:
  mode: offline-capable
  local_persistence:
    enabled: true
    path: /var/lib/redwood-gateway/buffer
    max_size_mb: 51200  # 50 GB (adjust per peak traffic)
    encryption: aes-gcm-256
  retention_hours: 72
delivery:
  endpoint: https://telemetry.redwood.example/v1/ingest
  batch_size: 1024
  max_concurrent_uploads: 4
  retry_policy:
    initial_backoff_s: 5
    max_backoff_s: 3600
    max_retry_window_hours: 72

Note: translate keys to the customer’s collector (Fluentd/Vector) equivalently.

6) Onboarding checklist (stages and acceptance criteria):
- Stage A: Pre-provisioning (customer completes)
  - Confirm storage path + encryption, agree on max retention sizing (artifact: sizing worksheet).
  - Confirm outbound egress or approved batch upload route.
  - Provide service identity/credentials to Redwood SE for test uploads.

- Stage B: Agent deployment (customer + SE)
  - Deploy agent in canary namespace/host (1–5% traffic).
  - Verify agent writes to local buffer; check permissions and disk usage.
  - Execute synthetic test for 1,000 events/min for 10 minutes.
  - Acceptance: agent persists events locally and marks events as queued.

- Stage C: Connectivity and delivery verification (customer + CS + Eng-SRE)
  - Run a simulated network partition (ingress blocked to Redwood endpoints) for 30 minutes.
  - Verify local buffer grows and no events are dropped.
  - Restore connectivity, verify backfill uploads complete and ingestion shows no duplicates or gaps.
  - Acceptance: Telemetry Continuity SLO met (all synthetic events ingested within 72 hours).

- Stage D: Scale and failure-mode tests (optional but recommended)
  - Simulate burst 5x peak for 1 hour; verify buffer headroom and upload behavior.
  - Test disk full condition: validate safe fail (agent rejects new events with clear logs) and recovery procedure.

7) Validation queries and dashboards (examples):
- Ingestion latency histogram (group by host/agent).
- Buffer utilization gauge per agent / host.
- Failed upload rate (5m rolling) > Alert at >= 0.5%.
- Backlog size in events and estimated hours to catch up.

Alert thresholds (recommended):
- P1: Backlog retention exceeds 80% of configured local persistence capacity OR estimated catch-up time > 48 hours.
- P2: Failed upload rate > 1% sustained for 15 minutes.
- P3: Agent process restarts > 3 times in 10 minutes.

8) Troubleshooting playbook (first 30 minutes):
1. Triage: Confirm whether issue is local (agent/host) or network (outbound to Redwood). Use agent status endpoint: curl http://localhost:9000/status
2. If network: capture tcpdump for outbound egress, check corporate proxy logs, verify DNS resolution to telemetry endpoint.
3. If local storage: df -h /var/lib/redwood-gateway; check agent logs for write errors and permissions.
4. Restart sequence: systemctl restart redwood-gateway-agent -> wait 30s -> check status. If restarts continue, escalate.

9) Escalation matrix (who to call and when):
- Level 1 (SE/CS handle) within 30 minutes: Collector misconfigurations, local disk warnings, authentication failures.
- Level 2 (Eng-SRE on call) within 2 hours: Large sustained backlogs, ingestion API 5xx responses, platform-side throttling.
- Level 3 (Platform Infra + Product) within 6 hours: Cross-region outage, storage corruption, data-loss risk.

Contact information (example):
- Customer Success: cs-team@redwood.ai (response target 60 minutes)
- Oncall Eng-SRE: eng-sre-oncall@redwood.ai (pager for P1)
- Platform Incident Slack: #platform-telemetry-incidents

10) Backfill and deduplication guidance:
- Backfill window: Redwood ingestion accepts up to 72 hours of delayed events with automatic idempotence when events include stable event_id and timestamp.
- Deduplication keys: event_id + source_host + timestamp. When using custom collectors, ensure event_id is stable across retries.

11) Customer acceptance and handoff to support:
- Deliverables before handoff: signed acceptance checklist, synthetic test logs, buffer sizing worksheet, and runbook with local contact.
- Handoff meeting agenda: final test replay, alert subscriptions, escalation points, QBR cadence.

12) QBR metrics to track post-onboarding:
- Weekly Telemetry Continuity compliance (% events ingested within 72h).
- Mean backfill time for any partition incident.
- Number of agent-side incidents and mean time to resolution (MTTR).

13) Appendix: Example incident scenarios and recommended actions:
- Scenario A: Proxy misconfiguration blocks HTTPS egress
  - Action: Temporarily switch agent to scheduled batch upload over SFTP to the prearranged S3 endpoint; mark incident and coordinate with customer network to restore egress.

- Scenario B: Disk corruption detected on host
  - Action: Fail agent to standby host (if HA enabled), copy partial buffer to quarantine storage, engage Eng-SRE for partial ingestion reconciliation.

- Scenario C: Platform ingestion throttling observed (5xx from telemetry API)
  - Action: Throttle client-side concurrent uploads to 1, open ticket with Eng-SRE, and enable priority routing for critical customer events (per contract).

Artifacts and templates (links to attach in Confluence):
- Buffer sizing worksheet (CSV template)
- Synthetic event generator (Python script)
- Acceptance checklist (PDF)

Notes and change history:
- 2026-01-12: Initial draft created by Marcos Delgado.
- 2026-03-04: Added retry policy and backlog alert thresholds per Eng-SRE feedback.
- 2026-07-14: Expanded verification tests and clarified deduplication guidance after two customer onboards.

End of document.

title: Session affinity fallback and observability adapter integration
content:
Summary
This guide describes the integration pattern and operational playbook for Session Affinity Fallback paired with the Observability Adapter. The goal is to maintain per-tenant session continuity (sticky routing + KV cache coherence) during model rollouts, capacity surges, and cross-environment (hosted -> dedicated -> private) handoffs while preserving telemetry fidelity for QBRs and incident investigations.

Context and problem statement
- Customers expect conversational continuity: the same persona, context, and KV cache should follow a tenant’s session even if the request is routed to a fallback or alternate deployment.
- During capacity pressure, routing changes, or version rollouts, naive failover breaks KV caches and makes tracing and quality regression analysis difficult.
- We provide an Observability Adapter that adds tenant-level metadata and reconciles distributed KV cache ownership during handoffs. This document explains the integration steps, config, and runbook for failure modes.

When to use
1) Enterprise tenants with strong SLAs for session continuity and traceable outputs.
2) Migration windows between hosted and dedicated/private deployments.
3) Canary or canary-surge auto-failovers where preserving context reduces user-facing quality regressions.

Architecture overview (text diagram)
- Client -> Ingress-proxy (sticky cookie / token) -> Routing-orchestrator -> [Primary pool: tenant-gateway -> model-pool, KV-store primary]
                                                                                                                        -> [Fallback pool: tenant-proxy -> model-pool, KV-sync sidecar]
- Observability Adapter (obs-adapter) is a sidecar in front of forwarders and emits tenant-scoped traces/metrics to the telemetry pipeline.
- KV-sync replicates prefix caches (KV cache) with configurable staleness windows.

Key components and responsibilities
- ingress-proxy: issues session tokens, enforces affinity hints (cookie, JWT claim), and marks requests with affinity headers. Owner: ingress team.
- routing-orchestrator: evaluates routing policy (latency vs cost vs tier) and decides fallback targets. Owner: routing team.
- tenant-gateway: primary request path for tenant; keeps authoritative KV ownership. Owner: tenant-platform.
- tenant-proxy + kv-sync sidecar: receives handoff requests; kv-sync attempts prefix/KV reconciliation with primary. Owner: private-deployments / dedicated ops.
- obs-adapter: injects tenant_id, session_id, model_version, fallback_reason into spans/metrics and emits structured logs for the QBR pipeline. Owner: telemetry team.

Prerequisites
- Tenant has a session token flow (cookie or bearer token) and tenant_id is present in request.
- KV sync endpoints enabled with TLS between primary and fallback pools.
- Observability Adapter image version >= 2.3.0 deployed alongside ingress-proxy and tenant-proxy.
- Routing-orchestrator supports fallback_reason codes and an affinity header (X-Redwood-Affinity).

Configuration examples
1) ingress-proxy affinity cookie (snippet):
- cookie_name: rw_session
- ttl: 3600 # seconds
- secure: true
- same_site: Lax

2) routing-orchestrator policy (YAML):
policy:
  - name: preserve-affinity-on-surge
    priority: 10
    conditions:
      - type: capacity-pressure
        threshold: 0.85
    actions:
      - type: fallback
        target_pool: fallback-pool-us-west
        preserve_affinity: true
        kv_reconciliation_window_sec: 30

3) kv-sync sidecar config (JSON example):
{
  "mode": "incremental",
  "max_prefix_bytes": 524288,
  "staleness_ttl_sec": 60,
  "consistency": "eventual",
  "reconciliation_interval_sec": 15
}

4) obs-adapter injection config (snippet):
- obs_adapter:
    emit_span_tags: ["tenant_id","session_id","model_variant","fallback_reason"]
    redact_fields: ["user_message.pii"]
    sample_rate: 1.0

Integration steps (high level)
1) Deploy obs-adapter v2.3.0 to ingress-proxy and tenant-proxy pods. Verify sidecar readiness.
2) Enable X-Redwood-Affinity header in ingress-proxy and set preserve_affinity: true in the routing-orchestrator policy used for the tenant.
3) Configure kv-sync TLS trust between primary and fallback clusters. Exchange certs using the private-deployments onboarding script.
4) Start a staged rollout: 10% traffic to fallback-pool with preserve_affinity and kv_reconciliation_window_sec=60.
5) Validate session continuity using the QA checklist below and observe traces in the telemetry dashboard.

QA and verification checklist
- Create a multi-turn session (10 turns) and note session_id.
- Force a controlled failover via routing-orchestrator API:
  curl -X POST "https://orchestrator.internal/api/v1/fallback" -H "Authorization: Bearer $RW_ADMIN_TOKEN" -d '{"tenant_id":"acme-corp","target":"fallback-pool-us-west","force":true}'
- Confirm the session_id is preserved in returned response headers (X-Session-Id).
- Inspect obs-adapter spans in Grafana/Tempo: ensure span tags contain tenant_id/model_variant/fallback_reason.
- Compare the produced response tokenization metadata for parity between primary and fallback (embedding dimensions, top-p, temperature).

Monitoring, alerts, and SLOs
- Telemetry emitted by obs-adapter: metric rw.session.handoff.count, rw.kv.reconciliation.success_rate, rw.handoff.latency_ms (p50/p95/p99).
- Recommended alert thresholds (pager):
  - rw.kv.reconciliation.success_rate < 95% for 5m -> page oncall (severity P1).
  - rw.handoff.latency_ms.p95 > 400ms for 10m -> notify routing and tenant-platform (P2).
  - rw.session.handoff.count spikes > 3x baseline per 5m -> alert capacity ops (P2).
- SLO targets for enterprise tenants using affinity:
  - Session continuity (session-id preserved across handoff): 99.9% monthly.
  - KV reconciliation success rate: 99% monthly.
  - Handoff latency p95: < 350ms.

Failure modes and runbook (step-by-step)
1) Symptom: KV_sync failing (error logs show TLS handshake failures) Runbook:
  a) Check kv-sync sidecar logs on fallback node: kubectl -n tenant-proxy logs -l app=kv-sync
  b) Validate TLS cert expiry: kubectl -n certs get secret tenant-kv-tls -o yaml | grep expiration
  c) If cert expired, follow cert-rotation playbook: update secret with new cert and restart pods.
  d) If network policy blocking, verify CNI rules and peering: run traceroute from fallback to primary on port 9200.

2) Symptom: Session ID not preserved after failover Runbook:
  a) Verify ingress-proxy is propagating X-Session-Id header.
  b) Inspect routing-orchestrator logs for preserve_affinity evaluation.
  c) If preserve_affinity=false, verify policy matches tenant label (policy may be scoped to enterprise-tier).
  d) If header present but lost downstream, check tenant-proxy header whitelist. Add X-Session-Id to allowed list.

3) Symptom: Observability spans missing tenant tags Runbook:
  a) Confirm obs-adapter sidecar is running and healthy. kubectl -n ingress get pods -l app=obs-adapter
  b) Check obs-adapter config: emit_span_tags includes tenant_id and session_id.
  c) If sample_rate < 1.0, temporarily set to 1.0 for a diagnostics window.

Rollout checklist and rollback plan
- Rollout (canary):
  1) Deploy obs-adapter to staging and run synthetic multi-turn sessions.
  2) Enable preserve_affinity for 5% of traffic to fallback. Monitor kv_reconciliation.success_rate and rw.session.handoff.count for 30 minutes.
