  3) Increase to 25% if metrics stable.
  4) After 2 hours at 25% and no P1s, expand to 100% for tenant.
- Rollback:
  - Immediate rollback: set routing-orchestrator policy to disable fallback (preserve_affinity=false) and redirect traffic to primary only.
  - If KV divergence occurred, run kv-sync reconciliation job with mode=full-sync (may incur cost/time). Track reconciliation job via job id returned by API.

Ownership and contacts
- Oncall (first-line): Customer Success Oncall (cs-oncall@redwood.ai)
- Escalation (P2+): Routing team (routing-eng@redwood.ai), Tenant Platform (tenant-platform@redwood.ai)
- Telemetry debugging: telemetry-observability@redwood.ai

Testing matrix for enterprise scenarios
- Scenario A: small multi-turn chat with immediate failover -> expected: session preserved, p95 latency increase < 150ms
- Scenario B: long context completion (2k tokens) with fallback -> expected: responses aligned but may have reduced caching efficiency; run embedding parity check post-handoff
- Scenario C: cross-region handoff (us-east -> eu-west) -> expected: increased latency but KV-sync allowed with staleness_ttl_sec >= 120

Operational notes and tips
- Prefer incremental kv-sync for low-latency workloads; schedule full-sync during maintenance windows.
- Use the obs-adapter structured logs to drive automated QBR sampling: tag sessions with product_feature and sample by tenant_impact_score.
- For private deployments behind air-gapped networks, provide a signed cert bundle using the private-deployments onboarding tool: scripts/certs/generate-bundle.sh

References and related pages
- routing policy reference: /confluence/eng-platform/routing-policy-reference
- kv-sync architecture: /confluence/eng-infra/gpu-fleet-and-capacity/kv-sync-architecture
- obs-adapter telemetry schema: /confluence/eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/obs-adapter-schema

Appendix: useful CLI snippets
- Force canary fallback via orchestrator:
  curl -X POST "https://orchestrator.internal/api/v1/fallback" -H "Authorization: Bearer $RW_ADMIN_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"tenant_id":"acme-corp","target":"fallback-pool-us-west","preserve_affinity":true}'

- Inspect reconciliation job status:
  curl -s "https://kv-sync.internal/api/v1/reconcile?job_id=JOB12345" -H "Authorization: Bearer $RW_ADMIN_TOKEN" | jq

- Quick validation script (python):
  python - <<'PY'
  import requests
  headers = {"Authorization":"Bearer $RW_ADMIN_TOKEN","Content-Type":"application/json"}
  r = requests.post("https://api.redwood.ai/v1/chat", headers=headers, json={"tenant_id":"acme-corp","session_id":"test-123","input":"hello"})
  print(r.headers.get('X-Session-Id'), r.json().get('response'))
  PY

Document lifecycle and maintenance
- Owners must review this guide quarterly or after any obs-adapter, routing-orchestrator, or kv-sync release.
- Major changes to preserve_affinity semantics require an update to enterprise SLOs and customer-facing documentation.

Feedback and improvements
- For integration gaps or missing telemetry fields, open an internal ticket in the #obs-adapter Slack channel and link the ticket to this page.
- Suggested improvements: automatic prefix reconciliation metrics per-session, stronger guarantees for bounded staleness in dedicated-private handoffs.

title: Customer telemetry schema harmonization and onboarding playbook
content:
Summary
-------
This playbook defines a standardized process for harmonizing customer telemetry schemas during enterprise onboarding, mapping telemetry to Redwood SLOs and QBR metrics, and validating ingestion pipelines. It is intended to reduce onboarding time, eliminate common mismatch failures, and ensure consistent downstream dashboards and billing attribution.

Scope
-----
- Applies to Dedicated and Private customers integrating with Redwood’s telemetry ingestion (telemetry-gateway, telemetry-transformer, metrics-collector).
- Covers event/metric/log schemas, required fields, sample transformations, validation steps, and escalation paths.
- Does NOT replace security/compliance data residency checks — coordinate with Security & Compliance for restricted customers.

Audience
--------
- Customer Success Engineers (CSEs) and Solutions Engineers running onboarding
- Customer platform engineers integrating telemetry
- Telemetry Platform team maintaining ingestion services

Goals and success criteria
--------------------------
- First ingestion success (schema accepted) within 5 business days for standard integrations.
- 99.9% telemetry ingest rate for onboarding test window (see validation SLOs).
- All QBR-critical metrics (latency p50/p95, error_rate, tokens_consumed) available in customer dashboard before go-live.

Prerequisites (customer)
-----------------------
- Network connectivity to telemetry-gateway endpoints (TLS 1.2+).
- Service account credentials and write-key provisioned by Customer Success.
- Sample event payloads (min 100 events across typical volume distribution).

Required fields and cardinality rules
-------------------------------------
The ingestion pipeline expects a canonical event JSON with these top-level fields. Missing required fields will trigger a schema rejection with HTTP 422.

| Field | Type | Description | Constraints |
|-------|------|-------------|-------------|
| tenant_id | string | Unique customer tenant identifier | max length 64, alphanumeric/-/_ |
| timestamp | ISO8601 | Event timestamp (UTC) | Acceptable skew: ±5m |
| source | string | Service/component name (e.g. web-ingress) | low-cardinality (<=100 per tenant) |
| event_type | string | One of: request, response, error, metric | enum |
| payload | object | Event-specific payload (see mappings) | size < 256 KB |

Note: High-cardinality values (user_id, session_id) must be nested under payload.user and should be hashed by the customer prior to send if retention is sensitive.

Telemetry -> SLO mapping reference
----------------------------------
We map incoming telemetry to Redwood SLOs used in QBRs. Ensure these metric names are produced, or provide a stable mapping during onboarding.

| Redwood metric | Type | Acceptable input names (customer) | Target SLO |
|----------------|------|----------------------------------|------------|
| request_latency_ms_p50 | gauge | request.latency.p50, latency_p50 | p50 <= 120 ms |
| request_latency_ms_p95 | gauge | request.latency.p95, latency_95 | p95 <= 450 ms |
| request_error_rate | ratio | request.errors.rate, error_rate | <= 0.5% |
| tokens_consumed_total | counter | tokens.used, tokens_consumed | N/A (billing) |

Onboarding checklist (step-by-step)
-----------------------------------
1. Kickoff: CSE schedules onboarding session, collects sample payloads and expected traffic profile.
2. Credentials: Provision write-key and test credentials in the customer sandbox project.
3. Schema draft: CSE and customer agree on a schema mapping table (use mapping template below).
4. Gatekeeper config: Telemetry Platform creates a temporary ingest gate (trial quota 10k events/day) and configures mapper rules.
5. Dry-run ingest: Customer sends 100 synthetic events across slow/fast paths. CSE validates ingestion receipts.
6. Validation suite: Run automated validators (see commands). Target: 95% pass in first run.
7. Dashboard wiring: Telemetry-Infra creates target dashboards and verifies dataflow for QBR metrics.
8. Readout and signoff: Customer PM and CSE confirm metrics and billing mapping.
9. Production enablement: Increase quota and flip to production write-keys.

Mapping template (example)
--------------------------
Provide a per-field mapping table for complicated sources. Example mapping for a web proxy: 

- tenant_id -> headers.x-tenant-id or query param tenant_id
- timestamp -> request.time (convert to ISO8601)
- source -> fixed value: web-proxy
- event_type -> map response.status >= 500 -> error, else response
- payload.request.latency_ms -> request.latency_ms (double)
- payload.tokens -> response.meta.tokens (int)

Example raw event (customer)
---------------------------
{
  "tenant": "acme-corp",
  "time_epoch_ms": 1680001234567,
  "svc": "edge-proxy",
  "status": 200,
  "latency": 95,
  "meta": {"tokens": 12, "session": "abc123"}
}

Transformer rule (example) - pseudo YAML
---------------------------------------
- match: source == "edge-proxy"
  transform:
    tenant_id: "$.tenant"
    timestamp: "to_iso($.time_epoch_ms)"
    source: "edge-proxy"
    event_type: "if $.status >= 500 then 'error' else 'response'"
    payload.request.latency_ms: "$.latency"
    payload.tokens_consumed: "$.meta.tokens"

Validation commands and CI checks
--------------------------------
- Ingest smoke test (curl):
  curl -X POST https://telemetry-gateway.redwood.internal/v1/ingest \\n    -H 'Authorization: Bearer <TEST_KEY>' \\n    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \\n    -d @sample-event.json | jq '.'

- Schema validator (local):
  python tools/schema_validator.py --schema canonical_schema.yaml --events sample-batch.json

- CI check: Add telemetry sanity test to customer onboarding harness. Required assertions:
  - all events accepted (no 422)
  - required Redwood metrics present in metrics-collector output stream

Validation SLOs for onboarding window
-------------------------------------
- Ingest success rate >= 99.9% for 24h trial window
- Metric freshness: p95 metric delay < 60s
- Cardinality safety: unique source tags per tenant <= 200 in trial window

Escalation and remediation matrix
--------------------------------
- If schema rejections > 1% over 1 hour: CSE to open Jira to Telemetry Platform (tag: telemetry-onboard) and notify #cs-onboard Slack.
- If metric freshness > 3m for p95: Telemetry oncall (@oncall-telemetry) to investigate collector lag.
- Billing attribution mismatch: open support ticket and CC Billing Ops.

Rollout and rollback steps
--------------------------
1. Canary: enable production write-key but limit traffic to 5% for 2 hours while monitoring ingest success and SLOs.
2. Verify: confirm dashboards populate and QBR metrics stable.
3. Promote: remove quota cap and update readme with production endpoints.
4. Rollback: if failure observed (ingest < 98% or missing critical metrics), revoke production key, revert gatekeeper mapping to previous version, and restore previous ingest config.

Troubleshooting common failure modes
-----------------------------------
- 422 schema rejections: Check required top-level fields and size limits. Use schema_validator to pinpoint missing keys.
- High cardinality errors (rate-limited): Identify tag producing high cardinality (source/user) and request a mapping to hash or truncate.
- Timestamp skew: If many events rejected for timestamp > ±5m, confirm client clock and apply to_iso conversion.

Ownership and contacts
----------------------
- Customer Success Onboarding (CS-Onboard): cs-onboard@redwood.ai, Slack #cs-onboard
- Telemetry Platform: telemetry-infra@redwood.ai, Slack #telemetry-ops, oncall @oncall-telemetry
- Billing Ops (attribution): billing-ops@redwood.ai

QBR artifacts to produce before go-live
--------------------------------------
- Dashboard: Ingest overview (success rate, p95 latency, errors)
- Mapping document: Final schema mapping spreadsheet (s3 link)
- Test run report: 24h validation run with pass/fail and anomaly notes

Appendix: quick check commands
-----------------------------
- Check latest ingest events in Kafka topic (dev-shared):
  kafka-console-consumer --bootstrap-server kafka.redwood.internal:9092 \\n    --topic tenant.telemetry.events --from-beginning --max-messages 50 | jq '.'

- Dump customer-level metrics filter:
  curl -s 'https://metrics-collector.internal/api/v1/query?query=request_error_rate{tenant_id="acme-corp"}' | jq '.'

Change log
----------
- 2025-09-15: Created initial playbook (Jordan Lee)
- 2026-02-10: Added SLO thresholds and rollback guidance (reviewers: Lina Gomez, Samir Rao)

End of playbook

title: Quota Protector Webhook Integration and Reconciliation Guide
content:
Overview
--------
This integration guide describes the Quota Protector webhook used by Redwood Inference to reliably surface customer quota events and automate protective credits and throttling adjustments during anomalous billing or rate-limit events. The document explains the webhook contract, delivery guarantees, recommended reconciliation workflow for enterprise customers, on-call runbooks for mismatches, and examples for implementing a receiver and reconciliation worker in third-party billing systems.

Goals
- Reduce false-positive quota rejections for enterprise customers during bursty or partial-failure conditions.
- Provide deterministic reconciliation steps to reconcile token usage vs. billing records within a 72-hour window.
- Support automated protective credits (temporary credits) and safe rollback actions with auditability.

When to use this integration
- Enterprise customers with reserved or committed capacity (Dedicated or Private) that need automated protective measures when perceived usage spikes or system anomalies occur.
- Partners who want proactive notifications and a standard reconciliation API for invoicing systems.

Prerequisites
- Customer must have a configured webhook receiver endpoint reachable from Redwood (HTTPS/TLS).
- Shared secret (HMAC-SHA256) provisioning via the console or SRE onboarding link.
- Access to your billing system’s ingestion pipeline (batch or streaming) for reconciliation.

Webhook contract (delivery semantics)
1) Event types (payload field event_type):
   - quota.alert: short-lived alert when usage approaches a quota threshold (INFO).
   - quota.protective_action: Redwood applied a temporary protective credit or soft-throttle (ACTION).
   - quota.reconcile_request: Redwood requests reconciliation for an identified discrepancy (RECONCILE).
   - quota.reconcile_result: Customer posts back reconciliation outcome (RESULT).
2) Delivery guarantees:
   - Redwood will attempt delivery with exponential backoff for up to 24 hours.
   - Events are delivered at-least-once; receivers must be idempotent (see Idempotency section).
   - Quota.reconcile_request is guaranteed to be emitted once per discrepancy case.
3) Security:
   - Each HTTP request includes X-Redwood-Timestamp and X-Redwood-Signature (HMAC-SHA256 of body + timestamp with shared secret).
   - Request body is application/json and UTF-8 encoded.

Example payloads
- quota.protective_action (abbreviated):
```json
{
  "event_id": "e7d1f2b8-9c7a-4a4b-8a6d-2f4a1a6c9b1e",
  "event_type": "quota.protective_action",
  "tenant_id": "enterprise-42",
  "timestamp": "2026-02-18T21:03:12Z",
  "action": "temporary_credit",
  "amount_tokens": 250000,
  "reason": "ingestion spike during redesploy",
  "correlation_id": "ops-rollback-20260218-1",
  "metadata": {"affected_routes": ["/v1/generate"], "instance_pool": "dedicated-prod-3"}
}
```
- quota.reconcile_request (abbreviated):
```json
{
  "event_id": "r2a9b4c5-44f6-4c9b-95d6-0b9f3a2c3d7b",
  "event_type": "quota.reconcile_request",
  "tenant_id": "enterprise-42",
  "timestamp": "2026-02-18T22:00:00Z",
  "window_start": "2026-02-18T20:00:00Z",
  "window_end": "2026-02-18T21:00:00Z",
  "reported_usage_tokens": 1200000,
  "observed_usage_tokens": 980000,
  "suggested_action": "credit_25000_tokens_or_manual_review",
  "details_url": "https://console.redwood.com/tenants/enterprise-42/recon/r2a9b4c5"
}
```

Idempotency and receiver best practices
- Use event_id as the primary idempotency key. Store event_id and processing result for 90 days.
- Design reconciliation handlers to accept repeated reconcile_request events and only create a single case per unique correlation_id.
- Return standard HTTP codes: 200 for success, 202 for accepted (async processing), 4xx for client errors, 5xx for transient failures. Redwood will retry on 5xx and network errors.

Sample receiver flow (recommended)
1) Verify signature and timestamp within +/- 5 minutes. Reject otherwise with 401.
2) Check local dedupe store by event_id; if found, return 200 with existing outcome.
3) For quota.protective_action: apply temporary internal protective credit and create an internal ticket with priority=high if action==temporary_credit.
4) For quota.reconcile_request: enqueue a reconciliation job that performs matching between reported_usage_tokens and your billing records for the provided window. Post a quota.reconcile_result when complete.

Reconciliation worker design
- Match level: ingestion-level (per request ID) if available; fallback to route-level aggregation by minute.
- Tolerance band: accept discrepancies <= 2.5% as noise; >2.5% and <=10% trigger automated protective credit up to suggested_action. >10% escalates to human review.
- Audit trail: include the Redwood event_id, your reconciliation_job_id, and links to raw records.

Automated protective credits and accounting flow
1) On reconcile_request that falls into the automated band, your system should:
   - Create a refundable credit entry tied to the tenant and reconciliation_job_id.
   - Post quota.reconcile_result with fields (event_id, job_id, outcome: auto_credit_applied, credit_amount_tokens, note).
2) Finance integration: reconcile refundable credit entries weekly against Redwood billing exports.
3) Auto-expiry: credits applied as protective must be stamped with expiry (default 30 days) and a reconciliation flag to convert to permanent credit only after human approval.

SLOs and monitoring
- Delivery SLOs: Redwood aims for 99.5% successful initial delivery (non-5xx) across webhook endpoints.
- Customer receiver SLOs: process reconcile_request within 8 hours or reply with 202+job_id to indicate longer processing windows.
- Alerting: customers should alert if more than 5 reconcile_request events are queued for >24 hours for a single tenant.

On-call runbook: unresolved reconciliation mismatch
1) Redwood emits quota.reconcile_request with suggested_action. Customer system posts back quota.reconcile_result. If no result after 24 hours, do:
   a) Check delivery logs (Redwood Console -> Integrations -> Webhooks -> Delivery).
   b) Confirm webhook receiver health (CPU, request queue depth, TLS cert validity).
   c) If receiver healthy but processing stuck, escalate to internal billing ops: create ticket with tags [recon-stuck, tenant:<tenant_id>] and assign to billing-ops on-call.
2) If the reconcile_result indicates disagreement (customer refutes observed usage), run a manual audit:
   a) Export raw request logs from Redwood for the window (Console -> Tenants -> Export Usage).
   b) Crosswalk timestamps and request IDs. If discrepancies persist, open a joint investigation with Redwood SRE via the enterprise support channel.
3) If finance disputes remain after 7 days, follow the contractual dispute process (see related_pages billing-credit-policy).

Troubleshooting common errors
- 401 Unauthorized: bad HMAC signature or clock skew. Verify shared secret and sync NTP.
- 422 Unprocessable Entity: missing required fields (event_id, event_type, tenant_id, timestamp). Confirm JSON schema.
- Repeated duplicates: confirm dedupe store retention and idempotency key correctness.
- Large backlog: increase worker parallelism and consider accepting 202 with job_id for long-running reconciliation.

Implementation examples and helper scripts
- Minimal Node.js receiver skeleton (pseudocode)
```js
const express = require('express');
app.post('/webhooks/rdw', verifySignatureMiddleware, async (req, res) => {
  const event = req.body;
  if (await alreadyProcessed(event.event_id)) return res.status(200).send({status:'duplicate'});
  enqueueReconcile(event).then(jobId => res.status(202).send({job_id: jobId}));
});
```

Operational recommendations for enterprise customers
- Keep a rolling 7-day window of raw request logs for quick manual audits.
- Configure alert thresholds on per-tenant queue depth and reconcile_request age.
- Regularly rotate webhook secrets and use mutual TLS for sensitive integrations.

Privacy and audit considerations
- Webhook payloads may contain tenant identifiers and usage aggregates. Do not log PII.
- All reconciliation actions must be recorded with who/what/when for billing audit trails.

Appendix: field reference
- event_id: UUID v4, unique per event.
- correlation_id: opaque string that groups related protective actions / reconcile flows.
- reported_usage_tokens: integer, tokens Redwood observed.
- observed_usage_tokens: integer, any computed alternate observation.
- suggested_action: free-text suggestion (credit_x_tokens | manual_review).

Contact and ownership
- Integration owner: Customer Success (Elena Park) — elena.park@redwood.com
- Escalation path: first-line CSM -> Billing Ops -> Redwood SRE (via enterprise Slack channel #eng-support-enterprise).

Revision history
- 2026-01-12: Created initial draft (Elena Park).
- 2026-02-20: Clarified idempotency and added tolerance bands for automated credits (reviewers: Marcus Li, Priya Nair).

Related artifacts and links
- Console integration page: https://console.redwood.com/docs/integrations/webhooks
- Billing export schema: https://console.redwood.com/docs/finance/billing-export-schema

title: Onboarding observability contracts for dedicated tenants
content:
Summary

This playbook defines the observability contract that Redwood and a customer agree on when provisioning a Dedicated tenant (reserved capacity or private deployment). The contract covers the telemetry signals, their schema, minimum retention and sampling guarantees, alerting baseline, SLO mappings, and a validation checklist used during onboarding. The goal is to ensure parity between Redwood operational expectations and the customer’s telemetry exports so that both parties can reliably triage incidents, verify SLAs, and run QBRs.

Who this is for

- Customer Success (CS) owners running onboarding
- Solutions Engineers and Integration Engineers
- Dedicated tenant SRE/Platform owners at Redwood
- Customer platform/observability engineers

Goals and non-goals

- Goals:
  - Agree and validate a minimum telemetry contract prior to production onboarding.
  - Prevent blind spots that block incident diagnosis (e.g., missing request trace ids, tenant_id labels).
  - Provide deterministic SLI extraction and alert thresholds for initial week-0 to week-12 SLOs.
- Non-goals:
  - Do not mandate customer-specific internal metrics beyond agreed labels and formats.
  - This is not an exhaustive observability design for the customer; it is a compatibility contract for Redwood’s support and SRE workflows.

Contract: required telemetry signals (table)

| Signal type | Canonical name (example) | Required fields/labels | Minimum frequency / retention | Notes |
|-------------|--------------------------|------------------------|------------------------------|-------|
| Request metric (histogram) | request.duration | service, route, model, tenant_id, status_code, request_id | 1s buckets; retention 90d for aggregates | Redwood expects histogram or Prometheus SUMMARY so p50/p90/p99 can be computed. |
| Request counter | request.count | service, route, model, tenant_id, status_code | delta COUNTER; retention 365d | Increment on request start/finish. Include status_code for error classification. |
| Token metric | tokens.generated | model, tenant_id, request_id | per-request sample; retention 90d | Optional for cost attribution but strongly recommended. |
| Traces / spans | span (OTel) | trace_id, span_id, parent_id, service, operation, route, model, tenant_id, request_id, sampling.priority | full traces for 1% of requests, tail-sampling for errors (100%) | Spans should attach request_id and tenant_id. Use semantic conventions below. |
| Logs | structured logs (JSON) | timestamp, level, service, tenant_id, request_id, message, err_code (optional) | 100% of errors; INFO sampling 1-10% | JSON structured logs preferred. Use consistent field names. |
| Synthetic checks | synthetic.transaction | check_id, tenant_id, route, latency_ms, success | run every 60s during cutover; retention 90d | Used for validation step and baseline alerts. |

Required labels and conventions

- tenant_id: string, immutable per tenant (required for all signals).
- request_id: UUID assigned by router / ingress for the request lifecycle (required).
- model: model id or family (e.g., gpt4o-small) when relevant.
- route: logical API route name (e.g., generation.v1, embeddings.v1).
- service: component name (e.g., ingress-proxy, inference-worker).
- status_code: canonical codes (200, 4xx, 5xx) or internal error categories.

OpenTelemetry/Prometheus examples

- Prometheus exposition example (histogram + counter):
  # HELP request_duration_seconds Request duration by route and status
  # TYPE request_duration_seconds histogram
  request_duration_seconds_bucket{le=\"0.1\",service=\"ingress-proxy\",route=\"generation.v1\",tenant_id=\"acct-abc\",status_code=\"200\"} 1234
  request_duration_seconds_sum{service=\"ingress-proxy\",route=\"generation.v1\",tenant_id=\"acct-abc\",status_code=\"200\"} 45.6
  request_duration_seconds_count{service=\"ingress-proxy\",route=\"generation.v1\",tenant_id=\"acct-abc\",status_code=\"200\"} 2500

- OTel span JSON (minimal):
  {
    \"trace_id\": \"4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736\",
    \"span_id\": \"00f067aa0ba902b7\",
    \"name\": \"request.process\",
    \"attributes\": {
      \"service\": \"inference-worker\",
      \"route\": \"generation.v1\",
      \"tenant_id\": \"acct-abc\",
      \"request_id\": \"8a1e6f3b-...\"
    },
    \"status\": {
      \"code\": \"OK\"
    }
  }

Sampling guarantees and error tail collection

- Baseline sampling: 1% uniform sampling of traces across traffic for 30d after go-live to collect representative traces.
- Error-tail sampling: 100% of traces that result in an error status (5xx or internal error) must be sent. This enables root-cause analysis regardless of base sampling.
- Synthetic journey traces: 100% of synthetic checks must export full spans.

Alerting and incident thresholds (default initial set)

- Pager/critical (Redwood SRE + CS on-call):
  - sustained p99 request latency > 4s for > 5m across > 5% of tenants
  - error rate (5xx) > 3% for > 5m across total requests
- High-priority (CS/SE + engineering on first response):
  - tenant-specific p99 > configured tenant SLO by 2x for > 10m
  - synthetic.check failures > 3 consecutive failures for a tenant
- Informational (Slack/ops):
  - tokens.generated 24h change > 50% vs baseline (cost-monitoring trigger)

SLO mapping and initial targets

- Recommended starter SLOs for Dedicated tenants (can be adjusted by contract):
  - Availability SLO: successful request rate >= 99.9% over rolling 30d (success = status_code < 500)
  - Latency SLO: p95(request.duration) <= 1.2s for generation routes (initial baseline)
  - Cost-awareness SLO: median tokens per request stable within 20% of baseline across 7d (informational)

Onboarding validation checklist (ordered steps)

1. Pre-cutover alignment call (SE + Customer observability lead + Redwood SRE): review contract and choose export method (Prometheus scrape vs OTLP push).
2. Export configuration: customer provides test endpoint or config; Redwood provides example scraping job / OTEL collector config (see snippets).
3. Smoke export test: send 1,000 synthetic transactions and validate metrics/labels arrive in Redwood tenant ingestion pipeline.
4. Trace validation: ensure at least 1% of traces appear, and 100% of error traces for test error injection.
5. Alert simulation: trigger synthetic failures and latency injection to verify alerts fire to CS channel.
6. QBR baseline capture: run 72h of production-equivalent traffic to capture baseline metrics for QBR and SLO tuning.
7. Production cutover sign-off: CS, SRE and Customer observability lead sign the checklist.

Onboarding example: OTEL Collector snippet (customer-hosted)

- Minimal OTLP exporter config (yaml block):
  receivers:
    otlp:
      protocols:
        http:
  exporters:
    otlp/redwood:
      endpoint: \"https://ingest.redwood.example.com:4318\"
      headers: {\"x-tenant-id\": \"acct-abc\"}
  service:
    pipelines:
      traces:
        receivers: [otlp]
        exporters: [otlp/redwood]
      metrics:
        receivers: [otlp]
        exporters: [otlp/redwood]

Troubleshooting common mismatches

- Missing tenant_id on metrics: verify collector includes resource attributes or the scraping job populates tenant_id via relabel_configs.
- request.duration is a gauge instead of histogram: the ingestion pipeline expects histogram buckets; either change to histogram or send summary with sufficient quantiles.
- Spans missing request_id: ensure the ingress assigns request_id and propagates it to downstream services via headers (x-request-id).
- No error traces: check tail-sampling config and error classification rules in the collector.

Rollout notes and risk mitigations

- Canary for telemetry: enable telemetry export for a low-volume tenant first for 48h to validate label cardinality and cost.
- Cardinality caps: Redwood reserves the right to request label normalization if cardinality exceeds 5k distinct values/day for tenant-scoped labels.
- Cost controls: if metrics/log egress costs exceed agreed thresholds, throttle sampling and re-run validation.

Owners and escalation path

- CS Onboarding Lead: Maya Patel (customer-success) — primary contact for checklist and sign-off.
- Redwood SRE: Ethan Brooks — validation, alerting, and production troubleshooting.
- Customer Integration Owner: provided at onboarding call — responsible for implementing exporters.

Validation artifacts to attach at completion

- 72h baseline metrics snapshot (Prometheus TSDB dump or CSV)
- Sample trace IDs and a small trace export file (OTLP JSON) showing request_id/tenant_id mapping
- Alert test logs and screenshots of notifications

Appendix: example SLO extraction PromQL

- p95 latency (generation route):
  histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket{route=\"generation.v1\"}[5m])) by (le))
- success rate over 30d:
  1 - sum(increase(request.count{status_code=~\"5..\"}[30d])) / sum(increase(request.count[30d]))

Document change log

- 2026-01-12: created by Maya Patel (initial contract draft).
- 2026-03-05: updated sampling guarantees and alert thresholds after SE feedback (Ethan Brooks).

Related reading

- Dedicated tenant cutover safety net playbook (link in related_pages).
- Tenant dashboard template (eng-platform): shows fields expected by Redwood dashboards.

Contact and next steps

Schedule the pre-cutover alignment call using the CS onboarding calendar. After sign-off, the integration engineer will share a tenant-scoped OTEL collector config and the Redwood validation script used to verify ingestion. For restricted customers (HIPAA/PCI), additional data redaction guidance will be appended to the contract per the Private deployment security checklist.

title: session-replay-and-request-correlation-integration-guide
content:
Overview

Purpose: This guide describes a recommended, low-risk approach for integrating session-replay and request-correlation telemetry into customer integrations with Redwood Inference. The goal is to enable deterministic post-hoc debugging of LLM response variance, accountable QBR-quality traceability, and safe data handling for enterprise customers.

Audience: Customer Success Engineers (CSEs), Integration Engineers, Platform Engineers, and partner SRE teams.

When to use this doc: Use during enterprise onboarding, troubleshooting escalations, or when customers request fine-grained request-level visibility for SLA/QBR evidence.

Key benefits
- Rapidly reproduce customer issues tied to specific requests and prompts.
- Correlate SDK requests, gateway routing decisions, model variant switches, and the runtime traces that produced the output.
- Provide customers auditable request timelines for QBRs while minimizing PII exposure.

Primary concepts and definitions
- Session ID: stable opaque identifier assigned by the client (or proxy) to group related requests (e.g., a user session or conversation).
- Request Correlation ID (rcid): short unique id assigned per logical request at the ingress gateway and propagated across service boundaries. Canonical header: X-RW-Request-Id.
- Replay Bundle: an anonymized package of inputs, metadata, and runtime trace references sufficient to recreate the inference call surface in a sandbox.
- Sampling Policy: deterministic rule used to mark which requests are retained at full fidelity (e.g., 1 in 1000 + on-error).

Minimum requirements
- Ingress must accept and forward X-RW-Request-Id and X-RW-Session-Id headers to Redwood front-line proxies and telemetry pipeline.
- Customer SDK or proxy must produce a stable client session id when available.
- Telemetry Gatekeeper must support three modes: none, sample, and full (configurable per tenant).
- Stored replay bundles must be encrypted at rest and available only to authorized roles.

High-level architecture
1) Client or sidecar assigns or forwards X-RW-Session-Id and X-RW-Request-Id.
2) Ingress gateway stamps and normalizes headers, adds route/model metadata (model-name, model-version, route-id).
3) Front-line proxy forwards request to runtime and emits a compact trace + request attributes to the telemetry pipeline.
4) Telemetry pipeline applies sampling policy; if retained, a replay bundle is persisted in replay-store and a short pointer is included in traces.
5) Customer Success and SRE teams use the correlation id to assemble the replay bundle and execute sandbox reproduction.

Headers and minimal telemetry schema (recommended)
| Header / field | Example | Purpose |
|---------------|---------|---------|
| X-RW-Request-Id | rw-req-20260218-7f9b | Primary correlation across services |
| X-RW-Session-Id | sess-42ab | Grouping for conversation-level analysis |
| X-RW-Model | redwood/loom-1.1 | Model identifier used for the request |
| X-RW-Model-Variant | quant-v2 | Variant / quantization profile |
| x-rw-latency-ms | 124 | End-to-end latency measured at ingress |

Configuration examples
1) Ingress gateway (NGINX sidecar snippet)
```
proxy_set_header X-RW-Request-Id $req_id;
proxy_set_header X-RW-Session-Id $http_cookie_session_id;
proxy_set_header X-RW-Model $upstream_model;
```
2) SDK side (Javascript example)
```
const rcid = generateRcId();
const sessionId = getActiveSessionId();
await fetch('/v1/generate', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: {
    'Content-Type': 'application/json',
    'X-RW-Request-Id': rcid,
    'X-RW-Session-Id': sessionId,
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({prompt})
});
```
3) Telemetry Gatekeeper policy (YAML)
```
tenantPolicies:
  tenant-123:
    sampling:
      default: 0.001 # 0.1% full replay
      on_error: 1.0   # capture all failed requests
    redact:
      fields: [user_email, credit_card]
    retention_days: 90
```

Replay bundle contents (anonymized)
- Request metadata: rcid, session id, model id/version, route id, timestamp, tenant id (hashed)
- Input artifacts: prompt text (redacted per policy) or prompt fingerprints (hashes), function call payloads (optional)
- Runtime trace pointer: object keys referencing distributed spans and per-worker kernel sampling logs (not full raw logs)
- Result snapshot: model tokenization, output tokens, confidence stats, and deterministic RNG seeds for reproducibility

Data protection and privacy checklist
1) Apply field-level redaction as per tenant policy before persisting replay bundles.
2) Replace any PII using deterministic tokenization and retain only hashed identifiers where necessary.
3) Ensure replay-store encryption (KMS) and access controls: CSEs require explicit RBAC grants and time-limited signed URLs for customer investigations.
4) Maintain an access audit trail for all replay retrievals; include reason and approver.

Rollout plan (recommended minimal-risk path)
1) Sandbox pilot (2 weeks): enable sample mode (0.1%) for non-production tenant test corpus. Validate header propagation and pointer integrity.
2) Expanded pilot (4 weeks): add on_error capture; involve 2–3 pilot customers with signed data handling agreements.
3) Canary to production (2–3 weeks): enable per-tenant sampling config at 1% for design partners; verify decryption and replay reconstruction flow.
4) GA: default sampling back to 0.1% with documented support SLAs for replay requests.

Operational playbook: reproducing a customer issue
1) Customer reports variance with rcid included in ticket.
2) Triage: validate rcid format and tenant mapping. Verify existence in traces via trace-search (owner: Observability team).
3) Pull replay pointer: request replay-store pointer and verify redaction markers.
4) Reconstruct: run sandbox replay using the replay runner (instructions below). Confirm deterministic seed and model variant used.
5) If reproduction fails: capture additional kernel traces (see escalation checklist) and open an internal incident with eng-serving-runtime on-call.

Sandbox replay runner (CLI example)
```
# replay-runner --replay-pointer s3://replay-store/tenant-123/rw-req-20260218-7f9b --kms-key projects/redwood/kms/replay
# returns: run-id 20260218-rr-02 (sandbox environment: sandbox-us-west)
```
Expected outputs: reconstructed prompt, tokenization map, output tokens, and a short deterministic diff report vs original output.

Common failure modes and mitigations
- Missing rcid in ingress: instruct customer to ensure SDK/sidecar headers are set; provide test curl snippet.
- Replay bundle redacted too aggressively: confirm sampling/redaction policy for tenant and, if necessary, request temporary elevated retention for a specific investigation (requires legal approval).
- Non-deterministic outputs on replay: capture model-variant and RNG seed; if different, escalate to model-onboarding for regression.

SLA & QBR considerations
- Support SLA: standard investigation turnaround for captured replays is 72 hours. Priority cases (customer production outage) follow the urgent escalation path.
- QBR evidence: exportable replay summaries (pointer + redacted prompt fingerprints + timeline) are acceptable artifacts for business reviews.

Ownership & responsibilities
- Customer Success (owner): coordinates replay requests with customer and verifies redaction/consent.
- Observability (traces): ensure trace search and pointer resolution.
- Eng/Serving-Runtime: support reproduction inside sandbox and provide kernel-level traces if needed.
- Security & Privacy: approve any policy exceptions for retention and elevated access.

Troubleshooting quick checklist
1) Verify headers present at ingress: curl -I -H 'X-RW-Request-Id: test' <customer-endpoint>
2) Confirm trace exists: trace-search --id rw-req-...
3) If trace present but no replay pointer: check gatekeeper sampling logs and on-error capture settings.
4) Request replay-store access: create ticket with access justification and time window.

Appendix: example support ticket template
- Customer: <tenant name>
- Reported time (UTC): <timestamp>
- RCID(s): <X-RW-Request-Id>
- Session id(s): <X-RW-Session-Id>
- Observed symptom: <short description>
- Attachments: minimal log extract, example prompt fingerprints, screenshot (if UI)

Contacts and escalation paths
- First-line CSE: customer-success-oncall@redwood.ai
- Observability lead: ethan.park@redwood.ai
- Runtime on-call rotation: see eng-serving-runtime on-call schedule (internal)

Change log
- 2025-11-12 Marisol Vega: initial draft and pilot checklist.
- 2026-02-18 Marisol Vega: updated sampling guidance, added replay-runner CLI example and expanded privacy checklist.

Related reading
- Telemetry Gatekeeper onboarding guide (integration-guides).
- Tenant retention and erasure policy (security-and-compliance).
- Sandbox replay-runner developer docs (eng-serving-runtime).

End of document

title: Adaptive ingress connection warmup for bursty tenants
content:
Overview

This guide describes the recommended adaptive connection warmup pattern for customers that exhibit highly bursty traffic at onboarding or after a policy change. The goal is to reduce 502/503 spikes, prevent ingress-proxy CPU spikes, and ensure steady, observable ramping of backend capacity for Dedicated and Private tenants. This is intended for Customer Success (CS), Solutions Engineering, and Eng-Infra/SRE teams who coordinate on new tenant cutovers, scale tests, or major product rollouts.

When to use this guide

- New enterprise customers expected to go from test traffic to production burst (e.g., sudden nightly batch, scheduled marketing sends, or unpredictable chatbots).
- Customers migrating to Dedicated instances where tenant-specific warmup helps autoscaler behavior.
- Known bursty workloads that previously caused connection churn, increased 5xxs, or token-processing backlog.

Goals and SLO alignment

- Keep ingress-level 5xx rate <= 0.2% during ramp windows.
- Ensure 95th percentile request latency at ingress proxy < 350 ms for short sequences during warmup (customer baseline may differ).
- Avoid cold-start-style resource contention that causes model-serving GPU preemption or long queueing.

Owner and stakeholders

- Primary owner: Customer Success (CS) - Onboarding & Escalations (owner: Priya Raman).
- Engineering partners: Eng-Infra (networking/ingress), Eng-Serving-Runtime (kernel/batching), Eng-SRE (autoscaling, capacity).
- Customer contacts: Solutions Engineer and Customer Platform/DevOps representative.

High-level approach

1) Classification: identify the tenant’s traffic profile (burst amplitude, events/s, average tokens per request).
2) Adaptive warmup policy: implement progressive connection and request rate increases using client-side and edge-side pacing.
3) Observability & gating: evaluate health via real-time dashboards and synthetic probes during each step.
4) Containment & rollback: automated throttles and failback paths if error thresholds exceed safe limits.

Pre-cutover checklist (CS + SE)

- Confirm tenant capacity profile: expected peak RPS, average token length, concurrency budget.
- Assign SRE on-call for the cutover window and notify Eng-Infra 24h ahead.
- Create a temporary warmup policy in the tenant config namespace (see examples below).
- Schedule synthetic traffic harness run and baseline snapshot 2 hours before cutover.

Example policy (edge-side):

This YAML snippet demonstrates an ingress-side warmup policy applied via the edge-sidecar config. Replace placeholder values with tenant-specific parameters.

---
apiVersion: redwood.io/v1
kind: WarmupPolicy
metadata:
  tenant: tenant-acme-inc
spec:
  initial_connection_limit: 20              # initial half-open connections allowed
  connection_ramp: [20, 50, 150, 500]      # connections by step
  step_duration_sec: 600                   # 10 minutes per step
  request_rate_cps: [5, 20, 80, 300]       # requests per second per connection pool
  health_gate:
    max_5xx_rate_pct: 0.2
    max_ingress_cpu_pct: 70
    max_queue_latency_ms: 500
  backoff_policy:
    on_threshold_breach: scale_down_step
    cooldown_sec: 300
---

Client-side recommendations

- Encourage the customer to use exponential backoff with jitter for retries (max 3 attempts) and a capped concurrency.
- Provide a lightweight reference client that respects server-supplied warmup tokens and per-connection rate hints. Example HTTP header: X-Redwood-Warmup-Window: step=2;allowed-cps=20.

Step-by-step warmup playbook

1) Step 0 — Preparation (T-120 to T-10 minutes)
   - Validate tenant config and warmup policy presence.
   - Start synthetic probe job hitting representative endpoints at low CPS (2–5 cps).
   - Take baseline telemetry snapshot (ingress 50/95/99 latencies, 5xx rates, edge CPU).

2) Step 1 — Initial connections (T=0 to +10 minutes)
   - Allow initial_connection_limit connections and enforce request_rate_cps[0].
   - Observe for anomalous 5xx increase or client retransmissions.
   - If health_gate breached: trigger backoff (see Containment).

3) Step 2 — Moderate ramp (+10 to +20 minutes)
   - Increase connection limit to connection_ramp[1] and CPS to request_rate_cps[1].
   - Validate KV cache hit ratios and runtime queue depths (should be trending down).

4) Step 3 — High ramp (+20 to +30 minutes)
   - Increase to connection_ramp[2] / request_rate_cps[2].
   - Confirm model-serving worker pools are scaling and GPU utilization <= 85%.

5) Step 4 — Full throughput (+30 to +40 minutes)
   - Allow final ramp step and monitor for steady-state metrics.
   - Mark warmup complete in tenant metadata and remove step header guidance to clients.

Containment and rollback

- Automated containment: edge-sidecar evaluates health_gate every 30s. If any metric breaches: reduce to previous stable step and set cooldown for cooldown_sec.
- Manual rollback: SRE can immediately flip tenant to safe-mode (hard throttle to 10 cps and single connection pool) and open an incident with CS and Eng-Serving-Runtime.

- Emergency isolation: If ingress proxy becomes unhealthy across nodes (ingress CPU > 90% for 2 minutes or 5xx rate > 2% for 1 minute), execute tenant isolation script: /ops/isolate-tenant --tenant tenant-acme-inc --mode drop-new-conns. Notify customer.

Observability and dashboards

Essential charts to have on the warmup dashboard (CS + SRE):
- Ingress: 5xx rate (1m/5m), 50/95/99 latency, connection counts, active streams.
- Edge-sidecar: per-tenant connection pools, queue depth, average request processing time.
- Serving runtime: request queue latency, GPU utilization, batching efficiency, KV cache hit ratio.
- Synthetic probes: success rate, median latency, token throughput.

Suggested Grafana queries (examples)

- 5xx rate: sum(rate(requests_total{status=~"5..",tenant=~\"tenant-acme-inc\"}[1m])) / sum(rate(requests_total{tenant=~\"tenant-acme-inc\"}[1m]))
- Ingress connections: sum(ingress_connections{tenant=\"tenant-acme-inc\"})
- Queue latency histogram: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_processing_seconds_bucket{tenant=\"tenant-acme-inc\"}[5m])) by (le))

Verification checklist (post-warmup)

- Latency: 95th percentile request latency below target (customer-specific, default 350 ms).
- Error rate: 5xx rate < 0.2% sustained for 30 minutes.
- Throughput: achieved >= 90% of projected peak RPS without queue growth.
- Resource: GPU utilization stable and not sustained > 88% for > 10 minutes.
- Client: client observed fewer than 1 retry per 1,000 requests.

Communication templates

- Pre-cutover email to tenant: short checklist, warmup window, expected behavior, contact on-call.
- Post-cutover summary: snapshot of key metrics, anomalies, and next steps.

Escalation path (if warmup fails)

1) CS Lead -> SRE on-call (pager) -> Eng-Serving-Runtime -> Eng-Infra networking lead.
2) If there is immediate customer impact (customer-reported errors affecting revenue), open a P1 and follow incident runbook.

Sample run-command for emergency isolation

# isolate tenant and reduce connections
redwood-ops tenant isolate --tenant tenant-acme-inc --conns 10 --reason "warmup breach"

FAQs and edge cases

Q: Customer uses third-party proxies that pre-open connections.
A: Recommend brokered warmup token returned via header; proxy teams must honor X-Redwood-Warmup to avoid pre-filling connection pools. If impossible, schedule longer step_duration_sec and smaller per-step ramp.

Q: Warmup causes autoscaler thrash (scale up and immediate scale down).
A: Increase scale stabilization window in the tenant autoscaler policy and rely on edge warmup to smooth the observed load.

Q: Token-based workloads vs. many short requests.
A: For token-heavy requests, prioritize KV cache priming: run representative synthetic requests that mirror real token lengths during the earlier warmup steps.

Appendix: quick links and scripts

- Tenants: /ops/tenants/{tenant-id} (view/add warmup policy)
- Warmup script: /scripts/warmup-injector --tenant tenant-acme-inc --pattern ramped --duration 40m
- Isolation runbook: /runbooks/tenant-isolation.md

Change log

- 2026-04-12: Initial draft and CS-Infra alignment.
- 2026-05-03: Added backoff policy examples, dashboard queries, and isolation script commands.

Contact

For questions or to request a custom warmup policy, contact the CS Onboarding lead (Priya Raman) or Eng-Infra (pager).

title: SDK embedding integration and operational playbook (Dedicated & Hosted)
content:
Summary:
This playbook describes a prescriptive integration and operational checklist for customers embedding Redwood Inference via SDKs (server-side embeddings, reranking, and generation) in Dedicated and Hosted modes. It covers prerequisites, step-by-step integration, production configuration recommendations, health checks and QBR telemetry, a tiered escalation matrix, common failure modes with workarounds, and a support bundle/rollback procedure. Use this doc during onboarding, handoff to SRE/Platform teams, and quarterly review preparation.

Scope and audience:
- Scope: Server-side SDK integrations for embedding/embedding pipelines, reranking flows, and generation endpoints. Includes both Hosted API and Dedicated capacity deployments.
- Audience: Customer Success Manager (CSM), Solutions Engineers (SE), customer's Platform/SRE, Redwood Support on-call, and Account Engineering.

Owners and SLAs:
- Primary owner: Customer Success (Aisha Patel)
- SE technical owner: Marco Nguyen
- Support escalation owner: Redwood Critical Incidents (on-call)
- Onboarding SLA (internal): 7 business days from kickoff to working POC; 30 days to first production rollout for standard integrations.

Prerequisites (customer & Redwood):
- Customer provides: API key or mTLS cert, VPC peering details (for Private/Dedicated), expected QPS/throughput profile, representative dataset (10–1000 prompts), and success criteria.
- Redwood provides: Dedicated capacity config proposal (GPU type, slots), SDK package (versioned), network allowlist entries, example pipeline repo, and an initial perf baseline.

Integration checklist (recommended order):
1) Kickoff & access
   - Verify contact list and escalation contacts (section: Escalation matrix).
   - Exchange API keys / service account or configure mTLS certificate.
2) Environment validation
   - Confirm network egress/ingress rules: TLS 1.2+, allow outbound 443 to api.redwood.ai and dedicated endpoint IPs/subnets as provided.
   - Validate time sync (NTP) on customer hosts.
3) Install SDK and example app
   - Use pinned SDK: pip install redwood-sdk==1.8.0 (example).
   - Run minimal embedding example against sandbox and verify response (min payload and latency).
4) Performance profiling with representative traffic
   - Run 1k sample requests with sequence length distribution matching production. Capture latency P50/P95, CPU/GPU utilization, and token-per-second throughput.
   - If Dedicated: validate pool size handles peak concurrency with <150ms P95 for embeddings (target depends on GPU tier).
5) Configure batching and cache
   - Recommended batching window: 5–20ms for short requests; for throughput-sensitive workloads use 50–100ms and larger batch sizes.
   - Enable prefix/KV cache when request reuse >10% to reduce token cost.
6) Integrate observability hooks
   - Add per-request trace_id and propagate: X-Request-ID header.
   - Emit metrics: request_count, request_error_count, tokens_consumed, batch_size_distribution, kv_cache_hit_rate, backend_latency_ms.
   - Push traces to our instrumented collector or export OpenTelemetry spans to the customer APM.
7) Run acceptance tests and quality checks
   - Run a small eval set (100–500 prompts) and compare generation/embedding similarity baselines.
   - Record and save failing prompts for regression alerts.
8) Staged rollout and canary
   - Start 5% traffic canary for 24–72 hours, monitor SLOs, then 25%, then 100%. Use automatic rollback on error budget breach.

Production configuration recommendations:
- Timeouts: client request timeout = 30s; token stream timeouts vary by model.
- Retries: exponential backoff with jitter; idempotency keys for safe retries.
- Batching: dynamic batching enabled in SDK; tune max_batch_tokens and max_batch_size per model.
- Quantization: if customer requires lower cost, recommend int8 quantized variant with quality regression tests.
- Rate limiting: set a per-key rate limit and a circuit breaker threshold at 5xx rate > 1% in 5-minute window.

Network & security checklist:
- TLS requirement: all traffic must use TLS; mutual TLS available for Private/Dedicated.
- IP allowlist: provide dedicated CIDR range for Dedicated deployments.
- KMS/HSM: for Private deployments, integrate keys via the customer KMS; confirm rotation cadence.
- Audit logs: enable request/response logging at 90-day retention for compliance customers (obfuscate PII per policy).

Observability, SLOs, and QBR telemetry:
- Recommended SLOs (example):
  - Availability: 99.95% (prod) measured as HTTP 2xx fraction per month.
  - Latency: Generation P95 < 500ms (small models) / < 1200ms (long-context models); Embedding P95 < 200ms.
  - Error rate: HTTP 5xx < 0.1% monthly, request timeouts < 0.5%.
- Daily/weekly dashboards:
  - Token consumption and cost by route/model, per-customer.
  - Latency distribution P50/P95/P99 and tail latencies by model and time window.
  - KV cache hit rate and batching efficiency.
  - Regression alerts: prompt-set accuracy drift over time.
- QBR metrics to report to customer: average monthly spend, 30/90/365 day latency trends, top 10 error classes, active prompts failing QA, planned infra changes.

Health checks and automated probes (examples):
1) SDK probe (every 60s): call /v1/health with minimal payload to verify auth and basic model response. Return codes: 200 OK => healthy; 429 => rate limited; 5xx => backend failure.
2) Latency probe (every 30s): send representative short request and measure P95 across 5 probes. Alert if P95 > configured threshold for 5-minute window.
3) KV cache probe (every 5m): prewarm and then measure cache hit for repeated request.

Severity & escalation matrix:
- Sev 1 (Critical): Production-wide outage or sustained SLO breach impacting >20% customers (or customer-critical path).
  - Response goals: acknowledge < 15 min, initial workaround in 30–60 min, continuous updates every 30 min.
  - Primary action: page on-call infra, notify CSM and SE, open incident ticket in PagerDuty and Incident Board.
- Sev 2 (High): Degraded performance for a single customer or partial capacity degradation.
  - Response goals: acknowledge < 1 hour, mitigation in 4 hours, updates every 2 hours.
  - Primary action: SE investigates tuning and config; consider temporary capacity increase or canary rollback.
- Sev 3 (Medium): Functional bug with workaround available; non-urgent customer impact.
  - Response goals: acknowledge < 24 hours, fix planned in next sprint or hotfix.
  - Primary action: Support creates JIRA, assigns to engineering backlog as appropriate.

Escalation path (contacts and steps):
1) Support Tier 1 (Customer Success/Support) – triage and gather support bundle.
2) Support Tier 2 (Solutions Engineering) – reproduce, check Dedicated pool health, batching, and cache.
3) On-call Runtime/Infra – kernel/runtime, GPU health, autoscaler.
4) Incident Commander (if Sev1) – coordinate cross-functional war room.

Contact template (use in every escalation ticket):
- Customer name, account id, contact mobile/email, environment (Hosted/Dedicated), observed impact, first seen timestamp (UTC), steps to reproduce, support bundle link, SLA target.

Support bundle (what to collect before Tier 2 handoff):
- Sample failing requests (max 100) and their timestamps.
- SDK version and client logs (including X-Request-IDs).
- Server-side metrics: GPU utilization, per-host CPU/memory, network egress, batch sizes, cache hit rates for the incident window.
- Topology: dedicated pool size and instance types, autoscaling events, recent deployments, rollback history.
- Logs: application + nginx/ingress + runtime logs (last 48 hours).
- Trace spans for 5 failed requests.

Common failure modes and mitigations (observed patterns):
- Symptom: sudden spike in 5xx errors after deployment.
  - Likely causes: model hot reload bug, kernel incompatibility, or bad quantized weights.
  - Mitigation: roll back to previous model version, disable new kernels, escalate to runtime team.
- Symptom: slow tail latencies for embeddings at peak.
  - Likely causes: insufficient batching, cold KV cache, noisy neighbors in Dedicated pool.
  - Mitigation: increase batching window, prewarm cache, scale pool or isolate workloads.
- Symptom: elevated token cost with low quality improvements.
  - Likely causes: model mismatch or prompt inflation.
  - Mitigation: A/B test smaller model or quantized variant; tighten prompt templates.

Rollback & remediation playbook (when to roll back):
- Criteria to rollback: error rate > 2% sustained for 15 minutes, latency P95 > 2x baseline for 10 min, or semantic regressions on saved prompt set.
- Rollback steps:
  1) Announce rollback to stakeholders and pause deployments.
  2) Trigger model/server rollback via Redwood Console (canary abort) or runbook script.
  3) Validate health probes and key metrics for 15 minutes.
  4) Reopen deployment only after stability confirmed or open a postmortem and mitigation plan.

Post-incident triage and QBR prep:
- After any Sev1/2 incident: run RCA within 72 hours, publish postmortem linked to the incident board, attach support bundle, and assign action items with owners and due dates.
- QBR prep checklist: gather monthly metrics, incident summary, cost optimization recommendations, and roadmap items affecting the customer.

Appendix: examples and snippets
- Minimal embedding request (curl):
  curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/embeddings \n    -H "Authorization: Bearer ${API_KEY}" \n    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \n    -d '{"input": "Redwood inference test prompt"}'

- Example SDK config (yaml):
  sdk:
    version: "1.8.0"
    batching:
      enabled: true
      max_batch_size: 64
      max_delay_ms: 25
    retries:
      max_attempts: 3
      backoff_ms: 200
    observability:
      enable_traces: true
      metrics_endpoint: "otlp://collector.local:4317"

- Quick support bundle collection (bash):
  #!/bin/bash
  set -e
  mkdir -p /tmp/support_bundle
  cp /var/log/redwood/*.log /tmp/support_bundle/ || true
  curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $API_KEY" "https://api.redwood.ai/v1/debug/metrics?since=48h" -o /tmp/support_bundle/metrics.json
  tar czf /tmp/support_bundle_$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ).tgz -C /tmp support_bundle

Change log (brief):
- 2025-11-10: Initial draft and internal review.
- 2026-01-12: Added KV cache probes and updated SLO targets for embeddings.
- 2026-02-18: Clarified escalation timeboxes and included support bundle script.

Notes and references:
- See related onboarding templates and the enterprise support lifecycle playbook for Dedicated-specific contract clauses.
- For Private deployments, confirm KMS integration and audit retention settings before enabling debug-level logging.

This playbook is intended to be a living document; please send suggestions and updates to the owner (Aisha Patel) or propose edits via the Confluence page comments.

title: Splunk HEC Audit Export (Beta) — Internal CS/SE Integration Guide
content:
## Purpose
This page is an internal Customer Success / Solutions Engineering guide for configuring **Splunk HTTP Event Collector (HEC)** as a destination for the **SIEM-ready audit export (beta)** feature in Redwood Inference. It covers:

- What to confirm with the customer before enablement
- How to configure Splunk HEC and Redwood’s destination settings
- How to validate events end-to-end (including dedup expectations)
- Troubleshooting common Splunk-side and Redwood-side errors
- Setting correct beta expectations (delivery semantics, backfill, limitations)

This doc is written for Hosted + Dedicated beta customers. Private/on-prem deployments are **out of scope for beta**.

---

## TL;DR (for fast enablement)
1) Confirm customer has Splunk HEC enabled and can provide: **HEC endpoint URL**, **HEC token**, **index**, and preferred **sourcetype/source**.
2) Ensure the customer’s networking permits inbound traffic to Splunk HEC from Redwood’s egress (customer may need allowlisting; see “Network & security prerequisites”).
3) Confirm Redwood tenant is **allowlisted** for the beta feature flag and the customer admin has the right RBAC permissions.
4) Create the Splunk destination in Redwood Console → **Audit Exports**.
5) Run **Test connection** in Console, then generate a known audit event (e.g., login, API key create, export config update) and verify it appears in Splunk.

---

## Beta expectations to set with customers (copy/paste)
Use this wording in email and calls to avoid misalignment:

- **Delivery semantics:** Audit export is **at-least-once**. During retries, the same event may be delivered more than once. Customers should deduplicate by **event_id**.
- **Ordering:** No strict ordering guarantees across categories/resources. Timestamps are included; use them for timelines.
- **Latency:** Typical delivery is near real-time, but short periods of lag can occur during downstream throttling/outages. Redwood provides export health and lag indicators.
- **Backfill:** Backfill is supported up to the configured window (beta limits apply per PRD). Backfill can increase throughput temporarily and may hit Splunk limits unless tuned.
- **Scope:** Hosted + Dedicated only (beta). Private/on-prem is not supported in beta.
- **PII:** Audit events follow Redwood’s audit schema and **PII minimization/redaction** policy; raw prompt or model output is not included in audit logs.

If the customer asks for exactly-once: “We provide at-least-once delivery; exactly-once is not guaranteed. Deduplication by event_id is the recommended pattern.”

---

## Prerequisites
### Redwood prerequisites
- Tenant must be enabled via the **SIEM audit export beta feature flag** (tenant allowlist).
- Customer user must have the correct RBAC permissions:
  - View export configs
  - Create/update export configs
  - Rotate credentials (if applicable)
  - View export health/status

If the customer cannot see the **Audit Exports** UI section, suspect **feature flag** or RBAC.

### Splunk prerequisites
Customer must:
- Have Splunk HEC enabled on Splunk Enterprise or Splunk Cloud
- Provide:
  - **HEC endpoint** (including scheme/port), e.g. `https://splunk.company.com:8088`
  - **HEC token** with permissions to write to the chosen index
  - Target **index** (e.g., `redwood_audit`)
  - Desired **source** and **sourcetype** (recommended below)
- Confirm HEC is reachable from Redwood’s egress (or an intermediary gateway/ingress they manage)

Recommended Splunk naming conventions:
- index: `redwood_audit` (or customer standard, e.g., `security_audit`)
- sourcetype: `redwood:audit:v2` (stable; do not include tenant name)
- source: `redwood-inference` or `redwood-audit-export`

---

## Network & security prerequisites
Splunk HEC is customer-hosted; most integration failures are network/security related.

Confirm with customer:
- **TLS required:** Redwood requires HTTPS endpoints for HEC.
- **Allowlisting / firewall:** Customer must allow inbound to HEC from Redwood’s egress. If the customer requires IP allowlisting, coordinate via the standard Security/Networking intake process. (Do not guess IP ranges in writing.)
- **Reverse proxy/WAF:** If they front HEC with a WAF or proxy, confirm it supports:
  - POST requests
  - Payload sizes consistent with batching
  - Optional gzip compression (if enabled)
- **Token handling:** HEC token is a secret. It should be stored as a secret reference in Redwood (Console/API will treat it as sensitive; do not paste tokens into tickets or Slack).

---

## Configuration steps
### 1) Configure Splunk HEC (customer-owned)
Ask the customer Splunk admin to:

1. Enable HEC (if not enabled)
   - Splunk Web → Settings → Data Inputs → HTTP Event Collector
   - Enable, choose a port (commonly 8088)
2. Create a new HEC token for Redwood Audit Export
   - Set a clear name, e.g., `redwood-audit-export-prod`
   - Limit index access to the intended index only
   - (Recommended) Disable “indexer acknowledgement” unless they explicitly require it; Redwood’s exporter uses its own retry + checkpointing model.
3. Confirm endpoint format
   - Standard endpoint: `https://<host>:8088/services/collector/event`
   - Some deployments accept `.../services/collector` as well; Redwood’s adapter targets the event endpoint behavior.

What we need from the customer:
- HEC base URL (host + port)
- HEC token
- Index
- Any required extra headers or proxy routing requirements (rare)

### 2) Configure the Splunk destination in Redwood Console (Redwood-owned)
In Redwood Console:

1. Navigate to: **Settings → Security & Compliance → Audit Exports**
2. Click **Create destination** → Choose **Splunk HEC (Beta)**
3. Fill in destination fields:
   - Destination name: e.g., `splunk-prod`
   - Endpoint URL: e.g., `https://splunk.company.com:8088`
   - Token: (store as secret)
   - Index: `redwood_audit`
   - Source: `redwood-inference` (optional; recommended)
   - Sourcetype: `redwood:audit:v2` (recommended)
   - Compression: leave default (generally ON if supported)
4. Configure filters (beta guidance):
   - Start with a minimal allowlist (e.g., authentication + admin/config changes) and expand after confirming throughput and indexing behavior.
   - Avoid overly broad exports on day 1 for high-volume tenants.
5. Set backfill window (if requested):
   - Keep initial backfill small (e.g., last 1–6 hours) to validate end-to-end.
   - Warn customer about potential burst volume and Splunk rate limits.
6. Click **Test connection**
   - This sends a lightweight test event (non-sensitive) to confirm authentication and connectivity.

If Test connection fails:
- Capture the UI error and export status details (do not capture token)
- See troubleshooting section below

---

## Validation checklist (end-to-end)
### A) Generate a known audit event
Recommended: generate an action that reliably emits audit events and is safe.
Examples:
- Create/update an audit export config (this itself is auditable)
- Create an API key (if policy allows)
- Change an RBAC role assignment (admin action)

### B) Validate in Redwood Console
In **Audit Exports → Destination → Status** confirm:
- Destination is **Enabled**
- Last success timestamp updates
- Lag is within acceptable range
- No sustained adapter errors

### C) Validate in Splunk search
Have customer run:

`index=redwood_audit sourcetype="redwood:audit:v2" earliest=-15m`

Recommended fields to spot-check:
- `event_id` (stable, unique per event; used for dedup)
- `timestamp` and/or `occurred_at`
- `tenant_id` / `workspace_id` (as applicable)
- `actor.*` (type/id; may include hashed/normalized identifiers per policy)
- `action` and `category`
- `resource.*` (type/id)
- `source_ip` and `user_agent` only when applicable and allowed by policy

### D) Deduplication guidance (Splunk)
Because delivery is at-least-once, duplicates may exist.

Customer can:
- Deduplicate in dashboards/searches using `event_id`
- Use Splunk’s search-level dedup, e.g.:
  - `... | dedup event_id`

Important: do not recommend dedup by timestamp alone.

---

## Data format notes (what Splunk receives)
- Payload: JSON events
- Each event includes stable identifiers and SIEM-friendly fields as defined in the Audit Event Schema v2
- Sourcetype/source/index are set per destination configuration

If a customer requests field mapping to Splunk CIM:
- Point them to the internal mapping guidance in: **Audit Event Schema v2 and SIEM mapping** (related page)
- In beta we prioritize stable schema + reliable delivery; custom per-customer field transforms are not included

---

## Common Splunk-side errors and fixes
### Quick reference table
| Symptom | Where seen | Likely cause | What to do |
|---|---|---|---|
| 401 Unauthorized | Redwood destination status / exporter logs | Wrong HEC token; token disabled; wrong endpoint path behind proxy | Ask Splunk admin to confirm token, re-create token if needed; confirm endpoint and proxy routing; rotate secret in Redwood |
| 403 Forbidden | Redwood status; customer ticket | Token scoped to different index; Splunk Cloud permissions; key restrictions | Confirm token permissions and target index; Splunk admin to adjust token/index settings |
| 404 Not Found | Test connection failure | Wrong URL (missing port, wrong base path), proxy misroute | Verify URL format and port; ensure HEC is enabled and reachable; check proxy configuration |
| 408/timeout / connection refused | Test connection failure / lag spikes | Firewall blocks, allowlist missing, TLS termination issues | Confirm network path; customer to allowlist Redwood egress; verify TLS cert chain; check WAF blocks |
| 429 Too Many Requests | Exporter errors; increased lag | Splunk HEC throttling / ingestion cap | Reduce backfill and filters; ask customer to raise HEC limits; Redwood exporter backs off and retries; duplicates may increase during retry windows |
| Events appear but fields are not extracted | Splunk UI/search | Sourcetype not configured for JSON, or props/transforms not enabled | Set sourcetype to JSON-friendly type or configure props.conf for JSON; confirm Splunk version and parsing rules |
| Large bursts overwhelm indexing | Customer reports missing/late events | Backfill too large; HEC queue/limits | Reduce backfill; stage rollout; consider separate index; monitor lag and throttle |

---

## Redwood-side troubleshooting (what CS/SE should check)
### 1) Is the tenant enabled for beta?
- If Audit Exports UI is absent or API returns “not found/disabled”, open an internal request to confirm the tenant is on the allowlist / feature flag enabled.

### 2) RBAC: does the user have permissions?
- If user can view but not edit, confirm they have export management permissions.

### 3) Destination health signals
Check the destination status panel:
- Last success
- Last error message (redacted)
- Current lag
- Retry counts

If lag grows and errors show 429/timeout:
- Treat as likely Splunk ingestion throttling or network instability
- Recommend reducing export scope temporarily (narrow filter, disable backfill)

### 4) Safe data handling while troubleshooting
- Do not request or paste HEC tokens in Slack.
- Use approved secret-rotation workflow if token must be replaced.
- When collecting evidence, capture:
  - Destination ID/name
  - Timestamp range
  - Error codes and summary
  - Exporter lag metrics screenshot (no sensitive payload)

### 5) Escalation
Escalate to on-call/SRE when:
- Export lag breaches agreed beta thresholds and persists
- Multiple tenants show similar failures (suspect platform regression)
- There is any sign of data leakage / misrouting

Reference: **Runbook — Audit Exporter Delivery Failures** (related page).

---

## Recommended customer enablement flow (SE-led)
1. Kickoff (30 min): confirm desired categories/filters and Splunk constraints (throttling, indexing rules).
2. Configure Splunk HEC token + index (customer admin).
3. Configure Redwood destination and run Test connection.
4. Validation (15–30 min): generate known audit events; confirm in Splunk.
5. Expand scope gradually:
   - Add more categories/actions
   - Add limited backfill if they need historical continuity
6. Set monitoring expectations:
   - Customer monitors Splunk ingestion and dashboards
   - Redwood monitors exporter health; weekly check-ins during beta

---

## FAQ (internal)
### Q: Does Redwood guarantee no duplicates?
No. Delivery is at-least-once. Dedup by `event_id`.

### Q: What if the customer demands exactly-once or Splunk ack?
In beta, we do not promise exactly-once. We also do not require Splunk indexer acknowledgement for correctness; Redwood’s exporter uses checkpointing + retries. If a strategic account requires ack semantics, capture as feedback for Product (Naomi Feldman) and Security (Marcus Lin) and do not commit.

### Q: Can the customer route to multiple Splunk HEC endpoints?
Not in the initial beta UI unless explicitly supported by destination configuration. Workaround is typically customer-side load balancing/ingress in front of HEC.

### Q: Can we send events to a customer-managed Splunk Cloud URL?
Yes if it is reachable and supports HEC; network allowlisting is usually the gating item.

### Q: Are prompts/model outputs included in audit events?
No. Audit events cover security-relevant actions and metadata per policy. If the customer requests payload-level logging, treat as a separate product conversation (and involve Security/Legal).

---

## Internal notes for CS/SE (do’s and don’ts)
- Do emphasize: stable schema, delivery guarantees (at-least-once), operational visibility.
- Do not promise: exactly-once, strict ordering, unlimited backfill, Private/on-prem support in beta.
- Do document in the account record:
  - Splunk endpoint type (enterprise vs cloud)
  - Throttling limits or ingestion caps mentioned
  - Index/sourcetype decisions
  - Any required allowlisting steps and current status

---

## Change log
- 2025-04-29: Updated troubleshooting table and added explicit dedup search example; aligned beta expectations language with Security FAQ.
- 2025-04-02: Added recommended sourcetype/source conventions and validation checklist.
- 2025-03-12: Initial version published for beta cohort enablement.

title: Tenant-heavy Ingest Surge Mitigation: Connector Patterns and Operational Playbook
content:
Overview

This playbook documents proven connector integration patterns and operator runbooks for handling tenant-heavy ingest surges against Redwood inference endpoints (hosted, dedicated, and private). It is intended for solutions engineers, customer success, SREs, and partner integrators who build connectors or bridges that forward high-volume telemetry, batched requests, or streaming job workloads into Redwood.

Goals
- Prevent noisy-tenant surges from degrading other tenants or customer SLAs.
- Provide single-source connector configuration templates for backpressure, graceful degradation, and safe failover.
- Define operational checks, monitoring signals, and an on-call escalation ladder.

Scope
- Applies to connectors that: ingest text payloads for generation, embeddings, or reranking; proxy tenant traffic; or batch large historical backfills.
- Covers both synchronous (API) and asynchronous (job/batch) ingestion patterns.
- Does NOT cover hardware-level GPU autoscaling (see eng-infra docs).

High-level Patterns (when to use each)
1) Client-side rate shaping (ideal for SaaS partners)
   - Best when you control the client SDK or agent.
   - Enforce tenant-level QPS/TPU caps and token limits proactively.
2) Connector-side adaptive throttling (recommended default)
   - Connector maintains per-tenant token counters and request queues; adjusts ingress windows based on downstream latency and error rates.
3) Burst cache + queueing with prioritized dispatch
   - For bursty workloads: short-term KV/prefix cache for repeated prompts + prioritized consumer queue to dispatch high-value requests first.
4) Degraded-mode fallback to lower-cost model variants
   - Fall back to quantized or smaller model variants when latency SLOs break. Useful in Dedicated and Private where model variants are available.
5) Backfill and bulk job isolation
   - Run large backfills on isolated routing paths and quota pools; never share production routing with real-time traffic.

Connector Architecture (text diagram)
- Ingress -> Per-tenant ingress limiter -> Priority queue (hot/warm/cold) -> Dispatch worker pool -> Redwood proxy (smart routing) -> Redwood inference endpoints
- Optional: Local caching layer and metrics exporter between queue and dispatch.

Required Preconditions
- Tenant quotas configured in Redwood console or via API (min and max token caps).
- Observability hooks configured: request tracing, per-tenant latency histograms, error counters, and token-metering.
- Circuit-breaker library available in connector runtime (examples use circuitbreaker v1.2).

Connector Configuration Examples
1) Per-tenant sliding window token limiter (pseudo-YAML)
---
# tenant rate limiter
window_seconds: 60
max_tokens_per_window: 10000
burst_allowance: 1.5
priority_buckets:
  - hot: 0.6    # 60% capacity reserved for high-priority routes
  - warm: 0.3
  - cold: 0.1
---

2) Adaptive dispatch strategy (pseudo-config)
---
autoscale:
  enabled: true
  target_latency_ms: 200
  min_workers: 2
  max_workers: 100
  cooldown_seconds: 30
backoff:
  initial_ms: 100
  max_ms: 5000
  factor: 2.0
---

Implementation recipes
A) Synchronous connector (recommended) - Validate incoming request size and tokens; reject with 429 when tenant quota exceeded.
- Maintain a token bucket per tenant persisted in Redis for cross-instance coordination.
- If downstream latency > target_latency_ms for 3 consecutive windows, reduce per-tenant throughput by multiplier 0.5 and emit event to telemetry.

B) Asynchronous large-batch worker - Accept job payloads, store in durable queue (SQS/Kafka), run preflight estimator that calculates token estimate, and schedule against a backfill queue with dedicated capacity pools.
- Mark job "low-priority" when it would exceed daily tenant quota; schedule to off-peak windows.

C) Prioritization example
- Tags: critical (SLAs), interactive (real-time), background (backfills).
- Dispatcher policy: always reserve 30% of capacity for critical and interactive. Background only consumes spare capacity or dedicated backfill pool.

Monitoring & Telemetry (what to track)
- Per-tenant token consumption (tokens/min, tokens/day)
- 95th/99th latency per tenant and per route
- 429 rate and quota rejections per tenant
- Queue depth by priority bucket
- Dispatch worker saturation (gpu_utilization, inflight_requests)
- Model fallback events and quality-regression alerts
- Cost metrics: estimated tokens billed vs allowed

Suggested SLOs and thresholds (connector owner to adopt)
- Target P95 end-to-end latency: 300ms for interactive routes, 1.5s for batch submission acceptance.
- Queue depth alert: queue_depth > 500 for 5m -> page oncall.
- Token spike alert: tenant token rate > 3x baseline for 5m -> create incident priority P2.
- Error ratio alert: 5xx_rate > 2% over 3m -> page P1.

Runbook: Surge detected (step-by-step)
1) Detection: Alert triggered (token spike OR queue_depth OR p99 latency).
2) Triage: Oncall examines per-tenant metrics, request traces, and Redwood console SLO page.
3) Immediate mitigation (5–15 minutes):
   - Throttle the offending tenant to safe cap (e.g., 50% of capacity) using Redis token bucket override.
   - If available, shift tenant to a dedicated low-priority pool or pause background jobs.
   - If customer has a go-live playbook, contact CS lead to coordinate intentional throttling.
4) Short-term containment (15–60 minutes):
   - Enable degraded-mode: route tenant to smaller model variant or quantized profile.
   - Add temporary rule in gateway to drop non-critical requests (e.g., trace-only or sampling).
5) Recovery & Postmortem (>60 minutes):
   - Maintain reduced cap until token rate returns to baseline for 30m.
   - Open RCA with customer and document actions in ticket; include traces and telemetry snapshots.

Escalation & Communication matrix
- If mitigation fails in 30 minutes escalate to Tier 2 SRE and CS Director.
- Customer communication template (first 30 minutes): acknowledge the surge, confirm an active mitigation, and provide ETA 60–90 minutes.
- Post-incident follow-up: share RCA and recommended client-side changes (e.g., batching, retry backoff).

Quality safeguards for degraded-mode fallbacks
