- If switching to smaller model variant, run a validation prompt set (20 representative prompts) and measure fidelity threshold (>= 90% acceptable). If below threshold: avoid fallback and instead tighten throttling.

Testing & QA checklist before enabling connector in production
- Load test with per-tenant mix: 80% interactive, 15% background, 5% critical.
- Verify token metering persists across restart and multiple instances.
- Chaos test: simulate network partition to Redis; ensure connector fails open-to-safe-mode (reject new requests with 503 rather than silently accept).
- Confirm alerts and dashboards surface tenant attribution in < 60s.

Operational notes and best practices
- Always prefer rejection (429) with clear error body for quota vs silent delay.
- Maintain a customer-specific throttle override table for known forged bursts (e.g., scheduled batch imports).
- Store per-tenant historical baseline metrics for anomaly detection rather than relying on global thresholds.
- Keep model fallback as a last-resort; measure downstream quality drift and notify customer when used.

Customer Success Playbook (how CS teams should engage)
- Pre-onboarding: document expected daily token volume and peak profile; agree on backfill windows.
- Go-live: run a pre-go-live surge simulation with the customer (30–60 minutes) and validate connector behavior.
- Post-incident: recommend engineering changes (batching, client SDK backoff), and schedule a follow-up health QBR focusing on inference economics.

Appendix: sample 429 response body
{
  "status": 429,
  "error": "quota_exceeded",
  "message": "Tenant token quota exceeded. Retry after backoff or contact your account team for quota increase.",
  "retry_after_seconds": 60
}

Owners and contacts
- Primary owner: Solutions Integration (Aisha Patel)
- Secondary owner: Customer Success Oncall (pager: #cs-oncall)
- Escalation: Eng SRE (pager: #eng-sre)

Related reading
- event-driven-batch-ingest-connector-guide-2026 (integration guide)
- tenant-stability-predictive-signals-runbook-2026 (support process)

Document history
- 2026-11-15: Created by Aisha Patel
- 2027-02-10: Expanded with runbook steps and testing checklist (reviewers: Marcus Lee, Elena Gómez, Samir Mehta)

title: Conversational feedback loop & labeling integration playbook
content:
Overview:

This playbook describes an end-to-end integration pattern for ingesting conversational feedback from customer applications, enriching and routing it to a labeling hub and model-eval harness, and surfacing high-quality signal into QBR reporting and model retraining pipelines. The goal is to make feedback ingestion reliable, auditable and cost-efficient while providing deterministic lanes for immediate remediation, quality telemetry and curated label sets for retraining.

Scope and intended audience:
- Audience: Customer Success Engineers, Integration Engineers, Observability owners and ML Ops.
- Out of scope: research-only annotation experiments and external crowdworker contracting.

Key owners and operational SLAs:
- Product Owner: Aisha Patel (Customer Success)
- Integration Owner: Marco Ruiz (Solutions Engineering)
- Telemetry Owner: Lina Chen (Eng Platform)
- Labeling Hub Owner: Diego Alvarez (Applied ML)
- Operational SLAs: ingestion availability 99.9% per region; median end-to-end latency (app event -> labeling queue) <2s, p95 <10s for streaming; 100% event storage for 72h, sampled subset retained for 2 years.

Prerequisites and required services:
- ingress-gateway: mTLS or token-auth endpoint customers post feedback to.
- telemetry-gatekeeper: JSON schema validation, deduplication and rate limiting.
- event bus: Kafka (telemetry-events-prod) or durable queue (PubSub/SQS) with DLQ.
- labeling-hub: supports API and web UI for human labeling and enrichment.
- model-eval-harness: nightly batch and online scoring harness.
- telemetry-archive: S3-compatible archive for long-term storage and legal hold.

Logical flow (text diagram):
Customer App -> ingress-gateway -> telemetry-gatekeeper -> telemetry-events-prod (feedback.raw) -> enrichment workers -> labeling-hub (labeling.inbound) -> human labelers/auto-labelers -> labeling-hub.outbound -> model-eval-harness -> eval.results -> telemetry-archive / qbr-dataset

Data contract and schema (required fields):
- event_id (string): globally unique id, e.g. evt_01F4YZ
- tenant_id (string): tenant-abc
- timestamp_iso (string): RFC3339 UTC, e.g. 2026-01-11T16:23:12Z
- source (string): enum {chat-widget, voice, api, webhook}
- feedback_type (string): enum {correction, rating, taxonomy_tag, ignore}
- payload (string): JSON-encoded payload, e.g. '{"correction":"Prefer X"}'
Optional fields: user_id (hash recommended), session_id, original_response (trimmed to 8k tokens), confidence (0..1).

Security & privacy controls:
- PII handling: user_id must be hashed at client or ingress-gateway (default SHA256 with tenant-managed salt) unless contract allows plaintext.
- Access controls: labeling-hub and telemetry-archive must be RBAC-restricted. Roles: viewer, labeler, curator, admin.
- Legal hold: telemetry-archive retention tags; events may be marked retention=legal_hold.

Ingestion examples (cURL):
1) Minimal rating event:
curl -X POST https://ingress.redwood.example/v1/feedback
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json'
  -d '{"event_id":"evt_01F4YZ","tenant_id":"tenant-abc","timestamp_iso":"2026-01-11T16:23:12Z","source":"chat-widget","feedback_type":"rating","payload":"{\"rating\":0}"}'

2) Correction event with original response (trim to 8k tokens):
POST /v1/feedback
{
  "event_id": "evt_01F4Za2",
  "tenant_id": "tenant-abc",
  "timestamp_iso": "2026-01-11T16:25:05Z",
  "source": "api",
  "feedback_type": "correction",
  "payload": "{\"correction\":\"Use product X instead of Y when context includes Z\"}",
  "original_response": "...",
  "session_id": "sess_9a2"
}

Validation and common rejection reasons (telemetry-gatekeeper):
- 400 INVALID_SCHEMA: missing required field(s)
- 401 AUTH_FAILED: token expired or invalid
- 429 RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED: per-tenant rate control
- 413 PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE: payload/original_response exceeds 64kB limit
- 422 DUPLICATE_EVENT: event_id seen in last 24h

Enrichment and automated labeling rules (examples):
- Enrichment adds tenant_plan, model_version, route.
- Auto-label rules:
  - rating <= 0 -> auto-label=low-quality
  - correction length < 30 chars -> short-corrections queue for curator review
  - banned-content regex match -> escalate to Safety queue

Sampling and retention policy for QBR datasets:
- Deterministic sampling: 10% of feedback events per tenant per week, stratified by feedback_type and model_version.
- High-signal retention: any event auto-labeled low-quality or routed to Safety retained 2 years.

Operational runbook (triage playbook):
1) Alert: labeling-hub throughput drop (LH_Throughput_p95_below_threshold)
   - Check telemetry-gatekeeper: error rates and 429s.
   - Verify consumer lag: kafka-consumer-groups --describe --group labeling-inbound-consumer --bootstrap-server kafka.prod:9092
   - If DLQ growth, inspect 413/413s for oversized payloads.
2) Duplicate-event storm
   - Mitigation: enable dedupe-mode=drop-duplicates on telemetry-gatekeeper, route ingest to fallback buffer endpoint returning 202 while investigating.
3) Suspected PII incident
   - Action: tag suspect tenant with legal_hold, export batch for secure wipe (follow data-erasure playbook), notify Legal.

Integration rollout checklist:
Preflight:
- Confirm tenant_id mapping and auth method (mTLS or token)
- Exchange public keys / JWKS endpoints
- Validate sample payloads against telemetry-gatekeeper staging endpoint
- Confirm labeling workflow and roles list
Canary (1 week):
- Route 1% traffic to feedback pipeline; monitor ingestion success, p95 latency and false-positive auto-label rate
- Weekly sync with Solutions Engineering and CS to tune rules
Full launch:
- Enable full traffic routing, enable stratified sampling for QBR and add tenant to retention dashboards

Model quality & QBR integration:
- model-eval-harness runs nightly jobs joining labeled items with model metadata to compute metrics (precision@k for corrections, conversion lift, false-positive rate).
- QBR outputs: weekly top-10 failure patterns; monthly curated dataset (~5k examples) for retraining candidates; quarterly executive summary with net quality delta and remediation plan.

Example consumer config (JSON represented as text):
{
  "consumer_name": "cs-labeling-consumer",
  "source_topic": "feedback.enriched",
  "batch_size": "50",
  "max_retries": "5",
  "dead_letter_topic": "feedback.dlq"
}

Troubleshooting cheatsheet:
- Ingest 401s: confirm JWT audience (aud) matches ingress-gateway expected_aud; check clock skew > 2 minutes.
- High 413s: clients sending full conversation traces; recommend client-side trimming and summaries.
- Sudden low-quality spike: check recent model-version rollout and latency regressions.

Suggested monitoring dashboard panels:
- Ingest: events/sec, p50/p95 ingestion latency, error rates (400/401/413/429), DLQ growth.
- Quality: auto-label precision (sample-verified), manual label throughput, median time-to-label.
- Business: tenant-level feedback rate normalized by MAU.

FAQ:
Q: Can we accept raw audio feedback?
A: Ingest audio only after transcription by a companion service; mark source=voice and include transcript in payload.

Appendix: useful commands and endpoints:
- Validate sample schema: curl https://telemetry-gatekeeper.staging/validate -d @sample-event.json
- Check consumer lag: kafka-consumer-groups --bootstrap-server kafka.prod:9092 --describe --group labeling-inbound-consumer
- Export suspect tenant batch: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <admin>" https://telemetry-archive/export?tenant=tenant-abc&since=2026-01-01 -o export.ndjson

Next steps:
- After integration, schedule a 30-day QBR with the CS manager to review weekly failure patterns and agree remediation runway.
- Related docs: telemetry schema guide (ingest schema), labeling-hub operator runbook, data-privacy-and-retention-policy.

title: Priority-proxy + Adaptive Backoff Connector Integration Guide
content:
Summary:
This guide describes recommended architecture, configuration, testing, and operational runbooks for integrating Redwood Inference with a customer or partner-side priority proxy. The pattern is intended for enterprise customers that run a multipurpose ingress layer that must: (1) prioritize latency‑sensitive inference requests, (2) handle large-volume background/async jobs without starving realtime traffic, and (3) implement an adaptive backoff strategy when Redwood responds with transient errors or capacity signals.

Goals:
- Preserve 95th/99th percentile latency SLOs for live inference routes.
- Maintain throughput for background pipelines without increasing cost to the customer.
- Provide clear telemetry and escalation hooks for degraded conditions.

Intended audience:
- Customer success engineers and integration engineers implementing ingress or API gateway policies.
- Customer platform and SRE teams responsible for on-prem or VPC deployments.

Key concepts and terminology:
- Priority Proxy: an edge or ingress proxy (e.g., Envoy, NGINX, API Gateway) that classifies and schedules requests based on route, header, or token attributes.
- Live route: low-latency user-facing inference endpoints (chat, completion, synchronously user-blocking).
- Background route: batch/async endpoints (embeddings indexing, bulk scoring) that can be queued or slowed to protect live SLOs.
- Adaptive Backoff: client-side or proxy-driven logic that reduces request rate to Redwood when observing specific signals (429s, 503s, elevated latency, or explicit capacity hints in response headers).

Architecture overview:
1) Classification: ingress annotates requests with X-Redwood-Priority: high | normal | background. Assignment should happen as early as possible (edge auth layer or API gateway).
2) Routing: priority header maps to separate internal queues/pools within the proxy. Live pool configured with fast-path (short timeouts, small queue depth). Background pool configured with large queue depth and longer retries.
3) Rate-limiting and token buckets: define separate token buckets for high and background priorities with configurable refill rates.
4) Backoff signals: Redwood will send one or more of the following signals when it detects load/capacity pressure: HTTP 429 with Retry-After, 503 Service Unavailable, X-Redwood-Capacity: degraded | constrained, and a latency-based heuristic (long tail latency > configured threshold). Proxy must translate these into adaptive backoff decisions.

Configuration reference (Envoy / Lua / NGINX examples):
- Example Envoy route filter snippet (YAML-like):

  - name: envoy.filters.http.lua
    typed_config:
      "@type": "type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.http.lua.v3.Lua"
      inline_code: |
        function envoy_on_request(request_handle)
          local priority = request_handle:headers():get("X-Request-Priority") or "normal"
          if priority == "background" then
            request_handle:headers():add("X-Redwood-Priority", "background")
          else
            request_handle:headers():add("X-Redwood-Priority", "high")
          end
        end

- Token-bucket policy table (recommended defaults):

  | Priority  | Token refill (tokens/s) | Burst capacity (tokens) | Max queued requests |
  |-----------|-------------------------|-------------------------|---------------------|
  | high      | 100                     | 200                     | 50                  |
  | normal    | 40                      | 80                      | 200                 |
  | background| 5                       | 50                      | 1000                |

Operational backoff algorithm (recommended):
1) On first 429 or 503 for a specific backend instance: multiply current per-route request allowance by 0.6 and set a soft cooldown timer T = 10s.
2) If Retry-After present: use Retry-After as initial T (capped at 60s).
3) Exponential grow-back: every T interval without further 429/503 events, increase allowance by factor 1.25 until original baseline is reached.
4) High-priority routes are exempt from aggressive multiply unless consecutive failure rate > 10% for 30s. In that case, failover to an alternate Redwood region/model variant (see Rollout & Failover).

Example proxy policy (pseudo-config):

  policies:
    - match: {header: {X-Redwood-Priority: "high"}}
      bucket: high
      backoff_strategy: conservative
    - match: {header: {X-Redwood-Priority: "background"}}
      bucket: background
      backoff_strategy: aggressive

Integration-specific headers to surface to Redwood and to watch for in responses:
- Outbound to Redwood: X-Redwood-Priority, X-Request-Id, X-Customer-Tenant, X-Client-Version
- Expected Redwood response headers: Retry-After, X-Redwood-Capacity, X-Redwood-Model-Variant

Telemetry and dashboards (minimum required):
- Per-priority request rate (RPS) and error rate (4xx/5xx)
- 95th/99th latency by priority and route
- 429/503 count and Retry-After distribution
- Queue depth per pool and token-bucket token consumption
- Model variant fallback counts and failover reasons

Suggested Grafana panels and alerts:
- Alert: High-priority 99p latency > 800ms for 5m -> Sev 2, notify customer SRE and CSM.
- Alert: High-priority error rate > 5% for 3m -> Sev 1, trigger incident process.
- Alert: Background queue depth > 75% capacity for 10m -> Pager to integration owner (warn).
- Alert: Adaptive backoff active for > 2 min and RPS still > 50% of baseline -> Ops review.

Testing and validation checklist (pre-go-live):
1) Functional test: verify X-Redwood-Priority header set correctly for all client types.
2) Failure simulation: Return 429 and 503 from a Redwood test backend and verify proxy reduces allowance per algorithm and that Retry-After is respected.
3) Load test: Run mixed workload that mirrors production split (example: 70% background, 30% live) and confirm high route p95/p99 latency remains within SLO at target baseline.
4) Chaos test: introduce model-variant failover and confirm client receives X-Redwood-Model-Variant header and traffic migrates per routing policy.
5) Telemetry validation: Ensure metrics show expected buckets and queue depth; test alert firing thresholds in staging.

Rollout and fallback steps:
1) Canary: Enable policies for 5% of traffic (by IP range or customer id). Monitor latency and error metrics for 30 minutes.
2) Ramp: 20% -> 50% -> 100% over incremental windows no shorter than 30 minutes after no alerts.
3) On alert (see conditions above): revert to previous proxy policy snapshot and open a ticket with Redwood CS with attached telemetry.
4) If Redwood signals capacity degraded for single region/model variant, initiate automatic failover to configured secondary region/model variant and notify stakeholders.

Operational runbook (play-by-play):
1) Detection: Alert fires for high-priority p99 latency.
2) Triage: On-call runs the following checks: per-route p99, queue depth, 429/503 spike, any active adaptive-backoff windows.
3) Short-term mitigation: Increase high-priority token refill by 10% (if safe), drain background tokens by 30%, and increase replica count for client-side frontends if autoscaling available.
4) Escalation: If mitigation fails within 10 minutes and error rates remain high, escalate to Redwood Customer Success and Eng SRE. Include: last 15m traces, p95/p99 history, and recent model variant headers.
5) Post-incident: Run RCA within 72 hours and update proxy policy with tuned thresholds.

Escalation contacts and ownership:
- Customer oncall/SRE: provided by customer (document here).
- Redwood CSM: Diego Alvarez (d.alvarez@redwood.example.com)
- Redwood Eng SRE escalation: eng-sre-oncall@redwood.example.com
- Priority escalation steps: open ticket at support.redwood.example.com -> tag as "priority-proxy" -> page oncall and CSM.

Common pitfalls and mitigations:
- Pitfall: Over-aggressive background throttling starves pipelines for hours.
  Mitigation: implement slow-fail queue drains with observable cutoff metrics and secondary offload to batch worker pool.
- Pitfall: Missing X-Request-Id header prevents tracing across systems.
  Mitigation: fail early and add generated request id at ingress if client absent.
- Pitfall: Relying only on latency heuristics can produce false positives under GC or networking blips.
  Mitigation: combine latency signal with 429/503 counts and Retry-After presence.

Appendix A — Example cURL smoke test:

  curl -i -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_KEY" -H "X-Redwood-Priority: high" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"input": "hello"}' https://api.redwood.example.com/v1/generate

Expected successful response headers:
- X-Redwood-Model-Variant: gptx-1.2
- X-Redwood-Capacity: available

Appendix B — Minimal policy JSON (example for integration with managed gateway):

  {"policies": [{"match": {"header": {"X-Redwood-Priority": "high"}}, "bucket": "high", "max_inflight": 50, "backoff": {"multiplier": 0.6, "cooldown_sec": 10}}, {"match": {"header": {"X-Redwood-Priority": "background"}}, "bucket": "background", "max_inflight": 1000, "backoff": {"multiplier": 0.25, "cooldown_sec": 30}}]}

Appendix C — Onboarding checklist (CS-led activities):
- Confirm ingress header mapping and token-bucket defaults.
- Run the testing and validation checklist with CSM present.
- Schedule QBR telemetries: include per-priority latency panels and adaptation history.
- Agree on escalation playbook and contact list.

Document history and notes:
- 2025-11-10: Initial draft authored by Diego Alvarez.
- 2025-12-05: Added Envoy snippet and token-bucket defaults after customer pilot.
- 2026-02-15: Finalized operational runbook and alerts with Eng SRE reviewers.

Related references:
- Streaming webhook retry and deduplication guide (integration-guides).
- Traffic shaping and queueing standards (eng-sre).
- Model switchover and fallback triage runbook (support-process).

Contact: Diego Alvarez — Customer Success, Redwood Inference

title: Proactive Telemetry & SLA Onboarding Checklist
content:
Overview
---------
This document is a pragmatic, step-by-step checklist for onboarding a new enterprise customer with proactive telemetry, SLO mapping, and QBR-ready artifacts. It is intended for Customer Success engineers, Solutions Engineers, and the customer engineering contact. The goal is to ensure that from day zero we have the signals, dashboards, and alerts required to operate the tenant within agreed SLAs and to produce reliable QBR metrics.

Scope
-----
- Applies to Hosted and Dedicated customers (Private deployments need network-specific gating described in the ‘Network & Security’ section).
- Covers: metric collection, trace and request tagging, SLO definition, alert thresholds, dashboarding, and QBR artifacts.
- Does not replace incident runbooks — use the incident-runbook specific to the service for live response.

Prerequisites (Customer / Redwood)
--------------------------------
1. Signed onboarding form with agreed SLOs and data-sharing consent.
2. Customer engineering contact has Redwoods' integration keys and sandbox tenant (if requested).
3. Access to customer's telemetry sink or permission to forward metrics/traces to Redwood telemetry gatekeeper.
4. Redwood onboarding engineer assigned and a shared Slack/Email channel established.

Key Telemetry Signals (required)
-------------------------------
Collect these signals with the tags described below. Each signal must be emitted with request_id and tenant_id (or dedicated_tenant) for correlation.

- Request counters: requests.total, requests.success, requests.error (label by model, route, tenant_id)
- Latency histograms: response.latency_ms (p50/p90/p99 buckets)
- Token counters: tokens.generated (per-model, per-route)
- Queue/backlog: serve.queue_length, serve.pending_batches
- Resource utilization: gpu.utilization, gpu.memory_free_mb, cpu.utilization
- Cache effectiveness: kvcache.hit, kvcache.miss, kvcache.evictions
- Retries and fallbacks: request.fallback_count, model.switch_count
- Error classes: error.type (rate-limited, infra, model_invalid_input, model_timeout)

Tagging and Naming Conventions
------------------------------
- tenant_id: required for multi-tenant customers. For Dedicated, use dedicated_tenant.
- model: canonical model id used by platform (e.g., gpt-j-8k-v2)
- route: api route or product feature (e.g., chat.generate, embeddings.index)
- env: prod | staging | canary
- shard/region: for geo routing visibility

SLO Mapping Template (example)
------------------------------
- Availability SLO: 99.9% successful_requests / total_requests measured monthly (error types: infra AND model_timeout count against SLO).
- Latency SLO: 95% of responses <= 300ms for short-sequence generation paths (<= 512 tokens).
- Token-cost guardrail (informational): average tokens.generated per request <= 120 for interactive route.

Instrumentation Checklist (step-by-step)
---------------------------------------
1. Verify SDK/sidecar instrumentation is deployed and reporting to telemetry-gatekeeper: run the sample curl below and confirm metrics appear in the metrics view.
   - Example curl: curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/demo -H 'Authorization: Bearer <key>' -d '{"prompt":"test"}'
2. Confirm request_id and tenant_id labels are present on all request metrics. Missing labels block tenant-level SLO calculation.
3. Ensure histogram buckets include 10ms..10s range for response.latency_ms.
4. Validate GPU telemetry: check gpu.utilization and gpu.memory_free_mb are reported by node exporter or GPU agent.
5. Enable KV cache metrics on the model-serving config if using prefix caching.
6. If streaming is used, instrument stream.chunk.count and stream.first_byte_latency_ms.

Dashboards to Create (minimum set)
----------------------------------
- Tenant SLO Overview (single panel with availability, latency p95 and p99 for primary routes)
- Model Economy (tokens.generated, cost_estimate_per_minute by model)
- Resource Pressure (gpu.utilization heatmap across nodes serving the tenant)
- Cache Health (kvcache hit ratio and evictions over time)
- Error Breakdown (top error types and top endpoints producing errors)
- Queue and Backlog (pending_batches and average batch size)

Alerting & Thresholds (recommended)
----------------------------------
Please treat thresholds as starting points that must be tuned with customer-specific traffic shape. Alerts are split into P1 (actionable immediate response) and P2 (investigate next business day).

P1 (page on-call):
| Signal | Condition | Notes |
| gpu.utilization | > 95% sustained for 3m | Risk of degraded tail latency |
| requests.error | error_rate > 0.5% over 5m AND error.type in (infra, model_timeout) | Blamable against SLO |
| serve.pending_batches | > 100 for 5m | Backlog causing latency spikes |

P2 (notify Slack Ops or owner):
| Signal | Condition | Notes |
| response.latency.p99 | > 1.5x SLO for 15m | Degradation trend |
| kvcache.evictions | > baseline*3 in 10m | Potential cache misconfiguration |
| tokens.generated.avg | > expected_per_request*2 over 30m | Cost anomaly watch |

Rollout & Validation Procedure
------------------------------
1. Dry-run: Enable telemetry collection on a canary subset (1–5% of traffic). Validate event schema and sample queries.
2. Full-rollout: Switch the production routing and enable SLO calculation.
3. Observe for 48–72 hours: confirm alerts noise is acceptable and dashboards show expected baselines.
4. Post-rollout review: produce a short onboarding summary for the QBR pack (see QBR Artifacts).

QBR Artifacts (what we deliver at first QBR)
-------------------------------------------
- Tenant SLO report (month-to-date and rolling-30d) with annotations for incidents.
- Cost-per-1k-tokens trend by route and model.
- Top 5 recommendations to improve latency/cost (batching, quantization, route split).
- List of action items and owners with ETA.

Validations & Sample Queries
---------------------------
Prometheus / M3 style examples:
- Availability: sum(rate(requests_success_total{tenant_id="TENANT_X"}[30d])) / sum(rate(requests_total{tenant_id="TENANT_X"}[30d]))
- P95 latency: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(response_latency_ms_bucket{tenant_id="TENANT_X"}[5m])) by (le))
- KV cache hit rate: sum(rate(kvcache_hit_total{tenant_id="TENANT_X"}[5m])) / (sum(rate(kvcache_hit_total{tenant_id="TENANT_X"}[5m])) + sum(rate(kvcache_miss_total{tenant_id="TENANT_X"}[5m])))

Example SQL for event store (clickhouse/postgres style):
SELECT tenant_id, count(*) as requests, sum(case when status = 'success' then 1 else 0 end) as success_requests, 100.0 * success_requests / count(*) as availability
FROM requests
WHERE ts >= now() - interval '30 day'
GROUP BY tenant_id;

Ownership Matrix (example)
-------------------------
- Customer Success (owner): onboarding coordination, QBR artifacts, SLO sign-off.
- Solutions Engineering: instrumentation support, sample queries, dashboard templates.
- Eng SRE: alert tuning and escalation owner for P1s.
- Customer Engineering Contact: provide access to telemetry sinks and validate sample runs.

Escalation Path (short)
----------------------
1. On-call SRE (P1) — page via PagerDuty.
2. Eng SRE runbook execution and mitigation.
3. Customer Success: notify customer success manager and schedule cross-team bridge.
4. CTO/VP Eng (if unresolved after 4 hours or business-impacting).

Network & Security Notes for Private Deploys
-------------------------------------------
- For Private deployments where telemetry cannot leave customer VPC, establish a signed collector (sidecar) that forwards aggregated metrics to Redwood’s metrics API over an approved egress path.
- Verify TLS mutual auth and KMS configuration prior to enabling telemetry export.

Onboarding Checklist (compact)
-----------------------------
- [ ] SLOs documented and signed by customer
- [ ] Instrumentation enabled and labels verified
- [ ] Dashboards created and shared with customer
- [ ] P1/P2 alerts configured and tested in canary
- [ ] QBR artifact skeleton ready (templates populated)
- [ ] Post-rollout review scheduled

Appendix: Common Gotchas & Troubleshooting Tips
----------------------------------------------
- Missing tenant_id label: SLOs will show as aggregated across customers — fix at SDK/sidecar config.
- Burst traffic causing batch queue growth: tune autoscaler target and batch_time_ms.
- Sudden token-cost spike: check client prompt changes, new feature releases, or retry loops.
- High GPU memory pressure: check model shard placement and local cache sizing.

Contacts & Links
---------------
- Onboarding template: /confluence/customer-success-and-support/enterprise-onboarding/onboarding-handback-and-first-90-days-ops-guide-2026
- SRE runbooks: /confluence/eng-sre/runbooks
- Dashboard templates repo: git@github.com:redwood-inference/dashboard-templates.git

Notes and change history:
- 2026-02-10: Created by Asha Patel.
- 2026-02-20: Added P1/P2 thresholds and private deployment notes (reviewed by Liam O'Connor, Priya Singh).

title: edge-telemetry-sidecar-onboarding-and-fidelity-guardrails-2026
content:
Overview

This guide describes the recommended onboarding flow, configuration guardrails, and troubleshooting ladder for deploying the Redwood Edge Telemetry Sidecar in enterprise Dedicated and Private deployments. The sidecar provides low-latency, filtered observability from customer ingress points to Redwood's telemetry pipeline while protecting PII, maintaining metric fidelity, and ensuring bounded resource impact on tenant gateways.

Who should use this guide

- Customer Success and Solutions Engineers onboarding dedicated/private tenants with custom ingress.
- Customer Platform Engineers responsible for sidecar installation and runtime validation.
- Observability/Telemetry Engineers verifying contract compliance and SLOs.

Goals and non-goals

- Goals: ensure telemetry completeness for critical signals, protect sensitive data at the edge, limit sidecar CPU/memory to avoid contention, provide clear rollback and escalation paths.
- Non-goals: full ingestion pipeline design; this guide assumes the customer's telemetry will route to Redwood's ingestion endpoints or a validated forwarder.

Key terms

- Sidecar: the telemetry agent deployed alongside an ingress/gateway service (Kubernetes DaemonSet / per-pod sidecar).
- Fidelity: percent of expected events/metrics retained after filtering and scrubbing.
- Contract: the documented set of events/metrics/logs the customer and Redwood agree to collect.

Quickstart checklist (high level)

1) Preflight: sign the Observability Contract SOW and verify CIDR allowlist.
2) Install sidecar in a staging namespace with sample traffic.
3) Validate signature TLS and auth with Redwood ingestion.
4) Run fidelity tests (see Validation section).
5) Approve production rollout, enable sampling/PII scrubbing rules, and monitor SLOs for 72 hours.

Required artifacts from customer before install

- Ingress topology diagram (service names, pods, expected peak RPS).
- Sample event/metric schema or example payloads.
- Accepted sampling targets and privacy constraints (fields to redact).
- Network egress rules (outbound to Redwood ingestion endpoints).

Sidecar configuration guardrails

The following guardrails are mandatory for Dedicated and Private environments unless an explicit exception is approved by Security and Compliance. Each item includes a rationale and recommended default.

- TLS-only transport to Redwood (rationale: prevent eavesdropping). Default: enforce mTLS, TLS 1.2+ with cert pinning.
- Max CPU per sidecar: 0.25 cores (rationale: avoid noisy neighbor on gateway pod). Default: request=100m, limit=250m.
- Max memory per sidecar: 256Mi (rationale: KV cache and buffers). Default: request=128Mi, limit=256Mi.
- Bounded local buffer: 10MB per sidecar, backpressure to client after buffer reach (rationale: avoid OOM and loss during downstream outages).
- PII redaction pipeline: apply schema-driven scrubbing before any logs/attributes leave the sidecar (rationale: regulatory compliance).
- Default sampling: 100% for error/latency traces, 10% for standard request traces, configurable per-route.
- Schema validation: drop fields that fail schema contract and emit a validation_error metric.

Example sidecar config snippet (kubernetes manifest fragment)

apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: telemetry-sidecar-config
data:
  sidecar.yaml: |
    transport:
      endpoint: https://telemetry-ingest.redwood.example
      tls: { enable: true, mTLS: true }
    resources:
      requests: { cpu: "100m", memory: "128Mi" }
      limits:   { cpu: "250m", memory: "256Mi" }
    buffer:
      max_bytes: 10485760
    sampling:
      default_trace_rate: 0.10
      error_trace_rate: 1.0
    pii_scrub_rules:
      - path: $.request.user.email
        action: redaction
      - path: $.request.body.credit_card
        action: drop

Validation and acceptance tests (executable steps)

1) Connectivity and auth (owner: customer-platform / Redwood Oncall)
   - curl -v --cert client.crt --key client.key https://telemetry-ingest.redwood.example/health should return 200.
2) TLS verification (owner: customer-platform)
   - Check peer certificate CN matches expected.
3) Resource containment (owner: customer-platform)
   - Deploy load generator with 50% of expected peak RPS for 10 minutes. Confirm sidecar resource usage <= configured limits.
4) Fidelity smoke tests (owner: customer-success)
   - Send 1,000 synthetic requests with seeded IDs. Confirm at least 995 IDs (>=99.5%) are observed in Redwood ingestion indexing within 30s.
   - For error conditions (50 injected 5xx responses), confirm all error traces arrive (100% capture).
5) PII scrubbing test (owner: customer-security)
   - Send payloads including known PII fields. Verify those fields are redacted/dropped in the ingested payloads.
6) Backpressure behavior (owner: eng-sre)
   - Simulate downstream outage by blocking egress; confirm sidecar exposes an http 429 to upstream when buffer > 80% and recovers when egress is restored.

SLOs and acceptance criteria

- Telemetry completeness: 99.5% of contract-required events are delivered to Redwood ingestion within 30s (measured per hour).
- Ingest latency: 95th percentile <= 2s from event emission to ingestion acknowledgment.
- Sidecar CPU: < 60% of configured limit under normal peak.
- PII leakage incidents: 0 per 90-day window.

Monitoring and dashboards

Required metrics to publish to the tenant's dashboard (suggested panel names):

- sidecar.event_delivery.success_rate (panel: "Telemetry Delivery Rate")
- sidecar.buffer.usage_bytes (panel: "Sidecar Buffer")
- sidecar.tls.handshake_failures (panel: "TLS Failures")
- sidecar.pii.redaction.count (panel: "PII Redactions")
- sidecar.validation.error_rate (panel: "Schema Validation Errors")

Alerting thresholds (examples)

- P0: sidecar.event_delivery.success_rate < 95% for 5m — page on-call SRE and Customer Success.
- P1: sidecar.buffer.usage_bytes > 80% for 10m — create incident and notify customer platform.
- P2: sidecar.tls.handshake_failures > 5 per minute for 5m — notify security and review cert rotation.

Rollback and canary strategy

- Canary Deployment: 1% of production pods for 30m, validate SLOs, increase to 10% for 1h, then 30% for 2h before full rollout.
- Fast rollback criteria (automated): any P0 alert or buffer > 95% for 5m should trigger an automated rollback to prior sidecar image config.
- Manual rollback: Customer Success must coordinate with customer platform and SRE; use documented runbook: "kubectl rollout undo" command and confirm traffic stability for 15 minutes.

Troubleshooting ladder (ordered)

1) Symptom: No telemetry received from tenant
   - Check sidecar pod status (kubectl get pods -n <ns> -l app=telemetry-sidecar).
   - Review sidecar logs for TLS errors and auth failures.
   - Confirm egress firewall rules include telemetry ingestion endpoints.

2) Symptom: High validation_error metrics
   - Compare incoming payloads to agreed contract. If contract has changed, route to Solutions for schema versioning.
   - If unexpected fields appear frequently, add transformation rule in sidecar config and patch via ConfigMap.

3) Symptom: PII observed in Redwood ingestion
   - Immediately circuit the pipeline: switch sidecar to fail-closed mode (drop all logs) and open an incident (see Escalation matrix).
   - Collect impacted sample messages and perform forensics with Security.
   - Temporary mitigation: enable additional regex-based scrub rules applied server-side until sidecar rule can be patched.

Escalation matrix (who to call)

- First contact: Customer Success Engineer (CSE) assigned to account — slack: #cse-<customer>-oncall
- If unresolved in 15 minutes: Observability Engineer (obs-eng) — slack: #obs-oncall
- If PII or regulatory exposure suspected: Security Incident Response — pager: sec-incident-pager and notify legal.
- If sidecar resource exhaustion threatens production: SRE pager.

Post-deployment ops and QBR inputs

For the first QBR after onboarding, Customer Success should prepare the following artifacts:

- Telemetry fidelity report (30/60/90-day buckets) showing delivery rate, latency, and redaction counts.
- Incident log summarizing any sidecar-related alerts, root cause, and mitigations.
- Resource utilization trend across the tenant's gateway fleet.
- Proposed optimizations (e.g., tune sampling or move heavy traces to async export).

Ownership and contacts

- Customer Success (primary owner for onboarding): Marcus Li (marcus@redwood.example)
- Observability Engineering (validation & dashboards): Priya Kapoor (priya@redwood.example)
- Security (PII rules & incident): Eleanor Chen (eleanor@redwood.example)
- SRE (rollouts & performance): Diego Marquez (diego@redwood.example)

Appendix A: Example fidelity test harness (shell)

# Produce 1k synthetic requests and record delivery IDs
for i in $(seq 1 1000); do
  id="test-$(date +%s)-$i"
  curl -s -X POST https://tenant-ingress.example/endpoint -d \"{\\\"id\\\":\\\"$id\\\",\\\"payload\\\":\\\"ping\\\"}\" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' &
done

# Query Redwood ingestion index (pseudo-API)
curl -s 'https://telemetry-api.redwood.example/search?tag=test' | jq '.hits | length'

Appendix B: Common exceptions and approvals

- Exception: Sidecar memory limit to 512Mi for heavy enrichment workloads. Approval required from SRE and Security with signed risk assessment.
- Exception: Sampling set to 100% for premium onboarding windows (72 hours) — document and timebox in the contract.

Change log

- 2026-02-10: Initial draft by Marcus Li.
- 2026-02-20: Added SLO targets and canary guidance (reviewers: Priya Kapoor).
- 2026-03-01: Final edits and publishing; added rollback automation criteria (reviewers: Eleanor Chen, Diego Marquez).

title: cross-account-metrics-and-traces-forwarding-playbook-2025
content:
Overview

Purpose:
This playbook documents an operational, secure approach for forwarding customer metrics and traces from a customer-managed AWS/GCP/Azure account into Redwood Console and an optional third-party observability backend (e.g., Splunk, Datadog, New Relic). It is intended for partners and enterprise customers who require cross-account telemetry collection without sending sensitive request payloads.

When to use this playbook:
- Customer has dedicated networking (VPC peering, PrivateLink, or firewall rules) and wants telemetry consolidated into Redwood Console.
- Customer requires audit-friendly cross-account forwarding with minimal footprint in customer environment.
- You need SRE-grade telemetry for QBRs, incident triage, and cost attribution.

Ownership and intent:
- Primary owner: Customer Success (onboarding team)
- Secondary owners: Eng-Infra (networking), Eng-SRE (alerting), Security (data handling)
- Goal: Reduce time-to-first-metric to < 4 hours for standard integrations; ensure data classification and retention meet customer SLA.

Prerequisites

Customer-side prerequisites:
1) Cloud account with the ability to deploy a small compute resource (Lambda/Cloud Run/VM) or install an agent on a telemetry gateway.
2) Network connectivity: one of the following: PrivateLink / VPC peering / IP allowlist for a Forwarder endpoint.
3) IAM/service account with least-privilege permissions to read metrics/traces and write to the forwarder resource.
4) List of metric namespaces and trace spans to be forwarded (sample set for initial onboarding).

Redwood-side prerequisites:
- Dedicated ingest endpoint (hosted) or customer-dedicated forwarder container image (for air-gapped/private deployments).
- Ingest API key scoped to metrics/traces ingest only. TTL and rotation policy to be agreed.

Architecture and flow

High-level flow (text diagram):
Customer telemetry source (Prometheus/OTel collector / vendor agent) --> Local forwarder (lightweight proxy) --> Cross-account secure tunnel / PrivateLink --> Redwood ingest endpoint --> Redwood Console (metrics store + traces index)

Security and data handling notes:
- Redact request-level payloads: Forward only metric names, numeric values, trace IDs, and safe tags. Customer must provide a redaction policy.
- TLS enforced mTLS where possible; fallback to TLS with mutual certificate pinning only if required by customer.
- KMS/HSM: For Private deployments, use customer-managed CMK to encrypt telemetry-at-rest.

Configuration reference (example table)

| Component | Minimum config (example) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| OTel collector | receivers: prometheus, exporters: otlp | Set resource.attributes.service to customer service name |
| Local forwarder | image: rdwd/telemetry-forwarder:1.3.0\nargs: --mode=proxy --dest=https://ingest.rdwd.internal:443 | Supports batching, backoff, and delta compression |
| Ingest endpoint | api_key: redwood-ingest-<customer>-2025\nrate_limit: 5000 metrics/s | Scales by reserved capacity on Dedicated customers |
\nStep-by-step integration (typical onboarding)

1) Discovery (Customer Success + Solutions Engineer)
   - Collect account IDs, preferred connectivity pattern, sample metric namespaces, and SPIFF for sensitive fields.
   - Confirm retention and PII policy (default: 90 days for metrics, 30 days for traces unless enterprise package purchased).

2) Provisioning (Infra/Solutions)
   - Create ingest-scoped API key in Redwood Console and send to customer via secure channel (1Password/secure email).
   - Provide container image and Helm/K8s manifest or Lambda snippet. Example Lambda (Node):

   ```javascript
   const https = require('https');
   exports.handler = async (event) => {
     // minimal forwarder example
     const payload = JSON.stringify(event);
     const req = https.request(process.env.INGEST_URL, { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Authorization': `Bearer ${process.env.INGEST_API_KEY}`, 'Content-Type': 'application/json' } }, res=>{});
     req.write(payload); req.end();
     return { status: 'forwarded' };
   };
   ```

3) Network setup
   - If PrivateLink: exchange service names and create VPC endpoint in customer account. Validate DNS and route tables.
   - If IP allowlist: provide list of Redwood egress IP ranges and validate with customer firewall.

4) Deployment and smoke test
   - Deploy forwarder with a conservative batch interval (e.g., 10s) and start with 1% sample rate for traces.
   - Verify connectivity and ingest using the test pipe: POST /v1/ingest/health with api key. Expected response 200 and JSON with ingest_ack:true.

5) Validation and ramp
   - Confirm metric counts, label cardinality, and top-10 costly metrics. Tune sampling for traces and scale forwarder CPU/memory.
   - Enable dashboard template in Redwood Console and add to customer team workspace for QBR reporting.

Operational runbook (SRE-focused)

Alert triggers (suggestions):
- Forwarder down > 5m: SEV-2
- Ingest 5xxs > 1% over 15m: SEV-2
- Cardinality spike > 3x baseline over 30m: SEV-3
- Ingest lag > 2x expected: SEV-2

Runbook steps for Forwarder down:
1) Confirm forwarder compute is reachable (SSH/Cloud logs).
2) Check forwarder logs for connectivity errors, auth failures, or OOM.
3) If auth failure: rotate API key and redeploy.
4) If network issue: validate PrivateLink/VPC peering status and security group rules.
5) Escalate to Redwood Eng-SRE if unresolved after 30 minutes.

Cost and cardinality controls

To protect customer and Redwood unit economics, apply the following safeguards:
- Default label whitelist: service, env, region, customer_id. All other labels blocked unless approved.
- Default max_series_per_minute: 50k (can be raised on Dedicated contracts).
- Auto-sampling rule: When series growth > 2x, apply 10% sampling to trace spans and alert customer.

Troubleshooting matrix (common issues)

1) No metrics visible in Console
   - Check forwarder logs for 401/403 (bad api key).
   - Validate network route: traceroute to ingest endpoint from customer network.
   - Confirm Prometheus scrape job status and local collector metrics.

2) High 5xxs from ingest
   - Check payload size (max 1MB per batch).
   - Verify forwarder version compatibility (upgrade to rdwd/telemetry-forwarder:1.3.0+).
   - Check rate limits: backoff settings in forwarder should respect Retry-After header.

3) Exploding cardinality after deploy
   - Identify newly introduced labels with high cardinality via /v1/metrics/cardinality API.
   - Apply drop_labels rule in OTel collector and redeploy.

QBR and health metrics (what to report)

For customer QBRs, include: 
- Key metrics ingested per day (time series count)
- P95 latency for ingest (ms)
- Trace sampling rate and traced requests/day
- Alert volume and MTTR for telemetry-related incidents
- Cost delta attributable to telemetry (tokens/metrics cost)

Suggested dashboard tiles for QBR:
- "Telemetry Ingest Overview": daily metrics/time series, error rates
- "Top Label Cardinality": top 20 labels by series growth
- "Trace Coverage": % requests traced per service

Compliance and data retention

- Default retention: metrics 90 days, traces 30 days. Extended retention available under enterprise contract.
- PII handling: Do not forward request bodies, headers with auth tokens, or any field classified as "sensitive" by the customer redaction policy.
- Audit trail: All API key rotations and configuration changes are recorded and available in Redwood Console audit logs.

Escalation and support contact matrix

- Customer Success Oncall (first 30 minutes): cs-oncall@redwood.ai
- Eng-SRE escalation (30–120 minutes): sre-escalation@redwood.ai
- Security escalation (data leak suspected): sec-incident@redwood.ai (phone pager)

Appendix: example OTel snippet (prometheus scrape + exporter)

```yaml
receivers:
  prometheus:
    config:
      scrape_configs:
        - job_name: 'app'
          static_configs:
            - targets: ['localhost:9100']
exporters:
  otlp:
    endpoint: '${INGEST_URL}'
    headers:
      'Authorization': 'Bearer ${INGEST_API_KEY}'
service:
  pipelines:
    metrics:
      receivers: [prometheus]
      exporters: [otlp]
```

References and related docs

- Redwood Console: telemetry ingestion docs (internal)
- Security: telemetry data classification and redaction playbook
- Eng-Infra: network connectivity patterns for PrivateLink and VPC peering

Change history

- 2025-03-12: Initial draft (Claire Nguyen)
- 2025-06-10: Added OTel snippets and sampling guidance (Ethan Morales)
- 2026-02-20: Updated forwarder image and alert thresholds (Priya Shah)

title: Telemetry Sampling & Privacy‑Balanced Onboarding Guide
content:
Purpose
This document explains a repeatable onboarding pattern for enterprise customers that need high-fidelity observability while honoring privacy constraints and cost budgets. It is intended for Customer Success engineers, SREs, and partner integration teams who run Redwood inference workloads in hosted, dedicated, or private environments.

Scope
- Applies to telemetry collected from production inference traffic: logs, traces, token-level telemetry, request/response payloads, and derived metrics.
- Covers sampling strategies, privacy filtering, acceptance criteria, telemetry assertions, and rollback triggers.
- Does not replace legal or Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIA); engage Security/Legal for regulated customers.

Goals
1. Ensure minimum observability to meet tenant SLOs and onboarding acceptance tests.
2. Minimize PII exposure and customer privacy risk by design.
3. Keep telemetry cost predictable and within customer / internal budget.
4. Provide clear operational runbook for escalation and rollback.

Key Terms
- High‑fidelity sample (HFS): full request/response payload, token-level timing, and traces.
- Metric-only sample (MOS): aggregated metrics and sampled traces but no payload.
- Privacy‑filtered: payloads with PII redacted or pseudonymized.

Recommended sampling matrix
Use this matrix to pick an initial sampling configuration based on customer tier and regulatory needs. Adjust during the onboarding runway.

| Customer tier | Default initial sampling | Privacy posture | Typical rate (requests/day) | Notes |
|---|---:|---|---:|---|
| Enterprise (regulated) | MOS + privacy-filtered HFS for canary | High: pseudonymize, redact | 0.1% HFS, 100% MOS | Use for PCI/PHI customers; review with Security |
| Enterprise (standard) | MOS + 1% HFS | Medium: redaction of known PII types | 1% HFS, 100% MOS | Good balance for SLAs + debugging |
| Growth/PLG | MOS | Low: redaction by default | 0% HFS, 100% MOS | Cost-conscious; escalate to HFS on incidents |

Guidelines for choosing sampling algorithm
- Deterministic reservoir sampling keyed by tenant_id + day for reproducibility.
- Priority-based sampling: elevate failed requests, high latency, or behavioral anomalies to HFS.
- Adaptive sampling: increase HFS during canary windows or after model upgrade events.

Privacy and PII handling
1. Default policy: redact known PII (SSNs, credit card numbers, unstructured PHI) from payloads before any HFS storage.
2. Use ephemeral pseudonymization when customer consents to richer telemetry. Store mapping in customer-managed KMS-backed vaults when required.
3. Tokenization logs: never store raw user-provided sequences for customers that opt out of raw telemetry. Use hashed prefixes for correlation.
4. Provide customers a telemetry expectations doc with clear opt-in/opt-out steps and retention windows.

Onboarding checklist (step-by-step)
1. Pre-onboarding: legal & security signoff for telemetry posture. Record consent level in tenant profile.
2. Define SLOs and acceptance criteria with customer (latency P50/P95, error rate, freshness of embeddings).
3. Baseline run: enable MOS for 7 days to collect metrics and establish normal ranges.
4. Canary window (7–14 days): enable priority-based 1% HFS for a small subset (0.5–2% traffic) and validate instrumentation.
5. Privacy validation: run redaction/pseudonymization tests against synthetic PHI fixtures.
6. Cost projection: run a 48‑hour HFS burst to estimate billing impact; record in tenant pricing sheet.
7. Go/No‑Go gates: must pass telemetry assertions (see below), security review, and cost approval.
8. Post‑go live: keep MOS enabled and scheduled HFS bursts for weekly quality checks.

Telemetry assertions (automated checks to run during acceptance)
- Coverage: 95% of routed requests produce metric envelopes and traces (MOS).
- Correlation: 100% of HFS samples have trace IDs that map to MOS metrics within 30s.
- Privacy: no raw PII found in HFS payloads for tenants with privacy opt-out. Run regex-based and ML-based detectors.
- Freshness: derived metrics and cost-attribution tags are visible in Redwood Console within 5m of ingestion.

Example sampling configuration (YAML)
```yaml
telemetry: 
  sampling_strategy: priority_adaptive
  default_metric_sample: 1.0         # 100% MOS (metrics + minimal traces)
  high_fidelity: 
    rate: 0.01                        # 1% HFS for canary by default
    triggers: [error, latency_p95_exceed, manual_tag]
  privacy: 
    redaction_profile: standard-2026
    pseudonymization: optional
  retention_days: 30
  owner: cs-integration-engineering@redwood.com
```

Example HFS JSON snippet (privacy‑guarded)
```json
{
  "request_id": "r-123456",
  "tenant_id": "t-abc",
  "trace_id": "trace-987",
  "payload": "<redacted>",
  "tokens_observed": 42,
  "latency_ms": 86,
  "sample_type": "HFS",
  "privacy_flags": ["pseudonymized"]
}
```

Operational playbook for incidents during onboarding
1. Detection: telemetry assertion failure alerts to CS/SRE channel.
2. Immediate action: reduce HFS rate to 0% for affected tenant, keep MOS at 100%.
3. Triage: run tool-assisted PII scan on most recent HFS window. If PII is found, follow the Sensitive Data Exposure Escalation (notify Security and Legal, preserve evidence, start customer notification timeline within 48h).
4. Recovery: re‑deploy privacy filter rule updates, run synthetic validation tests, and permit incremental HFS re‑enablement (start at 0.01%).
5. RCA: produce a short incident summary for the customer and an internal postmortem with action items and owners.

Escalation contacts and ownership
- Primary: CS Integration Lead — Aisha Patel (cs-integration@redwood.com)
- Secondary: Observability SRE — Liam Chen (sre-observability@redwood.com)
- Privacy Escalation: Security Analyst — Marcos Rivera (security-telemetry@redwood.com)

QBR & Health check integration
- Include telemetry baseline graphs in the go‑live QBR packet: MOS coverage, HFS sampling rate, privacy incidents (0 expected), and telemetry cost delta vs baseline.
- Suggested QBR cadence in first 90 days: weekly health reports for first month, biweekly for month 2–3, then monthly.
- Actionable metrics for QBRs: metric coverage %, median trace latency, number of HFS samples flagged for privacy review, and monthly telemetry spend by tag.

Documentation & APIs to use
- Telemetry Schema (internal): /docs/telemetry/schema-v2 (request via platform docs portal).
- Sampling control API (example): POST /admin/v1/telemetry/{tenant_id}/sampling
- Redaction rules repository: git://redwood/telemetry/redaction-rules  (access controlled)

Testing and validation matrix
- Unit tests: redaction rules must pass fixture suite for 200+ synthetic PII patterns.
- Integration tests: ensure MOS envelopes correlate with HFS samples across trace boundaries.
- Load test: run 48h of MOS + scheduled 1% HFS at production RPS; validate cost projection within 20% of estimate.

Common pitfalls & mitigations
- Overindexing on HFS early: keeps costs and privacy risk high. Mitigation: use MOS + targeted HFS triggers.
- Insufficient correlation keys: require tenant_id and request_hash in all envelopes.
- Drift in telemetry schema: enforce schema validations at ingest with automatic alerting.

Appendix: sample onboarding checklist (one‑page)
1) Legal/Security telemetry posture OK — checkbox
2) MOS enabled and baseline collected (7 days) — date: ________
3) Canary HFS configuration set (rate: __%) — window start: ________
4) PII redaction verification passed — tester: ________
5) Cost projection uploaded to tenant sheet — owner: ________
6) Go/No‑Go decision: ________ (CS lead, SRE, Customer)

Revision history
- 2026-03-15: Draft authored by Aisha Patel.
- 2026-06-10: Added adaptive sampling guidance and YAML example (reviewers: Liam Chen).
- 2026-08-02: Finalized privacy escalation flow and QBR integration notes (published).

Questions or feedback? Open a ticket to #cs-integration or email cs-integration@redwood.com.

title: Telemetry Gatekeeper: Onboarding & QBR Integration Guide
content:
SUMMARY

This guide defines the Telemetry Gatekeeper contract used during enterprise onboarding and quarterly business reviews (QBRs). It standardizes the telemetry, custom metrics, and validation checks we require before go-live and for QBR-ready reporting. The intent is to reduce onboarding time, prevent metric drift, and ensure customers and Customer Success (CS) teams have a shared, auditable signal set for availability, cost, latency, and quality.

SCOPE & AUDIENCE

- Scope: Redwood-hosted and Dedicated deployments where customers integrate service metrics or forward custom application signals. Covers metric schema, ingestion verification, dashboards, alert thresholds, and QBR-ready exports.
- Audience: Customer Success, Solutions Engineering, Enterprise Dev/Ops teams, Observability Engineers, and Account Execs preparing QBRs.

WHY A TELEMETRY GATEKEEPER?

Onboarding often stalls on mismatched telemetry expectations. Telemetry Gatekeeper provides a small, enforceable contract so we can:

1. Validate that SLAs and SLOs are measurable from day one.
2. Ensure consistent cost attribution (per-route/per-model) for enterprise billing.
3. Enable objective QBR metrics with minimal custom instrumentation.

OWNERSHIP & CONTACTS

- Telemetry Gatekeeper owner: Customer Success (Aisha Gupta)
- Platform integration contact: Eng Platform (Marcus Patel)
- Observability SME: Eng SRE (Leah Browne)
- Customer success lead (customer-side): provided during kickoff

PREREQUISITES BEFORE ONBOARDING CHECKPOINT

1. Customer can forward metrics to one of the supported collectors: Prometheus remote_write, Datadog, or a secure S3/Parquet export for batch ingestion.
2. Customer has agreed on the telemetry retention window for plant/usage signals (default 90 days).
3. Access: Redwood CS/Platform has read-only access to the metrics workspace or a credentials-based ingest token.

TELEMETRY GATEKEEPER CONTRACT (REQUIRED SIGNALS)

Required signals are grouped by category. Each metric must include labels/tags: customer_id, deployment_type (hosted|dedicated|private), region, model_name, route. Timestamps in UTC.

1) Availability & Capacity
- redwood.request.count (counter): total requests, labeled by route, model_name
- redwood.request.errors (counter): error_count segmented by code, route
- redwood.instance.healthy (gauge): 0|1 per server/pool id (optional for private)

2) Latency & P95/P99
- redwood.request.latency_ms (histogram or summary): per route and model_name
- redwood.request.kvcache_hit_rate (gauge): percentage [0-1] per model variant

3) Cost & Usage Attribution
- redwood.tokens.generated (counter): per request, with token_count label
- redwood.embedding.units (counter): if embeddings used, with vector_dim label
- redwood.batch.size (histogram): batch sizes for throughput analysis

4) Quality Signals (optional, recommended for QBR)
- customer.eval.score (gauge): application-level quality metric, tied to a named prompt-set
- customer.prompt.latent_failures (counter): domain-specific failure modes to surface regressions

SAMPLE METRIC SCHEMA (Prometheus exposition)

# HELP redwood_request_latency_ms request latency in ms
# TYPE redwood_request_latency_ms histogram
redwood_request_latency_ms_bucket{le="100",route="/v1/generate",model_name="gpt-j-quant",customer_id="acme-corp"} 42
redwood_request_latency_ms_sum{route="/v1/generate",model_name="gpt-j-quant",customer_id="acme-corp"} 8243
redwood_request_latency_ms_count{route="/v1/generate",model_name="gpt-j-quant",customer_id="acme-corp"} 123

INGESTION & VALIDATION STEPS (ONBOARDING CHECKPOINTS)

We break validation into three automated checkpoints and one manual review:

1) Collector connectivity check (Day 0-1):
- Verify connectivity with remote_write / Datadog API / S3 ingest.
- Expected result: first metric appears within 15 minutes.
- Tooling: telemetry-checker-cli send-sample --endpoint <endpoint> --customer acme-corp

2) Label & Schema validation (Day 1):
- Automated script validates presence of required labels and types.
- Expected: 100% of incoming series have customer_id and route labels.

3) Baseline signal sanity (Day 1-3):
- Compare incoming metrics to expected ranges. Example: request.count > 10/day for active customers.
- Flag anomalies for manual triage.

4) Manual dashboard + SLO review (Day 3-7):
- CS and SRE review dashboards and sign-off on go/no-go.
- Sign-off template included in this doc.

AUTOMATED VALIDATION RULES (EXAMPLES)

- Missing required label: FAIL
- Requests reported but tokens.generated missing: WARNING
- P95 latency > 2000ms for 10%+ of routes: ALERT (triage)

SAMPLE VALIDATION COMMANDS

# Validate schema and labels (CLI)
telemetry-checker validate-schema --source prom --customer acme-corp --required-labels customer_id,route,model_name

# Run baseline sanity check
telemetry-checker baseline --customer acme-corp --window 24h --expected-min-requests 10

DASHBOARDS & QBR METRICS (RECOMMENDED PANELS)

Minimum QBR-ready dashboards:
- Traffic & Errors: total requests, 7d trend, errors by code and route
- Latency Slices: P50/P95/P99 by model and route, broken down by region
- Cost Attribution: tokens.generated and embeddings.units per route and model, month-to-date
- Quality Signals: customer.eval.score trend and regressions by prompt-set
- Capacity & Autoscaling: instance utilization, queue lengths, batch sizes

SAMPLE PROMETHEUS QUERIES

- Total requests (7d): sum(increase(redwood_request_count[7d])) by (route)
- P95 latency: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(redwood_request_latency_ms_bucket[5m])) by (le, route, model_name))
- Token rate: sum(rate(redwood_tokens_generated[1m])) by (route, customer_id)

QBR SLIDE TEMPLATE (METRICS WE PULL)

1. Executive summary (uptime %, cost delta month-over-month, key wins)
2. Availability & Latency trends (P95, P99)
3. Cost per 1k tokens and cost drivers by route/model
4. Quality snapshot (customer.eval.score and top 3 prompt regressions)
5. Action items and runbook changes for next quarter

ALERTING & ESCALATION (TELEMETRY DISCREPANCIES)

Default thresholds (suggested; tune per-customer):
- Availability: redwood.request.errors / redwood.request.count > 0.02 for 5m -> P1 on-call
- Latency: P95 > 2s for 10% routes in 10m -> P1 on-call
- Token anomaly: token rate increase > 3x baseline in 15m without corresponding traffic -> P0 security/cost

Escalation steps:
1) Automated ticket created in Zendesk with metric snapshot and link to dashboard.
2) CS owns initial customer communication within 30 minutes.
3) If P1/P0, page SRE and Solutions Eng. Use dedicated escalation channel: #escalations-enterprise-telemetry.

HANDOFF CHECKLIST (GO-LIVE)

- [ ] Collector confirmed and sample data present
- [ ] Schema validation passed (labels/types)
- [ ] Dashboards created and shared with customer
- [ ] Alerts configured and SLOs mapped to on-call responders
- [ ] Cost attribution verified for top 5 routes
- [ ] CS sign-off documented

EXAMPLE CS SIGN-OFF NOTE

We, the undersigned, confirm that the Telemetry Gatekeeper contract is satisfied for customer ACME CORP. Dashboards: <link>. Alerts: <link>. Signed: Customer Success Owner (Aisha Gupta) & Customer Eng Lead (name). Date: YYYY-MM-DD.

DISCREPANCY TRIAGE RUNBOOK (WHEN METRICS LOOK OFF)

1) Confirm ingestion endpoint and timestamps (time skew issues are common).
2) Check labels: if missing customer_id, try re-ingest with relabeled source or apply relabeling rule in Prometheus remote_write.
3) If tokens.generated is zero but request.count > 0: check model routing and inference runtime for missing instrumentation (file a runtime bug).
4) For noisy spikes, compute request/token delta: spike in tokens without requests implies billing/abuse — escalate to security.

REPORTING & QBR PREPARATION (CS OPERATIONS)

- Weekly telemetry snapshot emailed to AE and customer 2 weeks before QBR.
- Pull standard artifacts 3 days before QBR: traffic CSV, cost CSV, quality eval exports (JSON), dashboard PDFs.
- Responsibility matrix: CS prepares executive summary; Solutions Eng prepares technical root cause slides; SRE validates production signals.

TEMPLATED ARTIFACTS (copy for CS)

1) Telemetry validation sign-off (Google Doc link template)
2) Dashboard export checklist (CSV of queries)
3) QBR metrics export script (CLI example):

# Export tokens per route last 30 days
telemetry-export --query "sum(increase(redwood_tokens_generated[30d])) by (route, model_name)" --format csv --customer acme-corp --out tokens_30d.csv

SECURITY & DATA SENSITIVITY NOTES

- Do not forward PII. All metrics must be anonymized; free-text prompt fields must be redacted.
- For private deployments, prefer VPC-native collectors and role-limited service principals.

TIMELINE RECOMMENDATION

- Day 0: Kickoff and collector access established
- Day 1-3: Connectivity + schema validation
- Day 3-7: Dashboard build and CS/SRE sign-off
- Week 2: Go-live and 7-day monitoring window

APPENDIX: COMMON TROUBLESHOOTING SNIPPETS

1) Prometheus relabel example to add customer_id:

- job_name: redwood_remote_write
  static_configs:
  - targets: ['collector.example.com:9091']
  relabel_configs:
  - source_labels: [__address__]
    target_label: customer_id
    replacement: acme-corp

2) Datadog forwarding note: ensure "host" tag is stable and not ephemeral. Use container_id label instead for grouping.

FEEDBACK & ITERATION

This guide is versioned by Customer Success. Send feedback or improvement requests to the Telemetry Gatekeeper owner or open a PR in the onboarding playbook repo.

RELATED RESOURCES

- Integration runbook: /confluence/customer-success-and-support/integration-guides/streaming-webhook-retry-and-deduplication-guide-2026
- Billing attribution: /confluence/finance-and-legal/revrec-and-billing/cost-attribution-models-2025

CHANGE LOG

- 2026-01-15: Initial published draft (Aisha Gupta)
- 2026-02-12: Added Prometheus examples, validated sample CLI commands, updated QBR checklist (reviewers: Marcus Patel, Leah Browne)

title: SLO telemetry corruption detection and repair runbook
content:
Summary:

This runbook describes detection patterns, triage steps, containment, and repair procedures for telemetry corruption that can affect SLO calculation and error‑budget decisions. Telemetry corruption includes any systematic integrity failure in metrics, traces, or logs that causes SLIs to be inaccurate (for example, missing labels, zeroed counters, duplicate events, stale timestamps, or aggregation compiler bugs). The runbook focuses on SLO correctness and making safe decisions when SLI data is unreliable.

Scope:
- In scope: aggregate SLI telemetry (Prometheus/Pushgateway metrics, pre‑aggregated counters, trace spans ingested into the tracing pipeline, logs parsed into the metrics pipeline), the SLO computation pipeline (aggregation jobs and rollup jobs), and the observability ingestion/ETL (Kafka topics, consumer groups, transform jobs).
- Out of scope: application code correctness unrelated to telemetry (e.g., business logic bugs causing real errors).

Why this matters:
- Incorrect telemetry can cause false SLO breaches or mask real outages, leading to improper capacity scaling, costly incident responses, incorrect billing/chargeback, and bad downstream product decisions.

Owner & escalation:
- Primary on‑call: Observability SRE rotation (pager: #sre-observability).
- Secondary: Runtime SRE (pager #sre-runtime).
- Escalation path: oncall -> Observability lead (Ava Martinez) -> Head of SRE (Nikhil Verma).

Definitions and mapping to SLIs/SLOs:
- Raw event: single telemetry event (metric sample, trace span, log line).
- Rollup job: scheduled aggregation that computes SLI numerator/denominator windows (1m, 5m, 1h).
- Corruption types: Missing samples, Stale timestamps, Label drift, Duplicate events, Aggregation regressions (off‑by‑one windows), Downstream truncation.

Key signals to watch (high level):
- Sudden drop to zero across many counters (indicates producer/ingestion issue).
- Large (>10%) divergence between raw rate and rollup rate over 5m windows.
- Increased cardinality of metric labels (new unexpected label values) or missing expected labels.
- Trace sampling rate collapse or identical trace IDs repeated.
- Log ingestion lag (consumer offset lag > 10m) or spikes in dropped messages.
- SLI backfill discrepancy: SLI computed from recent raw data differs from raw query by >5%.

Detection recipes (examples):
- PromQL: compare raw counter and rollup metric for a service (5m lookback):
  - raw rate query: rate(service_requests_total[5m])
  - rollup rate: service_requests_rollup_count[5m:5m] or an average of the preaggregated metric
  - anomaly indicator: (abs(rate - rollup) / max(rate, 1e-6)) > 0.05 for > 2 samples -> alert

- Missing labels detection (Grafana/LogQL):
  - query counts grouped by expected label set and assert presence: sum by(region,env)(service_requests_total)
  - If count for any expected env=="prod" drops to 0 while others remain, raise investigation.

- Trace duplication check (example with Jaeger/Tempo API):
  - curl "http://tempo/query?service=my-service&lookback=15m" and check for identical span IDs or repeated root trace IDs >100 occurrences -> suspect replay/consumer dedup bug.

- Consumer lag check (Kafka example):
  - CLI: kafka-consumer-groups --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --describe --group observation-etl | grep -E "^observation-etl"
  - alert threshold: partition lag > 1,000,000 messages or > 10 minutes backlog

Integrity matrix (reference table):
- Metrics: missing samples / label drift / zeroing / duplication.
- Traces: sampling collapse / duplication / missing service tag.
- Logs: parse failures / truncation / timestamp munging.

Immediate triage checklist (fast path):
1) Acknowledge alert and set incident type: TELEMETRY_CORRUPTION.
2) Record initial symptoms and time window (start Ts).
3) Snapshot current SLO dashboards and raw metrics (save GIFs or dashboard snapshots).
4) Check upstream producers: application metrics exporter status (service /metrics endpoints), exporter logs.
   - commands: curl -sS http://<host>:9100/metrics | head -n 50
5) Check ingestion/ETL layer: consumer group lag, transform job logs, error topics.
6) Check rollup jobs: job executor logs, recent job durations, and failures.
7) Decide containment action: Pause SLO alerts / mark SLO data as unreliable for window X, or switch to an alternate SLI source (fallback SLI).

Containment and immediate mitigation (safety-first):
- If telemetry corruption is confirmed and SLOs are used for automated throttles or billing, place SLO calculations into read‑only/failover mode and notify downstream consumers.
- Apply temporary flagging so that automatic remediation (capacity autoscaling, circuit breakers) does not act on corrupted SLI values.
- If possible, switch SLO computation to a secondary pipeline that uses raw events rather than rollups (see "fallback SLI sources" below).

Repair & recovery (detailed procedure):
Step A — Isolate the component:
1) Identify which layer is corrupted: producer, ingestion broker, transform job, rollup job, or SLO aggregator. Use the detection recipes above to localize.
2) If transform job is failing, cordon the job (k8s: kubectl cordon <node>/kubectl scale --replicas=0 deployment/etl-transform) and rerun a canary instance with debug flags.

Step B — Create reproducible snapshot and safe workspace:
1) Capture a time-bound snapshot of raw messages from the broker for the suspect window. Example (Kafka):
  kafka-console-consumer --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --topic telemetry-raw --partition 3 --offset 12345 --max-messages 1000 > /tmp/snapshot-part3.json
2) Export rollup outputs and job logs for the same window.

Step C — Integrity checks and repair actions (choose applicable):
- Label repair: if labels are missing due to transform bug, run idempotent label enrich job against snapshot and recompute rollups.
- Duplicate suppression: if duplicate events exist, deduplicate by unique_event_id and recompute aggregates.
- Timestamp repair: if timestamps truncated (e.g., second precision lost), reconstruct using broker offsets and producer time if available; otherwise mark affected window as unverifiable and proceed with backfill using application logs.
- Recompute rollups: run rollup job in a controlled backfill mode (dry run -> validation -> commit). Ensure the backfill is idempotent: use deterministic windowing and versioned rollup keys.

Example backfill sequence (bash):
- Step 1: run dry run (no writes)
  python etl/rollup.py --window-start="2025-02-18T14:00:00Z" --window-end="2025-02-18T14:05:00Z" --dry-run --source /tmp/snapshot-*.json
- Step 2: validate differences vs previous rollup
  python scripts/compare_rollup.py --old /data/rollups/2025-02-18-14-00.json --new /tmp/rollup-dryrun.json
- Step 3: commit if validated
  python etl/rollup.py --window-start=... --window-end=... --commit --source /tmp/snapshot-*.json

Verification after repair:
- Run gold‑standard queries against raw data and recomputed rollups and assert alignment within tolerance (default 0.5% for high‑volume SLIs, 2% for low‑volume).
- Recompute SLOs for the affected window and compare to pre‑incident values. Document differences.

Fallback SLI sources and practice modes:
- Maintain at least one alternate SLI path for each critical SLO: (a) raw query fallback (on-demand), (b) secondary rollup cluster (replicated), (c) application‑side telemetry snapshots.
- Practice: quarterly failover drill switching SLOs to fallback path and validating downstream dashboards and alerting.

Automated detectors & tooling suggestions:
- Add automated detectors that compare raw ingestion rate vs rollup rate and flag >5% divergence for 3 consecutive windows.
- Build a small CLI utility: telemetry-integrity-check that runs the integrity matrix and emits a succinct report and suggested remediation steps.
  - Example usage: telemetry-integrity-check --service my-service --window 2025-02-18T14:00:00Z/2025-02-18T14:05:00Z

Post‑incident evidence and postmortem checklist (required):
- Timestamped list of alerts and acknowledgements (who acknowledged and when).
- Snapshot of dashboards and raw queries used during triage.
- Consumer offsets, ETL job logs, and rollup job traces.
- Backfill artifacts (snapshots, dry‑run outputs, validation diffs).
- Root cause hypothesis, corrective actions, and follow‑ups (owner and due date).

Runbook drills & validation schedule:
- Monthly lightweight smoke tests: run telemetry‑integrity‑check for a random critical SLO window.
- Quarterly full backfill drill: intentionally reingest a 5m window in staging and practice rollup backfill and SLO re‑calculation.

Risk & mitigation notes:
- Backfills are costly and potentially destructive — always run dry‑run first and keep backfill operations gated by a single engineer with approval from the Observability lead.
- If timestamps are unrecoverable, prefer marking SLO window as unverifiable and document the rationale rather than making aggressive estimates.

Appendices:
A. Example PromQL anomaly alert (Grafana Alert / Alertmanager rule):
  ALERT TelemetryRollupMismatch
  IF abs(rate(service_requests_total[5m]) - service_requests_rollup_rate{job="rollup"}) / max(rate(service_requests_total[5m]), 1e-6) > 0.05
  FOR 3m
  LABELS { severity = "high", category = "telemetry" }
  ANNOTATIONS { summary = "Rollup vs raw mismatch for {{ $labels.service }}" }

B. Quick commands reference:
- Snapshot metrics endpoint: curl -sS http://<host>:9100/metrics | sed -n '1,200p' > /tmp/metrics-snapshot.txt
- Dump Kafka partition range: kafka-console-consumer --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --topic telemetry-raw --partition 0 --offset <start> --max-messages 10000 > /tmp/part0.json

C. Contacts & ownership (oncall rotation):
- Observability SRE rotation (primary): #sre-observability
- Runtime SRE (secondary): #sre-runtime
- Observability lead: Ava Martinez (ava@redwood.com)
- Head of SRE: Nikhil Verma (nikhil@redwood.com)

Document history and change notes:
- 2024-10-15: Created by Jordan Lee.
- 2024-12-02: Added backfill dry‑run enforcement and PromQL example (review: Kai Nguyen).
- 2025-02-20: Clarified containment gating and fallback SLI practice cadence (review: Ava Martinez).

Related reading:
- SLO observability pipeline design and validation (internal)
- Incident forensics evidence handoff procedure

End of runbook.

title: Telemetry Normalization and Fidelity Acceptance Playbook for Enterprise Tenants
content:
Overview

Purpose: This playbook defines the telemetry normalization, fidelity acceptance criteria, and handoff process for enterprise tenants onboarding to Redwood Inference. It ensures telemetry received from tenant environments maps cleanly into our observability pipeline (ingress-gateway -> telemetry-gatekeeper -> telemetry-pipeline -> metrics-aggregator), meets fidelity thresholds for QBR reporting, and contains cost attribution fields required for tenant-level billing.

Audience: Customer Success, Integrations Engineers, Observability/Monitoring, SRE, and the tenant technical contact.

Goals

- Provide a repeatable acceptance checklist for tenant telemetry during onboarding.
- Enforce minimum fidelity and completeness requirements so QBR metrics, cost attribution, and SLIs are trustworthy.
- Reduce back-and-forth during cutover by codifying normalization rules and validation queries.

Scope

Includes: metric names, label/tag normalization, span/trace expectations, required tenant metadata (tenant_id, environment, region, cost_center), retention and sampling guidance for dedicated/private tenants.
Excludes: application-level debugging not relevant to service-level SLOs (those are covered in the Tenant Debugging Playbook).

Key Definitions

- Fidelity: Percent of expected telemetry signals that are present and correctly formatted for a representative test traffic set.
- Normalization: The transformation rules applied to incoming metric names and labels so they align with Redwood canonical schema.
- Acceptance Window: The 72-hour validation period during which metrics are assessed against acceptance criteria before enabling compute-level billing and SLA reporting.

Acceptance Criteria (must all be met to mark telemetry as Accepted)

1) Ingestion and Latency
 - Metrics delivered to telemetry-pipeline ingestion topic within 60 seconds 95% of the time during the Acceptance Window.
 - Traces sampled at the agreed rate (default 1% for hosted, 5% for Dedicated during onboarding) with an end-to-end delivery latency < 120s for 99th percentile.

2) Metric Coverage & Fidelity
 - For the tenant's representative traffic replay (or production ramp), at least 98% of the expected metric families are observed (see required metric families table below).
 - Label fidelity: required labels (tenant_id, route_id, model_id, region, environment) must be present on >= 99% of tokens/requests metrics.

3) Naming & Normalization
 - Metric and label names conform to Redwood canonical names after normalization rules are applied (see Normalization Rules section).

4) Cost Attribution
 - cost_center and billing_tag labels populated on per-request or per-batch metrics, or alternate agreed mechanism validated via test traffic.

5) Data Retention & Access
 - Telemetry retention matches contract (default 90 days for enterprise onboarding window).
 - Observability roles for tenant contacts configured (read-only vs edit) and verified.

Required Metric Families (representative table)

| Category | Canonical metric name | Description | Min cardinality |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| Ingress | redwood.ingress.requests | per-request ingress counter (labels: tenant_id, route_id) | high |
| Latency | redwood.request.latency_ms | request latency histogram (labels: tenant_id, model_id) | high |
| Tokens | redwood.tokens.generated | tokens generated per request | medium |
| Errors | redwood.request.errors | 4xx/5xx error counter (labels: tenant_id, code) | medium |
