| VM/GPU Util | redwood.host.gpu.utilization | GPU utilization gauge for Dedicated hosts | low |

Normalization Rules (applied by telemetry-gatekeeper)

1) Metric name mapping: tenant metrics with prefixes are mapped to canonical names. Example mapping JSON (example shown inline):

  {
    "mappings": [
      {"source_prefix": "myapp.requests", "target": "redwood.ingress.requests"},
      {"source_prefix": "latency_ms", "target": "redwood.request.latency_ms"}
    ]
  }

2) Label canonicalization: alias labels are normalized (e.g., ns -> tenant_id, env -> environment). All tenant-generated labels are lowercased and sanitized to alphanumeric + underscore. Truncate labels > 128 chars to 128 to avoid storage blowup.

3) Cost tags: if tenant cannot add cost_center at request time, an ingress-side enrichment will attach a tenant-level cost_center label using the onboarding registry. This must be validated with a sample of 10k requests.

Implementation Steps (Integration Engineer + Tenant)

1) Pre-Work (week -1)
 - Customer Success schedules a 60-minute onboarding sync and assigns an Integrations Engineer (owner).
 - Tenant shares a telemetry sample (ndjson of 24-hour sample or replay harness) or grants access to a staging Kafka topic.

2) Configuration (day 0)
 - Integrations Engineer creates a temporary mapping rule in telemetry-gatekeeper for the tenant.
 - Gateway config: ensure tenant API key is present and routed to the correct ingress-gateway cluster (region matching tenant).
 - Apply retention/policy tags in telemetry-pipeline.

3) Validation Run (days 1-3) — Acceptance Window starts when valid traffic is observed
 - Run replayed traffic or coordinate a controlled production ramp.
 - Run the Validation Tests below hourly and collect artifacts (logs, sample traces, PromQL results).

4) Acceptance Handoff (day 4)
 - If all criteria met: integrator marks telemetry as ACCEPTED and notifies Customer Success.
 - If not met: mark as ACTION_REQUIRED, create a Jira ticket with remediation owner and 72-hour re-test window.

Validation Tests (automated & manual queries)

- Ingestion Latency check (PromQL): 100 * (sum_over_time(redwood.ingest.latency_seconds_bucket[5m]) / sum_over_time(redwood.ingest.requests[5m])) < 60 
- Label completeness check (example SQL against metrics store):
  SELECT count(*) AS total, sum(case when tenant_id IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS missing_tenant FROM metrics_raw WHERE timestamp > now() - interval '1 hour' AND tenant = '<tenant-marker>';
- Metric coverage report: run the canonical metric families list against observed metric sets and compute percent_present.
- Sample trace integrity: for 1,000 sampled traces, ensure trace_id continuity and presence of "ingress" and "backend" spans in >= 99% of traces.

Rollout & Risk Controls

- Canary Phase: enable telemetry-based billing and SLA reporting for 5% of tenant traffic for 24 hours. Monitor cost attribution and SLO divergence.
- Auto-fallback: if label fidelity drops < 95% or ingestion latency > 120s for 10 consecutive minutes, toggle telemetry-gatekeeper to enrichment-only mode (no normalization writes) and open PagerDuty alert to Integrations On-call.

Ownership and Escalation

- Integration Owner (first-line): Integrations Engineering (owner example: eng-integrations-team). PagerDuty: integrations-oncall@redwood.
- CS Owner: Customer Success Manager listed on the onboarding ticket.
- SRE Owner: observability-oncall for platform-level ingestion issues.

Escalation matrix

1) Integration Owner (2 hours) — fix mapping or config issue.
2) SRE (4 hours) — investigate pipeline/collector outages.
3) Platform Engineering (8 hours) — if root cause is kernel-level ingestion or Kafka/storage issues.

Artifacts to Collect for Acceptance

- Ingestion logs (telemetry-gatekeeper) for the Acceptance Window.
- Sampled traces (ndjson) with a failing example if any spans are missing.
- Prometheus/metrics-store queries showing metric coverage and label completeness.
- Screenshots of dashboards showing token/cost attribution.

QBR Deliverables (post-acceptance)

- Standard QBR deck attachments: metric coverage baseline, fidelity over time, cost attribution mapping, and recommended action items.
- One-time configuration export of the normalization rules (JSON) stored as a config artifact in the tenant onboarding folder.

Appendix: Example Normalization Mappings and Queries

Example mapping chunk (to copy into telemetry-gatekeeper):

  "mappings": [
    {"source_regex": "^app\\.requests\\.(.*)$", "target": "redwood.ingress.requests", "label_transforms": {"ns": "tenant_id"}},
    {"source_regex": "^app\\.latency_ms$", "target": "redwood.request.latency_ms"}
  ]

PromQL example — per-tenant p95 latency:
  histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(redwood.request.latency_ms_bucket{tenant_id=\"<TENANT>\"}[5m])) by (le, tenant_id))

Common Failure Modes and Workarounds

- Missing tenant_id: If tenants cannot emit tenant_id, use ingress API key enrichment and validate via the sample-count method (10k requests).
- High cardinality labels: apply label whitelist at telemetry-gatekeeper and normalize dynamic labels into "label_hash" to avoid metric cardinality explosion.
- Traces missing ingress spans: validate SDK/instrumentation version across services and ensure front-door proxy injects X-TRACE-ID header.

Onboarding Checklist (quick start)

1) Schedule kickoff and identify Integrations Engineer.
2) Tenant provides sample telemetry.
3) Gatekeeper mapping created and tested on staging.
4) Controlled traffic run, run validation tests every hour.
5) Acceptance decision and documentation artifacts uploaded.

Contacts

- Integrations Eng Lead: Arjun Patel (arjun@redwood.example)
- Customer Success: Maya Chen (maya@redwood.example)
- Observability Owner: Lina Morales (lina@redwood.example)

Document History

- 2026-02-15: Created by Maya Chen
- 2026-03-01: Reviewed and published after reviewer feedback (Arjun Patel, Lina Morales, Samir Gupta)

title: SCIM & SSO Provisioning: Validation and Operational Playbook
content:
Summary:
This playbook defines the standardized validation, testing, and operational steps for customer SCIM provisioning and OIDC/SAML SSO integrations with Redwood Inference. It is intended for Customer Success Engineers (CSEs), Solutions Architects, and the customer's identity/IT teams. Follow this document for pre-production validation, go-live checks, troubleshooting, and post-go-live monitoring items.

Scope and applicability:
- Applies to Dedicated and Private deployment customers implementing automated user provisioning (SCIM 2.0) and single sign-on (OIDC or SAML).
- Covers initial onboarding validation, periodic health checks, and playbooked escalation routes.
- Does NOT replace corporate security reviews or customer-specific legal controls; use alongside the Regulated Go‑Live Security Gates playbook.

When to use this playbook:
1. During the final phase of enterprise onboarding where users/groups are provisioned from the customer's Identity Provider (IdP).
2. When SSO authentication or SCIM provisioning errors are observed during canary or rollout.
3. When rolling out auto-provisioning to a larger user population (canary -> gradual ramp).

Prerequisites (customer and Redwood):
| Item | Required | Owner | Notes |
|---|---:|---|---|
| SCIM base URL and bearer token | Yes | Customer + CSE | Token with sufficient scopes for user/group CRUD
| IdP metadata (SAML) or OIDC client configuration | Yes | Customer | Include certificate or JWKS URL
| Firewall rules / allowlist | Yes | Customer + Infra | IP ranges or VPC peering as documented in Private deployments guide
| Test account(s) with admin and non-admin roles | Yes | Customer | One canary user per target group
| Test group(s) mapping plan | Yes | Customer | Map IdP groups -> Redwood roles (viewer/editor/admin)

Roles and responsibilities:
- Customer Success (owner): coordination, validation checklist, go/no-go recommendation.
- Solutions Architect: review mapping strategy, permission boundaries, and any custom attributes.
- SRE/Infra (for Private deployments): ensure network connectivity, firewall/NAT, and certificate trust.
- Customer IT/IdP team: provide test environment, tokens, and perform IdP-side tests.

Validation checklist (pre-canary):
1. Verify network connectivity: from IdP to Redwood SCIM endpoint for hosted customers, or the customer's SCIM endpoint (private). Use curl from a bastion host.
   - Example: curl -v -H "Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>" "https://scim.redwood.example.com/v2/Users"
2. Confirm token scopes and expiry: run a test PUT/POST and ensure 2xx response for valid payload.
3. Schema mapping review: confirm required attributes (userName, name.givenName, name.familyName, emails[type=work]) are mapped.
4. Group sync dry-run: perform a scoped sync of 5 users and compare expected role assignments.
5. SSO smoke test: authenticate via OIDC/SAML with a test user, assert role mapping and session creation.
6. Audit logging enabled: ensure provisioning events are emitted to the customer-visible audit log (or syslog for Private).

Step-by-step canary validation (1–3 days recommended):
1. Enable auto-provisioning for a single test group with 5–10 users. Document the exact group ID and filter.
2. Run an initial full sync (customer triggers) and confirm: user create events, group assignment, and correct role attachments.
3. Perform authentication tests for each user: internal UI login, API token minting (if permitted), and session termination.
4. Introduce controlled churn: change an attribute (email or displayName) in IdP and confirm delta sync updates the user in Redwood.
5. Revoke provisioning token (simulate rotation) and verify that failures are surfaced to the CSE dashboard and to the configured alert channel.
6. Expand to 25% of the user population after successful 24–48h stability window, then to 100% after 72h of stable metrics.

Operational SLOs and KPIs to track during rollouts:
- Provisioning success rate >= 99.5% (per-hour window).
- Average SCIM API latency < 350ms for 95th percentile for individual user operations.
- SSO authentication success >= 99.0% across test samples.
- Time-to-detect provisioning failures (alert to on-call) < 5 minutes.

Sample SCIM payloads and curl examples:
- Create user (minimal payload):
  curl -X POST
    -H "Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>"
    -H "Content-Type: application/json"
    https://scim.redwood.example.com/v2/Users
    -d '{"userName":"j.smith@example.com","name":{"givenName":"John","familyName":"Smith"},"emails":[{"value":"j.smith@example.com","type":"work","primary":true}],"active":true}'

- Sample OIDC client test (using oauth2-tool):
  oauth2-tool authorize --client-id <CLIENT_ID> --redirect-uri "https://app.redwood.example.com/_callback" --scope "openid email profile"

Common failure modes and troubleshooting steps:
- 401 Unauthorized from SCIM endpoints:
  1) Confirm token validity and scopes (check expiration).
  2) Confirm system time skew on IdP or Redwood gateway.
  3) Check for IP allowlist blocks.
- 400/422 on user import:
  1) Verify JSON structure against SCIM schema (common missing attributes: emails, userName).
  2) Inspect validation error in response body for attribute names.
- Duplicate user errors:
  1) Verify externalId mapping and ensure IdP and Redwood use same canonical identifier.
- Group mapping mismatches:
  1) Check case-sensitivity of group names and whitespace.
  2) Confirm that nested groups are supported/flattened according to customer's plan.

Debugging tools and logs to collect before escalation:
- SCIM request/response pairs (with sensitive fields redacted).
- IdP audit logs for the matching timestamp and user IDs.
- Application logs showing role assignment and session creation events.
- Network traces (tcpdump) for Private deployments if connectivity issues suspected.

Escalation matrix (when to escalate to Redwood SRE or Product):
- Escalate to SRE within 30 minutes if provisioning success rate < 95% after attempted remediation.
- Escalate to Product if schema or role mapping behavior appears inconsistent with product design (include sample payloads and expected vs actual).
- Contacts:
  - CSE on-call: customer-success-oncall@redwood.example.com
  - SRE Pager: +1-555-010-999 (use only for P1 affecting >50% users)
  - Product triage: product-integrations@redwood.example.com

Post-go-live monitoring and QBR metrics to report:
- Weekly: provisioning success rate, average latency, number of mapping exceptions, manual fix count.
- Monthly QBR slides should include a 90-day trend for: activated users, deprovisioned users, time-to-provision median, and incidents triggered by provisioning.

Rollout and rollback plan (canary -> full):
1. Canary: 5–10 users for 48–72 hours.
2. Ramp: 25% for 48 hours; 75% for 24 hours.
3. Full: remaining 100% after 72 hours stability.
4. Rollback: disable auto-provisioning and run a manual reconciliation to revoke recently-provisioned accounts; notify affected teams and attach incident ticket.

Security considerations and compliance notes:
- Never include cleartext tokens in shared logs; use redaction.
- Ensure audit trails are retained per the customer's retention policy (default 90 days) and documented in the compliance folder.
- For Private deployments, confirm HSM/KMS integrations for token storage.

Appendix A: Common SCIM response samples (redacted)
- Success: 201 Created with user resource including id, externalId, meta.version.
- Error: 409 Conflict with detail referencing externalId collision.

Appendix B: Quick checklist for customer-run tests (copyable)
- [ ] Obtain SCIM token and test curl against /v2/Users
- [ ] Create test user and verify created in UI within 30s
- [ ] Update attribute in IdP and confirm delta sync within 5 minutes
- [ ] Authenticate via SSO and verify role assignment
- [ ] Rotate token and confirm alerting and recovery

Change log:
- 2026-02-10: Document created by Aisha Patel.
- 2026-03-01: Added escalation matrix and OIDC test examples; updated SLO thresholds.

title: adaptive-telemetry-fallback-cost-control-integration-2026
content:
Overview

This integration guide describes how to connect a customer application or platform observability stack to Redwood Inference's adaptive telemetry fallback and cost-control system. The goal is to provide a resilient signal path for dynamic throttling, model switchover, and cost-protective actions while preserving customer SLAs. This page covers architecture, required telemetry, configuration examples, webhook payload formats, operational playbooks, and a suggested rollout plan.

When to use this guide

- Customers that need automated protection from sudden cost spikes (token/embedding usage) while maintaining availability.
- Multi-tenant products that require graceful degradation: model downshifts, reduced batch sizes, or regional routing when capacity or budget constraints appear.
- Integrations that must reconcile vendor billing/cost metrics with request-level telemetry for rapid mitigation.

Key goals

- Fast detection: <5s from anomalous pattern to initial mitigation signal.
- Minimal churn: avoid flapping between mitigation states with hysteresis and cooldown windows.
- Clear audit trail: each mitigation action is auditable with reason, metric snapshot, and operator context.

Architecture and signal flow

1) Telemetry sources (customer app, API gateway, edge-proxy, billing exports) -> centralized telemetry collector (Prometheus, Datadog, or internal agent).
2) Redwood telemetry gatekeeper: evaluates rules (SLOs, cost thresholds, rate anomalies) and emits actions via webhooks or direct control-plane API.
3) Redwood policy engine: decides mitigation type (soft-rate-limit, model-switch, route-to-fallback-region, or full throttle).
4) Enforcement: adaptive rate-limiter sidecar, API gateway rules, or tenant-shared proxy applies controls.
5) Observability: mitigation events are logged and surfaced to QBR and health dashboards.

Integration prerequisites

- A telemetry endpoint: Prometheus scrape, StatsD/Telegraf, or HTTP push gateway. Redwood supports Datadog, Prometheus, and OpenTelemetry traces/metrics.
- Ability to receive and act on webhooks from Redwood (HTTPS endpoint with TLS).
- RBAC service principal or API key (least privilege) for Redwood to call management endpoints, if using direct control-plane enforcement.
- A staging tenant or sandboxed environment to test behavioral rules before production rollout.

High-level integration steps

1) Define telemetry mapping: map your request-level metrics to Redwood's expected signals. Required metrics: requests_per_minute, avg_tokens_per_request, 95p_latency_ms, error_rate_5m, billing_rate_per_minute. Optional: model_confidence_low_rate, prefix_cache_hit_rate.
2) Configure Redwood gatekeeper: upload a rule set (JSON/YAML) to the Redwood Console or via API. See configuration examples below.
3) Provide a secure webhook endpoint for mitigation actions or configure Redwood to use your control-plane API.
4) Validate in staging: trigger synthetic scenarios to exercise each mitigation type and verify rollback/hysteresis.
5) Schedule a canary rollout: enable for a subset of tenants with monitoring dashboards and alerts.

Configuration reference (example)

Table: recommended rule fields and suggested defaults

| Field | Description | Suggested default | Notes |
|---|---|---:|---|
| rule_id | Unique identifier for the rule | telemetry-cost-protect-v1 | Required |
| trigger_window | Sliding window used to evaluate metric | 60s | Short windows for quick action; watch noise |
| metric | Telemetry metric to evaluate | billing_rate_per_minute | Required |
| threshold | Value that triggers the rule | 500 | Units: customer billing units/min |
| comparator | Comparison operator | gt | gt |
| severity | mitigation severity level | soft | soft, moderate, hard |
| action | Enforcement action | soft_rate_limit | soft_rate_limit, model_switch, regional_reroute, hard_throttle |
| cooldown | Minimum wait before re-evaluating after action | 300s | Prevents flapping |
| owners | On-call routing for alerts | cs-oncall@redwood.com | Comma-separated emails |

Example YAML rule (shortened)

---
rule_id: telemetry-cost-protect-v1
metric: billing_rate_per_minute
trigger_window: 60s
threshold: 500
comparator: gt
severity: moderate
action: model_switch
parameters:
  target_model: rwd-cost-slim-quantized-v2
cooldown: 300s
owners: cs-oncall@redwood.com
---

Webhook payload (POST) example

Content-Type: application/json

{
  "event_id": "evt_20260308_0001",
  "timestamp": "2026-03-08T15:12:34Z",
  "tenant_id": "cust-12345",
  "rule_id": "telemetry-cost-protect-v1",
  "decision": "apply",
  "action": "model_switch",
  "details": {
    "from_model": "rwd-llama-70b",
    "to_model": "rwd-cost-slim-quantized-v2",
    "metric_snapshot": {
      "billing_rate_per_minute": "612",
      "requests_per_minute": "1800",
      "95p_latency_ms": "210"
    },
    "reason": "billing_rate exceeded threshold",
    "cooldown_until": "2026-03-08T15:17:34Z"
  }
}
\nNote: the webhook consumer should validate the event_id and signature header (X-Redwood-Signature) using the shared webhook secret.

Direct control-plane API example (curl)

curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/tenants/cust-12345/actions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <REDACTED>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"action":"soft_rate_limit","limit_qps":15,"reason":"adaptive-telemetry-protection"}'

Operational playbook: mitigation and escalation

1) Detect: Gatekeeper triggers a mitigation action. Alert created in paging system.
2) Assess: CS on-call reviews the metric snapshot and recent deploys. If false positive, mark action as overridden and provide rationale.
3) Apply remediation: If mitigation is active > 10 minutes and customer impact is >10% error-rate increase, escalate to Engineering SRE.
4) Rollback: When metric returns below threshold for 2 consecutive evaluation windows (default 2 * trigger_window), the policy engine will auto-roll back. If not, manual rollback steps are in the next section.

Manual rollback steps (if auto-rollback fails)

1) Authenticate to Redwood Console (least-privilege account).
2) Navigate to Tenant -> Active Mitigations -> select event_id.
3) Click "Revert Action" and enter a justification.
4) Monitor the rollback for at least 20 minutes and notify customer contacts.

SLA mapping and SLO guidance

- Soft mitigations (rate reduce, small model switch): targeted to preserve 99% of successful responses for critical paths.
- Moderate mitigations (model downshift, reduced batch sizes): targeted SLO impact < 5% error increase for 30-minute windows.
- Hard mitigations (hard throttle): used only when cost/runaway usage threatens contractual limits; expected to impact availability and requires immediate escalation.

Suggested alert thresholds

- Billing anomaly alert: billing_rate_per_minute > threshold * 1.1 for 2 consecutive windows -> P2 alert to CS.
- Latency regression alert: 95p_latency_ms increases > 1.5x baseline and coincides with billing spike -> P1 to SRE.
- Flapping alert: more than 3 mitigations for same tenant in 1 hour -> P1 to Product & CS.

Testing and verification checklist

- [ ] Staging webhook receiver registered and validating signature header.
- [ ] Synthetic load test that increases billing_rate_per_minute above threshold.
- [ ] Validate actions appear in tenant audit log with event_id and payload.
- [ ] Confirm auto-rollback after cooldown period.
- [ ] Run rollback drill: CS performs manual revert with engineer supervision.

Monitoring dashboards and QBR artifacts

Include these panels in your tenant QBR dashboard (recommended):
- billing_rate_per_minute (real-time + 24h trend)
- model_variant_distribution (percent of requests by model)
- mitigations_timeline (events with reasons)
- request_success_rate_5m (before/after mitigation)
- cost_per_1M_tokens (normalized by model variant)

Rollout plan and canary checklist

1) Week 0: Deploy webhook endpoint and register in Redwood sandbox.
2) Week 1: Enable read-only mode (logging only) for 10% of traffic.
3) Week 2: Enable soft mitigations for 5 low-risk tenants.
4) Week 4: Broaden to 25% of traffic if metrics stable.
5) Post-rollout: include mitigation incidence and financial impact in next QBR.

Ownership and contacts

- Primary CS owner: Maya Reyes (maya.reyes@redwood.ai)
- CS on-call alias: cs-oncall@redwood.com
- Integrations engineer: Jun Park (jun.park@redwood.ai)
- SRE escalation alias: sre-escalate@redwood.ai

Related pages

- telemetry-gatekeeper-onboarding-and-qbr-integration-guide-2026 (integration-guides)
- tenant-stability-predictive-signals-runbook-2026 (support-process)

Revision history

- 2026-02-15: Draft created by Maya Reyes.
- 2026-03-08: Reviewed by Omar Singh and Jun Park; updated webhook schema and rollout plan.

Appendix: webhook signature validation (example pseudocode)

1) Compute HMAC-SHA256 of request body with shared secret.
2) Compare against X-Redwood-Signature header using constant-time compare.

Pseudo: verify_signature(body, header_signature, secret) -> boolean

If verification fails, return HTTP 401 and log attempt with headers for forensics.

title: Telemetry-driven SLA Calibration and Handoff for Enterprise Onboarding
content:
Summary

This playbook documents a telemetry-first approach to calibrating Service Level Agreements (SLAs) during enterprise customer onboarding, and the formal handoff from Customer Success (CS) to Production Operations / SRE. It is intended for CS leads, integration engineers, and production operations owners responsible for ensuring predictable inference economics and availability for new enterprise tenants.

Scope

- Applies to Hosted API and Dedicated (reserved-capacity) onboarding flows.
- Focuses on availability, tail latency, error rate, and cost signal alignment during the first 90 days post-provisioning.
- Does not replace contractual SLA language — this is an operational calibration & handoff procedure that maps telemetry to escalation and runbook actions.

Goals

1. Produce tenant-specific SLA targets informed by observed workload in the onboarding runway.
2. Define a deterministic, auditable handoff checklist from CS to SRE/Platform.
3. Ensure alerting and dashboards are in place with ownership and documented mitigation steps.

When to use this playbook

- Customer goes through enterprise onboarding and reaches the cutover/workload validation stage (typically week 2–6).
- Customer requests contract-level SLA profiling or has bespoke latency/cost targets.
- Early-production anomalies (cost spikes, tail latency regressions) require structured root-cause and adjustment of targets.

Roles and responsibilities

- Customer Success (CS) Lead: coordinates telemetry collection, customer communication, and initial run validation.
- Integration Engineer: implements telemetry tags, sample logs, and assists with synthetic tests.
- SRE / Production Ops Owner: configures final alerts, owns post-handoff incident response.
- Solutions Architect: recommends batching/quantization/routing changes when needed.

Key telemetry signals and mappings

- request_p95_latency_ms: primary latency indicator mapped to "SLO latency".
- request_p99_latency_ms: tail latency; escalation threshold mapping to incident response.
- request_error_rate_5m: 5-minute rolling error rate; triggers severity-2 at >=1%.
- tokens_per_second_per_tenant: throughput / cost proxy; used for cost-forecasting alerts.
- cache_hit_ratio_prefix: KV cache effectiveness; low values (>20% drop) trigger cache-investigation playbook.
- infra_utilization_gpu_pct: system-level signal — sustained >85% indicates capacity saturation.

Example mapping table (text table)

Metric | Observed threshold (onboarding) | Operational mapping
------ | ------------------------------ | ---------------------
request_p95_latency_ms | <= 250 ms (interactive apps) | Meet latency target: OK to hand off
request_p99_latency_ms | <= 800 ms | If >800ms for 3 consecutive days -> SRE review
request_error_rate_5m | < 0.1% | 0.1%–1% -> CS triage; >1% -> Page SRE
tokens_per_second_per_tenant | baseline from week-1 synthetic | Forecast cost and reserve capacity
cache_hit_ratio_prefix | > 70% | If drops by >20 percentage points -> investigate cache warming
infra_utilization_gpu_pct | < 65% | >85% sustained -> consider dedicated capacity / autoscale

Telemetry collection and tagging checklist (integration engineer)

1. Ensure all tenant-bound inference requests include tenant_id, route_id, model_variant, and flow_tags in telemetry headers and logs. Example JSON envelope: 

```
{
  "tenant_id": "acme-fin-001",
  "route_id": "chat-infer-v1",
  "model": "redwood-open-7b-q4",
  "flow_tags": ["interactive","high-priority"]
}
```

2. Emit per-request timing spans: client_enqueue, server_queue, decode_start, decode_end.
3. Emit token counts (prompt_tokens, completion_tokens) per request for cost attribution.
4. Instrument synthetic canary tests (see Synthetic test matrix below).

Synthetic test matrix (recommended)

- Warmup sequence: run 50 short inference requests (seq_len 32) to populate KV cache.
- Mixed load test: 10-minute run with 70% short (seq_len 32) + 30% long (seq_len 1024) at target TPS.
- Tail test: specific long-context requests (seq_len 4096) to confirm tail latency SLOs.

SLA calibration procedure (step-by-step)

1. Week-1 baseline (CS + integration engineer)
   - Run warmup and mixed synthetic tests at projected production TPS.
   - Collect 7 days of production-adjacent telemetry while customer runs in shadow/validation mode.
   - Compute baseline metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, 5m error rate, tokens/day, cache_hit_ratio.

2. Draft SLA targets (CS + solutions architect)
   - Use baseline metrics to propose tenant SLA bands: allow SLOs to be anchored to observed p95/p99 plus safety margin. Example: SLA_p95 = observed_p95 * 1.25 but capped to contract upper bound.
   - Document expected tail behavior for long-context requests and map to separate long-tail SLO (e.g., p99_long_seq).

3. Customer review and sign-off (CS + customer stakeholders)
   - Present telemetry summary, forecasted unit cost, and proposed SLOs in a short QBR-style deck.
   - Obtain explicit sign-off on targets or agreed-upon phase plan (e.g., Stage 1: soft SLOs for 30 days, Stage 2: hardened SLOs).

4. Handoff prep (CS + SRE) — minimum 48 hours before formal handoff
   - Ensure alert rules are implemented and tested in staging (see Monitoring queries).
   - Create tenant-specific dashboards and add to the SRE dashboard group.
   - Confirm on-call rotation and escalation contacts: primary SRE, secondary, CS on-call.

5. Formal handoff (SRE accepts ownership)
   - SRE runs synthetic verification and confirms alerts.
   - SRE documents runbook updates and acknowledges ownership in the handoff checklist.
   - CS schedules a 30-day checkpoint post-handoff for QBR alignment.

Acceptance criteria for handoff

- Required: 14 days of telemetry matching baseline behavior (no regressions >15% in p95 or error rate).
- Required: Tenant dashboard and 3 alerts configured (latency, error_rate, infra_utilization).
- Required: SRE runbook added to central runbook repo and owner acknowledged.
- Optional: Cost guardrails and quota caps configured if customer requires budget protection.

Monitoring queries (examples)

Prometheus-style example (replace label names as needed):

- p95 latency (ms):
```
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_ms_bucket{tenant_id="acme-fin-001"}[5m])) by (le))
```
- error rate (5m percent):
```
(sum(rate(request_errors_total{tenant_id="acme-fin-001"}[5m]))) / (sum(rate(requests_total{tenant_id="acme-fin-001"}[5m]))) * 100
```
- GPU utilization (avg 1m):
```
avg by (instance) (rate(gpu_utilization_percent_total[1m]))
```
- cache hit ratio (5m):
```
(sum(rate(kv_cache_hits_total{tenant_id="acme-fin-001"}[5m]))) / (sum(rate(kv_cache_hits_total{tenant_id="acme-fin-001"}[5m])) + sum(rate(kv_cache_misses_total{tenant_id="acme-fin-001"}[5m]))) * 100
```

Alerting thresholds (starter recommendations)

- Severity-1 (page): request_error_rate_5m > 3% for 5 minutes OR request_p99_latency_ms > 2000ms for 2 minutes.
- Severity-2 (notify + Slack): request_error_rate_5m between 1% and 3% for 10 minutes OR request_p95_latency_ms exceeds SLA_target by 30% for 10 minutes.
- Cost anomaly: tokens_per_hour increases by >150% relative to 7-day rolling average -> create investigation ticket.

Runbook excerpts (actions)

- On page (S1):
  1) Acknowledge page and add immediate note in incident tracker.
 2) Check tenant-specific dashboard for recent deploys, model variant, and queue depth.
 3) If infra_utilization_gpu_pct > 90% -> execute short-term scaling (burst or add capacity) and inform CS.
 4) If error spikes correlate with a specific model_variant -> fall back to last known-good variant using routing policy.

- On notify (S2):
  1) Post summary in tenant Slack channel and CC CS lead.
 2) Increase sampling of traces for affected route.
 3) Schedule triage within standard SRE response window (4 business hours).

Customer communications templates

- Pre-handoff sign-off confirmation (email):

Subject: [Action Required] SLA Calibration Summary & Handoff for {{tenant_name}}

Hi {{customer_contact}},

We completed 14 days of telemetry collection and synthetic validation for your environment. Attached is a short report with observed p95/p99 latency, error rates, and a cost forecast. Proposed operational SLAs: p95 <= {{SLA_p95}} ms; p99 <= {{SLA_p99}} ms; error rate < {{SLA_error}}%.

Please reply with approval or suggested changes. Once approved, we will schedule a formal handoff to our production ops team and enable tenant alerts.

Best,
{{cs_lead}}

Maintenance and post-handoff governance

- 30-day checkpoint: CS + SRE review telemetry and customer satisfaction.
- Quarterly reviews: incorporate QBR metrics and proposal for model/quantization changes that improve economics.
- Regression policy: any regression in p95 or error rate >20% post-handoff triggers an immediate joint triage and potential short-term rollback.

Operational notes and caveats

- Tail-sensitive workloads: for workloads that include sporadic long-context requests, maintain separate long-tail SLOs and make that explicit in the contract appendix.
- Warm caches: onboarded tenants that rely on prefix caching should expect a warm-up period; factor into SLA negotiation.

Appendix: Example dashboard widgets to include

- Tenant Overview: p50/p95/p99 latency trends (24h/7d), request rate, error rate.
- Cost attribution: tokens_per_hour, tokens_by_model, estimated $/hour.
- Capacity: GPU utilization, avg queue depth, instance count.
- Diagnostic traces: sample trace links for recent errors or high-latency requests.

Appendix: Quick CLI snippets for integration engineers

- Query recent tenant logs (example):
```
rdw logs query --tenant acme-fin-001 --from "-6h" --filter "route:chat-infer-v1" --limit 500
```
- Trigger synthetic test:
```
rdw synth run --tenant acme-fin-001 --test mixed-load --duration 10m --concurrency 10
```

Document maintenance and ownership

- Owner: Priya Shah (Customer Success) — maintain telemetry templates and sign-off checklist.
- Secondary owner: Miguel Torres (SRE) — owns alert rules and dashboard templates.
- Review cadence: biannual or when onboarding process changes materially.

Notes and references

- See related runbooks: tenant-stability-predictive-signals-runbook-2026.json for predictive signal definitions.
- See eng-platform dashboards for dashboard JSON templates.

End of document

title: Adaptive Telemetry Schema: Evolution & Backward Compatibility Guide
content:
Summary

This guide describes Redwood Inference's recommended approach for evolving customer telemetry contracts while preserving backward compatibility for enterprise onboarding and ongoing integrations. The target audience is Customer Success Engineers (CSE), Observability Engineers, and partner engineering teams responsible for telemetry ingestion and schema changes.

Goals
- Minimize customer downtime and avoid ingestion failures during schema updates.
- Provide a predictable, testable migration path for producers and consumers of telemetry.
- Maintain high-quality SLOs for telemetry ingestion and downstream dashboards.
- Provide clear ownership, automation playbooks, and rollback procedures.

When to use this document
- Customer is integrating Redwood agent, sidecar, or direct API and requests a schema extension.
- Product/engineering plans to add or deprecate telemetry fields for model-level metrics, cost-attribution labels, or tenant metadata.
- Observability team detects a breakage after a schema rollout.

Key terminology
- Telemetry contract: The JSON schema describing what telemetry events we accept on the ingestion API (ingest.v1.events).
- Producer: the service or customer component emitting telemetry.
- Consumer: Redwood services (observability pipelines, billing, alerting) that depend on specific fields.
- Soft-compat: New optional fields tolerated by consumers; old fields continue to be honored.
- Hard-compat: Required fields that, if missing, will cause ingestion rejection.

Compatibility strategy (overview)
1) Use semantic versioning for schema artifacts (e.g., ingest.v1 -> ingest.v2).
2) Strict compatibility rules:
   - Adding optional fields: allowed in minor version bumps (v1.1 -> v1.2).
   - Adding required fields or changing types: requires major version bump (v1 -> v2) and coordinated migration.
   - Deprecation: mark fields deprecated for one major-version cycle before removal.
3) Dual-write and dual-read support: ingestion pipeline should accept older and newer schemas for the duration of migration window.
4) Automated schema validation + canary ingestion for early detection.

Versioning policy (table)
| Change type | Version bump required | Rollout window | Notes |
| Add optional field | minor (vX.Y) | 1 week | Backwards compatible; consumers should ignore unknown fields |
| Add required field / type change | major (vX+1.0) | 8–12 weeks | Requires coordinated migration and explicit consumer opt-in |
| Deprecate field | minor + deprecation flag | 4–8 weeks | Emit deprecation telemetry to producers |

Example telemetry fragments and best-practices
- Canonical event envelope (ingest.v1):
  {
    "event_id": "string-uuid",
    "tenant_id": "TENANT-123",
    "timestamp": "2027-09-01T15:04:05Z",
    "type": "inference.request",
    "payload": { /* model-specific body */ },
    "meta": {"sdk_version": "1.4.2", "region": "us-west-2"}
  }

- Adding an optional field example (allowed in minor):
  {"meta": {"device_type": "edge-gpu"}}  // consumers ignore if absent

- Changing a field type (requires major):
  // Changing "timestamp" from string to integer epoch -> must follow major-version migration plan

Schema validation rules (operational)
- Ingest API returns 202 for accepted events, 400 for schema validation errors.
- Validation is enforced by the ingest-gateway service (team: eng-infra).
- Use feature-flagged validators during canary: validators.accept_old_schema = true

Onboarding checklist (CSE-run before enabling new schema)
1) Confirm change classification (optional vs required) with Observability owner.
2) Update schema registry entry and publish semantic version.
3) Create a synthetic event set (N >= 200) exercising new and old codepaths.
4) Run local contract tests using the schema-diff tool (see Appendix).
5) Configure canary ingestion: route 1% of production traffic from a staging tenant for 72 hours.
6) Monitor key signals (see Signals & thresholds).
7) Gradually increase traffic to 25% then 100% as green checks pass.
8) Post-rollout: notify stakeholders and schedule deprecation reminders.

Signals & thresholds (must be instrumented before rollout)
- Schema rejection rate (per-minute): alert if > 0.1% sustained for 10m.
- Ingestion latency p99: alert if > 3s over baseline.
- Missing critical field ratio: alert if > 0.05% (indicates producers not updated).
- Consumer downstream errors (billing/alerting): any error spike > 50% over baseline triggers immediate rollback.

Rollout and rollback playbook (step-by-step)
1) Pre-rollout (Owner: CSE + Observability):
   - Create rollout ticket and assign SLO owner.
   - Publish schema to registry and attach migration notes.
   - Create feature flag: ingest.validators.<schema_version>.enabled = false

2) Canary (Owner: Observability):
   - Enable feature flag for canary tenants.
   - Run the synthetic test harness: `./tools/schema-diff --baseline v1.0 --candidate v1.1 --run-synthetic ./tests/canary.json`
   - Observe dashboards for 72 hours.

3) Ramp (Owner: CSE):
   - If canary stable, increase to 25% for 48 hours, then 100% for 24 hours.
   - Update the release ticket with telemetry summaries at each step.

4) Immediate rollback criteria (triggered by SRE or Observability lead):
   - Schema rejection rate > 0.5% sustained for 5m
   - Ingestion p99 > 6s and downstream consumer errors spike > 2x
   - Any legal/PII incident discovered related to new fields

5) Rollback steps:
   - Flip feature flag: ingest.validators.<schema_version>.enabled = false
   - Revert gateway deployment to previous image tag (ingest-gateway:vX.Y-prev)
   - Re-route traffic to stable aggregator via traffic-manager CLI: `traffic-manager promote stable --target ingest-cluster`
   - Open incident ticket and perform RCA within 72 hours.

Detection, alerting, and remediation playbook
- Automated checks (Observability team):
  - Daily job: `./tools/telemetry-health-check --window 24h --report /tmp/telemetry-health.json` (alerts on anomalies)
  - Nightly diff reports comparing schema acceptance across tenants.
- Remediation common recipes:
  - If producers are missing required fields: contact CSM/CSE and provide code snippets and SDK upgrade instructions.
  - If ingestion gateway mis-parses new nested payloads: capture raw payload, file bug in runtime team (eng-serving-runtime) and escalate to SRE.

Known migration failure modes and mitigations
- Producer SDK lag: provide drop-in patch for v1.x to add optional wrapper fields.
- Legacy tenant proxies truncating large payloads: advise chunking or enable proxy passthrough.
- Ambiguous enum expansions: prefer additive enums with explicit unknown handling on consumers.

Ownership & escalation matrix
- Schema owner: Observability team (primary contact: Priya Raman).
- CSE on-call: Customer Success rotation (see /confluence/people-ops/oncall-rotations).
- Emergency escalation: pager to SRE -> Observability -> Eng Product (page the oncall rotation).
- Legal/security escalation: contact Security & Compliance (email security@redwood.ai) and mark confidentiality: restricted if PII is implicated.

Appendix A — Schema diff & test commands
- Basic schema diff: `tools/schema-diff --baseline ingest.v1 --candidate ingest.v1.2`
- Run contract tests locally: `./gradlew -Pschema=ingest.v1.2 :contracts:test`
- Generate synthetic payloads: `python tools/gen_synthetic.py --tenant TENANT-123 --schema ingest.v1.2 --count 500`

Appendix B — Example notice to customers (CSM template)
Subject: Planned telemetry schema update — action required by your engineering team

Hello <Customer Team>,

We will be deploying a non-breaking telemetry extension (ingest.v1.2) on 2028-02-15. No action is required immediately if you are on Redwood SDK >= 1.5.0. If you are using a custom integrator, please run the attached synthetic suite and confirm acceptance by 2028-02-01.

Steps to validate: 1) Run `python tools/gen_synthetic.py --tenant <your-tenant> --schema ingest.v1.2 --count 200` 2) Send results to your CSE.

Thank you,
Maya Patel (Customer Success Engineer)

Appendix C — References & related pages
- Customer telemetry schema harmonization playbook: /confluence/customer-success-and-support/integration-guides/customer-telemetry-schema-harmonization-and-onboarding-playbook-2026
- Telemetry ingestion SLA standard: /confluence/eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/telemetry-ingestion-sla-standards

Document history
- 2026-11-15: Created by Maya Patel
- 2027-03-02: Added canary thresholds and synthetic harness guidance (review: Diego Alvarez)
- 2028-01-10: Formalized rollback criteria and legal escalation steps (review: Priya Raman)

title: Enterprise Observability Contract Harmonization Playbook
content:
Overview
This playbook defines a repeatable process for harmonizing observability contracts across enterprise customer telemetry sources during onboarding. Harmonization reduces integration friction, ensures consistent SLO/SLA mapping, and shortens time-to-QBR readiness. Use this guide when integrating any new Dedicated or Private customer with custom telemetry, third-party agents, or legacy instrumentation.

Goals
- Provide a minimal required signal set for Redwood feature areas (ingress, request lifecycle, model inference, billing tokens, and error taxonomy).
- Define canonical metric/event names and recommended labels/tags.
- Specify retention, sampling, and privacy controls for regulated customers.
- Prescribe validation checks, ownership, and escalation points.

Scope
Applies to: Dedicated and Private customers onboarding into Redwood's monitoring and customer-facing SLO/Uptime reports. Not intended for ad-hoc product experiments.

Owners and stakeholders
- Customer Success (CS) — primary onboarding coordinator, responsible for acceptance criteria.
- Observability (Platform) — implements collectors, forwarders, and ensures schema conformity.
- SRE/Infra — verifies SLO mappings and alert routing.
- Customer Engineering — integrates customer telemetry; point-of-contact for schema questions.

Required signals (canonical contract)
The table below lists the minimum signals required to support production monitoring and QBR metrics. Provide all signals as either metrics (time-series) or structured events with the specified fields. If a customer cannot emit a field, mark the exception in the onboarding ticket.

| Signal | Type | Required fields / labels | Purpose | Acceptable fallback |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ingress.requests_total | metric (counter) | tenant_id, route, region, ingestion_type | Throughput and quota accounting | aggregated by tenant only (if per-route not available)
| request.latency_p50/95/99 | metric (histogram) | tenant_id, route, model_variant, sequence_length_bucket | Latency SLOs and perf trending | p95 only for initial acceptance
| inference.tokens_generated | metric (counter) | tenant_id, model_variant, prompt_hash | Inference economics, cost attribution | per-tenant token counts
| response.error | event | tenant_id, request_id, error_code, error_category | Error triage and classification | aggregated error rate by tenant
| kvcache.hits / kvcache.misses | metric | tenant_id, model_variant, prefix_cache_key | Cache efficiency and cost reduction | sample logs with cache-hit boolean
| billing.request_cost_usd | metric | tenant_id, billing_cycle, cost_type | Chargeback & QBR cost breakdown | estimated cost model from Redwood side
| telemetry.pii_exposure_alert | event | tenant_id, request_id, detection_ruleset_id | Data privacy monitoring | periodic sampling with redaction

Privacy and regulated accounts
For customers with data residency/regulation constraints (HIPAA, GDPR, FINRA):
- Never forward raw request/response text. Use hashed prompt IDs (prompt_hash) and token counts.
- Provide a privacy filter sidecar pattern: upstream collector masks or removes fields labeled pii_sensitive before forwarding.
- Retention: default 30 days for raw structured events, 365 days for aggregated metrics. For regulated customers, support options: 7/30/90-day retention tables.
- Document the KMS/HSM key ids used for redaction and provide evidence of encryption-at-rest and in-transit.

Sampling and cardinality guidance
- Low-cardinality tags: tenant_id, region, model_variant, route. Avoid user_id or free-text prompt content.
- For high-cardinality fields (prompt_hash) use bucketing: keep only first 8 characters of hash and limit distinct values per tenant to 10k/day.
- Sampling strategy: 100% for p95/p99 latency and error counters; 1–5% for raw example traces (for debugging) unless customer permits more.

Onboarding acceptance criteria (checklist)
1. Schema alignment: Customer telemetry emits all required signals with matching field names or mapped via an agreed adapter.
2. Ingestion validation: Observability platform ingests at least 7 days of representative traffic or synthetic replay.
3. SLO mapping: Latency and availability SLOs mapped to tenant dashboards.
4. Privacy gates: PII redaction and retention windows verified.
5. Cost mapping: Token & inference cost metrics available and reconciled with billing estimate.
6. Alerting: Alert rules for latent p95, elevated error_rate (>0.5% sustained 10m), and telemetry pipeline dropouts.
7. QBR readiness: Data populated for the last 30 days for the QBR template (see QBR readiness checklist).

Detailed onboarding procedure
Step 0 — Pre-engagement\- CS collects: customer account team, legal constraints, expected qps, list of models and regions in scope.\- Create an onboarding ticket in JIRA with "observability-contract" template and assign Observability engineer.

Step 1 — Schema discovery (2–3 days)\1. Run a short discovery call with Customer Engineering to list existing telemetry endpoints and formats (Prometheus, OTLP, Datadog, custom logs).\2. Ask for sample payloads (anonymized) and a list of current tag sets.\3. Produce a mapping document within 48 hours with fields either matched or flagged for adapter implementation.

Step 2 — Adapter & transport (1–2 weeks)
- If the customer uses a homegrown format, Observability team builds an adapter (Fluent Bit/Collector pipeline) to translate to canonical names. Document the adapter config as YAML in the ticket.
- Configure TLS and API key exchange. For Private deployments, confirm VPC peering or TLS proxy endpoints.

Step 3 — Validation (3–7 days)
- Run synthetic traffic that covers: high throughput, long sequences (>1024 tokens), and failure modes (timebox exceed, model OOM).
- Verify metrics: counters increase, histograms report expected buckets, events contain required fields.
- Execute the validation queries below and record results in the ticket.

Validation queries (examples)\- p95 latency by tenant: SELECT percentile(latency_ms, 95) FROM request_latencies WHERE tenant_id = '<TENANT>' AND time > now() - 1h\- error rate: SELECT sum(errors) / sum(requests) FROM (SELECT count_if(response.error = true) as errors, count(*) as requests FROM requests WHERE tenant_id = '<TENANT>' AND time > now() - 10m)

Step 4 — SLO mapping, alerts and runbooks (2–5 days)
- SRE maps the onboarded metrics to Redwood SLOs and creates runbook stubs. Example SLOs: request availability >= 99.95% monthly; p95 latency < 300ms for short sequence routes.
- Create alerts: (1) p95 latency increase > 30% over baseline for 10 minutes; (2) sustained error_rate > 0.5% for 10 minutes; (3) telemetry ingestion missing for 2 minutes.

Step 5 — Handback and QBR prep (1–2 days)
- CS verifies that all QBR metrics populate correctly for the prior 30 days.
- Produce an "Observability Acceptance" sign-off artifact with: mapping doc, adapter config, retention policy, SLOs, and runbooks.

Rollback and remediation steps
- If validation fails, revert the adapter config and pause ingestion for the tenant while preserving raw payloads for investigation (no raw text forwarded for regulated accounts).
- Escalation: Observability -> SRE -> CS -> Legal for PII incidents. Use the major-incident template in escalation-playbook.

Common integration patterns and sample configs
1) Prometheus scrape adapter (yaml):
- job_name: "redwood-tenant"
  static_configs:
    - targets: ['collector.local:9100']
  relabel_configs:
    - source_labels: [__meta_kubernetes_namespace]
      target_label: tenant_id

2) OTLP to Redwood-forwarder (cli example):
- otelcol --config /etc/otel/config.yaml --exporter.redwood.endpoint=https://telemetry.redwood.ai:443 --auth.token=<REDACTED>

3) Minimal JSON event example (privacy-preserving):
{
  "event_type": "response.error",
  "tenant_id": "acct-2b7f",
  "request_id": "r-9f1a",
  "error_code": "MODEL_TIMEOUT",
  "error_category": "timeout",
  "timestamp": "2026-02-15T14:03:22Z"
}

QBR readiness checklist (for CS owners)
- 30 days of latency, error, and cost metrics available
- Dashboards pre-populated and linked in the QBR template
- Cost attribution validated against billing estimates 
- Two example incident summaries (if any) with remediation notes
- Privacy and retention policy documented and agreed

Templates and artifacts to attach to the onboarding ticket
- telemetry-mapping.csv (field mappings)
- adapter-config.yaml (collector/exporter config)
- acceptance-signoff.md (one-pager with signatures from CS and Customer Engineering)
- slo-definition.json (SLOs and objectives)

References and related pages
- Observability onboarding checklist (internal link)
- QBR telemetry storyboard and action plan
- Escalation templates for PII or SLA incidents

Appendix: common troubleshooting commands
- Check ingestion pipeline: curl -fsS https://telemetry.redwood.ai/health || echo "pipeline down"
- Verify metric existence (example time-series store): SELECT count(*) FROM metrics WHERE name = 'ingress.requests_total' AND tenant_id = '<TENANT>' AND time > now() - 1d

Revision history
- 2026-01-15: Created by Maya Chen
- 2026-02-20: Added privacy gating guidance and additional validation queries (reviewers: Jasper Liu, Leah Martinez, Arjun Patel)

Contact
If you have questions about implementing the contract or need an adapter review, contact the Observability on-call channel (#obs-oncall) and assign ticket to the Observability team.

title: Event-driven batch ingest connector: enterprise integration guide
content:
Summary
This guide describes a recommended, production-ready approach for integrating event-driven batch ingestion pipelines with the Redwood Inference platform. It targets enterprise customers that ingest large volumes of user events (logs, suggestions, or telemetry) in batches and call Redwood models for enrichment, reranking, or embeddings. The pattern covers connector architecture, configuration, resiliency, monitoring, and an escalation matrix for operational issues.

Audience
- Customer Success Engineers (CSEs) onboarding enterprise customers
- Platform/ML Engineers building connectors to Redwood APIs
- SREs owning the ingestion pipeline and monitoring

Goals
1. Provide a deterministic, cost-effective pattern for batched inference with event-driven triggers.
2. Minimize per-token cost via caching and batching policies while preserving SLOs.
3. Document operational runbook for common failure modes and escalation.

Scope and non-goals
- This document focuses on event-to-batch pipelines that call Redwood’s REST API or Private Connector. It does NOT cover one-off interactive chat integrations or client-side SDK usage.

High-level architecture
1) Event producer: customer service emits events into a durable queue (Kafka topic, Kinesis stream, or SQS).
2) Batcher/connector: our recommended connector groups events by tenant/model and prepares batched requests using prefix/KV cache hints.
3) Redwood frontdoor: requests are sent to Redwood Routed API endpoint or Private connector (VPC) based on customer deployment.
4) Post-processing: enrichment service applies business logic, writes results to datastore (BigQuery/Snowflake/S3) and triggers downstream workflows.

Text diagram (logical)
Event producer -> Kafka (topic: events-ingest) -> Connector (batcher) -> Redwood API/Private -> Enricher -> Storage

Prerequisites and requirements
- Accounts: Customer must have a Redwood API key with batch ingestion scope and (for Private) VPN peering configured.
- Networking: outbound egress to Redwood endpoints or VPC peering for Private deployments. TLS 1.2+.
- Quotas: agreed throughput (tokens/sec) per tenant. Confirm Dedicated capacity commitments if > 10k concurrent tokens/sec.
- Security: KMS integration for any customer-managed keys when using Private.

Configuration checklist (table-style text)
- Connector concurrency: default 8 workers per vCPU (adjust after testing).
- Batch window: 250 ms or 1,000 events, whichever comes first.
- Max tokens per batch: 65,536 tokens (model-specific — align with model's sequence length).
- Retry policy: exponential backoff starting at 200ms, max 60s, 5 attempts.
- Circuit breaker: open after 50% error rate over 1-minute sliding window; rampdown to 10% traffic on fallback model.

Sample connector configuration (YAML)
```
connector:
  type: kafka-consumer
  topics:
    - events-ingest
  batch:
    max_events: 1000
    max_wait_ms: 250
    max_tokens: 65536
  concurrency: 8
  retry:
    max_attempts: 5
    base_backoff_ms: 200
    max_backoff_ms: 60000
  circuit_breaker:
    error_threshold_pct: 50
    window_sec: 60
    fallback_ratio: 0.1
  redwood_endpoint: "https://api.redwood-inference.com/v1/batch"
  api_key_source: "vault:kms/redwood-service-account"
```

Batch formation guidelines
- Group by tenant and model variant to maximize cache hits (same model+prompt structure yields KV cache reuse).
- Preserve ordering for time-series dependent events; otherwise process out-of-order to increase batching.
- Attach deterministic prompt templates to avoid quality variance across batches.

Call pattern and payload example
- Use Redwood batch endpoint with array-of-requests payload. Each item should include: tenant_id, request_id, prompt, hints (cache_prefix), and metadata.
- Example payload snippet:
```
POST /v1/batch
Authorization: Bearer <REDACTED_API_KEY>
Content-Type: application/json
{
  "requests": [
    {"tenant_id":"acct-123","request_id":"r-1","prompt":"Summarize: ...","cache_hint":"acct-123:summary-v1"},
    {"tenant_id":"acct-123","request_id":"r-2","prompt":"Summarize: ...","cache_hint":"acct-123:summary-v1"}
  ],
  "model": "redwood-rlhf-7b-v2",
  "max_tokens": 256
}
```

Monitoring and SLOs
- Recommended SLOs for batch ingestion:
  - Availability: 99.95% (API success responses within SLA window).
  - P99 end-to-end processing latency (producer -> storage): <= 2s for small batches, <= 10s for large batches.
  - Error budget: 0.05% monthly.
- Essential metrics to ship to dashboards:
  - redwood.requests.total, redwood.requests.success, redwood.requests.errors (4xx/5xx split), redwood.tokens.consumed, connector.batch.size, connector.latency_ms, connector.retries.count, connector.circuit_breaker_state
- Alerts (examples):
  1) P95 batch latency > 5s for 5m -> page on-call SRE.
  2) Error rate > 5% for same model for 3m -> open incident and escalate to Redwood CSE.
  3) Token consumption spike > 3x forecast -> notify Finance + Sales.

Logging and tracing
- Include request_id and batch_id in all logs.
- Trace Redwood API calls using X-Trace-Id: <guid> and link traces in Redwood Console -> trace view.
- Persist sample error payloads (redacted PII) for triage.

Cost optimizations and guardrails
- Use prefix/KV caching hints to reuse compute when prompts share prefixes.
- Prefer streaming where forwarded responses are large and single-threaded.
- Enforce per-tenant daily token caps via rate-limiter to avoid runaway costs.

Failure modes and workarounds
1) 5xx spikes from Redwood API
   - Short-term: activate circuit breaker and switch 10% traffic to a lower-cost fallback model (e.g., redwood-rlhf-3b-quant) configured in connector.
   - Long-term: collect request_ids and open a support ticket via Redwood Console with timeline, sample payloads, and relevant trace ids.
2) Partial batch failures (some items succeed)
   - Best practice: connector must implement item-level retries. Mark successful items as complete; enqueue failed items to retry queue with exponential backoff.
3) Network flaps / DNS issues
   - Workaround: implement client-side DNS caching and fallback to Private connector or alternate region endpoint.
4) Cost surge due to malformed prompts
   - Apply server-side schema validation to reject unexpectedly large prompts; alert product owner and block offending keys until fixed.

Testing and validation checklist
- Unit tests for batcher logic and token counting.
- Integration test: synthetic load test at 2x expected peak for 30 minutes. Verify token consumption, latency SLOs, and error behavior.
- Canary rollout: start at 1% traffic for 30 minutes, 5% for 2 hours, 25% for 24 hours, then 100%.
- Regression tests: prompt set-based QA to compare output distributions between model variants.

Operational runbook (step-by-step)
1) Detection: alert triggers or user report indicating high errors or latency.
2) Triage (5 minutes): check connector logs, batch failure rate, Redwood Console for downstream errors, token usage spike.
3) Immediate mitigation (10 minutes): reduce connector concurrency by 50%, enable fallback model at 10% traffic, increase batch window to 500ms to reduce API QPS.
4) Escalation (30 minutes): if errors persist, open Redwood support case (include request_ids, traces, sample payloads) and notify CSE and Account Exec.
5) Post-incident (72 hours): run RCA with customer and Redwood team, document mitigations and follow-up actions.

Escalation contacts and SLAs
- On-call SRE (customer): Pager duty team (customer side) — primary contact.
- Redwood CSE: cse-oncall@redwood.ai (weekday 08:00–18:00 PT) — response target 1 hour.
- Redwood SRE escalation: sre-escalations@redwood.ai — response target 30 minutes for P1.
- For Private deployments include VPN and account team contacts (see customer onboarding packet).

Known limitations and recommended workarounds
- Model sequence-length limits: extremely long concatenated contexts may require chunking; prefer semantic chunking and reassembly.
- KV cache misses on heterogeneous prompts: group by prompt template to improve hit rate.
- Batch size vs. latency tradeoff: large batches improve cost but increase tail-latency — use dynamic batch tuning tied to latency budgets.

Appendix A: Sample end-to-end curl test
```
curl -X POST https://api.redwood-inference.com/v1/batch \ 
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ${REDWOOD_API_KEY}" \ 
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ 
  -d '{"model":"redwood-rlhf-7b-v2","requests":[{"tenant_id":"acct-123","request_id":"t-1","prompt":"Short summary of text A","cache_hint":"acct-123:summ-v1"}] }'
```

Appendix B: Onboarding checklist for CSE
- Verify API keys + scopes and networking (egress or VPC).
- Confirm Dedicated capacity or Private SLA if required.
- Deploy connector in staging and run integration test harness.
- Review dashboards with customer: token burn, latency, failure rates.
- Schedule QBR in 30 days to review quality metrics and cost.

Ownership and follow-ups
- Connector template maintenance: Platform Eng.
- Customer onboarding operational owner: assigned CSE (see related page for handoff).
- Billing anomalies: Finance + Account Exec.

Revision history
- 2025-09-15: Document created by Maya Patel.
- 2025-12-03: Added circuit breaker recommendations and sample YAML.
- 2026-02-10: Expanded monitoring alerts and updated escalation contacts.

End of document

title: Observability Privacy Filter and Keyed Telemetry Onboarding Playbook
content:
Purpose:
This playbook describes the recommended process for onboarding enterprise customers to Redwood's keyed telemetry pipeline with a privacy-filtering layer ("Observability Privacy Filter") between customer data sources and Redwood observability systems. It is intended to ensure compliance with customer privacy constraints, minimize PII leakage, and preserve the fidelity required for SLO/QBR reporting and cost accounting.

Scope:
- Applies to Dedicated and Private customers integrating their application telemetry (request traces, token-level cost attributions, custom metrics) into Redwood observability.
- Covers contract schema negotiation, filter configuration, implementation patterns, validation, rollout, and post-onboarding handoff to customer ops and Redwood CS.
- Does not replace legal data processing agreements; coordinate with Security & Legal for restricted data.

Audience:
- Customer Success Engineers (CSEs) onboarding telemetry
- Integration engineers on the customer side
- Platform/SRE teams validating ingestion and SLOs
- Account teams preparing QBR telemetry bundles

Definitions:
- Keyed telemetry: telemetry records that include a tenant identifier (key) for attribution and routing.
- Observability Privacy Filter (OPF): a configurable filter service deployed at the customer edge or as a Redwood-managed middleware that redacts/replaces sensitive attributes while preserving routing keys and aggregates.
- Telemetry Contract: a schema agreement between customer and Redwood that defines field names, types, retention hints, and sensitivity labels.

Prerequisites (customer & Redwood):
1) Signed Data Processing Addendum (DPA) and any sector-specific addenda (finance, healthcare).
2) Approved telemetry contract draft and agreed retention windows.
3) Network ingress configured: IP allowlist, TLS certificates, and, if Private, VPC peering details.
4) Access to a staging project/tenant in Redwood with synthetic traffic capability.
5) Contact list: CSE, customer integration lead, customer security lead, Redwood SRE reviewer.

Roles and Ownership:
- Customer Success (owner): run onboarding, validate acceptance tests, and deliver QBR reporting templates.
- Customer Integration Lead (owner): implement client-side emitters and local filters.
- Security & Legal (reviewer): sign-off on privacy filter rules and DPA terms.
- Platform/SRE (reviewer): confirm ingestion capacity and SLO measurement hooks.

Step-by-step onboarding checklist (recommended timeline: 4–8 business days):
1) Kickoff (Day 0):
   - Introductions and objectives; share this playbook and telemetry contract template.
   - Confirm DPA status and desired retention/region constraints.
2) Contract negotiation (Day 0–2):
   - Exchange telemetry contract JSON schema (example below).
   - Mark sensitive fields with sensitivity labels: PUBLIC | CONFIDENTIAL | PII.
3) Filtering strategy workshop (Day 1–3):
   - Decide where OPF will run: customer-side agent (recommended for Private) or Redwood-managed ingress.
   - Choose operators: redact, hash (HMAC-SHA256 with tenant salt), truncate, pseudonymize.
4) Staging implementation (Day 2–4):
   - Customer deploys emitters to staging; OPF applied to traffic.
   - CSE runs acceptance suite including token-counting, latency sampling, and synthetic loads.
5) Validation and telemetry QA (Day 3–5):
   - Verify key preservation for routing and aggregation.
   - Assert no PII in fields labeled PII via automated scans (see validation commands).
6) SLO mapping and QBR dataset selection (Day 4–6):
   - Map telemetry fields to SLOs (latency, error-rate, token-cost).
   - Define QBR metrics and retention windows for executive dashboards.
7) Production go/no-go and rollout plan (Day 5–7):
   - Agree on canary % pattern, throttling/queue limits, and fallback to raw ingest for debugging windows.
8) Production rollout (Day 6–8):
   - Apply OPF to production canary; monitor for missing keys or metric gaps.
   - Gradual ramp with checkpoints at 10%, 50%, 100%.
9) Post-go monitoring and tuning (Week 1):
   - Monitor telemetry completeness, SLO drift, and cost attribution accuracy.
   - Tune filter rules to restore necessary fields if over-redaction occurs.
10) Handoff and QBR preparation (Week 1–2):
   - Deliver a QBR telemetry bundle and runbook for customer ops.

Telemetry contract (example snippet):
| field_name | type | example | sensitivity | retention_hint | notes |
| request_id | string | "req_01a7..." | PUBLIC | 7d | routing key for traces |
| tenant_id | string | "tenant:acme" | CONFIDENTIAL | 30d | must be preserved (hashed if required) |
| user_email | string | "alice@acme.com" | PII | 30d | must be redacted or pseudonymized unless DPA allows |
| prompt_tokens | integer | 12 | PUBLIC | 90d | used for cost attribution |
| response_tokens | integer | 64 | PUBLIC | 90d | used for cost attribution |
| model_id | string | "redwood/gptx-4b-q" | PUBLIC | 365d | model attribution for cost and debugging |

Telemetry contract JSON (recommended format):
{
  "fields": [
    {"name":"request_id", "type":"string", "sensitivity":"PUBLIC", "retention":"7d"},
    {"name":"tenant_id", "type":"string", "sensitivity":"CONFIDENTIAL", "retention":"30d"},
    {"name":"user_email", "type":"string", "sensitivity":"PII", "retention":"30d"},
    {"name":"prompt_tokens", "type":"integer", "sensitivity":"PUBLIC", "retention":"90d"}
  ]
}

Filtering operators (recommended patterns):
- redact: remove the field entirely from emitted telemetry. Use when customer policy prohibits storage.
- hash: HMAC-SHA256 with tenant-specific salt; preserves grouping but hides original value.
- pseudonymize: generate stable pseudo-id via keyed PRF; can be reversible only under strict legal control.
- aggregate: replace detailed values with buckets (e.g., token counts -> 0-32,33-64,...).

Validation commands and test harness (staging):
- Run the Redwood telemetry linter: rwd-telemetry-lint --schema telemetry_contract.json --sample sample_payloads/
- PII scan (simple grep approach for email): grep -E "[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\\.[A-Za-z]{2,}" logs/ingested/ || echo "PII-free"
- Request count verification: curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" https://staging-redwood/api/telemetry/tenant/<tenant_id>/counts

SLO and QBR mapping (example):
- Latency p50/p95 per model_id -> SLO 99.5% p95 < 350ms
- Token-cost attribution: daily delta per tenant -> used in finops QBR
- Ingest completeness: 99% of requests must include request_id and tenant_id

Troubleshooting and common failure modes:
1) Missing tenant_id after filter applied:
   - Symptom: Billing and routing gaps, alerts for missing-key ingestion spikes.
   - Cause: Filter misconfiguration replaced rather than hashed/preserved.
   - Remediation: Re-deploy OPF with tenant-preserve rule; run re-ingestion for the window if allowed.
2) Over-redaction causing SLO regression:
   - Symptom: Missing model_id or token counts; SLO dashboards show gaps.
   - Cause: Aggressive redact rules or wildcard match in OPF.
   - Remediation: Narrow rule scope, enable aggregated fallback (buckets) to preserve SLO signals.
3) Unexpected PII in ingestion:
   - Symptom: Automatic DLP scan flags stored records.
   - Cause: New emitters added fields that bypass the agreed contract.
   - Remediation: Freeze producer schema, run full scan, and engage Security & Legal per DPA.

Known issues and workarounds (current as of last_updated):
- Issue: HMAC salted hashing drift when tenant salt rotated causes broken grouping. Workaround: use versioned salt identifiers in emitted record and schedule a rehash job for recent windows.
- Issue: High-cardinality keys (full user_email hashed) inflates cardinality of metrics and increases cost. Workaround: pseudonymize to coarse buckets for analytics and preserve hashed emails only for reverse-lookup windows under strict access control.
- Issue: Edge OPF running on CPU-constrained appliances causes 200ms spike during peak ingest. Workaround: enable per-route sampling (1%) for detailed traces and send aggregated summaries for high-volume routes.

Acceptance criteria (must pass before handoff):
- No PII present in fields labeled PII in the agreed contract for production data (automated DLP scan).
- Ingest completeness >= 99% for required keys (tenant_id, request_id) across canary period.
- Token-cost attribution within 2% of staging baseline.
- SRE sign-off on ingestion capacity and fallback plan.

Handoff artifacts to provide to customer after onboarding:
- Telemetry contract JSON and final OPF rule-set
- Staging and production verification runbooks (commands and dashboards)
- QBR telemetry bundle and dashboard snapshot with sample queries
- Short operational runbook for rehash/rotation and emergency debug window steps

Appendix A: Example OPF rule (yaml)
- name: redact_user_email
  match: "event.user_email"
  action: "redact"
  reason: "Customer requested no email storage"
- name: hash_tenant_id
  match: "event.tenant_id"
  action: "hash:hmac-sha256:tenant-salt-v1"
  reason: "Preserve grouping without storing raw id"

Appendix B: Escalation path for data policy incidents:
1) CSE opens internal incident in PagerDuty with tag "telemetry-data-policy".
2) Notify Security & Legal immediately and place a temporary ingest halt if data exposure suspected.
3) Execute the containment checklist (snapshot, freeze schema changes, begin audit log collection).
4) If confirmed, follow DPA breach notification timelines; coordinate customer communications via Account team.

Contact and support matrix:
- Primary CSE: Leila Moreno (leila@redwood.example)
- Platform/SRE reviewer: Ethan Park (ethan@redwood.example)
- Security & Legal contact: Rima Gupta (rima@redwood.example)

Document maintenance:
- Owner: Customer Success (telemetry onboarding squad)
- Review cadence: Quarterly or on major stream changes

End of document.

title: Client-side Quota Guardrails: Rate Limiting, Grace Windows, and In-Product Nudges
content:
Overview:

This guide explains a pragmatic pattern for integrating client-side quota guardrails with Redwood’s server-side quota and rate-limiting signals. The goal is to reduce customer-reported overage incidents, improve perceived reliability during short bursts, and give product teams an easy path to deploy polite default rate limits, local backoff, and in-product nudges (warnings) while preserving server-side SLA enforcement.

Intended audience:
- Customer-facing SDK and frontend engineers
- Solutions engineers performing integration handoffs
- Customer Success and FinOps partners who configure quotas

Scope and objectives:
- Provide a recommended client-side token-bucket configuration for typical web apps and mobile clients
- Describe soft quota (grace window) semantics vs. hard quota enforcement
- Define API headers and signals customers should consume to present accurate usage/nudge UIs
- Offer rollout, testing, and observability checklist for safe deployment

Why client-side guardrails?
- Early throttling reduces noisy retries and downstream cost spikes.
- Grace windows enable short bursts (e.g., 5–15s) without immediate hard rejections, improving UX for interactive product flows.
- Coordinated nudges reduce support tickets and unexpected billing disputes.

Architecture and signal flow (text diagram):
1) Client SDK maintains a local token-bucket governor.
2) Client sends request to Redwood ingress.
3) Redwood responds with quota headers and may apply soft-throttle or hard-429.
4) Client updates local governor (replenish / reduce) and shows in-product nudge if remaining budget is low.

Example headers (returned on every successful/failed request):
- X-Redwood-Quota-Remaining: integer (approximate remaining units for the tenant in the current window)
- X-Redwood-Quota-Window: integer (window length in seconds, e.g., 3600)
- X-Redwood-Quota-Reset-At: ISO8601 timestamp for when the window resets (optional)
- Retry-After: integer seconds (when 429 returned)
- X-Redwood-Soft-Throttle: true|false (present when server has started soft-throttling to avoid hard failover)

Recommended local governor (token-bucket) reference configuration:
- bucket_capacity: min(tenant_rate_limit * 1.5, 200) tokens
- refill_rate: tenant_rate_limit / 60 tokens per second (convert per-minute policy to per-second refill)
- max_burst_seconds: 15 (protects against 1–15s interactive bursts)

YAML example (client SDK config snippet):

client_quota:
  bucket_capacity: 120
  refill_rate_per_sec: 2
  max_burst_seconds: 15
  behaviour_on_empty: "soft-nudge" # options: soft-nudge | block | allow-with-backoff

Behavior definitions:
- soft-nudge: allow the request but surface an in-app warning and apply progressive local backoff for subsequent immediate requests (recommended default for UI-heavy flows).
- block: immediately prevent request and return local error to the UI. Use for critical cost protection on low-trust clients.
- allow-with-backoff: allow request but increase refill delay to prevent repeated bursts.

Grace window vs. hard enforcement:
- Grace window: a short period during which the server returns 200/soft-throttle but sets X-Redwood-Soft-Throttle=true. Clients should downgrade non-essential requests (e.g., analytics, background embeddings) and show a subtle UI hint if end-user action triggers repeated consumption.
- Hard enforcement: server returns 429 with Retry-After header. Client MUST respect Retry-After and stop retrying until the window expires.

Nudge examples and recommended microcopy:
- Soft nudge (UI toast): "You're sending a lot of requests right now. Some features may slow down—try again in a few seconds."
- Billing/Quota banner (when remaining < 10%): "Your team is nearing its hourly quota. Contact [billing link] to increase capacity."
- Retry modal (after 429): "We’re temporarily limiting requests. Try again at {time}."

Customer-facing telemetry and SLOs (what to track):
- Client-side: local_throttle_count, local_block_count, nudge_shown_count
- Server-side: 429_rate_by_tenant, soft_throttle_rate, quota_warning_count, overage_events
- Business SLOs:
  - Support tickets for unexpected overages: < 1 per 100 customers / month
  - False-positive hard blocks (customer experiencing 429 but expecting allowed) < 0.5% of tenant requests

Rollout plan (recommended):
1) Internal canary: ship the client governor to internal test accounts and Redwood-provided demo tenants. Monitor local_throttle_count and 429_rate.
2) Partner pilot: enable for 3–5 opt-in enterprise customers. Collect UX feedback and billing deltas.
3) Gradual ramp: enable default soft-nudge behavior for 25% of new signups, then 100% after 4 weeks of telemetry review.

Testing checklist (pre-deploy):
- [ ] Simulate short bursts (1–10s) at 2x and 5x tenant rate and verify soft-nudge behavior
- [ ] Simulate sustained high traffic for >60s and verify server 429 and client obeys Retry-After
- [ ] Validate header propagation (X-Redwood-Quota-Remaining, Retry-After) across CDN and gateway caches
- [ ] Validate mobile offline/queued requests do not bypass server quotas when network resumes

Runbook: Handling a large number of customer overage disputes
1) Detect: alert when tenant overage events spike >5x baseline or >0.5% of requests return 429 in a 10m window. Owner: Customer Success (tiered alert to SE/Escalation).
2) Initial triage: check ingress logs for header signals and client governor telemetry. If X-Redwood-Soft-Throttle was present during burst, mark as "soft-throttle UX degradation".
3) Mitigation steps:
  a) For soft-throttle cases: share nudge timeline and adjustment options (increase local bucket, raise tenant rate limit temporarily, enable burst allowance).
  b) For hard 429 errors: validate expected quota and check for config drift (tenant plan vs applied quota). If quota misconfiguration: apply emergency fix and refund/credit if customer affected.
4) Post-incident: author a short incident note, update customer with timeline and remediation, and add a follow-up item to FinOps for any necessary credits.

Compatibility notes:
- Dedicated and Private deployments: these headers and soft-throttle semantics are supported but tenant rate limits may be enforced by customer-managed policy. Coordinate with private deployment teams to ensure header passthrough.
- SDK variations: server signals are identical across SDKs; only local governor implementation differs per platform (JS, iOS, Android, backend).

Operational knobs and admin controls (product-facing):
- Tenant rate window (per-minute vs per-hour)
- Soft throttle threshold (percent of window consumption to start soft throttle; default: 85%)
- Grace window length (default: 15 seconds)
- Emergency override: temporary increase of tenant limit (owner: FinOps or Customer Success)

Metrics / telemetry export (recommended tags):
- tenant_id, region, client_sdk, flow (interactive|batch|background), plan_tier

Example SDK pseudocode (JS):

class LocalGovernor {
  constructor(cfg) {
    this.capacity = cfg.bucket_capacity
    this.tokens = this.capacity
    this.refillRate = cfg.refill_rate_per_sec
    this.behaviourOnEmpty = cfg.behaviour_on_empty
  }
  attemptRequest(cost=1) {
    this.refillTokens()
    if (this.tokens >= cost) {
      this.tokens -= cost
      return {allowed: true}
    } else {
      if (this.behaviourOnEmpty === 'soft-nudge') {
        // allow but signal UI and start backoff
        this.startBackoff()
        return {allowed: true, softNudge: true}
      } else if (this.behaviourOnEmpty === 'block') {
        return {allowed: false}
      }
    }
  }
}

Ownership and contacts:
- Primary owner: Customer Success (Ayesha K. Patel)
- Engineering contact: Mateo Ruiz (SDKs)
- FinOps contact: Hannah J. Lee

References and related reading:
- telemetry-gatekeeper-onboarding-and-qbr-integration-guide (integration guides)
- enterprise-ratelimit-quota-adjustment-and-cost-protection-playbook (support process)

Appendix: sample incident communication template (short):
- Subject: "Incident: Temporary request limits observed for {tenant} on {date}"
- Body: bullet timeline, cause (soft-throttle vs hard limit), mitigation, actions taken, expected next steps

Document revision history:
- 2026-02-18: Initial draft by A. Patel
- 2026-03-02: Added rollout checklist and runbook steps after pilot feedback

title: SaaS Partner Integration Runbook and Onboarding Checklist
content:
Overview:
