This runbook describes the recommended process, technical requirements, and escalation paths for integrating a SaaS partner with Redwood Inference. It is intended for Customer Success Managers (CSMs), Solutions Engineers (SEs), and the partner's technical teams. Use this document during the initial 60-day integration window and as an operational checklist for ongoing partner maintenance.

Goals:
- Deliver a reproducible integration that meets security and performance SLOs.
- Ensure the partner can make production calls with predictable latency and cost.
- Define clear ownership, handoffs, and escalation routes.

Audience and ownership:
- Primary: CSM (owner), Solutions Engineering (technical lead), Partner Engineering (partner-owned).
- Secondary: Support (L1), Eng-SRE (L2), Eng-Serving-Runtime (L3).

Quick summary checklist (60-day timeline):
1) Kickoff & scope alignment (Day 0–3)
   - Confirm integration scope: API patterns (text gen, embeddings, chat), expected QPS, peak concurrency, data residency requirements.
   - Collect contact matrix (names, roles, SLAs).
2) Security & compliance (Day 3–10)
   - Validate network connectivity (VPC peering, IP allowlist, TLS requirements).
   - Verify contract attachments (DPA, SOC report references) and required audits.
3) Test environment setup (Day 5–14)
   - Provision sandbox API key, scoped to partner test workspace.
   - Provide sample prompts and token/usage quotas for benchmark tests.
4) Performance validation (Day 10–30)
   - Run throughput/latency tests against expected payloads and sequence lengths.
   - Confirm autoscaling behavior and cold-start characteristics.
5) UAT & cutover (Day 30–45)
   - Partner completes UAT with real traffic patterns.
   - Schedule gradual ramp and monitor usage & errors.
6) Post-cutover review & QBR prep (Day 45–60)
   - Finalize baseline metrics and agree on QBR cadence.

Prerequisites (technical):
- Partner-side: ability to make HTTPS requests, JSON parsing, retry/backoff logic, and optional websocket support for streaming.
- Network: IP allowlist or peered VPC, outbound HTTPS to api.redwood.ai (or private endpoint).
- Auth: API keys or OAuth client credentials (for private deployments, install-specific tokens).
- Data handling: Clarify PII vs non-PII, retention windows, and encryption requirements.

Technical configuration template (sample):
- API endpoint: https://api.redwood.example/v1/generate
- Authentication: Authorization: Bearer <REDACTED_KEY>
- Recommended headers: x-rw-customer-id, x-rw-environment

Sample cURL smoke test:
curl -s -X POST https://api.redwood.example/v1/generate -H "Authorization: Bearer TEST_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"model":"rw-large-1.0","input":"Hello, Redwood!","max_tokens":64}'

Performance validation checklist:
- Define representative prompt/sequence-length mix (e.g., 60% short prompts <128 tokens, 30% medium 128–512, 10% long >512).
- Run 1k request steady-state test at expected QPS. Capture p50/p95/p99 latency and token throughput.
- Validate KV cache benefits by running warm/cold cache scenarios.
- Targets: p95 latency <= 350ms for short prompts on hosted plan; p99 errors <0.5% (adjust by tier).

Security and compliance checklist:
- Confirm KMS integration details for Private deployment (customer-managed CMKs).
- Ensure audit logging is enabled and log retention meets partner requirements (enter retention policy in their contract).
- For restricted data: enable field-level redaction or on-prem option; document fields considered PII.
- MFA and SSO: require SAML SSO for admin console access on enterprise accounts.

Routing and fallback policy recommendations:
- Default routing: hosted model in closest region.
- Failure fallback: on 5xx/timeout, retry with exponential backoff up to 2 attempts, then fallback to smaller model variant or cached response.
- Cost fallback: for non-critical paths, route to quantized variant when cost/sla threshold exceeded.

Known integration pitfalls and workarounds:
- Pitfall: High variance in token length inflates latency and costs.
  Workaround: Add client-side prefiltering and token budget enforcement. Use streaming for long outputs.
- Pitfall: Unexpected 429s during bursts.
  Workaround: Implement client-side rate limiting with jitter; request Dedicated capacity if sustained high QPS.
- Pitfall: JSON-structured outputs failing strict parsers.
  Workaround: Use Redwood's structured output schema with schema-id header and validate with provided JSON Schema.

Escalation matrix (contact order):
1) Partner SE -> Redwood CSM (first 24–48 hours operational issues)
2) Redwood Support L1 (support@redwood.ai) -> triages logs and issues (within 4 business hours)
3) Eng-SRE on-call -> for incidents impacting SLOs (pagers for P1/P0)
4) Eng-Serving-Runtime -> for model runtime regressions or kernel-level bugs

Incident classification and SLA expectations:
- P0 (production down for >50% users): page Eng-SRE immediately, target TTR <2 hours.
- P1 (severe degradation): page Eng-SRE, target TTR <8 hours.
- P2 (partial impact): ticket to Support, target fix or mitigation within 72 hours.
- P3 (cosmetic): backlog grooming and triage in next sprint.

Monitoring and dashboards (must-have tiles for partner):
- Token usage by route (daily/7d/30d).
- Latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99) by model and prompt-length bucket.
- Error rate by status code and route.
- Cache hit rate and batching efficiency.
- Cost per 1k tokens vs baseline.

QBR template (recommended slides / sections):
- Executive summary (uptime, spend, actions)
- Usage and growth (top routes, peak concurrency)
- Performance (latency/SLO adherence, regressions)
- Cost and optimization opportunities (quantization, batching)
- Security & compliance updates (audit findings, open items)
- Roadmap / upcoming changes (model upgrades, infra migrations)
- Action items and owners (RACI for next quarter)

Post-onboarding handoff checklist:
- Confirm monitoring dashboards live and shared with partner.
- Transfer runbooks to partner Confluence space if requested.
- Schedule first operational QBR within 30 days of cutover.
- Set recurring support review cadence (monthly for first quarter, then quarterly).

Appendix A — Example alert thresholds:
- error_rate(route) > 1% over 5m -> severity P1
- p95_latency(model,short_prompts) > 500ms over 10m -> severity P1
- token_spend_day change > 30% day-over-day -> notify CSM

Appendix B — Example integration manifest (for partner config):
{"partner_id": "partner-acme", "environments": ["sandbox","production"], "endpoints": {"sandbox": "https://sandbox.api.redwood.example/v1", "production": "https://api.redwood.example/v1"}, "contact": {"technical": "eng+acme@partner.com", "business": "biz+acme@partner.com"}, "qps_expectation": "50", "data_sensitivity": "non-PII"}

Appendix C — Useful links and references:
- Developer quickstart: https://playground.redwood.ai/quickstart
- API reference: https://docs.redwood.ai/api
- Security & compliance overview: https://intranet.redwood.ai/security/compliance
- Support portal (create ticket): https://support.redwood.ai

If you have additions or local variations for a specific partner vertical (healthcare, finance, government), create a sibling page using this runbook as the template and label it with the vertical tag.

title: PRD: Developer Simulation Kit & Telemetry Bridge for Preflight Testing
content:
Summary

This PRD proposes a Developer Simulation Kit (DevSim) and a Telemetry Bridge that together provide engineers with an offline, high-fidelity preflight environment for: workload simulation, latency/cost forecasting, fidelity experiments, and telemetry capture that mirrors production signals. The goal is to reduce time-to-safe-deploy for engine and product teams by catching regressions and cost surprises earlier.

Context and motivation

- Teams repeatedly run into late-stage surprises when moving workloads from test harnesses to hosted/dedicated/private environments: unexpected tail-latency spikes, different token costs due to batching/caching behavior, and gaps in observability.
- Current sandboxes either (a) are lightweight and fast but underestimate cost/latency, or (b) are production clones that are expensive and slow to provision.
- DevSim + Telemetry Bridge is a developer-focused sandbox designed to be: portable (local/CI/cloud), inexpensive to run, and representative of production runtime behaviors (batching, KV cache warm-up, quantization variants).

Goals (what success looks like)

1. Provide a reproducible simulation that approximates hosted inference latencies and token cost within +/-10% for canonical workloads.
2. Surface fidelity regressions via synthetic and recorded prompt sets before production rollout.
3. Emit telemetry that is structurally compatible with production dashboards and alerts so preflight runs can be used in continuous gating.
4. Reduce mean time to detect cost/latency regressions during release validation from days to hours.

Non-goals

- Not intended to replace full private deployment validation for regulated customers.
- Not a replacement for long-duration soak tests or stress tests at production scale.

User personas

- Platform engineers: want to validate runtime kernel changes and batching policies.
- ML engineers: want to test quantization/fidelity changes against representative prompts.
- Product engineers: want quick cost/latency estimates for feature experiments.

High-level product concept

DevSim consists of three components:

1) Local Simulation Runtime (LSR)
- Lightweight containerized runtime that mimics production serving behavior: continuous batching, KV cache emulation (cold/warm cycles), quantization toggles, and failure injection.
- Configurable hardware profile (e.g., V100/RTX6000 equivalent timings) with pluggable latency/cost profiles derived from production benchmarking.

2) Workload Runner
- CLI and SDK for running recorded or synthetic workloads with control over concurrency, sequence length distributions, prompt sets, and session stickiness.

3) Telemetry Bridge
- Streaming adapter that maps DevSim events to the production telemetry schema and can either forward to a staging ingestion endpoint or write to a staging S3 bucket in the same format as production.

Detailed requirements

A. Functional requirements (MUST)
- FR-1: LSR must implement the same API surface as hosted inference (generate/chat/embeddings) with identical request/response contracts.
- FR-2: Workload Runner must accept a "recording" input (see Recording Format below) and replay with configurable timing and concurrency.
- FR-3: Telemetry Bridge must emit the following canonical event types: request_start, request_end, token_emitted, batch_formed, cache_hit, cache_miss, fallback_invoked, model_variant_selected.
- FR-4: DevSim must provide a cost model that estimates per-request token cost given batch size, quantization variant, and sequence length.
- FR-5: DevSim must be runnable in CI (Docker image < 2GB) and via a managed cloud offering for larger experiments.

B. Non-functional requirements (SHOULD)
- NFR-1: Simulation accuracy: mean latency and token-cost estimator for a standard benchmark (see Appendix A) must be within +/-10% of production for the 50th and 95th percentiles.
- NFR-2: Telemetry event schema must be 1:1 compatible with production staging ingestion endpoints to allow reuse of dashboards and alert rules.
- NFR-3: Default run should complete a 10k-request recorded replay in under 30 minutes on a 4-vCPU, 16GB host for cost/latency summary reports.

C. Operational requirements (MUST)
- OR-1: DevSim images and Telemetry Bridge must be signed and versioned; versions must map to production runtime versions.
- OR-2: Access to forwarding-to-production telemetry must be gated (RBAC) and require an approval workflow.
- OR-3: Telemetry retention for DevSim runs stored in staging must be at least 90 days.

Recording format (simple JSON schema)

- A recording contains: metadata (name, created_by, model_id), prompts (array of session objects), and annotations (optional ground-truth metrics). Example snippet: 

{
  "name": "checkout-flow-2026-10-01",
  "created_by": "ux-team",
  "model_id": "redwood-4x-q8",
  "sessions": [
    {"session_id":"s1","turns":[{"role":"user","text":"Find me the best deal on flights"},{"role":"system","text":"context: premium user"}]}
  ]
}

API & CLI examples

- Run a local replay with the CLI: 

redwood-devsim replay --recording checkout-flow-2026-10-01.json --concurrency 8 --profile v100-equivalent --telemetry forward://staging

- SDK usage (python): 

from redwood_devsim import Runner
runner = Runner.from_recording('checkout-flow.json')
report = runner.run(concurrency=4, duration_seconds=1800)
print(report.summary())

Telemetry Bridge event schema (fields)

All fields are sent as top-level keys in the event JSON (production-compatible).
- event_type (string): one of request_start|request_end|token_emitted|batch_formed|cache_hit|cache_miss|fallback_invoked|model_variant_selected
- timestamp (ISO8601)
- request_id (uuid)
- session_id (string)
- model_id (string)
- variant (string)
- batch_size (int)
- token_count (int)
- latency_ms (int)
- cost_estimate_micros (int)  # micro-units of currency for precision
- tags (array of strings)

Example event:

{
  "event_type": "request_end",
  "timestamp": "2026-10-20T15:23:12.123Z",
  "request_id": "a3f2-...",
  "session_id": "s1",
  "model_id": "rw-4x-q8",
  "variant": "q8-hybrid",
  "batch_size": 4,
  "token_count": 128,
  "latency_ms": 82,
  "cost_estimate_micros": 4200,
  "tags": ["preflight","checkout-flow"]
}

Dashboards and alerts (required)

- Dashboard: DevSim Preflight Summary
  - Panels: latency p50/p95, cost-estimate distribution, batch-size histogram, cache hit rate, model_variant distribution, mismatch-rate vs production baseline.
- Alert: preflight-latency-regression
  - Trigger: p95 latency deviation > 20% vs baseline AND absolute p95 > 400ms (over 1h window).
- Alert: cost-estimate-drift
  - Trigger: mean estimated cost deviation > 15% vs last production 7d rolling baseline.

Quality & acceptance criteria

- QC-1: Run three canonical recordings (chat-short, chat-long, embeddings-bulk). Each run must meet NFR-1 accuracy target.
- QC-2: Telemetry events from DevSim replay ingested into staging must be queryable with the same saved queries as production (no schema adaptation).
- QC-3: Developer onboarding: a new engineer can run the default replay and inspect the preflight dashboard within 20 minutes following README.

Rollout plan

1. Alpha (4 weeks): internal platform and ML teams. Manual sign-up for staging telemetry forwarding.
2. Beta (8 weeks): expand to product teams; add CI integration templates for GitHub Actions and GitLab.
3. GA (12+ weeks): public documentation, console integration to surface preflight reports in the deployment flow, Optimize integration for cost-optimization suggestions.

Rollout checklist

- [ ] LSR Docker images built and published to staging registry and versioned.
- [ ] Telemetry Bridge endpoint deployed to staging and covered by RBAC.
- [ ] Three canonical recordings validated and checked into recordings repo.
- [ ] Preflight dashboards (staging) and alert rules created.
- [ ] CI integration templates added to docs.

Dependencies & integrations

- Telemetry ingestion pipeline (observability team) — must accept staging forwarding with identical schema.
- Cost model calibration dataset from runtime benchmarking (runtime team).
- Console engineering to surface preflight run summaries and attach to rollout approvals.

Risks and mitigations

- Risk: Simulation diverges from production over time as runtime kernels evolve.
  - Mitigation: Enforce image/version parity; run an automated weekly calibration job that compares baseline recordings run in DevSim vs a small production cluster and produces calibration deltas.
- Risk: Telemetry forwarding misused and pollutes production metrics.
  - Mitigation: RBAC + tagging + require explicit approval for forwarding to any non-staging ingestion endpoint.

Ownership and contacts

- Product owner: Maya Chen (product)
- Tech lead: Aaron Li (platform engineering)
- Runtime interface: Priya Nair (serving runtime)
- Observability contact: Ethan Park (eng-platform)

Cost & licensing considerations

- Local DevSim is free for engineers. Managed cloud runs will consume credits; pricing model proposal: small runs (<=10k requests) free during alpha/beta, then a metered credit consumption model integrated into existing consumption billing for customers running large preflight experiments.

Appendix A: Benchmark workloads

- chat-short: 128 tokens avg, 1k sessions, concurrency 16
- chat-long: 1k tokens avg, 200 sessions, concurrency 8
- embeddings-bulk: 8k items, avg size 256 tokens

Appendix B: Example CI step (GitHub Actions)

name: Preflight replay
on: [push]
jobs:
  preflight:
    runs-on: ubuntu-22.04
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Setup Docker
        run: sudo systemctl start docker
      - name: Run preflight replay
        run: |
          docker run --rm -v ${{github.workspace}}:/data redwood/devsim:2026-11-01 \
            replay --recording /data/checkout-flow-2026-10-01.json --concurrency 8 --telemetry forward://staging

Appendix C: FAQs

Q: How closely will DevSim match spot GPU performance?
A: DevSim targets representative timings derived from benchmarking; it is not a real-time substitute for heterogeneous spot performance. Use DevSim to catch relative regressions and for cost trend estimation, not exact millisecond parity.

Q: Can DevSim mutate recordings (add noise, redact PII)?
A: Yes — the recording ingestion pipeline supports anonymization rules and synthetic perturbations to simulate user variance.

Next steps

- Approve scope and acceptance criteria (product review).
- Begin alpha implementation: containerized LSR + minimal Telemetry Bridge + three canonical recordings.

References

- Observability cost/latency guide: /confluence/product-docs/product-overview/observability-cost-latency-tradeoffs-guide-2025-06-09
- Offline cost estimator PRD: /confluence/product-docs/requirements/prd-offline-cost-estimator-sdk-and-simulation-playground-2025-10-12

title: Ingress Observability Bakeoff and Telemetry Declaration for Enterprise Cutovers
content:
Overview

Purpose: This document defines the standardized bakeoff and telemetry declaration process used during enterprise tenant cutovers and large customer integrations. The goal is to validate ingress observability, telemetry completeness, and SLA readiness before a production flip. This reduces incident churn, shortens the stabilization window, and provides a clear pass/fail decision path for the cutover gate.

Scope: Applies to Dedicated and Private launch cutovers and any Hosted onboarding with >1M monthly tokens or complex network topologies (VPC peering, private link, or regional egress controls). Not intended for small self-serve trials.

Audience: Customer Success Engineers, Solutions Engineers, Platform Oncall, Customer SRE, and Product Integration owners.

Summary of changes vs. previous practice:
- Formalizes a measurable bakeoff with explicit SLO thresholds and telemetry schema declaration.
- Introduces a compact "Telemetry Declaration" template that customers and Redwood must sign off on before canary.
- Defines ownership and escalation paths for failed observability checks to prevent ambiguous handoffs.

Roles & Responsibilities

- Customer Success (CSE): coordinates schedule, invites stakeholders, captures acceptance artifact.
- Solutions Engineering (SE): runs ingress tests, verifies request/response parity and header-level telemetry.
- Customer SRE / Network: validates network routing, TLS, and client certificate behavior.
- Platform Oncall: validates server-side traces, span naming, and alerts.
- Product Integration Owner: final sign-off for functional equivalence and rollout readiness.

Pre-bakeoff checklist (minimum required)

1) Provisioning and access
- Tenant configuration deployed (route table, DNS entries, certs, API keys).
- Red-team access account for SE & Platform Oncall active.
- Signed Telemetry Declaration draft (see template).

2) Baseline telemetry verified
- Metrics exposed: ingress_rps, ingress_error_rate, request_latency_p50/p95, token_count_per_request.
- Traces created for request start/end and model invocation with parent/child spans.
- Logs include request_id, tenant_id, route, and sampling flag.

3) Alerting and dashboards
- Canary dashboard created with the tenant tag.
- Alerts configured: ErrorRate >= 2% sustained for 5m, p95 latency > 2s for 10m, Token cost delta +30% vs baseline for 1h (optional).

Bakeoff procedure (90–120 minute window recommended)

Preparation (30m)
1. Confirm windows and invites; ensure stakeholders available for rapid decisions.
2. Seed simulated workload: run the standard ingress load generator for the workload class (examples in appendix).
3. Snapshot baseline: capture current dashboards, traces, and logs as the "pre-bakeoff" reference.

Phase A — Functional validation (20m)
1. Run 200–500 requests across core routes with representative payloads (short, medium, long).
2. Verify request/response parity for 100% of sampled requests (no silent truncation, correct streaming delim).
3. Validate header propagation: X-Request-Id, X-Tenant-Id, X-Region, X-Trace-Parent.
4. Record sample traces (3 successful, 1 with synthetic error) and attach to the bakeoff notes.

Phase B — Observability validation (30m)
1. Metrics: Confirm ingestion to Redwood telemetry or customer telemetry endpoint within 60s for meter points below.
2. Traces: Open a trace in APM and confirm model invocation spans contain span attributes: model.name, model.version, kv_cache_hit (true|false), quantized (true|false).
3. Logs: Search last 500 log lines for request_id mapping to trace_id.
4. Dashboard: Canary dashboard shows ingresses tagged by tenant and route.

Phase C — Stress and edge-cases (20–40m)
1. Burst test: 3x expected peak RPS for 60s to validate aggregation and sampling behavior.
2. Partial failure: Induce an artificial model timeout for 30s and confirm fallback policy is visible in traces and fallback_count metric increases.
3. Token and billing sample: Send a mixture of short/long prompts and compare per-request token metadata to billing token counters.

Acceptance criteria (pass/fail)

Pass requires ALL of the following: (explicit numeric thresholds)
- End-to-end request success rate >= 98% during functional validation.
- Observability latency: metrics ingestion lag <= 60s 95% of the time.
- Traces sampled and linkable: >= 95% of sampled request IDs must map to at least one trace with a model invocation span.
- Header propagation: 100% of sampled requests must contain X-Request-Id and X-Tenant-Id in both logs and inbound request headers.
- Alerts: No unacknowledged critical alerts fired during the bakeoff window (SRE may temporarily mute non-actionable alerts with approval).

Fail conditions (examples)
- Metrics ingestion lag > 120s or >5% metric points lost.
- Traces missing model invocation attributes in >=10% of sampled traces.
- Token accounting divergence >15% vs expected (requires immediate triage).

Telemetry Declaration Template (customer + Redwood sign-off)

Provide the following fields and confirm agreement before canary. Use the minimal JSON snippet below as the canonical declaration that will be attached to the cutover ticket.

--- JSON snippet (single-line friendly) ---
{ "tenant_id": "<tenant-id>", "telemetry_target": "redwood:observability-prod OR customer:apm-endpoint", "metrics": ["ingress_rps","ingress_error_rate","request_latency_p95","token_count_per_request"], "traces_required": true, "log_fields_required": ["request_id","tenant_id","route","status_code"], "ingestion_slo_seconds": 60 }

Notes on fields:
- telemetry_target: specify if telemetry should be forwarded to Redwood ingestion or to a customer-managed APM. If customer-managed, include endpoint and auth in related secure doc.
- traces_required: if false, bakeoff must be approved only for low-risk features; default is true.

Telemetry mapping recommendations

Metric name -> Redwood canonical mapping
- ingress_rps -> telemetry.ingress.rps
- ingress_error_rate -> telemetry.ingress.errors.percentage
- request_latency_p95 -> telemetry.ingress.latency.p95_ms
- token_count_per_request -> telemetry.billing.tokens_per_req

Span attribute recommendations
- model.name (string)
- model.version (string)
- model.invocation_time_ms (number)
- kv_cache_hit (boolean)
- quantized (boolean)
- request.priority (string)

Rollout decision matrix (example)

- Green: All acceptance criteria met -> Proceed to canary (10% traffic) and schedule 2-hour monitoring block.
- Yellow: One non-critical observability gap (e.g., missing optional span attribute) -> Defer canary until quick remediation or allow canary under compensating control (shorter canary, increased sampling). Must be approved by Platform Oncall and CSE.
- Red: Any metric or trace lag failures, token accounting divergence >15%, or missing header propagation -> Halt cutover and open a joint incident with SRE and SE.

Post-bakeoff artifacts (deliverable attachments)

- Bakeoff summary note (1–2 pages).
- Exported sample traces (3–10 traces) with trace IDs.
- Canary dashboard snapshot (PNG).
- Signed Telemetry Declaration JSON (attached to ticket).

Escalation & contact matrix

- First 15m: On-call Platform Engineer (pager) + SE lead slack channel (#se-platform-integration).
- 15–60m: Customer SRE + CSE primary.
- >60m or critical failure: Engineering Incident Lead and Product Integration Owner notified; declare joint incident with runbook id: OB-INGRESS-2028.

Appendix A — Example commands and snippets

Curl header propagation verification:

curl -s -D - -H "X-Request-Id: test-req-123" -H "X-Tenant-Id: tenant-prod-42" https://tenant.example.redwood.ai/v1/generate | jq '.

Telemetry sampling rule (Prometheus-style pseudo):

# Record per-tenant p95 in ms
record: tenant_request_latency_p95_ms = histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket{tenant=~"tenant-prod-.*"}[5m])) by (le, tenant))

APM query example (search traces for a request id):
trace_id = search_traces("attributes.request_id:test-req-123")

Appendix B — Workload generator reference

- Use the ingress-load-tool repo (internal): se-tools/ingress-load-generator. Recommended profile: "enterprise-chat-mixed" (50% short, 30% medium, 20% long).
- Command: ./loadgen --profile enterprise-chat-mixed --tenants tenant-prod-42 --rps 50 --duration 300

Governance and versioning

This document is the canonical bakeoff procedure for enterprise ingress observability. Any deviations must be recorded on the cutover ticket and approved by Customer Success and Platform Oncall. Changes to the Telemetry Declaration template must be reviewed by the Observability Standards working group.

Related documentation and links

- Onboarding post-provisioning stability checklist (internal)
- Observability fallback circuit and customer escalation protocol

Document history

- 2027-11-15: Draft created by Maya Chen.
- 2027-12-06: Added stress test and token accounting checks after SE field feedback.
- 2028-01-10: Revised telemetry SLO to 60s ingestion lag and formalized Telemetry Declaration template.

Contact for questions: Maya Chen (mchen@redwood.ai) or #customer-success-integrations on Slack.

title: WebSocket ingest backpressure & reconnect playbook
content:
Summary

This playbook describes recommended designs, operational controls, and a runbook for WebSocket-based ingestion integrations with Redwood Inference. It is intended for partner integrators, SDK teams, and Customer Success engineers onboarding customers that prefer persistent connection models (WebSocket, bidirectional HTTP/2, or similar). The guidance focuses on: graceful backpressure handling, reconnect and resume semantics, observable signals, and actionable escalation steps when connections degrade.

When to use this playbook

- Customers sending stream-oriented events with low per-message latency requirements (telemetry, conversational tokens, streaming embeddings ingestion).
- Integrations where long-lived client connections reduce overhead and improve responsiveness compared to polling or webhooks.
- Scenarios that must tolerate transient network issues and resume without duplicate processing.

Goals and success criteria

- Maintain end-to-end ingestion availability >= 99.9% (SLO) for customer traffic under normal network conditions.
- Avoid unbounded memory growth in brokers/ingest frontends when downstream is congested.
- Provide deterministic client behavior on reconnect: at-most-once delivery where required, or exactly-once semantics where customers implement idempotency keys.

Architecture patterns (recommended)

1) Terminate WebSocket at a lightweight edge proxy
- Edge (Layer 7) terminates TLS and authenticates the initial request. Use a proxy (Envoy/NGINX) that can do connection-level limits and graceful drain.

2) Forward to an ingestion front-end with internal queuing
- The front-end should accept frames and append to a bounded in-memory queue per-tenant. When limits are reached it applies backpressure by signaling clients (close frame or application-level flow-control message).

3) Decouple consuming workers from the front-end
- Worker pool processes queued messages and writes to durable storage or message bus (Kafka/Rabbit/Cloud Pub/Sub) with independent scaling.

Client best practices

- Authenticate once with a short-lived token and include a tenant id in the opening handshake.
- Support a small receive buffer and cooperative flow control: stop sending if the server sends a "PAUSE" control frame, resume on "RESUME".
- Implement exponential backoff with jitter for reconnect attempts and cap to a reasonable ceiling (e.g., 30s).
- Preserve in-flight message IDs and provide idempotency keys for operations that must be exactly-once.
- Segment large payloads into smaller frames and apply client-side rate limiting.

Server / Redwood-internal best practices

- Per-connection quotas: configure per-tenant and per-connection message and byte rate limits. Default: 200 messages/min and 2 MB/min per connection (tunable).
- Bounded queues: use per-tenant ring buffers with a configurable max (default 10k messages). When full, apply backpressure rather than unbounded allocation.
- Control frames: implement a minimal control protocol on top of WebSocket (CONTROL {type: "PAUSE" | "RESUME" | "ACK" | "NACK"}) to signal clients.

Reconnect and resume semantics

- Lightweight resume: clients include a resume_token assigned by the front-end in the opening handshake. The front-end keeps a short-lived in-memory window mapping tokens -> last-ack position (recommended TTL: 90s).
- Durable resume (for higher guarantees): instruct clients to checkpoint offsets into a durable store (e.g., tenant-state API) after receiving server ACKs.

Backpressure strategies (ordered preference)

1) Cooperative flow-control (preferred)
- Server sends "PAUSE" -> client throttles send rate. Server sends periodic "RESUME" to allow more data.

2) Token bucket token exchange
- Server grants credits to client; client can send up to credits. When depleted, client must stop until new credits arrive.

3) Explicit close with retry hint
- If a tenant exceeds absolute safety limits, close connection with a close code and a retry-after in the close payload. Example: Close(4001, "retry-after=15").

4) Drop oldest (safest for memory control)
- As a last resort, drop oldest messages in the per-tenant ring buffer and emit a metric and audit event. Documenting dropped events is required for customers.

Observable signals and metrics (recommended Prometheus names)

- websocket_connections_total{tenant} (gauge)
- websocket_active_connections{tenant,region} (gauge)
- websocket_messages_in{tenant} (counter)
- websocket_messages_dropped{tenant,reason} (counter)
- websocket_flowcontrol_paused{tenant} (gauge 0/1)
- websocket_resume_requests{tenant} (counter)
- websocket_resume_successes{tenant} (counter)
- websocket_reconnects{tenant} (counter)
- websocket_resume_latency_seconds{quantile="0.5|0.95|0.99"} (histogram)

Alerting thresholds (examples)

- P1: websocket_messages_dropped > 100/min for any enterprise tenant -> page SRE oncall.
- P2: websocket_reconnects increase 10x above baseline in 10m -> create incident and notify CSM.
- P3: websocket_flowcontrol_paused == 1 for > 2m for any top-10 tenant -> create Slack alert to #cs-ops and #platform-ops.

Operational runbook: triage steps

1) Initial intake (first 10 minutes)
- Validate tenant and region in the alert. Pull the last 15 minutes of websocket logs and metrics.
- Check if front-end CPU/memory is saturated, and inspect per-tenant queue occupancy and drop counters.

2) Customer-facing actions (10–30 minutes)
- Communicate immediately via the agreed channel (customer Slack or support ticket): "We have observed increased reconnects/drops. Our team is investigating. Please hold client restarts until we advise."
- If the client is aggressively reconnecting, ask the customer to temporarily increase reconnect jitter or disable immediate retry for 30–60 seconds.

3) Mitigation (30–90 minutes)
- Apply throttles or rate-limits at the edge for the tenant to prevent system-wide destabilization.
- If queue is full and safe, scale worker pool or increase retention for the tenant temporarily (follow capacity guardrails).

4) Root cause & follow-up (90m–7d)
- Correlate with downstream latency, storage write errors, or third-party queue instabilities.
- Produce an RCA for incidents meeting major-incident criteria; include impact, timeline, mitigations, and permanent fixes.

Escalation matrix (owners and contacts)

- First responder: Customer Success Engineer (owner_team: customer-success) -> Slack: @cse-oncall -> Pager: CSE rota.
- Platform on-call: Platform SRE -> Slack: #platform-oncall -> Pager duty: platform-sre.
- Product/ML OPS: for model or runtime regressions affecting throughput -> @mlops-lead.
- Exec escalation: Customer Success Manager -> escalates to Sales/Revenue Ops for high-impact SLAs.

Testing and validation checklist (pre-onboarding)

- Synthetic congestion test: run a client that increases message rate to 3x expected peak and verify backpressure triggers within 90s.
- Resume test: disconnect after N messages, reconnect using resume_token and validate no duplicates or gaps as per configured semantics.
- Chaos test: simulate transient backend errors (DB timeouts, message-bus spikes) and assert system remains within SLO with degradation modes well signaled.

Rollout checklist (for customers moving from webhooks to WebSocket ingestion)

1) Planning
- Confirm tenant capacity profile with Redwood CSM and ensure quotas are provisioned.
- Agree on monitoring workspace and alert routing.

2) Canary (single-tenant)
- Onboard a single production tenant into a canary pool. Run for 72 hours with synthetic traffic.

3) Scale (10% incremental)
- Increase the number of canary tenants in 10% increments while monitoring message_dropped and reconnects.

4) Production cutover
- Schedule a 2-hour maintenance window. Notify customer and Redwood stakeholders. Roll traffic gradually and observe for 2 maintenance windows before full cutover.

Appendix A: example handshake and control frames

- Opening handshake (client -> server):
{
  "type": "OPEN",
  "tenant_id": "tenant-1234",
  "auth_token": "redacted",
  "resume_token": "optional-client-token"
}

- Server PAUSE frame payload: 
{
  "type": "CONTROL",
  "control": "PAUSE",
  "reason": "upstream-backpressure",
  "retry_hint_seconds": 10
}

- Server close example (explicit):
Close code: 4001
Close payload: "retry-after=15;reason=tenant-rate-limit-exceeded"

Appendix B: sample Prometheus alert rule (YAML snippet)

- rule: HighWebsocketDrops
  expr: increase(websocket_messages_dropped[5m]) > 100
  for: 2m
  labels:
    severity: page
  annotations:
    summary: "High websocket message drops for {{ $labels.tenant }}"
    description: "Investigate per-tenant queue pressure and worker throughput."

Ownership and next steps

- Playbook owner: Aisha Rodriguez (Customer Success)
- Platform automation owner: Lucas Patel (Platform SRE)
- Review cadence: This playbook should be reviewed quarterly or after any major WebSocket-related incident.

Contact list

- Support inbox: support@redwood.ai
- CSE oncall rotation: linked in /confluence/people-ops/oncall-rotations
- Platform SRE pager: platform-pager@redwood.ai

Document history

- 2027-02-07: Initial published version by Aisha Rodriguez.
- 2027-03-01: Added Prometheus rule and clarified resume_token TTL (Aisha Rodriguez).

title: Adaptive rate limiter sidecar integration guide
content:
summary:
A prescriptive integration and ops playbook for teams integrating Redwood Inference with an adaptive rate-limiter sidecar (local proxy) to protect downstream capacity, preserve SLAs, and enable graceful degradation during surges.

body:
Overview

Purpose:
This guide describes recommended integration patterns, configuration examples, operational runbooks, monitoring signals, and escalation flow for deploying an adaptive rate-limiter sidecar in front of Redwood Inference API calls. The goal is to protect customer and Redwood capacity, maintain tail-latency SLOs, and provide deterministic degradation (reject/queue/fanout) during overload or degraded model availability.

Scope:
- Applies to enterprise customers and partners deploying a local sidecar in: VPC-hosted Redwood Private, Dedicated customers' edge proxies, or in-k8s service meshes for self-hosts.
- Covers per-tenant and per-route rate control, adaptive backpressure, token-bucket calibrations, and circuit-breaking behavior tied to Redwood response signals.

Intended audience:
- Customer success/solutions engineers implementing production integrations
- Customer SREs operating traffic shaping on the edge
- Redwood account engineers validating go-live readiness

Architecture summary:
Text diagram (request flow):
Client -> Local sidecar (adaptive limiter) -> Upstream Redwood egress (TLS + mTLS optional) -> Redwood ingress -> Model pool

Key design principles:
- Keep server-side throttling as a safety net; sidecar is the primary enforcement for burst smoothing.
- Prefer token-bucket + adaptive rejection over large client-side queues to avoid head-of-line blocking.
- Surface explicit reject responses with an RFC 8470 style guidance header so callers can implement exponential backoff.
- Use short-lived local metrics for fast detection and Redwood-provided upstream latency/error signals for adaptation.

Non‑functional requirements:
- Tail latency SLO (P99) for critical routes: <= 350ms under normal load
- Hard throughput cap per tenant enforced at the sidecar: configurable, default 500 requests/min for dev, 30k requests/min for enterprise (adjust per contract)
- Error budget policy: if 5xx fraction > 1% sustained for 3m, trigger gradual throttling and alerting

Prerequisites and assumptions:
1) Sidecar supports these features: token-bucket, dynamic config API, circuit-breaker, retry budget, rate limiting by route/model-version, and metrics export (Prometheus).
2) Upstream Redwood responses include: X-Redwood-Model, X-Redwood-Request-Latency-ms, X-Redwood-Quota-Remaining (recommended). If not available, work with Redwood enablement to add headers or telemetry forwarding.
3) TLS to Redwood with mutual auth for Dedicated/Private (customer-managed certs or Redwood provisioned).

Configuration examples

1) Token bucket baseline (YAML):

sidecar:
  global_rate_per_tenant: 18000 # requests per minute (example)
  burst_factor: 1.5
  refill_interval_ms: 1000
  min_reject_threshold: 0.85 # start rejecting at 85% of sustained capacity

route_overrides:
  - route: "/v1/generate"
    model_groups: ["small-latency", "medium-accuracy"]
    rate_per_minute: 6000
    burst_factor: 2

2) Adaptive backoff policy (JSON, for dynamic API):
{
  "policy_name": "latency_adaptive",
  "lookback_seconds": 120,
  "p90_latency_threshold_ms": 200,
  "scale_down_factor": 0.8,
  "scale_up_factor": 1.1,
  "min_rate_per_tenant": 1000
}

3) Retry budget config (CLI example):
# avoid retry storms; keep only N in-flight retries per tenant
redwood-sidecarctl set-retry-budget --tenant-id T123 --budget 50 --per-route "/v1/generate"

Operational checklist for go‑live (engineer-run):
1) Pre-check (customer): confirm TLS handshake and certificate validation to Redwood endpoints.
2) Validate metrics pipeline: sidecar -> Prometheus -> Grafana dashboard exists and shows request rate, reject-rate, 5xx-rate, p99 latency.
3) Baseline load test: run 1.2x expected sustained QPS for 15m and confirm P99 < 350ms and reject rate < 2%.
4) Canary rollout: enable sidecar rate limits for 5% traffic, monitor 30m, then 25%, 50%, 100% (standard canary windows).
5) Configure emergency fallback: if Redwood returns 503 or model-unavailable for >30s, sidecar should route to fallback model group or immediately return 429 with guidance header.

Deployment patterns and templates:
- In-k8s (recommended for Dedicated/Private): sidecar as a DaemonSet or per-pod sidecar injection; use ConfigMap for policies and a Deployment for control-plane that publishes dynamic updates.
- VPC edge: sidecar runs on a NATed EC2/GCE instance in the edge subnet with host networking and iptables capture.
- Hybrid: central rate manager that issues per-edge allocations via gRPC ACLs.

Monitoring and SLOs (what to alert on):
- Metrics to collect: requests_total, requests_per_second, rejects_total, retries_total, upstream_5xx_total, upstream_429_total, p50/p95/p99_latency_ms, queue_depth
- Alert thresholds (examples):
  - P99 latency > 500ms for 5m -> P2 (investigate upstream slowness/model pool)
  - Reject rate > 10% for 10m -> P2 (consider increasing tenant cap or route fallback)
  - Upstream 5xx rate > 1% for 3m -> P1 (escalate to Redwood oncall)
  - Queue depth > 1000 -> P2 (prevent unbounded queues; force rejects)

Troubleshooting playbook (step-by-step):
1) Symptom: sudden spike in reject-rate
   - Check sidecar metrics: is burst_factor exhausted? Is token refill rate lower than expected?
   - Check upstream latency headers on 2xx responses. If upstream p95 increased, throttle client or route to fallback model group.
   - If reject-rate persists, temporarily increase per-route rate by 10% for 5 minutes and monitor.

2) Symptom: increased upstream 5xx from Redwood
   - Verify network path (TLS, mTLS cert expiry).
   - Confirm Redwood regional health: call /health endpoint and check Redwood console.
   - If confirmed Redwood degraded, sidecar should enable conservative reject policy (return 429) and surface a user-facing header: X-Redwood-Fallback: true. Notify Redwood CS immediately.

3) Symptom: long tail latency with low QPS
   - Inspect model choice: certain model variants have much higher decoding latency. Match sidecar route to model-group latency profile.
   - If model change required, use blue/green route remap and a 10% canary first.

Escalation matrix and contacts:
- Triage owner (customer SRE): Primary on-call.
- Redwood CS AE: listed in the customer contract (include direct Slack #id and pager).
- Redwood oncall (platform): use Redwood paged channel when upstream 5xx > 1% and persists > 3m.
- Escalation procedure:
  1. Triage owner confirms issue and time window.
  2. If Redwood upstream suspected, open Redwood support ticket and tag with request-id examples.
  3. If degradation impacts SLAs, escalate to Redwood enterprise engineering via dedicated channel.

Sample status message template for customer comms:
- Subject: Service impact for Redwood inference (region us-west-2)
- Body: We observed elevated error rates between 14:03-14:28 UTC on 2026-02-03 impacting generative endpoints. The local rate-limiter enforced backpressure and served 429 responses to preserve P99 latency. We are investigating with Redwood engineering and will provide a 60m update.

Rollback and emergency mitigation steps:
1) Disable adaptive scaling and revert to conservative static limits while preserving reject behavior.
2) If sidecar misconfiguration is root cause, reload prior ConfigMap and restart pods in a controlled rolling manner (1 pod at a time).
3) As last resort, bypass sidecar for affected routes by updating service mesh traffic rules to route directly to upstream. Notify Redwood before bypassing to avoid capacity overrun.

Testing and validation checklist (post-deploy):
- Load tests covering steady-state and spikes (1s surge, 5m sustained)
- Chaos test: simulate 20% instance loss at upstream and validate sidecar rejects and fallback behavior
- Regression: verify headers X-Redwood-Request-Latency-ms and X-Redwood-Model are propagated to metrics and logs

FAQ and recommendations:
Q: Should we place the sidecar in front of every client or centralize at the edge?
A: Per-client sidecars offer finest-grained control and faster local adaptation; central edge proxies simplify operational ownership. Choose per-scale tradeoffs; for enterprise Dedicated we recommend edge placement with per-tenant logical quotas.

Q: How to handle bursty single-tenant traffic that risks collateral degradation?
A: Implement per-route burst caps and isolate high-risk tenants into their own rate domain or dedicated pool. Configure blackout windows for heavy background jobs.

Change log:
- 2026-01-12: Initial draft (Maya Chen)
- 2026-01-20: Added adaptive policy examples and monitoring thresholds (Diego Martinez)
- 2026-02-04: Finalized escalation matrix and rollout checklist (Lina Patel)

Appendix: Example Prometheus queries
- Reject rate: sum(rate(sidecar_rejects_total[5m])) by (tenant) / sum(rate(sidecar_requests_total[5m])) by (tenant)
- Upstream 5xx: sum(rate(sidecar_upstream_5xx_total[5m]))
- P99 latency: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(sidecar_request_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le))

Ownership and next steps:
- Primary owner: Customer Success - Integrations (Maya Chen)
- Engineering contact: Runtime Integrations (Arjun Rao)
- Next step: schedule customer go-live game day with Redwood enablement and run the Operational checklist above.

References:
- Related runbook: /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/traffic-shaping-and-throttling-standards
- Redwood header recommendations: please coordinate with Redwood account engineer to enable X-Redwood-* headers for telemetry enrichment.

title: edge-cache-consistency-and-embedding-sync-strategy-2026
content:
Overview
--------
This playbook describes an operational and engineering pattern for keeping edge caches, local CDN layers, and downstream embedding indexes (vector DBs) consistent for enterprise customers during normal operation, model upgrades, and bulk backfills. It is intended for integration engineers, customer success engineers (CSEs), and SREs working with enterprise tenants that maintain local inference front-ends, CDN caching layers, or dual-write ingestion paths to Redwood-hosted vector stores.

Goals
- Minimize end-user staleness for retrieval/semantic search use cases (target: median staleness < 30s for streaming ingest workloads).
- Provide clear invalidation and reconciliation primitives so Customer Success and Engineering can recover from divergence without data loss.
- Keep operational complexity reasonable for customers using a mix of Redwood-hosted vector stores and on-prem caching.

Scope and audience
- Applies to enterprise onboarding where customers integrate: local edge caches (Redis/ElastiCache/Memcached), CDN edge (Fastly/Cloudflare), and/or self-hosted vector databases with Redwood telemetry and webhook sinks.
- Not meant for simple read-only CDN caching of static assets (those are covered by CDN caching policy docs).

Key concepts and invariants
1) Source of truth: The canonical ingestion stream is the customer’s committed write to the canonical dataset (event platform, S3 object commit, or Redwood ingestion API). Vector stores and edge caches are derived stores.
2) Causal ordering: Ingest events must carry a monotonic sequence token (event_id or commit_ts) so that out-of-order delivery can be detected and reconciled.
3) Idempotency: All ingest APIs and webhook handlers must accept a client-generated idempotency_key or event_id.
4) Soft-state & TTL: Edge caches are soft-state and should have conservative TTLs that reflect ingestion velocity and desired staleness SLAs.

Recommended architecture patterns
- Dual-write with durable queue: Customer writes to their primary store and emits an event to a durable pub/sub (Kafka/Kinesis). Redwood subscribes to the durable queue. Edge caches and downstream vectorization pipelines consume from the same stream to ensure consistent ordering.
- Single-writer reconciliation: If the customer cannot dual-write, Redwood provides a periodic reconciliation job that compares the canonical dataset (via list-objects/manifest) with the vector DB index watermark.
- Watermark propagation: Each processed document must propagate a processing watermark (doc_id + commit_ts + model_hash) into the vector DB metadata and cache keys.

Configuration reference (recommended defaults)
| parameter | meaning | recommended default | rationale |
|-----------|---------|--------------------|----------|
| edge_cache_ttl_seconds | TTL for edge key | 45 | Balances low-latency reads with frequency of writes for typical chat/search workloads |
| reconciliation_interval_minutes | Interval for full index reconciliation job | 60 | Hourly ensures outliers are caught quickly without heavy compute |
| webhook_retry_policy | Exponential retry config for webhooks | 5 attempts, base 2s | Works with most customer endpoints behind load balancers |
| idempotency_key_ttl_days | How long to keep idempotency keys server-side | 14 | Allows safe replays during backlog windows |
| stale_threshold_seconds | Alert threshold for embedding staleness | 300 | Triggers investigation into backpressure or pipeline failures |

Example integration patterns and sample configs
- Sample webhook payload (customer -> Redwood ingestion):

{
  "event_id": "evt-20260501-0001",
  "doc_id": "tenant/123/doc/456",
  "commit_ts": "2026-05-01T14:22:07Z",
  "content_url": "s3://tenant-prod/objects/456.json",
  "metadata": {"tenant_id":"tenant-123","source":"app-frontend"},
  "idempotency_key": "uuid-v4-client-generated"
}

- Sample Redis cache key schema: 
  key: tenant:{tenant_id}:doc:{doc_id}:v{model_hash}:watermark:{commit_ts}
  value: {embedding_vector_base64, vector_ts, model_hash}

- Example webhook consumer pseudocode (idempotent):
  1. parse payload, validate auth signature
  2. if seen_event(event_id): ack and return 200
  3. fetch content_url for vectorization (or use payload embedding if provided)
  4. compute embedding (model_hash), upsert vector DB with metadata (id, vector, commit_ts, model_hash)
  5. write edge cache key with TTL and watermark
  6. ack event

Operational signals to monitor (SLOs and alerts)
- Ingest throughput: events/sec per tenant (alert if sustained > 2x baseline without scaling).
- Embedding processing backlog: number of events older than 2x median processing latency (alert: >500 events).
- Staleness metric: proportion of top-100 retrievals that read documents with vector_ts older than commit_ts by > stale_threshold_seconds (SLA: <1% daily).
- Edge cache miss spike: rate of cache misses per tenant per minute (alert threshold: 3x baseline).
- Reconciliation drift: percent of doc_ids mismatched during hourly reconciliation (alert: >0.5% for 3 consecutive runs).

Runbook: common incident scenarios and play actions
A. Missing embeddings for new documents (symptoms: retrieval returns older version or null)
1. Check ingestion stream health: verify upstream durable queue consumer lag (Kafka consumer lag metrics).
2. Confirm webhook delivery: check webhook delivery logs for 4xx/5xx responses. Look for recent retry storms.
3. If backlog present: kick off backfill job (one-off reprocess) scoped to tenant+time window. Use the safe backfill process below.
4. Post-backfill: run quick reconciliation (sample top 500 doc_ids) and validate retrieval quality. Communicate to CSE and affected product stakeholders.

B. Edge cache returns stale vectors after model upgrade
1. Verify model_hash propagated into new vector records. If model_hash mismatch between cache and vector DB, invalidate cache keys for affected tenant/model_hash combos.
2. Force soft invalidation via pub/sub invalidate topic: publish {tenant_id, model_hash, since_commit_ts}. Edge cache consumers should delete keys or set zero-TTL marker.
3. If invalidation publishing failed, run targeted keyscan and delete patterns (use guarded delete job with QPS limit to avoid thrashing).
4. Notify customer success and schedule a validation query batch.

C. Divergence after network partition (partial writes)
1. Identify diverged namespaces by comparing watermarks between canonical manifests and vector DB metadata.
2. Run snapshot reconciliation for namespaces with divergence, then queue up differential revectorization.
3. Coordinate a maintenance window with the customer if the reconciliation workload will cause increased latency or incur costs.

Safe backfill and throttled reconciliation procedure
1. Create a reconciliation manifest (list of doc_ids and commit_ts) for target tenant/time range.
2. Stage on a reconciliation worker fleet with rate limits configured (default: 100 docs/sec per tenant).
3. Use idempotent upserts to vector DB and do not evict cache until the worker completes the document and writes the new watermark key.
4. Emit progress metrics: processed_count, failures_count, average_latency. Alert if failure_rate > 1%.
5. When complete, publish completion event and run a sampling sanity check (n=100).

Communication & customer success playbook for divergence events
- Triage owner: Assigned CSE + oncall platform engineer.
- Initial customer comms (within 60 minutes): acknowledge, scope impact (estimated % of affected queries), mitigation steps underway.
- Follow-up (24–72 hours): provide RCA draft, remediation timeline, and any credit/compensation guidance (use enterprise SLA matrix).

Tooling and dashboards to ship with an integration
- Per-tenant ingestion lag dashboard (95th/median lag)
- Reconciliation job dashboard (processed rate, drift %, error rate)
- Recent invalidation events list (with status: queued, in-progress, completed)
- Top retrieval divergence samples (side-by-side vectors and commit_ts)

Troubleshooting checklist (quick)
- Are webhook signatures failing? Check shared secret rotation windows.
- Is the durable queue healthy? Check partition reassignment or hot partitions.
- Are reconciliations running and reporting zero progress? Inspect worker autoscaling and IAM permissions for reading canonical manifests.
- Are cache eviction patterns coordinated with model upgrades? Always deploy upgrade + invalidation together.

Owner & escalation path
- Integration lead (owner): CSE assigned in the onboarding engagement.
- Platform escalation (24/7): platform-sre oncall via Slack #sre-redwood and PagerDuty.
- Engineering escalation: eng-serving-runtime oncall for vectorization pipeline failures.

Appendix: example CLI snippets
- Trigger a targeted backfill for tenant-123 for last 6 hours:
  redwood-cli backfill start --tenant tenant-123 --from "2026-05-04T00:00:00Z" --to "2026-05-04T06:00:00Z" --rate 50

- Publish an invalidate event to pubsub (idempotent):
  curl -X POST https://pubsub.redwood.internal/invalidate \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer ${TOKEN}" \
    -d '{"tenant_id":"tenant-123","model_hash":"m-2026-05-01-a1b2","since_commit_ts":"2026-05-01T00:00:00Z"}'

Related reading
- embeddings-index-consistency-and-rollback-workarounds-2026 (internal)
- tenant-stability-synthetic-scenarios-and-mtr-playbook-2026 (internal)

Change log
- 2026-03-10: Initial draft by Lena Murray.
- 2026-04-12: Added watermark patterns and reconciliation defaults (reviewer: Diego Santos).
- 2026-05-04: Expanded runbook sections and added CLI examples (reviewer: Priya Nair).

title: adaptive-model-fallback-and-fanout-proxy-integration-playbook-2026
content:
Summary:
This playbook describes recommended integration patterns, configuration examples, and operational runbook items for customers that want to deploy an adaptive model-fallback strategy using a fanout/proxy layer in front of Redwood Inference endpoints. The goal is to provide resilient, cost-aware routing that maintains SLOs while exposing deterministic controls to platform engineers.

Scope and audience:
- Audience: Customer success engineers, platform engineers, SREs integrating Redwood inference into production services.
- Applies to: Hosted API, Dedicated, and Private deployments where a proxy/fanout layer is used for model routing, A/B, or capacity-tier fallbacks.
- Not covered: Internal kernel/runtime tuning; see eng-serving-runtime docs for low-level optimizations.

Motivation and outcomes:
- Reduce user-visible errors during model upgrades, regional outages, or capacity limits.
- Automatically route or fanout requests to secondary model variants when primary routes exceed latency or error thresholds.
- Provide cost control by routing non-critical workloads to cheaper quantized variants.
- Emit consistent telemetry for billing, evaluation, and QBRs.

Key concepts:
- Primary/Secondary model variants: Named endpoint or model version pairs configured with compatibility metadata (token limits, format expectations).
- Fanout proxy: The intermediary service that can replicate requests (read-only checks, shadowing) or route requests to a single back end.
- Adaptive policy engine: Evaluates runtime signals (latency p50/p95, error rate, token spend) and decides to failover, degrade quality, or throttle.
- Deterministic fallback: A predictable and auditable mapping (e.g., primary->fallback-quantized->fallback-llm2) so rollbacks and billing attribution are safe.

Pre-integration checklist (customer-side):
1) Identify primary request classes and SLOs (latency p95, availability target, max per-request cost).
2) Ensure model compatibility: prompt schemas, function-calling contracts, and tokenization behaviors.
3) Provision Redwood API keys and endpoint mapping for the primary and fallback model endpoints; record model versions.
4) Define telemetry tags that will be used by the proxy to annotate requests (tenant_id, route_id, fallback_reason, model_variant).
5) Agree on billing attribution policy with finance (how fallback calls are charged when triggered by the platform).

Architecture patterns (3 recommended):
A) Thin router with deterministic failover (low complexity)
- Behavior: Proxy routes single request to primary; upon configurable error/timeout/failure policy, sequentially retries to fallback variants.
- Use when: Small latency overhead budget, deterministic cost expectations.
- Pros: Predictable billing, simple tracing.
- Cons: Potential delay on failover path.

B) Concurrent fanout with race policy (parallel first-success wins)
- Behavior: Proxy issues parallel requests to primary and one or more fallback variants; first successful response is returned.
- Use when: Ultra-low tail-latency is critical and extra cost is acceptable for cold starts.
- Pros: Best p99 latency in many failure modes.
- Cons: Higher token cost and complexity in deduplication.

C) Shadowing + sampling for quality regression detection
- Behavior: Primary responses are returned to users; the same request is sent asynchronously (shadowed) to fallback/experimental variants for offline evaluation.
- Use when: Deploying new quantized models or tuned prompt sets; requires acceptance testing.
- Pros: Safe production testing; collects eval signals.
- Cons: Requires storage for shadow traces and eval pipeline.

Configuration examples
- Example router decision YAML (thin router):

router:
  default_policy: sequential_failover
  timeout_ms: 1200
  retries: 0
  model_priority:
    - name: redwood-prod/gptx-1.0
      max_tokens: 2048
      tag: primary
    - name: redwood-prod/gptx-quant-1.0
      max_tokens: 2048
      tag: fallback-quant
    - name: redwood-open/llm-lite-0.9
      max_tokens: 1024
      tag: fallback-lowcost
  signals:
    latency_p95_threshold_ms: 900
    error_rate_threshold_pct: 2.0
  telemetry_tags:
    - tenant_id
    - route_id
    - fallback_reason

- Example concurrent fanout JSON snippet (proxy):

{
  "strategy": "concurrent_fanout",
  "fanout_targets": [
    {"model": "redwood-prod/gptx-1.0", "weight": 0.7},
    {"model": "redwood-prod/gptx-quant-1.0", "weight": 0.3}
  ],
  "response_policy": "first_success",
  "dedupe_id_header": "X-Request-Id",
  "cost_cap_usd": "5.00"
}

Telemetry and SLOs to monitor (suggested):
- Per-route p50/p95/p99 latency (primary and fallback metrics separated).
- End-to-end error rate (4xx vs 5xx split) and fallback-trigger rate.
- Token spend per tenant per day and per-request token delta when fallback occurs.
- Shadow-eval regression rate: percentage of shadow requests that fail automated quality checks.
- Fanout duplicate suppression failures and occurrence of partial responses.

Suggested alert thresholds:
- Primary route p95 > 1.5x SLO for 5m -> P1 alert to SRE + CS on-call
- Fallback-trigger rate > 5% of total requests for 15m -> P2, investigate capacity or model degradation
- Token spend rate > expected burn rate by 20% -> Finance notification and temporary throttling

Operational runbook (triage steps)
1) If p95 spikes on primary route:
  a) Confirm if latency is localized (single region/tenant) or global via per-region dashboards.
  b) Check Redwood runtime health (model queue lengths, GPU load) and fanout proxy logs for timeout reasons.
  c) If primary is degraded and the proxy policy is sequential_failover, validate fallback responses are compatible with request schema.
  d) If immediate mitigation needed, update router to route to fallback-quant for affected routes and annotate in the incident.
2) If error rate increases and appears across variants:
  a) Pull recent prompts for top failing requests (use sampled traces).
  b) Validate prompt format/metadata changes from client code.
  c) Engage model-onboarding team if regression ties to model update.
3) If concurrency/deduplication failures observed in fanout:
  a) Inspect dedupe_id header propagation (X-Request-Id) and retry logic in client.
  b) Enable temporary sampling at 10% with shadowing disabled to reduce duplicate workload.

Compatibility and contract checklist
- Function/tool calling: ensure the fallback model supports invoked function schema or proxy will need to transform calls.
- Tokenization: annotate expected token usage per model in the router config.
- Response format: fallback variants must preserve critical structured fields or proxy must map/normalize them.
- Idempotency: client should set idempotency keys for non-idempotent side effects; proxy must forward key to all fanout targets if parallel.

Security and privacy considerations
- PII in shadowing: do not enable shadowing for requests flagged as sensitive unless destination model is permitted (see security-and-compliance/data-residency-and-retention).
- API keys: store Redwood credentials in a secrets manager; rotate keys per customer policy. Proxy should use short-lived tokens for upstream calls.
- Audit logging: annotate fallback_reason in audit logs and include model_variant to support billing and compliance requests.

Cost control knobs
- Cap fanout concurrency per tenant and enforce a per-tenant daily token cap.
- Use cheaper quantized models for sampled traffic and non-interactive routes (batch scoring).
- Configure the router with a cost_cap_usd to prevent runaway spend during incidents.

Testing and rollout plan
1) Local integration smoke tests: unit tests for header propagation, idempotency, and timeout handling.
2) Canary rollout: route 1% traffic through the proxy policy with shadowing enabled for secondary models. Verify metrics for 48 hours.
3) Incremental ramp: 1% -> 5% -> 20% over monitored windows, verifying shadow-eval pass rate and token spend.
4) Full switch with feature-flag toggle and ability to rollback in under 5 minutes.

Example test checklist (pass/fail criteria):
- 1000 synthetic requests: 0 critical schema mismatches returned by fallback.
- Shadow-eval difference in key metric (e.g., hallucination rate) < 3% over baseline.
- p99 end-to-end latency increase < 15% when concurrent fanout is enabled at 5% sampling.

Troubleshooting matrix (top issues):
- Symptom: Fallback returns truncated function-call JSON.
  Cause: Fallback model max_tokens lower than primary.
  Action: Increase max_tokens on fallback config or add post-processing normalization.

- Symptom: Unexpected cost spike during outage.
  Cause: Concurrent fanout without cost_cap or retries multiplied by proxies.
  Action: Disable parallel fanout; revert to sequential_failover and contact customer success.

- Symptom: Shadow-eval storage backlog.
  Cause: No downstream consumer or storage throttling.
  Action: Pause shadowing; provision temporary storage and backfill once consumer is restored.

Ownership and contacts:
- CS integration lead: Aisha Patel (author) — for playbook questions and live cutovers.
- Runtime escalation: eng-serving-runtime on-call (see runbooks).
- Model compatibility: Model Onboarding team (model-onboarding).
- Security review/approvals: security-and-compliance team.

Appendix A — Example proxy health check CLI
# curl health check to proxy
curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $PROXY_TOKEN" https://proxy.example.com/health | jq

Appendix B — Minimal sample router change for emergency rollback (CLI snippet)
# set route to fallback-quant immediately
redwood-routerctl set-route --route-id orders-completion --policy sequential_failover --model redwood-prod/gptx-quant-1.0 --annotation "emergency-rollback"

title: Streaming webhook retry strategies and deduplication guide
content:
Overview

This guide describes recommended patterns for delivering high-throughput streaming events from Redwood APIs (or any Redwood-backed pipeline) to customer webhook endpoints with robust retry behavior and deduplication. It is intended for technical owners on both Redwood and customer sides: customer-success engineers, integration engineers, SREs, and platform teams.

Goals

- Maximize end-to-end delivery success while maintaining predictable latency and avoiding duplicate side effects at customer systems.
- Provide concrete recommended retry schedules, idempotency semantics, and storage/TTL guidance for deduplication keys.
- Define observability, runbook steps, and escalation ownership for webhook delivery incidents.

Delivery semantics primer

- At-least-once: Redwood attempts delivery until success or an expiry condition; duplicates are possible and customers must guard against repeated processing.
- Best-effort exactly-once: Achieved by combining idempotency keys + deduplication windows at the recipient. The architecture below describes how to approach this pattern.

SLOs and thresholds (examples)

- Successful first-attempt delivery rate: >= 99.0% over 30d for customer endpoints with 200ms median response times.
- End-to-end success within retry window: >= 99.9% over 30d.
- Mean time to detect webhook delivery outage (alerting): <= 5 minutes.
- Duplicate delivery rate (observed duplicates processed): <= 0.05% for well-instrumented customers.

When to apply these patterns

- Recommended for event-driven integrations with side effects (billing, user notification, state mutation).
- Optional for purely idempotent / read-only consumers (batch analytics webhooks may accept relaxed deduplication).

Recommended architecture (high level)

1) Redwood outbound delivery service (owned by eng-infra/eng-platform): persistent queue, per-customer delivery workers, per-destination backoff and concurrency limits.
2) Delivery metadata: include a stable event_id, event_type, timestamp, and an idempotency_key header.
3) Recipient deduplication store: short-lived datastore (Redis, DynamoDB with TTL attributes, or Postgres table with TTL enforcement) keyed by idempotency_key/event_id.

Message contract (required fields)

- HTTP header: X-Redwood-Event-ID: <uuid-v4>
- HTTP header: X-Redwood-Event-Type: <string>
- HTTP header: X-Redwood-Idempotency-Key: <sha256 or custom>
- HTTP header: X-Redwood-Signature: sha256=HEX_SIGNATURE (see Security section)
- Body: JSON payload with an explicit "event_version" and canonical "payload" object.

Example payload

{
  "event_version": "1.0",
  "payload": {
    "user_id": "acct_123",
    "action": "model.inference.completed",
    "meta": {"model": "redwood-llm-v2", "latency_ms": 142}
  }
}

HTTP status mapping and recommendations

- 200 / 2xx: Success — Redwood marks delivery succeeded and stops retries.
- 429: Throttle — treat as transient. Retry using exponential backoff with jitter.
- 5xx: Transient server error — retry using exponential backoff with capped max interval.
- 408 / 499 / network errors: Transient — retry.
- 4xx (400, 401, 403): Permanent failure (client code issue or auth). Do not retry automatically; surface to integrations team and customer.

Recommended retry schedule (example)

- Immediate retry policy with exponential backoff + jitter. Conservative schedule used across Redwood: 

  Attempt 1: 0s (initial)
  Attempt 2: 5s + jitter (0-2s)
  Attempt 3: 30s + jitter (0-10s)
  Attempt 4: 2m + jitter (0-30s)
  Attempt 5: 10m + jitter (0-60s)
  Attempt 6: 1h + jitter (0-10m) — final attempt before expiry

- Default expiry window: 6 hours for non-critical events; 24–72 hours for business-critical events (negotiated in contract).
- Note: Customers may configure shorter windows in their destination configuration.

Idempotency and deduplication guidance

1) Idempotency key content: preferred: stable event_id (UUID v4) or sha256(event_id || tenant_id).
2) Deduplication window: set TTL = min(expiry_window + 10%, 7d). For typical 6h expiry, TTL ~7h. For 72h expiry, TTL ~4d.
3) Storage options:
   - Redis: fast checks, set NX with TTL. Good for sub-day windows.
   - DynamoDB: durable, can store more metadata; use TTL attribute and conditional put.
   - Postgres: use unique constraint on (event_id, tenant_id) with background cleanup; better if you already have transactional DB.
4) Accept-late-arrival semantic: if a duplicate arrives outside TTL, treat as new event or log as late duplicate per customer policy.

Example dedup pseudocode (Redis)

// pseudo-code
IF SETNX("dedupe:<idempotency_key>", "1", EXPIRE=ttl_seconds) == 1:
  // first-seen -> process
ELSE:
  // duplicate -> ack (200) and skip processing

Security: signature verification and replay protection

- Redwood signs payloads with HMAC-SHA256 using per-customer webhook secret. Signature is included in X-Redwood-Signature. Example header: 
  X-Redwood-Signature: sha256=4b6f...

- Verification example (pseudo-shell):
  expected=$(echo -n "$BODY" | openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac "$WEBHOOK_SECRET")
  if [ "$expected" != "$HEADER_SIG" ]; then reject (401)

- Replay protection: ensure idempotency_key and dedupe store are used. Optionally enforce timestamp freshness (X-Redwood-Timestamp) rejecting events older than a configurable window (default 24h).

Observability and metrics (instrumentation)

- Metrics to emit: delivery_attempts_total, delivery_success_total, delivery_failures_by_status_code, delivery_latency_ms_histogram, duplicate_events_acked_total, per_destination_concurrency, per_destination_queue_depth.
- Dashboards: per-customer delivery success rate, rolling-24h failure rate, average retry count, and top 10 failing endpoints.
- Alerts: trigger when a single destination has >1% failure rate over 10m and >100 attempts, or when delivery latency p50 > 5s for 5m.

Testing and validation checklist (for customers)

1) Provide a stable webhook endpoint that responds to GET or 200 to validate.
2) Share webhook secret for signature verification testing (use staging secret first).
3) Validate idempotency behavior by sending the same X-Redwood-Event-ID twice: first should be processed, second should be acknowledged without duplicate side effect.
4) Load test: exercise 10–50 rps for a sandbox destination to validate rate limiting and concurrency.

Sample curl test (signature omitted for brevity)

curl -X POST https://myendpoint.example.com/webhooks \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'X-Redwood-Event-ID: 9f8e7c1e-...-4a12' \
  -H 'X-Redwood-Idempotency-Key: 9f8e7c1e-...-4a12' \
  -d '{"event_version":"1.0","payload":{"action":"model.inference.completed","user_id":"acct_123"}}'

Operational runbook (common failure scenarios)

- Scenario: Large spike of 5xx errors from customer endpoint.
  1) Automatically increase backoff and reduce per-destination concurrency to 1 for 30m.
  2) Post incident in #cs-integrations with destination id, sample failures, and last successful timestamp.
  3) Notify customer success owner and schedule call if >30% messages failing after 1h.

- Scenario: Customer responding 4xx to all requests (401/403).
  1) Mark destination as "authentication error" in admin UI and suspend retries.
  2) Open a ticket to customer contacts, include sample request/response, and request resolution.

- Scenario: Duplicate processing observed by customer.
  1) Verify event IDs from logs and delivery requests.
  2) Confirm dedupe store TTL and existence.
  3) If Redwood caused duplicate replays (bug), escalate to eng-serving-runtime and run a hotfix rollout.

Rollout checklist for new customer webhook integration

- Pre-onboarding: confirm recipient supports HTTPS: TLS 1.2+, can verify HMAC signatures, provides a single stable URL, and has an owner + escalation contact.
- Sandbox phase (0–2 days): set up staging secret, run smoke tests, observe 100% first-attempt success in sandbox.
- Pilot phase (2–7 days): ramp to partial traffic (5–20%); monitor error rate and latency; exercise retries and dup detection.
- Go-live: switch route config to 100% traffic and maintain elevated monitoring for 72h.

Ownership and escalation

- Day-to-day owner: customer-success integrations engineer (CS Integrations).
- Escalation path: CS Integrations -> SRE oncall -> Eng Platform -> Eng Serving Runtime.
- Communication templates: include: event_id list, sample timestamps, last 10 delivery responses, and suggested action items.

Compatibility notes with Redwood features

- Batching and KV cache: if the webhook is triggered by a batched job (e.g., model inference group), events should include a batch_id in the payload to allow customers to coalesce processing.
- Model variant fallbacks: if Redwood automatically routes to a fallback model, event metadata will include fallback.reason and fallback.replaced_model. Customers should treat these events identically unless they filter by model.

Appendix A — Example headers and signature verification (Node.js snippet)

const crypto = require('crypto')
function verifySignature(body, headerSig, secret) {
  const expected = 'sha256=' + crypto.createHmac('sha256', secret).update(body).digest('hex')
  return crypto.timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(expected), Buffer.from(headerSig))
}

Appendix B — Example DynamoDB dedupe item (JSON)

{
  "EventId": "9f8e7c1e-...",
  "TenantId": "acct_123",
  "CreatedAt": "2026-01-20T15:12:34Z",
  "TTL": 1700000000
}

Change log

- 2025-09-14: Initial draft.
- 2025-11-02: Added example retry schedule and Redis pseudocode.
- 2026-02-03: Expanded runbook and ownership sections; added SLOs and metrics.

Related resources

- Integrations admin UI guide: confluence: /customer-success-and-support/integration-guides (see admin webhook config page).
- Eng-serving-runtime delivery queue design: confluence: /eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/delivery-queue-design.json

If you are integrating a Redwood webhook and need help during onboarding, contact CS Integrations (cs-integrations@redwood.ai) and include the destination id and a reproduction plan.

title: Adaptive ingress batching and error backoff guide
content:
Overview

Purpose
This guide describes recommended patterns, configuration defaults, and operational playbooks for adaptive batching and error backoff on inbound inference requests. It is intended for customer integration engineers, solutions architects, and SREs who implement or validate connectors that send traffic to Redwood Inference (hosted, dedicated, or private).

Scope and assumptions
- Applies to both streaming (chunked / websocket) and synchronous HTTP/REST ingest paths.
- Assumes a proxy or sidecar exists in the customer environment which can buffer, batch, and retry (e.g., Envoy, custom sidecar, or managed connector).
- Focus on reducing tail latency, preventing overload, and preserving SLOs during transient errors and capacity surges.

When to apply adaptive batching
- High request parallelism with many short requests (avg tokens < 80) where per-request overhead dominates cost.
- Periods of bursty traffic where dynamic batch sizing reduces GPU utilization variance.
- Environments where upstream rate-limits or quota errors are returned (HTTP 429 / 503) and a coordinated retry/backoff strategy is required.

Design goals
- Preserve p95/p99 latency SLOs for interactive flows while reducing per-token cost for bulk flows.
- Prevent cascade failures by bounding queueing and applying circuit-breaker logic.
- Maintain request ordering and idempotency guarantees where required by the customer workload.

Architecture (textual diagram)
Client -> Ingress proxy/sidecar (batcher) -> Rate limiter / circuit breaker -> Redwood edge -> Serving runtime

Key components and responsibilities
- Batcher: groups small requests into a single request payload when beneficial. Responsible for configurable max batch size, max waiting time, and priority queues.
- Retry controller: applies retry policy with exponential backoff + jitter, respects server-provided Retry-After headers and throttle signals.
- Circuit breaker: trips under elevated error rates or increased p99 serve latency to fail fast and avoid queue buildup.
- Metrics & tracer: emits per-batch and per-request metrics (see metrics section) and attaches trace ids for correlation.

Configuration recommended defaults (table)
Parameter | Default | Rationale
--------|---------|-------
max_batch_size | 16 | Fits typical GPU parallelism for small requests; tune upward for long-context models
max_batch_latency_ms | 30 | Limits additional wait introduced by batching to keep interactive latency under 200ms p95
min_batch_size | 1 | Allows passthrough for single request when latency-critical or when queue is empty
batch_priority_threshold_tokens | 120 | Requests longer than this are sent in dedicated batches to avoid head-of-line blocking
queue_capacity | 200 | Prevents unbounded memory growth; choose based on sidecar memory profile
circuit_breaker_error_pct | 20 | Trip if >20% of calls in sliding window fail (adjust per tenant SLA)
cb_window_seconds | 60 | Sliding evaluation window
retry_policy | exponential_jitter | Backoff base 200ms, multiplier 2, max 5 attempts
retry_on | 429, 503, 502, network_errors | Only retry transient errors; 4xx otherwise returned to caller
respect_retry_after | true | Honor Retry-After header from Redwood endpoints or upstream proxies
health_check_interval_s | 10 | Periodic probe to recovery endpoints when circuit open

JSON example: sidecar batcher config snippet
{
  "batch": {
    "max_batch_size": 16,
    "max_batch_latency_ms": 30,
    "min_batch_size": 1,
    "priority_token_threshold": 120
  },
  "retry": {
    "policy": "exponential_jitter",
    "initial_backoff_ms": 200,
