    "multiplier": 2.0,
    "max_attempts": 5,
    "retry_on": [429, 503, 502]
  },
  "circuit_breaker": {
    "error_percentage": 20,
    "window_seconds": 60
  }
}

Integration steps (recommended)
1) Validate call pattern: capture token distribution and request latencies for 48–72 hours in staging. Calculate median tokens and 95th percentile tokens.
2) Start conservative: enable batching with max_batch_size=8 and max_batch_latency_ms=50. Run traffic through sidecar to verify latency impact.
3) Ramp: increase max_batch_size incrementally (8 -> 16 -> 32) while monitoring p95 latency and GPU utilization.
4) Enable retry policy with max_attempts=3 and exponential backoff for staging tests against induced 429/503 responses.
5) Configure circuit breaker thresholds and test circuit open/close behavior via synthetic failures.
6) Go-live: adopt final config and schedule a monitored window (72 hours) with on-call coverage.

Operational runbook: alerts and triage
Primary metrics to monitor (metric names are Redwood conventions; map if using custom telemetry):
- ingress.batcher.active_batches (gauge)
- ingress.batcher.avg_batch_size (gauge)
- ingress.request.latency.p95 (histogram)
- ingress.request.errors.count (counter) broken down by status code
- ingress.sidecar.queue_length (gauge)
- ingress.sidecar.circuit_open (boolean)
- upstream.retry_after_rate (counter)

Primary alerts (suggested thresholds)
- High queue growth: ingress.sidecar.queue_length > 150 for 2m -> Severity: high -> Action: investigate traffic spike; scale sidecar replicas or reduce max_batch_size
- Increased client latency: ingress.request.latency.p95 > 500ms for 5m -> Severity: high -> Action: check batch latency, inspect avg_batch_size, and triage for hotspot model or throttling
- Elevated error rate: ingress.request.errors.count (4xx/5xx) > 5% for 3m -> Severity: critical -> Action: check circuit breaker status, inspect upstream 429/503 patterns, escalate to CS/Platform if widespread
- Circuit breaker open: ingress.sidecar.circuit_open == true -> Severity: medium -> Action: follow circuit-breaker remediation steps below

Circuit-breaker remediation steps
1. Confirm scope: determine whether circuit breaker is tenant-specific or global. Check sidecar logs and metric tags.
2. Inspect error distribution: are errors 429/503 from Redwood or network errors?
3. If transient upstream 429s: temporarily decrease request concurrency and enable longer backoff; notify Redwood CS if persistent.
4. If the circuit is open and healthy probes fail, scale sidecar and/or reduce ingress ingress rate at the client.
5. If issue persists >30 minutes, create an incident and escalate to Redwood Support per the escalation matrix below.

Escalation matrix (recommended)
- First-line: customer integration engineer / on-call platform engineer (0–15 minutes) — perform immediate triage and apply local mitigations (reduce concurrency, increase backoff).
- Second-line: Customer Success Engineering (15–60 minutes) — validate tenant config, run deeper traces, correlate with Redwood telemetry dashboards.
- Third-line: Redwood Platform SRE (60–240 minutes) — investigate serving capacity, GPU pressure, model fallback events.
- Executive/Account escalation: Customer Success Manager + Sales Engineering (>240 minutes) — coordinate client communications and SLA remedies.

Testing and validation checklist
- Synthetic load test at 1.5x normal peak while tracking p95/p99 latency and batch size behavior.
- Fault-injection: send a stream of 503s from a proxy to verify retry and circuit-breaker actions.
- Chaos test: restart sidecar replicas and confirm traffic re-routes without data loss.
- End-to-end trace verification: every request must carry a trace id that maps to Redwood edge trace id for easy triage.

Common failure modes and workarounds
1) Head-of-line blocking: large requests hold a batch and delay small interactive ones.
   Workaround: implement priority queues or token-threshold routing (send large requests in their own batch).
2) Unbounded queue growth during upstream outage.
   Workaround: enforce queue_capacity and fail fast (return 503 with guidance) when capacity exceeded; consider token-bucket rate-limiter upstream.
3) Retry storms causing more upstream load.
   Workaround: use exponential backoff with full jitter and respect Retry-After headers; limit max_attempts to 3–5.
4) Jitter in batching causing p95 regressions.
   Workaround: reduce max_batch_latency_ms or lower max_batch_size; prefer client-driven batching for ultra-low-latency paths.

Customer-facing error messaging guidance
When returning errors to downstream clients, include:
- stable error code (e.g., INGRESS_OVERLOADED)
- human-friendly summary of cause and expected retry window
- correlation id / trace id that maps to Redwood request id
Example HTTP 503 payload:
{
  "error_code": "INGRESS_OVERLOADED",
  "message": "Request dropped due to temporary ingress overload. Retry after 30s or contact support if persistent.",
  "trace_id": "rwd-9a2b-..."
}

Rollouts and change control
- Any change to batcher or retry defaults must go through a staged rollout: feature-flagged in staging -> 10% of traffic -> 50% -> 100%.
- Include automated canary checks measuring p95 latency, error rate, and avg_batch_size.
- Document configuration changes in the tenant change log and tag SRE owner.

Ownership and contacts
- Primary owner: Customer Success Engineering (Priya Nair)
- SRE escalation: Platform SRE on-call (rota: eng-sre)
- Redwood support contact: support@redwood.ai (include trace id and tenant id in subject)

Related resources
- Streaming webhook retry and deduplication guide (integration-guides)
- Tenant onboarding observability kit (enterprise-onboarding)
- Redwood edge API reference and Retry semantics (product-docs)

Appendix: quick tuning heuristics
- For high-throughput batch workloads (non-interactive): increase max_batch_size to 64–128 and increase max_batch_latency to 100–200ms for better throughput efficiency.
- For strict interactive SLAs: set max_batch_size <=8 and max_batch_latency_ms <= 20ms.
- If 429s are common at steady-state: coordinate with Redwood CS to increase quota or provision Dedicated capacity.

Document history
- 2026-11-10: Created by Priya Nair
- 2027-02-15: Updated with expanded circuit-breaker guidance and new metrics

title: Sensitive Data Retention & Pseudonymization Playbook — Enterprise Onboarding
content:
Overview

This playbook describes the recommended end-to-end handling of customer-sensitive data for enterprise customers during onboarding and recurring operations. It focuses on: retention policy mapping, pseudonymization approaches we support across deployment modes (Hosted API, Dedicated, Private), request and audit flows, verification steps for handback, and escalation paths for data incidents. Follow this playbook when a customer requires contractual controls over retention, deletion, or partial pseudonymization for compliance (e.g., GDPR, CCPA, sector regulations).

When to use this playbook
- New enterprise customers whose contract or security questionnaire includes data retention/deletion obligations.
- Customers requesting pseudonymization or reversible tokenization for specific data classes.
- During migrations or cutovers where data residency or retention windows change.

Owner & SLA targets
- Document owner: Customer Success (Samantha Lee)
- Technical owner: Platform Security (Diego Alvarez)
- Oncall escalation: Security oncall (rotation – see Security runbook)
- Target SLAs for requests originating from the customer security contact:
  1) Acknowledgement: within 4 business hours.
  2) Technical plan (for retention/pseudonymization changes): 48 business hours.
  3) Completed reversible pseudonymization request (up to 5M records): 7 business days.
  4) Full deletion requests (hosted metadata + cached keys): 48 hours for Hosted; 5 business days for Dedicated; customer-managed in Private (support assists with playbook).

Data classification matrix
| Customer data class | Typical location | Recommended treatment | Retention default | Notes |
|---------------------|------------------|-----------------------|-------------------|-------|
| PII (names, emails) | Request body, logs (redacted) | Pseudonymize + encrypted at rest | 365 days (configurable) | PII in logs must be redacted at ingestion
| Generated text (user prompts + responses) | Model input/output, cache zones | Respect customer policy: retain or delete on request | 180 days default | KV cache TTL configurable per customer
| Auth tokens & API keys | Secrets store / KMS | Never stored in plain form; rotate per policy | 90 days | Redwood does not index plaintext tokens
| Audit logs & traces | Observability backend | Aggregated and low-cardinality retention | 365 days | High-frequency logs sampled to meet cost SLOs

Architectural options and implications
- Hosted API: Redwood controls retention/keys; fastest path for contractual deletion. Provide retention profile in contract (standard/short/strict).
- Dedicated: Redwood-managed infra for customer; we operate deletion tools but must coordinate with Reserved Capacity Ops. Deletion time windows are longer due to bulk processing.
- Private (VPC/on-prem): Customer controls primary data plane; Redwood provides step-by-step scripts and verification checks for data erasure.

Selection guidelines
1) If customer requires sub-48-hour deletion, recommend Hosted with strict retention profile.
2) If customer requires on-prem isolation but needs Redwood assistance for migration, document reversible pseudonymization approach during handoff.

Operational request flow (high level)
1. Customer raises a retention/pseudonymization/deletion request through their designated CS contact or Support portal (ticket).
2. CS triages: confirm customer identity, scope (IDs, time window, data classes), and desired outcome (delete vs pseudonymize vs export).
3. CS opens a JIRA (tag: data-retention) and attaches signed authorization if required by contract.
4. Platform Security reviews and approves technical plan.
5. Ops executes plan in sandbox then prod.
6. Verification report produced and shared with customer; ticket closed after sign-off.

Detailed runbook: delete request example (Hosted)
1) Intake & validation
   - Required fields from customer: customer_id, record_ids OR retention window (ISO8601), contact email, signed auth (if contract requires).
   - Validate ticket owner against contract SSO groups.
2) Prepare rollback-safe snapshot (if requested by customer)
   - For Hosted, take a filtered snapshot of metadata only (no secrets) and store in retention vault for 30 days unless customer declines.
3) Execute pseudonymization or deletion
   - Use the data management tool (internal CLI: redwood-datactl) with dry-run first.
   - Sample command (dry-run):
     redwood-datactl delete --customer 12345 --window 2024-01-01:2024-12-31 --dry-run
   - Production run:
     redwood-datactl delete --customer 12345 --window 2024-01-01:2024-12-31 --confirm --audit=case-789
4) KV cache considerations
   - Invalidate affected KV cache prefixes and trigger background eviction if large.
   - Confirm no long-lived prefixes remain for pseudonymized records.
5) Post-process & verification
   - Run verification query to confirm zero results for scoped identifiers.
   - Generate signed verification report including run ids, hashes of affected record ids, and operator audit trail.

Escalation ladder (data handling incidents)
1) Customer Success Engineer (first responder) — <cs-oncall>@redwood.com — 4h SLA for acknowledgement.
2) Platform Security — sec-oncall@redwood.com — 2 business-hour escalation for suspected exposure.
3) Dedicated Ops Lead — ops-dedicated@redwood.com — for capacity/throughput constraints impacting deletion windows.
4) VP Customer Success — vp-cs@redwood.com — for contractual disputes or regulatory notices.

Verification checklist (required before closing ticket)
- [ ] Authorization verified and attached to ticket.
- [ ] Dry-run executed and approved by Platform Security.
- [ ] Production run complete; job IDs and timestamps recorded.
- [ ] KV cache invalidated and redis/edge eviction confirmed.
- [ ] Verification report generated and signed.
- [ ] Customer acknowledgment received or 7-day silent acceptance elapsed.

Sample pseudonymization approach (reversible tokenization)
- Tokenization step: replace sensitive fields with reversible token stored in a customer-scoped, envelope-encrypted store (KMS-wrapped).
- Token format example (JSON):
  {
    \"token\": \"tok_3G6aZ...\",
    \"method\": \"aes-gcm-kms\",
    \"kms_key_id\": \"projects/redwood/locations/global/keyRings/enterprise/cryptoKeys/ent-2025\"
  }
- Controls: token access requires explicit ACL entry and MUST be logged to audit trail.

Example API request for deletion (customer-facing support assist)
- Customer can initiate a scoped export or deletion via the Support portal or API (if enabled in contract). Example curl (support agent acting on behalf):
  curl -X POST \"https://api.redwood.ai/v1/admin/customers/12345/actions/delete\" \
    -H \"Authorization: Bearer ADMIN_TOKEN\" \
    -H \"Content-Type: application/json\" \
    -d '{\"scope\": {\"from\":\"2025-01-01\",\"to\":\"2025-06-30\"}, \"data_classes\":[\"generated_text\",\"pii\"], \"signed_auth\":\"<base64-pdf>\"}'

Telemetry & observability requirements
- Every retention/pseudonymization job MUST emit the following fields to the data-management metrics stream:
  - job_id, customer_id, operator, job_type (delete/pseudonymize/export), affected_count, start_ts, end_ts, outcome (success/partial/failure), verification_hash
- Alerting thresholds: failure rate > 3% across jobs in 24h window triggers an Ops incident.

Legal & compliance artifacts (required per enterprise contract)
- Signed Data Processing Addendum (DPA) with retention table
- Signed scope authorization for each deletion request (if outside DPA windows)
- Verification report (PDF) with audit hashes and operator signatures

Common failure modes & workarounds
- Large-volume deletion timeouts: schedule batched deletes during low-traffic windows and use background streaming deletions.
- Stale KV cache keys: force eviction and increment cache prefix version for affected customer.
- Missing authorization: route to CS Legal for expedited approval after identity proofing.

FAQ
Q: Can Redwood restore deleted data after a customer deletes?
A: For Hosted and Dedicated, Redwood maintains an optional short-lived snapshot only if customer requests a rollback window; otherwise deletion is irreversible after verification report. For Private, restoration depends on customer backups.

Appendix A — Example verification report outline
- Header: customer_id, case_id, operator, date
- Scope: retention window, data classes
- Execution summary: job_id, nodes used, duration, affected_count
- Hash table: list of hashed identifiers confirming deletion (salted hashing scheme)
- Signatures: operator and Platform Security approver

Change log
- 2025-11-12: Created by Samantha Lee.
- 2025-12-20: Added KV cache eviction guidance (review Diego Alvarez).
- 2026-01-28: Tightened SLA language and added telemetry fields (review Michael Chen).

Related links and references

- Security runbook: data-exposure-incident-playbook
- Product docs: retention-profiles-reference

title: Office plant care and decor guidelines
content:
Overview:

This page documents the recommended care, placement, and procurement guidelines for office plants and low-effort decor in Redwood Inference offices. The goal is to maintain a safe, healthy workplace, reduce allergens and pest risk, and ensure plants support wellbeing and culture without creating maintenance burden.

Scope:
- Applies to all shared indoor office spaces, meeting rooms, and communal areas in Redwood-managed offices.
- Does not cover employee personal desk plants (see "Personal desk plants" section).

Principles:
- Low-maintenance: prioritize species that tolerate office lighting and intermittent watering.
- Safety-first: avoid plants with known toxic sap or excessive shedding in high-traffic areas.
- Inclusive: accommodate allergies and scent sensitivities; avoid highly fragrant plants in shared spaces.
- Aesthetic coherence: plants and decor should be neutral and consistent with brand colors where practical.

Daily care checklist (facilities team):
1) Morning quick-check (mon-fri): inspect high-traffic common area plants for wilting, standing water, or pests.
2) Watering: follow the plant-specific schedule (see table below); avoid overwatering. Use saucers to prevent leaks.
3) Clean leaves monthly: wipe dust buildup to keep plants healthy and improve air quality.
4) Report issues: log major problems in #facilities with a photo and location.

Watering schedule by plant type (general guidance):
- Snake plant (Sansevieria): water every 4–6 weeks. Low light tolerant.
- ZZ plant (Zamioculcas zamiifolia): water every 4–6 weeks. Very low maintenance.
- Pothos/Devil's ivy: water every 10–14 days; trim vines if they encroach on walkways.
- Spider plant: water every 10–14 days; prefers bright, indirect light.
- Peace lily: water every 7–10 days; avoid placement where pollen may bother coworkers.
- Succulents/Cacti: water every 3–6 weeks depending on season.

Placement and safety guidelines:
- Do not place plants where they block egress, fire extinguishers, electrical panels, or sensors.
- Avoid hanging plants directly over desks where drips could occur.
- Ensure pots have trays; mopping and carpet damage incidents have previously come from unchecked overflow.
- Do not place heavily-shedding plants in meeting rooms or near shared keyboards and equipment.
- Plants with known mild-to-high toxicity (e.g., philodendron, oleander) are not allowed in common areas.

Personal desk plants (employee-owned):
- Allowed but must be maintained by the owner. If a plant becomes a nuisance (pests, mold, water damage) facilities may request removal.
- Use a waterproof tray and keep a small saucer under the pot.
- Notify facilities in case of spider/ant/pest sightings so coordinated treatment can occur.

Procurement and requests:
- To request a new plant or replacement, file a request in the Facilities request form (link in sidebar) with: proposed location, desired plant type (if known), and any accessibility concerns.
- Facilities maintains a small budget for replacements. For larger decorative refreshes, submit a ticket to People Ops with proposed spend and rationale.
- Preferred vendors: local nurseries and the approved vendor list (see Facilities vendor doc).

Decor guidelines (small items accompanying plants):
- Pots and stands should be neutral (matte blacks, grays, natural wood) unless coordinated as part of a themed refresh.
- No scented candles or oil diffusers in shared areas.
- Avoid porous pots that retain moisture directly against furniture; use trays and felt pads under stands.

Maintenance cadence and ownership:
- Facilities: weekly checklists, monthly leaf-clean, quarterly plant health review.
- People Ops: budget approvals, large refresh planning, and accommodation handling for allergies/sensitivities.
- Teams may volunteer to sponsor plants in their area (signup through People Ops); volunteer teams are responsible for basic watering on a shared rota.

Pest and allergy procedures:
- If pests (aphids, spider mites) are detected, quarantine the plant and notify #facilities immediately. Do not attempt over-the-counter pesticide sprays without coordination.
- For allergy complaints, People Ops will identify nearby plants and offer relocation/removal options. We prioritize non-confrontational resolutions and temporary workarounds (e.g., moving desks).

Exceptions and accommodations:
- If an individual requires a scent-free or plant-free workspace for medical reasons, People Ops will provide reasonable accommodation, including relocation or desk shields if needed.

Appendix: quick reference (contact & links)
- Facilities channel: #facilities (Slack)
- Facilities request form: /forms/facilities-request (internal link)
- Preferred vendor list: Confluence > Facilities > vendor-list (internal)

Revision history:
- 2025-11-04: Document created by Maya Chen.
- 2026-01-15: Updated watering schedules and added procurement budget note (reviewers: Jordan Reyes, Priya Kapoor).

Related pages:
- Office safety and emergency procedures (company-handbook)
- Facilities vendor list (facilities)

Feedback and questions: reach out to People Ops (people-ops@redwood.ai) or comment on this page.

title: office-art-and-plants-guidelines-2024
content:
Title: Office Art & Plant Guidelines

Summary:
This page documents lightweight guidelines for installing office art, plants, and temporary desk decorations at Redwood Inference offices. It is intended to balance aesthetic expression with safety, accessibility, and shared workspace norms. These notes are informal and maintained by People Ops.

Scope:
- Applies to common areas (kitchen, lounges, corridors) and individual desks in open offices.
- Does not replace formal safety or building management policies for structural changes or electrical work.

Guiding Principles:
1. Safety first: no obstructing egress, fire alarms, or emergency equipment. Avoid tripping hazards.
2. Respect shared spaces: avoid strong scents, noisy installations, or items that monopolize common areas.
3. Accessibility: ensure signage/art is hung at a height that does not impede mobility or visibility.
4. Temporary & reversible: most installations should be removable without tools or wall damage.

Approval & Ownership:
- Small desk plants and framed prints: no formal approval required.
- Larger items (floor-standing planters, freestanding sculptures, wall-hung installations > 30" in any dimension): submit a short request to people-ops@redwood.com with location, dimensions, weight, and installation method.
- People Ops is the owner for approvals and coordination with building management.

Installation Guidelines:
- Mounting: prefer adhesive strips rated for drywall where appropriate; for heavier fixtures require building-approved anchors and sign-off.
- Electrical: any installation requiring power must be scheduled with facilities and IT; do not run extension cords across walkways.
- Plants: prefer low-allergen, low-light tolerant species for shared spaces (e.g., snake plant, pothos). Avoid high-fragrance plants in kitchens and meeting rooms.
- ID tags: label any communal plant with owner name and watering cadence if not centrally maintained.

Maintenance & Removal:
- Owners are responsible for upkeep. Facilities may remove items that create hazards or persistent nuisances after one week's notice.
- For space reconfigurations, owners will be asked to relocate or remove personal/communal items within two weeks.

Temporary Exhibitions & Events:
- If a team wants to host a temporary exhibit (art show, maker fair, holiday display), submit a proposal at least 10 business days prior including insurance/waiver details if items are valuable.

Quick Checklist (for submitters):
- [ ] Location & footprint
- [ ] Estimated weight
- [ ] Mounting method
- [ ] Owner & contact
- [ ] Maintenance plan
- [ ] Needed approvals (building/facilities)

title: Office Plant Care and Desk Jungle Guidelines
content:
Overview:

This page documents lightweight, community-driven guidelines for caring for office plants and maintaining a pleasant desk-plant ecosystem. It is intended to keep shared spaces tidy, reduce plant mortality, and provide simple escalation paths for issues. These guidelines are informal and may be superseded by facility vendor contracts or building policies.

Scope:
- Applies to all plants in shared spaces (kitchen, conference rooms, lounge) and to potted plants kept at individual desks when they interact with shared facilities (water stations, plant shelves).
- Excludes customer office gardens and third-party contracted plant maintenance.

Principles:
1. Low-effort, resilient plants preferred: choose hardier species for communal areas (e.g., pothos, snake plant, ZZ plant).
2. Shared responsibility: facilities owns ordering and large maintenance; community volunteers do day-to-day checks.
3. Non-judgmental culture: if a plant is wilting, flag it; no shaming.

Roles & Responsibilities:
- Facilities (Facilities Manager): owns budget, vendor coordination, pest escalation, and the monthly supplies reorder.
- Desk Jungle Stewards (rotating volunteers): 1-2 people per floor who perform weekly checks and watering for shared-planter zones.
- Individual Employees: responsible for personal desk plants (follow desk guidelines below).

Weekly Care Schedule (recommended):
1. Monday: Steward inspects shared planters, notes soil moisture, and rotates plants if shade distribution is uneven.
2. Wednesday: Quick misting for humidity-sensitive plants (only in winter months).
3. Friday: Tidy loose soil, remove dead leaves, and record any pest signs in the shared Plant Log (Google Sheet link in related pages).

Desk Jungle Guidelines (for personal plants):
- Pot size: keep to 4–8 inch pots for desks; larger pots belong in floor planters.
- Watering: use a tray to prevent accidental spills; water at desk only in non-sensitive equipment areas.
- Lighting: if a plant requires bright light, place near windows; avoid blocking walkways.
- Allergies: pick hypoallergenic species when possible or keep plants contained inside cubicle boundaries.

Shared Planters & Conference Rooms:
- Labeling: all shared planter pots should have a small waterproof label with plant name and last-watering date.
- Rotation: every three months facilities will rotate plants to refresh displays and prevent one area bearing all sun/heat exposure.

Supplies & Ordering:
- Facilities will maintain a basic kit: peat-free potting mix, small pruning shears, plant food (low-dose), trays, and labels.
- To request supplies: submit a ticket in #facilities-requests Slack channel or file a help ticket (link in related pages). For emergency replacement (pests, floods), contact Facilities Manager directly.

Pests & Health Issues:
- Immediate action: isolate affected plant, take photos, and post to the Plant Log with time/date and steward name.
- Quarantine window: keep suspected plants isolated for 7–10 days; do not compost onsite without Facilities approval.
- Escalation: if pests persist or spread to multiple planters, Facilities will engage vendor or building management for treatment.

Event Use & Decorations:
- Temporary decorations (e.g., pot toppers, small plaques) allowed but must be removed within 48 hours after the event. No open flames or food-based decorations in shared planters.

Conflict Resolution:
- If a plant in a shared zone is being mistreated or over-cared (e.g., overwatered), leave a polite note on the shared Plant Log. If unresolved after one week, escalate to the Facilities Manager who will mediate.

FAQ:
- Q: Can I rehome my unhealthy desk plant into a shared planter?
  A: No — rehoming must be approved by a Steward after assessment to avoid introducing pests or disease.
- Q: Who pays for a replacement plant I broke?
  A: Personal desk plants are the owner’s responsibility; accidental damage to shared planters should be reported and may be covered by the facilities petty fund depending on circumstances.

Appendix (quick reference table):
Plant Type | Best Location | Water Frequency | Notes
Pothos | Low light zones, shelves | Every 10–14 days | Very tolerant of neglect
Snake Plant | Desks with very low light | Every 3–6 weeks | Avoid overwatering
Rubber Plant | Bright indirect light | Every 7–10 days | Trim to control size

Contacts:
- Facilities Manager: Lina Gomez (lina.gomez@example.redwood.com)
- Desk Jungle Coordinator: volunteer list maintained in Plant Log

- 2025-11-03: Updated watering cadence and quarantine instructions (Ethan Brooks)

Related artifacts and links:

- Facilities supplies page: /confluence/facilities/plant-supplies-ordering

title: Misc Office Ops and Runtime Quirks
content:
Overview:

This page is a deliberately miscellaneous collection of operational notes, small runbook fragments, and a handful of office logistics items that surfaced during on-call rotations and weekly runtime syncs. It is not a canonical architecture doc; treat items here as context-rich noise that may be useful when triaging odd runtime behaviours or planning small infrastructural housekeeping.

Purpose:
- Capture small, non-actionable observations about serving-runtime quirks.
- Keep a short checklist for low-cost office operations (vending, supplies) so on-call folks can avoid interruptions.
- Surface minor suggestions that don't yet warrant a full ADR or Confluence page.

Quick summary of notable runtime quirks (engineering context):
1) Occasional small-object GC pauses seen when background maintenance jobs overlap with burst traffic windows. Hypothesis: Python-based admin tasks touching model caches cause incremental memory pressure and CPU spikes on control-plane nodes.
2) Batching spikes when request size distribution shifts (more short queries than expected) leading to suboptimal packing. Temporary mitigation: reduce max-wait-ms in the inference router for affected prefix.
3) KV cache fragmentation after rolling restarts in mixed-quantization pools; increase measured tail latency by ~10–15ms for cold prefix workloads.

Actionable suggestions (short):
- For short-term GC pauses: schedule heavy control-plane jobs (snapshot, compliance exports) outside peak hours (US morning).
- For batching variance: add histogram metrics for request token-length by route to auto-detect distribution shifts.
- For KV fragmentation: include a lightweight post-rolling-check that validates KV consistency and warms the top N prefixes.

Office ops (non-technical but useful for continuity):
- Vending machine: restock request process: slack #facilities with photo, item list, and preferred vendor. Typical turnaround ~3 business days.
- Printer toner: shared_drives/engineering/_temp_uploads/toner-orders is the interim order sheet (legacy).

Runbook fragment: diagnosing a small spike in tail latency (<= 1 hour incident)
1) Check the Console SLO dashboard for the route and time range, confirm affected percentiles (p50/p90/p99).
2) Query recent deploys and rolling restarts: grep deploy logs for the service tag; correlate to control-plane maintenance jobs.
3) Inspect batching metrics: batching_queue_time_ms, batch_fill_ratio, and avg_tokens_per_request. If batch_fill_ratio < 0.6 and batch_size smaller than expected, consider temporarily lowering max-wait-ms on router.
4) Check KV cache hit rate and last_warm_timestamp for model variants. If hit rate < 85% and last warm < 2 hours, trigger a targeted warm-up (script: scripts/warm_prefixes.sh --top 50).
5) If CPU steal or I/O wait is high on nodes, check noisy-neighbor signals and recent dedicated capacity autoscaling events.

Small configuration table (example thresholds used by on-call)
- SLO target (route default): 95% requests <= 120ms, p99 <= 500ms
- Alert thresholds: p95 > 200ms for 5m OR p99 > 600ms for 1m
- Batching: default max-wait-ms = 12, max-batch-tokens = 4096
- KV cache warm threshold: < 85% hit triggers warm-up

Checklist for adding trivial housekeeping items to this page:
1) Add item with a short title and one-paragraph rationale.
2) If the item is clearly actionable in < 1 hour, move to eng-sre action list and assign.
3) If the item is long-form, draft an ADR and link from here.

Ownership and escalation:
- Maintainer: eng-serving-runtime on-call rotation (primary contact via PagerDuty).
- Triage owner for office ops items: facilities@redwood-inference (use internal alias).
- For anything tagged security or legal, escalate to security-and-compliance and stop; do not document sensitive details here.

Related artifacts and links:
- Deploy checklist: confluence/eng-serving-runtime/deploy-checklist
- Incident playbook: confluence/eng-sre/incident-response
- Warm-up script (repo): github/redwood/tools/warm-prefixes (note: small helper script, may be moved)

Notes and miscellaneous noise (explicitly informal):
- Coffee machine cycles correlate poorly with sprint deadlines but this is anecdotal.
- We keep a small spare HDMI->DP dongle in the engineering kitchenette labeled "borrow me." Return within 48 hours.
- If you find a half-eaten sandwich near the NUC rack, please notify facilities and remove before it attracts pests.

Revision history and authorship:
- 2023-11-15: Initial draft, Maya Chen.
- 2024-06-20: Added KV fragmentation notes, Lucas Patel.
- 2024-07-03: Minor edits and office ops checklist, Aisha Kapoor.

If something in this page looks like it should be a formal runbook, ADR, or incident postmortem, please create the canonical page and link it from here. This page intentionally accumulates small, cross-cutting notes that often get lost in ephemeral channels.

title: Oddball Office Procedures: Handling Miscellaneous Situations
content:
## Overview
This page documents a set of intentionally lightweight and occasionally whimsical procedures for small, real-world oddities that have occurred at Redwood Inference offices. The purpose is pragmatic: provide a repeatable, low-friction decision path for front-desk staff, people-ops, and any engineer who volunteers to handle the strange but non-critical situations that crop up.

These are not policies with legal force; they are pragmatic guidance and a place to capture low-risk defaults so we avoid ad-hoc escalation. Treat this page as an informal supplement to Office Guidelines.

## When to use this page
- The issue is non-safety-critical (no bodily harm, fire, major property damage).
- The situation is awkward, unexpected, and not covered by standard HR or security playbooks.
- You need a quick, sensible default to avoid micro-escalations (e.g., who takes custody of a found office cactus).

## Common scenarios and recommended handling (quick-reference)
1. Found items: keys, umbrellas, electronics
   - Put in the labeled "Found" basket at reception with date and finder initials.
   - Photograph item and post a single-line thread in #office-lost-and-found (photo + approximate location + date).
   - After 30 days unclaimed: donate (clothing) or recycle securely (storage devices) per IT disposal guidance.

2. A plant that clearly belongs to no one (the Rogue Plant)
   - Move it to the communal window bench and label with a sticky note: "Rogue Plant — survivor program."
   - If it’s thriving after 60 days and no owner identified, people-ops will adopt into the office green roster and assign a caretaker volunteer.

3. Persistent smell in the breakroom (non-emergency)
   - Ventilate windows/doors, check trash and forgotten food, log incident in the facilities queue.
   - If smell persists after two checks, escalate to facilities manager and note the date/time and area.

4. Small animal or insect guest (non-dangerous)
   - Safely trap or guide outside using a cup and paper or request facilities assistance.
   - For bees/wasps/large pests: do not attempt removal; contact facilities immediately.

## Step-by-step playbook: "Rogue Office Item"
1. Secure item and take a clear photo.
2. Label with date, finder initials, and a one-line description.
3. Place in reception "Found" basket or the secure bin for electronics.
4. Post notice in #office-lost-and-found with photo and location.
5. Record a 1-line note in the Facilities ticket system (ticket title: Found item — <short desc>).
6. After 30 days, follow disposal rules aligned to item type (electronics -> IT disposal; clothing -> donation).

## Table: Disposal guidelines (quick)
| Item type | Short-term home | 30-day outcome | Responsible owner |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Clothing | Found basket (closet shelf) | Donate | People-Ops |
| Keys / Wallets | Locked reception drawer | Security hold + attempt owner contact | Facilities |
| Electronics (phones, USB) | Secure bin (keyed) | IT erase / recycle | IT Ops |
| Houseplants | Communal bench | Assign caretaker or rehome | People-Ops |

## Communication templates
- Slack post (short): "Found a [item] near <location> at <time>. Photo attached. Putting it in reception. Please DM if it’s yours."
- Reception note (sticky): "Found: <item>. Date: <YYYY-MM-DD>. Finder: <initials>."

## Ownership and escalation
- Default owner for first 30 days: Reception / Facilities.
- If item appears high-value or clearly sensitive (e.g., labeled drives, encrypted devices): immediate escalation to IT and Security. Do not power on unknown devices.

## Related work and historical notes
- This page replaces a set of ad-hoc Google Docs that accumulated small anecdotes. It aims to reduce repeated ask/clarify cycles for reception staff.
- Past oddities that inspired this doc: a potted fern relocation, an unclaimed umbrella stash after a heavy rain day, and a mysterious jar of pickles left in a fridge (resolved by donation).

## Open questions / future items
- Should we add a short queue form for found electronics to capture serial numbers? (Tentative: yes — coordinate with IT.)
- Consider a quarterly "green roster" check to avoid plant turnover.

## Acknowledgements
Thanks to front-desk staff and the facilities volunteers for early feedback and for tolerating the majority of the experiments that motivated this page.

---
Notes: This page is intentionally light in formal language to encourage adoption. If an item is legally sensitive or safety-related, follow the standard incident or HR process instead of this guidance.

title: Cafeteria Beanbag and Ambient Noise Guidelines
content:
Summary

This page documents a lightweight, experimental set of guidelines for beanbag seating and ambient noise considerations in Redwood Inference shared spaces (cafeteria, lounge, and overflow areas). The goal is pragmatic: improve employee comfort and informal collaboration while keeping operational burden low.

Scope

- Applies to: cafeteria, adjacent lounge, satellite huddle areas on main campus and leased offices.
- Does NOT apply to: focus rooms, phone booths, secure rooms, or private customer meeting rooms.

Guiding principles

1. Respect for teammates: conserve shared spaces for implicit consent — assume people nearby prefer moderate noise levels.
2. Minimal ops: prefer low-maintenance furniture and sensors; avoid complex approvals for small purchases.
3. Data-informed: measure and iterate; use a simple decibel sampling process before large rollouts.

Furniture guidelines (beanbags and soft seating)

- Quantity: limit beanbag count per room to 6 units or 25% of casual seating, whichever is smaller.
- Placement: require at least 1.5m clear circulation path; do not block egress or access to kitchen equipment.
- Materials: choose wipeable, flame-retardant covers rated for commercial use.
- Procurement checklist (sample):
  1. Model spec and SKU
  2. Flame retardant certificate (pdf)
  3. Supplier lead time and return policy
  4. Estimated cost per unit
  5. Maintenance plan (wipe schedule)

Ambient noise guidance

- Target levels: daylight cafeteria 45-55 dB typical; lunchtime peaks allowed up to 65 dB for short periods.
- Quiet windows: designate 11:30-12:30 on Tuesdays as a quiet-lunch pilot in one lounge for two quarters and evaluate.

Quick decibel sampling procedure

1. Tools: smartphone with a basic dB meter app (note: consumer apps vary).
2. Sampling: take 6 samples across a 30-minute window during a target time (e.g., Wednesday 12:00-12:30).
3. Record: document median and max values. Store sample note on the facilities ticket with a short comment.

Example CLI-style sample (for reference in case teams use a measurement device):

# pseudo-command for a USB mic logger (example only)
# record 30s segments and write a simple CSV of RMS dB values
# recorder --device /dev/audio1 --interval 30 --out cafeteria-sample.csv

Operational checklist for pilot rollout (one-month pilot)

1. Facilities ops to order up to 4 beanbags for Pilot Location A.
2. People Ops to publish the pilot notice and expectations (quiet windows, cleanup).
3. Facilities to execute sampling on week 1 and week 4 and upload notes.
4. Survey: send a 3-question pulse survey after week 4 (comfort, noise impact, cleanup).

Safety, maintenance, and waste

- Cleaning: wipeable covers weekly; deep-clean monthly.
- Disposal: follow office recycling guidelines; avoid foam landfill where programs exist.

Decision and escalation

- If complaints > 10% of local headcount in pilot area, pause and review.
- Escalation owner: Facilities Lead (email: facilities@example.com).

Ownership and review cadence

- Document owner: People Ops (Aisha Khan).
- Review cadence: pilot review at month 1, full review at month 3.

Related artifacts and references

- See: Office space guidelines (Confluence) for building rules and safety.
- See: Facilities procurement template (Drive) for ordering checklist.

Attachments and sample forms

- Procurement sample checklist (attach to ticket)
- Decibel sampling notes (CSV)

Notes and known limitations

- This is intentionally lightweight and experimental. It is not a binding policy for client-facing meeting rooms or regulated spaces. If a space is used for interviews or customer meetings, revert to formal meeting-room standards.

Revision history

- 2024-11-07 initial draft by Aisha Khan
- 2025-01-15 pilot parameters updated after facilities review

title: Service energy and cost accounting metadata standard
content:
Overview

This page defines the company-wide standard for per-request energy and cost accounting metadata. The goal is to provide a consistent, compact envelope that services and proxies attach to requests and emitted telemetry so downstream billing, cost-optimization, SLO reconciliation, and sustainability metrics can reliably attribute spend and estimated energy consumption to tenants, models, and workload features.

Why this standard matters

- Unifies cost attribution across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.
- Enables low-latency routing decisions using cost hints without leaking raw pricing data.
- Provides the data foundation for chargeback, forecast, and energy-conscious routing features.
- Supports audits and compliance with per-tenant retention and redaction policies.

Goals and constraints

1. Keep the per-request envelope small (<= 2KB) to avoid adding significant network or serialization overhead.
2. Include stable, well-documented keys (snake_case) rather than free-form tags.
3. Ensure values are typed and bounded (e.g., currency amounts in micro-units, power in millijoules).
4. Make the envelope forward-compatible: allow vendor-specific extensions under a reserved prefix.
5. Avoid embedding per-token usage details in the envelope; use async telemetry for high-granularity events.

Scope

- Applies to: edge proxies (edge-router), inference routers (inference-router), runtime sidecars (runtime-sidecar), batch job submitters, and telemetry collectors.
- Does not mandate billing rates or conversion tables — those live in the billing service and are referenced by id.
- Includes both real-time headers for short-lived routing decisions and persisted JSON envelopes for telemetry records.

Metadata fields (canonical envelope)

Use the following canonical keys in the JSON envelope attached to telemetry events and the corresponding HTTP headers for routing. Types and example values are provided. Services must include the required fields; others are optional.

| Field | Required | Type | Description | Example |
|---|---:|---|---|---|
| request_id | yes | string | Global request UUID (trace-friendly). | "req_123e4567-e89b-12d3-a456-426614174000" |
| tenant_id | yes | string | Tenant (customer) identifier used for billing. | "acme-corp" |
| model_id | yes | string | Canonical model identifier (catalog/model-hash). | "redwood/gptx-7b:2025-03-01" |
| estimated_energy_mJ | no | integer | Estimated energy consumed by request in millijoules (best-effort). | "4120" |
| compute_microdollars | no | integer | Estimated compute cost in micro-dollars (USD * 1e6). | "125000" |
| cost_version | yes | string | Version of the cost-accounting envelope schema (v1, v2...). | "v1" |
| pricing_ref_id | no | string | Billing service reference to the pricing table used (opaque id). | "price-table-prod-2025-03" |
| priority_class | no | string | One of: realtime, interactive, batch, bulk. Used for routing decisions. | "interactive" |
| cache_hit | no | boolean | True if the request was served from a cache (impacts cost). | "true" |
| gpu_tier | no | string | GPU tier hint (e.g., a100-80gb, h100-80gb). | "a100-80gb" |
| inference_tokens | no | integer | Optional token estimate used for cost modeling (approx). | "120" |
| appended_by | yes | string | Service that appended/last-modified this envelope (service-name). | "inference-router" |
| routed_region | no | string | Region code used for routing (e.g., us-west1). | "us-west1" |

Header mapping for real-time routing

- For low-latency routing, services must propagate a minimal header: X-RW-COST (base64-encoded JSON) or the following individual headers when size is small: X-RW-REQ-ID, X-RW-TENANT, X-RW-MODEL, X-RW-PRIORITY.
- Runtime proxies should never include sensitive pricing_ref_id in headers forwarded to external/private deployments; use internal-only header flags.

Telemetry propagation and mutation rules

1. The first ingress service (edge-router or API-gateway) must create request_id and populate tenant_id and model_id.
2. Each service that materially changes estimated_energy_mJ or compute_microdollars must append itself to appended_by and set a local delta_{field} (telemetry only). Delta fields MUST NOT be included in routing headers.
3. Runtime-sidecars may update compute_microdollars after final token count; they must emit a separate telemetry record with final accounting and mark the envelope as finalized: "cost_finalized": "true".
4. If a proxy cannot compute estimated_energy_mJ, it must omit the field (do not set 0).

Schema versioning and compatibility

- Use the cost_version field to determine compatibility. Consumers must ignore unknown fields.
- When changing types or semantics, increment cost_version and publish a migration plan in this directory.

SLOs and accuracy expectations

- Energy estimate accuracy: median absolute error <= 20% for production real-time estimates vs finalized telemetry for 95% of requests over a rolling 7-day window.
- Cost estimate accuracy: median absolute error <= 10% for compute_microdollars vs billing-service reconciliation for 99% of requests within 24 hours.
- Envelope propagation SLA: 99.9% of in-flight requests must carry either the minimal header set or the base64 envelope between edge and runtime-sidecar.

Storage, retention and redaction

- Telemetry envelopes stored in observability must omit tenant_id for analytics buckets labelled "public-aggregate". Use hashed_tenant_id when sending to cross-team aggregate pipelines.
- Raw envelopes with tenant_id and pricing_ref_id are PII-adjacent; retention default is 90 days unless tenant contract requires longer retention.
- For privacy-sensitive tenants, support redaction at ingress: redact_fields=["pricing_ref_id","estimated_energy_mJ"].

Rollout plan (recommended)

1. Week 0: Publish spec and unit tests in infra-standards repository.
2. Week 2: Edge-router and API-gateway add generation of minimal headers (X-RW-REQ-ID, X-RW-TENANT, X-RW-MODEL, X-RW-COST-VERSION). Run compatibility tests.
3. Week 4: Runtime-sidecar and inference-router adopt envelope mutation rules and emit finalized telemetry.
4. Week 6: Billing-service subscribe to finalized telemetry and run reconciliation job; measure accuracy metrics.
5. Week 8: Enable opt-in energy-based routing experiments for a small percentage of traffic (5%).

Validation and testing

- Unit test: schema validator that rejects envelopes with wrong types or missing required fields.
- Integration test: synthetic workload where compute_microdollars from runtime matches the billing-service computed microdollars within <10%.
- Smoke test: request roundtrip through edge -> runtime -> telemetry collector must include X-RW-REQ-ID and the envelope in the final event.

Example envelopes

Minimal header-encoded JSON (for routing):

X-RW-COST: eyAicmVxdWVzdF9pZCI6ICJyZXFfMTIzZSIsICJ0ZW5hbnRfaWQiOiAiYWNtZSIsICJtb2RlbF9pZCI6ICJyZWR3b29kL2dwdHgtN2I6MjAyNS0wMy0wMSIsICJjb3N0X3ZlcnNpb24iOiAidjEiIH0=

Example telemetry JSON envelope (persisted):

{
  "request_id": "req_123e4567-e89b-12d3-a456-426614174000",
  "tenant_id": "acme-corp",
  "model_id": "redwood/gptx-7b:2025-03-01",
  "estimated_energy_mJ": "4120",
  "compute_microdollars": "125000",
  "cost_version": "v1",
  "pricing_ref_id": "price-table-prod-2025-03",
  "priority_class": "interactive",
  "appended_by": "runtime-sidecar",
  "routed_region": "us-west1",
  "cost_finalized": "true"
}

Operational runbook snippets

- Problem: Missing tenant_id in envelopes for a subset of traffic.
  1. Check edge-router logs for header generation failures (service: edge-router, log key: cost-envelope-generation).
  2. Validate ingress auth middleware configuration: ensure tenant extraction rules are up-to-date.
  3. If using hashed_tenant_id fallback, compare counts in realtime partition to determine scope.

- Problem: compute_microdollars differs from billing-service by > 20% (daily reconcile).
  1. Pull a sample of requests with request_id and compare runtime token counts vs billing charge pipeline.
  2. Verify pricing_ref_id mapping in billing-service and whether a new price-table was rolled without incrementing pricing_ref_id.
  3. Temporarily mark the envelope as "cost_override_reason": "investigation" in telemetry for debugging.

Governance and ownership

- Spec owner: eng-infra standards lead (Aisha Kapoor).
- Implementation owners: edge-router (team: eng-platform), inference-router (team: eng-serving-runtime), runtime-sidecar (team: eng-private-deployments).
- Review cadence: Quarterly review or when cost_version increments.

Backwards compatibility guidance

- Producer-first approach: when introducing new fields, producers may emit them flagged as optional. Consumers must tolerate absent fields.
- Deprecation: announce deprecation of a key at least 8 weeks prior and publish a migration playbook.

Open questions and future work

- Explore integrating energy models that use hardware telemetry (PState/PMU) for improved estimated_energy_mJ accuracy.
- Determine canonical hashed_tenant_id algorithm for cross-tenant analytics with privacy guarantees.
- Add support for multi-currency micro-units and per-region pricing overrides.

References

- Related playbook: /confluence/architecture-and-standards/infra-standards/resource-tagging-and-request-attribution-playbook-2024
- Metrics taxonomy: /confluence/architecture-and-standards/observability-standards/granular-metrics-taxonomy-and-dimension-catalog-2026

Appendix: CLI validator example

# Validate an envelope file
cat envelope.json | python -m rw_cost_validator --schema v1 --check-types

Exit codes:
- 0: valid
- 1: schema error
- 2: missing required field

If you have questions or need exceptions for a specific private deployment, open a request in #eng-infra-standards and tag the spec owner.

title: Data deletion and TTL enforcement standards
content:
## Purpose
This standard defines the minimum engineering requirements for implementing **data retention (TTL) and deletion** across Redwood Inference systems.

It exists to ensure:
- Retention controls are **enforceable** (not just configurable).
- Purge mechanisms are **safe, idempotent, and observable**.
- We can provide credible **evidence** for internal audits and customer security reviews (SOC 2/ISO-style).

This is a *must-follow* standard for any store or service that holds customer-affecting data classes subject to retention.

## Scope
Applies to:
- Control-plane and data-plane stores that persist any of the following (examples):
  - Request/response logs (where enabled)
  - Prompts/completions stored at rest (where enabled)
  - Audit logs
  - Traces/metrics/log aggregates
  - Artifacts (eval datasets, report packages, exported evidence bundles)

Does not replace:
- Data classification and logging standards (redaction, PII controls).
- Legal hold / exceptions policy (see Security & Compliance pages).

## Definitions
- **TTL (time-to-live):** Maximum time data is allowed to exist after its relevant timestamp (usually `created_at` / `ingested_at`).
- **Retention policy:** Tenant + data-class specific configuration describing TTL, residency constraints, and exception behavior.
- **Purge job:** Automated deletion process that enforces TTL by deleting records/objects past their expiry.
- **Idempotent deletion:** A purge job can run multiple times (retries, replays) and yields the same end state without causing incorrect deletions or operational harm.
- **Deletion verification:** A set of metrics and checks proving that expired data is actually removed within an allowed lag window.
- **TTL lag:** `now - max(deleted_cutoff_applied)` for a given store/tenant/data class. In other words, how far behind deletion is from the intended TTL boundary.

## Design principles
1. **Policy is evaluated centrally; enforcement is local.**
   - Policy evaluation source of truth is the control plane (see ADR-017).
   - Each store/feature must implement enforcement in the component that owns the data.

2. **Delete is a production operation.**
   - Purge paths must be designed for predictable load, backpressure, and safe retries.

3. **Verification is mandatory.**
   - If you can’t measure deletion, we treat it as not implemented.

4. **Prefer deterministic, incremental deletion over “big sweeps.”**
   - Use primary-key ordered pagination and bounded batch sizes.

5. **Respect legal hold and documented exceptions.**
   - Holds must be enforced consistently and be auditable.

## Required implementation checklist (all stores)
The following are minimum requirements for any TTL enforcement implementation.

### 1) Data model requirements
**Required fields (or equivalent):**
- `tenant_id` (or org/project/workspace id)
- `data_class` (explicit or implied by table/bucket)
- `created_at` or `ingested_at` timestamp (source-of-truth clock described below)
- Optional but strongly recommended:
  - `region` (if multi-region)
  - `policy_version_applied` (or last-evaluated policy reference)
  - `hold_status` / `hold_reason` (if holds apply at record/object granularity)

**Time source standard:**
- Use database/server-side timestamps for expiry decisions when possible (e.g., `NOW()` in SQL) to avoid clock skew.

### 2) Deletion semantics
You must document (in the owning system doc):
- Whether deletion is **hard delete** (required for retention enforcement unless explicitly approved otherwise).
- If soft-delete/tombstones exist for product needs, define:
  - When tombstones are permanently removed
  - Whether tombstones are themselves subject to TTL
  - How exports/reporting treat tombstoned records

**Not allowed as the only enforcement mechanism:**
- “We filter expired rows at read time.” (This is not deletion.)

### 3) Purge job requirements
All purge jobs must be:
- **Idempotent** (safe to re-run; deletes are repeatable).
- **Bounded** (limits per run to prevent DB/storage pressure).
- **Retryable** with exponential backoff.
- **Observable** (metrics + structured logs + run identifiers).
- **Multi-tenant safe** (no cross-tenant deletion).
- **Hold-aware** (legal hold / incident hold must prevent deletion when applicable).

### 4) Verification requirements
You must implement:
- TTL lag metric(s)
- Deletion success/failure metrics
- Backlog size estimates (where meaningful)
- Alerts (see below)
- A dashboard panel set (see “Dashboards”)

### 5) Runbook and ownership
Before GA:
- Create/extend a runbook describing how to monitor, throttle, re-run, and validate the purge.
- Explicitly assign an owning team and on-call escalation.

## Standard purge job pattern
### Recommended algorithm (SQL-backed stores)
**Key idea:** delete in small, ordered batches using an index that supports the filter.

**Required indexes (example):**
- `(tenant_id, created_at, id)` or equivalent.

**Batch delete pattern:**
1. Compute cutoff: `cutoff_ts = NOW() - ttl_duration` (from policy).
2. Select candidate ids using deterministic ordering and a strict upper bound.
3. Delete by id list (or range) with safeguards.
4. Emit metrics for deleted rows, runtime, and errors.

**Example (illustrative):**
- SELECT: `SELECT id FROM request_logs WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND created_at < $2 AND hold_status != 'HOLD' ORDER BY created_at, id LIMIT $3;`
- DELETE: `DELETE FROM request_logs WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND id = ANY($ids);`

**Safety requirements:**
- Enforce `LIMIT` and an absolute cap like `max_rows_per_minute`.
- Use statement timeouts and circuit breakers.
- If a batch repeatedly fails, the job must degrade safely (stop and alert) rather than spin.

### Object storage / blob stores
Prefer native lifecycle rules when compatible with policy semantics, but still implement **verification metrics**.

If lifecycle rules cannot express holds/exceptions, implement an explicit sweeper that:
- Lists objects by prefix including tenant and data class
- Compares object metadata timestamp to cutoff
- Deletes in bounded batches
- Tracks deletion results (including 404/not found as a successful idempotent outcome)

### Streaming/telemetry pipelines
For stores with compaction windows (e.g., metrics backends):
- Document the compaction/retention behavior and how it maps to customer TTL.
- Provide TTL lag as: `now - last_compaction_cutoff` or backend-specific equivalent.

## Idempotency requirements (what we test for)
A purge job must tolerate:
- Retry after partial success (some rows deleted, then crash)
- Concurrency (two workers overlap on the same range)
- Reordering (delayed scheduling, catch-up runs)
- Duplicate work (same batch processed twice)

Allowed outcomes:
- Attempted deletions of already-deleted data are treated as success.

Not allowed:
- Deleting outside the target tenant, region, or data class.
- “Cursor corruption” where later runs skip ranges permanently.

## Required metrics (minimum set)
All metrics must be emitted with **low-cardinality labels**. Do not label by request_id, user_id, or free-form strings.

### Metric names (standardized)
Use these canonical metrics for retention enforcement. If you must deviate, document it and provide mapping.

1) `ttl_lag_seconds` (gauge)
- Definition: How far behind TTL enforcement is for a given store.
- Required labels:
  - `store` (e.g., `request_logs_pg`, `audit_logs_pg`, `traces_clickhouse`)
  - `data_class` (e.g., `request_logs`, `audit_logs`, `traces`)
  - `region`
- Optional label:
  - `tier` (`hosted`, `dedicated`, `private`)

2) `purge_rows_deleted_total` (counter)
- Increment by number of records deleted.
- Required labels: `store`, `data_class`, `region`

3) `purge_failures_total` (counter)
- Increment on purge operation failure.
- Required labels: `store`, `data_class`, `region`, `failure_type`
- `failure_type` must be one of a bounded enum (examples): `db_timeout`, `rate_limited`, `permission_denied`, `serialization_failure`, `unknown`.

4) `purge_job_duration_seconds` (histogram)
- Required labels: `store`, `data_class`, `region`

5) `purge_backlog_estimate` (gauge) (when meaningful)
- Examples:
  - estimated rows older than cutoff
  - estimated bytes older than cutoff
- Required labels: `store`, `data_class`, `region`

### Structured logs
Each run must emit a single structured “summary log” event containing:
- `job_name`, `run_id`, `store`, `data_class`, `region`
- `cutoff_ts`, `batch_size`, `rows_deleted`, `rows_scanned` (if available)
- `duration_ms`, `status` (`success|partial|failed`)
- `error_code` (bounded enum) if failed

## Required alerts (baseline)
Alerts must be routed to the owning on-call with an escalation policy.

### Paging alerts (P1)
1. **TTL enforcement stalled**
- Condition: `ttl_lag_seconds` exceeds the maximum allowed lag for the store/tier.
- Default thresholds (unless documented otherwise):
  - Hosted: page at > 24h lag
  - Dedicated: page at > 12h lag
  - Private: page at > 24h lag (or as contractually required)

2. **Purge job error burst**
- Condition: `purge_failures_total` rate above threshold for 15 minutes AND `purge_rows_deleted_total` not increasing.
- Guidance: threshold depends on schedule; for hourly jobs, any consistent failure across 2 consecutive runs should page.

### Ticket alerts (P2)
3. **Backlog growing**
- Condition: `purge_backlog_estimate` increasing for > 6 hours.

4. **Job not running**
- Condition: missing `purge_job_duration_seconds` and `purge_rows_deleted_total` activity for > 2x expected schedule interval.

## Dashboards (required panels)
Create a dashboard (or extend the standard retention dashboard) with:
- TTL lag over time (`ttl_lag_seconds`) by region/store
- Rows deleted per run / per hour (`purge_rows_deleted_total` rate)
- Failure rate (`purge_failures_total` rate) with top `failure_type`
- Job duration (`purge_job_duration_seconds` p50/p95)
- Backlog estimate (if available)
- Overlay of deploy markers for the purge component (when supported)

## Performance and safety guardrails
### Database pressure controls
- Hard limit deletes per batch (e.g., 1k–10k rows) and per minute (environment dependent).
- Prefer primary-key pagination; avoid large OFFSET scans.
- Use read replicas for candidate selection only if correctness is preserved.
- Use statement timeouts and cancellation; do not allow long-running delete transactions.

### Scheduling
- Jobs should be scheduled at a cadence that matches TTL granularity and expected write volume.
- Stagger schedules by region to reduce peak load.

### Backfills and migrations
If adding TTL to an existing store:
- Provide a backfill plan for legacy rows without timestamps or without tenant attribution.
- Plan for initial backlog deletion (ramp slowly).
- Define success criteria (e.g., “ttl_lag_seconds < 6h for 7 consecutive days”).

## Legal hold and exceptions (integration requirements)
Retention enforcement must honor holds and exceptions as defined by Security & Compliance.

Minimum integration requirements:
- Purge evaluation must check for active hold at the correct scope:
  - **Tenant-wide hold:** all relevant data classes blocked.
  - **Case/incident hold:** specific data classes and time windows may be blocked.
- Hold decisions must be auditable (link to the policy version or hold record id).
- “Break-glass” exceptions must require:
  - explicit approval (per policy)
  - audit log entry indicating who/when/why

## Evidence and auditability requirements
For compliance reporting packs and internal audit readiness:
- The system must be able to export (or reconstruct) the effective retention configuration for a time window.
- Purge job runs must be traceable via run_id and summary logs.
- Demonstrate that metrics exist and alerts are configured.

## Testing requirements
Before enabling a retention control in production:
- Unit tests:
  - cutoff calculation, policy parsing, hold behavior
  - idempotency behavior (rerun same batch)
- Integration tests:
  - create expired records, verify deletion, verify non-expired not deleted
  - multi-tenant isolation
- Load tests:
  - ensure deletes do not exceed DB/storage SLO budgets
- Failure-mode tests:
  - injected timeouts, partial deletes, retry behavior

## Exceptions to this standard
Any exception (e.g., inability to hard delete due to third-party backend constraints) requires:
- Security review sign-off (Security & Compliance)
- SRE review for operational risk
- Documented compensating controls (e.g., crypto-shredding, lifecycle rules + verification)
- A clear timeline for remediation if the exception is temporary

## Reference implementation notes
- Prefer the shared purge job framework (see platform docs) to get:
  - run_id generation
  - retry/backoff defaults
  - metrics hooks
  - rate limiting

## Change log
- 2025-03-05: Standardized canonical metric names and default paging thresholds by tier; clarified hold integration requirements.
- 2025-02-03: Initial publication aligned with Retention Controls + Compliance Reporting Pack project requirements.

title: Tenant Safety Scorecard and Auto-Mitigation Patterns
content:
Overview
========
This document defines the Tenant Safety Scorecard (TSS) — a compact, production-focused scoring model and a library of automated mitigation patterns used to preserve platform SLOs while minimizing downstream customer impact. It describes: the metrics and weights for the scorecard, the ingestion and enrichment pipeline, operator thresholds, automated mitigation policies, observability and dashboards, runbook flows, and a safe rollout plan for enabling auto-mitigation in production.

Why we need a Tenant Safety Scorecard
------------------------------------
- Multi-tenant inference workloads can cause noisy neighbors: token spikes, KV cache pressure, GPU interference, or repeated misbehaving prompts.
- We must balance: preserving cluster SLOs (latency, availability) vs. customer-facing degradation and billing fairness.
- The TSS provides a single numeric signal per tenant that drives human alerts, automated actions, and retrospective analysis.

Goals
-----
1. Provide a deterministic, auditable score for tenant-induced platform risk.
2. Trigger graduated mitigations (informational -> soft limits -> hard limits) with human-in-the-loop gates.
3. Ensure mitigations are cost-aware and reversible with clear rollback primitives.
4. Provide dashboards and playbooks so oncall and SREs can quickly evaluate cause, customer impact, and remediation.

Scope and Non-Goals
-------------------
- Scope: realtime and 10m/1h aggregated signals affecting hosted and dedicated clusters. Applies to inference request routing, prefetched caches, and tenant-level autoscaling.
- Non-goal: tenant credit/billing dispute resolution (handled by billing workflows).

Definitions
-----------
- Tenant: account or API key group that owns requests and billing.
- TSS: Tenant Safety Scorecard, normalized 0.0 - 100.0 (higher = higher risk).
- Soft mitigation: non-blocking action (rate-limited responses, lower-priority queue).
- Hard mitigation: blocking action (temporary rate limit, model downgrade, or eviction).

Scorecard Components and Rationale
---------------------------------
We combine telemetry into compact sub-scores, each mapped to 0-100. The final TSS is a weighted sum, clipped to 100. Sub-scores:

1) Token Burst Score (weight 30)
- Measures percentile of short-window token rate vs. tenant baseline. Detects token storms.
- Signal sources: request_token_count, request_rate_1m, historical_7d_baseline.

2) GPU Interference Score (weight 20)
- Derived from GPU metrics: shared_p99_latency_increase, gpu_util_spikes, memory_swap_events. Correlates with tenant placement on noisy nodes.

3) KV Cache Pressure Score (weight 15)
- Tracks cache miss rate, prefix eviction rate, and hot-key skew. High score indicates evictions harming other tenants.

4) Quality-Stability Score (weight 15)
- Model-level errors: repeated malformed requests, function-calling misuses, and saturation of streaming channel errors.

5) SLO Burn Score (weight 20)
- Direct SLO impact: latency_p50/p95 increases attributable to tenant-weighted requests and error budget burn.

Scoring Table (example weights)
-------------------------------
| Component                | Weight | Nominal threshold | High-risk threshold | Notes |
|-------------------------|--------|-------------------|---------------------|-------|
| Token Burst             | 30     | +200% vs baseline | +800% vs baseline   | spikes in 1m window |
| GPU Interference        | 20     | p95+15ms increase | p95+50ms increase   | correlates with GPU metrics |
| KV Cache Pressure       | 15     | eviction_rate>5%  | eviction_rate>20%   | measured per-prefix |
| Quality-Stability       | 15     | repeated 5xx/400  | persistent 5xx/400  | per 1m and 1h windows |
| SLO Burn                | 20     | 5% SLO burn/1h    | 25% SLO burn/1h     | derived attribution engine |

How scores are computed (algorithmic outline)
---------------------------------------------
1. For each tenant, compute normalized sub-score S_i between 0 and 100 using piecewise-linear mapping with hysteresis.
2. Apply exponential smoothing alpha=0.2 to reduce jitter.
3. Final TSS = min(100, sum(weight_i * S_i / 100 * 100)). In practice: sum(weights * S_i) / sum(weights).
4. Persist 1m, 10m, 1h aggregates for retros and debugging.

Data pipeline and ownership
--------------------------
- Sources: ingress logs (request metadata), runtime telemetry (GPU metrics, cache metrics), router attribution, and anomaly-detector outputs.
- Pipeline: Kafka -> real-time scoring service (scoring-api) -> time-series store (VictoriaMetrics) and event sink (audit-events).
- Ownership: scoring-api owned by eng-platform/scoring team. Ingest schema managed in eng-platform/telemetry schema repo.

Operator thresholds and actions
------------------------------
The TSS triggers three classes of actions depending on score ranges and duration: informational (TSS 20-39), protective (TSS 40-69), and restrictive (TSS 70+). All actions are rate-limited and logged.

Informational (20-39)
- Alert: create a P1-Low pager (channel: #platform-tenant-safety) to inform tenant success and platform SRE.
- Action: add tenant to watchlist; increase sampling for detailed traces.

Protective (40-69)
- Automated action: apply adaptive backpressure for best-effort requests from tenant. Route tenant to lower-priority queue for non-critical routes.
- Operator action: open an incident review if TSS >50 for 15 consecutive minutes.

Restrictive (70+)
- Automated action (multi-step):
  1) Attempt soft mitigation: prefix-based throttling (reduce tokens/s by 30%), KV prefetch gating, and request batching enforcement. Wait 2 minutes to observe impact.
  2) If TSS persists >80 after 2 minutes, escalate to hard mitigation: temporary tenant rate limit (configurable, default 10% of baseline) and model downgrade to capped model variant.
  3) If TSS still >90 after additional 5 minutes, trigger eviction policy for the tenant from overloaded nodes and re-place to isolated capacity or dedicated pool if available.
- Human-in-loop: critical hard limits generate a page to the oncall SRE with a one-click rollback link in the incident UI.

Automated mitigation policy examples (YAML)
------------------------------------------
Example: soft-mitigation policy for token spikes\
```
policy_name: soft_token_backpressure_v1
match:
  tenant_id_regex: ".*"
  tss_range: [40, 80]
actions:
  - type: reduce_token_rate
    percent: 30
    duration: 120s
  - type: enable_high_sample_traces
    sample_rate: 0.05
audit: true
```

Example: hard-mitigation policy for repeated GPU interference\
```
policy_name: gpu_downgrade_and_eviction_v1
match:
  tss_range: [80, 100]
actions:
  - type: model_downgrade
    to_variant: quantized-small
  - type: tenant_rate_limit
    requests_per_minute: 100
  - type: node_eviction
    prefer_isolated_pool: true
escalate_to_oncall: true
audit: true
```
Observability and dashboards (owner: eng-platform/observability)
----------------------------------------------------------------
Required dashboard panels (reference names shown):
- TSS Overview (cluster heatmap): shows top 50 tenants by current TSS, sortable by sub-score composition.
- Tenant Detail: time-series for each sub-score + event timeline of policy actions.
- Mitigation Efficacy: percent reduction in SLO burn and token rate per mitigation policy.
- Incident Correlation: joins TSS events with GPU interference and placement changes.

Sample PromQL queries
---------------------
- Current tenant TSS (gauge): tenant_tss_current{tenant_id=~"$tenant"}
- Token burst component: tenant_token_burst_score{tenant_id=~"$tenant"}
- SLO burn attribution (1h window): increase_in_p95_attributable_to_tenant_1h{tenant_id=~"$tenant"}

Runbook: oncall first-responder flow (summary)
-------------------------------------------
1. Pager fires for TSS escalation (TSS >=70). Open the Tenant Detail dashboard and verify: 1m, 10m trends and recent policy actions.
2. Check the audit-events stream for policy decisions applied (scoring-api -> audit-events). Command:
   - kafka-console-consumer --topic audit-events --property print.key=true --from-beginning --max-messages=200 | jq 'select(.tenant_id=="$tenant")'
3. If mitigation is active and tenant impact is acceptable, coordinate with Customer Success to message the tenant and close the alert.
4. If mitigation is too aggressive or incorrectly applied: use the incident UI rollback button or run:
   - curl -XPOST "https://scoring-api.internal/v1/policies/rollback" -d '{"tenant_id":"$tenant","policy":"<policy_name>"}' -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPERATOR_TOKEN"
5. Open a post-incident ticket and tag with label tenant-safety and include the saved 1m/10m/1h aggregates.

SLA / Safety SLO mapping
------------------------
- Platform SLOs affected by tenant behavior: p95 latency < 250ms (critical routes), availability 99.95% monthly.
- Safety SLO obligations: TSS mitigations must not reduce a tenant's availability below 95% unless explicitly escalated to hard mitigation.

Testing and Rollout Plan
-----------------------
1. Simulation: run the TSS scoring service in a test cluster and replay synthetic tenant-traffic profiles using the tenant-sim harness. Evaluate false positive rate target < 1%.
2. Shadow mode: enable scoring and policy evaluation (no enforcement) for 4 weeks in prod; collect fidelity metrics and operator feedback.
3. Canary enforcement: select 5 low-risk tenants (opt-in) and enable full mitigation for 72 hours with manual observer oncall.
4. Phased increase: 10% -> 50% -> 100% of tenants, monitor Mitigation Efficacy and FP rate thresholds.

Postmortems and Retrospective Triggers
-------------------------------------
Create an automatic retrospective when any of the following occur:
- A mitigation rollback is performed more than twice in a single week.
- False positive rate >3% after enforcement.
- Any customer escalations >1 per month related to auto-mitigation.

Operational Metrics to Monitor
-----------------------------
- TSS FP rate (benign tenants receiving mitigation). Target: <1%.
- Mean time to mitigation (from TSS crossing threshold to policy applied). Target: <90s for automated actions.
- Mitigation efficacy: percent reduction in SLO burn within 5 minutes of action. Target: >60%.
- Eviction churn rate: number of tenant evictions per week. Target: <0.5% of tenants/week.

Security, Audit, and Compliance
------------------------------
- All scoring decisions and policy actions must be recorded to the audit-events sink for at least 180 days.
- Hard mitigations require two-person approval if tenant is tagged restricted-compute.
- Policy configuration changes must go through PR review and be signed by owners in the scoring-api CODEOWNERS file.

Ownership and Contact Matrix
---------------------------
- Scoring service & policy engine: eng-platform/scoring (primary).
- Observability dashboards and alerts: eng-platform/observability (primary).
- Operator runbook & oncall: eng-sre (first responder).
- Customer notifications: customer-success (for outreach).

Appendix A: Example debugging checklist (quick)
--------------------------------------------
- Verify tenant attribution: request logs contain correct tenant_id and api_key.
- Inspect GPU traces: nvidia-smi, grpc histograms, and runtime p95 deviation.
- Check KV prefix cache stats: eviction_rate, top-prefix heatmap.
- Recompute TSS locally using 1h raw traces for postmortem.

Appendix B: Data retention and sample sizes
-----------------------------------------
- 1m resolution scoring values: retain 14 days.
- 10m aggregates: retain 60 days.
- 1h aggregates: retain 1 year.
- Audit-events (policy actions): retain 180 days.

Change Log
----------
- 2025-11-12: Draft created by Aisha Patel.
- 2025-12-05: Added mitigation YAML examples and PromQL snippets (reviewers: Miguel Torres).
- 2026-01-20: Updated weightings and added canary rollout plan (reviewers: Priya Nair).
- 2026-02-08: Published with final operator flows and SLAs (reviewer: Daan van der Meer).

Notes and open decisions
------------------------
- Open decision: should hard eviction prefer dedicated pool allocation vs. live node eviction? Proposal: prefer isolated/dedicated pool when available; fall back to re-placement otherwise. Owner: eng-platform/scoring.
- Open action: run a 2-week shadow run during holiday traffic to measure holiday-specific FP rate. Owner: eng-platform/observability.

References
----------
- Tenant isolation economics playbook (internal): /confluence/eng-platform/systems-and-services/tenant-isolation-economics-playbook-2026
- Eviction and placement optimization spec: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/gpu-interference-detection-and-mitigation-playbook-2026

title: GPU graded-degradation and tenant fallback playbook
content:
Summary:

This playbook documents the decision matrix and operational run steps to perform graded degradation and tenant-level fallbacks for GPU-backed inference pools. Graded degradation is an automated + manual strategy to keep the service available with reduced feature set and preserved SLOs when the GPU fleet is under stress (high utilization, preemptions, network egress pressure, or supply loss). The goals are: preserve P95 latency for critical tenants, minimize cost spikes, and avoid hard failures or data loss.

Scope and applicability:
- Applies to inference GPU pools (hosted and dedicated) managed by the pool allocator service (allocator-svc).
- Targets tenant-facing request paths: predict/generate/chat/embedding.
- Not applicable to offline batch training or long-running checkpoint jobs. Those jobs should use the separate batch-queue runbook.

Owners and contacts:
- Primary runbook owner: eng-infra oncall (alias: eng-infra-oncall@redwood.com)
- Fallback policy maintainer: runtime-team (runtime-team@redwood.com)
- Escalation: oncall -> senior-sre -> head of infra (escalation matrix below)

When to run this playbook (signals):
1) Capacity signals (any of the following for > 5 minutes):
   - Cluster GPU utilization > 92% (sustained)
   - Warm-pool deficit > 30% (ten-second moving average)
   - Preemption/spike interruption rate > 1.8%
2) Latency signals:
   - P95 tail latency for critical routes > target + 40%
   - P99 errors or timeouts increasing > 3x baseline
3) Cost / billing signals:
   - Unexpected spot reclaim costs or burst egress charges > 2x projection for rollout windows
4) Multi-region degradation: regional capacity loss with cross-region failover saturation

Decision matrix (short):
- Priority customers (SLA tier: enterprise): try capacity reallocation and cross-region routing first; avoid feature degradation unless evacuation is unavoidable.
- PLG/self-serve tenants: prefer aggressive graded degradation earlier (model downscaling, token caps) and quota enforcement.
- New model rollouts: if rollout causes resource pressure, pause and revert to previous model variant.

Graded degradation levels (automated policy order):
Level 0 — nominal
- No changes. All routing normal.

Level 1 — soft cost/latency relief (automated):
- Lower per-request max_tokens by 20% for non-critical tenants (runtime flag: max_tokens_overcommit = 0.8).
- Aggressive KV-prefix cache reuse (cache-ttl bump).
- Increase batching window by up to 15ms if latency SLO still met.
