2. Replay must run in an isolated namespace with pinned kernel images matching the original kernel id or best-effort compatible variant.
3. Replay should produce a canonical result bundle: stdout JSON, kernel-trace.pb, telemetry-snapshot.json, and a fidelity-report comparing runtime signatures against the captured baseline.

Runbook: investigating a p99 spike with entropy samples
-----------------------------------------------------
1. Identify spike window and query telemetry: p50/p90/p99, sampler.decision ratio, reservoir usage.
2. Pull top N samples by score (N=200 by default) and surface the distribution by fingerprint, model, and tenant.
3. Triage by category: input-entropy dominant, kernel-hop dominant, kv-miss dominant, or mixed.
4. For kernel-hop cases: run replay-harness on the top 5 captures, compare kernel-trace.pb to stored baseline, and check for kernel version skew or NVLink remapping.
5. For kv-miss dominant: check kvcache hit rates across the cluster and warmup patterns; consult the kvcache-prefetch logs.
6. Draft incident note with root cause hypotheses and remedial actions (kernel patch, scheduler-rule, cache policy change).

SLOs and thresholds for sampling pipeline health
------------------------------------------------
- sampler.decision_latency: p95 < 2ms (impacting request tail should be negligible).
- capture.success_rate: >= 99% for declared samples.
- replay.harness.repeatability: >= 95% for deterministic kernels (document exceptions).

Storage, retention, and backfill guidance
----------------------------------------
- Target compressed capture size: median 3KB, 95th percentile < 1MB.
- Retention: high-priority captures (score > 0.95) keep 90 days; general captures keep 7–14 days depending on storage tier.
- Backfill: if replays require additional context we do not capture inline (e.g., larger KV snapshots) we store hooks to request ephemeral backfill runs against a temporary snapshot of tenant state under approved compliance process.

Privacy and compliance notes
---------------------------
- DO NOT capture full PII or customer content unless an explicit approved data-retention exception exists. Sampler must filter or redact fields defined in the global PII filter config.
- All captures are tagged with confidentiality: internal and logged in the audit service.

Operational checks and dashboards (recommended)
---------------------------------------------
- Dashboard: sampler overview (decisions/hour, avg score, reservoir fill).
- Dashboard: capture quality (size distribution, replay success over time, median time-to-replay).
- Alert: capture.success_rate < 98% for 10m, sampler.decision_latency.p95 > 5ms.

Appendix: CLI examples
----------------------
- Create a replay bundle from capture store (example):
  $ rcli capture fetch --id sample-2026-09-11-0001 --out ./bundle.tgz

- Run replay against staging:
  $ rcli replay run --bundle ./bundle.tgz --target staging --collect kernel-trace,telemetry --timeout 10m

FAQ
---
Q: How do we avoid capturing test traffic or repeated PLG samples?
A: Use fingerprint_fields to identify onboarding/test flows and set an explicit exclude policy.

Q: Does sampling add latency to production calls?
A: The in-line sampler must be asynchronous in critical-path if score calculation exceeds low-latency budget; prefer a fast-path estimate and deferred final capture.

Owners and contacts
-------------------
Primary: eng-serving-runtime/profiling (team alias).
Escalation: Aisha Patel (aisha.patel@redwood.ai), Marco Ruiz (marco.ruiz@redwood.ai).

Related reading
---------------
- Performance-regression-huntbook (see onboarding steps for replay harness)
- runtime-telemetry-sampling-cost-aware-profiling (design motivations and cost modeling)

Change log
----------
- 2025-02-10: initial draft and internal review.
- 2025-06-01: adjusted default weights after mixed-workload evaluation.
- 2026-08-12: added replay contract and PII compliance section.

title: GPU Kernel Latency Investigation Playbook
content:
Summary:

This playbook describes a repeatable, evidence-driven process for investigating request-level latency spikes attributable to GPU kernel behavior in the Redwood serving runtime. It is intended for on-call SREs, runtime engineers, and performance-focused ML engineers.

Goals:
- Rapidly determine whether a latency regression is caused by GPU kernel execution (vs. queueing, CPU scheduling, RPC, or networking).
- Produce actionable remediation (config change, kernel selector tweak, batching rule, or model fallback).
- Provide reproducible artifacts: kernel traces, flamegraphs, aggregated metrics, and a short root-cause summary.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to Redwood Dedicated and Private deployments where we control the GPU runtime.
- Assumes access to Prometheus, Grafana dashboards, node ssh, and container runtime metrics.
- Requires NVTX/NSYS instrumentation enabled on the runtime image (see section "Instrumentation checklist").

Key contacts / owners:
- Runtime Performance Lead: Maya Chen (author) — paged for escalations
- Serving Runtime Lead: Carlos Rivera — owner for rollout and kernel selector changes
- GPU Fleet Ops: Priya Kapoor — capacity and node-level remediation

SLOs and thresholds to guide triage:
- Per-request 95th percentile latency SLO: 1200 ms (text-generation default route).
- Alert firing threshold: 95p latency > 1400 ms for 5m or error rate increase > 1% relative baseline.
- Kernel suspicion rule: kernel_time_ratio > 0.5 for 95p requests (kernel_time_ratio = gpu_kernel_time / request_total_time).

High-level investigation checklist (fast path):
1) Confirm alert and scope in Grafana
   - Open route latency dashboard (dash: /dashboards/route-latency)
   - Identify affected routes, models, and regions.
2) Check server-side queueing and CPU stalls
   - Inspect metrics: request_queue_length, cpu_runqueue_length, worker_cpu_usage.
   - If queueing explains >50% of increased latency, follow runbooks/runbook-queue-surge (not this doc).
3) If CPU and queueing are normal, check GPU kernel dominance
   - Pull precomputed metric: gpu_kernel_time_total, request_wall_time_total, and compute kernel_time_ratio.
   - If kernel_time_ratio > 0.5 at 95p, proceed with kernel-level traces.

Instrumentation checklist (must be enabled before deep profiling):
- Runtime compiled with NVTX annotations around model forward passes and KV cache operations.
- Healthcheck job that can run a deterministic micro-benchmark per node (see snippet below).
- Container has nsys and ncu available (or a sidecar helper image).
- Prometheus exporters exposing per-gpu metrics: gpu_utilization_pct, gpu_compute_ms, gpu_memory_copy_ms.

Quick reproducible micro-benchmark (run from inside runtime container):

# Run a short deterministic workload against the model shard
python -c "from perf_utils import run_deterministic_batch; print(run_deterministic_batch('gpt-medium', batch_size=1, seq_len=128, steps=5))"

Expected output: JSON with timing breakdown: total_ms, cpu_ms, kernel_ms, memcpy_ms. Save to /tmp/prof-run-$(date +%s).json

Collecting traces (nsys) - safe, short captures:
- When possible, use a 10-20s capture window to reduce noise and storage.
- Prefer capturing a single node and single model shard to limit trace size.
- Example commands (run as root or container with host GPU access):

nsys profile --capture-range=nvtx --capture-range-end=stop --output=/tmp/trace-$(date +%s) --stats=true --trace=nvtx,cuda --duration=20s --processes=all --sample=none --sample-frequency=0

# Steps:
1. Start capture: nsys profile --output=/tmp/trace --trace=nvtx,cuda --capture-range=nvtx,...
2. Trigger a deterministic test load (see micro-benchmark).
3. Stop capture and pull .qdrep for analysis.

Key artifacts to extract from NSYS/NVPROF:
- Per-kernel latency distribution (mean, 50p, 95p, max)
- Kernel call counts per forward pass
- Memcpy times and patterns (H2D, D2H, P2P)
- NVTX region timelines (map to logical phases: tokenize→model_forward→KV_cache→postprocess)

What to look for (triage heuristics):
- Single large kernel dominating forward (e.g., attention_flop_kernel) with high variance: indicates kernel scheduling/preemption or data-dependent work.
- Many small kernels at high frequency causing scheduling overhead: candidate for kernel fusion or larger batch grouping.
- Long memcpy operations concurrent with compute: suggests PCIe contention or suboptimal tensor placement (host staging).
- High tail in kernel latency correlated with GPU context switches: check driver logs for TDR or preemption events.

Prometheus queries and Grafana panels to produce (examples):
- kernel_time_ratio by route:
  sum(rate(gpu_kernel_time_seconds_sum[5m])) by (route) / sum(rate(request_latency_seconds_sum[5m])) by (route)
- per-node kernel tail (95p):
  histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(gpu_kernel_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, node))
- memcpy vs compute scatter: use table panel with gpu_memory_copy_ms and gpu_compute_ms per node.

Example short RCA (what should be produced within 2 hours):
- Summary: High 95p latency on /api/generate caused by attention_kernel tail on shard-03 in us-west-2. Kernel_time_ratio=0.74.
- Evidence: NSYS trace (trace-167...), kernel latency histogram attached, Prometheus query snapshots.
- Root cause hypothesis: kernel performance regressed after CUDA driver upgrade -> changed scheduling granularity causing attention kernel to be preempted intermittently.
- Action taken: pinned driver to previous working version on shard-03; rolled canary to 10% to validate.
- Long-term fix: add kernel selector fallback to lower-compute granularities for affected models and add a preflight driver compatibility test.

Remediation options (ordered by speed/risk):
1) Node-level: Restart GPU driver / cordon and drain node (low-risk) — ops action.
2) Runtime config: Reduce max_concurrent_inflight_kernels (runtime param) to reduce kernel overlap and tail (medium risk, instant).
3) Kernel selector change: Prefer fused_kernel_variant_v2 for sequence lengths > 1024 (requires model-rebuild and canary, high risk).
4) Capacity: Shift affected traffic to Dedicated overflow pool (policy-based routing) while investigating (low-risk and immediate).

Rollback and rollout guidance for kernel selector changes:
- Use A/B canary: 5% -> 20% -> 50% -> 100% with 30m observe window at each step.
- Required telemetry: route-level 95p latency, gpu_kernel_time_ms 95p, error-rate.
- If 95p latency increases > 10% vs baseline or error-rate increases > 0.5%, stop rollout and revert.

On-call runbook (step-by-step):
1) Acknowledge alert and note affected routes and hosts.
2) Run quick checks (queueing, CPU busy, network) using dashboard checklist.
3) If GPU kernel suspected, trigger micro-benchmark and collect NSYS trace for one representative node.
4) Upload artifacts to /artifacts/perf/<incident-id>/ and create RCA draft in Jira ticket.
5) Execute short-term mitigation (drain node / reduce concurrency / shift traffic) and monitor.
6) If a kernel selector change is required, open PR in runtime repo and follow rollout guidance above.

Common symptoms -> probable causes (diagnostic table):
- Symptom: High tail only on long sequences. Probable cause: kernel variant with poor path for > seq_len threshold. Fix: switch selector, add regression test for long sequences.
- Symptom: High variance across identical hardware. Probable cause: PCIe contention or thermal throttling. Fix: check node-level metrics, migrate shards.
- Symptom: Small per-token slowdown but large aggregate. Probable cause: many tiny kernels. Fix: enable kernel fusion or increase batching.

Developer tips and primitives:
- Use NVTX ranges consistently in code; every logical phase should have a named NVTX annotation to ease capture filtering.
- Keep deterministic microbenchmarks checked into /infra/profiling/benchmarks with pinned seeds.
- When analyzing traces, always correlate nvtx timeline with top-level Prometheus traces to map request IDs to kernel timelines.

Post-incident checklist (complete within 48h):
- Produce an RCA doc with 1-2 figure summary, 3 evidence bullets, and 2 actionable follow-ups.
- Add a regression test to perf-suite if root cause is software (driver/runtime/model change).
- If hardware or driver was changed, add a canary job that runs perf smoke on the next upgrade.

References and tools:
- NVIDIA Nsight Systems (nsys): https://developer.nvidia.com/nsight-systems
- NVTX annotation best-practices: internal link /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/nvtx-guidelines (draft)
- Runtime config knobs: k_scheduling.max_concurrent_kernels, k_selector.prefer_fused, k_mem.copy_stride_threshold (see runtime-ops-config page)

Appendix A: Example ncu command for kernel stacks (more invasive)

ncu --target-processes all --launch-skip 0 --launch-count 10 --set full --output /tmp/ncu-report --sample 1000 --kernel-regex "attention|matmul|softmax" --trace-fork --target-pid <pid>

Note: ncu captures are large and should be reserved for offline analysis.

Appendix B: Minimal NVTX conventions (enforced by lint):
- NVTX names must include: component:model:phase (e.g., runtime:gpt-medium:forward)
- Push/pop nesting must be balanced; missing pop will break capture segmentation.

Appendix C: Example artifact checklist for RCA ticket
- Prometheus query snapshots (PNG) for route latency and gpu kernel metrics
- NSYS .qdrep and derived kernel latency histogram (CSV)
- Micro-benchmark logs and raw timing JSON
- Driver and kernel versions for affected nodes (nvidia-smi -q and uname -r)
- Short impact summary and mitigation steps taken

Notes and future work:
- We plan to add automated root-cause heuristics to the perf pipeline that flag kernel_time_ratio regressions and auto-attach the smallest representative NSYS trace.
- Propose adding a canary that runs a targeted NVTX-instrumented workload after every driver or CUDA change in the Dedicated fleet.

Document history:
- 2024-06-12: Initial draft
- 2024-09-05: Added NSYS examples and heuristics after attention-kernel regression
- 2025-01-20: Revised rollout guidance and added kernel selector remediation options

title: Quantization-Induced Timing Investigation Handbook
content:
Summary

This handbook codifies a standard investigation and mitigation workflow for latency regressions and high-variance tail behavior that correlate with quantized model kernels or mixed-precision execution paths. It is targeted at SREs, runtime engineers, and applied ML engineers responsible for rollout safeties and kernel scheduling.

Scope

- Applies to inference serving instances using int8/4/2 quantization paths, mixed FP16/FP32 kernels, and runtime kernel switching (auto, fallback, or staged rollout).
- Covers production incidents and reproducible lab investigations.
- Excludes model-quality hallucination investigation (see quality-guardrails space).

Symptoms that should trigger this playbook

1) Sudden increase in p99/p999 latency after a quantization rollout or kernel update.
2) Increased variance in kernel execution durations in kernel-duration histograms.
3) Elevated kernel error rates (timeouts/retries) coincident with quantized model variants.
4) Autoscaler thrash or queue buildup when quantized kernels are used.

Key telemetry to collect (minimum set)

- Per-request trace with kernel hints: kernel.name, kernel.variant, kernel.duration_ns, sequence_length, batch_size, tenant_id
- Percentile latency (p50/p95/p99/p999) for request surface and per-kernel breakdown
- Kernel-duration histogram (log-buckets, microsecond resolution)
- GPU occupancy / SM utilization per kernel (sampled)
- CUDA error counters and pending stream counts
- KV-cache hit/miss rates and cache-priming latencies
- Memory allocation / OOM events and fragmentation metrics

Recommended Prometheus alerting signals (examples)

- Alert: Quantization_Kernel_P99_Increase
  Expr: increase(runtime_request_duration_seconds_bucket{kernel_variant=~".*quant.*"}[5m]) > 0 and histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(runtime_request_duration_seconds_bucket{kernel_variant=~".*quant.*"}[5m])) by (le)) > 0.8

- Alert: Kernel_Error_Surge
  Expr: increase(runtime_kernel_errors_total{kernel_variant=~".*quant.*"}[1m]) / increase(runtime_requests_total[1m]) > 0.01

Investigation checklist (ordered steps)

1) Baseline verification
   - Confirm regression window and affected release / deployment (Git commit, container image, kernel package).
   - Query traffic slices: which model variants, routes, customer tiers are affected? Use time-windowed query and compare control vs. quantized slices.

2) Triage with shadowed traces
   - Enable shadow logging for a representative slice (non-prod routing or shadow channel) to collect per-kernel traces without impacting production.
   - If possible, mirror a small percentage (1–5%) of live requests to a canary pool running the quantized kernel for direct comparison.

3) Kernel-level profiling
   - Capture per-GPU kernel traces for the affected timeframe. Recommended tools and commands: 
     - Nsight Systems (batch capture): nsight-sys --trace=cuda --capture-range=pid:12345-12345 -o capture.qdrep
     - CUPTI / nvtx annotations: ensure runtime emits NVTX begin/end for kernel sections.
     - Lightweight sampler: collect 1s-5s stack-samples using perf or nsight-sys sampling to get occupancy hotspots.

4) Correlate kernel durations with sequence shape and batching
   - Use trace queries to pivot on sequence_length and aggregated batch_size. Look for skew: e.g., quantized kernel latency regresses for variable sequence segments > 512 tokens.

5) Check memory / dispatch interactions
   - Inspect memory allocation timelines for spikes that align with kernel duration climbs; quantized kernels may change workspace sizing.

6) Regression isolation using controlled replay
   - Re-run a production traffic slice through a replay harness in the lab that can toggle quantized vs. fp16 kernels deterministically. Measure per-kernel latencies and jitter.

7) If reproducible, instrument microbenchmarks
   - Create a microbenchmark (single request, controlled sequence length, controlled batch sizes) and run across kernel variants. Collect kernel duration histograms and occupancy.

8) Reach mitigation decision
   - If quantized kernel causes unfixable latency or tail variance (per SLO table below), trigger rollback policy. Otherwise, apply mitigations below and continue rollout in small cohorts.

SLO gating and decision table

| Severity | Condition | Action (owner) | Evidence required |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Sev 1 | p99 increase > 2x baseline AND errors > 0.5% | Immediate rollback to previous kernel (runtime-owner) | Pre/post histograms, trace slices, replay results |
| Sev 2 | p99 increase 1.2–2x OR p999 increase > 1.5x | Pause rollout and start triage (oncall + runtime) | Microbenchmark and kernel-level trace |
| Sev 3 | Minor p95 increase (<1.2x) but stable errors | Continue rollout with throttling and observability | Canary telemetry over 24h |

Mitigations and quick fixes

- Rollback: Revert to previous kernel / quantization profile via rollout CLI and route traffic away from canary pool.
- Kernel hinting: Pin to fallback kernel for high-seq-length cohort via routing rule (example below).
- Batching policy change: Force max-batch-size limit to reduce variation for mixed kernels.
- Prefetching: Increase async KV-cache prefetch window when memory allows.

Routing rule example (YAML fragment)

route_overrides:
  - name: pin-high-seq-to-fallback
    match:
      - field: request.sequence_length
        op: ">\""
        value: "1024"
    action:
      - set_kernel_variant: fallback-fp16

Runtime rollout CLI snippets

# List active kernel variants
redwood runtime kernels list --pool=canary
# Pin route to old kernel
redwood runtime route override apply --route-id=route-123 --kernel=fallback-fp16 --reason="rollback-quant-2026-11-05"

Controlled experiment: A/B quantized vs fallback (small cohort)

1) Select representative tenant cohort (low-volume but realistic shapes).
2) Create two canary pools: A (quantized) and B (fallback). Mirror identical traffic; ensure statistical power (minimum 5k requests per cohort).
3) Collect: per-request latencies, kernel durations, GPU utilization, and error rates.
4) Run a two-sample test on p99 and p999. Use bootstrap if distribution non-parametric.
5) If A shows significant tail degradation (p99 diff > 20% and p-value < 0.01), fail the gate.

Persistent-fix paths (when kernel is culprit)

- Kernel tune: collaborate with kernel-team to adjust tiling, loop unrolling thresholds, or quantization packing order.
- Workspace sizing: change temporary buffer allocation strategy to avoid fragmentation spikes.
- Scheduler hints: add admission control to avoid mixing large sequence requests with tight batches on quantized kernels.

Artifact and evidence collection policy

- Store all captures (nsight qdrep, trace logs) in S3 under s3://redwood-runtime-debug/{incident-id}/captures with read ACL to runtime-team and oncall.
- Include a triage.md summary with key graphs and the replay harness config.

Runbook checklist (quick actions for oncall)

1) Acknowledge alert and page runtime-owner.
2) Attach incident ID and take a short sample capture (30s) from impacted node(s).
3) Enable shadow capture for affected routes.
4) If clear regression and high customer impact: execute rollback steps.
5) If uncertain: create replay job and run microbenchmarks in the lab.

Ownership and escalation

- First responder: serving-runtime oncall (rotation: runtime-oncall@redwood.ai).
- Secondary: kernel-team lead (Sana Reddy).
- Escalate to SRE manager when rollback affects > 10% traffic or revenue-bearing tenants.

Appendix: Useful queries and artifacts

- Example trace store query (SQL-style):
  SELECT request_id, kernel_variant, histogram_quantile(0.99, kernel_duration_histogram) AS p99_kernel FROM traces WHERE timestamp BETWEEN TIMESTAMP_SUB(now(), INTERVAL 10 MINUTE) AND now() AND kernel_variant LIKE '%quant%' GROUP BY kernel_variant;

- Microbenchmark YAML example:
  bench_name: quant-510-test
  sequence_length: 510
  batch_sizes: [1,2,4,8]
  kernel_variants: [quant-int8, fallback-fp16]
  runs: 1000

- Preferred artifact naming: {incident-id}_{node-or-pool}_{capture-type}_{timestamp} e.g. INC-20261105_canary1_nsight_qdrep_20261105T0921.qdrep

Related reading

- Runtime profiling guidelines: /eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/runtime-profiling-playbook-guidelines-2025
- Quantization rollout safety: /eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/quantization-rollout-safety-and-quality-gate-playbook-2026

Contact and maintenance

- Doc owner: Aisha Thompson (aisha@redwood.ai)
- Next review cycle: 2027-06-01

End of handbook

title: developer-sandbox-benchmarking-playbook
content:
Summary
This playbook describes the developer-local runtime sandbox and associated benchmarking + profiling workflows used to reproduce key production behaviors without requiring full cluster access. The sandbox is intentionally lightweight and deterministic: it models the runtime dispatch, a KV cache shim, a kernel-proxy for scheduling experiments, and easy-to-run microbenchmarks. Use this guide to iterate on kernel scheduler patches, evaluate batching strategies, and validate optimization hypotheses before graduating changes to the full perf suite.

Scope
- Reproduce request lifecycle: API -> dispatcher -> kernel-proxy -> model executor (mock or quantized engine).
- Run microbenchmarks that mimic production prompt shapes (short, medium, long) and multi-turn chat traces.
- Exercise scheduling policies (fair-share, priority-driven, cooperative preemption) in a reproducible environment.
- Capture perf traces (CPU/GPU timelines), kernel occupancy, and per-token cost estimates.
- Limitations: does not emulate multi-tenant noisy neighbors at scale, and GPU topology is single-node only. See Known Differences section.

Prerequisites
1) Linux workstation with Docker 20.10+ or a macOS machine with Docker Desktop and a supported GPU passthrough (optional).
2) tools/runtime-sandbox repo checked out (internal): git clone git@repo.internal:redwood/tools/runtime-sandbox.git
3) Python 3.10+, pipenv or virtualenv for running harness scripts.

Sandbox Components (what runs locally)
- runtime-dispatcher-lite: lightweight HTTP front-end that accepts Redwood API-style requests and translates compute work into a scheduling request.
- kvcached-shim: in-memory KV cache with controllable hit-rate to simulate warm/cold sessions.
- kernel-proxy: process that implements a subset of production kernel selection + queuing logic; pluggable policies: simple_fifo, fair_share, priority_shepherd.
- model-mock: tunable latency stub or a real local quantized engine (GGML/onnxruntime path) for end-to-end verification.

Quickstart: run the sandbox (example)
1) Start the sandbox (default ports: 8080 dispatcher, 9090 proxy):
```bash
cd tools/runtime-sandbox
./scripts/start_sandbox.sh --workers 4 --policy priority_shepherd --kv-hit-rate 0.2
```
2) Run a short prompt microbenchmark (50 token generation, batch size 8):
```bash
./benchmarks/run_local_microbench.py --endpoint http://localhost:8080/generate --prompt-file examples/short_prompts.txt --batch-size 8 --tokens 50 --samples 100
```
3) Collect traces and open local report:
```bash
./scripts/collect_traces.sh --out=artifacts/run-$(date +%s)
open artifacts/run-*/index.html  # (Linux: xdg-open)
```

Benchmark Catalog (recommended microbenchmarks)
- short_prompt_50: 50 tokens, mean prompt length 12 tokens, simulates chat replies and low-latency assistant responses.
- medium_prompt_200: 200 tokens, mean prompt length 80 tokens, represents longer instruction completions.
- long_prompt_1024: 1024 tokens, stress test for KV cache and kernel memory usage.
- multi_turn_continuation: sequence of 4 calls with KV cache warmup between calls.
- mixed_priority_mixture: concurrent clients with priority labels (gold/silver/free) to exercise preemption.

Example benchmark command (mixed workload)
```bash
./benchmarks/run_local_mixed.sh \
  --clients 40 --gold-share 0.1 --silver-share 0.3 --policy fair_share \
  --duration 300 --output artifacts/mixed-$(date +%s).json
```

Kernel Scheduling Experiments
We expose the following knobs in kernel-proxy to emulate production scheduling behavior:
- batch_window_ms: how long to wait to form a batch before dispatch. Typical test values: 1, 4, 8, 16 ms.
- max_batch_tokens: maximum token budget allowed for a single batch.
- preempt_granularity: slice size used for cooperative preemption (in tokens).
- priority_weight: mapping table for gold/silver/free request weight.

Experiment template (compare batch_window_ms)
1) Start sandbox with identical worker count and model-mock latency profile.
2) Run short_prompt_50 with batch_window_ms set to 1, 4, 8, 16. Each run: 3 warmup minutes + 10 minute sampling.
3) Metrics to record: p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput (tokens/sec), mean batch size, dispatch queue depth.
4) Success criteria: for short_prompt_50, p95 <= 120ms and throughput drop <= 5% relative to baseline.

Profiling and Tracing Guidance
- Enable kernel telemetry: set env RUNTIME_TELEMETRY=1 in start_sandbox.sh to capture per-kernel timings and memory high-water marks.
- GPU traces: when running with a local GPU engine, enable CUPTI tracing via ./scripts/start_gpu_tracing.sh. For CPU-only runs, use perf and flamegraphs.
- Annotate traces with request provenance: the dispatcher attaches request_id and priority_tag to every scheduling event. Include these when uploading traces to the central trace collector.

Trace artifact format and required fields
When you upload a trace for triage, include the following in the artifact zip:
- run_metadata.json (fields: run_id, start_ts, policy, worker_count, kv_hit_rate, model_path)
- kernel_timings.csv (columns: timestamp, kernel_name, duration_ms, occupancy_pct, allocated_bytes)
- batch_events.ndjson (one line per batch event: request_ids[], batch_size, policy, outcome)
- system_monitor.log (CPU, GPU, memory samples at 1s resolution)

Example run_metadata.json (literal snippet)
```json
{
  "run_id": "local-20260210-001",
  "policy": "priority_shepherd",
  "worker_count": 4,
  "kv_hit_rate": 0.2,
  "model_path": "local-ggml/7b-q4_0.bin"
}
```

Runbook: triage workflow for an unexpected latency regression
1) Reproduce locally using the same artifact and policy. If you cannot reproduce, escalate to runtime-sre with full artifact.
2) Run `./benchmarks/run_local_microbench.py` with `--diagnostic=true` to produce kernel_timings and batch_events.
3) Check batch size distribution and batch wait times. If mean batch_size drops by >25% vs baseline, suspect batching regressions.
4) Inspect kernel_timings.csv for spikes in a specific kernel. If a single kernel shows >50% increase in median duration, flag as kernel regression and attach minimal repro to a kernel-owner PR.
5) If GPU memory HWM increased significantly, run the memory-fragmentation diagnostic script: `./scripts/gpu_memory_frag_diag.sh`.
6) Document findings in the triage template and update the related run in the benchmarking dashboard.

Known Differences vs Production
- Multi-node routing and remote shard topology are not modeled; cross-node latencies and NUMA effects may be missing.
- The sandbox runs a single GPU device; device-local scheduling differences and inter-GPU NVLink behaviors are not captured.
- Autoscaling and burst capacity behavior is not exercised.
- Real tenant-induced KV-cache conflicts are out of scope.

Best Practices for Developers
- Start with model-mock for rapid iterations; only switch to a local quantized engine (GGML/ONNX) when validating memory and kernel changes.
- Keep run_metadata for every experiment. It is the single source of truth when comparing runs.
- Use stable random seeds when benchmarking (pass --seed <n>) to reduce variance.
- Run at least 3 independent samples for each configuration and report median with IQR.

Onboarding Checklist (for new runtime contributors)
1) Read this playbook and the runtime profiling guidelines page.
2) Run the short_prompt_50 microbenchmark and verify baseline numbers (p95 <= 120ms on a dev workstation with model-mock).
3) Submit one small change (e.g., tweak batch_window_ms) and show the before/after artifacts in a PR.
4) Request review from kernel owners and runtime-sre for approval.

Troubleshooting common errors
- `Connection refused` on kernel-proxy: ensure the proxy is up (docker ps) and ports 9090/9091 are free.
- `Empty batches` warnings: check dispatcher logs; increase batch_window_ms by 2ms for noise-sensitive environments.
- `OOM on model-mock`: reduce model size or run with --simulated-memory=true flag.

Document changelog
- 2024-09-15: Initial draft and quickstart (Asha Patel).
- 2025-06-02: Added mixed_priority_mixture benchmark and new priority_weight knob (Marco Rivera).
- 2026-02-10: Added trace artifact schema and updated triage runbook (Elena Kim).

Owners and contacts
- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime/runtime-observability (Asha Patel)
- Runtime kernel owners: Marco Rivera (kernel mapper), Linh Tran (preemption infra)
- Escalation: runtime-sre on-call (see /confluence/eng-sre/oncall-rotations)

Appendix: example minimal policy YAML for kernel-proxy
```yaml
policy: priority_shepherd
params:
  batch_window_ms: 4
  max_batch_tokens: 2048
  preempt_granularity: 32
  priority_weight:
    gold: 3
    silver: 2
    free: 1
```

If you have questions about extending the sandbox or integrating additional telemetry hooks, reach out to the runtime-observability channel on Slack and attach run artifacts.

title: TP stall triage playbook (tensor-parallel hangs/timeouts)
content:
## Purpose
This playbook covers step-by-step triage for **tensor-parallel (TP) stalls** (a.k.a. hangs/timeouts) in the serving runtime. It is written for on-call SRE + runtime engineers to quickly answer:
- Is the stall **compute**, **NCCL/collectives**, or **scheduler/starvation**?
- Which replicas/ranks are stuck, and is it isolated or systemic?
- What data should we capture (metrics/logs/traces/NCCL debug) without making the incident worse?

This is **triage + profiling**. For mitigation actions (drain/replace, concurrency caps, feature flags), use the runbook: *Runtime TP hang mitigation*.

---

## Definitions (what we mean by “TP stall”)
A TP stall is a condition where a multi-GPU replica stops making forward progress for a request or decode loop. Typical external symptoms:
- Streaming responses stop mid-stream (client sees partial tokens then timeout).
- Request p99 and timeout rate spike for a subset of replicas (often a single model + HW type).
- GPU utilization becomes skewed by rank (one GPU at high util while others idle) or all GPUs look “busy” but throughput drops.

Internal signatures commonly fall into:
1) **Collective mismatch / ordering bug** (ranks enter different collectives or different order)
2) **Stream/event sync hazard** (collective enqueued but waits on an event never recorded / wrong stream)
3) **Scheduler starvation** (collectives or rank coordination starved by prefill-heavy batches or unfair queueing)
4) **Memory/KV cache pressure divergence** (rank divergence due to compaction/fragmentation edge cases)

---

## Before you start (scope + safety)
### Don’t worsen the blast radius
- Avoid enabling verbose NCCL debug on broad fleets. Prefer **single replica**, **short window**, **Dedicated-first**, and **off-peak** when possible.
- NCCL debug can create large logs and measurable overhead; it can also expose topology and environment details. Treat as internal-only.
- If customer traffic is impacted (timeouts), prioritize mitigation (drain/replace, cap concurrency) before deep profiling.

### What to capture (minimum useful packet)
Collect these for every suspected TP stall:
- Cluster/region, model name/version, runtime version, GPU type, TP degree (e.g., TP=4/8)
- Affected replica IDs + node IDs
- Time window (start, peak, end), and whether retries/fallback triggered
- Links to:
  - TP Stall & Timeout dashboard panels
  - Request trace IDs (at least 2–3 from timeouts)
  - Logs for the affected replica(s)

---

## Fast triage (5–10 minutes)
### Step 1: Confirm it’s TP-related vs generic overload
Use the dashboard: **TP stall and timeout dashboard**.

Look for:
- **Request timeouts** concentrated on TP replicas vs all replicas
- **TP rank heartbeat gaps** (per-rank progress stops)
- **Replica drain events** spiking (watchdog/abort path firing)
- **Scheduler queue depth** rising without corresponding throughput

If timeouts are uniform across all replicas, treat as broader capacity/overload and use standard overload playbooks.

### Step 2: Identify the blast radius
Answer:
- Is it **one replica** (likely wedged) or **many replicas** (likely systemic regression)?
- Is it tied to **one model**, **one GPU SKU**, **one cluster**, or **one recent rollout**?

Checklist:
- Compare Dedicated vs Hosted clusters
- Compare A100/H100/L40S pools
- Check recent runtime canary changes and feature flags

### Step 3: Determine stall class with 3 signals
Use these three signals together to classify quickly:

1) **Rank heartbeat age** (progress signal)
- Symptom: heartbeat age increasing on some/all ranks.

2) **In-flight collective counters** (comms signal)
- Symptom: collectives “in-flight” stuck (not decrementing) or ranks report different collective sequence.

3) **Scheduler queue depth / fairness** (scheduler signal)
- Symptom: queue depth grows; prefill-heavy batches dominate; decode iterations stop being scheduled.

If (1) is bad and (2) shows stuck collectives → suspect NCCL/collectives ordering or stream sync.
If (1) is bad but (2) is normal and (3) is bad → suspect scheduler starvation.
If (1) is bad and memory/KV errors appear in logs → suspect KV cache divergence/compaction.

---

## Metrics to use (names + interpretation)
Metric names may differ slightly by environment; prefer the dashboard panels as source of truth.

### Core TP health
- `runtime_tp_rank_heartbeat_age_seconds{model,replica_id,rank}`
  - **Actionable:** if > 10–30s sustained for any rank, suspect stall.
- `runtime_tp_stall_reason_total{model,replica_id,reason}`
  - **Reason codes** (common): `COMMS_COLLECTIVE_STUCK`, `SCHED_STARVATION`, `KV_ALLOC_WAIT`, `CANCEL_PATH_WAIT`, `UNKNOWN`.
- `runtime_tp_inflight_collectives{model,replica_id,rank,collective}`
  - Rising and never decreasing → stuck collective.

### Scheduler/backpressure
- `runtime_scheduler_queue_depth{queue,model}`
- `runtime_scheduler_prefill_decode_ratio{model}`
- `runtime_scheduler_starvation_events_total{model}`

### Timeouts + mitigations
- `api_request_timeouts_total{route,model,cluster}`
- `runtime_replica_drain_events_total{reason,model}`
- `runtime_overload_rejections_total{reason,model}`

---

## Logs (what to grep for)
### Structured runtime log fields to pull
For the suspected replica, gather logs around the stall window and extract:
- `replica_id`, `rank`, `tp_degree`, `model`, `request_id`, `trace_id`
- `stall_reason`, `collective_seq`, `collective_type`, `stream_id`, `cuda_graph_enabled`
- `kv_cache_bytes_free`, `kv_compaction_in_progress`, `oom/alloc_wait`

### Common log patterns
- Collective mismatch / ordering:
  - “collective sequence mismatch”
  - “rank entered ALLREDUCE but peer entered ALLGATHER”
  - “expected collective_id=X observed Y”
- Stream/event sync:
  - “waiting on cuda event” with long durations
  - “stream synchronize timed out”
- Scheduler starvation:
  - “prefill batch admitted while decode pending”
  - “fairness guardrail triggered” (if enabled)
- Cancellation path deadlock:
  - “client disconnected” followed by stuck collective / no further progress

---

## Traces (how to correlate stalls to collectives)
### What to look for in traces
For 2–3 timed-out requests:
- Identify the server-side spans for decode iterations.
- Check span attributes:
  - `tp.rank`, `tp.degree`
  - `tp.collective.inflight` counters
  - `tp.collective.seq` (if present)
  - `stall_reason` tag (if emitted)

### Minimal trace workflow
1) Pull a timeout request ID from API logs.
2) Find the associated `trace_id`.
3) Open trace and confirm where time is spent:
   - compute kernel spans vs NCCL spans vs scheduler wait spans.

If trace shows long gaps without spans, rely on heartbeat + logs; the process may be stuck below instrumentation.

---

## Node/replica inspection (commands)
The exact tooling differs by cluster. The commands below are representative for Redwood’s Kubernetes-based runtime clusters.

### Identify the pod and node
- Find pods for a model:
  - `kubectl -n runtime get pods -l app=redwood-runtime,model=<MODEL> -o wide`
- Filter to a specific replica:
  - `kubectl -n runtime get pod | grep <replica_id>`

### Quick GPU health (on the node)
If you have node access (or via privileged debug pod):
- `nvidia-smi -L`
- `nvidia-smi pmon -c 1`
- `nvidia-smi dmon -s pucvmt -c 5`

What you’re looking for:
- Rank imbalance (one GPU pegged while others idle)
- PCIe/NVLink issues (if visible)
- Memory near OOM or rapid allocation churn

### Collect pod logs around the stall
- `kubectl -n runtime logs <pod> --since=30m > /tmp/<pod>.log`
- If multi-container:
  - `kubectl -n runtime logs <pod> -c runtime --since=30m`

### Capture a lightweight runtime debug snapshot (preferred over heavy profilers)
If the runtime exposes a debug endpoint (varies by env):
- `kubectl -n runtime port-forward <pod> 6060:6060`
- Then (examples):
  - `curl -s http://localhost:6060/debug/tp/status`
  - `curl -s http://localhost:6060/debug/scheduler/queues`
  - `curl -s http://localhost:6060/debug/kv/summary`

If endpoints are unavailable, rely on logs + metrics.

---

## Safely capturing NCCL debug traces
### When to enable NCCL debug
Enable NCCL debug only when:
- The issue reproduces and **appears comms/collective-related**.
- The blast radius is controlled (single replica or small canary).
- You have a clear rollback plan and a short time window (10–30 minutes).

### Recommended NCCL debug settings (balanced)
Use the least-verbose settings that still show collective sequencing.

Suggested env vars:
- `NCCL_DEBUG=INFO`
- `NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=COLL,INIT`
- `NCCL_DEBUG_FILE=/var/log/redwood/nccl/%h_%p_rank%r.log`

Optional (only if needed):
- `NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=COLL,INIT,GRAPH`
- `NCCL_DEBUG=WARN` (if INFO is too noisy)

Avoid unless specifically requested by kernel team:
- `NCCL_DEBUG=TRACE` (very noisy)
- Broad `NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=ALL`

### Operational safety checklist
Before enabling:
1) Confirm **disk space** for logs on node/pod (NCCL logs can be large).
2) Confirm log retention and export path (avoid shipping huge logs to default pipelines).
3) Get explicit approval in the incident channel if customer impact is ongoing.

During capture:
- Keep capture window short.
- Prefer a canary replica with synthetic load or limited customer traffic.

After capture:
1) Turn off NCCL debug env vars.
2) Collect logs from the replica only.
3) Scrub and store logs in the incident artifact location (internal only).

### How to enable in practice
Preferred: use Redwood runtime config / feature flag mechanism for canary-only enablement.

If a rollout-based toggle exists (example):
- Enable flag: `runtime.nccl_debug_logging=canary` or `runtime.tp.nccl_debug=enabled` (exact names vary by release).
- Validate by searching logs for “NCCL version” and “NET/Topology” lines.

If you must patch a single deployment (last resort):
- Patch env vars on one replica deployment and restart only that replica.
- Coordinate with release/on-call owner to avoid triggering autoscaling thrash.

---

## Decision tree (compute vs comms vs scheduler)
### A) Suspect comms/collectives
Indicators:
- Heartbeats stop and `inflight_collectives` is stuck.
- Many timeouts cluster on a single replica; draining fixes temporarily.
- Logs show collective sequence mismatch or long waits on stream sync.

Next actions:
1) Capture NCCL debug logs (safe mode) on a canary replica.
2) Capture trace IDs for 2–3 timeouts.
3) Escalate to Kernel team with: model, TP degree, GPU type, runtime version, NCCL logs, and stall window.

### B) Suspect scheduler starvation
Indicators:
- Queue depth increases; prefill-heavy admission continues while decode progress halts.
- `stall_reason_total{reason="SCHED_STARVATION"}` increases.
- Switching workload mix (reduce long prefill / lower concurrency) improves.

Next actions:
1) Capture scheduler queue snapshot (`/debug/scheduler/queues`) if available.
2) Capture metrics: queue depth, prefill/decode ratio, starvation events.
3) Escalate to Scheduling team with workload distribution details (prompt length mix, streaming enabled, concurrency pattern).

### C) Suspect KV cache / memory pressure divergence
Indicators:
- Errors/warnings around compaction, allocation waits, or near-OOM.
- Stalls appear under long context + high concurrency.

Next actions:
1) Capture KV cache summary (`/debug/kv/summary`) if available.
2) Capture memory metrics + logs around compaction.
3) Escalate to KV/cache owner with stress suite parameters (context length, batch size, concurrency, cache settings).

---

## What to include in an escalation (copy/paste template)
**Subject:** TP stall suspected (comms/scheduler/KV) – <cluster> <model> TP=<N> GPU=<SKU> runtime=<ver>

- Cluster/region:
- Customer impact (Dedicated/Hosted, accounts):
- Model + version:
- Runtime version + recent changes/flags:
- GPU type + TP degree:
- Start time / peak / end:
- Symptoms:
  - Timeout rate:
  - p99 latency:
  - Streaming affected (yes/no):
- Suspected stall class: comms / scheduler / KV / unknown
- Evidence:
  - Dashboard links:
  - Metrics screenshots/exports:
  - Trace IDs:
  - Replica IDs / pod names:
  - Logs attached (runtime logs, NCCL logs if captured):
- Mitigations attempted (drain, caps, flags) + outcome:

---

## Common pitfalls
- Treating a wedged replica as overload: draining the replica may restore service but hides a systemic regression. Always capture artifacts first if feasible.
- Enabling NCCL TRACE broadly: can overload logging, increase latency, and create noisy data that’s hard to interpret.
- Failing to capture per-rank context: TP stalls are often rank-specific; always record `rank` and `replica_id`.

---

## Appendices
### A. Expected “healthy” baselines
These vary by model and workload, but generally:
- `runtime_tp_rank_heartbeat_age_seconds` stays near 0–2s with brief spikes under GC/compaction.
- `runtime_tp_inflight_collectives` oscillates but returns to baseline; it should not monotonically increase.
- Queue depth should correlate with throughput; sustained queue growth with flat throughput is suspicious.

### B. When to declare a suspected regression
Strong indicators of a regression (vs isolated node failure):
- Same stall signature across multiple replicas after a rollout
- Correlated with a specific GPU SKU or NCCL/CUDA change
- Reproducible in perf-canary or benchmark-lab using the mixed prefill/decode workload

If regression is suspected, coordinate with release owner to pause rollout and set a clear go/no-go checkpoint.

title: Runtime experiment feedback loop protocol
content:
Overview:
This page defines the experiment feedback loop protocol used by the Serving Runtime team to design, run, and act on profiling and kernel scheduling experiments that change runtime behavior. The protocol standardizes hypothesis framing, telemetry instrumentation, safety gates, analysis artifacts, and rollout rules. It is intended for engineers running microbenchmarks, shadow traffic experiments, and online canaries that touch the kernel scheduler, KV cache, batching heuristics, and model variant routing.

Why we have a formal protocol:
- Reduce noisy experiments and ensure reproducible results.
- Protect SLOs and customer traffic during investigations.
- Provide clear handoffs from experimenters to runtime operators and release engineers.

Scope:
Applies to experiments that: 1) modify kernel scheduler configuration or code paths, 2) alter request shaping / admission, 3) introduce new telemetry or sampling, or 4) change runtime fallback/degradation modes. Not intended for purely offline model evaluation.

Roles and ownership:
- Experiment Owner: engineer who proposes and executes the experiment (primary contact).
- Runtime Oncall: SRE responsible for live traffic safety gates (will have emergency rollback authority).
- Observability Owner: platform engineer who validates instrumentation and dashboards.
- Release Captain: release engineer who approves any rollout to Dedicated or Hosted clusters.

High-level workflow (5 phases):
1) Hypothesis & Safety Plan
   - Write a short hypothesis: "Changing kernel X threshold will reduce p99 latency by >=10% for short sequences without increasing p99 for long sequences."
   - Identify safety SLOs (see table below) and define abort thresholds.
   - Pre-validate on playground or shadow cluster.
2) Instrumentation & Baseline
   - Add required metrics and trace points.
   - Run baseline collection for at least 3 steady-state runs (48h recommended for production-like signals).
3) Controlled rollout (shadow -> canary -> ramp)
   - Start with offline shadowing, then small canary (1% traffic) with strict abort gates, then staged ramps.
4) Analysis and Signal Extraction
   - Produce an Experiment Report (templated). Include causal attribution, raw traces, and kernel-level timeline.
5) Action: revert, iterate, or promote
   - If passing gates, schedule full rollout and add config to runtime feature flags.

Safety SLOs and abort thresholds (default values):
| Signal | Baseline window metric | Abort threshold (quick abort) | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| p50 latency (inferred) | baseline median | +25% | Detects immediate regressions for short ops |
| p95 latency | baseline p95 | +15% | Sensitive to medium tail widening |
| p99 latency | baseline p99 | +10% | Critical — immediate abort if exceeded repeatedly |
| error rate (5xx/transport) | baseline error rate | +100% relative or absolute >0.5% | Transport / kernel faults |
| kernel watchdog restarts | 0 in baseline window | any occurrence | Immediate abort and system investigation |

Instrumentation checklist:
- Metrics: per-route p50/p95/p99, token-throughput, queue-depth per scheduler slot, kernel-run-time distributions (ms), kvcache-hit-rate, model-variant-fallback-count.
- Tracing: attach request-id, kernel-id, scheduling-decision-id, tenant-id, model-version.
- Logs: structured JSON with kernel signals (fields: timestamp, kernel_phase, gpu_id, free_mem_mb, queue_len).
- Sampling policy: pid-based stratified sampling + entropy-aware tail amplification.

Experiment Runbook (step-by-step):
1) Fill Experiment Form (template attached) with hypothesis, owner, safety SLOs, and rollback plan.
2) Create feature-flagged branch for runtime config changes; include toggle default=off.
3) Deploy to "dev-lab" and run benchmark harness (use: tools/bench/run_local.sh --profile=shadow --duration=60m).
4) Validate telemetry: ensure the new metrics appear in /observability/metric-registry and traces include kernel_id.
5) Start offline shadowing for 24–48h using replay tool (tools/traffic/replay --target=shadow --corpus=prod-corpus-2025).
6) If shadow looks stable, coordinate with Runtime Oncall to start canary: target 1% traffic for 30 minutes. Watch SLOs.
7) If canary passes, ramp to 5% for 2 hours, then 20% for 6 hours, then 100% with staged rollouts per region.
8) After any rollout step, produce a short update in the experiment thread and update the Experiment Report.

Experiment Report template (required fields):
- Title
- Owner
- Hypothesis
- Timeline (start/stop times)
- Baseline statistics (p50/p95/p99, error rates)
- Experiment statistics (same metrics, per-stage)
- Traces: 3 representative traces for each failure mode
- Kernel trace heatmap (attach image)
- Root cause analysis / attribution statement
- Decision and next steps (promote / iterate / rollback)

Quick CLI snippets and examples:
- Start local shadow run:
  ./tools/traffic/replay --target=shadow --dataset=playground-corpus --duration=3600
- Collect a kernel timeline for a trace (example):
  curl -sS -H 'X-Request-ID: <id>' 'https://obs-api.internal/trace/<id>' | jq .events[] | grep kernel
- Toggle feature flag via infra CLI:
  infra-ctl feature-flag set runtime.kv_prefetch_experiment --env=staging --value=true

Telemetry analysis cookbook (how to extract signal):
1) Use the "experiment" tag in metrics ingestion to separate experimented traffic.
2) Compute delta-series with a rolling baseline window using the last 24h outside experiment.
3) Use quantile-based comparison (not mean) for latency signals.
4) For kernel-level attribution, align request traces by kernel_start timestamp and compute occupancy vs. wait-time correlation matrix.

Fallout and rollback patterns:
- Immediate rollback: triggered by kernel watchdog restarts, large p99 increases, or >0.5% absolute error increase. Runtime Oncall will flip feature flag and open an incident if needed.
- Graceful rollback: if subtle regressions appear, pause ramp and revert config changes from the feature-flagged branch, then follow up with a targeted fix and re-proposal.

Postmortem and knowledge capture:
- For any abort or noticeable impact, the Experiment Owner must open an "experiment-pm" doc within 72 hours summarizing what happened and the reproduction steps.
- Attach kernel traces, metrics dashboards, and the final Experiment Report.

Safety guard examples (preset safe profiles):
- safe-lite: suitable for dev-lab and internal load tests. SLOs relaxed, fast rollback.
- safe-canary: default for canary on Hosted clusters; enforce p99 abort and error rate gates.
- safe-strict: used before Dedicated rollout; requires 7d baseline and extended shadowing.

Configuration table (example):
| field | safe-lite | safe-canary | safe-strict |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| canary_percent | 5 | 1 | 0.5 |
| shadow_duration_hours | 2 | 24 | 168 |
| baseline_days | 0 | 1 | 7 |
| abort_p99_increase_pct | 50 | 10 | 5 |

Related pages and artifacts:
- Kernel telemetry schema: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/kernel-telemetry-annotation-guidelines-2025
- Runtime feature flagging manual: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/runtime-feature-flagging-experimentation-contract-2026
- Experiment reporting dashboard: observability/dashboards/experiment-runbook

Appendix: common pitfalls and recommended mitigations:
- Pitfall: false positives from sampling imbalance. Mitigation: use stratified sampling aligned with tenant and sequence-length.
- Pitfall: backend cold-start noise. Mitigation: warmstart policy and avoid first-hour collection for baselines.
- Pitfall: conflating model quality regressions with scheduler changes. Mitigation: tag requests with model-version and run isolating experiments.

Contact and escalation:
- Primary owner: Asha Menon (asha@redwood.ai)
- Runtime Oncall: pager duty channel #runtime-oncall
- Observability: observability-team@redwood.ai

Document history:
- 2024-05-15: created (Asha Menon)
- 2024-11-02: added safe profiles and canary flow (review: Marco Alvarez)
- 2025-09-02: updated telemetry checklist and CLI snippets (review: Priya Shah)

End of document.

title: SRE Evidence-to-Action Handbook: From Incident Forensics to Capacity & SLO Remediation
content:
Summary
This handbook defines a prescriptive, auditable pipeline for converting incident evidence and post-incident findings into concrete SLO, error-budget, capacity, and tooling actions. The goal is to shorten the time from "discovery -> evidence -> decision -> remediation" while preserving blamelessness and traceability.

Audience
- SRE oncall and rotation leads
- Service owners and service reliability stewards
- Product managers responsible for tiered SLAs
- Capacity and forecasting teams

Why this exists
- We frequently collect high-quality forensic evidence in incident reviews but lack a standardized path that guarantees remediation (capacity, SLOs, tooling changes) is implemented and validated.
- This doc codifies who decides, how we prioritize, how we measure remediation success, and how evidence is stored and linked.

Key principles
- Evidence-first: every action must be linked to evidence items (logs, replays, synthetic canaries, graphs, sample tokens).
- Minimal viable remediation: prefer fast, reversible mitigations (traffic shaping, temporary headroom) while planning permanent fixes.
- Ownership and deadlines: each remediation item has an owner, ETA, verification steps, and a quality gate.
- Playbookable: run the same steps for incidents of similar class (latency spike, OOM cascade, model regression, capacity saturation).

High-level pipeline (4 stages)
1) Capture (During incident)
   - Assign an evidence recorder (oncall SRE) to collect: dashboards snapshot, p50/p95/p99 latency slices, error counts by tenant, representative request/response pairs, kernel/oom logs, Kubernetes pod events, heap/gc traces, KV cache usage, model cache hit/miss rates.
   - Use the incident evidence collector script: 
     curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $EVID_TOKEN" https://telemetry.internal/api/incident/capture?incident=$INCIDENT_ID > evidence_bundle.json
2) Triage (Post-incident 0-72 hours)
   - Run an evidence triage meeting within 72 hours; attendees: incident commander, service owner, one SRE steward, one oncall from runtime.
   - Classify root cause types: capacity headroom, model regression, infra degradation, config rollback, downstream outage, traffic spike, buggy client.
   - Produce an Evidence Summary doc (link to evidence_bundle) with minimal reproducible steps.
3) Remediate (7-30 days)
   - For each remediation candidate create a Remediation Item in the SRE action tracker. Each item must include: title, owner, priority (P0/P1/P2), blocking_flags, acceptance_criteria, expected cost/impact, rollback plan, and verification steps.
   - Example remediation types: capacity resize, autoscale tuning, token-priority throttle, model rollback/patch, patch to runtime kernel, cache warm pool augmentation, new synthetic canary.
4) Verify & Close (post-remediation)
   - Run the verification checklist in a production shadowed environment or using mirrored traffic. Verification must include: synthetic canary pass (7d), P95 latency return within X% of baseline, error rate below SLO by at least 95th percentile, unit-cost impact under budget.
   - Close the remediation item only after verification and update the incident review with links to the action and evidence.

Decision authority and cadence
- Day 0 triage decisions (fast mitigations): incident commander + SRE oncall may approve rolling back a model, enabling burst capacity, or applying a temporary traffic throttle. These require automated audit entries.
- Permanent capacity changes and SLO adjustments: require service steward approval + capacity planning representative + product manager sign-off for contractual SLOs.
- Emergency overprovisioning (>= 12 hours queue build): SRE Director must be notified and approval logged.

Remediation priority matrix
- P0: Customer-facing outage or sustained SLO breach > 4 hours, action must start within 4 hours.
- P1: Intermittent SLO breach or elevated burn rate, action must be planned within 72 hours and executed within 14 days.
- P2: Quality regressions or non-critical platform improvements, plan in next sprint.

SLO & Error-budget action guidelines (quick reference)
- If error-budget burn rate > 5x for 1 hour OR > 2x for 6 hours: open a P1 remediation item, enable conservative throttling for non-critical tenants, notify product.
- If sustained SLO breach (p95 latency > target for 3 consecutive measurement intervals): create rollback/fallback plan and schedule a canary of candidate fixes.
- For model-serving-specific SLOs: track token-rate headroom (tokens/sec capacity) and KV cache efficacy; if token-headroom < 20% for 1 hour, apply tenant priority gating.

Capacity planning integration
- Post-incident capacity action must be translated into an updated capacity forecast within the Capacity Ledger.
- Capacity change workflow: 
  1. Submit a Capacity Change Request (CCR) with inputs: observed peak qps, sustained 95th seq_len distribution, quantization mode, expected growth, business justification.
  2. Capacity team responds with: estimated hardware (GPU count/instance type), cost delta, lead time.
  3. Schedule deployment during off-peak (if possible) and create verification load test.
- Sizing heuristics (example):
  - Token throughput per A100-80GB (baseline serving runtime): ~1.2M tokens/sec for short sequences (<=64) under continuous batching; adjust by sequence-length multiplier = 0.8 + 0.02 * (avg_seq_len - 64)
  - Add safety headroom = max(20% of baseline, 2 * 99th token burst estimate)

Template: Capacity Change Request (CCR)
| field | example | notes |
|---|---|---|
| service | embed-service-prod | service id in catalog |
| observed_peak_tokens/sec | 320000 | 15-min sliding window |
| avg_seq_len | 128 | token estimate for requests |
| current_capacity | 3 x A100-80GB | units in inventory |
| requested_change | +2 A100-80GB | scaled up to absorb peak |
| justification | sustained p95 latency breach during sale event | attach incident link |
| requested_by | service-steward@example.com | |

Operational tooling: automated evidence and remediation SDKs
- Evidence Collector CLI (evidencectl)
  - capture: evidencectl capture --incident $ID --out incident-123.json\  - upload: evidencectl upload --file incident-123.json --project $SERVICE
- Remediation item creation via API:
  curl -X POST https://sre-actions.internal/api/items \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $SRE_TOKEN" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"title":"Increase model warm-pool","owner":"@oncall-alex","priority":"P1","related_incident":"INC-2025-456","acceptance_criteria":"p95 latency within 10% of baseline for 7d"}'

Runbook fragments (playable steps)
- Latency spike (p95) due to quantized-serving regression
  1. Evidence: collect p95 timeline, quantization flag distribution, node-level GPU utilization.
  2. Fast mitigation: disable quantized path for affected model (feature-flag) and roll forward to verified variant.
  3. Medium-term remediation: add canary pipeline for quantized kernels + add quantization-specific latency synthetic.
  4. Verification: synthetic canary run for 72 hours at production-like qps.

- Token headroom exhaustion (sustained)
  1. Evidence: per-tenant token consumption, token-priority queue lengths, model warm-pool utilization.
  2. Fast mitigation: apply token-priority gating for lower-tier tenants (using traffic-shepherd service).
  3. Capacity request: open CCR and schedule scale-up.
  4. Post-scaling verification: validate 7-day synthetic and spot-check customer flows.

Incident review standards (evidence and artifacts checklist)
- Required for all P0/P1 incidents:
  - Full packet: timeline, raw logs (redacted), grafana snapshots, heap/dump (if applicable), replay steps, representative request samples (masked PII), list of commands executed by responders.
  - Evidence retention: store immutable evidence bundle in SRE evidence bucket for 1 year (default) and link in incident doc.
  - Forensics owner: named SRE responsible for evidence integrity and replayability.

Acceptance criteria for remediation closure
- All remediation items must meet these gates before closure:
  1. Evidence link(s) attached and reproducibility steps documented.
  2. Synthetic or shadow verification executed and passing for configured window (default 7 days).
  3. If change affected billing/cost, finance-notify run and cost delta documented.
  4. Post-change SLO telemetry reviewed and thumbed by service steward.

Tracking & dashboards
- Required dashboards for every service (templated):
  - SLO dashboard: p50/p95/p99, error rate, burn rate, error-budget remaining (7d/30d).
  - Capacity dashboard: tokens/sec headroom, warm pool hit-rate, GPU utilization by cluster, pending scale requests.
  - Evidence catalog view: list of open remediation items linked to incidents and evidence bundles.

Change control and audit requirements
- Any fast mitigation performed by oncall must create an automated audit entry within 1 hour: who, what, why, linked evidence, revert plan.
- Permanent changes that affect SLOs or contractual obligations need change approval ticket and communication to affected customers.

Playbook for post-incident retrospective (2-week timeline)
1. Day 0-3: evidence capture + triage + create remediation items.
2. Day 4-10: implement short-term mitigations and schedule CCRs where necessary.
3. Day 11-14: verification runs and finalize action owners.
4. 2-week retro session to capture lessons and update runbooks.

Appendix A: Common CLI snippets and examples
- Collect a 15-minute Grafana snapshot and upload:
  grafana-snapshot --dashboard svc-slo --from -15m --to now --out svc-slo-15m.png && evidencectl upload --file svc-slo-15m.png --meta incident=INC-2025-456
- Sample token headroom query (PromQL):
  sum by(cluster) (rate(tokens_consumed_total[5m]))
- Example acceptance JSON for remediation API:
  {
    "title": "Add 2x A100 to embed-service-prod",
    "owner": "oncall-alex",
    "priority": "P1",
    "acceptance_criteria": "p95 latency <= baseline * 1.10 for 7d"
  }

Appendix B: Roles & Responsibilities (short)
- Incident Commander: owns evidence capture and highest-priority fast mitigations.
- Service Steward: owns long-term remediation and SLO contracts.
- Capacity Planner: translates CCR to procurement/resize.
- SRE Forensics Owner: ensures evidence bundles are reproducible and retained.

Feedback & improvements
- This handbook is reviewed quarterly by the SRE steering committee. To propose changes, open a PR against this page and tag the reviewers listed above.

Related policies and templates
- See: Incident Evidence Handoff Procedure, Capacity Onboarding Playbook, SLO Admission Checklist.

Contact
- For questions about this handbook, contact: asha.patel@redwood-inference.com

title: Trace augmentation and kernel causal linkage protocol
content:
Summary:
This document defines the Trace Augmentation and Kernel Causal Linkage Protocol (TACKL): a standardized pipeline and set of annotations for enriching runtime traces so that kernel-level events, scheduler decisions, and high-level request metadata can be correlated deterministically for attribution, triage, and experiment analysis. TACKL is intended to reduce mean-time-to-detect for performance regressions, support causal attribution of tail latency to kernel events, and provide a repeatable lab protocol for validating fixes.

Scope:
- Applies to all runtime components that emit execution traces and kernel telemetry: dispatcher, scheduler, kernel plugins, KV cache, and the GPU dispatcher layer.
- Covers production sampling, deterministic augmentation in canary environments, and the lab replay pipeline.
- Not intended to replace end-to-end distributed tracing standards (Zipkin/Jaeger) but to extend them with kernel-specific causal markers and deterministic linkage.

Definitions:
- trace_id: Global request identifier propagated across layers.
- causal_span: A span annotated with a causal tag pointing to a kernel decision or event.
- kernel_anchor: A short opaque token (8-char) representing a kernel-level event group (e.g., preemption, handoff, slow-kernel).
- decision_provenance: Compact encoded tuple showing scheduler policy, priority bucket, and timestamp.

Goals and success criteria:
- Link >= 95% of sampled request traces to a kernel_anchor when a kernel event influenced latency > 5ms.
- Reduce investigation time for kernel-related tail latency incidents by 40% within 3 months of roll-out.
- Provide reproducible lab replays where kernel anchors map to the same sequence of kernel events in the sandbox.

Protocol overview:
1) Instrumentation contract:
   - All services in the runtime must propagate trace_id and include a 3-field augmentation header when emitting kernel-facing requests: kernel-anchor (nullable), decision-provenance, and preface-timestamp (RFC3339).
   - Kernel modules emit event batches to the augmentation-forwarder with fields: kernel_anchor, event_type, local_timestamp_ns, metrics={latency_ns, occupancy_pct, memory_bytes}.

2) Augmentation-forwarder responsibilities:
   - Deduplicate and fold kernel events into the canonical trace stream.
   - Attach a compact event-sig (sha1 hex truncated to 12) to the trace as causal_span.signature.
   - Promote kernel_anchor to trace-level if any event in the batch exceeds configured thresholds.

3) Sampling and retention policy:
   - Default production sampling rate: 1% of requests.
   - Tail-path selective sampling: sample all requests that enter the >99th percentile latency or hit SLA fallback paths.
   - Full diagnostic retention window for augmented traces: 30 days for incidents, 7 days for general sampling.

Trace augmentation pipeline (components and flow):
- emitter (service) -> runtime-proxy -> kernel (events) + augmentation-forwarder -> trace-assembler -> observability-store
- The forwarder runs an enrichment worker that uses a lookback table of recent scheduler decisions to attach decision_provenance to event batches.

Attribution model (heuristic + causal tagging):
- Primary attribution heuristic: when kernel_anchor exists and event latency contribution > 5ms, mark causal_span.primary = true and increment kernel_blame_score by normalized latency percent contribution.
- Secondary attribution: if multiple anchors overlap, compute weighted attribution by (kernel_event_latency * occupancy_factor) and emit a sorted list of suspected causes.
- Confidence estimate: each attribution emits a confidence tag (high|medium|low) based on event coverage and correlation score.

Experiment lab and replay protocol (step-by-step):
1) Create a deterministic replay corpus using request-surface-replay tool with URI and tokenized prompt corpus. Example CLI:
   $ ri-replay --corpus requests.jsonl --seed 42 --output replay.sig
2) Enable full trace augmentation in the sandbox cluster and set sampling=100% for the replay namespace.
3) Record kernel anchors during the run and export augmentation bundles with:
   $ augmentation-export --run-id <id> --format ndjson --output augment.ndjson
4) Validate linkage: run the causal-link-checker to ensure each trace_id in augment.ndjson maps to at most one dominant kernel_anchor.
   $ causal-link-checker augment.ndjson --threshold-ms 5
5) Compare kernel event sequences between baseline and candidate kernels using event-sig diffs and produce a report.

Investigation runbook (when you see persistent tail latency):
1) Triage: identify representative traces from the 99.9th percentile from the observability-store (filter by model, seq_len, tenant).
2) Confirm augmentation: verify trace has kernel_anchor and causal_span.signature present. If not, increase sampling for the affected route and re-run.
3) Attribution: consult the attribution table (dashboard) to see top kernel anchors and their kernel_blame_score.
4) Reproduce: run the replay protocol in a sandbox pinned to the same kernel build and scheduler policy.
5) Hypothesis & patch: use the kernel anchor mapping to propose either a scheduler param change (see table below) or a kernel fallback patch.
6) Canary: deploy patch to a canary pool with 5% traffic and augmentation sampling=100% for 1 hour. Monitor kernel_blame_score and SLO.
7) Rollback criteria: if canary SLO breach > 2x baseline or kernel_blame_score worsens by >20%, rollback immediately.

Operational controls, dashboards, and alerts:
- Dashboard widgets to create: Top kernel_anchors by blame_score, kernel_anchor time series, per-route augmentation coverage, and attribution confidence distribution.
- Alerts:
  - alert_kernel_anchor_spike: trigger when kernel_anchor frequency increases > 3x baseline in 15m window.
  - alert_unlinked_tail_traces: trigger when >30% of 99.9th percentile traces are missing kernel_anchor.
  - alert_attribution_confidence_drop: trigger when average confidence for top causes drops below 60% for 30m.
Threshold suggestions:
- anchor spike: 3x baseline for 15 minutes.
- unlinked tail traces: 30% missing link in 1 hour.

Scheduler parameter table (common knobs to try during hypothesis patching):
| parameter | range | effect | suggested safe delta |
| priority_bias | -1.0..1.0 | shifts scheduler preference between latency-sensitive and economic throughput | +/-0.1 |
| preempt_window_ms | 0..200 | window that allows cooperative preemption to occur | -10ms to +20ms |
| kv_prefetch_budget | 0..10 | number of concurrent prefetch slots per shard | +/-1 |
| evict_grace_ms | 0..500 | extra grace for soft-evictions to complete | +50ms |

Example augmentation JSON snippet emitted by augmenter (ndjson line):
{"trace_id":"t-3f7c8a","kernel_anchor":"KA9b2f1d","causal_span":{"signature":"c1a9d3b7f2aa"},"decision_provenance":"sched=v2|bucket=high|ts=2026-02-02T15:04:05Z","events":[{"type":"slow-kernel","latency_ns":8200000,"occupancy":0.86}]}

Implementation notes and safety:
- The augmentation-forwarder is a best-effort component: it must not increase request tail latency. If augmentation queue lag exceeds 100ms, the forwarder will switch to async best-effort mode and emit a telemetry event.
- Avoid storing PII in augmented traces; strip user prompt content unless requested and approved under a support ticket.
- Encryption: augmented bundles at rest must be encrypted with the default KMS key for observability assets.

Ownership and rollout plan:
- Primary owners: Runtime Observability team (owner: Priya Nayar).
- Secondary owners: Scheduler team (reviewer: Ethan Blake), Kernel team (reviewer: Mariana Soto).
- Rollout plan:
  1. Implement forwarder prototype in sandbox (Q4 2025).
  2. Internal lab validation and 100% sampling replay (Jan 2026).
  3. Canary in production with 1% sampling (Feb 2026).
  4. Full rollout with dashboards and runbook training (Mar 2026).

Appendix A — common failure modes and mitigations:
- Missing trace propagation: ensure all HTTP/gRPC libraries include trace_id header and are upgraded to runtime 3.4+. Mitigation: emergency patch to inject trace_id at proxy layer.
- Forwarder overload: backpressure to kernel emitter and fall back to async ingestion. Monitor forwarder_queue_length > 2000 as critical.
- False positive anchors: refine anchor generation by tightening event grouping windows and requiring two corroborating signals (occupancy and latency).

Appendix B — related pages and artifacts:
- Links: (internal) /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/runtime-telemetry-sampling-cost-aware-profiling-2027 | /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-deployment-circuit-breakers-and-sla-fallback-playbook-2026
- Artifacts: replay tool, augmentation-forwarder helm chart, causal-link-checker binary.

Contact and questions:
- For implementation questions, contact priya@redwood-inference.internal or open an RFC in the runtime-observability repo.

Change log:
- 2025-11-12: Draft created (Priya Nayar).
- 2026-01-15: Added sampling policy and replay protocol (Ethan Blake review).
- 2026-02-03: Finalized rollout plan and alerts thresholds (published).

title: Cross-Layer SLO Validation & Benchmark Orchestrator
content:
Summary:
This document defines the Cross-Layer SLO Validation and Benchmark Orchestrator (CL-SVBO): a reproducible process and reference implementation for validating runtime SLOs end-to-end across scheduler decisions, kernel selection, and system-level telemetry. The goal is to provide a single authoritative workflow teams can run to certify that a code change, kernel rollout, or scheduler tune does not regress production SLOs.

Motivation and scope:
- Problem: We observe regressions that only appear when scheduler heuristics, kernel mappings, and telemetry interact under production-shaped load. Isolated microbenchmarks miss these interactions.
- Scope: CL-SVBO covers testing of latency SLOs, p99/p95 tail behavior, model-variant fallbacks, and degradation policies for the serving runtime. It is intended for: runtime engineers, kernel maintainers, SRE runbook authors, and release managers.

Key concepts (definitions):
1) SLO surface: per-route latency SLO (e.g., p99 <= 120ms for chat-range <512 tokens), throughput SLOs, and error budget burn rate thresholds.
2) Cross-layer signal: correlated observability traces that join scheduler decisions (slot allotment, kernel choice), kernel latency, and application-level token generation time.
3) Benchmark orchestrator: an automation harness that composes traffic shaping, shadowing, and controlled perturbations while recording deterministic traces.

Architecture overview (text diagram):
- Components:
  - runtime-orchestrator: control plane process that triggers experiments and records metadata (git sha, kernel version, scheduler profile).
  - benchmark-agent (fleet): distributed workload generators that mirror production traffic shapes.
  - telemetry-bridge: consumes traces, metric rollups, and scheduler decision logs; produces joinable event streams keyed by request_id.
  - experiment-coordinator: enforces perturbations (kernel slowdowns, affinity changes, NUMA noise).

Behavioral contract:
- Every experiment run produces an artifact with these sections: metadata.yaml, workload_manifest.json, traces.jl (line-delimited JSON), metrics.csv, and a verdict.json summarizing SLO pass/fail with per-bucket contributors.

Configuration table (recommended defaults):
| key | description | default |
|-----|-------------|---------|
| workload_profile | which production traffic shape to emulate (see profiles/*) | medium-burst-chat |
| duration_minutes | how long to run the steady-state portion | 30 |
| kernel_set | list of kernel builds to exercise | [stable, tuned] |
| perturbation | fault injection policy | none |
| collectors | telemetry endpoints to pull (traces, events, metrics) | telemetry-bridge:9411 |

Quick start (runbook):
1) Checkout the orchestrator repo and select the baseline and candidate kernels: git checkout && export BASELINE=stable && export CANDIDATE=experiment-2027-02.
2) Prepare metadata: ./rbench prepare --workload medium-burst-chat --save metadata.yaml
3) Dry-run (no perturbation): ./rbench orchestrate --metadata metadata.yaml --duration 20 --collect-only
4) Perturbation run (scheduler tweak): ./rbench orchestrate --metadata metadata.yaml --duration 30 --perturb scheduler:priority-window=20ms
5) Collect artifacts: ./rbench collect --run-id <id> --out ./artifacts/<run-id>
6) Analyze: ./rbench analyze --artifacts ./artifacts/<run-id> --report ./reports/<run-id>-report.md

Profiling playbook (when an SLO fails):
1) Verify experiment integrity: check metadata.yaml for correct git sha, kernel versions, and that agents were stable for at least the first 5 minutes.
2) Decompose tail: run the decomposition tool to join traces by request_id and produce a per-request timing waterfall. Command: ./rbench analyze --decompose --artifacts ./artifacts/<run-id>
3) Attribution checklist (ordered):
   a) Scheduler decision time: filter events for scheduler.* and compute median and p99 elapsed between arrival and kernel assignment. Threshold: p99 scheduler-decision < 8ms.
   b) Kernel latency: aggregate kernel.exec_ms by kernel_build and sequence_length_bin. Look for >15% increase in p99 vs baseline for specific bins.
   c) KV cache misses: join kvcache.hit=false events. If mis-hit rate > 3% correlating to latency spikes, escalate to model-onboarding.
   d) Network/dispatch noise: verify gRPC send/recv stalls; if present, open network incident and mark run as non-deterministic.
4) If step 3 finds a scheduler-related root cause, reproduce with microbench: a synthetic batch with identical concurrency and sequence bins and CPU/gpu affinity pinned.

Benchmark suite: workload profiles and acceptance gates:
- Profiles (examples):
  - small-chat-burst: 1–4 tokens per request; bursty arrival; target p99 < 30ms.
  - medium-burst-chat: seq_len 128–512, mixed streaming; target p99 < 120ms.
  - long-search: seq_len 512–2048, high KV miss rate; target p99 < 600ms.
- Acceptance gates (automated):
  1) Functional pass: request success rate >= 99.5%
  2) Latency pass: p95 and p99 within configured gates (see profiles/*).
  3) Regression cap: candidate must not exceed baseline p99 by more than 7% for any profile bin.

Release checklist (for kernel/scheduler changes):
1) Run CL-SVBO on baseline and candidate across all three profiles.
2) Run production canary mirroring at 10% traffic with shadow-mode telemetry for 24h.
3) If any SLO gate fails, halt promotion and file incident with tags: runtime-regression, kernel, scheduler, <owner-team>.

Operator runbook (triage steps):
1) Detect: alert fires for p99-sli-breach.<route> with >5% error-budget burn over 1h.
2) Snapshot: trigger ./rbench quick-snapshot --route <route> which launches a 10-minute capture and stores to S3 under artifacts/snapshots/<timestamp>.
3) Correlate: run ./rbench correlate --snapshot <path> --query 'scheduler.* OR kernel.exec_ms OR kvcache.*'
4) Mitigation options (ordered):
   - Revert scheduler profile to last-known-good: runtime-orchestrator apply --profile stable-slo-preserve
   - Pin model-variant to lower-latency quantized build: runtime-orchestrator update-route --route <route> --model <variant-id>
   - Temporarily increase concurrency headroom by scaling dedicated pool: autoscale set --pool <pool-id> --target-util 40%

Metrics and thresholds (extracted):
- p99 latency critical thresholds: small-chat-burst < 30ms, medium-burst-chat < 120ms, long-search < 600ms.
