- scheduler-decision p99: 8ms (soft) / 25ms (hard).
- kernel.exec_ms p99 regression cap: +7% over baseline per-bin.
- kvcache miss rate acceptable: <3% correlated to tail events.

Example artifacts (snippets):
- metadata.yaml:
  git_sha: "b1a2c3d4"
  baseline_kernel: "stable-2026-11"
  candidate_kernel: "tuned-priority-42"
  profiles: ["medium-burst-chat"]

- workload_manifest.json (excerpt):
  {
    "profile": "medium-burst-chat",
    "client_concurrency": 120,
    "arrival_pattern": "bursty",
    "seq_len_distribution": {"0-128": 0.2, "128-512": 0.7, "512+": 0.1}
  }

- analysis example (verdict.json):
  {
    "run_id":"2027-02-03-1234",
    "slo_results": {"medium-burst-chat": {"p99": 132.4, "baseline_p99": 119.1, "status":"FAIL", "dominant_cause":"kernel.exec_ms","confidence":0.86}}
  }

Ownership and escalation:
- Owners:
  - runtime-orchestrator: runtime-platform-team@redwood.com
  - scheduler-core: kernel-scheduler-team@redwood.com
  - telemetry-bridge: observability-team@redwood.com
- Escalation path: first responder -> scheduler owner -> runtime team -> SRE -> ENG execs. List oncall rotation lives in people-ops.

Guidelines for experiments that must be suppressed in public artifacts:
- Any run involving customer data or restricted models must be labeled confidentiality:restricted and stored in the private retention bucket. Do not include traces.jl in public decks.

Notes, limitations, and future work:
- CL-SVBO is designed to expose cross-layer interactions but cannot currently simulate under-specified hardware faults (e.g., NVLink partial degrade). A planned extension is the hardware-fault-injector (HFI) shim.
- We are piloting a regression classifier that highlights likely root causes automatically; currently the analyze step is semi-automated and requires human review.

Appendix: common investigation recipes (short):
- Spiking p99 with unchanged kernel: look for scheduler preemption spikes + dispatch queue depth.
- Kernel-specific driver regressions: reproduce with single-agent microbenchmark pinned to the same kernel and CPU/GPU affinity.
- High KV miss correlated tails: reproduce by clearing cache hints and re-running warmup sequences.

Related links and references:
- runtime release checklist: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-upgrade-validation-and-canary-matrix-2026
- telemetry contract: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/runtime-telemetry-annotation-guidelines-2025

If you are running a CL-SVBO experiment and need help, open a ticket under the "runtime-benchmarking" queue and tag it with the run_id and profile.

title: Runtime Fidelity: Onboarding & Consumption Playbook
content:
Overview

This playbook describes the recommended approach to onboard customers onto Runtime Fidelity profiles, how to measure and simulate consumption, and how to package pricing and SLAs for predictable economics. It combines a product overview, prerequisites, technical onboarding steps, pricing guidance, rollout milestones, and operational runbooks to enable cross-functional delivery (Product, Solutions, Sales, SRE, and Engineering).

Motivation

As customers adopt Redwood Inference across hosted, dedicated and private deployments they require: predictable latencies, clear fidelity tradeoffs, and transparent billing. Fidelity profiles (a bundle of model variant, quantization, and runtime configuration) enable customers to trade cost for output quality under well-defined SLOs. This doc standardizes onboarding and consumption simulation to reduce regressions and commercial disputes.

Scope

- Audience: Product managers, Solutions Engineers, Customer Success, Sales, Runtime Engineers, SRE.
- Applies to: Hosted API, Dedicated pools, and Private VPC deployments.
- Excludes: Marketplace third-party models (see reference design for third-party adapters).

Definitions

- Fidelity profile: Named configuration combining a model variant, quantization level, KV-cache behavior, batching target, and runtime kernel hints.
- Consumption unit: Token-equivalent used for billing and simulation (see Pricing section).
- Soft-fidelity SLO: Non-contractual quality target measured by eval prompts and acceptance thresholds.

High-level product overview

- Customers select a fidelity profile per route.
- The platform enforces runtime parameters and emits telemetry that maps to cost and quality.
- The Onboarding flow validates economics and quality via a Simulation Run, then issues entitlements (credits or SLO guarantees) as part of commercial packaging.

SLOs and acceptance criteria

- Latency (hosted): p95 <= 150ms for conversational short-turns (<=128 tokens).
- Latency (dedicated): p95 <= 120ms for pinned GPU pools.
- Availability: 99.95% monthly for Dedicated customers (see SLA appendix).
- Quality guardrail: regression < 2% on tenant preflight eval set (measured by ROUGE-like metric provided during onboarding).

Onboarding flow (recommended)

1. Discovery (Sales/SE): Collect target routes, expected qps, latency sensitivity, and example prompt sets.
2. Baseline capture (Customer+SE): Capture 24–72 hours of representative traffic samples or synthetic approximations.
3. Simulation run (Product): Run traffic through the Fidelity Simulator with 3 candidate profiles (High, Balanced, Low cost).
4. Acceptance test (Customer): Stakeholder reviews fidelity evals (10–50 prompts) and signs off on chosen profile.
5. Entitlements & packaging (Finance/Product): Map selected profile to pricing tier, SLA, and crediting (if applicable).
6. Rollout (Engineering/SRE): Canary deploy profile on 1–5% traffic, monitor signals for 72 hours, then expand.
7. Post-rollout (CS/Product): QBR + adjustments to profile parameters as usage stabilizes.

Simulation run: steps and checklist

- Inputs: representative request payloads, session distribution (session length histogram), expected concurrency, and acceptance prompts.
- Engine: Fidelity Simulator (internal tool: fidelity-sim). Use the following CLI to run a smoke simulation:

$ fidelity-sim run --profile balanced-2028 --input sample-traffic.json --duration 1h --out ./sim-results.json

- Required checks: token-per-response distribution, latency p95, model fallbacks triggered, cache hit rates.
- Output artifacts: sim-results.json (telemetry snapshot), fidelity-eval-report.md, cost-estimate.csv.

Packaging and pricing guidance

We recommend three packaged fidelity tiers for commercial offers. Table below shows suggested mapping; adjust for enterprise negotiations.

| Tier | Typical use case | Runtime config (example) | Expected relative cost | Commercial addon |
|------|------------------|--------------------------|------------------------|------------------|
| Fidelity:Premium | Latency-critical, high-Q | Model: variant-v3, quant: fp16, batching: low, KV-cache: full | 1.6x baseline | SLA 99.95%, priority support |
| Fidelity:Balanced | General-purpose conversational | Model: variant-v2, quant: int8, batching: adaptive | 1.0x baseline | Standard SLA, telemetry retention 30d |
| Fidelity:Economy | High-throughput, cost-sensitive | Model: variant-v1, quant: int8-q4, batching: aggressive | 0.55x baseline | Best-effort fallback to lower-cost models |

Pricing considerations (rules of thumb)

- Baseline unit: 1 consumption unit = 1k tokens equivalent for bundled pricing.
- Convert sim-estimate tokens -> consumption units and round up to nearest bundle.
- Offer warm capacity credits for dedicated customers to smooth bursts (recommended: 10–20% of committed qps).
- Preemptible or spot-backed capacity should have explicit crediting rules and shorter SLA windows.

Telemetry schema and signals to monitor

- Required telemetry fields: profile_name, route_id, tenant_id, tokens_in, tokens_out, model_variant, quantization_tag, batch_size, processing_time_ms, cache_hit, fallback_reason (nullable).
- Key derived metrics: cost_per_1k_tokens, p95_latency_ms, fallback_rate, quality_regression_score, kv_cache_hit_percent.
- Alert thresholds (sample): fallback_rate > 2% over 10m => SEV3; p95_latency increase > 40% vs baseline => SEV2.

Operational runbook: fidelity-related incidents

1. Detect: fidelity-alerts dashboard surfaces spikes in fallback_rate or quality_regression_score.
2. Triage: Check firmware/runtime kernel mismatch, quantization fallback logs, and capacity pressure metrics.
3. Mitigate: Temporarily route affected tenant to an alternative fidelity profile (canary rollback) using routing policy "fidelity-fallback-route".
4. Postmortem: Capture root cause, update profile compatibility matrix and add regression prompts to tenant's preflight set.

Developer API and SDK examples

- Example JSON route configuration (HTTP):

POST /v1/routes HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer <token>

{
  "route_id": "support-chat-v1",
  "default_fidelity_profile": "balanced-2028-01",
  "max_tokens": 1024,
  "model_hints": ["variant-v2","batching:auto"],
  "telemetry_enabled": true
}

- Sample SDK usage (pseudo-code):

client = RedwoodClient(api_key)
response = client.chat.create(route="support-chat-v1", messages=payload, fidelity_profile="balanced-2028-01")

Rollout roadmap and milestones (quarterly)

- Q3 2028: Launch public playbook and fidelity-sim v1.0; pilot with three enterprise customers.
- Q4 2028: Add automated fidelity-advisor suggestions in Console (beta).
- Q1 2029: Offer packaged warm-capacity credits bundled in Dedicated SKUs.

Governance and configuration control

- Fidelity profiles are versioned (semver-like): profile-name:major.minor (e.g., balanced-2028-01). Changes that impact model outputs require an approval from Product + Applied ML and must be accompanied by a regression report.
- All changes to commercial mappings must go through Finance & Legal review and SRE capacity signoff.

Quality & regression management

- Each tenant has a preflight prompt set (10–100 prompts) collected during onboarding. Every profile change runs the preflight set and reports delta metrics.
- If regression > 2% on the preflight set, the profile change is blocked from rollout.

Commercial escalation and credits policy

- If a fidelity profile causes a catastrophic regression (production-quality drop > 8% on customer preflight set), issue a remediation credit equal to 5% of that month’s consumption for the affected routes.
- Credits for degraded latency (p95 above contractual threshold for >72 hours) are tiered at 2% / 5% / 10% depending on SLA deviation.

Appendix A: Compatibility matrix (excerpt)

| Model Variant | Quantization | Supported runtimes | Recommended use |
|---------------|--------------|--------------------|-----------------|
| variant-v3 | fp16 | v3-runtime, dedicated GPUs | Premium conversational, long-context |
| variant-v2 | int8 | v2-runtime (hosted + dedicated) | Balanced conversational |
| variant-v1 | int8-q4 | v1-runtime (edge-friendly) | High-throughput, cost-sensitive |

Appendix B: Release notes (v1.0)

- Release date: 2028-07-14
- Highlights: Public playbook publication; fidelity-sim v1 with end-to-end token-cost simulation; three packaged fidelity tiers defined; default telemetry schema standardized.
- Known limitations: Quantization-aware evals are best-effort; hybrid private deployments may require additional network profiling during Simulation Run.

Appendix C: Owners and contacts

- Product owner: Priya Nambiar (product@redwood.ai)
- Runtime lead: Ethan Morales (eng-serving-runtime)
- Applied ML reviewer: Li Wei (applied-ml)
- Customer success liaison: Sophia Patel

Appendix D: Quick checklist for Solutions Engineers (deliverables)

- [ ] Capture sample traffic (24h).
- [ ] Run fidelity-sim and attach sim-results.json.
- [ ] Present fidelity-eval-report to customer and capture signoff.
- [ ] Apply profile and run 1% canary for 72h.
- [ ] Schedule QBR at 30 days.

If you have questions about mapping to contracts or need a custom fidelity profile, contact product@redwood.ai or open a ticket in #fidelity-onboarding.

title: Kernel Hint Propagation Profiling Pipeline
content:
Summary:

This document specifies the Kernel Hint Propagation Profiling Pipeline (KHPPP) — an end-to-end process used by the serving runtime team to capture, synthesize, and propagate lightweight kernel hints from production traces to the kernel selection and scheduler subsystems. The pipeline is optimized for low-overhead sampling, deterministic replay for hypothesis testing, and safe automated rollout of hint-driven kernel recommendations to the runtime.

Goals:
- Reduce unexpected kernel regressions by surfacing causal correlations between request shape and kernel latency.
- Provide repeatable profiling artifacts usable by scheduler and kernel teams for autotune jobs.
- Automate a canary rollout path for kernel hint changes with observable safety gates.

Scope and non-goals:
- Scope: inference request-level sampling -> trace enrichment -> hint extraction -> validation replay -> recommendation artifact -> canary rollout.
- Non-goals: full-model-level retraining or kernel code changes (those are handled by kernel engineering RFCs).

Owner and runbook contact:
- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime / Kernel Signals team (oncall: @kernel-signals).
- Secondary: eng-platform / Scheduler (oncall: @scheduler-op).
- On-call escalation ladder: pager -> lead kernel engineer -> runtime SRE.

Architecture overview:
1) In-proxy lightweight sampler (service: trace-sampler): attaches to request ingress and emits a sampled event with the following fields: request_id, model_id, route, token_len, prefix_hash, routing_decision, upstream_kernel_hint (if present). Sampling rate is configurable per-service (default 0.1%).

2) Enrichment & correlation (service: hint-enricher): enriches sampled events with kernel telemetry pulled from kernel-telemetry-store (per-GPU kernel latency percentiles, occupancy, kernel version). Correlation computes the candidate hint map for (model_id, sequence_bucket, route).

3) Hint extractor (service: hint-extractor): runs a lightweight causal check (Granger-inspired) to output a candidate hint: {hint_id, model_family, sequence_bucket, suggested_kernel_profile, confidence_score, sample_count, top_covariates}. Output written to artifact-store as a JSONL stream with TTL 90 days.

4) Replay & validation (service: hint-replay): replays a bounded subset of the original sampled traces in the internal replay lab (sandbox runtime) to validate latency delta, regression rate, and resource delta. Replay uses the same scheduler and kernel loader versions as production canary.

5) Recommendation and canary (service: hint-orchestrator): packages validated hints into a signed recommendation manifest and drives a staged canary rollout through the runtime configuration service (route-level config).

SLOs and thresholds (applies to the pipeline):
- End-to-end artifact availability: 99% within 15 minutes of sample capture.
- False-positive detection: target false-positive rate for deployed hints <= 2% measured over 7-day window.
- Canary safety: any canary that increases p99 latency for a route by > 3% or absolute +40ms must auto-abort.
- Resource delta: kernel profile must not increase GPU memory usage by > 6% without manual signoff.

Sampling configuration table (example):

| service | default-sampling | max-sampling | notes |
|---------|------------------:|-------------:|-------|
| public-api | 0.1% | 1% | Route override by SLA tier |
| internal-batch | 0.05% | 0.5% | High-throughput, low-latency sensitivity |
| dedicated-gpu | 0.2% | 2% | More signal for deterministic workloads |

Data retention and PII notes:
- Sampled traces omit prompt payloads by default. The pipeline stores prompt hashes and token counts only. Full payload capture is gated behind an explicit customer opt-in and legal review.

Trace enrichment schema (sample line):

{
  "request_id": "r_123abc",
  "model_id": "open-llama-13b",
  "route": "/v1/chat/completions",
  "sequence_bucket": "0-64",
  "kernel_versions": ["kv1.3.2"],
  "observed_p50_ms": "12.4",
  "observed_p99_ms": "73.1"
}

(Above is an example logged by hint-enricher; fields are stored as strings in artifact JSONL to simplify downstream joins.)

Validation replay checks (ordered step-by-step):
1) Replay subset selection: choose top 500 traces per candidate hint (or all if sample_count < 500).
2) Run replay with baseline kernel profile and with suggested kernel profile.
3) Capture metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, GPU memory, kernel occupancy, and error rate.
4) Apply decision rules (see decision matrix).

Decision matrix (simplified):
- Accept if: p99 improves by >= 4% AND resource delta <= 3% AND confidence_score >= 0.75.
- Tentative if: p99 improves 1–4% AND resource delta <= 6% -> schedule extended evaluation (72h).
- Reject if: p99 regresses > 0% OR error_rate increases > 0.1% OR resource delta > 10%.

Canary rollout procedure (operational checklist):
1) Create signed manifest via hint-orchestrator, include: hint_id, target_routes, advisory_notes, rollback_conditions.
2) Deploy to 1% of traffic in canary region (region: us-west2 by default).
3) Monitor canary dashboard for 30 minutes baseline, then 6-hour extended observation window.
4) Automated gates: if p99 delta > 3% or error_count delta > 0.05% -> immediate rollback. If any kernel panics or GPU OOMs -> immediate rollback and page oncall.
5) If canary passes extended window, increase to 10% for 24 hours, then 50% for 6 hours, then global rollout.

CLI and artifact examples:
- Inspect recent candidate hints:
```
$ rlctl hints list --since 2026-02-01 --filter model_family=open-llama-13b --min-confidence 0.6
ID        MODEL       SEQ_BUCKET  CONF  SAMPLES  STATUS
ht-8a2c   open-llama  0-64        0.78  1,240    validated
```

- Manifest sample (YAML):
```
hint_id: ht-8a2c
model_family: open-llama
sequence_bucket: 0-64
suggested_kernel_profile: wave-compact-v2
confidence_score: 0.78
validation:
  p99_delta_pct: -6.1
  resource_delta_pct: 1.8
  replay_samples: 500
canary_policy:
  initial_traffic_pct: 1
  region: us-west2
  abort_conditions:
    p99_delta_pct_gt: 3
    error_rate_delta_pct_gt: 0.05
```

Observability and dashboards:
- Dashboard: KHPPP / Candidate Hints Overview (service: grafana-khppp) shows candidate hint throughput, validation pass/fail rate, avg confidence, and top failing routes.
- Alerting rules:
  - khppp-artifact-delay-high: fires if >1% of artifacts are older than 15 minutes (SEV3).
  - khppp-canary-p99-abort: fires if any canary violates p99 delta > 3% (SEV2).
  - khppp-replay-failure-spike: fires if hint-replay job failure rate > 0.5% over 10m (SEV2).

Developer guidelines for writing kernel hints:
- Keep hints scoped: prefer sequence_bucket granularity (0-64, 65-256, 257-1024).
- Annotate top_covariates (e.g., prefix_hash, prompt_type) to help scheduler isolation policies.
- Provide a manual test plan in the artifact when confidence_score < 0.8.

Safety and rollback patterns:
- All manifests carry a 24h automatic rollback window if no explicit promotion is run.
- Rollbacks must be recorded in the audit log with cause and mitigation notes.
- For routes with strict SLOs (enterprise-tier), the pipeline is opt-in; hints will not be applied unless the customer has agreed to canary policy.

Troubleshooting playbook (quick steps):
1) Missing artifacts: check trace-sampler logs -> hint-enricher -> artifact-store. Rehydrate by running: `rlctl hints backfill --from 2026-02-10 --to 2026-02-11 --service public-api`
2) Replay failures: check sandbox runtime container logs (service: hint-replay) and kernel-telemetry-store ACLs. Common causes: missing kernel image or incompatible kernel loader.
3) Unexpected p99 regression in canary: immediate rollback via `rlctl canary abort --manifest-id <id>` and run `rlctl hints debug --id <hint_id>` to fetch top failing traces.

Runbook: immediate incident steps for kernel hint-induced outage:
1) Page kernel-signals and scheduler-op.
2) Abort running canaries and set global kernel manifest to baseline.
3) Capture traces for affected time window, escalate to kernel engineering.
4) Open postmortem and tag hint as rejected with root-cause.

Metric catalog (important signals):
- khppp.candidate.count (counter)
- khppp.validation.pass_rate (gauge, %)
- khppp.replay.latency_ms.p95
- khppp.canary.p99_delta_pct
- khppp.artifact.queue_time_seconds.p90

Related pages:
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/execution-stitching-and-fallback-orchestration-2026
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-observability-contract-and-simulated-injector-2026
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-deployment-circuit-breakers-and-sla-fallback-playbook-2026

Appendix: example decision rule JSON (flattened for automation):
```
{"rule_id":"dr-2026-11","min_confidence":"0.75","p99_improve_pct":"4","max_resource_delta_pct":"3","action":"promote"}
```

Notes and future work:
- Integrate KV-cache prefix signals to make hints prefix-aware rather than only sequence-length aware.
- Add a privacy-preserving differential sampling mode for regulated customers.
- Expose an internal UI for kernel engineers to triage top_covariates and request ad-hoc replays.

References:
- artifact-store schema: s3://redwood-artifacts/khppp/schema-v1.md
- scheduler contracts: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-observability-contract-and-simulated-injector-2026

Owner signoff:
- Jordan Patel (Kernel Signals)
- Priya Rao (Runtime SRE)

title: Interactive kernel latency surface mapping and lab protocol
content:
Title: Interactive kernel latency surface mapping and lab protocol

Overview
This document defines the lab protocol, tooling, and interpretation guide for interactive kernel latency surface mapping — a repeatable experiment to discover how scheduler decisions, kernel selection, and request shapes interact to produce the observed latency surface across our GPU fleet. The goal is to produce a compact, actionable artifact (the latency surface) for: triage, kernel hinting, scheduler tuning, and CI gating for kernel rollouts.

Why we need this playbook
- Compliments static microbenchmarks by exposing cross-layer effects (scheduling, batching, KV cache warmup, and transport).
- Produces a 2D/3D surface (example axes: concurrency x sequence length x kernel variant) that helps quantify non-linear tail behavior.
- Provides reproducible artifacts to attach to incident reviews and perf regression PRs.

Scope and assumptions
- Scope: production-like runtime and staging clusters only. Not intended for developer sandbox machines.
- Assumes trace-captured workload shapes (sequence length distribution, token rate, concurrency histogram).
- Requires telemetry stack: tracing enabled, kernel-hint annotations (k_hint), scheduler decisions logged, and KV cache hit-rate metrics.

Ownership and contacts
- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime/perf (on-call: Michael Chen)
- Kernel scheduling lead: Lena Ortiz
- SRE contact for fleet experiments: Tomás Rivera

Definitions
- Latency surface: a vectorized map of p50/p90/p99 generation latency over discretized axes (concurrency, sequence length, kernel variant, model shard count).
- Kernel variant: a named execution path (e.g., fast-attn-v2-fp16, sharded-kv-quant-8b).

High-level experiment steps
1) Select workload corpus
   - Use recent 7-day trace that matches the target customer profile. Export as request-surface.json following the format in Appendix A.
2) Provision experiment cluster
   - Create an isolated staging fleet subset (min size 8 GPUs, matching target hardware generation). Ensure same networking path as prod (VPC peering).
3) Apply instrumentation and deterministic seed
   - Enable full tracing (trace-level=debug), kernel hinting annotations, and set kvcache-deterministic=true for warmup runs.
4) Define axis grid
   - Concurrency: [1, 4, 8, 16, 32]
   - Sequence length: [8, 32, 128, 512]
   - Kernel variants: select 3–4 candidates under test
   - For heterogeneous pools, include shard counts [1, 2, 4]
5) Run warmup phase (10 minutes per grid point)
6) Execute measurement phase (3–10 minutes per grid point depending on noise)
7) Aggregate and synthesize the latency surface
8) Produce findings and suggested action items (kernel hints, scheduler policy changes, rollout gates)

Detailed commands and examples
- Provisioning (example using infra-tool):
  infra-tool create-experiment --name latency-surface-2027-11 --region us-west2 --gpus 8 --image runtime-experiment:v2027.03

- Trace replay command (local runner):
  trace-runner --input request-surface.json --concurrency 8 --sequence-length 128 --interval 0.01 --target http://staging-runtime:8080/generate --annotations k_hint=on

- Kernel probe invocation (on-node):
  sudo /opt/runtime/bin/kernel-probe --pid $RUNTIME_PID --duration 120 --out /tmp/kprobe.json

- Telemetry collection snippets (yaml):
  telemetry_capture: |
    capture: true
    metrics: ["latency_ms.p50","latency_ms.p90","latency_ms.p99","kvcache.hit_rate","kernel.exec_ns"]
    trace: true

Measurement considerations and guardrails
- Warmup is mandatory: discard first 120s of samples per grid point to avoid startup noise.
- Target request-rate should be bounded to avoid saturation outside interest range. Use rate limiter parameter to shape inputs.
- If node-level CPU steals or OOMs are observed, mark grid point as invalid and rerun after fixing interference.
- Use p99 over sliding window of 60s as primary tail metric.

Data model and artifact format
- Latency surface artifact is a newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON) file where each record has flat fields only:
  - timestamp, axis_concurrency, axis_sequence_length, kernel_variant, p50_ms, p90_ms, p99_ms, sample_count, kvcache_hit_rate, scheduler_decision
- Attach raw traces (zip) and kernel-probe outputs to the artifact bundle for deep dive.

Interpreting the surface: quick heuristics
- Sharp upward slope in p99 when going from concurrency 8 -> 16 suggests scheduler admission/backpressure tuning required.
- Diverging p90 vs p99 for the same kernel variant indicates tail amplification (likely inter-batch interference).
- If a kernel variant shows better p50 but worse p99 consistently, consider local hedging or slot reservation policies for latency-sensitive tenants.

Recommended actions matrix
| Symptom | Likely cause | Recommended quick action | Longer-term remediation | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| p99 spike at medium concurrency | Kernel blocking on NVLINK or serialization | Enable per-request kernel timeout / hedge | Patch kernel to reduce global locks; add preemption hints | Kernel team |
| p50 improves but p99 worsens | Inter-batch head-of-line contention | Add burst isolation for small sequences | Scheduler crediting by sequence-length class | Scheduler team |
| p99 increases with shard count | KV cache warmup inefficiency | Increase prefetch window for multi-shard requests | Rework KV prefetch algorithm to prioritize hot prefixes | Runtime team |

CI gates and rollout criteria
- Attach latency-surface artifact and p99 delta plots to every kernel rollout PR.
- Mandatory pass criteria for major kernel releases: p99 delta <= +3% across all grid points for the baseline customer corpus, and no grid point with >+10% increase.
- For canary: run abbreviated surface (concurrency [1,8,32], sequence lengths [8,128,512]) in canary fleet with 48h observation window.

Dashboarding and visualization
- Visualize as a 3D surface (concurrency x seq-length x p99) in Grafana using the latency-surface ndjson -> timeseries transformer. Provide a linked panel to sample traces for any selected grid point.
- Store artifacts in object-store prefix: s3://redwood-runtime-experiments/latency-surfaces/{YYYY}/{experiment-id}/artifact.ndjson

Known limitations
- Lab results are sensitive to cross-tenant noise and scheduler tuning; annotate experiments with cluster packing details.
- Results for highly heterogeneous models (different layer shapes) might not be comparable — restrict comparisons to similar model classes.

Reporting template (to attach to PRs/incidents)
- Experiment id: <uuid>
- Date run: <YYYY-MM-DD>
- Cluster: <region>/<flavor>/<k8s-version>
- Workload corpus id: <corpus-id> (link)
- Key findings (bulleted)
- Action items and owners
- Attached artifacts: latency-surface.ndjson, traces.zip, kprobe.json, dashboard-link

Appendix A — request-surface.json example (flattened NDJSON)
{"timestamp":"2027-02-28T14:23:00Z","req_id":"r-123","seq_len":"128","concurrency_bucket":"8","payload_sample":"<redacted>"}

Appendix B — minimal telemetry query examples
- p99 by grid point (promql):
  histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, kernel_variant, seq_len_bucket, concurrency_bucket))

Appendix C — quick trouble-shoot checklist
1) Confirm trace completeness and presence of k_hint annotations.
2) Inspect kernel-probe for long syscall blocking or NVLINK stalls.
3) Check scheduler decision logs for preemptions or admission rejects.
4) Validate KV cache hit rates at grid point; if <60% for expected hot prefixes, rerun with longer warmup.

Revision history
- 2026-11-14: Initial draft (Aisha Kapoor)
- 2027-01-08: Added CI gate thresholds and visualization guidance (Michael Chen)
- 2027-03-02: Clarified artifact schema and control plane commands (Lena Ortiz)

Links and references
- Runtime telemetry schema: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/runtime-telemetry-sampling-cost-aware-profiling-2027
- Kernel probe tool README: internal:/tools/kernel-probe/readme
- Scheduler policy language spec: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-policy-language-declarative-profiles-2026

End of document

title: Cache Telemetry Validation Checklist (Prefix + KV Cache)
content:
## Purpose
This checklist verifies that new prefix/KV cache telemetry is:
1) Correct (hit/miss attribution, counters/histograms consistent with request lifecycle),
2) Joinable (model/route/deployment identifiers present and stable),
3) Safe to operate (cardinality bounded, sampling behaves as intended), and
4) Low overhead (near-zero latency/throughput impact).

This is the required validation sequence for runtime changes touching:
- KV cache hit/miss counters and miss reasons
- Prefix cache reuse histograms
- Eviction/pressure indicators
- “Wasted prefill” metrics
- Trace span annotations for cache events

## Scope
Applies to: Hosted, Dedicated, and Private runtime builds that emit cache telemetry.

Out of scope: correctness of cache policy/eviction algorithms themselves (only their *telemetry*).

## Owners / when to run
- Primary owner: Runtime perf validation (Marcus Reed)
- Required reviewers for signoff: Runtime (Omar El-Sayed), Telemetry schema (Nadia Rahman), SRE observability (Allison Grant)
- Run for: every PR series that changes cache metrics semantics, tags/labels, sampling, or ingestion guards.

---

## Quick acceptance criteria (must pass)
### Correctness
- No systematic double-counting on streaming retries.
- Batched prefill attribution: per-request counters reconcile with batch-level spans.
- Partial reuse semantics are consistent (hit-rate is computed from the same numerator/denominator across dashboards).
- Wasted prefill increases when expected (forced misses/evictions), and stays low on stable repeated prompts.

### Joinability
- Each emitted metric/trace includes (or can be joined to) model identifier + model version, route identifier, deployment mode, and region.
- Join keys are stable across gateway logs, runtime metrics, and analytics aggregates.

### Cardinality & sampling
- No forbidden labels (raw prompt, request_id, user_id, tenant_id at high-cardinality) appear in metrics.
- Prompt length / token counts appear only as approved buckets.
- Sampling reduces event volume without biasing aggregate hit-rate beyond tolerance (see “Sampling bias check”).

### Performance
- p95 latency regression <= 0.5% in perf-canary at default sampling.
- Runtime CPU overhead <= 1% under representative throughput.
- Metrics emission does not increase tail latency variance (p99/p99.9) beyond alert thresholds.

---

## Definitions (what we mean by “correct”)
Use the definitions in the ADR (linked above). In practical validation, we check these invariants:
- A “request” flows through prefill then decode.
- Prefix cache reuse counts only reused prefix tokens that are actually applied to compute subsequent decode.
- KV cache hit/miss is attributed per request and is consistent across streaming and retries.
- Miss reasons are stable, mutually exclusive per miss event, and are not overloaded with transient internal states.

---

## Prerequisites
### Environments
- Staging (required)
- Canary (required for perf validation)
- Production (only after signoff)

### Required feature flags / config knobs
Verify the runtime supports enabling/disabling and sampling of cache telemetry. Names vary per deployment; use the effective config dump from the runtime.

Checklist:
- [ ] Cache telemetry enabled (metrics)
- [ ] Trace annotations enabled (if included in change)
- [ ] Sampling enabled and set to default (record the value)
- [ ] Rate limiter enabled (if implemented) and set to default

### Tools
- Metrics query access (Prometheus/Grafana or Redwood Console internal dashboards)
- Trace viewer (for span annotations)
- Load generator / replay tool for repeated prompts
- Runtime log access (structured logs only; do not log raw prompts)

---

## Step 1 — Verify build + rollout hygiene
1. [ ] Confirm the runtime image / build hash under test.
2. [ ] Confirm the feature flags are set as intended in the target env.
3. [ ] Confirm dashboards are pointing at the new metric names (if names were reconciled/renamed).
4. [ ] Confirm deprecated metric names (if any) are either still emitted with deprecation window or dashboards have migrated.

Record:
- Runtime version / commit:
- Deployment mode:
- Region:
- Telemetry sampling rate:

---

## Step 2 — Smoke test: metrics are present and non-zero
Generate traffic for 5–10 minutes with a mix of:
- Exact prompt repeats (high expected reuse)
- Slight prompt variations (low expected reuse)
- Two-turn chat (prefix reuse expected on turn 2 if canonicalization holds)

Checklist (observability):
- [ ] KV hit/miss counters increase
- [ ] Prefix reuse histogram buckets increase
- [ ] Eviction/pressure signals are present (may remain low)
- [ ] Wasted prefill is present and behaves plausibly
- [ ] Trace spans show cache annotations (if enabled) without high-cardinality tags

If any metric is missing:
- Validate config flags
- Validate metric allowlist in runtime emission
- Validate ingestion-side drop/guard behavior (see Step 6)

---

## Step 3 — Counter reconciliation (single-request invariants)
### 3A) Simple repeated prompt test (no streaming)
Procedure:
1) Send the same prompt N times (N>=50) to the same route/model/region.
2) Keep decode params constant.

Expected:
- Hit-rate increases after warm-up.
- Prefix reuse depth increases (distribution shifts right).
- Wasted prefill decreases after warm-up.

Checklist:
- [ ] After initial warm-up, KV misses per request trend down.
- [ ] Prefix reused tokens per request trend up.
- [ ] Wasted prefill per request trends down.

### 3B) Prompt mutation test
Procedure:
1) Append a random suffix to the prompt each request.

Expected:
- Hit-rate remains low.
- Reuse depth remains near zero.
- Wasted prefill may increase if prefill work is repeatedly not reused.

Checklist:
- [ ] Misses dominate; “hash_mismatch”/equivalent reason increases (if implemented).
- [ ] Reuse histograms concentrate in lowest buckets.

---

## Step 4 — Streaming + retry correctness (negative test)
Goal: ensure we do not double count when a stream is retried.

Procedure:
1) Initiate streaming responses.
2) Induce retry behavior (e.g., client disconnect/reconnect, simulated upstream retry, or known retry harness).
3) Repeat for a small set of prompts where reuse is expected.

Expected:
- Per-request cache metrics represent the logical request outcome, not the number of transport attempts.
- Retries should not inflate hit/miss totals disproportionately.

Checklist:
- [ ] KV hit/miss counters do not exceed expected request count by >2% (tolerance for in-flight edge cases).
- [ ] Wasted prefill does not spike solely due to retries.
- [ ] Trace spans show retry linkage without creating unique metric labels.

If failing:
- Check for duplicate “end-of-request” emission.
- Ensure retry instrumentation uses idempotent accounting.

---

## Step 5 — Continuous batching correctness (batched prefill attribution)
Goal: ensure that per-request counters are correct when multiple requests share a continuous batch prefill.

Procedure:
1) Enable a load profile that triggers continuous batching.
2) Send two cohorts concurrently:
   - Cohort A: repeated prompts (expected high reuse)
   - Cohort B: varied prompts (expected low reuse)

Expected:
- Cohort A shows higher hit-rate than Cohort B even under batching.
- Batch-level behavior does not “bleed” hits across requests.

Checklist:
- [ ] Metrics sliced by request-shape buckets show plausible separation.
- [ ] No systematic over-attribution of hits to shorter prompts.

---

## Step 6 — Sampling verification (volume + bias)
### 6A) Sampling is actually reducing volume
Procedure:
1) Run traffic at a fixed QPS for 10 minutes at sampling=1.0.
2) Run traffic at the same QPS for 10 minutes at sampling=default.
3) Compare emitted series rate / ingestion volume.

Checklist:
- [ ] Event/metric emission volume decreases roughly proportionally to sampling.
- [ ] Rate-limiting (if enabled) activates only under expected high-volume patterns.

### 6B) Sampling bias check (must not distort aggregates)
Compute hit-rate and reuse distributions for the same workload under sampling=1.0 vs default sampling.

Checklist:
- [ ] Aggregate KV hit-rate differs by <= 1.0 percentage point (or documented tolerance) between sampling modes.
- [ ] Prefix reuse histogram shape is not materially distorted (no bucket collapses due to sampling implementation).

If failing:
- Sampling must be applied uniformly at the correct event boundary (per-request, not per-token unless explicitly defined).
- Ensure denominators are sampled consistently with numerators.

---

## Step 7 — Cardinality safety checks (must pass before canary)
Goal: ensure we do not create a metric explosion.

Checklist:
- [ ] No metric includes raw prompt, canonical prompt hash (if high-cardinality), request_id, session_id, or user identifiers.
- [ ] Route/model/version tags are from strict allowlists (known route IDs, known model IDs).
- [ ] Prompt length / token counts appear only in pre-defined buckets.
- [ ] Tenant/customer identifiers are either absent or aggregated to an approved low-cardinality dimension (e.g., “tier” or internal/customer boolean) per policy.

Operational check:
- [ ] Validate ingestion logs for label-drop events are near zero.
- [ ] Validate series count for cache telemetry is within budget (compare to baseline; do not exceed 1.2x expected).

If you see a spike in “dropped labels”:
- Confirm allowlist config matches current route/model identifiers.
- Confirm gateway is populating join keys consistently (no new unexpected values).

---

## Step 8 — Miss reason taxonomy sanity
Procedure:
1) Force each miss reason in a controlled way (as feasible):
   - capacity/pressure: temporarily reduce cache budget or increase load
   - ttl_expired: configure a short TTL, wait, then repeat
   - policy_disabled: disable caching on a route
   - version_mismatch: roll model version and send repeated prompt across versions
   - hash_mismatch: prompt mutation
2) Observe miss reason breakdown.

Checklist:
- [ ] Each forced scenario produces the expected dominant reason.
- [ ] Reasons are mutually exclusive per miss event.
- [ ] “Unknown/other” remains low; if high, instrument a new explicit reason rather than overloading.

---

## Step 9 — Wasted prefill validation
Goal: ensure wasted prefill tracks “prefill work that does not contribute to subsequent decode due to cache misses/evictions” (as defined).

Procedure:
1) Baseline: repeated prompts with stable cache budget (expected low wasted prefill after warm-up).
2) Pressure: increase concurrency or reduce cache budget to trigger evictions.
3) Compare wasted prefill rates.

Checklist:
- [ ] Wasted prefill increases meaningfully under eviction pressure.
- [ ] Wasted prefill remains low in steady-state reuse.
- [ ] Wasted prefill does not increase simply due to longer decodes when reuse is still high.

---

## Step 10 — Trace annotations check (if included)
Goal: provide debuggability without high-cardinality metrics.

Checklist:
- [ ] Cache-related spans/annotations appear on the request trace.
- [ ] Attributes are bounded (e.g., booleans, enums, bucketed ints) and do not include prompt content.
- [ ] Trace sampling does not disproportionately exclude cache-miss traces (avoid only sampling “fast” paths).

---

## Step 11 — Overhead benchmarking (bench + perf-canary)
### 11A) Microbench / bench harness
Run a representative set of workloads:
- Short prompts (e.g., <256 tokens)
- Medium prompts (256–2k)
- Long prompts (>2k)
- Streaming on/off
- Continuous batching on/off

Checklist:
- [ ] Compare latency distributions with telemetry disabled vs enabled.
- [ ] Compare throughput (tokens/sec) with telemetry disabled vs enabled.
- [ ] Compare CPU utilization and allocator/memory overhead.

Acceptance:
- [ ] p95 latency regression <= 0.5% at default sampling
- [ ] p99 latency regression <= 1.0% at default sampling
- [ ] No measurable increase in GC/allocator churn attributable to telemetry tags

### 11B) Perf-canary gate
Procedure:
1) Enable telemetry on perf-canary workload.
2) Run for >= 30 minutes to include steady-state and burst patterns.

Checklist:
- [ ] Canary does not fail SLO gates.
- [ ] Tail latency variance does not increase unexpectedly.
- [ ] Metrics pipeline remains stable (no ingestion throttling alerts).

---

## Step 12 — Dashboard sanity + operational readiness
Checklist:
- [ ] Dashboards show expected patterns during the above tests:
  - Hit-rate trends respond to workload changes
  - Eviction/pressure correlates with wasted prefill
  - Model/region/route filters work and do not produce empty panels (unless truly no traffic)
- [ ] Alerts are either disabled in staging or tuned to avoid noise during validation.
- [ ] Runbook links from dashboards are correct.

---

## Common failure modes and how to diagnose
1) **All cache hits = 0**
   - Check: ingestion label-drop or cardinality guard dropping key labels
   - Check: caching policy disabled at route
   - Check: model version mismatch during rollout

2) **Hit-rate looks too good to be true (near 100%)**
   - Check: denominator not incrementing (missed “requests_total”)
   - Check: double counting hits due to retries

3) **Hit-rate collapse after model rollout**
   - Check: version_mismatch misses
   - Check: route now points to new model version without warm-up

4) **Series count explosion**
   - Check: route_id or model_version values not allowlisted
   - Check: prompt hash incorrectly tagged as metric label

---

## Signoff checklist (required before production rollout)
- [ ] Steps 1–10 completed in staging
- [ ] Step 11 completed (bench + perf-canary)
- [ ] Cardinality safety (Step 7) validated with Telemetry owner (Nadia Rahman or delegate)
- [ ] Dashboards/alerts validated with Observability owner (Allison Grant or delegate)
- [ ] Rollout plan reviewed with Release/canary coordination (Connor O'Brien)

Signoff notes (fill in):
- Runtime reviewer:
- Telemetry reviewer:
- SRE reviewer:
- Date:

---

## Appendix: recommended test workloads
Use these as standard reproducible workloads:
1) **Exact-repeat chat warm-up**: fixed system prompt + fixed first user turn repeated
2) **Two-turn chat**: same first turn, different second turn; verify partial reuse
3) **Suffix mutation**: same base prompt + random suffix
4) **Eviction pressure**: high concurrency long prompts to push cache budget
5) **Streaming retry**: simulated disconnect/reconnect during decode

Keep prompts synthetic or from approved test sets. Do not use customer prompts in staging/perf-canary.

title: Incremental Kernel Snapshot Profiling and Telemetry Deduplication Playbook
content:
Summary

This playbook describes an incremental snapshot profiling method for Redwood's serving runtime that reduces observability cost and noise by deduplicating telemetry at ingestion and by shipping compact kernel snapshots instead of full traces for every request. It is intended for engineers operating the runtime (runtime-manager, kernel-dispatcher, trace-collector, telemetry-processor) and for SREs investigating regressions.

Motivation

- Full-trace capture at high QPS produces excessive storage and processing costs and buries signals under duplicate events.
- Incremental snapshots preserve causal telemetry (kernel selection, queue wait, batch composition, KV-cache hits) while limiting volume.
- Deterministic deduplication reduces alert noise and increases signal-to-noise in regression hunts.

Scope and Audience

- Applies to: production runtime fleets (hosted and dedicated), dev sandbox fleets when sampling=on.
- Not for: air-gapped private deployments that have custom telemetry pipelines unless adapters are installed.
- Audience: runtime engineers, perf SREs, observability engineers.

Key Services & Components

- runtime-manager: orchestrates shard topology and rollout flags.
- kernel-dispatcher: assigns kernels and emits kernel-hint events.
- trace-collector: local agent on each instance, emits incremental snapshots.
- telemetry-processor: centralized aggregator that deduplicates, enriches, and stores compact records.

Goals and SLOs

- Profiling capture SLO: when sampling is enabled for a cohort, >=99% of sampled requests must produce an incremental snapshot within 1s of completion (99th percentile).
- Deduplication latency: telemetry-processor must deduplicate and index new unique signatures within 30s.
- Storage budget: sampled tracing must consume <= 1.5% of monthly observability spend for the fleet by default.

Terminology

- Snapshot: compact set of fields capturing request surfaces and kernel decisions (not a full span tree).
- Signature: a canonicalized hash of stable snapshot fields used for deduplication.
- Incremental diff: subset of fields that changed relative to the last seen signature for a tenant/cohort.

Design Overview

1) Local Collector Behavior (trace-collector)

- Capture points: request start/end, kernel selection, batch boundaries, KV cache warmup, GPU dispatch, kernel completion.
- Compose a baseline snapshot template per process at startup containing static metadata (instance_id, gpu_type, runtime_version).
- For each sampled request: produce an incremental snapshot consisting of {request_id, timestamp, seq_len, kernel_hint, batch_size, kvcache_hit_ratio, latency_buckets, runtime_flags}.
- Compute signature: SHA256(hex(pick_fields(kernel_hint,batch_shape,model_version,quant_profile,static_metadata))) truncated to 64 bits.

Example incremental snapshot (JSON line):

{
  "proc_id": "p-7f21",
  "req_id": "r-9b3e",
  "ts": "2026-02-03T15:12:21Z",
  "sig": "a3f4c1e2b8d9f6c7",
  "kernel": "sharded-attn-v2",
  "batch": 4,
  "seq_len": 128,
  "kv_hit": 0.78,
  "lat_ms": 72
}

CLI: capture a one-off snapshot from running instance

$ rctl instance snapshot capture --instance p-7f21 --tail 1 --out /tmp/snap.jsonl

2) Signature & Deduplication Strategy (telemetry-processor)

- Tiered signature keys:
  - primary_key: (tenant_id, model_version, quant_profile, kernel_hint, batch_shape)
  - secondary_key: (seq_len_bucket, kv_hit_bucket, runtime_flags_hash)
- Deduplication window: 15 minutes per tenant by default (configurable per cohort).
- Behavior: first occurrence of a signature produces a full record (indexed). Subsequent identical signatures emit only a counter increment event and a 1-line delta if a non-key field (e.g., tail latency) crossed a configured threshold.

Deduplication pseudocode (simplified)

store = TTLMap()  # TTLMap(signature->last_seen_ts, summary)

function ingest(snapshot):
  sig = snapshot.sig
  if sig not in store or now - store[sig].last_seen > dedup_window:
    index_full(snapshot)
    store[sig] = {last_seen: now, summary: summarise(snapshot)}
  else:
    delta = compute_delta(store[sig].summary, snapshot)
    if delta.significant:
      index_delta(snapshot.req_id, delta)
      store[sig].summary = merge_summaries(store[sig].summary, snapshot)
    else:
      increment_counter(sig)

3) Sampling and Cohorts

- Sampling policies are declared in runtime-manager as YAML cohort policies. Example:

cohorts:
  - name: production-critical
    sampling_rate: 0.01  # 1%
    dedup_window: 900   # seconds
    retention_days: 30
  - name: experimental-heavy
    sampling_rate: 0.10  # 10%
    dedup_window: 300
    retention_days: 7

- Default cohorts: baseline-sampled (0.1%), production-critical (0.01%), emergency-high (100% but short retention).

4) Storage schema & retention table

| Record type | Fields (primary) | Retention (default) | Size estimate | Owner |
| Full snapshot | sig, req_id, ts, kernel, batch, seq_len, kv_hit, latency_hist, flags | 30 days | ~1.2 KB | observability-team |
| Delta record | sig, req_id, ts, changed_fields | 90 days | ~200 B | observability-team |
| Counter event | sig, ts, count_inc | 365 days | ~50 B | cost-analytics |

5) Rollout checklist (how to enable on a fleet)

1. Create cohort in runtime-manager and set sampling_rate/dedup_window/retention. Owner: runtime-engineering.
2. Deploy trace-collector v2.4.1 to a 5% canary pool.
3. Verify snapshots flow to telemetry-processor test namespace, confirm signatures are computed (CLI: tproc inspect --ns test --sig a3f4...).
4. Confirm dedup counts vs full records ratio >= 20:1 for steady-state traffic.
5. Expand to 25% then 100% with 2h observation windows between stages.
6. Run the regression-hunt script (see Troubleshooting) against the new data.

Safety checks and thresholds

- If dedup ratio drops below 2:1 for 10m, rollback collector and open P0 incident.
- If average snapshot latency > 1s for 5% of instances, reduce sampling_rate by 50% and investigate kernel-dispatcher backlog.

6) Operational playbook: investigating a regression using incremental snapshots

1. Query telemetry-processor: find new signatures with sudden latency change:

$ tproc query --ns production --since 1h --filter "lat_ms>p95*1.5" --group-by sig --limit 50

2. For top signals run: tproc fetch-full --sig <sig> --limit 20 --out /tmp/full-samples.jsonl
3. Cross-reference with kernel-dispatcher logs:

$ kdis logs --sig <sig> --since 2m --follow

4. If root cause is a kernel change, trigger kernel-rollout-safety checks (see kernel-and-scheduling handbook).

7) Troubleshooting and common scenarios

- High cardinality due to noisy runtime_flags: canonicalize or map runtime_flags into coarse buckets in trace-collector config (example mapping in next section).
- Missing signatures: check process-level static metadata; ensure model_version and quant_profile are present.
- Signature collisions (rare): use extended signature (128-bit) temporarily and run forensic query to check variance.

Example trace-collector YAML (partial)

collector:
  sampling_rules:
    - cohort: production-critical
      rule: "request_path =~ /api/v1/complete"
      rate: 0.01
  canonicalization_map:
    runtime_flags:
      "debug_enabled": low
      "zero_copy": medium
      "hardware_bfloat": high

Performance experiments and benchmark plan

- Microbenchmarks: measure per-snapshot CPU and memory cost on representative instances (p4d-like and a100-like). Target: < 2% CPU and < 64MB additional RSS per 1% sampling of traffic.
- End-to-end: run load-synthesis with sampling on 1% baseline and measure dedup ratio, ingest latency, and storage delta.
- Regression tests: include snapshot capture and signature computation in CI perf-suite (benchmarking-and-perf-suite) with synthetic traces.

Security & Privacy considerations

- Redact PII at trace-collector using the redaction module (config key: redaction.enabled=true).
- For private deployments, provide an adapter that emits snapshots to customer-managed telemetry stores; deduplication runs can execute in a self-hosted mode.

Runbook links and ownership

- Runtime-engineering runbook: ../runbooks/runtime-hotpatch-and-quick-redeploy-playbook-2026.json
- Kernel scheduling handbook: ../kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-observability-contract-and-simulated-injector-2026.json
- Observability-team owner: observability@redwood.ai

Change log

- 2025-11-12: Initial draft and design review.
- 2025-12-08: Added deduplication pseudocode and cohort YAML examples.
- 2026-02-03: Published with rollout checklist and CLI commands.

Appendix: utility scripts

- regression-hunt.sh (pseudo):

#!/bin/bash
# Query for sigs with p95 jump and fetch examples
SIGS=$(tproc query --ns production --since 2h --group-by sig --filter "lat_ms>p95*2" --limit 20 --format ids)
for s in $SIGS; do
  tproc fetch-full --sig $s --limit 10 --out /var/tmp/snap-$s.jsonl
  kdis logs --sig $s --limit 100 > /var/tmp/klog-$s.txt
  echo "Saved $s"
done

End of playbook. For questions, contact the author or the observability team.

title: Runtime Energy-Aware Scheduling and Profiling Playbook
content:
Summary
-------
This playbook documents our approach to energy- and power-aware kernel scheduling for the Redwood serving runtime, and prescribes a repeatable profiling and benchmarking workflow for validating energy-related optimizations. The goal is to reduce total energy per inference (Joules/token) while preserving latency SLOs and model-quality constraints.

Scope
-----
Applies to: the serving runtime (scheduler, kernel mapper, and dispatch layers) and the GPU-hotpath kernel implementations. Covers: telemetry, local and cluster-level scheduling policies, profiling methodology, benchmark scenarios, rollout recipes, and incident runbook steps for energy regressions. Does NOT replace thermal/firmware actions performed by cloud providers.

Motivation
----------
- Our customer demand and operational costs require optimizing energy consumption for sustained workloads (e.g., embeddings, high-QPS chat).
- Naive throughput maximization can increase energy per token due to inefficient kernel choices and poor batching alignment.
- We need a documented, repeatable way to measure energy impact of runtime changes, and safe rollout patterns that respect latency SLOs.

Goals and success criteria
-------------------------
1. Reduce median Joules/token for production embedding workloads by >=15% in targeted fleets without increasing p99 latency by >5%.
2. Establish an energy-profiling pipeline that provides reproducible per-kernel and per-request energy attribution within ±10% measurement error.
3. Add automated benchmark scenarios to CI that flag >10% regression in energy-per-token relative to baseline.

Design overview
---------------
At a high level we extend the runtime with three cooperating components:

1) Energy Estimator (lightweight):
- Runs per-device and per-kernel cost models built from microbenchmarks (see Benchmark suite section).
- Inputs: kernel name, sequence length, batch size, quantization profile, GPU model and power cap.
- Output: estimated Joules for the predicted execution path.

2) Power-Aware Scheduler Layer (policy hooks):
- Policy types: power-capped admission, energy-windowing, and cost-weighted-priority.
- Scheduler consults estimator to compute cost delta when selecting kernel variant or slotting across GPUs.
- Policies can be per-tenant, per-model, or global.

3) Telemetry & Attribution:
- Fine-grained telemetry emitted for each request: kernel sequence, execution time, energy_estimate, actual_energy_reading (when available), and decision_reason.
- Telemetry schema additions are in the Team Wiki (see Related pages).

Scheduling policies (examples)
----------------------------
- Power-capped admission: refuse or re-route requests when aggregate expected power > cluster cap threshold. Use for burst isolation on constrained fleets.
- Energy-windowing: prefer kernel variants with lower energy for long-running batched requests even at slight latency cost.
- Cost-weighted priority: score each candidate placement by (priority_score / estimated_joules) to maximize useful work per Joule.

Policy configuration table
-------------------------
Key parameter | Description | Typical value
--------------|-------------|--------------
power_cap_pct  | Percent of device sustained power that scheduler will target | 80
energy_margin  | Allowed increase in Jain-style cost to trade energy for latency | 1.10
sample_interval_s | How often to sample device power sensors for calibration | 30
window_ms      | Energy-windowing decision horizon | 2000

Profiling methodology
---------------------
Objective: capture both model-level and kernel-level energy signals with reproducible noise bounds.

1) Environment requirements:
- Isolated host or pinned node to avoid cross-tenant noise.
- Node-level power telemetry enabled (NVML/AMDuProf/etc) with sampling frequency >= 10Hz.
- Soldered measurement (external PDUs) for fleet-level validation when available.

2) Signals to collect:
- Per-request: request_id, model, kernel_variant, batch_size, seq_len, start_ts, end_ts, gpu_power_series, gpu_temp_series, inferred_joules_estimate, actual_joules_measurement (if sampling available).
- Per-device: SKU, firmware version, driver version, CUDA/cuDNN/cuFFT versions (if applicable), clock settings, power-limit.

3) Sampling strategy and noise control:
- Run each microbenchmark 50+ times and report median and 95% CI.
- For end-to-end workload runs, replay production traces with at least 10 minutes sustained windows for steady-state measurement.
- Use A/B paired tests across identical hardware to factor out ambient variation.

4) Attribution technique:
- When device-level power is coarse, perform causal attribution by: (a) collect per-kernel execution intervals; (b) integrate power trace over intervals; (c) normalize by background idle baseline measured in the same experimental window.

Benchmark suite additions
------------------------
We extend the existing perf suite with energy-focused artifacts:
- microbench-energy-generator: microbenchmarks per kernel and per-sequence-length that emit time and power traces.
- steady-state-replay: component that replays production QPS traces with controllable slotting and power caps.
- energy-ci-checker: CI task that runs selected profiles and fails on >10% energy regression.

Sample CLI commands
-------------------
# Run a microbenchmark for a kernel variant and record power
$ tools/bench/microbench-energy --model gpt-3.5-small --kernel relu-fused --batch 8 --seq 512 --iters 100 --output /tmp/bench.json

# Run steady-state replay for 10 minutes under 80% power cap
$ tools/bench/steady-replay --trace traces/embeddings_jan.bt --duration 600 --power-cap 80 --out /tmp/replay.json

Expected baseline table (example)
--------------------------------
Workload | Baseline Joules/token | Median latency (ms) | Notes
---------|-----------------------|---------------------|------
Embeddings-512b | 0.18 | 12.4 | measured on A100-80W baseline
Chat-small-64 | 0.25 | 9.2 | small model optimized with fused kernels
Rerank-32 | 0.11 | 6.8 | heavily batched workload

Runbook: Investigation for energy regression
-------------------------------------------
When CI or production telemetry shows an energy-per-token regression >10%:
1. Confirm signal: validate CI artifacts and check paired baselines.
2. Check deployment: identify which kernel variants or scheduler changes rolled out in the window (use deployment trace).
3. Perform microbench isolation: run microbench-energy for the affected kernel variants on identical hardware.
4. Collect device telemetry: driver/firmware mismatches, thermal events, power-limit changes.
5. Rollback policy: revert scheduler policy flags (feature-flag ID) and/or kernel variant to last-known-good.
6. Postmortem: populate incident in the runtime incident tracker, include root cause, mitigations, and CI guard to prevent recurrence.

Rollout and safety
------------------
- Feature gating: energy-aware scheduling is behind a server-side feature flag per datacenter region.
- Canary matrix: run in 1% of serving capacity with both telemetry sampling and P99 latency guard rails for 24 hours before broader rollout.
- Automatic fallback: if p99 latency increases by >5% or energy-per-token regresses >20% in canary, disable policy and trigger alert to oncall.

Operational considerations
------------------------
- Telemetry storage: add sampling to limit retention cost; store high-fidelity traces for windows where anomalies are detected.
- Cost accounting: update per-tenant cost buckets to include energy_adjusted_charge = baseline_unit_cost * estimated_joules / baseline_joules.
- Security: energy telemetry is internal but may include customer request identifiers; mark as internal-only and scrub PII per data management policy.

Ownership and governance
------------------------
- Primary owner: serving-runtime kernel and scheduler squad (oncall-channel: #runtime-kernel).
- Measurement and benchmarking steward: perf-infra team.
- Review cadence: Quarterly review of energy baselines and policy thresholds.

Related pages and artifacts
--------------------------
- Kernel mapper and scheduling policy language docs (see kernel-and-scheduling folder).
- Microbench harness repository: git:github.com/redwood-inference/bench/microbench-energy
- Team wiki: telemetry schema and event names for energy profiling.

Appendix: energy-calibration JSON example
-----------------------------------------
{
  "device_sku": "A100-80W",
  "power_limit_w": "80",
  "microbench_median_joules_per_op": "0.0042",
  "calibration_ts": "2026-02-10T18:30:00Z"
}

Appendix: quick checklist for experiments
----------------------------------------
- Reserve isolated nodes and set consistent power limits.
- Use the microbench harness to build kernel cost table.
- Run steady-state replays with paired control experiments.
- Collect at least 10 minutes steady-state windows, repeat N=5.
- Commit a benchmark artifact to the energy-bench registry before PR merge.

Notes and open questions
------------------------
- We are still validating driver/firmware contributions to per-kernel energy variance: plan to run cross-firmware experiments in Q2 2026.
- GPU vendor APIs for per-kernel energy are still imperfect; fall back to interval-based attribution when necessary.

Contact
-------
For questions, reach out to the playbook author or ping #runtime-kernel on Slack.

title: fine-grained-causal-profiling-for-multi-kernel-paths-2026
content:
Summary:
This playbook describes a repeatable, low-risk process for performing fine-grained causal profiling across multi-kernel execution paths in the Redwood serving runtime. It targets cases where a single inference request may exercise multiple kernels (attention variants, fused matmuls, quantized vs FP16 paths) and where attribution of end-to-end latency or tail spikes to a specific kernel, combination of kernels, or scheduling interaction is uncertain.

Audience:
- Serving runtime engineers
- Oncall SREs investigating tail latency
- Profiling / performance owners evaluating kernel rollouts

Goals:
1) Produce a causal hypothesis ("kernel X caused tail at 99.9p") with an associated confidence score and required evidence.
2) Generate a minimal, reproducible profiling experiment that isolates the suspected kernel path and quantifies its impact on: p50/p95/p99 latency, GPU occupancy, SM stall time, and memory bandwidth.
3) Provide clear remediation guidance (rollforward/rollback, kernel knobs, scheduling policy changes).

When to use:
- New kernel variant rollout shows unexpected tail increase in canary or production shadowing.
- Mixed workload exposes previously unseen interference between kernels (e.g., sparse attention + fused softmax).
- Quantization rollout correlated with higher variance across cohorts.

Prerequisites:
- Access to trace IDs for affected requests and the consolidated trace store (trace-id -> kernel sequence).
- Profiling lab with the same accelerator family and driver stack as production.
- Baseline microbenchmarks for each kernel variant (available in /benchmarks/kernel-microbenchmarks).
- SLO targets and alert thresholds (example: p99 <= 1200ms for chat.route-alpha).

Procedure (step-by-step):
1) Triage and hypothesis formation
   a. Collect representative request traces for the incident window (use trace exporter: rwd-trace-export --start <ts> --end <ts> --label incident-42).
   b. Build a candidate list of kernels observed in the slow traces, ordered by aggregated kernel time.
   c. For each candidate kernel, capture: kernel name, variant tag, callsite (model shard id), observed kernel time distribution, and upstream queue wait time.

2) Causal probing via selective shadowing
   a. Create a shadow cohort in the profiling lab that replays the same trace corpus but forces a single kernel variant at a time (kernel override injection).
   b. Run 500–2000 replayed requests across varying concurrency shapes (1, 4, 16) and collect full-device perf counters (SM utilization, L2 read/write, DRAM BW).
   c. Compare distributions and compute delta metrics: delta_p99_ms, delta_occ_pct, delta_L2_miss_rate.

3) Interference experiments (pairwise)
   a. If multiple kernels are plausible, run pairwise interleaving experiments (A-only, B-only, A+B co-scheduled) to detect emergent interactions.
   b. Capture cross-correlation of latency with GPU scheduler backpressure signals and kernel start time jitter.

4) Controlled perturbations and causal inference scoring
   a. Apply small, safe perturbations: tensor packing/unpacking flags, reducing the kernel launch grid size by 10%, or enabling a single safety-fallback path.
   b. Use the following scoring rubric to assign confidence: EvidenceScore = 0.5*(delta_p99_normalized) + 0.3*(occupancy_change_normalized) + 0.2*(repro_rate). Normalization bounds are defined in the Appendix.

5) Remediation play
   a. If EvidenceScore >= 0.7: prepare an emergency canary rollback for the kernel variant with a one-hour monitor window.
   b. If 0.4 <= EvidenceScore < 0.7: open a kernel regression ticket, schedule a non-disruptive A/B test with shadow routing for 48 hours.
   c. If EvidenceScore < 0.4: capture experiment artifacts, label the hypothesis as low confidence, and schedule deeper instrumentation (see Appendix).

Observability checklist (data to collect):
- Full request trace with kernel sequence and timestamps (trace store id).
- Kernel-level histograms (start_time, duration, queue_wait).
- Device perf counters sampled at 10ms granularity: SM_util, warp_occ, DRAM_bw, L2_rd/wr, tensor_core_ops.
- Scheduler telemetry: slot assignment, preemption events, admission decisions.
- Execution environment: driver version, CUDA/cuDNN/ROCm versions, kernel build flags.

Safe lab commands and snippets:
- Start a deterministic replay with kernel override:
  rwd-replay --trace-corpus traces/incident-42.tar.gz --kernel-override attention:v2 --concurrency 8 --sample-rate 1.0 --out /tmp/replay-output

- Collect perf counters with rwd-prof (example):
  rwd-prof --pid <replay-pid> --counters SM_UTIL,DRAM_BW,L2_MISS --interval_ms 10 --out profiling/case-42.json

- Example kernel-override YAML used by the replay harness:
  overrides:
    - kernel: attention
      variant: v2
      force: true

Expected artifacts (attach to incident):
1) replay-output/log.json
2) profiling/case-42.json (perf counters)
3) delta-report.csv (p50/p95/p99 deltas, occupancy deltas)
4) experimental-runbook.md (chosen remediation path)

Decision matrix (condensed):
| EvidenceScore | Action | Rollout scope | Monitoring window | Owner |
|---------------|--------|---------------|-------------------|-------|
| >= 0.7 | Emergency rollback | Canary -> Prod stop | 1 hour | Kernel-owner |
| 0.4–0.7 | Targeted A/B | 5% traffic shadow | 48 hours | Runtime-release |
| < 0.4 | Deeper instrumentation | Lab only | N/A | Profiling team |

Appendix A — Normalization constants and thresholds:
- delta_p99_normalized = min(1.0, observed_delta_p99_ms / 300)  # 300ms maps to 1.0 for scoring
- occupancy_change_normalized = min(1.0, abs(delta_occ_pct) / 40)  # 40% occupancy swing maps to 1.0
- repro_rate = fraction of lab runs that reproduce > 90th percentile effect (0..1)

Appendix B — When to escalate to security/compliance:
- If the repro experiment required production customer data to trigger: mark confidentiality=restricted and notify security for data handling clearance.
- If remediation requires hotpatching customer-facing codepaths, open Change Management with at least one reviewer from Platform Security.

Appendix C — Recommended hooks to add for future incidents (owner: runtime-observability):
- Add kernel-variant tag to trace root and ensure sampling retains tag for 48 hours post-deploy.
- Emit per-kernel occupancy delta metrics to metrics store: runtime.kernel.occupancy.delta{kernel_variant}.
- Add an automated replay job that can reconstruct the top-100 slow traces for any 24h window.

Contact and ownership:
- Primary author: Priya Shah (serving-runtime perf)
- Reviewers: Evan Martinez (profiling), Lina Becker (SRE)
- Operational owner for playbook execution: runtime-oncall@redwood.com

Change history:
- 2025-11-05: Draft created by Priya Shah
- 2026-01-12: Added pairwise interference experiments (reviewer: Evan Martinez)
- 2026-03-02: Published with normalized scoring rubric and safe lab commands

Related artifacts and links:
- Kernel microbenchmarks: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/model-variant-selection-cost-latency-tradeoff-matrix-2024
- Trace storage spec: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/runtime-telemetry-sampling-cost-aware-profiling-2027

End of document.

title: Occupancy and Concurrency Audit Playbook for Serving Runtime
content:
Overview:

This playbook describes a repeatable audit process to assess and remediate GPU occupancy and request concurrency issues in the Redwood serving runtime. It is intended for on-call engineers, performance engineers, and SREs responsible for multi-tenant inference pools and kernel scheduler tuning. The goal is to detect pathological occupancy/concurrency patterns early, quantify their impact on latency/cost, and prescribe targeted mitigations.

Why this matters:

- Low GPU occupancy (SM utilization) or poor warp efficiency increases per-token cost and can drastically raise tail latency for short requests.
- Excessive concurrency without appropriate kernel crediting can cause kernel contention, eviction churn, and KV-cache thrash.
- Multi-tenant pools and dynamic batching increase the surface area for occupancy anomalies; automated audits help prevent regressions when we change kernel mappers, quantization profiles, or shard placement rules.

Scope and audience:

- Scope: GPUs used by Redwood-hosted runtime (heterogeneous pools), Dedicated clusters on RDW, and Private deployment models where we operate the inference stack.
- Audience: runtime performance team, serving runtime owners, SRE, release engineers.

Key concepts and metrics (short primer):

- SM Occupancy: fraction of Streaming Multiprocessor compute capacity active. Monitored with nvidia-smi dmon/ DCGM metric: gpu_sm_active and nvprof metrics like sm_efficiency.
- Warp Efficiency: fraction of executed threads performing useful work (warp_execution_efficiency).
- GPU Active Time / Kernel Time: total kernel execution time versus idle/wait time.
- CUDA Stream Utilization: concurrency of CUDA streams per process (useful for kernel overlap).
- Kernel Queue Length: number of enqueued kernels waiting execution per GPU.
- Token-per-second per-GPU and per-request token latency: application-visible metrics correlated with kernel metrics.

Acceptance thresholds (operational guidance):

- Avg SM Occupancy: target 30%–80% depending on model size. Small models (<=4B) should aim for >45% with batching; large models (>=70B) may be 20%–40% due to register pressure.
- Warp Efficiency: target >70%; investigate below 60%.
- Kernel Queue Length (p95): <= 8 for latency SLOs; if >16, treat as congestion.
- Kernel Preemption Events: zero preferred; any spike should be investigated.

Audit cadence and triggers:

- Scheduled audit: weekly automated run across production pools.
- Release-triggered audit: run after kernel mapper, quantization, or scheduler changes.
- Incident-triggered audit: triggered by sustained SLO degradation (p95 latency increase >20% or error spike).

Automated data collection (what to gather):

1) DCGM / Prometheus exporter snapshots for each GPU: sm_efficiency, sm_active, gpu_util, mem_used, sm_clock, power.
2) Kernel-level traces (perfetto / CUPTI) sampled for 60s across representative nodes.
3) Per-request runtime traces (trace-id keyed) including batch size, sequence length, model variant, and scheduling priority.
4) Kernel queue metrics and kernel metadata (kernel name, duration, per-kernel average latency).
5) KV-cache hit/miss rates and warmup time per request shard.
6) System-level metrics: NUMA statistics, PCIe throughput, nvlink/ nvlink errors.

How to run an audit (step-by-step):

1. Kick off collection:
   - Run the automated collector job (prod-audit-collector) for the target pool. CLI: 

   ```bash
   ./tools/profiler/run-audit --pool gpu-pool-2 --duration 60s --out /tmp/audit-gpu-pool-2.json
   ```

   - Ensure collector captures DCGM metrics at 250ms granularity and samples 1 CUPTI trace per physical GPU.

2. Baseline correlation (automated):
   - Run the baseline comparator tool to correlate p95 latency and per-GPU sm_efficiency. Example: 

   ```bash
   ./tools/perf/compare-baseline --current /tmp/audit-gpu-pool-2.json --baseline s3://perf-baselines/gpu-pool-2/2026-01-01.json
   ```

   - Output: CSV with columns (metric, current_p50, current_p95, baseline_p95, relative_change).

3. High-level triage (manual):
   - Open the generated dashboard link from the collector output. Inspect: SM occupancy heatmap, kernel queue length timeseries, per-model aggregated warp efficiency.
   - If p95 latency correlates with occupancy drop (sm_efficiency falls while kernel queue increases), flag as kernel contention.

4. Deep dive: kernel-level analysis:
   - Identify top 5 kernels by total time in the trace. Use the kernel map to attribute kernels to model layers (attention, MLP, softmax).
   - For each kernel, inspect duration distribution, occupancy-dependent latency (plot duration vs active warps).
   - Look for kernels with large variance or heavy tail (p99 > 4x median). Those are primary candidates for micro-optimization or fallback tuning.

5. Concurrency accounting check:
   - Verify kernel-credit accounting logs to ensure per-request credit consumption matches runtime expectations. Query: 

   ```promql
   sum by (pool) (increase(kernel_credit_consumed_total[5m]))
   ```

   - If observed concurrency > configured_max_concurrency by >20%, investigate admission control or credit leak bugs.

6. KV-cache correlation:
   - Join per-request latency with KV-cache hit rate. A simultaneous drop in hit-rate and SM occupancy often indicates aggressive eviction policies during high concurrency.

7. NUMA/PCIe check:
   - If occupancy low but GPU util high and kernel times are fragmented, inspect NUMA binding and transfer stalls. Use `numactl --hardware` and `perf record` to validate.

Automated remediation recommendations (ordered):

1) Apply immediate throttling: reduce admission concurrency for the affected model/pool by 20% (fast rollback).
2) Switch to a compatible lower-parallel kernel variant (runtime supports alternative kernel variants labeled fast-path, conservative).
3) Increase batching window for short-sequence workloads for 30s to evaluate impact.
4) Adjust kernel mapper hints to prefer fewer concurrent small kernels on the same GPU (see kernel mapper tuning snippet below).

Kernel mapper tuning example (config snippet):

- purpose: prefer sequential execution for kernels with low occupancy and high variance
- config keys (YAML):

  kernel_mapper:
    prioritize_small_kernel_serialization: true
    small_kernel_threshold_ms: 1.5
    concurrency_grouping_window_ms: 12
    backpressure_on_queue_length: 10

Metrics and dashboard recipes (Grafana/PromQL examples):

- SM occupancy heatmap: avg(sm_efficiency) by (gpu_id) over 5m
- Kernel queue alarm: (max_over_time(kernel_queue_length[5m]) > 12)
- Warp inefficiency alert (event): increase(warp_stall_cycles_total[5m]) / increase(instruction_issued_total[5m]) > 0.35
- Correlation panel: overlay p95(request_latency) with 1 - avg(sm_efficiency) (both normalized) to surface inverse relationships.

Incident play examples (short):

- Symptom: sudden p95 spike for short-text generation where throughput hasn't changed.
  Triage: run audit collector for 60s; find that kernel queue length jumped and sm_efficiency dropped to 18% on two GPUs.
  Remediation: throttle concurrency for model route, apply kernel mapper change to serialize small kernels. Result: p95 restored within 3 minutes.

- Symptom: slow cold-start for mini-batches after rollout of a quantized kernel.
  Triage: KV-cache miss surge and multiple small kernels with long tail.
  Remediation: revert to previous kernel variant for the model, schedule controlled rollout with traffic shadowing.

Decision criteria matrix (when to change runtime configs vs when to open a kernel engineering ticket):

- Quick config change (runtime): if issue is resolved by admission control, mapper hint flips, or batch-window adjustments and change reduces p95 by >15% in canary.
- Kernel engineering ticket: if top kernel p99 > 3x median and variance does not change with concurrency reduction or mapper hints, escalate to kernel team with trace bundle.

Ownership and escalation paths:

- Primary: serving-runtime-performance@redwood.internal (team lead: Priya Natarajan).
- Kernel engineering: kernel-core@redwood.internal (owner: Diego Morales).
- Oncall escalation: page SRE oncall if SLO breached after the second remediation step.

Artifacts to attach to the audit ticket:

- audit collector JSON and generated dashboard link
- top-5 kernel trace bundle (CUPTI/Perfetto) with timestamped ranges
- per-request trace subset (10–100 representative trace ids) with correlated KV-cache and scheduler decisions

Rollback playbook (if remediation regresses production):

1) Immediately revert the admission control change via runtime CLI: `runtimectl set-concurrency --pool <pool> --value <previous>`
2) Revert kernel mapper config using config rollback tag in S3 and trigger a config reload: `runtimectl reload-config --tag <previous-tag>`
3) If kernel variant was replaced, rotate traffic back to previous variant and monitor p95 for 10 minutes.

Checklist for a good audit report (what we expect in the ticket):

- Executive summary (one paragraph): impact, affected pools/models, summary of root cause.
- Data appendix: top graphs and a CSV of key metrics.
- Remediation applied and measurable effect (before/after numbers).
- Recommendations (short-term / long-term).
- Owner and ETA for follow-up (if kernel ticket created).

Related pages:

- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/adaptive-kernel-mapper-and-scaling-playbook-2026
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/numa-aware-shard-placement-eviction-playbook-2026
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/runtime-profiling-playbook-guidelines-2025
