- Reproduce against debug build with extended tracing
- If reproduction fails: request sampled prod replay (timeboxed)
- If reproduction succeeds: run git-bisect on kernel commits and mark candidate commit
- Patch, run probes, and submit fix with perf regression note

ownership-and-escalation:
Primary owners: eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling (on-call rotation). Secondary: eng-platform (capacity & infra), eng-sre (telemetry & incident comms). Escalation path: kernel-oncall -> runtime-arch -> eng-sre manager -> CTO on persistent high-severity regression. Contact aliases: #kernel-oncall, runtime-arch@redwood.com

title: Controlled Kernel Perturbation Playbook for Root-Cause Attribution
content:
Overview:

This playbook defines a controlled, repeatable experiment framework for perturbing kernel execution characteristics in the serving runtime to attribute latency, correctness, and fidelity regressions to kernel-level behavior. The goal is to support deterministic root-cause attribution for transient and steady-state regressions while preserving production SLOs and safety.

Who should use this document:
- Runtime engineers and system reliability engineers performing profiling or root-cause analysis.
- Kernel and scheduler owners validating changes to the kernel mapper, handoff, or fallback paths.
- Release engineers planning safety-guarded kernel rollouts.

Scope and non-goals:
- Scope: controlled perturbations of kernel latency, memory pressure injection, path toggles (fast-path vs fallback), and queue shaping for a selected tenant or shadow channel. Includes tooling, telemetry, safety checks, and interpretation heuristics.
- Non-goals: mass disruptive chaos testing at fleet scale (see accelerator-chaos playbook for those experiments); automated mutation testing of model weights.

Safety and approval checklist (required before any perturbation in a shared environment):
1) Perturbation run owner assigned and on-call notified.
2) Target workload scoped to a shadow/traffic-mirroring channel or single non-customer tenant.
3) SLA gate verified: choose experiments that guarantee p99 latency budget headroom >= 40% or use canary lane.
4) Runbook and rollback plan reviewed with SRE team.
5) Telemetry targets (metrics and dashboards) instrumented and smoke-tested.
6) Experiment window and blast radius (nodes, partitions) declared in the change ticket.
7) Emergency kill switch validated (runtime-dispatcher circuit-breaker to mute perturbation).

Ownership and key contacts:
- Playbook owner: Leah Park (runtime profiling)
- Kernel-scheduler SME: Marco Ruiz
- SRE safety lead: Priya Desai
- On-call channel: #runtime-sre

Experiment types and intent:
- Latency-injection (per-kernel): add deterministic delay to kernel callbacks to measure amplification to end-to-end p50/p95/p99. Use to identify sensitivity of request shapes to kernel latency.
- Memory-pressure-toggle: artificially reduce available device memory for a kernel to force smaller tiling/eviction paths and observe KV-cache churn.
- Path-forcing (fast-path vs fallback): force selection of fallback kernel variants to validate correctness and performance regressions.
- Queue-shaping: throttle kernel dispatch rate to validate admission and backpressure propagation to request surface.

Choosing a target and blast radius:
- Default: shadow channel only. For production-like signals, use request mirroring with 0% real traffic impact.
- Canary: single node pool with dedicated GPU slice (recommended when testing path-forcing changes).
- Full tenant: only with explicit business approval and multi-hour maintenance window.

Pre-run checks (automated):
- Confirm p95 and p99 baselines for the target feature and model variant (take latest 6-hour rolling baseline).
- Verify circuit-breaker endpoint responds within 1s.
- Ensure telemetry retention for experiment is at least 7 days to support postmortem.

Step-by-step procedure (example: controlled latency injection to a matrix-mul kernel)
1) Create a change ticket referencing this playbook and assign owner + reviewer.
2) Select target kernel: kernel_agent.matrix_mul_v2 in the kernel registry.
3) Prepare experiment config (example YAML):

experiment_name: controlled-latency-matrix-mul-2026
perturbation:
  type: latency_injection
  kernel_filter: "kernel_agent.matrix_mul_v2"
  delay_ms: 4
  mode: shadow
blast_radius:
  nodes: 3
  tenants: ["shadow-mirror-001"]
window_minutes: 45
rollback_trigger:
  - "p99_request_latency > baseline_p99 * 1.25 for 5m"
  - "error_rate > 0.5% for 2m"

4) Stage the experiment in the staging cluster and validate instrumentation (trace headers, kernel invocation traces).
5) Run a 5m micro-run with delay_ms=1 to validate plumbing and circuit-breaker. Collect traces.
6) Execute the full 45m run. Owner monitors dashboards and latency alerts.
7) If rollback triggers fire, press emergency kill (curl -X POST https://runtime-control.internal/experiments/<id>/kill) and follow rollback notes below.

Telemetry and signals to capture (minimum):
- end_to_end.p50/p95/p99 (per-route, per-model)
- kernel.invocation_count, kernel.latency_ms (histogram), kernel.cpu_ns, kernel.gpu_ns
- kvcache.hit_rate and kvcache.eviction_rate per session cohort
- scheduler.queue_length, scheduler.dispatch_rate, scheduler.preemptions
- error_rate (per-route and per-kernel) and transient_failure_count
- trace-level causal map: trace->kernel_invocations[] (use correlation_id header)

Interpretation heuristics (quick-reference):
- Amplification factor: if kernel.latency_ms increases by X ms and end_to_end.p99 increases by > 5*X, investigate request fanout and sequential kernel dependency chains.
- Memory-pressure signature: rising kernel.eviction_rate + kvcache.miss_rate strongly correlates with degraded throughput rather than single-request latency spikes.
- Path-forcing correctness: any non-zero error_rate introduced by forcing fallback indicates latent assumptions in the fast-path-fallback contract. Log stack traces and kernel-version hashes.

Data collection artifacts (what to attach to ticket):
- Out-of-band trace bundles (prototype: s3://runtime-dumps/experiments/<id>/traces.tar.gz)
- Kernel telemetry snapshot (JSON) taken at 1-minute resolution for the window
- Snapshot of scheduler state (queues, in-flight tokens, admission counters)
- Experiment config and git commit of kernel code & scheduler policy

Rollback plan and emergency procedures:
- Soft kill: toggle perturbation mode to "monitor-only" (does not alter running kernels). This is first step for non-critical regressions.
- Hard kill: runtime-control emergency kill endpoint to remove perturbation agent hooks and restore standard kernel selection path.
- Node remediation: if node-level resource exhaustion observed, cordon and drain the node, and trigger reprovisioning per standard runbook: /eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/node-reprovisioning-manual.
- Post-rollback: capture full telemetry for 30 minutes and compare to pre-run baseline before re-attempting a modified experiment.

Postmortem structure (required on any non-trivial result):
1) Summary: short statement of what was tested and main outcome.
2) Evidence: telemetry snapshots, top traces, kernel invocation timelines.
3) Root cause hypothesis and alternative hypotheses.
4) Action items and owners (code fixes, scheduler policy changes, test additions).
5) Roll-forward plan (if safe) or revert plan.

Common pitfalls and mitigations:
- Pitfall: running perturbations directly on production frontends. Mitigation: always use mirrored/shadow channels unless explicit approval.
- Pitfall: not correlating kernel-version hashes with telemetry. Mitigation: include build_id in kernel telemetry headers.
- Pitfall: choosing too-large blast radius. Mitigation: start single-node, single-tenant then scale.

Sample CLI and quick commands:
# list running experiments
$ runtime-experiments list --env=staging

# kill experiment (emergency)
$ curl -X POST https://runtime-control.internal/experiments/controlled-latency-matrix-mul-2026/kill -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'

# fetch kernel telemetry slice for experiment id
$ runtime-inspect kernel-telemetry --experiment-id=controlled-latency-matrix-mul-2026 --since=2026-01-12T15:00:00Z --output=telemetry.json

Recommended dashboards and queries:
- kernel.latency_ms{kernel="matrix_mul_v2"} by (node) -> heatmap across nodes
- top_traces_with_kernel("matrix_mul_v2", p99) -> list of traces with highest p99 contribution
- scheduler.queue_length_over_time / scheduler.dispatch_rate: look for sustained divergence when perturbation starts

Required tests before merging kernel-level changes:
- Unit-level deterministic kernel tests with latency bounds and flakiness thresholds documented in the test harness.
- Integration-level perturbation run in staging using this playbook for each scheduler or kernel change that touches decision logic.
- A documented canary matrix (node pool x model variant) must be exercised for at least 6 hours with traffic mirroring.

Appendix A — Example experiment log excerpt:
[2026-01-12T16:02:00Z] experiment=start id=controlled-latency-matrix-mul-2026 owner=leah.
[2026-01-12T16:10:00Z] kernel.matrix_mul_v2 delay_ms=4 applied to nodes: gnode-12,gnode-13,gnode-14
[2026-01-12T16:18:00Z] alert: end_to_end.p99 increased 18% vs baseline_p99 -> owner notified
[2026-01-12T16:20:00Z] action: soft-kill -> perturbation set to monitor-only
[2026-01-12T16:21:30Z] rollback: hard-kill executed; telemetry shows p99 returned to baseline within 3m

Appendix B — Minimal experiment configuration schema (table):
| field | type | required | notes |
| experiment_name | string | yes | unique identifier for run |
| perturbation.type | enum | yes | one of {latency_injection, memory_pressure, path_forcing, queue_shaping} |
| kernel_filter | string | yes | glob or exact kernel name |
| delay_ms | int | conditional | only for latency_injection |
| mode | enum | yes | one of {shadow, canary, full} |
| blast_radius.nodes | list[string] | yes | target nodes |
| rollback_trigger | list[string] | yes | boolean expressions on metrics |

Related reading and references:
- kernel-fuzz-suite and accelerator-chaos playbooks (profiling-playbook index)
- runtime-control API spec (internal)
- scheduler-observability-contract and kernel-handshake docs for contract obligations

Change history:
- 2026-01-12: initial draft and staging validation.
- 2026-02-18: added rollback triggers and sample CLI commands after a staging incident test.

If you have questions or need the playbook adapted for a third-party accelerator integration, contact the playbook owner or raise a ticket in #runtime-sre.

title: Shadow-channel Experimentation Framework and Telemetry Contract
content:
Summary

This document defines Redwood's Shadow-channel Experimentation Framework (SEF) and the accompanying telemetry contract used to run non-invasive experiments across the serving runtime. SEF lets engineers validate scheduler and kernel changes, batching strategies, and caching heuristics by mirroring live requests into an isolated execution path (the shadow channel) without affecting production responses.

Goals
- Enable high-confidence performance and correctness experiments using live traffic.
- Standardize telemetry so experiment results are comparable across kernels, schedulers, and topologies.
- Provide an operator-safe runbook for starting, observing, and rolling back experiments.

Non-goals
- SEF is not a canary rollout mechanism for user-facing traffic (use the rollout service for canaries).
- SEF does not modify customer-facing outputs; quality validation must use offline evals or compare-only decoders.

When to use SEF
1. Kernel-level performance patches that require realistic traffic shaping.
2. Scheduler policy changes impacting admission, preemption, or slot assignment.
3. KV cache prefetch/hint algorithms where hit/miss patterns are critical.
4. New batching heuristics or continuous-batching changes.

Architecture Overview

SEF has three main logical components: Mirror, Shadow Executor, and Aggregation/Verifier.
- Mirror (mirror-proxy): intercepts an incoming request and clones a deterministic copy of the request context and tokens. Mirrors run in the request ingress plane and annotate requests with a correlation_id.
- Shadow Executor (shadow-exec): a sandboxed runtime instance (container-level isolation) that consumes mirrored traffic. Shadow-exec may load alternative kernels, scheduler flags, or quantization profiles. It returns telemetry only; outputs are discarded or stored in a private experiment index.
- Aggregation/Verifier (exp-agg): aggregates shadow telemetry, computes experiment metrics (latency delta, kernel time, queue time, kvcache hit breakdown, token throughput), and performs quality checks. exp-agg produces a report stored in the experiments index and notifies Slack/Confluence hooks.

Key properties
- Non-intrusive: shadow paths must not alter production responses or resource quotas used for live serving.
- Budgeted: experiments must be assigned a budget (tokens/sec or % of cluster capacity). If the shadow budget is exceeded, the mirror-proxy drops mirrored traffic for that experiment.
- Deterministic correlation: all mirrored requests share a correlation_id prefix to link production and shadow telemetry.

Telemetry Contract (required fields)
Every shadow-exec must emit the following fields for each mirrored request (JSON lines to exp-agg):
- correlation_id: string (prefix links to production request)
- experiment_id: string
- timestamp_utc: iso8601 string
- stage_durations_ms: list (ingress, queue, kernel_dispatch, kernel_exec, decoder, kvcache_lookup) encoded as CSV of numbers
- kernel_signature: string (kernel name + variant + commit)
- scheduler_profile: string (policy name + profile hash)
- kvcache_stats: csv (hits, misses, prefetches, eviction_count)
- cpu_usec: integer
- gpu_usec: integer
- memory_bytes: integer
- status: ok | exec_error | resource_throttled | timed_out
- sampled_trace_id: optional string (links to full trace in tracing system)

Metric definitions (computed by exp-agg)
- shadow_p95_latency_ms: 95th percentile of end-to-end shadow latency
- delta_p95_ms: shadow_p95 - prod_p95 (linked by correlation_id)
- kernel_time_ratio: kernel_exec / end_to_end
- kv_hit_rate: hits / (hits + misses)
- resource_overhead_percent: (gpu_usec + cpu_usec equivalent) / prod_resource_usage

SLO and safety thresholds for experiments
- Max allowed delta_p95_ms: +5ms for latency-sensitive tiers, +20ms for best-effort experiments. Exceeding triggers automatic suspension.
- Max resource overhead percent: 25% (across aggregate traffic).
- Error budget for exec_error: 0.2% of mirrored requests per hour.

Experiment lifecycle (operator steps)
1. Create experiment metadata in experiments-service with experiment_id, owner, target clusters, budget (tokens/sec or %), and risk classification (low/medium/high).
2. Push experiment config to mirror-proxy: rdinfer-mirrorctl create --id <experiment_id> --budget 50rps --target shadow-cluster:shadow-v2 --policy sample:1/1000
3. Validate mirror can deliver minimal load by enabling a 0.1% sample on a low-traffic route.
4. Start shadow-exec job: k8s apply -f shadow-exec-<experiment_id>.yaml. Shadow-exec must run with nodeSelector=isolated-exec and resource limits set to the budgeted rate.
5. Wait for stable telemetry for 30 minutes. Run exp-agg quick-check: exp-agg check --experiment <id> --metrics delta_p95_ms,kernel_time_ratio,kv_hit_rate
6. Run benchmark harness (see Benchmark protocol below) or replay stored requests for reproducibility.
7. If metrics are within thresholds, scale up to the target budget incrementally (x2 every 30m). Monitor SLOs and resource overhead.
8. Conclude experiment and archive report. For negative results, follow the Rollback and postmortem procedure.

Operator runbook (quick actions)
- Suspend experiment: rdinfer-mirrorctl suspend --id <experiment_id>
- Resume experiment: rdinfer-mirrorctl resume --id <experiment_id>
- Emergency stop (immediate): rdinfer-mirrorctl kill --id <experiment_id> (drops mirror; does not delete artifacts)
- Collect traces for a sample: exp-agg collect-traces --experiment <id> --sample 100

Benchmark protocol (for synthetic verification)
Purpose: ensure shadow-exec results align with synthetic bench suite. Use the runtime benchmarking harness with mirrored request signatures.
Steps:
1. Rehydrate a 1-hour traffic window (production) into the benchmark harness: benchctl replay --source s3://prod-traces/2026-01-15/route-X --realtime=false --rate-scale 1.0 --target shadow-exec:5000
2. Run with the kernel variant under test and capture the same telemetry contract.
3. Compare bench outputs to exp-agg aggregated metrics using bench-compare: bench-compare --baseline prod --candidate shadow --metrics delta_p95_ms,kernel_time_ratio
Acceptance criteria:
- delta_p95_ms within the SLO defined above
- kernel_time_ratio difference < 10%
- no new exec_error class > 0.05%

Safety and resource isolation patterns
- Shadow-exec pods must be scheduled onto a dedicated taint:isolation=true node pool to prevent noisy neighbor effects. Use tolerations only for exp operator service account.
- ResourceLimits on shadow-exec pods: cpu=4, memory=16Gi, gpu=1 (or set GPU quota via device plugin).
- Throttling: mirror-proxy enforces an absolute max RPS per experiment to avoid runaway costs. Defaults: 100rps per experiment in hosted clusters.

Data retention and privacy
- Shadow payloads must strip PII before persisting to experiment indexes. Use the redact pipeline: redact-agent --policy exp-standard --in /tmp/exp-raw.json --out /tmp/exp-redacted.json
- Experiment telemetry retention: 90 days. Aggregated reports archived indefinitely.

Rollbacks and postmortem
- If an experiment breaches thresholds, suspend mirror immediately and mark experiment status=halted.
- Capture a forensics bundle: exp-agg bundle --id <experiment_id> --output /tmp/forensics.tar.gz
- Create an incident with severity matched to risk_classification. Notify owners and reviewers.

Appendix A: Example shadow-exec manifest (Kubernetes)
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: shadow-exec-<experiment_id>
  labels:
    app: shadow-exec
    experiment: "<experiment_id>"
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: shadow-exec
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: shadow-exec
    spec:
      nodeSelector:
        node-pool: shadow-isolated
      tolerations:
      - key: "isolation"
        operator: "Equal"
        value: "true"
        effect: "NoSchedule"
      containers:
      - name: shadow-exec
        image: rdinfer/shadow-exec:stable-2026-01
        resources:
          limits:
            cpu: "4"
            memory: "16Gi"
            nvidia.com/gpu: "1"
        env:
        - name: EXPERIMENT_ID
          value: "<experiment_id>"
---

Appendix B: Minimal exp-agg check output (JSON lines)
{"experiment_id":"exp-abc123", "metric":"delta_p95_ms", "value": 3.8, "threshold": 5.0}
{"experiment_id":"exp-abc123", "metric":"kernel_time_ratio", "value": 0.62}

Ownership and contacts
- Owners: eng-serving-runtime (pager: #infra-runtime-oncall)
- Experiment operator: Maya Chen (maya@redwood.ai)
- Observability reviewer: Diego Alvarez (diego@redwood.ai)

Related pages and references
- See also: runtime-execution-safety-matrix, kernel-handoff-and-decision-tracing-manual, and the benchmarking suite guide.

Revision history
- 2025-09-30: Draft created by Maya Chen.
- 2025-12-12: Added telemetry fields and safety thresholds (reviewer: Rina Patel).
- 2026-01-18: Incorporated exp-agg quick-check CLI and kube manifest example.

Notes
- This framework is under active iteration. Any changes to the telemetry contract must be coordinated with observability and oncall at least 2 weeks before rollout.

title: Runtime Observability Sleuthing and Probing Toolkit
content:
Overview

This page documents the toolkit, operational patterns, and safe procedures used by runtime engineers to perform rapid sleuthing (hypothesis-driven triage) and non-disruptive probing of the serving runtime in production and pre-production environments. The guidance balances signal fidelity with cost and safety constraints and provides concrete probe recipes, a sampling governor configuration, escalation paths, and ownership.

Summary / intent
- Goal: reduce mean-time-to-detect and mean-time-to-resolve for latency, fidelity, and kernel-related regressions while containing overhead to a safe telemetry budget.
- Audience: runtime oncall, profiling team, SRE, and feature owners who need to instrument kernels/scheduler and run targeted experiments.
- Non-goal: exhaustive academic profiling — this is a pragmatic, ops-first playbook for production-safe investigation.

Signal taxonomy (quick reference)
1) Traces: end-to-end request streams with kernel handoffs annotated. Use for causal chain reconstruction and tail-latency attribution.
2) Microprobes: high-frequency short-duration kernel timings (GPU dispatch, memcpy, kernel enqueue latency). Use for kernel regressions and scheduler jitter.
3) Counters & gauges: queue lengths, admission tokens, KV-cache hit rates, busy GPU percent, slot credits. Use for capacity and trend analysis.
4) Synthetic samples: replayed request surface (shadow) to reproduce behavior without impacting live traffic.

Sleuthing checklist (initial 10-minute triage)
1. Confirm symptom and scope: aggregate error/latency dashboards, which tenants/routes affected, and start time.
2. Correlate with deployments and config changes (canary rollouts, kernel changes, model swaps) using the deployment timeline.
3. Check kernel and scheduler health streams: kernel-failure-rate, kernel-queueing-latency, enqueue-to-start gap.
4. Validate resource & thermal indicators: GPU utilization, power capping events, PCIe/NVLink errors.
5. If the above are inconclusive, enable targeted microprobes (see Probe recipes).

Safe probing principles
- Principle 1: Budget first. Probes must respect the tracing budget (default 0.05% of total request CPU and < 1% of GPU extra work for a cohort).
- Principle 2: Non-blocking. Probes should not alter scheduling or kernel behaviour — use passive sampling and read-only metrics where possible.
- Principle 3: Scoped rollouts. Apply probes to a single small cohort (shadow or 0.5–2% of production tenants) and observe for 30–90 minutes before scaling.
- Principle 4: Fail-open. Add circuit-breaker guardrails: if P99 latency increases by > 10% or error rates double in the probed cohort, automatically disable the probing flag.

Probe recipes (practical, copy-paste)
1) Microprobe: kernel enqueue-to-start distribution - Purpose: detect scheduling stalls and handoff jitter - Target: one node in the affected pod group or a dedicated canary - Steps:
   1. Create feature flag "microprobe.enq_start" with cohort 0.5%.
   2. Configure runtime to emit microprobe events with 200ns timestamp resolution for each kernel enqueue and dispatch.
   3. Sampling: 1-in-N request sampling with N = 250 by default (adjust down to 50 for an active canary).
   4. Collect for 30 minutes and generate a heatmap of enqueue->start latency by kernel type.
   5. If enqueue->start P99 > 3x baseline, escalate and increase sampling to 1-in-25 for one node for 10 minutes.

2) Trace enrichment: correlated trace + KV-cache delta - Purpose: connect cache warmup/fidelity issues to end-to-end latency - Steps:
   1. Enable trace-enrichment flag for the affected route.
   2. For sampled traces, attach KV-cache hit/miss sequence and cache size at request start.
   3. Use the trace-joiner job to merge microprobe events with trace spans post-collection.
   4. Run the synthesized trace analysis to find patterns where cache miss bursts precede tail latency.

3) Shadow replay burst: safe synthetic stress - Purpose: reproduce a peaky failure surface without saturating live capacity - Steps:
   1. Mirror 0.5% of production traffic to a shadow cluster with strict admission caps (20% of node CPU/GPU used by shadow).
   2. Run the same request ordering but pause prefixes at the scheduler to test pre-emption and kernel churn.
   3. Capture both runtime-level telemetry and kernel microprobes.

Sampling governor and config (copy into config manifest)
| key | default | unit | meaning | safe bounds |
| sampling.global_rate | 0.0005 | fraction | fraction of total requests traced | 1e-6 .. 0.01 |
| sampling.microprobe_strategy | periodic | string | selection approach: periodic | periodic|adaptive|fingerprint |
| sampling.max_additional_cpu_pct | 0.05 | fraction | extra CPU budget for probes | 0.0 .. 0.1 |
| sampling.node_quota | 100 | items/s | per-node microprobe quota | 10 .. 1000 |

Example YAML snippet

sampling:
  global_rate: 0.0005          # 0.05% of requests
  microprobe_strategy: adaptive
  max_additional_cpu_pct: 0.05
  node_quota: 100

Telemetry retention & cost controls
- Keep high-resolution microprobe traces for 7 days by default. Aggregate rollups (histograms, heatmaps) are preserved for 90 days.
- If monthly trace ingestion exceeds 120% of budget, automatic downsampling triggers: reduce global_rate by 2x and notify owners.

Investigation playbook (step-by-step, 60–120 minutes)
1. Kickoff: capture hypothesis and assign a lead (Slack #runtime-oncall).
2. Snapshot: export dashboards, last 6 hours of traces, deployment timeline, and kernel-change list.
3. Execute targeted probes: enable "microprobe.enq_start" at cohort 0.5% and trace-enrich for the route.
4. Collect: wait 30–60 minutes or until 5–10k sampled events.
5. Analyze: run enqueue histograms, span waterfall visualizations, and correlate with KV-cache deltas.
6. Decide: if a kernel or scheduler regression identified, escalate to Kernel Team and open an investigation ticket with priority P1/P2 depending on impact.
7. Remediate & validate: apply rollback or hotfix, reduce probe cohort to 0.1% and observe for 60 minutes.

Escalation & ownership
- First responder: runtime-oncall (rotation).
- Profiler lead: assigned profiling-engineer on call (see team roster).
- Kernel owner: Kernel Team (kernel@redwood.ai).
- SLA triggers:
  - P99 latency increase > 25% across > 3 routes -> P0 incident page and cross-team warroom.
  - Reproducible regression localized to kernel variant -> open Kernel Team ticket and link telemetry snapshots.

Operational safety automations (what we enable)
- Automatic guardrail: probe circuit-breaker reacts to cohort latency signal and disables sampled flags.
- Budget monitor: monthly telemetry budget check with automated rate adjustments.
- Canary escalation: if a canary probe shows adverse change, the system auto-rolls to previous kernel variant for that canary.

Query and CLI examples
- Collect traces from timeframe (example CLI):
  rwi trace fetch --from 2026-02-10T02:00Z --to 2026-02-10T03:30Z --route /v1/generate --output traces.json

- Example microprobe event (JSON line):
  {"ts":1623345623123456789,"node":"node-15","kernel":"matmul_v2","phase":"enqueue","lat_ns":215}

- Join traces and microprobes (post-processing):
  python tools/join_traces_microprobes.py --traces traces.json --microprobes mp.json --out joined.json

Safety checklist before enabling a probe in production
1. Confirm owner and oncall contact listed.
2. Confirm cohort size, node quotas, and budget allowance in telemetry dashboard.
3. Define failure thresholds and circuit-breaker settings.
4. Add experiment to the experiment registry with start/stop times and intended metric signals.

Related pages and templates
- Runtime profiling playbook (template) — use the experiment template to register runs.
- Kernel rollout checklist — follow before toggling kernel variants.
- Incident runbook: runtime incident playbook (link to runbooks directory).

Appendix: quick heuristics
- If P99 enqueue->start spikes but raw kernel durations remain stable, suspect scheduler contention or admission-tokens scarcity.
- If kernel durations increase across the board, prioritize kernel variant rollback and test on replayed synthetic traffic.
- If only certain models/routes show degradation, focus on KV-cache and model-variant selection metrics.

Contacts & maintenance
- Doc owner: Marina Alvarez (marina@redwood.ai) — update cadence: quarterly or after any major telemetry change.
- Reviewers: Ethan Brooks, Priya Nair.

Change log
- 2025-11-02: created (initial cookbook).
- 2026-02-15: added sampling governor table, YAML examples, and automated safety checklist.

title: Perf Suite Profiling Playbook (Q1 2026 Baseline)
content:
## Purpose
This playbook describes how to reproduce a perf-suite result and capture the artifacts needed to attribute changes (runtime, scheduler, kernels, environment). It is intended for:
- Investigating perf-canary regressions (PR-level, nightly, or release-branch).
- Explaining deltas between baseline runs (Q1 2026 “golden” anchor) and candidate changes.
- Producing consistent traces/logs that can be shared across Runtime, Kernels, and SRE.

This page focuses on *how to profile* (traces, kernel timelines, scheduler logs) rather than *what workloads to run*. For workload definitions and required metrics, see the baseline plan and representative suite pages.

---

## What “good” looks like (minimum artifact set)
For any investigated run, attach or link the following artifacts (even if you also have dashboards):
1) Run manifest JSON (per ADR-0172) with *all* environment capture enabled.
2) Results JSON/CSV (p50/p95/p99 TTFT, TPOT, throughput, plus variance statistics if available).
3) Scheduler log bundle:
   - Queue wait time distribution
   - Batch assembly time distribution
   - Batch size histogram
   - Load-shed/drop counters (if any)
   - Correlation IDs / request IDs for trace alignment
4) Kernel selection debug dump (sampled) with fallback reasons (if any).
5) Nsight Systems (nsys) trace for at least one representative interval.
6) Optional but recommended: Nsight Compute (ncu) capture for the top 1–3 kernels (only when kernel-level regression is suspected).

---

## Measurement boundaries (so traces match reported metrics)
To avoid “apples to oranges,” ensure the profiling run uses the same boundaries as the perf suite metrics:
- **TTFT (Time To First Token)**: measured at the server boundary: request admitted → first token emitted to server streaming layer. Excludes client read/parse time.
- **TPOT (Time Per Output Token)**: measured at the server boundary for decode tokens only. Excludes prefill; excludes client overhead.
- **Throughput**: server-side tokens/sec or requests/sec depending on endpoint mode.

If you must deviate (e.g., reproducing a customer report with client-side timings), label the run explicitly as “client-inclusive” and do not compare to baseline dashboards without adjustment.

---

## Preconditions / Setup checklist
### A. Confirm you are targeting the same baseline anchor
Before profiling, confirm the baseline anchor for comparison:
- Runtime git SHA / tag (baseline)
- Benchmark harness version
- Model revision (weights + tokenizer)
- Scheduler profile and kernel-selection ruleset
- Region and GPU SKU

If you are unsure which build is the Q1 baseline anchor, check the baseline freeze thread and the baseline run tracker.

### B. Reduce variance (required for attribution)
These steps are required for “baseline-comparable” profiling runs:
1) Use a dedicated benchmarking node (no co-tenancy).
2) Lock GPU application clocks where permitted by fleet policy.
3) Pin CPU governor to performance.
4) Ensure consistent container image and driver/CUDA versions.
5) Run standardized warmup (see below).

If any variance-reduction step cannot be applied, mark the run as “non-baseline-comparable” in the run label and expect higher noise.

### C. Warmup standard (required)
Warmup reduces first-run variance from model load, JIT/compilation caches, allocator behavior, and KV cache initialization.
- Warmup duration: 3–5 minutes per (model, GPU, workload mode)
- Warmup workload: same request shape as the measured workload, but with lower concurrency
- Discard warmup metrics; only analyze traces taken after warmup completes

---

## Run labeling and naming conventions
Consistent naming is required so engineers can drill down from dashboard → manifest → traces.

### Run ID format
Use the following run_id format (single line, no spaces):
`perfq1_2026/<workload>/<model>/<region>/<gpu>/<runtime_sha>/<harness_ver>/<timestamp_utc>/<run_variant>`

Examples:
- `perfq1_2026/chat_streaming/llama3_1_70b/us-east/h100/7c3a91f/v1.8.2/2026-02-03T21-14-08Z/cold_cache`
- `perfq1_2026/long_prefill/qwen2_5_72b/eu-west/a100/7c3a91f/v1.8.2/2026-02-03T23-40-51Z/warm_cache`

### Required run_variant tags
Include at least these tags as part of the run_variant suffix:
- `cold_cache` or `warm_cache` (we report both; do not mix)
- `baseline_comparable` or `non_baseline_comparable`

Optional tags (use when relevant):
- `kernel_pin_<name>` (if pinning a kernel)
- `scheduler_override_<name>` (if changing scheduler knobs)
- `client_inclusive` (only if using client-side TTFT)

---

## Step-by-step: reproduce a perf suite run with profiling enabled
> The exact CLI flags may vary by harness version; the intent is to capture the same artifact set. If a flag below doesn’t exist in your harness build, file an issue in benchmark-lab and note it in the run summary.

### 1) Create (or locate) the canonical manifest
1. Start from the manifest used by the baseline run (from dashboards or the run tracker).
2. Copy it and increment `manifest_version` only if required by schema changes.
3. Verify these fields are present and accurate:
   - Model identifier + revision
   - Hardware: GPU SKU, GPU count, MIG settings (if any)
   - Region/zone
   - Runtime build SHA + build type
   - Driver/CUDA/Triton versions
   - Scheduler profile name + knobs
   - Kernel selection ruleset version
   - Workload seed and distribution parameters
   - Cache mode (cold/warm)

**Output:** `run_manifest.json`

### 2) Ensure environment capture is on
Enable full environment capture in the harness:
- GPU info (nvidia-smi dump)
- Driver/CUDA versions
- Container image digest
- Host kernel version
- CPU model, NUMA topology summary
- Power/clock settings (if available)

**Sanity check:** ensure the manifest “env” section is populated before you proceed. Missing env capture is a common reason runs can’t be compared later.

### 3) Run standardized warmup
Run warmup using the same workload generator but with reduced concurrency.
- Confirm warmup completes without errors (no OOM, no load-shed unless expected).
- Confirm steady-state GPU utilization.

**Output:** warmup logs (attach if investigating stability issues).

### 4) Run the measured workload and collect scheduler + kernel dumps
Run the measured workload with:
- Scheduler instrumentation enabled (queue wait, batch assembly time, batch size distributions).
- Kernel selection debug dump enabled (sampled is fine; 1–5% sampling is typical).

**Outputs:**
- `results.json` (metrics)
- `scheduler_metrics.jsonl` or equivalent
- `kernel_selection_dump.jsonl`

### 5) Capture an Nsight Systems (nsys) trace (required for attribution)
Capture nsys for a representative steady-state window. Recommendations:
- Trace window: 30–90 seconds during steady state.
- Capture CUDA + NVTX ranges.
- Minimize trace overhead: avoid tracing the full run unless necessary.

Operational guidance:
- If you control the runtime build, ensure key phases emit NVTX ranges:
  - request admitted
  - queue wait
  - batch assembly
  - prefill
  - decode
  - stream flush
- If ranges are missing, still capture the trace; file an issue for missing NVTX markers.

**Output:** `trace.nsys-rep` (or equivalent).

### 6) Optional: Nsight Compute (ncu) for kernel regressions
Use ncu only when:
- A regression correlates with a kernel selection change, or
- nsys shows kernel time dominated by one/few kernels, or
- Kernel-level variance is suspected (e.g., new fused attention path).

Guidelines:
- Profile a single process and short window to keep overhead manageable.
- Focus on top kernels by time; avoid broad “collect everything” profiles.

**Output:** `kernel_profile.ncu-rep` (or equivalent).

### 7) Upload artifacts and link them in the run summary
For every run you investigate, create a short run summary (Confluence comment, Slack triage thread, or ticket) that includes:
- run_id
- manifest link
- results link
- trace links
- “what changed” hypothesis
- whether the run is baseline-comparable

---

## Artifact checklist and where to find them
Attach links (preferred) rather than pasting raw files into Confluence.

Required artifacts:
- Run manifest: `run_manifest.json`
- Results: `results.json` (or results CSV exported by harness)
- Scheduler logs: `scheduler_metrics.jsonl`
- Kernel selection dump: `kernel_selection_dump.jsonl`
- Nsight Systems trace: `trace.nsys-rep`

Recommended context:
- Full runtime logs for the measured window (with correlation IDs)
- GPU clock/thermal readings during the run
- Harness configuration file used to launch

---

## How to align traces with reported metrics
When investigating TTFT p99 or TPOT p99 changes, align the following:
1) Pick a set of request IDs from the tail (p99 cohort) in the results export.
2) Locate those request IDs in scheduler logs:
   - Identify whether tail comes from queue wait, batch assembly, prefill, decode, or stream flush.
3) In the nsys trace, confirm:
   - GPU busy/idle patterns during the tail interval
   - Kernel timeline changes (different kernels, different durations)
   - CPU-side stalls that correlate with queue wait or dispatch
4) Cross-check kernel selection dump:
   - Ensure the expected kernel regime is selected for the sequence length bins
   - Investigate fallback reasons (often the root cause of step-function regressions)

Common interpretations:
- **Higher TTFT p99 with stable throughput:** often queueing/backpressure or batch-assembly changes.
- **Higher TPOT with stable TTFT:** often decode kernel changes, KV cache behavior, or reduced overlap.
- **Lower throughput with higher TTFT:** often saturation, contention, or poor batching efficiency.

---

## Common failure modes and quick triage
### 1) Trace shows client bottleneck (not server)
Symptoms:
- Server-side metrics look stable, but external client TTFT inflates.
Actions:
- Confirm you’re using server-boundary TTFT.
- Ensure streaming pacing is server-driven in the harness (avoid client read throttling).

### 2) Variance too high to attribute
Symptoms:
- Repeated runs differ by more than the regression threshold; p99 swings without code changes.
Actions:
- Verify clock locking and isolation.
- Increase sample size.
- Ensure warmup was performed.
- Check for node-level noise: thermal throttling, background jobs, noisy neighbor.

### 3) Kernel fallback
Symptoms:
- Step-function slowdown at particular sequence lengths.
Actions:
- Inspect kernel selection dump for fallback reasons.
- Compare to the kernel selection matrix for expected regimes.
- Consider pinning the baseline kernel temporarily for diagnosis; label run_variant accordingly.

### 4) Scheduler overload / load-shed
Symptoms:
- Elevated drop counters, timeouts, or long queue wait.
Actions:
- Confirm concurrency targets match workload spec.
- Validate backpressure thresholds (baseline vs overridden).
- Use scheduler metrics to determine whether overload is admission control vs batch assembly.

---

## When to open a ticket vs continue debugging
Open a Linear issue (or escalate to perf triage) when any of the following are true:
- Regression is reproducible in baseline-comparable conditions.
- Kernel selection changed unexpectedly vs matrix.
- Scheduler metrics show a clear regime shift (queue wait, batch size collapse) not explained by workload.
- Trace indicates a new stall in a known critical path (prefill/decode overlap, KV cache operations).

Include in the ticket:
- run_id(s)
- baseline comparison run_id(s)
- links to manifest/results/traces
- suspected component owner (scheduler/kernels/runtime infra)

---

## Owner / Questions
Primary owners:
- Benchmark harness & methodology: Rina Kobayashi, Claire Dubois
- Scheduler instrumentation: Sofia Ivanova
- Kernel selection & kernel timelines: Hiro Tanaka
- SRE benchmarking fleet stability: Sean Gallagher

If you encounter missing instrumentation (NVTX ranges absent, logs not emitted, schema fields missing), file an issue against the appropriate repo and link it in the run summary so the next investigation is faster.

title: Latency fingerprinting and kernel-sensitivity index: measurement and runbook
content:
Overview
--------
This page documents the Latency Fingerprinting methodology and the Kernel-Sensitivity Index (KSI) used by the serving runtime team to:
- Quantify per-kernel impact on P50/P95/P99 for representative text-generation workloads.
- Rank kernels by sensitivity so scheduling and preemption policies can be tuned without risking regressions.
- Provide a reproducible investigation runbook for tail-latency incidents attributed to kernel scheduling or kernel-level regressions.

Audience
--------
Primary: runtime engineers, SREs, performance QA, and release engineers. Secondary: product managers and infra owners who need a traceable cost/latency signal when evaluating kernel rollouts or quantization changes.

Why this matters
-----------------
We observe intermittent tail spikes that correlate with kernel version rollouts and heterogeneous job mixes. High-level SLOs are: P95 < 250ms, P99 < 800ms for short-sequence interactive routes; P50 < 30ms for control-plane fast-paths. Without a per-kernel sensitivity metric, rollouts rely on opaque aggregate telemetry and longer canary windows. KSI accelerates detection and points to a minimal remediation surface.

Definitions
-----------
- Latency fingerprint: a compact profile (histogram summary + contextual tags) describing how a specific workload shape (sequence length distribution, prompt tokenization class, decoding mode) maps to the latency curve observed on a given kernel build.
- Kernel-Sensitivity Index (KSI): a scalar in [-1.0, +1.0] representing the normalized change in tail latency attributable to a kernel compared with a baseline kernel. Positive KSI means the kernel increases latency.
- Workload shape: a tuple of {model_variant, avg_sequence_length, decoding_mode, batch_size_distribution}.

Measurement approach (high level)
--------------------------------
1) Select representative workload shapes from the operational workload catalog (see runtime-sandboxing lab manual). Each shape must include a seed prompt set (N=512) sampled from production anonymized traffic.
2) Run A/B microbenchmarks with deterministic seeds: baseline kernel (K0) vs candidate kernel (K1). Use traffic replay harness with request timing jitter to reflect production concurrency.
3) Collect per-request timing, kernel-name tag, compile flags, GPU occupancy, kernel queue depth, and full trace ids.
4) Compute the latency fingerprint (histogram quantiles plus conditional breakdowns) and the KSI per-shape.
5) Validate significance with bootstrap sampling (95% CI).

Detailed measurement protocol
-----------------------------
Prerequisites:
- Access to performance lab fleet with matching GPU family and driver version.
- Canary traffic replay harness (repo: infra/rl-replay) checked out at commit referenced in related_pages.
- Profiling agent v2.3+ installed (service: runtime-profiler).

Commands (example)
1) Install profiling agent and start harness:

$ git clone https://repo.internal/redwood/infra/rl-replay.git
$ cd rl-replay && ./setup.sh --gpu-family ampere --driver 555.40
$ ./replay --prompts seed_prompts_512.json --concurrency 128 --pacing jittered --profile --out /tmp/replay-output.json

2) Run candidate vs baseline pair with pinned kernel metadata:

$ ./replay --kernel-tag K0 --prompts seed_prompts_512.json --run-id baseline-2026-02-01 --profile --out baseline.json
$ ./replay --kernel-tag K1 --prompts seed_prompts_512.json --run-id candidate-2026-02-01 --profile --out candidate.json

3) Compute latency fingerprint and KSI (python tool):

$ pytools/latency_fingerprint/compute_ksi.py --baseline baseline.json --candidate candidate.json --out ksi_report.json

What the KSI output looks like
----------------------------
- ksi_report.json (example fields, abbreviated):
  - work_shape: "gpt-7b,avg_seq=64,topk=40"
  - ksi_value: "0.23"
  - p95_baseline: "312ms"
  - p95_candidate: "384ms"
  - p99_baseline: "820ms"
  - p99_candidate: "1102ms"
  - bootstrap_ci: "[0.18, 0.29]"
  - significant: "true"

Interpreting KSI
----------------
- KSI > +0.1: kernel is considered high-risk for the shape (investigate and block wide rollouts).
- +0.02 <= KSI <= +0.1: caution — prefer canary gating and extended sampling windows.
- -0.02 <= KSI <= +0.02: neutral — no action required beyond normal canary.
- KSI < -0.02: improvement — note in release notes and consider prioritized rollout.

Kernel-sensitivity matrix (example ASCII table)
------------------------------------------------
Each row is a workload shape; each column is a kernel candidate. Values are KSI (rounded).

| workload \t| kernel_K0 \t| kernel_K1 \t| kernel_K2 \t|
| short-chat \t| 0.00 \t| 0.23 \t| -0.04 \t|
| long-summarize \t| 0.00 \t| 0.07 \t| 0.12 \t|
| embeddings-batch \t| 0.00 \t| -0.02 \t| 0.01 \t|

This matrix is stored in the performance dashboard under: dashboards/ksi/matrix-latest (grafana).

Runbook: Investigate a kernel-attributed tail-latency incident
-------------------------------------------------------------
If an alert fires that correlates to a kernel rollout (alert name: kernel-sensitivity-p99-spike):
1) Triage: capture alert context, affected routes, and kernel-tag from the release event.
   - Owner: oncall-runtime (pager duty: runtime-team)
   - Initial data: timeframe, route(s), kernel-tag, % of traffic using kernel-tag.
2) Pull latency fingerprints for the top 3 affected shapes from the last 24h (dashboard query).
3) Run a quick A/B with the exact baseline and candidate on a staging replica using the seed prompts for the affected routes (10 minutes).
4) If KSI > +0.1 and bootstrap CI excludes 0: escalate to Kernel Rollout WG and block rollout. Create an issue: infra/kernel-rollout-blocker with the KSI report attached.
5) If KSI in (+0.02, +0.1): set temporary rate limit on the candidate kernel in the scheduler (see command below) and increase sampling to 4x for next 4 hours.
6) If neutral: continue monitoring and annotate release notes with the verification run id.
7) Record mitigations and postmortem if incident SLI impact exceeds threshold (sla-impact > 1 hour or customer-facing SLO breaches).

Commands to throttle candidate kernel in scheduler (example)
----------------------------------------------------------
- CLI (schedulerctl) to reduce slot weight for kernel-tag K1:

$ schedulerctl set-weight --kernel K1 --weight 0.2 --reason "ksi-quick-mitigation-2026-02-01"

- Revert:
$ schedulerctl set-weight --kernel K1 --weight 1.0 --reason "revert-ksi-mitigation"

Telemetry and observability contract
-----------------------------------
Every replay and production request must carry these trace tags:
- runtime.kernel_tag
- runtime.kernel_build_id
- runtime.kernel_variant (e.g., fp16-quant, int8-sym)
- runtime.kv_hit (true|false)
- runtime.queue_depth (integer)

Dashboards and alerts to check
-----------------------------
- dashboards/ksi/summary: KSI trend per kernel and workload shape.
- dashboards/latency/route-breakdown: per-route P50/P95/P99.
- alerting/kernel-sensitivity-p99-spike: triggers when KSI-based p99 delta > 150ms and traffic fraction > 5%.
- alerting/kernel-regression-ci-failure: flags if canary KSI exceeds +0.05 over three successive daily runs.

Guidance for release engineers
------------------------------
- Add KSI reports to the kernel candidate artifact in the release bundle under /artifacts/ksi/*.json.
- Require a KSI sign-off (responsible: perf-lead) for kernels with KSI > +0.02 on any production shape before global rollout.
- Use staged rollouts with weight 10% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100% with KSI checks at each gate.

Limitations and known caveats
----------------------------
- Small sample sizes for rare workload shapes inflate CI; prefer combining shapes with the same kernel hotpath.
- KSI attribution is sensitive to queueing effects; ensure queue depth tags are stable across A/B runs.
- Driver or compiler-level nondeterminism (JIT variability) can create noise — repeat runs and follow up with kernel-level deterministic tracing.

Maintenance and ownership
-------------------------
- Owner team: serving-runtime/perf (primary), eng-sre (secondary).
- Dashboard owner: telemetry-team.
- Review cadence: quarterly. Update this doc when the profiling agent or replay harness changes major versions (major semver).

Appendix: Quick checks and YAML example for CI gating
-----------------------------------------------------
YAML snippet (put into kernel-candidate CI job):

pipeline:
  steps:
    - name: run-ksi-smoke
      image: redwood/perf-tools:stable
      commands:
        - pytools/latency_fingerprint/compute_ksi.py --baseline baseline.json --candidate candidate.json --out ksi_report.json
        - if [ $(jq .ksi_value ksi_report.json) \u003e 0.02 ]; then echo "KSI exceeded"; exit 1; fi

If you have questions or need a dedicated pairing session to walk through the replay harness, ping the perf channel (#perf-runtime) or reach out to the doc reviewers listed above.

title: Kernel observability SLAs and profiling cadence
content:
Summary

This page defines a pragmatic, operationally focused observability SLA for the serving runtime kernel layer and specifies a profiling cadence and playbook for keeping kernel regressions visible and remediable. The goal is to ensure kernel-level performance signals (latency, dispatch/backpressure, memory pressure, and kernel success rates) are actionable by oncall and engineering, tied to benchmarking experiments, and budgeted within profiling cost constraints.

Why this matters

- Kernel regressions are the root cause of the majority of hard-to-diagnose tail-latency incidents.
- Observability at the kernel boundary is expensive; we need a cost-aware sampling strategy and a clear schedule so telemetry budgets are predictable.
- Tying profiling to the benchmarking suite and release gates reduces the chance of regressing a deployment unnoticed.

Scope

This document covers the manifest, SLOs, sampling & tracing cadence, profiling runbook, integration points with the benchmarking suite and release process, and known limitations. It applies to:

- The inference runtime kernel components (dispatcher, scheduler, kernel executor, KV cache interface).
- Host-level telemetry produced by kernel shim and GPU-side counters that we ingest via the kernel agent.

Key definitions

- Kernel sample: a single end-to-end kernel execution record (dispatch -> kernel launch -> completion) including timestamps, kernel variant id, request classification, memory footprint, and outcome code.
- Observability SLA: the target for alertable metrics derived from kernel samples (e.g., kernel_p99_duration, kernel_error_rate).
- Profiling window: an intentional time-bounded full-capture session used for deep analysis (trace-level).

Observability SLA (metrics and thresholds)

Table: metric | alert threshold | target (SLO) | runbook severity
- kernel_p95_execution_ms | > 80ms sustained 5m | SLO: p95 < 60ms over 24h | Sev2
- kernel_p99_execution_ms | > 200ms sustained 5m | SLO: p99 < 150ms over 24h | Sev1
- kernel_error_rate (non-transient) | > 0.5% over 10m | SLO: < 0.2% | Sev1
- kernel_dispatch_queue_depth | > 200 for 1m | SLO: median < 50 | Sev2
- kernel_memory_pressure_evictions_per_min | > 1/min | SLO: < 0.1/min | Sev2

Notes: thresholds are intentionally tighter than product-level SLA to detect regressions earlier. Alerting rules are configured in Monitoring (Grafana/Prometheus) under team "runtime-kernel-observability". Alerts map to runbook escalation in the Runbooks section.

Sampling policy and retention budget

- Continuous aggregated metrics: emitted for all kernels (high-cardinality fields are hashed). Retained for 90 days.
- Detailed traces (span-level, per-request kernels): sampled using hybrid sampling: deterministic sampling for top 1% traffic cohorts by token volume + probabilistic reservoir sampling (0.5% of all requests) to ensure long-tail visibility.
- Profiling windows (full capture): scheduled 3 times per week in production canaries and once weekly in a matched staging shard. Each profiling window is limited to 15 minutes per shard to keep cost bounded.
- Retention: full-trace artifacts retained for 30 days (aligned with the incident review window) and archived to cold storage (GCS) for 12 months for cross-release comparisons.

Profiling cadence (recommended schedule)

1) Daily lightweight probes (continuous):
   - Metric rollups + micro-histogram snapshots every minute.
   - Purpose: detect immediate shifts in medians and p95.

2) Weekly focused traces:
   - 2x profiling windows (15m each) in staging matched to production traffic shape.
   - Run: guided by the benchmark suite scenarios (see integration).

3) Release gating profiling:
   - For any kernel or scheduler change that lands in main and is tagged for canary, run a release profiling session (two 15m windows) in canary. Must pass the profiling gate (no new anomalies at p99 and no unexplained error-rate increase).

4) On-demand deep captures:
   - Triggered from an incident or a scheduled experiment. Can be 30–120 minutes, must be pre-approved by runtime leadership if > 30 minutes due to cost.

Profiling playbook (step-by-step)

Preconditions: you are oncall or the owner of a flagged release. Have access to the profiling orchestration tool (profilingctl) and the benchmark runner.

1) Validate the alert: confirm Prometheus/Grafana alert and cross-check with product-level SLOs.
2) Correlate: use the request-tagged rollups to identify cohorts (model variant, seq_length_bucket, priority_class).
3) If tail signals are present, promote a profiling window targeting the affected shard(s) for 15 minutes (profilingctl start-window --shard <id> --duration 15m --cohort <tag>).
4) Collect kernel samples and GPU-side counters. Verify the sample set exceeds the minimum capture size (>= 200 kernel samples for statistical validity).
5) Run the local analysis pipeline (profile-analyze) to generate: hotspot table, costly-kernel-variants, and cross-correlation with dispatcher queue depth.

- Hotspot table: top 10 kernel variants by p99 increase vs baseline.
- Costly-kernel-variants: kernel ids with a >2x increase in per-invocation GPU time.

6) Triage: if a single kernel variant explains >40% of the p99 shift, open an RFC and page the kernel owner. If no single variant emerges, escalate to sysinfra and kernel scheduling owners to look for admission/queueing interactions.

7) Mitigation options (short-term):
   - Rollback kernel patch; or
   - Switch offending cohort to a fallback model variant; or
   - Temporarily increase admission control for the priority class to shed non-critical traffic.

8) Postmortem: capture the artifact id of the profiling capture and link it to the incident ticket. Run a follow-up benchmark against the microbench suite to validate proposed fixes.

Integration with benchmarking suite

- The profiling orchestration integrates with the benchmarking suite via a shared experiment manifest. Each profiling window can be replayed against the benchmark harness to produce a reproducible microbench against the exact kernel variants observed.
- Benchmark experiments to run after a profiling session:
  - sequence-length-scaling scenario at 4 concurrency points
  - KV-cache-warmup profile to emulate long-session traffic
  - scheduler-priority-noise injection to validate admission controls

Release gating and automation

- Any release that touches: kernel code, scheduler, admission controller, or the dispatcher must include a profiling gate. The CI pipeline will schedule a canary profiling window automatically and fail the gate if:
  - kernel_p99_execution_ms increases by > 10% vs canary baseline; or
  - kernel_error_rate increases by > 0.05 percentage points.

Runbooks (high level)

- Sev1: (p99 spike or error rate)
  1) Page runtime-oncall and kernel-owner.
  2) Run profiling window (15m) targeted at canary shard(s).
  3) If profiling confirms a single kernel variant: apply emergency rollback and re-run profiling.
  4) If not, invoke admission-control escalation to shed traffic and restore SLOs.

- Sev2: (p95 or queue depth)
  1) Perform correlation and schedule a 15m profiling window.
  2) Tune admission control thresholds for the affected priority class.
  3) Schedule a follow-up benchmark to validate tuning.

Known limitations and gotchas

- Sampling bias: deterministic sampling of top cohorts improves reproducibility but can miss rare degradations in low-volume tenants. Use on-demand deep captures for those.
- GPU counters missing on legacy accelerator drivers: in those cases we fallback to host-side timing and increase sampling rate for statistical confidence.
- Profiling cost: full-trace windows are expensive; long captures require leadership sign-off. Abuse of on-demand windows has previously consumed >30% of monthly profiling budget — we now require ticketing and attach artifact ids.

Operational ownership and contacts

- Kernel observability ownership: runtime-observability@redwood.com (primary: Marcus Alvarez).
- Scheduler & kernel owners: see TEAM-OWNERS index in the runtime-team wiki.
- Oncall rota: runtime-oncall (primary) and kernel-secondary (secondary).

Appendix: handy commands and queries

- Start a short profiling window (CLI): profilingctl start-window --shard canary-3 --duration 15m --note "p99-burst-investigation"
- Generate a hotspot report: profile-analyze --capture-id <id> --output hotspots.csv
- Grafana query for kernel p99: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(kernel_execution_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, variant))
- Baseline comparison job: bench-runner --manifest capture-<id>.json --replay --compare baseline-2024-11-01.json

References and related pages

- Runtime profiling guidelines (internal): /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/runtime-profiling-playbook-guidelines-2025
- Benchmark suite catalog: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/microbenchmark-suite-variance-analysis-2025
- Release gating policy: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-upgrade-validation-and-canary-matrix-2026

Change log

- 2024-01-12: initial draft and schedule proposal.
- 2024-06-01: tightened sampling policy; added deterministic cohort capture.
- 2025-11-03: increased profiling window retention and clarified release gating thresholds.

title: observability-led-cost-and-fidelity-profiling-manual-2026
content:
Overview
========
This document defines the observability-driven profiling methodology used to measure and correlate runtime telemetry with operator cost and model fidelity. It is a cross-cutting manual intended for runtime engineers, SREs, and applied-ML teams who run fidelity-sensitive experiments, kernel scheduling changes, or cost optimizations (batching, quantization, caching). The goal is repeatable, low-noise profiling that produces actionable signal for rollouts and release gates.

Scope and goals
----------------
- Scope: production-like inference runtime across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.
- Goals:
  - Produce a repeatable experiment matrix that ties telemetry signals to per-token cost and fidelity deltas.
  - Provide a step-by-step runbook for incident-driven profiling and change verification.
  - Define an instrumentation contract for kernel schedulers and runtime components so signals are comparable across environments.
  - Integrate profiling outputs with the benchmarking suite and release gates.

Ownership and roles
-------------------
- Document owner: eng-serving-runtime observability group.
- Primary engineers: runtime-observability (oncall), kernel-scheduler team, profiling-lab.
- Reviewers: applied-ml (for fidelity metrics), cost-analytics (for cost-per-token alignment).

Key definitions and success metrics
----------------------------------
- Fidelity delta: measurable change in model output quality for a fixed prompt set (see fidelity prompts in the benchmarking suite). Expressed as a percent regression or score delta (ex: BLEU, embeddings cosine, or custom eval score).
- Cost-per-token: aggregated resource accounting for a request normalized to a token. Includes GPU dispatch time, per-kernel execution, and cross-layer overhead (dispatch, serialization).
- Probe SLOs for profiling runs:
  - Measurement noise: standard error of mean (SEM) < 3% across repeated runs.
  - Trace completeness: 100% of kernel boundaries annotated for target traces.
  - Cost correlation: telemetry-derived cost estimate within ±8% of accounting-WAL (billing-derived) for the same window.

Instrumentation contract (signals and semantics)
------------------------------------------------
This contract must be implemented by any runtime or kernel that participates in these experiments. Signals should be emitted using the runtime's telemetry pipeline with the following names and semantics:

- trace.request_id: unique request identifier (UUID).
- trace.model_variant: model name + quantization/precision tag (e.g., gptx2-8bit-v1).
- trace.sequence_len: integer, sequence length processed (input+generated).
- kernel.exec_ms: float, wall-time for the kernel execution in milliseconds.
- kernel.type: enum (attention, ff, matmul, kv_prefetch, decoder-step).
- kernel.queue_wait_ms: float, how long the request waited in scheduler queue.
- scheduler.slot_size: integer, number of requests batched together for that kernel invocation.
- kvcache.hits / kvcache.misses: integer counters for prefix reuse.
- network.serialized_bytes: integer, bytes transferred between runtime shards.
- accounting.gpu_ms: per-GPU accumulated ms attributed to request (derived by sampler).
- metadata.build_id / metadata.kernel_hash: strings to tie traces to binary artifacts.

Each signal must include a timestamp and be taggable with environment (prod/stage), region, and tenant-id (for Dedicated/Private).

Telemetry cardinality table (recommended retention)
--------------------------------------------------
Signal | Cardinality guidance | Reasoning
------ | --------------------- | ---------
trace.request_id | high | Required for trace reconstruction and causal attribution
kernel.exec_ms | high | Primary latency breakdown
kernel.type | medium | Grouping by kernel class for regression cause
scheduler.slot_size | medium | Batching and cost analysis
accounting.gpu_ms | low-medium | Cost reconciliation; sample-based can be used
metadata.* | low | Map to binary and rollout metadata

Profiling experiment matrix (high level)
--------------------------------------
Design experiments to isolate a single variable at a time. Examples:
1) Batch sizing impact on tail latency and per-token cost (vary scheduler.slot_size from 1,2,4,8).
2) Quantization rollout A/B: compare float16 vs 8-bit for the same model variant using identical prompts.
3) KV cache warmup dynamics: measure cold vs warmed kvcache hit rates and perf impact.
4) Kernel handoff regressions: insert synthetic latency into a specific kernel and validate scheduler behavior and cost delta.

For each experiment capture:
- hypothesis (one sentence),
- independent variable(s),
- fixed variables (hardware, sequence length distribution),
- sample size and run duration,
- success criteria (fidelity tolerance, cost delta threshold).

Standardized bench corpus and prompt sets
---------------------------------------
Use the canonical benchmarking corpus located in the benchmarking suite. For fidelity experiments include at minimum:
- 1000 short prompts (0–32 tokens)
- 500 medium prompts (32–256 tokens)
- 200 long prompts (256–1024 tokens)

Always run with deterministic seeds where applicable and capture random-number-generator state in metadata.

Profiling runbook (quick incident triage)
----------------------------------------
Follow these numbered steps when investigating a suspected regression or performing a focused profiling experiment: 
1) Reproduce the symptom in a staging mirror using traffic replay. Document the input corpus, build_id, and kernel_hash.
2) Activate high-fidelity tracing for the affected subset (enable kernel.exec_ms at trace level). Be careful to limit sampling to avoid production overhead.
3) Capture sample traces for 10,000 requests or until SEM target is reached.
4) Run data enrichment pipeline to compute per-request cost estimates and kernel contribution table.
5) Correlate fidelity changes using the canonical prompt set. If fidelity regression is observed, flag applied-ml and create a quality incident.
6) If cost regression without fidelity impact is observed, escalate to kernel-scheduler to review admission and slot accounting.
7) Apply targeted mitigations according to the mitigation table (see below).
8) For any binary/kernel change, run the bench-suite acceptance matrix (see 'Release gating' below) before rolling.

Mitigation table (common symptoms)
----------------------------------
Symptom | Likely cause | Immediate mitigation | Owner
--------|--------------|----------------------|------
Higher per-token GPU ms, no fidelity change | schedule/granularity change or unexpected sloting | Reduce slot_size to emergency smaller bin, throttle low-priority cohorts | kernel-scheduler
High tail latency | kernel queuing or NVLink saturation | Drain NVLink-heavy nodes, reroute traffic, enable backpressure | eng-sre / runtime-ops
Fidelity regression | quantization mismatch, kernel bug, wrong model variant | Roll back kernel binary, revert quantization rollout, engage applied-ml | runtime-release/applied-ml
Large network serialization bytes | sharded state transfer or incorrect serialization path | Enable compact serializer and route to local caches | runtime-network

Kernel scheduler considerations
------------------------------
- Scheduler must annotate slot_size and preemption events in telemetry.
- For reproducible profiling, scheduler should support a deterministic batching mode (fixed window) that can be enabled in staging.
- Provide a scheduler-level 'profiling-token' header that pins low-latency priority and disables best-effort preemption for the duration of the experiment.
- When evaluating new scheduling policies, run the 'slot-synthesis' synthetic workload from the benchmarking suite to validate fairness and cost envelopes.

Benchmarking suite integration
-----------------------------
- Bench runner should accept a --profiling-mode flag that:
  - pins the metadata.build_id and kernel_hash,
  - enables deterministic batching if requested,
  - provisions trace.request_id tags and collects kernel-level metrics.
- Output artifacts:
  - per-experiment metrics.csv with cost and fidelity aggregates,
  - raw-traces.tar.gz (sampled),
  - bench-report.html summarizing deltas and charts.
- Bench artifacts must be uploaded to the experiment storage bucket with a stable naming scheme: {bench}/{build_id}/{experiment_slug}/{timestamp}/

Release gating and signoff checklist
------------------------------------
Before rolling kernel or scheduler changes to production run the following: 
- Run bench-suite acceptance matrix against staging cluster.
- Verify no fidelity regression > 0.5% on canonical prompt set (applied-ml must sign off).
- Verify cost delta per-token within configured threshold (default 5%).
- Ensure tracing metadata is emitted and matches instrumentation contract.
- Confirm rollback automation is wired and smoke tests for connectivity pass.
- Approvers required: kernel-scheduler lead, runtime-observability owner, applied-ml approver.

Known issues (catalog and temporary workarounds)
-----------------------------------------------
- Issue: Sampled accounting.gpu_ms undercounts during mixed-precision kernels.
  - Workaround: Increase sampling rate or enable micro-instrumentation for affected builds.
  - Ticket: #INF-4721
- Issue: scheduler.slot_size unstable under sudden burst traffic leading to queue thrashing.
  - Workaround: engage the emergency admission controller to cap slot_size at 4 and enable backpressure for best-effort cohorts.
  - Ticket: #INF-5033
- Issue: kvcache hits reported but observed fidelity indicates stale cache usage in canary environments.
  - Workaround: purge kvcache on canary instances before experiment.
  - Ticket: #INF-4890

Appendix A: sample commands and example trace enrichment pipeline
-----------------------------------------------------------------
1) Run bench in profiling mode (example):
   ./bench-runner --suite canonical --build-id gptx2-8b-proto --profiling-mode --deterministic-batching --out /tmp/bench-output

2) Enable trace sampling (CLI to control-plane):
   curl -X POST "https://control-plane.internal/api/v1/tracing/sampling" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -d '{"rate":0.02, "filters": {"model":"gptx2*"}}'

3) Minimal enrichment pipeline (pseudocode):
   - ingest raw traces from /tmp/bench-output/raw-traces
   - group by trace.request_id, sum kernel.exec_ms, attach accounting.gpu_ms samples
   - compute per-token cost = accounting.gpu_ms / trace.sequence_len
   - join with fidelity evaluation results and output metrics.csv

Appendix B: experiment template (copy/paste)
-------------------------------------------
Title: Quant-AB-test-v2
Hypothesis: 8-bit quant reduces cost by >= 20% with <= 0.5% fidelity regression on canonical short prompts.
Independent variable: model variant (fp16 vs 8bit)
Fixed: same hardware (A100 80GB), traffic shape (50% short,30% mid,20% long), deterministic seeds
Sample size: 20k requests per cohort
Success: cost delta >= 18% and fidelity regression <= 0.5%
Artifacts: metrics.csv, raw-traces.tar.gz, bench-report.html

References and links
--------------------
- Benchmarking suite README: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/runtime-deployment-sanity-and-benchmark-suite-acceptance-2026
- Telemetry schema: internal telemetry catalog (link internal)
- Release gating policy: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/release-notes/release-readiness-integrated-checklist-technical-gate-2024

Change log
----------
- 2025-11-12: Initial draft (Aisha Patel)
- 2026-01-18: Added kernel scheduler deterministic-mode guidance (Marcelo Ruiz)
- 2026-02-03: Incorporated release gating thresholds and known issues (Priya Shah)

Contact
-------
For questions or to request an experiment run, ping #runtime-observability on Slack or email runtime-observability@redwood.com

title: Probabilistic latency attribution playbook (sampling-first approach) - 2026
content:
Summary:

This playbook describes a probabilistic approach to attributing observed request latency to runtime subsystems, kernels, and queueing stages when full-trace coverage is too expensive. The method combines lightweight sampling, sketch-based telemetry, and attribution heuristics to produce actionable signals for engineering and SRE teams.

Intended audience:
- Runtime engineers owning the scheduler and kernel mapper
- SREs and performance investigators
- Observability and telemetry engineers

When to use this playbook:
1) Production tail-latency events where full end-to-end tracing is disabled or introduces too much overhead.
2) When seeking fast, statistically plausible root-cause hypotheses across dozens of GPUs/nodes.
3) For continuous monitoring: convert the heuristics into alerts and periodic digests.

Definitions and conventions:
- request: a single API call delivered to the frontend routing layer.
- hotpath: the portion of request execution that executes on GPU for token generation.
- kernel step: atomic GPU kernel invocation (for example: attention, matmul, rotary).
- sample: a full, detailed trace captured for 1/N requests per bucket.
- sketch: compact aggregated metric (histogram, t-digest, count-min) emitted at 1s resolution.

Scope and constraints:
- This playbook focuses on inference serving runtime (GPU-backed path, KV cache, batching, and scheduler interactions). It does not replace detailed kernel profiling runs or microbenchmarks.
- Assumes telemetry pipeline supports: traces (sampled), metrics (prometheus-style counters/histograms), and log events with minimal schema.

Telemetry contract (required fields):
- request_id (string)
- model_family (string)
- model_variant (string)
- route (string)
- arrival_ts (ISO8601)
- dispatch_ts (ISO8601)
- kernel_start_ts (ISO8601) optional per kernel when sampled
- kernel_end_ts (ISO8601) optional per kernel when sampled
- gpu_id (string)
- shard_id (string)
- batch_size (int)
- tokens_generated (int)
- outcome (enum: success|fallback|error)
- trace_sampled (bool)

Sampling strategy recommendations:
- Baseline: 1/1000 sampled across all routes; increase to 1/100 for routes with observed tail greater than SLO threshold.
- Stratified sampling keys: model_family, route, batch_size_bucket (1, 2-4, 5-8, >8), gpu_pool_tier (hosted|dedicated).
- Burst sampling: when total 95th percentile latency exceeds configured threshold, temporarily increase sampling to 1/20 for the offending route for 10 minutes.

How sampling and sketches combine (high level):
1) Most requests emit lightweight sketches (per-minute histograms of request latency, queue wait, kernel execution) tagged by model_variant and route.
2) A small fraction of requests produce full traces with per-kernel timings and GPU occupancy snapshots.
3) Attribution uses samples to estimate distribution of per-kernel latencies within each sketch bucket using importance weighting.

Attribution algorithm (procedural):
1) Select window: choose the incident window (T0..T1) and the route/model to analyze.
2) Compute sketch deltas: obtain histogram of request latency and queue wait from sketches for the window.
3) Retrieve sampled traces: pull all sampled traces matching the same route/model and time window.
4) For each sampled trace, compute kernel fractions: f_k = kernel_k_time / total_gpu_time.
5) Use importance weights w = (count_histogram_bin / sample_count_bin) * adjustment_factor to scale sample fractions to the full histogram bins.
6) Estimate per-kernel latency contribution per bin: est_k_bin = f_k * median_latency_bin * w.
7) Aggregate across bins to produce: total_est_k, percent_contrib_k, and confidence intervals (bootstrap samples on the traces).

Example: if 95th requests have median latency 420ms and sampled traces show 60% time in attention kernels and 30% in KV cache sync, attribution reports attention approximately 252ms (60%), KV sync approximately 126ms (30%), remainder in queueing and overhead.

Practical investigation playbook (step-by-step):
1) Identify the symptom: route X, 95th latency 2x SLO, time window 13:02-13:22 UTC.
2) Pull three artifacts: sketches (1s resolution), sampled traces (all), node-level GPU metrics (occupancy, mem_bw).
3) Run attribution algorithm to produce per-kernel contributions and confidence bands.
4) If attention kernels are dominant: run quick kernel heatmap query and check recent kernel parameter changes or new model variants rolled out in that window.
5) If queue/warmup dominates: inspect autoscaling and pre-warm logs; check request arrival patterns and burst rates.
6) If KV cache sync shows up: correlate with cache miss rate and backend store latency.
7) Generate an incident hypothesis and log in the incident tracker, attaching top three contributing factors and suggested mitigations.

Automatable checks and quick queries (examples):
- PromQL: 5m rate of requests and 95th latency by route
  sum by (route) (histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le, route)))

- PromQL: kernel occupancy heatmap (approx):
  topk(20, sum by (kernel_name, gpu_id) (rate(gpu_kernel_time_seconds_sum[1m])))

- SQL (telemetry catalog): compute sample-weighted kernel fraction per route
  SELECT route, kernel_name, SUM(kernel_time * weight) / SUM(total_gpu_time * weight) AS frac
  FROM sampled_traces
  WHERE time >= '2026-02-01T00:00:00Z' AND route = 'inference-chat'
  GROUP BY route, kernel_name;

Confidence and caveats:
- Small sample sizes can bias the attribution; always report sample_count and bootstrap confidence intervals.
- Sampling bias: if sampling selection correlates with client size or request shape, stratify or reweight by the known metadata.
- Kernel durations measured on traces may vary across GPU types; normalize by hardware class when attributing across heterogeneous pools.

Mitigations and quick fixes mapped to root causes:
- Scheduler-induced queueing: lower batch_size cap for the route, enforce hard preemption window, or increase dedicated capacity for the tier.
- Attention kernel slowdown: revert recent kernel patch, change kernel mapper to fallback, or pin model to older compiled variant.
- KV cache sync latency: enable local cache warmup, increase async writeback threshold, or route reads to a faster replica.
- Memory fragmentation or OOM patterns: eject long-running allocations, increase malloc arena reuse, and schedule compaction during low-load windows.

Runbook checklist (for on-call):
1) Validate incoming alert: confirm sketch 95th greater than threshold and check recent deploys.
2) Run automated attribution job (script: tools/latency-attrib/run.sh) with window +/-30m.
3) Share initial results in incident channel with table: top-5 kernel contributors and sample_count.
4) If CI indicates kernel-level regression with high confidence (greater than 80% contribution and more than 50 sample traces), page runtime-owner and kernel-owner teams.
5) If no clear kernel signal, escalate to SRE to investigate infra (network, storage latencies).

Telemetry table (recommended emission cadence):
- Request sketches: per-route per-minute histograms (latency, queue_wait) - aggregation: t-digest/hd-pairs
- Sampled traces: per-request full trace JSON with per-kernel timings - 1/1000 baseline
- Node metrics: per-GPU 1s counters for kernel_time, kernel_count, occupancy, mem_bw
- Deployment events: model_variant_rollout, kernel_release tags as discrete events

Example sampled-trace (flattened representation):
- request_id: req-123
- route: inference-chat
- model_variant: gptx-7b-q4
- arrival_ts: 2026-02-08T13:14:05.123Z
- dispatch_ts: 2026-02-08T13:14:05.130Z
- gpu_id: gpu-az3-045
- batch_size: 4
- total_gpu_time_ms: 380
- kernels: attention_fwd=210ms, matmul_ffn=80ms, kv_sync=70ms

Ownership and escalation:
- Primary: eng-serving-runtime (runtime-kernel squad) - pager: #runtime-pager (oncall rotation)
- Secondary: eng-infra (GPU fleet) - pager: #infra-pager
- For storage/cache escalations: platform-storage team

Automation and dashboards to build (owners suggested):
- Attribution digest dashboard: per-route top contributors with CI bars updated every 5m. Owner: runtime-observability
- Sampling controller: auto-tune sampling rate per-route based on 95th latency and sample availability. Owner: telemetry
- Kernel heatmap: live matrix of kernel_time by kernel_name x gpu_model. Owner: runtime-performance

When to trigger a rollback or hotfix:
- If attribution shows greater than 50% regression attributable to a single kernel associated with a new kernel release or variant rollout and confidence greater than 90% (bootstrap), trigger rollback per deployment rollback runbook.

Post-incident follow-ups (template):
1) Hypothesis and evidence (sketches + traces + kernel heatmap).
