2) Actions taken and immediate outcomes (rollback, config change, capacity increase).
3) Root cause summary with supporting confidence interval plots.
4) Long-term fixes and owners (for example: increase sample rate for route X; create test harness for kernel Y).

Changelog:
- 2025-11-12: Initial draft and internal review.
- 2026-01-08: Added burst sampling and bootstrap CI guidance (reviewer: Marcus Lee).
- 2026-02-10: Added PromQL/SQL examples and automation recommendations.

References and related reading:
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/continuous-runtime-profiling-strategy-2026
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/tail-latency-investigation-and-mitigation-playbook-2026
- Telemetry schema docs: /confluence/eng-infra/team-wiki/telemetry-schema-v2

Appendix A - utility scripts:
- tools/latency-attrib/run.sh --window start end --route <route> --out results.json
- tools/latency-attrib/bootstrap.py --input results.json --iterations 1000 --out ci.json

Appendix B - quick checklist for product managers (non-technical):
- Is the incident tied to a model variant rollout? If yes, consider temporary pin to previous variant.
- Does the incident affect paying customers? If yes, notify customer success with summary and ETA.

End of document.

title: Scheduler Fuzz & Resilience Lab Manual
content:
Overview:

This lab manual documents the Scheduler Fuzz & Resilience Lab: the curated experiments, deterministic replay tooling, profiling practices, benchmark handoffs, and the operational runbook used by serving-runtime engineers to validate scheduler and kernel changes before canary and prod rollout. The lab targets regressions that are difficult to catch in unit tests and classical microbenchmarks, including priority inversion, eviction oscillation, NVLink-induced preemption stalls, and non-deterministic warmup losses.

Goals:
- Provide reproducible test recipes that catch subtle QoS and cross-tenant fairness regressions.
- Integrate fuzzed adversarial campaigns with deterministic replay for CI gating.
- Produce artifacts consumable by the benchmarking pipeline and release gates.

Lab topology and components:
- det-replay (deterministic replay harness): replays NDJSON trace records against a latency model and scheduler policy. Produces event-trace.log, per-tenant latency CSV, and kernel-usage CSV.
- sched-fuzzer: creates mutated traffic mixes and scheduler-parameter perturbations. Supports random, grid, and boundary sweep modes.
- prof-orchestrator: manages profiler agents, sampling windows, and full-trace collection on selected worker pools.
- chaos-injector: simulates node-level perturbations (thermal throttling, NVLink degradation, short network egress saturation).

Signals and artifacts produced (examples):
- event-trace.log (canonical, used for exact-replay checks)
- operational-signature.json (normalized SLO deltas and fairness metrics)
- kvcache-hit.csv (per-tenant cache hit ratios over time)
- kernel-calls.csv (callsite latency histogram)

Trace format (NDJSON example):
{"req_id":"r-0001","tenant":"t-acme","seq_len":64,"priority":"P1","arrival_ms":0}
{"req_id":"r-0002","tenant":"t-beta","seq_len":1024,"priority":"P3","arrival_ms":5}

Deterministic replay configuration snippet (YAML as string):
kernel_latency_profiles: small: {base_ms: 0.45, per_token_ms: 0.025} large: {base_ms: 2.0, per_token_ms: 0.075}
scheduler_policy: path/to/policy.json

Recommended experiment recipes:
1) Short-high vs long-low priority inversion sweep
- Setup: 80% long low-priority (seq_len >= 768), 20% short high-priority (seq_len <= 64) across 5 tenants.
- Run: sched-fuzzer --mode grid --param priority_ratio --values 0.01,0.05,0.1,0.2 --trace mixed-corpus.ndjson --out out/priority-sweep
- Instrumentation: prof-orchestrator annotate --full-trace on two worker nodes; enable scheduler decision debug logs.
- Acceptance: P1 median < 35ms, P95 < 140ms, preemption delay occurrences < 1 per 10k requests.

2) Eviction warmup boundary test
- Purpose: ensure model swap preserves prefix locality and prevents long-term cache thrashing.
- Steps: warm with N representative prefixes (N sweep: 1k, 10k, 50k), perform model rollout, replay warm set and measure hit ratio trajectory for first 30 minutes.
- Acceptance: hit ratio drop <= 6% after swap and rolling median latency <= 1.6x baseline within 5 minutes.

3) Admission-storm replay + NVLink perturbation
- Setup: 10x burst for 30s injected at t=0 while chaos-injector triggers a transient NVLink degradation for 5s at t=10s.
- Objective: reveal preemption stalls and kernel retry patterns.

Fuzz campaign modes and parameters:
- random (seeded) campaign: repeatability via seed stamping in metadata. Always record seed in event-trace.log.
- grid sweep: exhaustively vary one or two parameters (priority_ratio, slice_ms, preempt_window_ms).
- boundary sweep: test edge conditions (very small batches, extreme priority ratios).

CI and benchmark integration:
- CI job should run a short det-replay suite (canonical 12 scenarios) and 20 quick fuzz mutations as a fast pre-gate. Artifacts to persist: operational-signature.json, event-trace.log, kvcache-hit.csv.
- For a full merge validation (nightly): run sched-fuzzer campaign=200, run prof-orchestrator sampling on 3 nodes, upload artifacts to s3://lab-artifacts/scheduler-fuzz/$GITHUB_RUN_ID/.
- Bench mapping: operational-signature.json feeds the bench dashboard and is retained 90d; event-trace.log retained 180d for replay equality checks.

Release readiness checklist (kernel/scheduler change):
1) Unit tests and static analysis pass.
2) Deterministic replay: new policy passes canonical scenarios with no P99 regressions >20% relative to baseline.
3) Fuzz campaigns: no SEV-HIGH regressions across 200 mutation runs.
4) Profiling: primary kernel call latency mean change < 10%.
5) Bench: end-to-end throughput within tolerance defined in SLO matrix.
6) Canary: 1% traffic, 24h baseline monitoring, incremental ramp with automated rollback on SLO violation.

Severity taxonomy (lab):
- SEV-HIGH: P99 increase > 30% or cross-tenant fairness delta > 25%.
- SEV-MED: P95 increase 15-30% or sustained kvcache hit drop 6-15% for > 10m.
- SEV-LOW: transient deviations that resolve within 10m or small hit ratio drops < 6%.

Runbook: quick triage steps
1) Alert sources: CI gate failure, staging shadow mismatch, canary SLO alert.
2) First 10 min: fetch operational-signature.json from artifacts, compare to baseline using lab-tools bench-compare.
3) If repro exists in lab: run sched-fuzzer reproduce --id <campaign> --seed <seed> --out replay/<id>. If not reproducible, run det-replay with same seed and record mismatch.
4) Containment: rollback canary or revert scheduler preset via Admin API: POST $ADMIN/scheduler/preset/rollback with target stable tag.
5) Deep analysis: run prof-orchestrator collect --full-trace --annotate replay/event-trace.log and examine kernel-calls.csv for increased tail at specific callsites.

Known issues observed and mitigations (lab-tracked):
- NVLink transient stalls can trigger preemption retry loops. Mitigation: on NVLink error signals, scheduler applies exponential backoff for preemption and routes heavy long-running allocations away from degraded links.
- Replay inequality due to unrecorded seed metadata. Mitigation: stamp seed into event-trace.log header and validate replay equality in CI.

Metrics and dashboards to monitor:
- lab.sched_fuzz.campaign_count (counter)
- lab.det_replay.success_rate (gauge)
- lab.kvcache.hit_ratio (per-tenant time-series)
- lab.kernel.call_mean_ms (histogram)
Dashboards: Grafana IDs lab-sched-fuzz, lab-det-replay, lab-kernel-latency.

Operational ownership:
- Lab owner: Aisha Kumar (serving-runtime)
- Scheduler reviewer: Liam O'Connor
- Profiling automation: Sofia Martinez
- SRE escalation: Daniel Park

Appendix: sample quick commands
- Run a short deterministic check:
  det-replay run --scenarios canonical/* --out out/det
- Launch a seeded fuzz campaign:
  sched-fuzzer run --campaign 50 --trace samples/mixed-corpus.ndjson --seed 20260315 --out out/fuzz
- Reproduce a failing campaign:
  sched-fuzzer reproduce --campaign-id 1234 --seed 20260315 --out out/replay/1234

Artifact retention guidance:
- operational-signature.json: 90 days
- event-trace.log: 180 days
- kernel-calls.csv: 365 days

Change log:
- 2026-02-10: initial draft published by Aisha Kumar.
- 2026-03-15: added CI patterns, severity taxonomy, and expanded NVLink mitigation notes.

Contact and contribution:
Open issues and experiment requests: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime-lab/issues. For rapid coordination, ping #serving-runtime-lab on Slack or message Aisha.K.

title: Profiling → Benchmark Bridge Handbook
content:
Summary

This handbook describes the standard process and templates we use at Redwood to convert live runtime profiling traces and telemetry signals into repeatable benchmarking scenarios. The goal is to ensure that performance investigations produce benchmarks that faithfully reproduce observed production behaviours (latency shapes, tail events, kernel hotpaths, KV cache dynamics) so we can validate fixes, run regressions, and reason about cost/latency tradeoffs.

Audience

- Runtime engineers and SREs performing root-cause analysis.
- Performance/benchmarking owners who run controlled experiments.
- Release engineers validating performance gates.

When to use this playbook

1) You have an ongoing latency or cost regression and profiling traces show anomalous kernel/dispatch behaviour.
2) You must validate a kernel or scheduler change against a production-shaped workload.
3) You need a reproducible benchmark to demonstrate an SLA improvement or cost regression before rollout.

Key principles

- Fidelity over simplicity: preserve request concurrency shape, sequence length distribution, and KV cache warm/cold ratios when possible.
- Observability-driven knobs: derive benchmark knobs from telemetry signals (not arbitrary values).
- Small fast iterations: build a minimal reproducer first, then scale to full fidelity.
- Ownership and signalling: every benchmark run must list the owner, intent, and success criteria in the run metadata.

Mapping telemetry to benchmark knobs (quick reference)

- request_rate_rps -> target_concurrency / arrival_poisson_lambda
- sequence_length_p50/p90/p99 -> sample_length_distribution (file: lengths.csv)
- kv_cache_hit_ratio -> kv_cache_initial_warm_fraction and prefix_reuse_pattern
- kernel_exec_time_p50/p95 -> kernel_hint_profile (used to select mock kernel timeouts)
- batch_size_distribution -> concurrency_shaper.max_batch and batch_release_delay_ms
- tail_latency_spike_count -> interleaved_poisson_bursts / microburst_amplitude

Extraction procedure: from profile -> bench config (numbered steps)

1) Capture a canonical trace

- Command: rdwctl traces dump --trace-id <TRACE_ID> --format jsonl > production-trace.jsonl
- Capture matching logs: rdwctl logs fetch --trace-id <TRACE_ID> --since "-30m" > trace-logs.ndjson

2) Summarise the trace

- Run summariser: python tools/trace_summary.py production-trace.jsonl --output trace-summary.yaml
- Required output fields: request_rate_rps, concurrency_histogram, seq_len_p50_p90_p99, kv_cache_stats (hit_pct, hot_prefix_count), kernel_latency_p50_p95_p99, batch_dist_summary

3) Derive bench knobs

- Use tools/map_trace_to_bench.py --summary trace-summary.yaml --template templates/bench-template.json --out bench-config.json
- The script fills: arrival model (poisson or replay), concurrency target, sequence_length_sampler (with weights), kv_cache_warm_fraction, batch_release_delay_ms, runtime_model (real vs. synthetic kernel timings)

4) Create minimal reproducer

- Start with a single-node bench: bench/runner --config bench-config.json --scale 0.05 --replay-mode sample
- Validate that kernel hotpaths observed (kernel names/ids) match production summary within ±10% for p50/p95 kernel latencies.

5) Iterate to increase fidelity

- Gradually increase scale to full target. Add network noise, simulated NFS latency, and multi-tenant noise injection using bench/noise-injector.yaml.
- For KV cache dynamics, run a pre-warm phase: bench/warm_cache --pattern bench-config.kv_pattern --duration 300s then start primary run.

Bench config template (essential fields)

Content below is a representative JSON that our mapping script generates. Replace placeholders before running.

{
  "metadata": {
    "owner": "<owner-email>",
    "intent": "reproduce p99 latency spike for ModelX after kernel change",
    "created_at": "2028-01-11"
  },
  "workload": {
    "arrival_model": "poisson",
    "rps": "1200",
    "concurrency_target": "240",
    "sequence_length_sampler": "lengths.csv",
    "sequence_length_weights": "[0.6,0.25,0.1,0.05]"
  },
  "kernel_model": {
    "mode": "real",
    "kernel_select_hint": "attention-shard-3"
  },
  "kv_cache": {
    "warm_fraction": "0.36",
    "hot_prefix_count": "42"
  },
  "slo": {
    "target_p95_latency_ms": "85",
    "target_p99_latency_ms": "220"
  }
}

(When checked in, this config must be saved under bench/runs/<run-id>/bench-config.json)

Success criteria and validation checklist

- Visual parity: concurrency and RPS histogram match within 10% at p50/p90/p99.
- Kernel parity: top-3 kernel IDs have p50 and p95 within ±15% of production summary.
- KV cache behaviour: measured hit_ratio is within ±0.05 absolute.
- SLO gating: the change only passes the gate if p99 is improved or cost reduced without degrading p95 by >5 ms.

SLO thresholds (team defaults)

- p95 <= 120 ms (service-level)
- p99 <= 350 ms
- sustained cpu/gpu_util <= 85% (per instance)
- KV cache hit ratio >= 0.30 for warm-start dominated workloads

Mapping Bench outputs back to profiling for RCA

- Attach bench run traces to experiment ticket. Use tools/bench_to_trace.py to convert bench logs to the same trace schema as production so profiling tools can directly compare flame graphs and kernel timelines.

Common pitfalls and mitigations

- Error: bench shows lower latency than production despite similar summary metrics.
  - Cause: missing multi-tenant noise (other customers). Mitigation: enable noise_injector and rerun.
- Error: KV cache warm_fraction mismatch.
  - Cause: pre-warm pattern differs (prefix churn high). Mitigation: capture prefix histogram and port exact pattern into bench-config.kv_pattern.
- Error: kernel id mismatch (bench shows fallback kernel).
  - Cause: runtime feature flags differ. Mitigation: check runtime_feature_flags in bench metadata and align with prod.

Operator commands and utilities

- Capture traces: rdwctl traces dump --trace-id <id> --tail 0 --format jsonl
- Quick summary: python tools/trace_summary.py traces.jsonl --top-kernels 10 --out summary.yaml
- Map to bench: python tools/map_trace_to_bench.py --summary summary.yaml --out bench-config.json
- Run bench locally (docker): docker run --rm -v $PWD:/workspace redwood/bench:latest /workspace/bench/runner --config /workspace/bench-config.json

Rollout decision matrix (high level)

1) Local reproducer passes success criteria -> promote to staging with traffic shadowing (10% shadow). Run 3 x 30m replicates.
2) Staging parity holds -> schedule a canary: 5% traffic for 2h, monitor p99, kernel time series, and error rate.
3) If canary stable for 4h and post-canary audit shows no cost regression >3% -> proceed to 50% then 100% with standard cooldowns.
4) If at any step p99 worsens by >10% or errors rise by >0.2% absolute, rollback immediately and open incident runbook.

Runbook stub for failures during bench-driven rollouts

- Pager: runtime-oncall -> escalation to runtime-team and benchmarking-owner.
- Immediate steps: abort canary, revert runtime feature flags, pin model to previous version, and re-run bench to validate rollback.
- Postmortem: attach bench configs, production trace, and timeline.

Ownership and lifecycle

- Bench and mapping scripts owner: eng-serving-runtime/bench-team (primary contact: eng-bench@redwood.com).
- Long term artifacts (bench configs used for release gates) must be checked into git under bench/corpus/<named-workload>.

Appendix A — Example investigation timeline

1) 09:10 — Customer incident report p99 spike.
2) 09:20 — Capture trace id=trc-20281109-9911.
3) 09:30 — Summary produced: rps=1.2k, p99 kernel attention-shard-3=280ms, kv_hit=0.28.
4) 10:00 — Bench config generated and minimal reproducer confirms kernel p99 reproduces at scale factor=0.2.
5) 11:45 — Scheduler change tested: improved p99 from 280ms -> 210ms in bench. Canary runs initiated.

Appendix B — Useful links and references

- Runtime profiling playbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/runtime-profiling-playbook-guidelines-2025
- Bench templates: git@redwood:infra/bench-templates.git
- Production trace schema: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/runtime-telemetry-data-model-and-tracebook-2026

Notes and revision history

- 2026-11-15: initial draft (Anika Sharma).
- 2027-03-02: added bench_to_trace conversion utility and success criteria updates (Marcus Li).
- 2028-01-12: formalized rollout decision matrix and SLO defaults (Priya Nambiar).

title: Causal sampling and root-cause playbook for runtime latency anomalies
content:
Summary:
This playbook describes a repeatable, instrumentation-first approach to detect, sample, and perform causal root-cause analysis for runtime latency anomalies. It is intended for use by oncall engineers, performance SREs, and runtime owners when a service or model route shows unexplained tail-latency or degraded quality after ordinary triage. The goal is to produce actionable hypotheses and targeted remediation steps within a 3-hour incident window for most medium-severity incidents.

When to use this playbook:
- Sudden increase in p95/p99 tail latency for a production route (example SLOs: p99 < 120ms, p95 < 50ms)
- Regressions that are not explained by upstream traffic shifts or scheduled changes
- Persistent latency that fluctuates with workload shape (sequence length, batch size)

Prerequisites and quick checks (first 15 minutes):
1) Confirm the alert: verify the metric source (prometheus, metrics-aggregator) and the impacted routes. Note the time window and compare to deploy/change timeline.
2) Check rollout metadata: model version, kernel profile, kernel-release-tag, and scheduler policy.
3) Snapshot top correlates: kernel.name, gpu_dispatcher_shard, batch.size, seq.len, kvcache.hit, tenant_id.

Key terminology used in this document:
- Causal signal: a telemetry field that, when conditionally correlated with latency across controlled sampling, can be used to build a causal hypothesis. Examples: kernel.slot, kernel.version, kvcache.hit
- Sampling plan: deterministic subset of requests captured for deep traces and payloads to avoid full trace retention cost
- Shadow/sidecar channel: non-production path (or mirrored request) used for deeper instrumentation without affecting production latency

High-level approach:
1) Detect anomalous cohort(s) using light-weight filters.
2) Define a small number (1–3) of causal hypotheses.
3) Implement targeted sampling that isolates the hypothesis and captures enriched traces.
4) Run causal tests and confirm/deny hypotheses using pre-defined statistical checks.
5) Take mitigations mapped to the confirmed root cause.

Step-by-step triage and causal-sampling procedure (recommended cadence):
- 0–15m: Detection & context (owner oncall)
  1. Record symptom (metric, route, time window).
  2. Confirm no recent config/model/kernel rollout in last 30 minutes.
  3. Identify top-5 correlated tags from sparkline telemetry (e.g., kvcache.hit rate drop).
- 15–45m: Narrowing hypotheses & sampling plan (SRE lead)
  1. Form 1–3 hypotheses, e.g. “kv cache misses increased causing kernel warm-starts” or “a new kernel release has a serialization overhead for long sequences”.
  2. Choose sampling filters to isolate cohorts: by sequence length bucket, by kernel.version, by batch.size, by tenant or by route.
  3. Set targeted sampling rates (see sample configs below).
- 45–120m: Capture and analyze (profiling owner)
  1. Stream deep traces into ephemeral storage (max retention 72h) and ensure trace IDs correlate to request id in metrics.
  2. Run causal comparison queries (examples below).
- 120–180m: Confirm, mitigate, and close (incident commander + owner)
  1. If causal signal confirmed, perform mitigation (rollback kernel, increase autoscale, toggle fidelity).
  2. If not confirmed, increase sample breadth and repeat. Document next steps.

Sampling configuration examples (table):
| Use case | Filter | Initial sample rate | Retention | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| High-cost deep dive | route=/v1/generate AND p99>120ms | 100% for 30m | 72h | Only for critical incidents; consider sidecar mirroring |
| Kernel-version compare | kernel.version in [v2.3.1, v2.3.2] | 20% each | 48h | Balanced cost vs statistical power |
| Long sequences | seq.len >= 2048 | 50% | 48h | Sequence-length skew common source of degradation |

Instrumentation checklist (toggle per incident):
- Trace-level: ensure trace contains fields: request_id, route, kernel.version, kernel.slot, batch.size, seq.len, kvcache.hit, gpu_dispatcher_shard, kernel_latency_breakdown (decode/dispatch/compute/serialize).
- Metric-level: emit per-request histograms for kernel execution and batch queuing time.
- Kernel logs: enable 1–2 minutes of debug level for kernel-mapper and gpu-dispatcher where safe.
- Sampling guardrails: do not enable full-request payload capture for >5% of traffic without exec-approval.

Analysis recipes and example queries:
1) Kernel-version causal test (ClickHouse style pseudo-SQL):
```
SELECT kernel_version, quantile(0.99)(latency_ms) as p99
FROM traces
WHERE route = '/v1/generate' AND ts BETWEEN '2026-11-07 10:00' AND '2026-11-07 10:30'
GROUP BY kernel_version
ORDER BY p99 DESC
```
Interpretation: If p99 for new kernel_version exceeds baseline by >30% and batch.size distribution is comparable, this is strong evidence to favor kernel as root cause.

2) Causal kvcache hypothesis test (chi-squared style):
- Build two cohorts: kvcache.hit=true and kvcache.hit=false, control for seq.len and batch.size via stratified sampling. Compare p99 and p50 within matched strata. If difference persists across strata, treat kvcache miss as causal.

3) Bootstrapped confidence interval for p99 using sampled traces (Python snippet):
```
# pseudo-code
import numpy as np
p99_samples = [np.percentile(sample,99) for sample in bootstrap(traces_latencies, n=1000)]
ci = np.percentile(p99_samples,[2.5,97.5])
```
If the CI for suspected cohort does not overlap baseline CI, mark hypothesis confirmed.

Mitigation recipes mapped to common root causes:
- Kernel regression: rollback kernel.release or switch traffic to previous kernel.version via runtime routing policy.
- KV cache instability: trigger kvcache.prefetch for hot prefixes, restore warmup hints, or increase kvcache size for the affected shard.
- Burst-induced queuing: temporarily increase dispatcher slots for the shard, enable preemption policy or increase autoscale target.
- Sequence-length-driven cost: enforce hard route limits or return early-chunked responses for exceptionally long sequences.

Operational constraints and safety:
- No PII should be captured in deep traces unless explicitly approved; strip prompts and user identifiers. Use hash/tokenization when needed.
- Maintain cost ceiling: deep-trace budget per incident must not exceed $X (configured in FY26 runbook budget).
- Escalation: if sampling or debug toggles risk availability, consult SRE on-call before enabling.

Decision thresholds and SLO mapping:
- If p99 increases by >30% for core customer routes for >15 minutes, escalate to P1.
- If p95 crosses SLO but p99 unchanged, treat as degradation and open a P2.
- Map each confirmed root cause to a remediation owner and a timeline (immediate hotfix, 24h patch, or product/architecture change).

Ownership and run cadence:
- Oncall owner: lead triage, perform first 30m checks.
- Profiling owner: set up sampling and run deep analysis (45–120m).
- Runtime team: implement mitigations and rollback if needed.
- Postmortem: complete incident write-up within 72 hours; include sampling plan and validated causal test results.

Post-incident follow-ups (mandatory fields for postmortem):
- Root cause summary (one sentence)
- Evidence snapshot: key queries, CI results, and representative trace ids (redacted)
- Action items (owners + due dates)
- Test harness updates: add a regression-case to our microbenchmark suite to detect the issue early in future canaries

Appendix: quick commands and tracing pointers
- Enable debug logs on kernel-mapper (k8s): kubectl -n runtime annotate deploy/kernel-mapper debug=true --overwrite
- Selective trace export (example): curl -X POST https://trace-exporter.internal/ingest -d '{"filter":"route=/v1/generate AND seq.len>2048","sample_rate":0.5}'
- Example alert thresholds (prometheus):
  - runtime_route_p99_latency_seconds{route="/v1/generate"} > 0.12 for 5m -> page oncall

Related pages and references:
- See: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/probabilistic-latency-attribution-playbook-2026 for sampling theory background.
- See: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/execution-contracts-and-stable-fallbacks-2026 for routing mitigation patterns.

Document history:
- 2026-03-10: initial draft (Leah Morgan)
- 2026-06-18: added stratified sampling recipes and kvcache mitigation matrix (Diego Alvarez)
- 2026-11-08: clarified decision thresholds and added CI bootstrapping recipe (Maya Chen)

Contact: profiling@redwood-inference.internal for runbook questions and runbook budget approvals.

title: Event-sourced Observability: Correlation & Triage Runbook
content:
Overview:
This runbook defines the event-sourced observability model we use to correlate distributed runtime signals (traces, metrics, logs, kernel events) and perform fast, reproducible triage of inference incidents. It documents the canonical event envelope, enrichment rules, minimal required fields, triage playflow, example queries, and rollout checklist for instrumenting new runtime components.

Goals:
- Provide a single cross-team contract for events produced by runtime components (dispatcher, kernel, kvcache, allocator, model-swaps).
- Reduce mean time to resolution (MTTR) for performance regressions and correctness incidents by standardizing correlation keys and triage steps.
- Ensure low-cost, high-utility telemetry: bounding event size, pre-aggregation guidelines, and sampling rules.

Scope and when to use:
- Use this runbook for any incident that involves latency spikes, tail latency regressions, memory pressure OOMs, soft degradation, or model swap oscillations.
- Not intended for application-layer logic bugs (customer prompt-level bugs) unless they cause runtime-level resource anomalies.

Event model (canonical envelope):
Every runtime event MUST be an immutable envelope with the following fields (minimum set):
- event_id: globally unique id (uuid4)
- ts_iso: ISO8601 timestamp in UTC
- origin_service: short name (e.g., dispatcher, kernel, kvcache, allocator)
- host_id: node identifier (k8s node / instance id)
- shard_id: runtime shard or device id when applicable (e.g., gpu-0)
- request_id: upstream request trace id if present, otherwise generated
- route_tag: customer or route identifier (when applicable)
- phase: high-level phase (ingest, scheduling, dispatch, kernel_exec, postprocessing)
- level: INFO/WARN/ERROR
- payload: structured JSON blob with event-specific fields (see examples)

Minimal telemetry fields table (copyable):
| field       | type   | example                        | notes |
|-------------|--------|--------------------------------|-------|
| event_id    | string | 9f8b6aab-...                   | uuid4 |
| ts_iso      | string | 2026-02-14T18:03:23.123Z       | UTC |
| origin_service | string | kernel                      | short service name |
| host_id     | string | i-0a1b2c3d4e5f                 | k8s node id or instance |
| shard_id    | string | gpu-0                         | device/shard context |
| request_id  | string | req-4b123                      | correlates to client request |
| route_tag   | string | prod-chat-1                   | optional but highly recommended |
| phase       | string | kernel_exec                   | one of the canonical phases |
| level       | string | WARN                          | log level |
| payload     | object | {"lat_ms": 4.2}              | event-specific details |

Event envelope example (JSON):
{
  "event_id": "9f8b6aab-1234-4cde-8a7b-0abcde123456",
  "ts_iso": "2026-02-14T18:03:23.123Z",
  "origin_service": "kernel",
  "host_id": "node-42",
  "shard_id": "gpu-0",
  "request_id": "req-4b123",
  "route_tag": "prod-chat-1",
  "phase": "kernel_exec",
  "level": "INFO",
  "payload": {
    "lat_ms": 12.4,
    "seq_len": 256,
    "kv_hit": true,
    "kernel_variant": "vectored-tc"
  }
}

Enrichment rules (construction time):
1) Attach stable host_id and shard_id at process startup. Fail open: if shard unknown, set "shard_id": "unknown".
2) Propagate request_id from surface API through the dispatcher to the kernel; if absent, synthesize and mark with a "synthesized_request_id" boolean in payload.
3) Route tagging: upstream routers should add route_tag; if missing, call-site should derive route from model_id or team config.
4) Add deployment metadata (commit hash, kernel build id) to host-level heartbeat events produced every 5 minutes.

Sampling and retention guidance:
- Full tracing is expensive. Apply progressive sampling: 100% sampling for ERROR events, 10% for WARN, and reservoir sampling for INFO subject to label-based overrides (e.g., always sample requests tagged as "perf-eval").
- For high-volume kernels, emit aggregated rollup events per minute per shard with the fields: ts_minute, shard_id, kernel_variant, q1,q50,q95,q99,invocations,total_tokens. Use these for fast dashboards and cost-aware alerts.

Triage playflow (step-by-step):
1) Detect: alert triggers (e.g., p99 latency > SLO threshold on a route) should create an incident ticket with a link to the minute rollup and sample traces.
2) Initial burst analysis (5 min): run the minute rollup query filtered by route_tag -> check p50/p95/p99 delta, invocation count, token distribution.
3) Correlate with host-level signals: filter events by ts range and examine host heartbeats for thermal/power anomalies, collector reports for kernel build mismatch, and allocator warnings.
4) Expand to kernel-level events: pull kernel_exec events for the suspect shards and examine payload fields (lat_ms, seq_len, kernel_variant, tensor_core_util). Look for step changes in kernel_variant mix or sudden rise in seq_len.
5) Cross-check kvcache: look for kvcache miss spikes in the same time window using payload.kv_hit==false and kvcache warmup events. A kvcache miss storm often explains latency spikes.
6) If no kernel resource anomaly, inspect dispatcher and admission controller events for queue depth, preemption, or credit exhaustion.
7) If root cause unclear, collect a deterministic trace sample: set temporary sampling override to 100% for the offending route_tag for 2 minutes and capture full traces.
8) Containment: based on root cause, apply one of the quick mitigations (see Quick mitigations below), open a rollback or canary pause if needed, and annotate incident ticket with event ids of representative traces.

Quick mitigations (common):
- Increase per-route concurrency cap by +20% for 2 min via routing console (when admission controller is too restrictive).
- Temporarily pin route to a lower-fidelity model-variant to avoid kernel stalls.
- Evict cold kvcache on a small percentage of nodes to re-balance warm cache.
- Throttle low-priority background workloads on nodes reporting thermal or memory pressure.

Example KQL/SQL queries (schematic):
1) Minute rollup for route: SELECT ts_minute, shard_id, kernel_variant, q50, q95, q99, invocations FROM runtime_rollups WHERE route_tag = 'prod-chat-1' AND ts_minute BETWEEN x AND y ORDER BY ts_minute;
2) Kernel event histogram: SELECT bucket(lat_ms, [0,1,2,5,10,20,50,100]) AS lat_bkt, count(*) FROM events WHERE origin_service='kernel' AND ts_iso BETWEEN ... GROUP BY lat_bkt;
3) Correlate kvcache misses: SELECT request_id, ts_iso, payload.kv_hit, payload.seq_len FROM events WHERE origin_service IN ('kvcache','kernel') AND ts_iso BETWEEN ... AND route_tag='prod-chat-1' ORDER BY ts_iso LIMIT 500;

Investigation checklist (runnable):
- Reproduce local microbench with same kernel_variant and seq_len distribution.
- Compare kernel build id from host heartbeat to the canary fleet build id.
- Run a synthetic traffic replay using the request surface replay harness with identical token distribution.
- If memory pressure suspected, capture allocator diagnostic snapshot (see allocator-runbook).

Runbook for kernel regression rollback decision: (decision matrix)
- Severity: P0 (customer impacting or SLO breach > 1 hour): immediate rollback to last known good kernel_variant and schedule hotfix release.
- Severity: P1 (intermittent SLO breach < 1 hour): throttle traffic via routing and open detailed profiling ticket.
- Severity: P2: schedule follow-up experiment and kernel bisect.

Ownership, SLAs and notifications:
- Primary owner for this contract: Serving Runtime Observability (oncall): runtime-observability@redwood.ai.
- Oncall response SLA: acknowledge within 15 minutes for P0/P1, start triage within 30 minutes.
- Postmortem requirement: detailed incident postmortem for any event that caused > 1 hour SLO breach or > 5% customer error increase.

Rollout checklist for instrumenting a new component into the contract:
1) Add the canonical envelope producer to the component library with local validation.
2) Emit host-level heartbeat and attach deployment metadata.
3) Unit test event envelope, including synthesized request_id path.
4) Stage sampling rules and verify ingestion at low volume to the ingest cluster.
5) Add dashboard tiles: per-minute rollup, p95/p99 heatmap, kvcache-hit-rate, kernel_variant mix.
6) Run a 48-hour shadow run with sample-rate parity and measure telemetry cost.

Debugging utilities and commands (examples):
- Collect live kernel traces: rtr-collect --shard gpu-0 --since 2026-02-14T18:00Z --limit 200 --output /tmp/traces.ndjson
- Query rollups: rtql "SELECT * FROM runtime_rollups WHERE route_tag='prod-chat-1' AND ts_minute >= '2026-02-14T17:00'"

Appendix: Known anti-patterns and gotchas:
- Relying solely on p95 can hide p99 regressions that are caused by rare long sequences; always check p99 and the seq_len distribution.
- Missing request_id propagation from the gateway makes correlation much slower; instrument synthetic propagation in test harnesses.
- Overly aggressive INFO sampling can starve postmortem investigators of the causal chain.

References and related docs:
- Causal latency attribution playbook (see related_pages)
- Runtime rollup schema (runtime_rollup_schema.md)
- Allocator diagnostic runbook (allocator-runbook)

Contact and maintenance:
- Document owner: Aisha Patel (aisha.patel@redwood.ai)
- Review cadence: quarterly or after any major incident.

Change log:
- 2025-11-04: Created initial draft.
- 2026-01-10: Added sampling guidance and rollup schema.
- 2026-02-15: Finalized triage playflow and decision matrix.

title: KV Cache Compaction Profiling Playbook
content:
## Purpose
This page documents how to profile KV cache fragmentation and compaction behavior in the serving runtime. It focuses on:
- Capturing allocator state snapshots (fragmentation, freelists, per-sequence residency)
- Correlating compaction/eviction activity with tail latency (p95/p99) and scheduler phase boundaries
- Diagnosing “pathological fragmentation” cases (bursty churn, mixed sequence lengths, long-lived sessions)

This is an engineering playbook (not a runbook). If you are actively mitigating a production incident, follow the runtime operational runbook and use this page for deeper diagnosis.

## When to use this playbook
Use these steps when you see one or more of the following:
- p95/p99 decode latency spikes during burst traffic, especially with mixed prompt lengths
- Increased allocator overhead (alloc/free/defrag) or copy activity, without throughput gains
- Unexpected evictions or opportunistic shedding correlated with KV memory pressure
- Intermittent OOMs in high-churn chat workloads even when average utilization looks “safe”

## Prerequisites / access
- Access to the runtime host (Hosted canary or staging pool) via standard SRE SSH / debug workflow
- A trace viewer for Redwood distributed traces (Console → Tracing) and access to the “Serving Runtime” service
- Permission to use runtime debug endpoints (these are internal-only and may be disabled in some Dedicated/Private environments)

Recommended tooling (internal):
- `rwdctl` (runtime debug CLI) or equivalent admin RPC client
- `rwtrace` (trace export helper) or Console trace export
- `pprof` (CPU profiling) where enabled

## Safety and performance notes
- Allocator snapshots are designed to be low overhead, but they still walk allocator structures. Do not take snapshots at very high frequency in production.
- If you enable compaction debug logging, it can increase overhead and may distort latency measurements.
- Never capture request payloads or raw prompts in artifacts. Store only allocator state, counters, and trace IDs.

---

## Key concepts / what to look for
### Fragmentation vs utilization
High KV utilization is not necessarily bad. The key risk factor is fragmentation (free memory exists but cannot satisfy contiguous page/block needs without relocation).

Symptoms of pathological fragmentation:
- Fragmentation ratio stays high or increases over time even after load stabilizes
- Allocation failures/slow-path allocations rise while total free bytes are non-trivial
- Compaction bytes moved spikes repeatedly but fragmentation does not improve
- Eviction rate increases during bursts in a way that correlates with latency spikes

### Scheduler phases
Most deployments budget compaction around scheduler boundaries:
- Prefill → Decode transition
- Decode loop time-slices
- Background compaction worker (if enabled)

When correlating to tail latency, the question is: “Did compaction work happen on the critical path of decode?”

---

## Metrics to pull (minimum set)
Use these metric names/definitions as standardized in the metrics standard page. If names differ in your environment, consult the runtime metrics catalog.

Minimum set (per model + pool):
- `kv_cache_fragmentation_ratio` (gauge)
- `kv_cache_free_bytes` (gauge)
- `kv_cache_used_bytes` (gauge)
- `kv_cache_alloc_slowpath_total` (counter)
- `kv_cache_compaction_runs_total` (counter)
- `kv_cache_compaction_bytes_moved_total` (counter)
- `kv_cache_compaction_time_ms_total` (counter)
- `kv_cache_compaction_budget_exhausted_total` (counter)
- `kv_cache_evictions_total` (counter; with labels for reason/tier)
- `runtime_decode_latency_ms` (histogram; p50/p95/p99)

Helpful breakdowns:
- By tier (Hosted standard vs enterprise vs Dedicated)
- By scheduler phase (prefill vs decode)
- By model version and quantization profile

---

## Procedure A: Capture allocator state snapshots
Allocator snapshots should be captured at three times:
1) Baseline (steady state, before inducing burst)
2) During a latency spike / burst window
3) After compaction has run for a while (or after workload cool-down)

### A1) Snapshot via debug endpoint (recommended)
1. Identify a target runtime instance
   - Hosted: choose a canary instance in the target region/pool
   - Dedicated: choose a single replica where you can safely reproduce the behavior

2. Capture a snapshot
   Command (example):
   - `rwdctl runtime kv snapshot --format=json --include=freelist,arenas,sequences --output=/tmp/kv_snapshot_$(date +%s).json`

3. Collect instance metadata alongside the snapshot
   - Runtime version (e.g., `runtime-1.22.x`)
   - Model name + revision
   - GPU type + memory size
   - Feature flags (compaction enabled, background worker enabled)
   - Active limits (compaction budget time/bytes, trigger thresholds)

4. Upload artifacts
   - Store in the engineering perf artifact location for the project (follow your org’s artifact retention policy)
   - Include the trace IDs captured in Procedure B

### A2) Snapshot cadence guidance
- For investigation: no more than 1 snapshot every 30–60 seconds during a burst.
- For long soak tests: 1 snapshot every 5–10 minutes plus on event triggers (latency spike, eviction spike, OOM near-miss).

### A3) What a snapshot should contain (fields)
Snapshot should include (at minimum):
- Arena summary: total bytes, used bytes, free bytes
- Fragmentation summary: fragmentation ratio, largest contiguous free run
- Free-list histogram: free run sizes (p50/p95/p99)
- Relocation state (if compaction enabled): pending moves, in-flight moves
- Sequence residency summary: number of active sequences, pinned sequences, per-tier counts

If the snapshot does not include “largest contiguous free run” or free-run histogram, the snapshot is incomplete for diagnosing fragmentation.

---

## Procedure B: Correlate compaction/eviction to latency traces
### B1) Collect trace exemplars during spikes
1. Identify the time window where `runtime_decode_latency_ms` p99 increases.
2. Export trace exemplars for that window:
   - At least 10 traces near p99
   - At least 10 “normal” traces from an adjacent non-spiky window

3. For each trace, record:
   - Trace ID
   - Route / endpoint (chat vs generate)
   - Model + revision
   - Request shape (prompt length bucket, max_new_tokens bucket) — only as coarse buckets

### B2) Spans to look for
The runtime emits spans around compaction and eviction. Common span names:
- `kv.compaction.step`
- `kv.compaction.relocate_block`
- `kv.compaction.copy_kernels`
- `kv.eviction.select_candidate`
- `kv.eviction.evict_sequence`
- `scheduler.decode_tick`
- `scheduler.prefill`

What you want to determine:
- Whether compaction steps overlap decode critical sections
- Whether compaction “step” durations cluster around the spike window
- Whether eviction selection/eviction work is happening during decode bursts

### B3) Correlation checklist
For each spike window:
- Does `kv_cache_compaction_bytes_moved_total` slope increase?
- Does `kv_cache_compaction_budget_exhausted_total` increase (indicating we tried to compact but hit limits)?
- Does fragmentation ratio improve after bytes moved, or stay flat?
- Are evictions rising (especially for higher tiers or pinned sessions)?
- Do traces show compaction spans on the critical path of decode?

If traces show compaction on the decode critical path, confirm whether compaction is being triggered in the wrong scheduler phase or whether budgeting is too aggressive.

---

## Procedure C: Diagnose “pathological fragmentation” patterns
This section provides common patterns and how to validate them.

### Pattern 1: Mixed-length churn causes “Swiss cheese” freelists
Indicators:
- Free bytes are moderate/high
- Largest contiguous free run is small
- Free-list histogram is heavily skewed to small run sizes
- Slow-path allocations rise during bursts

Validation steps:
- Compare baseline vs burst snapshot: free-run histogram should shift toward smaller runs
- Check if compaction runs increase but largest run does not recover

Likely root causes:
- Block/page sizes mismatch common sequence length distribution
- Compaction trigger threshold too high (reactive instead of proactive)
- Compaction budget too low to “catch up” during churn

Next actions:
- Try lowering fragmentation trigger (canary only)
- Increase compaction budget slightly and confirm compaction stays off decode critical path
- Confirm scheduler hook placement (prefill/decode boundary vs continuous background)

### Pattern 2: Long-lived pinned sessions block compaction
Indicators:
- Many sequences marked pinned
- High fragmentation ratio localized to specific arenas
- Compaction repeatedly skips large pinned regions

Validation steps:
- Snapshot: verify pinned counts and pinned-byte totals
- Trace: evictions may spike for non-pinned sequences while pinned remain resident

Next actions:
- Confirm pinned semantics are correct (e.g., tool-calling sessions, Dedicated enterprise settings)
- Evaluate whether pinned sessions should be moved to separate arena/pool configuration
- Confirm eviction policy is tier-aware and respects pinned sequences

### Pattern 3: Compaction “thrash” (bytes moved high, no benefit)
Indicators:
- `bytes_moved_total` grows quickly
- Fragmentation ratio does not improve (or improves briefly then regresses)
- Copy kernels show up frequently in traces

Validation steps:
- Compare snapshots across 3 points (before/during/after): does largest run increase and stay increased?
- Check if eviction events immediately re-fragment the arena (churn after compaction)

Likely root causes:
- Workload churn rate is higher than compaction’s steady-state ability to maintain contiguity
- Compaction trigger oscillation (no hysteresis)

Next actions:
- Add/adjust hysteresis between “start compaction” and “stop compaction” thresholds
- Reduce compaction aggressiveness and rely more on eviction under overload, or vice versa, depending on tier goals

### Pattern 4: Budgeting misplacement causes decode stalls
Indicators:
- Traces show compaction spans nested under decode critical spans
- p99 spikes align with `kv.compaction.step` durations
- `budget_exhausted_total` may be low (we are doing work, but at the wrong time)

Validation steps:
- Inspect scheduler phase annotations in trace
- Check whether compaction is being called at every decode tick instead of at safe boundaries

Next actions:
- Move budget enforcement to safe scheduler boundaries
- Cap step duration more aggressively (time-based budget) rather than bytes-only

---

## Procedure D: Minimal reproducible benchmark in perf lab
When you need a reliable repro outside prod:

1) Use the fragmentation workload generator (benchmark-lab) configured for:
- Mixed prompt lengths (e.g., 128–8k)
- Mixed max_new_tokens (e.g., 64–2k)
- High cancellation rate (to mimic churn)
- A small proportion of long-lived sessions

2) Run two variants:
- Compaction OFF (baseline)
- Compaction ON with canary settings

3) Collect artifacts:
- p95/p99 decode latency
- Throughput
- Allocator snapshots at the same cadence for both runs
- Trace exemplars for spikes

4) Acceptance criteria (investigation phase):
- Compaction should reduce fragmentation ratio under the same workload without increasing steady-state p50 latency
- p99 should not show new spikes attributed to compaction spans

---

## Interpreting snapshot outputs (quick guide)
### Key derived values
- “Largest contiguous free run” matters more than “total free bytes” for avoiding slow-path alloc/defrag.
- A healthy steady state often looks like:
  - Fragmentation ratio stable or slowly improving
  - Largest free run not collapsing under burst
  - Slow-path allocations near zero except at ramp-up

### Red flags
- Largest free run collapses during bursts and does not recover after compaction
- Slow-path alloc counter increases monotonically in a steady workload
- Compaction bytes moved increases while fragmentation ratio stays flat
- Evictions spike for high-priority tiers or for pinned sequences (should not happen)

---

## What to attach to an investigation ticket
When opening a runtime investigation (Linear/Jira), attach:
- 2–3 allocator snapshots (baseline / spike / after)
- A metrics screenshot showing fragmentation ratio, bytes moved, evictions, and p99 over the same window
- 5–10 trace IDs around p99 and 5–10 trace IDs around baseline
- Runtime version + model revision + GPU type
- Feature flag state and compaction budget settings

Owners to @ for triage:
- KV cache / allocator: Omar El-Sayed, Samir Qureshi
- Scheduler integration: Sofia Ivanova, Julian Moore
- Metrics standardization: Allison Grant
- SRE escalation / canary guardrails: Sean Gallagher, Rafael Mendes

---

## Appendix: Debug toggles (engineering-only)
These are common toggles used during controlled canaries and lab testing. Do not change production defaults without the rollout owner and SRE approval.

- `kv_compaction_enabled` (bool)
- `kv_compaction_background_worker_enabled` (bool)
- `kv_compaction_trigger_fragmentation_ratio` (float)
- `kv_compaction_budget_max_ms_per_tick` (int)
- `kv_compaction_budget_max_bytes_per_tick` (int)
- `kv_eviction_enabled` (bool)
- `kv_eviction_policy` (enum: tier_aware_lru, …)

If you suspect compaction is contributing to an incident, use the kill-switch path documented in the runtime compaction runbook (do not attempt ad-hoc changes).

title: Workload Portrait & Sampler Playbook
content:
Overview

This playbook prescribes a compact, reproducible method for building workload portraits and converting those portraits into sampler policies used by the runtime. The goal is simple: capture the most diagnostically valuable traces given constrained storage and ingestion budgets, prioritize SLO-sensitive cohorts, and validate sampling choices via shadow replay before production rollout.

Audience

Runtime engineers, SREs, performance researchers, and platform product engineers who are responsible for profiling, kernel scheduling validation, and observability.

Goals

- Produce workload portraits: histograms, canonical traces, and impact statements per route/cohort.
- Generate versioned sampler policies that map cohorts to sample rates, triggers, and retention tiers.
- Validate sampling and capture fidelity through mirrored collection and shadow replay.

Core concepts (short)

- Workload portrait: short JSON/YAML summary containing p50/p95/p99 of sequence length, tokens, KV cache hit rate, and 3 canonical traces.
- Cohort: predicate for sampling (route, model, customer_tier, seq_bucket).
- Sampler policy: control-plane artifact (YAML) mapping cohorts -> sample_rate + triggers.
- Shadow replay: deterministic replay of captured traces against baseline and candidate kernels.

Principles

1) Discover before capturing: use cheap histograms (5m granularity) for discovery; escalate to full traces only where needed.
2) Keep policies limited and auditable: small set of cohort predicates that are easy to reason about and versioned in git.
3) Validate in staging: mirror, replay, and run explicit hypothesis tests before any policy changes go wide.
4) Privacy-first: redact/pseudonymize textual content by default; keep provenance metadata for debugging.

Process (step-by-step)

1) Discovery (7-14 days)
- Select anchor routes: 8-12 routes covering ~75% of token volume or SLA-bound endpoints. Include a mix of PLG and enterprise.
- Deploy histogram exporter (5m buckets) to collect seq_len, tokens_per_request, kv_cache_hit_pct, and response_size. Collect 14 days.
- Perform brief owner interviews (15-30m) to capture SLOs, fidelity tolerances, and known hotspots.

Deliverables: portrait.csv (route, p50/p95/p99 seq_len, tokens, owner, sla_flag), owner-notes.md.

2) Portrait synthesis (2-4 days)
- Cluster histogram vectors and business attributes into 3-6 portraits (examples: interactive-short, streaming-multi-turn, batch-embeddings).
- For each portrait produce: one-line impact statement, primary SLO metric, cost-sensitivity score (1-5), and sample density recommendation.

3) Sampler policy design (2-3 days)
- Baseline discovery rate: 0.05% to 0.5% depending on token volume.
- Portrait-driven rules: prioritize SLO-bound cohorts with higher baseline rates and escalation triggers.
- Retention tiers: full traces (14d default), escalated retention (up to 90d with approvals), aggregated histograms (365d).

Example sampler YAML (human readable)

sampler_version: 4
default_sample_rate: 0.0005  # 0.05%
cohorts:
  - id: interactive_short
    match: "route =~ '^chat:' and seq_len < 256"
    sample_rate: 0.01
    triggers:
      - metric: latency_p95_ms
        threshold: 250
        action: escalate_to_full_capture
  - id: streaming_multi_turn
    match: "archetype == 'streaming-multi-turn'"
    sample_rate: 0.005
    triggers:
      - metric: node_memory_util
        threshold: 0.9
        action: increase_sample_rate_to_0.05_ttl_180m
  - id: batch_embeddings
    match: "route =~ '^embed:'"
    sample_rate: 0.0002
    triggers:
      - metric: job_failure_count
        threshold: 1
        action: capture_failed_jobs_full

Implementation checklist (ops)

- Tagging: ensure request envelopes include route, archetype, customer_tier, seq_len_bucket.
- Provenance: every sampled record must include request_id, kernel_hash, node_id, model_variant, sampler_policy_version.
- Node-local sampler: a lightweight plugin that applies control-plane YAML and exposes /_internal/sampler/health and /_internal/sampler/policy endpoints.
- Telemetry: emit sample_rate_by_cohort, sample_loss_rate, policy_sync_lag to observability.
- Redaction: default pipeline must remove/replace any user prompt text fields before storage.

Validation (mirror + replay)

Stage A: Mirror (72h)
- Mirror sampled captures to validation cluster. Keep copies short-lived.

Stage B: Shadow replay
- Replay traces deterministically against baseline kernel and candidate kernels.
- Compute deltas: latency_p50/p95/p99, memory_alloc_per_request, token_cost_per_request, error_rate.

Acceptance thresholds

- SLO portraits: p95 delta <= 5% AND p99 delta <= 10%.
- Memory-sensitive portraits: OOM increase <= 0.1% absolute.
- Cost-sensitive portraits: token_cost delta <= 7%.

If a portrait fails validation, increase sample density for that portrait and re-run mirror + replay.

Operational runbook (abridged)

Trigger conditions:
- Coverage drop: sampler coverage decrease > 50% in 30 minutes.
- Sampler errors: sampler_error_rate > 0.2%.
- Config drift: policy_sync_lag > 2 minutes on >10% of nodes.

Oncall triage steps:
1) Check control-plane rollout logs and policy versions.
2) Query node sampler health: curl http://<node>:PORT/_internal/sampler/health
3) If coverage loss confirmed: enable emergency_full_capture for affected cohorts (TTL: 6h) and page runtime team.
4) Collect trace ids, attach to incident ticket, and escalate to runtime-observability.

CLI Snippets

- Emergency full capture via control-plane: 
  rctl sampler trigger --policy emergency_full --cohort interactive_short --ttl 360

- List sampled traces for route: 
  rctl traces list --route chat:widget --since 24h --limit 500

- Check node policy version: 
  curl http://<node>:PORT/_internal/sampler/policy | jq .version

Dashboards (recommended panels)

- Coverage matrix: cohort x hour showing sample_rate and total_traces.
- Sampler health: policy_sync_lag, sampler_errors_per_min, sample_loss_rate.
- Portrait regression panel: p95/p99 deltas by portrait.
- Cost vs visibility: daily storage cost for traces vs number of portraits captured.

Configuration & cost guideline (summary)

Item | Default | Rationale
Default discovery sample rate | 0.05% | Low-cost discovery for high-volume routes
Full-trace retention | 14 days | Enough for incident triage and replay
Histogram retention | 365 days | Useful for trend/seasonality analysis
Estimate storage | ~$90/day per 10k full traces | Varies with compression and redaction

Privacy and security

- Redact full prompt text fields and store only hashed identifiers for join operations.
- Restricted customers: capture only aggregated telemetry unless explicit approvals are present; always enforce KMS encryption for persisted traces.

Ownership & escalation

- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime
- Observability steward: runtime-observability
- Oncall: eng-sre
- Escalation path: runtime-oncall page -> #runtime-urgent -> create incident via opsbot

Experiment template (compact)

Hypothesis: "Kernel change X will reduce p95 by >=6% for interactive-short portrait."
Design: bump interactive_short sample_rate to 1% for 72h and mirror captured traces to staging.
Success: p95 reduction >= 6% OR p99 reduction >= 4% AND no OOM increase > 0.05%.
Rollout: successful experiments -> canary 5% traffic 24h -> 25% 48h -> 100%. Failures -> revert and document.

Related pages

- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/controlled-kernel-perturbation-playbook-2026
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/microbenchmark-suite-variance-analysis-2025

Document history

- created_at: 2025-03-18
- last_updated: 2026-01-12

Authors & reviewers

Author: Daniela Ruiz
Reviewers: Maya Chen, Liam O'Connor

Status: published

title: GPU memory fragmentation diagnostics and remediation playbook
content:
Summary:
This playbook defines a concrete, repeatable process for diagnosing and remediating GPU memory fragmentation observed in Redwood serving hosts. It consolidates telemetry to capture, commands and tooling to run during a live incident, thresholds we consider actionable, short-term mitigations to restore capacity, and long-term fixes to avoid recurrence.

Why this matters:
- Fragmentation can cause apparent out-of-memory (OOM) or allocation failures even when aggregate free memory looks sufficient.
- For inference workloads with persistent KV caches, allocator metadata, and mixed allocation sizes (small tensors, large KV pages), fragmentation reduces usable contiguous memory and increases tail latency / request rejection.
- Fast triage reduces customer impact and avoids unnecessary instance reprovisioning.

Scope / Audience:
- Applies to Redwood Dedicated and Private runtime nodes running CUDA-based inference backends (PyTorch/TVM/Rust CUDA runtime).
- Intended for oncall SREs, runtime engineers, and platform-hosting engineers.

Symptoms that point to fragmentation (not just peak usage):
1) Allocation failures or repeated cudaMalloc retries while nvidia-smi reports >20% free memory.
2) Rapid oscillation of free memory without matching process exit/creation events.
3) Frequent small free segments reported by allocator introspection (see "Telemetry to collect").
4) Successful large allocations after contiguous-space freeing (restart/evict/cache-trim).

Telemetry to collect (must be available on all runtime nodes):
- NVML / nvidia-smi samples (1s granularity if possible): memory.total, memory.used, memory.free, utilization.gpu, process PIDs and memory per process.
  - Command: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.total,memory.used,memory.free,utilization.gpu --format=csv -l 1
- CUDA allocator metrics (if enabled via runtime): per-process: allocated_bytes, reserved_bytes, allocation_failures, peak_reserved.
  - For PyTorch: TORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=enabled_stat=true or custom allocator hooks.
- CUDA malloc-async / mempool stats: free_count, reserved_count, largest_free_block_size (if runtime exposes).
- Host-level memory churn and OOM events: dmesg for oom-killer, system journal for process SIGKILL.
- GPU per-process mmap-style allocations: nv-hostengine / Nsight info or driver logs.
- Runtime-level KV cache metrics: shard_reserved_bytes, shard_active_bytes, eviction_count.
- Traces / flamegraphs around allocation calls during suspect windows.

Derived metrics and dashboard panels we recommend:
- Fragmentation ratio = 1 - (largest_contiguous_free_block / memory.free). (If largest_contiguous is unavailable, approximate using max single free chunk observed via allocator telemetry.)
- Allocation failure rate / minute per process.
- Average and P95 contiguous_free_block_size over 5m windows.
- % of memory held by long-lived allocations (> 10m).
- Eviction frequency and time-to-evict for KV cache.
- Requests rejected due to mem budget exceeded.

Actionable thresholds (initial defaults, tune per fleet):
- Fragmentation ratio > 0.6 for more than 2 minutes => investigate.
- Allocation failure rate > 3/min for any process => immediate mitigation.
- Largest_contiguous_free_block < model_max_allocation_size * 1.1 => urgent.

Immediate triage steps (ordered, meant for live incidents):
1) Confirm symptom: correlate API error logs (cuda OOM, allocation failed) with GPU telemetry timestamps.
2) Capture snapshot (do not reboot until snapshot taken):
   - sudo nvidia-smi --query-compute-apps=pid,process_name,used_memory --format=csv -f /tmp/gpu-proc-snapshot.csv
   - sudo nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.total,memory.used,memory.free --format=csv -f /tmp/gpu-snapshot.csv
   - Collect runtime allocator stats (endpoint /debug/alloc-stats or environment hooks).
   - If possible, run nsight systems quick snapshot: nsys profile --sample=none --trace=cuda --output=/tmp/nsys-snapshot
3) Identify long-lived owners: sort per-process used_memory and cross-reference process start times. If a single process holds a lot of small allocations, open a ticket for that service to examine pooling settings.
4) Apply safe short-term mitigations (pick in descending order of non-disruptiveness):
   - Trigger runtime cache trimming API for the affected shard(s). Example: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:9001/admin/cache/trim?target=20%
   - If allocator supports trimming (cudaMallocAsync pools), call the pool release function (approx: CUDA API cudaMemPoolTrim).
   - Reduce per-request cache prefetch length or per-request tensor pre-allocation via feature flags.
   - As last resort for single-host recovery: gracefully restart the offending process (preferred) rather than full host reboot. Use graceful drain/replica failover steps documented in the service's runbook.
5) If mitigations restore contiguous memory, keep the node in investigational mode: increase logging, take several post-mitigation snapshots.

If live mitigations fail (escalation path):
- If multiple nodes show fragmentation simultaneously, escalate to runtime+infra owners immediately.
- Reprovision with hot-swap of capacity: put node into drain in autoscaler, migrate traffic, then reboot host to reclaim whole GPU state. Reboot is last resort and requires labeling for postmortem.

Root cause analysis checklist (post-incident):
- Which allocator was in use (cudaMalloc, cudaMallocAsync, cub::DeviceMemoryPool, PyTorch caching allocator)?
- Were there mixed allocation sizes or a burst of very small allocations (tens to hundreds of KB)?
- Were there pinned host allocations interfering with DMA?
- Is there a mismatch between tensor pooling parameters (max_split_size_mb) and typical tensor sizes for this workload?
- Did kernel scheduling (concurrent kernels) leave many small allocations resident?
- Was quantization or model shard fragmentation causing many small mapping allocations (memcpy/backing pages)?

Long-term remediation patterns and engineering changes:
1) Enable allocator-level stats by default in canary fleets and add fragment metrics to runtime telemetry.
2) Switch heavy-allocation workloads to cudaMallocAsync + explicit mempool trimming where supported.
3) Tune TORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF settings for services with many small tensors. Example: export TORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=max_split_size_mb:32,garbage_collection_threshold:0.7
4) Introduce periodic background consolidation: low-priority background job that releases cached pools when utilization is low.
5) Add a shard-aware allocator: prefer coalesced large allocations for KV cache pages and compact small per-request allocations into batch arenas.
6) Add preflight allocation check: ensure largest_contiguous_free_block >= model_peak_allocation before scheduling a heavy request (fail fast/route to fallback).
7) Improve admission control: route requests that need large contiguous allocation to nodes with verified contiguous capacity.

Recommended config snippets and examples:
- PyTorch allocator stats enable (env):
  export TORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=enable_stat=true,max_split_size_mb:32

- Example pool trim via CUDA (pseudocode):
  // runtime exposes admin endpoint calling into CUDA mempool API
  cudaMemPoolTrim(memPool, bytesToTrim);

- Grafana / Prometheus query examples (PromQL-like pseudo):
  - frag_ratio = 1 - (gpu_largest_contig_free_bytes / gpu_free_bytes)
  - allocation_failures_per_min = increase(cuda_allocation_failures_total[1m])
  - p95_largest_free = histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (gpu_largest_free_block_size_bytes_bucket))

Ownership and SLAs for mitigations:
- First responder: runtime oncall (SRE) — initial triage and snapshot collection within 5 minutes of alert.
- Runtime engineering: implement short-term mitigations and coordinate safe process restarts within 30 minutes.
- Platform infra: if host reboot required, schedule and annotate, and complete within 60 minutes with approval.
- Post-incident RCA: assigned to runtime engineering, deliverable within 7 business days with action items.

Playbook for reproducibility tests (QA / dev):
1) Create a synthetic workload that alternates many small allocations with sporadic large allocations to mimic KV + request tensors.
2) Run on a canary node with allocator statistics enabled and measure fragmentation growth.
3) Test mitigations: trimming, adjusting max_split_size_mb, and using cudaMallocAsync. Measure time to recover and allocation failure counts.
4) Record results and add to the regression test harness (link in related pages).

Postmortem template fields to fill if fragmentation caused production impact:
- Incident start/end timestamps
- Symptoms observed and evidence (logs, snapshots)
- Short-term mitigations applied and timestamps
- Root cause hypothesis and evidence supporting it
- Long-term actions planned and owners

Appendix: quick commands and notes
- Snapshot GPU processes: sudo nvidia-smi --query-compute-apps=pid,process_name,used_memory --format=csv
- Continuous NVML sampling: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.used,memory.free --format=csv -l 1 > /tmp/gpu-sample.csv &
- Nsight quick trace: nsys profile --trace=cuda --output=/tmp/trace -t 10s <workload-cmd>
- PyTorch: print(torch.cuda.memory_stats()) and torch.cuda.memory_reserved()/memory_allocated() endpoints.

Notes and tradeoffs:
- Reboots clear fragmentation but hide underlying leaks/anti-patterns. Prefer tracing and allocator changes over reboot as the primary fix.
- Enabling allocator stats has a small perf overhead; start with a 1% canary population before fleet-wide rollout.
- Some hardware/driver combos expose more allocator metadata (e.g., newer CUDA runtimes). Maintain a compatibility matrix in the runtime wiki.

Contacts and escalation list:
- runtime-oncall@redwood.internal (primary)
- eng-serving-runtime@redwood.internal (engineering owners)
- infra-pool-management@redwood.internal (capacity and host reboots)

Document provenance and change log:
- 2026-01-18: initial draft by Aisha Patel.
- 2026-02-14: reviewed and published; added PromQL examples and explicit thresholds (reviewers: Marco Nguyen, Lena Hoffmann, Diego Alvarez).

title: Observability Correlates and Fidelity Sampling Handbook
content:
Summary:
This handbook documents a pragmatic, production-ready approach to sampling inference requests and correlating runtime observability signals while preserving fidelity for SLO-sensitive investigations. It is intended for runtime engineers, SREs, and profiling owners who need to collect richer traces without perturbing normal serving economics or introducing measurement bias.

Goals:
- Provide sampling strategies that retain representative high-fidelity examples for latency, kernel, and model-quality correlation.
- Define instrumentation and trace glue points required to map kernel-level metrics back to request context.
- Give a step-by-step runbook for enabling, validating, and rolling back sampling in production.
- Capture alert thresholds and dashboards to detect sampling regressions and cost spikes.

Scope and Out-of-scope:
- Scope: request-level sampling, KV-cache warmup probes, kernel trace correlation, time-series enrichment, offline replay gating.
- Out-of-scope: full distributed profiling of non-LLM services, low-level GPU driver fixes, kernel implementation details.

Owner and Contacts:
- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime observability team (Asha Patel).
- Pager: eng-serving-runtime oncall.
- Escalation: Miguel Ortega (runtime lead) -> Emily Chen (SRE manager).

SLOs and Acceptance Criteria:
- Sampling overhead added to P99 latency: < 2% relative increase for non-sampled requests.
- Cost budget ceiling for sampling: < 1.5x current telemetry spend in steady-state (configurable per-customer pool).
- Fidelity recall: sampled corpus must include >= 95% of tail-event types observed in unsampled production stream over 24h window.

Instrumentation checklist (required fields):
1) Request provenance header: x-rwd-request-id assigned at ingress.
2) Trace correlation key: rwd_trace_id propagated through RPC and kernel queues.
3) Kernel span attachment: attach rwd_trace_id to GPU kernel launch metadata.
4) KV-cache lineage tags: include cache-hit/miss and cold-warm indicators.
5) Sample metadata: sample_reason, sample_weight, sample_version.

Sampling strategies (choose one or combine):
- Deterministic stratified sampling by request class: partition by route/model/tenant and sample fixed ratios per bucket. Good for stable representation.
- Reservoir sampling for high-cardinality attributes: keep an unbiased rolling sample of N examples per minute for attributes such as prompt template hash.
- Priority sampling for anomalies: automatically sample requests that exceed preconfigured latency or error thresholds (e.g., kernel longer than 2s, model fallback triggered).
- Adaptive cost-aware sampling: increase sample probability during detected fidelity deviations and throttle during cost spikes.

Fidelity-preserving hybrid algorithm (pseudocode):
```
# every request R arrives with attributes A
if R.latency > tail_threshold OR R.error != OK:
    emit_sample(R, reason='priority')
else:
    bucket = hash(A.route, A.model_version) % B
    if reservoir[bucket].push(R):
        emit_sample(R, reason='reservoir')
    elif rand() < base_rate[bucket]:
        emit_sample(R, reason='stratified')
```
Notes: reservoir.push returns true when the item replaces a slot in the reservoir. base_rate per-bucket should be tuned from traffic fingerprints.

Data model and storage table (example):
| field | type | description |
| rwd_trace_id | string | global trace id for correlation |
| request_id | string | ingress-assigned id |
| sample_reason | string | priority|reservoir|stratified|
| sample_weight | float | inverse of selection probability |
| kernel_spans | list | compressed kernel span blob (base64) |
| prompt_fingerprint | string | hashed prompt template |
| kv_cache_state | string | cold|warm|hit|miss |

Operational runbook: enabling sampling in a fleet
1) Preflight: verify a/b namespace for telemetry ingestion and storage quota.
2) Deploy telemetry agent change in canary region with sampling disabled by default.
3) Enable low-rate stratified sampling (0.001) for non-critical routes + priority sampling enabled.
4) Monitor: dashboards for sampled rate, telemetry write latency, P95/P99 request latency for unsampled traffic.
5) Gradually ramp base_rate by x2 every 20 minutes until target corpus size reached or cost ceiling hit.
6) Validate fidelity: run offline congruence checks comparing attribute distributions (prompt_fingerprint, route, tenant) between sampled corpus and full stream.
7) If any metric exceeds thresholds (latency increase >2% or telemetry cost >budget), rollback to previous sampling config.

Validation checks (CLI examples):
- Count by route: rwd-observability-cli count-samples --start t0 --end t1 --group-by route
- Kernel-to-request join verification: rwd-observability-cli verify-join --trace-id <id>
- Sampling bias test: rwd-stats-tool compare-distribution --field prompt_fingerprint --sampled sampled-ds --full full-ds

Alerting rules (recommended):
- Sampling throughput spike: sampled-events/min > 5x rolling-mean -> page SRE.
- Join failure rate > 0.5% (kernel spans not attaching) -> page runtime-team.
- Fidelity drift: KL divergence(prompt_fingerprint) between sampled and full > 0.15 -> create investigation ticket.

Common pitfalls and mitigations:
- Bias from route-skew: ensure base_rate per-route to prevent small high-QPS routes from dominating sample.
- Cache-warming perturbation: do not enable aggressive cache-prefetch sampling in customer-dedicated pools without approval.
- Time-of-day effects: when validating fidelity, compare equivalent windows (weekday vs weekend).

Example trace annotation (JSON snippet):
```
{
  'rwd_trace_id': 'rwd-4f2a',
  'request_id': 'req-925',
  'sample_reason': 'priority',
  'sample_weight': '1.0',
  'kernel_spans': 'base64(... )',
  'kv_cache_state': 'cold'
}
```
(Production payloads use double-quoted JSON; snippet uses single quotes for readability.)

Rollback and emergency procedures:
1) Flip a central feature flag to disable all non-priority sampling.
2) Revert agent job to previous version that had sampling disabled.
3) If telemetry ingestion is saturated, reduce sample retention TTLs and purge debug indices older than 6 hours.

Postmortem checklist for sampling-related incidents:
- Timestamp of change and rollout window.
- Change-set (config keys and agent binaries).
- Telemetry capacity graphs and cost delta.
- Sampled corpus snapshot for the incident window.
- Action items for automation or guardrails.

Dashboard and queries to build:
- Sampled vs unsampled latency percentiles by model_version.
- Kernel span attach success rate by node.
- Sample weight distribution and effective coverage.

Appendix: tuning knobs and recommended defaults
- base_rate per-route: 0.001 (low-QPS 0.01, high-QPS 0.0005)
- reservoir size per-bucket: 2000 items/minute
- priority tail_threshold: 1.5x P95 latency or absolute 2s
- telemetry cost ceiling: 1.5x baseline budget

Related pages and references:
- See runtime telemetry sampling contract (link internal) for protobuf schema.
- See causal-latency-attribution playbook for techniques to attribute end-to-end latency to kernels.

Revision history:
- 2025-11-12: created by Asha Patel.
- 2026-01-15: added adaptive cost-aware sampling section (Miguel Ortega).
- 2026-02-20: clarified reservoir defaults and rollback steps (Emily Chen).

title: Kernel stability siege testing and metrics manifest
content:
Summary:

This document defines the 'siege testing' program for runtime kernel components: a repeatable, low-variability stress protocol designed to exercise kernel hot paths, handoff/fallback logic, allocator behavior, and scheduler admission/signaling. The goal is to produce deterministic signal surfaces and a small set of stable metrics that correlate with production regressions and that can be used as gates for kernel changes and experimental rollouts.

Scope:
- Components: kernel dispatcher, prefetch/hint path, batch slicer, KV cache eviction function, tensor allocator, cooperative preemption shim.
- Environments: synthetic lab cluster (staging-fidelity-1), canary pool, and a shadow-prod replay mode.
- Exclusions: network stack-wide failures, hardware thermal throttling (handled separately).

Why 'siege' testing?
- Traditional microbenchmarks miss cross-component contention; siege runs sustained, controlled contention across shared resources to reveal systemic instabilities (oscillation, runaway backpressure, allocator landlocks).

Testing matrix and workload catalog:

1) Workload classes (representative):
   a) Short-chat burst (seq_len 32, reply tokens 32): high qps, small KV reuse.
   b) Long-completion (seq_len 1024, reply tokens 512): memory-heavy, long kernel occupancy.
   c) Mixed-concurrency (50% short, 25% long, 25% moderate): mimics PLG mixed surface.
   d) Cold-start storm (many first-frame requests with empty caches).
   e) Model-switch churn (frequent model variants and quantization profile swaps).

2) Siege axes (vary these orthogonally):
   - Concurrency (clients): 100, 500, 2000
   - Batch-intent randomness: deterministic vs jittered arrival
   - Kernel variant set: baseline, opt-kernel-A, fallback-emu
   - KV cache hit ratio: 10%, 50%, 90%
   - Quantization mode: fp16, int8-quantized

Metrics manifest (canonical signals) - interpreted as single-line CSV-compatible columns for dashboards:

| metric_name                          | description                                                   | unit    | sampling_window |
|--------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------|---------|-----------------|
| kernel_dispatch_latency_p50          | kernel dispatcher processing latency (p50)                    | ms      | 1m              |
| kernel_dispatch_latency_p95          | p95 latency for kernel dispatch                               | ms      | 1m              |
| kernel_dispatch_latency_p99          | p99 (captures microbursts / hitch)                            | ms      | 1m              |
| kernel_cpu_busy_ratio                | % time CPU-bound in kernel control loops                      | pct     | 1m              |
| kernel_gpu_occupancy_ratio           | % GPU occupancy recorded during runs                          | pct     | 1m              |
| allocator_fragmentation_score       | normalized score (0..1) indicating fragmentation severity     | unitless| 5m              |
| kvcache_eviction_rate                | evictions per second                                          | /s     | 1m              |
| backpressure_retry_rate              | fraction of requests retried due to admission                 | pct     | 1m              |
| kernel_fallback_count                | number of fallback activations (kernel -> software-path)      | count   | 1m              |
| input_tail_response_time_p999        | e2e input->final-token latency p999                           | ms      | 1m              |
| kernel_stall_incidents               | counted 10s+ stalls identified by watchdog                     | count   | 1m              |
| error_budget_consumed_rate           | % of configured SLO budget used due to this test              | pct     | 1m              |

Pass / fail and stability criteria:
- Green: All p99 latencies < target for workload class, allocator_fragmentation_score < 0.3, kernel_fallback_count == 0 during steady-state 30m window.
- Amber: Any single metric crosses warning threshold (p99 > target*1.5 or fragmentation > 0.6), or >5 fallback activations in 30m. Requires immediate engineering review and localized bisect.
- Red: Recurring oscillation (latency spikes followed by capacity collapse) or kernel_stall_incidents > 3 in 10m. Block rollout and open P1 triage.

Example thresholds (should be tuned per-model):
- Short-chat: p99 < 120ms (green), warning if >180ms, critical >400ms.
- Long-completion: p99 < 900ms (green), warning if >1400ms, critical >3000ms.

Run procedure (operator-run; 20–60 minutes per configuration):
1) Pre-checks:
   - Ensure staging-fidelity-1 node labels and quotas are provisioned: 
     * kubectl get nodes -l env=staging-fidelity-1
   - Confirm telemetry ingestion: grafana/ingest check 'kernel_dispatch_latency_p95' has fresh datapoints.
2) Deploy test harness (siege-runner):
   - git clone git@internal:redwood/siege-runner.git && cd siege-runner
   - kubectl apply -f deploy/siege-runner-staging.yaml --record
3) Load scenario selection:
   - Edit scenarios/config.yaml: set workload_class, concurrency, kv_hit_target.
   - Example snippet:
     workload: short-chat
     concurrency: 500
     batch_jitter_ms: 5
     kv_hit_ratio: 0.5
4) Start run and tag with experiment metadata:
   - ./bin/siege-runner --scenario scenarios/config.yaml --tags kernel-experiment=stable-2026 --duration 30m
