5) Observe live dashboards: grafana dashboard id: runtime-kernel-siege-v2 (owner: eng-serving-runtime)
6) Collect artifacts at end: traces archive (traces.tar.gz), perf profiles (perf.data), allocator heap dumps (allocator-heap-*.bin), and the siege-runner events.json.
7) Upload to artifact store: rclone cp traces.tar.gz remote:kernel-siege/2026-02-03-<runid>

Instrumentation and telemetry guidance:
- Required tracing spans: kernel.dispatch, kernel.batch_slice, allocator.malloc, kvcache.evict, scheduler.admit. Ensure spans include kernel_variant, model_id, request_cohort labels.
- Sampling policy: 100% for p99 tail-trace capture during siege; annotated with 'siege_run_id'.
- Lightweight task-level counters should be emitted at 1s resolution to Prometheus push gateway for short retention.

Dashboards and alerting (deliverables):
- runtime-kernel-siege-v2 (Grafana): combined heatmap of p99 over concurrency sweep, allocator fragmentation trend, fallback waterfall chart.
- Alerts (temporary during siege): alert if kernel_stall_incidents > 1 in 2m or backpressure_retry_rate > 2%.

Analysis checklist (post-run):
1) Verify steady-state window (last 20m) has stable request rates.
2) Correlate p99 spikes with kernel_fallback_count and allocator_fragmentation_score.
3) Inspect traces for sequential blocking patterns (allocator->dispatcher->kvcache).
4) Run deterministic replay of top-5 tail traces with kernel variant toggles.
5) If amber/red observed, run a binary bisect: isolate last change (kernel commit range) and re-run siege with single-commit rollback.

Binary bisect protocol (fast safety bisect):
1) Narrow candidate commits to the minimal set by commit-time ordering and previous green runs.
2) Deploy candidate commit to a 2-node canary pool with identical siege workload.
3) Run 10m micro-siege focused on reproducing failing signal.
4) If failing, mark commit as suspect and iterate; if green, exclude commit and continue.

Artifacts to archive per run (minimum):
- siege-metadata.json (scenario + tags)
- traces.tar.gz (all collected spans)
- perf-summaries.csv (per-node p50/p95/p99)
- allocator-heap-*.bin
- kube-state-dump.yaml

Ownership and cadence:
- Program owner: runtime-reliability (eng-serving-runtime) — primary contact: Asha Patel (author).
- Siege maintenance: rotate workloads quarterly and review thresholds after each major kernel merge.
- Scheduled runs: weekly smoke (short 20m mixed-concurrency) and monthly deep-siege (full matrix).

Runbook: interpreting common failure modes:
- Symptom: p99 spikes + immediate kernel_fallback_count increase. Likely cause: kernel invariant assertion or slow path fallback. Action: check kernel logs (grep "fallback-activated" /var/log/kernel/*.log), collect first-tail trace, disable canary kernel variant.
- Symptom: allocator_fragmentation_score rising steadily with long-completion workloads. Likely cause: allocation patterns + tensor pinning. Action: trigger allocator-compact routine, capture heap dump, run reproducer with slab debugging flags.
- Symptom: oscillation between high occupancy and near-zero throughput. Likely cause: admission controller thresholds too aggressive combined with eviction storm. Action: reduce admission aggression, increase kvcache size for test, re-run.

Security and data handling:
- Siege runs must not use customer data. All test corpora reside in 'siege-corpus/public' and are sanitized.
- Artifacts containing telemetry are internal-only; upload paths are restricted to eng-serving-runtime group.

Appendix: example CLI recipes
- Start a short-chat siege locally (developer):
  ./bin/siege-runner --scenario scenarios/short-chat.yaml --concurrency 100 --duration 20m --local-debug

- Replay a trace against a kernel variant under test:
  ./bin/trace-replay --trace traces/tail-1234.json --kernel-variant opt-kernel-A --replay-speed real-time

Notes and future work:
- Add thermal/NRM (non-replayable memory pressure) axis to catch hardware-coupled flakes.
- Integrate automated bisect with CI as an optional post-merge siege gate for high-risk kernel changes.

References:
- See related: controlled-kernel-perturbation-playbook (link in related_pages).
- Runtime telemetry data model: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/runtime-telemetry-sampling-cost-aware-profiling-manual-2027.json

Document change log:
- 2024-11-12: Created by Asha Patel.
- 2025-07-10: Added allocator_fragmentation metric and bisect protocol (reviewers: Marco Li).
- 2026-02-03: Formalized pass/fail thresholds and added artifact manifest (reviewers: Priya Nambiar, Ethan Cole).

title: Kernel Interaction Correlation Lab and Investigation Checklist
content:
Overview

Purpose: This document defines a repeatable lab and step-by-step investigation checklist for diagnosing subtle kernel-level interaction issues in the serving runtime (contention, preemption races, KV cache coherence artifacts, and cross-kernel priority inversion). The intent is to provide a reproducible experimental harness, required telemetry fields, and a prioritized checklist on-call and SRE engineers can follow.

Audience: runtime SREs, performance engineers, kernel engineers, and on-call rotation members.

Scope and when to use this guide
- Use this playbook when: tail latency spikes (>99th percentile increases by >2x), unexplained GPU scheduler stalls, intermittent model-switch oscillations, or when a regression appears only under mixed-concurrency workloads.
- Out of scope: hardware-level power faults (use hardware incident runbook), application-level correctness bugs in the model code.

Background and rationale
- Modern inference workloads combine continuous batching, KV cache, and multiple kernel variants. Subtle interactions (e.g., a long-running kernel holding a tensor memory lock while preemption is attempted) can manifest as short-lived but high-impact latency spikes. These interactions are difficult to identify from high-level traces; causal correlation across runtime, kernel scheduler, and GPU dispatch telemetry is required.

Telemetry and signal catalog (required)
- Request-level signals:
  - request_id (string)
  - route/model (string)
  - timestamp_queued_ms (int)
  - timestamp_kernel_enqueue_ms (int)
  - timestamp_kernel_start_ms (int)
  - timestamp_kernel_end_ms (int)
  - cpu_thread (string)
  - kernel_variant (string)
  - batch_id (string)
  - kv_cache_hit_ratio (float)
  - tokens_generated (int)

- Kernel/dispatcher signals:
  - gpu_dispatch_time_ms
  - gpu_complete_time_ms
  - kernel_preempt_attempts (int)
  - kernel_preempt_duration_ms
  - occupancy_percent
  - tensor_memory_alloc_bytes
  - kernel_wait_queue_len

- System signals:
  - node_cpu_load_1m
  - node_gpu_temp_celsius
  - nvlink_retry_count
  - iommu_faults
  - cgroup_preempt_events

Quick reference thresholds (operational defaults)
- 99th percentile latency increase: alert if > 2x baseline for 5m window.
- Kernel preempt attempts: alert if > 10 attempts/min on a node.
- GPU occupancy: alert if > 95% for sustained 2m while tail latency increases.

Investigation checklist (ordered, prescriptive)
1) Triage and collect artifacts (first 10 minutes)
   - Capture high-level traces: request traces for the afflicted timeframe (trace ID or request_id).
   - Export kernel-level telemetry: gpu_dispatch_time_ms, kernel_variant per batch, preempt counters.
   - Snapshot node-level metrics: top process GPU memory, nvtop snapshot, nvidia-smi dmon 1s for 30s.
   - Preserve scheduler logs and admission controller decision logs for the period.

2) Fast correlation (10–30 minutes)
   - Correlate request trace timestamps with kernel start/end timestamps. Look for requests with long gap between kernel_enqueue and kernel_start (queueing at CPU/dispatcher).
   - Identify whether affected requests share model/version or batch shape. If yes, candidate a model-specific kernel variant.
   - Query: Prometheus example
     - promql: |
       increase(kernel_preempt_attempts_total[5m])
       
   - Quick grep on dispatcher logs for spike patterns: grep -E "preempt|handoff|wait_queue" /var/log/runtime/dispatcher.log | sed -n '1,200p'

3) Kernel-level deep-dive (30–120 minutes)\   - Reconstruct kernel timeline using kernel_trace_id map to request_ids.
   - If preemption attempts are present, examine preempt_duration_ms distribution. Long durations indicate stalled preempt handlers or unexpected GPU stall.
   - Run a focused microbenchmark: replay a small synthetic trace containing the same batch sizes and sequence lengths. Use the lab harness described below.

4) Hypothesis-driven fault injection (1–3 hours)
   - Hypothesis examples:
     - H1: A kernel variant with large scratch memory occasionally triggers a slow tensor allocation path causing long preempt durations.
     - H2: KV cache hot-skip path causes serialization on a shared mutex while kernel handoff waits, causing queue buildup.
   - For H1: deploy a canary variant with reduced scratch growth (quantized variant) and run shadow traffic. Observe preempt and tail latency.
   - For H2: run mutex contention stress test: deliberately increase concurrent KV hits on same keyspace and observe kernel_wait_queue_len.

5) Mitigation and rollback (if confirmed)
   - Immediate mitigations:
     - Route affected traffic to fallback kernel variant or smaller model variant.
     - Temporarily reduce max_concurrency for the node to shed potential long-running kernels.
   - Rollback checklist:
     - Validate fallback route maintains 95th/99th latency SLOs for a 10-minute observation window.
     - If stable, start a staged rollout of the stable kernel variant with 10/30/60 minute ramp steps.

Lab experiment protocol (reproducible)
- Goal: reproduce tail-latency spike deterministically in the lab, isolate kernel interaction sequence, and test mitigations.

Prerequisites:
- Lab cluster with identical GPU family and runtime build (container image tag).
- Corpus of requests: select real traffic sample (anonymized) with 1k requests covering observed sequence length distribution.
- Harness repo: git@internal:redwood/runtime-labs.git, branch: telemetry-repro-2024

Steps:
1. Environment setup\   - Deploy runtime image: docker run --rm -e RUNTIME_TAG=telemetry-repro-2024 redwood/runtime:telemetry-repro-2024\   - Ensure profiling sidecar enabled (ENV: ENABLE_PROFILE=1) and lightweight BPF tracing agent running (rbpf-agent).
2. Load injection\   - Use lab injector: ./injector --corpus=corpus/sample-telemetry-corpus.json --qps=target --concurrency=target --shape=traffic-shape.yaml --trace-prefix=test-repro\   - Example: ./injector --corpus=sample.json --qps=120 --concurrency=64 --shape=mixed-burst.yaml --trace-prefix=test-repro
3. Collect artifacts automatically\   - run: ./collect-artifacts --since "2024-07-15T00:00:00Z" --out ./artifacts/test-repro.tar.gz\   - Artifacts: traces/*.json, kernel_telemetry.csv, dispatcher.log, nvidia-dmon.log, rbpf-traces/*.perf
4. Repeatability notes\   - Run at least 5 iterations per configuration; seed injector with deterministic random seed.

Observability playbook: queries and examples\- Prometheus examples:
  - Tail latency spike detection (5m): |
    (histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, route)))
  - Kernel preempt heatmap: |
    sum by (node, kernel_variant) (increase(kernel_preempt_attempts_total[15m]))

- Trace join example (SQL-ish pseudocode for internal trace store): |
  SELECT r.request_id, r.route, t.kernel_variant, t.start_ms, t.end_ms
  FROM requests r JOIN kernel_spans t ON r.trace_id = t.trace_id
  WHERE r.timestamp BETWEEN '2024-07-15T10:00:00Z' AND '2024-07-15T10:10:00Z'
  ORDER BY t.start_ms DESC

Kernel-level capture snippets
- BPF tracer snippet (example): |
  sudo rbpf-agent --attach=nv_dispatch --out /tmp/rbpf-attach.log --fields pid,tgid,dispatch_timestamp,kernel_name,stack_id

- nvidia-smi sampling (30s high-fidelity window): |
  nvidia-smi dmon -s u -d 1000 -o TD > nvidia-dmon.log &

- Minimal script to extract slow kernel spans (bash): |
  awk -F',' '$6 - $5 > 50 {print $0}' kernel_telemetry.csv | head -n 200

Fault injection template (Caution: only run in lab or staging)
- Introduce artificial allocation latency at the runtime allocator path to emulate slow scratch growth:
  - Use LD_PRELOAD wrapper which sleeps on gpu_alloc path once every N allocations.
  - Invocation YAML snippet: |
    fault_injection:
      type: allocator-sleep
      sleep_ms: 25
      every_n: 1000

Acceptance criteria for mitigations
- Measured improvement: 99th latency returns to within 1.2x baseline and kernel_preempt_attempts drop by >= 60% in 15-minute window.
- No increase in error rate or model output degradation (compare eval prompts used in shadow traffic).

Runbook ownership and escalation
- Primary owner: runtime-sre@redwood.com (rotation: oncall-runtime).
- Secondary: kernel-team@redwood.com.
- Pager escalation: if mitigation not effective within 30 minutes, escalate to oncall-eng-lead and open a Sev-2 incident.

Post-incident hygiene
1. Tag all artifacts and traces with incident id: INC-YYYYMMDD-XXX.
2. Record principal hypothesis and final resolution in the incident doc.
3. Add a regression test to the microbenchmark suite (benchmarks/interaction-regressions) if the issue was root-caused to a kernel variant.

Appendix: example artifact file formats
- kernel_telemetry.csv (columns): timestamp_ms, node, gpu_id, batch_id, kernel_variant, start_ms, end_ms, preempt_attempts, preempt_duration_ms, tensor_alloc_bytes
- dispatcher.log entries: timestamp iso8601 | node | event | details

Appendix: common failure patterns (cheat sheet)
- Pattern: "enqueue drift" — long gap between kernel_enqueue and kernel_start; likely dispatcher saturation or priority inversion.
- Pattern: "preempt tail" — repeated preempt attempts with long preempt_duration_ms; likely kernel stall or driver-level hang.
- Pattern: "kv hotlock" — KV cache hit correlation with dispatcher mutex contention; look for high kv_cache_hit_ratio and mutex wait traces.

Related pages and artifacts
- Add links to the final artifacts tarball in the incident doc and tag the change with the runtime build that was running.

Maintenance and cadence
- This playbook is reviewed quarterly by the profiling team. Add new signal fields when the runtime or kernel telemetry schema changes.

Contact and feedback
- For clarifications or to propose changes to the checklist, open a pull request against runtime-labs/docs/kernel-interaction-checklist.md or ping Priya Nair on Slack (#runtime-profiling).

End of document

title: Runtime fidelity sprint handbook: profiling, kernel interactions, and rollback protocols
content:
Overview

This handbook describes the goals, lab protocol, measurement artifacts, and safe rollback procedures for a 'fidelity sprint' — a focused engineering sprint whose objective is to change or validate runtime fidelity (model variant, quantization, kernel variant, batching policy, or routing policy) without regressing customer-facing SLOs or quality metrics. It is intended for engineers, SREs, and applied ML practitioners who run experiments across the serving runtime.

Why a fidelity sprint?
- Reduce regressions: small behavioral changes in kernels, quantization, or batching can introduce subtle regressions in output quality or latency distribution.
- Reproducibility: define a repeatable lab protocol for new kernel rollouts and quantization profiles.
- Operational safety: codify rollback and guardrails that preserve availability and cost targets.

Scope
- Applies to changes that affect inference fidelity or execution internals: kernel variants, quantized weights/ops, KV-cache prefetch hints, scheduler admission policies, batching heuristics, and model-variant routing.
- Does NOT cover: API surface changes, control-plane-only feature flips, or customer-facing configuration changes that don't change execution fidelity.

Owners and stakeholders
- Sprint lead: owner of the change (name + pager) — typically a runtime or applied-ML engineer.
- QA / Evals: applied-ml team responsible for the prompt-suite and regression gates.
- Oncall SRE: responsible for rollout monitoring and rapid rollback steps.
- Product owner: for business risk decisions when rolling out to Dedicated/Private customers.

SLOs and acceptance criteria
- Latency SLOs: 99th percentile tail latency increase <= 10% relative to baseline for the same workload mix.
- Error budget: no more than 5% additional errors (5xx or runtime timeouts) during canary windows.
- Quality gate: prompt-eval pass-rate delta <= 0.5% absolute (for high-sensitivity tasks) or <= 2% for low-sensitivity tasks.
- Cost delta: per-token cost increase <= 5% (unless explicitly approved).

Labs and environment matrix (table)
- The lab matrix documents target hardware, kernel variants, and fidelity settings we exercise:

| Environment | GPU type | Kernel variant | Model variant | Typical sequence lengths | Notes |
|-------------|----------|----------------|---------------|-------------------------|-------|
| local-lab-rt | A100 80GB | v2-lowlat | fp16 | 32-128 | dev-only, limited concurrency |
| perf-lab-1 | A100S | v2-default | int8-q | 16-256 | synthetic replay of production traces |
| canary-region | T4/GPU | v2-explicit-prefetch | fp16 | 8-512 | small % of real traffic |
| dedicated-staging | H100 | v3-kernel-tiling | int8-q | 64-1024 | reserved for enterprise smoke tests |

Prerequisites (checklist)
1) Baseline capture: collect a 24-hour production trace and compute baseline SLOs and per-route token distribution.
2) Eval prompt set: ensure there is a labeled prompt set for at least three sensitivity tiers (high/medium/low).
3) Telemetry hooks: feature flags, kernel parameter tags, and tracing for kernel decisions must be enabled.
4) Canary plan: percentage targets, ramp schedule, and alert thresholds declared in the sprint ticket.

Experiment procedure (numbered steps)
1. Prepare artifacts\   a. Build the kernel/quantization artifact and tag with semver: kernel:vX.Y.Z-fidelity-sprint\   b. Generate a benchmark spec (JSON) that includes: route list, concurrency shape, sequence-length distribution, and sample prompt corpus. Example: {"routes": ["chat_v1","completion_short"], "concurrency": "Poisson(8)", "sample_corpus": "gs://redwood-evals/fidelity-sprint/"}
2. Run lab smoke tests (local-lab-rt)\   a. Execute unit-level smoke with trace replay: ./scripts/replay_trace.sh --trace=24h-baseline --kernel=kernel:vX.Y.Z\   b. Validate memory, no OOMs, and kernel logs for warnings.
3. Microbenchmark suite (perf-lab-1)\   a. Run throughput and tail-latency suite: python tools/bench_runner.py --spec fidelity_bench.json --out /tmp/bench-results.json\   b. Record: p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, GPU UTIL, kernel occupancy.
4. Offline quality evals\   a. Run the labeled prompt-set through both baseline and candidate artifacts: eval-runner --baseline s3://... --candidate s3://... --metrics rouge,bert-score,exact_match\   b. Produce a delta report and flag prompts with >X% change for manual review.
5. Canary rollout\   a. Start with 0.5% traffic in canary-region for 30 minutes. Monitor SLO and eval signal.\   b. If green, ramp to 2% for 2 hours, then to 10% for 4 hours.\   c. During each window, run shadow-mirroring to capture full outputs for offline eval.
6. Production ramp and final validation\   a. Only after meeting acceptance criteria for two independent canary windows do we proceed to full region or Dedicated rollout.\\n
Monitoring and telemetry (what to watch)
- Latency heatmap per route and per-sequence-length bin.
- Kernel decision rate: % of requests using new kernel vs fallback.
- Error types: kernel-timeout, OOM, scheduler-rejected, model-internal-errors.
- Output divergence fingerprints: fingerprint ID match rate between baseline and candidate outputs (approximate hash equality).
- Cost signals: per-route GPU time, kernel time breakdown, and billing samples.

Alert thresholds (sample)
- p99 latency increase > 12% for >5m -> page_oncall (P1)\- error-rate increase > 5% for >5m -> page_oncall (P1)\- eval-pass-rate drop > 1% absolute for high-sensitivity prompts (manual review) -> escalate to product + applied-ml

Rollback procedure (runbook)
1) Automated rollback trigger \   - If any P1 alert above fires during canary, the system must automatically flip routing to baseline kernel variant for the affected cohort.
2) Manual rollback steps (if automation unavailable)\   a. Oncall runs: curl -XPOST https://controlplane.internal/api/rollout/rollback -d '{"target":"kernel:vX.Y.Z","reason":"p99-latency"}'\   b. Confirm traffic reverts using: k get routes --selector fidelity-sprint=true -o wide\   c. Validate telemetry: confirm p99 returns to baseline within 3x of mean reversion time (typically 2 minutes).
3) Post-rollback actions\   a. Create a hotfix ticket, attach all trace artifacts and eval failure cases.\   b. Hold a 2-hour warroom with applied-ml and kernel-owner to triage.\\n
Quality analysis guidelines
- For each flagged prompt, capture: input, baseline output, candidate output, token-level alignments, and logits (where available).
- Use the scoring rubric: 1=identical, 2=minor wording difference (acceptable), 3=meaningful semantic change (requires escalation), 4=hallucination/regression (blocker).
- Tag each prompt with sensitivity and business impact.

Kernel scheduling interplay notes (short guide)
- Batching tradeoffs: larger batches improve throughput but increase latency tail for short-sequence requests. During fidelity sprints focus on sequence-length-aware batching (max_batch_size per-seqlen-bin).\- Preemption: enable preemption for priority traffic to avoid head-of-line latency for interactive routes. Validate preemption counters don't inflate kernel switch rate by >3x.\- KV-cache prefetching: for long chat sessions, prefetching reduces token latency but increases memory pressure. Add memory headroom checks and a soft cap of 80% GPU memory for prefetch cache.

Benchmarks and artifact naming convention
- Bench artifact names: fidelity-bench.{kernel_tag}.{model_tag}.{gpu}.{date}.json\- Always store raw traces, aggregated metrics, and the prompt-evaluation delta report in: gs://redwood-bench/fidelity-sprints/{sprint_id}/

Reporting and post-mortem
- After the sprint complete (success or rollback), the sprint lead must produce a 1-page summary with: baseline vs candidate summary table, failure cases, root cause hypothesis, and recommended next steps. Attach raw artifacts and the canary ramp timeline.

Appendices
A) Example benchmark spec (JSON)\\{
  "sprint_id": "fs-2026-07-23",
  "routes": ["chat_v1"],
  "shapes": [{"concurrency":10, "seq_len":64}],
  "duration_minutes": 60
}\\n
B) Quick commands\- Collect runtime traces: ./tools/capture_runtime_trace --duration 60 --out /tmp/trace.json\- Run bench: python tools/bench_runner.py --spec /tmp/fidelity_bench.json --kernel kernel:vX.Y.Z --out /tmp/results.json\- Trigger rollback (manual): ./scripts/rollback_kernel.sh --target kernel:baseline

C) FAQ\- Q: Can we skip shadow-mirroring during canary?\   A: No — shadow outputs are the primary artifact for post-rollout quality analysis.\- Q: Who signs off a Dedicated customer rollout?\   A: Product + Customer Success + Security (if private deployment).

Document maintenance
- Owner: Maya Chen (runtime). Update cadence: before every major kernel release or every 6 months.
- Record of changes: last major revision consolidated monitoring thresholds (2026-11-30).

Related links
- Runtime profiling guidelines: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/runtime-profiling-playbook-guidelines-2025\- Rollout orchestration: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/runtime-feature-flagging-experimentation-contract-2026

End of handbook

title: Trace Baggage and Locality Annotation Playbook
content:
Summary
=======
This playbook describes the convention, implementation points, rollout checklist and operational runbook for: 1) propagating lightweight trace baggage across internal runtime boundaries, and 2) annotating request locality signals for fast attribution of latency and fidelity degradations. The goal is to enable sub-second triage of tail-latency and fidelity regressions with minimal telemetry cost.

Why this exists
---------------
- Traces alone are insufficient when requests traverse multiple internal runtime surfaces (dispatcher, scheduler, per-GPU worker). Baggage and locality annotations let operators reconstruct: tenant, route, model-variant, kernel-hint, and shard-affinity without expensive full-span capture.
- We must keep sampling low (<=5% overall) to control telemetry egress costs while preserving high-fidelity signals for SLO-impacting traffic.

Goals & SLO impact
------------------
- Primary goal: reduce mean time to diagnose (MTTD) tail-latency incidents from 45m to <15m for P95+ incidents caused by scheduling or kernel mis-selection.
- Maintain telemetry cost increase <= 8% on production ingestion for a 5% sampling rate.
- Do NOT degrade request latency: all baggage operations must be O(1) and performed in allocation-hot paths with preallocated buffers.

Background and design constraints
--------------------------------
1. Baggage must be compact (<= 256 bytes per request including keys), ASCII-safe, and forward-compatible.
2. Locality annotations are short enumerated codes (see schema) emitted at key transitions and attached to the trace root as tags when sampled.
3. Any new annotation must have an owner and an explicit rollout plan (below).

Telemetry schema (fields and examples)
-------------------------------------
- Field name | Type | Example | Description
-------------|------|---------|------------
- tenant_id | string | t-acme | Canonical customer id used for cost partitioning
- route | string | /v1/generate | API route or internal route name
- model_variant | string | llama2-13b-q8 | Model family + quantization/variant tag
- kernel_hint | string | shard-fused | Scheduler-provided kernel hint used for execution
- locality_code | string | W1:S3:GPU-A | Encoded placement locality (warehouse:shard:device)
- priority_tier | string | burst | Economic priority assigned by governor
- fidelity_band | string | high | Chosen fidelity slice (high/medium/low)
- kvcache_status | string | warmed | kvcache state at request arrival

Note: the table above must be represented in the telemetry backend as top-level attributes to allow fast filtering in alert dashboards.

Locality codes and decoding guide
--------------------------------
Locality codes are human-readable tokens with three components separated by colons: W{rack}:S{shard}:{device-tag}. Examples:
- W2:S7:GPU-A — warehouse 2, shard 7, device A.
- W1:S3:CPU — fallback CPU execution.
Decoding should be implemented by the runtime operator CLI (see Commands).

Sampling strategy and cost controls
----------------------------------
1. Base-sample: stratified sampling giving 5% of all requests into traces. Stratification keys: tenant_tier (enterprise/standard/free) and route.
2. Tail-preserve: conditional up-sample of requests exceeding 90th latency percentile to 25% for 30s windows around detected tail spikes. Up-sampling is gated by an egress-budget token bucket (configurable).
3. Incident-sample: on a detected SLO breach the controller can enable request-level capture for offending route/model_variant for a configurable duration (default 15m). This capture mode includes full-span traces and physiological metrics.
4. Cost cap: per-cluster daily budget enforced by telemetry-proxy; if exceeded, tail-preserve and incident-sample are disabled until replenished.

Injection points (runtime locations to attach baggage/annotations)
----------------------------------------------------------------
- Frontend ingress (API gateway): attach tenant_id and route. Responsible: api-gateway service.
- Dispatcher layer: attach model_variant, priority_tier. Responsible: dispatcher-service.
- Scheduler/admission: attach kernel_hint, fidelity_band. Responsible: scheduler-service.
- Worker / GPU runtime: attach locality_code and kvcache_status (warmed/stale/empty). Responsible: worker-agent.

Implementation notes and code patterns
------------------------------------
- Use a single compact header X-RW-BAG (base64 of comma-delimited key=val pairs) for cross-process propagation. When possible, prefer binary-packed proto v1 to reduce size.
- Baggage encoding must be append-only by intermediate services; never rewrite tenant_id once set at ingress.
- Runtime helper API (pseudocode):
  - encode_baggage(map<string,string>) -> string
  - decode_baggage(string) -> map<string,string>
  - annotate_span(span, map<string,string>)
- Hot-path optimization: decoding should be lazy — decode only when the request is sampled OR when a local decision requires the field.

Runbook: Investigating a rapid P99 spike linked to kernel selection
------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Detect: Alert fired from per-route P99 > configured SLO (example: 1200ms).
2. Immediate actions (first 10 minutes):
   a. Check telemetry budget panel to ensure tail-preserve is enabled.
   b. Query the traces index for the route with attribute kernel_hint and locality_code for the offending window. Example query: "route:/v1/generate AND timestamp:[t-5m TO t] SORT BY latency DESC LIMIT 200".
   c. If traces available, aggregate by kernel_hint and locality_code. Look for a dominant kernel_hint associated with the tail.
3. Triage (10-30 minutes):
   a. If a kernel_hint shows >60% of tail samples, coordinate with kernel team to check recent kernel rollouts (see release notes index).
   b. Use worker-agent logs filtered by locality_code to inspect GPU telemetry (thermal throttling, mem fragmentation, OOM). CLI: 
      - rwi worker tail --locality=W1:S3 --since=15m 
   c. If locality shows cross-shard imbalance, escalate to scheduling team and consider transient rebalancing (see Rebalancing play).
4. Resolve (30m+):
   a. If kernel regression confirmed, trigger canary rollback following kernel rollback runbook.
   b. If kvcache coldness is root cause, engage warmup policy: increase prefix cache warmup for affected shards and enable asymmetric prefetch for the route for 2h.

Quick commands and examples
--------------------------
- Decode a baggage header locally: rwctl baggage decode --header "<base64>"
- Search traces by locality and kernel: rwctl traces query --route /v1/generate --filter "kernel_hint:shard-fused" --since 15m --limit 100
- List worker health for a locality: rwi worker list --locality W1:S3

Baggage key naming conventions
-----------------------------
- Keys MUST be lower_snake_case.
- Avoid long freeform values; prefer enumerations and short ids.
- Reserve prefix rw_* for runtime-owned keys (e.g., rw_kernel_hint).
- Example allowed keys: tenant_id, route, model_variant, rw_kernel_hint, rw_locality, kvcache_status

Security and privacy considerations
----------------------------------
- Do not propagate PII in baggage. Tenant identifiers must be opaque ids (no emails).
- Baggage header is signed by the ingress when crossing trust boundaries; internal hop-to-hop propagation is unsigned but validated for format.
- Review with legal for any new attributes that could be considered customer data.

Rollout checklist (feature flag gated)
-------------------------------------
1. Add baggage header encode/decode libs to api-gateway, dispatcher, scheduler and worker-agent. Unit tests + size regression tests.
2. Deploy library in canary region with base-sample enabled at 1%. Monitor header size distribution and egress impact for 48h.
3. Enable stratified base-sample at 5% and run for 7 days. Verify telemetry budget usage <= 8% increase.
4. Enable tail-preserve and validate tail-upsample correctness in staging with synthetic load.
5. Gradually roll to remaining regions, monitoring the telemetry budget and API latency metrics.

Safety gates and feature flags
----------------------------
- feature.runtime.baggage.enabled (bool) — global on/off
- feature.runtime.baggage.decode_lazy (bool) — lazy decode optimization
- feature.runtime.tracing.tail_preserve (bool) — enable tail up-sample
- rw.telemetry.max_daily_egress_bytes (int) — cap for cost control

Owner and escalation path
------------------------
- Primary owner: Runtime Observability (eng-serving-runtime) — Maya Patel
- Secondary owner: Kernel & Scheduler (Oliver Chen)
- Escalation: pager/runtime-sre -> oncall (see oncall roster)

Related pages and artifacts
--------------------------
- Runtime sampling and cost policies: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/runtime-telemetry-sampling-cost-aware-profiling-2027
- Kernel rollout notes: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/release-notes/kernel-variant-release-log-2025

Appendix: example encoded baggage (illustrative)
------------------------------------------------
- Raw kv pairs: tenant_id=t-acme,route=/v1/generate,model_variant=llama2-13b-q8,rw_kernel_hint=shard-fused,rw_locality=W1:S3:GPU-A
- Base64 header: <base64-of-utf8-bytes-of-comma-delimited-kv>

Glossary
--------
- baggage: small cross-process key/value header propagated with requests
- locality: encoded physical/logical placement token used for fast grouping in dashboards
- tail-preserve: conditional up-sampling of tail requests to increase signal during anomalies

Change log
----------
- 2024-11-04 — Initial draft (Maya Patel)
- 2025-02-12 — Added tail-preserve budget gating and rollout checklist; clarified lazy decode guidance (reviewer: Oliver Chen)

Contact
-------
For implementation questions or exceptions, ping #runtime-observability on Slack or email maya@redwood.ai.

title: Multimodal Burst Sculpting and Kernel Compatibility Playbook
content:
Purpose

This playbook documents an operational and profiling approach for handling short, high-concurrency multimodal bursts (text + embeddings + image preprocessing calls) while minimizing SLO violations and quantization/kernel compatibility regressions. It synthesizes: runtime admission-probing patterns, sculpting heuristics, a kernel compatibility checklist, profiling recipes, an e2e microbenchmark procedure, and an emergency rollback checklist.

Scope

- Audience: serving-runtime engineers, oncall, benchmarking team, release engineers.
- When to use: recurring tail spikes, sudden customer traffic bursts, onboarding new kernel variants, mixed-modes workload rollouts.
- Not covered: long-running batch offline training jobs or non-inference control-plane operations.

Background and motivation

We observe two recurring failure modes during multimodal bursts:
1) Admission storms that saturate kernel slots and trigger tail latency cascades.
2) New kernel variants (quantized or optimized tensor cores) that change memory patterns and produce silent fidelity regressions under burst conditions.

This playbook gives precise steps to identify which of the two is dominant and safe mitigations to restore SLOs while preserving throughput and unit cost.

Key SLOs and operational thresholds

- Short-request SLO (p95): 120 ms for <128 token text generations (hosted tier).
- Long-request SLO (p95): 1.2 s for sequences up to 2048 tokens.
- Embedding request SLO (p95): 60 ms.
- Kernel admission queue length: critical at > 200 pending kernel ops per GPU (investigate), emergency at > 400 (start mitigation).
- GPU kernel timeout failure rate: target < 0.01% 5m rolling.

Definitions

- Sculpting: active admission shaping that reduces concurrency or steers requests to compatible model variants during a burst.
- Admission probe: lightweight synthetic call that tests a kernel-path’s tail behavior without consuming full token budgets.
- Compatibility score: heuristic (0–100) combining memory pressure, float-precision support, and KV cache layout alignment.

Operational overview

1) Detection
- Alert triggers: sustained p95 breach for short-request SLO for 2 consecutive minutes OR kernel queue length above critical threshold.
- Dashboards: Burst Signatures dashboard (team: runtime-observability) shows per-model sequence-length histogram, per-GPU queue depth, kernel latency CDF, and KV cache hit ratio.

2) Triage (fast path)
- Step 1: Confirm burst shape. Oncall runs the lightweight probe (see CLI below) against affected model ID.
  - CLI: curl -s -X POST https://runtime-diagnostic.internal/api/v1/diagnose
    -d '{"model":"<model-id>","probe_type":"admission","seq_len":16,"modes":["text"]}'
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $DIAG_TOKEN"
- Step 2: Inspect kernel-level telemetry: top kernels by p99 latency, GPU mem utilization, and preemption events (from /metrics/kernel_events).
- Step 3: If kernel p99 spikes with normal request arrival, classify as admission saturation. If kernel p95 stable but per-request latency increases along with memory-related OOMs or soft-evictions, classify as kernel-compat/fidelity issue.

3) Immediate mitigations
- Admission saturation mitigation (fast):
  a) Ramp per-tenant concurrency limit down by 50% using the admission controller API: POST /runtime/admission/patch {"tenant":"<tenant-id>","max_concurrency":<value>}
  b) Enable short-path fallback: route requests with seq_len<=32 to low-latency variant (if model pinned variants exist).
  c) Turn on prefix-kv-cache bypass for bursty tenants to reduce KV cache pressure (command in runbook section).
- Kernel compatibility mitigation (fast):
  a) Disable the kernel variant tagged as experimental on affected pool: PATCH /runtime/kernels/<kernel-id>/state {"enabled":false}
  b) Switch to software-safeguarded kernel: set kernel_hint=legacy_safety on pool config.
  c) If memory ephemerality is suspected, reduce per-request beam/num_returned to shrink working set.

4) Recovery verification
- Run the admission probe and a short synthetic replay (10–20 requests across modes) to confirm p95 restored.
- Monitor rolling 10-minute window for regressions.

Profiling recipes (detailed)

A. Admission-probing recipe
1) Run the admission probe (as above) for the affected model across three modes: text-only (seq_len=16), text-long (seq_len=512), embeddings.
2) Capture the following traces: kernel selection path, scheduler decision, admission token. Annotate traces with request provenance tag: probe/admission/<run-id>.
3) Expected outputs: kernel queue depth waveform, preemption counts, per-kernel p50/p95/p99. Any kernel with p99 > 2x baseline flagged.

B. Memory-residency check (KV + activations)
1) For the offending node: run envoy/agent diagnostic endpoint to dump active KV footprint: GET /diagnostics/kv_footprint?node=<node-id>
2) Compare footprints across nodes to identify shard skew. If a node has >25% higher KV footprint than peers, mark for eviction and redistribute.

C. Kernel probe under synthetic microburst
1) Use the local microbench tool (examples below) to replay a 30s burst with configurable concurrency and inter-arrival jitter. Capture kernel traces and GPU metrics.
2) Run a grid of (concurrency: 2,8,32,128) x (seq_len: 16,128,512) and produce a CSV with p50/p95/p99 and memory high-water mark.

Example microbench (Python, simplified)
- python3 microbench/run_burst.py --model <model-id> --modes text,embed --concurrency 32 --seq-len 128 --duration 30 --output burst-run-<id>.csv

Kernel compatibility checklist (table)

| Kernel tag | Supported ops | Float precision | KV cache layout | Fallback severity |
|---|---:|---|---|---:|
| tensorcore-opt-v2 | fused-attn,matmul | fp16/amp | compact-interleaved | high |
| tc-legacy-safety | attn,matmul | fp32 only | legacy-offset | low |
| quant-int8-mode | matmul,quant-dequant | int8 | compact-interleaved | medium |
| hybrid-tc-async | attn,matmul,kv_prefetch | fp16/amp | split-shard | medium |

Interpretation notes:
- high fallback severity: disabling will likely increase token cost significantly or increase latency due to software fallback.
- Check the kernel runtime annotations for known issues (see related_pages).

Benchmarking and gating protocol for kernel rollouts

Before enabling a kernel variant across a pool, the rollout owner must execute the following in the staging footprint and record artifacts in the Benchmark Runbook:
1) Synthetic grid described in Profiling recipes, capturing p50/p95/p99, memory high-water marks, and preemption events.
2) Multitenant shadow run: replay 30-minute captured production trace with the kernel under test enabled on 10% of nodes. Measure SLO delta vs baseline.
3) Economic impact analysis: delta cost per token under realistic batching assumptions.
4) Compatibility matrix fill-out: confirm supported ops and kv cache alignment for all model families expected in the pool.

Rollout gates (must pass all)
- p95 regression < 2% relative to baseline for all seq_len bins.
- No new kernel-timeout errors in shadow run.
- Memory high-water mark < 90% of node RAM for 95% of runs.
- Quality regression tests: run canonical prompt set for the model family and ensure embedding cosine drift < 0.003 (or per-model guardrail).

Runbook snippets and commands

- Patch admission controller (safe):
  curl -X POST https://controlplane.internal/runtime/admission/patch
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $CP_TOKEN"
    -H "Content-Type: application/json"
    -d '{"selector":{"pool":"g4dn-multimodal"}, "patch":{"tenant_max_concurrency": 8}}'

- Disable kernel quickly (fast rollback):
  curl -X PATCH https://runtime.internal/kernels/tensorcore-opt-v2/state
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $OP_TOKEN"
    -H "Content-Type: application/json"
    -d '{"enabled": false, "reason":"auto-rollback:burst-induced-p99"}'

- Collect traces for a run id (example ktracer CLI):
  ktracer collect --run-id <run-id> --filters "model=<model-id>,tag=probe/admission" --out /tmp/traces.tgz

Escalation and ownership

- Primary owner: runtime-serving/team (oncall rotation). Contact: #runtime-oncall in Slack.
- Kernel rollout owner: release-kernel-team (owners list in kernel registry).
- If SLO remains violated after 20m of standard mitigations, escalate to SRE manager and Product (pages: /confluence/eng-sre/incident-review).

Post-incident tasks (postmortem checklist)

- Capture: traces, admission probe logs, microbench CSV, kernel registry state.
- Annotate: root-cause hypothesis: admission-saturation | kernel-compat | mem-skew | mixed.
- Action items: pinning changes, kernel-flag toggles, gating updates to rollout checklist.
- Run a targeted benchmark to validate fixes.

Artifacts and templates

- Microbench CSV template header: run_id,model_id,mode,concurrency,seq_len,p50_ms,p95_ms,p99_ms,mem_high_mark_mb,preemptions,kernel_id
- Postmortem template: incident-id,summary,timeline,root-cause,mitigations,actions,owners,due-dates

FAQ and troubleshooting tips

Q: Synthetic probes pass but production still sees p95 breach.
A: Check traffic shaping and tail correlation. Production may have correlated multimodal calls (image preprocessing + text gen) that the probe didn’t synthesize. Replay a live trace.

Q: Disabling kernel reduced throughput drastically.
A: Kernel had high fallback severity — use a gradual rollout policy and confirm a low-latency variant exists. Consider temporary additional capacity (spin-up dedicated burst nodes) while investigating.

Notes for future improvements

- Add an automated compatibility scoring service that computes compatibility score per model automatically and surfaces a per-pool warning when a kernel’s compatibility score drops under 70.
- Integrate microbench runs into CI as part of canary checks for kernel changes.

Appendix: useful internal endpoints and dashboards

- Burst Signatures dashboard: https://grafana.internal/d/burst-signatures
- Kernel events metrics: prometheus job name runtime-kernel-metrics
- Microbench tool repo: git@repo.internal:runtime/microbench.git
- Kernel registry: https://cargo.internal/kernels/registry

Document history

- 2026-01-12: created by Priya Nandakumar (initial draft)
- 2026-02-15: added rollout gates and microbench template, reviewers feedback incorporated

Owners and contact

- Document owner: Priya Nandakumar (runtime-serving)

title: Granular runtime energy accounting and telemetry playbook
content:
Summary:

This playbook documents the instrumentation, measurement methodology, and operational runbook for per-request and per-kernel energy accounting in the Redwood serving runtime. The goal is to provide a reproducible, low-noise measurement pipeline that ties energy consumption to SLOs, cost models, and regression gates used by runtime, infra, and perf teams.

Audience:
- Runtime engineers implementing kernel-level telemetry
- SRE and capacity teams performing capacity/cost forecasting
- Applied ML teams validating cost/quality tradeoffs for model variants

Goals and constraints:
- Provide request-level energy attribution within a bounded noise envelope (target: ±5% for steady-state long-running batches).
- Correlate per-token and per-request energy with kernel dispatch, kernel duration, and occupancy metrics.
- Avoid changes that materially affect scheduling behavior; default instrumentation must be low-overhead (<2% wall-clock overhead on p95 latency for typical workloads).
- Produce artifacts that feed into the benchmarking suite and release regression gates.

When to use:
- Baseline benchmarking for new kernel variants or quantized model builds.
- Cost regression detection during release and canary phases.
- Capacity planning when optimizing for energy-constrained regions or on-prem runtimes.

Telemetry model (schema):
Each emitted energy record is a single-line JSON event (or protobuf) with the following fields. The runtime telemetry collector should batch and compress these events for downstream storage.

| field | type | description | example |
|-------|------|-------------|---------|
| timestamp_utc | string | RFC3339 timestamp at sample emission | 2025-02-08T16:42:10.123Z |
| node_id | string | unique node identifier (hw+pool) | gpu-ec2-p4d-12-3 |
| gpu_index | integer | local GPU ordinal on the node | 0 |
| sample_type | string | one of: kernel_start, kernel_end, power_sample | kernel_start |
| sample_id | string | correlation id to join start/end/power samples | samp-abc-123 |
| request_id | string | optional request id when available | req-3d9f |
| model_variant | string | model id + quantization suffix | llama2-13b-q4 |
| kernel_name | string | runtime kernel or op name | attention_fused |
| wall_time_ms | number | duration in ms for kernel_start/kernel_end events | 2.6 |
| power_watts | number | instantaneous power measurement for power_sample | 210.5 |
| energy_joules | number | derived energy for the interval (if provided) | 0.55 |
| batch_size | integer | number of sequences/tokens in kernel invocation | 8 |
| seq_len | integer | sequence length payload for this kernel | 96 |
| tags | list[string] | additional labels (can include canary/cohort) | ["canary","gpu-fe"] |

Note: If the GPU vendor API yields only power samples, the ingestion pipeline must correlate power samples with kernel_start/kernel_end via sample_id and compute energy_joules = integrate(power_watts over time). The runtime should prefer hardware power sensors; fall back to model-based estimators when sensors are unavailable.

Measurement procedure (step-by-step):
1. Testbed setup
   - Use a dedicated cluster to avoid background noise (isolated queue, pinned GPUs, no other tenants).
   - Ensure node thermal state is stable: run a 15-minute warmup workload at target concurrency before measurement.
   - Disable DVFS or other dynamic power policies where possible; record firmware/driver versions.
2. Instrumentation
   - Enable kernel_start/kernel_end hooks around the kernel dispatch layer. Hooks must be high-resolution (microsecond clock).
   - Sample GPU power at 100Hz (or max supported) from hw telemetry; annotate with GPU clock/pstate where available.
   - Tag every request with a lightweight correlation id propagated from HTTP ingress to scheduler to kernel dispatch.
3. Data collection
   - Collect a minimum of N=1,000 similar request samples per model variant and shape to achieve stable aggregates.
   - Record the same workload under three concurrency shapes: low (single request), medium (SLO-target concurrency), and high (2x SLO concurrency) to capture contention effects.
4. Post-processing
   - Join kernel_start/kernel_end with power samples by sample_id and compute per-kernel energy in joules.
   - Aggregate per-request energy by summing kernel energies for all kernels attributed to a request_id.
   - Compute per-token energy by dividing per-request energy by generated tokens (or input+output tokens for inference accounting).

Benchmark protocol and acceptance criteria:
- Benchmark runs must be reproducible and declared in a manifest: workload description (prompt distribution), model commit, kernel build id, driver version, node topology, and network baseline.
- Reported metrics: median and p95 per-request energy (J), per-token energy (mJ/token), p95 latency, and delta from baseline (percentage).
- Acceptance gate for release: no >10% increase in median per-token energy without a commensurate latency or quality improvement. For targeted low-power builds, require p95 latency <= SLO and per-token energy reduction >= 15%.

Noise characterization and correction:
- Use paired experiments when comparing two variants on the same warmed cluster to reduce environmental variance.
- Apply a rolling median filter to power sample streams to remove transient spikes (e.g., fan spin-up).
- If ambient temperature shifts >3°C during a long run, invalidate the run and re-measure.

Operational runbook: energy-related SLO breach
1. Detection
   - Alert triggers: sustained >15% increase in per-token energy vs baseline on production traffic for 3 consecutive hours, or abnormal GPU power profile (fan at max, repeated thermal throttling events).
2. Triage steps
   - Identify affected nodes via node_id and cross-check driver/firmware changes in the last rollout.
   - Check kernel_build and model_variant tags for recent rollouts (use release manifest).
   - Run the short diagnostic job (see commands below) on a suspect node to confirm instrumentation readings.
3. Immediate mitigations
   - If a specific kernel variant is implicated, route traffic to previous kernel build using the runtime's rollout API (canary->stable rollback).
   - If thermal/firmware issue: cordon node, shift traffic, and notify infra to schedule remediation.
4. Postmortem and prevention
   - Add the failing trace and energy profile to the fidelity regression harness.
   - If root cause is scheduler-induced contention, update the scheduler hinting table to add a slot reservation for that workload shape.

Example diagnostic commands:
- Collect a 60s power trace on node: 
  sudo /opt/redwood/bin/gpu_power_capture --duration 60 --sample-rate 100 --out /tmp/power-$(date +%s).ndjson
- Run a local microbenchmark that replays the production sequence shapes: 
  /opt/redwood/bin/runtime_bench --model llama2-13b-q4 --shape-file shapes.yaml --iterations 200 --emit-energy --tag debug-2025

YAML manifest snippet (benchmark-declaration):

workload: "chat-short-prompts"
model: "llama2-13b-q4"
kernel_build: "kbuild-2025-03-12-rc3"
driver: "nvidia-560.12"
node_topology: "p4d-24x-gpu"
shapes: ["single-1","slo-8","burst-32"]
notes: "warmup 15m; ambient target 22C +/- 2C"

Appendix A — Example aggregation queries (pseudo-SQL):
- Per-token energy median: 
  SELECT model_variant, percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (energy_joules / tokens) AS median_mj_per_token
  FROM energy_events JOIN request_tokens USING(request_id)
  WHERE sample_time BETWEEN :start AND :end AND cohort='prod'
  GROUP BY model_variant;
- Kernel-level energy hotlist: 
  SELECT kernel_name, SUM(energy_joules) AS total_joules, COUNT(DISTINCT request_id) AS requests
  FROM kernel_energy_samples
  WHERE sample_time BETWEEN :start AND :end
  GROUP BY kernel_name
  ORDER BY total_joules DESC
  LIMIT 50;

Appendix B — Implementation notes for runtime engineers:
- Keep kernel_start/kernel_end as a minimal shim that only emits a correlation id and timestamp. Heavy processing must be deferred to the telemetry collector to avoid scheduler perturbation.
- Use asynchronous, lock-free buffers for power sample ingestion to avoid blocking kernel dispatch threads.
- When hardware sensors are not accessible (e.g., some on-prem vendors), implement a calibrated estimator that maps kernel duration and occupancy to energy. Calibration must be performed against hardware-sensor baseline across multiple shapes.

Appendix C — Known limitations and future work:
- Attribution across multi-GPU kernels (model parallel) increases complexity; current approach attributes energy to the initiating GPU and annotates cross-GPU spans for approximate redistribution. A planned follow-up (Q2 2025) will add cross-GPU energy stitching.
- NVLink and interconnect power contributions are currently excluded; roadmap includes capturing node-level PSU metrics in a future iteration.

Contacts and ownership:
- Playbook owner: Maya Chen (runtime perf)
- SRE escalation: Arjun Patel
- Kernel instrumentation: Sofia Martinez

Revision history:
- 2024-11-12: initial draft
- 2025-01-20: added acceptance gates and diagnostic commands (review Arjun, Sofia)
- 2025-02-08: clarified noise correction and updated schema examples

title: Profiling mixed prefill/decode contention (mixed-workload tail latency)
content:
## Purpose
This playbook documents how to reproduce and diagnose **mixed prefill/decode contention** that produces **user-visible p95 tail latency** regressions under mixed prompt-length distributions (e.g., short chat prompts interleaved with long-context prompts).

In steady-state homogeneous traffic, continuous batching tends to be stable. Under mixed workloads, we commonly see:
- **Head-of-line blocking**: long-prefill requests dominate GPU time and batch selection.
- **Scheduler instability**: rapid shifts between “prefill-heavy” and “decode-heavy” work.
- **Kernel selection thrash**: frequent switching of attention kernels/profiles as sequence lengths vary.
- **KV cache pressure**: eviction/compaction spikes that amplify decode latency.

This doc is written to be usable by Serving Runtime + Kernel teams and as a reference during canary triage.

---

## When to use this playbook
Use this playbook when you observe one or more of the following in Hosted or Dedicated pools:
- TTFT (time-to-first-token) p95 increases primarily during spikes of long-context traffic.
- Decode token latency looks fine in isolation, but p95 end-to-end increases due to queueing and/or prefill blocking.
- Per-GPU throughput remains similar, but p95 and p99 drift upward under mixed mixes.
- Increased variance in per-iteration batch composition and/or sequence-length distribution.

Not a good fit if the issue is clearly:
- Network or upstream API latency.
- Model-level regressions unrelated to serving (e.g., prompt changes, tool calling loops).
- GPU health / ECC / throttling incidents.

---

## Definitions (quick)
- **Prefill**: processing the prompt/context to initialize KV cache.
- **Decode**: iterative next-token generation using KV cache.
- **Mixed-workload contention**: prefill workload stealing scheduling budget from decode (or vice versa), creating tail amplification.
- **Kernel thrash**: repeated switching between kernels/profiles (often due to sequence-length variability) that reduces effective GPU utilization.

---

## Prerequisites and access
**Environments**
- Prefer a controlled staging pool or perf canary environment first.
- If profiling prod canary, coordinate with SRE (see “Operational safety”).

**Tools**
- Grafana dashboards for runtime + scheduler class metrics.
- Tracing (Tempo) and logs (Loki) access.
- Nsight Systems (nsys) and optionally Nsight Compute (ncu).
- Triton debug/autotune controls (if relevant for the deployed build).

**Build / flags**
- Runtime build with NVTX ranges enabled (recommended): `RUNTIME_NVTX=1` (or the equivalent runtime config toggle for the current release).
- Scheduler class metrics enabled (required for mixed-workload work): see metric names below.

---

## Operational safety (don’t skip in shared pools)
Profiling can be disruptive.
- Prefer capturing **short windows** (10–60s) during a stable reproduction.
- Do not run `ncu` in production pools unless explicitly approved; it can serialize kernels and distort latency.
- If you must profile on a shared canary GPU:
  1) Announce in `#eng-runtime` and `#eng-sre`.
  2) Ensure the canary guardrails are active (rollback triggers and p95/p99 thresholds).
  3) Use a single GPU or an isolated worker when possible.

---

## Step 1: Reproduce the issue reliably
### A. Synthetic mixed workload (recommended starting point)
Use benchmark-lab mixed scenarios (e.g., 80/20 short/long, 50/50, long-spike). Ensure the long prompts are long enough to create meaningful prefill cost (not just slightly longer chat prompts).

Reproduction checklist:
- Fix model version + runtime version.
- Fix GPU SKU and driver.
- Fix max batch / continuous batching settings.
- Fix request concurrency (start low; increase until p95 degradation begins).

What “good reproduction” looks like:
- p95 TTFT increases with long-traffic fraction.
- Queue time or scheduler wait time is a dominant contributor.
- Prefill duration p95 increases disproportionately (often due to batching side effects).

### B. Trace replay (closest to production)
Use anonymized production trace distributions and replay with the same short/long prompt-length mix.

Notes:
- Ensure the replay includes the same **arrival process** (bursty vs Poisson matters).
- Verify the prefill/decode ratio resembles production by comparing:
  - `prefill_latency_ms` distribution
  - average decode length and per-token decode latency

---

## Step 2: Confirm the signature in metrics before GPU profiling
Start with metrics; avoid Nsight until you know what you’re looking for.

### Key metrics to inspect (runtime + scheduler)
**Scheduler / queueing (per class if enabled)**
- `scheduler_queue_depth{class="short|long"}`
- `scheduler_time_in_queue_ms_bucket{class=...}` (focus p95)
- `scheduler_dispatch_share{class=...}` (how much GPU time/iterations each class gets)
- `scheduler_starvation_counter_total{class="long"}`
- `scheduler_aging_applied_total{class=...}`

**Prefill / decode breakdown**
- `prefill_latency_ms_bucket` (p50/p95)
- `decode_iteration_ms_bucket` (p50/p95)
- `ttft_ms_bucket` (TTFT p95 is typically the user-visible pain)
- `e2e_request_latency_ms_bucket`

**Batch composition and token budgeting**
- `batch_tokens_total{phase="prefill|decode"}`
- `batch_size{phase=...}`
- `scheduler_token_budget_overrun_total{class=...}`

**KV cache pressure**
- `kv_cache_hit_ratio` (trend matters more than absolute)
- `kv_cache_evictions_total`
- `kv_cache_compactions_total`
- `kv_cache_bytes_in_use`

**Kernel selection stability (if exposed by build)**
- `kernel_select_changes_total{op="attention_prefill|attention_decode"}`
- `kernel_profile_selected{op=..., profile=...}` (watch for oscillation)

### What to look for (common signatures)
1) **Head-of-line blocking**
- Long queue depth spikes coincide with rising short TTFT p95.
- Prefill latency p95 increases and consumes iteration budget.

2) **Decode starvation**
- Decode iteration p95 increases even when per-token compute is stable.
- Queue time dominates but GPU utilization stays high (GPU is busy, just on the “wrong” work).

3) **KV cache eviction spikes**
- Evictions/compactions spike during long-context bursts.
- Decode iteration latency increases shortly after eviction spikes.

4) **Kernel thrash**
- Kernel selection changes increase; latency variance increases.
- Effective throughput drops despite similar nominal GPU utilization.

If metrics do not show queueing / prefill dominance / cache pressure, do not proceed to GPU profiling yet; the bottleneck may be elsewhere (networking, upstream throttling, tokenization, etc.).

---

## Step 3: Capture traces (runtime + GPU)
### A. Runtime tracing (cheap, always do this first)
Recommended trace spans:
- `request.enqueue -> scheduler.classify -> prefill.start -> prefill.end -> decode.first_iteration -> first_token -> request.complete`

Minimum set of spans/attributes to verify are present:
- request_id, model, pool, region
- prompt_tokens, max_output_tokens
- class=short/long (if enabled)
- queue_time_ms
- prefill_time_ms
- decode_time_ms
- tokens_generated

If the trace shows large `queue_time_ms`, focus on scheduler policy and queue composition first.

### B. Nsight Systems (nsys) for timeline correlation
Use Nsight Systems to correlate:
- CPU scheduling and enqueue/dequeue behavior
- GPU kernel launches and gaps
- NVTX ranges for prefill vs decode

**Capture guidelines**
- Keep captures short: 10–30 seconds usually sufficient.
- Capture under stable load (after warmup; not during ramp).
- Prefer a dedicated worker.

**Suggested nsys command (example)**
- `nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt --sample=none --cpuctxsw=true --duration=20 --output=/tmp/mixed_contention_$(date +%s) --force-overwrite=true <run_command>`

NVTX naming conventions (what we expect to see):
- `rrt/prefill` ranges
- `rrt/decode` ranges
- `rrt/scheduler/dispatch` ranges

If NVTX ranges are missing, re-run with the correct runtime config (e.g., `RUNTIME_NVTX=1`) and confirm the build includes NVTX instrumentation.

### C. Nsight Compute (ncu) for kernel-level diagnosis (use sparingly)
Use `ncu` when you have strong evidence of kernel inefficiency or selection instability.

Recommended approach:
- Target a **single kernel** (attention prefill or decode) using regex filters.
- Capture a minimal set of metrics: occupancy, memory throughput, warp stall reasons.

Do not run `ncu` in production canary pools without explicit sign-off.

---

## Step 4: Interpret GPU timelines for mixed prefill/decode contention
### What “healthy” looks like
- Prefill bursts are present but bounded.
- Decode iterations are regular with limited jitter.
- Minimal gaps between kernel launches.
- Batch composition does not oscillate dramatically iteration-to-iteration.

### Red flags
1) **Prefill runs dominate long continuous windows**
- Timeline shows long unbroken sequences of prefill kernels.
- Short requests’ TTFT increases due to waiting behind long-prefill work.

2) **Kernel launch gaps / synchronization stalls**
- Gaps appear when switching between prefill and decode phases.
- Often coincides with memory pressure, cache management, or host-side batching logic.

3) **Kernel profile oscillation (thrash)**
- Attention kernel variants switch frequently.
- Increased CPU overhead for kernel selection/autotune or code paths that depend on shape buckets.

4) **Memory bandwidth saturation during cache events**
- Spikes in memory throughput correlate with KV cache compaction/eviction.
- Decode iterations immediately after eviction show higher latency.

---

## Triton + kernel selection debugging tips (when kernel thrash is suspected)
### Common causes
- Sequence lengths cross internal “bucket boundaries” frequently (short/long mixed in same batch).
- Autotuner evaluates multiple configs due to varied shapes.
- Runtime alternates between different attention implementations based on (seq_len, batch_size, head_dim, dtype, quant profile).

### What to enable (non-prod first)
If using Triton-based kernels or autotuned paths in your build:
- Enable autotune logging for a single run window.
- Pin or limit configurations if the build supports it.

Useful environment variables (names vary by release; treat as examples):
- `TRITON_PRINT_AUTOTUNING=1`
- `TRITON_CACHE_DIR=/tmp/triton_cache`
- `CUDA_MODULE_LOADING=LAZY` (to reduce module load stalls, depending on deployment)

What to look for:
- Repeated autotune entries for similar shapes.
- Frequent cache misses in the Triton cache directory (indicating cache eviction or non-reuse).
- Shape drift causing many unique compiled variants.

Mitigation patterns (to validate during experiments):
- Increase shape bucketing stability (larger buckets, fewer boundaries).
- Avoid mixing extreme seq lengths in a single batch when it forces worst-case kernel choice.
- Pin kernel profiles per SKU/model where supported.

---

## KV cache eviction/compaction debugging (cache pressure spikes)
### Symptoms
- `kv_cache_evictions_total` spikes during long-context bursts.
- `kv_cache_hit_ratio` drops and does not recover quickly.
- Decode iteration latency becomes noisy (high variance) after evictions.

### What to check
- Is the cache sized appropriately for the concurrency and max context length?
- Are long-context requests dominating concurrency in a way the pool wasn’t sized for?
- Is cache compaction running too frequently (small free segments, fragmentation)?

### Practical diagnostics
- Correlate eviction spikes with request mix changes and batch size changes.
- Confirm whether cache events align with prefill-heavy windows.
- Check if a new scheduling policy increased the number of “active sequences” in-flight and raised cache residency requirements.

---

## Common failure modes and how to confirm them
### 1) Kernel thrash due to sequence-length variability
**Confirm**
- Kernel selection changes increase (`kernel_select_changes_total`)
- Nsight timeline shows frequent switching between attention kernel variants
- Increased host overhead or gaps at transitions

**Next steps**
- Stabilize shape buckets; reduce boundary crossings
- Consider separate batching lanes for extreme long contexts
- Validate kernel profile pinning on the target SKU

### 2) Cache eviction spikes amplifying decode latency
**Confirm**
- `kv_cache_evictions_total` and/or `kv_cache_compactions_total` spikes
- Decode iteration p95 increases after eviction spikes

**Next steps**
- Reduce active sequences or cap long-context concurrency
- Re-check cache sizing assumptions and fragmentation behavior
- Validate whether scheduler changes increased cache churn

### 3) Host-of-line blocking from long-prefill dominating dispatch
**Confirm**
- Long prefill windows coincide with rising short TTFT p95
- Time-in-queue for short requests increases without a corresponding drop in GPU utilization

**Next steps**
- Test short/long class-based scheduling (two-queue) and token budgets
- Ensure aging/starvation prevention doesn’t swing too far (watch long starvation counters)

### 4) Instrumentation artifacts (profiling changes the workload)
**Confirm**
- Behavior only appears when Nsight is attached
- Latency shifts significantly with profiler on/off

**Next steps**
- Shorten capture; reduce trace categories
- Prefer nsys over ncu; avoid excessive logging

---

## Triage checklist (copy/paste into incident threads)
1) Workload: mix ratio, arrival pattern, concurrency, prompt token distribution, output token distribution.
2) Versions: runtime, model, driver, CUDA, SKU.
3) Metrics screenshots/links:
   - TTFT p95, e2e p95
   - prefill_latency p95, decode_iteration p95
   - scheduler_queue_depth + scheduler_time_in_queue (per class)
   - kv_cache_* (evictions/compactions/hit ratio)
   - kernel_select_changes_total (if available)
4) Trace sample: 5–10 representative requests showing queue/prefill/decode breakdown.
5) Nsight Systems: 10–20s capture with NVTX prefill/decode ranges.
6) Hypothesis: (HOL blocking | kernel thrash | cache pressure | other)
7) Proposed mitigation test: which knob, expected effect, rollback plan.

---

## Escalation and ownership
- If metrics point to **scheduler policy / queueing**: escalate to Serving Runtime Scheduling (Lena Fischer / Marcus Reed).
- If metrics + Nsight point to **kernel instability or attention kernel inefficiency**: escalate to Kernel team (Hiro Tanaka / Yuki Sato).
- If there is **prod canary impact** or guardrail/SLO questions: escalate to SRE sponsor (Sean Gallagher) and on-call.

---

## Appendix: Suggested configuration knobs to experiment with (controlled environments)
Note: knob names vary by release and deployment mode; confirm against the current runtime config schema.

Scheduler knobs (mixed-workload prototype builds):
- `scheduler.classification.enabled` (bool)
- `scheduler.classification.short_threshold_prompt_tokens` (int)
- `scheduler.dispatch.two_queue.enabled` (bool)
- `scheduler.dispatch.short_share_target` (float)
- `scheduler.dispatch.aging_ms` (int)
- `scheduler.dispatch.max_skew` (float)
- `scheduler.token_budget.per_iteration.short` (int)
- `scheduler.token_budget.per_iteration.long` (int)

Batching knobs:
- `batching.max_batch_size`
- `batching.max_prefill_tokens`
- `batching.max_decode_tokens_per_iter`

KV cache knobs:
- `kv_cache.max_bytes`
- `kv_cache.compaction.enabled`
- `kv_cache.compaction.target_fragmentation`

Kernel selection knobs (if supported):
- `kernels.attention.profile_pin` (by SKU/model)
- `kernels.attention.autotune.enabled` (bool)

---

## Appendix: Notes on avoiding false conclusions
- Always compare against a **single baseline** with identical load generator settings.
- Separate “prefill got slower” from “prefill waited longer” (compute vs queue time).
- Don’t rely on average GPU utilization alone. Mixed contention often keeps GPUs busy while users experience worse tail latency.
- Ensure you’re not mixing unrelated changes (scheduler + kernel + cache sizing) in a single experiment; change one variable at a time during diagnosis.

title: Proactive Thermal & Power Profiling Playbook
content:
Summary

This playbook describes the proactive profiling, telemetry collection, and remediation patterns for GPU power, thermal, and power-capping interactions with the runtime kernel and scheduler. It is intended for SREs, runtime engineers, and performance owners who operate the runtime-kernel-manager, gpu-dispatcher, and telemetry-collector stacks.

Why this matters

- Thermal events, power capping, and sustained TDP-related throttling account for intermittent high tail latency and elevated token cost in our hosted and dedicated fleets.
- Early, structured profiling improves our ability to: prevent service degradation, inform kernel scheduling hints, and craft safe rollout/rollback gates for quantization or kernel changes that alter power draw.

Scope and assumptions

- Applies to: G4/G5-like GPU nodes in hosted/dedicated pools and to supported on-prem accelerator types where Tegra/CUSTOM-HW telemetry is forwarded to telemetry-collector.
- Not covered: facility-level rack cooling changes (contact infra).
- Dependencies: telemetry-collector >= 2.3.0, runtime-kernel-manager >= 1.8.1, gpu-dispatcher >= 3.0.

Key metrics and thresholds

| Metric | Warning threshold | Critical threshold | Note |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| GPU junction temp (Tjunction, C) | 78 C | 88 C | sustained >1m triggers probe workflow |
| GPU power draw (W) | > 90% configured TDP for >30s | > 100% TDP (sustained or spiking) | power capping likely active |
| P99 runtime latency (ms) | > 250 ms | > 400 ms | across stationary workload sample |
| Kernel preemption count | > baseline + 50% | > baseline + 200% | indicates frequent kernel handoffs |
| Thermal throttling events | 1 per 10k requests | > 1 per 1k requests | immediate escalation |

Operational goals and SLO alignment

- Maintain fleet thermal-induced-degradation incidents to < 0.2% of customer requests per week.
- Ensure thermal-related rollbacks are executed within 30 minutes of detection for Dedicated customers.

Profiling procedures (lab and in-situ)

1) Synthetic lab profile (recommended before any kernel/quantization rollout)
   - Environment: perf-lab node with same SKU and driver stack as target fleet.
   - Steps:
     1. Deploy the exact model artifact and runtime-kernel-manager version to perf-lab.
     2. Run workload-sculptor to generate mixed-local-token workloads: `workload-sculptor --shape chat-heavy --concurrency 16 --duration 30m --seed <id>`.
     3. Collect GPU metrics: `telemetry-cli collect --node <node> --metrics gpu.temp,gpu.power,kernel.preempt --out ./lab-trace.json`
     4. Collect kernel traces: `sudo perf record -e sched_switch -a -- sleep 1800` then `perf script > perf-sched.txt`.
     5. Generate flamegraphs and power trace overlays: `flamegraph.pl perf-sched.txt > flame.svg` and `power-annotate --trace lab-trace.json --svg flame.svg --out annotated-flame.svg`.
   - Acceptance criteria: no sustained Tjunction > 85 C and P99 within 10% of baseline.

2) Controlled in-situ sampling (production shadow)
   - Use sampling window: 10 minute shadow runs covering 1% of traffic from a representative route.
   - Commands: `shadow-run orchestrator --route <route> --sample 0.01 --duration 10m --label thermal-probe-<date>`
   - Collect enriched traces via telemetry-collector and annotate with request provenance (trace id, model-version, kernel-hint).

3) Continuous low-cost probes
   - Probe config (telemetry-collector): sample-rate 0.001 for power/temp + priority-index annotation.
   - Drive alerts on rolling windows (5m/30m) for warning/critical thresholds.

Remediation runbook (elevated Tjunction or power capping detected)

Immediate steps (0–5 minutes):
1. Verify telemetry: `telemetry-cli query --since 5m --filter "node:<node> AND metric:gpu.temp>78" --out quickcheck.json`.
2. If confirmed, mark node as no-new-allocs: `gpu-dispatcher drain --node <node> --mode soft`.
3. Reduce concurrency for affected route(s) via runtime route-policy: set concurrency-limit = 0.5x for the route.
4. Notify on-call SRE team: channel #sre-runtime (post summary, node id, trace references).

Escalation (5–30 minutes):
1. If thermal persists after draining and cooling (5–10 min), trigger controlled model-fallback to lower-power variant (if available): `runtime-kernel-manager fallback --model <model-id> --variant quant-8bit --route <route> --canary 100% --reason "thermal_probe"`.
2. If no fallback and critical thresholds are crossed, escalate to infra to verify rack cooling; file ticket with `infra-ticket create --node <node> --symptoms thermal-critical` and CC runtime SRE.
3. For Dedicated customers, start the SLA incident flow and notify CS as per escalation-playbook.

Post-incident forensics (30–120 minutes)

- Rehydrate traces from telemetry-collector and link to perf-sched traces.
- Run kernel attribution to identify which kernel changes (recent kernel-hint rollouts, new preemption policies, or updated kernels) correlate with increased power draw.
- Produce an incident summary including: timeline, node-id, model-version, kernel-hint configuration, and remediation actions; publish to related_pages above and tag with label `thermal-incident`.

Integration with scheduler / kernel hinting

- Scheduler contract: scheduler may accept `power_budget_hint` and `therm_priority` attributes in the per-request routing header. These are surfaced in runtime-kernel-manager and should be used conservatively. Example header:

```
X-Runtime-Hints: power_budget_hint=120W;therm_priority=low
```

- Guidance:
  - Prefer `power_budget_hint` for long-form streaming requests where a slightly lower power draw trades off repeatable latency vs throughput.
  - Use `therm_priority=high` only during active degradation windows and with operator approval.

Benchmarking protocol additions

- Add a thermal dimension to our standard microbench: include a 45-minute sustained window with controlled ambient temps (if possible) and report: Tjunction time-series, P95/P99 latency vs time, and kernel preemption rates.
- Add a power-capping simulation test that artificially caps GPU power to 80% of TDP and measures latency and failure modes.

Operational tooling and saved queries

- telemetry-collector saved queries:
  - `thermal.warning.recent` => `metric:gpu.temp > 78` rolling 10m
  - `power.capping.detect` => `metric:gpu.power / tdp > 0.95` rolling 5m
- Grafana dashboards: `Runtime / Thermal` dashboard (owner: eng-serving-runtime/dashboard-dot) includes heatmap by rack, node trace links, and per-route thermal exposure.

Ownership and run cadence

- Primary owner: runtime-performance team (rotation: @oncall-runtime-perf).
- Secondary: infra-fleet for rack cooling liaison.
- Quarterly tasks:
  1. Run perf-lab thermal validation for any major kernel or quantization rollout.
  2. Revalidate thresholds after driver updates.

Release gating checklist (kernel or scheduling change impacting power draw)

- Checklist before canary deploy:
  1. Lab synthetic profile executed and passed acceptance criteria.
  2. 10m shadow probe executed against canary and no thermal warning.
  3. Telemetry saved queries configured and verified.
  4. Rollback plan documented and tested (automation for fallback to previously active kernel/hint enabled).

Appendix A: useful commands and snippets

- Quick telemetry query:
```
telemetry-cli query --node node-123 --metrics gpu.temp,gpu.power --since 15m
```
- Mark node soft-drain:
```
gpu-dispatcher drain --node node-123 --mode soft --reason "thermal_probe"
```
- Annotate trace with kernel-hint:
```
span.annotate("kernel_hint", "power_budget:120W")
```

Appendix B: Example incident summary template

1) Title: Thermal degradation — node-123 — 2026-02-27
2) Impacted routes: /v1/generate-chat, /v1/embed
3) Metrics at peak: P99 = 498ms, Tjunction = 91 C, gpu.power = 105% TDP (reported)
4) Actions taken: drained node, reduced route concurrency, triggered quant-8bit fallback for /v1/embed, infra engaged.
5) Root cause: regression in kernel preemption policy causing longer sustained active SM utilization spikes.
6) Follow up: revert policy 1.8.1 -> 1.8.0 on affected canaries; schedule perf-lab replay and driver review.

Related docs and references

- See related_pages for runbooks and scheduler observability contracts.
- Perf-lab runbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/developer-sandbox-benchmarking-playbook-2026

Change log

- 2024-11-12 — Created by Evelyn Chen (initial lab-driven protocol).
- 2025-06-08 — Added scheduler hint header examples and expanded remediation steps (reviewer Marco Liu).
- 2026-03-01 — Updated thresholds (Tjunction) and integrated automation commands for fallback (reviewer Aisha Patel).

title: Sequence runway sampling and batch fidelity playbook
content:
Summary

This playbook defines the Sequence Runway sampling method and operational guidance for measuring the interaction between request sequence-length distributions and batching fidelity. Sequence Runway is a structured sampling technique intended to produce representative micro-batches for performance profiling, kernel-sensitivity analysis, and fidelity regression detection across production-shaped traffic.

Why we built this

- Traditional uniform sampling under-represents transitions between short and long prefix lengths that trigger kernel path changes (attention tiling, KV cache hotness, quantized kernels).
- Ad-hoc sampling can miss edge cases where batch packing semantics significantly change per-token latency and model quality.
- Sequence Runway makes those transitions first-class, enabling repeatable benchmarking, better kernel hinting, and targeted mitigations (prefetching, backpressure tuning, or model-variant routing).

Goals

1. Provide a repeatable protocol for generating micro-batches that exercise kernel breakpoints and batching boundary cases.
2. Surface fidelity regressions introduced by batching or quantized-variant fallbacks.
3. Produce telemetry artifacts (trace + kernel tags + per-token latencies) consumable by the profiling pipeline and the benchmarking suite.

Scope and non-goals

- In scope: sampling and experiment protocol for online traffic replay, local synthetic corpus generation, expected telemetry schema, runbook for interpreting results.
