- request_id, model_version, prompt_hash, tokenized_input (safe-hashed), full kernel invocation timeline (per-kernel name, start_ns, duration_ns), batch_id, batch_composition (other request IDs in same batch), GPU index, device memory map, KV cache delta (keys evicted/inserted) as changelog, and environment tags (node, runtime-build).

Storage and retention policy (table):
| artifact | storage path | retention | rationale |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| sampled-metrics (aggregates) | s3://profiling/samples/yyyy/ | 90 days | rollups for alerting and SLO backfills |
| trace-on-demand raw | s3://profiling/traces/yyyy/ | 30 days | full replays are costly; short TTL |
| replay-recons | s3://profiling/replays/yyyy/ | 180 days | preserve repros tied to releases |
| kvcache-deltas | s3://profiling/kvcache-deltas/yyyy/ | 90 days | needed to reconstruct warmstart state |

Replay environment setup checklist:
1. Match runtime binary and kernel versions: use artifact tag from trace (runtime_build: tag).
2. Provision GPU nodes with identical or superset topology. For known NUMA-sensitive regressions, match node SKU and affinity masks.
3. Configure model weights path and quantization profile as recorded.
4. Seed KV cache from kvcache-deltas: apply changelog in order to an empty cache.
5. Configure batch scheduler to accept the recorded batch composition and arrival timings (use synthetic inter-arrival to reproduce burst/coalescing).

Reconstruction commands (examples):
- Export traces for replay run:
  redwoodctl profiling export --trace-id 1234abcd --out /tmp/replay_bundle.tar.gz
- Initialize replay environment:
  replayctl init --bundle /tmp/replay_bundle.tar.gz --runtime-tag release-2026-01-15
- Apply KV cache deltas:
  replayctl kvcache apply --bundle /tmp/replay_bundle.tar.gz --target replay-node-1

Deterministic replay run (example):
  replayctl run --trace-id 1234abcd --repeat 3 --compare-baseline /tmp/prod_timeline.json --output /tmp/replay_result.json

Validation and artifacts to collect from replay runs:
- Kernel timeline (per-step) and per-kernel duration distribution.
- GPU occupancy and SM utilization trace.
- CPU-to-GPU transfer timings (host staging times).
- Batch composition mismatch report (if scheduler coalesced requests differently).
- KV cache hit/miss timeline before and after warmstart.

Alert thresholds and triage heuristics:
- If replay kernel timeline matches production within 5% but latency differs > 15% -> investigate host-level interference (noisy neighbor) and network jitter.
- If kernel variance differs > 20% -> likely scheduling non-determinism or different concurrency mix in production. Check batch-size distribution over 1 hour window.
- If KV cache miss delta explains > 30% of token processing time -> treat as cache warmup issue and consider extending cache TTL for route.

Mitigations and runbook actions (ordered):
1. Validate runtime and kernel versions are identical. If mismatch, recreate replay with correct binary.
2. Re-run replay on node with isolated CPU/GPU (pinning) to rule out host noise.
3. Toggle kernel scheduling knobs: kernel_credit_limit, preemption_window_ms, eager_batching_enable. Use incremental changes and single-variable experiments.
4. If scheduling changes affect latency positively in replay, run small canary rollout with those knobs for 1% traffic and monitor sampled P95/P99.

Safe rollback guidance:
- Any kernel-level knob change must include an automatic rollback policy: revert if P99 increases > 10% or error rate increases > 0.5% within 30 minutes.

Example profiler config (YAML):
-----BEGIN CONFIG-----
profiling:
  sampling:
    default_rate: 0.005  # 0.5% of requests
    stratified_by: [model_version, sequence_length_bucket, route_tag]
  trace_on_demand:
    enabled: false
    global_cap_per_hour: 50
    per_node_rate_limit: 1/min
  artifacts:
    traces_bucket: s3://profiling/traces/{{YYYY}}/{{MM}}/{{DD}}
    replay_bucket: s3://profiling/replays/
-----END CONFIG-----

Security and privacy notes:
- Never store full prompt text for customer requests. Store tokenized inputs with reversible hashing disabled; keep a prompt_hash and only store cleartext for synthetic/internal test traces.
- Access to replay artifacts is restricted to eng-serving-runtime and incident response SSO groups. All exports are logged to audit.

Telemetry keys and dashboards to consult:
- profiler.sampled.latency.p99 (by model_version, route_tag)
- profiler.trace.count (successful captures)
- profiler.kvcache.hit_rate
- runtime.kernel.duration.per_kernel (heatmap)
- replay.compare.delta_ms (post-replay comparison)

Postmortem and documentation updates:
- If a replay produced a fixable action, attach the replay_result.json and a short remediation summary to the incident ticket and update the related kernel ADR if the fix changes scheduling guarantees.

Appendix: common troubleshooting nuggets
- If replay shows identical kernel durations but production is higher, instrument node-level cgroups & host IO (disk/NIC) — often a transient IO spike can amplify token latencies.
- For quantization-induced variance, compare matrix-multiplication microbenchmarks between prod and replay nodes; numerical noise can change control flow in rare models.

Contacts:
- Primary profiling lead: asha.menon@redwood.ai
- Runtime kernel SME: diego.ramirez@redwood.ai
- On-call SRE for replay infra: infra-oncall@redwood.ai

Change log:
- 2026-02-10: Created initial draft.
- 2026-02-18: Added retention table and replay commands (review feedback).
- 2026-02-28: Finalized thresholds and published.

title: Dynamic Sampling Orchestrator and Fidelity Proxy Playbook
content:
Overview

This playbook documents the Dynamic Sampling Orchestrator (DSO) and Fidelity Proxy components used by the serving runtime to coordinate low-cost, high-signal profiling. It describes the architectural intent, sampling contracts, fidelity downgrade/upgrade semantics, operational runbook for experiments, benchmarks to validate signal quality, and the rollout/rollback checklist. This doc is intended for runtime engineers, SREs, and applied ML engineers running fidelity experiments.

Motivation

- Profiling every request at full fidelity (full traces + KV captures + kernel timings) is too expensive at production scale.
- We need a way to: 1) sample requests adaptively to maximize root-cause signal, 2) ensure fidelity changes preserve SLOs, and 3) make sampling decisions auditable and reproducible for offline analysis.

Goals

1) Maintain production p95 latency SLO (default target: 95th <= 120ms for inference RPC) while collecting high-quality traces.
2) Allow experimenters to request arbitrary fidelity windows and get deterministic, reproducible sampling for evaluation workloads.
3) Provide a safe rollout path (canary -> cohort -> global) and automated safety checks (latency regressions, kernel slowdowns, cost delta).

Architecture (high level)

- Dynamic Sampling Orchestrator (service name: trace-orch): central policy engine; decides which requests to sample and at what fidelity.
- Fidelity Proxy (service name: fidelity-proxy): per-node agent that enforces sampling decisions and manages local buffering of high-fidelity payloads (KV snapshots, kernel timelines) to avoid backpressure on the request path.
- Telemetry Gateway (telemetry-gw): shuffles sampled payloads to the trace storage cluster (efficient path: ClickHouse for lightweight signals, Tempo for full traces, and S3 for archived kernel captures).
- Signal Bus (Kafka topic: profiling.signals): publish sampling decisions and metadata for downstream validation and audit.

Decision flow

1) Incoming request passes through request-classifier (runtime sidecar).
2) request-classifier sends a minimal decision-query to trace-orch (0.5ms p99 target).
3) trace-orch evaluates active policies and returns a sampling token with fidelity profile id (FPID).
4) fidelity-proxy receives token and applies local capture hooks. Large captures are stored to node-local disk and streamed to telemetry-gw asynchronously.

Sampling contracts and fidelity profiles

- Fidelity Profile (FPID): a small JSON manifest (versioned) describing captures and retention. Example fields: "trace_level": [light|standard|full], "kv_capture": [none|headers|prefix|full], "kernel_timings": [off|summary|full], "max_size_mb": n, "sample_weight": float.

- Contract guarantees:
  - If trace-orch returns an FPID, the fidelity-proxy will attempt to apply that profile; failures fall back to the next-fallback FPID(typically 'standard').
  - The orchestrator will not assign an FPID whose expected resource cost would exceed configured budget for the node or tenant.
  - FPID manifests are immutable after release; updates produce new FPIDs (semver).

- Default profiles we maintain:
  - low-signal: trace_level=light, kv_capture=none, kernel_timings=off, sample_weight=0.01
  - standard: trace_level=standard, kv_capture=headers, kernel_timings=summary, sample_weight=0.1
  - high-fidelity: trace_level=full, kv_capture=prefix, kernel_timings=full, sample_weight=1.0

Adaptive sampling algorithm (summary)

- Inputs: recent latency cohorts, kernel error rates, cold-start frequency, historical entropy of outputs.
- Outputs: an FPID assignment probability per request class.
- Key features:
  - Burst protection: stop increasing sampling during node-level thermal events.
  - Diversity heuristic: prioritize sampling across user cohorts to avoid measurement bias.
  - Reproducible seeding: sampling decisions derive from request_id + FPID salt so experiments can be replayed deterministically.

Fidelity Proxy internals

- Components: enforcer (applies FPID), capture buffer (capped circular buffer on local disk), uploader worker pool (streams to telemetry-gw), circuit-breaker (drop captures under pressure).
- Safety invariants:
  1) If disk usage > 65% of capture partition, circuit-breaker engages and downgrades to 'standard' for new captures.
  2) Uploader concurrency is rate-limited by node-configured egress bandwidth (default 25MB/s).
  3) Captures accepted for telemetry have an upper bound max_size_mb; oversized captures are truncated with metadata note.

Operational runbook: quick triage

1) Symptom: sudden increase in p95 latency correlated with deployment of a new FPID.
  - Step 1: Check trace-orch policy list: kubectl -n observability get cm fidelity-policies -o yaml
  - Step 2: Validate per-node circuit-breaker: kubectl logs fidelity-proxy-<node> | grep CIRCUIT_BREAKER
  - Step 3: Inspect sampling rate stream: kafka-console-consumer --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --topic profiling.signals --from-beginning | jq .fpid | uniq -c
  - Step 4: If majority of nodes report circuit-breaker engagements, revert latest FPID roll (trace-orch rollback API).

2) Symptom: missing high-fidelity traces for a specific tenant cohort.
  - Step 1: Confirm active FPID for tenant: curl -s http://trace-orch.internal/api/v1/tenant/<tenant>/fpids
  - Step 2: Check fidelity-proxy accept logs for that tenant: journalctl -u fidelity-proxy | grep <tenant-id>
  - Step 3: Verify telemetry-gw ingress metrics (telemetry-gw/metrics HTTP). If telemetry-gw is saturated, enable graceful backpressure mode (telemetry-gw API /v1/backpressure/enable).

Benchmarks and validation

- Purpose: ensure sampled traces have sufficient signal and that sampling scheme does not materially change runtime SLOs.
- Minimum validation suite:
  1) Replay fidelity parity test: sample N=10k requests with both 'standard' and 'high-fidelity' FPIDs in shadow mode and compare kernel timing distributions (KS-statistic < 0.05 target).
  2) Latency impact test: measure p95 with profiling enabled vs disabled under 95th percentile traffic; acceptable delta <= 5% or 50ms whichever is smaller.
  3) Cost delta analysis: compute storage and egress delta per million requests; abort rollout if > 2x planned budget.

Benchmark harness commands (examples)

- Start a shadow sampling run:
  curl -X POST http://trace-orch.internal/api/v1/experiments \
    -d '{"name":"shadow-fidelity-parity-2026-09","target": "tenant:all","mode":"shadow","fpids":["standard","high-fidelity"],"duration_minutes":60}'

- Export sample manifests:
  kafka-console-consumer --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --topic profiling.signals --timeout-ms 60000 | jq -r '
    "\(.request_id) \(.fpid) \(.timestamp)"' > /tmp/sampling-run.txt

Rollout and canary checklist

1) Pre-checks (automated):
  - All FPID unit tests pass.
  - Expected cost per 100k requests is under configured budget.
  - Shadow runs for 60 minutes show no p95 increase > 3%.
2) Canary (2% traffic, 4 nodes across zones):
  - Monitor: p95 latency, kernel_fails/sec, fidelity-proxy_truncations, telemetry-gw_ingress_errors.
  - Duration: min 2 hours at 99th percentile load.
3) Cohort rollout (20% traffic):
  - Run benchmark parity test on cohort traffic.
  - If any of the alerts fire (latency, cost, or disk pressure), immediately revert to previous FPID.
4) Global rollout: ramp to 100% over 6 hours with automated guardrails.

Automated safety checks (examples)

- Disk pressure alarm: node.capture_partition_free_bytes < 35% -> trigger fidelity-proxy downgrade
- Latency alarm: cohort_p95_delta > 7% AND absolute_delta > 60ms -> stop rollout
- Kernel error alarm: kernel_op_error_rate increased by factor > 3 -> hold rollout and notify kernel team

Operational APIs and quick commands

- Query current FPID for request class: curl http://trace-orch.internal/api/v1/query?class=chat-completion
- Start a canary: curl -X POST http://trace-orch.internal/api/v1/rollouts -d '{"fpid":"high-fidelity","traffic_pct":2}'
- Rollback last rollout: curl -X POST http://trace-orch.internal/api/v1/rollouts/rollback
- Inspect fidelity-proxy health: kubectl -n runtime get pods -l app=fidelity-proxy -o wide; kubectl logs fidelity-proxy-<pod> -c enforcer

Data quality and postmortem guidance

- When an experiment fails, collect: sampling.signals Kafka segment, fidelity-proxy logs (one hour before/after), telemetry-gw metrics, ClickHouse sample index for the period.
- Run signal quality checks: verify coverage across user cohorts, check kernel timing correlation with trace-level events, and compute reproducibility rate (fraction of replayed requests that get same FPID).

Appendix: example FPID manifest (YAML)

---
fp_id: "fpid.high-fidelity.v1"
version: "1"
trace_level: full
kv_capture: prefix
kernel_timings: full
max_size_mb: 16
sample_weight: 1.0
retention_days: 7
---

Appendix: sample CLI for fidelity-proxy dry-run

# Enable dry-run mode (no uploads)
kubectl -n runtime exec -it fidelity-proxy-<pod> -- fidelity-proxyctl --mode=dry-run --fpids=standard,high-fidelity

# Check upload backlog
kubectl -n runtime exec fidelity-proxy-<pod> -- fidelity-proxyctl status | grep backlog

Ownership, metrics and SLOs

- Owner: eng-serving-runtime / Observability subteam (primary: @asha.patel).
- SLOs to watch when running profiling experiments:
  - Runtime p95 latency: target <= configured tenant SLO (default 120ms).
  - Telemetry ingress error rate: < 0.1%
  - Fidelity-proxy truncation rate for accepted captures: < 0.5%
  - Reproducibility (replay match rate): > 98% for deterministic experiments

Related pages and references

- runtime-experimentation-blueprint-and-hypothesis-protocol-2026 (experiment gating)
- runtime-telemetry-sampling-cost-aware-profiling-manual-2027 (cost accounting)
- observability-bridge-and-execution-surface-manual-2026 (ingress and adapters)

Notes and open decisions

- Open: precise KS-statistic threshold for kernel timing parity is under review (current target 0.05).
- Open: centralized vs per-tenant sampling budgets — investigation ticket #ENG-9312.

Contact

For questions or to request a private profiling window for a customer engagement, ping #runtime-profiling on Slack or email asha.patel@redwood.ai.

title: Variance-driven Sampling and Cost-Latency Correlation Playbook
content:
Summary
-------
This playbook defines an operational pattern for using variance-driven sampling of runtime telemetries to detect and triage episodes where cost per inference increases without a corresponding improvement in quality, or where latency and cost diverge across model variants and request shapes. It describes instrumentation signals, adaptive sampling algorithms, alert thresholds, an investigation checklist, and recommended mitigations for common root causes (batching, KV cache misses, kernel fallbacks, and topology shifts).

Goals
-----
- Detect sustained or transient incidents where per-token cost increases by > 15% at p95 or where p99 latency regresses > 20% relative to baseline.
- Reduce alert noise by focusing on high-variance cohorts (request shapes, model versions, customer tiers).
- Provide a repeatable triage procedure that links telemetry to kernel-level causes and cost drivers.
- Recommend automated mitigations (sampling rate changes, fallback model routing, cache warmups) and manual runbook steps.

Scope and audience
------------------
- Audience: Runtime SREs, Serving Runtime Engineers, Performance Engineers.
- In-scope: Host-level and request-level telemetry, kernel selection traces, KV cache hit/miss streams, batching metrics, model variant rollouts.
- Out-of-scope: Model quality evaluation (use eval-harness), billing reconciliation (use finance tooling).

Key signals to collect
----------------------
1. Per-request fields (high-cardinality):
   - request_id, route, model_version, sequence_length, input_tokens, output_tokens, customer_tier
   - observed_latency_ms (end-to-end), kernel_latency_ms, queue_time_ms, batch_size_at_exec
   - kvcache_lookup_count, kvcache_miss_count, quantization_variant
2. Host & kernel telemetry (low-cardinality):
   - gpu_util_pct, sm_occupancy, memory_bytes_used, kernel_name, kernel_duration_ms
3. Cost proxies:
   - per-token_cpu_cycles_estimate, gpu_kernel_time_ms, amortized_gpu_seconds_per_call
4. Sampling metadata: sampling_bucket, sampling_score, sample_decision_reason

Design: variance-driven sampling
--------------------------------
Rationale: Static uniform sampling underweights rare but high-cost request cohorts (large seq len, model rollouts). The variance-driven sampler adapts sampling probabilities to prioritize cohorts with high observed variance in cost and latency so investigations capture explanatory examples with fewer total samples.

Algorithm (overview)
1. Define cohort key = hash(route, model_version, sequence_length_bin, customer_tier).
2. Maintain rolling window (W = 30m default) for each cohort with sample_count N and sample variance S^2 of cost-per-token and p95 latency.
3. Compute score = alpha * normalized(S_cost) + beta * normalized(S_latency) + gamma * recent_regression_indicator. (alpha=0.5, beta=0.4, gamma=0.1 default).
4. Map score -> sampling probability p = min(p_max, base_p * (1 + score)). Defaults: base_p=0.01, p_max=0.5.
5. Persist sampled traces to the central profiling sink for kernel traceback and storage.

Implementation notes
--------------------
- Use probabilistic reservoir per cohort to bound memory.
- Normalize variances using robust scaling (median absolute deviation) to avoid outlier blowup.
- Ensure sampling decisions are deterministic per request_id + sampling_window to prevent double-sampling across retries.
- Emit sampler telemetry: sampling_rate_by_cohort, missed_samples_due_to_quota, reservoir_overflow_count.

Configuration table (recommended defaults)
----------------------------------------
| parameter | description | recommended value | rationale |
|-----------|-------------|-------------------|-----------|
| W | rolling window length | "30m" | captures transient episodes without excessive state |
| base_p | baseline sampling probability | "0.01" | keeps storage costs low |
| p_max | sampling cap | "0.5" | ensures hot cohorts don't overwhelm storage |
| alpha,beta,gamma | score weights | "0.5,0.4,0.1" | weight cost more than latency |
| sequence_length_bins | bins for cohorting | "[<=32, 33-128, 129-512, 513+]" | separates short vs long requests |
| reservoir_size | per-cohort reservoir | "500" | memory bound per cohort |

Operational alerts and thresholds
--------------------------------
- Alert: "HighCostVarianceByCohort"
  - Trigger: cohort sampling variance in per-token cost increases > 15% and sampled p95 cost-per-token increases > 10% over baseline for W.
  - Severity: P2.
  - Pager: SRE on-call.

- Alert: "Cost-Latency Divergence"
  - Trigger: cohort where cost-per-token increases > 15% but p50 latency unchanged and kernel_latency_ms increased by > 30%
  - Severity: P3.

- Alert: "Sampling-Reservoir-Pressure"
  - Trigger: reservoir_overflow_count > 0 for > 5m.
  - Action: autoscale sampler or reduce base_p.

Investigation checklist (triage steps)
-------------------------------------
1. Validate alert and gather context: cohort key, time window, sample_count, top 10 sampled trace ids.
2. Compare with baseline: run cohort in benchmarking harness (use synthetic request replay) with identical model_version and input shape.
3. Examine kernel traces for sampled IDs: look for kernel_name fallback (ex: aten_attention_non_fused -> fused_attention) and increased kernel_duration_ms.
4. Check KV cache signals: high kvcache_miss_count correlating with increased model_compute_time implies cache warmup or shard misrouting.
5. Inspect batch dynamics: high variance in batch_size_at_exec can cause head-of-line latency spikes leading to inefficient kernel launches.
6. Cross-check recent rollouts and routing rules (route table changes, firmware/drivers, GPU topology reassignments).
7. If hardware-level (SM occupancy low, GPU underutilized) correlate with small batch sizes or poor kernel packing.

Mitigation playbook (ordered)
----------------------------
1. Short-term (automated):
   - If sampling indicates KV cache coldness: enable on-demand prefix caching for affected customer_tier or trigger a background warmup job (see Runbook: dynamic-kvcache-resilience-and-warmup).
   - If kernel fallback detected: route 10% of traffic to the previous model_variant until kernel mapper patch is deployed.
   - If reservoir pressure: reduce base_p by 2x for non-critical tiers.
2. Mid-term (manual, < 2 hours):
   - Increase batch window tolerance for the affected pool (increase batching latency SLO by 10–25% while monitoring error budget).
   - Rebalance KV cache shards to co-locate hot keys with serving shards.
3. Long-term (postmortem & dev work):
   - Add kernel fusion/optimization or adjust kernel-mapper heuristics to prefer fused kernels for the cohort shapes.
   - Add dedicated capacity for high-cost cohorts (Dedicated pool reservation) or surface cost-aware routing rules.

Playbook run example (commands)
-------------------------------
1) Query recent sampled traces via telemetry CLI:

```
redwood telemetry query --dataset=runtime_samples --filter "cohort=route:chat,model:v2,seq_bin:513+" --range "-45m" --limit 200 --output json > sampled_traces.json
```

2) Run local replay for top samples against bench harness:

```
bench-runner replay --input sampled_traces.json --model v2 --profile kernel-trace --out replay_results.json
```

3) Extract kernel summary:

```
jq -r '.traces[] | {trace_id, kernel_summary}' replay_results.json | less
```

Integration with benchmarking & release process
------------------------------------------------
- Any model or kernel mapper change that increases sample variance for any cohort by > 10% must be added as a checkpoint in the pre-release gating pipeline.
- Include a variance report (automated) in release notes: histogram of per-cohort sampling_score deltas versus baseline, top 3 regressing cohorts, and mitigation flags.

Example incident root cause matrix (quick reference)
--------------------------------------------------
| symptom | common root cause | first-check | short-term mitigation |
|--------|-------------------|-------------|----------------------|
| sudden p99 latency spikes for long-seq requests | kernel fallback to generic attention kernel | kernel_name in sampled trace | route to fallback-safe variant, roll back mapper change |
| increased per-token cost, stable latency | KV cache percent misses | kvcache_miss_count by cohort | enable cache warmup, rebalance shards |
| higher variance in cost across replicas | GPU topology change or firmware regression | recent node agent rollout | pin affected nodes out of pool, escalate to infra |

Ownership and SLAs
------------------
- Sampler service owner: eng-serving-runtime/perf-team.
- On-call: runtime-SRE rotation (see SLOs page).
- Sampling retention: sampled traces stored for 90 days in the profiling sink by default.

Metrics to report in QBRs
-----------------------
- median sampling_score across top 100 cohorts
- fraction of alerts triaged to kernel vs cache vs batching causes
- storage cost per 10k samples
- mean time to mitigative action (MTMA) for HighCostVarianceByCohort alerts

Appendix: recommended telemetry schema snippet
--------------------------------------------
(Illustrative example; actual schema enforced by telemetry ingestion service)
```
{
  "request_id": "uuid",
  "timestamp": "ISO8601",
  "route": "chat",
  "model_version": "v2",
  "sequence_length": 640,
  "sequence_length_bin": "513+",
  "input_tokens": 512,
  "output_tokens": 128,
  "observed_latency_ms": 422.1,
  "kernel_latency_ms": 391.3,
  "batch_size_at_exec": 4,
  "kvcache_lookup_count": 512,
  "kvcache_miss_count": 128,
  "kernel_name": "fused_attention_v3",
  "gpu_util_pct": 78.2,
  "sm_occupancy": 0.62,
  "sampling_bucket": "high_variance",
  "sampling_score": 3.4
}
```

Related reading
---------------
- Runtime: Dynamic KV cache resilience and warmup playbook (link above)
- Benchmarking: Mixed workload SLO simulation suite (link above)
- Profiling: Continuous runtime profiling strategy (internal)

Revision history
----------------
- 2025-11-03: Created by Maya Chen (initial design and defaults).
- 2026-01-12: Updated defaults for base_p and reservoir_size after pilot.
- 2026-02-14: Added mitigation step for kernel fallback routing and expanded alert definitions.

Contact
-------
For questions or to request an experiment slot for high-cost cohorts, contact eng-serving-runtime/perf-team or email maya.chen@redwood.com.

title: Execution Cohort Stabilization and Probing Playbook
content:
Summary:

This playbook documents the procedures, signals, and automated probes we use to detect, stabilize, and harden execution cohorts in the Redwood serving runtime. An execution cohort is a set of requests that share scheduling, kernel, and fidelity characteristics (for example: short-text-high-priority, long-sequence-batch, or embedding-burst). Cohort instability manifests as tail-latency spikes, throughput collapse, or fidelity regressions. This document provides detection heuristics, triage steps, remediation actions, and automation recipes for safe experimentation and production rollouts.

Scope and goals:
- Scope: per-region, per-cluster cohorts observed by the runtime scheduler and kernel dispatcher.
- Goals: detect cohort divergence within 2x of historical variance; restore stable latency SLOs (P95/P99) within the incident window; record a reproducible trace for postmortem.

Key definitions:
- Cohort: logical grouping of requests by route, model_variant, priority_class, and sequence_length_bucket.
- Stabilization: actions taken to restore steady-state (admit-rate tuning, kernel rollback, quota adjustments).
- Probing: controlled injection of synthetic/recorded traffic to validate remediation.

Signals to monitor (ranked):
1) Latency quantiles per-cohort: P50, P95, P99 sliding 1h/6h windows. Thresholds in the metric table (below).
2) Kernel execution time histogram for the cohort (microsecond buckets).
3) KV-cache hit ratio and miss spike events.
4) Slot reservation churn: rate of slot aborts per minute for cohort slots.
5) Backpressure indicators: queue depth, admission queue time, and admission rejection rate.
6) Model fidelity regressors: eval-set perplexity/accuracy delta if available.

Metric thresholds (operational table):
- P95 latency increase > 30% relative to 7d baseline -> severity: warning
- P99 latency increase > 50% relative to 7d baseline -> severity: incident
- KV-cache miss rate > baseline + 10ppt and sustained > 60s -> severity: action required
- Slot abort rate > 0.5/min/cohort -> severity: action required
- Admission rejection > 1% sustained over 5m -> severity: action required

(These thresholds are tuned per-customer; team owners should publish cohort-specific overrides to the Cohort Registry.)

Triage checklist (first 15 minutes):
1) Confirm signal: cross-check P99 spikes across both telemetry and shadow channels. Use ri-metrics query: 
   ri-metrics query "latency.quantile{cohort=\"$COHORT\",quantile=0.99} - baseline(7d)" --window=15m
2) Capture a live execution trace: 
   rictl trace collect --cohort $COHORT --duration 120s --priority high --label incident/$INCIDENT_ID
3) Determine scope: single node, shard, or cluster-wide. Inspect dispatcher logs for kernel handoffs: 
   rictl node inspect $NODE_ID --filter "handoff" --since 30m
4) Look for concurrent changes: kernel rollouts, kernel plugin activations, quantization-profile updates, or recent canaries.

Isolation & containment steps (minutes 15–45):
- If P99 > incident threshold and cohort is high priority: temporarily reduce concurrency cap for the cohort by 20%: 
  rictl cohort update $COHORT --max-concurrency $(calc 0.8 * current) --reason "auto-stabilize/$(date +%Y%m%d)"
- If slot aborts are high and localized to a node: cordon node from scheduler for new slot reservations (not evict running work) and migrate new reservations: 
  rictl node cordon $NODE_ID --drain=false
- If kernel hint mismatch detected (e.g., quantized kernel selected with incompatible sequence length): disable experimental kernel variant for the cohort: 
  rictl kernel variant disable --variant $VARIANT_ID --selector "cohort=$COHORT"

Probing and validation (45–120 minutes):
1) Re-run shadow traces while scaling concurrency down to validate that latency stabilizes. Use recorded request corpus where possible: 
   ri-playback run --corpus sprints/$COHORT/last-24h --mode shadow --concurrency 10 --duration 10m
2) Synthetic probing recipe (safe):
   - Start at 10% of baseline traffic, 1 minute run, verify P95 improvement.
   - Increase to 25% for 5 minutes with KV-cache warmup hints enabled.
   - If stable, ramp to 50% and mark cohort stable candidate.
3) Capture profiler artifacts for the window: kernel flamegraphs, GPU utilization, and host-level perf counters. Commands: 
   ri-probe collect --type kernel-flame --cohort $COHORT --out /tmp/$COHORT-flame.tgz
   nvtop-snapshot --output /tmp/gpu-$NODE_ID.json --duration 60

Remediation and rollback (2–6 hours):
- If a kernel variant causes regression: roll back kernel rollout for the affected pool and mark variant as quarantined in the kernel registry.
- If KV-cache miss storm: increase prefetch budget for the cohort and add a temporary prefix-caching policy for hot keys.
- If admission queueing is the root cause: reduce admission slice for long-sequence cohorts, and create a burst-allow list for short interactive cohorts.

Automation recipes (recommended):
1) Cohort Stabilizer (automated controller): declarative policy that can apply non-destructive throttles and probe injections. Policy example (YAML, conceptual):

  name: stabilize-short-interactive
  selector: cohort: short-text-high-priority
  triggers:
    - p99_latency_increase: 40
      window: 5m
  actions:
    - set_max_concurrency: 0.7
    - run_probe: \"shadow-corpus-stable-1m\"
    - notify: #on-call

2) Canary gating: require that every kernel variant rollout includes a cohort-probe plan that executes the above shadow probes before 10% traffic can be directed to the variant.

Investigation playbook (post-stabilization):
1) Collect and attach artifacts to incident: execution trace, kernel flamegraphs, dispatcher logs, admission metrics, KV-cache telemetry.
2) Run root-cause hypothesis checklist in order: 
   - Hypothesis A: scheduler mis-selection of kernel variant -> confirm by correlating kernel_id with increased latencies.
   - Hypothesis B: KV-cache eviction due to memory pressure -> confirm by cache eviction rate and node memory pressure events.
   - Hypothesis C: Traffic shape change (new route or prompt distribution) -> inspect request histogram and prompt length distribution.
3) If hypothesis confirmed: produce a remediation RFC (short) and schedule a targeted canary with explicit rollback criteria.

Runbook owner and escalation matrix:
- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime/scheduling-team
- Secondary: eng-sre/runtime-ops-oncall
- Pager escalation: paging policy (P1 -> 15m, P2 -> 60m) documented in oncall runbook.

Example incident timeline (annotated):
- 00:00 detect spike P99 elevated on cohort A
- 00:06 capture trace & begin containment (reduce concurrency)
- 00:18 identify node-local slot aborts correlated with kernel variant rollout
- 01:10 run shadow probe; latencies improve with concurrency throttled
- 03:30 rollout rollback completed, cohort stabilized

Post-incident hardening recommendations:
- Add cohort-specific kernel-compatibility matrix to the Cohort Registry.
- Instrument cohort-level admission slice metrics with earlier alerting thresholds (10m window).
- Expand shadow corpus coverage: preserve 7-day rolling windows for the top-20 cohorts by traffic.
- Publish a kernel-variant-failure annotation on the release notes for traceability.

Appendix: useful CLI snippets and queries
- List cohorts with recent P99 slope: ri-metrics list-cohorts --filter "p99_slope>0.2" --window 30m
- Fetch last trace for cohort: rictl trace get --cohort $COHORT --limit 1 --output /tmp/trace-$COHORT.json
- Quarantine kernel variant: rictl kernel quarantine $VARIANT_ID --reason "regression:$INCIDENT_ID"

Contact and ownership notes:
- For experimental kernel changes, the kernel owner must attach a cohort-probe plan to the rollout PR.
- All teams operating the Cohort Stabilizer must run weekly drills (see playbook schedule) and report a runbook-run summary in the runtime SRE weekly.

Related documents:
- Runtime decision graph and observed behaviour catalog (runtime-architecture)
- Kernel telemetry synthesis and proofing (kernel-and-scheduling)

Revision history:
- 2026-03-10: created by Priya Malhotra
- 2026-04-02: added automation recipes and probe recipes; reviewer feedback incorporated

End of document.

title: Asymmetric Kernel Fidelity Profiling  Guidelines and Experiment Matrix
content:
summary:
This playbook documents a repeatable approach to profile and evaluate asymmetric kernel variants used by the runtime: kernels that offer different fidelity or approximation levels (full-precision, quantized, approx-attention, mixed-kernel offloads). It provides an experiment matrix, instrumentation checklist, and interpretation guidance so kernel rollouts keep application-level quality and SLOs intact.

scope:
Applies to runtime kernel families used in production inference (attention, matmul, kv-cache ops). Focuses on profiling permutations where a request may fall back between kernel fidelity levels and on measuring the operational cost of transitions.

goals:
Detect fidelity regressions at prompt-set level; quantify latency and p99 tail per-kernel and per-sequence-length; validate graceful fallback behavior and measure reconfiguration costs; provide a go/no-go decision matrix for kernel rollout aligned with SLO thresholds.

definitions:
High-fidelity kernel: reference kernel prioritized for output quality (FP16/FP32). Economical kernel: optimized for cost/throughput (quantized, approximate) with potential quality delta. Fallback oscillation: repeated switching between kernels that causes latency spikes or quality divergence.

prerequisites_and_ownership:
Owned by eng-serving-runtime (profiling lead) with review from kernel maintainers and SRE. Required infra: profiling cluster with representative GPUs (A100/H100 and a low-cost pool like A10G), workload-replay service, and tracing hooks enabled. Provide access to artifact storage, a dashboard template (Grafana id: runtime.kernel.fidelity.profile), and the applied-ml-evals harness.

instrumentation_checklist:
Kernel-level timers per dispatch; request timeline markers (request_receive, model_load, kv_attach, kernel_dispatch(N), kernel_complete(N), response_stream_start); memory copy accounting between device regions; fidelity flag telemetry attached to kernel_dispatch events; quality trace linking prompt_id -> candidate_hash -> golden_eval_id.

sampling_strategy_and_telemetry_budget:
Stratified sampling by sequence length cohorts: short (<=64), medium (65-512), long (>512). SLO-aware sampling: increase sample rate during tail events and for high-sensitivity customers. Telemetry cost cap: profiling telemetry should not exceed 6% of production inference compute on the profiling cluster.

experiment_matrix:
1) Baseline characterization: reference kernels only; canonical prompt-set; metrics: latency p50/p95/p99, tokens/s, memory, energy, quality. 2) Single kernel substitution: replace one operator kernel with economical variant; run per cohort and measure quality drift and latency delta. 3) Mixed-mode (fallback) replay: enable runtime fallback policy and inject capacity events; track fallback frequency, transition time, oscillations. 4) Session-boundary stress: simulate long chat sessions to measure cache conversion/regeneration costs. 5) Canary with adversarial corpus: include prompts sensitive to approximation; run human eval gates for semantic regressions.

bench_commands_and_snippets:
replay-runner --corpus dev-corpus-v3 --cohort short,medium,long --kernel-policy ref_only --out results/baseline
replay-runner --corpus dev-corpus-v3 --cohort short,medium,long --kernel-policy economical_attention --out results/attn_sub
replay-runner --corpus dev-corpus-v3 --policy fallthrough --inject-load 0.7 --out results/fallback

Profiling-exporter config (YAML): trace_filters: include: [kernel_dispatch, kernel_complete, request_receive, kv_attach] tags: [kernel_variant, seq_len, tenant_id] sample_rate: 0.01 cohorts: [short, medium, long]

key_metrics_and_thresholds:
p50 delta (economical vs baseline) <= +10% for short/medium cohorts. p99 delta <= +15% for any cohort; above requires mitigation. Quality regression threshold: task-specific metric drop <= 1.5% absolute; for generative metrics use human review gate if >0.6% change. Fallback frequency expected <= 2% normal; >5% indicates misconfiguration. Transition cost target: <= 20ms avg; >100ms needs action.

interpreting_results:
Tail latency increase + low fallback rate -> suspect slow kernel micro-latency. Tail increase + high fallback rate -> policy thrashing or oscillation. Quality drop without latency improvement -> algorithmic regression in economical kernel. Memory spikes during switch -> examine device copy accounting and slab allocators; evaluate lazy-conversion or state-compat modes.

mitigation_patterns:
Narrow rollout with sequence-length gating; increase hysteresis in kernel selection policy; soft-fallback to non-critical routes or lower-tier tenants; convert state lazily (conversion-on-read) to reduce upfront cost.

reporting_template:
Experiment: economical_attention substitution; Date & cluster: <date> / profiling-h100-1; Workloads: dev-corpus-v3 cohorts; Key metrics: p50 +X%, p99 +Y%, quality delta -Z, fallback freq P%. Decision: example - proceed to canary with seq_len <= 256 gating and 1% traffic.

operational_runbook:
1) Create experiment ticket (JIRA epic: KERNEL-PROF-<ID>) with replay parameters and dashboard link. 2) Run baseline and upload trace tarball to artifact store (s3://redwood-profiling/<id>/). 3) Run candidate kernels until minimum sample (n>=5000 requests per cohort) or 6 hours. 4) Review automated report and trigger human evals for quality delta >0.3%. 5) If pass, approve staged canary: 0.1% -> 1% -> 5% with rollback gates. 6) Post-canary: 72-hour continuous monitoring focused on p99 and fallback frequency.

appendix_troubleshooting:
If p99 jumps: run trace-inspector --filter kernel_variant=approx-attn and inspect long kernel_dispatch events. If memory conversion dominates: capture nvprof and compare device copy bytes pre/post-switch. For quality diffs: run quality-diff --golden golden_id --candidate candidate_id --metrics ll,accuracy and schedule human review.

contact_and_escalation:
Slack: #runtime-profiling. Pager: eng-sre oncall for incidents during canary. Kernel regressions: assign to kernel-team@redwood.internal with trace tarball and report.

change_log:
2025-11-15: Created initial playbook and experiment matrix. (Asha Patel)
2026-01-20: Added canary gating thresholds and sample CLI snippets; clarified transition-cost threshold. (Asha Patel)

title: Operator profiling runbook for multi-model pipelines
content:
## Overview

This runbook guides operators and oncall engineers through focused profiling, triage, and mitigation for production inference pipelines that invoke multiple model variants within a single request path (for example: routing -> reranking -> generation). These multi-model pipelines have distinct failure and performance modes due to cross-model kernel contention, KV cache effects, and routing-induced burstiness. The goal is to localize dominant cost/latency contributors, validate fidelity regressions, and recommend safe mitigations.

Audience: SREs, runtime operators, performance engineers, and platform owners.

## When to use this runbook
- Incident symptoms: sudden p95/p99 latency increases, elevated per-token cost, regression alerts from fidelity monitoring tied to specific prompt sets, or increased model swap frequency.
- Pre-launch: run this profiling checklist before enabling new multi-model routing rules or model variants in production.

## High-level profiling objectives
1. Attribute latency to segment (frontend, router, model A, model B, post-processing).
2. Determine kernel-level contention or slow kernel regressions.
3. Measure KV cache hit/miss amplification across chained models.
4. Quantify cost impact (per-token GPU time and dispatched kernel time) and map to SLO risk.

## Signals and dashboards (reference thresholds)
| Signal | Source | Unit | Alert threshold | First action |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| p99 end-to-end latency | metrics.runtime.e2e_latency | ms | > 1200 | Start this runbook |
| p99 per-model inference latency | metrics.runtime.model_latency{model} | ms | > 400 | Inspect kernel traces |
| Kernel stall time | traces.kernel.stall_ratio | % | > 15% | Collect kernel samples |
| KV cache miss amplification | metrics.kvcache.miss_ratio | ratio | increase > 2x baseline | Check routing entropy |
| Per-token GPU time | metrics.gpu.token_time | ms/token | > 0.35 | Run microbenchmarks |
| Failure rate for fallbacks | metrics.runtime.fallback_rate | % | > 1% | Validate model compatibility |

Note: thresholds are a starting point. Tune per-customer/product SLO.

## Preparation steps
1. Notify stakeholders: channel runtime-ops and owning product team, record the incident ID in the investigation notes.
2. Capture a representative traffic window: enable request shadowing to staging or enable request sampling at 5% if live.
3. Ensure tracing level: set TRACE level for router and model-adapter services for a 10 minute window.
4. Reserve GPU profiling quota: request access to profiler nodes and ensure the kernel symbol map is current.

## Data collection checklist
1. Collect full traces for 500 representative requests spanning the bad window (or 10 minutes of high load).
2. Export kernel-level samples (nvprof/NSys or vendor equivalent) for the top 5 impacted GPUs.
3. Pull scheduler and admission logs for the timeframe (slot assignments, preemption events).
4. Gather KV-cache metrics per-shard and per-model for the same window.
5. Snapshot routing decisions and model variant assignment logs for sampled requests.

## Commands and snippets
Use these in the operator sandbox. Replace placeholders.

```bash
# sample trace export (internal cli)
redwoodctl traces export --start 2026-02-14T15:02:00Z --end 2026-02-14T15:12:00Z --service router,model-adapter,dispatcher --out /tmp/trace-window.json

# collect kernel samples from profiler node
ssh profiler-01 sudo nsys profile --trace=nvtx,cuda --output /tmp/prof-report

# query KV cache stats from metrics API
curl -sS "https://metrics.internal/api/query?m=kvcache.miss_ratio&from=2026-02-14T15:02:00Z&to=2026-02-14T15:12:00Z" > /tmp/kvcache.json
```

## Analysis steps and heuristics
1. Decompose end-to-end trace into segments and compute segment p99 contribution. If a single model consumes > 60% of p99, focus there.
2. Inspect kernel traces: look for increased stall_ratio, long memcpy peaks, or unexpected kernel serialization between models. Flag kernels with > 2x baseline latency.
3. Check scheduler logs for back-to-back preemptions or slot thrashing impacting KV cache locality.
4. Correlate routing entropy with KV cache miss amplification. A routing shift that increases model variance often drives cache misses.
5. Run targeted microbenchmarks to reproduce per-model per-shape latency using an isolated GPU: use the sample workload below.

Sample microbenchmark YAML (submit to perf-lab)
| field | value |
|---|---|
| job_name | mm-pbench-{{model}}-seq128 |
| model | model-a-v2,model-b-v1 |
| batch_shapes | [ {batch:1,seq:64}, {batch:1,seq:128} ] |
| duration | 10m |
| trace_level | kernel,scheduler |

## Mitigations (short-term)
- Apply routing rate limit for the upstream service to smooth burstiness.
- Increase admission capacity (if on Dedicated) for the affected pool for 10–30 minutes to reduce queueing.
- Temporarily pin requests to the stable model variant with known lower per-token GPU time.
- Disable non-critical post-processing (rerank stage) to measure its marginal impact.
- If kernel regression is confirmed, rollback the recent kernel or model runtime library change via the kernel rollback playbook.

## Long-term remediation recommendations
- Add model affinity tags to routing decisions to preserve KV cache locality.
- Introduce modeled per-request cost accounting to detect cost regressions alongside fidelity.
- Expand microbenchmark coverage to include chained-model scenarios and publish the benchmark manifests.
- Harden kernel rollout testing to include multi-model chain synthetic traffic.

## Known cross-model failure modes and mitigations
- Kernel serialization: concurrent model kernels serialize due to a scheduling bug. Mitigation: enable per-tenant kernel credit isolation and limit simultaneous kernels per-GPU.
- KV cache thrash: routing entropy leads to cold cache across chained requests. Mitigation: add short-lived prefix caching and warmup hints for high-entropy routes.
- Mismatched quantization paths: model A dispatches a quantized kernel incompatible with model B expectations. Mitigation: enforce variant compatibility matrix in the router.

## Triage decision tree (quick)
1. Is per-model latency the dominant contributor? Yes -> analyze kernel traces. No -> inspect router and network.
2. Are kernel stalls elevated? Yes -> capture kernel sample and escalate to runtime-kernel team. No -> look at queueing and admission.
3. Is KV cache miss ratio increased relative to baseline? Yes -> consider routing affinity and warmup. No -> check microbenchmarks for regression.

## Post-incident steps
1. Create an incident postmortem with timelines, root cause hypothesis, and actions.
2. Add a regression test to the microbenchmark suite that reproduces the identified mode.
3. Schedule a cross-team review if kernel or scheduler change was causal.
4. Update the routing and model-variant SLO documentation if thresholds were insufficient.

## Ownership and escalation
- Primary owner: runtime-ops oncall (runtime-ops rotation).
- Secondary: serving-runtime kernel subteam.
- Escalation: page runtime-sre lead for capacity changes; page runtime-kernel lead for kernel regressions.

## References and related artifacts
- Perf lab job templates: /ops/perf-lab/job-templates
- Kernel symbol map and upload guide: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/kernel-symbol-management-2025
- Routing policy manifest examples: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/delta-routing-and-cost-partitioning-architecture-2026

## Revision history
- 2026-02-15: created by Priya Nambiar.
- 2026-03-05: expanded mitigation checklist and added microbenchmark manifest.

title: Debugging kernel selection and launch config (profiling playbook)
content:
## Purpose
This page is the standard playbook for debugging **kernel selection** (v1 and v2) and **GPU launch configuration** in Redwood Serving Runtime.

It covers:
- Capturing kernel selection traces (telemetry + local dumps)
- Reproducing a mis-selection locally with the same inputs
- Comparing candidate kernels apples-to-apples
- Interpreting common GPU/perf counters for prefill vs decode
- Recognizing common failure signatures and the fastest mitigations

**Non-goals:** deep kernel implementation details or architectural rationale (see the design + ADR).

---

## When to use this playbook
Use this when you see any of the following:
- p95/p99 latency regression after enabling Kernel Auto-Selection v2
- Throughput instability on mixed workloads (short + long prompts)
- Unexpected fallback to a slower “generic” kernel
- GPU-SKU-specific regressions (A100 vs H100 vs L40S, MIG vs non-MIG)
- Suspected nondeterminism (same request → different kernel choice)

---

## Glossary (runtime terms)
- **Prefill:** processing the prompt/context (usually GEMM-heavy; long-context sensitive)
- **Decode:** token-by-token generation (latency sensitive; typically attention-heavy)
- **Seq bucket:** selector’s coarse regime classification (prefill/decode characteristics + token ranges)
- **Candidate kernels:** kernel implementations compatible with the request + model + GPU SKU
- **Launch config:** CUDA kernel launch parameters and runtime execution path configuration (e.g., split-K, CTA shape, persistent kernels, etc.)

---

## Quick-start triage checklist (10–15 minutes)
1) Identify **what changed**
   - Runtime version (e.g., 1.21 canary)
   - Selector version (v1 vs v2)
   - Driver/CUDA version
   - GPU SKU (including MIG)
   - Model version / quantization profile

2) Pull a single representative **trace**
   - Capture selection telemetry for the request(s)
   - Confirm chosen kernel, seq bucket, and fallback reason (if any)

3) Sanity check feature extraction
   - model_family correct?
   - prefill_tokens/decode_tokens estimates correct?
   - gpu_sku normalized correctly?

4) Compare with a forced kernel baseline
   - Force “known-good” kernel on same GPU SKU
   - Check prefill vs decode deltas; confirm regression is in the suspected phase

5) If customer-impacting
   - Apply runbook mitigation (disable v2 by model/GPU/region or pin kernel)
   - Then continue root-cause analysis offline

---

## Data you should collect (minimum)
For any debugging thread / ticket, include:
- **Model**: name + version hash (or Redwood model revision)
- **GPU**: sku (normalized), MIG mode (if present), driver + CUDA
- **Workload**: prompt tokens, max output tokens, streaming on/off, typical concurrency
- **Selector**: v1/v2 enabled, allowlist/denylist state, forced kernel overrides
- **Evidence**: 1–3 trace IDs and a short time window to query dashboards

Recommended extras:
- Nsight Systems (.nsys-rep) for one request
- Nsight Compute report for the dominant kernel (prefill or decode)

---

## Capturing kernel selection traces

### A) Using production telemetry (preferred)
Kernel selection emits a per-request event (sampled) when telemetry is enabled.

What to look for in the event payload:
- selector_version (v1 or v2)
- model, model_family
- gpu_sku, driver_version, cuda_version
- prefill_tokens, decode_tokens_est
- seq_bucket
- candidates (compact list)
- chosen_kernel
- fallback_reason (if any)
- decision_hash / determinism_fingerprint

**Recommended query pattern (Hosted/Dedicated):**
- Filter by model + gpu_sku + seq_bucket
- Compare selection distribution before/after the regression window
- Correlate with p95/p99 latency by the same dimensions

Sampling note:
- Sampling is intentionally low by default to control overhead and cardinality.
- If you need more coverage during a canary, coordinate with SRE/Observability to temporarily increase sampling for a narrow allowlist (model + region).

### B) Local dump (repro and deep debugging)
Use the runtime CLI flags to dump the selector’s decision record.

**Common flags (runtime 1.21+):**
- `--kernel-select.v2=0|1` (enable/disable v2)
- `--kernel-select.dump=/path/selector_dump.jsonl` (writes JSONL)
- `--kernel-select.sample-rate=0.0..1.0` (local only; do not use 1.0 in prod)
- `--kernel.force=<kernel_id>` (force a kernel; bypass selection)
- `--kernel-select.dump-candidates=1` (include candidate set; larger output)
- `--kernel-select.determinism-check=1` (assert stable decision_hash for repeated runs)

**Example: dump selection for a single run**
1. Start runtime locally with dumping enabled:
   - `rw-runtime serve --model llama-3.1-70b --kernel-select.v2=1 --kernel-select.dump=/tmp/sel.jsonl --kernel-select.sample-rate=1.0`
2. Send one request (use your normal client or `curl`).
3. Inspect `/tmp/sel.jsonl` and verify:
   - seq_bucket matches expectations
   - chosen_kernel is in candidates
   - fallback_reason is empty

**Expected dump line (shape, example fields):**
- `timestamp`
- `request_id`
- `model`
- `model_family`
- `gpu_sku`
- `driver_version`
- `cuda_version`
- `prefill_tokens`
- `decode_tokens_est`
- `seq_bucket`
- `candidates`
- `chosen_kernel`
- `fallback_reason`
- `selector_version`
- `decision_hash`

(Exact field names can change; treat this as the conceptual contract.)

---

## Reproducing a mis-selection locally
Goal: reproduce the same decision with the same inputs, then iterate quickly.

### Step 1: Pin the environment
To avoid false leads, match:
- GPU SKU (and MIG mode)
- Driver + CUDA
- Runtime build (commit hash)
- Model revision and quantization settings

If you cannot match GPU SKU exactly:
- Prefer the same architecture (e.g., H100 SXM vs H100 PCIe still differs; document it)
- Do not draw firm conclusions from cross-SKU comparisons without a controlled benchmark

### Step 2: Replay the request
Recommended approach:
- Use the request payload captured in logs/traces (prompt, params, max_tokens, sampling settings)
- Ensure tokenization is identical (same tokenizer/model revision)

Practical tips:
- Disable unrelated variability (temperature=0, top_p=1) when isolating perf/selection
- Warm the model (at least 10–20 requests) before measuring

### Step 3: Verify determinism
Run the same request N times (N=20 is usually sufficient) with:
- `--kernel-select.determinism-check=1`

If the decision_hash changes across runs, skip ahead to **Failure signatures → Nondeterministic selection**.

---

## Comparing kernels (A/B) correctly
Selection regressions are often “real” but can be misattributed due to measurement mistakes.

### Baseline method
1) Choose a workload profile
- Short: prefill ~256–1k tokens, decode ~64–256
- Long-context: prefill 8k–32k tokens, decode small/medium
- Mixed: alternating short and long requests (to stress cache/batching)

2) Compare two conditions on the same host/GPU
- Condition A: selector v2 normal
- Condition B: `--kernel.force=<known_good>` OR selector v1

3) Measure:
- End-to-end latency (p50/p95/p99)
- Prefill time and decode time (if you have phase breakdown)
- Throughput (tokens/sec) at a fixed concurrency

### Guardrails
- Keep concurrency and batcher settings fixed.
- Ensure compilation/warmup is not included (or include it consistently in both conditions).
- Watch for “silent” changes: different quantization path, different attention backend, different KV cache policy.

### Identifying kernel switch overhead
If you suspect selector overhead or frequent kernel switches:
- Use the selector dump to confirm how often the chosen kernel changes for similar requests.
- Measure CPU-side selector time (if exposed) and confirm it is not on the critical path.

---

## Interpreting perf counters (what matters for kernel selection)

### Tools
- **Nsight Systems (nsys):** timeline, kernel launch frequency, CPU/GPU overlap
- **Nsight Compute (ncu):** kernel-level metrics (occupancy, memory throughput, tensor core utilization)

### Prefill regressions (common with long context)
Typical indicators:
- Memory bandwidth saturation + poor L2 hit rate
- Excessive attention-related workspace allocations
- Reduced tensor core utilization (e.g., due to shape mismatch or fallback kernel)

What to check:
- Are we using the expected “long-context prefill” kernel variant?
- Did we accidentally select a kernel optimized for decode (small seq) for a large prefill?
- Is the launch config appropriate for the sequence length and head dimension?

### Decode regressions (common with small prompts, high QPS)
Typical indicators:
- Increased kernel launch count (too many small kernels)
- Lower occupancy due to small problem sizes or poor scheduling
- Higher CPU overhead per token (scheduling/selector/telemetry)

What to check:
- Are we selecting a decode-optimized kernel for short seq?
- Is continuous batching behavior consistent (same batch sizes)?
- Any sign that telemetry sampling is too high (CPU spikes)?

---

## Common failure signatures and fixes

### 1) Long-context p99 spikes after enabling v2
Symptoms:
- p50 unchanged, p99 worse
- Only affects large prefill (8k+ tokens)
- Selection traces show a “short/mid” seq bucket for long prompts or an unexpected kernel

Likely causes:
- Seq bucket misclassification at bucket boundaries
- Incorrect prefill token estimation (tokenizer mismatch, truncation, or streaming config)
- Missing long-context kernel for the GPU SKU → fallback to generic

Actions:
1) Confirm `prefill_tokens` and `seq_bucket` in the trace.
2) Force the known-good long-context kernel; verify p99 recovers.
3) If confirmed: add a temporary denylist rule for (model_family, gpu_sku, seq_bucket) and follow the rollback runbook.

### 2) GPU SKU mapping confusion (A100 variants, MIG)
Symptoms:
- Same instance type shows different sku strings across environments
- Selection differs unexpectedly between “same” GPU hosts
- Fallback_reason mentions “no compatible kernel for SKU”

Likely causes:
- SKU normalization mismatch (cloud naming vs PCI IDs)
- MIG partitions reported as distinct SKUs without mapping

Actions:
1) Capture raw GPU identifiers (from runtime startup logs).
2) Confirm normalized `gpu_sku` in selection traces.
3) If normalization is wrong, stop: comparisons are invalid until normalized.
4) Workaround: pin kernel or disable v2 on that SKU until mapping is corrected.

### 3) Unexpected fallback to generic kernel
Symptoms:
- chosen_kernel is a generic or “safe” kernel
- fallback_reason indicates denylist hit or missing kernel

Likely causes:
- Known-bad kernel/SKU combo is denied
- Kernel not built/registered for this runtime build + CUDA
- Driver/CUDA guardrail disables a kernel path

Actions:
1) Read fallback_reason; do not guess.
2) Check known-issues page for that SKU/driver.
3) Validate the kernel registry for the runtime build.
4) If it’s a new driver combo: treat as unsafe until validated; keep fallback.

### 4) Nondeterministic selection (same input, different kernel)
Symptoms:
- decision_hash changes across repeated runs
- kernel choice flips between two candidates without config changes

Likely causes:
- Unordered candidate iteration (map/set ordering)
- Floating-point scoring instability (if any scoring exists)
- Hidden dynamic inputs (e.g., scheduler hint updates mid-run)

Actions:
1) Enable determinism check flag locally.
2) Ensure scheduler hints are fixed for the test (or disable hints input).
3) Capture dumps for multiple runs and diff `candidates` ordering.
4) If confirmed: block rollout for the affected path; determinism is a hard requirement.

### 5) Telemetry/cardinality-induced overhead
Symptoms:
- CPU usage increases, minor but broad latency regressions
- Metrics ingestion/backends show increased series counts
- Alerts fire for “metric cardinality” changes

Likely causes:
- Sampling too high
- Candidate sets emitted too verbosely
- High-cardinality tags (e.g., request_id) accidentally included

Actions:
1) Reduce sampling immediately; keep only the dimensions required by the standard.
2) Confirm dashboards still work with reduced detail.
3) Coordinate with Observability for query/panel updates.

---

## Recommended debugging workflow (end-to-end)
1) **Validate** the regression is real
   - Same GPU SKU, same model rev, same concurrency

2) **Get a trace**
   - Confirm chosen kernel, candidates, seq bucket, fallback reason

3) **Reproduce locally**
   - Dump selector decisions and verify determinism

4) **A/B**
   - Selector v2 vs forced known-good kernel (or v1)

5) **Profile**
   - nsys: timeline and kernel launch patterns
   - ncu: dominant kernel metrics

6) **Mitigate** (if needed)
   - Disable v2 for (model/GPU/region) or pin kernel via runbook

7) **Close the loop**
   - Add/update known issue entry
   - If a rule threshold changes, add a regression test case (long-context boundary)

---

## Escalation and ownership
- If regression impacts Hosted canary or Dedicated pools: page **Runtime Oncall** and coordinate with **SRE** for rollback authority.
- Kernel selection logic issues: **Yuki Sato** (owner), **Hiro Tanaka** (kernels lead)
- Tail latency / observability issues: **Omar El-Sayed**, **Allison Grant**
- Perf suite additions / reproductions: **Marcus Reed**, **Claire Dubois**, **Sahana Iyer**

---

## Appendix: What “good” looks like
- For a fixed (model, gpu_sku, seq_bucket), chosen_kernel distribution is stable over time.
- p95/p99 deltas are within rollout budgets, with no long-context outliers.
- decision_hash is stable (deterministic) given identical inputs.
- Telemetry provides enough context to explain every fallback without additional logging.

---

## Appendix: Template for reporting a kernel selection bug
Copy/paste into a ticket:
- Runtime version / commit:
- Environment (Hosted/Dedicated/Private):
- Model + revision:
- GPU SKU + MIG + driver/CUDA:
- Selector: v1/v2, allowlist/denylist state, forced kernel?
- Workload: prefill tokens, decode tokens, concurrency, streaming:
- Trace IDs (1–3):
- Observed: (p95/p99 change, throughput change)
- Expected:
- Selection details: chosen_kernel, candidates, seq_bucket, fallback_reason:
- Mitigation applied (if any):

title: Profiling Synthetic Trace Injector and Scheduler Shadowing Cookbook
content:
Overview

Purpose: This cookbook documents a repeatable, low-risk process for reproducing, profiling, and quantifying scheduler- and kernel-sensitive performance behaviors using synthetic trace injection and scheduler shadowing. The goal is to create deterministic synthetic inputs that exercise known hot paths (KV cache thrash, long-sequence attention, quantized kernel fallbacks) and to run a scheduler shadow to evaluate policy changes without impacting production traffic.

Scope: covers tooling, safe injection channels, synthetic trace templates, experiment run matrix, telemetry correlation, post-run analysis, and rollback/cleanup. This playbook is intended for runtime engineers owning kernel scheduling, profiling, and the benchmarking suite.

Owner and contacts

- Doc owner: Maya Patel (runtime profiling team)
- Primary oncall for injections: runtime-sre rotation (see /confluence/eng-sre/oncall-rotations)
- Reviewers: Ethan Zhang (scheduler), Lina Fernández (observability), Jordan Kim (benchmarks)

When to use this playbook

- Investigating reproducible tail-latency spikes suspected to be scheduling interactions
- Validating scheduler policy changes (crediting, preemption thresholds) against representative workloads
- Debugging KV cache coherence regressions under composite load shapes
- Generating controlled regression candidates for the benchmarking and perf-suite

Safety model and constraints

- Never inject synthetic traces into live customer traffic channels. Use the dedicated shadow ingress (ingress-shadow.redwood.internal) or the local experiment harness.
- All experiments must run in the sandbox cluster or a reserved staging ring; do not point to Dedicated customer pools.
- Maximum allowed synthetic QPS: 25% of the node pool baseline for the targeted cluster (enforced by the shadow-admission controller).
- If any of the SLO gates (95p latency, error rate, GPU utilization) degrade by >20% compared to baseline within the first 5 minutes, abort automatically. Abort uses the circuit-breaker endpoint (POST /admin/experiment/{id}/abort).

Prerequisites

1) Access: experiment-runner role and shadow-cluster credentials (see /confluence/eng-sre/credentials).
2) Tooling: experiment-runner CLI (v1.14+) and trace-injector service binary. Install: curl -fsS https://internal.redwood/bin/experiment-runner | sh
3) Baseline capture: a 30-minute production shadow capture (compressed protobuf) representative of the workload you will emulate. See capture naming convention: capture-{service}-{date}-{env}.pb.gz

High-level flow

1) Derive synthetic trace templates from baseline capture using the extractor.
2) Augment templates to produce fault/edge cases (e.g., long prefix reuse, kvcache cold starts, model-variant switch).
3) Validate templates locally in the sandbox harness (dry run + trace-level assertions).
4) Launch scheduler-shadow run in a staging ring with the current scheduler and an alternate policy patched into the shadow controller.
5) Collect and correlate kernel traces, scheduler telemetry, and application observability.
6) Run benchmark-suite scenarios to quantify delta and generate regression tickets if necessary.

Step-by-step procedure

A. Generate synthetic traces from a capture

1. Fetch the baseline capture: experiment-runner capture fetch --id capture-frontend-20260104-staging --out /tmp/cap.pb.gz
2. Extract request surface and KV cache events: 

   trace-extractor --input /tmp/cap.pb.gz --output /tmp/template.json --include events:request,kvcache,session

   - The template.json contains arrays of request objects with fields: seq_len, prompt_token_counts, kv_key_prefixes, model_variant_hint.

3. Edit the template to add edge cases. Example additions (append to array):

   - a long-prefix case: {"seq_len": 4096, "prompt_token_counts": [1024, 3072], "kv_key_prefixes": ["user:prefetch-heavy"], "model_variant_hint": "llama-2-q8"}
   - kvcache cold-flush windows: add interval markers for forced cache eviction

B. Sanity-check templates in local harness

1. Start local harness (isolated docker image): docker-compose -f harness/docker-compose.yml up -d
2. Dry-run injection with assertions enabled: trace-injector --template /tmp/template.json --mode dryrun --asserts /etc/experiment/asserts.yaml
3. Expected dryrun outputs: per-request latency distributions and assertion report. If any assertion fails, modify template and repeat.

C. Schedule a shadow run with scheduler shadowing

1. Create experiment record: 

   experiment-runner create --name "sched-shadow-kvcoh-2026-06" --cluster staging-shadow --owner @maya --config experiments/sched-shadow-config.yaml

2. Example sched-shadow-config.yaml (annotated, included inline here for convenience):

   - name: sched_policy_patch
     type: patch
     description: "enable preemptive-shepherding at 80% GPU mem and lower affinity weight for best-effort"
     patch_location: runtime/scheduler/patches/preemptive-shepherding-v2.patch

   - name: injector_settings
     qps: 600
     concurrency_profile: bursty

3. Attach the template and set monitoring hooks: 

   experiment-runner attach --id <exp-id> --artifact /tmp/template.json --monitor hooks/sched-shadow-monitors.yaml

4. Start the experiment in dry-observe mode: 

   experiment-runner start --id <exp-id> --mode dry-observe --duration 00:45:00

   - dry-observe routes the synthetic traffic into the shadow admission pipeline and runs the scheduler patch in a non-invasive shadow controller; it does not alter live scheduling decisions but collects what would have happened under the patched policy.

D. Collect telemetry and kernel artifacts

Required telemetry buckets:

- scheduler-decision.trace (per-request decision log)
- kernel-invocations.ndjson (kernel start/stop with parameters)
- kvcache-events.pb (prefetch/evict/hit/miss counts)
- metrics.timeseries (prometheus-compatible)
- object-store: /experiments/<id>/profiles/ (profiling flamegraphs and pprof)

Collection command example: 

   experiment-runner collect --id <exp-id> --artifacts scheduler-decision.trace,kernel-invocations.ndjson,kvcache-events.pb,metrics.timeseries --out /tmp/exp-results

E. Correlate and analyze results

1. Run the correlation script: 

   scripts/exp-correlation --input /tmp/exp-results --output /tmp/exp-analysis.html

   The correlation script performs:
   - request-to-kernel join (match request id to kernel invocations)
   - compute latency delta window between baseline and shadow decisions
   - compute kernel utilization uplift and preemption counts

2. Key signals to inspect:

   - percent of requests that would have been preempted under the patched policy
   - changes to 95/99/99.9p token-latency
   - KV cache miss amplification due to preemption or affinity reduction
   - kernel queue length and average kernel execution time per sequence length bin

3. Example failure modes and diagnostic actions:

   - Observation: 20% increase in 99.9p token latency coinciding with preemption spikes.
     Action: examine kernel-invocations.ndjson for prolonged kernel cold-starts, verify whether preemption caused cache thrash; reduce preemption aggressiveness and rerun shadow.

   - Observation: increased tail correlated with model-variant switch events.
     Action: inspect scheduler-decision.trace to verify fallback routing and sequence-length misclassification; add model_variant hint alignment in template and re-evaluate.

F. Promoting changes and benchmarking

1. If shadow analysis is favorable, run a full benchmark suite against a tuning ring. Use the specific manifest for the suite: benchmarking/manifests/sched-fidelity-manifest.yaml
2. Launch: benchmark-runner run --manifest benchmarking/manifests/sched-fidelity-manifest.yaml --experiment <exp-id> --save results/sched-fidelity-2026-06-15.json
3. Required outputs: per-model per-route cost deltas, token-energy-profile, SLO-simulated pass/fail. Attach results to the experiment record and create a PR for scheduler patches with the artifacts.

Metrics, SLOs, and acceptance criteria

- Baseline SLOs for acceptance:
  - 95p token latency: <= baseline + 5%
  - 99.9p token latency: <= baseline + 10%
  - Error rate: no more than baseline + 0.1% absolute
  - GPU utilization: not increase > 8% sustained

- If the change improves cost per token by >7% while meeting SLOs, it is a candidate for staged rollout.

Observability and dashboards to check

- /dashboards/runtime/scheduler-shadow-overview
- /dashboards/runtime/kernel-hotpath-fingerprint
- /dashboards/benchmarks/sched-fidelity-comparison

Templates and example snippets

- Minimal inject template (JSON single line):
  [{"id":"synthetic-1","seq_len":512,"priority":"interactive","kv_prefix":"user:smallctx","model":"redwood-rlm-7b"}]

- Sample asserts.yaml (used in dryrun):
  - name: max-95p-latency
    metric: request.latency.p95
    threshold_ms: 200

- Recommended admission controller payload (YAML):
  admission_override:
    mode: shadow
    max_qps: 600
    owner: maya@redwood.internal

Post-experiment cleanup and artifacts retention

- Remove experiment artifacts older than 90 days unless attached to a release PR (policy enforced by exp-cleaner service).
- Archive approved experiments under /archive/experiments/{year}/{id} and tag in the benchmarking index.

Common gotchas and troubleshooting checklist

- If the scheduler shadow shows no decision differences but you see performance delta in kernel profiles: verify tracer clock sync (ntp/chrony) across nodes.
- For noisy baselines, increase capture window and apply stratified sampling before template derivation.
- When evaluating quantized kernels, ensure the profiler is launched with QUANT_PROF=1 to capture quantization fallback events.

Runbook snippets and quick recovery steps

- Abort an experiment quickly: curl -X POST -H \"Authorization: Bearer $(cat /etc/exp/token)\" https://api.internal/experiment/<id>/abort
- Revert a scheduler policy rollout: use rollout-manager revert --component scheduler --to-tag v2026-05-21 --force-annotate \"rollout-rollback due to tail-latency\"

Appendix: example analysis checklist (for experiment postmortem)

1. Experiment metadata: id, owner, start/end, cluster, patch applied.
2. Baseline vs shadow summary tables: p50/p95/p99/p999 deltas, error rate, GPU util, kernel invocation rate.
3. Top 5 correlated signals and their suspected causal path.
4. Suggested next steps (tune preemption thresholds, add KV warmup hints, revert affinity changes).
5. Attachment links: flamegraphs, kernel-pprof, scheduler-trace, benchmark manifest.

References and related pages

- Kernel telemetry model (see /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/kernel-telemetry-annotation-guidelines-2025)
- Benchmark manifest conventions (see /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/operational-workload-simulator-and-signature-guide-2026)

Document revision history

- 2026-01-12: initial draft by Maya Patel
- 2026-03-02: added dry-observe mode and admission constraints (reviewers: Ethan Zhang)
- 2026-06-15: expanded analysis checklist and acceptance criteria (reviewers: Lina Fernández, Jordan Kim)

title: Cross-Platform Tracing and Adaptive Sampler Strategy for Runtime
content:
Summary:

This document defines Redwood's recommended cross-platform distributed tracing architecture and a standardized adaptive sampling policy for the serving runtime. It describes how to collect correlated traces across user request paths, CPU/GPU kernel executions, and network transfers with bounded overhead, and how to configure adaptive and tail-aware samplers to maximize signal for debugging and regression detection.

Goals:
- Provide a single, operationally simple tracing model that works across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.
- Ensure traces capture: request route, model name and version, batch size, token counts, KV cache hit/miss, kernel ids, GPU kernel durations, and node-level context (NUMA, container id).
- Keep steady-state tracing overhead <= 2% CPU and <= 5ms p50 added latency for typical requests.
- Prioritize collection of rare/high-impact events via tail sampling and adaptive rules.

Scope:
- Applies to Redwood serving runtime components: frontend routers, request multiplexer, runtime workers, kernel execution layer, and the Redwood trace agent.
- Includes GPU-level instrumentation (CUPTI/NSYS), kernel telemetry annotations, NIC-level network timing (eBPF), and application-level context propagation (OTel).

Architecture Overview:
- Components:
  - redwood-trace-agent: lightweight sidecar that attaches to each node, collects local spans from the runtime and kernel probes, enriches with node metadata, and forwards to the OTEL collector.
  - otel-collector (shared): receives traces, performs sampling and tail sampling policies, and exports to our trace storage (Jaeger/Tempo + hot index in ClickHouse for fast queries).
  - kernel-probes: modules that emit short GPU/CPU kernel spans with standardized tags (kernel.name, kernel.id, gpu.sm_util_pct, memory_bytes).
  - eBPF collectors: capture NIC transmit/receive microspans and socket-level latencies to correlate network tail effects.

- Trace model conventions (required):
  - root_span: request:<route> with attributes: route, model, model_version, deployment_mode, env, user_token_id (hashed), batch_size, requested_max_tokens, client_latency_ms.
  - child spans: router, multiplexer, kv_cache (hit/miss boolean), kernel:<kernel_name> (with kernel.duration_ms), batching-window, emit-token-loop (per-100-token aggregated span).
  - IDs: span and trace ids must be 128-bit hex. Inject and propagate via W3C Trace-Context headers in HTTP and via metadata across internal gRPC.

Sampling Strategy (high level):
- Default global policy: Probabilistic reservoir sampling at 0.5% for steady-state production traffic. This keeps storage cost bounded while ensuring random coverage.
- Route-priorities: Override probabilistic sampler per-route. Important routes (e.g., admin endpoints, high-RPO customers, new-model routes) should be sampled at higher rates (2–20%).
- Tail-aware sampling: Implement tail-sampler in the OTEL collector that keeps a short window (5m) and promotes traces with high observed latency (> p95), error flags, or kernel anomalies to persisted storage regardless of initial sample decision.
- Adaptive sampler: Dynamically increase sampling for a route when its error rate or tail-latency growth exceeds thresholds. See algorithm below.

Adaptive Sampler Algorithm (pseudocode):
1) For each route R, maintain sliding metrics: rps(R), error_rate(R), tail_latency_p95(R). 5-minute windows.
2) Evaluate every 30s: if error_rate(R) > 0.5% AND rps(R) > 10 => sampler_rate(R) := min(0.2, sampler_rate(R) * 4).
3) If tail_latency_p95(R) increases by >25% vs baseline => sampler_rate(R) := min(0.1, sampler_rate(R) * 2).
4) Decay: every 10 minutes without triggers => sampler_rate(R) := max(default_rate, sampler_rate(R) * 0.7).
5) Ensure a global budget: sum(expected_spans_per_minute) <= configured_limit (configurable per-cluster).

Configuration Reference (OTel collector / redwood-trace-agent):
| key | example | description |
|-----|---------|-------------|
| sampling.global_default | 0.005 | global probabilistic default (fraction) |
| sampling.route_overrides | {"/chat/generate":0.02} | per-route overrides as JSON map |
| sampling.tail_window_secs | 300 | window for tail-sampler to keep candidate traces |
| sampling.max_spans_per_min | 50000 | safety budget for a cluster |
| trace_agent.buffer_size_mb | 32 | sidecar memory buffer before backpressure |
| gpu.probe_enabled | true | enable CUPTI/NSYS kernel spans |
| ebpf.nic_capture | drop | capture mode: drop|sample|full (avoid full in prod) |

Operational SLOs and Overhead Targets:
- Trace collection overhead: added p50 latency <= 5ms for normal 16k token requests when sampling <= 1%.
- Collector CPU budget: < 6 vCPU equivalent per 1K qps of traced traffic for full processing.
- Retention tiers: hot traces (30d, high-index) + cold traces (365d, compressed).
- Tail-sampling recall target: capture >= 95% of traces with request latency above configured p99 threshold.

Instrumentation Checklist (developer-facing):
1) Add span entry/exit for each high-level component: request router, multiplexer, model executor, kv-cache check.
2) Annotate spans with these required attributes: model.name, model.version, batch.size, requested_tokens, response_tokens, kv_cache_hit, kernel.id.
3) Emit kernel spans at kernel launch and kernel completion with start_ts and end_ts and resource tags (gpu_index, sm_util).
4) Expose a lightweight debug flag to force-sample traces for a request_id when doing customer debugging.
5) Ensure traces are scrubbed of PII by default; only hashed client ids and truncated prompt previews are allowed.

Rollout Procedure (recommended):
