1) Canary: enable redwood-trace-agent on 1% of nodes in a non-prod environment and validate basic end-to-end ingestion.
2) Staged prod rollout: 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100% with 1 hour observation windows. Verify overhead metrics after each step.
3) Enable Route overrides incrementally: start with low-risk routes, then business-critical routes.
4) Turn on GPU kernel probes separately: measure overhead with NSYS for 24h before enabling tail-promotion for kernel anomalies.
5) Full tail-sampler enablement only after tail recall verification in a loaded test environment.

Rollback Plan:
- If collector CPU or trace agent memory exceeds thresholds or p50 latency regressions > 10ms observed, roll back to previous sampling global_default and disable GPU/Net probes.
- Use the sidecar healthcheck endpoint (/health/trace-agent) to drain and stop forwarding.

Common troubleshooting patterns and remediation:
- Symptom: Many traces missing kernel spans.
  - Cause: CUPTI permission or probe not loaded on container runtime.
  - Action: Check redwood-trace-agent logs for "gpu-probe: init failed" and ensure container has CAP_SYS_ADMIN or appropriate device access; verify driver/ CUDA version compat.

- Symptom: Sudden spike in trace volume and storage pressure.
  - Cause: misconfigured route override or accidental debug-forced sampling.
  - Action: Temporarily set sampling.global_default to 0.001 and scale down overrides; throttle ingress to collector.

- Symptom: High tail latency captured but not correlated to kernel durations.
  - Cause: Network egress or kv-cache serialization.
  - Action: Enable eBPF NIC microspans for the suspected nodes and re-run tail-sampling for 1 hour.

Diagnostic CLI snippets and examples:
- Force a trace for a single request_id (debug only):
  curl -X POST \
    -H 'X-Redwood-Debug-Force-Trace: request:12345' \
    -d '{"input":"..."}' https://internal-router.local/chat/generate

- Example otel-collector sampling config fragment (YAML):
  receivers:
    otlp:
      protocols:
        grpc: {}
  processors:
    batch: {}
    tail_sampling:
      policies:
        - name: latency_high
          latency_threshold: 1s
          decision_wait: 30s
  exporters:
    jaeger:
      endpoint: jaeger.internal:14250

- Read GPU kernel spans in ClickHouse (example SQL):
  SELECT trace_id, span_name, kernel_name, span_duration_ms, tags
  FROM traces
  WHERE span_name LIKE 'kernel:%' AND event_ts > now() - INTERVAL 1 DAY
  ORDER BY span_duration_ms DESC
  LIMIT 500;

Appendix A — Minimal agent config example (redwood-trace-agent):
{
  "trace_endpoint": "otel-collector.internal:4317",
  "buffer_mb": 32,
  "sampling": {
    "global_default": 0.005,
    "route_overrides": {"/chat/generate":0.02}
  },
  "gpu_probe": true,
  "ebpf_nic_mode": "sample"
}

Appendix B — Ownership and SLAs:
- Owner: eng-serv-runtime / Observability subteam (primary: Maya Chen).
- SRE oncall: responsible for collector availability and scaling during rollout.
- Expected review cadence: Quarterly review of sampling budgets and route overrides.

Appendix C — Future enhancements (non-blocking):
- Kernel-level histogram sketches exported as metrics to avoid heavy trace storage for frequent short kernels.
- Better correlation between trace spans and token-level cost accounting (token-attribution spans).
- Automatic anomaly detectors that tune sampler rates using Bayesian change point detection.

If you implement or change instrumentation, add an entry to the "profiling-playbook/trace-instrumentation-register" index with components modified, owner, and a short note about expected overhead. For questions, reach out to the Observability channel (#obs-runtime) or directly to the document owner.

title: Compact trace annotation and causal latency map
content:
Summary
-------
This document describes the Compact Trace Annotation (CTA) format and the downstream Causal Latency Map (CLM) workflow we use to convert sparse, high-throughput traces into actionable latency attribution for inference requests. CTA+CLM provide a low-overhead instrumentation pattern suitable for production GPU pools and multi-tenant serving, enabling root-cause identification for P95/P99 regressions without capturing full trace payloads.

Why this exists
----------------
- Full-span tracing is too heavy for production inference: memory, disk, and network overheads degrade throughput and interfere with kernel scheduling.
- We need deterministic, reproducible attributions: whether latency comes from kernel contention, queueing, inter-node NVLink transfer, or KV cache misses.
- On-call and SRE teams require a compact artifact that can be stored for weeks and replayed into investigation tools.

Scope
-----
This doc covers:
- CTA schema (telemetry fields included and required)
- Collector configuration and rate controls
- CLI and pipeline to generate the CLM (processing and causal inference steps)
- Investigation runbook tied to SLO thresholds and alerts
- Dashboard and alert configuration snippets

Audience
--------
Primary: eng-serving-runtime, eng-sre, profiling engineers, incident responders. Secondary: product reliability, platform owners.

Telemetry contract: Compact Trace fields
-------------------------------------
We intentionally limit fields to keep artifacts small (~1–4KB per trace). Required fields are bold. Optional fields are encouraged when available. Keep field types primitive (string/number/boolean) to simplify downstream processing.

| Field | Type | Required? | Description |
|-------|------|-----------|-------------|
| request_id | string | yes | Global request identifier (UUID v4).
| ts_start | int | yes | Epoch ms when request first arrived at entry router.
| ts_end | int | yes | Epoch ms when response sent to client.
| stage_events | list<string> | yes | Ordered small tokens representing stage boundaries; see allowed tokens below.
| kernel_slots | list<int> | no | Compact histogram of per-kernel execution duration buckets (ms). Format: [count_lt1ms, count_1_5ms, count_5_10ms, count_gt10ms].
| kvcache_hits | int | no | Number of KV cache hits during request.
| kvcache_misses | int | no | Number of KV cache misses during request.
| shard_id | string | yes | Shard or node id handling primary compute for request.
| tenant | string | yes | Customer/tenant id (for multi-tenant pool attribution).
| kernel_hint | string | no | Optional model kernel hint (e.g. "fused-attn-v2", "triton-gemm").
| sampling_reason | string | yes | "p95-sample", "error-sample", "system-sample", "random".
| trace_version | string | yes | e.g. "cta-v1"

Allowed stage_events tokens (alphabetical): ENTRY, ENQUEUE, DEQUEUE, KERNEL_START, KERNEL_END, KV_LOOKUP_START, KV_LOOKUP_END, NETWORK_TX_START, NETWORK_TX_END, FALLBACK_SWITCH, RESPONSE_SEND

Compact Trace example (CTA payload)
----------------------------------
Example CTA (JSON single-line):
{"request_id":"b6f3c2d4-8e9f-4a2b-9cde-aa11bb22cc33","ts_start":1700000123456,"ts_end":1700000123590,"stage_events":["ENTRY","ENQUEUE","DEQUEUE","KERNEL_START","KERNEL_END","RESPONSE_SEND"],"kernel_slots":[0,1,0,0],"kvcache_hits":2,"kvcache_misses":0,"shard_id":"shard-eu-12","tenant":"acct-42","sampling_reason":"p95-sample","trace_version":"cta-v1"}

Collector configuration and rate controls
---------------------------------------
- Service name: inference-trace-collector (k8s: infra/observability).
- Default retention: compact traces stored in hot-s3 (14d), cold-s3 (90d).
- Sampling policy (k8s ConfigMap):
  1) p95-sampler: deterministic capture of requests where request_latency > 95th percentile (computed via streaming aggregator), priority 1.
  2) error-sampler: capture on any 5xx or model-runtime exception, priority 0 (always capture).
  3) system-sampler: capture 0.05% random traffic for long-term health signal, priority 2.
- Backpressure: if collector ingestion queue > 75% capacity, reduce system-sampler to 0.01% and drop random-samples older than 10s. Always preserve error-sampled traces.

Collector Config snippet (YAML)
-----------------------------
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: cta-collector-config
data:
  sampling.p95.threshold-ms: "200"
  sampling.system.rate-per-minute: "50"
  retention.hot-days: "14"
  retention.cold-days: "90"
  ingestion.queue-soft-limit: "0.75"

Processing pipeline to build the Causal Latency Map (CLM)
------------------------------------------------------
High-level steps:
1) Ingest CTA artifacts from hot-s3 for window W (typically last 6h).
2) Enrich each CTA with node-level kernel telemetry (kernel queue lengths, kernel dispatch times) from the kernel-metrics store (TSDB).
3) Group traces by shard_id + tenant + model_variant.
4) Build causal graph using stage_events ordering and per-stage timestamps: compute edge weights for queueing delay, kernel duration, network transfer, and kvcache penalty.
5) Aggregate graphs into a CLM that reports per-path contributions to request latency percentiles.

Command-line helpers (example)
-----------------------------
# Pull CTAs into local file for window 1h
redwoodctl trace fetch --from now-1h --to now --out ctas.ndjson --filter sampling_reason=p95-sample

# Enrich and build CLM
redwoodctl trace enrich --ctas ctas.ndjson --kernel-store tsdb://kernel-metrics --out enriched.ndjson
redwoodctl clm build --in enriched.ndjson --group-by shard_id,tenant,model_variant --out clm-20260218.json

Interpretation semantics
------------------------
- Edge weights are additive: total request latency ~= sum(edge weights on primary path) + residual.
- An edge labeled KERNEL_QUEUE indicates time spent waiting for kernel slot; KERNEL_EXEC indicates execution time.
- KV cache penalty: modeled as (miss_count * avg_kv_lookup_ms) + miss-induced-kernel-delay.

Investigation runbook (p95 alert)
--------------------------------
Trigger: alert runtime-p95-slo-violation firing (SLO: p95 < 180ms for hosted small).
1) Page on-call (primary SRE) and create incident in our tracker.
2) Run quick CLI to sample CTAs for the impacted window:
   redwoodctl trace fetch --from now-30m --to now --filter sampling_reason=p95-sample --out incident-ctas.ndjson
3) Run fast CLM build limited to tenant(s) in alert:
   redwoodctl trace enrich --ctas incident-ctas.ndjson --kernel-store tsdb://kernel-metrics --out incident-enriched.ndjson
   redwoodctl clm build --in incident-enriched.ndjson --group-by shard_id,tenant --out incident-clm.json --top-paths 10
4) Inspect incident-clm.json for primary contributors: queueing, kernel_exec, kv_miss, network.
5) If root cause is kernel contention on shard X:
   a) Check shard-level kernel queue length: grafana -> Kernel Dispatch -> shard X.
   b) If queue length > 5 for > 5m, consider immediate temporary mitigation: scale out shard pool or reroute low-priority tenants.
6) If root cause is KV cache misses:
   a) Confirm model variant and session affinity changes.
   b) Trigger KV cache prefetch for affected sessions (see KV prefetch playbook).
7) If root cause is network/NVLink transfer: verify network device errors and open infra incident.
8) Document findings on incident page and attach CLM artifact.

Escalation thresholds and ownership
----------------------------------
- SRE responder: pager duty -> eng-sre oncall.
- If CLM shows >40% contribution from kernel_queue across multiple shards for >10min, escalate to runtime-platform@redwood.com and CC oncall infra.
- If KV-miss contribution >30% for a tenant with reserved capacity, page the assigned solutions engineer.

Dashboards and alerts (suggested panels)
---------------------------------------
- CLM: stacked contribution chart (kernel_exec / kernel_queue / kv_penalty / network) per tenant.
- Kernel queue length heatmap by shard (alert if a shard has >5 queue length for 5m).
- CTA ingestion health: queue occupancy and dropped trace rate (alert if >1%).

Example Grafana alert (pseudo-YAML)
----------------------------------
alert: runtime-p95-slo-violation
expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le, model_variant)) > 0.18
for: 5m
labels:
  severity: critical
annotations:
  runbook: "/confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-deployment-circuit-breakers-and-sla-fallback-playbook-2026"

Performance cost and storage sizing guidance
-------------------------------------------
- CTA size: 1–4KB typical. Expect ~0.5GB/day per 10k p95-sampled requests at default sampling.
- Hot-s3 retention cost: plan for 14 days hot retention unless investigating large incidents; cold retention for months only on a per-need basis.
- CPU cost: enrichment step is CPU-heavy (TSDB lookups + graph building). For 1M CTAs, allocate at least 32 vCPU and 128GB RAM for the batch job.

Rollout checklist (safe deployment)
----------------------------------
1) Deploy collector config to staging with sampling p95 threshold at 2x current production baseline.
2) Validate CTA size and ingestion queue with canary traffic.
3) Run enrichment pipeline on staging CTAs and validate CLM graphs match synthetic ground truth.
4) Gradually reduce p95 threshold and move config to prod. Monitor ingestion queue and kernel-metrics tsdb latency.

Appendix: compact trace to full-trace mapping policy
---------------------------------------------------
- When on-call requires deep dive beyond CTA, create a short window full-span capture for the affected shard and tenant (max 100 requests, TTL 24h). Follow the full-trace capture playbook to avoid high production impact.
- Use CTA as first-line triage; full traces only for confirmed complex incidents.

Appendix: sample clm JSON (trimmed)
-----------------------------------
{"clm_window":"2026-02-18T14:00:00Z/2026-02-18T15:00:00Z","top_paths":[{"path":"ENTRY->ENQUEUE->DEQUEUE->KERNEL_QUEUE->KERNEL_EXEC->RESPONSE","p95_contrib_ms":45,"p95_share_pct":56,"example_request_ids":["b6f3c2d4-8e9f-4a2b-9cde-aa11bb22cc33"]}],"aggregate":{"kernel_exec_ms":40,"kernel_queue_ms":30,"kv_penalty_ms":5}}

Ownership and contacts
----------------------
- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime / profiling team.
- On-call: eng-sre (see PagerDuty roster).
- Contact list: runtime-platform@redwood.com, profiling@redwood.com

Related reading and links
-------------------------
- Runtime telemetry annotation guidelines: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/runtime-telemetry-annotation-guidelines-2025
- Full profiling playbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/runtime-profiling-playbook-guidelines-2025
- KV prefetching runbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/dynamic-kvcache-resilience-and-warmup-playbook-2026

Change log
----------
- 2025-11-12: Initial draft (A. Patel).
- 2026-01-08: Added CLM aggregation and pipeline commands (E. Liu).
- 2026-02-18: Clarified sampling/retention policy and rollout checklist (R. Khatri).

title: Latency Metric Synthesis and Normalization Guide
content:
Purpose
-------
This guide standardizes how we synthesize, normalize, and interpret latency signals across the serving stack so that dashboards, alerts, and post-incident analyses compare like-for-like. It documents the telemetry fields we require, the normalization math we use for cross-model and cross-hardware comparisons, and a step-by-step triage procedure for metric anomalies.

Scope
-----
- Applies to all runtime telemetry emitted by Redwood-serving components: dispatcher, scheduler, kernel dispatcher, KV cache, model-host pools, and the network fabric observed in the control plane.
- Target audiences: runtime SREs, profiling engineers, performance QA, and anyone authoring SLOs or dashboards.

Background and motivation
-------------------------
We observed repeated confusion when correlating percentiles across heterogeneous cohorts (different model sizes, sequence lengths, and GPU classes). Raw p95/p99 numbers are insufficient because:

- different workloads have different token distributions and tail behavior;
- kernels exhibit different steady-state vs warmup profiles;
- hardware differences (A100 vs H100 vs CPU) change latency skew and variance;
- sampling biases (e.g., production sampling favoring low-entropy requests) distort percentiles.

This document prescribes: a canonical telemetry contract, normalization transforms, recommended histogram bucketing, and an investigation checklist.

Key terms and definitions
-------------------------
- SLO unit: the atomic unit we measure against (e.g., per-token generation latency for hosted-api model X at seq_len=256).
- Cohort: grouping by {model, model_variant, region, accel_class, seq_len_bucket, customer_tier}.
- Normalized latency (L_norm): latency after applying transforms to remove known covariates used for cross-cohort comparison.

Required telemetry fields
-------------------------
All runtime spans/events used for latency synthesis must include the following attributes (table):

| field | type | description | retention/notes |
|-------|------|-------------|-----------------|
| request_id | string | unique per request | keep 30d indexed |
| customer_id | string | optional, helps cohorting | PII rules apply |
| model | string | model name + version | |
| model_variant | string | quantized/float/etc. | |
| seq_len | int | input sequence length (tokens) | use computed bucket if large |
| output_tokens | int | tokens generated | |
| accel_class | string | e.g., h100-80g, a100-40g, cpu | |
| kernel_id | string | identifier for kernel path executed | correlate to kernel telemetry |
| kernel_queue_ns | int | nanoseconds spent queued for kernel | |
| kernel_run_ns | int | nanoseconds kernel executed | |
| kv_cache_hit | boolean | true if KV cache served prefix | |
| cpu_network_ns | int | control-plane network time | |
| trace_start_ts | iso8601 | trace root start | |

(If a field cannot be present due to privacy or perf constraints, document why and propose a fallback.)

Histogram and bucket recommendations
-----------------------------------
- For raw span latency: use log-linear buckets from 0.1ms to 30s with finer granularity under 200ms.
- Emit both cumulative and delta histograms: cumulative for percentile computation, delta for rate-based anomaly detection.
- Ensure at least 100 buckets for sub-200ms region when using GPU-backed models (helps tail decomposition).

Normalization strategy (overview)
--------------------------------
We normalize in three stages: cohort alignment, per-request covariate adjustment, and variance stabilization.

1) Cohort alignment
- Define cohorts by model, accel_class, and seq_len_bucket. Only compare percentiles within cohorts by default.
- When comparing across cohorts (e.g., H100 vs A100), apply a hardware baseline multiplier derived from weekly calibration runs (see Calibration protocol below).

2) Covariate adjustment (per-request)
- Use a linear model: L_raw = beta_0 + beta_1 * seq_len + beta_2 * output_tokens + beta_3 * kv_cache_miss + epsilon.
- Fit model on a sliding 7-day window per-cohort; compute residual = L_raw - L_pred. The normalized latency L_norm = residual + cohort_median_baseline.
- For non-linear effects (e.g., seq_len^2), prefer GAMs when sample size permits; fall back to linear for small cohorts.

3) Variance stabilization
- Apply a robust transform to reduce heavy tails for visualization: use a log1p transform for dashboards but preserve raw percentiles in alerts.
- For alerting, use percentile bands on raw or residual latencies (do not alert on transformed values).

Calibration protocol (weekly lab runs)
-------------------------------------
Purpose: produce hardware multipliers and kernel mapping hints used for cross-hardware normalization.
Procedure:
1. Run synthetic trace generator against candidate hardware with canonical payload set (see /lab/bench/canonical-corpus).
2. Measure per-kernel mean and p95 across 1M tokens.
3. Compute multiplier: multiplier_h = median(p95_h) / median(p95_reference) where reference is h100-s-1.
4. Commit multiplier file to config repo: /configs/latency-calibration/<date>-<hardware>.yaml

Example calibration table
| hardware | p95 (ms) | multiplier | notes |
|--------:|---------:|----------:|-------|
| h100-80g | 12.4 | 1.00 | reference |
| a100-40g | 18.6 | 1.50 | higher variance for long seq |

Data collection checklist
-------------------------
- Ensure 100% of production API requests (for targeted services) include request_id and model.
- Turn on kernel_queue_ns and kernel_run_ns in kernel telemetry at least at sampling rate 10% for busy hosts.
- For small-volume customers, enable trace-shadowing for a 1-minute window per hour to get per-request fidelity.
- Retain high-fidelity traces for at least 14 days; aggregate histograms for 90 days.

Normalization and dashboard recipes
----------------------------------
1) Per-model dashboard (recommended):
- Panel: raw p50/p95/p99 for cohort (seq_len_bucket=128/256/512).
- Panel: normalized p95 (residual-based) plotted alongside raw p95.
- Panel: kernel queue vs run time heatmap (2D histogram).
- Annotation overlays: weekly calibration run timestamp and infra changes.

2) Cross-hardware comparison panel:
- For each hardware, plot L_norm * multiplier_h so that curves align if software effects are primary.
- Use bootstrapped confidence intervals (n=1000 resamples) for percentile estimates.

Alerting guidance
-----------------
- Avoid alerting on small cohorts (<1k requests/day) unless absolute latency is >5x SLO.
- Alert on: cohort p95 > SLO.p95 + max(3ms, 0.15 * SLO.p95) sustained for 5 minutes (or 3 minutes for high-severity routes).
- For kernel-queue spikes: alert when median(queue_ns) increases by >4x baseline and kernel_queue_ns contributes >30% of L_raw.

Investigation playbook: latency spike
------------------------------------
1) Confirm: Is the spike visible across similar cohorts? (model variant, seq_len_bucket)
2) Break down by kernel_id: query telemetry for top-5 kernel_ids by count and p95 contribution.
3) Check KV cache hit rate for the cohort during window.
4) Cross-reference infra events: GPU throttling, host OOM, noisy neighbors (see /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/known-issues).
5) If kernel_queue_ns dominates, escalate to kernel scheduler on-call with: sample trace + host_id + kernel_id + timeline.
6) Document findings and update calibration or normalization model if necessary.

Example investigation CLI snippets
--------------------------------
- Pull cohort percentiles (pseudo-CLI):
  curl -s "https://telemetry.query/api/query" -d '{ "q": "select percentile(hist,95) from latency where model=\'redwood-xl\' and seq_len_bucket=256 and timestamp>now()-5m" }' | jq

- Quick map of kernel queue share (pseudo-SQL):
  SELECT kernel_id, count(*) as n, p95(kernel_queue_ns) as q95_queue, p95(kernel_run_ns) as q95_run
  FROM traces WHERE model='redwood-xl' AND window='5m' GROUP BY kernel_id ORDER BY q95_queue DESC LIMIT 10;

Telemetry event example (single-line JSON for ingestion)
{
  "request_id": "r-9f2a3",
  "model": "redwood-xl-v2",
  "seq_len": 256,
  "output_tokens": 64,
  "accel_class": "h100-80g",
  "kernel_id": "k-embed-async-v3",
  "kernel_queue_ns": 1200000,
  "kernel_run_ns": 980000,
  "kv_cache_hit": false,
  "trace_start_ts": "2026-03-04T15:22:10.123Z"
}

Note: ingest as single-line JSON to minimize indexing cost; enrich later during batch pipeline.

Change control and versioning
-----------------------------
- Any change to the normalization model or cohort definitions must be recorded in the normalization registry: /configs/normalization-registry/<date>-<owner>.yaml and reviewed by profiling@redwood.com.
- Keep an audit column on dashboards noting the normalization version used.

Known limitations and caveats
----------------------------
- Residual-based normalization assumes covariates capture the majority of predictable latency. Residuals still include unobserved factors and should not be the only source for SLO enforcement.
- Calibration multipliers drift when firmware, driver, or microcode changes occur; schedule re-calibration after any infra upgrade.
- For very small cohorts, model-fitting is noisy; prefer cohort aggregation or basketed baselines.

Operational ownership and contacts
----------------------------------
- Primary owner: Runtime Profiling team (profiling@redwood.com).
- Escalation: runtime-scheduler-oncall@redwood.com (for kernel queue issues), infra-sre@redwood.com (for hardware incidents).

Appendix A — Normalization quick-reference table
--------------------------------------------------
| step | input | output | responsible |
|------|-------|--------|-------------|
| 1 | raw spans + histograms | cohorted percentiles | telemetry-pipeline |
| 2 | cohorted percentiles | fitted covariate model | profiling-job |
| 3 | residuals | L_norm time-series | dashboards |

Appendix B — Implementation notes
----------------------------------
- We prefer the profiling-job code in Go for performance; the models live in a shared library: internal/profiling/models.
- Persist fitted model coefficients to /meta/normalization/<cohort>/<date>.json for reproducibility.
- Unit tests: synthetic traces must exercise edge cases (kv cache thrash, long-tail kernels, sequence-length outliers).

Appendix C — Change log
------------------------
- 2026-01-10: Created by Aisha Patel (initial draft).
- 2026-02-02: Added calibration protocol (Marcus Li).
- 2026-03-05: Finalized alert thresholds and CLI snippets (Renee O'Connor).

If you have questions or want this applied to a new dashboard/cohort, ping profiling@redwood.com or open a PR against /configs/dashboard-samples.

title: Nsight Systems/Compute + CUPTI profiling for FP8/INT8 (quantized) kernels
content:
h1. Overview

This page is the step-by-step profiling playbook for *quantized kernel* work (FP8 / INT8) during the serving-runtime performance sprint. It focuses on:

* Capturing *repeatable* Nsight Systems (nsys) traces for end-to-end inference (prefill + decode) and isolating GPU vs scheduler/launch overhead.
* Capturing *actionable* Nsight Compute (ncu) reports for specific kernels/shapes to understand Tensor Core utilization, memory bandwidth, occupancy, and instruction mix.
* Using CUPTI-based counters (via runtime/benchmark instrumentation) to compare baselines vs FP8/INT8 variants without pulling full traces for every case.
* Comparing runs safely and consistently (same driver/CUDA/container, clocks, shape regime, and benchmark config).

This playbook is intended for engineers working on kernel integration (dispatch/registry) and scheduler interactions where quantized kernels show mixed outcomes.

h2. When to use this playbook

Use profiling when you observe one of the following in microbench or end-to-end serving benchmarks:

* FP8/INT8 shows *microbench wins* but *end-to-end* (TTFT/TPOT) regressions.
* FP8 attention path regresses *TTFT* for short prompts (suspected launch overhead / extra staging / scheduler interaction).
* INT8 matmul path is faster for some shapes but slower for others (suspected alignment/packing, memory bound, or fallback behavior).
* High run-to-run variance (suspected clock drift, thermal throttling, shared-node contention, or debug logging).

If the issue is primarily correctness (bad outputs, NaNs), start with the regression triage playbook and only profile after correctness is stable.

h1. Prerequisites & guardrails

h2. Access / tooling

You will need:

* Nsight Systems CLI: *nsys*
* Nsight Compute CLI: *ncu*
* CUDA toolkit compatible with the fleet image you are using (do *not* mix versions)
* Permissions to run on the benchmark fleet (H100/A100/L4 as applicable) and to upload artifacts to the benchmark bucket/Drive location

h2. Reproducibility requirements (do these first)

Before capturing any trace/report, ensure:

1. *Pinned container image* (same digest) and *pinned driver/CUDA* version (see benchmark runner pinning guidance).
2. *GPU clocks locked* when feasible (avoid boosting variability). If clocks cannot be locked, record clocks + power limits in the artifact metadata.
3. Dedicated node / no co-tenancy when collecting deep traces.
4. Stable benchmark configuration (prompt distribution, generation length, concurrency, batching window).

If you cannot guarantee these, your trace may be misleading and not comparable.

h2. Data handling

* Do not capture or upload customer prompts.
* Use the benchmark suite prompts only (approved internal sets) or synthetic prompts.
* Treat Nsight traces as *internal artifacts*; do not attach to customer tickets.

h1. Quick-start checklist (10 minutes)

*Goal:* Determine if a regression is GPU kernel time, launch overhead, memory bound, or scheduler-induced.

1) Reproduce the regression with the benchmark harness (same seed/config). Save the benchmark JSON config.

2) Capture a short *Nsight Systems* trace around a single run window (10–30s).

3) Inspect:
* GPU kernel time vs CPU time
* CUDA API call overhead (launches, memcpys)
* Stream utilization + overlap
* Context switches / host-side stalls

4) Identify the top 1–3 kernels by total time for the regressing case.

5) Capture *Nsight Compute* for those kernels only (filter by kernel name regex). Compare baseline vs quantized.

6) If kernel time is not the problem: look at scheduler metrics (queue depth, prefill/decode split, backpressure counters) and/or reduce launch count.

h1. Capturing Nsight Systems traces (nsys)

h2. What nsys is best for

* End-to-end timeline: CPU threads, CUDA API overhead, GPU kernel overlap, memcpy/memset, synchronization points.
* Diagnosing *launch overhead* and host-side stalls.
* Understanding if kernels are serialized due to stream usage or sync.

h2. Recommended capture profiles

*Short capture (default):* for most investigations
* Duration: 10–30 seconds
* Use case: identify where time is going, find top kernels

*Deep capture:* only when you need detailed CUDA API breakdown and NVTX ranges
* Duration: 30–90 seconds (keep it short; large traces are painful)

h2. Required NVTX ranges (benchmark + runtime)

To make traces comparable, ensure the run includes NVTX ranges (or equivalent annotations) for:

* request lifecycle: enqueue → schedule → prefill → decode → response
* per-phase ranges: prefill and decode
* kernel-mode tag: baseline / fp8 / int8

If ranges are missing, file an issue against the harness/runtime instrumentation (this is required for the sprint’s reproducibility bar).

h2. Command template (containerized benchmark run)

Replace placeholders in ALL CAPS.

1) Run the target benchmark case without profiling to confirm it reproduces:

*BENCH (no profiling)*

- Ensure you are using the same runner options used for the matrix.
- Save the resolved config and artifact metadata.

2) Run with nsys enabled (example):

nsys profile \
  --output nsys-QUANT-MODE-MODEL-GPU-CASE \
  --force-overwrite true \
  --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt,thread \
  --cuda-memory-usage=true \
  --sample=none \
  --capture-range=nvtx \
  --capture-range-end=stop \
  --stop-on-exit true \
  --export=sqlite \
  --stats=true \
  ./bench_runner \
    --model MODEL_NAME \
    --gpu-sku GPU_SKU \
    --quant-mode {baseline|fp8|int8} \
    --workload WORKLOAD_ID \
    --concurrency N \
    --seed SEED \
    --duration-seconds 20

Notes:
* Prefer *capture-range=nvtx* so you only capture the window around the benchmark iteration.
* Avoid CPU sampling unless needed; it increases overhead and file size.
* Keep profiling overhead in mind: always rerun a non-profiled case to confirm you didn’t change behavior.

h2. What to look for in nsys (common patterns)

h3. Pattern A: FP8/INT8 kernel is faster, but TTFT regresses

Look for:

* Increased *CUDA API call* time (lots of small launches)
* Additional memcpys/memsets (packing/unpacking, scale/zero-point transforms)
* Synchronization between streams causing serialization

Actions:

* Reduce launch count (kernel fusion, persistent kernels, larger tiles)
* Move preprocessing to GPU or fuse into matmul/attention epilogue
* Validate scheduler isn’t forcing smaller batch slices (which increases launches)

h3. Pattern B: Decode TPOT regresses only under concurrency

Look for:

* Increased time in scheduling/queueing ranges (NVTX)
* Kernel overlap decreases (GPU has bubbles)
* Frequent context syncs (cudaStreamSynchronize/cudaEventSynchronize)

Actions:

* Inspect scheduler metrics: queue depth histograms, backpressure counters, prefill/decode interleaving
* Validate that quantized decode doesn’t introduce extra sync points (e.g., KV cache alignment fixes)

h3. Pattern C: Kernel looks memory bound

Look for:

* High DRAM throughput but low SM/Tensor Core utilization
* Kernels dominated by global memory loads/stores

Actions:

* Move to Nsight Compute to confirm memory vs compute bound
* Evaluate layout changes, better vectorization, reduced precision/staging, or using Tensor Core-friendly formats

h1. Capturing Nsight Compute reports (ncu)

h2. What ncu is best for

* Per-kernel deep dive: Tensor Core utilization, achieved occupancy, memory throughput, instruction mix, launch configuration.
* Comparing baseline vs FP8/INT8 kernel variants for the *same shape*.

Use ncu only after you have identified *which* kernels matter from nsys (or from a kernel time breakdown in microbench).

h2. Keep ncu scoped

ncu overhead can be high. Always:

* Restrict to a single request or a small number of iterations.
* Filter kernels by name.
* Collect a limited set of sections first; expand only if needed.

h2. Command template (kernel-filtered)

Example: capture only attention and matmul kernels for a single benchmark iteration.

ncu \
  --set full \
  --target-processes all \
  --kernel-name-base function \
  --kernel-name "regex:.*(attention|gemm|matmul|wgmma|cutlass).*" \
  --launch-skip 5 \
  --launch-count 20 \
  --export ncu-QUANT-MODE-MODEL-GPU-CASE \
  ./bench_runner \
    --model MODEL_NAME \
    --gpu-sku GPU_SKU \
    --quant-mode {baseline|fp8|int8} \
    --workload WORKLOAD_ID \
    --concurrency 1 \
    --seed SEED \
    --max-iterations 1

If the run is too slow or generates too much output:

* Use a lighter set: `--set speedOfLight` or explicitly pick sections.
* Narrow the kernel regex.
* Reduce launch-count.

h2. Metrics & questions to answer (quantized kernels)

Use ncu to answer the following for each top kernel:

1) *Is it compute-bound or memory-bound?*
* Achieved memory bandwidth vs roofline
* Tensor Core utilization / HMMA/WGMMA usage

2) *Are we getting the expected Tensor Core path?*
* FP8: are we on Tensor Core FP8 instructions (architecture dependent)?
* INT8: are we using IMMA / Tensor Core INT8 paths or falling back to SIMT?

3) *Is occupancy limiting us?*
* Registers per thread, shared memory usage, occupancy
* Too-small tiles leading to low SM utilization

4) *Is the kernel dominated by type conversion/packing?*
* Excessive instructions for quant/dequant, scale application, or layout transforms

5) *Are launches too small (launch overhead dominated)?*
* Very short kernel durations repeated many times

h2. Common bottlenecks & fixes (cheat sheet)

h3. Launch overhead dominates (common for short prompts / small batches)

Symptoms:

* nsys shows lots of small kernels with gaps
* CPU thread shows heavy CUDA API time

Mitigations:

* Fuse epilogues / reduce intermediate kernels
* Increase work per launch (tile size, persistent scheduling)
* Ensure scheduler batching window is not too small for the target SLO

h3. Memory bound (common when quantization adds extra reads/writes)

Symptoms:

* High DRAM throughput, low Tensor Core utilization
* Many global loads/stores for scale/zero-point or layout conversion

Mitigations:

* Fuse quant/dequant with compute
* Prefer formats that avoid extra transposes
* Reuse scales/metadata from cache where possible

h3. Tensor Core underutilization (wrong path or shape misalignment)

Symptoms:

* Low HMMA/WGMMA/IMMA utilization
* ncu shows non-TC instruction mix

Mitigations:

* Validate alignment constraints (K dimension, leading dimensions)
* Confirm shape guardrails/fallbacks aren’t forcing a slower path
* Adjust kernel selection heuristic to pick baseline for unsupported regimes

h3. Occupancy limited by registers/shared memory

Symptoms:

* High registers per thread, low occupancy
* Performance sensitive to compiler flags / unrolling

Mitigations:

* Reduce register pressure (tuning, smaller unroll, different pipeline)
* Adjust shared memory staging strategy

h1. CUPTI-based profiling (lightweight counters)

h2. Why CUPTI counters

CUPTI-based counters provide a *low-friction* way to compare baseline vs quantized modes across many benchmark cases without collecting full nsys/ncu artifacts.

Use CUPTI counters to:

* Validate that a microbench win translates to higher GPU utilization end-to-end.
* Identify if regressions correlate with higher kernel launch counts, more memcpy/memset, or lower achieved occupancy.
* Gate canary decisions with supporting evidence.

h2. What to capture (minimum set)

For each run (baseline/fp8/int8), capture and record:

* GPU kernel time total (and top kernels if available)
* CUDA launch count
* memcpy/memset count and bytes
* SM utilization (or proxy) and achieved memory throughput (or proxy)
* Per-phase: prefill vs decode breakdown where available

If the harness provides “CUPTI summary” output, attach it to the run artifacts alongside the benchmark metadata.

h2. Recommended workflow

1) Run baseline vs fp8/int8 with CUPTI summary enabled (no nsys/ncu).
2) Compare deltas:
* If launch count increases meaningfully, suspect launch overhead / kernel fragmentation.
* If memcpy bytes increase, suspect packing/unpacking.
* If GPU utilization drops, suspect scheduler fragmentation or sync.
3) Only if needed, collect nsys/ncu for the top regressing cases.

h1. How to compare baseline vs FP8/INT8 runs (do this consistently)

h2. Pick apples-to-apples cases

When comparing modes:

* Same model revision / weights hash
* Same prompt distribution, generation length, and tool-calling/structured output settings
* Same concurrency and batching configuration
* Same GPU SKU and cluster (or same driver/CUDA/image)

h2. Compare at two levels

1) *Kernel-level* (microbench or isolated kernels)

* Compare time per kernel for identical shapes
* Verify the selected kernel path matches expectation (no hidden fallback)

2) *System-level* (end-to-end serving)

* TTFT and TPOT deltas
* Scheduler metrics (queue depth, prefill/decode split)
* Error rates/timeouts (quantized modes can surface new failure modes)

h2. Reporting template (paste into PR/issue)

Use this structure when posting results:

*Case:* MODEL / GPU / workload / concurrency / quant-mode

*Repro details:*
* container digest:
* driver/CUDA:
* clocks/power limits:
* git SHA:
* benchmark config link:

*Observed delta:*
* TTFT p50/p95:
* TPOT p50/p95:
* tokens/s:

*Profiling artifacts:*
* nsys trace: (link)
* ncu export: (link)
* CUPTI summary: (link)

*Conclusion:* (launch overhead / memory bound / TC underutilization / scheduler)

*Next action:* (kernel fix, heuristic update, scheduler tuning, or disable for shape)

h1. Artifact naming, storage, and metadata

h2. Naming convention

Use the following in all filenames:

`{tool}-{mode}-{model}-{gpu}-{workload}-{concurrency}-{date}-{gitsha}`

Examples:

* `nsys-fp8-llama3_70b-h100-mixA-c16-2026-02-18-a1b2c3d`
* `ncu-int8-mistral_7b-a100-decodeHeavy-c1-2026-02-18-a1b2c3d`

h2. Metadata file (required)

Alongside the trace/report, include a small text metadata file containing:

* model id + model hash
* quant mode + kernel selection flag states
* GPU SKU + MIG/partitioning status
* driver/CUDA/container digest
* clocks/power
* git SHA + build id
* benchmark config (resolved)

This is required for reruns and for variance investigations.

h1. Troubleshooting

h2. “My nsys trace is empty / no CUDA kernels show up”

* Ensure `--trace=cuda,nvtx` is set.
* Ensure the workload actually executed during the capture window.
* If using `--capture-range=nvtx`, confirm NVTX ranges are emitted and the capture stop event is reached.

h2. “ncu fails with permissions / attach issues”

* Check container capabilities and that you are allowed to access performance counters on the target node.
* If running in Kubernetes, ensure the pod has the required security context.
* Try `--target-processes all` if the process forks/execs.

h2. “Profiling changes performance too much”

* That is expected in some cases.
* Use CUPTI summaries first.
* Keep nsys duration short and avoid CPU sampling.
* Reduce ncu scope (fewer kernels, fewer launches).

h2. “Variance is still high even when profiling is off”

* Verify clocks are pinned and there is no thermal throttling.
* Confirm dedicated node / no background jobs.
* Check for debug logging paths and disable.
* Escalate to the variance investigation task if needed.

h1. Ownership & escalation

* Primary owner: Isabella Rossi (Serving Runtime)
* Kernel escalation: Hiro Tanaka / Grace Kim
* Scheduler instrumentation escalation: Julian Moore
* Perf regression architecture: Noah Patel

If you believe a quantized kernel should be disabled for a shape regime, open a runtime issue and link: the benchmark config, CUPTI summary, and at least one nsys trace for the problematic case.

title: Adaptive Observability and Kernel Hinting Playbook
content:
Summary

This playbook documents the Adaptive Observability & Kernel Hinting subsystem: the design, telemetry model, operational controls, and runbook for using kernel hints to steer the serving runtime. The goal is to reduce tail latency and per-token cost by leveraging request-level signals to select kernel execution paths and sampling strategies while keeping trace overhead bounded.

Why this exists

- Production inference workloads have widely varying sequence lengths, model architectures, and client SLAs. Static monitoring and static kernel selection produce suboptimal latency/cost tradeoffs.
- Kernel hints are lightweight signals (tagged on request metadata) that bias scheduler choices (kernel variant, prefetch, KV warmstart) for the current request cohort.
- Adaptive observability is necessary to validate that hints are safe, reduce false positives, and capture causal signals for regression detection.

Scope

This playbook covers:
- Design and components of the hinting + observability pipeline
- Data model, sampling policies, and trace budget rules
- Operational thresholds and incident runbooks for common failure modes
- Rollout and canary guidance for hinting rules and kernel profiles

Out-of-scope: model training, model quality evals, and on-device kernel internals beyond documented control signals.

Design overview

Architecture (text diagram)

Client -> Ingress Router -> Request Classifier -> Hint Enricher -> Hint Broker -> Scheduler/KV Prefetch/Kernels
                                         \u2022 Shadow Tracer -> Sampling Controller -> Observability Sink (TSDB / TraceDB)

Components

- Request Classifier: lightweight policy service that maps headers, route config, and proto attributes to request_cohort ids. Runs in the edge ingress so hint decisions travel with requests. Owned by serving-runtime/classification.
- Hint Enricher: attaches hint metadata (kernel_hint, prefetch_hint, expected_seq_len_bucket, sampling_weight) to the request context. Hints are cryptographically signed by the control plane to prevent tampering in dedicated/private deployments.
- Hint Broker: central service that resolves cohort->kernel_variant mappings and exposes a fast gRPC lookup for the scheduler. Supports versioned mappings and rollout tags.
- Scheduler Hooks: Scheduler reads kernel_hint and sampling_weight, consults runtime policy, and chooses a kernel variant, batch-slice, and prefetch action.
- Shadow Tracer & Sampling Controller: decides which requests get full end-to-end traces. Sampling is adaptive: when a hint is new or flips mapping, sampling weight temporarily increases for affected cohorts.

Data model and fields

Table: (rendered as text)
| field | description | type | examples |
|-------|-------------|------|----------|
| request_id | globally unique id for a request | string | r-0a1b2c |
| cohort_id | classifier-assigned cohort | string | search-embed-small |
| kernel_hint | suggested kernel profile tag | string | fast-fp16, stable-quant |
| prefetch_hint | kv cache warmstart preference | enum | none, aggressive, conservative |
| expected_seq_len_bucket | bucketed input length | string | short(<=64), med(65-512), long(>512) |
| sampling_weight | relative trace sampling weight | float (0.0-1.0) | 0.05 |

Operational invariants and SLOs

- Hint Safety: kernel_hint should not increase CPU GPU utilization > 5% above baseline for steady cohorts. Monitored via kernel_variant_resource_delta.
- Hint Efficacy: cohort p95 latency with kernel_hint-enabled should be <= 0.95x baseline p95 for the same workload when target is performance-optimized.
- Sampling budget: end-to-end trace capture should consume <= 0.5% of request airtime budget for high-volume cohorts.
- Rollout guard: any hint mapping change that increases p99 by > 10% triggers automatic rollback.

How sampling works (algorithmic summary)

1. Baseline sampling rate per cohort (configurable).
2. Change amplification: if a cohort's kernel mapping is changed, Sampling Controller increases sampling_weight by factor 5 for 30 minutes for that cohort.
3. Entropy hedging: if trace diversity drops (identical stack signatures exceed 90% of traces), controller reduces weight to focus on unique traces.

Config example (runtime hint controller YAML)

hint_controller:
  default_sampling_rate: 0.01
  change_amplification_factor: 5.0
  amplification_window_minutes: 30
  max_trace_budget_percent: 0.5
  cohort_overrides:
    - cohort: search-embed-small
      sampling_rate: 0.02
      allowed_kernel_variants: [fast-fp16, stable-quant]

(Place this in /etc/redwood/hint-controller.yaml on control plane nodes for Hosted; equivalent k8s ConfigMap for Dedicated.)

Trace schema example (JSON line format)

{
  "request_id": "r-0a1b2c",
  "cohort_id": "search-embed-small",
  "kernel_hint": "fast-fp16",
  "expected_seq_len_bucket": "short",
  "latency_ms": 12.3,
  "kernel_variant": "fast-fp16-v7",
  "cpu_pct": 23.4
}

Runbook: Tail-latency spike after hint rollout

Symptoms
- p99 latency for cohort X increases by > 15% within 10 minutes of hint rollout.
- Kernel variant CPU/GPU utilization delta > 7% vs baseline.

Immediate actions (1–10 minutes)
1. Identify affected cohort IDs from the alert payload.
2. Query trace sink for recent traces tagged with cohort_id and kernel_hint. Use the trace window 15m back.
3. If traces show higher kernel_cpu_pct or prefetch stalls, rollback the mapping in Hint Broker to previous version:

# rollback using hint-brokerctl
hint-brokerctl rollback --cohort search-embed-small --to-version v12

4. If rollback is not possible or unexpected: cascade to scheduler soft-fallback: set policy: honor_hint=false for affected nodes.

Post-incident analysis (within 48 hours)
- Run a fidelity experiment: replay representative requests against both kernel_variant A and variant B in the lab using the Operational Workload Simulator. Capture per-token cost, p95, and resource deltas.
- Update decision log with hypothesis and root cause.

Runbook: Missing or malformed hints observed

Symptoms
- Hints absent for > 0.1% of requests from an ingress cluster.
- Classifier latency spikes or returns default cohort frequently.

Immediate actions
1. Confirm ingress health and classifier logs for KeyError/timeout.
2. If classifier is degraded, switch ingress to classifier-fallback config: static cohort map.
3. Re-enable entropy-bounded sampling for the cluster to capture request variability until classifier is healthy.

Diagnostic commands (internal)
- kubectl -n serving logs deploy/ingress-classifier --since=10m | grep ERROR
- hint-brokerctl status --cohort search-embed-small
- tracesql 'select * from traces where cohort_id="search-embed-small" order by ts desc limit 100'

Testing and rollout guidance

Canary matrix
- Phase 0: lab validation (shadow run against replay corpus).
- Phase 1: 1% traffic canary for single AZ (monitor 30m).
- Phase 2: 10% traffic multi-AZ (monitor 2h).
- Phase 3: 100% traffic with gradual ramp (monitor 24h).

Gates to advance
- p95 change <= 3% on canary compared to baseline.
- kernel CPU/GPU delta <= 5% for the canary nodes.
- No increase in error rate or queueing indicators.

Telemetry and dashboards (recommended panels)
- cohort_p99_latency (split by kernel_variant)
- kernel_variant_cpu_pct and gpu_pct (time series with delta from baseline)
- hint_coverage_rate (percent requests with valid hints)
- trace_sampling_rate and trace_uniqueness_ratio
- sampling_controller_amplification_events

Security and safety notes

- Signed hints: in Dedicated/Private installs, hints must be signed by the control plane using the customer-managed KMS key (see security-and-compliance/rbac-and-auth for signing policy).
- Rate limits: the hint broker enforces a per-cohort mutation rate to avoid thrashing (default 1 change per 15 minutes).

Troubleshooting checklist (fast-reference)

1. Is hint coverage within expected range? If not, check classifier and ingress.
2. Are traces representative? Check sampling_controller_amplification events.
3. Is kernel_variant causing resource hotspots? Check kernel_variant_cpu_pct/gpu_pct panels.
4. If rollback needed, use hint-brokerctl rollback.

Owners and contacts
- Hinting & Sampling: runtime-observability team (team alias: #runtime-obsv). Primary oncall: Michael Chen.
- Scheduler integration: runtime-scheduler team. Contact: Sofia Alvarez.

Change log and decision trace

- 2026-09-15: Playbook created by Asha Patel.
- 2026-10-04: Added amplification window policy after canary experiment showed under-sampling.
- 2026-12-01: Safety guard added (automatic rollback on p99 regression > 10%).

References

- See runtime-architecture/dispatch-and-fidelity-bridging-playbook-2026 for routing policies.
- See kernel-and-scheduling/kernel-telemetry-annotation-guidelines-2025 for kernel metric naming.

Appendix: lightweight kernel hint examples

- fast-fp16: select FP16-optimized kernels, aggressive occupancy, hero prefetch enabled. Target: short sequences, latency-sensitive.
- stable-quant: select quantized kernels, conservative prefetch, disable speculative prefetching. Target: long sequences, cost-sensitive.

Appendix: example CLI snippets

# Inspect current mapping
hint-brokerctl get --cohort search-embed-small --output json

# Apply new mapping (creates versioned mapping)
hint-brokerctl apply --cohort search-embed-small --mapping '{"kernel_hint":"fast-fp16","allowed_variants":["fast-fp16-v7","fast-fp16-v8"]}' --author "asha.patel@redwood.ai" --message "canary fast-fp16 for search embed small"

End of playbook.

title: Caching & Batching Cost Signals (Serving Runtime Profiling Playbook)
content:
## Purpose
This playbook documents the serving-runtime signals we rely on to *explain* changes in unit cost (blended $/1M output tokens). It focuses on the three most common runtime drivers:

1) **Batching utilization** (how much GPU time is spent doing useful work vs waiting/underfilled)
2) **KV/prefix cache effectiveness** (how much compute we avoid by reusing previous work)
3) **Prefill vs decode mix** (how request shape and context length shift GPU cost per output token)

This page is referenced by the Unit Economics dashboard and the on-call discrepancy playbooks. It is intended for Serving Runtime, Telemetry/Analytics, and SRE.

---

## How runtime signals map to blended $/1M output tokens
### The mental model
At a high level:

**blended $/1M output tokens** ≈ (GPU $ + overhead allocations) / (output tokens) * 1,000,000

When the metric moves, one (or more) of these must be true:

- **Numerator increased**: we spent more GPU-hours for the same output tokens (e.g., lower batching efficiency, more prefill work, cache regression, slower kernels, lower quant efficiency).
- **Denominator decreased**: we reported fewer output tokens for the same GPU-hours (e.g., metering bug, streaming path undercount, increased truncation, more failures).
- **Mix shifted**: traffic changed in a way that makes output tokens more expensive (e.g., longer prompts → prefill-heavy, shorter generations with high prompt overhead, different model/quant profile, region/provider changes).

### Cost-driver decomposition (runtime-focused)
The unit cost typically correlates with the following derived factors:

- **Effective throughput:** output_tokens / GPU_second (higher is better)
- **Batching efficiency:** useful_compute_time / allocated_compute_time (higher is better)
- **Cache savings:** avoided_prefill_tokens (or avoided_attention_work) / total_prefill_work (higher is better)
- **Prefill load:** prefill_tokens / output_tokens (lower is better, but workload-dependent)

These are not accounting numbers; they are *explanatory signals* that should directionally match changes in blended cost.

---

## Required dimensions (to make signals actionable)
All runtime signals used for unit economics must be taggable by the dimensions the dashboard supports, within cardinality limits:

**Required dimensions** (where available):
- model_id (canonical)
- model_version (if pinned or surfaced via routing policy)
- quantization_profile (allowed-values only)
- region (normalized)
- customer_tier (self-serve / dedicated / private / enterprise)
- streaming (true/false)

**Important:** do *not* tag by customer_id, route_id with high uniqueness, or raw prompt hashes. See the cardinality standard referenced above.

---

## Signal 1: Batching utilization
### Why it matters
Continuous batching is the primary lever for improving GPU utilization for decode. Underfilled batches waste GPU cycles, increasing $ per output token.

Batching issues are one of the most common causes of sudden regional or model-specific unit cost spikes.

### Definitions
Use these terms consistently:

- **Batch size (decode):** number of active sequences decoded per step.
- **Batch occupancy:** batch_size / max_batch_size (or / capacity at the current kernel/sequence length).
- **Batching wait time:** time requests spend queued to form a batch.
- **Compute time:** time spent executing kernels.

### Recommended runtime metrics (names are illustrative)
Collect at least:

- redwood_runtime_decode_active_sequences_avg{model_id,region,quantization_profile,streaming}
- redwood_runtime_decode_max_active_sequences{...} (or configured max)
- redwood_runtime_batch_wait_ms_p50/p95{model_id,region}
- redwood_runtime_gpu_busy_ratio{region,cluster} (if available)
- redwood_runtime_decode_tokens_total{model_id,region,quantization_profile}

### Derived metrics & interpretation
- **Decode batch utilization** = active_sequences_avg / max_active_sequences
  - Healthy ranges vary by model/hardware, but sustained drops (e.g., 0.70 → 0.40) usually show up as a unit cost increase.

- **Queueing vs compute tradeoff**
  - If batch_wait_ms_p95 increases sharply while utilization remains low, we likely have fragmentation (many small pools), admission control issues, or a routing policy change.
  - If batch_wait_ms_p95 increases and utilization increases, we may have intentionally optimized cost at the expense of latency (confirm against SLOs).

### Common root causes
- Traffic fragmentation across too many pools (by model version, quant profile, region, tier)
- Overly strict routing/affinity rules preventing consolidation
- Misconfigured max_batch_size for new model or kernel regime
- Increased request concurrency variance (bursty traffic) + conservative batching windows
- Increased prefill pressure causing decode starvation

### What to do when batching utilization drops
1) Confirm the issue is real (not a missing-tag or sampling artifact).
2) Check for recent changes:
   - routing policy updates
   - canary rollout that split traffic
   - autoscaling events / pool resizing
   - model version pinning changes
3) Compare by dimension:
   - model_id + quantization_profile
   - region
   - customer_tier
4) Mitigation options (runtime-owned):
   - increase consolidation (reduce pool fragmentation)
   - adjust batching window/limits for affected pool
   - revisit admission control thresholds
   - consider fallback to a compatible model variant during capacity stress (if policy allows)

---

## Signal 2: KV cache and prefix cache hit rates
### Why it matters
Cache hits reduce prefill compute. Prefill can be a large fraction of GPU work for long-context workloads, so cache regressions can materially raise blended $/1M output tokens.

Important nuance: cache benefits can be workload-specific and may not show in all traffic (e.g., highly unique prompts).

### Cache types
- **Prefix cache (a.k.a. prompt cache):** reuses computed attention states for a shared prefix across requests.
- **KV cache reuse within session:** reuses per-sequence KV as decode progresses (normal decode state). This is not a “hit rate” in the same sense; the cost signal here is more about *KV cache pressure/evictions* and *context growth*.

### Definitions
- **Prefix cache hit:** request’s prefill can reuse a stored prefix representation, reducing prefill tokens processed.
- **Prefix cache hit rate:** hits / (hits + misses)
- **Cache saved tokens:** estimated prefill_tokens_avoided due to cache hits
- **Evictions / churn:** how often cached entries are removed due to memory pressure or TTL

### Recommended runtime metrics
Prefix cache:
- redwood_runtime_prefix_cache_hits_total{model_id,region,quantization_profile}
- redwood_runtime_prefix_cache_misses_total{...}
- redwood_runtime_prefix_cache_saved_prefill_tokens_total{...} (preferred; avoids inference from hits)
- redwood_runtime_prefix_cache_evictions_total{region,model_id}
- redwood_runtime_prefix_cache_bytes_in_use{region,model_id}

KV cache pressure (decode state / memory):
- redwood_runtime_kv_cache_bytes_in_use{model_id,region}
- redwood_runtime_kv_cache_oom_events_total{model_id,region}
- redwood_runtime_kv_cache_evictions_total{model_id,region} (if applicable)

### Derived metrics & interpretation
- **Prefix cache hit rate** = hits / (hits + misses)
  - Use as a qualitative indicator. It can be misleading if “hit” does not imply a large token savings.

- **Prefill tokens saved rate** = saved_prefill_tokens / total_prefill_tokens
  - Prefer this for cost attribution. A small hit rate can still save a lot if hits are on long prefixes.

- **Cost mapping**
  - When cache effectiveness drops, expect:
    - prefill_tokens / output_tokens to rise
    - GPU-seconds per output token to rise
    - blended $/1M output tokens to rise

### Common root causes of cache regressions
- Cache key changes (tokenization changes, prompt formatting changes, system prompt edits)
- TTL/size configuration changes reducing retention
- Memory pressure from longer contexts causing evictions
- Increased traffic diversity (fewer repeated prefixes)
- Region or pool split lowering reuse probability

### What to do when cache hit rate drops
1) Validate the workload changed (e.g., product launched new prompt template) vs system regression.
2) Compare cache signals alongside prompt length distributions:
   - rising average prompt length + falling cache savings often indicates evictions.
3) Check for a drop isolated to:
   - a region (config divergence)
   - a quantization profile (different cache capacity/behavior)
   - streaming vs non-streaming (request metadata differences)
4) Mitigations:
   - increase cache capacity (bytes) or TTL (if safe)
   - revert/adjust prompt formatting to stabilize prefixes
   - consolidate pools to increase reuse rate
   - fix cache key/versioning if mismatched between gateway/runtime

---

## Signal 3: Prefill vs decode ratio (request shape)
### Why it matters
Even if batching and caching are stable, unit cost can move due to request mix:

- Longer prompts increase **prefill** work.
- Shorter generations reduce **output tokens** per request, increasing overhead per output token.
- Tool calling / structured output may change average output length and stop conditions.

This is the most common explanation for “no regression found” in runtime code, but unit cost still increased.

### Definitions
- **Prefill tokens:** input tokens processed to build attention state before generating output.
- **Decode tokens:** output tokens generated.
- **Prefill/decode ratio:** prefill_tokens / decode_tokens (or / output_tokens).

### Recommended runtime metrics
- redwood_runtime_prefill_tokens_total{model_id,region,quantization_profile,streaming}
- redwood_runtime_decode_tokens_total{model_id,region,quantization_profile,streaming}
- redwood_runtime_request_count_total{model_id,region,streaming}
- redwood_runtime_prompt_tokens_histogram{model_id,region} (bucketed)
- redwood_runtime_output_tokens_histogram{model_id,region} (bucketed)

### Derived metrics & interpretation
- **Prefill/Output ratio** = prefill_tokens_total / decode_tokens_total
  - Rising ratio means each output token “costs” more prefill work.
  - Often driven by longer context windows or by product features that add system/tool context.

- **Output tokens per request** = decode_tokens_total / request_count
  - Falling output/request increases fixed overhead per output token (scheduler overhead, network, per-request setup).

- **Streaming vs non-streaming mix**
  - Streaming often correlates with shorter outputs (users stop early) and different cancellation patterns.
  - Ensure output token metering parity across streaming paths before drawing conclusions.

---

## Investigation workflow: explaining a unit cost change
Use this workflow when the Unit Economics dashboard shows a spike or drift in blended $/1M output tokens.

### Step 0 — Validate data integrity (before debugging runtime)
- Confirm output token metering completeness for the affected slice (especially streaming=true).
- Confirm dimension coverage (region/model/tier/quantization_profile not missing).
- Check the reconciliation report vs billing totals for the same time window.

If any of the above fail, follow the on-call guide and stop here.

### Step 1 — Determine if it’s numerator, denominator, or mix
For the same slice (model_id/region/tier), compare to previous period:
- GPU-hours (or allocated GPU cost proxy) trend
- output_tokens trend
- requests trend

Quick heuristics:
- output_tokens down but requests stable: likely metering, truncation, or behavior change.
- GPU cost up with tokens stable: likely utilization/efficiency regression.

### Step 2 — Check batching utilization
- decode batch utilization
- batch wait times
- GPU busy ratio (if available)

If utilization dropped, prioritize routing/pool fragmentation and autoscaling events.

### Step 3 — Check cache effectiveness
- saved_prefill_tokens / total_prefill_tokens
- hit/miss rate (secondary)
- evictions and cache bytes in use

If cache savings dropped, check prompt/template changes and cache config.

### Step 4 — Check prefill/decode mix
- prefill/output ratio
- prompt token distribution shift
- output tokens per request shift

If prefill/output ratio rose, look for product changes (system prompts, context injection), model changes (context window defaults), or customer-specific usage patterns.

### Step 5 — Tie back to unit economics narrative
Document the most likely driver(s) with:
- which signal moved
- magnitude of change
- impacted dimensions
- suspected cause
- next action + owner

This summary is what Product/Finance expects in an incident or exec readout.

---

## Practical guidance: what “good” looks like (directional)
These are not SLAs; they are sanity-checks.

- **Batch utilization (decode):** stable over time within a pool; abrupt step changes are suspicious.
- **Prefix cache savings:** should not drop to ~0 without an obvious prompt/template change or a cache outage.
- **Prefill/output ratio:** varies by use case; watch for week-over-week shifts, especially per customer tier.
- **Per-dimension stability:** if the aggregate metric moves but *no* per-model or per-region slice moves, suspect a reporting or dimension-mapping issue.

---

## Known pitfalls (do not mis-diagnose)
- **Hit rate ≠ savings:** use saved_prefill_tokens where possible.
- **Batch utilization can improve while unit cost worsens:** if prefill load rises dramatically, decode may be fine but total cost still increases.
- **Streaming cancellation:** early cancels can reduce output tokens per request; verify whether cancellation rate changed.
- **Quantization profile changes:** can change throughput and memory behavior; ensure telemetry tags the actual profile used at execution time.
- **Pool splitting for compliance/tier isolation:** expected to reduce batching/cache reuse; Finance/Product should be aware when interpreting tier-specific costs.

---

## Action items for instrumentation gaps
If you cannot explain a cost change because signals are missing or not dimensioned correctly, file a ticket with:
- which metric is missing
- required dimensions
- expected cardinality behavior
- how it supports unit economics drilldowns

Tag owners:
- Runtime signals: Serving Runtime
- Metering dimensions: Telemetry/Analytics (token metering)
- Dashboards/alerts: SRE/Observability

---

## Appendix: Suggested queries (warehouse-friendly)
Use warehouse views where available; do not query raw high-cardinality metrics for broad time ranges.

1) Prefill/output ratio by model and region:
- prefill_tokens_total / output_tokens_total grouped by (model_id, region, quantization_profile)

2) Cache savings rate by model:
- saved_prefill_tokens_total / prefill_tokens_total grouped by (model_id, region)

3) Batching utilization proxy (if exported):
- avg_active_sequences / max_active_sequences grouped by (model_id, region)

If these views do not exist yet, coordinate with Mei Lin (warehouse/views) and Logan Wright (Telemetry/Analytics) to materialize the minimum set needed for the Unit Economics dashboard drilldowns.

title: Telemetry-feedback kernel autotune playbook
content:
Summary
---
This playbook describes a telemetry-driven feedback loop used to automatically tune kernel selection and scheduling knobs in the serving runtime. It is intended for on-call engineers, runtime owners, and SREs who operate model-serving fleets. Unlike manual kernel tuning runbooks, this document specifies the signals, control loop design, safety gates, rollout and rollback procedures, and observability required to safely operate automated kernel autotuning in production.

Motivation
---
- Kernel characteristics and the optimal scheduling strategy can vary by model, sequence-length distribution, and traffic mix.
- Manual tuning is slow to react to changes (new models, workload shifts, infra upgrades).
- A closed-loop approach reduces human burden and improves unit-cost while preserving latency SLOs.

Scope and assumptions
---
- Applies to the inference serving runtime kernel-selection and minor scheduling parameters (batch-slice-size, prefetch-window, kernel-variant). Not in scope: major topology changes, shard rebalancing, or changes to global admission control.
- Requires the telemetry pipeline to deliver per-kernel latency histograms, occupancy, failed-dispatch counts, and end-to-end request traces with kernel attribution.
- Assumes we have an experiment framework for safe canary rollouts and immediate control-plane overrides.

Signals and telemetry (required)
---
1) Per-kernel latency histograms (P50/P90/P99) with labels: model_id, variant, sequence_len_bucket, gpu_type
2) Kernel occupancy (concurrent warps/threads) and utilization percentiles by GPU ID
3) Dispatch failures and fallback counts (native->fallback) per minute
4) E2E tail latency (request-level) with kernel attribution and route_id
5) Cost proxies: tokens_per_sec and GPU-time-per-token estimates
6) Sampled traces with kernel execution timeline (min 1 in 10k requests)

Design: control loop overview
---
- Control frequency: 10-minute decision windows (configurable).
- Candidate actions: switch kernel variant (e.g., aten->fused-attn), adjust batch-slice-size (-1/+1), +/- prefetch-window (ms), enable/disable quantized path.
- Optimization objective: minimize cost_per_token subject to SLO constraints (P99 latency < route-SLO AND error-rate < 0.1%).
- Policy engine evaluates candidates using a shadow-evaluation technique described below.

Shadow evaluation procedure
---
1) For each candidate action, generate a shadow configuration that runs in parallel on a small subset (default 2%) of requests for 10 minutes. Shadow runs must be CPU/GPU-isolated where possible to avoid perturbing production.
2) Collect the same telemetry for shadow runs. Compute deltas for P90 and P99 latency, error-rate, and estimated unit-cost.
3) Only consider promotion if:
   - latency delta at P99 <= +3% relative to baseline OR absolute P99 still under route-SLO, AND
   - error-rate delta <= +0.05pp, AND
   - estimated cost_per_token improves by >= 4% (configurable), AND
   - no regression signals flagged by quality monitors (see Guardrails).
4) When multiple candidates pass, rank by cost improvement / latency impact and select the top-ranked one for a staged rollout.

Staged rollout plan
---
- Stage 0: telemetry-only shadow (2%) — minimum 10 minutes.
- Stage 1: internal canary (10% of internal traffic) — 30 minutes.
- Stage 2: progressive ramp (25% -> 50% -> 100%) over a configurable window (default 3 hours).
- At each step, enforce automated checks (see Acceptance checks); if any check fails, abort and rollback immediately.

Acceptance checks (automated)
---
- P99 absolute must remain < route.SLO (hard gate).
- Relative P99 increase must be <= 7% at canary stage; <= 5% at progressive stage.
- Dispatch failure increase <= 0.1pp.
- Customer-impacting errors (500-level) must not increase above baseline + 0.02pp.
- Unit-cost improvement must be observed at the canary window for promotion to wider rollout.

Guardrails and safety mechanisms
---
- Kill-switch: Operators can flip a global flag to disable autotune; control plane respects immediate override.
- Emergency rollback: If any safety check trip is detected by the monitoring alert (SRE-alert), an automated rollback job reverses kernel selection within 60s.
- Rate-limited actions: no more than 3 kernel promotions per model per 24 hours.
- Staleness detection: if telemetry lag > 60s, suspend the control loop.

Operational runbook: step-by-step
---
1) If telemetry indicates a candidate passed shadow evaluation, the policy engine will post a pending action to /runtime/autotune/pending with details.
2) On-call receives an automated notification with diffs and the top-3 metrics to inspect.
3) Verify sampled traces for the canary population (use tracing panel: dashboard -> trace-sample -> filter model_id). Confirm no unexpected kernel fallbacks.
4) Approve or reject the stage-1 rollout via the autotune UI or `rtictl autotune approve <action-id>`; approval triggers the canary stage.
5) Monitor acceptance checks; if all pass, the system will continue ramping. If any check fails, the system will automatically rollback and create an incident ticket with correlated traces.
6) Post-deployment: run the performance-regression-huntbook checklist (link in Related pages).

Example CLI snippets
---
- Start a manual shadow run for diagnostics:
  rtictl profile shadow --model my-model-v3 --kernel fused-attn --sample-rate 0.02 --duration 10m

- List pending autotune actions:
  rtictl autotune list --state pending

- Approve an action (can be done from UI):
  rtictl autotune approve 5c2a8b9f

Configuration example (YAML)
---
autotune:
  decision_window: 10m
  shadow_fraction: 0.02
  cost_improvement_threshold_pct: 4
  max_promotions_per_day_per_model: 3
  rollback_on_telemetry_lag_seconds: 60

Metrics and dashboards to inspect
---
- Kernel latency heatmap (by model_id and sequence_len_bucket)
- Promotion pipeline dashboard: pending -> canary -> ramp -> success/fail counts
- Shadow delta table: candidate -> delta_P90 -> delta_P99 -> delta_cost
- Rollback events timeline (sensitive to operator action)

Alerting and SLOs
---
- SLOs consulted: route-SLO P99 (varies by product route), global error-rate target 0.1%
- Alerts fired when: automated rollback occurs, P99 increases > 10% absolute, dispatch failure spike > 0.2pp in 1m

Troubleshooting checklist (common failure modes)
---
- Symptom: P99 regressions after promotion
  - Inspect shadow delta metrics and sampled traces.
  - Check for sequence-length skew between shadow and production.
  - If regression confined to one GPU-type, restrict kernel variant by gpu_type label.
- Symptom: increased fallback counts
  - Verify kernel binary compatibility and model build flags.
  - Check for memory pressure or OOMs on canary nodes.
- Symptom: no cost improvement observed
  - Confirm cost estimator inputs (tokens/sec telemetry) and sample size.
  - Consider longer shadow windows or larger shadow fraction.

Ownership, release notes and roadmap items
---
- Primary owner: runtime-kernel-team (oncall alias: runtime-kernel@redwood.internal).
- Next roadmap items: integrate model-quality signals into autotune, add RL-based policy exploration, extend autotune to multi-tenant admission knobs.
- Ship notes: this playbook formalizes the telemetry-feedback pipeline for kernel autotune and documents the automated rollback behavior introduced in runtime release 2.14.0.

Appendix: short glossary and safe values
---
- kernel variant: a compiled execution path for attention/feed-forward operators (e.g., fused-attn-v2, aten-attn).
- prefetch-window: time in ms used to warm KV cache ahead of request.
- safe promotion thresholds: default cost_improvement_threshold_pct=4, p99_relative_threshold_promote=3%

Related pages
---
- Continuous runtime profiling strategy (link in Related pages)
- Performance regression huntbook
- Kernel build and compatibility matrix

Change log
---
- 2026-01-18: initial published draft by Maya Chen.
- 2026-02-12: clarified shadow fraction defaults and tightened rollback window.

title: Model chaining profiling and batch shaping playbook
content:
Overview

This playbook documents the recommended approach for profiling, benchmarking, and operationalizing multi-model request chains ("model chaining") in the Redwood serving runtime. Model chaining occurs when a single API request triggers sequential or conditional invocations across multiple model variants or pipelines (for example: classifier -> reranker -> generator). These patterns are increasingly common in production flows (routing, tool-calling, multimodal pre- and post-processing) and expose unique scheduling, caching, and batching interactions that require targeted profiling and shaping to meet latency and cost SLOs.

Audience
- Runtime engineers who implement scheduler/kernel changes
- Performance engineers owning microbenchmarks and end-to-end SLOs
- Oncall SREs and platform owners responsible for incident triage
- Solutions engineers validating customer workloads that chain models

Goals
- Provide a repeatable procedure to attribute latency and cost across a chained execution path.
- Offer batch-shaping and warmup recommendations that preserve p95 SLOs while minimizing per-token cost.
- Define benchmark scenarios and acceptance thresholds to gate releases that impact chained workloads.

When to use this playbook
- Adding a new chained pipeline to production
- Observed p95 regressions correlated with multi-model invocations
- Rolling out kernel or scheduler changes that affect batching/eviction logic

Key concepts and terms
- Link: one hop in the chain (e.g., token-classifier).
- Chain: ordered list of links that execute per request.
- Interlink latency: time window between link completion and next link start. Includes network, marshalling, and scheduling delay.
- Batch shaping: runtime techniques to control how requests in a chain are aggregated into kernel batches.
- Prefetch/warmstart: proactive loading of KV cache or kernels prior to link execution to reduce cold latency.

Observability checklist
- Per-link latency histogram (p50/p95/p99) with distinction of kernel vs scheduling vs marshalling time.
- Interlink gap histogram and correlation with kernel admission events.
- Kernel occupancy and batch size distribution per link.
- KV cache hit ratio per model link and warmup success rate.
- Cost per request and per-token cost tagged with chain-id and feature flags.

Suggested metrics (examples)
- chain.request.count (tags: chain_id, customer_tier)
- chain.latency.p95 (tags: chain_id, link_index)
- kernel.batch.size (tags: kernel_variant, link_index)
- kvcache.prefetch.success_rate (tags: chain_id, model)

Profiling procedure (step-by-step)
1) Identify representative chains
   - For the workload under investigation, extract the top 10 chain shapes by request volume and by p95 contribution. Use tracing to enumerate link types and their average token lengths.

2) Baseline capture (shadow/topology snapshot)
   - Capture a 10-minute tracing window in shadow mode with full span collection and kernel annotations. Use the replay harness to export the trace as a synthetic corpus.
   - Command example: 
     ./tools/trace-export --service=ingress --filter=chain_id:checkout_v2 --out=checkout_v2.trace

3) Microprofile each link in isolation
   - Replay links individually against the same model-variant to collect kernel-level latency and batch distributions. Use the microbenchmark agent with kernel annotation turned on.
   - Command example: 
     ./bench/replay --trace=checkout_v2.trace --link=2 --annotate-kernel --concurrency=50 --duration=60s --out=link2-profile.json

4) End-to-end chain replay with controlled shaping knobs
   - Re-run the synthetic chain while toggling shaping knobs: contiguous-batching, interlink-throttle, slot-reservation, kv-prefetch. Capture per-link breakdowns.
   - Command example: 
     ./bench/replay --trace=checkout_v2.trace --shaping='slot_reserve=2;interlink_throttle=50ms;kv_prefetch=on' --duration=600s --out=chain-run-1.json

5) Attribution and root cause analysis
   - For each chain run, compute: per-link kernel median/p95, interlink gap median/p95, batch-size vs latency correlation, and cost per request.
   - If p95 regressions are kernel-localized, open a kernel performance investigation. If regressions are due to interlink scheduling gaps, follow the Scheduler tuning steps below.

Batch shaping strategies (patterns and trade-offs)
- Tight slicing: enforce small, bounded batch slice per link to guarantee lower tail latency at higher per-token cost. Use when tail SLO is high priority.
- Opportunistic coalescing: allow larger batches across links when background load is stable to improve cost efficiency but monitor p95 drift.
- Slot reservation for sequential links: reserve N kernel slots across link boundaries for a chain to prevent preemption and eviction mid-chain. Useful for long KV warmup sequences.
- Interlink throttle: impose a minimal delay between links to allow the scheduler to co-locate subsequent link work into an opportunistic batch. Useful when immediate re-invocation results in wasted small batches.
- Adaptive prefetch: trigger KV/model prefetch for the next link when the probability of continuation exceeds a threshold. Tune by observing prefetch hit success and added upstream latency.

Configuration examples
- YAML example for batch shaper (runtime config):

| key | type | description | example |
|-----|------|-------------|---------|
| shaping.mode | string | One of: tight, opportunistic, reserved | reserved |
| slot_reservations | int | Number of kernel slots to reserve per chain | 2 |
| interlink_throttle_ms | int | Milliseconds to delay between link transitions | 30 |
