| kv_prefetch_enabled | bool | Enable prefetching for next-link models | true |
| prefetch_confidence_threshold | float | Trigger threshold (0-1) for prefetch | 0.65 |

Example YAML snippet:

shaping:
  mode: reserved
  slot_reservations: 2
  interlink_throttle_ms: 30
  kv_prefetch_enabled: true
  prefetch_confidence_threshold: 0.65

Kernel scheduling tuning checklist
- Ensure link affinity: tag chains with affinity labels so the scheduler prefers the same GPU/NUMA domain for adjacent links.
- Verify slot-reservation accounting: aggregated reserved slots should not exceed node capacity. The admission controller must expose a rejection metric for reservation overcommit.
- Prioritize prefetch I/O: prefetch requests should be admitted with lower admission latency guarantees to reduce cold-link penalties.
- Backpressure integration: interlink backpressure should surface as a chain-level signal to the admission controller.

Benchmarking suite additions (how to add chain tests)
1) Add synthetic corpus: export representative chain traces (see Baseline capture) to the corpus repo under benchmarks/chains/.
2) Define chain SLO matrix: for each chain define p50/p95/p99 thresholds and cost-per-request gates.
3) Add CI job: a nightly chain-run that executes the chains under variable background noise profiles and validates against the SLO matrix.

Sample SLO matrix (example)
| chain_id | p50 (ms) | p95 (ms) | cost/request (tokens) |
|----------|----------:|---------:|----------------------:|
| checkout_v2 | 60 | 220 | 1.8 |
| multimodal-qa | 120 | 420 | 3.6 |
| routing-fallback | 30 | 150 | 0.6 |

Release gating guidance
- Any change to kernel batching, admission controller, or slot-reservation logic must include a chained-workload benchmark in the release candidate validation matrix.
- Required artifacts: chain-run results (clean vs noisy), annotated traces showing per-link kernel attribution, and cost delta analysis.

Known issues (current)
- CHAIN-2321: Intermittent double-prefetch for conditional chains. Symptom: elevated upstream latency and duplicate KV reads. Mitigation: disable prefetch by setting prefetch_confidence_threshold to 0.9 for affected chain.
- CHAIN-2456: Slot reservation can starve small-batch tails under extreme node pressure. Symptom: increased rejection metric admission.slot_reservation_reject_count. Mitigation: reduce slot_reservations or enable opportunistic mode.
- CHAIN-2510: Tracing overhead at 100% span sampling increases measured interlink gap by ~8–12ms. Symptom: observed increase in chain latencies during full-trace captures. Mitigation: use 10% long-span sampling with synthetic replay for detailed kernel probes.

Runbook: p95 chain latency degradation
1) Triage
   - Check chain.latency.p95 and per-link histograms for the last 30m. Identify whether the p95 shift is isolated to a single link or distributed.
2) If single-link kernel regression
   - Open kernel perf ticket and roll kernel variant to previous stable using the kernel rollback playbook.
3) If interlink gap increase
   - Inspect admission.slot_reservation_reject_count and kernel.batch.size distributions. Temporarily enable reserved mode with slot_reservations=1 for the chain and measure impact.
4) If due to cold KV cache
   - Trigger a controlled warmup using the synthetic replay harness in warmup-only mode: 
     ./bench/replay --trace=checkout_v2.trace --warmup-only --repeat=500
5) Communication
   - Post an incident note on #runtime-alerts and notify owners: runtime-performance@redwood.com. Include the annotated per-link trace and recent commit IDs.

Operational ownership and contacts
- Primary owner: runtime-performance (team alias)
- Kernel lead: Marcus Chen
- Profiling/benchmarks steward: Priya Desai
- Oncall escalation: eng-sre rota (follow oncall directory)

Appendix: quick command reference
- Export chain trace: ./tools/trace-export --service=ingress --filter=chain_id:<chain> --out=<name>.trace
- Microprofile link: ./bench/replay --trace=<trace> --link=<n> --annotate-kernel --concurrency=<n>
- Full chain replay with shaping: ./bench/replay --trace=<trace> --shaping='<k=v;...>' --duration=600s
- Warmup replay: ./bench/replay --trace=<trace> --warmup-only --repeat=<n>

Related pages
- runtime-architecture/execution-stitching-and-fallback-orchestration-2026 (for fallback policy interaction)
- kernel-and-scheduling/slot-reservation-protocol-and-deferred-warmstart-manual-2026 (reservation economics)
- profiling-playbook/kv-prefetch-audit-and-experiment-guide-2026 (prefetch tuning)

Document change log
- 2025-09-10: Created by Elena Alvarez.
- 2026-01-18: Added slot reservation best-practices and SLO matrix examples (reviewer: Marcus Chen).
- 2026-03-01: Documented CHAIN-2510 tracing overhead observation and updated runbook steps.

title: Predictive Bundling & SLA Credit Algorithm Playbook
content:
Overview:

This playbook defines the predictive bundling model and SLA crediting algorithm used to (1) recommend bundled credit products for tenants, (2) apply automated SLA credits when latency or availability SLOs are missed, and (3) simulate the downstream financial impact of different bundling strategies. The goal is to enable predictable customer billing while preserving fairness and operational incentives across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployment modes.

Key objectives:
- Provide a transparent, auditable algorithm for SLA credit calculations tied to measurable telemetry signals.
- Surface predictive bundle recommendations that balance expected token consumption, latency SLOs, and cost-to-serve.
- Offer a simulation harness (offline and lightweight online mode) to estimate revenue and credit exposure before packaging changes.

Scope:
- Applies to all Hosted API customers and Dedicated plans that opt-in to usage-bundles. Private deployments may use the same algorithm as a reference but must explicitly opt into centralized billing behavior.
- Covers per-route and per-tenant SLOs for latency (p50/p95/p99) and availability (error budget burn).
- Excludes paper credits/goodwill adjustments which remain a manual CS workflow.

Definitions and primitives:
- Unit: a billing unit equivalent to 1,000 embedding tokens or 1,000 generation tokens depending on product SKU.
- Bundle: named package with N units + SLO promise (e.g., "Baseline-50k-20ms") and an associated monthly price and credit terms.
- Credit pool: per-tenant ledger where automatically applied SLA credits are deposited and visible on invoices.
- Exposure: estimated future credit liability (USD) under current observed SLO miss rates.

Algorithm overview (high-level):
1) Consumption forecast: estimate next-period token usage per tenant using exponential smoothing + feature adjustments (seasonality, recent growth spikes, marketing campaigns).
2) Cost projection: map forecasted consumption to expected cost-to-serve using model variant and quantization profile mapping (SKU->cost-per-unit matrix).
3) Bundle scoring: for candidate bundles compute a score = utility(consumption_coverage, cost_savings, latency_hedge) - risk(exposure, SLA-violation-rate).
4) SLA credit mechanism: when observed SLOs in a billing window fall below threshold, compute credit = min(max_credit_cap, severity_weight * usage_fraction * bundle_price).
5) Simulation: run monte-carlo scenarios for the next 12 billing windows and produce an expected credit liability distribution.

Telemetry inputs and sources:
- Primary signals: route latency histograms (p50/p95/p99), 5xx/4xx rates, sustained error budget burn (30-day), token counts by sku and route, model variant mapping, quantization profile labels.
- Data sources: Console telemetry: /metrics/latency-hist, /metrics/error-rate, billing ingestion: /billing/token-usage, runtime mapping: /service/variant-map.

Config table (algorithm knobs):
| config_key | description | default | allowed_values | owner |
|------------|-------------|---------|----------------|-------|
| forecast.window_days | lookback window for consumption forecast | 28 | 7-90 | product-data |
| forecast.alpha | smoothing factor for exponential smoothing | 0.25 | 0.01-0.5 | product-data |
| bundle.max_credit_ratio | max fraction of bundle price that can be auto-credited per billing period | 0.2 | 0.0-1.0 | pricing |
| sla.p95_threshold_ms | maximum p95 latency allowed for covered routes | 200 | 50-2000 | runtime-product |
| risk.exposure_decay_days | window over which past SLA misses decay for exposure calc | 90 | 30-365 | finance |
| scoring.weight_latency | relative importance of latency hedge in bundle score | 1.0 | 0.0-3.0 | product |
| scoring.weight_cost_savings | relative importance of cost savings in bundle score | 1.0 | 0.0-3.0 | product |
| simulation.scenario_count | monte-carlo scenario count | 2000 | 100-10000 | product-data |

SLA credit formula (detailed):
- Inputs: observed_miss_rate (fraction of requests in billing window that exceeded threshold), average_usage_in_window (units), bundle_price, severity_factor (0.5/1.0/1.5 for minor/major/critical).
- Raw credit = observed_miss_rate * average_usage_in_window * (bundle_price / bundle_capacity_units) * severity_factor.
- Credit applied = min(Raw credit, bundle_price * bundle.max_credit_ratio, tenant.credit_pool_balance + manual_adjustment_cap).
- Example: tenant T on a 50k-unit bundle at $12/month, observed_miss_rate = 0.06 over the month, average_usage_in_window = 30k units, severity_factor=1.0 => Raw credit = 0.06 * 30k * (12/50k) = $0.0432 * 30k? (See worked example below.)

Worked numeric example (simplified):
- Bundle: 50,000 units, price = $12/month. bundle_price per unit = $12 / 50,000 = $0.00024/unit.
- Tenant usage in window: 30,000 units. observed_miss_rate = 6% (0.06). severity_factor = 1.0.
- Raw credit = 0.06 * 30,000 * 0.00024 = 0.06 * 7.2 = $0.432.
- Assuming bundle.max_credit_ratio = 0.2 => max_credit = $12 * 0.2 = $2.40. Applied credit = min(0.432, 2.40) = $0.432.

Rollout and operational runbook (step-by-step):
1) Staging validation (product-data): run the prediction and simulation harness against last 12 months for a representative tenant cohort (20 tenants spanning small/medium/large). Validate prediction MAPE < 20% on usage and exposure estimate within 15% of observed credit payouts.
2) Canary pricing experiment (growth): publish opt-in bundles to 5% of newly onboarded tenants for one billing cycle. Monitor: credit payouts, change in churn intent, average ticket volume to CS.
3) Production enablement (pricing + finance): enable predictive bundling recommendation in Console for all self-serve tenants. Provide opt-out toggle.
4) Auto-credit enforcement (billing): enable automatic SLA crediting for bundles for tenants who explicitly accept terms. For those who do not accept, flag credits as "pending" for manual CS review.
5) Post-launch audits (quarterly): finance and audit run reconciliation comparing simulated exposure to realized credits and adjust scoring knobs if divergence > 20%.

Monitoring and success criteria:
- Primary metrics: monthly auto-credit payout (USD), credit frequency (percent of subscriptions receiving >0 credit), MAPE of consumption forecast, change in average per-unit realized price.
- SLOs for the algorithm: forecast_mape < 25% (target), applied_credit_false_positive_rate < 1% (customers disputing automatic credits), model_stability (no >10% score swings week-to-week for identical inputs).

Audit and dispute process:
- All automatic credits must generate a structured invoice line item and an audit record in /audits/sla-credits with keys: tenant_id, window_start, window_end, raw_credit_calc, applied_credit, reason_code, operator_override (if any).
- Disputes: CS agent receives an automated ticket if customer disputes > $5 or requests an explanation. The ticket must include the Monte-Carlo scenario snapshot for the billing window and the raw telemetry used for the calculation.

Implementation notes and pseudo-code snippet:
```
# Simplified pseudo-code for monthly credit calc
for tenant in billing_window.tenants:
  forecast = Forecast(tenant.usage_history, window=forecast.window_days, alpha=forecast.alpha)
  bundle = RecommendBundle(forecast, tenant.route_profile, scoring_weights)
  observed_miss_rate = ComputeMissRate(tenant.latency_histograms, sla.p95_threshold_ms)
  raw_credit = observed_miss_rate * tenant.avg_usage * (bundle.price / bundle.capacity_units) * SeverityFactor(tenant.incident_severity)
  applied_credit = min(raw_credit, bundle.price * bundle.max_credit_ratio)
  AuditLog(tenant, raw_credit, applied_credit, bundle.id)
  if tenant.accepts_auto_credit:
    ApplyCreditToInvoice(tenant, applied_credit)
  else:
    CreatePendingCredit(tenant, applied_credit)
```

Security and compliance considerations:
- Credit computation and simulated exposures are financial artifacts. Access to the simulation harness results and raw telemetry must be RBAC-controlled (roles: pricing-analyst, finance-auditor, cs-manager).
- Logs used for audits must be retained for 2 years to satisfy revenue recognition and potential disputes.

Open questions and future work:
- Should we allow negative credits (upsell penalties) when usage exceeds forecast by >200% and latency remains within SLO? (Finance requested a guardrail discussion.)
- Integrate model-based anomaly detection to tag consumption spikes that are non-billable (testing, bot traffic).
- Evaluate replacing exponential smoothing with a hierarchical time-series model for large enterprise tenants.

Ownership and contacts:
- Product: Nina Rao (playbook owner)
- Product-data / Forecasting: Lukas Meyer
- Pricing and Finance: Priya Desai
- Runtime / Telemetry: Marcus Lin
- Customer Success escalation: Talia Brooks

Appendices:
- Appendix A: Timeline for rollout (Gantt summary)
  - Week 0-4: Data integration and simulation validation
  - Week 5-8: Canary experiment with opt-in tenants
  - Week 9-12: Console UI exposure and opt-out paths
  - Week 13: Production enablement and audit window

- Appendix B: Simulation output sample (CSV columns): tenant_id, scenario_id, month, simulated_credit_usd, percentile(5/50/95), forecast_units, observed_miss_rate

- Appendix C: References and related pages
  - Pricing playbooks and previous bundles: /confluence/product-docs/pricing-and-packaging/preemptible-capacity-crediting-guidelines-2026-07-19
  - Consumption simulation toolkit: /confluence/eng-platform/systems-and-services/consumption-sim-harness

If you plan to implement changes to knobs in the live system, create a PR against infra-configs and include a simulation snapshot comparing baseline vs proposed within the PR description.

title: observability-driven-onboarding-runbook
content:
Overview

Purpose:
This runbook defines an observability-first approach to enterprise onboarding for Redwood Inference customers. It standardizes the telemetry contract, synthetic acceptance checks, escalation paths, and QBR handoff artifacts used during a customer go-live and the first 90 days of production.

Scope:
- Applies to Dedicated and Private deployments and to Hosted customers with enterprise SLAs.
- Covers telemetry-onboarding, pre-cutover validation, day-0 to day-14 stabilization, and QBR handoff.

Owners and Primary Contacts
- Customer Success (owner): Maya Chen (maya.chen@redwood.com)
- SRE / Platform escalation: Arjun Patel (arjun.patel@redwood.com)
- Serving Runtime SME: Sofia Martinez (sofia.martinez@redwood.com)
- Account Executive (commercial): Liam O'Connor (liam.oconnor@redwood.com)

Acceptance gates (must pass before route to production)
1) Telemetry contract validation (required)
   - Metrics: request_count, request_latency_ms_p50/p95/p99, token_consumption_total, kvcache_hit_ratio, active_connections_by_tenant
   - Traces: 95% of generation requests produce a trace with span for model-select and runtime-exec
   - Logs: structured request_id on all runtime logs with severity mapping (INFO/WARN/ERROR)

2) Synthetic scenario pass (3 independent runs)
   - Latency synthetic: 95th percentile end-to-end generation under 2.5s for the workload profile
   - Accuracy synthetic: pre-agreed prompt set map-of-outputs >= customer baseline (see "synthetic-prompt-set" artifact)
   - Failover synthetic: simulate a model-variant fallback and verify successful completion within 3s of fallback trigger

3) Cost and quota sanity check
   - Token burn projection for first 30 days within agreed threshold +/- 30%
   - Adaptive-rate-limiter integrated and returning 429s with observability tags when saturating

Telemetry contract: implementation checklist
- Instrumentation owners must ensure metrics emit at the tenant/request granularity. Required labels: tenant_id, region, model_name, route
- Preferred exporters: Prometheus (metrics), OpenTelemetry (traces), JSONL to S3 for long-term logs.
- Retention: 90d metrics, 30d traces, 365d logs (customer may opt for shorter).

Prometheus example queries (copy into onboarding dashboard)
- Total requests by tenant (30m): rate(request_count{tenant_id=~"TENANT_ID.*"}[30m])
- 95th percentile latency (10m): histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_latency_bucket[10m])) by (le))
- KV cache hit ratio: sum(rate(kvcache_hit_total[5m])) by (tenant_id) / sum(rate(kvcache_lookup_total[5m])) by (tenant_id)

Synthetic health checks and dashboard layout
- Dashboard sections: Overview, Latency & Throughput, Token Economics, Failure Modes, Instance Health, Rollout & Canary Status
- Widgets to include: p50/p95/p99 latency heatmap, request rate by tenant, token burn by route, cache hit ratio trend, recent errors table (parsed with error codes), live traces sample panel

Pre-cutover procedure (Day -3 to 0)
1) Day -3: Telemetry smoke test
   - Verify data arriving in Grafana and alerting pipeline.
   - Run the baseline synthetic suite; document results in the onboarding ticket.
2) Day -2: Load profile run
   - Ramp to expected steady-state TPS for 30 minutes, then peak to 2x for 15 minutes.
   - Confirm autoscaling/queueing behaves as expected, confirm no token anomalies.
3) Day -1: Canary rollout
   - 1% of traffic routed to the new tenant config. Monitor the canary for 60 minutes.
   - Check for errors, latency, and cost deltas. If any SLO breach detected, abort and roll back.
4) Day 0: Full cutover
   - Schedule 60 minute maintenance window. Notify stakeholders (email template provided below).
   - Enable full route, run post-cutover synthetic suite after 15 minutes, and validate telemetry contract.

Stability operations (Day 0–14)
- Daily cadence: 09:30 PST standup (CS + SRE + Runtime) for first 7 days, then every-other-day till day 14.
- Check list for standup:
  - Any SLO alerts fired in last 24h? (yes/no, link to alerts)
  - Token burn variance > 20%?
  - Customer reported LLM output quality regressions?
  - Any escalations initiated?

Escalation matrix and SLAs
- P1: Production-wide outage for customer's tenant (affects > 90% requests)
   - First response: SRE on-call (15m), followed by CS lead (30m)
   - Escalation: Paging to Engineering runtime leads at 60m, exec-brief within 2h
- P2: Severe degradation (p95 > target or error rate > 5%) for a single route
   - First response: CS + SRE (30m), resolution target 4h
- P3: Functional bug with workaround (non-blocking)
   - Response: Assigned support engineer within 8 business hours

Escalation contact table (use internal contact channel first, then email if needed):
- SRE on-call: PagerDuty roster (use paging code "RI-SRE-CUST")
- Platform lead: arjun.patel@redwood.com
- Runtime SME: sofia.martinez@redwood.com
- CS Lead: maya.chen@redwood.com

Communication and customer comms templates
- Pre-cutover notification (email):
  Subject: [Redwood] Scheduled go-live window for <tenant_name> on <date>
  Body: Short summary, expected window, primary contacts, rollback criteria, monitoring link (dashboard URL).

- Incident update template (customer-facing):
  1) What happened (concise)
  2) Impacted customers/tenants
  3) Mitigation steps taken
  4) ETA for resolution or next update

Rollback and safe-fail procedures
- Automatic rollback trigger conditions (examples):
  - p95 latency increase > 2x baseline for > 10 minutes
  - error rate > 5% sustained for > 5 minutes
  - token burn projection exceeds agreed cap by > 50% within next 24 hours
- Rollback steps:
  1) Use routing control to switch traffic back to previous deployment (CLI example):
     redwood route set --tenant <TENANT_ID> --route <ROUTE> --target previous
  2) Re-enable canary at 5% and rerun synthetic
  3) Open a post-rollback ticket and schedule a root-cause analysis (RCA) meeting

Postmortem and RCA handoff criteria
- Trigger an RCA when any of the following occur:
  - P1 incident
  - P2 incident that required > 4 hours to resolve
  - Any customer quiet-go-live rollback within first 14 days
- RCA ownership: SRE + Runtime + CS representative. Deliverable: written RCA (timeline, root cause, corrective actions) within 5 business days.

QBR handoff and artifacts (first QBR after go-live)
- Dashboard snapshot exported with:
  - Latency/Throughput trends since go-live
  - Token economics and cost delta vs projection
  - Error and degradation timeline with RCA links
  - Synthetic suite pass/fail history and prompt-set differences
- Customer Success playbook for the QBR:
  1) Review contract SLOs and whether we met them
  2) Share operational highlights and any outstanding risks
  3) Agree on quality/regression plan (if any)

Runbook annexes (copy into onboarding folder)
- Synthetic prompt set template: synthetic-prompt-set-v1.json
- Grafana dashboard JSON: onboarding-dashboard-template.json
- Prometheus alert rules: onboarding-alerts-rules.yml

Troubleshooting checklist (quick steps during an incident)
1) Identify affected tenants and routes: run request_count PromQL filter by tenant_id.
2) Check instance health and oom/killed events on nodes serving tenant.
3) Inspect traces to find whether slowdown occurred in model selection or runtime execution.
4) If KV cache hit ratio dropped significantly, flush affected prefix cache and monitor.
5) If error codes 5xx dominate, scale burst pool or reroute to fallback variant.

FAQ
- Q: What if synthetic checks pass but customers report poor output quality?
  A: Open a quality triage ticket and escalate to Applied ML; attach failing prompts and model version. Consider A/B rolling back to prior model variant.

References and links
- Onboarding dashboard template: //grafana.redwood/internal/dashboards/onboarding-dashboard-template
- Telemetry contract spec (internal): /confluence/eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/telemetry-contract-spec
- Canary playbook: /confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/canary-rollout-playbook

Revision history
- 2026-11-02: Created by Maya Chen
- 2027-01-12: Added synthetic failover scenario (reviewer Sofia Martinez)
- 2027-02-14: Added PromQL examples and expanded escalation matrix (reviewers Arjun Patel, Liam O'Connor)

title: Cohort Traffic Sculpting Lab Manual
content:
Overview

This manual describes the lab protocol for "cohort traffic sculpting" — a reproducible experiment set used to measure how the serving runtime (kernel scheduler, KV cache, and fallback routing) behaves when we apply controlled traffic perturbations across named cohorts. The goal is to produce deterministic signals for scheduler tuning, fidelity transitions, and fallback policies before making config changes in production.

Goals
- Produce repeatable performance and quality deltas for: latency P50/P95/P99, token throughput, kernel switch frequency, KV cache hit-rate per-cohort, and request-level quality (BLEU/embedding-similarity or domain-specific evals).
- Validate scheduler heuristics (priority decay, preemption thresholds) against realistic mixed workloads.
- Exercise fidelity transitions: quantization fallback, model swap, and degraded-routing modes.
- Provide a signed-off experiment matrix and a playbook for rolling safe runtime changes.

Scope and audience
- Audience: runtime engineers, performance SREs, and applied ML teams onboarding model variants.
- Scope: lab-run on the sandbox cluster (dev-fleet or sandbox-accelerator pool). DO NOT run these experiments directly on production clusters.

Prerequisites
1) Access: membership in group "runtime-lab" and SSH access to sandbox bastion.
2) Environment: sandbox GPU pool with at least 6 nodes of heterogeneous capacity (2x A100-40GB + 4x A10).
3) Artifacts: model bundles for three fidelity variants (full_fp16, int8_q, small_embed_quant) uploaded to /artifacts/lab/2026/cohort-sculpt.
4) Simulator: the operational workload simulator (owsim) installed at /opt/owsim/owsim-cli v0.9.1 or later.
5) Metrics: temporary Grafana board "lab/cohort-sculpt" and Prometheus scrape job for sandbox.

Experiment matrix
- Cohorts: baseline, premium, dev. Each cohort has a named traffic profile and SLA target.
- Shapes: steady, spike-10m, ramp-1h, bursty-5x.
- Fidelity transitions: off (no fallback), graceful (quantization fallback), aggressive (model swap to smaller variant).
- Scheduler knobs: preemption_threshold = [0.65, 0.8, 0.95], priority_decay_window = [30s, 120s, 600s].

Run each combination for 30 minutes (warmup 5m + measure 25m). For matrix coverage prioritize (premium -> baseline -> dev) ordering so premium path is warmed first.

Experiment config example (owsim YAML)
```yaml
version: 1
experiment_name: cohort-sculpt-ramp-2026-03
cohorts:
  - name: premium
    rate_qps: 120
    shape: ramp-1h
    token_length_dist: {p10:8, p50:32, p90:256}
    policy: {priority: 100, fallback: graceful}
  - name: baseline
    rate_qps: 60
    shape: steady
    token_length_dist: {p10:4, p50:16, p90:64}
    policy: {priority: 60, fallback: off}
  - name: dev
    rate_qps: 8
    shape: bursty-5x
    token_length_dist: {p10:2, p50:8, p90:32}
    policy: {priority: 10, fallback: aggressive}
scheduler_overrides:
  preemption_threshold: 0.8
  priority_decay_window_s: 120
metrics:
  - name: latency_p95
  - name: kv_hit_rate
  - name: kernel_switch_rate
  - name: model_swap_count
output: /tmp/owsim-results/cohort-sculpt-ramp-2026-03
```

Important configuration table (recommended lab defaults)

| Setting | Lab default | Description |
|---|---:|---|
| preemption_threshold | 0.8 | Fraction of kernel time at which preemption is permitted |
| priority_decay_window_s | 120 | How long strong priorities persist |
| kv_prefetch_enabled | true | Whether async KV prefetch hints are honored |
| cache_warmup_seconds | 300 | Warmup period for KV cache measurement |
| fidelity_transition_mode | graceful | Controls rollback/quality-first vs cost-first |

Runbook: executing a lab run
1) Prepare lab cluster: ensure node labeling for sandbox (kubectl label nodes --selector=pool=sandbox run=owsim).
2) Upload experiment artifacts and config to /tmp and validate checksums: sha256sum artifacts/* | tee checksums.txt.
3) Start the Prometheus scrape and Grafana board (scripts/lab/start-metrics.sh).
4) Start owsim: /opt/owsim/owsim-cli run --config config.yaml --dry-run to validate.
5) Execute with real run: /opt/owsim/owsim-cli run --config config.yaml --output /tmp/out --concurrency 4 &> /tmp/owsim.log &
6) Monitor: open Grafana "lab/cohort-sculpt" and Loki logs for owsim and runtime-exporter. Verify no node OOMs or GPU thermal events.
7) During run: capture kernel traces (trace-capture -o /tmp/trace-$(date +%s).pcap -t 1800) and scheduler debug snapshots via endpoint /debug/scheduler/snapshot.
8) Post-run: run analysis script scripts/lab/aggregate_metrics.py /tmp/out -> /tmp/analysis.json and upload to artifact store (gs://redwood-lab/experiments/).

Acceptance criteria and pass/fail rules
- Pass if for premium cohort: latency_p95 <= 200ms, kv_hit_rate >= 0.72, kernel_switch_rate <= 0.05 switches/sec per-kernel, model_swap_count == expected for fidelity policy.
- Fail if any node reports GPU memory > 92% for > 60s, or if scheduler enters preemption storm (>= 50 preemptions/min across cluster).
- Quality regression threshold: if reference eval on sample payloads shows > 2.5% drop in similarity metric for premium cohort relative to baseline model, mark as failed for rollout.

Telemetry and dashboards
- Provided Grafana panels: cohort_p95_by_priority, kv_hit_rate_by_cohort, kernel_switch_rate_heatmap, model_swap_timeline, per-node_gpu_memory.
- Tags to include in traces: experiment_id, cohort, request_priority, fidelity_variant, kernel_id. Ensure trace sampling rate is 100% for premium cohort during lab runs.

Troubleshooting and common failure modes
- Symptom: elevated kernel_switch_rate with small request sizes. Remediation: increase preemption_threshold by +0.1 and re-run a 10m smoke test.
- Symptom: KV hit-rate low for premium despite warmup. Remediation: verify session affinity and check prefix cache key construction; run tools/lab/kv-key-audit.py.
- Symptom: model_swap_count unexpected (too frequent). Remediation: check model health probes and disable aggressive fallback for a canary. Also examine runtime logs for version mismatch errors.

Safety and rollback guidance
- Never apply lab-derived scheduler changes straight to prod. Use the dedicated canary cluster flow: 1) apply to canary pool (10% traffic), 2) monitor 6 hours, 3) escalate to prod only after 3 successful canary windows. Document canary IDs and feature flags in the release ticket.

Ownership and contacts
- Lab owner: Aisha Patel (runtime experiments). Pager: #runtime-lab on Slack.
- Scheduler SME: Marcus Liu (kernel team).
- SRE contact: Sofia Ortega.

Appendix: sample commands and scripts
- Start a minimal smoke run:
  /opt/owsim/owsim-cli run --config smoke-config.yaml --output /tmp/smoke --duration 600

- Capture scheduler snapshot curl:
  curl -sS "http://runtime-sandbox:8080/debug/scheduler/snapshot" -H "X-Experiment-ID: sclpt-2026" > /tmp/snapshot.json

- Aggregate example (Python):
  python3 scripts/lab/aggregate_metrics.py /tmp/out --output /tmp/summary.json

Appendix B: expected artifact layout
/tmp/owsim-results/cohort-sculpt-ramp-2026-03/
  - run-001/ (raw traces and owsim output)
  - analysis.json (aggregated metrics)
  - scheduler_snapshots/
  - traces/

Related reading and links
- See also: Operational Workload Simulator guide (../benchmarking-and-perf-suite/operational-workload-simulator-and-signature-guide-2026)
- See scheduler observability contract (../kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-observability-contract-and-simulated-injector-2026)

Document change history
- 2025-11-12: initial draft by Aisha Patel.
- 2026-02-09: added acceptance criteria and runbook commands (review: Marcus Liu).
- 2026-03-02: updated lab defaults and example configs after sandbox infra changes (review: Sofia Ortega).

If you plan to run a long experiment that could affect shared sandbox capacity, please coordinate with #runtime-lab at least 48 hours in advance.

title: Runtime workload classifier and safety catalog
content:
Overview

This document defines the runtime workload classifier used by the serving runtime, catalogs safety-related workload types, and provides operational guidance for classifier changes, profiling, and benchmark integration. The classifier is the central input to: scheduler profiles, kernel selection hints, KV cache policies, batching windows, and quality-of-service (QoS) safety gates.

Scope
- Applies to hosted, dedicated and private chains of the runtime orchestration layer.
- Covers classifier taxonomy, schema for rules, rollout and canary testing, telemetry contracts, and runbook actions for misclassification incidents.
- Does NOT define model-level safety filters (those live in product filter pipelines); this is focused on runtime routing and fidelity safety.

Motivation
- Workloads present radically different cost/latency/fidelity trade-offs. A small mismatch (e.g., treating streaming responses as short interactive) increases tail latency and kernel contention.
- Explicitly declaring workload intent lets the scheduler / kernel mapper apply conservative or aggressive strategies while preserving SLOs and safety margins.

Classifier design principles
1. Deterministic, signal-first: classification must be derivable from request metadata and the first N tokens (N configurable); avoid reliance on model outputs.
2. Minimal changes to call paths: low-latency decision. The classifier runs inline in the ingress path or in the pre-routing sidecar for Private deployments.
3. Observable: emit classification events with version and feature flags to enable backfill analysis.
4. Safe defaults: unknown/ambiguous requests map to the most conservative profile.

Taxonomy (canonical classes)
| class_key | description | primary SLO | batch_target | kernel_hint | kv_cache_hint | typical examples |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|---|---|
| interactive-short | Single-turn, latency-critical (<200ms token) | P50 10ms / P99 120ms | 1-4 | fast-attn, tensor-core | warm | chat replies, completions from short prompts |
| streaming-long | Long streamed generations (>512 tokens expected) | sustained throughput  >=  token/sec target | 8-32 | streaming-optimized | strong-prefetch | audio transcription continuation, longform generation |
| embeddings-bulk | Offline or batch embedding jobs | throughput cost target | 64-1024 | vector-batch-kernel | n/a | dataset embedding jobs, periodic reindexing |
| rerank-latent | Short prompt, multi-candidate scoring | low-latency scoring | 4-16 | dense-matrix | cold | search reranking requests |
| multimodal-sync | Image+text interactive | interactive SLO / extra memory | 1-2 | mixed-precision | strong | vision QA, OCR + prompt |
| high-memory | Large context / long sequence buffers | P99 memory usage guard | 1-2 | memory-friendly | pin | document summarization w/ 100k tokens |
| regulated-sensitive | Data flagged as regulated (PII/PHI) | additional audit logging + KMS | conservative latency targets | conservative-kernel | disabled (no cache) | medical notes, SSNs |
| batch-notime | Best-effort, latency-insensitive background jobs | cost-minimize | 256+ | low-precision | disabled | nightly cleanup, offline scoring |

Classifier schema
- classifier_version: string (semver)
- rules: ordered list evaluated top-to-bottom
- rule: {id, predicates[], assign_class, confidence_threshold, metadata_hints}  # expressed as YAML/JSON in repo

Example rule (YAML):
```yaml
classifier_version: "1.3.0"
rules:
  - id: "regulated-header"
    predicates:
      - header_exists: "X-Customer-Regulated"
      - header_value: "true"
    assign_class: "regulated-sensitive"
    confidence_threshold: 0.95
    metadata_hints:
      kernel_hint: "conservative-kernel"
      kv_cache: "disabled"
  - id: "short-interactive-by-length"
    predicates:
      - estimated_tokens: "<64"
      - content_type: "text"
    assign_class: "interactive-short"
    confidence_threshold: 0.8
```

Runtime implementation notes
- Where: ingress proxy (hosted) or pre-routing sidecar (Private). The classifier is implemented as a small Go microservice (classifierd) with a 3ms median execution time under common rulesets.
- Caching: classifier decisions are cached per-session id for 5 minutes by default.
- Versioning: each decision emits header X-Runtime-Class:v=<version>|class=<class_key>. The header is read by downstream router and scheduler.

Telemetry contract
Emit the following events at INFO sampling 100% for canaries, 1% for production by default (configurable per tenant):
- runtime.classify.request (fields: request_id, class_key, classifier_version, decision_latency_ms, source, rule_id)
- runtime.classify.fallback (fields: request_id, fallback_reason, original_signals)
- runtime.classify.change (fields: old_class, new_class, diff_reason)

Profiling and benchmark integration
- Unit: every classifier change must have a microbenchmark that measures classifier latency and memory under representative rulesets. Use the benchmark harness: bin/classifier-bench --rules tests/rules/synthetic-large.yaml --qps 500 --concurrency 128.
- End-to-end: run standardized workload replays labelled with ground-truth: scripts/bench/run-replay --trace labelled-replay.json --compare baseline-release. Measure downstream P50/P95/P99 latency, kernel dispatches per second, and KV cache hit rate per-class.
- Experimental: for any rule that changes kernel_hint or batch_target, run the "Kernel Hint Validation" protocol (see Checklist).

Kernel Hint Validation checklist (numbered procedure)
1. Add the rule to a staging ruleset (classifier_version X.Y.Z+staging).
2. Deploy staging classifier to a small fraction (5%) of traffic or a dedicated shadow fleet.
3. Run the Kernel Hint Validation benchmark for 30 minutes: scripts/bench/kernel-hint-validate --class NAME --duration 1800s.
4. Compare baseline kernel utilization, tail latency, and throughput for the class. If P99 degrades >20% for the class or sibling classes, abort.
5. If safe, proceed to 25% traffic for 2 hours, then gradual ramp with automated SLO gates.

Operational runbook: misclassification incident
Trigger: sudden spike in runtime.classify.fallback, or increase in P99 for a class with no config changes.
Immediate steps:
1. Pager: owning runtime oncall (page).
2. Short-term mitigation: flip classifier to previous stable version (classifierd supports quick rollback: curl -XPOST http://classifier-control/reload?version=1.2.4).
3. If rollback not available, apply an emergency whitelist rule that routes to conservative class:
   - id: emergency-conservative
     predicates: [] # match all
     assign_class: interactive-short
     confidence_threshold: 1.0
4. Capture traces for 100% of a small sample of requests using trace-mode: curl -H "X-Debug-Trace:1" ... and upload to the runtime incident bucket.
5. Post-incident: run a classification audit job to compute false-positive/false-negative rates using ground-truth replays.

Change and release process (short bullets)
- Author creates classifier rule PR in infra/classifier-rules repo. Include YAML, unit tests, and a microbenchmark.
- Reviewer checklist: semantics, telemetry hooks, kernel_hint impact, caching implications.
- Staging rollout -> Kernel Hint Validation -> Canary (5/25/50/100) with SLO gates.

Security and privacy considerations
- Regulated-sensitive class must add KMS envelope tag and disable KV caching; operators must not allow cached payloads for these classes.
- All classification logs that include payload-derived signals must be redacted for tenants flagged with PII suppression.

Operational metrics and dashboards (table-like)
| metric | owner | alerting rule | baseline | notes |
| runtime.classify.latency.p50 | runtime | > 50ms p50 | 3ms | track per-version |
| runtime.classify.latency.p99 | runtime | > 200ms p99 | 30ms | investigate rule explosion |
| runtime.classify.event.rate | runtime | drop >10% | variable | sudden drops indicate infra issues |
| kvcache.hit.rate.by_class | infra/cache | <5% for interactive-short | target 70% | misclassification causes drops |

Ownership and contacts
- Primary owner: Runtime Orchestration (team: eng-serving-runtime/runtime-ops).
- Secondary: Kernel Mapping (team: eng-serving-runtime/kernel-scheduler).
- Oncall: see /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/serving-runtime-oncall-rapid-investigation-cheatsheet-2023.

Appendix: small debugging CLI snippets
- Validate current ruleset and version: curl -sS http://classifier-control/status | jq .
- Force reload (for emergency rollback): curl -XPOST http://classifier-control/reload?version=1.2.4
- Emit a self-test sample: bin/classifier-selftest --sample-file tests/samples/regression-suite.json

Appendix: example golden trace (JSON)
```json
{
  "request_id": "req-20260203-0001",
  "classifier_version": "1.3.0",
  "class_key": "interactive-short",
  "decision_latency_ms": 2.9,
  "rule_id": "short-interactive-by-length"
}
```

Revision notes
- 2025-11-12: initial draft (Maya Patel).
- 2026-01-08: expanded telemetry contract and kernel hint validation (Jordan Li).
- 2026-02-03: added emergency runbook steps and measurements for KV cache impacts (Aria Gomez).

title: runtime-cross-cutting-investigation-cookbook
content:
Overview

This cookbook collects cross-cutting investigation patterns used by the serving runtime team when incidents, regressions, or unexpected cost/latency changes span multiple subsystems (runtime architecture, kernel scheduling, profiling, benchmarking). It is intended for oncall, incident commanders, and engineers performing post-incident diagnostics. Follow the numbered procedures first; use the lookup tables and runbook snippets as shortcuts once familiar.

Key goals
- Rapidly triage impact vs root cause (latency SLO, error surface, cost delta).
- Preserve reproducible artifacts: traces, kernel profiles, synthetic replays.
- Provide a deterministic experiment matrix for validation (benchmarks + microtraces).

Pre-flight checklist (before you start)
- Confirm SLOs impacted and timeframe (10m/1h/24h). Typical SLOs: p95 <= 180ms, p99 <= 500ms for short prompt tier; throughput SLOs: 50 reqs/s per GPU pool.
- Capture a preserved span from distributed tracing covering router -> dispatcher -> kernel layer -> GPU.
- Lock configuration state for the timeframe: scheduler policies, kernel-version, model-variant, quantization profile, admission controller settings.
- Notify stakeholders: oncall lead, runtime owner, product oncall if customer-visible.

1) Rapid impact assessment (10–20 minutes)
1.1 Gather high-level signals
- Console: per-route latency change, token-level cost deltas.
- Telemetry: compute p50/p95/p99 deltas, error-rate change, queue length and slot occupancy.
- Billing signal: per-token cost change (if available).

1.2 Quick hypothesis mapping
Use the Signal -> Likely subsystem mapping (lookup table below) to generate 1–3 initial hypotheses. Prioritize by impact and reversibility.

2) Focused evidence collection (20–60 minutes)
2.1 Traces and causal spans
- Export a 10–30 minute trace window containing both normal and degraded requests. Annotate the span with request prototype (length, model, priority).
- Query example (internal trace UI): "service=kernel AND duration>100ms AND model=~'gpt-.*' | group_by(kernel_variant, node)"

2.2 Kernel profiling snapshot
- Collect one full kernel snapshot from an affected node: kernel traces (per-invocation micro-timeline), GPU occupancy, tensor core utilization, memory high-water marks.
- Commands (operator shell):
  - curl http://node.internal:1234/debug/kernel_snapshot?since=2026-11-05T10:00:00Z -o kernel-snap.json
  - rd-prof collect --node node-42 --duration 30s --output /tmp/kernel-prof.tgz

2.3 Scheduler and admission controller logs
- Pull last 500 scheduler decisions and admission controller responses for the pool. Look for sudden credit depletion, priority inversion, or policy churn.

2.4 Reproduce with microbenchmarks
- Use the microbenchmark runner to replay representative requests (same token lengths and model variant) against a shadow pool. Run three variants: (A) current production config, (B) previous kernel version, (C) previous scheduler policy. Compare p95/p99 and tail-samples.
- Commands:
  - bench-runner --profile replay-corpus.json --pool shadow-a --iterations 200

3) Isolation matrix (experiment plan)
- Change only one variable per experiment. Record the exact state and artifacts. Example matrix rows:
  - baseline (prod config)
  - kernel-old vs kernel-new
  - scheduler-policy-A vs policy-B
  - quantization-profile (int8 vs int4)
  - admission-controller thresholds (slot-limit +/- 10%)
- Record: synthetic traffic, observed trace, kernel snapshot, scheduler log extract.

Lookup table: signal -> probable root causes -> immediate mitigations
- sudden p99 spike + stable p50: probable root causes: rare kernel slow path (tensor core fallback), intermittent GPU thermal throttling, long KV cache misses. Immediate mitigations: route to a fallback model-variant, increase warmstart slots, enable short-circuit FPGA (if available).
- uniform latency increase across fleet: probable root causes: global config change (scheduler/admission), upstream router change, network fabric regression. Immediate mitigations: roll back recent policy change, shift traffic to unaffected region.
- increase in kernel queue length + drop in throughput: probable root causes: credit exhaustion, NUMA-induced memory pressure, preemption storm. Immediate mitigations: reduce admission rate, disable opportunistic preemption, scale up slot pool.
- token-level cost spike without latency changes: probable root causes: model variant upgrade with higher per-token cost, decoding beam-width change, tokenizer mis-configuration. Immediate mitigations: pin model version, revert decoding params.

Runbook snippets (quick actions)
- Eviction / warmstart play (fast, reversible)
  1) Identify hot nodes: telemetry shows >90% occupancy and >100ms extra scheduling delay.
  2) Drain new high-cost tenants via router tag: curl -X POST http://router/api/drain -d '{"tenant":"X"}'
  3) Trigger warmstart on replacement nodes: rd-runtime warmstart --pool pool-A --targets 3
  4) Monitor p95 and kernel error-rate for 15 minutes.

- Scheduler rollback (config-level)
  1) Check recent config commits: git log deploys/scheduler | head -n 10
  2) Apply previous policy (immutable snapshot id): rd-config apply --policy-id p-2026-10-21
  3) Monitor admission decisions and CPU wait times.

Telemetry and observability queries (examples)
- Kernel invocation latency by variant: metrics.query("kernel.invocation.latency{variant:*,model:*}").aggregate(quantiles=[50,95,99])
- Scheduler credit burn-down: metrics.query("scheduler.credit.delta{pool:pool-A}").rollup('1m')
- Trace correlation: select trace_id from spans where service='scheduler' and tag.key='decision' and tag.value='preempt'

Benchmarking integration (when to call the bench team)
- If microbenchmarks cannot reproduce the observed tail behavior within +/-10% at the same configuration, escalate to bench team. Provide: preserved trace window, kernel snapshot, sample inputs, and experiment matrix.
- Bench team checklist: run hardware-matched synthetic replay, run metrics correlation (scheduler vs kernel), and run stress for 2x production QPS for 30m.

Decision ledger (record what you change)
- Always create a short decision artifact stored in /incidents/<id>/decision.yaml with fields: who, why, start_time, end_time, actions, rollback_plan, confidence. Example line (as text): "action: rollback-scheduler-to-p-2026-10-21; who: Aisha; start: 2026-11-05T11:03:00Z; confidence: 0.65"

Post-incident: reproducibility recipe
- Reconstruct the exact experiment using the preserved inputs and pinned binaries (kernel-image hash, scheduler-policy id).
- Run three round-trip reproductions and collect: benchmark report, kernel profile tarball, scheduler decision log, and end-to-end trace. Attach to postmortem.

Appendix: common diagnostic heuristics
- "Kernel-only" signature: per-invocation timeline shows a long window inside the GPU kernel with high tensor-core idle time and memory copy stalls.
- "Scheduler-only" signature: spikes coincide with repeated admission-controller rejects and a diverging credit-accounting curve.
- "Network/IO" signature: long wait times in dispatcher->kernel RPCs, with socket retransmits observed.

Table: artifact types and retention (text table)
- artifact_type | retention | who-keeps
- trace_window (10–60m) | 90 days | runtime-oncall
- kernel-profile (snapshot) | 30 days | infra-team
- bench-report | 365 days | perf-team

Related resources
- Runtime runbooks: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks
- Profiling playbooks: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook
- Benchmarking suite repo: git@repo:redwood/benchmarks.git

Ownership and maintenance
- Owner: runtime reliability team (oncall rotation). Review cadence: quarterly.
- How to propose changes: open PR against this document in the docs repo (docs/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki) and add at least one reviewer from bench and one from kernel-scheduling.

Contact
- For immediate escalation: oncall@redwood.com and runtime-reliability slack channel (#runtime-reliability).

title: Stochastic Eviction Simulator and Heuristic Lab Manual
content:
Summary:
This document describes the design and operational playbook for the Stochastic Eviction Simulator (SES): a lab-grade emulator used by runtime teams to validate eviction heuristics, measure fidelity impact, and generate rollout-safe parameters for the production kernel-mapper and admission controllers. SES is intended to be the primary tool for preflighting any kernel, scheduler, or fidelity-degradation change that touches eviction, cache warmup, or admission policies.

Goals:
- Provide a repeatable experiment harness for eviction policy A/B testing under realistic traffic shapes.
- Quantify fidelity vs cost tradeoffs (quality regressions per eviction aggressiveness).
- Produce risk-bounded parameter sets for kernel rollouts and autoscaler admission controllers.

Scope:
- Includes simulations of: KV cache eviction, session warmup, slot preemption, admission backpressure, and tiered-fallback routing.
- Not for: full hardware-level GPU tracing or kernel micro-benchmarks (use runtime profiling playbook for kernel traces).

Quick concepts and definitions:
1) Eviction aggressiveness: numeric 0.0–1.0 controlling willingness to evict warm KV entries or preempt active slots. Higher = lower memory usage but more fidelity risk.
2) Fidelity score: a workload-anchored metric derived from evals (token-level logprob shift + task-level metric like Rouge/ROUGE-L or E2E pass rate). Represented as percent change from baseline.
3) Stochastic seed: SES can apply random jitter to eviction decisions to emulate real-world nondeterminism; seed should be recorded in experiment metadata.

Architecture (high level):
- Traffic generator (traffic-gen): replays traffic corpus or synthesizes session traces using shape profiles (burst, steady, diurnal).
- Resource model (resource-sim): models GPU memory, KV cache shards, per-tenant quotas, NUMA zones.
- Heuristic engine (heuristic-orch): executes eviction heuristics (LRU-window, recency+priority, cost-aware eviction, stochastic-probabilistic, ML-guided scorer).
- Fidelity model (fidelity-proxy): maps eviction events to expected quality delta using precomputed mapping tables from eval runs or an ML regressor trained on historical rollouts.
- Metrics collector (ses-metrics): aggregates SLOs, fidelity deltas, throughput, and cost proxies.

How SES integrates with runtime artifacts:
- Config inputs reference production feature flags and config keys from runtime-orch (e.g., runtime-orch.eviction.policy, kernel-mapper.slot-credit). Test configs should mirror the production JSON structure.
- SES can import a lightweight snapshot of kvcache-service metadata (shard counts, hit rates) exported from a production day and then replay traffic against that snapshot.

Simulator configuration example (YAML):
---
experiment_name: "evict-ml-scorer-stochastic-v2"
seed: 12345
traffic_profile: "customer-burst-30m"
duration_minutes: 180
num_tenants: 50
kvcache:
  total_memory_gb: 480
  shard_count: 64
  baseline_hit_rate: 0.82
eviction_policy:
  type: "ml-scorer-stochastic"
  aggressiveness: 0.46
  jitter_stddev: 0.12
  lookback_window_seconds: 900
fidelity_model:
  type: "regression-v1"
  trained_on: "canary-evictions-2025-10"
---

Common heuristics catalog (table-style in-line):
- LRU-window: deterministic, low CPU, baseline for comparisons. Params: window_seconds, victim_fraction.
- Cost-aware: prefers evicting low-cost tokens (shorter KV usage). Params: token_cost_weight.
- Priority-based: tenant/application-assigned priorities, used for enterprise isolation. Params: priority_decay_half_life.
- ML-scored: model predicts future hit probability and eviction risk. Params: model_version, score_threshold.
- Stochastic-probabilistic: base_prob = f(aggressiveness, recency); introduces randomness to smooth behavior.

Experiment metrics and targets (examples):
- Tail latency (p99 request latency): target <= 150ms for RLHF-chat workloads. Alert if > 180ms.
- Average throughput: baseline tokens/sec per-GPU, reported as tps/GPU. Degradation > 10% flagged.
- Fidelity delta: median evals score drop across prompt set. Acceptable rollback threshold: > 1.0% drop triggers fail.
- Cold-hit penalty: increase in average token compute due to cache misses; target < 6% uplift.
- Memory pressure events per-hour: target = 0 for gold configs, < 3 for canary.

How to run an SES lab experiment (step-by-step):
1) Select traffic corpus: pick one of {customer-burst-30m, steady-8h, mixed-diurnal-24h, stress-10x}.
2) Pick baseline: export current production config from runtime-orch and set as baseline_config in the YAML.
3) Choose eviction policies: include baseline and 1–3 candidate heuristics.
4) Run SES in multi-actor mode: ./ses run --config path/to/experiment.yaml --output-dir /tmp/ses-output/exp1
5) Sanity-check results: ./ses summarize /tmp/ses-output/exp1/ --metrics p99,throughput,fidelity_delta
6) If fidelity_delta > 0.5% but latency improves > 8%, schedule a focused eval run with the actual model on a held-out prompt set (see "Validation gating").

Validation gating (before production rollout):
- Must pass: fidelity_delta <= 1.0% AND p99 latency <= baseline + 10ms OR throughput improvement >= 7%.
- Must not: memory pressure events per node > 2 in a simulated 6-hour run.
- Secondary check: run a 2-node hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) smoke test with kvcache-service snapshots to validate non-linear cache effects.

Output artifacts produced by SES:
- per-tenant metric CSV: {tenant_id,timestamp,p99,throughput,fidelity_delta,mem_pressure_count}
- heatmap PNG of eviction incidence across shards and time
- simulated trace JSON lines (one event per eviction/preempt decision)
- decision log that can be loaded into runtime-devtools for replay

Rollout decision flow (how to act on SES results):
1) Blue/green parameter selection: pick candidate param set with lowest fidelity_delta under the SLO budget.
2) Canary: deploy to 1% traffic on dedicated canary pool (dedicated-capacity) with increased telemetry level.
3) Monitor: 24-hour watch for fidelity regressions, memory pressure, and p99 spikes. Use the checkpoint that records the SES seed to map back to simulated trace.
4) If canary passes, schedule staged ramp with throttles at 5%, 25%, 60%, 100% over 48–72 hours.
5) If failure at any stage, run the SES rewind harness to reproduce the incident and generate rollback patch.

Operational runbook snippets (quick actions during an experiment):
- To re-run an experiment with adjusted aggressiveness: ./ses patch --exp /tmp/ses-output/exp1 --set eviction_policy.aggressiveness=0.38 --rerun
- To extract top-k eviction keys for a shard: ./ses extract-keys --shard 12 --top 100 --out keys.txt
- To convert ses traces to runtime-devtools replay format: ./ses export --format runtime-replay --src /tmp/ses-output/exp1/trace.jsonl --dst /tmp/replay/

Table: recommended parameter bounds for candidate release profiles
Profile | aggressiveness | jitter_stddev | lookback_window_seconds | mem_pressure_tolerance
Gold    | 0.00 - 0.12   | 0.00 - 0.03   | 1800 - 7200             | 0
Stable  | 0.12 - 0.30   | 0.01 - 0.06   | 900 - 3600              | 1
Canary  | 0.30 - 0.55   | 0.05 - 0.12   | 600 - 1800              | 2
Aggressive| 0.55 - 0.95 | 0.08 - 0.20   | 300 - 900               | 3+

Troubleshooting and known limitations:
- SES approximates fidelity using regressors; it cannot catch model-architecture-sensitive regressions. Always pair with a micro-eval run against the actual model weights when fidelity_delta is close to threshold.
- NUMA and true GPU eviction ordering may yield non-deterministic hardware effects that SES models only approximately. HIL tests are required for high-risk kernels.
- SES uses a simplified network model; cross-node NVLink degradation scenarios must be profiled separately. See known-issues/nvlink-interconnect-degradation-and-remediation-2026.

Ownership and contact:
- Primary owner: runtime-performance team (owner lead: Chen Zhang).
- On-call escalation: eng-sre roster. For urgent simulator or data issues open: #runtime-simulator on Slack and tag @priya.menon.

Change log (high level):
- 2025-03-04: initial spec and prototype harness (seeded with canary traffic corpus).
- 2025-10-11: added ML-scored heuristic and fidelity regression model v1.
- 2026-01-18: formalized rollout gating and added HIL validation step.

Appendix A — Example SES output (JSON lines sample):
{"timestamp":"2026-01-18T03:22:11Z", "shard":12, "tenant_id":"T-42", "event":"evict", "key":"k_9f3a", "reason":"ml-score<0.12", "predicted_fidelity_delta":0.003}
{"timestamp":"2026-01-18T03:22:14Z", "shard":12, "tenant_id":"T-42", "event":"prefetch", "key":"k_12bb", "cost":0.0004}

Appendix B — Links and references:
- Runtime decision catalog: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/runtime-decision-graph-and-observed-behaviour-catalog-2026
- Kernel scheduler DSL: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-policy-language-declarative-profiles-2026
- Eviction rewind runbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/eviction-rewind-and-state-reconstruction-playbook-2026

If you are using SES for the first time, follow the "Getting started with SES" quickstart in the runtime-devtools repository and record the experiment metadata in the team experiment tracker (link in team wiki).

title: Runtime Execution Safety Matrix and Contraction Playbook
content:
Summary

This page defines the Runtime Execution Safety Matrix (RESM) — a prescriptive mapping from runtime signals to safe, deterministic mitigation actions — plus an operational playbook for 'execution contraction' (the controlled reduction of runtime concurrency and feature surface during incidents). RESM complements existing runbooks by codifying exact thresholds, owners, and automated vs manual actions for kernel scheduling, KV-cache, and model-variant routing subsystems.

Why this exists

- Reduce ambiguity during incidents where multiple subsystems degrade (e.g., kernel queuing + NVLink error flurries).
- Provide deterministic, tested contraction paths to preserve customer-facing SLOs while minimizing cost and blast radius.
- Standardize telemetry-to-action mappings so oncall, SRE, and runtime engineers share a single source of truth.

Scope and audience

- Audience: runtime engineers, SRE, oncall, release engineers, and incident commanders.
- Scope: serving runtime control plane, kernel scheduler, KV-cache layer, routing/fallback, and the integration points with autoscaler and Dedicated capacity. Not a replacement for low-level kernel docs — it references them.

Key concepts

1) Execution contraction

A controlled sequence of runtime state degradations designed to reduce resource pressure while preserving critical (customer-facing) traffic. Contraction is implemented by:
- narrowing concurrency windows (reduce max inflight requests per shard),
- tightening admission control (shortening queue depth),
- reducing model fidelity (switching to quantized / smaller variants),
- disabling non-critical features (structured output validation, large-context caching prefetch).

2) Safety matrix entries

Each entry maps: observable signal -> threshold -> categorical severity -> automated action -> oncall notification -> rollback condition.

Execution contracts (examples)

- Contract: "CPU-bound preemption storm"
  - Signal: kernel preemption failures (metric: kernel.preempt.fail.count)
  - Threshold: >= 20 failures / 30s on > 30% of shards
  - Severity: high
  - Automated action: apply kernel conservative mapper (priority: low), reduce concurrency target on affected shards to 40%
  - Notification: page oncall-sre@redwood (pagerduty) and post Slack #runtime-incidents
  - Rollback: kernel.preempt.fail.count < 2 / 5m AND p95 latency back within 120% of baseline

- Contract: "KV-cache storm (cold misses)"
  - Signal: kvcache.miss.rate > 0.85 for 10m AND kvcache.warmup.rate < 1.0
  - Severity: medium
  - Automated action: enable prefix-preservation mode, pause aggressive eviction heuristics, and increase prefetch window to 1.2x for identified tenant cohorts
  - Notification: post to #kvcache-observability; create triage ticket with runbook tag
  - Rollback: kvcache.miss.rate < 0.2 for 15m

Safety matrix table (text format)

| ID | Signal | Threshold | Severity | Automated Action | Owner | Metric to monitor |
|----|--------|-----------|----------|------------------|-------|------------------|
| RESM-01 | kernel.preempt.fail.count | >=20/30s on >30% shards | High | Conservative kernel mapper + concurrency reduce to 40% | kernel-team | p95_latency, kernel.preempt.fail.count |
| RESM-07 | kvcache.miss.rate | >0.85 for 10m | Medium | Prefix-preserve + pause eviction | storage-team | kvcache.miss.rate, kvcache.warmup.rate |
| RESM-12 | model.variant.switch.rate | >5/min across region | Low | Disable warm model swap; route to pinned stable variant | routing-team | model.swap.errors, route-err-rate |

Operational playbook: contraction flow (step-by-step)

1) Detect and classify
   - Automated monitors evaluate RESM entries every 30s (see monitoring rule bundles/resm-checks).
   - If an entry crosses 'automated' threshold, the automation enters a 'pre-commit' hold state for 20s to gather corroborating signals.

2) Execute minimal-impact mitigations (automated)
   - Apply the action in the Safety Matrix. Automation will:
     - run the scheduler control API: curl -X POST $SCHED_API/apply -d '{"shard": "shard-id", "concurrency_target": 0.4, "mapper_profile": "conservative"}'
     - set KV cache policy via admin cli: redwood-kvctl set-policy --shard shard-id --policy prefix-preserve --evict-pause true
   - Automation annotates rollback conditions and creates a short-lived incident (auto:RESM-<id>-auto).

3) Observe for 5–10 minutes
   - If rollup metrics improve to safe bounds, automation marks the incident resolved and records actions in incident index.
   - If still degraded or new signals appear, escalate to manual intervention.

4) Manual contraction and customer impact staging (human)
   - Oncall follows the manual contraction checklist below.
   - If customer-visible latency or error SLOs are at risk, initiate a canary traffic shift to Dedicated or fallback model region.

Manual contraction checklist (for oncall)

1. Verify correlated signals: kernel traces, NVLink errors, dispatch queue depths.
2. Lock the change window in the control plane (set change_window: locked).
3. Reduce global concurrency cap in 10% increments (max three steps). Command: redwood-runtimectl set-global-concurrency --pct 80
4. Pin critical customers to stable variants: redwood-routingctl pin --tenant-tenants=LIST --variant=stable-v1
5. Disable non-critical features: redwood-configctl toggle --feature structured-output-validation --off
6. Re-assess for 15 minutes between steps; document each action in the incident timeline.

Kernel scheduling interactions

- Priority mapping: RESM triggers may bump top-level request priorities for system-critical flows (health checks, control-plane requests). Use priority level 0 (highest) through 9 (lowest).
- Admission control: The scheduler supports dynamic queue depth per priority bucket. During contraction we prefer to reduce low-priority queue depths first.
- Cooperative preemption: On detected compute starvation, activate cooperative preemption window (default 200ms). This is a temporary measure to reduce tail latency but increases preemption overhead; used only when RESM-01 or RESM-03 active.

Profiling and instrumentation guidance

- Sampling policy: increase kernel-trace sampling from 0.5% -> 5% for affected shards during contraction. Use the profiling agent: redwood-profctl set-sampling --shard shard-id --rate 0.05
- Tag traces with RESM id: ensure every automated action attaches header X-RESM-ID: RESM-01 so traces can be filtered.
- Repro artifacts: collect a 10s GPGPU timeline, scheduler trace, and KV-cache histogram. Store under /artifacts/incidents/<incident-id>/ for postmortems.

Benchmarking matrix for contraction validation

- Validate contraction sequences on the staging bench using these controlled profiles before enabling automation:
  - Profile A: 90% short requests (<= 32 tokens), 10% long (>=1024 tokens). Target p95 latency 110% of production baseline.
  - Profile B: Mixed tenant concurrency with hotspot (10% tenants produce 60% load). Ensure eviction strategies do not thrash.
  - Failure injection: simulated NVLink flaps and kernel-preempt spikes. Automation must not raise error-rate above 0.5% for 5 minutes.

Release and rollout checklist for RESM automation

1. Unit and integration tests for each matrix entry (simulate signals and assert actions).
2. Run staged stress experiments on the bench (Profile A/B) for 48h.
3. Canary the automation to 2% of traffic for 24h with observability hooks.
4. Monitor key metrics for 72h and gather canary feedback.
5. Full rollout with 1-hour watch window and a designated rollback owner.

Operational metrics and SLOs referenced by RESM

- p95 latency (short seq): 120ms (SLO target), p99: 300ms (SLO target for hosted API).
- Error rate (5xx on inference path): <0.2% (SLA-sensitive).
- Kernel preemption failure: baseline <1 / 30s across fleet.
- KV-cache miss rate: baseline <0.15 for warmed cohorts.

Post-incident and continuous improvement

- Incident owners must attach a RESM review note to postmortems (template: RESM-review.md) capturing: why automated action triggered, what worked, false positives, and suggestions.
- Quarterly: kernel and scheduler teams run contraction drills (game days) with 1% production traffic mirrored to bench.

Appendix: sample configs and commands

- Scheduler apply (JSON payload):

  curl -X POST $SCHED_API/apply -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' -d '\n  {\n    "targets": ["shard-id-1","shard-id-2"],\n    "changes": {"concurrency_target": 0.4, "mapper_profile": "conservative"},\n    "annotation": "RESM-01 auto mitigation"\n  }'\n
- KV policy (CLI):

  redwood-kvctl set-policy --shard shard-id-1 --policy prefix-preserve --evict-pause true --note "RESM-07 auto"\n
- Profiling (increase sampling):

  redwood-profctl set-sampling --shard shard-id-1 --rate 0.05 --attach-header "X-RESM-ID:RESM-07"\n
- Example configuration table (text):

| config_key | default | RESM override | notes |
|-----------|---------|---------------|-------|
| scheduler.concurrency_global | 1.0 | 0.8,0.6,0.4 | Reduced in three steps during manual contraction |
| kvcache.eviction_aggression | 1.0 | 0.0 | Pause during prefix-preserve mode |
| profiling.sampling_rate | 0.005 | 0.05 | Increased for affected shards during investigation |
| kernel.mapper_profile | balanced | conservative | conservative reduces speculative work and preemption |

Contact and ownership

- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime (runtime-safety subgroup) — Aisha Patel (author)
- Kernel team contact: Marcus Liu
- KV/Storage contact: Priya Kannan
- Oncall escalation: see /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/oncall-rotations/ (internal link)

Change log

- 2026-01-12: Initial draft and internal review.
- 2026-02-18: Added KV-cache storm guidance and automated action payloads.
- 2026-03-01: Formalized rollback conditions and canary checklist (published).

title: Adaptive Degradation Safety & Verification Manual
content:
Summary:

This manual defines the safety contracts, verification checks, benchmarking protocols, and operational runbooks we use to validate adaptive degradation and fallback behavior in the Redwood serving runtime. It is intended for runtime engineers, SREs, and release owners who gate runtime and scheduler changes. The document consolidates architecture contracts, test harnesses, profiling playbooks, measurable acceptance criteria, and incident response steps into a single reference.

Scope:
- Covers adaptive degradation (fidelity staircases, model-variant fallback, burst shedding) and scheduler/kernel interactions.
- Includes verification checks executed in CI, pre-release staging, and canary phases.
- Prescribes profiling and benchmark procedures for SLO verification and performance regressions.
- Provides runbooks for on-call and release owners for graceful rollback and mitigation.

Principles and safety goals:
1) Observable and measurable: every degradation path must have a minimal observable signal (metrics, traces, events) and a single source-of-truth trace ID for forensic replay.
2) Fail open vs fail closed rationale: correctness-critical requests (enterprise-configured) should prefer fail-closed; non-critical/latency-sensitive requests can fail open to preserved throughput.
3) Bounded fidelity loss: fidelity steps should degrade quality predictably (quantified by eval sets) and be reversible.
4) Deterministic rollback: any automated fallback must expose a deterministic rollback path and human-confirmable guardrails.

Architecture contracts (high-level):
- Degradation tiers: primary (full model), degraded-1 (quantized), degraded-2 (short-context variant), fallback (smaller model / cached-embeddings). Each tier has an SLO budget and cost profile.
- Kernel scheduling contract: the scheduler must maintain per-request kernel affinity for the first N tokens and preserve KV cache affinity during tier transition windows (default N=16).
- Eviction and warmup contract: when a session is evicted from KV cache, a warmup window of configurable length (default 60s) is reserved to rehydrate frequently-seen prompts without degrading SLOs.

Verification matrix (summary table):
| Check ID | Purpose | Where executed | Acceptance threshold | Action on fail | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| VD-01 | End-to-end tail latency under 95th percentile SLO | CI staging + canary | p95 < 1200ms for interactive path | block release, auto-rollback in canary | runtime-sre |
| VD-02 | Kernel latency jitter for hot kernels | perf-lab | 95th/50th ratio < 3.0 | schedule throttling + revert kernel flags | runtime-kernel-team |
| VD-03 | Fidelity regression on golden prompt set | automated evals | task-specific metric delta < 1.5% | fail gating | applied-ml |
| VD-04 | KV cache hitrate during warmup | synthetic replay | hitrate > 70% after 120s | degrade to cached-response fallback | runtime-sre |
| VD-05 | Correctness of fallback routing (no request loss) | chaos lab | 0 dropped requests during routing switch | incident | runtime-oncall |

Verifiable artifacts for each check:
- Synthetic replay corpus snapshot (sha256) used in CI.
- Expected telemetry schemas (metric names, tags) and trace samples.
- Baseline benchmark outputs (binary artifacts) for diff-based gating.

CI and pre-release harnesses:
1) CI unit stage: microbenchmarks for individual kernels (latency, occupancy, memory). Thresholds are enforced as fast-fail rules.
2) Staging perf run: full-stack replay of production traffic sampled (1:1000) with degraded-tier injection. Output artifacts: histogram dumps, kernel traces, KV cache heatmaps.
3) Canary: traffic ramp with A/B model variants and automated rollback on VD-* failures. Canary policy: 1% -> 5% -> 20% over 30m windows with automated health checks every 5m.

Benchmarking protocol (detailed):
- Workloads to run:
  - Interactive short-chat (mean tokens=40, 90th=128) — target low-latency SLOs.
  - Streaming long-output (mean tokens=800) — target throughput and memory stability.
  - Embeddings burst (large batch sizes) — target batching efficiency and memory footprint.
- Metrics collected:
  - end_to_end_latency_ms (p50/p90/p95/p99), kernel_exec_time_ms per-kernel, gpu_mem_used_mb, kv_cache_hitrate_pct, tokens_per_second_per_gpu.
- Tooling & commands (examples):
  - Run synthetic replay: 
    ./perf-runner --profile=replay --corpus=sha256:abcd1234 --duration=15m --out=artifacts/replay-$(date +%s).tgz
  - Microbenchmark kernel: 
    python tools/microbench.py --kernel matmul --batch 1 --seq 128 --out json --repeat 50
  - Collect trace samples for a request: 
    curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $CI_TOKEN" https://staging.api.redwood.ai/v1/generate -d '{"prompt":"<<golden>>"}' -o /tmp/trace.json
- Acceptance criteria pattern:
  - No p95 regression > 8% vs baseline.
  - Kernel jitter (95/50) <= 3.0.
  - KV cache delta < 5% hitrate loss after warmup period.

Profiling playbook snippets (how-to):
1) Latency fingerprint collection (on perf-lab machine):
  - Start full instrumentation: export PERF_SAMPLER=on; ./runtime --enable-tracing --trace-sample-rate=0.01
  - Run workload for 10 minutes and collect traces: tar -czf traces.tgz /var/tmp/traces/*
  - Post-process: python tools/trace-aggregate.py --input traces.tgz --output traces-summary.json
2) Kernel causality mapping:
  - Use kernel-hint exporter to annotate kernels with request-id and token-index. Example PromQL to find kernel hotpaths: sum(rate(kernel_exec_time_ms_bucket[5m])) by (kernel_name)
3) Latency attribution checklist:
  - Confirm p95 skew aligns with a specific kernel or queue time via trace waterfall.
  - Check GPU utilization and eviction events within the window.
  - Validate KV cache hit/miss correlation with session affinity changes.

Runbook: Adaptive Degradation incident triage (short):
1) Detection: Alert triggers if p95 or error-rate breaches gating thresholds (see Verification matrix).
2) Initial triage (first 10 min):
  - Owner: oncall-runtime.
  - Query: run the baseline PromQL dashboards (listed below) and capture current vs baseline.
  - Commands:
    - promql: rate(request_latency_seconds_bucket[5m]) by (route)
    - runtime CLI: runtimectl list-sessions --filter=evicted=true --since=10m
3) Containment (10–30 min):
  - If caused by kernel regression: flip kernel rollout gate to previous stable tag (runtimectl kernel-set active:stable-<tag>) and pause canaries.
  - If caused by cache warmup regression: enable elevated pre-warm (config: prewarm_multiplier=2) and route new sessions to degraded-1 temporarily.
4) Remediation (30–90 min):
  - Roll back flagged config or kernel. Run perf-runner quick replay to validate.
  - If degradation persists, scale dedicated pool capacity for 15 minutes to reduce pressure and collect artifacts.
5) Post-incident verification: Ensure all VD-* checks pass in staging before re-enabling automated rollouts.

Release gating checklist (for runtime and scheduler changes):
- Code owner review and ADR reference.
- Automated CI checks: unit tests, lint, kernel microbenchmarks.
- Perf artifacts present: replay corpus, baseline histograms, and guard thresholds.
- Canary policy configured and health checks defined (list health checks and thresholds attached).
- Rollback plan and human approvers designated in the release ticket.

Instrumentation and metrics schema (quick reference):
- metric names: runtime.request.latency_ms, runtime.kernel.exec_ms, runtime.kv.hits, runtime.fidelity.tier, runtime.eviction.count
- required tags: service, model_name, model_variant, route, region, canary_id
- recommended tracing fields: request_id, session_id, token_index, kernel_name, warmup_phase

Ownership and escalation:
- Runtime architecture owner: runtime-arch@redwood.ai (primary: Sanjay Rao).
- Kernel scheduling owner: kernel-team@redwood.ai.
- Oncall rota: runtime-sre (see internal roster).
- Escalation path: oncall -> SRE lead -> runtime-arch -> Eng Director (timed escalation at 45m).

Appendices:
A) YAML example: adaptive degradation policy (example config to be applied via runtime fleet config)

  degradation_policy:
    tiers:
      - name: primary
        model_variant: v2-full
        slos:
          p95_latency_ms: 900
      - name: degraded-1
        model_variant: v2-quantized
        slos:
          p95_latency_ms: 700
      - name: degraded-2
        model_variant: v2-shortctx
        slos:
          p95_latency_ms: 350
    warmup:
      kv_cache_warmup_seconds: 120
      prewarm_multiplier: 1.5
    fallback:
      strategy: route-to-smaller-model
      max_inflight_fallback: 250

B) PromQL examples (quick):
- p95 latency for route: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(runtime_request_latency_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, route))
- kernel jitter index: (histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(kernel_exec_time_ms_bucket[5m])) by (le, kernel)))/(histogram_quantile(0.5, sum(rate(kernel_exec_time_ms_bucket[5m])) by (le, kernel)))

C) Minimal reproduction recipe for regressions:
1) Snapshot failing commit and baseline artifacts.
2) Run perf-runner with the failing kernel flag enabled and the baseline corpus.
3) Collect traces (traces.tgz) and microbench outputs.
4) Upload artifacts to /artifacts/regressions/<ticket-id>.

Related reading and references:
- See routing and fallback architecture ADR (link in related_pages).
- Profiling playbooks and telemetry contract (links in related_pages).

Notes and change log:
- 2026-01-15: Initial draft and adoption of verification matrix (S. Rao).
- 2026-03-10: Added canary ramp policy and refined kernel warmup contract; added runbook remediation steps (E. Hart, D. Alvarez).

If you are implementing a new scheduler or kernel change, follow this manual start-to-finish: 1) add microbench checks, 2) register threshold baselines, 3) run staging replay, 4) validate VD-* checks, 5) enable canary with the configured ramp, 6) monitor and be ready to rollback.

title: Deterministic Playback Manifest Format (v1)
content:
## Overview
This page defines the **Deterministic Playback Manifest** format (v1): a lightweight, self-contained JSON document intended to capture everything needed to deterministically replay an inference session (or an ordered set of requests) across model rollouts, runtime variants, kernel changes, and quantization profiles.

The primary goal is to make postmortems, regression triage, and model A/B comparisons reproducible **without requiring full environment cloning**.

## Non-goals
The manifest is intentionally not a full provenance ledger.

**Out of scope for v1**
- Capturing private customer data inline. Manifests must reference redacted payloads or point to approved secure storage locations.
- General-purpose data lineage, training provenance, or governance/audit trails.

## Design principles
- **Minimal**: reference large artifacts instead of embedding blobs.
- **Deterministic intent**: include all inputs that can affect output (tokenizer, seeds, runtime config, policies/hooks).
- **Portable**: JSON, human-readable, attachable to support tickets and GitHub issues.
- **Privacy-aware**: PII-bearing content must be referenced via controlled pointers and governed by a privacy policy token.

## Applicability and versioning
- This page defines **v1** of the format. Breaking changes require a new `manifest_version`.
- Forward-compatible additions must be optional and ignored by older runners.

## Required top-level fields (v1)
All top-level fields are JSON keys.

**Identity and metadata**
- `manifest_version` (required): must be `"1"`
- `manifest_id` (required): short stable id (UUID recommended)
- `created_by` (required): name/email of authoring agent (person or system)
- `created_at` (required): RFC3339 timestamp
- `source_context` (required): freeform string describing scenario (UI flow, API route, ticket)

**Artifacts and execution**
- `model_artifact` (required): model id + artifact digest
- `tokenizer` (required): tokenizer id + digest
- `environment` (required): runtime/environment snapshot string (see "Environment fields")
- `requests` (required): ordered list encoded as JSON array in the manifest; each element is a request descriptor (see below)

**Determinism controls**
- `runtime_flags` (required): list of `key=value` strings affecting execution (e.g., `use_kv_cache=true`)
