  - Use short-lived warmup traffic after deploy via internal warmup job: ./scripts/warmup.sh --model $MODEL.
- Short-term remediation:
  - Preload commonly used model variants into warm pools.
- Long-term remediation:
  - Optimize binary load path and introduce a lightweight shadow-warm-start path that avoids heavy memory copies.
- Owner: runtime-startup team.

9) Telemetry sampling gap / delayed traces
- Symptoms:
  - Lost traces with sampling rate drop; alerts missing for a class of errors.
  - Traces show large gaps in walltime or missing service spans.
- Immediate mitigation:
  - Re-enable fallback tracer and increase sampling rate to 100% for the affected service: OTEL_SAMPLER_PROBABILITY=1.0.
- Short-term remediation:
  - Fix the collector pipeline and replay buffered telemetry.
- Long-term remediation:
  - Harden exporter backpressure handling and add local persisted buffer for telemetry.
- Owner: observability team.

On-call quick playbook (ordered checklist):
1) Identify & classify: use grafana + traces to map symptoms to one of the catalog rows.
2) Contain: if host-level, drain or detach the host. If network-level, adjust proxy timeouts.
3) Mitigate: apply runtime feature flags or routing overrides that are documented in the failure row.
4) Notify: inform product owner and customer success for impacted tenants when SLOs look threatened.
5) Record: open incident ticket and tag with the catalog failure ID.
6) Run post-incident action: add test coverage or automation as listed in long-term remediation.

Example detection rules (Prometheus + alert templates):
- Kernel latency alert (high):
  - name: HighKernelLatency
    expr: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(runtime_kernel_latency_seconds_bucket[2m])) by (le, kernel, node)) > 2
    for: 2m
    labels:
      severity: page
    annotations:
      summary: "p99 kernel latency > 2s ({{ $labels.kernel }} on {{ $labels.node }})"

- GPU memory pressure alert:
  - name: GPUFreeBelow10pct
    expr: avg_over_time(node_gpu_memory_free_bytes[1m]) / node_gpu_memory_total_bytes < 0.10
    for: 1m
    labels:
      severity: page

Operational tooling & commands (handy snippets):
- Drain runtime host (orchestrator API):
  curl -X POST -H \"Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN\" \"$ORCH/api/v1/nodes/<node>/drain\"

- Validate kvcache shard (internal):
  curl -s -X POST \"$INTERNAL/kvcache/validate?shard=<id>\" | jq

- Temporary routing override (example):
  curl -X POST -H \"Content-Type: application/json\" -d '{"model": "gpt-large", "route": "fallback-quantized", "duration_s": 600}' \"$PLATFORM/internal/routing/override\"

Metrics and dashboards to check (recommended panels):
- kernel latency by kernel and node (p50/p95/p99)
- node GPU memory free pct over time
- kvcache checksum errors by shard
- connection lifetime distribution for gRPC clients
- scheduler queue depth by priority class

Runbook maintenance and ownership:
- Each failure mode row must be reviewed quarterly by the owning team.
- When a remediation is completed, add a follow-up line with JIRA id and date in the row and remove the H/M flag if priority changes.
- Owners are responsible for adding unit/integration tests to CI that exercise the short-term mitigations.

Priority actions for next quarter (engineering backlog recommendations):
- Kernel team: implement handshake protocol and ship kernel-level test harness (JIRA: RUNTIME-8421).
- Memory/allocator squad: implement preflight dynamic accounting (JIRA: MEMACC-330).
- Scheduler team: land preemptive slice rollout with integration test (JIRA: SCHED-214).
- Observability: add persisted telemetry buffer and 100% sampling toggle for incident windows (JIRA: OBS-120).

Appendices:
A) Example incident ticket template (copy into new ticket):
- Title: [INCIDENT] <short summary of failure mode>
- Affected services: runtime, scheduler
- Impact: routes, tenants, SLOs impacted
- Detection: Grafana panel + trace link
- Immediate mitigations applied: list commands and flags
- Owner: <owner-team>
- Next steps: short-term fix, long-term fix, test needed

B) Glossary of internal endpoints used in this doc:
- $ORCH: internal orchestrator API (https://orch.internal)
- $PLATFORM: platform control API (https://platform.internal)
- $INTERNAL: runtime internal admin API (https://runtime-admin.internal)

C) Change log:
- 2025-10-14: created — initial catalog of 7 failure modes (S. Martinez)
- 2025-12-02: added NVLink and telemetry gaps; clarified on-call steps (reviewers: A. Patel, L. Nguyen)
- 2026-02-09: updated mitigation commands and added short-term remediation for model-swap oscillation (M. Chen)

If you are on-call and this page does not match the incident you see, escalate to the runtime escalation channel (#runtime-ops) and update this page with the observed new signals so we can keep the inventory current.

title: Execution Inspection Proxy — Experimentation & Rollout Runbook
content:
Overview

This page defines the Execution Inspection Proxy (EIP): a lightweight, in-path inspection layer designed to enable low-overhead sampling, causal tracing, and feature experimentation against live inference traffic. The intent is to provide a safe way to surface execution-level signals (kernel selection, batching decisions, KV-cache warmup, and tail latency contributors) without modifying the core runtime or blocking production flows.

Goals and non-goals
- Goals:
  - Capture causal telemetry for sampled requests: kernel selection, batch composition, queue wait, dispatch, and kernel execution durations.
  - Support non-invasive shadow sampling and replay capture for downstream profiling.
  - Provide a controlled canary rollout pattern with clear safety gates and rollback criteria.
  - Emit structured events compatible with our observability pipeline (OTLP/jaeger-compatible spans + JSON payloads to kinesis).
- Non-goals:
  - This proxy is not a replacement for full kernel-level instrumentation. It intentionally samples and reconstructs rather than tracing every token event.

Architectural overview
- Deployment: the EIP runs as a co-located process on runtime nodes (container sidecar or host process) and accepts a mirrored subset of requests via the request-router. It has two logical components: the fast-path forwarder and the asynchronous inspector.
- Fast-path forwarder:
  - For mirrored/inspected requests, forward to runtime with TCP passthrough and minimal packetization to preserve latency characteristics.
  - Add only a single hop and a configurable metadata header (x-eip-sampled: id, sample-rate, sample-reason).
- Asynchronous inspector:
  - Receives sampling copies via the forwarder and enriches them by collecting decision traces from scheduler hooks and kernel handshake messages.
  - Persists captures to the profiling bucket and emits telemetry events.

Textual diagram
  Request Router --> [Runtime Node] --> (EIP forwarder) --> Runtime Core
                                     
                                     (copied sample) --> (EIP inspector) --> telemetry / profiling-bucket

Kernel scheduling interactions and safety considerations
- Priority propagation:
  1) The EIP must not change runtime scheduling priorities. To avoid priority inversion, the proxy only annotates metadata; it never adjusts request priority headers unless explicitly enabled in experiment mode.
  2) When experiment mode is enabled, a separate gating service (priority-gate) authorizes transient priority hints stored in a short-lived config (TTL 60s) to the scheduler.
- Backpressure and admission control:
  - EIP respects runtime admission controller signals. If the runtime returns HTTP 429 for a mirrored request, inspector drops additional enrichment traffic for that request to avoid amplification.
- Kernel handshake correlation:
  - The inspector consumes the kernel handshake stream (read-only subscription) to correlate kernel ID -> execution timings. This subscription path is throttled to 1% of live handshakes by default.

Profiling & benchmarking plan
- Success metrics for experiment:
  - End-to-end p50 overhead introduced by EIP on observed requests <= 0.5ms.
  - End-to-end p99 overhead <= 5ms and never larger than 5% relative increase over baseline p99.
  - CPU usage for EIP sidecar <= 3% of node CPU under typical traffic; memory overhead < 200MB.
  - Sampling fidelity: inspector correlates >= 95% of sampled requests to kernel handshake when sampling rate is 1/1000.
- Benchmarks to run:
  1) Baseline synthetic workload: 10k RPS mixed seq-lengths (8/64/512) using shadow-generator v2. Command: 
     ./shadow-generator --rps 10000 --mix "0.6:8,0.3:64,0.1:512" --duration 30m --dest <router>
  2) Canary real-traffic mirror: 0.1% live traffic mirrored for 24 hours with continuous telemetry checks.
  3) Load spike stress test: inject a 5x traffic spike for 10 minutes and observe EIP behavior under kernel negotiation churn.
- Measurement guidance:
  - Use histogram exports for latency (client-observed), EIP forwarder add-on latency, and inspector processing time.
  - Collect kernel handshake correlation rate and amount of additional memory allocated for captured artifacts.
  - Compare generation token throughput and tail latency against baseline snapshots collected immediately prior to EIP enablement.

Runbook: Canary rollout (step-by-step)
1) Pre-checks (owner: runtime-ops)
   - Confirm benchmark baseline snapshots exist (p50/p95/p99 for last 24h).
   - Ensure profiling-bucket has >= 5GB free and write policy enforces retention 30d.
   - Verify OTLP pipeline is green and downstream parsers accept EIP schema.
2) Deploy to 2% of fleet as sidecar in passive mode (sampling disabled, headers present) and run 2-hour smoke watch.
3) Enable sampling at 0.01% (1/10000) for 1 hour; run automated checks:
   - CPU delta per node < 2%
   - Additional p99 latency delta < 3%
   - No increase in kernel failure counts or eviction incidents
4) If automated checks pass, raise sample-rate to 0.1% and observe for 6 hours.
5) If still stable, raise to 1% for 24 hours and run the full profiling capture pipeline to produce sample artifacts for kernel team analysis.
6) If any safety gate fails, follow rollback procedure below.

Rollback procedure (critical)
- Trigger conditions (any):
  - Measured p99 latency increase > 5% absolute compared to baseline or > 10% relative increase.
  - Node-level CPU increase > 5% sustained for 10 minutes.
  - Any increase in error-rate or kernel OOM/invocations > threshold.
- Immediate steps:
  1) Toggle sampling to 0% via feature-flag (flag name: eip_sampling_rate) and set traffic routing to bypass EIP forwarder.
  2) If bypass fails, stop the EIP process using: systemctl stop eip-sidecar or kubectl delete pod <eip-pod> --namespace runtime-canary
  3) Open incident with runtime-sre and tag priority P1. Attach profiling artifacts.
  4) Follow post-incident diagnostics checklist (see Diagnostics section).

Diagnostics: investigation checklist
- Correlate any latency spike with:
  - Request-size mix changes in the router logs.
  - Kernel handshake error counts in the last 30 minutes.
  - Memory pressure events (dmesg/kernel logs) and GPU eviction traces.
- Useful queries (PromQL examples):
  - avg_over_time(eip_forwarder_latency_ms[5m]) by (node) > 1.0
  - rate(kernel_handshake_errors_total[5m]) > 0
  - sum(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{pod=~"eip-sidecar.*"}) by (node)

Known issues and mitigations
- Issue: occasional handshake desynchronization during heavy evictions.
  - Symptom: inspector cannot correlate kernel ID to request and marks sample as orphaned.
  - Mitigation: enable conservative sampling (lower rate) during high eviction windows; implement a short buffer (250ms) in inspector to wait for delayed handshake.
- Issue: small spikes in p99 when inspector writes large captures to disk synchronously.
  - Mitigation: use async write workers with backpressure (queue size 512). Limit per-request artifact size to 128KB.
- Issue: increased observability pipeline cardinality when sampling rate becomes large.
  - Mitigation: normalize dimension tags (drop high-cardinality request-id tag in telemetry; reserve it only for artifact payloads).

Telemetry & dashboarding (owner: observability)
- Minimum signals to emit:
  - eip.forwarder.latency_ms (p50/p95/p99)
  - eip.inspector.processing_ms (histogram)
  - eip.sample.correlation_rate (ratio of inspector->handshake correlates)
  - eip.disk.write_backpressure_events
  - eip.node.cpu_pct and eip.node.mem_bytes
- Suggested dashboards:
  - EIP Health overview (per-cluster): latency trends, CPU/mem, correlation_rate, artifact write volume.
  - Canary gate panel: real-time pass/fail indicators for sampling checks.

Ownership, contacts and escalation
- Feature owner: Jordan Li (eng-serving-runtime)
- Oncall escalation: runtime-sre pager (primary: smsg to #runtime-sre on PagerDuty)
- Observability contact: Priya Nair
- Kernel handshake analysis: Ethan Morales

Appendix: sample config (YAML)
```yaml
# eip-config.yaml
enabled: true
mode: canary # passive | canary | experiment
sampling_rate: 0.001 # fractional (0.001 = 0.1%)
max_artifact_size_bytes: 131072
artifact_write_workers: 4
handshake_subscribe_rate: 0.01 # throttle handshake subscription to 1% by default
forwarder_override_header: "x-eip-sampled"
backpressure_queue_size: 512
```

Appendix: quick CLI & debug commands
- Check status: kubectl -n runtime get pods -l app=eip-sidecar -o wide
- Tail logs (fast-path): kubectl -n runtime logs -f deployment/eip-forwarder
- Force disable sampling: curl -X POST $EIP_ADMIN/flags -d '{"eip_sampling_rate": 0}'

Notes & revision history
- 2026-01-15: initial draft and architecture sketch.
- 2026-02-10: added kernel handshake correlation plan and sample-rate gating.
- 2026-03-02: formalized rollout gates, added CLI commands and PromQL examples.

Related reading
- Runtime decision graph and observed behaviour catalog (for expected kernel handshake semantics)
- Kernel-team checklist: kernel-handshake-contract.md
- Observability adapter design notes

If you are preparing a canary for EIP or need help interpreting profiler artifacts, ping the feature owner in #eng-serving-runtime and schedule a 1:1 with the kernel team.

title: Session Affinity and Degraded Routing Playbook
content:
Summary

This playbook documents the recommended runtime configuration, operational runbooks, and troubleshooting steps for session affinity (sticky sessions) combined with graceful degraded routing for latency-sensitive tenants. It is intended for on-call engineers, runtime owners, and SREs operating Redwood's inference pools when we need to: preserve KV-cache locality, enforce soft SLOs for premium tenants, or gracefully degrade capacity during GPU pressure.

Goals

- Keep 99th-percentile tail latency within SLOs for latency-sensitive tenants while minimizing token-cost overhead.
- Preserve KV cache hit-rate for conversational sessions where possible.
- Provide deterministic failover behavior and clear rollout / rollback procedures.

Scope and applicability

- Applies to workloads classified as: conversational chat (KV-cache dependent), low-latency text-completion, and mixed chat + function-calling flows.
- Targets: Dedicated and Hosted routing layers that support kernel affinity and shard locality.
- Not intended for: batch embedding workloads or long-running non-interactive generation jobs.

Key concepts and behavior

1) Session affinity modes
   - strict: bind a session to a single runtime shard until explicit session end. Best for very small sessions and when KV cache is critical.
   - soft: preferential routing to the last-serving shard; allow fallback after a short backoff. Balances cache-hit vs availability.
   - stateless: no affinity; always route using policy (cost or region). Only for cache-less or idempotent workloads.

2) Degraded routing strategies (in order of preference)
   - local-evict-and-shed: if a shard is memory-starved, evict cold KV entries and continue serving with degraded cache-hit.
   - variant-fallback: route to a quantized/cheap variant of the model on the same or nearby shard.
   - inter-shard-redirect: if affinity cannot be preserved, redirect with a short-circuit session-transfer protocol.
   - best-effort-broadcast (last resort): fan-out to multiple shards and return the first response (used only for low-QPS, high-criticality flows).

SLOs and thresholds

- Primary SLO for premium latency-sensitive tenants: 99th percentile P99 latency <= 220ms for <512 token responses, and P99 <= 450ms for 512-1024 tokens.
- Cache hit-rate target: session-level KV-cache hit-rate >= 85% for conversational sessions.
- Degradation trigger thresholds (per shard):

| Metric | Warning | Critical | Action |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| GPU memory free (%) | 25% | 10% | issue local-evict-and-shed (step A) |
| Kernel queue depth | 80% of capacity | 95% | escalate to priority-preempt and trigger variant-fallback |
| KV-cache eviction rate (entries/s) | 50 | 200 | mark as degraded; prefer soft-affinity falls back |

Configuration examples

Example runtime routing policy (YAML)

```yaml
routing_policy:
  name: premium-session-soft-affinity-v1
  affinity_mode: soft
  max_sticky_duration_s: 3600
  fallback_sequence:
    - type: local-evict-and-shed
      max_evictions: 500
    - type: variant-fallback
      allowed_variants: [gptq-8bit, int8-fast]
    - type: inter-shard-redirect
      max_redirect_hops: 1
  priority: high
  sla_tags: [premium, chat]
```

Scheduler kernel hints (JSON blob used by kernel mapper)

```json
{"priority":"high","expected_seq_len":256,"kv_locality_weight":0.9,"preferred_kernel_profile":"low-latency"}
```

Operational runbook: automated response flow (on-call play)

1) Alert: "shard memory critical" (critical) or "kernel queue saturation" (critical). Pager to runtime-oncall.
2) Immediately mark incoming requests for the affected shard with route_hint:degraded. This activates soft-affinity-only routing.
3) Execute step A: local-evict-and-shed (automated):
   a) Run: /opt/redwood/bin/kvctl evict --policy=cold-first --max 500
   b) Monitor kv_cache_hit_rate and memory_free for 30s.
   c) If memory_free > 18% within 30s, continue monitoring; annotate incident.
4) If step A fails or kernel queue remains saturated for >60s, trigger variant-fallback: update Edge routing table with allowed_variants priority.
5) If variant-fallback does not restore P99 within 2 minutes, perform inter-shard-redirect for new sessions only. Sessions with strict affinity must be offered a graceful-transfer token (see API below).
6) If all above fail and P99 > 600ms for the premium tier after 5 minutes, activate cross-tenant shedding policy (move best-effort tenants off affected pool).

Session transfer protocol (graceful-transfer)

- Purpose: move a session's KV state to another shard without dropping the user's experience. Used when strict-affinity sessions must be migrated.
- Steps:
  1) Acquire ephemeral lock on session_id via rendezvous service: POST /internal/rendezvous/lock {"session_id": "<id>", "ttl_s": 30}
  2) Dump session delta: /opt/redwood/bin/kvctl dump --session <session_id> --format=json > /tmp/session-<id>.json
  3) POST /internal/shard-transfer/import {"target_shard": "s-1023", "payload": <file>}
  4) Update routing: PUT /internal/routing/sessions/<session_id> {"shard":"s-1023","affinity_mode":"strict"}
  5) Release lock.

Observability and dashboards

Required dashboards and panels:
- shard_overview: P50/P95/P99 latencies, kernel queue depth, GPU memory free, active_sessions, kv_cache_hit_rate.
- session_affinity_telemetry: session bind events, transfer attempts, transfer latency, transfer failures.
- degraded_routing_incidents: count and duration per shard, actions executed, rollback events.

Essential alerts (examples)
- alert: shard-mem-critical -> expr: gpu_memory_free_pct < 10 for 30s -> severity: critical -> runbook: this doc step 2
- alert: kernel-queue-saturated -> expr: kernel_queue_depth / kernel_capacity > 0.95 for 30s -> severity: critical -> runbook: escalate immediate preemption
- alert: session-transfer-failures -> expr: rate(session_transfer_failures[5m]) > 1 -> severity: high -> runbook: inspect rendezvous logs

Testing and benchmarking guidance

- Synthetic test to validate affinity benefit: run parallel A/B across same shard (sticky) vs random routing for 10k sessions, 95th-percentile delta should show >=8% latency improvement and >=20% KV-cache hit-rate improvement for typical chat workloads.
- Stress test for variant-fallback: overlay 50% additional burst and assert fallback switch completes within 45s and maintains functional correctness (no truncated JSON responses).

Maintenance and rollout checklist

1) Canary rollout schedule: 5% traffic (10 minutes) -> 25% (30 minutes) -> 50% (60 minutes) -> 100% (2h).
2) During canary watch: P50/P95/P99, kv_cache_hit_rate, error rates, model output quality (sample diff tests).
3) On failure during a stage: immediate rollback to previous routing_policy snapshot and file an incident.

Troubleshooting matrix

| Symptom | Likely cause | First-step action | Escalation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Rapid KV eviction spike | Memory pressure from a noisy tenant | Run kvctl top-sessions --sort=mem and throttle top 5 sessions | Engage runtime lead, consider tenant-shielding |
| Session-transfer failures | Rendezvous service timeouts / auth issues | Check rendezvous logs and auth tokens; retry manual import | Repro with local import and open ticket to infra |
| P99 regression after variant-fallback | Variant produces slower decode due to kernel mismatch | Revert variant order; re-run microbench; file kernel ticket | Temporary increase capacity (burst pool) |

Operational ownership and contacts

- Runtime service owner: eng-serving-runtime team (runtime-core subteam). Primary oncall: runtime-oncall rotation.
- Pager escalation: runtime-oncall -> runtime-sre -> infra-gpu-pager -> eng-platform lead.
- Runbook steward: Priya Raman.

Appendices

A. Example CLI snippets

- Trigger a soft-affinity toggle for a tenant:
  curl -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' -d '{"tenant":"acme","affinity_mode":"soft"}' https://internal-api.redwood/v1/routing/tenants/update

- Dump session payload for transfer:
  /opt/redwood/bin/kvctl dump --session s_abc123 --format=json | gzip > /tmp/s_abc123.json.gz

B. Quick reference config table

| Setting | Recommended value (premium) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| max_sticky_duration_s | 3600 | avoid unbounded affinity; use tokens for explicit renewals |
| affinity_mode | soft | default for most tenants; strict only when required |
| variant_fallback_timeout_s | 30 | time to wait before accepting variant answer |

C. Known caveats

- Session transfers increase transient network and CPU overhead; avoid during large-scale bursts.
- Variant-fallback may change model output characteristics. Always run sample-diff checks during rollouts.

Document change log

- 2025-11-05: Draft created by Priya Raman.
- 2025-12-10: Added session-transfer protocol & YAML examples (reviewer: Marco Silva).
- 2026-02-14: Expanded alerts and canary rollout guidance; added testing guidance (reviewer: Aisha Patel).

References

- Runtime decision graph: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/runtime-decision-graph-and-observed-behaviour-catalog-2026
- Runtime fallback playbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-fallback-and-degradation-playbook-2026

End of document.

title: runtime-load-synthesis-and-observable-signatures-2026
content:
Overview

Purpose: This page documents a reproducible library of synthetic load shapes and the observable telemetry signatures they produce on the Redwood serving runtime. The goal is to provide engineers and SREs with a shared vocabulary for diagnosing anomalies, designing targeted alerting, and tuning scheduler/kernel knobs.

Audience: runtime engineers, performance SREs, profiling team, and product teams running closed-loop experiments.

Summary of deliverables on this page:
- Catalog of canonical load shapes (definitions + generator commands)
- Observable signature matrix (metric patterns to expect)
- Fault-injection templates to augment load shapes (latency, NVLink, cache eviction)
- Experiment matrix and acceptance criteria for validating kernel/scheduler changes
- Quick triage playbook and ownership map

1) Canonical load shapes

Each shape is parameterized by: concurrency distribution (clients), typical sequence length, prompt entropy (deterministic vs high-entropy), and inter-arrival distribution. We provide the recommended stress generator (loadkit) commands and expected runtime flags to enable consistent runs.

A. Steady-state throughput (baseline)
- Definition: Constant QPS with uniform sequence length; used to calibrate nominal per-token overhead and bandwidth.
- Parameters: qps=50, seq_len=128, concurrency=25 clients, token_gen_model=llamav2-13b
- Generator example:
  loadkit run --shape steady --qps 50 --seq-len 128 --clients 25 --duration 15m --model llamav2-13b 
- Runtime flags: --kv-cache=on --batching=continuous --batch-max-tokens=8192

B. Bursty microspikes
- Definition: Short (30s-2m) bursts at 5–10x baseline QPS; tests kernel preemption and queue admission.
- Parameters: baseline_qps=50, burst_multiplier=8, burst_period=90s
- Generator example:
  loadkit run --shape bursty --qps 50 --burst-mult 8 --burst-period 90s --seq-len 64 --duration 10m

C. Ramp-and-hold (scale events)
- Definition: Linear ramp from low to high QPS (1x to 10x) over 10 minutes, hold for 5 minutes, then decay. Useful for scaling/autoscaler validation.
- Generator example:
  loadkit run --shape ramp --start-qps 5 --end-qps 500 --ramp-duration 10m --hold 5m --seq-len 256

D. Tail-heavy (sporadic large sequences)
- Definition: Mix of short (32 tokens) and long (2048 tokens) requests, with long requests at 2% frequency. Validates sequence-length-dependent kernel breakpoints.
- Generator example:
  loadkit run --shape tail-heavy --short 32 --long 2048 --long-rate 0.02 --qps 80 --duration 20m

E. Cold-fanout (many cold model initializations)
- Definition: Many clients create new sessions without sharing KV cache. Designed to exercise warmup/warmstart paths and model load latency.
- Generator example:
  loadkit run --shape cold-fanout --clients 500 --session-duration 10s --seq-len 64 --duration 15m

F. Mixed-tenant blend (multi-tenant interference)
- Definition: Two synthetic tenants with orthogonal SLOs: tenant-A (low-latency p99 < 150ms), tenant-B (high-throughput). Run with quota split and observe scheduler isolation.
- Generator example:
  loadkit run --shape mixed --tenant-a-qps 40 --tenant-b-qps 160 --seq-len 128 --duration 30m

2) Observable signature matrix (metrics -> patterns)

This table maps common runtime metrics to the signatures you should expect under each load shape. Use this when triaging a regression or validating a kernel/scheduler change.

Metric names (Prometheus / runtime telemetry):
- runtime_request_latency_seconds_bucket (histogram buckets)
- runtime_request_duration_seconds_count
- runtime_kernel_queue_depth
- runtime_kernel_preemptions_total
- runtime_gpu_kernel_execute_time_seconds_sum
- runtime_kvcache_miss_rate
- runtime_batch_size_distribution (histogram)
- runtime_dispatch_retries_total
- runtime_gpu_memory_fragmentation_ratio
- runtime_dispatch_backpressure_events_total

Signature examples (human-readable)
- Steady-state: stable p50/p95, batch_size_distribution mode ~ batch-max configured, kernel_queue_depth small and steady, kvcache_miss_rate low (<1%).
- Bursty spikes: p99 jumps, kernel_queue_depth spikes ahead of backpressure events, preemptions_total increases during burst, batch size distribution briefly collapses to single-digit sizes as slicing occurs.
- Ramp-and-hold: linear growth in dispatch_retries_total if admission control thresholds are too low; expected backpressure events at ramp inflection if autoscaler lag is present.
- Tail-heavy: p99/p999 driven by long sequences; per-token GPU utilization may remain steady but kernel_execute_time_seconds_sum climbs non-linearly and memory fragmentation_ratio may rise.
- Cold-fanout: increased model_load_latency (custom metric), kvcache_miss_rate ~ 100% for new sessions, p50 increases until caches warm.
- Mixed-tenant: tenant isolation failure shows as tenant-A p99 elevated while tenant-B throughput unchanged; kernel_credit accounting metrics will display negative drift if quota misapplied.

PromQL examples to surface signatures:
- p99 latency (overall): histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(runtime_request_latency_seconds_bucket[1m])) by (le))
- kernel queue depth per node: max(runtime_kernel_queue_depth) by (node)
- kvcache miss rate: sum(rate(runtime_kvcache_miss_total[2m])) / sum(rate(runtime_kvcache_request_total[2m]))
- preemption spike detector (alert candidate): increase(runtime_kernel_preemptions_total[5m]) > 5

3) Fault-injection templates

Inject faults in a controlled way to see how system signatures change. We use two layers: network-level (tc/netem) and runtime-level (chaos injector). Below are JSON templates for the chaos injector used in staging.

Example: NVLink degradation (chaos template)

{
  "name": "nvlink-degrade-15pct-60s",
  "target": "node-pool-gpu-1",
  "duration": "60s",
  "actions": [
    {"type": "nvlink-fault", "severity": "degrade", "rate": "15%"}
  ]
}

Example: artificial scheduler pause (runtime-level)

{
  "name": "scheduler-pause-500ms-30s",
  "target": "scheduler-instance-*",
  "duration": "30s",
  "actions": [
    {"type": "pause-loop", "delay_ms": 500, "scope": "dispatch"}
  ]
}

Notes on safe practice: always run fault injection in a staging cluster isolated from production telemetry ingestion. Each template must have a linked kill-switch and ownership assigned (see ownership map below).

4) Experiment matrix and acceptance criteria

Use this matrix when validating a scheduler or kernel change. The matrix is the canonical checklist for feature rollouts and performance PRs. Run each cell and record metric deltas.

Experiment columns: change-id, kernels toggled, scheduler flag, test-shape, measurement window, acceptance criteria

Example rows (text table):
- CHG-3821 | per-request-kernel-hedging=on | priority-synthesis=v2 | bursty | 30m | p99 delta <= 10% at baseline; preemptions not increased by >20%
- CHG-3914 | simplified-quant-kernel | batch-max-tokens=8192 | tail-heavy | 1h | token throughput +/- 5%; memory fragmentation ratio decrease >= 5%
- CHG-4070 | kvcache-warmup-prefetch=experimental | -- | cold-fanout | 20m | model_load_latency median reduced by >= 30%

Recording: attach standardized CSV export with columns: timestamp, node, metric, baseline_value, experimental_value, delta_pct, notes. Store results in the runtime-experiments bucket with naming convention experiments/{change-id}/{date}.csv

5) Quick triage playbook (when you see a signature)

- Symptom: sudden p99 spike across nodes during bursty test
  1. Check kernel queue depth and preemptions: PromQL provided above. If queue depth > configured_batch_capacity for >30s, open runbook "kernel-contention-throttling-and-backpressure-playbook".
  2. Verify batch size distribution collapsed: run query on runtime_batch_size_distribution. If yes, escalate to kernel team and reference CHG-3821 test results.
  3. Restart path: if a node shows sustained high queue depth and memory pressure, follow runbook: sigmoid drain -> graceful pod restart -> warmstart prefetch.

- Symptom: increased kvcache_miss_rate during mixed-tenant runs
  1. Confirm session affinity header in request provenance trace. If missing, trace request path to frontend.
  2. If affinity is present but miss rate high, inspect kvcache-shard-mapping indices and run shard rebalancer in dry-run.

6) Ownership and contacts

- Runtime telemetry & dashboards: SRE Observability (owner: Connor Blake)
- Kernel scheduling experiments and rollouts: Serving Runtime Kernel Team (owner: Marina Liu)
- Load generator & experiment infra: Perf Tools team (owner: Rashmi Verma)
- Chaos / Fault injection approvals: Safety Council (owner: Leila Ortega)

7) Dashboards and queries to add to shared boards

- Load Shape Overview: per-shape panes with qps, p50/p95/p99, batch_size_mode, kvcache_miss_rate
- Node Health pane: kernel_queue_depth heatmap, gpu_memory_fragmentation_ratio, dispatch_retries_total
- Experiment delta pane: precomputed delta panels for each active change-id

8) Known caveats and interpretations

- Kernel queue depth can transiently overshoot during admission-control recalculation; only treat >30s sustained increase as actionable.
- Large sequence tails will skew histogram-based aggregates; prefer quantile over sliding window and inspect per-sequence-length segments.
- Batch size distribution collapse is often a downstream symptom (e.g., kernel slicing), not a root cause — correlate with preemption and dispatch_retry metrics.

9) Templates and artifacts (links)

- Experiment CSV template: experiments/template-experiment-csv-v1.csv
- Loadkit repo: git@github.com:redwood/loadkit.git
- Telemetry queries: /dashboards/runtime-load-signatures

Appendix A — Sample experiment checklist (short)
1) Create experiment directory experiments/{change-id}/{date}/
2) Ensure staging cluster is isolated and telemetry ingestion tagged with label: experiments/{change-id}
3) Run baseline steady-state for 20 minutes and store CSV
4) Run target shape(s) per matrix and store CSVs
5) Run fault-injection template if applicable (single template per run)
6) Aggregate and compare metrics, fill out acceptance criteria form
7) Present findings at the weekly kernel-change sync and attach results to the PR

Appendix B — Useful CLI snippets

- Start a steady baseline and stream telemetry to CSV:
  loadkit run --shape steady --qps 50 --seq-len 128 --clients 25 --duration 15m | tee baseline.csv
\- Apply chaos template (staging only):
  chaosctl apply -f nvlink-degrade-15pct-60s.json --env staging --wait 10s

- Export Prometheus query to CSV (example p99):
  promql-to-csv "histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(runtime_request_latency_seconds_bucket[1m])) by (le))" --from now-30m --to now --step 15s > p99.csv

Document change history: initial publish 2025-11-12 by Marina Liu; added fault-injection templates and mixed-tenant guidance 2026-02-08 by Marina Liu.

End of document

title: Experimental Kernel Stability Matrix and Run Manifest
content:
Summary
======
This page defines the Experimental Kernel Stability Matrix and an associated run manifest used by the runtime, kernel, profiling, and benchmarking teams to systematically exercise kernel changes across production-like axes (model variants, quantization modes, sequence shapes, batching profiles, and hardware families). The intent is to provide a single-source-of-truth experiment catalog that: 
- Produces repeatable telemetry for stability/latency regressions
- Surfaces cross-layer interactions (KV cache, prefetch, schedule handoffs)
- Ties profiling artifacts to benchmark runs and release notes

Scope and goals
----------------
Scope:
- Controlled experiments for kernel and scheduler changes impacting inference runtime behavior.
- Not intended for full production canaries; those live in the release canary matrix.

Goals:
1) Detect kernel regressions before canary release by exercising representative fidelity points.
2) Produce annotated traces and profiling artifacts that map directly to performance/regression triage playbooks.
3) Provide a prioritized run-order and clear pass/fail criteria that teams can apply in CI and in lab runs.

Matrix concept and axes
-----------------------
We represent experiments as rows in the stability matrix. Each row is a single run configuration (manifest) and includes the following canonical axes:
- kernel_build: short tag for the compiled kernel set under test (e.g. k1.2026-02-05-rc3)
- model_variant: model name + size + tokenizer (e.g. openlm-mini-1B-v2, or redwood-1.3B-finetune)
- quant_mode: fp16 | int8 | q4_0 | q4_1 | q5_0
- hw_target: A100-80GB, H100-80GB, GPUTronX-64GB
- sequence_profile: short | median | long (see "Sequence blocks" table)
- batch_shape: continuous | bursty | single-token-heavy
- admission_profile: normal | preemptive | low_priority
- fidelity_flags: runtime flags that change fallback/kv behavior (e.g. async_prefetch=on, kv_persistence=sticky)
- pass_criteria: numeric SLOs and signal thresholds for this experiment

Example experiment row (table-friendly text)
------------------------------------------------
| row_id | kernel_build | model_variant | quant_mode | hw_target   | seq_profile | batch_shape | admission | fidelity_flags | pass_criteria |
| ESM-101 | k1.2026-02-05-rc3 | redwood-1.3B-finetune | fp16 | A100-80GB | median | continuous | normal | async_prefetch=on;kv_persistence=sticky | p50 < 28ms; p95 < 120ms; error_rate < 0.3% |

Sequence blocks (concrete shapes)
----------------------------------
- short: 8–32 tokens, typical chat assistant system+turns.
- median: 64–256 tokens, mid-length completion workload.
- long: 512–2048 tokens, long-form generation stress.

Run manifest schema (human-readable)
------------------------------------
Each JSON/YAML manifest used by the CI runner must include the following top-level fields (example below):

Example manifest (YAML snippet)
------------------------------
```yaml
id: ESM-101
kernel_build: k1.2026-02-05-rc3
model_variant: redwood-1.3B-finetune
quant_mode: fp16
hw_target: A100-80GB
sequence_profile: median
batch_shape: continuous
admission_profile: normal
fidelity_flags:
  - async_prefetch: true
  - kv_persistence: sticky
request_mix: |
  - 70% text-generation (n=1)
  - 20% chat (n=2 turns)
  - 10% embeddings (small)
metrics_export: prometheus,tracejson
artifacts:
  - perf-profile: /artifacts/esm-101/perf.pb.gz
  - trace: /artifacts/esm-101/trace.jsonl
pass_criteria:
  p50_latency_ms: 28
  p95_latency_ms: 120
  error_rate_pct: 0.3
```

Execution and instrumentation guidelines
----------------------------------------
1) Environment isolation: use dedicated test pool or namespace to avoid noisy neighbors. Document the pool id in the manifest.
2) Warmup: run a 10-minute warmup per row to stabilize kernels and KV caches. Capture pre- and post-warmup traces.
3) Telemetry levels: always enable kernel-level telemetry, request-level tracing, and GC/memory summaries. Use the profiling tag: "esm:row-id" for all exported signals.
4) Artifact naming: follow the artifact prefix convention: <row_id>/<kernel_build>/<hw_target>/
5) Repeats: run each row at least 3 independent times; compute median of medians for stable metrics.

Pass / fail and triage flow
----------------------------
- Automated pass/fail: CI runner evaluates pass_criteria after the median of runs. If any criterion fails, the entire row is marked failed and artifacts are uploaded to the experiment bucket.
- Triage steps on failure:
  1. Confirm environment (pool id, driver/kernel versions) against the manifest.
  2. Load last-good baseline artifact (baseline row id noted in matrix) and replay with the same trace.
  3. Run the profiler diff (script: tooling/esm/profiler-diff.sh) to generate a delta report.
  4. If regression maps to kernel latency (vs. scheduling), open a Kernel Regression Triage ticket and run the controlled-perturbation playbook (link in related_pages).

Integrations with other artifacts
--------------------------------
- Benchmarking suite: each row references a canonical bench workload id (bench-id) used by our throughput and cost simulations. Add bench-id to manifest when exporting to the benchmark catalog.
- Release notes: adds a short section for any failing rows that were run against release candidates. Use the release_notes tag in the manifest for automated aggregation.
- Profiling playbook: row artifacts feed directly into the profiling playbook’s replay harness. Include the sample-rate and trace-filter used.

Default run prioritization and scheduling rules
------------------------------------------------
We prioritize rows with the highest customer impact first:
1) Model families that are in production for top-20 customers
2) Quantization modes in active use (int8, q4_1)
3) Hardware families with active capacity commitments
4) Any kernel builds that change prefetch/prefetch eviction logic

Guardrails and noise budgeting
-----------------------------
- Define a noise budget per row (default: 5% for p95 latency). If observed within budget across repeats, mark as flaky rather than failed.
- Annotate known-noise sources in the manifest (network jitter, shared-NVLink traffic, scheduled maintenance windows).

Operational runbook excerpts (condensed)
---------------------------------------
1) If a run fails with intermittent GPU watchdog resets:
   a) Verify driver and BIOS match matrix-approved list.
   b) Capture core dump and log a kernel-watchdog incident.
   c) Re-run on isolated node; mark row as blocked until hardware is remediated.
2) If p95 deviates but p50 is stable:
   a) Check batch_shape and admission_profile for bursty spikes.
   b) Run a co-located latency corridor test (tool: tooling/esm/latency-corridor.sh).
   c) If batch-induced, add 'burst-hedge' policy to fidelity_flags and re-run.

Example triage table (quick reference)
-------------------------------------
| symptom | likely layer | first artifact to check | action |
| "p50 up, p95 up" | kernel scheduling or kernel op cost | perf.pb.gz, kernel-op-latency.csv | run profiler-diff, isolate kernel-builds |
| "high error rate (5%)" | model conversion/quant mismatch | model-checksum.txt, trace.jsonl | verify quant metadata, re-quantize model |
| "watchdog reset" | hardware/driver | dmesg, nvml logs | escalate to infra SRE, run hardware repro |

Retention and artifact storage policy
-------------------------------------
- Artifacts for passed rows: keep 30 days.
- Artifacts for failed rows: keep 365 days and pin in the experiment bucket.
- Golden baselines: keep indefinitely, rotate when a new release candidate is promoted and validated.

How this page fits into the org
-------------------------------
Primary owners: Kernel team (owners: @kernel-platform), Runtime performance (owners: @runtime-perf).
Secondary: Profiling team, Benchmarking, Release Engineering.
For urgent regressions, follow the incident path described in /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-incident-orchestration-and-capacity-decision-matrix-2026.json

Appendix: Quick commands and helper scripts
------------------------------------------
- Run a single manifest locally (example):
  ./tooling/esm/run_manifest.sh --manifest manifests/esm-101.yaml --pool test-pool-12

- Diff two profiles:
  ./tooling/esm/profiler-diff.sh /artifacts/esm-101/perf.pb.gz /artifacts/baseline-0401/perf.pb.gz --output /tmp/diff.html

- Generate manifest from bench-id:
  python tooling/esm/generate_manifest.py --bench-id bench-7 --kernel k1.latest --out manifests/auto-esm-###.yaml

Change log (selected)
---------------------
- 2026-01-12: Initial published schema and example manifests (Aisha Patel).
- 2026-02-10: Added noise budgeting rules and retention policy (Ravi Sundaram).
- 2026-02-25: Clarified warmup guidance and artifact prefixes; added triage table (Marta Kowalski).

If you have questions or want to add new rows to the public matrix, comment on this page or ping @Aisha Patel.

title: Runtime Experimentation Safety and Governance Checklist
content:
Overview

Purpose:
- Provide a practical, repeatable checklist and governance guidance for running experiments that touch the serving runtime (kernel scheduling, eviction behavior, batch shaping, quantization rollouts, routing/fallback policies, and instrumentation changes).
- Reduce risk to production SLOs and customer traffic while enabling safe iteration across runtime subsystems.

Scope:
- Applies to any change or experiment that affects: kernel selection/variants, scheduler policies, kvcache behaviour, batching/cohorting logic, fallback routing, runtime-invoked model variants, telemetry sampling strategy, and external benchmarking harnesses that mirror production traffic.
- Does NOT replace module-level ADRs or release sign-off; it complements release/runbook artifacts with gating criteria and experiment-specific guardrails.

Audience and Roles
- Experiment Owner: engineer running the experiment (responsible for checklist items, runbook, and artifact collection).
- Runtime Safety Reviewer: senior runtime engineer who approves gating thresholds and rollback criteria.
- Oncall Rotation Lead: SRE who will own paging/incident coordination if the experiment impacts production.
- Metrics Librarian: owner of benchmark & SLO dashboards who validates experiment telemetry.

Pre-experiment Proposal (required fields)
- Title and short description of the hypothesis.
- Components touched (pick from: scheduler, kernel mapper, kvcache, dispatch, routing, kv-epoch sync, telemetry pipeline).
- Risk tier (low/medium/high) — use the tier rules below.
- Target cohorts/tenants and whether experiment will touch Dedicated or Private clusters.
- Expected duration and window (start/end times).
- Safety owner and oncall paging contact.
- Rollout plan & rollback triggers (explicit thresholds).

Risk tier rules
1) Low: internal-only experiments in sandbox or staging; no production traffic and no changes to kernel binaries.
2) Medium: non-invasive production shadowing or non-stateful parameter tuning (e.g., sampling rate changes, telemetry tag additions) with canary traffic up to 1% and explicit latency/cost gates.
3) High: kernel variant rollouts, admission controller logic changes, quantization rollouts, or anything affecting multi-tenant eviction or persistent kvcache state. Requires extended approvals and a rehearsal in the experiment lab.

Preflight checklist (must be completed before start)
1) Safety doc published in the experiment backlog with owner and reviewers.
2) Experiment manifest committed to the experiment registry (example manifest snippet below).
3) Benchmarks: baseline performance and cost numbers captured from the benchmark suite for the target model and sequence-length distribution. Attach per-token latency, P99, and cost-per-1k-token.
4) Telemetry hooks: trace points, span names, and metric labels required by the profiling playbook are instrumented and reviewed. Sampling policy updated if necessary.
5) Canary cohort defined, <= 1% traffic for medium or <= 0.1% for high-risk changes initially.
6) Rollback automation tested in isolation (automated toggle that returns traffic to the previous policy or model variant).
7) Runbook authored with precise paging instructions, reproducible triage steps, and escalation contacts.
8) Owners of downstream systems (billing, analytics, deployments) notified.

Experiment manifest example (YAML)
- name: kernel-variant-hint-eta
  component: kernel-mapper
  risk_tier: high
  start_window: 2027-03-08T02:00:00Z
  duration_hours: 4
  canary_fraction: 0.001
  telemetry_required:
    - runtime/p99_latency_ms
    - runtime/error_rate_5m
    - kernel_dispatch/handoff_rate
  rollback_triggers:
    - metric: runtime/p99_latency_ms
      operator: ">"
      threshold: "+25% over baseline"
    - metric: runtime/error_rate_5m
      operator: ">="
      threshold: "0.5%"

Telemetry and profiling requirements
- Required spans and metrics (profiling-playbook alignment):
  - request.lifecycle.span (must include kernel_id, batch_size, tenant_id)
  - kernel.exec_time_ms (histogram with p50/p95/p99 buckets)
  - kvcache.miss_rate (per-tenant rolling 5m)
  - scheduler.admission_rejects (count + cause tag)
  - dispatch.queue_wait_ms (per-queue)
- Sampling: for high-risk experiments set trace sampling to 100% for canary cohort for the first hour, then 10% thereafter. Ensure traces are tagged with experiment_id and kernel_variant.
- Profiling: attach microbenchmark artifacts from the perf suite for the same model/config (binary/quantization level) used in the experiment. Include kernel-level profiles (CUDA/NVTX) and host-side wall-clock traces.

Benchmarking & gating (use the benchmarking suite)
- Minimum acceptance criteria (example):
  - End-to-end P99 increase <= 10% for low risk, <= 15% for medium, <= 5% absolute ms cap for high risk (owner must propose and safety reviewer approves).
  - Cost per token delta should be reported; for cost-first experiments set strict cost gates (e.g., cost change <= -5%).
  - Memory and GPU occupancy: no increase > 8% sustained or scheduled eviction must be disabled during the canary window.
- Shadow benchmarks: run a 30-minute synthetic replay with the production-shaped corpus and compare kernel time distributions to baseline. Attach the generated delta histogram.

Kernel scheduling and admission controller safety items
- Kernel variant selection: experiments that introduce new kernel variants must ship a compatibility whitelist. If the variant is non-deterministic under batching, flag as high-risk.
- Admission controller: any change to slot accounting or credit logic requires a simulation run using the scheduler emulator (include link to emulator run ID).
- Preemption and priority inversion: provide hypothesis and tests that show there is no new priority inversion path. Include a microburst stress test where high priority traffic is steadily increased to 2x normal for 5 minutes and confirm low-priority P50 remains below the specified cap.

Runbook (condensed)
1) Pager triage steps:
   a) Check "experiment_id" overlays in the SLO dashboard and confirm the canary cohort only.
   b) If error rate >= rollback trigger, run automated toggle to revert kernel_variant for the canary cohort (CLI: redwoodctl runtime experiment revert --id <experiment_id>).
   c) Collect top 10 traces (by latency) and attach to slack incident channel #runtime-incidents.
2) If toggle fails, scale canary down to 0 and divert traffic to fallback route: redwoodctl routing set-fallback --policy stable-default.
3) Escalation: after 4 consecutive failed toggles or if global P99 > 2x baseline, page Oncall Rotation Lead and safety reviewer.

Post-experiment artifacts and postmortem expectations
- Artifact checklist to attach to experiment entry:
  - Baseline and experiment benchmark CSVs (per-token latency, kernel time, queue time).
  - Trace bundle (ndjson) with experiment_id tag.
  - Kernel-level profiles and microbenchmark outputs.
  - Runbook timeline and any toggles applied.
  - Final decision: ship / revise / abandon with bullet justification.
- Postmortem: if experiment caused any customer-visible incident or SLO breach it requires a blameless postmortem within 3 business days with follow-ups tracked in the experiment backlog.

Known issues mapping and release notes guidance
- Any experiment that touches a subsystem with an active Known Issues entry must reference the issue ID and attach a short impact analysis.
- Release note snippet template to include in runtime release notes: "Experiment <name> ran against <component> on <date>. Result: <accept/reject>. Key signals: p99 latency delta, error delta, cost delta. Link: <experiment registry entry>."

Safe rollout patterns (recommended)
- Shadow -> Canary -> Ramp -> Hold: always run a shadow period long enough to collect representative telemetry (>= 30 minutes of production-shaped traffic) before allowing canary routing.
- Progressive kernel rollout: variant enabled for a single stable tenant first (if available), then a 0.1% multi-tenant canary, then incremental steps 0.1% -> 1% -> 5% with qualitative checks at each step.

Appendix: Operational commands & templates
- Toggle experiment (CLI): redwoodctl runtime experiment toggle --id <experiment_id> --state enable|disable
- Revert kernel variant (CLI): redwoodctl runtime kernel revert --node <node_id> --variant <variant_id>
- Collect traces (example): redwoodctl observability export-traces --experiment <id> --min-duration-ms 100 --output traces-<id>.ndjson
- Perf harness run (example): bench-suite run --profile production-shape --model <model> --seq-distribution <dist> --output bench-<id>.csv

Appendix: Quick checklist (single-line items for owners)
- [ ] Create experiment entry and manifest in registry
- [ ] Baseline benchmarks recorded and attached
- [ ] Telemetry spans/instrumentation reviewed
- [ ] Runbook and rollback automation tested
- [ ] Canary cohort scheduled and owners notified
- [ ] Oncall and safety reviewer assigned
- [ ] Shadow run completed (>=30m)
- [ ] Automated rollback exercises executed
- [ ] Post-experiment artifacts attached

Contact and escalation
- Primary safety mailbox: runtime-safety@redwood.ai
- Pager (Oncall Rotation Lead): see rota in the SRE team wiki
- Slack channels: #runtime-experiments (announce start/stop), #runtime-incidents (incident comms)

Revision history
- 2027-02-15: Initial draft by Marina Hsu
- 2027-03-02: Updated telemetry sampling guidance and added CLI snippets (reviewers: Samir Khan, Ellen Ruiz, Priya Nair)

This document is intended as a living checklist. If you are running an experiment that interacts with other spaces (dedicated, private deployments) add an explicit cross-space approval entry and notify the relevant customer owners.

title: Execution Telemetry Quorum and Sampling Policy
content:
Summary

This page defines the Execution Telemetry Quorum and Sampling Policy for Redwood's serving runtime. It explains the signals we collect, the quorum rules used to trigger high-fidelity capture, the sampling knobs available to runtime operators and SREs, and operational playbooks for incidents and benchmarks. The goal is to balance diagnostic fidelity for production incidents and regressions with telemetry cost and privacy constraints.

Why this matters

- Full-fidelity traces for all requests are prohibitively expensive (bandwidth, storage, ingestion cost).
- Certain failures and regressions only manifest under narrow execution cohorts; a simple uniform sampler reduces reproducibility.
- Kernel-level scheduling signals, KV-cache deltas, and cross-device handoff traces are high-value for root-cause analysis but high-cost to capture.
- We need a deterministic, auditable policy that: preserves SLO observability, limits cost, enables postmortem reproducibility, and supports controlled ramping during experiments.

Scope and definitions

- Execution telemetry: structured traces, kernel scheduling events, per-kernel latency histograms, KV cache hit/miss traces, device-to-device handoff events, and request provenance metadata.
- Quorum: a multi-signal predicate that determines whether a specific request execution should be elevated to high-fidelity capture.
- Sampling knob types: uniform, cohort-based, adaptive, and quorum-triggered.

Quorum signals (used in predicates)

1) SLO breach candidate: request latency > 95th percentile for route/model for the last 15 minutes.
2) Kernel anomaly: per-kernel execution time > kernel_baseline * 3 (fast local baseline).
3) Cross-tenant contention signal: GPU kernel preemption or eviction events observed within request lifetime.
4) KV cache warmup failure: expected cached prefix missing for an established session (session age > 1 minute).
5) Error family match: any 5xx or structured runtime error matching the incident regex list.

Quorum policy (default production)

- Elevate to high-fidelity capture when any two distinct quorum signals are true for the same request OR when a single critical signal is flagged (Error family match or GPU preemption).
- High-fidelity capture includes: complete kernel event stream, full per-token scheduler decisions, gpu telemetry slice, request input/output payloads (redacted), and KV cache deltas.

Sampling tiers and retention

- Baseline (always-on): lightweight request metrics and sparse trace IDs (1% uniform). Retention: 90 days aggregated metrics, 7 days indexed traces.
- Diagnostic (cohort-based): 5% of traffic per high-risk route (see table below) or cohort sampling determined by route annotations. Retention: 30 days indexed traces.
- Quorum-captured (elevated): retained for 90 days in compressed archive with access controls; access requires incident ticket and approval.

Operational table: sampling defaults by route profile

- low-latency-read: uniform 0.5% (embeddings, short completions).
- interactive-chat: uniform 1%, cohort 3% for power users.
- long-generation: uniform 2%, cohort 10% for pinned beta customers.
- batch-embedding-job: uniform 0.2%, cohort capture via job-id sampling 1%.

(Operators can override per-customer using route config in Redwood Console; see "How to override" below.)

Cost/benchmark impact guidance

- Turning on kernel-level event capture increases per-request telemetry payload by ~8–12KB and ingestion CPU by ~1.4x in our benchmarks. Expect storage 10x for full request-level captures vs. aggregated metrics.
- Benchmarks run with high-fidelity capture enabled should use the "telemetry-isolated" flag to prevent polluted baseline comparisons. See the CLI section below.

Implementation notes (runtime hooks)

- Kernel scheduler hooks: place a light-weight hook at kernel dispatch entry to emit a 64-byte token with request id and scheduling decision. Hooks must be non-blocking and batch-emitted at 50ms intervals.
- KV cache tracing: emit a compact diff (keys touched, miss/hit) with session id and hashed prefix. Do not include raw prompt text unless redaction pass is applied.
- Device handoff: emit handshake events with device ids, estimated queue depth, and kernel queue latency.

Sample quorum predicate (YAML)

quorum:
  version: 1
  rules:
    - id: slo_and_kernel
      description: "Latency spike + kernel abnormality"
      predicates:
        - signal: slo_breach_candidate
        - signal: kernel_anomaly
      require: 2
    - id: critical_error
      description: "Immediate capture on critical errors"
      predicates:
        - signal: error_family_match
      require: 1

How to override sampling in Console (step-by-step)

1) Navigate to Console > Runtime > Routes and select the route.
2) Click "Telemetry" tab.
3) Edit Sampling Profile: choose baseline/cohort/quorum-enabled.
4) Optional: attach a temporary experiment tag (telemetry.debug=true, expiry in 24h). Changes are audited and emitted as config diff to S3: s3://redwood-runtime-configs/telemetry-overrides.
5) Monitor cost impact: Console shows estimated daily ingestion delta before committing.

Runbook: incident capture and access flow (for SREs)

1) Triage: determine whether the incident is reproducible and whether quorum predicates would have captured examples.
2) If not captured, flip a cohort override for the affected route with a 10x cohort multiplier for 30 minutes. Use the CLI: redwood telemetry override --route <route> --multiplier 10 --duration 30m --reason "incident PID-<id>".
3) Collect captures: link to S3 tarball in the incident ticket. Retain copy in incident workspace (encrypted).
4) Postmortem: annotate the captured traces with kernel snapshot id, runtime version, and scheduler policy.

CLI examples

# Enable ephemeral high-fidelity capture for route
redwood telemetry override --route /v1/generate--chat --set quorum_enabled=true --duration 20m --owner sre-team

# Run benchmark without telemetry noise
redwood bench run --workload long-gen --telemetry-isolated=true --output ./bench-results

Privacy and redaction rules

- Request payloads are redacted by default: only prompt hashes and token counts are stored. Full text is captured only when: (a) customer consent is present, OR (b) explicit legal/incident approval is granted.
- PII redaction pipeline: apply token-level redaction that replaces probable PII tokens with <REDACTED_STRING> and emits confidence score.

Testing and rollout plan for changes to quorum policy

1) Developer preview: enable policy in the sandbox runtime (tag: telemetry-sandbox) for 1 week with 100% traffic in sandbox. Verify schema, CPU overhead <= +15%.
2) Canary: rollout 1% of production routes with telemetry-isolated benchmark. Monitor ingestion and per-token cost delta for 48h.
3) Gradual ramp: 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100% over rolling four-day windows. SRE gate: ingestion cost increase must be <= 30% of forecasted budget per stage.

Release notes (policy v1.2)

- 2026-01-18: v1.2 released. Key changes: added "cross-tenant contention" quorum signal, tightened default cohort rates for long-generation routes, introduced telemetry-isolated flag for benchmarks.

Known issues and mitigations

- #KT-1823: occasional race in kernel hook emission can drop the first scheduling token under high concurrency. Mitigation: bump batch flush window from 25ms to 50ms and retry on missing kernel snapshot.
- #KV-991: session-id collisions in high-throughput job batching caused misattribution in KV diffs. Mitigation: switch session-id generator to 128-bit random uuid and add job-id namespace.

Ownership and escalation

- Ownership: Observability Platform (owner) + Serving Runtime (maintainer). Primary contacts: observability@redwood.ai, runtime-oncall@redwood.ai.
- Escalation: if telemetry ingestion > 2x forecast, page Observability Platform lead and SRE. Use incident channel #telemetry-ops.

Appendix: schema snippets and sample JSON trace (compact)

- Compact trace example (fields explained):
{
  "trace_id": "abcd-1234",
  "route": "/v1/generate",
  "model": "rw-open-7b",
  "events": ["kernel_dispatch:ts:...","kv_cache_delta:...","handoff:..."],
  "meta": "schema_v1"
}

- Telemetry cost estimator quick lookup (Console): per-100k requests estimated delta with kernel_capture=on: +$1,200/day (region=us-west-2, as of 2026-01).

Related documentation

- Runtime tracing contract (internal): /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/kernel-telemetry-annotation-guidelines-2025.json
- Benchmarks: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/microbenchmark-suite-variance-analysis-2025.json

Contact and feedback

For questions or to propose changes to the policy, open a PR against the telemetry-policy repo in Git (gitlab.redwood.internal/git/telemetry-policy) and ping Eleanor Chen and Marco Ruiz for review.

Revision log

- 2025-09-15: Initial draft (Eleanor Chen)
- 2025-11-02: Added cohort default table and CLI examples (Aisha Patel)
- 2026-01-20: Formalized quorum signals and published v1.2 release notes (Marco Ruiz)

title: Kernel Heuristic Evolution & Compatibility Notes
content:
Overview

This document captures the working journal and operational notes from kernel heuristic experiments conducted between Q2 2025 and Q1 2026. It is intended for runtime engineers, kernel authors, and SREs who are responsible for scheduler hooks, kernel rollout, and profiling-to-benchmark translation. The goal is to document what changed, why it changed, compatibility tradeoffs we've observed, and the reproducible steps to validate behavior on staging and canary fleets.

Sections
- Summary of heuristic families and intent
- Compatibility matrix and known cross-variant issues
- Profiling experiment recipes (how to reproduce)
- Benchmark signatures and quick-check heuristics
- Minimal rollout / rollback runbook for kernel heuristics
- Investigation checklist and escalation paths

1) Heuristic families (short descriptions)

A. Admission heuristics
- Purpose: decide which slot/queue a request is admitted into (latency-tiered vs throughput-tiered).
- Key signals: request_sequence_length, token_budget_estimate, tenant_priority_score, kv_cache_hit_prob.
- Typical knobs: admission_timeout_ms (default 10ms), prefetched_kv_threshold (fraction), min_gpu_headroom_pct.

B. Kernel selection heuristics
- Purpose: pick the kernel implementation variant (e.g., tiled-attention-32, fused-attn-v2, sparse-approx) for a request at dispatch time.
- Signals: sequence_length, kv_cache_present, past_runtime_profile_id.
- Decision pattern: prefer lower-latency kernel for sequence_length <= 512 unless kv_cache_present==true and batch_size>1 then prefer batch-optimized kernel.

C. Eviction and prefetch heuristics
- Purpose: maintain KV cache / activations with minimal disruption for hot tenants.
- Signals: kv_access_frequency, slot_age_seconds, pending_warmups.
- Knobs: eviction_granularity (shard|page), prefetch_aggressiveness (0..10).

2) Compatibility matrix (summary table)

| Heuristic | Compatible kernel families | Known incompatibility | Mitigation |
|---|---:|---|---|
| aggressive-prefetch-v1 | fused-attn-v2, tiled-attn-32 | causes memory oversubscription on fractional-quant kernels | bound prefetch by quantization_profile memory cap |
| priority-admission-v2 | all CPU/GPU kernels | starvation observed for low-priority tenants under bursty load | enforce per-tenant minimal throughput token guarantees |
| kv-evict-cohorting-2025 | quantized kernels (int8/4) | rare KV corruption during async handoff on older dispatcher | require SDK handshake >= 1.7.3 or enable sequential handoff flag |

Notes: the matrix is intentionally conservative. When in doubt, run the profiling recipe in section 3 before enabling on Dedicated/Private fleets.

3) Profiling experiment recipes (repro steps)

Each recipe below produces an artifact (trace tarball + annotated flamegraph + request-level SLO CSV) that should be attached to the release ticket. Use the runtime profiling agent (rprof) with sample-rate 1/10 for microbursts and 1/100 otherwise.

Recipe A — Admission stress with mixed fidelity
1. Configure a 4-node staging pool with mixed kernels: [tiled-attn-32, fused-attn-v2, quant-int8].
2. Set admission policy: priority-admission-v2 with min_guarantee_tokens=1000 per minute.
3. Inject traffic: 60% short chat (seq <= 256), 30% completion (seq 512-1024), 10% long (seq 2048+). Burst pattern: 5000 req/min for 2m every 10m for 1h.
4. Run: rprof --pool staging-mixed --sample-rate 0.1 --outfile admission-stress.tar.gz
5. Post-process: run tools/trace-summarize admission-stress.tar.gz --quantize=kernel_variant > admission-stress-summary.csv

Recipe B — KV handoff integrity test
1. Deploy kv-evict-cohorting-2025 flag on a 2-node canary.
2. Warm-up: load 1M small sessions across tenants using kv-warmup tool.
3. Simulate preemption waves: send preempt signals to nodes (use node-chaos inject-preempt --pattern=short-burst).
4. Collect logs and run kv-checker against snapshot. Expected artifact: small list of inconsistencies (should be zero).

4) Benchmark signatures and quick-check heuristics

When evaluating kernel-heuristic changes, we look for three canonical signatures in the benchmark suite:
- Latency median shift > 5% for P50 or P95 on chat-short baseline.
- Tail-energy degradation: per-token GPU cycles increase > 4% for long sequences.
- Token-level QoR deviation: top-1 token distribution KL > 0.02 for generation tasks (indirect check for quant/approx kernel behavior).

Quick-check commands:
- Run the lightweight SLO smoke test: ./bench/slo-smoke --profile chat-short --runs 50
- Compute kernel-sensitive regressions: bench/regression-check --baseline v2025-04 --target HEAD --signal kernel_variant,kernel_latency,kvcache_hit

Example expected outputs:
- If a change regresses P95 by >7% or increases per-token cost by >6% we mark it -blocker and require detailed kernel traces.

5) Minimal rollout + rollback runbook for heuristic flips

Purpose: safe pattern to flip a heuristic gate and recover quickly if problems appear.

Prerequisites:
- Canary pool with telemetry baseline for last 24h.
- Canary alerting: P95 latency > baseline * 1.2, QoR-regression alert, error-rate > 0.5% absolute.

Steps to rollout (target: canary -> regional -> global):
1. Create a canary feature flag (ffctl create heuristic-X --scope canary-pool).
2. Enable on 1% of canary traffic for 30 minutes. Monitor: rprof traces + perf dashboards.
3. If stable, increase to 10% for 1 hour, then 50% for 2 hours.
4. Promote to regional pool and repeat the 10%/50% ramp.
5. Global enable only after 24h stability on regionals.

Rollback quick path (if any alert triggers):
1. ffctl disable heuristic-X --immediate.
2. Trigger rollback ticket and attach the canary artifact.
3. If errors persist, run node-repro replay using trace artifacts and escalate to kernel-oncall.

6) Investigation checklist and ownership paths

Initial triage (oncall):
- Collect artifacts: rprof archive, scheduler decision log, kernel dispatch trace.
- Validate compatibility: check quant_profile and dispatcher SDK version.
- Check metrics: per-tenant P95, kernel_variant distribution, kvcache hit rate.
- Run quick smoke bench against canary snapshot.

Ownership map:
- Kernel scheduling bugs -> kernel-team (oncall: kernel-scheduling@redwood.com)
- KV cache handoff -> runtime-cache team (oncall: runtime-cache@redwood.com)
- Dispatcher/Admission -> runtime-orch team (oncall: runtime-orch@redwood.com)

Escalation path: if investigation cannot conclude within 60 minutes, escalate to SRE lead and open an incident with severity determined by user impact. Attach the artifact bundle and the canary runbook link.

7) Example config snippets

Admission policy YAML (example):
```yaml
admission_policy:
  name: priority-admission-v2
  admission_timeout_ms: 12
  min_guarantee_tokens_per_min: 1000
  backpressure_slope: 0.6
  enforcement_mode: soft
```

Kernel selection override (runtime flag):
```json
{
  "selector_policy": "sequence_length_primary",
  "overrides": [
    {"if": "sequence_length > 1024", "use": "fused-attn-v2"},
    {"if": "kv_cache_present == true && batch_size >= 2", "use": "batch-optimized-quant"}
  ]
}
```

8) Postmortem learnings (short list)

- Heuristic changes that interact with quantized kernels require an explicit memory cap to avoid unexpected OOMs when prefetching is aggressive.
- Admission logic that uses only token budget without considering batch shape introduced per-tenant starvation in multi-tenant canaries. The fix: add a batch-aware floor to admission scores.
- Async KV handoff needs versioned handshakes; older dispatcher clients (pre-1.7.3) must be blocked or migrated.

9) Appendices: artifacts, dashboards, and links

- Recommended artifacts to attach to any heuristic change PR: rprof tarball, bench/regression-check output, kernel-variant flamegraph (SVG), canary alert timeline.
- Dashboards: kernel-variant-distribution, admission-latency-by-priority, kvcache-hit-heatmap.
- Helpful commands: ffctl status heuristic-X --history, rprof collect --pool <pool> --since 1h, bench/regression-check --target HEAD.

Contact and ownership
- Primary author: Maya Chen (maya@redwood.com)
- Kernel scheduling owners: kernel-team@redwood.com
- Runtime orchestration owners: runtime-orch@redwood.com

Revision history
- 2025-06-15: initial draft of heuristic families and recipes.
- 2025-10-09: added KV handoff integrity recipe and compatibility matrix updates.
- 2026-01-10: tightened rollout thresholds and added quick-check commands.

End of document

title: Execution Signal Grokking and Telemetry Orchestration Playbook
content:
Purpose:
This page documents the signal taxonomy and orchestration patterns we use to reason about end-to-end execution behaviour in the serving runtime. It is intended for runtime engineers, SREs, and performance analysts who need a repeatable way to:
- find the right signal when debugging kernel regressions or SLO violations,
- configure telemetry collection with cost-aware sampling, and
- run focused profiling and benchmarking experiments that map back to production observability.

Scope and goals:
1) Make multi-layer signal mapping explicit: request surface -> dispatch -> scheduler -> kernel -> device.
2) Provide a small, prioritized signal set for fast triage (the "fast five").
3) Standardize sampling and enrichment so production traces are high-signal for regression hunts.
4) Define a profiling playbook and benchmark checklist to validate fixes and measure cost/latency trade-offs.

Fast five signals (priority order):
1) request.timeline.total_ms — end-to-end wall-clock for the request.
2) kernel.exec_ms_p95 — kernel execution time, P95 per kernel type.
3) gpu.dispatch_queue_depth — instantaneous queue length at dispatcher.
4) kvcache.hit_ratio_prefix_ms — prefix KV cache hit latency and ratio for session keys.
5) preempt.count_per_min — count of scheduler preemptions per minute.

Signal taxonomy and where to instrument:
- API layer (dispatch-proxy): request.id, client_token, request.timeline.*. Instrument with HTTP middleware that injects X-Request-ID and logs entry/exit timestamps.
- Orchestrator / dispatcher (execution-orchestrator): queuing_delay_ms, dispatch_to_scheduler_ms, queue_depth. Emit counters and histogram aggregates at 1s granularity.
- Scheduler (kernel-scheduler): scheduling_latency_ms (queue->launch), slot_allocation_reason, preempt_* events. Attach a lightweight trace span for each kernel handoff.
- Kernel runtime: kernel.exec_ms, kernel.memory_bytes, kernel_variant (int8/float16/fp32). Export per-kernel histograms with bucket boundaries aligned to expected breakpoints (8ms, 16ms, 32ms, 64ms, 128ms, 256ms).
- Accelerator/device: device_util_pct (1s), thermal_events, nvlink_retries. Device exporter runs on node and tags metrics with node_id, rack_id.

Correlation keys and propagation rules:
- request.id must be propagated across RPCs and attached to kernel spans. Use header X-Request-ID and, inside the data plane, the 64-bit trace token `rt_trace` added to the first 8 bytes of the request header.
- session.id and kvcache.key_prefix should be attached to KV cache metrics and trace spans to correlate warm/cold behaviour.
- kernel_variant and model_version must be top-level tags on every telemetry object for cohorting.

Sampling policy (cost-aware):
- Baseline: sample 0.5% of requests for full-span traces with detailed kernel traces.
- Anomaly amplification: for any request where request.timeline.total_ms > p95_slo_threshold * 2, sample 100% of such requests for 30 minutes.
- Experiment switch: when running a kernel rollout experiment (flag: kernel_experiment=true), increase full-span sample to 5% for that cohort for the duration of the experiment.
- Heavy-path profiling: for requests routed to dedicated pools (redwood-dedicated-*), enable 2% always-on profiling to capture steady-state behaviour.

Telemetry configuration example (yaml):

telemetry:
  default_sample_rate: 0.005
  anomaly_amplify_factor: 100
  profiling:
    dedicated_pools_sample: 0.02
  enrichers:
    - rt_trace
    - kernel_variant
    - model_version

(This YAML is a minimal example for the dispatcher operator config.)

Tagging and metric naming conventions (summary table):
| Layer           | Metric prefix             | Key tags (examples)                  | Granularity |
|-----------------|---------------------------|---------------------------------------|-------------|
| Dispatch        | dispatch.*                | request.id, route, pool, region      | 1s          |
| Scheduler       | scheduler.*               | slot_id, priority, kernel_variant    | event + 1s  |
| Kernel runtime  | kernel.exec_*             | kernel_type, model_version, host_id  | histogram   |
| Device          | device.util_*             | node_id, gpu_index, thermal_state    | 1s          |

Profiling playbook (step-by-step):
1) Establish baseline: run the canonical benchmark suite (see Benchmark checklist) to capture baseline kernel.exec_ms_p50/p95/p99 for the target model and sequence profile.
2) Reproduce in staged environment: mirror 10% of production traffic to a canary dispatcher with identical telemetry sampling.
3) Isolate the layer: use request.timeline.* and scheduler.* spans to determine whether the latency is in dispatch, scheduling, kernel exec, or device.
4) If kernel.exec_ms_p95 increased: capture 100 full-span traces for the offending kernel_variant and run kernel microbenchmarks (kernel-only runner) with the same batch/seq shapes.
5) If device_util_pct high but kernel.exec low: investigate device contention (nvlink, PCIe stalls) using device exporters and nvlink_retries counter.
6) Patch hypotheses: apply targeted fixes (kernel parameter, prefetch hint, batching change) behind an experiment flag.
7) Validation: run the benchmark suite and mirrored traffic experiment; require no regression on p95 and a measured unit-cost delta within acceptable range before rollout.

Benchmark checklist (operational):
- Use workload generator with the production sequence length distribution.
- Run for 30 minutes steady-state + 10x microbursts to test tail behaviour.
- Collect: request.timeline.total_ms, kernel.exec_ms_* histograms, kvcache.hit_ratio, device.util_pct, preempt.count.
- Pass criteria: p95 latency <= production SLO (default 150ms for interactive models) and any p99 increase <= 10% relative to baseline.

Incident triage runbook (short):
1) Confirm SLO breach using incident dashboard (slo-oracle /alerts). Record time window and magnitude.
2) Run quick signal checklist: check request.timeline.total_ms, kernel.exec_ms_p95, gpu.dispatch_queue_depth.
3) If kernel.exec_ms_p95 elevated: collect 200 full traces (if sampling allows) and start an etl job to enrich traces with kernel_variant and model_version.
4) If gpu.dispatch_queue_depth > queue_depth_threshold (default 64): scale up dispatcher slots or divert low-priority cohorts.
5) If device_util_pct > 95% for > 60s on > 2 GPUs in the cluster: follow device incident playbook (see link in references).
6) Communicate: post initial summary to #runtime-ops channel with Runbook correlation_id and owner.

Regression hunt heuristics (pattern catalog):
- Pattern: sharp increase in kernel.exec_ms_p95 with no device_util_pct change -> likely kernel codepath regression or input shape distribution change.
- Pattern: rising preempt.count_per_min and growing tail -> scheduler policy or admission change causing churn.
- Pattern: kvcache.hit_ratio drop + increased dispatch latency -> session key format change or cache namespace collision.

Release notes template for runtime changes (short):
- Summary: one-line change.
- Impact: which customers/pools/models affected.
- Observability: list dashboards and key signals to watch (recommend adding p95 kernel.exec_ms, dispatch queue depth, and kvcache hit ratio).
- Rollout plan: canary %, duration, quick rollback criteria (e.g. p95 > 2x baseline or error rate increase > 0.5%).
- Owner and on-call rota.

Known issues (current):
| ID | Symptom | Likely cause | Mitigation | ETA for fix |
|----|---------|--------------|------------|------------|
| KS-2026-17 | Flaky preemption spikes on tiebreaker windows | Scheduler tie-break logic favors short-running slots causing handoffs | Temporarily increase preempt_grace_ms to 50ms; enable fairness governor | Patch in 2026-02-20 |
| KV-2025-09 | KV cache namespace collisions for long session IDs | New session-id encoding broke kv namespace prefix rules | Revert encoding or enable prefix-normalizer in dispatcher | Hotfix deployed 2026-01-11 |
| DEV-2026-03 | NVLink retry storms correlated with driver 525.x | GPU driver regression causing transient remap stalls | Pin driver to 520.x on affected fleet; schedule driver upgrade window | Fleet upgrade planned 2026-03-10 |

Operational ownership and contacts:
- Runtime Observability: Priya Anand (priya@redwood.ai)
- Kernel Scheduling: Marco Li (marco@redwood.ai)
- Device & Fleet: Aisha Thompson (aisha@redwood.ai)

Experiment and validation checklist (pre-rollout):
- Run canary for 48h against 5% production traffic.
- Confirm no >10% regression in p99 or >5% regression in p95 across replicated pools.
- Validate unit token cost delta using deploy-budget simulation (tool: cost-sim).
- Declare roll/no-roll in canary-embed PR with owner signoff.

Appendix: quick commands and snippets
- Collect 200 traces for a given request id:
