  curl -X POST "http://telemetry-api.local/trace/collect" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"request_id":"<id>", "limit":200}'

- Check scheduler queue depth (kubectl example):
  kubectl exec -n runtime svc/scheduler-metrics -- curl -s localhost:9102/metrics | grep scheduler_queue_depth | tail -n 10

- Kernel microbenchmark runner example (python):
  # runner.py (abridged)
  import runnerlib
  runnerlib.load_model('gpt-small', variant='int8')
  runnerlib.run_shapes(batch=1, seq=512, iterations=200)

title: Runtime Simulator Playbook and Operator Index
content:
Summary:
This playbook defines the canonical simulator suite, operator-facing index, and step-by-step validation checklist used to exercise degradation paths, canary rollouts, and SLA acceptance for runtime changes. It is intended for runtime operators, SREs, and experiment owners running pre-release canaries and postmortem reconstructions.

Scope and intent:
- Provide a repeatable simulation matrix that spans: latency tail, KV-cache warmup, kernel contention, memory pressure, quantization-induced quality drift, and mixed-cohort interference.
- Produce deterministic artifacts (replay traces, golden traces, acceptance matrices) that feed the release gating pipeline.
- Offer an operator index mapping common symptoms to simulator scenarios and corresponding escalation/runbook pages.

Ownership and roles:
- Author: Lina Ortiz (Runtime Infrastructure)
- Owners: eng-serving-runtime team (primary), eng-sre (secondary)
- Oncall contact (operator rotas): runtime-ops@redwood.ai; Pager: #runtime-oncall in Slack
- Escalation: follow SRE escalation ladder; see related_pages for circuit-breaker runbook.

Simulator suite overview (matrix):
The suite is composed of modular scenarios. Each scenario has: description, input corpus, traffic shape, hardware profile, kernel variants, and acceptance thresholds.
1) Latency-tail sculptor
   - Description: injects realistic bursts (90/95/99/99.9 quantiles) across sequence lengths and concurrency shapes.
   - Traffic shapes: steady, microburst (10s), diurnal ramp, randomized spike trains.
   - Hardware profiles: a2-highmem (single GPU), mixed pool (A100+T4), and dedicated-8x (reserved capacity).
   - Acceptance thresholds: 99.9p must not exceed baseline+120ms for production models; see Acceptance Criteria.

2) KV-cache warmup and prefetch simulation
   - Description: synthetic session mixes that reveal cold-start and warmup delta for prefix caching and prefetch heuristics.
   - Workload: long-session (avg 400 tokens), short-chat (avg 40 tokens), streaming token bursts.
   - Key metric: time-to-90%-hit-rate (T90) on KV cache, target <= 25s for dedicated pools.

3) Kernel contention and slot-saturation
   - Description: schedule overlapping kernel windows to exercise admission controller and preemption.
   - Variants: cooperative preemption on/off, batch-slicing enabled, credit accounting stress.
   - Safety checks: no priority inversion lasting >120s; kernel watchdog alerts must fire at 30s.

4) Memory-pressure and eviction cascade
   - Description: ramp synthetic multi-tenant memory growth to trigger cross-tenant eviction and compaction.
   - Acceptance: successful graceful eviction and resident set compaction without OOMs; failed reconcilers must be captured as incident tickets.

5) Quantization fidelity drift (greybox)
   - Description: compare generation quality across float16, int8, and hybrid-quantized kernels using a fixed prompt set.
   - Metrics: ROUGE/CHR-F/semantic-similarity delta, synthetic hallucination score.
   - Thresholds: any quality regression >4% on primary prompts triggers rollback gate.

6) Mixed-cohort interference
   - Description: run heterogeneous tenant mixes (high throughput + low-latency critical) to detect scheduling artifacts.
   - Observability: token-level trace correlation, kernel credit debits, admission latency heatmaps.

Runbook index (operator quick reference):
- Symptom: sudden 99.9p spike across all models
  - Simulator scenario: Latency-tail sculptor — microburst with high concurrency
  - Immediate checks: scheduler-queue-depth, kernel-queue length, NVLink saturation, GPU thermals
  - Playbook link: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/tail-latency-investigation-and-mitigation-playbook-2026

- Symptom: sustained increase in cold-start errors after deploy
  - Simulator scenario: KV-cache warmup
  - Immediate checks: KV-epoch sync logs, prefix-cache-miss-rate, prefetch worker backlog
  - Playbook link: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/dynamic-kvcache-resilience-and-warmup-playbook-2026

- Symptom: per-tenant quality regressions after quantization rollout
  - Simulator scenario: Quantization fidelity drift (greybox)
  - Immediate checks: eval-suite pass rates, sample outputs vs golden, embedding-similarity drift
  - Playbook link: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/quantization-rollout-safety-and-quality-gate-playbook-2026

Pre-release acceptance checklist (use when gating canaries or kernel rollouts):
1) Baseline capture: record golden traces for the target service and model (include token-level timing, kernel map, KV hits).
2) Scenario replay: run all simulator scenarios listed above at three scales: smoke (1x), nominal (1–2x), stress (5–10x nominal).
3) Observability validation: ensure telemetry pipelines capture token_id, kernel_id, slot_id, and admission_decision for every request.
4) SLA validation: compute quantile deltas vs baseline. Acceptance rule: for release to proceed, no critical SLA (99.9p latency, error rate, or KV warmup T90) may exceed baseline by >20% or hard thresholds (see numeric list below).
4a) Numeric thresholds (examples):
   - 50p latency delta <= +15ms
   - 95p latency delta <= +50ms
   - 99.9p latency delta <= +120ms
   - Error rate delta <= +0.1% absolute
   - KV T90 delta <= +40%
   - Quality regression >4% (primary prompt set) => block
5) Regression signals: automatic alerts must be raised to #runtime-ci and an incident template must be populated if any metric crosses gate.
6) Canary roll: progressive traffic ramp (5%, 25%, 50%, 100%) with a 30–60 minute hold and continuous SLO check. Abort conditions: any threshold breach or anomalous CPU/GPU error logs.

Operator procedures (step-by-step examples):
A) Running the simulator locally (developer sandbox)
   1. Checkout infra repo: git clone git@github.com:redwood-inference/runtime-sim.git
   2. Start environment: cd runtime-sim && scripts/start-sim --profile=dedicated-8x --corpus=golden-prompts.json
   3. Kick off a latency-tail run: ./bin/run-scenario --name=latency_tail --duration=10m --shape=microburst
   4. Collect artifacts: ./bin/collect-artifacts --out=/tmp/sim-artifacts/$(date +%F)-tail

B) Running a canary with simulator validation (CI pipeline)
   1. Trigger pipeline: ci/release/run_canary.yml with param SIM_RUN=true
   2. Pipeline stages: capture-baseline -> run-simulators -> compare-metrics -> gate/abort -> rollout
   3. On failure: pipeline creates an incident with prefilled fields: commit hash, artifact links, failing metric snapshots.

Observability and telemetry requirements (table):
- Field: token_timestamp — description: per-token timestamp emitted at kernel handoff — retention: 90d
- Field: kernel_id — description: identifier for kernel variant (eg: attention-sharded-v2) — retention: 90d
- Field: admission_decision — description: admission result (allowed/preempted/hedged) — retention: 30d
- Field: kv_hit — description: boolean and hit_latency_ms — retention: 30d
- Field: sample_flags — description: labels for sampled traces (canary/gold/control) — retention: 365d

Artifact management and storage:
- Golden traces stored in s3://redwood-ci/runtime-goldens/YYYY-MM-DD/ with metadata JSON including commit, model, and hardware profile.
- Simulator artifacts must include: metrics.csv, token_traces.jsonl (for 1% sample), kernel_profiles.pb, and an HTML perf-diff report.

Troubleshooting heuristics (common failure signatures):
- Kernel oscillation (symptom: repeated 500ms spikes correlated to kernel-switch events): inspect kernel-profile timeline and admission_decision traces; enable kernel debug mode and reproduce with microburst shape.
- KV epoch skew (symptom: high cache-miss across coordination window): check KV coordinator logs for epoch drift >5s and run kvcache-epoch-repair utility.
- Admission backpressure (symptom: queue length growth + drop in throughput): identify the admission controller heavy path; consider temporary increase in slot count or enable cooperative preemption.

Runbook links (operator navigation index):
- Tail latency investigation: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/tail-latency-investigation-and-mitigation-playbook-2026
- KV warmup & resilience: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/dynamic-kvcache-resilience-and-warmup-playbook-2026
- Quantization rollout gate: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/quantization-rollout-safety-and-quality-gate-playbook-2026
- Canary & rollback circuit: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-deployment-circuit-breakers-and-sla-fallback-playbook-2026

Data collection checklist (pre-run):
- Confirm model binary and kernel image checksums match golden (sha256).
- Validate telemetry ingestion end-to-end with a small smoke trace.
- Ensure SLO dashboards have synthetic baselines pinned for the test window.

Appendix A — example perf-diff command (CI):
- ./tools/perf-diff --baseline s3://redwood-ci/runtime-goldens/2026-06-01 --candidate /tmp/sim-artifacts --metrics latency_95,latency_999,error_rate --output report.html

Appendix B — emergency abort template (to be auto-filled by CI on gate breach):
- Title: CANARY ABORT: <service> <commit>
- Short description: Automatic gate breach detected during simulator validation.
- Failing metrics: list with quantile snapshots and links to artifacts.
- Immediate action: Revert route traffic, disable candidate kernels, and open P1 incident.

Notes and follow-ups:
- Simulation harness is intended to be conservative; always re-run failing scenarios at higher sampling to reduce false positives.
- Future work: add NVSwitch-level contention scenario and an asynchronous kernel-handshake injector.

Document change history:
- 2026-06-10: Created by Lina Ortiz (initial draft)
- 2026-09-14: Added KV warmup T90 thresholds and artifact schema (reviewers: Aisha Patel)
- 2026-11-30: Updated acceptance numeric thresholds and expanded operator procedures (reviewers: Jared Kim, Marco Silva)

title: Known issue: Tensor-parallel hangs under sustained load
content:
## Summary
Tensor-parallel (TP) replicas can intermittently **hang (no forward progress)** under sustained, mixed workloads (prefill + decode, long-context, bursty concurrency). This typically presents as **streaming responses stalling** and eventually **request timeouts**. In the worst case, one or more GPUs appear “wedged” until the replica is drained/restarted.

This page documents:
- Observable symptoms and common signatures
- Affected configurations (models, TP sizes, hardware)
- How to detect and confirm a TP stall
- Recommended mitigations (operational + config)
- Fix status by runtime version and feature flags

> If you are actively in an incident: jump to **Immediate mitigations** and then follow **Triage**.

---

## Impact / why we care
- **Customer impact:** Streaming completions stall; end-users see long hangs then timeouts. Enterprise Dedicated accounts are most affected due to higher sustained concurrency.
- **Operational impact:** Autoscaler thrash (p99 latency spikes trigger scale-up; wedged replicas never recover), elevated error rates, Sev1 potential.
- **Cost impact:** Stalled replicas waste GPU capacity and increase retry/duplicate compute.

---

## Symptoms (what you’ll see)
### External (API / client-facing)
- Streaming response starts and then stops emitting tokens mid-decode.
- Requests remain in-flight until client timeout (commonly 60–300s depending on route).
- Retry storms (client SDK retries or application-level retries) amplify load.

### Internal (replica-level)
- **No tokens produced** while GPU utilization may remain non-zero or drop unexpectedly.
- One TP rank appears stuck while others continue to enqueue work (or also stop).
- NCCL may not throw an explicit error; hangs can be “silent” without async error handling.

### Common failure signatures (taxonomy)
We currently bucket stalls into these high-level signatures (see `runtime.tp_stall_reason` below):
1. **collective_wait**: rank waiting for NCCL collective completion.
2. **collective_mismatch**: collective ordering divergence across ranks (often manifests as silent wait).
3. **scheduler_starvation**: collectives not scheduled fairly under prefill-heavy batching.
4. **stream_sync_gap**: CUDA stream/event ordering issue around NCCL boundary.
5. **kv_compaction_divergence**: KV cache compaction/fragmentation causes rank-side divergence.
6. **cancelled_stream_deadlock**: client disconnect/cancellation leaves ranks in inconsistent step state.

---

## Affected configurations
This issue has been observed most reliably under the following conditions.

### Workload characteristics
- Mixed prompt lengths (high variance) + streaming decode
- Long context (8k–32k) + high concurrent requests
- Bursty arrival patterns (spikes causing deep scheduler queues)
- Prefill-heavy traffic interleaved with ongoing decodes

### Deployment modes
- **Dedicated:** most common due to steady saturation and strict p99 expectations.
- **Hosted:** seen in a smaller number of high-throughput routes during peak bursts.

### Models and TP sizes (most affected)
| Category | Examples | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Large dense, long-context | Llama-70B class, Qwen-72B class | Higher risk when TP=4/8 and context > 8k |
| MoE models | Mixtral 8x7B class | Sensitive to scheduling/fairness under mixed prefill/decode |
| Any model with aggressive batching | Any high-throughput route | Risk increases with deep queues and long prefill batches |

### Hardware / topology
| Hardware | Topologies seen | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| A100 80GB | NVLink intra-node | Most reproductions and customer reports |
| H100 80GB | NVLink intra-node | Also observed; typically at higher throughput |
| PCIe-only multi-GPU | Mixed | Less common in production; higher sensitivity to comms latency |

### Runtime versions
- Observed most often on **runtime 1.18.x** in the presence of CUDA graph capture + mixed workloads.
- Some signatures also present on early **1.19.0 canaries** prior to watchdog + ordering hardening.

---

## Detection signals (metrics, logs, traces)
### Dashboards
- See: **TP stall and timeout dashboard** (Confluence: `tp-stall-and-timeout-dashboard`).

### Key metrics (authoritative)
> Metric names reflect the current standards agreed with SRE; older versions may differ.

1) **Per-rank heartbeat**
- `runtime_tp_rank_heartbeat_seconds{replica_id, tp_rank, model, cluster}`
- Signal: heartbeats stop updating for one or more ranks.
- Rule of thumb: **gap > 10s** during active traffic is suspicious; **gap > 30s** is a likely stall.

2) **Stall reason counters**
- `runtime_tp_stall_reason_total{reason, model, tp_size, cluster}`
- Watch for spikes in `collective_wait`, `scheduler_starvation`, `cancelled_stream_deadlock`.

3) **In-flight collective counters**
- `runtime_nccl_inflight_collectives{replica_id, tp_rank, collective}`
- Signal: counter remains >0 with no progress (and heartbeat gap).

4) **Scheduler pressure indicators**
- `runtime_scheduler_queue_depth{replica_id, queue}`
- `runtime_scheduler_prefill_decode_ratio{replica_id}`
- Signal: queue depth grows while decode throughput collapses.

5) **Customer-visible indicators**
- `gateway_request_timeout_total{route, model}`
- `gateway_streaming_disconnect_total{route, model}`
- `request_p99_latency_ms{route, model}`

### Logs (what to grep)
Look for structured fields (availability depends on runtime version):
- `tp_stall_detected=true`
- `tp_rank=<int>` and `tp_size=<int>`
- `stall_reason=<enum>`
- `inflight_collectives=<int>`
- `last_progress_ms=<int>`

### NCCL debug (use with care)
Use only for time-boxed windows due to verbosity/perf impact. Coordinate with SRE (see INT: enable extra NCCL debug logging).
Suggested minimal settings for targeted capture:
- `NCCL_ASYNC_ERROR_HANDLING=1`
- `NCCL_DEBUG=WARN`
- `NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=COLL`

Do NOT leave `NCCL_DEBUG=INFO` enabled broadly on production Dedicated clusters.

---

## Immediate mitigations (incident-safe)
These mitigations prioritize restoring service and preventing global GPU wedging.

### 1) Drain/replace suspect replicas
- Drain the affected replica(s) at the orchestrator level (preferred) rather than waiting for recovery.
- If multiple replicas show heartbeat gaps, drain in a staggered fashion to avoid full capacity loss.

### 2) Reduce concurrency and/or batch size (fastest risk reduction)
Recommended temporary caps (starting point; adjust per model/hardware):
- Reduce `tp.max_concurrency_per_replica` by **30–50%**
- Reduce `max_batch_prefill_tokens` (or equivalent) by **25–40%**
- Prefer limiting **prefill batch growth** over decode to preserve streaming responsiveness

### 3) Disable high-risk execution paths (if available)
Depending on runtime version and flags, consider:
- Disable CUDA graphs for TP decode on affected routes:
  - `runtime.tp.cuda_graphs_decode.enabled=false`
- Enable conservative stream/event synchronization around NCCL:
  - `runtime.tp.nccl_stream_sync_hardening=on`

### 4) Enable watchdog + safe abort (where supported)
If the watchdog feature is available in your runtime build, enabling it can prevent indefinite hangs:
- `runtime.tp_watchdog.enabled=true`
- `runtime.tp_watchdog.timeout_ms=<workload-specific>` (see below)

> Watchdog enables **controlled abort + replica drain** semantics instead of indefinite waits. This will increase error counts during true stalls but improves overall availability.

### 5) Load shedding / routing fallback (platform-level)
- If stall signals are present, enable overload protection to **reject/redirect new requests** away from the wedged replica pool.
- Prefer fallback to a compatible model variant/region if configured for Dedicated/Hosted.

---

## Recommended default mitigations (non-incident)
For clusters with frequent TP stall history, keep these guardrails enabled until runtime 1.19.2+ is fully deployed.

### Configuration guardrails
| Guardrail | Recommendation | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Concurrency cap | Set conservative `tp.max_concurrency_per_replica` | Reduces scheduler pressure and mixed-step divergence risk |
| Prefill batch cap | Limit `max_batch_prefill_tokens` | Prevents prefill-heavy batches from starving collectives/decodes |
| Async error handling | `NCCL_ASYNC_ERROR_HANDLING=1` | Surfaces errors sooner; reduces silent waits |
| Stream sync hardening | Enable if perf impact acceptable | Avoids event/stream ordering gaps around collectives |
| Watchdog | Enable with staged rollout | Converts indefinite hang into bounded failure + recovery |

### Watchdog timeout guidance
Use model/workload-specific defaults; avoid overly aggressive thresholds that create false positives under long-context.
- Small/medium (≤13B dense): start at **8–12s**
- Large dense (≥70B) TP=4/8: start at **15–25s**
- Long-context (≥16k): start at **25–40s**

Always stage changes:
1) Canary one cluster/route
2) Validate stall detection + error rate impact
3) Expand to Dedicated
4) Expand to Hosted

---

## Triage checklist (confirming a TP hang)
Follow the detailed steps in the playbook (Confluence: `tp-stall-triage-playbook`). Quick checklist:

1) **Confirm customer symptom**
- Streaming stuck mid-response, elevated timeouts, p99 jump.

2) **Check TP heartbeat gaps**
- Identify impacted `replica_id` and `tp_rank`.

3) **Correlate with in-flight collectives**
- `runtime_nccl_inflight_collectives` stuck >0 indicates comms boundary involvement.

4) **Check scheduler pressure**
- Queue depth rising while throughput drops suggests scheduler starvation component.

5) **Search logs for stall reason**
- Confirm `stall_reason` and `last_progress_ms`.

6) **Mitigate**
- Drain replica(s) and apply caps/flags.

7) **Capture artifacts** (only if safe)
- Minimal NCCL WARN logs
- Trace IDs for representative stuck requests
- Replica runtime logs around the stall window

---

## Fix status / roadmap
This is an active reliability initiative tracked in Linear: **ENG-4821**.

### Fixes delivered / in-flight
| Area | Status | References |
|---|---|---|
| Heartbeat + stall reason tagging | Landed | PR-21834; dashboard panels in observability pack PR-412 |
| Scheduler fairness / collective ordering guardrails | Landed | PR-21841; mitigates `scheduler_starvation` and ordering divergence |
| NCCL stream/event sync hardening | Landed (feature-flagged) | PR-21853; evaluate perf impact per model |
| Watchdog + safe abort + replica drain | Landed (feature-flagged) | PR-21860; ADR-0127 defines semantics |
| KV cache compaction safety | Landed | PR-21866; targets `kv_compaction_divergence` |
| Cancelled streaming deadlock fix | Landed | PR-21890; targets disconnect-triggered stalls |
| Improved NCCL error surfacing | In rollout | PR-21912; improves customer-facing diagnostics |
| Load shed on TP stall signal | In rollout | PR-21875 |

### Version guidance (operational)
| Runtime version | Guidance |
|---|---|
| ≤ 1.18.7 | Higher risk. Keep concurrency/prefill caps. Prefer disabling CUDA graphs for TP decode on affected routes. Drain-on-stall is primary recovery. |
| 1.19.0–1.19.1 | Use only with watchdog and stream sync hardening flags in canary first. Validate stall reasons and noise. |
| 1.19.2+ | Target stable baseline for Dedicated + high-throughput Hosted. Keep monitoring; reduce guardrails only after 2+ weeks without stall alerts on target workloads. |

### Rollout plan
- Dedicated-first rollout with explicit go/no-go gates: see Linear **ENG-4829**.
- Canary success metrics:
  - TP stall alerts reduced by **>80%** week-over-week (normalized)
  - Request timeouts attributable to TP stalls reduced to **<0.1%** of requests on canary routes
  - No sustained p99 regression > **5%** after enabling stream sync hardening/watchdog

---

## Customer communication notes (Support/CS)
When communicating with customers, avoid over-specifying a single root cause unless confirmed by artifacts. Recommended phrasing:
- “We have identified a class of TP forward-progress stalls under specific mixed workloads. We are rolling out runtime changes to improve collective ordering, stream synchronization, and add bounded-time watchdog recovery.”

If asking for customer artifacts, request:
- Affected model + TP size, GPU type, context length distribution
- Approx concurrency at time of stall
- Example request IDs / timestamps
- Whether stalls correlate with client disconnects

Support-facing summary and templated mitigations are maintained in: **customer-success-and-support/known-issues-and-workarounds/tp-timeouts-workaround-dedicated**.

---

## Owner / escalation
- Primary owner: **Eng Serving Runtime (Kernel + Scheduling)**
- Incident escalation: **#eng-sre** + **#eng-runtime** (include replica IDs, model, TP size, and stall reason metrics)
- Contacts:
  - Runtime TL: Noah Patel
  - Kernel: Hiro Tanaka / Grace Kim
  - Scheduling: Sofia Ivanova / Julian Moore
  - SRE lead: Rafael Mendes / Aisha Bello

---

## Changelog
- 2025-03-04: Updated version guidance for 1.19.2+ rollout gates; added cancelled-streaming deadlock signature and mitigation.
- 2025-02-20: Added heartbeat and stall reason metric names; linked dashboard and ADR.
- 2024-11-12: Initial publication based on Dedicated TP timeout reports and early repro findings.

title: Kernel telemetry annotation guidelines and observability cookbook
content:
Summary

Purpose: establish a consistent, low-overhead telemetry and annotation scheme for kernel-level events in the Redwood serving runtime so engineers can rapidly correlate performance anomalies to code, scheduling decisions, and hardware signals. This doc is a practical cookbook: schema, tagging rules, example dashboards, alert mapping, and step-by-step triage flows.

Scope
- Applies to all production and pre-production runtime kernels (attention kernels, kv-cache manager, batching scheduler, device transfers).
- Includes: span/tracing annotations, metric labels, log enrichment, histogram buckets, and example dashboard panels.
- Excludes: application-level business traces (those belong to product services).

Why this matters
- Kernels are the primary source of per-token latency variance. Without consistent annotations you cannot correlate tail latency to kernel selection, quantization path, or NUMA placement.
- Standardized telemetry reduces mean time to triage (MTTT) for SREs and runtime engineers and enables automated regression detection.

OWNER & ROUTING
- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime (runtime-observability subteam)
- Oncall routing: runtime-sre -> page if P0, slack #runtime-observability for P1/P2 context.

Telemetry primitives (schema)
- Traces/spans: all kernel entry points must emit a trace span with the following tags (attributes):
  - span.name: kernel.<family>.<op> e.g. kernel.attention.forward, kernel.kvcache.fetch
  - kernel.version: semantic version of kernel binary (e.g. 2025.10.3)
  - model.variant: redwood/gptq-7b-q4
  - quantization.path: fp16|int8|gptq
  - device: gpu-0|gpu-1|cpu
  - shard_id: shard-<id>
  - scheduling.policy: fair|priority|batching
  - batch_size: integer
  - seq_len: integer (input sequence length for this request)
  - kernel_rows_processed: integer (work metric)
  - kvcache.hit: true|false
  - fallback.triggered: true|false (if a higher-latency fallback path was used)
  - enqueue_time_ms: numeric (time spent waiting in software queue)

- Metrics: expose the following (Prometheus naming conventions recommended):
  - kernel_duration_seconds{kernel_family, kernel_op, device, model_variant} histogram
  - kernel_enqueue_seconds{...} histogram
  - kernel_work_units_total{...} counter
  - kernel_error_count{...} counter
  - kernel_qcache_hit_ratio{model_variant, shard_id} gauge (0..1)

- Logging: structured JSON logs at INFO/ERROR with fields: ts, span_id, trace_id, span.name, kernel.version, device, shard_id, batch_size, seq_len, msg. Avoid freeform stack traces in INFO.

Annotation rules (do this for every kernel entry/exit)
1) Small, deterministic tags only: prefer short keys (<=20 chars) and low-cardinality values. High-cardinality values (request_id, user_id, prompt_hash) should be attached only to span logs, not as metric labels.
2) Device and shard must use canonical identifiers (gpu-0..gpu-N, numa-0..). Mapping table maintained in /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/shard-id-lookup.
3) Quantization path: annotate all internal kernel branches that change numeric width. Use the canonical set: fp32, fp16, int8, gptq.
4) Scheduler policy: annotate the policy decision that scheduled the kernel run. If multiple policies applied, include the resolved policy and a comma-separated policy_stack attribute.

Sampling & cardinality controls
- Default sampling: 1% of all traces for production traffic; 100% for traces with kernel_duration_seconds bucket > 0.99 (99th percentile) or if fallback.triggered=true.
- High-variance buckets (seq_len > 2048 or batch_size > 64) must be sampled at 10% by default.
- Retention: raw traces retained for 14 days; aggregated histograms 90 days.

Recommended histograms & buckets
- kernel_duration_seconds buckets (seconds): [0.0001, 0.0005, 0.001, 0.002, 0.005, 0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.5]
- enqueue_time_ms (ms): [0.1, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 250, 500]
- These buckets are optimized for sub-1ms kernel latencies while still capturing pathological multi-second stalls.

Example instrumentation snippets
- C++ (span creation with OpenTelemetry):

  // create span at kernel entry
  auto span = tracer->StartSpan("kernel.attention.forward");
  span->SetAttribute("kernel.version", "2025.10.3");
  span->SetAttribute("model.variant", model_variant);
  span->SetAttribute("quantization.path", "gptq");
  span->SetAttribute("device", device_id);
  span->SetAttribute("shard_id", shard_id);

- Python (metrics export example):

  from prometheus_client import Histogram, Counter
  kernel_duration = Histogram('kernel_duration_seconds', 'Kernel latency', ['kernel_family','kernel_op','device','model_variant'])
  kernel_duration.labels('attention','forward','gpu-0','redwood/7b').observe(0.00072)

Telemetry enrichment and cross-product correlation
- Correlate model-level request traces (API spans) with kernel spans via trace_id. Ensure API-side instrumentation adds trace_id and root.span_id to request metadata so downstream kernel spans inherit it.
- Add a consistent prompt_hash tag (sha1 of normalized prompt) in the API span only. Kernel spans should reference prompt_hash only in logs, not as metric labels.

Dashboards: canonical panels (Grafana recommended)
- Kernel overview panel (heatmap): kernel_duration_seconds heatmap by kernel_family vs device; group by model_variant.
- Tail-latency waterfall: stacked bars showing enqueue, kernel, kvcache_fetch, device-transfer contributions for 50/90/99/99.9 percentiles.
- Scheduler policy impact: boxplots of kernel_duration_seconds by scheduling.policy.
- KVCache hit map: time-series of kernel_qcache_hit_ratio by shard_id.
- Regression indicator: change-point detector that compares 24h median kernel_duration_seconds to 7-day baseline; raises warning at >15% and P0 at >50%.

Example alerting table
| Alert name | Signal | Threshold | Severity | Runbook link | Owner |
| Kernel-tail-latency | kernel_duration_seconds 99.9p aggregated over 5m | > 60th baseline * 2 (or > 200ms absolute) | P1 | /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/kernel-high-tail-latency | eng-sre |
| Scheduler-queue-buildup | rate(kernel_enqueue_seconds_count[5m]) increasing & queue length > 200 | sustained 5m | P2 | /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/scheduler-queue-eviction | runtime-oncall |
| Fallback-rate-spike | ratio(fallback.triggered) > 1% | 1m | P0 if > 5% | /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/fallback-investigation | runtime-sre |

Triage playbook (step-by-step)
1) Detect: alert fires and oncall is paged.
2) Initial gather (5 min): collect: relevant traces, last 30m histograms, scheduler queue lengths, device-level metrics (GPU SM utilization, PCIe transfer latency), and kernel.version across hosts. Use the Diagnostic bundle collector: /scripts/collect-kernel-diagnostics.sh --trace-id <trace> --since 30m.
3) Correlate: find top kernel_family and kernel_op contributing to 99.9p. If enqueue_time_ms dominates, jump to scheduler playbook. If kernel_duration_seconds dominates, check kernel.version and quantization.path.
4) Isolate: toggle canary routing to an alternative kernel variant (if available) or pin model to previous kernel.version. For Dedicated clusters use: rctl route update --model <id> --kernel-version <previous>.
5) Mitigate: scale up capacity on the affected shard pool or switch routing policy to lower-latency fallback.
6) Post-incident: capture a regression report with before/after histograms and root cause. Link to regression in the changelog: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/release-notes/kernel-version-changelog.

Example diagnostic CLI outputs (simulated)

  $ collect-kernel-diagnostics.sh --since 10m
  HOST      GPU  kernel.attention.forward.p50  kernel.attention.forward.p99  enqueue-ms
  g-12-01   0    0.00072                      0.0048                       0.8
  g-12-02   1    0.00068                      0.0069                       4.2

Ownership & release rules
- Any kernel change that touches scheduling or quantization must include telemetry coverage: a signed checklist in the PR template (see PR checklist section below). Telemetry must be present in unit/integration tests prior to merge.

PR checklist (required fields)
1) Telemetry emitted for kernel entry/exit with required attributes.
2) Prometheus metric names and histogram buckets documented in PR description.
3) Load test run attached (link to perf run) demonstrating no >5% regression in median or 15% in 99.9p.
4) Reviewers: runtime + observability + performance owners.

Sample PR description snippet

  Telemetry: Emit span "kernel.attention.forward" with attributes [kernel.version: 2026.01.1, quantization.path: gptq, shard_id].
  Metrics: kernel_duration_seconds histogram (buckets: [..])
  Load test: https://perf.redwood.internal/runs/98765

Common troubleshooting patterns and fixes
- Symptom: 99.9p up but median stable.
  - Likely causes: device interference (noisy neighbor), sporadic kernel fallback, or small sample of large seq_len. Check kernel.version mismatch across hosts and fallback.triggered logs.
- Symptom: uniform latency increase across all percentiles.
  - Likely causes: resource saturation (GPU SM, memory bandwidth) or a model-level regression. Check device utilization and recent model rollout.
- Symptom: enqueue_time spikes without corresponding backend kernel duration increase.
  - Likely causes: scheduler misconfiguration or queue starvation. Apply scheduler debug flags and collect queue histograms.

Appendices
A) Example trace JSON (span-level)\n{
  "trace_id": "abcd1234efgh",
  "spans": [
    {"span_id":"s1","name":"api.request","attributes":{"prompt_hash":"...","model_variant":"redwood/7b"}},
    {"span_id":"s2","name":"kernel.attention.forward","attributes":{"kernel.version":"2026.01.1","device":"gpu-0","shard_id":"shard-7","batch_size":8,"seq_len":512,"kernel_rows_processed":1024}}
  ]
}

B) Common PromQL snippets
- 99.9p kernel latency for attention forward across GPUs:
  histogram_quantile(0.999, sum(rate(kernel_duration_seconds_bucket{kernel_op="forward",kernel_family="attention"}[5m])) by (le, device))
- Percent of kernels hitting fallback:
  sum(rate(kernel_error_count{reason="fallback"}[1m])) / sum(rate(kernel_work_units_total[1m]))

C) Migration notes for legacy telemetry
- Existing legacy spans (pre-2025) used keys like "kernel_type" and "lat_ms". A migration adapter will translate legacy keys to the canonical names for 12 months; new code must use canonical names immediately.

Contacts and escalation
- Runtime observability owners: Aisha Patel (author), Diego Martinez (runtime-sre), Evelyn Zhou (profiling).
- Pager: runtime-oncall (P0/P1). Slack: #runtime-observability.

Document change log
- 2025-05-14: created initial draft.
- 2025-10-02: added sampling and histogram recommendations (Evelyn Zhou).
- 2026-02-10: clarified fallback and scheduler policy annotations; tightened bucket defs (Samir Bhatt).

Related resources
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/runtime-profiling-playbook-guidelines-2025
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/numa-aware-shard-placement-eviction-playbook-2026
- Diagnostics script: /infra/tools/collect-kernel-diagnostics.sh

End of document

title: Runtime concurrency isolation and telemetry handbook
content:
Overview
========
This handbook describes Redwood Inference's conventions and operational practices for runtime concurrency isolation, lane-based request shaping, and the minimum telemetry required to detect and diagnose cross-tenant or cross-model interference. It consolidates architecture rationale, configuration examples, diagnostics runbooks, and rollout guidance for changing isolation or sampling policies in production.

Goals
-----
- Ensure noisy tenants or long-context workloads do not violate p95/p99 latency SLOs for other tenants sharing GPUs.
- Provide a consistent taxonomy (lanes, credits, isolation zones) for engineers and SREs to reason about scheduling and fairness.
- Define telemetry, sampling, and alerting so incidents can be triaged without deep kernel-level tracing for every case.

Scope
-----
This doc covers: request lanes, concurrency caps, credit accounting surface (what we expose to schedulers), required metrics, tracing annotations, recommended sampling rates, default configuration snippets for the runtime, and step-by-step operational procedures for common investigations. It does not attempt to re-specify kernel internals; refer to kernel mapper docs for low-level execution mappings.

Key concepts and terminology
----------------------------
- Lane: a logical request class (e.g., realtime, bulk-embed, batching-internal) that maps to priority and concurrency rules.
- Concurrency cap: the maximum number of inflight tokens/requests the runtime will accept for a given lane on a shard.
- Credit bucket: run-time accounting unit used for fair-share scheduling; credits are consumed per request based on model type and sequence length estimate.
- Isolation zone: grouping of shards and GPUs with stronger anti-affinity guarantees (used for Dedicated/Private customers).
- Soft preemption: a request can be signaled to yield before kernel dispatch when higher-priority work arrives; used to reduce tail latency.

Default lane taxonomy (recommended)
---------------------------------
1. realtime (default for host-api): low concurrency, highest priority, target p99 latency SLO.
2. interactive (chat UIs): medium concurrency, allow limited batching, mid priority.
3. bulk (embeddings, large generation jobs): high concurrency, low priority, throughput-optimized.
4. system (healthchecks, tracing-heartbeat): dedicated tiny lane, unthrottled internal access.

Default SLOs by lane
---------------------
| lane      | p50 latency | p95 latency | p99 latency | throughput expectation |
|-----------|-------------|-------------|-------------|------------------------|
| realtime  | < 20 ms     | < 60 ms     | < 200 ms    | low (1-10 rps per shard)|
| interactive | < 30 ms   | < 150 ms    | < 400 ms    | medium (10-200 rps)    |
| bulk      | variable    | variable    | variable    | high (hundreds rps)    |
| system    | < 10 ms     | < 20 ms     | < 50 ms     | negligible             |

Telemetry and instrumentation requirements
-----------------------------------------
At minimum, every request entering the serving runtime MUST emit the following fields as metrics or tracing tags:
- request_id (trace id or UUID)
- tenant_id (customer id or internal)
- lane (one of realtime/interactive/bulk/system)
- model_id (model artifact name + version)
- sequence_length_estimate (int; else -1)
- kernel_kind (e.g., attention-sharded, ffn-fused) when available
- shard_id and gpu_id
- admission_decision (accepted | rejected | queued)
- credit_cost_estimate (tokens * cost_multiplier)

Required metrics (per-shard, 30s resolution recommended)
- runtime.requests_total{lane,tenant,model} (counter)
- runtime.requests_rejected{reason,lane,tenant} (counter)
- runtime.latency_ms_bucket{le,lane,model} (histogram)
- runtime.inflight_requests{lane,shard,gpu} (gauge)
- runtime.credit_balance{tenant,shard} (gauge)
- runtime.kvcache_hit_rate{model,shard} (gauge)
- runtime.kernel_queue_length{kernel_kind,shard} (gauge)

Tracing and span annotations
- root span: runtime.request - tags: lane, tenant_id, model_id, sequence_length_estimate.
- latency spans: admission -> batching -> kernel_dispatch -> kernel_exec -> response_serialize.
- errors and preemption events must attach event annotations that include current_credit_balance and preempting_request_id.

Sampling policy (recommended defaults)
-------------------------------------
- 100% sampling for realtime lane traces for first 5 minutes following deploys or config changes (see Rollout guidance).
- 2% uniform sampling for interactive lane (min 1 trace per 10 minutes per model).
- 0.5% sampling for bulk (unless latency tail is elevated, then escalate to 5%).
- System lane: sample at 10% for health-periodic analysis.

Operational runbook: diagnosing cross-tenant interference (step-by-step)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Get context: incident time window and affected tenant(s). Correlate with deployment events in last 30 minutes.
2. Query metrics: runtime.inflight_requests and runtime.kernel_queue_length by shard for the time window. Look for queue spikes that align with latency regressions.
3. Check admission_rejected counters: if rejects increased for realtime lane, inspect which tenants are contributing to credit exhaustion (runtime.credit_balance).
4. If kernel_queue_length high but inflight low, suspect backend kernel stalls: pull kernel_exec span durations from tracing and grep for specific kernel_kind anomalies.
5. If preemption events recorded, find preempting_request_id and evaluate its tenant and model.
6. Mitigate:                                                       
   a. If a single tenant is noisy, apply per-tenant temporary concurrency caps: POST /admin/runtime/tenants/{tenant_id}/caps {"max_concurrency": 4, "lane":"bulk"} 
   b. If kernel stalls, switch the shard to a different kernel profile: POST /admin/shards/{shard_id}/kernel-profile {"profile":"low-latency"} (see Kernel scheduling interactions below).
   c. If kv-cache hot key miss storms present, enable request-level kvcache warmup for affected models.
7. Validate: watch p95/p99 and credit_balance for 10 minutes; if not recovered, escalate to SRE on-call.

Kernel scheduling interactions (practical notes)
----------------------------------------------
- The kernel scheduler consumes credits to assign kernels to SMs. When tuning lane caps, consider that lowering concurrency in the runtime can change observed kernel occupancy and shift breakpoints where attention kernels move between sharded and fused implementations.
- Suggested guardrails: do not reduce runtime concurrency for a shard below 2 concurrent kernel dispatches for models with sequence_length_estimate > 1024; below that risk of throughput collapse due to underutilized SMs.

Recommended configuration snippets
--------------------------------
JSON example: runtime admission policy (place in /etc/redwood/runtime/admission.json)

{
  "lanes": {
    "realtime": {"priority": 100, "max_concurrency_per_shard": 8, "credit_multiplier": 1.2},
    "interactive": {"priority": 80, "max_concurrency_per_shard": 32, "credit_multiplier": 1.0},
    "bulk": {"priority": 20, "max_concurrency_per_shard": 256, "credit_multiplier": 0.6},
    "system": {"priority": 110, "max_concurrency_per_shard": 16, "credit_multiplier": 0.1}
  },
  "per_tenant_default_credit": 1000
}

CLI sample commands (admin only):
- View per-shard inflight: redwood-admin runtime shards list --metrics inflight_requests --window 60s
- Apply temporary tenant cap: redwood-admin runtime tenant update --tenant 12345 --max-concurrency 6 --lane bulk
- Force immediate kernel profile: redwood-admin kernel set-profile --shard s-7 --profile low-latency

Rollout and change management guidance
-------------------------------------
1. Any change to admission.json that alters max_concurrency_per_shard or credit multipliers requires a staged rollout: 10% -> 50% -> 100% of shards over 30 minutes with 5-minute monitoring at each stage.
2. When increasing sampling rates for realtime traces, coordinate with Observability team to validate ingestion quotas.
3. Emergency rollback: restore previous admission.json via the runtime-configs artifact ID and POST /admin/runtime/reload-config.

Telemetry alert thresholds (suggested)
-------------------------------------
- Alert A1: realtime_lane_p95_exceeded -> trigger when p95 > 2x goal for 5 minutes. Severity: P1.
- Alert A2: inflight_spike -> runtime.inflight_requests{lane=realtime} increases > 3x baseline for 2 minutes. Severity: P2.
- Alert A3: credit_drain -> runtime.credit_balance{tenant} drops to 0 and requests_rejected increases > 10/min. Severity: P1.

Ownership and contacts
----------------------
- Runtime architecture owner: Jordan Kim (eng-serving-runtime).
- SRE on-call: see /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/oncall-rotation.
- Observability and metrics steward: Maya Lopez (eng-platform).

Appendix A — Sampling matrix (compact)
-------------------------------------
| lane | deploy-time sampling | steady-state sampling | spike escalation |
|------|----------------------|-----------------------|-------------------|
| realtime | 100% for 5m | 2% | up to 100% if p99 > target |
| interactive | 20% for 5m | 2% | 10% if p95 > target |
| bulk | 5% for 5m | 0.5% | 5% if throughput anomaly |

Appendix B — Troubleshooting quick commands
-------------------------------------------
- list top tenants by credit usage (last 10m):
  redwood-admin runtime tenants top-usage --window 10m --limit 20
- tail kernel spans for shard s-7:
  redwood-trace query --shard s-7 --service runtime.kernel --span kernel_exec --since 5m | jq '.duration_ms' | sort -nr | head -n 50

Related documentation
---------------------
See: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/continuous-runtime-profiling-strategy-2026, /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/adaptive-kernel-mapper-and-scaling-playbook-2026 for kernel-level details, and the admissions API spec in eng-developer-experience/api-examples/admissions-api-spec (internal link).

Change log
----------
- 2025-09-12: Created by Ava Chen.
- 2025-11-03: Added default sampling matrix and CLI commands (reviewers: Ravi Desai).
- 2026-02-08: Updated SLO guidance and rollout policy following Q4 experiments (reviewers: Maya Lopez).

title: Runtime experiment signal catalog and hypothesis matrix
content:
Purpose
-------
This document centralizes the signal definitions, collection guidance, and hypothesis matrix for runtime experiments across Redwood's serving stack. It is intended for engineers running controlled performance experiments, A/B rollouts, profiling campaigns, and benchmark suites. The goal is to reduce ambiguity about which telemetry to use for which kind of experiment and to standardize evaluation heuristics and rollback criteria.

Scope
-----
Applies to hosted, dedicated, and private runtime variants. Focused on: request path telemetry, kernel scheduling metrics, KV cache signals, batching utilization, and cost-attribution signals used by Redwood Optimize and runtime autoscalers. Not a replacement for incident runbooks; where an experiment reveals an incident, follow the incident playbooks in oncall_and_incident_response.

Quick summary (one-line)
----------------------
Use this catalog to: (1) select 3–5 core signals for hypothesis acceptance, (2) set primary/secondary thresholds, (3) follow the step-by-step experiment run, and (4) export the result to the benchmark suite for regression tracking.

Signal catalog and rationale
---------------------------
Each signal below includes: name, cardinality (per-request / per-slot / host-level), sampling guidance, expected distribution shape, primary/secondary use, and recommended alert thresholds for experiments.

1) request.latency_ms.{p50,p95,p99} (per-route, per-model)
- Cardinality: per-request aggregated by route/model/region.
- Sampling: full for release-level A/B; 10% for long-running smoke experiments.
- Distribution: heavy right tail; expect multiple modes if mixed sequence lengths.
- Use: Primary for latency SLO experiments.
- Experiment thresholds: delta(p95) <= +10% relative for canary acceptance; delta(p99) <= +20% triggers manual triage.

2) kernel.queue_depth_avg (per-device, per-kernel-type)
- Cardinality: device,kernel-type (attention, ff, matmul).
- Sampling: continuous at 1s resolution.
- Distribution: near-zero for elastic workloads; spikes indicate contention.
- Use: Secondary signal to explain latency regressions.
- Thresholds: sustained > 50% of peak slot count for >30s => consider reducing concurrency or increasing slots.

3) kvcache.hit_rate (session-id, per-model)
- Cardinality: session-level aggregated to route/model.
- Sampling: computed on write-window (1m).
- Distribution: dependent on prompt reuse; typical baseline for chat products is 0.35–0.85.
- Use: Primary when testing prefix caching or warmup strategies.
- Thresholds: drop > 15 percentage points relative -> expect token cost increase; auto-fallthrough if paired with latency increase.

4) batch_utilization_pct (executor-pod, per-1m)
- Cardinality: executor-pod.
- Sampling: 10s rolling window.
- Distribution: multi-modal depending on client batching.
- Use: Primary for cost-efficiency experiments; correlate with tokens/sec.
- Thresholds: sustained < 20% while throughput stable suggests misconfiguration (e.g., slice size mismatch).

5) kernel.exec_time_ms.{mean,95th} (per-kernel-type, per-device)
- Cardinality: kernel-type, device.
- Use: Diagnosing scheduling vs kernel inefficiency.
- Thresholds: > +25% mean vs baseline => flag for kernel rollout hold.

6) memory.gpu.free_mb and memory.gpu.fragmentation_pct (node-level)
- Use: Safety signals for private/on-prem experiments; fragmentation > 60% + free_mb < reserve -> OOM risk.

7) cost.per_token_usd (route, model_variant)
- Use: Primary for Optimize-driven experiments.
- Calculation: (infra_cost + reserved_amortization) / tokens_generated.

Instrumentation and collection guidance
-------------------------------------
- Services and names: rdx-runtime-dispatcher (ingest), rdx-kernel-agent (device-facing), rdx-kvcache (session store), rdx-metrics-aggregator, rdx-benchmark-runner. Tag metrics with: service, cluster, region, model, model_variant, route, experiment_id, canary_group.
- Metric format: Prometheus-style timeseries with labels above; export to metrics pipeline with 10s scrape where possible and 1s for kernel-level counters.
- Logs: include structured JSON request events with fields: request_id, route, model, seq_len_in, seq_len_out, kernel_hints, start_ts, end_ts. Example: 

```json
{
  "request_id": "r-7f3a2c",
  "route": "chat-default",
  "model": "open-vicuna-13b-quant-v2",
  "seq_len_in": 64,
  "seq_len_out": 128,
  "kernel_hints": "sharded-attn",
  "start_ts": "2027-02-10T15:12:03.123Z",
  "end_ts": "2027-02-10T15:12:03.379Z"
}
```

Benchmark config and expected artifacts
--------------------------------------
When converting an experiment to a benchmark, include a config file. Minimal example (YAML):

```yaml
benchmark_name: kvcache-warmup-vs-none
model: rdx-llama-30b-q4
routes: [chat-default]
workload_profile: production-sampled-2027-01
duration: 30m
concurrency: 64
metrics: [request.latency_ms.p95, kvcache.hit_rate, batch_utilization_pct, cost.per_token_usd]
export_to: perf-db://benchmarks/kvcache-warmup-vs-none-2027-02-10
```

Expected artifacts:
- raw telemetry (prometheus histograms + traces)
- per-request logs (parquet)
- experiment summary (markdown) with stat tests (see below)

Hypothesis matrix and statistical evaluation rules
--------------------------------------------------
Use the following convention for experiment outcomes: Primary signals (1–2) must meet acceptance thresholds; secondary signals should exhibit no regression beyond soft thresholds.

- Hypothesis example: "Enabling async kvcache prefetch will reduce p95 latency by >= 8% without increasing cost per token by > 5%."
- Primary signals: request.latency_ms.p95 (delta <= -8%) and kvcache.hit_rate (delta >= +6 percentage points).
- Secondary signals: cost.per_token_usd (delta <= +5%), kernel.queue_depth_avg (no sustained >75% saturation).

Statistical rules:
1) Use bootstrap resampling over per-request latencies; report 95% confidence intervals for deltas.
2) Accept only if delta and CI both exceed the acceptance threshold in the favorable direction.
3) For cost signals where variance is high, cap sample variance by stratifying on seq_len buckets: [0-64, 65-256, 257+].

Experiment runbook (step-by-step)
--------------------------------
1) Define experiment_id and register in the experiments board (team-wiki experiments index).
2) Select the core signals (max 5). Mark primaries.
3) Create benchmark config and a dedicated metrics dashboard with experiment_id filter.
4) Run warmup: 10 minutes at 25% target load to populate caches.
5) Execute canary: 5–10% traffic for 30 minutes.
6) Collect telemetry and run stats pipeline: 
   - Command: rdx-benchmark-runner analyze --experiment-id EXP123 --save-summary ./summary.md
7) Evaluate acceptance per hypothesis matrix.
8) If accepted, escalate to rollout plan (see rollout checklist). If rejected, capture triage notes and create a follow-up profiling ticket.

Rollout checklist and safety gates
----------------------------------
- Gate 1 (canary acceptance): primary signals meet thresholds; no kernel exec_time regression > 25%.
- Gate 2 (stability hold): run 2h at 50% traffic with continuous monitoring; no alerts fired.
- Gate 3 (full rollout): ramp to 100% over 3 steps (50%, 75%, 100%) with 10–20 minute hold per step.

Rollback criteria (automated and manual)
---------------------------------------
Automated rollback (preferred): any of:
- request.latency_ms.p99 increases > 40% for > 2 minutes.
- kernel.queue_depth_avg sustained > 80% for > 60s and accompanied by increase in request errors.
- memory.gpu.fragmentation_pct leads to OOM events.

Manual rollback: triggered by oncall if triage finds systemic regression in model quality (see eval signals) or client-facing error rates > 0.5% over 10m.

Tracing and attribution guidance
-------------------------------
- Ensure each request carries experiment_id, route, and model_variant. Span composition should include: dispatcher -> scheduler -> kernel-agent -> kvcache.
- For expensive experiments, enable 100% traces for canaries for 5–10 minutes to capture tail behaviors.

Examples: short triage checklist for a regression
------------------------------------------------
1) Confirm metric delta with raw per-request data (avoid dashboard smoothing artifacts).
2) Check kernel.exec_time_ms by kernel-type to see if new kernel hints caused regressions.
3) Inspect kvcache.hit_rate and warmup windows; check prefetch logs.
4) Run microbench: single-request microbench with the failing profile using rdx-runtime-local-runner.
5) If kernel-level, annotate a kernel snapshot and assign to kernel-team for kernel rollout revert.

Ownership and contacts
----------------------
- Document owner: runtime-performance guild (alias: #runtime-performance).
- Primary engineering owner: Aisha Patel (aisha@redwood.example.com).
- Secondary owners: Marco Chen (kernel), Dana Ortiz (profiling/telemetry).
- Pager: runtime-oncall (see oncall rotation page).

Appendix A — canonical metrics queries
--------------------------------------
PromQL examples (simplified):
- p95 latency: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_latency_seconds_bucket{route="chat-default",experiment_id=~"EXP.*"}[1m])) by (le))
- kvcache hit rate: sum(rate(kvcache_hits_total{model=~".*"}[1m])) / sum(rate(kvcache_requests_total{model=~".*"}[1m]))

Appendix B — experiment result template (markdown)
--------------------------------------------------
- experiment_id: EXP123
- hypothesis: text
- primary_signals: list with baselines and deltas
- secondary_signals: list
- raw_artifacts: link to perf-db
- statistical_summary: link
- verdict: accept | reject | inconclusive
- triage_notes: free text

Related pages and references
----------------------------
- Runtime profiling playbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/runtime-profiling-playbook-guidelines-2025
- Benchmarking suite guide: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/mixed-workload-slo-simulation-suite-2026
- Autotune framework: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/runtime-autotune-framework-spec-2026

Change log
----------
- 2026-11-15: created by Aisha Patel (first draft).
- 2026-12-21: added bootstrap rules and cost stratification (reviewer: Marco Chen).
- 2027-02-10: updated thresholds and rollout ramping guidance (reviewer: Dana Ortiz).

End of document

title: Cross-layer Experiment Matrix and Validation Checklist
content:
Summary:
This document is a consolidated experiment matrix and validation checklist for cross-layer runtime experiments that touch kernel scheduling, KV-cache behavior, profiling instrumentation, and benchmark acceptance. It's intended for engineiners running controlled experiments that may affect SLOs and cost. Use this as the canonical checklist and runbook for planning, executing, and validating experiments that modify scheduler policies, kernel variants, or observation sampling rates.

Scope and audience:
- Scope: experiments affecting serving runtime execution path, kernel selection, batching, KV cache prefetch, and telemetry sampling.
- Audience: runtime engineers, SREs, performance researchers, release engineers.

High-level experiment categories (matrix):
1) Scheduling policy changes
  - Example: priority-driven crediting -> opportunistic slot coalescing
  - Impact areas: tail latency, fairness, kernel queue depth, eviction rate
2) Kernel variant rollouts
  - Example: fast-attention-v2 vs safe-attention-v1 (reduced memory, different numeric stability)
  - Impact: per-token CPU/GPU time, p99 latency, EPS (errors per second)
3) KV-cache behavior and prefetch tuning
  - Example: asynchronous prefetch enabled/disabled, prefetch window size
  - Impact: cold-starts, token generation latency, cache warmup time
4) Telemetry and sampling changes
  - Example: full traces -> sampled traces with adaptive enrichment
  - Impact: signal fidelity, profiling cost, root-cause analysis windows
5) Quantization/Kernel-precision changes
  - Example: fp16 -> int8 with calibration profile B
  - Impact: model quality regressions, kernel numerical edgecases

Experiment planning checklist (pre-run):
- Define hypothesis in a single sentence. Example: "Opportunistic slot coalescing reduces average batch overhead by >= 8% without increasing p99 latency by > 5%."
- Identify owners and reviewer: owner (runtime-team), reviewer (profiling-team lead).
- Identify target canary cohort: (e.g., internal-dev, 5% routed to experimental pool).
- Required approvals: SLO-risk review (eng-sre), data-privacy signoff (if traces contain customer content).
- Safety gates: circuit-breaker thresholds (see table).

Safety gate thresholds (example):
- p50 latency: no increase > 15%
- p95 latency: no increase > 10%
- p99 latency: no increase > 5%
- Error rate: no absolute increase > 0.05% or > 2x baseline (whichever smaller)
- Observability signal: successful trace capture >= 60% of warm requests

Validation matrix (what to measure):
- Latency: p50/p95/p99 measured at token-level and end-to-end request-level
- Throughput: tokens/sec per GPU, requests/sec per slot
- Cost: per-token GPU time, energy proxy (W*ms) if available
- Correctness: model output diffs measured with eval prompt set (small fidelity harness)
- Resource signals: GPU SM util, memory alloc/peak, NVLink error rate
- Scheduler signals: queue depth, kernel startup time, preemption occurrences
- KV cache signals: hit rate, eviction churn, warmup time

Profiling playbook (short form):
1) Baseline capture: run 30-minute stable baseline with mirrored production trace. Collect: kernel traces, CPU/GPU counters, KV-cache logs, end-to-end latencies.
2) Change capture: enable experimental flag for 5% traffic with traffic mirror. Capture same signals and tag traces with experiment id.
3) Sampling strategy: use stratified sampling across sequence-length buckets: 0-64, 65-256, 257-1024, >1024. Target at least 1000 traces per bucket.
4) Trace enrichment: attach kernel-id, scheduler-decision, kvcache-cohort, slot-id, and model-variant tags to each trace.
5) Differential analysis: compute delta per metric per bucket and generate a hypothesis test (bootstrap CI).

Benchmarking protocol (operational):
- Use the canonical workload generator (redwood-bench 1.4) with the following profile file for acceptance tests. Always run bench in shadow-mode first (no live routing).

Sample bench invocation:
redwood-bench run --profile profiles/mixed-dialogue-2026.yaml --duration 30m --target-gpus 4 --mirror=true --tag exp-crosslayer-{{experiment_id}}

Example profile snippet (profiles/mixed-dialogue-2026.yaml):
---
name: mixed-dialogue-2026
sequence-distribution:
  short: 0.55
  medium: 0.30
  long: 0.15
concurrency: 120
  # simulated clients sending variable-length turn-taking dialogues

Acceptance criteria (bench):
- Stable p95 throughput within -5% / +6% of baseline for the same cost tier
- p99 latency no worse than baseline + 4%
- No numerical exceptions or OOMs across 1,000 long traces

Kernel scheduling guidance (operational rules):
- Prefer per-tenant credit buckets for Dedicated pools where business SLAs exist.
- Use opportunistic slot coalescing only if average sequence length > 128 in target workload.
- Avoid naive preemption on kernels marked as non-interruptible. Instead, use cooperative-yield signals.
- When testing new kernel variants, run the kernel under a synthetic microbench of 1-10 token sequences and 512-token sequences to surface divergences.

Runbook: experimental canary rollout (step-by-step):
1) Preflight (local): run bench shadow run and confirm metrics stable.
2) Canary 1 (internal-dev): route 0% -> 1% -> 5% over 30-minute windows. Monitor safety gates.
3) Canary 2 (internal-paid): route 10% for 2 hours. If metrics exceed thresholds, roll back to 0% and capture traces.
4) Controlled ramp: 10% -> 25% -> 50% over 24h windows with periodic smoke checks.
5) Full rollout: schedule during low-traffic maintenance window. Keep 30% rollback capacity for first 24h.
6) Post-mortem checklist: collect diffs, update experiment registry entry, and schedule follow-up regression tests if any signal exceeded warning thresholds.

Escalation and ownership:
- First responder: experiment owner (runtime team engineer).
- SRE on-call: Pager duty group "runtime-sre".
- If p99 latency threshold breached for > 15 minutes: escalate to on-call manager + product impact channel.
- If numerical regressions observed (BLEU/Rouge/embedding drift) above tolerance: involve applied-ml team and freeze rollout.

Appendix A — sample runtime feature flag YAML (deploy-time):
---
feature_flag:
  name: opportunistic_slot_coalesce
  enabled: false  # set true in canary
  rollout:
    strategy: gradual
    steps: [1,5,10,25,50,100]
  metrics_watch: [latency_p99, error_rate, kvcache_hit_rate]

Appendix B — common troubleshooting commands:
- Collect live traces for a slot: redwood-cli traces fetch --slot-id <slot> --from <time> --to <time> --format ndjson
- Dump scheduler queue state: kubectl exec -n runtime svc/scheduler -- schedulerctl queue-dump --output json | jq '.top10'
- Revert feature flag: redwood-cli flags set opportunistic_slot_coalesce --enabled=false --reason "slo-rollback"

Appendix C — minimal regression gating tests (CI):
- integration/e2e/fidelity-check: run 200 eval prompts generating at least 95% semantic similarity according to eval-harness v2.1
- perf/pipeline/smoke: run 30s microbench verifying kernel warmup time < 15ms on target hardware
- telemetry/sampling-check: confirm trace coverage >= configured target for each seq-length bucket

Notes and rationale:
- We prioritize conservative latency SLOs during canaries; cost improvements that cause small tail regressions should be debated with product if they affect user experience.
- The matrix enforces that any experiment that touches both kernel selection and KV-cache must include both microbench and end-to-end corpus fidelity tests.

Change log:
- 2026-02-11: initial draft (Priya N.)
- 2026-03-16: added acceptance criteria and bench profile examples (Marcus P.)
- 2026-05-03: expanded profiling sampling guidance and escalation steps (Leah Z.)

Related references:
- See runtime-decision-delegation-and-observer-patterns-2026 for observer tagging conventions.
- See causal-latency-attribution playbook for detailed statistical test recipes.

If you plan to run an experiment, create an entry in the experiments registry and assign the fields: hypothesis, owner, expected-safety-gates, mirror-run-id, and bench-tag. Attach the mirroring trace dataset to the registry entry before starting the canary.

title: Fidelity budgeting and runtime cost governor manual
content:
Overview
========
This document defines the Fidelity Budgeting model and the Runtime Cost Governor (RCG) — a declarative control plane that enforces per-tenant/route fidelity budgets at serving time. The goal of the RCG is to keep customer-visible SLOs within targets while bounding per-token and per-request spend across mixed workloads.

Intended audience
- Runtime and scheduler engineers
- Product owners for Dedicated/Private customers
- SRE and capacity-planning teams
- Benchmark and profiling engineers

Why this exists
- Inference cost is variable by model variant, sequence length, batching shape and kernel choices.
- We need a single, auditable mechanism to trade fidelity for cost under pressure (autoscale, thermal events, capacity constraints).
- RCG ties scheduling signals, kernel hints, and quantization/variant routing decisions to a budget and provides a deterministic downgrade strategy.

Principles
- Predictability: budget enforcement must be explainable and reproducible.
- Observability: every fidelity decision must be logged with provenance (trigger, score, pre/post metrics).
- Minimize user impact: preservation of critical tokens and short requests is prioritized over long/low-priority generation.
- Fast rollback: policy changes must be reversible within a single canary window.

Key concepts and terminology
- Fidelity budget: numeric allowance per time window (tokens or token-equivalents) that a tenant/route can spend.
- Fidelity credit: per-request currency derived from model variant cost and sequence projection.
- Degradation ladder: ordered list of fidelity actions (e.g., small-quantize -> shorter-prefix-cache -> model-variant -> response-truncation).
- Governor evaluation window: default 30s sliding window for budget accounting.

Metrics, signals and SLOs
- Primary SLOs: 99th-pct tail latency <= 250ms (interactive tier), ERR_RATE <= 0.5%
- Budget signals: token_consumed, credit_burn_rate, on_gpu_slots, queue_depth, kernel_wait_time_ms
- Observability artifacts: fidelity_decision events (json), pre/post latency histograms, regression score (quality delta vs baseline prompts).

Architecture overview
- Inputs: request classifier (priority, route), model catalog pricing table (tokens / cost), runtime telemetry (slot usage, kernel queue), profiling hints (sequence length distribution).
- Decision engine: lightweight policy evaluator that produces an ordered list of degradation actions and an urgency score.
- Enforcers: scheduler (admission control and slot assignment), kernel adapter (per-request kernel flags), router (model variant routing), kvcache layer (prefix eviction hints).
- Audit sink: fidelity-decision store and metrics exporter.

Budgeting controls and policy primitives
- static_budget: fixed tokens per-minute (example: 1e6 tokens/min)
- proportional_budget: fraction of cluster budget for shared pools (0.02 = 2%)
- emergency_buffer: reserved credits only used when latency or error budgets are breached

Simple policy example (YAML)
--------------------------
policy_name: interactive-default
owner: team-runtime
window_seconds: 30
budget_type: token_quota
budget_amount: 50000
degradation_ladder:
  - action: prefer-quantized-variant
    min_quality_delta: -0.02
  - action: reduce-max-output-tokens
    reduction_percent: 25
  - action: route-to-small-variant
    acceptable_loss: -0.05
priority_overrides:
  - route: /chat/completion
    min_reserve: 2000

Scheduler integration
- Admission checks use the RCG decision as a prefilter. If a tenant is above budget, admission returns PROBATION with a recommended action list.
- Scheduler applies soft-slot labels (e.g., fidelity=low) to place downgraded requests on consolidation pools to reduce interference.
- Kernel hints are conveyed via request metadata: {kernel_hint: "prefetch_off,quantize_a2"}.

Profiling & benchmarking guidance
- For each candidate policy change run:
  1) Local microbenchmark with synthetic sequences (short, medium, long) to measure latency and kernel divergence.
  2) Shadow traffic pass (1 hour minimum) to observe real distribution effects.
  3) Quality regression suite (prompt set) measuring ROUGE/BLEU and model-specific evals.
- Required artifacts to land a policy: before/after cost-per-token, latency p50/p95/p99, quality regressions per prompt set, and fidelity_decision trace samples.

Operational runbook: budget breach (quick triage)
1) Detection
  - Alert: fidelity_budget_burn_rate > 120% for 1 minute or fidelity_decision_failure_count > 5/min
2) Immediate actions (first 5 minutes)
  - Escalate to runtime-oncall and set channel #runtime-fidelity with incident tag.
  - Switch policy to safe-mode: static_budget=nominal/4, enforce-first-ladder-only.
  - Create shadow traces for 5 minutes: set header X-Trace-Fidelity-Detail=true.
3) Investigation (5–30 minutes)
  - Check recent deployments: kernel or scheduler changes in the last 30 minutes (kubectl/CI links).
  - Correlate with capacity metrics: GPU_utilization, kernel_wait_time_ms, queue_depth.
  - Run profiling job: sample 2% of traffic for deep trace (use trace-capture CLI below).
4) Mitigation (30–120 minutes)
  - If degraded by thermal or hardware: move high-priority tenants to reserved pools.
  - If caused by regression: revert policy or kernel flag and roll forward safe-mode config.
  - If intentional load spike: negotiate temporary budget increase with product (document in audit).
5) Postmortem requirements
  - Within 48 hours: publish summary, root cause, timeline, and any policy code changes.

Trace capture CLI (example)
- - -
# Capture 10k fidelity_decision events for tenant=acme
runtctl trace capture --tenant acme --events fidelity_decision --limit 10000 --out /tmp/acme-fidelity-trace.ndjson

Policy rollout checklist
1) Author policy with rationale and expected cost delta.
2) Unit tests for policy parser and fallback actions.
3) Local benchmark (p50/p99, cost delta).
4) Canary deploy (1% traffic, 30m), monitor fidelity_decisions and latency SLOs.
5) 10% shadow for 2 hours, examine quality regressions.
6) Gradual 20% -> 50% -> 100% steps with automated rollback thresholds (p99 latency +10% or error_rate > 0.2%).

Example governance matrix (text table)
- Name: interactive-default | Owner: team-runtime | Window: 30s | Budget: 50k tokens
- Rollout gate: p99_latency_delta <= +10ms & quality_regression <= 1%

Telemetry and audit
- fidelity_decision schema (logged): request_id, tenant_id, route, budget_window_start, budget_remaining, chosen_action, reason_code, decision_score, timestamp
- Export to: metrics (Prom), events (kafka topic: fidelity-decisions), long-term store for 90d.

Ownership & contacts
- Policy author: Ava Chen (runtime@redwood.ai)
- Scheduler integration owner: Marcus Patel
- Oncall for fidelity incidents: runtime-oncall rotation (oncall@redwood.ai)

Appendix A — configuration samples
- Governor config (JSON snippet):
{
  "policy_name":"interactive-default",
  "window_seconds":30,
  "budget_amount":50000,
  "degradation_ladder":["prefer-quantized-variant","reduce-max-output-tokens","route-to-small-variant"]
}

Appendix B — quality regression example
- For the "prefer-quantized-variant" action we allow a maximum QA score delta of -0.03 as measured on the interactive-quality prompt set. If measured delta exceeds threshold during canary, the canary aborts.

Related work and references
- See runtime-architecture predictive-prefetch doc for sequence projection inputs.
- See benchmarking suite docs for how to generate the required before/after artifacts.

Change log
- 2025-01-15: created (A. Chen)
- 2025-06-12: added emergency_buffer section and scheduler hints (M. Patel)
- 2025-10-02: clarified rollout gates and updated trace capture CLI (L. Ortiz)

End of document

title: Runtime fidelity experiment recipes and execution patterns
content:
Summary
-------
This page collects reproducible experiment 'recipes' and execution patterns for evaluating runtime fidelity (model output quality vs cost/latency) and how those choices interact with kernel scheduling, profiling instrumentation, and our benchmarking suite. The intent is to provide a small set of repeatable, reviewable experiments teams can run before changing default fidelity or scheduling policies in production.

Scope and goals
----------------
- Audience: runtime engineers, performance SREs, model-onboarding owners, and product owners evaluating tradeoffs.
- Goals:
  - Provide reproducible experiment steps that exercise fidelity tiers (high/medium/low) against representative workloads.
  - Capture instrumentation and profiling guidance so results are comparable across teams.
  - Describe the interaction surface between scheduling hints and fidelity fallbacks.
  - Include a triage checklist and runbook for common regression signals.

Owners and contacts
-------------------
- Page owner: Priya Raman (runtime-performance)
- Primary reviewers: Ethan Morales (serving-runtime), Lina Chen (profiling), Marco Alvarez (benchmarks)
- Slack channel: #runtime-fidelity

Experiment recipes (overview)
----------------------------
Each recipe below follows the same pattern: objective, prerequisites, configuration (as we-run YAML snippet), step-by-step procedure, metrics to capture, pass/fail criteria, and common failure modes.

1) Fidelity smoke: small-batch quality vs latency sweep
   Objective: Measure token-level latency and sample quality variation between fidelity tiers for a fixed prompt set.

   Prereqs:
   - model variant family loaded (e.g., redwood-open-8b, redwood-v2-7b-quant)
   - bench client >= 1.4.0 on bastion
   - golden prompt set s3://redwood-experiments/fidelity/golden-100.txt

   Config (example runtime route override, minimal YAML):
   ---
   route: fidelity-smoke-test
   model_variant: redwood-open-8b
   fidelity_profiles:
     high: {quantize: false, kv_cache: write-through, decode_samples: 1}
     medium: {quantize: int8, kv_cache: writeback, decode_samples: 1}
     low: {quantize: int4, kv_cache: disabled, decode_samples: 1}
   concurrency: 16
   sequence_p95_limit: 256
   ---

   Steps:
   1. Deploy route override using `rctl apply -f fidelity-smoke.yml --env=staging`.
   2. Warmup: run `bench client warmup --route fidelity-smoke-test --duration 3m`
   3. Run sweep: for each fidelity profile run `bench run --route fidelity-smoke-test --prompts golden-100.txt --concurrency 16 --duration 10m --trace`
   4. Collect outputs to s3: `bench collect --dest s3://redwood-results/fidelity/smoke/$profile/`

   Metrics to capture:
   - per-request p50/p95/p99 latency (server-side and client-side)
   - tokens-per-second and GPU utilization (nvidia-smi per-host + runtime kernel counters)
   - sample-level quality: BLEU/ROUGE and task-specific scorer (or human eval sample set)
   - trace IDs for any requests > p99 latency

   Pass criteria:
   - High->medium quality delta < 4% by primary scorer while medium latency reduction >= 20% and cost-per-token improves >= 18%

2) Kernel hint A/B: preemption vs cooperative windowing
   Objective: Evaluate effect of scheduler hinting (preemptive-priority vs cooperative-window) on tail latency under mixed short/long workloads.

   Prereqs: scheduler feature flag `hint:kernel_priority_v2` enabled on test fleet pool.

   Config (policy snippet):
   ---
   scheduler_policy: |
     priorities:
       - name: interactive
         credit: 100
         preemptive: true
         window_ms: 20
       - name: batch
         credit: 10
         preemptive: false
         window_ms: 200
   ---

   Steps:
   1. Create two test pools with identical hardware; enable policy A (preemptive for interactive) in pool-1 and policy B (cooperative windowing) in pool-2.
   2. Use `rbench mixed-shape --short 50% --short-rt 10-50ms --long 50% --long-rt 400-800ms --duration 30m --trace` to reproduce mixed traffic.
   3. Compare p95/p99 tail and kernel queue length metrics from runtime kernel telemetry.

   Expected observations:
   - Preemptive policy typically lowers p95 for short requests but may increase kernel churn (kernel-switch counts rise by 15–40%).
   - Cooperative windowing reduces overall context-switch churn at the expense of longer p99 for short requests under high long-request load.

   Triage tip: If kernel-switch counts increase dramatically (>100% baseline) and GPU occupancy drops, enable `kernel_backpressure_sampling` and collect detailed traces as described in the Profiling section.

3) KV-cache warmstart experiment
   Objective: Quantify warmup period and hit-rate dynamics for KV cache strategies across fidelity profiles.

   Steps:
   1. Start with empty pool; route requests that mimic conversational traffic (session affinity on).
   2. Run for 90 minutes and record per-session hit-rate, mean latency, and memory pressure stats.

   Metrics to capture: hit-rate over time (per-session and aggregate), byte-eviction rates, model-serving p50/p95 over warmup window.

Instrumentation and profiling guidance
------------------------------------
- Baseline profiling flags (recommended): `--telemetry=full --kernel-sampler=1/100 --trace-mode=shadow`
- Flamegraph capture: run `rt-prof --trace-id $TRACE --output flame-$TRACE.svg`. Use the sampled user+kernel timeline to identify kernel scheduling hot spots.
- When collecting traces for regression triage include the following: runtime logs (json), kernel telemetry export (prometheus snapshot), GPU metrics (nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,memory.used --format=csv), and bench client logs.

Sample CLI snippet (end-to-end):
```
rctl apply -f fidelity-smoke.yml --env=staging
bench client warmup --route fidelity-smoke-test --duration 3m
rbench mixed-shape --route fidelity-smoke-test --concurrency 16 --duration 10m --trace > mixed.out
rt-prof collect --trace-file mixed.out --out /tmp/rtprof
rt-prof flame /tmp/rtprof -o /tmp/flame.svg
```

Benchmarking suite integration
------------------------------
- Use the canonical harness `rbench` and the workload signatures in s3://redwood-bench/signatures. When adding new signatures:
  1. Include a short, medium, and long sequence template.
  2. Provide an expected token distribution and a golden scorer if applicable.
  3. Register the signature in the benchmark catalog with owner and date.

- Example benchmark config table (plain CSV view):
  name,concurrency,duration,seq_p95_limit,workload_signature,owner
  fidelity-smoke,16,10m,256,golden-100.txt,priya
  mixed-longshort,64,30m,512,mixed-shape-v2,marco

Runtime config requirements (table)
--------------------------------
- Minimum: 8 vCPU job agent, 64GB host RAM, 32GB GPU ram (A100-40G recommended)
- Kernel telemetry: telemetry-v2 enabled (retain 72h)
- Profiles: capture at least 1/100 sampled traces for production parity

Regression triage runbook (short)
--------------------------------
1. Observe signal: elevated p95/p99, increased error-rate, or quality regression.
2. Check deployment diff: recent route overrides, scheduler policy changes, model-variant swaps.
3. Run `bench replay --trace-ids <p99-trace-ids> --baseline <prev-run>` to reproduce in a shadow pool.
4. Collect artifacts: trace + runtime logs + kernel telemetry + GPU metrics.
5. Run `rt-diff` to get per-span latency deltas and `kvcache-hitrate-report` for cache regressions.
6. If kernel scheduling is implicated: escalate to kernel-scheduling owners (label: kernel-scheduling) with artifacts and short summary (include p95 delta and kernel-switch counts).

Common failure modes and mitigations
-----------------------------------
- Short-run sampling bias: If sequence lengths < 16 tokens, sampler under-represents hot paths. Mitigation: increase `--kernel-sampler` to 1/10 for short-run experiments.
