- Small-batch oscillation under swap pressure: small batches cause frequent kvcache eviction thrashing on memory-constrained hosts. Mitigation: pin session affinity to fewer hosts and increase `kvcache.reserve_mb` by 30%.
- Kernel-hint bitmask misapplication: observed where a plugin sets a priority bit but forgets to clear on error leading to permanent elevated priority. Mitigation: add guard in FFI shim to reset hint on error path (PR template included below).

Quick PR template for kernel-hint guard
---------------------------------------
- Title: kernel: guard-clear-hint-on-error (short description)
- Description: ensure scheduler hint bitmask is cleared on all error return paths for FFI calls to kernel_hint_set.
- Test plan: unit tests for error path, integration smoke with `rbench mixed-shape` to ensure no increased priority leak.

Release note snippet (if experimental becomes default)
----------------------------------------------------
- Added fidelity experiment recipes and scheduler interaction guidance. Teams should run the fidelity smoke before flipping `default_fidelity=medium` to avoid unexpected quality regressions.

Appendix: example JSON result artifact layout
--------------------------------------------
- results.json (metadata + aggregated numbers)
- traces/ (directory of trace JSONs)
- flamegraphs/ (SVGs)
- bench-raw/ (raw bench client stdout)

Notes and references
--------------------
- See also: execution-contracts-and-stable-fallbacks-2026 (runtime execution guarantees)
- Profiling playbook: telemetry-feedback-kernel-autotune-playbook-2026 for autotune loop guidance

If you use these recipes please add a short note under this page (EDIT history) with your experiment id and a 2–3 line outcome.

title: Request Timeline & Determinism Playbook
content:
Purpose

This document defines a reproducible approach to mapping an end-to-end request timeline through the Redwood serving stack, explains sources of non-deterministic latency and behavior, and provides a playbook for profiling, benchmarking, and mitigating determinism regressions. The goal is to enable engineers and SREs to quickly triage and resolve incidents where identical request inputs do not produce stable latency envelopes or consistent processing paths.

Scope

- Applies to hosted, dedicated, and private deployments where the runtime codebase is shared.
- Covers request ingress -> routing -> batching -> kernel dispatch -> KV cache -> model execution -> network egress.
- Does NOT cover model stochasticity (sampling temperature/top_k) or application-level business logic differences.

Background and motivation

We observed a growing class of incidents where median latency is stable but per-request timelines diverge (e.g., 95th/99.9th spikes) without obvious capacity pressure. Root causes frequently involve timing interactions across kernel scheduling, KV cache warmup, and ephemeral network backpressure. Deterministic request timelines make capacity planning, autoscaling, and SLO enforcement reliable. This playbook codifies instrumentation and procedures to diagnose and reduce nondeterministic behavior.

High-level dependency map

Component | Responsibility | Owner | Key telemetry
----------|----------------|-------|--------------
API gateway | Authentication, rate limit, initial routing | api-gateway | api.gateway.request_duration_ms, api.gateway.route_decisions
Router/Orchestrator | Policy-based routing (latency/cost/region) | routing | routing.request_dispatch_ms, routing.fallback_count
Batcher | Windowing, priority mixing, slice formation | runtime-batcher | batch.size, batch.slice_latency_ms
Scheduler / Kernel mapper | Kernel selection, GPU mapping, preemption tickets | kernel-scheduler | kernel.dispatch_latency_ms, kernel.preempt_events
KV cache | Prefix/KV cache lookup, miss/warmup | kvcache | kv.hit_rate, kv.miss_latency_ms
Model execution | Compilation & kernels, attention state | model-exec | model.step_latency_ms, model.kv_memory_pressure
Network/Transport | Client socket, streaming backpressure | transport | transport.send_queue_ms, transport.socket_write_retries

Determinism-sensitive subsystems and how they break determinism

- Kernel scheduler: non-deterministic preemption ordering and fairness heuristics can reorder slices across tenants, causing high tail latency for otherwise identical requests.
- Batching: dynamic slice formation (size-based timeouts + priority mixing) can cause similar requests to hit different batch boundaries.
- KV cache: cold misses introduce variable latency; inconsistent shard-affinity (NUMA placement changes) amplifies variance.
- GPU memory fragmentation: transient OOMs and page migration can introduce stalls not visible in average metrics.
- Networking: TCP retransmits, streaming backpressure or socket write stalls cause long-tailed egress.

SLOs and jitter budgets (recommended)

- 50th latency SLO: median request end-to-end < 30ms (sample workload).
- Tail latency SLO: 99.9th < 300ms for standard small response workloads; jitter budget for run-to-run variance (stability) is 10% at 99th.
- Determinism alert: when the standard deviation of 99th percentile across 1-minute windows > 15% for 30 minutes.
- Cache warmup budget: first 100 requests on a model variant should not exceed 5x median if traffic steady; >10x indicates warmup misrouting.

Instrumentation and telemetry checklist (minimum)

- Per-request tracing spans across: ingress -> route -> batch-window -> kernel-dispatch -> kv-lookup -> model-step -> egress. Use trace tags: request.id, model.version, kernel.variant, batch.id, tenant.id.
- Metrics to emit per component: see dependency map above. Add cardinality-limited labels: model_family, seq_len_bucket, priority.
- Span duration histogram (exponential buckets) for kernel.dispatch and model.step.
- Emit an event when a request is preempted, including preempting_ticket_id and reason string.

Example PromQL queries for quick triage

- 99.9th end-to-end latency (1m):
  histogram_quantile(0.999, sum(rate(api_gateway_request_duration_seconds_bucket[1m])) by (le))
- Variance of 99th over past 30m (one-liner):
  stddev_over_time(quantile_over_time(0.99, api_gateway_request_duration_seconds_bucket[30m])[30m:1m])
- Preemption events rate:
  sum(rate(kernel_preempt_events_total[5m])) by (node)

Profiling playbook: reproduce, collect, analyze

1) Reproduce with a deterministic harness
   - Use the gated harness mode in the perf repo: set RNG seeds and use fixed workload trace. Example run:

   ```bash
   PERF_SEED=1234 ./perf/harness/run_workload.sh --trace samples/seq_32_fixed.json --parallel 8 --warmup 200
   ```

2) Record full trace with dependent spans (30s window around the offending request id). Use the runtime debug trace API:

   ```bash
   curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
     https://internal-debug.redwood/api/v1/runtime/trace?request_id=<REQUEST_ID> \
     -d '{"window_ms":30000, "include_kernel_samples": true}'
   ```

3) Collect kernel-level GPU samples (NVTX/CUPTI) from the node running the kernel mapping. Sample policy (recommended YAML):

   sampling_policy:
     profile_duration_ms: 30000
     sample_rate_per_ms: 0.5
     include_nvtx: true
     include_cpu_stacks: true

4) Correlate traces and GPU samples by timestamp and batch.id. Look for: long idle gaps between spans, unexpected preempt events, or repeated KV misses in the same request path.

Benchmarking suite: adversarial recipes

- Seeded homogeneous bursts: sequences of identical small requests with controlled inter-arrival jitter [0–10ms]. Measure batch boundary sensitivity.
- Mixed-priority storms: interleave priority=high and priority=low with 80/20 ratio to exercise scheduler fairness.
- KV churn profile: rotate prefix keys every N requests to force cache eviction and validate warmup budget.

Example wrk-style scenario to create edge-case jitter (bash):

   ```bash
   # run for 10 minutes, spawn 64 connections, random sleep to mimic jitter
   wrk -t8 -c64 -d600s --latency --script scripts/jitter.lua http://runtime-redwood/api/v1/generate
   ```

Runbook: triage steps for nondeterministic tail latency

1) Gather a representative request id and time window. Ensure you have traces and request headers (model.version, seq_len, priority).
2) Check routing decisions for that time: routing.fallback_count and route.dispatch_latency_ms. If >0 fallback, proceed to step 6 (fallbacks).
3) Inspect batcher logs for batch.size and slice_latency_ms around the request. If request landed in different sized batches across runs, note weight of adaptive timeouts.
4) Query kernel.preempt_events for the node and tenant. If preemption occurred, capture the preempting_ticket_id and escalate to kernel-scheduler owners.
5) Check KV cache metrics for the model/version shard: kv.hit_rate and recent misses. If miss pattern aligns with spikes, run cache-warmup script and consider pinning shard affinity.
6) Fallback and route-mismatch: if routing routed to a cheaper/remote variant, annotate the trace and consider rollout policy changes to prefer latency-stable variants during canaries.
7) If GPU-level stalls suspected, request GPU profile (NVTX/CUPTI) and look for CUDA synchronization points or long memcpy operations.

Quick remediation actions (temporary)

- Enable deterministic-batching-mode for the model variant (forces fixed batch window and disables dynamic priority mixing) via runtime flags. Note: increases average latency for small workloads.
- Pin request affinity to a node group to avoid NUMA rebalancing during incident.
- Increase kernel preemption grace period to reduce preemption churn while investigating.

Recent release notes (high-level)

Release: determinism-mode v0.7 (Feb 2026)
- New: deterministic-batching-mode flag (per-model). When enabled, the batcher uses fixed windows and sequence-aware packing.
- New: kernel.dispatch_span_id included in traces for robust cross-correlation.
- Fixed: race condition in preemption accounting that underreported preempt_events under high multiplexing.
- Known limitation: deterministic-batching-mode may increase average latency for seq_len <= 16 workloads.

Known issues and recommended mitigations

- ISSUE-6721: Intermittent kernel.preempt_events surge on A100-80GB nodes after driver upgrade. Mitigation: pin driver to 525.60 or roll back kernel mapper policy to conservative_crediting. Owner: kernel-scheduler.
- ISSUE-6842: KV shard skew after rolling upgrade leads to miss storms. Mitigation: run shard-rebalance with dry-run and then schedule gradual rebalance during low-traffic window. Owner: runtime-batcher/kv-team.
- ISSUE-7015: Tracing gaps for high-throughput streaming clients. Mitigation: increase tracing sampling window and use combinatorial span deduplication. Owner: observability.

Ownership and escalation

- First responder: team oncall (eng-serving-runtime).
- Kernel scheduling issues: kernel-scheduler team (pager: kernel-sched@sre).
- KV cache and shard issues: runtime-batcher and kv-team.
- Observability / tracing gaps: observability team.

Appendix: handy CLI snippets and scripts

- Fetch recent 5 preempt events with context (kubectl):

  ```bash
  kubectl logs -n runtime -l app=kernel-scheduler --tail=200 | rg "preempt" -n | tail -n 5
  ```

- Pin model variant to deterministic batching (admin CLI):

  ```bash
  redwood-admin model set-flag --model my-model:v2 --flag deterministic_batching=true
  ```

References

- See kernel scheduler spec: ../kernel-and-scheduling/preemption-aware-batch-slicing-spec-2026.json
- Profiling playbook: ../profiling-playbook/variance-driven-sampling-and-cost-correlation-playbook-2026.json

Action items

- [ ] Add a synthetic test to CI that runs seeded-burst scenario nightly and fails on >20% 99.9th variance. Owner: eng-serving-runtime perf.
- [ ] Instrument preempting_ticket_id in rollout dashboards. Owner: observability.

Document history

- 2025-11-12: Created by Priya Nair
- 2026-02-20: Added deterministic-batching-mode runbook steps and release notes

title: Execution surface containment and observability guardrails
content:
Summary:

This document defines the execution-surface containment policy and the accompanying observability contract for Redwood's inference runtime. It codifies the containment 'rings' (execution tiers), scheduling constraints, telemetry requirements, and safe-experiment controls that teams must follow when deploying kernel, scheduler, or runtime experiments. The goal is to preserve customer SLOs while enabling controlled experimentation and rapid incident triage.

Scope:

- Applies to: runtime-dispatcher, kernel-shepherd, slot-admission, kv-cache, and any execution plugins that affect GPU scheduling or memory.
- Does not apply to: client-side SDK experiments, control-plane UI-only changes (see related policy: /confluence/policies-and-process/change-management).

Definitions:

1) Containment ring: logical execution tier that constrains resources and visibility for workloads.
2) Escrowed experiment: an experiment that runs in a restricted ring with strict telemetry and rollback windows.
3) Observability contract: the required metrics, traces, and log annotations an artifact must emit to be allowed in production rings.

Containment rings (high level):

- Ring 0 (Hotpath): production-critical, low-latency workloads. Strict SLOs: p50 < 20ms, p99 < 150ms for short-seq gen workflows. No experimental kernel hooks allowed.
- Ring 1 (Managed Experiment): production-like capacity with strict limits (max 2% of requests, tied to tokens). Allowed for A/B experiments with automatic rollback.
- Ring 2 (Sandboxed Fallback): degraded-fidelity paths and canary logic. Higher latency acceptable; used for fallback routing and load-shedding testing.
- Ring 3 (Escrowed Lab): long-running experiments, large-profile kernels, or new accelerator integrations. Runs isolated from customer traffic by default.

Enforcement controls (how containment is implemented):

- Admission controller (service: slot-admission): enforces per-experiment quotas, tenant isolation labels, and routing policies. Integrates with RTS policy engine.
- Kernel flags: kernel-shepherd exposes explicit feature flags (example: kernel-shepherd.enable_waveform_orchestration=false). Any change to these flags must be behind an experiment descriptor with metadata and telemetry hooks.
- cgroup-like isolation + GPU slot reservation: we allocate 'soft' and 'hard' limits at the dispatcher level; hard limits are protected via SLOT_HARD_LIMIT env and rejected if exceeded.
- Network and I/O throttles for Ring 3 to keep lab experiments from saturating disk or NVLink.

Observability contract (v1): required signals for any artifact to be assigned to Ring 0 or Ring 1. All fields below are required with specified collection frequency or sampling rate.

- Metrics (emit at 10s rollup unless noted):
  - runtime.request.count (per-model, per-route)
  - runtime.request.latency_ms.p50/p90/p95/p99 (per-model, per-route)
  - runtime.kvcache.hit_rate (1m)
  - kernel.dispatch.time_ms (histogram)
  - kernel.queue.length (gauge, 5s)
  - kernel.error_rate (1m), broken down by error_class
  - memory.gpu.free_bytes and memory.gpu.total_bytes (10s)
  - admission.rejected_requests (1m)

- Traces:
  - Distributed trace per request with these required span attributes: "route_id", "model_version", "kernel_variant", "ring_id", "slot_request_id".
  - Sample rates: 1% system-wide shadow sampling; 100% for requests that trigger timeouts or errors > 5xx.

- Logs: structured JSON logs with keys: timestamp, level, service, host_id, trace_id, request_id, ring_id. Sensitive fields must be redacted (PII tokens must be hashed).

- Alerts (must be wired to PagerDuty for owner teams):
  - SLO breach projection: predicted p99 > 200ms for 5m (SEV-1)
  - Kernel OOMs rate > 0.5% 5m (SEV-2)
  - Admission rejections > 1% of total requests 1m (SEV-2)

Policy: experiment preflight checklist (must be completed before assigning to Ring 1 or higher)

1) Metrics & tracing: artifact emits all required metrics and trace attributes in a staging environment.
2) Canary matrix: define canary percent, escalation steps, and rollback criteria (see example below).
3) Load profile: provide synthetic benchmark that shows no >10% degradation in p99 under representative load.
4) Failure injection plan: document how to safely inject kernel timeouts or queue saturation and expected behavior.
5) Owner and runbook: list oncall owner and confirm runbook presence in /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks.

Example canary matrix (text table):

| step | traffic % | duration | success criteria | action |
|------|-----------|----------|------------------|--------|
| baseline | 0% | 10m | stable | none |
| canary-1 | 0.5% | 15m | p99 <= baseline*1.1, errors <= 0.1% | promote or rollback |
| canary-2 | 2% | 30m | p99 <= baseline*1.15, no new error classes | promote or rollback |

Safe experimentation flow (detailed steps):

1) Open an experiment RFC in the runtime experiments tracker with artifact build id and feature flags.
2) Run local & staging validations: metrics emitted, e2e traces flow to telemetry-bridge, unit tests pass.
3) Create an escrowed experiment descriptor with ring target = Ring 2 and reviewers set to runtime-owners.
4) After 72h stable in Ring 2, request promotion to Ring 1 with canary matrix and automatic rollback configured in slot-admission.
5) Monitor both the telemetry contract and resource quotas; abort immediately on any SLO projection alert.

Profiling & benchmarking playbook pointers:

- For kernel latency regressions: use profiler bundle script: 
  ./tools/profiler/collect_kernel_trace.sh --bundle-id EXP123 --duration 60 --target hosts@dispatchers
- Use the synthetic benchmark harness (service: workload-sim) to replay representative request corpus with model_token_distribution.json. Ensure experiment does not increase per-token energy by >20% in our cost envelope.
- Sample profiling recipe: stratified-sample 1% system traces + 100% error traces; correlate kernel.queue.length spikes with dispatch.latency.histogram.

Operational runbooks (short-form):

- Incident: sustained p99 latency spike for Ring 0
  1) PagerDuty trigger (SLO-projection alert) — oncall acknowledges.
  2) Run quick triage: fetch last 15m of runtime.request.latency histograms, kernel.queue.length, kernel.dispatch.time_ms.
  3) If kernel.queue.length correlated with specific kernel_variant: set slot-admission to divert to fallback kernel_variant via: 
     curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" https://runtime-admin/route/divert \n       -d '{"route_id":"/v1/generate","from_variant":"kvq-quant","to_variant":"kvq-fallback","percent":100}'
  4) If memory OOMs observed: scale down kernel concurrency and trigger evictions: 
     kubectl patch deployment kernel-shepherd -n runtime --type='json' -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/env/0/value","value":"CONCURRENCY=4"}]'
  5) If no immediate mitigation: engage runtime-sre and escalate to oncall infra.

- Incident: admission.rejected_requests spike
  1) Check admission.rejected_requests by tenant and policy id.
  2) If caused by quota misconfiguration: increment tenant soft quota via admin UI and monitor.
  3) If caused by runaway experiment: identify experiment_id in slot logs and disable via: 
     curl -X POST https://slot-admin/experiments/EXP123/disable -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN"

Ownership and escalation:

- Runtime experiments steward: eng-platform/runtime-experiments (alias: #runtime-experiments).
- Oncall for Ring 0: runtime-sre PagerDuty.
- Kernel/scheduler escalation: kernel-team oncall.

Rollout checklist (short):

- [ ] Unit tests and smoke tests pass
- [ ] Metrics emitted at expected cardinality
- [ ] Tracing attributes present and validated in staging
- [ ] Canary matrix defined and reviewed
- [ ] Failure-injection plan uploaded
- [ ] Runbook page created and linked

Appendix: sample artifact metadata (YAML)

---
artifact_name: kernel-wave-1
build_id: build-20231012-987
ring_target: Ring 1
owner: aisha.patel@redwood.ai
telemetry_contract: v1
canary_matrix:
  - step: canary-1
    traffic_percent: 0.5
    duration_mins: 15
    pass_criteria: "p99 <= baseline*1.1 and error_rate <= 0.1%"
rollback_criteria: "error_rate > 0.2% or p99 > baseline*1.2"
---

CLI examples:

- Check ring assignment for a route:
  rcli runtime describe-route --route /v1/chat --fields ring_id,model_version,active_variants
- Create escrowed experiment descriptor (example):
  rcli experiments create --name kernel-wave-1 --ring Ring-2 --owner aisha.patel --manifest /tmp/manifest.yaml

Further reading and links:

- Runtime decision graph (internal): /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-decision-graph-and-observed-behaviour-catalog-2026
- Scheduler observability injector: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-observability-contract-and-simulated-injector-2026
- Continuous profiling strategy: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/continuous-runtime-profiling-strategy-2026

Revision history:

- 2023-10-12: Document created by Aisha Patel (initial draft)
- 2024-04-11: Expanded telemetry contract and added canary matrix examples (reviewers: Marco Li, Sophie Nguyen)

If you plan to run an experiment touching kernel scheduling, create the RFC and ping #runtime-experiments at least 48 hours before any Ring 1 promotion.

title: Runtime signal conciliation and latency cohorting
content:
Summary
This page defines a single, operationally actionable taxonomy for runtime signals (conciliation) and a pragmatic approach to grouping traffic by latency cohorts (cohorting). The goal is to standardize how the runtime reconciles competing signals — SLOs, kernel pressure, KV cache warm state, and cost guidance — and how the scheduler harmonizes execution decisions across those cohorts to reduce tail latency while preserving throughput and cost targets.

Intended audience
- Runtime engineers (kernel, scheduler, dispatch)
- SREs and oncall engineers owning latency SLOs
- Performance and profiling owners

Why this exists
We observed repeated flapping between priority policies during mixed workloads: short chat requests bouncing against long generation jobs; KV cache warmup causing transient tail spikes; and adaptive batching oscillations that increase mean latency. Those issues trace back to inconsistent interpretation of telemetry signals across components. This doc prescribes: 1) a shared signal vocabulary, 2) cohorting rules, 3) a scheduler harmonization contract, and 4) an operational playbook for experiments and incidents.

Key concepts
- Signal conciliation: the deterministic process by which the runtime reduces multiple, possibly conflicting telemetry inputs into an ordered set of actions (e.g., throttle, preempt, hedging, fallback).
- Latency cohort: a stable label assigned to a request (or request class) representing its expected latency distribution and tolerance (e.g., interactive-50ms, elastic-200ms, batch-1s). Cohorts are used to drive scheduling, admission, and caching policies.
- Steering signals: canonical telemetry used for conciliation. See table below.

Steering signals (canonical)
- SLO_gap: (SLO_target_ms - observed_p95_ms) normalized by SLO_target_ms. Positive = healthy.
- Queue_depth: per-queue pending requests count and age histogram (0-10ms, 10-100ms, >100ms).
- Kernel_pressure_index (KPI): weighted sum of GPU occupancy, active kernels, enqueue latency, and memory stall rate. Range [0,100].
- KV_warm_fraction: fraction of requests expected to hit prefix/KV cache (0-1).
- Cost_signal: per-token cost estimate and priority cost budget remaining for the route/customer.
- Error_rate: percent of responses that triggered fallback/retry in the last minute.

Latency cohorts (recommended defaults)
1) interactive-50ms: requests with strict p50/p95 targets (e.g., UI autocompletion).
2) interactive-150ms: session chat turns that can tolerate modest tail but expect snappy median.
3) elastic-400ms: longer generations where batching accelerates cost efficiency.
4) background-batch-1s: large offline or low-priority requests eligible for queueing and high batching.

Cohort assignment rules
1. Assign cohort at ingress based on route metadata and model profile (explicit route overrides default).
2. If request includes max_latency_ms or max_tokens, map to cohort using the mapping table in Appendix A.
3. Dynamic reclassification: on warmstart/kvcache-warmup events, mark requests as "warming-elastic" for up to 2s to bias toward nodes with warm cache.

Scheduler harmonization contract (short)
- Purpose: give a deterministic algorithm for turning conciliated signals into actions across the admission-controller, slot allocator, and kernel dispatcher.
- Input: steering signals + cohort label + route SLA tier + model-variant cost guidance.
- Output: admission decision (accept/defer/redirect), slot allocation (slots, preemptible flag), kernel hints (preferred kernel ID, quantization path), and fallback instruction (model-variant or queue route).

Decision precedence (ordered)
1. Safety blocks (OOM, watchdog) — immediate reject/evict.
2. SLO preservation for interactive cohorts when SLO_gap < 0.1 — apply hedging, reduce batch size, reserve non-preemptible slot.
3. KPI escalation — if KPI > 80, favor elastic/background cohorts for eviction or delayed admission.
4. Cost_controls — if cost budget is exhausted for a high-cost route, redirect to quantized variant or lower-fidelity model.
5. KV_warm_fraction optimization — prefer nodes with warm fraction >= 0.7 for cohorts that benefit from cache; otherwise allow warmup cohort routing.

Operational playbook (incident / experiment flow)
1. Detection: Alert triggers if p95_interactive > SLO_target * 1.2 for 3 minutes OR KPI > 85 for 2 minutes.
2. Triage rapid checks (2 min):
   - Check SLO_gap, KPI, Queue_depth, KV_warm_fraction across affected nodes.
   - Identify cohort skew (which cohorts show disproportionate latency).
3. Rapid mitigation (5–15 min):
   - If KPI high and elastic/background load is > 40% of active kernels, temporarily drain new batch routes and redirect to spare pool.
   - If KV_warm_fraction low and interactive cohorts are affected, enable warm-prefetch for interactive routes and nominate warm nodes using routing tag warm-preferred=true.
   - Apply emergency hedging for interactive cohorts: spawn second probe request on separate slot and cancel slower completion.
4. Follow-up (post-mitigation):
   - Run microbenchmark traffic shaped to reproduce cohort mix that triggered incident (see Benchmarking protocol section).
   - Capture full traces for 30 minutes and export to profiling lab.

Benchmarking protocol (cohort-aware replay)
- Purpose: validate scheduler decisions under realistic mixed cohorts.
- Core steps:
  1. Build a traffic shape with 3 lanes: interactive-50ms (40% qps), interactive-150ms (30% qps), elastic-400ms (30% qps).
  2. Run three scenarios: baseline (no harmonization), harmonization-lite (conciliation but no preemptive evict), harmonization-full (all rules enabled).
  3. Measure: p50/p95/p99 per cohort, mean tokens/sec, kernel context-switches, KPI, KV hit delta, cost_per_1k_tokens.
  4. Acceptance criteria: interactive-50ms p95 improvement >= 20% vs baseline and overall cost increase <= 8%.

Profiling playbook (fast experiment loop)
- Sampling: mark 1% of interactive requests and 0.5% of elastic as deep-sampled for full trace collection.
- Instrumentation: include kernel_id, batch_size, slot_id, kv_hit, enqueue_time_ms, kernel_start_ms, kernel_end_ms, total_response_ms.
- Replay: use the captured traces to run stepwise synthetic replays in the profiling lab with and without harmonization – compare kernel dispatch histograms.

Configuration reference (examples)
Table: Scheduler conciliation thresholds (human-readable)
- interactive_reserve_slots: 20% (reserve always-available non-preemptible slots per node for interactive cohorts)
- hedging_probe_delay_ms: 30 (time after which hedging probe is launched for interactive when queue_age > 10ms)
- kpi_preempt_threshold: 80
- warm_preferred_fraction_threshold: 0.7
- cost_redirect_threshold_usd_per_1k: 2.50

Example YAML snippet (route-level override)
- route: /api/chat/fast
  cohort: interactive-50ms
  reserve_slots: 0.25
  max_batch_size: 8
  fallback_variant: model-lite-quantized-v2

Runbook excerpt: latency spike play actions (cheat sheet)
1. Acknowledge alert and post on #runtime-incidents.
2. Run `runtime-cli get-signals --nodes affected` and snapshot KPI/queue/kv.
3. If KPI > 85: scale out spare-pool by +10% and enable batch-drain on background pools.
4. If interactive p95 > target*1.2 and KV_warm_fraction < 0.6: set routing tag warm-preferred=true for interactive routes and re-route 10% traffic to warm nodes.
5. If no improvement in 10 minutes: failover to regional fallback model family (defined in Release Playbook).

Dashboards and alerts (minimum)
- Dashboards: cohort-latency-heatmap, KPI-over-time, kv-warm-fraction-by-node, admission-decision-by-cohort.
- Alerts: High KPI, cohort p95 breach, sustained hedging rate > 5%, sudden KV_warm_fraction drop > 0.2 in 5m.

Ownership and contacts
- Runtime scheduler owner: Marcus Lee (pager: eng-runtime-scheduler)
- Kernel infra owner: Elena García (pager: eng-kernel)
- Profiling & benchmarks: Jordan Kim (profiling@redwood.ai)

Appendix A — cohort mapping guidelines
- max_latency_ms <= 50 -> interactive-50ms
- 50 < max_latency_ms <= 200 -> interactive-150ms
- 200 < max_latency_ms <= 600 -> elastic-400ms
- max_latency_ms > 600 or large token budgets -> background-batch-1s

Appendix B — experiment checklist for safe rollout
1. Feature-flagged rollout (10% traffic) for 48h with continuous monitoring.
2. Canary cluster with identical HW profile and KV warm snapshot.
3. Compare p99 and error delta vs baseline; gate at 2% p99 regression or 0.5% error rate increase.

Change log
- 2025-09-14: Document created (Aisha Patel).
- 2025-11-02: Added hedging parameters and KPI definition (Marcus Lee).
- 2026-02-03: Tuned benchmark acceptance criteria and added warm-preferred routing guidance (Elena García).

Related artifacts
- Synthetic replay harness: repo: infra/perf/replay/cohort-replay
- Profiling lab dashboard: dashboards/runtime/cohort-profiles

Finally
This doc is normative for any scheduling or admission change that touches cohorted traffic. If you propose a change that modifies the conciliation algorithm, update the decision precedence table and run the cohort-aware benchmark suite described above prior to rollout.

title: Runtime Sandboxing Experiment Lab Manual
content:
Overview

This manual describes the lab-grade sandboxing environment used by the runtime team to run invasive performance experiments, kernel-scheduler patches, and mixed-workload benchmarks without risking production stability. It documents the sandbox architecture, isolation model, step-by-step experiment runbook, profiling and telemetry requirements, benchmark invocation patterns, known issues encountered during experiments, and incident runbooks specific to lab activities.

Goals

- Create a reproducible, auditable environment for risky runtime changes.
- Ensure experiments are isolated from production control planes and do not leak telemetry or credentials.
- Provide a standard profiling and benchmarking workflow so results are comparable across runs.
- Capture failure modes and required mitigation steps.

Audience

- Runtime engineers doing kernel and scheduler work.
- Performance engineers running comparative benchmarks.
- SREs supporting lab infrastructure.

High-level sandbox architecture

Components

- lab-gateway: Lightweight ingress that routes experiment traffic and enforces quotas.
- kernel-orchestrator: Service that deploys custom kernel/kernelspecs into lab nodes.
- sandbox-runner: Per-node agent that configures cgroups, MIG partitions and GPU modes, and applies kernel module overrides.
- kvcache-sim: A synthetic KV cache used to emulate prefix / session caching behavior.
- telemetry-proxy: Collects and stamps telemetry for lab runs, marks data with lab_run_id, and writes to the lab telemetry bucket.

Isolation model

- Network: Lab runs live in the lab VPC (vpc-lab-1). No cross-VPC peering with prod. All egress is via nat-lab with explicit allow lists.
- Compute: Nodes are labeled "lab:true" and exist in a separate autoscaling group. Node OS images include the debug kernel and a signed kernel module whitelist.
- GPU: Two isolation modes supported: NVIDIA MPS per-experiment (for multi-process concurrency experiments) and MIG partitions (for perf isolation). sandbox-runner toggles these per experiment.
- Storage and secrets: Lab runs use ephemeral PVCs. Secrets are provided by the lab KMS with a short TTL and are not replicated to production KMS.

Kernel-scheduling considerations for lab experiments

- Scheduler variants: The lab supports several scheduler builds under kernel-orchestrator: baseline, preemptive-slice, adaptive-slice, and priority-decoupled. Each build is tagged and has a known compatibility matrix for driver and CUDA versions.
- Mapping priorities to runtime classes: Use the experiment configuration to map Redwood priority classes to kernel priorities. For example: "interactive" -> SCHED_RR with 10ms quantum; "batch" -> SCHED_DEADLINE with ED=50ms/1s.
- Fairness accounting: When testing cooperative preemption, enable kernel credit accounting (lab flag: enable_credit_accounting=true) to observe queue-smear effects.

Experiment environment provisioning

1) Request sandbox allocation

- Open RFC in the experiments tracker with: title, hypothesis, required node types, GPU mode, expected run time, and roll-back criteria. Example: "RFC: preemptive-slice latency reduction vs baseline".
- On approval, run the allocation script: ./scripts/request-lab --project runtime --nodes 4 --gputype a100 --duration 8h --labels preemptive-test

2) Provisioning checklist (automated but must be validated)

- Confirm nodes in ASG have label lab:true.
- Confirm kernel-orchestrator has deployed the requested kernel tag.
- Verify sandbox-runner applied requested GPU mode: kubectl get nodes -l lab=true -o json | jq '.items[].metadata.annotations.gpu_mode'
- Ensure telemetry-proxy is configured with lab_run_id and bucket path.

Step-by-step experiment runbook

1. Prepare experiment config (YAML)

- Minimal example (save as experiment-config.yaml):

experiment_name: preemptive-slice-compare-2026
environment: staging-sim
node_selectors:
  - lab:true
kernel_tag: preemptive-slice-v3
gpu_mode: MIG-1g.5gb
workload_profiles:
  - name: interactive
    qps: 120
    seq_length_p95: 320
  - name: batch
    qps: 2
    seq_length_p95: 2048
measurement_windows_s: 300
telemetry_bucket: s3://lab-telemetry/runtime/2026/experiment-123

2. Start with a short smoke run (10 min)

- Validate functional correctness, all services respond, and telemetry tags are present.
- Commands: ./lab-runner start --config experiment-config.yaml --smoke

3. Full run

- Start bench: ./lab-runner start --config experiment-config.yaml --duration 3600 --trace-sampling 0.1
- Monitor: kubectl top nodes -l lab=true; ./observability/quick-check --run-id=experiment-123

4. Collect artifacts

- Kernel traces: /var/log/lab/experiments/experiment-123/kernel-trace.tar.gz
- Flamegraphs: s3://lab-telemetry/runtime/2026/experiment-123/flamegraphs/
- Perf counters (per-node): s3://lab-telemetry/runtime/2026/experiment-123/perf/
- Telemetry manifest: s3://lab-telemetry/runtime/2026/experiment-123/manifest.json

Profiling playbook (lab-specific)

- Sampling strategy: Start with probabilistic sampling at 10% for p50/p95 slices and 100% sampling for all p99+ traces during the first 5 minutes and then drop to 1% for the remainder. This accelerates root-cause collection without overloading telemetry.
- Metrics to capture: per-request wall_time, kernel_queue_time, kv_cache_hit, gpu_busy_time, gpu_memory_alloc, context_switches/sec, scheduler_runqueue_length.
- Tracing hooks: Ensure runtime-gateway and kernel-orchestrator include lab_run_id and experiment_name in trace root spans.
- Perf tooling: Use perf + Nsight CLI for A100 profiling. Example: sudo perf record -a -g -- sleep 300; perf script | ./FlameGraph/stackcollapse-perf.pl | ./FlameGraph/flamegraph.pl > flame.svg

Benchmarking suite invocation

- Use the canonical runner that wraps the microbenchmark harness.
- Example command: ./bench-suite/run --profile latency --shards 4 --concurrency 64 --model redwood-v0.9-quant --seed 42 --out s3://lab-telemetry/runtime/2026/experiment-123/bench

- Config table (CSV-like text)

config_key,description,default,lab_override
shards,number of client shards,4,4
concurrency,total outstanding requests per shard,32,64
sequence_distribution,which lengths to sample,prod-like,tail-enhanced
model_variant,model binary to run,baseline,preemptive-slice-v3

Data hygiene and retention

- All lab telemetry must be tagged with lab_run_id and have a retention of 90 days by default. If an experiment is deemed sensitive, adjust confidentiality to 'restricted' and contact security.
- Do not import lab telemetry into production dashboards. To compare to production, export aggregated metrics only (no traces, no raw kernel profiles).

Release notes for this manual (v1.2)

- 2026-01-12: v1.0 initial release documenting the sandbox architecture and minimal runbook.
- 2026-01-25: v1.1 added kernel scheduling mappings and new perf counter list.
- 2026-02-03: v1.2 added MIG / MPS guidance and bench-suite invocation examples.

Known issues and mitigations (lab-specific)

- GPU driver mismatch causing node panic: Always pin driver version to node image and verify with ./scripts/verify-driver.sh. Mitigation: cordon and reprovision node with driver-consistent AMI.
- Telemetry proxy dropping spans at >2k RPS: Reduce trace sampling or scale telemetry-proxy (HPA target cpu 70%).
- kvcache-sim inconsistent TTL behavior under heavy load: Increase kvcache-sim replica_count to at least 3 and enable read-through logging.

Incident runbooks for lab activities

1) Node panic during experiment

- Step 1: Pause experiment: ./lab-runner pause --run-id=experiment-123
- Step 2: Cordon node: kubectl cordon <node-id> && kubectl describe node <node-id> | tee /tmp/node-diagnostics.txt
- Step 3: Capture kernel oops: sudo journalctl -k -b -1 > /tmp/kernel-oops.txt; attach to incident.
- Step 4: Reprovision using: ./scripts/reprovision-node --node <node-id> --ami ami-lab-debug-20260101

2) Telemetry corruption detected

- Verify manifest integrity: aws s3 cp s3://lab-telemetry/.../manifest.json - | jq .status
- If manifest shows missing files, escalate to telemetry team (owner: telemetry-eng@redwood.com) and mark run as partial.

Safety and approvals

- Any experiment that modifies kernel scheduling semantics that could change tenant isolation must have a security review and an SRE sign-off. Use the experiment-approval workflow in the tracker and attach the signed checklist.

Ownership and contacts

- Primary owner: runtime-experiments@redwood.com (team: Runtime Performance)
- On-call for lab infra: eng-sre-oncall@redwood.com (pager duty)
- Telemetry owner: telemetry-eng@redwood.com

Appendix: quick reference commands

- Request nodes: ./scripts/request-lab --nodes 4 --duration 8h
- Start bench: ./bench-suite/run --profile latency --out <s3path>
- Smoke run: ./lab-runner start --config experiment-config.yaml --smoke
- Collect kernel trace: sudo tar czf /var/log/lab/experiments/<run>/kernel-trace.tar.gz /sys/kernel/debug/tracing

Document history and contributors

- Written by: Maya Alvarez (runtime-experiments)
- Contributors: Arjun Patel, Sofia Lin, Liam O'Connor

Feedback

- Add comments on this page or open an issue in the experiments tracker with the label "lab-manual".

title: Inference Operational Handbook — Pragmatic Guides (2026)
content:
Summary:
This handbook collects applied, operational guidance for running inference reliably and cost-effectively across Redwood's serving runtime. It consolidates practical heuristics for kernel scheduling, profiling and sampling workflows, benchmark interpretation, and a concise incident response playbook for common production failure modes. The goal is to provide on-call and platform engineers a single, short reference that balances prescriptive steps with rationale and metric thresholds.

Scope:
- Relevant components: scheduler daemon (schedulerd), kernel plugin manager (kpm), request-router (route-proxy), kv-cache service (kvcache), and the telemetry ingestion pipeline (telemetry-ingest).
- Workloads: multi-tenant hosted API, Dedicated GPU pools, and Private deployments using the same runtime binary.
- Not covered here: billing reconciliations, model quality regression procedures (see eval-harness pages).

Owners and escalation:
- Primary owner: Serving Runtime Team (oncall rotation: runtime-oncall).
- Secondary owner: Platform SRE (platform-oncall).
- Pager escalation path: runtime-oncall -> platform-oncall -> runtime-eng lead (Marco Ramirez) -> SRE manager.

High-level operational goals:
- Latency SLOs: 95th < 120ms for short-turn chat (<=64 tokens), 99th < 320ms for generation (<=256 tokens) on Dedicated tier.
- Error budget: 0.1% 5xxs per minute window across API routes.
- GPU memory pressure threshold: start eviction at 78% usage; force reclaim and better-fit sharding at 92%.
- Bounding cost: track per-token cost delta after kernel changes; aim for <=8% unit cost increase post-rollout.

Runtime architecture primer (brief):
1. Request ingress: route-proxy performs request classification (route, priority, model-family).
2. Scheduling layer: schedulerd maps requests to candidate kernels and slots. It uses kernel hints, model-shape fingerprints, and tenant-priority weights.
3. Kernel execution: kpm loads kernel binary into shards and runs the optimized attention/ML kernels on the selected GPU.
4. KV-caching: kvcache maintains prefix KV for active sessions and provides asynchronous prefetch hints to kpm.
5. Telemetry flow: per-request trace + kernel annotations are emitted to telemetry-ingest and stored under runtime-telemetry.

Kernel scheduling heuristics (practical rules):
- Prefer single-kernel fast-path for requests with <=64 tokens and batchable shapes. This reduces context-switch overhead.
- For long context sequences (>=1024 tokens) route to segmented-attn kernels; mark request as "non-interactive" priority unless user-specified.
- When concurrency > 1.4x target, enable cooperative preemption: slice long-running kernels at 50ms quantum boundaries.
- Kernel selection priority: latency-optimized variant -> balanced variant -> quantized-low-memory variant. Only downgrade to quantized when memory pressure > 85% and latency SLO for the route allows it.

Scheduling policy table (quick reference):
| Condition | Action | Owner | Metric to watch | Threshold |
| --- | --- | ---:| --- | ---: |
| Burst of small requests (P95 rising) | Increase batch slot size for small-shape path by 2x; cap at 8 | schedulerd | small-path P95 latency | >120ms for 3 consecutive minutes |
| GPU memory > 78% | Reduce batch depth, enable preemption | schedulerd | GPU memory util | >=78% |
| Tail latency > SLO | Switch to latency-optimized kernel variant; enable KV-prefetch | runtime-oncall | 99th latency per route | >SLO for 5m |
| Frequent kernel timeouts | Disable experimental kernel plugin | kernel-owner | kernel timeout rate | >0.05% over 10m |

Profiling and sampling playbook (step-by-step):
1) Alert triage: correlate the alert with topology (shard id, gpu id) using the request trace id.
2) If per-kernel latency spike is observed, capture full kernel trace sample (use profiler tool: profiler capture --trace-id <trace> --duration 30s).
3) Run bounded microbenchmarks from the developer sandbox to reproduce: sandbox-bench --model <model> --shape <seq> --batch <b>. Compare with golden baseline stored in benchmark-manifests.
4) If discrepancy > 20% on P95/P99, collect the following artifacts: scheduler logs, kernel plugin logs, GPU driver dmesg, nvprof trace (or ROCm equivalent). Attach to incident.

Sampling and telemetry guidance:
- Global sampling: 2% of all requests capture full kernel timeline. Increase to 10% for routes in active experiments or incidents.
- Stratified sampling: ensure at least 5 captures per tenant per hour for tenants with >1k qps.
- Annotate samples with kernel-variant, scheduling-decision, and prefetch-hints. These three fields are necessary to correlate regression root causes.

Benchmark suite interpretation (how to use numbers):
- Use the operational benchmark suite under benchmarking/operational-v1 to compute unit cost and latency envelope. Each change to scheduler, kernel, or kpm must run the smoke-profile (20k small requests; 5k long requests) and compare three signals: P50, P95, P99, and cost-per-token.
- Regression thresholds: P95 increase >10% or P99 increase >8% or unit cost increase >6% requires a rollback candidate or a corrective patch before releasing to Dedicated.
- Report format: include CSV with columns [model, shape, batch, kernel_variant, P50, P95, P99, cost_per_token, notes].

Common incident runbooks (concise):
A) High tail latency across a model-family:
- Step 1: Identify affected shards: query telemetry "select top shards by p99 where model_family='X' and time>now-15m".
- Step 2: If a single GPU/host is hot, cordon node in the scheduler (schedulerctl cordon <node>). Begin draining long sessions with graceful 60s window.
- Step 3: Switch affected route to latency-optimized variant: schedulerctl set-route <route> --kernel=latency-opt --reason=\"incident-mitigation\".
- Step 4: Re-run operational benchmark smoke-profile against the node to confirm restoration.
- Step 5: Post-incident, run kernel trace diff and open PR tagging kernel-owner.

B) Kernel plugin memory leak suspected:
- Step 1: Confirm by checking kernel plugin resident set trend via telemetry (plugin_name.resident_set / 1h).
- Step 2: Increase sampling and capture heap profile: profiler heap-dump --plugin <name> --duration 60s.
- Step 3: Restart plugin with --mem-safemode flag on a staged shard. Observe delta. If restart reduces leak, schedule full rollout of patched plugin.

C) Frequent preemption spikes causing jitter:
- Step 1: Verify cooperative preemption quantum metrics (preempt.quantum_ms distribution).
- Step 2: Lower quantum to 30ms for affected pool: schedulerctl set-pool <pool> --quantum-ms=30.
- Step 3: If jitter persists, temporarily reduce pool concurrency limit by 15% and open monitoring ticket.

Telemetry and dashboards (operational checklist):
- Core dashboards to keep on-call pinned:
  - runtime / latency-by-route (P50/P95/P99 over 30m)
  - scheduler / memory-pressure (per-host GPU memory %)
  - kernel / timeout-and-exceptions (counts and per-plugin rates)
  - kvcache / hit-rate-by-session (prefetch success and eviction churn)
  - cost / per-token-cost (by model and by kernel-variant)
- Useful example queries (pseudo-SQL):
  - 99th latency per model: SELECT model, percentile(latency_ms, 99) FROM runtime_traces WHERE ts > now() - 10m GROUP BY model
  - Kernel timeout by plugin: SELECT plugin, count(*) FROM kernel_exceptions WHERE error_type='timeout' and ts > now()-1h GROUP BY plugin ORDER BY count DESC

Configuration snippets (examples to copy):
- schedulerd policy snippet (YAML):
```yaml
pools:
  - name: latency-pool
    concurrency_limit: 64
    quantum_ms: 50
    kernel_preference: [latency-opt, balanced]
  - name: cost-pool
    concurrency_limit: 128
    quantum_ms: 80
    kernel_preference: [balanced, quantized-lowmem]
```

- kernel plugin safe-start CLI:
```bash
kpmctl start --plugin my-kernel-v2 --safe-start --max-shards=2
```

Release and rollout guidance for kernel changes:
- Required gates before rollout: CI microbench green; operational benchmark smoke-profile; telemetry sampling increased to 5% during canary; rollback playbook documented.
- Canary strategy: 3-phase
  1) Dev sandbox validation (dev environment) — smoke-profile vs golden baseline.
  2) Staged canary (5% of traffic across 3 nodes) — 1h observation window; track P95, P99, kernel-exception-rate, and cost-per-token.
  3) Gradual ramp (5% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100%), gating each step on zero regressions for 30 minutes.

Post-incident checklist and postmortem template (short):
- Incident summary, impact window, metrics, owner, immediate remediation, root cause (hypothesis), timeline of key actions, data artifacts (links to traces/logs), follow-ups and owners, whether we need change to SLOs or scheduling heuristics.

Developer ergonomics and experimentation guidance:
- For kernel experiments, include an experiment manifest with: name, hypothesis, traffic split, metric targets, rollback criteria, baseline commit, and benchmark CSV. Keep experiment duration to <=48 hours in production.
- When requesting telemetry schema changes, coordinate with telemetry-ingest and include a migration plan. Backward-compatible fields only for 90 days.

Appendix: quick diagnostic commands and artifacts to attach
- profiler capture: profiler capture --trace-id <id> --out /tmp/trace.tar.gz --duration 30s
- collect node snapshot: node-collect --node <node> --include=dmesg,nvidia-smi,top,gpu-metrics --out /tmp/node-snapshot.tar.gz
- run smoke-profile: benchctl smoke --manifest benchmarking/operational-v1/smoke-manifest.yaml --out /tmp/smoke.csv

FAQ (short):
Q: When should we prefer quantized kernels?
A: Only when memory pressure consistently prevents meeting concurrency limits, and latency SLOs for the route allow a modest degradation. Quantized kernels must pass the smoke-profile with cost gain >8% to justify tradeoff.

Q: How long do we keep sampled kernel traces?
A: Full kernel traces retained for 30 days in hot storage and archived for 365 days if tied to a Sev incident. Aggregated metrics remain in hot storage for 90 days.

References and links:
- operational benchmark manifests: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/operational-v1-manifests
- scheduling policy language spec: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-policy-language-declarative-profiles-2026
- continuous profiling strategy: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/continuous-runtime-profiling-strategy-2026

Document history:
- 2026-01-12 created by Aisha Patel (initial draft)
- 2026-02-04 added kernel scheduling heuristics and scheduling policy table (reviewers: Marco Ramirez)
- 2026-03-02 finalized sampling quotas and canary guidance (reviewers: Liang Chen, Sofia Martinez)

End of handbook.

title: Request Classification and Observability Contracts for Runtime Routing
content:
Summary

This page defines the request classification model and the corresponding observability contract used across the serving runtime. The goal is to produce deterministic routing decisions, consistent SLO mapping, and standardized telemetry that enables rapid triage and automated policy enforcement (e.g., cost-aware routing, fallback decisions, and quality guards). This is an engineering-facing spec intended for runtime, router, and telemetry consumers.

Scope

- Applies to all inbound inference requests processed by Redwood public and dedicated runtimes.
- Covers: request tagging, workload classes, priority heuristics, routing attributes, required telemetry fields, and common debugging workflows.
- Excludes: IAM/auth schemes, billing pipeline (except for reference label mapping), and model content inspection for privacy.

Why this matters

Inconsistent request semantics produce noisy SLO attribution, incorrect capacity decisions, and inaccurate cost signals. Aligning on a single classification scheme reduces variance in routing outcomes and enables reusable dashboards, alert rules, and automated remediation.

Definitions

1) Workload class: A short label describing the expected performance and quality envelope for the request. Examples: "realtime", "interactive", "batch", "embedding-internal", "low_priority_scrape".
2) Priority: Discrete integer (0..9) used by schedulers to shape kernel allocation and preemption policies. 0 is highest priority (system-critical).
3) Route intent: High-level objective for the request (e.g., "low_latency", "low_cost", "high_quality").
4) Fingerprint: Stable hash of request properties used to group similar requests across telemetry and cache keying.

Contract: Required request attributes

Every request that enters a runtime path must include at minimum the following envelope attributes. If missing, the router will fill with conservative defaults and emit a visibility warning (see Debugging section).

- request_id: UUID v4
- client_id: team or org identifier
- model: model name or alias (string)
- model_version: semver-like or sha tag
- workload_class: one of (realtime, interactive, batch, embedding, maintenance)
- priority: integer 0..9
- route_intent: one of (low_latency, low_cost, high_quality, degrade_gracefully)
- sequence_hint: expected token count (optional but recommended for long-form workloads)
- fingerprint: hex encoded sha1 of canonicalized attributes (see fingerprinting rules)
- provenance: origin (api, console, sdk, internal)
- ttl_ms: optional time-to-live for queued work

Fingerprinting rules (stable, language-agnostic)

1) Canonicalization order: client_id, model, model_version, workload_class, route_intent, sequence_hint (empty values omitted).
2) Normalization: lowercase strings, trim whitespace, replace multiple spaces with single space.
3) Hashing: sha1(canonical_string) and hex-encode.
4) Example canonical string: "acme:bert:2026-01-02:interactive:low_latency:512" -> fingerprint: "e6f3..."

Workload class semantics and SLO mapping

- realtime: Target p95 latency <= 120ms; used for websockets, streaming endpoints. Priority default 3.
- interactive: Target p95 latency <= 350ms; used for chat-like UX. Priority default 4.
- batch: No strict latency SLO; throughput and cost are primary. Priority default 7.
- embedding: Target p95 latency <= 300ms for dedicated embedding endpoints. Priority default 5.
- maintenance: For scheduled background tasks; can be preempted aggressively. Priority default 9.

Routing policy precedence (ordered)

1) Explicit route bindings (customer-specified pin)
2) SLO-driven routing (map workload_class -> compatible model variants)
3) Cost policy (if route_intent == low_cost)
4) Capacity availability fallback (regional/variant fallthrough)
5) Canary/rollout overrides (if in canary window and route matches)

Telemetry contract (required fields for ingestion)

Telemetry must be emitted at three points: router-in (accept), runtime-start, runtime-complete. Each emission is a JSON line with the following flat keys. All keys are strings unless noted. Timestamp fields are ISO8601 UTC.

Required fields (all events):
- ts_iso: timestamp
- event_type: router-in | runtime-start | runtime-complete
- request_id
- fingerprint
- client_id
- model
- model_version
- workload_class
- priority (stringified int)
- route_intent
- selected_variant (the variant/kind chosen or "none")
- region
- node_id (when available)
- seq_len_hint (if present)

Additional fields (runtime-complete):
- latency_ms (integer)
- tokens_out (integer)
- tokens_in (integer)
- error_code (empty if success)
- preempted (true|false)
- cost_estimate_usd (string)

Example telemetry lines:

router-in:
{
  "ts_iso": "2026-02-12T20:34:12.123Z",
  "event_type": "router-in",
  "request_id": "4a1f...",
  "fingerprint": "e6f3...",
  "client_id": "acme",
  "model": "gpt-redwood-3b",
  "model_version": "v2026-02-01",
  "workload_class": "interactive",
  "priority": "4",
  "route_intent": "low_latency",
  "selected_variant": "gpu-v1",
  "region": "us-west-2",
  "node_id": "node-42"
}

runtime-complete:
{
  "ts_iso": "2026-02-12T20:34:12.501Z",
  "event_type": "runtime-complete",
  "request_id": "4a1f...",
  "fingerprint": "e6f3...",
  "latency_ms": 378,
  "tokens_out": 120,
  "tokens_in": 24,
  "error_code": "",
  "preempted": "false",
  "cost_estimate_usd": "0.0032"
}

Derived metrics and dashboards (minimum set)

- p50/p95/p99 latency per workload_class x model_variant
- success_rate (1 - error_rate) per priority bucket
- preemption_rate per client_id and workload_class
- cost_per_1k_tokens by model_variant and region
- queue_depth and wait_time distributions for batch queues

Alerting guidelines

- Latency SLO breach: if p95(realtime) > 120ms for 10m with volume > 10 req/s -> P1 page and trigger fallback routing to low-latency variants.
- Unexpected preemption spike: preemption_rate increase by 5x relative to 1h baseline -> P2 investigate kernel fairness and priority inversion.
- Fingerprint drift: sudden >40% increase in unique fingerprints for a client in 30m -> P2 check client SDK changes or bot traffic.

Debugging checklist (fast path)

1) Confirm router-in event exists for request_id. If absent, check ingress hooks and SDK instrumentation.
2) Validate fingerprint consistency across router-in and runtime-complete. Mismatches indicate canonicalization bugs.
3) If high latency, query node_id and run quick diagnostics: gpu utilization, kernel queue length, eviction_count.
4) For preemptions, inspect kernel-scheduler logs and priority queues for inversion traces.
5) If cost unexpectedly high, check selected_variant and route_intent; ensure quantized variant was eligible.

Common misconfigurations and remediations

- Missing sequence_hint: For long-form interactive tasks, omission causes kernel to select conservative unbatched path. Remediation: Upgrade SDK to v1.8+ or set default seq_len_hint on the route.
- Incorrect workload_class mapping from SDK: Use migration script provided in tools/routing-migrate.sh.
- Fingerprinting version skew: Ensure all SDKs use fingerprint spec v2.0 (see appendix) or enable compatibility header "Fingerprint-Version: v1".

Operational playbook: automated remediation examples

1) Auto-fallback on SLO breach:
   - Trigger: p95(realtime) > 120ms for 10m
   - Action: Router attaches tag "fallback_low_latency" and re-routes new requests to cached low-latency variants for 5m.
   - Postmortem: Create alert ticket and run throughput simulation against captured traces.

2) Auto-throttle noisy client:
   - Trigger: unique_fingerprints_per_minute(client_id) > threshold AND error_rate > 1%
   - Action: Inject rate-limit header, shadow route to cost-tiered variant, notify account owner.

Appendix A: Configuration examples

YAML: route binding example

routes:
  - name: acme-realtime
    client_id: acme
    workload_class: realtime
    default_priority: 3
    allowed_variants: ["gpu-v1", "gpu-small-v2"]
    route_intent: low_latency
    fallback_order: ["gpu-small-v2", "cpu-quantized"]

CLI snippet: emit a router-in test event

$ ./tools/emit-test-telemetry --type router-in --request-id 0000-1111 --client acme --model gpt-redwood-3b --workload interactive

Appendix B: Fingerprint compatibility table

| SDK version | fingerprint spec | notes |
|-------------|------------------|-------|
| 1.x         | v1               | legacy: canonicalization omitted sequence_hint |
| 2.0         | v2               | current: canonicalization includes sequence_hint and route_intent |
| 2.1+        | v2               | adds optional deterministic client-salt header |

Ownership and rollout plan

- Owner: runtime-routing team (primary), telemetry-shared (secondary)
- Rollout: SDK + router integration to be staged across canary -> region-wide over 6 weeks.
- Migration windows: SDKs older than 2.0 will be supported with compatibility headers for 90 days.

Open items and future work

- Formalize a bounded vocabulary for route_intent to support programmatic policy synthesis.
- Investigate compact binary telemetry envelope for high-throughput short events.

Related reading

- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/request-multiplexing-backpressure-architecture-2026
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/runtime-observability-data-model-and-tracebook-2026

Document revision history

- 2025-11-12: created by Aisha Patel
- 2026-01-18: added preemption alert thresholds (Daniel Kwon)
- 2026-02-15: clarified fingerprinting canonicalization and telemetry example formats (Marco Ruiz)

title: runtime-qualification-circuit-and-chaos-lab-manual-2026
content:
Runtime qualification circuit and chaos lab — manual

Purpose
This document defines the standard experimental qualification circuit we use to validate changes to the serving runtime surface (kernel patches, scheduler policy changes, fallback routing, KV cache logic, and runtime config knobs). It pairs structured benchmarks with deterministic and stochastic chaos experiments and provides a single, reproducible gating checklist for releases.

Scope
- Applies to any code or config change that affects: kernel selection/execution, request scheduling/admission, KV cache behaviour, batching/packing logic, or telemetry/trace collection paths.
- Includes both pre-merge CI sanity tests and staged canary/qualification runs in the chaos lab.

Outcome and acceptance criteria (high level)
- No P0 regressions in production SLOs during the canary window: 99th percentile tail latency ≤ pre-change baseline + 15% and p75 ≤ baseline + 8%.
- Resource efficiency: per-token GPU micros (measured by kernel-time-trace) must not exceed baseline by more than +12% for default load shapes unless feature flagged (requires business signoff).
- Quality / fidelity: when applicable, outputs must pass the regression prompt set acceptance suite with zero critical regressions.
- Observability contract: all new signals introduced by the change must be emitted and documented before rollout.

Qualification circuit: phases and expected artifacts
1) Local dev and unit-level profiling
   - Fast path: run microbenchmarks from the repo /bench/local and the kernel unit harness. Capture single-GPU kernel latencies and memory footprints.
   - Artifacts: kernel latency CSV, memory allocation timeline, and a short explanatory note.

2) CI integration smoke and deterministic benchmark
   - CI runs the integration harness that replays a fixed request corpus (low-entropy synthetic + replayed production traces) across the runtime in a containerized fixture.
   - Pass/fail gates: no increased assertion failures, no trace reordering, and a per-test latency regression threshold.

3) Chaos-lab qualification (isolated cluster)
   - Target: a dedicated qualification cluster (tag: chaos-qualifier) sized to match the smallest production cluster.
   - Runbook steps (numbered):
     1. Deploy change to 5% of nodes behind a controlled load generator.
     2. Run the benchmark harness (see Benchmarks below) under three traffic shapes: steady, burst, and mixed latency-sensitive.
     3. Inject deterministic kernel perturbations: add a synthetic 10–50ms delay in the slowest attention kernel and verify scheduler hedging/timeout behaviour.
     4. Run stochastic chaos phases: network partitions (0.5–2s jitter), NVMe fault injection (simulated stalls), and transient GPU throttling simulation.
     5. Monitor telemetry dashboard (Latency, Error-rate, Kernel-queue-depth, GPU-utilization) and the qualification acceptance checklist.
   - Artifacts: full benchmark results, crash dumps, kernel traces, and an incident-style summary for any anomaly.

4) Canary + rollback validation (production-but-controlled)
   - Canary window: 24–72 hours depending on change size and risk profile.
   - Traffic steering: start with 1% of traffic, progress to 10% only if all SLOs and checks pass at each step.
   - Rollforward rules: automatic at each step if: (a) no P0 signals for 2h, (b) error-rate delta < 0.1% absolute, and (c) tail latency within acceptance bound.
   - Automatic rollback triggers: error-rate > 3x baseline for 15 minutes, p99 latency > baseline + 50% for 10 minutes, OR any kernel watchdog crash.

Benchmarks and test corpus (what to run)
- Baseline corpora:
  - small-chat: median length 60 tokens, mostly streaming, latency-sensitive.
  - long-completion: median length 1,200 tokens, throughput focused.
  - multi-turn-chat: mixes prefix cache reuse patterns to exercise KV cache.
- For each corpus run: record per-token kernel time, scheduler queue metrics, GPU occupancy, and memory high-water marks.
- Statistical reporting: p50/p75/p95/p99/p999 for latency; mean and 95% CI for per-token kernel micros.

Profiles and telemetry required
- Mandatory telemetry emitted during qualification run:
  - kernel.exec_time_ms (per-kernel tag), kernel.exec_count, kernel.queue_depth
  - request.latency_ms (per-stage: queue, kernel, postprocess), request.path (route tag), request.trace_id
  - gpu.utilization_pct, gpu.memory_used_mb, gpu.temp_celsius
  - kvcache.hit_ratio_prefix, kvcache.hot_evictions, kvcache.repopulation_latency_ms
- Tagging: all metrics for a qualification run must include qualifier_id and experiment_label.

Observability & dashboards
- Create a temporary dashboard for each qualification run that includes:
  - Time-series for p99 tail latency, request error-rate, kernel queue depth heatmap, and GPU memory pressure.
  - A waterfall view (textual) of the top 5 slow requests with kernel traces attached.
- Logging: increase kernel-level debug logging only for the qualification run (env var RK_QUAL_DEBUG=true) and ensure logs are retained for 14 days in the qualification workspace.

Experiment catalogue (example matrix)
- The following table (described) maps experiment types to goals and pass criteria:
  - kernel-change | goal: ensure no kernel-time regressions; pass: p99 per-kernel exec_time <= baseline * 1.12
  - scheduler-policy | goal: preserve tail SLOs under mixed load; pass: tail latency + queued requests within budget and no starvation events
  - kvcache-tuning | goal: reduce median latency for multi-turn; pass: prefix hit_ratio increases by >=10% without >5% memory overhead
  - tracing-addition | goal: increase observability; pass: all traces sampled and attached to traces in the dashboard with <=1% additional latency overhead

Runbooks (quick reference)
- If p99 spike during chaos-lab:
  1. Run quick filter: slice telemetry by qualifier_id and experiment_label to isolate the change.
  2. Collect top 3 kernel traces and inspect queue-depth histograms.
  3. If one kernel is dominant, revert the kernel change to kernel-fallback profile and re-run the step.
- If canary induces elevated error-rate:
  1. Pause traffic ramp.
  2. Execute automated rollback (route traffic back to baseline revision).
  3. Capture full core dumps and attach to an incident ticket with replication script.

Release gating checklist (must be red/green before promoting to general release)
- [ ] Unit and integration CI: green
- [ ] Qualification lab run: documented and green with artifacts uploaded to /s3/qualifier/<qualifier_id>/
- [ ] Observability signals updated and dashboards created
- [ ] Regression prompt-set run: human-reviewed failures triaged
- [ ] Rollback playbook validated in staging
- [ ] Security review (if change touches data plane or auth paths)

Operational notes and common pitfalls
- Memory fragmentation: small kernel-side allocator changes can change high-water marks without changing average usage — always inspect allocator heatmaps.
- NVMe stalls: some lab simulations surface stalls only at longer run durations — include at least one 6-hour endurance run for storage-dependent changes.
- Telemetry overhead: adding fine-grained per-kernel counters can increase CPU load; qualify sampling rate before enabling in canary.

Appendix: example CLI snippets and reproducibility tips
- Launch local qualifying harness (Docker):
  - docker run --rm -e RK_QUAL_DEBUG=1 -v $(pwd)/bench:/bench redwood/runtime-qualifier:latest /bench/run --corpus small-chat --out /tmp/qual.csv
- Quick telemetry export (prometheus query example):
  - prometheus_query 'histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_latency_bucket{qualifier_id="Q-20260215"}[5m])) by (le))'
- Replaying production slice to replica cluster:
  1. Generate curated trace: tools/trace_slice --start=2026-02-01T00:00Z --duration=1h --pattern=mixed > /tmp/slice.avro
  2. Replay: bench/replay --target=chaos-qualifier --trace /tmp/slice.avro --rate 200rps

Ownership and contacts
- Qualification steward: Priya Desai (runtime-experiments)
- Chaos-lab infra owner: Marco Alvarez (infra-platform)
- Oncall contact for canary window: serving-runtime oncall runbook (alias: #runtime-oncall)

Related documents and references
- See the per-kernel telemetry contract in the team wiki and the release gating templates in the release-notes folder.
- For scheduler policy language examples, consult the scheduler-policy DSL spec in kernel-and-scheduling.

Revision history
- 2025-11-12: Created (Priya Desai)
- 2026-02-15: Added stochastic chaos recipes and canary rollback thresholds (Marco Alvarez)

title: Kernel Signal Catalog and Experimental Hook Manifest
content:
Overview

Purpose: Provide a single, practical reference for all kernel-level signals, experimental hook points, and safe experiment templates used by runtime engineers when validating scheduler changes, kernel rollouts, or fallback policies. This document is intended for runtime, infra, and applied-ML engineers who run controlled experiments or require a repeatable instrumentation manifest.

Scope

- Signals covered: kernel lifecycle, dispatch credits, eviction events, preemption indicators, KV cache warmup/evict traces, and per-request kernel hints.
- Hook points: places in the runtime where lightweight, gated instrumentation or short-circuit behavior can be installed for experiments (no PLT changes required).
- Safety: rollout-gates, SLO checks, and automated rollback criteria are included.

Signal catalog (short-form)

Note: field names below map to telemetry keys emitted by kernel-agent v3+ and the runtime-scheduler. Use these keys in dashboards, span tags, and experiment metadata.

| Signal key | Source component | Semantics | Typical cardinality | Severity / priority |
|------------|------------------|----------:|--------------------:|--------------------:|
| kernel.alloc.lat_us | kernel-agent | microsecond latency to allocate kernel slot | per-kernel | high |
| kernel.dispatch.credit_delta | runtime-scheduler | change in token credits for a dispatch cohort | per-dispatch | high |
| kernel.handoff.attempts | kernel-agent | number of handoff attempts between kernels | per-request | medium |
| kv.prefetch.hit_ratio | kv-cache | rolling hit ratio for prefetch hints | per-session | medium |
| kernel.preempt.marker | kernel-agent | boolean marker when preemption path invoked | per-kernel | high |
| runtime.fidelity.level | orchestrator | current fidelity mode (low/med/high) | per-tenant | medium |
| scheduler.queue.depth_p50_p95 | runtime-scheduler | queue depth percentiles used for admission decisions | per-pool | high |
| kernel.quant.hint | kernel-agent | kernel-level quantization mode hint (int8/int4/float16) | per-model | low |
| eviction.reason | eviction-controller | canonical reason string (pressure/tenant-limit/fragmentation) | per-eviction | medium |
| kernel.sticky_affinity | scheduler | affinity token used for stickiness heuristics | per-instance | low |

Full telemetry mapping and JSON schema for these keys is maintained in the telemetry repo (see related_pages for links).

Experiment hook manifest (safe pattern)

High-level contract for hooks:

1) All hooks must be gated behind feature flags in the runtime-config service; flags must include an EXPERIMENT_ID and an OWNER.
2) Hooks are read-only by default: they emit telemetry and optionally short-circuit a non-critical code path. Any mutation requires an explicit canary plan.
3) Hooks must attach an experiment metadata header to outgoing spans: experiment.id, experiment.variant, experiment.owner.

Common hook types and usage examples

- Probe (telemetry-only): Inserted at allocation/handoff boundaries to emit signal snapshots. Use when you want visibility without behavior change. Example span tags: {"probe.phase":"alloc-end", "kernel.alloc.lat_us": 123}.
- Shadow-invoke: Call a new kernel path in parallel but do not use its result for production. Good for measuring compatibility cost. Ensure shadow result sampling < 0.1% to limit overhead.
- Weighted path selection toggle: Allow deterministic routing to alternate kernel for a percentage of traffic (A/B by request-id hash). Must have automatic failback after 10m if error rate delta > 0.5%.
- Soft-fallback: On kernel preempt marker, route to a lower-fidelity path maintaining a durable mapping to the original request for tracing.

Experiment template (example)

Title: Kernel-credit-hedge (weighted rollout)
Owner: Elliot Zheng
Experiment id: KCH-2026-11
Objective: Measure tail latency and error delta when applying a credit-borrowing heuristic in the scheduler for small requests.

Steps:
1) Create feature flag KCH-2026-11.enabled with 0% rollout.
2) Instrument hook at runtime-scheduler::allocate() to emit kernel.dispatch.credit_delta and kernel.alloc.lat_us.
3) Start with 0.5% traffic (random by request-id). Validate telemetry for 15 minutes.
4) Bump to 2% if no SLO violations. Continue sampling and run a 2-hour plateau.
5) If p99 latency delta > +10% OR error_rate_delta > +0.3% (vs baseline), immediately rollback to previous flag value and mark the experiment as failed.
6) If metrics stable, expand in geometric phases (2% -> 10% -> 40% -> 100%) with 1-hour observation windows.

SLOs and safety gates

- Latency: p50/p95/p99 measured at the token-generator boundary. Gates: rollback if p99 delta > +10% for more than 10m.
- Error rate: rollback if error_rate_delta (absolute increase) > +0.3% sustained for 5m.
- Cost: estimate per-token cost delta; abort experiment if cost increase > +12% without commensurate quality improvement.
- Resource pressure: if GPU memory pressure > 70% cluster-wide and eviction rate spikes > 2x baseline, pause rollout.

Profiling and data collection checklist

- Low-overhead profiling: enable tiered sampling at 0.5% for kernel traces using profiler-sidecar; capture stack + kernel tags for sampled requests.
- Deterministic microbench: use the op-bench harness with --seq-len=64 --batch=1 --count=10000 to measure kernel.alloc.lat_us stable baseline.
- End-to-end regression: run shadow-replay of 10k production traces in the sandbox with both paths enabled; collect token-per-ms and memory footprint.

CLI snippets and monitoring queries

- Toggle feature flag (example):
  rdw-ff toggle KCH-2026-11.enabled --percent=2 --owner=elliot.zheng@redwood.ai

- Start low-overhead sampling:
  rdw-profiler set-sample --target kernel-agent --rate 0.005 --dest telemetry-prod-lz

- Grafana example (PromQL):
  increase(kernel_alloc_attempts_total[5m]) / increase(kernel_alloc_success_total[5m])

- Alerting rule (pseudo-YAML):
  - alert: KernelCreditHedge_p99_regression
    expr: (histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(kernel_alloc_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le)) - baseline_p99) / baseline_p99 > 0.10
    for: 10m
    labels: {severity: page}

Operational playbook (quick triage)

1) Detection: Alert fires for p99 regression or preempt marker spike.
2) Initial triage (first 5 minutes):
   - Confirm the experiment ID in recent spans.
   - Check feature flag state and rollout percent.
   - Look at kernel.dispatch.credit_delta distribution and kernel.alloc.lat_us percentiles.
3) Immediate mitigation:
   - If experiment traffic > 0, roll flag back to previous percent.
   - If rollback not possible, add an ingress rule to divert traffic from affected pool to fallback pool.
4) Deeper investigation:
   - Replay sampled traces in the lab with debug logging ON for kernel-agent.
   - Run microbench for kernels observed with high alloc latencies.
   - Correlate infra metrics: GPU memory, NVLink errors, host load.
5) Postmortem:
   - Owner files an incident note and attaches experiment logs, replay artifacts, and the decision timeline.

Run governance and ownership

- Experiments must have a single owner and at least one technical reviewer from SRE or Kernel team.
- A QA signoff must exist for experiments that mutate data paths.
- All experiments must be tracked in the experiment registry with tags: owner, risk, baseline_hash, expected_resource_delta.

Appendix: lightweight JSON manifest for experiments (example)

{
  "experiment_id": "KCH-2026-11",
  "owner": "elliot.zheng@redwood.ai",
  "variants": ["control", "credit-hedge"],
  "telemetry_keys": ["kernel.dispatch.credit_delta", "kernel.alloc.lat_us"],
  "safety_gates": {"p99_latency_pct": 10, "error_rate_abs_pct": 0.3},
  "start_percent": 0.5
}

(When you create a registry entry paste this JSON into the experiments board; the registry will expand it into CI/CD hooks.)

Notes and caveats

- Do not use hooks that increase per-request memory by > 100KB in hot paths.
- Shadow-invoke should not be enabled for HS (highly stateful) models without explicit approval.
- Kernel signal names are semi-stable; use the telemetry-schema repo for canonical names in dashboards.

Ownership and contacts

- Primary owner: Elliot Zheng (runtime kernel team)
- SRE reviewer: Maya Thompson
- Kernel reviewer/approver: Ravi Iyer
- Telemetry: Ana Gómez

Related artifacts and links

- Telemetry schema: /repos/telemetry/schema/kernel-signals.yaml
- Experiment registry: /tools/experiments/board/KCH
- Profiler playbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/telemetry-feedback-kernel-autotune-playbook-2026

Revision history

- 2025-11-12: Created by Elliot Zheng (initial catalog and templates).
- 2026-01-08: Added soft-fallback template and SLO gates after pilot.
- 2026-02-18: Clarified sampling guidance and added CLI snippets.

title: Runtime Instrumentation Catalog and Incident Playbook
content:
Summary

This page defines the canonical runtime instrumentation catalog for the serving runtime, the metric and trace contracts teams must follow, and an investigation playbook for the most common performance incidents. It merges runtime architecture signal expectations, kernel scheduler hooks, profiling runbooks, and how the benchmarking suite should be used to validate instrumentation changes.

Scope and audience
- Audience: runtime engineers, SREs, profiling engineers, and release owners who change execution, kernels, or observability.
- Scope: production and canary environments for Redwood Inference hosting and Dedicated clusters. Does not cover client SDK metrics.

Key goals
- Provide a small, stable set of metric and trace contracts that are cheap to collect and sufficient for SLO ownership.
- Standardize kernel-level signals that scheduler engineers must expose to telemetry.
- Offer a reproducible profiling and benchmarking workflow for validating changes to instrumentation and scheduler behavior.
- Provide step-by-step incident triage for tail latency and kernel hang patterns.

Metric and trace contract catalog (single-table view)
Note: this table is the ground truth for dashboards, SLOs, alerts, and benchmarking assertions. Keep stable names; rename only via ADR and release notes.

| Service | Metric name | Interpretation | Owner | SLI window | SLO | Alert threshold |
| Serving Runtime | runtime.request.p95_ms | p95 end-to-end runtime request latency excluding queue time | runtime-observability | 5m | p95 < 120 ms | p95 > 250 ms for 3m |
| Serving Runtime | runtime.kvcache.hit_rate | fraction of token-level KV cache hits | runtime-cache | 1h | > 0.75 across traffic | drop > 0.15 relative to baseline in 15m |
