| Kernel Dispatcher | kernel.dispatch.utilization | GPU kernel dispatch utilization (0-1) | kernel-scheduler | 5m | 0.35-0.85 is healthy | sustained > 0.95 or < 0.15 for 10m |
| Kernel Dispatcher | kernel.preempt.count | number of cooperative preemptions per minute | kernel-scheduler | 1h | < 5/min averaged | > 20/min in 10m |
| Network | grpc.connection.reuse_rate | fraction of reused connections | infra-network | 1h | > 0.8 | drop below 0.5 for 30m |

Instrumentation guidance and conventions
- Metric naming: dot-separated domain.prefix.metric. Use lower case and underscores only for labels.
- Units: always append units in metric descriptions (ms, bytes, percent). Avoid unitless counters unless absolute counts.
- Cardinality: labels are limited to runtime, model_family, model_variant, region. Do not introduce free-form user identifiers.
- Sampling: traces default to 0.5% in production; increase to 2% on canaries. For kernel events, use deterministic sampling for error paths and probabilistic sampling for happy-path events.
- Baggage and spans: top-level span name must be request_id. Span tags: model, sequence_length, route.

Kernel scheduler signals and hooks
- Exposed signals: kernel.dispatch.start, kernel.dispatch.end, kernel.kernel_hint (quantization_level, preferred_slice), kernel.kvcache.prefetch_hits, kernel.handoff.reason.
- Hook semantics: kernel.dispatch.start must be emitted before any GPU work. kernel.dispatch.end must include kernel.wall_ms and kernel.tokens_produced. kernel.handoff.reason must be one of: preemption, eviction, migration, thermal_throttle.
- Backpressure indicator: runtime.queue.depth_by_priority. Use this with kernel.dispatch.utilization to compute admission decisions.

Profiling playbook: when and how to profile
1) Trigger conditions
   - Regression alert fires for runtime.request.p95_ms or kernel.dispatch.utilization anomalies.
   - Release candidate that introduces kernel or scheduler code.
2) Safe sampling plan
   - Start with live sample at 0.5% using tracing agent. Collect 10k requests or 1 hour minimum.
   - For kernel-level deep samples, schedule a controlled profiling job on canaries with overlay traffic at 10% of production QPS.
3) Commands and artifacts to collect
   - tcpdump and connection logs around the incident window (if networking suspected).
   - Kernel traces: enable kernel hook logging level 3 and collect 60s of GPU metrics via nvidia-smi or platform agent.
   - Use the profiling harness: ./tools/profiler/run_sampled_capture --trace-rate 0.01 --duration 3600 --tag regression-YYYYMMDD
4) Analysis checklist
   - Decompose latency by span: pre-queue, queue, kernel dispatch, post-process. If kernel dispatch dominates, open kernel investigation.
   - Correlate kvcache.hit_rate drops with sequence length changes.
   - Look for sudden increases in kernel.preempt.count or kernel.handoff.reason=thermal_throttle.

Benchmarking suite integration
- Purpose: validate that instrumentation changes do not skew SLOs or increase overhead beyond threshold.
- Baseline rules: every PR that changes metric emission or adds tags must run the microbenchmark suite that asserts per-token CPU overhead < 1.2x baseline and p95 latency variance < 5%.
- Synthetic corpus: use workload lanes defined in workloads/catalog.yaml where lanes include short-chat, long-infer, embedding-batch. Always run short-chat and long-infer.
- Representative test matrix: model families (small, medium, large), sequence lengths (32, 256, 1024), batch shapes (1x1, 8x8).

Release notes snippet (example for instrumentation changes)
- v2.4.0-instrumentation: Added kernel.handoff.reason field and reduced default trace sampling to 0.5% in prod. Backwards compatibility: dashboards continue to read runtime.request.p95_ms. Migration: update any alert rules that used deprecated tag "kernel_phase".

Known issues and guidance
- Issue: transient kvcache hit_rate drop on warm startups. Workaround: enable kvcache.warmup_hint for canaries to prefetch top 10k prefixes.
- Issue: occasional nvlink interconnect flapping shows as kernel.dispatch.utilization oscillation. Guidance: treat as infra/networking incident and escalate to infra-network team.
- Issue: high preemption counts after scheduler changes. If kernel.preempt.count > 20/min, rollback scheduler commit or apply temporary admission controller to reduce concurrency by 30%.

Incident triage playbook: high tail latency (p95 spike)
Step 0: Declare incident if p95 > 250 ms for 3 consecutive minutes and SLO burn expected. Notify oncall and post to channel #runtime-incident.
Step 1: Immediately check top-line signals
   - runtime.request.p95_ms, runtime.request.error_rate, kernel.dispatch.utilization, runtime.queue.depth_by_priority
Step 2: Narrow to span that increased
   - Use trace sample drilldown to find whether queue or kernel dispatch increased. If queue increased, jump to Step 4. If kernel dispatch increased, go to Step 3.
Step 3: Kernel investigation
   - Check kernel.preempt.count, kernel.handoff.reason, kernel.kernel_hint distributions.
   - If preemptions are high, run a canary with reduced concurrency. If handoffs show thermal_throttle, open hardware ops ticket.
Step 4: Queue and admission control
   - Inspect request arrival rate and admission controller logs.
   - If backpressure misconfiguration suspected, apply emergency admission policy: reject low-priority routes and reduce max tokens per request by 20%.
Step 5: Mitigation and rollback
   - If a recent deploy is implicated, follow the runtime deployment circuit breaker and rollback matrix. If not, apply temporary circuit breakers and schedule deeper profiling.
Step 6: Postmortem
   - Fill incident template: impact, root cause hypothesis, timeline, remediation, monitoring changes, action items. Assign a 2-week follow-up for regression test addition.

Ownership and escalation
- Primary oncall: runtime SRE rotation. Secondary: kernel-scheduler rotation. Tertiary: infra-network oncall.
- Pager duty runbook link: docs/pagerduty-runtime (internal link).

Related pages and anchors
- runtime-architecture/execution-stitching-and-fallback-orchestration (architecture contract)
- kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-observability-contract-and-simulated-injector (scheduler test harness)
- profiling-playbook/controlled-kernel-perturbation-playbook (kernel perturbation lab)

Appendix: common CLI snippets
- Quick latency decomposition using trace sampler: curl -X POST https://canary-api.internal/trace/decompose -d '{ request_id: R123 }'
- Start a controlled profiling capture on canary: ./tools/profiler/start_capture --env canary --tag perf-capture --duration 300

Document maintenance
- This document is the central catalog for metric and kernel signal contracts. Any change to names, units, or cardinality requires an ADR and a release-note entry.
- Owner: runtime-observability. Review cadence: quarterly or ahead of any major scheduler release.

title: Runtime precursor signal catalog and escalation checklist
content:
Overview
--------
This document is a cross-cutting catalog of PRECURSOR signals the runtime team uses to detect emerging problems across the serving runtime, kernel scheduler, profiling pipeline, and benchmarking surface. It pairs each signal with a short investigation checklist, automated queries (PromQL / SQL / CLI examples), threshold guidance, and structured escalation steps. The goal is to surface problems earlier than full SLA violations and standardize triage across on-call, SRE, and runtime engineers.

Scope
------
- Applies to hosted, dedicated, and private deployments where the runtime agent and dispatcher emit telemetry into the telemetry stack.
- Covers signal classes: scheduler contention, kernel regressions, KV cache cold/warm signals, sequence-tail latency drift, single-tenant hot-spotting, resource fragmentation, profiling anomalies, and benchmark/regression triggers.
- Does NOT replace existing runbooks for full outages; this doc is a precursor checklist and routing map.

Owner & Contacts
------------------
- Document owner: Lara Chen (runtime reliability)
- Primary on-call: runtime-oncall rotation (pager duty group: RD_runtime)
- Secondary escalation: eng-sre@redwood.com
- Model-serving kernel owner: Miguel Santos
- Observability steward: Asha Kapoor
- Slack channels: #runtime-oncall, #runtime-observability, #kernel-dev

Signal Catalog (by subsystem)
----------------------------
1) Scheduler and kernel signals
   - Symptom: Per-project kernel queue length climbs steadily and queue drain rate drops.
     - Why this matters: indicates admission or kernel-backpressure misprediction causing latency stacking.
     - PromQL example: 
       sum(rate(runtime_kernel_queue_length[1m])) by (kernel_variant, project) / sum(rate(runtime_kernel_dispatches[1m])) by (kernel_variant, project)
     - Threshold guidance: sustained ratio > 3 for 2m for a single project => investigate.
     - Quick checks:
       1. Check kernel variant logs: kubectl logs -n runtime kernel-<id> --since=5m
       2. Confirm admission tokens and quota-balance: GET /admin/quota?project=<id> (internal API)
       3. Inspect preemption events: PromQL: sum(increase(kernel_preempt_events_total[5m]))
   - Escalation: if ratio persists > 3 for 10m or 50% of requests to that project exceed 95th p50 latency SLO, escalate to kernel-owner.

2) KV cache and session signals
   - Symptom: KV cache hit-rate drops and cold-start ratio increases for median session length > 4 tokens.
     - Why: high cold cache rates increase per-token cost and tail latency.
     - Query examples:
       - Embedding of hitrate: rate(kvcache_hits_total[5m]) / rate(kvcache_lookups_total[5m])
       - Cold start indicator: rate(session_warmup_failures[5m])
     - Thresholds: hit-rate < 80% sustained for 15m bucket on a top-10 route => schedule kvcache warmup investigation.
   - Checklist:
     1. Compare session fingerprint distribution with baseline (last 7d).
     2. Verify async prefetcher logs and backpressure conf (see config table).

3) Latency drift and tail amplification
   - Symptom: P95/P99 shows divergence from P50 by more than historical variance.
     - Diagnostic query:
       - p50: histogram_quantile(0.5, sum(rate(runtime_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, route))
       - p95/p99 similar.
     - Guideline: If (p99/p50) increases > 4x baseline for a route for two consecutive 5m windows, run tracer-based decomposition.
   - Quick triage:
     1. Grab a compact trace (trace id sampling endpoint) for a sample of slow requests.
     2. Run `trace-replay --sample <trace-id>` in the dev sandbox to reproduce.

4) Kernel regression and microbenchmark signals
   - Symptom: Microbenchmark suite shows a >3% regression on token throughput for a kernel variant between consecutive releases.
     - Why: kernel-level regression often causes subtle production degradation under burst load.
     - Bench protocol: run microbenchmark generator with synthetic token sequences (stable seed), measure tokens/s median and p99.
     - Promoted action: Block release if regression persists after a quick bisect.

5) Profiling pipeline and telemetry health
   - Symptom: Profiling sampler drop rate > 20% or trace baggage missing fields (kernel_id, slot_id).
     - PromQL: rate(profiling_samples_dropped_total[5m]) / rate(profiling_samples_total[5m])
     - Checklist: verify agent version compatibility, check sidecar obfuscation rules, confirm sampling egress to observability pipeline.

6) Benchmarking/Regression gate signals
   - Symptom: Canary benchmark shows fidelity gap > configured gate or cost per token rises > 8% for top workload.
     - Table: Benchmark gate example thresholds:

   | Metric                      | Gate threshold (minor) | Gate threshold (blocker) | Action         |
   | --------------------------- | ---------------------- | ------------------------ | -------------- |
   | Median tokens/s (workload)  | 3% drop                | >6% drop                 | Triage / Block |
   | Per-token median cost       | 5% increase            | >10% increase            | Block release   |
   | Synthetic P95 latency       | 5% rise                | >12% rise                | Triage / Block |

   - Release rule: If any blocker thresholds hit on canary cluster, stop rollout and open a regression ticket.

Known-issue precursors (examples)
--------------------------------
- NVLink flapping: precursor is increased nvlink_error_rate metric plus asymmetric GPU dispatch times. Mitigation: cordon host and drain sessions with graceful transfer.
- Async kernel deadlock patterns: precursor is sustained increase in kernel_lock_wait_time_avg with no corresponding increase in dispatch rate. Immediate mitigation: escalate and apply emergency kernel patch.

Runbook: rapid triage checklist (on-call)
----------------------------------------
1. Verify alert vs precursor: confirm telemetry source and time window.
2. Scope: Isolated to single project, single cluster, or global? Use these queries: 
   - Projects impacted: topk(10, sum(rate(runtime_request_errors_total[5m])) by (project))
   - Clusters impacted: sum by (cluster) ...
3. Quick containment: apply temporary degradation policy for impacted project (API: POST /admin/degradation?project=<id>&mode=graceful)
4. Collect artifacts: kernel logs, compact traces (up to 10 samples), kvcache snapshots, microbenchmark run used for gating.
5. If > 10% of traffic to any route is impacted and duration > 10m, follow full incident process and notify eng-sre.

Escalation matrix
------------------
- Level 1: runtime-oncall (investigate, collect artifacts, apply containment)
- Level 2 (after 10m of sustained impact or major customers affected): paging to kernel-owner + eng-sre
- Level 3: Pager to oncall-lead and product/security if customer data or SLA breach risk exists

CLI & Admin commands (examples)
------------------------------
- Fetch kernel queue status: curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://admin.redwood.internal/runtime/kernel_status?kernel=KERNEL_ID
- Temporary route degradation: curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -d '{"project":"proj-123","mode":"best-effort","ttl":600}' https://admin.redwood.internal/runtime/degradation
- Force kvcache warmup for route: rdc kvcache warmup --route /chat/stream --count 200 --timeout 120s

Post-incident handoff & RCA starter template
-------------------------------------------
- Minimum required artifacts: list of traces (IDs), a reproducible microbenchmark script and seeds, snapshot of kernel variant config, and the canary benchmark run that first flagged the regression.
- RCA template fields: Summary, Timeline (UTC), Root cause hypothesis, Evidence, Corrective actions, Preventative actions, Owners, and Follow-up verification steps.

Automation & Dashboard suggestions
----------------------------------
- Add a combined "pre-cursor index" dashboard that weights signals (scheduler queue ratio, kvcache dip, profiler drop rate, microbenchmark delta) and surfaces top-10 routes/projects with the highest risk score.
- Add automated synthetic trace replays when the pre-cursor index breaches medium threshold for a route.

Appendix: config table (sampling and kvcache)
----------------------------------------------
| Config key                       | Default    | Notes                                   |
|----------------------------------|------------|-----------------------------------------|
| profiling.sampler.rate           | 0.01       | fraction of requests sampled            |
| profiling.max_inflight_traces    | 200        | guard to avoid pipeline saturation      |
| kvcache.async_prefetch.enabled   | true       | improves warmup for conversational apps |
| kvcache.prefetch_concurrency     | 8          | tuned per-cluster based on latency SLOs |

Related pages
-------------
- See: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-incident-orchestration-and-capacity-decision-matrix-2026
- See: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/model-variant-selection-cost-latency-tradeoff-matrix-2024

Revision history
----------------
- 2024-11-15: Created by Lara Chen
- 2025-01-12: Added canary benchmark gates and CLI snippets (reviewers: Maya Alvarez)
- 2025-06-10: Updated escalation timings and thresholds after Q1 incident retro (reviewers: Ethan Park, Jonah Patel)

title: Experiment Governance and Release Gates Playbook
content:
Overview

This playbook defines governance, metric gates, and operational procedures for running experiments that change the serving runtime surface: kernel selection, scheduling policies, KV cache heuristics, quantization rollouts, and runtime admission controllers. It consolidates requirements from runtime architecture, kernel scheduling, profiling, benchmarking, and release runbooks into a single actionable checklist for engineers and release managers.

Purpose and audience

- Purpose: Ensure safe, measurable, and auditable runtime experiments with clear release gates and rollback criteria.
- Audience: Runtime engineers, SREs, release managers, experiment owners, and applied ML engineers validating model-serving changes.

Scope

Applies to any change that touches the serving runtime execution path including but not limited to:
1) New or updated kernel implementations or kernel hints.
2) Scheduler policy changes (priority, preemption, admission).
3) Prefetch/KV cache algorithm changes or cache layout.
4) Quantization profile rollouts and mixed-fidelity execution.
5) Changes to batching logic and slotting/credit accounting.

Key concepts and decision model

- Risk tiering: Every experiment must be classified into Low / Medium / High risk. Classification factors: blast radius (cross-tenant potential), SLO sensitivity, frequency of affect, and revert complexity.
- Canonical metrics: latency P50/P95/P99, errors per 1000 requests, kernel-failure-rate, token-cost (per-1000 tokens), tail-kernel-duration, queue-depth distribution, successful-prefetch-rate, and fidelity-regression-score (from eval harness).
- Gate types: Canary gating (traffic slice + duration), Shadow gating (mirrored traffic), Microbench gating (isolated bench harness), and Staged rollout (percent-based ramp).

Experiment lifecycle and checklist

1) Proposal and classification (owner creates an experiment RFC with: description, affected services, implementation plan, risk tier, feature flag path, and target metrics).

2) Automated prechecks (CI):
   - Linting and static safety checks on kernel code.
   - Unit tests and deterministic scheduler simulation pass.
   - Performance microbench: baseline vs candidate on representative model snapshot (script provided below).

3) Offline evaluation:
   - Run the candidate through the benchmarking harness with the same request surface as prod for 1M synthetic tokens or 24h of replay, whichever is earlier.
   - Record per-token cost and throughput delta.
   - Run the fidelity suite (prompt set) and capture quality signals: F1, BLEU (if applicable), and our fidelity-regression-score.

4) Canary plan:
   - Canary size: start at 0.5% traffic for High risk, 1% for Medium, 5% for Low.
   - Canary duration: minimum 4 hours and until at least 10k live tokens have been served.
   - Observability hooks: enable detailed tracing (kernel spans), increase sampling of tail traces to 100% for canary cohort.

5) Gate evaluation:
   - Pass conditions (all must hold):
     a) Latency: P95 no worse than +10% relative to baseline and P99 no worse than +15% (configurable by risk tier).
     b) Errors: error-rate increase <= +0.05 errors/1k requests.
     c) Kernel reliability: kernel-failure-rate < 0.01% and no escalation events in runtime watchdog.
     d) Cost: per-token cost delta <= +8% for throughput-optimized rollouts.
     e) Fidelity: fidelity-regression-score <= 0.5 points drop (or owner-provided SLA).
     f) Observability: required traces and metrics flowing and not sampling-masked.

   - Fail conditions (any triggers immediate rollback):
     a) P99 latency regression > +25% or P95 > +40% for High risk experiments.
     b) Error-rate increase > +0.2 errors/1k.
     c) Any kernel panic/watchdog node hang.
     d) Model-quality regressions above threshold defined in the RFC.

6) Staged rollout and primary release:
   - Ramp schedule: exponential ramp doubling every 6–12 hours with metric-level check at each step.
   - Final gate: full cluster performance benchmark on a representative mixed-workload shadow for 6 hours with no critical threshold breaches.

Rollback and incident interaction

- If a fail condition is observed, the oncall or experiment owner must:
  1) Flip the feature flag to revert candidate.
  2) Notify SRE and runtime owners in #runtime-incidents with a short post including metrics and trace links.
  3) Open a postmortem stub (template below) within 24 hours.

- For partial degradations (e.g., localized node issues), consider throttling the rollout, isolating faulty topology (node affinity), and running targeted kernel telemetry collection rather than full rollback.

Telemetry and required signals

Minimum telemetry the experiment must produce:
- metric.runtime.latency.{p50,p95,p99}.percentile (per-model and per-route)
- metric.runtime.errors.perk (errors per 1k requests)
- metric.kernel.failure_rate
- metric.kvcache.hit_rate
- trace.kernel.span with attributes: kernel.name, kernel.variant, seq_len, request_id
- metric.token.cost.per_1000
- sample.trace.tail (100% for canary cohort)

Profiling and targeted investigation steps

When a threshold is near a gate limit, follow this profiling recipe:
1) Reproduce with microbench harness: use the candidate build and the 'production-replay-corpus' with: 
   ./bench/run_microbench --build=canary --model=gpt-compat --tokens=200000 --concurrency=32 --kvcache=true

2) Attach kernel tracer and collect 1k tail traces:
   - Enable kernel debug span: curl -X POST $OBS_API/trace-config -d '{"sampling": "100%", "filters": ["kernel.span.tail"] }'
   - Use kernel-timeline tool: kernel-timeline --input traces.json --group-by kernel.name --percentiles 50,95,99

3) Heap/fragmentation and GPU diagnostics: run the GPU memory profiler and the allocator snapshotter: 
   - gpu-prof --pid $RUNTIME_PID --duration 60s > gpu-snapshot.json
   - allocator-dump > alloc-$(date +%s).json

4) Scheduler contended path: replay the canary trace with the scheduler-sim binary to observe admission drops and preemption events:
   scheduler-sim --replay traces.json --policy candidate.json --output sim-report.json

Benchmarking harness and pass/fail example YAML

Example benchmark job snippet for CI (yaml as text):
---
job: runtime-microbench
build: canary
model: llama-13b
corpus: production-replay-corpus
tokens: 1000000
concurrency_profiles: [burst, steady, poisson]
measurements:
  - latency_p95
  - p99_tail_latency
  - tokens_per_sec
  - kernel_fallbacks
pass_criteria:
  latency_p95: "<= baseline * 1.10"
  p99_tail_latency: "<= baseline * 1.15"
  tokens_per_sec: ">= baseline * 0.95"
  kernel_fallbacks: "<= 0.005%"
---

Release orchestration and roles

- Experiment owner: authors RFC, tracks the gate, owns rollback.
- Runtime SRE: configures canary traffic split, escalates to infra on hardware issues.
- Observability owner: ensures traces/metrics are enabled and dashboards available.
- Release manager: signs off on staged roll when canary gates pass.

Template: RFC/Canary plan (text fields to include)

- Title
- Summary and motivation
- Affected paths (services, kernels, schedulers)
- Risk tier and justification
- Telemetry required (list)
- Microbench baseline results (attach artifact link)
- Canary size & ramp schedule
- Pass/fail gates (numeric thresholds)
- Rollback plan and estimated revert time
- Post-rollout monitoring window

Known issues catalogue excerpt (how to document and label)

When filing a known issue for an experiment, include these labels in the ticket: [runtime, kernel, experiment-{id}, sla-impact-{low|medium|high}]. Use the following template in the ticket body:
- Observed behaviour
- First-seen timestamp and canary ID
- Affected topology/nodes
- Reproducer steps (ideally microbench command)
- Attached traces and trace IDs
- Immediate mitigation taken

Postmortem and continuous improvement

- Create a concise postmortem that includes timeline, root cause hypothesis, remediation, and preventative actions. Tag the experiment RFC and link the microbench artifacts and dashboards.
- Quarterly review: the runtime team will review all High and Medium risk experiments for pattern detection (SLO regressions, kernel instability patterns) and update the gate thresholds or CI microbench profiles accordingly.

Appendices

A. Example quick rollback CLI
- Toggle feature flag: curl -X POST $FF_API/flags/candidate-kernel -d '{"state":"off"}'
- Evict canary session cohort: ./runtime-admin evict --cohort canary-2026-01-18

B. Postmortem stub (plain text)
- Title:
- Summary (1–2 sentences):
- Timeline:
- Impact (SLOs breached, customer-visible):
- Root cause:
- Remediation and follow-ups:
- Owner:

C. Observability dashboard checklist
- Canary overview tile (p50/p95/p99 over time)
- Kernel variant heatmap (counts and failures)
- KV cache hit-rate and eviction rate by prefix length
- Token-cost and throughput by model and route

D. Escalation contacts (roles)
- Runtime oncall: @runtime-oncall (rotation)
- Kernel lead: Diego Martinez (diego@redwood.com)
- SRE lead: Ava Chen (ava@redwood.com)
- Observability lead: Rohit Singh (rohit@redwood.com)

E. Related documents
- Runtime decision graph and behaviour catalog (internal)
- Continuous profiling strategy (internal)
- Microbench harness README (repo link)

If you are preparing an experiment and need a quick sanity review, ping #runtime-experiments and attach the RFC link and the benchmark artifact URL.

title: runtime-contributor-onboarding-lab-guide-2026
content:
Summary
-------
This lab-style guide is intended to onboard new contributors and rotating engineers into the serving runtime team. It consolidates the minimum safe workflow for making experimental changes, running targeted profiling and benchmarks, exercising scheduler/kernels in sandboxes, and shipping small iterate-able improvements with maintained SLOs. The guide is written for engineers with prior Linux and Python experience; no prior kernel-development experience is required.

Audience
--------
- New members of eng-serving-runtime (runtime, kernel, scheduler, and tooling subteams)
- Rotating SREs and performance engineers who will run experiments or triage incidents

Why this exists
----------------
- Reduce time-to-meaningful-contribution while minimizing risk to production pools
- Establish reproducible experiments and artifact capture for each change
- Ensure every contributor follows the same safety, observability, and rollback gates

Prerequisites (local and cloud)
------------------------------
1. GitHub account with repo access: request via infra-oncall ticket if missing.
2. Bastion + kubectl access to dev clusters: dev-serving-1 and dev-serving-2.
3. GPU-enabled dev nodes (tag: runtime-lab) provisioned by infra.
4. Python 3.10 environment with dev dependencies: pip install -r tools/requirements.txt
5. Familiarity with the following playbooks: the runtime profiling playbook, kernel scheduling contract, and the canary-run matrix (links in "Related pages" above).

Quick environment setup (copy-paste)
-----------------------------------
# Create virtualenv and install
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -U pip setuptools
pip install -r tools/requirements.txt

# Configure kube context and dev cluster port-forwarding
export KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/config
kubectl config use-context dev-serving-1
# port-forward dispatcher for local profiling UI
kubectl -n runtime port-forward svc/dispatcher 8080:8080 &

Local sandbox: starting a single-shard runtime for experiments\-----------------------------------------------------------
We maintain a lightweight developer runtime image that mirrors production behavior but restricts capacity. Use this to iterate fast:

# start a single-node sandbox (local dev box must be in dev cluster)
kubectl -n runtime apply -f infra/k8s/sandbox-single-shard.yaml
kubectl -n runtime rollout status deploy/sandbox-runtime --timeout=120s

Once the sandbox is up, you can push model binaries to the sandbox bucket and point the runtime at them for kernel experiments.

Experiment lifecycle (minimum viable experiment)
------------------------------------------------
1) Hypothesis & test plan (commit to a small MD file under experiments/): include the expected metric delta and the signal source (trace, histogram, microbenchmark).
2) Local reproduction: run an isolated microbenchmark against sandbox using workload-replay tool.
3) Capture artifacts: profiling traces, kernel counters, target traces, and the synthetic corpus used. Attach artifacts to the experiment PR.
4) Peer review: request at least one reviewer from the kernel or runtime team depending on the change.
5) Canary run: run change in canary pool with trace sampling enabled and compare SLOs.
6) Rollout gate evaluation: use the rollout checklist (section below).
7) Roll forward or rollback based on gate results.

Profiling quick-start (what to collect and why)
------------------------------------------------
- Flame traces (CPU path) — to attribute host scheduling cost.
- GPU kernel timeline (nsight/metric export) — to find stalls or serialization.
- Kernel dispatch histograms (per-kernel latency P50/P90/P99).
- KV cache hit/miss counters and session lifecycle traces.
- Request and token level latency breakdown (dispatcher, kernel queue, kernel run).

Collecting a trace (example commands)
------------------------------------
# run the replay harness for 5 minutes and collect traces
replay --config experiments/basic-replay.yaml --duration 300 --trace-out artifacts/trace-$(date +%s).zip

# extract kernel counters from the node (requires node SSH)
ssh gpu-dev-node-1 sudo /opt/runtime/bin/pull-counters --out artifacts/counters-$(date +%s).json

Benchmarks: recommended suite and how to run
-------------------------------------------
We maintain a curated benchmark suite that mirrors common customer workloads. Benchmarks are separated into three categories: micro (kernel-level), meso (single-model end-to-end on a shard), and e2e (multi-tenant dispatcher+shard).

Running a microbenchmark (example)
1. Build kernel hint artifact: make -C runtime/kernel artifacts/bench_hint.o
2. Run microbench: python tools/microbench.py --kernel bench_hint.o --iters 1000 --out artifacts/micro-$(date +%s).json

Running the meso benchmark (dispatcher + single shard)
1. kubectl -n runtime apply -f infra/k8s/bench-meso.yaml
2. python tools/bench_driver.py --scenario meso-latency --duration 600 --sample-rate 100

SLOs and safety gates for experiments
------------------------------------
- Baseline SLOs (applies to all experiments unless otherwise noted):
  - P99 end-to-end latency (single-token): <= 250ms on dev shards
  - P95 inference latency (per request): <= 180ms
  - Error rate (HTTP 5xx): <= 0.05% in canary
  - Kernel regressions: no increase > 5% P99 kernel-run-time vs baseline for the same sequence-length distribution

Gate checklist (before canary)
1. Unit tests and microbench suite pass locally.
2. Profiling artifacts attached to PR.
3. Performance regression test (meso benchmark) within threshold.
4. Observability: trace sampling enabled and dashboards updated.
5. Rollout plan with timeboxed canary and rollback TTL.

Canary run matrix (example)
--------------------------
- Canary group A: 1 shard, 10% production trace sampling, 12-hour run, synthetic and shadow traffic.
- Canary group B: 2 shards, real production traffic at 1%, 24-hour run, enhanced telemetry.

Rollback triggers (automated/manual)
------------------------------------
- Automated: error rate exceeds 0.1% OR P99 latency regresses by > 10% sustained for 5 minutes.
- Manual: on-call or owning engineer observes customer-visible degradation or fidelity regression.

Making kernel changes: additional cautions
------------------------------------------
- Kernel patches must include deterministic microbench and counter-driven rationale.
- Avoid changes that alter kernel ABI or input serialization without explicit compat notes.
- Include a fallback path (config flag) to switch back to previous kernel implementation at runtime.

Example CI job for kernel change (YAML snippet)
------------------------------------------------
ci-jobs:
  kernel-change-check:
    steps:
      - name: run-unit-tests
        run: make test
      - name: run-microbench
        run: python tools/microbench.py --iters 200 --out artifacts/ci-micro.json
      - name: upload-artifacts
        run: ./tools/ci/upload-artifacts artifacts/ci-micro.json
      - name: auto-profile-compare
        run: python tools/ci/compare_profiles.py --baseline s3://bench-baselines/kernel-p99.json --candidate artifacts/ci-micro.json
\nPost-merge observability and ownership
--------------------------------------
- Ownership: the author owns the change for a 72-hour burn-in period. The oncall takes secondary watches.
- Dashboards: add a dashboard panel named feature/<pr-number> to the Runtime Canary folder.
- Alerts: for short-lived experiments use an alert muting policy; create a tagging rule to ensure faster triage.

Runbook snippets and playbook links
----------------------------------
- If kernel stall is suspected: follow the "kernel-stability-siege-testing" playbook (see Related pages) and collect GPU timelines, host traces, and allocator stats.
- For cross-tenant noise: consult the "multi-tenant-affinity-noise-mitigation" benchmark procedures.

Checklist for turning an experiment into a permanent change
----------------------------------------------------------
1. Confirm that artifacts, benchmarks, and canary runs are reproducible and archived.
2. Update runtime feature flags or configuration schema.
3. Add automated microbench to CI with the new baseline.
4. Document the change in release notes and link to experiment artifacts.
5. Schedule a follow-up verification run after 30 days.

Roles & responsibilities (table)
--------------------------------
| Role | Responsibility | Escalation |
|---|---|---|
| Author | Write experiment plan, implement change, run local CI | Team lead |
| Reviewer | Validate benchmarks and safety gates | Senior runtime engineer |
| Oncall | Monitor canary, trigger rollback if thresholds hit | SRE lead |
| Bench steward | Maintain benchmark baselines and runner infra | Performance lead |

Common pitfalls and how to avoid them
------------------------------------
- Pitfall: running benchmarks with mismatched sequence-length distributions.
  Remedy: verify input corpus stats with tools/corpus_stats.py and attach results.
- Pitfall: forgetting to enable trace sampling in canary.
  Remedy: use the canary template from infra/canary-templates/canary-config.yaml.
- Pitfall: not including a fallback flag for kernel ABIs.
  Remedy: always add a runtime toggle and document expected behavior.

Appendix A: Useful commands and tooling paths
--------------------------------------------
- replay: tools/replay/README.md
- microbench: tools/microbench.py
- profiler UI: http://localhost:8080 (port-forward to dispatcher)
- trace archive convention: experiments/<pr-number>/artifacts/<timestamp>.zip

Appendix B: On-call contacts and escalation matrix
--------------------------------------------------
- Runtime oncall (primary): #eng-runtime-oncall Slack
- Performance lead: lena@redwood.ai
- Kernel lead: theo@redwood.ai

Related pages
-------------
See the profiling playbook, kernel scheduling contracts, and the benchmarking suite for deeper reference material. This page is the operational glue that explains how to safely move through the change lifecycle from idea to production.

Revision history
----------------
- 2026-02-18: Initial draft by Aisha Romero.
- 2026-04-12: Added canary matrix and CI YAML by Theo Martinez.
- 2026-09-10: Clarified SLO thresholds and added rollout checklist by Aisha Romero.

title: Slot Reservation Protocol and Deferred Warmstart Manual
content:
Overview

This manual documents the Slot Reservation Protocol used by the Redwood serving runtime and the Deferred Warmstart mechanism that reduces first-token latency for interactive requests without excessive pre-warm cost. It is written for oncall engineers, scheduler and worker owners, and product owners who need an operational contract for admission and warmstart behavior.

Goals
- Reduce tail latency for interactive routes by pre-reserving execution slots for requests judged latency-sensitive.
- Limit wasted GPU cycles by deferring full warmstart work until a reservation is confirmed and a short pre-execution checkpoint is reached.
- Provide clear admission semantics, deadlines, and observable signals for SRE runbooks and automation.
- Define safe fallback behavior so requests are served cold if warmstart is unavailable, with telemetry to measure impact.

Key terms
- Slot: a single execution unit on a worker that can be bound to one inference request at a time.
- Reservation: a soft hold on a slot that can be confirmed, released, preempted, or expired.
- Warmstart: preparing KV prefix state and kernel activation so generation can start with reduced latency.
- Deferred Warmstart or DWS: the practice of delaying full warmstart actions until after reservation confirmation and a final readiness checkpoint.

High-level flow
1) Frontend classifies incoming request into a tier such as interactive, best-effort, or batch.
2) For interactive requests, the frontend asks the admission component to reserve a slot using the SRP API. The request includes an affinity fingerprint, sequence length hint, and kernel hints.
3) Admission forwards a reserve request to the scheduler with a short deadline; the scheduler attempts tentative reservation on candidate workers.
4) Workers reply confirmed if they can honor the reservation within the deadline. On confirmation, admission returns a reservation acknowledgement to the frontend.
5) After confirmation, admission starts DWS: it sends a compact KV hint and kernel activation request to the assigned worker. DWS has a configurable soft time budget.
6) If DWS completes before its budget, the frontend sends the request payload to the warmed slot. If DWS aborts or times out, the payload is sent to the worker for cold execution and fidelity is recorded.

Reservation states and transitions
- Pending becomes Confirmed when the worker accepts.
- Pending becomes Expired if the deadline is missed.
- Confirmed may become Released after use or be Preempted by higher priority work.

Admission API summary
The reserve call carries the following fields in plain text: affinity fingerprint (tenant, model, route), sequence length hint, a deadline in milliseconds, a priority level, and a set of kernel hints. The response includes a status token that indicates confirmed, queued, or expired plus an optional slot identifier and ETA.

Deferred Warmstart semantics
- DWS is executed only after reservation confirmation and when affinity trust conditions are met. The default trust threshold is one previous affinity hit but is configurable per-customer.
- DWS has three logical phases: compact KV hint injection, kernel activation, and a final readiness checkpoint.
- The default DWS budget is 30 milliseconds. If the worker cannot finish within the budget the system aborts DWS and falls back to cold execution. Abort events are recorded.

Recommended configuration defaults
- reservation.deadline_ms = 15
- warmstart.time_budget_ms = 30
- affinity.trust_threshold = 1
- preempt.policy = preempt-by-priority
- reservation.max_pending_per_node = 64

Operational runbook: common failure modes
- Symptom: Elevated DWS abort rate
  1. Inspect metrics: reservation latency percentiles and worker KV prepare latency percentiles.
  2. If admission latency exceeds reservation deadline, investigate control plane saturation and network latency.
  3. If worker KV prepare latency is high, check GPU utilization, kernel unload events, and memory pressure.
  4. Short-term mitigation: increase warmstart.time_budget_ms to a conservative value such as 60 milliseconds for affected pools.

- Symptom: Confirmations frequently expire for interactive traffic
  1. Examine scheduler pending counts per node and the scheduler queue length.
  2. If pending counts approach the per-node maximum, scale worker pools or reduce the per-node pending limit.
  3. Review preemption logs; if frequent, tune preemption policy or raise priority for critical routes.

- Symptom: Preemption causes missing warmstarts and SLO misses
  1. Correlate request trace ids with scheduler event logs for the preceding window.
  2. If preemptions align with traffic bursts, enable a short holdback window so confirmed slots complete first-token generation before preemption.

Telemetry, metrics and alerts (minimum set)
- Counters and histograms to export:
  - admission_reservation_attempts_total
  - admission_reservation_confirm_rate
  - admission_reservation_latency_ms p50 p95 p99
  - worker_warmstart_success_rate
  - worker_kv_prepare_latency_ms p95
  - runtime_first_token_latency_ms p95 tagged by fidelity warmstart or coldstart
- Recommended alerts:
  - reservation_failure_rate exceeds 3 percent over 5 minutes -> P1 paging for runtime oncall
  - dws_abort_rate exceeds 1 percent over 10 minutes while cost exceeds budget -> P2 investigate kernel churn and memory pressure

Quality versus cost considerations
- Aggressive warmstarting yields the lowest latency but increases GPU active time and memory pressure. Use the affinity trust threshold and per-customer warmstart budgets to constrain warmstarts for cost-sensitive tenants.
- For low-priority traffic, prefer lazy strategies with background prefetchers rather than immediate DWS.

Safety and fallback patterns
- If a worker fails during DWS, scheduler marks pending reservations as expired and attempts reseating to an alternate worker under a secondary deadline, default 25 milliseconds.
- For customers requiring strict confidentiality, DWS is opt-in and warmth requires explicit permission to prefetch cached prefixes.

Rollout checklist
1. Add feature flags: admission.srp.enabled and worker.dws.enabled, defaulting to disabled.
2. Canary the reservation API in a single region and enable DWS for internal test routes only. Monitor confirmation rates and first-token latency.
3. Run synthetic traffic with mixed affinity distribution to validate worker KV prepare latency at target load.
4. Increment traffic exposure and enable preemption holdback.
5. At intermediate exposure, enable for a small set of low-revenue tenants while collecting cost telemetry.
6. Proceed to full rollout after 72 hours stable operation at each stage and absence of sustained alerts.

Ownership and contacts
- Primary owner: serving-runtime scheduler team, runtime-scheduler-oncall channel.
- Secondary owner: serving-runtime worker team, runtime-worker-oncall channel.
- Product contact for SLA decisions: Priya Shah.

Troubleshooting commands and examples
- Tail reservation traces for a node in the last 15 minutes: redwoodctl reservations tail with node filter and status filter.
- Inspect recent worker kernel and warmstart logs using remote access and the worker inspect tool to show warmstart history.

Engineering test guidance
- Unit tests should mock reserve responses for confirmed and expired states and assert admission behavior on timeouts.
- Integration tests should replay production fingerprints for at least five minutes and require warmstart success rate above 90 percent for interactive tier under nominal load.
- Load tests should use the benchmark harness with affinity skew to verify per-node pending limits and reservation saturation behavior.

Security considerations
- KV hints must never contain plaintext customer PII; admission scrubs hints and rejects any payload that exceeds configured size limits.
- Reserve API requires internal mutual TLS and scoped tokens with reserve write permission.

Appendix: simplified worker-side behavior pseudocode described in prose
- On tentative reserve, the worker marks a slot tentative and evaluates whether it can confirm the reservation within the configured deadline. If it can, it confirms; otherwise it queues or expires the tentative reservation.
- On DWS start, the worker checks for memory pressure and may abort early. If resources permit, it prepares KV using hints and activates kernels from idle state. The worker records prepare latency metrics and responds ready or abort.

Example configuration snippet represented as key value pairs
- reservation.deadline_ms: 15
- reservation.max_pending_per_node: 64
- warmstart.enabled: true
- warmstart.time_budget_ms: 30
- warmstart.trust_threshold: 1
- preempt.policy: preempt-by-priority
- preempt.holdback_ms: 10

Related references
- Runtime rejection and backpressure SLA in the eng-sre space.
- Coldstart warmup strategies in the eng-serving-runtime runbooks.

Revision history
- 2026-02-15: Draft created by Asha Ramanathan
- 2026-02-20: Incorporated reviewer feedback on preemption behavior
- 2026-03-01: Published with rollout checklist and alert guidance

title: Fallback Synthesis and SLA Preservation Handbook
content:
Summary:
This handbook consolidates guidance for synthesizing graceful fallbacks across the serving runtime while preserving customer SLAs. It covers the decision graph, kernel scheduling considerations, a profiling/playbook for investigating performance regressions that lead to fallbacks, an operational benchmarking protocol to validate fallback behavior, and concrete runbook steps for mitigation and postmortem.

Purpose and scope:
- Purpose: Reduce customer-visible SLA breaches by providing a repeatable playbook for when fallbacks, degradations, or variant swaps are triggered by runtime anomalies.
- Scope: Applies to all hosted and dedicated executions managed by the serving runtime (production fleets, canaries, and pre-production mirrors). Excludes private on-prem deployments where the customer owns local network/infra.

Intended audience:
- Oncall SREs and runtime engineers
- Runtime product owners and release engineers
- Observability/telemetry engineers and performance researchers

Key concepts and definitions:
- Fallback: Any automated or manual change that routes a request to a different model variant, region, or degraded execution path intended to preserve latency or error SLAs.
- SLA preservation target: Primary SLOs we attempt to preserve are p99 latency and availability per-customer route.
- Variant: Model quantization/size/compiled-kernel variant that is functionally compatible.
- Eviction vs fallback: Eviction is a resource reclaim action on a worker; fallback is a traffic-routing reaction at the decision layer.

SLO thresholds and mapping (operational values):
- Availability SLO: 99.9% over 30 days.
- Latency SLOs: p50 <= 50ms; p95 <= 120ms; p99 <= 320ms for short-chat routes (<=256 tokens). Long-form routes have route-specific p99s.
- Fallback trigger thresholds (examples):
  - p99 observed > 1.5x configured SLO for five consecutive 1-minute windows -> candidate fallback.
  - Error rate (5xx) spike > 3x baseline for 3 consecutive windows -> immediate evaluation.
  - GPU kernel queue depth > 85% for sustained 30s -> trigger conservative admission.

Fallback decision flow (high-level):
1) Detect anomaly: telemetry alert fires (latency/error/queue depth).
2) Correlate signals: match trace ids, kernel-level metrics (kernel latency, occupancy), and recent config changes.
3) Classify cause: kernel regression, model artifact, traffic surge, network degradation, or hardware failure.
4) Action selection: pick from the fallback catalog (model variant swap, route-level throttling, regional reroute, or degrade features).
5) Apply fallback with canary: route 5% -> fallback for 60s, observe p99 and error delta.
6) If successful: gradually ramp to 100% over 10 minutes.
7) If unsuccessful: rollback and escalate to incident channel.

Decision heuristics (rules of thumb):
- Prefer model-variant fallback when kernel CPU/GPU stalls or kernel timeout errors are observed.
- Prefer region-level reroute when network egress/ingress errors are correlated to region telemetry.
- Avoid functional-degrading fallbacks (e.g., remove tool-calls) for routes marked "high-fidelity" unless explicitly approved by product.
- Maintain conservative prefactors: use 1.5x–2x thresholds for latency-based fallbacks to avoid oscillation.

Kernel scheduling considerations during fallback:
- Preemptive eviction policy: mark fallback traffic as low-priority so kernels initiated by fallback traffic are subject to cooperative preemption.
- Kernel selection: when falling back to a quantized variant, ensure the kernel mapper chooses the relaxed-precision kernels with the same attention sharding to minimize KV-cache incompatibilities.
- KV cache handling: ensure session affinity mapping is preserved; if KV cache rehydration will introduce large cold-starts, prefer routing to a compatible variant that can share cache where possible.
- Admission throttles: apply admission tokens per-GPU to prevent fallback traffic from thrashing host queues.

Profiling playbook (quick triage):
1) Capture trace: enable 100% sampling on impacted route for a 5-minute window using trace tag: fallback-triage-<incident-id>.
2) Collect kernel-level histograms: per-kernel execution times, queueing durations, occupancy, and memory allocs for affected hosts.
3) Run lightweight reproducer: using the operational workload replayer, mirror a 10s slice of production traffic into a sandbox with kernel debug flags enabled.
4) Compare to baseline: use the last-successful-stable profile from the execution-profile-registry and compute delta percentiles.
5) Hypothesis checklist: kernel regression, bad kernel rollout, model weight mismatch, GPU thermal/driver regress, or system-level overload.
6) Apply mitigations: kernel rollback, model-variant swap, or admission controller limit.

CLI examples and snippets:
- Mark route for 5% fallback:
  redwoodctl routes update --route-id r-abc123 --fallback-variant quant-8bit --canary-percent 5 --canary-duration 60s

- Snapshot kernel histograms (host):
  curl -sS http://internal-metrics/hosts/host-23/kernelsnapshot | jq .histograms > /tmp/host-23-kernel.json

Benchmark protocol for validating fallback behavior:
- Objective: quantify the latency, error, and cost delta when switching to a fallback variant under representative load.
- Setup: use the operational-workload-simulator against a mirror stack with the same model catalog and kernel builds.
- Steps:
  1) Baseline: run 10m at expected steady QPS (S) and collect p50/p95/p99 and kernel histograms.
  2) Induce fallback: apply target fallback configuration (variant/region/quantization).
  3) Ramp workload: run a 30m scenario with 2x momentary spikes to simulate burst behavior.
  4) Measure: p50/p95/p99, error budget consumption, per-token GPU time, and per-request memory allocations.
  5) Pass criteria: p99 <= 1.2x baseline p99 and error rate increase <= +0.5 percentage points.

Configuration reference (examples):
| key | default | recommended for fallback testing |
|-----|---------|---------------------------------|
| admission.max_inflight_per_gpu | 1024 | 512–768 (reduce during fallback) |
| kernel.mapper.relaxed_precision | false | true for quantized variants |
| routing.canary.percent | 0 | 5–10 |
| kvcache.rehydrate_timeout_ms | 30000 | 15000 (for aggressive fallbacks) |

(When converting to the Confluence table UI, use the same three columns.)

Runbook: immediate mitigation steps (for oncall)
1) Acknowledge pager and post incident banner on #runtime-ops.
2) Gather: alert context, affected routes, recent releases (kernel/model), and top-5 affected hosts.
3) Execute safe fallback: route 5% to fallback variant using redwoodctl (see CLI example).
4) Monitor 60s canary: p99, 5xx rate, kernel queue_depth.
5) If canary improves SLA metrics -> follow ramp plan.
6) If canary fails -> rollback and execute isolation steps (drain hosts, cordon, and trigger host repair runbook).
7) Open incident with priority P1 and assign owners: runtime-oncall, kernel-author, model-oncall.

Post-incident checklist and postmortem triggers:
- Trigger a postmortem if SLA breach > 1 hour or customer-impacting errors exceed 1,000 requests.
- Include: timeline with kernel-level latency charts, decision rationale for fallback, and action items (e.g., kernel rollback automation).

Release notes and known issues matrix (short form):
- Release 2026.01.12: introduced conservative fallback orchestrator. Known: initial rollout underestimates KV cache rehydration cost for large sessions (work item assigned: PERF-876).
- Release 2025.10.30: relaxed_precision kernels added for several quantized variants. Known: a minority of kernels show 8–12% p99 regression under mixed-length sequences (mitigation: adaptive kernel selector flag).

Operational runbook annex (troubleshooting cheatsheet):
- Symptom: sudden p99 spike with no deploys
  - Check kernel histogram for long-tail spikes
  - If kernel spikes present -> try model-variant fallback to quant-8bit
  - If queue depth high and no kernel spike -> check admission throttles and increase preemption window

- Symptom: 5xx surge correlated to a recent kernel rollout
  - Rollback kernel bundle on affected hosts
  - Apply route-level canary to fallback variant

Ownership and escalation paths:
- Runtime oncall: first responder for detection, canary application, and short-term mitigation.
- Kernel team: authoritative owner for kernel rollbacks and performance fixes.
- Model onboarding: owner for validating functional compatibility of fallback variants.

References and related pages:
- execution-contracts-and-stable-fallbacks-2026 (execution contracts and compatibility matrix)
- runtime-deployment-circuit-breakers-and-sla-fallback-playbook-2026 (circuit breaker policies and automation)
- runtime-telemetry-sampling-cost-aware-profiling-2027 (sampling guidance)

Appendix: example incident timeline (fictional)
- 10:02 UTC: p99 alert fires for route chat-realtime-prod (observed p99 = 670ms).
- 10:03 UTC: oncall captures traces, correlates to kernel build k-7b2 which was rolled out at 09:58.
- 10:06 UTC: apply 5% fallback to quant-8bit variant; canary p99 -> 180ms.
- 10:20 UTC: ramp to 100% over 8min; monitor for regressions.
- 10:45 UTC: incident closed, follow-up action: pin k-7b2 rollout and queue a kernel hotfix.

Contact and feedback:
- For updates to this handbook, open a PR in the runtime-team-wiki repo and ping reviewers listed above.
- If you encounter a scenario not covered here, tag #runtime-ops with the label "fallback-gap" and file an architecture request.

Document history:
- 2025-11-03: initial draft by Aisha Patel
- 2025-12-12: added benchmark protocol and config reference (reviewers: Jonah, Priya)
- 2026-02-15: clarified kernel scheduling heuristics and added CLI snippets (reviewer: Marco)

title: Experimental runtime sandbox: safety, benchmarking, and observability manual
content:
Overview
--------
This manual documents the Experimental Runtime Sandbox ("Sandbox") used by engineering to safely run kernel scheduling experiments, profiling campaigns, and microbenchmark families against production-like stacks without exposing customer traffic. The goal is to provide repeatable processes, safety checks, telemetry expectations, and benchmark recipes so experiments can be run with minimal risk and high signal quality.

Intended audience
- Runtime engineers running kernel or scheduling experiments
- SREs validating performance/operational impact
- Research/Applied ML teams onboarding model variants into experiments

Key principles
- Isolation: sandbox instances must not be able to reach production control planes or persist customer data.
- Observability parity: the sandbox must expose the same telemetry surfaces (traces, metrics, kernel counters) as production.
- Incremental blast radius: start tiny (1-2 nodes) and scale only after passing guardrails.
- Reproducibility: each experiment must include a reproducible workload definition and seed set.

Quick reference SLOs for Sandbox test runs
- Synthetic latency target (sample workload): p95 < 120ms, p99 < 300ms.
- Throughput stability: mean throughput drift < 8% over 30-minute window compared to baseline.
- Kernel error rate: GPU kernel launch failures < 0.01% per-minute.
- Resource leakage: no orphaned processes or pinned memory > 5 MB per minute after tear-down.

Sandbox environments and naming conventions
- dev-sbx-<engineer>-<yyyymmdd>-vN (short-lived, free-form experiments)
- qa-sbx-chaos-<id> (used by SRE for fault-injection tests)
- perf-sbx-<model>-<profile> (used for benchmarking/model variant comparison)

Environment creation checklist
1. Verify the experiment has an associated ticket and owner.
2. Create sandbox VPC with egress-only NAT; no peering to prod.
3. Provision GPU nodes from the sandbox pool with node labels: sandbox=true, owner=<owner>.
4. Ensure KMS keys used are test keys; do not reuse customer KMS material.
5. Deploy runtime under feature-flagged build and enable extra logging (TRACE=kernel,harness).
6. Confirm Prometheus and tracing collectors point to sandbox ingestion endpoints.

CLI snippets
- Create sandbox cluster: redwoodctl sandbox create --name perf-sbx-bert-20241015 --gpu-type a100 --nodes 2
- Deploy runtime: redwoodctl deploy runtime --cluster perf-sbx-bert-20241015 --image gcr.io/redwood/runtime:exp-kernel-20241015
- Start workload generator: ./sbx-loadgen --profile=chat_short --concurrency=16 --duration=1800s --seed=42

Experiment config example (YAML)
- name: kernel-waveform-test-1
  owner: @ava
  cluster: perf-sbx-bert-20241015
  model: bert-base-384k
  build: exp-kernel-20241015
  workload: chat_short
  telemetry: [metrics, traces, kernel_counters]

Telemetry and observability checklist
- Metrics: request_latency_ms (p50/p95/p99), tokens_per_second, kernel_launch_errors, gpu_mem_free_bytes, kvcache_hit_rate.
- Traces: full request timeline including kernel dispatch spans and kernel_id annotation.
- Kernel counters: per-kernel CUDA duration, SM occupancy, warp-efficiency estimates, L2 cache misses.
- Logs: runtime.INFO and runtime.DEBUG logs shipped to sandbox logging bucket.
- Sampling guidance: for medium experiments (10k requests) sample 5% full traces; for small experiments (1k requests) sample 100% for triage.

Profiling playbook (how to collect high-signal profiles)
1. Baseline run: 10-minute steady-state run of the chosen workload with the current stable kernel. Collect metrics and a 1% trace-sample.
2. Instrumented run: enable kernel-level tracing and nvprof capture for 120s at the 5-minute mark.
3. Differential comparison: generate flamegraphs for both runs and diff by kernel name and sequence length bucket.
4. Hypothesis validation: if increased latency maps to specific kernels, run microbenchmarks that pin sequence length and batch shapes to reproduce.
5. Regression triage: if latency is > 15% vs baseline at p95, stop and move to incident-style runbook (section: Failed experiment escalation).

Microbenchmark recipes (recommended canonical workloads)
- chat_short: 1–4 tokens prompt, typical PLG latency-sensitive route; concurrency 8–32; sequence length 256.
- long_context: 1–8 tokens prompt with 16k context retrieval; concurrency 2–6; sequence length 8192.
- search-embeddings: batch-size 128, measure tokens/s and memory footprint.
- rerank-burst: bursty pattern, 100 requests over 10s, then idle 50s; used to test cold-start behaviors.

Kernel scheduling knobs to test (and safe ranges)
- preemption_granularity: [ms] allowed range 1–50ms. Start at 10ms.
- batch_slice_target_ms: 5–40ms. Lower values reduce p99 but lower throughput.
- cooperative_yield_backoff: 0.5–4 (multiplier). Use 1.0 baseline.
- kernel_credit_limit: integer per-tenant limit; recommended test values 1, 4, 8.

Table: safe test matrix (examples)
Name | Nodes | Concurrency | Duration | Safety gates
-----|-------|-------------|----------|-------------
mini-smoke | 1 | 4 | 10m | kernel_launch_errors < 0.01%
stability-run | 2 | 16 | 60m | throughput drift < 5%
stress-burst | 4 | 64 | 30m | p99 < 3x baseline or auto-abort

Release-style checklist for promoting changes from Sandbox to Canary
1. Confirm experiment reproducibility and attach baseline vs experiment artifacts (metrics, traces, profiles).
2. Create a change request including kernel binary hash, config diff, and expected impact matrix.
3. Run a 4-hour stability-run in sandbox and pass SLOs.
4. Run canary in isolated prod tenant with 0.1% traffic and close monitoring for 6 hours.
5. If canary passes, increment traffic via automated rollout with automated rollback threshold: p95 increase > 20% or error rate increase > 0.1%.

Runbook: failed experiment escalation (step-by-step)
1. Immediately stop experiment traffic (redwoodctl sandbox stop --name <name>).
2. Snapshot pods and kernel logs: redwoodctl logs collect --cluster <cluster> --since 15m --output /tmp/snapshot.tgz
3. If kernel_launch_errors > threshold, mark experiment "unsafe" and alert runtime-alerts@redwood.com.
4. Triage owners: runtime-oncall -> experimental-owner -> applied-ml.
5. Reproduce in a clean sandbox cluster; if reproducible, open a kernel regression bug with reproducer and attach nvprof output.

Known limitations and common pitfalls
- Telemetry skew: sandbox ingestion pipeline can introduce up to 2–4% metric distortion due to sampling; account for it during comparisons.
- NVProf overhead: nvprof captures can add 10–30% latency during capture windows — never run nvprof in production.
- Resource packing differences: sandbox GPU instances may have slightly different NUMA locality vs prod fleet; include NUMA annotation when comparing.

Safety primitives implemented in the Sandbox runtime
- admission-controller sandbox-enforcer: blocks any deployment that references production secrets or KMS ARNs.
- runtime-feature-flag: experiments must be deployed with runtime.env.EXPERIMENT_ID set.
- automated abort: sidecar monitors p95 and kernel errors; if thresholds exceeded, triggers teardown.

PromQL queries to use for dashboards
- p95 latency: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le))
- kernel errors per minute: sum(increase(kernel_launch_errors_total[1m]))
- kvcache hit rate: sum(rate(kvcache_hits_total[5m])) / sum(rate(kvcache_requests_total[5m]))

Post-experiment artifacts required
- workload definition (seeded generator config) as a checked-in yaml.
- raw metrics tarball (Prometheus scrape or pushgateway export).
- sampled traces (trace IDs list and span export).
- nvprof and flamegraph artifacts.
- experiment retrospective: short doc with conclusions and recommended next steps.

Ownership and contacts
- Sandbox environment owner: @ava (eng-serving-runtime).
- Runtime kernel owner: @rohan (eng-serving-runtime).
- SRE validation @emily (eng-sre).
- Security contact for sandbox network reviews: security-oncall@redwood.com

Appendix: sample experiment retrospective template
1. Title and owner
2. Purpose and hypothesis
3. Baseline vs experiment: key metrics (table)
4. Profiles: top 5 kernels by added latency
5. Reproducibility checklist
6. Decision and next steps

Example decision snippet
- Decision: Roll forward cooperative_yield_backoff=0.8 in staged canary.
- Rationale: 12% p95 improvement on chat_short, no increase in kernel errors over a 4-hour stability run.
- Rollout plan: 0.1% -> 1% -> 10% traffic increments with 6-hour observation windows.

Notes and references
- See runtime-architecture/execution-stitching-and-fallback-orchestration-2026 for fallback policies.
- See profiling-playbook/telemetry-feedback-kernel-autotune-playbook-2026 for autotuning loops.

This manual should be updated whenever a new telemetry surface is added or sandbox safety primitives change. For editorial changes, reach out to the document owner (author listed above).

title: Operator Economics and Fidelity Gating Manual
content:
Purpose
-------
This document codifies operator-facing economics and fidelity-gating controls used by the serving runtime. It explains the decision surface between cost, latency, and output fidelity and provides prescriptive operator procedures, telemetry checks, and safe rollback paths. Intended audience: SREs, runtime engineers, and platform owners.

Summary and scope
-----------------
- Scope: runtime-level controls (scheduler quotas, kernel selection hints, KV cache warmup, model variant fallback) and the observability/benchmark artifacts needed for safe gating.
- Goal: keep production SLAs while minimizing incremental cost and preserving highest-possible fidelity for priority traffic.
- Not covered: model training or offline eval pipelines (see /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals).

Key concepts and definitions
---------------------------
- Fidelity band: discrete levels of model execution quality we expose to the runtime: high, balanced, economical. Each band maps to kernel variants, quantization profile, KV cache eviction aggressiveness, and max sequence length.
- Cost delta: estimated additional $/token or $/request when upgrading fidelity band.
- Fidelity gate: a runtime policy (per-route or global) that controls which fidelity bands are eligible for a request.
- Operator budget: a time-boxed cost allocation (e.g., additional $5000/week) used to permit temporary fidelity upgrades for experiments.

Architecture overview (operator view)
------------------------------------
The runtime exposes a Fidelity Controller service that synthesizes signals and programs the scheduler/kernels and routing plane. High-level flow:
1) Request classification: route-level tags + customer tier + dynamic QoS (latency headroom, token budget).
2) Fidelity scoring: small in-rack scorer computes a score (0..100) using historical latency, delta cost, and a lightweight quality estimate from the shadow-eval service.
3) Gate decision: score mapped to fidelity band using configured thresholds.
4) Program runtime: scheduler receives a per-request execution profile (kernel hints, max tokens, kvcache hint).
5) Observability: fidelity decisions are annotated in traces and roll up to the Fidelity Controller dashboard.

Operators should understand these contracts before changing thresholds or kernel hints.

Operator configuration reference
-------------------------------
Below are the canonical fields and recommended defaults stored in the runtime config service. Change via the control-plane API (see CLI examples).

Table: Fidelity gating fields (canonical)
| field | description | recommended default | units | owner |
|-------|-------------|---------------------|-------|-------|
| fidelity_threshold_high | score above which high fidelity is allowed | 90 | score | runtime-scheduler |
| fidelity_threshold_balanced | lower bound for balanced band | 60 | score | runtime-scheduler |
| kv_warmup_ms | recommended prefetch window to warm KV for high band | 1200 | ms | kv-team |
| quant_profile | quantization profile applied per band | q8_0 (balanced), q4_0 (economical) | string | runtime-optimizer |
| max_sequence_override | hard cap for economical band | 512 | tokens | runtime-scheduler |

CLI and API examples
--------------------
To view current gating config:

```
redwoodctl runtime fidelity get --env prod --cluster us-west-2
```

To set balanced->high threshold to 85:

```
redwoodctl runtime fidelity set --env prod --cluster us-west-2 --fidelity_threshold_high 85
```

Rollback example (aka emergency revert):

```
redwoodctl runtime fidelity rollback --to revision=2025-11-03 --reason "regression: increased hallucination in route /compose"
```

Operational runbook: fidelity gate changes
----------------------------------------
Prerequisites: owner on-call, runbook approvals from product and SRE, and a small canary percentage (1%).

Steps:
1) Create a canary blueprint: pick 1% traffic and a single model variant. Record baseline metrics (tail P99 latency, quality eval on golden prompts, cost-per-token).
2) Apply gate change to a named canary (control-plane API).
3) Monitor 0-20 minutes: using the fidelity-dashboard, watch for regressions in quality signals and tail latency. Abort if P99 > baseline + 40ms or quality-signal drop > 3% absolute.
4) If stable at 1% for 1 hour, escalate to 10% for 2 hours. Watch cost burn rate; abort if projected weekly cost delta exceeds operator budget (see cost calc below).
5) Full rollout by doubling cadence (10% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100%) with at least 2x the stabilization window at each step.

Quality rollback triggers (automated):
- Shadow eval regression: +5% failure on golden prompt set.
- Customer-facing error increase: >0.5% increase in partial/invalid responses.
- Latency SLO breach: sustained P99 > SLO + 50ms for 15 minutes.

Cost calculus and projection examples
-----------------------------------
Operators should use the projection helper to estimate weekly cost deltas. Example calculation (simplified):
- Baseline: 10M tokens/day at $0.0003/token = $3,000/day.
- High fidelity increases per-token cost by estimated 12%. Projected increase: +$360/day -> $2,520/week.

Command to run projection locally (developer helper):
```
python tools/cost_projection.py --tokens-per-day 10000000 --delta-pct 12
```

Profiling & benchmarking tie-ins
--------------------------------
When changing kernel hints or scheduler admission, always run the local microbenchmark suite with identical sequence-length distributions. The canonical benchmark command (CI lab):

```
./benchmarks/run_workload.py --profile fidelity-gate-candidate --samples 1000 --seq-dist heavy-long
```

Record these outputs into the bench-results store and link them in the rollout ticket. Bench checklist:
- steady-state throughput (rps)
- p50/p95/p99 latency
- kernel occupancy and context-switch rate
- tail jitter across nodes

Kernel scheduling considerations
--------------------------------
The Fidelity Controller can influence three scheduler knobs per request: priority class, batch-slicing hint, and kernel-variant preference. Operator guidance:
- Do not change priority caps for the production shared pool without SRE approval.
- When adjusting batch-slicing hint for economical band, prefer conservative slice_count values (>=4) to avoid preemption storms.
- Prefer kernel-variant toggles during low-traffic windows (00:00-04:00 PST) and never during scheduled major releases.

Table: Safe kernel toggle window
| toggle type | recommended window | reason |
|-------------|--------------------|--------|
| experimental SIMD kernel | 00:00-04:00 PST (weekends prefer) | stability unknown for mixed workloads |
| quantized-fallback kernel | rolling 20% canary during low traffic | monitor quality regressions |

Telemetry and dashboards
------------------------
Essential metrics to watch when performing fidelity changes:
- fidelity_decision.count (per band)
- fidelity_rollback.count (by reason)
- runtime.p99_latency (by band)
- kvcache.hit_rate (by band and model)
- kernel.handoff_errors
- cost.estimated_delta_per_hour

Tracing keys to inspect: fidelity_decision_id, request_cohort, kernel_variant, kv_prefetch_id. Tag traces with the causal_change_id for rollback tracing.

Known issues and mitigations (operator-focused)
-----------------------------------------------
1) Symptom: intermittent hallucination spike after enabling high-fidelity on a compositional route.
   - Likely cause: model variant mismatch (high-fidelity kernel uses slightly different positional handling).
   - Mitigation: revert gate for that route and run the golden-prompt regression harness.

2) Symptom: sudden drop in KV hit_rate after reducing kv_warmup_ms.
   - Cause: aggressive eviction and unoptimized prefetch policy for long-tail contexts.
   - Mitigation: increase kv_warmup_ms by +400ms on the affected cohort and bump prefetch parallelism by +1.

3) Symptom: scheduler credit starvation for small but latency-sensitive customers when enabling balanced band globally.
   - Cause: priority class leakage and insufficient credit isolation.
   - Mitigation: activate per-tenant cap and enable emergency backstop (route-level hard cap on concurrent high-fidelity slots).

Release checklist (when delivering fidelity-controller changes)
-------------------------------------------------------------
- Unit and integration tests for fidelity scoring logic (coverage >= 85%).
- Microbenchmarks for the affected kernels and quant profiles attached to PR.
- Canary plan and explicit abort conditions documented on the PR.
- Audit log entry created and reviewed by security for changes to quant_profile.
- Post-release 24-hour watch shift assigned.

Safety-first experiments: example lab plan
----------------------------------------
1) Lab hypothesis: switching balanced->high reduces BLEU-like failures by 2% on summarization route.
2) Minimal footprint: replicate 10k requests from production trace in CI lab with shadow scoring enabled.
3) Acceptance criteria: 2% improvement on golden set with <10ms median latency increase.
4) If acceptance criteria met, move to 1% canary in prod (see runbook).

Operational play: emergency rollback and postmortem template
---------------------------------------------------------
Emergency rollback steps (quick):
1) Run redwoodctl runtime fidelity rollback --to last-known-good and annotate incident in PagerDuty.
2) Open an incident ticket and tag "fidelity-rollback". Include causal_change_id and affected routes.
3) Initiate golden-prompt regression run and attach outputs to the incident.
4) If rollback was triggered by quality regression, schedule a cross-team triage (runtime + applied-ml) within 24 hours.

Postmortem template fields (required):
- summary (one-paragraph)
- timeline of events
- root cause hypothesis (with artefacts)
- detection vector and detection latency
- mitigation and permanent fix plan with owners and ETA

Appendices
----------
A. Example JSON request profile (what the scheduler receives)
```
{
  "request_id": "req-20260110-7f2a",
  "route": "/compose",
  "cohort": "tier-enterprise",
  "fidelity_score": 92,
  "fidelity_band": "high",
  "kernel_hint": "sliced_simd_v2",
  "kv_prefetch_ms": 1200
}
```

B. Checklist for safe kernel-variant rollouts
- Canaries in a dedicated low-impact shard.
- Performance counters enabled and live alerting for increased kernel.handoff_errors.
- A/B shadow evaluation against golden prompt set.

C. Contact and ownership
- Fidelity Controller owner: runtime-scheduler team (pager: #runtime-scheduler-oncall).
- KV team SME: @meera (Meera Iyer).
- Applied ML contact for quality regressions: @luca (Luca Martinez).

D. References and links
- Fidelity scoring proto: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/fidelity-orchestrator-telemetry-contract-runbook-2026
- Benchmarking lab guide: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/runtime-deployment-sanity-and-benchmark-suite-acceptance-2026

If you are planning a fidelity or kernel change and do not have a template for the canary plan, copy the checklist under "Operational runbook" and open a draft change ticket in the runtime change board.

title: Scheduler Shadowplay and Telemetry Convergence Playbook
content:
Summary
This playbook defines the 'Scheduler Shadowplay' experiment pattern and a telemetry convergence protocol for validating scheduler and kernel-scheduling changes against production-like traffic. It combines parallel (shadow) scheduling runs, targeted profiling, and a gated quality checklist so teams can iterate on scheduling policies without risking customer SLAs.

Why this exists
- Scheduler changes (admission, preemption, kernel hints) can introduce subtle latency and fidelity regressions that are hard to detect with unit tests or synthetic microbenchmarks.
- Shadowing real traffic through a non-authoritative (shadow) scheduler lets us compare end-to-end observables while keeping live traffic untouched.
- Telemetry convergence defines statistical checks and gating rules so rollouts proceed only when measurable signals align with safety thresholds.

Scope and assumptions
- Applies to changes in: scheduler policy DSL, kernel selection heuristics, priority mapping, preemption thresholds, and admission controllers.
- Assumes: shadow scheduler can be run in parallel to production pods (no write-side-effects), tracing headers are propagated (trace-id/kvcache-hash), and a profiling instrumentation sidecar is available.

Owners and contacts
- Playbook owner: eng-serving-runtime Scheduling Guild (primary: Maya Chen)
- On-call escalation: runtime-sre team (pager: #runtime-sre)
- Reviewers: listed in metadata above

High-level pattern
1) Prepare shadow environment
   - Deploy a shadow scheduler instance that consumes mirrored decision requests. Shadow scheduler MUST NOT affect traffic (read-only decision path).
   - Ensure shadow pods have the same kernel build (or explicitly labeled if testing kernel changes).
2) Collect baseline
   - Run shadowplay with baseline scheduler to establish reference telemetry for 48h (recommended) or one production peak cycle.
3) Deploy candidate scheduler
   - Switch shadow cluster to candidate scheduler and run for an identical period.
4) Telemetry convergence checks and gating
   - Compute delta metrics (candidate vs baseline) and run statistical tests.
5) Profiling and targeted instrumentation
   - On any significant divergence, run focused profiler sessions using the profiling sidecar.
6) Decision and rollout
   - If all gates pass, proceed to canary with controlled traffic. If not, collect diagnostics and iterate.

Metric and signal catalog
- Latency: p50/p90/p95/p99 for request end-to-end (ms). Primary gating metric: p95.
- Errors: 4xx/5xx within runtime, kernel faults, NVLink reprobes.
- Kernel switch count: average kernel flips per request (should not increase >10%).
- KVCache hit ratio: prefix/KV cache hit % (should not degrade >1.5ppt for high-fidelity cohorts).
- Token throughput: tokens/sec aggregated per shard.
- Resource signals: GPU SM occupancy, memory allocs/sec, swap activity (on-host), CPU steal.
- Cost proxy: normalized per-token GPU utilization estimate.

Gating thresholds (default)
- p95 latency: candidate <= baseline + 10 ms OR no statistically-significant increase (p-value > 0.05 for Mann-Whitney U test)
- Error rate: candidate <= baseline + 0.1% (absolute)
- KVCache hit: no decrease greater than 1.5 percentage points for workloads with >10% cacheable prefixes
- Throughput: candidate >= 95% of baseline under matched load
- Cost delta: normalized per-token cost increase <= 8% (ops must approve >8%)
- Stability: no kernel panics, watchdog resets, or GPU timeout events during the shadow period

Statistical procedures
- Use paired comparisons where possible: align requests by trace-id to compute per-request deltas and run a Wilcoxon signed-rank test for latency deltas.
- For non-paired aggregated signals, use bootstrap confidence intervals (95%) to judge convergence.
- Require at least N=10k matched requests for meaningful p95 comparisons; otherwise extend the shadow window.

Data sources and dashboards
- Primary time-series: runtime.metrics.{latency,end_to_end}_p95, runtime.errors.count, runtime.kvcache.hit_ratio, kernel.switch_rate, gpu.utilization_pct
- Traces: trace.span.runtime_request -> annotate with scheduler.variant and kernel.hints (tag names: scheduler.variant, kernel.tag, shadow.play_id)
