- Dedicated dashboards: "Scheduler Shadowplay Convergence" (Grafana) and "Scheduler Shadowplay Diff" (Heatmap). Ensure diff dashboard shows per-cohort comparisons.

Runbook: immediate remediation flow (if candidate fails during shadow)
1) Abort: stop candidate shadow traffic and revert shadow scheduler to baseline.
2) Snapshot: capture a 10-minute high-fidelity profile (pprof + GPU traces) and save a trace sample set with trace-ids.
3) Notify: post summary to #runtime-ops including key deltas and linking the snapshot.
4) Triage: schedule a focused investigation within 4 business hours with scheduling, kernel, and SRE.
5) Rollback plan: candidate must remain off the production decision path until the issue is resolved and a new shadow run passes gates.

Profiling playbook (when divergence detected)
- Step 1: Reproduce in controlled shadow window with load-sculpting tool (load-sculptor-cli).
  Example: load-sculptor-cli replay --corpus=samples/peak-1H --concurrency=120 --trace-ids=./trace-seed.json
- Step 2: Enable sidecar collection: set env SHADOW_PROFILING=enabled and increase trace sampling to 100% for 5 minutes.
- Step 3: Capture: GPU traces (nsys), kernel timeline (ktrace), and runtime CPU flamegraphs.
- Step 4: Annotate: tag traces with reason tags (e.g., preemption-regression, kernel-selection) and add kernel hint dumps.
- Step 5: Analyze: correlate p95 latency spikes with kernel switch counts and NVLink activity. Use causality checklist below.

Causality checklist (common root causes)
- Kernel hint mismatch: candidate suggested a heavier kernel path for mid-length sequences.
- Increased kernel churn: frequent kernel switches per request due to sequence length fragmentation.
- Admission backpressure: new admission thresholds caused head-of-line blocking at dispatcher.
- KV cache coldspots: candidate ordering increases cold-start requests for popular prefixes.
- Resource contention: increased SM occupancy leading to longer kernel enqueue latencies.

Example scheduler policy snippet (YAML)
- name: test-candidate-policy
  admission:
    max_slots_per_shard: 48
    queue_timeout_ms: 120
  preemption:
    enabled: true
    debt_threshold_ms: 5
  kernel_hints:
    prefer_quantized: true
    max_kernel_switches_per_request: 2
  priority_synthesis:
    economic_weight: 0.7
    fidelity_weight: 0.3

CLI example: start a shadow run (ops)
1) Create play:
   rwd ctl shadow create --name=scheduler-shadow-2026-06 --source=mirror-prod --target=shadow-cluster-03 --duration=48h --note="candidate kernel: v2-opt-hint"
2) Switch policy:
   rwd ctl shadow set-policy --play=scheduler-shadow-2026-06 --policy-file=policies/test-candidate-policy.yaml
3) Watch progress:
   rwd ctl shadow status --play=scheduler-shadow-2026-06 --format=wide

Acceptance checklist before promoting candidate to canary
- All gating thresholds satisfied for target cohorts for a minimum of 48 hours (or one peak cycle).
- Telemetry pipelines show <5% missing trace propagation during the shadow window.
- No kernel-level faults or GPU watchdog events recorded.
- Profiling artifacts and a short investigation note uploaded to the shadowplay artifact bucket: s3://redwood-shadowplay/artifacts/{play_id}/
- Approval from runtime-sre and Scheduling Guild leads.

Rollout matrix (recommended)
- Shadow -> Canary 1 (5% traffic, 4h) -> Canary 2 (20% traffic, 12h) -> Gradual ramp to 100% over 72h if no regressions.
- If canary shows divergence, follow rollback immediate remediation flow above.

Operational tips and anti-patterns
- Tip: Align shadow windows to production peak hours for more representative load.
- Tip: Use cohort labels (e.g., small-seq, long-seq, embeddings-heavy) to avoid signal dilution.
- Anti-pattern: Short (15–30 minute) shadow runs; these often miss tail behaviour.
- Anti-pattern: Ignoring KV cache observables; many scheduler changes shift ordering and indirectly alter cache hit rates.

Appendix A — Example diff report fields
- total_matched_requests
- p95_baseline_ms, p95_candidate_ms, p95_delta_ms, p95_pvalue
- errors_baseline, errors_candidate, errors_delta_pct
- kvcache_hit_baseline_pct, kvcache_hit_candidate_pct, kvcache_delta_pp
- gpu_util_baseline, gpu_util_candidate, util_delta_pp
- artifact_link (S3)

Appendix B — Troubleshooting quick hits
- If p95 increases but kernel switch count unchanged: look for NVLink queueing or host CPU starvation.
- If KV hits drop: verify request ordering and any implicit batching changes.
- If errors spike with no latency change: prioritize investigating kernel-level assertions and runtime error wrapping.

References and related docs
- Runtime decision graph and observed behaviour catalog (link in metadata)
- Profiling: causal latency attribution playbook (link in metadata)
- Runtime runbooks: eviction, warmstart, and graceful degradation playbooks

Change log
- 2026-01-15: Initial draft (Maya Chen)
- 2026-03-22: Added statistical procedure guidance and default gating thresholds (reviewers: Priya Nair)
- 2026-06-30: Expanded profiling playbook and added CLI examples; set publication status to published

End of document

title: Runtime fidelity surgeon manual
content:
Summary
-------
This manual describes the end-to-end process and operational discipline we use to change inference fidelity inside the runtime: any deliberate change that affects numeric precision, kernel selection, batching policy, KV-cache warmup, model variant selection, or routing heuristics that we expect to change latency/cost/quality tradeoffs. The document combines architecture rationale, kernel scheduling implications, profiling playbook steps, benchmarking commands, an acceptance gate checklist, and example release-note scaffolding.

Scope
-----
- Applies to hosted, dedicated, and private deployments for production traffic.
- Covers automated changes (autotune controller), manual operator interventions, and canary rollouts.
- Excludes model training changes, prompt-level A/B experiments, and customer-visible prompt edits.

When to perform fidelity surgery
-----------------------------
Perform a fidelity change only when one or more of the following are true: 
1) measurable unit-cost savings (>5% projected) with acceptable quality risk;
2) latency SLO headroom is low and a fidelity change is required to meet tail SLOs;
3) a hardware constraint (GPU memory, thermal ceiling) necessitates an alternate execution path;
4) quality regressions are explicitly tolerated for degraded tiers (e.g., fallback fast path).

Before you start (preflight checklist)
------------------------------------
- Ownership: confirm an owner from runtime-ops and an owner from applied-ml (names and PagerDuty rotation).
- Ticketing: create a ticket with hypothesis, target metric delta, and rollback conditions.
- Canary targets: identify traffic cohorts and snapshot corresponding request surfaces.
- Baseline captures: collect 1 hour of traces for the target cohort including kernel traces, KV-cache hit rates, per-token cost, and example outputs (min 100 sessions).
- Evaluation prompts: select at least 200 prompt/test pairs from the eval harness tagged for quality regressions.

Architecture considerations that inform changes
----------------------------------------------
- Kernel selection is orthogonal to model architecture; the runtime maps model ops to kernel families at dispatch time. Changes in kernel hints may increase occupancy and change preemption behavior.
- Prefetch and KV-cache warmup interact with quantized execution: warmup patterns that assume FP16 cache layouts may be less effective for int8 kernels.
- Priority-driven scheduler treats fidelity-change traffic as "deferred candidate" until canary passes; this prevents accidental priority inversion.

Operator runbook: step-by-step
-----------------------------
1) Prepare canary image/config: increment feature flag and attach a unique trace tag (fidelity-surgeon-<ticket-id>).
2) Dry-run locally: use the shadow harness to replay captured traces against the new kernel/code path with shadow traffic enabled (no live responses).
   - Command: 
     ./bin/shadow-replay --trace-file=baseline-traces.tar.gz --kernel-hint=int8-micro --concurrency=20 --output=shadow-report.json
3) Run microbenchmarks on the intended hardware slice (3 runs):
   - Per-token latency (p50/p95/p99)
   - Kernel invocation time distribution (collect CUDA/NVTX traces)
   - Memory high-water mark and fragmentation sample
4) Canary rollout: begin with 0.5% traffic to a stable pool with increased logging and a non-blocking guard. Monitor for 30 minutes.
5) Expand canary: if health signals remain green, expand to 5% for 2 hours, then to 25% for 12 hours.
6) Full rollout: gradually promote to 100% using the rollout matrix in the Acceptance section.

Key monitoring signals (must be green during canary)
---------------------------------------------------
- SLOs: request p99 latency relative delta <= 10% and absolute p99 inside SLA target.
- Errors: request error rate increase <= 0.01% absolute; business-critical routes require 0 increase.
- Quality: BLEU/ROUGE/embedding-sim metrics on eval prompts must be within the regression gate (default: < 1.5% quality loss).
- Cost: per-token CPU/GPU time reduction >= projected threshold.
- Kernel health: no new kernel OOMs, kernel launch errors, or NVML thermal spikes.

Profiling playbook excerpts
--------------------------
- Sampling plan: stratified sampling across short/medium/long sequences, chat vs. single-call, and top-ten customer tenants.
- Tools and commands:
  - nvprof/Nsight: capture GPU kernel timelines for the benchmark trial. Example: 
    nsight-sys profile --output=nsys-report.nsys --trace=cuda,nvtx --duration=120 ./serve-bench --profile-target=canary-pool
  - Kernel traces: ensure kernel names are mapped to canonical IDs using the kernel-mapper utility: 
    python tools/kernel-mapper.py --input nsys-report.nsys --output kernel-latency.csv
  - Per-request trace: use the trace-correlator to stitch system-level traces to request IDs: 
    ./trace-correlator --trace-dir traces/ --tag fidelity-surgeon-1234 --out stitched.json

Benchmarking suite: what to run and why
--------------------------------------
- Microbenchmarks: single-batch synthetic runs to measure kernel latency and occupancy at fixed sequence lengths.
- Replay benchmarks: replay captured production traffic with preserved inter-arrival timing. This shows end-to-end behavior (queueing, batching).
- Shadow A/B: run new path in shadow mode with sampling of produced outputs for offline quality scoring.
- Cost simulation: feed kernel-level latencies into the cost model to project monthly delta.

Example bench commands
----------------------
- Synthetic micro: 
  ./bench/micro --model rwind-7b --batch-size 1 --seq-len 256 --kernel-profile > micro-256.log
- Replay: 
  ./bench/replay --trace traces/capture-20261001.tar.gz --scale 1.0 --inject-tag fidelity-surgeon-5678 --out replay-report.json

Kernel scheduling knobs and notes
--------------------------------
- Admission window: reduce admission window for int8 kernels to avoid long head-of-line blocking with high-occupancy kernels. Typical knob: runtime.scheduler.admission_ms (default 3ms) -> 1.5ms for micro-kernel heavy workloads.
- Priority decay: lower priority decay to bias warmup cohorts into prefetch success for cache-sensitive flows.
- Cooperative preemption: enable for high-mix pools when deploying new kernels to help prevent starvation. Flag: runtime.scheduler.coop_preempt=true.
- Kernel crediting: track kernel cost units per-request and enforce soft quotas to limit noisy-neighbor impact.

Acceptance criteria (canary gates)
---------------------------------
Table: acceptance thresholds (must be strings per JSON schema but presented in a table-like block)

- SLO_p99: "<= baseline_p99 * 1.10"
- Error_rate_delta: "<= 0.0001 (absolute)"
- Eval_quality_pass: ">= 98.5% of baseline score on eval set (configurable)"
- Cost_delta: ">= projected_savings OR documented justification for cost-neutral change"
- Kernel_stability: "0 kernel OOMs, 0 new kernel launch errors in canary window"

Rollback plan
-------------
- Immediate rollback triggers: any of the following should trigger an automated rollback and pager:
  1) p99 latency > acceptance threshold for 3 consecutive measurement windows (5-minute windows).
  2) quality regression detected above tolerance on sampled outputs.
  3) kernel crash, OOM, or interconnect fault.
- Rollback procedure:
  1) Flip feature flag to previous image using the rollout controller: 
     ./rolloutctl promote --target previous --tag fidelity-surgeon-1234 --reason "auto-rollback"
  2) Confirm system converges and monitor the same signals for 30 minutes.
  3) Create incident ticket and attach all artifacts (nsys report, stitched traces, shadow-report.json).

Known issues and mitigation notes
--------------------------------
- Int8 microkernels show sporadic latency spikes at p99 on sequence length > 1024 due to tensor-slice alignment. Mitigation: apply kernel alignment patch (K-alignment-v2) or restrict int8 to seq<=1024.
- KV-cache warmup mismatch: quantized kernels may interpret KV padding differently; run the kv-warmup-mapper job during canary.
- Scheduler hysteresis: rapid fidelity flips can cause scheduler thrashing; enforce a 30-minute minimum cool-down on pool-level knob changes.
- Observability gaps: early int8 rollouts may not tag kernel names correctly in legacy telemetry; ensure kernel-mapper version >= 2.12.

Release note template (for product/release notes)
------------------------------------------------
Summary: "Runtime: deploy int8 microkernel path for rwind-7b on production pools. Expected improvements: ~7% unit GPU cost reduction at p50 latency parity. Rollout: staged canary with automated rollback."
Impact: "Lower per-token cost; potential small quality drift in edge cases (long sequences)."
Rollout: "0.5% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100% over 48 hours if gates pass."
Monitoring: "SLOs: request p99, kernel health, eval-quality snapshot for top 20 customers."
Known limitations: "Do not enable for on-prem clusters with older cuDNN versions (see compatibility table)."

Compatibility table (text)
- cuDNN >= 9.0: supported
- CUDA >= 12.2: recommended
- kernel-mapper >= 2.12: required for accurate telemetry

Operational ownership and contacts
----------------------------------
- Primary owner: runtime-ops (team alias: runtime-ops@redwood.com)
- Applied ML owner: applied-ml-evals@redwood.com
- PagerDuty escalation: runtime-pager (P1)

Postmortem and retrospective triggers
-------------------------------------
If a rollout hits an automated rollback or an unexpected quality regression, initiate a 72-hour postmortem with the following deliverables:
- Timeline of events (minute-level)
- Traces and profiles (NSYS, kernel-latency.csv)
- Hypothesis and test plan for next patch
- Action items and owners

Appendix: useful commands and scripts
------------------------------------
- Shadow replay harness: ./bin/shadow-replay --help
- Kernel mapper: python tools/kernel-mapper.py --help
- Rollout controller: ./rolloutctl status --tag fidelity-surgeon-1234
- Cost delta estimator: python tools/cost-sim.py --input replay-report.json --output cost-estimate.csv

References
----------
- Runtime scheduler decision fabric (internal): /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-decision-fabric-and-telemetry-playbook-2024
- Profiling playbooks: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/telemetry-feedback-kernel-autotune-playbook-2026
- Benchmarking suite docs: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/runtime-deployment-sanity-and-benchmark-suite-acceptance-2026

Document history
----------------
- 2026-02-15: created by Alexandra M. Rivera
- 2026-04-12: added KV-cache warmup notes (Priya Kaur review)
- 2026-10-03: clarified acceptance thresholds and added rollback automation steps (Daniel S. Cho review)

title: Runtime experimentation blueprint and hypothesis protocol
content:
Overview

Purpose: This document defines a standardized, repeatable blueprint for formulating hypotheses, instrumenting experiments, and executing cross-layer runtime experiments that span runtime architecture, kernel scheduling, profiling playbooks, benchmarking suites, runbooks and release verification. It codifies guardrails for safety, data collection contracts, and an escalation path for regressions detected during experiments.

Audience: runtime engineers, SREs, performance researchers, release managers, and solutions engineers who run or consume inference experiments.

Scope and high-level principles

- Keep experiments scoped to a single independent variable wherever possible (e.g., scheduler policy, kernel variant, KV warmup window).
- Measure both application-visible metrics (p50/p95/p99 latency, error rate, token cost) and internal kernel signals (occupancy, kernel queue depth, preemption count, batch composition).
- Use shadow channels and low-risk canaries for disruptive changes; require automatic fallback for any change affecting P99 by >25% or cost by >15% in production-like traffic.
- Maintain reproducibility: every experiment must have an ID, input corpus, and synthetic traffic profile attached to the run artifact.

Roles and ownership

1. Experiment owner (single point): responsible for hypothesis, orchestration, runbook, and final report. (Typically the engineer proposing the change.)
2. Observability owner: ensures traces, metrics and sampled traces are available and annotated with experiment_id.
3. SRE reviewer: verifies safety windows, capacity headroom, and rollback plan for production canaries.
4. Release manager: gates experiment-to-release handoff and signs off acceptance criteria.

Hypothesis lifecycle (protocol)

1. Formulate hypothesis: 1–2 sentence statement (e.g., "Switching kernel-variant X to f32->int8 delta path reduces P50 by 18% for short sequences without increasing P99 by >5%.")
2. Define primary/secondary metrics: primary = P99 tail latency; secondary = token cost per million tokens, preemption rate, GPU stall time.
3. Create experiment specification: include traffic corpus, seed RNG, workload mix (inference/generation/chat/embedding), concurrency shape, and warmup steps. Use the experiment template.
4. Baseline capture: run at least three baseline runs across different cluster nodes (same family) and record statistical distribution.
5. Run treatment: execute change with identical traffic; collect same signals.
6. Statistical test: use non-parametric comparison (e.g., Mann–Whitney U) for latency distributions and bootstrap confidence for cost metrics.
7. Acceptance rules: pre-declared thresholds (see acceptance table). If a treatment fails, follow rollback runbook.

Experiment specification template (text)

- experiment_id: REX-2026-<short-id>
- hypothesis: short sentence
- target_cluster: hetero-gpu-pool-eu
- model_variant: gptx-2b-quantized-v2
- scheduler_profile: experimental-low-latency-priority
- traffic_profile: mixture {chat:40%, gen:40%, embedding:20%}, seed: 42
- synthetic_corpus: s3://redwood-experiments/corpora/voice-assistant-2025-v2
- duration: 30m warmup + 60m measurement
- observability_tags: [experiment_id, run_id, owner]

Telemetry contract (required signals)

Every experiment run must include the following time-aligned signals:

- request: request_id, timestamp, route, model_variant, sequence_length_in, sequence_length_out, token_count
- latency: service_pod_p99/95/50, kernel_dispatch_latency_ms, kernel_execution_ms, queue_wait_ms
- kernel: kernel_variant, batch_size_at_dispatch, preempted (bool), preemption_reason, occupancy_percent
- resource: gpu_util_percent, gpu_mem_free_mb, nvlink_errors, node_temperature_celsius
- cost: internal_token_cost_usd_per_1m, kernel_cuda_time_ms
- traces: sampled_trace (include kernel span IDs)

Scheduling & kernel test harness

- Use the harness utility at tools/runtime-experiments/harness to define: workload mix, artificial jitter, and backpressure injection. Example CLI:

  ./harness run --experiment REX-2026-001 --profile mixed-chat-gen --duration 5400 --seed 42 --trace-sample-rate 0.02

- Kernel-scheduler knobs to exercise: priority-weight (0–100), batch-slice-ms, preemption-window-ms, admission-rate-per-sec. Record each knob change in the run metadata.

- Synthetic failure injection: in non-prod clusters, run controlled preemption bursts to observe contention behavior: inject_preempt --rate 5/s --duration 60s --target kernel-variant=kv-prefetch

Benchmarking acceptance criteria (table as text)

| Metric | Baseline target | Treatment pass requirement | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| P50 latency (ms) | 12–20 | No increase >10% (prefer decrease) | Short-sequence workload |
| P95 latency (ms) | 32–60 | No increase >15% | Multi-tenant noise tolerant |
| P99 latency (ms) | 110–220 | No increase >5% (hard gate) | If >5%, require canary-only rollout & SRE approval |
| Error rate (5xx) | <0.05% | No increase >2x baseline | Hard gate |
| Token cost per 1M | $1.20 | No increase >10% | Estimate from kernel_cuda_time |
| Preemption rate | 0–2% | No increase >3x | Investigate starvation |

(Note: treat the P99 gate as blocking for production rollouts.)

Profiling playbook integration

- When an experiment exercises kernel changes, attach a profiling run using the standard profiler: profiler run --experiment <id> --collect kernel-metrics,trace-heap,occupancy --duration 10m
- Capture at least 1s-resolution kernel spans and a sampled set of full-request traces (1 trace per 5k requests).
- Use the profiler output to create a causal latency map and annotate preemption/splice points.

Runbook: regression triage (high-level steps)

1. Detect: alert triggers when P99 > baseline * 1.05 or error-rate spikes. Tag alert with experiment_id.
2. Contain: immediately stop the experiment traffic or throttle to 10% of original. If production canary, initiate immediate rollback.
3. Collect: gather last 15 minutes of metrics, 100 sampled traces, kernel occupancy histograms and recent scheduler decisions.
4. Hypothesis stack: compare dispatch batch sizes, kernel_variant usage, and preemption_events between baseline and treatment.
5. Mitigate: apply mitigation recipes in order: a) revert scheduler profile to stable, b) enable admission-limiter, c) pin to previous kernel_variant.
6. Postmortem: owner writes incident note within 48 hours with root cause and remediation plan.

Release notes checklist (for changes touching runtime stack)

- Include experiment IDs used for benchmarking.
- Summarize acceptance metrics and whether any additional SRE mitigations were required.
- Highlight known limitations and observed anomalies.
- Attach reproducible run artifacts: traffic profile, synthetic corpus, raw profiler output.

Known issues and workarounds (examples)

- ID KI-2026-42: Intermittent kernel handoff timeout when batch_slice_ms <= 3. Symptoms: elevated P95 and occasional request timeout (upstream grpc deadline). Workaround: set batch_slice_ms >= 5 or enable cooperative-preempt fallback.
- ID KI-2026-57: KVCache warmup misalignment on heterogeneous pools. Symptoms: cold-start P50 spikes for embedding-heavy routes. Workaround: pre-warm KV cache using warmup traffic job; use kv_warmup_hint in deployment config.
- ID KI-2026-88: Trace sampling amplification under high concurrency causing trace-collector backpressure. Symptoms: missing kernel spans in profiler output. Workaround: reduce trace-sample-rate to 0.005 during high concurrency and rely on shadow channels for full fidelity.

Safeguards for production experiments

- Any experiment running on production-labeled pools must:
  - have an SRE reviewer with signed approval,
  - be limited to max 5% of production traffic during initial canary,
  - include an automated fallback plan that triggers on P99 violation or error-rate > 2x baseline.

Artifact retention and reproducibility

- Store experiment run artifacts under s3://redwood-experiments/runs/<experiment_id> including: run_metadata.json, profiler.tgz, metrics.csv, sampled_traces.tgz, baseline_snapshot.json.
- Attach a short reproducibility note summarizing exact cluster topology, seed, and version pins for the runtime, scheduler, and kernels.

Quick examples

- Example kernel config snippet (YAML):

  scheduler:
    name: experimental-low-latency-priority
    priority_weight: 80
    batch_slice_ms: 6
    preemption_window_ms: 12
    admission_rate_per_sec: 1200

- Example rollout CLI to start a canary (production-safe):

  ./orchestrator rollout --cluster prod-eu --deployment my-model:v2026-07 --canary-percent 3 --monitor-metrics p99,errors --fallback revert --experiment-id REX-2026-101

Post-experiment reporting structure

- Executive summary (1 paragraph)
- Baseline vs treatment metric tables and distribution plots (P50/P95/P99)
- Key profiler findings and kernel-level causal map
- Acceptance decision (Pass/Fail/Conditional) and recommended rollout path
- Artifacts: links to s3 run folder, dashboards, and traces

References and links

- Profiling playbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/telemetry-feedback-kernel-autotune-playbook-2026
- Benchmark suite: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/runtime-deployment-sanity-and-benchmark-suite-acceptance-2026
- Runbooks: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-upgrade-validation-and-canary-matrix-2026

Appendix: experiment scoring rubric (how to pick winners)

- Score components (weights): latency improvement (40%), cost improvement (30%), stability (20%), operational complexity (10%).
- Score interpretation: >70 = recommended rollout; 50–70 = gated rollout with more shadow testing; <50 = discard and iterate.

Contact and escalation

- Primary contact: Maya Chen (runtime-experiments@redwood.com)
- SRE on-call: see eng-sre/schedule for rotation
- Slack channels: #runtime-experiments, #runtime-incidents

End of document.

title: Runtime plugin safety and deployment checklist
content:
Overview
-------

Purpose: This page documents a prescriptive checklist, gating criteria, and automated tests required to safely introduce runtime plugins (kernel adapters, scheduler plugins, or sidecar instrumentations) into Redwood's inference runtime. It is intended for runtime engineers, kernel authors, and release owners.

Scope: applies to any code that executes inside the serving runtime process or modifies kernel scheduling behavior, including:
- third-party kernel drivers or accelerator adapters
- custom scheduler plugins and admission controllers
- observability sidecars that inject telemetry or sampling hooks
- experimental serialization/deserialization modules that touch request/response flows

Goals
-----
- Minimize production blast radius for plugin rollouts.
- Ensure deterministic performance and memory behaviour under peaky traffic.
- Guarantee observability and fast rollback on regressions.
- Provide reproducible benchmarking and profiling steps for acceptance gates.

Key risks and failure modes
-------------------------
- Non-deterministic kernel latency growth (tail latency spikes).
- Memory fragmentation or soft-ooms from plugin state leaks.
- Priority inversion introduced by scheduler hooks.
- Telemetry amplification causing control-plane overload.
- Silent semantic changes to model inputs/outputs (format drift).

Pre-deployment checklist (must pass all gates)
--------------------------------------------
1) Code & static safety
   - PR has clear README describing purpose, public interfaces, and intended failure modes.
   - Static analysis run: no unsafe deserialization, no unbounded allocations without guardrails.
   - Third-party dependencies reviewed for license and CVEs (security team sign-off for >= moderate).

2) Unit and integration tests
   - Unit coverage >= 80% for new code paths.
   - Integration tests exercise: request lifecycle (begin, KV cache lookup, kernel dispatch, response), error injection (timeouts, kernel failure), and graceful degradation.
   - Fuzz harness enabled for parser/serializer plugins.

3) Performance and resource budgets
   - Microbenchmarks added to the repo with the submitter-provided baseline and expected overhead.
   - Memory budget defined: max RSS delta <= 5% on steady-state synthetic workload; peak transient <= 15% with GC/eviction verified.
   - Max per-request added latency budget: p50 <= 1ms, p95 <= 5ms (defaults; product/route owners may tighten).

4) Profiling & observability hooks
   - Traces: plugin exposes span(s) with standardized tags: plugin.name, plugin.version, request.id, kernel.variant.
   - Metrics: must emit per-plugin counters for invocations, errors, and duration histogram (Prometheus format).
   - Logs: structured JSON logs with level, timestamp, request.id, and short context.

5) Canary and rollout plan
   - Canary matrix prepared (traffic slices, model variants, sequence lengths).
   - Rollout strategy defined: staged percentages 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100% with 30m observation windows.
   - Automatic rollback rules enumerated (see SLO gates below).

6) Security and data handling
   - No write access to persistent customer data outside defined KV caches unless explicitly approved.
   - KMS/HSM integration validated if plugin requests keys.

Acceptance gating: telemetry & SLOs
--------------------------------
The plugin rollout must satisfy these gating rules during every canary window:
- Error rate: plugin-specific error_rate <= baseline_error_rate + 0.2% absolute AND service-level errors not increased.
- Latency regressions: p95 latency of route using plugin must not exceed baseline p95 + 10% or +50ms (whichever smaller).
- Resource signals: node memory pressure and GPU memory delta stable (no increase in OS OOM kills).
- Kernel health: no increase in kernel queue length > 2x baseline sustained > 5 minutes.
- Observability completeness: 99% of requests must include plugin spans and metric emission.

If any gate fails, the automated rollout must immediately revert to the previous release and file an incident.

Canary and rollout step-by-step procedure
---------------------------------------
1) Pre-canary (run in staging):
   - Deploy plugin build to staging runtime cluster.
   - Run synthetic benchmark plan: 30m steady-state, 5m microburst at 10x, and 10k unique prompt corpus replay.
   - Validate telemetry completeness and that integration tests pass on the canary lab.

2) Canary 1% (production shadow+1%):
   - Route 1% of production traffic through the plugin-managed path; mirror requests to comparison path.
   - Monitor gates for 30 minutes.
   - If green, promote to 5%. If not, rollback and open triage.

3) Canary 5% and 25%:
   - At each stage, run targeted microbenchmarks for the active model variants and sequence length distributions.
   - Run the profiling playbook (see Profiling section).

4) Full rollout:
   - Once at 100% for 60 minutes with no gate violations, mark feature as GA.

Profiling and benchmarking playbook (quick reference)
---------------------------------------------------
- Tools: perfbench (internal), microtrace (span collector), nvprof/nvtx (for accelerator plugins), pprof (CPU), jemalloc statistics.
- Synthetic load: use the inference-workload-replay tool with the golden corpus of route-specific prompts. Example command:
  ./inference-workload-replay --route my-route --duration 30m --qps 250 --seq-distribution seq-dist.json --compare baseline-build:12345

- Kernel-level profiling: run a 10-minute mixed workload and collect nvtx ranges labelled plugin:entry and plugin:exit. Example nvprof invocation:
  NVPROF_LOGFILE=nvlog.json nvprof --profile-child-processes --export-profile nvprofile.nvprof -- ./runtime --plugin path/to/plugin.so

- Memory and allocator checks:
  - Capture jemalloc stats pre/post using: curl localhost:9100/allocator/stats | jq '.'
  - Ensure active fragment count delta < 3% for steady-state runs.

- Tracing validation: verify every request has plugin span and that duration histogram aligns with microbenchmarks. Use microtrace query:
  microtrace query "service=runtime AND plugin.name=MY_PLUGIN" --stats p50,p95,p99

Test matrix (text table)
----------------------
Route | Model variant | Seq lengths | QPS profile | Required checks
------|---------------|------------|------------|----------------
search-low | base-merged | [8,32] | 200 | latency p95, mem delta, spans
chat-long | llama-xl | [64,512] | 50 | p95, kvcache correctness, distributional checks
batch-embed | embedder-v2 | [1,1] | 800 | throughput, batching overhead, histogram stability

Rollback and incident triage playbook
-----------------------------------
1) If automatic rollback triggered:
   - Oncall patches route to prior build and escalates to runtime-oncall and plugin owner.
   - Collect artifacts: traces (microtrace TTL 7d), nvprof logs, jemalloc dumps, kernel queue length logs, and pod-level logs.

2) Triage checklist (first 30 minutes):
   - Reproduce failure in canary lab with identical traffic profile.
   - Check for memory leaks: run 15-minute soak with heap snapshot.
   - Confirm whether failure is semantic (input/output differences) or performance (latency/memory).

3) Post-incident:
   - Fill incident template with root cause hypothesis, mitigation, test to prevent regressions, and owner for follow-up.
   - Schedule a 2-hour postmortem within 72 hours if customer impact occurred.

Operational runbook extracts (for oncall)
---------------------------------------
- Quick checks when alerted:
  1) Query: Prometheus - plugin:errors_total{plugin=\"MY_PLUGIN\"} by (instance) over 10m.
     Alert threshold: > 1% of total requests.
  2) Kernel queue depth: runtime_kernel_queue_length{instance} > 2x baseline for 5m.
  3) Memory: node_memory_available_bytes and container_memory_rss_bytes trend.
  4) Trace sampling: microtrace sample rate and presence of plugin spans; if missing, fail closed (treat as regression).

Ownership, signoff and documentation requirements
------------------------------------------------
- Code owner: must be an engineering team with 24/7 oncall coverage.
- Release owner: a named engineer responsible for canary monitoring and rollback.
- Documentation: README, deployment manifest, schema for metrics and spans, and example benchmark artifacts must be committed to the plugin repo.

Appendix A: sample deployment fragment (Kubernetes)
-------------------------------------------------
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: runtime-plugin-myplugin
spec:
  template:
    metadata:
      annotations:
        runtime.redwood.com/plugin-name: "myplugin"
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: runtime
        image: ghcr.io/redwood/runtime:canary-2028-01-10
        args: ["--plugin", "/opt/plugins/myplugin.so", "--plugin-metrics-prefix", "plugin_myplugin_"]
      - name: plugin-sidecar
        image: ghcr.io/redwood/plugin-sidecar:1.0.0
        env:
        - name: PLUGIN_MODE
          value: "sandboxed"

Appendix B: sample validation script (bash snippet)
-------------------------------------------------
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
# run quick smoke and collect traces
./inference-workload-replay --route search-low --duration 5m --qps 100 || { echo 'replay failed'; exit 1; }
microtrace query "service=runtime AND plugin.name=myplugin" --stats p95 || { echo 'tracing missing'; exit 1; }

Appendix C: FAQ
---------------
Q: What qualifies as a plugin vs an integration?
A: Plugins execute inside the runtime or affect scheduling. Integrations that run externally (e.g. separate microservices) are treated as normal service integrations and follow a different checklist.

Q: How do I request higher latency budgets for experimental features?
A: Submit a feature request to the runtime-product channel with workload benchmarks and target routes. Product must approve any SLO changes before canary.

Contacts
--------
- Runtime oncall: runtime-oncall@redwood.ai
- Runtime product manager: elena.park@redwood.ai
- Security review: security-reviews@redwood.ai

Related documents
-----------------
- Kernel scheduler contract and telemetry spec (see related pages).
- Profiling playbook for nvprof and microtrace.

Change log
----------
- 2028-01-12: Created (Asha Verma).
- 2028-02-20: Added automated gating criteria and sample Kubernetes fragment (reviewers: Marco Diaz, Elena Park).

title: Cross-layer Observability & Diagnostics Playbook — Burst and Degradation Incidents
content:
Summary
-------
This playbook describes a cross-layer, repeatable approach for detecting, diagnosing, and mitigating short-duration bursts and progressive degradation in the Serving Runtime. It bridges runtime architecture, kernel scheduling signals, profiling playbooks, and benchmarking checks so oncall and runtime engineers can quickly restore SLOs and reduce mean time to innocence (MTTI).

Scope and audience
------------------
- Scope: Hosted + Dedicated runtime clusters and the operator-facing control-plane paths (Dispatcher, SlotAllocator, KernelRunner, KVCache, and Runtime Router).
- Audience: Serving runtime oncall, runtime engineers, release owners, and performance SREs.

Goals and SLO references
------------------------
- Primary detection SLOs: 95th token-latency < 100ms, 99th token-latency < 300ms for default small-model profile. (See per-model SLO sheet.)
- Operational goals: initial triage within 5 minutes, mitigation (fallback or ramp) within 15 minutes, restore to within 10% of baseline P95 within 60 minutes.

How this playbook fits with other docs
-------------------------------------
This is an operational layer that references: profiling playbooks for telemetry sampling, kernel-scheduler design docs for decision points, benchmarking suite for reproducible load, and existing runbooks for fallback and warmstart. Use this playbook when alerts indicate sudden tail-latency or progressive throughput drop.

Key concepts and system components
----------------------------------
- Dispatcher: user-facing ingress that performs request classification and route affinity. Primary source of request-level traces.
- SlotAllocator: assigns execution slots (cohort/priority) used by the scheduler. Tracks queue lengths and admission metrics.
- KernelRunner: GPU process pool executing kernels. Emits kernel_latency_hist, kernel_qps, kernel_error_rate, and kernel_memory_pressure.
- KVCache: per-session prefix cache. Key signals: hit_rate, eviction_rate, and warmup_latency.
- Runtime Router / Graceful Fallback: orchestrates model variant fallbacks and cross-region routing.

Signal catalog and quick thresholds
----------------------------------
(Use these to prioritize initial checks.)

| Signal (metric)                      | Type         | Quick threshold (when to escalate) |
|--------------------------------------|--------------|------------------------------------|
| dispatch.request_p95_ms              | latency      | > baseline * 1.2 or > 200ms       |
| kernel_latency_p95_ms                | latency      | > 1.5x baseline                   |
| kernel_queue_depth                   | gauge        | > 80% of max slots                |
| slot_allocator.queue_wait_time_p95   | latency      | > 50ms                            |
| kvcache.hit_rate                     | ratio        | drop > 15 percentage points       |
| grpc.reconnect_rate                  | rate         | sustained > 5/min                 |
| node_gpu_utilization                 | utilization  | > 95% (thermal risk)              |
| infra.network_rtt_p95                | latency      | > baseline + 20ms                 |

Note: baseline is the rolling 7-day median for the service and model profile.

Triage checklist (first 5 minutes)
----------------------------------
1) Validate alert and scope
   - Confirm alert: check Alerting UI + trace sample in the last 2 minutes.
   - Determine scope: single node, single pool, entire region, or global. Use the Dispatcher topology view.
2) Quick telemetry pull
   - Pull P95/P99 for dispatch.*, kernel_*, kvcache.* and slot_allocator.* for last 30m vs 3h.
   - Commands (on the runbook box):
     ```bash
     rmetric query --service=dispatcher --metrics="dispatch.request_p95_ms,dispatch.request_p99_ms" --range=30m
     rmetric query --pool=kernerrunner --metrics="kernel_latency_p95_ms,kernel_queue_depth" --range=30m
     rlog fetch --trace-id $(rmetric top-traces --service=dispatcher --limit=1) --follow=1m
     ```
3) Fast isolation heuristics
   - If kernel_queue_depth high and kernel_latency rising: likely kernel scheduling or admission.
   - If kvcache.hit_rate collapsed and kernel P95 is higher: consider cache warmup cascade.
   - If node_gpu_utilization is low but kernel queue depth is high: investigate scheduler admission/NUMA balance.

Isolation procedures (15–30 minutes)
-----------------------------------
A. Kernel scheduling checks
   - Check scheduler decision log: `rkctl scheduler inspect --pool <pool> --window 10m`
   - Look for recent policy changes (priority weights, admission caps). If there was a rollout in the last hour, rollback to the previous scheduler config.
   - Check GPU mismatch signals: `rkctl node inspect --node <id>` -> note nvlink errors, thermal events.
B. Admission and backpressure
   - Validate admission thresholds: `SlotAllocator.admit_rate` vs observed arrival rate.
   - If admission is overly conservative, temporarily increase soft-cap by +10% and monitor.
   - If admission is broken, flip to the safe fallback profile: `rkctl route set-fallback --route <route> --profile reduced-memory`
C. KV cache warmup cascade
   - If kvcache.eviction_rate spiked, trigger a targeted prefetch job for the affected sessions:
     ```yaml
     apiVersion: redwood.io/v1
     kind: KVPatchJob
     spec:
       model: <model-name>
       sessions: [session-ids-file]
       concurrency: 4
     ```

Mitigation patterns (approved temporary actions)
------------------------------------------------
- Short term (minutes): route to warm fallback model variant in-region; increase admission soft-cap by 5–10%; reduce batch size target to lower per-call kernel time.
- Medium term (hours): evict peaky low-util priority cohorts; initiate rolling restart of KernelRunner pool if drivers show instability; apply kernel restart mitigation which drains pending short calls first.
- Long term (post-incident): schedule simulation in the benchmarking suite to reproduce the burst, add synthetic traffic signature to the mixed-workload SLO test, and create a scheduler policy change with canary and rollout plan.

Diagnostic playbook for kernel-level regressions
------------------------------------------------
1) Reproduce with a targeted microbenchmark
   - Use the perf harness: `bench-run --profile kernel-latency --model <model> --sequence 256 --concurrency 8 --duration 5m`
   - Collect kernel traces: `kerntrace collect --pool <pool> --out /tmp/kerntrace.pb`
2) Compare kernel signature to baseline
   - Run diff against golden: `kerntrace diff /tmp/kerntrace.pb gs://benchmarks/kernel-gold/<model>.pb`
3) If reproducible, tag as kernel-regression and create a hotfix branch with kernel config rollback. Include the diff and perf artifacts in the PR.

Benchmarks and quick acceptance tests
------------------------------------
Use the standard benchmarking suite to validate mitigations before full rollout. Minimum test matrix:
- Mixed workload replay (30m): baseline QPS, 30% long sequences, 20% high-concurrency short sequences.
- Kernel microbench: 1–8 batch sizes, sequence 16/128/512.
- Admission and fallback test: inject synthetic saturating arrival and assert fallback triggers within 10s.

Sample benchmark run (CLI)
```bash
benchctl run --suite mixed-workload --tag incident-capture-$(date +%s) --params "qps=500,duration=30m,seqmix=0.3:512,0.5:128,0.2:16"
benchctl collect --artifact incident-capture-1234 --to gs://bench-results/incident-capture-1234
```

Release notes and change correlation
-----------------------------------
- Always check the Deployment Log (release-control) for any scheduler or kernel config changes in the 60 minutes before incident start.
- Use the release correlation query: `rctl releases list --since 1h --component scheduler,kernerrunner,kvcache`
- If a canary rollout is present, pause or rollback the canary immediately and re-evaluate.

Known issues to consider (fast checks)
------------------------------------
- NVLINK flapping on a subset of nodes causes intermittent kernel stalls (workaround: cordon nodes with nvlink_errors > 0 and drain after cooldown).
- Kernel memory fragmentation causing soft OOMs under interleaved batches (mitigation: apply compacting GC in 2.3.1-hotfix and restart KernelRunner).
- GRPC connection recycling leading to small head-of-line stalls at the Dispatcher (workaround: increase connection pool size temporarily).

Runbook appendices and artifacts to collect
-------------------------------------------
Collect these during the incident and attach to the postmortem:
- Top 20 traces (dispatch) during incident window.
- kernel_trace.pb files for affected KernelRunner nodes.
- SlotAllocator decision log for the interval.
- Bench artifacts if a reproduction was run (benchctl outputs).
- Release correlation snapshot (release-control export).

Post-incident actions (owner: runtime-performance squad)
-------------------------------------------------------
1) Assign postmortem owner within 24h.
2) Reproduce incident in bench lab with identical traffic signature within 72h.
3) Create follow-up tickets: scheduler policy change, kernel tuning, KVCache prefetch improvements, or infra remediation (if hardware).
4) Add a synthetic SLO probe to the mixed-workload suite for future detection.

Operational contacts and escalation
----------------------------------
- Oncall (runtime): #runtime-oncall Slack, Pager schedule in PagerDuty
- Kernel squadra: kern-team@redwood.com
- Infra hardware: infra-hw@redwood.com

Maintenance checklist (for release owners)
-----------------------------------------
- Before rolling scheduler changes: run the canary matrix (3% traffic) for 60 minutes against mixed workload.
- Attach bench artifacts and kernel diffs to the PR.
- Notify SRE and runtime performance reviewers 24h prior to rollout.

Revision history
----------------
- 2025-11-12: initial draft (Aisha Kapoor)
- 2026-01-18: added KVCache warmup cascade procedures and benchmark commands (reviewers: Marco Ruiz)
- 2026-03-01: expanded kernel-level diagnostics and known issues section; published (reviewers: Evelyn Park, Daniel Kim)

Related resources and links
-------------------------
- Dispatcher traces dashboard: /dashboards/dispatcher/traces
- Mixed-workload bench suite: /tools/benchctl/doc
- Scheduler policy language reference: confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-policy-language-declarative-profiles-2026
- Kernel tracing guide: confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/kernel-observability-sla-profiling-cadence-2024

If you have questions or need a walkthrough, ping the runtime-performance squad in #runtime-performance and request a live lab replication session.

title: Operational Signal Fabric and Cohorted Scheduler Handbook
content:
Summary
-------
This handbook describes the Operational Signal Fabric and the Cohorted Scheduler approach used by Redwood's serving runtime to map runtime observability signals to scheduler decisions, incident triage actions, profiling experiments, and benchmarking checks. It is written for runtime engineers, SREs, and subsystem owners responsible for scheduler policies, telemetry alignment, and production rollouts.

Goals
-----
- Define a single signal taxonomy (the Signal Fabric) that is consumed by scheduling heuristics, alerting rules, and profiling experiments.
- Describe how execution cohorts are derived, annotated, and persisted for deterministic investigations.
- Provide concrete runbooks for common scheduler/resilience incidents and profiling experiments.
- Give a rollout checklist for scheduler policy changes that minimizes regressions in latency, cost, and fidelity.

Scope
-----
Applies to: all runtime scheduler components (priority governor, admission controller, kernel mapper), kernel plugins that expose telemetry hooks, and the profiling/benchmarking suites that validate scheduling changes. This document does NOT specify kernel implementation details; it focuses on operational mapping between signals and scheduler behavior.

Core concepts
-------------
1) Signal Fabric: canonical names, units, and retention for runtime signals consumed by scheduling logic. Signals are emitted at three layers: request-surface (API/router), kernel-dispatch (runtime kernels), and infra (node/accelerator).
2) Cohorts: deterministic classification of requests into buckets based on stable attributes (model_id, model_variant, sequence_length_bucket, client_tier, route_flags). Cohorts allow targeted profiling and rollback.
3) Decision Bindings: declarative rules that map signal thresholds and cohort identities to scheduler actions (prioritize, throttle, preempt, fallback to variant).
4) Fidelity Guards: safety checks (quality/eval) attached to any scheduler action that can change model variant/quantization.

Signal Fabric (canonical table)
--------------------------------
| Signal name                     | Layer           | Unit           | Cardinality | Producer                 | TTL   | Use cases |
|---------------------------------|-----------------|----------------|-------------|--------------------------|-------|-----------|
| request.p90_latency_ms          | request-surface | milliseconds   | per-route   | router                   | 90d   | SLO monitoring, alerts |
| kvcache.hit_rate                | kernel-dispatch | fraction (0-1) | shard       | kvcache                  | 30d   | batching hints, warmup |
| kernel.queue_depth              | kernel-dispatch | integer        | shard       | dispatcher               | 14d   | admission control, preempt decisions |
| node.gpu_util_pct               | infra           | percent        | node        | node_agent               | 60d   | capacity planning, admission |
| token.emission_rate_per_s       | request-surface | tokens/s       | tenant      | runtime_router           | 30d   | billing/cost throttles |
| request.sequence_bucket         | request-surface | enum (S/M/L/XL) | per-request | router                   | 90d   | cohorting, kernel hints |
| kernel.latency_per_op_ms        | kernel-dispatch | ms/op          | kernel      | kernel_profiler          | 90d   | kernel selection, canary gating |

Note: Cardinality indicates the level at which the signal is indexed. Keep high-cardinality signals off the hot path unless sampled.

Cohort definition and lifecycle
-------------------------------
- Cohort keys: model_id, model_variant_id, sequence_bucket, client_tier, route_tag.
- Generation: router computes the cohort_key at request admission and attaches headers: X-Runtime-Cohort: model=v3.1;var=quant-8bit;len=XL;tier=gold;route=chat_inline
- Storage: cohort annotations are copied into trace/span baggage and a lightweight cohort index (redis-backed) for 72 hours to simplify postmortem replay.
- Decay policy: if a cohort observes < 0.1% of traffic over 24h, mark as transient and expire cohort metadata to reduce index noise.

Decision bindings (examples)
---------------------------
Decision bindings are simple JSON-like rules (stored in policy-service) that map signal predicates to actions. Example binding: 

```
{
  "binding_id": "bind-high-queue-preempt-2026-01",
  "predicate": "kernel.queue_depth > 120 AND node.gpu_util_pct > 85",
  "cohort_filter": "*",
  "action": "preempt_background_slots",
  "action_params": {"max_preempt_per_node": 2, "backoff_minutes": 5},
  "safety_check": "fidelity_guard_alpha"
}
```

- Predicates are evaluated by the decision engine at 10s cadence. Keep predicates simple to avoid evaluation amplification.
- Actions include: increase_priority, decrease_priority, admit_burst, preempt_background_slots, route_to_variant, throttle_tenant.

Scheduler resilience runbooks (triage-first)
-------------------------------------------
1) Symptom: sudden p99 latency increase for a high-traffic route.
   - Owner: runtime-oncall
   - Steps:
     1. Query recent cohorts for the route: kubectl run query-cohorts --route=<route> --since=1h
     2. Check request.p90_latency_ms and kernel.queue_depth across cohorts.
     3. If kernel.queue_depth > 100 on > 3 nodes, execute emergency admission: policy-service apply emergency-admit=throttle-background
     4. If queue depth is concentrated in a cohort with sequence_bucket=XL, enable sequence-length-capping variant: policy-service route cohort -> variant=shortened-context
     5. Open incident with SRE and attach cohort index snapshot and the last 3 kernel.profiler traces.

2) Symptom: kernel plugin experiencing increased op failure rate.
   - Owner: kernel-team
   - Steps:
     1. Collect kernel.latency_per_op_ms and kernel.plugin_errors by kernel version.
     2. If error rate > 0.5% for 5m, pin runtime to previous kernel and trigger canary rollback: rollout-service rollback kernel-plugin --to=stable-20260201
     3. Run controlled profiling (see Profiling experiments) for the failing kernel on a replay corpus.

Profiling experiments: structure and templates
--------------------------------------------
Purpose: isolate scheduler and kernel interactions for targeted cohorts.
Template steps:
1. Select cohort(s) and timeframe (use cohort index).
2. Construct replay corpus (use request-surface traces and synthetic sequences to reproduce distribution).
3. Baseline: run 3x baseline runs with current scheduler policy, collect kernel.latency_per_op_ms, kvcache.hit_rate, and tail latency distribution.
4. Apply one policy change at a time (decision binding tweak), re-run 3x, and compare deltas.
5. Metrics to record: p50/p90/p99 latency, per-token energy (if available), kvcache warmup time, variance across runs.
6. Tag experiment with experiment_id and attach results to policy change PR.

Profiling CLI snippets
---------------------
- Build replay corpus: 
  ./tooling/replay-builder --cohort "model=v3.1;len=M" --since 2026-02-14T00:00:00Z --out corpus.tgz
- Run replay with scheduler override (local lab):
  ./tooling/runtime-replay --corpus corpus.tgz --scheduler-overrides ./overrides/policy-test.json --repeat 3 --collect-traces

Benchmark and validation checklist for scheduler change
-----------------------------------------------------
- Unit gates (automated):
  - scheduler-policy-lint: no circular bindings
  - predicate-safety-check: no policy that can reduce admitted capacity below 60% for any tenant without a manual guard
- Staging gates (synthetic):
  - run mixed-load benchmark against production-like mix for 30m; verify p90 delta < 8% and p99 delta < 15% for stable cohorts.
  - run capacity burst test to verify no kernel plugin regressions.
- Canary gates (shadow & live):
  - enable policy for 5% tenant shadow for 24h, compare decisions and ensure no negative action rate > 0.1%
  - live canary on non-critical region for 4h; require rollback if any cohort exceeds fidelity-guard threshold.

Release and rollout checklist (scheduler policy changes)
-----------------------------------------------------
1. Author creates policy change PR with decision bindings and rationale.
2. Automated policy lint and unit tests pass.
3. Run profiling experiments and attach results to PR.
4. Execute staging benchmark checklist and attach artifacts.
5. Reviewer sign-off from kernel-team and SRE.
6. Staged canary (shadow + 5% live) for 24h.
7. If canary is green, ramp to 25% for 12h, then 100% with monitoring.
8. Post-rollout 48h observation window; capture cohort-indexed telemetry and store artifacts under /artifacts/scheduler-rollouts/<pr-number>.

Safety and fidelity guards
-------------------------
- Any action that routes to a lower-fidelity variant must require an active fidelity_guard check that validates the last known eval delta < configured threshold (default 0.03 quality drop).
- Quality-eval integration: policy-service must call eval-api with a short prompt set for the affected cohort before allowing auto-variant-routing in production.

Operational telemetry dashboards and alerts (recommended)
------------------------------------------------------
- Dashboard: "Scheduler Decision Surface" (node-level tiles, cohort heatmap, decision-rate chart).
- Essential alerts:
  - A1: kernel.queue_depth > 150 for > 3 nodes (P0)
  - A2: preempt_action_rate > 5% sustained for 10m (P1)
  - A3: fidelity_guard_failures > 0.1% for 30m (P1)
  - A4: cohort.latency_regression_delta_p99 > 20% (P0)

Ownership and contacts
---------------------
- Scheduler policy service: owner "runtime-policy-team" (pager: #runtime-policy)
- Kernel plugins: owner "kernel-team" (pager: #kernel-team)
- Oncall escalation path: runtime-oncall -> runtime-sre -> kernel-lead -> eng-manager

Appendix A: sample decision binding catalog (short)
--------------------------------------------------
1) Background fairness governor (default): throttle tenants consuming > 75% of background credits in 5m window.
2) Sequence-length capper: for cohorts with median_sequence_length > XL and p99 queue_depth > 100, cap to L variant.
3) Opportunistic admission: if node.gpu_util_pct < 35% and queue_depth < 20, allow burst admissions up to 50 concurrent short jobs.

Appendix B: common investigation commands and scripts
-----------------------------------------------------
- cohort index dump for route: ./tools/cohort-dump --route=chat_inline --since=2h --out=cohort-dump.json
- decision binding dry-run: curl -X POST https://policy-service.internal/v1/dry-run -d @overrides/policy-test.json -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
- collect trace bundle for a node: ./tools/collect-trace --node node-123 --since 2026-02-17T12:00:00Z --out node-123-traces.tgz

Related reading and links
-------------------------
- Kernel telemetry synthesis (internal): /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/kernel-telemetry-annotation-guidelines-2025
- Runtime decision graphs and behavior catalog: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/runtime-decision-graph-and-observed-behaviour-catalog-2026

Change history
--------------
- 2025-11-13: created by Ava Martinez (initial draft)
- 2026-02-18: added profiling templates and updated cohort decay policy (Samir Patel review)

Contact and feedback
--------------------
Send feedback to #runtime-policy or email avam@redwood-inference.example."

title: Runtime design intent and contracts catalog
content:
Overview

This page captures the design intent and service-level contracts that govern the Redwood serving runtime. It is a team-catalog (reference) describing: service boundaries, RPC/HTTP contracts, scheduling expectations, shard isolation invariants, backpressure signals, preferred observability points, and canonical configuration recommendations. The goal is to provide engineers and oncall responders with a single, readable source of truth about what components are expected to guarantee under normal operation and during degraded modes.

Audience

- Runtime engineers (serving runtime, kernel, scheduler)
- SREs and oncall responders
- Platform/product engineers integrating with the runtime APIs

Design principles (short)

1. Explicit contracts: every surface exposes a minimal set of semantic guarantees (latency/throughput/failure modes).
2. Fail-fast / graceful-fallback: components should fail in a way that preserves upstream routing decisions and provides clear telemetry.
3. Observable invariants: critical invariants are always exported as metrics and trace annotations.
4. Backwards-compatible changes: new fields/flags are opt-in; defaults preserve existing behaviour.

Canonical component names and responsibilities

- request-router: accepts external HTTP/SDK requests, enforces quotas, tags request priority, and routes to batch-aggregator or kernel-executor.
- batch-aggregator: forms batches by model/variant/priority window and hands over to kernel-executor. Performs KV-prefix cache lookup and prefetch hints.
- kernel-executor: runs the optimized kernels on GPUs (or emulated CPUs); exposes kernel health and memory accounting.
- kv-cache-proxy: global LRU cache front for shared KV-prefix entries; supports per-customer namespace isolation.
- shard-manager: decides shard placement, migration, and eviction; owns shard-level leases.

Service contracts (summary)

Each contract is expressed as a set of expectations (what the caller can rely on) and obligations (what the callee must do).

1) request-router -> batch-aggregator
- Protocol: HTTP/1.1 JSON body or internal gRPC (preferred). Required fields: request_id, customer_id, model_variant, priority, max_latency_ms, seq_hint (optional).
- Expectations: batch-aggregator will acknowledge receipt within 5ms (p50) and either accept for batching or reject with BACKPRESSURE with a human-readable reason.
- Obligations: if the aggregator accepts, it must surface an accept_trace_id and the estimated enqueue_delay_ms. If rejecting, it must return retry_after_ms if applicable.

2) batch-aggregator -> kernel-executor
- Protocol: internal gRPC with a binary batch payload and per-request metadata.
- Expectations: kernel-executor will either start execution within the configured scheduling window (default 8ms) or return a PREEMPTION token explaining why (e.g., memory pressure, higher-priority workload).
- Obligations: executor must persistently record kernel_start and kernel_end timestamps for each batch and expose per-kernel memory_high_water_mark bytes.

Scheduling contract (kernel-level)

- Priority levels: system (highest), interactive (default), background (lowest).
- Scheduling window: default 8ms for interactive traffic; configurable per-deployment. Kernels should honor the window and not block longer than window + 2ms for integration steps.
- Max tokens per scheduling slice: 2048 tokens per GPU slice for transformer-based models unless overridden by model_profile.
- Fairness: no single customer may consume more than 30% of kernel credits on a shard unless explicitly reserved.
- Preemption semantics: preemption returns PREEMPTED status with reason code and a deterministic backoff recommendation. Preemption must be idempotent: re-submitting the same request_id within the recommended backoff window must be safe.

Shard isolation invariants

- Lease model: shard-manager grants a lease token to the kernel-executor to operate a shard; leases are renewed every 2s. Loss of lease triggers a soft-eviction where the kernel drains active batches for up to 250ms before halting new accepts.
- Memory isolation: each shard has a soft_limit and hard_limit (bytes). The soft_limit is 80% of hard_limit and triggers eviction/gc policies. Hard_limit must never be exceeded; kernel must fault instead of corrupting other shards.
- Namespace separation: kv-cache-proxy provides tenant namespaces. Cross-tenant cache affinity is prohibited unless explicitly whitelisted.

Telemetry and observability contract

Every runtime binary must export the following metrics and trace annotations:

- metrics (prometheus style):
  - runtime.request.router.latency_ms.p50/p95/p99
  - runtime.batch.aggregator.batch_size_distribution
  - runtime.kernel.executor.kernel_latency_ms.p50/p95/p99
  - runtime.kernel.executor.mem_high_water_mark_bytes
  - runtime.shard.lease_renewal_success_rate
  - runtime.kvcache.hit_ratio_last_5m
  - runtime.scheduling.preemptions_total{reason}
- traces: annotate spans with request_id, accept_trace_id, kernel_start, kernel_end, kernel_slice_id, and preemption_reason.

Suggested alerting thresholds (baseline)

- Alert A1 (request backlog): batch_aggregator.enqueue_depth > 1000 for 2m -> SEV2.
- Alert A2 (kernel memory pressure): kernel.mem_high_water_mark > 90% of hard_limit -> SEV1.
- Alert A3 (preemption spike): preemptions_total increases by > 5x baseline in 5m -> SEV2.
- Alert A4 (lease renewal failures): shard.lease_renewal_success_rate < 99% for 5m -> SEV1.

Configuration catalog (example table)

| config_key | purpose | recommended_default | notes |
|---|---|---:|---|
| scheduling.window_ms | target kernel scheduling window | "8" | tuned per-region/instance-class |
| kernel.max_tokens_slice | hard max tokens per slice | "2048" | model_profile may override |
| shard.memory.soft_limit_pct | when to trigger eviction | "80" | percent of shard hard_limit |
| kvcache.eviction_policy | global eviction policy | "segmented-lru" | supports namespace weights |
| router.priority_override | allow special customers to bypass | "disabled" | requires compliance review |

Sample YAML (deployment-level)

deployment: production-us-east-1
components:
  request-router:
    replicas: 6
    max_in_flight_per_replica: 1200
  batch-aggregator:
    scheduling_window_ms: 8
    max_batch_size: 64
  kernel-executor:
    gpu_type: a100-80gb
    max_tokens_slice: 2048
    memory_hard_limit_bytes: 85899345920 # 80 GiB

Behavioral expectations during upgrades

- Backward compatibility: new executor features must accept both old and new request_meta fields. Default behaviour for unspecified fields must match the old implementation.
- Rolling upgrades: shard-manager will move new workloads onto upgraded nodes gradually (10% per 10 minutes) to validate kernel behavior under mixed-version conditions.
- Graceful draining: before terminating a node, the shard-manager should mark shards draining and allow up to 1s for active kernels to complete; any remaining batches should be moved or aborted with clear diagnostics.

Oncall quick runbook (first 10 actions)

1. Check primary dashboards: kernel_latency (p95), kernel_mem_hwm, batch_enqueue_depth.
2. If enqueue_depth > 1000 and growing, scale batch-aggregator replicas or reduce window_ms temporarily: curl -X POST "https://ops-api/deploys/scale?component=batch-aggregator&delta=+2".
3. If kernel.mem_hwm > 90%: identify offending shard via mem_high_water_mark metric and query shard-manager: 
   curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPS_TOKEN" "https://internal-api/shards?min_hwm=80" | jq .
4. If preemptions spike: check recent trace samples for preemption_reason tag and cross-reference customer_id. If caused by noisy tenant, apply rate limit or kernel credit cap.
5. If lease renewals failing: restart shard-manager replica on same AZ and monitor lease_renewal_success_rate.

Recovery play snippets

- Emergency evict and remap (when node unrecoverable):
  1) shard-manager mark-evict --node-id <node> --force
  2) kernel-executor drain --shard <shard-id> --timeout 250ms
  3) shard-manager remap-shard --shard <shard-id> --target <node2>

- Quick cache warmup after failover: run kvcache-prefetcher job with preapproved keys from recent hot prefix telemetry. Example CLI: 
  ./prefetcher --namespace tenant-123 --prefixes-file /tmp/hot-prefixes.json --concurrency 16

Compatibility notes & extension points

- Model profiles: model_onboarding must publish a model_profile JSON (schema v2) listing preferred max_tokens_slice, quantization_hint, and kv_prefixes. Runtimes must consult model_profile before enforcing hard caps.
- Custom schedulers: teams may implement a custom scheduling plugin provided they implement the SchedulingPlugin interface (method signatures listed below) and pass integration tests (scheduling-plugin-conformance).

Integration checklist for downstream teams

- Provide request examples (with request_id and priority) and a 48h synthetic load trace during onboarding.
- Confirm required SLO class with platform: interactive (p95 < 120ms), latency-sensitive (p95 < 80ms), batch (throughput, cost-optimized).
- Verify that any cache namespace sharing is approved and conforms to data residency rules.

Appendix: SchedulingPlugin interface (summary)

- on_batch_ready(batch_metadata) -> scheduling_decision{slice_tokens, priority_override, estimated_wait_ms}
- on_preemption(slices, reason) -> reschedule_hint{backoff_ms, allow_retry}
- health_check() -> {ok|degraded, diagnostics}

Appendix B: Change log (summary)

- 2024-11-05: initial catalog authored.
- 2025-02-12: added preemption idempotency requirement and backoff recommendations.
- 2025-08-10: clarified lease renewal invariants and increased default scheduling_window to 8ms (from 6ms) for interactive workloads after real-world tuning.

If you are adding or changing a contract on this page: update the change log, increment the compatibility note, and add a reviewer from SRE and Scheduling team.

Document owners and contacts

- Primary owner: lena.thompson@redwood.ai
- Secondary: eng-sre@redwood.ai

References

- See also: runtime-architecture/request-multiplexing-backpressure-architecture (detailed backpressure flow)
- Kernel scheduling guidelines (kernel-and-scheduling)

title: Runtime Inference Cost Model and Simulation Workbook
content:
Overview

Purpose
This workbook documents the inference cost model used by the runtime team, the accompanying simulation harness, and practical runbooks for diagnosing cost regressions. It ties together kernel scheduling behavior, profiling signals, and benchmarking inputs so engineers can reason about per-request unit economics and make configuration decisions that respect latency SLOs.

Scope
- Serving runtime cost components: GPU compute, memory, CPU-side batching, KV-cache hit behavior, overheads (RPC, serialization).
- Interaction surface with kernel scheduler (preemption, slot accounting, slice sizing).
- Guidance for running simulations, interpreting results, and a short incident triage procedure for cost regressions.

Intended audience
- Runtime engineers tuning kernel parameters
- SREs and capacity planners validating reserved capacity sizing
- Product/Finance engineers reconciling unit economics with pricing models

Owner and SLAs
- Document owner: Asha Patel (runtime-performance)
- Reviewers: Miguel Rios, Tara Singh, Luca Moretti
- Target cadence: review after any major scheduler change or model-variant onboarding; mandatory update if unit cost deviates by >10% for 3 consecutive production days.

Principles and assumptions
1) Costs are additive along a critical path, with caching and batching providing multiplicative reductions for token-level work.
2) Latency SLOs are primary constraints; cost optimizations must not increase p95 beyond target without explicit approval.
3) Simulations should mirror production traffic mixes (session lengths, model variants, priority classes).

Core cost model (conceptual)
TotalCost(request) = ComputeCost(tokens, model_variant, quant_profile) + MemoryShareCost(request_share) + SchedulingOverhead(request_profile) + IOOverhead
Where:
- ComputeCost = sum over slices (GPU_time(slice) * GPU_cost_per_second)
- MemoryShareCost = (allocated_memory_fraction * GPU_hour_cost) amortized over active sessions
- SchedulingOverhead = context-switch and preemption penalties (measured via kernel telemetry)
- IOOverhead = network + serialization (measured at ingress/egress proxies)

Example: per-token compute estimate (pseudocode)
- base_flops_per_token = model_variant.flop_estimate * quant_scale
- gpu_time_per_token = base_flops_per_token / effective_kernel_throughput
- ComputeCost(tokens) = gpu_time_per_token * tokens * GPU_COST_SEC

Key telemetry signals (metrics)
- gpu_kernel_time_seconds (per kernel type)
- slice_wait_time_seconds (time a request waits in scheduler queue)
- preemption_count{request_id}
- kvcache_hit_ratio (session-scoped)
- batch_size_distribution (time-windowed histogram)
- tokens_generated_per_request

Kernel scheduling interactions
- Slot accounting: scheduling config exposes two knobs — slot_capacity and fair_share_weight. The effective GPU_time_per_request is a function of allocated slot_size and slice_duration.
- Preemption penalties: empirically measured as additional 8–40ms depending on model state size and KV cache reconciliation. Use the preemption_penalty table below for planning.

Preemption penalty table (typical values)
| scenario | measured penalty (ms) | notes |
|---|---:|---|
| small model (<=2B) | 8–12 | lightweight kernel reloads |
| medium (2B–13B) | 15–25 | shard rebind + lightweight KV reconciliation |
| large (>=70B) | 30–40 | memory copy + kernel reinitialization costs |

Profiling and data collection playbook
1) Collect: enable the continuous micro-trace sampler for 10% of production traffic for 6 hours (see sampling flags below).
2) Aggregate: reduce traces by kernel signature, request class, and model variant. Export to the performance data lake with tags: runbook=cost-simulation, trigger={upgrade, regression, experiment}.
3) Sanity checks: assert kvcache_hit_ratio variance < 5% across replicas and batch_size_distribution stdev < 2 tokens for single-model experiments.

Sampler CLI snippet
```
runtimectl sampling set --policy proportional --rate 0.10 --tags runbook=cost-simulation --duration 6h
runtimectl trace export --filter "tag=runbook:cost-simulation" --output s3://redwood-perf/cost-sim/2026-02-01
```

Benchmarking suite: inputs and canonical workloads
- Canonical mixes: interactive-chat (short sessions, many small requests), assistant-batch (long sessions, many tokens with few concurrent sessions), embedding-bursts (short CPU-heavy requests).
- For each mix, define: session_length_distribution, tokens_per_request_distribution, concurrency_profile, priority_mix.

Sample workload YAML (used by the simulator)
```
name: interactive-chat-v1
concurrency: 120
session_length_dist: {type: pareto, alpha: 1.5, min: 3, max: 200}
tokens_per_request_dist: {type: lognormal, mu: 2.2, sigma: 1.1}
priority_mix: {standard: 0.85, premium: 0.12, system: 0.03}
model_variants: [{name: rdl-13b-fp16, share: 0.6}, {name: rdl-6b-q4, share: 0.4}]
```

Running a simulation (worked example)
1) Prepare profiles: export kernel-throughput hints and kvcache hit maps for the target model variants.
2) Configure simulator: point to the workload YAML and the metric sinks for GPU_time and scheduling traces.
3) Run: runtimectl simulate --workload interactive-chat-v1 --duration 4h --seed 42 --output results/json/interactive-chat-v1-4h.json
4) Postprocess: generate cost breakdown and p95 latency charts via scripts/sim-report.py

Interpreting simulation outputs (priorities)
- Primary: p95 latency across the standard priority band must remain <= configured p95_slo (e.g., 120ms).
- Secondary: per-token unit-cost reduction versus baseline; flag >10% regressions.
- Tertiary: preemption frequency and tail of slice_wait_time.

Regression triage runbook (cost increase >10%)
1) Confirm: reproduce with the same simulator seed and at least 2 independent runs.
2) Isolate variable: switch off recent kernel changes (rollback to previous kernel image) and re-simulate. If cost returns to baseline, schedule a kernel revert and open a high-priority patch.
3) Profile differential: run full micro-trace on the top 5 slowest kernels; compute delta in gpu_kernel_time_seconds.
4) Fix options (choose one): adjust slot_capacity downward to reduce preemption, increase slice_duration to improve kernel amortization, or pin to a quantized variant. Document chosen mitigation in the incident tracker.

Quick mitigation template (to paste in incident ticket)
- Symptom: measured per-token compute increase of +12% during interactive-chat workload.
- Immediate action taken: reduced slot_capacity from 32 -> 24 on pool gpu-pool-us-west-2-a.
- Expected impact: reduce preemption by ~18%, estimated unit-cost return ~7% within 10 minutes.
- Owner: runtime-oncall (pager duty)

Known issues and caveats
- KV cache cold-starts in bursty onboarding: observed when a large fraction (>30%) of traffic is new sessions. Simulation underestimates cold start cost unless kvcache_fill_latency is included. Workaround: warm-fill by routing a small fraction of sessions to a prewarm pool.
- Nonlinear quantization interactions: q4->q3 transitions can change kernel selection heuristics, causing unexpected kernel fallout. When evaluating quantization savings, run the simulator with kernel_hint_override to match the kernel mapper.
- Edge-case: undersized slice_duration combined with high-priority churn leads to starvation for medium-length requests. Detectable by increased slice_wait_time spike at 99.9p.

Table: Recommended simulation fidelity levels
| fidelity | when to use | config notes |
|---|---|---|
| low | early design estimates | 5% sampling, single-region, analytical kernel model |
| medium | pre-rollout validation | 10% sampling, 2 regions, empirical kernel profiles |
| high | release candidate | 25% sampling, full trace replay, multi-tenant mixes |

Appendix A — Example JSON output (trimmed)
```
{
  "workload": "interactive-chat-v1",
  "duration_s": 14400,
  "results": {
    "p95_latency_ms": 118.4,
    "unit_cost_per_1000_tokens_usd": 0.72,
    "kvcache_hit_ratio": 0.82,
    "preemption_rate_per_hour": 3.6
  }
}
```

Appendix B — Scheduler knobs cheat sheet
- slot_capacity (int): max concurrent slices per GPU. Lower => less multiplexing, fewer preemptions, but higher idle time. Default 32.
- slice_duration_ms (int): target runtime of a slice before yielding. Higher => better kernel amortization, worse latency for small requests. Default 64ms.
- fair_share_weight (map): per-priority weight used by the slot allocator. Example: {premium: 2.0, standard: 1.0, system: 4.0}.

Appendix C — References and related pages
- See benchmarking suite: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/mixed-workload-slo-simulation-suite-2026
- Runtime decision surfaces: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/runtime-decision-graph-and-observed-behaviour-catalog-2026
- For kernel telemetry schema: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/kernel-telemetry-annotation-guidelines-2025

Change log
- 2026-01-12: initial draft (Asha Patel).
- 2026-01-20: added sampling CLI and preemption penalty table (reviewers: Miguel Rios).
- 2026-02-18: updated simulation fidelity guidance and regression-runbook (Tara Singh).

Contact
For questions or help running simulations, ping #runtime-cost-sim on Slack or contact Asha Patel (asha@redwood.ai).

title: Holistic Inference Observability Patterns
content:
Summary
-------
This playbook consolidates patterns we use to observe, profile, benchmark, and operate the Redwood serving runtime end-to-end. It bridges runtime architecture, kernel scheduling signals, profiling playbooks, the benchmarking suite, release-note requirements, common known issues, and short runbooks for on-call responders. The goal is to provide a single, pragmatic reference for engineers instrumenting new routes, kernels, or model variants to ensure consistent SLO alignment and actionable telemetry.

Audience
--------
- Serving runtime engineers
- SREs and capacity planners
- Applied ML and model-onboarding engineers
- Devs instrumenting SDKs and SDK-facing endpoints

Design principles
-----------------
- Observability must answer the three questions: What happened? Why did it happen? What should I do next?
- Prioritize pay-for-value telemetry: high-cardinality traces for failures, aggregated metrics for trends.
- Instrument along the request path boundaries: ingress, routing/decision, kernel scheduling, kvcache, hw-dispatch, egress.
- Telemetry must be actionable within 2 minutes (alerts) and diagnostic within 30 minutes (traces + flamegraphs).

Key services and signal owners
-----------------------------
- runtime-gateway (owner: runtime-api) — ingress latencies, auth errors
- dispatchd (owner: kernel-scheduler) — kernel queue lengths, slot utilization, preemptions
- kvcache-service (owner: kvcache) — hit/miss, warmup rate, eviction pressure
