- runtime-exec (owner: runtime-core) — per-kernel exec time, memory high-water marks
- telemetry-ingest (owner: observability) — sampling, event drop rate, pipeline lag

Minimum SLOs and alert thresholds
---------------------------------
- Short-response generation (<= 128 tokens): p95 latency < 130ms, p99 < 250ms.
- Long-response generation (>= 512 tokens): p95 latency < 1200ms, p99 < 2200ms.
- Kernel queue depth: alert when avg queue depth > 80% of capacity for 5 minutes.
- kvcache hit rate: warn when hot-prefix hit-rate drops > 10% vs baseline.
- Telemetry ingestion lag: page when pipeline lag > 2 minutes for 5m window.

Observability patterns (practical)
--------------------------------
1) Transactional tracing per request
   - Propagate a single trace_id across components: runtime-gateway -> routing -> dispatchd -> kernel -> telemetry-ingest.
   - Use tags: model.name, model.variant, sequence_length_bucket, customer_tier, kernel_hint, gpu_type.
   - Attach sampling hint: sample on errors and on tail latencies (p99 triggers).

2) Two-tier metrics approach
   - Aggregated metrics (prometheus): qps, token/s, p50/p95/p99 latencies, kernel_slot_occupancy, kvcache_hit_rate.
   - High-cardinality logs and traces: request payload hashes, input signature, failure stack.

3) Kernel-level observability
   - Expose per-kernel metrics: kernel.exec_ms, kernel.wait_ms, kernel.preempt_count, kernel.context_switches.
   - Maintain a kernel-health triple: (avg_exec_ms, exec_variance_ms, preempt_rate).

4) Workload-aware sampling
   - Always sample 100% of 5xx errors and any request with kernel.exec_ms > p99_threshold.
   - Use probabilistic sampling by customer_tier: 0.5% for free, 5% for standard, 25% for enterprise.

Telemetry schema (table)
-----------------------
Metric name | Type | Retention | Notes
----------- | ---- | --------- | -----
request.latency_ms | histogram | 90d | label: model, variant, route
kernel.exec_ms | histogram | 30d | label: kernel_name, gpu_family, shard_id
kvcache.hit_rate | gauge | 180d | 1m and 1h resolutions
telemetry.pipeline_lag_ms | gauge | 30d | alerts when > 120000 ms
dispatchd.queue_depth | gauge | 14d | per-pool view

Example trace span model (text)
-------------------------------
- span: ingress.request (service=runtime-gateway)
  - tags: {trace_id, request_id, model.name, client_id}
- span: route.evaluate (service=routing)
  - tags: {routing_policy, fallback_used}
- span: kernel.schedule (service=dispatchd)
  - tags: {kernel_hint, slot_id, scheduled_delay_ms}
- span: kernel.exec (service=runtime-exec)
  - logs: {flamegraph_blob_id}

Profiling playbook (step-by-step)
--------------------------------
1) Pre-checks before profiling
   - Confirm test harness: bench-client v2.3.1 and that model/version pinned.
   - Ensure telemetry-ingest is sampling errors at 100% and enabled for p99 tail traces.
2) Reproduce or collect baseline
   - Run synthetic workload: bench-client --profile-shape mixed_short_long --duration 15m --concurrency 64
   - Record p50/p95/p99, token/s, kernel.exec_ms distributions. Save baseline id.
3) Controlled sampling & flamegraph capture
   - Flip kernel debug flag: dispatchd/admin api PATCH /debug/kernel-trace?duration=60s&sample_rate=1.0
   - Collect flamegraph blob from runtime-exec: curl -s http://runtime-exec:8080/debug/flame?id=<blob_id> > flame.svg
4) Diagnose
   - Compare kernel.wait_ms vs exec_ms: if wait_ms >> exec_ms, focus on scheduling and preemption.
   - Use trace waterfall to find serialization points (eg. bottleneck at kvcache warmup).
5) Mitigate and verify
   - Small mitigations: increase dispatchd slot_count by 15% for the affected pool, enable prefix caching for hot routes.
   - Re-run bench-client for 10m and compare to baseline.

Benchmarking suite integration notes
----------------------------------
- Add new kernel variants to the regression suite by creating a descriptor under /bench/descriptors with fields: name, model_compat, input_shape_samples, expected_p99.
- Bench script example: ./bench/runner --descriptor small-llama-13b-quant --iterations 500 --report-to bench-results/serviceX/2026-02-01
- Bench result table (example)

Model Variant | p50 (ms) | p95 (ms) | p99 (ms) | tokens/s | notes
------------- | -------: | ------: | -----: | -------: | -----
llama-13b-8bit-quant | 42 | 110 | 210 | 480 | tuned-kernel-v2
llama-13b-bf16 | 55 | 140 | 320 | 420 | high-precision path

Release notes checklist (for runtime releases)
---------------------------------------------
- Document kernel changes and expected perf delta (p50/p95/p99) per variant.
- List config toggles with safe defaults and rollout plan (canary matrix).
- Add required telemetry fields and their schema versions.
- Add a smoke-runbook with exact bench commands and thresholds.

Known issues and mitigations (operational)
----------------------------------------
1) Symptom: sudden p99 spike for short-response routes
   - Likely causes: kernel preemption, kvcache cold miss, network tail on telemetry-ingest.
   - Quick checks: `kubectl top pods -n runtime | grep dispatchd` ; check dispatchd.queue_depth > 0 ; check kvcache hit rate.
   - Mitigation: increase dispatchd slots for pool, temporarily enable kvcache-prefetch for hot-prefix, lift per-tenant concurrency cap.
2) Symptom: dispatchd OOM during heavy mixed workloads
   - Cause: kernel slot memory accounting drift after recent kernel-change.
   - Mitigation: drain node, restart dispatchd, roll back kernel commit, open PR to add stronger accounting and unit tests.

Operational runbooks (quick actions)
----------------------------------
- Runbook: tail-latency spike
  1. Pager triggers alert: p99 latency > configured threshold.
  2. On-call: query `prometheus` for kernel.exec_ms distribution and `dispatchd.queue_depth`.
  3. If queue_depth is high, increase slot_scale for the affected pool (dispatchd/admin scale).
  4. If preempt_rate increased, roll back recent kernel rollout in the canary matrix.
  5. If kvcache hit-rate dropped, trigger kvcache warmup script: `tools/warmup-prefixes --prefix-file /tmp/hot-prefixes.csv`

- Runbook: telemetry pipeline lag
  1. Check telemetry-ingest pods and SQS/Kafka backlog.
  2. If backlog present, temporarily reduce sampling rate for standard/free tiers via admin API.
  3. If ingestion still behind, admit reduced retention for metrics to reduce ingestion pressure.

Appendix: example telemetry event (JSON)
--------------------------------------
{
  "trace_id": "9f1d3a2b4c",
  "request_id": "r-123456",
  "timestamp": "2026-02-14T15:04:22Z",
  "model": "llama-13b-8bit-quant",
  "variant": "tuned-kernel-v2",
  "metrics": {
    "request.latency_ms": 218,
    "kernel.exec_ms": 182,
    "kvcache.hit": false
  },
  "tags": ["enterprise", "route:chat"]
}

Appendix: common CLI/debug commands
-----------------------------------
- Check node-level GPU utilization: `kubectl top nodes --selector=gpu=true --containers`
- Check dispatchd queue: `http :8080/dispatchd/metrics | jq .queue_depth`
- Fetch flamegraph: `curl http://runtime-exec:8080/debug/flame?id=<blob_id> -o flame.svg`
- Run benchmark: `bench-client --descriptor small-llama-13b-quant --concurrency 32 --duration 600`

Notes and next steps
--------------------
- We will iterate on the schema versioning strategy for telemetry (v1 -> v2) to make kernel tags backwards compatible.
- Short-term roadmap items: enrich kernel spans with GPU SM occupancy, add cross-tenant memory eviction metrics, and automate warmup for top-100 hot prefixes.

If you are adding new instrumentation or a kernel variant, follow the checklist in "Release notes checklist" and file a PR that includes updated telemetry schema and a bench descriptor. For questions, ping #runtime-observability on Slack or assign to the owner team (observability).

title: Runtime autotune framework: telemetry contracts and tuning playbook
content:
summary:
Specification and operational playbook for the Runtime Autotune Framework: telemetry contracts, experiment design, safety controls, and oncall procedures for automated kernel and batching parameter tuning.

body:
Overview

This page documents the Runtime Autotune Framework (RAF): an orchestrated system that ingests workload telemetry, runs controlled optimization experiments, and produces validated parameter updates (kernel selection, batch sizing, concurrency caps, and quantization profiles) that can be rolled out to production runtime clusters. The goal of RAF is to improve per-token cost and tail latency while preserving correctness and customer-visible SLOs.

Goals and non-goals

- Goals:
  - Automate routine tuning for stable workloads to reduce manual effort and cost by 10–30% over time.
  - Maintain or improve 95/99/99.9 latency SLOs; never trade away SLOs for cost without an explicit human approval step.
  - Provide clear telemetry contracts so experiments are reproducible and auditable.
- Non-goals:
  - RAF does not perform model-level parameter changes (weights) or retrain models.
  - RAF is not intended to replace incident response; automated rollbacks exist for safety but oncall intervention is required for complex degradations.

High-level architecture

1) Telemetry ingestion: continuous metrics stream and structured trace events are ingested into the RAF experiment service.
2) Workload profiler: synthesizes request distributions (sequence length, prompt prefix similarity, token-per-request distribution, function-calls frequency).
3) Hypothesis generator: maps workload fingerprints to candidate tuning vectors (e.g., kernel A for short sequences, mixed-kernels for long tails).
4) Controlled experiment runner: executes traffic-shaping A/B/canary experiments in isolated slices.
5) Validator and safety checker: compares aggregated metrics against acceptance criteria and generates signed decisions.
6) Rollout manager: applies changes according to rollout policy (canary -> gradual -> global) with automatic rollback triggers.

Telemetry contract (required fields)

Every signal used by RAF must implement the following contract. Signals are exported as Prometheus metrics or annotated traces with the following stable names and labels. Table reflects canonical names used across customers and internal deployments.

- Metric namespace: redwood_runtime_autotune_* (Prometheus)

| Metric name | Type | Description | Required labels | Collection frequency | Notes |
|-------------|------|-------------|-----------------|----------------------|-------|
| redwood_runtime_autotune_request_seq_length | histogram | Request input token count distribution | model, region, shard | 1m | Buckets: 0-32,33-64,65-128,129-256,257-512,512+ |
| redwood_runtime_autotune_latency_seconds | summary | End-to-end request latency (s) including network + kernel exec | model, region, shard, priority | 10s | Quantiles: 0.5,0.95,0.99,0.999 |
| redwood_runtime_autotune_kernel_cpu_ms | counter | Cumulative CPU ms used by kernel selection per request | model, kernel_variant, shard | 1m | Reset on process restart |
| redwood_runtime_autotune_kvcache_hit_ratio | gauge | KV-cache prefix hit ratio (0..1) | model, shard | 30s | Critical for batching decisions |
| redwood_runtime_autotune_error_counts | counter | Categorized error counts (parse, model-mismatch, oom, timeout) | model, error_type, region | 10s | Must increment consistently |

Operational semantics for metrics

- Label cardinality: model and region are required; additional labels (customer_id) may be included but cardinality must be capped using the cardinality policy (see related page).
- Aggregation window: RAF uses sliding windows with configurable length (default 5m for short experiments, up to 30m for conservative validation).
- Fidelity: samplers must preserve rare-tail behaviour; use stratified sampling when downsampling traces.

Hypothesis generation and candidate vector format

- Candidate vector is a fixed schema JSON (stored in experiment metadata) with string keys and scalar values. Example keys: kernel_variant, batch_max_tokens, batch_max_items, concurrency_limit, kvcache_policy, quant_profile.

Example candidate vector (YAML for readability):

---
kernel_variant: "fused-attn-v2"
batch_max_tokens: 2048
batch_max_items: 8
concurrency_limit: 12
kvcache_policy: "prefetch-on-hot-prefix"
quant_profile: "int8-mixed"
---

Experiment design and traffic shaping

1) Canary slice (default 0.5% traffic) for 30 minutes.
2) If canary passes acceptance, expand to staged rollout: 1% -> 5% -> 20% with minimum dwell time of 10 minutes per stage.
3) Each stage runs with an active control arm (unchanged parameters) and returns pre/post metrics.

Acceptance criteria (validator rules)

- Latency (tail) regression: 95th percentile tail must not increase by more than +5% relative to control.
- Error budget: error_counts.total must not exceed control by more than +10% absolute or 2x relative (whichever is smaller).
- Cost delta: expected per-token cost must improve or remain within -2% (no >2% cost increase allowed).
- Resource safety: GPU memory usage must not exceed 90% of baseline.
- Guard for degenerate behaviour: if kvcache_hit_ratio drops by >0.05 absolute in canary, abort.

Automated rollback triggers

- Instant rollback on any of the following during a stage:
  - 99.9 latency regressed >10% absolute.
  - OOM errors observed in >0.1% of canary requests.
  - Unhealthy node count increases by >1 per shard.

Experiment telemetry retained for audit

- Every experiment stores: candidate vector, start/end timestamps, aggregated metrics for control and treatment windows (as JSON blobs), decision (approve/reject), operator (automated or user id), git sha for runtime binaries, and rollout graph.
- Retention: 90 days hot, 2 years archived (compliance requirement).

Safety and human-in-the-loop controls

- Any candidate that touches quant_profile or kernel_variant requires an explicit human review for models with customers in restricted compliance tiers.
- Tiered approvals:
  - Low risk: kernel parameter tuning that does not change quant_profile and passes canary -> auto-approve.
  - Medium risk: changes that touch quant_profile but are only conservative adjustments -> require 2 engineering reviewers.
  - High risk: any change that reduces replication or changes memory layout -> product and security review required.

Runbook: how to launch a manual experiment

1) Create a new experiment record in RAF UI or via CLI. Example CLI snippet:

raf experiment create --name "short-seq-batching-optim" --vectors '{"batch_max_tokens":1024,"concurrency_limit":10,"kernel_variant":"fused-attn-v2"}' --canary-percent 0.5 --dwell 30m --owner "team-runtime"

2) Observe RAF dashboard for the canary window (link: /raf/ui/experiments).
3) If validator shows PASS, promote to staged rollout. If FAIL, inspect raw traces and open an incident if necessary.

Troubleshooting checklist (first 60 minutes)

- If canary FAILS:
  1) Check redwood_runtime_autotune_error_counts for error_type=oob/oom/timeout.
  2) Inspect per-shard latency histograms to detect skew.
  3) Compare kvcache_hit_ratio between control and treatment.
  4) If resource saturation is suspected, run ephemeral profiler (profctl snapshot --target shard-X) and capture GPU kernel traces.

- If intermittent tail spikes only during peak traffic, abort staged rollout and reopen with a narrower sequence-length targeted candidate.

Operational responsibilities and ownership

- RAF service owner: eng-serving-runtime team. Primary oncall: runtime-platform-sre.
- Experiment approvers: runtime-performance SIG (listed in team roster).
- Auditing and compliance: security-and-compliance owns retention and access policies for experiment artifacts.

Safety-oriented telemetry sampling policy

- Always keep a separate high-fidelity tail-sampler stream (1 in 100 requests by default) with full traces and raw input signatures (redacted per privacy policy). Do not apply downsampling before safety checks.

Example validation query (Prometheus-like pseudo-query)

"(histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(redwood_runtime_autotune_latency_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le)) )"

Configuration table (defaults and recommended ranges)

- batch_max_tokens: default 1024, allowed range [32, 8192]
- batch_max_items: default 8, allowed range [1, 64]
- concurrency_limit: default 12, allowed range [1, 128]
- quant_profile: default "int8-mixed", allowed values ["fp16", "int8-mixed", "fp32-conservative"]

Release cadence and compatibility

- RAF uses semantic releases aligned with runtime major versions. Each release includes a compatibility matrix: supported kernel variants, required telemetry schema version, and minimum runtime binary git sha. The RAF service rejects experiments that declare an incompatible runtime binary.

Audit and postmortem expectations

- Any automated rollout that triggers a rollback must create an experiment postmortem within 72 hours. The postmortem must include: root cause hypothesis, data artifacts, and corrective action plan (owner and ETA).

Appendix: quick references

- Related runbooks: session-lifecycle-kvcache-consistency-guidelines-2024, kernel-contention-throttling-and-backpressure-playbook-2026
- Helpful CLI commands: raf experiment list; raf experiment status <id>; profctl snapshot --shard <shard-id>
- Contacts: runtime-sig@redwood.ai, oncall runtime-platform-sre

Document change log

- 2025-09-10: Draft by Priya Nair.
- 2025-11-18: Added telemetry contract and candidate vector schema. Reviewer: Marco Liu.
- 2026-02-15: Finalized acceptance criteria, rollout policy, and retention rules. Reviewed by Samira Patel.

End of document.

title: Economic Fidelity Controller and Safeguards — design manual
content:
Overview

This document specifies the Economic Fidelity Controller (EFC): a runtime subsystem that dynamically balances model fidelity, latency, and per-token cost across hosted and dedicated deployments. The EFC is a control plane component embedded in the serving stack that enforces cost and quality guardrails through real-time signals to the scheduler and kernel selection layer.

Goals
- Enforce organization-level cost targets (per-customer and aggregated) while preserving user-facing quality SLOs.
- Provide a transparent, auditable policy surface for degradations and fidelity regressions.
- Make runtime fidelity decisions reversible and safe: all changes must be observable, attributable, and subject to automatic rollback.
- Integrate with existing runtime scheduler and kernel mapper without adding undue tail-latency risk.

Scope and non-goals
- In-scope: model variant selection, dynamic quantization profiles, request routing to cheaper device pools, short-lived fidelity steps (e.g., sequence-length bucketing, KV cache hints), telemetry and alerting.
- Out of scope: training-time quantization decisions, model architecture changes, long-term contractual pricing.

High-level architecture

Components:
- runtime-efc (control loop service) — computes per-cohort fidelity actions every 5s by default.
- scheduler-proxy — receives EFC actions and converts them to scheduler admission rules / kernel hints.
- kernel-guard — lightweight in-node agent that applies kernel variant selection and enforces per-request fidelity caps.
- telemetry-bridge — aggregates fidelity decisions, token/cost deltas, and model quality signals for dashboards and audits.

Data flows (textual diagram)
1) telemetry -> runtime-efc: raw signals (per-route latency P50/P95/P99, per-token cost, embed/call counts, quality regressions from evals) flow to runtime-efc via the telemetry-bridge.
2) runtime-efc -> scheduler-proxy: actionable policy (e.g., reduce high-cost customer cohort fidelity to F-2 for 60s; route low-priority cohort to econ-gpu-pool).
3) scheduler-proxy -> kernel-guard: concrete kernel variant and admission instructions.
4) kernel-guard -> runtime (per request): tag request with fidelity metadata; enforce runtime caps.

Control loop semantics
- Decision cadence: default 5s decision window with exponential backoff on oscillation.
- Safety multiplier: every action carries a safety_multiplier (0.0–1.0); actions with multiplier < 0.25 require manual approval for tenant-broad changes.
- Confidence scoring: runtime-efc assigns confidence based on sample size and historical stability. Actions with confidence < 0.5 are restricted to shadow mode.

Policy primitives
- fidelity-step: an atomic change (e.g., quantize to int8, switch model variant to compact-v2, reduce max_tokens from 1024 -> 512).
- cohort-selector: matches requests to cohorts using route, customer_tier, token_budget, and tags.
- duration: TTL for the fidelity-step (e.g., 30s, 5m, 1h).
- escalation: if action persists > escalation_window, EFC escalates to an owner and can trigger rollback policies.

Telemetry and signals
Key signals (ingested via telemetry-bridge):
- latency_p50, latency_p95, latency_p99 (ms) per route and per cohort
- tokens_consumed and cost_per_token (USD) per model variant
- quality_score_{promptset} (0..1) from continuous evals and prompt-set checks
- kv_cache_hit_rate and sequence_length_distribution
- kernel_switch_rate and kernel_error_rate
- packing_efficiency and batch_size_distribution

SLOs and thresholds (examples)
| signal | target | warning | critical | owner |
|--------|--------|---------|----------|-------|
| route_latency_p95 | <= 450ms | > 550ms | > 800ms | runtime-sre |
| per_token_cost (30m window) | <= $0.0009 | > $0.0012 | > $0.0020 | finance-eng |
| quality_score_regression | delta <= -0.03 | delta <= -0.06 | delta <= -0.12 | applied-ml |

Integration with scheduler and kernels
- API handshake: runtime-efc exposes a gRPC action stream to scheduler-proxy: Action { cohort_id, fidelity_step, ttl_s, safety_multiplier, cause_id }
- Scheduler-proxy resolves conflicts between multiple controllers (e.g., operator-initiated vs EFC) by priority: manual > experiment > EFC > default.
- Kernel hinting: fidelity_step maps to kernel tags (e.g., quant-int8, split-attn-low, kv-prefetch-disabled). kernel-guard translates tags into in-node flags.

Kernel selection pseudocode (simplified)
1) request arrives with cohort_id
2) kernel_tag = kernel-guard.lookup(cohort_id) 
3) selected_kernel = kernel_catalog.best_match(kernel_tag, request.shape)
4) if selected_kernel.unavailable -> fallback to nearest-fidelity kernel and report metric efc.kernel_fallback

Example policies
- Cost cap policy: if per_token_cost (30m) for a customer > $0.0012 AND kv_cache_hit_rate < 0.3 -> apply fidelity-step: compact-v2 for 15m with safety_multiplier=0.6.
- Latency preservation: if route_latency_p95 degradation > +150ms -> temporarily reduce batching for the affected cohort and escalate to SRE.

Rollout checklist (canary-driven)
1) Merge feature branch to canary runtime-efc service (canary tag: efc-canary-202602).
2) Enable EFC in shadow mode for 48h on canary cluster; compare hypothetical actions to baseline.
3) Metric guard checks (must pass): no more than 0.5% increase in route_p99, no knock-on increase in kernel_error_rate.
4) Release to 5% of traffic by cohort and run for 2h. Verify cost deltas and quality-signal drift.
5) Expand to 25%/2d, 67%/24h, global after 72h if stable.

Operational runbook: fidelity-induced incident
(Owner: runtime-sre)
1) Detect: Alert fired for quality_score_regression critical or per_token_cost critical.
2) Triage: Check EFC action timeline (telemetry-bridge -> EFC decisions). Identify cohort_id and action_id.
3) Immediate mitigation: disable EFC (runtime-efc -> pause) for impacted tenant cohort or set safety_multiplier=0.0 to force rollback.
4) Containment: if kernel_error_rate correlated, instruct kernel-guard to revert to baseline kernel tag.
5) Root cause: run hypothesis list (network contention, quantization misestimate, eval false-positive). Use request traces (trace_id) and shadow logs.
6) Postmortem: produce PM with signal graphs (pre/post), action timeline, and an action to add new test prompts if regression was genuine.

Testing and benchmark plan
- Unit tests: decision engine determinism, hysteresis math, TTL expiry.
- Integration tests: runtime-efc -> scheduler-proxy gRPC mocking with fault injection.
- E2E perf: run mixed-workload tracer across three synthetic cohorts (chat-short, chat-long, embedding-heavy). Measure: per_token_cost, p99 latency, quality-score drift.
- Regression tests (daily): run a 1h mini-run against the baseline cluster using representative prompt-sets and assert quality_score >= baseline - 0.02.

Sample test matrix (human-readable)
| workload | mocked signal | expectation |
| chat-short (50k reqs) | spike in tokens_consumed | EFC recommends compact-v2 for low-priority cohort; no p99 increase > 5% |
| embedding-burst (10k reqs) | sudden cost uplift | EFC routes to econ-gpu-pool; verify latency change within 20% |

Auditing and compliance
- Every EFC action is logged as immutable event: {action_id, timestamp, cohort_id, pre_state_hash, post_state_hash, actor=efc, reason_code}. Events are retained 365 days in audit-store.
- For enterprise customers with private deployments, EFC can be configured in read-only (advisory) mode.

Dashboards and alerts (owner mappings)
- EFC Decisions dashboard: lists active fidelity-steps, safety_multiplier, and confidence scores (owner: runtime-ops).
- Cost drift dashboard: per-customer cost trends (owner: finance-eng).
- Fidelity regressions: quality-score delta alerts to applied-ml slack channel and paging for critical regressions.

Ownership and contacts
- EFC design owner: Arjun Mehta (runtime-platform)
- Runtime SRE: Sofia Kwon
- Applied ML owner (quality signals): Maya Rodriguez
- Scheduler integration lead: Tomás Alvarez

Change log
- 2026-01-12: Initial draft and design review created.
- 2026-01-28: Added kernel-guard integration and safety_multiplier semantics after SRE review.
- 2026-02-14: Finalized rollout checklist and incident runbook; set retention policy for action events.

Appendix: practical examples and CLI snippets
- Inspect active EFC actions (CLI):
  $ rctl efc list --cluster canary --format json | jq '.active_actions[] | {action_id, cohort, fidelity_step, ttl_s, safety_multiplier}'

- Simulate a cost cap policy (pseudo-YAML):
  policies:
    - id: cost-cap-01
      selector: {customer_tier: silver, route_tag: public-chat}
      condition: 'per_token_cost_30m > 0.0012 and kv_cache_hit_rate < 0.3'
      action: {fidelity_step: compact-v2, ttl_s: 900, safety_multiplier: 0.6}

- Example audit event (log line):
  2026-02-10T15:02:03Z efc.action CREATED action_id=ac_7b9f cohort=tenant-124 pre_hash=ha1 post_hash=ha2 reason=cost_cap_01

Glossary
- fidelity-step: concrete runtime change that reduces compute/precision to save cost.
- cohort: a request grouping key (route + customer_tier + tags).
- kernel-guard: in-node enforcement agent.

References
- See also: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/concurrency-shape-calibration-and-cost-envelope-2026 for workload definitions.
- Scheduler policy language: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-policy-language-declarative-profiles-2026

Feedback
For questions, feature requests, or to schedule a walkthrough, ping #runtime-efc on the internal Slack or contact Arjun Mehta (arjun@redwood.ai).

title: runtime-failure-scenario-simulator-and-capture-format-2026
content:
Summary
-------
This document defines the Runtime Failure Scenario Simulator (RFSS): a deterministic, configurable simulator and a compact capture format for recording real production requests and environment signals so we can reliably reproduce and reason about failures, regressions, and scheduling anomalies in the serving runtime. RFSS is intended for engineering teams working on kernel scheduling, shard placement, eviction, and KV-cache warmup logic.

Motivation
----------
We frequently observe complex multitenant failures and regressions that are hard to reproduce in a lab because:
- Production request mixes, ordering, and interleaving matter (prefix caching, KV hits).
- Heterogeneous GPU topology and eviction interactions vary by tenant co-location.
- Timing-sensitive scheduler decisions (preemption, handoff) only manifest at specific concurrency shapes.

RFSS gives a small, portable way to:
1) Capture a faithful snapshot of request traces + environment signals (compact capture format).
2) Re-run the captured workload in a simulator that models kernel queueing, KV-cache state, and tenant credit accounting.
3) Produce deterministic diagnostics (latency decomposition, kernel timeline, eviction traces) to accelerate triage and root cause analysis.

Scope and non-goals
-------------------
Scope:
- Multitenant inference request captures (HTTP/gRPC metadata + token-level lengths + decision traces).
- Runtime signals required for scheduling decisions (queue depths, current kernel credits, per-shard memory headroom).
- Deterministic simulator that approximates kernel dispatch latencies, backpressure, and preemption effects.

Non-goals:
- Full-cycle GPU microarchitectural simulation (we rely on parametric latency models derived from microbenchmarks).
- Privacy-sensitive payload retention (customer prompt text is redacted by default; refer to Data Handling section).

Design overview
---------------
- Capture layer (edge-side hook): lightweight capture that samples requests and enriches them with provenance: tenant_id, model_variant, seq_len, request_timestamp, and scheduler-decision-snapshot (priority, affinity, quota_token_balance).
- Compact capture format (.rfscap): newline-delimited JSON records with a header describing environment parameters and a sequence of request events. Each event contains token counts and pointers to anonymized prompt hashes if full text is not stored.
- Simulator core: event-driven discrete-time simulator with components: KernelQueue, KVCacheModel, ShardTopology, AdmissionController. Each component exposes a minimal state API to load snapshot values and emit time-annotated events.
- Output artifacts: kernel-timeline.tsv, eviction-log.ndjson, latency-decomposition.txt, deterministic replay log (.rfsreplay).

Capture format (compact, human-reviewable)
----------------------------------------
Top-level header (single JSON object, required):
| key | description | example |
|-----|-------------|---------|
| version | capture schema version | "1.0" |
| cluster_profile | named cluster profile used during capture | "gpc-prod-eu" |
| seed_time | UTC timestamp of capture start | "2026-02-10T12:05:23Z" |
| topology_snapshot | short token summarizing shard mapping | "shardmap-v12" |

Each subsequent line is a JSON event record. Example event fields:
- ts: absolute timestamp (ms since epoch)
- req_id: opaque id
- tenant: tenant short id (redacted)
- model: model id and variant
- seq_len: user token length (int)
- kv_hint: small set of cache keys touched (list of short strings)
- scheduler_snapshot: {priority, aff_group, credit_balance} (stringified map)
- probe_meta: optional performance probes captured at edge (latency_ms)

Note: because JSON objects in the capture events must be single-line, the format is NDJSON-style with escape conventions.

Simulator components and models
-------------------------------
1) KernelQueue
- Model: token-based service time model: service_time_ms = kernel_base_ms + per_token_ms * seq_len * kernel_multiplier(model_family).
- Admission: takes scheduler priority and kernel credits into account. If credits insufficient, sim emits "deferred" event and queues.

2) KVCacheModel
- Tracks warm/cold key sets per shard. Cache hit reduces per_token_ms by a hit_reduction_factor. Eviction follows LRU with configurable bucket sizes.

3) ShardTopology
- Abstracts the mapping of requests to physical shards and NUMA domains. Topology file is loaded from the capture header and supports simulating NUMA-induced transfer penalties.

4) AdmissionController / Scheduler
- Implements the same priority/credit semantics as production: token-bucket crediting, preemption thresholds, and cooperative yielding. The simulator exposes knobs: preemption_grace_ms, max_inflight_per_tenant, kernel_credit_decay_window_ms.

Operational runbook: capture -> reproduce -> triage
--------------------------------------------------
1) When to capture:
- Any persistent latency regression (>2x p99 observed vs baseline) or kernel-related error spikes (GPU watchdog, kernel OOM).
- Every failed canary during runtime rollout.

2) Capture procedure (engineer-facing):
1. From the incident page, request capture slot and mark timeframe.
2. Enable RFSS capture for 5–20 minutes with sample rate conservatively set (default 1:1000) or higher for targeted tenants.
   - CLI: rfsctl capture start --profile gpc-prod-eu --duration 600 --sample-rate 0.01 --tenants=T123,T456
3. Wait capture window, then stop and securely upload to the sandbox bucket: rfsctl capture stop --upload s3://redwood-sandbox/rfscaps/2026-02-10/
4. Create a simulator job: rfsctl simulate --cap s3://.../capture.rfscap --profile lab-simulator-small --seed 12345 --output s3://.../replays/

3) Reproduce steps:
1. Run simulator in deterministic mode using the capture header seed.
2. Compare simulator output artifacts to production traces (latency histograms, kernel-timeline).
3. If mismatch beyond tolerance, iterate by adjusting cluster_profile parameters (kernel_base_ms, per_token_ms, numav_penalty_ms).

4) Triage checklist (results-driven):
- If the simulator reproduces the regression: extract the earliest divergent event and trace back to scheduler_snapshot differences.
- If simulator shows eviction storms, flag "eviction-correlated-latency" and assign to kernel-scheduler oncall.
- If simulator fails to reproduce any backlog but production had tail latencies, escalate to SRE for topology-level investigation (nvlink issues, node-level watchdogs).

Example config table (simulator knobs)
| knob | default | description | safe-range |
|------|---------|-------------|-----------|
| kernel_base_ms | "0.4" | base kernel dispatch overhead in ms | "0.1 - 2.0" |
| per_token_ms | "0.03" | additional per-token work in ms | "0.01 - 0.1" |
| hit_reduction_factor | "0.55" | multiplier applied when KV cache hits | "0.3 - 0.95" |
| preemption_grace_ms | "8" | delay before preemptible tasks are yielded | "1 - 50" |

Data handling and privacy
-------------------------
- By default, prompt_text is omitted. Captures contain prompt_hash and short tokenized fingerprint. Teams may request full text for escalations; access requires security approval and an audit entry.
- Captures are TTL'd to 90 days in the sandbox and archived only with explicit owner approval.

Acceptance criteria for a good capture
-------------------------------------
- Contains at least 10k request events across affected tenants or 1 hour of contiguous traffic, whichever is smaller.
- Includes topology_snapshot that matches the production cluster profile used in the incident.
- Sampled scheduler_snapshot fields are present for >95% of events.

Integration and tooling roadmap (next 12 months)
------------------------------------------------
- Q2: Add automated diff tool that highlights scheduler_snapshot deltas aligned with latency spikes.
- Q3: Expose a web UI to playback kernel-timeline and zoom to eviction hot spots.
- Q4: Add a lightweight on-host collector that records fine-grained NVLink/temperature signals to improve NUMA modeling.

Ownership and SLAs
------------------
- Owner: Kernel & Scheduler team (primary), Observability team (secondary).
- Oncall routing: kernel-scheduler oncall receives alerts when simulator reproduces an "eviction storm" label.
- Expected turnaround: 48 business hours from new capture uploaded to a first diagnostic pass.

Appendix A: Example capture event (single-line NDJSON)
{"ts":164+000, "req_id":"r-9f3b", "tenant":"T123", "model":"redwood-7b.q4", "seq_len":234, "kv_hint":["k:lice-23"], "scheduler_snapshot":"p=high;aff=zone-a;credits=12", "probe_meta":{"edge_latency_ms":3}}

Appendix B: Troubleshooting notes
- If simulation fails with inconsistent kernel_base_ms, run the microbenchmark harness to recalibrate the model: tools/kernel-microbench --profile gpc-prod-eu --out calib.json
- For persistent mismatches with production, add a focused production-run with "shadow-mode" simulation to capture unresolved variables.

Contact and further reading
-------------------------
- RFC: runtime-replay-and-capture-rfc-2025 (internal link)
- Owners: Asha Natarajan (kernel & scheduling), Liam Chen (observability)
- Slack channel: #rfs-sim

title: Resilience Scenario Lab Notebook
content:
Overview

This lab notebook captures a set of reproducible resilience experiments for the Redwood serving runtime. It is intended to standardize how we exercise fallback, graceful degradation, kernel scheduling perturbations, and observability plumbing in a controlled environment so that results are comparable across releases and hardware types. The notebook cross-references profiling playbooks and benchmarking suites and provides explicit run instructions, telemetry targets, and postmortem templates.

Goals
- Establish a repeatable experiment matrix to validate runtime behavior across failure domains.
- Produce telemetry-based acceptance criteria for degradation modes (latency SLOs, degradation SLOs, error budgets).
- Provide runbook actions and mitigation patterns for observed failure classes.
- Capture kernel-scheduler-specific knobs and their observable side effects.

Audience
- Runtime engineers running kernel scheduler experiments.
- SREs validating release gates for degradation behavior.
- Benchmarking and profiling teams creating long-running simulations.

Experiment matrix (high level)
| Scenario ID | Fault injected | Target surface | Primary metric | Secondary metrics | Expected outcome |
|-------------|----------------|----------------|----------------|-------------------|------------------|
| R-01 | KV cache miss storm (eviction) | KV cache subsystem | p50/p95 tail latency | per-token cost, kernel occupancy | graceful warmup, bounded p95 increase < 2x |
| R-02 | Kernel slow-path insertion | kernel execution pipeline | kernel execution time (ms) | global request queuing, GPU utilization | detect and isolate slow kernel to degraded slot |
| R-03 | Network partition to region | smart routing / fallback | request success rate | failover latency, extra cost | automated region fallback within configured policy |
| R-04 | Mixed-tenant noise (burst) | scheduler admission controller | SLA-preserving fraction | token throughput, eviction rate | admission controller sheds best-effort traffic, preserves priority SLOs |

Prerequisites and lab topology
- Kubernetes cluster with node pools representing heterogeneous accelerators (A100, H100).
- Canary model bundle named `gpt-lite-canary:v3` pinned for test.
- Runtime image with experimental scheduler flags built: `redwood/runtime:test-experiments-2023-11`
- Access to the synthetic workload generator (`/opt/bench/synth-load`) and the profiling collector (`/opt/bench/trace-collector`).
- Telemetry stack: Prometheus remote write to test TSDB, Jaeger for traces, Loki for logs.

Environment variables and config snippets
- Example scheduler config (yaml):

apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: scheduler-experiment-config
data:
  admission_policy: |
    priority_classes:
      - name: interactive
        weight: 100
      - name: background
        weight: 10
    kernel_hints_enabled: true
    max_cohort_size: 64

- CLI to deploy synthetic traffic: 
/sbin/benchctl --target http://runtime-canary.test --concurrency 120 --qps 400 --profile mixed_length_corpus.json --ramp 60s

Injection recipes (step-by-step)
1) KV cache eviction storm (R-01)
   1. Start baseline capture (prometheus job: `baseline-run`, 5m).
   2. Launch synth workload at 60% p95 load for 3 minutes.
   3. Force eviction: `kubectl exec -it kvcache-controller -- ./evict --rate 5000 --duration 120`
   4. Observe warmup trajectory in `runtime.kvcache.hits` and `runtime.kvcache.evictions`.
   5. If p95 latency > 2x baseline for > 10m, record as failure and follow mitigation playbook.

2) Kernel slow-path perturbation (R-02)
   1. Enable fault injection in kernel plugin: set `KERNEL_FAULT_INJECTION=enabled` on canary pods.
   2. Apply an experimental kernel that introduces a 15–50ms tail in attention compaction: `kubectl set env deployment/runtime-canary KERNEL_VARIANT=slowpath-test`
   3. Run the microbenchmark harness: `/opt/bench/kernel-bench --model gpt-lite --seq 1024 --iters 1000`
   4. Collect traces and annotate slow kernel spans with `kernel.name` tag.

3) Admission controller overload (R-04)
   1. Configure admission thresholds: `max_slot=512`, `background_share=0.08`.
   2. Create a background blast: `benchctl --tenants background --concurrency 800 --qps 1200 --duration 600` while keeping interactive load steady.
   3. Verify that `scheduler.admitted_by_priority` shows interactive preserved > 95%.

Telemetry signals and dashboards
- Primary signals (Prometheus metrics):
  - `runtime.request.latency_seconds{quantile}` (p50/p95/p99)
  - `kernel.exec_time_ms` (histogram)
  - `runtime.kvcache.hits` and `runtime.kvcache.evictions`
  - `scheduler.admitted_requests_total{priority}`
  - `gpu.utilization_percent` and `gpu.memory.allocated_bytes`
- Traces: span annotations for `kernel.exec`, `kvcache.lookup`, `request-routing`.
- Log patterns to watch for (Loki):
  - \"kernel-slow-path\" entries with stack context
  - \"eviction-threshold-crossed\" events

Acceptance criteria (per scenario)
- R-01: After cache-storm ends, p95 should return to baseline within 5x median warmup time and not exceed 2x baseline for more than 10 minutes.
- R-02: Slow kernel must be isolated to experimental cohort; global p95 must not exceed SLA target (200ms) for interactive tier.
- R-04: Priority-preservation target >= 95% for interactive requests; background throttled to maintain SLO.

Profiling playbook excerpt (when experiment diverges)
1. Snapshot kernel-level histograms (use `kernel-bench --dump-histogram`).
2. Correlate kernel spans with GPU metrics over the same timestamp window.
3. Increase tracing sampling to 100% for suspect cohort for 10 minutes and collect full spans.
4. Run a controlled microbenchmark that isolates sequence length and batch size to reduce confounders.
5. Annotate the experiment run with `experiment_id` and add to the experiment registry.

Runbook actions (triage ladder)
1. Detect: Alert fires for p95 > SLO for two consecutive 1m windows.
2. Contain: Flip `admission.shed_noninteractive=true` and reduce `max_cohort_size` by 50%.
3. Isolate: Move suspect kernel variant to a canary node pool with `kernel_taint=experimental`.
4. Recover: Roll back the kernel image or increase the admission reserve for interactive priority.
5. Remediate: Create a ticket and schedule a root-cause profiling run with relevant owners.

Known issues catalog (excerpt)
- Issue K-117: Intermittent NVLink degradation causes higher than expected kernel exec variance. Workaround: enable `nvlink-probe` and auto-evacuate pods with > 2% packet-loss. Status: monitoring.
- Issue R-204: Admission controller miscalculates slot cost when session KV prefetch is enabled. Workaround: disable prefetch for background classes. Status: mitigated in 2024-01 patch.

Release gating checklist (for runtime release candidate)
- Run R-01 through R-04 matrix against target release image on both A100 and H100 node pools.
- All acceptance criteria met for interactive priority on both hardware types.
- No new entries in known issues catalog with severity P0/P1.
- Profiling artifacts (trace and kernel histograms) uploaded to experiment registry and linked from release notes.

Postmortem template (use for any failed run)
1. Summary: one-sentence description of what failed.
2. Timeline: ordered list of events with timestamps.
3. Impact: customers/tenants affected, SLO burn observed.
4. Root cause hypothesis and evidence.
5. Actions taken: contain/isolate/recover.
6. Long-term fixes and owners.
7. Regression test to prevent future recurrence.

Ownership and contacts
- Experiment owner: Asha Patel (runtime reliability).
- SRE liaison: Michael Chen.
- Kernel scheduling SME: Olivia Ruiz.

Appendix A — Example synthetic workload (json)
{
  \"name\": \"mixed_length_corpus\",
  \"shapes\": [
    {\"seq\": 64, \"weight\": 0.6},
    {\"seq\": 512, \"weight\": 0.25},
    {\"seq\": 1024, \"weight\": 0.15}
  ],
  \"behavior\": \"bursty\"
}

Appendix B — Common troubleshooting commands
- Stream request traces for a given request id: `kubectl logs runtime-canary --follow | jq -r \'select(.request_id==\"<id>\")\'`
- Dump kernel histograms: `kubectl exec -it kernel-agent -- /opt/bin/kernel-stats --dump`
- Force scheduler admission snapshot: `curl -X POST http://scheduler.test/admin/snapshot`

Notes and next steps
- Add R-05 (region failover under partial DNS outage) to next quarter's matrix with a focus on client retry behavior.
- Formalize exact graph panels and dashboard ids referenced here and add them to the shared dashboard library.
- Convert the lab harness into an automated CI job that runs on each candidate release image.

Document history
- 2023-11-07: Created by Asha Patel.
- 2024-02-15: Expanded acceptance criteria and added R-04 admission controller scenario.

title: Async KVCache Prefetch and Adaptive Kernel Selection Playbook
content:
Summary
This playbook describes the design, operational controls, profiling guidance, benchmarking recipes, and incident runbooks for the asynchronous KV cache (KVCache) prefetcher and the adaptive kernel selection subsystem. The document explains how the prefetching pipeline integrates with the request classifier and kernel selector to reduce token-era latency for long-context and multi-shot workloads while preserving cost and fairness SLOs.

Why this exists
- Root cause: Tail latency often originates from sequential KV loads and conservative kernel choices for requests with uncommon sequence profiles.
- Goal: Reduce P95/P99 generation latency by prefetching KV segments and selecting kernels tuned to the observed request pattern without increasing average GPU occupancy or costs by more than 8%.

Scope
- Included: Async prefetch coordinator, request classification heuristics, kernel selection policy, metrics and alert thresholds, profiling steps, benchmarking recipes, rollout and rollback steps.
- Excluded: Model architecture changes, quantization profiles (see quantization-profiles directory), network-level transport changes.

High-level architecture (text diagram)
- Ingress -> Request Classifier -> Routing & Prefetch Coordinator -> Kernel Selector -> GPU Dispatcher -> KVCache (per-shard) -> Runtime Executor
- Feedback loop: Runtime Telemetry -> Adaptive Policy Engine -> Prefetch & Kernel Policy Store

Components and responsibilities
1) Request Classifier
- Tag requests at ingress with a sequence profile: typical length distribution, presence of tool/function calls, streaming flag, and priority class. Uses lightweight sampling models (logistic model trained on historical traces).
- Responsible for assigning a prefetch hint (none, soft-prefetch, eager-prefetch) and candidate kernel families (A/B) for the Kernel Selector.
2) Prefetch Coordinator
- Receives hints and maintains per-session prefetch state. Issues non-blocking KV reads to co-locate likely KV pages before the request reaches the hot kernel path.
- Uses backpressure-aware dispatch: prefetch requests are priority-0 and are throttled by an adaptive token bucket per-GPU to maintain tail SLOs.
3) Kernel Selector
- Maintains a policy table indexed by (model-variant, sequence-profile, priority). Each entry contains candidate kernels with expected latency & cost vectors.
- Uses a bandit-style experiment framework for online exploration (epsilon-greedy by default) with decay windows tied to model version rollouts.
4) Adaptive Policy Engine
- Periodically (5m) retrains lightweight policies from telemetry. Generates updated thresholds for prefetch aggressiveness and kernel switching.

Key design tradeoffs and safeguards
- Safety first: Kernel switches are allowed only if the candidate improves expected latency without exceeding a configured cost delta (default +8%).
- Backpressure integration: Prefetch-level throttles yield immediately under GPU memory pressure or when per-GPU kernel saturation > 85%.
- Gradual exploration window: exploration rate is capped to avoid noisy regressions in canaries.

Operational metrics and dashboards (minimum required)
- Prefetch hit rate (per model, per region): percent of requests where prefetched KV page satisfied first KV fetch.
- Prefetch to primary fetch latency delta (ms).
- Kernel selection distribution: percent usage of each kernel family by model-version.
- P50/P95/P99 generation latency (token complete) by kernel family and sequence-profile.
- GPU occupancy and queue length by kernel family.
- Cost-per-token delta by kernel family.

SLO guardrails (observable thresholds)
- P95 generation latency: target 120ms, alert if >160ms sustained for 3m.
- Prefetch hit rate: target >= 70% on long-context workloads, warning if <50%.
- Kernel-induced cost delta: warn at >+8% sustained 30m, page at >+12%.

Profiling playbook (how to investigate quality/latency regressions)
1) Initial triage
- Verify if latency spike correlates with: recent kernel rollout, prefetch policy change, model-version rollout, or GPU pool capacity event.
- Query traces: filter by request classifier tag and kernel family.
2) Reproduce with developer sandbox
- Use the sandbox driver with the same sequence-profile and batch shape. Run microbenchmarks with and without prefetch: ./bench_driver --model vX --profile long-context --prefetch on/off --kernel A/B.
3) Telemetry collection
- Capture a full trace set for 5 minutes: kernel dispatch times, KVCache miss/hit events, per-token latency, and GPU occupancy. Use the runtime trace sampler: rt-sample --duration 300 --labels kvcache,prefetch,kernelselect.
4) Root-cause patterns and fixes
- High KV miss & low prefetch hit -> increase conservative prefetch window and examine classifier false negative rate.
- Kernel family P99 regressed -> disable exploration flag for that family; roll back canary.
- GPU memory pressure during prefetch -> reduce per-GPU prefetch tokens or restrict eager-prefetch to dedicated pools.

Benchmarking suite (recipes and canonical configs)
- Objective: quantify cost/latency tradeoffs for prefetch aggressiveness and kernel families across representative profiles.
- Canonical workload set: short-chat (avg len 30), long-instruction (avg len 512), multi-shot session (avg len 800 with KV locality).
- Benchmark config table (text):
  - Test name: long-kv-prefetch-scan
    concurrency: 200
    seq_profile: long-instruction
    prefetch: eager
    kernels: [A-optimized, B-latency]
    duration: 30m
  - Test name: mixed-plg-burst
    concurrency: 500
    seq_profile: mixed
    prefetch: soft
    kernels: [A-optimized]
    duration: 60m
- Key result artifacts to capture: per-token latency histograms, GPU occupancy heatmaps, prefetch hit/miss timelines, and cost-per-token estimations. Store outputs as parquet with schema: trace_id, timestamp, model_version, kernel_family, cpu_ms, gpu_ms, kvcache_event, cost_units.

Release and rollout plan
1) Local QA: unit tests + microbench suite.
2) Canary: enable soft-prefetch + adaptive kernel selection in a 1% canary pool with exploration rate 1%. Monitor the following for 30m: P95 latency, prefetch hit rate, kernel cost delta.
3) Staged expansion: 1% -> 5% -> 20% -> global. At each stage the policy engine must show no adverse impact on SLOs for 30m before advancing.
4) Automatic rollback triggers: sustained P95 regression > 20% or prefetch hit rate drop > 30% vs baseline for 15m.

Runbook snippets (incident steps)
- Symptom: sudden P99 spike for long-context model
1) Check recent policy changes: /ops/deploy-log or policy-store update id.
2) Query prefetch hit rate and kernel distribution for the last 10m.
3) If prefetch hit rate dropped > 40%: immediately flip prefetch to conservative mode for the affected model-version: rt-cfg set prefetch.policy conservative --model vX --scope pool:us-east-1-canary
4) If a kernel family shows P99 > baseline by >50%: reroute to fallback kernel family: rt-route set --model vX --kernel-family B --scope pool:us-east-1-canary
5) Engage runtime-oncall and kernel-owner (see ownership section).

- Symptom: elevated GPU memory pressure correlated with prefetch activity
1) Reduce per-GPU prefetch tokens: rt-cfg set prefetch.tokens 4 --scope pool:eu-west-1
2) If memory pressure persists, disable eager-prefetch globally for the affected pool: rt-cfg set prefetch.enabled false --scope pool:eu-west-1
3) Schedule a postmortem and attach sampled traces.

Observability and tracing guidance
- Span instrumentation: add spans for prefetch.issue, prefetch.wait, kvcache.load, kernel.select, kernel.dispatch.
- Sampling: keep deterministic sampling for requests in canary pools and stratified random sampling across sequence profiles (target 1% global, 10% for canaries).
- Annotation: annotate spans with request_classifier tag, prefetch_hint, kernel_family, and kvcache_page_id.

Ownership and contacts
- Primary owners: Serving Runtime - Kernel and KV team (team slack: #runtime-kv-kernel)
- Secondary: Eng-SRE for capacity events (#eng-sre)
- Pager duties: runtime-oncall@redwood.ai

Open issues and known limitations
- Prefetch heuristics still misclassify some nested tool-calling sessions; leads to wasted KV reads in low-locality sessions. Tracking work item: RUNTIME-1126.
- Kernel exploration can oscillate under non-stationary traffic patterns; mitigation: add per-model decay windows (WIP: RUNTIME-1183).

Appendices
A) CLI snippets
- Re-run microbench: ./bench_driver --model vX --profile long-context --prefetch eager --kernel-family A --out results.parquet
- Toggle conservative prefetch: rt-cfg set prefetch.policy conservative --model vX
B) Suggested alert definitions (PromQL-like, text form)
- prefetch_hit_rate < 0.5 for 10m -> severity: warning
- p95_generation_latency{model="vX",kernel_family!="fallback"} > 160ms for 3m -> severity: page

C) Related experiments and artifacts
- Experiment: kernel-A vs kernel-B bandit logs (s3://redwood-experiments/kernelselect/bandit/2025-11)

Document history
- 2025-07-15: Initial authoring (Anya Patel)
- 2025-11-02: Added benchmarking recipes and rollout thresholds (reviewers: Marco Ruiz)
- 2026-02-03: Clarified GPU backpressure behavior and added CLI snippets (reviewers: Priya Shah, Evan Chao)

End of document

title: Third-party accelerator compatibility and dependency matrix (compatibility manifest)
content:
Summary:
This page is the canonical compatibility and dependency matrix for third-party accelerators that the runtime supports or plans to support. It codifies driver/runtime/library versions, expected kernel features, known incompatibilities, required CI smoke tests, ownership, and an automated manifest format (JSON) used by our onboarding toolchain. Use this when: planning support for a new accelerator, triaging inference regressions on a new hardware class, or validating release gates before a runtime rollout.

Goals:
- Capture the minimal set of platform packages (drivers, runtimes, libs) required for the serving runtime to deliver production SLOs.
- Provide reproducible test matrix entries used by CI and the hardware lab.
- Surface common failure modes and triage steps specific to each vendor.
- Define rollback and mitigation procedures when a hardware-specific kernel or driver causes regressions.

Scope and conventions:
- This document covers: NVIDIA (CUDA/NVML/NCCL), AMD (ROCm/MIOpen), AWS accelerators (Inferentia/Trainium), Intel/OneAPI-backed accelerators, Graphcore/Poplar, and other partner ASICs where we have lab access.
- Each matrix row includes: vendor, model family, required host kernel ABI, driver/runtime version range, critical libraries, recommended Docker base images, CI test IDs, owner, and known-risk flags.
- Version ranges are inclusive. Entries marked "experimental" must pass the experimental-canary CI suite, not just the smoke suite.

Compatibility matrix (text table):
Note: use this table as a quick reference. The source-of-truth is the JSON manifest in the repository at infra/accelerator-manifests/compatibility-manifest.json.

| Vendor | Family / Models | Host kernel ABI | Driver / Runtime | Critical libs / plugins | Recommended image tag | CI test(s) | Owner | Risk notes |
|--------|------------------|-----------------|------------------|-------------------------|------------------------|-----------|-------|------------|
| NVIDIA | A100, H100 (Tensor) | linux-5.15+ (glibc ABI stable) | CUDA 12.2 - 12.4, NVIDIA driver 535+ | cuBLAS, cuDNN, NCCL, NVML | redwood/runtime-nvidia:cuda12.4-rt-2026 | ci-accel-nvidia-smoke, ci-nvlink-stress | runtime-hw | NVLink firmware mismatch causes memory teleport errors (see known issues) |
| AMD | MI250, MI300 | linux-5.15+ (ROCm-ready ABI) | ROCm 5.8 - 6.0 | MIOpen, ROCm NCCL-compatible libs | redwood/runtime-amd:rocm5.8-rt-2026 | ci-accel-amd-smoke, ci-rocm-memory-fft | runtime-hw | GPU page table fragmentation risk under high concurrency |
| AWS | Inferentia | linux-5.10+ (aws kernel) | Neuron SDK 2.3+ | neuron-libs, neuron-runtime | redwood/runtime-aws:neuron2.3-rt | ci-aws-inferentia-smoke | platform-partner | Binary ABI for Neuron is sensitive to compiler flags; require vendor-signed kernels |
| Intel | Gaudi/ Habana (Partner) | linux-5.15+ | Poplar / OneAPI stacks | poplar-rt, onednn | redwood/runtime-intel:oneapi-2026-rt | ci-intel-accel-smoke | runtime-hw | Driver installer writes kernel modules to non-standard paths; watch mknod/udev permissions |
| Graphcore | IPU-M2000 | linux-5.15+ | Poplar 2.x series | poplar-plugins | redwood/runtime-ipu:poplar2-rt | ci-ipu-smoke | runtime-hw | High cold-start memory usage; require warmup harness |

(For an up-to-date machine-readable matrix, see infra/accelerator-manifests/compatibility-manifest.json in the infra repo.)

Manifest format (example JSON snippet):
This is the canonical object the onboarding automation consumes. Store one file per vendor-family in infra/accelerator-manifests/.

{
  "vendor": "nvidia",
  "family": "h100",
  "models": ["h100-sxm", "h100-pcie"],
  "host_kernel_min": "5.15",
  "driver_version_range": "12.2:12.4",
  "required_packages": ["nvidia-driver>=535", "cuda-toolkit>=12.2", "libnccl>=2.15"],
  "recommended_image": "redwood/runtime-nvidia:cuda12.4-rt-2026",
  "ci_gate": "ci-accel-nvidia-smoke",
  "risk_flags": ["nvlink_firmware_sensitivity"]
}
(When editing the manifest, increment the manifest_version field and attach the matching lab test run id.)

CI and lab test design:
- Smoke suite (ci-*-smoke): quick boot, telemetry, single-request inference for canonical models, KV cache sanity, and basic memory pressure. Completes in < 5 minutes per node. Required for all PRs that touch runtime scheduler or kernel selection.
- Stress suite (ci-*-stress): multi-concurrency sustained runs, NVLink/PCIe saturation tests, rendezvous N random seeds to detect numerical drift. Runs in ~2 hours across our lab pool. Used for release gating on major driver bumps.
- Fidelity suite (ci-*-fidelity): compares output distributions against golden corpora, quantization toggles, and mixed-precision paths. Used when enabling quantization profiles.

CI matrix YAML example (used by our GitHub Actions):

name: Accelerator Compatibility Matrix
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  matrix-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-22.04
    strategy:
      matrix:
        vendor: [nvidia, amd, aws]
        model_family: [h100, a100, mi300, inferentia]
    steps:
      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Launch lab node (or mock)
        run: ./infra/labctl/launch_node --vendor ${{ matrix.vendor }} --family ${{ matrix.model_family }}
      - name: Run smoke tests
        run: ./infra/ci/run_compatibility_smoke.sh --manifest infra/accelerator-manifests/${{ matrix.vendor }}-${{ matrix.model_family }}.json

Known failure modes and triage playbook (quick reference):
1) Driver mismatch at startup (symptoms: driver load failures, NVML unavailable, crate reports "missing kernel symbols").
   - Commands: sudo dmesg | tail -n 200; nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name,driver_version --format=csv; rocminfo; sudo modinfo nvidia
   - If driver ABI mismatch: pin to the last known-good driver (see infra/accelerator-manifests/last-known-good) and trigger a canary rollout.
2) NVLink firmware mismatch (symptoms: inter-GPU copy hang, elevated kernel errors, OOMs during large KV cache warmups).
   - Triage: check nvidia-smi -q -d LINK; check firmware version table in infra/hardware-inventory/firmware.csv. If mismatch detected: set scheduling policy to avoid cross-socket NVLink paths (see mitigation below) and file an infra ticket for firmware alignment.
3) Host kernel OOPS when loading vendor kernel modules (symptoms: kernel oops, machine reboots, module load stacktrace).
   - Triage: capture vmcore if possible; collect /var/log/kern.log; isolate kernel version and report to partner. Revert kernel update and boot previous AMI.
4) Inference numerical drift after driver update (symptoms: fidelity alerts, increased model perplexity).
   - Triage: run ci-*-fidelity suite on the same commit+driver to confirm; if deterministic, mark driver as blocked for quantized paths and force fallback to float kernels; open follow-up with research and vendor.

Mitigations and operational knobs:
- Scheduler-level mitigation: 'evict-across-nvlink' boolean in scheduling profiles. When true, the scheduler will prefer cross-socket placement only for requests that are tagged as high-throughput and tolerant of additional latency.
- Kernel selection fallback: runtime keeps a per-node kernel-hint file produced by the onboarding manifest. If a kernel path is missing at startup, runtime will: 1) degrade to a compatible kernel plugin (if available), 2) reduce concurrency quota for the tenant, and 3) emit an operational alert with a suggested rollback.
- Container image pinning: all production pools use image digests (sha256) instead of tags. The manifest includes recommended image digests under recommended_image_digest.

Rollback and canary process for driver/runtime changes:
1) Staging validation: the proposed driver/runtime version must pass the smoke and stress suites in staging (staging-lab with 3 nodes) and not regress more than 1% on 95th p99 latency for canonical prompts.
2) Canary: roll to 5% of production traffic in a single region with canary telemetry enabled. Observe per-model fidelity metrics for 24 hours.
3) Rollback criteria: any of the following triggers a rollback: p99 latency increase >10% vs baseline, fidelity regression >0.5% for golden prompts, GPU hardware errors >0.1% of requests.
4) Rollback steps (operator):
   - Set scheduling policy to avoid affected pool(s): curl -X POST $RUNTIME_API/pools/scale -d '{"pool":"h100-rt-prod","target":0.9}'
   - Trigger node drain: infra/labctl/drain_node --node h100-rt-12
   - Re-image node with last-known-good driver image: infra/ami-bootstrap/reimage --ami ami-xyz --manifest infra/accelerator-manifests/last-known-good/nvidia-h100.json
   - Monitor: validate smoke-suite; close incident if green.

Ownership and contact matrix (text):
- runtime-hw (owner): Priya Nambiar, Luis Ortega — Responsible for manifests, smoke tests, and lab coordination.
- infra (owner): Jonah Park — Responsible for AMIs, kernel builds, and lab node boots.
- research/applied-ml: Maya Chen — Responsible for fidelity suite, golden corpora, and drift triage.
- platform-partner: Partner PM / Partner Eng — vendor-specific escalation.

Lab checklist before declaring full support:
1) Run full stress and fidelity suites for 48 hours across 3 nodes.
2) Validate billing/chargeback hooks for the pool (cost attribution).
3) Document warmup and eviction behaviors in the runtime pool README.
4) Add entries to hardware-inventory, include firmware and BIOS versions.

Operational examples and debug commands (cheat sheet):
- Check basic GPU health (NVIDIA): nvidia-smi -q -d MEMORY,UTILIZATION,LINK
- Check NVLink details: nvidia-smi -q -d LINK | egrep -A4 "Link"
- ROCm diagnostics: /opt/rocm/bin/rocminfo; /opt/rocm/bin/rocm-smi -d 0 --showtemp
- Container runtime test: docker run --rm --gpus all --privileged redwood/runtime-nvidia:cuda12.4-rt-2026 nvidia-smi -L
- Kernel module info: sudo modinfo nvidia | head -n 40

Appendix A — Example compatibility test case (text):
- Test id: ci-accel-nvidia-smoke-001
- Purpose: Validate A100/H100 basic inference path and KV cache warmup under 8 concurrent workers.
- Steps:
  1) Boot node with manifest infra/accelerator-manifests/nvidia-h100.json
  2) Pull recommended image digest and run containerized test harness: infra/ci/harness/run_infer_test.sh --image sha256:abcd... --concurrency 8 --model gpt-redwood-small
  3) Assert: 95th latency < 200ms, memory growth < 2GB/worker after 30s warmup, no GPU driver errors in dmesg.

Appendix B — How to update this manifest:
1) Edit infra/accelerator-manifests/<vendor>-<family>.json and bump manifest_version.
2) Run ./infra/ci/run_compatibility_smoke.sh --manifest <path> locally against a mock node or in the lab.
3) Create a PR against infra with the manifest and the lab run id attached. Tag runtime-hw and infra teams as reviewers.

Change log (brief):
- 2026-05-12: initial published manifest and CI matrix (Priya Nambiar).
- 2026-08-16: added ROCm 5.8 compatibility entries and stress test IDs (Luis Ortega).
- 2026-10-03: added Graphcore IPU entry and expanded rollback procedure (Priya Nambiar).

Related resources (internal):
- infra/accelerator-manifests/ (repo)
- infra/hardware-inventory/firmware.csv
- infra/ci/ (compatibility test harness)
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/runtime-onboarding-for-third-party-accelerators-2026
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/seamless-model-swap-and-kv-consistency-guide-2025

If you are adding a new accelerator family and do not have lab access, open an infra-lab request with subject: "New accelerator onboarding - <vendor> <family>" and attach expected manifest draft.

End of document.

title: runtime-observation-enrichment-and-labeling-guidelines-2025
content:
Overview:
This document defines the canonical approach for enriching runtime telemetry (traces, kernel events, request metadata) with contextual labels and cost tags so downstream consumers (alerting, billing, profiler, experiments) can reliably join signals. The goal is consistent, low-cost enrichment that enables accurate SLO attribution, cost-per-inference accounting, and fidelity-aware debugging across hosted, dedicated and private deployments.

Why this matters:
- Inconsistent labels are the single largest source of signal fragmentation when debugging tail latency and kernel regressions.
- Cost and energy tags let product and finance teams reconcile per-route economics without pulling raw traces.
- Enriched, compact traces speed triage for oncall by surfacing the minimum causal set of attributes needed to reproduce or route incidents.

Principles:
1) Minimal, stable keyset: restrict primary labels to a small set that is unlikely to change (see Label Taxonomy).
2) Schema-first: all labels follow the canonical key names and types in this doc; any extension requires a review.
3) Cost-aware sampling: enrich higher-value requests at a higher sampling rate; inexpensive warmup traces sampled low.
4) Privacy & minimal PII: do not attach user PII or raw prompt text to traces. Use hashes or prompt-ids where needed.
5) Low-latency enrichment: enrichment must not add more than 1 ms on the request path in p95. Use asynchronous enrichers for non-blocking attributes.

Label taxonomy (canonical keys):
- request.id: stable UUID for the user request (string)
- route.name: product route or API path (string)
- model.variant: model name and variant (e.g., gptx-16q8) (string)
- kernel.path: kernel family / variant invoked (string)
- hw.pool: accelerator pool identifier (e.g., a100-pool-3) (string)
- cost.token_estimate: integer estimated token count (stringified integer)
- fidelity.flag: one of [full, approximate, degraded] (string)
- kvcache.hit_ratio: float (0.0-1.0) represented as string
- customer.tier: free | standard | enterprise (string)
- region: cloud region (string)
- trace.version: schema version (string)

Note: store numeric values as strings for telemetry pluggability and to avoid downstream parsing discrepancies.

Table: retention and storage hints (recommended):
- traces.enriched.retention: 30d (for fully enriched traces used in oncall workflows)
- traces.minimal.retention: 7d (for minimal traces used only for perf sampling)
- aggregated.metrics.retention: 365d
- cold-storage.export: weekly snapshots to S3 for compliance (retention 2y)

Sampling policy (high-level):
1) Baseline sampling: 0.5% of all requests capture minimal trace (spans + request.id + route.name).
2) Enriched sampling tiers:
   - High-value routes (customer.tier=enterprise or routes flagged by product): 20% enriched.
   - Potential-regressions: traffic flagged by the anomaly-detector (see procedure) gets 100% enrichment for 1h.
   - Manual oncall escalations: toggle enrich=true via /api/operator/enrich-toggle for the given route for immediate 15-minute capture.
3) Dynamic cost weighting: If cost.token_estimate > 10k, escalate enriched sampling by +5x for that request bucket.

Enrichment pipeline (component roles):
- Request Ingress (lightweight): attaches request.id, route.name, and region synchronously.
- Async Enricher (nonblocking): fetches model.variant, hw.pool membership, kvcache.hit_ratio from the runtime metadata service; annotates trace with these fields.
- Cost Estimator (streaming): estimates token count using header hints and concise tokenizer lookup; writes cost.token_estimate into trace.
- Privacy Redactor: replaces prompt text with prompt.id before long-term retention.

CLI examples:
- Toggle enrichment for route for 15m (operator):
  curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $OP_TOKEN" 
    https://internal-api.redwood.local/operator/enrich-toggle 
    -d '{"route":"/v1/chat/llm", "enrich": true, "duration_m":15}'

- Query enriched trace sample (example using internal tracer):
  rtr-cli get-trace --id 8a7f3c2b --compact=true

JSON example of a canonical enriched trace (compact):
{
  "trace.id": "8a7f3c2b-9c1d-4f8d-bf3a-abcdef012345",
  "route.name": "/v1/generate/completion",
  "model.variant": "redwood/longformer-32k-16q8",
  "kernel.path": "attention-sharded-v2",
  "hw.pool": "a100-pool-3",
  "cost.token_estimate": "1200",
  "fidelity.flag": "full",
  "kvcache.hit_ratio": "0.82",
  "customer.tier": "standard",
  "trace.version": "v1"
}

Enrichment performance budget:
- Synchronous enrichment: <1 ms p95
- Full async enrichment completion: <50 ms median, <200 ms p99
- Failure modes: if enricher times out, record enricher.timeout=true and proceed without fields to avoid on-path tail inflation.

Debugging and incident workflows (runbook excerpt):
1) If tail latency breach detected for route X:
   a) Check sampled enriched traces for route.name==X in the last 15m.
   b) Filter traces where fidelity.flag != full and compare kernel.path distributions.
   c) If kernel.path change or hw.pool migration is visible, escalate to runtime-kernel-oncall and attach 5 representative traces (use rtr-cli sample-attach).
2) If cost-per-inference anomalies observed:
   a) Aggregate cost.token_estimate by model.variant and route.name for the window.
   b) If sudden token estimate inflation, run tokenizer audit (tokenizer-audit --route X --window 1h).
   c) Notify SRE and product: add label incident.cost_inflation.

Extension and governance process:
- To add a new canonical label or change type, open an ADR and include: motivation, schema change, migration plan, and storage impact estimate.
- Small labels (non-critical) may be trialed as optional.enricher.* keys for 4 weeks before approval.

Table: enforcement thresholds and alerts:
- Missing trace.version on >1% enriched traces for 1h -> P2 alert to observability team.
- enricher.timeout > 0.5% of enriched traces in 5m -> P1 to runtime infra.
- prompt-id absent on any trace stored beyond 7d -> security incident, restrict retention immediately.

Operational rollout checklist (numbered):
1) Deploy async enricher v1 to canary fleet (10% traffic).
2) Run canary for 72h, monitor enricher.timeout and enrichment-completion latency.
3) Validate label presence against schema for 95% of enriched traces.
4) Run tokenizer-audit on canary traffic to confirm cost estimates alpha accuracy within 15%.
5) Gradual ramp to 100% canary-to-prod over 48h if all checks pass.

Ownership and contacts:
- Observability Infrastructure (primary): Marcus Lee (oncall rotation: infra-observe@redwood.com)
- Runtime Telemetry Enricher owner: Elena Rodriguez
- Security & Privacy reviewer: Aisha Patel

Appendix A — Example instrumenter snippet (Python):
# pseudo-code, meant for the runtime's tracer shim
from internal_tracer import start_span, annotate
span = start_span('request')
span.annotate('request.id', request_id)
span.annotate('route.name', route_name)
# schedule async enricher task
async_enricher.schedule(request_id, context_headers)

Appendix B — Migration notes for older schemas:
- Older traces used trace.schema v0 and stored model and kernel under model_info.*; ingestion pipeline must map model_info.name -> model.variant and kernel.variant -> kernel.path at read time. Backfill of trace.version=v1 is optional; if required, create a daily job to migrate high-value route traces first.

Related artifacts and reading:
- runtime-telemetry-sampling-cost-aware-profiling-2027 (sampling rules)
- kernel-telemetry-annotation-guidelines-2025 (kernel-specific annotation practices)
- privacy-redaction-spec-2024

Document change log:
- 2024-11-12 (Elena Rodriguez): created initial draft.
- 2025-02-10 (Marcus Lee): clarified sampling multipliers for token-heavy requests.
- 2025-04-02 (Aisha Patel): added privacy enforcement thresholds and updated retention hints.

title: Runtime operator observability and diagnostic playbook
content:
Summary
-------
This playbook consolidates operator-facing observability patterns, diagnostic procedures, and escalation steps for the Redwood serving runtime. It bridges runtime architecture concepts (request routing, kernel scheduling, KV cache), profiling techniques, benchmarking checks, and runbook actions used during incidents and routine validation. The intended audience is oncall operators, SREs, and runtime engineers.

Scope
-----
- Host-level and service-level telemetry required to diagnose perf and correctness issues
- Kernel scheduling and admission controller signals relevant to prioritization and preemption
- Profiling commands and sampling recipes for reproducing tail-latency and memory-pressure scenarios
- Benchmarks and quick smoke checks to validate rollouts and hotfixes
- Clear owner / escalation steps and related documentation links

Roles & ownership
-----------------
- Oncall (Triage): first responder for alerts; run the checklist and collect traces/metrics.
- Runtime Engineers (RTE): perform kernel-level debugging, implement mitigations, and ship canary fixes.
- SRE: adjust global admission and capacity, coordinate capacity-driven fallbacks.
- Release owner: coordinate rollouts and postmortem.

SLOs and quick thresholds
-------------------------
- P99 generation latency per model route: 300ms (hosted), 150ms (dedicated).
- Error rate (5xx) per service: < 0.2% over 5m.
- Kernel queue length (per GPU): alarm if > 90th percentile of baseline for 10m.

Operational traces and telemetry to collect (minimum)
--------------------------------------------------
- Request timeline trace (edge -> orchestrator -> kernel dispatcher -> GPU execution) with span tags: model, seq_len, kernel_variant, priority, tenant_id.
- Kernel-level counters: active_kernels, preemptions, eviction_events, kv_cache_hits, kv_cache_misses.
- GPU telemetry: memory_used, sm_utilization, mem_alloc_latency, temperature_C.
- Admission signals: queue_depth_by_priority, available_slots, predictive_warmstart_score.

Fast triage checklist (first 10 minutes)
----------------------------------------
1) Validate alert context and affected routes: check Console route dashboard for increased 5xx or latency.
2) Capture representative traces: use trace-id from alert and run `rtrace fetch <trace-id>` to pull the full timeline.
3) Metrics snapshot: export the following queries to a file (Prometheus / Cortex):
   - promql: rate(runtime_request_errors_total[5m]) by (service, model)
   - promql: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(runtime_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, route))
   - promql: sum(active_kernels) by (gpu_id)
4) Check kernel scheduler status: `kubectl -n runtime get pods -l app=kernel-dispatcher -o wide` and `kubectl logs <dispatcher-pod> | tail -n 200`.
5) If GPU memory pressure observed (memory_used > 95% sustained for 1m) — start memory-pressure runbook (below).

Kernel scheduling knobs and their operational meaning
---------------------------------------------------
| knob_name | default | intent | operator action |
|-----------|---------|--------|----------------|
| preemption_budget_pct | 20 | maximum percent of task budget allowed for preemptions | reduce to 5–10 for critical low-latency routes during incident |
| admission_backpressure_threshold | 0.85 | queue fullness fraction after which admission starts rejecting | increase by +0.05 to allow burst if healthy slots exist |
| kernel_variant_preference | [fast_fp16, econ_int8, cpu_fallback] | ordered fallback chain | pin to fast_fp16 for SLA routes during canary |
| kvcache_warmup_concurrency | 8 | number of parallel prefetch workers | increase to speed warmstarts on cold-model rollouts |

(When editing knobs, follow the change-management window noted in infra-standards.)

Profiling recipes (commands + sampling plan)
------------------------------------------
- Lightweight live sample (5–15 minutes):
  - Enable `adaptive_latency_sampler` at 10% target rate for affected route.
  - Run: `rprof sample --route <route> --duration 10m --output /tmp/prof-route.json`
  - Produce flamegraph: `rprof flamegraph /tmp/prof-route.json > /tmp/flame.svg`
- Deterministic micro-replay (devlab):
  1. Capture representative request set (see benchmarking section).
  2. Run `rreplay --corpus ./corpus.json --concurrency 8 --model-version vX.Y` against canary runtime.
  3. Collect `nvprof` or vendor-specific traces on the accelerator host.

Benchmarking smoke tests (quick checks for rollouts)
--------------------------------------------------
- Purpose: confirm no obvious latency regressions and that scheduling decisions match expected cost envelope.
- Minimal checks (3–15m):
  1. Small synthetic burst: 1000 short requests (seq_len <= 64) at T=200 RPS. Confirm P95 < 120ms on dedicated nodes.
  2. Mixed-size steady test: 5m run with 60% short, 30% medium (seq_len 64–256), 10% long. Observe kernel_variant distribution and kv_cache hit-rate > 60%.
  3. Cold-model warmup: redeploy model and measure cold-start 50th/95th percentiles. Expected cold-start P95 < 1.2s for pinned pin-size models.
- Example curl-based generator (replace tokens and route):
  - bash snippet:
    for i in $(seq 1 1000); do curl -s -X POST \"https://api.redwood.internal/v1/generate?route=insights\" -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' -d '{"prompt":"hi","max_tokens":16}' & done; wait

Release note snippet (how to validate a runtime patch)
