-----------------------------------------------------
- Patch summary: short description of kernel or scheduler change, risk classification (low / medium / high), and rollback plan.
- Validation steps included in the PR: smoke benchmark results (before/after), unit tests for scheduler policy language, and canary traffic matrix.
- Communication: post to #runtime-release with roll-forward time and rollback steps.

Known issues index (active)
--------------------------
- ISSUE-2026-118: `kvcache_shard_serialization_delay` — symptom: sporadic 5xx on long-sequence workloads when shard repair triggers under high eviction. Mitigation: temporarily increase `kvcache_warmup_concurrency` and apply shard-rebalance. Owner: Cache Team. Link: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/known-issues/kvcache-shard-skew-quantization-interaction-2026.
- ISSUE-2026-212: `dispatcher-latency-spikes-on-burst` — symptom: dispatcher queue stalls after burst followed by sudden kernel preemption storms. Mitigation: lower preemption_budget_pct, enable burst_smoothing_policy, escalate to kernel-scheduler oncall if persists. Owner: Scheduler Team.

Memory-pressure triage runbook (short form)
------------------------------------------
1) Confirm with metrics: GPU memory_used_pct > 95% for 60s and mem_alloc_latency increase > 5x baseline.
2) Reduce admission for non-critical routes: `kubectl exec -n runtime <admission-controller-pod> -- patch ...` (follow safe change template).
3) Trigger eviction of low-priority sessions: `rctl evict --priority low --gpu <gpu-id> --grace 5s` and monitor for recovery.
4) If eviction fails or node unstable, cordon the node and drain: `kubectl cordon <node>` and `kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets`.
5) Post-incident: gather kernel-level debug bundle: `rdiag collect --since 30m --traceids <list> --output /tmp/diag-bundle.tgz` and attach to postmortem.

When to escalate to kernel-scheduler oncall
------------------------------------------
- Repeated kernel preemptions > 50/minute without corresponding queue depth increase.
- Kernel dispatch logs showing repeated ‘variant_mismatch’ errors.
- Any situation where immediate knob changes fail to restore latency within 10 minutes.

Template: investigation timeline (first 90 minutes)
---------------------------------------------------
- 0–10m: Triage checklist, gather traces, confirm SLO breach and scope.
- 10–30m: Apply minimal mitigations (admission control, knob tweak), capture before/after metrics.
- 30–60m: If still unresolved, start canary rollback or constrained routing to fallback model variants.
- 60–90m: Decide incident severity level, call for cross-team coordination, open postmortem.

Artifacts to attach to a postmortem
----------------------------------
- Trace bundle (rtrace), profiler output (rprof), benchmark job outputs, manifest of knob changes, PR references, and timeline of alerts/commits.

Appendix: handy queries and CLI snippets
---------------------------------------
- Top erroring routes: promql: topk(10, sum(rate(runtime_request_errors_total[5m])) by (route))
- Kernel busy GPUs: promql: topk(5, sum(active_kernels) by (gpu_id))
- Representative trace fetch: `rtrace fetch --service runtime --filter route=insights --limit 5`
- Kernel dispatcher health: `kubectl -n runtime exec svc/kernel-dispatcher -- /usr/local/bin/dispatchctl status`

Related documentation and runbooks
--------------------------------
- Runtime deployment circuit-breakers and SLA fallback playbook — link in related_pages.
- Latency fingerprint & kernel sensitivity index — profiling-playbook (refer reviewer list).
- Kernel scheduler design intent and contracts catalog — runtime-architecture team wiki.

Revision history
----------------
- 2026-02-08: created by Aisha Patel.
- 2026-03-01: updated with memory-pressure runbook and new kernel knobs table (reviewers: Miguel Ortega, Priya Shah).

Contact
-------
For urgent escalations: #runtime-oncall (pager duty) and runtime-scheduler@redwood.internal for kernel-scheduler oncall.

title: Observability → Cost Signal Mapping and Ownership Roster
content:
Overview:
This document defines a pragmatic mapping between runtime observability signals and the cost / SLO consequences they imply. It consolidates ownership for each signal, provides concrete alert thresholds, investigative playbooks, and sample queries to accelerate incident triage and cost attribution. The goal is to make cost-impacting signals actionable for oncall, SREs, runtime engineers, and product stakeholders without repetitive context-switching.

Why this exists:
- We observe recurring incidents where telemetry is present but responsibility and cost mapping are unclear.
- Kernel-level events (slow kernels, preemption, fragmentation) generate telemetry that must be translated into cost signals (excess GPU-hours, increased tail-latency retries, failed inference units).
- This doc standardizes naming, ownership, and initial remediation steps so pager fatigue and finger-pointing decrease.

Signal taxonomy (high level):
1) Resource & capacity signals
   - gpu_util_pct: instantaneous GPU utilization per node
   - gpu_steal_pct: fraction of GPU cycles lost to eviction/preemption
   - host_mem_pressure: OS-level memory pressure on serving nodes
2) Kernel & scheduler signals
   - kernel_latency_p50/p95/p99: per-kernel execution latencies
   - kernel_queue_depth: queued kernel invocations waiting on scheduler slot
   - kernel_handoff_count: number of handoffs between kernels/plugins during a request
3) KV / model caching signals
   - kvcache_hit_rate: ratio of requests served from KV cache
   - kvcache_warmup_time: average time to populate cache after model swap or scale event
4) Request surface & fidelity signals
   - observed_brevity: fraction of responses truncated due to eviction or timeout
   - model_variant_switch_rate: rate of runtime fallback to lower-fidelity variants
5) Cost-correlated aggregates
   - token_cost_rate: modeled $/token over 1m windows (see cost-model section)
   - excess_gpu_hours: measured GPU-hours above steady-state baseline

Signal → Cost mapping (annotated table):
Note: This table is intended to be human-readable. For programmatic mapping, see the appendix sample SQL/PromQL.

| Observability Signal | Immediate Cost Impact | How to interpret | Primary Owner | Escalation owner |
|----------------------|-----------------------|------------------|---------------|------------------|
| gpu_steal_pct > 5% (5m) | Excess GPU-hours due to preemption (retries + lower throughput) | Often caused by noisy neighbor or infra reclaim | infra-fleet (eng-infra) | eng-sre-oncall |
| kernel_latency_p99 increase by > 2x (30m) | Increased tail latency -> client-side retries -> higher token_cost_rate | Could be kernel regression or scheduler congestion | serving-runtime (eng) | runtime-incident-lead |
| kvcache_hit_rate < 70% (5m) | Increased per-request compute -> higher unit cost | May indicate cache invalidation after deploy or model swap | runtime-caching (eng) | eng-platform |
| model_variant_switch_rate spike | Switches to cheaper variants may hide SLO regressions but lower revenue/quality | Intentional during degradation, but unexpected spikes indicate routing misconfig | routing-and-fallbacks (eng) | product-ops |
| host_mem_pressure sustained | Node-level OOMs, increased evictions, workload redistribution -> excess infra spend | Investigate recent deploys, container limits | node-ops (eng-infra) | eng-sre |

Ownership roster (quick reference):
- serving-runtime (primary): Hannah Chen, Arjun Patel
- infra-fleet (primary): Miguel Ortega
- runtime-caching (primary): Priya Natarajan
- routing-and-fallbacks (primary): Carlos Vega
- eng-sre (escalation/human ops): Devon Brooks
- product-ops (business impact): Maya Singh

Alert thresholds and rationale (recommended starting points):
- gpu_steal_pct (5m avg) >= 5% -> Severity: P2. Rationale: sustained steal causes throughput loss across tenants; triage within 30m.
- kernel_latency_p99 (per-model) >= baseline * 2 for 30m -> Severity: P1 (if traffic > 5% of production) or P2 otherwise.
- kvcache_hit_rate drop >= 15 percentage points for 10m -> Severity: P2.
- model_variant_switch_rate > 3x baseline and > 0.5% absolute -> Severity: P2 (investigate misrouting or rollout).

Sample triage runbook (first 30 minutes):
1) On alert, capture current window traces and the following dashboards: kernel-latency-per-model, gpu-util-and-steal, kvcache-heatmap, routing-variant-metrics.
2) Run quick attribution queries:
   - PromQL: avg_over_time(gpu_steal_pct[10m]) by (node)
   - SQL: SELECT model, count(*) as requests, avg(kernel_latency_p99) FROM traces WHERE ts >= now() - interval '10 minutes' GROUP BY model ORDER BY requests DESC LIMIT 20;
3) If kernel_latency_p99 is elevated and confined to a subset of models: tag the suspect model(s) and check recent model-rollout commits and quantization profiles.
4) If gpu_steal_pct is high across nodes: check cloud provider preemption events, node autoscaler logs, and recent infra changes.
5) If kvcache_hit_rate is low across many models: verify kvcache warmup logs, recent cache eviction policies, and any config change in cache TTLs.
6) Document findings in the incident ticket and implement temporary mitigations (scale out read cache nodes, pin model variants, shift traffic) before long-term fix.

Cost model quick reference (how signals feed $):
- token_cost_rate = base_token_cost * (1 + kernel_overhead_factor + retry_factor)
- excess_gpu_hours = sum_over_nodes(steal_pct * node_gpu_capacity * window_hours)
Example calculation (pseudocode):
  base_token_cost = $0.0000005
  kernel_overhead_factor = kernel_latency_p50 / baseline_p50 - 1
  retry_factor = observed_retries / successful_requests
  token_cost_rate = base_token_cost * (1 + kernel_overhead_factor + retry_factor)

Configuration table (what to hook up where):
| Signal Name | Collector | Typical retention | Dashboard | Alert channel |
|-------------|-----------|-------------------|-----------|---------------|
| gpu_steal_pct | node-exporter + agent | 30d (raw), 90d (rollups) | infra/gpu/steal | #infra-ops (PagerDuty P2) |
| kernel_latency_p99 | trace-collector (open-telemetry) | 90d (indexes), 365d (samples) | runtime/kernel/latency | #runtime-oncall (PagerDuty P1/P2) |
| kvcache_hit_rate | metrics-proxy | 60d | runtime/cache/hit-rate | #runtime-oncall |
| model_variant_switch_rate | routing-metrics | 90d | routing/variant-switches | #product-ops (notify) |

Signal enrichment examples (useful tags):
- model=*, model_version=*, kernel_name=*, node=*, tenant_id=*, request_path=*, quant_profile=*

Sample PromQL / SQL snippets (copy-paste friendly):
- PromQL: topk(10, sum by (model) (increase(kernel_exec_count[10m]) * increase(kernel_latency_sum[10m]) / increase(kernel_exec_count[10m])))
- SQL (clickhouse-like):
  SELECT model, percentileExact(0.99)(kernel_latency_ms) AS p99, count() AS requests
  FROM traces
  WHERE ts >= now() - INTERVAL 15 MINUTE
  GROUP BY model
  ORDER BY p99 DESC
  LIMIT 50;

Runbook: when to escalate to runtime-incident-lead (P1 path):
1) Any kernel_latency_p99 regression for a model responsible for >5% of token_cost_rate for >30 minutes.
2) A sudden cross-tenant spike in gpu_steal_pct causing >10% throughput degradation across multiple tenants.
3) Sustained kvcache mass-invalidations affecting >10 models and causing >20% token_cost_rate increase.

Ownership & playbook contact matrix (condensed):
- infra-fleet: node preemptions, GPU allocations, cloud autoscaler interactions. Contact: @Miguel Ortega, #infra-ops.
- serving-runtime: kernel performance, scheduler policies, per-model kernel regressions. Contact: @Hannah Chen, #runtime-oncall.
- runtime-caching: kvcache policies, TTLs, cache node scaling. Contact: @Priya Natarajan, #runtime-cache.
- routing-and-fallbacks: model variant routing, canary logic, fallback mapping. Contact: @Carlos Vega, #routing.

Rollout checklist for new kernel or scheduler change:
1) Preflight: 72h synthetic run with representative traffic (see synthetic-corpus-runbook).
2) Canary: 0.5% traffic for 2h, collect kernel_latency_p50/p95/p99, gpu_steal_pct.
3) Observe: no p99 regression > 1.3x baseline and no increase in gpu_steal_pct > 2 percentage points.
4) Gradual ramp: 5% -> 25% -> 100% with automated abort if any alert fires.
5) Post-mortem: mandatory if any alert triggered during rollout.

Appendix A — Example incident timeline (realistic condensed case):
- 10:03: Alert: kernel_latency_p99 for model X increased 2.8x (30m window). PagerDuty P1 triggered.
- 10:06: Oncall collects traces; finds kernel_handoff_count spike that correlates with a new kernel plugin rollout.
- 10:14: Mitigation: rollback new plugin for model X. p99 returns to baseline by 10:22.
- 10:45: Post-incident owner: serving-runtime. Root cause: plugin introduced unexpected lock in KV prefetch path.

Appendix B — Glossary (short):
- kernel_handoff: an executed context switch between kernel implementations or accelerator adapters during a single request.
- gpu_steal: cycles lost due to preemption/reclamation or other system-level scheduling.
- kvcache: prefix/KV cache used to avoid recomputing model context.

Notes and future work:
- Integrate a machine-readable mapping (YAML/JSON) into the alerts pipeline so that runbooks are surfaced in the alert payload.
- Build a cost-attribution job that regularly computes token_cost_rate and posts to the cost dashboard.
- Add correlation widgets in dashboards that join traces to infra events (node reboots, preemption).

Related resources:
- runtime/kernel-telemetry-annotation-guidelines (team-wiki)
- runtime-oncall-playbook (runbooks)
- synthetic-corpus-runbook (benchmarking suite)

If you find gaps in ownership or unclear signal definitions, please open a ticket with label "observability:signal-mapping" and tag @Hannah Chen for triage.

title: Runtime Experiment Scorecard and Telemetry SLA
content:
Summary
-------
This document defines a unified experiment scorecard and a minimal telemetry SLA for runtime experiments, kernel-level canaries, and benchmark-driven rollouts. It bridges architecture, kernel scheduling, profiling, benchmarking, release gating, and on-call runbooks so that engineers and SREs can run reproducible experiments with clear pass/fail criteria.

Scope
-----
- Applies to: runtime feature experiments, kernel variant canaries, quantization rollouts, and model-variant A/B tests run in hosted and dedicated deployments.
- Excludes: user-facing product A/B tests unrelated to inference runtime behavior.

Why this exists
----------------
We observed variability between bench microbenchmarks and live traffic (tail latency regressions, subtle token-cost changes, KV-cache warmup differences). That undermines rollouts. The scorecard + telemetry SLA ensures experiments have signal fidelity, observability, and clear remediation steps.

Scorecard: pass/fail axes
------------------------
Each experiment run must record a scorecard. Minimum axes (all numeric, reported at 99th, 95th, and mean as indicated):

1) Latency (ms)
   - p99 latency vs baseline (target: <= +5% delta)
   - p95 latency vs baseline (target: <= +3% delta)
   - mean latency (target: <= +2% delta)
2) Throughput (req/s)
   - Sustained throughput under canonical load (target: >= 98% of baseline)
3) Token unit cost (USD/token or internal cost units)
   - Per-token cost change (target: <= +4% delta)
4) Failure rate (5xx/timeout)
   - Error rate (target: < 0.1% absolute increase)
5) Kernel preemption count / backpressure events
   - Absolute counts and rate per 10k requests (target: no increase beyond historical 95th percentile)
6) KV-cache hit rate and cold-start warmup curve
   - Hit-rate curve and time-to-90%-steady-state (target: within baseline envelope)
7) Quality-relevant regressions (output-level metrics, tying to evaluation harness)
   - BLEU/ROUGE/embedding-sim delta or application-specific eval set pass rate (target: no regression beyond alert threshold)

Each axis is graded as: pass / warn / fail with a short rationale field. The final decision is: fail if any axis is fail OR more than two axes are warn.

Telemetry SLA (minimal contract)
--------------------------------
The experiment telemetry must be available in the canonical observability stack within the following windows:
- Metrics (timeseries): within 1 minute of generation.
- Traces (sampled detailed traces): available in trace storage within 5 minutes.
- Kernel-level events (preempt, handoff, slot-abort): ingested and queryable within 30 minutes.
- Bench artifacts (microbench outputs, raw traces, sample payloads): uploaded to experiment object store within 1 hour.

Required telemetry labels/tags (schema)
- experiment_id: string
- run_id: string
- kernel_variant: string
- model_variant: string
- node_pool: {dedicated, hosted, private} (string)
- kvcache_epoch: integer (stringified)
- sequence_length_bucket: {short, medium, long} (string)
- traffic_cohort: string

Example metric naming conventions (timeseries)
- runtime.latency.p99.{kernel_variant}.{model_variant}
- runtime.kvcache.hit_rate.{node_pool}.{sequence_length_bucket}
- runtime.kernel.preempt.count.{kernel_variant}
- runtime.cost.per_token.{model_variant}

Experiment orchestration (procedural checklist)
------------------------------------------------
1) Define hypothesis and scorecard (owner: experiment author).
2) Register experiment in experiment ledger with experiment_id and target cohorts.
3) Provision canary capacity (node_pool and kernel_variant pinned) and record kernel_variant metadata.
4) Run synthetic benchmark (bench harness) for at least N=3 sustained loops; collect microbench metrics.
5) Shadow traffic or low-percentage real traffic for 24 hours (or N requests if traffic low).
6) Collect telemetry and compute scorecard axes.
7) If pass, promote to wider canary (30% traffic) and repeat step 6 for 48 hours.
8) If pass again, initiate rollout with staged increments and continuous monitoring.
9) If any stage fails, follow rollback runbook immediately.

Benchmarking harness: minimum requirements
----------------------------------------
Table: harness config (as a simple ASCII table)

| key                     | expected value / example                             | rationale |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------|-----------|
| workload_profile        | conversational-chat, short-completion, reranking      | cover common shapes |
| request_rate            | synthetic: 100–200 RPS per node; canary: mirror live  | stress check |
| sequence_length_dist    | short: 1–32, medium: 33–256, long: 257+              | bucket coverage |
| replication_factor      | 3                                                  | reduce sample noise |
| telemetry_sampling_rate | 100% metrics, 10% traces, 1% full kernel traces      | cost tradeoff |
| run_duration           | microbench: 15m; full: 24h                          | warmup capture |

Benchmark outputs (artifacts)
- summary.json (scorecard axes, percentiles)
- traces.tar.gz (sampled traces mapped to requests)
- microbench.csv (per-run detailed timings)
- kernel_events.log (preempt/handoff records)

Kernel scheduling considerations for experiments
------------------------------------------------
- Avoid mixing kernel variants with very different preemption semantics in the same node pool during an experiment. This creates hard-to-interpret backpressure signals.
- When testing preemptive kernel variants, include a control cohort pinned to a non-preemptive kernel to differentiate scheduler-side artifacts from upstream workload variability.
- Record kernel credit accounting deltas and slot occupancy histograms. These must be included in the scorecard telemetry.

Profiling playbook (quick-action steps)
--------------------------------------
1) Detect: anomaly triage starts when p99 latency delta > +8% or error rate delta > +0.2%.
2) Collect: increase trace sampling for experiment_id to 100% for 10 minutes and trigger immediate kernel_events collection.
3) Snapshot: create a bench snapshot (replay corpus of 10k requests captured from canary).
4) Isolate: replicate offending workload in sandbox with a 1:1 traffic replay. Capture GPU occupancy, kernel latencies, preempt counts.
5) Hypothesize: use heap map and NVLink counters to check for interconnect or memory-copy hotspots.
6) Mitigate: throttle offending traffic cohort or fallback to baseline kernel_variant.
7) Remediate: iterate on kernel parameter, or revert rollout; document in the experiment ledger.

Sample CLI snippets
-------------------
- Run bench harness:
  
  ./bench-runner --experiment-id exp-2025-0423 --profile conversational-chat --rps 150 --duration 15m --output ./artifacts/exp-2025-0423/

- Increase trace sampling for experiment:
  
  rb-control telemetry set-sampling --experiment exp-2025-0423 --traces 100 --duration 10m

- Pull kernel events for run:
  
  rb-control events fetch --run exp-2025-0423 --type kernel_events --out kernel_events.log

Release gating and rollbacks
-----------------------------
Release gates are evaluated against the scorecard and telemetry SLA. Gate rules:
- Canary -> 30% -> wide rollout. Each gate requires: telemetry SLA met, scorecard pass, no outstanding high-severity known issues.
- Automatic rollback triggers:
  - p99 latency regression > 12% sustained for 10 minutes
  - error-rate increase > 0.5% absolute sustained for 5 minutes
  - kernel preemption rate spike beyond 5x baseline with correlated tail-latency increase

Known issues to monitor during experiments
-----------------------------------------
- KV-cache cold-start nonlinearity: some large-context workloads exhibit long tail warmup spikes. Mitigation: pre-warm cache with shadow traffic and set warmup threshold in deployment config.
- Slot-abort cascade under microburst: certain scheduler configurations can trigger cascading slot aborts, visible as short-lived error bursts. Mitigation: admission-controller smoothing and burst token bucket.
- NVLink blips impacting cross-GPU attention kernels: monitor nvlink_retransmit_rate metric and correlate with kernel latency. Mitigation: fall back to single-GPU execution for affected kernels.

Runbooks (links to actionable pages)
-----------------------------------
- Immediate rollback runbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-upgrade-validation-and-canary-matrix-2026.json
- Kernel preemption investigation: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/priority-inversion-detection-and-mitigation-playbook-2026.json

Owner and escalation
--------------------
- Experiment owner: author listed in experiment registration (primary contact).
- Runtime oncall: first escalation for perf regressions.
- Kernel scheduler engineering: secondary escalation for kernel-level anomalies.

Appendix: artifact examples
--------------------------
Example summary.json (minimal):

{
  "experiment_id": "exp-2025-0423",
  "run_id": "r1",
  "latency": {"p99": 152.3, "p95": 83.1, "mean": 31.4},
  "kvcache": {"hit_rate": 0.86, "time_to_90": 420},
  "kernel_preempt_count": 23
}

Contact and ownership
---------------------
For questions or to propose changes to the scorecard or telemetry SLA, open a PR against this doc and notify reviewers. For operational exceptions, request a documented exception with a proposed compensating control from runtime SRE.

Revision history
----------------
- 2024-04-15: initial draft (Asha Mehta)
- 2024-09-02: added kernel-event ingestion SLA and sample naming conventions (Ethan Park)
- 2025-11-02: tightened canary gating thresholds and added CLI snippets (Sofia Ruiz)

title: Cross-Layer Execution Audit & Escalation Playbook
content:
Purpose
This playbook defines a repeatable cross-layer audit and escalation process for execution anomalies that cross scheduler, kernel, runtime, and networking boundaries. It is intended for oncall engineers and runtime owners who need to triage incidents impacting latency, correctness, or cost SLOs.

Scope
- Applies to hosted, dedicated, and private deployments managed by the runtime.
- Covers anomalies that cannot be diagnosed from a single layer (for example: a spike in p95 latency that coincides with increased kernel queue depth and model variant swaps).
- Does not replace single-service runbooks; it coordinates them.

Summary of responsibilities
- First responder: serving-runtime oncall (primary).
- Secondary: kernel-scheduler team.
- Tertiary: infra/networking team (for cross-host or NVLink issues).
- Communication: SRE/incident commander if SLO impact > 30 minutes or customer escalation.

Key SLOs & alert thresholds (reference)
- p95 request latency (inference): 150 ms (alert at 200 ms sustained for 5m).
- error rate (5xx): 0.5% (alert at 1% sustained for 5m).
- GPU kernel queue depth: baseline varies by family, critical if > 90th historical quantile and rising.
- KV-cache warmness: < 80% warm triggers quality-check pipeline.

High-level investigation flow (quick checklist)
1. Confirm scope and impact
   - Confirm if the issue is global, per-region, or per-tenant. Use:
     - Dashboard: "Per-region latency by model"
     - PromQL: sum by(region) (increase(request_duration_seconds_bucket{job=\"runtime\"}[5m]))
2. Capture short-term forensic snapshot (first 10 minutes)
   - Collect traces, scheduler telemetry, kernel metrics, and node-level system stats.
   - Commands:
     - redwoodctl trace fetch --start "-15m" --filter "service:runtime" --limit 1000 > /tmp/trace-snapshot.json
     - redwoodctl telemetry slice --metric kernel.queue_depth --start "-15m" --end "now" --out /tmp/kqueue.json
     - kubectl top node --heapster > /tmp/node-top.txt
3. Correlate signals across layers
   - Match trace IDs across: API gateway -> request router -> runtime dispatcher -> kernel trace.
   - Look for common request attributes (model, sequence length, prompt size, routing policy).
4. Run quick hypotheses (examples)
   - Hypothesis A: a bad model variant rollout increased token compute. Verify: sudden rise in tokens-per-request and kernel time per token.
     - Query: rate(runtime_tokens_processed_total[1m]) by(model_variant)
   - Hypothesis B: NVLink degradation increased cross-host transfer time. Verify: network egress/intra-node bandwidth and per-GPU pci errors.
     - Query: increase(node_network_transmit_bytes_total[5m]) and dmesg /var/log/kern.log for NVLink errors.
   - Hypothesis C: Scheduler starvation from a noisy tenant. Verify: kernel slot accounting and priority debt.
     - Query: runtime_scheduler_priority_debt_seconds{tenant=~".*"}

Detailed collection recipes (what to collect and where)
- Trace artifacts (store under /incident/<INC_ID>/traces): JSON traces from redwoodctl, full headers for 10 representative requests (p95/p99).
- Kernel telemetry (store under /incident/<INC_ID>/kernel): kernel.latency.histogram, kernel.queue_depth, kernel.context_switches, kernel.kv_prefetch_hits.
- Scheduler logs (store under /incident/<INC_ID>/scheduler): admission decisions, preempt events, slot allocations for last 30 minutes. Sample collector:
  - redwoodctl scheduler dump --since "-30m" --format json > /incident/$INC_ID/scheduler_dump.json
- Node diagnostics (store under /incident/<INC_ID>/nodes): nvidia-smi topo, nvlink status, gpu temperatures, dmesg. Commands:
  - nvidia-smi topo --matrix > /incident/$INC_ID/gpu-topo.txt
  - nvidia-smi --query-gpu=temperature.gpu,utilization.gpu,memory.used --format=csv -l 1 -f /incident/$INC_ID/gpu-sample.csv & (stop after capture window)

PromQL / Metrics recipes (copy-paste)
- P95 latency (approx): histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(runtime_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, model))
- Kernel queue depth by shard: sum(rate(kernel_queue_depth_total[1m])) by (shard_id)
- Preempt events: increase(runtime_preempt_events_total[5m])
- KV-cache hit ratio: sum(runtime_kvcache_hits_total) / sum(runtime_kvcache_requests_total)

Escalation matrix and decision rules
- Tier 1 (oncall): can resolve in 30–60 minutes with runbook actions (restart kernel shard, adjust admission knobs).
- Tier 2 (kernel-scheduler): escalate if root cause points to kernel regressions, fairness policy violation, or kernel-level resource leaks.
- Tier 3 (infra/hardware): escalate for NVLink, host-level memory pressure, or cloud provider networking incidents.
- Emergency (exec + customer success): if customer-facing SLA breach > 1 hour or sensitive customer data impacted.

Safe remediation actions (ordered, low-risk -> high-risk)
1. Reroute to a healthy model variant or region via routing policy (no restart).
2. Adjust admission controller temporary thresholds: reduce burst admission for noisy tenants.
   - Example: redwoodctl admission set --tenant noisy-tenant --max-burst 0.5
3. Restart a kernel shard (graceful): follow runtime shard restart checklist (drain, snapshot KV-cache if needed, warm start).
   - Command: redwoodctl shard restart --shard-id shard-17 --graceful
4. Rollback recent kernel patch (Tier 2 involvement).
5. Full node recycle (Tier 3) for hardware-linked anomalies.

Post-incident tasks (within 24–72 hours)
- Runbook update: add the exact reproduction steps and any new queries that were useful.
- Regression test: add a synthetic test to the benchmark suite covering the failing scenario (e.g., long-context small-batch tails).
- RCA: owner writes a concise RCA and assigns follow-up tickets with owners and SLA for fixes.
- SLA customer comms: coordinate with Customer Success for affected accounts.

Example incident timeline (template)
- 00:00 — Alert triggers: p95 > 200 ms for 12m.
- 00:03 — Oncall collects traces and kernel telemetry snapshot.
- 00:12 — Correlation found: model-variant v2 rollout coincident with token/time-per-token increase.
- 00:18 — Remediation: rollback model-variant and reduce admission for v2.
- 00:25 — Latency returns to baseline.
- 00:55 — Postmortem scheduled; artifacts uploaded to /incidents/INC-1234.

Quality gates and bench additions (for product/bench team)
- Add a benchmark that mirrors the incident: sequence-length distribution, per-tenant concurrency, and small-batch microbursts.
- Add kernel-level fuzz tests for queue-depth edgecases.

Templates and copyable snippets
- Incident folder naming: /incidents/INC-<YYYYMMDD>-<short-tag>
- Redaction checklist before sharing logs externally: remove Authorization headers, PII from prompts, customer IDs.

Ownership matrix (who does what)
- Oncall (serving-runtime): initial triage, trace collection, safe remediations.
- Kernel-scheduler: kernel telemetry interpretation, kernel rollbacks, scheduler policy updates.
- Infra: hardware health, NVLink, node-level diagnostics.
- Bench/product: add regression tests and synthetic workloads to prevent reoccurrence.

Appendix A — Useful queries and sample JSON
- Example PromQL for noisy-tenant detection: topk(10, sum by(tenant) (rate(runtime_request_duration_seconds_count[5m])))
- Example trace-filter (redwoodctl syntax): redwoodctl trace fetch --filter 'span.service:\"kernel\" AND error:true' --start '-30m'
- Example minimal trace JSON snippet: {
  \"trace_id\": \"abcd1234\",
  \"spans\": [
    {
      \"id\": \"s1\",
      \"service\": \"api-gateway\",
      \"duration_ms\": 12
    },
    {
      \"id\": \"s2\",
      \"service\": \"runtime-dispatch\",
      \"duration_ms\": 85
    },
    {
      \"id\": \"s3\",
      \"service\": \"kernel\",
      \"duration_ms\": 320
    }
  ]
}

Related runbooks and playbooks

title: Runtime Debt Playbook and Remediation Roster
content:
Summary:
This playbook centralizes identification, scoring, and remediation of persistent technical debt affecting the serving runtime. It is intended to be actionable: each roster item contains an owner, reproducible test, remediation steps, CI/observability gates, and verification criteria. Use this document as the single source for planning debt sprints and for informing SRE/incident prioritization.

Audience and scope:
- Audience: runtime engineers, SREs, program managers, and product owners who approve runtime changes.
- Scope: core runtime components (dispatcher, scheduler-agent, kernel-coordinator, slot-synth, kv-cache shards, observer-collector). Excludes client SDKs, documentation debt outside runtime, and infra account billing items.

Taxonomy and risk model:
- Taxonomy: Code debt, Test/CI debt, Observability debt, Operational process debt, Data/migration debt.
- Risk model: compute a numeric score (1-25) = Severity x Exposure x Reproducibility, where each factor is 1-5.
  - Severity: SLO impact if left unresolved (1 low - 5 catastrophic).
  - Exposure: percent of traffic or customers affected (1 <1% - 5 >50%).
  - Reproducibility: how easy it is to trigger in test (1 hard - 5 trivial).
- Priority bands: Low 1-6, Medium 7-12, High 13-18, Critical 19-25.

Remediation lifecycle (required for every roster item):
1) Triage: Owner documents symptoms, evidence, and a minimal reproducible case.
2) Scoring: Owner assigns Severity, Exposure, Reproducibility and computes score.
3) Plan: Author a remediation plan with an estimate (Quick, Small, Medium, Large), rollback plan, and validation checklist.
4) PR & CI: Changes must include unit tests, an integration test where feasible, and a CI job tag referencing this roster item.
5) Shadow & Canary: For High/Critical items, run 24-72h shadow traffic followed by staged canary rollouts (5% -> 25% -> 100%) with automated rollback criteria.
6) Close: Owner posts retrospective, updates the roster status to Resolved, and records measured SLO/cost impact.

Verification and gating requirements (minimum):
- Unit and integration coverage for modified code paths.
- New or extended metrics and an alert (metric, baseline, threshold, window).
- A synthetic reproducible harness entry in the benchmarking suite for items that affect latency or throughput.
- Post-deploy check: 72h shadow or mirrored run for High/Critical items, compare p50/p95/p99 and cost per token to baseline.

Remediation roster (examples):
- ID: ROSTER-101
  Title: Asymmetric kvcache invalidation after point-upgrade
  Component: kv-cache shards
  Owner: Lena Zhou
  Created: 2025-01-15
  Status: open
  Risk score: 17
  Symptoms: Some shard nodes show kvcache_miss_spike after staggered kafka replays; affected routes show p99 increases for 30-90 minutes.
  Repro steps: Controlled rolling upgrade on staging with staggered restart and synthetic multi-turn traces.
  Remediation plan: Stabilize invalidation protocol, persist prefetch hints, and add a graceful drain handshake between dispatcher and shard.
  CI gates: Integration test simulating staggered restarts; metric kvcache_hit_rate must not drop >10% in test.
  Validation: 48h shadow and a 3-stage canary.

- ID: ROSTER-112
  Title: Priority inversion under mixed short/long requests
  Component: scheduler-agent
  Owner: Ravi Patel
  Created: 2025-06-02
  Status: in_progress
  Risk score: 20
  Symptoms: Under sustained mixed traffic, low-latency workload p99 balloons due to long-running batches delaying preemption.
  Repro steps: Mixed-workload harness that sends 1:5 ratio of short:long requests at sustained qps.
  Remediation plan: Implement preemptive batch slicing and a credit rebalancer; introduce backpressure signals from kernel-coordinator.
  CI gates: New scheduler simulator regression tests, end-to-end latency lab.
  Validation: Shadow two production routes for 72h, expect p99 reduction >30% for short requests.

- ID: ROSTER-123
  Title: Kernel plugin lifecycle leak (third-party accelerators)
  Component: kernel-coordinator
  Owner: Marco Delgado
  Created: 2025-08-10
  Status: backlog
  Risk score: 12
  Symptoms: Memory growth on nodes using experimental accelerator plugin after repeated model loads.
  Repro steps: Repeated model load/unload loop on testbed with mixed quantization variants.
  Remediation plan: Add reference counting to plugin lifecycle and defensive cleanup paths; add integration test in plugin sandbox.
  CI gates: Plugin sandbox memory regression test.
  Validation: No growth over 48h soak in canary.

- ID: ROSTER-137
  Title: Dispatcher GRPC channel reuse policy causes short-lived connection thrash
  Component: dispatcher
  Owner: Ava Martinez
  Created: 2025-11-01
  Status: open
  Risk score: 14
  Symptoms: Connection churn and brief spikes in CPU during microbursts.
  Repro steps: Burst traffic harness and connection churn monitor.
  Remediation plan: Implement connection pooling and tuned keepalive/backoff; add stress test to burst harness.
  CI gates: Stress test with connection churn metric reduced by >= 70%.
  Validation: Canary with burst simulation in production shadow channel.

Operational playbook for items that cause incidents:
- Immediate action: If a roster item is implicated in an SLO breach or incident, mark it P0 and trigger an incident review; assign a short remediation runway (hotfix or mitigation) with an SRE owner.
- Communication: Notify Customer Success and affected customers within the incident timeline if the issue is user-visible.
- Follow up: Add remediation item to next sprint and track completion in retrospective.

Dashboards and queries (examples to copy into Grafana/BigQuery):
- kvcache_hit_rate_by_shard: SELECT shard, avg(kvcache_hit) FROM runtime_metrics WHERE job='kvcache' AND time > now() - 1h GROUP BY shard
- scheduler_pending_credit_balance: derive credit imbalance and alert when > 80th percentile for 10m.
- connection_churn_rate: rate(grpc_conn_create_total[1m]) by dispatcher_zone

Quarterly KPIs and reporting:
- Publish a quarterly debt report with: open items by priority band, average time to remediation, observed SLO improvement post-remediation, estimated cost delta.
- Target: reduce Critical items by 40% QoQ until Critical <= 3.

Templates and checklist (copy into Jira ticket or PR):
- Summary, Repro steps, Benchmark harness name, Risk score, Remediation steps, Validation checklist (unit/integration/shadow/canary), Rollback criteria, Observability changes (metrics/alerts), Related runbooks, Owner.

Appendix: example rollback criteria (must be machine-readable in deploy system):
- If p99 latency on route X > baseline * 1.5 for 10m, rollback.
- If kvcache_hit_rate drops > 15% for 30m after change, rollback.

Contacts and ownership roster:
- Runtime tech lead: Ava Martinez (ava.martinez@redwood.ai)
- SRE liaison: Diego Rivera (diego.rivera@redwood.ai)
- Program manager: Sasha Novak (sasha.novak@redwood.ai)
- General runtime channel: runtime-team@redwood.ai

Change log:
- 2025-04-02: Playbook created and baseline roster seeded.
- 2025-06-03: Added ROSTER-112 and updated scoring guidance.
- 2025-11-02: Added dispatcher connection churn entry.
- 2026-02-10: Updated gating requirements and verification checklist.

End of document.

title: Lighthouse Serving Roundtable: Rollout Readiness Checklist (Canary A / Quantized v2)
content:
## Overview
This page standardizes what we review in the Lighthouse Serving Roundtable before changing the Canary A rollout percentage for the quantized v2 serving path. It is intended to keep the weekly discussion focused on decision-quality inputs: customer impact risk, capacity readiness, instrumentation coverage, and rollback safety.

This document replaces ad-hoc personal prep notes and should be used as the pre-read template for the roundtable thread.

---

## Meeting format
**Cadence:** Weekly (Tuesday) 30 minutes

**Expected attendees:**
- Serving runtime core
- Infrastructure (capacity / cluster)
- Console (route configuration / UX)
- SRE on-call (rota)
- Product PM (as needed for release gating)

**Primary goal:** Make (or defer) a clear decision to (a) proceed to the next canary step, (b) hold at current %, or (c) roll back.

---

## Scope
**In scope**
- Canary A (quantized v2) rollout readiness and gating checks
- High-risk regressions that could change rollout decisions (latency tail, error rates, warm-start behavior)
- Fallback policy configuration for route-level safety

**Out of scope**
- Deep debugging during the 30-minute slot (schedule a dedicated 60-minute deep dive with traces/logs preloaded)

---

## Current rollout target
- **Release target:** Serving Runtime **0.9.3** (updated from earlier 0.9.2 plan)
- **Canary stream:** Canary A (quantized v2)
- **Proposed next step:** 10% → 25% (only if all gates below are met)

---

## Decision gates (must pass to increase canary percentage)
### 1) Customer impact gates
Proceed only if all are true for the last 24 hours in each primary region (at minimum: us-west-2, us-east-1):
- **p99 latency:** ≤ **900 ms** for small-sequence workloads (median ~128 tokens) OR no more than **+20%** versus float32 control on matched traffic.
- **Error rate (5xx + timeouts):** ≤ **0.30%** and not increasing week-over-week.
- **Retry rate:** no anomalous increases attributable to quantized path.

Notes:
- The p99 tail is the primary customer-risk metric. If p99 is above gate but p50/p95 are healthy, treat as a hold condition and require a concrete remediation plan.

### 2) Capacity gates (Infra/SRE)
- Confirm **≥ 20% spare capacity** in the dedicated canary pool for the full rollout window.
- Confirm an **emergency scale** procedure is on-call owned and tested within the last 30 days.
- Confirm cluster autoscaling safeguards do not conflict with pinned canary nodes.

### 3) Observability gates (Runtime/SRE)
- 7-day latency histograms are available and reviewed (p50/p95/p99), segmented by:
  - region
  - workload size (short vs long sequences)
  - model variant (quantized v2 vs float32)
- Canary dashboards include:
  - token cost metrics (avg and distribution)
  - memory pressure signals (RSS, OOM events)
  - queueing time vs compute time breakdown
- Alerts exist and are actionable for:
  - p99 latency regression
  - warm-start throughput degradation
  - error rate spikes

### 4) Rollback and fallback gates (Console/Runtime)
- Rollback plan has been reviewed and is executable in **< 15 minutes**.
- Route-level fallback behavior is documented and tested:
  - Manual fallback to float32 variant is validated.
  - Auto-fallback is allowed only if telemetry is sufficient to avoid oscillation (see below).

---

## Known issues and current status
### RED-2147: HTTP/2 p99 latency spike
**Original symptom (observed early March):** p99 for small-seq workloads increased substantially under HTTP/2 traffic.

**Updated status (as of 2026-03-21):**
- Root cause narrowed to an HTTP/2 connection management interaction in the sidecar/proxy path.
- Mitigation implemented via runtime + proxy tuning; fix tracked in **GH PR 497**.
- Current p99 in us-west-2 for the same segment is down from the earlier peak and has been stable over the last 48 hours.

**Roundtable requirement:**
- Mikael (runtime) confirms the fix is in the candidate build for 0.9.3 and shares a short before/after comparison.

### RED-2199: KV cache invalidation after quantized warm-start
**Original symptom:** stalled throughput for multiple minutes after node restart.

**Updated status (as of 2026-03-21):**
- Instrumentation added for warm-start duration and cache rebuild time.
- Throughput drop duration reduced; remaining issue is variance during peak queue depth.

**Roundtable requirement:**
- Priya (runtime) confirms alerting thresholds and links to the dashboard panel used for the gate.

---

## Metrics snapshot (what to include in the roundtable pre-read)
Provide the following bullet summary (one line each) plus links to dashboards:
- **Latency (quantized v2 vs float32):** p50 / p95 / p99, by region
- **Cost:** avg token cost delta (target: negative) and any variance by workload class
- **Errors:** 5xx, timeouts, retries (absolute + change)
- **Stability:** OOMs, restarts, warm-start duration

Recommended one-liner format:
- "Canary A: token cost -20%, p50 +6%, p95 +9%, p99 +14% (stable), error rate 0.18% (flat), no new OOMs."

---

## Fallback policy (route-level)
### Policy intent
Fallback exists to preserve customer experience if the quantized path regresses (tail latency, errors) while limiting churn and avoiding oscillation.

### Current stance (updated)
- **Manual fallback:** Supported and required to be tested each rollout step.
- **Auto-fallback toggle:** Not GA by default until we have:
  1) per-route telemetry surfaced in Console (error/latency deltas), and
  2) a cooldown mechanism to prevent flip-flopping.

### Console requirements
- Add a route-level quick link to canary metrics (dashboard deep link).
- Display the current model variant and canary status on the route page.

Owner: Zara Thompson (Console)

---

## Standard agenda (30 minutes)
1) **Quick wins since last sync (3m)**
   - Each team: one sentence
2) **Incidents / regressions (8m)**
   - RED-2147 HTTP/2 p99 status
   - RED-2199 warm-start/cache status
3) **Rollout readiness decision (10m)**
   - Review decision gates (customer impact, capacity, observability, rollback)
   - Decision: proceed to next step vs hold vs roll back
4) **Console / UX readiness (4m)**
   - Route metrics link status
   - Fallback UI status
5) **Action items & owners (5m)**

---

## Action items template (capture during meeting)
Use this structure in the meeting thread:
- **Decision:** Proceed / Hold / Roll back
- **Actions:**
  - Owner — Deliverable — Due date — Link
- **Customer comms (if needed):** Owner — Audience — When

---

## Current action items (carried forward)
- Omar Ruiz: publish weekly one-pager with p50/p95/p99 graphs + cost delta for Canary A (includes region segmentation). Due: 2026-03-22.
- Mikael Andersson: close out investigation for RED-2147 with fix summary and verification evidence (includes perf traces). Due: 2026-03-24.
- Priya Nair: validate RED-2199 alert thresholds and add runbook link to the alert description. Due: 2026-03-25.
- Zara Thompson: implement route page link to canary metrics and propose copy for fallback controls (manual only for now). Due: 2026-03-26.
- SRE rota: confirm capacity cushion for next canary step and link the emergency scale playbook. Due: 2026-03-22.

---

## References
- Latency response guidance: confluence:serving-runtime/latency-playbook
- Tickets: JIRA:RED-2147, JIRA:RED-2199
- Recent PRs: GH PR 482 (historical graphs), GH PR 497 (current mitigation)

---

## Change log
- 2026-03-13: Created checklist from prior roundtable prep notes.
- 2026-03-18: Updated release target to 0.9.3 and formalized decision gates.
- 2026-03-21: Updated known-issue status and clarified auto-fallback stance pending telemetry.

title: Cohort Latency Heatmap Cookbook and Incident Playbook
content:
Overview

This cookbook describes how we construct, maintain, and operate cohort-level latency heatmaps for the Redwood serving runtime. The document includes: rationale, data collection and aggregation guidance, a canonical generation pipeline, visualization and dashboard conventions, alerting thresholds, and an incident response playbook tied to heatmap signals.

Audience

- Runtime engineers
- SREs responsible for inference SLOs
- Performance and profiling teams

Problem statement and motivation

Tail and cohort-specific latency behavior frequently hide inside aggregate p99 metrics. A heatmap that slices latency by request cohort (e.g., model variant, sequence_length bucket, batch size, customer_tier) gives us a richer signal to:

- Quickly identify emergent hotspots (e.g., a model variant regressions for long sequences)
- Prioritize kernel rollouts and scheduling policy changes by impacted cohorts
- Correlate kernel pressure, kv-cache hit-rate, and GPU occupancy with cohort-level latency shifts

Scope and definitions

- Cohort: a single dimension or combination of dimensions used to group requests. Canonical fields: model_name, model_variant, sequence_length_bucket, batch_size_bucket, customer_tier, route.
- Heatmap cell: distribution summary for a (cohort, latency_bucket, time_bucket) tuple; we store p50/p95/p99 and count.
- Time resolution: default 1m for operational dashboards, 5m for long-term retention.

Prerequisites and telemetry sources

- Traces: request-level spans emitted by runtime-dispatcher and kernel-orchestrator with tags for model_name, variant, seq_len, batch_size, route_id, customer_tier.
- Metrics: Prometheus counters/gauges for kernel_queue_depth, kernel_active_count, gpu_occupancy_percent, kv_cache_hit_ratio, request_count_total by labels.
- Logs: structured JSON request logs (request_id, cohort labels, elapsed_ms, status_code).
- Storage: long-term heatmap aggregates live in the performance-timeseries cluster (Influx/Clickhouse) with 5m rollups.

Canonical cohort bucketing scheme (recommended)

| Field | Buckets | Rationale |
|---|---:|---|
| sequence_length_bucket | 1-32, 33-64, 65-128, 129-256, 257-512, 513+ | Kernel breakpoints and attention memory patterns occur at these ranges |
| batch_size_bucket | 1, 2-4, 5-8, 9-16, 17+ | Shapes typical for interactive vs batch workloads |
| customer_tier | free, standard, enterprise | Routing and capacity policy differences |
| model_variant | base, q8_0, q4_0, distilled | Distillation/quantization affects kernel choice |

Heatmap generation pipeline (end-to-end)

1. Instrumentation: ensure every request writes a short request-level record to the request-log with the canonical labels. Use runtime tracing to populate model and kernel hints.
2. Ingestion: pipeline-job (k8s job: heatmap-ingest) consumes request logs and spans; performs label normalization, applies bucketing rules, and emits per-minute aggregates: count, p50, p95, p99, sum.
3. Storage: write per-minute aggregates into performance-timeseries cluster using keys: ts, model, variant, seq_bucket, batch_bucket, tier, route.
4. Rollup: a scheduled job performs 5m/30m/1h rollups and computes historical baselines (7d median and 28d median) for each cohort.
5. Visualization: Grafana dashboard 'Cohort Latency Heatmap (runtime)' renders a timeseries heatmap using p95 latency with cohort on Y axis, time on X axis.
6. Alerting: apply anomaly detectors on per-cohort p95 and on the delta-from-baseline metric (see alert thresholds).

Prometheus & Clickhouse queries (examples)

- PromQL (short-term):
  - p95 latency for a specific cohort (1m): histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_latency_bucket{model_name="gpt-lite",sequence_length_bucket="65-128"}[1m])) by (le))
- Clickhouse example (aggregation over logs):
  - SELECT toStartOfInterval(timestamp, INTERVAL 1 minute) as t, sequence_length_bucket, quantileExact(0.95)(elapsed_ms) as p95, count() as n FROM request_logs WHERE model_name='gpt-lite' AND t >= now() - INTERVAL 1 DAY GROUP BY t, sequence_length_bucket ORDER BY t ASC

Visualization conventions and dashboard layout

- Single dashboard panel per tenant slice: aggregated (all tiers) + enterprise-only panel.
- Heatmap colors: green (p95 < 200ms), amber (200–500ms), red (>500ms). Use a bivariate tooltip that shows p50/p95/p99 and request count.
- Cohort ordering: stable sort by historical 7d median p95 descending so noisy cohorts float to the top.

Alerting thresholds and incident signal rules

- Severity P1 (Immediate)
  - Rule: any cohort with p95 > 1s AND request_count >= 50 in 1m window OR delta-from-baseline > 250ms sustained for 3 consecutive 1m buckets.
  - Pager duty: on-call runtime-sre 
  - Runbook: follow "Heatmap-P1 runbook" below.

- Severity P2 (Investigate)
  - Rule: cohort p95 between 500–1000ms with request_count >= 20 in 5m window OR delta-from-baseline > 150ms.
  - Slack notify: #runtime-observability

- Noise suppression: ignore cohorts with request_count < 5 in 5m unless the customer_tier==enterprise.

Heatmap-P1 runbook (play-by-play)

1. Acknowledge the alert and open an incident channel in #runtime-incidents with alert details.
2. Pull the heatmap panel and filter to the top-5 cohorts by request_count.

Quick triage checklist (ordered):

1. Is this localized to a single model_variant? If yes, check kernel rollout recent deployments: kernel-orchestrator release history and canary health.
2. Are kernel_queue_depth or kernel_active_count elevated? Prometheus: rate(kernel_queue_length[1m]) and kernel_active_count. If yes, investigate admission controller and scheduling policy EQS.
3. Check kv_cache_hit_ratio for the cohort. A sudden drop often explains long-tail runtime stall due to kv cache warmup.
4. Confirm GPU throttling or thermal events (GPU driver logs + node-exporter gpu_temp, gpu_throttle_count). Thermal-induced slowdowns appear as gradual p95 increase with high GPU occupancy.
5. Correlate with infra events: autoscaler activity, node restart, or AZ/region events.
6. If customer_tier==enterprise and service SLA impacted, page CSM on-call.

Mitigation strategies (fast):

- Immediate fallback: route impacted cohort to a compatible, lower-fidelity model_variant via delta-routing when kernel pressure is observed. See "tiered-fallback-routing-and-eviction-architecture-2026" for config steps.
- Temporary throttling: apply per-route concurrency cap for the cohort to reduce kernel queueing.
- Cache prewarm: trigger async KV prefetch job for the model and sequence length range.
- Evict/scale: if GPU occupancy is saturated and autoscaler has capacity, scale dedicated-pool by +20% and monitor.

Post-incident follow-up (blameless)

- Owner: the on-call who acknowledged the alert must file an incident summary within 48h. The summary must include: impacted cohorts, estimated customer impact, root cause hypothesis, mitigation applied, and recommended changes (patch/observability/runbook update).
- Run an experiment: recreate cohort traffic in the synthetic workload builder and run the profiler-microbench for the implicated kernel path.
- If root cause is a kernel regression, follow the kernel rollback procedure (see kernel-snapshot-observability-contract-2026).

Operational hygiene and scheduled jobs

- Weekly: validate bucket definitions and mapping rules; if model lineup changes add new variant mappings.
- Daily: ingest job health check — ensure no >1% of logs are dropped for the last 24h.
- Monthly: review dashboards and baselines; retire cohorts with <1000 requests/month.

Troubleshooting annex (common patterns)

- Pattern: sudden p95 bump for high sequence buckets only
  - Likely causes: new kernel change that increases memory working set or introduces extra synchronization; KV cache effectiveness drops for long prefixes.
  - Actions: capture a kernel flame trace, compare occupancy and workspace allocation between baseline and current, roll back kernel patch if confirmed.

- Pattern: scattered red cells across many cohorts with high GPU occupancy
  - Likely causes: noisy neighbor or autoscaler insufficient to absorb batch bursts.
  - Actions: inspect scheduler admission logs, review batch-slicing policy, increase burst capacity for Dedicated pools.

Ownership and contacts

- Dashboard owner: runtime-observability team (runtime-observability@redwood.com)
- On-call: runtime-sre rotation (see team roster)
- Kernel escalation: kernel-maintainers@redwood.com

Appendix A — sample heatmap color scheme (Grafana friendly)

- Value mappings: 0-200 -> #2ECC71 (green); 200-500 -> #F1C40F (amber); 500-1000 -> #E67E22 (dark amber); >1000 -> #E74C3C (red).

Appendix B — example heatmap-ingest job config (k8s snippet)

apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: heatmap-ingest
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: heatmap-ingest
        image: gcr.io/redwood/heatmap-ingest:stable
        args: ["--log-source=s3://ingest/request-logs/", "--out-db=clickhouse://perf-ts:9000/heatmaps", "--interval=1m"]
      restartPolicy: OnFailure

Appendix C — related dashboards and runbooks

- Grafana dashboard: Cohort Latency Heatmap (runtime)
- Related runbooks: runtime-deployment-circuit-breakers-and-sla-fallback-playbook-2026, quantization-rollout-safety-and-quality-gate-playbook-2026

Change log

- 2025-02-12: Initial draft and acceptance test harness described.
- 2025-05-03: Added PromQL + Clickhouse examples and rollout mitigations.
- 2026-01-18: Refined alert thresholds and added post-incident follow-up requirements.

End of document.

title: Runtime experiment registry and reproducibility protocol
content:
Summary

This page defines the canonical registry, metadata contract, and execution protocol for all runtime-level experiments at Redwood Inference. It covers experiment registration, required metadata, how to capture and store traces, profiling and benchmarking steps, kernel-scheduler configuration checkpoints, runbook hooks for anomalies, and a release-note template for experiments that affect production runtime behavior.

Why this exists

Teams run many experiments that touch the serving runtime: new kernel rollouts, scheduler-policy changes, KV-cache warmup heuristics, quantization variants, and fallback routing alterations. Without a single registry and reproducible protocol we lose provenance, can’t compare results reliably, and risk unsafe rollouts. This doc is the operational contract for reproducible runtime experimentation.

Scope

- Applies to all experiments that change behavior of services under sources/confluence/eng-serving-runtime (runtime-router, kernel-dispatcher, kv-cache, prefetcher, admission-controller).
- Includes lab runs, canary rollouts, and production toggle experiments.
- Excludes purely model-only experiments (those belong to applied-ml-and-evals/model-onboarding).

Definitions and identifiers

- Experiment ID: EXP-YYYY-NNN (e.g., EXP-2025-042). Unique across the registry.
- Artifact snapshot: git commit + container image digest (sha256).
- Kernel version: runtime kernel semantic tag (e.g., k-2.4.1-hotfix).
- Trace bundle: compressed trace file containing request-level events (trace.jsonl.gz).

Required metadata for registry entry

Every experiment must be registered before execution in the experiments table in the Registry service. Minimum fields:

| Field | Example | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| experiment_id | EXP-2025-042 | Assigned by registry UI/CLI |
| owner | eng-serving-runtime/runtime-team | Team and primary oncall |
| hypothesis | "Reduce p95 by < 10% for short-text gen by enabling kernel-waveform v2" | One-line hypothesis |
| artifacts | repo:infra@abcdef, image:runtime:v2025.09@sha256:... | List of artifact snapshots |
| kernel_version | k-2.4.1-hotfix | Kernel and kernel-extensions |
| quant_flags | q4_0, fp16-cache | Quantization flags used |
| traffic_shape | short-gen:60%, long-gen:40% | Traffic mix for synthetic runs |
| seed_traces | s3://exp-bundles/EXP-2025-042/traces/seed-20250912.jsonl.gz | Location of trace bundle |
| benchmark_suite | evbench-v3 | Name of benchmark harness used |
| rollout_plan | canary-5%-24h -> 25%-48h -> 100% | Rollout steps (if planned) |
| sros | runtime-p95:120ms, runtime-p99:450ms, cpu-util:80% | Target SLOs for the experiment |

Registering an experiment

1. Create registry entry via /internal/experiments API or the Registry UI.
2. Attach artifact snapshots and upload seed trace bundle to S3 using cli:infra exp upload-trace --id EXP-XXXX --file traces/seed.jsonl.gz.
3. Add reviewers and link related playbooks (runbooks or chaos scenarios).

Execution protocol (lab run)

1. Reserve a lab-cluster via infra-tag: runtime-lab-XX for the exact kernel and image.
2. Replay seed traces using the Benchmark Harness (evbench-v3):
   - CLI: evbench run --suite evbench-v3 --trace s3://... --concurrency 8 --out s3://exp-results/EXP-2025-042/
3. Collect traces and profiles:
   - runtime-trace-collector --output /tmp/traces --sample 100%
   - perf-kernel-capture --kernel k-2.4.1-hotfix --out /tmp/kernel-profiles
4. Perform profiling: capture GPU counters, kernel dispatch latencies, KV-cache hit breakdowns.
5. Run the standard benchmark matrix: cold-start (10 retries), warm-start (1000 requests), microbursts (10x peak QPS for 10s).

Kernel-scheduler checkpoint and configuration snapshot

Before making scheduler changes, save a checkpoint record that includes:
- Scheduler policy YAML (scheduler-policy.yaml)
- Priority buckets and token rates
- Admission-controller thresholds (tokens per-second)
- Kernel credit accounting config

Store the checkpoint alongside the experiment under s3://runtime-checkpoints/EXP-YYYY-NNN/. Example snippet (scheduler-policy.yaml):

```yaml
priority_buckets:
  - name: interactive
    weight: 100
    token_rate: 200
  - name: batch
    weight: 20
    token_rate: 20
admission:
  max_concurrent: 250
  preemption_enabled: true
```

Observability checklist (required for canary/production experiments)

- p50/p95/p99 latency dashboards for impacted routes
- Kernel dispatch histogram by request_size and model_variant
- KV-cache hit ratio and warmup curve
- Error budget burn rate alert (notify eng-sre)
- Trace correlation ID consistent between runtime-router and kernel-dispatcher

Runbook hooks and anomaly handling

If any of the following occur during a canary:
- latency p95 > target by > 25% for 10m OR
- error-rate > 0.5% absolute increase OR
- kernel crash rate > 0.1%
Then:
1. Pause rollout and scale down canary traffic to 0% (automatic via admission-controller).
2. Trigger experiment incident: tag EXP-XXXX in incident channel #runtime-incidents.
3. Collect last 1h traces and kernel profiles: infra collect-exp-bundle --id EXP-XXXX --window 60m.
4. Engage oncall (owner listed in metadata) and follow the Incident Triage runbook.

Profiling playbook distilled steps

1. Start a controlled replay with sample rate 100% for 1k requests.
2. Capture: compact traces, nvprof counters, kernel-dispatch latency, scheduler token queues.
3. Annotate traces with kernel_version, scheduler-policy hash, and artifact digest.
4. Run causal-attribution script: tools/causal-attrib --before before.tar.gz --after after.tar.gz --out analysis.json

Benchmark mapping and acceptance criteria

- Map each experiment to at least one benchmark in the central suite (evbench-v3, microburst, tail-latency).
- Acceptance: p95 must not regress > 5% for the primary route; p99 regressions require a manual review and explicit approval.

Known-issues capture and linking

When an experiment surfaces a reproducible issue, create an issue entry in the runtime known-issues board and add the following tags: experiment_id, kernel_version, severity (sev1-3). Example known-issue entry fields: [issue_id, experiment_id, summary, repro_steps, traces, owner, mitigation]. Always link the known-issue id back to the experiment registry entry.

Release notes template for experiments that progress to production

- Title: EXP-YYYY-NNN: <short description>
- Summary: one paragraph
- Impacted services: runtime-router, kernel-dispatcher, kv-cache
- SLO deltas observed in canary: p95 before -> after
- Rollout plan: (same as registry)
- Revert instructions: kubectl rollout undo ...; admission-controller rollback command: infra rollback-exp --id EXP-YYYY-NNN
- Contact: owner (email) and oncall rotation

Retention and provenance

- All experiment artifacts (registry entry, traces, kernel checkpoints, profiles) are retained for 540 days in s3://exp-retention/ by default.
- Ownership: the owner field on registry entry is responsible for clean-up and long-term follow-up.

Appendix: quick CLI reference

- Register: infra exp create --id EXP-2025-042 --owner eng-serving-runtime/runtime-team --hypothesis "..."
- Upload trace: infra exp upload-trace --id EXP-2025-042 --file seed.jsonl.gz 
- Start lab run: infra exp run --id EXP-2025-042 --cluster runtime-lab-03 --suite evbench-v3
- Collect bundle: infra exp collect-bundle --id EXP-2025-042 --out s3://exp-results/EXP-2025-042/bundle.tar.gz

Owners and points of contact

- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime/runtime-team (Aisha Patel)
- SRE: Diane Chen
- Applied ML liaison: Omar Haddad

If you plan an experiment that touches kernel scheduling, profiling, or rollout mechanics, register it here first and follow this protocol end-to-end. This ensures we preserve reproducibility, reduce blast radius, and make results comparable across runs.

title: Kernel Health Index and Oncall Investigation Playbook
content:
Summary:
This page defines the Kernel Health Index (KHI) — a composite signal used to detect regressions and degradation in the serving runtime’s kernel layer — and provides a step-by-step oncall investigation and remediation playbook. The KHI aggregates kernel-level telemetry (latency, error rates, kernel queue lengths, preemption events, and GPU memory pressure) into a single, interpretable score per scheduler cohort. The goal is early, actionable detection with minimal false positives and clear escalation steps.

Why we need KHI:
- Kernels are a frequent choke point for tail latency and cross-tenant interference.
- Single-signal alerts (e.g., p50 token latency) are noisy when mixed workloads or rolling deploys are active.
- KHI provides a stable, cohort-scoped index that surfaces meaningful kernel-level change while preserving correlation to user-visible SLOs.

Scope and ownership:
- Scope: GPU kernel operations and the scheduler/handoff surface inside the runtime (kernel invocation, queueing, preemption, kernel handoff errors, kernel timeouts).
- Owning team: eng-serving-runtime (runtime kernel and scheduling subteams).
- Oncall escalation: runtime oncall -> kernel scheduling rotate -> runtime performance owners.

KHI definition (high level):
- KHI is a normalized, weighted sum of standardized component signals for a cohort and 1-minute window:
  - Latency sensitive kernel tail (K_tail): percentile-based tail of kernel execution time (e.g., 99th percentile of measured kernel time).
  - Kernel error spike score (K_err): count of kernel-level errors (failed launches, launch timeouts) normalized by request volume.
  - Queue pressure index (K_q): average queue length / slot capacity ratio in scheduler queues.
  - Preemption churn (K_preempt): count of preemption events per minute normalized by active kernels.
  - Memory pressure index (K_mem): fraction of kernels that triggered OOM/soft-OOM or elevated allocation/reclaim events.

- Simplified score formula (illustrative):
  KHI = 100 * (0.35*norm(K_tail) + 0.25*norm(K_err) + 0.15*norm(K_q) + 0.15*norm(K_preempt) + 0.10*norm(K_mem))
  where norm(x) maps the raw metric to [0,1] using cohort-specific baseline percentiles (historical 7d median + MAD).

Interpretation buckets:
- KHI < 15: healthy. No action required.
- 15 <= KHI < 40: watch. Add to daily telemetry digest and correlate with SLO deltas.
- 40 <= KHI < 70: alert to oncall. Start triage checklist.
- KHI >= 70: high-priority incident. Execute mitigation matrix and page kernel scheduling owners.

PromQL and query recipes (examples):
- 99th percentile kernel exec time per cohort (example):
  histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(kernel_exec_duration_seconds_bucket{cohort="web-embeddings"}[5m])) by (le, cohort))

- Kernel error spike (5m):
  sum(rate(kernel_launch_errors_total{cohort="web-embeddings"}[5m])) / sum(rate(kernel_invocations_total{cohort="web-embeddings"}[5m]))

- Queue pressure (1m avg):
  avg_over_time(scheduler_queue_length{queue=~"kernel-.*",cohort="web-embeddings"}[1m]) / scheduler_queue_capacity{cohort="web-embeddings"}

- Preemption churn (1m):
  sum(rate(kernel_preemptions_total{cohort="web-embeddings"}[1m])) / max(1, sum(rate(kernel_invocations_total{cohort="web-embeddings"}[1m])))

- Memory pressure (ratio):
  sum(rate(kernel_memory_pressure_events_total{cohort="web-embeddings"}[5m])) / sum(rate(kernel_invocations_total{cohort="web-embeddings"}[5m]))

Alerting rules (recommended thresholds):
- KHI Alert (page): KHI >= 40 for 2m sustained OR KHI delta >= 25 in 5m. Severity: P2 (first responder), escalate to P1 if sustained > 10m or correlated SLO breach.
- Kernel error rate guide: kernel_launch_error_rate > 0.005 (0.5%) sustained 5m -> generate paging alert.
- Queue pressure guide: scheduler_queue_length / capacity > 0.7 for 3m -> fire warning; >0.9 -> page.

Oncall investigation checklist (ordered):
1) Confirm alert and scope
   - Look at KHI time series and cohort tag. Is the spike localized to one cohort or global?
   - Check related SLO dashboards (token latency, request success rate) for correlation.
2) Immediately gather fast artifacts (first 2 minutes)
   - grep or use trace UI to collect 5–20 traces that hit altered kernels.
   - Snapshot kernel metrics: kernel_exec_duration_seconds, kernel_launch_errors_total, scheduler_queue_length, kernel_preemptions_total, kernel_memory_pressure_events_total.
   - Capture top-10 affected hosts/pods and GPU IDs.
3) Triage for common fault classes (parallelizable):
   - Regression in kernel binary/driver: check recent kernel-related rollouts or kernel-variant canaries in the last 30m. Command: git rev-list --since="30 minutes ago" -- kernel/
   - Resource exhaustion: look at node GPU memory util and host-level OOM logs. CLI examples: kubectl top pod -n runtime | sort -k3 -nr; ssh to host and check nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.used,utilization.gpu --format=csv
   - Scheduler misconfiguration: check admission-controller and credit buckets for cohort. Query admission metrics and recent config pushes.
   - Hot-path kernel slowdown due to sequence length change: correlate request sequence_length histogram to kernel latency.
4) Apply fast mitigations (choose applicable, run one at a time):
   - Route affected cohort to safe model variant or lower fidelity model to reduce kernel load. (Console route change; follow routing rollback checklist.)
   - Increase scheduler slots or temporarily widen admission (if SLO permits).
   - Abort rollout: revert recent kernel or kernel-config change via canary rollback.
   - Evict noisy tenant(s) if cross-tenant noise is identified (follow eviction authority policy).
5) If mitigations fail, page kernel scheduling owner and SRE with incident severity.

Post-incident diagnostics and writeup (10 steps):
1) Capture full 1h/24h metric windows and annotate the KHI spike and mitigations applied.
2) Replay sample traces with throttling reproduction harness (use the replay-runbook below).
3) Run targeted microbenchmarks against suspected kernels (see section: microbenchmark recipes).
4) Check for correlated infra events (network blips, cloud NPU maintenance notices, host reboots).
5) Extract kernel flame graphs and differential profiles against a pre-incident baseline.
6) If a new kernel variant is implicated, run the compatibility test matrix and kernel-safety smoke tests.
7) Update KHI normalizers if the baseline has shifted legitimately due to new model mix.
8) Produce a short incident summary with root cause, corrective actions, and preventive work.
9) Link a follow-up ticket with owners and target dates for any code/config change.
10) Verify remediation by validating KHI and SLOs for 48–72 hours.

Microbenchmark recipes (quick):
- Controlled invocation: run the kernel microbench driver with varying sequence lengths and batch shapes to reproduce tail behavior. Example command: 
  ./kernel_microbench --model=decoder_v2 --batch-shape=1x64x512 --sequence=1024 --repeat=200

- Kernel launch stress: synthetic parallel launch script to exercise launch paths. 
  python tools/parallel_launch.py --workers=128 --ops=2000 --cohort=web-embeddings

Observability changes to implement (backlog):
- Add KHI cohort breakdown to the daily perf digest email and Console uptime dashboard.
- Store 7d sliding baseline histograms per cohort to make normalization robust to diurnal patterns.
- Introduce automatic root-cause candidate ranking: link top correlated signals and host/pod lists in alert payload.

Known limitations and caveats:
- KHI can be biased during large deployments or A/B experiments; always annotate major rollouts and use rollouts tag to mute alerts during coordination windows.
- The normalization function requires 7d stable baseline; newly onboarded cohorts with <24h data should use default baseline.
- Cross-tier routing events can create transient KHI spikes; correlate routing events to avoid unnecessary paging.

Example incident timeline (short):
- 09:02 KHI crosses 40 for cohort web-embeddings.
- 09:03 Oncall investigation started; top 5 hosts show GPU memory pressure.
- 09:05 Route impacted cohort to quantized variant; KHI falls to 22 within 6 minutes.
- 09:30 Root cause identified: canary kernel variant introduced a memory growth regression.
- Postmortem: canary gate tightened; new safety test added to microbenchmark suite.

Appendix A — Sample alert payload (suggested fields):
- alert_name: kernel_health_index_high
- cohort: web-embeddings
- khi_value: 73
- khi_delta_5m: 38
- top_metrics: {k_tail: 0.99, k_err: 0.007, k_q: 0.85, k_preempt: 0.12, k_mem: 0.22}
- top_hosts: [ip-10-1-12-3, ip-10-1-13-9]
- recent_rollouts: [kernel-variant-1.7.2, scheduler-config-2026-11-12]

Appendix B — Example canary mute policy (operational):
- During a scheduled kernel canary (window: 30m), KHI alerts are muted if canary_rollout_tag=true AND KHI increase is restricted to canary cohort only. Non-canary cohort impact always pages.

Appendix C — Links and references:
- Runtime telemetry data model: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/runtime-telemetry-sampling-cost-aware-profiling-2027
- Scheduler admission matrix: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/kernel-admission-matrix-and-signal-negotiation-manual-2026
- Microbenchmark suite: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/microbenchmark-suite-variance-analysis-2025

If you are oncall and unsure, follow the checklist under 'Confirm alert and scope' and escalate immediately. This playbook will be iterated on after each incident and quarterly review by the kernel scheduling team.

title: cross-layer-failure-taxonomy-and-healing-playbook-2028
content:
Summary:
This document defines a cross-layer failure taxonomy for the Redwood serving runtime and prescribes a prioritized set of automated and manual healing patterns. It ties failure classes to observable signals, SLO impact estimates, kernel-scheduler interactions, and a validation protocol (simulation + benchmarks) to verify healing effectiveness. The goal is to reduce MTTI (mean time to impact resolution) and minimize customer-visible SLA violations while retaining explainability for operators and on-call engineers.

Scope:
- Systems covered: serving runtime (scheduler, kernel plugins, KV cache, model swapping path, request multiplexer), GPU nodes, and control-plane routing that affects inference.
- Not covered: provisioning infra (cloud provider account-level failures), storage backend outages unrelated to KV cache persistence.

Key definitions:
1) Failure mode: a discrete class of root cause (e.g., kernel starvation, KV cache thrash, model swap oscillation).
2) Signal: an observable metric or event correlated with a failure mode (e.g., per-gpu-run-queue-latency, kernel-backpressure-count).
3) Healing pattern: an automated or manual mitigation action (e.g., graceful model downgrade, preempt-and-slice, kernel rollback).

Cross-layer failure taxonomy (compact):
- Hardware Degradation:
  - Examples: NVLink flapping, thermal throttling, ECC corrections escalations leading to GPU driver resets.
  - Typical signals: thermal_temperature_gpu > 85C sustained, nvlink_error_rate > baseline, driver-restart events, unexpected GPU offline.
  - Immediate impact: abrupt token latency spikes, increased tail latency, node removal from pool.

- Kernel-level Regression / Latency Inflation:
  - Examples: new kernel release with suboptimal tiling for medium sequence length; per-kernel code-path takes 2x cycles for specific ops.
  - Signals: kernel_duration_p50/p95 increase for impacted kernel id, kernel-inflight-queued, kernel-error-ratio.
  - Interaction: scheduler may increase backpressure, leading to higher queueing latency across tenants.

- Scheduler Misconfiguration or Policy Conflict:
  - Examples: aggressive fairness policy resulting in starvation of high-priority SLOs; priority inversion with ephemeral plugins.
  - Signals: queue-depth-by-priority, delayed-scheduler-invocations, starvation-duration>threshold.

- KV cache evictions & cold-start storms:
  - Examples: bulk tenant requests after model swap cause cache churn and repeated warmups.
  - Signals: kvcache-hit-rate drop, warmup-requests-per-minute spike, per-request-additional-latency-with-warmup.

- Model-variant oscillation / continuous fallback churn:
  - Examples: routing policy repeatedly swaps between quantized and full-float model variants under marginal quality regressions.
  - Signals: model-switch-count, transient-quality-regression-alerts, per-session-inconsistency.

- Control-plane routing instability:
  - Examples: region-level routing flaps, misapplied rollout policy, bad canary rules.
  - Signals: route-change-events, sudden shift in capacity-utilization across regions, <route>-fallback-invoked.

Severity matrix and SLO correlation (short):
- Sev 1 (customer-impacting steady): sustained 50% increase in tail-99 latency, >5% error rate for >5 minutes.
- Sev 2 (degraded but partially functional): 20–50% tail-99 increase, transient errors affecting <5% of requests.
- Sev 3 (anomalous but within SLO): localized kernel latency bump, single-node thermal throttling with graceful failover.

Observable signals catalog (recommended):
- infra.*: gpu_temp_celsius, nvlink_errors, driver_restarts, node_oom_kills
- kernel.*: kernel_exec_time_ms{kernel_id}, kernel_error_count, kernel-inflight
- scheduler.*: queue_depth{priority}, time_to_schedule_ms, preemptions_per_minute
- kvcache.*: hit_rate, warmup_ops_per_minute, eviction_rate
- model.*: model_swap_count, variant_latency_ms, quality_regression_delta
- request.*: per_request_tail_latency_ms{p50,p95,p99}, request_error_rate

Automated healing patterns (ordered by safety):
1) Protective throttling and admission control (safe):
   - When queue_depth{all} > Q_HI and p99_latency > L_HI, trigger per-tenant admission-shed at 5–20% increments with exponential backoff.
   - Purpose: immediately reduce queuing amplification and allow kernels to drain.

2) Kernel safety-net rollback (safe with guardrails):
   - Trigger conditions: kernel_exec_time_p95 exceeds baseline * 1.6 AND kernel_error_increase > X.
   - Action: flip the kernel feature-flag to the previous stable kernel variant on affected shard group; increment kernel-rollback-counter; notify runtime-ops.
   - Validation: quick microbenchmark run (10s, sample requests) against canary path to confirm p95 return.

3) Model variant staged fallback (safe for quality):
   - Trigger: model_latency_multiplier > 1.5 OR kvcache-hit-rate < 0.2 for > 30s.
   - Action: route new requests to a fallback variant (quantized or smaller context) using session-preserving redirect; enable quality-guardrail sampling for first 100 requests.

4) KV cache conservative mode & priming (safe):
   - Action steps: reduce cache target size for new sessions, enable proactive priming background job for top-N prefixes, temporarily exempt high-SLA tenants from eviction until priming completes.

5) Node isolation & graceful eviction (higher disruption):
   - If node-level GPU errors or thermal thresholds persist, mark node in draining state; initiate graceful eviction of live sessions with session-transfer when supported; prevent new allocations for 5 minutes; coordinate with fleet-autorepair.

6) Scheduler quick-slice preemption (experimental):
   - Use when kernel-backed stalls cause broad queueing but kernels still launch. Create short preemption slices (50–100ms) to interleave low-latency tenants. Only enabled under controlled flags and rollouts.

Decision heuristics and guardrails:
- Do not perform model-variant fallback if quality-monitoring signals show >2% quality degradation in last 30s.
