- Kernel rollback requires at least one successful microbenchmark verification and should record an audit event with a trace id.
- Admission-shed must be tenant-scoped and rate-limited; global sheds are an emergency-only action.

Manual triage and runbook (for on-call):
1) Initial detection (0–5 minutes):
   - Pull SLO dashboard for affected route/model.
   - Check node health (gpu_temp_celsius, driver_restarts), kernel errors, and scheduler queue depths.
2) Quick containment (5–15 minutes):
   - If spike is noise, observe for additional 5 minutes.
   - If persistent, enable tenant-scoped admission-shed at 10% and monitor p99.
3) If kernel regression suspected (15–30 minutes):
   - Trigger kernel-rollback play (via runtime admin cli): runtime-admin rollback-kernel --shard-group <id> --cause "p95-regression-<id>"
   - Run microbenchmark: bench-tool --target sh://<shard> --template warmup_short --duration 10s
4) If KV cache storm (15–45 minutes):
   - Apply kvcache-conservative-mode for affected shards: runtime-admin set-kvcache-mode --shards <list> --mode conservative
   - Kick off priming job: priming-svc start --strategy top-prefixes --window 10m
5) Escalate to runtime-core if cross-shard rollback needed or if node isolation fails.

Kernel scheduling interactions (guidance):
- Preemption semantics: preemption should avoid inflight KV mutations; prefer slice boundaries at request or token boundaries where possible.
- Batching trade-offs: increased batching increases throughput but amplifies kernel regressions across tenants; include batch-size hysteresis in scheduler policy to quickly reduce batch size on p95 inflation.
- Priority inversion detection: monitor latency deltas by priority band; automated alert if p95_low_priority improves while p95_high_priority worsens beyond threshold.

Simulation & validation recipe (must-run for any new healing policy):
1) Test harness: use the operational workload simulator with a blended-client-corpus (from request-surface-replay) and inject fault primitives (thermal_increase, kernel_slowdown_x2, kvcache-eviction-spike).
2) Benchmarks to run:
   - pre/post p95/p99 delta test (steady state 5m window)
   - tail amplification ratio under 5% error injection
   - model-quality-sampling to validate fallback fidelity (1000 sampled completions compared via eval-set).
3) Success criteria: automated healing must reduce p99 to <=1.2x baseline within 120s for Sev2 and within 300s for Sev1 while quality regression remains within policy bounds.
4) Regression checks: ensure no >0.5% increased error surface for unrelated tenants during tests.

Operational playbook for release validation (Autonomous Recovery v1):
- Feature description: Autonomous Recovery v1 implements kernel-rollback, kvcache-conservative-mode, and tenant-scoped admission-shed as coordinated automated responses.
- Staged rollout: 1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% over 3 days with automated rollback on predefined SLO regressions.
- Acceptance tests for each stage: run the simulation recipe for 15m and confirm success criteria.
- Rollback criteria: p99 latency regression > 1.5x baseline OR quality-sampling failure > 2% in two consecutive windows.

Telemetry and observability additions required:
- Add a healing-events stream: healing_event{type, target, trigger, actor, trace_id}.
- Annotate request traces with healing_hint when fallback/rollback applied.
- Add a dashboard: "Healing Effectiveness" showing time-to-heal histograms, success-rate by type, and per-tenant impact.

Troubleshooting checklist (fast):
- If rollback didn't reduce p95: verify microbenchmark runner executed against same shard; confirm kernel-side metrics were ingested.
- If admission-shed did not apply: confirm policy sync to edge routing; check policy-eval-latency.
- If kvcache priming thrashed memory: inspect priming job concurrency and rate-limit to avoid OOM.

Ownership & escalation:
- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime (pager: runtime-oncall@redwood.com).
- Secondary: eng-sre (pager: eng-sre-oncall@redwood.com).
- Escalation path: on-call -> runtime-core -> infra-platform lead -> engineering director.

Appendix A — Example CLI snippets:
- Rollback kernel:
  runtime-admin rollback-kernel --shard-group sg-17 --kernel-id k-2027-11 --reason "p95_regression_20270302"
- Set kvcache conservative mode:
  runtime-admin set-kvcache-mode --shards sg-17,sg-18 --mode conservative --ttl 10m
- Start priming job:
  priming-svc start --strategy top-prefixes --sample-size 500 --shard sg-17

Appendix B — Minimal YAML policy sample (human-readable):
  healingPolicies:
    - name: kernel-safety-net-v1
      conditions:
        - metric: kernel_exec_time_p95
          comparator: ">"
        - threshold: 1.6
      actions:
        - type: rollback-kernel
          cooldown: 120s

References and related pages:
- Runtime incident orchestration and capacity decision matrix (internal)
- Kernel safety net and rollback playbook
- Runtime observability data model and tracebook

Document history:
- 2026-11-15: doc created (Maya Chen)
- 2027-01-18: added simulation recipe and success criteria (Rafael Ortiz)
- 2027-03-02: updated rollout acceptance tests and telemetry requirements (Priya Kapoor)

Credits:
This playbook was authored by Maya Chen with contributions from Rafael Ortiz, Priya Kapoor, and the serving runtime on-call rotation.

title: Service Surface and Scheduler Interop Playbook
content:
Overview
========

Purpose: This playbook defines the service surface contract between the serving runtime and kernel scheduler components, specifies an interop handshake, and provides operational guidance for profiling, benchmarking, and incident response when scheduler/runtime mismatches cause latency or cost regressions. It is intended for runtime engineers, scheduler authors, SREs, and platform product managers.

Why this exists
- We frequently observe subtle regressions when a new scheduler or kernel mapping is rolled out without a clearly defined contract (e.g., unexpected preemption behavior, missed cache affinities).
- A small, testable interop specification and an operational checklist reduce rollout risk and speed investigation.

Scope
- Applies to the primary GPU serving runtime, the kernel scheduling layer, and their integration surface (request admission, priority propagation, KV cache hints, slot accounting).
- Out of scope: low-level device driver patches, third-party accelerator SDK internals (these should have their own adapter docs).

Actors and Ownership
- Runtime API/serving team: owns the public-facing runtime service surface, telemetry annotations, and stability SLOs.
- Kernel/scheduler team: owns scheduling decisions, admission controller, and kernel hints.
- Eng-SRE: owns alerts, incident runbooks, and canary gating criteria.

Key Goals and Invariants
1) Deterministic Metadata: requests must carry a minimal, normalized header bundle (priority, estimated_seq_len, model_variant_hint) so scheduler decisions are reproducible.
2) Idempotent Handshake: scheduler must acknowledge accepted admission units and provide an opaque allocation token that the runtime will return on completion.
3) Observability Parity: both sides must emit a matching correlation_id and timestamped lifecycle events for each request path (admit, queue, slice_start, kernel_enqueue, kernel_complete, complete).
4) Graceful Degradation: when the scheduler cannot honor a request-level quality hint, it must return a structured fallback suggestion that the runtime will act on (e.g., select lower-fidelity variant, apply shorter seq cutoff).

Service Surface Specification (compact)
- Request headers (required):
  - X-Runtime-Correlation: <uuid> (opaque, generated by fronting service)
  - X-Priority: integer (0=low .. 10=critical)
  - X-Estimated-Seq: integer (tokens)
  - X-Model-Variant: string (optional hint)
  - X-Cache-Affinity: string (optional prefix fingerprint)

- Admission response (scheduler -> runtime): JSON body with fields - status, allocation_token, granted_fidelity_profile, queue_position (nullable), eviction_constraint (nullable), telemetry_tags. Example:

  {
    "status": "granted",
    "allocation_token": "alloc_9f2a...",
    "granted_fidelity_profile": "vocab-trim-quant8",
    "queue_position": null,
    "eviction_constraint": null,
    "telemetry_tags": ["kernel-A", "slot-42"]
  }

Handshake and Admission Protocol (textual flow)
1) Runtime wraps incoming client request with X-Runtime-Correlation and normalized headers.
2) Runtime sends admission call to scheduler: /admit (POST) with request headers + estimated_runtime_budget_ms field.
3) Scheduler responds synchronously (<=50ms aim) with the admission response JSON above.
4) Runtime begins prefetch/KV hinting based on granted_fidelity_profile and allocation_token.
5) On kernel enqueue the runtime includes allocation_token and correlation id; on completion it posts /release with allocation_token and final telemetry payload.

Configuration Example (YAML)
- Scheduler policy snippet (declarative)

policy: "redwood-default"
preemption: true
max_slots_per_tenant: 12
priority_bands:
  - band: 9
    min_slots: 2
    preemptable: false
  - band: 5
    min_slots: 1
    preemptable: true

- Runtime admission call (curl example)

curl -X POST https://scheduler.internal.redwood/v1/admit 
  -H 'X-Runtime-Correlation: 6f8d7c8b-2d6b' 
  -H 'X-Priority: 5' 
  -d '{"model_variant_hint": "redwood-7b-quant", "estimated_runtime_budget_ms": 120}'

Telemetry and Observability Contract
- Required metrics (emitted by both sides with correlation_id tag):
  - admit.latency_ms
  - queue.length (gauge)
  - kernel.enqueue_ms
  - kernel.exec_ms
  - allocation.tokens.active (gauge)

- Events timeline (example table represented as pipe-delimited rows):
  | event_name | emitter | description | required_fields |
  | admit.request | runtime | serialized admission call | correlation_id, priority, est_seq |
  | admit.response | scheduler | decision payload | allocation_token, granted_fidelity |
  | kernel.enqueue | runtime | request enters accelerator queue | allocation_token, kernel_hint |
  | kernel.complete | kernel | kernel finished execution | allocation_token, exec_ms |
  | request.complete | runtime | final response sent to client | correlation_id, total_ms, tokens |

- Trace span guidelines:
  - Every admission call must create a span named runtime.admit with tags: priority, model_variant, est_seq, scheduler_decision.
  - Kernel spans must annotate kernel type (attention, matmul-batched), memory usage, and peak SM utilization.

Profiling Playbook (when scheduler-induced latencies occur)
1) Reproduce with synthetic traffic: use the workload-replay tool with exact header bundle (priority, est_seq, model_variant).
2) Enable 1% continuous tracing on both runtime and scheduler for the offending route for 30 minutes.
3) Collect kernel-level counters and runtime svc-level histograms. Export to profiling bucket named profiling/<correlation-id>.
4) Run the latency attribution script: tools/latency-attrib --bucket profiling/<correlation-id> --group-by allocation_token, kernel_type.
5) If kernel.exec_ms shows heavy variance tied to allocation_token, escalate to kernel team with attached trace and stripped pcap of scheduling RPCs.

Benchmarking Guidance
- Benchmark goals: reproduce production mix of sequence lengths and priority bands. Target metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec per GPU, preemption rate.
- Synthetic benchmark command example (k8s job):

kubectl run bench-replay --image=redwood/bench-replay:stable -- 
  --corpus s3://bench/corpus/mix-aug-2026.json --qps 200 --priority-dist "0:10,5:70,9:20" --duration 30m

- Cost-aware bench: run two passes with and without prefix caching enabled and compare tokens/sec and average cost-per-token.

Release and Canary Checklist (integration of scheduler/runtime)
1) Unit tests: admission serializer/deserializer (coverage >=95%).
2) Integration tests: local docker-compose full-handshake scenario.
3) Canary (10% traffic for 24h) with telemetry gating: if admit.latency_p95 increases >10% or preemption_rate>3% pause rollout.
4) Run the benchmarking job (above) against canary; compare baseline against canary with an automated diff report.

Incident Runbook (quick triage)
1) Alert triggers: spike in admitted.queue_length or admit.latency_p95.
2) Run quick probe: curl /debug/admit?sample=100 on scheduler to check policy state.
3) Correlate allocation_token churn to runtime kernel_complete events. Command: tools/trace-correlate --from now-15m --tag correlation_id --agg by allocation_token.
4) If scheduler is returning fallback fidelity frequently, temporarily toggle runtime to conservative_fallback_mode via feature flag: runtime.fallback.mode=static-low-fidelity.
5) Escalation: if issue persists >30m open incident and page kernel and scheduler oncall. Attach traces and the benchmark replay command used for repro.

Known Limitations and Mitigations
- Limitation: Allocation tokens are opaque and prevent cross-cluster visibility. Mitigation: add hashed cluster_id in telemetry_tags.
- Limitation: Scheduler response latency can amplify tail latency. Mitigation: local admission cache in runtime with TTL 200ms for frequent identical requests.
- Limitation: Priority inversion when many low-priority, long-seq requests occupy non-preemptable slots. Mitigation: implement aging-based slot rebalancer (see roadmap item).

Appendix: Example diagnostic payload (JSON)
{
  "correlation_id": "6f8d7c8b-2d6b",
  "allocation_token": "alloc_9f2a",
  "timeline": [
    {"event":"admit.request","ts_ms":1672500000000},
    {"event":"admit.response","ts_ms":1672500000042},
    {"event":"kernel.enqueue","ts_ms":1672500000200},
    {"event":"kernel.complete","ts_ms":1672500000420},
    {"event":"request.complete","ts_ms":1672500000450}
  ]
}

Change log
- 2025-11-12: Draft created (Maya Chen).
- 2025-12-18: Added profiling checklist and YAML examples (Arjun Patel review).
- 2026-02-03: Finalized telemetry contract and canary gating thresholds (published).

Related reading
- See scheduler policy language reference (kernel-and-scheduling).
- See runtime admission telemetry schema (eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/runtime-telemetry-sampling-cost-aware-profiling-2027.json).

Contacts
- Runtime API owner: @maya.chen (paging: maya-oncall)
- Scheduler lead: @arjun.patel
- Eng-SRE: eng-sre-oncall@redwood.internal

End of document.

title: Request Provenance & Decision Trace Patterns
content:
Overview:
This document defines our patterns and operational guidance for request provenance and decision trace capture in the serving runtime. The goal is a compact, actionable trace that records the sequence of deterministic and policy-driven decisions made for each request (routing, kernel selection, quantization path, cache behavior, priority/crediting), and ties those decisions to profiling events and benchmark artifacts for fast triage.

Why we need this:
- Reduce time-to-blame for performance regressions and correctness incidents by exposing causal decisions.
- Enable reproducible investigations: the same request + recorded decisions should allow offline replay/tests.
- Provide inputs to cost accounting, model rollout analysis, and automated fallback validation.

Design goals:
- Minimal runtime overhead: target median added latency <= 0.5% and p99 < 1.0% for traced requests.
- Deterministic schema with optional enrichment fields to allow incremental rollouts.
- Sample-aware: full traces for 0.1% of requests by default, dynamic sampling for incidents or experiments.
- Privacy-conscious: do not record raw user inputs; record hashes/prefixes and model identifiers.

Trace model (canonical fields):
- trace_id: unique 128-bit hex string
- request_id: the per-request correlation id seen by the control plane
- sample_rate: sampling multiplier when trace was captured (e.g. 0.001)
- timestamp: ISO-8601 receive time
- origin: source type (api, dedicated, private)
- route: API route name or model route id
- tenant: tenant id (internal opaque id)
- user_data_hash: sha256 prefix (first 8 hex chars) of request content OR "masked" when not available
- seq_length: requested max tokens / prompt length bucket
- decisions: ordered list of decision events (see example below)
- kernel_profile_ref: short id linking to the kernel profiling snapshot (if available)
- kvcache_hits: number of KV cache prefix hits observed
- cost_estimate_units: token-equivalent units used for quick billing breakdown
- fallback_path: list of fallbacks invoked (empty if none)
- outcome: success | degraded | failed

Implementation note: the primary trace object must be a single JSON blob no larger than 4KB in production sampling; enrichment objects (large kernel profiles, microprofiles) are referenced by id and stored separately.

Decision event schema (textual table):
| field | description | examples |
|---|---|---|
| ordinal | integer ordering for causal sequence | 0,1,2 |
| ts | event ISO time relative to trace start | +3.2ms |
| actor | subsystem making decision | router, policy-engine, kernel-mapper, kvcache |
| decision | short token representing choice | route:region-us-east-1, kernel:fp16-q5 |
| reason | concise reason or rule id | capacity-constrained, latency-slo |
| metadata | small key=value pairs (flat) | core_count=1;quant_profile=q5 |

Instrumentation points (where to emit decision events):
1) Ingress routing: record top-k route candidates, selected route, and rule id.
2) Auth/tenant resolution: tenant id derivation and any policy overrides.
3) Model variant selection: model id, version, quantization profile, and compatibility hint.
4) Kernel mapper: chosen kernel binary id, block size, and shard topology.
5) Scheduling crediting: priority class, kernel credit debit snapshot.
6) KV cache layer: prefix lookup result, partial fill, eviction hint.
7) Batching window decisions: batch size, wait time, and cause (idle/burst).
8) Fallback decisions: model swap, region fallback, or feature flag disable.

Sampling and retention policy:
- Default sampling: 0.1% global for production requests.
- On-incident sampling: increase to 10% for affected routes via runtime flag.
- Experiment sampling: per-release experiment tags allow targeted 5% sampling for test cohorts.
- Retention: full trace records retained for 90 days; referenced kernel profiles retained for 365 days.
- Access controls: traces are internal-only; any trace access must be via RBACed consoles and audited.

Trace telemetry SLOs and overhead budget:
- Trace emission error rate: < 0.01% of traced requests may fail to persist.
- Max added latency (median): 0.5% of request median latency.
- CPU overhead: prefer async, batched persist writes; budget 0.2 vCPU per 1000 RPS of traced streams.
- Storage budget: estimate 3MB per 1k full traces per day (adjust by enrichment usage).

Correlating traces with profiling and benchmark artifacts:
1) Kernel profiling snapshot linkage: include kernel_profile_ref (short id) in trace that maps to a per-node microprofile (occupancy, register use, latency histogram).
2) Benchmark run mapping: records produced during A/B tests must include experiment_id and commit hash in trace metadata.
3) Offline replay input: traces flagged with reproducible=true must include sufficient bucketed inputs and model version to run the same code path in staging.

Operational runbook: triage using decision traces (short):
1) Reproduce the incident window: collect traces for the problem window (use on-incident sampling to increase capture).
2) Identify decision divergence: look for traces where decision sequences differ from baseline (kernel change, fallback trigger, scheduling policy).
3) Correlate with kernel_profile_ref and node telemetry (GPU temp, stall counters).
4) If kernel choice changed unexpectedly, run targeted microbenchmark using the same kernel_profile_ref and seq_length bucket.
5) Mitigation options (ordered by safety): roll back kernel mapping change, temporary increased sampling + capture full profiles, enable fallback to previous variant, scale dedicated pool.
6) Post-incident: attach relevant traces to incident page, rerun small replay suite to validate regression fix.

Incident-specific procedures (detailed):
- High tail latency on hosted API:
  1) Increase tracing to 5% for the affected route for 15 minutes.
  2) Run an automated trace-diff: group by (kernel binary id, batch size, seq_length).
  3) If group with higher p99 has a common kernel id, escalate to kernel-owner.
- Unexpected fallback storms:
  1) Query traces with fallback_path length > 0 and group by reason.
  2) If reason is capacity-constrained, consult capacity-dashboard and consider temporary autoscale bump.

Best practices for developers and SREs:
- Prefer referencing trace ids in PRs that touch kernel selection or routing logic.
- When adding a new decision point, add a single event and avoid verbose metadata; use a separate enrichment store for large objects.
- Use hashing and bucketing for any user content stored in traces to preserve privacy.

Implementation checklist (minimal viable trace support):
- [ ] Add trace emission hook at ingress with trace_id and request context.
- [ ] Add decision event writer library (lightweight, flat map API).
- [ ] Implement async tracer to persist to internal trace store with batching.
- [ ] Add kernel_profile_ref generation and store microprofiles separately.
- [ ] Add runtime flags for sampling multipliers per route.
- [ ] Add console query that links from request_id -> trace_id -> kernel_profile_ref.

Ownership and contacts:
- Product owner: Connor Wu (Runtime Observability)
- Primary owners: Runtime-observability team (eng-serving-runtime)
- Secondary owners: Kernel-mapper team, Scheduler team
- Pager for critical tracing pipeline failures: oncall-runtime-observability@redwood.com

Appendix A — Example lightweight trace JSON (for reference):
```json
{
  "trace_id": "9f2a1e7b9c4d2f001234abcd5678ef90",
  "request_id": "r-20260211-17a2",
  "sample_rate": "0.001",
  "timestamp": "2026-02-11T17:22:03.123Z",
  "origin": "hosted",
  "route": "text.generate.v1",
  "tenant": "t-834",
  "user_data_hash": "a3f4b2c1",
  "seq_length": "<=512",
  "decisions": [
    {
      "ordinal": 0,
      "ts": "+0.2ms",
      "actor": "router",
      "decision": "route:us-east-1",
      "reason": "latency-region-preference",
      "metadata": "score=0.78"
    },
    {
      "ordinal": 1,
      "ts": "+1.5ms",
      "actor": "kernel-mapper",
      "decision": "kernel:fp16-q5-compact-v2",
      "reason": "latency-slo",
      "metadata": "shards=2;block=256"
    }
  ],
  "kernel_profile_ref": "kp-20260211-17a2-03",
  "kvcache_hits": "3",
  "cost_estimate_units": "12",
  "fallback_path": [],
  "outcome": "success"
}
```

Appendix B — Frequently asked questions:
Q: Will traces include prompt text?
A: No. We record hashed prefixes and bucketed lengths only to avoid sensitive data in traces. If a tenant requests full content capture for a private deployment, that must be enabled under a restricted policy and stored in an encrypted enrichment store.

Q: How do we avoid trace storming when an incident spike occurs?
A: Sampling multipliers are capped and require an ops-token to exceed 10% for a route. The tracing pipeline has a backpressure mechanism that drops the lowest-priority enrichment payloads first.

Related work and references:
- Runtime observability data model (team wiki) — see related_pages above.
- Kernel mapping policy doc — kernel-and-scheduling folder.

Revision history:
- 2025-11-03: Initial draft by Lena Park.
- 2025-12-18: Added sampling policy and storage estimates (Diego Morales).
- 2026-02-12: Finalized SLOs and triage runbook steps (Aisha Kapoor).

title: Telemetry rollup and sampling strategies for the serving runtime
content:
Summary:
This document describes the telemetry aggregation (rollup) and sampling strategies used by the Redwood serving runtime. It gives concrete rollup policies, sampling heuristics for traces/requests, cardinality guidance, example ingestion configurations (Prometheus/OTLP/agent), and migration/runbook steps to reduce telemetry cost while preserving SLO-aligned visibility.

Goals:
- Keep operational dashboards and SLO alerting robust while lowering metric cardinality and storage costs.
- Standardize rollup windows and aggregation keys across runtime services to make cross-service joins reliable.
- Provide deterministic sampling rules for traces and high-frequency events so debugging remains possible for class-of-failures.
- Preserve fine-grained telemetry for canaries and high-priority customers (Dedicated/Private) while applying stronger rollups for best-effort workloads.

Audience:
- Observability engineers, runtime/infrastructure owners, SREs, and oncall responders.

Principles and tradeoffs:
1) SLO-driven fidelity: choose retention and granularity so that any alertable SLO has the required percentile and time-window fidelity. If a 10-minute p99 is an SLO target, ensure that rollups keep 1s/10s resolution-derived p99 for the relevant signal.
2) Limit cardinality at the ingestion layer: drop or hash low-value tags before series creation. Use label allowlists per metric.
3) Separate control-plane vs data-plane telemetry: control-plane operations (deploys, rollouts) keep full labels; high-volume data-plane metrics use coarser keys.
4) Deterministic sampling: sampling decisions should be stable (based on deterministic hash of request id / customer id) when possible so traces for a customer are consistent across retries and fallbacks.

Metric naming and canonical tags:
- Metric prefix: runtime_<component>_<metric> (e.g., runtime_shard_kernel_latency_seconds).
- Canonical tags (allowlist order of importance): service, model, model_variant, region, shard, priority_tier, customer_tier.
- Non-canonical / scrubbed tags: request_id, user_prompt_digest (hashed), raw_input_size (binned: small/medium/large).

Rollup windows and retention (recommended defaults):
- 15s raw ingestion retention: 7 days (default for critical metrics tied to SLO).
- 1m rollups: 30 days.
- 5m rollups: 90 days.
- 1h rollups (aggregated summaries): 1 year.
Notes: For Dedicated/Private customer lanes, maintain 15s raw for 30 days when contract requires longer retention.

Aggregation semantics:
- Counters: standard delta aggregation.
- Gauges: last-sample aggregation for rollup window, plus min/max.
- Histograms: keep exemplars where available; rollup histograms by merging buckets using consistent bucket boundaries. Avoid dynamic buckets per-instance.
- Summaries: discouraged for cross-host rollups; prefer histogram-based approach for pXX calculations.

Cardinality control and label strategies:
1) Enforce label allowlists at the ingestion client (agent): only forward tags in canonical list.
2) Hash low-entropy user identifiers when they must be retained, and annotate the metric with hashed_id_bucket (e.g., hashed_customer_bucket=0..1023).
3) Use per-metric label limits: if unique label values exceed 1000 in a 5m window, trigger autoscrub mode for that metric and remove the offending label.
4) Example denylist: full_text, prompt_blob, kvcache_key.

Sampling rules (traces and request spans):
- Default sampling: 1% deterministic trace sampling (by stable hash of request_id) for production best-effort workloads.
- Priority sampling: 100% for errors (HTTP 5xx, internal error flags), timeouts, and requests contributing to tail-latency (e.g., if token-generation time > 2x median).
- Canary and customer lanes: 100% traces for canary clusters and Dedicated customer_tier requests.
- Adaptive spike sampling: when trace storage budget exceeded for the minute, reduce best-effort sampling to preserve error+tail capture. Implementations should lower non-error sampling stochastically but keep deterministic sampling for a fixed seed segment.

Example agent configuration (OTel/Prometheus hybrid):
- Rollup policy (YAML):
  rollup_policy_version: v1
  metrics:
    - name: runtime_kernel_latency_seconds
      rollup_windows: [15s, 1m, 5m, 1h]
      labels_allowed: [service, model, model_variant, region, priority_tier]
      cardinality_limit: 2000
    - name: runtime_requests_total
      rollup_windows: [15s, 1m, 5m]
      labels_allowed: [service, region, shard, customer_tier]
      cardinality_limit: 1000
  trace_sampling:
    default_rate: 0.01
    priorities:
      - condition: error_or_status_5xx
        rate: 1.0
      - condition: customer_tier == "dedicated"
        rate: 1.0
      - condition: canary == true
        rate: 1.0

PromQL and query examples (for dashboards/alerts):
- p50/p95/p99 from histogram (Prometheus):
  histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(runtime_kernel_latency_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, service, model, model_variant))
- request rate (per-region):
  sum(rate(runtime_requests_total[1m])) by (region)

SLO mapping examples (how metrics map to SLOs):
- Inference latency SLO (small_seq): objective: p99 < 150ms over 10m window.
  Signal: runtime_kernel_latency_seconds histogram filtered by model_variant=small_seq.
  Required retention: 15s raw or 1m rollup that preserves histogram buckets.
- Request success SLO: 99.95% success over 1h.
  Signal: 1 - (sum(increase(runtime_requests_total{status!~"2.."}[1h])) / sum(increase(runtime_requests_total[1h])))

Alert thresholds (examples):
- P99 latency breach: when 99th percentile > target for 3 of 5 consecutive 1m windows -> P0 alert.
- Error-rate spike: when error rate increases 3x baseline or > 0.5% absolute for 15m -> P1.

Dashboards and slices to maintain:
- Service overview: throughput, p50/p95/p99 latencies, error rate, autocost estimates.
- Kernel health: per-shard GPU utilization, kernel queue length, average kernel execution time.
- KV cache impact: cache hit ratio, warmup rate, cache-size-by-shard.
- Customer-tier slices: Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private.

Runbook excerpt: handling a sudden cost spike from metric churn
1) Detect: Alert triggers for cardinality explosion (metric series growth > 15%/min).
2) Triage: Identify metric and offending label via series cardinality query (example query: topk(10, increase(prometheus_tsdb_head_series_total[5m]))).
3) Mitigate: Apply ingress label drop rule for the offending metric (agent config push): remove label or replace with hashed bucket.
4) Validate: Confirm series count stabilizes and dashboard panels return to expected series counts.
5) Postmortem: Create incident note with root cause and owner, adjust label allowlist or client instrumentation accordingly.

Compatibility and migration guidance:
- Backfill approach: do not backfill histograms by merging old dynamic-bucket histograms; instead regenerate from raw request logs where necessary.
- Rolling agent update: deploy rollup/allowlist changes via the config service in a canary->region->global rollout with feature flag to revert.
- Coordinate with telemetry-cost team for major label changes (expected cost delta estimation required) before global rollout.

Cost estimation guidelines:
- Use 5k series per node as a budgeting heuristic for standard best-effort nodes.
- Estimate trace storage: 1% sample of 10k rps with average 10 spans/request -> ~1MM spans/day; use compression and exemplar policies to reduce long-term retention.

Ownership, escalation, and contacts:
- Ownership: Observability team owns ingestion pipelines and rollup infra. Runtime infra (serving-runtime) owns metric naming and client-side allowlist.
- Oncall: Observability rotation for ingestion issues; runtime SRE rotation for metric correctness and SLO alerts.
- Contacts: obs-oncall@redwood.ai, runtime-sre@redwood.ai.

Open action items and future work:
- (Action) Define per-model bucket schemas for histograms to avoid bucket mismatches during rollup. Owner: Priya Nair. Target: 2026-04-01.
- (Action) Implement adaptive sample-rate controller that lowers sample rate during ingestion spikes but preserves deterministic sampling for hashed buckets. Owner: Jordan Li. Target: 2026-06-15.
- (Research) Evaluate compressed histogram encodings (t-digest / HDR) for long-term retention cost savings.

Appendix: quick CLI examples
- Force an ingress allowlist update (example):
  curl -X POST https://config.redwood.internal/v1/rollup-policies \\n    -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' \\n    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \\n    -d '{"policy_name": "reduce-cardinality-2026-02", "updates": [{"metric": "runtime_requests_total", "drop_labels": ["raw_prompt"]}]}'

- Check current top series by growth:
  promql: topk(20, increase(prometheus_tsdb_head_series_total[5m]))

References:
- Related: runtime-observability-data-model-and-tracebook-2026 (data model and tracebook)
- Related: production-rollout-tuning-checklist-2026 (rollout steps for infra changes)

Document history:
- 2024-11-12: initial draft
- 2025-03-10: added deterministic sampling rules and cost heuristics
- 2026-02-18: finalized rollup windows and added runbook steps

title: Runtime failure inoculation and experimentation manual
content:
Overview

This document defines Redwood's recommended practice for failure inoculation experiments against the serving runtime. The goal is to run controlled, measurable experiments that surface weak points in: kernel scheduling, KV-cache consistency, model swap safety, preemption and eviction, cross-tenant interference, and network/service mesh degradations — while preserving customer SLAs and ensuring fast rollback.

Scope and motivation

- Scope: hosted, dedicated, and private runtime topologies. Focus area for this manual: experiments that exercise the inference serving stack layers (dispatcher, scheduler, kernel, kvcache, model loader, and network fabric).
- Motivation: proactively discover degradations and channel findings into kernel/scheduler hardening, autoscaling rules, runtime admission policies, and fidelity fallback contracts.

Definitions

- Failure inoculation: deliberate, controlled introduction of adverse conditions to observe system resilience and recovery behavior.
- Experiment runbook: documented steps for preflight, execution, measurement, and rollback.
- Safety envelope: pre-declared constraints that must not be violated (SLO breach thresholds, impacted tenants, time windows).

Safety policy and gating

Before any experiment is scheduled the following gates must be satisfied:

1) Business and customer gate
- No running experiments against paid enterprise Dedicated clusters without explicit customer approval.
- Hosted experiments must restrict to synthetic tenants and test API keys; production traffic must not be targeted.

2) SLO safety envelope (hard thresholds)
- Global p95 API latency must not exceed baseline p95 + 30% for more than 5 minutes.
- Error rate (5xx) must remain below 0.5% of baseline traffic during the experiment window.
- Token-generation fairness: no single synthetic tenant may consume > 10% of cluster dispatch capacity unless previously authorized.

3) Operational staffing
- At least two on-call engineers from eng-serving-runtime must be present during the experiment (primary + observer).
- SRE must be notified and on standby if the experiment could affect cross-tenant routing.

Experiment types and intent

A. Scheduler perturbation
- Intent: validate scheduler credit accounting, priority inversion detection and graceful backpressure.
- Action examples: artificially throttle kernel dispatch for a priority tier; inject slot starvations to simulate device contention.
- Key metrics: kernel queue length, per-priority p99 latency, kernel rejection rate, scheduler admission counters.

B. KV-cache warm/cold transition
- Intent: exercise cache warmup paths and eviction ripple effects during model swap.
- Action examples: evict selected tenant shards, simulate cold model swap (flush local cache + remote fetch delays).
- Key metrics: kvcache miss rate, model load time, tail latency during first 100 tokens after swap.

C. Model swap and fallback orchestration
- Intent: verify canary/rollout safety, fallback to lower-fidelity model variants, and KV consistency post-swap.
- Action examples: trigger a staged model push to a small cohort, then force a full-swap while artificially raising checksum mismatch errors in the loader.
- Key metrics: successful fallback count, consistency reconciliation time, error surface for model artifact validation.

D. Network fabric degradation
- Intent: validate RPC timeouts, gRPC retry behavior, and graceful degradation when inter-node latency increases.
- Action examples: introduce 50-250ms RTT between dispatcher and GPUs inside the test topology, or inject packet loss of 0.5-2%.
- Key metrics: request retry rate, end-to-end token latency, CPU scheduling spikes attributable to increased RPC stalls.

E. Thermal and power throttling simulation
- Intent: emulate GPU thermal throttling and observe kernel preemption/backoff reactions.
- Action examples: reduce available compute quota to a worker to simulate thermal step-down.
- Key metrics: kernel reschedule rate, preemption counts, impact on concurrent tenants.

Experiment design template (always populate)

- Experiment ID: runbook-{YYYYMMDD}-{short-name}
- Owner(s): (name, pager)
- Objective: one-sentence hypothesis
- Target topology: (hosted/dedicated/private) and cluster IDs or labels
- Safety envelope: list of SLO thresholds and excluded tenants
- Steps: numbered preflight -> inject -> observe -> withdraw -> analysis
- Measurement sheet: queries and dashboards to collect (see example observability queries)
- Rollback criteria: explicit conditions that trigger an immediate abort and remediation steps
- Postmortem required: Y/N (postmortem required for any experiment that triggers a safety-envelope violation)

Preflight checklist (must be completed and signed off)

1) Create Experiment ticket in the experiments board and link the runbook.
2) Confirm synthetic tenants and test api-keys are configured; validate routing isolation.
3) Ensure TTL and billing freezes for synthetic tenants to avoid unexpected charges.
4) Record baseline metrics for at least 15 minutes pre-injection: p50/p95/p99, 5xx rate, kernel queue depth, kvcache hitrate.
5) Notify SRE and product ops with time window and pager contacts.

Execution procedure (sample)

1) Start live observability snapshot: run the collection job to capture high-resolution traces for the next 30 minutes. Command: curl -X POST https://observability.internal/api/snapshots -d '{"scope":"experiment-run"}' -H 'Authorization: Bearer $OBS_TOKEN'

2) Apply failure injection via the chaos service:
- Scheduler throttle example:
  curl -X POST https://chaos.internal/v1/inject \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $CHAOS_TOKEN" \
    -d '{"type":"scheduler-throttle","target":"priority=low","duration_s":300,"params":{"drop_rate":0.15}}'

3) Monitor critical dashboards: kernel queue depth, scheduler admission logs, per-priority tail latency.

4) Observe for the pre-declared timebox (suggested 5 minutes for initial smoke). If any rollback criteria met, execute rollback (step 6).

5) Withdraw injection: call the chaos service to remove the perturbation.

6) If rollback criteria met, escalate following the runtime incident process:
- Immediate action: cancel injection and run remedial script to re-stabilize dispatchers:
  kubectl -n runtime-system rollout restart deployment/dispatcher --selector=cluster=test-cluster
- Notify affected owners in #runtime-incidents and switch on emergency traces (increase sampling to 100% for 5 minutes).

Rollback criteria (examples)

- latency.p99.global > baseline.p99 * 1.5 for more than 3 minutes
- 5xx rate spike to > 1% sustained for 2 minutes
- model loader error rate > 0.2% for any active model group

Observability and measurement examples

- Required dashboards: "Experiment control plane" (admission counters, chaos events), "Kernel surface" (queue depth, execution latency), "KV-cache" (hit/miss, eviction churn).
- Example queries (Prometheus-like):
  - kernel_queue_depth{cluster=\"test-cluster\",priority!="system"}
  - histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(kernel_exec_duration_seconds_bucket[2m])) by (priority)
  - sum(rate(kvcache_miss_total[1m])) by (shard)

- Trace collection: enable distributed traces with tags: experiment_id, injector, owner. Use trace span enrichers to attach kernel hint and scheduler decisions.

Analysis and acceptance criteria

- Post-experiment analysis must include: timeline graph aligned to injection start, delta vs baseline for p50/p95/p99, error annotation, and any kernel-level anomalies (excess preemptions, stalls, failed kernel launches).
- Acceptance: if all metrics return within the safety envelope within 10 minutes of withdrawal and no undetected data corruption is observed, mark experiment as "non-disruptive". Otherwise, mark for follow-up remediation and potential code fixes.

Channeling findings into engineering workflow

- Findings are filed as "Experiment Findings" tickets with tags: experiment_id, severity (S1-S4), component (scheduler/kernel/kvcache). Include reproducible script and minimal repro trace link.
- Remediation priority: P0/P1 (blocker/regression) mapped to oncall and relevant code owners.

Experiment catalog (example entries)

| Experiment ID | Focus area | Short description | Blast radius | Last run | Owner |
|---------------|------------|-------------------|-------------:|---------:|-------|
| runbook-20260115-sched-throttle | scheduler | throttle low-priority kernel dispatch to validate admission | small (test cluster) | 2026-01-15 | Marcus Liu |
| runbook-20260201-kv-evict | kvcache | evict tenant shard to observe warmup penalty | small | 2026-02-01 | Priya Natarajan |
| runbook-20260122-model-swap-fuzz | loader | staged model swap while injecting checksum mismatches | medium | 2026-01-22 | Evelyn Cho |

Practical tips and anti-patterns

- Tip: prefer short, repeated pulses over a single long blast. Short pulses reveal transient cascading effects with lower blast radius.
- Tip: pair every experiment with a synthetic probe that asserts correctness (e.g., deterministic prompt set with golden responses for fidelity checks).
- Anti-pattern: running wide blast experiments during major releases or when kernel-rollout is in progress.

Integration with release and canary process

- Canary experiments should include at least one failure inoculation scenario (scheduler perturbation or kvcache cold start) in the pre-release gate when enabling new kernel variants.
- Release checklist item: confirm the canary cluster has passed the designated inoculation scenarios within the last 72 hours.

Templates and artifacts to attach to experiment tickets

- experiment-runbook.yaml (example below)

  id: "runbook-{{date}}-{{short}}"
  owner: "team/person"
  topology: "test-cluster"
  safety_envelope:
    p99_latency_multiplier: 1.5
    max_5xx_rate: 0.01
  inject_steps:
    - name: "scheduler-throttle"
    - name: "wait-5m"

- observation-query-list.txt containing the PromQL queries and trace sampling instructions.
- representative trace and kernel log bundle upload link.

Frequently asked questions

Q: Can I run these on Dedicated customer clusters?
A: Only with written customer consent and a scoped, agreed blast radius. For Dedicated clusters we recommend using a cloned environment or staging VPC.

Q: What if my experiment causes a regression that only manifests after 24 hours?
A: If a delayed regression is suspected, mark for extended monitoring and create a long-running regression ticket. Increase retention of relevant traces and logs for at least 72 hours.

Ownership and contacts

- Experiments steward: eng-serving-runtime-experiments@redwood.ai
- On-call escalation: see /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/eng-sre/runbooks for the oncall roster and escalation matrix.

Versioning and audit trail

- Every experiment ticket must attach the exact chaostool manifest and experiment-runbook.yaml. The experiment control plane persists start/stop events and injector logs to S3://experiments-buckets/{experiment-id}/. Maintain a short audit summary in the ticket including who approved and who executed.

Appendix: quick checklist (one-line)

- Create ticket -> Confirm synthetic tenancy -> Baseline metrics -> Notify SRE -> Run with observer -> Withdraw -> Validate metrics -> File findings.

Contact and feedback

Send questions or proposed additions to the manual to Evelyn Cho (evelyn@redwood.ai) or open a PR on the team wiki page.

title: Experiment Safety and Metric Harmonization Compact Manual
content:
Summary

This compact manual documents a cross-cutting, reproducible approach for running runtime experiments that touch kernel scheduling, profiling, benchmarking, and production runbooks. It prescribes safety gates, harmonized metrics, and a short remediation checklist for rapid rollback. This doc is intended for runtime engineers, oncall responders, and experimentation owners running controlled changes to scheduling policies, kernel variants, or telemetry sampling.

Scope

- Applies to: any experiment that modifies kernel selection, kernel hint propagation, admission controllers, or runtime-level batching/eviction parameters in the serving runtime.
- Excludes: model parameter changes, user prompt set changes, or user-visible model content experiments (those are handled by Model QA and Product).

Goals

1. Keep production SLOs intact during experiments (95th and 99th latency, error rate, token throughput).
2. Ensure metric comparability across runs (common tags, sampling strategy).
3. Provide fast, well-documented rollback and recovery steps if safety gates fail.

Ownership and Roles

- Experiment Owner: creates experiment charter and runs the change.
- Runtime Operator: oncall engineer responsible for monitoring and rollback.
- Telemetry Owner: maintains metric instrumentation and sampling configuration.
- SRE Reviewer: approves capacity and failure-domain checks prior to canary.

Pre-experiment Checklist (must pass before enabling traffic)

1. Charter (one paragraph) posted to the experiment tracker with expected impact, duration, and rollback criteria.
2. Runbook attached with clear sign-off columns for Experiment Owner and Runtime Operator.
3. Canary plan defined: affected zones, percent traffic, duration per step.
4. Baseline snapshot collected: 24-hour sliding window for key metrics.
5. Trace sampling and live profiling configured: enable lightweight trace at 1% and high-fidelity on shadow channels.

Metric Harmonization Guidelines

- Canonical metric names (use these exactly):
  - runtime.request.latency_ms.p50, p95, p99
  - runtime.request.error_count
  - runtime.token.throughput
  - kernel.switch.count
  - kvcache.hit_rate
  - scheduler.admission.rejected_count

- Required tags/labels on every metric: environment, deployment_id, experiment_id, kernel_variant, region
- Sampling policy: production baseline sampling must remain unchanged during experiment windows. Additional high-fidelity samples should be routed to shadow channels only.

Experiment Safety Gates (automated and manual)

Automated gates (fail experiment immediately if any triggers):
- > 3x increase in runtime.request.error_count in 5-minute rolling window
- p99 latency increase > 30% vs baseline over 10 minutes
- Token throughput drop > 25% sustained for 5 minutes

Manual escalation triggers (operator decides rollback after assessment):
- p95 latency increase between 15% and 30% sustained for 10 minutes
- Kernel.switch.count spike without matching change in request load
- Unexplained increase in scheduler.admission.rejected_count

Kernel / Scheduler Impact Table (quick reference)

| Change           | Likely short-term impact           | Observability signals to watch               | Recommended canary step |
|------------------|------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|------------------------|
| batch_size_up    | lower throughput variance, higher latency for short requests | p50/p95 latency divergence; kernel.dispatch.wait_ms | 1% traffic, 5m        |
| prefetch_hint_en | improved warmstart; higher memory pressure | kvcache.hit_rate up; memory_pressure metric | 0.5% shadow, then 2%  |
| preemptive_split | reduces long-tail by interrupting heavy kernels; risk of more kernel.switch | kernel.switch.count; p99 latency | 0.1% stage, monitor 15m |
| admission_tight  | protects latency SLOs, may reject low-priority work | scheduler.admission.rejected_count; error_count | 1% canary, 10m       |

Profiling Playbook (short)

1. Baseline capture: collect 5-minute microtraces for representative routes prior to change.
2. Warm shadow profiling: route 0.5% of traffic to the experimental binary with full trace baggage.
3. Aggregation and diff: use the profiling pipeline to compare kernel-level CPU/GPU time and serialization stalls between baseline and experiment.
4. Rapid hypothesis loop: if a kernel shows +25% GPU time, pin to kernel variant A and re-run a micro-canary.

Benchmarking and Acceptance Protocol (quick runbook)

- Bench harness: use the accepted workload manifest (manifest_id: workload/production-replay/v2) with token distribution and concurrency matrix.
- Acceptance criteria: no increase in p99 latency > 20% under matched concurrency; no regression in kvcache.hit_rate < -5 percentage points; kernel errors remain zero.
- Experiment can graduate to broader canary only after 3 successful acceptance runs spaced at least 2 hours apart.

Rollback and Recovery Procedure (explicit)

1. Immediate: disable experiment toggle or revert scheduler config using the emergency toggle endpoint: curl -XPOST https://ops-api.internal/v1/exp-toggle/{experiment_id}/disable -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN'
2. Recompute capacity: if eviction pressure observed, run: ./ops-scripts/redistribute-shards --grace-period=60s
3. Verify: confirm p95 and p99 back to baseline within 15 minutes. If not, escalate to SRE Reviewer.

Quick Troubleshooting Decision Tree

- Symptom: p99 latency spike without error_count rise
  1) Check kernel.switch.count -> if high, consider scaling back preemptive_split.
  2) Check memory_pressure -> if high, disable prefetch_hint_en.

- Symptom: error_count spike
  1) Inspect scheduler.admission.rejected_count and recent config changes.
  2) If errors map to a single kernel variant, revert that kernel at the service control plane.

Postmortem and Data Retention

- If any automated gate fired or manual rollback was executed, an incident-lite postmortem should be produced within 48 hours. Include: baseline snapshot, experiment logs, trace samples, kernel timings, and decision rationale.
- Retain experiment traces for 90 days. Summaries and roll-forward decisions must be recorded in the experiment tracker.

Checklist for Safe Rollout Phases (canary -> ramp -> full)

1. Canary (0.1% - 1%): 30m min per step, automated gates live, operator present.
2. Ramp (1% - 10%): 1h min per step, increased trace sampling to 5% in shadow channels.
3. Full (10%+): staggered regional enablement, capacity verification with SRE, monitoring page in console set to shared view.

Appendix: Useful Commands and Probes

- Toggle an experiment: curl -XPOST https://ops-api.internal/v1/exp-toggle/{experiment_id}/(enable|disable) -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN'
- Collect a microtrace from node: ssh ops-node-1 -- sudo /usr/local/bin/collect-trace --pid $PID --duration 30s > /tmp/trace.json
- Quick kernel health query (PromQL): sum(rate(kernel_exec_time_ms[5m])) by (kernel_variant) / sum(rate(kernel_exec_count[5m])) by (kernel_variant)

Contacts and Escalation Path

- Primary Runtime Owner: asha@redwood.ai
- Oncall Runtime Operator: runtime-oncall@redwood.ai
- Telemetry Owner: telemetry@redwood.ai
- SRE escalation pager: +1-555-0101 (use for >15m unresolved SLO regressions)

Change Log

- 2025-11-17: Created (Asha Menon).
- 2026-02-26: Clarified automated gate thresholds and added kernel impact table (reviewed by Diego Ramirez and Claire Chen).

Related references

- See profiling playbook for trace enrichment patterns and trace baggage conventions.
- See benchmark acceptance suite for the workload manifest and harness details.

End of document.

title: Runtime operator handoff and shared observability contract
content:
Overview

Purpose: This page defines the operator handoff checklist and the shared observability contract used by runtime engineers, SREs, and oncall to run, tune and troubleshoot Redwood's serving runtime. The contract covers the set of metrics, traces, profiling artifacts, benchmark markers, release-note signals, and known-issue flags that must be produced and consumed during a feature rollout or operational incident.

Scope
- Applies to runtime components that live in the serving process: dispatcher, kernel dispatcher, KV cache, scheduler, admission controller, telemetry adapter.
- Intended consumers: oncall SRE, runtime owners, release engineers, customer-facing support.

High-level principles
1) Contract-first telemetry: every feature must document the telem signals it produces and the expected shapes before canary.
2) Lightweight by default: default collection is cheap; heavy profiling is opt-in and gated by the profiling playbook.
3) Deterministic handoff: deployments must meet the handoff checklist before they are considered live for SRE ownership.

Operator handoff checklist (must be completed by owning team before SRE takeover)
1. Architecture summary and README: service-level diagram, primary components, and request path.
2. SLOs and budgets: Token-level P50/P95/P99, request success rate, and error budget allocation. See SLO table below.
3. Runbook links: runbooks for slow kernels, memory pressure, eviction, and graceful shutdown (links).
4. Baseline benchmarks: representative benchmark IDs and artifact links produced by the benchmark suite.
5. Observability contract: list of metrics/traces/logs produced and required alerts.
6. Profiling recipe: sample profiling command and storage location for artifacts.
7. Feature flags and gating matrix: flags to revert/disable and required rollout steps.
8. Known issues: documented regressions and mitigations.
9. Oncall contact and escalation path.

SLO summary (example table)
| Metric | Target | Measurement window | Owner |
| Token latency P95 (generation) | <= 140ms | 1h | runtime-kernel |
| Request end-to-end P99 | <= 350ms | 1h | runtime-dispatch |
| Request success rate | >= 99.92% | 24h | runtime-sre |
| Kernel error rate (per kernel) | <= 0.05% | 1h | runtime-kernel |

Required observability signals
- Metrics (timeseries):
  - runtime.requests.total, runtime.requests.latency_ms{p50,p95,p99}, runtime.kvcache.hits, runtime.kvcache.miss_rate, runtime.kernel.queue_length, runtime.kernel.active_kernels, runtime.kernel.evictions, runtime.dispatch.admission_rejections.
- Traces: distributed trace with root span = request.dispatch, child spans: route.resolve, kernel.execute[slice], kvcache.lookup, response.serialize. Each kernel.execute span must annotate kernel_id, input_seq_len, output_tokens, and kernel_hint_version.
- Logs: structured JSON logs with fields {request_id, trace_id, kernel_id, error_code, node_id, cohort}.
- Profiling artifacts: flamegraphs, nvprof summaries, kernel latency histograms, and memory-snapshot tarballs. Must include commit hash and benchmark id in filenames.

Profiling playbook (quick recipe)
1. When: trigger profiling when P95 exceeds baseline by > 25% for 3 consecutive 5-minute buckets, or when kernel error rate spikes.
2. Sampling mode: start with lightweight sampling (1% of requests) using adaptive tracer.
3. Escalation: if signal persists, run an isolated micro-benchmark using the benchmark ID from the baseline (see example command).
4. Artifact retention: upload artifacts and add link to incident. Retain for 90 days by default.

Command examples
- Lightweight trace sampler (k8s job):
  kubectl -n runtime exec -it profiler -- /bin/sh -c "profiler collect --sample-rate=0.01 --duration=15m --out=/tmp/prof-$COMMIT-$ID.tgz"

- Micro-benchmark run (local dev):
  ./benchctl run --suite=echo-mixed --concurrency=16 --seq-dist="(8:0.6,64:0.3,512:0.1)" --commit=$COMMIT --artifact=bench-$COMMIT-$(date +%s).tgz

Benchmark suite manifest (required fields for baseline artifact)
- bench_id: short identifier of benchmark (e.g., echo-mixed-20241112)
- commit_hash: runtime sha
- hardware_profile: e.g., a100s-40g, h100-80g.pci, t4-dense
- seq_distribution: brief summary
- batch_config: {batch_size, max_latency_ms} (recorded as YAML in artifact metadata)

Example artifact metadata (YAML snippet)
commit_hash: "a1b2c3d4"
hardware_profile: "h100-80g.pci"
bench_id: "echo-mixed-20241112"
seq_distribution: "8:60%,64:30%,512:10%"
batch_config:\n  batch_size: 8\n  max_latency_ms: 120

Kernel scheduling tracing contract
- Kernel spans must include: kernel_id (stable id), kernel_version, kernel_hint, requested_seq_len, observed_concurrency, dispatch_slot_id.
- Scheduling decisions (admit/reject/hedge) must emit an event to the scheduling bus and write a trace annotation with decision_reason.
- Scheduler-level metrics to emit: kernel.wait_time_ms, kernel.exec_time_ms, kernel.preemptions, kernel.hedges_initiated.

Release note and canary signals
- Every runtime release must include a release note that lists: changed kernels, new scheduler heuristics, observability deltas (new metrics/traces), and benchmark regressions measured against the acceptance suite.
- Canary acceptance criteria (example): no P99 latency regression > 10% vs baseline, error rate <= baseline + 0.02%, no new disk or memory OOMs observed during canary window.

Known issues reporting format
- Include short description, impacted components, reproducibility steps, temporary mitigation, owner, and ETA for permanent fix. Example: 
  - ID: KVC-2026-07
  - Summary: infrequent KV cache shard imbalance under multi-tenant spikes
  - Impact: increased cold misses and P95 latency blips
  - Mitigation: scale KVC shards or enable per-tenant eviction policy.
  - Owner: runtime-kv-team
  - ETA: 2026-02-28

Operational runbooks and playbook links (must be present)
1. slow-kernel-detection-and-hotfix-playbook (link)
2. memory-pressure-incident-triage-and-recovery-playbook (link)
3. runtime-deployment-circuit-breakers-and-sla-fallback-playbook (link)
4. quantitative-burst-slo-simulation-and-cost-sampling (benchmarks)
5. graceful-shutdown-and-session-drain-runbook (link)

Owner & escalation matrix
- Primary owner: runtime-platform (pager: oncall-runtime-platform)
- Secondary (kernel): runtime-kernel (pager: oncall-runtime-kernel)
- SRE escalation: follow standard oncall escalation (1st hour - page primary, 1-3 hours - page secondary, >3 hours - page eng manager).

Checklist for post-incident follow-up (postmortem inputs)
1. Collect baseline benchmarks (pre/post) and profiler artifacts.
2. Annotate traces with incident timeline and decision points.
3. Run regression bench suite to validate fix.
4. Update runbooks and observability contract if gaps discovered.

Appendix: quick reference (search tokens)
- Search metric prefixes: runtime.*, kernel.*, kvcache.*
- Benchmark artifact prefix: bench-
- Profile artifact prefix: prof-
- Incident label: runtime-incident-YYYYMMDD

Related docs and references
- Profiling playbook (recommended sequence): /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/runtime-profiling-playbook-guidelines-2025
- Benchmark acceptance suite: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/runtime-deployment-sanity-and-benchmark-suite-acceptance-2026
- Scheduler design notes: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-policy-language-declarative-profiles-2026

End of document

title: Runtime resource annotation taxonomy and signal enrichment
content:
Summary

This document defines a canonical taxonomy for resource annotations used across the serving runtime, plus the enrichment pipeline that turns raw telemetry + config into scored signals used by the scheduler, admission controller, and autoscaler. The goal is to standardize names, types, semantics, and operational practices so that components can interoperate without brittle ad-hoc mappings.

Motivation

- Multiple teams (scheduler, kernel mapper, autoscaler, Observability) require consistent, machine-readable metadata about model-serving resources (GPUs, shards, model variants, containers, and requests).
- Inconsistent annotation names caused mismatches in fallback routing and incorrect prefetch decisions during Q3 incidents.
- A small, well-documented set of canonical fields reduces cognitive load for owners and speeds rollouts of policy changes.

Scope

- This taxonomy applies to: GPU nodes, runtime shards, model-variant instances, session tokens (provenance), and request classes.
- Out of scope: long-term billing tags (managed by Finance) and user-level semantic labels (managed by product teams).

Core principles

1) Backwards-compatible: existing annotation keys must continue to be supported; new keys should have clear deprecation paths.
2) Idempotent enrichment: repeated enrichment runs should produce identical signals for the same inputs.
3) Typed and validated: each key has a strict type and acceptable value range.
4) Explainable scores: any composite score must be reproducible and accompanied by its component weights.

Canonical annotation table (summary)

| key | type | description | primary consumers | default/notes |
|---|---:|---|---|---|
| resource_type | string | one of [gpu-node, shard, model-variant, session, request-class] | all | required |
| affinity | string | affinity class: one of [high, medium, low] used for co-location heuristics | scheduler, autoscaler | default: medium |
| eviction_priority | integer | 0 (never) - 100 (highest) eviction ranking, lower = safer to evict | scheduler, runtime | default: 50 |
| kvcache_hotness | float | 0.0-1.0 locality score for KV cache reuse | kernel-mapper, scheduler | computed by enrichment pipeline |
| kernel_hint | string | preferred kernel execution path (e.g. attention-sliced-v2, fused-mlp) | kernel-mapper | optional |
| fidelity_profile | string | fidelity target: [max_quality, balanced, cost_saver] | autoscaler, rollout | impacts quantization and fallback policies |
| estimated_tps | float | estimated tokens-per-second capacity for this resource | admission, autoscaler | derived from microbenchmarks and telemetry |
| thermal_headroom | float | 0.0-1.0 available thermal headroom; <0.2 triggers soft-limits | scheduler, SRE | pulled from node sensors |
| model_variant_compat | list | list of variant ids this resource is compatible with | orchestrator | canonicalized to short ids |
| provenance | string | origin id of last configuration change | all | helps audit and debugging |
| isolation_class | string | [best_effort, strict, dedicated] determines multi-tenancy isolation | scheduler, infra | default: best_effort |
| prefetch_hint | string | [none, small, aggressive] KV prefetch strategy expected | kernel-mapper | influences warmstart behavior |
| billing_bucket | string | internal billing categorization | billing, finance | optional, tie-breaker only |

Full field definitions and validation rules

- resource_type (string, required): must be one of the canonical values. Reject unknown types during ingestion and route to owner for classification.

- affinity (enum): used by the placement policy to express co-location sensitivity. Implementation note: treat affinity high as an additive score +30 in placement ranking.

- eviction_priority (int 0-100): lower values protected; eviction_policy: pick candidate with highest eviction_priority first. For multi-tenant nodes, maintain per-tenant min_protected_threshold.

- kvcache_hotness (float 0.0-1.0): computed by enrichment pipeline using a sliding-window merge of request provenance + access patterns. See Enrichment pipeline section. Values <0.15 are considered cold.

- kernel_hint (string): free-form but validated against KernelHintRegistry (see Operational pointers). Unrecognized hints fall back to kernel auto-selection with telemetry annotation.

- fidelity_profile (enum): toggles quality/cost tradeoffs; must be supported by model_variant. If a requested fidelity_profile is unsupported, admission rejects with a 409 and details recommended alternatives.

Enrichment pipeline (architecture)

The enrichment pipeline converts raw inputs into canonical annotated-resource records. Design choices: streaming-first but compact, idempotent, and vectorizable for fast scoring.

Inputs
- Telemetry: hot-prefix traces, KV access logs, per-request latency and token counts, node sensor readings (temp, power), kernel failure traces.
- Config/state: model manifests, node labels, feature flags, recent rollout history.
- Microbenchmarks: per-variant short-run throughput/latency profiles stored in the Benchmark Catalog.

Stages (high-level)
1) Ingest and canonicalize keys: map vendor-specific labels (e.g., nvidia.gpu.type -> resource_type/gpu_model) using Canonicalizer map.
2) Join time windows: create sliding windows (default 5m, 1h) for hotness and latency measures.
3) Compute primitive signals: mean_ttfb, median_tokens, kv_access_rate, error_rate, thermal_percentile.
4) Normalize & clamp: scale signals into canonical ranges, clamp outliers (z-score guardrails).
5) Composite scoring: calculate kvcache_hotness, estimated_tps, eviction_priority_delta using weighted sums. Weights are stored in the ScoreConfig repo and are versioned.
6) Publish annotated record: write to Annotated Resource Store (a lightweight document store with versioned entries).

Example enrichment rule (pseudocode)

# kvcache_hotness calculation - pseudocode

window = last_15_minutes(requests.filter(model==X))
kv_hits = sum(window.map(r -> r.kv_hit ? 1 : 0))
kv_accesses = sum(window.map(r -> r.kv_accesses))
hotness = (kv_hits + 0.5 * kv_accesses) / max(1, window.request_count)
normalized_hotness = sigmoid_scale(hotness, scale=0.8)  # clamp to 0..1

Operational notes on enrichment weights
- ScoreConfig is a Git-backed JSON with simple schema: {"kv_weight": "0.6", "latency_weight": "0.3", "thermal_penalty": "0.1"}. Changes require a review and a CI gate that replays enrichment on a representative sample.

Storage and API

- Annotated Resource Store: path /annotated-resources/{resource_id}, JSON document with last_enriched_at and version tag. The store supports conditional writes (ETag) to avoid stomping concurrent enrichments.
- Read API: /api/v1/annotated-resources?filter=... supports predicates on canonical fields and returns stable snapshots.

Consumers and contracts

- Scheduler: consumes annotated records and uses affinity + kvcache_hotness + thermal_headroom to rank placement. Contract: annotated record must be <5s old for scheduling decisions.
- Kernel-mapper: consumes kernel_hint + kvcache_hotness to pick kernel and prefetch budget. Contract: if kernel_hint missing, mapper must annotate chosen kernel back into resource record.
- Autoscaler: consumes estimated_tps and error_rate; expects monotonicity of estimated_tps across enrichment runs unless a flagged recalibration event occurred.

Sample annotation (JSON example)

{
  \"resource_id\": \"shard-az2-gpu-47\",
  \"resource_type\": \"shard\",
  \"affinity\": \"high\",
  \"eviction_priority\": \"20\",
  \"kvcache_hotness\": \"0.73\",
  \"kernel_hint\": \"attention-sliced-v2\",
  \"fidelity_profile\": \"balanced\",
  \"estimated_tps\": \"120.5\",
  \"thermal_headroom\": \"0.62\",
  \"model_variant_compat\": [\"rv1-small-int8\", \"rv1-small-fp16\"],
  \"last_enriched_at\": \"2026-11-03T14:22:11Z\"
}

(Consumers should parse the types—this example renders numbers as strings for Transport-level simplicity; the API schema documents native types.)

Producer guidelines (how to add or change annotations)

1) Create a proposal in the ScoreConfig repo for new fields or weights and add a small integration test that exercises enrichment.
2) Add a validator in the Enrichment Validator module with a clear error message and remediation steps.
3) Increment the scoreconfig version and open a changelist referencing this Confluence page.
4) Run enrichment replay on the low-cost sample corpus (CI job) and upload diff report.

Common failure modes and mitigations

- Symptom: kvcache_hotness drops suddenly for a shard after rollout.
  - Check: recent model_variant rollout, kernel_hint change, and cold-start events in warmup logs.
  - Mitigation: increase prefetch_hint for the shard, and re-run warmup job for 1-2 minutes.

- Symptom: scheduler rejects placement citing thermal_headroom < 0.2 unexpectedly.
  - Check: node sensor telemetry, recent firmware updates, and thermal_headroom normalization params.
  - Mitigation: temporarily lower thermal_penalty in ScoreConfig and trigger prioritized drain if needed.

Versioning, deprecation, and migration

- New keys must include a deprecation plan in the PR: alias mapping, 90-day dual-write window, and a one-time migration job for historical entries.
- ScoreConfig versions are semver: enrichment-runner uses the highest-stable tag unless an override is present.

Rollout checklist (for ScoreConfig or field additions)

1) Draft ScoreConfig change and unit tests.
2) Reviewer sign-off (2 reviewers including one SRE).
3) Run enrichment replay against sample corpus.
4) Deploy to enrichment-staging and run a 1h shadow pipeline.
5) Monitor divergence metrics: annotated-record-delta-rate < 1% and scheduler-placement-change-rate < 0.5% for safe rollout.
6) Promote to production with a 10-minute canary window, monitor live SLOs.

Operator runbook snippets

- Quick check: get last enriched record for a shard

curl -sS -H \"Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN\" \
  https://internal-api.redwood.local/api/v1/annotated-resources/shard-az2-gpu-47 | jq .

- Replay enrichment for a single resource (local dev)

# assumes enrichment binary in PATH and SCORECONFIG env set
ENRICHMENT_CONFIG=s3://scoreconfig/prod.json enrichment-runner --resource-id shard-az2-gpu-47 --window 15m --dry-run

Operational ownership and contacts

- Owners: Serving Runtime Observability & Enrichment squad (primary)
- Oncall escalation: runtime-oncall -> eng-sre -> platform-eng lead.

title: Runtime Decision Replay and SLO Forensics Manual
content:
Overview
========

This document describes the decision-replay pipeline and a structured forensic playbook for investigating SLO violations that originate in the serving runtime. It ties scheduler/kernel choices, KV cache hits/warmness, model variant routing, and cross-tenant admission decisions to downstream SLO impact. The goal is to provide a repeatable investigation path for engineers on-call and owners of runtime subsystems.

Scope
-----
- Applies to Hosted, Dedicated, and Private runtimes managed by the Redwood serving runtime.
- Focuses on latency and availability SLOs for synchronous generation / streaming endpoints (per-request SLOs: p50/p95/p99).
- Excludes model quality regressions; see quality-guardrails docs for signal correlation.

Key concepts and services
-------------------------
- runtime-dispatcher: front-line routing service that maps requests to execution slots and chooses model variants.
- slot-manager: tracks GPU resources and admission credits across heterogeneous pools.
- kernel-orchestrator: selects kernel/attention plan and preemption policy per request.
- kvcache-proxy: global KV cache coordinator for prefix and session caches; exposes cache_warmness metadata.
- replay-indexer: storage + query layer for deterministic decision replays (see Decision Replay format section).

Required telemetry and artifacts (must be present for replay)
---------------------------------------------------------
1) request-trace (full event timeline, request_id) — retention: 30d
2) scheduler-decision-record (slot, priority, preemption_token) — retention: 90d
3) kernel-hint-record (kernel_id, tile_plan, estimated_cycles) — retention: 90d
4) kvcache-stats (hit/miss, warmness, evicted_keys) — retention: 7d (aggregates) / 30d (per-session)
5) system-metrics at 1s resolution (GPU utilization, mem pressure, nvlink errors) — retention: 14d
6) request-payload (prompt length, sequence length, truncated flag) — retention: 7d

Decision Replay format (canonical JSON)
--------------------------------------
A single replay bundle is stored as newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON). Each line is a flat object, sample keys below; the replay-indexer exposes a /replay API that returns NDJSON to feed local deterministic replays. Example snippet: 

{
  "request_id": "r-20251201-6843",
  "timestamp": "2025-12-01T14:23:45.123Z",
  "dispatcher_decision": "pool-a:slot-42",
  "kernel_choice": "matmul-tiling-v3",
  "kvcache_warmness": "cold",
  "estimated_tokens": "512",
  "observed_latency_ms": "1245"
}

(Keep fields flat and string-typed to simplify ingestion across languages.)

Triggering conditions for a forensics replay
-------------------------------------------
- Automated: SLO alert fires (p95 or p99 breach sustained for 5m) and the incident playbook triggers replay-indexer ingestion.
- Manual: engineer on-call suspects an event (e.g., sudden p95 spike correlated with kernel rollout). Use the manual replay steps below.

Forensic investigation playbook (step-by-step)
----------------------------------------------
1) Triage and scope (5–15 minutes)
   - Pull the SLO alert timeline from alerting-dashboard (time window T = alert start - 10m to alert end + 10m).
   - Identify a representative set of request_ids (prefer p99 offenders and a small sample of p95/p50).
   - Record business impact: request types, customers affected, percent traffic impacted.

2) Bulk metadata unlock (5 minutes)
   - Query replay-indexer for the request_ids: /api/v1/replay?ids=r-...
   - Confirm required artifacts exist for each request (scheduler record, kernel hint, kv state). If missing, mark as partial replay; annotate possible blind spots.

3) Deterministic local replay (10–30 minutes)
   - Use the replay harness (runtime-replayer CLI) which accepts NDJSON. Example: runtime-replayer --input bundle.ndjson --mode dry-run
   - Validate the harness reproduces the observed kernel_choice and dispatcher_decision. If divergence occurs, capture the divergence snapshot: 
     - runtime-replayer --input bundle.ndjson --emit-divergence=divergence.log

4) Attribution pass (30–60 minutes)
   - Compare baseline vs observed: create a delta matrix across factors: kvcache_warmness, kernel_choice, slot_latency, preemption events.
   - Use the causal scoring heuristic (see table below) to rank likely root causes.

5) Hypothesis testing (minutes to hours)
   - If kvcache coldness is top candidate: re-run replay with kvcache_warmness forced to "warm" and measure simulated latency delta.
   - If kernel_choice is suspect: re-run with previous kernel (kernel-v2) and compare per-step cycle counts.
   - If scheduling/preemption suspected: re-run multiple requests in a batch to surface contention effects.

6) Remediation and rollback (variable)
   - If a kernel rollout caused regression: open an urgent kernel-rollback PR to kernel-orchestrator and schedule canary rollback.
   - If admission policy misconfiguration: update slot-manager policy and monitor SLOs for 30m.

Causal scoring heuristic (illustrative)
-------------------------------------
Score factors (0-100 each):
- kvcache_delta_score: function(hit_rate_change, warmness)
- kernel_regress_score: function(est_cycles_increase, memory_pressure)
- schedule_contention_score: function(queue_depth_change, preemptions)
- infra_fault_score: function(nvlink_errors, gpu_throttle_count)

Rank = weighted_sum([kvcache:0.25, kernel:0.35, schedule:0.25, infra:0.15])

Quick reference SLO thresholds (applies to core-generation-route)
---------------------------------------------------------------
| SLO metric        | Target   | Alert threshold          | Escalation window | Owner          |
|-------------------|----------|-------------------------|-------------------|----------------|
| p50 latency       | 60ms     | >120ms for 5m           | Pager (P1)        | runtime-sre    |
| p95 latency       | 220ms    | >350ms for 3m           | Pager (P0)        | runtime-sre    |
| p99 latency       | 850ms    | >1200ms sustained 2m    | Pager (P0)        | runtime-sre    |
| availability      | 99.95%   | drop 0.2% in 1h         | Incident (P0)     | runtime-sre    |

(These thresholds are per-route and subject to per-customer SLA overrides; always check route-level overrides in token-config DB.)

Common root causes and signposts
--------------------------------
- Cold KV cache (signs: kvcache_warmness==cold, cluster-wide recent evictions, per-session miss spikes)
- Kernel regression (signs: kernel_hint shows new kernel id, estimated_cycles >> baseline, p95 increase tied to rollout window)
- Admission pressure (signs: queue_depth spike, preemption_count increment, allocation_timeouts)
- Infra flakiness (signs: nvlink/PCIe errors, GPU thermal throttling alarms)
- Telemetry sampling artifacts (signs: trace gaps, missing scheduler records)

Playbook checklists and commands
-------------------------------
- Commands:
  1) Fetch replay bundle: curl -sS "https://replay-indexer.internal/replay?range=2026-02-09T10:00:00Z,2026-02-09T11:00:00Z&route=core-gen" > bundle.ndjson
  2) Run deterministic replay: runtime-replayer --input bundle.ndjson --log-level debug --emit-metrics
  3) Query kv cache state: redis-cli -h kvcache-proxy-01 info | grep Evicted
  4) Inspect kernel rollout timeline: ksctl rollout history kernel-orchestrator | tail -n 50

- Minimal investigation checklist (tick-box):
  - [ ] Representative p99 request_ids collected
  - [ ] Replay bundle exists and replays without missing artifacts
  - [ ] Divergence snapshot captured (if any)
  - [ ] Ranked causal candidates and hypothesis list documented in incident ticket
  - [ ] Remediation planned and annotated with rollback plan

Testing the replay pipeline (how to validate a new trace source)
----------------------------------------------------------------
1) Add synthetic trace producer: runtime-test-harness can emit controlled divergence scenarios (flags: --fault kvcache-evict --burst 100).
2) Run in staging: inject 1K synthetic requests from the harness for 30s.
3) Validate replay-indexer stores NDJSON bundles and the runtime-replayer reproduces the divergence.
4) Add a unit test in replay-indexer that asserts schema completeness for required keys.

Operating agreements and ownership
----------------------------------
- runtime-sre: incident lead and primary pager for production SLO breaches. Responsible for running this playbook during incidents.
- runtime-serving: owner for dispatcher_decision logic, kernel-orchestrator changes, and rollout gating.
- infra-stability: owns hardware-related investigations (nvlink, thermal, EC errors).
- telemetry-platform: maintain replay-indexer SLAs (ingest latency <30s) and schema stability.

Rollout guidance for changes that affect decision-collapse surface
----------------------------------------------------------------
- Always include a deterministic replay diff in PRs that touch dispatcher, slot-manager, or kernel-orchestrator. The PR template must include: before.ndjson, after.ndjson, and a 1-page summary of delta.
- Canary policy: run kernel and dispatcher changes at 0.5% traffic for 30 minutes, compare causal score distributions.

Appendix A: Example incident timeline (annotated)
------------------------------------------------
1) 10:03 UTC - Alert: p99 latency exceeds 1200ms
2) 10:04 UTC - runtime-sre triage: fetch 200 p99 request_ids
3) 10:06 UTC - replay-indexer returns bundle; 40% of reqs missing kvcache state -> mark partial
4) 10:12 UTC - deterministic replay shows kernel-v3 increased estimated_cycles by 2.8x relative to baseline
