5) 10:22 UTC - rollback of kernel-v3 to v2 initiated; p99 improves toward baseline within 12 minutes

Appendix B: Troubleshooting tips
--------------------------------
- If replay diverges immediately: check schema version mismatches between runtime and replay-indexer (header field: replay_schema_v).
- If kvcache artifacts missing for customers on Private deployments: confirm replay-agent sidecar is enabled in the customer manifest.
- If preemption_count is high but queues are not deep: investigate cross-tenant quota bleed; consult tenant-throttle logs.

References and related reading
----------------------------
- runtime-dispatcher design doc (internal link): /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/delta-routing-and-cost-partitioning-architecture-2026
- Kernel rollout policy: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/kernel-handshake-and-adaptive-fallback-patterns-2026
- SLO runbook canonical page: /confluence/eng-sre/slo-and-error-budgets/p99-slo-handbook

Contact and escalation
----------------------
- Primary on-call: runtime-sre rotation (pager duty team: @runtime-sre)
- Slack channels: #runtime-ops, #kernel-rollouts, #kvcache
- Emergency escalation path: runtime-sre -> Head of Infra -> CTO (as per incident policy)

Change log
----------
- 2025-11-12: Created by Jordan Matthews (initial draft).
- 2026-01-08: Added causal scoring heuristic and replay CLI examples (reviewed by Ava Martinez).
- 2026-02-10: Finalized SLO thresholds and testing protocol; published.

title: systematic-load-profiles-and-scaling-experiments-2026
content:
Overview:

## Purpose
This playbook documents a repeatable, engineering-focused approach to construct, run, and interpret end-to-end load and scaling experiments for the Redwood serving runtime. The goal is to give engineers a single, well-scoped procedure for validating autoscaling policies, kernel scheduling knobs, KV cache warmup behavior, and cost/latency tradeoffs across realistic workload shapes.

## Scope and when to use this doc
- Validating autoscaler configuration changes prior to a production rollout.
- Quantifying latency vs. cost impact of new kernel scheduling heuristics.
- Reproducing and debugging SLO regressions tied to workload distribution shifts.
- Benchmarking model-variants or quantization profiles under mixed concurrency.

## High-level experiment design
1. Define the hypothesis (explicit). Example: "Adaptive batching with max_batch=64 reduces 95th percentile latency by >=15% for short-sequence chat workloads at 300 qps."
2. Select a small set of representative traffic profiles (see Profiles table).
3. Establish stable baseline (3 successful runs with current config).
4. Apply change under test.
5. Re-run identical experiment suite and collect telemetry.
6. Analyze deltas against baseline using the analysis checklist below.

## Representative traffic profiles (canonicalized)
| Profile name | Composition | Avg seq len | Burst pattern | Target qps | Notes |
|--------------|-------------|------------:|---------------|----------:|-------|
| Chat-short   | 85% chat + 15% system prompts | 96 tokens | Poisson bursts, CV=1.2 | 300 | Typical webchat PLG use-case
| Assist-long  | 40% long-form completions | 1024 tokens | Steady ramp with periodic spikes | 40 | Notebook / code gen workloads
| Embedding-burst | 100% embedding (batchable) | 1 token | High-frequency microbursts (100ms inter-arrival) | 400 | Tests batching & coalescing
| Mixed-enterprise | 60% chat, 20% completion, 20% embeddings | variable | Diurnal with hourly spikes | 120 | Representative enterprise route mix

## Pre-experiment checklist
- Owner: assign an experiment lead and a verifier.
- Environment: use a non-production cluster matching the target capacity profile (same GPU generation & kernel build).
- Config snapshot: save current model.json, kernel-mapper.yaml, autoscaler policy JSON, and routing rules. Example:

Save command examples:
```
kubectl -n runtime get configmap kernel-mapper -o yaml > kernel-mapper.prechange.yaml
aws s3 cp s3://redwood-experiments/configs/model.json model.json.prechange
```

- Monitoring hooks: ensure traces, per-token cost, and KV cache hit-rate metrics are enabled. Required metrics:
  - runtime.request.latency.p50/p95/p99
  - kernel.queue.depth, kernel.active_batches
  - kvcache.hit_rate, kvcache.evicts
  - gpu.utilization, gpu.memory.used
  - autoscaler.desired_replicas, autoscaler.actual_replicas

## Execution steps (detailed)
1. Baseline run
   - Deploy a tagged Canary stack: runtime image tag = stable/2026-01-12-canary
   - Warmup KV cache: replay 20,000 representative prefixes at production token distribution.
   - Duration: run steady-state for 30 minutes plus a 10-minute spike window.
   - Run 3 trials separated by 15 minutes idle.
2. Change under test
   - Apply change (examples: kernel scheduling policy flip, max_batch increase, new quantization kernel).
   - Restart runtime nodes using rolling restart with 1 node at a time.
   - Repeat warmup and trials as for baseline.
3. Safety guardrails during runs
   - Abort if p99 latency exceeds baseline p99 by 2x or absolute p99 > 5s for > 60s.
   - If GPU OOM occurs, collect node logs and capture heap/profile then revert.

## Data collection and artifact list
- Raw telemetry (Prometheus TSDB snapshot) for window start..end.
- Traces: sampled 1:50 with full token span for at least 10% of requests.
- Kernel executor logs and per-kernel timing histograms.
- Autoscaler event log and provisioning timeline.
- Workload generator logs (k6/Locust) and input request corpus.
- Cost estimate: GPU-hours * on-demand cost + estimated inference token cost.

Create an artifacts folder naming convention: experiments/<YYYYMMDD>-<profile>-<change>/

## Analysis checklist
- Verify experiment parity: identical request corpus and seed across baseline and variant runs.
- Primary checks (pass/fail):
  - p95 improved/worsened (quantify absolute ms and percent).
  - p99 behavior during spikes.
  - Mean GPU utilization delta.
  - KV cache hit-rate delta and warmup time.
  - Autoscaler oscillation or thrash events.
- Secondary checks:
  - Per-model token cost changes.
  - Number of kernel preemptions or queue overflows.
  - Any increase in tail queue depth indicating head-of-line blocking.

## Typical experiment failure modes and remediations
- Observation: p99 improves at steady-state but regresses during spike.
  Remediation: reduce max_batch or enable fast-path for short-sequence requests.
- Observation: autoscaler overshoots and causes thrash.
  Remediation: increase stabilization window and add rate limit to scale-up.
- Observation: KV cache hit-rate drops after change.
  Remediation: review shard placement, increase warmup traffic, or adjust cache eviction policy.

## Quick reference: CLI snippets
k6 synthetic profile example (chat-short):
```
k6 run --vus 40 --duration 30m --out influxdb=http://metrics:8086/chat-short.js
```
Locust swarm with custom payload:
```
locust -f locustfile.py --headless -u 300 -r 50 --run-time 30m
```
Extract prom snapshot:
```
kubectl -n monitoring exec prometheus-0 -- promtool snapshot /prom/data /tmp/snapshot.tar.gz
kubectl cp prometheus-0:/tmp/snapshot.tar.gz ./artifacts/snapshot.tar.gz
```

## Config matrix (example)
| Variable | Baseline | Variant A | Variant B | Notes |
|----------|----------|-----------|-----------|-------|
| max_batch | 32 | 64 | 16 | Larger batch reduces per-token overhead but increases latency for short seqs
| kernel-map | default | priority-driven | numa-aware | Kernel mapping strategy to GPUs
| autoscaler.min_replicas | 2 | 2 | 4 | Minimum pool size
| autoscaler.scale_up_window_s | 60 | 120 | 30 | Stability vs responsiveness

## Reporting template (what to publish after an experiment)
- Title: short, change under test, profile name, date
- One-paragraph summary of outcome (latency vs cost tradeoff).
- Key metrics table (baseline vs variant): p50/p95/p99, GPU util, cost estimate, cache hit-rate.
- Graphs: latency heatmap, kernel-level time series, autoscaler timeline.
- Action items: accept / iterate / rollback / require more tests.

## Ownership and escalation
- Experiment owner: runtime performance engineer (assign in doc frontmatter).
- Verifier: senior SRE or runtime tech lead.
- Escalate to oncall if incident occurs during run (follow oncall runbook link).

## Appendix: reproducible artifacts and example corpus format
- Request corpus JSON schema (newline-delimited):
```
{"route":"/v1/chat/completions","model":"rwd-small-v2","prompt":"<...>","max_tokens":256,"seed":42}
```
- Acceptable image: a timeline diagram text description: "Diagram shows warmup -> steady-state -> spike -> cooldown with autoscaler adjusting replicas at t+8m".

## Related pages and reading
- See: Mixed workload SLO simulation suite (internal link)
- See: Runtime observability data model and traceback (internal link)
- See: Production rollout tuning checklist (internal link)

Last updated by Nora Chen on 2026-02-14.

title: Runtime telemetry sampling and cost-aware profiling policy
content:
Summary
-------
This document defines Redwood's standardized policy for runtime telemetry sampling and cost-aware profiling. It describes which signals to collect, how to sample requests to meet SLOs while controlling telemetry costs, recommended storage/retention tiers, and an operational runbook for changes or incidents that require higher-fidelity traces. The goal is to preserve diagnostic signal for engineering and SRE workflows while bounding observability costs and avoiding unbounded ingestion/ingress spikes.

Motivation and goals
--------------------
- Reduce observability spend growth while retaining high utility for performance and regression investigations.
- Provide deterministic, auditable sampling behavior across runtime components (dispatcher, kernel dispatcher, kvcache, model-handler).
- Make profiling decisions workload-aware: bursty clients, tail-heavy routes, canary experiments, and high-cost model variants should get more coverage.
- Define safe escalation and rollback paths when increased telemetry is required during incidents or experiments.

Telemetry signals (priority list)
--------------------------------
1) High-value, low-volume (always-on)
   - Per-request SLO metadata: request_id, route, model_variant, tenant, priority_class, latency_ms, status_code
   - Aggregated token-level counters: tokens_requested, tokens_emitted per model_variant (1s rollup)
2) Medium-value (sampled)
   - Traces for inference lifecycle across runtime components (dispatcher -> kernel -> device)
   - Kernel queue times and kernel execution durations (p50/p95/p99 histograms)
3) Low-value / expensive (adaptive sampling)
   - Full step-level GPU kernel traces (PTX/cupti-level) and per-op GPU timelines
   - Full request payloads and user prompt text (redaction rules apply)

Sampling strategy overview
--------------------------
We use a hybrid deterministic+adaptive sampling strategy: a low base sample rate plus deterministic upsampling for classes of requests that historically produce high-value signals.

Base rates (default global policy)
- Trace sampling (end-to-end request spans): 1 in 200 requests (0.5%)
- Kernel-level detailed tracing: 1 in 10,000 requests (0.01%)
- Heavy payload capture (prompts > 2k tokens): 1 in 500 requests (0.2%)

Deterministic upsampling rules (always evaluated before random sampling)
1) Canary/experiment routes: 100% tracing for canary cohorts during rollout window.
2) Error-class upsampling: any request with status != 200 is captured at 100% for at least 10 minutes after first occurrence, then decays to base rate over an hour.
3) Tail-latency upsampling: requests that exceed route p95 latency are marked for additional traces for the next N=100 matching requests.
4) High-cost models: model_variants with per-token cost > X (configurable) increase trace sample to 1% by default.

Adaptive, cost-aware throttling
------------------------------
- Observability budget: each runtime cluster (per-region) has a monthly ingestion budget measured in "trace-equivalent-units" (TEUs). TEU is defined as a weighted unit that normalizes traces, kernel traces, and payload captures.
- When projected weekly TEU consumption reaches 60% of budget, the system reduces non-essential sampling rates by 30% and notifies owners. At 85% projected consumption, further reductions occur and only high-priority deterministic sampling remains.
- An emergency override allows SRE to enable 100% tracing for up to 2 hours for incident triage; this must be logged and tagged to an incident ID.

Retention and storage tiers
--------------------------
- Hot (7 days): full-span traces and per-request metadata stored in tracing backend (used for immediate triage and dashboards).
- Warm (30 days): aggregated histograms and reduced traces (kept with sampling metadata).
- Cold (365 days): token counters, aggregate model_variants cost metrics, and sampling logs for audit.

Table: storage and retention
| signal_type | retention | storage_location | downstream_exports |
| trace_full | 7d | trace-cluster-hot | alerting/dashboards |
| trace_reduced | 30d | trace-cluster-warm | performance-reports |
| aggregates | 365d | metrics-db | billing/simulation |

Dashboarding and alerting
-------------------------
- Critical SLO dashboards should use sampled-corrected histograms. Sampling-corrected estimators must be applied to p95/p99 calculations when sampling != 100%.
- Alerts:
  - Incoming trace TEU rate > cluster budget_projection_rate * 1.2 -> paged to eng-sre.
  - Spike in kernel-level error rate (>=5% of kernel calls in 10m) -> pager.
  - Sampling configuration drift (any change to deterministic rules) -> notify runtime config-owners and security for scrutiny.

Operational runbook (when more fidelity is needed)
--------------------------------------------------
1) Triage phase: Validate the failure mode using existing traces and aggregated metrics.
2) If insufficient signal, escalate to temporary upsampling: update cluster sampling override policy to increase trace sampling to 5% for affected routes for a maximum of 90 minutes.
3) If kernel-level detail required, enable kernel-level tracing for a dedicated rolling node pool with isolated TEU accounting.
4) After capture: revert overrides, tag traces with incident ID, and run cost reconciliation.
5) Produce a post-incident note listing why higher fidelity was required and whether sampling policies should be adjusted.

Change management and rollout process
-----------------------------------
- Sampling policy lives in a declarative feature flag repo: repo: infra/observability/sampling-policies, file: runtime-defaults.yaml.
- Changes require:
  1) Design doc (1 page) describing reason and measurement plan.
  2) PR with unit tests + simulation against synthetic workloads (see tools/telemetry-sim).
  3) Canaried rollout to 2% of clusters for 24 hours; check TEU impact and correctness.
  4) Gradual rollout with metric-based gates.

Config examples
---------------
YAML example for route-level policy (runtime-defaults.yaml excerpt):

---
routes:
  - name: /v1/generate
    default_trace_sample: 0.005 # 0.5%
    upsample_rules:
      - name: canary_cohort
        matcher: "route:generate AND cohort:canary"
        sample: 1.0
      - name: tail_latency_boost
        matcher: "route:generate AND latency>p95"
        sample: 0.2

CLI snippet: enable temporary override
$ ri telemetry override set --cluster=us-west-2 --trace-sample=0.05 --duration=90m --reason="incident-INC-1234"

Example queries (Appendix)
--------------------------
- Estimate true p95 from sampled histograms: use the per-bin weight correction factor included in each span (example SQL-like pseudocode):
  SELECT corrected_percentile(histogram_bins, sample_rate) FROM traces WHERE route='/v1/generate' AND ts BETWEEN ...;
- TEU projection snippet (pseudocode):
  projected_teu = current_week_teu + (average_daily_teu * remaining_days)

Ownership and contacts
----------------------
- Policy owner: Priya Nair (runtime-observability)
- On-call for telemetry ingestion: eng-sre on-call (pager duty team: infra-sre)
- Budget owner: Finance-ML (for cross-checks and chargebacks)

Appendix: privacy and redaction rules
------------------------------------
- No full prompt text is stored in hot traces by default. Prompts are redacted at capture time using redaction ruleset v2. See infra/observability/redaction-rules.md.
- PII found during capture triggers immediate encryption with customer-specific KMS per Private deployment and will be excluded from exported datasets.

Appendix: quick checklist for a high-fidelity capture request
-------------------------------------------------------------
1) Create a short incident doc and assign incident ID.
2) Open PR in infra/observability with sampling override.
3) Confirm TEU budget availability with eng-sre.
4) Apply override and monitor TEU spikes for first 5 minutes.
5) Revert and annotate results.

Related references
------------------
- telemetry-rollup-and-sample-strategies-2026 (internal)
- continuous-runtime-profiling-strategy-2026 (internal)

Change log
----------
- 2026-11-10: Created initial draft.
- 2027-01-12: Added TEU projection and retention tiers.
- 2027-02-15: Clarified deterministic upsampling rules and added CLI snippets.

For questions or requests for exceptions, contact the policy owner listed above.

title: Cross-layer inference audit and synthesis manual
content:
Overview:
This manual defines a repeatable, cross-layer approach for auditing inference requests that hit Redwood's serving runtime and for synthesizing findings into actionable mitigations and experiments. It codifies: runtime architecture checkpoints, kernel scheduling guardrails, profiling playbooks, benchmark integration, release gating, runbook mappings, and a short known-issues catalog with triage paths.

Audience:
- Runtime engineers owning kernels and scheduler policies
- SRE and performance owners who operate production fleets
- Applied ML engineers validating model serving fidelity
- Product/QA engineers running end-to-end latency/cost regressions

Goals and scope:
- Provide a standard investigation lifecycle from signal to mitigation (Detect -> Isolate -> Reproduce -> Diagnose -> Remediate -> Verify).
- Bridge observability signals (traces, kernel telemetry, scheduler events, KV cache hits) with actionable kernel-level and orchestration-level fixes.
- Ensure benchmark artifacts and canary results map back to concrete rollout decisions.
- Cover multi-tenant and dedicated pools; on-prem private deployments may adapt the steps but keep the contract.

Ownership and contact matrix:
- Runtime kernel scheduler: ownership: runtime-kernel-team; primary oncall: @runtime-kernel-oncall; escalation: @eng-sre
- Observability and tracing: ownership: observability-team; contact: Marco Chen
- Benchmarking and gold corpus: ownership: benchmark-ops; contact: Asha Patel
- Quality + model fidelity: ownership: applied-ml; contact: Diego Rivera

Key concepts and definitions:
- Execution fan-out: number of kernels / shards invoked to satisfy a single request token. High fan-out correlates with increased tail latency and NVLink pressure.
- Kernel isolation level: the degree to which a kernel's resources and tensors are logically partitioned (full, fractional, soft-isolated).
- Fidelity tiers: {high: exact floating-point kernels; balanced: mixed quantized kernels; low-cost: quantized/approx kernels}.
- Prefix/KV caching policy: TTL and eviction semantics for cached KV entries.

Observability contract (telemetry fields every request must include):
- request_id, tenant_id, model_variant, sequence_length, prompt_prefix_hash, kernel_map_version, kernel_id_sequence, kvcache_hit_rate (percent), batch_size, scheduling_priority, pci_e_latency_ms, queue_time_ms, execution_ns, end_to_end_latency_ms, token_count
- SLOs to monitor:
  - p50 end_to_end_latency_ms: <= 120ms for interactive class;
  - p95 end_to_end_latency_ms: <= 250ms;
  - p99 end_to_end_latency_ms: <= 800ms;
  - kernel_error_rate: < 0.2%
  - kvcache_hit_rate (global): target >= 72% for production workloads

Profiling playbook (step-by-step):
1) Detect: automated alert triggers or benchmark drift reports list anomalies. Primary signals: sudden p99 latency jump, step-change in kernel execution_ns, increased queue_time_ms, or drop in kvcache_hit_rate.
2) Capture: spin a time-bound capture (recommended 5–10 minutes) using the live trace sampler:
   - CLI: `rwictl trace capture --req-filter 'tenant=TENANT_ID & model=MODEL' --duration 600s --sampler=adaptive`
   - Ensure kernel-level hooks are enabled (kernel-map + per-kernel counters).
3) Classify: use the classification checklist to map the dominant contributor:
   - Queueing backlog (queue_time_ms dominates) -> scheduler or admission controller misconfiguration
   - Kernel slowdown (execution_ns spike across kernel_id_sequence) -> kernel regression, thermal throttling, or memory contention
   - Fan-out change (kernel_id_sequence length increased) -> topology or model sharding change
   - KV cache drop -> cache eviction regression or prefix-hash skew
4) Reproduce: use the local sandbox replay:
   - `rwictl replay --trace <trace_id> --sandbox-profile small-gpu --max-requests 200`
   - If the repro is noisy, pin the kernel-map version and disable prefetchers to isolate the kernel path.
5) Diagnose: combine kernel latency flamegraphs (per-operator) with NVLink / PCIe counters and occupancy metrics. Typical checks: GPU occupancy sudden drop, memcpy stalls, or long kernel launches due to scheduler preemption.
6) Mitigate:
   - Short-term: adjust admission control thresholds (reduce concurrency for affected pool), enact per-tenant priority throttling, or shift traffic to compatible model variant.
   - Medium-term: rollback kernel change, tune kernel launch parameters, increase KV cache TTL for the affected prefixes.
   - Long-term: implement scheduler rewrite (see Scheduler Guardrails) or rework model shard topology.
7) Verify: re-run bench harness with the same corpus and target SLOs (see Benchmarks integration).

Scheduler guardrails (recommended safety checks for any policy change):
- Any new admission rule must declare maximum concurrency (slots), preemption_weight (0–100), and safe_fallback_variant.
- Rollout checklist for scheduler policy change (minimum):
  1. Unit tests for admission rule semantics
  2. Canary: 1% traffic with shadow tracing for 1 hour
  3. Monitor: p99 latency, kernel_error_rate, queue_time_ms, and per-kernel execution_ns
  4. Abort if p99 increases by >15% or kernel_error_rate > 0.5%

Benchmarks suite and automation (how to integrate audit findings into bench artifacts):
- Gold corpus: store representative request traces and their expected fidelity checksums in the benchmark-ops artifact store. Each corpus item is annotated with sequence length, expected kvcache_hit boolean, and latency budget.
- Sample benchmark job YAML (text representation):
  name: inference-regression-check
  target_pool: prod-balanced
  corpus: gs://bench-artifacts/gold-corpora/2026-09/recall-5000
  concurrency_profile: [1, 4, 8, 16]
  validation:
    - latency_p95_ms: 250
    - fidelity_checksum: expected-v1.4

- Run locally: `benchctl run --job-file job.yaml --report-path ./reports/job-$(date +%F).json`
- Integrate with CI: benchmark artifacts are required for any kernel or scheduler PR that touches the runtime; failures must create a blocking defect in the PR pipeline.

Release notes and rollout gating (operational checklist):
- Every runtime release must include:
  - kernel-change summary (diff of kernel ids and a rationale)
  - scheduler policy change log (human-readable intent + machine-enforced guardrails)
  - benchmark run artifacts: canary and control groups with p50/p95/p99 and fidelity checksums
  - a short rollback playbook with command snippets and ownership

Example rollback snippets:
```
# Demote scheduler policy and drain new kernels
rwictl scheduler apply --policy-id OLD_POLICY_ID --force
rwictl node drain --selector 'kernel_map_version=new_2026_11' --timeout 600s
```

Runbooks (incident triage map):
- P99 latency spike (tier: high): follow Profiling playbook. Immediate actions: reduce admission concurrency by 30% for affected pool, enable shadow-routing to fallback variant, page runtime-kernel-team.
- Kernel OOMs (tier: critical): cordon affected nodes, mark kernel_id as quarantined, revert kernel image rollout, patch kernel memory accounting in the next patch.
- KV cache correctness regression (tier: high): disable prefix-based eviction, switch to TTL-based fallback, and run cache-consistency validation against the gold corpus.

Known issues (short catalog and mitigation pointers):
- Issue: intermittent NVLink retransmits increase memcpy stalls (ticket: RT-2026-344). Mitigation: adaptively throttle cross-GPU fan-out and schedule co-located shards where possible.
- Issue: quantized-kernel launch path increased p50 by ~12% on T4-like hardware (ticket: RT-2026-410). Mitigation: maintain a hardware compatibility matrix and pin balanced variant for T4 pools until kernel patch 2026.11.05.
- Issue: scheduler preemption pulses cause short-lived lat spikes when preemption_weight > 60. Mitigation: lower preemption_weight to 40 and increase soft-reserve slots.

Appendix A — Config reference (text table):
- admission_rule max_concurrency: integer (1..1024) — cap on concurrent requests per-slot
- admission_rule preemption_weight: integer (0..100) — higher favors higher-priority preemption
- kernel_map_version: string (semantic tag) — must be included in release notes
- kvcache_ttl_seconds: integer — default 300; increase for conversational workloads

Appendix B — Quick commands and debug snippets:
- Live small trace capture (5m): `rwictl trace capture --duration 300s --filter 'model:gemma-v2 & tenant:benchmark' --sampler=adaptive`
- Replay trace in sandbox with pinned kernel map: `rwictl replay --trace <id> --sandbox small-gpu --kernel-map 2026-11-05`
- Generate benchmark report: `benchctl report --input ./reports --format html --output ./reports/summary.html`

Appendix C — Change log and who to notify:
- 2026-02-13: initial draft — Leah O'Connor
- 2026-06-21: added scheduler guardrails and benchmark YAML examples — Marco Chen
- 2026-11-08: expanded known-issues and added rollback CLI snippets — Asha Patel

References and related pages:
- See the runtime decision graph for execution pathways, per-kernel telemetry contract, and the benchmark gold-corpus directory for canonical traces.

Notes and next steps:
- Short-term: adopt the observability contract across all capture agents (target Q1 2027).
- Medium-term: add a machine-readable policy schema and an automated canary gating job that fails PRs if p99 worsens by > 10%.
- Long-term: integrate kernel-safety proofs into CI for critical kernel changes.

If you have questions or need help applying this manual to a live incident, page the runtime-kernel-team and attach trace IDs and benchmark report links.

title: Cross-layer fidelity and cost accounting manual
content:
Summary:
This document defines a reproducible, cross-layer approach for measuring, attributing, and validating "execution fidelity" (quality of model outputs and execution correctness) against token-level and kernel-level cost accounting. It is intended for runtime engineers, performance SREs, and applied ML teams. The manual describes metrics, instrumentation requirements, a validation lab protocol, CI/QA gates, and recommended runbook actions when drift or regressions are detected.

Scope and motivation:
- Scope: hosted, dedicated, and private deployments where the Redwood serving runtime is responsible for kernel selection, KV cache management, batching, and quantization.
- Motivation: teams often treat fidelity (quality) and cost (GPU cycles, token pricing) as separate concerns. Engineering changes (kernel updates, scheduler policies, quantization profiles) create cross-cutting effects that can reduce quality while improving cost or vice versa. This manual provides a standard contract for measuring both and for validating regressions prior to rollout.

Key concepts and definitions:
1) Execution fidelity: a composite of functional correctness checks (deterministic outputs for fixed seeds and prompts), quality evaluation (task-specific metrics like BLEU/ROUGE, embedding cosine retention, or user-defined evals), and runtime consistency (KV cache correctness, repeatable logits for pinned RNG seeds).
2) Cost accounting units:
   - token_compute_ms: per-token kernel time measured in wall-clock milliseconds in the kernel execution path.
   - host_latency_ms: per-request host-side latency excluding kernel execution (scheduling, serialization, network).
   - memory_pressure_score: percentile-based indicator of GPU memory fragmentation affecting eviction rates.
   - kernel_credit_units: abstracted unit mapping per-kernel to normalized cost; used in cost-allocation reports.
3) Cross-layer attribution: mapping from token/response quality deltas to kernel-level events (kernel selection changes, quantization boundaries, batch slice sizes) and to infrastructure events (GPU throttling, NVLink errors).

Instrumentation contract (minimum):
- Traces: every request must emit a trace containing request_id, model_variant, kernel_id, kernel_start_ms, kernel_end_ms, batch_size, sequence_lengths, kvcache_hit_ratio, and rng_seed when provided.
- Metrics: per-kernel counters for invocations, avg_exec_ms, p50/95/99_exec_ms, gpu_util, and transient_error_count.
- Logs: deterministic kernel logs must include stable kernel signature and quantization profile id.
- Probes: a lightweight fidelity probe that can be run on a small sample of requests to compute a quick quality score (see Validation Lab below).

Measurement model and schema (example):
- Reporting key: {date, region, cluster, model_family, model_version, deployment_tier} -> values: [tokens_processed, token_compute_ms_total, host_latency_ms_p50, fidelity_probe_score_p50, kernel_credit_units_total].
- Store rollups at 1m, 15m, 1h granularity.

Validation Lab: reproducible experiment protocol
Purpose: run deterministic workloads (synthetic and live-sampled) through candidate runtime changes and produce a signed report that combines fidelity and cost tradeoffs.
Prerequisites:
- Canary cluster with same kernel-build-id and same model artifacts as candidate.
- Seed corpus: 10k prompt-set with labeled expected behaviours (include edge cases, long-context examples, and hallucination-sensitive prompts).
- Eval harness configured to produce both numeric metrics and qualitative examples.

Protocol steps:
1) Baseline capture (24h): collect baseline metrics on current runtime and model_version for 24 hours using production traffic shadowing OR synthetic replay. Persist kernel traces and fidelity_probe outputs.
2) Controlled candidate run (6h): deploy candidate kernel/scheduler/quantization to canary cluster and replay the identical workload. Ensure identical seed RNG and request ordering when possible to maximize comparability.
3) Compute delta report:
   - For each prompt in the seed corpus compute: quality_delta = candidate_score - baseline_score.
   - Compute cost_delta = (candidate_token_compute_ms_total - baseline_token_compute_ms_total) / baseline_tokens_processed.
   - Flag any prompt with quality_delta < -0.02 (example threshold) and cost_delta < -10% as high-risk.
4) Inspect top 50 negative quality_delta cases with kernel traces attached.
5) Run targeted kernel bisection: if negative cases correlate to a single kernel_id or quantization_profile, run a binary rollback across those kernels to isolate the regression.
6) Sign-off criteria: no more than 0.5% of prompts exceeding the quality_threshold and no regressions in canonical smoke tests; cost improvements > 15% may be accepted if regression cases are triaged and mitigated with fallback policies.

CI/QA gates and automated checks:
- Unit tests: deterministic kernel unit-tests must pass for signed kernels.
- Integration checks: a lightweight fidelity_probe run (sample size 200) with automated alert if probe_score drops below baseline by >1%.
- Pre-merge: bundles that change kernel selection logic require an attached canary-compatibility matrix.
- Pre-release: performance annex must include token_compute_ms delta and the signed Validation Lab report.

Example experiment config (YAML-like inline):
---
experiment_name: "kv-cache-reshard-q3"
seed_corpus: "s3://redwood-evals/kv-reshard-seed/2026-01"
canary_cluster: "canary-eu-west-1-3"
metrics: [fidelity_probe_score, token_compute_ms, host_latency_ms]
rollback_policy: "immediate-on-fidelity-drop"
duration: "6h"
---

Practical checklist for triage when fidelity regressions appear:
1) Confirm measurement integrity: validate that the same seed corpus and RNG seed were used, check trace completeness.
2) Correlate with kernel_id and quantization_profile: use the top-5 kernel attribution table.
3) Check infra signals: GPU thermal and NVLink counters, OOM events, or driver resets during the candidate window.
4) If kernel-level cause: annotates the kernel in the kernel registry and tag as "suspect". Run kernel bisection.
5) If scheduling or batching cause: re-run with reduced batch-size and disabled preemption to compare.
6) Action: rollback, deploy per-route fallback to previous model_variant, or apply a targeted kernel patch.

Operational dashboards and reports (recommended):
- Fidelity vs Cost heatmap: x-axis = fidelity_probe_score delta, y-axis = cost_delta_per_token. Color = incidence count.
- Per-model fidelity anomaly stream: streaming alerts when rolling 1h fidelity_probe_score deviates by >2 sigma.
- Kernel-level ledger: per-kernel deploy history with quick links to Validation Lab reports.

Ownership and responsibilities:
- Runtime SRE (oncall): monitoring, immediate triage, runbook execution for infra failures.
- Runtime Platform: produce Validation Lab report and maintain the experiment harness.
- Applied ML / Model Onboarding: define seed corpus and acceptance thresholds for each model_family.
- Release owner: responsible for including the validation report in the release bundle.

Runbook excerpts (quick actions):
1) Fidelity-alert-fire:
   - Notify: @runtime-sre, @applied-ml; open incident with tag fidelity-regression.
   - Snapshot: capture 1h of kernel traces and the Validation Lab delta report.
   - If kernel_credit_units spike with fidelity drop -> immediate canary rollback.
2) High-cost-variance:
   - If token_compute_ms_per_token > baseline*1.25 for 3 consecutive 5m windows, reduce admission concurrency for affected model_family.

Guidelines for progressive rollouts (canary -> gradual -> global):
- Small canary (1% traffic) with automatic shadowing and deterministic replay.
- Gradual expansion gates: fidelity_probe_score stability and cost_delta within defined envelope for 6 successive evaluation windows.
- Fallback: maintain a per-route automatic fallback policy that can route a small percentage to a stable lower-cost variant for mitigation while preserving availability.

Appendix A: fidelity_probe quick implementation (pseudo):
- Input: list of prompts with expected artefacts.
- Steps:
  1) Send prompts with fixed rng_seed and streaming disabled.
  2) Compare token-level logits for seeded outputs; compute cosine similarity for embeddings and task-specific metrics.
  3) Produce probe_score in [0,1] aggregated as a trimmed mean (drop top/bottom 5%).

Appendix B: example CLI commands
- Run local replay harness: ./tools/replay --cluster canary-eu-west-1-3 --seed s3://... --out report.json
- Generate delta: ./tools/delta-report --baseline baseline.json --candidate candidate.json --out signed-delta.json

Appendix C: common pitfalls and mitigations
- Non-deterministic scheduling: use request ordering locks in the Validation Lab to minimize noise.
- Sampling bias: ensure seed corpus mirrors production tail behaviours (very long contexts, multi-turn chats).
- Metric-churn: adopt trimmed-mean and per-prompt significance testing to avoid false positives.

References and next steps:
- Owners should schedule a quarterly Validation Lab for each major model_family and any kernel release that touches quantization or scheduling.
- See related operational playbooks: runtime-upgrade-validation-and-canary-matrix-2026 and runtime-deployment-circuit-breakers-and-sla-fallback-playbook-2026 for rollout mechanics.

Contact: Maya Chen (runtime-platform) — for implementation support and experiment templates.

title: Runtime integration service contracts and debugging cookbook
content:
Overview:

This document specifies the operational contracts between the Redwood serving runtime and the wider platform (API surface, console, Dedicated/Private control planes, and developer tooling) and provides a pragmatic debugging cookbook for the most common oncall scenarios. The goal is to reduce mean time to mitigation (MTTM) by standardizing observability signals, log schemas, escalation steps, and safe remediation patterns for kernel and scheduler changes, profiling runs, and benchmark integrations.

Scope and audience:
- Audience: runtime engineers, platform engineers, SREs, SDK and developer-experience owners, and solutions engineers running Dedicated/Private deployments.
- Scope: request lifecycle contracts, kernel scheduling signals, profiling/playbook guidance, benchmark integration points, runbook steps for 3 common incidents, and a release/rollout checklist for kernel or runtime changes.

1) Service contract (request lifecycle)

Short summary: every inbound request into the runtime must carry a minimal set of headers and context for observability, routing, and cost accounting. The runtime must emit canonical telemetry during the five canonical phases: ingress, scheduling, kernel execution, KV/cache interactions, and egress.

Required request headers/context (in order of importance):
1. X-Request-Id: unique 128-bit hex string (UUID4 accepted).
2. X-Customer-Id: numeric tenant id or anonymous-token for hosted flows.
3. X-Route-Id: API route or model route identifier (string).
4. X-Desired-SLO-ms: integer SLO target (ms) to drive admission and priority decisions.
5. X-Experiment-Id (optional): A/B/canary identifier for rollout correlation.

Telemetry emission contract (every request):
- Ingress span: tags {request_id, customer_id, route_id, desired_slo_ms, payload_tokens} emitted at reception.
- Scheduling events: queue_enqueue, queue_dequeue, scheduling_decision (reason=priority/affinity/overloaded).
- Kernel span(s): per-kernel traces with attributes {kernel_variant, shard_id, sequence_length, effective_batch_size, kernel_latency_ms}.
- KV/cache events: kvcache_lookup, kvcache_hit/miss (include key pattern categories e.g., prompt-prefix/hash).
- Egress span: final status code, response_tokens, total_token_ms, tail_lat_ms.

2) Observability contract (metrics, logs, traces)

SLOs and key metrics to be exported to the metrics platform (Prometheus/OTLP):
- runtime_request_success_rate (1m, 5m windows) per route_id; SLO target 99.95% for hosted-critical routes.
- runtime_p50_latency_ms, runtime_p95_latency_ms, runtime_p99_latency_ms per (route_id, kernel_variant).
- runtime_queue_depth and runtime_enqueue_rate per scheduling pool (labels: pool_name, priority_level).
- kernel_cpu_utilization_percent, kernel_gpu_utilization_percent per shard.
- kvcache_hit_ratio and kvcache_eviction_rate per shard.
- kernel_oom_count and kernel_memory_pressure_events.

Suggested PromQL queries (store as saved queries):
- P95 latency for route r: topk(10, histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(runtime_request_duration_seconds_bucket{route_id="r"}[5m])) by (le)))
- KVCACHE MISS STORM: increase in miss rate: increase(kvcache_lookup_total{shard="*"}[5m]) - increase(kvcache_hit_total{shard="*"}[5m]) > 1000

Logging schema (single-line JSON log each major event):
| timestamp | level | component | request_id | event | payload | details |
Example log (kernel span start):
{
  "ts":"2026-03-02T15:24:18.123Z",
  "level":"INFO",
  "component":"kernel-runtime",
  "request_id":"8f7a4b2e-1c6b-4a2d-b9d3-4f2c7a1a9f2e",
  "event":"kernel_start",
  "kernel_variant":"kv-quant-int8-v2",
  "shard_id":"shard-21",
  "sequence_length":1024,
  "effective_batch_size":6
}

Tracing contract: every request must be traceable end-to-end with a 128-bit trace id and per-span attributes matching the telemetry contract above. Span names should be stable: ingress, schedule, kernel:<variant>, kvcache:<op>, egress.

3) Kernel and scheduler change rollout checklist (safe rollout and rollback)

Pre-rollout (dev->canary):
- Benchmarks: run microbenchmark suite for candidate kernel against baseline using the stable-run harness (sample config block below).
- Static checks: kernel binary signature, schema validation for kernel hints, and deterministic unit tests for small sequences.
- Canary matrix: select 2% traffic across 3 route shapes (short chat, long-form synthesis, embedding).

Canary config sample (YAML):
---
canary: true
traffic_fraction: 0.02
routes: ["chat-short","text-gen-long","embeddings-avg"]
monitoring: ["p95_latency","error_rate","kvcache_hit_ratio"]
thresholds:
  p95_latency_increase_pct: 15
  error_rate_increase_pct: 0.1
---

Rollout steps (numbered):
1. Start canary with traffic_fraction and attach shadow-mirroring to baseline for fidelity checks.
2. Observe for 30 minutes minimum; validate p95, error rate, kvcache metrics.
3. If anomalies detected beyond thresholds, abort and roll back using the canary_abort endpoint.
4. If stable, ramp to 25% for 2 hours, then to 75% for 6 hours before global.
5. Post-rollout: run a fidelity evaluation against 100 golden prompts and verify token-level output similarity >= 98.5%.

Rollback quick commands:
- redwoodctl runtime canary abort --id <canary_id>
- redwoodctl runtime kernel rollback --variant <baseline_variant> --force

4) Profiling and benchmarking playbook (high level)

Profiling cadence and instrumentation:
- Continuous lightweight sampling: 1% of requests are sampled for full traces and kernel-level microtraces (sufficient for trend detection).
- Full profiling runs for a target route should be scheduled weekly for high-traffic routes and on-demand for incident triage. Use the profiling pipeline with an export window of 72h.
- Budget: keep continuous sampling overhead under 2% CPU/GPU cycle impact.

Benchmark harness integration (developer instructions):
1. Create a scenario YAML describing request surface (percent short/long, concurrency, token distribution). Example:
   - name: long-form-synthesis
     qps: 15
     sequence_length: 1024
     concurrency: 64

2. Run harness against candidate kernels:
   ./bench-runner --scenario scenarios/long-form-synthesis.yaml --kernel kv-quant-int8-v2 --duration 30m --out results/kv-int8-march2026.json

3. Generate comparison report (bench-compare):
   bench-compare --baseline results/baseline.json --candidate results/kv-int8-march2026.json --metrics p95,p99,cost_per_token

Expected pass criteria (example):
- end-to-end p95 <= baseline.p95 * 1.12 for long sequences
- cost_per_token <= baseline.cost_per_token * 0.95 (if claim is cost-reducing)
- no kernel_oom events during 30m run

5) Troubleshooting cookbook (three prioritized incidents)

A. Scenario: sudden spike in p99 tail latency on a model route
Symptoms: p50 stable, p95 up 8%, p99 up 3x, queue_depth rising, kernel_latency_ms shows long tail for kernel_variant kv-quant-int8-v2.

Step-by-step response:
1. Identify affected route and time window (Prometheus query: increase(runtime_request_duration_seconds_count{route_id="<r>"}[10m]) and p99 series).
2. Check scheduling queue for backpressure: runtime_queue_depth{pool_name!~"default"} and recent scheduling_decision events.
3. Inspect kernel spans for tailing latency: filter traces where kernel_variant==kv-quant-int8-v2 and span.duration > 500ms.
4. If kernel spans are long and present across many shards, mark kernel variant as degraded and route to fallback using routing policy: set route override to baseline kernel (redwoodctl route update --route <r> --kernel <baseline>).
5. Kick off a controlled kernel rollback per checklist.
6. After mitigation, capture a reproducible trace (use shadow traffic replay) and file an issue with trace id + top 5 offending spans.

B. Scenario: KVCACHE miss storm after model swap
Symptoms: sudden tail latency and increased GPU utilization; kvcache_hit_ratio drops from ~0.82 to <0.1; high eviction_rate observed.

Steps:
1. Confirm model swap event/time via deployment events store.
2. Run kvcache lookup logs: grep for kvcache_miss events in the window and sample keys.
3. If miss pattern indicates prefix variance, run prefix-hash audit (script: tools/kvcache/prefix-audit.py --trace <trace-id>) to identify mismatched prompt normalization.
4. If prompt normalization is the root cause, roll forward with normalization patch or enable kvcache_warmup mode for affected shards: redwoodctl kvcache warmup --shard <shard-id> --seed-corpus 10k --rate 200/s.
5. If eviction_rate is high due to memory pressure, temporarily increase kvcache capacity for the shard (config change), and schedule a full warmup run.

C. Scenario: intermittent kernel OOMs on heterogenous GPU pool
Symptoms: kernel_oom_count increments scattered, node-level OOM events in node_exporter, some dispatch failures and SIGKILL.

Steps:
1. Identify offending nodes: query kernel_oom_count by node and cross-check node memory pressure metrics.
2. Isolate workload: taint node or cordon it from scheduling to stop new kernels landing: kubectl cordon <node>; redwoodctl runtime drain --node <node> --mode cordon-no-evict
3. Retrieve kernel logs and coredumps for analysis (redwoodctl runtime collect-diagnostics --node <node> --since 1h).
4. If reproducible with specific kernel_variant and sequence_length, schedule immediate rollback of that variant and run a patch: kernel memory request increase or limit tuning.
5. Reintroduce node once validation passes; monitor kernel_oom_count for 2h.

6) Incident handoff and ticketing template

When an incident is triaged and a mitigation applied, create an internal ticket with the following fields (ticket template):
- Title: short summary (route/kernel/incident-type)
- Severity: Sev1/Sev2/Sev3
- Start time / detection time
- Detection signal & link (prometheus/trace id)
- Mitigation applied (commands, canary id, rollback id)
- Root-cause hypothesis
- Owner for RCA and ETA for fix

7) Runbook for oncall rotation owners (quick actions)

Immediate triage checklist (first 15 minutes):
- Confirm scope and blast radius (routes/customers).
- Capture a reproducible trace id and attach to the incident ticket.
- If SLO impact > 0.05% breach projected, escalate to senior SRE and paging policy.
- Execute mitigation (route override, kernel rollback, or kvcache warmup) and note command history.

Escalation matrix:
- Oncall engineer -> runtime-sre lead (pagess) -> runtime eng manager -> product security if customer data affected.

8) Known issues (current catalogue)

- KV-prefetch warmup not idempotent for normalized prompts (INC-2026-0423): symptom is duplicate warmup entries and poor hit stabilization. Mitigation: run warmup with dedupe flag (tools/kvcache/warmup --dedupe). Owner: runtime-cache team.
- Intermittent scheduler preemption hang on GPUs with mixed tensor cores (TICKET-2026-0311): transient preemption leads to long kernel tails; mitigation: apply scheduling fallback to partitioned pool. Owner: scheduler team.
- GRPC connection churn under high multiplex (BUG-2025-2117): affects connection reuse and increases enqueue latency; mitigation: increase per-process connection pool and enable keepalive tuning. Owner: grpc-proxy team.

9) Release notes template for runtime/kernels (to be included in release notes channel)

- Summary: one-sentence summary of change.
- Risk: low/medium/high (reasons).
- Canary plan: traffic fractions, routes in canary.
- Observability: metrics to watch (p95, error_rate, kvcache_hit_ratio, kernel_oom_count).
- Rollback plan and commands.

10) Developer integration checklist (for SDKs and console)

- Ensure SDKs propagate required headers (X-Request-Id, X-Customer-Id, X-Desired-SLO-ms).
- Provide developers a debug helper in SDK (redwood.sdk.debug.capture_trace(request_id)) to attach annotated logs.
- Console must surface route-level canary controls and saved metric views (p95, p99, error_rate) for each canary.

Appendix A — Example configs and commands

1) Example bench-runner command to run mixed workload:
./bench-runner --scenario scenarios/mixed-prod-shape.yaml --kernel kv-quant-int8-v2 --duration 45m --concurrency 128 --out /tmp/kv-int8-run.json

2) redwoodctl quick debug commands:
- redwoodctl runtime traces get --request-id <id> --format json
- redwoodctl runtime metrics snapshot --route <route> --window 15m --out snapshot.json

3) Minimal trace correlation in logs (recommended):
Log line must include: request_id, trace_id, shard_id, kernel_variant, step. Example: "req=%s tid=%s shard=%s kernel=%s step=schedule"

Appendix B — Ownership and SLAs

- Runtime SRE: primary pager for runtime incidents; SLA to acknowledge Sev1 within 5 minutes.
- Kernel & Scheduler team: responsible for kernel rollouts, 24-hour patch turnaround for regressions in canary.
- Developer experience: ensure SDKs carry headers and provide debug helpers.

Appendix C — Where to look next (related docs)

- See runtime-architecture playbooks for deep dive on fallback orchestration.
- See profiler-runner readme for trace collection and analysis steps.

If you have an improvement to this cookbook or an additional triage scenario to include, add a PR to the team-wiki folder or ping @Priya on Slack.

title: On‑Call Rapid Investigation Cheatsheet — Serving Runtime
content:
Purpose

This one-page cheatsheet is designed for first responders on the serving-runtime oncall rotation. It emphasizes fast, high-confidence checks to determine whether a user-visible degradation is: 1) a routing/capacity incident, 2) a kernel or accelerator-level regression, 3) a model/quantization quality issue, or 4) a networking/storage problem. Use this as the initial investigation path to minimize mean time to mitigation (MTTM).

When to use

- Any alert with SLO impact: 95th/99th token latency breach, error rate spike > 1% absolute, or token cost anomaly.
- Customer-reported failures affecting multiple tenants or a Dedicated pool.
- Sudden increase in timeouts, streaming truncations, or model-variant fallbacks.

Quick triage checklist (1–10 minutes)

1) Validate user-facing signal
   - Confirm whether the symptom is global or cohort-specific (hosted vs Dedicated vs Private).
   - Check primary dashboards: "Routes SLO Overview" and "Token Latency by Model Variant" for immediate spikes.

2) Confirm impact scope
   - Isolated to one region? One model? One capacity pool?
   - Look at per-route and per-tenant panels. If only one tenant -> follow customer escalation playbook.

3) Surface network and infra alarms
   - Fast check on infra alerts: node reboots, GPU watchdogs, NVLink errors, cloud network flaps.
   - If there are node-level alerts, mark as likely infra and contact infra-sre.

4) Kernel / scheduling symptoms
   - Identify: concurrent kernel queue growth, long queue times, repeated preemption events.
   - If kernel queue depth correlates with latency, apply admission-control throttle (see Temporary Mitigation).

5) Model & quantization fallbacks
   - Check model swap events and fallback logs: "model_swap_reason" and "quantize_fallback" tags in traces.
   - Correlate recent deployments/rollouts to timing of incident.

6) Caching and KV warmup
   - Look for high miss rates on KV cache and cold-start traces. If a mass warmup is in progress, expect transient latency as caches populate.

Immediate data sources (quick links)

- Observability dashboards: /dashboards/runtime/routes-slo-overview, /dashboards/runtime/kernel-queue, /dashboards/runtime/kvcache-hitrate
- Tracing: Jaeger/Tempo -> Search by trace tags: service=runtime, event=dispatch|kernel|evict, model=<name>
- Logs: central-log (fluentd) queries: "level>=WARN AND (kernel OR eviction OR model_swap)" within last 15m
- Metric queries (Graphite/Prometheus):
  - runtime_dispatch_queue_length{pool="<pool>"}
  - kernel_execution_time_seconds{kernel="attention"}
  - kvcache_hit_rate{shard="*"}
  - per_route_error_rate{route="<route>"}

Fast instrumentation queries (copy-paste)

- Prometheus: max_over_time(runtime_dispatch_queue_length[5m]) > 100 -> indicates queue saturation
- Prometheus: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(kernel_execution_seconds_bucket[1m])) by (le,kernel))
- Fluentd (CLI): 
  curl -s "https://logs.redwood.internal/query?q=level%3D%3DWARN%20AND%20(kernel%20OR%20evict%20OR%20model_swap)&from=-15m" | jq -r '.results[] | .message'

Temporary mitigations (safe, quick)

- Canary route diversion: divert 50% of traffic from affected route to the stable model-variant for 10m. Use console -> Routing -> Temporary divert.
- Admission throttles: apply soft admission limit on the afflicted pool to target queue depth <= 50. Command (operator CLI):
  rwdctl pool throttle set --pool-id <pool> --max-queue 50 --reason "oncall-mitigation"
- Increase autoscale burst for Dedicated pool (if allowed by contract) to blunt sudden throughput surges.
- Retry policy tweak: temporarily set per-request client retry to linear backoff 200ms x 3 to reduce concurrent pressure.

When to escalate

- Escalate to Eng-SRE within 10 minutes if any of: GPU watchdogs present, node OOMs, NVLink bit errors, or >2% sustained 5m SLO breach.
- Escalate to Serving Runtime Kernel team if kernel queue growth remains after admission throttles or if kernel execution time 99th increases by >2x.
- Escalate to Model Onboarding if model fallback/quality regressions coincide with a new model rollout.

Escalation contacts (fast list)

- Eng-SRE Pager: +1-555-0100 (pager) / #eng-sre-oncall
- Serving Runtime Kernel team: @kernel-oncall (Slack) / email kernel-oncall@redwood.ai
- Model Onboarding: @model-oncall / model-oncall@redwood.ai

Investigation play (30–90 minutes)

1) Capture canonical traces: use sampling label "oncall-rapid" and capture 200 traces across affected routes.
2) Run head-to-head microbenchmarks for suspect model-variant on a sandbox node to reproduce elevated kernel exec times. Use the local perf harness:
   ./perf/harness/run_bench --model <model> --sequence 512 --batch 1 --profile
3) If KV miss rate high: run kvcache-prefetch for top 10 prefixes for the route:
   rwdctl kvcache prefetch --route <route> --prefix-file top_prefixes.txt
4) If networking suspected: correlate pod/node network metrics (qdisc drops, retransmits) and cross-check cloud VPC flow logs.

Post-incident steps (ownership and timeline)

- Owner: first responder creates incident ticket and assigns to kernel or infra with summary, key traces, metric snapshots, and mitigation steps taken.
- Within 48 hours: postmortem draft with timeline, root cause hypothesis, and proposed corrective actions.
- Within 7 days: implement one low-effort fix (config, throttle change, or alert tuning).

Quick reference table: SLO thresholds and first responder targets

| Signal | SLO | First-responder target | Typical owner |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 95th token latency (global) | <= 400ms | Acknowledge in 5m, mitigate in 30m | Eng-SRE / Runtime |
| 99th token latency (route) | <= 800ms | Acknowledge in 5m, mitigate in 60m | Runtime Kernel |
| Error rate (per-route) | <= 0.5% | Acknowledge in 5m, mitigate in 30m | Runtime / CS |
| KV cache hit-rate | >= 95% | Identify warmup in 10m | Runtime Ops |

Appendix: Useful snippets and dashboards

- Example trace tags to search:
  - span.tags: {"runtime.phase": "dispatch"}, {"kernel.name":"matmul"}, {"model.variant":"v2-quant"}
- Console actions (UI):
  1. Routing -> Route Health -> Open incident divert
  2. Pools -> Select pool -> Throttles & Autoscale -> Apply temporary change
- Local helper scripts (location): /ops/oncall-scripts/fast_summaries.sh

FAQ / gotchas

- "Why did admission throttle not reduce latency?" -> If kernel execution is the dominant contributor (not queueing), throttling won't help; check kernel_execution_time.
- "We see many model_swap events but no deploys" -> Check quantization autoswitch policy and per-tenant override config.

Owners and maintenance

- Primary owner: Serving Runtime Oncall rotation (team wiki -> rotation calendar).
- Document maintainer: Aisha Patel (serving-runtime-observability team). Please update this cheatsheet after any change to Route SLOs, dispatch instrumentation, or oncall runbook.

Revision history

- 2023-11-15: Initial draft (A. Patel).
- 2024-06-18: Added KV-prefetch quick step and Prometheus queries (D. Morales).
- 2024-12-05: Updated escalation thresholds and automation commands (P. Shah).

title: Runtime change impact matrix & experimentation cookbook
content:
Overview:

This document defines a single, consistent process for assessing the operational impact of changes to the serving runtime and for running controlled experiments (feature gates, kernel rollouts, scheduler tuning, quantization profiles, and routing policies). It combines a lightweight impact matrix with an experimentation cookbook and the minimal runbook snippets required to triage regressions introduced by change. The goal is to reduce blast radius, speed detection, and make rollbacks predictable.

Scope:
- Applies to changes that modify: runtime binary (C++/CUDA), kernel selection mapping, scheduler policy, KV cache behavior, batching heuristics, and routing/fallback rules.
- Excludes purely client-side SDK changes or docs-only updates (those follow a different lightweight process).

Who should use this:
- Release engineers and runtime owners for planned rollouts
- SREs on-call during canaries and business hours
- Performance engineers running microbenchmarks and cost simulations

Owners and Contacts:
- Runtime owner: Alyssa Chen (runtime@redwood.example.com)
- Scheduler lead: Diego Morales
- SRE oncall escalation: pager RUNTIME_PGM

Change impact matrix (summary):

| Change class                         | Primary subsystems affected                 | Risk vector(s)                                     | SLOs to watch                         | Suggested canary scope                  | Rollback threshold (alert-driven)        |
|--------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------|------------------------------------------|
| Kernel mapping or new kernel binary  | kernel scheduler, GPU dispatcher, telemetry | increased tail latency, OOM, kernel hangs         | P99 latency < 250ms; error rate <0.1% | 1% traffic, single region, dev tenants  | P99 > 350ms for 5m OR error% > 0.5%      |
| Scheduler policy change              | request router, admission control, metrics  | priority inversion, head-of-line blocking         | P95 latency < 150ms; queue depth SLAs | 5% traffic, shadowing only               | sustained queue growth > 30%            |
| KV cache eviction/format change      | kvcache, model swap, warm start             | cold-start regressions, model consistency issues  | cold-start P90 < 400ms                 | internal tenants only, off-peak hours    | cold-start P90 > 800ms                  |
| Quantization profile (exec change)   | kernel execution paths, memory footprint     | accuracy regressions, per-token latency increase  | embedding similarity drift < 0.02      | batch replay + 0.5% production traffic   | quality alert (eval) OR latency > 2x    |
| Routing/fallback policy              | routing, model catalog, tracing             | oscillation, request misrouted, capacity overrun  | availability 99.9%                     | canary on non-critical routes            | availability < 99.7% OR oscillation >3x |

Notes:
- SLOs here are global defaults. Product teams may define tighter per-route objectives; include those in the rollout ticket.
- Canary scope should prefer low-risk tenants (internal or dev).

Experimentation cookbook (step-by-step):

1) Plan & impact assessment
   - Create a runtime change card in Jira with: change summary, binary/flag, owner, rollback plan, required observability, required benchmark and eval suites to run.
   - Fill the light-weight impact matrix (use the table above as a template).
   - Required artifacts: perf microbenchmark results, unit tests, regression eval with golden prompts (for quantization or model changes).

2) Lab validation (developer sandbox)
   - Run isolation microbenchmarks from the perf-suite (see section "Benchmarks to run").
   - Run deterministic unit-level CUDA reproducer if applicable.
   - Run the policy through synthetic load generator using the "operational-workload-simulator" harness.

3) Canary (staged)
   - Canary configs: 1% of traffic, single region, low-variance time window (preferably off-peak).
   - Enable verbose telemetry at canary endpoints: kernel traces, kvcache hit rates, scheduler queue depth, per-request decision trace id.
   - Monitor these dashboards: Runtime-P99-Latency, Kernel-Error-Rate, Scheduler-Queue-Depth, Canary-Health.
   - Run automated smoke checks every 30s (example PromQL provided below).

4) Evaluate canary
   - Wait for at least 30 minutes of steady traffic or a minimum of 10k requests (whichever is larger).
   - Evaluate: latency P50/P95/P99, error rate, queue depth percentile, memory growth, GPU SM utilization, and regression eval if applicable.
   - If any rollback threshold breached (see matrix), execute rollback immediately and file an incident.

5) Rollout to broader population
   - If canary passes, increase scope to 10% for one hour, then 30% for two hours, then full rollout.
   - At each step, confirm no regressions and that rollbacks are wired and tested.

6) Post-rollout verification
   - Run the full benchmark suite and a dedicated quality eval within 24h.
   - Update release notes template (see below) and mark the change as stable.

Benchmarks to run (minimum set) :
- Microbench: per-kernel latency (single-threaded) across sequence lengths [8,64,256,1024] on target instance types.
- Mixed workload SLO simulation: run the mixed-workload simulator with tenant mix matching last 7d production sample.
- Burst SLO test: synthetic bursts to validate admission control and backpressure.
- Token-cost regression: end-to-end token cost comparison vs baseline.

Example PromQL smoke checks (copy into canary job):
- Kernel error rate (30s): sum(rate(runtime_kernel_errors_total[30s])) / sum(rate(runtime_requests_total[30s]))
- P99 latency (1m): histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(runtime_request_duration_seconds_bucket[1m])) by (le))
- Scheduler queue depth (1m avg): avg(runtime_scheduler_queue_depth)

Profiling and telemetry checklist during rollout:
- Enable sampling rate to at least 10% for compact traces; ramp to 30% if small regressions are suspected.
- Attach kernel-level timestamps and cuda-kernel ids to traces.
- Collect a small set of full-trace captures (5–10 requests) for failed or slow requests.
- Ensure perf counters (SM utilization, memory bw) and NVLink error counters are surfaced to dashboards.

Release notes template (to be included in the change ticket):
- Title: short summary (single sentence)
- Change id: runtime/commit/hash or flag name
- Jenkins/CI build: link + artifact hash
- Canaries: date/time, scope, passing checks
- Benchmarks: key numbers (P95/P99 vs baseline, token cost delta)
- Known limitations: any outstanding caveats and owners

Runbook snippets (quick triage):

Symptom A: sudden P99 spike (>100% increase) shortly after enabling change
1) Look up canary decision trace IDs and correlate kernel ids.
2) Check kernel error rate query (above) and GPU watchdog alerts.
3) Capture 5 slow traces and compare kernel execution time per segment.
4) If cause is kernel hang or long SM stall, trigger rollback and file incident.

Symptom B: queue depth steadily grows while throughput flatlines
1) Check scheduler policy change flag and admission control metrics.
2) Inspect top-N slow requests by route and trace decision path.
3) If root cause is priority inversion, roll back scheduler change; otherwise tune admission settings.

Symptom C: spike in cold-start latency after KV cache change
1) Validate kvcache hit ratio and warmup hooks.
2) Run canary replay for warmstart paths and compare warmup traces to baseline.
3) If eviction policy regressions found, revert to previous retention and run a targeted warmup job.

Known issues and detection signatures (current):
- Intermittent kernel-side deadlock on Ampere+ 80GB nodes when executing fused attention path under large batch shapes. Signature: occasional 100% SM utilization but zero progress at host level; kernel_timeouts increased. Workaround: disable fused attention for affected kernel patch; fix scheduled for next kernel release.
- KVcache shard skew when tenant affinity mixing changes: detection signature is per-tenant warmup time drift > 3x baseline and increased model-swap events. Workaround: enforce soft-affinity during canaries.

Telemetry queries and dashboards (examples):
- Basic canary dashboard widgets:
  - Request P50/P95/P99 over time (per model variant)
  - Kernel error rate and error types (OOM, kernel-crash, watchdog)
  - Scheduler queue depth histogram (per priority class)
  - KVcache hit rate and average warmup time
- Suggested alerting thresholds:
  - Canary-P99>350ms sustained 5m -> Sev2
  - Kernel error rate >0.5% for 5m -> Sev1
  - Queue growth > 30% for 10m -> Sev2
Example canary CLI steps (for runtime binary + flag rollouts):
```
# build and upload runtime artifact
bazel build //runtime:server --config=release
artifacts upload ./bazel-bin/runtime/server.tar.gz --tag runtime/2026-02-18

# create canary rollout with 1% traffic
redwoodctl rollout create --service runtime --artifact runtime/2026-02-18 --scope canary --percent 1 --region us-west-2 --flag enable-new-sched=true

# watch logs and metrics
redwoodctl rollout watch --id <rollout-id>
```

Quality eval example (for quantization changes):
- Run golden prompt set (1000 prompts) and compute: exact-match, BLEU if applicable, and embedding drift (cosine) with baseline. Alert if embedding mean drift > 0.02 or exact-match drops > 1.5%.

Postmortem and learning loop:
- If a rollback occurs, create an incident review within 72h describing: what changed, what triggered detection, timeline, root cause, and at least two action items (one for technical fix, one for process improvement).

Appendix A — Small impact matrix (CSV for ticket copy-paste):
ChangeClass,Subsystems,PrimaryRisk,SLOToWatch,CanaryScope,RollbackCondition
KernelBinary,kernel-scheduler;gpu-dispatcher,tail-latency;oom,P99<250ms,1%/dev,P99>350ms or error%>0.5%
SchedulerPolicy,router;admission-control,queue-growth,P95<150ms,5%/shadow,queue_growth>30%
KVCache,kvcache;model-swap,cold-starts,coldstart_P90<400ms,internal-only,coldstart_P90>800ms
QuantProfile,kernel-exec;memory,quality-drift;latency,embedding_drift<0.02,batch-replay,eval_alert_or_latency>2x
Routing,router;catalog,availability;oscillation,availability>99.9%,non-critical_routes,availability<99.7%

Appendix B — Links and references:
- Runtime decision graph (internal): /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/runtime-decision-graph-and-observed-behaviour-catalog-2026
- Continuous profiling strategy: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/continuous-runtime-profiling-strategy-2026
- Mixed-workload simulator: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/mixed-workload-slo-simulation-suite-2026

If you have feedback on this cookbook or find missing telemetry hooks, please tag the runtime team and create an improvement ticket (label: runtime-rollout-improvement).

title: Execution Cohort Playbook and Experiment Journal
content:
Purpose
-----
This document describes the "execution cohort" concept we use to group similar inference requests for improved latency predictability and cost efficiency. It combines architecture notes, scheduling policy pseudocode, a profiling playbook for cohort-related regressions, a benchmarking experiment design, a release checklist, a curated known-issues list, and incident runbooks.

Audience
--------
- Runtime engineers implementing or tuning the scheduler and kernel selection.
- SREs owning runtime availability and alerting.
- Applied ML engineers designing workload-fit experiments.

Goals and success criteria
--------------------------
- Reduce P99 tail latency variance for small/interactive models by >= 20% versus baseline.
- Maintain per-tenant throughput within 10% of historical baseline while reducing per-token cost.
- Provide deterministic, reproducible experiment artifacts for every scheduling change.

Scope and non-goals
-------------------
- In scope: cohort creation heuristics, scheduling policy, kernel dispatch interaction, profiling and benchmark plans, runbook steps for cohort incidents.
- Not in scope: model quantization strategy, private-deployment network setup (see eng-private-deployments docs).

Architecture overview (text diagram)
-----------------------------------
Key services and components involved:
- runtime-cohort-manager (component that classifies incoming requests into cohorts)
- kernel-dispatcher (maps scheduled slots to GPU kernels/queues)
- kv-cache-proxy (shared KV cache service for prefix reuse)
- scheduler-ledger (global admission controller and capacity accounting)
- telemetry-ingest (traces, events, metrics pipeline)

Simple ASCII diagram:

  client -> ingress-router -> runtime-cohort-manager --+--> scheduler-ledger --> kernel-dispatcher --> GPU
                                                       |\
                                                       +--> kv-cache-proxy (hot prefix reuse)

Design intent:
- Cohorts are immutable for the lifetime of a request. Classification is cheap and stable (hash + lightweight fingerprint).
- Scheduler decisions are made at cohort granularity (batching, priority, slot reservation).
- The kernel-dispatcher uses cohort metadata to select optimized kernels and execution paths (e.g., fused-attention, reduced-precision path).

Cohort definition and metadata fields
------------------------------------
Each cohort record contains flat fields used by multiple subsystems:
- cohort_id (string)
- workload_family (string, e.g., "chat-short", "embedding-long")
- model_variant (string)
- target_slo_ms (numeric as string, e.g., "120")
- prefer_low_latency (true/false as string)
- suggested_batching (string, e.g., "auto|max_tokens:64|min_batch:1")
- kv_cache_key_hint (short string)
- owner (team/email)

Cohort lifecycle
----------------
1. Classification: runtime-cohort-manager computes fingerprint and assigns cohort_id.
2. Admission: scheduler-ledger evaluates slot credits and admission rules.
3. Dispatch: kernel-dispatcher picks the kernel path and queue.
4. Post-process: telemetry-ingest tags traces with cohort_id and quality signals.

Priority and fairness policy (plain-language)
-------------------------------------------
- Priority is a function of (SLO attainment delta, observed tail risk, tenant SLAs).
- Fairness is enforced by token-based credit accounting in scheduler-ledger.
- Emergency preemption rules: high-priority control-plane traffic and SLA-protected cohorts can preempt best-effort cohorts up to a configured cap (default 15% of active slots).

Scheduling policy pseudocode
----------------------------
// Simplified view used in design discussions
function admit_request(request):
  cohort = classify(request)
  credits = ledger.peek_credits(cohort.owner)
  if credits < cohort.min_credit_threshold:
    if cohort.prefer_low_latency == "true":
      // try fast-path hedging up to X times
      return try_fast_path_hedge(request, cohort)
    else:
      return queue_in_backlog(request, cohort)
  // apply latency headroom check
  estimated_latency = kernel_dispatcher.estimate_latency(cohort, request.tokens)
  if estimated_latency <= cohort.target_slo_ms * 1.2:
    ledger.consume(credits, estimate_cost(request))
    return schedule_on_queue(request, cohort.preferred_queue)
  else:
    return fallback_to_variant_or_degrade(request)

Key tunables (table)
--------------------
- min_credit_threshold: smallest credit bucket to allow admission (default "5").
- hedging_max_attempts: max hedges for low-latency cohorts (default "2").
- preemption_cap_pct: percentage of slots reclaimable for SLAs (default "15").
- kv_prefetch_window_ms: how far ahead to warm prefix cache (default "200").

Profiling playbook for cohort regressions
---------------------------------------
When a cohort shows increased tail latency or error rate, follow these steps:
1. Capture a deterministic traffic sample (10k requests) by inserting a traffic mirror rule for cohort_id.
2. Run lightweight traces: set telemetry-ingest sampling to 100% for cohort_id for 1 minute.
3. Collect kernel-level timelines: use kernel-trace-tool "ktctl sample --cohort <id> --duration 60s --out /tmp/kt.json".
4. Correlate traces with ledger events: ledger.trace_id -> kernel-trace -> application trace.
5. If KV cache miss rate > 30% for the cohort, run kv-cache-warmup script and re-evaluate.
6. If kernel queuing time accounts for >50% of tail latency, escalate to kernel team with attached kt.json and sampled traces.

Profiling commands and quick checks
----------------------------------
- Check admission backlog: curl -s http://scheduler-ledger.local/metrics | jq '.backlog_by_cohort["<cohort_id>"]'
- Kernel queue times: ktctl histogram --cohort <id> --metric queue_ms
- KV cache hit ratio: curl http://kv-cache-proxy/metrics | grep cohort_<id>_hit_ratio

Benchmarking experiment design (template)
---------------------------------------
Objective: evaluate impact of cohort-aware scheduling on tail latency and cost.
Experiment matrix (examples):
- Variables: batch_size {1,4,8}, concurrency_shape {steady, bursty-10s, spiky-1s}, model_variant {v1, v1-quant}  
- Metrics: P50, P95, P99 latency, CPU/GPU utilization, tokens/sec, tokens/cost, cohort_kv_hit_ratio, queue_time_ms.

Sample YAML workload config:
```yaml
workload_name: chat-short-burst-test
model: gptx-chat-v1
cohort_label: chat-short
duration_s: 900
phases:
  - name: warmup
    qps: 50
    duration_s: 120
  - name: burst
    qps: 1200
    duration_s: 30
  - name: steady
    qps: 200
    duration_s: 660
request_shape:
  avg_tokens: 48
  seed_variability: high
batch_policy:
  enabled: true
  max_batch_tokens: 256
  max_batch_requests: 8
```

Benchmark collection checklist:
- Mirror production ingress for the cohort (shadow-mode)
- Collect kernel-trace logs (ktctl) and telemetry traces for entire run
- Snapshot scheduler-ledger state before/after test
- Record cost estimate via runtime-cost-sim tool

Release checklist for scheduler/cohort changes
--------------------------------------------
1. Update unit tests for scheduler policy language and cohort classification.
2. Run local microbenchmarks (microbench-suite) and record baseline artifacts.
3. Create canary branch with new policy and schedule canary deployment across 1% of requests for 24 hours.
4. Monitor KPIs: P95, P99, queue_time_ms, kernel_queue_depth, error_rate.
5. If regressions are detected, revert using feature-flag rollback or scale down new variants.
6. Post-mortem experiment: reproduce with synthetic workload within 72 hours.

Known issues (curated)
---------------------
1) Cohort oscillation under mixed bursty traffic
- Symptom: cohort membership toggles for identical request fingerprints leading to cache fragmentation.
- Probable root cause: fingerprint window too short (default 30s).
- Mitigation: increase fingerprint stability window to 5 minutes for high-throughput cohorts; schedule a follow-up stability test.

2) Hedging-created duplicate kernel load
- Symptom: hedged fast-path attempts increase GPU occupancy and raise queue times for best-effort cohorts.
- Root cause: lack of cross-cohort hedging circuit-breaker.
- Mitigation: enforce global_hedge_inflight limit and introduce per-node hedging accounting.

3) KV prefetch storm on rollout
- Symptom: massive KV warmups when a variant is rolled out, causing transient I/O saturation.
- Root cause: naive prefetch for all cohorts on deploy.
- Mitigation: stagger kv_prefetch_window and use probabilistic prefetch sampling (10% initially).

4) Scheduler-ledger stale view after partial-network-partition
- Symptom: admission decisions based on outdated credits causing over-admission.
- Root cause: optimistic-local-ledger without timely reconciliation.
- Mitigation: enable short reconciliation heartbeat (default 2s) and fall back to conservative admission if heartbeat missed > 3x.

Runbook: Cohort starvation incident
----------------------------------
Trigger: alert "cohort_p99_latency > 2x target for 5 minutes" or backlog growth > 5000 requests.
Immediate steps (0–5 minutes):
1. Pager to oncall runtime engineer.
2. Run quick health checks:
   - curl http://scheduler-ledger.local/health
   - ktctl histogram --cohort <id> --metric queue_ms --last 5m
3. If kernel queue_ms > 300ms and backlog growing, scale temporary admission down: curl -XPOST http://scheduler-ledger.local/actuate "{\"action\":\"throttle_cohort\",\"cohort\":\"<id>\",\"pct\":\"50\"}"
4. If KV miss ratio > 40%, trigger kv-cache warmup and allocate one prefetch worker: kvprefetchctl start --cohort <id> --workers 1
5. If situation persists beyond 15 minutes, revert recent scheduler changes (feature flag) and roll back canary.

Post-incident actions (within 72 hours):
- Run profiling playbook and attach artifacts to incident ticket.
- Schedule a postmortem and update cohort stability parameters.

Telemetry and dashboards (recommended)
-------------------------------------
Essential metrics (metric names follow internal conventions):
- cohort.<cohort_id>.p50_ms, p95_ms, p99_ms
- cohort.<cohort_id>.queue_time_ms
- cohort.<cohort_id>.kv_hit_ratio
- scheduler.ledger.backlog_by_cohort
- kernel.queue_depth, kernel.exec_time_ms_histogram
- runtime.coalesced_batch_size_by_cohort

Suggested alert thresholds (example)
- cohort.<id>.p99_ms > target_slo_ms * 2 for 5m -> P1
- cohort.<id>.kv_hit_ratio < 0.5 for 10m -> P2
- scheduler.ledger.backlog_by_cohort > 1000 -> P1

Experiment journal template (copy into new experiment ticket)
------------------------------------------------------------
- experiment_id: (auto)
- lead: name/email
- hypothesis: short sentence
- cohort_ids: list
- config_snapshot: (link to S3 / artifact)
- benchmark_matrix: (variables & ranges)
- start_time / end_time
- raw_artifacts: list of links (ktctl, traces, ledger snapshots)
- outcome: pass/fail/observations
- followups: actionable items

Ownership and contacts
----------------------
- runtime-cohort-manager: @runtime-team (primary)
- kernel-dispatcher: @kernels-team (secondary)
- scheduler-ledger: @sre-runtime
- telemetry and traces: @observability

Appendix: quick reference commands
---------------------------------
- classify example: curl -XPOST http://runtime-cohort-manager/classify -d '{"request": "..."}'
- ledger peek: curl http://scheduler-ledger.local/credits?owner=<team>
- start a focused trace: tracectl start --filter cohort_id=<id> --duration 60s
- canary rollback: ffctl disable feature.scheduler_new_policy

Notes and change history
------------------------
- 2026-02-15: Created by Aisha Khatri.
