- 2026-03-01: Added hedging limits and incident runbook; reviewers Marcus Li, Sofia Alvarez, Dmitri Petrov.

Related reading
---------------
- See runtime-architecture/runtime-decision-graph-and-observed-behaviour-catalog-2026 for decision graphs.
- See kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-policy-language-declarative-profiles-2026 for policy language reference.

End of document.

title: Runtime Observability Data Model and Tracebook
content:
Overview

This page defines the canonical telemetry/trace data model for the Redwood serving runtime, and collects pragmatic recipes (the "Tracebook") for diagnosing common kernel-scheduling and runtime-performance incidents. The goal is a single reference that: (1) standardizes events/labels emitted by runtime components, (2) specifies trace/span correlation conventions, and (3) provides step-by-step debugging playbooks for triaging GPU/CPU contention, KV-cache hotlines, and kernel fallback behavior.

Scope

- Components: dispatcher, rserv (user-level runtime), k-scheduler, kvcache-shard, loader, trace-collector.
- Signals: traces (OpenTelemetry), metrics (Prometheus), kernel events (perf/kern logs), GPU-side counters (NVIDIA DCGM where available).
- Not in scope: application-level prompts, customer PII, non-runtime business metrics.

Key principles

1) Consistent IDs: every request must carry request_id, route_id, and shard_id tags.
2) Lightweight single-sample events: emit small structured events at scheduling boundaries rather than large stack dumps.
3) Correlatable traces: attach source=client and model_variant labels to spans.
4) Dual-plane visibility: metric-derived alerts (SLOs) and trace-first investigations (root-cause).

Canonical fields (string keys emitted on spans/metrics)

| Field | Type | Meaning | Example |
|-------|------|---------|---------|
| request_id | string | Global request UUID injected at ingress | req_2026-03-01_7f3a |
| route_id | string | API route or customer route identifier | route:chat-completion-v2 |
| model_variant | string | Model identifier + quantization tag | gptj-16k-q8_0 |
| shard_id | string | Serving shard identifier (node:gpu index) | shard-usw2-12:gpu3 |
| kernel_path | string | Kernel execution path annotation | attention/sharded_fused |
| sched_policy | string | Scheduling policy used | preemptive/priority-bucket |
| kv_cache_hit | boolean | Hit/miss indicator for prefix cache | true |
| queue_time_ms | number | Time waiting to enter GPU queue | 4.2 |
| exec_time_ms | number | Kernel execution duration on GPU | 1.8 |
| fallback_reason | string | Why a fallback path executed | quant_conv_unavailable |

Trace/span conventions

- Tracer: OpenTelemetry (OTel) format. All internal services must use the Redwood OTel SDK wrapper which ensures:
  - Sampling: adaptive sampling that retains all traces flagged by alert rules (see section below).
  - Exporter: to the internal trace-collector — endpoint: https://trace-collector.internal:4317.
  - Baggage: request_id, route_id, model_variant.

- Span hierarchy (recommended):
  - ingress.span (generated by dispatcher)
    - request.routing.span (route decision + model variant lookup)
      - k-scheduler.enqueue.span (time added to scheduling queue)
        - k-scheduler.schedule.span (scheduling decision, includes policy)
          - gpu.exec.span (kernel execution; attach kernel_path, exec_time_ms)
          - kvcache.lookup.span (if prefix cache involved)

Instrumenting kernel scheduling details

Attach the following attributes to k-scheduler spans: sched_policy, priority_bucket (0-7), preemptible (true/false), soft_deadline_ms, queue_time_ms. Use numeric buckets for quick aggregation: priority_bucket: 0 (lowest) .. 7 (highest).

Kernel event taxonomy

- Normal exec: kernel_path includes architecture and fused-op indicators (e.g., attention/axial_fused_fp16). exec_time_ms reflects wallclock time on GPU.
- Fallback exec: fallback_reason present; often accompanied by increased exec_time_ms and a kernel shim label (kernel_path: attention/fallback_cpu_sync).
- OOM/Retry: emit event oom_attempts (int) on gpu.exec.span and increment metric runtime.kernel.oom_attempts.

Metric naming and SLOs

- Metrics (Prometheus):
  - runtime.request.latency_p50_ms, runtime.request.latency_p95_ms, runtime.request.latency_p99_ms
  - runtime.kernel.exec_time_ms_bucket (histogram)
  - runtime.kvcache.hit_ratio (gauge by route/model)
  - runtime.scheduler.queue_time_ms_summary
  - runtime.kernel.fallback_count_total

- Example SLOs (for hosted API):
  - 95th percentile end-to-end latency <= 300ms for short-text route (<=256 tokens).
  - kernel fallback rate < 0.5% per model_variant over 24h.
  - KV cache hit_ratio >= 0.70 for conversational workloads in dedicated pools.

Tracebook: triage recipes

1) Symptom: sudden spike in request p99 for route:chat-completion-v2
- Step 1: open dashboard -> route latency -> filter route_id=chat-completion-v2 and time range last 30m.
- Step 2: check metric runtime.scheduler.queue_time_ms_summary and runtime.kernel.exec_time_ms_bucket. If queue_time_ms increased sharply -> contention at scheduling layer.
- Step 3: search traces by route_id + tag priority_bucket. Run query: resource.attributes.route_id:chat-completion-v2 AND k-scheduler.enqueue.span.queue_time_ms:>50.
- Step 4a: If many traces show priority_bucket==0 and preemptible==true, check autoscaling and pool utilization (gpu-fleet dashboard). Action: temporarily raise priority for recent canary traffic or route to dedicated pool.
- Step 4b: If exec_time_ms increased while queue_time small, inspect kernel_path for fallback_reason and kernel metrics. Common causes: quantization kernel not available on this GPU driver build -> fallback to CPU. Open host logs /var/log/rserv/kernel-fallback.log.

2) Symptom: elevated kernel fallback_count_total for model_variant=gptj-16k-q8_0
- Step 1: grep traces: fallback_reason and kernel_path. Look for recurring reason strings (e.g., quant_conv_unavailable, fused_op_missing).
- Step 2: correlate with node labels: hardware_capability and driver_version. Query node exporter: node_gpu_driver_version{model_variant=~"gptj.*"}. If failure concentrated on specific driver range -> roll forward driver or pin compatible variant.
- Step 3: rollback plan: pin affected route to older model_variant or disable aggressive quantization profile in the route config (console -> model routing -> override quant_profile).

3) Symptom: KV cache hit_ratio drop for a customer on dedicated pool
- Step 1: examine kvcache.shard metrics: runtime.kvcache.hit_ratio by shard_id and route_id.
- Step 2: inspect shard placement: k8s label shard_affinity and rough cache_size usage. If one shard shows >80% eviction_rate, run cache diagnostics: curl http://kvcache-shard-$SHARD/diagnostics | jq .eviction_histogram.
- Step 3: mitigation: increase per-shard cache_size (config map: kvcache-shard.size_mb) or rebalance routes to spread hot prefixes.

Investigating GPU kernel stalls and preemption

- Signals to collect: long-running gpu.exec.span (> 10ms for small kernels), per-GPU utilization (DCGM: sm_util), power draw spikes, and GPU-side queue depths.
- Recommended command on onprem nodes: 
  - dcgmi dmon -e 0 -s 200ms --format csv > /tmp/gpu-dmon.csv
  - ncu --target-processes all --kernel-name-base demangled --sample 200ms (only in controlled debug environments)

- If kernel exec_time_ms is high but SM utilization low, suspect memory-bound ops or PCIe stalls. Check node dmesg for pci errors and nvidia-smi pmon.

Trace and metric retention and sampling policy

- Retention: spans retained for 30 days in trace-store for production; high-fidelity traces for flagged incidents kept for 90 days.
- Sampling: default 1% head-sampling, adaptive increase to 100% for traces that hit any of these conditions: runtime.request.latency_p99>2*SLO, any kernel.fallback_reason present, or runtime.kvcache.hit_ratio<0.4.

Alerting examples

- Alert: runtime-kernel-fallback-rate-high
  - Query: increase(rate(runtime.kernel.fallback_count_total[5m])) by (model_variant) > 0.005
  - Severity: P2
  - Runbook: follow Tracebook recipe 2 (fallback investigation) and open a ticket with infra if driver incompatibility suspected.

- Alert: scheduler-queue-growth
  - Query: increase(runtime.scheduler.queue_time_ms_summary{quantile=\"0.95\"}[10m]) > 50ms
  - Severity: P1 if sustained for >5m
  - Runbook: see Tracebook recipe 1. Consider emergency scaling or temporary routing to dedicated pools.

Implementation checklist for instrumenters

- [ ] Use Redwood OTel SDK wrapper and ensure request_id is propagated across RPCs.
- [ ] Emit the canonical fields on k-scheduler and gpu.exec spans.
- [ ] Attach lightweight numeric tags (priority_bucket) for efficient aggregation.
- [ ] Add a top-level metric runtime.kernel.fallback_count_total with label fallback_reason.
- [ ] Add unit-tests that assert span attribute presence in end-to-end integration tests (see test/observability/integration in repo).

Dashboard and queries (examples)

- Grafana panels to build:
  - Per-route latency waterfall: groups by queue_time_ms vs exec_time_ms.
  - Kernel fallback heatmap: model_variant x driver_version -> fallback_count_total.
  - KV cache occupancy and eviction rate by shard.

- Example PromQL: 
  - p95 latency: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(runtime_request_latency_bucket{route_id=\"chat-completion-v2\"}[5m])) by (le))
  - fallback rate by model: increase(runtime_kernel_fallback_count_total[10m]) / increase(runtime_requests_total[10m])

Ownership and escalation

- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime ( observability squad )
- Oncall escalation: SRE -> runtime infra -> applied-ml (for model-specific regressions)

Appendix A: example trace JSON (OTel-like, trimmed)

{
  "traceId": "4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736",
  "spans": [
    {
      "name": "ingress.span",
      "attributes": {
        "request_id": "req_2026-03-01_7f3a",
        "route_id": "chat-completion-v2",
        "model_variant": "gptj-16k-q8_0"
      }
    },
    {
      "name": "k-scheduler.schedule.span",
      "attributes": {
        "sched_policy": "preemptive",
        "priority_bucket": "3",
        "queue_time_ms": "72.4"
      }
    },
    {
      "name": "gpu.exec.span",
      "attributes": {
        "kernel_path": "attention/fallback_cpu_sync",
        "exec_time_ms": "28.9",
        "fallback_reason": "quant_conv_unavailable"
      }
    }
  ]
}

Appendix B: quick CLI snippets

- Search traces in trace-collector (OTel query API):
  curl -sS -H \"Content-Type: application/json\" -X POST https://trace-collector.internal:4318/api/traces/search -d '{"query":"resource.attributes.route_id:chat-completion-v2 AND resource.attributes.model_variant:gptj*"}' | jq .hits

- Inspect kvcache shard diagnostics:
  export SHARD=shard-usw2-12
  curl -sS http://kvcache-shard-$SHARD:8080/diagnostics | jq

- Spin a high-priority scheduling test (internal loadgen):
  rloadgen run --route chat-completion-v2 --qps 200 --priority 7 --duration 5m

Changelog

- 2025-11-12: initial draft (Asha Kapoor).
- 2026-01-08: added adaptive sampling and retention policy (Rina Patel).
- 2026-02-18: extended Tracebook with fallback investigation steps and CLI snippets (Miguel Santos).

If something in this model prevents practical instrumentation or causes cardinality explosion, contact observability@redwood.ai and propose a compact alternative.

title: third-party-accelerator-onboarding-and-runtime-integration-2026
content:
Overview

Purpose: This document defines the engineering process, interface contracts, testing checklist, performance profiling playbook, and runbook steps required to safely onboard third-party accelerator kernels (vendor-provided or community plugins) into Redwood's serving runtime. It is intended for runtime engineers, kernel maintainers, release engineers, and partners delivering binary kernels.

Scope: Includes ABI/handshake, scheduling delegation, telemetry requirements, automated benchmarks, release gating criteria, and emergency rollback procedures. Does NOT cover dedicated/hardware procurement policies or vendor commercial agreements.

Key goals
- Protect production SLOs (p95 latency, p99 tail, and throughput) when new kernels are introduced.
- Ensure predictable fallbacks and fast mitigation for regressions.
- Provide a repeatable onboarding checklist for partner kernels.
- Integrate kernel-level telemetry into profiler and benchmark suites.

1) Architecture and contracts
1.1 High-level flow
- Client request -> Router -> Kernel-aware Scheduler -> Accelerator Driver -> Kernel Binary -> Execution -> KV Cache / Memory Manager -> Response
- The scheduler exposes a lightweight delegation API to accept or decline work based on kernel-reported capacity hints.

1.2 Required contracts (must be implemented by any third-party kernel)
- ABI handshake: JSON manifest exchanged at registration time containing: kernel_id, supported-ops, max_sequence_length, preferred_batch_shape, memory_reservation_bytes, suggested_concurrency, quantization_support (none/int8/fp16), version, and signature (SHA256).
- Health API: /kernel/health -> { status: ready|degraded|unavailable, current_load: int, available_slots: int } (gRPC or HTTP as configured).
- Telemetry hooks: emit tracing span with tag kernel.id, provide per-call token_count and per-buffer memory_usage metrics.
- Fallback hints: on degradation kernel must supply a suggested fallback model_variant or indicate graceful-degradation behavior.

2) Scheduling & delegation model
- Scheduler roles: admission control, prioritization, and preemption signaling.
- Delegation handshake: scheduler sends a PROBE (100–200ms budget) to allow kernel to confirm readiness and advertise capacity. If no response within the probe window, scheduler treats kernel as unavailable for that allocation.
- Priority mapping: requests carry route_priority (0=system,1=premium,2=default,3=best-effort). Kernel must accept or reject based on a priority bitmap advertised in the manifest.
- Preemption signal: scheduler may send PREEMPT_WITH_INTENT to request graceful early termination of lower-priority in-flight work. Kernels must support checkpointing of KV cache state if execution spans >500ms.

3) Profiling playbook for new kernels
- Baseline collection steps (automated pipeline)
  1. Deploy kernel in isolated sandbox cluster with synthetic traffic that mirrors target route shapes (short-form-chat, long-sequence-completion, embeddings).
  2. Run 3 x 30-minute runs per workload shape at steady concurrency targets: low (10%), nominal (100%), and burst (300%).
  3. Capture full traces, kernel internal counters, GPU occupancy, PCIe/NVLink bandwidth, host CPU steal, and memory fragmentation metrics.
- Key signals to evaluate
  - mean_token_latency, p95/p99 token generation latency, kernel_dispatch_time, kernel_queue_wait, kernel_compute_time, kvcache_hit_ratio, memory_alloc_failures.
  - cost proxy: tokens/sec per accelerator-hour and estimated $/1M tokens using current price model.
- Failure modes to flag automatically
  - sudden increase (>20%) in p99 with no corresponding CPU or request-shape delta.
  - unbounded growth in memory ( > 5% per minute over 5 minutes).
  - frequent short bumps in kernel_queue_wait correlated with NVLink retransmits.

4) Benchmarking suite integration steps
- Add kernel to perf-registry: a YAML entry in the benchmarking repo with fields: kernel_id, node_type, driver_version, regression_thresholds. Example table:
| field | example | description |
| kernel_id | vendorX-int8-v2 | unique id used in manifests |
| node_type | g10x-48GB | validated hardware profile |
| driver_version | 4.2.1 | expected driver / runtime combo |
| p99_threshold_ms | 42 | absolute gating p99 for nominal workload |
| throughput_tokens_per_sec | 12_000 | expected steady-state throughput |

- Bench harness requirements
  - Must run the kernel under the same batching and prefix-caching configs used in production.
  - Mirror request provenance (token lengths, system prompts, function call patterns).
  - Produce an artifact: annotated trace (.zip) plus a normalized perf JSON that includes histograms.

5) Release gating and validation
- Mandatory checks (all must pass for canary rollout)
  1. Unit trust: manifest signature verified and integration tests pass (functional correctness).
  2. Canary perf: benchmark harness p99 and throughput within 95% of golden baseline.
  3. Telemetry conformity: kernel emits required spans and metrics.
  4. Graceful-fallback test: simulated node failure triggers scheduler fallback without client error rate > 0.1%.
- Progressive rollout plan
  1. Sandbox -> internal canary (5% infra) for 24h -> expanded canary (25%) for 72h -> production (100%) with 2-week monitoring holds.
  2. Automatic rollback if: p99 increases by >25% or error rate increases by >0.5% over baseline within the observation window.

6) Known issues and mitigation patterns (for this kernel onboarding flow)
- Issue: kernel reports low available_slots intermittently causing oscillation. Mitigation: enable probe backoff to 2s and increase scheduler probe timeout for the node pool.
- Issue: memory fragmentation leads to OOM on long sequences. Mitigation: enable slab compaction on host and tune kernel memory_reservation_bytes in manifest.
- Issue: degraded telemetry fidelity (missing token_count). Mitigation: fail the canary and require kernel debug build with logging enabled; add temporary sidecar to enrich traces.

7) Runbook: emergency rollback (fast path)
- Preconditions: alert fires for rolling-p99-regression OR >0.2% client errors for >5 minutes.
- Fast rollback steps (under 15 minutes target)
  1. Runbook initiator (oncall) adds "kernel-quarantine" tag to affected node group in cluster manager.
  2. Drain new kernel variant from router by toggling route-level kernel preference to previous kernel_id via feature toggle service.
  3. Trigger scheduler-level evict-and-failover: call /scheduler/evict?kernel_id=<id>&grace=30s on impacted pool.
  4. Revert driver-level configuration if driver update applied within last 6h.
  5. Roll forward mitigation: re-run perf smoke tests on a mirrored sandbox; if passes, perform controlled reintroduce at 5% for 2 hours.
  6. Document incident in postmortem with timeline, traces, and kernels artifacts.

Checklist quick-reference (for on-call)
- [ ] Is the manifest signature valid?
- [ ] Are health pings returning `ready` from all nodes?
- [ ] Is p99 > baseline by threshold? (check dashboard)
- [ ] Apply kernel-quarantine tag if failing
- [ ] Start rollback sequence and notify ops@redwood.com

8) Ownership & contacts
- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime (runtime-kernel-onboarding squad)
- Secondary owners: infra-release, eng-platform-observability
- Pager escalation: runtime-oncall -> kernel-oncall -> eng-platform SRE lead
- Documentation owner: Aisha Kumar

9) Appendix: sample manifest (stringified)
| key | example | notes |
|-----------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------|
| kernel_id | vendorx/gemm-int8-2026-04 | must be globally unique within perf registry |
| supported_ops | ["matmul","attention","layernorm"] | operator subset; runtime will reject ops not listed |
| preferred_batch_shape | [1, 8, 2048] | suggested batch shapes for best throughput |
| memory_reservation_bytes | 40000000000 | reserve 40GB to avoid fragmentation |
| telemetry_version | 1.1 | matches runtime tracer contract |

CLI snippets
- Register kernel manifest: redwoodctl kernel register --manifest=vendorx-manifest.json --pool=canary-pool
- Run benchmark: redwood-bench run --kernel=vendorx/gemm-int8-2026-04 --profile=long-seq --output=artifacts/vendorx.zip
- Quarantine pool: redwoodctl pool tag add --pool=canary-pool --tag=kernel-quarantine

Change log / release notes (template)
- 2026-03-01: Initial draft and checklist published (Aisha Kumar)
- 2026-03-10: Updated profiling thresholds and added emergency rollback steps (reviewers: Miguel Santos, Priya Nair)

Related artifacts
- Benchmarking repo: git@internal:redwood/serving-benchmarks.git (perf-registry / kernel-entries)
- Telemetry schema: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/runtime-telemetry-sampling-cost-aware-profiling-2027 (see event schema v1.1)

Notes and next steps
- Short-term: automate manifest signature checks as a pre-commit hook in the perf-registry.
- Mid-term: build a simulator that replays scheduler-probe patterns to detect oscillations before canary.
- Long-term: extend ABI to support multi-accel fused kernels and dynamic quantization negotiation.

End of document

title: Cohort Sampling Governor and Kernel Lifecycle Playbook
content:
Summary
-------
This playbook documents the Cohort Sampling Governor (CSG) — the runtime component that determines how we sample live inference traffic for profiling and fidelity checks — and the kernel lifecycle safeguards that control how kernel changes are rolled out against sampled cohorts. The goal is to keep profiling cost bounded while ensuring representative coverage and safe kernel change rollouts that preserve SLOs.

Scope and intended audience
- Audience: serving runtime engineers, oncall, profiling team, runtime SREs, and release engineers.
- Scope: live sampling policies, cohort definitions, governor tuning knobs, kernel lifecycle states, rollout/rollback procedures, validation queries, and incident remediation.

Why this matters
- Sampling informs quantization, batching and kernel selection decisions. Incorrect sampling bias -> bad kernel hints -> fidelity regressions at scale.
- Kernel rollouts must be coordinated with sampling to avoid unobserved regressions impacting production SLOs.

Key concepts and definitions
- Cohort: a stable grouping of requests (by client, route, model_version, or token-rate percentile) used for sampling.
- Governor: dynamic service that assigns a sampling probability to each cohort based on budgets, recent coverage, and anomaly score.
- Kernel lifecycle states: "canary", "shadowed", "gradual", "broad", "paused", "rollback".
- Fidelity sample: a captured trace that includes prompt, response, kernel version, and annotations (latency, token counts, cost).

High-level architecture
1. Ingress: request classification service tags request with cohort_id (rules: route, model, customer_tier, token_count_bin).
2. CSG: computes sample_prob in realtime using policy inputs (budget, entropy, last_seen, anomaly_score).
3. Shard router: duplicates requests to profiling pipeline if sampled; otherwise normal path.
4. Profiler pipeline: stores traces, computes fidelity metrics, runs automated evals.
5. Release controller: consults sampling coverage before moving kernel lifecycle forward.

Sampling policy and knobs
- Global budget: maximum profiling QPS allowed (default 50 QPS for hosted clusters).
- Per-cohort min/max probability: ensures low-volume customers still sampled and high-volume customers capped.
- Entropy-driven boost: increase sample_prob for requests with surprising model output (high perplexity / low confidence).
- Decay window: weight recent coverage more heavily (default 24h).

Recommended baseline policy (table)
| cohort_type | rule | min_prob | max_prob | rationale |
|-------------|------|----------|----------|-----------|
| enterprise-high | customer_tier = "enterprise" AND SLA = "gold" | 0.005 | 0.02 | guarantee representation for high impact customers |
| public-api | route startswith /generate | 0.001 | 0.01 | common surface area sampling |
| tail-token | request_length_percentile >= 99 | 0.02 | 0.1 | capture long-sequence regressions |
| experimental-model | model_tag in ["alpha","exp"] | 0.05 | 0.5 | prioritize new variants |

Dynamic adjustments
- If global budget saturated, CSG reduces probabilities proportionally, maintaining every cohort's min_prob floor.
- If an anomaly detector triggers for a cohort (latency or error spike), sample_prob is boosted by factor (2x by default) for 1h.

Telemetry and metrics to monitor
- Sampling QPS per-cohort (gauge) — expected vs actual.
- Profiled-fidelity-lag (histogram): time between request and availability of trace in profiler. Target: p95 < 90s.
- Coverage-entropy (gauge): fraction of distinct cohorts sampled in last 24h; target >= 0.85.
- Kernel-impact delta (histogram): change in p95 latency post-kernel-change on sampled cohort. Trigger alert if delta > 15% absolute.

Example telemetry alert rules (PromQL-like)
1) Coverage drop: 1 - (sum(sampled_cohorts_last_24h) / sum(known_cohorts)) > 0.15 -> Sev2
2) Profiling backlog: increase(profile_queue_depth) > 2000 for 5m -> Sev2
3) Kernel-regression signal: increase(kernel_impact_delta_bucket{le=\"0.15\"}[15m]) / increase(kernel_impact_delta_count[15m]) > 0.2 -> Sev1

Config snippet: cohort sampling YAML (example)
---
version: v1
global_budget_qps: 50
cohorts:
  - id: enterprise-high
    match: "customer_tier == 'enterprise' and sla == 'gold'"
    min_prob: 0.005
    max_prob: 0.02
  - id: tail-token
    match: "request_length_percentile >= 99"
    min_prob: 0.02
    max_prob: 0.1
policy:
  anomaly_boost_factor: 2.0
  decay_hours: 24
---

Runbook: adjusting governor parameters (oncall)
1. Verify alerts in PagerDuty and Slack (#runtime-incidents).
2. Check sampling QPS and profile queue depth:
   - kubectl -n runtime exec -it csg-0 -- /bin/csgctl metrics --cohort-metrics
   - grafana dashboard: "CSG / Sampling Overview"
3. If global_budget_qps is saturated and profile_queue_depth > 1000, increase global_budget by +10 qps:
   - curl -X POST https://config.internal/api/v1/sampling/budget -d '{"global_budget_qps":60}' -H 'Authorization: Bearer $CONFIG_TOKEN'
4. If coverage drops (coverage < 0.7), temporarily increase per-cohort max_prob for underrepresented cohorts:
   - Update YAML and push to config service (see CI validation below).
5. Monitor consequences (p95 profiling lag, storage ingestion rates) for 30 minutes.

Kernel lifecycle and safe rollout guardrails
- Precondition: for a kernel to move from "canary" -> "gradual", coverage_entropy must be >= 0.8 for cohorts exposed to the kernel and no regressions flagged in the last 72h.
- Canary phase: 0.5% of traffic from targeted cohorts; run for minimum 6 hours.
- Shadowed mode: shadow execution on 5% of sampled requests (no external user impact) for fidelity comparison.
- Gradual phase: linear ramp to 20% over 24h if metrics stable.
- Broad: >80% traffic only after 7 days of stable metrics and at least 10k sampled traces.

Kernel rollout checklist
1. Create a release with kernel metadata and associated cohort whitelist.
2. Ensure profiler pipeline healthy (profile_queue_depth < 200).
3. Start canary and notify #kernel-rollouts channel.
4. Run automated fidelity checks (see validation queries) and manual spot checks.
5. If any Sev1/Sev2 alerts triggered, invoke rollback.

Validation queries and spot checks
- SQL: sample extraction to validate canonical traces (run against profiler DB)
  SELECT cohort_id, count(1) AS traces, avg(latency_ms) AS avg_latency
  FROM profiler.traces
  WHERE kernel_version = 'k-v2.4.1' AND ts >= now() - interval '24 hours'
  GROUP BY cohort_id
  ORDER BY traces DESC;

- Automated evaluation: run prompt set suite against new kernel using shadowed mode and compare metrics (exact_match, leniency_score, p95 latency).

Incident remediation: kernel regression detected
1. Pause rollout (controller -> state=paused).
2. Immediately increase sampling for impacted cohorts (min_prob -> min(min_prob*3, 0.5)).
3. Collect 5k failing traces or 30 minutes of incidents, whichever comes first.
4. Open an incident with tags: runtime, kernel, regression. Include trace set, diff of eval metrics, and host telemetry.
5. If rollback criteria met (p95 delta > 10% or error_rate increase > 0.5pp), perform automated rollback to last green kernel.

Rollback command (example)
- curl -X POST https://release-controller.internal/api/v1/rollback -d '{"kernel_id": "k-v2.4.0", "reason": "p95-latency-regression"}' -H 'Authorization: Bearer $RC_TOKEN'

Safe experimentation guidelines (for engineers)
- When adding a new cohort rule, test in staging with a synthetic traffic generator.
- Avoid cohort rules that overlap ambiguously (use priority ordering).
- New kernel builds require a sampling policy declaration (YAML) that lists expected cohorts and initial min_prob.

Ownership and contact points
- CSG service owner: runtime-profiling (pager oncall: @runtime-profiling-oncall).
- Release controller and kernel rollout: runtime-releases (oncall: @runtime-releases-oncall).
- Profiler pipeline: profiling-data-team.

CI validation for sampling config changes
1. Lint: config linter rejects overlapping cohort match expressions.
2. Simulator: run a 1h synthetic run that checks coverage_entropy >= 0.75 under expected QPS.
3. Safety gate: changes that increase global_budget_qps > 100 require engineer + SRE approval.

Troubleshooting tips and common gotchas
- Gotcha: high sampling for experimental-model cohorts can overwhelm ingestion. Counter: set an ingestion cap flag per-cohort.
- Gotcha: cohort rule regression after route refactor. Counter: add a stable attribute (model_family) to cohort rules.
- Gotcha: profiler storage spike during kernel-broad rollouts. Counter: enable short-term retention and archive pipeline.

Appendix: quick reference commands
- csgctl show-config: kubectl -n runtime exec -it csg-0 -- /bin/csgctl config\- csgctl set-budget 60: kubectl -n runtime exec -it csg-0 -- /bin/csgctl set-budget 60
- Release inspect: curl -s https://release-controller.internal/api/v1/releases/k-v2.4.1 | jq

Change log
- 2025-07-12: initial draft and baseline policy (Priya Rangan).
- 2025-11-01: added entropy-driven boosting and decay policy (Ethan Morales).
- 2026-02-03: tightened preconditions for canary->gradual transitions and added CI validation steps (Sofia Chen).

Related reading
- Profiling playbook: variance-driven-sampling-and-cost-correlation-playbook (internal link).
- Scheduler design: predictive-slotting-and-quota-orchestration (internal link).

End of document.

title: Runtime Cohesion and Integration Manual
content:
Overview
--------
This manual describes how the serving runtime components must integrate to preserve predictable inference SLAs while enabling safe experimentation. It consolidates architecture contracts, scheduler integration expectations, a compact profiling playbook, benchmarking guidance, release checklists, and concise runbook actions. The audience is runtime engineers, platform owners, and SREs who operate or extend the inference stack.

Scope
-----
Covers the following subsystems and artifacts: inference-router, kernel-coordinator, kernel-manager, kv-cache, fidelity-orchestrator, batching-service, telemetry-adapter, and the benchmarking harness (op-sim). It intentionally excludes SDK-level API ergonomics and customer Console UI.

Design principles
-----------------
- Observable contracts: every handoff between components must carry an event with correlation_id and causality_trace.
- Fail-fast, degrade-safe: fallbacks must preserve API success (200s) with explicit fidelity headers when possible.
- Testability: each integration point must be exercised via the op-sim harness before rollout.
- Bounded blast radius: experimental scheduler plugins run in sandbox cohorts with quota-limited traffic.

Architecture components and responsibilities
------------------------------------------
- inference-router: performs tenant routing, request classification, and initial priority tagging. Must attach request.metadata.priority and request.metadata.expiry_ts.
- kernel-coordinator: authoritative placement decision-maker; returns allocation tokens and kernel_hint (e.g., "segmented-attn-v2", "quantized-8bit").
- kernel-manager: asserts kernel version compatibility, triggers handoff to the GPU dispatcher, and surfaces kernel telemetry with kernel_signature and kernel_commit.
- kv-cache: manages prefix caches per-session; emits cache_warmup events and provides warmup_score (0..1).
- fidelity-orchestrator: maps workload -> model_variant with policy evaluation (latency vs cost vs quality).
- batching-service: consolidates requests, exposes queue_depth and current_burst_size metrics.
- telemetry-adapter: normalises and annotates traces for downstream SLO dashboards.

Scheduler integration contract (must be implemented on every kernel path)
------------------------------------------------------------------------
Table: Required fields on kernel allocation response
| field | type | meaning | example |
| correlation_id | string | mirrors router trace | rtr-01b2.. |
| allocation_token | string | ephemeral token to acquire GPU slot | tok-3ef4.. |
| kernel_hint | string | suggested kernel variant | segmented-attn-v2 |
| estimated_tail_ms | int | estimated tail latency for this request shape | 45 |
| fallback_variants | list | ordered fallbacks when capacity misses | [lrg-8q, lrg-4q] |

Behavioral expectations:
1) kernel-manager must validate allocation_token within 200ms of issuance.
2) If kernel-manager cannot satisfy kernel_hint, it must return first compatible fallback_variants and set response.header.x-fidelity-degraded = true.
3) Any allocation that waits > 2s must be annotated with queue_backpressure=true and emit an alert to the SLO monitoring stream.

Profiling playbook (compact)
---------------------------
Purpose: enable fast root cause between request-shape, kernel choice, KV hit-rate, and tail-latency.
Quick steps:
1) Reproduce under op-sim with identical request distribution (seeded corpus).
2) Enable full trace on a 1% sampleset (trace_level=full) for 10 minutes.
3) Correlate kernel_signature -> kernel_latency_ms histogram and kv_hit boolean.
4) If tail > SLO (95p > 120ms), run microbench: single-tenant kernel warmstart and memory-pressure sweep.
Useful commands:
- ./op-sim run --profile-corpus corpuses/production-seed-2026.json --sampling 1%
- curl -H "X-Debug-Trace: capture" https://inference-router/api/v1/debug/trace?request_id=<id>

Benchmarking suite guidance
--------------------------
- Baselines: maintain L1 baselines for the following canonical shapes: short-chat (<=64 tokens), long-completion (>=512 tokens), embedding-batch (batch_size=128).
- Metrics to capture: p50, p90, p95 token latency, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, CPU steal, KV hit-rate, and per-token cost_estimate_usd.
- Canary policy: new kernel builds must pass the op-sim synthetic corpus with <=+5% p95 regression and <=+2% cost increase versus baseline.
- Repro steps for suspect builds: 1) pin commit, 2) run three independent op-sim runs at scaled load (0.25x, 0.75x, 1.25x), 3) run kernel microbenchmark with isolated device.

Release and rollout checklist (runtime component)
------------------------------------------------
1) Feature branch: include integration tests that validate allocation_token flow.
2) Pre-merge: create a canary matrix (tenants, shapes, model-variants) and run op-sim.
3) Canary: deploy to 5% traffic in region-us-west1 for 24 hours. Monitor: p95 latency, error-rate, kernel-failure-rate.
4) Gradual roll: 25% -> 60% -> 100% with 1h gates and automated rollback on SLO breach.
5) Post-mortem: collect trace samples and a kernel-perf snapshot.

Known issues and mitigations
--------------------------
- Symptom: sporadic 500s on long-completion shapes when KV cache warmup_score is low.
  Mitigation: enable prefetch for sessions with entropy_score < 0.15 and increase kv-cache prewarm concurrency.
- Symptom: kernel-manager reports transient kernel_commit mismatch after rolling kernel update.
  Mitigation: adopt dual-run intersection checks: kernels serve concurrently for 30 minutes while allocation_token includes kernel_commit_v2.
- Symptom: burst-traffic leads to request prioritisation inversion.
  Mitigation: enforce priority drain windows and apply reserve slots for high-SLA tenants (reserve ratio 0.12).

Runbook (quick actions)
----------------------
1) P95 latency spike (owner: runtime-oncall):
   a) check telemetry-adapter for sudden drop in kv_hit_rate and burst in queue_depth.
   b) if kernel failures > 0.5% in last 10m, flip canary fallback routing (set routing.policy.fallback_rate=0.4).
   c) scale up dedicated burst-pool by +20% for 15 minutes.
2) Kernel deadlock (owner: kernel-team):
   a) identify affected host via kernel-heartbeat missing.
   b) set host to drain and restart kernel-manager process with core-dump enabled.
   c) redirect traffic via inference-router override to alternate pool.

Ownership, escalation and docs
-----------------------------
- Primary owner: Runtime Platform team (runtime-platform@redwood.ai).
- Oncall rotation: runtime-oncall (pager duty) handled by eng-sre and runtime engineers.
- Escalation matrix: runtime-oncall -> kernel-team lead -> eng-sre manager -> CPE.

Appendix: sample config snippets
-------------------------------
1) kernel-allocation response (JSON example):
{
  "correlation_id": "rtr-01b2abcd",
  "allocation_token": "tok-3ef4xyz",
  "kernel_hint": "segmented-attn-v2",
  "estimated_tail_ms": "45",
  "fallback_variants": "[lrg-8q,lrg-4q]"
}

2) op-sim command to run canary corpus:
./op-sim run --corpus corpuses/canary-may-2026.json --concurrency 64 --capture-traces yes --output results/canary-may-2026.json

Document history
----------------
- 2026-02-15 authored by Sofia Martinez
- 2026-03-04 reviewed and updated threshold values (Amit Rao)
- 2026-06-10 added runbook quick actions and profiling command examples (Claire Jensen)

Related reading and links
-------------------------
See also: runtime-decision-graph-and-observed-behaviour-catalog-2026 (architecture), latency-sensitivity-and-graceful-migration-playbook-2026 (scheduling), runtime-profiling-playbook-guidelines-2025 (profiling).

title: Runtime release readiness manifest and engineering gates
content:
Purpose

This page defines the cross-functional release readiness manifest and engineering gates for any major or minor runtime change that touches the serving stack: kernel scheduler, GPU dispatch path, K/V cache, telemetry surface, or client-facing runtime gateway. The goal is a single, repeatable checklist that combines architecture review, kernel scheduling safety, profiling and benchmarking artifacts, release notes, known-issues enumeration, and runbook activation criteria.

Scope

Applies to: runtime-gateway, kernel-scheduler, gpu-dispatcher, kvcache-service, telemetry-collector, runtime-agent.
Excludes: control-plane-only changes (console UI, billing) unless they alter routing or model selection logic.

Quick summary of gates

1) Architecture review complete and signed off.
2) Scheduler kernel tests green on canary hardware profile.
3) Profiling and regression benchmarks executed; no >5% tail-latency regressions without mitigation.
4) Benchmark suite (unit, integration, e2e) completed and artifacts uploaded.
5) Runbooks updated + pager paths validated.
6) Known issues triage completed and mitigations documented.
7) Release notes prepared and release artifact zipped.

Owners & responsibilities

| Area | Primary owner | Secondary owner | Acceptance criteria |
|------|---------------|-----------------|--------------------|
| Architecture & API contract | Sanjay Rao | Hannah Li | ADR recorded; compatibility matrix updated |
| Kernel scheduling changes | Dmitri Ivanov | Lee Chen | Scheduler unit tests + scheduling-safety fuzzing pass |
| Profiling & regression | Aisha Kumar | Priya Natarajan | Profiling report produced; root-cause analysis for any regression |
| Benchmarking & cost | Marcus Perez | Owen Wright | Bench harness artifacts uploaded; cost delta <= budget gate |
| Runbooks & Ops playbooks | Renee O'Connell | SRE oncall | Runbook publishes TTLs and escalation paths |

Pre-release checklist (detailed)

1) Architecture and design
   - Add/update ADR or design note with backward compatibility section.
   - Document expected behavior under degraded resources (eviction semantics, model swap).
   - Confirm model variant routing policies and fallback order.

2) Kernel & scheduler safety
   - Run scheduler unit tests (fast): ./tools/test-scheduler --unit --filter=priority_*
   - Run cooperative preemption simulation: ./tools/sim-scheduler --scenario=preempt-coop --iterations=500
   - Execute safety fuzzing: ./tools/sched-fuzz --duration=4h --seed=stable
   - Validate kernel handoff traces: trace_id = <sample>; verify no missing commit markers.
   - Acceptance: no assertion failures and <0.1% missed deadline events on canary pool.

3) Profiling & microbenchmarks
   - Produce before/after profiling bundle for the change: perf-bundle --baseline=main --candidate=feature/branch --out=perf-bundle.zip
   - Required profiler outputs: occupancy.csv, kernel-latencies.json, kv-cache-hitrates.csv, p99_token_latency.tsv
   - Focus tests: short (<=32 tokens), medium (128 tokens), long (1024 tokens), streaming scenarios.
   - Gate: p99 token latency regression <=5% on canonical workloads; any higher requires mitigation plan.

4) Benchmarking suite (integration + e2e)
   - Run mixed-workload harness: ./bench/run-mixed --profile=prod-sim --duration=30m --concurrency=100
   - Run SLO simulation: ./bench/slo-sim --traffic-profile=canary --seed=42
   - Cost sensitivity: ./bench/cost-delta --quant=quant-8 --baseline=main
   - Upload artifacts to perf-lab artifacts bucket: gs://perf-artifacts/runtime/releases/<release-tag>/
   - Gate: no >10% cost-per-token increase vs baseline without corresponding quality improvement.

5) Observability & telemetry
   - Ensure new metrics registered in telemetry-collector and dashboard panels created: runtime.kernel.commit_latencies_ms, runtime.kvcache.hit_rate, runtime.scheduler.preempt_events_total
   - Validate traces are sampled at p=1% for production-like jobs and p=100% on canaries for 24h.
   - Ensure tracing spans include kernel_id, shard_id, request_class, token_count.

6) Runbooks and operational readiness
   - Update runbook sections: "eviction-reconstruction", "scheduler-deadline-exceedances", "kvcache-warmup".
   - Add step-by-step remediation with commands, expected side-effects, and ownership. Example command: kubectl -n runtime rollout restart deploy/gpu-dispatcher --grace-period=60
   - Pager test: run a simulated incident drill with oncall and confirm escalation chain works.

7) Known issues and mitigations
   - Add any pre-existing known issues that could interact with the change (e.g., NVLINK degradation profile, nvdriver-compatibility-510).
   - Provide mitigation matrix: severity, mitigation steps, rollback hints, communication template.

Sample mitigation table

| Issue | Severity | Immediate mitigation | Runbook link |
|-------|----------|----------------------|--------------|
| NVLINK interconnect degradation on p4d | high | Move non-critical workloads, enable slot isolation | /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/known-issues/nvlink-interconnect-degradation-and-remediation-2026 |
| K/V cache cold-start regression | medium | Increase warmup-provisioning for canary; prefill common prefixes | /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/dynamic-kvcache-resilience-and-warmup-playbook-2026 |

Release artifact and notes template

- Artifact name: runtime-release-<tag>.zip
- Contents: binary images, perf-bundles/, benchmark-results.csv, profiling/ (occupancy/latency), release-notes.md, runbooks/updated_runbooks.pdf

release-notes.md (boilerplate)

Title: <release-tag> — short summary\\nAffected Services: runtime-gateway, kernel-scheduler\\nSLO impact: none expected; if any, see SLO section below.\\nMigration steps: none (runtime-internal) / manual rollout matrix attached.\\nKnown regressions: list here (if any) and mitigation.

SLO gates and metrics (hard)

- p50 token latency: no change >3% (informational)
- p95 token latency: no change >5% (investigate)
- p99 token latency: no change >5% (blocker unless mitigated)
- Error rate (user-visible 5xx): <0.1% increase allowed during canary window
- Scheduler missed-deadlines: <0.05% over 24h on canary pool

Kernel change rollback procedure (fast path)

1) Trigger canary rollback: kubectl -n runtime set image deployment/kernel-scheduler kernel-scheduler=registry.redwood/runtime/kernel-scheduler:<previous-tag>
2) Restart dependent daemons in order: gpu-dispatcher -> kvcache-service -> runtime-gateway (graceful drain between each with 60s).
3) Re-run smoke checks: ./tools/runtime-smoke --endpoints=smoke-list.txt
4) If rollback fails, escalate to platform-release@redwood and open an incident with "runtime-kernel-rollback" template.

Post-release tasks

- Monitor telemetry for 72 hours at increased sampling (p=5%).
- Run cost sampling job to detect any regression in GPU utilization or per-token cost.
- Retain perf artifacts for 180 days.
- Conduct a 2-week retrospective with owners and capture follow-ups.

Checklist sign-off (required fields)

- [ ] Architecture review (owner + date)
- [ ] Kernel safety tests (owner + date)
- [ ] Profiling bundle uploaded (artifact path)
- [ ] Benchmark suite passed (artifact path)
- [ ] Runbooks updated and linked (URLs)
- [ ] Release notes published (link)
- [ ] Release artifact uploaded (path)

References and useful commands

- Profiling: perf-bundle --baseline=main --candidate=feature/x --out=/tmp/bundle.zip
- Mixed workload benchmark: ./bench/run-mixed --profile=prod-sim --duration=30m --concurrency=100 --out=results.csv
- Scheduler fuzz: ./tools/sched-fuzz --duration=4h --out=fuzz-results.json
- Upload artifact: gsutil cp -r perf-bundles/<tag> gs://perf-artifacts/runtime/releases/<tag>/

Contact list

- Release owner: Aisha Kumar (aisha@redwood.ai)
- Kernel lead: Dmitri Ivanov (dmitri@redwood.ai)
- SRE lead: Renee O'Connell (renee@redwood.ai)

Appendix: Minimal verification script (example)

# Minimal smoke script (bash excerpt)
# 1) Check health endpoints
# 2) Run 50 short token requests and assert no 500s

set -e
for ep in $(cat smoke-list.txt); do
  status=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' $ep/health)
  if [ "$status" != "200" ]; then
    echo "Health check failed for $ep"; exit 1;
  fi
done

python - <<'PY'
import requests
urls = open('smoke-list.txt').read().splitlines()[:5]
for u in urls:
    r = requests.post(u + '/v1/generate', json={'input': 'hello', 'max_tokens': 8}, timeout=5)
    assert r.status_code == 200
print('smoke ok')
PY

End of document.

title: Runtime Integration Gateway & Operator Playbook
content:
Summary

This page documents the design, operational contract, and runbooks for the Runtime Integration Gateway (RIG) and the Operator component used by Redwood’s serving runtime. The RIG is the control plane facade that mediates decisions between the API surface, routing layer, and the kernel scheduler. The Operator is the local agent that implements prefetch/eviction hints, capacity decisions, and safety checks on a per-host basis. Together they enable consistent fallback behavior, cache coordination, and safe kernel handoffs across deployments (hosted, dedicated, private).

Scope

- Cross-cutting: runtime architecture, kernel scheduling hints, profiling instrumentation, benchmark protocols, evacuation/eviction runbooks, and release guidance.
- Intended audience: runtime engineers, SREs, oncall, platform/ops teams, and partners owning Private deployments.

Design overview

Key goals:
- Preserve latency SLOs while maximizing throughput and cache hit ratios.
- Provide safe, observable prefetch and eviction signals to kernels without exposing internal kernel details.
- Offer a deterministic handshake for model swap, graceful degradation, and fast rollback.

Core components:
1) Runtime Integration Gateway (RIG): global control plane component that synthesizes routing policy, historical telemetry, and fidelity budgets to produce per-tenant hints (prefetch score, target warmup priority, eviction budget).
2) Operator agent: host-local agent that receives hints and enforces them via kernel scheduler APIs and kvcache controls.
3) Kernel Scheduler: GPU-local execution layer that exposes a narrow set of safe primitives (reserve_slot, prefetch_token, soft_evict, priority_boost).

Behavioral contract (high level)

- Hints are advisory: Operator must never trigger kernel state transitions that break in-flight requests. All transitions are atomic and checkpointed.
- Backpressure loop: if Operator observes a >10% SLO degradation coincident with hint enforcement, it must throttle hint application and report a delta to RIG.
- Revisioning: every hint includes a version token; kernels reject stale tokens.

Kernel scheduling integration patterns

Recommended primitive semantics (stable API):

| Primitive | Inputs | Expected behavior | Safety checks |
|---|---:|---|---|
| reserve_slot | model_id, seq_len_est, ttl | Reserve a logical GPU slot for expected new sequence starts. Not a physical allocation. | Reject if host soft-oom or thermal throttling active. |
| prefetch_token | kv_key, priority, expected_live_ms | Start asynchronous KV prefetch and stage to warm cache. | Limit bytes prefetched per-second by host budget. |
| soft_evict | kv_key, reason | Mark entry for eviction; kernel may defer until safe window. | Respect in-flight references; must not kick out active session entries. |
| priority_boost | tenant_id, boost_level | Raise kernel scheduling priority for specific tenant's packets. | Must honor fairness quotas and not exceed token budget. |

Integration notes:
- Use request timeline annotations (trace_id + event_ids) when translating prefetch into kernel operations to permit traceability.
- All kernel APIs return an op_result and telemetry tag; Operators should emit both as structured logs.

Profiling & observability guidance

Required telemetry flows (minimum):
- Hint lifecycle traces: RIG:hint:generate -> Operator:hint:apply -> Kernel:hint:ack.
- Prefetch stats: bytes_initiated, bytes_completed, success_rate, tail_latency_p95/p99.
- Eviction surface: evict_attempts, evict_success, delayed_eviction_count, in_flight_blocker_reasons.

Sampling policy:
- 100% of hint lifecycle events must be annotated and sampled at 10% for full trace capture.
- Stratified sampling: always capture 100% when SLO > breach_threshold or when evictions coincide with model-swaps.

Profiling playbook excerpt (investigation steps):
1) Identify symptom: increased generation tail latency or token error rate.
2) Correlate with hint application windows (RIG/Operator traces).
3) If evictions increased: pull kvcache-backed references and examine in-flight reference counts.
4) If prefetch failures: check network I/O metric (prefetch throughput) and per-host prefetch budget exhaustion.
5) Deploy a controlled canary: disable prefetch for a single tenant cohort and compare SLA slices; report delta to RIG.

Benchmarking protocol (how to validate changes safely)

- Objective: measure delta in per-token cost, tail latency, and cache hit ratio after any change to hint heuristics or Operator enforcement.
- Minimum benchmark matrix:
  - Workloads: short-chat (mean seq_len 32), long-chat (mean seq_len 512), embedding-bulk (batch-size 128), mixed-burst (poisson arrivals lambda=200).
  - Metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens-per-second, cache_hit_rate, kernel_preemption_count, host_cpu_percent, GPU_util.
  - Duration: each profile run = 2h steady-state after 20m warmup. Repeat 3x and report median.

Bench commands (example):
- Synthesize traffic: ./benchctl --profile mixed-burst --tenant test-tenant --duration 02:00 --seed 42
- Collect traces: benchctl collect --trace-filter "RIG:hint* OR Operator:hint*" --out bench-2026-02-collect.json

Release & rollout guidance

- All Operator changes must pass a green gate on the benchmark matrix above with no >5% regression in p95 for the short-chat workload across three replicate runs.
- Rollout strategy: staged canary by affinity cohort (10% -> 30% -> 60% -> 100%) with automated rollback on >3s sustained p95 regression or 2x increase in eviction-induced request failures.
- Release note template: include exact benchmark artifact links, canary cohort ids, and throttling parameters.

Known issues (current summary)

| ID | Symptom | Impact | Workaround | Owner |
| KVO-2025-11 | Prefetch storms on model swap causing network saturation | Elevated tail latency for embedding workloads | Stagger prefetch by 2s buckets via RIG hint windowing | eng-serving-runtime |
| OP-2025-07 | Operator sometimes double-applies soft_evict after transient disconnect | Elevated evict_attempts and unnecessary cache churn | Blacklist consecutive soft_evicts within 500ms per-kv | kernel-team |
| THERM-2025-02 | Thermal-induced GPU throttles reject reserve_slot calls | Rejection leads to rapid fallback to lower-capacity kernels | Preemptively lower prefetch budget when thermal_throttle > 0 | infra-sre |

Eviction & prefetch runbook (operational playbook)

When customers report latency regressions possibly tied to prefetch/eviction:
1) Triage: capture traces across RIG, Operator, and kernel for the suspect timeframe.
2) Check host budgets: run `rigctl host-status --host <node>` and inspect prefetch_budget and eviction_backlog.
3) If prefetch_budget_pressure > 80%: temporarily reduce RIG prefetch window for the affected cohort: `rigctl hint-update --cohort <id> --prefetch-window-ms 200`
4) If eviction churn > 100/min: enable soft-eviction-mitigation mode on Operator: `operatorctl set soft-evict-delay 1200` (ms).
5) If step 3–4 restore SLOs: schedule a follow-up bench run and root-cause analysis. If not, escalate to oncall kernel-team.

Escalation matrix

- Oncall runtime (pager): Triage and apply immediate mitigations.
- Kernel team (pager): For kernel API misbehavior or invariant violations.
- Infra SRE: For network, thermal, or host-level resource saturation.

Ownership and maintenance

- RIG control plane: eng-serving-runtime/core-routing (primary).
- Operator agent: eng-serving-runtime/operator (primary); kernel-team (secondary for API changes).
- Bench harness and artifact storage: benchmarking-team.

Appendix: sample Operator config (yaml)

```yaml
operator:
  prefetch:
    enabled: true
    max_bytes_per_sec: 250000000 # 250MB/s
    per_tenant_limit: 50MB
  eviction:
    soft_evict_delay_ms: 1000
    max_concurrent_evictions: 16
  safety:
    slo_throttle_threshold_pct: 10
    telemetry_sampling_pct: 10
```

FAQ and change log

- Q: Why are hints advisory not mandatory?
  A: Kernels have richer context about in-flight requests and memory graphs; advisory model preserves safety and prevents hard failures.

Change log (high level):
- 2024-11-12 initial draft and prototype Operator integration.
- 2025-04-03 added prefetch budget enforcement and hint versioning.
- 2026-02-18 added canary gating rules and expanded benchmark matrix.

Related reading

- See runtime-execution-safety-matrix-2026 for safety invariants.
- See kvcache-epoch-synchronization-and-repair-procedures-2026 for epoch reconciliation procedures.

If you implement or modify the Operator or RIG, update this playbook and attach benchmark artifacts to the release notes before rolling past 30% canary.

title: Observability Adapter Sidecar: Design Manual and Onboarding Guide
content:
Overview

This document describes the design, operational contracts, and onboarding checklist for the Observability Adapter Sidecar (OAS)—a lightweight per-node sidecar that attaches to serving runtime processes and provides production-safe, low-overhead instrumentation for per-request fidelity signals, adaptive sampling, and enriched traces. It is intended for runtime engineers, profiling owners, and SREs who will operate and extend the OAS.

Goals

- Provide a stable, low-latency mechanism for enriching requests with fidelity metadata (kernel hints, kv-cache hit/miss, quantization variant).
- Support adaptive, policy-driven sampling that balances observability coverage with cost and privacy constraints.
- Decouple heavy signal processing from the hot runtime path via asynchronous sinks and backpressure-aware queues.
- Offer clear contracts so runtime teams can consume telemetry without coupling to probe implementations.

Scope and Non-Goals

- In scope: sidecar API contract, sampling controller protocol, configuration schema, rollout checklist, security constraints, and troubleshooting playbook.
- Not in scope: changes to kernel scheduling heuristics, evaluation algorithms for model quality, or storage-side analytics pipelines (those are handled by telemetry-backend teams).

Design Principles

1. Non-blocking hot path: sidecar must not add synchronous latency to inference token emission or RPC response paths.
2. Bounded memory & predictable cost: local queues have strict bounds; policies exist to drop or aggregate when saturated.
3. Policy-driven behavior: sampling and enrichment governed by remote policy controller with health-fallback to cached defaults.
4. Minimal privileges: run with least privilege; network egress only to approved telemetry endpoints.
5. Observable and debuggable: expose health, queue-length, and sampling-rate metrics for immediate SLO correlation.

Architecture (text diagram)

- Serving process (runtime) <--> Local IPC socket (unix/grpc) <--> Observability Adapter Sidecar (OAS) 
  
  OAS components:
  - Ingress listener: small sync layer to accept lightweight event envelopes (<= 1KB) over unix socket.
  - Adaptive sampler: local policy engine + short-lived remote policy cache (refresh TTL 30s).
  - Local aggregator & aggregator worker pool: batch events and flush asynchronously to sink.
  - Backpressure manager: implements admission/drop + p99 tail guard for sync APIs.
  - Telemetry sink: pluggable output (http/gRPC to telemetry backend, local file for debug).

Component Contracts

1) Ingress contract
- Envelope format: JSON lines or protobuf-lite. Required fields: request_id, model_variant, shard_id, event_ts_iso, event_type, token_count, kernel_hint (optional), kvcache_status (hit/miss/partial), extra_tags (map).
- Max envelope size: 1024 bytes. Larger events must be truncated and flagged.

2) Sampling controller contract
- Policy model: simple JSON with rules (matchers on route/model/metadata) and actions (sample_rate 0.0-1.0, aggregate:true/false, redact_fields:list).
- Local behavior: if controller unreachable, fall back to baked-in policy at start-up and operate in degraded mode.

3) Sink contract
- Accept batched payloads via HTTP POST application/json with Authorization: Telemetry-Key header.
- Retry policy: exponential backoff capped at 5 retries, then drop and increment metric oas.sink.drop_count.

Configuration (example YAML)

-- oas-config.yaml --
listen: 
  unix_socket: "/var/run/oas.sock"
  max_concurrent_ingress: 64
sampler:
  policy_url: "https://telemetry-policy.internal/api/v1/policy"
  refresh_interval_seconds: 30
  default_policy: 
    - matcher: "route == '/v1/completions' and model_variant =~ '.*-quant'"
      action: 
        sample_rate: 0.05
        aggregate: false
queue:
  max_items: 20000
  max_bytes: 50MB
sink:
  url: "https://telemetry-ingest.internal/v1/ingest"
  auth_header: "Telemetry-Key: ${OAS_KEY}"
  batch_max_size: 100
  flush_interval_ms: 200
security:
  allowed_egress_hosts: ["telemetry-ingest.internal"]
  run_as_user: "oas-agent"
  restrict_capabilities: true

Operational Signals and Metrics (as a text table)

Metric name | Type | SLI indication | Alert threshold
oas.health | gauge | service up | health == 0 for 3m
oas.queue.length | gauge | admission pressure | queue.length > 80% for 5m
oas.sampler.effective_rate | gauge | observability coverage | effective_rate < configured - 10%
oas.sink.latency_p50/p95 | histogram | sink performance | p95 > 5s
oas.sink.drop_count | counter | data loss | drop_count increase > 100/min

Deployment and Rollout Checklist (numbered)

1. Pre-flight validation:
   a. Verify unix socket permissions and SELinux/AppArmor policy.
   b. Confirm OAS container resource limits: CPU 200m, mem 128Mi to start.
   c. Validate policy endpoint reachable from canary nodes.
2. Canary (5% nodes):
   a. Enable OAS in 'observe-only' mode (sample_rate=0, aggregate=true) and flow to debug sink.
   b. Check oas.queue.length and oas.sink.latency_p95 for regressions.
   c. Confirm no increase in serving p99 latency beyond 1%.
3. Progressive ramp: 5% -> 25% -> 100% over 72h observing signals; adjust sample rates if sink latency increases.
4. Enable adaptive sampling live with conservative initial policies (global sample_rate <= 0.02).

Validation Tests (quick list)

- Latency regression: run synthetic replay with representative token distributions and ensure p99 latency delta < 2%.
- Failure injection: block sink and verify OAS backpressure behavior and that serving continues with bounded memory.
- Policy mismatch: deploy an invalid policy payload and confirm OAS rejects it and reverts to cached default.

Troubleshooting Runbook (step-by-step)

1. Symptom: increased serving p99 at peak.
   - Check oas.queue.length and oas.sink.p95. If both spike, scale sink or reduce sample_rate.
2. Symptom: oas.health == 0 on node.
   - Examine sidecar logs /var/log/oas/*.log for startup failures, permission errors, or TLS issues.
   - If crashloop, isolate with strace and check for blocked socket binds.
3. Symptom: high oas.sink.drop_count.
   - Verify telemetry backend auth and rate limits. Rotate keys if auth failures are observed.
4. Symptom: privacy violation flag from telemetry-backend.
   - Immediately enable redact_fields in policy and trigger a 'flush-and-scrub' protocol (contact telemetry-backend runbook).

Security and Data Protection

- PII redaction: sidecar must support policy-driven redaction of fields and should never transmit raw user_prompt unless expressly allowed by customer config.
- Egress controls: OAS must respect allowed_egress_hosts and refuse any unexpected DNS resolutions.
- Keys & secrets: use instance-level KMS-wrapped keys, not environment-injected plaintext secrets.
- Auditing: emit audit events for every policy change and policy fetch with timestamp and signature verification.

Extension Points for Runtime Teams

- Kernel hint schemas: runtime owners can add new kernel_hint keys but must submit a schema bump PR to runtime-telemetry contract repo and add mapping to the downstream ingest pipeline.
- Aggregation plugins: teams can propose a custom aggregator (e.g., histogram summarizer) that implements the aggregator gRPC signature. These plugins must pass the plugin-safety CI suite.

Onboarding Checklist for New Runtime Projects

- Implement a small adapter client that serializes envelopes to the unix socket. Example snippet: 

curl -s --unix-socket /var/run/oas.sock -X POST http://localhost/enqueue -d '{"request_id":"r1","model_variant":"redwood-7b","event_ts_iso":"2026-03-01T12:00:00Z","event_type":"response","token_count":24}'

- Add OAS sidecar to your Pod spec with resource limits and a readiness probe:

containers:
  - name: oas-agent
    image: registry.internal/infra/oas:2026-02-01
    resources:
      limits:
        cpu: "200m"
        memory: "128Mi"
    readinessProbe:
      exec:
        command: ["/usr/bin/oasctl","health"]
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
      periodSeconds: 10

Ownership and SLAs

- Primary owner: runtime-observability team (pager: oncall-runtime-obsv).
- Support escalation: send to infra-sre@redwood.ai and telemetry-backend oncall if sink outages exceed 5 minutes.
- Operational SLO: OAS health >= 99.5% monthly and effective sampling coverage within 10% of policy target.

Change Management and Policy Review

- All policy schema changes must be reviewed by telemetry-backend and privacy team.
- Major behavioral changes (e.g., switching to synchronous enrichments) require a canary plan and sign-off from runtime performance sig.

Appendix: Example Sampling Policy JSON

{
  "version": "1",
  "rules": [
    {"matcher": "model_variant =~ '.*-quant'","action": {"sample_rate": 0.02,"aggregate": false}},
    {"matcher": "route == '/v1/chat' and tenant in ['enterprise-a']","action": {"sample_rate": 0.2,"aggregate": false}},
    {"matcher": "default","action": {"sample_rate": 0.005,"aggregate": true}}
  ]
}

Frequently Asked Questions (short)

Q: Will enabling OAS slow down my model?
A: When configured per the rollout checklist, OAS is bounded to add <1% p99 latency. If you observe larger regressions, check queue saturation and sampler policies.

Q: How do I add a new telemetry field?
A: File a schema PR to the telemetry-contracts repo, include a migration plan for existing ingestion pipelines, and coordinate with telemetry-backend for parsers.

Related pages and next steps

- Implement the client adapter template in runtime-examples repo and submit for review.
- Coordinate with telemetry-backend to register your model_variant mapping.

Document history

- 2026-01-12: Initial draft by Maya Patel.
- 2026-02-10: Added rollout checklist and sink contract after SOC review.
- 2026-03-01: Final edits and published.

title: Runtime Playground Operator Handbook
content:
Overview

This handbook documents the operator workflows, safety gates, telemetry contracts, and procedural recipes for running the Runtime Playground — a curated staging cluster where runtime, kernel, and scheduler experiments are carried out end-to-end. The Playground is the canonical environment for: kernel prototype rollouts, scheduling-policy stress tests, profiling and latency-attribution experiments, and candidate benchmarking suites prior to canarying into production.

Goals
- Provide a low-friction but safe path to run destructive/performance experiments.
- Preserve fidelity to production execution surfaces while isolating blast radius.
- Ensure experiments produce reproducible artifacts (traces, tracesets, golden benchmarks).
- Make rollbacks and postmortems fast and deterministic.

Audience
- Runtime engineers implementing kernel or scheduler changes.
- SREs validating capacity/eviction behaviors.
- Applied ML engineers testing model-variant cost/latency tradeoffs.
- Performance engineers authoring benchmarks and profiling harnesses.

Key Concepts
- Playground Cluster: A dedicated tenant-aware runtime cluster with production-like GPUs, reduced traffic, and explicit circuit breakers.
- Shadow Traffic: Mirrored production request surface used for fidelity tests without impacting users.
- Decision Trace: A serialized, linkable trace that captures routing and scheduler decisions for every experimental run.
- Fidelity Gate: A quality threshold (latency/cost/quality) that must be met for an experiment to advance.

Ownership and Contacts
| Role | Team | On-call / Primary | Escalation |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Playground Owner | Eng - Serving Runtime | Jonah Kim | Pager: eng-runtime-oncall |
| Kernel Sandbox Custodian | Eng - Kernel | Marta Alvarez | Slack: #kernel-sandbox |
| Observability Lead | Eng - Platform | Ethan Zhou | Pager: observability-oncall |

Environment Layout
- Cluster name: playground-us-west-2 (k8s namespace: playground-runtime)
- GPU mix: 8x A10G (evaluation), 4x H100 (reserved testbeds)
- Network: Isolated VPC with egress-only to infra systems (S3, telemetry-api)
- Data retention: experiment artifacts stored 30 days by default; long-term artifacts archived to experiments-bucket with TTL policy.

Pre-flight Checklist (must be green before any experiment)
1. Create an Experiment Issue and link to this handbook (template: EXP-PLAYGROUND).
2. Confirm resource quotas with Capacity Owner (Slack: #capacity).
3. Confirm tracking keys for telemetry: experiment_id, run_id, operator, hypothesis.
4. Smoke test baseline traces: run 100 requests of the target profile and capture Decision Traces.
5. Ensure canary circuit breaker flags are configured: playground.allow-destructive (bool), playground-kernel-override (list).

Experiment Lifecycle
1) Plan
- Hypothesis: short phrase describing expected change (e.g., "sharded attention reduces p95 by >= 8ms for seq=1024").
- Metrics: primary (p50/p95 latency), secondary (token throughput, kernel queue length), safety (error rate, OOM count).
- Acceptance criteria: numeric thresholds and max allowed regressions.

2) Authoring
- Add experiment config (YAML) to experiments/ directory in git. Example: 

```yaml
experiment_id: exp-2025-4623
description: "priority-aware kernel sharding test"
variants:
  - name: control
    kernel_profile: v2
  - name: shard-12
    kernel_profile: v3-sharded
traffic: shadow-mirror
traffic_weight: 0.0 # mirrored only
duration: 2h
telemetry: decision-trace,perf-sample,kvcache-dump
rollback_on:
  - error_rate > 0.5%
  - p95_control - p95_variant > 10ms
```

3) Scheduling and Execution
- Submit experiment via cli: `rk experiment submit --file exp-2025-4623.yaml --owner asha.patel`
- The scheduler assigns to a sandboxed node group with admission-controller policy applied.
- Use `rk experiment status <id>` to follow progress.

4) Profiling and Data Capture
- Enable continuous profiler snapshot: `rk profiler start --experiment <id> --sample-rate 1/1000`
- For kernel-level traces enable kernel-hint logging: set KGLOG=debug in experiment env.
- Ensure prefix/KVcache dumps are captured at run start and end: `rk kvcache dump --experiment <id> --bucket experiments-bucket`

5) Analysis and Artifact Collection
- Golden artifacts to collect: Decision Traces (JSON), perf-samples (parquet), microbench histograms (txt), kernel logs (tar.gz).
- Use artifact aggregation script: `scripts/collect_artifacts.sh <experiment_id> > artifacts/<experiment_id>.tar.gz`
- Run bench-compare tool: `bench-compare --left=control --right=shard-12 --metrics=p95,p50,tokens/s --output=reports/<id>.html`

6) Post-run Review and Gates
- Populate the experiment issue with: summary, artifacts link, pass/fail against acceptance criteria, and next steps.
- If gates fail, tag `regression` and assign to owner. For failures with unknown root cause, follow the Incident Triage Runbook (section below).

Safety and Blast Radius Controls
- Admission policies: no experiment may allocate > 30% of a sandbox node group's memory or > 50% of GPU cycle credits.
- Circuit breakers: automatic abort on sustained OOM > 3 within 10 minutes or kernel panic observed.
- Network egress: disallowed to customer endpoints; only infra endpoints permitted.
- Identity: experiments run under a limited service account with no access to production secrets.

SLOs and Monitoring for Playground
- Uptime: 99.5% cluster level for experimental scheduling controller.
- Telemetry latency: Decision Trace publish latency < 30s 95th percentile.
- Artifact availability: experiment artifacts available for download within 5 minutes of run completion.

Runbook: Incident Triage for Regressions in Playground
1. Detect
  a. Alert triggers: bench-compare flags p95 regression > acceptance threshold; profiler shows CPU or kernel queue saturation; artifact pipeline fails.
2. Contain
  a. Stop the experiment: `rk experiment abort <id>` (immediate).
  b. Quarantine node(s): mark nodes unschedulable and collect kernel-state snapshot.
3. Diagnose
  a. Pull Decision Traces: `rk trace fetch --id <run_trace_id>` and open in Trace Viewer.
  b. Correlate perf-samples with kernel logs (time-aligned).
  c. If OOM suspected, run `rk memory-audit --node <node> --since <ts>` to get allocation flamegraphs.
4. Remediate
  a. If regression is kernel-level, revert kernel candidate using `rk kernel rollback --name <candidate>` and re-run smoke-tests.
  b. If scheduling policy error, restore previous scheduler policy from policy-store tag `stable`.
5. Postmortem
  a. Create a postmortem document with links to artifacts and hypothesis tests.
  b. Run a mini-experiment that increments in smaller steps to validate fix.

Benchmarks and Reproducibility
- Benchmark templates live in `benchmarks/templates/` and must declare: workload profile (concurrency, sequence distribution), model variant, kernel hints, and warmup protocol.
- Reproducibility note: always seed the request generator and record seed in Decision Traces.

Kernel and Scheduler Experiment Patterns
- Priority Staircase Test: Verify priority decoupling by stepping traffic through priority buckets (0->1->2) and measuring cross-priority interference.
- Sharded-KV Warmup Pattern: Pre-warm KV shards deterministically using synthetic prefix sequences to avoid cold-start noise.
- Kernel Hedging Probe: Inject low-latency hedged kernel calls to test preemption and cooperative handoff.

Example Kernel Rollback Command (safe pattern)

```bash
# verify artifacts before rollback
rk kernel candidate inspect --name v3-sharded --artifacts \
  --expect-files kernel.so,kernel-meta.json
# promote previous stable
rk kernel promote --from-tag stable --to active --confirm
# monitor health
rk health watch --filter kernel,eviction,oom --duration 10m
```

Release Notes and Change Log (playground-specific)
- 2024-11-12: Initial handbook and cluster provisioning template.
- 2025-01-18: Added automated decision-trace enrichment and bench-compare output format.
- 2025-02-03: Updated safety thresholds for GPU credit usage and artifact TTL policy.

Common Known Issues (Playground)
- Artifact pipeline stalls when S3 throttling observed: mitigation — reduce parallel uploads and add exponential backoff (see scripts/collect_artifacts.sh).
- Kernel candidate fails with assert in `kv_shard_indexer`: usually due to mismatched shard map; mitigation — run `rk kvcache validate --map` then replay warmup.
- Shadow traffic skew: if production sampling is not representative, use synthetic traffic generator with recorded seed and distribution to improve fidelity.

Appendices
A. Experiment Issue Template (EXP-PLAYGROUND)
- Title, hypothesis, acceptance criteria, duration, resource request, telemetry keys, owner, reviewers.

B. Artifact Naming Convention
- `<experiment_id>.<run_id>.decision-trace.json`
- `<experiment_id>.<run_id>.perf-samples.parquet`
- `<experiment_id>.<run_id>.kvcache.tar.gz`

C. Quick CLI Cheat Sheet
- `rk experiment submit --file <yaml>` — submit an experiment.
- `rk experiment status <id>` — status.
- `rk experiment abort <id>` — abort.
- `rk profiler start --experiment <id>` — enable continuous profiler.
- `rk trace fetch --id <trace_id>` — fetch decision trace.

D. Post-experiment Retention Policy
- Short-term: artifacts retained 30 days.
- Long-term: curated artifact sets (postmortem-critical) archived for 365 days.

E. Related Playbooks
- runtime-upgrade-validation-and-canary-matrix-2026 (for production rollout)
- kernel-handshake-and-adaptive-fallback-patterns-2026 (kernel-level behavior reference)

If you have questions or an experiment need, open an EXP-PLAYGROUND issue and tag @playground-ops.

Document history: Asha Patel (author), initial publish 2024-11-12; safety updates and telemetry enrichment 2025-02-03.

title: Fractional Kernel Coexistence Handbook
content:
Overview

This handbook documents the design, operational guidance, profiling procedures, benchmark suite, and incident runbooks for Fractional Kernel Coexistence (FKC) — the runtime pattern that allows multiple kernel implementations and fidelity levels to share physical accelerator capacity with fine-grained isolation and graceful degradation. It consolidates architecture intent, scheduler contracts, rollout checklist, and actionable troubleshooting flows so engineers and oncall SREs can operate FKC safely in production.

Goals

- Enable multiple kernel implementations (full-precision, quantized, sparse, optimized attention variants) to run concurrently on the same GPU(s) without violating latency SLOs for critical routes.
- Provide bounded performance isolation: define and enforce resource shares, preemption semantics, and degradation fallbacks.
- Make kernel transitions observable and revertible with low blast radius.
- Instrument profiling and benchmark workflows that reflect production co-location effects.

Audience

- Runtime engineers, scheduler owners, serving SREs, release engineers, and applied ML engineers onboarding new kernels.

Design summary

1) Principle: soft-isolation via fractional allocation and latency budgets
   - We do not rely on hardware partitioning exclusively; runtime allocates fractional execution slots and soft-resources (tensor memory caps, tensor-core credit buckets) and enforces latency budgets per request class.

2) Components
   - Kernel Registry: metadata store mapping model_variant -> kernel_tag, stability_grade, observed_seq_len_profile.
   - Fractional Admission Controller (FAC): decides admission and slot sizing per incoming request. Implements token-accounting (credits) per kernel_tag.
   - Kernel Handshake Protocol (KHP): short RPC between scheduler and kernel container to request/return fractional slots, handshake includes kernel_hints and kernel_fidelity_flags.
   - Graceful Fallback Orchestrator: on admission failure or SLO violation, reroutes to compatible kernel variant or reduces fidelity according to policy.

Scheduling model and contracts

- Request classes: realtime-critical, background-batch, best-effort-async. Each class has a latency SLO, credit refill rate, and eviction priority.
- Slot size: logical unit (fraction) representing amortized token throughput and memory footprint. Slot sizes are mapped to kernel categories (e.g., fp32-large, q4-small).
- Preemption semantics: preemption is cooperative where possible. If kernel cannot yield (long-running large sequence generation), FAC will avoid new admissions for lower-priority classes and use fallback routing. Immediate preemption (hard kill) is reserved for safety-critical incidents and requires manual approval.

Kernel handshake protocol (KHP) - message contract

- handshake.request { request_id, kernel_tag, required_slots, max_latency_ms, kvcache_hint }
- handshake.accept { allocation_id, granted_slots, preemption_token, expected_release_ms }
- handshake.reject { reason_code, suggested_fallback_tags }
- release { allocation_id, actual_duration_ms, observed_peak_mem_mb }

Note: KHP messages are carried on the scheduler's local RPC bus and annotated in traces. Handshake defines fields but transport is protobuf-over-grpc in current implementation.

Admission controller configuration (recommended defaults)

| Parameter | Default | Description |
|---|---:|---|
| realtime.credit_rate | 500 credit/s | Refill rate for realtime routes |
| batch.credit_rate | 200 credit/s | Refill rate for background batch |
| small-slot-mem-cap_mb | 512 | Soft memory cap for q4-small category |
| large-slot-mem-cap_mb | 16384 | Reserve for fp32-large |
| preemption.grace_ms | 250 | Time to allow cooperative yield |

Sample FAC policy (YAML)

```
admission_policies:
  realtime:
    min_slots: 2
    max_concurrent: 600
    credit_rate: 500
  background:
    min_slots: 0
    max_concurrent: 200
    credit_rate: 200
kernel_categories:
  q4-small:
    slot_mem_mb: 512
    priority: 30
  fp32-large:
    slot_mem_mb: 16384
    priority: 10
```

Profiling playbook (co-located kernels)

1) Objective: measure interference and performance coupling when two or more kernel variants run concurrently on the same physical GPU set.
2) Inputs: production-like request traces (sequence distribution, prompt prefix patterns), representative models for each kernel variant, and noise traffic generator.
3) Steps:
   a) Reserve a test GPU pool with identical HW to production.
   b) Deploy kernel variants with FAC enabled and set deterministic credits (freeze refill rates).
   c) Start baseline: run single-kernel load for 30 minutes to capture baseline latency P50/P95/P99, GPU SM utilization, power, memory high-water mark.
   d) Add second kernel mix slowly using traffic ramping (10% increments) until steady state. Collect traces.
