   e) Run adversarial microbursts (3x normal qps for 60s) targeting the lower-priority kernel to validate eviction and fallback.
   f) Run a slot starvation injection where large-slot kernels hold allocations for longer than expected to validate FAC backpressure behavior.

4) Telemetry to capture (metric names):
   - runtime.admission.granted_slots_total
   - runtime.admission.rejected_by_fac_total
   - runtime.kernel.allocation_duration_ms (histogram)
   - runtime.kernel.peak_mem_mb
   - gpu.sm_util_pct (per device)
   - runtime.latency.route.<route>.p50/p95/p99
   - runtime.fallback.reroutes_total

5) Success criteria:
   - Critical realtime routes: p95 within SLO +10% overhead vs baseline.
   - No memory OOMs; observed_peak_mem_mb < configured slot_mem_mb * 0.95.
   - Reroute rate <= 0.5% for sustained load.

Benchmark suite additions (co-location scenarios)

- Add cross-kernel interference benchmarks to the perf-suite. Each benchmark is parameterized by: kernel_pair (primary, secondary), mix_ratio, sequence_length_quantile. The suite must run with at least three seeds and report: latency quantiles, per-device SM tail, and reroute/fallback rate.

- Bench metadata example (JSON lines - user-facing test harness accepts NDJSON):

```
{ "name": "fkcoexist_q4-small_fp32-large_80-20_seq95_seed1", "primary":"q4-small","secondary":"fp32-large","mix_ratio":"80-20","seq_quantile":95 }
```

Release notes snapshot (v1.3 - FKC-alpha)

- Feature: Fractional Kernel Coexistence alpha enabled behind feature-flag runtime.fkc.alpha.
- Performance: observed median latency regression of 3% on realtime routes at 20% co-located load; p99 remained stable under controlled profiling.
- Known limitations: hard preemption not implemented; rare allocation thrashing under pathological slot-starvation patterns.
- Migration: default scheduling remains single-kernel; to opt-in see rollout checklist below.

Known issues and mitigations

- Issue: occasional allocation thrash when several large-slot kernels start simultaneously.
  - Symptom: bursts of handshake.reject(reason=ALLOCATION_STARVATION), followed by high retry rate and elevated p99s.
  - Mitigation: enable queue_smoothing_seconds=15 in FAC; stagger kernel container startups by 10s.

- Issue: observed tenant isolation bleed-through when secondary kernel uses NVLINK heavily.
  - Symptom: neighboring nodes see increased PCIe stalls and higher inter-node latency for control-plane RPCs.
  - Mitigation: limit secondary kernel nvlink_bandwidth_pct to 30% via kernel hints; route heavy NVLINK kernels to dedicated node pools.

Operational runbook (incident flows)

Severity classification:
- Sev1: Realtime p99 > SLO + 250ms for > 5 minutes and reroute rate > 5%
- Sev2: Realtime p99 > SLO + 250ms for 2–5 minutes or reroute rate between 1%–5%
- Sev3: Deployment or benchmark failures without immediate customer impact

Sev1 quick steps:
1) Page oncall runtime/sre and kernel owner.
2) Run quick diagnostics:
   - curl -s http://scheduler.local/health | jq .allocations_active
   - kubectl -n runtime get pods -l app=kernel -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name} {.status.phase} {.metadata.annotations.kernel_tag}\n'
3) Check FAC metrics in Grafana dashboard 'FKC - Admission' for rejected_by_fac_total spike and runtime.fallback.reroutes_total.
4) If allocation thrashing: toggle feature flag runtime.fkc.safe-mode=true which enforces single-kernel policy for affected pool (immediate but safe fallback).
5) If thermal/SM saturation across devices: run node eviction script to drain lower-priority cohorts, see commands below.

Draining lower-priority cohorts (script snippet)
```
# mark nodes for low-priority eviction
curl -XPOST http://operator.local/nodes/mark-evict -d '{"label":"fkcoexist-evictable","reason":"sev1-protect-realtime"}'
# scale-down background admission
kubectl -n runtime patch configmap fac-config --type merge -p '{"data":{"background.max_concurrent":"0"}}'
```

Rollback checklist (kernel rollout rollback)

1) Disable rollout: runtime.fkc.rollout_enabled=false
2) Revert kernel registry entries for staged nodes to previous kernel_tag via: POST /kernel-registry/v1/patch with previous_tag
3) Restart scheduler processes in the affected pool with 60s stagger to avoid thundering herd.

Onboarding checklist for new kernel variants

- Owners: Kernel author, runtime-scheduler owner, applied-ml reviewer.
- Pre-launch requirements:
  - Pass unit kernel conformance tests (latency and mem invariants).
  - Run FKC compatibility microbench (local) with sequence distribution matching production route.
  - Submit benchmark NDJSON (see example) and get approval from scheduler owner.
  - Add kernel_tag and fidelity metadata to Kernel Registry.
- Launch: deploy to staging pool for 48h with FAC credit scaling at 10% traffic slice.
- Post-launch: run profiling playbook and look for regressions in p95/p99; if any are > 10% over baseline, escalate.

Ownership and contact list

- Runtime scheduler: Marco Liu (marco@redwood.ai)
- Kernel onboarding / applied ML: Evelyn Ortiz (evelyn@redwood.ai)
- Serving SRE: Diego Fernandez (diego@redwood.ai)
- Release engineering: Priya Nair (priya@redwood.ai)

References and related pages

- Kernel admission and signal negotiation manual — internal link in team library.
- Runtime profiling playbooks (see profiling-playbook directory).
- Benchmark suite contributor guide — follow perf-suite/README for NDJSON conventions.

Appendix A — quick verification checklist (pre-merge gate)

- [ ] Kernel tag registered with stability_grade >= canary
- [ ] FAC policy set for pool and credit_rate validated
- [ ] Benchmarks (3 seeds) show p95 within +10% of baseline for realtime route
- [ ] Observability: tracing annotations for KHP added and sampling enabled
- [ ] Release note entry drafted

Appendix B — sample trace annotation snippet (pseudo-JSON)

```
{
  "trace": {
    "request_id": "r-abc123",
    "events": [
      {"ts": 167000000, "name": "fac.handshake.request", "kernel_tag": "q4-small"},
      {"ts": 167000130, "name": "fac.handshake.accept", "allocation_id": "alloc-42"},
      {"ts": 167000780, "name": "kernel.execute.start", "kernel_variant": "q4-small-v2"},
      {"ts": 167001200, "name": "kernel.execute.end", "duration_ms": 420}
    ]
  }
}
```

If anything in this handbook is unclear or you encounter behaviours not covered here, file a ticket in the runtime backlog and tag scheduler-owner and serving-sre for prioritization.

title: Dispatch Telemetry Schema and Fallback Playbook
content:
Summary
-------
This document defines the canonical telemetry schema emitted at the dispatch layer, describes the signal->decision mapping used by the runtime to enact fallbacks, and provides an operational playbook for on-call and engineering teams to diagnose and remediate dispatch-induced degradations. The intent is to ensure consistent instrumentation, make fallback triggers auditable, and provide a reproducible validation and benchmarking process prior to rollout.

Scope
-----
Applies to: dispatch-svc (request router), kernel-orchestrator, runtime-admission-controller, and the observability pipelines that consume their telemetry.
Excludes: user-facing application logs, customer prompts, and post-hoc analysis performed by product analytics.

Why this matters
-----------------
- Dispatch is the first decision point that affects latency, model fidelity, and per-token cost.
- Inconsistent telemetry or opaque fallback decisions have caused missed SLAs and customer surprises in previous incidents.
- This playbook standardizes signals so automated escalation and incident playbooks can be deterministic.

Telemetry Schema (dispatch layer)
--------------------------------
Emit these fields on every request event (JSON schema example):

Example event (flattened JSON):
{
  "timestamp": "2026-02-03T14:11:22Z",
  "req_id": "req_6a2f9b",
  "tenant_id": "team-alpha",
  "route": "/v1/generate",
  "model_variant": "rw-13b-quant-a",
  "dispatch_decision": "scheduled",  // scheduled | fallback | queued | rejected
  "kernel_id": "k-03",
  "kernel_queue_time_ms": 12.4,
  "kernel_exec_time_ms": 78.2,
  "end_to_end_latency_ms": 142.8,
  "token_count": 64,
  "cost_estimate_units": 0.024,
  "priority": "standard",
  "cohort": "mixed-burst",
  "prefetch_hit": false,
  "kv_cache_hit_rate": 0.0,
  "fallback_reason": "kernel-unavailable", // optional string when dispatch_decision == fallback
  "decision_trace": ["slot-claim","kernel-hedge"],
  "sampling_score": 0.63
}

Signal catalog and semantic definitions
--------------------------------------
- dispatch_decision: high-level outcome of routing. Values and semantics in table below.
- kernel_queue_time_ms: time spent waiting in kernel dispatch queue (critical for tail latency).
- kernel_exec_time_ms: wall time of in-kernel execution. Excludes queue time
- end_to_end_latency_ms: total time from HTTP ingress to response commit
- prefetch_hit: whether a prefetcher predicted and warmed the KV cache for this session
- decision_trace: ordered list of decision checkpoints (useful for replay and audit)

Alerting thresholds and SLO mappings
-----------------------------------
We maintain per-tenant and global SLOs. The dispatch layer maps signal anomalies to alerts and automated fallbacks. Use the following baseline thresholds (table):

| Metric | Warning threshold | Critical threshold | Action | Owner |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| p95 end_to_end_latency_ms (global) | 120 ms | 180 ms | Trigger latency-alert, cascade to autoscaler and runtime fallback policy | eng-sre |
| kernel_queue_time_ms (p99) | 50 ms | 150 ms | Increase priority for pinned kernels; enable hedging; if persists >5m -> fallback to compressed variant | runtime |
| dispatch_decision == rejected (rate) | 0.5% | 2% | Backpressure review; open incident if sustained >1m | eng-sre |
| fallback_rate (tenant, 1m) | 1% | 5% | Page product on degrading quality, run triage | runtime/product |
| kv_cache_hit_rate (cohort) | - | <10% sustained | Trigger KV cache warmup re-eval; run prefetcher audit | runtime |

Decision categories and recommended policies
-------------------------------------------
1) scheduled: proceed with selected kernel/model variant.
2) queued: admitted but awaiting slot. If queue exceeds 250ms (p95), enable short hedging to an opportunistic kernel.
3) fallback: routed to lower-cost or lower-fidelity variant to preserve latency SLO. Record fallback_reason.
4) rejected: admission controller refused due to quota or emergency backpressure. Return 429 with debug code.

Fallback decision matrix (example)
--------------------------------
If a decision point detects an anomaly, use tenant tier and request priority to calculate allowed fallback strategies.

- High priority (enterprise SLA): prefer region fallback before fidelity fallback.
- Standard: prefer fidelity fallback (quantized or distilled variant) before cross-region.
- Low: allow admission rejection if autoscaler capacity unavailable.

Matrix (simplified):

| Trigger | Enterprise | Standard | Low |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| kernel-unavailable | cross-region swap -> scheduled | model-quantized fallback -> scheduled | reject |
| kernel-thermal-throttle | migrate to warm node -> scheduled | model-quantized fallback -> scheduled | fallback -> reject if persists |
| sustained-high-queue | burst-scale slots + hedging | fidelity fallback + hedging | queue or reject |

Operational playbook (step-by-step)
-----------------------------------
The following steps assume an alert was raised for p99 kernel_queue_time_ms above critical for multiple kernels.

1) Triage (first 5 minutes)
  a) On-call reviews the alert, pulls the live dispatch dashboard (Dash: Dispatch/Kernel Queues).
  b) Check correlation between queue spike and recent deployments (check /releases and kernel-rollout feed).
  c) Inspect decision_trace sample stream for pattern (e.g., repeated "slot-claim-timeout").
2) Immediate mitigations (5--20 minutes)
  a) If spike is caused by a specific kernel_id and thermal/host issues: mark kernel node as drain-candidate and migrate sessions (CLI snippet below).
  b) Increase short-lived hedging for affected routes: set hedging multiplier to 2 for 10 minutes.
  c) Enable fidelity fallback for standard tenants: config change in runtime-admission-controller config map.
3) Root cause and resolution (>20 minutes)
  a) Capture representative traces (use sampling_score >0.5) and upload to incident artifact store.
  b) Run targeted microbenchmarks against kernel_id with synthetic corpus.
  c) If code regression suspected, roll back kernel/driver rollout per the kernel rollback playbook.
4) Post-incident
  a) Update incident report with timeline, decision_trace snippets, and corrective config changes.
  b) Propose adjustments to thresholds and fallback rules if behavior was expected under new traffic patterns.

Commands and examples
---------------------
Drain a kernel node (cli):

$ ri-runtimectl kernel drain --kernel-id k-03 --reason "thermal-throttle" --deadline 300s

Increase hedging for route (api):

POST /admin/runtime/hedging
Content-Type: application/json
{
  "route": "/v1/generate",
  "multiplier": 2,
  "duration_s": 600
}

Patch admission controller to enable quantized fallback (kubectl patch example):

kubectl -n runtime patch configmap admission-config --patch '{"data":{"enable_quantized_fallback":"true"}}'

Benchmarks and validation before rollout
---------------------------------------
Before changing any dispatch decision logic or adding a new fallback path:
- Run the dispatch synthetic workload harness (see runbook: dispatch-synthetic-harness).
- Execute a fidelity-vs-latency sweep: quantify quality delta (BLEU/ROUGE/LLM-eval metric) vs latency improvements for the candidate fallback.
- Validate end-to-end SLOs using the mixed-workload-slo-simulation suite with the same traffic signatures produced by our production traffic mirror.

Validation checklist (must pass all):
1) No more than 0.5% increase in error rate for enterprise tenants.
2) p95 latency improvement >= 10% in overloaded scenarios.
3) Rollback path tested in staging and rehearsal performed with chaos injection.

Observability and auditing
-------------------------
- Decision_trace must be retained for 30 days for all requests sampled with sampling_score > 0.5; store in compressed parquet in observability cluster.
- Fallbacks must emit a structured event (fallback_event) with metadata: {req_id, tenant_id, original_variant, fallback_variant, reason, latency_before, latency_after}.
- Maintain a daily fallback-rate report by tenant and route (automated job).

Ownership and contact list
--------------------------
- Dispatch service: runtime-dispatch@redwoodinternal (owner: Marcus Chen)
- Runtime admission controller: runtime-admission@redwoodinternal (owner: Priya Rao)
- Eng SRE on-call: see oncall roster

Rollout checklist (pre-deploy)
------------------------------
- [ ] Schema validated by telemetry team and CI schema checks pass.
- [ ] Synthetic harness pass at 10% and 100% load profiles.
- [ ] Canary rollout to 1% traffic for 4 hours with live metrics.
- [ ] Audit log retention and decision_trace retention configured.
- [ ] Runbook links and owner tags added to release notes.

Diagnostics tips and common failure modes
----------------------------------------
- Symptom: many fallbacks recorded with fallback_reason == "kernel-unavailable" but kernel hosts show healthy metrics.
  - Likely cause: admission-controller slot accounting mismatch. Check slot-claim timeout in decision_trace.
- Symptom: p95 latency improves after fallback but product quality complaints spike.
  - Action: revert fidelity fallback for affected tenant cohort and open product escalation.

Appendix: Lightweight schema registry (how to evolve)
---------------------------------------------------
1) Add new fields as optional and increment telemetry schema minor version.
2) Update CI schema-lint job to validate new fields against the registry.
3) Consumers must declare compatibility: any consumer that depends on a field must list it in the registry.
4) Deprecation policy: mark field deprecated for 60 days before removal; provide a migration adapter.

References
----------
- Execution contracts and stable fallbacks (see related pages)
- Kernel rollout and rollback playbook (kernel-and-scheduling)
- Mixed-workload SLO simulation suite (benchmarking-and-perf-suite)

If you find gaps or ambiguous signal semantics, open a PR against this page and ping the reviewers listed above.

title: Serving Runtime Feature Flag Cleanup Plan
content:
h1. Overview
This page describes the plan to clean up and remove legacy feature flags in the Serving Runtime related to experimental batching and KV-cache heuristics. The goal is to reduce configuration surface area, remove dead code paths, and simplify rollout logic without regressing latency, throughput, or correctness.

This work originated as *ENG-5842* and has been updated to reflect the 2025H2/2026Q1 serving architecture changes (Adaptive Micro-batching v2 and KV-cache policy unification).

h1. Goals
* Remove unused or permanently-enabled flags.
* Replace “behavioral” flags with explicit, versioned runtime configuration where needed.
* Eliminate rollout branching that is no longer exercised.
* Maintain safe canarying and rollback hooks during the removal window.

h1. Non-goals
* Redesign batching scheduling (owned by the batching roadmap).
* Change default model-level cache settings (owned by Model Perf).
* Rework customer-exposed API parameters.

h1. Scope
The cleanup targets flags that historically controlled:
* Experimental batching (now superseded by *Adaptive Micro-batching v2*).
* KV-cache heuristic selection and fallback behavior (now consolidated into a single policy engine).

h2. Repos / services affected
* serving-runtime (core runtime)
* gateway (request shaping / headers)
* fleet-config (runtime config distribution)
* console (admin UI surfacing of flags)

h1. Flag inventory and decisions
The table below lists the most common legacy flags and the current disposition.

|| Flag || Previous use || Decision (2026) || Notes ||
| enable_experimental_batching | Toggle early micro-batching experiment | *Remove* | Adaptive Micro-batching v2 is the only supported path. |
| experimental_batching_max_tokens | Limit batch size in experiment | *Replace* | Move to fleet-config key: runtime.batching.max_tokens (validated range, no branching). |
| experimental_batching_max_delay_ms | Scheduler delay cap | *Replace* | Move to fleet-config key: runtime.batching.max_delay_ms. |
| kv_cache_heuristics_mode | Select heuristic set (A/B) | *Remove* | Policy engine now selects based on model profile; legacy modes unused since 2025-10. |
| kv_cache_force_recompute | Force bypass cache for debugging | *Keep (restricted)* | Remains available only in restricted admin tooling; not a general runtime flag. |
| kv_cache_skip_reuse_on_miss | Fallback behavior in early cache | *Remove* | Redundant with unified policy engine; code path deleted. |

h2. Notes on what changed since the original ticket
* Experimental batching flags were originally planned for canary removal only; as of *2025-11*, the runtime defaults to Adaptive Micro-batching v2 and the legacy implementation is no longer exercised in production.
* KV-cache heuristics have been unified; selection is now driven by model profile + runtime policy rather than ad-hoc flags.

h1. Deprecation and removal timeline
* 2025-12 to 2026-01: Mark flags as deprecated in runtime logs and console.
* 2026-02: Stop reading deprecated flags (soft removal) while still accepting them in config payloads to avoid hard failures.
* 2026-03: Delete legacy code paths and remove flags from config schemas.
* 2026-04: Remove any remaining UI surfacing and docs references.

h1. Implementation plan
# Audit and enumerate flags
## Search for reads and writes across repos; produce a single source-of-truth list (this page).
## Identify flags that are:
* Dead (never read)
* Always-on
* Equivalent to a stable config knob
# Deprecation notices
## Runtime:
* Emit a warning when deprecated flags are present.
* Include a single-line migration hint to the replacement fleet-config keys.
## Console:
* Mark as deprecated with removal date.
* Hide deprecated flags from default view.
# Removal patches behind feature branches
## Land changes in small PRs:
* Introduce replacement fleet-config keys (validated, documented).
* Stop reading legacy flags (soft removal).
* Delete dead/legacy modules (hard removal).
# Testing and validation gates
## Microbenchmarks:
* Throughput (tokens/sec) must not regress > 1%.
* p95 end-to-end latency must not regress > 2%.
## End-to-end smoke tests:
* Streaming and non-streaming inference.
* Multi-turn sessions (cache reuse).
* High-concurrency workloads.
# Rollout and coordination
## Coordinate canary rollout with Eng-SRE and QA.
## Use dedicated canary pools and automatic rollback hooks.

h1. Rollout procedure
h2. Canary pools
* sr-canary-a (1% traffic)
* sr-canary-b (5% traffic)

h2. Success criteria
* Error rate increase <= 0.1% absolute (5xx and runtime-level failures).
* p95 latency increase <= 2% relative.
* Cache hit-rate does not drop > 3% relative for cache-eligible routes.

h2. Rollback
* Roll back by reverting to last known good runtime build and re-enabling legacy read path only if necessary.
* Note: once hard removal lands (code deletion), rollback requires reverting the runtime commit; this is why soft removal precedes hard removal by at least one release.

h1. Ownership and tracking
* Primary owner: Rajat Patel
* Doc owner: Maya Thompson
* Eng-SRE partner: Elena Park

Tracking:
* Original ticket: ENG-5842 (runtime-maintenance)
* Follow-on hard removal checklist: ENG-9137 (serving-runtime)

h1. Risk assessment
Overall risk is *low*, but requires careful canarying due to:
* Configuration drift across dedicated pools.
* Hidden dependencies in older customer deployments that may still set deprecated flags.

Mitigations:
* Soft removal phase (warn + ignore) before hard deletion.
* Canary pools with automated regression detection.
* Clear rollback path while soft removal is active.

h1. References
* confluence/eng-serving-runtime/flag-deprecation-plan
* github/redwood/pr-7812
* github/redwood/pr-9074
* confluence/eng-sre/canary-rollout-standard

title: Observability Bridge and Execution Surface Manual
content:
Purpose

This document defines the Observability Bridge: the cross-cutting contract between the serving runtime execution surface, kernel scheduler, and the observability/benchmarks systems. It is a practical manual for engineers who implement instrumentation, create profiling experiments, debug production SLO regressions, and author synthetic benchmarks.

Scope and audience

- Scope: runtime telemetry schema, kernel scheduling knobs that affect signals, profiling/playbook templates, benchmarking harness integration, incident runbook steps for SLO regressions, and a short release-notes checklist for telemetry changes.
- Audience: runtime engineers, platform SREs, profiling owners, and applied ML engineers onboarding to inferencing performance work.

High-level goals

1. Provide a stable, low-cost telemetry surface that supports causal latency attribution and cost-per-token accounting.
2. Ensure kernel scheduler decisions are visible and actionable in traces, metrics, and sample profiles.
3. Reduce investigation time for tail latency and regression hunts by 50% through standardized probes and playbooks.

Key concepts and terminology

- Execution surface: API boundary between the front-end request router and the per-GPU kernel worker. Includes request metadata (route, priority, model-variant), session affinity hints, and requested QoS profile.
- Kernel epoch: a contiguous sequence of kernel launches that service a single logical request (can include kernel hedges, fallback kernels, and prefetch kernels).
- Decision trace: a compact, append-only event bundle attached to each request that records scheduling choices, cache hits/misses, kernel variant selection, and routing fallbacks.
- Observability Bridge: the canonical set of telemetry artifacts (metrics, traces, event logs, binary samples) and the mapping rules from runtime artifacts to downstream stores (Prometheus, Jaeger/OTel, ClickHouse).

Observability Bridge: telemetry contracts

1) Minimal per-request trace model (OTel-compatible)

- Required attributes (always present):
  - request.id (string)
  - request.route (string)
  - user.tier (string)
  - model.name (string)
  - model.variant (string)
  - sequence.length (int)
  - priority (int)
  - kernel.epoch_id (string)
  - kernel.epoch_stage (enum: enqueue|dispatch|kernel_start|kernel_end|postprocess)

- Important events (emit as spans or events inside the request trace):
  - kvcache.hit / kvcache.miss (include shard_id and approximate latency_ms)
  - kernel.selection (selected_variant, heuristics_triggered)
  - kernel.hedge (hedge_target_ms)
  - routing.fallback (reason_code, fallback_variant)
  - admission.control (slot_granted, preemption_note)

2) Lightweight counters and histograms (Prometheus)

- Counters: requests_total{route,model,variant,priority}, kvcache_hits_total{shard}, kernel_launches_total{variant}, preemptions_total{reason}.
- Histograms/Summaries: request_latency_ms_bucket{route,percentile}, kernel_exec_ms_bucket{variant,slot_type}, kv_latency_ms_bucket{shard}.

3) Binary sample capture (for root-cause)

- Samples must be probabilistic and cost-aware. Default policy: sample 0.1% of requests globally, 1% of requests in the 95–99.9th latency percentile, and 100% of requests marked as incidents. Captured artifacts: full trace, kernel microprofile (CUDA CUPTI / ROCm HSA), and model logits snapshot (first 64 tokens).

Mapping and retention

- Mapping rules: traces -> Jaeger/OTel; counters/histograms -> Prometheus/Thanos; binary samples -> ClickHouse S3-backed archive with TTL 90 days for non-incident samples, 540 days for incident samples.

Kernel scheduler observability patterns

Make scheduling decisions visible without exposing implementation internals:

- Annotate every kernel launch with kernel.metadata tags: slot_type (dedicated|burst|preemptible), kernel_priority, preemptible_till.
- Emit scheduling decisions as events in the request trace with reason codes mapped to stable enum values.
- Surface per-slot occupancy metrics with 1s resolution and 1m rollups.

Example kernel decision trace (OTel pseudo-JSON)

{
  "trace_id": "...",
  "spans": [
    {"name": "request.dispatch", "attributes": {"kernel.epoch_id": "e-6bd3"}},
    {"name": "scheduler.decide", "attributes": {"slot_type": "preemptible", "decision": "queued", "reason": "burst_quota"}},
    {"name": "kernel.launch", "attributes": {"variant": "int8-fastpath", "exec_ms": 12}}
  ]
}

Profiling playbook (quick start)

Purpose: binary reproducible steps to attribute tail latency to one of the common buckets (queuing, kvcache, kernel, postprocess/IO).

1. Reproduce load shape in the local benchmark harness. Use the Operational Workload Simulator (see benchmarking catalog).
2. Run fast-path sampling: collect request traces at 1% sampling for 15 minutes with kernel microprofiles.
3. Run deterministic microbenchmarks: kernel alone, shader-only with identical input sizes, and KV cache-only hit/miss experiments.
4. Apply the causal attribution checklist: correlate request-level latency with kernel.exec_ms, kvcache latency, and scheduler.queue_ms.

Benchmarking harness integration

- Standard artifact: workload YAML describing request distribution, concurrency, model variant mix, and token-length histogram. Example:

workload: "chat-service-small-burst"
concurrency: 120
model_mix: {"gpt-like-xxs": 0.7, "gpt-like-slim": 0.3}
percentile_targets: [50, 95, 99, 99.9]
sequence_length_histogram: "path/to/histogram.json"

- Run sequence:
  1) dry-run (validate connections and KV cache priming)
  2) steady-state ramp to target concurrency over 180s
  3) 10m stable measurement window with live counters and trace sampling
  4) cool-down and artifact collection

- Cost accounting: ensure the harness reports per-token GPU-time and model-variant per-token energy. Use the runtime cost plugin to collect per-token CUDA ns.

Release notes and telemetry changes checklist

- If a PR changes any emitted attribute, add an entry to the telemetry changelog and bump the schema minor version. Mandatory reviewer: Observability Platform (Maya Patel).
- Backwards compatibility rule: new attributes may be added; renaming or removing attributes requires a deprecation cycle of at least 30 days and a coordinated rollout across consumers.

Known issues and mitigations (engineers should copy these patterns into incidents)

1. Symptom: Intermittent 99.9th latency spikes with high kvcache misses.
   - Probable cause: Shard imbalanced eviction or prefetch turned off during burst.
   - Mitigation: Temporarily increase kvcache.repair_concurrency to 8 and enable shard-prefetch for affected route.

2. Symptom: Kernel launch queue grows but kernel.exec_ms stays constant.
   - Probable cause: Admission control or slot exhaustion.
   - Mitigation: Check slot occupancy metrics, temporarily enable burst capacity pool, and scale Dedicated pool if sustained.

3. Symptom: Traces show many scheduler.decide events with reason=preemption_expected.
   - Probable cause: aggressive priority shaping or degraded NVLink.
   - Mitigation: Lower preemption aggressiveness, kick off NVLink health-check job, and route critical traffic to reserved slots.

Incident runbook (SLO regression — high-level)

1) Triage
  - Confirm SLO breach (duration, route, model). Pull top-100 traces for the breach window.
2) Classify
  - Run the profiling playbook reproduction for the same load shape. Compute attribution across queuing, kernel, kv, postprocess.
3) Short-term mitigations
  - Route critical customers to alternate variant/model (prefer lower-latency variant). Throttle bulk routes. Increase sample rate.
4) Root-cause and fix
  - If kernel-related: apply kernel rollback or tuning and run canary. If kvcache-related: rebalance shards and pre-warm hot keys.
5) Postmortem and follow-up
  - Publish incident notes, update telemetry mapping if additional attributes were required, and add a permanent alert if the event repeats.

Operational dashboards and alerts (recommended)

- Dashboards:
  - Runtime Overview: requests/s, 95/99/99.9 latencies, kernel_launch_rate, kvcache_hit_rate, slot_occupancy
  - Scheduler Health: per-slot occupancy heatmap, preemption_rate, queue_length trend
  - Sampling Explorer: sampled-traces-per-minute, tail-sample-conversion-rate (sample -> binary sample)

- Alerts (suggested):
  - P1: 99.9 latency breach for >10m AND tail-sample-conversion-rate < 0.1% -> page oncall
  - P2: slot_occupancy > 95% for 3m -> message runtime-scaling channel
  - P3: kvcache_hit_rate drop > 20% in 5m -> create auto-ticket for kvcache-repair job

Contributions and ownership

- Observability Bridge steward: Maya Patel (Observability Platform)
- Runtime telemetry owner: Priya Nambiar (Serving Runtime)
- Profiling playbook owner: Diego Alvarez (Performance)

How to onboard a consumer (team) to the bridge

1. Request access to the telemetry schema and sample traces (file a ticket to observability-platform).
2. Verify client can parse required attributes and run the compliance test harness (small binary producing sample traces).
3. Run a joint benchmark with a runtime engineer to validate the mapping.

Appendix A — telemetry attribute enum table

| Attribute | Type | Description | Stable values / notes |
| request.route | string | Logical route name | freeform but align to routing service naming |
| kernel.epoch_stage | enum | Stage within epoch | enqueue, dispatch, kernel_start, kernel_end, postprocess |
| slot_type | string | Slot allocation type | dedicated, burst, preemptible |
| preemption_reason | string | High-level reason code | quota_burst, topology_eviction, maintenance |

Appendix B — example CLI snippets

# Run a local sampling session (harness)
redwood-bench run --workload path/to/workload.yaml --sample-rate 0.01 --collect-traces

# Export top traces to local dir
redwood-observe export --time-window "2026-02-08T14:00:00Z/2026-02-08T14:10:00Z" --filter "route=chat-service" --dest ./samples

Further reading / related pages

- Runtime decision graph and observed behaviour catalog (internal)
- Causal latency attribution playbook
- Kernel telemetry annotation guidelines

Document change log

- 2025-09-14: Initial draft (Priya Nambiar)
- 2025-11-02: Added binary sample policy and benchmarking YAML example (Diego Alvarez)
- 2026-02-10: Formalized release-notes checklist and retention policy (Maya Patel)

title: Runtime Phase Diagram and Fidelity Operational Playbook
content:
Summary

This playbook defines a compact operational contract for how the serving runtime transitions across deterministic phases during normal operation, stress, and failure modes. It codifies: a phase diagram (textual + ASCII timeline) for decision points; fidelity modes and their safe transitions; kernel-scheduler hooks and minimum telemetry signals required for automated decisions; a step-by-step runbook for human intervention; and a lightweight experiment checklist for validating policy changes. This document is intended for runtime engineers, on-call SREs, and product owners responsible for SLOs and quality budgets.

Goals

- Ensure predictable and auditable transitions between runtime fidelity modes (Full, Graceful Degraded, Conservative, Emergency).
- Define the minimal signals and thresholds needed to trigger automated transitions and operator alerts.
- Provide a safe rollback and validation checklist for kernel/scheduler policy changes that affect fidelity.

Scope

- Applies to the primary serving runtime (gpu-dispatcher + kernel-shephard) and the orchestration layer that performs routing/fallback.
- Covers request-level fidelity changes (response length truncation, sampling temperature changes, model variant swap, quantization tiering) and execution-level controls (batch slicing, preemption, slot revocation).
- Excludes client-side retry/backoff policies and upstream model training pipelines.

Phase Diagram (textual)

We model runtime state as a small set of phases that the operator or automation may transition between. Each phase has a clear intent, allowed actions, and required observability.

1) Full (green)
   - Intent: Serve requests at configured model and kernel fidelity with SLO headroom.
   - Allowed actions: Normal batching, full KV cache retention, prefetch enabled, latency SLO = 95th < configured threshold.

2) Graceful Degraded (amber)
   - Intent: Reduce cost/pressure while preserving correctness for high-priority requests.
   - Allowed actions: Apply per-tenant degradation (e.g., lower sampling N, transient model variant with smaller context), reduce prefetch aggressiveness, coalesce small batches, enable fast-path quant kernels.

3) Conservative (orange)
   - Intent: Stop non-essential work, prioritize tail-latency sensitive traffic and safety-critical routes.
   - Allowed actions: Disable background KV prefetch, evict cold KV shards, reduce maximum output tokens, enable stricter admission control quotas.

4) Emergency (red)
   - Intent: Maintain basic availability for critical customers or routes, accept higher unit cost.
   - Allowed actions: Route only to SLA-backed capacity, reduce model size aggressively (e.g., prune/condense context), enable synchronous hedging to reduce tail risk, lift batching to reduce memory pressure.

ASCII timeline (simplified)

  Normal -> (pressure rises: sustained queue depth > Q_high) -> Graceful Degraded -> (kernel errors or memory pressure) -> Conservative -> (data-plane outage or severe capacity loss) -> Emergency
  Emergency -> (capacity restored and health heuristics pass) -> Conservative -> (stability sustained) -> Graceful Degraded -> (fully recovered) -> Normal

Signals and thresholds (minimum set)

- Queue metrics: request_queue_depth (per node), sustained_window = 120s, Q_high = 500, Q_critical = 1500.
- Kernel metrics: kernel_p95_latency (per kernel family), slow_kernel_rate > 2% over 5m -> escalate.
- Memory: gpu_memory_utilization > 92% for 60s -> trigger Conservative.
- Error rates: model_inference_errors > 0.5% 1m OR grpc_stream_resets > 1% 1m -> evaluate for Emergency.
- SLO degradation: observed_p95_latency > target * 1.35 for 3 consecutive evaluation windows (1m windows) -> transition to Graceful Degraded.

Telemetry contract (required fields for automation)

- request.surface: route_id, priority_score, user_tier
- request.metrics: queue_depth, arrival_rate, last_trace_id
- kernel.signals: kernel_family_id, p50/p95/p99, queue_drain_rate
- host.metrics: gpu_mem_pct, cuda_error_count, nvlink_errors
- runtime.health: consul_health, agent_heartbeat, time_since_last_config_apply

Kernel scheduler hooks (implementation notes)

- admission_controller.on_phase_change(phase_name): idempotent call invoked by orchestration layer. Handlers must complete within 2s and return a short summary.
- kernel_mapper.suggest_variant(route_id, phase_name, sample_context): returns kernel_variant_id and expected_resource_delta.
- kvcache.adaptive_eviction(phase_name, eviction_fraction): synchronous call to reduce memory footprint with consistent eviction markers.

Operational runbook: automated transition flow

1) Detection (automation)
   a) Rolling windows: compute windowed aggregates for queue_depth, kernel latency, memory utilization.
   b) If any threshold crossed (see Signals table), automation sends an entry to the decision log and evaluates safe transition rules.
2) Policy evaluation
   a) Run admission policies (priority-aware): ensure top 20% high-priority routes do not drop below configured fidelity threshold.
   b) Compute candidate actions (e.g., enable quantized fast-kernel for model X on pool A).
3) Staging (pre-commit)
   a) Try non-invasive controls first: increase batch coalescing, lower sampling, alpha throttle non-critical routes.
   b) Wait 30s; if improvements observed in p95 latency and queue depth, keep staged changes and record in decision log.
4) Commit
   a) Execute idempotent kernel and routing changes with atomic config tags (config.apply_id).
   b) Emit audit event and notify on-call via Slack pager and runbook link.
5) Monitor
   a) Observe for 5 minutes. If metrics improve, continue; otherwise escalate to human operator for Conservative/Emergency escalation.

Human escalation playbook (short)

- If automation fails to stabilize after a single commit and 2x staging attempts (total 2m), page on-call SRE with subject: "Runtime phase escalate -> node group X". Include decision log id.
- On-call responsibilities:
  1. Verify decision log and applied config changes.
  2. If memory pressure is root cause: run the GPU eviction helper and cross-check NVML diagnostics.
  3. If kernel stalls present: trigger graceful drain of affected node(s) and activate a recovery kernel roll (see Kernel Roll procedure below).

Kernel roll procedure (safe patch for slow kernel family)

1) Quarantine: mark kernel_family.K as quarantine=true in scheduler metadata. Stop assigning new slots.
2) Shadow canary: deploy candidate kernel K' to 2 nodes in shadow pool, mirror a 1% traffic sample (low-priority traffic) for 10 minutes.
3) Compare latencies and error rates against historical baseline using the bench harness (bench-run-id) and the microprobe profile.
4) If K' passes (p95 <= baseline * 1.05 and errors <= baseline), promote K' to 10% traffic, then 30%, then full, with 5m observation windows.
5) If K' fails at any step, roll back immediately and run postmortem tag.

Minimum validation checklist for any scheduler/config change

- Unit tests for mapper and admission_controller change: green.
- End-to-end bench: synthetic replication of traffic shape (spike and tail) using the runtime synthetic runner.
- Canary traffic: 2 nodes, 1% traffic for 10m, metrics inbound to bench-run-id.
- Observability: new signals annotated in telemetry index, alert rule added with known owner.
- Rollback plan: pre-recorded config.apply_id for immediate revert.

Config table (example values)

| Parameter | Recommended default | Notes |
| request_queue_probe_window | 120s | Window used to compute sustained pressure |
| Q_high | 500 | Node-level queue depth for guarded staging |
| Q_critical | 1500 | Escalation to Conservative |
| staging_wait | 30s | Wait time after staging change before commit |
| observe_commit_window | 5m | Monitor after commit before marking resolved |
| high_priority_preserve_pct | 20% | Minimum traffic share preserved at higher fidelity |

(Represented above as a markdown-style table for readability; our telemetry UI expects these params in runtime-config service under /configs/phase_control)

Experiment checklist (for policy changes)

- Define hypothesis and metric delta (p95 latency, error rate, SLO loss) and minimum detectable effect.
- Build synthetic load profile that captures burst shape (spike length, inter-arrival tail).
- Run NOMINAL baseline bench (3 runs) and record bench-run-id.
- Deploy change behind flag; run shadow canary for 15m collecting p50/p95/p99, cuda errs, queue_depth.
- Automatic gating: stop if p99 increases by > 30% or error rate doubles.

Common failure scenarios and suggested mitigations

- Symptom: Sustained high queue depth with low GPU utilization.
  Mitigation: Increase batching and coalesce small requests; verify admission_controller is not misclassifying priorities.

- Symptom: High kernel p95 with bursty small requests.
  Mitigation: Enable fast-path quantized kernels for small-context routes; reduce scheduling jitter by pinning core threads.

- Symptom: Frequent NVML OOMs after deployment.
  Mitigation: Revert recent kernel changes, evict cold KV shards, and enable conservative phase to protect high-priority routing.

Ownership and links

- Primary owner: Runtime Platform (eng-serving-runtime). Pager: runtime-oncall@redwood.ai.
- Related docs:
  - /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-upgrade-validation-and-canary-matrix-2026 (upgrade gating)
  - /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/kernel-snapshot-observability-contract-2026 (kernel observability)
  - /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/runtime-deployment-sanity-and-benchmark-suite-acceptance-2026 (bench harness)

Appendix A — Example config footprint (YAML snippet)

---
phase_control:
  window_seconds: 120
  q_high: 500
  q_critical: 1500
  preserve_tiers:
    - tier: enterprise
      preserve_pct: 50
    - tier: standard
      preserve_pct: 20
  staging_wait_seconds: 30
  observe_commit_minutes: 5
---

Appendix B — Quick CLI helpers

- Show decision log: rw-runtimectl decision-log show --limit 50 --since 1h
- Force a phase: rw-runtimectl phase set --node-group gpu-pool-3 --phase graceful-degraded --reason "manual-test"
- Rollback config: rw-runtimectl config revert --apply-id <id>

Notes and change history

- 2025-10-15: Created by Priya Raman to consolidate phase controls and automation contract.
- 2025-12-09: Added kernel roll procedure and quarantine pattern (review by Diego Alvarez).
- 2026-02-18: Added explicit telemetry contract and tightened thresholds for Q_high/Q_critical following a production incident (postmortem ref: PM-2026-03).

This playbook is expected to evolve. If you propose changes, open a PR to the runtime playbook repo and ping the reviewers listed above.

title: SLO-driven Scheduler Autotune Playbook
content:
Summary:
This playbook describes the SLO-driven Scheduler Autotuner: a control loop that adjusts runtime scheduling parameters and kernel selection preferences to meet tenant and global SLOs while minimizing cost. It covers architecture, signals, tuning procedures, canary/rollout steps, observability dashboards, and triage steps for common failure modes.

Goals and scope:
- Primary goal: keep per-route and per-model latency SLOs (p50/p95/p99) within target while maximizing throughput and minimizing per-token GPU cost.
- Secondary goals: avoid oscillation, preserve fairness across tenants, and provide deterministic rollback.
- Scope: inference request scheduler, kernel mapper hints, batching window, prefetching hints, and priority shaping. Not in scope: model parameter changes, quantization format changes, or hardware auto-scaling (handled by capacity-control).

Context and assumptions:
- Runtime exposes the following knobs: batch_max_tokens, batch_time_ms, kernel_hint (preferred kernel profile), kvcache_prefetch=true/false, priority_boost (integer), and graceful_preempt_timeout_ms.
- Telemetry: scheduler emits per-route aggregated metrics every 10s; per-request traces are sampled at 0.1% by default.
- SLOs can be defined at route, model, and tenant levels. Autotuner operates bottom-up: route -> model -> tenant.

Signals and telemetry (observable list):
- Latency.P50.route.<route> (ms)
- Latency.P95.route.<route> (ms)
- Latency.P99.route.<route> (ms)
- TailQueueDepth.route.<route> (requests)
- KernelExecutionTime.avg (ms) by kernel_hint
- BatchSize.mean and BatchSize.p95
- KVCacheHitRate.route.<route> (ratio)
- GPUUtilization.device (percent)
- SchedulingDecision.count.policy.<policy> (counter)
- AutotuneAction.events (counter with labels: action=scale_batch/time/kernel_hint)
- Cost.per_token.estimate (USD)
- ErrorRate.route.<route> (5xx + 4xx as separate series)

Key SLO examples (company defaults):
- Soft SLO: Latency.P95.route.* < 120ms
- Hard SLO: Latency.P99.route.* < 300ms
- Availability SLO: ErrorRate.route.* < 0.5% (rolling 1h)
- Cost target: per_token_cost.delta <= +20% from baseline for non-critical routes

Autotuner decision policy overview:
- Policy input: last 5m rolling metrics, traffic shape (sequence length histogram), GPU capacity, current batch stats, and recent autotune actions.
- Priority: preserve Hard SLO > Soft SLO > cost minimization.
- Action set (atomic): increase/decrease batch_time_ms by up to 20%, increase/decrease batch_max_tokens by up to 2x/0.5x, switch kernel_hint to compatible alternative, enable kvcache_prefetch on warm routes, apply priority_boost for short burst latency reduction.
- Cooldown: minimum 5 minutes between actions targeting the same route.

Control loop pseudo-algorithm (high level):
1. Aggregate metrics for each route for the last 5m.
2. If Latency.P99 > Hard SLO -> take emergency fallback action: reduce batch_time_ms by 50% and apply priority_boost=2.
3. Else if Latency.P95 > Soft SLO -> conservative action: reduce batch_time_ms by 20% or switch to lower-latency kernel_hint.
4. Else if Latency.P50 << SLO and GPUUtilization < 60% and Cost.per_token too high -> increase batch_time_ms up to 20% to improve cost efficiency.
5. Propose action -> run local simulation (see section "local simulation harness") -> score expected impact -> if score positive apply action with step and start cooldown.

Components and responsibilities:
- Scheduler Autotuner service (autotuner-svc): evaluates metrics, recommends actions, delegates to runtime-config API. Owner: serving-runtime/scheduling team.
- Runtime-config service: accepts config patches and enforces validation & safety. Owner: runtime-core.
- Telemetry bridge (telemetry-proxy): supplies metrics and sample traces to autotuner. Owner: telemetry-infra.
- Canary orchestrator: runs per-route canaries when enabled. Owner: rollout-planning team.

Config schema (example YAML):
---
policy_name: slo_latency_balancer_v1
routes:
  - id: \/v1\/generate
    hard_slo_ms: 300
    soft_slo_ms: 120
    cost_sensitivity: low
    allowed_kernels: ["opt-low-latency", "opt-balanced"]
  - id: \/v1\/embed
    hard_slo_ms: 400
    soft_slo_ms: 200
    cost_sensitivity: medium
global:
  cooldown_minutes: 5
  max_concurrent_actions: 2
  emergency_action:
    reduce_batch_time_pct: 50
    priority_boost: 2
---

CLI examples and debug commands:
- Enable autotuner for a policy: rdwctl runtime autotune apply --policy slo_latency_balancer_v1 --env prod
- Disable autotuner: rdwctl runtime autotune disable --policy slo_latency_balancer_v1 --env prod
- Force an emergency rollback: rdwctl runtime config rollback --policy slo_latency_balancer_v1 --to-revision 42
- Query recent actions: curl -sS "https:\/\/runtime-api.internal.autotune\/actions?route=\/v1\/generate" | jq

Local simulation harness (developer workflow):
1. Pull 10m of production metric slices (export via telemetry-proxy) for the route under test.
2. Run autotuner-sim --policy policy.yaml --metrics sample.json --simulate-horizon 10m --output scoring.json
3. Review scoring.json for expected p50/p95/p99 and cost delta.

Canary & rollout plan (recommended):
1. Dry-run: schedule autotuner in dry-run mode for 30 minutes to collect proposed actions without applying them. Validate proposed actions against canary rules.
2. Canary (2% traffic): apply only kernel_hint and batch_time_ms conservative adjustments. Observe for 1h.
3. Canary (10% traffic): apply full action set but limit to max_concurrent_actions=1. Observe 2h.
4. Ramp to 50% traffic and then 100% if metrics are stable and no hard SLO violations.

Deployment success criteria (example):
- No Hard SLO violations during 4h post-rollout.
- AutotuneAction.events with action=reduce_batch_time count <= 0.1% of requests.
- Per-token cost changes within policy-defined limits.

Roll forward / rollback triggers:
Roll back immediately if any of the following occur within the post-rollout observation window:
- Any route hits Hard SLO for > 5m sustained.
- ErrorRate increases by > 0.3 percentage points versus baseline.
- Unexplained GPU saturation (utilization > 95% with no matching throughput increase).

Debugging checklist (fast triage):
1. Check autotuner action logs: rdwctl runtime autotune actions --recent 50 --route \/v1\/generate
2. Inspect last-applied runtime-config revision and diffs.
3. Correlate with sampled request traces (trace-id from action log).
4. If kernel_hint switch coincided with regression, revert kernel_hint before other actions.
5. If batch_time_ms reductions created instability, scale back to previous revision and increase cooldown.

Common failure modes and mitigations:
- Oscillation (autotuner bounces knobs repeatedly): raise cooldown_minutes, increase hysteresis thresholds, add action dampening (apply fractional steps).
- Cold-route regression: enable kvcache_prefetch only after route warmup (threshold: 100 successful inferences within last 10m).
- Unhandled kernel incompatibility: autotuner must validate allowed_kernels list; runtime-config rejects incompatible kernel_hint by returning 422. Fallback action: revert kernel_hint and mark route for manual review.

Runbook: emergency response (p99 breach detected):
1. Acknowledge alert on #runtime-ops and tag oncall.
2. Run rdwctl runtime autotune emergency --policy <policy> --route <route> (this applies emergency_action).
3. Monitor p99, GPUUtilization, and ErrorRate for 15 minutes.
4. If still exceeding Hard SLO after emergency action, scale to reserved capacity pool (see oncall runbook: eng-sre/capacity-planning).
5. Open incident with severity=SLO-Breach and include autotuner action timeline and traces.

Observability & dashboards (must-have panels):
- Per-route SLO panel: p50/p95/p99 with thresholds overlaid.
- Autotune Actions timeline: actions annotated on latency charts.
- BatchSize distribution heatmap and queue depth.
- Kernel execution time by hint and by model version.
- Cost per token trend vs baseline.
- Action-to-latency correlation scatter (expected delta).

Prometheus example queries (appendix):
- p99 for route: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_latency_seconds_bucket{route=\"\/v1\/generate\"}[5m])) by (le)) * 1000
- KVCache hit rate: sum(rate(kvcache_hits_total{route=\"\/v1\/generate\"}[5m])) / sum(rate(kvcache_requests_total{route=\"\/v1\/generate\"}[5m]))
- Autotune actions: sum(rate(autotune_actions_total[5m])) by (action, route)

Appendix: example runtime-config patch (JSON):
{
  "route": "\/v1\/generate",
  "changes": {
    "batch_time_ms": 12,
    "kernel_hint": "opt-low-latency",
    "priority_boost": 1
  },
  "metadata": {
    "trigger": "autotuner",
    "policy": "slo_latency_balancer_v1"
  }
}

Ownership and contacts:
- Owner: scheduling/autotuner team (oncall: @scheduling-oncall).
- Primary contacts: Maya Chen (author), Jordan Lee (scheduler lead).
- Escalation: Eng SRE -> Runtime Core -> CTO on persistent unresolved SLO breach.

Related pages and references:
- Kernel scheduler ABI spec (see internal kernel mapper docs).
- Runtime observability data model (telemetry contract).
- Canary orchestration runbook.

Notes and future work:
- Planned: add reinforcement-learning–based estimator for longer-horizon traffic patterns; until validated this remains a disabled experimental branch.
- Planned: per-tenant cost-aware objectives to allow pay-for-performance priorities.

Document revision history:
- 2025-11-02: Draft authored by Maya Chen.
- 2026-01-10: Updated with canary cadence and emergency_action defaults (review Jordan Lee).
- 2026-02-14: Published with example queries and rollout checklist (review Priya Nambiar).

title: Execution Fidelity Smoothing and Adaptive Slot Coalescer
content:
Summary:
This doc describes the design, operational guidelines, and measurement recipes for the Execution Fidelity Smoothing system and the Adaptive Slot Coalescer (ASC). The ASC is a scheduler-layer component that dynamically merges short-lived slots to improve packing efficiency while the fidelity smoother ensures gradual changes to numerical execution fidelity (quantization/precision and batch size) to avoid abrupt quality regressions in production.

Who should read this:
- Runtime scheduler engineers (ownership for ASC)
- Profiling and benchmarking team (validation and SLO tuning)
- Oncall and SRE (runbook and dashboards)

Goals and motivation:
- Reduce per-token cost by 6–20% for bursty, short-sequence workloads without increasing p95 latency beyond SLOs.
- Avoid sudden fidelity drops visible to customers by smoothing transitions across quantization levels or hybrid-kernel fallbacks.
- Make coalescing decisions observable and recoverable with minimal blast radius.

Design overview:
1) Adaptive Slot Coalescer (ASC)
   - Coalescing window: ASC observes slot lifetimes and merges adjacent idle/short slots when the projected latency impact is within a configurable budget.
   - Decision inputs: slot occupancy distribution, model-variant latency profile, KV cache hit ratio, tenant priority, inferred tail-sensitivity.
   - Safety checks: predicted p95 delta threshold, memory headroom check, kernel-compatibility matrix.

2) Fidelity Smoother
   - Purpose: when the scheduler or the economic governor recommends a lower-fidelity execution (e.g., int8 quantized kernel or smaller max-seq trim), the smoother phases the change across N requests or T seconds to detect quality regressions early.
   - Modes: time-based ramp, quantile-based ramp (by model output distribution), request-count ramp.

Key algorithm (pseudocode):
```
function consider_coalesce(slot_a, slot_b):
  if not same_device(slot_a, slot_b): return false
  predicted_p95 = predict_p95_after_merge(slot_a, slot_b)
  if predicted_p95 > p95_budget: return false
  if memory_usage_after_merge() > memory_limit: return false
  if kernel_compatibility(slot_a.model, slot_b.model) == false: return false
  return true

function apply_fidelity_smooth(node, target_fidelity):
  stage_count = config.smoothing_stages
  for stage in 1..stage_count:
    apply_partial_fidelity(node, stage / stage_count, target_fidelity)
    wait(config.stage_interval_seconds)
    if quality_regression_detected(node):
      rollback_to(node, previous_safe_fidelity)
      alert("fidelity-regression", node)
      break
```

Configuration matrix (recommended defaults):
| Parameter | Default | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| p95_budget | 1.10 (10% headroom) | Multiplier over baseline p95 per model-profile |
| smoothing_stages | 4 | Number of discrete steps when ramping fidelity |
| stage_interval_seconds | 15 | Wait time between stages |
| coalesce_max_slot_gap_ms | 20 | Max difference in start times to consider merge |
| memory_limit_fraction | 0.85 | Prevent merges reducing free memory below this fraction |

Operational playbook (step-by-step):
1) Preflight (development & staging):
   - Enable ASC in simulator mode for 48h using shadow traffic capture. Validate predicted cost reduction and p95 impact.
   - Run fidelity-smoother experiments against a curated prompt set (see 'Benchmarking' below).
2) Canary rollout (small % of production tenants):
   - Release to 5% tenants (low-latency-tolerance cohort). Monitor: p95, p99, error-rate, logical-output-quality (BLEU/ROUGE or task-specific metric).
   - Criteria to proceed to 25%: no >5% relative increase in p99 and automated quality checks passing for 1h window.
3) Full rollout:
   - Increase gradually to 100% with staged toggles and rollout-exempt list for known-sensitive tenants.

Runbook (incident scenarios):
- Symptom: p95 rises above SLA after ASC enabled
  1) Inspect ASC decision logs: find merges executed in last 5m. Query: \"asc_decisions{outcome=\"merged\"}\".
  2) If merged slots correlate with p95 spikes, toggle config: coalesce_enabled=false for affected pool.
  3) If toggling not immediately available, increase p95_budget by +0.05 to relax merging aggressiveness.
  4) Rollback fidelity-smoother staged transitions if they coincide with quality alerts.
  5) Post-incident: capture traces and run local simulation with the exact sequence distribution.

Profiling & benchmarking recipes:
- Synthetic microbenchmarks:
  - Sequence-length sweep: 8, 16, 32, 64 tokens; run 60s at 200 qps each; measure packing delta with and without ASC.
  - Burst packing: 1s microbursts at 500% baseline qps; measure tail amplification.
- Real traffic shadowing:
  - Shadow 24h production traffic into a sandbox runtime with ASC_enabled toggled; compare per-tenant cost and fidelity metrics.
- Quality guard prompts (suggested set):
  - 200 prompts: generation (open-ended), code-completion, summarization, instruction-following. Evaluate automated metrics and a 5-person human panel for edge cases.

Data and dashboards to create (Grafana / Explore queries):
- asc_coalesce_rate = sum(asc_decisions{outcome=\"merged\"}) / sum(asc_decisions_total)
- asc_predicted_p95_delta (histogram) by model_variant
- fidelity_smoother_stage_{0..N} counts and rollback rate
- cost_saved_by_coalescer = baseline_token_cost - observed_token_cost (rolling 1h)

Configuration table (YAML example to apply per-pool):
```
asc:
  enabled: true
  p95_budget: 1.10
  coalesce_max_slot_gap_ms: 20
  smoothing:
    enabled: true
    stages: 4
    stage_interval_seconds: 15
  safety:
    memory_limit_fraction: 0.85
    disable_for_tenant_labels: [\"sensitive\", \"real-time\"]
```

Quality validation (automated checks added to CI):
1) For each smoothing experiment run, CI must compute a quality delta for the benchmark set; fail the experiment if any metric regresses beyond threshold (default 1.5%).
2) Synthetic latency regression simulation using the observed distribution; fail if p99 grows by >10%.

Known interactions and edge cases:
- KV cache warmup: aggressive coalescing may reduce effective prefix-sharing and temporarily lower KV-hit rates; include a hysteresis timer to avoid oscillation.
- Mixed-variant coalescing: merging slots executing different model variants can trigger kernel fallbacks. ASC uses the kernel_compatibility matrix to avoid cross-variant merges unless safe_fallback is configured.
- On-prem GPU fragmentation: ASC merges can increase fragmentation if coalesced groups exceed allocator soft caps; monitor allocator.fragmentation by node.

Testing checklist before enabling in production:
- Unit tests for coalescer decision logic under random distributions.
- Integration tests with runtime telemetry injection (trace+metrics).
- End-to-end shadow-run against production traffic for 72h.

Rollout and kill-switch knobs:
- Per-pool config switch asc.enabled (fast toggle via config service).
- Global emergency-toggle feature flag: runtime.asc.global_mode = OFF.
- Per-tenant exemption labels: runtime.asc.safelist_labels.

Ownership and contacts:
- Primary: Marina Kovács (scheduler team) — owner for design and code.
- Secondary: Daniel Park (profiling) — benchmarking and validation.
- Oncall escalation: eng-sre team (pager on-call) — for incidents caused by p95/p99 regressions.

Postmortem guidance (if a rollout causes customer-visible degradation):
1) Capture decision traces and sampled payloads for all merges in the incident window.
2) Re-run simulation locally with identical slot timelines.
3) Iterate on smoothing_stages and p95_budget, prefer more conservative ramps.

Appendix: example Grafana panel queries and CLI toggles
- Toggle ASC for pool 'us-west-asc' via CLI:
  curl -X POST https://control-plane.internal/api/pools/us-west-asc/config -d '{\"asc\":{\"enabled\":false}}' -H 'Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN'

- Example Prometheus query for ASC rollback rate:
  sum(rate(asc_smoother_rollbacks_total[5m])) / sum(rate(asc_smoother_attempts_total[5m]))

References and related reading:
- See the scheduler decision provenance spec for how ASC appends decision metadata to trace spans.
- Cross-reference: predictive-slotting-and-quota-orchestration-2026 (decision heuristics) and sequence-runway-sampling-and-batch-fidelity-playbook-2026 (profiling recipes).

This doc will be updated as we collect more production evidence. For feature requests or to join the profiling study, ping @marina.kovacs on Slack.

title: Scheduler Compatibility Dependency Graph and Safety Orchestrator
content:
Summary

This document defines the Scheduler Compatibility Dependency Graph (SCDG) and describes the Safety Orchestrator that enforces compatibility, graceful degradation, and safe rollouts between kernel variants, scheduler plugins, and runtime subsystems. It combines a static dependency model with dynamic runtime checks and an automation layer that performs remediation and controlled fallback.

Why this exists

- Kernels and scheduler plugins are evolving rapidly (new quantization paths, sparse-attention kernels, fractional residency modes). We need a machine-readable compatibility model to avoid accidental unsafe pairings.
- Incidents historically involve combinations of kernel variants + admission-controller policies that produce deadlocks, soft OOMs, or priority inversion. The SCDG lets automation surface risky pairings before they reach production.

Scope and assumptions

- Space: eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling and runtime-architecture operational surface.
- Assumes per-cluster kernel metadata is available via kernel-manifest service (artifact: /artifacts/kernels).
- Not a replacement for unit/interop tests; it augments CI and runtime safety checks.

Key concepts

1) Node: a component (kernel, plugin, admission-controller, cache-manager). Each node has attributes: name, semantic-version, capabilities, resource-profile, affinity-tags.
2) Edge: a directional compatibility relation between nodes. Edge metadata includes: compatibility-level (compatible | advisory | incompatible), min-version, known-issues-ref.
3) Cohort: a small set of nodes commonly updated together (e.g., {tensor-core-kernel-v2, prefetch-plugin-1.4}). Cohorts are used for canaries and rollback groups.
4) Safety Orchestrator: runtime daemon that consumes the SCDG and enforces policy: rejects incompatible combos, synthesizes safe fallbacks, and coordinates rolling remediations.

Design overview

- Authoring: kernel owners publish node descriptors as YAML under kernel-manifest; CI validates descriptor JSON schema.
- Graph materialization: a scheduled job (scdg-builder) consolidates manifests from clusters, runs compatibility heuristics, and persists a canonical SCDG snapshot to the metadata DB.
- Runtime enforcement: Safety Orchestrator subscribes to snapshots. On each model-serving slot allocation, it verifies requested kernel + plugin pair against SCDG. If advisory or incompatible, orchestrator applies configured policy (block | warn-and-audit | auto-fallback).
- Telemetry: every verification emits a verification event (verif_id) with context: request_id, node-pair, compatibility-level, decision, and matched-cohort. These events feed the scheduler-telemetry pipeline.

Compatibility matrix (example table)

| Component A | Component B | Min A ver | Min B ver | Compatibility | Action on incompatible |
|-------------|-------------|----------:|----------:|--------------:|-----------------------:|
| tensor-core-kernel | prefetch-plugin | 2.1.0 | 1.4.0 | compatible | none |
| tensor-core-kernel | sparse-attn-plugin | 2.0.0 | 0.9.0 | advisory | warn-and-audit |
| fp8-quant-kernel | nvlink-allocator | 1.0.0 | 2.3.1 | incompatible | block-and-fallback |

Authoring schema (YAML snippet)

```yaml
# kernel-manifest/<kernel>/descriptor.yaml
name: tensor-core-kernel
version: 2.1.0
capabilities:
  - attention:sparse
  - quantization:fp16
resource_profile:
  vram_min_mb: 12288
affinity_tags:
  - high-throughput
compatibility:
  - with: prefetch-plugin
    min_version: 1.4.0
    level: compatible
  - with: sparse-attn-plugin
    min_version: 0.9.0
    level: advisory
```

Safety Orchestrator policies (examples)

- block-on-incompatible: refuse to schedule and return HTTP 409 with a diagnostic payload to the dispatcher.
- warn-and-audit: allow scheduling but attach a high-severity audit event and tag the request for shadow replay.
- auto-fallback: transparently substitute the nearest compatible kernel variant from the same cohort and attach a warning in response metadata.

Operational runbook: incompatible-pair-detected

1. Trigger: Safety Orchestrator emits event type SCDG.VERIF.INCOMPATIBLE with decision=block-and-fallback.
2. Immediate actions (0-5m):
   a. Orchestrator will reject new allocations for the offending cohort.
   b. Paging is sent to oncall-scheduler (channel: #oncall-scheduler).
   c. Short-circuit: route new requests for impacted model routes to fallback pool (if configured).
3. Triage (5-30m):
   a. Oncall inspects SCDG snapshot id and the verif_id, then runs scdg-debug --verif <verif_id> to get contextual pair traces.\   b. If a recent change is implicated, use canary-rollback playbook (section: Canary rollback matrix).
4. Remediation (30m-4h):
   a. If safe fallback exists, perform automated cohort-rollback or kernel-substitute using orchestrator's action plan.\   b. If no fallback, escalate to kernel owner and schedule expedited patch.
5. Post-incident (4h+):
   a. Add an advisory edge entry describing observed behavior and mitigation steps.
   b. Schedule a focused interop run in the CI lab with the failing pair (see test matrix below).

Canary and rollout matrix

- Canary cohort size: 1–3 nodes (1% traffic from a control tenant, randomized across zones).
- Canary pass criteria (automated): 99.95% success rate for 10k requests, median latency delta < 5% vs baseline, no new SLO error budget burn > 2%.
- Rollout steps (recommended):
  1. Publish kernel descriptor and update SCDG snapshot in staging.
  2. Run interop suite: scdg-interop --staging --cohort <name>. Expect green.
  3. Canary deploy to production cohort (1% traffic) with orchestrator policy=warn-and-audit.
  4. Monitor for 6 hours. If green, advance to 10% with auto-fallback enabled.
  5. Full rollout after 72-hour quiet window.

Test matrix (short)

| Test | Target | Expected outcome |
|------|--------|-----------------|
| admission-safety | kernel + admission-controller | pass (no rejection) |
| memory-pressure | kernel + allocator | no soft-ooms under baseline burst profile |
| latency-cohort | kernel + plugin | p99 < configured p99 SLO |

Observability and alerts

- Verification events feed: scheduler.verify.events -> kafka/topic:scheduler-verify.
- Alert: SCDG.IncompatibleRate > 5/min for 5m -> PagerDuty to scheduler oncall.
- Dashboard: "Scheduler Compatibility" with heatmap of advisory/incompatible edges by cohort and 24h trend.

Developer workflows and CLI tools

- scdg-author validate <descriptor.yaml>  # local schema validation
- scdg-builder --snapshot-id auto         # produces canonical SCDG
- scdg-debug --verif <verif_id>          # human-readable decision trace
- scdg-simulate --pair A:B --load-file burst-profile.json  # run lab interop

Configuration table (defaults)

| Key | Default | Notes |
|-----|--------:|-------|
| scdg.snapshot.interval | "1h" | Frequency scdg-builder runs; lower intervals increase churn |
| orchestrator.policy.default | "warn-and-audit" | Default enforcement policy for advisory edges |
| canary.cohort.size | "1-3" | Number of nodes in a canary cohort |
| canary.traffic.percent | "1" | Starting canary traffic percent |

Safety trade-offs and notes

- Conservative defaults avoid silently shipping incompatible combos; teams that opt into faster innovation should register cohorts and accept increased advisory warnings.
- The SCDG is only as good as manifests and telemetry. Encourage owners to include comprehensive capability tags and reproduction steps in manifests.
- Known blind spot: cross-cluster NVLink topology constraints are not inferred automatically; add explicit edges when topology matters.

Ownership and contact points

- Scheduler Compatibility steward: Ava Martinez (author).
- Kernel manifest service owner: Priya Natarajan.
- Oncall escalation: eng-serving-runtime/scheduler rotation.

Related pages and artifacts

- Kernel manifests: artifact store /artifacts/kernels (read-only for non-owners).
- CI interop harness: repo infra/ci/scdg-interop.
- Telemetry schema: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/runtime-telemetry-data-model-and-tracebook-2026.

Appendix A: example incident query (KQL)

```
// sample query: find incompatible failures in last 6h
service=="safety-orchestrator" and event_type=="SCDG.VERIF.INCOMPATIBLE" | where timestamp > now() - 6h | top 50 by count()
```

Appendix B: minimal manifest checklist (owner must verify before publish)

1. version and checksum present
2. resource_profile.vram_min_mb accurate
3. affinity_tags reflect intended scheduling
4. compatibility edges include at least: allocator, admission-controller, common-plugin-cohort

Document change log

- 2026-01-15: Draft created by Ava Martinez.
- 2026-02-03: Added runbook steps and CLI examples after reviewer feedback.

title: Runtime Scheduler Decision Fabric and Telemetry Playbook
content:
Summary

This document defines the "Decision Fabric" concept for the runtime scheduler: a structured set of decision points, the telemetry signals required to make those decisions, and a practical playbook for evaluating, rolling out, and debugging scheduler policy changes. It is intended for runtime engineers, SREs, and owners of scheduling policy components.

Goals

- Make scheduling decisions auditable and reproducible.
- Ensure telemetry is sufficient to explain why any request took the path it did.
- Provide safe rollout and rollback steps for scheduler changes.
- Define incident triage and escalation steps when scheduling misbehavior impacts SLOs.

Scope

Covers: kernel scheduling policy decision points, admission controllers, priority tags, preemption windows, kernel selection hints, and the telemetry & alerts that validate these decisions.
Does not cover: low-level GPU kernel source code changes or vendor driver instrumentation (those belong to kernel-and-scheduling code docs).

1. Decision Fabric: concepts and nodes

The Decision Fabric is a logical DAG of discrete decision nodes that operate on enriched request context and produce actions or routing hints. Nodes are micro-decision units intended to be small and testable. Example nodes:

- Request Classification: maps incoming request attributes to a class (e.g., interactive, batch, background).
- Admission Gate: enforces concurrency & slot availability budget for class and tenant.
- Priority Arbiter: resolves conflicts between competing requests (SLA, customer tier, emerging emergency).
- Kernel Selector: picks the kernel variant and quantization profile.
- Prefetch/KV Hint: decides whether to fetch KV cache for a session.
- Fallback Router: chooses alternate model variant/region on capacity or error.

Each node emits a standardized Decision Event (see Telemetry section). Nodes are composed into runtime pipelines.

2. Decision Event schema (telemetry contract)

All scheduler decision nodes MUST emit a Decision Event at the moment a decision is made. This makes decisions traceable end-to-end. The near-term schema (text representation):

Example Decision Event (single-line JSON text for logs; the runtime also emits structured proto for the tracing pipeline):
{
  "request_id": "string",
  "timestamp": "2026-01-15T14:12:03Z",
  "node": "PriorityArbiter:v2",
  "input_signals": ["tenancy_tier:standard","seq_len_estimate:32","recent_error_rate:0.002"],
  "decision": "grant:slot-id=slot-42, kernel_hint=gptq-4bit-fp16",
  "reason_codes": ["tenancy_quota_ok","latency_target_50ms"],
  "latency_ms": 0.42,
  "cost_weight": 1.0
}

- Note: Events should be JSON-encoded when landing in structured logging systems; they must also exist as compact binary in the tracing pipeline for high-cardinality sampling.

Required fields (text form): request_id, timestamp (ISO8601), node (string), decision (string), reason_codes (list), latency_ms (number), cost_weight (number), input_signals (list).
Optional but recommended: model_version, kernel_revision, tenant_id, route, sampled_trace_id.

3. Minimal telemetry to support common investigations

To triage scheduling issues within 5–15 minutes, the following telemetry streams are required:

- Decision Events (high cardinality, sampled): ~1 per decision; sample strategy below.
- Request Timeline Trace (distributed trace spanning API -> admission -> kernel dispatch).
- Per-kernel execution metrics: queue_time_ms, kernel_exec_ms, retry_count.
- Admission & slot pool stats: available_slots, inflight_by_tier, eviction_count.
- Request classification histogram: seq_len, token_budget, request_surface_type.

Suggested retention and sampling:

| Stream | Sampling | Hot retention | Cold retention |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
|Decision Events|100% for tier=enterprise; 5% for standard/free|7d|180d|
|Request Traces|100% for p99+ tail traces, 1% baseline|14d|90d|
|Kernel exec metrics|Aggregate per-min buckets 100%|30d|365d|

4. Reason-coding taxonomy (short list)

Decision nodes should attach reason codes. We maintain a canonical set to avoid free-form strings. Examples:

- quota_exhausted
- latency_slo_risk
- high_seq_len
- emergency_preemption
- kernel_incompatible
- kvcache_miss
- model_swap_fallback

5. Playbook: safe rollout of scheduler changes

This is the sequential process you must follow when deploying a scheduler policy change (e.g., new PriorityArbiter logic, admission thresholds, kernel selector rules):

1) Design review and unit tests
- Create an ADR (link to decision record). Include decision fabric impact map (which nodes change).
- Unit tests: determinism tests for decision nodes and reason_code coverage matrix.

2) Local and integration testing
- Run deterministic replay of representative request corpus (use the operational workload simulator) and compare Decision Event diffs.
- Validate no new reason codes introduced unintentionally.

3) Canary rollout (safety gates)
- Canary cohort: 0.5% baseline requests or a narrow tenant set of non-critical accounts.
- Observability checks (automated):
  - p50/p95 request latency for canary <= baseline + 5%
  - decision_event.reason_code change rate <= 2x baseline for any single reason code
  - admission.rejection_rate <= baseline + 0.1% absolute
  - kernel_exec_ms median unchanged or improved

4) Gradual ramp and policy checks
- Ramp to 5% after 30m if canary signals pass for 15m rolling windows.
- Run the differential tracer extractor to verify decision path similarity (expectation: >95% of canary decisions match legacy for non-experimental paths).

5) Full rollout and post-mortem observation
- After 24 hours at 100% observe metrics for 72 hours.
- If any SLO regressions occur, trigger automatic rollback and open a postmortem.

6. Incident triage checklist (scheduling-related)

When customers observe increased latency or error rates that trace to scheduler behavior:

1. Confirm alert and scope: check SLO dashboards for elevated p99 and per-route errors.
2. Correlate with Decision Event spike: query decision_event.node aggregated by reason_code in last 15m.
3. Inspect admission pool state: available_slots, pool_eviction_count, queue_time_ms.
4. Query kernel health: dispatch_fail_rate, nvlink_errors, watchdog_restarts.
5. If decision nodes show a sudden change in reason_code distribution (e.g., quota_exhausted spikes), identify the upstream change (policy, config, traffic surge).
6. If root cause is policy regression, execute rollback (see Rollback snippet).

Rollback CLI snippet (example):

# Roll back to last stable policy bundle
redwood-schedctl rollback --bundle-id=rb-2026-0007 --reason="p99-latency-regression"

Wait for slot metrics and decision_event reason_code to normalize, then annotate the incident.

7. Debug recipes and quick checks

- "Why did my request get preempted?"
  1) Search Decision Events by request_id -> look at PriorityArbiter and Admission Gate nodes.
  2) Check reason_codes: if emergency_preemption present, check active incident tags and owner.

- "Why was kernel_variant X chosen?"
  1) Inspect KernelSelector decision event; cross-check input_signals for sequence length and model_version.
  2) Look at kernel_revision compatibility table (see table below).

Kernel compatibility table (text):
| kernel_revision | model_family | quant_profile | notes |
| kv1.4 | gpt-j | 8bit | legacy; higher latency for long seqs |
| gq-2025-4b | llama-family | gptq-4bit-fp16 | low cost; prefer for background tasks |
| vbench-rc2 | opt | int8 | experimental; disable for enterprise tenants |

8. Metric and alert definitions (examples)

- sched.decision.rate (counter): decision events per second. Alert: sustained drop >30% over 5m -> scheduler stall investigation.
- sched.admission.rejection_rate (gauge %): Alert if >0.5% absolute above baseline for 10m.
- sched.kernel.queue_time_p99 (ms): Alert if >250ms for 5m.
- sched.reasoncode.quotas_exhausted.rate (counter): Alert if sudden spike (>5x expected) during deployment windows.

9. Sampling and storage plan for Decision Events

We recommend a two-path approach:
1) High-fidelity path (tracing infra) stores sampled full traces and Decision Events for a narrow sample of requests and all p99 tail traces.
2) Low-cost aggregated path stores per-minute aggregated counters and histograms for long-term analytics.

Sampling knobs (examples):
- sample_by_tier: {enterprise: 100%, standard: 5%, free: 1%}
- tail_capture: p99+ of request_latency || error_rate -> force sample.

10. Ownership and escalation

- Primary owner: runtime-scheduler team (oncall rota: runtime-scheduler@pagerduty).
- Secondary owner: eng-sre (for capacity, node-level issues).
- Incident severity mapping:
  - Sev-1: customer-facing outage (SLO > 30m breach) -> notify exec-oncall, start incident bridge.
  - Sev-2: p99 latency spikes without complete outage (SRE & scheduler oncall).

11. Compatibility and migration notes
