- topology_proximity (0.5 weight): 1.0 for GPU on same NUMA socket + NVLink; 0.6 for same server different NUMA; 0.2 for different host.
- free_memory_fraction (0.25 weight): fraction free after reserving estimated KV cache + prompt payload.
- kernel_compat_score (0.15 weight): historical success ratio for model-variant + quantization combo.
- recent_error_rate (0.10 weight, inverted): recent failure rate (lower is better).

Final score = weighted_sum; ties broken by LRU of last_use_timestamp to improve locality.

Affinity Profiles (examples)
- latency-first: topology_proximity=0.8, free_memory=0.1, kernel_compat=0.05, errors=0.05
- cost-first: topology_proximity=0.2, free_memory=0.3, kernel_compat=0.3, errors=0.2
- isolation-first: prefers devices with low cross-tenant memory usage, adds +0.2 safety bonus to devices with isolation flags set.

Scheduler integration and kernel handoff
--------------------------------------
- The rcd integrates with the global scheduler using a lightweight RPC (gRPC) interface: AllocateDevice(request_meta) -> DeviceLease. DeviceLease includes device_id, kernel_hint, lease_ttl_ms.
- Kernels are loaded lazily. Kernel Broker supports two strategies: optimistic prefetch (load on ranking) and conservative (load on assignment). Use optimistic for latency-first profiles and conservative for cost-first.
- Handshake sequence (simplified):
  1. rcd -> kernel broker: reserve kernel on device X
  2. kernel broker -> device agent: pin kernel and return success/failure
  3. If success, rcd marks device as reserved and dispatches request; otherwise rcd increments kernel_compat_bad counter and retries.

Kernel hinting and contract
--------------------------
- Requests may carry an X-Runtime-Kernel-Hint header: format "model:variant:quantization". The coordinator uses this to prefer kernels but validates compatibility.
- Kernel Broker exposes kernel metadata: {kernel_id, compiled_for_sm, quantized_bits, expected_workspace_bytes}.
- Compatibility rules: compiled_for_sm must match device.sm_family OR kernel is marked multi-sm compatible. workspace_bytes <= device.free_workspace_limit.

Profiling recipes (developer/SRE guidance)
------------------------------------------
Prerequisites: nsys, ncu (or ROCm equivalents), runtime debug build, traces enabled.

1) Kernel-level latency hotspot
- Step 1: Capture short trace at production traffic (10–60s) with sampling: `nsys profile --sample=cpu,gpu -o /tmp/rcd-kernel-trace`
- Step 2: Use the trace to map kernel launch times to request ids (rcd correlator). Look for repeated long launches (>95th percentile).
- Step 3: If kernel stalls appear on specific SM families, collect `ncu --target-processes=all` to inspect tensor core utilization and register spilling.

2) PCIe / host-side stalls
- Step 1: Inject a synthetic heavy-kv-evict workload using the benchmark harness (see Benchmarking Guidance) across co-tenants in a staging cluster.
- Step 2: Collect perf counters on the host PCIe root port: `perf record -e pci:*` and cross-correlate with device telemetry.

3) End-to-end latency attribution
- Use the runtime's correlator to produce a waterfall trace. If kernel handoff retries are >1% of requests, the coordinator is a dominant contributor.

Benchmarking guidance (how to validate changes)
------------------------------------------------
Goals: validate SLOs (p50/p95/p99), kernel success rates, and cost per token under representative mixes.

Benchmark steps:
1. Build synthetic workload with sequence-length distribution matching production (we provide a corpus builder tool: workload-corpus-gen).
2. Run three profile passes: micro (single-GPU), rack (topology-aware, NVLink present), cluster (mixed types). Each pass should run 30 minutes minimum for stable percentiles.
3. Metrics to collect: token/sec, p50/p95/p99 latency, kernel_fallback_rate, KV_cache_hit_ratio, device_multiprogramming_index (DMI).
4. Validation gates: any change that increases p99 by >7% or kernel_fallback_rate by >0.5pp must be blocked and reviewed.

Sample benchmark command (example)
```
benchmark-runner --corpus /bench/corpora/seq-dist-512.json --parallelism 200 --profile rack --out /tmp/bench-rcd-202609
```

Configuration table (recommended defaults)
----------------------------------------
|| config_key || default || notes ||
| affinity.profile | latency-first | can be overridden per-tenant |
| coordinator.max_retries | 3 | kernel reservation retries before fallback |
| kernelbroker.prefetch | optimistic | set to conservative for cost-first experiments |
| coordinator.lease_ttl_ms | 8000 | typical request TTL; tune for longer generation workloads |
| affinity.topo_bias_threshold | 0.12 | minimum score delta to prefer topology |

Release notes (rcd v1.3.0)
-------------------------
- New: Affinity profiles (latency/cost/isolation) configurable per-tenant.
- New: Kernel hint header support and explicit fallback logging.
- Improvement: Kernel Broker prefetch heuristics reduce p99 by 6% in mixed NVLink racks (internal benchmark).
- Fix: Prevented a race where two rcd instances double-reserved the same kernel after a lease renew failure.

Operational runbook: affinity-related incidents
----------------------------------------------
Incident type A: sudden p99 regression with high kernel_fallback_rate
1. Detect: Alert when kernel_fallback_rate > 0.5% for 10m and p99 > baseline + 7%.
2. Immediate mitigation: Switch tenant to conservative affinity profile (API call: `POST /v1/tenants/{id}/affinity?action=switch&profile=conservative`).
3. If mitigation fails: Drain the affected device pool using the scheduler's drain API and route new requests to fallback pool.
4. Postmortem: Collect traces, Kernel Broker logs, and device telemetry for the 30 minutes before incident.

Incident type B: device-level OOM during assignment
1. Detect: Device telemetry shows sudden free_memory_fraction drop and kernel_compat_score falls to 0.
2. Mitigate: Immediately revoke leases to the device (rcd -> kernel-broker revoke) and trigger eviction script: `rcdctl evict --device {id} --grace 120s`.
3. Recovery: Reimage device agent if OOM persists after eviction; escalate to HW team if host-level memory errors persist.

Incident type C: PCIe saturation causing multi-tenant latency spikes
1. Detect: host_pcie_util > 85% correlated with crostalk in tenant latencies.
2. Mitigate: Reduce parallelism for co-located tenants via token-based admission: `rcdctl set-parallelism --tenant {id} --value 0.6` (reduces allowed concurrent slots).

Known issues (short catalog)
---------------------------
- PCIe-root-port-saturation-eviction(2026-07): observed when large KV cache flushes are scheduled simultaneously with cross-host prefetch. Mitigation: stagger prefetch windows and apply host-level preemption.
- ephemeral-kernel-compile-time-deadlock(2026-03): rare deadlock in the kernel compilation pool leading to stalls when two incompatible quantization requests race. Workaround: restart kernel-broker service; patch in v1.3.1 planned.
- nvlink-failover-delay(2025-11): NVLink path failover can add 1–3ms to p95 during hardware link reconfiguration; translated into affinity score jitter. We added smoothing in the scoring logic to avoid thrash.

Signals and SLOs to watch
------------------------
- SLOs: p50 <= 15ms (small models), p95 <= 60ms, p99 <= 150ms (production defaults; tenant configs may differ).
- Signals: kernel_fallback_rate, kernel_reserve_latency, device_eviction_rate, kvcache_hit_ratio, device_pcie_util.

Rollout checklist for affinity changes
-------------------------------------
1. Add unit tests for score vector math and tie-breaking.
2. Run microbench + rackbench in staging with production traffic replay.
3. Deploy canary to 5% of traffic with conservatively higher telemetry sampling.
4. Wait 48 hours, validate gates (p99, fallback rate, cost delta).
5. Gradually ramp to 25%, 50%, 100% while monitoring.

Operational ownership and contacts
----------------------------------
- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime (pager: #eng-runtime-oncall).
- Secondary escalation: infra-gpu-team.
- Performance review contact: Priya Nair (priya@redwood.ai).

Related pages and artifacts
---------------------------
- Runtime observability contract (link internal: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/runtime-observability-data-model-and-tracebook-2026)
- Kernel Broker API spec (internal link: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/kernel-broker-api-2025)
- Benchmark corpora (s3://redwood-bench/corpora/seq-dist-512.json)

Appendix: example affinity profile YAML
-------------------------------------
```
# latency-first profile
profile_name: latency-first
weights:
  topology_proximity: 0.8
  free_memory_fraction: 0.1
  kernel_compat_score: 0.05
  recent_error_rate: 0.05
preferences:
  prefetch: optimistic
  prefer_nvlink: true
  max_retries: 3
```

Notes and next steps
--------------------
- Short-term: ship kernel-broker v1.3.1 with the compile-deadlock fix and improved lease renewal telemetry.
- Medium-term: prototype a learned-scoring variant that incorporates request-level latency predictions from a lightweight model.
- Long-term: integrate with Dedicated capacity planner so that affinity profiles can be used as a placement hint for reserved pools.

Document history
----------------
- 2026-02-12: initial draft by Sofia Ramirez.
- 2026-04-20: profiling recipes expanded (Liam Chen).
- 2026-09-04: updated scoring weights and release notes (Priya Nair).

title: Cooperative Kernel Waveform Orchestration Spec
content:
Summary
-------
This spec describes the Cooperative Kernel Waveform Orchestration (CKWO) design: a scheduling abstraction and operational playbook for coordinating short-lived inference kernels across heterogeneous GPU pools to reduce tail latency and improve packing efficiency while preserving isolation guarantees. CKWO is intended for the high-concurrency, mixed-model workloads that characterize Redwood’s hosted API and Dedicated clusters.

Goals
-----
- Reduce 95th/99th percentile token-generation latency by coordinating micro-batches across kernels.
- Improve kernel packing to reduce per-token GPU cycles without increasing head-of-line blocking.
- Make kernel coordination observable and debuggable with explicit wave metadata.
- Provide safe degradation modes that never violate customer SLOs (latency/COST isolation).

Scope and non-goals
-------------------
- In-scope: inter-kernel coordination for attention/matmul kernels, batching signals, KV-cache-aware warmup, and telemetry annotations for wave events.
- Out-of-scope: model architecture changes, driver-level preemption, and tenant-level admission control policy (higher-level quota layer handles admission).

Conceptual overview
-------------------
CKWO organizes short-lived kernel executions into "waves". A wave is a logical grouping of kernels that can be co-scheduled with cooperative guarantees:
- Wave phases: PREPARE -> PACK -> EXECUTE -> COMMIT -> CLEANUP.
- Each wave carries a Wave ID (UUID), priority class (low/normal/high), and waveform hints (expected sequence length, kv-cache affinity, quantization tag).
- Waves may be single-tenant or multi-tenant depending on affinity and isolation constraints.

Architecture components
-----------------------
- Wave Controller (service): creates and coordinates waves per GPU node. Runs in the runtime control plane.
- Kernel Coordinator (in-runtime agent): local to each GPU process, executes the waveform phases and enforces packing and fairness.
- Wave Metadata Bus (lightweight pub/sub): transports wave lifecycle events (wave-start, pack-complete, exec-complete) to telemetry and tracing.
- Admission shim: lightweight hook at request enqueue time that emits waveform hints and SLO tags.

Scheduling primitives and contracts
---------------------------------
1. Slot promises: a kernel can promise a time-limited slot to the wave controller when it has partial readiness (e.g., token prefix loaded). The promise includes expected slot duration and token budget.
2. Cooperative preemption token: short consensus token to allow higher-priority waves to reclaim unused slots during PACK phase (fast-path only).
3. Quiesce boundary: kernels must implement a quiesce handler to checkpoint the KV cache pointer and return consistent partial outputs on preemption.

Wave orchestration lifecycle (detailed)
-------------------------------------
1) PREPARE
   - Admission shim validates hints and annotates the request.
   - Wave Controller assigns preliminary Wave ID and target node(s) based on affinity and SLOs.
   - Telemetry: emit wave.prep.{wave_id}.
2) PACK
   - Kernel Coordinator gathers ready kernels and evaluates pack candidates using waveform hint heuristics.
   - Pack decision includes which kernels will run together and estimated duration.
   - Telemetry: emit wave.pack.{wave_id} with pack composition and estimated duration.
3) EXECUTE
   - Kernels execute with coordinated start. Micro-batching may be performed only if all kernels meet packing constraints.
   - Cooperative preemption may be triggered if a higher-priority wave claims slots.
   - Telemetry: wave.exec.{wave_id} including per-kernel timing and kernel IDs.
4) COMMIT
   - Outputs are merged, cache pointers advanced; per-tenant quotas updated.
5) CLEANUP
   - Memory and ephemeral allocations released; pack accounting updated.

Observability contract (what to emit)
------------------------------------
- Required events: wave.created, wave.pack_attempt, wave.pack_commit, wave.exec_start, wave.exec_end, wave.preempt_request, wave.preempt_granted, wave.cleanup_complete.
- Each event must include: wave_id, node_id, kernel_id(s), priority, estimated_duration_ms, actual_duration_ms, pack_reason (latency/cost/affinity), and a diagnostic tag.
- Correlate with existing traces: append wave_id to the request trace root.

Config knobs (table)
--------------------
| name | default | description | operator guidance |
| wave.max_pack_size | 8 | Max kernels in a single pack | Start at default, tune downward for high tail latency |
| wave.max_pack_latency_ms | 8 | Max time to wait while assembling a pack | Lower to prioritize latency; increase for better efficiency |
| wave.priority_strictness | medium | How strongly controller prefers higher-priority waves | Set to high for SLO-critical clusters |
| wave.coop_preempt_window_ms | 2 | Time window where cooperative preemption can be claimed during PACK | Keep small to minimize instability |
| wave.kv_affinity_threshold | 0.7 | Confidence threshold to colocate wave with warm KV cache | Use 0.8+ for latency-sensitive traffic |

Example pack decision pseudocode
-------------------------------
```
// simplified pack selection logic
candidates = gather_ready_kernels()
score(candidate) = affinity_score*0.6 + priority_score*0.3 - est_duration*0.1
selected = top_k(candidates, wave.max_pack_size, score)
if max_est_duration(selected) > wave.max_pack_latency_ms: fallback_to_singleton()
```

Safe degradation and fallbacks
------------------------------
- If pack assembly time exceeds wave.max_pack_latency_ms, controller falls back to executing available kernels immediately (singletons).
- If cooperative preemption fails repeatedly for >3 waves in 60s for a node, disable PACK on that node for 60s (circuit breaker).
- If observed 95th latency increases by >20% after a rollout, rollback the new controller and enable conservative packing config.

Runbook: investigating long PACK times
-------------------------------------
1. Alert triggers: packing_latency.node > 99th percentile threshold for 5m.
2. Triage steps:
   a) Query last 10 wave.pack_attempt events for the node: composition, estimated vs actual durations.
   b) Check node GPU utilization and dispatch queue lengths (node/gpu/{id}/utilization, dispatch.queue.length).
   c) Verify kv-cache hit ratio for packed kernels — low affinity increases waiting.
   d) If packing contention due to small kernels, reduce wave.max_pack_size or increase priority_strictness.
3. Mitigation:
   - Temporarily set wave.max_pack_latency_ms to 3ms for high-priority traffic.
   - Trigger node-level PACK-disable circuit breaker if pack attempts > 100 and mean wait > 15ms.
4. Postmortem: record root cause, pack composition, and correlate with traffic mix.

Benchmarks and validation strategy
---------------------------------
- Microbenchmarks: synthetic mixes of (short, medium, long) sequences at concurrencies [10, 50, 200] measuring p50/p95/p99 for token latency and per-token GPU cycles.
- A/B rollout: shadow CKWO with pack disabled for 24h; compare cost-per-token and tail latency. Staged rollout matrix described below.

Rollout plan and metrics
-----------------------
1) Canary (5% traffic, internal customers): run CKWO controller in parallel mode (no-enforce) for 48h. Monitor wave packing ratio and tail latency.
2) Limited (20%): enable CKWO with conservative knobs; monitor 1h and 24h windows.
3) Gradual (50% -> 100%): increase over days if both cost and latency show improvement or remain within 3% of baseline.

Key success metrics (track weekly)
- pack_efficiency_ratio: (tokens served under packs)/(tokens total) target > 0.35 after warmup.
- p95_token_latency change <= +3% during rollout.
- per_token_gpu_cycles delta <= -5% (cost savings target).

Telemetry dashboards and alerts (minimum)
- Wave overview: pack rate, average pack size, pack latency distribution.
- Node health: pack_attempts, pack_failures, preempt_requests/grants.
- Alerts: pack_latency.node.high, pack_preempt.failure_spike, wave.exec.error_rate.

Instrumentation examples
-----------------------
- Example Wave event JSON (annotate into existing trace):
{
  "event": "wave.pack_commit",
  "wave_id": "wf-2a7d9c1e",
  "node_id": "node-gpu-34",
  "kernels": ["k-124", "k-125"],
  "priority": "normal",
  "est_duration_ms": 4,
  "actual_duration_ms": 3
}

- Example runtime config snippet (YAML):
wave:
  max_pack_size: 6
  max_pack_latency_ms: 6
  priority_strictness: medium
  coop_preempt_window_ms: 2
  kv_affinity_threshold: 0.75

Operational ownership and contacts
----------------------------------
- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling team.
- Oncall rotation: runtime-sre (pager: see oncall roster).
- Design/implementation contacts: Asha Patel (author), Diego Morales (kernel lead).

References and related work
---------------------------
- Predictive slotting and quota orchestration (related decisions).
- Telemetry feedback kernel autotune playbook for continuous tuning loops.
- Runtime packing experiments in /playbooks/bench/ckwo-experiments-2025 (internal notebook).

Appendix: experiment checklist
-----------------------------
1. Prepare synthetic load generator with realistic prompt length distribution.
2. Baseline run (no CKWO) for 12h, record p50/p95/p99, cost.
3. Enable CKWO in no-enforce mode for 24h, compare signals.
4. Enable conservative CKWO config on a single node pool for 6h, validate correctness and tail behaviour.
5. Execute A/B run for 24h with 20% traffic, evaluate.

End of spec. For implementation RFC, see the kernel-and-scheduling team wiki space and open the design PR referenced in related_pages.

title: Graceful Degradation Orchestrator: Design, Telemetry Contract, and Validation
content:
Purpose

This document defines the Graceful Degradation Orchestrator (GDO): the runtime subsystem that coordinates fidelity reduction, kernel variant switching, and routing fallbacks when capacity, thermal/power or kernel regressions threaten SLOs. It specifies the telemetry contract between the orchestrator and downstream subsystems (scheduler, kernel mapper, network router, kv-cache and model manager), describes configuration primitives, and provides a validation and incident-runbook for operators.

Summary (short)

- Why: Keep customer-facing latency and success-rate SLOs while minimizing cost and output-quality regression during resource-constrained events.
- What: A declarative orchestrator that synthesizes signals and executes a prioritized set of mitigation actions (local kernel switch, model fidelity stepdown, prioritized admission, cross-region reroute).
- Who: Owned by eng-serving-runtime (scheduler + runtime-ops collaboration).
- When to use: automatically in production via policies; manually for targeted customers via orchestration console.

Design goals

1) SLO-first: Preserve p50/p95 latency objectives and success-rate (generation completion) where possible.
2) Observable: Every mitigation must emit structured telemetry and be reversible.
3) Progressive fidelity: Minimize perceptible quality regression by ordering mitigations from least-visible to most-visible.
4) Safe and auditable: All policy changes are versioned and subject to canary gates.

Key terms

- Fidelity step: Discrete quality reduction (e.g., int8 quantized variant, sequence-length cap, sampling temperature clamp, max_tokens cap, offload to smaller model).
- Kernel variant: Implementation variant of an operator (tensor-core optimized vs. scalar fallback).
- Mitigation action: Single atomic change that the orchestrator can apply and revert.
- Mitigation plan: Ordered list of mitigation actions with exit criteria.

Architecture overview

Components and interactions (high level)

- GDO controller (stateless service)
  - Receives aggregated signals and policy input.
  - Plans and issues actions via runtime control-plane APIs.

- Signal ingestion (streaming)
  - High-frequency telemetry from scheduler, kernel telemetry, GPU power/thermal, model-serving trace.
  - Low-frequency business signals: customer tier, active QBR or experiments.

- Execution agents (on-node agents)
  - Apply kernel switches, update config flags, trigger model variant swap, adjust admission tokens.

- Audit & Reconciliation service
  - Records planned vs applied actions, detects drift and attempts automated revert if mismatches persist.

Sequence diagram (textual)

1) Telemetry breach detected (p95 latency > 1.2x SLO for 30s)
2) GDO evaluates candidate mitigations based on policy and current state
3) GDO issues an optimistically-scoped mitigation (e.g., drop kernel launch priority; enable kernel low-latency codepath)
4) Observability checks evaluate effect for 20s; if improved -> commit; else escalate to next mitigation (e.g., quantized model variant or sequence-length cap)
5) If a mitigation causes quality regression beyond policy thresholds, revert and try alternative path or route to dedicated capacity tier.

Policy primitives (JSON example)

```json
{
  "policy_id": "gd-policy-2025-01",
  "priority": 100,
  "target_scope": {
    "model_id": "redwood-llama-70b-cpu-fallback",
    "tenant_ids": ["*"],
    "region": "us-west-2"
  },
  "slo_constraints": {
    "p95_latency_ms": 250,
    "success_rate": 0.995
  },
  "mitigation_plan": [
    {"action": "kernel_priority_tweak","params": {"kernel_id": "attn_v2","priority": "lower"},"exit_on": {"p95_latency_ms": 1.05}},
    {"action": "enable_kernel_variant","params": {"kernel_id": "attn_v2","variant": "nvcc_fast_f32"}},
    {"action": "fidelity_step","params": {"step": "quantize_int8"},"quality_guard": {"semantic-preservation": 0.92}},
    {"action": "limit_sequence_length","params": {"max_tokens": 256}},
    {"action": "route_to_dedicated","params": {"pool": "dedicated-500g"}}
  ]
}
```
Telemetry contract (signals, semantics, retention)

Table: signal -> producer -> semantics -> recommended sampling

| signal | producer | semantics | sampling |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| kernel_queue_depth | node-scheduler | number of pending kernel launches | 1s aggregated per node |
| token_emit_latency_ms | kernel-runtime | per-token emit time (median/95) | 1s sliding, store 30d aggregated |
| kernel_variant_switch_latency_ms | node-agent | time to move to variant and stabilize | report per switch (trace) |
| gpu_power_watts | hw-metrics | instantaneous power draw | 5s avg, store 90d samples |
| kvcache_hit_rate | kv-cache | fraction of requests served from persistent cache | 10s aggregate |
| request_failure_rate | api-gateway | fraction of requests that failed before completion | 1s aggregate |

Contract rules (plain language)

- All signals must include: timestamp (RFC3339), node_id, shard_id (if applicable), model_id, request_cohort (experimental/dedicated/hosted).
- Signal producers must maintain >= 30s retention in hot storage for high-frequency signals used by GDO decision window.
- Each mitigation action must emit a START/END event with correlation_id and pre/post snapshot of the small set of signals (queue_depth, p95 token emit latency, kvcache_hit_rate).

Mitigation action taxonomy and safe limits

- Non-invasive (fast revert): kernel priority tweak, scheduler backpressure adjustments, queue preemption. (Immediate revert safe)
- Moderate (short-term quality impact): change kernel variant to lower-latency optimized build, apply small quantization profile. (Guarded by sampling)
- Invasive (visible quality impact): hard sequence-length cap, route significant traffic to smaller model. (Require reviewer approval when touching enterprise tiers)

Table: action -> visible impact -> max duration (auto) -> revert criteria

| action | impact | max_auto_duration | revert_criteria |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| kernel_priority_tweak | none | 300s | no improvement in p95 after 30s |
| enable_kernel_variant | low | 600s | token error rate > 0.1% or p95 worsens 10% |
| fidelity_step (quantize) | medium | 900s | semantic_preservation_score < policy threshold |
| limit_sequence_length | high | 1800s | business metric drop > 2% |

Validation and preflight suite

Preflight tests that must pass before enabling a mitigation policy in production:

1) Canary microbenchmark: apply mitigation to a 1% shadow of production (shadow-not-serve) and evaluate p50/p95 and semantic-preservation (using an automated prompt set).
2) Regression fuzz: run a synthetic workload shaped to the target tenant's recent traffic (sequence-length distribution, tokens per request) and measure kernel stability for 10 minutes.
3) Stability soak: ensure no memory leaks or steady-state increased memory usage over 30 minutes.

CLI snippets (examples for operators)

- List active policies

$ rdoctl policies list --region us-west-2 --format table

- Trigger policy dry-run (canary 1%):

$ rdoctl policies apply --policy gd-policy-2025-01 --canary 0.01 --dry-run

- Force revert mitigation on node

$ rdoctl nodes revert-mitigation --node node-15 --correlation-id abcd-1234

Quality and semantic-preservation checks

- Redwood uses an internal prompt-set for fidelity checks. For GDO policy changes that perform quantization or model swaps, require the semantic_preservation metric to be >= 0.90 for public tiers and >= 0.95 for enterprise-tier policies.
- Semantic preservation is computed as: 1 - (normalized embedding distance between golden and mitigated outputs) aggregated across the prompt set.

Observability & dashboards

Minimum required dashboards for GDO operations:

- Mitigation action timeline: list of START/END events with correlated latency and success_rate lines.
- Quality delta panel: semantic_preservation over time split by tenant tier.
- Signal heatmap: token_emit_latency_ms p95 across nodes with kernel variants annotated.

Runbook: Incident triage (SRE playbook)

1) Alert: GDO escalates with priority P1 if p95 latency > 1.3x SLO and mitigation plan reaches invasive actions.
2) Immediate steps (0-5m):
   - Verify alert in dashboards.
   - Check GDO decision log (correlation_id) and list of applied mitigations.
   - If mitigation was applied in last 60s, run quick revert for the latest action and observe impact.
3) Next steps (5-20m):
   - If revert improves latency, keep reverted state and schedule a targeted canary for alternatives.
   - If revert does not help, escalate to runtime kernel leads and consider cross-region routing.
4) Recovery and postmortem (post 2 hours):
   - Record timeline events, include all START/END and signal snapshots.
   - Run semantic-preservation audits for any automatic quantize actions.
   - Publish RCA and update policy safe limits if necessary.

Safety and governance

- Enterprise customer exemptions: Policies that change model fidelity for enterprise customers must include an "exempt" flag in the policy or have an explicit allowlist.
- Change control: All policy edits are audited and require a single-engineering approval and a product reviewer for changes that alter semantic thresholds.

Testing & benchmarking guidance

- Use the benchmarking suite to generate a representative request corpus (see service-profile builder). For each mitigation candidate:
  - Measure delta_p95 and delta_semantic_preservation over 10k requests.
  - Measure CPU/GPU utilization and memory delta for each node type.
  - Produce a mitigation scorecard: {p95_delta_pct, sem_pres_mean, cost_delta_pct}.

Appendix A: Example mitigation scorecard (table)

| mitigation | p95_delta_pct | sem_pres_mean | cost_delta_pct |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| kernel_priority_tweak | -8 | 0.99 | -0.5 |
| enable_kernel_variant nvcc_fast_f32 | -12 | 0.995 | +1.2 |
| quantize_int8 (aggressive) | -25 | 0.88 | -33 |

Appendix B: Correlation IDs and event schema (example)

Event payload (single line JSON for logs):

{"ts":"2025-11-01T16:24:32Z","correlation_id":"gdo-7f4a","node_id":"node-15","action":"quantize","phase":"start","policy_id":"gd-policy-2025-01","snapshot":{"p95_token_ms":312,"kvcache_hit":0.62}}

Appendix C: Ownership and contacts

- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime (runtime-ops subteam)
- Oncall escalation: runtime-oncall -> runtime-kernel-rotation -> eng-sre
- Design/approvals: Marco Reyes (kernel lead) and Jordan Kim (runtime infrastructure)

Notes and future work

- Integrate language-model-aware quality metrics (hallucination detection) to make quality_guard criteria more robust.
- Add ML-driven mitigation ranking (currently rule-based) to reduce human tuning.
- Expose a per-tenant simulation sandbox in the Console for product and CS to preview potential mitigations.

Change log

- 2025-03-12 initial draft by Aisha Patel
- 2025-06-18 added validation suite and CLI snippets (review by Marco Reyes)
- 2025-11-01 clarified telemetry contract and event schema; tightened revert criteria (review by Jordan Kim)

Related artifacts and links

- Runtime decision graph (internal): /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/runtime-decision-graph-and-observed-behaviour-catalog-2026
- Scheduler telemetry synthesis: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-telemetry-synthesis-and-proofing-2025
- Mitigation test harness: git repo internal: git@code.redwood:redwood/runtime/gdo-harness.git

title: Adaptive Kernel Mapper and Capacity Scaling Playbook
content:
Summary:

This playbook describes the Adaptive Kernel Mapper (AKM) and associated capacity-scaling procedures used by the Redwood serving runtime to dynamically select execution kernels and right-size GPU capacity for diverse LLM workloads. The AKM is a runtime component that maps model characteristics and live workload signals to a kernel/quantization/placement profile and triggers scale decisions or fallback policies when thresholds are crossed.

Purpose and scope:
- Document how the AKM makes decisions (inputs, scoring, policies).
- Provide concrete configuration examples and CLI commands for ops.
- Prescribe runbook procedures for performance regressions and capacity incidents.
- Link to profiling and benchmarking artifacts used to tune AKM heuristics.

Intended audience:
- Serving runtime engineers (primary)
- SRE and capacity planners
- Model onboarding and perf benchmarking teams

Key concepts (brief):
- Kernel candidate: a specific combination of operator implementation (CUDA/cuBLAS/cutlass), data type/quantization (fp16/int8), and fusion knobs.
- Profile: measured perf/latency/cost numbers for a model + sequence length distribution + batch shape.
- Cost-utility score: composite metric combining tokens/sec (throughput), p95 latency, and estimated cloud cost per token.
- Mapping policy: a set of rules that prefer lower-latency kernels for low-concurrency, and higher-throughput kernels for high-concurrency.

Architecture overview:
1) Telemetry inputs to AKM:
   - Model metadata: architecture family, layer count, head size, weight dtype (fp32/ptq/q4).
   - Serving signals: current concurrent requests per model, average request size, observed prefix cache hit rate.
   - Perf probes: fast microbenchmarks executed in the background on warm workers to validate kernel latency for target sequence length.
   - Historical profiles: offline benchmark results indexed by model hash and quantization profile.

2) Decision pipeline (high-level):
   - Normalize signals -> derive workload fingerprint.
   - Fetch candidate kernels from catalog filtered by model compatibility.
   - Score candidates using cost-utility function.
   - Run safety checks: memory headroom, kernel stability records, mismatch with policy exclusions (e.g., avoid int8 if regression alert exists).
   - Commit selection to local worker and report to central control-plane for observability and rollouts.

Scoring function example (pseudo):
   score = w1 * norm(tokens_per_sec) - w2 * norm(p95_latency) - w3 * norm(cost_per_token)
Weights (w1..w3) are configurable per customer tier (e.g., enterprise might set w2 higher to prioritize latency).

Kernel catalog (recommended fields):
| kernel_id | dtype | impl | ideal_seq_len | mem_delta | notes |
| KERN_CUTLASS_F16 | fp16 | cutlass-v3 | 512 | +0.2GB | good single-stream latencies |
| KERN_INT8_FUSED | int8 | fused-ops-v2 | 1024 | -1.0GB | best throughput at high concurrency |

Configuration file example (YAML):
```yaml
akm:
  scoring_weights:
    tokens_per_sec: 0.5
    p95_latency_ms: 0.35
    cost_per_token: 0.15
  concurrency_thresholds:
    single_stream: 1
    medium: 4
    high: 32
  safety_filters:
    - max_memory_overcommit: 0.85
    - banned_kernels: [KERN_INT8_FUSED] # temporary blocklist if regression detected
```

Operational runbook: when to invoke the AKM incident procedure
1) Alert types that trigger the runbook:
   - p95 latency breach for a model route > SLO for 10 minutes.
   - Sudden drop in tokens/sec per GPU of > 25% over 5 minutes without matching traffic drop.
   - Repeated OOMs on a worker (>= 3 in 12 hours).

2) Immediate triage steps (first-responder, 0–15 mins):
   1. Check service dashboard: model route, worker hostids, recent kernel changes (control-plane audit).
   2. Run quick perf probe against affected worker: akmctl probe --worker <id> --seq 512 --batch 1 --kernel all.
   3. If probe shows kernel regression vs baseline, add kernel to temporary blocklist and restart worker:
      - akmctl block-kernel --kernel KERN_XYZ --reason "p95 regression"
      - systemctl restart redwood-runtime@<worker>
   4. If OOMs present, reduce per-worker concurrency and enable fallback profile: akmctl set-profile --worker <id> --profile conservative

3) Escalation (15–60 mins):
   - Notify capacity-oncall and SRE (pager duty).
   - Spin up dedicated burst capacity pool for the model (if autoscale failed):
     - terraform apply -var "burst_pool_for=model-abc" ... (link to runbook snippet)
   - If root cause appears to be a kernel regression from a recent rollout, initiate rollback of AKM rollout: akmctl rollback --rollout <id>

4) Post-incident (60+ mins):
   - Collect traces: kernel-specific traces, perf probes, flamegraphs.
   - Run A/B microbenchmarks against candidate kernels offline to validate production behavior.
   - Open a regression investigation (link to regression-triage playbook) and add labels and owners.

Profiling and microbenchmarks (how to reproduce locally)
- Use the perf harness to generate representative requests and measure per-kernel latencies.
- Example command to run a microbenchmark on a dev node:
```bash
python perf/harness/run_microbench.py \
  --model /models/llama-70b/ --sequence 1024 --batch 1 \
  --kernels KERN_CUTLASS_F16,KERN_INT8_FUSED --measure p50,p95
```
- Record results into the benchmark catalog JSON and tag with commit/hash.

Benchmarking suite tie-ins:
- The AKM relies on the benchmarking catalog (benchmarks indexed by model fingerprint). When adding a new model or quant profile, the onboarding pipeline must run the benchmark suite at scale and publish profiles. See related_pages for the canonical onboarding docs.

SLOs and operational thresholds (suggested defaults):
- p50 latency target: <= 30ms for single-stream configs; p95 <= 120ms.
- Throughput target: configurable per model; default tokens/sec >= baseline_profile * 0.85.
- Kernel stability: <= 0.5% error/exception rate in a 24-hour window.

Observability (metrics the AKM emits):
- akm.selected_kernel{model,worker} -> kernel_id
- akm.score_breakdown{model,kernel} -> tokens_per_sec, p95_ms, cost_per_token
- akm.probe_status{worker,kernel} -> ok|regression|oom
- akm.rollback_events -> rollout_id, reason, initiated_by

Common troubleshooting scenarios:
1) p95 spike after kernel swap:
   - Rollback kernel selection and re-run probes. Check NVTX traces for unexpected operator fusion costs.
2) Throughput drop under high concurrency:
   - Ensure batching logic is not constrained by small max_batch_size; inspect batching histograms.
3) Memory headroom dangerously low after selecting int8 path on certain models:
   - Verify quantization table match; fall back to fp16 profile for that model.

Controlled rollouts and safety knobs:
- Rollouts are performed by control-plane and are slow by default (10% of workers every 10 minutes).
- Safety rollback triggers:
  - kernel p95 > baseline * 1.4 for 5m
  - error rate spike > 1% for 10m
  - manual abort by oncall

Example rollout command (ops):
```bash
akmctl rollout --kernel KERN_INT8_FUSED --models "llama-13b,redwood-turbo" --rate 10% --monitor p95:120ms
```

Ownership and contacts:
- Component owner: Priya Nair (serving runtime)
- Supporting teams: perf-benchmarks, model-onboarding, eng-sre
- Oncall rotation: runtime-oncall (see eng-sre oncall roster)

Maintenance and tuning cadence:
- Quarterly review of scoring weights and kernel catalog (Q1/Q2/Q3/Q4).
- Monthly automated probes running across representative model set to detect silent regressions.

Appendix A — Useful CLI references:
- akmctl probe --worker <id> --seq <n> --batch <b> --kernel <id|all>
- akmctl set-profile --worker <id> --profile {conservative,balanced,aggressive}
- akmctl block-kernel --kernel <id> --reason "<text>"
- akmctl rollout --kernel <id> --models "<csv>" --rate <pct> --monitor "<metric:threshold>"

Appendix B — Example audit log snippet (control-plane):
[2026-02-18T09:12:34Z] rollout: id=rl-20260218-003 kernel=KERN_INT8_FUSED models=[llama-13b] initiated_by=ci-bot status=partial
[2026-02-18T09:18:05Z] probe: worker=w-130 akm.probe_status=regression kernel=KERN_INT8_FUSED p95_ms=162 baseline_p95=98

Appendix C — Quick checklist for model onboarding teams:
1. Run full benchmark suite (seq 128/512/1024, batch 1..16) and publish catalog entries.
2. Attach profiling traces and memory maps to the profile artifact.
3. If quantizing, run stability validation for 72 hours at low load.
4. Provide recommended default profile for AKM.

Notes and future work:
- Planned: add ML-driven scoring function that learns from production regressions to adjust weights automatically.
- Planned: finer-grained per-operator fallbacks to allow mixed-precision within layers.

References:
- See runtime-architecture and kernel scheduler spec for deeper details on placement and preemption semantics.
- Regression triage playbook for root-cause workflow (related_pages).

title: Predictive Warmstart and Cache-Hinting Architecture for Low-Latency Serving
content:
summary:
This document defines the Predictive Warmstart and Cache-Hinting architecture (PWC Architecture) designed to reduce observable tail latency and cold-start variability for multi-tenant model serving. The design couples an inference-side predictive planner with the KV-cache prefetcher and the runtime's kernel scheduler to proactively populate hot state and shape scheduling hints based on traffic predictions.

goals_and_non_goals:
Goals:
- Reduce 95th and 99th percentile request latency for cold or low-traffic model variants by pre-populating KV caches and tensor allocator state before request arrival.
- Provide a low-risk canary and rollout path that can be throttled per-customer or per-model.
- Expose telemetry for cost vs latency trade-offs and enable automated tuning.
Non-goals:
- This design does not replace hardware-level warmup that requires model weight preloading. It focuses on runtime-level warmstart (KV cache, allocator priming, kernel hints) and workload-level caching policies.

scope:
Applies to: hosted and dedicated runtime pools where multi-tenant scheduling and KV-cache are active.
Out of scope: on-prem private deployments with strict air-gapped constraints unless customer opts in; deep model weight transformer warmups that require offline preparation.

background_and_motivation:
Operational observations (2024-Q4 to 2025-Q2) showed that mixed workloads with bursty conversational sessions produce repeated cold-like tails: small sessions that skip cache priming cause disproportionate tail-latency spikes and GPU kernel mispredictions. Existing approaches (heuristic ttl-based caching, on-request prefetch) either over-provision memory or introduce request-time overhead. Predictive warmstart aims to move the decision upstream to a planner that learns short-term traffic patterns and coordinates safe prefetches.

architecture_overview:
High level components:
- Predictive Planner: time-series and event predictor that emits warmstart candidates (tenant, model, session signature, TTL recommendation).
- Cache Hint Broker: lightweight control plane that accepts predictions and converts them into cache-prefetch jobs and kernel-hint annotations.
- Prefetch Worker (on-node): receives jobs, enqueues KV-cache prefetch, tensor allocator prime, and lightweight kernel micro-benchmarks to 'touch' critical code paths.
- Scheduler Integration Layer: exposes a hint API that the kernel scheduler uses to preferentially schedule warmstart jobs during free slots and to avoid starving priority traffic.
- Telemetry and Cost Estimator: aggregates prefetch effectiveness and cost (tokens, memory, kernel time) for feedback to Planner's policy optimizer.

data_flow_and_interactions:
1) Runtime telemetry (session arrives, token distribution, model variant) flows to the Planner via a time-series ingestion stream (Kafka topic: runtime.session.signals).
2) The Planner produces candidate warmstart events in the 'pwc.candidates' topic. Each event has: tenant_id, model_id, signature_hash, preferred_node_affinity, estimated_score, ttl_seconds. Example payload (JSON): {
  "tenant_id": "cust-123",
  "model_id": "redwood-v2-small",
  "signature_hash": "sha256:abcd...",
  "preferred_node": "poolA-6",
  "score": 0.78,
  "ttl": 120
}.
3) Cache Hint Broker validates, rate-limits, and enqueues Prefetch Worker jobs.
4) Prefetch Worker issues prefetch calls to the local KV-cache API, primes allocators (page-touch) and runs microkernel invocations with a capped budget.
5) Scheduler uses annotation flags on these jobs to schedule during slack periods; if server load exceeds threshold, prefetch jobs are evicted gracefully and rescheduled.

prefetch_and_warmstart_algorithms:
Core heuristics and policies:
- Scoring function: score = alpha * recency_score + beta * session_prob + gamma * model_cost_factor - delta * mem_pressure_penalty. We empirically set alpha=0.5, beta=0.3, gamma=0.15, delta=0.05 for initial rollout.
- Signature selection: prefer shortest canonical token prefix that maximizes reuse; prefer session-level signatures for chat workloads, request-level signatures for retrieval/embedding workloads.
- Budgeting: each node has a prefetch budget (cpu_millis, gpu_ms, mem_mb) and a soft_cost_limit. Prefetch jobs are charged to the originating tenant's cost center.
- TTL adaptation: if repeated hits observed, TTL is extended multiplicatively up to an upper cap (configurable). If misses exceed a threshold within window W, the Planner reduces score for that signature.

node_level_components:
Prefetch Worker responsibilities:
- KV-cache prefetch API call example: POST /internal/kvcache/prefetch {
  "model": "redwood-v2-small",
  "signature": "<signature>",
  "context": ["The user's last message summary..."]
}
- Allocator prime: touch pages and pre-allocate GPU tensors of expected size. CLI helper: runtime-prime --model redwood-v2-small --tensor-shape 1x2048 --budget-ms 20.
- Microkernel probe: run a 5-10ms inference warm call with deterministic random seed using quantized path where applicable.
Notes: Prefetch operations must be idempotent and safe on repeated application.

scheduler_integration_and_fallbacks:
Integration points:
- Hint API: schedule.hint_register(job_id, priority_hint, preferred_window_ms).
- Admission control: scheduler consults node prefetch_budget and current load. If CPU or GPU util > 75%, hints are deprioritized.
Fallbacks:
1) If prefetch failed due to mem pressure, mark signature as 'expensive' and reduce Planner score for 10 minutes.
2) If kernel microbenchmark reveals slow path on a variant, the runtime will annotate model_variant as 'compat_slow' and Planner will prefer alternative variant ids for warmstarts.

slo_cost_and_configuration_table:
Configuration key/value (presented as a table in prose):
- pref.max_concurrent_prefetch_per_node: 8 (integer) - Maximum concurrent prefetch jobs on a node.
- pref.cpu_budget_millis_per_min: 5000 (ms) - CPU budget per node per minute.
- pref.gpu_budget_ms_per_min: 300 (ms) - GPU warmstart budget per node per minute.
- pref.kv_prefetch_ttl_default_s: 60 (seconds) - Default TTL for prefetch entries.
- pref.score_threshold: 0.6 (0-1) - Planner emits only scores >= threshold.
SLO/Target metrics to track: 95th token latency (-10% target vs baseline), 99th token latency (-5% target), Prefetch success hit rate >= 70% for emitted jobs, Prefetch cost per saved-latency ms under configured cost cap.

telemetry_and_observability:
Required telemetry (exported to metrics and traces):
- metric: pwc.prefetch.emitted_total (labels: tenant, model, node, variant)
- metric: pwc.prefetch.hit_total (labels identical)
- metric: pwc.prefetch.cpu_ms_consumed
- metric: pwc.prefetch.gpu_ms_consumed
- trace: pwc.candidate.lifecycle (events: created, broker_validated, dispatched, completed, evicted)
- logs: prefetch-worker INFO/ERROR with structured fields (tenant_id, model_id, signature_hash, reason)
Dashboards to create:
- Prefetch efficiency: hit/emit over 1h/24h windows
- Node budget exhaustion heatmap
- Per-tenant cost impact dashboard (rolling 7d)

runbook_incident_playbook:
Incident: Unexpected spike in prefetch CPU usage and scheduler thrashing.
Severity: P1 if impacting user latency, P2 otherwise.
Immediate steps:
1) Disable Planner emission for affected node pools: POST /internal/pwc/control -d '{"action":"pause_pool","pool":"poolA"}'.
2) Evict prefetch jobs: runtime-cli prefetch evict --node poolA-*.
3) Revert score_threshold to 0.9 as temporary mitigation: PATCH /config/pref.score_threshold -d 0.9.
4) Collect debug traces: pwc.dump-trace --since 15m --out /tmp/pwc-trace.json.
Postmortem checklist:
- determine root cause (planner mis-estimation, model change, telemetry lag).
- run retrospective experiment to tune alpha/beta parameters.
- update planner training windows if needed.

safety_and_security_considerations:
- Prefetches must not access customer PII or external connectors; only use deterministic context hashes and minimal context summaries.
- All control plane calls are authenticated via mTLS and signed tokens.
- Budget accounting must be auditable: prefetch cost charged back to tenant's usage ledger.
- Provide an opt-out signal for customers who require strict cost isolation (tenant_prefetch=false).

rollout_and_canary_plan:
Phased rollout recommendations:
1) Internal dogfooding (2 nodes, non-critical pools) for 2 weeks. Monitor hit rate and 95p latency.
2) Canary graduates to 5% of traffic in a dedicated pool for a set of model families for 4 weeks.
3) Increase to 25% after verifying cost caps and no regression in tail-latency.
4) Global rollout with adaptive TTL and per-tenant opt-in within 12 weeks.
Canary health matrix (pass/fail):
- 95p latency regression <= 0%
- Prefetch hit rate >= 65%
- Prefetch cpu_ms_consumed per node < configured budget

troubleshooting_and_known_failure_modes:
Common failure modes and detection:
- High miss-rate: indicates Planner misprediction. Detect by pwc.prefetch.hit_total / pwc.prefetch.emitted_total < 0.4. Mitigation: increase signature windows or reduce emission frequency.
- Mem pressure evictions: detected via kernel eviction traces and node-level OOM counters. Mitigation: lower pref.kv_prefetch_ttl_default_s and reduce concurrent prefetch.
- Scheduler starvation: detect by node idle vs kernel queue backlog mismatch. Mitigation: raise scheduler hint backoff and reduce pref.max_concurrent_prefetch_per_node.

operational_ownership_and_contacts:
Primary owner: Runtime Performance Team (oncall alias: #rt-perf-oncall).
Secondary owner: Serving Scheduler Team.
Escalation path:
- Pager: runtime-perf-pager (P1)
- Slack: #rt-perf-alerts
- Email: runtime-performance@redwood.ai

compatibility_and_backward_compatibility:
The PWC architecture is designed to be additive: safe defaults ensure no prefetch by default (score_threshold default=0.95). Older runtime nodes ignore hint headers gracefully (they accept but do not act on hints). Config migration scripts exist to mark legacy nodes with 'hintable:true' during gradual upgrades.

open_questions_and_future_work:
- Integrate with Redwood Optimize: use historical cost/quality trade data to auto-tune alpha/beta weights.
- Explore model-aware microbenchmarks that exercise attention kernels more precisely.
- Study cross-tenant prefetch sharing heuristics for identical signature reuse with privacy-preserving aggregation.

references_and_related_artifacts:
- See runbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/cold-start-warmup-strategies-and-entropy-reduction-2025
- Kernel telemetry guidelines: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/kernel-telemetry-annotation-guidelines-2025
- Prefetch control plane proto: internal git repo path: //git.redwood/internal/pwc/proto (link in internal repo browser)

changelog:
2026-02-08: Published initial stable spec and added detailed runbook and canary matrix.
2025-12-12: Draft approved by runtime performance review; adjusted default score weights.
2025-10-15: Created initial design doc.

appendix_examples:
Example Planner emission (Kafka event) JSON string:
{
  "tenant_id": "acme-inc",
  "model_id": "gptx-8b",
  "signature_hash": "sha256:ef01...",
  "preferred_node": null,
  "score": 0.72,
  "ttl": 90
}
CLI: Retrieve prefetch metrics:
$ metrics-cli query 'pwc.prefetch.hit_total{model="gptx-8b"}' --window=1h
YAML example: default planner config:
planner:
  emit_interval_s: 5
  score_threshold: 0.6
  alpha: 0.5
  beta: 0.3
  gamma: 0.15
  delta: 0.05

title: Latency Sensitivity Classification and Graceful Migration Playbook
content:
Summary:
This playbook defines a pragmatic classification for request latency sensitivity, maps scheduling and kernel strategies to each class, and prescribes a repeatable, observable migration procedure for moving traffic between kernel/runtime variants or GPU pools with minimal customer impact. It synthesizes runtime architecture considerations, kernel scheduling knobs, profiling steps, benchmark targets, runbook actions, and known failure modes.

Why this exists:
- We operate a heterogeneous serving fleet with multiple kernel variants and GPU shapes.
- Some workloads are extremely latency-sensitive (user-facing chat), while others (batch embeddings, async jobs) favor throughput/cost.
- Incorrect migration or mismatched scheduling leads to p99 spikes, ordering anomalies, and cache warm-up regressions.

Intended audience:
- Serving runtime engineers, SREs, platform engineers, and release owners performing model/kernel migrations or pool consolidations.

1) Latency Sensitivity Classification (quick reference)

- Class A - Interactive-critical:
  - Target: client-facing features where p99 user-perceived latency must meet SLOs. Default SLO: p50 < 50ms, p95 < 120ms, p99 < 250ms.
  - Typical workloads: real-time chat, API sync completions with tight SLAs.
  - Scheduling strategy: strict prioritization, preemptible background throttling, smallest batch sizes, KV cache pinning.

- Class B - Latency-aware background:
  - Target: near-real-time pipelines where occasional p99 bursts are tolerable but median latency matters. SLO example: p50 < 150ms, p95 < 400ms.
  - Typical workloads: autocomplete, user-notification generation.
  - Scheduling: opportunistic batching, intermediate batch cap, allow limited co-tenancy with backpressure.

- Class C - Throughput-first / best-effort:
  - Target: optimize tokens/sec and unit cost. No strict user-facing latency constraints.
  - Typical workloads: offline embeddings, large-batch reranking, async summarization.
  - Scheduling: high batching, quantized kernels, pre-warmed large sequence kernels, deferred KV loads.

2) Sensitivity Matrix (quick table)

Columns: class | batch size cap | preemption | cache policy | default kernel | rollout risk
- Class A | 1-8 | preemptible (high) | KV pin to hot shards | low-latency kernel (fp16/optimized attention) | medium
- Class B | 8-64 | soft preemption | opportunistic cache | balanced kernel (small-opt batching) | low
- Class C | 64-2048 | non-preemptible | deferred cache | throughput kernel (int8/quantized) | low (cost tradeoffs)

3) Telemetry signals to evaluate sensitivity and migration health

Primary signals (real-time):
- p50/p95/p99 request latency per route/model variant
- GPU active SM utilization and crate-level burst (1s and 1m)
- Kernel queue length and average batch size (tokens/request)
- KV cache hit ratio and warmed-frontier age
- End-to-end tail error rate (5xx / model fallback count)

Secondary signals (profiling):
- Per-kernel microsecond latency histogram (attention, matmul, softmax)
- Memory allocator success/failure / OOM attempts
- PCIe saturation and inter-device memcpy spikes

Synthetic indicators for migration safety check:
- p99 delta on canary < 10% absolute or 15% relative (whichever is smaller)
- GPU utilization delta not exceeding +12 percentage points for sustained 1 minute
- KV hit ratio decline < 5 percentage points

4) Profiling & Benchmark Steps (pre-migration)

Required artifacts before migration begins:
- Representative trace capture for 1 hour of production traffic (covering sequences and prompt lengths).
- Microbenchmark suite run for the target model on both kernel variants: 10K requests, sequence lengths [32, 128, 512, 1024] with mixed batch sizes.
- Cost model estimate: per-token ops and measured tokens/sec -> projected cost change.

Commands/examples:
- Capture live traces (agent CLI):
  redwood-trace capture --service=serve-ingress --route=chat-completion --duration=3600 --out=chat-jan-trace.json

- Run microbench (local GPU harness):
  ./bench/run_microbench --model=redwood-xc-3b --kernel=lowlat --seqs=32,128,512,1024 --iters=10000 --out=bench-lowlat.json

Interpreting results: look for kernel-level outliers where a specific op takes >35% of end-to-end compute time (indicates kernel specialization opportunity). If memory-copy time >10% of total on 1024 sequences, investigate PCIe/NUMA placement.

5) Canary & Gradual Migration Plan (runbook)

Preconditions:
- Canary capacity reserved: 3% of total traffic or at least 2 GPUs identical in SKU to target pool.
- Observability: dashboards for primary signals wired and alerting pages configured.
- Rollback hooks present in rollout system with 5-minute circuit breaker.

Step-by-step:
1. Create canary deployment pinned to target kernel variant and attach the trace-capture hook.
2. Inject 0.5% of traffic for 15 minutes. Monitor primary signals for 30 minutes after injection and ensure synthetic indicators pass.
3. If pass, increase to 2% for 30 minutes. Re-run microbench on-canary for short sample.
4. If still green, increase to 10% with automated progressive ramp (10 -> 25 -> 50) with 10 minute holds and a final 1-hour hold at 50% before full cut.
5. During each hold evaluate: p99 delta, error rate delta, KV hit ratio, GPU utilization.
6. If any alarm trips or synthetic indicator thresholds exceeded, immediately pause ramp and rollback to previous stable variant.

Automations to enable:
- Automatic rollback when p99 delta > 25ms absolute for Class A routes.
- Autoscale target pool up by +15% if GPU utilization crosses 80% for >5 minutes during ramp.

6) Rollback Criteria and Postmortem Checklist

Immediate rollback triggers:
- p99 delta > configured threshold (Class A: 25ms absolute)
- Error rate increase > 2x baseline or > 0.5% absolute
- OOM / kernel crash observed on canary instance

Post-rollback actions:
1. Lock the previous variant as the default; mark rollout as failed with a ticket.
2. Capture full diagnostic bundle: kernel traces, dmesg, GPU metrics, allocator logs.
3. Run focused microprofiles to reproduce the issue.
4. Convene a triage meeting within 24 hours; assign owners, timeline, and hotfix plan.

7) Known Interactions and Mitigations

- KV cache warmup: moving to a different kernel shard topology can lower hit ratios for minutes to hours. Mitigation: stagger migrations by user cohort and pre-warm hot keys using synthetic requests.
- NUMA/PCIe shifts: migrations that change device placement may cause memcpy bursts. Mitigation: run a 2-minute memcpy synthetic test preflight and schedule migrations in low-traffic windows.
- Small-batch latency cliffs: some throughput kernels optimize large batch paths and disable small-batch fast-paths. Mitigation: force small-batch branch via a kernel flag: kernel_config.force_small_batch_fastpath=true.
- Quantized-kernel numerical drift: for Class A routes require regression evals on canonical prompt-set with strict tolerance rules (see Quality Guardrails).

8) Benchmarks to include in acceptance criteria

- Stability run: 6 hours @ 50% traffic on target kernel with production sequence mix. Metrics: p99, error rate, memory headroom.
- Cost run: measure tokens/sec and cost-per-1M-tokens comparison.
- Regression eval: run 200 prompt-set against both kernels to ensure model output divergence < 0.3 BLEU-ish / heuristics defined per-model.

9) Observability Dashboard templates (fields to include)

- Top row: p50/p95/p99 latency, request rate, error rate.
- Middle row: GPU utilization, avg batch size, kernel queue depth, KV hit ratio.
- Bottom row: per-kernel hot op latency histograms, memcopy rate, per-instance OOM counters.

10) Ownership, cadence, and archive

- Migration owner: the engineer or oncall who initiates the rollout. Must be tagged in rollout plan and remain the escalation contact for 24 hours post full cut.
- Required reviews: runtime platform peer review and SRE approval for Class A migrations.
- Archive artifacts: attach bench outputs, trace captures, and final decision doc to rollout ticket. Keep for 180 days.

Appendix A - Example YAML fragment for rollout policy (text):

rolloutPolicy: |
  name: 'kernel-variant-rollout'
  targetRoutes: ['/v1/chat', '/v1/complete']
  canary: 
    initialPercent: 0.5
    steps: [2, 10, 25, 50, 100]
    holdMinutes: 10
  alarms: 
    p99DeltaMs: 25
    errorRatePercent: 0.5

Appendix B - Quick Troubleshooting Cheatsheet:
- If p99 spikes but GPU utilization low: suspect KV-cache pressure or network jitter. Check kv.hit_ratio and p99 by shard.
- If p99 and GPU utilization both increase: consider kernel path regression; run microprofile on representative sequences.
- If errors increase only in one AZ: check device driver/version diffs and PCIe errors in system logs.

Appendix C - Release note blurb (for runtime release notes):
- Added 'Latency Sensitivity Classification' and an automated migration playbook that prescribes canary quotas, telemetry thresholds, and rollback criteria. This reduces Class A rollout incidents by targeting safe traffic ramps and automated circuit breakers.

Owners and contacts:
- Document owner: Priya Nair (runtime-platform)
- SRE lead: Marco Alvarez
- Applied ML reviewer: Jinsoo Park

Revision history:
- 2026-02-10 created by PN
- 2026-02-18 added synthetic indicator thresholds and YAML fragment (reviewers: MA, JP)
- 2026-03-01 clarified rollback deltas for Class A and added automation recommendations

Related reading:
- See request-multiplexing-backpressure-architecture-2026 for how routing interacts with scheduling.
- See mixed-workload-slo-simulation-suite-2026 for simulation recipes to validate ramp policies.

title: Paged KV: Compact Sweep + Granular Pin Coordinator Rollout Guide
content:
summary:
This page describes how to safely roll out (and roll back) the paged-KV compact sweep reclamation pass and the granular pin coordinator in production. These changes reduce fragmentation and pin-induced allocator stalls, improving 99p latency under mixed workloads. The guide includes recommended configs, feature gates, dashboards, canary procedure, and known failure modes.

body:
## Background
Long-lived pins and coarse reclamation can cause tail-latency spikes and fragmentation in the paged KV backend. The compact sweep pass opportunistically coalesces sparse blocks; the granular pin coordinator tracks mini-span pins inside blocks to avoid head-of-line blocking during eviction/reuse contention.

This guide is a production-facing update to the implementation that landed in redwood#91534. Since the PR merged, rollout controls, metric names, and default gating have been updated based on perf-canary and two real-world regressions (see “Known issues & mitigations”).

## What changed (operator view)
### Compact sweep
- Runs opportunistically when the allocator reports sufficient slack.
- Moves live mini-spans into denser blocks and releases empty blocks back to the global pool.
- Adds bounded background CPU work to reduce fragmentation and improve reuse.

### Granular pin coordinator
- Exposes per-mini-span pin tokens.
- Fast-path acquisition via atomic bitmap/refcount; fallback path uses a short wait strategy before parking.
- Integrates with eviction scoring (frecency + pin density) to prefer reclaim candidates with fewer pinned spans.

## Feature gates and current defaults
The original PR introduced a scheduler gate named `kv.background_pin_lane`. During rollout hardening (Dec 2025–Jan 2026), we standardized flags and changed defaults.

### Gates
1) Scheduler background lane for long pins
- Old key (deprecated): `kv.background_pin_lane`
- New key: `kv.pin_coordinator.background_lane_enabled`
- Current default: true in canary, false in general production unless explicitly enabled by service config (see “Rollout procedure”).

2) Compact sweep enablement
- Key: `kv.compact_sweep.enabled`
- Current default: true for paged-KV enabled services.

3) Compact sweep aggressiveness
- Keys: `kv.compact_sweep.min_free_ratio`, `kv.compact_sweep.max_cpu_pct`, `kv.compact_sweep.max_move_bytes_per_run`
- Notes: `max_move_bytes_per_run` was added after perf-canary feedback to cap worst-case relocation bursts.

## Recommended configuration (2026-02)
Use these as baseline values. Adjust per cluster based on workload mix and SLO sensitivity.

### Baseline (safe)
- `kv.compact_sweep.enabled=true`
- `kv.compact_sweep.min_free_ratio=0.18`
- `kv.compact_sweep.max_cpu_pct=1.0`
- `kv.compact_sweep.max_move_bytes_per_run=268435456`  (256 MiB)
- `kv.pin_coordinator.enabled=true`
- `kv.pin_coordinator.background_lane_enabled=false`

### Performance-optimized (after canary success)
- `kv.compact_sweep.enabled=true`
- `kv.compact_sweep.min_free_ratio=0.12`
- `kv.compact_sweep.max_cpu_pct=2.0`
- `kv.compact_sweep.max_move_bytes_per_run=536870912`  (512 MiB)
- `kv.pin_coordinator.enabled=true`
- `kv.pin_coordinator.background_lane_enabled=true`

## Observability
### Key metrics (current names)
Metric names were normalized after the PR. If your dashboard uses older names, update it.

Compact sweep:
- `kv.compact_sweep.runs_total`
- `kv.compact_sweep.coalesced_blocks_total`
- `kv.compact_sweep.moved_bytes_total`
- `kv.compact_sweep.run_duration_ms`
- `kv.compact_sweep.throttled_total` (incremented when CPU budget or move cap prevents additional work)

Pin coordinator:
- `kv.pin_coordinator.active_tokens`
- `kv.pin_coordinator.wait_latency_ms` (histogram)
- `kv.pin_coordinator.waiters`
- `kv.pin_coordinator.fallback_path_total`

Allocator / fragmentation:
- `kv.paged_allocator.fragmentation_index` (0..1)
- `kv.paged_allocator.free_ratio`
- `kv.paged_allocator.eviction_stalls_ms` (histogram)

Scheduler lane (when enabled):
- `scheduler.background_lane.queue_depth`
- `scheduler.background_lane.run_latency_ms`

### Traces / logs
- Traces: `compactSweep()` spans include tags `moved_bytes`, `coalesced_blocks`, `throttled`.
- Pin acquisition traces include tags `fast_path=true|false`, `wait_ms`.
- Log sampling: keep at <= 0.1% for pin wait warnings; otherwise high-QPS services can flood.

### SLO signals to watch during canary
- Serving 99p/99.9p latency
- OOM / RSS growth rate
- Token cost or GPU utilization (service-dependent)
- `kv.pin_coordinator.wait_latency_ms` p99
- `kv.paged_allocator.eviction_stalls_ms` p99

## Rollout procedure
### 0) Preconditions
- You are on a runtime build that includes the post-merge config normalization (>= runtime v1.19.3).
- You have dashboards updated to the metric names above.
- You can revert flags without redeploy (dynamic config or config-map reload).

### 1) Canary: enable compact sweep only (recommended order)
1. Set `kv.compact_sweep.enabled=true` (if not already).
2. Start with baseline settings:
   - `min_free_ratio=0.18`, `max_cpu_pct=1.0`, `max_move_bytes_per_run=256MiB`.
3. Run for 24 hours.
4. Success criteria:
   - Fragmentation index drops by >= 20% relative to baseline over comparable traffic.
   - No sustained increase in tail latency (> 2% at p99) and no elevated eviction stall p99.

### 2) Canary: enable granular pin coordinator (if not already default)
1. Set `kv.pin_coordinator.enabled=true`.
2. Keep `kv.pin_coordinator.background_lane_enabled=false` initially.
3. Run for 24 hours.
4. Success criteria:
   - Reduction in `kv.paged_allocator.eviction_stalls_ms` p99 (target: 10–25% depending on workload).
   - `kv.pin_coordinator.fallback_path_total` stable or decreasing after warm-up.

### 3) Canary: enable background lane for long pins (optional)
1. Set `kv.pin_coordinator.background_lane_enabled=true`.
2. Run for 24–72 hours.
3. Success criteria:
   - No throughput regression on continuous batching.
   - Background lane queue depth remains bounded (no persistent growth).

### 4) Ramp-up
- Ramp 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100% by cluster, holding at least 12 hours per step.
- Use the same step schedule for enabling background lane.

## Rollback procedure
If any of the following occurs, rollback the most recent step first:
- Sustained p99 latency increase > 5% for 30 minutes.
- OOM events increase or RSS growth accelerates unexpectedly.
- `kv.pin_coordinator.wait_latency_ms` p99 increases > 2x baseline.

Rollback order:
1) Disable background lane: `kv.pin_coordinator.background_lane_enabled=false`
2) If still bad, disable pin coordinator: `kv.pin_coordinator.enabled=false`
3) If still bad (rare), disable compact sweep: `kv.compact_sweep.enabled=false`

Notes:
- Disabling compact sweep may increase fragmentation over hours; plan for a follow-up defragmentation window if needed.

## Expected performance impact (field data)
The original microbench numbers in redwood#91534 remain directionally correct, but production outcomes vary by workload.

Observed ranges in canary (Nov 2025–Feb 2026):
- 99p latency: 12–25% improvement for short-sequence / mixed hot-cold traffic; minimal change for long-context dominated traffic.
- Fragmentation index: 25–45% reduction after 6–24 hours of steady traffic.
- Token cost: 3–7% improvement where eviction/reuse contention was a limiter.

## Known issues & mitigations
1) Burst relocation causing short CPU spikes
- Symptom: `kv.compact_sweep.run_duration_ms` and host CPU jump, correlated with small latency blips.
- Mitigation: lower `kv.compact_sweep.max_cpu_pct` or `kv.compact_sweep.max_move_bytes_per_run`.

2) High contention pin waits under pathological micro-span churn
- Symptom: `kv.pin_coordinator.wait_latency_ms` p99 increases and `fallback_path_total` climbs.
- Mitigation: ensure background lane is disabled initially; if enabling, confirm background lane queue depth stays bounded. Consider raising allocator free ratio target (service-specific).

3) Config key mismatch after standardization
- Symptom: changes to `kv.background_pin_lane` have no effect.
- Mitigation: migrate to `kv.pin_coordinator.background_lane_enabled`. The old key is ignored in runtime >= v1.19.3.

## Ownership & support
- Primary owner: Serving Runtime (Kernel & Scheduling)
- Escalation: #eng-serving-runtime-oncall
- Related work items: ENG-7342, ENG-7460

## Appendix: quick validation checklist
- [ ] Confirm `kv.paged_allocator.free_ratio` is stable after enabling compact sweep.
- [ ] Confirm fragmentation index trends downward over a full diurnal cycle.
- [ ] Confirm eviction stalls p99 is not worse than baseline.
- [ ] Confirm pin coordinator wait latency p99 is stable.
- [ ] If background lane enabled, confirm scheduler queue depth is bounded.

title: Runtime Scheduler Testbed and Quality Assurance Manual
content:
Overview

This manual describes the runtime scheduler testbed we maintain for validating scheduler policy changes, kernel rollouts, and fidelity-preserving degradation strategies. It documents the architecture of the testbed, the QA workflows, acceptance criteria, regression detection heuristics, and step-by-step procedures to run experiments safely against synthetic and shadow production workloads. The goal is to catch behavioral regressions (latency, fairness, tail-risk), prevent production impact, and provide reproducible evidence for signoff.

Scope

- Kernel and scheduler policy changes (priority changes, preemption rules, admission controller tweaks)
- Scheduler-agent and slot-allocation algorithms
- Admission and backpressure logic (credit accounting, slot reclamation)
- Fidelity/staircase degradation policies and fallback composition
- Telemetry contract validation for scheduler signals

Testbed architecture (high level)

1) Components
- Experiment orchestrator: coordinates scenario provisioning, traffic shaping, and result collection.
- Shadow router: mirrors production request streams into isolated clusters with controlled time offset.
- Synthetic workload generator: produces deterministic mixes for unit tests (see workload catalog below).
- Local kernel harness: runs candidate kernel/scheduler binaries inside container sandboxes with tracer hooks.
- Observability sink: Elasticsearch / Clickhouse for metrics, Jaeger for traces, and artifact store for profiling bundles.

2) Isolation guarantees
- Hardware isolation: testbed uses dedicated GPU pool (label: qa-gpu) to avoid noisy neighbors.
- Network isolation: mirrors run through a VPC peering path with egress-only NAT; no writeback to production control plane.
- Config sandboxing: runtime config is loaded from experiment-specific namespaces; no global flag flips without explicit signoff.

Workload catalog (examples)

- w-small-chat: 95% short prompts (<64 tokens), 5% long (>512 tokens), concurrency 50
- w-bursty-chat: Poisson bursts with 500 rps for 10s every 5m, baseline 20 rps
- w-multi-tenant-mix: 30 tenants, skewed qps distribution, KV cache hit rate target 65%
- w-seq-heavy: long decoding tails, average response 800 tokens, continuous low QPS

Acceptance criteria and QA gates

Run-level acceptance must produce PASS for all checks below before any scheduler change proceeds to staged rollout. Each check has a pass/fail threshold and an owner.

| Check | Metric | Threshold | Owner |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Latency SLO | p99 end-to-end generation | <= 1.15x baseline | SRE - Runtime
| Kernel sensitivity | per-kernel 95th percentile op time | <= +15% vs baseline | Runtime Perf
| Fairness | 95th percentile ratio tenant A / tenant median | <= 2.0x | Runtime Ops
| Throughput | sustained tokens/s under nominal load | >= 0.95x baseline | Capacity Planning
| Regression signal | anomaly score (ensemble detector) | < 0.8 (no alarm) | Observability

Note: Baseline is the last released scheduler binary that passed production canary.

QA workflows and procedures

A. Preflight validation (developer)
1. Create an experiment branch and upload candidate scheduler binary to the artifact store.
2. Populate experiment namespace with config: prioritization rules, admission thresholds, and preemption windows. Example YAML: 

apiVersion: v1
kind: SchedulerExperiment
metadata:
  name: qa-priority-test-2025-02
spec:
  admission:
    max_slots_per_tenant: 8
    credit_replenish_ms: 500
  priorities:
    - name: realtime
      weight: 100
    - name: background
      weight: 10

3. Run unit harness: ./tools/sched-harness --binary=artifact://... --workload=w-small-chat --verify-signals
4. Verify trace-level invariants: no kernel preemption loops, no unbounded queue growth.

B. Shadow-validation (engineer + oncall)
1. Schedule a shadow run mirroring a 5% sample of production traffic for 2 hours. Use shadow router config: 
- mirror_ratio: 0.05
- offset: 300s
- bind_to: qa-gpu-pool
2. Monitor the dashboards (links in Observability section).
3. Execute acceptance checks from the table. Block if any check fails.
4. If minor regressions appear (kernel latency increase < 10% but within SLO), tag for controlled canary and schedule remediation experiments.

C. Canary rollout (SRE-led)
1. Canary percentage cadence: 1% -> 5% -> 20% -> 100% (min 30m per step and performance stable for 3 consecutive windows).
2. Automated rollback triggers: any of the following -> abort and roll back to baseline.
   - p99 latency > 1.25x baseline for two consecutive windows (5m windows)
   - Kernel error rate increases by >0.5% absolute
   - Unrecoverable fairness violation (tenant starvation detected)
3. Post-canary signoff: runtime product manager + release lead.

Observability and telemetry contract

Minimum telemetry required for any experiment: token-level timing, kernel_id, kernel_phase, scheduler_decision (admit, queue, preempt), tenant_id, queue_depth, slot_allocations. All fields must be present in trace or metric envelopes. Missing fields cause experiment to be rejected.

Suggested dashboards (links are placeholders):
- Scheduler QA Overview: /dashboards/scheduler-qa-overview
- Kernel Heatmap: /dashboards/kernel-heatmap
- Tenant Fairness Matrix: /dashboards/tenant-fairness

Regression detection heuristics

We employ an ensemble of detectors: moving-window z-score, seasonal decomposition residuals, and causal-signal attribution that correlates kernel changes to downstream latencies. Key rules:
- Flag when z-score(p99) > 4 sigma over baseline for 10m
- Correlate kernel_id spikes with p50->p99 divergence using Granger-style causality test (implemented in analysis pipeline)
- Use controlled perturbation runs (see perturbation lab) to map sensitive kernels.

Perturbation lab (controlled experiments)

Purpose: rapidly probe kernel and scheduler behaviour by injecting micro-perturbations and observing knock-on effects. Typical perturbations:
- Small increase in kernel op latency (+5–20%) via CPU throttling per container.
- Forced preemption events every Nth request.
- Synthetic cache misses by clearing kvcache hints.

Procedure:
1. Tag experiment as perturbation-run and ensure artifact retention.
2. Run baseline, then incrementally apply perturbation levels (0%, 5%, 10%, 20%).
3. Collect kernel flamegraphs and trace bundles for each level.
4. Submit a perturbation report (template below) to the experiment tracker.

Perturbation report template (plain text)
- Experiment id: EXP-YYYYMMDD-xxx
- Perturbation type: latency-injection / preemption / cache-eviction
- Affected kernels: kernel_42, kernel_37
- Metrics delta: p50:+3%, p95:+18%, p99:+24%
- Interpretation: kernel_37 has non-linear sensitivity at >10% perturbation; consider moving to fallback kernel variant.

Runbook: Investigate scheduler regression (quick triage)

1. Confirm experiment or production alert: check p50/p95/p99 and kernel error rates.
2. Gather recent artifacts: latest experiment bundle, trace sample, flamegraph, and scheduler decision logs.
3. Reproduce in testbed using the same workload spec. If reproduction fails, escalate to Observability for sampling validation.
4. If reproduced, run bisection: deploy last-known-good scheduler/kernel and progressively switch flags to isolate change.
5. Create incident ticket with severity and owner, schedule rollback if safety thresholds exceeded.

Escalation matrix

- Tier 1 (oncall runtime): initial triage and short-term rollback (first 30 minutes)
- Tier 2 (runtime engineers): in-depth bisection and remediation (30m–4h)
- Tier 3 (product + SRE leadership): customer communication and permanent fixes (>4h)

Operational checklist before any production rollout

- [ ] Experiment artifacts uploaded and retained for 90 days
- [ ] Telemetry contract validated (no missing fields)
- [ ] Synthetic and shadow runs executed with acceptance checks PASS
- [ ] Canary policy pre-configured with rollback hooks
- [ ] Owners and oncall notified with runbook link and signoff list

Ownership and contacts

- Testbed steward: Priya Kapoor (runtime-quality@redwood.ai)
- Scheduler QA lead: Evan Li (evan.li@redwood.ai)
- Observability owner: Marcus Hernandez (obs-owner@redwood.ai)

Appendices

A. CLI recipes
- Launch a local harness: 
  ./tools/sched-harness run --binary artifact://scheduler:v2025-02 --workload w-bursty-chat --collect-traces --out /tmp/exp-bundle
- Submit experiment to orchestrator: 
  curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"experiment":"qa-priority-test-2025-02","binary":"artifact://scheduler:v...","workload":"w-small-chat"}' \
    https://orchestrator.internal/api/v1/experiments

B. Example synthetic workload snippet (YAML)
workload:
  name: w-bursty-chat
  phases:
    - type: steady
      qps: 20
      duration: 2400
    - type: burst
      qps: 500
      duration: 10
      cadence: 300
  token_distribution:
    short: 95
    long: 5

C. Artifact retention and privacy
- All experiment bundles are retained for 90 days in the QA artifact store. Sensitive payloads must be redacted before public sharing. See data-retention policy.

D. Templates and links
- Perturbation report template: /templates/perturbation-report
- Experiment tracker: /tools/experiment-tracker
- Release checklist: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-deployment-circuit-breakers-and-sla-fallback-playbook-2026

Revision history

- 2024-11-12: Initial draft and testbed spec (Priya Kapoor)
- 2025-01-07: Added perturbation lab procedures and acceptance criteria (Evan Li)
- 2025-02-08: Finalized canary cadence and telemetry contract; published (Priya Kapoor)

title: Kernel variant split-testing and safety contract
content:
Summary

This document defines the safety contract, telemetry requirements, and a step-by-step split-testing procedure for rolling out new kernel variants in the serving runtime. It is intended for runtime engineers, release owners, and on-call SREs.
