- harness-agent: small in-process shim that can toggle SDK behavior (sync vs async logging, sample rate) at runtime.
- replay-corpus: directory of sampled request traces and generated synthetic workloads.
- assertion-library: a set of reusable checks (latency budgets, kernel-signal presence, KV cache warmup checks).

Operational diagram (text)
-------------------------
1. harnessctl launches a controller (k8s job or local process).
2. Controller schedules N parallel kernel drivers against a test runtime cluster or a mocked harness runtime image.
3. Observability injector instruments the runtime via harness-agent and network proxies to inject delays or drop events.
4. Assertion engine gathers metrics via Prometheus, traces via Jaeger/OTLP collector, and logs from stdout.

Key test scenarios
------------------
|| Scenario || Perturbation || Acceptance criteria || Owner ||
|| Span amplification || Add 2x span annotations per token (500B payload) || No more than +7% P95 token latency; no missing kernel handshake spans; no increase >3% in GPU stall time || runtime-kernel-team ||
|| Sampling skew || Vary sampling rate from 100% -> 0.1% during steady traffic || Reconstruction of request lineage must succeed for at least 95% of sampled traces; SLO change <5% || observability-team ||
|| Sidecar headroom loss || Sidecar adds 10–250ms per span on a configurable fraction of calls || System remains within degradation budget and fallback policy triggers correctly when latency > 200ms || infra-team ||
|| SDK sync-blocking || Toggle agent to synchronous flush on process-critical path for 1 minute || No kernel-level timeouts or watchdog escalations; error rate delta <0.5% || sdk-team ||

Example harness configuration (YAML)
----------------------------------
```yaml
experiment_name: observability-span-amplification
duration: 15m
parallel_clients: 48
replay_corpus: gs://redwood-test-corpus/kernels/seq-len-tail
observability_injection:
  span_amplification:
    enabled: true
    extra_annotation_size_bytes: 512
    fraction_of_requests: 0.25
  sidecar_delay:
    enabled: true
    p99_delay_ms: 120
assertions:
  - type: latency_budget
    p95_ms: 70
  - type: span_presence
    required_spans:
      - kernel.handshake
      - kernel.eviction
```

Running the harness (CLI examples)
---------------------------------
- Dry run locally (fast validation):
  ```bash
  harnessctl plan --config=./observability-span-amplification.yaml --dry-run
  ```
- Full experiment against staging cluster (k8s):
  ```bash
  harnessctl apply --config=./observability-span-amplification.yaml --namespace=staging-runtime
  harnessctl watch --experiment observability-span-amplification
  ```
- Tail assertion output:
  ```bash
  harnessctl logs --experiment observability-span-amplification --assertion-stream
  ```

Assertion engine: common checks
-------------------------------
- Latency budgets: P50/P95/P99 token and request latency thresholds.
- Span integrity: presence of kernel.* spans, consistent correlation_id propagation, and incremental sequence numbers for kernel events.
- Telemetry volume sanity: ensure instrumentation doesn't increase Prometheus scrape cardinality >10x for the run.
- Resource counters: GPU SM utilization, memory stall counters, and kernel execution time histograms.
- Detected anomalies: signature for KV-cache warmup regressions, cold-start variance, and kernel handshake timeouts.

Automated gating and rollout policy
----------------------------------
1. Every kernel or scheduler change must be validated with the OIKVH in known-good staging and with 3 targeted experiments: baseline (no injection), moderate injection (10–20% request fraction), and heavy injection (50% fraction).
2. Gating criteria: all assertions pass or are explained by a documented change. Failures must open a ticket in the runtime backlog and block rollout.
3. For critical kernels (attention, kv-cache, dispatcher), require a k-change postmortem for any P95 increase >10% under moderate injection.

Telemetry assertions and dashboard queries
----------------------------------------
The assertion engine publishes a results bundle (JSON) and a short summary to the harness dashboard. Example PromQL checks the P95 token latency: 
```promql
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(runtime_token_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le))
```
Check for missing kernel.handshake spans using trace counts: ensure trace_count(kernel.handshake) / requests_sampled > 0.9 for sampled requests.

Failure modes and mitigation guidance
-----------------------------------
- Symptom: P95 increases only when tracing enabled.
  Action: Reduce tracing payloads, switch SDK to async flush, rerun harness to isolate span that correlates.
- Symptom: Prometheus scrape cardinality explosion.
  Action: Revert instrumentation that creates high-cardinality labels; add label aggregation; schedule a follow-up microbenchmark.
- Symptom: Kernel handshake missing under head-of-line injection.
  Action: Increase kernel handshake timeout and add a non-blocking hedging path; validate with targeted harness test.

Ownership and lifecycle
-----------------------
- Primary owner: runtime-kernel-team (oncall: runtime-kernel-oncall).
- Observability integration and support: observability-team.
- SDK shim maintenance: client-sdks team.
- Quarterly: run the full corpus across latest staging image and publish an experiment digest to the Runtime QA channel.

Runbook: quick steps for a failed experiment
------------------------------------------
1. Inspect harnessctl logs and the assertion output. Identify the first failed assertion timestamp.
2. Correlate with Prometheus and tracing timeslices.
3. If impact is limited to instrumentation metrics (cardinality/latency) and kernel functional metrics are unaffected, open a follow-up with sdk-team and mark experiment as ‘investigated – non-blocking’.
4. If kernel SLOs are violated, page runtime-kernel-oncall, capture a diagnostic packet (harnessctl gather --since <ts>), and escalate per incident runbook.

Appendix: example minimal assertion JSON output
----------------------------------------------
```json
{
  "experiment": "observability-span-amplification",
  "result": "failed",
  "failed_assertions": [
    {"id": "latency_p95_token", "observed_ms": 78, "threshold_ms": 70},
    {"id": "span_presence_kernel_handshake", "missing_pct": 12}
  ],
  "attachments": ["s3://redwood-test-artifacts/harness/2026-11-07/exp-1234.tgz"]
}
```
Appendix: quick checklist before a kernel rollout
-------------------------------------------------
- [ ] Run OIKVH baseline, moderate, and heavy injection experiments.
- [ ] Confirm no assertion regressions or file tickets for each failure.
- [ ] Publish experiment digest and reviewers’ signoff.
- [ ] Include instrumentation delta summary in release notes.

References and related pages
---------------------------
- Runtime profiling guidelines: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/runtime-profiling-playbook-guidelines-2025
- Kernel handshake patterns: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/kernel-handshake-and-adaptive-fallback-patterns-2026
- Canary and SLA gate matrix: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-upgrade-validation-and-canary-matrix-2026

If you are implementing or extending the harness, contact the runtime-kernel-team channel and add your experiment to the replay-corpus index (gs://redwood-test-corpus/index.yaml).

title: scheduler-observability-contract-and-simulated-injector-2026
content:
Overview:

This document defines the Scheduler Observability Contract for Redwood's serving runtime and describes an accompanying Simulated Injector tool used to validate telemetry pipelines end-to-end. The goal is to make scheduler behavior (admission, batching, kernel mapping, preemption, and handoff) observable through a small, stable set of events and metrics so SRE, runtime, and profiling teams can reliably detect regressions, diagnose incidents, and run automated acceptance tests during rollouts.

Audience:
- Runtime engineers (owners of kernel/scheduler code)
- SRE and oncall teams
- Profiling and benchmarking teams
- Observability and telemetry platform owners

Contract principles (high level):
1) Minimalism: Emit a compact set of structured events that capture decisions and state transitions. Avoid duplicating high-volume token-level logs.
2) Deterministic schemas: Every event must follow a documented JSON schema with stable field names (snake_case). Changes require cross-team review.
3) Cost-aware sampling: High-frequency internal traces are sampled; key transition events must be unsampled or sampled with guaranteed floor rates for SLO monitoring.
4) End-to-end testability: A simulator must be able to inject synthetic traces that exercise normal and pathological scheduler flows; observability owners are responsible for ingest test harnesses.

Event taxonomy (summary):
- scheduler_decision: Admission decision for an incoming request (accept/reject/defer).
- batch_formation: When the scheduler assembles a batch (includes batch shape, kernel_hint).
- kernel_dispatch: When a kernel is selected and dispatched to an accelerator.
- preemption_event: When a running kernel is preempted or split.
- handoff_event: When request ownership moves between worker threads or nodes.
- resource_pressure: Node-level signals (gpu_memory_pct, active_streams, nvlink_health).

Event schema examples (JSON):
1) scheduler_decision sample:
{
  "event_type": "scheduler_decision",
  "request_id": "req-20260223-7c9b2",
  "tenant_id": "team-optimizer",
  "priority": "P0",
  "decision": "accept",
  "reason": "admitted_to_slot",
  "timestamp": "2026-02-23T17:12:03.123Z"
}

2) batch_formation sample:
{
  "event_type": "batch_formation",
  "batch_id": "b-4491",
  "shape": "[1,8,64]",
  "kernel_hint": "attention_v2_fp16",
  "requests": ["req-7c9b2", "req-8a1d0"],
  "queued_ms": 12,
  "timestamp": "2026-02-23T17:12:03.135Z"
}

Metric table (concrete list for dashboards and alerts):
| metric_name | unit | description | floor_sampling | alert_threshold | owner |
| scheduler.admit_rate | requests/s | Rate of accepted requests post-admission | unsampled for P0/P1 | sustained < 5th percentile baseline for 5m | runtime-sre |
| scheduler.queue_latency_p95 | ms | 95th percentile time between enqueue and batch dispatch | 100% for P0 traces | > 200 ms increase vs baseline | runtime-sre |
| scheduler.batch_size.avg | requests | Rolling average batch size per kernel | sampled 10% | step-change > 30% | runtime |
| scheduler.preempt_rate | events/s | Number of preemption events | unsampled for P0 | > expected floor for 10m | runtime |
| node.resource_pressure | pct | Node-level memory utilization | sampled 5% | > 90% for 3m | infra |

Sampling rules and guarantees:
- P0 (latency-critical) requests: all scheduler_decision and batch_formation events must be emitted unsampled and preserved for 72 hours.
- P1: floor sampling 10% for high-volume events; core transition events unsampled.
- Node-level telemetry: aggregated at 1s resolution, retained 14 days.
- If budget / ingestion pressure is detected, the horizon for batch_size.avg and resource_pressure can be downsampled but scheduler_decision for P0 must remain.

Trace and span conventions:
- Each request carries a trace_id and request_id in all emitted events. Spans are tagged with: service=scheduler, kernel=..., slot_id=..., tenant_id=...
- Parent-child relationships: scheduler_decision -> batch_formation -> kernel_dispatch -> kernel_execution_span (if available).

Simulated Injector (overview):
The Simulated Injector (sim-injector) is a lightweight binary and set of test harness scripts that synthesizes scheduler events and metrics to validate the entire telemetry ingestion, enrichment, and alerting pipeline. The injector supports:
- Normal steady-state profiles (latency-sensitive and throughput-oriented shapes)
- Pathological cases (burst admission storms, opaque kernel failures, preemption cascades)
- Configurable tenant-mix, sequence-length distributions, and kernel-hint compositions

Key features:
- Deterministic replay mode: replays a seed corpus to reproduce prior incidents.
- Fuzz mode: randomizes batch shapes and decision jitter to stress sampling invariants.
- Backpressure faucet: emits resource_pressure events under operator control to exercise degradation paths.

How to run (local quickstart):
Prereqs: go 1.20+ or prebuilt binary; access to dev telemetry ingestion endpoint (env var TELEMETRY_ENDPOINT).

1) Build or fetch binary:
$ go build ./cmd/sim-injector -o sim-injector

2) Run a simple steady-state profile (10 tenants, 100 rps):
$ TELEMETRY_ENDPOINT=https://dev-telemetry.redwood.internal:443 
  ./sim-injector --profile steady --tenants 10 --rps 100 --duration 300s

3) Run a preemption cascade scenario and persist traces to local file for debugging:
$ ./sim-injector --scenario preempt-cascade --out-file preempt-trace.json --duration 120s

4) Replay a saved trace against staging ingestion to validate alerting rules:
$ ./sim-injector --replay preempt-trace.json --target staging

Acceptance tests (gating a scheduler change):
- Unit: New decision code emits scheduler_decision with new field kernel_version (if added) and passes JSON schema validation.
- Integration: Run sim-injector steady profile at 10% of production RPS for 30m into staging; no increase in queue_latency_p95 > 10% and no unhandled preemptions.
- Observability smoke: All P0 traces appear in the P95 latency dashboard and sample logs link back to request_id.

Rollout checklist for scheduler changes that affect the contract:
1) Update this document and add schema diff (PR).
2) Coordinate with telemetry owners and alerting oncall.
3) Add compatibility shim to runtime that emits legacy fields for 14 days.
4) Run sim-injector compatibility runs against staging ingestion and dashboards.
5) Canary deploy scheduler change to 1% traffic with active sim-injector shadowing.
6) Verify metrics and tracing invariants for 24h, then expand canary.

Ownership and escalation:
- Scheduler telemetry contract owner: Priya Raman (runtime observability).
- Ingestion and enrichment: Observability Platform (owner: Ethan Cole).
- Oncall escalation: runtime-sre rotation (page: #runtime-sre).
- For schema changes: require review by Observability Platform and Runtime leads.

Appendix A — JSON Schema (abridged):
{
  "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#",
  "type": "object",
  "required": ["event_type", "timestamp", "request_id"],
  "properties": {
    "event_type": {
      "type": "string",
      "enum": ["scheduler_decision", "batch_formation", "kernel_dispatch", "preemption_event", "handoff_event", "resource_pressure"]
    },
    "timestamp": {
      "type": "string",
      "format": "date-time"
    },
    "request_id": {
      "type": "string"
    }
  }
}

Appendix B — Common troubleshooting scenarios and quick checks:
- Missing P0 events in dashboards: verify tracer injection, check trace sampling policy, confirm TELEMETRY_ENDPOINT and auth tokens, and run sim-injector --replay for a P0 trace.
- High preempt_rate after change: run sim-injector preempt-cascade and compare kernel_dispatch vs preemption_event counts.
- Alert noise due to downsampling: confirm sampling floor is honored for P0; if not, escalate to Observability Platform.

Change log (summary):
- 2025-11-12: Initial draft created (Priya Raman).
- 2026-01-15: Added sampling guarantees and metric definitions (Maya Gupta).
- 2026-02-28: Introduced Simulated Injector quickstart and rollout checklist (Priya Raman).

Related artifacts:
- sim-injector repo: git@github.com:redwood/injector.git (internal)
- Dashboards: /grafana/d/runtime/scheduler-health
- Alerts: /alerts/runtime/scheduler-queue-latency

If you modify any event names or fields, update the schema in Appendix A, notify reviewers listed above, and run the sim-injector compatibility suite before merging.

title: Quota Reshaping and Graceful Priority Revocation — Spec + Runbook
content:
Summary

This document specifies the Quota Reshaping and Graceful Priority Revocation feature for the Redwood serving runtime scheduler. The goal is to allow the scheduler to rebalance per-tenant and per-route resource allocations under sustained pressure without causing sharp fidelity drops, SLO violations, or oscillatory eviction behavior. The doc contains: design intent, scheduling state machine, metrics & instrumentation, operational runbook for incidents, config examples, rollout checklist, and ownership.

Why this exists

- Problem: sudden quota exhaustion, tenant burst consolidation, or hardware degradation can force hard evictions that break KV cache consistency, invalidate warmstart assumptions, and produce large P95/P99 latency regressions.
- Goal: implement a controlled, observable sequence to reshape quotas and softly revoke priority (i.e., gradually reduce slot weights / kernel credits), providing smooth fidelity degradation and clear recovery paths.

Design overview

1) Principle: degrade gracefully, prefer admission control and shaping over instantaneous preemptive evictions.
2) Surface: extends scheduler admission controller and kernel admission (credit) layer. Two coordinated actions: 
   - Quota Reshaping: modify per-cohort quotas (GPU slots / kernel share) based on observed usage and backlog.
   - Priority Revocation (soft): decrement per-request priority multiplier and re-evaluate kernel assignment; do not forcibly preempt running kernels unless safety thresholds exceeded.
3) Safety: hard-eviction remains a last resort behind multiple guarded checks.

Terminology

- slot: logical allocation unit for GPU kernel execution (existing).
- credit: kernel-level CPU/GPU time accounting token.
- cohort: grouping (tenant-route-model-version) used for quota accounting.
- soft-revoke: transient decrease of effective priority multiplier used by the scheduler when scoring requests.

State machine (high level)

1) Detect: Async monitor observes backlog growth, queue latency, kernel queue length, and GPU occupancy.
2) Candidate selection: pick cohorts with highest excess tail-impact score (see scoring below).
3) Reshape proposal: synthesize a target quota delta for each selected cohort. Proposal includes: delta_percent, grace_period_s, rollback_condition_expression.
4) Soft-apply: apply soft-revoke by reducing cohort priority by X% in increments (step size configurable). Track the impact for 'observation_window_s'.
5) Confirm/rollback: if P95 latency or fidelity metric regresses beyond configured tolerance, automatically rollback the change. If improvement persists and allowed budget used, commit the reshape to quota service.

Scoring and selection

Use a weighted score combining: queue_growth_rate (50%), p99_latency_increase (30%), recent_error_rate (10%), coldstart_fraction (10%). Normalise each signal and compute: score = 0.5*g + 0.3*l + 0.1*e + 0.1*c. Higher score -> higher candidate priority.

Key metrics & instrumentation (names are authoritative)

- scheduler.quota_reshaper.proposals.count (counter)
- scheduler.quota_reshaper.applied.count (counter)
- scheduler.priority_revocation.step_applied (gauge) — current step for cohort
- scheduler.priority_revocation.rollback.count (counter)
- runtime.kv_cache.hit_ratio (gauge) — use when deciding safe reshaping targets
- runtime.p95_latency_ms (histogram) — per-cohort, per-route
- scheduler.backlog.size_by_cohort (gauge)
- scheduler.soft_revoke_active (gauge boolean)
- alerts: alert if scheduler.quota_reshaper.rollback.count > 3 within 30m for same cohort

Config example (YAML)

--8<-- CONFIG START
quota_reshaper:
  enabled: true
  max_concurrent_proposals: 5
  detection_window_s: 60
  observation_window_s: 120
  step_size_percent: 10      # reduce priority by 10% per step
  max_steps: 5               # at most 50% soft revoke
  min_grace_period_s: 30
  rollback_criteria:
    p95_latency_increase_pct_threshold: 15
    fidelity_regression_score_threshold: 0.08
    error_rate_absolute_threshold: 0.01
  selection_weights:
    queue_growth: 0.5
    p99_latency: 0.3
    errors: 0.1
    coldstart: 0.1
  hard_evict_thresholds:
    gpu_ooms_in_window: 1
    sustained_gpu_occupancy_pct: 98
--8<-- CONFIG END

Notes on tuning: step_size_percent and max_steps balance rapid recovery vs fidelity risk. Default values are conservative.

Kernel-level integration

- When the soft-revoke step changes, the scheduler attaches a priority_multiplier to the request descriptor that the kernel admission subsystem reads. Kernel admission then de-queues lower-scored requests first.
- The kernel must not preempt in-flight execution unless hard_evict_threshold is met. Instead, new admissions are biased away from revoked cohorts.

Rollout / Fallback strategy

1) Canary: enable in canary runtime region with max_concurrent_proposals=1 and observation_window_s=300. Monitor the following dashboards for 48h: p95 latency, kv_cache.hit_ratio, scheduler.quota_reshaper.* metrics.
2) Graduated rollout: increase traffic to canary cohorts and raise max_concurrent_proposals progressively.
3) Fallback: automated rollback if any rollback_criteria tripped. Manual rollback option for oncall via CLI: rshctl quota-reshaper rollback --cohort <id>

Operational runbook: immediate steps for incidents

Title: High tail latency suspected due to quota reshaping
Severity: Sev2
Owner: Serving-runtime oncall (primary)

1) Check dashboard: runtime.p95_latency_ms (global and per-cohort), scheduler.quota_reshaper.applied.count in last 30m.
2) If applied.count > 0 for suspect cohort: run rshctl quota-reshaper list --recent 30m to view proposals and steps.
3) Soft rollback (automated) will occur if criteria met. If automated rollback has not triggered and P95 > SLA threshold (see below), manually rollback: rshctl quota-reshaper rollback --cohort <id> --reason "oncall-rollback"
4) If rollback succeeds but latency remains high: escalate to runtime-sre and open PAGER channel. Collect traces: occtl traces query --cohort <id> --window 15m and attach to incident.
5) If system is oscillating (repeated apply->rollback loops): disable quota_reshaper globally: rshctl feature toggle quota_reshaper --off and file a follow-up investigation ticket.

SLA and thresholds

- Platform latency SLO (hosted tier): p95 < 150ms, p99 < 400ms for text-generation endpoints under nominal load.
- Acceptance guard for changes: no single cohort should see p95 increase > 15% relative to baseline for longer than observation_window_s.

Safety considerations and edge cases

- KV cache thrash: avoid reducing priority for cohorts with kv_cache.hit_ratio > 0.70 unless backlog growth is extreme — we prefer shaping other cohorts first.
- Coldstart-heavy cohorts: coldstart_fraction used to downweight candidates to avoid punishing transient spikes.
- Multi-tenant entanglement: changes applied for one cohort must be visible to cross-tenant routing decision (so that downstream routing can reroute to fallback model variants).

Audit logs and governance

- Every proposal, step application, commit, and rollback is written to audit-service with fields: {proposal_id, cohort_id, author=system|user, delta_percent, steps_applied, timestamps, reason}.
- Retention: audit records retained 90 days by default; retention for enterprise private deployments configurable via policy.

Testing and benchmark plan

- Unit tests for scoring and selection (deterministic stubs).
- Integration tests: synthetic traffic generator (benchgen) produces sustained vs spiky patterns; run across hardware types and validate no more than 2% increase in cost/throughput envelope.
- Benchmark: run mixed-workload-slo-simulation-suite (see benchmarking-and-perf-suite) for 1000 trial seeds to measure false-positive reshapes. Target false-positive rate < 1 per 1000 trials.

CLI & debugging commands

- rshctl quota-reshaper status --cohort <id>
- rshctl quota-reshaper explain --proposal <proposal_id>
- rshctl quota-reshaper rollback --cohort <id> [--force]
- rshctl metrics tail scheduler.priority_revocation.step_applied

Example proposal record (JSON)

--8<-- EXAMPLE START
{
  "proposal_id": "qr-20250901-77a3",
  "cohort_id": "tenant-234/route/text-gen/v2",
  "delta_percent": -20,
  "steps_planned": 2,
  "applied_steps": 1,
  "status": "observing",
  "created_by": "automated-detector",
  "created_at": "2025-09-01T12:34:00Z"
}
--8<-- EXAMPLE END

Ownership and follow-ups

- Primary owners: runtime-scheduler team (pager: runtime-scheduler-oncall)
- Secondary owners: runtime-kernel team (for kernel admission integration), runtime-observability (dashboards & alerts)
- Follow-up work: add cohort-impact simulation harness to benchgen; cross-validate reshaper decisions vs offline explainer scores.

Rollout checklist (preflight)

1) Unit tests green; integration tests pass locally
2) Canary dashboard created and shared with SRE and runtime product (links provided to stakeholders)
3) Set conservative defaults (step_size_percent=5, max_steps=2) for initial canary
4) Ensure audit logs visible in Splunk / Loki and retention confirmed
5) Coordinate release window with SRE (low-traffic period recommended)

Appendix: failure-mode examples

- Failure: reshaper reduces priority for cohort with 95% KV hit ratio -> causes cache miss storm -> increased p99 -> rollback. Action: add a KV-hit safeguard and raise coldstart/caching score weight.
- Failure: oscillation due to noisy signals -> add hysteresis: require two consecutive observation windows of improvement before commit.

If you have questions or want to run a localized experiment, ping Aisha on Slack (#runtime-scheduler) or open an RFC in the runtime-experiments board.

title: Kernel safety net and automated rollback playbook
content:
Summary:
This playbook defines the safety nets, observability gates, and automated/manual rollback procedures for kernel and runtime patch deployments to Redwood’s serving runtime. It combines release-stage benchmarking gates, profiling hooks, SLO monitoring, and a decision tree for automated rollback and staged remediation. Use this document when rolling out any change that affects GPU kernels, batching paths, KV cache interaction, or kernel scheduling policies.

Why this exists:
- Kernel-level changes can cause fast, system-wide regressions (tail latency, GPU hangs, memory corruption).
- Rolling backwards quickly and predictably limits customer impact and reduces incident scope.
- Provide consistent signals that integrate the benchmarking suite, continuous profiler, and runtime telemetry.

Scope and out-of-band exceptions:
- Applies to all kernel changes merged to the runtime branch and promoted to staging/production clusters.
- Hotfixes that only touch non-execution control-plane code may follow the lighter release checklist, but safety net monitors still apply.
- For air-gapped Private deployments, local operators must run the equivalent benchmarking and profiling steps listed below before approval.

Ownership and contacts:
- Release owner: engineering-release@redwood.com (primary: Priya Menon)
- Kernel SME: Ethan Caldwell
- Runtime SRE oncall: runtime-sre@redwood.com
- Observability/telemetry owner: Marina Lopez
- Escalation path: oncall -> kernel-sme -> eng-manager -> director-of-runtime

Preconditions (gates before canary):
1) Green unit and integration tests for scheduler and kernel modules.
2) Microbenchmarks: no regression > 1.5% in mean latency for core kernels, and no regression > 5% in p95/p99 token throughput on the synthetic-batcher (run locally).
3) Static safety checks: memory boundary sanitizers on in-tree test harness, kernel ABI compatibility checks.
4) CI-generated artifact tagged with build metadata and kernel-compat matrix.

Staging canary process (recommended matrix):
- Canary cohort sizes: 1% -> 5% -> 20% traffic buckets. Advance only after each gate passes for 30 minutes of steady-state and no alerting.
- Run the following in parallel at each step:
  - Canary synthetic smoke run: payloads from the mixed-workload-slo-simulation-suite for 15 minutes.
  - Profiling capture: 30s sampling of kernel traces and NVTX spans, uploaded to the profiling bucket.
  - Benchmark run: run "bench-runner --profile kernel --suite canary-gates" to generate per-kernel latency and occupancy csv.

Release gating thresholds (must be instrumented and evaluated automatically):
- Latency:
  - p50: regression <= 3% vs baseline
  - p95: regression <= 5% vs baseline
  - p99: regression <= 10% vs baseline
- Error budget signals:
  - GPU kernel failure rate (CUDA errors / kernel launches) must be < 0.02% absolute increase
  - RPC retransmits or GRPC error spikes > 3x baseline are blocking
- Resource metrics:
  - GPU memory high watermark increase <= 5% absolute
  - Scheduler pending queue growth: consistent > 10% sustained for > 2m is blocking
- Observability health:
  - Missing KV cache hits or sudden drop in prefix cache hit rate > 7% absolute is blocking

Automated detection rules (implemented in alerting/monitoring):
- alert: KernelLatencyRegression
  expression: increase(runtime_kernel_p99{job="serving",kernel=~".*"}[5m]) > scalar(0.10 * baseline_p99)
  runbook: follow this playbook (section: Automated rollback decision).
- alert: KernelCrashSpike
  expression: increase(runtime_kernel_crash_total[1m]) > 5
- alert: GpuMemoryPressureHigh
  expression: runtime_gpu_memory_utilization > 0.95 for 60s

Automated rollback decision (CI -> staging -> prod CI process integration):
1) If any blocking alert fires during a canary window, the deployment controller will automatically mark the canary as FAILED and initiate a rollback to the previous kernel artifact.
2) The controller will attempt a graceful revert: notify SRE channel, pause further promotions, and schedule a revert job with a 5-minute cooldown.
3) If revert job fails or the cluster is unhealthy, the oncall must escalate to kernel SME for a manual rollback plan (see manual rollback below).

Manual rollback and mitigation steps (ordered):
1) Quarantine the offending cohort: redirect new routing for the canary cohort to fallback model variant and mark cohort draining (API: "redwood-router --drain-cohort <cohort-id>").
2) Execute cluster revert job: "deployctl promote-artifact --to=prod --artifact=<previous-artifact> --reason=kernel-rollback".
3) Run immediate smoke tests:
   - toolchain: "smoke-check --gateway <prod-gateway> --mini-scenarios"
   - confirm p95/p99 latency falls back to baseline within 10 minutes.
4) If smoke tests fail, cut traffic to Dedicated fallback tier and enable read-only mode for high-risk endpoints until further mitigation.

Profiling playbook integration (what to capture and how to interpret):
- Capture points: kernel entry/exit spans, NVTX annotated sections for batch assembly, KV cache stats, GPU utilization counter snapshots.
- Recording commands (example):
  - docker run --rm --privileged profiling-tool --target http://canary-host:8080 --trace 30s --out s3://profiling/canary/<build-id>.tgz
  - nvprof/nvtrace capture for suspect kernel: "nvidia-trace --pid <pid> --duration 20s --output /tmp/trace.nvt"
- Short interpretation checklist:
  1) Is there a measurable shift in kernel occupancy or warp divergence? If yes, suspect kernel code path change.
  2) Are there repeated GPU stalls (SM stalls) co-incident with tail-latency spikes? If yes, verify memory barriers and atomic usage.
  3) Compare sample heatmaps vs baseline using the profiling diff tool: "prof-diff baseline.nvt canary.nvt".

Benchmarking-suite gate (how to run before promotion):
- Command (CI): "bench-suite run --suite=promote-gates --artifact=<build> --compare-to=baseline --report /tmp/report.json"
- Required outputs (CI verifies):
  - per-kernel CSV including mean/p50/p95/p99 and sample count
  - occupancy and concurrency heatmap images
  - end-to-end token throughput measurement with identical synthetic trace input
- Gate pass criteria:
  - No blocking regressions per Release gating thresholds section.
  - Bench variance: coefficient of variation for p95 across 5 runs < 6%

Known failure modes and mitigations (quick reference):
- Symptom: sudden p99 jumps with no increase in qps.
  - Likely causes: kernel codepath regression, memory bank conflicts, or scheduler mis-prioritization.
  - Mitigation: scale canary to 0, capture profiles, and revert.
- Symptom: intermittent GPU watchdog timeouts on certain nodes.
  - Likely causes: driver mismatch or concurrent host process contention.
  - Mitigation: cordon node, repro on a clean node, check driver and CUDA versions.
- Symptom: KV cache miss storms after kernel change.
  - Likely causes: cache invalidation behavior changed or shard affinity drift.
  - Mitigation: temporarily force rewarm on stable kernel or revert; run kv-warmup utility.

Post-incident actions and required artifacts (if rollback happened):
1) Create an incident page in the incident tracker with timeline, build id, and cohort IDs.
2) Attach profiling bundles, bench-suite reports, and alert graphs.
3) Owner (release owner) must schedule a deep dive within 72 hours and assign remediation owners.
4) Update the kernel test harness with a targeted regression test before the next attempt.

Operational runbook snippets (copy/paste safe):
- Promote previous artifact: "deployctl promote-artifact --to=prod --artifact=redwood-runtime-kernel:v1234 --reason=rollback"
- Drain cohort: "redwood-router --drain-cohort canary-2027-02 --timeout 300s"
- Collect profile bundle: "collect-profile --target http://<pod-ip>:9100 --duration 30s --out /tmp/bundle.tgz && aws s3 cp /tmp/bundle.tgz s3://profiling/incident/<incident-id>/bundle.tgz"

Telemetry & dashboards to monitor during rollout (must be on the canary dashboard):
- Kernel p50/p95/p99 by kernel_name and node (timeseries and heatmap)
- GPU error counters (illegal-instruction, illegal-memory-access, oob)
- Scheduler queue length and average wait time
- KV cache hit rate by prefix length and class
- Deploy controller state and promote/rollback events stream

Checklist before reattempting rollout:
- Root cause identified and a test added reproducing regression (unit or benchmark)
- Patch is submitted and reviewed with kernel-SME approval
- Bench-suite baseline updated if change is expected (documented in release notes)
- Canary cohort will be limited in size and have a longer observation window (recommended: 2x)

Release notes guidance (what to record for kernel change):
- Build id, git sha, target kernel modules and API changes
- Bench-suite summary and explicit pass/fail lines for gate metrics
- Profiling bundle id and link to S3
- Known risks and mitigation knobs (e.g., toggle to force old kernel, scheduler flags)

Appendix: quick decision tree (text form)
1) Alert fires during canary -> automated controller attempts revert (wait 5m)
2) Revert succeeded -> run smoke tests, close incident, schedule RCA
3) Revert failed or cluster unhealthy -> escalate to kernel SME, gather profiles, cordon nodes as needed
4) If failure reproducible on single node type -> stop rollout globally and open P0 incident

Related documentation and runbooks:
- See /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/for detailed trace collection and profiler tooling
- See /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/runtime-scaling-experiment-protocol-and-benchmark-checklist-2026 for bench-suite details
- See /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-upgrade-validation-and-canary-matrix-2026 for promotion mechanics

Contact and feedback:
If you find gaps in this playbook or observe a new failure mode, please file an RFC in the runtime team board and tag the owner (Priya Menon).

title: Execution contracts and stable fallbacks — runtime handbook
content:
Summary
-------
This document defines the execution contracts between serving runtime components and the recommended, tested fallback/degradation modes to preserve customer-facing SLOs during resource contention or partial failure. It is intended for runtime engineers, SREs, and product owners who need clear invariants when changing the scheduler, kernel selection logic, or deployment topology.

Scope
-----
- Applies to: runtime-proxy, gpu-dispatcher, kernel-mapper, kvcache-svc, execution-allocator, and canary routing.
- Environments: hosted API, dedicated capacity, and private deployments.
- Goals: maintain 99th percentile latency SLOs for interactive endpoints while maximizing throughput and minimizing silent correctness regressions.

Key execution contracts (high level)
----------------------------------
1) Latency envelope contract
   - "Interactive" requests (priority band P0) must target p99 <= 250 ms for generation-only requests up to 512 tokens when in steady state.
   - "Background" requests (P2) may be queued or batched; expected p95 <= 3s; no hard p99 requirement.

2) Preemption and kernel semantics
   - Kernels must expose a preemption token: preemptible=true/false. The kernel-mapper will not assign non-preemptible kernels to capacity that services P0 unless explicit reservation exists.
   - Preemption must preserve partial KV cache state on eviction and provide a best-effort resume hook.

3) KV cache consistency
   - KV entries are considered ephemeral per session. Strong consistency is not required across model swaps, but the runtime will attempt in-place migration of compatible KV formats.
   - If model swap occurs and KV migration fails, the contract requires the session be downgraded to a new cold-start path with a documented telemetry event (kvcache.migration_failed).

4) Model swap contract
   - Model swaps triggered by routing or autoscaler must be atomic per request: either the request completes on the original model or is routed and restarted on a compatible variant (not partially executed).

5) Observable control plane signals
   - The allocator exposes: free_slots, reserved_slots, preemptions_pending, eviction_pressure. These MUST be present in the allocator/metrics endpoint.

Degradation modes (ordered by preference)
----------------------------------------
- Transparent fallback to compatible model variant (same tokenizer / comparable LM family).
- Partial output with structured disclaimer: return earliest stable token and a field: "partial=true" and a reason code. Use only for low-safety internal endpoints.
- Throttling with HTTP 429 and Retry-After header; prefer this for non-critical background tasks.
- Canary redirect to Dedicated or Alternate region when capacity or NVLink issues detected.
- Soft-failure to an n-best cached response if prefix match > 95% and data residency/compliance permits.

Kernel scheduling interactions (detailed)
----------------------------------------
- Priority bands: P0 (interactive), P1 (nearline), P2 (batch). Each band's scheduler policy includes concurrency cap, slot weight, and eviction tolerance.
- Kernel hints provided by model onboarding: {preferred_kernel:list, min_batch_size:int, max_latency_ms:int, memory_safety_margin_percent:int}. The kernel-mapper uses these hints to select kernel and decide whether to co-locate competing kernels.
- Cooperative preemption handshake:
  1) Allocator sets preempt_request=true for target slot.
  2) Kernel runtime receives SIG_PREEMPT and replies with remaining_work_estimate.
  3) If remaining_work_estimate <= preemption_cutoff_ms, kernel completes; otherwise kernel checkpoints and releases slot.

Example scheduler policy (YAML)
------------------------------
# declarative policy snippet consumed by allocator and verifier
policy_version: v1
priority_bands:
  - name: interactive
    id: P0
    concurrency_cap: 8
    slot_weight: 100
    eviction_tolerance_ms: 50
  - name: nearline
    id: P1
    concurrency_cap: 16
    slot_weight: 50
    eviction_tolerance_ms: 300
  - name: batch
    id: P2
    concurrency_cap: 64
    slot_weight: 10
    eviction_tolerance_ms: 5000

Operational observability and telemetry (must-haves)
---------------------------------------------------
- Core metrics (per deployment and per model variant):
  - runtime.request_latency_p50/p95/p99
  - runtime.request_error_rate
  - allocator.free_slots, allocator.reserved_slots
  - kernel.preemptions_total, kernel.preemption_success_rate
  - kvcache.hits, kvcache.misses, kvcache.migration_failed
  - slot.eviction_pressure
- Tracing: span names should follow: runtime:[proxy|allocator|kernel|dispatcher].<operation>. Include tags: request_id, session_id, model_variant, priority_band, kernel_hint.
- Logs: structured JSON with level, component, event_code, human_message, and stable fields: request_id and shard_id. Example event_code: KERNEL_CHECKPOINT_FAILED.

Incident triage playbook (step-by-step)
--------------------------------------
1) Detect: alert on p99 latency breach for interactive endpoints for >5 minutes or error_rate > 0.1% over 10 minutes.
2) Correlate: check allocator.free_slots, preemptions_pending, nvlink.error_rate, and recent kernel.rollouts.
3) Quick containment (first 10 minutes):
   - If allocator.free_slots < 10% and eviction_pressure high: enable conservative-mode via feature-flag (allocator.conservative_mode=true) which reduces concurrency caps per band by 40%.
   - If preemption failures are the cause: temporarily disable non-preemptible kernels on P0 and drain affected nodes.
4) Stabilize (10–60 minutes):
   - Shift traffic to canary region or Dedicated pool if policy allows. Use the routing API: curl -X POST https://controlplane/api/v1/routing/shift -d '{"from":"us-west-2","to":"us-east-1","percent":30}'.
   - Roll back recent kernel or kernel mapper changes using the kernel-deploy rollback CLI: ./kernel-deploy rollback --release <tag> --confirm
5) Post-incident: create incident summary, attach timeline with span-level traces and allocation snapshots. Run the regression test matrix (see Benchmark checklist).

Runbook commands and useful CLIs
-------------------------------
- Inspect allocator state:
  curl -s http://allocator.internal/metrics | jq '.free_slots, .reserved_slots, .preemptions_pending'
- Force-safe-mode on allocator:
  kubectl exec -n runtime deploy/allocator -- /bin/allocatorctl set-safe-mode true
- Trigger model-variant fallback for a session (debug-only):
  curl -X POST http://runtime-proxy/internal/debug/fallback -d '{"session_id":"<sid>","variant":"gptx-1-quant"}'

Benchmark checklist (for change validation)
-----------------------------------------
- Baseline capture: record p50/p95/p99 for 5k live-sampled requests and a synthetic mix: 40% short (<=64 tokens), 50% medium (65–512), 10% long (>512).
- Kernel upgrade: run synthetic microbenchmarks for each kernel hint permutation (min_batch_size x sequence_length x concurrency).
- Eviction and preemption test: emulate heavy P2 batch contamination and assert P0 p99 remains <=250ms under 95% of runs.
- KV migration test: trigger model swap and assert kvcache.migration_failed rate < 0.1%.
- Chaos profile: NVLink degradation (packet loss emulation) for 3 minutes and assert routing fallback succeeds without request duplication over 99.9% of requests.

Rollout and canary guidance
---------------------------
- Any scheduler or kernel-mapper change must follow the four-step rollout: dev -> staging -> canary(1%) -> canary(10%) -> gradual (50%) -> full.
- Canary health gates: runtime.request_error_rate delta < 0.02% and p99 delta < +20ms relative to baseline.
- If kvcache.migration_failed events appear >0.5% in canary, abort and rollback.

Ownership and escalation
------------------------
- Primary owner: runtime-platform team (oncall: runtime-platform-primary).
- Kernel-mapper owner: serving-runtime-kernels team.
- SRE escalation: use PagerDuty escalation path "runtime-slo-pager" for P0 SLO breaches.

Appendix A: sample trace annotation schema
-----------------------------------------
All traces must include these attributes as tags: request_id, session_id, start_token_count, end_token_count, model_variant, kernel_name, priority_band, allocator_slot_id, kvcache_hit_ratio. Example (textual):
Span: runtime:kernel.execute
Tags: {"request_id":"r-123", "model_variant":"gptx-1-quant", "kernel_name":"attn_fused_v3", "priority_band":"P0"}

Appendix B: compatibility table for fallback decisions
----------------------------------------------------
- Fallback allowed if: tokenizer_compat=true AND (model_family == model_family OR embedding_compat=true).
- Disallowed fallback if preserves privacy/residency restrictions or if model variant differs by >2B parameters and no regression test exists.

Change log
----------
- 2025-07-15: Initial draft by Priya Nandakumar.
- 2025-11-02: Added cooperative preemption handshake (Jin Park).
- 2026-01-30: Clarified telemetry keys and added canary health gates (Ethan Morales).

Related documents
-----------------
- Runtime upgrade validation and canary matrix (internal).
- Scheduler policy language (declarative profiles).
- Runtime observability data model and tracebook.

Contact
-------
For questions or proposed changes, open a PR against confluence source and tag @runtime-platform or email runtime-platform@redwood.ai.

title: GPU job failure-injector and scheduler robustness manual
content:
Summary:

This document describes the GPU Job Failure-Injector (GJFI) and an operational playbook for validating scheduler robustness. It covers design, safe execution procedures, configuration templates, observable signals, typical experiment matrices, and rollback controls. The intended audience is runtime engineers, SREs, and test owners who run scheduled or ad-hoc resilience validation on the serving runtime.

Objectives:
- Validate scheduler decisions under realistic failure modes (GPU device errors, NVLink degradation, driver stalls, container OOM, kernel timeouts).
- Measure SLA impact (tail latency, error rate, throughput) for degradation scenarios.
- Confirm graceful degradation and fallback routing behavior across model variants and capacity tiers.
- Provide reproducible experiment artifacts and safety gates for production-adjacent testing.

Scope and guarantees:
- Scope: production-like staging fleets, can be used in controlled production with approval.
- Guarantees: all injections are reversible; the injector uses non-destructive signals (cgroup throttles, simulated driver fault via kernel module toggle, network packet blackhole) where possible. Permanent hardware damage is out-of-scope and explicitly avoided.

Ownership and contacts:
- Owner: Runtime Resilience Team (runtime-resilience@redwood.ai)
- Primary on-call: Marcus Nguyen (runtime-sre)
- Safety reviewer: Lin Zhao

High-level architecture of the GJFI tool:
- Controller (gjfictl): orchestrates experiments and applies injection recipes to target nodes/groups.
- Injector agent (gjfi-agent): lightweight daemon that executes local manipulations (cgroup memory/CPU caps, kill/pause tasks, iptables rules, soft-unbind NVLink path).
- Measurement harness: integrates with our benchmarking suite to replay request traces and collect metrics (latency distributions, kernel queue lengths, KV cache miss rate).
- Audit & rollback: every action is recorded in Experiment Log (JSON), and rollback is an atomic two-step: stop injection and rewarm caches.

Key failure modes covered (short descriptions):
1) Synthetic GPU stall: pause CUDA kernels for X ms using driver shim to simulate transient stall.
2) NVLink packet loss: drop a percentage of packets on nvlink path to simulate inter-GPU slowdown.
3) Device OOM simulation: throttle cgroup memory to provoke eviction and GPU memory pressure.
4) Driver watchdog wake: toggle GPU watchdog controls to force a soft-reset path.
5) Host-level IO saturation: stress block device and observe scheduling queuing side-effects.
6) Network ingress blackhole: drop or delay incoming RPCs to scheduler node to simulate partial control-plane partition.

Safety controls and preconditions (must be satisfied before any experiment):
1) Approval: Test plan must be approved in RFC linked in Experiment Log and signed off by on-call owner.
2) Canary target: Run on dedicated canary pool (label: canary-fidelity) unless explicit prod approval.
3) Capacity headroom: Ensure >20% spare capacity in the region; otherwise abort.
4) Alerting: Temporary SLO overrides are set and a high-priority alert channel (pager) is configured.
5) Time window: Run during a low-traffic window unless testing production failover behavior.
6) Automated kill-switch: experiment controller must be reachable and can stop injection within 10s.

Experiment catalog and matrix (example):
- Variables: injection_type, intensity (low/medium/high), duration, target_pool, traffic_profile (spiky/steady/chatty).

Sample experiment table (CSV-style):
| id | injection_type | intensity | duration | target_pool | expected_primary_metric |
| E100 | synthetic_gpu_stall | low | 120s | canary-fidelity | p99_latency +10% |
| E101 | nvlink_loss | medium | 5m | multi-gpu-inference | throughput -15% |
| E102 | device_oom | high | 2m | memory-tight-pool | error_rate +5% |
| E103 | network_blackhole | medium | 3m | control-plane-nodes | fallback_routing_occurs |

Observability checklist (metrics & traces to collect):
- Application: p50/p90/p99 latency, success_rate, tokens_per_sec (per model variant)
- Runtime internals: kernel_queue_depth, GPU_busy_fraction, kvcache_miss_rate, batch_size_distribution
- Network: rpc_latency, retransmit_rate, connection_errors
- Host: OOM_kills, dmesg watchdog entries, GPU_reset_count
- Logs: experiment_id tag attached to all emitted traces and logs.

CLI quick-start examples:
- Dry-run: gjfictl plan --recipe nvlink_loss --intensity medium --targets label:canary-fidelity --trace replay:latest --dry-run
- Execute: gjfictl run --recipe synthetic_gpu_stall --intensity low --duration 120s --targets nodepool:canary-fidelity --notify oncall@redwood.ai
- Abort: gjfictl abort --experiment E101 --reason "observed p99 > 3x baseline"

Recipe YAML example (safe default):
---
experiment_id: E200-safe-nvlink
recipe: nvlink_loss
intensity: low
duration_seconds: 180
target_selector: label==canary-fidelity
metrics_to_sample: [p99_latency, throughput, kernel_queue_depth]
safety_controls:
  max_error_rate: 0.02
  max_p99_increase_pct: 25
  abort_on: [node_oom, gpu_reset]
---

Run procedure (step-by-step):
1) Prepare: create RFC summarizing goal, acceptance criteria, and rollback steps. Add reviewers and obtain approval.
2) Baseline: capture a 15-minute baseline run with traffic replay and collect metric snapshots.
3) Dry-run: execute plan in dry-run mode (controller validates targets and resources).
4) Execute: run experiments at low intensity for short durations with active monitoring.
5) Observe & record: collect trace bundles and update Experiment Log immediately.
6) Scale intensity: if results are stable and within acceptance, step intensity to medium/high per matrix.
7) Post-check: run a 10m warmup phase to rehydrate kvcache, and check for lingering resource pressure.
8) Report: publish findings to the RFC thread and mark experiment closed with tags.

Rollback and remediation playbook:
- Immediate abort: gjfictl abort --all --reason "safety threshold exceeded". The controller runs rollback hooks in parallel: remove iptables, restore cgroup limits, re-enable driver paths.
- Cache warmup: run a short warm replay of representative traffic with reduced concurrency to re-populate KV cache and warm CUDA kernels.
- Diagnostic capture: collect kernel logs, /var/log/nv-hostmanager, and a focused sample of traces for causal attribution.

Acceptance criteria examples (example for E100):
- p99 latency increase <= 10% for 5 consecutive minutes during the injection window.
- No increase in client-visible 5xx rate above 0.5%.
- Kernel queue depth transient spike < 2x baseline and recovers within 120s of rollback.

Common failure signatures and suggested remediation:
- Symptom: persistent p99 elevation after rollback.
  - Likely cause: cache eviction or kernel memory leak.
  - Remediation: run targeted rewarm with small batch sampling, escalate to runtime-dev if no recovery in 15m.
- Symptom: increase in GPU_reset_count.
  - Likely cause: driver instability at this firmware level.
  - Remediation: mark node as quarantined and schedule firmware rollback; inform hardware team.
- Symptom: controller cannot reach gjfi-agent on multiple targets.
  - Likely cause: control-plane partition or agent crash.
  - Remediation: use host-level ssh multiplex to run rollback script and redeploy agent.

Test artifacts and reproducibility:
- Every experiment must include: experiment_id, recipe YAML, baseline metrics snapshot, trace bundle (min 10k requests or 15 minutes), and a roll-forward/rollback transcript.
- Store artifacts under: s3://redwood-experiments/{experiment_id}/

Integration with benchmarking and perf-suite:
- The measurement harness plugs into the replay engine used by the benchmarking suite. Use replay labels like replay:prod-sample-2027 to run realistic traces.
- Post-experiment analysis uses the perf-suite notebook templates in /notebooks/resilience-analysis to produce p99 deltas and heatmaps.

Release notes and versioning for GJFI:
- v1.0 (2026-06-10): initial rollout, supports cgroup throttles, iptables blackholes, and synthetic kernel stalls.
- v1.1 (2026-11-12): NVLink loss simulation via shim, audit log schema v2, automated kill-switch.
- v2.0 (2027-01-12): safe production mode, scheduler API hooks for non-invasive metadata tagging, improved rollback performance.

Appendix A: Example experiment output (trimmed):
{
  "experiment_id": "E101",
  "status": "aborted",
  "reason": "p99 exceeded threshold",
  "metrics": {"p99_latency": "480ms (baseline 140ms)", "throughput": "85% of baseline"}
}

Appendix B: Quick checklist before running in production-adjacent fleets:
- RFC with reviewers: yes
- Canary pool allocated: yes
- Pager configured: yes
- Automated rollback tested: yes
- Experiment id reserved: yes

Related pages and references:
- Kernel scheduler policy language (link internal)
- Runtime fallback and degradation playbook (see runbooks directory)

Document history:
- 2026-06-10: created by Asha Patel (v1.0)
- 2026-11-12: NVLink support added (v1.1)
- 2027-01-18: production-safe mode & scheduler hooks documented (v2.0)

End of document.

title: Hybrid accelerator integration and fidelity guidelines
content:
Summary
This document defines the integration contract, quality/fidelity guidelines, and operational runbook for bringing hybrid accelerator resources (on-host GPUs + third‑party accelerators such as NPUs/DPUs/TPUs via remote attach) into Redwood’s serving runtime. It covers compatibility decisions, kernel-scheduling boundaries, profiling and benchmark requirements, preflight checks, rollout criteria, and rollback gates. The goal is to enable safe, measurable performance improvements while preserving inference fidelity and SLOs.

Scope and audience
- Scope: hybrid accelerator attachments that extend the runtime’s kernel execution layer (e.g., hardware with different numeric formats or reduced FP precision, remote-attached inference ASICs).
- Audience: runtime engineers, kernel scheduling owners, platform SREs, profiling engineers, and release engineers who validate new accelerator integrations.

Goals and design principles
1) Safety-first: no automatic traffic routing to a new accelerator variant without passing fidelity & stability gates.
2) Observable fidelity: every accelerator variant must emit a fidelity profile and regression signals tied to canonical prompt sets.
3) Isolated scheduling: scheduler must treat hybrid accelerator pools as distinct resource classes with explicit mapping rules.
4) Deterministic fallbacks: runtime must be able to fall back to a verified CPU/GPU kernel variant with bounded latency and output drift.

Definitions
- Accelerator variant: a compiled kernel implementation or model quantization that executes on a particular accelerator type/version.
- Fidelity profile: per-model/per-prompt metrics comparing outputs vs a golden baseline (semantic similarity, token-level divergence, hallucination indicators).
- Degradation event: fidelity drop or p95 latency breach after activation.

Compatibility matrix (example)
| Accelerator class | Min firmware | Supported quant formats | Expected max seq_len | Verified models (examples) | Notes |
|-------------------|--------------:|------------------------|----------------------:|---------------------------|-------|
| Remote NPU v1     | 2025-04-12    | int8, int8-with-scale   | 2048                 | Llama-2-13B, MPT-7B      | supports KV cache via proxy, 1.8x throughput gain |
| On-host A100-48GB | n/a           | fp16, bf16, int8        | 4096                 | Llama-2-70B              | native CUDA kernels, priority pinning required |
| ThirdParty-TPU    | 2024-12-01    | bfloat16                | 4096                 | Flan-T5-large            | network-attached, higher cold-start penalty |

Pre-integration checklist (must be completed before any staged traffic)
- [ ] Hardware and firmware versions recorded in the accelerator registry.
- [ ] Provider compatibility tested with the kernel mapper test harness.
- [ ] Baseline golden outputs produced using the canonical baseline environment (host-GPU fp16) for each target model and prompt set.
- [ ] Fidelity profile generation job configured and passing (see ‘Profiling and fidelity tests’).
- [ ] Scheduler policy authored: pool label, admission control thresholds, priority groups.
- [ ] Monitoring & alerting configured: fidelity-alert (>=3% semantic drop), latency-alert (p95 breach > configured SLOs).
- [ ] Rollout and rollback playbook drafted with owners identified.

Scheduler integration guidelines
- Resource classification: hybrid accelerators must be mapped to one of three scheduler resource classes: dedicated-accel, shared-accel, network-accel. Code-level tags: accel.class = {dedicated,shared,network}.
- Admission control signals: each pool exposes available_credits, max_concurrency, and warm_ratio (fraction of warmed KV sessions). Inject these into the request admission flow.
- Kernel hints: kernels must advertise fallback_compat set (list of compatible kernel variants) and deterministic_fallback_cost (approx ms). The scheduler consults fallback_compat before routing.
- Priority synthesis: combine request priority, SLO sensitivity, and customer tier to produce a scheduling key. For hybrid pool admission require: request_priority >= pool_min_priority and warm_ratio >= pool_min_warm.

Profiling and fidelity tests (playbook)
1) Canonical prompt set generation
   - Use the internal prompt-set-builder to produce 3 prompt cohorts: short-chat (<=128 tokens), multi-turn (3 turns, average 400 tokens), long-context (>=2048 tokens).
   - Save the seed corpus and store the job ID in the release ticket.

2) Golden baseline collection
   - Command (example):
     run-benchmark --model Llama-2-13B --backend host-gpu-fp16 --prompts prompts/llama13b-canonical.json --out baseline/llama13b-host-fp16.json

3) Accelerator run and raw trace capture
   - Command (example):
     run-benchmark --model Llama-2-13B --backend remote-npu-v1 --prompts prompts/llama13b-canonical.json --trace raw-traces/npu-v1/

4) Automated fidelity metrics job
   - Compare outputs with baseline and compute: ROUGE-L, BLEURT, token-level KL, and a semantic-similarity embedding score (cosine).
   - Thresholds (example):
     - Embedding cosine >= 0.92 vs baseline for short-chat cohort
     - BLEURT delta <= -0.03 for multi-turn cohort
     - No hallucination rate increase > 0.5% (see hallucination-detector v2)

5) Statistical significance and A/B harness
   - Run paired A/B for n >= 500 samples per cohort. If metrics are borderline, collect n >= 2000.

Benchmarking suite requirements
- Microbenchmarks: per-kernel latency histogram for 1..4096 sequence lengths, token throughput (tokens/s) under 1, 4, 16 concurrent sessions.
- End-to-end benchmarks: p50/p95/p99 for representative routes (completion, chat, embeddings).
- Cost model: estimate cost-per-token based on observed util and amortized kernel credits. Provide delta vs baseline.
- Energy estimate: if hardware monitoring available, include watt-seconds/token.

Release validation matrix
| Check | Pass criteria | Owner |
|-------|---------------|-------|
| Functional smoke | No errors on 100 sample requests | Release engineer |
| Fidelity | Embedding cosine >= 0.92 AND BLEURT delta within threshold | Profiling owner |
| Latency SLO | p95 <= configured SLO (route specific) | SRE |
| Stability | No OOMs, no kernel crashes for 24h soak | Kernel owner |
| Observability | Traces, metrics, and traces contain accel tags | Observability team |

Runbook: activate new accelerator pool (staged rollout)
1) Canary: enable pool for internal/beta customers only (5% of traffic). Monitor fidelity and latency in 1m buckets for 2 hours.
2) Expand: move to 20% if no alerts. Validate via A/B test comparing golden baseline metrics.
3) Ramp: move to 50% over 6-12 hours if rolling windows show steady state.
4) Full switch: 100% only after 48h of production stability and business sign-off.

Rollback gates and automated safety breakers
- Fidelity-alert: configured to trigger if embedding cosine drops by >= 0.03 on rolling 30-minute window across the canonical prompt set. Immediate automated action: pause routing to the accelerator pool and shift to fallback kernel for affected models.
- Latency SLO breach: if p95 breaches SLO for 3 consecutive 5-minute windows, reduce accelerator pool traffic by 50% automatically and notify SRE on-call.
- Crash circuit: 3 kernel crashes within 10 minutes triggers full evacuation and disables pool.

Investigation playbook (if degradation observed)
1) Capture failing requests using trace IDs from the fidelity job and store full KV state.
2) Re-run failing inputs locally against: baseline, accelerator variant, and deterministic fallback to compare token-by-token diffs. Use internal tool: fidelity-inspect --baseline baseline.json --variant variant.json --output diffs/
3) Check kernel telemetry: kernel-latency-distribution, kernel-mem-residency, and hardware-err logs.
4) If hardware fault suspected, quarantine node and escalate to hardware vendor with collected traces and firmware versions.

Kernel developer checklist for accelerator-targeted kernels
- Export deterministic_fallback_cost and fallback_compat metadata.
- Provide a regression harness (Docker image) that reproduces microbenchmark and includes a mock KV cache.
- Ensure deterministic seeding for ops that rely on RNG or beam search.
- Provide a smoke vector of at least 200 canonical prompts with expected output hashes.

Telemetry and dashboards (minimum required panels)
- Accelerator pool health: uptime, crash_count, avg_warm_ratio
- Fidelity rollup: embedding_cosine_rolling_30m, BLEURT_delta_30m, hallucination_rate_24h
- Cost & throughput: tokens/s, util_percent, estimated_cost_per_1M_tokens
- Observability traces: sample request traces with accel.* tags and kernel version metadata

Contacts and ownership
- Kernel integration owner: Priya Nambiar (pri@redwood.example.com)
- Scheduler policy owner: Ethan Morales (ethan@redwood.example.com)
- Profiling and fidelity owner: Sofia Chen (sofia@redwood.example.com)
- On-call SRE escalation channel: #sre-accelerator (pager: SRE on-call rotation)

Appendix A — Example scheduler policy snippet (YAML)
policy_name: \"npu-v1-weighted-pool\"
pool_label: \"remote-npu-v1\"
accel:
  class: network-accel
  max_concurrency: 64
  warm_ratio_threshold: 0.6
admission:
  min_priority: 20
  fallback_compat: [\"host-gpu-fp16\",\"on-host-a100-int8\"]

Appendix B — Common failure signatures and first actions
- High token-drop: look for quantization saturation (check kernel counter: q_saturation_rate). Action: reduce batch size and fall back.
- KV mismatch after warmstart: indicates proxy state desync. Action: flush session and force cold restart with warm hint disabled.
- Increased hallucination: compare hallucination_anchors and run hallucination-detector; run A/B with baseline.

Document maintenance and cadence
- This page is reviewed quarterly by the kernel integration guild.
- Any production incident that involves a hybrid accelerator must attach an incident note and suggested updates to this doc.

Related resources
- Kernel mapper test harness (internal repo)
- Fidelity evaluator job spec (link in related_pages)
- Scheduler policy language reference

Revision history
- 2025-11-12: Created (Priya Nambiar)
- 2026-02-18: Added automated safety breaker thresholds and YAML policy example (Priya Nambiar)

title: Priority Decoupling and Preemptive Shepherding for Kernel Scheduling
content:
Summary:
This document describes the design, configuration, and operational runbook for Priority Decoupling and Preemptive Shepherding — a scheduling pattern used by Redwood's serving runtime to meet tight p95/p99 latency SLOs while maximizing throughput. The pattern separates how priorities are assigned from how GPU kernels are chosen, and introduces a lightweight preemption shepherd that migrates or degrades low-priority work to background execution paths when kernel pressure threatens SLOs.

Audience:
- Runtime engineers (kernel & scheduler teams)
- SREs oncall for inferencing clusters
- Performance researchers tuning SLOs

Goals and motivation:
- Keep high-priority, interactive requests within configured latency SLOs (p95 <= 150ms for short-chat flows; p99 <= 400ms across mixed workloads).
- Avoid priority inversion where low-priority batching choices delay high-priority requests.
- Allow non-critical work (bulk embeddings, long-batched offline jobs) to consume spare capacity without impacting interactive tails.
- Enable graceful degradation (quantized fallback kernels, truncated generation) rather than outright request drops.

Key concepts:
1) Priority decoupling:
- Priority is an attribute on the request (e.g., priority=interactive, priority=batch, priority=background).
- Kernel selection is done by the Kernel Mapper service (kernel-mapper), which considers model variant, sequence length, and GPU topology.
- Decoupling means kernel-mapper ignores priority when computing feasible kernel candidates but exposes metadata about kernel latency and preemption cost to the Preemptive Shepherd.

2) Preemptive Shepherd:
- A lightweight controller running colocated with the scheduler (preempt-shepherd) that monitors kernel queue depth, tail-latency estimates, cache warmness, and current SLO burn-down.
- When p95/p99 projections exceed thresholds, the shepherd triggers targeted actions: migrate in-flight low-priority requests to background kernels, reduce batch sizes for candidate kernels, enable quantized variants, or route affected requests to fallback model variants.

Architecture overview (text diagram):
- API Gateway -> router -> request-priority-evaluator -> scheduling-queue -> kernel-mapper -> preempt-shepherd -> runtime-worker (GPU)
- Telemetry: metrics flow to metrics-backend; traces flow to jaeger; kernel telemetry to timeline-db.

Operational details and metrics:
- SLOs:
  - interactive_short (<=128 tokens): p95 <= 150ms, p99 <= 350ms, error_rate <= 0.5%
  - interactive_long (<=1024 tokens): p95 <= 450ms, p99 <= 900ms
  - embeddings (batchable): throughput target 30k emb/s per A100x8 node (baseline)

- Key metrics exposed by preempt-shepherd:
  - shepherd.p95_projection (ms)
  - shepherd.p99_projection (ms)
  - shepherd.kernel_queue_depth (count)
  - shepherd.low_priority_evictions (count/min)
  - kernel-mapper.candidate_latency_estimates (ms, histogram)
  - kvcache.hit_ratio_by_priority (0..1)

Configuration table (knobs and defaults):
| knob_name | description | default | safe-range | owner |
|-----------|-------------|---------|------------|-------|
| shepherd.enabled | enable the preemptive shepherd control loop | true | true/false | runtime-scheduling |
| shepherd.p95_target_margin | trigger margin over p95 SLO (ms) | 30 | 10-100 | runtime-scheduling |
| shepherd.max_evictions_per_min | max low-priority migrations per minute per node | 20 | 0-200 | runtime-scheduling |
| kernel-mapper.quantized_threshold | if kernel latency > threshold -> allow quantized variant | 400 | 200-1200 | kernel-team |
| scheduler.priority_age_limit_ms | promote aged low-priority tasks after this time | 1500 | 500-5000 | scheduler-team |

Example YAML runtime config (used by scheduler agent):

shepherd:
  enabled: true
  p95_target_margin_ms: 30
  max_evictions_per_min: 20
kernel_mapper:
  quantized_threshold_ms: 400
  prefer_shallow_batches_for: [interactive]

Notes on quantization and fallbacks:
- The shepherd prefers applying model quantized variants (int8 or q4_0) for low-priority request migration if the quality budget allows it. Quality checks are gated by the Optimize team’s per-model regression flags (optimize.quality_blocklist).
- If KV cache warmness < 0.25 for a request (i.e., cold start), shepherd favors warmstart prioritization instead of eviction to avoid extra compute.

Preemptive actions (ordered by preference):
1) Slow-path migration: move request to a background kernel variant that runs with lower kernel priority (non-preemptible OS niceness + lower kernel scheduler credits).
2) Batch-size reduction: reduce batch aggregator window for affected kernels to reduce latency at the expense of throughput.
3) Quantized fallback: switch to quantized model variant for the request.
4) Truncated generation / partial response: cap output tokens (operator-configurable) and queue continuation as background job.
5) Reject with graceful HTTP 202 + background job token (last resort for overloaded systems).

Behavioral examples:
- Scenario A: Spike of interactive requests plus concurrent large embedding job.
  - Shepherd sees kernel_queue_depth rising and p95_projection > SLO + margin.
  - It migrates queued embedding batches to background kernels and reduces their batch sizes, freeing slots for interactive flows.

- Scenario B: A cache-cold large interactive conversation triggers long latency estimates.
  - If kvcache.hit_ratio_by_priority for interactive < 0.25, shepherd prioritizes warmstarts by assigning dedicated prewarmed slot for the conversation's worker shard (if prewarm budget available).

Runbook: Investigating an SLO burn (oncall steps)
1) Alert: shepherd.p95_projection > SLO_threshold for > 1 minute.
2) Triage: query timeline-db for kernel-level latencies:
   $ curl -s "https://metrics.internal/api/query?metric=kernel_latency&node_id=$NODE&from=-15m" | jq .
3) Inspect preempt-shepherd decisions:
   $ kubectl logs deployment/preempt-shepherd -n runtime --since=15m | grep Decision
   Look for fields: decision_type, affected_priority, recommended_action, eviction_count
4) Check kvcache health:
   $ curl http://kvcache-$NODE.internal/metrics | grep hit_ratio
5) If shepherd.eviction_count is saturated and errors increased, consider immediate mitigation: temporarily set shepherd.max_evictions_per_min to 100 (via configmap) to allow rapid rebalancing, or toggle shepherd.enabled=false to fall back to conservative scheduling while investigating.
6) Post-incident: capture a flamegraph of GPU kernels from the time window and attach to incident page. Use nvprof or nsight-capture on an affected node (see profiling section).

Profiling checklist and commands:
- Lightweight traces (first call): enable per-request tracing: trace_sample_rate=0.1 on the router.
- Kernel level profiling (when SLO-critical):
  - On affected node, capture a 60s capture:
    $ sudo /opt/runtime/tools/gpu-trace-capture.sh --duration 60 --out /tmp/gpu-trace.tgz
  - Convert to flamegraph:
    $ /opt/runtime/tools/convert-trace /tmp/gpu-trace.tgz --flame /tmp/flame.svg
- NVPROF / Nsight examples (run in maintenance window):
  - nv-nsight capture for a specific worker PID: nv-nsight-cu-cli --target-processes all --duration 30s --output /tmp/trace.nv
- Collect kernel-mapper debug dump:
  $ curl -s "http://kernel-mapper.$NS.internal/debug/dump" > /tmp/kernel-mapper-dump.json

KPIs to include in postmortem:
- p95 and p99 before/after mitigation
- shepherd.eviction_count and eviction_success_rate
- kernel_queue_depth and batch_size distribution
- kvcache hit ratio by priority

Rollout checklist for shepherd changes (careful staged rollout):
1) Feature branch & unit tests covering decision logic and safe-fail behaviors.
2) Canary on internal perf cluster (min 10% capacity) with synthetic mixed workload replay that includes: 60% interactive_short, 20% interactive_long, 20% embeddings.
3) Collect metrics for 24h: p95/p99, error_rate, eviction_count, mean_batch_size. Set automatic rollback if p99 increases by >10% absolute.
4) Gradually increase to 50% then 100% over 72h with checks at each step.
5) Post-rollout: run 7-day monitoring dashboard and escalate if shepherd.low_priority_evictions > 5% of requests consistently.

Known limitations and caveats:
- Priority decoupling can increase overall tail variance if kernel latency estimators are stale. Ensure kernel-mapper latency profiles are refreshed every 6 hours for production models.
- Preemptive migration costs: moving an in-flight request often discards warmed KV cache (if not preserved) causing additional compute; the shepherd prefers migrating queued—not running—work.
- Quantized fallbacks may cause quality regressions; Optimize team must maintain per-model regression thresholds in optimize.quality_blocklist.

Ownership and escalation:
- Owner: runtime-scheduling@redwood.com (primary contact)
- Secondary: kernel-team@redwood.com
- Oncall: runtime-sre rotation (see /confluence/eng-sre/oncall-rotations)
- If quality regressions observed after shepherd actions, tag the Optimize team (optimize@redwood.com) and create a severity-2 incident.

Appendix: example alert rules (prometheus-style)
- ALERT ShepherdP95ProjectionExceeded
  IF shepherd.p95_projection > (interactive_short_p95_slo_ms + 30)
  FOR 1m
  LABELS {severity="page"}
  ANNOTATIONS {summary="Shepherd projecting p95 > SLO+margin", runbook="/confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/runtime-priority-decoupling-and-preemptive-shepherding-2026#Runbook"}

References:
- See kernel-mapper design: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/priority-driven-kernel-scheduler-spec-2026
- Fallbacks & degradation playbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-fallback-and-degradation-playbook-2026

Change log:
- 2026-01-15: Initial authored draft by Priya Anand.
- 2026-02-03: Updated rollout checklist and added profiling commands (reviewed by Ethan Liu).

title: Plugin Sandbox Hardening and Scheduler Contract
content:
Summary
This document defines the security and isolation model for runtime plugins ("extension modules"), the scheduler contract that governs plugin execution and preemption, and operational guidance for hardening, profiling and benchmarking plugin-enabled runtime paths. It is intended for runtime engineers, SRE, and security reviewers.

Goals
- Allow safe, resource-bounded extensions to the serving runtime (e.g., custom token preprocessors, routing adapters, feature gates) while preserving tenant isolation and SLOs.
- Define a clear scheduler contract so plugin authors and kernel/scheduler teams share expectations about CPU/GPU/IO budgets, preemption, and observable signals.
- Specify profiling and benchmarking methodology for plugin-enabled experiments to avoid blind spots in latency/cost analyses.

Scope
- Applies to: ephemeral plugins loaded into the runtime process or per-request sandboxes (WASM, subprocess, container), scheduler hooks that influence kernel selection, and the profiling/canary paths used during deploys.
- Excludes: long-lived persistent sidecars with separate process governance (see appendix for cross-process patterns).

Definitions
- Plugin: a modular extension that executes during various stages of request processing (preprocess, postprocess, routing).
- Sandbox: the isolation boundary for a plugin (WASM runtime, seccomp + cgroup, or container).
- Execution slot: logical budget allocated by the scheduler for a plugin invocation (time + CPU + GPU hints + ephemerality flag).
- Kernel: the runtime component that executes model inference.

Security & Isolation Model (high level)
1) Default isolation: all third-party or untrusted plugins must run in a sandboxed environment. Approved internal plugins may run in-process only after security review and feature-flag gating.
2) Resource cgroups: every sandboxed plugin invocation must be instantiated with a cgroup (CPU quota, memory limit, blkio throttle). Suggested defaults are in the config table below.
3) Syscall filters: use seccomp policies tailored to each sandbox type; prohibit network access unless explicitly requested and approved.
4) Filesystem access: sandboxes must mount read-only data volumes; write access limited to ephemeral tmpfs with size caps.
5) Cryptographic keys: plugin code must not receive plaintext customer keys. Any KMS/HSM access must be proxied by a runtime RPC that performs auth checks and enforces audit logging.
6) Network egress: deny by default. Egress rules require an allowlist and audit trail (team + ticket id).

Recommended cgroup defaults (table)
| parameter | recommended default | rationale |
|-----------|--------------------:|----------|
| cpu_quota | 100ms per invocation | bounds CPU tail latency when many small plugin calls occur |
| memory_limit | 64MB | prevents per-request memory blowups; increase only with review |
| blkio_weight | 50 (out of 1000) | limits disk pressure from plugins during retries or dumps |
| pids_max | 32 | prevents fork bombs from exhausting node resources |
| ephemeral_tmp_size | 8MB | prevents uncontrolled temp file growth |

Scheduler contract (concise)
- Scheduler shall advertise per-invocation execution slots with the following attributes: {slot_id, cpu_budget_ms, wall_time_deadline_ms, priority_class, preemptible:true/false, affinity_hint}. Plugin runtime must accept these attributes at start and enforce budget locally.
- Plugins must check remaining_budget_ms on each yield point (documented below) and abort gracefully returning a standardized status: "plugin.timeout" or "plugin.preempted".
- Preemption semantics: when the scheduler reclaims a slot, the plugin process/wasm runtime must receive a soft-signal (SIGUSR1-equivalent) and begin controlled shutdown within soft_shutdown_ms (default 20ms). If soft shutdown does not complete, the hard-kill path triggers after hard_kill_ms (default 150ms).
- Affinity and locality: plugins that request GPU hints must annotate affinity_hint; the scheduler may reject or remap hints to keep kernel scheduling deterministic.

Plugin lifecycle and API checklist
1. Manifest: every plugin bundle must include a manifest.yaml with: name, version, author, declared_api_surface (pre/post/routing), declared_resource_hints, required_capabilities (network, file_write), and signing_checksum. Example manifest snippet: 

manifest.yaml
---
name: redwood.token-filter
version: 0.3.1
author: internal:token-team
api: [preprocess]
resource_hints:
  cpu_ms: 20
  memory_mb: 16
capabilities: [network:false, file_write:false]
signature: "sha256:..."

2. Signing & provenance: plugin bundles must be signed by an approved build pipeline. The runtime verifies the signature against a rotation-aware public key list at load time.
3. Static analysis: run the plugin through the sandbox-targeted static analyzer (see pipeline job: eng-serving-runtime/plugin-static-check).
4. Canary: deploy plugin in a canary with 1% of traffic, run the profiling and tail-latency checks described later, and only escalate to broader rollout after meeting SLOs for 48 hours.

Yield points and cooperative preemption
