- Yield points are the only safe locations where user code may check budgets: after deserialize, after tokenization, and before issuing kernel offload. For WASM plugins, provide a host function check_budget() which returns remaining_budget_ms and allows early return.
- Cooperative window: plugin code must assume that a hard preemption may occur at any syscall boundary; keep critical sections small and idempotent.

Observability & Profiling requirements
- Telemetry emitted per invocation: plugin.id, invocation.id, slot_id, start_ts, end_ts, cpu_ms_user, cpu_ms_sys, memory_peak_mb, decision_trace (max 512 chars), status.
- Traces: span naming convention: runtime.plugin.<plugin-name>.<phase>. Include kernel hint tags when applicable.
- Sampling: for production, sample all plugin failures and 0.5% of successful calls; during canary increase sampling to 100% for the first 10k invocations or 24h.
- Profiling: capture wall time + CPU time histograms; keep p90/p99 deltas before and after plugin enablement as part of the benchmark report.

Benchmark & Canary checklist (step-by-step)
1) Baseline: run a 24h synthetic run of the target workload without the plugin. Capture per-route p50/p90/p99 latency, tokens/sec, and cost-per-token.
2) Synthetic plugin run: enable plugin on a shadow copy of traffic at 0x cost impact and measure overhead with production kernels.
3) Canary rollout: 1% traffic (multi-az). Monitor plugin metrics + runtime SLOs for 48h. Key thresholds: p99 increase <= 5% absolute and error-rate increase <= 0.1 percentage points.
4) Scale test: run a 6-hour stress with burst emulation (2x normal peak) and validate eviction and preemption paths.
5) Postmortem criteria: if any kernel timeouts, oom-kill, or scheduler-induced rollbacks occur, halt rollout and run rollback checklist.

Runbook: plugin-induced latency spike (operational steps)
1) Detection: alert fires for route X when p99 > baseline + 5% sustained for 2 minutes.
2) Immediate mitigation: disable plugin routing flag for affected route (CLI: rwdctl runtime plugin disable --route X --plugin name).
3) Trace collection: snapshot last 500 traces with trace-ids tagged plugin=true and upload to /var/tmp/plugin-triage/<inc_id>.
4) Revert decision: if disabling returns SLOs to normal within 3 minutes, keep disabled and create P0 incident. If no change, escalate to scheduler oncall.
5) Post-incident: run the profiling checklist and attach findings to incident record.

Runbook: plugin resource runaway (memory or cpu)
1) Pager triggers on node-level oom_kill or cpu_throttle > 70% sustained.
2) Isolate: scheduler should mark node as cordoned_for_plugins and start draining plugin-invocations to new nodes.
3) Kill policy: notify plugin owner_team via automated page; issue soft-kill to plugin processes and escalate to hard kill after hard_kill_ms.
4) Recovery: autoscale replacement nodes if needed and run kernel-level health checks.

Hardening checklist for security review
- Ensure manifest signature validated and build provenance recorded.
- Verify seccomp/capabilities are the minimal set for declared features.
- Confirm no direct KMS keys are provisioned into plugin environment.
- Run fuzzing for 72h using the runtime plugin-fuzz harness (job: eng-serving-runtime/plugin-fuzz-72h).
- Confirm telemetry contains at least 8 fields listed in Observability section and uses redaction policy for PII.

Example scheduler-policy fragment (YAML)
---
policy_name: plugin-defaults
priority_classes:
  - name: latency-sensitive
    cpu_budget_ms: 50
    preemptible: false
  - name: background
    cpu_budget_ms: 100
    preemptible: true
hard_kill_ms: 150
soft_shutdown_ms: 20
max_concurrent_plugins_per_node: 64

Testing harness commands
- Build and sign plugin: tools/plugin_builder --build ./pkg --sign --key-id ci-plugin-key-02
- Run unit sandbox locally: tools/sandbox_runner --bundle ./out/redwood.token-filter.tar.gz --profile debug --max-invocations 1000
- Canary enable: rwdctl runtime plugin enable --plugin redwood.token-filter --route reviews-api --percent 1 --reason "canary token-filter v0.3.1"

Ownership & SLA
- Plugin runtime and scheduler teams own the enforcement code and telemetry emitters.
- Plugin authoring teams own their manifests, static analysis fixes, and canary configuration.
- SLOs preserved: no plugin deploy should increase route p99 by more than 5% absolute or add >0.1pp error-rate without explicit senior eng approval.

Appendix A: Cross-process plugin patterns
If a plugin requires long-lived resources or external network egress, prefer a separate service with an authenticated, audited RPC. The RPC should be rate-limited and expose a per-request cost budget. This pattern isolates faults and allows independent scaling.

Appendix B: Troubleshooting quick reference
- Symptom: plugin not starting under cgroup -> check journalctl for cgroup OOM messages and policy mis-match in manifest.resource_hints.
- Symptom: plugin preempted frequently -> increase cpu_budget_ms in manifest for canary only and surface details via trace.
- Symptom: signature verification failed -> validate the public key rotation list and confirm the plugin bundle was built in the approved CI job.

Notes & change log
- 2026-02-10: initial draft by Lina Chen.
- 2026-04-13: added cooperative preemption semantics and yield-point list (review: Marcus Rivera).
- 2026-10-05: tightened canary thresholds and added hardening checklist (review: Aisha Patel, Tom Novak).

Links and references
- Plugin static analysis job: ci.redwood.internal/job/eng-serving-runtime/plugin-static-check
- Plugin fuzz harness: eng-serving-runtime/tools/plugin-fuzz/README
- Scheduler control API: /internal-api/runtime/scheduler/v1/docs

End of document

title: Kernel selection matrix (Q1 2026 baseline)
content:
## Purpose
This page defines the **kernel auto-selection rules** used for the **Q1 2026 performance baseline runs**. It is the canonical reference for:
- Which attention/GEMM kernels are expected for each **model family**
- Which fallbacks are acceptable (and when they are considered “unexpected”)
- Known performance cliffs and required **driver/CUDA/Triton** constraints for reproducibility

The goal is to make baseline results **attributable**. If a perf delta is observed, the first question should be: *did kernel selection change?*

---

## Scope
**In scope**
- Attention kernel selection (prefill + decode)
- KV-cache layout implications (paged vs contiguous) as they affect kernel eligibility
- Common model families: **Llama-family**, **Qwen-family**, **Mistral-family** variants used in baseline sweeps
- Hardware: **H100 (SXM/PCIe)**, **A100 80GB**, **L40S**

**Out of scope**
- Detailed scheduler knobs (see scheduler baseline)
- Compiler passes beyond kernel eligibility (tracked separately)
- Customer-facing or marketing benchmark guidance

---

## Definitions and measurement boundaries
- **Prefill length (P):** number of input tokens processed before first generated token.
- **Decode length (D):** number of output tokens generated.
- **TTFT (time-to-first-token):** server-side time from request admitted to scheduler → first token available to stream (see ADR-0172 for canonical boundary).
- **TPOT (time-per-output-token):** server-side per-token latency for decode tokens after TTFT.

---

## Baseline environment constraints (must match for “golden” runs)
Baseline kernel behavior is only considered comparable when the following constraints are met.

### Required versions (Q1 2026 baseline)
| Component | Baseline requirement | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| NVIDIA Driver | >= 550.54 | Must be consistent across the benchmark fleet per SKU. Do not mix minor driver versions in the same baseline sweep. |
| CUDA Runtime | CUDA 12.3 | CUDA 12.2 is allowed only if noted in the run manifest; kernel eligibility differs for some fused paths. |
| cuBLASLt | bundled with CUDA 12.3 | Used for GEMM/autotune; ensure deterministic mode as described below. |
| Triton | 2.1.x (pinned) | Triton minor bumps can change codegen and autotune decisions. |
| Redwood runtime build | baseline tag as per baseline plan | Must be recorded in run manifest (git SHA + build ID). |

### Runtime flags (baseline defaults)
These flags affect kernel selection and must be captured in the run manifest:
- `RWD_KERNEL_AUTOTUNE=baseline` (disables cross-run autotune drift; uses pinned profiles)
- `RWD_ATTENTION_BACKEND=auto` (selection rules in this document)
- `RWD_KV_LAYOUT=paged` for baseline runs unless explicitly running the contiguous variant
- `RWD_ENABLE_FP8=off` for baseline (FP8 work is tracked separately; not part of Q1 2026 golden)

### Determinism and noise control (minimum)
- GPU clocks should be locked or constrained (see SRE benchmark fleet guidance); otherwise kernel timing-based heuristics can “flip” on borderline cases.
- Warmup is mandatory (see perf suite profiling playbook).

---

## Kernel families (names used in logs and debug dumps)
These are the kernel identifiers we expect to see in the **kernel selection debug dump** and perf run metadata.

### Attention kernels
- **FA3_PREFILL / FA3_DECODE**: FlashAttention v3 variants (H100-optimized). Lowest TPOT when eligible.
- **FA2_PREFILL / FA2_DECODE**: FlashAttention v2 variants (A100/L40S primary path).
- **PAGED_ATTENTION_DECODE**: Paged KV cache decode attention (robust under fragmentation / long-running serving).
- **TRITON_ATTENTION_FALLBACK**: Triton attention fallback (functional, but usually slower; allowed only in specific edge cases).

### GEMM / fused MLP kernels
- **CUBLASLT_GEMM**: cuBLASLt-selected GEMM.
- **TRITON_FUSED_MLP**: Triton fused MLP for certain shapes.
- **FUSED_ROPE**: fused RoPE application when supported.

---

## Selection principles (high-level)
Kernel selection is based on a combination of:
1) **Hardware capability** (SM version, shared memory, BF16 support)
2) **Data type** (BF16/FP16; quantization modes)
3) **Attention shape regime** (P and D; head dim; GQA/MQA)
4) **KV layout** (paged vs contiguous)
5) **Sequence length regime** (context window boundaries)

The baseline target is to maximize **TPOT** for decode-heavy workloads while protecting **p99 TTFT** for long-prefill workloads.

---

## Kernel selection matrix (Q1 2026)
The tables below represent **expected** kernel choices when the baseline environment constraints are satisfied.

### A) Llama-family (e.g., Llama 3.x class; GQA variants common)
Assumptions:
- DType BF16 preferred
- GQA supported by FA2/FA3 paths only when head configuration matches supported patterns

| Hardware | Regime | Expected attention kernel | Expected KV layout | Allowed fallback | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| H100 | P <= 4k, D any | FA3_PREFILL + FA3_DECODE | paged | FA2_* only if FA3 disabled | FA3 is baseline on H100. If FA3 not selected, treat as investigation unless run manifest indicates override. |
| H100 | 4k < P <= 16k | FA3_PREFILL (may switch to FA2_PREFILL for some head dims) + FA3_DECODE | paged | TRITON_ATTENTION_FALLBACK for unsupported head dim | Known cliff if head dim unsupported: prefill can drop to Triton; TTFT p99 increases sharply. |
| H100 | P > 16k | FA2_PREFILL + PAGED_ATTENTION_DECODE | paged | TRITON_ATTENTION_FALLBACK | FA3 prefill not guaranteed beyond 16k in baseline; decode remains FA3 if eligible, otherwise paged decode. |
| A100 | P <= 8k | FA2_PREFILL + FA2_DECODE | paged | PAGED_ATTENTION_DECODE | If KV fragmentation high, decode can prefer paged kernel for stability. |
| A100 | P > 8k | FA2_PREFILL + PAGED_ATTENTION_DECODE | paged | TRITON_ATTENTION_FALLBACK | Long-prefill TTFT is sensitive; ensure scheduler backpressure settings align with baseline. |
| L40S | P <= 4k | FA2_PREFILL + FA2_DECODE | paged | PAGED_ATTENTION_DECODE | L40S is more likely to flip to paged decode under high concurrency due to memory pressure. |
| L40S | P > 4k | FA2_PREFILL + PAGED_ATTENTION_DECODE | paged | TRITON_ATTENTION_FALLBACK | Treat Triton fallback as “allowed but undesirable”; file an issue if common. |

### B) Qwen-family (often long-context; attention shapes vary)
Assumptions:
- Long-context workloads are common; P in 8k–32k appears in representative suite

| Hardware | Regime | Expected attention kernel | Allowed fallback | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| H100 | P <= 8k | FA3_* | FA2_* | Baseline target is FA3 end-to-end. |
| H100 | 8k < P <= 32k | FA2_PREFILL + FA3_DECODE (if eligible) OR PAGED_ATTENTION_DECODE | TRITON_ATTENTION_FALLBACK | Some variants prefer FA2 prefill due to shared-memory constraints; this is considered “expected” for baseline. |
| A100 | P <= 16k | FA2_* (prefill+decode) | PAGED_ATTENTION_DECODE | Decode may switch to paged at high P to avoid OOM / fragmentation. |
| A100 | P > 16k | FA2_PREFILL + PAGED_ATTENTION_DECODE | TRITON_ATTENTION_FALLBACK | If Triton is used for decode at scale, investigate eligibility regression. |
| L40S | P <= 8k | FA2_* | PAGED_ATTENTION_DECODE | L40S is sensitive to batch size; ensure workload concurrency targets match suite definitions. |

### C) Mistral-family (mix of standard + MoE variants)
Assumptions:
- Standard dense models behave similarly to Llama-family
- MoE variants introduce additional GEMM/dispatch pressure; attention selection still follows rules below

| Hardware | Regime | Expected attention kernel | Expected GEMM/MLP | Allowed fallback | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| H100 | P <= 8k | FA3_* | CUBLASLT_GEMM + TRITON_FUSED_MLP (if eligible) | FA2_* | MoE routing can increase variance; ensure warmup includes expert paths. |
| A100 | P <= 8k | FA2_* | CUBLASLT_GEMM | PAGED_ATTENTION_DECODE | If fused MLP not selected, treat as neutral unless perf delta is large. |
| L40S | P <= 4k | FA2_* | CUBLASLT_GEMM | PAGED_ATTENTION_DECODE | L40S memory bandwidth can make paged decode preferable under load. |

---

## Sequence length regimes and “cliff” boundaries
These are the boundaries where we most commonly observe kernel selection flips that affect TTFT/TPOT.

### Common boundaries (baseline guidance)
- **P ~ 4k:** Some models switch from FA decode to paged decode under concurrency due to KV growth.
- **P ~ 8k:** A100 and L40S often show increased fallback rates if batch size is high.
- **P ~ 16k:** Eligibility constraints become more pronounced; prefill kernels may change; TTFT p99 becomes sensitive.
- **P > 32k:** Not part of the Q1 2026 representative suite v1 “must-pass” set. If included in ad-hoc runs, expect non-golden behavior.

### Known performance cliffs (tracked issues)
1) **Unexpected Triton fallback on H100 for supported head dims**
   - Symptom: FA3 expected, but TRITON_ATTENTION_FALLBACK appears in dump.
   - Impact: TPOT degradation (often 15–40%), higher p99.
   - Usual cause: Triton version drift or a disabled capability flag.

2) **Paged decode overuse at moderate P (<= 4k)**
   - Symptom: PAGED_ATTENTION_DECODE selected despite low KV pressure.
   - Impact: TPOT drop; throughput regression in chat streaming.
   - Usual cause: KV allocator fragmentation from prior runs (fix by isolation + warmup; confirm via run manifest and allocator stats).

3) **cuBLASLt autotune instability across runs**
   - Symptom: GEMM algo changes without code change.
   - Impact: Throughput noise; can look like a regression.
   - Mitigation: Use baseline autotune mode and ensure consistent GPU clocks.

4) **GQA/MQA edge-case eligibility**
   - Symptom: FA2/FA3 not selected for certain head configs; fall back to Triton.
   - Impact: TTFT and TPOT regression concentrated in specific models.
   - Action: Treat as “expected only if documented in model profile”; otherwise investigate.

---

## Expected fallback hierarchy (by component)
When `RWD_ATTENTION_BACKEND=auto`, the runtime should follow this hierarchy:

### H100
1) FA3
2) FA2
3) PAGED_ATTENTION_DECODE (decode only)
4) TRITON_ATTENTION_FALLBACK

### A100 / L40S
1) FA2
2) PAGED_ATTENTION_DECODE (decode only)
3) TRITON_ATTENTION_FALLBACK

**Policy for baseline runs:**
- Falling below (2) requires a note in the run manifest and is **not eligible** for baseline “golden” publishing unless explicitly waived.

---

## Operational requirements for baseline publishing
A run is eligible to be included in the Q1 2026 baseline report only if:
- Kernel debug dump is present (or kernel telemetry sample rate is >= baseline requirement)
- No unexpected fallback below the expected tier for the model/hardware/regime table above
- Environment versions match baseline constraints (or deviations are clearly annotated and approved)

**Artifacts to attach/link**
- Run manifest (schema per ADR-0172)
- Kernel selection dump (per-run or sampled)
- Summary metrics (p50/p95/p99 TTFT, TPOT, throughput) and variance panels

---

## How to validate kernel selection (quick procedure)
1) Confirm the run manifest records:
   - Driver/CUDA/Triton versions
   - `RWD_*` kernel/autotune/KV flags
   - Model identifier + dtype/quantization mode
2) Open the kernel selection dump and verify:
   - Attention kernels match the matrix for the given P regime
   - Any fallback includes a reason code (unsupported head dim, KV layout constraint, disabled capability, etc.)
3) If mismatch:
   - Re-run once on the same node (after warmup) to rule out transient noise
   - If persistent, file a perf triage issue and attach dump + manifest

---

## Notes on quantization and “non-golden” modes
For Q1 2026 baseline runs, the default publishing set is **BF16**.

Quantized runs (INT8/INT4) are allowed for exploratory tracking, but:
- Kernel eligibility differs substantially (especially for fused GEMMs)
- Results are not comparable unless the same quant profile is pinned and declared

If you must run quantized baselines, create a separate baseline cohort and document:
- Quantization format and calibration/pinning
- Any altered attention backend selection

---

## Ownership and change control
- **Owner:** Hiro Tanaka (kernels)
- **Co-owner:** Yuki Sato (kernel auto-selection stability)

Changes to this page must be paired with:
- A corresponding change to the kernel debug dump reason codes (if new rule introduced)
- An update to the baseline plan if the expected kernel for a published cohort changes
- A note in the perf-canary threshold config if the change is expected to shift metrics

---

## Appendix: Reason codes (expected in kernel selection dump)
- `ELIGIBLE_FASTPATH`: selected highest-tier kernel
- `FALLBACK_UNSUPPORTED_HEAD_DIM`
- `FALLBACK_KV_LAYOUT_INCOMPATIBLE`
- `FALLBACK_SEQ_LEN_OUT_OF_RANGE`
- `FALLBACK_DISABLED_BY_FLAG`
- `FALLBACK_TRITON_VERSION_MISMATCH`
- `FALLBACK_AUTOTUNE_PROFILE_MISSING`

If a dump contains `UNKNOWN_REASON`, treat as a tooling bug and file against kernel telemetry.

title: Heterogeneous GPU Pool Consolidation and Topology-aware Batching Guidelines (2026)
content:
Summary:
This document defines operational guidelines for consolidating heterogeneous GPU pools and applying topology-aware request batching in Redwood's serving runtime. It captures objectives, safe rollout steps, benchmarks to validate cost/latency trade-offs, kernel-selection constraints, telemetry queries, and troubleshooting guidance.

Context and Motivation:
- We operate multiple GPU types (A100 80GB, A100 40GB, H100 80GB, and 4/8-bit quantized T4/NVNeon instances in partner clouds). Running separate pools for every SKU is wasteful for mid- and tail workloads; consolidation improves utilization and reduces unit cost.
- However, naive consolidation increases tail latency due to differing kernel characteristics, memory layouts, and NUMA/topology effects. Topology-aware batching and kernel routing preserve SLOs while realizing consolidation benefits.

Goals and Non-goals:
- Goals:
  - Reduce average GPU utilization variance across fleets by 10–25% for mixed model workloads.
  - Achieve >=15% nominal token cost reduction for multi-tenant serving clusters without regressing p50/p95 latency SLOs.
  - Provide a safe rollout path that can be reverted in 15 minutes of an automated policy.
- Non-goals:
  - This is not a complete replacement for dedicated pools for high-security or extremely low-latency tenants.
  - Not intended to optimize offline training workloads.

Assumptions and Preconditions:
- Runtime must support kernel variants per device family and a per-request device affinity label.
- KV cache sharding must be accessible to batch router to prevent cross-shard hotkeys in a single micro-batch.
- Observability must provide per-model, per-device-type token-level latency and kernel selection traces for the last 72 hours.

Key Concepts (short):
- Device bucket: group of GPUs with compatible kernels / memory footprint (e.g., A100-80 / A100-40 are separate buckets).
- Topology tag: node-level metadata (NUMA groups, PCIe switch domains) supplied at node registration.
- Topology-aware micro-batcher: runtime component that forms micro-batches considering both sequence-length distribution and device topology to avoid cross-switch memory transfers.

Policy Matrix (when to consolidate):
| Tenant class | Recommended pool | Consolidation allowed? | Fallback policy | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| Free / Trial | Consolidated heterogeneous pool (best-effort) | Yes | Auto-fallback to hosted small CPU-backed instances on overload | Accept higher variability |
| Mid-market | Consolidated w/ topology awareness | Yes (soft) | Canary to tenant-dedicated on SLA breach | Monitor p95 closely |
| Enterprise (SLA) | Dedicated GPU pool or pinned device family | No | N/A | Requires contractual sign-off |

Application-level Kernel Constraints:
- When serving autoregressive models with long KV caches (>128k tokens), prefer device buckets that support large contiguous memory kernel paths (A100-80, H100).
- For quantized 4-bit variants with fused kernels, avoid mixing with non-fused kernel devices in the same micro-batch.
- If a request's model variant requires FP16 kernels, do not route to devices flagged as quant-optimized-only.

Benchmarking and Validation Checklist (before rollout):
1) Microbenchmarks
   - Generate synthetic request traces using the production sequence-length histogram (use workload >= 24 hrs).
   - Run 3 full-pass simulations over mixed-device pools and collect p50/p90/p99 token latency and kernel-selection distribution.
   - Tools: ./benchmark/simulate_pool.sh --trace=prod_hist.json --devices=A10080,A10040,H100 --runs=3
2) End-to-end canary
   - Route 5% of traffic for non-SLA tenants for 48 hours.
   - Monitor: p50/p95 increase, error rate, kernel-variant churn metric.
3) Cost analysis
   - Compare token cost normalized per-device and extrapolate monthly savings; ensure no >5% p95 regression.

Suggested Experiment Metrics (tracked as dashboards):
- kernel.selection.rate: count by device_bucket, kernel_variant
- request.latency.token_p95_by_device: histogram per device family
- batching.deadline-missed: micro-batches that exceeded latency target due to waiting for topology alignment
- kv.cache.hit_ratio_by_pool: ensure cache effectiveness unchanged

Topology-aware Batching Rules (implementation constraints):
- Prefer intra-switch micro-batches: assemble requests whose assigned devices share a switch or PCIe root complex.
- Batch co-location window: 2ms default; if insufficient co-located requests form a fallback batch limited to size N_fallback (configurable, default 4).
- Batch size guidance: prioritize latency SLOs — for p95-sensitive models, cap micro-batch at 8 tokens/requests; for throughput-first jobs, allow up to 32 where kernels are linear-scaling.

Runtime Configuration Snippets (examples):
- device-buckets.yaml (excerpt):
  - name: a100-80
    families: ["A100-80GB"]
    supported_kernels: ["matmul-fused-v2","kv-sharded-contig"]
    preferred_topology_tags: ["pci-socket-0","numa-0"]
  - name: h100-80
    families: ["H100-80GB"]
    supported_kernels: ["matmul-fused-h100","kv-sharded-contig"]

- batcher-config.json (excerpt):
  { "co_location_window_ms": "2", "max_microbatch_size": "16", "fallback_batch_size": "4" }

Rollout Procedure (step-by-step):
1) Preparation (T-72h): signal to infra and run a dry-run of simulations; collect baseline dashboards.
2) Canary (T-48h): enable topology-aware batching for 5% trial tenants and route synthetic traffic that mimics heavy tail sequences.
3) Observe (T-24–48h): verify kernel.selection.rate stabilizes and p95 delta < 5%. If not, revert.
4) Incremental ramp (T+72h): ramp to 25% then 50% over several days with automated health gates.
5) Full roll (T+7d): consolidate pools for eligible tenants and deprovision redundant dedicated nodes.
6) Post-roll review (T+14d): cost savings report, incident log, and lessons learned.

Automated Health Gates (examples):
- Abort if request.latency.token_p95_by_device increases >7% for 1h.
- Abort if batching.deadline-missed rate > 0.5% for 30m.
- Auto-fallback: if kernel.selection.churn > 3 variants per minute for a device node, reroute the node to dedicated small-pool mode.

Observability Playbook (alerts and dashboards):
- Dashboard: "Consolidation Health" showing per-device p50/p95/p99, kernel selection heatmap, kv cache hit ratio, microbatch sizes.
- Alerting rules:
  - P95 regression: trigger paging to eng-serving-runtime on >7% sustained p95 regression for 15 minutes.
  - Kernel-fallback storms: low-severity Slack alert to #runtime-kernels when churn triggered.

Troubleshooting (common failure modes):
- Symptom: sudden p95 increase after consolidation
  - Check: kernel.selection.rate for new device variants; if many requests falling back to slower kernels, mark node for probe and reduce co_location_window_ms to 1ms.
  - Action: temporarily move affected tenant to prior pool via routing-policy and drain node for device-level profiling.
- Symptom: high batching.deadline-missed on a subset of racks
  - Check: node topology tag registration mismatch (PCIe root reported mismatches). Reconcile tags via: ./infra/topology-sync --node <id> --resync
  - Action: Restart micro-batcher on affected agents to flush pending co-location buffers.

Operational Runbook Commands (examples):
- Simulate production trace: ./benchmark/simulate_pool.sh --trace=prod_hist.json --devices=A10080,H100 --runs=5
- Reconfigure batcher on fleet: ./infra/ctl batcher update --config batcher-config.json --selector "pool=consolidated-1"
- Force fallback for node: ./infra/ctl node set-mode --node <node-id> --mode dedicated

Ownership and Contacts:
- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime / Priya Nair (runtime performance)
- Secondary owners: Kernel team - Ethan Morales; GPU infra - Ling Zhao

Compatibility and Future Work:
- Planned: integrate kernel-selection ML policy that predicts fastest kernel variant per-request (Q3 2026).
- Research note: explore per-tenant dynamic quantization routing to allow mixed micro-batches while preserving fused-kernel requirements.

Appendix A — Example telemetry queries:
- p95 by device (PromQL):
  histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_latency_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, device_family))
- kernel selection proportion (Influx/SQL-like):
  SELECT device_family, kernel_variant, count(*) FROM kernel_events WHERE time > now() - 1h GROUP BY device_family, kernel_variant

Appendix B — Safety checklist before decommissioning dedicated nodes:
1) Validate no tenant has explicit affinity labels to decommissioned device families.
2) Confirm kv.cache.empty_rate < 1% on impacted pools.
3) Ensure rollback script tested: ./infra/ctl pool restore --snapshot <timestamp>

Document Change Log:
- 2024-11-12: Initial draft (Priya Nair).
- 2025-06-01: Added automated health gates and telemetry examples (Ethan Morales review).
- 2026-02-15: Updated per-device batch size guidance after H100 rollout (Ling Zhao review).

Related reading:
- Priority-driven kernel scheduler spec (kernel-and-scheduling).
- NUMA-aware shard placement and eviction playbook (runbooks).

End of document.

title: Scheduler telemetry synthesis and proofing playbook
content:
Overview

Purpose: This playbook defines the instrumentation contract, synthetic proofing pipeline, and troubleshooting runbook used to validate scheduler changes (policy, kernel hints, admission controller) before and during production rollout. It unifies metrics, traces, and synthetic benchmarks into a single reproducible proofing flow so we can confidently ship scheduler updates without regressions to SLOs.

Scope: scheduler policy changes, kernel hint propagation, admission signals, request shapers, and scheduler-side telemetry. This does NOT cover GPU driver upgrades or infra-level NIC/MTU changes — see infra runbooks for those.

Owner and stakeholders
- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling (on-call: kernel-scheduling team)
- Secondary owners: eng-sre (alert and incident ownership), eng-infra (capacity & hardware), eng-platform (observability ingestion)
- Review cadence: policy changes must be reviewed by two reviewers and validated with a full proofing run (see Proofing pipeline).

Contract: required telemetry signals and their semantics
Each scheduler change must produce or be compatible with the following signals. These are required for canary gating and alerting. Put this table in the change PR checklist and ensure synthetic jobs export the same metric names.

- scheduler.request_start_ts (histogram): time request entered scheduler queue
- scheduler.kernel_dispatch_latency_ms (histogram): kernel dispatch to first kernel-execution microsecond
- scheduler.kernel_queue_length{priority,cohort} (gauge): instantaneous queue depth per priority and cohort
- scheduler.kv_cache_hit_ratio{model_variant} (gauge): prefix/KV cache effective hit ratio seen by scheduler
- scheduler.kernels_inflight (gauge): number of kernels currently running on GPU(s) attributable to this scheduler shard
- scheduler.preemption_events_total{reason} (counter): count of preemption events and labeled reasons
- scheduler.admission_drop_total{reason,policy} (counter): dropped/short-circuited requests
- scheduler.latency_p50_ms, scheduler.latency_p95_ms, scheduler.latency_p99_ms (gauges): aggregate observed tail latency per window

Instrumentation checklist (pre-merge)
1) All metric names match the canonical contract above and are emitted for dev/prod canaries.
2) Metrics include the required labels: priority, cohort, model_variant, node_id, gpu_type.
3) Traces: every request must have a root span with scheduler:enqueue, scheduler:dispatch, kernel:launch, kernel:complete. Spans must propagate request_id and cohort tags.
4) Logs: scheduler-level events (admission decisions, preemptions, eviction reasons) must be structured JSON with timestamp, request_id, node_id, and decision_code.
5) Test harness: unit tests for policy logic + integration test that replays production-like traces with mocked kernel latencies.

Proofing pipeline (automated)
Purpose: run synthetic experiments that exercise the scheduler at representative load shapes and compare key metrics to a baseline. The pipeline runs locally in dev, then on a dedicated proofing cluster, and finally as a canary against a shadow production feed.

Steps (automated):
1. Build and instrumented image: build the scheduler change in an image tagged proofing/<change-id>.
2. Baseline snapshot: select the last known-good baseline snapshot (metrics and traces) from artifact storage.
3. Synthetic job generation: generate three workload shapes (steady, spike, long-tail) using the workload-builder. Each job produces: token length distribution, concurrency shape, and KV cache warmness profile.
4. Inject deterministic kernel latency perturbations: apply three perturbation profiles (nominal, 10% slow kernels, 1% slow outliers).
5. Run paired experiments: baseline vs candidate run for N=3 iterations each. Capture metrics, traces, and full request logs.
6. Compute differential report: compare p50/p95/p99 latency, admission_drop_total, preemption_events_total, and kv_cache_hit_ratio. Generate effect sizes and bootstrap confidence intervals.
7. Gate decision: if p99 regresses by >5% and admission_drop increases by >2x or preemption_events increase by >50%, fail gate. Otherwise, produce a human reviewable report.

Manual canary steps (if pipeline passes)
1. Deploy candidate to a 5% canary pool with traffic shadowing for 2 hours.
2. Activate synthetic short-burst test against canary nodes and verify matching telemetry.
3. Monitor the canary dashboard for 6 hours (metrics below). If any hard alert fires, trigger rollback.

Key proofing queries and example PromQL
- p95 latency for a cohort/variant: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(scheduler.latency_bucket[2m])) by (le, cohort, model_variant))
- admission drops rate: sum(rate(scheduler.admission_drop_total[1m])) by (policy)
- preemption spike detection (rule): increase(scheduler.preemption_events_total[5m]) > 0.5 * avg_over_time(increase(scheduler.preemption_events_total[1h])[1h:])

Alert thresholds and SLOs (gating & production)
- SLOs: latency_p95 <= 120ms for interactive small-chat cohort; p99 <= 400ms.
- Soft gate alerts (canary): p99 increase > 10% sustained for 10m OR admission_drop_total rate > 2x baseline for 15m. These trigger human review.
- Hard gate alerts (automatic rollback): p99 increase > 25% for 5m OR preemption_events_total increase > 100% for 5m OR kernel_queue_length per-GPU > 90% capacity for 3m.

Table: recommended sampling rates for proofing and production
- service_trace_sample_rate: proofing=1.0, canary=0.5, production=0.02
- scheduler_metric_resolution: proofing=5s, canary=10s, production=30s
- request_log_sampling: proofing=100%, canary=10%, production=0.1%

Diagnostic runbook: investigating scheduler-induced latency regression
1. Confirm regression window using p99 change detector (compare recent 10m to previous 1h).
2. Identify cohorts impacted: run per-cohort p99 query and list top-3 affected model_variant.
3. Check admission_drop_total and preemption_events_total for correlated spikes.
4. Attach traces: pull 20 traces sampled during the regression window for the affected cohort. Look for: long scheduler:enqueue spans, repeated preemption, or kernel:launch retries.
5. Inspect kernel metrics: kernel_dispatch_latency_ms and kernels_inflight. If kernel_dispatch_latency_ms increased while kernels_inflight unchanged, suspect kernel queuing within GPU driver or interconnect. If kernels_inflight jumped, suspect scheduling admission miscalibration.
6. Cross-check KV cache metrics: a sudden drop in kv_cache_hit_ratio often amplifies p99 due to longer decode generation chains.
7. If root cause points to policy change, disable the policy flag (feature-flag rollback) and observe metric reversion for 10 minutes. If rollback undoes regression, open an incident with severity P1 and follow incident process.

Quick commands and snippets
- Pull traces for a request_id (example):
  curl -s "https://traces.internal/api/trace?request_id=abcd-1234" | jq '.'
- Export scheduler metrics snapshot (example):
  promtool snapshot query 'sum(rate(scheduler.latency_bucket[5m])) by (le, cohort, model_variant)' --output json > /tmp/scheduler_snapshot.json
- Run synthetic local job (workload-builder):
  wb run --shape spike --concurrency 120 --model small-chat --kv-warmness 0.7 --out artifacts/run-<id>

Visibility and dashboards
- Canary dashboard must include: p50/p95/p99 by cohort, admission_drop rate, preemption_events, kv_cache_hit_ratio, kernel_queue_length heatmap by node.
- Proofing report components: paired-differential graphs (latency, drops, preemptions), trace waterfall samples, and an artifacts section with raw logs and run configuration.

Rollout gating matrix (summary)
1. Unit tests + instrumentation checks: required before merge.
2. Automated proofing pipeline: must pass.
3. Canary deployment (5%): must pass soft gates for 6 hours.
4. Gradual rollout: 25% -> 50% -> 100% with monitoring windows at each step (30m, 1h, 2h).

Rollback procedure (fast rollback)
1. Set feature flag to baseline (feature-flag disable <change-id>).
2. Restart scheduler processes on canary nodes with baseline image: kubectl rollout restart daemonset/scheduler -n serving-canary
3. Validate metric reversion: p99 returns to within 3% of baseline in 10 minutes.
4. If not recovered, escalate to eng-sre and open emergency bridge.

Appendix: proofing artifact naming conventions
- proofing/<change-id>/run-<iteration>/<workload-shape>/<snapshot-timestamp>
- Each artifact dir must include: metrics.json, traces.jsonl, run-config.yaml, raw-logs.jsonl, compare-report.html

FAQ and notes
- Why synthetic proofing? Production traffic can be noisy; synthetic proofing isolates scheduler logic against repeatable inputs and controlled kernel perturbations.
- How to add new telemetry? Add metric to contract and update instrumentation checklist. New metrics require at least one synthetic job that validates cardinality and label density.
- Expected time for a full proofing run: 45–90 minutes depending on artifact upload times.

Contacts and escalation
- Kernel-scheduling on-call: #kernel-scheduling (Slack)
- Eng-SRE incident channel: #sre-incident
- Observability infra: eng-platform-observability@redwood.internal

Document history
- 2025-04-12: initial draft (Miguel Santos)
- 2025-07-01: added proofing pipeline automation steps (Asha Nair)
- 2026-09-02: tightened gate thresholds and added canary sampling guidance (Kai Huang)

End of document.

title: Accelerator Fallback Translation Layer and Bindings Spec
content:
Overview:

Purpose
- Define the translation layer and binding registry that enable safe automatic fallback and translation between heterogeneous accelerator backends and the reference GPU kernel paths in the Redwood serving runtime.
- Provide operational policies, SLO impact modeling, telemetry contract, and rollout steps for enabling the feature across hosted and Dedicated pools.

Scope
- Applies to kernel dispatch paths that may execute on: NVIDIA GPUs (cuda/cuBLAS/cuDNN tensor cores), AMD ROCm, third-party accelerators with vendor SDKs (e.g., Habana, Graphcore), and CPU-quantized fallback paths.
- Includes design for a runtime translation shim, per-accelerator binding manifests, quality gating, and scheduler integration points.
- Excludes model training and developer SDKs; covers inference-only serving runtime and operator interactions.

Background and Motivation
- Our runtime must support a growing set of accelerator types while preserving predictable latency and correctness. Different accelerators expose different kernel semantics (data layout, tile sizes, fused op availability).
- Rather than maintaining fully separate codepaths per accelerator, the translation layer provides:
  - deterministic, validated translations of dispatch descriptors (shard shapes, datatype, op flags) into vendor-specific kernel hints,
  - a bindings registry describing capability levels and quality-compatibility for each accelerator, and
  - fallback policies the scheduler uses to preserve SLOs when preferred backends fail or degrade.

Design Goals
1. Safety: never violate model numerical correctness guarantees beyond a bounded epsilon defined per-model/config.
2. Observability: every translation and fallback decision must emit structured telemetry for SLO attribution and regression detection.
3. Locality: translation must be cheap (<=200us median on control plane path) to avoid adding tail latency.
4. Composability: support chained fallbacks (e.g., Habana -> CUDA-compat shim -> quantized-CPU) with clear rollback semantics.

High-level Architecture
- Components:
  - translation-shim: a lightweight service in the serving process that maps canonical dispatch descriptors to backend-specific call signatures and kernel hints.
  - binding-registry: static manifests that enumerate per-accelerator capability (supported dtypes, fused ops, effective throughput, fidelity tier).
  - bind-manager (scheduler plugin): consults binding-registry at placement time and annotates requests with ordered backend candidates and max-fidelity constraints.
  - fallback-orchestrator: runbook-aware state machine that executes recovery sequences (rebind, degrade quantization, divert to regional pool).

Architecture diagram (textual):
- Client -> ingress -> request-classifier -> bind-manager -> kernel-dispatcher -> translation-shim -> vendor-kernel -> accelerator
- Fallback path: translation-shim -> fallback-orchestrator -> (alternate vendor-kernel | quantized-CPU)

Binding Registry Format (YAML example)
- Purpose: machine-readable capability manifest used by bind-manager and translation-shim.

binding_manifest: |
  accelerator_id: nvidia-a100-80gb
  vendor: nvidia
  capability_version: v1
  supported_dtypes: [fp16, bf16, int8-quantized]
  fused_ops: [layernorm_fused, attention_fused]
  performance_profile:
    - sequence_len: 512
      tokens_per_sec: 12k
      tail_p95_ms: 5.2
  fidelity_tier: high
  fallback_compatible_with: [cuda-compat-shim, cpu-quantized-path]

Compatibility Matrix (samples)
| accelerator_id         | fp16 | bf16 | int8 | fused-attn | gpu-kernel-compat |
|------------------------|------|------|------|------------|-------------------|
| nvidia-a100-80gb       | yes  | yes  | no   | yes        | native            |
| amd-mi250              | yes  | partial | no | partial    | shim              |
| habana-gaudi-2         | no   | partial | yes | no         | shim              |

Capability levels in the registry are annotated with one of: native, shim, partial, none.

Translation Shim Responsibilities and API
- Input: canonical dispatch descriptor (model id, op sequence id, tensor shapes, dtypes, requested fidelity).
- Output: vendor-specific call descriptor (kernel id, workspace bytes, launch grid), plus a quality-estimate score.
- Local checks: validate workspace fits memory budget, simulate small representative kernels on a cached microprofile to update per-request latency expectation.
- API (pseudo-CLI):
  curl -X POST http://localhost:3123/translate 
    -d '{"model":"gpt-small","op":"attention","shape":[1,512,4096],"dtype":"bf16"}'

Telemetry contract (events emitted)
- translation.requested {model, op, requested_fidelity, bind_candidates}
- translation.resolved {chosen_backend, affinity, estimated_latency_ms}
- fallback.invoked {original_backend, fallback_backend, reason_code}
- translation.quality_delta {model, delta_metric, threshold}
- performance.sample {observed_latency_ms, backend, kernel_hint}

Each event MUST include correlation_id and trace_id and be indexed to the request token bucket.

Fallback Policies and SLO Impact Matrix
- Policy precedence (high-level):
  1) Retry on same backend with jittered backoff if transient error (<=2 retries).
  2) If kernel is unavailable or slow (p95 observed > policy_threshold), attempt alternative backend from bind-manager list.
  3) If alternative backend supports only partial fidelity, apply model-specific fidelity transform (e.g., reduce beam size, lower temperature clamp, int8 path) and annotate response with fidelity metadata.
  4) If no backend acceptable, route to regional Dedicated capacity or return 503 with structured degradation reason.

SLO impact table (example):
| Action                                | Expected added latency | Probability of success | Notes |
|---------------------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|-------|
| Retry same backend (1 retry)          | +20–80ms               | +30%                   | transient network or driver hiccup |
| Switch to shim path (different vendor)| +5–50ms                | +90%                   | depends on compatibility |
| Degrade to int8 quantized CPU path    | +60–300ms              | +99%                   | quality regression possible |

Quality Gate and Regression Checks
- Every translation change must be accompanied by:
  - unit tests (shape/dtype permutations),
  - microbench replay on representative traces,
  - shadow comparison against canonical GPU path for at least 72 hours on a 1% shadow sample,
  - automatic regression alerts if model-level metrics (perplexity/accuracy/top-k) degrade beyond configured thresholds.

Rollout and Validation Plan
1. Unit-level: integration tests in CI for each binding manifest.
2. Canary: enable translation-shim in read-only shadow mode on 5% traffic; compare outputs and emit translation.quality_delta events.
3. Partial-run: Allow shim to serve low-impact tenant cohorts flagged in bind-manager for 2 weeks with daily review.
4. Broad rollout: Enable for all non-critical pools, monitor telemetry; enable broad for Dedicated pools after 30 days and SLA verification.

Operational Runbook (summary)
- Symptom: sudden spike in translation.fallback.invoked events
  1) Run query: SELECT count(*) FROM telemetry WHERE event = 'fallback.invoked' AND backend = '<accelerator>' AND timestamp > now() - 10m
  2) Check binding-registry version and recent deployments (git tag).
  3) Inspect vendor driver health on nodes (node-sys healthcheck: /opt/runtime/bin/driver-check).
  4) If widespread, activate fallback-orchestrator to divert new placement to next-ranked backend and notify SRE oncall.

- Symptom: quality_delta alerts for a model
  1) Pause automatic fallback for that model via model-fidelity-overlay in bind-manager.
  2) Escalate to model-owner and ML-ops to determine acceptable fidelity transforms.

Configuration knobs (table)
| knob_name                      | default | description |
|--------------------------------|---------|-------------|
| binding_registry_version       | v1      | current manifest applied by bind-manager |
| translation_timeout_ms         | 200     | timeout for translation-shim path |
| fallback_max_retries           | 2       | retry attempts before switching |
| fidelity_degradation_threshold | 0.03    | max allowed quality delta (relative) |

Testing Checklist (pre-merge)
- Compliance tests: ensure binding manifest contains no fields marked 'experimental' in production registries.
- Performance: translation-shim median <200us on supported platforms.
- Telemetry: all four core events emitted with correlation ids.
- Safety: shadow-run fails <0.01% for regression thresholds.

Ownership and Contacts
- Design owner: Ravi Kapoor (eng-serving-runtime)
- Implementation lead: Maya Chen
- SRE contact: Elena Morales
- ML contract reviewers: Jonah Lee, Priya Srinivasan

References and Related Docs

- See kernel scheduler API: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-telemetry-synthesis-and-proofing-2025.json

Appendix: example quick commands
- Validate manifest: ./bin/bind-validator --manifest bindings/a100-v1.yaml
- Enable shadow translation on pool "dev-shadow": ./opsctl pools annotate dev-shadow --feature translation_shim=shadow

Change log

title: Kernel compatibility matrix and rolling upgrade playbook
content:
Summary:
This document defines the kernel compatibility matrix and the step-by-step rolling upgrade playbook for Redwood's serving runtime kernels. It codifies preflight checks, compatibility rules, canary and phased rollout procedures, automated and manual verification gates, telemetry thresholds, rollback criteria, and post-rollout validation. The goal is to enable safe roll-forward of kernel builds across heterogeneous GPU pools with minimal customer impact.

Audience:
- Runtime engineers
- SREs and oncall
- Release and QA engineers
- Integrations/Private deployment teams

Owners and escalation:
- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime/kernel-scheduling team (oncall: @kernel-scheduler)
- Release coordinator: Maya Thompson
- SRE escalation: Pager duty (SRE-oncall)

1) Compatibility matrix (purpose and format)
The compatibility matrix captures which kernel binary versions are allowed to run against which runtime control-plane versions, model-ABI versions, and accelerator families. It is the single source of truth for rollout decisions.

Matrix columns (canonical):
- kernel_version (e.g., kv1.4.2)
- runtime_api_version (e.g., rapi-2.1)
- model_abi_tag (e.g., v10-kv-shape)
- supported_accelerators (comma-separated; e.g., A100-80GB, H100-80GB)
- mandatory_feature_flags (comma-separated; e.g., async-handshake, prefetch-v2)
- safe_for_canary (yes/no)
- known_incompatibilities (short note)

Example row (ASCII table):
| kernel_version | runtime_api_version | model_abi_tag | supported_accelerators | mandatory_feature_flags | safe_for_canary | known_incompatibilities |
| kv1.4.2 | rapi-2.1 | v10-kv-shape | A100-80GB,H100-80GB | async-handshake,prefetch-v2 | yes | none |

Location:
- Canonical file persisted in git: infra/serving/kernel-compatibility/canonical-matrix.csv
- A human-readable exported copy lives in Confluence attachments and the release ticket.

Maintenance rules:
- Any kernel build must include a compatibility entry before scheduling to production pools.
- Entries are created by the kernel owner and reviewed by the runtime API owner (two approvals).
- When a control-plane change increments runtime_api_version, affected kernel entries must be audited within 48 hours.

2) Preflight checklist (automated + manual)
Automated checks (CI must pass):
- Unit and integration test suite: PASS
- Kernel self-smoke: can load model artifacts and run a short end-to-end generation for 512 tokens with NVTX tracing enabled
- ABI verifier: static check for model_abi_tag compatibility
- Telemetry instrumentation present: success/failure counters, heap/gpu mem gauges, and critical trace spans
- Artifact signing and provenance: SHA256 + build metadata present

Manual checks (release engineer):
1. Confirm compatibility matrix entry and required feature flags.
2. Verify canary image tag exists in registry and matches signed SHA256.
3. Confirm automated preflight reports are green and that a representative model from the canary corpus completes end-to-end generation within baseline latency + 15%.
4. Check known-issues tracker for regressions against this kernel family.

3) Canary rollout plan (recommended default)
Objective: validate new kernel in small, representative traffic with full observability and automatic halt on regressions.

Phases:
- Phase A (lab canary): 0% production. Deploy to lab pool with synthetic traffic generator. Duration 4 hours. Gate: no critical errors, tail latency p50/p95 within target, no increase in GPU OOM events.
- Phase B (shadow canary): shadow production traffic (mirror) to canary instances; no responses used for serving. Duration 6 hours. Gate: match semantic outputs for a 1k prompt sample (fidelity >= 98%), no unbounded latency spikes.
- Phase C (live canary): route 3% of production requests by weighted routing to canary nodes. Duration 2 hours. Gate: token error rate < 0.05%, p95 latency within 1.2x baseline, no kernel-level panic or GPU watchdog events.
- Phase D (ramp): if gates pass, double canary traffic every 30 minutes (3% -> 6% -> 12% -> 24% -> 48% -> 100%). Each step has a 30-minute observation window and explicit automated checks.

Automated gating checks (examples):
- Error budget burn for the kernel cohort: > 10% of allocated error budget -> halt and rollback
- Token-level error rate delta > 0.02% above baseline-> halt
- SLO latency p95 delta > 25% -> halt
- GPU memory OOM events rate > 0.01 per 10k requests -> halt

4) Roll-forward and fallback mechanics
Artifact naming and deployment:
- Kernel artifacts use a deterministic tag: <kernel_version>-<build_date>-<sha8>
- Release job publishes signed artifact and updates a canary deployment manifest in k8s (or internal deployment coordinator for Dedicated pools)

Routing controls:
- Weight-based routing controlled by the routing-service with per-pool overrides. Canary group is isolated by pool labels (kernel:kv1.4.2-canary).
- Fallback policy: on detection of a kernel-level failure, the router automatically re-routes impacted requests to the last-known-good kernel version in the same pool (prefer local fallback) and triggers enrichment events.

State and KV cache handling:
- New kernel must be able to reconcile KV cache formats. If cache format changes are non-backward-compatible, the canary entry must include a migration plan (see section "KV migration patterns").
- Best practice: versioned cache keys and a two-step reconciliation where new kernels accept old keys and write with a new versioned prefix for a configurable warmup window (default 1 hour).

5) KV migration patterns (examples)
- Read-compatible migration: new kernel reads both old and new key namespaces; writes only new namespace. Safe for rolling upgrade without global cache flush.
- Full rekey migration: requires coordinated drain-and-repopulate. Procedure:
  1) Schedule maintenance window for dedicated pools.
  2) Drain incoming new sessions, allow existing sessions to finish.
  3) Run rekey job that migrates hot keys first (top 5% heat).
  4) Bring new kernels online and monitor cache hit rate and latency.

6) Observability and runbook automation
Essential dashboards and alerts (owner: telemetry/runtime-observability):
- Kernel cohort dashboard: p50/p95/p99 latency, token error rate, GPU OOMs, CPU steal, nvml_temperature, kernel_crash_count
- Canary gating dashboard: automated gate results, canary routing weight history, payload fidelity scorecards
- Deployment health alerting rules (examples):
  - kern_crash_rate > 0.5 per minute for 5m -> Sev-1
  - token_error_rate_delta > 0.02% for 15m -> Sev-2
  - canary_p95_latency_delta > 25% for 10m -> Sev-2

Standard automated remediation play actions (CI/CD hooks + operator):
1. Automatic immediate weight rollback to previous kernel on kern_crash detection.
2. Create a rollback release ticket with diagnostics bundle (trace samples, nvml counters, kernel logs, artifact sha).
3. If rollback fails or broader pool degradation observed, escalate to oncall SRE and initiate incident process per oncall-and-incident-response docs.

7) Rollout validation checklist (post-100%):
- 24h stability: no Sev-1 incidents tied to kernel, <10% error budget burn vs baseline
- 72h fidelity: sample prompt set outputs validated against golden set for regression drift (automated diffing)
- Cost/efficiency check: per-token GPU time within expected envelope (±10%)
- Telemetry maturity: histogram buckets for latency show no new unexpected long tail spikes

8) Rollback decision tree (condensed):
- Immediate rollback triggers (automated): kernel_crash_rate spike, GPU driver panic, mass OOM, unhandled kernel watchog reset
- Conditional rollback (requires manual review): sustained p95 latency > 1.5x baseline for 30m, widespread fidelity regressions on important customers
- If rollback performed, collect a full post-rollback artifact bundle and open a postmortem if incident severity >= Sev-2.

9) Testing matrix (must be green before canary):
- Unit tests: 100% green
- System tests: conv/generation/embeddings path tests with sample models on each target accelerator type
- Interop tests: runtime_api_version compatibility tests across last 3 API versions
- Chaos tests: simulated GPU preemption, NVLink transient error replay, kernel-level random failures (in lab)

10) Release notes content model (what goes into the release ticket and Confluence excerpt):
- What changed: brief bullet list of functional changes and safety mechanisms
- Compatibility impacts: matrix excerpt showing affected runtime_api_versions, models, and accelerators
- Known limitations: short list and mitigation recommendations
- Migration steps: KV migration or config toggles required
- Owners and rollback instructions

11) Examples: quick commands and verification queries
- Check canary weight: curl -sS https://routing.internal/api/v1/weights | jq '.pools["kv1.4.2-canary"]'
- Fetch kernel logs: rlog fetch --pool kernel:kv1.4.2-canary --since 1h --grep kern_crash
- Automated gate status: /infra/cicd/gates/latest?artifact=kv1.4.2

12) Post-deployment retrospective checklist (within 7 days):
- Release owner schedules a 30m review: verify metrics, confirm no hidden regressions, and capture lessons learned
- Update compatibility matrix if any implicit constraints were discovered
- If migration was required, document performance delta and any customer communication that occurred

Appendix A: Emergency rollback quick commands
1) Immediate zero-weight (global): routingctl set-weight --cohort kernel:kv1.4.2-canary --weight 0 && routingctl promote --cohort kernel:kv1.3.9-stable
2) Force restart pool nodes: deployctl restart --pool kernel:kv1.4.2-canary --grace 30s
3) Collect diagnostics bundle: diag-collector --pool kernel:kv1.4.2-canary --out /tmp/diag-kv1.4.2.tgz

Appendix B: Glossary
- Kernel: native GPU execution binary and support shim used by the serving runtime
- Model ABI: serialized contract between runtime and model execution kernels
- Canary cohort: isolated set of nodes running a target kernel for validation

References:
- infra/serving/kernel-compatibility/canonical-matrix.csv (git)
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-upgrade-validation-and-canary-matrix-2026 (related runbook)
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/kernel-handshake-and-adaptive-fallback-patterns-2026 (handshake spec)

Contact: Maya Thompson (mthompson@redwood.ai) for questions or to request a matrix exception.

title: Token-Aware Scheduler: Telemetry, Safety Checks, and Fallback Playbook
content:
Summary

This playbook documents the Token-Aware Scheduler (TAS) telemetry contract, production safety checks, and step-by-step fallback and mitigation procedures used by the serving runtime. TAS is the scheduler layer that considers request token counts, sequence-length distributions, and per-request SLO budgets when assigning kernels and shaping batching windows. The goal of this document is to make the scheduler-to-runtime observable, auditable, and safe for rapid rollouts without surprising regressions in tail latency or model fidelity.

Goals and scope

- Define the telemetry signals required by the scheduler and runtime for token-aware decisions.
- Enumerate deterministic safety checks and thresholds for automatic fallback or throttling.
- Provide an operational runbook for incidents caused by token-shape variability, kernel mismatches, or batching anomalies.
- Give test-and-rollout recipes for canarying TAS versions and new kernel handoff behaviors.
- Scope: applies to hosted and dedicated clusters running v2 scheduler runtime API. Does not prescribe cloud-provider specific autoscaling settings.

Actors and ownership

- Owner (operational): eng-serving-runtime/scheduler-team (engineering)
- Primary oncall: runtime-sre
- Secondary: inference-platform-team
- Reviewer group: perf-eng, observability

Key concepts and definitions

- Request token shape: observed pair {prompt_tokens, completion_budget} used to pick batching window and kernel hints.
- Kernel hint: metadata tag passed to runtime indicating preferred execution variant (float16/quantized/sharded-attn variant).
- Batching window: the time horizon TAS holds requests to form a batch; adaptive to token shape and SLO.
- Fidelity clamp: policy that gracefully reduces model variant (e.g., smaller model or lower precision) to preserve SLOs.

Required telemetry (contract)

All signals must be emitted at request decision time and at kernel completion. These are structured as key/value tags in the trace and as metrics in Prometheus/OTel.

- request.id (string)
- request.arrival_ts (epoch-ms)
- request.token_estimate (int)
- request.completion_budget_tokens (int)
- request.priority_tier (string) — {critical, standard, best_effort}
- scheduler.decision_ts (epoch-ms)
- scheduler.batch_id (string|null)
- scheduler.chosen_batching_window_ms (int)
- scheduler.kernel_hint (string) — e.g., "kv-sharded-ep10-q4",
- scheduler.predicted_latency_ms (int)
- scheduler.predicted_cost_micros (int)
- runtime.kernel_start_ts (epoch-ms)
- runtime.kernel_end_ts (epoch-ms)
- runtime.kv_cache_hit_rate (float)
- runtime.actual_tokens_emitted (int)
- runtime.memory_pressure_level (low|medium|high)
- runtime.fidelity_action (none|quantize|model-fallback|rate-limit)

Metric families (Prometheus)

- tas.request_token_distribution{tenant,model} histogram (buckets by 1,8,32,128,512,2048)
- tas.batch_size{pool,model} gauge
- tas.predicted_vs_actual_latency_ratio histogram
- runtime.kernel_handshake_failures counter (labels: reason)
- runtime.fidelity_actions_total counter (labels: action,reason)
- tas.batch_window_ms gauge

Safety thresholds and deterministic rules

The scheduler enforces these safety constraints before committing a request to a batch and emitting the kernel_hint.

1) Kernel compatibility gate
- If runtime reports kernel_handshake_failures > 5 in last 1m for chosen kernel_hint, mark hint as degraded and pick next compatible variant. If no variant available, fallback to model-fallback.

2) Token-window SLO guard
- If scheduler.predicted_latency_ms > SLO_target * 0.9 for the request.priority_tier, reduce batching_window_ms by 50% for the next 30s for that tenant-model pair.

3) Memory-pressure guard
- If runtime.memory_pressure_level==high on the target node, route new requests to alternative pool or trigger fidelity_action: quantize for best_effort only.

4) KV cache instability guard
- If runtime.kv_cache_hit_rate drops >20% vs baseline over 2 minutes, disable long-prefix batching for affected model for 5 minutes.

Fallback and mitigation actions (ordered by severity)

- Soft fallback (no fidelity change): reduce batching_window_ms, increase preemption priority for critical requests, spin up additional execution slots.
- Quantization fallback: switch kernel_hint to a quantized execution path (q4/q8) if the model variant has been validated for the tenant. Label action in telemetry: fidelity_action=quantize.
- Model fallback: route to a smaller/compatible model variant. Must attach a quality-warning header to downstream callers for auditing.
- Rate-limit fallback: for best_effort tier only, apply 429 with retry-after and emit runtime.fidelity_action=rate-limit.

Runbook: Incident response for elevated tail latency attributed to token-shaped bursts

Initial detection
1) Alert threshold: tas.predicted_vs_actual_latency_ratio > 1.4 for p99 over 5m for a tenant.
2) Pager triggers to runtime-sre oncall.

Triage steps (oncall)
1) Pull recent traces for sample request.id showing predicted latency and actual kernel durations.
2) Check scheduler.batch_window_ms and tas.batch_size trends.
3) Query runtime.memory_pressure_level and kernel_handshake_failures for 10m window.
4) If kv_cache_hit_rate dropped: identify whether a model rollout or cache eviction happened.

Immediate mitigations
1) If kernel_handshake_failures > 5: temporarily blacklist faulty kernel_hint (CLI below) and restart canary kernel pool.
2) If memory_pressure_level==high: trigger eviction policy, and if unavoidable, set tenant policy to quantize for next 10m.
3) If batch_window_ms is large and predicted latency is underestimated: reduce batch_window_ms by 40% for affected tenant-model via dynamic policy API.

CLI commands and examples

- Blacklist kernel hint (safely):
  rdsctl scheduler blacklist-kernel --kernel "kv-sharded-ep10-q4" --reason "handshake-failures" --duration 10m

- Set tenant-model dynamic policy (reduce batching):
  rdsctl scheduler set-policy --tenant acme-corp --model t-rxl-3b --batch-window-ms 25 --reason "tail-latency-mitigation"

- Force quantized fallback for best_effort:
  rdsctl runtime set-fidelity --tenant acme-corp --model t-rxl-3b --action quantize --duration 15m

Validation checklist (post-mitigation)

- Confirm tas.predicted_vs_actual_latency_ratio returns <1.1 at p99 for 10m window.
- Confirm runtime.fidelity_actions_total increments are expected and labeled properly.
- Run 1000 synthetic requests matching the original token shape via loadsculptor and compare responses for quality regressions (automated evaluation harness).
- Confirm related customer-facing routes show no 5xx spikes.

Canary and rollout recipe for new TAS kernel handoff behavior

1) Unit + integration tests: scheduler decision simulator with synthesized token-shaped workloads.
2) Private canary: enable on 1% of traffic with strict shadow tracing enabled (emit scheduler.* telemetry but route to stable path).
3) Observability gates for promotion (all must pass):
   - p99 latency difference <+5% vs baseline
   - kernel_handshake_failures == 0 sustained for 60 minutes
   - fidelity_action model-fallback count == 0
4) Progressive rollout: 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100% with 30–60 minute observation windows and auto-rollback on gate failure.

Testing guidance and bench harness

- Use load profiles that mirror long-tail token shapes: create corpora with 1%, 5%, 20%, 50% tails at 512+ tokens.
- Run A/B fidelity checks using our eval harness repository: refer to related_pages below.
- Synthetic chaos: inject kernel handshake failures and KV cache eviction events while running the bench to validate deterministic fallbacks.

Operational notes and best practices

- Prefer proactive KV cache warming for models with long-prefix reuse; TAS will prefer longer batching windows only after hit rate >70%.
- Annotate model variants with compatibility matrix: kernel capabilities, max_sequence_length, quantization validated flags.
- Maintain an "execution-compatibility" manifest per model in the model-onboarding catalog so TAS can enumerate fallbacks deterministically.

Related pages

- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/model-variant-selection-cost-latency-tradeoff-matrix-2024
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/kv-prefetch-audit-and-experiment-guide-2026
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/quantization-rollout-safety-and-quality-gate-playbook-2026

Appendix: quick policy YAML example

policies:
  - tenant: "acme-corp"
    model: "t-rxl-3b"
    batch_window_ms: 40
    kernel_hints_priority:
      - "kv-sharded-ep10-q4"
      - "kv-sharded-ep10-fp16"
    emergency_fallbacks:
      - action: "quantize"
        allowed_for_tiers: ["best_effort"]
      - action: "model-fallback"
        allowed_for_tiers: ["standard","best_effort"]

Contact and escalation

- Oncall: runtime-sre Slack (#runtime-oncall)
- Pager duty: runtime-sre primary
- Engineering owners: scheduler-team@redwood.com

Document history

- 2027-11-15: Created by Aisha Park
- 2027-12-10: Added canary recipe and metric gates (reviewers: Diego Marquez)
- 2028-01-22: Updated telemetry contract with new kernel_handshake_failures counter (reviewers: Evelyn Chen)

title: Economic Priority Governor and Degradation Scenarios: design & runbook
content:
Overview

Purpose: This document describes the Economic Priority Governor (EPG) — a scheduling policy component that combines token-cost signals, per-tenant budgets, SLOs, and priority tiers to make admission, throttling, and graceful-degradation decisions in Redwood's serving runtime. It includes design rationale, policy examples, a rollout/test plan, observable contract, and a practical incident/runbook for when degradation modes trigger.

Audience: runtime engineers, SREs, product owners for Dedicated/Private tiers, and on-call responders.

Summary of behavior

- The EPG takes as input: request priority, tenant token-budget metadata, model variant cost estimate, current per-GPU/KV cache pressure, and SLO health signals.
- It evaluates a scoring function that yields one of: allow, delay (micro-burst queue), degrade (route to cheaper model variant or quantized path), or reject.
- Degradation modes are tiered and reversible; the governor records decisions and exposes a decision trace for postmortem.

Design goals and constraints

1) SLO preservation: keep p95 latency and error-rate SLOs for high-priority users where feasible.
2) Cost predictability: prevent runaway cost from low-priority or uncontrolled workloads.
3) Graceful degradation: prefer fidelity stair-step (model->quantize->cached-response) rather than blackholing traffic.
4) Observability: each decision must emit a DecisionTrace event with inputs and reason codes.

Decision inputs and data model

- request.priority: enum (urgent, interactive, background)
- tenant.budget_window_usd_per_hour: numeric (configured per-tenant)
- model.variant.cost_per_ktoken_usd: numeric (runtime catalog metadata)
- gpu_utilization_pct: rolling 30s average
- kvcache_hit_rate: rolling 1m average
- slo_health: derived boolean from SLO engine (true=healthy)

Scoring function (high-level)

score = w_p * priority_score + w_c * cost_risk - w_s * slo_headroom + w_r * resource_pressure

Interpretation: lower score -> more aggressive degradation. We tune weights (w_*) via A/B simulation experiments documented below.

Policy configuration (example table, expressed in prose)

- admission_thresholds: numeric thresholds for allow/delay/degrade/reject decisions. Example: allow if score >= 0.7, delay if 0.5<=score<0.7, degrade if 0.2<=score<0.5, reject if score<0.2.
- degradation_order: [model_variant, quantize_profile, cached_prefix, approximate_rerank] (applies in sequence)
- preemption_policy: immediate for urgent over background; background requests can be preempted after 120ms of queuing.
- budget_burn_rate_limit: per-tenant burn-rate cap (e.g., 3x hourly average). Exceeding triggers soft-degrade, repeated exceed triggers strict reject.
- safety_gates: absolute p95 latency floor (e.g., 800ms) — if exceeded for 3 consecutive 1m windows, governor shifts to stricter degrade mapping for all non-urgent traffic.

Configuration example (YAML snippet)

policy:
  admission_thresholds:
    allow: 0.7
    delay: 0.5
    degrade: 0.2
    reject: 0.0
  degradation_order:
    - model_variant
    - quantize_profile
    - cached_prefix
    - approximate_rerank
  preemption:
    urgent_over_background_ms: 120
  budget_controls:
    max_burn_multiple: 3.0
    warning_window_minutes: 10
  safety_gates:
    p95_latency_floor_ms: 800
    sustained_window_minutes: 3

Operational observables (metrics, logs, traces)

Emit and dashboard these metrics at tenant and cluster level:
- epg.decisions.allow_total, delay_total, degrade_total, reject_total (counters)
- epg.degrade_by_type{model_variant,quantize,cached} (counters)
- epg.budget_overage_count (gauge, tenants currently over budget)
- epg.decision_latency_ms (histogram)
- request.p95_latency_ms, request.p50_latency_ms (runtime request metrics)
- cost.estimated_usd_per_minute (cluster estimate)
- slo_health (boolean per-service)

Each decision should also produce a DecisionTrace JSON attached to the request trace with fields (flattened key/value in logs): decision, score, inputs:[priority,cost_estimate,budget_headroom,gpu_util,kv_hit], applied_degradations, reason_code.

Runbook: incident flow when safety_gates trigger

Purpose: step-by-step actions for on-call to restore SLOs, assess cost impact, and roll back unintended degradation.

1) Alert symptoms and triage
  - Pager triggers when cluster-level p95 > 850ms for 3 consecutive minutes AND epg.degrade_total increased by >200% vs baseline.
  - On-call examines: cluster GPU utilization, epg metrics, per-tenant budget_overage_count, and DecisionTrace samples.

2) Initial mitigation (fast)
  - Temporarily widen admission_thresholds (allow->0.6) for 5 minutes to favor throughput over cost while diagnosing: CLI: redwoodctl epg set --path /policy/admission_thresholds.allow --value 0.6 --team runtime --ttl 300
  - If widening reduces p95 under floor, keep open and continue root-cause. Otherwise revert.

3) If broad widening is unsafe, quick-targeted mitigations:
  - Pin high-value tenants to reserved capacity (switch routing policy to dedicated pool) via routing API. Example: curl -XPOST $ROUTER/api/v1/route/pin -d '{"tenant":"acme","pool":"dedicated-us-west-1"}'
  - For top offending tenants (by DecisionTrace), apply temporary per-tenant throttle: redwoodctl tenant throttle --tenant-id <id> --qps 10 --duration 15m

4) Deeper diagnosis
  - Replay DecisionTrace logs via the EPG simulator (see Testing and simulation) to reproduce policy decisions.
  - Check for model catalog mis-priced variants (cost_per_ktoken drift) and measurement anomalies in cost model.
  - Confirm KV cache hit-rate; low hit-rate may force model re-exec and drive up cost.

5) Restore & follow-up
  - Roll back any ephemeral policy changes using redwoodctl epg rollback --reason "post-incident".
  - Open postmortem referencing DecisionTrace correlation ids for affected requests.
  - If mis-pricing found, publish corrected model cost metadata and run full canary.

Testing and simulation plan (before rollout)

1) Unit tests: deterministic scoring inputs -> expected action (allow/delay/degrade/reject). Store cases in the scoring test matrix repo.
2) E2E EPG simulator: a lightweight harness that replays real request traces and asserts that SLOs, cost, and per-tenant budgets behave as expected for policy parameter sweeps.
3) A/B rollout in sandbox (recommended matrix):
  - 5% traffic with canary weights for 24h across three traffic shapes: interactive-heavy, background-batch, and bursty-chat.
  - Measure p50/p95 latency, epg.degrade_by_type, and cost.delta_usd/hr.
4) Chaos tests: inject KV cache TTL expiration spikes, and GPU slow-path latency increase to validate degradation order and safety gates.

Simulation commands (examples)

- Start simulator with historic trace: ./epg-sim --trace traces/2026-02-22/interactive.json --policy policy/epg-canary.yaml --report reports/canary-interactive.json
- Run parameter sweep: ./epg-sim --sweep policy/param_grid.yaml --out reports/sweep-summary.csv

Rollout plan and gating

- Stage 0 (dev): unit tests + simulator run (green)
- Stage 1 (canary): 5% production traffic, 24–48h. Must show no >2% regression on p95 for urgent tier and cost delta within expected band.
- Stage 2 (regional expansion): 25% traffic for 48h with alternate hardware templates.
- Stage 3 (full): 100% with gradual scale over 6h and a 1h fallback window.

Acceptance criteria (example)

- Urgent-tier p95 change <= +2% versus baseline.
- Background-tier cost reduction >= 10% in high-burn traces without increasing urgent-tier p95.
- DecisionTrace sampling success >= 99%.

Known risks and mitigations

- Mis-priced model variants: mitigate by batching a catalog refresh job and adding canary tags on cost changes.
- DecisionTrace overload: sample at 1% by default; increase when debugging but watch storage cost.
- Tenant UX regressions: add visible headers in API responses when degraded: X-Redwood-Degraded: quantized-profile-3 so customers can failover.

Operational ownership and contacts

- Primary owner: Runtime Scheduling team (on-call alias: runtime-scheduling@redwood.ai)
- Escalation: Eng SRE (pager: eng-sre@redwood.ai) -> Head of Runtime (Marco Ruiz)
- Change approvals: runtime-architecture SIG and Security review for policy changes that expose tenant metadata.

Appendix A: example DecisionTrace (flattened log line)

timestamp=2026-08-02T14:12:33Z decision=degrade score=0.34 priority=background cost_est_kusd=0.003 tenant_headroom_usd=2.5 gpu_util=92 kv_hit=0.21 applied=[model_variant:fast-quant,quantize:8bit] reason=budget_burn_high trace_id=abc123

Appendix B: quick CLI reference

- Inspect current policy: redwoodctl epg get --path /policy --format yaml
- Set a temporary threshold: redwoodctl epg set --path /policy/admission_thresholds/degrade --value 0.25 --ttl 600 --author "oncall"
- Revert latest change: redwoodctl epg rollback --last 1 --author "oncall" --reason "mitigation"

Appendix C: simulation test cases (human-readable table)

1) Interactive low-cost: high urgent fraction, low average sequence length -> expect allow rate >95% for urgent tier.
2) Bursty batch: many background jobs arriving in bursts -> expect degrade for background and stable urgent p95.
3) Cache-thrash + expensive model: low kv_hit + high model cost -> expect degrade to cached_prefix or quantize earlier.

title: Kernel capacity safeguards and quality delegation playbook
content:
Summary
-------
This playbook describes the capacity safeguard and quality delegation mechanisms the runtime scheduler uses to preserve customer SLOs while minimizing cost. It is intended for runtime engineers, on-call SREs, and product owners responsible for routing and tiering policies. The document covers design intent, concrete admission-control configurations, emergency mitigation steps for spikes and noisy tenants, and a test matrix for rollout validation.

Goals and scope
----------------
- Preserve 95th/99th latency SLOs for paid tiers under bursty traffic.
- Minimize unnecessary fidelity drops for important customers while enforcing cost controls.
- Provide clear runbook actions for incidents related to slot exhaustion, prolonged degradation, and cross-tenant interference.
- Apply to hosted, dedicated, and private modes (differences noted).

Terminology
-----------
- Slot: logical GPU time window available to a request; unit used by admission controller.
- Fidelity: an abstraction combining model variant (e.g., base/quantized/ distilled), token budgeting, and sampling temperature.
- Quality delegation: controlled, policy-driven decision to lower fidelity for non-critical traffic to preserve SLOs for higher-tier traffic.
- Safeguard pool: reserved slots (percentage of cluster) kept aside for high-priority traffic and emergency backfills.

Design overview
---------------
1) Two-tier slot accounting
   - Fast path slots: low-latency, prewarmed kernels with KV cache affinity. Targets 1–2 GPU hops.
   - Bulk slots: high-throughput, higher-latency buckets for best-effort work (large batches, background embedding jobs).

2) Safeguard pool and soft-reservation
   - Default: 8% of capacity marked as safeguard pool cluster-wide. This is configurable by offering and region.
   - Soft-reservation semantics: safeguard pool drains preferentially to fast-path requests when utilization > 92%.

3) Quality delegation policy engine
   - Decision inputs: request_priority, customer_tier, model_variant_cost, current_latency_headroom, recent_error_rate, KV_cache_hit_rate.
   - Delegation actions: model downgrade (e.g., 8-bit quantized variant), reduce max_output_tokens, switch to cached-prefix generation, or return synthetic fallback.

Configuration examples
----------------------
Below is a representative admission controller policy (YAML). Use the runtime CLI to push to the cluster: `redwoodctl scheduler apply -f policy.yaml`

YAML example:

---
policy_name: cost-aware-quality-delegation-v1
defaults:
  safeguard_percent: 8
  fast_path_threshold: 0.92   # fraction of fast-path capacity
  bulk_slot_backoff: 0.65
rules:
  - name: premium-preserve
    match:
      customer_tier: premium
    action:
      reserve_from_safeguard: 0.5   # allow premium to consume half of safeguard if needed
      max_fidelity_drop: 0.0       # do not downgrade fidelity for premium
  - name: general-peak-control
    match:
      customer_tier: standard
    action:
      max_fidelity_drop: 0.5       # allow downgrades up to 50% perceived quality
      fallback_variant_sequence: ["quantized-v2","distilled-v1"]
      token_cut_percent: 20
  - name: background-bulk
    match:
      route_tag: background
    action:
      route_to: bulk_slots
      batch_preference: true
      max_latency_slo: 2000
---

Operational thresholds and SLO mapping
-------------------------------------
- Cluster-wide fast-path utilization alarm: > 88% sustained for 2 minutes -> evaluate safeguard pressure.
- Safeguard depletion alarm: safeguard consumption > 75% -> trigger pre-emptive quality delegation for non-premium tiers.
- Customer-level degradation target: keep premium 99th latency < 600ms; standard 95th < 1.5s.
- Eviction aggressiveness scale (0–10): default 4. Increase to 7 when KV cache miss rate > 40% and fast-path latency > 90th historical.

Runbook: fast-path slot exhaustion
