----------------------------------
Detection signals (automated):
1) fast_path_util >= 0.9 for 90s
2) per-model 99th latency crossing threshold
3) safeguard pool usage > 0.75
4) sustained increase in preemption events

Immediate mitigation steps (SRE primary)
1) Verify signals in the Scheduler dashboard and correlate with tracing: services/scheduler -> cluster/slots -> traces.
2) If safeguard pool is near exhausted, set a temporary override: `redwoodctl scheduler patch --set=policy.defaults.safeguard_percent=12` (will persist to audit log).
3) Enable aggressive quality delegation for standard tier: `redwoodctl policy apply --name=cost-aware-quality-delegation-v1 --override=general-peak-control.max_fidelity_drop=0.7`
4) If preemptions spike, throttle new long-running requests: `redwoodctl admission throttle --route-pattern="/v1/generate" --window=30s --max-inflight=150`
5) Notify product/support channels with incident tag: `#runtime-incident` and include the following fields: cluster, region, safeguard_usage, top-3 tenants by slot consumption.

Escalation (within 10 minutes if no improvement)
- Team: Runtime Pager -> MTL (Multi-tenant lead) -> Oncall infra.
- Action: shift best-effort background jobs to bulk_slots forcibly: `redwoodctl route set --tag=background --dest=bulk_slots`

Post-incident recovery
---------------------
1) Gradually revert temporary overrides after 15 minutes of stable fast_path_util < 0.7. Use canary revert: revert 20% of changes every 5 minutes.
2) Run the incident analysis job: `scripts/slot-usage-histogram.sh --window=1h` and upload to /incidents/<id>/artifacts.
3) Create follow-up work item if safeguards were insufficient: add to scheduler backlog with priority P1 if premium latency violated SLO.

Testing and rollout matrix
-------------------------
- Unit tests: policy engine rule evaluation table with 1000 synthetic requests.
- Integration tests: simulate 3x spike with mixed tiers; verify premium 99th < 600ms in 95% of runs.
- Chaos tests: simulate KV cache partial outage and confirm eviction aggressiveness moves to >=7 and fallback config triggers.
- Canary rollout: deploy policy to single region, run two-hour soak while monitoring: fast_path_util, safeguard_usage, premium_99p, standard_95p.

Representative simulation commands
----------------------------------
# Local load generator (example)
./tools/loadgen --cluster staging-eu --mix=30:70 --premium_qps=200 --standard_qps=300 --background_qps=100 --duration=15m

# Collect metrics after test
redwoodctl metrics query --cluster staging-eu --metric=fast_path_util --start=-20m | tee fast_path_util.csv

Quality metrics to track (dashboard prescriptive)
-----------------------------------------------
- premium_99p_latency_ms (goal < 600)
- standard_95p_latency_ms (goal < 1500)
- safeguard_percent_consumed (goal < 0.75)
- model_variant_switch_rate (goal < 0.05/min)
- failed_fidelity_delegations (count where delegation aborted due to model incompatibility)

Private and Dedicated deployment differences
-------------------------------------------
- Private: customer-managed KMS and audit policy require that any automatic downgrade to a different model_variant be explicitly logged and reversible. Policy must be shipped to the customer control plane as `policy-shim.yaml`.
- Dedicated: default safeguard_percent is negotiated in the contract and reflected in the runtime config (`contract.safeguard_percent`). Administrative override requires CA-signed approval in the audit log.

Known caveats and hard edges
---------------------------
- Cross-variant token accounting: downgrading to a quantized variant changes per-token CPU/GPU cost; heuristic cost estimates may underreport when sequence length variance is high. Monitor `per_token_energy_estimate` and adjust policy parameters.
- Fairness vs. latency: aggressive safeguard borrowing by premium customers can starve standard customers during sustained high-utilization windows. Use `reserve_from_safeguard` carefully and monitor per-tenant fairness index.
- Cold KV cache effects: policy may erroneously downgrade traffic that would have been fast-path after a warmup. Consider a short probation window (30s) where newly warmed sessions get temporary protection.

Operational play examples (CLI snippets)
--------------------------------------
# Increase safeguard to 12% in region us-west-2 for 30 minutes
redwoodctl scheduler patch --region=us-west-2 --set=policy.defaults.safeguard_percent=12 --ttl=30m

# Force route background jobs to bulk slots
redwoodctl route set --region=global --tag=background --dest=bulk_slots --reason="incident-mitigation"

# Temporarily raise eviction aggressiveness
redwoodctl scheduler patch --set=policy.defaults.eviction_aggressiveness=7 --note="KV cache miss spike"

Ownership and contacts
----------------------
- Primary owner: Runtime kernel & scheduler team (team@redwood.com)
- Oncall rotation: runtime-sre@redwood.com (follow escalation policy)
- Product contact: Maya Lin (product-inference@redwood.com)
- Compliance/enterprise approvals: eng-private-deployments@redwood.com

Change history and audit guidance
--------------------------------
- All policy changes must be codified in the policy repo and reference a changelist: `policies/scheduler/*.yaml` with a linked PR.
- Short-term overrides must be applied with `--note` and `--ttl` so the audit service automatically expires them. Long-term changes must go through config review and performance testing.

Appendix A: Test scenarios and acceptance criteria
--------------------------------------------------
- Scenario A: 2.5x premium spike for 10 minutes with standard baseline unchanged -> acceptance: premium_99p stays < 600ms, standard_95p may increase up to 2s but not exceed 2.5s.
- Scenario B: KV cache cold-start during 30-minute peak -> acceptance: quality delegation triggers within 45s and reduces expensive kernel invocations by at least 30%.
- Scenario C: sustained mixed noise (top 5 tenants consuming > 60% of slots) -> acceptance: scheduler must identify noisy tenants and apply soft-rate-limits within 5 minutes, with documented rationale in incident ticket.

Appendix B: Example observability panels to include in dashboard
---------------------------------------------------------------
- Cluster: fast_path_utilization, safeguard_consumption, eviction_rate, preemption_events/min
- Tenant: slot_consumption_by_tenant (top 50), tenant_fidelity_switches/min, tenant_99p_latency
- Kernel: kernel_queue_length_by_priority, average_kernel_hold_time_ms

Appendix C: Frequently asked operational questions
--------------------------------------------------
Q: What do we do if a private deployment customer forbids automatic fidelity downgrades?
A: Ship a differentiated policy-shim that only performs non-destructive throttles (token caps and batch delays). Document the trade-offs and surface them in the onboarding questionnaire.

Q: How long should temporary overrides remain active?
A: Default TTL is 30 minutes. If the override is still required after TTL expiry, a documented manual re-approval with justification should be required (create a ticket and attach logs).

Change log (this page)
----------------------
- 2025-11-10: Created by Aisha Patel.
- 2026-01-15: Added simulation commands and private deployment guidance (reviewer: Diego Marquez).
- 2026-02-18: Clarified escalation timelines and added safeguard_percent example (reviewer: Priya Nair).

Related reading
---------------
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/eviction-rewind-and-state-reconstruction-playbook-2026
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/predictive-slotting-and-quota-orchestration-2026
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/runtime-scaling-experiment-protocol-and-benchmark-checklist-2026

End of document

title: L40S tuned hardware profile reference (memory + batching presets)
content:
## Purpose
This page documents the **L40S tuned runtime profile** in the Hardware Tuning Profiles Pack. It focuses on:
- **Memory constraints and KV-cache behavior** on L40S (48GB class, PCIe)
- **Safe-by-default batching / queue / backpressure presets**
- Guidance for **cost-sensitive workloads** where L40S is used to reduce $/token while maintaining predictable latency

This is a reference doc ("expected behavior"), not a contractual guarantee. For operational rollout steps and rollback criteria, use the rollout runbook.

---

## Target hardware and assumptions
**GPU SKU:** NVIDIA L40S (PCIe)

**Key constraints vs H100-class fleets**
- **Tighter memory headroom** for long-context + high concurrency workloads. OOM risk is dominated by KV cache growth and fragmentation.
- **Lower peak prefill throughput** than H100; aggressive batching can improve $/token, but must be bounded to avoid tail latency spikes.
- Typically deployed as **single-GPU nodes** in Redwood pools. Multi-GPU collectives tuning is generally not applicable.

**Software assumptions (minimum tested)**
- Runtime: `runtime-1.18.x` or newer (see startup compatibility log)
- CUDA: 12.4+ (driver compatible)
- NCCL: default runtime bundle (no special overrides expected for L40S)

If your stack differs (especially Private), confirm via `runtime --dump-effective-config` and validate against the workload matrix.

---

## Profile identifiers
The profile pack ships multiple L40S profiles. Names are stable; values may change across pack versions.

**Current recommended defaults (pack v1.3.x)**
- `l40s/balanced` (default) — general-purpose, streaming-friendly, bounded batching
- `l40s/throughput` — cost/throughput prioritized, may increase p95 under bursty traffic
- `l40s/long-context-guarded` — more conservative KV-cache budgeting; for long-context-heavy routes

> Note: Fleet defaults may select `l40s/balanced` unless overridden per pool/route.

---

## When to use L40S profiles
Use L40S profiles when you prioritize **cost efficiency** and can tolerate slightly higher latency relative to H100, while still needing stable tail latency (no periodic OOM/restart thrash).

Recommended for:
- High-volume, moderate-context chat (e.g., ~1–4k input tokens, ~0.2–1.5k output tokens)
- Embeddings/rerank or short-generation routes where prefill dominates and batching is effective
- Dedicated/Private deployments where L40S is the primary cost lever and memory guardrails are essential

Not recommended for (without explicit validation):
- Sustained **8k–32k context** workloads at high concurrency without route-level limits
- Traffic with highly variable prompt lengths (very long tail) without queue caps and admission control
- Workloads requiring the lowest possible token latency (consider H100/B200)

---

## Workload envelope (what the profile is tuned for)
The tuned defaults assume:
- **Concurrency:** steady-state moderate concurrency with occasional short spikes
- **Sequence length distribution:** mostly short/medium prompts; limited long-context outliers
- **Streaming:** supported and expected; the profile tries to preserve inter-token latency stability by limiting micro-batch growth

Validation sources:
- Workload matrix runner results (see: workload matrix page)
- L40S OOM triage outcomes and mitigations (see: known issues page)

---

## Key knobs and recommended defaults
Below are the key knobs that materially impact memory stability and batching behavior on L40S. Exact config key names may differ slightly across runtime versions; treat these as the *effective* settings as reported by `--dump-effective-config`.

### Summary table (effective defaults)
| Category | Knob (effective) | `l40s/balanced` | `l40s/throughput` | Why it exists |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| KV cache | `kv_cache.max_bytes` | `34GiB` | `36GiB` | Caps KV cache growth to preserve headroom for activations + fragmentation |
| KV cache | `kv_cache.watermark_high` | `0.92` | `0.94` | Starts backpressure before hard OOM; higher allows more usage but increases risk |
| KV cache | `kv_cache.eviction_policy` | `age_lru` | `age_lru` | Prefers keeping active streams; evicts oldest prefixes first |
| Admission | `admission.max_inflight_requests` | `96` | `128` | Prevents concurrency-driven KV blowups |
| Scheduler | `scheduler.continuous_batching.enabled` | `true` | `true` | Improves utilization on cost-sensitive GPUs |
| Scheduler | `scheduler.prefill_decode_fairness` | `balanced` | `decode_biased` | Avoids starving decode (streaming) while still batching prefill |
| Batching | `batch.max_batch_tokens` | `8192` | `12288` | Upper bound on batch growth to protect tail latency |
| Batching | `batch.max_batch_size` | `48` | `64` | Limits request count per batch to avoid fragmentation/overhead |
| Queue | `queue.max_depth` | `256` | `512` | Prevents unbounded queueing that inflates p95/p99 |
| Queue | `queue.max_wait_ms` | `35ms` | `60ms` | Caps coalescing delay for streaming responsiveness |
| Backpressure | `backpressure.mode` | `shed_on_watermark` | `shed_on_watermark` | Rejects new work earlier to preserve node health |
| Memory | `memory.fragmentation_guard.enabled` | `true` | `true` | Adds conservative headroom and triggers early-shed when fragmentation risk rises |

Notes:
- KV cache headroom is intentionally conservative on `l40s/balanced` to reduce restart loops.
- `l40s/throughput` increases batching limits and inflight caps; validate p95 and error rates before broad rollout.

### KV cache budgeting (L40S-specific)
**What tends to fail on L40S:** a small number of long-context or long-generation requests can drive KV growth quickly, leading to:
- allocator fragmentation
- sudden OOM during prefill spikes
- repeated pod restarts (which often looks like "random" latency spikes)

The L40S profiles therefore:
1) cap KV cache (`kv_cache.max_bytes`)
2) apply a high-watermark backpressure mechanism
3) favor eviction that keeps active streams stable

**Operational guidance**
- If you see OOMs under realistic traffic, do **not** first increase `kv_cache.max_bytes`. Start by:
  - reducing route max context
  - switching the route/pool to `l40s/long-context-guarded`
  - lowering `admission.max_inflight_requests`
  - lowering `batch.max_batch_tokens`

### Batching and queueing defaults
L40S cost efficiency comes primarily from keeping the GPU busy via continuous batching. However, L40S tail latency can degrade if batching is allowed to grow without bounds.

**Balanced profile intent**
- Keep **p50** close to baseline while improving throughput moderately
- Bound **p95** via queue wait caps and batch token limits

**Throughput profile intent**
- Improve tokens/sec and $/token under steady concurrency
- Accept higher p95 during bursty arrivals (queue coalescing + larger batches)

### Scheduler fairness
We bias L40S toward **stable streaming**:
- `balanced`: fairness tuned to avoid decode starvation when prefill bursts arrive
- `throughput`: decode-biased to maintain streaming, while prefill may be chunkier

If you observe "bursty" streaming (long gaps between tokens), check:
- fairness mode
- queue wait caps
- whether the route is dominated by long prefill prompts (consider route-level partitioning)

---

## Expected behavior (observed trends)
These are typical patterns from the workload matrix runs; exact deltas vary by model family and prompt mix.

**What usually improves**
- Higher steady-state GPU utilization
- Better throughput at moderate concurrency
- Fewer OOMs / restarts compared to untuned (overly permissive) KV settings

**What may regress**
- p95 under bursty traffic if `throughput` is used without queue caps
- Very long-context requests may see increased rejection/429 due to admission control (by design)

**Key principle:** on L40S, we prefer **predictable survival** (no restart loops) over squeezing the last 3–5% throughput.

---

## Enabling and overrides (quick reference)
Profile selection follows the override order defined in the ADR (fleet default → pool → deployment → route → explicit runtime env override). Common patterns:

### Hosted / Dedicated pools
- Default: fleet chooses `l40s/balanced`
- Pool override: set pool-level profile to `l40s/throughput` only after canary is green

### Private (Helm)
- Use the Helm values from the runtime chart (see helm chart docs) to set:
  - `hardwareProfile.name: l40s/balanced`
  - optional per-route overrides for long-context endpoints

Verification:
- Check startup log line: `HardwareProfile selected=l40s/balanced source=pool_default pack=v1.3.2`
- Query metrics: `runtime_profile_selected{profile="l40s/balanced"}`
- Run: `runtime --dump-effective-config | grep -E "kv_cache|max_batch|queue|admission"`

---

## Troubleshooting
### Symptom: OOMs during long-context tests
Likely causes:
- inflight cap too high for the prompt distribution
- KV cache budget too large (fragmentation) rather than too small
- route-level max context is not enforced

Mitigations (in order):
1) Move long-context routes to `l40s/long-context-guarded`
2) Lower `admission.max_inflight_requests` by 15–30%
3) Lower `batch.max_batch_tokens`
4) Reduce route max context and/or enforce max output tokens

### Symptom: p95 spikes during traffic bursts
Likely causes:
- `queue.max_wait_ms` too high for the workload
- `queue.max_depth` too high (queueing instead of shedding)
- throughput profile enabled on a latency-sensitive route

Mitigations:
1) Switch to `l40s/balanced`
2) Lower `queue.max_wait_ms` (e.g., 60ms → 35ms)
3) Ensure backpressure is shedding (not unlimited queueing)

### Symptom: Streaming feels "chunky" (token gaps)
Likely causes:
- fairness mis-tuned for your arrival pattern
- batches growing too large

Mitigations:
- Use `l40s/balanced`
- Reduce `batch.max_batch_tokens`
- Validate that prefill-heavy requests aren’t co-located with latency-critical streaming routes

---

## Change management notes
- L40S profiles are especially sensitive to **prompt distribution drift**. When a major route changes (longer prompts, tool-calling, larger outputs), re-run the workload matrix subset and re-validate.
- Do not treat pack upgrades as "free" on L40S; always canary and watch memory + restarts + tail latency.

---

## Contacts
- Scheduling/batching: **Sofia Ivanova**, **Lena Fischer**
- KV cache / memory behavior: **Omar El-Sayed**, **Samir Qureshi**
- Perf methodology: **Claire Dubois**, **Rina Kobayashi**
- Rollout and guardrails: **Neha Kapoor (SRE sponsor)**, **Sean Gallagher**

For incidents/regressions during rollout, follow the rollout runbook and page eng-oncall + eng-sre with the selected-profile metrics and a `--dump-effective-config` excerpt.

title: Model-aware Request Shaper — Design and Operations
content:
Overview

This document defines the design, operational procedures, and observability requirements for the Model-aware Request Shaper (MARS): a cross-layer runtime component that adapts admission, batching, and kernel hints based on the target model variant, request class, and active fidelity constraints.

MARS is intended to reduce SLA violations and improve unit cost by making shaping decisions informed by model characteristics (sequence length distribution, KV cache friendliness, quantization profile) rather than treating all requests uniformly. This page covers: design goals, architecture diagrams, scheduler interactions, telemetry and profiling playbook, benchmark procedure, rollout checklist, runbook for common incidents, configuration reference, and ownership.

Goals and non-goals

Goals:
- Reduce 95th/99th token-latency SLO violations for multi-model fleets by coordinating batching and kernel selection per model variant.
- Preserve strict fairness across tenants while enabling cost-aware prioritization for Reserved/Dedicated pools.
- Provide actionable telemetry and knobs for on-call and SRE to react to model-specific regressions quickly.
- Allow per-customer/model feature flags (prefetching, aggressive batching, relaxed latency window) and safe fallbacks.

Non-goals:
- MARS does not replace global admission controllers that enforce account-level rate limits; it augments them with model-aware signals.
- MARS does not attempt to change model weights or quantization at runtime; it surfaces suggestions to the Optimize team only.

High-level architecture

(ASCII diagram)

Client -> API Gateway -> Router -> MARS -> Admission Controller -> Scheduler -> Kernel Executor

Components:
- Model Hint Registry: Stores per-model metadata (expected token distribution, hot prefix likelihood, kv-cache sensitivity, preferred kernel families). Populated from model-onboarding pipeline and updated by profiling jobs.
- Request Classifier: Lightweight classifier that attaches a request signature (model_id, prompt-length-bucket, customer-tier, op_type) to each request. Runs in the front-line router.
- Shaping Policy Engine (MARS Core): Evaluates policies to decide shaping actions: permit/queue/reject, batch slicing keys, kernel hints, kv-prefetch directives, and expected tail-fallthrough rules. Uses declarative policy profiles authored by scheduler team.
- Telemetry Enricher: Adds model-aware fields to traces and metrics (model.variant, hint_version, predicted_sequence_bucket, chosen_kernel_hint).
- Feedback Loop: Periodic job that reconcilies actual latency/cost vs predicted and updates Model Hint Registry (signal back to Profiling Playbooks).

Policy model and examples

Policies are expressed in our scheduler policy DSL (see scheduler-policy-language-declarative-profiles) and are composed of conditions and actions. Example policies (pseudo-DSL):

1) Low-latency small prompt policy:
when model.family == "redwood-compat-tiny" and prompt_bucket in [0-64]:
  - set kernel_hint = "fast-small-ctx"
  - max_batch_size = 16
  - admission_priority = "interactive"

2) Cost-sensitive long-seq policy for batch windows:
when model.quant_profile == "int4" and median_length > 256:
  - enable_kv_prefetch(true)
  - set_kernel_hint = "concat-friendly"
  - target_batch_latency_ms = 120
  - admission_priority = "best-effort"

Scheduler interactions and kernel handshake

MARS communicates intent to the scheduler and kernel executor via:
- Kernel hint header: structured token the scheduler maps to kernel families (sharded vs fused attention, prepacked weights).
- Batch-slice key: chosen to optimize packing (e.g., same prompt_bucket + kv-cache affinity).
- Preferred prefetch directive: instruct kernel to pre-issue KV cache lookups or to use lazy prefetch.

The scheduler must validate kernel hints against the current kernel compatibility matrix. If a hint is incompatible with the node (e.g., missing kernel plugin), the scheduler will either map to a nearest compatible hint or follow the MARS-declared fallback priority list.

KV cache coordination

MARS can request coordinated KV prefetch windows for long-running sessions. Coordination rules:
- Prefetch is gated by per-node memory watermarks (see config table below).
- Prefetch concurrent limit default: 4 per-GPU.
- When prefetch window is enabled, MARS will mark the request as heavy; admission priority may be lowered unless the customer tier is Reserved.

Telemetry and profiling playbook (operational)

Purpose: ensure model-aware shaping decisions are observable and profile their impact on latency, cost, and fidelity.

1) Enrichment fields (required):
- model.id, model.variant
- request.predicted_seq_bucket (0-64, 65-256, 257-1024, >1024)
- kernel_hint, hint_version
- batch_slice_id, batch_size_actual
- kv_prefetch_enabled (bool), kv_prefetch_duration_ms
- scheduling_latency_ms, kernel_enqueue_ms, kernel_exec_ms

2) Key dashboards and alerts:
- Model-level SLO rollup: 95th/99th token-latency per model.variant. Alert if 95th > SLO*1.1 for 5m.
- Hint-compatibility mismatch: rate of rejected/translated kernel hints > 0.5% over 10m.
- Prefetch OOM signal: memory.watermark_eviction_count > 0 in window. Critical alert.
- Batch-slice starvation: fraction of requests assigned to native batch < 90% for an active model.

3) Profiling procedure (when suspect model-level regression):
- Step 1: mirror 1% of production traffic for the target model into the profiling cluster (shadow-run) with same MARS policy.
- Step 2: collect 1,000 representative requests per prompt_bucket for 30 minutes.
- Step 3: run kernel-level microbenchmarks for the exact kernel_hint variants observed (use microbenchmark-suite).
- Step 4: analyze traces to attribute latency to scheduling vs kernel vs serialization (use causal-latency-attribution playbook).
- Step 5: propose policy adjustment (e.g., reduce target_batch_latency_ms, change kernel_hint) and run A/B shadow test for 24 hours.

Benchmark protocol for validating MARS effects

Objective: quantify cost/latency/fidelity tradeoffs introduced by MARS policies.

Benchmark setup:
- Use the operational workload simulator (service: workload-synth) and a corpus of request templates grouped by prompt_bucket and op_type.
- Baseline: scheduler with model-agnostic shaper (current mainline).
- Treatment: scheduler + MARS with policy profile X.
- Metrics: p50/p95/p99 token latency, per-token GPU utilization, per-request cost estimate, kernel queue time distribution.

Run script (short):
1) seed the model hint registry with profile X.
2) run 60-minute steady-state at target QPS for mid-tier pool.
3) collect traces and aggregate.
4) compute relative delta and run statistical significance (t-test) per metric.

Acceptance criteria:
- p95 delta <= -10% (reduced) or <= +2% (acceptable increase) AND per-request cost delta <= -5% OR there is a documented product tradeoff.

Configuration reference (example table)

| key | default | description | notes |
|-----|---------|-------------|-------|
| mars.max_prefetch_per_gpu | 4 | Max concurrent kv-prefetch per GPU | Soft limit enforced by scheduler |
| mars.max_batch_latency_ms | 150 | Maximum batch formation latency target | Lower improves latency, raises cost |
| mars.policy_reload_interval_s | 60 | How often MARS refreshes policy and hints | Use 60s in prod |
| mars.hint_fallback_ttl_s | 300 | Time to trust a mapped fallback hint | Set to 5m to allow smooth conversions |
| mars.prefetch_memory_watermark_pct | 0.7 | Node-level watermark to allow prefetch | 0.7 recommended |

Operational runbook (common incidents)

Incident: Elevated model p99 for model.variant A after policy rollout
1) Immediately open a remediation incident and tag "mars-incident".
2) Check alert dashboard: confirm p95/p99 increase and affected prompt_buckets.
3) Abort rollout: set policy flag to previous version via policy rollback API:
   curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPS_TOKEN" \
     https://internal-control-plane/api/mars/policy/rollback 
   Confirm policy reload succeeded (logs in /var/log/mars/reloader.log).
4) Run profiling replay for 15 minutes using captured requests for each affected bucket.
5) If kernel_hint mismatch rate non-zero: check kernel plugin health on nodes (svc: kernel-plugin-manager).
6) If kv-prefetch caused OOMs: drain prefetch windows by toggling mars.max_prefetch_per_gpu=0, then roll forward with reduced prefetch.
7) Postmortem scope: include hypothesis, root cause (policy misclassification/kernal incompatible/misprofiled), timeline, and mitigations.

Incident: Hint-compatibility spike (translated-to-fallback count rising)
- Check Model Hint Registry: ensure hint_version is the same across front-line routers. If not, force reload:
  kubectl rollout restart deployment/mars-reloader -n runtime
- If nodes lack plugin: schedule kernel-plugin-manager restart on affected node pool.

Rollout checklist (safe rollout matrix)

- Canary: deploy policy to 0.5% traffic for model variant; monitor 1h.
- Shadow: mirror 1% traffic to a MARS-enabled staging cluster and compare traces for 24h.
- Gradual increase: 0.5 -> 1 -> 5 -> 20 -> 100% with 1h holds and automated rollback if p95 > SLO*1.1.
- Post-rollout validation: run benchmark protocol for 60m.

Ownership and contacts

- MARS Core Owner: Maya Patel (eng-serving-runtime).
- Scheduler integration: Daniel Chen (kernel-and-scheduling).
- Profiling and lab: Sofia Martinez (applied-ml-and-evals).
- On-call: runtime-sre rotation (link to oncall page).

Appendix: sample policy JSON (examples)

{
  "policy_name": "interactive-small-ctx-v1",
  "conditions": ["model.family == 'rwd-tiny'", "prompt_bucket == '0-64'"],
  "actions": {
    "kernel_hint": "fast-small-ctx",
    "max_batch_size": "16",
    "target_batch_latency_ms": "30",
    "admission_priority": "interactive"
  }
}

Notes and future work

- Integrate MARS with Optimize to allow policy suggestions based on cost budgets.
- Explore per-tenant adaptive learning of target_batch_latency using automatic feedback.
- Work with Private Deployments team to expose a restricted subset of MARS policies for self-hosted customers.

Related resources

- scheduler-policy-language-declarative-profiles (internal)
- runtime-microbenchmark-suite and kernel-hinting-matrix
- profiling-playbook/causal-latency-attribution-and-signal-enrichment-playbook-2026.json

Revision history

- 2026-02-14: Created (Maya Patel)
- 2026-04-07: Added telemetry enrichment and runbook sections (Daniel Chen)
- 2026-06-01: Tuned rollout thresholds and benchmark acceptance criteria (Sofia Martinez)

title: Kernel Sandboxing, Bandwidth Controls, and Cooperative Shepherding Manual
content:
Overview:

This document defines the design, operational controls, and incident procedures for the Kernel Sandboxing and Cooperative Shepherding subsystem (KSCS). KSCS is the combination of: the sandbox controller that constrains per-cohort resource "bandwidth", an admission/governor layer that enforces soft and hard limits, and a cooperative shepherding protocol between the scheduler and kernel plugins to enable graceful handoff, preemption-friendly slices, and prioritized progress for latency‑sensitive requests.

Scope and intent:
- Scope: Applies to the runtime kernel and scheduler integrations used by Redwood’s hosted and dedicated inference clusters.
- Intent: Reduce noisy-neighbor and runaway kernel behavior while preserving tail latency for high-priority tiers and enabling safe experimental kernel rollouts.

Design goals:
1) Safety: prevent single tenant/cohort from starving others; avoid node OOMs and GPU hangs.
2) Latency preservation: keep high-priority request P99 within SLOs where possible.
3) Observability: expose deterministic telemetry for allocation and handoff decisions.
4) Replayability: allow deterministic replay of scheduling decisions for investigation.

Architecture overview:
- Components:
  - Sandbox Controller (sandboxd): central agent per node that negotiates quota windows, issues bandwidth tokens, and exposes an RPC for kernel plugin sync.
  - Kernel Plugin Interface (KPI): light-weight ABI inside each kernel that accepts token credits, preemption hints, and cooperative-shepherding callbacks.
  - Bandwidth Governor: admission service in the scheduler that translates request characteristics into bandwidth profiles (tokens/sec, max-slice-ms, priority).
  - Shepherd Agent: cross-node coordinator for multi-stage requests (e.g., multi-shard KV cache warmups) that requests temporary credits and releases them on completion.

How it works (high level):
1) Request classified by admission -> bandwidth profile assigned (e.g., interactive-high, batch-background).
2) Scheduler requests token allocation from sandboxd for the chosen cohort. sandboxd enforces cohort global windows using a leaky-bucket model.
3) Kernel receives tokens and can run a slice up to configured max-slice-ms. If a higher priority request arrives, kernel uses cooperative callback to yield at a safe boundary.
4) Shepherd Agent mediates long-running handoffs (for example, model swap or large KV prefetch) to avoid long blocking of interactive slots.

Terminology:
- token: smallest unit of bandwidth credit (represents a short amount of GPU work permissable).
- cohort: a classification of traffic (customer-tier + workload-class).
- slice: contiguous execution window inside a kernel invocation (bounded by max-slice-ms).
- shepherding: cooperative handoff process where a running kernel segment coordinates with scheduler to release or re-acquire credits gracefully.

Modeled policies and examples:
- Leaky-bucket parameters (default):
  - bucket_size_tokens: 10_000
  - refill_rate_tokens_per_sec: 5_000
  - max_burst_tokens: 15_000
- Priority mapping (example):
  - interactive-high: tokens/sec 5_000, max-slice-ms 6, preemption-grace-ms 2
  - interactive-low: tokens/sec 2_000, max-slice-ms 8, preemption-grace-ms 4
  - batch-background: tokens/sec 1_000, max-slice-ms 50, preemption-grace-ms 20

Config table (YAML sample for sandboxd per-node):

node_id: node-az1-gpu-123
sandboxd:
  bucket_size_tokens: 10000
  refill_rate_tokens_per_sec: 5000
  max_burst_tokens: 15000
  cohort_defaults:
    interactive-high:
      tokens_per_sec: 5000
      max_slice_ms: 6
      preemption_grace_ms: 2
    interactive-low:
      tokens_per_sec: 2000
      max_slice_ms: 8
      preemption_grace_ms: 4
    batch-background:
      tokens_per_sec: 1000
      max_slice_ms: 50
      preemption_grace_ms: 20

Important telemetry and metrics (exposed via /metrics and traces):
- sandboxd_cohort_tokens_total{cohort, node} (counter)
- sandboxd_cohort_tokens_available{cohort, node} (gauge)
- kernel_slice_duration_ms{cohort, kernel_variant} (histogram)
- shepherd_handoff_success_total (counter)
- preemption_yield_count{cohort} (counter)
- kernel_blocked_on_tokens{node} (gauge)
- p99_latency_by_cohort{cohort} (derived)

Alerting thresholds (recommended):
- sandboxd_cohort_tokens_available drops below 10% for more than 30s for interactive-high -> P1 oncall paging.
- kernel_blocked_on_tokens spikes > 3 nodes in 1m -> P0 investigation (potential global throttling).
- shepherd_handoff_success_total failure rate > 2% over 10m -> P2 ticket.

Scheduling hooks and API (summary):
- RequestClassification(request) -> cohort, profile_id
- SandboxRequestTokens(profile_id, amount) -> granted_tokens, lease_ms
- KernelYieldHint(current_slice_ms, grace_ms) -> ok_to_yield
- ShepherdAcquire(resource_id, expected_duration_ms) -> temporary_credit_handle
- ShepherdRelease(handle) -> release_ack

Rollout checklist for kernel-side changes (safe deployment):
1) Create a feature flag for KPI changes and ensure sandboxd reads dynamic config.
2) Run unit tests and KPI ABI checks in kernel-sandbox CI.
3) Canary deploy with 0.5% traffic, monitor kernel_slice_duration_ms and preemption_yield_count.
4) If p99 latency regression > 8% or shepherd_handoff failures > 1% in 30m, rollback.
5) Gradually increase traffic in doubling steps (0.5%, 1%, 2%, 4%, 8%, 16%) with 30m steady windows.

Incident triage runbook (fast path):
1) Symptoms: high P99 for interactive-high with kernel_blocked_on_tokens > 0 and tokens_available < 5%.
2) Run: kubectl exec to sandboxd on affected node(s) and run admin /debug/token-state.
3) If a single cohort is consuming > 80% of tokens, identify the tenant and either:
   a) Apply temporary cohort-hold via admission to reduce tokens/sec by 50%, or
   b) Evict long-running background batch pods from the node.
4) If multiple nodes show kernel_blocked_on_tokens, trigger global mitigation: scale dedicated GPU pool up by +20% and enable degraded-routing policy to fallback model-variant with lower memory.
5) Create an incident page, attach sandboxd token dumps, kernel traces, and shepherd agent logs.

Experiment & benchmark protocol (how to measure effects):
1) Goal: validate that KSCS reduces cross-cohort interference while maintaining P99 SLO for interactive-high.
2) Synthetic corpus: mix of short interactive requests (median tokens 40, 90% < 120 tokens) and long prefetchs (median 2k tokens).
3) Bench steps:
   a) Baseline: run workload on current kernel w/o KSCS active for 1 hour. Capture p50/p95/p99 and per-cohort token consumption.
   b) Activation: enable KSCS sandboxd with conservative refill rates and run for 1 hour.
   c) Stress: drive a background cohort to 300% of normal rate and measure regressions.
4) Success criteria:
   - interactive-high p99 delta <= +5% compared to baseline under normal load.
   - Under stress, interactive-high p99 should degrade less than baseline (target < +30% delta).
   - shepherd_handoff_success_total >= 99.5%.

Testing checklist (local/dev):
- Unit tests for KPI ABI compatibility.
- Local sandboxd simulator with configurable leak rates.
- Synthetic trace replay harness (see related pages) to reproduce burst shapes.

Operational notes and ownership:
- Owners: Runtime Scheduling Team (primary), Runtime Observability (secondary).
- Slack channels: #runtime-schedule, #runtime-ops. Use the incident template when paging.

Known limitations and caveats:
- Some third-party kernel plugins may not implement cooperative yield hooks; we provide a compatibility shim that converts hard preemption to softer slice truncation but may increase tail variance.
- Token accounting introduces small overhead (~1–2% CPU per sandboxd node) and additional trace volume; budget observability accordingly.
- KSCS reduces but does not eliminate cross-node emergent backpressure when NVLink or PCIe saturation occurs; use combined network+sandboxd alarms in those cases.

Appendix A — Troubleshooting commands:
- sandboxd debug token summary:
  curl -sS http://sandboxd.local/debug/token-state | jq .
- show recent yields and preemptions from kernel traces:
  <internal-trace-query> | filter event:kpi_yield | sort -desc timestamp | limit 200

Appendix B — Short FAQ:
Q: What happens if shepherding fails mid-handoff?
A: The shepherd agent rolls back the temporary credit and marks the resource as "quarantined" for 60s; background cohorts are deprioritized and telemetry recorded for follow-up.

Q: Can we bypass KSCS for emergencies?
A: Yes — emergency flagging route exists but requires sign-off from SRE/Runtime leads and leaves an audit trail; misuse will trigger automatic review.

Related reading and links:
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/execution-stitching-and-fallback-orchestration-2026
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/kv-prefetch-audit-and-experiment-guide-2026

Revision history:
- 2026-02-15 — initial draft by Aisha Patel
- 2026-04-01 — added shepherding API and rollout checklist (reviewer: Marco Liu)
- 2026-08-20 — finalized telemetry metrics and incident thresholds (reviewer: Daniel Ortega)

title: Tenant-aware Kernel Ladder: Architecture, Profiling, and Runbook
content:
Summary:
This handbook documents the tenant-aware kernel ladder: a runtime subsystem that adaptively promotes and demotes kernel configurations per-tenant to meet latency SLOs while optimizing GPU utilization and cost. It combines architecture rationale, kernel scheduling rules, profiling playbook, benchmarking plan, rollout checklist, and an incident runbook.

Purpose and scope:
- Audience: serving runtime engineers, SREs, on-call, and performance engineers.
- Scope: design and operational procedure for the kernel ladder (promotion/demotion, telemetry signals, safety guards, and rollback).
- Non-goals: hardware provisioning, global autoscaler policies, and model architecture changes.

1) High-level design
Overview:
- Kernel ladder is a discrete set of kernel profiles (K0..K4) that trade throughput/cost for worst-case latency. Each profile is a precompiled kernel bundle + scheduler hints (batch slice size, preemption score, qcache warmup).
- Per-tenant control plane maps tenant -> ladder policy. Policy attributes: base_profile, min_profile, max_profile, promotion_cooldown_s, demotion_cooldown_s, telemetry_weights.
- Runtime components:
  - Ladder controller (per-node): watches incoming telemetry and per-tenant session state, emits profile-change intents.
  - Kernel activation agent (per-GPU): applies profile bundles and issues kernel handshake; ensures safe rollback if activation fails.
  - Quota crediter: ensures profile changes respect slot accounting and kernel credits.
  - Telemetry exporter: publishes promotion/demotion events and rationale to metrics and traces.

Architecture diagram (text):
- Request -> Request-classifier -> Tenant policy lookup -> Ladder controller -> Kernel activation agent -> GPU dispatcher -> Kernel execution -> Telemetry sink

2) Policy model and scheduling rules
Policy fields (table):
| field | type | description | example |
|---|---|---|---|
| base_profile | string | default kernel profile for tenant | K1 |
| min_profile | string | lower bound allowed | K0 |
| max_profile | string | upper bound allowed | K3 |
| promotion_metric | string | telemetry metric used for upshift | tail_latency_99ms |
| promotion_threshold | string | threshold to trigger promotion | 150ms |
| demotion_metric | string | metric used for downshift | avg_tokens_per_second |
| promotion_cooldown_s | int | min seconds between promotions | 60 |
| demotion_cooldown_s | int | min seconds between demotions | 300 |

Scheduling rules (short):
- Prefer non-disruptive profile changes: when possible, move only new allocations to the higher profile and let existing sessions finish (soft promotion).
- Hard promotion: if tail latency > promotion_threshold for 3 consecutive 1-min windows, force immediate kernel swap for hot sessions with warm-up prefetch.
- Demotion: only demote when sustained over a 10-minute window and GPU utilization headroom > 25%.
- Safety: at most 20% of a node's kernels can be in an experimental (K4) profile concurrently.

3) Telemetry & SLOs
Canonical metrics (exported to metrics namespace rwd.runtime.ladder):
- tenant.tail_latency_99_ms (gauge, ms)
- tenant.avg_latency_ms (gauge, ms)
- tenant.token_throughput_tps (gauge)
- node.gpu_utilization_pct (gauge)
- ladder.promotion_events_total (counter)
- ladder.failed_activations_total (counter)

SLO guidance (example tenant class):
- Enterprise interactive: p99 latency <= 180ms for requests <= 256 tokens, availability >= 99.95%.
- Standard API customers: p99 latency <= 300ms, availability >= 99.9%.
- Background batch: p99 latency <= 2s, availability >= 99.5%.

Alert thresholds (examples):
- Pager (SEV2): tenant.tail_latency_99_ms > 250ms sustained for 5m AND ladder.promotion_events_total increased by > 30% in 10m.
- Ops (SEV3): ladder.failed_activations_total > 5 in 10m on a single node.

4) Profiling playbook (how to collect targeted signals)
Objective: gather representative traces and microprofiles to decide ladder step definitions and promotion thresholds.
Steps:
1. Identify representative tenants: choose 3 tenants per SLA class (interactive, standard, batch).
2. Use sampled tracing at 1% of requests for 24h with request context "ladder-prof"; capture kernel dispatch timings, batch shapes, KV cache hit ratio, and prefetch latencies.
3. Run microbenchmarks on candidate kernel bundles: run 10k synthetic short requests (32–64 tokens) and long requests (512 tokens) across K0..K4. Collect p50/p95/p99 and memory working set.
4. Create a ladder-definition artifact (YAML) for each tenant class. Example: 

---
tenant_class: interactive
ladder_steps:
  - id: K0
    description: minimal-latency (low-batch, high-priority, small kernels)
    expected_p99_ms: 120
    cost_factor: 1.8
  - id: K1
    description: balanced
    expected_p99_ms: 160
    cost_factor: 1.0
  - id: K2
    description: throughput-optimized
    expected_p99_ms: 260
    cost_factor: 0.6
---

5. Validate ladder offline using the workload replay harness in benchmarking suite (see section 5).

5) Benchmarking plan and acceptance criteria
- Bench harness: use the operational-workload-simulator with recorded traces. For each ladder candidate, measure: node throughput, tail latency, GPU idling, kernel switching time, and cost-per-token estimate.
- Acceptance criteria (release gating):
  - p99 latency improvement for promoted tenants >= 25% vs base_profile under matched load, AND
  - Cost uplift per-token <= 40% for interactive tenants (for enterprise customers with higher SLOs), OR
  - No more than 5% increase in node-level tail latency for mixed-tenant workloads.

6) Release & rollout checklist
Pre-flight:
- Generate ladder YAML artifacts and commit to repo rwd/ladder-defs.
- Run full bench harness and attach results to release ticket.
- Code review and canary gate: enable ladder in canary region with traffic fraction 0.5% for 2 hours.
Gradual rollout:
1. 0.5% traffic - 2h - check metrics and failed_activations_total.
2. 2% traffic - 4h - validate p99 and GPU utilization headroom.
3. 10% traffic - 6h - watch cross-tenant tail latencies.
4. 50% traffic - 24h - if stable, escalate to 100%.
Rollback criteria (automated):
- Any single-node ladder.failed_activations_total > 10 in 5m -> immediate rollback of ladder on that node.
- Cross-tenant node p99 latency regressions > 15% sustained for 15m -> rollback to previous kernel bundle set.

7) Operational runbook (on-call playbook for SEV2/SEV3)
When triggered: detect via alert or manual observation.
A. Initial triage (first 10 minutes):
1. Check ladder.failed_activations_total and node.gpu_utilization_pct graphs.
2. Identify affected tenants and node(s) via trace ids and metrics.
3. If failed_activations_total spikes on a node: ssh to node and inspect /var/log/rwd/kernel-activation.log for handshake errors; run `rwdctl kernel status --node $NODE`.

B. Mitigation steps (10-30 minutes):
1. Soft demote affected tenant(s): `rwdctl ladder set --tenant $TID --profile K1 --mode soft`.
2. If kernel activation handshake fails repeatedly, drain node from scheduler and trigger a rolling restart of kernel agent: `rwdctl node cordon $NODE && rwdctl agent restart kernel-agent --node $NODE`.
3. If cross-tenant p99 regressions: temporarily enable global conservative policy: `rwdctl ladder set-global --max_profile K1` (admin only).

C. Post-incident actions (30m+):
1. Collect the following artifacts and attach to incident ticket: kernel-activation.log, last 30m of ladder telemetry, sample traces (ladder-prof), bench-run summary.
2. Open a performance regression ticket if ladder caused regressions, assign to kernel-scheduling team.

8) Known limitations and issues
- Kernel activation latency: some legacy kernels require a cold handshake that can take 120–250ms. Workaround: prefer soft promotions and warm-prefetch for affected models.
- Cache-skew edge-case: per-tenant promotions may create KV cache fragmentation; mitigation: periodic KV compaction job (daily) and prefetch heuristics.
- Rollout oscillation: naive promotion/demotion based solely on p99 can oscillate. The ladder uses cooldown windows and hysteresis, but complex multi-tenant bursts may still cause flapping. Future fix: add predictive smoothing using short-term AR models.

Known issues table (brief):
| id | symptom | workaround | owner |
| KLD-101 | failed kernel handshake on A100p 2.0 nodes | cordon node and restart kernel-agent | kernel-scheduling team |
| KLD-112 | tenant p99 spike after hard promotion | revert tenant to previous profile and soft-warm | SRE/perf |
| KLD-117 | KV cache fragmentation for >1000 active tenants | run kv-compact and limit concurrent promotions | runtime-infra |

9) Postmortem and metrics to track after rollout
- Reduction in tenant-tail-p99 per SLA class
- ladder.promotion_events_total/k (normalized) vs failed_activations_total
- Node-level avg GPU-ptime (time kernels are active) and idle fraction
- Cost per token estimates before/after ladder

10) Ownership, contacts and escalation
- Primary maintainers: kernel-scheduling (team alias: team-kernel-sched@redwood.com)
- On-call rotation: kernel-scheduling SRE and runtime-platform SRE (see oncall roster link: /confluence/eng-sre/oncall-roster)
- Pager escalation: SEV2 -> oncall SRE, then engineering manager.

References and artifacts:
- rwd/ladder-defs repository (internal)
- Benchmark runs: /artifacts/bench/ladders/2026-01 (links attached to release ticket)
- Related pages: predictive-slotting-and-quota-orchestration-2026, delta-routing-and-cost-partitioning-architecture-2026

Appendix: Useful CLI snippets
- Check a tenant's current profile:
  rwdctl ladder get --tenant $TID
- Force soft promotion for debugging:
  rwdctl ladder set --tenant $TID --profile K2 --mode soft --reason "debug/latency-test"
- Dump last activation logs for node:
  sudo journalctl -u rwd-kernel-activation -n 500 | tee ~/activation-tail.log

Revision history:
- 2026-01-15: Initial draft (Ava Martinez).
- 2026-02-10: Add acceptance gating criteria and bench harness steps (Daniel Cho).
- 2026-03-02: Update rollout steps and rollback automation triggers (Marcus Flynn).

title: Per-request Credit Accounting and Economic Priority Scheduler — Design & Runbook
content:
Summary:

This document specifies the Per-request Credit Accounting model and the Economic Priority Scheduler (EPS). The EPS attaches a short-lived "credit" budget to each incoming inference request to make admission and scheduling decisions that trade off latency, cost, and fairness across tenants and routes. The design combines kernel-cost estimates from the profiler, per-route SLAs, and configurable economic policies to preserve customer SLOs while minimizing operator cost.

Goals and non-goals:
- Goals:
  - Provide deterministic admission decisions for mixed workloads (interactive + batch) that respect per-route latency budgets and global cost targets.
  - Allow runtime to prioritize requests when capacity is constrained using an explicit credit currency.
  - Surface a small, inspectable config and telemetry surface for cost attribution and debugging.
- Non-goals:
  - This is not a replacement for the long-term scheduling fabric; EPS is an admission and intra-node prioritization layer.
  - EPS does not currently reassign credits between live requests; credits are assigned at admission and can be topped only by explicit policy hooks.

Design overview:
1) Credit currency and accounting
- Each request is assigned a numeric credit at admission. Credits are consumed by execution events (kernel dispatch, attention passes, KV cache fetch).
- Credit consumption map is derived from the profiler cost model (see "Profiling integration" below). Credits measure operator cost (approximate GPU milliseconds weighted by tensor compute intensity) rather than tokens or bytes to better correlate to real running cost.
- Credits are opaque to customers but logged in tracing and metrics with per-request credit_assigned and credit_remaining fields.

2) Admission policy and thresholds
- Admission uses a two-step check: (A) SLO guard: ensure the request's declared max-latency and model variant are compatible with current node tail-latency (p99) and slot availability; (B) Economic guard: request credit <= route_max_credit OR global_background_budget allows burst credits.
- Default thresholds (can be overridden per-tenant/route):
  - route_max_credit: 300 (default)
  - background_burst_budget_pct: 10% of spare capacity
  - min_credit_reserve: 20 (to prevent very small requests from starving kernels for bookkeeping)

3) Priority synthesis and preemption
- Priority key is a tuple: (tier, credit_price, latency_slack).
  - tier: explicit customer tier (hosted / dedicated / private).
  - credit_price: derived from route pricing config to favor higher-commit customers when cost is constrained.
  - latency_slack: (declared_slo - expected_runtime_latency) / declared_slo. Negative slack indicates likely SLO violation.
- When slots are contended, EPS sorts runnable requests by effective_priority_score = credit_price * (1 + max(0, -latency_slack)*SLA_WEIGHT) / sqrt(credits_assigned). This formula is tunable; see config table below.
- Preemption: soft preemption is supported for queued requests only (we avoid kernel-level preemption except for cooperative handoff). Soft preemption cancels queued low-priority requests and returns HTTP 429 with credit_refund.

4) Profiling integration
- The EPS consumes kernel-level cost hints from the continuous profiler pipeline. Key inputs:
  - kernel_average_ms_by_shape: mapping of (model,seq_len,batch_size) -> ms per token
  - attention_factor and kv_fetch_penalty per model family
- A local estimator converts declared request properties (model, prompt_len, expected_generated_tokens) into a credit estimate using the profile mapping. The estimator includes a conservative safety multiplier (default 1.25) to account for variability.

5) Telemetry and observability
- Per-request tags emitted to tracing and metrics: credit_assigned, credit_consumed, admission_decision, priority_score, preempted_by (request id).
- Dashboards to build:
  - Credit burn heatmap: credits_consumed / minute by node and model family.
  - Admission waterfall: requests accepted/rejected by reason (SLO, economic, malformed).
  - Priority inversion alarms: if lower priority requests are consistently served while higher-priority ones wait > 2x expected latency.

Config table (defaults):
| key | default | description |
|---|---:|---|
| eps.route_max_credit | 300 | Max credit per request for non-enterprise routes |
| eps.safety_multiplier | 1.25 | Multiplier applied to profiler estimate |
| eps.sla_weight | 8.0 | Weight for latency slack in priority_score |
| eps.background_burst_pct | 10 | Percent of idle capacity allowed for bursts |
| eps.min_credit_reserve | 20 | Minimum credit unit for the scheduler |
| eps.preempt_grace_ms | 1500 | Time allowed for soft preemption handlers |

Operational runbook (for oncall / SRE):
- Symptom: sudden spike in 429 rejections for interactive routes.
  1) Check "Admission waterfall" dashboard: confirm whether rejections are ECONOMIC or SLO.
  2) If ECONOMIC: inspect recent changes to eps.route_max_credit and global credit pool. Roll forward to previous config if an accidental drop occurred.
  3) If SLO: check node p99 latency and kernel watchdog logs. If p99 elevated > 2x baseline, escalate to runtime team and execute the "node-remediate-and-drain" procedure.
  4) Mitigation: temporarily raise background_burst_pct to 20% for 5–15 minutes using: 
```
redwoodctl runtime set-config --path eps.background_burst_pct --value 20 --expiry 15m
```
- Symptom: priority inversion alert firing.
  1) Inspect traces for preempted_by field. Identify request causing inversion.
  2) Check whether credit_price was misconfigured (billing or pricing service outage can zero a price).
  3) If misconfiguration, set a safe default: `eps.default_credit_price = 1.0` and re-evaluate.

Release and rollout checklist (canary strategy):
1) Unit tests for estimator and priority scoring.
2) Integration tests with profiler stub (simulate worst-case kernel-cost variance +15%).
3) Canary rollout to non-critical region (region-us-west-2-canal) with 2% traffic. Monitor credit-burn, 95th latency, and 429 rates for 30 minutes.
4) Gradual ramp to 25% then 100% with staged config updates.

Benchmarks and profiling harness to validate EPS:
- Synthetic scenarios to run in the benchmarking suite:
  1) Mixed-interactive: 70% short prompts (<64 tokens), 30% long streaming (>512 tokens) with standard concurrency. Measure admission rate and p95 latency.
  2) Peaky-burst: bursts of 10x baseline traffic for 2 minutes to verify background_burst_pct behavior and credit refunds.
  3) Priority-contest: mix of free-tier and enterprise-tier requests at 1:1 ratio under constrained capacity to validate economic ordering.
- Expected KPIs:
  - p95 latency for interactive routes <= configured SLO + 20ms during steady state.
  - 429 rate < 0.5% under steady state.

Debugging recipes (common queries):
- Find requests with high credit burn but low token count:
```
SELECT request_id, model, prompt_len, generated, credit_assigned, credit_consumed
FROM trace.requests
WHERE credit_consumed > 1000 AND generated < 32
ORDER BY credit_consumed DESC
LIMIT 50;
```
- Recompute estimator for a single request locally (Python snippet):
```
# estimator.py (snippet)
def estimate_credits(model, seq_in, gen, batch):
    base_ms = profile.get((model, seq_in+gen, batch), 0.8)
    credits = base_ms * (seq_in+gen) * eps.safety_multiplier
    return int(max(eps.min_credit_reserve, credits))
```

Ownership and escalation:
- Owner: Runtime Performance Team (runtime-performance@redwood.com)
- Primary oncall escalation: runtime-sre -> runtime-platform -> runtime-performance. See oncall rota in /people-ops/oncall.

Open questions and future work:
- Should credits be refundable in-part for aborted streaming requests? (tradeoff: bookkeeping cost vs user UX)
- Explore kernel-level cooperative credit donation for live re-prioritization.
- Integrate cost-based credits with billing so credits can be surfaced to customer dashboards for explainability.

Appendix: Config example (YAML)
```
# eps-config.yaml
eps:
  route_max_credit: 300
  safety_multiplier: 1.25
  sla_weight: 8.0
  background_burst_pct: 10
  min_credit_reserve: 20
  preempt_grace_ms: 1500
```

Links and references:
- Profiling pipeline: /eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/continuous-runtime-profiling-strategy-2026.json
- Scheduler policy language: /eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-policy-language-declarative-profiles-2026.json
- Admission runbooks: /eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-deployment-circuit-breakers-and-sla-fallback-playbook-2026.json

This doc will be updated as EPS matures — major revisions should include new benchmark runs and an updated release checklist.

title: Slot-abort Contract and Graceful Recovery Protocol
content:
SUMMARY

This document specifies the Slot-abort Contract and Graceful Recovery Protocol used by the serving runtime scheduler and kernel plugins. It formalizes the signals, invariants, telemetry, operator runbook, and verification tests required for safe slot abortion, state preservation, and deterministic recovery paths. The goal is to minimize user-visible SLO impact during kernel-level preemption, eviction, or forced termination while keeping the runtime auditable and testable.

INTENDED AUDIENCE
- Runtime kernel and scheduler engineers
- Oncall and SRE teams
- Release engineers validating scheduler behavior
- Performance and profiling teams

GOALS AND NON-GOALS
Goals:
- Define a single contract for how a running request slot may be aborted or suspended.
- Ensure deterministic state handoff for recoverable requests (KV cache, partial logits, decoding state).
- Provide telemetry and traces needed to map aborted slots to user-level tail latency/regressions.
- Standardize operator recovery steps and automated remediation.

Non-goals:
- This is not a doc for admission control or long-term placement policies (see scheduler-policy-language-declarative-profiles).
- Does not change model-serving API semantics for clients; all changes are internal to runtime.

BACKGROUND
Redwood’s serving runtime supports preemptive slot reclamation to maintain capacity and QoS. Historically, ad-hoc slot killing led to state loss, user-visible 5xxs, and noisy post-incident debugging. The Slot-abort Contract aims to normalize this behavior across kernel variants (synchronous kernels, async handoff kernels, multi-GPU shards).

TERMINOLOGY
- Slot: a runtime-execution reservation associated with a request pipeline (may span kvcache + token generation).
- Abort: an intentional termination of a slot prior to natural completion (categories below).
- Suspend: a low-latency serialization of in-flight state to persistent or shared memory for later resume.
- Handshake: the two-phase protocol between scheduler and kernel for safe slot transition.

ABORT CATEGORIES (with examples)
1) Planned Abort (managed): graceful eviction intended for maintenance or preemption windows. Example: drained node for upgrade.
2) Priority Preemptive Abort (policy): scheduler reclaims slot to satisfy a higher-priority request (e.g., enterprise dedicated pool overrides best-effort).
3) Forced Abort (emergency): kernel or host signals unrecoverable state (OOM, NVLINK fatal) and cannot complete handshake.
4) Latency-offload Abort: scheduler chooses to cut low-value tail requests to preserve p50/p95 for paying customers.

SIGNALING AND CONTRACT
- Outgoing abort request from scheduler to kernel: an RPC call AbortSlot(slot_id, reason_code, deadline_ms).
- Kernel must reply within handshake_deadline_ms with one of: ACK_SUSPEND, ACK_TERMINATE, NAK_RETRY.
- If ACK_SUSPEND: kernel emits a resume_token and writes minimal state to the shared suspension store (S3-like or in-cluster memstore).
- If ACK_TERMINATE: kernel attempts a best-effort flush of outputs (streamed partials) then perform local cleanup.
- If no reply before handshake_deadline_ms: scheduler marks slot as ForceKilled and increments ForceKill counter for telemetry.

Default timeouts (configurable):
| Config key | Default | Notes |
| ---------- | ------- | ----- |
| handshake_deadline_ms | 250 | Time allotted for kernel to respond to AbortSlot.
| suspend_write_ms | 100 | Time allowed to persist suspend state.
| resume_call_timeout_ms | 350 | Timeout for resume RPC when restoring a suspended slot.

STATE MODEL AND PERSISTENCE CONTRACT
- Minimal resume_token payload (string) must include: slot_schema_version, kernel_variant, kvcache_keys_hash, partial_decode_cursor, bytes_written_checksum.
- Suspension store contract: put(resume_token, binary_snapshot) must be idempotent and versioned. Failure modes must return explicit error codes (STORE_EWRITE, STOREFULL).
- On resume, kernel must validate token schema_version and kvcache_hash; mismatch -> FAIL_RESUME and surface as recoverable shim error.

TELEMETRY & TRACE SIGNALS (REQUIRED)
Emit standardized tracing annotations and metrics for every abort flow:
- trace/span tags: slot.id, abort.reason, abort.initiator (scheduler/kernel/host), kernel.variant, resume.token.present (true/false).
- counters: slot.abort.total, slot.abort.forcekill, slot.suspend.success, slot.resume.success, slot.resume.fail.
- histograms: suspend_write_latency_ms, resume_latency_ms, abort_handshake_latency_ms.

SLO IMPACT & ALERTING THRESHOLDS
Use these as initial operational thresholds (tunable per pool):
- If slot.abort.forcekill / slot.abort.total > 0.05 for 1h -> SEV2.
- If slot.resume.fail rate > 0.01 over 30m -> SEV2 and rollback any enabling rollout.
- If suspend_write_latency_ms p95 > 200ms -> investigate storage layer; create SEV3.
- Tail-latency correlation: if p99_request_latency increases by >15% coincident with increased slot.aborts -> open incident.

OPERATOR RUNBOOK (investigation and remediation)
1) Detect: receive alert (e.g., slot.resume.fail > 1%).
2) Gather context:
   - kubectl logs of kernel pod(s) with slot.id; retrieve trace span from tracing UI.
   - Query suspension store for resume_token existence: curl -X GET https://suspend-store/api/v1/tokens/<token>.
   - Check node GPU health: nvidia-smi -q; verify ECC/warnings.
3) Triaging steps (ordered):
   a) If ForceKill counter increased across many slots -> suspect handshake_deadline tuning or kernel blocking. Temporarily increase handshake_deadline_ms in canary to 500ms and observe.
   b) If store errors (STORE_EWRITE / STOREFULL) -> free space or fail fast to ensure kernel falls back to ACK_TERMINATE path.
   c) If resume validation fails (schema mismatch) -> mark resume_token as invalid; schedule automated metric to failback to full retry path and roll back kernel variant that introduced schema change.
4) Remediation:
   - For storage latency: route suspend writes to fallback in-cluster memstore and flag for storage team.
   - For kernel stalls: trigger runtime profiling (see PROFILE: gstack capture command below) and scale up auxiliary worker threads.
   - For node-level failures: cordon node and migrate slots via scheduler handoff policy.
5) Communication: create incident with slot.id examples, attach traces and last 50 lines of kernel logs, and tag oncall team.

EXAMPLE COMMANDS AND SNIPPETS
- AbortSlot RPC pseudo-call (go):
  client.AbortSlot(ctx, &pb.AbortRequest{SlotId: "slot-12345", Reason: pb.AbortReason_PREEMPT, DeadlineMs: 250})

- Inspect suspend store:
  curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $SUSPEND_STORE_TOKEN" https://suspend-store.internal/api/v1/tokens/slot-12345-token | jq '.'

- Quick local debug: capture the last 2MB of kernel logs and upload to S3:
  kubectl logs -n runtime kernel-pod-abc --tail=10000 > /tmp/kernel-logs.txt && aws s3 cp /tmp/kernel-logs.txt s3://redwood-debug/$(hostname)-kernel-logs.txt

TEST SUITE AND BENCHMARKS
We require a set of unit and integration checks for any change to scheduler or kernel:
- Unit tests: verify resume_token schema round-trip, idempotency of store operations, and handshake timeouts.
- Integration tests (CI): simulate Planned Abort, Preemptive Abort, Forced Abort under mixed load and assert percent of forcekills < 0.5% at p95 concurrency.
- Chaos test: orchestrated kernel stall injection (sleep in abort handler) combined with storage latency injection; assert system maintains p95 SLO for high-priority pool.
- Benchmark target: suspend_write_ms p50 < 20ms, p95 < 120ms on production-like suspension store.

INSTRUMENTATION GUIDANCE FOR PROFILING TEAMS
- Add a labeled trace span around AbortSlot/Handshake with sampling rate 100% for first 5 minutes of any canary rollout.
- Attach stack snapshots when handshake latency exceeds 2x median. Use the profiling pipeline:
  - capture: runtime-profiling agent collect --span=abort-handshake --limit=3
  - analyze: upload to internal profiler and mark as abort-handshake digest.

CANARY AND ROLLOUT CHECKLIST (pre-deploy gate)
- Unit and integration tests green.
- Canary rollout (10% of nodes) for 24h with 100% trace sampling on abort flows.
- Verify metrics: slot.suspend.success > 99.5%, slot.resume.success > 99.9% for canary.
- Confirm no increase in customer-facing 5xxs or p99 latency beyond 5% baseline.
- Approve by runtime lead and SRE reviewer.

IMPLEMENTATION NOTES FOR KERNEL AUTHORS
- Keep suspend payload minimal; avoid serializing entire kvcache — instead persist key hashes and rely on shared kvcache invalidation/refresh on resume.
- Prefer async suspend writes: serialize-to-local-buffer then background upload; ensure background uploader is bounded and contributes to backpressure metrics.
- For multi-GPU shards: two-phase suspend where master shard coordinates a quorum ack before returning ACK_SUSPEND.

OWNERSHIP, ESCALATION AND ADDITIONAL RESOURCES
- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime/kernel-scheduling team (SL: Jordan Lee).
- Oncall escalation: eng-infra SRE -> runtime platform -> kernel-scheduling.
- Related pages: tuning guidance for handshake_deadline (see related_pages) and suspend-store SLA page (internal link).

CHANGE HISTORY
- 2026-11-15: Draft authored (Evelyn Cho).
- 2026-12-08: Added telemetry counters and initial SLO thresholds (review by Priya Ramanathan).
- 2027-03-02: Finalized operator runbook and canary checklist; published after two-week canary validation.

APPENDIX A: RESUME TOKEN EXAMPLE (JSON-LIKE)
{
  "token": "slot-v1-abcd1234",
  "slot_schema_version": "1",
  "kernel_variant": "async-shard-3",
  "kvcache_keys_hash": "sha256:...",
  "partial_decode_cursor": "tokpos:1024",
  "crc32": "0x9af3b1"
}

APPENDIX B: QUICK-REFERENCE TABLES
- Abort reason codes:
  - PREEMPT: policy preemption
  - MAINTENANCE: planned maintenance
  - OOM: out-of-memory detected on device
  - HW_FATAL: hardware fatal (nvlink/ecc)
  - SUSPEND_TIMEOUT: kernel did not complete suspend in allowed window

- Handshake outcomes and downstream action:
  - ACK_SUSPEND -> persist state -> scheduler marks slot as Suspended -> possible resume later.
  - ACK_TERMINATE -> best-effort emit partial outputs -> mark request as Aborted.
  - NAK_RETRY -> scheduler may retry abort after backoff.
  - NO_RESPONSE -> ForceKilled; allocate replacement slot and increment alerting counters.

If there are questions about edge cases or proposals to change timing/config, open a design RFC in the kernel-scheduling team space and reference this document.

title: Scheduler Resource Tagging and Precedence Manifest
content:
Overview

Purpose: This document specifies the resource-tagging and precedence manifest used by Redwood's scheduler to make deterministic decisions about kernel assignment, admission control, and graceful degradation. Resource tags let higher layers add lightweight metadata to requests (workload characteristics, cost-sensitivity, fidelity budget, retry semantics) that the scheduler uses together with telemetry to make per-request placement and preemption choices.

Goals
- Make scheduling decisions predictable and auditable by standardizing tags and precedence rules.
- Expose controllable levers to product and platform teams to express cost vs fidelity tradeoffs.
- Ensure backward compatibility: untagged requests follow current best-effort policies.
- Provide operator runbooks and profiling guidance for tag-driven regressions.

Scope and Non-Goals
- Scope: runtime admission controller, scheduler policy layer, kernel hinting, and observability fields.
- Non-Goals: model selection logic, API surface changes for customers (tags are internal to Redwood and derived from routing policies or per-tenant config).

Key Concepts and Terminology
- Resource Tag: structured label attached to a request at the service boundary. Tags are short key:value tokens.
- Precedence Manifest: ordered rule set that maps tag combinations to scheduling actions (admit, queue-with-sla, degrade-mode, preemptible).
- Degradation Mode: a policy action that reduces fidelity (quantized model variant, prefix cache usage, early cutoff).
- Kernel Hint: annotation passed to kernel mapper that influences kernel selection (e.g., preferred kernel family or tight latency bound).

Design Principles
1) Keep tags small and typed: allow exactly the tag keys documented in the manifest.
2) Deterministic precedence: rules are evaluated top-to-bottom; earlier rule wins.
3) Least-privilege impact: tags can only reduce resource footprint or request priority, never increase allocation.
4) Observability-first: every evaluation emits a traceable event containing the matched rule id and rationale.

Resource Tag Schema (canonical keys)
- fidelity: {high, standard, economical}  # fidelity budget for the request
- cost_sensitivity: {low, medium, high}  # willingness to use expensive kernels or CPU fallback
- latency_class: {interactive, best_effort, batch}  # latency tolerance
- preemptible: {true, false}  # candidate for preemption under pressure
- cache_hint: {kv_prefetch, prefix_cache_ok, no_cache}  # cache preferences
- isolation: {tenant_dedicated, tenant_shared}  # tenancy isolation; impacts shard placement

Example Tagging Table (ascii)
| Tag key | Purpose | Default | Notes |
| fidelity | fidelity budget | standard | high=use highest-quality model variant if latency allows |
| cost_sensitivity | operator cost tolerance | medium | low=prefer quantized kernels and batching |
| latency_class | scheduling latency target | interactive | impacts admission timeout |
| preemptible | preemption candidacy | false | true allows background eviction under pressure |

Precedence Manifest (human-readable sample)
1) rule_id: P-01-critical-interactive
   match: fidelity=high AND latency_class=interactive AND isolation=tenant_dedicated
   action: admit_prefetch, kernel_hint=low-latency, preemptible=false
   rationale: SLA-backed dedicated tenant traffic must be prioritized; kernel hint prefers kernels tuned for short sequences

2) rule_id: P-02-econ-background
   match: fidelity=economical OR cost_sensitivity=high OR preemptible=true
   action: queue-with-sla(200ms), kernel_hint=quantized-prefer, allow_batched_execution=true
   rationale: background tasks should use cost-optimized paths and accept higher latency

3) rule_id: P-03-standard-shared
   match: isolation=tenant_shared AND latency_class=interactive
   action: admit_with_quota, kernel_hint=balanced, preemptible=true

4) rule_id: P-99-default
   match: catch-all
   action: best-effort admit, kernel_hint=balanced

Manifest Format and Storage
- Manifest is stored as a versioned YAML in the control plane: /manifests/scheduler/resource-precedence/{version}.yaml
- Each manifest publishes: id, created_by, created_at, rules[], validation_hash.
- Validation: control plane runs static validation on update (no contradictory rules, explicit default rule present).

YAML Example (extracted)
---
version: v1.2
created_by: scheduler-team
created_at: 2026-02-01
rules:
  - id: P-01-critical-interactive
    match: "fidelity == 'high' && latency_class == 'interactive' && isolation == 'tenant_dedicated'"
    action: "admit_prefetch, kernel_hint=low-latency, preemptible=false"
  - id: P-02-econ-background
    match: "fidelity == 'economical' || cost_sensitivity == 'high' || preemptible == 'true'"
    action: "queue-with-sla(200ms), kernel_hint=quantized-prefer, allow_batched_execution=true"
---

Runtime Evaluation Flow (per-request)
1) Request enters ingress; routing layer attaches derived tags (from customer config, route labels, or system defaults).
2) Admission controller fetches latest precedence manifest and evaluates rules top-to-bottom.
3) Matched action produces an Admission Decision object containing: target kernel_hint, admission_bucket, preemptible flag, degradation plan id.
4) Admission decision is persisted as an event and attached to the request trace for auditing.
5) Kernel mapper consumes kernel_hint and schedules kernel execution; preemption decisions are handled by the quota controller.

Observability and Telemetry Changes
- New telemetry fields to include in traces/metrics: precedent_rule_id, admission_decision, computed_slot_cost_estimate, kernel_hint, preemptible_flag.
- Exported metrics: precedence_rule_match_count{rule_id}, precedence_rule_latency_ms{rule_id}.
- Alerting: sudden shift in matches to P-02-econ-background for a high-SLA tenant triggers an incident.

Profiling and Benchmarking Guidance
- Profiling playbook change: when benchmarking slot consumption, record matched precedence_rule_id for each trace. Use this to correlate rule effects on tail latency.
- New microbench: tag-sensitivity-stressor. Procedure:
  1) Generate synthetic traffic with identical payloads but differing tag sets (high vs economical).
  2) Measure kernel selection distribution, per-token latency, and per-request cost.
  3) Validate that economical tags reduce per-token cost by >= 20% vs standard baseline for same model family.

Operator Runbook: Precedence Regression (critical)
- Symptom: production latency spike coinciding with increased matches to P-02-econ-background for interactive routes.
- Quick triage steps:
  1) Query traces for precedence_rule_match_count where rule_id==P-02-econ-background over last 15m.
     CLI: rquery metrics precedence_rule_match_count --filter "rule_id=P-02-econ-background" --range 15m
  2) Identify affected tenant_ids from traces with tag isolation=tenant_shared and latency_class=interactive.
  3) Roll back manifest to previous version: control-plane-cli manifest rollback --name resource-precedence --to-version v1.1
  4) If rollback not possible, apply emergency override: control-plane-cli manifest patch --set "rules[0].action='admit_with_quota, kernel_hint=balanced, preemptible=false'"
  5) Post-incident: run profiling microbench and annotate the root cause in the incident ticket.

Release Notes (short entry)
- 2026-06-15: Introduced Resource Tagging & Precedence Manifest v1.2.0.
  - Adds fidelity/cost_sensitivity/latency_class tags.
  - Default manifest contains deterministic precedence and observability hooks.
  - Telemetry fields added: precedent_rule_id, kernel_hint.

Backward Compatibility and Migration
- Untagged traffic is matched by P-99-default and behaves like existing scheduler logic.
- Migration plan for Dedicated customers: gradually attach isolation=tenant_dedicated at routing-layer; this unlocks lower-latency kernels and disables preemption.

Security and Privacy Considerations
- Tags contain no PII and are generated by routing logic or internal policy.
- Manifest changes are restricted to scheduler-admin role with audit logging enabled.

Known Limitations and Issues
- K-101: Under multi-tenant noise, the "queue-with-sla(200ms)" action can lead to unpredictable slot entanglement. Mitigation: add explicit per-tenant queue caps in next manifest.
- K-102: Kernel_hint favors quantized kernels for economical tags; regression found on short-sequence chat where quantized kernel introduces hallucination regressions under specific logits threshold. Tracking ticket: SCHED-4793.

Testing and Validation Checklist for Manifest Changes
1) Static validation: lint manifest, ensure default rule present.
2) Unit tests: rule matching semantics, short-circuit precedence ordering tests.
3) Integration canary: deploy to canary pool for non-critical tenants for 48h.
4) Benchmark gate: run tag-sensitivity-stressor and verify cost/latency deltas against baseline.
5) Beta rollout: enable for 10% traffic of new tenants, monitor precedence_rule_match_count and tail latency.

Operational Metrics to Monitor After Rollout
- precedence_rule_match_count by rule_id (trend and sudden shifts)
- admission_decision_latencies P50/P90/P99
- kernel_selection_entropy (higher indicates varied kernel churn)
- per-tenant preemptions per-minute

Owner and Contact
- Primary owner: eng-serving-scheduler team (oncall alias: eng-serving-scheduler@redwood.ai)
- Document steward: Asha Patel (asha.patel@redwood.ai)

Appendix A: Example Trace Snippet (annotated)
- trace_id: 0001
- tags: fidelity=high, latency_class=interactive, isolation=tenant_dedicated
- precedence_rule_id: P-01-critical-interactive
- admission_decision: admit_prefetch; kernel_hint=low-latency; preemptible=false
- kernel_selected: kernel-family-v2-lowlatency

Appendix B: FAQ
Q: Can customers influence tags?
A: Not directly. Tags are derived from routing rules and customer's plan mapping (dedicated vs shared, SLAs), and from internal cost-sensitivity mappings.

Q: Will tags slow down admission?
A: Tag matching is optimized and cached per route; additional latency is under 200us in canary measurements.

Document History
- 2026-02-10: Draft created by Asha Patel
- 2026-03-05: Internal review and telemetry additions by Miguel Ortega
- 2026-06-15: Published (v1.2) with schedule-team approved changes

End of Document

title: SLA-aware Admission Controller and Backpressure Playbook
content:
Summary:

This playbook defines the SLA-aware Admission Controller and Backpressure strategy for Redwood's serving runtime. It describes the design, configuration, operational runbook, and recommended testing/benchmarking steps to ensure tenant-level SLOs are respected under mixed workloads and overload scenarios. The playbook targets runtime-admission (service), kernel-scheduler (service), and dispatcher components and is intended for on-call, runtime engineers, and SREs.

Goals and scope:

- Ensure per-tenant and per-route latency SLOs are prioritized when system capacity is constrained.
- Provide deterministic admission behavior that is auditable and testable.
- Define backpressure signals exposed to clients and internal services.
- Offer a practical operational runbook for detecting, mitigating, and rolling back admission policy changes.

Out of scope:

- Model-level quality regressions (handled by Optimize/evals).
- Long-term capacity provisioning (handled by capacity-planning team).

Background and motivation:

As traffic patterns diversify and multi-tenant traffic mixes (short-chat, long-generation, embeddings), the runtime must protect defined SLOs (p95/p99 for latency) for high-priority tenants. Simple FIFO queues allow noisy tenants to consume disproportionate kernel slots and drive SLO violations.
