An admission controller that incorporates SLA buckets, dynamic scoring, and token budgets prevents this while enabling graceful degradation for best-effort traffic.

Design overview (high level):

1) Components
- runtime-admission: front-line HTTP/gRPC gateway that accepts requests, validates routing, and evaluates admission score.
- kernel-scheduler: allocates kernel slots and issues low-level backpressure when GPU resources are saturated.
- dispatcher: routes admitted requests to worker shards and observes queueing metrics.

2) Signals and inputs to admission decision
- Tenant SLA tier (platinum/gold/silver/best-effort).
- Real-time queue depth and queue wait time (per-tenant).
- Recent kernel eviction/timeout rates and per-shard utilization.
- Token budget consumption (per-tenant per-window).
- Experiment/canary overrides (for rollout testing).

3) Outcome actions
- Admit immediately and assign priority metadata.
- Defer (hold in bounded waiting queue with estimated wait).
- Reject with structured payload (429 with retry-after and fallback model suggestion).
- Route to best-effort fallback pool (quantized/low-cost variant).

Admission algorithm (practical rules):

- Each tenant has a configured SLA bucket: {tier, p95_ms_target, burst_tokens_per_minute, steady_tokens_per_minute}. Example tiers: platinum (p95 120ms), gold (p95 200ms), silver (p95 500ms), best-effort (no p95 SLO).

- Score calculation (simplified):
  score = (tier_weight / (1 + queue_wait_ratio)) * available_token_ratio - penalty(kernel_eviction_rate)
  where values are normalized to [0,1]. The admission threshold is configurable per-service.

- Token budgets are refilled on a leaky-bucket; requests consume budget proportional to estimated token cost (sequence length * model_cost_factor).

Backpressure signals and API:

- kernel-scheduler exposes gRPC stream /v1/backpressure with messages: {shard_id, congestion_level, suggested_drain_ms, affected_models}.
- runtime-admission subscribes and translates congestion_level to per-tenant queue caps and admission thresholds.
- HTTP response header additions for observability and client behavior: X-Redwood-Admission: admitted|deferred|rejected, X-Redwood-Estimated-Wait: <ms>, X-Redwood-Policy-Id: <id>.

SLOs and thresholds (examples):

- Default per-tenant p95 targets (example): platinum 120ms, gold 200ms, silver 500ms.
- Maximum admission queue depth per shard: 512 requests.
- Defer-to-reject pivot: if average estimated wait > 2 * p95_target for tier AND kernel_eviction_rate > 0.05, switch to reject for best-effort.

Configuration examples (YAML):

# admission-policy.yaml
policy:
  name: sla-aware-default
  tiers:
    - name: platinum
      p95_ms: 120
      tier_weight: 1.0
      burst_tokens_per_minute: 60
      steady_tokens_per_minute: 20
    - name: gold
      p95_ms: 200
      tier_weight: 0.7
      burst_tokens_per_minute: 40
      steady_tokens_per_minute: 12
    - name: silver
      p95_ms: 500
      tier_weight: 0.4
      burst_tokens_per_minute: 20
      steady_tokens_per_minute: 6
    - name: best-effort
      p95_ms: 0
      tier_weight: 0.1
      burst_tokens_per_minute: 10
      steady_tokens_per_minute: 2

# kernel backpressure thresholds
kernel:
  congestion_levels:
    - level: 0
      util_pct: 0-70
    - level: 1
      util_pct: 71-85
    - level: 2
      util_pct: 86-95
    - level: 3
      util_pct: 96-100
  level_actions:
    0: no_action
    1: tighten_admission_by: 10%
    2: tighten_admission_by: 25%
    3: reject_non_critical: true

Operational runbook (oncall) - overload detection:

1) Detect: Alerts to pager when aggregated kernel_utilization > 92% for > 60s OR p95 per-tenant latency > configured p95_target for two consecutive 30s windows.
2) Triage: Use dashboards: Runtime -> Admission -> Per-tenant queue depth, Kernel -> shard_utilization and eviction_rate, Dispatcher -> per-route latency heatmap.
3) Short-term mitigation (fast, <5m):
   a) Increase admission strictness: curl -XPOST http://runtime-admission/internal/policy/tighten -d '{"factor":0.25}'
   b) Apply emergency routing to fallback pool: kubectl patch svc dispatcher -p '{"spec": {"selector": {"pool":"fallback"}}}' (use only for best-effort heavy traffic).
   c) If single tenant causing noise, temporarily throttle via: POST /internal/tenants/{id}/throttle with {"rate": "5 rps"}.
4) Medium-term mitigation (5-30m):
   a) Temporarily increase worker replicas for fallback pool if capacity available.
   b) Engage capacity-planning if average utilization remains > 85% for > 30m.
5) Communication: Post status on #runtime-ops with subject [Admission Overload] and include quick metrics snapshot: top 5 tenants by queue depth, kernel_eviction_rate, affected models.

Runbook: admission policy rollback and canary steps:

- Canary rollout matrix: 1% traffic for 15m, observe p95/p99 and kernel_eviction_rate. If no regression, progress to 10% for 30m, then 50% for 60m, then full.
- Rollback command: POST /internal/policy/activate with previous_policy_id or kubectl apply -f admission-policy-previous.yaml.
- Safety gates automated: If p95 for any platinum tenant degrades by >20% vs baseline or kernel_eviction_rate > 3%, automatically rollback to last stable policy.

Diagnostics and telemetry to collect (minimum):

- Per-request: tenant_id, route_id, estimated_token_cost, admission_outcome, estimated_wait_ms, kernel_shard_id.
- Aggregates: per-tenant queue depth, average wait, admitted rate, rejected rate, kernel_eviction_rate per shard.
- Traces: end-to-end trace from runtime-admission to kernel-scheduler with 5% sampling for normal, 50% for overload.

Testing and benchmarking plan:

- Synthetic scenarios in the perf harness: mix of short (<=64 tokens) chat, medium (256 tokens) generation, long (>=1024 tokens) generations, and embedding streams.
- Run 6h soak tests with 70/20/10 mix (short/medium/long) at 1.5x expected peak to validate admission fairness and SLO preservation.
- Validate canary using shadow traffic: compare admitted outcomes and latency deltas against baseline.

Example troubleshooting checklist (quick):

- If many deferred requests but low admitted latency: inspect token budgets and refill rates.
- If kernel_eviction_rate high: check large-sequence tenants and apply temporary model-variant routing.
- If single shard hot: verify shard affinity and consider rebalance (see runtime-shard-placement playbook).

Ownership and escalation:

- Primary owner: runtime-scheduling team (oncall: runtime-sched-rotations).
- Secondary: eng-sre.
- For capacity issues escalate to capacity-planning lead.

Compatibility notes / Release considerations:

- Admission changes are backward compatible for clients; runtime will continue to return structured 429 responses.
- When introducing new header fields (X-Redwood-Estimated-Wait), coordinate with SDK team and document in SDK changelog.

Related artifacts and links:
- Perf harness job: perf/sla-admission-harness (internal CI)
- Telemetry dashboard: /dashboards/runtime-admission-sla
- Kernel backpressure gRPC proto: proto/runtime/backpressure.proto

Appendix: sample 429 response payload (JSON)

{
  "error": "capacity_exceeded",
  "reason": "platinum-sla-protect",
  "retry_after_seconds": 8,
  "suggested_fallback": "gpt4-small-quantized"
}
Notes and future work:

- Research item: incorporate model-level estimated compute (measured in flops or kernel cycles) into token budget calculation.
- Explore reinforcement learning approach for dynamic admission thresholds.

Document history:
- 2027-02-14 created by Priya Natarajan
- 2027-03-01 updated: clarified backpressure API and added automatic safety rollback gate.

title: Kernel ABI & Quantization Kernel Compatibility Guidelines
content:
Summary

This document describes the compatibility matrix and operational guidelines for kernel ABIs and quantization-optimized kernels used by the Redwood serving runtime. It covers version mapping, supported GPU microarchitectures, recommended fallback strategies, preflight tests, safe rollout and rollback procedures, and required telemetry for forensic analysis. The goal is to make kernel selection predictable across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments and to reduce upgrade risk for private (VPC / on-prem) customers.

Scope

- Kernel ABIs exposed by the runtime (cuda/cudnn/cuBLAS, ROCm, oneAPI-compatible kernels)
- Quantization-aware kernels (int8, int4, dynamic-float16 paths) and heuristics that select them
- Compatibility across accelerator generations (NVIDIA Ampere, Hopper, Ada; AMD CDNA2/CDNA3; Intel Gaudi/ARC where applicable)
- Runtime-level rollback and canary test procedures for private deployments

Audience

This is intended for: runtime engineers, kernel maintainers, private-deploy field operators, SREs, and solutions engineers who run customer rollouts.

1) High-level compatibility principles

- ABI-first: prefer stable runtime ABI targets (e.g., CUDA 11.x vs 12.x). Kernel optimizations should be feature-gated, not ABI-breaking.
- Architecture-aware selection: kernels must declare supported architectures (e.g., sm_80, sm_90, gfx110x) and a minimum driver/firmware requirement.
- Graceful fallback: for any quantized kernel that fails validation, the runtime must fall back to the next-safe kernel (e.g., int8 -> fp16 -> fp32) while preserving request semantics.
- Telemetry and evidence preservation: every kernel switch must emit structured telemetry (see "Telemetry requirements" section) to support post-incident forensics.

2) Kernel compatibility table (summary)

| Kernel type | Typical ABI / Driver req | Supported HW (examples) | Quant modes | Notes |
|-------------|-------------------------|-------------------------|-------------|-------|
| high-throughput-mha-optim (CUDA) | CUDA 12.1+, driver 535+ | NVIDIA Ada (RTX 40x0/ GH200 variants), Hopper (H100) | fp16, bf16 | Uses Tensor Cores; requires cuBLAS/cuDNN GPU kernels; prefers workspace memory >= 8 MB |
| int8-mha-fastpath | CUDA 12.1+, driver 540+ | NVIDIA Hopper (H100) with int8 tensor cores | int8 | Only for models validated to <1% quality delta; must be feature gated per-customer |
| rocm-mha-optimized | ROCm 5.6+ | AMD CDNA2 (Instinct MI100), CDNA3 | fp16, bf16 | Requires ROCm kernel packages; falls back to CPU-hosted fp32 path if missing |
| oneapi-bf16-path | oneAPI 2023.4+ | Intel Gaudi/ARC experimental | bf16 | API experimental; enabled only in internal QA and by explicit customer opt-in |

(Full machine-readable matrix is stored in the kernel registry: /internal/registries/kernel-compat-2026.csv)

3) Preflight checks (private deployments)

Before enabling a new kernel set on a private deployment, run the checklist below. These steps must be automated and recorded in the release ticket.

Preflight checklist (ordered):
1. Inventory: collect accelerator model, driver version, firmware revision and OS kernel (uname -a) from every node.
2. Sizing: ensure ephemeral workspace and pinned GPU memory meet kernel requirements (example: 8 MB workspace recommended for mha-optim).
3. Driver validation: verify drivers meet minimum versions listed in the compatibility table.
4. Artifact attestation: verify kernel artifacts signatures using the internal signing key (see CLI snippet).
5. Unit kernel smoke: run the kernel smoke harness (tools/kernel-smoke-runner) on a representative node.
6. Regression eval: run a small, deterministic prompt set against the canary cluster (N=1k tokens) and check quality regressions (absolute delta thresholds per model).
7. Telemetry gating: ensure telemetry hooks are deployed and forwarding to the evidence sink.

Example CLI snippets:

# retrieve GPU inventory (Linux)
$ sudo /opt/redwood/bin/gpu-inventory --output json > gpu-inventory.json

# verify kernel artifact signature
$ /opt/redwood/bin/artifact-verify --artifact /opt/kernels/mha-optim-v2.tar.gz --trusted-keys /etc/redwood/trusted-keys.pem

4) Canary rollout plan (safe pattern for private/VPC deployments)

Principles: small blast radius, automatic quality gates, rollback hooks, and customer notification where required.

Step-by-step canary plan:
1. Create a canary pool: reserve 2–4 nodes (must be isolated from production tenant traffic).
2. Apply kernel bundle to canary nodes and restart runtime components using the operator's safe-restart hook.
3. Run functional smoke and deterministic evals. Must pass model-level quality gates:
   - Top-level service SLOs (p95 latency, error rate) must remain within 10% of baseline.
   - Quality regression per-model must be <= configured delta (default 0.8% absolute token-level difference).
4. Run load-validation: replay recorded production traces at 1x and 2x QPS for 30 minutes. Monitor CPU/GPU utilization and latency tails.
5. If all gates pass, promote kernel bundle to a staged subset (10% of production nodes) and run the same checks for 2 hours.
6. Gradually increase to 50% and then 100% using automated health checks.

If any gate fails, follow the rollback procedure immediately. Notify the customer and create a postmortem if customer-affecting.

5) Rollback procedure (operator-safe)

Goals: restore previous stable kernel, preserve forensic evidence, avoid data loss.

Immediate rollback steps:
1. Abort ongoing promotions using the operator: /opt/redwood/bin/operator promote --abort <bundle-id>
2. Mark the canary nodes read-only for new model swaps: /opt/redwood/bin/node-ralm --set read-only
3. Revert kernel artifacts to the last-known-good bundle: /opt/redwood/bin/artifact-apply --bundle-id <last-good>
4. Restart runtime components with --preserve-kv to avoid KV cache loss when possible.
5. Run validation smoke and replay a 10-minute production trace.
6. Collect forensic evidence: kernel logs, telemetry spans, driver stack traces. Package them with the rollback ticket.

Operator CLI example for rollback:

# revert to last known good bundle
$ /opt/redwood/bin/artifact-apply --bundle-id rwbundle-2026-09-12 --force && sudo systemctl restart redwood-runtime --preserve-kv

6) Forensic telemetry and required traces

Minimum telemetry emitted on kernel switch events (every value must be present):
- event_type: KERNEL_SWITCH
- timestamp_utc
- node_id
- bundle_id
- previous_kernel_id
- new_kernel_id
- driver_version
- firmware_revision
- validation_signatures (artifact sig id)
- smoke_results: pass/fail and short hash of the test output
- quality_eval_summary: per-model numeric deltas

Retention: for private deployments, preserve full forensic packages for 90 days (customer contract permitting). Evidence bundles must be stored in the customer-specific evidence bucket with immutability flags when requested by compliance.

7) Quality gating configuration (suggested defaults)

- latency_p95_increase_threshold: 10%
- error_rate_absolute_threshold: 0.5%
- per_model_quality_delta: 0.8% absolute token-level difference
- smoke_harness_timeout: 300s

8) Known incompatibility patterns & mitigation recipes

Pattern: int8 kernel yields subtle hallucination drift on long prompts.
Mitigation: restrict int8 to short-sequence inference or enable per-model calibration. If a customer requires long-context fidelity, prefer bf16 or fp16 kernels.

Pattern: ROCm kernel fails on nodes with older firmware microcode.
Mitigation: require firmware >= vendor-specified minimum; if not possible, mark nodes as non-candidate for this bundle.

9) Customer-facing configuration knobs (private deploys)

Operators can expose the following flags to customers during onboarding (document in the customer-runbook template):
- enable_experimental_kernels: boolean (default false)
- per_model_quantization_profile: URL to customer-approved profile
- max_latency_slo: integer (ms) to allow tuning fallback aggressiveness

10) Post-incident checklist and postmortem template

1. Preserve evidence bundle and copy to secure forensic store.
2. Populate postmortem with timeline, root cause hypotheses, and customer impact.
3. Run replays using isolated sandbox and test candidate fixes.
4. Share corrective action plan with stakeholders and schedule follow-up.

Appendix A — Kernel artifact signing and verification

- All kernel bundles must be signed by the release pipeline using the Redwood release key. Artifacts without a valid signature are rejected by the operator.
- Signing command (CI):
$ gpg --batch --yes --armor --sign --detach-sign --local-user redwood-release-key artifacts/mha-optim-v2.tar.gz

- Verification (operator):
$ /opt/redwood/bin/artifact-verify --artifact artifacts/mha-optim-v2.tar.gz --trusted-keys /etc/redwood/trusted-keys.pem

Appendix B — Minimal test matrix (smoke harness samples)

| Test name | Purpose | Expected result | Run time |
|-----------|---------|-----------------|----------|
| kernel-basic-launch | Validate kernel loads and exports expected symbols | success, no segfault | 30s |
| inkernel-inference | Basic generate for short prompt (N=3 tokens) | exact output hash match | 45s |
| stress-multi-stream | 8 concurrent streams for 60s | p95 latency < configured threshold | 60s |

Appendix C — Ownership and escalation

- Primary owner: kernels team (eng-serving-runtime) — Mateo Alvarez
- Secondary: SRE on-call for serving runtime
- Escalation: if rollback required and customer impact > 10% of SLO, page Director of Platform (on-call list) and notify Customer Success lead for the affected account.

Related documents and artifacts

- Kernel compatibility registry: /internal/registries/kernel-compat-2026.csv
- Kernel smoke harness: git@internal:redwood/tools/kernel-smoke-runner.git
- Artifact signing key rotation policy: /confluence/security-and-compliance/crypto-agile-key-rotation-2026

Change log

- 2026-02-15: Created (initial draft)
- 2026-06-01: Added canary rollout timings and telemetry fields (Priya Rangan)
- 2026-08-12: Clarified rollback commands and preserved-kv restart semantics (Janelle Park)

title: Per-request Kernel Hedging and Lazy Activation Guide
content:
Overview
-------
This guide documents the design, operator configuration, and runbook for the per-request kernel hedging and lazy activation mechanisms implemented in the Redwood inference runtime. These features are targeted at reducing tail latency caused by kernel cold-starts, kernel contention, and cross-tenant kernel churn without sacrificing average throughput or fair resource sharing.

Goals and non-goals
-------------------
- Goals:
  - Reduce 99th and 99.9th percentile latency for short and medium-length generation requests by enabling hedged fallbacks and lazy kernel activation.
  - Limit additional cost and kernel churn by constraining hedging concurrency and using heuristics to trigger lazy activation only when beneficial.
  - Provide clear telemetry and operator controls to tune behavior per-tenant, per-model, and per-runtime-pool.
- Non-goals:
  - Replace the scheduler or admission control; these features are orthogonal and intentionally conservative.
  - Change core cost accounting semantics; hedged requests are tracked for chargeback and forecasting but billed according to existing token accounting.

Architecture and high-level flow
-------------------------------
1. Request classification: incoming RPCs are annotated with request hints (sequence_length_estimate, priority_class, model_variant_hint). The classifier runs in the front-end (service: router-proxy) and tags requests that are "hedge-eligible."
2. Kernel lookup & probe: the runtime consults the kernel catalog for the requested model_variant. If the preferred kernel instance is unavailable or in a cold state, the runtime triggers lazy activation and marks a soft deadline (hedge_deadline_ms).
3. Hedged probe: at hedge_deadline_ms, the scheduler may launch a hedged request to an alternative kernel variant or a pre-warmed lightweight kernel shim (see Kernel Variants below).
4. Fast-path response: whichever path returns first wins; the other hedged request is cancelled and its metrics are recorded for hedging efficiency calculations.

Key components and services
---------------------------
- router-proxy: tags requests with hints and enforces per-route hedging policy (config in /etc/redwood/router/hedge-policy.yaml).
- kernel-manager: maintains kernel lifecycle (active, warming, idle) and exposes activation APIs.
- scheduler-core: decision engine that evaluates hedging eligibility against slot quotas and queue length signals.
- telemetry-collector: emits hedging metrics and traces (see Observability section).

Kernel variants and fallbacks
----------------------------
We recommend a small hierarchy of kernel variants to hedge against:
- optimized-kernel: fastest path, may require quantized kernels and certain hardware features.
- lite-kernel-shim: reduced feature set (no KV cache) but very fast to activate; used as the first hedged fallback for short requests.
- cpu-emulation: last-resort fallback for durability, used only when GPU options are saturated.

Configuration examples
----------------------
Default per-tenant configuration (router/hedge-policy.yaml):

---
# Hedge policy tokens per-tenant
tenant_id: "*"
hedge_enabled: true
hedge_deadline_ms: 40
max_hedge_concurrency_per_tenant: 4
lite_kernel_activation_timeout_ms: 120
allow_cpu_fallback: false
---

Scheduler policy snippet (scheduler/policy.d):

policy "hedge-lazy-activation" {
  when request.is_short_sequence and kernel.state in [idle, cold]
  and tenant.hedge_quota.available > 0
  then schedule.lazy_activate(kernel) |> set.deadline(40ms) |> allow.hedge(alternative = lite-kernel-shim)
}
Observability and metrics
-------------------------
Required metrics (emitted by kernel-manager and scheduler-core):
- hedging.attempts (counter)
- hedging.successes (counter, hedged request returned first)
- hedging.failures (counter)
- hedging.cancellation_overhead_ms (histogram)
- kernel.activation.latency_ms (histogram) by kernel_variant
- kernel.usage.active_slots (gauge)
- tenant.hedge_quota.available (gauge)

Recommended tracing spans:
- router-proxy.classify -> kernel-manager.lookup -> scheduler-core.decision -> kernel.<variant>.execute

Dashboards and alerts
---------------------
Create a dashboard with the following panels:
- Hedge hit rate: hedging.successes / hedging.attempts (target >= 0.6 for short sequences)
- Hedge cost ratio: tokens_consumed_by_hedged_requests / tokens_consumed_total (warn if > 0.15)
- Kernel activation P95/P99 per-variant (warn if p99 > 250ms for lite-kernel-shim)

Alerts (examples):
- hedging.error-rate > 5% sustained for 5m -> page oncall (pagerduty: runtime-core)
- hedging.cost-ratio > 20% for 10m -> notify runtime-costs slack channel

Operational runbook (tail-latency incident)
------------------------------------------
1. Pager fires for high 99th latency.
2. Open runtime dashboard, filter by route and tenant. Check hedging.attempts and kernel.activation.latency_ms.
3. If hedging.attempts are high but hedging.successes are low:
   a. Reduce hedge_deadline_ms by 10ms increments to avoid launching costly hedges.
   b. Consider increasing the limit on lite-kernel pre-warmers for the affected pool (see Pre-warm section).
4. If hedging.cost-ratio is high (>15%):
   a. Temporarily disable hedging for low-value tenants via router-proxy config.
   b. Schedule capacity bump for the affected kernel_variant.
5. If kernel.activation.latency_ms p99 spikes:
   a. Inspect kernel-manager logs for OOMs or driver errors.
   b. Roll back recent kernel or driver rollouts (see Rollout and compatibility).

Pre-warm and capacity controls
-----------------------------
- Pre-warm clusters: dedicated lightweight pools of lite-kernel-shim instances. Use prewarm.policy.yaml to define min_ready_count per-pool.
- Adaptive pre-warm heuristic: if short_sequence_rate > 60% and prewarm_utilization > 70% then scale pre-warm by +20%.

Table: example pre-warm config
Name | min_ready | max_ready | scale_increment
short-request-pool | 8 | 32 | 4
medium-request-pool | 4 | 12 | 2

Rollout and compatibility notes
------------------------------
- Feature gates: hedging and lazy activation are behind feature flags (runtime.feature.hedging, runtime.feature.lazy_activation). Enable in canary clusters only.
- Kernel ABI: lite-kernel-shim implements a subset of runtime kernel-ABI v2.2. Ensure model_variant compatibility before enabling for production.
- Driver versions: Linux kernel module rwinf-v3+ is required for lazy activation memory hotplug optimizations.

Testing and benchmarking guidance
--------------------------------
- Synthetic acceptance: run short-sequence synthetic benchmarks with sequence length distribution set to p25=8, p50=12, p75=24, p95=128. Measure hedging.hit-rate and total cost delta.
- Chaos testing: introduce transient node reboots and verify hedged requests maintain SLOs for 99% of traffic.
- Cost simulation: use the runtime cost-sim tool to simulate hedged request overhead across 7-day traces (tool: tools/runtime-cost-sim).

SLO and recommended targets
---------------------------
- Short-sequence SLO (<=64 tokens): p95 latency <= 80ms, p99 <= 220ms.
- Hedge subsystem targets: hedging.success_rate >= 60% and additional token overhead <= 15%.

Ownership and escalation
------------------------
- Feature owner: Maya Chen (eng-serving-runtime).
- Pager owner for incidents: runtime-core SRE rotation (runbook reference: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/eng-sre/runbooks/slo-and-error-budgets).
- Changes to default tenant policy must be reviewed by: Ravi Patel, Kernel Scheduling team.

Implementation notes for engineers
---------------------------------
- API: kernel-manager exposes POST /v1/kernels/{id}/activate with body {"mode":"lazy","timeout_ms":120}. Example curl:
  curl -X POST https://kernel-manager.internal/v1/kernels/12345/activate -H \"Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN\" -d '{"mode":"lazy","timeout_ms":120}'

- Metrics emission: use telemetry-client.emit_counter("hedging.attempts", 1, {"tenant":tenant_id, "variant":variant})

- Scheduler policy DSL example (complete):
  when request.is_short_sequence and kernel.state in [idle, cold] and tenant.hedge_quota.available > 0 then schedule.lazy_activate(kernel, prewarm_hint=true) |> set.deadline(40ms) |> allow.hedge(alternative=lite-kernel-shim, max_concurrency=2)

Open questions and future work
-----------------------------
- Should hedging apply to streaming/long-lived chat requests (current recommendation: disabled for streams).
- Integrate ML-based hedging deadline prediction using sequence_length_estimate + historical activation latency. Pilot planned for Q4 2026.

Appendix: YAML snippets and quick checks
---------------------------------------
Quick check script (bash):

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Check hedging feature flag and health
FLAG_URL=https://config.internal/v1/flags/runtime.feature.hedging
HEALTH_URL=https://kernel-manager.internal/health
curl -s $FLAG_URL | jq '.'
curl -s $HEALTH_URL | jq '.'

Example hedge-policy (full):
---
tenant_policies:
  fast-startups:
    hedge_enabled: true
    hedge_deadline_ms: 35
    max_hedge_concurrency_per_tenant: 3
    allowed_fallbacks: ["lite-kernel-shim"]
  default:
    hedge_enabled: false
---

References
----------
- scheduler-policy-language-declarative-profiles (internal)
- runtime-fallback-and-degradation-playbook (internal)
- telemetry-rollup-and-sample-strategies-2026 (internal)

Document history
----------------
- 2026-02-10: Draft created by Maya Chen.
- 2026-04-02: Added pre-warm heuristics and metrics by Ravi Patel.
- 2026-09-20: Clarified rollout notes and added SLO targets by Maya Chen.

title: Scheduler Policy Baseline (Q1 2026 Perf Suite)
content:
## Purpose
This page defines the **scheduler configuration baseline** used for the **Q1 2026 Perf Baseline & Representative Workload Suite** runs.

The baseline is the set of scheduler knobs (and guardrails) that are considered “default-correct” for benchmarking and regression detection across:
- Regions: **us-east**, **eu-west**
- GPU SKUs: **H100 / A100 / L40S** (where applicable)
- Workloads: chat streaming, tool/function calling, long-context prefill, embeddings high-QPS

The intent is to:
1) Make perf results comparable over time (reproducible, attributable).
2) Represent production behavior (no benchmark-only shortcuts that hide real latency sources).
3) Keep the scheduler explainable under tail latency (p95/p99) investigations.

This baseline is referenced by the run manifest schema (see ADR-0172) and is expected to be applied verbatim in baseline sweeps unless explicitly noted in the manifest.

---

## Non-goals
- This is not a design doc for new scheduling algorithms.
- This does not define kernel selection (see **Kernel Selection Matrix (Q1 2026)**).
- This does not prescribe customer-specific tiering policies. It defines a stable *benchmark* policy that is compatible with production semantics.

---

## Glossary (scheduler-adjacent)
- **TTFT**: time-to-first-token (server-side, first token committed to the streaming transport / response body).
- **TPOT**: time per output token (server-side; excludes client read/backpressure unless explicitly testing client pacing).
- **Prefill**: prompt processing phase.
- **Decode**: token generation phase.
- **Continuous batching**: dynamic batch assembly across time while tokens are being decoded.
- **Queue wait**: time request spends waiting in scheduler prior to admission into a batch.

Metric boundaries for perf suite runs must follow the definitions in ADR-0172 and the metrics dictionary. This page only specifies the scheduler inputs that influence those metrics.

---

## Baseline versioning
**Baseline name:** `sched-baseline-q1-2026-v1`

**Baseline anchor runtime tag (for baseline sweep signoff):** `runtime-q1-2026-baseline`
- The exact runtime commit SHA and container digest are captured in each run manifest.

**Policy on changes:** Any change to baseline defaults requires:
- Updating this page (and bumping baseline name suffix),
- A short rationale in the change log section, and
- A perf-suite re-calibration run if the change is expected to affect p95/p99.

---

## Scheduler architecture assumptions (as exercised by the perf suite)
The baseline assumes a standard Redwood serving topology:
- **Ingress → Admission control → Per-endpoint queues → Batch assembler → GPU dispatch**
- Requests are categorized by **route/workload mode** (chat streaming vs non-streaming; embeddings) and by **model**.
- The batch assembler supports:
  - Separate prefill and decode micro-batches,
  - Overlap of prefill/compute with decode where supported,
  - KV cache accounting and guardrails.

This baseline uses **deterministic policy choices** where possible, to minimize “scheduler randomness” as a variance source.

---

## Baseline policy principles
1) **Tail latency protection first, then throughput**
   - Baseline aims to keep p99 TTFT stable under representative traffic shapes.
   - Throughput optimizations must not introduce unbounded queue growth.

2) **Fairness without starvation**
   - Under mixed concurrency, smaller requests should not be permanently blocked behind long-prefill requests.

3) **Explicit overload behavior**
   - When capacity is insufficient, the scheduler should degrade predictably via backpressure and load-shed rules, not via timeouts.

4) **No hidden “warm cache only” assumptions**
   - Baseline supports both cold and warm cache scenarios; the scheduler policies must behave safely in both.

---

## Baseline defaults (summary table)
The table below lists the baseline knobs. Exact field names in the run manifest are provided in the next section.

| Category | Knob | Baseline default | Rationale |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Queue discipline | `queue_discipline` | `wfq_cost_aware` | Balances fairness and throughput by approximating work-conserving WFQ with cost estimates. |
| Fairness | `fairness_scope` | `per_tenant_per_model` | Prevents a single tenant/model pair from dominating a GPU pool in benchmarks with mixed mixes. |
| Fairness | `age_boost_half_life_ms` | `2000` | Avoid starvation under long-prefill + streaming mixes. |
| Admission | `max_queue_time_ms` | `800` | Keeps p99 TTFT aligned with SLO expectations; avoids “queue inflation” hiding saturation. |
| Admission | `max_queue_depth` | `2x max_concurrency_target` | Bound memory/latency under spikes; tuned to representative suite ramps. |
| Admission | `reject_status_code` | `429` (rate/overload) | Makes overload explicit; avoids long tail timeouts. |
| Batch assembly | `continuous_batching` | `true` | Matches production scheduling and is required for realistic throughput. |
| Batch assembly | `batch_assembly_interval_ms` | `2` | Low assembly cadence reduces TTFT without thrashing. |
| Batch assembly | `max_batch_size` | `auto_by_sku` | Avoids pathological batches on smaller SKUs while remaining throughput-competitive. |
| Batch assembly | `max_batch_tokens_prefill` | `auto_by_sku` | Controls prefill latency cliffs and KV allocation spikes. |
| Batch assembly | `max_batch_tokens_decode` | `auto_by_sku` | Keeps decode batching stable; avoids long per-step lat spikes. |
| Batch assembly | `prefill_decode_overlap` | `true` | Represents production runtime behavior for prefill-heavy workloads. |
| KV cache | `kv_high_watermark` | `0.90` | Start backpressure before OOM and paging-like behavior. |
| KV cache | `kv_eviction_policy` | `lru_by_session` | Predictable in multi-turn / tool-calling workloads; mirrors typical prod semantics. |
| Streaming | `stream_flush_interval_ms` | `20` | Avoids measuring client-read bottlenecks while preserving realistic streaming cadence. |
| Overload | `load_shed_policy` | `drop_oldest_in_queue` (after hard limits) | Minimizes time spent on requests likely to violate TTFT SLO; keeps system responsive. |
| Observability | `scheduler_metrics_sampling` | `1.0` in perf suite | Full fidelity for attribution; production uses lower sampling. |

Notes:
- “auto_by_sku” means the value is computed from GPU SKU + model max context limits using the rules below and recorded explicitly in the manifest.
- The perf suite must capture resolved values (post auto-resolution) to ensure reruns are identical.

---

## Canonical scheduler config block (as recorded in run manifests)
The benchmark harness records this config block in each run manifest under `scheduler_config` (stringified JSON). Below is the baseline configuration in YAML for readability.

```yaml
baseline_name: sched-baseline-q1-2026-v1
queue_discipline: wfq_cost_aware
fairness_scope: per_tenant_per_model

# Cost model used by WFQ and admission scoring
cost_model:
  unit: tokens
  prefill_weight: 1.0
  decode_weight: 1.2
  streaming_overhead_ms: 3
  long_prefill_penalty_threshold_tokens: 4096
  long_prefill_penalty_multiplier: 1.4

# Anti-starvation
age_boost:
  enabled: true
  half_life_ms: 2000
  max_boost_multiplier: 3.0

admission_control:
  enabled: true
  max_queue_time_ms: 800
  max_queue_depth_multiplier: 2.0
  reject_status_code: 429
  reject_reason_tag: scheduler_overload

batching:
  continuous_batching: true
  batch_assembly_interval_ms: 2
  prefill_decode_overlap: true
  max_batch_size: auto_by_sku
  max_batch_tokens_prefill: auto_by_sku
  max_batch_tokens_decode: auto_by_sku
  min_decode_microbatch_size: 1

kv_cache_guardrails:
  kv_high_watermark: 0.90
  kv_hard_limit_action: shed
  kv_eviction_policy: lru_by_session

streaming:
  stream_flush_interval_ms: 20
  server_push_only: true

overload_behavior:
  load_shed_policy: drop_oldest_in_queue
  shed_after_queue_time_ms: 1000
  shed_after_queue_depth_multiplier: 2.5

instrumentation:
  metrics_sampling_rate: 1.0
  emit_queue_wait_histogram: true
  emit_batch_assembly_histogram: true
  emit_batch_size_histogram: true
  emit_load_shed_counters: true
  trace_correlation_ids: enabled
```

Implementation note: the perf suite must store both:
- the config **as provided**, and
- the config **as applied** (after resolving `auto_by_sku` and any model-specific caps).

---

## SKU-specific resolution rules (auto_by_sku)
To reduce “baseline drift,” we define deterministic resolution rules for the key batching caps. These are designed to be conservative for tail latency, while leaving throughput competitive.

### Inputs
- GPU SKU class: H100 / A100 / L40S
- Model context limits and hidden-size dependent memory scaling
- Workload mode (chat streaming vs long-prefill vs embeddings)

### Resolved caps (baseline)
The resolved caps below are defaults; per-model adjustments are allowed only when documented in the run manifest and baseline plan.

**H100 (80GB class)**
- `max_batch_size`: 48
- `max_batch_tokens_prefill`: 65536
- `max_batch_tokens_decode`: 8192

**A100 (80GB class)**
- `max_batch_size`: 32
- `max_batch_tokens_prefill`: 49152
- `max_batch_tokens_decode`: 6144

**L40S (48GB class)**
- `max_batch_size`: 16
- `max_batch_tokens_prefill`: 24576
- `max_batch_tokens_decode`: 4096

Guardrail: if KV cache watermark exceeds `kv_high_watermark` during admission, the scheduler must reduce effective `max_batch_size` by 25% increments until the watermark is below threshold or until `min_decode_microbatch_size` is reached.

Rationale:
- Prefill caps are set to avoid long-prefill p99 TTFT cliffs caused by over-aggregation.
- Decode caps constrain per-step latency spikes that disproportionately affect streaming TTFT+TPOT tails.

---

## Queue discipline and fairness policy
### Selected discipline: `wfq_cost_aware`
We use a cost-aware Weighted Fair Queuing approximation over (tenant, model) flows.

**Why WFQ-like behavior vs FIFO?**
- FIFO amplifies tail latency under heterogeneous request sizes (especially long-prefill mixed with short chat prompts).
- Cost-aware selection improves mean throughput while preventing “elephant requests” from blocking “mice requests” indefinitely.

### Fairness scope: `per_tenant_per_model`
Each (tenant, model) is treated as a fairness group. This matches our production need to prevent a single tenant’s workload mix from monopolizing one model’s capacity while still allowing different models to saturate different pools.

### Anti-starvation: age boost
Each queued request receives an age-based multiplier to its effective priority score.
- Half-life: 2000ms
- Max boost: 3x

This is specifically to keep multi-turn tool calling and long-prefill workloads from starving behind high-QPS short chats in mixed mixes.

---

## Backpressure and admission control
Admission control is enabled and must be treated as part of the baseline (not an optional optimization).

### Key thresholds
- **Soft bound:** `max_queue_time_ms = 800`
  - Requests predicted to exceed this are rejected early with `429 scheduler_overload`.
- **Hard bound:** `shed_after_queue_time_ms = 1000`
  - If the queue contains requests older than this threshold (e.g., burst beyond expected mix), the scheduler begins load shedding by policy.

### Why early reject (429) is the baseline behavior
- Prevents “silent” TTFT blowups that turn into ambiguous client timeouts.
- Keeps benchmark results interpretable: once saturation occurs, the system expresses overload explicitly.
- Aligns with SRE guidance that overload should page/alert based on **rate of rejects** rather than **tail latency explosions**.

### Queue depth bound
`max_queue_depth_multiplier = 2.0` relative to the workload’s declared concurrency target.

Rationale:
- Deep queues may make throughput look stable while TTFT becomes non-representative.
- Bounding queue depth makes saturation visible in both dashboards and manifests.

---

## Overload behavior
When overloaded (queue and/or KV watermark), the scheduler transitions through these stages:

1) **Backpressure via admission control**
   - Reject new requests once queue-time prediction exceeds bounds.

2) **Adaptive batching reduction**
   - Reduce effective batch size to control TTFT tails (especially for long-prefill).

3) **Load shedding**
   - Policy: `drop_oldest_in_queue`
   - Rationale: If a request has already waited long enough to violate the TTFT budget, completing it is less valuable than keeping the system responsive for newly arriving short requests.

4) **Hard stop / safety**
   - If KV hard limit is reached: `kv_hard_limit_action = shed` (never OOM the worker during baseline runs).

Note: the perf suite must tag overload events in results (reject rates, shed counts). Any baseline run where overload dominates the sample must be marked “invalid for baseline comparison” unless the workload explicitly tests overload behavior.

---

## Streaming-specific behavior
Streaming adds two common sources of measurement confusion: server flush policy and client-read backpressure. The baseline defines server behavior to reduce variability:

- `server_push_only: true`
  - The server emits tokens on its own schedule; it does not attempt to synchronize with a benchmark client’s read cadence.
- `stream_flush_interval_ms: 20`
  - Chosen to approximate production streaming “smoothness” while limiting flush overhead.

Guidance for the perf harness:
- Client must read continuously and avoid introducing backpressure.
- TTFT is measured at “first token committed on server side,” per ADR-0172.

---

## Instrumentation requirements (baseline runs)
For Q1 2026 baseline runs, instrumentation is considered mandatory (sampling = 1.0). The goal is attribution, not lowest overhead.

The scheduler must emit at minimum:
- Queue wait time histogram (per workload + model)
- Batch assembly time histogram
- Batch size distributions (prefill and decode)
- Counters: rejects, sheds, KV watermark excursions
- Correlation IDs that link:
  - workload generator request → scheduler queue event → batch event → model execution trace

This is required to support triage playbooks (see perf suite profiling playbook).

---

## Known trade-offs and rationale notes
- **Cost model simplicity:** The token-based cost model is intentionally simple to reduce drift. It will not perfectly predict runtime cost across model families, but it substantially improves fairness vs FIFO.
- **Aggressive queue-time bounds:** We prefer explicit overload signals. This can reduce “apparent throughput” in extreme bursts, but makes tails interpretable and matches production expectations.
- **Overlap enabled:** Prefill/decode overlap is enabled to reflect real runtime behavior. If overlap changes between releases, that should be treated as a first-class perf change and investigated (not papered over by policy tweaks).

---

## Operational checklist (for baseline sweeps)
Before running a baseline sweep, confirm:
1) Run manifest includes `scheduler_config.baseline_name = sched-baseline-q1-2026-v1`.
2) All `auto_by_sku` fields are resolved and recorded in the manifest.
3) Metrics sampling is 1.0 and scheduler histograms/counters are present.
4) Any deviations are explicitly documented in the run manifest `notes` field and flagged in the run tracker.

---

## Change log
- **2026-01-28:** Clarified SKU-specific batching caps and added explicit `shed_after_queue_time_ms` to separate admission reject vs shed phases.
- **2026-01-14:** Set `stream_flush_interval_ms` to 20ms for consistency across regions; aligned TTFT measurement boundary with ADR-0172.
- **2025-12-08:** Initial publication of Q1 2026 scheduler baseline (WFQ cost-aware, admission control, KV guardrails).

title: Hardware Tuning Profiles Pack (H100/B200/L40S) — Project Overview
content:
## Summary
Redwood Inference will deliver a **hardware tuning profiles pack** for the serving runtime focused on **kernel + scheduler performance** across the current and near-future NVIDIA fleet: **H100, B200, L40S**.

The pack consists of **curated, versioned runtime configuration profiles** that are:
- **Safe-by-default** (guardrails, compatibility checks, sane fallbacks)
- **Measurable** (benchmarked against a workload matrix with tracked deltas)
- **Operationally rollout-friendly** (canaries, regression gates, rollback semantics)
- **Consistent across deployment modes** (Hosted, Dedicated, Private)

This page defines the project goals, non-goals, target SKUs, success metrics, ownership, and the milestone plan.

---

## Why we’re doing this
As our model catalog expands and fleet heterogeneity increases, performance issues increasingly come from **serving configuration mismatch** rather than model quality. Today, “best settings” are often:
- discovered ad-hoc,
- embedded in code defaults,
- inconsistently applied across pools/regions,
- and hard to rollback when they regress tail latency.

This pack operationalizes “Redwood-verified performance profiles” as a repeatable, versioned artifact.

---

## Goals
1) **Ship a versioned profile pack** for H100, L40S (GA) and B200 (experimental/gated) with clear intended workload envelopes.
2) Provide a **profile schema + loader** that supports:
   - hardware detection and normalization (SKU string variance),
   - explicit compatibility with runtime releases,
   - a deterministic override/precedence order,
   - and validation/guardrails (reject unsafe combos; fallback safely).
3) Improve production economics while protecting user experience:
   - raise tokens/sec and reduce cost per 1M tokens,
   - maintain or improve p50 latency,
   - and cap p95 regressions via guardrails + canary gates.
4) Make changes **easy to observe and debug**:
   - expose selected profile + override source in metrics/logs,
   - provide a “dump effective config” mechanism for oncall and Support.
5) Establish a **benchmark and regression framework**:
   - representative workload matrix,
   - standardized reporting artifacts,
   - pre-merge and post-deploy perf-canary gates.

---

## Non-goals (initial release)
- Writing entirely **new kernels** from scratch (we tune selection and toggles; we don’t build net-new kernel families in this initiative).
- Major public API changes to Redwood API/SDKs.
- Customer-by-customer bespoke tuning as part of the pack release (handled via Solutions/Support follow-ups; the pack is for standard supported presets).
- Guaranteeing contractual performance/SLO improvements (docs will describe **expected behavior** and known trade-offs, not guarantees).

---

## Target hardware SKUs
We are targeting the following NVIDIA SKUs across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private. Profiles must account for common fleet variance (HBM size, PCIe vs SXM, clocks, MIG/partitioning, multi-GPU nodes).

### H100 (GA)
- Primary production workhorse for latency-sensitive + throughput workloads.
- Profile family: **balanced** default + optional throughput-first mode (guardrailed).

### L40S (GA)
- Cost-sensitive workloads; more stringent memory constraints.
- Profile emphasizes KV cache budgeting, OOM prevention, and stable batching.

### B200 (Experimental, gated)
- Early enablement with limited fleet access.
- Profile is gated behind an explicit feature flag and strict stack/version checks.
- Must include a clear fallback plan (H100-compatible behavior where applicable, or “disable profile” to runtime defaults).

---

## Scope: what a profile can tune
Profiles are allowed to set knobs in these categories (final supported keys are defined in the schema doc):

1) **Kernel selection + execution toggles**
- Sequence-length bucket heuristics
- Attention/kernel selection toggles
- Quantization-friendly execution path toggles (when compatible)

2) **Scheduling + batching presets**
- Continuous batching settings
- Prefill vs decode fairness and backpressure
- Queue limits and admission control
- Streaming vs non-streaming handling (where runtime supports separate policies)

3) **Memory + KV cache behavior**
- KV cache budgeting and caps
- Fragmentation-aware behavior (where available)
- Safe defaults for long-context workload buckets

4) **Collectives / NCCL / multi-GPU (where applicable)**
- Conservative tuning only; must be safe across topology variance

5) **CPU-side runtime settings**
- Threading/concurrency settings that materially affect scheduling and end-to-end latency

---

## Success metrics
We measure success via benchmark deltas on the workload matrix and production signals during canary rollouts.

### Primary metrics (bench + canary)
| Metric | How it’s measured | Success target (pack v1) |
|---|---|---|
| **Throughput (tokens/sec)** | per model + workload bucket; steady-state | +5–15% in targeted buckets, with explicit notes where neutral |
| **Latency p50** | end-to-end request latency; streaming includes TTFT + per-token | No regression in p50; ideally modest improvement in high-concurrency |
| **Latency p95** | end-to-end tail latency | Guardrails: p95 should not regress >3–5% in “balanced” profiles; throughput-first may allow limited regression with explicit labeling |
| **Cost per 1M tokens** | GPU-time-derived unit cost proxy (bench) + production allocation | Downward trend proportional to throughput gains; documented per SKU |

### Secondary metrics (safety + operability)
- OOM / allocation failure rate (must not increase; L40S specifically must improve under long-context workloads)
- Retry rate / fallbacks triggered (should remain stable; increased fallbacks indicate unsafe tuning)
- Error budget consumption during canary pools
- Profile selection correctness (rate of “unknown SKU” and fallback-to-default)
- Config drift: “effective config” should match expected profile + overrides

### “Definition of done” for the pack
- Profiles are versioned and shipped per the distribution ADR.
- Schema validation prevents invalid/unsafe configs from starting.
- Perf-canary gates exist for each SKU profile with noise-reduced thresholds.
- Rollout runbook is complete and has been exercised at least once in a controlled canary.
- Expected-behavior docs are published for H100/L40S and experimental guidance for B200.

---

## Owners and stakeholders
### Program and executive sponsorship
- **Program lead:** Talia Benson
- **Executive sponsor (Runtime):** Mateo Alvarez

### Engineering owners
- **Kernel tuning:** Hiro Tanaka (lead), Grace Kim, Yuki Sato, Isabella Rossi
- **Scheduling/batching:** Sofia Ivanova (lead), Lena Fischer, Marcus Reed
- **Runtime architecture / regression strategy:** Noah Patel
- **KV cache / memory behavior:** Omar El-Sayed, Samir Qureshi
- **Schema + guardrails:** Ethan Park
- **Loader + rollout primitives:** Benji Okafor, Diego Santos, Quentin Harris

### Perf + infra + reliability
- **Benchmark methodology:** Claire Dubois
- **Benchmark harness:** Rina Kobayashi
- **Perf regression detection tooling:** Kira Volkov
- **Infra/fleet rollout sponsor:** Irene Choi; with Vanessa Ortiz, Keiko Yamamoto, Nina Petrova
- **SRE sponsor:** Neha Kapoor; rollout + oncall coordination via Sean Gallagher
- **Dashboards / canary gates:** Aisha Bello, Allison Grant

### Applied ML review
- **Applied ML sponsor:** Dr. Maya Srinivasan
- Reviewers: Arjun Desai, Jonas Weber

---

## Milestone plan (8–10 weeks)
Dates are illustrative and shift with fleet access (especially for B200).

1) **Kickoff + requirements (Week 1)**
- Confirm target SKUs and known fleet variance.
- Define “safe-by-default” constraints and acceptance metrics.
- Align on doc language: “expected behavior” vs guarantees.

2) **Baselines (Weeks 1–2)**
- Lock benchmark suite inputs and workload matrix.
- Collect baseline curves per GPU SKU (and key instance variants where relevant).

3) **Schema + implementation (Weeks 2–5)**
- Profile schema, inheritance/versioning, and validation.
- Loader + hardware detection and normalization.
- Implement initial presets and safe fallback behavior.

4) **Validation + staged canary rollout (Weeks 5–8)**
- Add/adjust perf-canary gates; reduce flake/noise.
- Stage rollout by region/pool; observe production metrics.
- Triage regressions; add targeted fixes and regression tests.

5) **Documentation + release (Weeks 7–10)**
- Publish reference pages per SKU: knobs, deltas, workload envelope, trade-offs.
- Ship rollout runbook and oncall playbook; training for SRE/CS.
- Release checklist and sign-offs.

---

## Rollout strategy (high level)
All rollouts must be reversible quickly at the pool/region level.

1) **Pre-merge gates**
- Microbench sanity checks (kernel selection changes)
- Workload-matrix subset for fast signal
- Schema/override precedence integration tests

2) **Post-deploy canaries**
- Enable profile pack in a small canary pool per SKU
- Monitor latency (p50/p95), throughput, errors, OOMs
- Require dashboards to segment by selected profile + override source

3) **Staged expansion**
- Expand by region/pool tiers
- Avoid simultaneous multi-SKU changes unless explicitly approved

4) **Rollback semantics**
- Disable the profile at the pool/region level (revert to runtime defaults or previous profile version)
- For B200, keep the profile gated (opt-in) until stability is proven

(Operational steps and thresholds live in the rollout runbook.)

---

## Key risks and mitigations
1) **Tail latency regressions from throughput tuning**
- Mitigation: balanced vs throughput-first modes; explicit guardrails; p95 canary gates; fairness/backpressure limits.

2) **Hardware variance (HBM size, PCIe/SXM, MIG, multi-GPU)**
- Mitigation: conservative defaults; detection normalization; compatibility rules; safe fallback when detection is ambiguous.

3) **B200 limited access + evolving stack requirements**
- Mitigation: experimental gating; strict driver/CUDA checks; pool-scoped enablement; explicit disable plan.

4) **Perf-canary noise/flakiness**
- Mitigation: runner stability work, robust aggregation, threshold tuning, and “investigate” vs “block” severity tiers.

5) **Config drift between runtime defaults and profile pack**
- Mitigation: normalize defaults; log effective config; enforce precedence tests; document override order.

---

## Communication + where to look
- Canonical design docs:
  - Profile schema and compatibility rules
  - Distribution + override-order ADR
- Operational docs:
  - Rollout runbook
  - Perf-canary gates and dashboards
  - Known issues and mitigations
- Per-SKU reference:
  - H100 tuned profile reference
  - L40S tuned profile reference
  - B200 tuned profile reference (experimental)

For questions or changes to scope/targets, contact **Talia Benson** (program), **Hiro Tanaka** (kernels), or **Sofia Ivanova** (scheduling).

title: Traffic Mirroring End-to-End Benchmark Protocol
content:
Summary

This document defines the canonical end-to-end (E2E) benchmark protocol for measuring runtime performance using traffic mirroring. Traffic mirroring benchmarks run real production traffic in read-only mode against candidate runtime builds, model variants, or kernel scheduling configurations. The goals are to:

- Obtain representative latency and correctness signals with minimal production risk.
- Compare candidate changes to a baseline across cost and tail-latency envelopes.
- Produce reproducible artifacts suitable for release gating and perf regression detection.

Scope

Applies to: eng-serving-runtime teams running hosted, dedicated, and private deployments. This protocol is intended for:
- New kernel scheduling releases
- Runtime build changes that touch request routing or batching
- Model-variant rollout validation (e.g., quantized vs float variants)
- Autoscaling/slotting policy experiments

Excludes: experiments that mutate customer-visible state or alter traffic semantics (see safety checklist).

Key Concepts

- Mirrored traffic: a copy of production requests sent concurrently to the candidate system without forwarding responses back to the user.
- Shadow target: an isolated cluster or pool that processes mirrored traffic for measurement and logging.
- Replay-safe: traffic transformed to remove sensitive PII and non-idempotent operations.

Roles and Ownership

- Benchmark Owner: person who schedules and signs off the run (example: Priya Shah).
- Runtime Owner: service-level owner of the candidate runtime build.
- Observability Owner: responsible for ensuring required dashboards and traces are available.
- SRE Approval: SRE must sign off for any run that exceeds baseline resource consumption thresholds.

SLOs and Acceptance Criteria

Baseline: production cluster A (stable). Candidate: cluster B (mirrored). Acceptance requires:
- P50 latency delta <= +10% compared to baseline under same load shape.
- P95 latency delta <= +15%.
- P99 tail-latency delta <= +25% OR absolute p99 < 3000ms (whichever is stricter for the workload).
- Throughput: candidate must sustain 95% of baseline sustained QPS without queue growth.
- Error rate (5xx): candidate <= baseline + 0.1 percentage points.
- Semantic parity: for deterministic workloads, token-level equality >= 98%. For non-deterministic outputs, use embed-similarity thresholds (cosine >= 0.985).

Safety Checklist (must be completed before any mirror run)

1) Sanitize inputs: remove Authorization headers and any customer PII using the request-sanitizer pipeline.
2) Ensure the candidate is strictly read-only: no upstream writes, no metrics emitted to billing systems.
3) Mirror traffic rate scaling: start at 1% of production QPS and increase only after SRE approval.
4) Resource isolation: shadow target must have separate autoscaling group / node-pool and no shared persistent storage with prod.
5) Alerting: create temporary alert suppressions to avoid noisy page storms and ensure critical alerts still page.

Procedure: Run Plan

1) Prepare candidate build and environment:
   - Deploy candidate runtime to shadow cluster B with identical network topology and model pins.
   - Ensure KV cache behavior is reset unless intentionally testing cache warmup.
   - Tag build with bench-run/<YYYYMMDD>/<run-id> for trace correlation.

2) Configure mirroring:
   - Use the traffic-mirror service (internal) to configure rule: mirror-rule:<service>-<route>-<run-id>.
   - Example rule config (YAML):

     mirror_rule: 
       name: chat-completions-shadow-2027-01
       source: prod-gateway
       match: path_prefix: "/v1/chat/completions"
       sampler: fixed_rate
       rate: 0.01
       sanitizer: request-sanitizer-v2
       targets: ["shadow-cluster-b"]

   - CLI to apply (internal):
     $ traffic-mirror apply --from prod-gateway --to shadow-cluster-b --path-prefix /v1/chat/completions --rate 0.01 --sanitizer request-sanitizer-v2 --name chat-completions-shadow-<run-id>

3) Warmup and ramping:
   - Start with 0.1% mirror rate for 10 minutes to validate pipeline. Confirm no errors and resource headroom.
   - Ramp to target mirror rate (commonly 1% or 5% depending on risk classification) in exponentially increasing steps (0.5%, 1%, 2%). Each step: hold for 5–15 minutes and observe metrics.

4) Data collection windows:
   - Short-run benchmarking: 30–60 minutes. Use when kernel or kernel-parameter changes are small.
   - Long-run benchmarking: 6–24 hours. Use for model-variant comparisons or autoscaling policy changes.
   - Capture request/response timeline traces, kernel metrics, GPU utilization, per-token latency histograms, KV cache hit rates, and queue length series.

5) Instrumentation and required telemetry

Required traces/metrics (minimum):
- request.timeline: trace spans for gateway->router->runtime->kernel->executor
- runtime.latency_ms: p50/p95/p99 histograms by route and model
- kernel.queue_length: 1s resolution time-series per GPU slot
- kernel.dispatch_time_ms: per-request quantiles
- gpu.utilization_pct: per-GPU
- kvcache.hit_rate: rolling 1m and 5m
- embed-similarity: sample of 200 request pairs comparing baseline vs candidate outputs

Tagging: all metrics must include bench.run_id and bench.build_tag dimensions.

Artifacts to persist

- Raw traces: stored in obs.test-bench/traces/<run-id> (retention 90d)
- Aggregated histograms: obs.test-bench/histograms/<run-id>.json
- Representative sample of requests and candidate responses (sanitized): s3://bench-artifacts/<run-id>/samples.jsonl.gz
- Perf report: s3://bench-artifacts/<run-id>/report.html (generated by bench-reporting tool)

Analysis and Reporting

1) Automated report generation:
   - After the run finishes the bench-orchestrator will produce a summary report containing latency deltas, resource deltas (GPU-hours used), and semantic similarity.
   - The report includes waterfall diagnostics for slow tail requests and a heatmap of queue growth over time.

2) Manual triage checklist:
   - If p99 delta > acceptance, run failure mode triage: inspect kernel dispatch traces, check for blocking allocations, and examine kernel-runloop starvation.
   - Compare kvcache.hit_rate trends: a sudden drop suggests cache population mismatch or differing shard keys.
   - Check for dispatcher backpressure events and kernel preemption counts.

3) Release gating:
   - Candidate passes if all acceptance criteria are met and no new critical incidents were generated during the run.
   - For marginal cases, run a focused replay of suspect requests with increased sampling (100–500x) to amplify differences for debugging.

Troubleshooting and Common Failure Modes

- Symptom: Elevated p95 with normal GPU utilization
  Action: Inspect kernel.queue_length and dispatch_time_ms for contention; verify batch-slicing thresholds and preemption windows.

- Symptom: Higher error rate on candidate
  Action: Check sanitizer pipeline for malformed transformed requests; validate model version pins; look for OOMs in runtime logs.

- Symptom: Semantic drift (embed-similarity drop)
  Action: Confirm identical tokenizer and model quantization parameters; check for off-by-one sequence padding differences.

- Symptom: Large cost delta with similar latency
  Action: Analyze per-token GPU cycles using kernel-cycle counters; check for degenerate scheduling producing small, inefficient kernels (e.g., repeated tiny-attention launches).

Operational Controls and Cost Limits

- Default mirror rate cap for non-critical patches: 1% of prod QPS.
- For kernel/platform team experiments that intentionally stress resources, a waiver must be obtained from SRE and Finance for temporary increased cloud spend (submit bench-cost-waiver/<run-id>).

Automation recipes and scripts

- bench-orchestrator job spec (short):
  - name: mirror-bench-<run-id>
  - baseline_cluster: prod-a
  - candidate_cluster: shadow-b
  - routes: ["/v1/chat/completions"]
  - mirror_rate: 0.01
  - sanitizer: request-sanitizer-v2
  - artifact_bucket: s3://bench-artifacts/<run-id>

- Example invocation:
  $ bench-orchestrator run --spec ./specs/mirror-bench-<run-id>.yaml --notify @eng-runtime --tag bench.run_id=<run-id>

Postmortem and Artifact Retention

- All run artifacts are retained for 90 days by default. Stakeholders must archive essential artifacts to the release retro bucket for multi-year retention if used for compliance.
- Any unexpected production-facing incident correlated to a mirroring run triggers a full incident review and possible rollback of mirror permissions.

Notes on Privacy and Compliance

- The request-sanitizer pipeline must run in-line before the mirror emitter. It should: strip auth tokens, normalize or redact PII fields, and replace customer ids with stable pseudonyms.
- For customers with restricted data residency, mirroring is disabled unless an explicit contractual exception is documented.

Appendix A: Example artifact schema (samples.jsonl line)

{
  "bench.run_id": "<run-id>",
  "timestamp": "2026-12-08T14:22:12Z",
  "route": "/v1/chat/completions",
  "sanitized_input": "{...}",
  "baseline_output_meta": {"latency_ms": 120, "tokens": 48},
  "candidate_output_meta": {"latency_ms": 160, "tokens": 48},
  "embed_similarity": 0.992
}

Appendix B: Quick checklist for small patch owners

1) Run preflight unit perf tests in sandbox.
2) Schedule 30min mirror at 0.5% and validate no increased error rate.
3) Expand to 1% for 60min and evaluate report.
4) If candidate is clean, request staging rollout.

References

- Traffic mirror service README (internal): /tools/traffic-mirror/README
- Bench-orchestrator docs: /tools/bench-orchestrator/guide
- Request sanitizer config templates: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/request-sanitizer-templates

Contact

For questions or help running a mirror benchmark, ping #eng-runtime-perf or email perf@redwood.example.com.

title: Mixed-size Model Co-scheduling and Traceable Kernel Affinity Guide
content:
Overview

This document describes a pragmatic design and operational playbook for co-scheduling mixed-size LLM inference requests (small models, medium backbone models, and large-context LLMs) on heterogeneous GPU pools while preserving predictable latency SLOs and providing traceable kernel-to-request affinity for incident investigation. It complements the scheduler language profiles and heterogeneous-pool guidance; its aim is prescriptive: how to set affinity, observe it end-to-end, and run safe rollouts.

Scope

- Applies to hosted and Dedicated clusters that share the same scheduler control plane.
- Covers inference-only workloads (token-generation and chat) and does not cover training jobs.
- Targets co-location of models with different memory/compute footprints on the same compute nodes and multi-model pipelines where a single request touches more than one model.

Motivation

Co-scheduling increases GPU utilization but introduces contention that impacts tail latency and quality (eviction of KV cache, kernel serialization). Engineering teams need:

1. A predictable model for assigning kernel affinity so traces map to requests.
2. Runtime choices (slotting, preemption policy) that preserve latency budgets.
3. A rollout/runbook for experiments and regressions.

Key concepts and definitions

- Model size class: SMALL (<=3B), MEDIUM (3B-13B), LARGE (>13B or long-context variants).
- Kernel affinity: declarative hint that binds a request's kernel selection to a set of kernel implementations and GPU slot properties (tensor cores, persistent kernel lanes, quantized fast-paths).
- Slot reservation: transient GPU resource reservation for latency-sensitive requests (duration measured in ms/tokens).
- Traceable affinity token (AFT): a unique trace id propagated from API gateway through the scheduler to kernel telemetry so all runtime artifacts can be correlated to the originating request.

Design overview

1) Affinity-first routing

- In the routing layer, requests declare the expected model-size-class and latency tier (critical / best-effort). The route's configuration converts these into scheduler affinity tags: model_class=SMALL/MEDIUM/LARGE, latency_tier=critical|standard|background.
- The scheduler maps affinity tags to kernel profiles and slot classes. Example mapping:

| model_class | latency_tier | kernel_profile | slot_class | preemption_allowed |
|-------------|--------------|----------------|------------|--------------------|
| LARGE       | critical     | large-opt-v2   | reserved_hq| false              |
| MEDIUM      | standard     | medium-quant   | shared_mid | true               |
| SMALL       | background   | small-fastpath | opportunistic | true            |

2) Kernel profile hints

- kernel_profile is a scheduler-side label that selects an ordered list of kernel implementations (e.g., tensorcore-fused, int8-quantized, fallback-generic). The runtime evaluates the list, preferring earlier entries but falling back safely.
- Kernel profiles are versioned (kernel_profile: name@vN) to allow safe rollouts and telemetry rollbacks.

3) Traceable affinity propagation

- The API gateway assigns an AFT (traceable affinity token) to each request: AFT format: r_<route-id>_<timestamp>_<rand4>. This token is:

  - logged at ingress (gateway)
  - attached to RPC metadata to scheduler and runtime
  - emitted in kernel telemetry as kernel.affinity_token

- Example (pseudo-HTTP header):

  X-AFFINITY-TOKEN: r-chat-v2_20260302T141200Z_7f9a

Operational primitives and controls

1) Slot classes

- reserved_hq: pre-allocated slices with strict CPU+GPU memory limits for large-critical requests; no preemption.
- shared_mid: dynamically multiplexed slots with fair scheduling and bounded preemption.
- opportunistic: lower priority, bursty work; can be preempted or pushed to packer nodes.

2) Preemption policy knobs

- preemption_window_ms: how long the scheduler delays preemption to let short sequences finish (default 100ms).
- evict_kvcache_only: Boolean; when true, preemption evicts KV caches first instead of killing kernels.

3) Kernel profile rollout gates

- Canary cohort (1% traffic), shadow validation (replay requests), and compare metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, token-per-second throughput, top-5 kernel fallbacks.

Telemetry and profiling guidance

- Required telemetry keys to emit for every kernel invocation:

  - kernel.affinity_token (AFT)
  - kernel.profile.name@version
  - kernel.impl (implementation id)
  - kernel.exec_time_ms
  - request.model_class
  - request.route_id
  - node.gpu_id

- Traces must join gateway logs, scheduler decisions, and kernel events with the AFT as the join key. The recommended retention for affinity traces during rollouts is 30 days.

- Profiling playbook snippet: how to measure co-scheduling impact on tail latency

  1. Baseline: Measure p50/p95/p99 with only the target model class in the pool for 24 hours.
  2. Add co-located class: introduce SMALL or MEDIUM classes to 10% of capacity.
  3. Run synthetic and shadow traffic for 4 hours. Capture kernel.affinity_token and kernel.exec_time_ms.
  4. Compare distributions and identify increased kernel fallback rates. If p99 increases by >15%, abort and rollback kernel_profile.

Synthesis debugging workflow (incident triage)

1) Assemble the AFT from the erroring request (gateway logs).
2) Query scheduler decisions for that AFT to find the slot_class and kernel_profile chosen.
3) Pull node/gpu telemetry for the kernel.affinity_token window to see co-located kernels and memory pressure events.
4) Look for observable signals: increased kernel.fallback_count, kvcache.evictions, gpu.sustained_power_capping.

Example diagnostics query (pseudo-SQL)

SELECT trace_id, kernel_impl, exec_time_ms, fallback_count, node_gpu_id
FROM kernel_telemetry
WHERE kernel_affinity_token = 'r-chat-v2_20260302T141200Z_7f9a'
ORDER BY ts ASC;

Runbook: safe co-scheduling experiment (step-by-step)

1. Define hypothesis and success criteria (latency delta thresholds, quality metrics).
2. Reserve a canary pool (5% capacity) and mark with label: cosched_canary_<date>.
3. Deploy kernel_profile name@v1 to canary; route 1% traffic.
4. Enable AFT propagation and shadow-mode tracing; do not affect responses.
5. Monitor metrics for 2 hours: p50/p95/p99, kvcache.eviction_rate, kernel.fallback_rate.
6. If metrics exceed thresholds: revert kernel_profile, roll back scheduling weight, and file a triage ticket.
7. If stable for 24 hours, increase canary capacity and repeat until full rollout.

Configuration examples

YAML: route affinity declaration example

- route: /v1/chat
  model_class: LARGE
  latency_tier: critical
  affinity: |
    model_class=LARGE
    latency_tier=critical
    kernel_profile=large-opt-v2@v3
    slot_class=reserved_hq\n

Scheduler policy snippet (pseudo DSL)

policy "cosched-affinity" {
  when model_class == LARGE and latency_tier == "critical" {
    bind slot_class = "reserved_hq"
    bind preemption_allowed = false
  }
  when model_class == MEDIUM {
    bind slot_class = "shared_mid"
    bind kernel_profile = ["medium-quant@v2", "medium-generic@v1"]
  }
  metrics_to_emit = ["kernel.exec_time_ms", "kvcache.eviction_rate", "kernel.fallback_count"]
}

Safety and fallback modes

- Soft-fallback: if a preferred kernel is not available, the runtime uses the next profile entry and emits kernel.fallback_count. Set alert if fallback_rate > 0.5% for critical routes.
- Degradation policy: for sustained high contention, scheduler can switch reserved_hq to degraded_hq which reduces concurrency and pins single-request kernels to dedicated lanes. This mode requires an SRE approver and a recorded decision.

Operational checklist (daily/weekly)

- Daily: check canary cohorts for any kernel.fallback_count spikes; validate AFT join success rate (>99%).
- Weekly: run co-scheduling shadow experiments with synthetic traffic and publish short report to the runtime QA channel.
- Monthly: review kernel_profile adoption matrix and prune unused profiles older than 90 days.

Ownership and contacts

- Primary owner: Runtime Scheduling Team (runtime-scheduler@redwood.ai)
- Oncall escalation: Runtime SRE rota (page: /confluence/eng-sre/oncall)
- Related teams: Model Onboarding, Benchmarks, Kernel Engineering.

References and links

- Scheduler policy language (related page)
- Kernel profile registry (internal service: kernel-registry)
- Telemetry contract: runtime-observability (see team wiki)

Appendix: common troubleshooting scenarios

- Symptom: p99 latency spike for LARGE-critical routes after adding SMALL opportunistic workloads.
  Action: check kvcache.eviction_rate and kernel.fallback_count for AFTs. If eviction_rate increased, enable evict_kvcache_only during preemption.

- Symptom: unexplained GPU thermal throttling causing degraded throughput.
  Action: correlate node.gpu_id events with kernel.exec_time_ms and offload opportunistic workloads using node-label packer-enabled=false.

Change log

- 2026-01-18: Initial draft (Aisha Patel).
- 2026-02-10: Added trace token format and rollout gates (Daniel Kim).
- 2026-03-02: Telemetry keys and operational checklist added (Mateo Alvarez).

title: Preemption-aware Batch Slicing: Spec and Operational Playbook
content:
summary:
This document defines the design and operational guidance for "preemption-aware batch slicing" — a kernel-scheduler-adjacent feature that slices large inference batches into smaller execution windows aligned to expected preemption boundaries and GPU occupancy windows. The goal is to reduce tail-latency spikes caused by mid-kernel preemption, long-running kernels blocking higher-priority work, and KV-cache warmup penalties while preserving throughput and unit-cost efficiency.

introduction:
Large requests and long-sequence generation can produce kernel executions that exceed preemption windows on shared GPU pools. When preemption occurs mid-kernel, it can cause: lost progress for KV cache priming, long tail latencies for higher-priority requests, and noisy GPU utilization signals that complicate autoscaling. Preemption-aware batch slicing inserts low-overhead slice boundaries and scheduling hints so the kernel mapper and dispatcher can make better trade-offs between latency and efficiency.

scope:
- Applies to: runtime dispatcher + kernel mapper + per-shard executor on heterogeneous GPU fleets (hosted and Dedicated modes).
- Not in scope: model-architecture-level sequence truncation, offline compilation changes, or business-layer client batching policies.

motivation_and_goals:
- Reduce 95th/99th percentile latency regressions caused by preemption during long kernels.
- Minimize KV-cache thrash from repeated long preemptions.
- Preserve (or gracefully trade) throughput for improved latency predictability.
- Provide knobs for operations to tune behavior per service / customer tier.

core_design_principles:
- Non-invasive: default behavior should be conservative (opt-in per route or model bundle).
- Scheduler hints: expose slice boundary hints to kernel mapper and GPU dispatcher rather than forcing a single global policy.
- Cheap slicing: slices add minimal overhead (<2–4% per-token CPU overhead in microbenchmarks) and leverage existing continuous-batching state (KV cache re-use across slices).
- Observability-first: emit slice metrics (counts, preemptions, latency per slice, warmup penalty) for actionable alerts.

runtime_semantics_high_level:
1. Request classification: the dispatcher categorizes incoming requests by expected kernel duration (microbenchmark model estimate + runtime sampler). If estimated kernel > slice_threshold_ms, candidate for slicing.
2. Slice generation: generate a sequence of slice descriptors. Each slice descriptor contains: slice_token_budget, expected_execution_ms, priority_hint, and cache_warmup (boolean).
3. Execution model: slices are enqueued to shard executors. The kernel mapper may coalesce slices from different requests if compatibility and priority allow, subject to slice size upper bounds.
4. Preemption and recovery: if a slice is preempted mid-execution, runtime records a "preempted_slice" event and restarts the slice respecting cache_warmup. Recovery strategy prefers resuming from last KV checkpoint if supported; otherwise slice is retried and warmup penalty is recorded.
5. Completion semantics: final response is reassembled from slice outputs. The runtime ensures deterministic ordering and idempotency of slice execution.

interactions_with_existing_systems:
- KV cache: slices should be sized to preserve meaningful KV reuse. The runtime tags warmup slices to avoid evicting critical entries.
- Adaptive kernel mapper: uses slice.expected_execution_ms to choose different kernel implementations (fast-preemptible kernels vs high-throughput kernels).
- Priority and credit accounting: slice_priority is charged against the original request budget and interacts with kernel-credit-accounting and fairness systems.
- Autoscaler: emits slice-level throughput and preemption rates to autoscaler to help scaling decisions (see metrics section).

configuration_reference_table:
Parameter | Default | Description
slice.enabled | false | Master kill-switch. Must be enabled per route or model via config blob.
slice.threshold_ms | "120" | Estimate threshold above which requests become slicing candidates (ms).
slice.max_tokens | "2048" | Maximum token budget for a single slice; influences kernel execution time.
slice.min_tokens | "16" | Minimum slice token size to avoid excessive overhead on tiny requests.
slice.timeout_ms | "200" | Wall-clock timeout to cut a running slice for fairness and preemption sensitivity.
slice.priority_policy | "inherit" | inherit | explicit-priority | preemptible-first — how a slice chooses priority.
slice.warmup_policy | "sticky" | sticky | fresh — whether slices assume prior KV warmup is valid.
slice.coalesce_window_ms | "10" | Micro-window where compatible slices can be coalesced by the dispatcher.
slice.metrics_sampling | "1.0" | Fraction of slices for detailed telemetry (0.0–1.0).

sample_yaml_route_level_configuration:
route: /v1/generate-heavy
model: redwood/turbo-large-8k
slice:
  enabled: true
  threshold_ms: 120
  max_tokens: 1024
  min_tokens: 32
  timeout_ms: 250
  priority_policy: inherit
  warmup_policy: sticky
  coalesce_window_ms: 8

observability_and_metrics_required:
Emit the following metrics (prometheus-style names):
- runtime_slice_total{route,model,priority}
- runtime_slice_preempted_total{route,model}
- runtime_slice_latency_ms_p50/p90/p95/p99{route,model}
- runtime_slice_warmup_penalty_ms_avg{route,model}
- runtime_slice_coalesce_rate{route,model}
- runtime_slice_resume_success_ratio{route,model}
- runtime_slice_estimation_error_ms{route,model}

alerting_guidance_example_rules:
1) High preempted slice rate
- Trigger: increase in runtime_slice_preempted_total over 5m such that rate > 0.5% of runtime_slice_total AND p95 latency for route increases > 30% relative to baseline.
- Severity: P2
- Action: follow "slice preemption triage" runbook (below).

2) Warmup penalty regression
- Trigger: runtime_slice_warmup_penalty_ms_avg > 30ms for 10m for a paid-customer route.
- Severity: P3
- Action: Consider increasing slice.min_tokens, enabling sticky warmup, or moving customer to dedicated pool if persistent.

operational_runbook_slice_preemption_triage:
1. Identify affected routes
- Query: top 5 routes by runtime_slice_preempted_total in last 30m and correlated p95 latency.
2. Verify cluster-level preemption activity
- Inspect kube/gpu-proxy preemption events and cloud provider preemption logs.
