function select_kernels_v2(request, model, hw, scheduler_hint, config):
  feats = extract_features(request, model, hw, scheduler_hint)
  cfg_hash = hash(config.selector_rules, config.allowlist, config.denylist)

  candidates = registry.get_candidates(
      model_family=feats.model_family,
      gpu_sku=feats.gpu_sku_norm,
      seq_bucket=feats.seq_bucket)

  candidates = apply_denylist(candidates, feats, config.denylist)

  for k in candidates.attention:
    if supports(k, feats) and passes_gates(k, config):
      selected = k
      reason = "NONE"
      break

  if selected is null:
    selected = registry.get_baseline_attention()
    reason = "FALLBACK_BASELINE"

  emit_telemetry_sampled(feats, selected, candidates, reason, cfg_hash)
  return selected
{code}

h2. 17) Changelog
- 2026-01-14: Initial draft (Yuki Sato)
- 2026-02-03: Added explicit determinism + replay requirements (Noah Patel review)
- 2026-02-12: Added SKU normalization rules + MIG notes (Isabella Rossi input)
- 2026-02-21: Updated fallback reason taxonomy + telemetry sampling guidance (Omar El-Sayed, Allison Grant)

title: Scheduler Policy Language (SPL) and Declarative Profile Library
content:
Overview

This page introduces the Scheduler Policy Language (SPL): a compact, declarative format for expressing kernel scheduling and resource partitioning intent in the Redwood serving runtime. SPL is intended for runtime operators and product/infra owners who need predictable SLOs, multi-tenant fairness, and reproducible rollbackable scheduling changes without modifying code paths in the dispatcher or kernel selector.

Goals
- Provide a human-readable policy DSL that maps to runtime kernel scheduling primitives (priority, batch slicing, preemption windows, kernel selector hints).
- Make tenant-level SLOs, cost tiers, and fallback policies first-class and auditable.
- Enable safe staged rollouts via validation, dry-run, and automatic fallback to default profiles.
- Support observability mapping: each policy declares the metrics and traces it depends on and the telemetry it will emit.

Quick summary
- SPL is YAML-first (examples below) with a strict type schema enforced by the runtime controller.
- Policies live in the configstore (git-backed), validated by the policy service, and pushed to dispatchers as signed bundles.
- Key concepts: profile, rule, target, threshold, kernel_hint, preempt_window, admission_bucket.

When to use SPL
- Constraining latency for high-priority endpoints (e.g., chat-completion interactive)
- Guaranteeing fair GPU time slices across customers in Dedicated clusters
- Implementing cold-start soft-limits and warmup priorities
- Expressing region/instance-specific kernel selection preferences for cost-saving quantized variants

SPL primitives (human description)
- profile: a named collection of rules and defaults. Profiles are versioned.
- target: selector expression that matches request attributes (route, model, customer_tier, region).
- rule: an ordered policy clause (match -> action) with a priority and safety guard.
- action parameters: priority_level, batch_cap, preempt_window_ms, kernel_hint, cache_weight, fallback_sequence.
- threshold metrics: p50, p95, cpu_ms_per_token, token_rate, queue_length.

Example policy (YAML)
# Enforce interactive-latency profile for platinum customers using gpt-4x variants
profile: interactive-platinum-v1
description: Preserve 99th percentile tail latency for interactive endpoints owned by platinum customers
version: "2026-02-01"
rules:
  - target:
      route: "/v1/chat/completions"
      customer_tier: platinum
      model_family: "gpt-4x*"
    match: true
    actions:
      priority_level: 1        # 1=highest, larger numbers lower priority
      batch_cap: 8
      preempt_window_ms: 12
      kernel_hint: "fp16-low-latency"
      cache_weight: 0.9
    safety_guards:
      - metric: p95_latency_ms
        operator: "<"
        value: 120
      - metric: gpu_memory_util_pct
        operator: "<="
        value: 92
  - target:
      route: "/v1/embeddings"
      customer_tier: platinum
    match: "request_tokens < 1024"
    actions:
      priority_level: 2
      batch_cap: 32
      kernel_hint: "int8-quant-emb"

Compatibility note: actions.kernel_hint is advisory; runtime will map to the closest supported kernel variant for the host GPU. The mapping is visible in the kernel catalogue.

Simple JSON equivalent (used by controller)
{
  "profile":"interactive-platinum-v1",
  "rules":[{"target":{"route":"/v1/chat/completions","customer_tier":"platinum"},"actions":{"priority_level":1}}]
}

Policy grammar (abridged)
- selector := attribute (== | != | match | in | < | > | <= | >=) value
- target := { attribute: value, ... }
- match := boolean or expression combining selectors with AND/OR
- action := { priority_level: int, batch_cap: int, preempt_window_ms: int, kernel_hint: str, cache_weight: float }
- safety_guard := { metric: string, operator: one-of(<, <=, ==, !=, >=, >), value: number }

Validation matrix (controller checks)
1) Schema validation: required fields present, types correct.
2) Semantic validation: batch_cap within [1, 256], preempt_window_ms within [0, 2000], cache_weight in [0.0,1.0].
3) SLO collision check: if two profiles target same route+tier with overlapping windows, require explicit decision (priority or merge).
4) Kernel hint compatibility: warn if kernel_hint maps to an unsupported kernel on the target pool.

Table: Allowed ranges and default values
- priority_level: int, allowed 1..100, default 50
- batch_cap: int, allowed 1..512, default 16
- preempt_window_ms: int, allowed 0..2000, default 100
- cache_weight: float, allowed 0.0..1.0, default 0.5
- admission_bucket: string, allowed [interactive, burst, batch, low_cost], default batch

Runtime behavior and mapping
- The dispatcher reconciler converts an SPL profile into a policy bundle per node pool. A bundle contains: compiled match tree, action table, and telemetry hooks.
- Priority levels are translated to scheduler lanes; lower numeric priority is scheduled ahead of higher numbers.
- preempt_window_ms defines the soft window in which a running kernel can be preempted and requeued with cooperative preemption handshake. Values larger than 500ms are reserved for long-running batch jobs.
- batch_cap interacts with the kernel-slicer to decide whether to use continuous batching (low-latency path) or slice-per-batch (throughput path).

Operational concerns and playbook steps (change management)
1) Author policy in the policy repo branch. Add unit tests using the policy validator harness.
2) Open PR and assign "eng-serving-runtime" and "sre" reviewers.
3) Run `policylint` and `policysim` locally: `./tools/policylint policy.yaml` then `./tools/policysim --profile policy.yaml --trace sample-trace.json`
4) Dry-run deploy to Canary pool: push bundle with tag `canary` and enable dry-run mode (no active enforcement, emits telemetry).
5) Observe metrics for 24-72 hours (p50/p95 latency, queue_length, eviction_rate, preempt_count).
6) If metrics are within expected bounds, promote to staged rollout (10% -> 50% -> 100%) with automated rollback triggers defined below.
7) On rollback, use `policyctl rollback <profile> --to <version>`; controller will resume previous bundle atomically.

Automated rollback triggers (recommended defaults)
- p95 latency increase > 15% sustained for 15 minutes.
- preempt_count increase > 3x baseline in 10 minutes.
- gpu_memory_util_pct > 95% for longer than 2 minutes.

Testing and benchmarks
- Each policy should include representative trace inputs in `policies/test_traces/`. Use the benchmarking harness to simulate traffic across sequences (long-form, short-chat, bursty embeddings).
- Recommended benchmark matrix:
  - short interactive: 8k requests, seqs 32 tokens avg, target p95 < 120ms
  - long-halting: 1k requests, seqs 5k tokens avg, target p95 < 2.5s (for batch lanes)
  - embeddings-burst: 5k requests, seqs 1024 tokens avg, cost per 1k req < budgeted baseline
- Use the `bench-runner` with `--policy` flag to evaluate policy-level effects on throughput and tail latency. Example: `bench-runner --config bench.yaml --policy policy.yaml --out results.json`

Observability contract
- Every applied SPL profile must declare at least these emitted metrics: `slo.p50_ms`, `slo.p95_ms`, `slo.queue_length`, `slo.preempt_count`, `slo.eviction_rate`, `slo.gpu_mem_pct`
- Traces must include policy_id and rule_id tags for per-rule attribution.
- Telemetry sampler targets: 1% traces for general traffic, 10% for canaries and affected routes.

Fallback and graceful degradation rules
- If controller detects kernel_hint mismatch for > 5% of dispatched kernels in 1 minute, it will automatically replace kernel_hint with the nearest compatible variant and emit `policy.kernel_hint_fallback` event.
- A profile can declare a fallback_sequence (ordered list of profile names). When resource pressure triggers, runtime will progressively demote the request to the next profile in sequence.

Security and signing
- Policy bundles are signed with the policy service key. Dispatchers reject unsigned or expired bundles.
- Access to the policy repo is RBAC-gated: only owners in `infra-schedulers` and `platform-owners` may merge to `main`.

Migration notes for existing configs
- The controller will import legacy priority JSONs via `policyctl import-legacy --source legacy-priorities.json` and map top-level fields to a profile with version `migrated-<date>`. Manual review is required for kernel_hint translation.

Ownership and contacts
- Primary author: Aisha Patel (eng-serving-runtime)
- Operational owner: SRE (oncall rotation, contact via pager duty team `SRE-Serving`)
- Kernel-variant mapping owner: Kernel Team (kernel-team@redwood.ai)

Appendix: Example policysim output (abbreviated)
- Summary: 95th latency delta: +4.2% (expected)
- Preempt events: 12 per minute -> stable under threshold
- Kernel fallback events: 2 (kernel_hint -> fp16-fallback)

CLI snippets
- Validate: `./tools/policylint path/to/policy.yaml`
- Simulate: `./tools/policysim --policy path/to/policy.yaml --trace traces/platinum-chat-2026.json`
- Deploy (canary): `policyctl apply --profile interactive-platinum-v1 --env canary --dry-run=false`
- Rollback: `policyctl rollback --profile interactive-platinum-v1 --to interactive-platinum-v0`

Change log (high level)
- 2025-11-03: Draft created and initial grammar specified.
- 2025-12-14: Added safety guards and validation matrix after internal review.
- 2026-01-20: Canary support and telemetry contract finalized.
- 2026-02-12: Publishing the first stable SPL spec and profile library.

Related artifacts and repo locations
- Policy repo: git@repo.redwood.ai:infra/scheduler-policies.git
- Validator: //tools/policylint (internal binary)
- Simulator: //tools/policysim
- Controller service: infra/policy-service (k8s namespace: infra-policy)

Notes and open items
- Draft an automated test that injects a kernel_hint mismatch and verifies fallback semantics.
- Consider adding cost-aware policy expressions (cost_per_token < X) in the next SPL revision.
- Evaluate integration with Optimize recommendation engine so product tiers can be automatically suggested SPL profiles.

End of document

title: KV Cache Compaction Improvements — Design Doc (Runtime 1.22)
content:
h1. Overview
This document proposes KV cache compaction + tier-aware eviction for Redwood’s serving runtime to reduce GPU memory fragmentation and mitigate burst-driven tail latency (p95/p99) during sustained decode workloads with mixed sequence lengths.

The design adds:
* A measurable definition of *fragmentation* for the KV arena
* A compaction mechanism (incremental, budgeted) integrated with the scheduler
* A safe eviction strategy (tier-aware LRU + pinned-session handling)
* Feature flags / kill-switches for staged rollout and rapid disable
* Observability standards (metrics + tracing) and rollout guardrails

h2. Context and problem statement
The runtime maintains a GPU-resident KV cache for active sequences (and optionally cached prefixes). Under mixed prompt lengths and high churn, long-lived allocations + frequent frees can create holes in the allocator arena. Over time, the allocator may fail to find contiguous blocks for new KV pages, causing:
* Increased allocator overhead (free-list scanning, defragment bookkeeping)
* Opportunistic evictions at high pressure moments
* Copy/relocation work occurring at inopportune times
* Worst case: OOM/forced request shedding or large p99 latency spikes

We see the most pronounced issues in:
* Bursty chat traffic (many short sessions, some long sessions)
* Mixed decode lengths, long-running streams, and frequent cancellations
* Dedicated pools with high utilization and limited headroom

h2. Goals
* Reduce memory fragmentation in the KV arena without harming steady-state throughput.
* Reduce tail latency under burst traffic (p95/p99) and mixed length distributions.
* Add an eviction policy that is safe (correctness), observable (metrics), and configurable (tier/model/profile).
* Provide guardrails: compaction budgets/limits, backpressure integration, and kill-switches.

h2. Non-goals (initial release)
* Customer-facing configuration UI in Console (flags/config only).
* Major kernel rewrites unrelated to KV movement (minimal copy/pack kernels allowed).
* Changing the semantic contract of KV residency (i.e., no “approximate” KV).

h2. Stakeholders / owners
* Tech lead (KV): Omar El-Sayed
* Allocator/compaction: Samir Qureshi
* Scheduler integration: Sofia Ivanova
* Architecture/correctness: Noah Patel
* Observability standards: Allison Grant
* SRE guardrails/rollout: Sean Gallagher, Rafael Mendes
* Kernels (if needed): Hiro Tanaka, Grace Kim, Yuki Sato

h1. Current KV allocation model (as of runtime 1.21)
h2. High-level model
* KV is stored in a GPU “arena” split into fixed-size pages (per layer, per head layout), allocated per sequence.
* A sequence holds a list of pages per layer (or a compact per-seq structure pointing into per-layer slabs, depending on model profile).
* Allocation is primarily driven at two points:
  # Prefill: reserve initial KV pages proportional to prompt length
  # Decode: allocate more pages as tokens append
* Free occurs when:
  * Sequence completes
  * Sequence is cancelled
  * Sequence is evicted due to memory pressure

h2. Allocator details (simplified)
* Arena is sized per GPU and model profile (varies by hosted tier / dedicated pool).
* Free space is tracked in a free-list keyed by contiguous ranges of pages.
* Allocation uses “first-fit”/“best-fit-ish” heuristics tuned for speed.
* Coalescing occurs on free where adjacent ranges are merged.

h2. Why fragmentation happens
Fragmentation emerges because allocation requests are not uniform:
* Mixed sequence lengths: some sequences grow slowly, others rapidly
* Long-lived sessions: hold pages for long time, forcing new allocations to fit around them
* High churn: frees create holes that are too small for subsequent requests
* Cancellation edge cases: mid-decode cancellation can free non-uniformly across layers, increasing small holes

Net result: free space exists but is split into many small ranges, increasing allocator overhead and raising the probability of forced eviction or OOM when new contiguous ranges are needed.

h1. Definitions and fragmentation measurement
We standardize the following key terms (see metrics standard page for canonical names):

h2. Key terms
* *Arena bytes*: total bytes managed by KV allocator for a model profile.
* *Free bytes*: total bytes currently free.
* *Largest free span*: the largest contiguous free range.
* *Fragmentation ratio*: 1 - (largest_free_span_bytes / free_bytes), with 0 meaning perfectly contiguous free space.

Notes:
* We compute this per device and per model profile (and, where feasible, per pool).
* We also track “free spans count” (count of free ranges) as a secondary indicator.

h2. Health thresholds (initial)
These are starting points and will be tuned via canary:
* Warn: fragmentation_ratio > 0.55 AND free_bytes > 2 GB
* Critical: fragmentation_ratio > 0.70 AND free_bytes > 1 GB

Rationale: fragmentation is only actionable if meaningful free space exists; otherwise pressure is “real” and eviction may be required.

h1. Proposed design
We propose a two-part approach:
* Compaction: relocate KV pages to reduce fragmentation, performed incrementally with budgets.
* Eviction: tier-aware eviction when pressure is high and compaction cannot recover sufficient contiguous space quickly.

The compaction mechanism is integrated with the scheduler to avoid decode stalls and to allow backpressure/guardrails.

h2. Design principles
* Correctness first: relocation must preserve per-seq KV content and ordering.
* Budgeted work: bound compaction by *time* and/or *bytes moved* per scheduling cycle.
* Avoid tail spikes: do not perform large relocation inside latency-sensitive decode inner loops.
* Observable: export metrics + tracing spans to correlate compaction/eviction with tail latency.
* Safe-by-default: feature flags + kill-switch + staged rollout.

h1. Compaction mechanism
h2. What we compact
We compact at the granularity of allocator “pages” (or blocks) used for KV storage. Compaction moves live pages to earlier (lower) addresses in the arena to create larger contiguous free spans.

We do not attempt to change the logical layout of KV within a page; we only relocate pages and update indirections.

h2. Preconditions / invariants
During relocation we must preserve:
* A sequence’s KV pointer table must not point to freed/moved pages.
* Reads during decode must see a consistent view of the KV pointers.
* Cancellation/free racing with relocation must not leak pages or double-free.

We enforce these with:
* A per-sequence “relocation lock” (logical lock in scheduler state; not a heavy mutex).
* A relocation state machine (see kv-cache-memory-layout-overview page).
* A two-phase commit for relocation:
  1) Copy live page(s) to new location
  2) Atomically swap pointer(s)
  3) Release old page(s) back to free-list

h2. Incremental compaction (primary)
Incremental compaction runs as a small step each scheduler cycle, bounded by budgets.

Algorithm sketch:
1) Determine if compaction should run:
   * fragmentation_ratio above threshold
   * free_bytes above minimum actionable free
   * allocator under “pressure soon” or “pressure now” signals (see integration)
2) Choose relocation candidates:
   * Prefer sequences with pages scattered across many spans
   * Prefer low-priority tiers first (Hosted Free/Dev > Hosted Pro > Dedicated)
   * Avoid sequences marked as pinned or “latency critical”
3) Choose destination:
   * Allocate a contiguous target span near the “front” of the arena
   * If no contiguous destination exists, compaction step becomes no-op
4) Copy pages:
   * Use GPU memcpy/pack kernel as appropriate
   * Update indirections
5) Update allocator metadata and emit metrics

Budgets:
* bytes_moved_budget_per_tick (default varies by tier)
* time_budget_per_tick_ms (hard cap)

A step stops when any budget is exhausted or when scheduler enters a latency-critical boundary.

h2. Background compaction (secondary; optional)
We support an optional background compaction worker thread that can perform additional relocation when:
* The scheduler indicates the system is in a low-utilization window
* Or when a pool is in “stabilize” mode after a burst

This worker is strictly lower priority than request processing and must also respect global budgets. Initial rollout will keep background compaction disabled by default; incremental compaction is the primary mechanism.

h2. Compaction triggers
We trigger compaction when any of the following are true:
* fragmentation_ratio > trigger_threshold
* free_span_count > span_count_threshold
* allocator_failures_recent > 0 (failed allocations that required fallback/eviction)
* tail_latency_guardrail engaged (SRE signal; see guardrails doc)

We also include hysteresis to avoid oscillation:
* Trigger on threshold_high; stop when below threshold_low.

h2. Candidate selection and fairness
We maintain a small priority queue of candidate sequences. Each sequence is scored by:
* scatter_score (number of spans touched)
* bytes_to_compact (estimated)
* tier_weight (lower tiers more eligible)
* pinned_penalty (pinned sequences typically ineligible)

We also enforce fairness:
* No single sequence can consume > X% of a tick budget.
* Round-robin across candidates to avoid starvation.

h2. Kernel requirements
Most moves can use device-to-device memcpy. For some layouts (paged KV with interleaved head dimension), we may need a lightweight pack kernel to maintain alignment/coalescing.

Initial plan:
* Start with memcpy for page-aligned moves.
* Add pack kernel only if benchmarks show significant regression due to misalignment or if page strides require transformation.

h1. Eviction policy
Compaction reduces fragmentation but cannot create memory out of thin air. When true memory pressure exists (or compaction cannot quickly produce a contiguous span), we must evict.

h2. Policy summary
We implement tier-aware LRU eviction at the sequence level:
* Evict whole sequences (freeing all KV pages for that sequence).
* Prefer evicting:
  * Lower-tier traffic first (e.g., Hosted Free/Dev)
  * Older/idle sequences (LRU by last_token_timestamp)
  * Sequences not marked pinned

We do not evict partial layers or partial KV for a sequence in the initial release.

h2. Pinned sessions and correctness
Some sessions are pinned:
* Dedicated customer pinned sessions (contractual / product requirements)
* Internal canary/test sessions

Pinned sessions are ineligible for eviction unless:
* emergency_oom_mode is enabled (explicit, off by default)
* and SRE oncall flips the kill-switch policy (see runbook)

h2. Prefix cache interaction
If prefix caching is enabled for a model profile:
* Prefix cache entries are separately tracked and are more evictable than active sequences.
* Under pressure we evict prefix cache entries before evicting active sequences.
* Compaction does not move prefix cache entries in v1 unless they share the same arena; if shared, they participate as low-priority candidates.

h2. Customer-facing behavior
Eviction of an active sequence manifests as:
* Request error (e.g., RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED) or retryable overload signal depending on caller type
* Or graceful degradation if routing can retry on a different replica/region (when enabled)

We will not silently drop tokens.

h1. Scheduler integration
The scheduler is the control point to ensure compaction does not cause tail latency spikes.

h2. Integration points
We integrate compaction into scheduler phases:
* End of prefill phase: safe window to do small relocation steps
* Decode boundary between token steps: only if budget is tiny and queue depth is low
* After completion/cancellation processing: coalesce + small compaction step

h2. Budget enforcement
Budgets are enforced by the scheduler, not solely within allocator code:
* The scheduler provides a per-tick budget context:
  * time_budget_ms
  * bytes_budget
  * max_sequences_to_touch
* The allocator/compactor must check the context and return early.

This is intentional to keep latency control centralized and consistent with other runtime maintenance tasks.

h2. Backpressure and overload signals
When overload is detected:
* Prefer shedding new work over doing heavy compaction.
* Compaction should enter “stabilize” mode:
  * perform minimal work required to prevent allocator failure
  * rely on eviction if needed

Signals:
* queue_depth_high
* decode_utilization_high
* p99_latency_rising
* allocator_failures_recent

h2. Safety: cancellation and concurrent events
Cancellation can race with relocation. We handle with:
* Sequence state transitions guarded by scheduler state machine.
* Relocation “epoch” per sequence:
  * cancellation waits for relocation swap to complete or aborts relocation at a safe point
* Allocator operations must be idempotent for the old page free after pointer swap.

We will add targeted stress tests for cancellation during relocation (see validation plan).

h1. Configuration and feature flags
All controls are runtime config flags (no Console UI in v1).

h2. Feature flags (names are internal; subject to config registry constraints)
* runtime.kv_compaction.enabled (default: off initially)
* runtime.kv_compaction.mode = off | incremental | incremental_plus_background
* runtime.kv_compaction.trigger_fragmentation_ratio_high (default: 0.70)
* runtime.kv_compaction.trigger_fragmentation_ratio_low (default: 0.55)
* runtime.kv_compaction.min_actionable_free_bytes (default: 2GiB hosted; 1GiB dedicated)
* runtime.kv_compaction.bytes_budget_per_tick (default: hosted 128MiB; dedicated 256MiB)
* runtime.kv_compaction.time_budget_per_tick_ms (default: hosted 0.35ms; dedicated 0.50ms)
* runtime.kv_compaction.max_sequences_per_tick (default: 2)

Eviction:
* runtime.kv_eviction.enabled (default: on; existing behavior refined)
* runtime.kv_eviction.policy = tier_aware_lru_v1
* runtime.kv_eviction.allow_evict_pinned (default: off)
* runtime.kv_eviction.prefer_prefix_cache_first (default: on)

Kill-switch:
* runtime.kv_compaction.kill_switch (default: false)
  * When true: disables compaction immediately and blocks new relocation steps.

h2. Tier defaults (proposal)
* Hosted Free/Dev:
  * compaction enabled after canary
  * smaller budgets to minimize latency risk
  * aggressive eviction permitted (non-pinned only)
* Hosted Pro:
  * compaction enabled after hosted subset validation
  * slightly higher budgets
* Dedicated:
  * compaction enabled last
  * higher budgets allowed, but stronger guardrails on eviction (pinned sessions common)

Final defaults will be set after benchmark + canary results (see experiment tracker).

h1. Observability
We add:
* Metrics
* Tracing spans
* Dashboards and alerts (SRE-owned)

h2. Metrics (high level)
Allocator health:
* kv_allocator_fragmentation_ratio
* kv_allocator_free_bytes
* kv_allocator_largest_free_span_bytes
* kv_allocator_free_span_count
* kv_allocator_allocation_failures_total

Compaction activity:
* kv_compaction_bytes_moved_total
* kv_compaction_time_ms_total
* kv_compaction_steps_total
* kv_compaction_aborted_steps_total

Eviction:
* kv_evictions_total{reason,tier}
* kv_evicted_bytes_total{tier}
* kv_eviction_candidates_scanned_total

Correlations:
* Export exemplars linking compaction spans to latency traces.

h2. Tracing
We add spans around:
* compaction_step
* relocation_copy
* relocation_pointer_swap
* eviction_selection
* eviction_execute

Each span includes attributes:
* model_profile
* gpu_id
* bytes_moved
* sequences_touched
* fragmentation_ratio_before/after (sampled)

h1. Performance and correctness validation
h2. Benchmark plan
We extend the benchmark suite with scenarios designed to induce fragmentation:
* Mixed prompt lengths (p50 short, p90 long)
* High churn (frequent cancellations)
* Long-lived decode sessions (streaming)
* Bursty arrival patterns (traffic spikes)

KPIs:
* p50/p95/p99 latency (prefill and decode)
* throughput (tokens/s/GPU)
* fragmentation_ratio time series
* compaction_bytes_moved and overhead
* eviction rate

Acceptance criteria (initial):
* No more than 1–2% steady-state throughput regression at equivalent load.
* p99 tail latency improvement in burst/mixed-length scenarios, or at minimum elimination of the worst spikes.
* Compaction overhead stays within budget, with no sustained scheduler stalls.

h2. Correctness and stress tests
Add/extend tests:
* Cancellation during relocation (including repeated cancel/retry)
* Concurrent completion + eviction
* Long-running sessions with intermittent backpressure
* Adversarial patterns: alternating small/large allocations to maximize fragmentation

h2. Failure modes and mitigations
* Decode stalls due to heavy compaction:
  * Mitigation: strict scheduler-enforced budgets, disable background compaction by default
* Copy overhead increases GPU utilization:
  * Mitigation: limit bytes moved; tune thresholds; add pack kernel only if needed
* Pointer swap race leading to incorrect KV:
  * Mitigation: relocation state machine + invariants + stress tests + tracing
* Increased evictions:
  * Mitigation: compaction first when actionable; tier-aware eviction; prefix cache evicted first

h1. Rollout plan
We will follow staged rollout with explicit guardrails and rollback triggers.

h2. Stage 0 — Internal dev & perf lab
* Enable compaction in controlled benchmarks and staging clusters.
* Validate metrics dashboards and trace exemplars.
* Validate cancellation stress tests.

Exit criteria:
* Benchmarks meet acceptance criteria.
* No correctness regressions.

h2. Stage 1 — Internal canary (small %)
* Enable on a small internal canary pool.
* Watch:
  * p99 decode latency
  * allocator_failures
  * bytes_moved/time_ms per tick
  * eviction spikes

Rollback criteria:
* p99 sustained regression beyond guardrail for > N minutes
* allocator_failures increase significantly
* suspected correctness issue (immediate disable)

h2. Stage 2 — Hosted subset (tier-limited)
* Enable for a subset of Hosted (starting Free/Dev, then Pro).
* Tight budgets; aggressive monitoring.

h2. Stage 3 — Dedicated pools (opt-in, then default)
* Start with one dedicated pool with known burst issues.
* Allow per-customer override via config registry.

h2. Communications
* Runtime release note (Runtime 1.22) includes:
  * What changed
  * What metrics to monitor
  * How to disable (oncall)
* Support/CS enablement:
  * How to interpret p99 improvements and eviction errors

h1. Rollback / kill-switch plan
Oncall/SRE can disable compaction within minutes via:
* runtime.kv_compaction.kill_switch = true
* runtime.kv_compaction.enabled = false

Expected behavior on disable:
* No new relocation steps start.
* In-progress relocation steps complete or safely abort at a barrier.
* Allocator continues without compaction (existing behavior).

If eviction policy changes contribute to incidents, we can revert eviction policy to previous behavior via:
* runtime.kv_eviction.policy = legacy

h1. Alternatives considered
* Full stop-the-world defragmentation:
  * Rejected due to unacceptable tail latency impact.
* Pure eviction-only strategy:
  * Rejected because it increases customer-visible errors and is avoidable when free space exists but is fragmented.
* Changing to a completely different allocator (buddy allocator / slab by size classes):
  * Deferred; more invasive, higher migration risk.

h1. Open questions
* Do we need a pack kernel for specific KV layouts (e.g., interleaved heads) to avoid alignment regressions?
* What is the best default fragmentation trigger per model profile (7B vs 70B) given very different KV footprints?
* Should we expose compaction controls in Console for Dedicated customers in a later release?
* How should we treat cross-replica routing retries when an active sequence is evicted (product behavior vs pure infra behavior)?

h1. Appendix: Pseudocode (illustrative)
Compaction step (simplified):
1) if !enabled or kill_switch: return
2) if fragmentation_ratio < low_threshold: return
3) budget = scheduler.get_compaction_budget()
4) candidates = allocator.select_candidates(max_sequences_per_tick)
5) for seq in candidates:
   a) if budget.exhausted(): break
   b) if seq.pinned: continue
   c) plan = allocator.plan_relocation(seq)
   d) if plan.none: continue
   e) bytes_moved = relocate(plan, budget)
   f) allocator.commit(plan)
   g) emit metrics

Eviction (simplified):
1) if allocation fails or free_bytes < min_free_bytes:
2) evict prefix cache entries first (if enabled)
3) if still pressure:
4) select seq by tier-aware LRU, excluding pinned
5) evict seq, emit reason and tier

---
Changelog:
* 2026-01-23: Initial draft (O. El-Sayed)
* 2026-02-02: Added scheduler budgeting section + trigger hysteresis (S. Ivanova)
* 2026-02-09: Updated metrics list + tracing attributes (A. Grant)
* 2026-02-16: Added tier defaults + rollback criteria aligned with SRE guardrails (S. Gallagher)

title: Mixed-Precision Token Billing and Telemetry Playbook
content:
Summary

This playbook defines the telemetry, tagging, measurement, and investigation process required to bill GPU inference usage at token granularity for mixed-precision and quantized execution paths. It is intended for infra engineers, billing/data platform, and SREs who operate the inference runtime and chargeback pipeline.

Goals

- Produce accurate token-level billing that reflects real execution cost differences between FP16/FP32/BF16 and INT8/4-bit quantized paths.
- Map runtime telemetry to billing dimensions without double-counting KV-cache reuse, cached prefixes, or streaming re-requests.
- Provide a reproducible investigation checklist for cost anomalies and reconciliations.
- Minimize instrumentation overhead and avoid exposing customer prompt text to billing systems (PII-sensitive).

Scope and non-goals

- Scope: hosted & dedicated deployments; applies to on-prem when telemetry bridge is enabled.
- Non-goals: prompt content collection, model-quality metrics, or per-token content inspection. This playbook is strictly about resource attribution and cost telemetry.

Ownership

- Runtime telemetry schema and collectors: infra/serving-runtime team (owner: Aisha Patel)
- Billing pipeline mapping & ETL: finance-data (owner: Marcus Lee)
- Billing validation & reconciliation: infra-sre + finance ops (owner: Sofia Gomez)

High-level approach

1) Emit a compact per-request telemetry envelope from the runtime that includes resource-attribution fields (not raw text). Telemetry must be signed and batched to avoid high cardinality.
2) Enrich telemetry in the ETL with model flavor, quantization profile, and effective execution kernel.
3) Convert tokens to a normalized token-charge unit using a kernel-cost table and per-region GPU cost factors.
4) Post-process to deduplicate cached tokens (prefix/kv hits) and to apply tenant-level discounts/credits.

Telemetry envelope (contract)

- Emit at request completion and for mid-stream checkpoint (for long streaming sessions). Envelope fields (compact):
  - request_id: opaque UUID
  - tenant_id: tenant-opaque-id
  - model_id: model name + pinned version (e.g., "llama-2-70b-v1")
  - kernel_id: runtime kernel identifier (e.g., "attn_v2_bf16_k8")
  - precision_path: one of [FP32, BF16, FP16, INT8, INT4]
  - input_tokens: integer (tokens in prompt sent to runtime)
  - output_tokens_emitted: integer (tokens emitted to user)
  - tokens_served_from_kv_cache: integer
  - continuous_batch_group: optional string (if request batched)
  - seq_len_distribution: short histogram string (buckets: <=32, 33-128, 129-512, 513+)
  - gpu_micros: integer (microseconds spent on GPU kernels attributable to request)
  - gpu_memory_bytes_peak: integer
  - region: cloud region code
  - instance_flavor: e.g., "p4d.24xlarge" or on-prem SKU
  - timestamp: ISO8601

Example (JSON emitted by runtime):

{"request_id":"f83c9a1e-...","tenant_id":"t-acme-42","model_id":"redwood-rlm-30b@v3","kernel_id":"attn_v2_bf16_k8","precision_path":"BF16","input_tokens":48,"output_tokens_emitted":96,"tokens_served_from_kv_cache":12,"gpu_micros":230000,"gpu_memory_bytes_peak":2147483648,"region":"us-west-2","instance_flavor":"g5dn.12xlarge","timestamp":"2025-10-05T17:12:09Z"}

Note: Runtime MUST NOT emit user prompt text or raw outputs in this envelope. Any enrichment requiring prompt length should only use token counts.

Kernel cost table and normalized token units

- Maintain a kernel cost table (canonical source: infra-config repo) that maps (kernel_id, instance_flavor, region) -> cost_per_micros and amortized overhead_per_request.
- Billing unit: normalized_token_cost = base_token_charge * precision_multiplier * kernel_efficiency_factor
  - base_token_charge is a global value per model family and region (configurable)
  - precision_multiplier examples: FP32=1.0, BF16=0.75, FP16=0.7, INT8=0.42, INT4=0.29 (numbers derived from profiling; updated quarterly)
  - kernel_efficiency_factor is derived from gpu_micros / output_tokens_emitted to capture kernel-level variance

Telemetry to billing pipeline mapping (ETL steps)

- Ingest raw envelopes into telemetry lake (Kafka -> minio).
- Enrich with model family tags and quantization profiles (from model-service metadata).
- Convert per-request fields into normalized_token_cost and token_count_for_billing = output_tokens_emitted - tokens_served_from_kv_cache.
- Aggregate per tenant per day/hour and write to billing ledger (append-only).

Deduplication & KV-cache handling

- Rule: Tokens served from KV cache do not incur full generation cost; they are charged at cache_retrieval_rate (configurable, default 10% of base token charge) unless the KV cache warmup was a paid generation by another tenant.
- If tokens were seeded by the same tenant earlier in the session, mark as internal cache hit -> charge at cache_retrieval_rate.
- If tokens were restored from a global warm-pool seeded by evaluation infra (non-customer), the ETL should flag this and drop charges (or route to evaluation billing codes) using warmpool_tag in telemetry.

Chargeback reconciliation rules

- Daily reconciliation: compare telemetry-derived spend vs. GPU utilization cost allocation. If delta > 3% absolute or > $2,500/day, trigger an automatic investigation ticket.
- Weekly sampling audit: pick 0.1% of requests, validate telemetry fields against raw runtime logs (only counts, never text).

Alerting thresholds (SRE + Finance)

- anomaly_spend_rate: 20% increase in normalized_token_cost per tenant vs. 7-day rolling baseline -> create high-priority alert.
- kernel_efficiency_regression: a kernel_id with median gpu_micros/output_token > baseline * 1.35 over 30 minutes -> pager to runtime-oncall.
- telemetry_backfill_lag: if ETL ingestion lag > 2 hours for > 10% partitions -> page data-platform.

Investigation runbook (step-by-step)

1) Triage ticket created automatically by reconciliation or manual alert.
2) Owner: infra-sre oncall. Attach tenant_id and the offending time window.
3) Query examples:
   - Prometheus: GPU kernel micros per request: sum(rate(runtime_gpu_micros_total{tenant_id=~"t-.*"}[5m])) by (kernel_id, tenant_id)
   - SQL (bigquery-like): SELECT tenant_id, SUM(gpu_micros) as gpu, SUM(output_tokens_emitted) as tokens, kernel_id FROM telemetry_enriched WHERE timestamp BETWEEN X AND Y GROUP BY tenant_id,kernel_id
4) Calculate normalized_token_cost_delta = current_cost_per_token / baseline_cost_per_token. If delta > 1.2, proceed.
5) Check for: model change (new model_id), kernel rollout, quantization override, instance flavor change (spot->on-demand). Cross-check with deploy history and rollout tags.
6) If kernel_efficiency_regression: roll back kernel rollout (see kernel rollback playbook) or engage runtime engineers.
7) If billing mis-attribution suspected: freeze ledger writes for the tenant for the time window and perform manual discounts/adjustments. Finance ops to approve crediting.

CI/CD & Terraform patterns for instrumentation rollout

- Instrumentation code lives in serving-runtime repo. Releases must follow canary promotion policy: 5% canary -> 25% -> 60% -> 100% with 12-hour observation windows.
- Terraform: add option to enable/disable enriched telemetry at tenant scope via terraform module parameter (module: tenant-gpu-config.enable_cost_telemetry).
- A sample Terraform snippet (HCL):

resource "redwood_tenant_config" "acme" {
  tenant_id = "t-acme-42"
  enable_cost_telemetry = true
  telemetry_retention_days = 30
}

Performance and privacy constraints

- Telemetry aggregation must be batched with max payload size 512KB and no more than 1 request/sec per inference process to the telemetry endpoint.
- All telemetry must be obfuscated at source: tenant IDs are hashed with a rotating salt when exported to datasets used by non-finance teams. Full tenant mapping is restricted to finance-data.

Operational play scenarios

- Scenario A: Sudden spike in per-token cost for a single tenant -> run Investigation runbook; if caused by accidental model pin to FP32, recommend a customer-facing configuration change and offer temporary credit.
- Scenario B: Kernel rollout caused fleet-wide 10% cost uplift -> immediate rollback and create postmortem with cost delta table.
- Scenario C: ETL lag causes underbilled tenants -> run backfill procedures (see "backfill-procedure" internal doc id) and communicate adjustments with finance ops.

Metrics dashboard (recommended widgets)

- Per-tenant normalized token cost (7d, 30d)
- Kernel efficiency heatmap (kernel_id x model_family) showing median gpu_micros/output_token
- KV-cache hit ratio by tenant and by model
- Daily delta: telemetry-derived spend vs. infra allocation cost

Quarterly governance

- Every quarter: update precision_multiplier table based on micro-benchmarking across representative model families.
- Finance and runtime lead to sign-off on multiplier changes; changes are annotated and backdated for historical comparability.

Appendices

A. Example ETL pseudo-SQL for deriving billing rows

INSERT INTO billing_ledger (tenant_id, day, normalized_tokens, amount_usd)
SELECT tenant_id, DATE(timestamp) as day, SUM((output_tokens_emitted - tokens_served_from_kv_cache) * precision_multiplier * kernel_efficiency) as normalized_tokens, SUM((output_tokens_emitted - tokens_served_from_kv_cache) * precision_multiplier * kernel_efficiency * base_rate) as amount_usd
FROM telemetry_enriched
WHERE timestamp BETWEEN @start AND @end
GROUP BY tenant_id, day;

B. Common troubleshooting checks (quick list)

- Did the tenant pin to a new full-precision model?
- Was a kernel rollout in the affected region?
- Did instance flavor change to an expensive SKU (spot->on-demand)?
- Are cache warmups being misattributed as paid generations?
- Is ETL normalizing tokens incorrectly (off-by-one in output token counts)?

C. Contact matrix

- runtime-oncall: #runtime-oncall (pager)
- infra-sre: infra-sre@redwood.com
- finance-data: finance-data@redwood.com
- billing-ops (customer credits): billing-ops@redwood.com

D. Change log

- 2024-11-12: Document created (Aisha Patel)
- 2025-04-01: Added kernel_efficiency_regression alert thresholds (Marcus Lee)
- 2026-01-20: Updated precision_multiplier recommendations after Q4 benchmarking (Sofia Gomez)

End of document

title: Perf Regression Canary (Prod) — Design: Runtime + Kernel/Scheduler Attribution
content:
## 1. Summary
We will deploy a lightweight, always-on **performance canary** in production to detect and alert on **per-model** serving regressions before they broadly impact customers. The canary continuously runs a **synthetic, privacy-safe workload** against a curated model list in each enabled region/tier and evaluates results against **versioned baselines**.

Primary regression signals:
- **p95 end-to-end latency** and **p95 runtime-only latency**
- **tokens/sec** (throughput)

Secondary signals used for attribution and fast triage:
- Prefill vs decode latency
- Scheduler **queueing time** and batch size distribution
- KV cache hit rate (where applicable)
- Runtime build id, kernel selection id, scheduler config id

This document covers the architecture, workload model, metrics, baseline strategy, regression evaluation, attribution, and rollout plan.

## 2. Problem statement
Runtime performance regressions are often introduced by:
- Kernel changes (new fused kernels, attention paths, quantization kernels)
- Scheduler/batching heuristic changes (continuous batching decisions, token budget changes)
- Model config updates (rope scaling, max context, kv cache settings)
- GPU fleet changes (new driver, MIG layout, SKU mix)
- Release/rollout sequencing and region-specific differences

Customer traffic is too noisy and privacy-sensitive to use directly for early detection. We need a controlled, repeatable signal that is:
- **Low overhead** (<0.5% GPU capacity per region for covered models)
- **Low noise** (anti-flap, minimum sample sizes)
- **Actionable** (clear attribution: kernel vs scheduler vs infra)
- **Integrates** into dashboards, incident-bot, and rollout gates

## 3. Goals / non-goals
### 3.1 Goals
1) Detect per-model regressions in production with low noise:
- Latency: p95 and p99 (end-to-end and runtime-only)
- Throughput: tokens/sec drop (decode throughput)

2) Provide fast triage signals to classify regressions:
- Kernel-level vs scheduler-level vs model-config-level vs infra/fleet-level

3) Integrate into existing tooling:
- Grafana dashboards and trace/log links
- Alert routing to #eng-runtime and SRE on-call (tiered)
- Rollout workflow gates (pause / rollback criteria)

4) Keep overhead and risk low:
- Strict QPS and token budgets
- No customer prompts, no user identifiers

### 3.2 Non-goals (initial)
- Shadowing or sampling real customer prompts/traffic
- Coupling to quality regression evaluation (handled by Applied ML eval harness)
- GPU microbench replacement (this is an always-on canary; microbench remains pre-merge / pre-release)

## 4. High-level architecture
### 4.1 Components
**Service:** `perf-canary`
- Stateless service deployed per region
- Generates synthetic requests (seeded workload)
- Calls internal inference endpoints using restricted auth scope
- Emits metrics + structured events
- Evaluates regressions against baselines
- Sends alert webhooks to incident-bot

**Control plane config:** `canary_targets` (validated + audited)
- Which models/versions per region/tier are covered
- Workload profile to use (prompt buckets, target output lengths)
- Safety limits (QPS/tokens budget)

**Baseline store:** `perf-baseline-store`
- Versioned baseline artifacts keyed by (model_id, model_version, runtime_build, hardware_sku, region?)
- Read path: perf-canary fetches the baseline summary needed for regression evaluation
- Write path: baseline generation job produces artifacts after controlled load runs

**Telemetry pipeline:** Prometheus-compatible metrics + trace sampling
- Metrics: histograms and counters (guarded cardinality)
- Traces: limited sampling of canary requests only (no customer data)

**Dashboards + alerts:** Observability pack + incident-bot
- Grafana dashboards per model with breakdowns
- Warning and paging alert rules with dampening
- Incident-bot dedupe keys and runbook links

### 4.2 Request flow (text diagram)
1) `perf-canary` loads `canary_targets` for region `R` and tier `T`.
2) For each enabled model target, it generates a synthetic prompt (seeded) and calls:
   - `inference-gateway.internal/v1/chat/completions` (or equivalent internal route)
3) Runtime emits request-scoped metrics including:
   - runtime build id, kernel selection id, scheduler config id
   - queueing time, batch size, prefill/decode timing
4) `perf-canary` aggregates samples into a rolling window and evaluates against baseline.
5) On regression, `perf-canary` posts a structured alert payload to `incident-bot`.
6) Incident-bot posts to Slack and links to:
   - Grafana dashboards
   - Baseline artifact
   - Runbook

## 5. Canary workload model (synthetic, privacy-safe)
### 5.1 Design principles
- Represent common **shape** of production requests (prompt lengths and decode lengths) without using any customer content.
- Be reproducible: deterministic seeding so changes are attributable.
- Avoid pathological prompts that trigger unusual tokenization variance.
- Cover multiple buckets because regressions often appear at specific sequence length or batch behavior.

### 5.2 Prompt distribution (v0)
We use a small set of prompt templates that are semantically inert and stable (e.g., “system: You are a helpful assistant.” + generated filler). The content is non-sensitive and generated in-service.

Buckets are defined by **input tokens** (approximate) and **target output tokens**.

Table: v0 buckets
- Bucket A (short): input 32–64 tokens, output 64 tokens
- Bucket B (medium): input 256–384 tokens, output 128 tokens
- Bucket C (long prefill): input 1,024–1,536 tokens, output 64 tokens
- Bucket D (long decode): input 256–384 tokens, output 512 tokens

Target mix (initial): A 35%, B 35%, C 15%, D 15%

Rationale:
- A/B cover common chat sizes and batch behavior.
- C is prefill-heavy and catches attention/prefill kernel regressions.
- D is decode-heavy and catches tokens/sec and decode kernel regressions.

### 5.3 Generation parameters
Defaults (can be overridden per model target):
- Temperature: 0.0 (reduce stochasticity)
- Top_p: 1.0
- Presence/frequency penalty: 0
- Stop sequences: none
- Streaming: off for primary canary (avoid client-side streaming variance). We may add a streaming track later.

### 5.4 Scheduling and rate limiting
The canary must be “always-on” but not disruptive.

Per region, per model target:
- Max QPS: 0.05–0.2 QPS (tuned by model cost)
- Concurrency: 1 (initial)
- Token budget guardrail: max 25k tokens/min/model (input+output)

Global guardrails:
- Hard cap of total canary tokens/min per region (config default: 200k tokens/min)
- Automatic backoff on elevated error rates or increased queueing

### 5.5 Isolation and routing
- The canary uses an internal route that is isolated from customer auth scopes.
- Targets are pinned to a specific **capacity tier** where possible (Hosted/Dedicated pools differ).
- Requests include `x-redwood-canary: perf-regression` header for traceability and filtering.

## 6. Metrics captured
### 6.1 Required metrics (per model target)
All metrics must be emitted for canary traffic only (filterable by header/service identity).

Latency (histograms):
- `canary_e2e_latency_ms` (client-observed; includes gateway + scheduler + runtime)
- `runtime_total_latency_ms` (runtime-observed; excludes gateway)
- `runtime_prefill_latency_ms`
- `runtime_decode_latency_ms`
- `scheduler_queueing_latency_ms`

Throughput:
- `runtime_tokens_generated_total` (counter)
- `runtime_tokens_per_second` (derived; or emit as gauge per request)

Batching / scheduler behavior:
- `scheduler_batch_size` (histogram)
- `scheduler_microbatch_count` (histogram or summary)
- `scheduler_active_requests` (gauge; optional)

Caching:
- `runtime_kv_cache_hit_rate` (gauge; where applicable)
- `runtime_prefix_cache_hit_rate` (gauge; where applicable)

Reliability (for safety + correlation):
- `canary_request_errors_total` labeled by error class (timeout, 5xx, 429)
- `canary_request_timeouts_total`

### 6.2 Required dimensions (labels) and cardinality rules
We keep labels minimal and bounded.

Required labels:
- `model_id` (canonical)
- `model_version` (canonical)
- `region`
- `capacity_tier` (hosted|dedicated|private where applicable)
- `hardware_sku` (e.g., h100-sxm, a100-80gb, l40s)
- `runtime_build_id` (short hash)
- `kernel_selection_id` (bounded id, not raw kernel name list)
- `scheduler_config_id` (bounded id)

Explicitly not allowed:
- request ids
- tenant/customer ids
- prompt hashes
- raw prompt lengths as labels (use buckets/quantiles)

Note: `kernel_selection_id` and `scheduler_config_id` must be stable enums with bounded cardinality (see §8).

## 7. Baseline strategy
### 7.1 Baseline keys
Baselines are versioned and stored per:
- `model_id`
- `model_version`
- `runtime_build_id`
- `hardware_sku`
- `capacity_tier`
- optionally `region` (see §7.4)

We intentionally do NOT baseline purely by “model” because:
- Performance is sensitive to runtime build and hardware
- Model version pinning matters for consistent expectations

### 7.2 Baseline contents
For each metric, the baseline artifact includes:
- p50/p95/p99 estimates
- dispersion/variance estimate (e.g., MAD or stddev) for noise-aware thresholds
- sample size used and collection window metadata
- reference links: baseline job run id, runtime release id

### 7.3 How baselines are generated
Baselines are produced by a controlled load job (benchmark-lab) that runs the same workload profile against a prod-like pool:
- Warmup phase (discard)
- Measurement phase (target N requests per bucket)

Acceptance criteria to publish a baseline:
- Minimum sample size per bucket (initial: 200 requests/bucket)
- No elevated error rate (>0.5%)
- Stable queueing (p95 queueing under defined cap for “baseline-quality”)

### 7.4 Region handling
Initial policy:
- Baseline is **hardware SKU + tier scoped**, and region is treated as an attribute for monitoring.
- We only split baselines by region when we have evidence of consistent region deltas (driver versions, fleet composition).

Operationally:
- The evaluator can apply region-specific multipliers if needed (config-based) without exploding baseline cardinality.

### 7.5 Baseline updates and drift
Baselines are updated when any of the baseline keys change (new runtime build, new model version, new hardware SKU).

We avoid continuously rolling baselines in the first iteration because it can hide slow regressions and caused alert storms in prior systems. Instead:
- Baselines are **fixed per release key** and explicitly advanced.
- We monitor drift separately via a “baseline freshness” dashboard panel and a “slow drift” warning (non-paging).

(See ADR: baseline computation and thresholds.)

## 8. Regression evaluation and anti-flap logic
### 8.1 Windowing and minimum samples
`perf-canary` aggregates observations in a rolling evaluation window.

Defaults (per model target):
- Evaluation window: 30 minutes
- Minimum samples: 80 total requests AND at least 15 requests in each of the top 2 buckets by weight
- Cooldown: 45 minutes after an alert resolves before re-alerting on the same key

### 8.2 Regression definitions (initial)
We evaluate multiple conditions. A regression is raised if ANY “paging” condition is met, otherwise warning if “warning” conditions are met.

Definitions use percent change from baseline:
- Latency regression: `(observed_p95 / baseline_p95 - 1)`
- Throughput regression: `(baseline_tokens_per_sec / observed_tokens_per_sec - 1)`

Initial thresholds (subject to calibration):
Warning:
- p95 e2e latency >= +10% for 2 consecutive windows
- OR p95 runtime latency >= +10% for 2 consecutive windows
- OR tokens/sec drop >= 8% for 2 consecutive windows

Paging (top models only; controlled by target list):
- p95 e2e latency >= +20% for 2 consecutive windows
- OR tokens/sec drop >= 15% for 2 consecutive windows

Guardrails:
- If scheduler queueing p95 increases by >30% AND runtime latency is flat (<= +5%), classify as “capacity/scheduler” and route as warning unless sustained > 90 minutes.

### 8.3 Noise controls
- Use histograms and compute quantiles server-side (Prometheus/Grafana) and evaluator-side using stable quantile estimator.
- Apply a small smoothing factor for p95 comparisons (EWMA across windows) but never smooth raw metric emission.
- Enforce “two-window confirm” for warning/paging.
- Deduplicate alerts by: (model_id, model_version, runtime_build_id, hardware_sku, region, tier, metric_class).

## 9. Attribution and triage signals
When a regression triggers, we want immediate evidence pointing to the likely root cause.

### 9.1 Kernel-level vs scheduler-level heuristics
The alert payload includes a classification based on these decision rules:

A) Likely kernel/runtime execution regression
- `runtime_total_latency_ms` p95 increases materially (>= threshold)
- AND `scheduler_queueing_latency_ms` is flat or minor
- AND `kernel_selection_id` changed recently OR correlates with runtime_build_id change

B) Likely scheduler/capacity regression
- `scheduler_queueing_latency_ms` p95 increases materially
- AND `runtime_total_latency_ms` p95 is flat or minor
- AND batch size distribution shifts (lower effective batch) OR active requests increases

C) Likely model-config regression
- Regressions are isolated to a single model_version
- AND kernel_selection_id and runtime_build_id unchanged
- AND prefill/decode split changes consistent with config (e.g., max context / rope)

D) Likely infra/fleet regression
- Regressions correlate with hardware_sku or a single region
- Increased variability + increased queueing + increased error rates
- Correlated fleet signals (driver rollout, MIG config changes) if available

### 9.2 Required tags for attribution
To support the above, runtime telemetry MUST expose:
- `runtime_build_id`
- `kernel_selection_id` (bounded enum; e.g., “attn_v3_fp16”, “attn_v4_flash”, “int8_decode_v2”)
- `scheduler_config_id` (bounded enum; ties back to scheduler heuristics)

Implementation detail:
- Do not emit raw kernel names or dynamic combinations as labels.
- Maintain a mapping table in runtime code for stable ids.

### 9.3 What goes in the alert payload
Alert payload fields (sent to incident-bot):
- model_id, model_version, region, tier, hardware_sku
- runtime_build_id, kernel_selection_id, scheduler_config_id
- baseline p95 and observed p95 (e2e and runtime)
- baseline tokens/sec and observed tokens/sec
- queueing p95 and batch size deltas
- confidence level (based on samples and variance)
- links: dashboards, baseline artifact, recent runtime release notes, runbook

## 10. Dashboards (what we expect to see)
For each model target, the dashboard provides:
- p50/p95/p99 time series for e2e latency and runtime latency
- Prefill/decode/queueing breakdown
- tokens/sec and tokens/request
- batch size histogram (over time)
- KV cache hit rate (when enabled)
- Annotation overlays for runtime releases and kernel flag flips

Dashboards must include a single-click “Compare to baseline” panel showing percent deltas.

## 11. Deployment, safety, and privacy
### 11.1 Identity and permissions
- `perf-canary` runs under a restricted service account scope: inference read + metrics write.
- No access to customer metadata stores.
- Config reads are audited.

### 11.2 Data handling
- Synthetic prompts only.
- No prompt or completion text is persisted.
- Logs are redacted and include explicit assertions:
  - never log request payload
  - never log auth tokens
  - only log bucket id and token counts

### 11.3 Overhead budget
Target: <0.5% GPU capacity per region for covered models.

Operational budget model (initial):
- Per model target token budget: 25k tokens/min
- If a region runs 10 covered models, total = 250k tokens/min
- Convert to GPU utilization using measured tokens/sec per SKU and average batch behavior; enforce hard cap per region.

Safety valves:
- Global disable switch in control plane (`canary_enabled=false`)
- Automatic backoff on:
  - queueing p95 exceeding threshold
  - elevated 429s
  - elevated 5xx

## 12. Rollout plan
### Phase 0: Staging and prod-like bake
- Run canary against staging pools and a prod-like dedicated environment
- Validate metric correctness, label cardinality, and baseline stability
- Acceptance: variance characterization complete, no unexpected overhead

### Phase 1: Prod enablement (single region, small model set)
Target: `us-east`
- Enable 2–3 models:
  - 1 “top model” (high traffic)
  - 1 “high-risk model” (recent kernel/scheduler changes)
  - 1 long-context model (prefill heavy)
- Start with warning-only alerts for 7–14 days
- Tune min sample sizes and dampening

### Phase 2: Enable paging for top models
- Gate on: low false positive rate and on-call readiness
- Paging only for top-model list
- Confirm incident-bot dedupe and runbook links

### Phase 3: Expand coverage
- Expand to top 10 models and additional regions (e.g., eu-west)
- Re-evaluate whether region-specific baselines are needed

### Phase 4: Rollout gates integration
- Use canary as an automated signal in release workflow:
  - “Pause expansion” when paging-level regression in canary
  - Optional auto-rollback for runtime build when confidence is high

## 13. Failure modes and mitigations
- Canary causes queueing / interference:
  - Mitigation: strict QPS/token caps, backoff on queueing, per-region hard caps

- False positives due to baseline drift:
  - Mitigation: fixed baselines per release key, drift monitoring as separate non-paging signal, two-window confirm

- Metric label explosion:
  - Mitigation: bounded enums for kernel/scheduler ids; no high-cardinality labels

- Telemetry pipeline latency causes late alerts:
  - Mitigation: evaluator uses direct client-observed metrics for quick checks; dashboards annotate ingestion delay

- Canary fails silently:
  - Mitigation: heartbeat metric `canary_runs_total` and “canary stopped” warning alert

## 14. Open questions
1) Should we maintain separate baselines for hosted vs dedicated pools when the hardware SKU is the same but scheduling policies differ?
2) Do we need a streaming-mode canary track to catch gateway/streaming regressions (separate from runtime)?
3) How should we represent and validate `kernel_selection_id` when kernel selection is partially dynamic?
4) What is the long-term policy for baseline freshness (e.g., monthly re-baseline even without release key changes)?

## 15. Ownership
- Design/implementation lead: Noah Patel
- Scheduler attribution + queueing metrics: Sofia Ivanova
- Kernel tagging + correlation: Hiro Tanaka
- Runtime instrumentation: Omar El-Sayed
- Telemetry + baselines pipeline: Logan Wright, Nadia Rahman
- Alerting standards + dashboard consistency: Allison Grant
- SRE readiness + paging policy: Sean Gallagher, Rafael Mendes

## 16. Appendix: Terminology
- E2E latency: client-observed time from request submission to full response completion
- Runtime latency: time measured inside the model runtime (excludes gateway)
- Queueing latency: time spent waiting for scheduler admission / batch formation
- Tokens/sec: generated tokens divided by decode time (or runtime decode phase time)

title: Sharded Attention Execution Guidelines
content:
Summary:
This guide describes recommended execution patterns, kernel scheduling strategies, profiling steps, benchmark integration notes, and operational runbook actions for sharded-attention execution in the Redwood serving runtime. It is intended for engineers who implement or tune shard-aware kernels, SREs triaging performance regressions, and platform owners running the benchmarking suite.

Goals:
- Provide a compact, actionable checklist to achieve predictable latency and throughput for sharded attention workloads.
- Describe scheduling primitives and policy knobs the runtime exposes and when to use them.
- Outline profiling and benchmark procedures that produce reproducible performance artifacts.
- Document triage/runbook steps for common regressions and known mitigations.

Context and background:
Sharded attention (tensor-parallel splits across KV shards) is used for large-decoder models and some encoder-decoder variants to scale state and computation. In our fleet, sharded attention adds interaction points with: GPU memory placement, KV cache routing, communication schedules (all-reduce / reduce-scatter), and kernel selection (FP16 vs int8 mixed paths). Mistuned scheduling or batching can produce amplified tail latency and cross-request interference.

Architecture overview (high level):
- Logical components:
  - Request router: assigns incoming requests to shard groups based on model-version and shard topology.
  - Execution orchestrator: slices requests into micro-batches for compute kernels and coordinates cross-shard comms.
  - Kernel mapper: selects kernel variant based on seq_len distribution, quantization profile, and available comm topology.
  - KV cache manager: handles prefix cache hits, partial cache reuse and eviction across shards.

- Dataflow sketch:
  1) Request arrives -> route to shard-group leader
  2) Orchestrator computes micro-batch plan (batch size, slice offsets)
  3) KV indices resolved; cross-shard comm plan computed
  4) Kernels invoked on each shard with coordinated comm primitives

Key scheduling primitives and policies:
- Priority lanes: per-tenant/per-route numeric priority (0..7). Use lanes to isolate high-SLO customers from best-effort workloads.
- Deadline-aware slicing: requests with tight latency budgets can be sliced into smaller micro-batches that avoid queueing behind large batches. Config knob: scheduler.deadline_slicing.enabled (boolean) and scheduler.deadline_slicing.max_slices (int).
- Backpressure thresholds: two soft thresholds (queue_soft_ms, queue_hard_ms). If queue latency exceeds queue_soft_ms the scheduler reduces auto-batched slice sizes by 25% until below threshold. If queue_hard_ms is exceeded the request is re-routed to fallback model variant.
- Affinity constraints: pin hot shard leaders to NIC/GPU pairs to reduce cross-host comm overhead for latency-sensitive flows. affinity.policy can be set to host-local | spread | packed.

Kernel selection heuristics (how mapper picks kernels):
- Inputs considered: seq_len distribution (p50/p95/p99), effective micro-batch size, quantization profile, active comm topology.
- Heuristic examples:
  - If p95_seq_len < 64 and micro-batch >= 8 -> choose fused-attention-kernel-v2 for stable throughput.
  - If quant_profile == int8 and there are frequent prefix-cache-hits -> prefer int8-kernel-with-cache-optimized-path to reduce decode overhead.
  - If all-reduce latency > 120us -> choose locality-optimized kernels that favor reduce-scatter + overlap-compute.

Profiling and investigation playbook (step-by-step):
1) Reproduce on staging with the same model-version and shard-topology. Record the exact git commit / runtime image.
2) Capture end-to-end traces for 5k requests across representative traffic: use agent tracing (trace level = debug) and kernel-level telemetry. Commands:
   - rwinfctl trace start --model my-model:2026-02-01 --duration 10m --level debug --out /tmp/trace-$(date +%s).zip
   - nvprof (for local reproduce) or perf on host; capture GPU kernel timelines.
3) Produce flamegraphs for the orchestrator and per-GPU kernel timelines. Tools and scripts: scripts/perf/trace_to_flame.sh /tmp/trace.zip > /tmp/flame.svg
4) Validate comm microbench: run inter-shard all-reduce ping-pairs to measure baseline latency (expected < 80us in colocated racks).
5) Compare metric deltas vs baseline: p50/p95/p99 latency, token throughput, GPU occupancy, SM utilization, PCIe bandwidth.
6) Run focused microbench with synthetic seq_len slices to isolate kernel selection boundaries. Use the benchmarking harness: 
   - benchctl run --workload sharded-attn-sweep --model my-model --seq-lens 8,32,128 --micro-batch-sizes 1,4,8 --out ./bench-results.json
7) If kernel hotpath spans >20% of observed latency and comms are under budget, open a kernel ticket and include reproducible microbench steps (see "Ownership and escalation").

Benchmarking suite notes (integration and expectations):
- Canonical workloads: sharded-attn-sweep (sweeps seq lens and micro-batches), long-prefix (emulates long prefix reuse), mixed-traffic (production mix weighted by route).
- Metrics to publish per run (JSON fields required): run_id, model_version, shard_topology, seq_len_p50/p95/p99, tokens_per_sec_mean, tail_latency_ms_p99, gpu_utilization_mean, comm_latency_us_mean.
- Acceptance criteria for a candidate kernel change: tokens_per_sec >= baseline * 1.02 OR tail_latency_p99 <= baseline * 0.98, with no increase in memory-footprint > 5%.
- Artifact retention: keep raw traces and kernel timelines for at least 90 days for any benchmark that triggers a perf regression alert.

Operational runbook snippets (common incidents):
Incident: sudden p99 spike for sharded models across a rack
  1) Check scheduler queue depth and queue_soft_ms/queue_hard_ms events in the last 30 minutes.
  2) Validate inter-shard all-reduce latency from telemetry. If > 150us, escalate to networking and check NIC interrupts/traffic shaping.
  3) If comms healthy, inspect kernel selection logs for unexpected switch to slow kernel variant (kernel_mapper.log).
  4) Hot mitigation: enable priority lane for affected routes (rwctl route update <route> --priority 1) and reduce batch windows for that node group (set scheduler.batch_window_ms = 3).
  5) If mitigation fails, failover affected routes to fallback model variant with local (non-sharded) execution: route->fallback:model:local-encoder-compat.

Incident: long running fragmentation / OOMs on shard GPUs
  1) Run host-diagnostics to capture GPU memory fragmentation metrics.
  2) If fragmentation ratio > 0.65, schedule a rolling drain of the host, trigger unified-allocator defrag (adminctl allocator defrag --target gpu0).
  3) If OOM persists, reduce per-shard KV cache retention for that model (kvcache.retention_ms = 600000).

Known issues and current mitigations (as of runtime v3.4.x):
- Issue: intermittent 10–20% p99 degradation when sequence-length distribution shifts suddenly toward long prefixes.
  - Mitigation: enable adaptive_kernel_mapper.seq_len_smoothing to avoid thrashing kernel selection.
- Issue: all-reduce tail latency anomalies correlated with kernel preemption on mixed workloads.
  - Mitigation: set affinity.policy=packed for latency-critical routes and move large-batch offline traffic to dedicated nodes.
- Issue: int8 cache-path regressions when cache eviction patterns align with quantized tile boundaries.
  - Mitigation: use fallback quantization profile int8-stable for models with >10% prefix reuse until kernel patch is released.

Release notes snapshot (runtime v3.4.2):
- Improved locality-optimized kernels for 8x shard topologies; expected comm latency reduction ~18% for colocated racks.
- Added deadline_slicing scheduler knob and two new telemetry counters: scheduler.slice_count and scheduler.slice_drop_rate.
- Fixed memory leak in fused-attention-kernel-v1 when micro-batch size == 1.

Ownership and escalation:
- Kernel mapper and scheduling primitives: Runtime Core team (team lead: Miguel Santos).
- Benchmarks and profiling harness: Bench Team (owner: Sofia Ramos).
- SRE operational playbooks: Platform Reliability (lead: Liam O'Connor).
- Escalation path: On-call runtime engineer -> Runtime Core -> Networking -> Kernel dev. Use the incident-runbook channel for urgent comms.

Adding a new kernel variant (developer checklist):
1) Implement kernel and add feature flag kernel.<name>.enabled=false by default.
2) Add unit-level microbench in bench/harness (sharded-attn-sweep).
3) Run full benchmark matrix on staging and publish artifacts to /bench-artifacts/<run_id>.
4) Open a PR with documentation entry in this guide and a migration note for operators.
5) Iterate on heuristics and land default enablement only after 2 successful benchmark runs with artifacts reviewed by Bench Team.

References and links:
- Kernel mapper design doc: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/adaptive-kernel-mapper-and-scaling-playbook-2026
- Shard topology reference: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/runtime-op-pathways-and-shard-topology-2024
- Benchmarking harness README: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/throughput-latency-workload-catalog-2026

Appendix: Quick config table (YAML-like example)
| key | example value | description |
| scheduler.deadline_slicing.enabled | true | enable slicing for tight-latency routes |
| scheduler.deadline_slicing.max_slices | 6 | max micro-slices per request |
| scheduler.batch_window_ms | 6 | how long to wait for auto-batching (ms) |
| affinity.policy | host-local | affinity placement policy (host-local|spread|packed) |
| kvcache.retention_ms | 600000 | default per-model KV cache retention |

If you make changes to this doc, update the related_pages list and add the bench run_id that validates the change.

title: Eviction–Kernel Coordination Protocol and Signal Handbook
content:
summary:
A practical handbook describing the protocol and operational guidance for coordinating memory eviction (KV cache, model weights/shards) with kernel scheduling signals to prevent tail-latency spirals and preserve throughput SLOs.

content:
Overview
========
This document defines the Eviction–Kernel Coordination Protocol (EKCP), a lightweight control plane and operational playbook that synchronizes cache/shard eviction decisions with kernel scheduling hints and backpressure signals emitted by the serving runtime. The goal is to avoid reactive thrashing (concurrent eviction + heavy kernel activation) and reduce tail latency regressions when the system rehydrates caches or migrates shards under load.

Scope
-----
- Applies to: KV cache eviction, session/sequence eviction, model shard migration, and kernel activation scheduling in the serving runtime.
- Excludes: higher-level routing policies (tiered fallback routing) and customer-side session management.

Why this matters
----------------
During mixed workloads we observed sequences of events that amplify tail latency:
1) Memory pressure triggers mass eviction of KV cache and/or lightweight session state.
2) Immediately after eviction, the scheduler admits high-priority requests that require cache rehydration and heavy kernel execution.
3) Kernel queue saturation and memory reallocation cause long-tail latencies and increased error rates.

EKCP provides a modest coordination layer of signals and policies to:
- Stagger and rate-limit rehydration work.
- Prefer low-fidelity fallbacks until caches are warmed.
- Prioritize small, cheap inference requests during warmup windows.

Design principles
-----------------
- Backwards-compatible: Defaults are conservative; behavior toggled via config flags per cluster/pool.
- Signal minimal: Only a few semantic signals to avoid high cardinality.
- Observability-first: Emit clear metrics and traces for every decision.
- Experiment-friendly: Feature flags + canary ramp plan included.

Protocol summary (high level)
----------------------------
EKCP uses three coordinated signal channels between eviction manager and kernel scheduler:
- EvictionIntent: emitted when a tenant/pool plans mass eviction (soft signal).
- WarmupWindow: a timeboxed period after eviction where rehydration is rate-limited and scheduler favors cheap kernels.
- RehydrationProgress: incremental reports of cache warm percentage (0-100) and shard residency counts.

State machine (per-pool)
------------------------
States: IDLE -> EVICTING -> WARMUP -> NORMAL
Transitions:
1) IDLE -> EVICTING: EvictionIntent(true) issued when free_memory < threshold_low and reclaim_plan applies.
2) EVICTING -> WARMUP: Once eviction completes, WarmupWindow opens for N seconds (configurable).
3) WARMUP -> NORMAL: When RehydrationProgress >= warmup_target OR warmup timeout expires.
4) Any state -> IDLE: Manual override or pool drain event.

Message formats (examples)
-------------------------
All messages are lightweight JSON blobs carried over the internal control plane (gRPC or internal pub/sub). Example payloads: 

EvictionIntent example:
{
  "pool_id": "gpu-pool-23",
  "initiator": "eviction-manager:v2",
  "reason": "memory-pressure",
  "estimated_evicted_mb": 15360,
  "timestamp": "2026-06-11T13:22:08Z"
}

WarmupWindow example:
{
  "pool_id": "gpu-pool-23",
  "warmup_seconds": 45,
  "priority_policy": "favor-l2-small-requests",
  "rehydration_target_percent": 30,
  "timestamp": "2026-06-11T13:22:18Z"
}

RehydrationProgress example:
{
  "pool_id": "gpu-pool-23",
  "cache_percent": 22,
  "shard_residency": {"model-A": 3, "model-B": 7},
  "timestamp": "2026-06-11T13:22:42Z"
}

Operational policy parameters (recommended defaults)
--------------------------------------------------
| Parameter | Default | Description |
|---|---:|---|
| memory_threshold_low | 0.15 | Fraction free memory that triggers soft eviction |
| warmup_seconds_default | 30 | Default warmup window length |
| warmup_rehydrate_target | 25 | Percent of important cache that should be present to exit warmup |
| rehydrate_slowdown_factor | 0.6 | Rate limiter: reduce parallel rehydration tasks by this factor during warmup |
| allow_high_fidelity_during_warmup | false | Whether to allow heavy kernels during warmup |

Scheduler integration points
----------------------------
The kernel scheduler consumes EKCP signals and implements the following behaviors while warmup is active: 
- Admission shaping: lower concurrency for kernels requiring > X MB scratch or > Y streams. 
- Kernel hinting: prefer quantized or small-batch kernels for a configured percent of early requests. 
- Soft-fallback: route to cheaper model variant (if available) for non-critical requests until warmup passes.

Observability contract
----------------------
Every EKCP event must produce:
- trace/span with event tags: pool_id, state, initiator, reason, warmup_seconds
- metrics (per-pool): ekcp_evictions_total (counter), ekcp_warmup_seconds (histogram), ekcp_rehydrate_percent (gauge), ekcp_warmup_blocked_requests_total (counter)
- logs: structured JSON logs with correlation_id for cross-service debugging

Suggested dashboard widgets
---------------------------
- Warmup windows active (count) by pool (heatmap)
- 95p/99p latency vs EKCP state time series (line)
- Rehydration percent vs throughput (scatter)
- Eviction triggers trend (bar)

Runbook: triage when tail latencies spike after evictions
---------------------------------------------------------
1) Verify recent EKCP events: query ekcp_evictions_total and ekcp_warmup_seconds for pool in question.
2) Check RehydrationProgress: if cache_percent < warmup_rehydrate_target, warmup is ongoing. Decide if you should extend warmup.
3) Examine kernel queue depth and GPU occupancy. If occupancy > 90% and warmup is active: reduce admission for heavy kernels.
4) Apply quick mitigations (ordered):
   a) Increase warmup_seconds for the pool by +30s.
   b) Enable allow_high_fidelity_during_warmup=false (if toggled).
   c) Temporarily divert non-critical traffic to cheaper variant or fallback region.
   d) If kernel queue remains saturated, scale up ephemeral burst capacity (if available).
5) Post-incident: run a targeted replay of representative requests to validate recovery and update the eviction threshold if repeated.

Benchmarking and validation protocol
-----------------------------------
Goal: ensure EKCP reduces 99p latency regressions without materially reducing 50p latency or throughput.
Procedure:
1) Baseline capture: capture normal steady-state for 30m, record latency distribution and cache hit ratio.
2) Controlled eviction injection: simulate 2x the memory pressure to trigger eviction and observe behavior with EKCP OFF.
3) EKCP ON: repeat the eviction injection with EKCP enabled.
4) Compare: 99p latency, throughput, cache rehydration time, and error rates.
5) Run stress matrix across tenant mixes (pure chat, embeddings-heavy, mixed short-long sequence).

Sample synthetic driver commands
-------------------------------
# Start a warmup-aware eviction test
redwood-testctl simulate-eviction --pool gpu-pool-23 --pressure 1.5 --duration 90
# Observe samples and metrics
redwood-metrics query "ekcp_rehydrate_percent{pool_id=\"gpu-pool-23\"}" --since 5m

Rollout plan (canary -> regional -> global)
------------------------------------------
1) Feature flagged, default disabled. Enable EKCP in 1 canary pool (non-critical workloads). Run for 48 hours.
2) If canary is stable, enable for backup pools for 7 days.
3) Enable in 20% of production pools for 72 hours.
4) Gradually roll to 100% with continuous monitoring of 95/99p latency and throughput.

Testing checklist before global rollout
--------------------------------------
- Unit tests for state transitions and message validation.
- Integration tests with a stubbed scheduler and eviction manager.
- End-to-end replay testbench with synthetic traffic.
- Observability verification (metrics, traces, logs).

Ownership and contacts
----------------------
- Primary owner: Runtime Scheduling team (oncall: #runtime-scheduling).
- Secondary: Kernel Performance team (oncall: #kernel-perf).
- Escalation: Eng SRE lead (pager).

Troubleshooting examples (short)
