-------------------------------
Symptom: Warmup window never completes and cache_percent stalls at 1-5%
Likely cause: Rehydration tasks are being rate-limited too aggressively or blocked by admission shaping.
Remediation steps:
- Inspect rehydrate_slowdown_factor and temporarily set to 1.0
- Temporarily increase warmup_seconds to allow background rehydration workers to catch up
- Check for kernel hot-path saturation and enable additional background worker slots

Appendix A: Example cluster config snippet
-----------------------------------------
# ekcp config for a GPU pool (YAML)
ekcp_config:
  enabled: true
  memory_threshold_low: 0.12
  warmup_seconds_default: 45
  warmup_rehydrate_target: 30
  rehydrate_slowdown_factor: 0.7
  priority_policy: "favor-l2-small-requests"
  allow_high_fidelity_during_warmup: false

Appendix B: Telemetry queries (promql examples)
----------------------------------------------
# warmup windows currently active
sum(ekcp_warmup_seconds_count) by (pool_id)
# 99p latency correlated with warmup state
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, pool_id, ekcp_state))

Change log
----------
- 2026-01-15: Initial draft.
- 2026-04-02: Added RehydrationProgress payload and warmup_rehydrate_target param.
- 2026-07-02: Published after canary; updated default parameters and troubleshooting steps.

Related reading
---------------
- NUMA-aware shard placement and eviction playbook (see related_pages).
- Scheduler admission shaping guidelines (internal kernel scheduling doc).

Notes and future work
---------------------
- Explore probabilistic warmup targets based on request shape prediction.
- Add cross-pool coordination to avoid simultaneous warmups in colocated pools.

End of document

title: Sandboxed Scheduler: Economic Admission & Canary Playbook
content:
Summary:

This playbook documents the experimental scheduler sandbox (sched-sandbox) used to validate cost-aware admission policies, economic priority governor behaviors, and safe canary rollouts for kernel changes. It is intended for runtime engineers, oncall, and performance owners running safety-limited experiments against production-like traffic.

Purpose and scope:
- Reduce risk when introducing scheduler/econ changes by running them in an isolated decision plane that mirrors production inputs.
- Capture SLO regressions, cost deltas, and fidelity impact before full rollout.
- Provide a concrete runbook for activation, monitoring, rollback, and postmortem.

High-level architecture overview:
- sched-sandbox (service): an in-cluster decision plane that accepts a copy of dispatch metadata and returns admission/priority decisions for sampled traffic. It does not affect real dispatch; instead it annotates decisions for comparison.
- kernel-admitter (component): produces observed kernel slot allocations and credits. Sandbox mirrors the API and uses the same kernel hints.
- econ-governor (component): configurable economic model (weights for latency vs cost vs fidelity) used by sched-sandbox to synthesize priority.
- profiling-agent: collects trace fragments, kernel timing, and cost estimates for sandboxed requests.

Design principles:
1) Non-invasive: sandbox must never affect live routing or admission. Make-change-by-annotation only.
2) Deterministic inputs: ensure sampled requests have the same input features (sequence length, model variant, tenant tier, token budget).
3) Low-noise sampling: prefer stratified sampling by tenant and route to ensure representation across latency-sensitive and batchy workloads.
4) Telemetry parity: capture the same telemetry tags as production (kernel_id, slot_count, credit_charge, model_variant, origin_region).

Operational SLOs (for sandbox observability):
- Sample coverage: >= 0.5% of all requests per active route OR at least 5 QPS per route for 95% of time.
- Trace fidelity: 99% of sandbox traces must include kernel_id, kernel_latency_ms, and credit_cost_estimate.
- Canary detection latency: sandbox must detect a statistically significant SLO shift within 30 minutes for a sustained regression lasting 5 minutes.

Admission policy and economic model (econ-governor):
The econ-governor computes a numeric priority score P per request: P = w_L * normalized_latency_sensitivity + w_C * normalized_cost_sensitivity + w_F * fidelity_penalty.
- Weights are declared per-experiment and can be tuned in the sandbox UI.
- Normalization uses percentiles from a 7-day rolling window (p50..p99.9) per route.

Configuration table (canonical knobs):
| knob | description | default | safe-range |
|------|-------------|---------|------------|
| sampling_rate | Fraction of requests mirrored to sandbox | 0.005 | 0.001 - 0.02 |
| econ_weights | [w_L,w_C,w_F] vector | [0.6,0.3,0.1] | each 0.0 - 1.0, sum>0 |
| admission_queue_limit | Max concurrent sandboxed admissions queued | 200 | 50 - 1000 |
| drift_alert_threshold | Relative delta from production decision rate to trigger review | 5% | 1% - 20% |
| canary_window_minutes | Sliding window for canary decision aggregation | 30 | 5 - 120 |

Canary and experiment lifecycle (step-by-step):
1) Plan: create experiment entry in the experiments registry with objectives, owner, and primary metrics (cost per token delta, p99 latency, fidelity rollback rate).
2) Baseline capture: run sandbox with current production econ_weights for 24–72 hours to capture baseline decision distribution and kernel hints.
3) Pilot: deploy modified econ_weights or scheduler policy to sched-sandbox only at sampling_rate = 0.5%.
4) Shadow analysis: run automated comparison job that computes the following per-route metrics every 10 minutes:
   a) Decision flip rate (fraction of requests where sandbox decision differs from production).
   b) Delta cost estimate (sandbox_est - production_est) per-token and per-request.
   c) SLO delta (p50,p95,p99) predicted from kernel_latency models.
5) Canary escalation: if metrics within acceptance band for 4 consecutive windows, increase sampling_rate to 2% and repeat.
6) Live canary: with approval, route 1% real traffic to new scheduler policy (controlled canary). If safe, scale to 10% then full rollout.

Acceptance bands (default):
- Cost per-token increase: <= 3%
- p99 latency predicted increase: <= 5% absolute ms or <= 10% relative (whichever larger)
- Decision flip rate: <= 8% for high-volume routes, <= 15% for low-volume routes

Automated analysis and alerts:
- Daily experiment report summarizing cost and SLO deltas (owner: runtime-experiments@redwood.com).
- Immediate alert (pager) if predicted p99 latency increases by > 50ms or decision flip rate > 25% sustained for two windows.
- Drift alert when sandbox decisions diverge from production at > drift_alert_threshold; this triggers an investigation ticket.

Profiling and benchmarking protocol for experiments:
1) Synthetic fidelity replay: replay a slice of production traffic (stored in request-corpus) through the sandbox with and without the change to compute kernel occupancy differences.
2) Microbench patch: run kernel-level microbenchmarks with stress harness to estimate worst-case slot contention and thermal influence.
3) Shadow benchmarks: run the bench-suite (bench-run) with the candidate scheduler policy against a mirrored cluster to measure throughput and tail-latency under mixed workloads.

Example CLI snippets:
- Enable sandbox for experiment EX-123:
  rctl experiments create --id EX-123 --owner aisha --weights 0.5,0.4,0.1 --sampling 0.005
- Increase sampling rate:
  rctl experiments update --id EX-123 --sampling 0.02
- Fetch last 30m comparison summary:
  rctl experiments summary --id EX-123 --window 30m --format table

Runbook: urgent triage (if sandbox flags a regression):
1) Acknowledge alert and page runtime-sre and the experiment owner.
2) Immediately pause the experiment sampling (set sampling_rate=0).
3) Capture a forensic sweep: export sandbox traces, kernel snapshots, and bench-suite results for the last 60 minutes.
4) Rollback any canary routing if in live canary stage.
5) Triage with the kernel team: inspect kernel_id distribution and credit exhaustion signals.
6) If root cause is econ weights, revert to baseline weights and re-run baseline capture for 24 hours.
7) Produce a postmortem within 72 hours if the incident impacted production latency or cost beyond escalation thresholds.

Ownership, roles and contacts:
- Runtime experimentation owner: Aisha Patel (aisha@redwood.com)
- Kernel instrumentation: Jonah Kim (jonah@redwood.com)
- SRE paging rota: eng-sre-oncall@redwood.com

Safety checklist before promoting a scheduler change to production:
1) Baseline capture completed and reviewed.
2) Shadow and synthetic replay show cost delta within acceptance band.
3) Bench-suite shows no >10% regression in throughput for critical routes.
4) Canary plan documented with rollback windows and owners.
5) Alerts and dashboards created (grafana urls inserted in the experiment page).

Metrics and dashboards to create for each experiment (minimum):
- Decision flip rate by route (1m, 5m quantiles)
- Estimated cost delta per-token (rolling 1h)
- Kernel occupancy heatmap (by kernel_id x slot_count)
- Predicted vs observed p99 latency (compare model estimate and production measurement)

Post-experiment checklist and follow-up:
- If promoted: update runtime-contracts and scheduler-policy registry with new weights and policy id.
- If rejected: archive experiment and note root-cause, suggested mitigations, and next steps.
- Add a short summary to the weekly runtime experiment digest.

Appendix: example experiment metadata YAML:
---
experiment_id: EX-123
owner: aisha
change: "econ_weights: [0.5,0.4,0.1] and admission_queue_limit: 150"
sampling_rate: 0.005
acceptance_criteria:
  cost_per_token_pct: 3
  p99_latency_ms: 50
  decision_flip_pct: 8
canary_steps: [0.005, 0.02, 0.1]
notes: "Baseline capture performed 2026-01-12 to 2026-01-14"
---

References and related reading:
- Runtime telemetry contract: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/observability-adapter-sidecar-design-manual-2026
- Scheduler telemetry synthesis: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-telemetry-synthesis-and-proofing-2025
- Bench-suite guide: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/operational-workload-simulator-and-signature-guide-2026

Change log:
- 2026-01-10: Draft created by Aisha Patel.
- 2026-02-18: Added automated alert thresholds and canary escalation flow after pilot run.
- 2026-03-02: Clarified acceptance bands and sampling guidance.

title: Fairness Observability and Quantile Audit Guide
content:
Summary

This guide defines how the runtime and scheduler teams observe, detect, and audit tenant-level fairness regressions using quantile-based metrics. It describes the telemetry, dashboard views, alerting rules, and a step-by-step reproducible audit procedure for fairness incidents (unbalanced slot allocation, credit drift, or sustained latency skew across tenants).

1. Purpose and Scope

- Purpose: Provide a single operational runbook for detecting fairness issues in the serving runtime and performing a reproducible quantile audit that produces evidence useful for triage and rollbacks.
- Scope: Applies to multi-tenant serving clusters (hosted + dedicated), scheduler credit systems, kernel admission controllers, and cross-layer tracing. Does NOT cover quota- or billing-related disputes (handled by finance).

2. Background & Definitions

- Fairness regression: a sustained (>10 minutes) deviation where a tenant's critical SLO quantiles (p95 or p99) degrade relative to their baseline and cannot be explained by customer-driven workload changes.
- Baseline window: 7-day rolling window ending 24 hours before incident start.
- Quantile audit: compare matching quantiles (p50/p95/p99) per-tenant against baseline and population to detect outliers.

3. Key metrics and instrumentation (concrete names)

- scheduler_credit_balance{tenant_id, pool, region} — per-tenant scheduler credit balance (tokens).
- scheduler_credit_rate{tenant_id, pool, region} — credit accrual rate.
- request_latency_ms_bucket{tenant_id, route, le} — histogram for request latency (ms).
- runtime_kv_prefetch_hit_rate{tenant_id} — cache hit rate affecting effective latency.
- kernel_dispatch_utilization{gpu_id, kernel_variant} — GPU-side utilization by kernel.
- request_trace_id and request_provenance labels are captured and persisted to trace-store (ClickHouse) for sample reconstruction.

4. Quantile calculation examples (PromQL and ClickHouse)

- PromQL p95 by tenant (30m):
```
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_latency_ms_bucket[30m])) by (tenant_id, le))
```
- PromQL fairness score (p95 ratio vs population median):
```
( histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_latency_ms_bucket[30m])) by (tenant_id, le)) )
/
( scalar(quantile_over_time(0.5, sum(rate(request_latency_ms_bucket[7d])) by (le))[7d:1h]) )
```
- ClickHouse example: compute per-tenant p95 latency over a window and join to baseline
```
SELECT
  tenant_id,
  quantiles(0.5, 0.95, 0.99)(latency_ms)[2] AS p95
FROM requests_local
WHERE timestamp >= toDateTime('2026-07-01 12:00:00')
  AND route IN ('/v1/generate','/v1/chat')
GROUP BY tenant_id
ORDER BY p95 DESC
LIMIT 200
```

5. Dashboards & suggested panels

Create a "Fairness Observability" dashboard with at minimum:
- Per-tenant quantiles (p50/p95/p99) heatmap (time x tenant).
- Top-k tenants by p95 deviation vs baseline (sparkline + % change).
- Scheduler credit balance timeline for affected tenants.
- Kernel dispatch utilization overlayed with request p95 by tenant.
- Trace sample picker panel that links to trace-store filters (tenant + time window + route).

6. Alerting rules (severity, thresholds, and rationale)

- alert:Tenants_P95_Fairness_Deviation
  severity: page
  condition: tenant_p95 / median_population_p95 > 2.0 AND increase(unavailable_errors[10m]) < 1
  window: 10m
  rationale: A 2x gap suggests scheduling or kernel starvation rather than workload shift.

- alert:Credit_Drift_High
  severity: ticket
  condition: rate(scheduler_credit_balance[5m]) < -0.1 for any tenant_id in production pool
  window: 15m
  rationale: Rapid credit depletion can indicate runaway batching or accounting bug.

7. Reproducible audit procedure (ordered steps)

1) Triage intake: record incident start time, alert ids, impacted tenant_ids, route(s), and correlation trace ids.
2) Run baseline comparison (ClickHouse query above) for incident window vs baseline window. Save CSV of results to: s3://redwood-inference-audit/<incident-id>/quantile-diff.csv
3) Inspect scheduler_credit_balance and scheduler_credit_rate for tenants and neighbors (±15 minutes around start). Pull minute-level time series and save as JSON.
4) Reconstruct top-n representative traces: use trace-store query to pull 30 traces per tenant that are above the 95th percentile latency, include full request provenance and kernel variant annotations. Save traces to s3://redwood-inference-audit/<incident-id>/traces/
5) Correlate kernel_dispatch_utilization and GPU metrics: export 1s-sampled utilization for GPUs serving the tenants for the window.
6) Run root-cause hypothesis checklist (below). Mark which hypotheses are confirmed/ruled out.
7) If scheduler misallocation is suspected, run controlled replay of a synthetic workload in sandbox to reproduce credit drift (use QA cluster).
8) Produce an executive audit summary with a 1-page summary, a 3-page technical appendix, and a list of recommended mitigations; publish to the incident tracker and tag the oncall rotation.

8. Root-cause hypothesis checklist (fast triage)

- H1: Workload change (sudden token/sequence-length increase) — check usage telemetry and customer release notes.
- H2: Scheduler credit accounting bug — inspect ledger events and compare accrual vs consumption.
- H3: Kernel variant regression (new kernel promoted) — correlate kernel_variant label with p95 bump.
- H4: Hot GPU/numa/thermal noise — check node-level watchdog and thermal metrics.
- H5: Cross-tenant noisy neighbour — inspect co-located tenant metrics and admission logs.

9. Runbook for oncall when fairness page fires (quick actions)

- Step 1: Acknowledge the page; create incident with severity and attendees (scheduler, runtime, observability).
- Step 2: Run the quantile baseline query and upload CSV to the incident S3 path.
- Step 3: Pin dashboards and grab the trace samples.
- Step 4: If evidence indicates kernel regression, follow the kernel rollback playbook (link in related_pages).
- Step 5: If evidence indicates scheduler misallocation and impact is severe, enact short-term routing policy to divert affected tenant(s) to a safe pool (use the routing console with canary config).
- Step 6: Document all steps and escalate to PL when customer SLAs are violated.

10. Evidence packaging and retention

- Required artifacts for any audit: quantile CSV, timeseries JSON (credits + latency), trace package (ndjson), kernel-utilization CSV, and incident notes.
- Retention: keep packaging in s3://redwood-inference-audit/<incident-id>/ for 90 days by default; mark longer retention with finance/legal approval.
- Hash evidence archives and attach SHA256 to the incident ticket.

11. Post-audit reporting template (to include in incident tracker)

- Title / Incident id
- Summary (1 paragraph)
- Impacted tenants and routes (list)
- Measured regression (p95 change, absolute values, duration)
- Root cause hypothesis and supporting evidence
- Actions taken (mitigations, rollbacks, routing changes)
- Long-term recommendations and owners

12. Ownership and escalation matrix

- Primary owner: runtime-team/scheduler-subteam (oncall rotation lead: @runtime-oncall)
- Observability contact: observability-team (dashboard maintainers)
- Kernel engineering: serving-runtime/kernel-team (for kernel variant rollbacks)
- Customer escalation: customer-success-escalations (for billing/contract questions)

13. Sample scheduler observer config (appendix)

A small JSON snippet that the observer runs to sample and emit per-tenant quantiles to Prometheus remote write. Replace <ENV> and <BUCKET> with runtime config values.
```
{
  "observer_name": "fairness-quantile-observer",
  "scrape_interval": "30s",
  "tenants": "production",
  "export": {
    "prometheus_remote_write": "https://remote-write.service.prod",
    "s3_audit_bucket": "s3://redwood-inference-audit/<ENV>/"
  },
  "sampling": {
    "window": "30m",
    "quantiles": [0.5, 0.95, 0.99]
  }
}
```

14. FAQ and pitfalls

- Q: How do we avoid false positives when a tenant deploys a new model?
  A: Cross-check the tenant release notes, sequence-length distribution changes, and recent model-version labels in traces; if model rollout is the cause, mark as "customer-change" and route to success.

- Pitfall: Triggering mitigation too early (diverting traffic) can obscure evidence. Prefer collecting a 10–15 minute evidence set before aggressive mitigations, unless customer SLA requires immediate action.

15. Appendices and links

- Related runbooks: kernel rollback, priority inversion mitigation, runtime-fallback-orchestration. See related_pages for direct links.
- Contact list: runtime@s.redwood.com, observability@s.redwood.com, scheduler-leads (see team roster).

Document history

- 2026-03-15: Created by Riley Chen (initial draft).
- 2026-05-10: Added PromQL examples and alert tuning after a field incident.
- 2026-07-03: Finalized retention policy and added evidence packaging conventions.

title: Scheduling Feedback Loop: Operator Handbook
content:
Overview:

This handbook describes the scheduling feedback loop used by the serving runtime to preserve SLOs while optimizing cost and utilization. It is intended for on-call operators, runtime engineers, and release leads who need to understand how telemetry is translated into scheduler adjustments, how automated and manual controls interact, and how to safely intervene.

Goals and scope:
- Keep 99th percentile token latency below SLO targets per tier (see SLO table).
- Maintain per-node GPU utilization in the operational band to avoid thermal or NVLink contention (recommended 60–85% during normal traffic).
- Limit regression risk by constraining automated changes behind safe guardrails and staged rollouts.
- Cover both automated autotune flows and manual operator interventions.

Quick reference SLOs and thresholds:
| SLO / Metric | Target | Operator alert threshold | Action level |
|--------------|--------|--------------------------|--------------|
| 99p token latency (hosted-prod) | <= 120ms | >= 140ms for 5m | P1 |
| 99p token latency (dedicated) | <= 80ms | >= 100ms for 5m | P1 |
| GPU thermal throttle events / node | 0 per 1h | > 3 in 10m | P1 |
| GPU memory fragmentation ratio | < 0.25 | > 0.4 | P2 |
| Scheduler change fail rate (canary) | < 1% | > 2% | P2 |

Key concepts:
- Feedback loop inputs: aggregated traces (99p latency), kernel queue lengths, per-shard KV cache hit rates, sequence length distribution, per-GPU occupancy, and admission controller reject rates.
- Controller outputs: kernel slot allocations, batch slicing targets, priority weight adjustments, per-tenant quota limits, and hint signals for KV cache prefetch.
- Guardrails: change rate limit (max 5% of slots per minute), rollback window (10 minutes), and canary sampling (5% traffic by default).

Roles and ownership:
- Runtime Scheduling Team: primary owners for the feedback controller and policy language.
- SRE on-call: monitors alerts and executes runbook actions.
- Release lead: approves non-automated policy changes and coordinates canaries.
- Observability team: owns metric definitions and dashboards used by the loop.

Automated feedback path (high level):
1. Signal ingestion: streaming metrics from the collector (grpc-traces, kernel-metrics-pipeline).
2. Signal enrichment: causal attribution service enriches latency spikes with kernel and tenant context.
3. Decision engine: policy engine evaluates rules and candidate adjustments.
4. Safety checks: simulated dry-run against the simulator and quota check.
5. Apply: change is committed to the scheduler with a versioned change id and canary rollout.

Safety and simulation:
- All automated changes are run through the local decision simulator. The simulator must flag potential >3% expected 99p latency regressions or >5% drop in throughput.
- Canary matrix: default is 5% traffic for 10 minutes, 20% for 20 minutes, then full roll. The decision engine will abort if any stage shows alert violations.

Operator runbook: incident triage and mitigation steps:
1. Confirm the alert: check 99p latency, kernel queue backlogs, and recent scheduler change IDs. CLI: redwoodctl metrics query --range 10m --metric 99p_token_latency --service serving-runtime
2. Identify correlated signals: correlate with deployment events, kernel rollout flags, or thermal events. Use dashboard: Serving Runtime / Scheduling Feedback Loop / Recent Decisions.
3. If automated change is in progress and latency regressed:
   a. Rollback automated change: redwoodctl scheduler rollback --change-id <id> --reason "latency-regression-rollback"
   b. Pause auto-rollouts: redwoodctl scheduler set-guardrail --auto-rollout false
   c. Open an incident and tag the runtime-scheduling Slack channel (#runtime-scheduling) and page SRE.
4. If no automated changes present, apply manual mitigation: reduce admission controller concurrency for affected model variant(s). Example:
   a. redwoodctl admission update --route /v1/generate --concurrency 8
   b. Expand canary to divert to fallback model variant if available: redwoodctl routing set-fallback --route /v1/generate --variant small-llm-quant --weight 0.25
5. Observe for 10 minutes, collect traces: redwoodctl traces fetch --filter "change_id:<id>" --out /tmp/traces.json
6. If mitigation stabilizes, stage a gradual safe change using the policy language (see Applying manual scheduler changes).

Applying manual scheduler changes (recommended safe pattern):
- Always create a change proposal: scheduler-change create --description "<reason>" --patch-file ./patch.yaml
- Validate against simulator: scheduler-change simulate --proposal <id> --duration 30m
- Submit as canary: scheduler-change submit --proposal <id> --canary-percent 5 --canary-duration 10m
- Monitor canary: automated checks will run; responsible engineer must review dashboards and approve promotion.

Example scheduler patch (YAML snippet):
---
scheduler_patch_version: v1
patches:
  - path: /kernel_slots/global
    op: replace
    value: 0.92
  - path: /priority_weights/model_variants/large
    op: add
    value: 0.05
  - path: /batch_slicing/max_slice_length
    op: replace
    value: 256

Knobs and recommended ranges (table):
- kernel_slot_adjustment: +/- 20% per change, recommended step 5%
- batch_slicing.max_slice_length: 64–1024 (default 512), reduce for tail latency when cold KV cache prevalence > 0.35
- priority_weights: 0.0–1.0 (normalize to 1.0 across weights), avoid >0.6 single-tenant weight in multi-tenant pools
- admission_controller.concurrency: 1–32 per shard, typical 8 for high-latency-sensitive routes

Telemetry and dashboards to check:
- Serving Runtime / Scheduling Feedback Loop / Decision Log (primary)
- Serving Runtime / Kernel Queue Depths by Node
- Serving Runtime / 99p Latency Attribution (model variant, user segment, sequence length)
- Infra / GPU Health / Thermal and ECC events

Alerting playbook (when to page):
- Page SRE immediately (P1) for Hosted 99p latency > alert threshold sustained for 5 minutes or >3 simultaneous thermal throttle events.
- P2: scheduler canary failure rates or simulator mismatch > 2%.

Post-incident: required artifacts and timeline
- Incident summary within 24 hours including timeline, decision IDs, traces, and root cause hypothesis.
- Attach the simulator run output and the final rollback or change id.
- Required reviewers: scheduling team lead and observability owner.

Runbook test plan (game day checklist):
1. Inject simulated queue pressure on a canary node using load-generator (tool: perf-lab/gen_load).
2. Validate the feedback controller proposes a slot reallocation within 2m.
3. Confirm simulator prediction matches observed 99p delta within 10%.
4. Execute simulated rollback and verify system returns to baseline within 10m.

Operational notes and best practices:
- Prefer incremental slot adjustments instead of large swings — aim for stability and predictable canary behavior.
- Use the policy language labels to scope changes (e.g., production, dedicated, gpu-pool-a).
- Avoid adjusting batch slicing and kernel slot allocations simultaneously in the same proposal.

Appendix A: common failure modes and quick diagnostics:
- Symptom: sudden 99p spike with low GPU utilization -> likely KV cache cold or admission spike. Check kvcache hit rate and sequence length distribution.
- Symptom: rising kernel queue + high occupancy -> kernel is starved; consider raising kernel_slot allocation or preempting low-priority workloads.
- Symptom: canary passes but gradual regression at 100% -> investigate cross-node noise and topology mismatch; consider staged topology-aware rollout.

Appendix B: contacts and escalation path:
- Runtime Scheduling on-call: pager duty schedule (internal)
- Slack: #runtime-scheduling, #sre-oncall
- Pager: SRE primary, then Runtime Scheduling lead

Related artefacts and links:
- Policy language spec: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-policy-language-declarative-profiles-2026
- Decision simulator code repo: git@redwood:runtime/scheduler-simulator.git
- Metrics catalog: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/runtime-telemetry-rollup-and-sample-strategies-2026

Revision history:
- 2026-02-10: Created by Sofia Patel.
- 2026-03-01: Clarified canary timings, added CLI snippets and YAML patch example (Evelyn Zhang).

End of handbook.

title: Production rollout: runtime operational tuning checklist
content:
Summary
=======
This page is an operational tuning checklist and companion runbook for production model rollouts and routine performance tuning of the Redwood serving runtime. It consolidates cross-cutting checks (kernel scheduling, batching, KV cache, quantization, profiling, canary steps, and monitoring) that should be validated pre-rollout and during live operation.

Purpose
-------
- Provide a reproducible, checklist-driven process for small/medium production changes (model size, quantization profile, batching strategy, shard topology).
- Reduce time-to-detect regressions and ensure SLO alignment (p50/p95/p99 latency, token cost).
- Share concrete commands, dashboards, and rollback criteria for on-call and SRE.

Owner and scope
----------------
- Primary owner: Serving Runtime (runtime-svc) team.
- Secondary owners: SRE, Observability, Model-Onboarding.
- Applies to hosted, dedicated, and private deployments where the runtime binary and orchestration layer are used.

Pre-rollout checklist (gated)
-----------------------------
1) Canary plan drafted and approved
   - Canary % (recommended start: 1%).
   - Traffic routing policy (region-aware, fallback fallback-model).
   - Rollout duration: minimum 24h for steady-state metrics; extend for long tails.
2) Performance smoke tests
   - Run microbenchmarks for target model shape (prompt length distribution).
   - Validate throughput target (TPS) and p95 latency within budget.
3) Kernel & scheduling sanity
   - Ensure kernel mapper selection matches model arch (GELU/FlashAttention variant).
   - Check priority-driven scheduler tags for canary service.
4) Batching and queue configuration
   - Verify max_batch_tokens, max_batch_size, and latency_budget values.
   - Confirm batching policy overrides for high-priority routes.
5) KV cache validation
   - Confirm cache sharding aligns with NUMA topology.
   - Validate prefix cache population strategy and TTL.
6) Quantization profile validation (if used)
   - Run quality regression evaluation on representative prompts.
   - Validate QAT/INT8/FP16 performance delta and check for hallucination increase.
7) Observability and alerts
   - Create/verify dashboards for latency distribution, OOMs, kernel queue length, effective batch sizes, and cache hit ratio.
   - Configure regression alerting: 15% increase in p95 or 5% drop in cache hit ratio triggers oncall.
8) Safety and fallback rules
   - Ensure fallback model variant available and compatibility table updated.

Commands and diagnostics (examples)
----------------------------------
- Start a targeted canary (CLI):
  rdmctl rollout create --service runtime-svc --model-id model-v3-int8 --traffic 1 --duration 24h --route canary-eu

- Run microbenchmark (local):
  ./perfbench --model ./models/model-v3-int8 --seq 512 --concurrency 8 --batch-packing auto

- Inspect runtime scheduler state (prometheus labels available via API):
  curl -s http://runtime-svc.internal/api/v1/scheduler/state | jq

- Dump KV cache stats from a shard:
  rdmctl debug kvcache stats --shard 2 --output json

- Collect GPU kernel traces (short window):
  rdmctl trace start --duration 30s --filters kernel,memcopy && rdmctl trace download --out trace-$(date +%s).zip

Key metrics to validate
-----------------------
- Latency: p50/p95/p99 (global and per-route)
- Throughput: tokens/sec and requests/sec by model and route
- Effective batch size: mean and histogram
- Kernel queue depth: per-device and per-priority class
- KV cache: hit ratio, evictions/sec, eviction latency
- Memory: GPU resident set and fragmentation indicators
- Errors: OOMs, model-incompatible exceptions, RPC timeouts

Configuration reference table (common knobs)
--------------------------------------------
Parameter | Typical value | Notes
max_batch_tokens | 2048 | Upper bound on combined token length in a batch
max_batch_size | 32 | Max number of concurrent requests batched together
latency_budget_ms | 120 | Soft SLO for request assembly before flush
scheduler_priority | high/normal/low | High for interactive routes, low for background generations
kv_cache_ttl_sec | 300 | Tune based on prompt reuse pattern
quant_profile | int8/float16/fp32 | Use int8 for cost-sensitive workloads after quality checks

(Represented above as plain text table to keep confluence export-friendly.)

Profiling playbook (when anomaly detected)
-----------------------------------------
1) Identify symptom grouping\   - High p95 with steady p50 -> tail queuing or occasional slow kernels.\   - p50 and p95 both elevated -> overall resource contention (CPU/GPU throttling or batching misconfig).
2) Capture traces\   - Start kernel traces for 60s on affected devices.\   - Collect per-request timing, kernel durations, memcopy times.
3) Check scheduling hotspots\   - Look for priority inversion where low-priority bulk jobs starve interactive queues.
4) Inspect cache behavior\   - If cache miss spike correlates with latency spikes, check shard skew and TTL churn.
5) Quick mitigations (order of ops)\   - Temporarily reduce batch size (max_batch_size -> max(8, current/2)).\   - Raise scheduler priority for interactive routes.\   - Pin affected model shards to different NUMA nodes.\   - If OOMs observed, reduce kv_cache_ttl or decrease model batch packing.
6) Post-mortem actions\   - Add a synthetic workload to test candidate fix before re-enabling full traffic.\   - Update the runbook entry with root cause and long-term mitigation.

Release gating and rollback criteria
------------------------------------
- Automatic rollback triggers:
  - p95 latency increase > 25% sustained for 15 minutes.
  - Error rate increase > 3x baseline for 10 minutes.
  - Cache hit ratio drop > 10% with correlated latency increase.
- Manual rollback triggers (owner judgement):
  - Unexplained memory fragmentation growth.\  - Significant model quality regression identified by eval jobs.

Rollout / rollback steps (high level)
------------------------------------
1) Initiate canary with 1% traffic for 24h.
2) Monitor key metrics for 30m stability window then every hour.
3) If anomalies appear, promote mitigations (see profiling playbook).
4) If mitigations fail or rollback triggers hit, revert traffic:\   - rdmctl rollout rollback --service runtime-svc --to stable --reason "p95 regression"
5) After rollback, collect full traces of canary window and open incident ticket.

Dashboards and alert links (examples)
-------------------------------------
- Runtime / Latency Overview: dashboards/runtime/latency-overview
- Kernel telemetry: dashboards/runtime/kernel-telemetry
- KV Cache Health: dashboards/runtime/kvcache-health
- Perfbench trends: dashboards/perfbench/model-trends
- Alerts: alerting/runtime/perf-regressions

Operational run notes and tips
-----------------------------
- For small models, batching tends to dominate latency economics; be conservative when increasing max_batch_tokens.
- Prefer small canaries but run them long enough to exercise tail behavior and daily traffic patterns.
- Use synthetic prompt bundles that mimic real user distributions (include short/long prompts and multi-turn sessions).
- When experimenting with quantization, always run automatic evals tied to the prompt set and check CEILING/LOWER threshold differences.

Common pitfalls and how to avoid them
------------------------------------
- Overpacked batches: can reduce throughput and spike p99 due to stragglers. Test effective batch size distribution.
- Unbalanced shard placement: causes cache skews and cross-node memcopies. Use shard placement tool before rollout.
- Silent kernel fallback: some kernels may fall back to a slower implementation without clear error—check kernel selection logs.

Post-rollout checklist
----------------------
- Confirm steady-state for 72 hours for customer-facing models.
- Record observed effective batch size, kernel mix, and cache hit ratio in the release note.
- Schedule follow-up perf benchmark after 1 week of full traffic.

Appendix: useful commands and scripts
------------------------------------
- Quick effective batch histogram:
  rdmctl metrics query --expr 'histogram_quantile(0.9, sum(rate(runtime_effective_batch_size_bucket[5m])) by (le))'

- Shard placement planner (dry run):
  rdmctl planner plan-shards --model model-v3 --nodes node[1..8] --dry-run

- Kvcache reshard (safe mode):
  rdmctl kvcache reshard --target 8 --grace-period 600 --plan-file plan.json

- Quality smoke eval (small):
  python evals/run_smoke_eval.py --model model-v3-int8 --prompt-set prompts/enterprise-critical.json --out smoke-2026-$(date +%s).json

Contact and escalation
----------------------
- Runtime oncall: #oncall-runtime (pager duty link in handbook)
- Owner: Maya Chen (maya@redwood.ai)
- Observability lead: Arjun Patel (arjun@redwood.ai)

Change log
----------
- 2025-11-10 (Maya Chen) - created initial checklist.
- 2026-02-12 (Maya Chen) - added automated rollback criteria and profiling playbook section.

References
----------
- Runtime architecture: ../runtime-architecture/runtime-op-pathways-and-shard-topology-2024.json
- Tail latency playbook: ../benchmarking-and-perf-suite/tail-latency-investigation-and-mitigation-playbook-2026.json
- GPU memory diagnostics: ../profiling-playbook/gpu-memory-fragmentation-diagnostics-playbook-2026.json

End of document.

title: Cross-Domain Evidence Orchestration: RBAC, Audit, Residency & SDLC Controls for Inference Pipelines
content:
Overview

This handbook describes a cross-domain process for producing, packaging, and validating compliance evidence for model inference pipelines at Redwood Inference. It ties together RBAC decisions, audit logging artifacts, data residency markers, SDLC gates, and incident response artifacts so that we can: 1) respond to auditor requests within 48 hours, 2) run forensics after incidents, and 3) automate evidence assembly for external compliance assessments.

Scope

- Applies to: hosted API, dedicated capacity endpoints, and private (VPC/on-prem) inference deployments.
- Services referenced: inference-gateway, authz-service, audit-streamer, evidence-orchestrator, residency-proxy, ci-release-gate.
- Not in scope: non-inference user account provisioning (separate HR/IdM flows).

Goals and success metrics

- Auditor response SLA: provide curated evidence packet within 48 hours for Level-1 requests (customer-facing incidents) and 7 days for Level-2 (policy reviews).
- Evidence completeness target: 95% of artifacts in automated evidence bundles for routine rollouts.
- Forensics readiness: mean time-to-correlate (MTTC) cross-service traces < 3 hours.

Responsibilities and owners

- Security (owner): overall evidence packaging rules, retention policies, and chain-of-custody checklist.
- Eng-SRE: ensure audit-streamer health, 99.9% ingestion success, alerting on dropped events.
- Eng-Private-Deployments: ensure residency-proxy tagging and local retention configs for on-prem customers.
- Eng-Serving-Runtime: instrumentation of request/response context and KV cache telemetry.
- Product/Legal: define compliance scope for customer contracts and any redaction requirements.

Key concepts and artifacts

1) RBAC snapshot (rbac-snapshot.json)
- Contains: role bindings, entitlement timestamps, approval ticket IDs, and justification notes.
- Generated: daily by authz-service at 02:00 UTC, on-demand via /internal/v1/authz/snapshot.
- Retention: 3 years by default, 7 years for regulated customers (labelled 'residency=long-term').

2) Audit streams (audit.*)
- Source: inference-gateway -> audit-streamer -> immutable-audit-store (S3/GCS BCP with WORM).
- Minimum event schema (example):

  {
    "event_id": "uuidv4",
    "timestamp": "2026-03-02T15:12:00Z",
    "service": "inference-gateway",
    "principal": "service:customer-a:svc-account-1234",
    "action": "model.generate",
    "resource": "model:open-llama-7b:v2",
    "result": "success|error",
    "context": {"seq_len": 512, "kv_cache_hit": true, "route": "dedicated-us-west-2"}
  }

- Retention buckets: short-term (90 days), standard (3 years), archival (7+ years). Retention varies by data residency labels.

3) Residency markers and data movement manifests
- residency-proxy annotates requests with country and region tags: region=eu-west-1, residency=customer_geofence.
- Movement manifest (CSV/JSON) shows transfers between clouds for cross-region failover; signed by residency-proxy and stored in evidence-bucket/manifest/.

4) SDLC release evidence (release-evidence.tar.gz)
- Contents: build artifacts, SBOM, dependency checksums, CI/CD run logs, signed canary roll decisions, and pre-deploy security gate results.
- Generated by ci-release-gate via pipeline variable: EVIDENCE_PACKAGE=true.

Evidence packaging workflow (high-level)

1. Trigger (automated or manual)
- Automated triggers: nightly packaging, post-deploy (successful production rollout), and weekly retention audits.
- Manual triggers: SOC request, external auditor request, or incident triage lead.

2. Orchestration steps (evidence-orchestrator)
- Step 1: collect rbac-snapshot.json from authz-service API.
- Step 2: query immutable-audit-store for event ranges (by timestamp or event_id). Use the audit-query CLI: 
  $ audit-query --service inference-gateway --from 2026-03-01T00:00:00Z --to 2026-03-02T00:00:00Z --format ndjson > events.ndjson
- Step 3: obtain residency manifest(s) and signed movement statements from residency-proxy.
- Step 4: fetch release evidence from ci-release-gate artifact store: release-evidence.tar.gz
- Step 5: run evidence validator (sha256 checks) and produce evidence-manifest.json containing checksums and a minimal chain-of-custody ledger (signed by evidence-orchestrator using KMS key arn:aws:kms:us-west-2:123456789:key/eo-2024).

3. Packaging rules
- All artifacts must be hashed (SHA-256) and signed.
- Sensitive PII must be redacted prior to packaging unless the request explicitly requires full-content for legal reasons. Redaction patterns are controlled by redaction-rules.yml in security repo.
- Evidence packet structure (flat storage layout):
  /evidence/<case-id>/rbac/
  /evidence/<case-id>/audit/
  /evidence/<case-id>/residency/
  /evidence/<case-id>/release/
  /evidence/<case-id>/chain-of-custody.json

4. Delivery and audit trail
- Delivery channels: secure SFTP endpoint (sftp.redwood-secure.com), signed presigned URL with one-time token (expires in 72 hours), or internal ticket attachment on Legal's CASE system.
- Evidence-orchestrator posts an immutable audit event to audit-streamer: action=evidence.package.created, includes case-id, package-hash, and delivery-method.

Operational runbooks (condensed)

A. Fast responder (48-hour auditor request)
1. Triage: Security on-call creates case-id and marks request level.
2. Orchestrate: run evidence-orchestrator --case <id> --scope last_30_days --redact auto.
3. Validate: run evidence-validate --package <path> (checksums + access log).
4. Deliver: upload package and update ticket.
5. Post-action: schedule a 2-week follow-up to archive any exported copies and update retention policy for customer if requested.

B. Post-incident forensic collection
1. Lock down ingestion windows (SRE): freeze audit-streamer retention compaction for the incident window.
2. Snapshot: authz-service snapshot + runtime KV telemetry dump (kv-dump --since <ts>).
3. Correlate: use cross-service trace ID and match events in events.ndjson with rbac snapshot.
4. Package & preserve: evidence-orchestrator --preserve-immutable --notes "incident <id>".

Technical checks and SLOs to monitor

- Audit ingestion success: audit-streamer.ingest_rate >= 99.9% over 24h. Alert: PagerDuty P2 if below.
- Snapshot freshness: authz-service.snapshot_age <= 4 hours. Alert: P3.
- Evidence packaging time: median packaging time (last 30 days) <= 90 minutes for automated runs.
- Evidence validation failures: retry logic (3 attempts) then escalate to security-oncall.

Sample CLI and API examples

- Create authz snapshot (API):
  POST https://internal.redwood/api/v1/authz/snapshot
  Headers: Authorization: Bearer <service-token>

- Query audit events (CLI):
  $ audit-query --service inference-gateway --from 2026-03-01T00:00:00Z --to 2026-03-02T00:00:00Z --format ndjson
\- Orchestrate evidence (CLI):
  $ evidence-orchestrator --case rwd-2026-031 --scope last_7_days --delivery sftp --redact auto

Data residency nuance and legal controls

- If residency=eu (customer label), all artifacts must remain in eu-* storage endpoints; cross-region transfer requires explicit legal sign-off and must appear in the movement manifest.
- For on-prem customers, Eng-Private-Deployments must provide a signed retention covenant that maps local retention configuration to Redwood's evidence retention manifest.

Secure SDLC integrations

- Pre-deploy gate: ci-release-gate runs dependency scanning (SNYK), SBOM generation, and a minimal runtime instrumentation smoke test. Gate output is stored as release-evidence.tar.gz.
- Post-deploy guardrails: canary telemetry must be retained for 14 days before being eligible for automatic purge; any canary security alarms will pin release artifacts for 90 days.

Risk and exceptions process

- Approval flow for evidence exceptions (e.g., extend retention beyond default): 1) engineer requests via Exceptions Tool; 2) Security reviews and attaches a compensating control; 3) Legal approves for customer contracts; 4) record in the exception register with TTL and owner.
- Emergency exception (for incident response): Security may invoke a 72-hour emergency clause documented in the case artifact; post-incident a formal exception request must be created within 7 days.

Frequently encountered scenarios and playbook snippets

1) Customer asks for full audit log for 6 months (EU customer)
- Required: residency legal sign-off, scoped evidence where PII is redacted if not requested, and delivery via EU-only storage.
- Steps: open case -> tag residency=eu -> run evidence-orchestrator with --residency eu -> produce manifest -> legal sign-off -> deliver via sftp.eu.redwood-secure.com.

2) Entitlement discrepancy discovered during audit
- Steps: pull rbac-snapshot for the requested window, identify change-event in audit stream (action=authz.change), pull approval ticket and check identity of approver, escalate to IAM owner, and create remediation ticket with rollback plan.

Appendices

A. Minimal schema reference for audit events
- event_id, timestamp, service, principal, action, resource, result, context.seq_len, context.route, trace_id

B. Example evidence-manifest.json (minimal)
  {
    "case_id": "rwd-2026-031",
    "package_hash": "sha256:abcd...",
    "items": ["rbac-snapshot.json","events.ndjson","release-evidence.tar.gz"],
    "signed_by": "arn:aws:kms:us-west-2:123456789:key/eo-2024",
    "notes": "auto-generated by evidence-orchestrator 2026-03-02T12:00:00Z"
  }

C. Contact matrix
- Security on-call: #sec-oncall (PagerDuty)
- Eng-SRE on-call: #sre-oncall (PagerDuty)
- Legal: legal-internal@redwood.ai

References and related docs

- See also: audit-schema-versioning-and-evidence-tagging-2026 (audit-logging), service-identity-rotation-and-evidence-playbook-2026 (rbac-and-auth), inference-data-flow-deidentification-and-audit-correlation-standards-2026 (data residency).

Change history

- 2026-02-11: Created by Aisha Patel.
- 2026-03-02: Reviewed and updated packaging checksums and delivery TTLs (reviewers: Marco Ruiz, Tessa Nguyen, Daniel Kim).

End of document

title: Runtime Trace Correlator and Event Reconciliation Playbook
content:
Summary
-------
This runbook describes the recommended operational process and commands to correlate end-to-end request traces with low-level kernel dispatch events and GPU timeline samples, detect event mismatches ("reconciliation failures"), and perform remediation and post-incident analysis. It is intended for SREs and runtime engineers responding to tail-latency, unexplained cost spikes, or transient model-swap oscillations where higher-level traces (API/ingress) do not match kernel-level telemetry.

When to use
-----------
- Persistent or recurring tail latency (>99.9th percentile) with no clear API-level throttling.
- Cost anomalies where per-token compute does not match expected kernel time.
- Model swap or variant fallback events observed in control plane logs but no downstream kernel activity.
- Kernel timeouts, stalled GPUs, or delayed KV cache warmups that manifest as opaque request slowdowns.

Owner & escalation
------------------
- Primary on-call: eng-sre/runtime-sli on-call.
- Secondary: runtime-kernel team (pager) if kernel or GPU hang suspected.
- Escalate to infra on-call for suspected hardware/driver issues.
- Post-incident owner: person who closes the incident must schedule a postmortem in 72 hours.

Prerequisites and telemetry
--------------------------
Ensure the following telemetry streams are available and not in degraded mode before starting:
- request-traces (sampled via trace-collector; trace-id present in headers x-rw-trace-id)
- kernel-events stream (kernel-dispatcher -> event bus) with event_id and parent_request_id
- gpu-timeline samples (per-device microsecond timestamps)
- kvcache-metrics and session-affinity logs
- runtime-proxy and model-router logs at info level

Minimum retention and sampling recommendations:
- request-traces: 1% deterministic sampling for production; increase to 10% during investigation
- kernel-events: full capture for at least 6 hours around incident window
- gpu-timeline: rolling 1-hour window, sampled at 100Hz aggregation for latency spikes

Quick reference SLOs and thresholds
----------------------------------
Table: Primary triggers used in the playbook (text table)
| Signal | Alert threshold | Triage priority | Notes |
| API p50/p95/p99 | p99 > 2x baseline | P1 | Typical entry signal |
| Kernel queue depth | > 85% sustained 5m | P1 | Indicates backpressure |
| GPU utilization vs kernel time | GPU util < 30% while kernel time high | P2 | Possible serialization or stall |
| KV cache miss ratio | > 10% | P2 | Warmup or affinity break |

Step-by-step procedure
----------------------
1) Capture incident window and identify a representative trace
   - Timebox: pick 5 minutes around alert onset and 30 minutes before for baseline.
   - Query traces:

   ```bash
   # increase sampling if possible for live investigations
   curl -s "https://obs-api.internal/v1/traces?start=2025-09-10T12:10:00Z&end=2025-09-10T12:15:00Z&min_duration_ms=200" \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBS_API_KEY" | jq . | less
   ```

   - Identify a trace with full path: ingress -> runtime-proxy -> model-router -> kernel-dispatcher. Note the x-rw-trace-id and request_id (request-id header).

2) Map high-level trace spans to kernel events
   - Kernel events contain fields: {event_id, parent_request_id, kernel_name, start_us, end_us, device_id, reason}. Use parent_request_id to map to request_id.
   - Example kernel-events query (Elasticsearch/ESQL):

   ```sql
   SELECT event_id, parent_request_id, kernel_name, start_us, end_us, device_id, reason
   FROM kernel-events
   WHERE parent_request_id = 'req-1234' AND timestamp BETWEEN '2025-09-10T12:09:30Z' AND '2025-09-10T12:15:30Z';
   ```

   - If parent_request_id is missing: search by trace timestamp +/- 50ms on same host/slot and correlate by kernel start_us approximate to span.start_timestamp_us.

3) Reconciliation rules and heuristics (event matching algorithm)
   - Exact-match: trace.request_id == kernel.parent_request_id -> mark reconciled.
   - Heuristic match: if exact-match absent, match by host, GPU device_id, and kernel start timestamp within +/- 2500us of span boundary.
   - Unmatched span classification:
     - Missing-kernel: high-level span present, kernel event absent => suspect routing/fallback or kernel dispatch failure.
     - Orphan-kernel: kernel event with no active high-level trace => likely system-level background task or delayed trace sampling.
     - Delayed-commit: kernel start occurs but no end_us recorded -> suspect watchdog or driver hang.

4) Run automated reconciliation query and produce summary report\
   - Use the provided connector script (trace-correlator) on the runbox:

   ```bash
   ./tools/trace-correlator --trace-id req-1234 --window 30s --output /tmp/recon-req-1234.json
   cat /tmp/recon-req-1234.json | jq .summary
   ```

   - Expected output: counts for reconciled, missing-kernel, orphan-kernel, delayed-commit.

5) Remediation actions by category\
   - Missing-kernel:
     1. Check model-router logs for "no-capacity" or "variant-mismatch" for the affected trace-id.
     2. If routing indicates fallback to another region/tier, verify that cross-region routing is completing and that kernel-dispatcher is reachable.
     3. If model was swapped mid-request, run the model-swap audit:

   ```bash
   curl -s "https://control-plane.internal/v1/rollouts?request_id=req-1234" -H "Authorization: Bearer $CP_API" | jq .
   ```

     4. If routing and control-plane look healthy, raise a kernel-dispatcher debug request to capture next 100 dispatch attempts and escalate to kernel team.

   - Orphan-kernel:
     1. Check whether the kernel was part of a background eviction, prefetch, or garbage collection by inspecting kernel_name and reason.
     2. If orphaned kernel time is significant (>100ms), investigate whether tracing sampling missed the parent due to rate limits. Consider increasing request-traces sampling temporarily.

   - Delayed-commit / GPU hang:
     1. Immediately check GPU watchdog metrics and driver logs on node.
     2. If kernel end_us missing, perform a soft-reset on the dispatcher lane (non-destructive) by toggling lane draining: `curl -X POST https://admin.internal/dispatcher/lane/drain?lane=lane-7`
     3. If soft-reset fails, escalate to infra; capture a full GPU dump and attach to incident.

6) Short-term mitigations to restore SLOs\
   - Activate canary fallback: route to pre-warmed smaller variant (model-small-quant) for new inbound requests for the affected customers.
   - Increase continuous-batching windows for short period to absorb variance if kernel queue depth is high.
   - Temporarily raise trace sampling to 10% to improve reconciliation signal.

7) Post-incident diagnostics and artifacts\
   - Required artifacts to attach to postmortem:
     - Representative trace(s) x-rw-trace-id(s) and request-id(s).
     - /tmp/recon-<id>.json output.
     - Kernel-event dump for the incident window.
     - GPU timeline sample slice (.timeline.gz).
     - Control-plane rollout events for model-variants.
   - Run a delta analysis comparing expected kernel time vs observed kernel time across the 1-hour window around incident. Include token counts and model variant in analysis.

Operational tools and snippets
----------------------------
- trace-correlator usage: `./tools/trace-correlator --window 30s --sample-rate 10% --trace-id <id>`
- quick ES aggregate to get reconciliation rates by host:

  ```sql
  SELECT host, COUNT(*) as total_traces, SUM(case when reconciled then 1 else 0 end) as reconciled_count
  FROM trace-recon-results
  WHERE timestamp BETWEEN '2025-09-10T12:00:00Z' AND '2025-09-10T13:00:00Z'
  GROUP BY host
  ORDER BY reconciled_count ASC
  ```

- Kernel dispatch debug mode (non-prod first):

  ```yaml
  debug_mode: true
  capture_count: 100
  include_backtrace: true
  filter: "device_id=nvA100-07 and kernel_name contains 'attn'"
  ```

Telemetry tuning & sampling guidance
-----------------------------------
- Increase kernel-events retention to 24 hours for clusters with 1000+ qps.
- For noisy customers, add request-id sticky sampling so heavy users get 100% trace sampling for a rolling 15-minute window when an anomaly starts.
- Add a reconciliation metric: `recon.mismatch_rate` (percent of spans that did not reconcile) with 1-minute resolution to use in alerting.

Common investigation scenarios (examples)
---------------------------------------
- Scenario A: p99 spike with many Missing-kernel classified traces.
  - Likely cause: transient model-router GC cleared routing table. Look for model-router logs: "slot reaped". Mitigation: increase routing-table TTL or add warm probes.

- Scenario B: Orphan-kernel dominated by background prefetch kernels during peak.
  - Likely cause: aggressive prefetch; add prefetch-rate-limit per tenant and move prefetch work to separate non-urgent queue.

- Scenario C: Delayed-commit on a single device.
  - Likely cause: intermittent driver hang/firmware bug. Escalation: infra kernel/GPU vendor support with timeline and logs.

Postmortem template and action items
-----------------------------------
Include the following fields in every postmortem derived from this playbook:
- Incident summary (what happened, impact)
- Timeline with reconciled/unreconciled counts per 5-minute bucket
- Root cause hypothesis and evidence (link to recon JSON and kernel dumps)
- Remediation actions (what fixed it) and long-term fixes (owner + ETA)
- Telemetry improvements (sampling, metrics to add)
- Runbook updates (this doc should be updated if new heuristics are discovered)

Appendix: example trace-correlator output (abbreviated)
----------------------------------------------------
{
  "summary": {
    "trace_id": "req-1234",
    "reconciled": 12,
    "missing_kernel": 3,
    "orphan_kernel": 1,
    "delayed_commit": 2
  },
  "mismatches": [
    {
      "span": "model-router:dispatch",
      "reason": "missing_kernel",
      "notes": "model-router logged fallback to region-us-west-2"
    }
  ]
}

Related reading and links
-------------------------
- request-provenance-and-decision-trace-patterns (design intent)
- probabilistic-latency-attribution-playbook (profiling heuristics)
- kernel-dispatcher debug docs (internal)

Change log
----------
- 2024-11-15: Initial draft (Maya Chen).
- 2025-03-12: Added heuristics for timestamp-based matching and sample CLI (Arjun Patel).
- 2025-09-10: Added GPU hang remediation steps and sample ES queries (Lena Sørensen).

Notes and caveats
-----------------
- This playbook focuses on telemetry correlation, not on kernel kernel-level patching. If a kernel bug is suspected, coordinate with the kernel team for safe reproduction in staging.
- Reconciliation will never be perfect due to sampling; use heuristics and representative samples for investigative confidence.

title: Adaptive cohort probing and handoff runbook
content:
Summary

This runbook describes the adaptive cohort probing and handoff process used by the Redwood serving runtime to detect per-cohort fidelity degradation, orchestrate kernel handoffs, and safely probe changes under production traffic. It defines telemetry signals, thresholds, automated decision steps, and operator procedures for investigation and rollback. The goal is to allow dynamic handoffs (e.g., between quantized kernel A and fallback kernel B) while preserving SLOs and minimizing cost impact.

Scope

- Applies to multi-tenant inference pools running heterogeneous kernels (FP16, 8-bit quantized, sparse-aware kernels) on GPU clusters.
- Covers automated probing, graceful handoff, telemetry required, manual intervention steps, and validation/benchmarking checklist.
- Excludes model packaging and build processes (see model-onboarding docs).

Audience

- Oncall SREs and runtime engineers responsible for scheduler and kernel rollouts.
- Benchmarking and profiling engineers validating kernel variants.

Background and motivation

Redwood supports multiple kernel implementations with different performance/cost/quality characteristics. When the scheduler considers swapping a cohort to a new kernel variant (for cost saving or fallback), naive switchovers can introduce regressions (tail latency spikes, token errors) that impact customer SLAs. Adaptive probing lets us sample production traffic for a small and controlled cohort, gather fidelity and latency signals, and make a conservative decision to expand, hold, or rollback.

Key terminology

- Cohort: A logical group of requests defined by model, route, or customer label.
- Probe window: The time-bounded sampling period used to evaluate a kernel change for a cohort (default 5 minutes).
- Handoff: The act of routing cohort traffic from one kernel variant to another.
- Fidelity regression: Any measurable reduction in output quality against a defined prompt-suite (e.g., Rouge/BLEU/embedding-similarity drop or increased hallucination rate).

Architecture overview (textual diagram)

Serving runtime components involved:

- Dispatcher: request classifier and cohort router (policy engine)
- Scheduler: allocates kernel slots and performs handoff orchestration
- Kernel Registry: metadata and compatibility matrix for kernel variants
- Probe Engine: lightweight mirroring and sampling sub-system for probe windows
- Telemetry Pipeline: streaming traces, percentile latencies, fidelity probes, error rates

(Imagine a horizontally stacked diagram: Dispatcher -> Scheduler -> Kernel instances; Probe Engine forks short-lived shadow requests to probe kernels and emits enriched traces into Telemetry Pipeline.)

Signals to collect

Collect these signals at 1s/10s/60s granularities depending on signal type:

- Latency: p50/p95/p99 for token generation and end-to-end request time
- Error rates: gRPC/HTTP 5xx, codec errors, kernel panics
- Fidelity metrics: embedding cosine similarity to baseline, token-level divergence, special token counts (UNK/UNK-like), model-specific eval score on a small prompt set
- Resource signals: GPU SM utilization, memory pressure, kernel queue depth
- Queueing indicators: queuing_time_ms, active_slots, preempt_count

Decision thresholds (defaults)

- Latency: p99 increase > 15% for probe cohort compared to baseline => fail probe
- Error rate: absolute increase > 0.5 percentage points or relative > 2x => fail probe
- Fidelity: embedding similarity drop > 0.015 absolute or relative quality delta > 5% on validation prompts => fail probe
- Resource: sustained (30s) GPU mem pressure > 90% or SM utilization pegged at 98% => fail probe

Config table (example values)

- probe_window_minutes: 5
- probing_fraction_initial: 0.01 (1% of cohort)
- probing_fraction_step: 0.05 (increase to 5% on success)
- max_probe_fraction: 0.20
- telemetry_aggregation_interval_seconds: 10
- required_consecutive_success_windows: 2

Automated probe lifecycle (high-level steps)

1) Candidate selection: Release pipeline marks kernel variant K2 as candidate for kernel K1 on cohort C.
2) Canary allocation: Scheduler selects a probe subset P (probing_fraction_initial) of cohort C and routes those requests to K2 for probe_window_minutes.
3) Shadow probing (optional): For fidelity-sensitive cohorts, the dispatcher sends a non-blocking shadow request to K2 in parallel; results are compared against the primary path.
4) Aggregation: Probe Engine aggregates telemetry for P and computes delta vs baseline.
5) Decision: If all thresholds are satisfied and required_consecutive_success_windows are met, increase probing_fraction by probing_fraction_step and continue. If probe reaches max_probe_fraction and passes final checks, promote K2 for cohort C. Otherwise, abort and revert to K1.

Manual escalation playbook (when automated probe fails but metrics are borderline)

1) Pager triggers: If failure threshold crossed for production cohort above severity threshold (see SLO incident taxonomy), page runtime-oncall.
2) Initial triage (5 min):
  - Confirm the cohort identity and affected customers.
  - Check recent kernel release events, model version swaps, infra incidents.
  - Run ktrace for an exemplar request (see commands below).
3) Containment (10 min):
  - Quarantine cohort: change cohort routing policy to pin to stable kernel K1 for all non-probe traffic.
  - Increase telemetry sampling to 100% for affected cohort for 15 minutes.
4) Root cause and remediation (30–90 min):
  - If kernel bug suspected, open kernel rollback and mark variant as unsafe in Kernel Registry.
  - If resource pressure, expand capacity or move cohort to different node pool.
  - For fidelity regressions, trigger a focused validation replay (see benchmarking steps) and notify model quality team.

Investigation commands and examples

- Capture a short trace for a failed sample:
  curl -s -H \"Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN\" \
    -d '{\"model\":\"X-small\",\"input\":\"<repro prompt>\",\"trace_id\":\"probe-debug-$(date +%s)\"}' \
    https://dispatcher.internal/v1/execute

- Query probe aggregates (PromQL example):
  sum(rate(kernel_request_duration_seconds_bucket{cohort="$COHORT",kernel_variant="K2"}[5m])) by (le)

- Compare embeddings (quick python snippet):
  from numpy import dot
  from numpy.linalg import norm
  def cos(a,b):
    return dot(a,b)/(norm(a)*norm(b))

Profiling and synthetic replay checklist

- Before large cohort promotions, run the following:
  - Microbench: run 1k synthetic requests with mixed sequence lengths (16/64/256) using the benchmark harness. Record p50/p95/p99 and compare to baseline.
  - Shadow replay: replay a 10k-sample window from production tracing storage through candidate kernel in sandbox.
  - Fidelity run: execute cohort-specific prompt set (50–200 prompts) and compute embedding similarity + model-specific metrics.

Benchmark commands (example harness invocation)

- ./bench_harness --kernel K2 --model X-small --sequences 1000 --mix \"16:0.5,64:0.3,256:0.2\" --concurrency 8 --report out/K2-microbench.json

Kernel scheduling policy examples

Use this sample policy to prefer memory-efficient kernels for cohorts with high concurrency:

- policy name: cohort_memory_preference
- selectors: cohort.labels.fidelity_tolerance <= 0.02 and avg_seq_length > 128
- preferred_kernel_order: [quantized_lowmem, fp16_sparse, fp16_full]
- admission: max_slots_per_node 32

Validation and rollout checklist (pre-promotion)

- Automated probe passed for required_consecutive_success_windows.
- Microbench p99 no more than 10% increased vs baseline.
- Fidelity metrics within thresholds on the validation prompt set.
- No related infra incidents in last 60 minutes.
- Release notes entry added to runtime release notes and Kernel Registry annotated with risk level.

Rollback policy

- Immediate auto-rollback on: p99 latency > 2x baseline or absolute error-rate jump > 2 percentage points.
- Automated partial rollback: if probe window fails but not catastrophic, revert probing_fraction to 0 and annotate Kernel Registry with failure reason.

Operational run scenarios (short examples)

- Scenario A: New quantized kernel shows 3% p99 improvement but 0.02 drop in embedding similarity.
  1) Probe small cohort (1%). 2) Fidelity delta borderline — hold probe and escalate to model-quality team. 3) After validating prompt set, either accept with a soft-fidelity gate or rollback.

- Scenario B: Kernel passes fidelity but causes GPU mem pressure.
  1) Probe fails on resource signal. 2) Quarantine cohort, move to larger nodes, re-run microbench.

Ownership and escalation contacts

- Runtime oncall: runtime-oncall@redwood.ai (primary)
- Kernel release owner: arjun.patel@redwood.ai
- Model quality: lena.rodriguez@redwood.ai

Operational metrics to track (dashboards)

- probe_success_rate by kernel_variant and cohort
- cohort_p99_latency and cohort_fidelity_delta
- kernel_panic_count and kernel_retry_rate

Safety notes and guardrails

- Never promote a kernel that showed any instance of deterministic correctness error (e.g., tokenization mismatch) in probe windows.
- For regulated cohorts (confidentiality=restricted), shadow probing is disabled unless explicitly approved by security/compliance.

Audit and postmortem requirements

- Any automated rollback must generate an incident record with: timeline, probe aggregates, decision rationale, and remediation plan.
- For rollouts that change >10% of cohort volume, perform a 72-hour post-rollout review and record in related_pages.

Appendix: troubleshooting quick hits

- If probe_latency spikes but resource signals are normal: collect detailed kernel traces and map to kernel queue depth; suspect scheduling contention.
- If fidelity drops only for long sequences: check kvcache eviction settings and kernel-specific KV handling toggles.

Related artifacts

- Kernel Registry schema: see /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/kernel-registry-spec (internal)
- Benchmark harness: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/operational-workload-simulator-and-signature-guide-2026

Change log

- 2026-01-12: Created by Maya Chen.
- 2026-02-10: Added kernel scheduling sample policy and expanded telemetry thresholds (review by Arjun P.).
- 2026-03-02: Clarified rollback policy and added synthetic replay checklist (review by Lena R.).

title: Runtime hotpatch and quick redeploy playbook
content:
Summary

This playbook captures step-by-step guidance for applying small, targeted hotpatches to the serving runtime (kernel or scheduling components) and for performing a fast emergency redeploy when a hotpatch is not possible or has failed. It targets oncall engineers and runtime SREs who must restore service within the next 15–60 minutes while preserving customer SLOs and minimizing blast radius.

When to use this playbook

- Critical kernel or scheduler bug causing elevated 99th-percentile latency or hard errors (5xx) for >1 minute and automatic mitigations have not restored SLOs.
- Memory corruption or a known safe patch exists that can be applied without a full image build.
- Emergency patch path is documented in the kernel safety-net and approved by the runtime owner.
- If the issue is a broader configuration, refer to the deployment circuit-breakers playbook instead.

Owners and escalation

- Primary: runtime-oncall (pager duty) — first responder.
- Secondary: runtime-sre (pager) — 10 minutes escalation if unresolved.
- Tertiary:serving-runtime-eng (email/Slack) — for cross-team rollout coordination.

Required checks before hotpatching (preflight)

1) Confirm actual customer impact:
   - Check per-route 99th latency spikes and 5xx rate in the last 5 minutes.
   - Verify error budgets: if < 10% remaining for the hour, proceed with caution.

2) Validate trace and kernel signal presence:
   - Look up last 100 traces that hit the failing path (trace tag: runtime.kernel.failure=true).
   - Confirm root cause candidate aligns with a supported hotpatch (see Acceptable Hotpatch Types table below).

3) Confirm rollback path and canary target nodes are available:
   - Identify a canary cohort of 5–10% of nodes in the affected pool (minimum 3 nodes).
   - Ensure at least one warm spare pool is ready for immediate slot migration.

Acceptable Hotpatch Types (short table)

| Hotpatch Type | Allowed when | Risk |
|---|---|---|
| JIT config tweak (no binary change) | Fixes runtime flags or scheduler thresholds | Low |
| Lua/JS actuator script swap | Script corrects route matching / backoff | Low–medium |
| Binary function-level hotfix (approved diff) | Small critical logic change with signed patch | Medium |
| Kernel microservice restart with staged image | When binary replacement is required but can be canaried | Medium–high |

Note: Full binary rebuilds that change kernel ABI are NOT eligible for hotpatch and require a standard canary image rollout.

Hotpatch procedure (fast path) — target time 15–25 minutes

1) Announce intent (1 minute)
   - Post to #runtime-incidents with: incident id, short description, target nodes, and expected time window.

2) Quiesce auxiliary load (2 minutes)
   - Use the admission controller to shift non-critical burst traffic: 
     redwoodctl route-weight --scope affected --weight 0.1 --duration 5m
   - Enable temporary cache bypass for debug traces: 
     redwoodctl debug cache-bypass --routes debug-* --on

3) Apply the hotpatch to canary cohort (3–5 minutes)
   - For config/script changes: push via the config service: 
     curl -X POST https://config.redwood.internal/v1/hotpatch -d '{"patch":"<base64>"}' -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN'
   - For signed binary microfix: use the runtime hotpatch signer: 
     redwoodctl patch-kernel --cohort canary --patch-file /tmp/patch.bin --signature /tmp/patch.sig
   - Confirm deployment status: 
     redwoodctl cohort-status --cohort canary --wait 60s

4) Observe telemetry for 10 minutes (minimum)
   - Dashboards to watch: per-node 99th latency, per-route 5xx rate, kernel-exception-rate.
   - Run smoke query: 
     curl -sS https://svc-internal/health-check -H 'x-test-trace: hotpatch-canary' | jq .status

5) If stable -> progressive expand (10–20 minutes)
   - Expand cohort in steps: 10% -> 30% -> 60% -> 100%, with 5–10 minute observation windows between steps.
   - Use automated rollout: 
     redwoodctl rollout expand --strategy progressive --interval 5m --steps 10,30,60,100 --cohort affected

Emergency redeploy procedure (when hotpatch fails or not allowed) — target time 30–60 minutes

1) Abort any in-flight hotpatch and mark canary as failed:
   - redwoodctl patch-kernel --cohort canary --abort --reason "hotpatch failed"

2) Prepare a fast redeploy image (prebuilt emergency image recommended)
   - If a prebuilt emergency image exists, tag it as emergency: 
     redwoodctl image tag --image-id img-2026-11-09-emergency --tag emergency-<incident-id>
   - If not, build minimal image with the exact production ABI and only the required fix. Use the fast-build profile: 
     ./build-image --profile fast --include runtime:hotfix-module --tag emergency-<incident-id>

3) Canary redeploy to the canary cohort (5–10 minutes)
   - Deploy the emergency image to the canary cohort: 
     redwoodctl deploy --image emergency-<incident-id> --cohort canary --max-concurrency 3
   - Attach observability hooks: trace-sampling=100%, metric-enrichment=hotpatch-incident.<id>

4) Automated smoke and runbook checks (10–15 minutes)
   - Run the smoke suite against the canary: 
     redwoodctl smoke-run --cohort canary --tests core-latency,kv-consistency,session-stability --timeout 600s
   - Verify no increase in memory RSS, no new 5xx, and no kernel panics.

5) Expand or rollback (progressive)
   - Follow the same progressive expansion steps as the hotpatch procedure.
   - If at any point the 99th latency or 5xx rates regress above pre-incident thresholds, trigger rollback immediately.

Rollback and containment

- To rollback a hotpatch to the previous known-good state: 
  redwoodctl patch-kernel --cohort affected --rollback-to stable-<timestamp> --force-checks
- To rollback a redeploy: 
  redwoodctl deploy --image stable-image-<timestamp> --cohort affected --force
- Containment steps if rollback is not possible quickly: 
  1) Shift traffic away from affected pool using route weights.
  2) Attach fallback routing: 
     redwoodctl routing fallback --policy model-variant --target variant-stable --duration 30m

Telemetry and post-incident tasks

- During the operation ensure the following metrics are captured at 10s granularity for at least 30 minutes: per-node cpu/gpu utilization, per-node memory RSS, kernel-exception-rate, per-route 99p latency, per-route 5xx rate, kvcache-hitratio.
- Create an incident bridge note with timeline and include command transcripts.
- Postmortem: owner is runtime-sre; draft within 72 hours; public summary to go-to-market within 7 days if customer-facing.

Command reference (common commands)

- redwoodctl patch-kernel --cohort <cohort> --patch-file <file> --signature <sig>
- redwoodctl patch-kernel --cohort <cohort> --abort --reason <text>
- redwoodctl deploy --image <image-tag> --cohort <cohort> --max-concurrency <n>
- redwoodctl rollout expand --strategy progressive --interval <min> --steps <csv> --cohort <cohort>
- redwoodctl smoke-run --cohort <cohort> --tests <list> --timeout <s>
- redwoodctl cohort-status --cohort <cohort> --wait <s>

Safety thresholds (must abort and rollback if any triggered)

- Per-route 5xx rate increases by >200% vs baseline for a sustained 3 minutes.
- Per-route 99p latency increases by >50% vs baseline for a sustained 3 minutes.
- Any kernel panic or OOM observed on >1% of nodes in cohort.

Configuration snippets and examples

- Example emergency rollout policy (YAML):

  apiVersion: redwood/v1
  kind: RolloutPolicy
  metadata:
    name: emergency-fast-expansion
  spec:
    strategy: progressive
    steps: [10, 30, 60, 100]
    intervalMinutes: 5
    maxConcurrency: 5
    safetyChecks:
      - metric: kernel-panic-count
        threshold: 1
        windowSeconds: 60

- Example smoke test list (JSON array):

  ["core-latency","kv-consistency","session-stability","model-fidelity-basic"]

Post-incident hygiene checklist

1) Record the exact patch artifact and commit hash used.
2) Create a test matrix entry that reproduces the failure in the sandbox.
3) Schedule a controlled rebuild and standard canary for the patch (no emergency tags) within 72 hours.
4) Update the kernel hotpatch whitelist if the hotpatch type will be reused.
5) Update runbook: add any missing steps or commands discovered during the incident.

Appendices

A. Quick diagnostics commands
- tail -n 200 /var/log/runtime/kernel.log | grep -i panic
- redwoodctl metrics query "avg(99p_latency) by route" --from -10m
- redwoodctl traces query --tag runtime.kernel.failure --limit 100

B. Canary cohort sizing guidance
- For small pools (< 100 nodes) use minimum 3-node canary.
- For large pools (> 1000 nodes) prefer 5–10% but cap canary at 200 nodes.

C. Links and references
- Kernel safety and rollback playbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/kernel-safety-net-and-rollback-playbook-2027
- Deployment circuit breakers: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-deployment-circuit-breakers-and-sla-fallback-playbook-2026
- Canary matrix and validation: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-upgrade-validation-and-canary-matrix-2026

If you are the oncall taking this action: add your name to the incident timeline and ping runtime-sre for audit and postmortem ownership.

title: Latency-Fidelity Governor and Experimentation Playbook
content:
Summary
-------
This playbook describes the Latency-Fidelity Governor (LFG): an operational component that mediates runtime scheduling decisions to balance client-facing latency SLOs against model output fidelity and cost. It bundles architecture notes, scheduler integration patterns, profiling/benchmark procedures, rollout & release guidance, and an incident runbook.

Audience
--------
- Runtime owners and engineers implementing scheduling policies
- Oncall SREs responding to latency/fidelity incidents
- Applied ML engineers running fidelity regressions during quantization or model swaps

Goals
-----
1. Define a repeatable, observable control loop that enforces latency SLOs while minimizing fidelity regressions.
2. Provide concrete experimentation and rollout steps so teams can validate LFG changes in staging and production-like environments.
3. Standardize telemetry and profiling artifacts used in decisions and post-incident analysis.

Scope and non-goals
-------------------
- Scope: scheduling policy surface (admission, preemption, kernel hints), governor controller, observability signals, benchmark harness, and incident playbook.
- Non-goals: model training, user-facing prompt engineering, or billing systems.

Design overview
---------------
High level: LFG is a control plane component that consumes real-time telemetry (latency quantiles, kernel queue lengths, token-throughput, KV cache hit rates, and quality metrics from evaluation hooks) and outputs: per-route admission thresholds, priority weights, and model-variant fallback directives.

Key concepts
------------
- Latency target (SLO): per-route 95p service time target (example: 95p <= 120 ms for short-completion routes).
