- Fidelity budget: allowable delta in downstream eval metrics (e.g., Rouge-L, BLEU, hallucination P@K) vs baseline after model or quantization changes.
- Degradation modes: reduced beam size, fallback to larger model variant that runs on different kernel, or lower token-sampling temperature.
- Cost knob: quantization level and batching (higher batching reduces cost but increases tail latency).

Component interactions (text diagram)
-----------------------------------
1) Ingress router -> 2) Admission controller -> 3) LFG controller (observability inputs) -> 4) Kernel scheduler / slot allocator -> 5) Serving runtime (kernels + KV cache) -> 6) Eval hook (async quality probe) -> back to 3).

Controller behavior and ruleset (condensed)
-------------------------------------------
- Every 30s sliding window evaluate: 95p latency, avg queue length, KV hit rate, and sample eval success rate.
- If 95p > SLO by 15% and queue length high: lower admission rate for low-priority routes by 25% and escalate heavy requests to Dedicated pool (if configured).
- If async eval shows fidelity delta > budget and cost per token < configured cap: reduce batching aggressiveness and prefer higher-precision quantization profile for affected model route during peak windows.
- Always maintain a safety floor: preserve at least 5% capacity for high-priority low-latency routes.

Kernel scheduler integration
---------------------------
- Policy tokens: LFG emits kernel-hints as metadata on requests: {priority: P0|P1|P2, kernel_hint: fast_fwd|stable_prec, admission_deadline_ms: X}.
- Scheduler consumes these hints to decide slot assignment, preemption windows, and co-location affinity.
- When kernel switching is required (e.g., switch from quantized kernel to fp16 kernel for fidelity), controller triggers a gradual ramp using the runtime's canary matrix (see "Rollout checklist").

Telemetry and observability contract
-----------------------------------
Required signals (sample names):
- runtime.latency_ms.{route}.{quantile} (p50,p90,p95,p99)
- runtime.queue_length.{pool} (gauge)
- runtime.kv_hit_rate.{model} (ratio)
- runtime.kernel_dispatch_latency.{kernel_variant} (histogram)
- runtime.quality_probe.{route}.{metric} (value)
- runtime.cost_per_token.{route} (gauge)

When to run profiling and benchmarks
-----------------------------------
- Pre-merge: any code that touches admission, scheduling, or kernel selection must include unit tests and a microbenchmark showing performance delta.
- Pre-production canary: run the benchmark suite with the target synthetic load and the fidelity probe corpus.
- Rolling upgrade: for kernel or quantization changes run a 72-hour shadow-run against a 10% traffic mirror and collect fidelity and latency traces.

Profiling playbook (short)
-------------------------
1. Baseline capture: collect 1 hour of trace from production for the target route under normal load (traces must include kernel ids and KV cache annotations).
2. Micro-run: replay baseline with single-tenant microbench harness to reproduce tail artifacts. Command: 
   runtimectl profile --route /v1/generate --sample-hour 2026-07-09T14:00Z --out /tmp/trace.pb
3. Kernel-sensitivity sweep: iterate kernel variants with sequence-length buckets [8, 32, 128] and collect dispatch and execution times.
4. Fidelity probe: run evaluation harness with the same prompts used for quality gates. Command: 
   runtimectl eval --corpus corpora/latency-fidelity-corpus.jsonl --model v2.1-quantized --metrics rouge-l,bertscore --out /tmp/eval.json
5. Report: produce a combined PDF with latency quantiles, kernel breakdown, and fidelity deltas. Use the runtime-report tool.

Benchmark suite guidance
------------------------
- Run the system-wide benchmark harness (shell snippet):
  export BENCH_PROFILE=latency_fidelity_experiment
  benchctl run --config benchmarks/profiles/latency-fidelity.yml --duration 30m --collect-traces
- Benchmark profile should include: mixed route weights, client-side pacing, and session-affinity churn. Use three load shapes: steady, spike (x3 for 90s), and decay.
- Acceptance criteria: 95p latency within target and fidelity delta <= configured budget over 30m. If violated, abort rollout.

Runbook: incident response for sustained 95p regression
-----------------------------------------------------
- Trigger: alert runtime.latency_ms.{route}.p95 > SLO * 1.15 for 5m.
- Primary oncall steps (0–5m):
  1) Acknowledge and tag incident in PagerDuty with "LFG: latency regression".
  2) Check synthetic shadow-run status and recent admission changes.
  3) If admission throttles were applied in last 5 minutes, rollback last policy change.
- Triage (5–30m):
  1) Pull runtime.trace for top 10 slow requests; look for: kernel_dispatch_latency spikes, KV miss bursts, or increased preemption events.
  2) If KV miss rate > 10pp from baseline: trigger kvcache-warmup pipeline (see runbook kvcache-warmup).
  3) If kernel_dispatch_latency for a kernel variant is elevated by >25%: move traffic to an alternate kernel with the governor directive: LFG:set kernel_hint=stable_prec for route X.
- Mitigation (30–120m):
  1) Reduce batching target by 20% for affected pool.
  2) If capacity saturation is root cause, request Dedicated pool burst (for customers with Dedicated) or swap to a lower-cost model variant that preserves latency.
  3) Monitor fidelity probes continuously; if fidelity regressions exceed budget during mitigation, revert to baseline model.

Rollout checklist (for a new LFG policy or kernel variant)
--------------------------------------------------------
1. Unit tests and microbench coverage added (PR required).
2. Run local benchmark profile with synthetic load (pass).
3. Stage canary: 1% production traffic shadow + 0.5% live traffic, 24h collection.
4. Shadow run fidelity delta must be <= budget and 95p latency <= SLO + 5%.
5. Gradual ramp: 1% -> 5% -> 20% -> 50% -> 100% with 30–60m observation windows and automated rollback on policy triggers.
6. Release note snippet example: 
   - "LFG v1.3: Adds per-route dynamic batching and stable_prec kernel preference. Default fidelity budget: 0.5% BLEU delta. Auto-rollback on p95>120ms*1.15"

Known issues and mitigations (picked examples)
--------------------------------------------
- Intermittent KV-cache ripple: After large model swaps, initial KV misses cause higher tail latency. Mitigation: kvcache prewarm and staged model swap with traffic drain.
- Kernel scheduler misclassification: rare cases where multitenant co-location causes credit starvation. Mitigation: enable quota isolation for top 3 high-priority routes.
- Fidelity probe sampling bias: small corpora can underrepresent failure modes. Mitigation: expand corpus with adversarial prompts and stratified sampling across customers.

Operational metrics to publish weekly
----------------------------------
- % routes meeting p95 target
- Median fidelity delta across active experiments
- Number of automatic rollbacks initiated by LFG
- Cost per 1M tokens for routes using adaptive batching

Ownership and contacts
----------------------
- LFG proto team: Maya Thompson (owner), Ravi Kapoor (scheduler lead), Elena García (profiling/benchmarks).
- PagerDuty: runtime-oncall team (primary).

Appendix: example LFG config snippet
----------------------------------
(Place under /etc/runtime-governor/policies/latency-fidelity.yml)

```yaml
policy_name: latency_fidelity_default
routes:
  - name: /v1/generate-short
    slo_p95_ms: 120
    fidelity_budget: 0.005   # allowed relative delta
    admission_share: 0.9
    kernel_preferences:
      - stable_prec
      - fast_fwd
  - name: /v1/completions-long
    slo_p95_ms: 600
    fidelity_budget: 0.02
    admission_share: 0.7
    kernel_preferences:
      - fast_fwd
```

Appendix: minimal experiment commands
------------------------------------
- Start an experiment: 
  runtimectl experiment start --name latfidelity-july --policy /etc/runtime-governor/policies/latency-fidelity.yml --traffic-split 0.01 --shadow true
- Collect traces for 1h: 
  runtimectl collect --exp latfidelity-july --duration 1h --out /tmp/latfidelity-trace.tar

Change log (summary)
--------------------
- 2026-02-15: Initial draft created.
- 2026-05-02: Added kernel hint metadata contract and runbook mitigations.
- 2026-07-10: Expanded profiling playbook and clarified rollout windows.

Related references
------------------
- Runtime decision graph and observed behaviour catalog (see related_pages)
- Scheduler telemetry synthesis and proofing
- Runtime profiling playbook and microbenchmark catalog

End of document

title: Runtime Integrated Experimentation Playbook
content:
Summary:
This playbook describes the integrated experimentation framework used by the runtime, kernel scheduling, profiling, and benchmarking teams to design, run, and validate production-impacting experiments. It codifies an observability-first approach that ties kernel and scheduler changes to measurable signals (latency, cost, kv-cache health, queueing) and defines guardrails for safe rollout across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private environments.

Goals and scope:
- Enable low-risk kernel and scheduler experiments that yield reproducible performance and cost delta measurements.
- Provide a single source of truth for experiment lifecycle: design, stage validation, canary rollouts, full rollout, and rollback.
- Ensure experiments are observable end-to-end and tied to SLO and cost budgets.
- Apply to changes affecting: kernel selection logic, batch slicing, preemption policies, KV cache heuristics, quantized execution paths, and routing/fallback rules.

Owners and roles:
- Experiment Lead: owner of the change (usually runtime or kernel eng).
- Instrumentation Lead: observability or profiling owner responsible for telemetry coverage.
- Benchmarks Owner: benchmarking team contact who runs controlled traffic and cost simulations.
- SRE Reviewer: approves rollout policy and SLA gating.
- Oncall rotation: runtime-oncall for the day of canary and 24h after full rollout.

Required telemetry and dashboards (minimum coverage):
- request.timeline.kernel_exec_ms (histogram)
- request.queue.wait_ms (histogram)
- kernel.dispatch.queue_depth (gauge)
- gpu.occupancy.percent (gauge)
- kvcache.hit_rate.prefix (ratio)
- tokens.per_request (summary)
- per_token_cost_usd (derived counter)
- request.error_rate (rate)
- model.variant.fallback_rate (rate)
- cpu_p95_sys/user_ms (histogram)
- p95_latency_ms, p99_latency_ms, p999_latency_ms (quantiles)

SLOs and experimental thresholds (example):
- Production latency SLO: p99 < 300ms for text-generation small models (configurable per model family).
- Error budget: no more than 1% of p99 variance attributable to experiment in the first 24 hours.
- Cost target: measured per-token cost delta must be within +/- 5% of predicted.
- Fallback bound: model variant fallback rate must not exceed 0.1% during canary.

Experiment lifecycle checklist:
1) Proposal and hypothesis
   - Document hypothesis (what change, why, expected delta on latency/cost).
   - Include experiment lead, reviewers, and owners in doc metadata.
   - Define success criteria in both statistical and operational terms.
2) Instrumentation and smoke tests (pre-merge)
   - Add telemetry points and expose counts/metrics as above.
   - Local microbench smoke runs must pass (no new failures).
   - Add unit tests for kernel selection edge-cases.
3) Synthetic benchmark / offline validation
   - Run microbench suite mirroring representative sequence-length distributions.
   - Produce delta report: p50/p95/p99, throughput, GPU occupancy, and token cost estimate.
   - Benchmarks Owner signs off on data quality.
4) Staging canary (internal traffic)
   - Deploy to isolated staging pool (10% of staging capacity).
   - Run the system for 24-72 hours with synthetic replay and limited real traffic.
   - Monitor the experiment dashboard and Slack alert channel.
   - Abort if: error rate increases > 0.05 absolute, fallback rate > 0.2%, or p99 increases > 50ms above baseline.
5) Production canary (small customer/region)
   - Gradually enable 1% -> 5% -> 20% traffic over 6–24 hours with verification at each step.
   - Post-step checks: run automated smoke suite, compare telemetry windows (30min, 3h, 24h).
   - Require manual approval from SRE Reviewer before entering >20% traffic.
6) Full rollout and post-rollout validation
   - Proceed if all gating checks pass for 24h at 20% traffic.
   - Monitor error budget burn, cost prediction, and fallback behaviors for 72h.
   - Complete rollout only after Benchmarks Owner and SRE Reviewer sign-off.
7) Postmortem and learnings
   - Capture results in the experiment page: data, dashboards, replay tokens, and decision rationale.
   - If rollout fails, follow the rollback playbook (see section below).

Gating criteria (explicit):
- Safety gates (fail fast): request.error_rate increase > 0.05 absolute, p99 increase > 2x baseline for more than 10 minutes, queue_depth sustained increase > 3x baseline for 5 minutes.
- Quality gates (manual): fallbacks above target, increased hallucination rate on eval prompts (if applicable), or new error classes.
- Cost gates: per-token cost regression > +10% (auto pause) or > +5% requiring manual approval.

Rollback and mitigation steps (runbook):
Immediate actions (first 15 minutes):
1) Pause the experiment via feature-flag:  featurectl set kernel_experiment=false --env=prod --region=<region>
2) Route affected traffic to the previous model variant with fallback policy: set-route-priority --route=default --priority=stable
3) Notify SRE and Experiment Lead in #runtime-experiments and page runtime-oncall.
4) Capture full profiler snapshot and save to /artifacts/experiments/<id>/snapshot-<ts>.json
5) If GPU OOMs or watchdog trips observed, cordon nodes and escalate to infra (tag node with reason: experiment-rollback).

Post-rollback analysis (24–72 hours):
- Run reconstruction using captured traces and synthetic replay.
- Correlate kernel.exec_time spikes with dispatch.queue_depth and kvcache hit-rate.
- Produce a triage report: root cause, potential mitigations, and next steps.

Experiment types and recommended precautions:
- Kernel mapping changes (e.g., switching to fused attention kernel): low-latency risk; require synthetic replay with varied sequence-lengths and gating on p99.
- Scheduler policy changes (preemption thresholds, batch slicing): test in staging for queueing regressions. Use stress profiles with mixed-priority workloads.
- KV cache heuristics (eviction threshold, prefetch window): verify with long-running chat sessions and ensure session-affinity preserved.
- Quantization and mixed-precision rollouts: include correctness evaluation on unit prompt set and monitor token-level quality regressions.

Benchmarking and validation recipes (examples):
- Latency heatmap generation: replay 1M requests sampled from the last 7 days stratified by sequence length and model variant. Produce matrix: rows=seq_length_bins, cols=model_variants, cells=median/p99 latency.
- Cost-sensitivity sweep: run the same workload across model variants and quantization profiles, report per-token cost and normalized latency.
- Priority inversion stress test: create synthetic mix with 80% background low-priority requests and 20% high-priority short requests; measure high-priority p99 under kernel changes.

CLI examples and YAML manifests (for reproducibility):
- Feature flag example:
  {
    "flag": "kernel_experiment",
    "enabled": false,
    "scopes": ["staging", "canary-region-us-east-1"]
  }

- Canary rollout manifest (simplified):
  rollout: |
    - step: enable
      percent: 1
      wait: 30m
    - measure: latency_p99, error_rate
      threshold: {"p99_delta_ms": 20, "error_rate_delta": 0.005}
    - step: increase
      percent: 5
      wait: 2h

Data recording and artifacts to retain:
- Microbenchmark CSVs and raw traces (retain for 90 days).
- Profiler snapshots and GPU kernel timelines (retain for 365 days for variance analysis).
- Experiment ticket and final triage report (permanent).

Known issues and caveats (current):
- Intermittent kernel selection thrash: observed when multiple kernel hints exist for the same model/seq-length bin. Mitigation: add cooldown of 60s before switching kernel variant.
- Observability gaps for Private deployments: telemetry sampling rates are lower in some on-prem installs; include replay artifacts when operating in these environments.
- Quantized-execution correctness edge cases with long context windows (>16k): require guardrail tests and lower rollout percentage.

Runbook snippets for common alerts:
- Alert: kernel.exec_time.p99 spike
  1) Check dispatch.queue_depth and kvcache.hit_rate.
  2) If queue_depth elevated and kvcache hit_rate low, suspected warmup/eviction issue: trigger async kvcache prefetch for affected sessions.
  3) If dispatch backlog persists, enable emergency congestion-control: set-congestion-mode --level=throttle

- Alert: GPU occupancy drop with latency increase
  1) Validate kernel selection logs to see if a slower kernel was chosen.
  2) Roll back kernel selector or reduce concurrency on affected nodes.

Team wiki and experiment catalog guidance:
- Every experiment must have a short wiki page under /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/experiments/<experiment-id>. That page must include: hypothesis, bench reports, canary manifest, dashboards (links), artifact URIs, and final decision.
- Maintain an experiments index with metadata columns: id, title, owner, status, start_date, end_date, delta_p99_ms, delta_cost_pct, notes. Example CSV header: id,title,owner,status,start_date,end_date,delta_p99_ms,delta_cost_pct,notes

Release cadence and communication:
- Major kernel/scheduler changes should be communicated as part of the monthly runtime release notes with a short impact statement and links to the experiment pages.
- For high-impact internal rollouts, publish a pre-rollout note to #infra-announce with expected windows and rollback contact.

Appendix A: Example hypothesis (realistic)
- Hypothesis: Switching to fused-attention-v2 reduces p95 by 12% for sequence lengths 512-2048 with an expected per-token cost reduction of 6%, without increasing p99 by more than 10ms.
- Validation plan: microbench suite (3k synthetic samples across seq bins), staging canary 48h, production canary 5% for 24h.

Appendix B: Quick checklist (one-page)
- [ ] Hypothesis documented and reviewers assigned
- [ ] Telemetry instrumented and dashboard created
- [ ] Microbench reports attached
- [ ] Staging canary passed (24h)
- [ ] Production canary gates passed (30m, 3h, 24h)
- [ ] Post-rollout report published

Contacts and escalation
- Runtime Engineering: runtime@redwood.com (primary)
- Observability / Profiling: telemetry@redwood.com
- Benchmarks team: benchmarks@redwood.com
- Oncall rotation: see /confluence/eng-sre/oncall-rotations

References and related docs
- Runtime decision graph and observed behaviour catalog (internal page)
- Continuous runtime profiling strategy (profiling-playbook)
- Kernel telemetry annotation guidelines

Document history:
- 2026-01-15: Created by Evan Garcia
- 2026-02-02: Added synthetic stress tests section (Priya Kapoor)
- 2026-03-02: Finalized gating thresholds and included rollback CLI snippets (Lena Morris)

title: Runtime Adapter Playground: Authoring Kit, Telemetry Stubs, and Canary Templates
content:
Overview

This document describes the Runtime Adapter Playground Authoring Kit — a lightweight, reproducible developer experience for building, testing, and canarying SDK adapters and runtime integrations against Redwood’s local sandbox. The kit bundles:

- opinionated repo layout and templates for new adapters (HTTP, gRPC, and local shim).
- telemetry stub server and example event schemas so adapters emit stable contract telemetry.
- canary deployment templates and a short runbook for gradual rollout with automated rollback.
- troubleshooting checklist of top support issues and canonical fixes for adapter authors.

Goal and audience

- Goal: Reduce time-to-first-success for adapter authors (internal teams and third-party integrators) by providing a single, documented playground and set of templates that cover the most common failure modes.
- Audience: SDK engineers, integrator partners, and platform engineers validating runtime shims.

When to use this kit

- Authoring a new adapter to translate third-party model runtime APIs to Redwood’s runtime API.
- Adding telemetry to an existing adapter and validating it against the telemetry contract.
- Performing a canary rollout of an adapter bundle to Dedicated/Private deployments.

Contents of the kit

1) Repo layout (recommended)

- /adapter/ — adapter source (language-specific).
- /stubs/telemetry/ — telemetry stub server (node/python).
- /templates/ — canary manifests, CI examples, and example feature flags.
- /examples/local-run/ — docker-compose for local sandbox + adapter.
- /docs/ — quickstart and runbook snippets.

2) Telemetry contract (summary)

- Required events: adapter.start, adapter.request, adapter.response, adapter.error, adapter.metrics.snapshot
- Core fields (all events): request_id, timestamp_iso, adapter_id, adapter_version, env, host_id
- P95 latency metric is expected on adapter.response: latency_ms (number)

Example JSON event (adapter.response):

{
  "event_type": "adapter.response",
  "request_id": "req-1a2b3c",
  "timestamp_iso": "2027-01-10T15:32:12Z",
  "adapter_id": "llm-http-adapter-v1",
  "adapter_version": "0.3.0",
  "env": "local",
  "host_id": "vm-023",
  "status": "ok",
  "latency_ms": 42,
  "tokens_in": 32,
  "tokens_out": 96
}

3) Telemetry stub server (quickstart)

- Purpose: receive adapter events on a local endpoint and validate schema, sample rate, and required fields.
- Start (node example):

$ cd stubs/telemetry && npm ci && node server.js

- Default listen port: 9911 (configurable via TELEMETRY_PORT). The stub returns 200 for valid events, 400 for schema violations, and logs to stdout.

4) Local sandbox run (docker-compose)

Steps to run the playground locally:

1. Clone kit: git clone git@internal:redwood/runtime-adapter-playground.git
2. Start the telemetry stub and local sandbox:

$ docker-compose -f examples/local-run/docker-compose.yml up --build

3. Build adapter image (example for Go adapter):

$ docker build -t rwd/adapter-go:dev ./adapter/go

4. Attach adapter to sandbox (local manifest):

$ kubectl apply -f templates/local/adapter-binding.yaml --context=kind-local

5. Exercise the adapter with the included curl script: templates/local/requests.sh

5) Canary rollout template and steps

We provide a Kubernetes manifest and a short CI snippet for a staged canary. The template uses traffic-splitting via ingress weights and automated monitoring checks that gate promotion.

Canary SLOs (suggested thresholds):

- Latency: p95 < 250ms (adapter.response.latency_ms)
- Error rate: < 0.5% (adapter.error events / total requests)
- Observability: telemetry ingestion success > 99% (stub acceptance rate)

Canary promotion sequence (numbered):

1. Push adapter image and tag: rwd/adapter-<name>:canary-<sha>
2. Create canary Deployment with 10% traffic weight.
3. Monitor for 30 minutes with automated checks: p95, error rate, and telemetry ingestion.
4. If checks pass, increase to 50% for 15 minutes.
5. Final promotion to 100% or rollback if any check is violated.

Automated gate example (Jenkins/GitHub Actions snippet):

- run: ./scripts/check-canary.sh --endpoint https://canary.local --window 30m --p95 250 --error-rate 0.005

check-canary.sh performs:

- queries telemetry stub for adapter.response/p95 and adapter.error counts
- computes failure conditions and returns non-zero exit to fail CI

6) Common adapter authoring patterns and templates

- Idempotent request handling: adapters must include request_id handling and be safe for retries. Template provides a small Redis-backed dedupe helper.
- Graceful partial failures: adapters should emit adapter.error with error_code and fallback_reason and return a graceful 200 with a structured error payload to the caller when downstream model fails.
- KV cache hints: include recommended cache TTLs in adapter metadata to allow the runtime to leverage prefix caching.

7) Troubleshooting and canonical fixes (top support issues)

A. Missing API key or 401 from Redwood host
- Symptom: adapter.request receives 401 from runtime or requests fail immediately.
- Canonical fix: Validate environment variable REDWOOD_API_KEY is present in adapter pod and the adapter signs requests using the standard header Authorization: Bearer <key>. Use the included diagnostic script: templates/local/check-credentials.sh

B. Telemetry sample rate lower than expected
- Symptom: production monitoring shows ingestion < 90% of events.
- Canonical fix: Ensure telemetry client is not dropping events on full buffers. Increase telemetry queue size (TELEMETRY_QSIZE env var) and switch to async flush on shutdown. See stubs/telemetry/README.md for recommended values (qsize=500, flush_interval_ms=250).

C. Streaming truncation or mis-ordered chunks
- Symptom: Client observes partial streaming responses or chunks arrive out of order.
- Canonical fix: Confirm adapter is using connection: keep-alive and sets chunked transfer semantics per the streaming guideline (templates/streaming/README). Add sequence_id to adapter.response events and validate order in the telemetry stub.

D. Elevated p95 latency after canary promotion
- Symptom: p95 jumps beyond threshold after migration to new adapter.
- Canonical fix: Rollback using canary manifest, capture pprof/trace from the adapter instance, and validate kernel scheduling and batch sizing. The troubleshooting checklist includes commands to capture CPU, GPU, and network stats: 

$ kubectl exec -it <pod> -- /bin/sh -c "curl -s localhost:6060/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=30 > /tmp/profile.pprof"

8) Example adapter-binding manifest (local)

| Field | Example | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| adapter_id | llm-http-adapter-v1 | unique id used in telemetry.adapter_id |
| health_check_path | /healthz | runtime uses for liveness probing |
| max_concurrency | 8 | cap per instance, used by autoscaler |
| telemetry_endpoint | http://host.docker.internal:9911/events | local stub address |

9) Access and ownership

- Kit owner: eng-developer-experience (doc); runtime-adapter-team (code).
- Escalation: open an issue in the runtime-adapter-playground repo and tag @runtime-adapter-team and @devx-oncall. For production incidents contact eng-sre via PagerDuty.

10) Appendices

A. Quick CLI snippets

- Build and push canary image:
$ docker build -t rwd/adapter-example:canary-$(git rev-parse --short HEAD) .
$ docker push rwd/adapter-example:canary-$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)

- Apply canary manifest (k8s):
$ kubectl apply -f templates/canary/adapter-canary.yaml

B. YAML example for canary scaling (templates/canary/adapter-canary.yaml):

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: adapter-example-canary
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: adapter-example
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: adapter-example
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: adapter
        image: rwd/adapter-example:canary-abc123
        env:
        - name: REDWOOD_API_KEY
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: redwood-credentials
              key: api_key

C. Contacts and runbook links

- Runtime Adapter team Slack: #rwd-runtime-adapter
- DevX docs: /confluence/eng-developer-experience/docs-site/sdk-local-proxy-sandbox-strategies-2026.json
- Incident runbook: /confluence/eng-oncall-and-incident-response/runbooks/adapter-incident-runbook

If you are contributing templates or fixes, open a PR against the runtime-adapter-playground repo and add one of the reviewers listed at the top. The templates are designed to be minimal but extensible; include a short integration test in /examples/local-run/tests that exercises both telemetry emission and the runtime request path.

title: Kernel continuity and state reconciliation manual
content:
Purpose:
This manual describes the operational controls, instrumentation, and step-by-step runbooks for maintaining kernel continuity across live kernel handoffs, preemptive evictions, and cross-node failover. It focuses on deterministic state reconciliation of KV caches, token-level prefix state, and quantization metadata to avoid model drift, duplicate generation, or silent correctness regressions during runtime transitions.

Scope and audience:
- Audience: runtime oncall, runtime engineers, release engineers, and SREs responsible for kernel rollouts and incident recovery.
- Scope: live kernel swaps, preemption and eviction events, cross-NUMA/node handoffs, and scripted rollback scenarios. Does NOT cover model-level content validation or developer sandbox experiments (see related pages).

Goals and SLO constraints:
- Preserve deterministic generation for pinned sessions where possible: session_replay_agreement >= 99.9% within 2s of handoff under nominal load.
- Maintain 99th percentile latency SLOs within configured degradation targets (see table "Operational thresholds").
- Avoid silent semantic regressions: any handoff that changes generation tokens for >0.1% of validation prompt set must trigger an audit and canary rollback.

Definitions (quick):
- Kernel instance: runtime binary + kernel plugins that schedule and execute attention kernels.
- KV state: Key/value caches (kv_cache) containing past key/value tensors and session metadata used to accelerate autoregressive generation.
- Continuity window: time range where in-flight requests must be consistent across old and new kernel variants.
- Deterministic reconcile: process that ensures two kernel instances produce identical logits for an identical prefix.

Architecture overview (text diagram):
- Ingress -> Request classification (priority, session pin) -> Kernel router -> Kernel pool (GPU shards)
  - Each kernel has local KV cache + shared persistent session index (Session Index backed by Redis/etcd).
  - Handoff path: kernel A (source) -> cooperative drain -> state snapshot -> kernel B (target) -> verify -> commit -> update router.

Key invariants to enforce:
1) Snapshot completeness: all active KV ranges referenced by sessions must be included in the snapshot (no partial references).
2) Sequence monotonicity: session token counters must not decrease across handoffs.
3) Quantization metadata fidelity: quantization scale/zero-point and per-layer layout metadata must accompany tensors.
4) Observability trace IDs must be preserved across Gs (gateway) to kernel transitions.

Operational thresholds (table):
- SLO / Threshold / Action
- session_replay_agreement >= 99.9% / auto-verify pass -> commit handoff
- session_replay_agreement 95%-99.9% / mark as degraded, produce regression diff report, require engineer signoff
- session_replay_agreement < 95% / automatic rollback and incident page creation
- handoff-duration-target < 2s (median) / if > 5s then fail fast to fallback pool

Instrumentation and required metrics (minimum):
- kernel.handoff.attempts (counter)
- kernel.handoff.success (counter)
- kernel.handoff.duration_ms (histogram)
- kernel.kv.snapshot_size_bytes (gauge)
- kernel.kv.missing_keys_during_replay (counter)
- kernel.replay.agreement_pct (gauge per session sampled)
- kernel.quant.meta_mismatch (counter)
- trace.session_id preserved (boolean per handoff)

Observability queries (examples):
- Reconciliation failure rate last 1h:
  - PromQL: sum(increase(kernel_replay_agreement_failures_total[1h])) / sum(increase(kernel.handoff.attempts[1h]))
- Sessions with missing KV keys:
  - PromQL: sum by (kernel_id) (increase(kernel_kv_missing_keys_during_replay_total[15m]))
- Latency impact of handoff:
  - LogQL: | json | handoff=false OR handoff=true | compare percentile(latency_ms,95, kernel)

Pre-check checklist (automated gating before any kernel rollout):
1) Canary cohort traffic mirror is configured (mirror ratio >= 0.02).
2) Snapshot size distribution within historical 95th percentile for target model.
3) Quantization profile compatibility matrix verified for target kernel version.
4) Observability sampling and tracing propagated for all canary requests.
5) Canary health probes (see health probe list) passing for 15 minutes.

Health probes (example list):
- probe /healthz/kernel -> returns OK + kernel_version + kv_snapshot_epoch
- probe /healthz/replay -> runs deterministic replay on a synthetic prefix corpus and returns agreement pct
- probe /metrics -> Prometheus scrape endpoint

Runbook: graceful kernel handoff (cooperative) - for SRE / oncall
1) Intent: move sessions from kernel A to kernel B for planned upgrade or maintenance.
2) Preconditions: B has been validated in staging, gating pre-checks passed, canary mirror warm.
3) Steps:
   a) Mark kernel A as "draining" in router config: set routing.weight(A)=0 over 30s window; router will forward new requests to other kernels while allowing in-flight to finish.
   b) Trigger snapshot: POST /internal/kernel/{A}/snapshot -> returns snapshot_id.
   c) Verify snapshot completeness: GET /internal/snapshots/{snapshot_id}/verify -> expect {"missing_keys":0, "meta_ok":true}. If missing_keys > 0 go to troubleshooting below.
   d) Transfer snapshot to B: POST /internal/kernel/{B}/ingest-snapshot {"snapshot_id": "..."}.
   e) Run local deterministic replay on B for sample prefixes: POST /internal/kernel/{B}/replay-sample -> returns agreement scores per prefix.
   f) If agreement >= 99.9% for sampled prefixes, mark commit: POST /internal/kernel/{B}/commit-handoff {"snapshot_id":"..."}. Router update: atomically swap session index pointers to B.
   g) Monitor for 15 minutes: replay.agreement_pct, kv.missing_keys, 95/99 latency. If any threshold violated, trigger rollback (see rollback flow).
4) Post-mortem: record snapshot_id, durations, sample diffs, and link to incident tracker.

Runbook: emergency handoff (preemptive eviction) - for critical capacity events
1) Intent: evict and migrate sessions from an overloaded node when cooperative drain not possible.
2) Preconditions: immediate capacity pressure, automated graceful drain failed or impossible.
3) Steps:
   a) Select victim kernel(s) using eviction scorer (eviction_score > configured_threshold).
   b) Create partial snapshot including most-recently-used KV ranges prioritized by active sessions. Limit snapshot duration to 500ms to bound tail latency.
   c) Ingest into fallback kernel pool (a pool running conservative kernels that accept smaller snapshots).
   d) Run targeted replay on highest-priority sessions only (top 1% traffic by token-volume).
   e) If replay agreement < 95% for any top-priority session: mark for immediate re-run with full snapshot and escalate to runtime-engineer.

Rollback flow (automated and manual)
- Automated rollback trigger: replay.agreement_pct < 95% OR kv.missing_keys_during_replay > 10 for any affected session cohort. System will:
  1) Re-point router session index back to source kernel snapshot_id (atomic pointer swap).
  2) Mark target kernel instance as failed and add to quarantine list.
  3) Create incident ticket and populate required fields (snapshot ids, sample diffs, metric deltas).
- Manual rollback requires engineer signoff and is used when automated rollback cannot be executed (e.g., persistent index corruption).

Troubleshooting matrix (common failure modes):
- Symptom: missing keys during replay
  - Likely causes: partial snapshot, metadata mismatch (namespace/versioning), or RPC truncation.
  - First actions: examine snapshot verification output, check transport logs for truncated payloads (s3/redis clamp errors), check kernel.kv.snapshot_size_bytes variance.

- Symptom: quantization metadata mismatch -> scaled logits differ
  - Likely causes: kernel compiled with different quantization layout, per-layer quantization rounding change, or precision-promote in kernel config.
  - First actions: compare kernel.build_metadata.quant_profile between A and B. If mismatch, abort commit and roll back.

- Symptom: replay agreement slightly degraded (99.0-99.8%)
  - Likely causes: non-determinism in floating ops at fringe layers, timing differences in fused kernels, or sampling variance in test corpus.
  - First actions: increase sample size for replay check, run deterministic microbench on fused kernel path, and if persistent, capture kernel traces for triage.

Reconciliation algorithm (recommended pseudocode):
```python
# high level pseudocode for deterministic reconciliation
def reconcile_snapshot(source_snapshot, target_kernel):
    # 1. validate metadata
    assert source_snapshot.model_id == target_kernel.model_id
    assert source_snapshot.quant_profile == target_kernel.quant_profile

    # 2. stream keys and apply in deterministic order (lexicographic by session_id, then seq_num)
    for session_id in sorted(source_snapshot.sessions):
        for ev in sorted(source_snapshot.sessions[session_id].events, key=lambda e: e.seq_num):
            target_kernel.apply_event(session_id, ev)

    # 3. run sampled deterministic forward passes and compare logits
    diffs = []
    for prefix in sample_prefixes():
        out_src = source_snapshot.simulate_forward(prefix)
        out_tgt = target_kernel.simulate_forward(prefix)
        diffs.append(cosine_similarity(out_src.logits, out_tgt.logits))

    return aggregate_agreement(diffs)
```
Upgrade and rollout policy (recommended):
1) Canary (1% mirrored traffic, 30m) -> 2) Extended canary (5% mirrored traffic, 2h) -> 3) Progressive roll (20% -> 50% -> 100%) with health gates at each step.
2) Automatic rollback gates for any step if replay.agreement drops below configured threshold for the cohort.
3) All rollouts must include a replay corpus and the snapshot archive stored with provenance tags.

Developer guidance for kernel authors (short):
- Maintain backward-compatible quant_profile changes; add feature flags and opt-in toggles for new fused kernels.
- Implement deterministic seeds for any non-deterministic code paths used during snapshot application and replay.
- Provide a unit-test harness: unit_replay_suite that can be executed with "./tools/unit_replay_suite --snapshot <id> --kernel <target>".

Post-incident checklist and artifacts required:
- snapshot_id(s), sample prefixes used, replay diffs, kernel build hashes for source and target, Prometheus metric snapshots (15m pre/post), traces (OTel) correlated to trace.session_id, and incident timeline.

Appendix A: Example CLI snippets
- Trigger snapshot (operator):
  curl -X POST http://runtime-internal/api/v1/kernel/alpha/snapshot -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' -d '{"reason":"canary-rollout-2026-02"}'
- Verify snapshot:
  curl http://runtime-internal/api/v1/snapshots/<id>/verify | jq
- Ingest snapshot into target:
  curl -X POST http://runtime-internal/api/v1/kernel/beta/ingest-snapshot -d '{"snapshot_id":"<id>"}'

Appendix B: Minimum config example (YAML)
- gate:
    replay_sample_size: 50  # number of prefixes to check per snapshot
    min_agreement_pct: 99.9
    emergency_min_agreement_pct: 95.0
- snapshot:
    max_transfer_bytes: 1_200_000_000
    transfer_timeout_ms: 5000
- routing:
    graceful_drain_window_s: 30
    fallback_pool: "conservative-pool-v1"

Contacts and ownership:
- Primary owner: Priya Ranganathan (runtime infra)
- Secondary: Elliot Brooks (serving runtime)
- Pager: runtime-oncall@redwood.ai (follow escalation playbook)

Change log (short):
- 2025-06-10: Initial draft and baseline procedures created by Priya Ranganathan.
- 2025-11-02: Added emergency handoff flow and automated rollback gating.
- 2026-02-15: Updated instrumentation list and minimum config with transfer limits after field incidents.

Related reading and links:
- Execution stitching and fallback orchestration (architecture)
- Seamless model swap and KV consistency guide
- Quantization rollout safety playbook

End of document

title: Adaptive Fidelity Decision Log & Playbook
content:
Summary:
This document captures the decision rationale and operational playbook for adaptive-fidelity behavior in the serving runtime. It is intended for oncall engineers, runtime operators, and product owners who must make or review changes to fidelity-orchestration policies (quality <-> cost <-> latency tradeoffs) and eviction/topology actions during normal operations and incidents.

Why this exists:
- Adaptive fidelity (also known as fidelity orchestration) is the runtime component that reduces model or execution fidelity to preserve SLOs (latency/availability) during capacity pressure or incident scenarios.
- Without a documented decision trail and safe runbook, fidelity changes risk causing silent quality regressions or customer-impacting rollbacks.

Scope and systems referenced:
- fidelity-orchestrator (service): policy engine that issues fidelity-advice (quantize, half-precision, variant-switch, reduce-beam) and hard actions (route-to-variant, throttle, shed).
- runtime-orchestrator: accepts fidelity advice and performs routing/eviction as well as kv-cache coordination.
- scheduler-gw / kernel-shepherd: component responsible for admission control and kernel selection.
- eviction-operator: cross-node component that enacts shard-level evictions and reports consistency fences.

Decision log (chronological highlights):
1) 2025-07-21 — Adopted a two-tier fidelity policy: advisory (soft) and enforced (hard). Rationale: allow safe observability and gradual rollouts. Owner: Runtimes team.
2) 2025-11-03 — Introduced "fidelity-budget" per tenant to bound economic impact during long incidents. Rationale: protect high-value tenants from repeated large-quality shifts. Owner: Finance+Runtimes.
3) 2026-01-10 — Default policy change: prefer model-variant-switch to kernel-level quantization for burst-induced latency SLO preservation. Rationale: empirical regressions in long-form generation when live-quantizing. Owner: Applied ML + Runtimes.

Operational guarantees and SLO mappings:
- Safety boundary: any enforced fidelity change must be logged and include a validated rollback path (automated or documented manual steps).
- Quality SLO: per-model baseline eval_score (internal eval harness metric). Hard guard: enforced fidelity must not reduce eval_score by > 3 percentage points without explicit stakeholder signoff.
- Latency SLOs (examples):
  - short-response 95th pctl <= 120ms (route preference: low-latency variants)
  - completion 99th pctl <= 1s for <512 tokens on dedicated pools
- Cost guardrails: fidelity-budget throttle at 30% monthly overspend triggers notification and limits further enforced fidelity changes.

Playbook: when fidelity-orchestrator recommends a change (automated or manual)
1) Triage and context (owner: oncall/runtime):
   - Confirm trigger: kernel queue length > Q_HIGH (default 4x baseline) OR node-eviction-in-flight OR NVTHERMAL alert.
   - Pull recent traces: runtime-orchestrator/traces/<request_id> and fidelity-orchestrator/decision/<decision_id>.
   - Check related KPIs: 95p latency, kernel-queue-depth, model-kvcache-hit-rate.

2) Advisory mode (first 10 minutes):
   - Apply advisory-only advice in fidelity-orchestrator (no enforced routing).
   - Create a short-lived traffic mirror (shadow) to the advised variant for perf/quality verification. Use CLI:
     rdxctl fidelity advise --tenant $TENANT --policy burst-preserve-latency --mode advisory --duration 10m
   - Observe: latency, token-cost delta, eval-score proxy (short sample prompt set).

3) Enforce-only after verification (manual or automated conditional):
   - If advisory mirror shows latency improvement >= 30% on key cohorts and eval-score proxy degradation <= 1.5 points, proceed to a staged enforce:
     a) Canary group (1% traffic) for 5 minutes
     b) Gradual ramp: 1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% over 30 minutes if KPIs healthy
   - rdxctl fidelity enforce --tenant $TENANT --policy model-variant-switch --canary 1% --rollback-window 30m

4) Rollback and emergency revert:
   - Automated rollback conditions (runtime-orchestrator): 95p latency increases by > 20% vs baseline OR error-rate spike > 5x
   - Manual rollback steps (oncall):
     1. rdxctl fidelity rollback --decision <decision_id>
     2. Validate KV-consistency: rdxctl kvcache check --shard <shard_id> and wait for fence=clear (max 2m).
     3. If kvcache fence fails, escalate to eviction-operator owners and follow "KV recovery and rehydration" runbook (link below).

Safety checklist before any enforced policy is applied:
- Owner and reviewer listed in fidelity decision record (email + ticket).
- Corresponding canary health dashboards created: latency, error-rate, cost-per-token, eval-proxy.
- Rollback automation verified and tested in the last 72h (smoke).

Runbook: emergency fidelity hard-stop (when incident requires immediate preservation of availability)
- Trigger: simultaneous NVTHERMAL + kernel-watchdog + 95p latency > SLO and burst length > 10s.
- Action (immediate):
  1) Oncall executes: rdxctl fidelity emergency-hold --global --reason "thermal+queue"
  2) runtime-orchestrator will immediately switch affected routing to pre-approved low-fidelity variants (predefined set) and disable new long-running kernels.
  3) Notify impacted tenants via incident channel and open incident ticket with tag runtime-fidelity-emergency.
  4) Begin 15-minute observation window. If stability returns, begin staged re-enable per "Playbook" above.

KV cache and eviction coordination notes:
- Eviction ordering: eviction-operator must ensure kvcache fence idempotency: eviction-operator -> runtime-orchestrator: POST /eviction/start -> include fence_id -> runtime-orchestrator acknowledges -> proceed.
- If an enforced fidelity change requires variant swap with incompatible KV layout, follow this sequence:
  1) Advisory mirror (no kvcache writes)
  2) Quiesce writes to kvcache shard: rdxctl kvcache drain --shard <id> --timeout 60s
  3) Perform variant swap and warmstart new kernels
  4) Rehydrate cache via background replay (rate-limited)

Example policy config (JSON snippet to be used in fidelity-orchestrator):
{
  "policy_id": "burst-preserve-latency-v2",
  "triggers": {
    "kernel_queue_multiplier": 3.5,
    "node_cpu_usage": 0.85
  },
  "actions": [
    {
      "type": "model_variant_switch",
      "variants": ["variant-latency-1", "variant-latency-2"],
      "scope": "tenant"
    }
  ],
  "guards": {
    "max_eval_drop_pct": 3.0,
    "cost_budget_pct": 30
  }
}

Smoke tests (pre-deploy validation):
- Synthetic microburst: simulate 10s 10x traffic spike against staging clusters with fidelity-budget=unbounded and ensure auto-advisory path runs without errors.
- KV compatibility test: run variant-swap + cache-drain + rehydrate sequence in a local 3-node staging cluster. Verify no dropped requests and latency within 2x baseline.
- Canary rollback test: force an error-rate spike and verify the automated rollback completes within the configured rollback-window.

Dashboards and alerts (minimum set):
- fidelity-orchestrator/decisions (counts by type, avg latency benefit, avg eval-proxy delta)
- runtime-orchestrator/95p-latency-by-tenant (alert: > SLO*1.25 for 5m)
- kvcache/eviction-fence-failures (alert: >0 in 10m)
- scheduler-gw/kernel-queue-depth (warning: > baseline*3)

Ownership and escalation:
- Primary owners: Runtimes team (oncall rotation: runtimes-oncall@redwood.com).
- Secondary owners: Applied ML (quality regressions), SRE (eviction/cluster stability), Finance (fidelity budget overrun).
- Escalation path: oncall -> service-owner -> SRE lead -> VP Eng. Use incident tag: runtime-fidelity.

Post-incident analysis and required artifacts:
- Decision record update: add reason, traces, metrics and signed-off owner within 48 hours.
- Eval-run: run the canonical eval set for affected models (mark baseline vs post-change) and store results in /evals/fidelity/<decision_id>.
- Experiment: if an enforced policy was used, create an experiment ticket to test alternate mitigations (e.g., latency-aware batching) within 14 days.

Appendix A — Quick CLI cheatsheet:
- Advise (advisory-only): rdxctl fidelity advise --tenant $TENANT --policy $POLICY --duration 10m
- Enforce with canary: rdxctl fidelity enforce --tenant $TENANT --policy $POLICY --canary 1% --rollback-window 30m
- Rollback: rdxctl fidelity rollback --decision <decision_id>
- KV drain: rdxctl kvcache drain --shard <shard_id> --timeout 60s

Appendix B — Example staging test matrix (table):
- Test | Goal | Pass criteria
- Synthetic microburst | ensure advisory path triggers | advisory decision recorded, no errors
- Variant-swap + rehydrate | KV compatibility during swap | no requests dropped, cache warm within 10m
- Canary rollback | verify rollback automation | rollback completes within 2x rollback-window

References:
- Runtime decision delegation patterns: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/runtime-decision-delegation-and-observer-patterns-2026
- KV cache lifecycle: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/session-lifecycle-kvcache-consistency-guidelines-2024
- Fidelity containment experiment notes: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/fidelity-containment-and-cost-feedback-playbook-2026

Last reviewed: 2026-03-10 by Jonah Kim and María Torres.

title: Serving runtime hotfix procedure (Hosted API)
content:
# Overview
This runbook describes how to execute an emergency hotfix or emergency rollback for the *Hosted API serving runtime*. It is optimized for speed while preserving safety (blast-radius control, verification, rollback readiness).

**Applies to:** runtime pods (model-server), runtime scheduler, runtime sidecars, runtime config/feature flags, and kernel selection/quant profiles when delivered via runtime image/config.

# Preconditions
- If there is active customer impact: declare an incident (Sev1/Sev2) and use the incident channel for coordination.
- Confirm EPC approvals per the Emergency production change policy.
- Identify the rollout target: region(s), tier(s), and route(s). Default is: one region canary first.

# Required dashboards (open before changing anything)
- Hosted API: request success rate (2xx/4xx/5xx) by region
- Runtime: p50/p95/p99 end-to-end latency and time-to-first-token
- Runtime: crash-loop rate / container restarts
- GPU fleet: utilization + queue depth
- Error taxonomy: top runtime error codes (oom, kv_cache_eviction, stream_disconnect)

# Decision tree (hotfix vs rollback vs mitigation)
1. If regression started after a known deploy and rollback is available: **rollback** is preferred.
2. If rollback is not available or doesnt address the issue: apply a **mitigation** (feature flag off, reduce max tokens, adjust batch limits).
3. If issue is correctness/security: prefer **hotfix** with minimal diff and targeted rollout.

# Step-by-step: emergency rollback
1. Identify last known good runtime version (tag) from: release notes, deploy history, or the incident timeline.
2. Validate rollback artifacts exist: image tag present in registry and deployment tool can reference it.
3. Roll back in this order:
   1) One canary cell in us-east
   2) Full us-east
   3) One canary cell in eu-west
   4) Full eu-west
4. Verification after each step (must pass before proceeding):
   - 5xx rate returns to baseline
   - p95 latency improves or is flat (no >10% regression)
   - restarts trending down
   - no new error signature dominates
5. Post in incident channel: what changed, where, and observed effect.

# Step-by-step: emergency hotfix
1. Reduce scope: minimal code/config change that addresses the issue. Avoid refactors.
2. Build + publish hotfix artifact per Release Engineering checklist (emergency path).
3. Deploy sequence:
   - Canary: 1 cell / 1 region / 10 minutes minimum observation
   - Expand: 25% of region
   - Expand: 100% of region
   - Repeat for next region
4. Monitoring gates (stop/rollback if any occurs):
   - error rate +0.3% absolute sustained for 5 minutes
   - p95 latency +15% sustained for 10 minutes
   - restart rate doubles for 10 minutes
   - GPU OOM events increase >20%
5. Record the following in the EPC record: version/tag, flags changed, cells/regions impacted, approvals, and verification evidence.

# Common mitigations (preferable to code changes when possible)
- Disable experimental scheduler features: `RW_SCHED_EXPERIMENTAL=0`
- Reduce max batch tokens: `RW_BATCH_MAX_TOKENS`
- Reduce max concurrent streams per pod
- Force conservative kernel selection (turn off fused attention for impacted arch)
- Temporarily lower max output tokens for affected routes

# Rollback triggers (hard)
Immediately rollback if any of the following are observed and attributed to the change:
- elevated 5xx correlated with rollout expansion
- widespread stream disconnects increase
- crash-loop / OOM increases
- customer escalations spike tied to the rollout region

# Customer comms reminders
- If the mitigation is visible (rate limits, reduced max tokens), coordinate with Support/CS and post status update when required.
- Avoid promising exact recovery times; provide next update cadence.

# Appendix: What to link in the incident timeline
- GitHub PR + merge SHA (or rollback tag)
- Deploy command / job link
- Dashboards used for verification

title: Runtime Experimentation: Safety, Isolation, and Rollback Runbook
content:
Summary
-------
This runbook defines the safety, isolation, rollout, and rollback procedures for running experiments that touch the serving runtime surface: kernel changes, scheduler policy updates, quantization rollouts, and affinity/topology experiments. It is intended for runtime engineers, SREs, and experiment owners who run controlled experiments against live traffic.

Purpose and scope
-----------------
- Purpose: limit blast radius, provide deterministic rollback, and ensure experiment telemetry is sufficient to detect regressions to latency, error rate, and fidelity.
- Scope: changes to kernel selection, scheduling policy, K/V cache heuristics, admission controller parameters, runtime flags that alter execution fidelity.
- Exclusions: application-layer prompt tuning, customer prompt datasets, or non-runtime model artifacts (see product docs).

Owner and escalation
--------------------
- Runbook owner: Runtime Experiments Guild (oncall: runtime-experiments@redwood).
- Primary contacts: Priya Nambiar (runtime experiments lead), Ethan Brooks (SRE lead).
- Pager escalation: follow standard eng-sre incident process; if experiment causes SLA degradation escalate to Eng SRE oncall.

When to use this runbook
------------------------
Use this runbook for any runtime change that could impact per-token latency, tail latency, or model fidelity in production. Examples:
1) Kernel hint changes or new kernel rollout.
2) Scheduler credit/accounting policy adjustments.
3) Enabling a new prefetch/prefill strategy for KV cache.
4) Introducing a quantized-op fallback path.

Pre-flight checklist (must-pass before injecting traffic)
--------------------------------------------------------
1) Approval: experiment approved by a runtime owner and an SRE reviewer. Add approval comment to the experiment ticket.
2) Benchmarks: local and canary synthetic benchmarks executed; baseline and candidate run data attached to ticket.
3) Canary resources: dedicated canary pool provisioned (min 2 nodes/GPUs) and network isolation validated.
4) Observable hooks: dashboards, alerts, and traces created and reviewed. See Observability configuration section below.
5) Abort signals: a named alert and a quickstop playbook are configured (alerts must map to concrete thresholds).
6) Safety timeout: automatic experiment pause set to 60 minutes if manual approval not received.

Isolation matrix (traffic & environment)
---------------------------------------
| Experiment Type | Isolation step | Traffic fraction | Notes |
|-----------------|----------------|------------------|-------|
| Kernel rollout | Canary pool w/affinity | 1-5% | Ensure canary nodes are not used by customer-critical tenants |
| Scheduler policy | Simulated shadow + 0.5% live | 0.5-2% | Use shadow routing first then small live sample |
| KV cache heuristic | Shadow + canary | 1% | Measure hit/miss and warmup behavior |
| Quantized fallback | Offline validation + 0.5% | 0.5% | Validate fidelity using held-out prompts |

Observability configuration (required)
------------------------------------
- Dashboards: create or update a dashboard with the following panels: P50/P95/P99 latency, per-request kernel selection distribution, kernel queue depth, kernel preemption rate, KV cache hit rate, error rate (5xx + internal errors), model output fidelity metrics if applicable.
- Alerts (examples):
  - runtime.latency.p99 > 150ms over 5m for canary -> Severity: critical; automatic pause.
  - runtime.error.rate > 0.5% over 5m -> Severity: critical; automatic pause.
  - kernel.preemptions.per_min > 20 on any GPU -> Severity: warning.
  - kvcache.miss_rate.delta > 10pp vs baseline -> Severity: warning.
- Tracing: Ensure request traces sample rate >= 1% for experiment cohort and include kernel selection and scheduler decision tags.
- Logs: Enable DEBUG-level kernel-selection logs for canary nodes for the duration of the experiment (rotated out after collection).

Telemetry thresholds and automated stop conditions
--------------------------------------------------
- Hard stop (immediate rollback):
  - p99 latency increase > 40% relative to baseline for 5m window.
  - Total error rate > 1% for 5m.
  - Model fidelity regression: automatic detection based on eval prompts showing > 5% drop in correctness/score.
- Soft stop (pause and investigate):
  - p99 latency increase between 20% and 40% for 10m.
  - Error rate between 0.5% and 1% for 10m.
  - kvcache.miss_rate delta > 7pp.

Canary rollout sequence (recommended)
-----------------------------------
1) Offline lab validation: run candidate kernels or policy in lab with replay corpus. Record microbenchmarks and end-to-end latency traces.
2) Shadow experiment: enable shadow routing for 1–2 hours at production concurrency; collect traces and compare decisions.
3) Tiny live canary: route 0.5–1% live traffic to canary pool for 30–60 minutes. Check thresholds.
4) Small ramp: increase to 5% over 1–2 hours if metrics stable.
5) Progressive ramp: 5% -> 25% -> 50% over multiple hours/days with manual gates between steps.
6) Full rollout: only after SRE signoff and 48h stable at 50%+.

Emergency rollback procedure (immediate actions)
------------------------------------------------
1) Hit hard-stop alert.
2) Execute immediate pause: set routing rule to revert canary/cohort to baseline model/kernels. Example command for routing service: 

```
# Revert canary cohort by name
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $ROUTE_API_TOKEN" \
  -d '{"cohort":"canary-123","action":"revert"}' \
  https://routing.internal.redwood/v1/cohorts/revert
```

3) Scale down canary pool to zero or detach nodes from serving plane. Example k8s label patch: 

```
kubectl label node gpu-canary-01 experiment=false --overwrite
kubectl cordon gpu-canary-01
kubectl drain gpu-canary-01 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data
```

4) Notify oncall, SRE, and experiment owner via standard incident channel. Create incident ticket referencing experiment.
5) Preserve artifacts: collect traces, kernel logs, and profile dumps and attach to the incident.

Post-incident triage and artifact collection
-------------------------------------------
- Required artifacts to attach to postmortem:
  - Full dashboard snapshots for experiment window (timestamps).
  - Traces with kernel selection tags and sampled request payloads (redact PII).
  - Kernel profiles (nvprof/metrics) and occupancy reports.
  - Scheduler logs and admission controller events.
  - Repro corpus and steps used for offline replay.

Minimum artifact retention: keep all experiment-related artifacts for 90 days in the runtime experiments S3 bucket.

Observability onboarding template (checklist)
-------------------------------------------
- Panels to create: latency(p50/95/99), error rates per route, kernel-selection histogram, queue depth heatmap, per-GPU temperature and throttling, KV cache hit/miss and warmup curve.
- Alerts to wire: p99 latency, error rate, preemption spike, cache-miss delta.
- Traces: 1% sample for production, 5% for canary cohort.

Data privacy and compliance
--------------------------
- Do not store raw customer prompts or outputs in experiment buckets unless explicitly approved. Use anonymized or synthetic corpora for fidelity checks.
- If collecting traces that include request text, apply the redaction pipeline before long-term storage.

Troubleshooting common failure modes
----------------------------------
- Symptom: sudden p99 spike with no error-rate increase. Likely cause: kernel queueing or preemption.
  - Action: check kernel.queue_depth and kernel.preemptions. Reduce admission credits for the cohort.
- Symptom: fidelity regression on quantized path.
  - Action: enable shadow fallback to float path for the failing requests and collect diffs for top 50 prompts by frequency.
- Symptom: KV cache warmup causing high tail latency during rollout.
  - Action: increase warmup traffic, use traffic shaping or temporary routing to warm required prefixes.

Experiment audit & signoff
--------------------------
- All experiments must have a ticket with: hypothesis, metric targets, isolation plan, observability plan, rollback criteria, and owner.
- Signoff: runtime owner + SRE reviewer must explicitly approve before any live traffic changes. Approval should be recorded in the ticket.

Example YAML snippet: canary routing policy
-----------------------------------------
```yaml
apiVersion: routing.redwood/v1
kind: CanaryPolicy
metadata:
  name: canary-runtime-policy-2025-09
spec:
  cohort: canary-123
  initialFraction: 0.005
  steps:
    - wait: 30m
      fraction: 0.005
    - wait: 60m
      fraction: 0.05
    - wait: 120m
      fraction: 0.25
  healthChecks:
    - name: p99_latency
      threshold: 150 # ms
    - name: error_rate
      threshold: 0.005 # 0.5%
```
Change log
----------
- 2025-03-01: Created (Priya Nambiar).
- 2025-06-15: Added KV cache warmup guidance and soft stop thresholds (Ethan Brooks).
- 2025-09-12: Clarified artifact retention and added explicit hard-stop thresholds for model-fidelity regression (Sofia Martinez).

Related reading
---------------
- Runtime upgrade validation and canary matrix (guideline).
- Continuous runtime profiling strategy.

Appendix: quick diagnostic CLI commands
--------------------------------------
- Check canary p99 from metrics API:
```
curl -s "https://metrics.internal.redwood/api/query?expr=histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket{cohort=\"canary-123\"}[5m])) by (le))" | jq
```
- List kernel selection distribution from traces index:
```
curl -s "https://tracing.internal.redwood/api/traces?service=runtime&cohort=canary-123&limit=100" | jq '.[] | {trace_id:.id, kernel: .tags.kernel}'
```

Contact and ownership
---------------------
- Runtime Experiments Guild (owner): runtime-experiments@redwood
- SRE escalation: sre-oncall@redwood
- Product/Model fidelity contact: model-evals@redwood

End of document.

title: GPU thermal throttling: detection, profiling, and graceful mitigation playbook
content:
Overview:

This runbook describes how to detect, profile, and mitigate incidents where thermal-induced GPU throttling causes elevated latency or error rates in the Redwood inference runtime. Thermal throttling is a distinct failure mode that reduces sustained clock frequency (core/memory), disrupts kernel latency distributions, and can trigger backpressure cascades that violate tail-latency SLOs.

Scope and intent:
- Covers production clusters (hosted and Dedicated) and Private deployments where node-level GPU telemetry is available.
- Focuses on detection heuristics, quick mitigations to preserve customer-facing SLOs, and deeper profiling steps for post-incident RCA.
- Not a hardware repair guide; coordinate with datacenter/cloud provider and HW ops for long-term remediation.

Symptoms (common signals):
1) Sudden p99/p999 increase for generation or chat routes with no corresponding request-rate surge.
2) Drop in per-GPU reported core clock or memory clock (nvml nvmlDeviceGetClockInfo) while temperature remains high (>80–85C).
3) Spikes in kernel execution time samples in traces: kernel_seen_time increases for attention or GEMM kernels while queue length is stable.
4) Multiple nodes in a rack show similar thermal signatures (possible ambient/CRAC failure).

Telemetry and detection rules (recommended):
- Primary metrics to collect: "gpu.temperature_c", "gpu.core_clock_mhz", "gpu.memory_clock_mhz", "gpu.power_w", "gpu.utilization_pct", "runtime.kernel_latency_ms_p95", "runtime.kernel_latency_ms_p99", "runtime.request_latency_ms_p99", "node.ambient_temp_c".
- Heuristic alert (suggested):
  - Condition A: gpu.temperature_c > 86C for > 30s AND gpu.core_clock_mhz has dropped by >= 20% vs baseline for > 15s
  - Condition B: runtime.request_latency_ms_p99 increases > 2x baseline while qps change < 15% over same window
  - Fire a P1 alert if A and B both occur on >= 2 nodes in a pool within 5 minutes.
- Grafana/PromQL example (conceptual):
  - "(avg_over_time(gpu_core_clock_mhz[1m]) < 0.8 * avg_over_time(gpu_core_clock_mhz[1h])) and (avg_over_time(gpu_temperature_c[30s]) > 86)"

Immediate automated mitigations (fast, reversible):
1) Drain new-green traffic from affected nodes: mark node as SCHEDULING_DRAIN and stop assigning new sessions for 60s.
2) Reduce batching: temporarily set batch_max_tokens to 0 for vulnerable model pools to force single-request preemption-friendly execution.
3) Route low-priority and background requests to warm spare pools or to lower-tier quantized model_variants.
4) If cluster admission controller available, lower concurrency slots for the affected node group by 30% to reduce sustained thermal load.
5) Where available, request a hot-swap: move critical tenants to sibling nodes with healthy thermal headroom (automated via edge routing rules).

Runbook for on-call (step-by-step):
1) Triage and confirm
   a) Verify alert timeline in PagerDuty and open incident in the incident tracker.
   b) Confirm telemetry: check GPU temperatures, core/memory clock histories, and request latency graphs for the node(s). Collect last 10 minutes of metrics.
   c) Validate no upstream cooling change or maintenance: check datacenter CRAC alerts and cloud provider health messages.
2) Apply fast mitigations (10–15 minutes)
   a) Execute: POST /internal/cluster/nodes/{node_id}/drain with reason="thermal-throttle"
   b) Adjust per-pool batching: PUT /internal/config/pools/{pool_id} {"batch_max_tokens": 0} (example CLI below).
   c) Rebalance traffic: run routing job to move sessions off the node.
3) Observe (15–45 minutes)
   a) Watch request latency p95/p99 and kernel trace tail. If metrics recover, keep node drained for at least 30 minutes.
   b) If continued degradation, escalate to hardware ops and proceed to cross-node evacuate.
4) Evacuation and remediation
   a) If the node does not recover, mark node for maintenance: POST /internal/cluster/nodes/{node_id}/maintenance_lock
   b) Schedule hardware inspection or provider ticket with collected nvml logs and timestamps.

Diagnostic commands and examples (on-runner / on-host):
- nvml (NVIDIA examples):
  - nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,temperature.gpu,clocks.current.graphics,clocks.current.memory,power.draw,utilization.gpu --format=csv -l 5
  - Example output snippet:
    "0, 88, 1177, 4008, 210 W, 92 %"
- Core clock history via NVML (Python):
  - python snippet:
    """
    import pynvml
    pynvml.nvmlInit()
    h = pynvml.nvmlDeviceGetHandleByIndex(0)
    print(pynvml.nvmlDeviceGetTemperature(h, 0))
    print(pynvml.nvmlDeviceGetClockInfo(h, 0))
    """
- Lightweight kernel tracing: collect a 30s nsys profile around an incident window and upload to perf-s3-bucket with tag thermal-incident-{incident_id}.
- Runtime trace checks: correlate trace_id -> kernel spans where kernel_duration > historical 95th. Use tracing service query: "trace.duration_ms{service:runtime, span:kernel} by (kernel_name)"

Profiling playbook (post-incident deeper analysis):
1) Collect datasets
   - NVML per-second logs (last 60m), nsys captures, runtime traces, kernel-level histograms, and process-level perf samples.
2) Reconstruct workload
   - Replay workload in an isolated staging pool mimicking same concurrency/sequence-length distribution. Use saved request payloads from the incident window.
3) Kernel attribution matrix
   - Build a table mapping kernel_name -> median latency, p95, p99 during baseline and incident windows. Highlight kernels with > 2x p99 regression.
4) Thermal signature analysis
   - Check delta between ambient and GPU temps, analyze power draw curves. Determine if throttling is due to gradual thermal ramp vs immediate power cap enforcement.

Benchmark and reproduction guide (safe staging only):
- Purpose: reproduce thermal-induced throttling on a single node to validate mitigations and scheduler changes.
- Synthetic load harness (conceptual):
  - Run a sustained generator with long context and repeated heavy GEMM kernels for 60–90 minutes. Example script: 
    """
    #!/bin/bash
    for i in {1..180}; do
      python synthetic_infer.py --model modelA --context 512 --batch 1 --repeat 20 &
      sleep 20
    done
    """
  - Monitor nvml metrics and ensure cooling is intentionally limited (only in lab / sanctioned racks).
- Acceptance criteria for reproduction: sustained drop in core clock >= 20% with p99 request latency increase > 50% vs baseline.

Scheduler and kernel-level mitigations (longer-term):
- Conservative slot admission: add a thermal headroom factor to the admission controller so that nodes with temp > 75C accept fewer long-sequence requests.
- Kernel scheduling hint: prefer smaller batch slices when node.temp > 78C and limit fused-kernel activation for large-context workloads.
- Priority-aware eviction: implement a short-lived preemption window to evict non-critical batch jobs when temp thresholds crossed.
- Example config table (values are defaults and can be tuned per pool):

  | parameter                     | default | mitigation intent                                   |
  | ----------------------------  | ------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
  | thermal_headroom_pct          | "20"   | reserve 20% of scheduling capacity above baseline  |
  | throttle_temp_c               | "86"   | temperature to start aggressive draining policies  |
  | batch_slice_limit_when_hot    | "32"   | maximum tokens per slice when node.hot              |
  | quantized_fallback_threshold  | "70"   | % of node pool usage to trigger quantized routing  |

Post-incident RCA checklist and owners:
- Engineering runtime owner: triage kernel attribution and scheduler tuning (owner: Marcus Chen).
- Capacity and fleet: verify cluster-level cooling events and coordinate with infra/custops (owner: Elena García).
- HW ops / provider ticket: include NVML logs, nsys captures, and node asset IDs.
- Follow-up actions: update admission controller config, add or change alert thresholds, and schedule canary to validate tuning.

Example CLI snippets (internal APIs):
- Drain node: curl -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' \n  "https://internal-api.redwood/v1/cluster/nodes/host-0123/drain" -d '{"reason":"thermal-throttle","duration_mins":60}'
- Adjust pool batching: curl -X PUT -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' \n  "https://internal-api.redwood/v1/pools/large-gen/config" -d '{"batch_max_tokens":0}'

Known limitations and caveats:
- Not all thermal events are symmetric: some GPUs may show normal temperature with localized die hotspots; NVML may not expose per-die microhotspots.
- Private/on-prem racks may have different cooling telemetry semantics; validate metric names before relying on thresholds.
- Automated mitigation that reduces batching will increase per-request cost; weigh economic impact for each customer tier.

Contacts and escalation path:
- On-call runtime (primary): runtime-oncall@redwood.internal
- Fleet & infra: fleet-ops@redwood.internal
- Hardware ops: hw-ops@redwood.internal
- If incident affects >= 3 customers or SLAs: notify SRE manager and CS lead.

Appendix: example incident timeline (realistic sample)
1) 2027-01-18 03:12 UTC: alert fired for pool-gen-a p99 spike and core clock drop on host-0123.
2) 03:14 UTC: node drained and batching disabled for pool-gen-a. P99 begins to fall by 03:25 UTC.
3) 03:40 UTC: node marked for maintenance; provider ticket created.
4) 2027-01-20: provider confirmed CRAC unit failure in rack; remediation scheduled and nodes returned to service after hardware swap.

Revision notes:
- 2027-02-15: expanded detection heuristics and added scheduler tuning table (Aisha Patel).
- 2026-11-02: initial draft and tested in dedicated cluster labs (Aisha Patel).

Related reading and references:
- NVML API reference: https://developer.nvidia.com/nvml
- nsys quickstart and capture guides: https://developer.nvidia.com/nsight-systems
- Runtime admission controller design doc: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-policy-language-declarative-profiles-2026

title: Priority inversion detection and mitigation playbook
content:
Summary
-------
This playbook defines detection, profiling, and step‑by‑step mitigation for priority inversion and related starvation scenarios in the Redwood serving runtime (components: runtime-shepherd, kernel-mapper, request-router, kv-cache). It is intended for oncall SREs, runtime engineers, and release owners responsible for kernel scheduling and request orchestration.

Scope
-----
- Applies to all production clusters running the inference runtime (hosted + dedicated pools).
- Targets cases where low-priority long-running requests cause high-priority short requests to miss SLOs (p95/p99 latency regressions, queue growth).
- Includes detection signals, live profiling actions, short-term mitigations, and long-term scheduler fixes.

Background and definitions
--------------------------
- Priority inversion: higher-priority requests being delayed because resources are held by lower-priority work (e.g., long decode kernels, blocking I/O).
- Kernel scheduling: the runtime-mapped ordering of GPU kernels invoked by requests; implemention lives in kernel-mapper and runtime-shepherd.
- Starvation: sustained inability of a priority class to make forward progress for a defined window.

Detection (alerts and observability)
----------------------------------
Primary alerts (Prometheus):
1) High-priority latency breach alert (P95)
   - Query: rate(app_request_duration_seconds_bucket{priority="high"}[5m]) and histogram_quantile(0.95, ... ) > 120ms 
   - Alert threshold: p95 > 120ms for 3m
2) Kernel queue skew
   - Query: increase(kernel_invocations_total[1m]) grouped by priority / shard; if low-priority invocation rate is >150% of high-priority for same shard and high-priority queue depth > 10 -> fire
3) GPU nowait stalls
   - Signal from trace-agent: gpu_kernel_enqueue_latency_seconds{status="queued"} p99 > 20ms
4) Owner breach: request-router drop rate > 0.5% for priority=high over 5m

Diagnostic dashboards and traces to open on alert:
- Runtime queue heatmap: request-router > queues by priority and shard
- Kernel invocation waterfall: kernel-mapper traces for last 5 minutes
- KV-cache hot vs cold access by request signature
- GPU utilization and active-kernel-count

Profiling and data collection (first 10 minutes)
------------------------------------------------
1) Capture a 60s flame trace (distributed) from trace-agent: POST /admin/trace?duration=60s on runtime-shepherd admin port.
   - Example: curl -s -X POST http://runtime-shepherd-admin:9090/admin/trace -d '{"duration":"60s","tags":["priority"]}'
2) Snapshot kernel queues: curl http://kernel-mapper:9100/debug/queues -> save as kernel-queues-<timestamp>.json
3) Collect Prometheus range for the last 15m for these metrics: request_duration, kernel_invocations_total, kernel_queue_depth, gpu_active_kernels. Use grafana-export or promql curl.
4) If pprof is enabled for C++ agents, run pprof for the shard experiencing skew: ssh to node -> /usr/local/bin/pprof -http=:8080 /var/profiler/shard-XX.pb.gz

Immediate mitigations (order of operations)
-----------------------------------------
Goal: restore high-priority SLOs within 5–15 minutes while preserving safety. Escalate to runtime engineers if mitigation cannot be applied within 10 minutes.

1) Canary fallback to alternate model variant (stateless mitigation) — 0–2 minutes
   - Use request-router policy to reroute priority=high to a compatible model variant with lower kernel latency (e.g., gpt-q4_0 -> gpt-q8_0).
   - API example: PATCH /admin/routing/policy
     Payload (example):
     {
       "route":"/v1/generate",
       "selector":{"priority":"high"},
       "fallback":"gpt-q8_0-small",
       "timeout_ms":1000
     }
   - Verify: p95 for high priority drops within 2 minutes.

2) Force preemption window (kernel-shepherd soft shrink) — 2–6 minutes
   - Enable soft-preempt on the affected pool: curl -X POST http://kernel-mapper:9100/admin/soft_preempt -d 'shard=shard-7&window_ms=50'
   - This instructs kernel-scheduler to allow eviction points after each kernel batch to service high-priority queue.
   - Monitor: kernel_enqueue_latency p50/p95 and high-priority p95.

3) Drain or throttle low-priority long tail requests — 3–10 minutes
   - Apply a per-route throttle: /admin/quotas -> add token-bucket for low priority: rate=5rps, burst=10.
   - For sessions with known large sequence lengths, mark as "background" and move to background queue via request metadata tag.

4) Emergency scale-up (if latency continues) — 5–15 minutes
   - Temporarily allocate additional shard capacity: increase desired_shards for pool-id in autoscaling API. Example: PATCH /admin/pool/pool-4/scale {"desired_shards": 8}
   - Note: scaling takes 2–8 minutes depending on available nodes. Use only if fallback/preempt fail.

Long-term fixes and scheduler patches (post-incident)
-----------------------------------------------------
- Implement priority-aware kernel credit accounting (design doc reference in related_pages).
- Add bounded preemption points in long-running kernels (op-level changes) to reduce blocking windows > 50ms.
- Improve request-router hinting: attach estimated-kernel-cost to incoming requests (model-size, sequence length) so kernel-mapper can make informed placement.
- Add acceptance tests in benchmarking suite to simulate priority-inversion patterns (see Benchmarking and Validation).

Benchmarking and validation
--------------------------
Purpose: ensure mitigations bring back SLOs and regression tests prevent reintroduction.

Required benchmarks to run after mitigation and before merge:
- Priority inversion synthetic test (recommended harness: perf-bench/priority-inversion):
  - Scenario: 20% high-priority short requests (seq_length 32), 80% low-priority long requests (seq_length 1024) for 10 minutes.
  - Assertions: high-priority p95 < 120ms, overall GPU utilization < 90%, kernel_queue_skew < 2x for >2m windows.
- Kernel preemption microbench: measure kernel context-switch overhead after adding preemption points; target p50 additional overhead < 8ms.

Configuration matrix (example table):
| variable | accepted threshold |
|---|---|
| high-priority p95 | < 120ms |
| high-priority p99 | < 300ms |
| kernel_queue_depth (per-shard) | < 25 |
