| gpu_active_kernels | < 16 |
| kernel_enqueue_latency p99 | < 40ms |

Release notes and changelog template
-----------------------------------
When shipping scheduler changes include the following fields in the runtime release notes:
- Summary of change (one line)
- Impacted components: kernel-mapper, runtime-shepherd
- Behavioral change: preemption, credit accounting, queue ordering
- Feature flags required and safe rollout steps
- Benchmarks run and results (attach CSV)

Example entry:
- Title: Add bounded preemption windows to kernel-scheduler
- Date: 2026-02-04
- Rollout: feature flag runtime.scheduler.preempt_v2, canary 10% pools -> 50% -> 100% over 6 hours
- Benchmarks: priority-inversion synthetic passed; high-priority p95 improved from 220ms -> 96ms; overhead p50 +4ms.

Known issues and caveats
-----------------------
- Preemption can increase tail latency for low-priority requests if preemption frequency is too high. Use conservative windows.
- KV-cache hot state (hot prefixes) may hold GPU kernels indirectly via synchronous reads. If kv-cache is the causal chain, throttling requests or warming prefixes is recommended rather than kernel preemption.
- Hardware-level constraints (older CUDA drivers) may not support fine-grain preemption; fall back to routing-level mitigations.

Runbook: play-by-play checklist (for oncall)
-----------------------------------------
1) Acknowledge alert and page runtime oncall.
2) Collect traces and kernel queue snapshot (Profiling and data collection).
3) Apply routing fallback to alternate variant and observe (Immediate mitigation #1).
4) If not resolved in 2 minutes, enable soft-preempt (Immediate mitigation #2).
5) If p95 still > threshold after 10 minutes, apply throttles and notify infra to scale shards.
6) When resolved, note incident, attach collected artifacts to Jira incident, and create post‑mortem if SLOs were missed for >30 minutes.

Ownership, SLAs and escalation
------------------------------
- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime oncall (rotation: runtime-oncall@redwood.com).
- Secondary owner: runtime-platform team (pager: runtime-platform-leads).
- Escalation: after 10 minutes without improvement escalate to Senior Runtime Engineer (pager) and schedule a conference bridge.
- SLOs referenced: hosted API p95 goal = 80ms (small sequences), hard SLO = 200ms; see product docs for customer-facing thresholds.

Post-incident actions and tickets
--------------------------------
- Create a ticket in PROD-OPS with label priority-inversion and link traces + kernel queue snapshots.
- If mitigation involved feature-flag changes, submit a PR that reverts the quick fix and replaces with long-term scheduler patch behind the flag.
- Add a new unit/regression test to perf-bench suite that reproduces the incident pattern.

References and related pages
----------------------------
- Kernel scheduler spec: see related pages above.
- Runtime profiling guidelines: see related pages above.
- Perf harness: git://repo/perf-bench (priority-inversion harness).

Appendix: common PromQL and CLI snippets
---------------------------------------
- High-priority p95 (example):
  histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(app_request_duration_seconds_bucket{priority="high"}[5m])) by (le))

- Kernel queue depth per shard:
  sum(kernel_queue_depth) by (shard, priority)

- Snapshot kernel queues:
  curl -sS http://kernel-mapper:9100/debug/queues > /tmp/kernel-queues-$(date +%s).json

- Enable feature flag on canary:
  curl -X POST http://featuregate:8080/api/v1/flags -d '{"flag":"runtime.scheduler.preempt_v2","state":"on","target":"canary-pool-*"}'

Contact and maintenance
-----------------------
- Maintainers: Lena Ortiz (runtime-shepherd), Priya Nair (kernel-mapper).
- Quarterly review: schedule after any two incidents or post-major-release.

End of document.

title: Seamless model swap and KV consistency guide
content:
Summary:
This playbook describes a prescriptive, low-risk procedure for swapping active model variants and migrating KV cache shards without violating session consistency guarantees or significantly degrading tail latency. It combines a verified orchestration recipe, telemetry checks, and rollback criteria suitable for Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments.

Scope & audience:
- Audience: runtime engineers, release engineers, SRE on-call, platform integrators.
- Applies to: model binary swaps, kvcache layout migrations, topology changes that rebind session affinity (shard moves, NUMA rebinds).
- Not covered: full cluster reboots, GPU firmware upgrades, application-layer prompt changes.

Goals & success criteria:
- Zero user-visible correctness regressions for in-flight sessions (consistency goal).
- No more than 2x degradation of P95 latency during controlled canaries.
- Automatic, deterministic rollback path on defined error thresholds.

Key definitions and guarantees:
- Strong session consistency: a session's KV prefix and cache must remain readable for the lifetime of a conversation until explicit eviction.
- Live-swap: replacing the active model binary for a shard without terminating incoming connections.
- Drain-and-rebind: moving session ownership by draining new requests from a source shard, replaying KV as needed, and binding to a destination shard.

Architecture overview (concise):
- Orchestration layer (Orch): issues swap commands, coordinates canaries, and sets routing policies.
- Shard controller (SC): enacts bind/unbind, coordinates KV replication, and performs drain.
- KV layer: multi-tiered prefix cache with ephemerality flags and fast-lookup index.
- Frontdoor router: routes requests by session token -> shard map; can be flipped to prefer new shard when canary progresses.

Consistency models and tradeoffs:
- Option A (Strong): Synchronous KV snapshot+handshake with two-phase commit. Guarantees no missing keys at cost of higher latency during swap windows.
- Option B (Eventually consistent): Shadow-replication with read-fallback to source shard. Lower latency, but requires careful time-bounded fallbacks and observability.

Recommended default for production: hybrid approach. Start with Option B during canary periods with strict telemetry; for full rollout switch to Option A for final cutover when load is predictable.

Preflight checklist (automatable):
1) Validate model artifact checksum and signature: sha256sum and k8s image signature present.
2) Confirm destination shard has >= 1.5x memory headroom for KV warmup.
3) SLO budget check: current error budget >= planned swap budget (default 0.5%).
4) Open on-call window and post runbook link to #runtime-ops.
5) Gather baseline telemetry (P50/P95/P99 tokens/latency, error-rates, kv-miss-rate).

Step-by-step migration playbook (operational steps):
1) Prepare canary routing rule:
   - Orch: create canary route rule (1% traffic) mapped to destination shard with "shadow-read: true" and "write-back: false".
   - Confirm no destructive flags set.
2) Warmup and shadow replication (10-30 minutes typical):
   - Trigger KV prefetch: SC issues async prefetch for top-10% hottest prefixes via background task.
   - Monitor kv-warmup-progress: expect >80% hot prefix residency within window.
3) Telemetry gating during canary (continuous):
   - p50/p95 latency delta <= +30% and p99 delta <= +60% vs baseline.
   - kv-miss rate on destination <= 2x baseline.
   - error-rate increase <= 0.2% absolute.
   - No functional anomalies in downstream evals (sampled prompts).
   - If any gate trips, abort canary and rollback to previous routing.
4) Incremental ramp (phased percentages):
   - 1% -> 5% -> 20% -> 50% -> 100% over multiple verification steps (15-60m between steps).
   - At each step, run automated smoke tests and fuzzed prompt validation against responses to detect semantic drift.
5) Final cutover (atomic rebind):
   - Switch routing map atomically: Orch flips session token assignment and marks source shard for graceful deprecation.
   - If Option A chosen: perform synchronous KV handshake before flipping (blocking window).
   - Wait 3x observed median warmup latency before marking migration complete.
6) Post-cutover validation and tidy-up:
   - Mark source shard as "standby" for 1 hour to serve any read-fallbacks and then evict.
   - Run integrity-check job to confirm no missing session prefixes.
   - Update catalog/version metadata and notify product/clients if required.

Rollback criteria and steps:
- Auto-rollback triggers (any one):
  * sustained p99 latency > 2x baseline for 15m.
  * error-rate spike > 1% absolute for 5m.
  * kv-miss rate on destination > 5x baseline for 10m.
  * semantic-eval failures (failing >3 out of 20 sampled prompts).
- Rollback procedure:
 1) Orch reassigns routing map back to source shard (atomic).
 2) Destination shard switches to read-only and begins cache eviction.
 3) Post-rollback alerting: tag incident and capture traces for triage.

Operational knobs and configuration examples:
- CanaryRoute YAML example:
  ---
  kind: CanaryRoute
  metadata:
    name: model-swap-canary-1
  spec:
    percent: 1
    shadow_read: true
    write_back: false
    metrics_gates:
      - latency_p95_delta_ms: 100
      - kv_miss_rate_ratio: 2.0

- Shard binding config snippet:
  shard_bind_timeout_ms: 30000
  kv_sync_mode: "shadow_async" # options: shadow_async | synchronous_two_phase
  max_prefetch_prefixes: 2000

Observability & required dashboards:
- Canary health panel: p50/p95/p99 latency, ingest QPS, kv-miss-rate, error-rate, session-affinity-violations.
- Integrity panel: orphaned-prefix-count, prefix-staleness-hrs, fallback-read-count.
- Tracing: ensure spans include orch.request_id, shard_id_old, shard_id_new, kv_sync_mode.
- Logs: structured event for steps (canary-start, warmup-complete, cutover-inflight, rollback).

Alerting thresholds (recommended):
- Sev1: p99 > 3x baseline for 10m OR sustained error-rate > 2% for 5m.
- Sev2: p99 > 2x baseline OR kv-miss > 5x baseline for 10m.
- Sev3: p95 > 1.5x baseline OR smoke-test failures during ramp.

Troubleshooting matrix (common symptoms -> checks -> mitigation):
- Symptom: sudden p99 spike after 20% ramp.
  Checks: inspect kv-miss-rate, kernel queue depth, GPU memory pressure.
  Mitigation: pause ramp, reduce percent, initiate partial rollback, increase destination shard headroom.
- Symptom: session-level 500s and missing responses.
  Checks: trace request lifecycle for missing KV reads, check for deserialization errors on new model.
  Mitigation: roll back routing, tag failing model artifact for analysis.
- Symptom: high fallback-read-count from frontdoor.
  Checks: verify prefix ingestion pipeline on destination, examine network egress errors between shards.
  Mitigation: restart prefetch workers, rerun KV replay on subset of prefixes.

Diagnostics commands and snippets:
- Show current canary rules:
  # rctl canary list --namespace prod
- Force a single-session rebind for testing:
  # rctl session rebind --session-id <SID> --to-shard shard-42 --mode dry-run
- Inspect shard health and kv stats:
  # shardctl status shard-42 --format json | jq '.kv_stats | {miss_rate,hot_prefixes,mem_used}'

Postmortem data collection (prescribed):
1) Export span traces for the migration window +/- 15 minutes.
2) Export kv-metrics timeline and compare hot-prefix residency before/after.
3) Snapshot sample requests and responses for semantic regression testing.
4) Correlate scheduler/kernel metrics (GPU occupancy, kernel latency) with tail latency spikes.

Ownership and escalation:
- Primary owner: runtime-serving-team@redwood.com (oncall rotation in #runtime-oncall).
- Secondary owner: infra-sre@redwood.com.
- Escalation path: oncall -> runtime tech lead -> SRE manager -> Eng Director.

Appendix A: example smoke tests (automated):
- Test 1: top-20 prompts from prod anonymized corpus; assert token-level edit distance < 5% vs baseline.
- Test 2: prefix read/write roundtrip: perform 100 session-rewind operations, assert no missing keys.

Appendix B: known-risk checklist before private deployments:
- KMS key ACLs validated for destination host.
- Network egress rules between shards in VPC are permissive for replay channels.
- HSM-backed signing available if two-phase commit is used.

Related runbooks and docs:
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-upgrade-validation-and-canary-matrix-2026
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/preemption-aware-batch-slicing-spec-2026

Revision history:
- 2025-03-12: initial draft by Riley Chen.
- 2025-06-18: added telemetry gating thresholds and CLI snippets (Asha Menon).
- 2025-10-08: expanded rollback criteria and appended private deployment checklist (Diego Alvarez).

Contact for questions: Riley Chen (riley.chen@redwood.ai)

title: End-to-End Latency Decomposition and Kernel Hinting Playbook
content:
Summary:

This playbook describes a standard, repeatable process for decomposing end-to-end inference latency into measurable components and using those signals to drive kernel hinting changes in the runtime. It combines observability queries, targeted profiling, an action checklist, and a safe rollout procedure for kernel-hint configuration updates. The goal is to reduce 95th/99th percentile latency regressions while preserving throughput and fairness across tenants.

Scope and intent:
- Applies to hosted and dedicated serving clusters running the Redwood serving runtime.
- Targets interactive text-generation and chat workloads (typical seq_len 16–2048).
- Focuses on per-request latency; does not replace per-token cost optimization playbooks.

When to use this playbook:
1) Sudden increase in p95 or p99 latency for a model route.
2) Regressions observed after a kernel rollout, quantization change, or autoscaler tuning.
3) Persistent tail latency despite normal kernel telemetry.

Owner and escalation path:
- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime oncall team (primary: @runtime-oncall).
- Secondary owner: Serving Runtime Kernel SIG (rotation: kernel-sig@redwood).
- Escalation: If changes affect >2x latency or traffic outage, escalate to SRE Pager and Product (use internal pager flow).

Key concepts and definitions:
- E2E latency: measured at edge proxy from request start to final byte.
- Scheduling latency: time spent waiting in runtime scheduler queue before kernel dispatch.
- Kernel execution latency: GPU kernel time (inclusive of kernel launch and completion).
- KV prefetch / warmup time: additional per-shard I/O or KV cache population time that occurs before kernel execution.
- Serialization / networking: edge, reverse-proxy, and inter-node serialization + network transfer time.

Observability checklist (quick diagnostic):
1) Open the route dashboard (Grafana): route.latency.p95, route.latency.p99, route.success_rate.
2) Split E2E into spans: proxy_span, scheduler_queue_span, kernel_exec_span, kv_warmup_span. Grafana panels exist with these derived metrics.
3) Run a time-range query (last 15m and last 6h) to check whether the tail event is transient or sustained.

Useful PromQL and sample queries:
- p95 E2E: quantile_over_time(0.95, histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(runtime_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, route)))
- Avg scheduling queue time: avg_over_time(runtime_scheduler_queue_seconds_sum[5m]) / avg_over_time(runtime_scheduler_queue_seconds_count[5m])
- Kernel execution 99th: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(kernel_exec_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, kernel_name))
- KV warmup rate spike: increase(kv_warmup_ops_total[5m]) / increase(runtime_request_total[5m])

Initial triage steps (ordered):
1) Confirm signal: validate the alerting query and look for correlated error spikes (grpc errors, resource saturation).
2) Isolate scope: is the regression single-route, model-variant, or cluster-wide? Filter by route, model_id, shard_id.
3) Compare to kernel telemetry: check kernel_exec_seconds histogram and per-kernel concurrency.
4) Check scheduler telemetry: per-priority queue lengths, wait-time distributions, and preemption events.
5) Inspect GPU host metrics: GPU utilization, memory pressure, nvlink error counters, PCIe throughput.
6) If kernel_exec latency is stable but queue times increased -> suspect scheduler/backpressure or KV warmup.
7) If kernel_exec latency increased -> suspect kernel regressions, new kernel rollout, instruction set mismatch, or memory thrashing.

Profiling playbook (when deeper analysis needed):
1) Capture a targeted trace using the runtime trace-sampler for the affected route (sample rate 100% for a 2 minute window):
   - CLI: redwood-runtime trace capture --route <route> --duration 120s --out /tmp/trace.json
2) Run offline trace decomposition tool (trace-decompose) to split timings by span and annotate kernel traces with CUDA timestamps.
   - Example: trace-decompose /tmp/trace.json --output /tmp/decomposed.csv
3) If kernel exec is dominant -> collect CUPTI and kernel-level samples on the node (coordinate with infra oncall).
4) If KV warmup is dominant -> enable kvcache debug logs at INFO for the route for 10 minutes and gather sample logs.

Kernel hinting: intent and mechanics
- Kernel hinting lets the high-level scheduler bias scheduling decisions for a request: e.g., prefer fused attention kernels, prefetch KV cache, or mark as latency-sensitive so it bypasses large-batch queues.
- Hint sources: static model profile, dynamic telemetry rule, manual override via rollout. Hints are attached to request metadata and consumed by the scheduler and kernel mapper.

Example kernel-hint configuration (YAML snippet):
```
kernel_hint_profiles:
  - id: short-chat-low-latency
    match:
      max_seq_len: 256
      model_family: "redwood-chat"
    hints:
      prefer_kernel: "fused_attn_v3"
      priority: high
      kvcache_prefetch: true
      prefetch_window_ms: 50
```

Interpreting hint effects:
- prefer_kernel: if the preferred kernel is available on the node, scheduler will route to matching nodes first.
- priority: routes the request into a priority queue; high-priority queues are policed to preserve SLOs.
- kvcache_prefetch and prefetch_window_ms: cause asynchronous KV prefetch before kernel dispatch to reduce warmup latency.

Safety constraints for hint changes (must be followed):
- Any new hint profile must have an automated canary with traffic fraction <= 2% for 24 hours and p95/p99 compared to baseline before rollforward.
- Run an A/B test with traffic mirroring for at least 2 hours and collect per-token tokenization parity checks.
- Ensure hint profiles are scoped by route or tenant to avoid cross-tenant performance impact.

Rollout procedure for kernel-hint adjustments (step-by-step):
1) Create a kernel-hint PR in infra-configs with: rationale, telemetry baselines, YAML snippet, and rollback plan.
2) Apply to canary pool (label: canary-hint) at 1% traffic. Observe for 1 hour.
3) If no regressions: increase to 2% for 24 hours while running differential metrics and trace capture.
4) Run targeted load tests from benchmarking suite: replicate production p95 with synthetic load to validate scaling behavior.
5) If stable: increase to 10% for 2 hours, then 50% for 2 hours, then full rollout.
6) On any regression, immediately rollback by removing the canary hint profile; trigger postmortem.

Playbook for common symptoms and recommended actions:
- Symptom: p99 latency increase but kernel_exec stable -> Action: investigate scheduler queueing. Consider creating a temporary priority hint for affected routes or enabling limited prefetch to avoid queue spike.
- Symptom: kernel_exec p99 spike on specific kernel -> Action: pin route to alternative kernel (prefer_kernel override) or revert recent kernel rollout. Collect CUPTI traces.
- Symptom: KV warmup spikes on cold-starts -> Action: increase prefetch_window_ms for small window; evaluate pre-warm policies in autoscaler.
- Symptom: NVLink or PCIe-related variance -> Action: move traffic away from affected nodes via decommission flag; open infra ticket for hardware investigation.

Observability artifacts to collect when filing an incident:
- Route ID, model ID, user-visible error/latency windows, p50/p95/p99 baseline and during incident.
- 2–5 representative decomposed traces (decomposed.csv) and corresponding raw trace.json.
- Kernel histograms and queue length time-series for the incident window.
- Node-level GPU metrics and recent kernel-rollout history.

Postmortem guidance and experiment tracking:
- Any hint-profile change that affects latency by >10% p95 or p99 requires a short postmortem (owner: author of the config PR).
- Track experiments in the runtime experiment dashboard with traffic fractions, start/end times, and success criteria.

Appendix A — Example Grafana panels and what they show:
- Scheduler queue heatmap: shows per-priority queue depth over time (useful for burst/backpressure).
- Kernel selection vector: fraction of requests using preferred kernel vs fallback kernels.
- KV prefetch hit rate: percent of requests that served from warm KV.

Appendix B — Troubleshooting quick commands:
- Tail runtime logs for route: kubectl logs -l route=<route> -c runtime --tail=500
- Capture traces: redwood-runtime trace capture --route <route> --duration 120s --out /tmp/trace.json
- Apply hint config locally (dry-run): infra-configctl apply --file hint.yaml --dry-run

Related pages and references:
- Benchmarking playbooks for synthetic p95 simulation (see related pages).
- Kernel mapping and policy language specification (kernel mapper docs in kernel-and-scheduling).

Notes and rationale:
- Kernel hinting is a surgical lever: it should be used to rescue latency-sensitive routes where global kernel changes would harm throughput-critical workloads. The playbook prioritizes measurement, small canaries, and observability to avoid cross-tenant regressions.

Change history:
- 2026-01-12: Initial draft by Maya Chen.
- 2026-02-03: Added canary percentages and PromQL examples (reviewed by Diego Martinez).

title: Emergency rollback: Serving Runtime (Hosted + Dedicated)
content:
h1. Purpose
This runbook describes how to perform an *emergency rollback* of the Serving Runtime release across *Hosted* and *Dedicated* fleets. It focuses on restoring SLOs safely and quickly while preserving evidence for later analysis.

h1. When to rollback (triggers)
Rollback is appropriate when one or more is true and mitigation is not available within ~30 minutes:
* p95 *time-to-first-token (TTFT)* regression > 30% in 2+ regions for 10+ minutes
* error rate > 2% on generation routes due to runtime (5xx, timeouts, OOM)
* canary cohort shows sustained degradation and traffic shift cannot be halted cleanly
* repeated GPU OOM or kernel crash loops attributable to the new runtime build

*If unsure*: declare an incident and page Runtime + SRE (see incident process) and start preparing rollback steps in parallel.

h1. Preconditions
* An incident has been declared if customer impact is confirmed or likely (see SEV process page).
* Runtime oncall has identified *candidate rollback target* (prior runtime release tag).
* Release engineer or infra oncall is available to execute the pipeline rollback (see CI/CD rollback doc).

h1. Ownership and roles
* Incident Commander (IC): owns the decision to rollback and comms cadence.
* Runtime oncall: validates technical root cause hypothesis and rollback target.
* Release/Infra oncall: executes the rollback in deployment tooling.
* SRE: monitors fleet-level SLOs and regional health signals.

h1. Rollback decision checklist
Before executing rollback, capture in the incident channel:
# Current runtime release identifier (e.g., runtime-release-2025.02.01)
# Intended rollback target (e.g., runtime-release-2025.01.17)
# Blast radius (Hosted regions; Dedicated clusters/tenants)
# Primary symptom (TTFT, throughput, 5xx, OOM)
# Confirm the prior release is known-good (at least 24h stable in prod)

h1. Step-by-step procedure

## 1) Freeze rollout / stop further progression
* If a rollout is in progress, *pause* it immediately (do not continue canary expansion).
* Ensure no automated progressive delivery job will re-advance the rollout.

## 2) Hosted rollback (global fleets)
Follow the CI/CD rollback doc to pin the Hosted runtime to the rollback target, then:
* Roll back in this order:
  # non-critical region (if any still on canary only)
  # remaining canary cohort
  # all regions currently on the bad release
* After each region completes, verify:
  * 5xx rate normalizes
  * GPU utilization returns to expected
  * TTFT and token/s recover to baseline

Hosted verification queries (Console):
* Dashboard: "Hosted Inference / Runtime Release Health"
* Metrics to watch: request_error_rate, ttft_p95_ms, tokens_per_sec, gpu_oom_count

## 3) Dedicated rollback (tenant clusters)
Dedicated rollbacks must consider customer-specific change windows and comms. In emergencies, proceed under the emergency change policy.
* Identify impacted Dedicated clusters/tenants:
  * Check "Dedicated / Runtime Release Adoption" dashboard
  * Confirm whether each tenant is on the bad release
* Execute rollback per cluster using the pipeline rollback procedure.
* For high-sensitivity tenants, coordinate with CS for outbound comms and approvals (see comms guide).

## 4) Post-rollback validation
* Keep the incident open until metrics are stable for 30 minutes (Hosted) / 60 minutes (Dedicated)
* Confirm request latency distributions return to baseline and no new error modes appear
* Ensure autoscaling stabilizes (watch for over-provisioning due to the regression)

h1. Guardrails and common failure modes
* If rollback target also shows elevated OOMs, stop and reassess (may be traffic pattern or model mix).
* If only one model family is impacted, consider temporarily routing to a compatible variant instead of fleet rollback (requires IC approval).
* Avoid rapid flip-flopping between releases; if you must re-roll forward, document the reason and require runtime lead approval.

h1. Required artifacts (for later review)
Capture links in the incident channel:
* CI/CD job link(s) for rollback
* Affected regions / clusters
* Metrics screenshots or dashboard permalinks
* Any customer comms sent

h1. References
* SEV process for runtime regressions (incident roles, paging, timelines)
* Runtime release pipeline rollback procedure (exact CI/CD steps)
* Emergency change policy (approvals and documentation)
* Customer/status comms guide (templates and approval chain)

title: Soft Failure Synthesis and Routing Playbook
content:
Summary:

This playbook documents the end-to-end design, operational guidance, and engineering procedures for synthesizing and routing soft failures in the Redwood serving runtime. Soft failures are controlled degradations (reduced fidelity, alternative kernels, fallbacks to smaller model variants, or increased batching/timeout tradeoffs) used to preserve availability and SLOs when a hard failure or capacity exhaustion is imminent.

Goals and scope:

- Define the runtime-level signals, thresholds, and scheduler policies used to trigger soft-failure modes.
- Provide profiling and benchmarking scenarios to validate degradations preserve user-facing SLAs.
- Document concrete runbook steps for detection, triage, mitigation, and rollback of soft-failure events.
- Capture release compatibility constraints and known issues related to soft-failure orchestration.

This playbook applies to hosted, dedicated, and private deployments that use the Redwood serving runtime. It covers kernel scheduling hooks, routing policies, KV cache behavior, telemetry instrumentation, and operator runbooks.

Definitions and key concepts:

- Soft failure: a deliberate, well-scoped reduction in fidelity or compute that keeps requests progressing rather than failing hard (errors). Examples: reduced beam size, lower-precision kernels (int8), model-variant downgrade, function-call truncation, or increasing allowed latency window.
- Fidelity stair-step: an ordered list of degradation modes (Tier 0: full fidelity; Tier 1: quantized kernels; Tier 2: smaller model; Tier 3: cached response / static fallback) used for predictable escalations.
- SLO-preserving route: a request routing outcome that aims to keep p95 latency and error rate within SLO by preferring lower-cost alternatives over returning 5xx errors.

Architecture overview (how soft-failure flows through runtime):

1. Signal sources: kernel latency spikes, GPU memory pressure, queue depth, per-tenant error budget depletion, cross-region capacity alerts. Each signal is emitted to the runtime decision-plane.
2. Decision layer: the Decision Fabric evaluates rules (SLO rules, tenant priority, current fidelity state) and emits a policy action (e.g., apply Degradation Profile G: quantize-kernel + allow-extra-20ms-latency).
3. Scheduler & Kernel Mapper: the kernel scheduler receives the policy and maps incoming requests to appropriate kernel binaries/runner pools, adjusting batching hints and preemption windows.
4. Routing & Fallbacks: Router chooses between local degraded pool, remote region, or model variant. A weighted hedge (default 80/20) is maintained during progressive rollouts to validate quality metrics before widening.

Diagram (text): Decision Fabric -> Scheduler -> Kernel Pool(s) -> Router -> Client responses (fidelity stair-step applied at Scheduler/Router boundary).

Kernel scheduling and routing policy details:

Policy units and primitives:
- PolicyDefinition: name, priority, trigger_signals, actions, rollback_window_seconds.
- Actions (examples): set_kernel_hint=quantized_int8, set_model_variant=compact-1.3B, extend_timeout_ms=20, enable_kv_prefetch=true.
- Priority semantics: higher priority policies preempt lower ones within the same tenant; cross-tenant isolation enforced via kernel-credit accounts.

Default production policy (summary):
- Trigger: per-GPU queue depth > 85% OR p95 kernel latency > 1.4x baseline for 90s.
- Action sequence (applied sequentially every 30 seconds until safe):
  1) Hint quantized kernels for non-critical tenants.
  2) Increase batching window by 10ms for background routes.
  3) Swap to smaller model-variant for new sessions only.
  4) Route 10% of traffic to remote region (longer network latency tradeoff).

Telemetry and profiling playbook (what to collect and how to act):

Signals to collect (minimum):
- Kernel dispatch latency histogram (per kernel id, per shard).
- GPU memory headroom gauge per node and per process.
- Queue depth and queue wait time per route.
- KV cache hit ratio and reconstruction time.
- Decision Fabric action logs with correlation IDs.
- Sampled request traces (1 in 5k for production baseline, 1 in 200 for degraded periods).

Profiling procedure when a degradation policy fires:
1) Increase trace sampling to 1 in 200 for the affected tenant and route.
2) Capture 60s of full kernel-level traces and stack annotations.
3) Run an accelerated microbenchmark run simulating the observed concurrency shape (see Benchmark scenarios).
4) Produce a short profiling ticket with attached traces, affected kernels, and suggested mitigations.

Example CLI to collect kernel histogram from node: (shell snippet)

sudo redwoodctl node-telemetry --node gpu-17 --metrics kernel_dispatch_histogram --window 60s > traces/kernel_hist_60s.json

Benchmark scenarios and acceptance criteria:

We maintain a small canonical suite used by Decision Fabric to validate degradations. Each scenario is a replay corpus + traffic shape + expected quality delta. Execute using the runtime benchmark harness: redwood-bench.

Scenarios (representative):
- Interactive chat (burst): median seq_len 40, concurrency 250, baseline p95 latency target: 350ms. Acceptable soft-fail p95: 700ms, quality drop measured by prompt eval: <4% absolute BLEU/ROC-AUC delta.
- Long-form generation (sustained): median seq_len 800, concurrency 40, baseline p95 latency target: 900ms. Soft-fail allowed to increase latency to 1600ms but quality metric drop must be <6%.
- Embedding bulk: 1k documents over 60s, throughput target 20k embeddings/s. Soft-fail fallback to batched-async must keep throughput >= 65% of baseline and error rate <0.5%.

Benchmark metadata table (text):
- Column headers: scenario, baseline_p95_ms, degraded_p95_ms_limit, max_quality_loss_percent, runbook_test_command
- Row example: Interactive chat | 350 | 700 | 4 | redwood-bench --scenario=chat-burst --degrade=quantize-int8 --duration=120s

Runbook: detection, triage, and mitigation steps:

Detection (automated):
1) Alert triggers when Decision Fabric emits more than 5 degradation actions for a tenant within 5 minutes OR node-level GPU memory headroom < 10% sustained for 60s.
2) Pager duty: on-call SRE receives pager if combined signal results in p95 latency > SLO threshold * 1.5 or total errors > 0.5%.

Triage checklist (first 10 minutes):
1) Acknowledge alert and capture top-of-trace logs: decision-fabric events and kernel histograms.
2) Identify scope: tenants affected, routes, kernels, regions.
3) Validate if degradation mode is intentional (rollout, experiment). If intentional, skip to Monitoring - verification.
4) If unintentional, determine quickest reversible mitigation: temporarily widen rollback_window_seconds to 0 and ask Decision Fabric to cancel policies via the control plane.

Mitigation recipes (ordered by safety):
A) Conservative rollback: cancel active degradation policies for the affected tenant and force full-fidelity kernel mapping on a small set of canary nodes.
B) Capacity unlock: evict background batch jobs (eviction priority policy) to recover headroom.
C) Cross-region spill: route 25% of traffic to a warmed remote region with identical model variant.
D) Emergency throttling: apply rate-limiter to low-priority routes only until headroom is restored.

Example control-plane command to cancel a policy:

redwoodctl policy cancel --policy-id df-policy-2026-09 --force --reason "Auto-triggered soft-failure during unexpected kernel regression"

Post-mitigation verification (10-30 minutes):
- Monitor p95 and error rate for affected routes.
- Ensure Decision Fabric logs show no further degradation actions.
- Re-run a focused benchmark replay (30–60s) to ensure the kernel regression is not persistent.

Rollback and patching guidance (for engineering owners):
1) If mitigation reveals an underlying kernel regression, generate an Incident JIRA and assign to kernel team.
2) Patch plan: include minimal reproduction, a small patch branch, unit tests for kernel selection logic, and canary rollout plan (5% -> 25% -> 100% with 30m observation windows).
3) Release notes must include: changed kernel mapping heuristics, new policy IDs, and user-visible behavior notes for tenant support.

Release notes compatibility matrix (short):
- Runtime v2.8.x: supports policy primitives {set_kernel_hint, extend_timeout_ms, set_model_variant}. Known limitation: remote routing hedges require v2.8.3+.
- Runtime v2.9.0+: adds per-tenant rollback-window overrides and improved decision trace correlation.

Known issues and temporary mitigations (operational):
- Issue: kv-cache warmup delay after model-variant swap leads to repeated short degradations. Mitigation: stagger model-variant swaps across shards and pre-warm KV cache via async prefetch (enable_kv_prefetch).
- Issue: quantized kernels show higher variance on very short sequences (<12 tokens). Mitigation: avoid quantized fallback for routes with median seq_len < 20; add exclusion in PolicyDefinition.
- Issue: scheduler preemption can cause priority inversion under heavy spill. Mitigation: enable scheduler credit-bucket smoothing and set preemption_grace_ms=5.

Owner, SLAs, and contacts:
- Primary owner: Runtime Scheduling Team (owner alias: runtime-scheduler@redwood.dev).
- Secondary owner: Observability & Telemetry (telemetry@redwood.dev).
- On-call rota: see /confluence/eng-sre/oncall-and-incident-response/oncall-rotations.
- Production SLOs referenced: p95 latency per-route (service-level), error rate < 0.1% global. Soft-failure SLO relaxation: permitted p95 inflation up to 2x for up to 15 minutes when a controlled policy is active.

Post-incident actions and measurement:
- Create a post-incident summary capturing: root cause hypothesis, timeline of Decision Fabric actions, kernel IDs impacted, mitigation steps applied, and customer impact estimate.
- Add a benchmark replay to the runtime benchmark TV (tracking board) demonstrating before/after metrics and the validated quality delta.
- If mitigation included code changes, add a regression test to the benchmark harness to prevent recurrence.

Suggested follow-ups for engineering teams:
- Kernel team: add unit test for short-sequence variance for quantized kernels.
- Decision Fabric: instrument action confidence and optional A/B rollout percent metadata on each decision.
- Observability: add a derived metric: Decision-Fabric-Action-Rate / minute per tenant and make it a first-class alert.

Appendices:
A. Degradation policy JSON example (control-plane payload):

{
  "policy_name": "quantize-on-high-queue",
  "priority": 120,
  "trigger_signals": ["gpu_queue_ratio>0.85", "kernel_p95>1.4x"],
  "actions": [
    {"type": "set_kernel_hint", "value": "quantized_int8", "scope": "non-critical"},
    {"type": "set_model_variant", "value": "compact-1.3B", "scope": "new-sessions-only"}
  ],
  "rollback_window_seconds": 900
}

B. Quick checklist for runbook runners:
- Capture Decision Fabric event IDs and attach to incident ticket.
- Confirm whether a rollout or experiment could be the source.
- If patching kernels, verify canary nodes have full trace sampling enabled.

Related pages and references:
- Runtime topology and shard placement (runtime-op-pathways-and-shard-topology-2024)
- Runtime deployment circuit breakers (runtime-deployment-circuit-breakers-and-sla-fallback-playbook-2026)
- Kernel selection observability contract (kernel-telemetry-annotation-guidelines-2025)

Document maintenance:
- Owner (Runtime Scheduling Team) reviews annually and after any major kernel or Decision Fabric change.
- Minimum revision cadence: when runtime major version bumps or when new policy primitives are added.

End of document.

title: Runbook: Cutting a Runtime LTS Patch Release (Serving Runtime)
content:
## Purpose
This runbook describes the end-to-end procedure to cut a **Runtime LTS patch release** (example: `1.18.1-lts`) from an LTS branch (example: `runtime-1.18-lts`). It is designed for Release Engineering + Runtime + SRE to produce:
- A patch containing **approved backports only** (security, Sev1/Sev2 reliability, correctness fixes)
- **Reproducible, auditable** artifacts (checksums/signatures/provenance; SBOM where applicable)
- **Perf-validated** binaries (gated benchmark suite + waiver workflow)
- Enterprise-grade **slower-change release notes**
- Coordinated rollouts across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private packaging

## Scope
Applies to:
- LTS patch releases for the serving runtime (kernel + scheduling + runtime core)
- Standard monthly cadence patches and out-of-band security hotfixes

Not covered:
- Cutting a new LTS branch (see ADR-027)
- Feature releases on `main`

## Roles and responsibilities (RACI)
**Release Manager (RM)**: Connor O'Brien (primary), Devon Price (backup)
- Owns timeline, patch contents lock, gate status, final go/no-go, publication

**Runtime Approvers**
- Kernel: Hiro Tanaka
- Scheduling: Sofia Ivanova
- Architecture: Noah Patel

**CI/Build**: Sahana Iyer
- Release-branch CI, deterministic builds, provenance/signing key workflow

**Perf Gates**: Marcus Reed (owner), Claire Dubois / Jonas Weber (advisors)
- Benchmark execution, noise analysis, threshold/waiver recommendation

**SRE**: Sean Gallagher (primary), Rafael Mendes (escalation manager)
- Release readiness review, rollout monitoring, incident-driven backport escalation

**Docs/Release Notes**: Elliot Price
- Release notes compilation, taxonomy compliance, known issues alignment

**Customer-facing comms**
- Support: Dev Patel
- Enterprise CS: Rachel Kim
- AEs: Avery Johnson / Hannah Schmitt

## Definitions
**Sev1**: Crash/data corruption/security-critical issue causing production outage or unsafe operation for customers.
**Sev2**: High-impact correctness/availability issue with significant customer impact or high likelihood of escalation.
**LTS patch**: `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH-lts` (example: `1.18.1-lts`) released from `runtime-<MAJOR>.<MINOR>-lts`.

## Preconditions / Required access
Before starting, verify:
1) You have release permissions for:
   - `redwood` runtime repo release branches
   - Artifact publishing buckets/registries (Hosted + Private)
   - Signing/checksum pipeline (key access via least-privilege job or break-glass approval)
2) Perf runner capacity is available for the patch window (coordinate with Infra/SRE if capacity constrained).
3) Backport candidates for the patch have:
   - `backport-candidate` label
   - an approved risk score + test plan per LTS policy
   - named approvers from Runtime + Release Eng + (if perf risk) Perf owner

## Patch cadence and calendar
Default cadence (steady state):
- Patch week runs Monday–Thursday (publish Thursday)
- Out-of-band security patch: publish as soon as gates and approvals complete (see "Emergency security hotfix" section)

Recommended timeline (standard patch):
- **T-7 days**: candidate list frozen for perf-risk changes; start cherry-picks
- **T-4 days**: CI green on release branch; RC build cut
- **T-2 days**: perf gates complete; release notes draft circulated
- **T-0**: publish artifacts + notes; begin rollout

---

## Step 0 — Identify target branch + version
1) Confirm the LTS line:
   - Example: `runtime-1.18-lts`
2) Determine next patch version:
   - If current is `1.18.0-lts`, next is `1.18.1-lts`
   - If re-cut is needed, use `1.18.1-lts+rebuild.<N>` **internally** (do not expose to customers) and only publish a single canonical `1.18.1-lts` externally.
3) Open a release tracking ticket (or update the existing epic) and link:
   - candidate list
   - perf gate run IDs
   - release notes draft

RM checklist (Step 0):
- [ ] Branch + version agreed
- [ ] Release window communicated to Runtime + SRE + Support/CS

---

## Step 1 — Create/refresh local release workspace
Commands (example; adjust remote names as needed):
1) Fetch latest:
   - `git fetch origin --prune`
2) Checkout LTS branch:
   - `git checkout runtime-1.18-lts`
   - `git pull --ff-only origin runtime-1.18-lts`
3) Ensure release tooling is up to date:
   - `./tools/release --version`
   - `./tools/backport-helper --help`

If the release branch is newly created or CI secrets were rotated, verify CI passes on a no-op commit before proceeding.

---

## Step 2 — Finalize patch candidate set (content lock)
Goal: lock the list of backports early enough to avoid churn and perf noise.

Input sources:
- `lts-backport-candidate` tracker (sheet)
- Support/CS escalations (Sev mapping + repro)
- SRE incident review outcomes

Rules of thumb:
- Prefer minimal diffs. A small correctness fix beats a broad refactor.
- Avoid kernel autotune or scheduling heuristic changes unless they are explicitly justified as stability fixes and are perf-gated.
- Any change that could impact throughput/latency must include a perf plan and expected deltas.

RM procedure:
1) Export candidate list into the release ticket (PR links + summary).
2) For each candidate, record:
   - severity (security/Sev1/Sev2)
   - expected impact
   - tests added/updated
   - perf risk (low/med/high)
   - required approvers
3) Announce **content lock** in `#eng-releases` and tag approvers.

Content lock message template:
- "Content lock for `runtime-1.18.1-lts` at <time>. Any additions require RM approval + updated perf plan + SRE acknowledgment."

---

## Step 3 — Cherry-pick backports onto the LTS branch
Preferred method: automation helper.

### 3.1 Create backport PRs (recommended)
1) For each approved PR on main, run:
   - `./tools/backport-helper --target runtime-1.18-lts --pr <PR_NUMBER>`
2) The helper should:
   - create a backport branch
   - cherry-pick commits
   - open a PR with backport template
   - apply labels (`lts`, `backport`, `security` if relevant)

### 3.2 Manual cherry-pick (only when needed)
1) `git checkout -b backport/<topic>-to-runtime-1.18-lts`
2) `git cherry-pick -x <commitSha>`
3) Resolve conflicts. Keep the patch minimal; avoid opportunistic cleanups.
4) Push and open PR.

### 3.3 Backport PR requirements (must-haves)
- PR description includes:
  - Root cause
  - Risk assessment
  - Test plan and evidence (CI link)
  - Perf expectations (if any)
- Includes or references a regression test when feasible.
- Approvals:
  - Code owner(s)
  - RM sign-off
  - SRE sign-off for operational risk OR customer-impacting changes

RM checklist (Step 3):
- [ ] All backports merged to `runtime-1.18-lts`
- [ ] No open high-risk backport without explicit waiver plan

---

## Step 4 — Release branch CI and deterministic build gates
Goal: ensure the branch is green with release-branch-specific workflows.

### 4.1 Kick CI on the branch head
1) Confirm required workflows are enabled for release branches:
   - unit/integration
   - scheduler smoke suite
   - build reproducibility job
   - container image build (staging)
   - SBOM generation (or stub where supported)
2) Run/verify:
   - "Release Branch CI" workflow is green on HEAD commit

### 4.2 Deterministic build validation
Requirements:
- Build artifacts must be traceable to:
  - git SHA
  - toolchain version
  - build recipe inputs
- Checksums produced for each published artifact.

If deterministic build check fails:
- Stop the release.
- Engage Sahana Iyer + Infra support (permissions/secrets/toolchain mismatch are common causes).

---

## Step 5 — Cut an RC (release candidate) build
Purpose: a stable snapshot for perf gates and final verification.

Procedure:
1) Choose the RC tag (internal):
   - Example: `runtime-1.18.1-lts-rc.1`
2) Create tag on the release branch head:
   - `git tag -a runtime-1.18.1-lts-rc.1 -m "RC 1 for 1.18.1-lts"`
   - `git push origin runtime-1.18.1-lts-rc.1`
3) Trigger build pipeline for RC artifacts (staging only).
4) Record artifact URIs (staging) in the release ticket.

RC verification checklist:
- [ ] Version string in runtime reports `1.18.1-lts-rc.1`
- [ ] Basic smoke (startup, model load, simple generation) passes
- [ ] No unexpected dependency bumps

---

## Step 6 — Run perf gates (required for publish)
Perf gates are mandatory for LTS patches unless explicitly waived by RM + Perf owner + SRE.

### 6.1 Gate inputs
- Base: last published LTS patch (example `1.18.0-lts`)
- Candidate: current RC (example `1.18.1-lts-rc.1`)
- Canonical workloads:
  - short prompts / high QPS (batching sensitivity)
  - mixed prompt lengths (scheduler fairness)
  - long context (KV cache pressure)
  - tool-calling/structured output (tokenization + streaming)
- GPU coverage (minimum): A10, L4, A100, H100 (or current fleet equivalents)

### 6.2 Thresholds (summary; see perf gates doc for full details)
Default fail thresholds (unless workload-specific):
- p50 latency regression: > 2% (fail)
- p95 latency regression: > 3% (fail)
- Throughput regression (tokens/s): > 3% (fail)
- Error rate increase: any statistically significant increase (fail)

Noise handling:
- If results are borderline and known noisy, rerun once on isolated runners.
- If still borderline, document variance analysis and request waiver (see below).

### 6.3 Waiver workflow (exception)
Waivers are rare for LTS. If needed:
1) Provide:
   - gate output artifacts
   - rerun evidence
   - analysis (why acceptable)
   - customer impact assessment
   - rollback plan
2) Approvals required:
   - RM
   - Perf owner (Marcus Reed)
   - SRE (Sean Gallagher or delegate)
3) Note waiver explicitly in release notes under "Performance".

RM checklist (Step 6):
- [ ] Perf gates PASS (or approved waiver recorded)
- [ ] Gate artifacts linked in the release ticket

---

## Step 7 — Compile and validate release notes (LTS format)
Release notes for LTS must be "slower-change" and enterprise-friendly.

### 7.1 Generate initial notes
1) Run the release notes generator in LTS mode:
   - `./tools/release-notes --lts --from 1.18.0-lts --to runtime-1.18.1-lts-rc.1`
2) Ensure each change is categorized:
- Security
- Reliability/Correctness
- Performance
- Operational/Observability
- Known issues / Workarounds
- Compatibility / Upgrade notes

### 7.2 Curate summaries
Requirements:
- No raw internal jargon without context.
- Include customer-facing symptom + impact + mitigation.
- Include whether change is behavior-preserving or not.

### 7.3 Update known issues
- Add any discovered RC issues that will not be fixed in this patch.
- Ensure the known-issues page links from release notes.

### 7.4 Review and approvals
- Elliot Price owns editing.
- RM + Runtime leads sign off on accuracy.
- Support/CS provides a quick scan for clarity and “what do I tell a customer?”

Release notes must include:
- Patch identifier and date
- Git SHA(s) and artifact IDs
- Compatibility matrix pointer (runtime ↔ installer/Helm ↔ model catalog constraints)
- Rollback guidance summary

---

## Step 8 — Build final artifacts and sign/checksum/provenance
Publishing requires auditable artifacts.

### 8.1 Promote RC to final
If no code changes since RC:
- Use the RC commit SHA as final.
If changes are required:
- Cut a new RC (`rc.2`) and rerun gates impacted by the change (minimum: CI; perf if perf-sensitive).

### 8.2 Final tag
1) Create final tag:
- `git tag -a runtime-1.18.1-lts -m "Runtime 1.18.1-lts"`
- `git push origin runtime-1.18.1-lts`

### 8.3 Artifact build (production)
- Build runtime containers/images for Hosted, Dedicated, and Private distribution channels.
- Generate:
  - checksums (SHA256)
  - signature (per signing standard)
  - provenance metadata (build attestation)
  - SBOM (where supported)

### 8.4 Verification (must-do)
RM (or CI/build owner) verifies:
- Checksums match downloaded artifacts
- Signature verification passes using documented verification method
- Artifact metadata includes:
  - git tag and SHA
  - build timestamp
  - builder identity
  - dependency/toolchain IDs

If verification fails:
- Stop release.
- Treat as Sev2 internal process incident (auditable artifacts are a core LTS promise).

---

## Step 9 — Publish release notes and internal distribution
### 9.1 Publish release notes
- Publish in the LTS release notes area and link:
  - artifact download locations
  - checksums/signature instructions
  - known issues page

### 9.2 Internal announcement (required)
Post to:
- `#eng-releases`
- `#support`
- `#customer-success`
- `#sales` (if relevant to open deals)

Announcement template:
**Subject:** Runtime `1.18.1-lts` released
- Summary: 2–5 bullets of what changed
- Impact: who should upgrade and why
- Rollout plan: Hosted/Dedicated schedule; Private availability
- Known issues: link
- Verification: checksums/signature link
- Support guidance: “If customer asks X, say Y” link to Support playbook

### 9.3 External/customer comms (as applicable)
Coordinate with CS/AEs for customers pinned to LTS:
- Provide release notes link
- Provide upgrade + rollback guidance link
- Provide whether the patch is **mandatory** or **optional**

Criteria for “mandatory”:
- Security patch with credible exploitation risk
- Sev1 affecting a meaningful fraction of LTS deployments
- Data corruption/correctness bug with silent failure mode

---

## Step 10 — Rollout execution and monitoring
Rollout must be staged and observable.

### 10.1 Hosted
- Start with internal canary traffic (or dedicated canary project) for 30–60 minutes.
- Expand to small percentage by region.
- Monitor:
  - error rate
  - p50/p95 latency
  - throughput
  - GPU memory/fragmentation metrics
  - scheduler queue depth/backpressure
- If stable, proceed to full rollout.

### 10.2 Dedicated
- Notify SRE + CS of rollout start window.
- Roll out by customer tier/region according to change-control agreements.
- If a Dedicated customer has strict change windows, schedule upgrade explicitly.

### 10.3 Private
- Ensure installer/Helm pinning references the new tag.
- Publish artifact verification instructions (checksums/signature/SBOM notes) in the Private upgrade guidance.
- Ensure rollback path is validated (previous LTS patch remains available).

### 10.4 Rollback criteria
Rollback immediately if:
- Crash loop or elevated fatal errors in canary
- p95 latency regression exceeds threshold and is reproducible (not noise)
- correctness regression identified

Rollback procedure (high level):
- Hosted/Dedicated: revert runtime image tag to previous patch; drain/rotate
- Private: instruct customers to pin back to prior patch (provide exact tag + checksums)

RM checklist (Step 10):
- [ ] Rollout started with canary and monitored
- [ ] Rollout completed or paused with documented rationale
- [ ] Any rollback executed is communicated to Support/CS immediately

---

## Step 11 — Closeout and post-release hygiene
Within 24–48 hours:
1) Update the LTS patch tracking ticket with:
- final tag + SHA
- links to artifacts + checksums
- perf gate artifacts
- rollout notes
2) Ensure known issues list is current.
3) If any waivers were used, open follow-up tasks to reduce future need (benchmark stability, targeted tests, etc.).
4) If release had incident/near-miss, schedule a lightweight retro in `#eng-releases`.

---

## Emergency security hotfix procedure (out-of-band)
When a security issue qualifies for LTS patching (per security policy):
1) Establish a secure coordination channel (restricted Slack/Doc as appropriate).
2) Content lock is immediate; only security fix and directly required support commits allowed.
3) Shorten gates only with explicit sign-off:
   - CI must still be green
   - Perf gates: run minimum representative subset unless the fix is clearly perf-neutral
4) Approvals required:
   - RM
   - Runtime lead (Mateo Alvarez delegate acceptable)
   - Security sponsor (Dr. Aisha Rahman or Hanae Suzuki delegate)
   - SRE
5) Release notes:
   - include CVE or internal identifier
   - describe impact and mitigation clearly
   - state whether patch is mandatory
6) Comms:
   - notify Support/CS immediately
   - provide customer-ready language and verification instructions

---

## Appendix A — Quick “Release Manager” checklist (printable)
Pre-flight
- [ ] Version + branch confirmed
- [ ] Candidate list finalized + content lock announced
- [ ] Required approvers identified

Build + test
- [ ] All backports merged
- [ ] Release branch CI green
- [ ] RC tag created and artifacts built (staging)
- [ ] Perf gates PASS (or waiver approved and documented)

Docs + publish
- [ ] Release notes generated + curated + approved
- [ ] Known issues updated
- [ ] Final tag created
- [ ] Production artifacts built
- [ ] Checksums/signature/provenance verified
- [ ] Release notes published with artifact links

Rollout
- [ ] Hosted canary + monitoring
- [ ] Dedicated rollout plan executed/communicated
- [ ] Private artifacts available + pin/rollback guidance verified

Close
- [ ] Ticket updated with links and outcomes
- [ ] Retro scheduled if needed

---

## Appendix B — Common failure modes and what to do
1) **Release-branch CI fails but main is green**
- Likely: secret permissions, toolchain mismatch, release workflow differences
- Action: engage CI/build owner; avoid bypassing release-branch checks

2) **Perf gate flake/noise**
- Rerun once on isolated runners
- Compare against baseline variance
- If still noisy, escalate to perf owner; do not publish on ambiguous results

3) **Cherry-pick conflicts on scheduler/kernel code**
- Stop and reassess whether the backport is still minimal
- Prefer rewriting as a smaller targeted patch on LTS rather than forcing a large conflict resolution

4) **Artifact verification mismatch**
- Treat as blocking
- Rebuild from clean environment; confirm tag/SHA match; validate signing pipeline inputs

---

Contact points
- Release Eng: Connor O'Brien (primary), Devon Price (backup)
- CI/Build: Sahana Iyer
- Perf gates: Marcus Reed
- SRE: Sean Gallagher / Rafael Mendes
- Support workflow: Dev Patel

title: Fidelity containment and cost-feedback playbook
content:
Overview
--------
This playbook defines a structured, testable approach for containing output fidelity regressions while responding to cost and capacity signals in Redwood's serving runtime. The goal is to preserve customer-visible quality within defined tolerances while allowing the runtime to reduce unit cost and maintain latency SLOs under stress.

Intended audience
- Runtime SREs and oncall engineers
- Serving runtime product engineers
- Applied ML / model-onboarding engineers responsible for model variants
- Solutions engineers running Dedicated/Private rollouts

Scope and definitions
- Fidelity: measurable customer-facing quality of generated text or embeddings (proxy signals include embedding cosine similarity drift, eval-set pass rate, hallucination detectors, and automated eval metrics like ROUGE/BLEU/EM/accuracy on canned checks).
- Cost signal: per-request (or per-token) cost estimate derived from kernel accounting and model variant price multipliers.
- Containment action: an automated or manual change that reduces runtime resource use or switches model variant to a cheaper/less-fidelitous option (examples: quantized variant, shorter max tokens, trimmed sampling temperature, fall back to smaller model).
- Allowed fidelity window: policy-defined bounds (absolute or relative) that define tolerable degradation for a given customer tier/route.

Key principles
1. Prioritize customer-facing quality over short-term cost savings. Containment actions must be reversible and accompanied by quality monitoring.
2. Make containment decisions observable and auditable: every automated action must produce a traceable event and justification.
3. Apply progressive containment: prefer parameter tuning and cache/batching before model-variant switch.
4. Keep inexpensive, fast rollback paths and an explicit manual escalation path for high-impact customers.

Observable signals and thresholds
- Primary signals: p50/p95 latency, p99 latency, tokens/second served, per-token-cost estimate, model variant error-rate on canary prompt set, embedding drift (cosine similarity delta), auto-eval pass rate.
- Secondary signals: kernel queue length, GPU occupancy, KV cache hit ratio, request retries, gRPC error rates.

Minimum policy thresholds (example defaults)
| Signal | Warning threshold | Containment threshold | Notes |
|--------|-------------------:|----------------------:|-------|
| p95 latency (route) | 350 ms | 600 ms | measured at route-level aggregation over 1m windows |
| p99 latency | 900 ms | 2s | escalation if sustained >5 minutes |
| Per-token cost (moving 5m avg) | +15% vs baseline | +40% vs baseline | baseline is 30d rolling median |
| Embedding drift (cos sim drop) | 0.03 | 0.07 | evaluated on route-specific reference corpus |
| Canary eval pass-rate drop | 5 ppt | 15 ppt | ppt = percentage points |

Containment matrix (progressive actions)
1. Soft tuning (no model change): reduce max_response_tokens by 10–30%, reduce sampling temperature or top-p, tighten repetition_penalty, enable prefix/KV cache prefetch for hot routes.
2. Batch and cache aggression: increase batching window by 10–25% for non-interactive routes, enable shared prefix caching when identity-safe.
3. Model micro-variants: switch to quantized or 8-bit floating variant of the same model.
4. Model downgrade: route to smaller model family with documented fidelity/cost tradeoff.
5. Route-based rate limiting: apply slow-path throttle to non-critical traffic classes.
6. Emergency low-fidelity fallback: deterministic n-gram based summarization or templated replies for extreme outages.

Automation policy template (YAML-like example)
```
# policy_name: fidelity-cost-feedback-2026
triggers:
  - metric: per_token_cost_5m
    comparator: ">="
    threshold: 1.40  # 1.0 = baseline
    window: 300
    severity: high
  - metric: p95_latency_route
    comparator: ">="
    threshold: 0.6  # seconds
    window: 60
    severity: medium
actions_sequence:
  - id: "soft_tune_1"
    action: "reduce_max_tokens"
    params: { percent: 20 }
    rollback_on: ["canary_eval_drop_ppt >= 10"]
  - id: "enable_batching_aggressive"
    action: "increase_batch_window_ms"
    params: { add_ms: 15 }
  - id: "variant_quantized"
    action: "switch_model_variant"
    params: { variant: "quant-8bit" }
  - id: "variant_downgrade"
    action: "switch_model"
    params: { model_family: "redwood-lite" }
  - id: "emergency_template_fallback"
    action: "apply_template_fallback"
    params: { template_id: "low_fidelity_fallback_v1" }
```

Operational runbook (play-by-play)
1) Detection and initial triage (Oncall)\- Review alert payload: identify affected routes, model variants, and customer tiers.\- Confirm signal: check p95/p99 windows, per-token cost spike, and kernel-level metrics (GPU queue length, occupancy).\- Run quick baseline: compare to rolling 30d baseline and to same-window previous day.

2) Canary evaluation (automated/manual)\- Run the canonical canary prompt set for each impacted route against current runtime and candidate containment variants. Canary outputs to be scored by automated eval harness.\- Pass criteria: no more than X ppt drop in canary pass-rate for Standard tier; less strict thresholds for internal/beta routes.

3) Apply progressive containment\- Execute actions in the containment matrix one step at a time. After each step, wait a stabilization window (default 60–180s for soft tuning; 5–10 minutes for model variant switches) and re-evaluate canary metrics and the primary signals.\- Required observability: annotate the deployment/trace with the containment_action id and reason.

4) Monitor and iterate\- If metrics recover within thresholds, retain the change for a policy-defined cooldown (default 30 minutes) while running a more comprehensive quality sweep (10–30m).\- If metrics do not improve or quality regression exceeds rollback_on conditions, immediately roll back the last action and escalate to oncall escalation path.

5) Escalation path
- Pager duty: runtime-sre@redwood.com (primary)
- If repeat-size event or large customer impact: paging product-eng lead and solutions engineering for affected customers.
- For legal/security impact (data exposure): notify security@redwood.com immediately.

Manual rollback checklist
- Identify exact action to rollback (action id and timestamp).
- Ensure no upstream automation will re-apply the action during rollback window. Use the feature-flag lock: \"runtime.containment.lock\" = true.
- Execute rollback and validate canary and live traffic metrics for 15 minutes.
- Note the rollback in incident timeline with justification.

Testing and preflight requirements
- Every containment action must have an associated unit test in the runtime-autotest suite and a canary-run scenario in the benchmark harness.
- Poison tests: synthetic low-fidelity queries must be included to ensure fallback templates don’t leak sensitive info.
- Load test runbook: schedule a weekly simulated event where containment policies are exercised end-to-end in staging using traffic replays.

Observability and dashboards (minimum set)
- Route health dashboard: per-route p50/p95/p99 latency, per-token-cost trend, request volume, KV cache hit rate.
- Canary quality dashboard: rolling pass-rate for canary prompts per route and per-customer-tier.
- Containment actions log: chronological view of automated/manual actions, actors, and outcomes (success/failure, rollback).
- Kernel telemetry correlation: cross-filter by trace id to observe kernel-level queue depth, GPU occupancy, and active kernel variant.

Audit and compliance
- All containment decisions (automated or manual) must emit an audit event with: action_id, actor (automation or user), triggered_by (metric id and value), route, affected_customers, pre_action_metrics, post_action_metrics, canary_results. Events are retained 365 days by default.

Ownership and contacts
- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime (runtime-sre rotation), contact runtime-oncall@example.redwood.com
- Model variant owner: applied-ml-and-evals/model-onboarding team
- Product escalation: product-engineering lead for affected product line (contact list in team wiki)

Post-incident analysis (required for any containment that persisted > 1 hour or affected > 5 customers)\- Produce a short incident summary with root cause hypothesis, timeline of containment actions, observed impact on quality/cost, and recommended permanent mitigations (e.g., model retraining, kernel tuning, new model variant).\- Required metrics: cost delta, customer-visible fidelity delta, number of rollbacks, time-to-stabilize.

Playbook example: small incident walkthrough
Scenario: sudden token cost spike on "chat-completion" route causing p95 latency to rise to 750ms and per-token cost +60%
1. Alert fired (policy: per_token_cost_5m >= 1.4)
2. Oncall runs canary set: small drop in canary pass-rate (6 ppt)
3. Apply soft_tune_1 (reduce_max_tokens 20%)
4. Re-evaluate 90s later: p95 reduced to 420ms, per-token cost reduced to +18%, canary drop stable at 7 ppt (within Standard threshold)
5. Place containment on 30m cooldown and notify product for customer comms if effected customers > 2
6. Post-incident: schedule a variant benchmark comparing quant-8bit and redwood-lite on the exact request surface.

Appendix A: sample CLI commands
- Query affected routes:
  rcli routes list --filter "metric:per_token_cost>1.2" --since 10m
- Run canary prompt set (local harness):
  python infra/tools/canary_runner.py --route chat-completion --variant current --output /tmp/canary.json
- Apply containment action (manual override):
  rcli runtime contain apply --route chat-completion --action reduce_max_tokens --percent 20 --note "manual containment by oncall"
- Lock automation to prevent reapplication:
  rcli feature-flag set runtime.containment.lock true --expiry 30m --note "incident rollback in progress"

Appendix B: policy parameter guidance
- Window sizing: prefer shorter windows (60–300s) for latency-driven triggers, longer windows (5–15m) for cost signals to avoid transient noise.
- Canary set construction: include 15–50 prompts per route with a mix of short/long sequences, edge-case tokens, and privacy-sensitive examples that must never be returned in fallback templates.
- Tiered thresholds: enterprise customers have half the allowed fidelity-degradation window compared to standard/free tiers.

Appendix C: related artifacts and links
- Execution stitching and fallback orchestration (design doc) — see related_pages for link id
- Canary harness repository: git@github.com:redwood/canary-harness
- Runtime containment audit sink: kafka://infra.events.runtime.containment

Revision history
- 2026-02-15: created by Priya Desai
- 2026-05-20: added automation template and extended escalation with security contact (Marcus Chen review)
- 2026-11-30: tightened default thresholds and added audit retention note (Ana-Maria Popescu review)

End of document

title: Cold-start Quality Degradation Detection and Recovery Runbook
content:
Summary:
This runbook describes how to detect, triage, and recover from quality degradations that are correlated with cold-start events in the runtime (examples: increased hallucination rate, lower QA pass rate, deterministic prompt-prefix regressions after model swap, or output truncation tied to KV cache misses). It is focused on production incidents where client-facing correctness metrics drop following service restarts, model swaps, autoscaler-driven scale-ups, or routing to undersized warm pools.

Scope and intent:
- Scope: hosted/Dedicated/Private deployments running the Redwood serving runtime. Applicable to model swaps, node restarts, autoscaling events, or any scenario where a high proportion of requests experience cold execution (empty KV/embedding caches, unprimed kernels).
- Intent: detect regressions quickly, preserve customer-facing SLOs, and restore previous-quality behavior with minimal disruption. This runbook prioritizes safe, reversible actions and clarifies ownership.

Who owns this runbook:
- First responder: serving-runtime oncall (eng-serving-runtime team)
- Escalation: runtime-sre lead, model-onboarding owner, customer-success for impacted customers

Key signals to monitor (detection):
1) Behavioral quality metrics (primary):
   - QA pass rate on synthetic prompt-sets (rolling 5m and 1h buckets). Alert if 1h pass rate drops >20% relative to 6h baseline.
   - Hallucination indicator: fraction of responses matching negative heuristics (nonsense score, repeated tokens). Alert if >5% of responses exceed hallucination threshold and correlated with cold-start tags.
2) Telemetry and execution signals (correlated with cold-start):
   - KV cache miss rate: per-shard and per-model KV miss rate spike (Prometheus: runtime_kvcache_miss_rate). Alert if >= 80% of requests for a cohort are cold for >10min.
   - Prefix latency spike: token-latency for first N tokens (token_index <= 32) up by >2x baseline.
   - Model swap events: recent model variant switch or kernel rollouts (eventlog entries).
3) Sampling-based checks (low-volume but high fidelity):
   - Shadow evaluation: sample requests shadowed to previous model/variant; if shadowed outputs differ on correctness checks by >15% relative to live, flag as regression.

Detection playbook (automated alerts and triage):
- Automated alerts to page oncall when any primary signal triggers. Alerts should include:
  - affected model(s)/variant(s) and cohort IDs
  - recent autoscaler/node events in last 10 min
  - KV cache miss heatmap and per-shard error rate
  - attached sample of 10 failed responses (anonymized)

Initial triage (oncall checklist):
1) Validate alert: confirm metric anomalies using PromQL and sampling endpoints. Quick PromQL queries: 
   - QA pass rate: sum(rate(eval_qa_pass_total[5m])) / sum(rate(eval_requests_total[5m]))
   - KV cold fraction: increase(runtime_kvcache_miss_rate[10m]) > 0.2
2) Correlate with infra events: check cluster events, node restarts, pod reschedules, and model rollout timestamps (kubectl get events, /ops/eventlog).
3) Isolate scope: check whether issue affects single model variant, model family, single region, or all customers. Use per-route and per-token tagging.
4) Collect traces & dumps: capture 30s full trace for a failing request pattern (trace-id), and export kernel telemetry and KV warmup state for the affected shard(s). CLI snippets below.

Immediate mitigations (order of preference — safer first):
1) Route traffic to warm pool or previously healthy variant:
   - Use routing policy to send impacted percentage to warm pool while keeping the rest on primary for canary validation.
   - Command (control plane): redwood route update --model <model> --variant prev-stable --percent 30 --reason "cold-start-quality-rollback"
2) Force KV prefill for high-impact cohorts: schedule an immediate prefill job for affected keys (see prefill command below). Prefill avoids cold KV misses that often trigger hallucination in long-context models.
   - Prefill CLI: redwood runtime prefill-kv --shard <shard-id> --keys-file /tmp/prefill-keys.json --priority high
3) Temporarily widen quality SLO to reduce batching/fusion: reduce concurrency and batching for the affected variant to reduce kernel cold micro-behavior that affects output shape.
   - config patch (example YAML snippet):
     batcher:
       max_batch_tokens: 4096
       target_latency_ms: 50
       enable_prefill: false
4) Rollback model variant if the degradation coincides with a recent variant rollout and automated canary validation fails. Rollback is disruptive; prefer routing to warm pool when customer impact is partial.

Commands & data-collection recipes:
- Capture a full trace (oncall machine with access):
  curl -sS "https://obs-api.redwood.internal/trace/collect?model=<model>&window=30s&sample=1" -H "Authorization: Bearer $OBS_KEY" > /tmp/trace.json
- Export KV state for shard:
  redwood infra kvcache dump --shard <shard-id> --output /tmp/kvcache-shard-123.dump
- Run batch of synthetic QA prompts against previous-stable variant:
  redwood eval run --model <model>:prev-stable --prompt-file qa-failure-sample.json --concurrency 5 --out /tmp/eval-prev.json

Operational controls (threshold table — editable):
- This table lists the default thresholds used by the detection engine. Operate conservatively and update only after post-incident review.

| signal | alert threshold | severity | default action |
|---|---:|---|---|
| 1h QA pass drop vs baseline | >20% absolute drop | Sev2 | page oncall; run shadow eval |
| KV cold fraction (cohort) | >80% cold requests for 10m | Sev1 | route to warm pool; prefill KV |
| Prefix token latency change | >2x for token_idx < 32 | Sev2 | decrease batch size; reduce concurrency |
| Shadow-vs-live correctness delta | >15% | Sev1 | immediate rollback or route to prev-variant |

Note: The table above should be managed in the runtime-config repo (config/runtime/coldstart-detection.yaml). Sample YAML fields: 

signal_thresholds:
  qa_pass_drop_pct: 20
  kvcold_fraction_threshold: 0.8
  prefix_latency_multiplier: 2.0
  shadow_delta_pct: 15

Recovery playbook (step-by-step):
1) If KV cold fraction is main driver: run prefill job, validate reduced KV miss rate, then gradually increase traffic to variant.
2) If model swap is root cause and prior variant performs better on shadow eval: route 100% to previous variant and open a rollback change in the deployment tracker.
3) If the issue is due to kernel rollout or scheduling change: pause the kernel rollout, set scheduler to conservative profile, and engage kernel owner to examine kernel changes.
4) If widespread and unknown: enable temporary degradation mode that firms up safety heuristics (shorten response length, add conservative decoding params like top_p=0.8) while engineers investigate.

Post-incident actions (postmortem checklist):
- Create a postmortem within 72 hours with: timeline, contributing causes, sampling artifacts, KV dump, traces, rollout IDs, and remediation owner.
- Update the thresholds table if alert was noisy or too lax.
- Add targeted integration tests to the benchmark suite: shadow-evaluation scenarios that mimic the failed cohort shape.
- Schedule a follow-up: kernel scheduling replay across recorded traces to reproduce the behavior in the lab.

Runbook escalation matrix and SLA:
- Sev1 (customer-impacting correctness): page oncall immediately, 15 min ack, 1 hour mitigation or rollback.
- Sev2 (degraded QA but limited subset): page oncall, 30 min ack, mitigation within 4 hours.

Known gotchas and heuristics:
- Small cohorts (low traffic) produce noisy QA signals; require a minimum sampling floor of 200 requests/hour before auto-alerting.
- Not every KV miss spike implies hallucination — cross-check with decoding entropy and repeated token heuristics.
- Prefill can be expensive. Use prioritized prefill for high-value cohorts only.

Examples and case studies (short):
- Case: Model-variant X rollout (2025-08-13) produced a 35% QA pass drop for long-context summarization requests. Root cause: optimistic kernel fusion that skipped boundary prefetch for windowed attention. Recovery: immediate rollback to prev-stable, patch to prefetch check in kernel 2.1. Patch released with canary and shadow checks.

References and links:
- Prefill job operator docs: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/prefill-job-operator-manual
- Cold-start warmup patterns: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/cold-start-warmup-strategies-and-entropy-reduction-2025
- Observability data model: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/runtime-observability-data-model-and-tracebook-2026

Appendix: quick checklist card (for oncall)
1) Verify alert artifacts and sample 10 failing traces.
2) Check KV cold fraction and prefill if >80%
3) Shadow-eval prev-stable variant (5m)
4) Route traffic to warm pool or prev-stable variant (30% -> 100% if good)
5) If kernel rollout correlated, pause rollout and contact kernel owner
6) Open postmortem and attach kvcache dump + traces

Contact list:
- serving-runtime oncall: #oncall-serving-runtime (Slack)
- runtime-sre lead: diego.alvarez@redwood.ai
- kernel owners: kernel-team@redwood.ai
- model-onboarding: models@redwood.ai

Document maintenance:
- Owner: eng-serving-runtime runbooks guild (rotate quarterly)
- Review cadence: quarterly or after any Sev1 incident tied to cold-start quality

End of document.

title: Operator live-trace collection and rollback playbook
content:
Summary

This runbook describes the on-call operator workflow for collecting live inferences traces (live-traces), extracting high-fidelity kernel/dispatch telemetry, performing a safe canary or full rollback of runtime/kernel changes, and verifying SLA preservation. It is intended for SREs and runtime engineers running live incidents where a kernel, scheduler, or runtime rollout is suspected of degrading latency, throughput, or correctness.

Scope

- Applies to the production inference runtime (service: inference-runtime-v2) across Hosted and Dedicated clusters.
- Covers: live-trace capture, short-term retention, signal triage, automated rollback criteria, manual rollback steps, verification, and post-incident actions.
- Does NOT cover model artifact rollbacks or customer data access procedures. See the release gating doc for those flows.

Ownership and escalation

- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime oncall (team roster: runtime-sre@redwood.com).
- Fallback: runtime-core engineers (runtime-core@redwood.com).
- Pager escalation: follow the oncall rotation. If SLA impact > 5% error budget within 30m, notify on-call manager and SRE lead.

Signals / When to run this playbook

Run this playbook when one or more of the following are observed:

- Tail P99 latency for text.generate or chat.stream exceeds baseline by > 40% for 10+ minutes.
- Error rate (5xx or RPC timeouts) increases above 0.5% absolute and persists 5+ minutes.
- Sudden spike in kernel-level timeouts or NVLink retransmits reported by kernel telemetry.
- Canary or experimental rollout shows divergent latency/cost compared to control group.

Prerequisites and quick checks

- Ensure you have kube and opscli access: kube-context with cluster-admin and opscli >= v1.12.
- Confirm active trace retention window: default retention for live-traces is 2 hours. If the incident is older, check archived trace store (s3://redwood-runtime-traces/archived).
- Check current rollout state: opscli rollout status inference-runtime-v2 --environment=prod
- Confirm SLOs: generation P95 < 200ms, P99 < 850ms, error rate < 0.5%.

Step A — Rapid triage: collect lightweight indicators (0–5 minutes)

1) Pull high-level SLO metrics and recent deployment metadata:

- Grafana panels: inference/slo-overview-prod, kernel/dispatch-health, scheduler/admission-rate.
- CLI queries (examples):
  - opscli metrics query "sum(rate(inference_generation_latency_ms_p99[5m]))" --env=prod
  - kubectl -n runtime get pods -l app=inference-runtime-v2 -o wide

2) Identify suspect deployment(s) and kernel artifact versions:

- opscli rollout list --service=inference-runtime-v2 --env=prod
- If a kernel or runtime image was deployed in the last 30–120 minutes, note the image tag and rollout id.

3) Open a live incident channel and annotate: #inc-runtime-prod and add the rollout id, observed metric deltas, and time window.

Step B — Live-trace capture (5–30 minutes)

Goal: capture a set of 200–500 representative trace samples covering slow tails and error cases. Keep captures focused to reduce overhead.
