1) Select 2–3 representative frontends or routes (e.g., /v1/generate, /v1/chat/stream).
2) Use the trace capture command to start an on-host sampler:

- opscli trace start --service inference-runtime-v2 --routes "/v1/generate,/v1/chat/stream" --duration 30m --sampler=error-first --max-samples 500 --label incident=<INCIDENT_ID>

3) For immediate collection (when rollout is live), prefer error-first sampling to ensure tokenization/kernel failures are captured. For tail-latency troubleshooting, use tail-latency sampler: --sampler=latency-tail --threshold-ms=500.

4) Monitor capture progress and backpressure:

- opscli trace status <trace-id>
- If capture fails due to agent overload, reduce duration to 10m and retry.

5) After capture completes, snapshot raw trace bundle to archive for triage:

- opscli trace export <trace-id> --dest s3://redwood-runtime-traces/incidents/<INCIDENT_ID>/raw.zip

Step C — Signal enrichment and quick attribution (30–90 minutes)

1) Enrich traces with kernel and scheduler telemetry (automatic for live-traces). Use the trace viewer filters:

- Kernel step durations: kernel.exec_ms, kernel.kv_lookup_ms, kernel.copy_ms
- Scheduling signals: scheduler.queue_ms, admission.rejected_count, preempt.count

2) Run the quick attribution queries (examples):

- opscli trace query --trace-id <trace-id> --filter "kernel.exec_ms > 200" --aggregate "count(),p99(kernel.exec_ms)"
- jq filter for trace bundle: jq '.spans[] | select(.tags.kernel_exec_ms>200) | {pod:.host, span:.name, t:.duration_ms}' traces.json

3) Look for these common failure modes:

- Kernel regression: p99 kernel.exec_ms increased while scheduling queue_ms stays stable.
- Admission/backpressure: admission.rejected_count spike, long scheduler.queue_ms leading to timeout.
- KV-cache hot miss storm: many large kv_lookup_ms peaks correlated with model switching.

Decision point: do we rollback?

Rollback is recommended when:

- A deterministic regression is attributed to a specific kernel or runtime image AND
- The regression meets business impact thresholds (P99 > 40% above baseline or error delta > 0.3% absolute for 15+ minutes) OR
- Canary group divergence > 25% on cost/latency and automated rollback policy (canary-fidelity-policy) tripped.

Step D — Automated canary rollback (safe, fast)

If the rollout was governed by opscli and automatic canary policies are enabled, trigger the automated rollback first so the system can restore traffic gradually:

- opscli rollout abort --rollout-id <id> --reason "auto-rollback: runtime P99 regression"

Verify progress: opscli rollout status <id> should show traffic shifting back to previous replica set. Monitor SLOs for 5–20 minutes after rollback completion.

Step E — Manual rollback (when automated path is not available or failed)

1) Pre-rollback checks:

- Ensure the prior image is available in registry: docker pull registry.redwood.com/runtime:<previous-tag>
- Confirm db/config compatibility for hot rollback (consult runtime-hot-compat-list).

2) Manual rollback via opscli (preferred):

- opscli rollout promote --service inference-runtime-v2 --image registry.redwood.com/runtime:<previous-tag> --env prod --strategy=rolling --max-unavailable=1 --max-surge=1 --annotate "rollback:incident=<INCIDENT_ID>"

3) K8s direct rollback (only if opscli path unavailable):

- kubectl -n runtime set image deploy/inference-runtime-v2 inference-runtime=registry.redwood.com/runtime:<previous-tag>
- kubectl -n runtime rollout status deploy/inference-runtime-v2 --timeout=10m

4) If the rollback cannot complete due to image pull or resource constraints, follow the escalation steps:
  - Open a high-priority ticket to infra-ops and ping #infra-urgent. Include deployment error logs and node pressure reports.

Step F — Verification and validation (5–30 minutes)

1) Immediate checks (0–5 minutes after new pods become Ready):

- smoke: run integration smoke suite against canary endpoints (smoke-cli run runtime/basic-smoke --env=prod --sample=20)
- sanity logs: kubectl -n runtime logs -l app=inference-runtime-v2 --tail=200 | grep -i error | head -n 50

2) SLO and telemetry validation (5–30 minutes):

- Confirm P95/P99 and error rate trending back to baseline via Grafana.
- Verify kernel metrics: kernel.exec_ms p99 reduced to baseline.
- Validate admission queue and preemption counters normalized.

3) If metrics do not stabilize after rollback, revert the rollback and trigger deep investigation with runtime-core (see Post-incident actions).

Step G — Post-incident actions

1) Record incident timeline and actions in the incident tracker; attach trace bundle and opscli logs.
2) Create an action item to run replay experiments against the archived trace set in the lab environment (lab replay tag: incident-<INCIDENT_ID>-replay).
3) If rollback was caused by a kernel change, schedule a kernel-stage regression hunt: owner runtime-kernel-team, priority P1, due within 3 business days.

Configuration reference (threshold table)

- Metric | Alert threshold | Operator action
- P99 latency (generation) | > 40% baseline for 10m | Run this playbook, collect traces, consider rollback
- Error rate (5xx) | > 0.5% absolute for 5m | Collect traces, check canary, consider rollback
- Admission rejects | > 1000/min | Inspect scheduler, consider capacity adjustments
- Kernel exec p99 | > 200 ms 

Quick commands and parsable examples

- List recent rollouts:
  - opscli rollout list --service inference-runtime-v2 --limit 10 --env=prod
- Start trace capture (JSON example):
  - opscli trace start --json '{"service":"inference-runtime-v2","routes":["/v1/generate"],"duration_mins":20,"sampler":"latency-tail","max_samples":300,"label":"incident-1234"}'
- Export and unzip traces locally:
  - aws s3 cp s3://redwood-runtime-traces/incidents/incident-1234/raw.zip ./ && unzip raw.zip

Known limitations and safety notes

- Live trace captures produce additional overhead on runtime pods; prefer short captures and avoid simultaneous capture on all nodes.
- Rollback does not revert model artifacts; ensure model compatibility with previous runtime.
- For multi-region incidents, rollback by region to limit blast radius.

Verification checklist to close the incident (all items required)

- [ ] Trace bundle captured and archived (s3 path noted)
- [ ] Rollback (automated or manual) executed if criteria met
- [ ] SLO metrics returned to baseline for 30 minutes or incident escalated
- [ ] Incident channel annotated with rollout id and action history
- [ ] Post-incident replay scheduled and owner assigned

Appendix: helpful queries and field definitions

- kernel.exec_ms: time spent executing kernel compute (ms)
- kernel.kv_lookup_ms: average per-request KV cache lookup time (ms)
- scheduler.queue_ms: time spent waiting for slot assignment (ms)
- admission.rejected_count: count of requests rejected by admission controller

- Example Kibana/Kusto query for tail traces:
  - "service:inference-runtime-v2 AND span.duration_ms:>400" | sort by @timestamp desc | limit 500

- Artifact registry locations: registry.redwood.com/runtime:<tag> and registry.redwood.com/kernel:<tag>

Related reading

- Runtime rollout and canary policy (link): /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/runtime-feature-flagging-experimentation-contract-2026
- Trace format and viewer guide (link): /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/trace-viewer-and-format-spec-2026

Contact matrix

- Runtime SRE oncall: runtime-sre@redwood.com
- Runtime kernel team: runtime-kernel@redwood.com
- Infra ops: infra-ops@redwood.com

Document history

- Created by Lena Ortiz 2026-11-12
- Reviewed by Arjun Rao and Priya Singh 2026-12-03
- Updated to include automated canary commands and verification checklist 2027-02-03

title: quantization-rollout-safety-and-quality-gate-playbook
content:
Summary
=======

This playbook defines a standardized, safety-first process for rolling out quantized model variants across Redwood's serving runtime. It balances unit-cost benefits from lower-precision weights with product-quality and reliability commitments. The document describes metrics, quality gates, phased rollout procedures, observability requirements, automated test harness commands, and rollback criteria.

Goals
-----
- Protect customer-facing SLOs and output quality while enabling quantization as a cost-optimization lever.
- Ensure reproducible validation and fast failure-detection for regressions introduced by quantization.
- Provide clear, actionable rollout steps for engineers, SREs, and product owners.

Scope
-----
Applies to: model variants served by the runtime (hosted, dedicated, private). This playbook covers post-onboarding quantized variants (post-model-onboarding perf validation). It does not replace model training/finetuning practices; coordinate with Applied ML for model-level regressions.

Definitions
-----------
- Quantized variant: A model binary converted to reduced numeric precision (e.g., int8, nf4, 4-bit) used as a drop-in serving variant.
- Canary cohort: A small subset of traffic or dedicated test tenants used for early validation.
- Quality gate: An automated or manual threshold check that must pass before increasing exposure.
- Determinism variance: A measure of how often output tokens or decisions differ between baseline and variant given the same prompt and RNG seeds.

Prerequisites
-------------
1. Variant artifact uploaded to model registry with metadata: quantization-profile, hash, expected memory, and kernel hints.
2. Benchmark jobs executed in synthetic harness (latency, throughput, mem).
3. Offline quality evaluation completed against production prompt set (see "Evaluation harness commands").
4. Dashboards and alerting (per-variant) created in Grafana and routed to the SRE rotation.
5. Runbook stub created and linked in the deployment change.

Quality gates and thresholds
---------------------------
All quantized rollouts must pass the following gates. The thresholds are conservative defaults and can be tightened by product owners per model.

| Gate | Metric | Baseline | Allowed delta | Enforcement | Notes |
|------|--------|----------|---------------|------------|-------|
| Latency SLA | p99 inference latency | baseline p99 | +20% | Automated | If baseline p99 <= 150ms, allowed delta = +15% |
| Tail error rate | 5xx & 429 per-minute | baseline error rate | +0.2% abs | Automated | Any spike above 0.5% absolute triggers immediate rollback |
| Generation quality (LM) | Mean MAU (macro) or human-eval proxy: ROUGE/bleu surrogate | baseline score | -2.0% rel | Manual review | Use automatic metrics for fast gating, manual if near threshold |
| Embedding fidelity | Cosine similarity (mean) on eval set | 0.98 | >= 0.97 | Automated | Monitor distribution tails (5th percentile) |
| Determinism variance | Token sequence edit distance (median) | baseline ~0 | <= 2 tokens median | Automated + manual | For deterministic models, tolerate <=1 token diff |
| KV cache hit-rate | Session-level kvcache hit rate | baseline | -3% abs | Automated | Degraded kvcache reduces perf benefits |

Note: Product owners may add workload-specific gates (e.g., code-completion exact match, hallucination rate on QA prompts).

Phased rollout procedure
------------------------
1) Static verification (done before any traffic)
   - Confirm artifact signatures and runtime kernel compatibility.
   - Run unit tests and microbenchmarks.
   - Execute offline eval: accuracy, embedding similarity, stop-token behavior.

2) Canary (shadow or routed) — 1–2% traffic or dedicated canary tenants for 24–72 hours
   - Deploy variant to canary pool with request-mirroring enabled to compare outputs without impacting users (shadow mode) where possible.
   - Enable variant-level telemetry (latency, memory, kernel metrics).
   - Run continuous diff-sampling: sample 1:1000 requests for side-by-side comparison.
   - Evaluate quality gates hourly; if automated gates fail, circuit-break immediately.

3) Controlled ramp — 10–30% over 48–96 hours
   - If canary is stable, increase exposure in increments (10% -> 30%).
   - Add human-in-the-loop checks at each increment: SE/PM sign-off if quality metrics degrade near thresholds.

4) Broad rollout — 100% over 3–7 days with capacity fallback
   - Ramp to 100% only when sustained passing of gates and no trend violations.
   - Keep automatic fallback policy in place to rollback to baseline variant if sudden regression occurs.

Decision matrix example
-----------------------
- If latency p99 increases by >25% at canary: abort rollout and revert artifact.
- If embedding mean cosine drops below 0.95: abort and open a regression ticket with Applied ML.
- If generation quality metric drops between -1% and -2%: pause and schedule manual human eval.
- If 5xx spikes by >0.5% absolute: immediate rollback.

Monitoring and alerts
---------------------
Essential dashboards (per-variant):
- Latency (p50/p95/p99) and distribution heatmaps
- Error rates (5xx/4xx/429) with per-tenant breakdown
- Output-diff sampling logs (side-by-side diffs)
- Embedding similarity distribution and 5th percentile
- KV cache hit-rate and eviction count
- GPU kernel stalls and retry counts

Alerting tiers:
- Sev-1 (auto-rollback): error rate spike >0.5% abs, p99 > baseline +50%
- Sev-2 (investigate): p99 > baseline +20% for 10 minutes, embedding 5th percentile < 0.94
- Sev-3: gradual drift in sample diffs (trend of increasing edit distance over 24h)

Automated rollback and safeties
------------------------------
- Circuit-breaker service must have per-variant policies. If any automated gate trips, the cluster autoswitch will point traffic back to previous baseline variant and mark the rollout failed.
- Rollback must be executed within 2 minutes of automated trigger by the circuit-breaker.
- SRE Runbook: on rollback, capture diagnostic snapshot: variant logs, sample diffs, kernel traces, GPU counters, and upload to the incident bucket.

Test harness examples
---------------------
Run offline eval suite (example commands):

# Run token-level comparison harness
eval_harness compare --baseline model:openai/baseline-v1 --variant model:redwood/quantized-v1 --prompt-corpus ./prod_prompts/sample_10k.json --seed 42 --out ./out/diff_report.json

# Compute embedding similarity distribution
eval_harness embed-compare --baseline model:openai/baseline-v1 --variant model:redwood/quantized-v1 --corpus ./prod_prompts/embeddings_eval_5k.json --metric cosine --out ./out/embed_stats.json

Example deployment manifest (YAML)
-------------------------------
(The runtime config fields below are used by the rollout automation service)

---
variant: redwood/quantized-v1
quantization_profile: nf4-ptq-v2
max_concurrency: 128
kernel_hints: [int8-fast-matmul, cached-embedding-path]
canary_percentage: 1
auto_rollback: true
sampling_rate: 0.001 # fraction of requests for side-by-side diff
quality_gates:
  latency_p99_delta_pct: 20
  embedding_cosine_min: 0.97
  generation_quality_min_rel: -0.02

Operational checklist (pre-rollout)
----------------------------------
- [ ] Model artifact signed and checksum verified.
- [ ] Canary pool provisioned and capacity checked.
- [ ] Dashboards created and linked in the changelist.
- [ ] Side-by-side diff exporter enabled.
- [ ] Alerting endpoints for SRE rotation configured.
- [ ] Rollout ticket with owner and rollback owner assigned.

Rollback and post-rollback procedures
------------------------------------
1. Immediate steps (within first 5 minutes):
   - Invoke automated rollback via circuit-breaker.
   - Notify SRE rotation and the variant owner on Slack + PagerDuty.
   - Collect diagnostics: attach traces, telemetry snapshots, sample diffs.
2. Triage (within 2 hours):
   - Reproduce regression with offline harness.
   - Determine cause: quantization algorithm, kernel mismatch, runtime decode differences, or dataset boundary.
   - If fix is trivial (config/tuning), schedule hotfix canary. Otherwise, revert to baseline and open a cross-team incident.
3. Postmortem:
   - Owner must produce a 48-hour incident summary if rollback affected >=5% traffic or triggered Sev-1. Include root cause, mitigation, and action items.

Governance and permissions
-------------------------
- Only authorized owners (model owner + release engineer) can start a production quantization rollout.
- SRE on-call has the authority to abort or rollback without owner approval.
- Product must approve any relaxation of quality gates for cost experiments.

Examples of past findings and mitigations
----------------------------------------
- Case: int8 quantization caused subtle stop-token shift for a conditional generation model. Mitigation: adjust tokenizer rounding heuristics and add targeted stop-token tests to the eval set.
- Case: NF4 variant produced identical embeddings but increased decode latency due to kernel mismatch. Mitigation: update kernel hint to 'fast-matmul-v2' and rebench.

Appendix: quick reference commands
---------------------------------
- Create canary rollout:
  rcli rollout create --model redwood/quantized-v1 --canary 1 --auto-rollback
- Suspend sampling:
  rcli rollout update --id <id> --sampling_rate 0.0
- Force rollback:
  rcli rollout rollback --id <id> --reason "auto-gate:embedding-drop"

Contacts and ownership
----------------------
- Playbook author: Lena Alvarez (serving-runtime)
- Primary reviewers: Marcus Chen (SRE), Priya Natarajan (Applied ML)
- Escalation: SRE PagerDuty (oncall@sre.redwood.com)

Related reading
---------------
- Performance regression huntbook (benchmarking team)
- Fidelity containment and cost feedback playbook
- Model onboarding checklist (applied-ml)

Revision history
----------------
- 2026-01-18: Created by Lena Alvarez
- 2026-02-10: Added automated embedding gate and sampling guidance (review by Priya)
- 2026-03-02: Clarified alert thresholds and added CLI commands

title: Inferno Lab: Kernel Fuzz & Recovery Runbook
content:
Summary:

This runbook describes the Inferno Lab protocol: a controlled kernel fuzzing and recovery exercise designed to validate runtime-scheduler, kernel-shim, and dispatch recovery mechanics under adversarial kernel perturbations. The goal is to exercise defensive surface area (preemption, cooperative handoff, KV cache reconciliation, and admission controller backpressure) while ensuring safe, observable, and automatable rollback.

Scope
- Services in scope: runtime-scheduler, kernel-shim, dispatcher, kvcache-agent, slot-reservation.
- Environments: staging, canary, then targeted production cohorts (only after green canary).
- Not in scope: customer UI, billing pipeline, external storage control plane.

Why this runbook exists
1. Detect latent kernel-handoff deadlocks that do not appear in deterministic unit tests.
2. Validate operator recovery scripts and timings (SLO preservation under degraded kernel behavior).
3. Measure end-to-end fidelity loss and rollback safety for quantization- or kernel-level regressions.

Safety controls and preconditions
- Approval gate: Experiment must be approved by the SRE lead and the runtime owner. Record approval in the experiment ticket.
- Canary guardrails: Only run against a 1% traffic cohort in prod; stop if any of the following triggers: p95 latency > 2x baseline, error rate > 0.5% absolute increase, or customer-facing SLA alarms fire.
- Automated kill-switch: An orchestration job (inferno-guardian) will automatically revert the kernel patch when the canary guardrails are breached.
- Time window: Execute experiments in a 02:00–06:00 UTC window for production cohorts.
- Observability: Ensure traces, kernel telemetry, and dispatch sampling are enabled and sampled at 100% for canary runs.

Metrics and observability contract
- Latency: p50, p95, p99 (token-gen and end-to-end). Baseline p95 for indexed canary must be recorded before experiment start.
- Error signals: 4xx/5xx surface on API, scheduler-retries, kernel-timeouts.
- Kernel signals: kernel-handoff-duration, kernel-eviction-count, kvcache-warmup-latency.
- Recovery metrics: time-to-first-successful-request, number-of-revert-attempts, rollback-latency.

Experiment matrix (templates)
| Variant | Perturbation | Target | Expected impact | Safety threshold |
|---|---:|---|---|---|
| A | Slow context-switch (add 50–200us jitter to kernel scheduler) | kernel-shim | Increased p95, potential backpressure | Stop if p95 > 2x baseline |
| B | Partial KV cache corruption (drop 1% of prefetch hints) | kvcache-agent | Increased cold starts, cache warmup | Stop if kvcache-warmup-latency > 5x |
| C | Cooperative-preempt stall (simulate one cooperative preempt stall per node) | runtime-scheduler | Head-of-line blocking | Stop if queue-length > 10x |
| D | Randomized slow kernel calls (10% of calls delayed by 5ms) | kernel-shim | Microburst tail latency | Stop if error rate +0.5% absolute |

Pre-run checklist (every execution)
1. Create an experiment ticket referencing this runbook and link to monitoring dashboards.
2. Snapshot baseline metrics (last 24h) and attach to ticket.
3. Ensure alerting runbooks are assigned and primary/secondary on-call are notified.
4. Verify canary routing policy to route exactly N% traffic to canary cohort.
5. Validate inferno-guardian is configured with appropriate thresholds and test kill-switch in a dry-run mode.

Step-by-step run procedure
1. Staging validation
   a. Deploy kernel perturbation to staging cluster with same config as planned for canary.
   b. Run synthetic user traffic generator (inferno-sculpt) for 30 minutes.
   c. Collect traces, perf profiles, and kernel telemetry.
   d. Run automated post-check script: ./tools/inferno-postcheck --baseline <snapshot> --report out/report-staging.json
   e. Proceed to canary only if staging report passes all checks.

2. Canary deployment
   a. Deploy perturbation to canary nodes (1% traffic cohort).
   b. Start a 15-minute warmup with low traffic to let kvcache stabilize.
   c. Increment to full canary load and start continuous monitoring.
   d. If guardrails are violated, inferno-guardian will trigger a rollback; document the event.

3. Production cohort expansion (optional)
   a. Expand in 1% increments with 15-minute observation windows.
   b. Stop expansion if any safety threshold is breached.

Rollback and recovery procedures
- Automated rollback (preferred): inferno-guardian reverts kernel-shim to previous image and triggers a rolling restart of kernel-shim pods. Monitor rollback-latency and p95 recovery.
- Manual rollback steps:
  1. Pause traffic to affected nodes: kubectl label nodes <node> inferno-paused=true
  2. Revert kernel image: kubectl set image daemonset/kernel-shim kernel-shim=redwood/runtime-kernel:stable-20260501
  3. Trigger graceful eviction: kubectl rollout restart daemonset/kernel-shim --grace-period=60
  4. Run reconciliation: ./tools/kvcache-reconcile --nodes <node-list> --force-resync
  5. Unpause traffic when metrics show p95 within 10% of baseline for 10 minutes.

Operator commands and snippets
- Run the inferno-guardian dry-run locally:

```bash
# dry-run will simulate threshold breaches but not revert
python infra/inferno_guardian.py --experiment inferno-2026-05 --dry-run
```

- Deploy kernel-shim perturbation image (canary):

```bash
kubectl set image daemonset/kernel-shim kernel-shim=redwood/runtime-kernel:inferno-canary-2026-05
```

- Post-check example (JSON output):

```json
{
  "p95_before_ms": 120,
  "p95_during_ms": 280,
  "error_rate_delta": 0.002,
  "kvcache_warmup_factor": 3.1
}
```

Alerting rules to validate before start
- runtime.p95.above_baseline_multiple (alert if p95 > 2x baseline for 5m)
- runtime.api.error_rate.spike (alert if error rate uplift > 0.5% for 3m)
- scheduler.queue.length.high (alert if average queue length > 10x baseline)

Escalation path
1. On-call SRE gets page.
2. If automated rollback fails, call runtime-owner (pager) and handoff to emergency kernel team.
3. If rollback succeeds but residual errors persist > 30 minutes, open a Sev2 and follow incident runbook.

Post-experiment analysis and required artifacts
- Attach to experiment ticket: staging report, canary logs, full perf traces, tracer flamegraphs, kprobe captures.
- Required evaluation:
  - Fidelity delta report (sample prompts vs baseline)
  - Cost impact analysis (per-token CPU/GPU trend during perturbation)
  - Root-cause hypothesis and next steps (actions to harden scheduler or kvcache)

Ownership and RACI
- Responsible: runtime-ops (execution), kernel-shim eng (perturbation code), SRE (monitoring & rollback orchestration).
- Accountable: Head of Serving Runtime.
- Consulted: Security (for risk acceptance), Product (if customer-impacting).
- Informed: Customer Success for enterprise customers in cohorts.

Common failure scenarios and quick mitigations
- Scenario: KV cache warmup never completes
  - Mitigation: Revert perturbation, run kvcache-reconcile, and increase prefetch multiplier.
- Scenario: Scheduler preempt stall causes head-of-line blocking
  - Mitigation: Evict affected slots, escalate to kernel-shim team to toggle cooperative preempt flag.
- Scenario: Inferno-guardian fails to revert automatically
  - Mitigation: Manually trigger rollback and mark guardian incident for follow-up.

Postmortem template (to copy into ticket)
1. Title and experiment id.
2. Timeline of events with timestamps.
3. Metric deltas vs baseline.
4. Root cause hypothesis.
5. Action items (owners and due dates).
6. Lessons learned and prevention steps.

Appendix: injector config examples
- Sample injector YAML (staging):

```yaml
injector:
  perturbation_name: slow-context-jitter
  target_component: kernel-shim
  jitter_us: 120
  occurrence_rate: 0.05
  rollout_strategy:
    mode: canary
    canary_percentage: 1
    step_delay_minutes: 15
```

- Example monitoring query (Prometheus):

```
# p95 latency during experiment window
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le))
```

Revision history
- 2026-03-10: Created by Aisha Patel.
- 2026-04-15: Added inferno-guardian CLI examples and canary expansion guidance (reviewer: Daniel Kim).
- 2026-06-01: Added appendix and escalation path; clarified safety thresholds (reviewer: Marta Rodriguez).

Related links
- Kernel rollback automation: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/kernel-safety-net-and-rollback-playbook-2027
- Kernel perturbation harness code: gitlab:redwood/runtime/inferno-harness

title: Runtime Fallback & Graceful Degradation Playbook
content:
summary:
Operational runbook and engineering guidance for automatic fallback and graceful degradation behaviors in the Redwood serving runtime. Covers triggers, architecture interactions, scheduler implications, profiling and benchmarking guidance, and step-by-step incident remediation.

body:
Overview:

This playbook describes the intended behavior and operational steps for runtime-level fallback and graceful degradation across Redwood Inference deployments. It targets on-call SREs, runtime engineers, and platform product owners who must ensure applications meet latency and availability SLOs under degraded conditions (e.g., spot evictions, model OOMs, regional capacity constraints, extreme tail-latency events).

Goals and SLO impact:

- Primary goals:
  - Keep requests successful and bounded in latency by applying controlled degradation rather than failing hard.
  - Maintain transparency to customers (logs, metrics, traces) when fallbacks occur.
  - Provide deterministic, testable fallback policies that interact cleanly with kernel scheduler decision-making.
- SLO considerations:
  - Availability SLO: keep request success rate >= 99.9% across primary+fallback flows.
  - Latency SLO: p95 <= 250ms and p99 <= 600ms for standard small-response routes; fallback flows may relax latency SLO but must be documented in per-route dashboards.
  - Error budget accounting: fallback-induced higher latency counts against the latency error budget but not necessarily the availability budget if response semantics are preserved (200 OK with degraded payload).

When to engage fallback layer:

Fallback layer should be applied when one or more of the following triggers fire (automated):
1) Serving node failure modes: GPU OOMs, VMM crashes, container restarts above threshold (>=3 in 5m).
2) Resource saturation: queue length > config.queue_threshold or CPU/GPU utilization sustained > 92% for 60s.
3) Tail-latency surge: p99 request latency for a model > configured model.p99_threshold for 60s.
4) Regional capacity shortage: target region has < 10% of baseline free capacity and cross-region failover policy exists.
5) Model regression detection: quality monitoring signals output regression (eval set drop > 3% absolute) and defined auto-fallback rule is enabled.

Architecture integration (how fallback fits in the runtime):

- Placement: Fallback logic lives in the routing and execution orchestration layer (service: runtime-router). The runtime-worker accepts policy decisions (serve, downgrade, cache-hit, reject) returned by router.
- Policy store: Policies (per-route) are defined in the control plane config-store and propagated as immutable rollout keys. Each policy key maps to a fallback strategy bundle.
- Execution paths:
  - Normal path: route -> schedule -> worker -> model -> response.
  - Fallback path examples:
    - Model-variant downgrade: route -> schedule -> worker -> quantized-or-smaller-model -> response.
    - Cached-prefix reply: route -> cache-check -> cached-response -> response.
    - Short-circuit: route -> runtime-synthesizer -> short-summary response (used for long-running synth).
    - Regional fallback: route -> alt-region-router -> remote-worker -> response.
- Observability: All fallback decisions emit a fallback.reason tag and fallback.variant tag on traces and metrics. Billing and cost analytics receive a fallback.flag to attribute cost differences.

Fallback strategies and recommended order (policy template):

1) Prefetch & Cache (least-visibility change)
  - Serve cached completion or prefix when TTL not expired.
  - Use for high-QPS, low-variance routes (embeddings, re-ranking).
2) Quantized / Smaller model variant
  - Serve from a model variant with smaller memory footprint or int8 quantization.
  - Keep model-variant performance profile available in model catalog.
3) Partial-response / Synthesis
  - Return partial tokens up to configured token limit + summary flag.
  - Mark response with metadata: degraded: true, reason: partial-response.
4) Cross-region routing
  - Use only when network latency increase is acceptable vs local unavailability.
5) Hard reject / 503 fallback
  - Final resort when no compatibility policy exists; provide diagnostics link in body.

Kernel-scheduler considerations:

- Prioritization policy: The kernel scheduler should expose preemption hints for fallback flows. For example, models used in fallback (smaller quantized variants) receive lower CPU/GPU priority class so that primary models reclaim resources first.
- Eviction thresholds: Scheduler must support two eviction windows: graceful and immediate. Graceful eviction attempts to flush in-flight KV caches and migrate small models; immediate eviction kills the process when node health is compromised.
- Continuous batching interaction: When switching to smaller model variant, kernel should recompute batching windows (batch_size, batch_timeout) because per-token latency and throughput profiles change. The runtime must trigger a batching reconfigure hook on model-switch.

Profiling & benchmarking guidance during fallback mode:

- Benchmark plan: Run a paired A/B microbenchmark comparing normal variant vs fallback variant across the following axes: cold-start latency, steady-state latency, p99, throughput at target concurrency, memory footprint, and token throughput.
- Profiling checklist (oncall):
  1) Capture perf traces (nvprof / nsight) and runtime traces (OpenTelemetry) for both normal and fallback variants.
  2) Compare KV-cache hit rate and batching efficiency before/after fallback.
  3) Measure syscall and GPU kernel latencies; look for stall patterns indicating memory pressure.
- Metrics to surface on dashboards: fallback.count, fallback.latency.delta, fallback.impact_pct_of_requests, fallback.model_variant, fallback.trigger_reason.

Operational runbook (step-by-step):

Detection:
1) Alert fires: FALLBACK_POLICY_TRIGGERED OR model.p99_exceeded.
2) Oncall acknowledges and posts to incident channel (ops/runtime-fallback).

Immediate triage (first 10 minutes):
1) Confirm scope: run queries:
   - curl -sS "https://runtime-metrics.internal/api/v1/route_status?route=<route>"
   - rtfctl route inspect <route> --fields=queue_len,model_variant,uptime
2) Check node and scheduler health:
   - kubectl get pods -n runtime -l app=runtime-worker -o wide 
   - k8s node metrics: kubectl top nodes | sort -nr -k3
3) Determine fallback type currently in use via logs/traces (search for fallback.reason tag).
4) If fallback variant is active and correctness is acceptable, follow stabilization steps below.

Stabilization steps (10–60 minutes):
1) If queue backpressure is root cause, temporarily increase per-route max_workers or enable short-burst scaling (config: autoscale.burst=true) for up to 30 minutes. Document change and set timer.
2) If model OOMs triggered fallback, scale up node group (add nodes) or enable model eviction order: evict large non-critical models first.
3) If degradation due to bad model quality (detected by eval alerts), toggle model.quality_block to stop rollout and enable previously-validated variant.
4) Apply temporary route-level policy: set fallback.strategy=cache-first, max_tokens=128, respond_with_degradation_flag=true.

Rollback and permanent fix (1–24 hours):
1) If configuration/rollout caused the issue, revert the rollout using the control-plane rollback CLI: cpctl rollout revert <rollout_id>.
2) If capacity is root cause, schedule a capacity bump and update scaling policy: infra-iac PR to increase gpu_pool.capacity by recommended amount.
3) If kernel scheduler misbehavior suspected, collect scheduler dump and escalate to runtime-scheduler team: runtime-scheduler@redwood.ai. Include scheduler dump path and most recent kernel-profile tarball.

CLI and debug commands (common):
- rtfctl policy get <route>
- rtfctl model variants <model_id>
- curl -sS https://runtime-router.internal/healthz
- kubectl logs -n runtime <pod> -c worker --since=15m | grep fallback
- oc promql 'sum(rate(fallback_total[5m])) by (route)'

Config snippet (example policy - YAML):

---
route: /v1/generate/summarize
policy_key: minor-degrade-v1
fallback_policy:
  order: [cache, quantized_variant, short_response, cross_region]
  cache_ttl_s: 30
  quantized_variant: model-xy-q8
  short_response_max_tokens: 64
  cross_region: us-west-2
  circuit_breaker:
    consecutive_errors: 5
    reset_after_s: 300
---

Post-incident checklist:
- Create incident summary and link telemetry artifacts (traces, perf tarballs, scheduler dump).
- Run regression tests for the route(s) impacted.
- Schedule a postmortem within 3 business days.
- Add unit/e2e tests for new fallback behavior to prevent regressions.
- Review related model onboarding checks (ensure quantized/variant profiles exist).

Ownership and escalation:
- Primary oncall: runtime-sre team (alias: oncall-runtime@redwood.ai).
- Scheduler and kernel issues: runtime-scheduler@redwood.ai.
- Model quality regressions: applied-ml-and-evals@redwood.ai.
- Product and customer notifications: customer-success@redwood.ai.

Release notes and change history: 
- 2025-11-10 (Lena Hart): Initial draft of playbook.
- 2026-01-08 (Marisol Vega): Added kernel-scheduler preemption guidance and batching reconfigure hook.
- 2026-02-14 (Priya Nair): Expanded operational runbook and added config examples and CLI debug commands.

Appendix A — Known edge cases and mitigation: 
- Cached prefix staleness: Ensure cache invalidation hooks run on model rollout. Add checks: cache_version == model_variant_version.
- Quantized variant mismatch: Validate outputs with a lightweight semantic-similarity check before enabling in routed traffic.
- Cross-region data residency: Cross-region fallback must be disabled for routes marked with confidentiality: restricted.

Appendix B — Test plan for changes to fallback policies:
1) Unit tests for policy evaluation logic.
2) Integration tests simulating node failures and verifying fallback paths (run in staging with chaos tests).
3) Performance benchmark: 48-hour soak with periodic simulated OOMs to verify no latent memory leak in fallback variants.

Related artifacts: 
- Telemetry dashboards: runtime/fallbacks-overview, runtime/fallback-latency-impact.
- Perf artifacts stored at: s3://redwood-test-artifacts/runtime/profiles/fallback-tests/
- Playbook canonical ID: RBWF-2026-04

Contact & feedback:
If you find gaps or incorrect thresholds, please file a PR against this page or email the document owner (Lena.Hart@redwood.ai). For urgent escalations contact oncall-runtime@redwood.ai.

title: Cold-start Warmup Strategies and Entropy Reduction Playbook
content:
Summary:
This playbook describes recommended approaches for reducing cold-start latency and request output entropy during model/worker startup in Redwood’s serving runtime. It consolidates operational patterns, automated warmup recipes, example configs, and runbook steps for diagnosing and recovering from cold-start–related SLO breaches. The guidance applies to hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.

Scope:
- Applies to long-lived model workers and ephemeral worker pools (autoscaled GPUs).
- Focus on first-token latency, tail latency during burst scaling, and early-session output quality variability caused by incomplete KV cache or lazy kernel initialization.
- Excludes model training workflows and offline batch workloads.

Background and problem statement:
Cold starts in the runtime manifest in three measurable ways:
1) high first-byte/first-token latency before kernels and memory paths are hot,
2) increased variance/entropy in early outputs when KV caches or sampled attention layers are empty or not warmed, and
3) transient resource throttling when many warmup tasks coincide with customer traffic.
These symptoms complicate SLOs for developer-facing APIs and drive poor user experience for PLG customers who exercise new endpoints.

Goals and SLOs:
- Bring median first-token latency for a cold worker within 1.2x of steady-state median within the first 60 seconds of start.
- Keep 99th-percentile first-token latency below 250ms for dedicated pools and 500ms for ephemeral workers on typical L-inference models (L ~ 512 tokens) during warmup windows.
- Ensure early-output perplexity / BLEU (where applicable) is within 10% of steady-state model output on canonical prompt sets after warmup sequence completes.

Principles:
- Make warmup deterministic and measurable. Synthetic sequences should mimic real user distributions.
- Minimize interference with live traffic: warmup must be rate-limited, backpressure-aware, and preemptible.
- Favor progressive warming over wholesale parallel warmup when capacity-constrained.
- Prefer cached-prefix warming for popular prompt prefixes and KV cache seeding for chat-style sessions.

Warmup techniques (catalog):
1) Kernel and CUDA warmup
- Purpose: JIT kernels, populate driver memory mappings, load PTX/CU into GPU.
- Recipe: run a minimal forward pass with sequence_length=32 and batch_size=1 across major model ops.
- Observability: kernel load time traces, CUDA module load events.

2) KV-cache seeding (chat and long-context models)
- Purpose: fill per-shard KV caches with realistic key/value vectors for reused prefixes.
- Recipe: replay top-N canonical prefixes derived from traffic analytics (N=20 default) at target sequence lengths.
- Implementation note: use offline precomputed embeddings for synthetic prefixes to avoid model compute where possible.

3) Token-distribution annealing (entropy reduction)
- Purpose: reduce early output variance by briefly constraining temperature/top-k during first few tokens.
- Recipe: during warmup requests set temperature=0.7 -> 0.5 -> 0.2 over first 5 tokens, then restore customer-configured sampling.
- Guardrail: only apply to internal warmup requests; do not alter customer-visible sampling.

4) Layerwise micro-batching for kernel priming
- Purpose: exercise large-matrix paths at small batch sizes to prime GEMM kernels and memory allocator.
- Recipe: run micro-batches of 1–4 across sequence lengths [8,32,128] in series.

5) Prefix-aware KV prefetching for multi-tenant pools
- Purpose: avoid polluted global KV spaces by quarantining tenant-specific warmup prefixes.
- Recipe: allocate transient warmup KV buckets tagged by tenant and promote buckets into the main tenant shard once validated.

Warmup orchestration patterns:
- Passive: warmup triggered on scale-up completion but paused if ingress TPS > threshold.
- Active: proactive warmup before traffic shifts (e.g., scheduled deploys, predictable traffic spikes).
- Hybrid: run a minimal passive warmup on boot, then schedule active warmup in off-peak windows.

Configuration examples (YAML snippet):
```
warmup:
  enabled: true
  mode: hybrid
  prefix_list_source: traffic-analytics/top-prefixes-v2
  sequence_profile:
    - length: 32
      count: 10
    - length: 128
      count: 5
  kvbucket: tenant_quarantine
  rate_limit_rps: 5
  max_concurrency: 2
  sampling_anneal_steps: 5
```

Suggested default parameters:
- rate_limit_rps: 5 requests per worker during warmup
- max_concurrency: 2 synthetic warmup threads per GPU
- prefix_list N: 20 top prefixes per model/tenant
- anneal_steps: 3–8 tokens depending on model sensitivity

Automated warmup pipelines (implementation notes):
- Warmup controller integrates with orchestration service (k8s operator / Redwood scheduler).
- Controllers must observe the pool SLO token bucket before issuing warmup requests.
- Warmup requests are flagged at trace-level with tag: "warmup=true" for downstream trimming and auditing.
- Use per-model warmup manifests stored in the model catalog for reproducibility.

Runbook: diagnosing a warmup-related incident (SLO breach)
1) Detect
  - Alerts: increased first-token latency (p99_first_token > threshold) or high early-output perplexity for a small but growing percentage of sessions.
  - Query: filter traces where trace.tag[warmup] != true to exclude synthetic runs.
2) Triage
  - Check cluster events: scale-up, OOMs, GPU driver reloads within last 10 min.
  - Check warmup controller logs: failures, rate-limit kicks, preemption events.
  - Inspect KV cache hit rates (per-shard): missing hits indicate improper seeding.
3) Immediate mitigation (0–15 min)
  - Pause active warmup pipeline (toggle warmup.enabled=false).
  - If high latency correlates with kernel loads, roll back to previous runtime image with known kernel warm state.
  - Reduce warmup concurrency or rate limits: set max_concurrency=1 and rate_limit_rps=1.
4) Recovery (15–60 min)
  - Perform controlled progressive warmup: one worker at a time with monitoring hooks.
  - If KV caches were corrupted, evict and reseed using validated prefix lists.
  - Re-run synthetic sampling with telemetry to validate output perplexity.
5) Post-incident actions
  - Collect root cause: automation bug, driver regression, noisy prefix set, or capacity storm.
  - Update model warmup manifest and increase test coverage in CI for cold-start scenarios.

Scripting and CLI examples:
- Trigger an on-demand warmup for model "mosaic-v2" with tenant "acme":
  - rctl warmup start --model=mosaic-v2 --tenant=acme --sequence-profile="32:10,128:5" --rate=2
- Query warmup progress:
  - rctl warmup status --run-id=warmup-20250304-01

Observability and dashboards (minimum set):
- Warmup controller: run-state, queued tasks, failures per minute.
- Worker-level: first_token_latency (median/p99), kernel_load_time, kvcache_hit_rate by shard.
- Traffic-adjacent: percentage of sessions in first-30s window with early-output flags.
- Anomaly detector: sudden spike in kernel_load_time correlated with image or driver changes.

Acceptance tests and CI checks:
- CI should include a synthetic cold-start validation stage that spawns a worker, runs warmup manifest, and validates: p50_first_token < 1.2x baseline and 99th_first_token < threshold defined per model.
- Regression tests for sampling-anneal must assert that internal warmup requests do not leak sampling params to customer-visible telemetry.

Operational limitations and tradeoffs:
- Warmup CPU/GPU cost: synthetic warmup consumes real compute; use off-peak and rate limits.
- Over-warming: unnecessary warmup reduces global capacity for live traffic; monitor overall SLO budget.
- Prefix-selection sensitivity: wrong prefixes bias KV caches and can reduce quality for tail users.

Ownership and rollout checklist for implementing model warmup manifest:
1) Author a model warmup manifest and add to model-catalog (owner: model-onboarding).
2) Add warmup job to the fleet operator (owner: eng-platform).
3) Create dashboards and alerts (owner: eng-sre).
4) Add CI cold-start test (owner: eng-serving-runtime).
5) Small canary rollout to <5% of new workers, verify metrics for 48 hours.

Appendix A — Example warmup manifest (JSON):
```
{
  "model": "mosaic-v2",
  "tenant": "default",
  "prefix_source": "traffic-analytics/top-20-v1",
  "sequence_profile": [{"len":32, "count":10}, {"len":128, "count":5}],
  "rate_limit_rps": 3,
  "max_concurrency": 2,
  "anneal_steps": 5
}
```

Appendix B — Troubleshooting checklist (quick):
- If p99_first_token spikes: check kernel_load_time and recent image rollouts.
- If early-output perplexity high: inspect prefix list validity and kvcache_hit_rate.
- If warmup tasks failing: inspect controller auth and rate-limiter errors.

Related pages and references:
- See runtime-architecture diagram for worker lifecycle and shard boundaries.
- See telemetry-rollup page for metric names and dashboards.

Document maintenance:
- Owner: eng-serving-runtime team.
- Review cadence: quarterly or after any runtime image/driver upgrade.

Change log:
- 2024-11-12 created by Aisha Patel (initial draft).
- 2025-01-08 updated: added sampling-anneal pattern and YAML examples (reviewers: Marco Reyes).
- 2025-03-04 updated: tuned SLO numbers and added CLI commands for rctl (Ethan Cole).

title: Runtime upgrade validation and canary matrix
content:
Overview

Purpose: This document defines a repeatable, telemetry-driven validation matrix and automated canary procedure for runtime component upgrades (kernels, schedulers, KV-cache variants, and compilation artifacts). It combines benchmark gating, live-canary thresholds, and automated rollback criteria to reduce risk while enabling faster iteration.

Scope: applies to server-side runtime components deployed to hosted and dedicated environments. Excludes customer-managed Private deployments unless explicitly opted into Redwood upgrade automation.

Audience: runtime engineers, infra SRE, release managers, product reliability.

Goals

- Standardize evidence required before a kernel/scheduler change is promoted.
- Automate canary progression based on concrete telemetry signals.
- Provide clear, reproducible rollback gates to prevent production regressions.

Key definitions

- Candidate: A build artifact (kernel binary, scheduler config, quantized weights + kernel hints) targeted for rollout.
- Canary cohort: Fraction of traffic routed to candidate.
- Validation matrix: Cross-product of workload classes and required checks (benchmarks, profiling, live SLOs).

Validation matrix (summary table)

Workload class | Benchmarks required | Profiling artifacts | Live telemetry thresholds
---------------|---------------------|--------------------|----------------------
Light chat (seq <= 128) | microbench p50/p95 throughput, token-per-second | kernel traces, occupancy profile | p95 latency delta <= +10ms, error rate delta <= +0.05% absolute
Long-form gen (seq 512–4096) | tail-latency simulation, memory growth test | allocation flamegraph, KV-cache hit-ratio | p99 latency delta <= +15%, OOM events == 0
High-concurrency embeddings | throughput-saturation, queuing model test | concurrency contention traces | throughput delta >= -7%, queue length growth <= 15%
Cold-start heavy | cold-start latency benchmark | warmup hit-rate and init-cost trace | cold-start p95 delta <= +25% of baseline

Pre-flight checklist (CI / bench stage)

1) Automated performance benchmarks complete and pass thresholds in isolated test harness (see matrix above).
2) Profiling artifacts uploaded to internal profiling store: kernel traces, NVidia counters, KV-cache hit heatmaps.
3) Static analysis and safety checks: no non-deterministic memory accesses reported; sanitizers pass on debug builds.
4) Automated canary plan generated (JSON) with target filters (model families, customer tiers, regions). Example plan snippet:

{
  "candidate": "kernel-v2.3.1",
  "cohorts": [{"pct": 1, "duration_min": 60}, {"pct": 5, "duration_min": 30}, {"pct": 20, "duration_min": 30}, {"pct": 50, "duration_min": 60}],
  "gates": {"p95_latency_pct": 110, "error_rate_absolute": 0.0005}
}

(Above JSON is illustrative; CI generates canonical plan stored at "/releases/runtime/canary-plans/<candidate>.json")

Live canary progression policy

- Start: 1% traffic for 60 minutes. Collect signals from telemetry backend.
- Metrics evaluated: latency p50/p95/p99, request error rate, kernel-level metrics (warp occupancy, SM utilization), GPU memory fragmentation events, KV-cache hit ratio, GC/alloc stalls.
- Evaluation windows: rolling 5m and 30m windows. Candidate must satisfy both short and mid windows.
- Progression: If all gates pass for the mid window, advance to next cohort. Otherwise hold for remediation and re-evaluate after operator intervention.

Automated gating thresholds (default)

- p95 latency: candidate <= baseline * 1.10 (10% relative increase allowed)
- p99 latency: candidate <= baseline * 1.15
- Error rate (4xx/5xx): absolute increase <= 0.05% (0.0005)
- OOM / GPU watchdog events: 0 allowed
- Memory growth (over 2h): <= 5% relative
- Kernel launch failures: 0 allowed

Custom gates per change type

- Kernel micro-optimizations: tighten p95 to 1.05 and require occupancy within 3% of baseline.
- Scheduler policy changes: require queue-length regression < 10% and throughput regression < 5%.
- Quantization / compilation changes: require accuracy-preserving regressions flagged in model-evaluations <= acceptable threshold (team-specific).

Rollback criteria and automation

1) If any hard gate (OOM, kernel-launch-failure, watchdog) triggers, immediately abort canary and trigger rollback automation to previous stable artifact. 2) If soft gates (latency or error delta) fail consecutively for two mid-windows, pause and notify on-call and release manager. Automated snapshot of traces, flamegraphs, and sample requests is captured. 3) Rollback steps (automated):
   a) Set routing weight of candidate to 0 via traffic-controller API.
   b) Post-deploy job: restore previous kernel artifacts to nodes that had changed (idempotent).

Operational runbook (step-by-step)

1) Prepare candidate: verify CI artifacts and upload profiling bundles. 2) Create canary plan via release CLI:

$ rdeploy canary create --candidate kernel-v2.3.1 --plan /releases/runtime/canary-plans/kernel-v2.3.1.json

3) Kick off canary:

$ rdeploy canary start --candidate kernel-v2.3.1 --env prod-us-east-1

4) Monitor dashboards for the first 60 minutes. Required checks in parallel:
- Latency dashboard (p50/p95/p99)
- Error-rate heatmap by customer tier
- Kernel-level telemetry panel: warp occupancy, kernel duration histogram
- Memory fragmentation and allocation stalls panel

5) If gates pass, approve progression via CLI or UI:

$ rdeploy canary progress --candidate kernel-v2.3.1 --to 5

6) If any gate fails, abort:

$ rdeploy canary abort --candidate kernel-v2.3.1 --reason "p95 delta breach"

Observability and required dashboards

- Canary overview: candidate, cohort, routing %, evaluation status.
- Signal breakdown: latency, errors, throughput, kernel traces, memory metrics.
- Rollforward / rollback audit log.

Benchmarking hygiene

- Benchmarks must be seeded with production-like request mixes; synthetic single-query microbenchmarks are insufficient alone.
- For each candidate, attach the benchmark run id and the commit SHA to the canary plan.

Profiling artifact requirements

- Kernel traces (per-shard, per-GPU) for representative workloads; include nvprof / CUPTI counters.
- KV-cache heatmaps: hit ratio by prefix and warmup curves.
- Memory allocator profiles (jemalloc stats or equivalent).

Failure investigation checklist (if canary fails)

1) Re-run microbench with same load profile from bench harness and compare traces. 2) Capture top-N slow requests and replay in local dev cluster. 3) Check kernel/build differences (diff .cubin/.ptx metadata). 4) Inspect scheduler metrics for throttling or priority inversion. 5) If a fix requires configuration change, create a follow-up candidate and attach a root-cause summary to the original canary record.

Roles and ownership

- Runtime team: prepares candidates, ensures profiling artifacts, makes fixes.
- Infra SRE: approves global canary windows, supervises rollbacks, validates capacity.
- Release manager: coordinates cross-team communications, authorizes canary progression beyond 20% for high-risk changes.
- On-call: responds to automated alerts triggered by failed gates.

Related automation endpoints (examples)

- Traffic controller: POST /api/v1/traffic/control {candidate, weight}
- Canary controller: POST /api/v1/canary/start {candidate, plan}
- Telemetry query job: GET /api/v1/telemetry/query?query=canary_signals

Post-release requirements

- 72-hour monitoring window: run automated regression check at 24h and 72h and record results.
- Publish release note summarizing canary outcome, telemetry snippets, and any mitigations. Include links to profiling bundles.

Appendix A — Example canary plan (complete)

candidate: kernel-v2.3.1
filters:
  regions: ["us-east-1", "us-west-2"]
  model_tags: ["chat-light", "embeddings-small"]
  customer_tiers: ["free", "standard"]
cohorts:
  - pct: 1
    duration_min: 60
  - pct: 5
    duration_min: 30
  - pct: 20
    duration_min: 30
  - pct: 50
    duration_min: 60
gates:
  p95_latency_pct: 110
  p99_latency_pct: 115
  error_rate_absolute: 0.0005
  max_oom_events: 0

Appendix B — Example telemetry queries

- p95 latency delta (5m):
  baseline = metric("runtime.latency.p95", tag: baseline)
  candidate = metric("runtime.latency.p95", tag: candidate)
  query: 100 * (candidate / baseline)

- error-rate absolute: count(errors)/count(requests) over 5m window

Appendix C — FAQ

Q: When should we tighten gates?
A: For any change that touches memory allocation or scheduling, tighten p95 to 1.05 and require no more than 2% memory growth.

Q: Who can abort a canary?
A: On-call and Infra SRE have automated abort privileges; runtime owners and release manager should be notified immediately.

Q: Can we run a canary scoped to a single customer?
A: Yes — use customer filters in the canary plan, but for high-risk internal-only fixes prefer canarying on internal test tenants first.

Document history and links

- First published: 2025-11-12 by Emily Chen.
- Major revision (gate tightening for kernels): 2026-02-03 (Emily Chen)

Related pages: see internal benchmarking catalog and profiling playbooks for workload definitions.

title: Session lifecycle and KV-cache consistency: design, diagnostics, and operational playbook
content:
Summary:
This document defines the session lifecycle model used by the Redwood serving runtime, describes KV-cache consistency guarantees we target, and provides an operational playbook for diagnosing and remediating common failures. It consolidates architecture decisions, scheduling implications, profiling guidance, and runbook procedures into a single reference for on-call and runtime engineers.

Scope:
- Applies to the hosted, dedicated, and private runtime variants that implement per-session KV caching and request multiplexing.
- Covers session creation/teardown, KV-cache warmup, cache eviction/rehydration, cross-shard consistency failure modes, and relevant kernel-scheduling interactions.
- Excludes higher-level prompt rewriting policies, user-auth flows, and storage-layer backup/restore (see references).

Context and motivation:
- Our processing model uses per-client sessions with an in-memory KV cache (attention key/value cache) to avoid re-computation across streaming tokens. Correctness and latency depend on cache hits being logically consistent with the active session state.
- Recent production incidents (see related_pages below) showed subtle race conditions during fast session migration, autoscaling-driven eviction, and preemption. This guide codifies safe invariants and pragmatic mitigation steps.

Design goals and invariants:
1) Strong last-writer-wins within a single shard: updates to a session's KV cache must reflect the most recent token generation on that shard.
2) Session affinity for low-latency paths: warm sessions should prefer the same worker to preserve cache locality.
3) Bounded staleness across fallback: when falling back to a compatible model variant, staleness must be identifiable and handled (e.g., by a re-roll or explicit re-population).
4) Observable transitions: each lifecycle transition emits annotated telemetry to allow precise post-hoc attribution.

Session lifecycle (state machine):
- States:
  - INIT: session placeholder created during first request; no KV cache populated.
  - WARMING: first generation(s) are populating prefix cache; partial hit rate expected.
  - HOT: cache hit rate above configured threshold; session eligible for latency-optimized routing.
  - MIGRATING: session being transferred between workers (scale-out/maintenance).
  - EVICTED: cache cleared due to memory pressure or policy; session remains logically valid but warmup required.
  - CLOSED: session terminated and resources freed.

- Transitions (high level):
  1. INIT -> WARMING on first generate call.
  2. WARMING -> HOT when hit_rate >= 85% for the last N tokens (see config table).
  3. HOT -> MIGRATING when autoscaler moves workload or node is drained; a dup-sync protocol begins.
  4. MIGRATING -> HOT (fast-path) if migration succeeds without loss.
  5. MIGRATING -> EVICTED if migration fails or eviction threshold crossed.
  6. Any -> CLOSED on explicit session end or TTL expiry.

KV-cache consistency guarantees and semantics:
- Within-shard operations: atomic append semantics for kv-update events. Kernels consuming KV must use the latest indicated sequence number stamped by the session coordinator.
- Cross-shard handoff: we use a two-phase snapshot-and-ack protocol for handoff: source worker snapshots KV segments, destination worker applies snapshot and acknowledges. Only after ACK does routing flip.
- Best-effort reordering protection: sequence numbers prevent reordering when network duplicate packets occur; however, packet loss during handoff can yield partial snapshots that must be detected and retried.

Configuration table (default thresholds and rationale):
| config_key | default | unit | rationale |
|-----------|---------:|------:|----------|
| session.hot_hit_rate_threshold | 85 | percent | Balances warmup cost and latency benefit (empirical). |
| session.hot_window_tokens | 512 | tokens | Window used to compute moving hit rate. |
| session.eviction_low_water_mb | 256 | MB | Memory threshold to trigger targeted eviction of cold sessions. |
| session.eviction_grace_seconds | 30 | seconds | Allow in-flight requests to drain before eviction completes. |
| kvcache.snapshot_chunk_size | 4 | MB | Chunk size for snapshot transfer to limit memory spikes. |

Kernel scheduling and interaction notes:
- Priority synthesis: HOT sessions are marked as latency-sensitive and scheduled onto low-latency kernels with preemption disabled for short windows; avoid long-running background kernels during hot generation.
- Warmup profiling: when WARMING sessions exceed expected warmup time, collect microprofiler traces (see profiling section) and annotate traces with hit-rate and kernel flags.
- Cooperative eviction: scheduler should coordinate with kvcache manager to preferentially evict sessions with low routing stickiness and low recent QPS.

Known failure modes and diagnostics (quick reference):
1. Symptom: sudden drop in per-session hit rate and latency spike after autoscale event.
   - Likely cause: incomplete handoff (MIGRATING -> EVICTED).
   - Immediate checks:
     - worker logs for snapshot/ack errors.
     - kvcache.transfer.* telemetry for failed chunks.
   - Remediation steps:
     1. If snapshot retries are failing due to network timeouts, increase snapshot_chunk_timeout and re-run the handoff (or route new requests to fallback model briefly).
     2. If eviction was forced, trigger an async background warmup using recent token prefix (see warmup playbook).
2. Symptom: Incorrect output ordering or hallucinated tokens after migration.
   - Likely cause: stale KV segment applied out of order.
   - Diagnostics:
     - Verify sequence numbers on outgoing tokens vs the applied sequence on destination worker.
     - Check for duplicate or delayed ACKs.
   - Remediation:
     1. Revert routing to source worker if still alive, then re-initiate snapshot with stricter consistency (pause generation).
     2. If source is gone, mark session as EVICTED and request client-side retry with explicit session reset.
3. Symptom: Frequent small evictions causing churning and high CPU.
   - Likely cause: aggressive eviction_low_water_mb misconfiguration or fragmentation.
   - Remediation:
     - Increase eviction_low_water_mb, or tune allocator compaction.
\Operational playbook: step-by-step (oncall)
1) Triage and scope: identify if incident affects single session, worker, or region. Use /observability/session-search with session_id to get state machine events within the last 5 minutes.
2) If session in MIGRATING longer than config.session.eviction_grace_seconds, check kvcache.transfer.* metrics.
3) If snapshot errors are present, capture the following artifacts and attach to incident: worker logs, kvcache snapshot traces, profiler sample for the migration window.
4) Apply mitigation: for hot customer-facing traffic, follow fast mitigation order: (a) route to fallback variant with identical semantics, (b) spin up dedicated worker with same model variant pinned, (c) throttle low-priority batch work to free memory.
5) Post-incident: run warmup job to pre-populate caches for impacted sessions (see Warmup recipe).
\Warmup recipe (automated job)
- Objective: restore cache state for evicted sessions using stored recent prefix tokens (last 1024 tokens).
- Steps:
  1. Lookup recent user prefix from opt-in session-history store (TTL 24h).
  2. Submit a synthetic generate request with the prefix to a warm worker using 'cache-only' mode to populate KV segments.
  3. Validate by reading kvcache.hit_rate for the session and confirm > session.hot_hit_rate_threshold.
\Profiling guidance and targeted metrics to collect:
- Always collect these during warmup/migration windows: kvcache.hit_rate (per-session), kvcache.size_bytes, kvcache.snapshot.chunk_latencies, kernel.dispatch.latency_p50/p95, worker.memory.used_mb, and kernel.preempt_events.
- Recommended profiler captures:
  - 30s microprofiler (wall-clock) around migration boundary.
  - Kernel-level GPU traces if dispatch latencies exceed expected thresholds.
- Useful sampling queries (example CLI):
  - redwood telemetry query "kvcache.hit_rate{session_id=\"<id>\"} | last 1m"
  - redwood trace fetch --session <id> --window 00:00:30
\Testing and benchmark guidance:
- Synthetic scenarios to include in the perf-suite:
  1. High-churn sessions: 100k sessions with TTL=60s to exercise eviction.
  2. Large-prefix warmups: 10k sessions with 2k token prefixes to measure warmup tails.
  3. Migration storm: simultaneous drain of a 100-worker AZ to validate snapshot throughput.
- Bench metrics to capture: session warmup tail latency (p99/p999), steady-state hit rate, snapshot transfer throughput (MB/s), and CPU/GPU cost per warmup.
\Safety and rollout checklist (for changes to session/KV code):
- Unit tests for sequence-number semantics and snapshot chunk retries.
- Integration test: simulated migration with induced chunk timeouts.
- Canary rollout steps:
  1. Deploy change to a single non-prod zone and run migration storm workload for 2h.
  2. Promote to canary region with 5% of production traffic for 24h, monitor kvcache.* and kernel.preempt_events.
  3. Full rollout with autoscaler observation window enabled.
\Owners and contacts:
- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime-session (team alias)
- Secondary: eng-serving-runtime-kernels
- Pager: oncall-runtime (see oncall rota)
\Related pages:
- eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/request-multiplexing-backpressure-architecture-2026
- eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/dynamic-kvcache-resilience-and-warmup-playbook-2026
- eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/sequence-length-scaling-and-kernel-breakpoints-2026
\References and artifacts:
- Design doc: internal link to kvcache-handoff-protocol (v2)
- Kernel scheduling ADR: priority-decoupling-and-preemptive-shepherding (2026)
- Incident writeups: migration-failure-incident-2025 (postmortem)
\Appendix A: example kvcache snapshot CLI (pseudo)
```
# snapshot transfer (pseudo)
redwood kvcache snapshot --session <id> --chunk-size 4MB --timeout 2s --retries 3 --dest-worker <worker>
```
\Appendix B: useful log search terms
- kvcache.snapshot.error
- session.transition.migrating
- kernel.preempt.requested

Revision history:
- 2024-11-12: created by Maya Chen (initial draft).
- 2025-07-01: replaced snapshot chunking defaults after field trial (Aisha Patel).
- 2026-02-03: added profiling sections and benchmark scenarios (Tomás Rivera).

title: Scheduler Injection and Fidelity Rollback Lab Manual
content:
Overview

Purpose
- This document defines a reproducible lab procedure for injecting scheduler-level perturbations against the serving runtime, observing fidelity regressions, and executing an automated rollback of fidelity-reducing changes. The intent is to provide a safe, auditable experiment protocol that engineering and SRE teams can run in the staging and canary environments.

Scope
- Applies to runtime scheduler, kernel admission controller, and the fidelity orchestration layer.
- Environments: staging (required), canary (recommended), production (only for validated runbooks and with approval).

When to use this runbook
1. Before rolling out a new scheduler policy or kernel variant that affects priority, preemption, or coalescing.
2. When reproducing a customer-facing fidelity regression trace.
3. To benchmark rollback and fallthrough guarantees under controlled degradation.

Background and rationale
- Recent work on predictive slotting and admission controllers introduced priority-reshaping heuristics. These heuristics can inadvertently change effective model fidelity under bursty traffic (e.g., quantization swap or kernel variant downgrade). The lab manual captures a safe method to simulate scheduler mis-behaviour, measure fidelity impact using our eval harness, and validate rollback safety.

High-level testbed architecture (text diagram)
- Components:
  - Traffic generator (tg-load) -> Request router -> Scheduler/Admission controller -> Kernel variants on GPU nodes -> Observability collectors (trace/metrics) -> Eval harness and fidelity oracle
- Text diagram: [tg-load] -> [router] -> [scheduler-admission] -> [gpu-kernel-pool: vA/vB] -> [observability: otel, runtime-metrics, fidelity-evals]

Prerequisites (environment and access)
| Item | Required | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Staging cluster | yes | kube context: staging-runtime-admin |
| Canary namespace | recommended | canary runtime-namespace: redwood-canary |
| Experiment CRD installed | yes | chart: runtime-chaos/1.3.0 |
| Telemetry hooks enabled | yes | traces + metrics (otel + prometheus) |
| Eval harness snapshot | yes | prompt-set: fidelity-smoke-v3 |
| Owner on-call | yes | listed in ownership section below |

Safety rules and approvals
- Never run injection on production without written approval from Eng SRE and Product Security.
- Maintain an experiment ticket in the Experiment Registry with start/end times and rollback criteria.
- Quotas: inject only up to 20% of scheduler decision streams during a single test.

Success criteria and SLOs to watch (staging/canary baseline)
- Latency SLO baseline: p50 < 60ms, p95 < 150ms, p99 < 300ms for generator workload.
- Error rate: application-level 5xx < 0.1% above baseline.
- Fidelity: pass rate on fidelity-smoke-v3 >= baseline - 2 percentage points. If regression > 2pp, trigger rollback.
- GPU utilization: sustained increase > 30% above baseline for > 3 minutes -> investigate kernel thrash.

Experiment types supported
1. Priority inversion injection: re-label incoming requests with low priority after scheduler decision to simulate admission misclassification.
2. Kernel downgrade bloom: force a subset of requests to be routed to a lower-fidelity kernel variant (vB) for an interval.
3. Prefetch delay: add artificial delay in kvcache prefetch path to emulate missing warmups.
4. Admission flood: increase admission GC frequency to create eviction churn.

Safe experiment template (YAML)
- Example CRD (apply to staging only):
  apiVersion: chaos.redwood.ai/v1
  kind: SchedulerInjection
  metadata:
    name: fidelity-downgrade-smoke-1
    namespace: staging-experiments
  spec:
    type: kernel-downgrade
    targetPercentage: 10
    duration: 10m
    injectionWindow: 09:00-09:20Z
    rollbackCondition:
      fidelityDropPct: 2.0
      p95IncreaseMs: 50

Step-by-step procedure
1. Create experiment ticket in Experiment Registry and notify on-call. Include start/stop window and rollback policy.
2. Verify telemetry: run quick smoke to collect baseline metrics (run for 5 minutes). Command: kubectl --context staging-runtime-admin run tg-load --image=redwood/tg-load:stable -- ... (see quickstart args in the experiment repo).
3. Deploy experiment CRD to staging: kubectl apply -f scheduler-injection-smoke.yaml -n staging-experiments.
4. Monitor the observability dashboard (link below) and the fidelity runner.
5. If fidelity regression exceeds rollbackCondition, execute rollback (automated by the experiment controller) or manual rollback: kubectl delete schedulerinjection fidelity-downgrade-smoke-1 -n staging-experiments.
6. Run post-experiment eval: curl -X POST https://staging-evals.internal/api/run -d '{"suite":"fidelity-smoke-v3"}' -H 'Authorization: Bearer $EVAL_TOKEN'

Observability checklist (metrics and traces)
- Metrics (Prometheus names):
  - runtime_request_latency_seconds{quantile="0.95"}
  - runtime_request_errors_total{code=~"5.."}
  - scheduler_decision_latency_seconds
  - kernel_variant_served_total{variant="vA|vB"}
  - gpu_kernel_thrash_events_total
- Traces: correlate a sample of slow requests with scheduler.trace_id and kernel.variant tag.
- Logs: watch for admission-controller WARN entries: "eviction-loop" and "kernel-fallback".

Automated rollback detection rules (experiment controller)
- Primary triggers (immediate rollback):
  - fidelityDropPct >= 2.0 for the eval suite window.
  - p95 latency increase >= configured p95IncreaseMs (default 50ms).
  - sustained 5xx delta >= 0.2% over 60s.
- Secondary triggers (escalation):
  - GPU utilization > 95% for > 2 minutes.
  - Kernel handshake failures > 5/min.

Manual mitigation playbook (if automation fails)
1. Pause ingress to the canary namespace: kubectl scale deployment/router --replicas=0 -n redwood-canary
2. Force route to baseline kernel variant: curl -X POST https://runtime-admin.staging.internal/routing/set -d '{"force_variant":"vA"}' -H 'Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN'
3. Rebalance kvcache shards: runtime-opctl rebalance --scope=canary --shards=8
4. If nodes are unstable, cordon and drain affected GPU nodes: kubectl cordon <node>; kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data

Post-experiment analysis and artifacts
- Required artifacts to attach to the experiment ticket:
  - baseline and during-run Prometheus snapshots (5m each).
  - 50 representative traces (trace-ids or zipped spans).
  - Eval harness results (JSON), including per-prompt failure reasons.
  - Kernel variant counters and admission-decision logs.
- Template for postmortem summary (1 paragraph plus bullets):
  - What we changed (experiment spec)
  - What we observed (metrics & fidelity delta)
  - Root cause hypothesis
  - Remediation / follow-ups (owners and due dates)

Ownership and contacts
- Experiment owner: Maya Thompson (runtime experiments) - pager: maya-pager
- Eng SRE escalation: Arjun Patel - pager: arjun-pager
- Kernel oncall owner: Operator Team - ops-oncall@redwood.ai

Runbook maintenance and versioning
- Keep the experiment CRD examples in the runtime-experiments repo under /manifests/lab-playbooks.
- This doc is versioned by last_updated. For any changes that relax rollback thresholds, require SRE approval and update the Experiment Registry entry.

Links and references
- Observability dashboard (staging): https://grafana.staging.redwood.ai/d/runtime-inject
- Experiment Registry: https://experiments.redwood.ai/browse
- Eval harness docs: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/applied-ml-and-evals/eval-harness
- Scheduler fuzz lab: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-fuzz-resilience-lab-manual-2026

Appendix A — Example quick commands
- Baseline snapshot: kubectl run tg-load --image=redwood/tg-load:stable --command -- /bin/sh -c 'tg-run --profile=small-burst --duration=300' --context=staging-runtime-admin
- Trigger manual downgrade via admin API:
  curl -X POST https://runtime-admin.staging.internal/experiments/manual-downgrade -H 'Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN' -d '{"percent":10, "variant":"vB", "reason":"test"}'

Appendix B — Common failure modes and troubleshooting notes
- Symptom: fidelity drop without latency increase. Likely root cause: routing mislabeling or eval harness mismatch. Check kernel_variant_served_total and request-tag propagation.
- Symptom: p95 spikes but fidelity stable. Likely cause: kernel thrash or prefetch delays. Check gpu_kernel_thrash_events_total and kvcache-miss rates.
- Symptom: automation fails to rollback. Check experiment controller logs (controller-manager) and the event stream: kubectl -n staging-experiments get events --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp

Revision log
- 2025-11-12: Created by Maya Thompson.
- 2026-01-20: Added automated rollback thresholds (Arjun Patel).
- 2026-03-05: Clarified GPU utilization secondary trigger and updated command examples (Sofia Ramirez).

End of document

title: Elastic Fidelity Debt Amortization — Operational Playbook
content:
Summary
-------
This playbook describes the Elastic Fidelity Debt Amortization pattern: a deterministic, observable procedure to reduce latency/cost SLO debt by gradually stepping application fidelity (model variant, quantization, batch sizing, caching aggressiveness) using a staircase profile. The goal is to preserve user-facing availability while amortizing the operational and quality cost of emergency fidelity drops over a controlled time window.

When to use
-----------
- High short-term load or capacity pressure where immediate full-fidelity fallback causes unacceptable cost or instability.
- Post-incident recovery when we want to converge back to nominal fidelity without causing new tail-latency spikes.
- Release windows for quantization/kernel rollouts where a fast rollback would cause excess cost or churn.

Intended guarantees and SLOs impacted
------------------------------------
- Availability: no more than 1% user-facing errors during transition windows.
- Latency: p95 should remain below configured emergency SLO (example: 450ms).
- Quality budget: aggregated eval-score degradation limited to -3% per 10 minutes during amortization.
- Cost smoothing: avoid >2x immediate per-token cost increase when restoring fidelity.

Key concepts and terminology
----------------------------
- Fidelity Step: a named configuration applying a set of runtime knobs (model_variant, quant_profile, batch_max, kvcache_mode, kernel_variant).
- Debt Window: the time budget to recover (e.g., 30m).
- Amortization Staircase: ordered fidelity steps applied at deterministic intervals.
- Safety Gate: quality and latency checks that must pass before launching the next step up.

Example Staircase (recommended baseline)
---------------------------------------
1) emergency-low: small quantized variant, aggressive batch coalescing, KV cache only prefix mode. (immediate)
2) safety-hold: medium quantized variant, conservative batch increase, KV caching warmed, kernel spec fallback. (+5 minutes)
3) gradual-restore-1: larger variant with per-tenant token cap lift, reduced quantization. (+10 minutes)
4) gradual-restore-2: near-nominal variant, speculative prefetching enabled. (+20 minutes)
5) nominal: full-fidelity model variant and runtime knobs. (+30–60 minutes)

Operational configuration (policy sample YAML)
--------------------------------------------
- name: elastic_fidelity_amortization
  debt_window_minutes: 30
  steps:
    - id: emergency-low
      duration_minutes: 5
      model_variant: "gptx-mini-q4"
      quant_profile: "q4-agg"
      batch_max_tokens: 1024
      kvcache_mode: "prefix-only"
      accept_quality_drop_pct: 5.0
    - id: safety-hold
      duration_minutes: 5
      model_variant: "gptx-small-q4"
      quant_profile: "q4"
      batch_max_tokens: 2048
      kvcache_mode: "normal"
      accept_quality_drop_pct: 3.0
    - id: gradual-restore-1
      duration_minutes: 10
      model_variant: "gptx-base-q8"
      quant_profile: "q8"
      batch_max_tokens: 3072
      kvcache_mode: "normal-warmup"
      accept_quality_drop_pct: 1.5
    - id: nominal
      duration_minutes: 10
      model_variant: "gptx-base"
      quant_profile: "fp16"
      batch_max_tokens: 4096
      kvcache_mode: "full"
      accept_quality_drop_pct: 0.2

Telemetry signals to watch (real-time)
-------------------------------------
- runtime.p95_ms (by route and model_variant) — target: < emergency_slo_ms
- runtime.error_rate (5m rolling) — immediate abort threshold: >1%
- runtime.kvcache_hit_ratio (by tenant) — expected to increase through steps; flag if < 20% after step 2
- cost.per_1k_tokens (approx) — should not spike >2x baseline when moving steps
- eval_shadow.delta_score (shadow eval harness) — must stay within accept_quality_drop_pct

Runbook: emergency execution (operator path)
-------------------------------------------
1) Detect: Pager triggers (high p95 or GPU OOM alerts). Open incident in Slack channel #runtime-incidents and create an incident stub.
2) Immediate action (0–2 min): set policy to emergency-low. CLI: redwood runtime apply-policy --policy elastic_fidelity_amortization --start-step emergency-low --force
3) Observe (2–7 min): watch runtime.p95_ms, runtime.error_rate, kvcache_hit_ratio. If error_rate >1.5% after emergency-low, escalate to oncall and consider capacity-side mitigations (resume fallback region or scale up dedicated capacity).
4) Controlled staircase (5–30 min): allow policy to advance per configured durations. Before each advance, execute Safety Gate checks (see below). If a gate fails, halt and execute remedial actions (warm caches/evict/prefetch or re-enforce batching).
