5) Converge to nominal: once nominal step passes all gates for two consecutive intervals, mark incident resolved and create a post-incident note with metric deltas.

Safety Gate checks (pre-step promotion)
--------------------------------------
- Promoted if:
  - p95 improved or stable (within 10% of previous step)
  - error_rate <= 1%
  - shadow eval delta_score >= -accept_quality_drop_pct for step
  - no GPU OOMs in the past 3m
- If any check fails, run corrective sequence:
  - run: redwood runtime profile-collect --tenant <T> --duration 60s --tags step-promote
  - increase kvcache prefetch multiplier: redwood runtime set-kvcache --prefetch-multiplier 2 --tenant <T>
  - re-run safety gate after 2 minutes

Automated validation (CI gating)
-------------------------------
Before enabling Elastic Fidelity in production for a route, the following automated checks must pass in the staging environment:
- Ladder replay: run end-to-end request replay for 30 minutes covering the staircase transitions and verify p95 and error_rate projections.
- Shadow-eval: run prompt set shadow evaluation across steps and ensure aggregated delta_score within configured accept thresholds.
- Kernel compatibility test: validate kernel_variant fallbacks do not raise lane-level tail latencies beyond 25% of baseline.

Testing checklist (on-call drills)
----------------------------------
- Create a synthetic overcapacity event using the operational workload simulator and run the full amortization staircase in sandbox.
- Validate metrics ingestion and dashboarding for the key signals above.
- Time-boxed rollback: practice invoking immediate revert to nominal-low-cost fallback and verify rollback completes in < 60s.

Rollbacks and aborts
--------------------
- Immediate rollback: CLI: redwood runtime apply-policy --policy elastic_fidelity_amortization --start-step nominal --force
- Partial abort: set --hold-on-step <id> to prevent promotions while investigating.
- If operator cannot recover within debt_window_minutes, escalate to platform oncall for capacity scaling and perform emergency region failover if configured.

Ownership and handoff
---------------------
- Primary owners: runtime-operator (oncall rotation) and scheduling team (for kernel_variant toggles).
- Post-incident: assign a runbook owner to update policy thresholds and record lessons in the incident postmortem.

Observability and dashboards (recommended panels)
------------------------------------------------
- Elastic Fidelity Console: composite view showing current step per route, time-in-step, and per-step telemetry deltas.
- Step health chart: p95 / error_rate / kvcache_hit_ratio overlayed with step annotations.
- Shadow-eval trend: rolling delta_score for top 100 prompts.

Appendix: useful CLI snippets
----------------------------
- Show active policy and current step:
  redwood runtime get-policy --name elastic_fidelity_amortization --format table

- Force start a specific step:
  redwood runtime apply-policy --policy elastic_fidelity_amortization --start-step safety-hold --reason \"operator emergency\"

- Collect a 60s trace for step-promote troubleshooting:
  redwood runtime profile-collect --route <route> --duration 60s --output /tmp/trace.json

- Example alert rule (Prometheus):
  ALERT ElasticFidelityErrorSpike
    IF increase(runtime_error_total[2m]) > 0.01
    FOR 5m
    LABELS {severity=\"critical\"}
    ANNOTATIONS {summary=\"Error rate spike during amortization\"}

Notes and rationale
-------------------
- Why amortize? Immediate full-quality restores create hot-path costs and may re-trigger capacity instability. Gradual promotion reduces sudden spikes, lets caches warm, and provides measurable quality checkpoints.
- Why deterministic staircase? Human-friendly timeboxes improve predictability for oncall and allow automation to assert safety gates.

Document history
----------------
- 2025-11-02: Drafted by Priya Shah.
- 2025-12-10: Safety gate criteria refined after sandbox drills (Marco Li).
- 2026-01-18: Published with standardized YAML schema and new telemetry anchors (Sofia Gonzales).

title: Degradation Probing and Load‑Shed Orchestration Manual
content:
Overview
========
This document describes the design, operational contracts, and runbook for Redwood's runtime-level degradation probing and load‑shed orchestration subsystem (the Shedder + Probe Controller). It explains how the system detects overload or fidelity regressions, safely degrades throughput/quality, probes for capacity recovery, and executes fallbacks to preserve customer‑facing SLOs. Intended audience: SREs, runtime engineers, oncall responders, and anyone running canary/rollout experiments against the serving runtime.

Scope and goals
----------------
- Scope: host runtime components that make admission and fidelity decisions (shedder, probe controller, router policies, kernel scheduler hooks). Includes metrics, alerting, config knobs, and incident procedures. Does NOT cover dedicated customer‑side capacity contracts or API client behavior.
- Goals:
  - Keep p99 tail latency below configured SLOs during partial failure modes.
  - Minimize error amplification from naive hard‑shutdowns.
  - Provide deterministic probing detection windows (so automated rollbacks/canaries behave reliably).
  - Offer clear observability signals for triage and postmortem.

Ownership
---------
- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime (runtime-sre squad)
- Secondary owners: eng-platform (routing), eng-infra (autoscaler)
- Pager: runtime-sre oncall

Key terminology
---------------
- Shedder: admission component that rejects or defers incoming requests based on runtime signals and configured policies.
- Probe: a controlled low‑volume request used to test component health/fidelity during or after a degraded state.
- Degradation window: period during which the runtime accepts reduced throughput or fidelity (e.g., lower token budget, quantized model variant) to remain within resource bounds.
- Fidelity fallback: deliberate swap to a cheaper/compact model variant to preserve latency at the expense of some output quality.

High‑level architecture (text diagram)
-------------------------------------
Ingress -> Per‑route Router -> Admission Layer (Shedder) -> Scheduler/Kernels -> Execution
                              ^                                      |
                              |                                      v
                        Probe Controller <--- Health Aggregator <-- Kernel Telemetry

Design principles
-----------------
1. Graceful and measurable degradation: prefer smooth fidelity reductions (batch size limits, prefix caching, model variant swap) over abrupt connection resets.
2. Explorable recovery: when shedding, emit probes at controlled cadence to test recovery; probes must be tagged and isolated for observability.
3. Multi‑signal decisions: admission uses a weighted decision of kernel latency, GPU queue length, KV cache miss ratio, and model‑swap health. No single metric triggers an irreversible fallback.
4. Safety first: all automated fallback actions are rate‑limited and subject to automatic rollback if probe failure rate exceeds threshold.

Runtime components and contracts
--------------------------------
- Shedder (runtime component):
  - Inputs: per‑GPU queue depth, p99 kernel latency (1s window), slot exhaustion events, memory pressure flag.
  - Outputs: admit / queue / reject decisions + shed_reason tag.
  - Contract: decision latency <= 2ms; decisions annotated with trace_id and shed_reason.

- Probe Controller:
  - Inputs: health signals from telemetry, manual override from console, experiment flags.
  - Behavior: when degradation begins, schedule periodic probes (default cadence 1 probe/10s per cohort) that exercise the full model path including KV cache warmups.
  - Contract: probes must not exceed 0.5% of normal traffic and must be isolated from user billing metrics.

- Fidelity Orchestrator (model variant switcher):
  - Inputs: probe success ratio, runtime pressure score.
  - Outputs: model variant assignment per route/session.
  - Contract: variant switch must be atomic at the session token boundary and revertible within 30s when probes pass recovery thresholds.

Observability contract (metrics and logs)
-----------------------------------------
The following metrics must be emitted for every runtime shard and aggregated per cluster. Use these exact metric names for alerts and dashboards.

Metrics table (CSV style)
metric_name,description,unit,cardinality
runtime.shedder.admit_rate,Requests admitted after admission logic,req/s,route+shard
runtime.shedder.reject_rate,Requests rejected due to shedding,req/s,route+shard
runtime.shedder.queue_depth,Admission queue length,requests,shard
runtime.kernel.p99_latency,Kernel p99 latency over 1s window,ms,shard
runtime.kernel.queue_wait,Time spent waiting for kernel slot,ms,shard
runtime.kvcache.miss_ratio,KV cache miss ratio,percent,route
runtime.probe.success_ratio,Fraction of probes that returned expected status,percent,cohort
runtime.fidelity.variant,Active model variant id,string,route+session

Alerting thresholds (recommended)
- Sev 1: runtime.kernel.p99_latency > 1200ms for > 2m AND runtime.shedder.reject_rate > 0.1req/s aggregated across cluster.
- Sev 2: runtime.probe.success_ratio < 80% over a 5m window.
- Sev 3: runtime.kvcache.miss_ratio > 30% for a route over 10m.

Runbook: detection -> containment -> probe -> recovery (step‑by‑step)
-------------------------------------------------------------------
1) Detection:
   - Pager triggers on Sev 1 alert. Open incident channel and claim.
   - Confirm p99 latency, drop rate, and any kernel OOM/slot errors in the trace stream.
2) Containment:
   - If admit decisions are saturating kernels, temporarily raise shedder aggressiveness to target 20% reject until further analysis. Command:
     - rctl shedder set --route <route> --aggressiveness 0.2 --reason "temporary‑containment"
   - Document the change in the incident timeline and tag affected customers in the console.
3) Probe:
   - Initiate manual probe run to validate execution path:
     - curl -H "X-Redwood-Probe: true" -X POST https://runtime-probe.local/healthcheck --data '{"route":"<route>","model":"<variant>"}'
   - Inspect runtime.probe.success_ratio and kernel traces for failed probes.
4) Recovery:
   - If probe success_ratio >= 95% for 2 consecutive 1m windows: gradually rollback shedder aggressiveness by 10% every 30s.
   - If probe failure persists, trigger model variant swap to a lower‑cost variant (see fidelity table below) with a canary cohort (1% traffic) for 5m before wide rollout.

CLI and diagnostic commands
---------------------------
- List shedding state per route: rctl shedder list --output table\- Set aggressiveness (0.0–1.0): rctl shedder set --route <route> --aggressiveness 0.3\- Trigger a manual probe: rctl probe run --route <route> --variant <variant> --count 10\- Dump last 5 kernel traces for a shard: rctl trace tail --shard <id> --limit 5\- Temporarily pin model variant: rctl model pin --route <route> --variant <id> --ttl 10m

Sample PromQL alerts
--------------------
- High p99 latency with shedding:
  sum by(cluster) (rate(runtime.kernel.p99_latency_sum[1m])) / sum by(cluster) (rate(runtime.kernel.p99_latency_count[1m])) > 1200
- Probe failure rate:
  1 - (sum(runtime.probe.success_ratio) by(cohort) / count(runtime.probe.success_ratio) by(cohort)) > 0.2

Configuration knobs and recommended defaults (table)
---------------------------------------------------
knob,default,description
shedder.window_size,1000ms,Time window for smoothing decision signals
shedder.min_admit_rate,10req/s,Minimum guaranteed admission per route (soft)
shedder.max_probe_fraction,0.005,Max fraction of traffic that can be probes
probe.cadence,10s,Minimum interval between probes for same cohort
variant.canary_fraction,0.01,Fraction of traffic used to canary a variant swap
fallback.max_duration,15m,Maximum continuous duration for an automatic fallback before human review

Safety & rollout constraints
---------------------------
- Any automated model variant swap must pass the probe gate for the canary cohort for at least three consecutive probe windows.
- Fallbacks that persist longer than fallback.max_duration must open a ticket in the runtime backlog and notify the release owner.
- All shedder aggressiveness changes performed by automation are rate limited to 10% change per minute to avoid oscillation.

Testing and validation matrix
----------------------------
- Unit tests: shedder decision logic and probe tagging (CI enforced).
- Integration tests: synthetic load profiles that simulate cache coldstart, kernel saturation, and degraded interconnect (run by perf CI nightly).
- Chaos tests: injected kernel hang and NVLink degradation scenarios with controlled shedding to validate graceful degradation behavior (game day quarterly).

Known limitations and tradeoffs
------------------------------
- Probes are small by design and can pass even when larger normal traffic fails due to queue ordering differences; use probe traces as one signal among many.
- Model variant swaps reduce latency but may cause downstream semantic regressions; every variant includes a quality delta estimate that must be considered for enterprise customers.
- The shedder cannot (currently) account for cross‑shard KV cache warming heuristics perfectly; this can lead to transient higher miss_ratio after recovery.

Post‑incident checklist
----------------------
- Export probe traces and kernel traces for the incident window.
- Compute probe success_ratio and compare to probe baseline.
- If fallback triggered, run fidelity regression suite for affected prompt sets.
- File a follow‑up action in the runtime backlog with owner and target date.

Appendix A: Example YAML policy fragment
---------------------------------------
# admission policy for high throughput text-generation route
admission_policy:
  route: "/v1/generate"
  shedder:
    aggressiveness: 0.15
    window_size_ms: 1000
    min_admit_rate: 10
  probe:
    cadence_s: 10
    max_fraction: 0.005
  fidelity_fallback:
    canary_fraction: 0.01
    variants:["gptx-8b-q4","gptx-8b-q2a"]

Appendix B: Quick reference for oncall responders
--------------------------------------------------
- First 5 minutes: confirm alerts, set temporary containment to 20% reject if kernels saturated.
- 5–20 minutes: run manual probes and escalate to runtime-sre if probe fail rate > 20%.
- >20 minutes: if automated rollback does not stabilize, trigger manual canary variant swap and route pin.

Document history and changes
--------------------------
- 2026-02-10: created (Priya Nandakumar)
- 2026-04-18: tightened probe cadence and added canary constraints (reviewers: Ethan Park)
- 2026-09-15: updated alert thresholds and added PromQL examples (reviewers: Marcus Li, Sofia Alvarez)

Related docs and links
----------------------
- Runtime decision graph: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/runtime-decision-graph-and-observed-behaviour-catalog-2026
- Backpressure playbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/sla-aware-admission-controller-and-backpressure-playbook-2027
- Kernel telemetry contract: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/kernel-telemetry-annotation-guidelines-2025

title: memory-pressure-incident-triage-and-recovery-playbook-2026
content:
Summary:

This runbook describes detection, triage, mitigation, and recovery procedures for GPU and host memory pressure incidents affecting the Redwood serving runtime. It centralizes observable signals, automated mitigations, manual steps, rollback guidance, and post-incident analysis templates. It is intended for on-call SREs, runtime engineers, and the serving runtime owners.

Scope and intent:
- Applies to production and pre-prod clusters running the runtime (hosted and dedicated).
- Covers transient memory spikes, sustained memory leaks, KV cache bloat, and OOMs that surface as request failures, elevated tail latency, or node instability.
- Does NOT replace component-specific leak-fix investigations (those belong in an RCA). This is an operational triage and recovery playbook.

Key signals (primary metrics and thresholds):
- gpu_memory_utilization_pct > 92% (sustained for > 60s) => warning
- cuda_free_bytes < 0.1 * cuda_total_bytes (free < 10%) => critical
- host_mem_free_pct < 8% => critical
- node_oom_kills > 0 in last 5m => critical
- kvcache_eviction_rate == 0 while kvcache_size growing => suspicious
- request_rejection_rate > 0.5% & tail_p95_latency > SLO => operational impact

Recommended alert definitions (examples):
- ALERT RuntimeGpuMemoryPressure
  - expr: avg_over_time(gpu_memory_utilization_pct[1m]) > 92
  - for: 1m
  - severity: page

- ALERT HostMemoryExhaustion
  - expr: avg_over_time(node_memory_free_percent[2m]) < 8
  - for: 2m
  - severity: page

Quick detection checklist (what to look at first):
1) Is the alert noisy or isolated? Check cluster scope and pod cardinality.
2) Are requests failing with OOM or CUDA errors? Check logs for "OutOfMemoryError", "cudaErrorUnknown", "CUBLAS_STATUS_ALLOC_FAILED".
3) Correlate with recent deploys/rollouts or model variant switches in the last 10 minutes.
4) Confirm whether KV cache warmup or bulk-replay jobs are running.

On-call escalation matrix (who to call):
- Primary: runtime-oncall (pager duty) -> owns immediate remediation
- Secondary: serving-platform (Slack: #serving-platform)
- Tertiary: runtime-kernel-team (for suspected kernel/cuda issues)

Automated mitigations (automatically triggered by the control plane):
- Soft eviction: decremented KVCACHE retention per tenant by 20% for 2 minutes. This frees pinned prefixes preferentially.
- Request shedder: temporarily reject low-priority background requests and batch-jobs for 30s.
- Model fallback: route to smaller model variant with identical interface (e.g., 13B->7B) for impacted routes if configured.
- Slot reduction: reduce per-tenant concurrency slot allocation by 25% to avoid head-of-line memory bloat.

When automated mitigations run, on-call must verify impact within 60–120s and whether further manual action is required.

Manual triage and remediation steps (ordered):
1) Triage & scope
   - Identify impacted nodes via alert dashboard: query node labels and pod assignments for the high-mem nodes.
   - Grafana queries to run:
     - gpu_memory_by_node: avg(gpu_memory_alloc_bytes) by (node)
     - kvcache_size_by_tenant: sum(kvcache_bytes) by (tenant)
     - recent_deploys: increase(time() - deploy_timestamp_seconds < 600)

2) Immediate mitigation (safe, low-risk first)
   - Trigger soft eviction manually if automated path not already run: POST /admin/evict?scope=soft&fraction=0.2
   - Disable non-critical background jobs: apply label "no-batch" to pods via kubectl or patch the job controller.
   - Flip model-route to fallback variant for the tenant: use routing API -> PATCH /routes/{route}/variant -> {"variant":"fallback-small"}

3) Step-up mitigation (if memory continues rising)
   - Drain requests from the most memory-taxing nodes: kubectl cordon && kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --force <node>
   - Evacuate long-lived sessions: signal runtime to gracefully terminate sessions with > N cached tokens. (runtime admin CLI: runtime-admin sessions terminate --idle-gt 3600)
   - Reduce per-request max_sequence_length via runtime config for affected routes.

4) Emergency mitigation (if OOMs continuing or node instability)
   - Scale down concurrency aggressively for the cluster or move tenants to lower-memory pools.
   - Power-cycle affected GPU nodes through the node pool API (last resort).

Rollback and recovery guidance:
- If the incident started with a deploy/rollout, immediately roll back the deploy using the canary matrix in the deployment dashboard. Record rollback ID and time.
- After memory metrics stabilize (gpu_memory_utilization_pct < 65% for 5m and host_mem_free_pct > 20%), reverse mitigations in reverse order: uncordon nodes, restore background jobs, re-enable higher-concurrency slots, and re-route traffic to primary model variants gradually (canary 10% -> 50% -> 100% with 5m observation window).

Root cause hypotheses and evidence checklist (collect before altering state):
- Memory leak in kernel-level allocator: evidence = steadily increasing GPU reserved bytes even with low request rate, kernel update in last 24h.
- KV cache pinning: evidence = kvcache_size growing with zero eviction_rate & tenants with long-running sessions.
- Bursty large-batch traffic (client-side): evidence = sudden spike in batch_size distribution and request aggregation metrics.
- Model switch oscillation causing multiple variants to instantiate simultaneously: evidence = near-simultaneous model_load events and peak in model_startup_allocations.
- Driver / CUDA bug: evidence = correlated driver update + node-level coredumps or CUDA errors across heterogeneous hardware.

Forensic commands and useful log snippets:
- kubectl get pods -o wide --field-selector status.phase=Running -l service=runtime --all-namespaces
- journalctl -u runtime.service --since "10 minutes ago" | grep -E "OutOfMemory|cudaError|CUBLAS"
- nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.total,memory.free,memory.used --format=csv -l 1
- runtime-admin metrics dump --node <node> --out /tmp/metrics.json

Suggested dashboards and panels to check:
- Cluster memory overview (node+gpu) – panel: node_free_pct, gpu_free_bytes
- Top tenants by GPU memory (table) – kvcache size, session count, recent model loads
- Request pipeline telemetry – queue_depth, batch_size_distribution, p95/p99 latency
- Recent driver and kernel deploy timeline overlay

Playbook of short CLI snippets (examples):
- Force soft eviction for tenant 'acme':
  curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" https://controlplane.internal/admin/evict?tenant=acme&scope=soft&fraction=0.25
- Drain a node safely:
  kubectl cordon gpu-node-17
  kubectl drain gpu-node-17 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --force
- Patch a route to smaller variant:
  curl -X PATCH -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" https://controlplane.internal/api/routes/my-chat-route -d '{"variant":"13b-to-7b-fallback"}'

Owner and responsibilities table (informal table):
- Incident owner: runtime-oncall (page) => triage, run mitigations, escalate.
- Kernel/pool issues: runtime-kernel-team => kernel-level fixes, kernel rollback.
- KV cache behavior: serving-platform => cache policies, eviction tuning.
- Post-incident RCA: runtime-techlead => lead investigation and publish RCA.

Post-incident checklist and RCA template (to run within 48h):
1) Save all monitoring data slices (5m before start, during incident, 30m after) and upload to incident folder.
2) List timeline with exact timestamps for deploys, mitigations, and observed metric changes.
3) Hypotheses considered and tests run (include commands and results).
4) Root cause conclusion and long-term mitigations (code fixes, config changes, alert tuning).
5) Action owners and deadlines.

Example mitigation proposals (long term):
- KVCACHE adaptive eviction policy: implement per-tenant LRU aging + memory headroom target.
- Slot-aware allocation: use per-GPU soft quotas and proactive slot shedding when headroom < 20%.
- Memory-safety CI job: inject synthetic leaks in a staging harness ("oom-injector-simulator") to validate auto-eviction and draining behavior.
- Runtime memory accounting improvements: instrument allocator to report per-session and per-model allocation breakdowns.

Related pages and references:
- runtime-telemetry-schema (dashboard link)
- kernel-and-scheduling/preemption-aware-batch-slicing-spec-2026
- runbooks/cold-start-warmup-strategies-and-entropy-reduction-2025

Appendix: quick decision table (text table)
| Symptom | First action | When to escalate | Likely owner |
|---------|--------------|-------------------|--------------|
| Rapid GPU mem rise but requests normal | Soft-evict KVCACHE; check for background jobs | If mem stays >90% for 3m | serving-platform |
| Frequent OOM kills | Cordons + drain node; migrate tenants | Immediate page | runtime-kernel-team |
| Model load storms during deploy | Rollback deploy canary; enable model fallback | If reoccurs on rollback -> page | runtime-release |

Contact and runbook updates:
- Keep this doc current: runtime-oncall updates after every major kernel or routing change.
- Add any new remediation commands or endpoints to the Playbook CLI list above.

End of document.

title: Slow Kernel Detection and Hotfix Playbook
content:
Overview

This playbook describes detection, automated containment, and manual hotfix procedures for incidents where a GPU kernel (or small set of kernels) regress in latency or CPU/GPU time and produce sustained throughput degradation. It focuses on actionable detection signals, escalation thresholds, immediate mitigations to protect SLAs, and validated release steps for kernel hotfixes.

Scope

- Applies to production inference runtime kernels (attention, fused-matmul, kv-cache ops, rotary/rope ops) across hosted and dedicated clusters.
- Does NOT cover hardware faults (power/thermal fails) or driver-level crashes — those are handled by infrastructure runbooks.

Ownership and contacts

- Incident owner: eng-serving-runtime oncall (primary).
- Kernel lead: @Maya Chen (runtime-kernels).
- Escalation: runtime-arch-sre@redwood.internal.

When to use this playbook

Use this playbook when:
1) Kernel latency spike or variance is correlated with increased end-to-end p95/p99 serving latency for >5 minutes.
2) Throughput drop or request queuing increases by >30% while GPU utilization is not saturated.
3) Automated regression detection (see Alerting rules) fires.

Detection signals and telemetry

Primary metrics to monitor (examples):
- kernel.exec_time_ms (histogram per kernel): sudden shift in median or tail.
- kernel.cpu_time_ms and kernel.gpu_time_ms: divergence indicates scheduling/serialization issues.
- runtime.request_queue_depth: sustained increase suggests backpressure.
- gpu_utilization_pct: if <85% while queue depth grows => kernel stalls/serialization.
- kernel.retry_count / kernel_ejection_count: raised ejection counts.

Suggested alert rules (promQL-like pseudocode):

- name: KernelTailLatencyExceeded
  expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(kernel_exec_time_ms_bucket[2m])) by (le,kernel)) > 12
  for: 4m

- name: KernelVarianceSpike
  expr: (quantile_over_time(0.95, kernel_exec_time_ms[10m]) / quantile_over_time(0.5, kernel_exec_time_ms[10m])) > 4
  for: 3m

- name: QueueGrowthWithLowUtil
  expr: (increase(runtime_request_queue_depth[5m]) > 30) and (avg_over_time(gpu_utilization_pct[5m]) < 85)
  for: 5m

Investigation timeline (first 30 minutes)

1) Triage (0–5m):
   - Acknowledge alert in PagerDuty and tag with incident channel.
   - Attach the alert graph and note the affected model(s)/cluster(s).

2) Quick checks (5–12m):
   - Confirm whether regression is per-kernel or broad: query kernel.exec_time_ms grouped by kernel_name and host.
   - Check recent releases or kernel rollouts in the last 60 minutes.
   - Inspect kernel ejection logs and driver warnings.

3) Decide containment (12–20m):
   - If kernel impact is limited to a subset of workers, use targeted quarantine (see Automated mitigations).
   - If impact is global or affects control-plane operations, follow full degradation playbook and notify product & CS.

Automated mitigations (safe by default)

We prefer automated, reversible actions to avoid manual intervention during noisy transient spikes. Typical automated mitigations:

- Kernel quarantine: mark kernel variant as degraded and route traffic to next-compatible variant (e.g., fallback quantized kernel or older kernel build).
- Per-host kernel disable: use runtime-agent to toggle kernel blacklist on affected hosts.
- Graceful request shed: temporarily reduce concurrency for affected hosts and redirect to healthy pools.

Automation pseudocode (internal operator):

# Example internal CLI commands
redwood-runtimectl quarantine-kernel --kernel-name fused_attn_v2 --reason "p95 regression 2026-02-28" --scope hosts=pool-3b
redwood-runtimectl set-concurrency --host host-12 --max-concurrency 2

Containment decision matrix (summary):
| Impact pattern | Immediate action | Rationale |
|---|---:|---|
| Single-host / single-kernel | Kernel quarantine + local restart | Limits blast radius |
| Multi-host same kernel | Route to fallback variant + scale healthy pool | Prevents large SLA violations |
| Global performance regression | Activate degradation SLOs and roll back recent kernel rollout | Protect customer-facing SLAs |

Manual hotfix procedure (if automation insufficient)

1) Create incident branch and patch:
   - Branch from release-tag: git checkout -b hotfix/kernel-<id>-<date> release/<tag>
   - Add guard-logging (timestamps + kernel id) and revert recent non-essential optimizations if needed.

2) Build and smoke test in staging:
   - Build: make -C runtime kernels && ./tools/build-kernel --name hotfix-kernel --ccache
   - Unit smoke: ./tools/smoke-runner --kernel hotfix-kernel --profile micro-latency
   - Perf microbench: ./bench/kernel-bench --kernel hotfix-kernel --seq-lens 8,64,512 --shots 200

3) Canaried rollout (targeted pattern):
   - Canary to 2–3 hosts with mirrored traffic for 10m.
   - Metrics to watch during canary: p50/p95 kernel.exec_time_ms, request_queue_depth, gpu_utilization, error_rate.
   - Canary acceptance criteria: no >5% regression vs baseline on p50 and <3% change in p95.

4) Gradual ramp: 20% -> 50% -> 100% or by host pools depending on topology. Evaluate at each step for 10–15 minutes.

Rollback criteria and steps

Rollback if any of the following occurs during canary or ramp:
- p95 increases by >10% relative to the pre-incident baseline.
- request queue depth increases by >2x.
- error rate (5xx) increases above SLO thresholds.

Rollback steps:
1) Immediately set routing to previous kernel variant using runtime controller.
2) Drain canary hosts and reboot agent if necessary: systemctl restart runtime-agent on canary hosts.
3) Mark hotfix branch for postmortem and revert patch in mainline if necessary.

Verification checklist after rollback/hotfix

- Verify kernel.exec_time_ms histograms have returned to baseline over 30 minutes.
- Validate no increase in request_retries or request_timeouts.
- Confirm logs show no new driver warnings.
- Close incident with updates to relevant oncall and product teams.

Post-incident follow-up

- Owner prepares postmortem within 72 hours: root cause, timeline, mitigations, action items.
- If kernel regression was caused by a code change, add mandatory microbench in CI for the offending kernel with 95th percentile assertions.
- Schedule a retro with kernel authors and SRE to adjust thresholds or automation if false positives/negatives caused disruption.

Testing and benchmark additions

When a kernel shows instability add these tests to the CI pipeline:
- Deterministic microbenchmark for sequence lengths: 8, 32, 128, 512 (200 iterations each).
- Telemetry spike test: inject synthetic jitter and assert no >2x increase in hardware stall markers.
- Multi-host soak test: run 60-minute concurrent-run against a mirrored traffic profile.

Quick reference commands

- Query per-kernel tail latency (internal monitoring):
  curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $MONITOR_TOKEN" "https://monitoring.internal/api/query?q=kernel_exec_time_ms%7Bcluster%3D%5C\"prod%5C\"%7D"

- Quarantine kernel: redwood-runtimectl quarantine-kernel --kernel-name <kernel> --scope hosts=<pool>
- Re-enable kernel: redwood-runtimectl unquarantine-kernel --kernel-name <kernel>
- Canary rollout: redwood-runtimectl deploy-kernel --image hotfix-kernel:canary --hosts host-12,host-13

Appendix: recommended thresholds (editable)

| Setting | Default value | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| p95_kernel_latency_alert_ms | 12 | Trigger for KernelTailLatencyExceeded rule |
| kernel_variance_ratio_alert | 4 | Ratio of p95/p50 over 10m window |
| queue_growth_pct_alert | 30 | Percent growth over 5 minutes |
| canary_observe_window | 10m | Observation window for canary acceptance |

Related artifacts and links

- Kernel perf harness: git:/repo/runtime/kernels/bench/
- Quarantine controller docs: /eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/quarantine-controller-2025
- Incident tracker template: /oncall-and-incident-response/postmortem-template

Revision history

- 2026-01-15: Initial draft by Maya Chen.
- 2026-02-10: Added automated mitigation examples and CLI snippets.
- 2026-02-28: Finalized thresholds and canary acceptance criteria (published).

title: Serving Runtime Hotfix Runbook (Emergency Patch Release)
content:
h2. When to use this runbook
Use this runbook when a serving-runtime change must be shipped quickly to mitigate an active incident (typically Sev-1). This covers code change, build, validation, and handoff to rollout owners.

h2. Preconditions
* Emergency change approvals recorded per /policies-and-process/change-management/emergency-change-policy-v3
* Incident channel exists (or a dedicated Slack thread) with IC identified
* A rollback plan exists (previous runtime image tag + restart procedure)

h2. Step 1 — Cut a hotfix branch
1. Create branch naming: hotfix/runtime-<YYYYMMDD>-<short-issue>
2. Cherry-pick the minimum fix commit(s) only.
3. Update CHANGELOG entry under 'Runtime Hotfixes'.

h2. Step 2 — Create PR and get emergency reviews
1. Open GitHub PR targeting release branch (preferred) or main if release branch is not available.
2. Required reviewers: runtime on-call + SRE on-call (or IC).
3. Include in PR description: incident link, hypothesis, risk, rollback, rollout owners.

h2. Step 3 — Build + sign artifacts
Follow /eng-infra/ci-cd-and-build/hotfix-build-and-signing. Minimum artifacts:
* runtime container image (multi-arch if applicable)
* SBOM (CycloneDX)
* provenance attestation

h2. Step 4 — Validate the fix
*Minimum* validation required even in an incident:
* Unit tests for affected module
* One perf-canary run for representative model (e.g., Llama 3.1 70B)
* One stress test at the incident-triggering pattern (sequence length + concurrency)

Validation checklist (record results in PR):
* Error rate improves or eliminates the triggering error
* p95 latency does not regress > 10% compared to previous runtime image for the same workload
* No increase in OOM or GPU reset counters

h2. Step 5 — Prepare rollout notes
In the incident channel, post:
* New runtime image tag
* Expected impact during rollout (restarts, brief connection resets)
* Canary target (Hosted region or Dedicated cluster)
* Rollback criteria (metrics + customer symptom)

h2. Step 6 — Handoff to rollout owners
* Hosted: hand off to Platform/SRE per /eng-platform/runbooks/hosted-rollout-and-rollback-procedure
* Dedicated: hand off to Infra + CSEM per /eng-infra/gpu-fleet-and-capacity/dedicated-cluster-hotfix-rollout-notes

h2. Rollback reminder
If rollback triggers are met, roll back immediately; do not wait for a full incident update cadence. Announce rollback in incident channel and update status page wording to reflect mitigation change.

h2. Appendix — Common pitfalls
* Fix includes unrelated refactors (reject; keep minimal).
* No canary defined (must be explicitly waived by IC).
* Artifact unsigned or missing SBOM (must not ship).

title: Runbook: Runtime overload mitigation (Hosted API)
content:
## Purpose
This runbook describes how to detect, triage, and mitigate **Serving Runtime overload** for Redwood Hosted API. It focuses on the runtime layer (scheduler, batching, KV cache, GPU utilization signals) and how to apply mitigations safely without causing retry storms or noisy-neighbor regressions.

This runbook is used when:
- p95/p99 latency spikes and/or timeouts correlate with runtime saturation.
- Error rates increase due to runtime admission rejecting work (shed) or the gateway/routing breaker opening.
- One or more GPU pools show persistent queue growth or memory pressure.

## Scope
In scope:
- Runtime overload symptoms and saturation metrics
- Runtime mitigations (throttle/admission, batching caps, feature reduction toggles exposed to runtime)
- When/how to coordinate with Gateway and Smart Routing

Out of scope:
- Customer comms/status page updates (see Hosted circuit breaker runbook)
- Long-term capacity changes / procurement

## Roles and escalation
- **Runtime oncall (primary):** serving-runtime engineer on rotation
- **SRE oncall (incident commander):** for SEV2+ or multi-region impact
- **Gateway/control plane:** for admission-layer changes
- **Smart Routing:** for fallback routing / regional steering

Escalate when:
- Multi-tenant impact in a region for >10 minutes
- Shed rate > 2% sustained for a tier that should not shed under normal bursts (Enterprise Hosted)
- Suspected regression (post deploy) correlates with overload signals

## Safety principles (read first)
1. **Prefer early shedding over tail-latency collapse.** If runtime is overloaded, accepting more work usually makes recovery harder.
2. **Avoid retry storms.** Any change that increases 429/503 must ensure stable Retry-After behavior at the edge (Gateway) and bounded retries in clients.
3. **Change one thing at a time.** Apply a single mitigation, wait 3–5 minutes, then evaluate.
4. **Preserve tenant isolation.** Do not globally increase batching to “fix” one tenant if it degrades others.

## Quick decision tree
Use this to choose the right mitigation quickly.

### A) Queue depth climbing and latency increasing; GPU utilization high
Likely **compute saturation** (tokens/sec bound) or under-provisioned pool.
- First actions: tighten admission / reduce concurrency; confirm gateway breaker is protecting.
- Secondary: reduce max_tokens caps / streaming concurrency; adjust batching caps conservatively.

### B) Queue depth climbing; GPU utilization moderate; memory usage high / OOMs
Likely **KV cache pressure** / memory fragmentation / long-context load.
- First actions: cap max_context or max_prefill_tokens; reduce parallelism for long prompts.
- Secondary: adjust KV cache policy; reduce batch size or prefill concurrency.

### C) Queue depth stable; latency spikes; error rate increases in bursts
Likely **dependency brownout** (model storage, tokenizer service, auth, or routing) or **scheduler stall**.
- First actions: identify dependency errors; consider temporary feature reduction that reduces dependency load.
- Secondary: coordinate with SRE; consider draining affected shards.

### D) Shed rate high but saturation metrics look normal
Likely **bad thresholds** or **bad signal** / instrumentation issue.
- First actions: validate signal freshness and aggregation; check if a single shard is bad.
- Secondary: roll back threshold changes; page runtime instrumentation owner.

## Where to look (dashboards & logs)
### Dashboards
Open the “Overload Protection” dashboard and then drill into “Serving Runtime” panels.
Recommended views (filters): `region`, `cluster`, `pool`, `model_family`, `tier`.

Key panels to review (names may vary by region):
- **Runtime admission / shed rate** (requests rejected at runtime)
- **Prefill queue depth** (pending prefill jobs)
- **Decode queue depth** (pending decode steps)
- **Scheduler backlog / loop time** (scheduler tick latency)
- **Token throughput** (tokens/sec by pool)
- **GPU utilization** (avg and p95 across replicas)
- **KV cache pressure** (usage ratio, eviction rate)
- **GPU memory usage** and **OOM count**
- **P99 end-to-end latency** split by stage (gateway, routing, runtime)

### Logs / traces
- Runtime service logs: `serving-runtime` (and model-specific workers)
- Look for: `OOM`, `cuda out of memory`, `scheduler lag`, `queue full`, `admission denied`, `kv_cache` warnings
- Trace a few slow requests to see whether time is spent in prefill, decode, or waiting.

## Metrics glossary and how to interpret
Use these to confirm you are dealing with runtime overload (vs gateway/routing/dependency).

### 1) Prefill queue depth
What it means: number of requests waiting for prefill (prompt processing).
Interpretation:
- Rising steadily with increasing prefill latency indicates prefill saturation (often long prompts).
- If prefill queue grows but decode queue is flat, you are prefill-bound.

### 2) Decode queue depth
What it means: backlog of decode steps (streaming generation) waiting for compute.
Interpretation:
- Rising decode queue with high GPU util indicates tokens/sec saturation.
- Rising decode queue with moderate GPU util can indicate scheduler overhead or throttling.

### 3) Token/sec saturation
What it means: measured throughput approaching pool’s steady-state ceiling.
Interpretation:
- If tokens/sec is near ceiling and p99 worsens, prioritize shedding / concurrency reduction.
- If tokens/sec is low but queues grow, suspect stalls, memory, or dependency issues.

### 4) KV cache pressure
Signals:
- `kv_cache_usage_ratio` high (near configured limit)
- high `kv_cache_evictions` and increasing latency
Interpretation:
- High KV usage correlates with long contexts and many concurrent streams.
- Evictions can cause performance cliffs; prefer limiting long-context concurrency rather than only increasing batching.

### 5) Memory pressure / fragmentation proxy
Signals:
- increasing allocation failures / “reserved but unavailable” patterns
- frequent OOM recoveries/restarts
Interpretation:
- Treat as urgent; restarts can cause thundering herd if the gateway keeps admitting.

## Standard triage procedure
### Step 1 — Confirm impact and scope (2–3 minutes)
1. Identify region(s), model(s), and tiers affected.
2. Confirm if the gateway breaker is open and shedding is happening at the edge.
3. Check whether impact is localized to a pool/shard or systemic.

Record in the incident doc (or Slack thread):
- Start time
- Affected region + model + tier
- Current shed rate and p99 latency

### Step 2 — Determine saturation type (5 minutes)
Use the “Metrics glossary” above to classify as:
- Compute saturation (decode-bound)
- Prefill saturation (prompt-bound)
- Memory/KV pressure
- Dependency brownout / scheduler stall

### Step 3 — Apply the least risky mitigation
Prefer mitigations in this order (lowest blast radius first):
1) Tighten admission for the impacted pool/route
2) Reduce expensive features (streaming concurrency, tool-calling complexity)
3) Reduce max_tokens / max_context caps (tier-aware)
4) Tune batching caps
5) Drain/cordon bad replicas/shards

### Step 4 — Validate recovery
After each change:
- Wait 3–5 minutes (longer for long-context workloads)
- Confirm queue depth trends down
- Confirm p99 latency improves
- Confirm shed rate stabilizes (not oscillating)
- Confirm no new error class/regression is introduced (e.g., missing Retry-After at edge)

## Mitigation actions (how-to)
Notes:
- Exact knobs vary by deployment. When in doubt, coordinate with Gateway oncall before changing customer-visible behavior.
- All changes should be logged in the incident timeline with time, actor, knob, previous value, new value.

### Mitigation 1 — Reduce runtime admission / concurrency (preferred first response)
Goal: stop backlog growth and allow queues to drain.

Common actions:
- Reduce `runtime_max_inflight_requests` for the impacted pool.
- Reduce `decode_concurrency_per_gpu` or `streams_per_replica`.

Operational guidance:
- If queue depth is climbing: cut concurrency by 10–25% first.
- If OOMs are occurring: cut concurrency by 25–50% and reduce long-context traffic.

Example (illustrative) command patterns:
- View current pool config:
  - `rwctl runtime pools get --region us-east --pool hosted-a10g-1`
- Patch concurrency cap:
  - `rwctl runtime pools patch --region us-east --pool hosted-a10g-1 --set decode_concurrency_per_gpu=6`

Rollback:
- Restore previous values after queues stabilize for at least 30 minutes.

### Mitigation 2 — Feature reduction toggles (reduce expensive work)
Goal: reduce per-request cost while keeping service available.

Supported feature reduction modes (must be policy-guarded):
- Lower streaming concurrency (limits concurrent active streams per tenant)
- Reduce tool-calling complexity (e.g., cap tool calls or tool schema size)
- Apply stricter `max_tokens` caps during overload

When to use:
- Decode-bound saturation (tokens/sec ceiling)
- Tenant with unusually heavy tool-calling causing noisy-neighbor behavior

How to execute:
- Confirm the feature flag is enabled for overload mode (policy engine / gateway).
- Apply only to affected tier/route/model if possible.

Notes:
- Customer-visible behavior may change. Ensure error semantics remain stable and documented (ADR-014).

### Mitigation 3 — Cap long-context prefill (KV/memory pressure response)
Goal: reduce KV cache footprint and avoid OOM/fragmentation.

Actions:
- Reduce `max_context_tokens` (or `max_prompt_tokens`) for the affected model route.
- Reduce parallel prefill concurrency (if exposed separately).

When to use:
- Prefill queue depth + memory pressure rising
- OOMs correlated with long prompts

Tradeoffs:
- More requests may be rejected early (prefer 429/503 overload with clear guidance) rather than timing out.

### Mitigation 4 — Adjust continuous batching caps (use with caution)
Goal: improve throughput efficiency without causing latency cliffs.

Actions:
- Increase `max_batch_tokens` slightly (5–15%) if GPU util is high but scheduler overhead is low.
- Decrease `max_batch_tokens` if tail latency is exploding due to too-large batches.

When to use:
- Stable traffic with predictable sequence lengths
- You have clear evidence of batching inefficiency rather than pure saturation

Warnings:
- Over-aggressive batching can worsen p99, especially with mixed prompt lengths.
- Changing batching interacts with KV cache behavior.

### Mitigation 5 — Drain/cordon unhealthy replicas or shards
Goal: remove pathological workers (memory leak, bad GPU, driver issues) that create localized overload.

Indicators:
- One replica shows abnormal queue depth, errors, or restarts.
- Pool-wide metrics look fine but tail latency remains high.

Steps (generic Kubernetes pattern; adapt to your environment):
1. Identify unhealthy pods:
   - `kubectl -n serving-runtime get pods -l pool=<pool> -o wide`
2. Check logs for repeated OOM or crash loops.
3. Cordon/drain (if supported via runtime orchestration):
   - `rwctl runtime replicas cordon --replica <id> --reason "oom-loop"`
4. Verify load rebalances and queues recover.

### Mitigation 6 — Coordinate with Smart Routing for fallback/steering
Goal: shift load away from an overloaded region/pool or to a compatible model variant.

When to page Smart Routing:
- Region capacity dip persists >10 minutes
- Shed rate remains >1–2% after local mitigations
- You see a single hot model family saturating a region

What to provide:
- Region/pool/model impacted
- Current saturation signals (queue depth, tokens/sec)
- Desired action (regional shift vs model fallback)

Constraints:
- Ensure loop prevention and bounded retries are working (routing should not bounce between regions/models).

## Common failure modes and fixes
### Failure mode: Shed rate oscillation (flapping)
Symptoms:
- Breaker opens/closes repeatedly; queues never fully drain.
Fixes:
- Add hysteresis: raise close threshold, increase min-open duration.
- Reduce concurrency slightly more to create headroom.
- Confirm signal is smoothed (avoid reacting to 10–30s spikes).

### Failure mode: Timeouts increase but shed rate is low
Symptoms:
- Requests pile up; gateway keeps admitting; runtime queues spike.
Fixes:
- Coordinate with Gateway to increase edge shedding and set Retry-After.
- Ensure runtime admission is wired to saturation signals (not just static caps).

### Failure mode: OOM storm after a deployment
Symptoms:
- Frequent worker restarts; partial outage.
Fixes:
- Reduce max_context and concurrency immediately.
- Roll back the offending runtime change if correlated with a specific deploy.
- Keep gateway shedding on until restart rate normalizes.

### Failure mode: Metric cardinality / delayed signals
Symptoms:
- Dashboards stale; decisions based on old data.
Fixes:
- Check metric freshness panels.
- Use aggregated pool-level metrics rather than per-request labels.
- Page telemetry platform if ingestion is degraded.

## Verification checklist (post-mitigation)
- Queue depths trending down (prefill and/or decode)
- OOMs stopped; restart rate normal
- p95/p99 improved and stable for 15+ minutes
- Shed rate stable (not flapping) and within acceptable tier policy
- No spike in client retries / upstream request rate amplification
- Correlation IDs present in overload responses (spot-check sample logs)

## Post-incident follow-ups (required)
Create follow-up tasks when any of the below occur:
- Shed rate exceeded tier expectations
- False positive overload (shed without saturation)
- Missing Retry-After or inconsistent error payloads observed
- Need for new/clearer dashboards or better signal smoothing

Capture:
- Peak queue depth, peak tokens/sec, max KV usage ratio
- Time-to-recovery after mitigation
- Which mitigation(s) were applied and their effect

## Appendix A — Reference thresholds (starting points)
These are *guidelines*; actual thresholds vary by model family and GPU type.
- Sustained rising queue depth for >3 minutes + p99 rising: treat as overload
- OOM count > 0 in 5 minutes: treat as urgent; reduce concurrency and long-context caps
- KV cache usage ratio > 0.90 sustained: reduce long-context concurrency/caps
- Scheduler loop time p95 > 2x baseline: suspect scheduler stall or pathological batching

## Appendix B — What to tell SRE/Gateway when you need help
Provide:
- Region + pool + model route
- Saturation classification (compute vs prefill vs memory vs dependency)
- Current mitigations attempted
- Requested change (increase edge shedding, enable fallback, adjust tier policy)

## Document history
- 2025-10-21: Initial publication for overload protection dark launch.
- 2025-11-29: Added feature reduction modes and coordination notes for canary rollout.
- 2026-02-14: Updated triage decision tree and post-incident checklist based on winter traffic spikes.

title: KV cache consistency and degraded-read backoff guide
content:
Overview: This guide defines the detection, containment, and remediation patterns we use when the LLM KV (key-value) cache exhibits consistency or availability problems that cause degraded reads (stale or missing KV state). It explains automated degraded-read backoff behavior, operator remediation steps, configuration knobs, and dashboards/alerts to ensure predictable failover without violating tenant SLOs. Scope: - Applies to the distributed LLM KV prefix cache used by the serving runtime (global name: runtime-kv-cache). - Covers transient network partitions, metadata index corruption, leader election flaps, and partial shard availability. - Excludes full model binary corruption and hardware-level memory errors (see eng-serving-runtime/known-issues). Owner and responders: - Primary owner: eng-platform (runtime-ops squad) - Oncall rotation: platform-operator (pager) -> eng-sre escalation -> runtime-infra engineering - Notification channels: #platform-ops, #oncall-pager, paged phone roster Definitions and failure modes: 1) Missing-KV reads: requests that expect a cached KV entry but receive a cache-miss where a valid entry should exist. 2) Stale-KV reads: reads that return older prefix state due to replication lag or divergent leadership. 3) Partial-shard-unavailable: a subset of shards return 5xx or time out. 4) Consistency-mismatch: divergence between metadata index and stored shard contents resulting in incorrect routing or invalid tokenization offsets. Detection signals (metrics & logs): - metric/runtime_kv_read_error_rate (per-shard, p95) - metric/runtime_kv_stale_read_ratio (synthetic checks comparing authoritative source to cache) - metric/runtime_kv_replication_lag_seconds (95/99) - logs: "KV_MISMATCH", "KV_SHARD_OOS", leader-change events in audit logs - synthetic canaries: canary-prefix-check- (compare authoritative prefix store -> cache) Alerting rules and dashboard guidance: - Alert: KV-SHARD-ERROR-CRITICAL - Trigger: shard error rate > 0.5% for 5m AND p95 latency > 250ms - Severity: P1 (page) - Alert: KV-READ-DEGRADED-WARN - Trigger: aggregated stale_read_ratio > 0.2% for 10m OR replication_lag_seconds p99 > 3s - Severity: P2 (slack) - Dashboard panels to include: - per-shard read error heatmap - multi-region canary diff (ratio of mismatches) - recent leader-change timeline annotated with deploys - operator mitigation knobs (current backoff multiplier, degraded-serving-mode) Containment and automated degraded-read backoff pattern (high level): 1) Detect anomalous shard behavior using the synthetic canary and metric gates. 2) Automatically place affected shard(s) into "degraded-read-backoff" mode rather than immediate eviction when: - read_error_rate spike OR replication_lag > configurable threshold AND - model SLO indicates a better UX serving slightly stale responses vs 5xx errors. 3) In degraded-read-backoff mode, the runtime will: - apply exponential read delay/queuing for new requests targeting that shard (config: backoff_base_ms, max_backoff_ms) - fall back to last-known-good (LKG) prefix state if the request decoder accepts slightly older KV state (config: allow_stale_prefix=true for non-strict routes) - stream partial outputs with a header: X-Redwood-KV-State: degraded/LKG
This behavior reduces 5xx storms, prevents cascading load onto healthy shards, and buys time for automated healing. Config table (recommended defaults): | knob | description | default | |------|-------------|---------| | backoff_base_ms | base backoff delay applied on first degraded read | "20" | | max_backoff_ms | maximum per-attempt backoff to avoid request starvation | "2000" | | backoff_multiplier | exponential multiplier per retry | "2.0" | | allow_stale_prefix | whether to serve last-known-good prefix on degraded read | "true" | | degraded_mode_min_duration_s | minimum time to stay in degraded mode before re-eval | "30" | | degraded_mode_probe_interval_s | frequency of probes to check shard recovery | "10" | | stale_tolerance_seconds | maximum age of LKG prefix allowed | "5" | (Operator note: the runtime accepts these via the /api/v1/ops/kv-config endpoint. Example YAML below.) YAML example (ops config push): ```yaml kv_backoff: backoff_base_ms: 20 max_backoff_ms: 2000 multiplier: 2.0 allow_stale_prefix: true min_duration_s: 30 probe_interval_s: 10 stale_tolerance_seconds: 5 ``` Automated remediation actions (order of operations): 1) Probe: controller runs an immediate consistency probe against the shard (reads canonical store and compares prefixes). 2) Soft-redirect: route a percentage of traffic to compatible model-variant replicas in the same region (variant-candidates list maintained by model-onboarding). See routing policy example below. 3) If probes pass -> transition out of degraded mode. 4) If probes fail for > 3 probes spaced by probe_interval -> start controlled re-synchronization job for shard (resync ownership -> rehydrate cache from authoritative store). 5) If re-sync fails or OOS count > threshold -> schedule shard replacement/rehoming (operator intervention required). Routing policy example (OPA / policy hint): - Prefer: same-region compatible-variant -> preferred-latency < 50ms - Fallback: cross-region cold-variant (only when allow_cross_region_fallback=true and tenant policy allows) Operator runbook (step-by-step): 1) Triage 1. Acknowledge page. Post immediate summary in #platform-ops with shard and region, include alert runbook link. 2. Check dashboard panels: per-shard heatmap, leader-change log, probe history. 2) Immediate containment (automated but verify): 1. Confirm degraded-read-backoff mode enabled for affected shard via API: curl -sS https://ops.internal/v1/kv/shards//status 2. If not enabled, enable with: curl -X POST https://ops.internal/v1/kv/shards//degraded -d '{"mode":"backoff"}' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' 3) Investigate root cause: - Review shard logs for KV_MISMATCH and leader-election flaps. - Run a targeted probe: /tools/kv_probe --shard --compare-authoritative true --output json 4) Repair path options (pick one): A) Quick rehydrate: trigger cache rehydrate job for shard (if probe shows missing entries). Command: /ops/bin/rehydrate_shard --shard --type incremental B) Rehome: if leader flapping, reassign leader and wait for stable leader epoch. Command: /ops/bin/rehome_shard --shard --target-node C) Full resync: schedule full resync job during low-traffic window and notify SRE. Use: /ops/bin/full_resync --shard --window_start --dedupe true 5) Monitor recovery: probe-to-success ratio should reach 1.0 for three consecutive probes spaced by probe_interval_s before clearing alerts. 6) Post-incident checklist: create retrospective (template below), tag runbook with lessons and any configuration changes. Escalation matrix and SLAs: - If P1 persists > 15 minutes without improved probe results -> page runtime-infra lead and eng-sre manager. - If degraded mode remains > 2 hours -> schedule customer-impact investigation with customer-success for tenants impacted by strict-consistency routes. Testing and validation (pre-deploy & chaos): - Unit tests: simulate kv-backoff with synthetic requests asserting that no more than 1% of requests see 5xx under injected 10% shard error. - Chaos tests: orchestrate shard flaps via canary chaos runner: cause leader-flap, confirm degraded-mode triggers and traffic falls back to LKG without customer-visible 500s. - Load tests: verify degraded backoff increases tail latency by < 20% for affected routes and reduces 5xx rate by > 95%. Dashboard and alert implementation details (Grafana/Prometheus): - Query examples: - Read error rate per shard: sum(rate(runtime_kv_read_errors_total[5m])) by (shard) / sum(rate(runtime_kv_reads_total[5m])) by (shard) - Stale read ratio (canary diff): sum(canary_mismatch_total) / sum(canary_probe_total) - Alert escalation note: alerts should include a direct link to the probe job and the current degraded-mode flags to reduce cognitive load. Release, rollout, and operator training: - Feature flag: kv-degraded-backoff-v2. Roll out in three phases: internal canary -> regional canary -> global. - Training: 45-minute ops workshop for platform-operators covering: runbook walk-through, probe tools, and rehome commands. Record session and attach to team-wiki. Retrospective template (to complete after incidents): 1) Incident summary (one-paragraph) 2) Timeline of key events (alerts, mode changes, operator actions) 3) Root cause analysis (technical) 4) Detection gaps and suggested metric additions 5) Configuration changes made and rationale 6) Action items, owners, due dates 7) Follow-up verification steps and cost/latency impact post-remediation Appendix: example incident timeline snippet - 2027-02-03 03:14 UTC: KV-READ-DEGRADED-WARN alert fired for shard-12 (us-west) - 03:16 UTC: controller enabled degraded-read-backoff for shard-12 automatically - 03:17 UTC: probe failed (missing prefixes), rehydrate job scheduled - 03:28 UTC: rehydrate completed, probe green at 03:30 UTC -> degraded mode cleared Contacts and links: - Runtime-ops runbook index: /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks - Oncall rota: /confluence/eng-platform/team-wiki/operator-oncall-quick-reference-shell-helpers-and-scripts-2026 - Tooling: /internal/tools/kv_probe (README attached on team drive) Change history: - 2027-01-14: created by Maya Patel (draft) - 2027-02-01: rewrote containment strategy to prefer LKG + backoff (reviewers Diego Martinez, Hannah Lee) - 2027-02-09: published after chaos-tests and led a training session

title: Execution provenance, replay, and hash specification
content:
Overview

This document defines the execution provenance format, canonical hash scheme, and replay artifact requirements used by Redwood Inference runtime for deterministic reproduction of inference executions. It standardizes what data to capture at request ingress, kernel selection, KV-cache decision, routing, and final token emission to enable: post-incident forensics, fidelity regression repro, and deterministic replay in the sandbox.

Goals

- Make a minimal, fixed set of fields that allow deterministic replays at the same or compatible runtime version.
- Ensure artifact size is bounded and classified so privacy-sensitive payloads can be redacted before long-term storage.
- Provide a reproducible hashing strategy to detect non-deterministic divergence between production and replayed runs.

Scope and non-goals

- Scope: inference request path from API gateway -> runtime-coordinator -> kernel-router -> GPU shard(s) -> response assembly. Includes model variant metadata, kernel hints, and runtime decisions.
- Non-goal: this is not a full telemetry retention policy; refer to observability for retention windows and PII rules.

Specification: execution provenance artifact

An execution artifact (E-Artifact) is a newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON) file with three reserved top-level records in order: METADATA, DECISIONS, EVENTS. Additional records (LOG / TRACE / PAYLOAD) are optional and flagged. Each line is a single JSON object with primitive values only. Nested objects are flattened with dot notation in keys (see examples).

Required records (order matters):

1) METADATA record (type: "metadata")
- artifact_version: text (current: "v1")
- runtime_version: semantic version string (e.g., "2.14.0")
- model_id: catalog identifier (e.g., "redwood/open-13b-v2")
- model_variant: text (e.g., "int8-fast")
- request_id: global request UUID (X-Request-Id)
- timestamp_utc: ISO8601
- ingress_cluster: region/cluster id
- route_name: API route name
- fidelity_profile: label used by fidelity-orchestrator (e.g., "balanced")

Example METADATA line:
{
  "type": "metadata",
  "artifact_version": "v1",
  "runtime_version": "2.14.0",
  "model_id": "redwood/open-13b-v2",
  "model_variant": "int8-fast",
  "request_id": "b6b7e2f2-8a72-4f1a-9c7b-1a2d3e4f5a6b",
  "timestamp_utc": "2026-01-10T15:34:21Z",
  "ingress_cluster": "us-west-2-prod-1",
  "route_name": "/v1/generate",
  "fidelity_profile": "cost-optimized"
}

2) DECISIONS record (type: "decisions")
- kernel_selection: text (kernel id chosen)
- kernel_flags: comma-separated short flags (e.g., "prefetch,kvcache")
- kvcache_hit_bitmap: base64-encoded bitset (optional)
- scheduler_cohort: text (cohort id used by job scheduler)
- routing_path: pipe-separated list of nodes/shards (e.g., "coord-3|shard-12|shard-15")
- batch_size_at_dispatch: integer
- quantization_profile: text
- fallback_invoked: boolean string ("true"|"false")
- fallback_reason: text (if fallback_invoked)

Example DECISIONS line:
{
  "type": "decisions",
  "kernel_selection": "kvm-attn-v2-16",
  "kernel_flags": "kv-prefetch,continuous-batch",
  "scheduler_cohort": "cohort-22",
  "routing_path": "coord-3|shard-12",
  "batch_size_at_dispatch": "8",
  "quantization_profile": "q4_0",
  "fallback_invoked": "false"
}

3) EVENTS record(s) (type: "event")
- Sequence of deterministic events with monotonic event_index starting at 0.
- event_type: one of {ingress, kernel_enter, kernel_exit, kv_write, kv_read, token_emit, error}
- event_index: integer
- elapsed_ms: integer (ms since METADATA.timestamp_utc)
- note: short text (max 256 chars)
- checksum_hint: short hex string (optional, used during correlation)

Example event line:
{
  "type": "event",
  "event_type": "kernel_enter",
  "event_index": "3",
  "elapsed_ms": "37",
  "note": "dispatched to shard-12"
}

Optional record types (flagged via "type"):

- payload (type: "payload"): request prompt and redaction mask. If present, store only after automated PII redaction; payloads > 8KB must be stripped and replaced with a reference to secure blob store.
- trace (type: "trace"): block of stack frames/execution markers for kernel; base64 compressed.
- log (type: "log"): supplemental runtime logs, one-per-line semantics.

Hashing and divergence detection

Purpose: determine if replay diverges from production execution due to runtime non-determinism or model-level changes.

Canonical hash construction (SHA256):
- Inputs concatenated in this exact order (UTF-8): METADATA.request_id + "|" + runtime_version + "|" + model_id + "|" + model_variant + "|" + decisions.kernel_selection + "|" + serialized-events-hash
- serialized-events-hash = SHA256 of the concatenation of event lines exactly as persisted (preserve order and whitespace).
- Final hash (execution_hash) = SHA256 hex of the entire concatenated string.

Store the final execution_hash in the METADATA record under key execution_hash. Replays compute their own execution_hash and compare. Differences are classified as:
- MATCH: identical hash -> deterministic replay success
- KERNEL_DIFF: kernel_selection differs (indicates routing or scheduler change)
- EVENT_MISMATCH: same kernel but serialized-events-hash differs (indicates non-determinism or missing telemetry)
- METADATA_MISMATCH: any other metadata field mismatch (e.g., model_variant change)

Replay workflow (operational runbook)

Prerequisites: sandbox runtime matching runtime_version (within same minor), model artifact available, kernel plugin versions compatible.

Steps:
1) Fetch E-Artifact by request_id from archive or hot-store.
2) Validate METADATA.execution_hash present.
3) Start replay in isolated sandbox with environment variables: RUNTIME_REPLAY_MODE=1, REPLAY_REQUEST_ID=<request_id>.

CLI example to start a replay job via runtime-coordinator-controller (rcctl):

# start a replay with the archived artifact attached
rcctl start-replay --artifact-id b6b7e2f2-8a72-4f1a-9c7b-1a2d3e4f5a6b --sandbox-profile small --env "RUNTIME_REPLAY_MODE=1"

4) On completion the sandbox computes execution_hash and writes a small replay-summary JSON to /artifacts/<request_id>/replay-summary.json containing: request_id, original_execution_hash, replay_execution_hash, status (MATCH/KERNEL_DIFF/EVENT_MISMATCH/METADATA_MISMATCH), divergence_hint.

Replay triage matrix (quick decisions)

- MATCH -> close forensics ticket as reproducible; attach summary and annotated trace.
- KERNEL_DIFF -> escalate to kernel-scheduling owners: include DECISIONS record, compare scheduler_cohort and kernel_flags.
- EVENT_MISMATCH -> run delta-trace analysis: compare event_index sequences and run "event-aligner" tool (see tools section).
- METADATA_MISMATCH -> check rollout history; likely model or runtime upgrade caused mismatch.

Retention and privacy guidance

- E-Artifacts for high-severity incidents: retain for 180 days. Other artifacts: 30 days by default.
- Sensitive fields: payload.prompt and payload.user_text must be redacted before long-term storage unless a legal hold is present. Use the redaction tool:

# redact and upload to secure archive
redact-and-archive --input artifact.ndjson --pii-policy p0 --output s3://secure-archive/provenance/ --tag incident-1234

Tooling and utilities

- event-aligner: CLI tool to diff two EVENTS streams and present minimal edit script. Usage: event-aligner --original orig.ndjson --replay replay.ndjson --out diff.html
- hash-inspector: prints the canonical concatenation used to compute execution_hash for auditing.
- repro-runner: helper utility that spins a sandbox with model artifacts pinned.

Diagnostic fields and common failure modes

Table: common divergence indicators

| symptom | likely root cause | first action |
|---|---|---|
| kernel_selection mismatch | scheduler policy change or kernel deprecation | check scheduler rollout timeline, kernel-compat table |
| missing events or truncated artifact | transport/archiver dropped lines | run archive validation and re-ingest from hot-store |
| checksum_hint mismatches on token_emit events | non-deterministic token sampling | validate sampling RNG seed and temperature config |
| kvcache_hit_bitmap differences | cache eviction or timing | compare kv cache warmup windows and eviction logs |

Versioning and compatibility rules

- artifact_version evolves (v1 -> v2) whenever any required record schema changes. Replays must refuse artifacts with artifact_version > supported_max.
- runtime minor upgrades (2.14.x -> 2.15.0) are allowed if kernel plugin compatibility matrix flags "replay-safe". Major version mismatch requires model-owner approval.

Housekeeping and ownership

- Owning team: eng-serving-runtime (runtime-observability subteam). Primary contacts: Priya Rao (runtime-observability), Samir Gupta (scheduler), Leah Ortiz (forensics).
- SLA for requested replay artifact retrieval: 24 business hours for P1/P0 incidents, 5 business days for routine requests.

Appendices

A. Minimal example E-Artifact (NDJSON):

{"type":"metadata","artifact_version":"v1","runtime_version":"2.14.0","model_id":"redwood/open-13b-v2","model_variant":"int8-fast","request_id":"b6b7e2f2-8a72-4f1a-9c7b-1a2d3e4f5a6b","timestamp_utc":"2026-01-10T15:34:21Z","ingress_cluster":"us-west-2-prod-1","route_name":"/v1/generate","execution_hash":"<sha256-hex>"}
{"type":"decisions","kernel_selection":"kvm-attn-v2-16","kernel_flags":"kv-prefetch","scheduler_cohort":"cohort-22","routing_path":"coord-3|shard-12","batch_size_at_dispatch":"8"}
{"type":"event","event_type":"ingress","event_index":"0","elapsed_ms":"0","note":"received at api-gateway"}
{"type":"event","event_type":"kernel_enter","event_index":"1","elapsed_ms":"18","note":"dispatched to shard-12"}
{"type":"event","event_type":"token_emit","event_index":"6","elapsed_ms":"320","note":"emitted token: 0x4f"}

B. Quick checklist for oncall when a replay request is opened:
1) Confirm artifact retrieval path and manifest checksum.
2) Ensure sandbox runtime matches runtime_version (minor ok).
3) Trigger repro-runner with explicit --seed if replay uses sampling.
4) Save replay-summary and attach to incident.
5) If divergence, tag the incident with divergence class and notify owners.

C. References and related standards
- telemetry-data-model-and-tracebook (see team-wiki)
- runtime-decision-replay-and-slo-forensics-manual (operational patterns)
- data-management/pii-redaction-policy

Document change log

- 2025-03-12 (Marcos Lin): created initial draft v1 of spec.
- 2025-09-01 (Priya Rao): added retention and redaction rules.
- 2026-02-14 (Samir Gupta): clarified canonical hash algorithm and added replay triage matrix.

Contact and escalation

For urgent questions about failing replays or missing artifacts, page: #runtime-observability on Slack and email runtime-observability@redwood.ai.

title: Fallback validation and chaos test plan for graceful runtime fallbacks
content:
Purpose
-------
This document defines a repeatable validation and chaos-testing plan for the runtime's graceful fallback paths. It is intended to: verify correctness and SLA-preservation when primary kernels, model variants, or regions become unavailable; exercise fallthrough policies and automated rollback; and validate telemetry/alert fidelity used for automated mitigation. The goal is to catch correctness, performance regressions, and observability gaps before customer impact.

Scope
-----
- Components: kernel selector, request router, model-variant manager, KV cache coordination, shard handoff logic, admission controller, and routing fallbacks (region/model/tier).
- Test goals: functional correctness (response validity), latency SLO preservation (p50/p95/p99 targets), cost/capacity boundary behavior, and signal hygiene (trace/span/metric availability).
- Exclusions: hardware-level power failures and long-lived data-plane networking partitions (these are handled by infra-chaos).

Success Criteria (pass/fail)
--------------------------
1) Functional correctness: 100% of golden prompt set must return syntactically valid responses for the active fidelity target, with no malformed tokens or KV desync artifacts.
2) Latency preservation: during fallback exercises, p95 must not exceed configured fallback-SLO-multiplier x baseline p95 (default multiplier = 2.5) for more than 60s continuously.
3) Error budget preservation: fallback exercises must not consume >1% of monthly error budget for the affected tenant pool.
4) Observability: every fallback action must emit a correlated trace/span and a metric tag (fallback_type + reason) within 2s of policy firing.
5) Rollback/Recovery: automatic rollback to previous stable variant must succeed within 5 minutes for canary rollouts that experience degraded quality.

Test Plan Overview
------------------
1) Canary/Unit tests (CI): validate logic paths with deterministic mocks. Run for every kernel-scheduler or fallback-policy change.
2) Staging validation (integration): run the full plan against a staging cluster that mirrors production routing and telemetry collection.
3) Controlled chaos in canary prod (low-traffic window): short, scheduled experiments that validate production signals and playbook correctness.
4) Escalation rehearsals: practice runbook steps with oncall and SRE to measure human response and timing.

Test Types and Procedures
-------------------------
A. Kernel Unavailability Simulation
- Purpose: ensure the kernel mapper and admission controller fall back to compatible kernels or model variants without corrupting KV cache or client sessions.
- Pre-conditions: baseline throughput at 20% of steady-state; golden prompt set loaded and pinned.
- Steps:
  1. Inject kernel SIGSTOP via test harness on a subset of worker processes (3 nodes) to simulate a hung kernel.
  2. Observe: request router should divert new requests away from affected kernels after 3 failed scheduling attempts.
  3. Verify: no KV cache corruption events in logs; sessions tied to affected kernels are migrated or retried.
  4. Metrics to monitor: kernel_failure_count, kernel_schedule_retries, kvcache_migration_events, request_reroute_ratio.
- Pass/Fail:
  - Pass if golden prompts succeed within retry policy and no cache mismatches are observed.

B. Model Variant Fallback and Quality Validation
- Purpose: validate that downgrading fidelity (e.g., 16k->8k context, quantized variant) preserves semantic correctness and that the quality monitoring pipeline will detect regressions.
- Steps:
  1. Trigger variant swap for a small subset (1% traffic) using the deployment controller to a quantized variant.
  2. Feed continuous golden prompt set and synthetic adversarial prompts aimed at edge-cases.
  3. Capture outputs and run automatic evaluation (embedding-similarity + token-level diff + custom assertions).
  4. Assert alerts are fired by the quality monitor if quality drop > configured threshold (default 6% drop in embedding similarity).
- Tools: rollout-cli, quality-eval-harness, embeddings-service, diff-checker script.

C. Regional Failover and Routing Policy Exercise
- Purpose: verify smart routing and cost-aware fallback preserves SLOs when a region is slowed or unreachable.
- Steps:
  1. Simulate increased regional latency by adding artificial delay on the regional egress (tc/netem) in staging.
  2. Confirm tiered routing policy triggers (region_fallback_count metric increments) and traffic is rebalanced to alternate regions according to configured policy.
  3. Validate that per-tenant token cost does not spike beyond policy limits and that route trace contains fallback annotations.

D. KV Cache Warmup and Eviction Race Scenario
- Purpose: confirm that when primary shard evicts and fallback uses cold cache, responses are still correct and warmup telemetry is produced for downstream autotune.
- Steps:
  1. Force eviction on a KV shard by lowering memory watermark through the admin API.
  2. Route live sessions and verify fallback returns coherent responses while autoscaler warms new copies.
  3. Confirm warmup_latency, kvcache_miss_ratio, and kvcache_prefetch_hints metrics are emitted.

E. Admission Backpressure and Queue-Starvation
- Purpose: ensure admission controller rejects or queues work as designed and that graceful degradation path (reduced tokens, partial response) is triggered for overload.
- Steps:
  1. Generate synthetic burst (10x normal p50 throughput) to the cluster.
  2. Verify admission decisions, queue lengths, and that the partial-result fallback path returns truncated but valid outputs with a clear header "X-Redwood-Fallback-Reason: partial-response".

Observability & Telemetry Requirements
--------------------------------------
Every experiment must validate the following signals:
- Traces: fallback.<type>.decision (contains request_id, policy_version, reason_code, target_variant)
- Metrics (per-tenant and per-route): fallback_count, fallback_latency_ms, fallback_success_ratio, fallback_recovery_time_s
- Logs: structured JSON logs containing fallback_type, node_id, kernel_id, kv_shard_id, and experiment_tag
- Dashboards: a temporary experiment dashboard must exist for the run including p50/p95/p99, error_rates, fallback_count, and quality_eval_score

Experiment Tagging Convention
-----------------------------
Use the tag: "chaos-fallback-{YYYYMMDD}-{short-owner}" in all telemetry, e.g., chaos-fallback-20260615-priya. This ensures artifacts are searchable and excluded from production SLO calculations where appropriate.

Automated Validation Scripts (examples)
--------------------------------------
- Verify fallback emitted trace:
  curl -s "${TRACE_API}/search?tag=chaos-fallback-20260615-priya&event=fallback.decision" | jq '.hits | length'

- Run embedding similarity check:
  python3 tools/quality_eval.py --gold staples/golden_prompts.jsonl --candidate outputs/experiment_run.jsonl --threshold 0.94

Run Schedule and Roles
----------------------
- Preflight (SRE + Runtime owner): 1 week before run - verify staging mirrors production and golden sets are recent.
- Dry run (Runtime + Observability): 48 hours before - run full plan in staging.
- Production canary window (SRE lead, Runtime lead, Oncall): scheduled low-traffic window (UTC 02:00 - 05:00).
- Postmortem / Debrief: within 48 hours, include action items and telemetry gaps.

Ownership and Contacts
----------------------
- Runtime Owner: Priya Natarajan (runtime-owner@redwood.example.com)
- SRE Lead: Ethan Morales (sre-lead@redwood.example.com)
- Observability: Lina Zhang (obs@redwood.example.com)
- Quality/Applied ML: Carlos Rivera (quality@redwood.example.com)

Post-experiment Runbook (if failure observed)
--------------------------------------------
1. Immediate containment: revert to previous stable routing policy or pause the rollout (rollout-cli rollback --name <rollout> --reason "chaos-fallback-failure").
2. Triage: collect traces, kernel logs, kvcache snapshots, and raw request/response pairs for a 30-minute window around the failure.
3. Hotfix: if the issue is a missing trace/metric, re-enable telemetry flags and re-run short smoke test. If the issue is correctness (tokenization, alignment), pause rollout and open a quality incident.
4. Communication: notify customer-facing teams if user-visible SLOs were affected and update status page if >5% of tenants impacted.
5. Retrospective: schedule a 1-hour postmortem within 72 hours and assign action owners.

Artifacts to Produce
--------------------
- Experiment run artifact bundle: traces, metrics snapshots (prometheus dump), logs, and evaluation outputs (embedding similarity scores and diffs).
- Short executive summary (1 page) with pass/fail and recommended actions.
- Open ticket list with ownership and SLAs for remediation.

Appendix: Sample configuration matrix
------------------------------------
| Experiment | Traffic fraction | Baseline p95 multiplier | Max duration | Owner |
