| Kernel hang | 2% | 2.0 | 15m | Runtime |
| Variant swap | 1% | 1.5 | 30m | Quality |
| Region degrade | 5% | 2.5 | 10m | SRE |
| KV eviction | 3% | 2.0 | 20m | Runtime |
| Admission overload | 10% | 3.0 | 5m | SRE |
Notes and best practices
------------------------
- Always run against a pin-provisioned canary tenant to avoid accidental large-scale customer impact.
- Keep golden prompt sets versioned and representative (include adversarial edge-cases).
- Ensure experiment tags are excluded from billing and SLO retrospectives via query filters.
- Prefer short, iterative experiments over long-running undifferentiated chaos.

Revision history
----------------
- 2026-03-10: Created by Priya Natarajan (initial draft).
- 2026-05-12: Added embedding similarity thresholds and automated validation scripts (reviewer: Lina Zhang).
- 2026-06-30: Expanded observability requirements and post-experiment runbook (reviewer: Ethan Morales).

Related pages
-------------
See also runtime decision graphs, fallback playbooks, and canary rollout guidelines: the related_pages list at the top contains the primary references.

End of document

title: OOM cascade and memory throttling runbook
content:
Summary:
This runbook defines the operational play for diagnosing and recovering from OOM (Out Of Memory) cascades and memory-pressure-induced throttling in the serving runtime. It covers detection signals, immediate mitigation (fast-path recovery), medium-term capacity and configuration changes, and post-incident SLO/error-budget reconciliation. This is intended for SREs on-call for model-serving and runtime engineers supporting quantized and multi-tenant GPUs.

When to use this runbook:
- Multiple worker processes failing with OOM within a short window (minutes).
- Sustained memory pressure across a node pool leading to eviction or throttling signals (OOM_kill, slow-model spins).
- Unexplained latency spikes correlated with memory metrics or KV cache growth.
- Alerts: memory.node.high (>= 90% for 3m), worker.oom.rate (>5% of workers in 2m), kvcache.evictions.rate (>10% in 5m).

Key metrics and thresholds (single-pane reference):
- node.memory.utilization (gauge): warn at 75%, critical at 90% measured across 1m aggregates.
- worker.oom.count (counter): alert if >= 3 within 5 minutes in same cluster zone.
- kvcache.size.bytes (gauge): action if growth rate > 10%/minute sustained for 5 minutes.
- request.tail_latency_99_ms (histogram): correlate when increases > 2x baseline for 5+ minutes.
- slo.error_budget_burn_rate (gauge): if burn_rate > 2x and memory alerts active, escalate to tier-2.

Quick triage (first 10 minutes) — Tier 0 (on-call responder):
1) Confirm alerts and scope:
   - Query service map: which services/tenants are affected?
   - Grafana/Observe: check node.memory.utilization and OOM events.
   - Run: kubectl get pods -n model-serving -o wide --field-selector=status.phase=Running | grep <suspect-node>
2) Identify immediate impact on SLOs:
   - Check per-route error and latency dashboards (last 15m).
   - Pull error budget burn rate for affected SLOs.
3) If OOM events are ongoing, execute mitigation steps below immediately.

Immediate mitigation steps (fast-path) — Tier 1 (SRE with runtime privileges):
A) Soft remediation (non-disruptive, prefer first):
   - Remove heavy queries from the live traffic gate: update /traffic-gates route rules to reject or sample-down very large requests (> max_tokens threshold).
   - Enable per-request memory limits where supported: set request.max_kv_bytes=128MB for affected model routes.
   - Apply priority class to critical routes to preserve control-plane operations.
B) Node-level containment (if soft remediation insufficient):
   - cordon the affected node(s): kubectl cordon <node>
   - migrate non-critical pods off the node: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --force
   - scale up transient capacity (if autoscaler policy allows burst): trigger autoscaler burst: POST /internal/autoscaler/v1/burst?policy=oom-emergency&count=2
C) Worker restart pattern (when a single process is leaking or stuck):
   - Rolling restart of model-worker on the node: kubectl rollout restart deployment/model-worker --namespace=model-serving --field-selector=spec.nodeName=<node>
   - Use restart guard to ensure not to thrash: wait 60s between restarts and monitor worker.oom.count.

Medium-term recovery and remediation — Tier 2 (SRE + Runtime Eng):
1) Capture forensic evidence before any destructive action:
   - Collect coredumps (if enabled), dmesg logs, /var/log/messages, and container logs for the time window (t0-10m to t0+10m).
   - Snapshot process memory maps: pmap/pidstat or jmap for JVM-based model processes.
   - Save KV cache metrics and a sample of cache keys (respecting PII constraints).
2) Analyze root cause hypotheses (quick checklist):
   - Genuine workload spike (larger prompts / more concurrent long-context requests).
   - KV cache runaway due to misconfigured prefix retention or tenant key duplication.
   - Memory leak in new model binary or a third-party dependency (libsomething).
   - Node-level hardware degradation (failing NUMA behavior or GPU driver memory accounting bug).
3) Remediation options by cause:
   - Workload spike: enforce request size guardrails, add token-based admission control, and advise product/CS to throttle heavy tenants.
   - KV cache runaway: reduce retention window, enable max_entries limit and promote explicit cache eviction policy. Example config change (YAML):
     kvCache:
       enabled: true
       maxEntries: 250000
       evictionPolicy: LRU
       retentionSeconds: 1800
   - Memory leak in binary: pin to previous version and schedule canary deploys with heap/proc-accounting instrumentation.
   - Hardware/driver: isolate to node pool, tag and retire suspect hosts; file vendor ticket with kernel/OEM vendor.

Capacity planning triggers and actions:
- If we observe node.memory.utilization > 75% baseline frequently (>= 3 days of >40% of daily peaks above 75%), schedule capacity runway provisioning for the service and increase reserve by 15% for that service's cluster pool.
- For models with >100 active concurrent long-context requests, request dedicated GPU pools via Dedicated capacity quota.
- Maintain a 10% memory headroom buffer on all serving node pools running quantized models due to heavier KV-backed footprints.

Operational tooling and commands (copy-paste safe snippets):
- Identify recent OOM events:
  kubectl logs -n model-serving --since=15m -l app=model-worker | grep -E "OOM|OutOfMemory|KilledProcess"
- Correlate with node memory metrics (Prometheus):
  sum by(instance) (rate(node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes[2m]))
- Force-cache-eviction RPC (internal service):
  curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" https://internal-api.redwood/v1/cache/evict?scope=tenant:<tenant-id>&policy=soft
- Burst autoscaler API (internal):
  curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" -d '{"policy":"oom-emergency","count":3}' https://internal-api.redwood/internal/autoscaler/v1/burst

Incident review and SLO/error-budget reconciliation:
1) Assign the incident a severity label and owner within 48 hours.
2) Collect timeline and evidence: alerts, key metrics, tool commands executed, and configuration changes.
3) Calculate SLO impact: compute time-windowed error budget consumption and attach to incident record.
4) If error budget burn > 25% for the impacted SLO, require a corrective action plan and capacity provisioning proposal within 7 days.
5) Include the following in the post-incident report:
   - Exact root cause (or top hypotheses) and evidence for each.
   - List of mitigation steps taken and the time to restore.
   - Long-term fixes, owner, and ETA.
   - SLO impact summary (tokens affected, estimated customer impact, error budget consumed).

Runbook for recurring / chronic memory events (continuous-improvement loop):
1) If the same cause reappears more than twice in 30 days, open a reliability initiative ticket (RI) and prioritize a fix in the next SRE cycle.
2) RI deliverables should include: automated canary with memory leak detection, KV cache instrumentation, and a traffic-shepherd rule to limit large requests.
3) Add synthetic canaries that exercise long-context flows at low volume but regular cadence to detect growth in memory footprint.

Incident checklist (to attach to incident ticket):
- [ ] Node(s) cordoned and drained where appropriate
- [ ] Forensic logs archived to incident bucket (s3://redwood-incidents/<id>/logs)
- [ ] Core dumps collected and uploaded (if policy allows)
- [ ] KV cache snapshot collected
- [ ] Autoscaler actions documented
- [ ] SLO impact computed and attached
- [ ] Owners assigned for short and long term fixes

Appendix: example alert rule (Prometheus-style pseudo):
- alert: NodeMemoryPressureHigh
  expr: (node_memory_MemTotal_bytes - node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes) / node_memory_MemTotal_bytes > 0.9
  for: 3m
  labels:
    severity: critical
  annotations:
    summary: "Node memory > 90% for >3m"

Appendix: KV cache config table (human-readable):
| parameter | default | recommended for quantized-serving | rationale |
| maxEntries | 100000 | 250000 | Quantized models maintain larger key footprints; raise default carefully |
| retentionSeconds | 3600 | 1800 | Shorter retention reduces runaway growth during spikes |
| evictionPolicy | LRU | LRU | Proven policy for tenant fairness |
| trackPerTenant | false | true | Helps prevent a single tenant from polluting global cache |

Ownership and escalation:
- Primary on-call: model-serving SRE rotation (pager) — first responder.
- Secondary: runtime-engineering (pager).
- Triage lead: SRE duty lead or on-call manager for multi-tenant incidents.
- Escalate to incident commander for Sev2+ when burn rate > 2x or when > 5% of customers report functional degradation.

Document maintenance:
- Owner: Priya Nair (runtime SRE lead).
- Review cadence: quarterly or after any Sev1/Sev2 OOM incident.
- Change log: last major update 2026-06-15 — added KV cache retention guidance and autoscaler burst policy.

References and related pages:
- Internal autoscaler API docs: /confluence/eng-platform/operational-tooling/autoscaler-api
- KV cache design doc: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/kv-cache-design-2025
- Incident postmortem standard: /confluence/eng-sre/incident-review/postmortem-automation-and-causal-mapping-standard-2026

End of runbook.

title: GPU affinity and eviction strategies for high-density inference
content:
Summary:
This runbook defines recommended GPU affinity, placement, and eviction strategies for Redwood’s serving runtime when operating high-density multi-tenant inference fleets. It is intended for on-call SREs, runtime engineers, release engineers, and platform owners who configure tenant isolation, capacity packing, and preemption policies.

Scope:
- Applies to Redwood Hosted and Dedicated pools that share GPUs across model deployments.
- Covers affinity labeling, node packing heuristics, eviction triggers, graceful preemption, and post-eviction recovery.
- Does NOT replace tenant-level quota or billing policies; those are handled by the billing & quota service.

Why this matters:
High-density packing improves utilization and reduces unit cost, but increases risk of tail-latency spikes and OOM-induced kernel failures. A clear affinity and eviction policy balances cost and reliability by:
- Preserving SLOs for latency-sensitive customers (p99 < configured target).
- Ensuring memory-heavy workloads do not cause noisy-neighbor OOMs.
- Allowing controlled preemption for lower-priority workloads during capacity pressure.

Key concepts and terminology:
- Affinity label: a runtime label attached to a workload that constrains placement (e.g., "affinity:latency-critical", "affinity:batch-heavy").
- Hard affinity: placement must satisfy the label or request is rejected/queued.
- Soft affinity: placement prefers matching nodes but falls back if needed.
- Eviction: the act of terminating or pausing a workload to reclaim resources.
- Preemption: a planned eviction triggered by a higher-priority request.
- Graceful drain: process to checkpoint and resume model state (KV cache/weights) before killing a process.

Policy overview (recommended defaults):
1) Affinity tiers:
   - latency-critical: p99 SLO tighter than 250ms; hard affinity to isolated pools (1–2 models per GPU).
   - standard: p99 SLO 250–600ms; soft affinity with controlled packing (3–6 models per GPU depending on quantization and KV usage).
   - best-effort: batch/async jobs and low-SLA workloads; packed aggressively and preemptible.

2) Memory headroom thresholds (per GPU):
   - WARNING: 75% memory usage -> emit alert to capacity dashboard.
   - THROTTLE: 85% memory usage -> stop admitting soft-affinity placements; begin queueing new requests.
   - EVICT: 95% memory usage OR repeated kernel OOMs (>=3 within 5m) -> trigger eviction policy.

3) CPU/IO headroom: systems-level throttle triggered at 80% CPU on the host or when PCIe tx/rx saturates sustained > 120s.

Operational runbook: detection and automated response
1) Detection (automatic):
   - Metric sources: gpu.memory.used, gpu.memory.total, runtime.kernel.oom_count, host.cpu.utilization, kvcache.eviction_rate.
   - Alert rules (examples):
     - ALERT RuntimeGPUHighMemory: gpu.memory.used / gpu.memory.total > 0.75 for 2m -> Severity: P3
     - ALERT RuntimeKernelOOMSpike: runtime.kernel.oom_count >= 1 for 30s or >=3 within 5m -> Severity: P2

2) Immediate automated responses (system):
   - At WARNING: emit alert, mark node as "packing-candidate: low" in scheduler metadata, do not evict.
   - At THROTTLE: switch scheduler to "admit-restricted" mode: only hard-affinity and latency-critical workloads are allowed on node; soft-affinity attempts go to other nodes or queue.
   - At EVICT: begin eviction pipeline (see Eviction flow). If kernel OOMs are observed, route traffic to fallback model variants in <region> if configured.

Eviction flow (automated, with manual override):
1) Evaluate candidates (automated):
   - Rank running tasks by eviction_score = (priority_weight * tenant_priority) + (mem_factor * gpu_mem_used_ratio) + (slo_factor * p99_violation_count). Lower score -> preferred to keep.
   - Preferred eviction candidates: best-effort workloads, long-running batch jobs without checkpointing, and tenants with explicit preemption=true.

2) Graceful preemption attempt (30s window):
   - Notify container: POST /runtime/v1/tasks/<task_id>/preempt?deadline=30s
   - Container should respond with status: checkpointing / draining / refused. If checkpointing: wait for checkpoint success (<=30s) and then terminate. If refused or timeout: proceed to force-kill.

3) Force-kill fallback (immediate):
   - kill -9 <pid> (as last resort). Record cause in task metadata and emit event to audit log: "eviction.forced".

4) Post-eviction healing:
   - Mark node as under-healing for 10s and block new soft-affinity placements for 60s to allow memory stabilisation and kernel cache cleanup.
   - If repeated evictions (>=3) happen on a single node within 10m, mark node as cordoned for manual investigation and escalate to runtime on-call.

Manual triage checklist (on-call):
1) Verify alert context: check graph of gpu.memory.used, kernel.oom_count, kvcache.eviction_rate, and host.cpu.utilization for the previous 30m.
2) Identify which tasks were evicted: runtime audit log -> search events with "eviction.*" and cross-reference task IDs to tenant and model.
3) If eviction of latency-critical tenant occurred: immediately open incident and run rollback (route traffic to designated standby model or region).
4) If node shows repeated kernel failures: collect traces (see Telemetry section) and capture kernel logs: journalctl -u runtime-service, nvidia-smi pmon, /var/log/nvml.log.
5) If cluster-level resource pressure: consider expanding dedicated pool or enabling burst capacity per capacity plan.

Configuration reference (sample table):
- Name | Default | Purpose
- affinity.labels | ["latency-critical","standard","best-effort"] | Affinity categories used by scheduler
- memory.warning_threshold | "0.75" | Memory usage fraction to emit warning
- memory.throttle_threshold | "0.85" | Memory fraction to stop admitting soft-affinity placements
- memory.evict_threshold | "0.95" | Memory fraction to trigger eviction pipeline
- eviction.preempt_timeout_s | "30" | Seconds to wait for graceful checkpointing
- node.healing_block_s | "60" | Seconds to block new soft-affinity placements after eviction

Example CLI and API snippets:
- List affinity labels for a node:
  rcli node describe --id node-123 --fields affinity_labels,mem_used,mem_total

- Trigger a manual preempt for a task:
  curl -X POST "https://runtime.internal/api/v1/tasks/<task_id>/preempt?deadline=30s" -H "Authorization: Bearer $RUNTIME_TOKEN"

- Sample policy YAML (appendix contains full example):
  scheduler:
    affinity:
      tiers:
        - name: latency-critical
          hard: true
        - name: standard
          hard: false
    thresholds:
      memory_warning: 0.75
      memory_throttle: 0.85
      memory_evict: 0.95
    eviction:
      preempt_timeout_s: 30
      node_healing_block_s: 60

SLOs and thresholds (operational impact):
- Latency-critical pools: p99 <= 250ms (target), error budget 99.9% uptime.
- Standard pools: p99 <= 600ms, error budget 99.0% uptime.
- Eviction tolerance: latency-critical tenants should have eviction_rate < 0.01% monthly. Best-effort eviction_rate can be up to 20% monthly.

Telemetry and dashboards (what to monitor):
- Per-node: gpu.memory.used, gpu.memory.total, kernel.oom_count, host.cpu.utilization, pci.tx/rx, container_start_failures.
- Per-task: task_id, tenant_id, model_version, kv_cache_size, last_checkpoint_time, p50/p95/p99 latency buckets.
- Dashboards to check: "Runtime / Node Health", "Eviction Events by Tenant", "KV Cache Pressure", "Admission Control / Requeued Requests".

Testing and rollout plan for policy changes:
1) Canary (1% of capacity): deploy new thresholds to a small labeled pool with synthetic workloads that simulate KV-heavy and latency-critical traffic.
2) Observe key metrics for 6h: p99 latency, admission_rejects, eviction_count.
3) Gradual ramp: 1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% over 48–72h with human gating and automated rollback if p99 or eviction rate increases > 2x baseline.

Escalation and ownership:
- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime (oncall: runtime-oncall rotation).
- Secondary: eng-sre (oncall: sre-runtime-rotation).
- Escalate to runtime-sre leads (Diego Alvarez) for repeated node cordons or unexplained kernel OOMs.
- For customer-impacting events (latency-critical evictions), follow incident process in oncall-and-incident-response/postmortems.

Helpful troubleshooting commands and artifacts to attach to incidents:
- rcli node top --id node-123 --window 30m --metrics gpu.memory.used,host.cpu.util
- docker inspect <container_id> | jq '.State, .Config'
- sudo cat /var/log/dmesg | tail -n 200
- nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.used,memory.total,utilization.gpu --format=csv -l 5

FAQ and common scenarios:
Q: A node is repeatedly hitting 95% memory and evicting best-effort tasks. Should we cordon it?
A: Not immediately. Confirm whether pack density or a new model caused increased memory. Cordoning recommended after 3 forced evictions in 10m.

Q: A latency-critical tenant was evicted. What to do?
A: Immediately open an incident, run rollout to standby model/region, and start a hotfix: reduce packing on latency-critical pool and increase headroom by +10% temporarily.

Appendix: sample eviction policy YAML:
---
scheduler:
  affinity:
    tiers:
      - name: latency-critical
        hard: true
      - name: standard
        hard: false
      - name: best-effort
        hard: false
  thresholds:
    memory_warning: 0.75
    memory_throttle: 0.85
    memory_evict: 0.95
  eviction:
    preempt_timeout_s: 30
    node_healing_block_s: 60
    candidate_selector: |
      # Python-like expression evaluated by scheduler to rank eviction candidates
      (tenant_priority * 100) + (gpu_mem_used_ratio * 100) + (p99_violation_count * 1000)

Related pages:
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/production-rollout-tuning-checklist-2026
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/dynamic-request-orchestration-and-fallthrough-2026

Document change log:
- 2025-11-10: created by Maya Patel (initial draft).
- 2026-02-15: expanded eviction flow and added node healing block; reviewer feedback incorporated by Priya Nair.

title: Dynamic KV-Cache Resilience and Warmup Playbook
content:
Summary
-------
This playbook describes our recommended architecture, operational procedures, and diagnostic workflows for handling dynamic KV cache (prefix / KV cache) resilience and warmup in the serving runtime. It synthesizes kernel scheduling interactions, profiling steps, benchmark configurations, and automated runbooks to: reduce cold-start latency, mitigate cache-eviction storms, and preserve SLOs under bursty traffic and model rollouts.

Scope
-----
- Applies to all hosted and Dedicated serving runtime clusters using the v2 KV-cache layer (sharded prefix KV cache across inference shards).
- Includes guidance for Private deployments where runtime configuration parity is required.
- Does NOT replace per-customer onboarding docs for Private (see eng-private-deployments).

Why this matters
----------------
- Cold KV-cache regimes can add 10–40% tail latency for short sequences and increase GPU cost by 15–60% during warmup windows.
- Improper eviction + kernel scheduling interference leads to thrashing: high kernel contention, repeated model recomputation, and increased rate of transient OOMs.

Goals and SLO impact
--------------------
- Target median additional token latency from cold-kvcache: <= 5 ms for standard Llama-like models.
- Tail (p99) increase during warmup events: < 20% of baseline.
- Reduce warmup token count to reach steady-state cache hit rate by 50% vs uncontrolled rollout.

Architecture overview
---------------------
High-level components:
- KV Cache Shard Manager: responsible for shard ownership, lease renewal, and local warmup policy.
- Warmup Coordinator: broadcast mechanism (gossip/leader) used to coordinate aggressive prefix caching after a model variant rollout.
- Kernel Scheduler: enforces priority bands for warmup vs production requests to avoid preemption storms.
- Local LRU/Adaptive Evictor: per-shard eviction policy with heuristics for token frequency, request recency, and model-fingerprint awareness.

Interaction diagram (text)
1) Model rollout triggers Warmup Coordinator to mark new model-variant shards CAN_WARMUP.
2) Warmup Coordinator signals subset of traffic nodes to send protocol-safe prefetch requests (synthetic prefixes) to populate KV shards.
3) Kernel Scheduler temporarily assigns warmup requests to a separate priority band with controlled concurrency to avoid kernel inversion.
4) KV Cache Shard Manager tracks warmup progress with hit-rate metrics and signals a ramp-down once steady-state hit-rate achieved.

Operational knobs and recommended defaults
---------------------------------------
| Setting | Default | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| warmup.enabled | true | Enable coordinated warmup post-rollout |
| warmup.max_parallel_prefetch | "8" | Max concurrent synthetic warmup streams per node |
| warmup.prefetch_window_seconds | "180" | Window to complete aggressive warmup |
| kvcache.eviction_threshold_mb | "8192" | Per-shard soft threshold to start adaptive eviction |
| scheduler.warmup_priority_band | "low" | Lower priority than live production but higher than background maintenance |
| scheduler.concurrent_warmup_limit | "16" | Global per-GPU limit enforced by kernel scheduler |

Note: values are intentionally strings here to match internal config APIs that accept env var strings.

Profiling playbook: diagnosing warmup and eviction issues
---------------------------------------------------------
When you observe increased tail latency or unexpected token generation costs, follow these steps:
1) Snapshot telemetry for the affected interval (use timeframe covering 2x warmup_window):
   - metrics: kvcache.hit_rate, kvcache.evictions/sec, kernel_queue_length, gpu_utilization, request_latency_p50/p95/p99
   - traces: end-to-end request trace including kvcache calls and kernel scheduling annotations

2) Run targeted profiler on affected GPU nodes:
   - CLI: `redwood-profile --nodes <node-list> --duration 60s --tags kvcache,warmup,kernel`
   - Expect to capture: repeated model layer recomputations, KV fetch stalls, kernel enqueue spikes.

3) Inspect kernel scheduler counters:
   - `curl http://<node>/debug/kernel-scheduler/stats` (JSON)
   - Look for: warmup_priority_band queue depth > scheduler.concurrent_warmup_limit or frequent task preemptions.

4) Heap/Memory checks:
   - `nvidia-smi` and runtime allocator stats. Watch for abrupt free/alloc cycles that coincide with eviction spikes.

Common root causes and mitigations
---------------------------------
- Symptom: High eviction rate immediately after a canary rollout.
  - Cause: Warmup coordinator disabled or misconfigured; synthetic prefetch not triggered.
  - Mitigation: Re-enable warmup.enabled, increase max_parallel_prefetch to 12 for initial ramp, then reduce.

- Symptom: Kernel priority inversion (live traffic starved) during warmup.
  - Cause: Warmup requests scheduled at same or higher priority as production.
  - Mitigation: Ensure scheduler.warmup_priority_band < production; apply throttling: scheduler.concurrent_warmup_limit=8.

- Symptom: Warmup completes but hit-rate decays rapidly under bursty traffic.
  - Cause: Eviction policy too aggressive for mixture of short/long sequences.
  - Mitigation: Switch to adaptive evictor with model-fingerprint hysteresis and increase kvcache.eviction_threshold_mb by 20%.

Benchmarks and validation harness
--------------------------------
We validate warmup changes with two benchmark profiles stored in the perf repo:
- warmup-prefill-suite: simulates rollout with synthetic prefixes, measures time-to-80%-hit-rate and cost delta.
- mixed-burst-suite: 90% short-seq low-latency requests + 10% long-seq heavy KV usage to validate eviction behavior.

Example benchmark invocation:
```
perf-runner --suite warmup-prefill-suite --nodes 10 --concurrency 120 --duration 300 --model llama-3-8b --kvcache-enabled
```
Expected outputs (asserted by CI):
- time_to_80_hit_rate < 120s
- p99_latency during warmup < baseline_p99 * 1.25
- additional GPU-seconds < 1.5x baseline for warmup period

Runbook: automated remediation steps
-----------------------------------
Trigger conditions (automated):
- kvcache.evictions/sec > 50 for > 60s OR
- kvcache.hit_rate < 0.5 for > 180s post-rollout OR
- kernel_queue_length[warmup_band] > scheduler.concurrent_warmup_limit for > 30s

Automated remediation sequence (scripted):
1) Throttle warmup: set scheduler.concurrent_warmup_limit = 4 via config push and notify SRE.
2) Temporarily raise kvcache.eviction_threshold_mb by 25% for affected shards.
3) If eviction rate remains high after 2 minutes, pause rollout (Warmup Coordinator: PAUSE_WARMUP) and failover 10% of traffic to previous model.
4) Create incident with severity: high and attach profiling artifacts.

Manual escalation checklist for oncall
------------------------------------
1) Confirm the automated remediations executed successfully.
2) Take heap+KV cache core dump: `postmortem-tool collect --type kvcache --duration 30s`
3) Validate kernel scheduler policy file (path: /etc/redwood/kernel-scheduler/policy.yaml) for unintended overrides.
4) If root cause unclear, escalate to runtime-kernel team and attach profiler snapshot.

Release notes (behavioral changes to track)
------------------------------------------
- 2026-02-18: Enabled Warmup Coordinator by default for Canary rollouts.
- 2026-02-25: Kernel Scheduler: new warmup_priority_band added; default concurrent_warmup_limit=16.
- 2026-02-28: Adaptive Evictor v1.2 rolled out to 10% of clusters; adds model-fingerprint hysteresis.

Known issues and workarounds
---------------------------
- Issue: kvcache hit-rate metric can lag by up to 30s under heavy aggregation (observed 2026-01-10). Workaround: use raw per-shard counters for real-time gating.
- Issue: Synthetic prefetch increases billing for Dedicated customers. Workaround: limit prefetch_window_seconds and scope warmup to sample nodes.
- Issue: On certain GPUs (driver <= 535.54), kernel enqueue stalls observed when many small kernels are scheduled concurrently. Workaround: pin warmup kernels to separate CUDA streams and upgrade driver.

Telemetry and dashboards to monitor
---------------------------------
Must-have panels:
- KV Cache: per-shard hit_rate, evictions/sec, memory_used_mb
- Scheduler: queue_depth by priority_band, preemptions/sec, avg_hold_time_ms
- Cost: warmup_gpu_seconds by cluster and model_variant
- Alarms: automated trigger conditions (see Runbook)

Diagnostics snippets
-------------------
- Quick hit-rate query (PromQL):
```
rate(kvcache_hits_total[1m]) / (rate(kvcache_hits_total[1m]) + rate(kvcache_misses_total[1m]))
```
- Kernel scheduler queue snapshot (example):
```
curl -s http://<node>/debug/kernel-scheduler/queues | jq .
```

Testing and rollout guidance
---------------------------
- Canary strategy: 5% initial traffic with warmup.prefill enabled for 5 minutes, then 25% for 15 minutes, then 100% if metrics stable.
- Benchmarks must be run in isolated capacity to avoid noise. Attach perf-run output and raw profiler captures to rollout ticket.

Team responsibilities and ownership
---------------------------------
- Runtime-kernel team: kernel scheduler changes and API for priority bands.
- Serving-runtime team: KV Cache Shard Manager, Warmup Coordinator and adaptive evictor.
- Eng-sre: alerting, automated runbooks, capacity overrides during incidents.
- Observability: dashboards, perf-suite maintenance.

Appendix: example config snippets
--------------------------------
Warmup Coordinator YAML (example):
```
warmup:
  enabled: true
  max_parallel_prefetch: 8
  prefetch_window_seconds: 180
  coordinator_type: "gossip"
```
Kernel scheduler policy excerpt:
```
priority_bands:
  - name: production
    priority: 10
  - name: warmup
    priority: 5
    concurrency_limit: 16
  - name: background
    priority: 1
```

Contacts and escalation links
----------------------------
- runtime-kernel Slack: #runtime-kernel
- serving-runtime Pager: /pagerduty/service/serving-runtime
- Perf repo: git@internal:redwood/perf-suites.git (folder: warmup-prefill-suite)

Revision history
----------------
- 2026-02-12: Drafted by Maya Thompson.
- 2026-02-18: Warmup Coordinator defaults note added (Diego Alvarez).
- 2026-02-25: Scheduler policy excerpt and automated remediation steps (Priya Shah).
- 2026-03-01: Finalized and published (Jonas Müller).

End of document.

title: Serving Runtime Patch Rollback & Dependency Compatibility Runbook (2026)
content:
## Purpose
This runbook standardizes how we review, roll out, and (if necessary) roll back patches that touch Serving Runtime request routing, batching, configuration parsing, or client-compatibility behavior. It is intended for on-call engineers, patch authors, and reviewers.

## Scope
Applies to changes in:
- Batching router and queueing logic
- Legacy config parsing and request header parsing
- Dependency upgrades that can affect wire formats, caching formats, or client interoperability
- Observability/metrics naming changes that can break dashboards or alerting

Out of scope: database schema migrations owned by other teams (follow the owning team’s migration runbook), unless the runtime change includes an embedded migration step.

## Background / Common Risk Profile
A recurring high-risk pattern is a small router or parser change that is logically correct but fails under concurrency or with older clients. Typical symptoms include intermittent 5xx spikes during high concurrency runs and unexpected 4xx responses when optional client headers are missing.

Recent example category (tracked under INF-2293):
- Change touched split-batching fast-path and legacy config parsing.
- Older clients did not send a new optional header; initial implementation returned 415 for some request shapes.
- Staging saw intermittent 502s during batching boundary transitions due to a race in router queue-length calculation.

## Definitions
- "Old client": any client version that predates the optional header behavior (see Client Compatibility Contracts page).
- "Compatibility shim": minimal patch that restores old behavior when the optional header is absent or malformed.
- "Canary": small traffic slice routed to a dedicated pool or deployment for early detection.

## Pre-Merge Checklist (Reviewer + Author)
### 1) Compatibility behavior
- Confirm unit tests cover the header-absent case with safe defaults.
  - Required cases: no-header, bad-header, extra-field/unknown value.
  - If the parser previously accepted missing header, it must continue to do so unless there is an approved deprecation.
- Confirm the API/contract is updated if behavior changes.
  - If behavior is conditional on header presence/absence, document it explicitly and include a deprecation timeline.

### 2) Tests and CI gating
- Integration test required for split-batching + old-client compatibility.
  - Must run in CI (may be tagged as slow), and must include a mixed workload where a subset of requests omit the optional header.
  - Current standard: 30 minutes minimum for the long-run stability test on the canary build.
- Ensure the change does not introduce new flakiness.
  - If it does, address flakiness before merge or add a temporary feature flag + follow-up ticket.

### 3) Observability and metrics
- Validate metric naming backwards compatibility.
  - Do not rename existing metrics without providing a migration plan and updating dashboards.
  - If new metrics are added, ensure they are clearly scoped and labeled.

### 4) Dependencies and formats
- Verify no changes to tokenization, KV cache format, or any persisted on-disk format.
  - If any format change is unavoidable, block until a versioned migration strategy is defined.
- Verify no new DB migrations or schema changes.
  - If present, ensure rollback is explicitly documented and ownership is confirmed.

### 5) Rollout controls
- Prefer a feature flag for behavior changes.
  - Requirement (2026 standard): any router behavior change that could affect latency/5xx must be behind a flag or must have a documented safe fallback.

## Known Failure Modes to Test For
### A) Batching boundary race (high severity)
Symptom:
- Spikes of 502/503 during batching boundary transitions under high concurrency.

What to validate:
- Router queue-length calculation is atomic/consistent.
- Boundary update logic does not produce transient invalid state.

### B) Missing optional header triggers 4xx (moderate severity)
Symptom:
- Some internal clients return 415/400 when the optional header is missing.

What to validate:
- Missing header defaults to the prior safe behavior.
- Malformed header fails gracefully (ideally warning + fallback) unless explicitly a hard error.

### C) Metrics/dashboard break (low-medium severity)
Symptom:
- Dashboards missing data; alerts silent/noisy due to renamed metrics.

What to validate:
- Existing metric names remain stable.
- Any additions include a dashboard update plan.

## Repro / Validation Procedure (Local + Staging)
### Local repro
1) Start runtime with staging-like config and reduced batching thresholds.
2) Run load script with mixed client population (at least 50% old-client simulation that omits the optional header).
   - Recommended: scripts/loaders/split_batch_test.py
3) Inspect logs for batching boundary update events and correlate with any 5xx.
4) If latency jumps, enable router/queue debug logs and collect a CPU profile.

### Staging validation
1) Deploy to staging pool with debug logging enabled for the router component only.
2) Run the same mixed client load for at least 20 minutes.
3) Confirm:
   - No header-related warnings at steady state.
   - No sustained 5xx above baseline.

## Canary Rollout Plan (Standard)
1) Deploy to canary pool.
2) Start at 5% traffic for 12 hours.
   - If the change is high-risk (router/batching logic), extend to 24 hours.
3) Monitor:
   - Error budget burn and 5xx rate (page if >1% over a 5-minute window)
   - p50/p99 latency, especially tail latency on hot routes
   - Any increase in 4xx related to parsing/headers
4) If stable, promote incrementally (e.g., 25% -> 50% -> 100%).

Notes:
- Small canaries can hide statistically significant regressions; if traffic is low, extend duration rather than increasing percentage too quickly.

## Rollback Plan
### Fast path (preferred)
- Revert the merge commit and redeploy.
  - Command guidance: use a standard git revert of the merge SHA and deploy hotfix to canary, then production.
- Communicate in #sre-oncall and #serving-runtime if the rollback is due to customer-visible impact.
  - Open an incident channel if >1% error rate over 5 minutes or if tail latency breaches SLO.

### If revert is blocked by dependent PRs
- Deploy a compatibility shim:
  - Accept missing optional header and fall back to old behavior.
  - Keep the shim minimal and well-tested.
- Promote shim via canary first.

### Rollback decision thresholds (operational)
Initiate rollback if any of the following holds during canary:
- 5xx > 1% for 5 minutes and attributable to the change
- p99 latency regression > 15% sustained for 15 minutes on critical routes
- Any new systematic 4xx for old-client population (header missing/malformed)

## Backport Guidance (Stable Branch)
- Backport only the minimal safe subset.
  - Typical backport contents: parser default behavior + compatibility tests + feature flag plumbing.
  - Avoid backporting batching optimizations unless explicitly approved by release owner.
- Current stable target (as of last update): release/2026-03-stable.
- Label backports with: backport/stable and link to the original PR.

## Post-Deploy Manual Verification
After canary promotion (and again after full rollout):
- Verify p50/p90/p99 latencies per route.
- Run a small synthetic workload:
  - 100 requests/sec
  - at least 40% old-client simulation (no optional header)
  - confirm zero parsing-related 4xx/5xx
- Check logs for header-related warnings.
  - Target: zero occurrences of "unknown-client-header" (or equivalent warning string for the current parser).

## PR Review Talking Points (Copy/Paste)
- Does the optional header default to a safe value in all call sites?
- Is conditional behavior documented in the client compatibility contract?
- Is there a feature flag (or equivalent rollout control) for risky behavior changes?
- Are metrics backwards compatible, and is there a dashboard migration plan if needed?
- Are before/after performance numbers provided (p50/p99 under representative load)?

## Post-Incident / Follow-ups
If a rollback occurs:
- Create a short blameless postmortem within 2 business days.
- Add a regression test that would have caught the issue.
- Update this runbook if the rollback path was unclear or slow.

## Ownership
- Runbook owner: Eng Serving Runtime
- Primary maintainer: Evan Blake
- Canary monitoring rotation: Serving Runtime on-call (coordinate with SRE for paging thresholds)

title: Execution Degradation Simulator and Recovery Procedures
content:
Summary
-------
This document describes the Execution Degradation Simulator (EDS) — a lab-grade harness and operational runbook for reproducing, characterizing, and automatically recovering from runtime degradation modes that affect execution coordination, kernel scheduling, KV cache warmup, and tail-latency amplification. The guide contains: architecture interactions, supported simulation scenarios, telemetry requirements, step-by-step recovery procedures, benchmark acceptance criteria, and post-test analysis templates.

Goals
-----
- Provide a deterministic, auditable way to inject realistic degradation into the serving runtime so teams can validate detection and recovery logic.
- Reduce time-to-detection for complex degradation classes (scheduler thrash, kernel saturation, KV cold miss storms).
- Validate automated mitigation policies (backpressure, model fallback, admission control) without impacting production.

Scope and intended use
---------------------
- Target: internal staging clusters and dedicated canary pools only. Never run EDS against production clusters unless authorized by SRE with a staged blast radius plan.
- Components in scope: Execution Coordinator, Scheduler, Kernel Handoff, KVCache layer, Dispatch layer, Telemetry collectors, and Autoscaler hooks.
- Not in scope: third-party accelerator firmware updates and hardware-level electrical faults.

High-level architecture interactions
-----------------------------------
- Execution Coordinator: central decision point for slot assignment and handoff. Simulations should exercise coordinator decisions (reject/accept), delayed handoff, and inconsistent state reconcilers.
- Scheduler: drives kernel admission and batch composition. Injected noise should include burst queueing, priority inversions, and synthetic long-running kernel reservations.
- Kernel Handoff: emulate slow kernel activation (warm-up latency), deliberate kernel failures, and fallback activation to software kernels.
- KVCache: simulate cold start storms, targeted shard eviction, and inconsistent session lookup latencies.

Prerequisites
-------------
1. Access to staging cluster with labeled nodes: eds-canary-*.
2. A snapshot of representative traffic (shadow replay corpus) stored at s3://redwood-eds/corpus/<name>.
3. EDS binary and manager CLI installed (see install section below).
4. Alerting subscribers and a post-test channel created (#eds-results).

Install (one-time)
------------------
# install EDS manager in your environment
kubectl -n eds-system apply -f https://internal-assets.redwood.com/eds/install/eds-manager-2027-02.yaml
edsctl auth login --token $EDS_TOKEN --cluster eds-canary-01

Simulation harness overview
--------------------------
- Components:
  - eds-controller: orchestration service that schedules scenario runs and controls blast radius.
  - eds-injector: surface for fault injections (latency, cpu-steal, kernel-delay, kv-evict).
  - eds-replayer: traffic replayer that feeds the runtime using recorded traces and synthetic load shapes.
  - eds-observer: aggregator that composes traces, kernel telemetries, and SLO metrics for the scenario timeline.

Supported fault injection primitives
----------------------------------
- latency-add(ms) — adds N ms latency to targeted RPCs (dispatch, coordinator, kv).
- cpu-steal(percent) — consumes CPU cycles on chosen process groups to emulate noisy neighbors.
- kernel-hold(ms) — delays kernel activation to simulate slow NVLink or kernel cold starts.
- kv-evict(pct,shard) — evict a percentage of keys from a KV shard to create cache coldness.
- batch-break(probability) — randomly split batches with given probability to simulate batching failure.

Standard test scenarios (examples)
--------------------------------
1) Coordinated KV Cold Storm
   - Objective: validate autoscaler + admission policy under KV cache miss amplification.
   - Steps: replay 3x peak traffic with kv-evict(80,shard-07) + latency-add(25) on KV RPCs for 10 minutes.
   - Pass criteria: median P50 latency < 300ms and P99 < 1.2s after mitigation policies engage; no dropped requests > 0.5% over 1 minute.

2) Priority Inversion and Kernel Starvation
   - Objective: ensure scheduler crediting and per-request SLOs remain enforced when a long-running kernel locks slots.
   - Steps: inject kernel-hold(4500) on selected kernel_id, replay mixed traffic ramp (50% short chat, 50% long completion) for 8 minutes.
   - Pass criteria: short requests P95 meets target (< 400ms) after preemption or cooperative handoff; scheduler logs show credit redistribution.

3) Handoff Oscillation (flapping model swap)
   - Objective: detect oscillatory fallback between model variants and verify hysteresis/backoff controls.
   - Steps: alternate model-variant health toggles with 30s cadence while sending steady traffic.
   - Pass criteria: no more than 2 model switch cycles per 5 minutes; fallback proportion < 10% of all requests.

Runbook: controlled execution and recovery (step-by-step)
-------------------------------------------------------
1. Prepare: notify #eds-results and owners; tag run in eds-controller (run-id generated).
2. Lock: ensure no other e2e/chaos jobs are running on the canary pool.
3. Snapshot: save current autoscaler config and coordinator routing table:
   kubectl -n runtime get configmap autoscaler-config -o yaml > /tmp/autoscaler-config.$RUNID.yaml
   kubectl -n runtime get configmap coordinator-state -o yaml > /tmp/coordinator-state.$RUNID.yaml
4. Start replay: edsctl run --run-id $RUNID --scenario kv-cold-storm --corpus s3://redwood-eds/corpus/weekday-peak
5. Monitor (first 5 minutes): watch streaming dashboard: Grafana -> /d/eds/eds-scenario?orgId=1&run=$RUNID. Key panels: P50/P95/P99, kernel-queue-len, coordinator-pending-ops, kv-miss-rate.
6. If P95 exceeds threshold (see thresholds table) for 2 consecutive minutes, proceed to automated mitigation; otherwise let the scenario run its full duration.

Automated mitigation sequence (triggered by watcher)
1) Step 0 (detect): eds-observer fires alert EDS-AUTO-MIT-01 when P95>threshold and kv-miss-rate > 5x baseline.
2) Step 1 (soft): temporarily tighten admission controller by 20% (admit-rate reduction). Command:
   edsctl mitigation apply --run-id $RUNID --policy admit-reduce-20pct
3) Step 2 (scale): request a fast scale up of dedicated slots:
   kubectl -n runtime annotate deployment serving-runtime autoscaler-request=\"fast-scale-$RUNID\" --overwrite
4) Step 3 (fallback): enable model-variant fallback (degraded quantized variant) for affected routes:
   edsctl variant set --route /chat --fallback-variant redwood-chat-q4f --ttl 900
5) Step 4 (observe): wait 90s and observe P95; if still > threshold, proceed to manual escalation to SRE.

Manual recovery checklist (if automated mitigation fails)
1. Pause scenario: edsctl run stop --run-id $RUNID
2. Revert admission changes: edsctl mitigation rollback --run-id $RUNID
3. If coordinator is unresponsive, restart coordinator replicas sequentially with zero-downtime replacement:
   kubectl -n runtime rollout restart statefulset coordinator --strategy=RollingUpdate
4. If kernel binary is suspect, pin a previous kernel version using the runtime-plugin manifest:
   kubectl -n runtime apply -f /manifests/kernel-plugin-pin-$KNOWN_GOOD.yaml
5. Post-recovery: collect full traces from eds-observer and run the postmortem checklist.

Telemetry and alert thresholds (reference)
----------------------------------------
| Metric                          | Warning threshold          | Critical threshold         | Recovery target |
|---------------------------------|---------------------------|---------------------------|-----------------|
| route.p95_latency_ms           | > 450ms for 2m            | > 900ms for 1m            | < 400ms         |
| kernel.queue_length            | > 120 (per device)        | > 200 (per device)        | < 80            |
| kv.miss_rate                   | > 3x baseline (2m)        | > 10x baseline (1m)       | baseline ±10%   |
| admission.rejected_rate        | > 2%                      | > 5%                      | < 1%            |
| error.rate                     | > 0.5%                    | > 2%                      | < 0.2%          |

Benchmarks and acceptance criteria (post-test)
----------------------------------------------
- Each scenario run must produce a benchmark artifact (JSON) with the following fields: run_id, scenario, corpus, p50,p95,p99, kernel_utilization_mean, kv_miss_rate, mitigation_steps_taken. The eds-controller automatically uploads these to s3://redwood-eds/results/<run_id>.
- Acceptance is defined per scenario; a two-stage pass is required:
  - Detection pass: alerts fire within 90s of the injected degradation.
  - Mitigation pass: P95 returns to recovery target within 5 minutes after automated mitigation.

Artifacts and analysis commands
------------------------------
- Fetch artifacts:
  aws s3 cp s3://redwood-eds/results/$RUNID/ /tmp/eds-results-$RUNID --recursive
- Summarize run (quick):
  jq '.metrics | {p50: .p50, p95: .p95, p99: .p99, kernel: .kernel_utilization_mean}' /tmp/eds-results-$RUNID/summary.json
- Generate timeline heatmap (local):
  edsctl analyze timeline --input /tmp/eds-results-$RUNID/traces.json --output /tmp/heatmap-$RUNID.html

Post-test reporting and checklist
--------------------------------
1. Upload run summary to Confluence under the test-results space and link to artifacts.
2. Create a short postmortem if either detection or mitigation pass fails. Include: root cause hypothesis, steps to reproduce, changes to telemetry or thresholds, and action items.
3. If kernel or scheduler adjustments were made, schedule a canary dry-run and sign-off with Runtime PM.

Ownership and escalation
------------------------
- Scenario owner: runtime-e2e (oncall: runtime-e2e-oncall@redwood.com)
- Telemetry owner: observability-infra
- Escalation: SRE -> Runtime leads -> CTO (only for cross-region incidents)

Safety and blast-radius controls
-------------------------------
- Automatic safeguards in eds-controller: max_nodes_affected default = 2; cooldown between mitigations = 60s; manual escalation required if rollback rate > 10%
- Always run with the --dry-run flag first to validate expected actions without changing cluster state.

Appendix: example alert rule (Prometheus format)
------------------------------------------------
- name: EDS-AUTO-MIT-01
  expr: |
    histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(route_request_duration_bucket[1m])) by (le, route)) > bool 0
  for: 2m
  labels:
    severity: warning
  annotations:
    summary: "EDS scenario {{ $labels.route }} p95 high"

Appendix: sample mitigation policy (YAML)
----------------------------------------
apiVersion: eds.redwood/v1
kind: MitigationPolicy
metadata:
  name: admit-reduce-20pct
spec:
  action: adjust-admission
  parameters:
    admit_rate_multiplier: 0.8
    duration_seconds: 600

Contact and feedback
--------------------
For questions, improvements, and post-test reviews contact: priya.raman@redwood.com. Add suggested improvements to the doc as a PR in the confluence-docs repo.

title: Observability Bootcamp & Triage Runbook for Inference Runtime
content:
Overview:

This document is an onboarding-focused observability bootcamp and operational runbook for engineers and on-call SREs who will diagnose, triage, and mitigate production issues in the inference serving runtime. It distills the most common failure modes we see across kernel scheduling, KV cache, dispatch, and networked request surfaces and provides standard dashboards, playbooks, and example queries for pragmatic, repeatable investigations.

Audience:
- New runtime SREs and on-call engineers
- Backend engineers owning scheduler/kernel changes
- Applied ML engineers supporting model-onboarding incidents

Goals:
- Reduce mean time to detect (MTTD) and mean time to restore (MTTR) for runtime incidents
- Provide a repeatable cognitive checklist for triage across latency, correctness, and capacity classes
- Normalize telemetry and annotation conventions for rollouts and experiments

1) Quickstart: first 10 minutes on call
1.1 Triage checklist (prioritized):
1) Confirm alert context: alert name, fired time, route/model affected, severity, and any active rollout/experiment tags (see "Annotations & Tags" below).
2) Check global SLO dashboards (latency P50/P95/P99, error rate, per-route request rate) for correlated spikes.
3) Inspect kernel scheduler health panel for queue backlog and kernel backlog per-GPU.
4) Query trace samples for slow requests and check span breakdown (queue -> kernel dispatch -> inference -> postprocess).
5) If CPU/network saturation is suspected, inspect host-level metrics and network errors.

2) Observability primitives and conventions
- Service names: runtime-orch (orchestration), infer-gate (request ingress), kernel-gate (kernel manager), kvproxy (KV cache proxy), obs-collector (metrics/traces/log ingress).
- Alert naming convention: runtime.<component>.<symptom>.<severity> e.g., runtime.kernel-gate.queue-depth.critical
- Annotation keys (must be attached to requests and stored in trace attributes): rollout_id, variant (quantized|fp16|baseline), experiment, customer_tier, route_id.

3) Dashboards to open (ordered)
- Runtime: Global SLO Overview (P50/P95/P99, error budget burn)
- Kernel Scheduler: Per-GPU queue depth, kernel wait time, kernel dispatch rate, preemption count
- KV Cache: hit ratio (global & per-tenant), warmup rate, negative hit diffusion
- Network & IO: gRPC errors, connection churn, retransmits
- Cost & Throughput: tokens/sec, GPU utilization, model-replica counts

4) Standard queries and examples
4.1 PromQL examples (Grafana datasource):
- Per-route P95 latency (5m):
  
  histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(runtime_request_duration_seconds_bucket{route=~"$route"}[5m])) by (le))

- Kernel queue backlog (per GPU):
  
  sum(runtime_kernel_queue_depth) by (gpu_id)

- KV cache global hit ratio (1h window):
  
  sum(increase(kvproxy_hits_total[1h])) / sum(increase(kvproxy_requests_total[1h]))

4.2 Trace/Span patterns to look for (examples):
- Symptoms: long queue time with short kernel execution -> scheduler bottleneck
- Symptoms: long kernel execution and short queue time -> kernel optimization/degradation or wrong kernel variant
- Symptoms: high postprocess time -> downstream client or serialization issues

Example Jaeger-like span JSON snippet (single slow trace):
{
  "traceID": "abc123...",
  "spans": [
    {"operation": "ingest:parse", "duration_ms": 5},
    {"operation": "queue:kernel", "duration_ms": 450, "tags": {"gpu_id":"gpu-a12"}},
    {"operation": "kernel:forward", "duration_ms": 35, "tags": {"kernel_variant":"quant-fuse"}},
    {"operation": "postprocess:serialize", "duration_ms": 10}
  ]
}

5) Structured triage playbook (latency incident)
5.1 Step 0 — gather context
- Record incident ID, start time, alert thresholds
- Document active rollouts or quantization changes in the last 72 hours

5.2 Step 1 — isolate the layer
- If queue: queue depth and dispatch rate increased -> escalate to scheduler owners (kernel-scheduling team).
- If kernel: kernel execution time rose without queue increase -> collect recent kernel-release tags and CPU/GPU driver churn.
- If kvcache: hit ratio dropped -> check kvproxy error logs and cache warmup rate; examine recent model version swaps that invalidate prefixes.

5.3 Step 2 — quick mitigations (ordered by impact/risk)
1) Roll back recent kernel hint rollout (if annotated in traces and flagged in release chaperone).
2) Temporarily increase admission threshold for best-effort traffic and preserve reserved slots for SLO-critical routes. CLI example: 

  # Increase reserved slots for tiered routes (runtime-orch CLI)
  rdoctl admission update --tier critical --reserved-slots 30

3) Disable preemption for affected GPUs for 5–15 minutes if preemption churn correlates with latency spikes.
4) Enable shadow-routing of suspect route to a stable, lower-throughput model variant.

5.4 Step 3 — deep collection (when quick mitigations insufficient)
- Enable request-level debug sampling (increase trace sample rate to 100% for route-id X for 10 minutes).
- Collect full kernel traces: kernel_gcov, kernel_dispatch_profile, and executor logs from affected GPU hosts.
- Export recent microbenchmarks used by the scheduler for the current time window.

6) Runbook for error storms and connection churn
6.1 Symptoms: Sharp spike in gRPC UNAVAILABLE or connection resets
- Immediate checks: service endpoint health (kube probe), node-level TCP retransmits, ulimit of open files.
- Mitigation steps: temporarily shift traffic away from affected AZ/region, increase gRPC max-connections on fronting proxies, restart infer-gate pod after draining.

6.2 Example commands and logs to collect:
- Kubernetes pod status: kubectl -n runtime get pods -o wide --selector app=infer-gate
- Netstat summary: ss -s; ss -p | grep runtime-orch
- gRPC logged error snippet (example):
  
  E 2026-02-10T12:23:44.123Z infer-gate runtime: request failed: rpc error: code = Unavailable desc = connection closed by peer

7) Escalation matrix and ownership
- Level 1: On-call runtime SRE (primary) — initial triage and short mitigations (15–30m).
- Level 2: Kernel-scheduling owners / Inference runtime team — deep kernel and scheduler changes (30–120m).
- Level 3: Infra/Cloud/Networking — cross-host issues (120m+), driver or NVLink problems.

Contact roster (primary contact tags):
- runtime-oncall: #runtime-oncall in Slack
- kernel-scheduling: @kernel-sched-leads
- infra: #infra-ops

8) Post-incident follow-up checklist
- Create a postmortem within 72 hours for any incident > 3 hours or that breached an error budget.
- Include reproduction steps, top contributing causes, and a concrete remediation plan with owners and completion dates.
- Add instrumentation gaps found to the telemetry backlog and tag with "telemetry-gap".

9) Observability hygiene and instrumentation guidance (for PRs)
- Always add these trace attributes in request path: route_id, rollout_id, model_variant, request_priority.
- Use the standardized histogram buckets for request_duration_seconds (see table below).

Histogram buckets (recommended):
| bucket (s) | rationale |
|------------|-----------|
| 0.005 | parse/ingest micro-latency |
| 0.02  | fast responses |
| 0.1   | typical token-level requests |
| 0.5   | larger generation or batched flows |
| 2.0   | slow operations; investigate |
| 10.0  | gateway/backpressure expiry |

10) Example alert definitions (templates)
- kernel-gate.queue-depth.warning: runtime.kernel-gate.queue-depth.warning
  - Condition: sum(runtime_kernel_queue_depth) by (cluster) > 1000 for 5m
  - Runbook pointer: this doc -> section 5
- kvproxy.hitratio.critical
  - Condition: (sum(increase(kvproxy_hits_total[15m])) / sum(increase(kvproxy_requests_total[15m]))) < 0.5
  - Runbook pointer: section 5 & 6

11) Release and experiment annotation workflow (short)
- Before any kernel or scheduler hint rollout, create an experiment entry in the release tracker with an annotation token (e.g., rollout_id=rb-20260210-kh). The runtime orchestration will emit rollout_id on all traces so incidents can be correlated automatically.
- Toggle dark launches with runtime-orch feature flags and ensure the feature flag name is included as 'experiment' on traces.

12) Common debugging recipes (quick snippets)
A) Find top slowest routes in the last 15 minutes (PromQL):
  topk(10, histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(runtime_request_duration_seconds_bucket[15m])) by (le, route)))

B) Find hosts with highest kernel execution time per GPU: 
  topk(10, sum(runtime_kernel_exec_time_seconds) by (host, gpu_id))

C) Dump recent kvproxy error logs for tenant X: 
  rdoctl logs kvproxy --tenant X --since 30m --grep "ERR"

13) Appendix: instrumentation snippets and SDK examples
- OpenTelemetry span example (pseudocode):
  span = tracer.startSpan("kernel:forward")
  span.setAttribute("gpu_id", gpu_id)
  span.setAttribute("kernel_variant", "quant-fuse")
  span.end()

- Runtime-orch admission override example (YAML):
  apiVersion: runtime.redwood.ai/v1
  kind: AdmissionPolicy
  metadata:
    name: critical-reserved-slots
  spec:
    tier: critical
    reservedSlots: 30
    backoff: 10s

14) Ownership and maintenance cadence
- Owner: runtime-observability squad (rotating oncall: see team wiki for roster)
- Quarterly hygiene tasks:
  - Audit dashboards and remove unused panels
  - Validate alert thresholds against synthetic load profile
  - Run the observability runbook drill (game-day) once per quarter

15) Frequently seen root causes (historical examples)
- Kernel fingerprint regression after a fused-kernel rollout (fixed by rollback and kernel autotune).
- KV cache invalidation after model prefix change (mitigated by warming and routing tag).
- Preemption storms caused by mis-sized admission controller thresholds (fixed by adding hysteresis).

Related resources and links:
- Runtime telemetry sampling and cost playbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/runtime-telemetry-sampling-cost-aware-profiling-handbook-2027
- Kernel scheduling ADRs: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-policy-language-declarative-profiles-2026
- On-call Slack channel: #runtime-oncall

If you are new on call, run the quickstart checklist at the top of this doc on every page load until you have handled 3 real incidents. That practice significantly reduces cognitive load during the first live incident.

Change log:
- 2026-02-10: Initial authored by Priya R. Natarajan
- 2026-03-01: Clarified triage steps and added PromQL examples (reviewed by Liam Chen)

title: KVCache Chaos Validation and Reconciliation Manual
content:
Overview

This document defines the validation, chaos experiments, and reconciliation playbook for the KVCache subsystem in the serving runtime. It is intended to give on-call engineers, SREs, and runtime owners a prescriptive set of experiments and verification steps to catch, reproduce, and remediate KV cache consistency issues that can affect fidelity, tail latency, and customer-facing correctness.

Background and Motivation

- The KVCache holds per-session and per-shard prefix state used to accelerate autoregressive decoding.
- Incorrect eviction, stale reads, or shard re-assignment can produce hallucinations, token repetition, or increased generation latency while silently degrading quality.
- We run periodic chaos validation to: surface rare race conditions, validate reconciliation logic, and ensure safe rollouts of kernel/scheduler changes that affect warmstart paths.

Scope

- Subsystem: kvcache-manager, kvcache-shard-proxy, runtime-dispatcher, and scheduler-adaptor.
- Environments: staging and canary production clusters only. Do NOT run destructive experiments on global production without coordinating with Platform Ops and Customer Success.
- Tests covered here: eviction race, stale-read windows, shard-migration replay, partial-ack loss, and reconciliation under GC pressure.

Ownership and Contacts

- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime/runtime-team (oncall: #runtime-oncall).
- Secondary: eng-sre (page: /confluence/eng-sre/incident-review).
- Pager escalation: follow oncall rota; if experiment impacts SLAs, notify SRE lead.

Service-level verification (SLOs to monitor during experiments)

- Tail P95 generation latency for canary model: must remain < 150 ms (baseline).
- Token-quality regression: measured by prompt-set A->B BLEU-like eval; target: no >1.5% degradation vs baseline.
- Error rate: RPC error rate <= 0.1% for the test window.

Before you start (prechecks)

1. Ensure a clean baseline snapshot: collect 10 minutes of production-like traffic replay into the staging cluster using shadow-proxy.
2. Confirm toggle flags: kvcache-reconciliation enabled, eviction-delay-ms default set (see sample config).
3. Notify stakeholders and schedule a 60-minute maintenance window for canary.
4. Validate observability: dashboards loaded, tracing enabled, and trace-sampler set to 100% for mirrored traffic.

Validation matrix (tests, intent, success criteria)

- Eviction race injection
  - Intent: simulate overlapping eviction and read to detect stale-pointer windows.
  - Injection: pause kvcache-shard-proxy apply loop for X ms while allowing reads.
  - Success: no incorrect token sequences in generation corpus; no RPC panics; reconciliation loop repairs state within 500 ms.

- Stale-read window
  - Intent: verify upper bounds on how long a stale entry can be served.
  - Injection: insert artificial network latency between dispatcher and shard proxy (200-800 ms).
  - Success: stale-read count <= 0.05% of requests; each stale read triggers a reconciliation event annotated in traces.

- Shard migration replay
  - Intent: ensure kvcache warmup when a shard moves nodes during a canary rollout.
  - Injection: schedule a controlled shard eviction and immediate reassignment.
  - Success: warmstart hit-rate recovers to >90% within 30 seconds and no QoS regressions observed.

- Partial-ack loss and backpressure
  - Intent: detect the dispatcher behaviour when partial ACKs are lost and retry semantics cause duplication or reordering.
  - Injection: drop 30% of ACK packets from shard proxy for 10 seconds.
  - Success: no duplicate token emission; dispatcher metrics show retry spikes but bounded.

- GC pressure reconciliation
  - Intent: measure reconciliation under memory compaction/fragmentation events.
  - Injection: trigger memory compaction on a subset of GPU nodes and force minor GC on node-side components.
  - Success: no unbounded latency; reconciliation completes within configured window and produces a summary trace.

Runbook: step-by-step experiment procedure (example: Eviction Race)

1. Preparation (10 min)
   - Load the test corpus (see Appendix A) via shadow-replay into staging.
   - Start baseline traces: `curl -X POST https://internal-telemetry/api/start-snapshot -d '{"name":"kvcache-e2e-eviction-YYYYMMDD"}'`
   - Ensure alerting temporarily muted for the canary namespace.
2. Start experiment (5 min)
   - Deploy the chaos job in namespace `runtime-chaos-staging` with label `experiment=eviction-race` using the script below.
   - Command (example): `kubectl apply -f kvcache-eviction-pause-job.yaml -n runtime-chaos-staging`
3. Observe (10 min)
   - Monitor dashboards: KVCache Recon Events, dispatcher.rpc.errors, generation.tail-latency.
   - Run the automated verifier: `./tools/kvcache-checker --replay-id kvcache-e2e-eviction-YYYYMMDD --asserts eviction-no-regression`
4. Reconciliation validation (5 min)
   - Verify reconciliation logs: search traces for `reconcile::success` and `reconcile::duration_ms < 500`.
   - If reconciliation fails, execute manual reconciliation: `kubectl exec -it kvctl -- /bin/kvctl reconcile --shard <shard-id>`
5. Teardown and post-checks (10 min)
   - Remove chaos resources and allow systems to stabilize for 5 minutes.
   - Collect traces and export telemetry: `scripts/export-traces.sh kvcache-e2e-eviction-YYYYMMDD`
   - Run diff analyzer: `python tools/compare-generation-corpora.py baseline.json after.json`

Automated harness sample (k8s job manifest snippet)

# kvcache-eviction-pause-job.yaml (snippet)
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: kvcache-eviction-pause-001
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: pause-eviction
        image: internal/chaos:kvcache-v1
        args: ["--target=kvcache-shard-proxy","--pause-ms=400","--shard-selector=region=canary"]
      restartPolicy: Never

Validator CLI examples

- Check for stale reads:
  ./tools/kvcache-checker --mode stale-read-detect --window 60 --threshold 0.0005 --trace-output stale-read-traces.json
- Aggregate warmstart hit-rate:
  ./tools/metric-agg --metric warmstart.hit_rate --group-by shard_id --window 30s

Observability and queries

- Critical dashboards (links internal):
  - KVCache Health Overview: /dashboards/kvcache-health
  - Recon & Warmstart: /dashboards/kvcache-recon
  - Dispatcher Effects: /dashboards/dispatcher-impact

- Recommended metric queries (PromQL-like):
  - Stale reads per minute:
    sum(increase(kvcache_stale_reads_total[1m])) by (shard_id)
  - Recon duration 99th:
    histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(kvcache_reconcile_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le))
  - Warmstart hit-rate:
    1 - sum(rate(kvcache_miss_total[1m])) / sum(rate(kvcache_request_total[1m]))

Instrumentation and trace expectations

- Every request touching KVCache must produce a trace span: `kvcache.access` with tags: shard_id, session_id, op=(read|write|evict), outcome=(hit|miss|stale|error).
- Recon spans: `kvcache.reconcile` must include `reconcile.reason` and `reconcile.result`.
- Traces of failed reconciliation must attach a `reconcile.snapshot` file reference for offline analysis.

Failure modes and immediate remediation (short triage)

- Symptom: Continuous `reconcile::failure` spikes with duration > 2s across shards  Remediation: scale kvcache-reconciler replicas up by 2, enable debug logging, and pause any non-essential canary traffic.
- Symptom: Duplicate token emission observed in generation samples  Remediation: immediately disable dispatcher-retry for the affected shard group and run `kvctl reconcile --repair-duplicates` then escalate.
- Symptom: Slow warmstart recovery (>60s) after migration  Remediation: increase warmstart prefetch parallelism and re-run shard-warmup script; follow with postmortem.

Rollout gating and acceptance criteria

- For any kernel, scheduler, or reconcilation code change that touches kvcache paths, the change must pass:
  1) Automated chaos validation in staging (all tests pass).
  2) Canary run with reduced traffic: warmstart hit-rate drop <= 10%, no token-quality regression >1.0%.
  3) No new `reconcile::failure` alerts for 24 hours post-canary.

Post-test report template (deliverables)

- Title
- Date and experiment id
- Environment and cluster
- Test matrix results (pass/fail + short notes)
- Key telemetry artifacts (links to dashboards, trace-snapshot ids)
- Actions required (bug, mitigation, rollout decision)

Appendix A: Test corpus and generator

- A curated set of 2k prompts that represent session seeds for product features (chat, summarization, completion). Stored at: s3://redwood-test-corpora/kvcache/2026-q1/{baseline.json,edgecases.json}
- Generator invocation:
  python tools/generate-replay-corpus.py --profiles chat,short-complete --size 2000 --out baseline.json

Appendix B: Sample config (kvcache manager)

# yaml snippet for kvcache manager
reconciliation:
  enabled: true
  concurrency: 8
  max_reconcile_duration_ms: 1000
eviction:
  default_ttl_ms: 600000
  backlog_pause_ms: 50

References and related pages

- Runtime reconciliation design spec: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/execution-stitching-and-fallback-orchestration-2026
- Session lifecycle & kvcache guidelines: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/session-lifecycle-kvcache-consistency-guidelines-2024

Change log

- 2026-02-10: Created by Asha Patel (initial draft).
- 2026-09-15: Added GC pressure experiment and updated reconciliation thresholds (A. Patel).

title: Asynchronous Kernel Handoff Simulation and Safety Playbook
content:
Summary

This playbook describes the simulation-driven, safety-first approach for introducing and validating asynchronous kernel handoffs in the runtime scheduler. It complements the scheduler contract and kernel handoff design docs by providing step-by-step simulation recipes, invariant checks, telemetry baselines, and an incident recovery checklist for live rollouts.

Intended audience
- Runtime engineers implementing scheduler/handoff changes
- SREs validating rollouts and runbooks
- Performance engineers and profiling owners

Scope and definitions
- Asynchronous kernel handoff: transferring control of a kernel or execution slot from one worker / kernel instance to another without blocking incoming requests synchronously; may include prefetching of KV cache and lazy state reconciliation.
- Simulation harness: an isolated environment that replays production-like traces and injects failure modes deterministically.
- Safety invariants: conditions that must hold before, during, and after handoffs (listed below).

Goals
1. Validate correctness: ensure no token duplication, KV cache divergence, or session corruption occurs across handoffs.
2. Preserve SLOs: keep p50 and p99 latency within the rollback guard rails during canonical handoff scenarios.
3. Enable deterministic root cause: simulation traces must reproduce handoff failures with >=95% fidelity to production traces.
4. Provide a concise checklist for safe rollout and emergency rollback.

Safety invariants (explicit)
- Invariant A: No request may be acknowledged to the client more than once.
- Invariant B: KV cache consistency: for any session id, post-handoff output must be deterministic given the same prompt and pre-handoff KV state.
- Invariant C: Memory safety: no kernel may hold references to evicted memory regions after handoff.
- Invariant D: Backpressure preservation: handoff must not exceed a 10% transient increase in queuing for any request class.

Simulation harness overview
- Components:
  - Trace replayer: injects request timeline events (arrival times, priorities, session ids, token budgets).
  - Fault injector: simulates partial failures (GPU preemption signals, process SIGTERM, nvlink transient errors, slow KV prefetch).
  - Kernel proxy: mediates handoff by providing deterministic serialization/deserialization of kernel runtime state.
  - Metrics collector: exports the same telemetry schema we use in staging (request_timeline, kernel_events, kvcache_diff_ratio, handoff_duration_ms).

Quick start (local staging)
1. Provision the harness cluster: ./infra/scripts/provision-sim-cluster.sh --type=staging-small 
2. Load trace corpus: ./tools/trace_importer --source s3://redwood-prod-traces/2025-11 --filter "route:chat, seq_len>64, entropy>0.2"
3. Start trace replayer: ./sim/replayer --traces ./corpus --concurrency 200 --compress-traffic
4. Start fault injector (dry-run): ./sim/fault_injector --profile handoff-basic --mode dry
5. Run baseline: ./sim/run_experiment --scenario baseline --duration 10m --collect prometheus,otel
6. Run handoff scenario: ./sim/run_experiment --scenario async-handoff --handoff-window 200ms --faults "gpu-preempt:50ms"

Suggested simulation parameter table
| parameter | example | purpose | acceptance threshold |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| concurrency | 200 | concurrent in-flight requests to simulate mixed traffic | p99 latency <= baseline * 1.10 |
| handoff-window | 200ms | allowed window where both origin and target may race | no token duplication, kvcache_diff_ratio < 0.001 |
| fault-injection-rate | 5% | fraction of handoffs where a fault is injected | recovery completes or rollback triggers 100% |
| replay-fidelity | 0.95 | percentage match of timeline events to production trace | >= 0.90 for acceptance |

Key telemetry and alerts to monitor during simulation
- Metrics to chart live:
  - handoff_attempts_total (by scenario, kernel_variant)
  - handoff_success_total / handoff_failure_total
  - handoff_duration_ms (p50/p90/p99)
  - kvcache_diff_ratio (per-session rolling 1m)
  - duplicate_response_detected_total
  - request_retries_total (automated retry policy triggered)
  - downstream_slo_violation_count (per-service)
- Alerts to configure for canary/staging:
  - P1: duplicate_response_detected_total > 0 in 5m window -> stop rollout
  - P1: handoff_failure_total / handoff_attempts_total > 0.01 over 10m -> investigate
  - P2: p99 end-to-end latency > baseline p99 * 1.2 for 5m -> throttling rule

Acceptance criteria for simulation runs
- Functional: duplicate_response_detected_total == 0 and kvcache_diff_ratio < 0.001 across all traces.
- Performance: p99 latency <= baseline p99 * 1.10 and CPU/GPU utilization delta <= 15% compared to baseline.
- Observability: full trace sampling with trace-id correlation for at least 80% of simulated handoffs.

Experiment scenarios (examples)
1. Graceful prefetch handoff: origin prefetches KV to target before releasing slot (no faults).
2. Interrupted migration: origin receives SIGTERM during prefetch and target must reconcile partial KV state.
3. Transient interconnect loss: nvlink jitter causes target to receive delayed KV chunks; simulate reordering.
4. Priority inversion under load: high-priority requests arrive during handoff causing preemption to requeue.

Step-by-step simulation validation checklist
1. Start baseline run and capture baseline snapshots for 10m.
2. Run scenario with handoff enabled and no faults. Validate functional invariants, then capture telemetry.
3. Introduce single-fault injections and assert invariants still hold or run compensating recovery.
4. Scale fault-injection to 5% and validate rollback triggers and operator automation.
5. Run full mixed-workload run and validate acceptance criteria.
6. Produce a short experiment report and attach trace bundles for reviewers.

Runtime-safe rollout procedure (canary -> ramp)
1. Canary: enable async handoff for 1% of traffic routed to a dedicated pool for 2 hours.
2. Verify: run the simulation acceptance suite against canary traces and monitor P1 alerts for 30m.
3. Ramp: 1% -> 5% -> 15% -> 50% over successive deployments, each step with a 2h monitoring window and automatic rollback on P1 alerts.
4. Full rollout guard: require sign-off from owner (runtime scheduler) and observability owner before >50%.

Emergency rollback checklist
1. Trigger: P1 alert firing (duplicate_response_detected_total>0 or handoff_failure ratio > threshold).
2. Actions:
   a. Flip feature flag: infra/flags set async_handoff=false for affected pool.
   b. Drain: start draining canary pool (no new handoff attempts) using /ops/drain-pool --pool <id> --mode gentle
   c. Rehydrate: ensure in-flight requests are allowed to complete under origin kernels.
   d. Postmortem: collect handoff trace bundles, kernel logs, and the fault injector script used.
3. Communicate: status-page update and paging to runtime-oncall channel (#runtime-oncall).

Runbook: triage recipe for a single handoff failure
1. Identify trace-id(s) from handoff_failure events. 2. Pull the correlated kernel_event timeline and kvcache snapshots. 3. Re-run the small-trace repro in the harness with identical fault injection. 4. If repro succeeds locally, create a hotfix branch to add additional guards (e.g., stricter prefetchcks, idempotency tokens). 5. If repro fails to reproduce, escalate to scheduler + kernel owners with a seeded simulation trace and full telemetry bundle.

Developer guidance: safe coding patterns for handoff logic
- Always attach monotonic idempotency tokens to outbound token-write ops.
- Serialize kernel runtime state with a compact checksum field to quickly validate deserialized state.
- Prefer append-only handoff logs for state replay to avoid in-place mutation issues.
- Add defensive backoff and re-check logic for KV prefetch acknowledgements.

SLOs and impact budget for rollout
- Target: end-to-end p99 latency regression <= +10% during steady-state handoffs.
- Error budget: no more than 0.1% of requests may be retried due to handoff (counted toward service SLO).

Ownership and contact list
- Scheduler owner: Daniel Kim (daniel.k@redwood.ai)
- Kernel runtime owner: Priya Natarajan (priya.n@redwood.ai)
- Profiling & telemetry: Evan Martinez (evan.m@redwood.ai)
- SRE oncall: see rotation in /ops/oncall-schedule

Artifacts to produce after an experiment
- Experiment report (one-page): hypothesis, configuration, graphs, acceptance pass/fail, decision.
- Trace bundle: named <scenario>-<date>-<gid>.tar.gz uploaded to s3://redwood-sim-results/<team>/
- Hotfix or roll-forward plan if acceptance failed.

References and related material
- Kernel handoff decision tracing manual (link above)
- Compact trace annotation and causal latency map (profiling-playbook)
- Runtime decision graph and observed behaviour catalog

Appendix: example commands and JSON config
```
# simulate a graceful prefetch handoff scenario
```
