```
./sim/run_experiment --scenario async-handoff --handoff-window 200ms --concurrency 200 --faults "none" --output s3://redwood-sim-results/handsoff-2026-03-02

# sample experiment config (JSON stored in /infra/experiments)
{
  "name": "async-handoff-graceful-200ms",
  "scenario": "async-handoff",
  "concurrency": 200,
  "handoff_window_ms": 200,
  "faults": [],
  "sampling": {
    "trace_sample_rate": 0.8
  }
}
```

Notes and future work
- Next iteration: integrate kernel-level snapshot diffs to reduce trace bundle sizes and speed up repro.
- Long term: bake this harness into CI gating for scheduler changes that touch handoff paths.

Change log
- 2026-01-12: Initial draft by Sofia Patel.
- 2026-02-05: Added acceptance table and telemetry alerts (reviewers Daniel, Priya).
- 2026-03-02: Finalized rollout procedure and emergency rollback steps (published).

End of document

title: Crossplane fallback & profiling playbook: diagnosing fused fallbacks across scheduler layers
content:
Summary
-------
This playbook documents how to diagnose, triage, and remediate cross-layer fallback events in the serving runtime when the router, kernel-dispatcher, and kv-cache layers interact to trigger graceful degradations. It focuses on a class of incidents we call 'fused fallbacks' — when multiple subsystems independently activate fallback policies and the system degrades more than intended (e.g., model swap + kernel downgrade + cache eviction).

Audience
--------
- Oncall SREs and runtime engineers handling production incidents.
- Performance engineers running microbenchmarks and regression hunts.
- Release engineers validating canaries for new scheduler or kernel rollouts.

Why this is different
--------------------
Existing runbooks cover single-layer fallback (router or kernel) or warmstart strategies. This document covers the combined behavioral surface: how fallback signals propagate, what telemetry to collect to see the causal chain, and an ordered mitigation sequence that minimizes user-visible SLO impact.

Key goals and SLOs
------------------
- SLOs to use during triage: p50 < 60ms, p95 < 220ms, p99 < 700ms for short-text generation (seq<=128) on hosted tier.
- Fallback budget: total degraded token-rate should be <5% of baseline over 5m rolling window.
- Alert thresholds: sustained 2x increase in kernel-handled-slow-calls with concurrent model-variant-swaps > 10/min.

Primary services and signals to inspect
-------------------------------------
- inference-router: routing decisions, chosen-tier, model-variant-id, timestamped route decisions (field: route_decision.trace_id).
- kernel-dispatcher: kernel_version, queue_depth, dispatch_latency_ms, kernel_error_rate.
- kv-cache-manager: hit_rate, warmup_ratio, eviction_rate, per-tenant cache_size_bytes.
- fallthrough-agent: fused-fallback-events log (proto), reason codes (NETWORK_PRESSURE, KERNEL_TIMEOUT, CACHE_WARMUP_FAIL).
- telemetry-ingester / traces: trace spans linking router -> dispatcher -> kernel.

Immediate triage checklist (first 15 minutes)
-------------------------------------------
1) Verify customer impact and scope. Query the status dashboard for affected routes and tenants.
2) Fetch correlated alerts: kernel_timeouts, model_swap_rate, cache_evictions.
3) Run a targeted synthetic request against the same route with trace headers enabled. Example: 

   curl -s -H "X-Trace-Enable: 1" 
        -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_DEBUG_TOKEN" 
        -d '{"input":"hello"}' 
        https://inference-router.internal/v1/generate?model=redwood-small

   Capture trace_id and inspect trace spans in the trace UI.

4) Check fallthrough-agent logs for fused-fallback-events in the 5m window.

Causal diagnosis matrix
-----------------------
Use the following matrix to map observed symptoms to likely root causes. The matrix is intentionally conservative — multiple cells can be true.

| Symptom | Likely root causes | Quick check |
|---------|--------------------|-------------|
| sudden model variant swap + p99 spike | router policy fallback due to capacity + kernel preemption | router logs: route_decision.reason == CAPACITY_CONSTRAINT; kernel-dispatcher.preemption_count > 0 |
| progressive latency increase + kv hit-rate drop | cache warmup failing over eviction threshold | kv-cache-manager.eviction_rate > 100/s; warmup_ratio < 0.6 |
| repeated kernel timeouts + model downgraded | kernel-side OOMs or kernel update causing regressions | kernel-dispatcher.kernel_error_rate > 1%; node-level GPU OOM events present |
| multi-tenant p95 regressions with low per-tenant qps | admission controller misconfigured quota spillover | admission-controller.metrics.queue_weight_rebalance > 0.7 |

Longer investigation (15–90 minutes)
------------------------------------
- Stitch traces: find the earliest fallback signal in router traces and follow downstream spans to kernel and cache. Identify which component first emitted a fallback decision (router fallthrough vs kernel probe failure).
- Gather microbenchmarks: run the microbenchmark harness matching the production shape (concurrency, sequence length, input distribution). Compare against the last known-good baseline stored in the benchmarking suite.

  Example microbenchmark command (internal harness):

  ./bench/run --target https://inference-router.internal --model redwood-medium --shape concurrency=8,seq=256,inputs=1000 --trace --output /tmp/bench.out

- Capture kernel telemetry snapshot: /api/v1/internal/kernel/metrics?snapshot=true. This returns a compact JSON array of kernel occupancy, active-calls, and per-kernel latency histograms. (The endpoint is internal-only and requires service-to-service auth).

Observed pattern -> ordered mitigations
--------------------------------------
When fused fallbacks are observed, apply mitigations in this order. The goal is to limit cascading side-effects and keep the customer-visible latency within SLO while preserving safety.

1) Rate-limit non-critical tenants: temporarily reduce burst allowance to free slots. CLI: 

   redwoodctl quota apply --tenant experimental --burst=0 --policy=reduce-by-75

2) Pin affected routes to a conservative model-variant (not a lower-quality model) using the router override to avoid triggering kernel variant swaps: 

   redwoodctl router override --route /v1/generate --model redwood-medium:v1-pin --duration 15m --reason "fused-fallback triage"

3) Increase kernel dispatch retry budget to avoid OOM-triggered swaps while kernel team investigates: 

   curl -X POST -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $SVC_TOKEN" 
     https://kernel-dispatcher.internal/admin/retry-config 
     -d '{"max_retries":3,"backoff_ms":150}'

4) If cache warmup is failing, temporarily enable conservative cache replication for the affected tenant: 

   api: POST /api/internal/kvcache/replicate?tenant=TENANT_ID&mode=shadow

5) If kernel-side regressions are suspected and rollback is available, rollback kernel to last-good version with canary disabled for that node pool. Follow the kernel rollback runbook after trusting the rollback assessment.

Instrumentation and data to collect for postmortem
--------------------------------------------------
- Full traces for a sampling of 30 failed requests including the router route_decision span.
- Kernel dispatch snapshots (as above) for the 30 requests and a 10m period surrounding the event.
- kv-cache-manager metrics and per-tenant cache keys eviction traces for the 30 requests.
- Fallthrough-agent fused-fallback-event protos.
- Microbenchmark run output and diff against baseline.

Quick reference tables
----------------------
Fallback reason codes and recommended triage owner:

| Reason code | Primary owner | Triage action |
|-------------|---------------|---------------|
| KERNEL_TIMEOUT | runtime/kernel | collect kernel snapshot, raise kernel regression alert |
| CACHE_WARMUP_FAIL | runtime/cache | inspect eviction/warmup metrics, replicate cache if necessary |
| CAPACITY_CONSTRAINT | platform/router | check autoscaler activity, reduce non-critical burst allowances |
| NETWORK_PARTITION | infra/networking | verify link health, throttle regional routing |

Escalation matrix (when to page)
--------------------------------
- Page runtime-kernel oncall if p99 > 2x SLO and kernel_error_rate > 5% for 5m.
- Page infra-networking if fallthrough-agent reason == NETWORK_PARTITION.
- Page platform-availability if model_swap_rate > 50 swaps/min or global autoscaler failed.

Runbook for reproducing fused fallback in staging (step-by-step)
---------------------------------------------------------------
1) Prepare a staging cluster configured to mimic the production admission-controller weights.
2) Deploy a kernel test build with instrumentation flags: KERNEL_DEBUG=1, PROBING_ENABLED=1.
3) Seed the kv-cache with a warm working set using the cache warmup harness: 

   ./tools/cache-seed --tenant test-tenant --keys 100000 --payload-size 512

4) Run synthetic load: 

   ./bench/run --target https://staging-router.internal --model redwood-medium --shape concurrency=32,seq=128,inputs=20000 --faults kernel-slow=0.15,cache-evict-burst=0.2

5) Observe the fused-fallback events via fallthrough-agent and iterate mitigation steps in a non-production safe mode. Ensure you capture the timeline of first fallback emission.

Benchmark artifacts to collect
----------------------------
- baseline.json: last-known-good microbenchmark output for the same model/shape.
- current-run.json: the run performed in step 4.
- kernel-diff.txt: human-readable diff of kernel histogram deltas.
- trace-archive.tar.gz: collected traces for all sampled requests.

Postmortem template (required fields)
------------------------------------
- Summary of impact (routes, tenants, duration).
- Timeline with the first fallback emission timestamp and causal chain.
- Root cause analysis and evidence (traces, kernel snapshots, eviction logs).
- Short-term mitigations applied and timeline.
- Long-term action items (owners + target dates).
- Monitoring changes and new alerts added.

Ownership and contacts
----------------------
- Runtime: @runtime-oncall (rotation page) — primary triage.
- Kernel: Carlos Mendes (carlos@redwood.ai) — kernel profiling and rollback.
- Cache: Aisha Khan (aisha@redwood.ai) — eviction and warmup tuning.
- Router & policies: Ethan Liu (ethan@redwood.ai) — routing policy tuning.

Appendix A — common diagnostic queries
--------------------------------------
1) List fused-fallback events in the last 10m:

   gcloud logging read 'resource.type="k8s_container" AND jsonPayload.component="fallthrough-agent"' --limit 50 --project redwood-prod | jq '.jsonPayload | select(.event=="fused-fallback")'

2) Kernel snapshot fetch (internal curl):

   curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $SVC_TOKEN" https://kernel-dispatcher.internal/api/v1/internal/kernel/metrics?snapshot=true | jq '.'

3) Compare benchmark histograms using the internal comparator: 

   ./tools/bench-compare --base baseline.json --current current-run.json --out /tmp/bench-diff.html

Appendix B — safe defaults for emergency toggles
-------------------------------------------------
| Toggle | Safe default during triage | Notes |
|--------|----------------------------|-------|
| router.model_swap.enabled | false | prevents mass variant swaps while retaining current model mapping |
| kernel.autotune.enabled | false | prevents aggressive kernel selection changes during live incidents |
| kvcache.eviction_aggressiveness | 0.2 | reduces churn; may increase memory usage temporarily |

Appendix C — glossary of new terms used here
----------------------------------------------
- fused fallback: coordinated or coincident fallback actions from multiple runtime layers that lead to larger-than-expected degradation.
- fallthrough-agent: internal daemon responsible for aggregating fallback decisions and emitting fused-fallback-events.
- kernel-probe: periodic kernel health probe used by the dispatcher to decide whether to switch kernel implementations.

Notes and change history
------------------------
- 2025-08-15 (Priya Nambiar): initial playbook draft.
- 2025-10-02 (Ethan Liu): added benchmark artifact checklist and safe toggles.
- 2026-02-10 (Priya Nambiar): expanded escalation matrix and added CLI examples for router overrides.

Related runbooks and reading
---------------------------
- runtime-deployment-circuit-breakers-and-sla-fallback-playbook-2026 (for circuit-breaker policy knobs).
- telemetry-feedback-kernel-autotune-playbook-2026 (for kernel autotune interactions).

End of document

title: SIGTERM Connection Drain and Graceful Shutdown Playbook
content:
Purpose
-------
This playbook describes the operational procedure, runtime integrations, and verification steps for performing graceful shutdowns of inference runtime workers in response to SIGTERM (or equivalent orchestration signals). It covers: connection draining, inflight request completion, kernel-scheduler handoff, KV cache persistence, observability checks, and rollback. The goal is to avoid user-facing 5xx/timeout spikes and to preserve SLOs for p99 latency and error rate during deployments and preemptions.

Scope
-----
- Applies to: runtime worker processes (redwood-runtime-worker), shard proxies (kv-shard-proxy), and the request-router service.
- Deployment modes: Hosted API, Dedicated nodes, and Private single-tenant installs (behavior differs slightly; see "Mode differences" below).

Ownership and Contacts
---------------------
- Runbook owner: Runtime Operations (runtime-ops@redwood.internal)
- Primary on-call: eng-sre/runtime team (page: /oncall-and-incident-response/incident-process)
- Escalation: Runtime Lead — Arjun Patel, and Kernel Scheduling Lead — Lina Gomez

Key SLOs to preserve during shutdown
----------------------------------
- p99 request latency for text-generation endpoints: 300ms target degradation window
- 5xx error rate: < 0.5% global increase tolerated during drain windows
- Maximum queue length per worker: 8 (if exceeded, router will re-route)

Principles
----------
- Prefer draining over immediate process kill. Allow inflight generation to finish up to a configurable soft timeout (default 10s).
- Prevent new requests: stop accepting new upstream connections and signal the router to stop routing new sessions to the instance.
- Give kernel scheduler and batcher time to flush batched work and spill KV cache if storing to shared cache is necessary.
- Instrument every step with metrics and trace spans so SREs can verify correctness automatically.

Sequence: Graceful Shutdown (recommended)
----------------------------------------
1) Orchestrator signals SIGTERM to redwood-runtime-worker. This may be from k8s (preStop), autoscaler, or a manual kill.
2) Worker transitions to DRAINING state and publishes event: runtime.instance.drain_start (tags: instance_id, node_pool, model).
3) Worker removes itself from service-discovery / load-balancer via Router API: POST /router/v1/instances/{id}/set-drain with payload {"drain": true, "soft_timeout_ms": 10000}.
4) Router ceases assigning new requests. Any sessions already routed continue until completion. Router emits router.instance.eviction and begins rebalancing.
5) Kernel scheduler is notified to finish current kernel runs but avoid scheduling new batches for this worker. Scheduler sets kernel-credit to 0 for new kernels on that worker.
6) If a batch is currently running, the runtime allows up to soft_timeout_ms for completion. If batch overruns, the batcher signals preemption checkpoints: write KV cache to ephemeral storage (if configured) and surface incomplete token count in traces.
7) After inflight work completes or the soft timeout expires, worker flushes KV cache shards that are configured for warm-start persistence. Use CLI: /usr/local/bin/rw-kv-flush --shard <id> --dest /mnt/ephemeral/kvcache/<id>.
8) Worker publishes runtime.instance.drain_complete and transitions to SHUTTING_DOWN.
9) Perform final telemetry flush: flush traces, metrics, and event logs to central collector (otel-collector:4317).
10) Worker exits with code 0. Orchestrator can then terminate the VM or detach the GPU.

Abort path (forced kill)
-----------------------
- If a SIGKILL or 30s post-SIGTERM timeout occurs, worker must attempt one last telemetry flush. The forced-kill event runtime.instance.forced_kill must be emitted with reason and inflight_count.
- The router should detect dropped connections and increment a router.eviction.dropped counter; automated mitigation routes traffic to fallback model variants within 2s.

Mode differences
----------------
- Hosted API (multi-tenant): router enforces aggressive re-routing. soft_timeout_ms default=10s
- Dedicated (reserved capacity): more lenient soft timeout, default=30s, because throttling downstream is under customer contract.
- Private (on-prem): operator-configurable; document recommends aligning to Dedicated defaults unless operator constraints require shorter windows.

Kernel-scheduler interactions and knobs to tune
-----------------------------------------------
- kernel_credit_window: how many kernel launches are permitted during the drain window. Set to 0 to prevent new launches.
- batcher_drain_mode: when true, batcher stops aggregating new requests into kernels destined for this worker.
- preempt_checkpoint_interval_ms: interval for writing a consistent preemption checkpoint inside long-running kernels (recommended 500ms for generation workloads > 2s).
- Example config YAML snippet (runtime config):

  ---
  runtime: 
    shutdown:
      soft_timeout_ms: 10000
      flush_kv: true
      preempt_checkpoint_interval_ms: 500
    scheduler: 
      kernel_credit_window: 0
      batcher_drain_mode: true
  ---

Observability and verification checklist (pre- and post-shutdown)
----------------------------------------------------------------
Pre-shutdown (automated):
- Verify instance has active sessions: gauge runtime.sessions.active > 0. If none, immediate shutdown OK.
- Emit drain_start event and confirm router acknowledgement (router.instance.ack_drain == true).
- Record current p99 latency baseline for the model.

During shutdown:
- Monitor: runtime.inflight.count, runtime.kernel.active_batches, kvcache.flush.latency_ms.
- Traces: Ensure spans include drain_start and drain_complete and that root span duration <= soft_timeout_ms + 2s.
- Alerts to watch: router.eviction.dropped > 0 persist for > 10s (trigger paged alert).

Post-shutdown verification (automated smoke):
1) Run a canary traffic test that sends 50 requests distributed across same model and compares p99 latency to baseline. Pass criteria: p99 <= baseline + 20%.
2) Confirm no unexplained 5xx spike: metrics.delta(api.errors.5xx) < 0.5%
3) Check telemetry logs for runtime.instance.forced_kill — if present, trigger a postmortem.

Runbook: manual operator procedure (fast path)
-------------------------------------------
1) On-call receives alert about scheduled maintenance or faulty node.
2) SSH to controller and note instance id: curl -s http://metadata.internal/instance-id
3) Trigger drain via Router API: curl -X POST "https://router.internal/api/v1/instances/<id>/action" -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" -d '{"action":"drain","soft_timeout_ms":10000}'
4) Wait for runtime.instance.drain_complete event (timeout: 60s). If not complete, inspect runtime logs: journalctl -u redwood-runtime-worker -n 200
5) If kernel batch stuck > soft_timeout_ms: request kernel-team to inspect live kernel stacks: /usr/local/bin/rw-kernel-dump --pid <pid> > /tmp/kernel-dump.txt
6) If unable to recover, trigger failover: tag instance as unhealthy in service-discovery and scale up replacement nodes via autoscaler.
7) After replacement nodes are up and passing smoke tests, decommission old instance.

Testing and validation matrix
---------------------------
- Unit tests: runtime integration tests simulate SIGTERM and validate sequence transitions.
- Integration tests: run on staging release lanes with variable latency models including long-running generation (20–60s) and check KV flush artifacts land in expected S3 prefix s3://staging-runtime-kv/<instance>/
- Chaos tests: scheduled preemptions injected at random phases of kernel execution (see: benchmarking-and-perf-suite/synthetic-chaos-stress-profiles-2026)

Dashboards and Alerts
---------------------
Recommended dashboards:
- Instance Drain Overview: shows runtime.instance.* events, inflight counts, kernel active batches, kv flush latency, and router ack status.
- Eviction Impact Dashboard: p99 delta vs baseline, error rate delta, dropped connection count.

Suggested alerts (pager for PRD-impacting metrics):
- router.eviction.dropped > 10 in 60s AND p99 delta > 25%
- runtime.instance.forced_kill > 0
- kvcache.flush.latency_ms > 5000

Post-incident analysis (if forced_kill observed)
--------------------------------------------
- Owner: Runtime incident responder. Timeline to collect: kernel dumps, router routing table at time of event, traces with drain tags, and orchestrator event stream (k8s events or cloud provider preemption log).
- Metrics to include: inflight_count, active_batches, kernel_wait_time_histogram, and router.retry_count.
- Output: short-form incident report with root cause, mitigation, and action items (file to /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/incident-review/).

Compatibility notes and caveats
-----------------------------
- Some older models that rely on pinned KV state may need longer soft_timeouts; consult model-onboarding docs before changing defaults.
- In air-gapped Private installs, ensure the KV flush destination is reachable (NFS or operator-provided S3-compatible store).
- Draining behavior for GPU co-located processes: if multiple runtime workers share a GPU, prefer in-place workload migration with kernel scheduler support rather than draining all workers simultaneously.

Appendix: Helpful CLI snippets
----------------------------
- Trigger router drain (example):
  curl -X POST "https://router.internal/api/v1/instances/<id>/action" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -d '{"action":"drain","soft_timeout_ms":10000}'

- Check last drain events for instance:
  curl -s "https://events.internal/query?instance_id=<id>&event=runtime.instance.drain_*" | jq '.'

- KV flush (example):
  /usr/local/bin/rw-kv-flush --shard 4 --dest s3://runtime-kv-backups/staging/<id> --sync

- Kernel dump (debug only):
  /usr/local/bin/rw-kernel-dump --pid $(pgrep -f redwood-runtime-worker) > /tmp/kernel-$(date +%s).dump

References
----------
- Runtime architecture overview: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/request-multiplexing-backpressure-architecture-2026
- Kernel scheduler contracts: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/runtime-priority-decoupling-and-preemptive-shepherding-2026
- Eviction and eviction strategies: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/gpu-affinity-and-eviction-strategies-2026
- Chaos and stress profiles: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/synthetic-chaos-stress-profiles-2026

Change log
----------
- 2024-11-01: Created by Maya Chen (initial draft).
- 2025-01-10: Added kernel-scheduler knobs and CLI examples (reviewer: Lina Gomez).
- 2025-02-20: Finalized mode-specific defaults and added postmortem checklist.

title: Serving runtime resilience field guide and operator playbook
content:
Overview:

This field guide consolidates operator-facing runbook actions, calibration guidance for chaos and resilience tests, and deterministic fallback recipes for common partial-failure modes in the Redwood serving runtime. It is written for SREs and runtime engineers who must keep inference SLOs during hardware flakiness, kernel regressions, and network partitions.

Goals:
- Restore or preserve 95th/99th latency SLOs or provide acceptable graceful-degradation behavior within 10 minutes for production incidents.
- Validate that fallback chains (model variants, quantized fallbacks, regional draining) trigger with predictable, auditable steps.
- Provide reproducible chaos calibration recipes so experiments are safe and informative.

Who should use this doc:
- Oncall SREs executing incident playbooks.
- Platform engineers validating rollout gates and kernel rollbacks.
- Release engineers preparing canary plans for scheduling/kernel changes.

Key runbook sections (quick links):
1) Triage heuristics and immediate mitigation (p.1)
2) Deterministic fallback invocation recipes (p.4)
3) Hardware/network partial-failure drills (p.7)
4) Chaos calibration lab guide (p.11)
5) Post-incident follow-ups and RCA template (p.15)

1) Triage heuristics and immediate mitigation

Symptoms -> quick checks (first 5 minutes):
- Elevated 95th/99th tail latency
  - Check per-kernel P95/P99 in runtime-kernel telemetry dashboard (panel: kernel-latency-by-workload).
  - Query: `SELECT kernel, p95_latency_ms, p99_latency_ms FROM runtime_latency WHERE window=5m`
- Increased retry counts or gRPC stream resets
  - Check connection reset rate across dispatcher nodes and frontends.
- Drop in throughput with stable input traffic
  - Check GPU utilization, and kernel queue length on the affected pool.

Immediate mitigations (order matters):
1. Short-term routing: shift traffic off the suspected pool regionally using the routing control API. Command: `redwoodctl routing weight --pool <pool-id> --set 0.0 --reason "emergency-drain"`
2. Enable conservative admission controller: flip the admission gate to `slo-conservative` for affected service. CLI: `redwoodctl admission set --service <svc> --profile slo-conservative`
3. Activate model-variant fallback for critical endpoints only (see section 2). Use `--scope` to avoid global behavioral changes.
4. If kernel-specific traces exist (trace-id), collect live kernel trace bundles and attach to the incident ticket: `redwood-trace collect --trace-id <id> --output /tmp/trace.tgz`

2) Deterministic fallback invocation recipes

Fallback types supported (and recommended use-cases):
- Model-variant fallback: swap to a smaller model shard or lower-fidelity quantized variant to preserve latency for critical endpoints. Use when latency spikes but correctness can be marginally reduced.
- Local KV-prefetch bypass: disable speculative KV prefetch on the pool to reduce queuing in cold paths. Use when kernel stalls are queue-related.
- Regional reroute: move traffic to a healthy region replica when a hardware domain (rack/NVLink island) is implicated. Use when interconnect errors appear in telemetry.

Activation steps: Model-variant fallback (safe scoped):
1. Identify endpoint route(s) affected: `redwoodctl route list --filter "p95>200ms"`
2. Create a scoped policy:
```
redwoodctl policy create --name "emergency-variant-fallback-<incident-id>" \  --scope routes=<route-id1>,<route-id2> \  --action model_variant --variant smaller-llm-q4_1 --ttl 30m
```
3. Verify traffic is handled by checking `model_variant_switch{policy="emergency-variant-fallback-<incident-id>"}` in metrics within 2 minutes.
4. Escalate to runtime owners if P95 does not improve within 10 minutes.

Rollback steps:
- Revoke the policy: `redwoodctl policy delete --name <policy>`
- Confirm traffic returns to baseline model by checking the model catalog assignment (`redwoodctl model assign --route <route-id> --catalog-entry <id>`) and validating end-to-end latency.

3) Hardware/network partial-failure drills

Common failure patterns and operator steps:
A) NVLink flap / interconnect errors (symptoms: kernel retries, partial model swap churn)
- Quick checks: `nvidia-smi topo --matrix` (on node), `dmesg` for PCIe/NVLink errors, runtime telemetry `nvlink_error_count`
- Mitigation: reduce batch concurrency on affected nodes (`redwoodctl node set --node <id> --batch-concurrency 1`) and move traffic away from the node pool. Consider a controlled rolling reboot if hardware vendor recommends it.

B) GPU thermal-induced throttling (symptoms: sustained throughput drop + GPU freq drop)
- Check GPU telemetry: `gpu_temperature_celsius`, `gpu_power_draw_watts`, `gpu_clocks_mhz`
- Mitigation: mark node `cordon` and route collector jobs away, allow graceful termination of in-flight requests, then perform cooling window and manual hardware inspection.

C) Rack-level network partition (symptoms: partial dispatcher connectivity, cross-rack p95 increases)
- Use `redwoodctl network diag --rack <rack-id>` to collect connectivity graphs.
- Mitigation: enable cross-region fallback policy and set `max_inflight_per_route` lower to avoid head-of-line blocking.

4) Chaos calibration lab guide (safe, repeatable experiments)

Purpose: calibrate the amount and kind of fault injection to surface realistic resilience gaps without producing noisy or unsafe outages. All experiments must run in a dedicated staging fleet.

Principles:
- Start small and increment: inject low-frequency faults and step up based on verified metrics.
- Use traffic shadowing for realistic request shapes.
- Always have an abort button (policy to immediately revert routing/admission) and a telemetry watch (automated alert that halts the experiment).

Sample calibration protocol: NVLink stress calibration
1. Environment: staging pool with representative models and request trace replay (shadow traffic).
2. Baseline: run replay for 30 minutes, capture p50/p95/p99, kernel retries, and throughput.
3. Inject: use the chaos harness to flip a virtual NVLink error rate on target nodes at 0.1% of packets for 10 minutes. YAML snippet for the harness:
```
chaos_test:
  name: nvlink-perturbation-calibration
  targets:
    - node_selector: pool=staging-gpu
  injection:
    type: nvlink_error_rate
    rate: 0.001
    duration: 600s
  abort_on:
    - metric: runtime.p99_latency
      threshold: 1.5x_baseline
```
4. Observe: If P99 > 1.5x baseline or kernel retry rate > 10x baseline, stop the injection and capture traces.
5. Increment: increase rate to 0.5% only if safety thresholds are not breached.

Measuring experiment value:
- Record the minimal injection rate that produces consistent P99 degradation — this is the fleet fragility index for NVLink. Track over time.

5) Post-incident follow-ups and RCA template

Minimum deliverables after any production intervention:
- Incident timeline (wall-clocked) with actions and actor names.
- Telemetry extracts: pre-incident, incident window, and 2x recovery period.
- Minimal actionable root cause (hardware/kernel/operator) and one prioritized remediation (short, medium, long-term).
- Test plan to validate the remediation in staging (include chaos calibration adjustments).

RCA template (copy/paste):
- Title: Short sentence summarizing outage
- Impact: SLOs breached, customer visible impact, duration
- Timeline: bulletized timeline with timestamps and actions
- Root cause analysis: primary cause and supporting evidence (logs, traces, kernel dumps)
- Mitigations: what we did during the incident and why it helped
- Fixes: short/medium/long term with owners and ETA
- Postmortem checklist items: capacity, monitoring, runbook updates, PRs created

Operational tooling and queries (cheat sheet)
- See current admission profile: `redwoodctl admission get --service <svc>`
- Force a model-variant switch for a route (scoped): `redwoodctl policy create --name emergency-switch --scope routes=<route> --action model_variant --variant <id>`
- Collect kernel trace: `redwood-trace collect --trace-id <id> --query 'kernel:*' --output /tmp/kernel-trace.tgz`
- Cordon node from scheduler: `redwoodctl node cordon --node <id> --reason "investigation"`

Ownership and escalation
- First responder: Oncall SRE (runtime-sre rotation) — execute triage and immediate mitigations.
- Secondary: Runtime kernel lead — investigate kernel traces and decide on kernel rollback.
- Tertiary: Platform owner — approve regional failover and cross-region policy changes.
- Pager escalation matrix: follow the team directory in People Ops; aim to escalate to kernel lead within 20 minutes if mitigations fail.

Safety and governance
- All production policy changes triggered by this runbook must be backed by an incident ticket and remain auditable.
- Chaos experiments must be registered in the experiment registry with a runbook link, expected metrics and abort conditions.

Appendix A — Example dashboard panels to check
- kernel-latency-by-workload: stacked p50/p95/p99 per kernel
- nvlink_error_count: NVLink errors per node, 1m/5m windows
- model_variant_switch: counts and policy labels
- admission_profile_effectiveness: admitted vs rejected requests per profile

Appendix B — Quick glossary
- Kernel: execution unit (e.g., attention-shard, kv-prefetch, softmax-quant) scheduled on GPU.
- Admission controller: runtime component that shapes inbound requests by policy profiled to SLOs.
- Model-variant: a functionally similar served artifact with different fidelity/cost characteristics.

Contact and feedback
- Document owner: Aisha Patel (runtime reliability) — please add suggested improvements as comments on this page or open a PR to `eng-serving-runtime/runbooks` repo.

title: Eviction Rewind and State Reconstruction Playbook
content:
Overview
========
This playbook documents the procedure to recover from kvcache eviction events that cause request-level state divergence or incomplete KV reconstruction during model swaps, preemption, or kernel handoffs. It covers triage, automated rewind and state reconstruction action sequences, verification checks, rollback criteria, and safety tests. The intended audience is oncall SREs, serving-runtime engineers, and incident responders.

Why this matters
-----------------
- Eviction-induced state gaps can lead to incorrect completions, user-facing hallucinations, or repeated model fallbacks.
- Fast, deterministic reconstruction preserves SLOs and avoids large-scale reroutes to lower-fidelity fallback models.
- This playbook provides a safe, repeatable sequence to reconstruct per-session KV state and safely resume traffic.

When to run this playbook
-------------------------
Run this playbook when one or more of the following are observed:
- Sudden spike in kvcache_reconstruction_failures (> 10/min sustained for 5 minutes)
- Increase in tail latency correlated with eviction_rate or kernel_handoff_rate
- Model swap incidents where > 0.5% of sessions show token regression or repeated left-pad artifacts
- Automated canary signals mark warmup_failure=true during rollout

Impact and SLOs
---------------
- Target: recover affected sessions and restore p95 inference latency within 10 minutes of start of remediation.
- Acceptable interim error budget consumption: up to 2x normal error budget for the affected service for a single incident.
- Escalate to incident commander if reconstruction extends beyond 30 minutes or if reconstruction failures exceed 1% of total affected sessions.

Ownership and permissions
-------------------------
- Primary owner: Serving Runtime (runtime-sre)
- Secondary owner: Kernel Scheduling Team (kernel-scheduler)
- Required permissions: ability to trigger kvcache reconstruction jobs, pause model-swap-agent rollouts, and modify scheduler admission controls.
- Contacts: runtime-oncall@redwood.ai, kernel-scheduler@redwood.ai, runtime-release@redwood.ai

Pre-incident checklist (quick)
-----------------------------
- Confirm current SLA window and active deployments.
- Check if any maintenance or known rollouts are in progress (model-swap-agent, kernel rollouts).
- Ensure a recent snapshot of kvcache index exists (last 24h).
- Open a dedicated incident channel and note affected clusters/regions.

Immediate triage (first 10 minutes)
-----------------------------------
1) Tag and isolate: Identify affected shard sets and tag them in the incident channel. Use the runtime incident tool:  `rtctl shards list --filter=\"eviction_rate>0.1\"`
2) Confirm metric correlations: Dashboard: Runtime / KVCACHE / Reconstruction. Check metrics: eviction_rate, kvcache_reconstruction_failures, kvcache_warmup_seconds, kernel_handoff_rate, p95_latency.
3) Stop compounding actions: Pause any model-swap-agent rollouts for affected model-versions: `rtctl rollout pause --model vX --clusters shard-a,shard-b`.
4) Reduce admission pressure: Temporarily tighten admission control to reduce new sessions to affected shards: `schedulerctl admission set --target 60% --scope shard-a`

Automated reconstruction flow (recommended)
------------------------------------------
Use the automated reconstruction pipeline (recon-runner) to attempt fast rewind and state rebuild before manual steps. Steps it performs:
- Fetch latest durable prefix snapshots from persistent-store (S3 / object-store).
- Rehydrate session KV caches using checkpointed KV deltas.
- Replay last N tokens from request logs (N default 32) into warmed kernel contexts to re-establish KV validity.
- Validate by running synthetic trace assertions.

Command to start automated run on a shard set:
- `recon-runner start --shards shard-a,shard-b --max-parallel 4 --replay-window 32 --dry-run=false`

Manual reconstruction procedure (if automated runner fails)
---------------------------------------------------------
1) Stop accepting new traffic to affected shards: `schedulerctl drain --shard shard-a --mode immediate`
2) Snapshot live kernel state (if available): `rtctl kernel snapshot --shard shard-a --out /tmp/shard-a-snap.tgz`
3) Extract last-request logs for affected sessions: `logql query \"{service=\"runtime-gpu-proxy\", shard=\"shard-a\"} | json | last(5000)\" > /tmp/shard-a-requests.ndjson`
4) Run replay tool in isolated reconstruction cluster (no external traffic):
   a) `replay-tool --input /tmp/shard-a-requests.ndjson --model-model-path gs://models/vX --kv-checkpoint gs://kvcache/snapshots/shard-a/latest --replay-window 64 --out /tmp/shard-a-replay-results.json`
   b) Inspect replay failures: `jq '.failures | length' /tmp/shard-a-replay-results.json`
5) Apply KV deltas to in-memory cache with controlled rate-limiter: `kvcachectl apply-deltas --shard shard-a --source /tmp/deltas --rate 1000/s`
6) Re-enable traffic with traffic shaping: `schedulerctl admission set --target 30% --ramp 10m --scope shard-a`

Verification checks (post-reconstruction)
----------------------------------------
- Metric convergence: kvcache_reconstruction_failures -> 0/min; kvcache_hit_rate >= previous baseline - 2% within 15 minutes.
- Synthetic assertion: run 100 representative prompts (from canary prompt-set) against reconstructed shards and assert token-by-token parity >= 99.5% (or within acceptable fidelity reg thresholds).
- Latency: p95 within 10% of baseline for reconstructed shards.
- Error logs: no new kernel panics or repeated model-fallback events for 30 minutes.

Rollback and fallback policy
---------------------------
If reconstruction fails or fidelity is unacceptable:
- Immediately revert model swap (if the swap caused the state divergence) using: `rtctl rollout revert --model vX --to vX-previous --scope shard-a`
- If revert is not possible, route affected traffic to a hardened fallback pool (fallback-tier-2) with conservative admission limits.
- Mark incident as "stalled reconstruction" and escalate to runtime product and kernel-scheduler leads.

Post-incident actions (within 72 hours)
--------------------------------------
- Run a formal postmortem with causal timeline, including kernel handoff signals and eviction bursts.
- Bake-in new canary checks if missing: add warmup_failure assertion to canary pipeline.
- Create a blocker ticket for any persistent root cause (e.g., persistent NVMe contention, faulty eviction heuristics).

Testing and canary protocol for recon changes
--------------------------------------------
1) Unit tests for recon-runner with synthetic KV deltas and deterministic replay.
2) Integration test: deploy recon-runner in canary A (single shard) with traffic mirror of 2% for 2 hours. Assert: warmup_success=true, reconstruction_latency < 300s.
3) Rollout: gradual - 5% clusters -> 25% -> 100% with automated rollback on warmup failure.

Telemetry and dashboards to consult
----------------------------------
- Runtime / KVCACHE / Eviction Rate (eviction_rate)
- Runtime / KVCACHE / Reconstruction Failures (kvcache_reconstruction_failures)
- Runtime / KVCACHE / Warmup Duration (kvcache_warmup_seconds)
- Runtime / Kernel / Handoff Rate (kernel_handoff_rate)
- APIGW / Inference / p95 latency (p95_inference_latency)
- Runtime / Synthetic / Canary Fidelity (canary_token_parity)

Diagnostic commands and snippets
-------------------------------
- List active recon jobs: `reconctl list --status active`
- Tail kernel logs for shard: `kubectl -n runtime logs -l shard=shard-a -c kernel --since=20m | grep -i eviction`
- Inspect last kvcache checkpoint manifest: `gsutil cat gs://kvcache/snapshots/shard-a/manifest.json | jq`

Config table (important params)
------------------------------
Parameter | Default | Purpose / Impact
--------- | ------- | ------------------
replay_window | 32 | Number of tokens replayed to reconstruct KV. Increasing improves fidelity but increases time.
max_parallel_recon | 4 | Maximum parallel reconstruction jobs per region. Higher value speeds recovery but raises load.
apply_delta_rate | 1000/s | Rate at which KV deltas are applied to in-memory kvcache to avoid memory spikes.
snapshot_ttl | 24h | How long persistent snapshots are kept. Longer TTL increases recovery surface but costs storage.
warmup_assertion_threshold | 0.995 | Minimum token parity to consider reconstruction successful.

Example reconstruction config (YAML)
-----------------------------------
reconstruction:
  shards: ["shard-a", "shard-b"]
  replay_window: 64
  max_parallel_recon: 2
  apply_delta_rate: 750/s
  synthetic_canary_set: "canary-recon-v2"
  notify_on: ["success","failure"]

Safety notes and caveats
------------------------
- Never apply deltas across model-version boundaries unless the model architecture and tokenizer are compatible. Cross-version KV application will produce corruption.
- If kernel snapshot feature is unavailable for a shard, prefer routing traffic away rather than performing blind reconstruction.
- Reconstruction may surface latent bugs in quantization path; watch for sudden increase in soft-errors from kernel telemetry.

Appendix: quick checklist (one-pager)
------------------------------------
1) Pause rollouts and tag shards.
2) Run recon-runner (dry-run first if time permits).
3) If recon-runner fails, drain shard and run replay-tool in isolated cluster.
4) Apply KV deltas with rate-limiter and re-enable traffic with ramp.
5) Verify fidelity with canary prompt-set and metrics.
6) Revert or fallback if fidelity/latency unacceptable.

Related links and artifacts
--------------------------
- Kernel signal handbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/eviction-coordinate-protocol-and-kernel-signal-handbook-2026
- Reconstruction automation repo: git@github.com:redwood-inference/recon-runner
- Canary prompt sets: gs://runtime-canaries/canary-recon-v2/prompts.ndjson

Document history
----------------
- 2026-01-15: Created by Sophie Chen (initial draft).
- 2026-04-08: Added automated recon-runner section and YAML config (Marco Alvarez).
- 2026-07-02: Updated verification thresholds and telemetry lists (Dmitri Sokolov).

title: Runtime cost-fidelity incident response cookbook
content:
Overview

This runbook documents a pragmatic, operator-focused decision tree and checklist for incidents where cost, latency SLOs, and inference fidelity interact (for example: a sudden traffic spike that forces aggressive batching or a regression in quantized kernels that increases token cost). The goal is to restore acceptable SLOs and predictable unit economics while protecting application-level quality.

Scope

- Applies to serving runtime incidents involving: unexpected cost spikes, fidelity regressions tied to runtime changes, and mixed-fidelity routing failures.
- Not intended for model-training incidents or purely upstream network failures.

Key definitions

- Fidelity breach: measurable drop in application-level quality (examples: decreased BLEU/ROUGE on eval prompts, increased hallucination rate, user-reported quality regression) tied to a runtime or config change.
- Cost spike: per-token or per-request cost increases >25% baseline sustained for >15 minutes without corresponding traffic growth.
- Performance SLO breach: p95 or p99 latency crossing defined SLOs for a route for more than two consecutive 5-minute windows.

SLO and alert thresholds (example values; confirm for customer tiers)

| Signal | Alert threshold | Pager | Owner |
|---|---:|---|---|
| p95 latency (production route) | >200ms above route SLO for 10m | P1 | runtime-oncall |
| Token cost (per-route) | +25% vs 24h rolling baseline | P2 | cost-ops |
| Fidelity regression (eval set) | Significant drop vs shadow baseline (>3% absolute) | P1 | applied-ml |

Incident triage checklist (first 10 minutes)

1. Confirm signal provenance
   - Check route-level telemetry in Console: per-token cost, batching histograms, kernel variant counters.
   - Verify alerts (PagerDuty / Opsgenie) and correlate with traces (trace id examples).
2. Identify scope and last change
   - Which routes / tenants are affected? Use cohort selector by model_id and route tag.
   - Has there been a release / kernel rollout / quantization profile change in last 60 minutes? Check: `git log` of the release tag and the runtime canary matrix.
3. Decide immediate containment action (choose one):
   - If latency SLOs are broken for critical routes: apply admission controller throttle to non-critical tenants and enable degraded-fidelity mode for best-effort routes.
   - If cost spike without latency issue: roll back recent quantization or kernel change and increase KV cache retention to reduce token re-computation.
   - If fidelity regression is observed: switch affected routes to verified high-fidelity model variants and pin to the previous model-version.

Containment commands and quick actions

- Scale down admission windows for background tenants (CLI):
  - `redwoodctl admission set --policy background:0.2 --policy critical:1.0 --until 2026-02-15T16:00Z`
- Pin route to earlier model (console or CLI):
  - `redwoodctl route update --route my-chat --model redwood-chat-v1.3 --pin`
- Force kernel variant fallback for a node pool:
  - `redwoodctl nodepool patch --name gpu-pool-eu --kernel-variant stable-2025-11`
- Temporarily increase KV cache TTL to avoid recompute storms:
  - `redwoodctl runtime config set --kv-cache-ttl 1800`  # seconds

Decision tree (high-level)

- Does the incident include fidelity regression?
  - Yes -> Is there a canary baseline?
    - Yes -> Re-run shadow baseline against canary, capture difference, escalate to applied-ml + product; pin routes to previous variant; open rollback PR.
    - No -> Switch traffic to high-fidelity model variant, enable emergency A/B with very small fraction of traffic to validate rollback integrity.
- Is the incident primarily cost-driven?
  - Yes -> Evaluate batching distribution and KV cache hit-rate: if batching increased without improved throughput, reduce batch windows and enforce per-tenant batch caps. Consider temporary quantization rollback.
- Is latency SLO impacted?
  - Yes -> Prioritize latency SLO remediation: reduce concurrency, favor low-latency kernels (even at higher cost), and isolate noisy tenants.

Operator checklist for rolling rollback (if needed)

1. Confirm rollback candidate and verify artifacts in release registry.
2. Start canary: 1% traffic to rollback build with health checks; monitor p95/p99, token cost, and eval prompt fidelity. 3 minutes minimum.
3. If canary acceptable, expand to 10% with 15-minute monitoring window.
4. If metrics stabilize, run full rollout with automated surge control and a 30-minute watch.

Quality validation suite (must run during canary)

- Small eval set (50 prompts) covering intent, hallucination, and safety checks. Must run in parallel to the canary traffic using shadow routing. Capture per-prompt deltas.
- Latency microbenchmarks for the chosen kernel variant (short/median/long sequence lengths).
- Token-cost microbenchmarks for sample workload slices.

Post-containment investigation (owner: runtime + applied-ml)

- Evidence collection checklist:
  - Pull kernel telemetry from affected nodepools (kernel version, kernel counters, CUDA metrics).
  - Retrieve sample traces where per-token compute time spiked.
  - Collect KV cache hit/miss logs for affected sessions.
  - Archive canary and prod corpora snapshots for replay.
- Hypothesis-driven analysis steps:
  1. Reproduce with a replay harness using recorded traces and traffic shapes.
  2. Toggle kernel variants and quantization settings to find the regression boundary.
  3. If a kernel is implicated, open kernel-telemetry issue and tag kernel owners.

Operator escalation matrix

- Oncall runtime engineer: initial triage and containment (0–15m).
- Senior runtime engineer: rollback coordination and canary expansion (15–60m).
- Applied ML lead: fidelity regression analysis and evaluation validation (30–120m).
- Product / Customer Success: notify impacted customers and coordinate postmortem if customer-facing degradations occurred.

Configuration reference table (common knobs)

| Config | Typical safe range | Fast-check command |
|---|---|---|
| Batch window (ms) | 10-200 | `redwoodctl runtime get --route my-chat | jq .batch_window_ms` |
| Per-tenant concurrency cap | 1-16 | `redwoodctl tenant describe --id tenant-123` |
| KV cache TTL (s) | 60-3600 | `redwoodctl runtime get --kv-cache-ttl` |
| Kernel variant | stable-YYYY-MM | `redwoodctl nodepool get --name gpu-pool-eu | jq .kernel_variant` |
| Quantization profile | int8/float16/mixed | `redwoodctl model inspect --model-id redwood-chat-v1` |

Runbook examples (real incident patterns)

- Case A: Sudden cost spike after kernel rollout
  - Symptoms: per-token cost +40%, latency unchanged, token compute counters show higher flops per token.
  - Containment: pin routes to previous kernel variant; increase KV cache TTL.
  - Postmortem focus: kernel micro-ops change, verify tensor layouts and cuBLAS usage.
- Case B: Fidelity regression after quantization profile change
  - Symptoms: hallucination rate increased, eval delta >5%, negligible latency change.
  - Containment: revert quantization profile for affected model; route affected traffic to high-fidelity variant; run eval suite.
  - Postmortem focus: compare quantized weight diffs and calibration dataset coverage.
- Case C: Latency SLO breach during traffic surge
  - Symptoms: p99 latency spike, batch latency histograms show oversized batches forming under new batching heuristics.
  - Containment: reduce batch window, enforce per-tenant batch caps, enable degraded routing for background tenants.
  - Postmortem focus: refine batching shaping heuristics and admission controller thresholds.

Communication and customer notifications

- Internal: update incident Slack channel every 15 minutes while P1. Include short bullets: scope, containment actions, next steps, owner.
- Customer-facing: coordinate with Customer Success for customers with dedicated contracts. Provide: summary, impact window, mitigation applied, and ETA for rollback or permanent fix.

Post-incident actions and metrics to track

- Short term (24–72 hours): verify cost returns to baseline, no residual fidelity regressions on replications, update canary tests to cover regression vector.
- Mid term (2–4 weeks): kernel and quantization rollout policy updates (add more orthogonal canaries, require shadow-fidelity runs on new quantization profiles).
- Long term: add regression-capture rules to telemetry suite and add synthetic prompts to the eval harness that reflect observed failure modes.

Appendix A — Playbook quick cheat sheet

1. Identify: scope, last change, affected routes.
2. Contain: pin model/kernel, adjust KV TTL, reduce batch windows, isolate tenants.
3. Validate: run 50-prompt eval, latency microbenchmarks, token-cost checks.
4. Rollback if canary shows improvement.
5. Investigate and document findings, add tests to prevent recurrence.

Appendix B — Suggested dashboards & queries

- Console dashboard: Route Overview (p95/p99, throughput, token-cost, kernel_variant)
- Query examples: `sum(rate(token_compute_ops[5m])) by (kernel_variant, nodepool)` to spot kernel-level spikes.

Contacts and ownership

- Runtime oncall: #runtime-oncall (PagerDuty)
- Applied ML: applied-ml@redwood.ai
- Cost Ops: cost-ops@redwood.ai

Document change history

- 2025-06-10: Created by Marisol Chen.
- 2026-02-15: Revised containment commands and added cost-driven decision branch (Marisol Chen).

title: Runbook: Perf canary rollout for new kernels (FP8/INT8 and beyond)
content:
## Purpose
This runbook defines the operational procedure for enabling new inference kernels (e.g., FP8/INT8 attention + matmul paths) behind flags and rolling them out safely via perf canary before broader enablement.

The goals are:
- Detect latency/throughput regressions early (TTFT/TPOT/tokens/s) with enough statistical power.
- Minimize customer impact through cohorting, automatic rollback, and clear comms.
- Provide a repeatable, auditable checklist (what we changed, where it ran, what we observed).

## Scope
Applies to:
- Hosted API serving runtime rollouts (multi-tenant).
- Dedicated pools **only** when explicitly scheduled with Infra/SRE and customer success coordination.

Not covered:
- One-off benchmarking runs (see benchmark runner / sprint plan).
- Model catalog policy decisions (see quantization profile policy + ADR).

## Owners and on-call
- Primary operational owner (SRE): **Rafael Mendes**
- Runtime kernel owner: **Hiro Tanaka**
- Runtime scheduling owner: **Sofia Ivanova**
- Dashboards/alerts: **Allison Grant**
- Release coordination: **Connor O'Brien**

Escalation channels:
- #eng-sre (rollout execution, incident response)
- #eng-runtime (kernel/runtime debugging)
- #eng-ml (quality regressions / quantization concerns)
- #incidents (if rollback/impact crosses incident thresholds)

## Definitions
- **TTFT**: time-to-first-token (ms). Primary user-perceived latency for streaming.
- **TPOT**: time-per-output-token (ms/token) or decode latency proxy.
- **Prefill**: prompt processing stage (often attention-heavy, longer sequence lengths).
- **Decode**: token generation stage (often KV-cache + small matmuls, sensitive to cache alignment and launch overhead).
- **Perf canary**: controlled enablement of a change to a small cohort (region/model/GPU/traffic slice) with automated regression detection and rollback.
- **Kernel mode**: baseline vs INT8 vs FP8 (and variants).

## Preconditions (must be true before starting)
1) **Change is behind a flag** (server-side, remotely configurable) and supports fast rollback.
2) **Metrics are correctly dimensioned** by at least:
   - model
   - region
   - GPU SKU (e.g., H100/A100/L4)
   - kernel_mode (baseline/int8/fp8)
   - route type (chat/generate/embeddings if applicable)
3) **Perf canary thresholds exist** for the target model+SKU (or have been created) with a known baseline window.
4) **Correctness gates passed** (unit tests + CI smoke bench for quantized kernels).
5) **Applied ML sign-off** if the default enablement changes quantization behavior or could affect output quality.
6) **Capacity guardrails confirmed** with Infra/SRE (no collision with Dedicated pools; no overbooking on canary clusters).

## Inputs you need (collect before rollout)
- Runtime version / git SHA:
  - Release tag (e.g., runtime 1.22.0-rcX or 1.22.0)
  - Git SHA for the serving runtime image
- Flag names and intended values (per cohort)
- Target cohort definition:
  - Region(s)
  - Model(s)
  - GPU SKU(s)
  - Traffic %
- Expected impact range from benchmark matrix (e.g., “TTFT -5% to +1%, TPOT -10% to -3% on H100; neutral on A100”)
- Rollback owner and rollback path (flag-only vs image rollback)

## Standard flag model (reference)
We use a layered approach:
- Global kill switch (highest priority)
- Per-model enablement
- Per-region enablement
- Optional shape-guard exceptions / denylist

Common patterns:
- runtime.kernels.fp8_attention.enabled = true|false
- runtime.kernels.int8_matmul.enabled = true|false
- runtime.kernels.autoselect.enabled = true|false
- runtime.kernels.fp8_attention.denylist_shapes = <pattern list>

Notes:
- Prefer **positive allowlists** during canary; move to broader default only after stability.
- Ensure **fallback behavior** is explicit: unsupported shapes must route to baseline kernel path.

## Canary stages (recommended)
**Stage 0: Dry run in staging**
- Environment: staging cluster with representative GPUs if available.
- Traffic: synthetic + low-volume internal.
- Duration: 30–60 minutes after warmup.
- Exit criteria: no crash-looping, no elevated error rate, metrics dimension tags present.

**Stage 1: Single-region, single-model canary (1–5% traffic)**
- Pick a region with:
  - Good observability coverage
  - Low blast radius
  - Stable baseline history
- Duration: minimum 2 hours, ideally covering at least one traffic peak.

**Stage 2: Expand within region (10–25% traffic)**
- Expand traffic % once Stage 1 is green.
- Duration: 4–24 hours depending on variance and customer sensitivity.

**Stage 3: Multi-region canary**
- Add 1–2 additional regions (avoid enabling all regions at once).
- Duration: 24–72 hours.

**Stage 4: Broad enablement**
- Expand to all eligible cohorts.
- Keep kill switch armed for at least 7 days.

## Step-by-step procedure
### 1) Preflight checklist (T-1 day or earlier)
1. Confirm release artifact is ready:
   - Runtime image published
   - Config/flag mechanism tested
2. Confirm dashboards exist and are correct:
   - TTFT p50/p95
   - TPOT p50/p95
   - tokens/s (or throughput proxy)
   - GPU util + memory
   - error rate (HTTP + model/runtime)
   - restart/crash-loop indicators
3. Confirm baseline window:
   - At least 24h of baseline data for the same cohort dimensions.
4. Confirm thresholds:
   - Threshold profile loaded for model+SKU+region (or defaults reviewed).
5. Confirm comms owner and schedule:
   - Who posts start/stop updates
   - Who triages alerts

### 2) Announce rollout start (Slack templates below)
- Post in **#eng-runtime** and **#eng-sre** with:
  - what is changing
  - where it is changing
  - how to roll back
  - dashboards to watch

### 3) Enable flags for Stage 1 cohort
- Apply flags to the smallest viable cohort.
- Validate config propagation:
  - Confirm a sample of requests are running with kernel_mode=fp8/int8.
  - Confirm baseline cohort remains unaffected.

Operational verification (first 10–15 minutes):
- Error rate is flat (no spikes in 5xx/timeouts).
- TTFT does not jump immediately.
- GPU memory does not show sustained step increases.

### 4) Monitor canary (steady-state)
Monitoring window guidance:
- Minimum: 2 hours.
- Prefer: 1 full traffic cycle (peak + off-peak) for high-variance workloads.

What to monitor (order of priority):
1. **Customer-facing latency**
   - TTFT p50/p95 by model/GPU/region/kernel_mode
2. **Decode performance**
   - TPOT p50/p95 by model/GPU/region/kernel_mode
3. **Throughput**
   - tokens/s and/or requests/s normalized by concurrency
4. **Stability + correctness signals**
   - error rate
   - OOM rate
   - crash loops
   - elevated retries
5. **Scheduler health indicators**
   - queue depth histograms
   - backpressure counters
   - prefill/decode split changes

Noise handling:
- Prefer comparing canary vs baseline using the same time window.
- If sample size is small, do not overreact to single-window spikes; require sustained breach per the canary gate policy.

### 5) Expand canary (Stages 2–3)
- Expand traffic % or add regions **only** if:
  - No threshold breaches during Stage 1
  - No unresolved anomalies
  - Kernel owners agree the observed deltas match expected benchmark direction

### 6) Broader enablement (Stage 4)
- Increase eligibility (models/regions/SKUs) gradually.
- Keep a weekly review slot for the first two weeks to revisit:
  - denylist shapes
  - scheduler knob interactions
  - model-specific regressions

## Automatic rollback triggers (policy)
Perf canary should be configured to auto-rollback on sustained breaches. Use these as default triggers unless a per-model profile overrides them.

### Rollback severity levels
**Immediate rollback (auto + page on-call)**
- Error rate increase: +0.25% absolute (or +50% relative), sustained 10+ minutes
- TTFT p95 regression: ≥ +7% sustained over 15+ minutes
- TPOT p95 regression: ≥ +8% sustained over 15+ minutes
- OOM rate increase: any sustained non-zero OOMs attributable to kernel change

**Rollback after confirmation (auto rollback allowed; human confirm within 15 minutes)**
- TTFT p50 regression: ≥ +5% sustained 30+ minutes
- TPOT p50 regression: ≥ +5% sustained 30+ minutes
- tokens/s regression: ≥ -5% sustained 30+ minutes

**Do not rollback on perf alone (investigate first)**
- Improvements smaller than noise floor
- Single-bin spikes with low sample size
- Variance correlated with driver/CUDA mismatch or thermal throttling events

## Manual rollback procedure
Use manual rollback when:
- Canary gating is disabled or misconfigured
- Regression is severe but doesn’t match current threshold logic
- A correctness bug is suspected (e.g., output corruption)

Rollback steps:
1) **Flip kill switch / disable kernel mode for affected cohort**
   - Prefer the smallest change: disable fp8_attention or int8_matmul for that cohort.
2) Confirm propagation (5–10 minutes)
   - kernel_mode returns to baseline
   - TTFT/TPOT start trending back to baseline
3) Post rollback update in #eng-runtime and #eng-sre
4) If customer impact occurred:
   - Follow incident policy (open incident thread in #incidents)
   - Create support-facing note for CS if needed

If flag rollback is insufficient (e.g., crash-loop due to init):
- Roll back runtime image in the affected region/cluster per release tooling.

## Triage guide (first 30 minutes)
When a regression alert fires:
1) Confirm scope:
   - Which model(s), region(s), GPU SKU(s)
   - Which kernel_mode
   - Which route types (chat vs generate)
2) Confirm it is real (not instrumentation drift):
   - Check metric tags: model/gpu/kernel_mode present and consistent
   - Compare request volume baseline vs canary
3) Check “classic” causes:
   - Driver/CUDA mismatch across nodes
   - Thermal throttling or clocks not pinned
   - Contention from other jobs or noisy neighbors
   - Debug logging accidentally enabled
   - KV cache alignment edge cases (decode-specific)
4) Decide:
   - Roll back immediately if severe or correctness-related
   - Otherwise capture evidence (dash snapshots, logs) and proceed to deeper debugging

Artifacts to capture:
- Grafana snapshots (canary vs baseline)
- Runtime logs around alert window
- Node-level GPU telemetry for affected cohort
- If needed: Nsight trace for one representative case (use profiling playbook)

## Post-rollout tasks (definition of done)
Within 24 hours of broad enablement:
- Update release notes (what enabled, where, how to disable)
- Update denylist/guardrails if any edge cases were discovered
- File follow-up issues for:
  - shape guard improvements
  - scheduler interactions
  - metric dimension gaps
- Ensure perf canary thresholds are updated based on observed noise

## Communication templates
### A) Rollout start (post in #eng-runtime and #eng-sre)
Subject: [perf-canary] Starting kernel rollout: <FP8 attention / INT8 matmul> for <model> on <GPU> in <region>

Message:
- Change: enabling <flag(s)> to turn on <kernel_mode> for <model> on <GPU SKU>
- Cohort: <region>, <traffic %>, <route types>
- Expected impact: TTFT <range>, TPOT <range>, tokens/s <range> (from benchmark matrix)
- Dashboards: <link to Grafana dashboard> (filter: model=<>, gpu=<>, kernel_mode=<>)
- Rollback: flip <kill switch flag> or disable <flag> for cohort
- On-point: <name> (SRE) / <name> (runtime)

### B) Canary green / expansion notice
Subject: [perf-canary] Canary green — expanding <FP8/INT8> to <traffic %> / adding <region>

Message:
- Stage completed: <Stage 1/2>
- Observed deltas vs baseline (p50/p95):
  - TTFT: <x%>
  - TPOT: <x%>
  - tokens/s: <x%>
  - error rate: <no change / details>
- Next step: expanding cohort to <details> at <time>
- Rollback remains: <kill switch flag>

### C) Rollback announcement (include cause + next steps)
Subject: [perf-canary] Rollback executed — <kernel_mode> for <model> in <region>

Message:
- Action: disabled <flag> / flipped kill switch at <time>
- Reason: <TTFT p95 regression / error rate / OOM / correctness concern>
- Impact: <estimated scope, duration>
- Current status: <metrics recovered / monitoring>
- Next steps:
  - <owner> capturing traces/logs
  - <owner> filing issue + proposed fix
  - Re-canary plan: <when / conditions>

### D) Incident escalation (if needed)
Subject: [INCIDENT] Perf regression during kernel canary — Sev?<proposed>

Message:
- Summary: <one line>
- Start time: <UTC>
- Affected: <region/model/percentage>
- Symptoms: <TTFT/TPOT spike, errors>
- Mitigation: <rollback done / in progress>
- Owner: <incident commander>

## Safety notes and anti-patterns
- Do not enable new kernels globally without a canary stage.
- Do not canary during known fleet instability or major infra migrations.
- Avoid mixing multiple major changes in one canary (e.g., new kernel + scheduler knob overhaul) unless explicitly planned with separate attribution metrics.
- Do not rely on microbench wins alone; always validate end-to-end with realistic prefill/decode mixes.

## Appendix: Recommended default thresholds (starting point)
These are starting points; use per-model profiles when available.
- TTFT p95 regression: +7% (15 min sustained)
- TPOT p95 regression: +8% (15 min sustained)
- TTFT p50 regression: +5% (30 min sustained)
- TPOT p50 regression: +5% (30 min sustained)
- Error rate: +0.25% absolute or +50% relative (10 min sustained)

If thresholds are “too noisy”:
- Increase minimum sample size requirement
- Switch to longer evaluation windows
- Ensure kernel_mode tagging is correct (mis-tagging looks like noise)

---
Changelog
- 2026-02-26 (Rafael Mendes): Updated for FP8/INT8 sprint; added staged rollout guidance, rollback severity levels, and standardized Slack templates.
- 2025-11-14 (Rafael Mendes): Initial version for kernel feature-flag rollouts via perf canary.

title: Runtime Execution Orchestra: Scheduler Synthesis, Profiling Playbook, and Benchmarking Matrix
content:
Overview

This playbook synthesizes cross-cutting runtime concerns into a single, experiment-driven operational guide: how the Scheduler (scheduler-service) integrates with the Execution Orchestra (runtime-orchestrator), how we profile scheduler and kernel behaviour end-to-end, and a compact benchmarking matrix to validate tuning changes before rollout. It is intended for runtime engineers, SREs, and profiling squad members.

Goals

- Provide deterministic, repeatable steps to evaluate scheduler changes and their impact on tail latency, cost, and kernel utilization.
- Standardize profiling hygiene for scheduling experiments so results are comparable across clusters.
- Define a lightweight benchmark matrix that exercises common production shapes and quantization variants.

Service & Component Inventory

- runtime-orchestrator: control plane that composes kernel dispatch plans and routes requests to kernel-dispatcher.
- scheduler-service: admission controller and slot allocator; implements priority buckets and credit accounting.
- kernel-dispatcher: GPU-side dispatcher that executes mapped kernels.
- kvcache-service: shared KV cache with warmup and eviction telemetry hooks.
- request-classifier: sidecar component that assigns incoming requests to pre-configured execution cohorts.

Key Performance Targets (SLOs)

- Stability SLO (short requests, seq <= 64): p99 latency <= 250ms; p95 <= 80ms.
- Long-sequence SLO (seq 512): p99 <= 2.2s; p95 <= 1.1s.
- Kernel tail safety: no single kernel should have >15% invocation rate variance across active slots for a sustained 10-minute window.
- Cost SLO: per-token GPU time change <= +10% after scheduler changes for steady-state mixed workloads.

Experiment Matrix and Benchmarking Table

Run each experiment in a dedicated canary cluster or shadow lane. The matrix below covers three canonical workload shapes: interactive chat (short), document summarization (long), and embeddings mix (small dense batches).

| Workload               | Seq len | Concurrency | Kernel hint    | Quant profile | Key metrics collected               |
|------------------------|---------|-------------|----------------|---------------|-------------------------------------|
| Interactive Chat       | 8-64    | 50-300      | small-attn     | q4f           | p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec     |
| Document Summarization | 256-1024| 10-40       | sharded-attn   | fp16 / q8_1   | p95/p99 latency, kernel-util, evicts|
| Embeddings Mix         | 1-32    | 100-1000    | dense-matmul   | fp16          | throughput, kernel-queue-length     |

Benchmarking notes:
- Use the operational-workload-simulator with the same request provenance headers used in prod to ensure equivalence.
- For each cell run: 10m warmup, 30m steady-state sampling, 5m cool-down.

Profiling Playbook (step-by-step)

1) Prepare the environment
   - Reserve a canary GPU pool (tag: canary-scheduler-experiment).
   - Deploy the candidate scheduler binary behind a feature flag (flags: scheduler.new_priority_map=true).
   - Ensure kvcache-service telemetry is at debug level for the experiment window.

2) Baseline capture (control)
   - Run the benchmark matrix against current production scheduler.
   - Collect kernel traces (ktrace), scheduler traces, and kvcache hit-rate histograms.
   - Commands (example):

   # Start a profiler capture (example CLI)
   infra-cli profiler start --service scheduler-service --session experiment-run-001 --duration 40m

   # Start kernel dispatcher trace (on canary nodes)
   node-ctl trace start --target kernel-dispatcher --label canary-scheduler-experiment --out /tmp/ktrace-control.pb

3) Candidate capture (treatment)
   - Flip the feature flag and re-run the same benchmark cells. Keep all other infra constants identical.
   - Capture the same traces and aggregate.

4) Signal extraction
   - Extract the following per-request signals: scheduler_decision_time_ms, kernel_enqueue_delay_ms, kvcache_lookup_time_ms, and overall_end_to_end_latency_ms.
   - Use the trace-correlation utility:

   trace-corr --input /tmp/ktrace-control.pb,/tmp/ktrace-treatment.pb --keys request_id --out /tmp/trace-diff.json

5) Attribution checks
   - For any latency regression >10% at p95 or p99: construct causal hypothesis and search for correlated spikes in kernel_enqueue_delay_ms or priority-rebalancing events.
   - Check kernel utilization per-GPU and per-kernel type. If a single kernel shows >25% uplift in p99 execution time, tag as kernel-regression.

6) Quality gates
   - Block rollout if: p99 regression > 15% on short workloads OR kernel tail safety SLO violated.
   - Soft rollout allowed if cost delta <= +5% and p99 regression < 10%, with live monitoring for 24h.

Observability & Telemetry Contract

Every scheduler experiment must emit the following metrics at 10s and 1m resolution:
- scheduler.admit_latency_ms.p95, p99
- scheduler.slot_fill_ratio (0-1)
- scheduler.priority_rebalances.count
- kernel.dispatch_queue_length.avg
- kvcache.evictions_per_minute
- request.cohort_end_to_end_latency.p50,p95,p99

Trace annotations (required):
- scheduler_decision_id: unique id for scheduler decision that can be correlated to kernel events.
- kernel_dispatch_id: id assigned by kernel-dispatcher.
- cohort_label: the request-classifier cohort name.

Runbook: Incident Triage (scheduling-related)

Symptoms: sudden p99 rise in short requests, excess scheduler.rebalance events, disproportionate kernel queue length on a subset of nodes.

Immediate actions (0-10m)
1. Page runtime-oncall and @runtime-platform Slack channel.
2. Activate runbook channel (ops-channel: #runtime-incidents).
3. Toggle scheduler -> safe-mode: infra-cli flag set-scheduler-mode safe (falls back to admission-by-cost).
4. Re-route new traffic to backup GPU pool (tag: fallback-dedicated) using runtime-orchestrator policy: runtime-orchestrator route --policy fallback-dedicated --reason "incident".

Diagnostic steps (10-45m)
- Capture a 15m trace of scheduler decisions and kernel dispatch traces.
- Run quick histogram diff: trace-diff-analyzer --metric scheduler.admit_latency_ms --window 15m
- Check for: priority inversion signals, KV cache coldness, node-level GPU thermal throttling (node-ctl metrics).

Mitigations (45m-3h)
- If priority inversion: temporarily disable low-priority bursting (scheduler-service config: allow_burst_low_starve=false).
- If kvcache cold: trigger targeted prefetch for top-10 keys per cohort (kvcache-service API: prefetch --cohort <name> --keys-file /tmp/top10.json).
- If node thermal: cordon affected nodes and shift batches using runtime-orchestrator node-drain policy.

Post-incident (3h-72h)
- Run the full profiling playbook and compare control vs incident traces.
- Create an incident postmortem with the following sections: timeline, impact, root cause hypothesis, remediation plan, roll-forward/rollback plan, owners.
- If change was due to scheduler code, revert to previous release and open a regression ticket with kernel team.

Rollout & Release Guidance

- Canary phases: alpha (1 node), small-canary (5 nodes), canary-pool (20 nodes), fleet-rollout (gradual 5% increments every 6h).
- Required sign-offs: runtime-platform lead, kernel-owner, SRE on-call.
- Monitoring checklist before each percentage bump: p95 and p99 within thresholds, no new error signatures in scheduler logs, eviction rate stable.

Configuration Examples

1) scheduler-service config (YAML snippet)

scheduler:
  mode: "priority"               # priority | cost | safe
  slot_size_ms: "8"            # nominal slot unit
  max_slots_per_gpu: "64"
  allow_burst_low_starve: "true"
  rebalance_window_s: "30"
  credit_decay_s: "300"

2) runtime-orchestrator route policy (JSON example)

{ "policy_name": "fallback-dedicated", "criteria": ["latency>200ms","load>0.85"], "actions": ["reroute_pool:dedicated-03","notify:sre-team"] }

Known Issues & Short-term Workarounds

- Issue: transient priority oscillation when slot_size_ms is less than kernel microbatch latency.
  Workaround: increase slot_size_ms to 12ms for affected kernel families and enable slot coalescing.

- Issue: kvcache prefetch storms during synchronized warmups cause eviction spikes.
  Workaround: stagger cohort warmup by 10-30s using request-classifier delay window.

- Issue: scheduler metrics undercount when trace sampling is set below 2%.
  Workaround: temporarily raise sampling to 10% during experiments.

Ownership & Contacts

- Author: Priya Shah (runtime-platform)
- Owners: runtime-platform (primary), kernel-team (secondary), eng-sre (oncall)
- Slack: #runtime-platform, #runtime-incidents
- Pager: runtime-oncall rotation

Appendix: Experiment templates and expected artifacts

- Required artifacts for every scheduler experiment: control and treatment ktrace pb, aggregated trace-diff.json, metric rollup CSV (10s/1m), experiment runbook with hypothesis, and JIRA ticket linking artifacts.

- Template command to upload artifacts to experiment bucket:

  infra-cli artifact upload --session experiment-run-001 --files /tmp/ktrace-control.pb,/tmp/trace-diff.json --bucket gs://runtime-experiments/2025-03-12/experiment-run-001

- Minimum artifact retention: 90 days for cross-reference during regressions.

Revision History

- 2025-03-12: Initial draft (Priya Shah)
- 2025-06-02: Added kernel tail safety gate and bench matrix tweaks (reviewers: Marco Alvarez)
- 2026-01-15: Updated rollout cadence and added thermal node mitigation steps (Ethan Brooks)

Related pages

See also: scheduler-policy-language reference, continuous-runtime-profiling-strategy, runtime-inference-cost-model-and-simulation-workbook.

title: Cross-tenant failure domain mitigation and kinetic fallback patterns
content:
Summary

This document defines operational patterns, scheduling knobs, profiling and benchmarking steps for mitigating cross-tenant failure domains and implementing kinetic fallback behaviors in the runtime. It consolidates architecture intent, kernel scheduling recommendations, specific runbooks for incidents, and a minimal benchmarking protocol to validate mitigations before rollout.

Audience

- Runtime engineers (kernel and scheduler owners)
- SREs who operate GPU pools and admission controllers
- Platform product managers planning fallbacks and SLAs

Context and problem statement

Cross-tenant failure domains occur when a fault (hardware, thermal, driver, model regression, or noisy neighbor) degrades quality-of-service for multiple tenants sharing a GPU node, a rack, or a scheduler queue. Without explicit mitigation, symptoms include elevated p95/p99 latency, KV-cache churn, kernel timeouts, and degraded throughput. Traditional single-tenant isolation strategies are expensive; instead we use kinetic fallback patterns — adaptive, fast-acting fallbacks that proactively reduce fidelity or change routing to preserve SLOs for unaffected tenants while isolating failure impact.

Goals and SLOs

- Preserve tenant-facing availability: 99.95% uptime per customer pool (monthly).
- Maintain latency SLOs under degraded conditions: p95 <= 60ms, p99 <= 200ms for standard generation routes; critical routes p95 <= 40ms, p99 <= 120ms.
- Contain token cost increase for unaffected tenants to <= 10% during mitigation windows.

Principles

1. Fast detection — prioritize cheap, high-signal telemetry (kernel queue latency, GPU utilization spikes, KV cache miss-rate) for initial decisioning.
2. Graceful degradation — step down fidelity in controlled stages (e.g., quantized variant, smaller context window, prefix cache warmup) instead of abrupt circuit breakers.
3. Isolation by policy — prefer routing heuristics and tenant-weighted admission controls over full-host quarantine where possible.
4. Observable and reversible — every fallback must emit a decision trace and be reversible via automatic rollback or manual operator action.

Key components and service names

- runtime-scheduler: admission control, slot allocation, kernel hint emitter.
- kernel-agent: per-GPU kernel selector / binder and health checker.
- kvcache-manager: prefix KV cache owner, warmup controller.
- fallback-router: policy engine to reroute requests to alternative variants/regions.
- telemetry-pipeline: high-frequency telemetry ingestion and decision-triggering alerts.

Decision graph (high level)

1) Detect anomaly — telemetry-pipeline raises condition (e.g., node_kernel_timeout_rate > 0.5% over 1m).
2) Evaluate impact window — runtime-scheduler queries kvcache-manager and kernel-agent for eviction rates and kernel latencies.
3) Apply kinetic fallback Stage A (non-disruptive): increase per-tenant slot circuit cap, enable local KV cache aggressive rewarm, issue kernel preference hints (prefer fused-kernel-lite).
4) If condition persists, Stage B (fidelity reduction): fallback-router switches non-critical tenants to quantized model_variant-q8 and reduces max-generation-length to 512 tokens.
5) Stage C (isolation): runtime-scheduler enacts tenant-weighted throttling and migrates hot tenants off the degraded node.
6) Recovery: reverse stages in order; verify telemetry returns below thresholds for 5m.

Kernel scheduling guidance
