- Do not roll back a change that was part of a security patch without approval from Security and Product — instead perform targeted mitigations while preserving the security patch if possible.
- Automated rollback needs an explicit changelog entry created by CI/CD; otherwise the safety checks will refuse to act.
- For Dedicated and Private environments, follow the environment-specific rollback authorization steps (see related_pages).

Ownership and contacts
- Primary oncall (runtime): runtime-oncall@redwood.ai
- SRE lead: Arjun Patel (arjun@redwood.ai)
- Release owner (deploy pipeline): Luis Ortega (luis@redwood.ai)
- Profiling / experiments: Maya Chen (maya@redwood.ai)

Appendix A — Example queries and snippets
- List recent model swaps: rt-query audit --type model_swap --since 1h | jq '.[] | {time,change_id,actor,new_variant}'
- Quick p95 per-route table: runwayctl metrics table --metric p95_latency --group-by route --from "T0-15m" --to "T0+15m"

Appendix B — Change log for this runbook
- 2025-03-12 (Maya Chen): Initial creation.
- 2025-09-02 (Arjun Patel): Added automated rollback triggers and heatmap-gen workflow.
- 2026-01-18 (Luis Ortega): Tightened thresholds for kernel rollbacks and added safety note for security patches.

Related resources
- Runtime rollout API spec: ../runtime-architecture/runtime-feature-flagging-experimentation-contract-2026.json
- Canary orchestration patterns: ../runbooks/runtime-upgrade-validation-and-canary-matrix-2026.json
- Profiling playbook: ../profiling-playbook/causal-latency-attribution-and-signal-enrichment-playbook-2027.json

End of document

title: Incident readiness matrix and runbook synthesis
content:
Overview

This document synthesizes the canonical runbooks for high-impact services and provides a compact readiness matrix used to prioritize runbook coverage, on-call mentorship, and game-day simulations. It is intended for on-call engineers, SRE leads, and incident commanders who own restoration playbooks and training for the rotation.

Goals
- Reduce time-to-recovery for Sev1/Sev2 events by 30% via consolidated playbooks and targeted game-days.
- Ensure every service has a tested primary runbook, a fallback plan (compatible model variant or degraded-mode), and a responsible owner.
- Provide repeatable communication templates for customer-facing and internal status updates.

Key concepts
- Readiness Score (0-100): single numeric summarization of a service’s incident preparedness. Calculated from: runbook completeness (40%), SLO instrumentation & alerts (30%), recent test coverage (20%), owner availability (10%).
- Playbook Synthesis: canonical extraction of critical actions from team-specific runbooks into a one-page triage ladder.
- Escalation Ladders: explicit contacts and times-to-escalate (5m, 15m, 60m) for each class of incident.

Readiness Matrix (sample)

Service | Primary Owner | SLO (availability / p95) | Runbook status | Readiness Score
api-gateway | Platform API | 99.95% / p95 < 250ms | canonical + tested (2026-01-12) | 88
inference-runtime | Serving Runtime | 99.9% / p95 < 350ms | canonical, partial simulated test | 72
kv-cache | Redis-cluster | 99.99% / p95 < 50ms | legacy runbook, needs update | 58
router | Smart Router | 99.9% / p95 < 200ms | canonical + canary plan | 82

(When authoring, use this table and export regularly to the team dashboard.)

Service Triage Ladder (one-page synthesis)
Example: inference-runtime (high cost / customer impact)
1) Detect and score impact
   - Alert: inference-runtime.cpu_ready_ratio > 0.85 for 2m OR request-error-rate > 2% for 3m.
   - Immediate check: /observability/dashboards/runtime/overview -> continous_failures panel.
2) Containment (first 10 minutes)
   - Switch routing policy to fallback-model variant: `redwood-cli route set --policy degraded --service inference-runtime --duration 20m`
   - If GPU OOMs: temporarily set model.max_batch_size=1 via remote config service.
3) Mitigation (10-45 minutes)
   - Drain new requests from impacted pool: `kubectl cordon pod/<pod-name>` and `kubectl scale deployment inference-runtime --replicas 0` for affected ASG.
   - Redeploy last-known-good image: `helm upgrade --reuse-values inference-runtime ./charts/inference --set image.tag=v2026-01-22`
4) Recovery and verification
   - Run smoke harness: `scripts/smoke/inference_smoke.py --model small --n 50` (pass >=95% success).
   - Confirm p95 latency back under SLO for 10m window.
5) Post-incident actions
   - Create postmortem entry within 24h; link to runbook if gaps were found.

Decision thresholds and SLO breakpoints
- Green: error budget > 30% — follow standard incident cadence.
- Yellow: error budget between 5% and 30% — notify product and SRE leads; prepare mitigations.
- Red: error budget < 5% or any multi-region outage for >5 minutes — page engineering leadership and open an incident channel.

Escalation matrix (condensed)
- 0-5 minutes: on-call primary (page via PD)
- 5-20 minutes: on-call secondary (if unresolved)
- 20-60 minutes: service owner and SREEM (SRE escalation manager)
- 60+ minutes: engineering director and product owner; consider exec notification if customer impact is severe

Customer-facing status templates
- Initial status (first 20 minutes)
  Subject: Incident: [service] degraded — initial update
  Body: We are investigating elevated errors for [service]. Impact: a subset of API requests may fail or experience elevated latency. Affected regions: [us-west-2]. Actions under way: switching routing and validating fallback models. We will update within 30 minutes.

- Follow-up (30-90 minutes)
  Subject: Incident update: progress on [service]
  Body: We have applied a temporary routing policy to reduce failures and begun a targeted rollback to a known-good image. Error rates have dropped from X% to Y%. We continue validation and expect another update in 60 minutes.

- Resolution
  Subject: Incident resolved: [service]
  Body: The issue impacting [service] has been resolved. Root cause (preliminary): [brief]. Actions taken: [routing fallback, rollback, config change]. Next steps: a full post-incident review will be published in 48 hours. If you experienced customer-visible data loss, contact support at support@redwood.com.

Internal status channel templates
- Triage header: [INC-ID] [service] [sev] — short summary — owner: @user
- Short update cadence: 5m until containment, then 15m until stable, then 60m until recovery.

Runbook hygiene checklist (to keep readiness high)
- Owner assigned and on-call escalation lines declared.
- Runbook < 3 pages summary + detailed steps & rollback commands.
- Test harness that exercises the mitigation path present in CI.
- Playbook contains clear telemetry queries for impact scoring.
- Postmortem template link included at top of runbook.

On-call Rotation Mentorship program
- Pairing: new on-call engineers are paired with a mentor from SRE for first 90 days of rotation. Mentor responsibilities: review runbook with mentee within first week, run two shadow incidents, conduct a simulated restore together at week 4.
- Competency milestones: read-only access to incident channel -> small triage actions -> execute containment -> lead a canary rollback under supervision.
- Evaluation: at the end of each rotation, the mentor fills a short readiness assessment (pass/fail + notes). Failure triggers a remediation plan with extra game-days.

Game-day syllabus (90-minute template)
- Objective: validate runbook actions for top 3 readiness-score-lacking services.
- Roles: facilitator (SRE lead), incident commander, primary on-call, secondary on-call, customer comms, observer.
- Timeline: 10m brief, 30m simulated incident, 20m remediation & rollback, 30m after-action and capture of improvements.
- Deliverables: updated runbook snippet, action items with owners, updated playbook test cases.

Postmortem template (to paste into the PM doc)
- Title: [INC-ID] — short descriptive title
- Timeline: minute-by-minute summary of key events
- Impact: customers affected, regions, measurable metrics (error rate, requests lost, latency regression)
- Root cause: technical explanation and detection path
- Contributing factors: people/process/tech factors
- Resolution: steps taken to restore service
- Corrective actions: owner + ETA, verification steps, and follow-up game-day if applicable
- Severity rationale and learning notes

Example CLI and Observability snippets
- Check rolling restarts: `kubectl get pods -l app=inference-runtime -o wide`
- Grep recent errors in logs: `stern inference-runtime --since 1m | grep -i "OOM\|error\|failed"`
- Run smoke script in CI: `python tests/smoke/run_smoke.py --suite runtime_quick --repeat 3`

Configuration sample (YAML snippet to be placed in runbooks)
```yaml
alert_rules:
  - name: inference_high_error_rate
    expr: sum(rate(http_request_errors_total[2m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total[2m])) > 0.02
    severity: page
    runbook: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/runbooks/inference-runtime
```
Governance and review cadence
- Quarterly runbook audit: owners must update runbook and score on readiness matrix.
- After any Sev1 incident, the implicated runbook must be updated within 7 days; if not, an SRE lead escalates to engineering director.
- Game-days schedule: every team should run at least two focused game-days per year; teams with readiness score <70 must run an additional game-day.

Appendix: quick references
- Runbook location convention: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/runbooks/<service-name>
- PagerDuty escalation policy: Redwood-Core-Oncall (primary -> secondary -> SREEM)
- Slack incident channel naming: #incident-<service>-<INC-ID>

If you are an on-call engineer and notice any missing item in the readiness matrix, file a `runbook-update` ticket under the SRE board and tag the service owner.

End of document

title: KVCache epoch synchronization and repair procedures
content:
Overview
--------
This page documents the operational contract, detection signals, and step-by-step repair procedures for KV cache (kvcache) epoch divergence across runtime shards and kernels. The document is intended for oncall SREs, runtime engineers, and release engineers executing maintenance or incident mitigation related to kvcache epoch drift, partial corruption, or replay divergence.

Intro and intent
- The kvcache is a soft-state prefix/KV cache used by the serving runtime to avoid recomputing early key/value activations for long-context workloads.
- An epoch is an integer monotonic marker stamped into shard-local kvcache state at the time of checkpoint or warmstart. Epochs must be aligned for a shard group to accept replayed prefix tokens and to safely resume session continuation across host failovers.
- This runbook covers: detection signals, triage, safe repair patterns (resync, targeted purge, rehydrate), verification checks, and automated mitigation best practices.

Fast summary (TL;DR)
1) If the alert "kvcache_epoch_mismatch" fires, do not mass-purge immediately. Run the inspection steps below to determine divergence scope (single shard, cohort, or cluster).
2) For single-shard epoch mismatch with low error rate: attempt soft resync (admin API epoch bump + passive replay) -> verify hashes -> promote.
3) For cohort-level drift or corruption: perform coordinated epoch rotate with drain and staged rehydrate (detailed below).
4) If disk-backed checkpoint is corrupted, engage oncall runtime-owner and disable cross-shard routing until fixed.

Observability signals and thresholds
- Alerts (Prometheus/Alertmanager):
  - kvcache_epoch_mismatch (firing when >0.5% shard request failures referencing mismatched epoch over 5m)
  - kvcache_rehydrate_failure_rate (>1% failed rehydrates per shard over 5m)
  - kvcache_hash_divergence (binary alert when checksum mismatch detected during meta-replay verification)
  - kvcache_eviction_surge (when eviction rate increases >5x baseline for a shard cohort)

- Key metrics to inspect (PromQL examples):
  - Rate of epoch mismatch: sum(rate(kvcache_epoch_mismatch_events[5m])) by (shard)
  - Hash divergence ratio: sum(kvcache_hash_mismatch_total) / sum(kvcache_hash_checks_total)
  - Rehydrate latency P95: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(kvcache_rehydrate_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le))

Telemetry artifacts to collect before repair
1) kvcache meta dump (HTTP API): curl -sS http://admin.{env}.local:9090/kvcache/meta?shard={shard} > meta-shard-{shard}.json
2) kvcache local checksum: rwi kvcache inspect --shard {shard} --checksum > checksum-{shard}.txt
3) short trace covering a mismatched request: trace id from logs and link to tracing UI
4) node runtime logs (last 1h) and kernel handshake logs

Triage flow (detailed)
1) Scope detection (3 quick checks)
   a) Is the mismatch limited to a single shard? Query meta for epoch values across the shard group:
      - admin API: /kvcache/meta?cohort={cohort_id}
      - If only one shard shows a different epoch, proceed with single-shard repair.
   b) Does the hash divergence alert also fire? If no, consider epoch misstamp (clock skew or delayed checkpoint) rather than corruption.
   c) Check shard health: rehydrate errors, OOM logs, kernel panic, disk IO errors. If hardware symptoms present, escalate to infra SRE.

2) Impact assessment
   - Compute affected request percentage (use kvcache_epoch_mismatch events correlated with request counts). If <1% of requests and only warm path, prefer rolling/soft options. If >5% or critical customer routes affected, escalate to incident severity and use coordinated rotate.

Repair procedures
-----------------
A. Safe soft resync (preferred when divergence is minor and single-shard)
1) Preconditions:
   - Divergence confirmed on single shard only.
   - No disk corruption indicated.
   - Rehydrate latency within normal bounds.
2) Steps:
   1. Put shard into passive mode: curl -X POST http://admin.{env}.local:9090/kvcache/mode?shard={shard}&mode=passive
   2. Bump epoch via admin API (this triggers a soft checkpoint boundary):
      - curl -X POST http://admin.{env}.local:9090/kvcache/epoch?shard={shard}&action=force_bump
   3. Allow the shard to receive passive replay traffic for 30s to 2m to rehydrate prefixes from normal request flow.
   4. Run checksum verification: rwi kvcache inspect --shard {shard} --verify
   5. If checksums match cohort leader, set mode back to active: curl -X POST http://admin.{env}.local:9090/kvcache/mode?shard={shard}&mode=active

3) Post-verify steps:
   - Monitor kvcache_epoch_mismatch and kvcache_hash_divergence for 10m. If no recurrence, close incident.

B. Targeted purge and rehydrate (use when some prefixes are corrupted)
1) Preconditions:
   - Hash divergence localized to identifiable prefix ranges or key patterns
   - Customer request impact moderate
2) Steps:
   1. Identify offending prefix hash set from meta dump.
   2. Use targeted purge API: curl -X POST http://admin.{env}.local:9090/kvcache/purge?shard={shard} --data '{"prefixes":["hk:abc...","hk:xyz..."]}'
   3. Wait for background rehydrate to repopulate from canonical model execution or forward the next N matching requests through bypass path to rebuild state.
   4. Verify each purged prefix checksum after rehydration.

C. Coordinated epoch rotate (cohort-level)
1) Preconditions:
   - Multi-shard or cohort-level epoch mismatch or corruption
   - Rolling soft options failed or not applicable
2) Safety checklist (pre-rotate)
   - Notify customers via incident channel if >5% request impact
   - Confirm backups of disk checkpoints available and validated
   - Verify automated rollback playbooks present and tested in lab
3) Coordination steps (sequence)
   1. Set cohort to read-only routing (no new sessions anchored to this cohort).
   2. For each shard in cohort, in parallel: mark passive -> drain existing requests -> snapshot meta -> force epoch bump -> restart kvcache process if necessary. Use the orchestration tool: rwi kvcache rotate-cohort --cohort {cohort_id} --mode coordinated
   3. Wait for rehydration and cross-shard checksum convergence. Allow at least 5m for warm paths and up to 30m for long-prefix workloads.
   4. Re-enter cohort into active routing and ramp traffic using a 5-step circuit: 5% -> 20% -> 50% -> 80% -> 100% with 3–5 minute observation windows.

D. Disk checkpoint repair (when checkpoint file corrupted)
1) Preconditions:
   - Checkpoint verification fails, file-level corruption detected
   - There's a recent healthy checkpoint on another replica or in object store
2) Steps
   1. Pause cross-shard routing for cohort.
   2. Copy healthy checkpoint from s3://redwood-kvcache-checkpoints/{cohort}/{shard}/latest to node (use signed URL).
   3. Verify file checksum locally: sha256sum checkpoint.bin | grep {expected_hash}
   4. Replace corrupted file atomically: mv checkpoint.bin checkpoint.bin.bak && mv checkpoint.bin.new checkpoint.bin
   5. Restart kvcache service: sudo systemctl restart rw-kvcache && monitor startup logs.

Verification and tests (post repair)
- Functional checks (runbook)
  1) Run kvcache meta diff across cohort: rwi kvcache meta-diff --cohort {cohort_id} > meta-diff.txt
  2) Run sample replay test suite (contains 50 canonical prefix scenarios): ./tools/replay-suite/run.sh --shard {shard} --cases sample-50
  3) Hash agreement test: rwi kvcache verify-hash --cohort {cohort_id}
- Performance checks
  - Ensure rehydrate latency P95 back within 10% of baseline within 30 minutes.
- Safety observation window
  - Maintain elevated monitoring for 60 minutes. If any of the following recur, escalate to Runtime Incident:
    * kvcache_epoch_mismatch firing again
    * kvcache_rehydrate_failure_rate > 1%
    * kvcache_hash_divergence reappears

Automation and tooling notes
- rwi (runtime ops CLI) has commands used above. See rwi help for subcommands and flags. Example: rwi kvcache rotate-cohort --help
- The orchestration job uses a preflight check that validates checkpoint availability and verifies storage IOPS before starting coordinated rotate.
- A small Lambda/cron job performs nightly checksum sampling and records a digest manifest to object storage. This is used for fast verification during repairs.

Rollout and release considerations
- Changes to the kvcache serialization format or epoch semantics must be accompanied by:
  1) A compatibility test in the benchmark suite that performs cross-version meta-diff using shadow cohorts.
  2) A staged rollout: dev -> canary (5%) -> regional canary (20%) -> global (100%) with the kvcache epoch rotate orchestration able to abort mid-rotation.
- Release note template snippet:
  - Component: runtime.kvcache
  - Change: bump epoch marker to 64-bit and add robust checkpoint CRC
  - Safety: automated coordinated rotate orchestration and nightly checksum manifests
  - Rollback: restore previous checkpoint from s3 and rotate cohort back.

Known issues and caveats
- Clock skew can cause false-positive epoch mismatch alerts if leader shard epoch bumps while follower is slightly behind; always check NTP health and kernel clock offset before repair.
- Very long prefix workloads may require up to 30m for full rehydrate convergence; do not prematurely escalate if inspection shows slow but steady convergence.
- Partial serialization changes without back-compatibility will cause cross-version epoch mismatch; ensure model-serving and kvcache serialization version are co-deployed.

Escalation matrix and ownership
- First responder: serving-runtime oncall (pager duty)
- Secondary: runtime-kvcache owner (Asha Kapoor)
- Tertiary: infra-sre (for disk or hardware IO issues)
- Legal/Customer-Sensitive: if a customer reports data leakage correlated with kvcache keys, tag confidentiality=restricted and escalate to security oncall.

Appendices
A. Example commands
- Inspect meta for cohort:
  curl -sS http://admin.prod.local:9090/kvcache/meta?cohort=cohort-42 | jq '.' > cohort-42-meta.json
- Force epoch bump for shard 7:
  curl -X POST http://admin.prod.local:9090/kvcache/epoch?shard=7&action=force_bump
- Targeted purge (JSON body escaped for shell):
  curl -X POST http://admin.prod.local:9090/kvcache/purge?shard=7 \\--header 'Content-Type: application/json' \\--data '{"prefixes":["hk:abc123","hk:def456"]}'

B. Checksum manifest format (nightly)
- A nightly manifest (JSON) stored at s3://redwood-kvcache-checksums/{date}.json with records: 
  - {"cohort_id":"cohort-42","shard":7,"epoch":12345,"sha256":"ab..."}

C. Quick decision table
| Symptom | Likely cause | Recommended action | Owner |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Single-shard epoch mismatch, no hash divergence | delayed checkpoint / clock skew | soft resync (force bump) | serving-runtime oncall |
| Hash divergence on multiple shards | serialization/corruption | coordinated epoch rotate + restore checkpoint | runtime-kvcache owner |
| Disk IO errors + rehydrate failures | node hardware or disk corruption | escalate to infra-sre, isolate shard | infra-sre |

D. Contact links
- Runtime runbook Slack: #runtime-oncall
- Incident bridge template: https://incidents.redwood.ai/template/kvcache-epoch

Document history
- 2026-02-10: Created by Asha Kapoor
- 2026-03-21: Expanded verification section and added automation notes (reviewed by Miguel Alvarez, Ruth Chen)

Related reading
- session-lifecycle-kvcache-consistency-guidelines-2024 (session consistency specifics)
- kv-prefetch-audit-and-experiment-guide-2026 (profiling and rehydrate experiments)

title: Mixed-workload scheduler prototype — rollout runbook
content:
## Purpose
This runbook describes how to safely enable and ramp the mixed-workload scheduler prototype (short/long prompt-aware scheduling) in production pools.

Primary goal: reduce user-visible p95 tail latency (TTFT and end-to-end) under mixed prompt-length distributions without materially regressing throughput or fairness.

This runbook covers:
- Preconditions and required sign-offs
- Feature flag enablement and safe parameter ramps
- Monitoring checklist and known-bad signals
- Rollback procedure
- Owner rotation and escalation

---

## Scope
Applies to runtime version(s) that include the prototype scheduler (currently: runtime-1.18+ candidate builds where the feature flag is present).

In-scope deployment targets:
- Hosted API: a single canary region/pool first (typically us-east)
- Dedicated: a small, opt-in subset of Dedicated GPU pools with mixed-workload symptoms

Out of scope:
- Multi-tenant QoS tier productization
- Broad admission-control redesign (only minimal coupling to existing backpressure)

---

## Definitions (quick)
- **Short vs long class**: request classification based on prompt/context length and/or predicted prefill cost.
- **Two-queue dispatch**: separate queues for short/long with a policy bias toward short while guaranteeing progress for long.
- **Aging/starvation prevention**: long requests accrue priority with time-in-queue, preventing indefinite delay.
- **Token budgets**: per-iteration limits (especially for long-prefill dominance) to avoid tail amplification.

---

## Ownership and escalation
### Primary owners (during canary windows)
- Rollout driver / on-point: **Rafael Mendes (SRE/Canary Ops)**
- Runtime scheduling on-call / implementation: **Marcus Reed** (backup: **Omar El-Sayed**)
- Scheduler policy TL: **Lena Fischer**
- SRE sponsor / guardrails: **Sean Gallagher**
- Observability: **Allison Grant** (backup: **Logan Wright**)
- Release coordination: **Connor O'Brien**

### Escalation rules
Escalate immediately to #incidents and page SRE on-call if any rollback trigger fires (see “Rollback triggers”).

If symptoms are contained and do not breach rollback triggers:
1) Ping #eng-runtime with dashboard links + parameter snapshot
2) If suspect instrumentation or dashboard integrity: ping #eng-sre and @Allison Grant
3) If suspect kernel thrash/selection instability: ping kernel on-call and @Yuki Sato

### Comms channels
- Coordination: #eng-runtime, #eng-sre, #eng-releases
- Incidents: #incidents

---

## Preconditions (must be true before enabling)
### 1) Code + config readiness
- Feature flag is present and off by default in target pools.
- Config validation bounds are deployed (prevents unsafe parameter values).
- Per-class metrics are emitting in the target environment.

### 2) SRE guardrails and dashboards ready
- Dashboard for class metrics is live and verified in the target region/pool.
- Tail latency guardrails (allowed drift) are agreed for the canary window.
- Rollback procedure is tested (dry-run) in staging.

### 3) Canaries and baseline established
- Baseline measurements captured for at least 24h (or one full traffic cycle) with flag OFF:
  - p50/p95/p99 TTFT
  - p50/p95 end-to-end latency
  - throughput (tokens/sec and requests/sec)
  - error rates (timeouts, cancellations)
  - queue time distribution
- Perf-canary nightly job is green for mixed workload scenarios (or explicitly waived with justification).

### 4) Approvals
- Runtime Scheduling EM (Sofia Ivanova) approves the canary enablement.
- SRE sponsor (Sean Gallagher) approves guardrails + rollback triggers.
- Release coordinator (Connor O'Brien) acknowledges the ramp window and comms plan.

---

## Feature flag and configuration
### Feature flag name
- `runtime.scheduler.mixed_workload.enabled`

Flag scope:
- Can be enabled per pool.
- Should NOT be enabled globally during prototype.

### Core knobs (prototype)
These are the minimum knobs expected to be exposed for safe ramps. Exact names may differ slightly by runtime build; verify in runtime config docs for the current release.

1) Classification
- `scheduler.mixed.classification.mode`: `tokens` | `prefill_cost`
- `scheduler.mixed.classification.short_prompt_tokens_threshold`: e.g., 256
- `scheduler.mixed.classification.long_context_tokens_threshold`: e.g., 2048 (optional override)

2) Dispatch policy
- `scheduler.mixed.dispatch.short_weight`: bias for short queue selection (e.g., 3)
- `scheduler.mixed.dispatch.long_weight`: baseline for long queue (e.g., 1)
- `scheduler.mixed.aging.enabled`: true/false
- `scheduler.mixed.aging.half_life_ms`: e.g., 2000–6000ms

3) Token budgets / guardrails
- `scheduler.mixed.budget.enabled`: true/false
- `scheduler.mixed.budget.max_prefill_tokens_per_iter_long`: e.g., 4096–8192
- `scheduler.mixed.budget.max_decode_tokens_per_iter_long`: e.g., 1024–2048
- `scheduler.mixed.budget.max_skew_ratio_short_to_long`: e.g., 6.0 (prevents starving long)

4) Safety bounds
- `scheduler.mixed.safety.burst_cap_short_queue`: e.g., 2–4 iterations of preferential short dispatch before forcing a long opportunity
- `scheduler.mixed.safety.max_queue_wait_ms_long`: e.g., 15000 (if exceeded, the system should prioritize long)

---

## Rollout strategy overview (recommended)
### Principles
- Ramp in two dimensions separately:
  1) Enable flag for a very small traffic slice (or a small pool subset)
  2) Increase policy bias/weights gradually (do not jump to aggressive settings)
- Prefer parameter changes over code changes during canary.
- Keep rollback simple: flip the flag OFF first; only then consider reverting config.

### Standard ramp plan (Hosted API canary)
1) **Stage 0: Baseline** (flag OFF)
   - Duration: 24h
   - Output: baseline dashboard snapshot + notes on known mix (% long contexts)

2) **Stage 1: Enable with conservative params**
   - Scope: 1 canary pool (or lowest viable slice)
   - Duration: 2–4h
   - Goal: validate correctness + no regressions, confirm metrics

3) **Stage 2: Increase bias modestly**
   - Duration: 4–8h
   - Goal: observe p95 improvement for short class without long starvation

4) **Stage 3: Overnight soak**
   - Duration: 12–24h
   - Goal: cover diurnal mix changes, capacity shifts, and autoscaling events

5) **Stage 4: Expand scope**
   - Add one more pool OR increase slice in same region
   - Only after meeting success criteria + no near-miss rollbacks

### Dedicated ramp plan
Dedicated pools may have workload-specific sensitivity. Use opt-in pools with active mixed-workload pain. Keep initial enablement to a single pool and do not overlap with customer-side releases when possible.

---

## Parameter presets (starting points)
Use these as starting points; do not treat as universal defaults.

### Preset A (Conservative)
- short_weight=2, long_weight=1
- aging.enabled=true, aging.half_life_ms=6000
- budget.enabled=true
- max_prefill_tokens_per_iter_long=4096
- max_decode_tokens_per_iter_long=1024
- short_prompt_tokens_threshold=256
- burst_cap_short_queue=2

### Preset B (Balanced)
- short_weight=3, long_weight=1
- aging.enabled=true, aging.half_life_ms=4000
- budget.enabled=true
- max_prefill_tokens_per_iter_long=8192
- max_decode_tokens_per_iter_long=2048
- short_prompt_tokens_threshold=256
- burst_cap_short_queue=3

Guidance:
- Start with Preset A for first enablement in a new environment.
- Move to Preset B only after confirming long-class queue wait and starvation counters remain stable.

---

## Step-by-step procedure
### A) Pre-flight checklist (T-60 to T-15)
1. Confirm change window and on-point coverage.
   - Rollout driver + runtime scheduling + SRE on-call available for the full ramp.
2. Verify target pools and current runtime version.
   - Ensure runtime build includes mixed scheduler flag + metrics.
3. Validate dashboards are live and correct (no missing labels).
   - Queue depth by class
   - Time-in-queue by class
   - TTFT p50/p95 by class
   - End-to-end p95 by route/model
   - Starvation counters
4. Capture baseline snapshot links (flag OFF):
   - 30m window and 6h window
5. Confirm rollback path:
   - Who flips the flag
   - Where to flip it
   - How to confirm it propagated

### B) Enablement (Stage 1)
1. Apply Preset A (Conservative) to the target pool(s).
2. Enable the feature flag for the target pool(s):
   - Set `runtime.scheduler.mixed_workload.enabled = true`
3. Confirm propagation:
   - Within 5–10 minutes, verify per-class metrics show non-zero dispatch share in both classes.
   - Confirm the scheduler reports the active policy in runtime logs (expected once per process start or config reload).

### C) Ramp (Stage 2/3)
1. If stable after 30–60 minutes (no rollback triggers), adjust toward Preset B:
   - Increase `short_weight` by +1 (max one adjustment per hour).
   - Optionally reduce `aging.half_life_ms` by 10–25% to improve long progress.
2. After each change, wait a full observation window:
   - Minimum: 30 minutes
   - Preferred: 60–120 minutes if traffic is bursty
3. Do not change classification thresholds and weights in the same step.

### D) Expansion (Stage 4)
Only expand scope after:
- At least one full soak period (overnight preferred)
- Documented results vs baseline
- No starvation incidents and no near-miss rollback triggers

---

## Monitoring checklist (what to watch)
Monitor the following at minimum.

### Latency
- Short-class TTFT p95 (primary)
- Overall TTFT p95/p99 (guardrail)
- End-to-end latency p95 by route/model
- Long-class latency p95 (guardrail; should not drift beyond allowed limits)

### Queueing
- Queue depth by class
- Time-in-queue p95 by class
- Long-class max time-in-queue (watch for creeping ceilings)

### Fairness / starvation
- Starvation counters (long)
- Dispatch share short vs long (should remain within configured skew bounds)

### Throughput and utilization
- Tokens/sec per GPU
- Requests/sec
- GPU utilization stability (watch for oscillation)

### Errors
- Timeouts (client and server)
- Cancellations / aborted requests
- OOM / KV-cache allocation errors

---

## Known-bad signals (stop-the-line indicators)
Any of the following should trigger a pause and likely rollback, depending on severity and duration.

### Immediate rollback triggers (do not wait)
- Sustained p99 TTFT regression > SRE guardrail for the region/pool (per SRE doc).
- Any evidence of long-class starvation:
  - Starvation counters increasing steadily for >5 minutes, OR
  - Long-class time-in-queue max exceeding `scheduler.mixed.safety.max_queue_wait_ms_long` for >10 minutes.
- Error-rate spike attributable to scheduler change (timeouts/cancellations) beyond normal variance.
- Kernel selection instability / thrash that causes visible jitter:
  - Rapid oscillation in kernel choice correlated with latency spikes
  - GPU utilization seesawing with no capacity change

### Investigate and consider rollback
- Overall throughput regression > ~3–5% sustained (unless explicitly accepted in the canary plan).
- Long-class p95 increases materially even if short-class improves.
- Queue depth growth without matching traffic increases (possible scheduling dead zone).

---

## Rollback procedure
Rollback should be fast, reversible, and documented. Prefer flipping the flag OFF before modifying multiple parameters.

### Rollback steps
1) Announce rollback in #eng-runtime and #eng-sre with:
- Pool/region
- Time window
- Dashboard links
- Current parameter snapshot

2) Disable feature flag:
- Set `runtime.scheduler.mixed_workload.enabled = false` for the target pool(s).

3) Confirm rollback took effect:
- Within 5–10 minutes:
  - Dispatch share by class should collapse to baseline behavior (class metrics may remain but should show no policy bias).
  - TTFT should begin trending back toward baseline.

4) If latency does not recover:
- Check for confounders: capacity events, autoscaling, upstream traffic changes, model rollout.
- If required, revert the config knobs to baseline defaults (last known good).

5) Create follow-up action items:
- File a runtime bug for the observed failure mode, include parameter snapshot and reproduction hints.
- If starvation-related, link to the regression test coverage and validate it ran.

### Post-rollback notes
- If rollback was triggered by guardrails, treat as a canary failure: do not re-enable in that pool until a fix or parameter revision is reviewed by Scheduling TL + SRE sponsor.

---

## Troubleshooting guide (common failure modes)
### Symptom: short improves, long gets “stuck”
Likely cause: overly aggressive short bias or insufficient aging.
Actions:
- Verify starvation counters and long time-in-queue.
- Increase long opportunities:
  - Reduce `short_weight` by 1, OR
  - Increase aging aggressiveness (lower `aging.half_life_ms`), OR
  - Reduce `burst_cap_short_queue`.
- If already near limits or unclear, rollback.

### Symptom: TTFT jitter / sawtooth patterns
Likely cause: kernel auto-selection instability when mixing sequence lengths or token budgets causing batch composition oscillations.
Actions:
- Check kernel selection logs/metrics for oscillation.
- Temporarily increase long token budget caps (avoid too-tight budget that fragments work) OR return to Preset A.
- If jitter causes p95 regression beyond guardrail, rollback and engage kernel team.

### Symptom: throughput drops but latency improves
This can be an acceptable trade-off only if explicitly aligned to the canary success criteria.
Actions:
- Quantify: tokens/sec delta and cost impact.
- Check whether the token budgets are too conservative (causing under-filled batches).
- If throughput regression is sustained and > agreed bounds, rollback.

---

## Documentation requirements (during rollout)
During each stage, the rollout driver must capture:
- Pool(s), region(s), runtime version
- Parameter snapshot (before/after)
- Start/end timestamps for each stage
- Dashboard links: baseline vs canary windows
- Any incidents/near-misses and actions taken

Store links in the Linear initiative (ENG-2417) and update the results summary page if outcomes are meaningful.

---

## Appendix A: Example configuration snippet (illustrative)
NOTE: Field names may differ by build; use runtime config schema for your release.

```
# pool: hosted-us-east-canary
runtime:
  scheduler:
    mixed_workload:
      enabled: true
      classification:
        mode: tokens
        short_prompt_tokens_threshold: 256
      dispatch:
        short_weight: 2
        long_weight: 1
      aging:
        enabled: true
        half_life_ms: 6000
      budget:
        enabled: true
        max_prefill_tokens_per_iter_long: 4096
        max_decode_tokens_per_iter_long: 1024
      safety:
        burst_cap_short_queue: 2
        max_queue_wait_ms_long: 15000
```

---

## Appendix B: Canary “go/no-go” checklist
GO if all are true for the prior observation window:
- Short-class TTFT p95 improved or neutral
- Overall p95/p99 within SRE drift guardrails
- No rising starvation counters
- Long-class max time-in-queue stable and below cap
- Errors within normal variance
- Throughput within acceptable bounds

NO-GO / Rollback if any trigger is met (see “Known-bad signals”).

title: Rollout Runbook: Hardware Tuning Profiles Pack (H100/B200/L40S)
content:
h1. Purpose
This runbook describes the operational procedure for safely rolling out the *Hardware Tuning Profiles Pack* for the serving runtime across *Hosted, Dedicated, and Private* deployments. It covers:

* Staged rollout by pool/region
* Required dashboards and gates
* Alert thresholds and stop/rollback criteria
* Triage and incident response playbook for regressions

The profiles pack provides curated, versioned runtime configuration presets per GPU SKU (*H100, B200, L40S*) and a consistent override model across fleet defaults and per-deployment overrides.

h1. Scope and assumptions
h2. In scope
* Enabling a specific *profile pack version* as the fleet default (or per-pool override)
* Enabling/disabling the profiles feature at runtime
* Rolling forward/back profile versions
* Handling expected failure modes: performance regressions, OOMs, elevated error rate, queueing/backpressure anomalies, profile mis-detection

h2. Out of scope
* Customer-specific bespoke tuning beyond supported overrides (route-level overrides handled via Support/Solutions)
* Writing new kernels (kernel changes should have separate rollout/guardrail docs)

h2. Definitions
* *Profile pack* — Versioned bundle of hardware tuning profiles.
* *Selected profile* — The runtime’s chosen profile after hardware detection and compatibility checks.
* *Override order* — Precedence rules (fleet default, per-pool, per-deployment Helm values/env, per-route policy, etc.). See ADR.
* *Canary pool* — Small percentage of traffic/capacity used for early validation.

h1. Ownership and escalation
* Primary oncall: *eng-oncall* (Serving Runtime)
* SRE escalation: *eng-sre* (Neha Kapoor org) and *#eng-sre-oncall*
* Infra/fleet escalation: Irene Choi / Vanessa Ortiz
* Runtime scheduling escalation: Sofia Ivanova / Lena Fischer / Marcus Reed
* Kernel tuning escalation: Hiro Tanaka / Yuki Sato / Grace Kim

h2. Change approvers (rollout sign-off)
* SRE: Sean Gallagher
* Infra/Fleet: Irene Choi
* Runtime: Noah Patel (or delegate)

h1. Preconditions (must be true before any rollout)
1) *Compatibility checks are green*
* Runtime release includes profile loader + compatibility matrix logging at startup.
* Profile pack version is declared compatible with the runtime release target.

2) *Observability is in place*
* Dashboards and alerts for:
  * latency (p50/p95/p99) segmented by profile
  * throughput/tokens-per-second segmented by profile
  * error rate and retry rate
  * OOM / CUDA out-of-memory / allocator failures
  * queue depth / backpressure / drop rate
  * profile selection metrics (selected_profile, override_source)

3) *Perf canary gates are configured*
* Pre-merge or pre-deploy canary job runs the workload matrix on the target GPU SKU.
* Canary thresholds updated for the profile-enabled build.

4) *Rollback mechanism is tested*
* Confirm we can disable profiles per pool within 10 minutes.
* Confirm we can pin profile pack to prior version within 20 minutes.

h1. Required dashboards and where to look
h2. Dashboards (must be open during rollout)
* *Serving Runtime Overview* (global + by region/pool)
  * Request rate, error rate, p50/p95/p99 latency
* *Profile Selection & Overrides*
  * selected_profile (by pool)
  * override_source (fleet default vs per-pool vs deployment override)
  * mismatch/unknown-sku count
* *Perf & Unit Economics*
  * tokens/sec, GPU utilization, kernel time
  * cost-per-1K tokens (Hosted), effective throughput (Dedicated)
* *Scheduler Health*
  * queue depth, batch sizes, prefill/decode fairness, backpressure events
* *Memory & Stability*
  * KV cache usage, fragmentation indicators, OOM count, CUDA errors

h2. Logs (minimum)
* Runtime startup log line: profile pack version + compatibility matrix
* Per-request debug sampling (if enabled): batch size, seq len bucket, decode concurrency

h2. Debug tools
* CLI: dump effective runtime config after selection and overrides (useful for Private/Dedicated).
* Runtime debug endpoint: expose selected profile + effective key knobs.

h1. Rollout strategy overview
We roll out in stages, per GPU SKU, per region/pool, and per deployment mode. *Stop-the-line* if any stop criteria is met.

h2. Recommended order
1) H100: Hosted canary → Hosted 25% → Hosted 100% → Dedicated pilots → wider Dedicated
2) L40S: Hosted canary → Hosted 50% (smaller fleet) → Hosted 100% → Dedicated
3) B200: *Experimental only*, gated by feature flag + limited regions; do not enable fleet-wide defaults until maturity criteria is met.

h2. Rollout stages
* Stage 0: Dry run (no traffic)
* Stage 1: Canary (1–5% capacity or traffic)
* Stage 2: Limited expansion (10–25%)
* Stage 3: Majority (50–75%)
* Stage 4: Full enablement (100%)
* Stage 5: Post-rollout validation + documentation

h1. Stage 0 — Dry run (no customer impact)
Goal: confirm profile selection, override order, and basic stability in a controlled environment.

Checklist:
1) Deploy runtime build + profile pack to a non-prod or shadow pool.
2) Verify startup logs include:
   * runtime_version
   * profile_pack_version
   * sku_detection_result
   * selected_profile
   * compatibility_result
3) Run smoke workload:
   * short prompts, long prompts, streaming on/off
   * tool-calling style (if supported)
4) Confirm no elevated:
   * OOM / CUDA errors
   * error rate > baseline

Exit criteria:
* Zero OOMs in smoke runs
* Error rate within baseline noise
* selected_profile matches expected SKU profile

h1. Stage 1 — Canary rollout (1–5%)
Goal: validate real traffic behavior with strict rollback readiness.

h2. Setup
* Choose canary pools per region (at least one high-traffic and one representative low-traffic region).
* Ensure oncall coverage for the full canary window.
* Disable concurrent major changes (driver upgrades, scheduler refactors, autoscaling policy changes) in canary pools.

h2. Steps
1) Enable profiles in canary pool only.
2) Confirm profile selection is stable (no flapping between profiles across restarts).
3) Monitor for 60–120 minutes (minimum) or 2 peak traffic cycles (recommended).

h2. Canary success criteria (must hold)
* Latency:
  * p95 <= baseline + 5% (same route/model cohort)
  * p99 <= baseline + 8%
  * No new long-tail spikes correlated with profile selection
* Errors:
  * 5xx rate <= baseline + 0.1% absolute
  * Retry rate <= baseline + 0.2% absolute
* Stability:
  * OOM count == 0 for canary window (or <= baseline if baseline non-zero due to known noisy workloads)
* Throughput:
  * tokens/sec >= baseline - 2% (we accept small drops if latency improves)

h2. Stop criteria (immediate)
Trigger rollback if any of the below persists for >10 minutes (or is severe immediately):
* p95 latency regression >= 10% (same route/model cohort)
* p99 latency regression >= 15%
* 5xx rate regression >= +0.25% absolute
* Any OOM burst (>= 3 OOMs within 15 minutes) on L40S pools
* Scheduler health degradation:
  * sustained queue depth above alert threshold (see below)
  * request drop/backpressure events above baseline by 2x

h1. Stage 2–4 — Expansion rollout (10% → 25% → 50%+ → 100%)
Goal: expand while preserving the ability to correlate regressions with the rollout.

h2. General rules
* Expand one dimension at a time:
  * either increase traffic share in one region, or add one new region at same share.
* Hold each stage for at least:
  * 2 hours during business hours, or
  * 1 peak window for that region (recommended)
* Record a short change note in the release channel including:
  * profile pack version
  * pools/regions affected
  * any notable metric shifts

h2. Expansion checklist (repeat at each stage)
1) Confirm selected_profile distribution matches plan.
2) Compare latency/throughput segmented by:
   * region
   * pool
   * model family
   * streaming vs non-streaming
3) Watch for cohort-specific regressions (often only long-context or high-concurrency cohorts).
4) Confirm autoscaling and backpressure behavior is unchanged or improved.

h1. Alert thresholds (rollout-time)
These are rollout-time thresholds used to decide whether to pause/rollback. They are *not* contractual SLOs.

h2. Latency thresholds (per route/model cohort)
* Warning:
  * p95 +7% vs trailing 7-day baseline (same time-of-day)
  * p99 +10%
* Critical / rollback consideration:
  * p95 +10% sustained 10 minutes
  * p99 +15% sustained 10 minutes

h2. Error thresholds
* Warning:
  * 5xx +0.15% absolute vs baseline
  * retry rate +0.2% absolute
* Critical:
  * 5xx +0.25% absolute sustained 10 minutes
  * specific error signatures: CUDA OOM, illegal memory access, NCCL errors

h2. Memory/OOM thresholds
* H100:
  * Critical: >= 2 OOMs in 30 minutes in same pool
* L40S:
  * Critical: >= 3 OOMs in 15 minutes (lower headroom; treat as urgent)
* Any GPU:
  * Critical: allocator failures or fragmentation warnings correlated with profile enablement

h2. Scheduler/queueing thresholds
* Warning:
  * queue depth p95 +25% vs baseline
  * backpressure events 1.5x baseline
* Critical:
  * drop rate > 0 (if system previously configured to never drop)
  * sustained queue depth p95 +50% for 10 minutes

h1. Rollback and mitigation
h2. Rollback hierarchy (prefer least disruptive)
1) *Disable profiles for the affected pool/region* (feature toggle)
2) *Pin to previous profile pack version* for the affected pool/region
3) *Revert runtime release* (only if issue is in loader/selection logic)

h2. Rollback targets
* Per pool/region rollback (preferred)
* Per GPU SKU rollback if issue is SKU-specific (e.g., L40S memory guardrails)
* Per deployment-mode rollback (e.g., Private customers pinned differently)

h2. Rollback procedure (pool/region)
1) Declare rollout paused in the release channel and tag SRE oncall.
2) Disable profiles in the affected pool/region.
3) Confirm within 10–15 minutes:
   * selected_profile metric drops to “none/default” (or expected fallback)
   * latency/error metrics return toward baseline
4) If not recovering, pin to last-known-good runtime config (pre-profile defaults) and escalate to Runtime oncall.

h2. Version rollback procedure (profile pack)
1) Update pool configuration to pin *profile_pack_version = last_known_good*.
2) Restart or roll nodes according to pool policy.
3) Verify at startup:
   * profile_pack_version matches pinned
   * compatibility_result == ok

h2. Mitigations short of rollback
Use only when rollback is costly and regression is localized.
* Reduce max batch size / tighten queue limits (protect tail latency)
* Reduce KV cache budget / enable stricter KV cache guardrails (prevent OOM)
* Disable specific kernel-selection toggles (if the regression signature matches known issue)
* Adjust prefill/decode fairness knobs (if p95 tail regresses under streaming/tool-calling mixes)

h1. Incident response playbook (profile-related regression)
Use this when *stop criteria* is met or customer impact is reported.

h2. Step 1 — Identify blast radius (5–10 minutes)
1) Confirm whether issue correlates with:
   * profile enablement time
   * specific pool/region
   * specific GPU SKU
   * specific model family or context-length cohort
2) Check selected_profile / override_source metrics for anomalies:
   * unknown SKU
   * unexpected override source
   * profile flapping after restarts

h2. Step 2 — Stabilize service (10–20 minutes)
1) If error rate or OOMs are elevated: *disable profiles* in affected pool immediately.
2) If tail latency is elevated but errors stable:
   * prefer disabling profiles first
   * alternatively reduce batching/queue knobs (if disabling profiles is not possible due to policy)
3) Confirm stabilization on dashboards.

h2. Step 3 — Collect evidence (while stabilization occurs)
Collect and attach to incident ticket:
* pool/region list, SKU
* runtime version + profile pack version
* selected_profile distribution snapshot
* top error signatures and counts
* representative request cohorts (seq len bucket, streaming on/off)
* runtime startup logs (compatibility + selection)

h2. Step 4 — Triage root cause (30–90 minutes)
Common root causes:
* *Profile selection mismatch*: SKU string variant not normalized; wrong profile applied.
* *Tail-latency regression*: prefill/decode fairness or queue limits too aggressive for traffic mix.
* *OOM/regression on L40S*: KV cache budget too large; fragmentation; long-context cohorts.
* *B200 experimental instability*: driver/CUDA mismatch; kernels not mature; must remain gated.

h2. Step 5 — Follow-up actions
* File/associate issue with:
  * profile pack version
  * runtime version
  * dashboards
  * mitigation applied
* Add/adjust perf-canary gate if regression was not caught.
* Update known-issues page with signature + mitigation.

h1. Private and Dedicated deployment notes
h2. Dedicated pools
* Prefer pool-level enablement with clear rollback path.
* Ensure customer-facing SLAs are not described as “guaranteed improvements”; use “expected behavior”.

h2. Private deployments
* Customers may pin profile versions and override select knobs via Helm values.
* Supportability requirement: customer overrides must remain within documented guardrails.
* When troubleshooting:
  * request the output of “dump effective runtime config”
  * verify the override order and which layer introduced the change

h1. B200-specific guardrails
* B200 profile is *experimental* until the maturity criteria is met.
* Must be behind an explicit feature flag.
* Only enable in approved pools/regions with Infra + SRE sign-off.
* Default fallback must be defined (e.g., “no profile / safe defaults”) when compatibility check fails.

Maturity criteria (minimum):
* 2 consecutive weeks of canary with no critical incidents
* workload matrix green for representative models and seq length buckets
* stable driver/CUDA baseline documented

h1. Post-rollout checklist
Within 2 business days of full enablement:
1) Publish a short summary:
   * perf deltas (latency/throughput) per SKU
   * any trade-offs observed
   * final pinned versions
2) Confirm dashboards are updated to segment by selected_profile.
3) Ensure oncall playbook links are current.
4) Update the “expected behavior” docs and known issues list.

h1. Appendix A — Quick decision tree
* Elevated 5xx or CUDA errors? → Disable profiles in affected pool immediately.
* OOM burst on L40S? → Disable profiles or tighten KV cache budget; treat as urgent.
* Tail latency up (p95/p99) with stable errors? → Disable profiles first; if not possible, reduce batching / adjust fairness.
* Only one region affected? → Roll back only that region/pool; keep others unchanged.
* Only one SKU affected? → Roll back SKU profile or pin to prior pack version.

h1. Appendix B — Standard change note template
Use in #eng-releases and #eng-runtime (or equivalent):

*Change:* Enable Hardware Profiles Pack
*Runtime version:* <runtime-x.y.z>
*Profile pack version:* <profiles-a.b.c>
*Scope:* <region/pools>, <SKU>
*Stage:* Canary / 25% / 100%
*Dashboards:* <links>
*Owner:* <name>
*Rollback:* Disable profiles in <pool> / pin to <previous version>

h1. Appendix C — Contact checklist
When paging or escalating, include:
* pool/region + SKU
* runtime + profile pack versions
* regression type (latency / throughput / errors / OOM)
* time window + graphs
* mitigation already attempted

title: Scheduler inspection and repro lab manual
content:
Summary

This runbook describes a reproducible lab process for inspecting scheduler-related anomalies in the serving runtime. It is intended for oncall engineers, SREs, and runtime devs who need to: detect a regression, reproduce the failure in a controlled environment, collect deterministic traces and kernel-level telemetry, and run targeted benchmarks to validate fixes.

Scope

- Components covered: dispatch, slot-manager, kernel-coordinator, prefetch-orchestrator, kvcache-agent
- Environments: staging (recommended), canary, and dev-lab nodes
- Not covered: hardware-level root cause analysis for faulty accelerators (separate HW Playbook)

Why this doc exists

Scheduler issues manifest as: elevated p99 latency, increased enqueue-to-dispatch time, unfair slot allocation, or kernel contention that appears as slowper-token regressions. Those symptoms often require coordinated tracing and a lab repro to validate kernel fixes, admission policy adjustments, or scheduler-profile changes.

Signal detection (what to watch for)

- Metric thresholds (alerts):
  - dispatch.enqueue_to_dispatch_p95 > 120ms for 5m
  - kernel-queue-depth spike > 3x baseline for 1m
  - per-gpu-active-slots variance (stddev) > 2.0 across hosts
  - request-abort-rate > 0.5% while throughput steady
- Correlated signs: elevated kernel tail latency, OOM churn, or frequent kernel-handoff logs with WARN level

Quick triage checklist (first 10 minutes)

1. Identify impacted cohort: model, route, and tenant tags (use observability route filters).
2. Confirm alert signals across both control-plane and data-plane: traces, kernel metrics, and host-level metrics.
3. Flame graph quick check: run `rbctl trace tail --service dispatch --filter "route=<route>" --last 2m` to capture high-level traces.
4. If the symptom is reproducible in staging, proceed to the repro lab steps below. Otherwise gather traces and escalate owner.

Repro lab: create a deterministic experiment

Goal: reproduce the observed pathology on an isolated set of nodes so we can iterate on kernel/scheduler changes. Follow these numbered steps.

Prerequisites
- Staging cluster with identical runtime binaries to production (tagged `prod-like-<date>`).
- Access to the experiment cluster and `rbctl` CLI with `trace:write` and `bench:run` roles.
- Synthetic workload generator `inference-loadgen` (v2.3+) available in staging.

Steps to repro

1. Snapshot current scheduler config: `rbctl config get scheduler --cluster staging > scheduler.snapshot.yaml`
2. Reserve 3 nodes for experiment: `rbctl node claim --cluster staging --nodes 3 --label lab=inspector`
3. Deploy a controlled model instance: `rbctl deploy model --name repro-model --image model-prod:sha --replicas 1 --routes "/test-repro" --cluster staging`
4. Start kernel/hotpath trace collection on the claimed nodes:
   - `rbctl trace start --targets kernel-coordinator,slot-manager --duration 180s --out /tmp/kernel-trace.json`
5. Run `inference-loadgen` with the recorded workload signature (use the original tenant's traffic shape if available)
   - Example: `inference-loadgen --route /test-repro --qps 80 --burst 200 --seq-dist gaussian --seed 1729 --duration 5m`
6. Capture kernel metrics and host state during the run:
   - `rbctl metrics collect --targets gpu:* --interval 1s --duration 6m --out /tmp/gpu-metrics.csv`
7. If the failure reproduces, record the exact command, config, and time window and move to deterministic tracing.

Collecting deterministic traces and artifacts

- Required artifacts: kernel-trace.json, dispatch-traces.json, gpu-metrics.csv, scheduler.snapshot.yaml, loadgen-config.json, and system dmesg/secure logs for the timeframe.
- Deterministic trace commands: 
  - `rbctl trace export --trace-id <id> --format ndjson > /tmp/trace.ndjson`
  - `rbctl kernel-snapshot --node <node> --out /tmp/kernel-snap.pb` (binary snapshot but referenced in the bug ticket)
- Tag all artifacts with experiment id `sched-lab-<YYYYMMDD>-<run>` in the ticket and storage.

Instrumentation checklist (what to enable)

- High-frequency kernel telemetry: kernel.dispatch_latency_ns, kernel.queue_depth, kernel.slot_acquire_latency
- Scheduler signals: admission_score, prefetch_hint_hit_ratio, slot_steal_count
- Host metrics: GPU_util, GPU_mem_alloc, nvlink_error_count, cpu_iowait
- KV cache metrics: kvcache.miss_rate, kvcache.prefetch_latency

Profiling and trace snippets (examples)

- Example: identify slot starvation from trace
  - In kernel-trace.json, find events `slot_acquire_attempt` -> `slot_acquired` and compute delta. A median > 10ms and p99 > 200ms indicates contention.
- Example `rbctl` commands to get a concise summary:
  - `rbctl trace summarize --in /tmp/trace.ndjson --group-by kernel_id,route --agg p50,p95,p99 --out /tmp/trace-summary.csv`
  - `jq -r '.events[] | select(.name=="slot_acquire") | [.ts, .node, .duration_ns] | @csv' /tmp/kernel-trace.json | head -n 50`

Benchmarking guidance to validate fixes

- Microbench: use `bench:kernel-sim` to run small, deterministic sequences that exercise kernel handoff and preemption. Target size: 1–8 concurrent sessions per GPU.
- End-to-end: `inference-loadgen` with full token generation to validate per-token latency under representative QPS. Use the same seed and sequence-length distribution as the incident.
- Acceptance criteria (example):
  - p99 end-to-end latency reduces by at least 20% vs baseline for the repro workload
  - slot_acquire_p99 < 80ms
  - kernel.queue_stall_time < 5s per minute aggregated

Common failure modes and focused mitigations

- Mode: kernel handoff thrash (many aborted handoffs)
  - Mitigation: increase slot handoff backoff from 20ms to 50ms; enable `slot-handoff-jitter=true`
- Mode: admission policy starvation for low-priority routes
  - Mitigation: add short-lived admission credits for low-priority routes during bursts; adjust economic-priority-governor thresholds (see related pages)
- Mode: prefetch thrash causing KV cache churn
  - Mitigation: tighten prefetch window heuristics and enable conservative prefetch profiling for the tenant

Escalation and ownership matrix

- Tier 1 (oncall runtime): initial triage, run reproducibility lab, collect traces
- Tier 2 (runtime dev): implement scheduler config adjustments, prototype kernel patch, run microbenchmarks
- Tier 3 (platform SRE/hw): if nvlink/gpu ECC errors or host-level anomalies are present, coordinate with infra and cloud provider

Postmortem and experiment hygiene

- Create an incident experiment ticket with: hypothesis, repro steps, artifacts, bench results, and selected fix candidate.
- Every experiment must have a rollback plan: restore scheduler.snapshot.yaml and redeploy the original config.
- Tag the experiment with the causality label and link to the regression-run in the benchmarking suite.

Appendix: quick-reference commands and sample config table

Commands
- rbctl config get scheduler --cluster staging > scheduler.snapshot.yaml
- rbctl node claim --cluster staging --nodes 3 --label lab=inspector
- rbctl trace start --targets kernel-coordinator,slot-manager --duration 180s --out /tmp/kernel-trace.json
- inference-loadgen --route /test-repro --qps 80 --burst 200 --seq-dist gaussian --seed 1729 --duration 5m
- rbctl metrics collect --targets gpu:* --interval 1s --duration 6m --out /tmp/gpu-metrics.csv

Sample config table (fields to capture as YAML or record in ticket)
| field | description | example |
| scheduler.policy | Admission and priority policy blob | economic-priority-governor v2 |
| scheduler.slot_handoff_backoff_ms | Backoff between handoff attempts | 50 |
| prefetch.window_ms | Prefetch lookahead window | 300 |
| kernel.kv_prefetch_enabled | Enable kvcache prefetch | true |

Related pages and references
- Scheduler policy language (internal) and admission governor design notes (see related_pages)
- Kernel telemetry contract: runtime-telemetry-sampling-policy (team-wiki)

Ownership and contact
- Primary owner: Anika Patel (runtime infra)
- SRE escalation: Marcus Liu
- Kernel owner: Sophie Nguyen

Revision history
- 2025-11-12: created by Anika Patel
- 2026-01-18: updated repro lab steps and added benchmark acceptance criteria

title: Known issue note: KV-cache pressure mitigation via model fallback (2025-06)
content:
h2. Issue
Under certain prompt distributions (high variance in context length), KV-cache memory pressure can cause abrupt throughput collapse on some A100 pools, leading to queue amplification and increased tail latency.

h2. Symptoms
* Rising GPU memory utilization with frequent allocator churn
* Increasing queue wait time and p95 latency
* Occasional 503 spikes from admission control

h2. Recommended mitigation (temporary)
If you observe KV-cache pressure and cannot immediately reduce context length or reconfigure batching, you may activate *automatic model fallback* to a smaller compatible model for the affected route(s) to maintain availability.

Suggested policy parameters:
* Trigger: queue_wait_ms > 300 OR gpu_mem_utilization > 92%
* Primary: rw-llama-3.1-70b-instruct
* Fallback: rw-llama-3.1-8b-instruct
* Disable once the pool is stable for 30 minutes

h2. Permanent fix
We are rolling out a KV-cache eviction tuning change and improved allocator settings in runtime release rr-2.18.

h2. References
* Runtime profiling playbook: KV cache section
* Related incident patterns: fallback activation during latency events

title: Allocator bump and soft-OOM simulation report
content:
Summary:

This document describes a reproducible simulation and postmortem of a class of incidents we call "allocator bump" leading to soft-OOM symptoms in mixed tenant GPU nodes. The goal is to provide:
- A concise defect description and root-cause hypothesis.
- A repeatable test harness and config used for simulations.
- Observable signatures (metrics, traces, kernel logs) for fast detection.
- Mitigations, short-term runbook steps, and long-term remediation options.

Background and impact:

We observed intermittent increases in per-request allocator reservation (an "allocator bump") during mixed workloads involving long-context chat and short-shot embed requests. The bump causes cross-tenant eviction churn and transient soft-OOM: allocation failures that do not immediately kill processes but trigger repeated kernel preemption and degraded latency for 3–10 minutes. Impacted customers experienced increased tokenization latency, higher error rates (502/504) on heavy tails, and elevated cost due to repeated KV-cache warmups.

Key symptoms observed in production:
- Sudden rise in node-level "reserved_bytes" (>20% above baseline) without corresponding increase in active sessions.
- Rapid eviction events across shards: eviction_rate increase by 5–15x.
- GPU CUDA OOM-type warnings followed by scheduler preemption events (see kernel logs).
- Traces show repeated cold-kv cache hits and model swap churn.

Root-cause hypothesis (short):

A combination of a kernel-level allocator regression and an uncommon sequence pattern (many concurrent short-lived requests interleaved with a few long-context generations) causes the allocator to allocate larger contiguous blocks for attention state than expected. The allocator fragmentation / rounding policy then prevents efficient compaction, bumping the effective reserved footprint and triggering eviction cascades. Regression window: kernel runtime change v2.14.1 -> v2.15.0.

Repro harness and test plan (exact steps):

Prerequisites:
- Test cluster with 4 heterogeneous GPU nodes (A100x4 and A10x4 mixed pool).
- Load generator: runtime-loadgen v0.9.0 (local binary).
- Model bundles: long-context chat (context 8192, model: redwood-7b-fast-ql) and short embed endpoint (seq_len 32, redwood-embed-small).
- Node config: kvcache_enabled=true, allocator_compaction_threshold=0.65, prefetch=on

1) Baseline run (validate steady state):
   - Start 100 concurrent short requests (qps 200) for 10m.
   - Start background 2 long-context sessions (persistent approach) each producing 2–3 generations per minute.
   - Collect metrics: node/reserved_bytes, eviction_rate, kernel_logs, tracer spans.

2) Stress run (trigger bump):
   - Increase short request concurrency to 600 (qps 1200) maintaining the 2 long-context sessions.
   - Run for 20m.
   - Observe reserved_bytes and eviction spikes.

Commands used (examples):

# start short-run generator
./runtime-loadgen --mode embed --qps 200 --concurrency 100 --model redwood-embed-small --duration 600

# start long-context sessions (simplified)
./runtime-loadgen --mode chat --persist-sessions 2 --model redwood-7b-fast-ql --context 8192 --rate 3/m --duration 1800

Collecting traces and kernel logs:
- Enable kernel debug level 3 on test nodes: sudo sysctl -w runtime.kernel.debug=3
- Start continuous trace sampling for allocation events: tracerctl start --events allocator:alloc,allocator:free,kernel:preempt --out alloc-trace.json

Repro results (observed):
- Baseline: reserved_bytes stable at ~12GB per node; eviction_rate low.
- Stress: reserved_bytes climbed to 18–22GB on A100 nodes over 2–5 minutes; eviction_rate spiked 8x.
- Traces show a recurring pattern: a long-generation allocation grabs a contiguous block, short jobs request many small allocations; allocator rounds small allocations into larger blocks when a fragmentation threshold is hit, then compaction does not free those blocks immediately (compaction gated by idle window), producing the bump.

Detection signatures (for alerting):
- Metric alert: node.reserved_bytes > node.reserved_bytes_p99 * 1.25 for 2m AND node.eviction_rate > 3x baseline.
- Trace signature: repeated allocator:alloc followed by kernel:preempt within 2s for the same process id, >50 occurrences in 5 minutes.
- Log grep pattern: "Allocator: compact skipped (idle_window)" repeated for multiple shard ids.

Short-term mitigations (runbook steps):
1) On detection, immediately increase compaction aggressiveness on affected nodes:
   - sudo runtimectl set allocator.compaction_policy aggressive
2) Temporarily drain new long-context sessions from the node: mark node cordon for long-context routes by updating routing policy:
   - runtime-router update-pool --node node-12 --route-pattern "/generate-long" --weight 0
3) If eviction churn is high, enable conservative admission for short requests: limit concurrency to 300 per node.
4) Collect full alloc-trace and kernel logs, attach to incident ticket.

Long-term remediation options (prioritized):
- P1: Fix kernel allocator rounding (release patch v2.15.1) to avoid rounding small allocations into large contiguous chunks under mixed load.
- P2: Add proactive compaction triggers tied to eviction_rate rather than only idle windows.
- P3: Improve routing heuristics to co-locate long-context and long-lived KV cache sessions on denser nodes and avoid mixing with high-churn short embedding lanes.
- P4: Metric-level SLOs for reserved_bytes and proactive autoscaling triggers for mixed pools.

Design notes and tradeoffs considered:
- Aggressive compaction has CPU/latency cost; we recommend gating it to nodes exhibiting sustained eviction > 3x baseline.
- Preventing allocator rounding will improve fragmentation but requires careful testing across kernels/accelerators (NV and AMD).

Telemetry and dashboards to add:
- New panel: Allocator footprint heatmap (reserved_bytes by shard, 1m resolution).
- Alert: "Allocator bump in mixed pool" with runbook link.
- Trace quicklink to the "allocator-alloc" event stream in the incident view.

Appendix A — Compact reproduction config (YAML):

cluster:
  pools:
    - name: mixed-gpu-pool
      nodes: 4
      types: [A100, A10]
runtime:
  allocator:
    compaction_threshold: 0.65
    rounding_granularity: 256KB
    compaction_policy: conservative
  kvcache: true
loadgen:
  short_embed:
    qps: 1200
    concurrency: 600
    seq_len: 32
  long_chat:
    sessions: 2
    context_len: 8192
    rps_per_session: 0.05

Appendix B — Example kernel log excerpt (sanitized):

[2025-03-12T14:05:03Z] allocator:alloc shard=shard-7 pid=2103 size=24MB rounded=32MB
[2025-03-12T14:05:03Z] allocator:alloc shard=shard-9 pid=4157 size=4KB rounded=256KB
[2025-03-12T14:05:04Z] kernel:preempt victim=pid=4157 reason=eviction
[2025-03-12T14:05:04Z] allocator:compact skipped shard=shard-7 reason=idle_window

Appendix C — Ownership and follow-ups:
- Incident owner: Aria Chen (serving-runtime)
- Kernel patch owner: Mei Tanaka (kernel-and-scheduling)
- Runbook update: SRE (oncall) to add detection signature and immediate compaction command.
- Timeline: aim to ship allocator rounding fix in 2 weeks (v2.15.1) with canary in non-production pools, 1–2 week observability validation window.

Contact and escalation:
For questions or to run the reproduction locally, ping #serving-runtime on Slack and add the tag "allocator-bump". For urgent customer impact, follow the oncall escalation in the oncall roster and attach the alloc-trace.json artifact.

Document history:
- 2024-11-12: created by Aria Chen (initial simulation notes).
- 2024-12-05: added production traces and mitigation commands after incident INC-2024-714.
- 2025-03-18: expanded runbook steps and shipped detection rule draft.

title: Workaround: 429 quota mismatch and rate‑limit headers
content:
## Summary
Customers may receive HTTP **429 Too Many Requests** while their dashboard (or internal estimates) suggest they are under quota. In most cases, this is expected behavior caused by **short-window rate limits** (requests/minute, tokens/minute, concurrent requests) rather than **plan quota** (daily/monthly token or embedding allotment). In a smaller set of cases, the confusion is due to:
- Misinterpreting response headers (rate limit vs quota signals)
- SDK retry behavior causing unintentional traffic amplification
- Header inconsistencies that were addressed in an engineering fix (see “Status / ongoing fix”)

This article provides customer-safe troubleshooting steps, common misconfigurations, and Support validation steps.

---

## What a 429 means at Redwood
A **429** indicates the request was blocked by an enforcement policy. The most common categories are:
1) **Rate limit exceeded (short window)**
   - Per API key / workspace limits such as requests per minute (RPM), tokens per minute (TPM), or concurrent in-flight requests.
2) **Quota / budget exceeded (longer window)**
   - Monthly/daily allotments, contract caps, or account-level safety caps.
3) **Protective throttling** (rare)
   - Temporary throttles during partial degradation to protect overall availability.

Important: A customer can be “under quota” for the month and still hit 429 due to short-window limits.

---

## Symptoms
Customers typically report one or more of:
- Increased 429s after an SDK upgrade (without intentional traffic increase)
- 429s occurring in bursts (e.g., at the top of the minute, after job fan-out, or during batch processing)
- Dashboard shows “quota remaining” but requests fail
- Rate limit headers appear inconsistent across endpoints or responses

---

## How to interpret rate limit / quota headers
### Headers you should look for
Depending on endpoint and deployment tier, responses may include some combination of:
- **Retry guidance**
  - `retry-after` (seconds) when the server can provide a safe retry window
- **Rate limit signals (short window)**
  - `x-redwood-ratelimit-limit-requests`
  - `x-redwood-ratelimit-remaining-requests`
  - `x-redwood-ratelimit-reset-ms`
  - (In some cases) token-based variants such as `x-redwood-ratelimit-limit-tokens`
- **Quota / budget signals (long window)**
  - `x-redwood-quota-remaining-tokens` (or similar account budget indicators when enabled)

### Practical rule of thumb
- If the response includes **rate limit remaining/reset** headers, treat the 429 as a **rate limit** event.
- If the response indicates **quota remaining = 0** (or an explicit “quota exceeded” classification in the error body), treat it as a **quota/budget** event.
- If headers are missing or unclear, rely on:
  - The structured error body classification (if present)
  - `retry-after`
  - Support-side telemetry confirmation using request IDs

### Why headers can look confusing
- Different endpoints may enforce different limit dimensions (e.g., chat completion vs embeddings).
- Concurrent usage across environments (prod + staging) with the same API key can deplete short-window limits unexpectedly.
- Client retries can multiply request volume, making the limit appear “too low”.

---

## Common customer-side causes (and fixes)
### 1) Concurrency spikes / fan-out jobs
**Pattern:** A batch job or queue consumer increases parallelism (threads/processes) and triggers 429.

**Fix (recommended):**
- Add client-side throttling:
  - Cap concurrent in-flight requests
  - Use a token bucket limiter at the application edge
- Stagger job starts (avoid synchronized bursts)
- For batch workloads, prefer larger batches where supported (and avoid micro-batches that increase RPM)

### 2) Auto-retry amplifying traffic
**Pattern:** After an SDK upgrade, 429 increases because the client retries aggressively and creates a feedback loop.

**Fix (recommended):**
- Ensure 429 retries respect `retry-after` when present.
- Use exponential backoff with jitter.
- Cap retries (do not retry indefinitely).
- Ensure retries are not happening at multiple layers (SDK + gateway + application).

**Guidance:**
- For non-idempotent operations, retries must be handled carefully. For chat/text generation, retries are generally safe if you:
  - Include an idempotency key (if supported by your integration)
  - Or ensure the request is safe to re-run from your business logic perspective

### 3) Mis-scoped API keys (shared across teams/environments)
**Pattern:** One API key used across prod/staging and multiple services.

**Fix (recommended):**
- Use separate API keys per environment and per workload class.
- If you must share a key, implement per-service client-side rate limiting.

### 4) Using streaming reconnect logic as “retry” without backoff
**Pattern:** Client reconnects repeatedly and quickly after a failure and unintentionally drives RPM/TPM.

**Fix (recommended):**
- Treat reconnect as a retry: backoff + jitter + max attempts.
- Log and surface request IDs for Support.

---

## Customer-safe troubleshooting checklist
Ask the customer to provide the following (copy/paste into an email or ticket):
1) **Time range** of the issue (with timezone)
2) **Region** (e.g., us-east, eu-west)
3) **Endpoint** (chat/completions/embeddings/rerank)
4) **Model** + model version pin (if applicable)
5) **SDK name + version** (or raw HTTP)
6) **2–3 request IDs** from failed 429 responses
7) The **full response headers** for a 429 (redact auth)
8) Current **client concurrency** and any recent deploys/config changes

### Recommended customer action
- Reduce concurrency by 50% for 15 minutes and observe whether 429s drop.
- Enable logging of request IDs and `retry-after` values.
- Confirm whether multiple environments share the same API key.

---

## Workaround patterns we recommend
### A) Implement standard 429 handling
- If `retry-after` is present: wait that duration, then retry.
- Else: exponential backoff starting at 250–500ms with jitter; cap at ~10–30s.
- Stop retrying after a small number of attempts (e.g., 3–5) and surface an error to the caller.

### B) Add a client-side limiter
- Concurrency limiter (max in-flight)
- Request-rate limiter (RPM)
- For token-heavy workloads: throttle by estimated tokens per request

### C) Upgrade to latest SDK / apply patch guidance
If the customer is on an older SDK version and seeing confusing 429/header behavior, recommend upgrading to the latest Redwood SDK release. If they cannot upgrade immediately, advise:
- Disable aggressive automatic retries
- Log headers and request IDs for Support verification

---

## Support validation steps (internal)
Use these steps to confirm whether the 429 is rate-limit vs quota vs an inconsistency.

### 1) Confirm classification from telemetry
Using the request IDs and timestamps:
- Check gateway/request logs for the enforcement reason
- Confirm which limiter fired (RPM/TPM/concurrency/quota/budget)
- Verify the customer workspace tier and configured limits

### 2) Cross-check customer-visible usage signals
- Compare:
  - Console usage charts (long-window)
  - Enforcement events (short-window)
- If the customer is “under monthly quota,” verify whether they hit:
  - Per-minute token or request caps
  - Concurrency caps

### 3) Look for retry amplification
Signals:
- Multiple near-identical requests within seconds
- Elevated request counts from a small number of client IPs/user agents
- SDK version change immediately preceding the spike

### 4) Header consistency spot-check
If the customer reports inconsistent headers:
- Collect 2–3 raw responses (headers + body) across endpoints
- Confirm whether responses include both quota and rate limit headers, and whether reset/remaining values are plausible
- If inconsistency is confirmed, link to the active engineering workstream addressing rate-limit header consistency and attach examples to the ticket

### 5) Decide whether to escalate
Escalate to Platform/On-call if:
- 429s spike across multiple customers/keys/regions (possible protective throttling)
- The enforcement reason in telemetry does not match headers returned to the customer
- The customer is enterprise/dedicated/private and impact meets P0/P1 criteria per the severity matrix

---

## When to escalate (customer-facing guidance)
Escalate to Redwood Support (or request a priority escalation) if any of the following apply:
- 429 rate is sustained and blocking production traffic for >15 minutes
- You are retrying with `retry-after` and still see persistent 429s at low concurrency
- Headers suggest quota is available but errors explicitly claim “quota exceeded,” or vice versa
- You can provide request IDs showing inconsistent header values between responses

---

## Status / ongoing fix
We have an engineering follow-up to improve consistency of rate-limit/quota headers and reduce ambiguity in 429 responses (including tests to prevent regressions). Until the fix is fully rolled out across all tiers/regions:
- Treat `retry-after` as the primary retry signal when present.
- Use request IDs for Support verification if header values appear contradictory.

---

## Appendix: Quick macros (Support)
**Request to customer (headers + IDs):**
“Please send 2–3 example request IDs that returned 429, the exact timestamp (with timezone), region, model, and the full response headers (redacting Authorization). This lets us confirm whether the 429 is caused by short-window rate limits (RPM/TPM/concurrency) vs account quota/budget.”

**Suggested mitigation:**
“Most 429s are short-window rate limits. Please reduce concurrency and implement exponential backoff with jitter (and honor `retry-after` when present). If you share an API key across prod/staging or multiple services, consider splitting keys or adding a client-side limiter.”

title: Mixed-workload scheduler prototype: known issues and edge cases
content:
## Overview
This page tracks known issues, edge cases, and operational pitfalls for the mixed-workload scheduler prototype (short/long classification + two-queue dispatch + token budget guardrails). It is intended for runtime engineers and SREs during benchmarking and canary.

**Scope:** scheduler behavior under mixed prompt-length distributions, interactions with the prefill/decode pipeline, KV cache pressure, and hardware/runtime-specific anomalies.

**Non-goal:** this is not a full QoS/tenancy policy document. For intended behavior and configuration semantics, see the design doc.

## Quick triage checklist (when something looks wrong)
1. Confirm the issue is actually *mixed-workload* related:
