   - If fast-path utilization > 92%: enable fast-path autoscale +20% surge for 15 minutes.
   - If burn-rate projection > 110%: enable tenant-level cost caps and trigger Budget_Exceeded_Predicted alert flow.
3) Mitigate (15–60 minutes)
   - Apply model downgrade for non-critical tenants.
   - If latency remains violated, consider regional routing to alternative region with spare capacity and notify customers of degraded latency with ETA.
4) Post-incident (within 72 hours)
   - Create a postmortem with traffic profile snapshots, decisions taken, and a recommended roadmap item if recurring.

Telemetry and instrumentation checklist
- Per-request: tenant_id, model_id, tokens_in, tokens_out, routing_path, kv_cache_hit, queue_wait_ms, worker_id.
- Aggregates: tokens/sec (1m/5m), p50/p95/p99 latencies, queue depth, fast-path utilization per-region.
- Cost attribution: cost per token by model variant and by routing_path; daily/weekly projection exports.

Dashboard template (short example instructions)
1. Create a multi-row dashboard titled: "SLO Economics — <tenant>"
2. Row 1: Latency heatmaps and p95 sparkline (time window 1h, step 30s)
3. Row 2: Token throughput + cost-per-1k-requests gauge with forecast annotation
4. Row 3: Routing breakdown (fast-path vs bulk-path) with percent and absolute tokens

Roadmap items (beyond scope)
- Q2 2026: Integrate budget projections into route decision engine for proactive throttling.
- Q3 2026: Per-tenant micro-A/B test harness to validate quantized variant quality before full rollout.
- Q4 2026: ML-driven prediction of short-term tail events for pre-warm scheduling.

Ownership and contacts
- Primary owner: eng-platform (Priya Iyer, eng-platform lead) — operational ownership for runbook and alarms.
- Runtime policy implementation: eng-serving-runtime (Marco Alvarez).
- Cost instrumentation and billing integration: finance-and-legal (Elena Novak).
- Escalation: oncall-sre rotation -> platform-oncall -> eng-platform-manager.

Change log (summary)
- 2025-09-15: Initial draft (Aisha R.).
- 2025-11-07: Added automated remediation recipes and decision thresholds (Miguel T.).
- 2026-02-18: Finalized dashboard templates and roadmap items, moved to published.

Appendix A — Example tenant policy YAML
```yaml
tenant_policy_id: tenant-6421
priority_profile: interactive
fast_path_capacity_pct: 75
fallback_grace_ms: 200
budget_saturation_pct: 85
quantized_variant: gptx-8q
```

Appendix B — Quick CLI snippets
- view burn-rate projection (internal): rdx metrics query "sum(token_cost_last_24h) * 30 / 24 by (tenant)"
- force enable grace queue for tenant: rdx control set-tenant-policy tenant-6421 --grace-ms 200 --force-apply

Related reading
- See: /eng-platform/runbooks/cold-start-warmup-orchestration-runbook-2026 for warmup patterns
- See: /eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/token-cost-attribution-and-explainable-trace-playbook-2026 for token cost instrumentation examples

End of document

title: CUDA sparse-attention degradation under burst load (investigation & mitigations)
content:
Summary
-------
This page documents a recurring production degradation mode observed in inference fleets running CUDA-accelerated sparse-attention kernels under short, high-intensity request bursts. Symptoms include elevated 99th/99.9th percentile token latency, sudden KV-cache thrashing, and transient GPU SM saturation that persists longer than the burst window. We describe detection signals, reproducible steps, short-term mitigations (runbook), and the engineering plan for a permanent fix.

Background
----------
We onboarded a custom sparse-attention kernel (sparse-cuda-v2) in Q4 2025 to reduce memory pressure and token compute for long-context models. In low-to-moderate steady-state traffic the kernel performs as expected. Over the last two months, multiple SRE and runtime teams observed repeated incidents where microbursts (50–300 concurrent short requests, <200 tokens) cause a 3–6x jump in tail latency and an increase in dropped streaming connections.

Scope and impact
----------------
- Affects: heterogeneous GPU pool types using sparse-cuda-v2 kernel (A100 and H100 variants tested).
- Percent of fleet observed: ~12% of nodes in west-2 region over Jan–Feb 2026.
- Customer impact: elevated tail latency for hosted API routes using these model variants; some enterprise customers observed timeouts against strict 500ms SLOs.

Observed symptoms & measurements
--------------------------------
- 99.9th token latency increases from baseline ~420ms to 1.8s during incidents.
- GPU SM util jumps to sustained 95–100% for 2–8s after a burst.
- Average batch size drops (due to preemption/priority shuffling) while in-flight kernels show increased warp serialization.
- KV-cache churn rate metric (kvcache.churn_rate) spikes by 5–12x.

Repro recipe (lab)
------------------
1. Use a test driver to send 250 concurrent 80-token requests over a 1s window to the model variant with sparse-cuda-v2. Example:

   sh ./tools/loadgen/run_burst.sh --concurrency 250 --tokens 80 --duration 1s --host inference-west-2.internal --model my-sparse-model:v2

2. Collect GPU traces (nsys) on a target node and record the kernel timeline:

   nsys profile --stats=true --output burst-profile %PID%

3. Capture runtime traces and KV metrics via the runtime tracer:

   curl -sS http://localhost:9080/debug/trace > /tmp/trace.json

4. Confirm the same signature: tail-latency spike aligned to a burst window and sustained SM saturation.

Telemetry & detection rules
--------------------------
We recommend the following production detectors to triage quickly. Add to alerts and dashboards where missing.

Table: Detection thresholds (text table)
Metric | Alert threshold | Recommended action
kvcache.churn_rate | > 8x baseline (5m) | Route to SRE, enable burst-mitigation runbook
gpu.sm_utilization | > 90% (1m sustained) combined with tail latency | Auto-scale eligible pool/shift traffic
model.tail_latency.99.9 | > 1200ms (5m) | Trigger rolling routing policy to fallback model-variant

Example Prometheus alert rule (yaml snippet):

ALERT SparseAttentionBurst
IF increase(kvcache_churn_rate_total[2m]) > 8
AND avg_over_time(gpu_sm_utilization[1m]) > 0.9
FOR 2m
LABELS {severity="page", team="runtime"}
ANNOTATIONS {summary="Sparse-attention burst signature: kvcache churn + gpu saturation"}

Immediate mitigations (runbook)
------------------------------
These steps are for on-call SREs to contain customer impact quickly. Follow the numbered procedure.

Runbook: emergency containment (SRE)
1) Identify affected nodes: query fleet telemetry for nodes with matching model variant and sm_utilization > 90%.
   - CLI: curl -sS http://telemetry-api.internal/query?query="gpu_sm_utilization>0.9 and model_variant=\"sparse-cuda-v2\""
2) Temporarily shift traffic for the impacted routing key to the dense fallback model-variant (dense-cuda-v1) via the routing API:
   - curl -X POST https://routing.internal/v1/route-shift -d '{"route":"/v1/generate","from_variant":"sparse-cuda-v2","to_variant":"dense-cuda-v1","percent":100}'
3) If shifting traffic is not possible, enable per-node burst backpressure by setting admission_controller.max_burst_inflight=50 on the node agent and trigger a graceful drain:
   - kubectl patch daemonset runtime-node-agent -n runtime --type=json -p '[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/env/0/value","value":"50"}]'
4) If nodes remain saturated, scale the pool by +20% capacity or enable emergency autoscale for the dedicated pool.
5) After mitigation, collect traces and attach to the incident ticket. Note any repro artifacts and timestamps.

Short-term engineering remediation (2–4 weeks)
----------------------------------------------
- Hotfix A (config): Reduce the eager thread concurrency in sparse-cuda-v2 kernel launcher when per-GPU concurrent requests exceed 96. Configuration patch: set kernel_launch.max_worker_threads = 64 for burst conditions. This reduces thread oversubscription and warp serialization.
- Hotfix B (runtime): Add a rapid cool-down slot for KV-cache eviction to avoid over-eviction during bursts: kvcache.eviction_cooldown_ms = 5000.
- Monitoring: Add per-kernel warp-serialization counters and expose them through kernel telemetry.

Long-term engineering plan (Q2–Q3)
----------------------------------
1) Kernel rewrite: introduce cooperative micro-scheduling within sparse kernel so that kernel work yields when global stream stalls are detected (non-blocking cooperative yield). Goal: reduce post-burst SM hang time by >50%.
2) Admission-controller enhancement: predictive admission controller that uses short-term traffic forecasts (burst detector) to apply temporary batching policies and pre-warm KV-cache for hot keys.
3) Scheduler: extend GPU scheduler to prefer batch-consolidation over preemptive micro-batching when the burst is predicted to finish within X seconds (configurable X).
4) Regression tests: add a burst-sculpting synthetic test to the benchmarking suite that asserts tail latency and kvcache churn bounds.

Root cause hypothesis
---------------------
Our working hypothesis is a compound interaction: a) the sparse kernel's internal thread-launch strategy aggressively spans SM warps to improve utilization under steady-state; b) during a microburst the host enqueues many small kernel launches causing kernel serialization and increased register pressure; c) combined with aggressive KV-cache eviction policy, the runtime thrashes cache and prolongs kernel busy signals, leading to sustained SM saturation beyond the burst window.

Data to collect for RCA
-----------------------
- nsys timeline and kernel launch parameters (grid, block, shared mem) for affected windows.
- kvcache.events (evict, fetch, miss) with per-key provenance.
- per-kernel warp-serialization and occupancy metrics.
- host-side thread pool statistics and kernel launch latencies.

Acceptance criteria for a permanent fix
--------------------------------------
- Tail latency 99.9th reduced to <= 750ms under the same synthetic burst profile.
- kvcache.churn_rate under bursts reduced to <= 2x baseline.
- No regression in steady-state throughput (within 5% of current).

Open action items and owners
---------------------------
- SRE: add detection alert and dashboard — Miguel Torres (owner) — due 2026-03-05
- Runtime: implement eviction_cooldown and config gate — Chen Li (owner) — due 2026-03-12
- Kernel: prototype cooperative-yield in sparse-cuda-v3 — Rina Sato (owner) — due 2026-04-02
- Bench: add burst-sculpting test to perf-suite — Priya Bhandari (owner) — due 2026-03-22

Related artifacts and logs (examples)
------------------------------------
- Example kernel launch line from nsys:
  Kernel: sparse_attention_v2 grid=(128,1,1) block=(256,1,1) shared=64KB regs=64
- Sample kvcache event: {timestamp: 2026-02-04T16:03:12.123Z, node: gpu-12, key: "sess:abcd1234:prefix", event: "evict", reason: "memory_pressure", age_ms: 12}

Operational notes and follow-ups
-------------------------------
- When shifting routes to a dense variant, watch for memory pressure on dense nodes; do not exceed 70% memory utilization per GPU.
- Add a scheduled run of the lab repro every week to catch regressions.
- Document kernel-exported telemetry fields in the telemetry contract docs before v3 rollout.

Appendix: quick detection checklist (for on-call)
------------------------------------------------
1. Check alerts: SparseAttentionBurst firing?
2. Inspect gpu.sm_utilization and model.tail_latency.99.9 aligned to burst timeframe.
3. If confirmed, run mitigation runbook steps 1–4.
4. Attach traces and escalate to Runtime oncall if Hotfix A/B needed.

If you have additional logs or repro traces, attach them to the incident ticket and ping #runtime-incidents with the ticket link.

-- Priya Bhandari, Runtime Performance Engineering

title: airgap-gpu-image-promotion-and-hsm-signing-pipeline
content:
Overview:

This page documents the recommended CI/CD and promotion pipeline for GPU runtime images and Terraform artifacts intended for air-gapped / on-prem Redwood Private deployments. The design balances secure provenance (HSM-backed signing and offline attestation), reproducible image promotions, and fast rollback semantics while remaining operable in environments with limited or no outbound network access.

Scope:
- Build and sign GPU node images, container runtimes, and inference runtime bundles.
- Produce Terraform module release artifacts and a promotion flow to on-prem registries/artifact stores.
- Provide an offline verification and attestation process for customer-side import.
- Define rollback and patching runbooks for emergency CVE or kernel regressions.

Intended audience:
- Infra/Platform engineers responsible for Redwood Private on-prem packaging.
- SRE and Security engineers who review supply-chain and signing controls.
- Customer deployment engineers who operate air-gapped cluster ingestion.

Key goals and constraints:
- Cryptographic signing of images and Terraform state/artifacts using HSM (cloud HSM for hosted builds, portable HSM/Nitro enclave for partner builds).
- Minimal trust bootstrap: customers verify signatures and a concise provenance bundle prior to activation.
- Offline-friendly artifact export formats (OCI image tarballs, signed sbom + provenance file, terraform module bundles).
- Fast rollback within a 30-minute window for node image revert with no remote registry access.

High-level architecture (text diagram):

Buildkite/CI --> Build Agents (GPU-enabled) --> Image Signing Service (HSM) --> Artifact Staging (S3/GCS) --> Promotion Orchestrator --> Airgap Export Package

Components and responsibilities:
- CI (Buildkite): orchestrates reproducible builds, runs unit/e2e tests, and produces SBOMs. Uses ephemeral GPU runners with cached dependencies.
- Image Builder: Packer / Kaniko / buildx pipelines that output OCI image manifests and tarballs.
- Signer Service: centralized signing service with HSM (AWS CloudHSM or YubiHSM in SOC2 ops room). Creates detached signatures and a signed provenance JSON (build id, git commit, artifact hashes, sbom hash, signing key id).
- Promotion Orchestrator: a lightweight operator (go) that gamely moves artifacts from staging to the on-prem bundle builder, records promotions in the release ledger (signed), and triggers export packaging.
- Export Package: zip/tar containing images (OCI tarballs), signed provenance.json, sbom.json, terraform-module.tar.gz, and an import-manifest.md with verification steps.

Prerequisites and security controls:
- Attestation keys rotate quarterly via KMS with automated key rotation playbook.
- CI runners must be ephemeral and attested (node attestation) before build job runs.
- All build outputs have SBOM (CycloneDX) and are linked to a reproducible build-id.
- Terraform modules and tfstate schemas are hashed and signed along with images.

CI/CD flow (detailed):
1) Trigger: PR merge to release branch (release/*) or manual release ticket.
2) Build stage (Buildkite):
   - Checkout pinned commit.
   - Run container/image builds with deterministic build args (BUILD_DATE, SOURCE_COMMIT).
   - Produce SBOM and layer hashes (cyclonedx + har).
   - Run unit tests and a small inference smoke test on a canary dataset (sec 60 sec limit).
3) Attestation & Signing:
   - Upload artifacts to a secure staging bucket (private).
   - Invoke Signer Service: request HSM-signed detached signatures and produce provenance.json (signed with a CI release key identifier).
   - Signer returns signature, signing_key_id, and timestamp.
4) Promotion Orchestrator:
   - Default policy: after successful sign and smoke test, mark artifact as candidate.
   - Human approval gate for air-gapped export (2 approvers: Security + Platform).
   - On approval, orchestrator builds Export Package and writes an entry to the release ledger (signed ledger record).
5) Export Packaging:
   - Create OCI tarball with images and include provenance.json + sbom.json + terraform bundle.
   - Run checksum (sha256) for package and sign final package manifest.
6) Delivery:
   - For customer self-pull: provide signed package and instructions for offline import.
   - For partner-managed import: deliver via encrypted removable media and provide HSM public key for verification.

On-prem import and verification (customer steps):
1) Verify package signature using provided public key (commands):
   - sha256sum package.tar.gz && openssl dgst -sha256 -verify public.pem -signature package.sig package.tar.gz
2) Unpack and verify image manifests against provenance.json.
3) Load OCI tarballs into private registry (registry restore commands provided).
4) Apply Terraform module bundle to control plane in a dry-run (terraform plan) and verify provider plugin hashes.
5) Run importer verifier script (sh importer-verify.sh) which validates SBOM/ signatures and performs sample inference test on a staging GPU node.

Rollback and emergency patching:
- Rollback windows: we target 30-minute rollback to previously signed image. Achieved by: keeping last three signed images in local cache + enabling offline revert script on node provisioning host.
- Emergency CVE process:
  1. Create hotfix branch and trigger emergency build (fast-path CI).
  2. Sign and package with expedited approvals (automated security scan + single approver from Security on-call).
  3. Distribute hotfix bundle using the same airgap process and follow immediate apply with accelerated cluster drain window.
- Rollback runbook steps (abridged):
  1. Identify bad promotion id in release ledger.
  2. On the provisioning host, run revert script: ./revert-to-image.sh --promotion-id <id> --nodes <node-group>.
  3. Verify node rejoin and warm KV cache seed (run kv-cache-warmup job).
  4. Monitor errors for 15 minutes; if degradation persists, escalate to SRE on-call.

Testing matrix and CI gates:
- Required gates for promotion: unit tests, deterministic-image-hash-check, SBOM completeness, kernel compatibility check, inference smoke test (latency < 300ms, output sanity pass), security static scan (SCA) pass.
- Optional gates for expedited path: allow skip of non-blocking long-running integration tests with explicit human acknowledgement.

Terraform + IaC considerations:
- Terraform module bundles are versioned with semver and a signed CHANGES.md.
- The Orchestrator embeds a ‘tf-lock.json’ snapshot to ensure providers and plugin binaries match the promoted artifact.
- For customers who cannot run provider plugins from public registries, we include a provider plugin bundle with SHA256 and signature.

Operational runbook snippets (actionable):
- Verify a package: ./tools/verify-package --package ./package.tar.gz --key ./public.pem  # exits non-zero on mismatch
- Load images to local registry: ctr image import images.tar  # followed by registry sync script
- Import terraform bundle: tar -xzf tf-modules.tar.gz && terraform init -plugin-dir=./plugins && terraform plan
- Force revert of nodes: ./scripts/force-node-revert.sh --group infra-gpu-01 --image-id <signed-image-id> --reason "kernel-regression"

SLOs and operational thresholds for private deployments (recommendation):
- Promotion time-to-deliver (signed package ready): <= 2 hours for standard releases, <= 30 minutes for hotfixes.
- Verification time (customer import verification): <= 60 minutes (documented walk-through helps).
- Rollback completion: <= 30 minutes to restore previously known-good image on affected node group.

Ownership and escalation:
- Primary owner: infra-release-team (Platform) — paged via #infra-release and on-call rotation.
- Security owner: sec-supply-chain — must approve airgap promotions.
- Escalation path: on-call infra -> infra-release lead -> sec lead -> CTO if cross-customer outage.

Open decisions and follow-ups:
- Decide whether to embed signed kernel modules in the image or provide separately as a module bundle for customers who require FIPS/HSM validation.
- Evaluate using in-toto for richer provenance (action: prototype Q4 2025).
- Pilot local YubiHSM workflow with two customers in EU (action: schedule workshops).

References and related pages:
- Preflight acceptance checklist: /confluence/eng-private-deployments/deployment-guides/preflight-private-deploy-acceptance-checklist

title: Paged Attention Memory Spikes (OOM) — Allocator & Block Manager Tuning Guide
content:
## Overview
This page documents a recurring production failure mode for paged-attention model shards: GPU memory spikes and occasional OOMs under high concurrency and long KV cache lifetimes. The issue typically manifests as allocation storms (cudaMalloc/cudaFree) triggered by frequent block-manager compaction sweeps, leading to fragmentation and latency tail regressions.

This guide consolidates what we learned from the initial canary regressions (runtime rollout around commit f3a9b2c) and subsequent fixes shipped in later runtime releases.

## Symptoms
### What you’ll see
- Sudden GPU memory spikes on specific shards (often correlated with high QPS and long-running sessions).
- Latency tail regression (p99/p999) coincident with allocator activity.
- OOMs shortly after a series of compaction events.

### Representative log snippet
```
W blockmgr: compacting 24 blocks -> moved 18, freed 6, compaction_cost_ms=42
I kvcache: reserve_block(0x7f8c) -> size=256k
E allocator: cudaMalloc failed after 3.1s, retrying
OOM on device 0, requested 1.2GB
```

## Root causes (most common)
1. **Fragmentation + small allocation churn**
   - Default allocator path issues many device allocations when compaction moves blocks and temporary attention buffers are not reused.
2. **Allocator arena/pool too small for workload**
   - A small arena leads to frequent device allocations under sustained load.
3. **Aggressive compaction behavior**
   - Compaction that attempts to move too many blocks in a single sweep can create a cascading allocation burst.

## Immediate mitigations (recommended order)
### 1) Enable CUDA async pool allocator (cudaMallocAsync)
**When to use:** Any paged-attention deployment where compaction frequency is non-trivial (most high-QPS clusters).

**Why it helps:** Reduces cudaMalloc/cudaFree storms by routing allocations through a pool.

**Caveats:**
- cudaMallocAsync changes lifetime semantics. Buffers must be returned promptly to avoid pool bloat.
- Pool fragmentation is still possible when block sizes are highly variable.

### 2) Increase allocator arena size
Empirically, increasing the per-GPU arena/pool reserve reduces allocation hot-path noise.

**Current guidance (2026-02):**
- Start at **256MB** per GPU for mid-size models (e.g., OPT 2–7B class).
- Use **512MB** per GPU for very high concurrency or long session lifetimes.

Note: Our runtime defaults were raised after the initial incident; confirm your deployed version before overriding.

### 3) Tune paged-attention block size
Block size is a tradeoff:
- Smaller blocks => more blocks => more compaction activity and allocation churn.
- Larger blocks => fewer compactions and fewer allocations, but more internal slack (wasted memory in partially filled blocks).

**Current recommendation:**
- Prefer **512KB** blocks for most production workloads.
- Avoid **1MB** unless allocation call counts dominate and you have headroom for internal slack.

## Tuning results (reference)
The following benchmark matrix (originally reproduced on redwood/opt-2.7b, seq_len=2048, steady QPS ~1200 on prod-ish canary) shows typical trends:

```
results:
- block=256k + default alloc: p99=120ms, mem_peak=18.1GB, alloc_calls=1780
- block=256k + async pool:   p99=90ms,  mem_peak=15.9GB, alloc_calls=320
- block=512k + async pool:   p99=68ms,  mem_peak=16.8GB, alloc_calls=210
- block=1MB   + async pool:  p99=72ms,  mem_peak=18.9GB, alloc_calls=140
```

Interpretation:
- **Async pool** produces the biggest win by reducing allocation call volume.
- **512KB blocks** typically minimize latency tail with acceptable memory footprint.
- **1MB blocks** may reduce alloc calls further but can increase wasted memory.

## Standard configuration (recommended starting point)
### Runtime config (JSON)
```
{
  "allocator": "cuda_async_pool",
  "arena_size_bytes": 268435456,
  "enable_workspace_reserve": true,
  "paged_attn_block_size_bytes": 524288,
  "compaction_max_relocate_fraction": 0.60
}
```

Notes:
- `arena_size_bytes`: start at 256MB; increase to 512MB if pool high-water repeatedly hits the cap during sustained traffic.
- `paged_attn_block_size_bytes`: 512KB default is recommended unless a model has extreme KV sparsity.
- `compaction_max_relocate_fraction`: safety guard to prevent compaction from attempting a massive sweep. Earlier experiments used 0.75; production experience showed 0.60 is safer under bursty loads.

### Canary rollout guidance
1. Enable flags on a small canary set (e.g., 5 nodes / <5% traffic).
2. Observe for 24 hours:
   - allocator call count (rate)
   - pool high-water mark
   - compaction runs and compaction duration
   - OOM count and retry logs
   - p99/p999 latency for affected routes
3. If stable, roll out gradually in 25% increments.

## Observability: what to measure
Track these metrics (names may differ by runtime version; use the closest equivalent):
- `alloc_call_count` (or `cuda_alloc_calls_total`)
- `pool_high_water_bytes`
- `pool_current_bytes`
- `compaction_runs_total`
- `compaction_cost_ms` (histogram)
- `kvcache_reserved_blocks`
- `oom_events_total`

Red flags:
- Rising `pool_high_water_bytes` with flat traffic suggests buffers are not being returned.
- `compaction_runs_total` spiking during steady-state suggests block size too small or compaction thresholds too aggressive.

## Troubleshooting checklist
1. Confirm allocator mode
   - Ensure the deployment is actually using `cuda_async_pool` (misconfigurations commonly fall back to default).
2. Check arena/pool sizing
   - If pool high-water reaches the configured max repeatedly, increase `arena_size_bytes`.
3. Validate block size
   - If compaction runs are frequent and move many blocks, try 512KB.
4. Audit temporary buffers
   - Ensure attention workspace buffers and temporary blocks are reused rather than reallocated each request.
5. Compaction safety
   - Confirm compaction guard is enabled to avoid single-sweep relocation bursts.

## Release notes / behavioral changes
- Enabling `cudaMallocAsync` changes how memory reuse behaves. Include a release note when toggling this on for customer-facing clusters.
- Block-size changes can shift memory footprint slightly (often upward due to slack) even while reducing OOM risk.

## Ownership and escalation
- Owner: Serving Runtime (eng-serving-runtime)
- Escalate to: #eng-runtime with (a) model name, (b) seq_len / concurrency, (c) allocator config, (d) compaction metrics snapshot, and (e) a 10-minute profiler capture if available.

title: KV Cache Compaction: Known Risks, Failure Modes, and Mitigations
content:
## Summary
KV cache compaction reduces GPU memory fragmentation and mitigates burst-driven tail latency under mixed sequence lengths. This page documents known risks, failure modes we have observed or expect in production-like conditions, and the required mitigations/guardrails.

This is not a design doc; it is an operator- and reviewer-oriented risk register meant to be referenced during:
- rollouts (internal canary → hosted subset → dedicated pools)
- incident response / oncall
- perf regressions (p95/p99 spikes)
- correctness investigations

For operational steps, use the runbook: **Runtime KV Cache Compaction Runbook**.

---

## Scope and assumptions
Applies to runtime versions shipping KV compaction + tier-aware eviction behind feature flags (runtime-1.22 train).

Assumptions:
- Compaction is **budgeted** (time and/or bytes moved) and integrated with scheduler phases.
- Eviction may be enabled as a safety valve when fragmentation or capacity pressure persists.
- Metrics and tracing are present per the fragmentation metrics standard.

---

## Risk register (known risks → signals → mitigations)
The table below is intended as a quick index. Details and kill-switch guidance follow.

| Risk / failure mode | Primary impact | Likely signals | Default mitigation | Immediate operator action |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Compaction stalls decode (budget too large or wrong phase) | p95/p99 latency spike, throughput dip | p99 jumps correlated with compaction spans; increased scheduler loop time; compaction_time_ms spikes | Enforce compaction budgeting at safe boundaries; cap per-step time/bytes | Reduce budget; disable background compaction; if severe, disable compaction |
| Copy/pack overhead too high at steady state | Token cost increase, throughput regression | tokens/sec drop; GPU memcpy/LDST utilization spikes; bytes_moved high even when fragmentation low | Trigger only above frag threshold; hysteresis; limit moved bytes per minute | Raise frag trigger; lower budget; ensure eviction isn’t thrashing |
| Thrash cycle: compact ↔ evict ↔ reallocate | Instability under burst traffic | evictions_per_min high; bytes_moved high; frag ratio oscillates; queueing/backpressure increases | Add hysteresis; cap evictions; tie eviction to overload state | Temporarily disable eviction OR raise eviction thresholds; evaluate workload/policy |
| Rare correctness hazard during relocation (stale mapping / race) | Wrong outputs, crashes, leaks | CRC/assert failures; KV page refcount anomalies; intermittent wrong tokens (hard to detect) | Strict relocation state machine; pinning rules; cancellation handling; stress tests | Disable compaction immediately; preserve traces and allocator snapshots; escalate to Runtime |
| Cancellation during relocation edge case | Page leak, stall, inconsistent allocator state | Increased “orphaned pages” counter; stuck relocation state; elevated OOM risk | Two-phase commit relocation; cancellation-aware rollback path | Disable compaction; drain pool if allocator health degraded |
| Model-specific behavior (long context / high KV footprint) | Earlier eviction, higher compaction pressure | Eviction triggers at lower QPS; OOM risk when bursts overlap | Per-model defaults; tier-aware policy; more conservative budgets | Apply model/profile overrides; consider dedicated capacity |
| Interaction with prefix/KV caching policies | Unexpected evictions of cached prefixes; cost increase | prefix hit-rate drop; cache miss spikes; evictions attributed to prefix pages | Mark prefix pages as preemptible with separate caps; tier-aware selection | Disable prefix eviction class or raise caps; coordinate with routing policy |
| Metrics overhead / tracing overhead | Small but real perf regression | p50/p95 regression after enabling spans; CPU overhead increases | Sampling; conditional spans; perf gates in CI | Reduce sampling; disable verbose spans in hot paths |
| Kill-switch propagation delay | Slow mitigation during incident | Kill-switch flipped but behavior persists for minutes | Define propagation SLO; support “local override” | If delay exceeds SLO, use pool-level config override / drain |

---

## Detailed risks and mitigations

### 1) Compaction-induced latency spikes (scheduler stalls)
**What happens:** If compaction work (bytes moved, copy kernels, metadata updates) is executed in the wrong place or with excessive per-step budget, decode can stall. This tends to show up as p95/p99 spikes during sustained decode, especially when churn is high.

**Where we’ve seen it:**
- When compaction ran during decode loops rather than at prefill/decode boundaries.
- When background compaction did not respect a global per-GPU time budget.

**Signals to watch (must be on dashboards):**
- `kv_compaction_time_ms` (per-step and total)
- `kv_compaction_bytes_moved_total` and bytes moved per minute
- scheduler loop time / “scheduler iteration” latency
- trace exemplars: compaction spans overlapping with long request spans

**Mitigations/guardrails:**
- Budget compaction by **time and bytes** and enforce budgets at scheduler integration points.
- Prefer incremental compaction at safe boundaries; keep background compaction strictly capped.
- Add hysteresis: do not repeatedly compact if fragmentation is already below the “clear” threshold.

**Operator guidance:**
- First response: reduce per-step budget (time/bytes) and confirm p99 stabilizes.
- If p99 continues to rise or correctness is uncertain: disable compaction (see kill-switch section).

---

### 2) Increased copy overhead (throughput regression)
**What happens:** Compaction does real work: device-to-device copies and metadata updates. If triggered too aggressively, compaction can reduce tokens/sec and increase cost.

**Common root causes:**
- Fragmentation trigger threshold set too low for the workload.
- No hysteresis: compaction runs frequently even when benefits are marginal.
- Compaction target selection causes excessive movement (e.g., moving “hot” pages repeatedly).

**Signals:**
- tokens/sec down with stable request mix
- `kv_compaction_bytes_moved_total` grows continuously even when `kv_fragmentation_ratio` is stable/low
- GPU copy engine / memory bandwidth saturation during compaction windows

**Mitigations:**
- Trigger compaction only above a fragmentation ratio threshold and require sustained breach for N seconds.
- Add “bytes moved per minute” ceiling to prevent runaway overhead.
- Validate default budgets separately for Hosted vs Dedicated pools.

---

### 3) Thrash between compaction and eviction
**What happens:** Under burst traffic, the system may compact (to reclaim contiguous space), then evict (to meet capacity), then reallocate, causing oscillations. This is more likely when:
- fragmentation is high,
- headroom is low, and
- eviction selection removes sequences that immediately re-enter decode.

**Signals:**
- `kv_evictions_total` rising rapidly
- `kv_compaction_bytes_moved_total` rising rapidly at the same time
- fragmentation ratio oscillating rather than trending downward
- backpressure events increase (queue length and/or admission control triggers)

**Mitigations:**
- Introduce hysteresis and cooldown windows for both compaction and eviction.
- Cap eviction rate per GPU/pool and prefer evicting the least disruptive classes first.
- Tie eviction activation to overload/backpressure states rather than raw fragmentation alone.

**Operator guidance:**
- If p99 spikes correlate with high eviction rate: temporarily raise eviction thresholds or disable eviction first.
- If allocator health is degrading (or OOM risk is elevated): disable compaction and drain/rotate capacity.

---

### 4) Correctness hazards during relocation (rare but highest severity)
**What can go wrong:**
- Stale mapping from sequence → KV pages after relocation.
- A race between scheduler ownership and allocator relocation state.
- Refcount underflow/overflow causing premature reuse.
- Partial copy + metadata commit leading to “torn” KV state.

**Why it’s hard:** Wrong-output failures are intermittent and can look like model nondeterminism. Treat any suspected correctness issue as **Severity 0** for the feature and disable compaction until proven otherwise.

**Must-have invariants (review checklist):**
- Relocation must be atomic from the perspective of consumers (two-phase commit: copy → validate → swap mapping).
- Cancellation must not leave sequences with mixed old/new KV pointers.
- Pages must not be returned to free lists until no consumers remain (refcount correctness).
- “Pinned” sessions (or protected classes) must not be relocated/evicted unless explicitly allowed.

**Signals / indicators:**
- allocator invariants/asserts firing
- `kv_orphaned_pages` or equivalent health counter increases
- crashes in relocation code path
- unexplained token anomalies correlated with compaction spans (strong but rare)

**Mitigation:**
- Keep compaction behind a feature flag with a fast disable path.
- Require stress tests that include cancellations, partial streaming, and adversarial churn.

**Operator guidance:**
1) Disable compaction immediately.
2) Preserve evidence: allocator snapshots, traces with exemplars, request IDs.
3) Escalate to Runtime TL (Omar) and correctness reviewer (Noah).

---

### 5) Cancellation during relocation (known edge case class)
**What happens:** A request cancellation can occur while relocation is copying or before metadata commit. If not handled, this can leak pages, stall compaction state machines, or leave allocator metadata inconsistent.

**Signals:**
- elevated cancellation rate + elevated compaction retries
- allocator “in progress relocation” counters never return to zero
- GPU memory usage increases without a corresponding increase in active sequences

**Mitigations:**
- Cancellation-aware rollback path that returns pages to a consistent state.
- Timeouts: relocation must not hold locks/ownership beyond a bounded window.

**Operator guidance:**
- If allocator health metrics trend negative (or OOM risk increases), disable compaction and consider draining the pool.

---

### 6) Model- and workload-specific behaviors
Some workloads make compaction/eviction more sensitive:
- **Long-context chat**: larger KV footprint per sequence → less headroom; fragmentation hurts earlier.
- **Mixed prompt lengths + bursty arrivals**: worst-case fragmentation patterns.
- **High concurrency on small GPUs**: compaction/eviction triggers more frequently.

**Model-specific considerations to document in overrides:**
- GQA/MQA vs full attention: different KV shapes can change page packing efficiency.
- Very large hidden sizes: more expensive copies per token of KV.
- Extremely long max sequence settings: compaction may help, but eviction risk rises if headroom is mis-estimated.

**Mitigations:**
- Tier/model/profile overrides for:
  - fragmentation trigger and hysteresis
  - per-step budget (ms/bytes)
  - eviction enablement and rate limits
- Dedicated pools may use higher budgets if latency SLO allows and throughput stability is the goal.

---

### 7) Interaction with prefix cache / cached prompts
If prefix caching is enabled, compaction/eviction policies must treat cached prefixes as a distinct class:
- Evicting prefixes can reduce hit-rate and increase prefill cost.
- Relocating prefix pages too aggressively can increase bytes moved without improving fragmentation.

**Mitigations:**
- Separate accounting/metrics for prefix pages vs active decode pages.
- Class-based eviction (prefer evicting lowest priority and most safely recomputable data first).

---

### 8) Observability and “silent failure” risks
Compaction can fail silently if:
- metrics are missing or mislabeled
- dashboards don’t correlate compaction to latency
- sampling is too low to capture exemplars during rare spikes

**Requirements:**
- All required metrics must match the naming/definition standard.
- Dashboards must include correlation panels: fragmentation vs p99, bytes moved vs p99, evictions vs p99.
- Tracing spans must include request IDs and allocator state tags sufficient to debug.

---

## Kill-switch and safe-disable guidance
This section is intentionally explicit for oncall use. Exact flag names may differ by environment; confirm current names in the runbook.

### Recommended kill-switch hierarchy
Disable in this order depending on symptoms:
1) **Eviction** (if thrashing or customer-visible behavior suggests excessive session drops)
2) **Background compaction** (if p99 spikes correlate with compaction windows)
3) **All compaction** (if correctness is suspected, allocator health degrades, or p99 is severe)

### Common runtime config flags (reference)
- `runtime.kv_compaction.enabled` (bool)
- `runtime.kv_compaction.background_enabled` (bool)
- `runtime.kv_compaction.budget_ms_per_step` (int)
- `runtime.kv_compaction.budget_bytes_per_step` (int)
- `runtime.kv_compaction.bytes_moved_ceiling_per_min` (int)
- `runtime.kv_compaction.frag_trigger_ratio` (float)
- `runtime.kv_compaction.frag_clear_ratio` (float)
- `runtime.kv_eviction.enabled` (bool)
- `runtime.kv_eviction.max_evictions_per_min` (int)
- `runtime.kv_eviction.tier_protection` (enum/bitmask)

Notes:
- Hosted and Dedicated defaults may differ; do not assume one pool’s safe budget is safe for another.
- Some pools enforce guardrails via rollout policy in addition to runtime flags.

### Safe-disable semantics (what to expect)
- Disabling compaction should stop new relocation steps quickly, but in-flight steps may complete.
- Disabling eviction should stop selecting new victims; existing sequences should continue.
- If allocator health is compromised (e.g., suspected leaks), disabling may not recover memory; draining capacity may be required.

### Config propagation risk
During incidents, the impact depends on how fast flags reach GPU workers.
- If the kill-switch does not take effect within the expected propagation window, use pool-level override tooling (or drain) per runbook.
- Escalate to platform/control-plane if propagation delay is abnormal.

---

## Rollout gating (risk-driven)
Block rollout or auto-rollback if any occur in the canary cohort:
- sustained p99 regression beyond the guardrail threshold
- compaction bytes moved ceiling exceeded repeatedly
- allocator health counters degrade (orphaned pages, refcount anomalies)
- any suspected correctness issue

Refer to: **Hosted API tail latency guardrails** for the current SLO/threshold values used by rollout automation.

---

## Escalation and ownership
Primary owners:
- KV cache / compaction: **Omar El-Sayed**
- Scheduler integration: **Sofia Ivanova**
- Correctness review: **Noah Patel**
- SRE guardrails + rollout automation: **Sean Gallagher**
- Oncall readiness / runbooks: **Rafael Mendes**

If you suspect correctness:
- Disable compaction immediately.
- Page Runtime TL and correctness reviewer with allocator snapshots + trace IDs.

---

## Changelog
- 2026-02-26: Added explicit thrash pattern section (compaction↔eviction) and updated kill-switch hierarchy.
- 2026-02-18: Added cancellation-during-relocation indicators and evidence preservation steps.
- 2026-02-10: Initial publication for runtime-1.22 rollout readiness.

title: transient-model-switch-oscillation-incident-and-mitigation-2026
content:
Summary:

This document describes a recurrent production phenomenon we observed in Q4 2025–Q1 2026 that we have labeled 'Transient Model Switch Oscillation' (T-MSO). Symptoms include a rapid sequence of model routing changes for the same logical request stream, causing repeated KV-cache invalidations, throughput collapse, and elevated tail latency for 20–40s bursts. The behavior was visible across multiple tenants and both Hosted and Dedicated modes.

Purpose and audience:

- Audience: runtime engineers, oncall SREs, platform reliability, and product teams coordinating model rollout policies.
- Purpose: document root cause analysis, reproduction steps, mitigation and long-term fixes, and monitoring/alerting recipes.

Incident timeline and impact:

1) First escalations: 2025-11-12 — intermittent customer reports of long tail latencies (95th–99.9th spike) during midday traffic.
2) Pattern recognition: 2025-11–2026-01 — telemetry showed recurring multi-second oscillations coincident with model rollout events and autoscaling bursts.
3) Root-cause CVE to product: production incidents impacted 3 high-throughput tenants (2 enterprise, 1 AI-startup).
4) Severity: P2 on affected tenants; burst loss of throughput and 2x token-cost increase due to repeated re-warmups.

Observed symptoms (signals):

- Per-request traces show routing decisions flip between Model-A (quantized) and Model-A-v2 (float) multiple times during a single conversation session.
- KV cache miss-rate spikes from baseline ~5% to ~70% for affected sessions.
- Kernel scheduling shows alternating allocation of shard ownership across NUMA nodes leading to extra cross-node memcpy and dispatch delays.
- Autoscaler logs show a short-lived scale-up then immediate scale-down (<45s) before traffic stabilizes.

Root cause analysis (summary):

Contributing factors (combined):

1) Route-policy hysteresis gap: the routing policy that chooses model variants had insufficient hysteresis for transient capacity signals. It used a simple threshold on per-model GPU utilization and a last-eviction timestamp without multi-sample confirmation.
2) Fast autoscale + conservative warmup policy: autoscaler reacted to short spikes by adding nodes; warmup and placement logic attempted to place the preferred model variant on newly provisioned nodes without synchronized cache warming.
3) Fallback policy collision: the fallback mechanism to switch to a cheaper variant when capacity is constrained did not lock per-session routing decisions. Multiple concurrent components (router, fallback controller, and per-tenant policy agent) raced to reconcile the model id.
4) Model-version affinity: model variants shared the same model family id but had incompatible KV cache representations (different quantization metadata), which forced cache invalidations when a session switched variants.

Put together, a short traffic spike would trigger autoscale -> router attempted to move traffic to new nodes -> fallback policy evaluated capacity and flipped model variant -> per-session routing did not persist a decision -> router flipped variant again when observed latency on new nodes rose -> oscillation continued until traffic dropped or a manual kill-switch engaged.

Reproduction steps (sanitized, deterministic):

1) Environment: use a staging cluster with two-node initial pool (GPU A1, GPU A2) and the same autoscaler policy used in production (scale-step: +1, cool-down 30s).
2) Models: upload Model-A (8-bit quantized) and Model-A-v2 (fp16) with distinct model_variant_ids and the same model_family tag. Ensure model_variant metadata has different cache_schema fields.
3) Traffic generator: run sustained baseline QPS 120 with short spikes: every 90s inject 30s burst of 600 QPS.
4) Observe: within 1–3 burst cycles, routing flips per-session multiple times, KV cache miss-rate spikes, and tail latency increases.

Temporary mitigations (applied Nov 2025–Jan 2026):

- Hysteresis increase: increased routing decision confirmation window from 3s to 45s (multisample policy). Deployed as a stop-gap to reduce flip frequency.
- Per-session sticky routing: introduced sticky-routing flag for at-most-once routing decisions for session TTL = 120s to keep sessions bound to the same model_variant_id while warming caches.
- Autoscaler hold: added a 60s 'placement-quarantine' after scale-up during which routing avoids moving sessions to newly provisioned nodes for that tenant.
- Fallback locking: implemented an optimistic lock in fallback controller; fallback changes now require acquiring per-session key for the TTL duration.

These mitigations reduced oscillation frequency by ~90% in canaries and restored tail latency to acceptable SLOs for affected tenants.

Permanent fixes and design proposals (owner & timeline):

1) Stronger routing contract (owner: runtime-routing team). Timeline: Q2 2026.
- Implement a small state-machine per-session: {PreferredVariant, FallbackVariant, Transitioning} with explicit TTL, and expose it to router + fallback controller via a single authoritative store (Redis cluster/sharded snapshot).
- Ensure routing decisions are idempotent and can be reconciled from traces.

2) Cache schema compatibility registry (owner: model-onboarding). Timeline: Q2–Q3 2026.
- During model onboarding, compute a compatibility signature for KV cache schema. Reject variant pairings that are incompatible unless a migration plan is provided.

3) Autoscaler grace API (owner: eng-sre + autoscaler). Timeline: Q3 2026.
- Autoscaler should expose placement state for new nodes and allow the routing layer to query 'ready_for_session_migration' boolean.
- Add 'soft-add' option where capacity bookkeeping increases but routing waits until warmup script returns success.

4) Observability: enhanced traces and derived metrics (owner: telemetry team). Timeline: Q2 2026.
- New tracing span: routing.decision.{evaluate|commit} with tags model.family, model.variant, decision.ttl, decision.reason.
- Telemetry to emit 'session_routing_flip' event with sample of request ids.

Monitoring and alerting recipes (immediate and long-term):

- Immediate alert (P95 spike correlated with session-flip rate):
  Condition: p95_latency(service:inference) > 2x baseline AND rate(session_routing_flip) > 5/min for 5m.
  Pager: oncall-runtime primary.

- PromQL example (sample):
  # session flip rate per tenant
  sum(rate(session_routing_flip_total[1m])) by (tenant_id)

- Grafana dashboard panels to add:
  - per-tenant routing flip heatmap (time vs tenant)
  - KV-cache miss-rate and miss-to-hit ratio overlayed with routing flips
  - autoscaler events timeline aligned with routing.decision spans

Operational runbook (short):

1) When alerted, run quick triage (5m):
  a) Query session_routing_flip_total for affected tenant.
  b) Check autoscaler events: list recent scale-up/scale-down events.
  c) Identify if fallback controller applied variant change events (via event log).
2) Mitigate (10–20m):
  a) If flip rate is high and autoscaler churn is observed, activate 'routing-hysteresis-override' for tenant to 120s via console.
  b) If particular model variants are involved, mark the newer variant as 'do-not-route' until canary is analyzed.
  c) If on Dedicated, coordinate with SRE to hold node termination/scale-down.
3) Post-incident (24–72h):
  a) Capture traces and attach to the incident with key spans highlighted.
  b) Run the deterministic reproduction in staging and file a follow-up ticket to implement missing design fix.

Ownership matrix (short):

- Runtime-routing team: lead = Omar Lewis — authoritative for routing contract, sticky routing, and hysteresis tuning.
- Model-onboarding: lead = Priya Natarajan — schema compatibility registry and model metadata.
- Autoscaler: lead = Samir Patel — expose placement readiness API and scale behavior.
- Telemetry: lead = Maya Chen — new tracing spans and metrics.
- Oncall SRE: rotation owners — incident triage and manual mitigations.

Backwards compatibility and customer communication:

- We will send an incident summary to affected customers with an explanation of the cause and the applied mitigations. The summary will include recommended tenant-level options (enable routing session stickiness, request canary windows) and a support contact.
- No data loss or model output correctness issues were observed; impact was limited to latency and cost.

Appendices:

A) Example routing-decision trace span (pseudo-JSON):

routing.decision.evaluate {
  trace_id: "abcd-1234",
  tenant_id: "acct_9876",
  session_id: "sess_42",
  candidate_variants: ["A-q8", "A-fp16"],
  chosen: "A-q8",
  reason: "capacity_low",
  timestamp: "2026-01-13T18:03:21Z"
}

routing.decision.commit {

title: KV-cache shard skew and quantization interaction: investigation, mitigation, and runbook
content:
Summary:
This document captures an investigation into a recurring class of production incidents where uneven KV-cache (prefix/KV) distribution across shard workers combined with aggressive post-training quantization (8-bit asymmetric) produced high tail latency and occasional OOMs. It includes root-cause evidence, detection queries, a short-term mitigation runbook, recommended scheduler and quantization configuration changes, and a checklist for long-term fixes and testing.

Scope and impact:
- Affects: hosted and dedicated serving pools using split-shard KV routing + quantized model families (q8_a and q8_b).
- Symptom window: intermittent p99/p999 spikes (200–800ms over baseline), spikes concentrated during synthetic-batched workloads and long-context chat sessions (>= 2048 tokens).
- Frequency: 3 incidents between 2025-09 and 2025-11 in US-east-1 GPU pools; reproduction locally with shard skew simulator.
- Business impact: API error rate increased 1.4–2.3x during events; customers on Dedicated saw throughput degradation prompting support escalations.

Key findings (short form):
1) Shard assignment heuristic allowed up to 2.5x more active KV-entries on certain workers for common long-prefix prompts, causing memory pressure and slower KV lookups.
2) Quantized kernels (8-bit asymmetric) for recent model variants introduce nonuniform per-layer memory layout that increases temporary workspace allocation variance per token. When combined with prefetching, this exacerbated peak memory use.
3) Kernel scheduler prioritized throughput over memory headroom during steady-state autoscaling; under high skew this led to transient OOM kills and a cascade of request retries that amplified tail latencies.

Relevant metrics and alerting thresholds:
- kv_cache_local_entries_per_shard (gauge) — alert if max_shard / median_shard > 1.6 for 5m
- kv_cache_hit_rate (percent) — warn if < 92% for 10m on a model route
- gpu_mem_headroom_pct (gauge) — critical if any device < 12% for 1m
- request_latency_ms{route} p99 and p999 — critical if p999 > baseline_p999 * 3 for 5m
- kernel_scheduler_pending_queue_length — warn if > 1000 for 2m

PromQL examples (Grafana):
- Shard skew ratio:
  max(kv_cache_local_entries_per_shard{pool="us-east-1-prod"}) / avg(kv_cache_local_entries_per_shard{pool="us-east-1-prod"})
- GPU headroom percentage (device-level):
  100 * (1 - (avg_over_time(nvidia_gpu_memory_used_bytes[1m]) / avg_over_time(nvidia_gpu_memory_total_bytes[1m])))

Investigation artifacts (evidence):
- Kernel traces showing repeated cudaMalloc failure -> fallback path for q8 kernels (attached as trace IDs: trc-20251004-42, trc-20251021-08).
- Heap dumps from affected workers demonstrating 60–80% of incremental allocations were temporary layer workspaces tied to the quantized fused-kernel (dump ids: heap-20251004-a, heap-20251102-b).
- Repro script: scripts/kv-skew-sim/runner.py (internal repo: infra/sim) — reproduces p99 spike by driving long-prefix variety and forcing unbalanced shard assignment.

Immediate mitigation (short-term runbook) — use during incidents:
1) Detect: confirm shard_skew_ratio PromQL > 1.6 and gpu_mem_headroom_pct any device < 12% or p999 > baseline*2.
2) Quarantine affected model route: add a temp-route override to route requests to a non-quantized fallback model (e.g., model-xv2-fp16) via the routing control plane.
3) Throttle synthetic-heavy customers: apply per-client rate limit for 10m windows on routes causing skew.
4) Rebalance shards: trigger targeted shard-respin for the worker pool (CLI):
   - rcli shard rebalance --pool us-east-1-prod --strategy uniform --drain=true --concurrency=2
5) If OOM persists, scale up a hotfix worker-sized pool with higher-memory instances:
   - terraform: apply -var='pool_size=4' -target=module.hotfix-us-east1
6) Monitor: ensure kv_cache_local_entries_per_shard ratio returns < 1.2 and gpu_mem_headroom_pct > 18% before resuming normal routing.

Commands and ops snippets:
- Check shard skew quickly (kubectl + prom):
  kubectl -n serving exec -it svc/prom-query -- curl -sG 'http://localhost:9090/api/v1/query' --data-urlencode 'query=max(kv_cache_local_entries_per_shard{pool="us-east-1-prod"}) / avg(kv_cache_local_entries_per_shard{pool="us-east-1-prod"})' | jq
- Force scheduler to prefer memory headroom (onbox flag):
  echo 'MEMORY_FIRST=1' > /etc/redwood/runtime_flags.d/priority.conf && systemctl restart redwood-runtime-scheduler.service

Root-cause analysis (detailed):
- Allocation pattern: the quantized fused attention kernel uses dynamic temporaries sized to sequence length and per-layer hidden-size alignment. Some hardware-specific kernel variants pad workspace to 64-byte boundaries; combined with our allocator metadata this produced a 20–40% bloat versus FP16 kernels under long sequences.
- Shard topology and assignment: the greedy prefix hash used for low-latency routing did not incorporate current KV cache size or recent allocation footprint. That optimization favored route-affinity but ignored memory balance.
- Scheduler policy: the priority-driven scheduler groups tasks into batches by estimated token cost but uses static headroom thresholds. In skewed scenarios it allowed many high-cost requests to land on a single worker because affinity minimization lowered request hop cost metric.

Design decisions and trade-offs considered:
- Option A — Always prefer FP16 fallback for long-context (>2048) requests: reduces cost/throughput but increases latency per token slightly for some model families.
- Option B — Update shard assignment to be headroom-aware: requires global KV size propagation (adds 200–400ms route lookup overhead unless cached).
- Option C — Kernel change: adjust quantized kernels to pre-reserve workspace conservatively, reducing dynamic allocation churn (engineering cost high, long lead time).
Recommendation: Combine B + short-term A during rollout. B provides the most sustainable operational improvement with tolerable lookup overhead if we cache single-key headroom info in the routing plane.

Planned short-to-medium term fixes (owners and ETA):
- Immediate (SRE / eng-serving-runtime) — Implement a headroom-aware shard assignment flag and enable in canary pool (owner: Ravi Patel) — ETA: 2026-03-10.
- Near-term (runtime team) — Add memory-first scheduler mode toggles and expose on control-plane flags (owner: Aisha Kumar) — ETA: 2026-04-01.
- Medium (kernel team) — Rework q8 fused-kernel workspace allocation to use pooled temporaries and deterministic preallocation (owner: Lena Schwartz) — ETA: 2026-07-15.

Testing and benchmarking plan (how we will validate):
1) Add a new scenario to the perf-suite: long-context mixed-prefix workload with intentional skew (workload id: long-prefix-skew-2026). Benchmarks: p50/p95/p99/p999 latency, tokens/sec, retry rate, GPU util, mem headroom.
2) Unit tests for shard assignment: simulate 10k concurrent prefixes and assert skew ratio < 1.3 under headroom-aware policy.
3) Kernel perf run: compare q8_old vs q8_pooled on sequence lengths 512/1024/2048 measuring workspace allocations (nvprof traces).
4) Canary rollout: enable headroom-aware routing in dedicated canary pool of 5 workers for 72h; if p999 regressions occur > 10% abort.

Acceptance criteria for rollout:
- Canary p999 latency does not increase by more than 10% relative to baseline for the same traffic mix.
- kv_cache_local_entries_per_shard ratio <= 1.3 sustained for 24h.
- No device reports gpu_mem_headroom_pct < 10% for more than 1 minute.

Operational notes and playbook tips:
- When rebalancing, prefer graceful drain (drain=true) to avoid losing KV in-flight; allow 60s for KV transfer per shard.
- Avoid enabling both memory-first scheduler and aggressive batching in the same pool simultaneously—conflicting objectives can hurt throughput.
- Document temporary route fallbacks in the routing change log with the incident tag (inc-20251004-kv-skew).

Developer checklist for implementations:
- Add integration tests in infra/sim for skewed KV distributions and quantized kernel stress.
- Add end-to-end benchmark in perf-suite with automated alerting hook comparing new runs to historical baselines.
- Update the Runtime Scheduler config schema (runtime-configs/scheduler_v2.yaml):
  # example excerpt
  scheduler_mode: \"memory_first|throughput_first\"
  memory_headroom_threshold_pct: 18
  shard_assignment_cache_ttl_ms: 250
  headroom_propagation: true

Change log (brief):
- 2026-02-18: Published doc and runbook; added PromQL detection query and immediate mitigation steps.
- 2025-11-12: Initial post-incident analysis draft created.

Related resources:
- perf-suite workload definitions: infra/perf/long-prefix-skew-2026.yaml
- Kernel trace bundle: s3://redwood-internal/traces/kv-skew-q8-2025/
- Simulation runner: git@internal:redwood/infra/sim.git (branch: kv-skew-fixes)

Appendix A — Example alert runbook (short):
1) Pager triggers: SRE oncall receives p999 alert for route X.
2) Triage: confirm shard_skew_ratio > 1.6 and check pool memory headroom.
3) Action: apply temporary route override to FP16 fallback and trigger shard rebalance.
4) Post-incident: run heap-dump collector on affected workers and upload to s3 with tag inc-YYYYMMDD-kvskew.

Appendix B — Experimental notes from local reproducer:
- On an AWS p4d-like instance: sequence length 4096 + q8 kernel -> temporary allocations peaked at 64MB per layer; reducing per-layer workspace alignment to 32 bytes reduced peak by ~18%.

Owner contact and escalation:
- Primary owner: Marco Delgado <marco@redwood.ai>
- SRE escalation: oncall@redwood.ai (pager duty)

If you make changes to scheduler flags or shard assignment heuristics, add a short design note in eng-serving-runtime/decision-records and tag reviewers: Aisha Kumar, Lena Schwartz, Ravi Patel.

title: adaptive-route-token-bundles-prd-2026-05
content:
Summary:

This PRD describes Adaptive Route Token Bundles (ARTB), a product initiative to let customers buy, assign, and manage token bundles that are scoped to a specific route (or set of routes). ARTB targets two customer needs: predictable unit economics for high-volume routes, and controlled burst capacity without manual intervention. The feature covers purchase flows, per-route assignment, auto-topup, billing treatment, Console/UI controls, API surfaces, and telemetry requirements.

Context and motivating problems:
- Teams running production LLM features (recommendations, search, chat support flows) want cheaper predictable units for sustained heavy usage rather than pay-as-you-go variability.
- Platform and finance teams need guardrails for bursty routes (embeddings, vectorization jobs) to avoid surprise bills.
- Dedicated customers require on-contract pricing constructs and audit trails for route-level spending.

Goals:
- G1: Enable customers to purchase token bundles (named bundles) and assign them to one or more routes with clear billing visibility.
- G2: Support automatic topups when a bundle dips below a threshold with configurable topup methods (prepaid charge, invoice hold, or disable topup).
- G3: Provide per-route consumption accounting, real-time bundle usage dashboards, and alerting for low-balance and over-consumption.
- G4: Ensure compatibility with Dedicated, Hosted, and Private deployments (with reasonable limitations for air-gapped environments).

Success metrics (30/60/90 days post-launch):
- Adoption: 25% of new Dedicated customers assign at least one token bundle within 60 days.
- Spend predictability: Average month-to-month variance in per-route spend for bundle-backed routes drops by 40% for adopters.
- Customer satisfaction: CSAT for billing related inquiries decreases by 20% for customers using ARTB.
- Operational: Billing disputes related to burst tokens decrease by 50% for customers on ARTB.

Must-have requirements:
- R1: Purchase API and Console flow to create a token bundle with parameters: name, token_count, effective_start, effective_end (optional), price_plan_reference, auto_topup_policy.
- R2: Route assignment API: assign/unassign bundle_id to route_id(s), with validation that the caller has route.admin permission.
- R3: Real-time accounting: every routed token consumption must decrement the assigned bundle in near-real-time (<5s propagation to UI).
- R4: Auto-topup policies: support three modes: prepaid_charge (instant charge to payment method), invoice_on_cycle (defer to next billing cycle), and topup_disabled (stop serving when depleted).
- R5: Billing integration: bundle usage must be reflected in monthly invoices with line-item granularity: bundle_purchase, topup_events, overage_charges.
- R6: Audit logs: purchases, assignments, auto-topups, and overage events must emit audit entries that include actor_id, route_id, bundle_id, tokens_consumed, and timestamp.

Nice-to-have requirements:
- N1: Bundle sharing: ability to share a bundle across multiple routes with consumption weighting rules.
- N2: Per-route priority class that consumes from bundle first, then falls back to pay-as-you-go.
- N3: Console visualization of projected exhaustion date given recent consumption patterns.

Non-goals / explicitly out of scope:
- Long-term credit trading or marketplace for bundles between customers.
- Fine-grained token-level reservation for single-request pinning.

User journeys:
- Purchase & assign (admin): In Console, Billing -> Token Bundles -> Create Bundle -> enter token count and pricing plan -> choose auto-topup -> Create. Then navigate to Routes -> select route -> Assign Bundle -> choose bundle_id and priority -> Save.
- Auto-topup flow (prepaid_charge): When bundle balance < topup_threshold, billing-service charges saved payment method, creates topup_event, and increases bundle balance. Audit log emitted.
- Depleted bundle with topup_disabled: When balance reaches zero, route-level behavior follows config: either reject requests (HTTP 402) or fall back to pay-as-you-go if configured. System emits RouteCostCapExceeded alert.

High-level design notes:
- Data model additions:
  - token_bundles table: bundle_id (UUID), name, owner_org_id, tokens_total, tokens_available, price_plan_ref, auto_topup_policy, topup_threshold, created_at, expires_at
  - route_bundle_assignments: route_id, bundle_id, priority, assigned_at

- Billing model and pricing behavior:
  - Bundles are sold as pre-sized token packs with a configured price_plan_ref which maps to per-token amortized price and revenue recognition rules.
  - Auto-topup prepaid_charge applies standard per-token rate for the purchased topup, not the bundle amortized rate unless the customer selects a matching promo.
  - When both a bundle and pay-as-you-go are enabled, bundle tokens are consumed first according to assignment priority.
  - Overages (consumption when bundle exhausted and topup not available) billed at standard pay-as-you-go rates and flagged for dispute if configured.

- Consumption path (runtime):
  - routing-proxy attaches route_id to each request. At token emission, a token-accounting service checks route_bundle_assignments in-memory cache, decrements tokens_available using an optimistic concurrency update, emits usage_event, and returns billing_token_id to runtime for invoice correlation.
  - For high-throughput routes, we support chunked attribution: runtime requests a token-reservation batch (n tokens) to reduce per-token RPCs. Reservations expire in 30s if not consumed.

APIs and CLI:
- POST /v1/bundles {name, tokens_total, price_plan_ref, auto_topup_policy, topup_threshold, expires_at}
- POST /v1/routes/{route_id}/bundle-assign {bundle_id, priority}
- GET /v1/bundles/{bundle_id}/usage
- CLI examples: redwood bundles create --name "search-bulk-1" --tokens 1000000 --price-plan enterprise-2026 --auto-topup prepaid_charge --topup-threshold 0.15

Console UX / product surface:
- Billing -> Token Bundles: list view with balances, projected exhaustion, linked routes, recent topup events.
- Route Settings: assign/unassign bundle, set consumption priority, set depletion behavior (deny or fallback to pay-as-you-go).
- Alerts: prebuilt alert template BundleLowBalance and BundleTopupFailed.

Telemetry and observability:
- New metrics: bundle_tokens_available (gauge, tagged by bundle_id), bundle_tokens_consumed_total (counter), bundle_topup_events_total (counter), bundle_reservation_failures (counter).
- Logs: bundle_audit_event containing actor_id, action, bundle_id, delta_tokens, route_id, request_ids (when applicable).
- Dashboards: Bundle Health (per-bundle: balance, 7-day burn rate, projected exhaustion), Route-Bundle Correlation.

Data and consistency guarantees:
- Consistency: tokens_available is strongly consistent for assignment and reservation operations. We use a leader-sharded token accounting service per org to avoid cross-DC races.
- Performance: bulk reservation path supports up to 10k tokens reservation per RPC. Per-token debit operations optimized with batched writes to ledger.

Compatibility and deployment considerations:
- Hosted: full feature set including auto-topup prepaid_charge.
- Dedicated: full feature set with contractual price_plan_refs; finance must provision price keys per customer.
- Private: auto-topup prepaid_charge disabled by default for air-gapped installs; topup_invoiced_on_cycle supported. Manual billing hooks required.

Security and compliance:
- Only users with billing.admin or route.admin can create/assign bundles.
- Bundle events must be retained for 2 years for audit purposes.
- Sensitive billing operations (prepaid charging) require 2FA for the initiating user in Console.

Migration plan for existing customers:
1. Offer an opt-in migration for high-spend routes: export existing monthly usage summary and generate suggested bundle sizes (Console wizard).
2. Pilot with 10 existing Dedicated customers for 6 weeks. Learn pricing acceptance and topup defaults.
3. Provide a bulk-assign CLI to map bundles to routes for customers with many routes.

Rollout plan and release gates:
- Phase 1 (internal + 5 pilot customers): API + Billing integration + Console list view. Pass gate: accurate near-real-time balancing (<5s) and successful topup charging in sandbox.
- Phase 2 (Beta): +25 customers, add reservation path and projected exhaustion UI. Pass gate: no regressions in billing reports and <1% reservation failure rate.
- Phase 3 (GA): general availability for Hosted and Dedicated, Private on request.

Safety checks & failure modes:
- Topup charge failure: emit BundleTopupFailed alert, fall back to invoice_on_cycle if configured, or set route to depletion_behavior as defined.
- Reservation expiration: tokens reserved but not consumed return to bundle; high expiration rates surface on dashboard.
- Under-billing risk: reconcile daily ledger dumps between token-accounting service and billing-service; discrepancies >0.1% trigger automatic investigation.

Open questions for product decisions:
- Q1: Should we allow peer-to-peer bundle transfers between orgs (currently set to No)?
- Q2: Discounting policy for auto-topup amounts vs initial bundle purchase (do we allow promo-consistent topups?): Finance to advise.
- Q3: Default topup_threshold percentage and whether it should be configurable per-org or per-bundle?

Dependencies:
- Billing-service: invoice line-item support and topup charging endpoint.
- Routing-proxy & token-accounting service: fast path integration for reservations.
- Console: Billing UI and Route assignment panel updates.
- Finance & Legal: price_plan_ref creation and revenue recognition guidance.

Ownership and stakeholders:
- Product: Sofia Martinez (owner)
- Engineering lead: Marco Silva (eng-serving-runtime)
- Billing & Finance: Alexis Nguyen (finance-and-legal)
- DX/SDKs: Evan Cho (eng-developer-experience)
- SRE: Priya Raman (eng-sre)
- Security & Compliance: Omar Haddad (security-and-compliance)

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: Unexpected billing disputes due to asynchronous accounting. Mitigation: strong consistency for token debits and daily ledger reconciliation.
- Risk: Customer confusion around pricing differences between bundle amortized rate and topup rate. Mitigation: Console explanations and pre-purchase simulator.

Appendix: sample bundle YAML export
---
bundle_id: bundle-4c9b
name: search-high-volume-1
tokens_total: 1000000
tokens_available: 720000
price_plan_ref: enterprise-2026
auto_topup_policy: prepaid_charge
topup_threshold: 0.15
created_at: 2026-05-10T14:00:00Z

Change log:
- 2026-05-10: Draft created by Sofia Martinez
- 2026-05-16: Added reservation path and UI mock notes (reviewed with Marco Silva)
- 2026-05-20: Updated billing integration details and sample YAML; set status to in_review

title: OpenAI-compat streaming truncation (missing [DONE]) - suspected gateway idle timeout
content:
## Summary
We are tracking intermittent truncation of SSE streams on the OpenAI-compatible route (`/v1/chat/completions` with `stream=true`). The observed symptom is that clients receive some token events and then the connection closes without the terminal `[DONE]` event. Clients often see HTTP 200 with partial content.

This has been reported by multiple customers and correlates with a spike in client disconnect telemetry in **eu-west** (INC-2025-02-13-STREAM).

## Root cause hypothesis
The OpenAI-compat streaming stack can exhibit brief upstream quiet periods (no tokens emitted) during generation. When the upstream is quiet long enough, the API gateway/proxy may trigger a read/idle timeout and close the downstream connection, which appears to the client as a truncated SSE stream.

Contributing factors we suspect:
- OpenAI-compat uses HTTP/1.1 SSE with chunked transfer; some intermediaries are sensitive to idle gaps
- Current `proxy_read_timeout` for this route in eu-west is lower than we expect for long generations
- We do not currently emit heartbeat comments when the upstream is quiet

## Mitigation
### 1) SSE heartbeat comments
Emit an SSE comment line periodically when upstream is quiet to keep the connection active. Example payload (comment):
`: heartbeat

`

Proposed settings:
- heartbeat interval: 5s
- only when no downstream bytes have been sent in the interval

### 2) Gateway timeout tuning
Increase read timeout for OpenAI-compat streaming route in eu-west. (Coordinate with Eng Platform; see confluence://eng-platform/runbooks/api-gateway-timeouts.)

## Customer-facing guidance
Support/CS can recommend:
- Treat missing `[DONE]` as a failure and retry
- Capture `x-request-id`, region, and last SSE event for investigation

## References
- SUP-2481 (AsterixPay)
- SUP-2490 (OrchidCRM; also BluePeak Analytics comms)
- Slack incident thread 1739443389 in #incidents

## Rollout plan
1. Canary heartbeat in eu-west for OpenAI-compat streaming only.
2. Bump gateway timeout in eu-west.
3. Expand to other regions after confirming disconnect rate decreases and no client parsing regressions.

title: async-kernel-deadlock-patterns-and-mitigation-2026
content:
Summary:

This document catalogs recurring async-kernel deadlock patterns observed in the runtime between 2024–2026, diagnostic signatures, short-term mitigations, and durable remediation paths. It is intended for oncall engineers, runtime kernel authors, scheduler owners, and SREs.

Scope and impact:
- Affects the serving runtime's asynchronous kernel handoff and cooperative preemption paths.
- Symptoms range from elevated tail latency (p99.99 spikes) to full request stalls on specific model variants, sometimes causing partial loss of capacity on a GPU node for minutes.
- Customers: observed primarily under mixed workloads (long-context chat + short embeddings) and during kernel rollouts or topology changes.
- Business impact: can exceed alerting SLOs (p95 latency > 2x target) and trigger failover cascades in the orchestrator.

High-level patterns (observed signatures):
1) Handoff-starvation deadlock
   - Trigger: a kernel A holding a per-shard mutex waits for a KV cache warmup callback that is scheduled on the same worker thread which is blocked on A’s completion.
   - Telemetry: kernel_handoff_wait_ms for shard X increases; kernel_active_threads==0 while gpu_dispatch_queue_depth>0; repeated trace annotations: "handoff:await-kv-warmup".

2) Interleaved-batch lock inversion
   - Trigger: two concurrent request cohorts (cohort-long and cohort-short) acquire locks in opposite orders during batch assembly and commit; when a preemptible kernel tries to preempt a non-cooperative kernel, both wait for slot credits.
   - Telemetry: increasing lock_contention_count, per-kernel credit_backoff_ms, and a correlated rise in per-request queue_time.

3) Async-callback-livelock from external IO
   - Trigger: a plugin or sidecar performing model-variant lookup issues synchronous filesystem or network calls within an async callback that is expected to be non-blocking; the callback holds scheduler-internal state and prevents kernel completion.
   - Telemetry: long-running callback traces labeled "sidecar-sync-io"; blocked thread stack traces show user call into sidecar library.

Detection rules and useful queries:
- Metrics to monitor (recommended):
  - kernel_handoff_wait_ms (histogram)
  - kernel_dispatch_backpressure_ratio (gauge)
  - lock_contention_count (counter) broken down by lock name
  - gpu_dispatch_queue_depth (gauge)
  - kernel_active_threads (gauge)
  - kernel_stall_retries (counter)

- Example alert condition (immediate page):
  - WHEN: 5m avg(kernel_handoff_wait_ms{p99} > 500ms) AND gpu_dispatch_queue_depth > 4
  - WHY: indicates persistent handoff slippage with backpressure building on dispatch queue
  - ACTION: page runtime-oncall, include node id and recent trace ids

- Useful log search patterns:
  - "handoff:await-kv-warmup" OR "sidecar-sync-io" OR "lock_acquire_timeout"
  - Example logQL: {app="runtime"} |= "handoff:await-kv-warmup" | json | line_format "{{.shard}} {{.kernel_id}} {{.duration_ms}}"

Repro steps (minimal, non-customer data sandbox):
1) On the dev cluster, deploy the synthetic-deadlock-replayer service (see repo infra/synthetic-deadlock).
2) Configuration snippet (YAML) for reproducer:
   - concurrent_long_cohorts: 6
   - short_cohort_rate: 200/s
   - enable_sidecar_sync_io: true
   - kv_warmup_latency_ms: 200

3) Run: `./replayer --target-node=node-7 --duration=600s --profile=handoff-starvation`
4) Observe metrics: p99 kernel_handoff_wait_ms > 500ms and kernel_active_threads drop to near 0 while gpu_dispatch_queue_depth rises.

Live investigation playbook (oncall):
1) Triage and scope
   - Identify affected nodes (metric: gpu_dispatch_queue_depth > 0 for > 60s).
   - Gather recent traces (trace IDs indicated by trace_sampler for the node).
2) Quick mitigations (fast, reversible)
   - If pattern is handoff-starvation: disable KV-prefetch warmup (runtime flag: --kv-warmup=false) for the node or toggle to low-concurrency mode.
   - If pattern is plugin IO: flip plugin sandboxing mode to async (flag: --plugin-sync-to-async=true) or unload the plugin (if safe).
   - If lock inversion suspected: enable priority-boost (flag: --sched-priority-boost=on) to break inversion while preserving safety.
3) Evacuate traffic (if mitigations insufficient)
   - Evacuate the node from the pool using orchestrator: drain node with graceful timeout 120s, failing fast if operator needs to reclaim capacity.
4) Capture artifacts
   - Collect full core dumps (gcore), runtime thread stacks, and kernel dispatcher traces and attach to incident. Use `collect-runtime-artifacts --node node-7 --since 2026-10-03T10:00:00Z`.

Long-term remediations and design recommendations:
- Contract-level changes
  - Enforce async-safety contracts: any callback executed in the runtime must be annotated and rejected at load-time if it performs sync IO or acquires runtime locks. Introduce linker-time or load-time checks for common blocking syscalls.
  - Introduce cooperative timeout windows for long kernels: kernels must periodically yield within a configured window (default 50ms) or be preempted at a safe checkpoint.

- Scheduler improvements
  - Deterministic lock ordering: define and enforce a global lock ordering table for the most frequently contended locks (kv-warmup-lock, batch-assemble-lock, checkpoint-lock). See proposed table below:

  +----------------------+----------------------------+
  | Lock name            | Ordering priority (lower=first) |
  +----------------------+----------------------------+
  | scheduler-global     | 1                          |
  | kv-warmup-lock       | 2                          |
  | batch-assemble-lock  | 3                          |
  | kernel-state-lock    | 4                          |
