  - Kernel handoff grace protocol: when a kernel attempts handoff, a small rendezvous token is acquired; if rendezvous cannot be satisfied inside 100ms, the originator will release non-critical locks and retry to avoid circular waits.

- Observability and testing
  - Add a dedicated deadlock detector stage in the nightly microbenchmark suite that runs the synthetic-deadlock-replayer across combinatorial cohort ratios and kernel variants.
  - Add deterministic unit tests for priority-boost and lock ordering with a simulated scheduler.

Safe rollout guidance for fixes:
- Canary algorithm: start with 1% canary traffic on patched scheduler + kernel (min 3 nodes). Validate metrics for 6 hours. Gate criteria: no p99.9 kernel_handoff_wait_ms regression, lock_contention_count reduced by >= 50% on canary.
- Fallback: automatic rollback if canary sees kernel_active_threads drop by > 30% or if dispatcher error rate increases > 0.5% above baseline.

SOP snippets (commands):
- Disable kv warmup on a single node (useful temporary mitigant):
  kubectl -n infra exec node-agent--node-7 -- sh -c 'svcctl set-flag runtime --kv-warmup=false && svcctl restart runtime'

- Collect kernel dispatcher traces:
  curl -s "http://node-7.internal:9090/debug/dispatcher/traces?since=10m" > dispatcher-traces-node-7.json

- Minimal gdb backtrace capture (if the node is unresponsive):
  sudo gcore $(pgrep runtime) && sudo gdb --batch --pid $(pgrep runtime) -ex 'thread apply all bt' -ex 'quit' > bt-node-7.txt

Owner and escalation:
- Primary owner: runtime-kernel-team (oncall alias: runtime-kernel-oncall)
- Secondary: eng-sre (alias: eng-sre-oncall)
- For customer-impacting incidents, page customer-success-sre and the PM for the affected model tier.

Related pages and artifacts:
- See synthetic-deadlock test harness: git://repo/infra/synthetic-deadlock (internal)
- Trace examples attached to this page: trace-2026-06-11-node-7 (internal)

Appendix: example stack snapshot (sanitized) showing common deadlock layout:
- Thread 1: runtime::kernel::kv_warmup_wait() -> runtime::kv::lock() -> waiting for checkpoint-lock
- Thread 2: runtime::scheduler::batch_commit() -> runtime::kernel::lock() -> waiting for kv_warmup-lock
- Thread 3: plugin::variant_lookup() -> sync DNS resolve -> holds scheduler-global context

Notes and caveats:
- Many deadlock signatures are transient and only appear with a precise mix of cohort shapes; synthetic replayer helps reproduce but may not capture third-party plugin-induced deadlocks.
- Changes that add preemption points must be verified against model fidelity experiments to ensure they do not materially regress latency stability for long-context workloads.

Change history:
- 2026-05-12: Document created (Maya Chen)
- 2026-07-01: Added quick mitigation flags and example commands (Ethan Park)
- 2026-10-03: Expanded detection queries and added canary gating thresholds (Rina Patel)

End of document.

title: Interleaved-batch memory safety & soft-GC: detection and mitigations
content:
Summary:

This document describes a class of hard-to-reproduce memory-safety failures that we observed in production during sustained mixed workloads: a combination of interleaved (asynchronous + synchronous) batching, aggressive KV-cache soft garbage collection (soft-GC), and fast slot recycling can produce illegal memory accesses and occasional kernel crashes. The net result is transient instance instability, sporadic OOMs on GPUs, and elevated tail latency as affected shards restart.

Background: why this class appears

- Our runtime performs continuous batching with two execution paths: synchronous (hotpath) and asynchronous (background coalesced batches).
- A soft-GC subsystem attempts to reclaim KV-cache memory opportunistically when host- or device-memory pressure grows; it marks entries stale and reclaims in the background without global synchronization to avoid latency cliffs.
- Worker slot recycling reclaims CPU/GPU slot metadata aggressively to maximize throughput. When these three systems interleave at the wrong time, reclaimed GPU-side buffers or stream handles can be referenced by an in-flight kernel, leading to illegal memory access and CUDA driver errors.

Observed symptoms (production signals)

- Sporadic GPU kernel failures (CUDA errors logged: UNKNOWN or illegal memory access) without obvious memory growth prior to failure.
- Increase in tail latency and 5xx error spike in model-serving routes that use long KV cache lifetimes (chat sessions).
- Short-lived pod restarts on a small percentage (~0.3%–1%) of nodes; restart reason = crashloop at the GPU driver layer.
- Traces show kernel launch times overlapped with cache-evict markers and slot-reuse timestamps.

Known reproducibility steps (local repro)

1. Use a synthetic client that alternates short synchronous requests (prompt length 16–32) with long-generation asynchronous requests (prompt length 512+) to force mixed batching paths.
2. Configure a small device-memory headroom to trigger soft-GC: set kv_cache_soft_gc_threshold = 0.78 and kv_cache_eviction_batch_size = 16.
3. Reduce slot_reuse_delay_ms to a small value (10ms) to emulate aggressive recycling.
4. Run the workload with a high concurrency driver until you observe intermittent CUDA errors.

Telemetry and detection rules

- Important signals to capture (add to node-level dashboards):
  - cuda_error_count (per GPU): alerts when > 0 in 5m window
  - kv_cache_eviction_rate and kv_cache_reclaim_time_p50/p95
  - slot_reuse_rate and slot_reuse_delay_ms distribution
  - kernel_launch_overlap_ratio: fraction of launches that overlap with a cache-reclaim marker (sampled)

- Detection rule (recommended):
  - Alert if cuda_error_count > 0 OR kernel_launch_overlap_ratio > 0.1 for a given shard AND kv_cache_eviction_rate_p95 > baseline + 3 sigma.

Immediate mitigations (for oncall)

1. Throttle soft-GC: admin API

   curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN" -d '{"kv_cache_soft_gc_threshold": 0.92, "kv_cache_eviction_batch_size": 4}' https://admin.internal/runtime/config

   Effect: reduces background reclaim aggressiveness and gives in-flight kernels more time to complete.

2. Increase slot reuse delay to force explicit fencing:

   curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN" -d '{"slot_reuse_delay_ms": 250}' https://admin.internal/runtime/config

   Effect: prevents immediate reuse of CPU/GPU slot structs while kernels or stream callbacks may still hold references.

3. If alerting indicates a specific node / shard: cordon the node and redeploy the runtime with the mitigations above; optionally drain and restart the affected pod to clear dangling state.

Long-term fixes (engineering roadmap)

- Short-term (sprint-scale):
  1) Add explicit device-side fencing and reference counting for KV cache buffers. Before reclaiming, ensure all stream callbacks have executed and kernel completion fences are observed.
  2) Make soft-GC cooperative: transition from blind background reclamation to a token-based protocol where a limited number of concurrent reclaims can happen per-shard.
  3) Add stronger sanitizers in the dev profiling harness to catch races (e.g., ASAN-like host checks and CUDA memcheck in staging).

- Mid-term (quarter-scale):
  1) Introduce a kernel-scheduling handshake that timestamps reclaim windows and prevents kernel launches that would reference recently reclaimed buffers.
  2) Improve batch planner to prefer contiguous execution (avoid interleaving synchronous launches with async coalesced batches when soft-GC is active).
  3) Add automated tests in the benchmarking suite that run mixed-workload tortures for >8 hours and report divergence metrics.

Impact to release & rollout notes

- Releases that change KV cache layout, soft-GC heuristics, or slot metadata must include:
  - Benchmark matrix results for mixed-sync/async workloads (see Mixed-Workload Stress Matrix).
  - Profiling traces demonstrating zero kernel-reclaim overlap for p99 windows.
  - New canary policy requiring 48h of shadow traffic with injected GC pressure.

Benchmarking & profiling guidance

- Use the 'mixed-batcher-stress' scenario in the benchmark suite with these knobs:

  - concurrency: 64
  - sync_fraction: 0.35
  - generation_length: 512
  - kv_cache_hard_limit_fraction: 0.82

- Profiling checklist:
  1) Capture kernel launch timestamps and GC marker timestamps in high-resolution traces.
  2) Export per-kernel stream id and buffer UUID (instrumentation) to facilitate matching.
  3) Run CUDA memcheck on a small sample to detect illegal access (use in staging-only due to perf overhead).

Scheduler & kernel implications

- Scheduler adjustments to consider:
  - Introduce a soft barrier token that prevents certain asynchronous batch types from starting while a reclaim token is held.
  - Track per-shard outstanding device-side references and decrement at kernel callback completion; disallow reclaim until zero.

Minimal config reference (table)

| key | suggested safe default | description |
|-----|------------------------|-------------|
| kv_cache_soft_gc_threshold | 0.90 | fraction of device memory used before soft-GC steps up |
| kv_cache_eviction_batch_size | 4 | number of entries evicted per async GC cycle |
| slot_reuse_delay_ms | 200 | delay before a freed slot can be reused |
| max_concurrent_kernels | 128 | cap on concurrent kernel launches per GPU |

Runbook: triage checklist (oncall)

1. Confirm signal: check cuda_error_count and kernel_launch_overlap_ratio.
2. If cuda errors present: flip mitigations (throttle soft-GC and increase slot_reuse_delay_ms).
3. Isolate affected node(s): mark unschedulable; rotate traffic if more than one node impacted.
4. Collect traces: attach last 15 minutes of kernel/GPU traces and KV GC logs and upload to incident artifact store.
5. If errors persist after mitigations: open high-priority SEV and page runtime-kernel team.

Post-incident follow-ups

- Create a dedicated test in the benchmark suite labeled mixed-gc-safety and run in CI-nightly until flakiness is resolved.
- Add regression alert: any release that modifies kv_cache_* or slot_* config keys must run the mixed-gc-safety scenario.
- Schedule an architecture review to approve the kernel-scheduling handshake proposal.

Owners and escalation path

- Primary owner: runtime-kernel (eng team) — Laura Kim (author)
- Secondary: runtime-observability — Diego Morales
- Escalation: oncall -> runtime-kernel lead -> eng-sre -> CTO pager if > 3h impact on customer SLAs.

References and artifacts

- Reproducer repo: //git.internal/repro/mixed-gc-safety (staging-only)
- Relevant dashboards: GPU / KV Cache / Kernel Overlap (dash IDs in related_pages)
- Follow-up ADR: (planned) kernel-fence-and-refcount-adr (link to be added after review)

Appendix: quick debug commands

- Tail summarized kernel overlap events:
  kubectl -n runtime logs -l app=serving -c kernel-inspector --since=15m | grep OVERLAP | jq -r '.msg' | head -n 200

- Increase soft-GC threshold temporarily from kubernetes config map:
  kubectl edit cm runtime-config -n runtime
  # set kv_cache_soft_gc_threshold: 0.92

Contact the runtime-kernel team in #runtime-kernel on Slack for fast assistance.

title: Hardware tuning profiles: known issues and mitigations (living)
content:
## Purpose
This page is a living list of issues we have observed (or can reliably reproduce) when enabling the **hardware tuning profiles pack** for the serving runtime (H100, B200, L40S). Each issue includes:
- Symptoms you can validate quickly (what customers/oncall will see)
- How to detect (metrics/log signatures)
- Immediate mitigation steps (safe toggles/flags)
- Longer-term fix status (when known)

This is *not* an incident log. It is intended to reduce time-to-triage during rollouts and prevent repeated regressions.

**Primary audience:** Runtime oncall, SRE, Infra rollout owners, Support/Solutions.

**Owner:** Serving Runtime (Scheduling + Kernels). Operational upkeep coordinated by SRE.

---

## How to use this page during an incident
1) Identify the deployment + pool + GPU SKU (H100/B200/L40S) and confirm whether a profile is selected.
2) Check if the symptom matches one of the patterns below.
3) Apply the mitigation in the order listed (prefer “revert to baseline/default profile” over ad-hoc knob edits).
4) If mitigation requires disabling profiles for a pool/region, follow the rollout runbook and record the toggle + time window.

**Fast checks (recommended order):**
- Runtime startup logs: profile version + compatibility matrix (runtime version vs profile pack)
- Metrics: `runtime_profile_selected{sku,profile}` and `runtime_profile_override_source{source}`
- Tail latency: p95/p99 by route/model, segmented by profile
- OOM/restart rate and GPU memory headroom

---

## Common mitigations (safe-by-default toggles)
These are the mitigations referenced throughout the issue list.

### A) Disable profile selection (force baseline)
- **Use when:** unknown regression, ambiguous GPU detection, widespread tail-latency increase.
- **Effect:** runtime falls back to built-in baseline defaults.
- **Notes:** Use per-pool override first; avoid global unless impact is broad.

### B) Force a specific profile mode (e.g., H100 balanced)
- **Use when:** throughput-first mode causes tail latency or streaming instability.
- **Effect:** keeps profile benefits while restoring fairness/backpressure.

### C) Reduce batching / tighten queue limits
- **Use when:** tail latency spikes, request queue growth, streaming stutter.
- **Effect:** reduces queueing delay at the cost of throughput.

### D) Constrain KV cache budget
- **Use when:** OOMs, frequent restarts, memory fragmentation, long-context workloads.
- **Effect:** caps memory reserved for KV cache; may reduce max concurrency for long contexts.

### E) Disable experimental B200 profile
- **Use when:** any regression in B200 pools; if driver/CUDA mismatch suspected.
- **Effect:** revert to H100-like baseline or “generic” safe config.

(Exact flag/env/Helm key names vary by deployment mode; see the rollout runbook and the profile schema doc for current canonical names.)

---

## Known issues (by category)

### 1) Pathological prompt distributions / workload mismatch

#### KI-PP-001: Long-prefill-heavy workloads regress tail latency under throughput-first scheduler presets
**Applies to:** H100 (primarily), sometimes B200 when experimental mode is enabled.

**Symptom(s):**
- p95/p99 latency increases (often 20–60%) while average tokens/sec improves.
- Queue depth increases; “time-to-first-token” (TTFT) regresses most.
- Customers report “slow start” on long prompts, especially during load spikes.

**Likely trigger:**
- Workload skewed to long prefill (e.g., large context ingestion, retrieval-heavy prompts, tool-call scaffolding) combined with high concurrency.

**How to detect:**
- Segment by request type: prefill vs decode (if available).
- Look for disproportionate increase in TTFT and “prefill queue wait time.”
- `scheduler_fairness_adjustments_total` trending up (if instrumented) alongside tail latency.

**Mitigation:**
1) Switch pool to **balanced** mode profile (B).
2) Tighten max queue depth / reduce batching (C).
3) If still regressing: disable profiles for the pool (A) and proceed with rollback criteria.

**Status / notes:**
- A similar tail-latency regression was previously fixed in the prefill/decode fairness logic; if this appears after a profile pack update, treat as a candidate regression and compare to prior profile pack version.

---

#### KI-PP-002: “Too-clean” benchmark prompt mix hides streaming instability
**Applies to:** H100, L40S.

**Symptom(s):**
- Benchmarks pass; real traffic shows intermittent streaming stalls (“chunky” streaming) and elevated partial-response retries.
- p50 steady; p95 spikes correlate with peak concurrency.

**Likely trigger:**
- Real prompts include tool-calling patterns, high variance in output length, or client-side disconnects; these stress backpressure/streaming buffers.

**How to detect:**
- Increase in `stream_send_blocked_seconds` (or equivalent), and `client_disconnects_total` correlated with latency spikes.
- Elevated `request_retries_total{reason="upstream_timeout"}` on streaming routes.

**Mitigation:**
1) Reduce max in-flight streams per worker / tighten backpressure settings (C).
2) Prefer balanced mode (B) for streaming-heavy pools.
3) If stability issues persist, rollback profiles for the pool (A) and file an issue to expand workload matrix coverage.

**Status / notes:**
- Treat as a “workload matrix gap” if it passes canary but fails in prod; update the workload matrix with a representative streaming mix.

---

### 2) KV cache, memory fragmentation, and OOM patterns

#### KI-MEM-001: L40S OOMs under long-context + high concurrency due to KV cache over-reservation
**Applies to:** L40S.

**Symptom(s):**
- Sudden OOMs during prefill on long contexts; pods restart.
- GPU memory headroom oscillates; fragmentation increases over time.
- p95 latency spikes preceding OOMs (retries and warm-up effects).

**Likely trigger:**
- L40S has tighter memory constraints; aggressive KV cache budgeting that is safe on H100 can be unsafe on L40S.

**How to detect:**
- `gpu_oom_events_total` increases.
- `gpu_memory_free_bytes` trends downward across hours even at similar QPS (fragmentation pattern).
- Runtime logs mention KV cache allocation failure or emergency eviction.

**Mitigation:**
1) Enforce L40S profile with explicit KV cache budget constraints (D).
2) Reduce max batch size and/or max queued requests (C).
3) If OOMs continue: disable profiles (A) and set conservative runtime memory defaults until re-validated.

**Status / notes:**
- If you see “creeping” fragmentation, capture an hourly memory snapshot and attach to the tracking ticket; this typically indicates a reuse/allocator behavior mismatch for this workload.

---

#### KI-MEM-002: Memory fragmentation leading to degraded throughput after several hours (allocator behavior)
**Applies to:** L40S (most common), occasionally H100 in high churn traffic.

**Symptom(s):**
- Tokens/sec gradually declines over time; p50 stable but p95 creeps.
- No explicit OOMs; instead, more frequent small allocations and cache thrash.

**Likely trigger:**
- High variance in sequence lengths and frequent cancellations time-slice allocations differently than the benchmark harness.

**How to detect:**
- `kv_cache_evictions_total` increases without QPS growth.
- `gpu_memory_fragmentation_ratio` (if available) increases.
- Elevated `cuda_malloc_retry_total` / allocator warning logs.

**Mitigation:**
1) Reduce KV cache target utilization (D).
2) Prefer settings that reduce churn: cap max concurrent long-context requests (C + D).
3) If impact is severe: roll pool and disable profiles (A) pending deeper allocator analysis.

**Status / notes:**
- Often shows up only on specific traffic mixes; request a traffic replay / prompt distribution sample (sanitized) to reproduce.

---

### 3) Kernel selection mismatches and micro-architecture assumptions

#### KI-KRN-001: Kernel auto-selection chooses a suboptimal path for short sequences, causing TTFT regression
**Applies to:** H100; can affect B200 if heuristics borrowed.

**Symptom(s):**
- TTFT regresses for short prompts (e.g., <256 tokens input) while long prompts improve.
- Overall throughput may appear neutral, but UX impact is high for chat-like workloads.

**Likely trigger:**
- Heuristic bucket boundaries (sequence length bins) don’t match the real distribution; “short” bucket gets a kernel optimized for different occupancy characteristics.

**How to detect:**
- Segment TTFT by prompt length buckets.
- Compare `kernel_selected{bucket=...}` distribution pre/post profile.

**Mitigation:**
1) Switch to balanced mode or the “general” kernel selection preset for that SKU (B).
2) If available, enable adaptive kernel selection rather than pinned selection for short buckets.
3) If no safe option: disable profiles (A) for the affected pool.

**Status / notes:**
- When filing a follow-up, include bucket histograms (input/output length) and the kernel selection stats.

---

#### KI-KRN-002: Kernel mismatch when GPU SKU string detection is ambiguous (provider-specific strings)
**Applies to:** All SKUs; most common in mixed fleet environments and during provider expansion.

**Symptom(s):**
- Runtime selects “generic” profile unexpectedly, or selects the wrong SKU profile.
- Performance deviates from expectations; in worst cases, stability issues if an incompatible toggle is applied.

**Likely trigger:**
- GPU model strings differ across drivers/providers/instance types (e.g., formatting or suffix variations).

**How to detect:**
- Startup log shows `gpu_sku_raw` and `gpu_sku_normalized` mismatch; profile selection metric shows fallback.
- Increased rate of `profile_selection_ambiguous_total`.

**Mitigation:**
1) Force explicit SKU/profile via pool override (B) until detection is fixed.
2) If forced override is not possible: disable profiles (A) and run with baseline.
3) File an Infra ticket with the raw strings and node types involved; add to normalization allowlist.

**Status / notes:**
- This should be treated as a correctness issue, not “just performance.” Incorrect profile selection can invalidate canary results.

---

### 4) Scheduler/backpressure edge cases

#### KI-SCH-001: Queue growth + timeouts during burst traffic due to queue limit mismatch with upstream timeouts
**Applies to:** H100, L40S.

**Symptom(s):**
- Requests time out upstream; runtime appears healthy but queue depth spikes.
- p99 latency spikes; retries increase; effective throughput drops.

**Likely trigger:**
- Profile queue limits allow too much buffering relative to gateway/client timeouts; burst traffic fills queue faster than it drains.

**How to detect:**
- `request_queue_depth` increases; `gateway_timeouts_total` increases.
- `queue_wait_ms` becomes dominant contributor to latency.

**Mitigation:**
1) Reduce queue limits and tighten backpressure (C).
2) Align per-route timeout budgets with expected max queue wait.
3) If customer impact persists, rollback profile for pool (A) and re-validate burst behavior.

**Status / notes:**
- Prefer smaller queues and more explicit load shedding for customer-visible endpoints; large queues hide overload until timeouts cascade.

---

#### KI-SCH-002: Multi-tenant interference in Dedicated pools when throughput-first batching is enabled
**Applies to:** Dedicated H100 pools with mixed tenant traffic.

**Symptom(s):**
- One tenant’s long-context or high-output requests dominate batching windows.
- Other tenants see tail-latency regressions and inconsistent TTFT.

**Likely trigger:**
- Batching parameters optimized for aggregate throughput without sufficient per-tenant fairness constraints.

**How to detect:**
- Latency segmented by tenant spikes for “small” tenants during another tenant’s traffic burst.
- Batch composition metrics show high skew.

**Mitigation:**
1) Switch pool to balanced profile mode (B).
2) Apply stricter per-tenant concurrency limits (if configured via routing/gateway).
3) If needed, split tenants to separate pools (operational action) and re-run perf validation.

**Status / notes:**
- Treat as a product/SLA concern; do not “optimize away” fairness unless the pool is explicitly single-tenant.

---

### 5) B200 experimental profile (maturity and compatibility)

#### KI-B2K-001: Driver/CUDA mismatch causes silent fallback or instability
**Applies to:** B200 only (experimental gated).

**Symptom(s):**
- Profile not applied even when enabled; runtime logs show version guardrails tripping.
- In some cases: increased error rate, sporadic kernel launch failures.

**Likely trigger:**
- B200 profile requires minimum driver/CUDA stack; partial fleet upgrades lead to mixed compatibility.

**How to detect:**
- Startup logs show “incompatible stack” warning and selected fallback.
- `profile_compatibility_violation_total{sku="B200"}` increases.

**Mitigation:**
1) Disable experimental B200 profile for the pool (E).
2) Verify driver/CUDA versions match the B200 bring-up checklist; upgrade fleet before re-enabling.
3) Re-enable only with canary gating and a rollback plan.

**Status / notes:**
- Default posture for B200 remains “gated + explicit enablement.” Treat any enabling as a staged change with extra SRE oversight.

---

#### KI-B2K-002: Cross-region regression requiring pool-level disable (known precedent)
**Applies to:** B200 (experimental) in specific pools/regions.

**Symptom(s):**
- Immediate p95 regression post-enable; canary gate triggers or customer reports.

**How to detect:**
- Perf canary gate breach for B200 pools; increased tail latency segmented by region.

**Mitigation:**
1) Disable experimental B200 profile for the impacted pool/region (E).
2) Leave other regions unchanged until root cause is understood.
3) Capture: node type, NCCL/topology characteristics (if multi-GPU), and driver stack details.

**Status / notes:**
- Regional differences (network topology, firmware, provider) can invalidate assumptions. Ensure each region has baseline curves.

---

## Observability: what to capture when filing a follow-up
When escalating to Runtime (Scheduling/Kernels) or Infra, include:
- Deployment mode (Hosted/Dedicated/Private), region, pool name, GPU SKU, MIG status (if any)
- Runtime version + profile pack version
- Selected profile and override source (fleet default vs per-pool vs per-deployment vs manual)
- Before/after comparison window and traffic level (QPS, concurrency)
- Workload characteristics: prompt length distribution, output length distribution, streaming vs non-streaming share
- Key metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, TTFT, tokens/sec, queue wait, OOM/restart rate
- Relevant logs: startup compatibility matrix, kernel selection summary, allocator warnings

---

## Update process (for maintainers)
- Add a new entry when: (a) reproducible in perf suite, (b) observed in prod and confirmed profile-related, or (c) known hazard with a clear mitigation.
- Retire an entry only when the mitigation is no longer needed *and* the fix is present in the supported runtime/profile versions.
- Keep entries terse and operational. Link deeper analysis to the relevant PR/ADR/ticket.

**Maintainer rotation:** Kira Thompson (Docs/Runbooks) with quarterly review by Noah Patel (Runtime architecture) and Aisha Bello (SRE dashboards).

---

## Changelog (high level)
- 2026-02-20: Added B200 compatibility and regional disable guidance; expanded observability capture checklist.
- 2026-01-14: Added kernel auto-selection TTFT regression pattern and detection steps.
- 2025-12-09: Added L40S KV cache budgeting/OOM patterns and recommended guardrails.
- 2025-11-26: Initial publication (bootstrap list from rollout triage and perf suite findings).

title: gRPC connection reuse and pipeline regeneration: root causes, triage, and mitigations
content:
Summary

This page documents a recurring class of production issues we tag as \"gRPC connection reuse / pipeline regeneration events\" that affect the serving runtime's frontproxy -> worker (dispatcher/gpu-proxy) communication path. The problem manifests as sudden latency spikes, increased CPU on frontproxy, and a transient drop in request throughput for a subset of tenants. These incidents have been observed across heterogeneous pools (A100 and H100) and correlate with high client churn, long tail responses, or server-initiated stream resets.

Goals

- Provide a clear symptom checklist and deterministic triage workflow.
- Identify short-term mitigations and longer-term remediation patterns.
- Standardize monitoring, tests, and release guidance to prevent regressions.

Scope and assumptions

- Applies to gRPC multiplexed HTTP/2 connections used by frontproxy and internal GPU-side proxies.
- Does not cover public API client SDKs (separate doc).
- Assumes HTTP/2 flow control, stream reset (RST_STREAM), and GOAWAY semantics are in play.

Observed symptoms (production signature)

1) Sudden P50->P99 latency divergence for affected route(s). P99 increases by 3x+ while median increases modestly.
2) Frontproxy CPU climbs to >75% in the cluster pool while worker GPU utilization remains stable.
3) Error burst of grpc.StatusCode.UNAVAILABLE and INTERNAL with message fragments like \"RST_STREAM\" or \"REFUSED_STREAM\".
4) Connection-level metrics show spike in active connection churn (connections/sec) and TCP retransmits.
5) Streaks of reorders in request ids in the trace logs due to stream reassignments.

Root cause taxonomy (how this happens)

- A: Client churn + stream reuse exhaustion: large number of short-lived clients exhausts MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS and triggers RST_STREAM or REFUSED_STREAM; frontproxy retries rebuild pipelines to other worker connections causing in-flight reorder and temporary head-of-line blocking.
- B: Server-side keepalive and GOAWAY miscoordination: worker-side GOAWAY to drain leads frontproxy to open new connections while in-flight streams are aborted due to aggressive RST semantics.
- C: Middlebox path MTU or TLS renegotiation causing short disconnects: connection rekeying or PMTU events cause transport resets and pipeline re-creation.
- D: Backpressure-induced stall: GPU-side request processing stalls (long decode/attention spike) causing HTTP/2 flow-control window exhaustion; frontproxy treats stall as connection failure and rebuilds session.

Immediate triage checklist (ordered)

1) Identify affected routes and tenants. Query the request log aggregator for spikes in grpc UNAVAILABLE/INTERNAL for last 15m.
   - Kibana query: service:frontproxy AND grpc.code:(UNAVAILABLE OR INTERNAL) AND @timestamp:[now-15m TO now] AND route:<ROUTE>
2) Check frontproxy connection churn: connections_opened_per_min and connections_closed_per_min for frontproxy pool.
   - Grafana panel: frontproxy.connections_opened_rate / frontproxy.connections_closed_rate
3) Inspect trace spans for RST_STREAM, REFUSED_STREAM, and GOAWAY markers. Correlate trace ids across frontproxy -> worker hops.
4) Validate server keepalive and window sizes in worker logs. Look for GOAWAY frames with last_stream_id < current_stream_id.
5) CPU vs GPU utilization: if frontproxy CPU high but GPU healthy, likely pipeline rebuild churn.
6) Confirm whether error pattern follows a config change or deploy within the last 30 min.

Short-term mitigations (operational playbook)

- Apply an emergency rate limit per-source IP for the affected route to reduce churn. Example: edge-bind limit 150 rps per ephemeral client for the route.
- Temporarily increase MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS and flow-control window on frontproxy-worker connection endpoints (config knobs below). Note: increasing streams increases memory and per-connection CPU.
- Disable aggressive keepalive or delayed GOAWAY on the worker to allow graceful stream completion.
- If the issue correlates with a recent kernel or runtime patch, rollback using the runtime rollback matrix.

Permanent fixes and engineering changes

- Connection leasing: implement short-lived connection leases that reduce per-client connection churn while enforcing per-lease stream accounting. This avoids opening new TCP/TLS connections for every client burst.
- Adaptive MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS: runtime-side controller that increases allowed streams when measured per-connection CPU overhead is low and decreases during overloads.
- Improved GOAWAY semantics: coordinate GOAWAY issuance with stream-level graceful window to avoid aborting in-flight streams.
- Flow-control heuristic: detect in-flight compute stalls (GPU-side stalls > threshold) and advertise smaller initial windows so frontproxy spreads streams across more connections rather than piling onto a blocked connection.
- Health-aware routing: extend the smart routing policy to avoid using worker connections with elevated stall signals; prefer routing new streams to underutilized connections.

Config knobs and recommended safe ranges

| config_key | default | recommended emergency | tradeoffs |
|------------|---------|------------------------|-----------|
| grpc.max_concurrent_streams | 100 | 200 | higher concurrency reduces connection churn but increases memory/CPU per-connection |
| grpc.initial_window_size | 65535 | 65535 | very large windows can worsen head-of-line blocking when stalls occur |
| grpc.stream_idle_timeout_ms | 60000 | 120000 | longer idle avoids premature RST from transient spikes but delays resource reclamation |
| worker.goaway_grace_ms | 500 | 2000 | larger grace means fewer aborted streams during drain at the cost of slower rollouts |

Note: the table above is presented as text in this page; apply changes during low risk windows or use canary first.

Monitoring and alerting recipes

- New composite alert: GRPC_PIPELINE_REGEN_HIGH
  - Trigger: frontproxy.connections_opened_rate > 5x baseline AND frontproxy.grpc_unavailable_rate > 3x baseline in 3m window.
  - Severity: P2 when affecting <5% tenants, P1 when >5% tenants or SLO breaches.
  - Runbook link: this page.

- Dashboards to add:
  - Connection churn per route (heatmap)
  - Stream reset reason breakdown (REFUSED_STREAM / RST_STREAM / GOAWAY) by worker pool
  - Average outstanding streams per connection and avg stream lifetime

Reproduction procedure (dev sandbox)

1) Test harness: grpc-client-spammer (internal tool). Start with N=500 concurrent short-lived clients sending 1-2 requests and terminating.
2) Vary MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS to 20, 50, 100 and observe when REFUSED_STREAM increases.
3) Introduce artificial GPU-side stalls by injecting a sleep in the decoder path for a subset of requests and observe frontproxy behavior.
4) Capture tcpdump and http2 frame logs to confirm GOAWAY and RST frames.

Fix rollout guidance and canary strategy

- Any change to grpc.max_concurrent_streams or worker.goaway_grace_ms must be canaried: apply to 5% of worker nodes for 2 hours under production-like synthetic traffic.
- For code changes (connection leasing, adaptive controller): feature-flag and side-by-side deployment with telemetry gates. Telemetry gates must include stream-reset rate, per-connection CPU, and P99 latency for canary tenants.

Testing checklist for PRs and releases

- Unit tests for new state machines (lease lifecycle, goaway-coordination).
- Integration test: simulated churn harness with deterministic verification of no stream loss above threshold.
- Load test: scaled to 300k streams/min with mixed short/long sessions showing <=3% REFUSED/RST under steady state.
- Chaos test: inject GOAWAY and RST under load and assert graceful completion percent >= 95%.

Ownership and contacts

- Primary owner: runtime-networking (oncall: @runtime-networking-oncall).
- Secondary owner: frontproxy-team.
- SLT escalation: runtime-eng-manager@example.redwood.com

Post-incident analysis template

1) Incident timeline: collect timestamps for first error spike, detection, mitigation, and recovery.
2) Affected tenants: list tenant ids and approximate request volume during window.
3) Root cause evidence: trace screenshots, tcpdump snippets, worker logs with GOAWAY/RST frame dumps.
4) Remediation actions taken and time to implement.
5) Follow-ups and code patches assigned with owners and ETA.

Appendix: example diagnostic commands and snippets

- grpc tranlogs: curl -s \"https://logs.internal/api/search?q=grpc.code:REFUSED_STREAM%20AND%20service:frontproxy&from=now-15m\"
- tcpdump: sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w /tmp/conn-regen.pcap host <worker_ip> and port 443
- http2 frame log extract (dev tool): ./http2-frame-dump --file /tmp/conn-regen.pcap --filter 'GOAWAY|RST_STREAM'
- quick config bump (kubectl patch): kubectl -n runtime patch configmap frontproxy-config --type merge -p '{\"data\":{\"grpc.max_concurrent_streams\":\"200\"}}'

Revision history

- 2025-04-10: Created by Sofia Martinez.
- 2025-05-02: Expanded mitigation list and added monitoring alert recipe (Ravi Menon).

References

- HTTP/2 GOAWAY semantics: RFC 7540 section 6.8
- Internal: frontproxy connection metrics schema: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/runtime-telemetry-data-model-and-tracebook-2026

If you see an ongoing incident matching the symptom checklist, follow the triage checklist first and notify runtime-networking. For long-term work, file a tracking ticket in the runtime backlog with label \"grpc-pipeline-regen\" and link to this doc.

title: NVLink interconnect degradation and remediation playbook
content:
Summary:
This page describes symptoms, detection signals, triage steps, and remediation actions for NVLink / GPU interconnect degradation observed in the runtime fleet. NVLink issues typically present as increased tail latency and elevated per-request GPU-to-GPU copy times for sharded models or multi-GPU kernels. The goal of this playbook is to provide a repeatable oncall and engineering triage path, automated mitigations where safe, and guidance for permanent fixes or vendor escalation.

Scope and impact:
- Affects multi-GPU model shards, cross-GPU KV cache fills, and kernels that perform peer-to-peer communication (e.g., sharded attention, distributed KV cache updates).
- Typical customer impact: 99.9th percentile generation latency spikes (5x–20x), increased error rates due to kernel timeouts (grpc errors, TPU-like watchdog resets), and occasional node-level GPU panic requiring node restart.
- Known affected subsystems: gpu-dispatcher, shard-orchestrator, kvcache-sync-job, and the runtime kernel layer.

When to use this playbook:
1. Alert fires: "nvlink_transfer_time_p95 > 10ms for 5m" or "gpu_p2p_error_rate > 0"
2. Tail latency regressions correlated with multi-GPU allocations in Grafana panel 'Model Shard Latency by Node'
3. Post-deploy increase in intra-node memcpy or nvlink error counters in node exporter

Detection signals (ranked):
1. Telemetry (high confidence):
   - PromQL: sum(rate(nvlink_transfer_time_sum[5m])) / sum(rate(nvlink_transfer_time_count[5m])) > 0.01 // mean > 10ms
   - PromQL alert: increase(gpu_nvlink_link_error_total[10m]) > 0
   - Perf counters: PCIe DMA stall events and increased memcpy latency in per-kernel telemetry
2. Runtime traces:
   - Trace span 'p2p-copy' duration spike on request trace
   - Traces show 'wait-for-peer' subspan dominated in GPU scheduler traces
3. Node metrics:
   - nvlink_utilization / nvlink_throughput drop while local GPU utilization remains high

Immediate oncall triage (0–15 minutes):
1. Confirm alert context and scope:
   - Determine affected node(s) and model(s) using 'alert.labels.node' and 'alert.annotations.models'.
   - Run quick queries: 
     - kubectl -n runtime get pods -o wide --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node>
     - prometheus query: topk(10, rate(nvlink_transfer_time_sum[1m]) / rate(nvlink_transfer_time_count[1m]))
2. If the issue is isolated to a single node and no kernel panics: divert new multi-GPU allocations off the node.
   - Command: curl -X POST https://internal-scheduler/api/v1/drain-node -d '{"node":"<node>","reason":"nvlink_degradation"}'
3. If kernel panics / GPU watchdog resets observed: escalate to SRE and set short maintenance window for node reboot.
   - Oncall runbook: run 'sudo nv_peer_sync_check.sh' (see diagnostics below) before reboot; collect logs to /tmp/nvlink-diagnostics-<timestamp>.tar.gz

Automated mitigations (safe defaults):
- Auto-fallback policy (configured in dispatcher): when nvlink_transfer_time_p95 > 10ms for a node for 3m, do not schedule multi-GPU shards to the node; allow single-GPU fallbacks. See 'fallback-routing-config' below.
- KV cache sync throttle: reduce kvcache-sync parallelism from 64 -> 8 for nodes with nvlink anomalies. Controlled by the 'kvcache.sync_parallelism_per_node' feature flag.

Deep triage (15–90 minutes):
1. Reproduce telemetry in isolation: run a synthetic cross-GPU memcpy microbenchmark against the node:
   - test tool: /opt/runtime/tools/p2p_transfer_test --size 256MB --iters 200 --target-node <node>
   - Expected baseline: p2p latency median < 2ms, p95 < 5ms. If p95 > 10ms, then NVLink degradation confirmed.
2. Collect GPU and NVLink counters:
   - nvidia-smi dmon -s u -d 1 -o DUMP > /tmp/gpu-dmon-<ts>.log
   - nvlink error counters (via nvidia-smi nvlink) or vendor tool: nvlink-smi --show-errors > /tmp/nvlink-errors-<ts>.log
3. Kernel-level profiling: capture a short runtime profile (10–30s) with tracing enabled:
   - curl -X POST http://localhost:15000/api/v1/trace/start -d '{"duration_s":30, "include":"p2p-copy,kernel-launch"}'
   - Save trace: /tmp/trace-nvlink-<ts>.json and open in TraceUI. Look for long queues at 'gpu-mem-copy' spans.
4. Check OS-level messages: dmesg, kernel logs may show peer-to-peer DMA errors or nvlink faults.
   - sudo journalctl -u nvidia-node-manager -n 500 | grep -i nvlink

Diagnostics scripts and snippets:
- nv_peer_sync_check.sh (runs basic nvlink and p2p checks):
  #!/bin/bash
  node=$1
  timestamp=$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)
  nvidia-smi nvlink --query-gpu=all > /tmp/nvlink-summary-${timestamp}.txt
  nvidia-smi dmon -s u -d 1 -c 10 > /tmp/gpu-dmon-${timestamp}.log
  /opt/runtime/tools/p2p_transfer_test --size 32MB --iters 50 --target-node ${node} > /tmp/p2p-test-${timestamp}.log
  tar -czf /tmp/nvlink-diagnostics-${timestamp}.tar.gz /tmp/nvlink-summary-${timestamp}.txt /tmp/gpu-dmon-${timestamp}.log /tmp/p2p-test-${timestamp}.log
  echo "/tmp/nvlink-diagnostics-${timestamp}.tar.gz"

Recommended alert definitions (Prometheus):
- Alert: NVLink_P2P_Latency_High
  expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(nvlink_transfer_time_bucket[5m])) by (le,node)) > 0.01
  for: 5m
  labels: { severity: page, subsystem: runtime }
  annotations: { runbook: "/confluence/eng-serving-runtime/known-issues/nvlink-interconnect-degradation-and-remediation-2026" }

Fallback routing config (example YAML):
- name: fallback-routing-config
  version: 2
  rules:
    - when: nvlink_transfer_time_p95 > 0.01 and nvlink_error_rate > 0
      action: avoid_multi_gpu_on_node
      ttl: 15m
      owner: runtime-scheduler-team

Operational thresholds and SLO impact guidance:
- If a single node exhibits nvlink p95 > 10ms for > 10 minutes, mark node as 'degraded' and avoid new multi-GPU allocations.
- If >= 3 nodes in a single AZ show degradation for 15m, open an incident (sev2).
- SLO impact: a single degraded node hosting large model shards can increase per-request cost by 30% and tail latency by up to 10x for affected customers.

Permanent remediation checklist (owner: hardware-ops / infra-eng):
1. Validate hardware: reseat NVLink bridges, check physical connectors, and run vendor diagnostics.
2. Firmware: ensure GPUs have vendor-recommended firmware revision (vendor_firmware >= 2025.12.1).
3. OS driver: verify NVIDIA driver >= 535.x where known nvlink fixes exist.
4. Replace unit: if nvlink errors persist after reseat + firmware + driver, schedule GPU or node replacement with priority 'P1 hardware' queue.

Escalation matrix:
- Oncall SRE (first): notify via #sre-runtime and tag runtime-oncall (pager if sev1).
- Hardware ops: if nvlink error counters persist after reboot/resync, create ECC ticket with vendor and include diagnostics tarball.
- Product/Customer Success: if major customers are affected, inform assigned CSM and prepare a customer-facing incident summary.

Post-incident analysis and permanent mitigations (RCA template):
1. Timeline of detection, mitigations, and service impact.
2. Root cause hypothesis (hardware / firmware / OS driver / workload pattern).
3. Evidence: telemetry graphs, diagnostics tarball, vendor response.
4. Action items with owners and ETA (firmware rollouts, alert tuning, scheduler constraints).

Appendix: Useful queries and dashboards
- Grafana panels: 'NVLink topology and errors', 'Model shard p2p latency by node', 'KVCache cross-gpu sync latency'.
- PromQL quicklist:
  - nvlink_error_total: increase(gpu_nvlink_link_error_total[10m])
  - nvlink_p95: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(nvlink_transfer_time_bucket[5m])) by (le,node))
  - p2p_wait_traces: sum(rate(runtime_p2p_wait_seconds_count[5m])) by (node) / sum(rate(runtime_p2p_wait_seconds_sum[5m])) by (node)

Contacts and ownership:
- Primary: runtime-infra (pager: pagerduty runtime-infra)
- Secondary: gpu-hardware-ops (slack: @gpu-hw-ops)
- Documentation owner: Lina Park (lina.park@redwood.ai)

Change history:
- 2026-02-14 (Lina Park): initial draft
- 2026-06-07 (Marcus Chen): added automated fallback policy and alert examples
- 2026-11-03 (Aisha Bello): updated firmware and driver recommended versions, clarified diagnostic commands

Notes and references:
- Vendor NVLink troubleshooting guide (internal link stored in hardware-ops drive)
- See related runbooks: 'gpu-affinity-and-eviction-strategies', 'gpu-memory-fragmentation-diagnostics-playbook' for mitigation overlap.

End of document.

title: PCIe Topology Fragmentation and Runtime Fallback Mitigation
content:
Summary:

This page documents a class of production incidents we have observed where PCIe / host topology fragmentation (uneven NUMA/PCIe root complex attachments and NVLink islands) produces unpredictable kernel scheduling outcomes, degraded throughput, or cascaded fallbacks to lower-fidelity execution paths. The doc explains symptoms, root causes, automated detection heuristics, immediate mitigations, and medium-term fixes plus an incident runbook for oncall.

Why this matters:
- Manifestation: single-tenant or multi-tenant kernels exhibit large variance in tail latency and per-token GPU time (20–400% increases) under certain placement patterns.
- Impacted features: large autoregressive generation, streaming responses, batching-heavy endpoints, multi-model pipelines with chained KV cache usage.
- Business impact: SLA violations on 99th percentile latency, elevated per-token costs, and repeated model fallback/eviction cycles that reduce quality for users.

Scope and applicability:
- Affects clusters with mixed PCIe/NVLink topologies (common in our Dedicated and Private deployments when mixes of A100, H100, and earlier generation cards are used).
- Observed when node-level device allocation policies route co-resident critical kernels to devices across distinct PCIe root complexes or across an NVLink boundary.

Symptoms (observable signals):
1) Stepwise increase in kernel wall-time correlated with specific placement decisions (per-kernel wall-time jump of 3–10x).
2) Elevated scheduler preemption and reroute events (trace tags: scheduler.reassign, kernel.handoff).
3) Rapid increase in fallback-to-lower-fidelity model variants or disabled tensor-core paths.
4) Device-to-device throughput variance visible in node telemetry (NVLink bandwidth metrics asymmetry).

Quick triage checklist (oncall):
1) Identify affected pod/workload: check request trace and model variant.
   - Commands:
     - kubectl -n redwood get pods -o wide | grep <instance-id>
     - rg "request-id=<id>" /var/log/serving/requests.log
2) Correlate with node device topology: run on suspected host:
   - lspci | rg -A1 -i nvidia
   - sudo nvidia-smi topo -m
   - | Example output: "GPU0 GPU1 CPU0 CPU1
     GPU0 X NVLINK SYS SYS
     GPU1 NVLINK X SYS SYS"
3) Inspect runtime kernel traces and scheduler events (trace tags):
   - curl http://localhost:8100/debug/trace?request=<id> | jq .events | rg topology
4) Check for recent placement changes or cluster autoscaler events in the same timespan.

Root cause patterns (typical):
- Placement across PCIe root complexes: co-scheduled sub-tasks of a single request land on GPUs with expensive host hops.
- NVLink island mismatch: pinned KV cache or attention cache spans GPUs without high-bandwidth interconnect, forcing expensive host-mediated transfers.
- Fragmented allocator state: per-device memory fragmentation makes the scheduler attempt split allocations that require cross-device coordination.
- Healed device affinity fallthrough: the admission controller moves work to an available GPU that is topologically distant to reduce queueing, which worsens latency.

Table: symptom => short-term mitigation => medium-term fix
| Symptom | Short-term mitigation | Medium-term fix |
|---|---|---|
| Kernel wall-time spike when GPU hops cross NVLink | Evict non-critical background cohorts from affected host; enable same-node placement policy for the request | Topology-aware allocator and routing policy (see design below) |
| KV cache misses due to remote device eviction | Increase ephemeral routing priority for cached session tokens or pin cache to single NVLink island | Cache-aware placement + capacity reservation for cache-heavy cohorts |
| Scheduler reassign thrash | Raise preemption threshold and enable backoff window 30s | Admission-control refinement: topology penalty scoring + binding reservations |

Immediate mitigations (playbook actions):
- Emergency stabilization (2–5 minutes):
  1) Put the affected node(s) into cordon state to prevent new allocations: kubectl cordon <node>.
  2) Identify and migrate non-critical low-priority cohorts off the node (evict pods with priorityClassName: low).
  3) If the node hosts canary or experimental kernels, roll them back to the previous runtime version (release tag).
- Short window guard (10–30 minutes):
  1) Flip the scheduler flag runtime.scheduler.topology_penalty_multiplier=2.0 (temporary) via config-svc: curl -X PATCH $CONFIG_SVC/api/v1/flags -d '{"topology_penalty_multiplier":2.0}'.
  2) Enable topology-aware binding for the service route: patch route config to bindingMode: strict-local for critical endpoints.
  3) Monitor 99p latency, kernel wall-time, and NVLink drop counters.

Runbook: step-by-step incident handling
1) Detect
   - Alert trigger: 99th-percentile generation latency > SLO * 1.5 for 5 minutes AND scheduler.reassign events > 50/min across a host cluster.
2) Contain
   - Action: Cordon and drain non-critical pods; set node annotation redwood/isolated=true to prevent autoscaler reattachment.
3) Diagnose
   - Collect: nvidia-smi topo -m, dmesg | tail -n 200, runtime trace for request IDs, allocator map: curl $RUNTIME/api/v1/allocator/slots?node=<node>&json=true
   - Note: allocator map endpoint returns a large JSON; save to /tmp/alloc-<node>-YYYYMMDD.json for postmortem.
4) Mitigate
   - If KV-cache eviction found: restore pinned cache by restarting cache-manager with parameter --pin-to-island=GPU0,GPU1.
   - If scheduler is reassigning across root complexes: set runtime.scheduler.force_coalition_binding=true for the affected cohort.
5) Restore
   - Uncordon hosts once stable for 10 minutes; revert temporary flags after rolling config change to final topology-aware policy.
6) Postmortem
   - Assign engineer to root cause investigation and timeline; attach traces and config diffs; classify severity and action items.

Debugging artifacts to collect (commands):
- sudo nvidia-smi topo -m > /tmp/topo-<node>.txt
- sudo lspci -vvv | rg -A3 -i nvidia > /tmp/lspci-<node>.txt
- curl $RUNTIME/debug/trace?node=<node>&range=10m > /tmp/trace-<node>.json
- cat /var/log/syslog | rg -i "nvlink|pci|nvidia|oom" > /tmp/syslog-device.txt

Medium-term design proposal (owner: runtime kernel team):
1) Topology-aware scheduler scoring: augment the current scheduler score with a topology penalty term computed from an undirected graph of device connectivity. Score = base_score - alpha * locality_bonus + beta * topology_penalty.
2) KV-cache affinity reservations: allow session tokens to create light-weight reservations within an NVLink island. Reservation semantics: soft_hold (30s) and hard_hold (configurable per-cohort).
3) Allocator compaction and defragmentation daemon: periodic compaction job per node that coalesces free blocks and emits health metrics.
4) Admission controller policy: route requests through a topology advisory function that returns a placement recommendation; fallback to cost-based placement only if advisory cannot satisfy SLO.

Configuration examples:
- Scheduler flag patch (example curl):
  curl -X PATCH https://config.redwood-internal/v1/flags
    -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json'
    -d '{"runtime.scheduler.topology_penalty_multiplier":"1.5"}'

- Example admission policy snippet (YAML):
  apiVersion: redwood/v1
  kind: RouteBindingPolicy
  metadata:
    name: cache-heavy-binding
  spec:
    bindingMode: "prefer-local-island"
    topologyHints:
      nvlink_weight: 10
      pcie_weight: 5
    reservations:
      soft_hold_seconds: 30
      hard_hold_seconds: 300

Metrics and dashboards to monitor (suggested panels):
- Kernel wall-time by placement type (local-island vs cross-root): 99/95/50 percentiles.
- NVLink utilization and per-link asymmetry heatmap.
- Scheduler reassign / handoff rate per host.
- KV-cache miss ratio per session cohort.
- Incident guard: nodes with recent topology_penalty overrides.

Testing and benchmark guidance:
- Synthetic reproduction: use our workload-synth harness with --placement-pattern topology_cross and --burst-shape {microburst, sustained}. Benchmark matrix should include: sequence lengths 64, 512, 2048; batch sizes 1, 8, 32; and model variants with and without KV cache.
- Kernel-level microbench: run schedule_with_topology_probe binary on target host; collect microtraces and compare median kernel launch latencies across islands.

Rollout plan for topology-aware scheduler (phased):
1) Canary (QA): small internal cluster with mixed topologies; run 48-hour soak with workload-synth corpora.
2) Beta (limited customer): enable on Dedicated regions with annotation-based opt-in.
3) Gradual ramp: 10% -> 50% -> 100% traffic over 2–4 weeks with rollback gates on 99p latency and per-token cost.

Ownership and escalation path:
- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime/kernel-scheduling (rotation: @kernel-oncall).
- Secondary: eng-infra/gpu-fleet (pager: @gpu-oncall).
- Escalation to SRE and Product if SLA risk > 4 hours.

Related pages:
- runtime-architecture/execution-stitching-and-fallback-orchestration-2026
- kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-telemetry-synthesis-and-proofing-2025

Post-incident action items (examples):
- Add topology-awareness unit tests to scheduler CI (owner: kernel team).
- Instrument allocator to surface fragmentation percentiles per-device.
- Document preferred hardware mixes for Dedicated offers (product + infra).

Appendix: diagnostic outputs (example snippets)
- Example nvidia-smi topo -m excerpt:
  "GPU0   GPU1   CPU0   CPU1
   GPU0    X    NVLINK SYS   SYS
   GPU1  NVLINK    X   SYS   SYS"
- Example trace event line: trace_event{timestamp:162..., tag:"kernel.handoff", payload:"from=GPU0,to=GPU3,reason=affinity_fallback,delta_ms=245"}

Notes and rationale:
- We prefer conservative short-term mitigations that prioritize availability and predictable latency over immediate throughput gains. The topology-aware scheduler balances quality with economics by default but can be tuned per-customer.

Document history:
- 2026-02-10: initial draft by Asha Patel.
- 2026-05-03: added KV-cache reservation semantics and early implementation notes (Liang Zhou).
- 2026-08-15: finalized runbook steps and rollout plan (reviewers Diego Morales, Maya Singh).

End of document.

title: Dispatcher memory leak and connection-window exhaustion — investigation & mitigation
content:
Summary
-------
This page documents a recurring failure class observed in the dispatcher service where long-running connection windows and an unbounded buffer growth lead to pod memory exhaustion and partial request loss. The doc covers: detection signals, short-term mitigations, permanent fixes planned, rollout steps, post-incident verification, and ownership.

Context and scope
------------------
- Affected service: dispatcher-service (grpc frontend + connection multiplexer)
- Secondary impact: kernel-manager and grpc-proxy pods observed elevated tail latency due to request drops and retries.
- Customer-visible symptoms: increased 5xx rates on hosted API routes, transient model swap failures, and elevated p99 latency.
- Root hypothesis summary: under sustained backpressure (long KV cache fetches / slow kernel warmstarts), the dispatcher accumulates connection windows and request buffers that are not compacted, causing memory pressure and eventual OOM/kube eviction.

Why this matters
------------------
- SLO impact: incidents breached the 99.9% availability SLO for several customer routes for 4–17 minutes in observed incidents.
- Cost/operational: repeated restarts mask the underlying problem and create downstream load spikes (thundering herd) when services recover.

Detection and alerting
----------------------
Create or verify these signals in Grafana / Prometheus: 
1) Memory growth slope alert (dispatcher pod level):
- PromQL (example):
  increase(container_memory_working_set_bytes{job="dispatcher-service"}[15m]) > 150e6
- Alert intent: signal sustained memory growth > 150MB over 15 minutes.

2) Connection-window count spike:
- Instrumentation metric: dispatcher_connection_windows_total (gauge of active per-client windows)
- PromQL: sum(dispatcher_connection_windows_total) by(cluster_zone) > 5000

3) Request buffer backlog:
- Metric: dispatcher_request_buffer_depth (histogram buckets or gauge). Alert when avg > 400 per pod for 10m.

4) Error surface correlation: correlate 500s spike with buffer metrics using dashboards. Create a combined panel that shows: 5xx_rate, dispatcher_memory_working_set, request_buffer_depth

Investigation checklist (fast triage)
------------------------------------
1) Identify affected pods: kubectl -n inference get pods -l app=dispatcher-service --field-selector status.phase!=Running
2) Check last OOM reason: kubectl describe pod <pod> | grep -i oom
3) Check top memory consumers inside the pod: kubectl exec -it <pod> -- pmap /proc/1/maps || ps aux --sort=-rss | head -n 20
4) Query metrics: use the PromQL alerts above to identify trend and onset time windows.
5) Grab heap profile (if enabled): curl -sS http://<pod-ip>:6060/debug/pprof/heap > heap-<pod>.pb.gz
6) Correlate with kernel-manager traces: tracer id / request ids in logs. Use the trace-id header to find full request timeline.

Immediate mitigations (stop-gap, low-risk)
------------------------------------------
Apply these in order to reduce customer-visible impact while preserving diagnostics: 
1) Scale horizontally: kubectl scale --replicas=+2 deploy/dispatcher-service (add pods to lower per-pod backlog).
2) Enable admission backpressure: set config dispatcher.max_inflight_per_client to 50 (from default 200) via config map and rolling restart. This limits per-client window growth.
3) TTL/Compaction: reduce dispatcher.window_idle_ttl from 10m to 90s to force faster window tear-down.
4) Controlled rolling restart: restart the pods with highest memory slope first, one at a time, with 3m drain between restarts. Use the readiness probe to ensure no traffic is sent to the pod during restart.
5) Route heavy customers to Dedicated capacity or lower-priority model variants temporarily (use routing policy to steer by customer tag).

Permanent remediation plan (engineering work items)
--------------------------------------------------
Priority and owner: platform/runtime team (owner: Maya Singh)
Planned tasks and rationale: 
- Task A (P0): Fix buffer compaction logic — when downstream kernels take long to accept data, dispatcher should compact or spill oldest requests to disk-backed buffer with explicit backpressure. (PR: #5482)
- Task B (P1): Add bounded request queue per-client with adaptive eviction policies (evict smallest/least-progressing items).
- Task C (P1): Improve heap visibility — enable continuous heap sampling and add an automated heap-diff alert with sample retention for 72 hours.
- Task D (P2): Add a new telemetry label to trace all requests carrying dispatcher_window_id for easier cross-service correlation.
- Task E (P2): Scheduler change — enforce admission controls earlier in edge proxies to stop untrusted clients from opening many logical windows.
Estimated timeline: P0 in 3 weeks (hotfix + canary), P1/P2 in 6–10 weeks with review cycles and integration tests.

Patch / hotfix notes
--------------------
- Hotfix branches: hotfix/dispatcher/buffer-compact-2026-06 (contains limited compaction and conservative defaults).
- Canary plan: deploy to canary zone (us-west-canary) with 5% traffic shadowing for 48 hours and run the playback suite from benchmarking repo (endpoint: /health-playback).
- PR references: #5482 (compaction), #5510 (window-id telemetry).

Rollout checklist (post-PR merge)
--------------------------------
1) Deploy hotfix to staging and run the synthetic backlog test from benchmarking suite: benchmarks/runtime/dispatcher-backlog-sim (expected max memory < 1.2x baseline).
2) Canary deploy to us-west-canary with traffic-split=5% and monitor alerts for 24–48 hours.
3) If no regressions, lift to 25% traffic for another 24 hours.
4) Gradually roll to remaining regions with guardrails: watch for memory-slope alert, request_buffer_depth, and 5xx_rate.
5) Complete rollout and mark release in release-tracker: release-id: rdr-runtime-2026-06-compact.

Rollback plan
-------------
- If memory slope increases by > 50% vs baseline or 5xx rate increases > 1% absolute during canary: rollback to previous deploy using kubectl rollout undo deployment/dispatcher-service --to-revision=<rev> and revert config changes (max_inflight_per_client, window_idle_ttl).
- For severe regressions, scale down the hotfix replicas and revert config through the operator to restore previous behavior.

Post-incident verification and monitoring additions
--------------------------------------------------
- Add a derived metric: dispatcher_active_window_memory_ratio = dispatcher_memory_used_by_windows / container_memory_working_set_bytes. Alert if > 0.6 for 10m.
- Add an automated dashboard row in the dispatcher incident dashboard: memory slope, buffer depth, active windows, 5xx rate, kernel-manager inflight.
- Add unit and integration tests in the runtime bench suite that simulate slow kernel acceptance and verify compaction does not exceed memory targets.

Ownership and escalation
------------------------
- Primary owner: Runtime Platform (oncall rotation: runtime-platform-oncall).
- Secondary owner: Serving Runtime SRE.
- Pager escalation: runtime-platform-oncall -> platform-lead -> eng-sre-lead.
- Slack channels: #runtime-ops, #serving-incident-escalations

Postmortem and follow-ups
-------------------------
1) Run a two-week incident review with stakeholders: runtime, SRE, kernel-team, customer-success for any impacted customers.
2) Deliver a short RCA doc that enumerates timeline, root causes, and action items with target dates.
3) Close or convert any temporary mitigations (shorter TTLs, stricter admission) into configuration toggles that default to safe values.

Appendices
---------
A) Example PromQL snippets
- Memory slope (per pod): increase(container_memory_working_set_bytes{pod=~"dispatcher-service-.*"}[10m])
- Buffer depth agg: avg_over_time(dispatcher_request_buffer_depth[5m])
- Combined alert rule sample:
  - name: DispatcherMemorySlope
    expr: increase(container_memory_working_set_bytes{job="dispatcher-service"}[15m]) > 150e6
    for: 10m

B) Diagnostic commands
1) pod list and memory usage: kubectl top pod -n inference | grep dispatcher-service\2) fetch heap profile: kubectl exec -n inference -c dispatcher <pod> -- curl -sS localhost:6060/debug/pprof/heap > /tmp/heap.pb.gz\3) extract top alloc sites from heap: go tool pprof -top /tmp/heap.pb.gz\\n
C) Impact table (sample from incident 2026-06-18)
| Region | Duration | Peak affected pods | Customer routes impacted | Notes |
| us-west-2 | 00:17 | 3 | /v1/generate, /v1/chat | sustained KV fetch failure from remote cache |
| eu-central-1 | 00:04 | 1 | /v1/embed | transient kernel warmstart stutter |

Related pages
-------------
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-deployment-circuit-breakers-and-sla-fallback-playbook-2026 (for fallback policies)
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/gpu-memory-fragmentation-diagnostics-playbook-2026 (for GPU memory correlation)
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/runtime-deployment-sanity-and-benchmark-suite-acceptance-2026 (benchmarks to run)

Contact and next steps
----------------------
If you are paged, follow the Investigation checklist, apply Immediate mitigations as needed, and notify runtime-platform-oncall. For changes to telemetry or alerting, open an RFC in the runtime-team repo and tag reviewers: @EthanB, @LeahM.

Document history
----------------
- 2026-02-12: created by Maya Singh
- 2026-06-19: hotfix branch created and canary started (notes added)
- 2026-07-03: permanent remediation plan and rollout checklist added

title: Release Readiness: Integrated Technical Gate for Runtime, Kernels, and Benchmarks
content:
Overview

Purpose
This page defines the integrated technical gate that merges runtime architecture checks, kernel-scheduler validation, profiling smoke tests, and benchmark acceptance criteria into a single, repeatable release-readiness workflow. The gate is intended for major runtime releases, kernel rollouts, scheduler policy changes, quantization/format migrations, and any change that may materially affect latency/cost SLOs.

Scope
- Applies to changes merged into the runtime/main branch that will be deployed to production pools or dedicated capacity.
- Covers: kernel binary changes, scheduler policy DSL changes, KV-cache adjustments, batching/autotune algorithm updates, and observability/telemetry agents added to runtime.
- Not in scope: pure UI/console changes and non-runtime-facing documentation updates.

When to use
- Major version bumps (>=1.0.0 -> 1.1.0)
- Kernel ABI changes or accelerator/driver updates
- Scheduler policy changes that alter admission/backpressure behavior
- New autoscaling or eviction heuristics shipped to production

Roles & Ownership
- Release Lead: coordinates execution and signoff (Release Engineer on-call).
- Runtime Lead: technical owner of runtime arch and kernel compatibility (assigned eng owner).
- SRE: validates production-mirroring canaries, monitors post-deploy SLOs.
- Benchmarks Owner: runs and interprets perf suite and approves threshold passing.
- Observability Owner: verifies trace/metric sampling and budget configuration.

Quick reference table (contacts)
| Role | Primary | Escalation |
|---|---|---|
| Release Lead | Diego Alvarez | Maya Chen |
| Runtime Lead | Maya Chen | Jonah Kim |
| Benchmarks Owner | Priya Nair | Bench Team Pager |
| SRE | Jonah Kim | SRE Lead |

Integrated Gate checklist (automated + manual steps)
1) Pre-merge automated checks (CI) — must be green
   - Unit tests and integration tests with full mock KV and scheduler stubs.
   - Linting and static analysis for scheduler DSL changes.
   - Kernel ABI compatibility check (binary signature + interface tests).
   - Smoke profiling: 90-second microprofile run against a canary image.
     * Failure if P50 deviates >10%% from baseline or memory growth >15%%.

2) Controlled perf-suite run (pre-release) — automated but gated
   - Jobs: throughput_sustained, tail_latency_99_9, concurrency_scaling, mixed_workload_mirror.
   - Minimums: throughput within -6%%/+10%% of baseline; tail-99.9 latency not worse than +12%%.
   - Run on the same hardware class and driver versions intended for rollout.
   - Use synthetic corpus representing 60%% short chat, 30%% long completion, 10%% embeddings.

3) Scheduling & kernel handoff validation
   - Execute scheduler simulation harness for 12 hours with synthetic customer cohorts. Look for:
     * Priority inversion signals (request wait-time spikes correlated to lower-priority pods).
     * Kernel contention hotspots and cross-tenant interference.
   - Validate preemption/handoff latency is within configured guard rails (default: 150ms median handoff, 95th < 400ms).

4) Profiling and determinism checks (developer + perf engineer)
   - End-to-end profile capture (trace + GPU kernel timeline) for representative requests.
   - Determinism smoke: replay 50 trace samples, compare execution graph hash and KV cache warmup patterns.
   - Investigate if kernel ordering reorders >5%% of calls relative to baseline.

5) Flakiness & regression mitigation (benchmarks owner)
   - If any benchmark fluctuates between runs beyond historical variance band, perform: 3 additional runs, median wins.
   - Label results with run metadata (driver, kernel-commit, scheduler-flag snapshot, seed corpus version).

6) Canary deployment (SRE) — staged rollout to production-like pool
   - Canary size: 2%% of global production traffic or fixed slot count for Dedicated (whichever partitions to similar mix).
   - Monitoring window: 45 minutes steady-state + 3 hours accelerated traffic probing.
   - Abort rules (automatic): error-rate increase > 0.5pp absolute or token-cost spike > 20%% sustained for 10 minutes.
   - Manual abort: any SRE/release lead can stop and rollback immediately.

7) Observability & trace budget verification
   - Confirm span sampling is set to "release_high" for canary for the 3-hour window.
   - Verify traces produced include: kernel_id, scheduler_decision, execution_slot_id, kvcache_hits, quantize_profile_version.
   - Confirm metric rollups appear in the release dashboard within 5 minutes of traffic.

Acceptance criteria (final signoff)
- All CI gates green and no outstanding blocking defects.
- Perf-suite median results within acceptable deltas (throughput, tail).
- Scheduler simulation shows no priority inversion or catastrophic handoff regression.
- Canary window meets SLOs for 3x monitoring intervals and no auto/manual aborts.
- Observability traces and metrics verified and annotated.
- Release Notes drafted and peer-reviewed (incl. compatibility caveats).

Runbook: quick rollback steps
1. Trigger controlled traffic divert to previous runtime image (routing flag: runtime.fallback.image=sha256:<previous>).
2. Scale down new pods using staging selector and scale up previous replica set.
3. Invalidate caches on nodes where kernel artifacts changed: run node-tool flush-kvcache --node <id>.
4. Re-run minimal benchmark smoke to confirm restored baseline.
5. Open incident and attach perf capture and top-line metrics.

CLI snippets and configs
- Launch perf-suite job (example):
  ./bench/run-suite --suite mixed_workload_mirror --drivers nvdriver/2.1 --runtime-image registry/redwood/runtime:canary-20260301 --seed-corpus v3

- Sample perf job JSON (annotate with metadata):
  {
    "suite": "throughput_sustained",
    "driver": "nvdriver/2.1",
    "runtime_commit": "<sha>",
    "scheduler_flags": ["econ-priority-v2", "prefetch-on"],
    "seed_corpus": "2026-02-mix-v2"
  }

Observability budgeting and cost controls
- For any canary or perf-suite run lasting >2 hours, request a temporary trace-budget uplift via Observability Owner. Default trace-budget for routine canary: 10%% sampling on production traces, release_high: 50%% sampling for canary window.
- Annotate runs with label: release:<version> so sampling retention and export rules can be applied post-hoc.

Known caveats & interoperability notes
- Kernel change that touches 'direct-copy' path may temporarily increase PCIe transfers; expect short-lived memory-pressure signals. Plan to run memory-fragmentation diagnostic after any direct-copy kernel change.
- Scheduler policy 'async-preempt' can change handoff ordering; verify that KV-cache prefetch hints are still honored.
- Quantization profile upgrades must be tested for token-level quality regressions with the eval harness before committing to the gate.

Post-release hygiene
- Merge performance artifacts and annotated traces to the release artifact bucket: s3://redwood-release-artifacts/<release>/perf/
- Schedule a 1-week post-release review meeting to capture any slow-burn regressions.
- Add retro notes to runtime/team-wiki and link to this gate for future improvements.

Appendix: Example acceptance thresholds (editable table)
| Metric | Baseline threshold | Pass condition | Notes |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Throughput (rps) | 10000 | >= 9400 (-6%%) | Measure under same driver & hw class |
| Tail latency 99.9 | 1.2s | <= 1.344s (+12%%) | Percentile computed over 30-minute window |
| Memory growth (per pod) | 0MB | <= +15%% | Measured during 1h warmup + 30 min steady |
| Error rate | 0.2%% | <= 0.7%% absolute | Abort if exceeded >10 minutes |

References
- See profiling playbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/runtime-profiling-playbook-guidelines-2025.json
- Benchmark suite: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/runtime-deployment-sanity-and-benchmark-suite-acceptance-2026.json
- Canary policies: /confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/slo-and-error-budgets (internal link)

Change log
- 2026-02-10: created by Maya Chen (initial draft).
- 2026-03-02: updated acceptance thresholds and added automated abort rules (reviewers: Diego Alvarez, Priya Nair).

Contact & feedback
If you have suggestions to improve this gate or want the gate extended for a new class of changes (e.g., experimental accelerator fleets), open a ticket in the runtime team board and mention the Release Lead.

title: Automatic fallback policy behavior (Hosted API)
content:
# Summary
This page documents the behavior of **automatic fallback** in the Redwood serving runtime for the **Hosted API**. This policy is used during normal operations and is often enabled during model rollouts to reduce customer-visible errors during capacity or instability events.

# What fallback does
When fallback is enabled on a route, the router may send requests to a **fallback model** instead of the primary model based on defined triggers. The request remains a standard Hosted API request; the router modifies the upstream target only.

# Fallback triggers
Fallback can activate for these reasons (not exhaustive):
- **Capacity pressure**: primary pool is saturated (queue time above threshold).
- **Elevated error rate**: primary 5xx above threshold over a short window.
- **Cold start or rollout warmup**: primary replicas not ready or still ramping.
- **Regional impairment**: a subset of instances in a region failing health checks.

# Default rollout-time trigger thresholds (recommended)
For fallback-enabled rollouts, recommended initial thresholds are:
- Queue time (primary) > **250 ms** p95 over 3 minutes
- Primary 5xx > **0.8%** over 5 minutes
- Primary timeout rate > **0.3%** over 5 minutes

Teams may tune these thresholds, but must record the change in the release ticket and return to defaults after the rollout window unless there is an explicit follow-up task.

# Compatibility requirements
Fallback is safe only when primary and fallback are compatible for the routes expected client behavior. In particular:
- The API surface must match: tool calling enabled/disabled should be consistent, and structured output constraints must be compatible.
- Tokenization changes can affect downstream parsing and should be validated with smoke tests.
- Context length and max output token limits should not be materially lower on the fallback model for high-traffic routes.

# Observability
When fallback is active, metrics include:
- `router.fallback_activated_count` (tagged by reason)
- `router.fallback_share` (percentage of requests served by fallback)
- `inference.latency_ms` by model_version (primary vs fallback)

Logs: routing decisions are annotated with `fallback_reason` and `selected_model_version`.

# Known sharp edges
- Fallback can mask quality regressions: if the primary produces degraded outputs, overall error rates might stay low while user experience becomes inconsistent. Rollback is still required.
- Tool-calling: if the fallback model has different function-call style, clients may see inconsistent tool selection.
- Streaming: fallback can increase time-to-first-token if the fallback pool is colder than primary.

# Operational guidance
- During model rollouts, keep fallback enabled at least through the canary and the first 24 hours at 100% unless there is a known incompatibility.
- If fallback share exceeds **20%** for more than 10 minutes during a rollout, treat it as a signal to pause the ramp and investigate capacity or error spikes.

title: Integration & Release Orchestration Playbook for Inference Runtime
content:
Summary
This playbook defines the cross-cutting requirements and step-by-step orchestration for integrated releases of the Redwood inference runtime. It bridges runtime architecture decisions, kernel scheduling rollouts, profiling/benchmark gates, runbook rehearsals, and the final release note artifact. Use this document for minor to major releases (feature flags, kernel variants, scheduler changes, quantization profile updates).

Goals
- Reduce production regressions by standardizing preflight and canary criteria.
- Ensure observability and cost telemetry are sufficient to diagnose degradation within 10 minutes.
- Provide a repeatable, auditable sequence for rollouts with clear owners and rollback criteria.

Scope and applicability
Applies to: serving runtime service (runtime-coordinator), kernel dispatcher (kernel-dispatcher), KV cache controller (kvcache-controller), scheduler API (schedulerd), and integration components (orchestrator-api, perf-runner). Notably this playbook includes: kernel scheduling policy changes, kernel binary rollouts, runtime feature flags (continuous batching, predictive-prefetch), and changes to telemetry retention that affect profiling.

Who should read this
- Release engineers coordinating the deploy (owner: runtime-release).
- Kernel and scheduler owners (team: kernel-scheduling).
- Profiling and benchmarking leads (team: perf-eng).
- Oncall SREs and maintainer of the canary and chaos tooling.

High-level release flow (summary)
1) Design and risk assessment (RFC + ADR entry)
2) Local developer verification (unit tests + e2e in sandbox)
3) Controlled bench runs (perf-runner + shadow replay)
4) Canary release (progressive percentages) with automated gates
5) Ramp and monitoring window (24–72 hours depending on risk)
6) Full release and release note publish

Preflight checklist (must pass all items)
| Check | Command / Location | Acceptable value | Owner |
|---|---|---:|---|
| ADR linked | confluence RFC link | RFC+ADR present | feature-owner |
| Unit + integration tests | CI: runtime-ci/pipeline | green | eng-ci |
| Kernel binary signature | sigstore verify kernel-v*.sig | verified | kernel-scheduling |
| Perf warm-run | perf-runner --profile=warm --runs=100 | p95 < 120ms | perf-eng |
| Synthetic tail test | perf-runner --profile=tail --duration=30m | p99 < 350ms | perf-eng |
| Memory regression check | kvbench --alloc-check | no >10% reg | runtime-release |
| Telemetry schema validation | telemetry-lint schema/runtime-telemetry.yaml | ok | observability |
| Runbook rehearsal | playbook-runner simulate --incident=latency-spike | success | eng-sre |

Design and risk assessment
- For any kernel/scheduler change the author must produce a concise risk assessment with: affected models, sequence length distribution shift, expected kernel path changes, and potential memory/regression vectors.
- Attach the following artifacts to the RFC: microbenchmark results (csv), kernel trace samples (gzip), and a short rollout plan.

Local verification (developer sandbox)
- Use the runtime sandbox image: registry.redwood.internal/runtime-sandbox:dev-<sha>.
- Commands to run basic verification:
  1. Start local runtime: docker compose -f runtime-sandbox/docker-compose.yml up --build
  2. Run unit e2e: ./scripts/e2e_local.sh --model=llama-mini --seq=256 --concurrency=4
