This doc formalizes a pragmatic, testable econometric model and a simulation protocol to estimate those effects using production traces + controlled synthetic workloads.
- Who should use this: runtime engineers, performance analysts, SREs, product owners evaluating cost-optimization proposals.
- Outcome: A reproducible vector of sensitivity metrics: delta P50/P95/P99 latency per unit change, marginal cost per 1k tokens, and joint probability of SLO violation under traffic variance.

2) Model specification and assumptions
- Model form (high level): latency ~ alpha + beta1 * effective_batch_size + beta2 * kernel_choice_factor + beta3 * seq_len + beta4 * kvcache_hit_rate + beta5 * quant_level + epsilon
- Cost proxy: per_token_cost_estimate = fixed_dispatch_cost / expected_tokens + dispatch_amortization(batch_size) + kernel_compute_cost(kernel_choice, seq_len, quant_level) + infra_markup
- Interpretability: beta coefficients are marginal effects; we prefer GLM with log-link for latency and cost when distributions are skewed. Use robust standard errors clustered by trace session.
- Key assumptions to record before running experiments:
  - Trace representativeness: sampled traffic should match production distribution for sequence lengths and request inter-arrival times within 5–10% L2 distance.
  - Stationarity window: workload period chosen should be short enough to avoid major model drift (recommended 4–24 hours) unless explicitly modelling diurnal effects.
  - Kernel comparability: kernel_choice_factor encodes candidate kernel implementations that satisfy semantic parity for outputs (validation gate required).

3) Required telemetry and inputs
- Mandatory fields from production traces (per request):
  - timestamp (ms), request_id, model_id, model_variant, kernel_id, batch_size, seq_len, token_count, kvcache_hit (bool), kernel_start_ms, kernel_end_ms, total_latency_ms, host_id, accelerator_type
- Aggregates needed for modelling:
  - session_id-level prefix counts, per-host occupancy, infra_cost_tags (spot vs reserved), network RTTs
- Additional signals to collect for sensitivity attribution:
  - scheduler_decision_tag, admission_reason, preemption_count, soft_degradation_flag
- Recommended sampling/retention policy for experiments: retain full traces for 90 days in the lab bucket; keep 7-day high-fidelity window for direct replay.

4) Simulation lab setup and dataset construction
- Data sources: production trace snapshot (anonymized), synthetic corpus (diverse seq_len and prompt shapes), and microbenchmarks for each kernel variant (cold, warm, high-concurrency).
- Dataset construction steps (summary):
  1. Select representative day(s) and extract 4-hour windows covering peak and off-peak traffic.
  2. Resample requests to produce target QPS shapes (steady, ramp, burst) preserving inter-arrival distribution at 10ms resolution.
  3. Inject controlled variance: scale seq_len distribution by +/- 20% in separate cohorts; create an extreme-burst cohort (10x for 30s every 5 minutes).
  4. Annotate each request with kernel hints and quant_profile tags for the simulation scenarios.
- Lab topology: use a small isolated cluster that mirrors production instance types (same accelerator families). Use network shaping to emulate production RTT and packet loss if relevant.

5) Runbook: experiment steps (numbered)
1. Preflight checks (owners: experiment lead, runtime owner)
   a. Confirm trace window selection and anonymization complete.
   b. Verify kernel builds are semantically equivalent (unit test and model-output diff below threshold).
   c. Validate lab cluster health and telemetry ingestion.
2. Baseline collection
   a. Run baseline scenario: production kernel + current batching + quant profile; collect 2 full runs (steady + burst) to measure variance.
   b. Compute baseline metrics: mean/median/std for latency quantiles, per_token_cost_estimate (see formula), kernel utilization, queue lengths.
3. Candidate configuration injection
   a. For each candidate change (kernel variant, batch reshaping, quant level), run 3 independent repeats across identical QPS shapes.
   b. Capture microbenchmarks before and after: cold-path start, warm-path P50 kernel time, kernel tail.
4. Sensitivity estimation
   a. Fit the GLM to pooled run data with scenario tags. Use clustered robust errors at host-level.
   b. Produce coefficient table and marginal effect plots (delta latency per +1 batch, per quant step, per kernel switch).
5. Stress and edge-case probing
   a. Run chaos-scenarios: preemption bursts, eviction-induced cold starts, and simulated NVLink degradation.
   b. Record joint SLO violation frequency and time-to-recovery.
6. Regression attribution and anomaly hunting
   a. If any scenario raises tail latency > baseline P99 + 15% or increases per-token cost > 10% with no quality gain, mark as failed and collect full traces for RCA.
7. Signoff matrix and rollout plan
   a. If sensitivity metrics fall within acceptance envelope (see section 6), prepare canary rollout plan with automatic rollback triggers and observability dashboards.

6) Analysis and decision criteria
- Primary acceptance envelope (default):
  - P95 latency increase <= 5% and P99 <= 10% relative to baseline for expected traffic;
  - Marginal per-token cost delta <= +3% for hosted pricing-sensitive tiers;
  - No increase in observed model output divergence beyond validation tolerance.
- Escalation thresholds (immediate abort):
  - P99 increases by > 25% or joint SLO violation probability increases > 2x under burst scenarios;
  - Any increase in error rate / silent degradation flag set by runtime checks.
- Statistical checks:
  - Use bootstrapped confidence intervals for marginal estimates; require 95% CI not crossing zero for performance improvements to be considered significant.
  - For tail metrics use peak-over-threshold EVT-inspired checks plus sample quantile CI.
- Economics view:
  - When comparing two candidates with similar latency, prefer the one with lower estimated cost-per-1M tokens, but apply a product-weighted factor (weight latency more for interactive products; see appendix for weight table).

7) Example configs and sample output
- Example simulation scenario (YAML):
  scenario_name: kernel-led-quant-test
  qps_shape: burst-peak-2x
  kernel_candidates: [kernel_v1_float16, kernel_v2_int8_opt]
  batch_policy: [auto, target_batch=16, max_latency_ms=120]
  quant_profiles: [q4_0, q8_1]
  replay_window: 2025-11-04T02:00:00Z/2025-11-04T06:00:00Z

- Example result snippet (CSV-friendly summary):
  metric,baseline, candidate_v2,delta,ci_low,ci_high
  p50_latency_ms,24,22,-8.3%,-9.5%,-7.1%
  p95_latency_ms,78,85,+9.0%,+6.1%,+11.8%
  p99_latency_ms,210,250,+19.0%,+12.0%,+26.5%
  estimated_cost_per_1M_tokens,$420,$385,-8.3%,-10.1%,-6.2%

8) Ownership and escalation
- Primary owner: runtime-performance team (team contact: runtime-performance@redwood.example.com).
- Experiment lead: listed per-run on the experiment ticket; responsible for preflight, results, and rollout proposal.
- SLA owner and SRE review: required before any production canary that affects P95.
- Escalation route: experiment lead -> runtime tech lead -> SRE oncall -> VP of Engineering if unresolved.

9) Appendix: quick CLI snippets and sanity checks
- Replaying a trace to lab cluster (sanitized):
  cat trace.jsonl | jq -c '. | del(.user_data)' | lab-replay --cluster lab-west-1 --qps 120 --seed 42
- Simple GLM fit command (python/pandas/statsmodels):
  python -c "import pandas as pd, statsmodels.formula.api as smf; df=pd.read_csv('runs.csv'); m=smf.glm('np.log(total_latency_ms) ~ batch_size + C(kernel_id) + seq_len + kvcache_hit', data=df).fit(cov_type='cluster', cov_kwds={'groups':df['host_id']}); print(m.summary())"
- Sanity checks before signoff:
  - Kernel unit tests pass and model-output-diff < 0.1% of tokens differing.
  - Telemetry ingestion shows no missing kernel tags for >99% of requests in the run.
  - Canary dashboard widgets prewired: P50/P95/P99, per-token-cost, kernel-utilization, queue-lengths, and a per-host heatmap.

Frequently asked questions (short)
- Q: How long does a full experiment take?
  A: End-to-end from baseline to signoff usually 6–18 hours depending on repeats and stress tests.
- Q: Can I rely only on microbenchmarks?
  A: No. Microbenchmarks are necessary but insufficient because they do not model admission, scheduling, or KV cache effects under real traffic shapes.

Change log
- 2025-11-12: Initial draft and baseline model spec (Priya N.).
- 2026-02-07: Added bootstrapped CI guidance and canary acceptance envelope; tightened preflight checks (Priya N., reviewed by Marcela G.).

Related artifacts to attach to the experiment ticket:
- baseline_runs.csv (zipped), candidate_runs.csv (zipped), kernel_microbenchmarks.tar.gz, dashboard_snapshot.png, signed-off validation diff report.json

Notes and caveats
- This model is intentionally pragmatic: do not treat coefficients as structural causal estimates without additional causal identification work. For changes with product-level impact (e.g., new quantization profiles that alter model outputs), engage Applied ML for an evaluation gate before rollout.

If you have questions or want this runbook adapted for Private deployments (VPC/on-prem), contact the runtime-performance team for a tailored lab topology and cost-tag mapping.

title: Service-mesh impact and networked-fidelity benchmarks
content:
Overview

This document captures the rationale, experiment design, sample configurations, and runbook for benchmarking how different service-mesh and network topologies affect inference fidelity and operational SLOs. It is intended for engineers running distributed Redwood Private or Dedicated clusters where network pathing (sidecars, mTLS, mesh proxies, ingress controllers) may interact with runtime components (frontends, routers, model shards, kvcache, and tracing).

Why this matters

- Network pathing can add microsecond-to-millisecond tail latency that changes batching behaviour and kernel scheduling decisions.
- Proxies and sidecars may buffer, reorder, or aggregate requests which alters sequence arrival patterns and therefore KV cache hit rates and generation quality for stateful chat sessions.
- mTLS and service-mesh observability can introduce CPU overhead on nodes hosting lightweight services and affect co-located scheduler performance.

Scope

- Topologies: direct (no mesh), mesh sidecar (Envoy-like), ingress+mesh (gateway + sidecar), and cross-region overlay.
- Workloads: interactive chat (median tokens 40, tail 1024), streaming token-by-token generation, and bulk embeddings (batched).
- Hardware: A40/RTX/T4 pools and mixed GPU pools used in Dedicated clusters.
- Not covered: model-level quantization effects (handled in quantization-profiles).

Success criteria / SLOs

- Median generation latency (token emission) delta vs direct baseline <= 8% for interactive workloads.
- 95th percentile latency delta <= 20% for streaming workloads.
- KV cache hit-rate deviation <= 3 percentage points.
- Fidelity regressions: BLEU/ROUGE-like drops or hallucination-rate increases must be <= 1.5% absolute vs baseline for canary pass.

Experiment design

1) Controlled variables
   - Same model binary and runtime kernels across runs.
   - Fixed token budget and prompt corpus (prompt-sets-and-benchmarks corpus v2026-09).
   - Identical request surface (headers, chunking, streaming flags).

2) Independent variables
   - Network topology (direct, sidecar, ingress+sidecar, overlay).
   - TLS on/off (and session reuse policy).
   - Proxy concurrency and buffer sizes.
   - Placement variants: co-located sidecar on GPU node vs sidecar on separate infra node.

3) Metrics collected (minimum set)
   - Service-level: median, p95, p99 for request latency; queue length; dropped requests.
   - Runtime-level: per-kernel execution time, kernel scheduling latency, kv cache hit rate, batch size distribution.
   - Network-level: RTT distribution, sidecar CPU/memory, open connections, TLS handshake rate.
   - Fidelity: token-level log-prob deltas, output differences against golden responses, hallucination rate, semantic-similarity score.

Environment matrix (example)

| Test ID | Topology | TLS | Proxy CPU | Node placement | Notes |
|---------|----------|-----|----------:|----------------|-------|
| T01     | direct   | off | 0%       | none           | baseline |
| T02     | sidecar  | on  | 10%      | co-located     | typical small mesh sidecar CPU cgroup 10% |
| T03     | ingress+sidecar | on | 12%  | gateway on infra node | gateway does TLS termination + routing |
| T04     | overlay cross-region | on | 15% | mixed | simulates inter-region hops (~20-40ms) |

Benchmark harness and step-by-step procedure

1) Provisioning
   - Use the workload-sim tool (internal) to instantiate traffic replay. Example: 
     ./workload-sim --corpus=prompt-sets/chat-2026.json --qps=250 --shape=poisson --seed=202602 --streaming=true --out=run-T02

2) Deploy topology
   - Direct: disable sidecar injection and point frontend to runtime service.
   - Sidecar: enable mesh injection; apply sidecar resource limits using sidecar-cgroup.yaml (sample below).
   - Ingress+sidecar: install gateway config and route to mesh; enable TLS passthrough vs termination variants.

3) Run baseline and experiments
   - Run baseline (T01) for 60 minutes to warm caches and collect stable metrics.
   - For each topology, run 3 x 30-minute trials. Restart the runtime between each trial to reinitialize KV cache when testing cold-cache effects.

4) Data collection and verification
   - Export telemetry to the benchmarking S3 bucket with tags: topology, trial, seed, model-version.
   - Verify trace correlation IDs are preserved end-to-end. If trace sampling removes tail events, increase sampling to 100% for test windows.

Sample sidecar resource YAML (sidecar-cgroup.yaml)

apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: sidecar-cgroup
data:
  CPU_LIMIT: "100m"
  CPU_REQUEST: "50m"
  BUF_SIZE: "65536"

Network measure snippets

- To measure RTT and handshake overhead: 
  time curl -w "RTT:\t%{time_connect}\tTLS: %{time_appconnect}\n" -o /dev/null -s https://runtime-host/api/gen

- To surface out-of-order or reordering statistics we use tcpdump + reorder-detector: 
  sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w /tmp/run-T02.pcap &
  ./reorder-detector --pcap /tmp/run-T02.pcap --out /tmp/reorder-summary.json

Interpretation guide

- Small median deltas with large p99 deltas typically indicate buffering/queueing inside proxies or gateway resource saturation.
- A decreased KV cache hit rate with identical prompt distribution indicates request reordering or session affinity breakage: check sticky-session configuration and cookie/session-id propagation.
- Token-level log-prob deltas correlated with increased per-token latency usually point to batching changes (smaller effective batches) or kernel time-slicing; reconcile with batch-size histograms.

Example analysis queries

- Query: p99 latency by topology and kernel-version: 
  SELECT topology, kernel_version, percentile(latency_ms, 99) FROM inference_traces WHERE run_tag = 'T02' GROUP BY topology, kernel_version

- Query: kv cache hit rate drop traces and session-affinity mismatch: 
  SELECT session_id, kv_hit, request_ts FROM kv_cache_events WHERE run_tag='T03' ORDER BY request_ts DESC LIMIT 1000

Runbook: when networked topology causes production regressions

1) Detection: automated canary monitors should flag the fidelity alert (>=1% absolute drop in semantic-similarity) or SLO breach.
2) Immediate mitigation (0-15 minutes):
   - Reduce proxy buffer sizes and disable request aggregation on the gateway: set BUF_SIZE=16384 and reload gateway.
   - If sidecar CPU is saturated, enable automatic sidecar eviction policy for canary cohort.
3) Secondary actions (15-60 minutes):
   - Repoint traffic to the direct path (bypass mesh) for the affected cohort. Use routing policy: 
     curl -X POST https://controlplane/api/route-adjust -d '{"match":"account:1234","route":"direct"}'
   - If session-affinity is broken, rotate to sticky-session fallback using jwt-subject header as affinity key.
4) Post-incident analysis (>60 minutes):
   - Re-run the controlled experiments to reproduce and capture kernel-level traces. Document config deltas and upload to the benchmark bucket.

Ownership and contacts

- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime perf team (Ava Martínez).
- On-call contact: runtime-sre@redwood.ai.
- Escalation: Priya Rao (Runtime Platform), Oliver Singh (SRE).

What to log and attach to tickets

- Benchmark run tags and S3 path.
- Topology YAMLs and k8s manifests used.
- Pcap and reorder-summary if reordering suspected.
- Kernel trace slices (timestamps aligned with trace IDs).

Limitations and caveats

- This harness assumes uniform client-side TLS termination where applicable. Real client diversity (mobile vs server) can show different handshake and multiplexing behavior.
- Overlay cross-region tests must account for background internet noise; use VPC-peered emulation where possible.

Next steps and proposed improvements

- Add a synthetic jitter injector to emulate tail network spikes and observe scheduler response.
- Automate a compare-committee that runs fidelity checks in CI when gateway or sidecar versions are changed.
- Integrate result dashboards into the Redwood Console benchmarks view so product owners can see topology sensitivity when evaluating Dedicated/Private options.

Appendix: quick checklist for running a gated canary

1) Confirm model-version pinned and binary checksum matches baseline.
2) Run baseline T01 for 1 hour and archive metrics.
3) Run mesh topology trials (T02/T03) with same seed and warmup.
4) Run fidelity checks against golden corpus and send results to reviewers.
5) If failures observed, follow the runbook above and open a postmortem ticket with attachments.

End of document

title: Tail Latency Investigation and Mitigation Playbook
content:
Overview:

This playbook describes a reproducible, prioritized workflow for investigating, mitigating, and preventing tail-latency regressions in the Redwood serving runtime. It covers measurement methodology, diagnostic commands, quick mitigations, kernel-scheduler knobs, benchmark repro recipes, canary/rollout guidance, alerting rules, and a checklist for post-incident follow-up.

Why tail latency matters:

- SLO impact: p99 and p99.9 directly affect user-facing latency for streaming and non-streaming workloads; a small number of high-latency requests can cause downstream timeouts and user-visible errors.
- Cost and capacity: excessive tail latency reduces effective throughput and increases idle GPU time (KV cache churn, smaller batch efficiency).
- Regression vectors: model changes (longer context), quantization shifts, kernel changes, misconfigured batchers, network spikes, and KV cache thrash.

SLOs and thresholds (company-standard baseline):

- p50 <= 35ms (token generation path, hosted small models)
- p95 <= 120ms
- p99 <= 450ms
- p99.9 <= 1200ms
- Return-to-service target for critical customer routes: p99 < 500ms within 30 minutes of detection unless escalated.

Measurement and instrumentation guidelines:

- Use downstream, request-scoped tracing (trace events: request_enqueue, batch_start, kernel_launch, kvcache_lookup, kvcache_miss, dll_fetch, response_stream_start).
- Emit microsecond-resolution histograms for request_duration_seconds and per-substage timers (enqueue, batch_wait, kernel_exec, kvcache_latency).
- Label dimensions: model_name, model_variant (quant/float), deployment_zone, backend_node_id, route, request_size_tokens, client_tier.
- Define rolling windows: 1m / 5m / 1h for alerts/analysis.

Key Prometheus / Thanos queries (examples):

- p99 latency (5m):
  histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, model_name))

- Tail contribution by substage (5m):
  sum(rate(kernel_exec_seconds_sum[5m])) by (model_name) / sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_sum[5m])) by (model_name)

- Hot-node identification (p99 per backend):
  topk(10, histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, backend_node_id)))

Diagnostic workflow (ordered):

1) Confirm alert and scope: identify affected routes, model variants, and time range.
2) Pull dashboards: p50/p95/p99 heatmap over zones and backend_node_id.
3) Correlate upstream events: deployments, kernel rollouts, autoscaler events, config changes.
4) Triangulate using traces: filter traces for requests with duration > p99 threshold, inspect span timeline for long gaps.
5) Reproduce with targeted load: run the micro-workload for the failing route at 2x p99 arrival rate to reproduce.
6) Mitigate (see quick mitigations).
7) Root-cause analysis and permanent fix.

Quick mitigations (emergency steps to restore SLOs):

- Route-level rollback: pin the route to previous model_variant (fastest rollback if regression due to model or quantization).
- Backpressure tuning: reduce max_concurrency for the route to reduce batching head-of-line blocking (example: max_concurrency 32 -> 16).
- Autoscaler pulse: scale up dedicated pool by +20% capacity for 10–30 minutes to absorb tail churn.
- Batcher drain and restart: rotate batcher workers on affected nodes one-at-a-time to clear strays.
- Fallback policy: switch to a lower-context / smaller model variant with preserved semantic behavior.

Emergency CLI snippets:

- Rollback a route to pinned variant:
  redwood routes update --route-id r-1234 --model-variant stable-v1

- Temporarily reduce concurrency on route (examples):
  redwood routes update --route-id r-1234 --max-concurrency 16

- Force autoscale increase (dedicated pools):
  redwood pools scale --pool-id p-12 --desired-instances 12 --reason "tail-latency mitigation"

Kernel / scheduler tuning matrix (guidance):

- If p99 kernel_exec is dominating and kernel shapes are small (short seq): favor smaller-launch latency-optimized kernels: kernel.flags = ["low-launch-latency"] and kernel.batch_size_hint = 8.
- If batch wait contributes > 20% to p99: increase max_batch_size and reduce batch_timeout_ms to prioritize throughput: max_batch_size += 50%, batch_timeout_ms -= 10ms (observe cost).
- If KV cache miss ratio > 2% and kvcache_latency contributes to tail: enable per-node hot-key prefetch and reduce kvcache_eviction_pressure: kvcache.eviction_target = 0.6 -> 0.75.

Example scheduler tune table (text-representation):

- Scenario: Single-node hot tail due to kernel spikes\  Action: reduce kernel-concurrency on node, set kernel.flags to low-launch-latency\  Expected effect: reduced p99 kernel latency, lower throughput efficiency
- Scenario: Global increase in batch_wait\  Action: increase batch_timeout_ms by 5–15ms, raise max_batch_size for non-latency routes\  Expected effect: shifts work to larger batches, improves token cost and average latency

Profiling playbook (what to collect):

- Collect a minimal trace set for 50 failing requests (p99 class) and 50 matching successful requests. Use distributed tracing export and local perf tools (nsys for NVIDIA).
- For GPU traces: nsys capture focused on kernel launch and memcpy with --trace=cuda,nvtx and symbols for runtime.
- For CPU/batcher: perf record --call-graph dwarf -p <pid> for 60s on affected batcher process.

Profiling commands (examples):

- Trace collection (request scoped):
  redwood debug collect-trace --request-id <req-id> --out /tmp/trace-<req-id>.json

- GPU capture (container):
  docker exec -it runtime-worker bash -c "nsys profile -o /tmp/nsys --trace=cuda,nvtx --sample=none -- ./bin/runtime-worker --trace-target <backend_node_id>"

- Aggregated flamegraphs (CPU):
  perf script | FlameGraph/stackcollapse-perf.pl > out.folded
  FlameGraph/flamegraph.pl out.folded > perf.svg

Benchmarking repro harness (step-by-step):

1) Isolate route in an internal staging deployment with the same model_variant and quantization flags.
2) Seed KV cache with representative prefixes using seed-client:
   seed-client --model my-model --prefix-file samples/prefixes.txt --parallelism 8 --rate 50/s
3) Replay a recorded production arrival trace (5m) at 1x/2x p99 rate using replay-tool:
   replay-tool --trace artifacts/prod-2026-01-11.trace --replay-rate 2.0 --concurrency 4 --route r-1234
4) Monitor metrics (Prometheus + runtime traces) and capture traces on failing runs.

Canary and rollout mitigation plan (safeguards):

- Canary settings for kernel/scheduler changes:
  - Canary size: 2% of traffic or <= 2 instances in each zone.
  - Canary observation period: 30 minutes with p99 and error rate gating.
  - Roll forward criteria: no p99 regression > 15% and error rate increase < 0.05% over baseline.
  - Rollback criteria: p99 > 25% above baseline or error rate delta >= 0.1%.

- A/B and gradual ramp guidance: use step ramps of 5–10% every 15 minutes with automated rollback hooks.

Alerting rules (examples):

- Critical: p99(past 5m) > SLO by 30% for two consecutive evaluation windows (5m) -> page SRE and runtime-oncall.
- Warning: p99 increase > 15% -> slack channel #runtime-performance for triage.

Example alert rule (pseudo-Prometheus):
  ALERT TailLatencyCritical
  IF histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, route)) > (slo_route_p99 * 1.3)
  FOR 10m
  LABELS {severity="page"}
  ANNOTATIONS {runbook="/confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/tail-latency-investigation-and-mitigation-playbook-2026"}

Post-incident checklist and RCA steps:

- Save raw traces and profiling captures to the incident artifact bucket with tags (incident_id, route, timeframe).
- Record all mitigation steps in the incident timeline (who did what and why).
- Run the reproducible benchmark recipe and attach artifacts to RCA.
- Identify preventative engineering work: kernel patch, batcher improvement, KV cache policy, rollout gating changes.
- Schedule an engineering task with owner and target ETA; include automated regression test in the perf-suite pipeline.

Ownership, escalation, and runbook contacts:

- First responder: runtime-oncall (rotating SRE)
- Secondary: serving-runtime team (pager: @serving-runtime)
- Tertiary: profiling-and-evals team for deep kernel work

Dashboards and recommended panels:

- Route performance overview: p50/p95/p99 horizon chart by route and model_variant.
- Node hotlist: table of p99 by backend_node_id, memory pressure, gpu_utilization, kvcache_eviction_rate.
- Substage waterfall: stacked bar showing percent time spent in enqueue/batch_wait/kernel_exec/kvcache.

Appendix A — Example JSON trace filter (for trace-collector):

{
  "filter": {
    "min_duration_ms": 450,
    "labels": {"route": "r-1234", "model_variant": "candidate-v2"}
  },
  "limit": 200
}

Appendix B — Frequently observed root causes and remedies:

- Kernel launch variance due to JIT/kernel selection: roll back recent kernel mapper changes or pin kernel profile for the model.
- KV cache churn after model size increase: enlarge node-local cache or change eviction policy.
- Batcher stall caused by skewed client arrival patterns: enable adaptive batching per-client and cap single-client concurrency.

Contacts & references:

- Runtime profiling guidelines: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/runtime-profiling-playbook-guidelines-2025.json
- Throughput & latency workload catalog: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/throughput-latency-workload-catalog-2026.json
- Fallback and degradation playbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-fallback-and-degradation-playbook-2026.json

Change log (high level):

- 2025-11-12: Document created by Nina Patel (initial published draft).
- 2026-01-20: Added kernel tuning matrix and canary gating criteria (reviewers: Jonah Kramer, Priya Menon).
- 2026-02-10: Added emergency CLI snippets and appendix JSON filter example.

End of playbook.

title: Policy-driven load probe and scheduler feedback protocol
content:
Summary
-------
This page documents the Policy-driven Load Probe and Scheduler Feedback Protocol (PLP-SFP). The protocol is designed to safely surface scheduler and kernel behavior under controlled, policy-shaped load while providing deterministic feedback signals that the runtime scheduler can consume to adjust admission, backfill, and priority heuristics.

Intended audience
- Runtime engineers
- Benchmarking and perf-sig members
- Oncall and SRE rotation responsible for scheduler incidents

Goals
- Provide a reproducible method for injecting targeted load shapes into the serving runtime without violating customer SLAs.
- Produce canonical telemetry artifacts (probe reports) that map directly to scheduler decision signals.
- Define automated feedback actions the scheduler can take when probes indicate a regression or resource pressure.

Scope and non-goals
- In scope: admission/backfill behavior, KV cache warmup under shaped bursts, per-kernel latency distribution under mixed-concurrency, slot coalescing effectiveness.
- Out of scope: long-running model training, hardware-level failure injections (handled by infra chaos team).

Glossary
- Probe: controlled synthetic traffic pattern exercised against a target model and route.
- Fingerprint: compact summary of latency/cost distribution for a probe (see Probe fingerprint format).
- Decision signal: normalized metric emitted by the probe runner that the scheduler consumes (e.g., kernel contention score, slot-utilization drift).

Architecture overview
1) Controller: probe-runner service (bench-probe) that schedules probes and collects traces. Owned by benchmarking team.
2) Collector: high-throughput telemetry pipeline that annotates traces with request-provenance and kernel hints. Uses the runtime trace bus.
3) Aggregator: offline/nearline job that produces a probe fingerprint and decision signals. Runs in namespace perf-aggregator.
4) Consumer: scheduler decision fabric subscribes to decision signals via the signal bus and maps signals to policy actions (admit/reject/backfill/tier-shift).

Probe types and recommended usage
- Smoke probe: short (30s) steady QPS at nominal concurrency. Use for CI verifications.
- Burst probe: 5–60s high-intensity spike aimed at stressing KV cache and kernel preemption. Use for degradation mode tests.
- Ramp probe: linear ramp from 10% to 110% nominal QPS over 5–10 minutes to find nonlinear breakpoints.
- Cohort probe: multi-route correlated traffic that exercises cross-tenant memory eviction and kernel-sharing.

Probe configuration (recommended defaults)
| field                  | description                                              | default        | notes |
|------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------|----------------|-------|
| model                  | model variant to exercise (e.g., gptx-3-8b-quant)        | required       | pick a representative variant |
| duration_seconds       | probe wall time                                           | 60             | adjust for probe type |
| qps_target             | aggregate queries per second                              | 50             | expressed at client ingress |
| concurrency_target     | target in-flight requests                                 | 8              | prefer 1–32 |
| input_seq_length       | input token length distribution (CSV of percentiles)      | 8,32,128       | used to exercise kernel breakpoints |
| trace_level            | trace/detail (none|header|full)                           | header         | full increases telemetry cost |
| allow_fallbacks        | whether probe may trigger model fallback                  | false          | keep false for fidelity baseline |

Probe fingerprint format
- single-line canonicalization: <probe-name> | <median-lat-ms> | <p95-lat-ms> | <cost-per-token-µs> | <kv-hit-rate> | <kernel-contention-score>
- store fingerprints in perf-store keyed by probe id and commit sha.

Operational procedure: running a scheduled probe
1) Author probe manifest and check against policy validator: bench-probe validate <manifest.yaml>.
2) Schedule in bench-probe: bench-probe run --manifest manifest.yaml --dry-run (dry-run verifies signal wiring without emitting traffic).
3) Execute during a controlled window (must coordinate with SRE). Add marker to rollout calendar.
4) After run, wait for aggregator job to publish the fingerprint artifact.
5) Review report in perf-dashboard and file any anomalies in the perf-issue tracker with tag "plp-sfp".

Example probe manifest (manifest.yaml)
---
probe_name: "kv-warmup-burst-az1"
model: "redwood/gptx-3-8b-quant-v2"
duration_seconds: 45
qps_target: 250
concurrency_target: 12
input_seq_length: "8,32,128"
trace_level: "header"
allow_fallbacks: false
---

Telemetry and key metrics to collect
- request_latency_ms (p50/p90/p95/p99) broken out by kernel and end-to-end
- kernel_queue_depth and kernel_dispatch_time_ms
- kv_cache_hit_rate and kv_locality_ratio
- token_throughput and token_cost_estimate_us
- kernel_contention_score: synthetic metric combining kernel-wait time and preemption counts

Automated feedback and mapping to scheduler actions
- If kernel_contention_score > 0.45 for sustained 30s: reduce admit rate for affected slot by 30% and enable slot-coalescing for that cohort for 2 minutes.
- If kv_cache_hit_rate falls below 0.6 during burst probe: prioritize pre-warmed slots (warmstart=true) and temporarily prefer slot affinity to nodes with warm caches.
- If p99 request_latency exceeds configured SLO + 2x baseline during a smoke probe: mark the latest deployment as suspect and open a canary rollback action.

Policy validation rules (validator checks)
- Probes must not target production tenant routes unless a written SLA waiver exists.
- qps_target * duration_seconds must be within the probe window budget assigned to the bench namespace.
- allow_fallbacks must be false for fidelity-critical probes.

Scheduler mapping examples
- Decision signal: {kernel_contention: 0.52, cohort: "search-heavy"} -> Action: cohort_priority -= 1; trigger_backfill_threshold=0.65; run eviction-smoothing for 90s.
- Decision signal: {kv_hit: 0.45, node_affinity: [n1,n2]} -> Action: nominate pull-warmslot job for nodes n1,n2; increase preferred_affinity_weight for 60s.

Runbook: probe-caused outage mitigation (oncall steps)
1) Identify active probes via bench-probe events and correlate with perf ingest times.
2) If production SLOs are impacted: disable probe by ID immediately (bench-probe cancel <id>).
3) Escalate to scheduler-owner and runtime-oncall. Attach probe fingerprint to the incident ticket.
4) If degradation persists after probe cancellation, run the rollback matrix: a) reduce admission to reserve 20% capacity for critical routes b) enable coarse-grained fallback routes for enterprise customers.
5) Post-incident: run a shaded replay of the probe in a canary namespace and collect aggregated artifacts for root cause analysis.

Reporting and dashboards
- perf-dashboard/plp-sfp: single-pane view showing live probe status, fingerprint changes over time, vulnerable cohorts, and aggregated decision signals.
- Alerting: probe-failure (job failed to complete), probe-sla-impact (if probe correlates to any route SLO breach within 1m), probe-signal-spike (kernel_contention > 0.5).

Automation and CI integration
- Short smoke probes run on every runtime scheduler merge to main. CI job: bench-probe ci-run --manifest ci-smoke.yaml.
- Longer ramp and burst probes are gated behind an internal release window and require SRE approval.

Ownership and contacts
- Primary owner: Benchmarking team (owner group: eng-serving-runtime-benchmarking).
- Scheduler consumer: Runtime Scheduler team (contact: @arjun.patel).
- Oncall escalation: runtime-oncall rotation.

Related artifacts and references
- Probe runner implementation: git://repo/bench-probe (internal)
- Fingerprint schema: perf-store/docs/fingerprint-spec.md
- Scheduler signal bus contract: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-telemetry-synthesis-and-proofing-2025.json

Change log
- 2026-01-12: Draft created by Maya Chen.
- 2026-03-02: Added probe fingerprint schema and initial mapping rules.
- 2026-09-04: Updated automated feedback thresholds and example manifest; added runbook steps for probe-caused outages.

Appendix: troubleshooting checklist
- If aggregator fails to produce fingerprint: verify telemetry pipeline health, ensure bench-probe wrote trace ids to perf-ingest, check S3 bucket for raw traces.
- If scheduler ignored decision signals: confirm signal bus ACLs, confirm consumer subscription, validate schema version alignment.
- If KV warmup did not occur: check warmstart job logs and node affinity assignments.

---
Please reach out to the reviewers listed above for review requests or to schedule a probe window.

title: Slot Synthesis Simulator and SLA Fuzz Playbook
content:
Overview

This playbook describes the Slot Synthesis Simulator (S3) — a reproducible lab harness used to synthesize GPU slot allocation, kernel contention, and scheduler behavior to fuzz-test SLA boundaries. The purpose is to find edge cases where our scheduler, kernel selection, or cache warmup interacts to cause SLO regressions or degraded output fidelity. S3 is intended for benchmarking, pre-release safety gates, and targeted post-incident verification.

Why we built S3

- Production traffic has complex concurrency shapes, prefix-sharing, and mixed model families (FP32/INT8/quantized). Traditional replay and unit microbenchmarks miss combinatorial scheduling interactions.
- S3 allows us to simulate: heterogeneous accelerators, slot preemption, admission spikes, varying sequence length distributions, and KV-cache warmup patterns.
- Results feed into kernel/operator rollouts, scheduler policy tuning, and gating decisions for quantization/feature releases.

Glossary

- slot: logical GPU allocation unit used by the scheduler (can map to CUDA context / compute slice).
- slot synthesis: creating synthetic slot occupancy patterns over time to emulate real request mixes.
- SLO fuzz: intentionally varying traffic and system parameters beyond expected ranges to find brittle decision boundaries.
- fidelity cliff: abrupt quality degradation (latency or output) when scheduler or kernel changes occur.

High-level architecture of S3

1) Input generator: consumes a workload profile (sequence-length histogram, model mix, KV-cache hit curves) and emits a timeline of synthetic requests.
2) Slot modeler: maps requests to slot occupancy using configurable policies (co-location, isolation, preemption windows).
3) Kernel stressor: simulates kernel handoffs, warm/cold kernel latencies, and queueing at kernel dispatcher granularity.
4) Metrics sink: collects per-request synthetic metrics (simulated service time, queue delay), aggregates into SLO windows, and emits experiment reports.

Simulator configuration reference (key fields)

- experiment_name: short id for the run
- duration_seconds: wall-clock duration of the simulation
- models: ordered list of model stubs with per-model latency and token-cost distributions
- slot_topology: definition of slot counts, types (cpu, gpu_a100, gpu_h100, tpu), and heterogeneity mapping
- admission_policy: policy id (e.g., conservative, balanced, aggressive) to exercise scheduler branches
- preemption_profile: probability/time-window parameters to synthesize preemption events
- kv_warmup_curve: mapping from time to hit-rate for prefix cache
- sequence_length_distribution: empirical histogram or parametric (p95, mean)

Sample YAML experiment (copy/paste into simulator CLI)

---
experiment_name: "s3_sla_fuzz_canary_2026_02"
duration_seconds: 3600
models:
  - name: "lm-medium-quant"
    mean_token_ms: 6.8
    token_std_ms: 1.2
    kv_sensitivity: 1.6  # relative slowdown when kv miss
  - name: "chat-large"
    mean_token_ms: 12.3
    token_std_ms: 3.1
    kv_sensitivity: 1.0
slot_topology:
  - type: "gpu_h100"
    count: 8
    slots_per_gpu: 4
  - type: "gpu_a100"
    count: 12
    slots_per_gpu: 2
admission_policy: "balanced"
preemption_profile:
  probability: 0.08
  min_interval_ms: 5000
  max_drain_ms: 12000
kv_warmup_curve: "linear:0.2->0.85:900"
sequence_length_distribution: "empirical:seq_hist_2026_q1.json"
---

CLI examples

- Dry run (no metric sink):
  ./s3 run --config examples/canary.yaml --dry-run

- Full run with metrics upload: 
  ./s3 run --config examples/canary.yaml --metrics gs://redwood-s3/experiments/2026/

Primary metrics and acceptance criteria

- p50 / p95 / p99 tail latency (per-model and global) — baseline delta tolerated: p95 <= baseline_p95 * 1.15 for a non-blocking release; p95 <= baseline_p95 * 1.05 for a kernel rollout gate.
- SLO violation rate (requests exceeding latency SLO) — gating threshold: < 0.5% for general release, < 0.1% for high-risk kernel changes.
- Queue growth rate: slope of queue length over 60s windows (alert if > 15 req/s/min sustained).
- Preemption-induced failure probability: fraction of preempted requests that miss deadline (>1% requires investigation).
- Cost signal (simulated GPU-seconds): used to catch regression in per-token cost.

Experiment recipes (start here depending on intent)

1) Canary kernel rollout simulation (safety gate)
   - Purpose: measure effect of new kernel variant on tail latency under mixed traffic.
   - Steps: pick production model mix; set 10% of slots to new_kernel profile; run S3 for 1 hour with several admission_policy values (conservative, balanced, aggressive); compare per-model p99 and p95 to baseline.
   - Gate: no model-level p99 regression > 10% and global SLO violation < 0.1%.

2) Affinity breakdown stress test
   - Purpose: validate slot co-location rules under hot-model concentration.
   - Steps: synthesize a hot-spot where 30% of requests target a single model; force co-location policy to pack slots; inject KV cache cold start at t=0.
   - Gate: queue growth rate must stabilize within 120s. If not, mark admission_policy for tuning.

3) Preemption fuzz (edge-case discovery)
   - Purpose: discover corner cases where preemption ordering and kernel handoffs cause starvation.
   - Steps: set preemption_profile.probability to 0.2 and reduce min_interval_ms to 1000; run for 30 minutes and log any request hitting >2x latency SLO.
   - Gate: debug any observed requests, capture decision traces and slot assignment timeline.

Runbook: executing a baseline S3 experiment

1) Prepare baseline artifacts: workload profile, seq_hist, and baseline_p95 numbers (from production telemetry).
2) Upload config to experiments bucket and mark experiment_name with owner prefix (e.g., se-runtime/alice-s3-2026-02).
3) Start dry-run locally to validate config: ./s3 run --config ... --dry-run.
4) Run full experiment with metrics sink.
5) Publish report: include aggregated graphs, regression table (models vs baseline), and raw traces link.
6) If failure gates hit, open a bug in JIRA and tag owner_team: eng-serving-runtime.

Safety and preconditions (must be satisfied before risky runs)

- All kernel rollout experiments must be run with a baseline reference and known-good commit id.
- Long-running fuzz runs (>6h) must be signed off by the runtime lead and scheduled to avoid infra contention.
- Secrets and PII: S3 must never be run with production user data; use anonymized or synthetic request shapes only.

Interpreting S3 outputs

- Regression matrix: rows = models, cols = metrics (p50/p95/p99, SLO rate, cost). Flag cells that exceed gate thresholds.
- Decision trace artifacts: a sequence of slot assignment events + kernel hints. Use the trace viewer (link in appendix) to step through abnormal requests.
- Heatmaps: slot occupancy over time; look for correlated increases in kernel queue time and KV-miss spikes.

Common failure modes and troubleshooting checklist

- Symptom: p99 regressions concentrated on quantized models
  - Likely cause: kv_sensitivity underestimation or inadequate kernel warmup for INT8 kernels.
  - Actions: increase kv_warmup_curve, re-run GPU affinity packing test.

- Symptom: sustained queue growth under "balanced" policy
  - Likely cause: admission_policy implementation mismatch with production (policy parameters differ).
  - Actions: export production admission snapshot, reconcile parameter differences, re-run.

- Symptom: flakiness between runs (non-deterministic results)
  - Likely cause: RNG seeds not pinned or sequence_length_distribution referencing mutable live corpus.
  - Actions: pin seeds in config and use archived seq_hist files.

Ownership and escalation

- S3 maintainer: runtime-simulations@redwood (primary: Priya Nair)
- Escalation path: if experiment shows SLO regressions that could impact customers, notify runtime-oncall -> eng-sre -> product-security if customer data concerns.

Appendix A — Example regression report table (text)

Model | baseline_p95_ms | experiment_p95_ms | delta% | gate_pass
----- | --------------- | ----------------- | -----: | :-----:
lm-medium-quant | 150 | 163 | 8.7% | PASS
chat-large | 320 | 365 | 14.1% | FAIL
reranker-small | 90 | 95 | 5.6% | PASS

Appendix B — Debugging commands and artifacts

- Capture decision trace id from experiment report and open viewer: http://internal-trace-viewer/trace/<TRACE_ID>
- Convert a trace to CSV for offline analysis: ./s3 export-trace --id <TRACE_ID> --format csv --out /tmp/trace.csv
- Run a focused synthetic microbursts test to reproduce: ./s3 run --config examples/microburst.yaml --duration 600

Appendix C — Known limitations of S3

- S3 models kernel cost and queueing but does not currently simulate low-level GPU thermal throttling; regressions caused by temperature-induced frequency scaling must be validated on hardware labs.
- Network cross-node RPC timing variance is approximated; multi-node scatter/gather effects should be validated with shadow traffic tests.

Appendix D — Links and artifacts

- Binary: gs://redwood-tools/s3/v0.6.4/s3-linux-amd64
- Trace viewer: http://internal-trace-viewer/
- Experiment examples: gs://redwood-s3/examples/2026/
- Run ownership playbook: ../runbooks/runtime-deployment-circuit-breakers-and-sla-fallback-playbook-2026.json

Contact and feedback

For questions, feature requests, or if results indicate a potential production impact, file an issue in the runtime-simulations board and add reviewers: Ethan Brooks, Marta Iglesias, Linus Kwan.

title: SDK Connection Pooling and Fanout Quickstart
content:
Overview

This quickstart describes recommended connection pooling and request fanout patterns for Redwood SDK clients. It targets backend services that make high-throughput calls to the Redwood API (generation, embeddings, reranking). The goal is to reduce tail latency, avoid connector saturation at the network layer, and provide predictable token-cost accounting when fanout is required.

Use cases covered

- High QPS microservices that call Redwood for short-lived generation requests.
- Batch/parallel embedding workloads (concurrent tenants).
- Fanout workflows where a single user action triggers 3–10 parallel model calls (e.g., multi-hypothesis generation + reranker).

Principles and tradeoffs

1) Keep a modest, bounded pool per process — prefer many small pools over one global unbounded pool.
2) Prefer async concurrency primitives with backpressure (semaphores, rate limiters) over naive thread-per-request models.
3) When fanout > N (where N is configurable), consider sequential or staged execution to preserve latency SLOs and cost budgets.
4) Instrument both pool usage and request-level downstream metrics so capacity issues are observable before customers notice.

Quickstart patterns

Pattern A — Single-host connection pool (recommended for stateless API servers)

- Maintain a fixed-size HTTP/HTTP2 connection pool to the Redwood endpoint.
- Per-process pool size = min(64, max(8, CPU_cores * 8)) as a starting heuristic.
- Combine with an async semaphore to cap in-flight API calls to the pool size.

Example: Node.js (axios + generic-pool)

const axios = require('axios');
const genericPool = require('generic-pool');
const HttpsAgent = require('https').Agent;

const agent = new HttpsAgent({ keepAlive: true, maxSockets: 64 });
const client = axios.create({ baseURL: process.env.REDWOOD_URL, httpsAgent: agent, timeout: 30000 });

// Simple semaphore (toy example)
const { Sema } = require('async-sema');
const poolSemaphore = new Sema(32); // in-flight cap

async function callRedwood(payload) {
  await poolSemaphore.acquire();
  try {
    const res = await client.post('/v1/generate', payload, { headers: { 'Authorization': `Bearer ${process.env.REDWOOD_KEY}` } });
    return res.data;
  } finally {
    poolSemaphore.release();
  }
}

Notes: tune maxSockets to match process-level CPU and expected concurrency. Keep separate agent/client instances for long-running worker vs short-lived request handlers.

Pattern B — Controlled fanout (recommended for multi-call UX flows)

- Limit simultaneous branch calls with a bounded concurrency pool.
- Stagger start times slightly to avoid synchronized bursts across instances.
- If branches are independent but result sizes vary, prefer pessimistic token budgeting + adaptive early cancellation.

Staged fanout algorithm (recommended)

1) Sort branches by predicted cost (if available) or worst-case estimate.
2) Reserve slot tokens equal to branch concurrency cap (K).
3) Start first K branches in parallel; as each completes, start the next.
4) If cumulative token usage exceeds a configured budget, cancel lower-priority branches and return partial results.

Example: Python (asyncio + aiohttp + asyncio.Semaphore)

import asyncio
import aiohttp

REDWOOD_URL = "https://api.redwood.ai"
REDWOOD_KEY = "${REDWOOD_KEY}"

async def fetch(session, payload):
    async with session.post(REDWOOD_URL + '/v1/generate', json=payload, headers={'Authorization': f'Bearer {REDWOOD_KEY}'}) as resp:
        return await resp.json()

async def staged_fanout(branches, concurrency=4, token_budget=10000):
    semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(concurrency)
    results = []
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession(connector=aiohttp.TCPConnector(limit=concurrency*2, force_close=False)) as session:
        async def run_branch(branch):
            async with semaphore:
                return await fetch(session, branch['payload'])
        for coro in asyncio.as_completed([run_branch(b) for b in branches]):
            res = await coro
            results.append(res)
            # token tracking pseudo-code: if tokens_used > token_budget: break
    return results

Pattern C — Dedicated worker pool for heavy throughput (batching-friendly)

- For embedding and batching workloads, use dedicated worker processes with larger connection pools and explicit batching logic.
- Worker pool size should match GPU/CPU and memory footprint; keep API request backpressure at the entrypoint.

Configurations table (recommended starting values)

| Component | Setting | Rationale | Starting value | Notes |
|---|---:|---|---:|---|
| Per-process max sockets | maxSockets | Network concurrency to Redwood | CPU_cores * 8, capped at 64 | Reduce if using many processes on same host |
| In-flight API semaphore | concurrency cap | Limits RPC concurrency | 32 | Tune down if 503s/connection errors rise |
| Fanout concurrency (K) | per-request parallel branches | Limits parallel branches | 4 | Increase for low-latency critical flows |
| Token budget | per-request token cap | Cost control for fanout | 8k tokens | Used for early-cancellation logic |
| Request timeout | per-call | Avoid hung sockets | 30s | Shorter for latency-sensitive endpoints |

Telemetry and instrumentation (must-haves)

- Metrics to emit from SDK or service:
  - redwood.pool.max_sockets (gauge)
  - redwood.pool.in_flight (gauge)
  - redwood.request.latency_ms (histogram)
  - redwood.request.status_counts (counter, by status code)
  - redwood.fanout.active_branches (gauge)
  - redwood.fanout.cancelled_branches (counter)
  - redwood.token.usage_per_request (histogram)

- Important derived alerts:
  - pool_in_flight / max_sockets > 0.9 for > 5m -> investigate pooling saturation
  - 5xx rate > 1% and > 50 requests/min -> possible API throttling or misconfigured timeouts
  - average token usage per-request trending up > 25% week-over-week -> check prompt changes

Common failure modes and canonical fixes

1) Symptoms: sudden spike in connection resets and 5xx for many clients.
   Fixes: verify keepAlive agent is enabled, reduce pool size if host-level limits (ulimit / ephemeral ports) are reached, increase TCP TIME_WAIT reuse on busy hosts.
2) Symptoms: high tail latency with large fanout jobs.
   Fixes: enable staged fanout, add per-branch time budget and early cancellation, enforce token budget.
3) Symptoms: intermittent auth errors when rotating credentials in mid-flight.
   Fixes: implement safe key rotation: preload new key into pool handshake or restart worker processes at controlled cadence.

Operational runbook (triage flow)

1) Confirm scope: are errors scoped to one service or pervasive? Check redwood.request.status_counts by service.
2) Check pool metrics: are in_flight near max_sockets? If yes, reduce concurrency cap and investigate upstream load.
3) Check downstream network: increased TCP retransmits or socket exhaustion on host level. Use netstat/ss and dstat.
4) If fanout-related, look at redwood.fanout.active_branches and cancelled_branches. Consider toggling fanout staging.
5) If token-cost spike, locate deployments with sudden prompt changes using telemetry and revert/mitigate.

Rollout guidance for applying changes

- Canary steps for concurrency tuning:
  1. Deploy new setting to 1 instance group (5% traffic).
  2. Monitor pool saturation and 5xx over 15 minutes.
  3. If healthy, increase to 25% and repeat.
  4. At 100%, run a synthetic load test for 1 hour.

- Safe fallback: configuration should be feature-flagged or env-var driven so rollback requires only a config change or process restart.

Checklist for SDK authors (must ship with all language SDKs)

- Default client uses connection keep-alive and a configurable maxSockets.
- Expose a concurrency/semaphore primitive or helper class for staged fanout.
- Built-in telemetry hooks (emit the metric names above) and a pluggable metrics sink.
- Documentation example for both per-request and worker-process usage patterns.
- Clear guidance on key rotation best practices.

Example configuration snippets (YAML)

server:
  redwood_client:
    base_url: "https://api.redwood.ai"
    max_sockets: 48
    in_flight_limit: 32
    request_timeout_seconds: 30
    fanout:
      max_parallel_branches: 4
      per_request_token_budget: 8000

Troubleshooting quick hits

- If you see a spike in TIME_WAIT sockets: reduce per-process pool and increase number of worker processes, or enable socket reuse at OS level.
- If you observe 429s: verify client-side rate limiting; introduce jitter and exponential backoff on retries.
- If embedding batch latency is high: increase batch size on worker and reduce network concurrency at entrypoint; consider colocating workers.

Ownership and contacts

- SDK patterns owner: Eng DX (Priya Raman)
- Runtime/infrastructure contact: Serving Runtime (Dmitri Kozlov)
- SRE on-call: see /confluence/eng-sre/runbooks

References and related reading

- API contract: /confluence/eng-developer-experience/api-examples/api-deterministic-output-samples-and-canonical-fixes-2025
- Fanout patterns reference: /confluence/eng-developer-experience/quickstarts-and-templates/client-request-shaping-and-local-fallback-playbook-2026
- Pooling and kernel-level notes: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling

Appendix — small checklist before a major rollout

1) Add telemetry for redwood.pool.* and redwood.fanout.* in your feature branch.
2) Run load test that matches production percentiles (p50/p90/p99) and observe connection reuse rates.
3) Validate safe key rotation in a staging environment.
4) Confirm that configuration is env-var controllable and that SRE can remotely rollback.

Document history

- 2026-08-15: initial draft by Priya Raman
- 2026-09-01: reviewer feedback incorporated (Maya Chen)
- 2026-10-01: published after SRE review

title: Shadow Cohort Fidelity Stitching Protocol
content:
Summary
--------
This document defines the Shadow Cohort Fidelity Stitching Protocol: an experiment and analysis pattern for running mirrored (shadowed) production traffic across multiple runtime cohorts to validate fidelity, kernel-scheduling and quantization impacts, and end-to-end user-visible regression risk before rollout. The protocol is designed for validating changes that affect execution kernels, scheduler policies, KV cache behavior, quantization profiles, or model variants.

Scope
-----
- Applies to runtime experiments that change kernel selection, scheduler configuration, quantization profile, or model variant.
- Intended for mid-to-large scale shadow runs (from single-node to fleet-wide depending on risk).
- Not for synthetic microbenchmarks; this protocol relies on production-shaped traffic.

Objectives
----------
1. Detect regressions in output fidelity (semantic divergence, hallucination rate) introduced by kernel/scheduler/quantization changes.
2. Measure operational impact: latency p50/p95/p99, tail amplification, token cost delta, and memory pressure.
3. Provide clear pass/fail criteria tied to SLOs and risk budgets.
4. Produce automation-friendly artifacts: config snippets, analysis queries, and dashboard templates.

Definitions and terms
---------------------
- Primary cohort: live production serving path receiving real user traffic.
- Shadow cohort: non-responding mirrored path that receives copies of requests for analysis only.
- Stitching: aligning outputs from primary and shadow for token-level and semantic comparison.
- Fidelity delta: measured difference in quality metrics (embedding similarity, logprob delta, downstream evals).
- Cohort window: contiguous time range used for comparison (recommended 60–120 minutes per experiment).

Ownership and roles
-------------------
- Experiment owner: eng-serving-runtime feature lead (creates config, runs experiment).
- Observability owner: eng-platform (dashboards, sampling traces).
- Quality owner: applied-ml-and-evals (defines fidelity metrics and acceptance thresholds).
- Oncall / Runbook owner: eng-sre (prepared to abort if operational thresholds are breached).

Pre-requisites
--------------
- Canary availability of shadow cohort image/version with kernel/scheduler/quantization change.
- Traffic mirroring capability at the dispatch layer with request context preservation (headers, timestamps).
- Stable sampling and replay hooks in tracing and KV cache to capture divergent behaviour.
- Baseline corpus of prompts and a lightweight eval harness to run offline checks for severe regressions.

Experiment matrix and cohorts
----------------------------
Use a combinatorial matrix to cover realistic differences:
| Cohort name | Model variant | Kernel set | Quantization | Scheduler profile | Notes |
| Primary | redwood-v1.4 | stable-kernels-1 | q8_compat | standard | baseline production |
| Shadow-A | redwood-v1.4 | new-kernel-optim | q8_compat | standard | tests kernel changes |
| Shadow-B | redwood-v1.4 | new-kernel-optim | q4_ffnx | adjusted-batching | tests quantization + scheduler |
| Shadow-C | redwood-v1.5 | stable-kernels-1 | q8_compat | priority-synth | tests model variant + scheduler |

Sampling strategy
-----------------
- Mirror 100% of a low-risk subset (e.g., read-only assistant queries) for correctness experiments.
- Mirror 5–20% of general traffic with deterministic hashing (request_id mod N) for operational metrics to limit cost.
- Ensure session affinity keys are preserved so session-level KV cache behavior is comparable.

Instrumentation and telemetry
----------------------------
Collect the following per-request:
- request_id, timestamp, cohort_id, model_version, kernel_tag, quant_profile, scheduler_profile
- latency_ms (dispatch, kernel, end-to-end), token_count_in, token_count_out
- model_logprob_sum, per-token logprobs (sampled), response_embedding (128–1024 dim depending on model)
- runtime signals: GPU_util_pct, cuda_mem_free_mb, cpu_load, kvcache_hit_ratio

Metrics and acceptance thresholds
-------------------------------
Quality metrics (primary gates):
- Embedding cosine similarity median ≥ 0.995 and 5th percentile ≥ 0.95 between primary and shadow responses (for single-turn responses).
- Mean per-token logprob delta ≤ 0.15 nats/token across stitched tokens.
- Downstream task AUC / exact-match must not degrade > 1.5% relative.
- Severe hallucination rate (as flagged by eval harness or heuristics) increase ≤ 0.1 percentage point.
Operational metrics (secondary gates):
- delta p99 latency ≤ +12 ms (absolute) OR relative increase ≤ 15% (whichever is smaller).
- p95 latency amplification factor ≤ 1.25.
- Increase in GPU tail stalls > 10% requires immediate abort and triage.
- Token cost delta per 1M tokens ≤ 5% for production budget-sensitive customers.

Procedure: runbook-style steps
-----------------------------
1. Preparation (owner + 2 reviewers):
   - Create experiment config and register cohort IDs in dispatch.
   - Pre-run offline golden-corpus checks (1000 prompts) using the shadow image.
   - Confirm observability dashboards (latency, embeddings, traces) are available.
2. Ramp stage (10–30 minutes):
   - Start mirroring the low-risk hashed subset to shadows at 1% of traffic.
   - Monitor p50/p95/p99, memory, and kvcache heatmap.
   - If operational thresholds breached, pause mirroring and escalate to eng-sre.
3. Validation stage (60–120 minutes):
   - Increase mirror to target sampling rate (5–20%).
   - Persist request/response pairs to stitched storage with retention 14 days for analysis.
   - Run automated fidelity-check jobs every 15 minutes (embedding similarity, LM logprob deltas).
4. Analysis stage (post-run):
   - Aggregate metrics by cohort, request class, model_version, and kernel_tag.
   - Run stratified analysis by sequence length (short/medium/long), session-affinity (cold/warm), and request type.
   - Generate a report with pass/fail and recommended mitigations.
5. Decision & rollout:
   - If all gates pass: prepare canary rollout (10% traffic to new cohort) following standard canary checklist.
   - If any gate fails: create issue with reproduction artifacts and assign to kernel/scheduler owners.

Analysis recipes and queries
---------------------------
- Stitching key: use (request_id || request_timestamp || session_id) to join primary and shadow. If multiple shadow responses exist, align by token offset.
- Example SQL-like aggregation (pseudo):
```
SELECT cohort, percentile(latency_ms, 50) AS p50, percentile(latency_ms, 95) AS p95, 
  avg(embedding_cos_sim) AS mean_emb_sim, percentile(embedding_cos_sim,5) AS emb_sim_p5
FROM stitched_responses
WHERE run_id = 'shadow-2027-02-10'
GROUP BY cohort;
```
- Semantic regression triage: for requests where emb_sim < 0.9, run difference-aware diffing (top-k token alignment + LM delta) and capture the turn-level trace for manual inspection.

Dashboard and reporting templates
--------------------------------
- Live dashboard tiles to prepare: cohort throughput, cohort p50/p95/p99, emb_sim median/p5, lm_logprob_delta distribution, kvcache_hit_ratio, GPU tail stall rate.
- Automated PDF report (generated nightly while experiment runs) with a one-page summary and a detailed appendix containing top 50 low-similarity examples.

Safety and rollback guidelines
----------------------------
- Abort criteria (immediate stop of mirroring): sustained p99 latency increase > 25% OR GPU error rate spike > 3x baseline OR emb_sim cohort median < 0.90.
- Fast rollback: terminate shadow image and clear cohort registration; if changes are in the primary path, execute a canary revert.
- For ambiguous failures, perform a targeted replay of failing requests in isolated environment with full tracing enabled.

Known pitfalls and mitigation notes
----------------------------------
- KV cache non-determinism: session key hashing differences can produce spurious divergence; ensure session-affinity keys are identical across dispatches.
- Sampling bias: avoid mirroring only low-latency traffic; introduce stratified sampling by request type.
- Quantization-induced subtlety: q4 variants can change tokenization margins leading to marginally different token boundaries; stitch by canonicalized token IDs where possible.
- Scheduler preemption effects: high-priority preemption can change runtime ordering and amplify tail latency; include preemption count in telemetry.

Example automation config (dispatch snippet)
-------------------------------------------
```yaml
# shadow cohort registration example
shadow_cohorts:
  - id: shadow-a-kernel-opt
    image: redwood-serving:2027-02-kernel-opt
    mirror_fraction: 0.05 # 5% deterministic via request_id hash
    preserve_headers: ["x-session-id", "x-request-id", "x-original-timestamp"]
    tags: ["kernel_opt", "q8_compat"]
```

Appendix: sample stitched result JSON (single line per request)
--------------------------------------------------------------
```json
{"request_id":"r-123","cohort":"primary","tokens":["Hello","there"],"embedding": [0.001, 0.9, ...],"logprob_sum":-12.4,"latency_ms":34}
```
(When stored, truncate per-token logs for retention; keep full artifacts for the top 500 divergent requests.)

Postmortem and release linkage
-----------------------------
- If this protocol discovers production-impacting regressions, the experiment owner must create a postmortem following the standard incident template and link it to the release notes for the kernel/scheduler/quantization change.
- Include prescriptive mitigations (kernel fallback gating, scheduler guardrails, quantization tuning) and update the rollout playbook.

References and related docs
--------------------------
- Runtime observability contract and telemetry guide (see related_pages).
- Quantization rollout safety playbook.
- Runtime canary and rollout checklist.

Questions and feedback
---------------------
For questions about implementing this protocol, contact the owner team (engineering) or reviewers listed above. Report anomalies to eng-sre via the standard channel with the experiment run_id and top divergent request IDs.

title: runtime-deployment-sanity-and-benchmark-suite-acceptance-2026
content:
Summary:

This document defines the deployment sanity acceptance criteria and the canonical benchmark suite used by the runtime team to gate runtime changes (kernels, scheduler, orchestration). It is intended for engineers running release validation, SREs owning rollout decisions, and release managers approving canaries.

Goal:

- Provide a compact, reproducible benchmark suite that exercises the common hot-paths across models, sequence lengths, batching shapes, and third-party accelerators.
- Define clear pass/fail acceptance criteria and automated checks that can be executed in CI or on pre-deploy staging clusters.
- Ensure performance regressions (latency, throughput, and cost-per-token) are caught before platform rollouts beyond canary.

Scope:

Applies to: kernel patches, scheduler policy changes, orchestration control plane releases that affect request routing/eviction, and quantization/runtime memory layout changes. Does not replace long-form lab benchmarks (see references).

Owner and Escalation:

- Suite owner: Runtime Performance Team (primary contact: Aisha Patel)
- On-call escalation: runtime-sre@redwood.ai -> Pager duty escalation per SRE rota

Acceptance Criteria (high level):

1) Functional: all sample generation and embedding endpoints return valid responses for the test corpus (no 5xx/errors)
2) Latency: p95 generation latency must not regress more than 10% vs baseline for the same commit, absolute p95 thresholds below: see table.
3) Throughput: end-to-end throughput for batched inference must remain within -15% of baseline on identical hardware profiles.
4) Cost: measured per-token GPU cycles (proxy: aggregate GPU utilization normalized by tokens/s) must not increase >8%.
5) Memory: peak GPU memory used must not exceed baseline + 50 MB for small models, +200 MB for large models.

Sanity matrix (text table):

| Test name | Model class | Sequence lengths | Concurrency / Batch shapes | Primary metric | Threshold |
|-----------|-------------|------------------|----------------------------|----------------|----------|
| gen-short-seq | small (7B) | 32 / 128 | 1, 8 | p95 latency | < 120ms (p95) |
| gen-long-seq | medium (13B) | 512 / 1024 | 1, 4 | p95 latency | < 650ms (p95) |
| batch-encoder | embedding (2B) | 128 | 32/64 | qps | >= baseline*0.85 |
| kv-cache-warm | session-heavy (7B) | 256 | 1 steady | tail latency | <= baseline + 10% |
| quantized-fidelity-check | quantized 4-bit (13B) | 128 | 4 | output match | top-5 token agreement >= 98% |

Note: baseline values are taken from the last green release tag (recorded in the benchmark registry). Absolute thresholds are pragmatic safety nets; primary gating is percentage regression relative to baseline.

Benchmark suite components and runner:

- bench-runner v2: our canonical harness (Go binary) used by CI. Configs live in repo: infra/benchmarks/bench-runner/configs/
- trace-collector: sidecar process that collects kernel timings, GPU utilization, and NVLink stats.
- shadow-replayer: replays production request surface for fidelity checks (sampled traces).
- model-profiles: YAML files describing model input shapes, cache-hit scenarios, and expected KV-cache behavior.

Example bench-runner config (YAML snippet):

-- bench_config:
   name: gen-short-seq-7b
   model: redwood/small-7b:2026-01
   seeds: 100
   sequence_lengths: [32, 128]
   concurrency: [1, 8]
   gpu_profile: p4d.24xlarge
   metrics: [p50, p95, p99, gpu_util, tokens_per_second]
   run_duration: 180

CI integration and automated checks:

- Pull request pipeline will run a lightweight subset (smoke) of the suite on a single accelerator host (duration ~15m).
- Merged commits to the release branch trigger a nightly full sanity run against the current baseline.
- Release candidate builds must pass the full suite in staging (see "Release gating" below) before canary rollout.

How to run locally (developer guide):

1) Checkout infra/benchmarks and build bench-runner: make bench-runner
2) Start a staging node with the same accelerator profile used in CI (use dev-k8s cluster): ./scripts/provision-staging --profile p4d
3) Upload the model bundle to the staging model registry: scripts/push-model --model redwood/small-7b:local
4) Run bench-runner with a config: ./bin/bench-runner --config configs/gen-short-seq-7b.yaml --collect-traces
5) Upload results to the benchmark registry: ./scripts/upload-results --run-id=local-$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)

Measurements and signal definitions:

- p95 latency: end-to-end wallclock time from request accept to final token (includes network hop to sidecar).
- token-rate: measured as tokens / GPU-second, aggregated over the run (proxy for cost per token).
- kernel-latency profile: distribution of kernel launch times collected by trace-collector (used for attributions).

Pass/fail automation rules (applied by bench-compare tool):

1) If any functional test returns non-2xx: FAIL
2) If p95 regression >10% on any generation test: WARNING (auto-fail unless triage-approved)
3) If throughput regression >15% or token-cost increase >8%: FAIL
4) If peak GPU memory exceeds the memory budget (per model): FAIL
5) Small regressions (p95 5-10%) open a performance ticket with attached traces; release can proceed only with a documented mitigations plan approved by the runtime performance lead.

Release gating and canary choreography:

- Staging green -> Canary 1 (1% traffic, 4 hours) -> Canary 2 (10% traffic, 8 hours) -> Gradual ramp to 100% (24–48 hours)
- Canary approval requires: pass of full sanity suite in staging, no SLO breaches in Canary 1, and no kernel exceptions in trace logs.
- If any SLO breach occurs during canary, rollback immediately to previous stable tag and open incident with the severity determined by the breach impact table below.

Severity and rollback table (text):

- Sev-1: total p95 regression >50% or >=1 service-wide 5xx per 1000 requests for 15m -> immediate rollback, stop rollout, incident declared.
- Sev-2: p95 regression >25% or sustained token-cost increase >20% for 30m -> pause rollout, mitigation plan within 4 hours.
- Sev-3: isolated regression for a single model class or marginal p95 regression 10–25% -> require patch and re-run of suite before reattempting rollout.

Runbook: triage steps on failing benchmark run:

1) Gather artifacts: bench-runner logs, trace-collector bundle, GPU-health metrics, bench-compare report.
2) Run bench-compare to produce diff vs baseline: ./bin/bench-compare --baseline last-green --run current-run-id
3) If failure maps to kernel hotspots, tag kernel-team and include kernel traces.
4) If failure maps to scheduler/policy (e.g., increased tail latencies under mixed shapes), repro in local lab with shadow-replayer and run scheduler-debug script.
5) For memory regressions, capture heap/profile: /scripts/capture-gpu-mem-snapshot.sh <node> and file a memory regression bug.

Known limitations and caveats:

- This suite intentionally focuses on representative shapes; it can miss rare production edge-cases. Use production shadow traces to complement the suite.
- External cloud neighbor noise (noisy GPUs) can affect throughput numbers; we mitigate by running three repeats and using median.
- Third-party accelerator quirks (driver versions and NVLink topology) must be documented per-hardware in infra/benchmarks/hardware-profiles/

Operational housekeeping:

- Bench results retention: raw traces stored for 90 days, aggregated metrics indefinitely in the benchmark registry.
- Baseline rotation: After a major release, the baseline is re-recorded. Baselines must be signed off by runtime performance lead.

References and links:

- infra/benchmarks/README (bench-runner usage)
- runtime-architecture/execution-stitching-and-fallback-orchestration-2026
- runbooks/runtime-upgrade-validation-and-canary-matrix-2026

Appendix: example bench-compare output (abridged):

{
  "run_id": "2026-02-18-rc1",
  "model": "redwood/small-7b:2026-01",
  "p95_baseline": 110.2,
  "p95_current": 129.7,
  "p95_delta_pct": 17.7,
  "token_rate_delta_pct": -12.3,
  "status": "FAIL"
}

Notes for reviewers:

- Please review the memory budgets table in infra/benchmarks/hardware-profiles and confirm the small/large model cutoffs align with recent capacity planning.
- Confirm that the quantized fidelity test (top-5 token agreement threshold) is still appropriate for our customer SLAs.

Change log:

- 2026-01-12: initial draft by Aisha Patel
- 2026-02-18: added CI integration details, simplified pass/fail automation rules (Aisha Patel)

title: Request Surface Replay & Synthetic Corpus Builder
content:
Summary
-------
This document describes the canonical process and tooling to produce replayable request surfaces and synthetic request corpora for benchmarking, profiling, and regression tests of the Redwood inference runtime. The corpus builder produces privacy-validated payloads, stratified sampling artifacts, and annotated replay manifests that drive the microbench, end-to-end, and kernel-level perf suites.

Goals
-----
- Provide reproducible, representative request sets that reflect production request shape (tokens, context windows, multimodal markers, KV cache patterns).
- Enable deterministic replay for latency, tail analysis, and kernel-sensitivity tests.
- Produce anonymized synthetic variants for open benchmarking and distributed perf teams.
- Integrate with existing perf harnesses and the profiling playbook to link input tokens to kernel execution traces.

Scope and non-goals
-------------------
In scope:
- Extraction and normalization of request metadata from live sampling channels (telemetry/ingress-proxy).
- Sampling strategies that preserve per-tenant request distributions.
- Tools to synthesize requests that preserve statistical properties while removing PII.
- Output formats and manifests consumed by the benchmarking suite and runtime profilers.

Out of scope:
- Full conversational session reconstruction (this builder targets single-request / short-session replay).
- Long-term storage policy (see data-residency-and-retention policy).

When to use this builder
------------------------
- Before kernel rollouts to verify sensitivity across representative inputs.
- Prior to model-variant release to simulate cost/latency tradeoffs.
- During incident postmortems where a reproducible input is needed for hypothesis testing.

High-level design
-----------------
1) Ingress sampling: live request sampler emits lightweight records to the sampling pipeline (ingest topic: perf-samples).
2) Normalizer: canonicalizes fields (prompt, metadata, token counts), computes derived features (prompt_length, kv_hits_est), and marks candidate PII spans.
3) Sampler & stratifier: chooses records by tenant, model, time-of-day, and sequence-length bucket; produces a replay_manifest.json.
4) Anonymizer & synthesizer: replaces PII using deterministic synthetic replacement; can optionally generate paraphrases and temperature variations.
5) Exporter: writes artifacts to artifacts/perf-corpora/<corpus-name>/ with a defined structure for the benchmark harness.

Data model and manifest format
----------------------------
The pipeline emits two artifact types: raw_sample_records (for internal debugging) and replayable_corpora (used by benchmarks). A sample replay manifest (replay_manifest.json) has these top-level fields (text form):

- name: string (corpus ID)
- created_at: ISO timestamp
- sample_count: integer
- stratification: list of {dimension:bucket-definition}
- files: list of {path:relative/path.jsonl, compression:gzip|none, record_schema: v1}
- privacy_level: none|anonymized|synthetic
- producer_version: semver

Record schema (line-delimited JSON): each line is a request record with flattened fields to simplify ingestion. Example (single line):
{\n  \"request_id\": \"r-01234\", \"tenant\": \"t-company-x\", \"model\": \"redwood-7b-v1\", \"prompt\": \"Summarize the quarterly KPIs...\", \"prompt_tokens\": 124, \"max_tokens\": 256, \"response_expected\": true, \"kv_cache_hint\": 0.2, \"metadata\": {\"route\": \"/generate\", \"region\": \"us-west-2\"}\n}

Note: the manifest and record schema are stored as flat JSONL; nested maps in \"metadata\" must be stringified to keep ingestion tooling simple.

Sampling and anonymization guidance
----------------------------------
- Minimum sample sizes: for per-tenant test corpora aim for 10k requests or 1% of tenant traffic, whichever is smaller.
- Buckets: use token-length buckets {0-32, 33-128, 129-512, 513-2048, 2049+} and priority buckets (real-time, background, batch).
- Differential privacy step: for public synthetic exports, apply a DP noise layer to counts (epsilon configurable; default 1.0) before publishing aggregate summaries.

Anonymization modes:
1) anonymized: redact or replace email/phone/account ids with deterministic tokens (user_00001).
2) synthetic: generate paraphrases that preserve language features (POS distribution, length) but not original content; used for customer-sharable corpora.

Anonymization table (example)
Field | Action | Notes
------|--------|------
email | replace | deterministic hash -> user_{n}
phone | redact | replace with \"<PHONE>\"
account_id | token -> ACC_{n} | preserve stable id mapping for replay correlation
