free_text_prompts | PII detect + paraphrase | optional paraphrase to preserve token shape

Pipeline: step-by-step runbook
-----------------------------
Prerequisites:
- Access to sampling topic (infra role: perf-sampler-reader).
- S3 write access to artifacts bucket: s3://redwood-perf-artifacts/<team>/

1) Create a new corpus definition:
   - File: pipelines/corpus-defs/<corpus-name>.yaml
   - Required fields: name, target_window (UTC), privacy_mode, stratification_rules, sample_goal

2) Dry-run extract (no PII transformation):
   $ tools/corpus-builder extract --config pipelines/corpus-defs/<corpus-name>.yaml --mode dry-run --out /tmp/corpus-dryrun
   - Verify sample_count and bucket distribution in /tmp/corpus-dryrun/preview.json

3) Commit anonymization policy and run full build:
   $ tools/corpus-builder build --config pipelines/corpus-defs/<corpus-name>.yaml --out s3://redwood-perf-artifacts/benchmarks/<corpus-name>/ --anonymize

4) Validate artifacts with harness smoke test (local runner):
   $ perf-harness run --corpus s3://redwood-perf-artifacts/benchmarks/<corpus-name>/replay_manifest.json --verify-schema

5) Schedule the corpus for perf runs (Jenkins or prow job): add to nightly-bench.yaml with job label corpora/<corpus-name>.

CLI examples and tips
---------------------
- To generate a small dev corpus (100 records) focused on long prompts:
  $ tools/corpus-builder extract --config pipelines/corpus-defs/long-prompts.yaml --sample-goal 100 --filter \"prompt_tokens>512\" --out ./dev-corpora/long-100

- To create a synthetic public corpus with paraphrases and DP on aggregates:
  $ tools/corpus-builder build --config corpora/public-synthetics.yaml --privacy synthetic --dp-epsilon 0.8 --out s3://redwood-public-benchmarks/synthetics/v1

Storage layout and artifact naming
--------------------------------
Artifacts must follow this layout in the artifacts bucket: 

s3://redwood-perf-artifacts/benchmarks/<corpus-name>/
  - replay_manifest.json
  - records.v1.jsonl.gz
  - integrity.sha256
  - summary.statistics.json
  - annotations/kernel-hints.csv
  - provenance/build-metadata.json

Naming conventions: use lowercase, dashes, and a date suffix for iterative builds (e.g., retail-2025-11-03).

Integration points with profiling and benchmarking suites
---------------------------------------------------------
- perf-harness consumes replay_manifest.json and maps each record to a bench case. The harness will optionally attach kernel hint annotations to tracer spans using annotations/kernel-hints.csv.
- runtime-tracer expects the corpus to include \"kv_cache_hint\" and \"prompt_tokens\" fields to optimize tracing bucketization.
- Use the \"profiling:enrich\" step to precompute per-record kernel selection expectations (tools/corpus-builder enrich --out annotations/).

Metrics and SLOs we track for corpora-driven runs
------------------------------------------------
- baseline_throughput_rps: expected throughput for the mixed workload (target is corpus-specific).
- p50, p95, p99 generation_latency_ms: compare to declared baseline; regression threshold = +20% p95 or +50% p99.
- kernel_error_rate: percentage of runs that triggered fallback kernels; regression threshold = 2% absolute increase.
- trace_coverage: fraction of records that produced full kernel traces (target >= 90%).

Ownership and responsibilities
------------------------------
- Producer: perf-platform team (owner: Ravi Singh) — defines sampling windows and maintains extractors.
- Maintainer: serving-runtime/benchmarking (owner: Aisha Nguyen) — maintains corpus-builder tooling and manifests.
- Privacy reviewer: security-and-compliance (owner: Lena Hofstad) — approves synthetic/public exports.

Rollout checklist for a new corpus
----------------------------------
- [ ] corpus definition YAML checked into pipelines/corpus-defs/
- [ ] dry-run sample preview reviewed (buckets, tenant balance)
- [ ] anonymization policy approved by privacy reviewer
- [ ] artifacts built and verified by perf-harness smoke test
- [ ] job added to nightly-bench and merged
- [ ] metrics alerts configured for regression thresholds

Troubleshooting common failures
-------------------------------
- Missing records in manifest: confirm the sampler had permissions; check perf-samples topic lag.
- Schema verification fails: run tools/corpus-builder lint --schema v1 and inspect errors.
- Low trace_coverage: ensure profiler sidecar is enabled for the target bench job and tags (kernel-hints) are present in annotations.

Appendix: example corpus-def YAML
--------------------------------
name: dev-long-prompts-2025-03
target_window: 2025-03-01T00:00:00Z/2025-03-01T06:00:00Z
privacy_mode: anonymized
stratification_rules:
  - dimension: prompt_tokens
    buckets: [\"0-32\", \"33-128\", \"129-512\", \"513-2048\"]
sample_goal: 10000
filters:
  - expression: \"model==\\\"redwood-7b-v1\\\" and region==\\\"us-west-2\\\"\"

Contact and related resources
-----------------------------
- Perf-platform: #perf-platform on Slack
- Benchmarking repo: github.com/redwood-inference/perf-harness
- Data retention policy: /confluence/policies-and-process/data-management/retention-guidelines-2024

Change log
----------
- 2025-03-12 — initial draft (Aisha Nguyen)
- 2025-09-04 — added DP guidance and synthetic mode (reviewers: Ravi Singh)
- 2026-01-10 — clarified manifest schema and added troubleshooting section (Lena Hofstad)

title: GPU Dispatcher Topology and Stability Protocol
content:
Overview:

This document defines the GPU Dispatcher Topology and Stability Protocol (GD-TSP) — a cross-cutting operational spec for how the serving runtime maps inference requests to GPU execution resources, how we validate topology changes with controlled benchmarking and profiling, and the runbooks to recover from topology-induced instability. It consolidates architecture intent, kernel scheduling implications, profiling playbook steps, benchmark protocols, release notes conventions for topology changes, and a curated list of known issues with pragmatic mitigations.

Intended audience:
- Runtime engineers responsible for dispatcher, scheduler, and kernel mapping
- SREs and oncall responders for inference fleet
- Performance engineers running micro/scale benchmarks
- Private deployment engineers planning topology configuration changes

Goals and invariants:
- Maintain tail-99 latency SLOs under mixed workloads (default SLO: 99th percentile <= 120ms for small-chat profile, see benchmark section).
- Keep graceful degradation semantics: requests should fallback to lower-cost model variants or queued/burst paths before hard rejecting.
- Ensure dispatcher topology changes are reversible and validated by automated benchmark and profiling gates.
- Provide an action-oriented runbook for common stability regressions caused by topology changes.

1) Topology primitives and terminology:
- GPU pool: a named group of homogeneous or compatible GPUs (e.g., g.pool.a100-80gb-q8).
- Dispatcher shard: logical unit inside the dispatcher mapped to a GPU pool shard (1:many mapping possible).
- Hotpath connector: low-latency path (no preemption) reserved for priority requests (priority class >= 100).
- Coldpath connector: higher-throughput, preemptible pool used for background or low-priority requests.
- Kernel affinity profile: a selected set of kernels (FP16/INT8/Triton fallback) and launch parameters pinned per GPU pool.
- KV-cache partitioning policy: descriptor for how KV caches are split across shards (range, hash, or LRU-slab).

2) Topology design guidelines (high level):
- Prefer narrower shards for high-priority low-latency workloads. Narrow shards = fewer concurrent requests per GPU; reduces queuing variance.
- Co-locate coldpath workloads on quantized kernels to save memory and throughput; avoid mixing with hotpath FP16 kernels on same physical GPU when latency SLOs are tight.
- Use NUMA-aware placement for on-prem racks: ensure dispatcher shards respect PCIe locality and do not cross NUMA domains for KV-heavy models.
- Configure dispatcher to expose a per-shard concurrency cap and a soft-threshold for admission (default soft-threshold = 0.75 * concurrency_cap).

3) Kernel scheduling implications and constraints:
- Kernel preemption cost: long-running fused kernels (e.g., long-sequence rotary attention fused kernels) increase preemption penalty. Documented rule: if average kernel_time > 12ms, prefer non-preemptive placement for hotpath.
- Continuous batching policy interacts with shard width. Wider shards yield larger effective batch sizes; use batch size caps to avoid OOM and increased p99.
- Kernel selection ramp: when upgrading kernels, ramp through alpha->canary->general with checkpointed perf baselines. Kernels must pass microbenchmarks for latency, tail, and throughput before rollout.

4) Profiling playbook for topology changes (step-by-step):
Pre-change checklist:
1. Record current topology manifest and active dispatcher routing table (CLI: redwoodctl dispatcher export --namespace <ns> --output json).
2. Capture baseline traces for 30 minutes using the standard sample policy (trace-level: request, kernel, and NVML counters).
3. Run the lightweight synthetic smoke test for correctness (single-turn, deterministic prompt).

Change-and-profile steps:
1. Apply topology change in a canary shard (apply to 1–3 GPUs) during low-traffic window.
2. Start continuous microbenchmark runner against canary for 60 minutes: 5 workload profiles (small-chat, assistant-long, embedding-batch, rerank, multimodal-lite).
3. Collect the following telemetry: per-request latency histograms, kernel latency distributions, GPU utilization, memory clocks, power draw, NVLink traffic, KV-cache hit ratios, and preemption counts.
4. Correlate sudden p99 jumps with kernel-time percentiles and preemption_count spikes.
5. If p99 delta > +20% or average GPU DRAM rising > 10% relative to baseline, automatically roll back.

Profiling artifacts to produce:
- Canary-report-YYYYMMDD.csv (rows: timestamp, workload, p50, p95, p99, qps, avg_gpu_mem_mb, kv_hit_ratio)
- Flamegraphs for kernel stacks (symbolized)
- NVML time-series segments clipped to incident window

5) Benchmark suite protocol (how we validate topology changes end-to-end):
Purpose: Provide reproducible, comparable results to gate dispatcher topology changes in CI and pre-prod.

Benchmark harness configuration (table):
- scenario: small-chat | assistant-long | embedding-batch | rerank | mixed-burst
- seq_len: 32 | 512 | 512 | 128 | variable
- concurrency: 200 | 40 | 16 | 80 | variable
- duration: 10m | 20m | 10m | 15m | 30m
- metrics: p50,p95,p99,tail-qps,token-cpu-ms,token-gpu-ms,cost-per-token

Run protocol (numbered):
1. Provision an isolated pre-prod cluster matching the target topology (exact GPU models, A/B IP ranges, same kernel libs).
2. Seed with representative KV-cache warmup traffic for 20 minutes.
3. Execute bench harness with the scenario matrix above. 5 replicates per scenario to reduce variance.
4. Aggregate metrics and run statistical significance test (paired t-test on p99 across replicates).
5. Approve topology change if: p99 delta <= +5% and cost-per-token delta <= +3% and no memory OOM observed.

6) Release notes conventions for topology/kernel changes:
- Title: [Dispatcher Topology] <short summary> (e.g., "[Dispatcher Topology] Split hotpath shards for chat-v2").
- Body must include: rationale, list of affected clusters, benchmark artifacts links, canary rollout schedule, rollback conditions, owner and oncall rota.
- Must attach: canary-report CSV, microbench baseline JSON, and profiler flamegraphs.

7) Runbooks (quick actions for common symptoms):
Symptom A: sudden p99 spike across a single shard- Quick triage:
1. Verify alert and scope (redwoodctl metrics query --expr 'p99_latency{shard="<shard>"}').
2. Fetch latest kernel latency histogram from tracing service.
3. If preemption_count increased > 10x, toggle preemption_policy=soft for affected shard and re-run microbench.
4. If GPU memory increased abnormally, temporarily shrink concurrency_cap by 25% and initiate KV-cache eviction.
5. If immediate mitigation fails, reassign traffic off shard to fallback pool (CLI: redwoodctl dispatcher reroute --from <shard> --to <fallback>) and open incident.

Symptom B: OOMs observed on mixed workloads after topology change- Quick triage:
1. Inspect kernel allocations in the last 10 failures (tracing id list).
2. If new kernel introduced (kernel_version mismatch), revert kernel on shard.
3. Reduce batch size caps and restart worker process for shard.
4. Escalate to runtime-core-owner if OOM persists after 2 restarts.

8) Known issues catalog (selection with mitigations):
- Issue: KV-cache slab fragmentation causing steady growth of memory usage on long-lived shards.
  - Symptom: slowly increasing GPU memory footprint (~1-2% per day) without workload change.
  - Mitigation: schedule periodic slab compaction (cron: /opt/redwood/bin/kv_compact --shard <s> --threshold 0.6).

- Issue: NVLink saturation when cross-rack shard affinity incorrectly configured.
  - Symptom: decreased throughput and increased kernel latency during multi-query KV-syncs.
  - Mitigation: pin shards to same-rack GPUs or throttle KV-sync frequency; add NVLink utilization alarms.

- Issue: Incompatible quantized kernel causing subtle token-level regressions (micro hallucinations).
  - Symptom: rare semantic drift in assistant-long scenarios after kernel swap.
  - Mitigation: run evaluation prompt-set (eval-suite: semantic-coherence-001) in canary and require zero false positives before general rollout.

9) Ownership, SLAs and metrics to monitor:
- Owners: dispatcher-service -> runtime-dispatcher-team; kernel library -> runtime-kernel-team; top-level oncall -> eng-sre-inference.
- Critical metrics (monitor every minute): p50_latency, p95_latency, p99_latency, qps, gpu_mem_used_mb, gpu_util_pct, preemption_count, kv_cache_hit_rate, tail_retries
- Alert thresholds (examples): p99_latency > 1.2x baseline for >5m -> P1; OOM count > 3 in 1m -> P1; preemption_count spike > 50% -> P2.

10) Post-incident and improvement actions:
- For any topology-induced P1 incident, produce an incident summary with: timeline, root cause, perf artifacts, remediation steps, and a 30/60/90 day mitigation plan.
- Quarterly: run chaos experiments that randomly permute shard-to-GPU mappings in pre-prod and validate benchmark suite resilience.

Appendix A — Useful commands and examples:
- Export current dispatch topology:
  redwoodctl dispatcher export --namespace prod-east-1 --output json > topology-prod-east-20260214.json

- Temporarily reduce concurrency cap on shard:
  redwoodctl shard update --shard s.chat.hotpath.3 --concurrency-cap 24 --soft-threshold 18

- Canary-run microbench (example):
  bench-runner --scenario small-chat --target https://canary.dispatcher.prod --concurrency 150 --duration 10m --out canary-small-chat.csv

- Sample shard manifest snippet (YAML textual example):
  ---
  shard_id: s.chat.hotpath.3
  gpu_pool: g.pool.a100-80gb-q8
  concurrency_cap: 32
  preemption_policy: hard
  kernel_profile: fp16_fused_v2
  kv_partition: hash:mod-1024

Appendix B — Release checklist for topology changes (quick):
1. Create a change PR with topology manifest and bench plan attached.
2. Run unit/integration tests locally and in CI.
3. Execute benchmark harness in pre-prod (5 replicates).
4. Upload canary reports and request approval from runtime-kernel-team and eng-sre.
5. Schedule canary rollout and monitor gating metrics for 60m.
6. Proceed to staged rollout if gates pass; otherwise revert and file RCA.

Document changelog:
- 2024-09-12: Initial draft authored by Asha Patel.
- 2025-11-04: Added KV-cache slab compaction mitigation and preemption soft toggle. Reviewer: Daniel Kim.
- 2026-02-14: Updated benchmark gating thresholds and added NVLink guidance. Reviewer: Priya Nambiar.

References and links:
- See runtime design intent and contracts catalog: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/runtime-design-intent-and-contracts-catalog-2025
- Kernel mapper ADR: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/priority-driven-kernel-scheduler-spec-2026
- Benchmarking micro-suite: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/microbenchmark-suite-variance-analysis-2025

If you are making a topology change and need a quick consult, tag @runtime-dispatcher-team on the internal Slack channel #runtime-performance and attach the canary CSV and flamegraphs.

title: Workload-to-Hardware Fit & Scheduler Evaluation Manual
content:
Overview
=======

This manual describes a repeatable process for characterizing production inference workloads, mapping them to appropriate accelerator classes, and evaluating scheduler/kernel policies to meet SLOs while minimizing cost. It consolidates profiling playbook steps, benchmark harness configuration, acceptance criteria for rollouts, common failure modes, and lightweight runbook actions for operational teams.

Goals
-----
- Produce a deterministic workload fingerprint (latency shape, token density, sequence distribution, KV-cache affinity).
- Map fingerprints to a small set of hardware classes (e.g., H100-80GB, A100-80GB, L40s-48GB, T4-16GB) with expected cost and tail-latency envelopes.
- Evaluate scheduler knobs (batching, slotting, preemption, kernel hints) and quantify their impact on per-token cost, p50/p95/p99 latency, and GPU utilization.
- Provide a decision checklist for model-variant selection and fallback policies.

Scope and audience
------------------
This doc targets SREs, runtime engineers, and applied ML engineers responsible for: model onboarding, canary design, Dedicated capacity sizing, and private deployment sizing. It assumes familiarity with the runtime tracing tooling (trace-proxy, kernel-hint annotations) and the benchmarking harness in tools/perf-harness.

Key definitions
---------------
- Request shape: immutable properties of a request — prompt tokens, expected response token cap, streaming vs non-streaming.
- Sequence distribution: histogram of input+output lengths across a sample window.
- Affinity: the probability that successive requests share KV cache entries (session/conv affinity).
- Fidelity class: mapping of model/quantization/profile that yields a certain output quality and cost.

1) Workload fingerprinting (profiling playbook)
------------------------------------------------
Step-by-step (safe for production):
1. Identify a representative capture window (3–6 hours of typical traffic or per-release 24h). Prefer business-hours and a 24h weekend slice for consumer apps.
2. Shadow-capture requests using trace-proxy with disabled side-effects. Capture fields: timestamp, user/session id, model, route, seq_len_in, seq_len_out_cap, kv_cache_hit_estimate, tokens_generated, latency_ms, error_code, kernel-hints. Use JSONL at 1k/s sampling for high-volume routes.

Recommended capture command:
```
trace-proxy capture --router $ROUTE --write /tmp/captures/$ROUTE-2026-02-01.jsonl --sample-rate 0.01 --fields timestamp,request_id,session_id,model,route,seq_in,seq_out_cap,kv_hint,latency_ms,error
```

Normalization and derived signals:
- tokens_per_request = seq_in + median(seq_out_observed if available else seq_out_cap)
- burstiness = count(requests within 1s windows) distribution
- continuity_index = fraction(session_id consecutive requests share model/version)

Output artifact: workload-profile.json (canonical format used by perf-harness). Example snippet:
```
{
  "route": "search-completions",
  "time_window": "2026-02-01T08:00:00Z/2026-02-01T12:00:00Z",
  "seq_len_p50": "48",
  "seq_len_p95": "224",
  "tokens_p_request_avg": "132",
  "kv_affinity": "0.72",
  "burst_percentile_99": "34"
}
```

2) Benchmark matrix & experiment design
---------------------------------------
Design an experiment that spans: hardware classes, model variants (fp16, q4_k, q8_0), kernel configurations (continuous batching on/off, slot size, preemption policy), and traffic shapes (steady, microburst, session-affine).

Minimum matrix entries for a production acceptance test:
- Hardware: {H100-80GB, A100-80GB, L40s-48GB}
- Model variants: {fp16, q4_k, q8_0}
- Scheduler presets: {latency-tilt, throughput-tilt, balanced}
- Traffic shapes: {baseline-day, microburst-peak, long-seq-synth}

For each run collect: p50/p90/p95/p99 latency, throughput (tokens/s), GPU utilization (SM%, mem%), kernel queue length, kernel dispatch time histogram, energy-per-token estimate.

Acceptance criteria (example):
- p99 <= declared SLO + 15% (safety buffer) on latency-tilt config for baseline-day shape.
- tokens/sec per GPU meets committed reserve for Dedicated customers within 10%.
- model-quality regression: automatic eval set must show BLEU/ROUGE/semantic-similarity delta < defined threshold.

3) Scheduler & kernel evaluation checklist
-----------------------------------------
Primary knobs to sweep and why:
- batch_size_max: affects amortized kernel overhead and tail latency. Sweep 1, 4, 8, 16 for short sequences.
- batch_wait_ms: tradeoff between latency and throughput for bursty traffic.
- preemption_policy: eager | cooperative | disabled. Use cooperative on multi-tenant pools.
- slot_quota / tenant_credits: enforces fairness under contention.
- kernel_hint: prefer fused_attention | sharded_attention | memory_opt; used to surface specialized kernels.

Evaluator actions:
1. Run low-load baseline to establish kernel latency floor per kernel_hint.
2. Inject mixed-priority synthetic load to measure priority inversion and starvation risk.
3. Toggle preemption to gauge warm-start cost vs p99 improvement.
4. Measure KV-cache warmup curve: cold -> 30m -> 2h to estimate steady-state cost savings.

Suggested result table (example lines):
"Hardware | Kernel_hint | batch_size | p50 | p95 | p99 | tokens/s | SM% | Notes"
"H100 | fused_attention_v2 | 8 | 22ms | 48ms | 120ms | 4200 | 73% | Best for long seqs"

4) Profiling recipe (trace to remediation)
-----------------------------------------
Trigger: p99 regression or new kernel rollout.

Rapid triage steps (first 20 minutes):
1. Confirm scope: route(s) affected, time window, customer impact. Use kibana/route-dashboard.
2. Pull canonical workload-profile for the route. If production profile changed >10% on seq_len_p95 or burstiness, mark as traffic-shift.
3. Enable detailed trace-proxy sampling for the affected route (raise sample rate to 1%).
4. Correlate trace IDs with runtime kernel traces (kernel-trace tool) to determine slow kernels.
  - kernel-trace aggregate --start TS1 --end TS2 --group-by kernel_hint --metric mean_dispatch_ms,p95_dispatch_ms
5. If kernel dispatch time increased but SM% unchanged -> suspect kernel regression (new codepath or compilation change).
6. If SM% spiked and memory pressure rose -> suspect increased concurrency or larger batch sizing; check eviction logs.

Common remedial actions:
- Rollback kernel rollout via feature-flag: runtime-flag set kernel_selector=stable
- For memory pressure: reduce batch_size_max and enable eager-eviction for ephemeral caches
- For priority inversion: temporarily raise tenant_credits for affected route or enable emergency quota-exemption for critical traffic

5) Cost & capacity guidance (back-of-envelope models)
-----------------------------------------------------
Unit economics inputs:
- tokens_per_request (from fingerprint)
- tokens_per_second_per_GPU (measured in benchmark)
- cloud GPU $/hr (from procurement table)
- target utilization (70–80% for Dedicated pools)

Example calculation (string form):
"Provisioned GPUs = ceil(peak_tokens_per_sec / tokens_per_second_per_GPU / target_utilization)"

Quick example: average tokens/sec required = 500k -> tokens_per_gpu = 4k -> target_util 0.75 -> GPUs = ceil(500000 / 4000 / 0.75) = 167 GPUs

6) Canary and rollout matrix for scheduler/kernel changes
--------------------------------------------------------
Principles:
- Small fast canaries: 0.5–1% traffic for 30 minutes with full traces enabled.
- Gradual ramp: 1% -> 5% -> 20% -> 50% -> 100%, validate p99/p95 and per-route cost after each step.
- Safety gates: automatic rollback if p99 increases >20% or tokens/sec drops >15% vs baseline.

Recommended telemetry to watch during canary:
- route-p99, route-error-rate, kernel-dispatch-p95, gpu-eviction-rate, kv-warmup-slope.

Canary checklist (playbook):
1. Start at 0.5% for 30m, inspect traces and run the profiling recipe.
2. If all checks pass, extend to 5% for 1h, run full benchmark matrix for that period.
3. If any safety gate trips, rollback to previous kernel_selector and escalate to runtime-oncall.

7) Known issues inventory (operational notes)
-------------------------------------------
- Large-LLM microbursts causing slot exhaustion: mitigate with per-route burst_alloc and smaller batch windows.
- KV-cache skew across shards: drains during scale-up cause increased cold hits; schedule staggered warms on scale events.
- GPU memory fragmentation after quantization rollouts: periodic compaction job recommended during maintenance windows.
- Kernel regression from clang update: always run the hidden-kernel-regression-probe-suite before rollout.

8) Runbook extracts (for Pager/Slack responders)
------------------------------------------------
Symptom: sudden p99 increase for route X
- Pager owner: runtime-oncall
- Initial actions (within 10m):
  1. Confirm impact (dashboard p99 spike > configured alert threshold).
  2. Identify whether spike correlates with deployments or traffic-shift: check deploy-log and trace-capture.
  3. If deployment correlates, flip kernel_selector to previous stable tag and monitor for 10m.
  4. If traffic-shift, apply emergency throttles or temporary scaling policy to Dedicated pool.
  5. Open incident ticket with kernel traces attached and assign to oncall-engineer.

Symptom: elevated GPU OOMs during rollout
- Steps:
  1. Suspend rollout.
  2. Reduce batch_size_max by 50% across affected pool.
  3. Kick maintenance compaction job: gpu-mem-compact --pool $POOL --max-run 2h
  4. If OOMs persist, escalate to infra-gpu team.

9) Release notes template for runtime changes
-------------------------------------------
Use this compact template for each runtime release (kernel/scheduler/runtime binary):
- Release tag: x.y.z
- Owners: runtime-team
- Summary: one-sentence summary of user-facing impact
- Benchmarks run: matrix summary (hardware, routes, model variants)
- Canary plan: percentages + safety gates
- Known limitations: e.g., issues with T4 under long sequences
- Rollback steps: clear commands and feature-flag names
- Relevant artifacts: links to workload-profile(s) and perf-harness logs

10) Operational ownership and links
--------------------------------
- Primary owners: runtime-team (oncall rotation), perf-engineering for benchmark harness, infra-gpu for hardware incidents.
- Related pages and artifacts:
  - perf-harness repo: //git.internal/redwood/perf-harness
  - trace-proxy runbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-trace-correlator-and-event-reconciliation-playbook-2025
  - canonical workload storage: s3://redwood-perf/workloads/

Appendices
----------
A. Example scheduler policy (YAML)
```
policy_name: latency-tilt-small-batches
batching:
  max_batch_size: 8
  batch_wait_ms: 6
preemption:
  policy: cooperative
  preempt_check_interval_ms: 50
quota:
  tenant_credit_mode: burstable
  default_quota_tokens_per_minute: 60000
kernel_hints:
  preferred: [fused_attention_v2, sharded_attention]
```

B. Quick commands (profiling)
- Pull kernel traces for window:
```
kernel-trace aggregate --route search-completions --start 2026-02-01T08:00:00Z --end 2026-02-01T09:00:00Z --out /tmp/kt.json
```
- Run synthetic microburst generator:
```
perf-harness loadgen --profile workload-profile.json --shape microburst --duration 15m --out /tmp/run-01
```

C. Contact list
- Runtime oncall: runtime-oncall@redwood.com
- Perf engineering: perf-eng@redwood.com
- Infra GPU: infra-gpu@redwood.com

Change history
--------------
- 2025-09-14: Document created by Priya Nair (initial draft)
- 2025-11-03: Added canary checklist and cost model example (review: Ethan Kim)
- 2026-02-12: Expanded profiling recipe and known issues, added example YAML policy (review: Sofia Martins)

End of document

title: Batching SLO Tier Benchmark Methodology
content:
## Overview
This document defines the benchmark methodology used to validate the three customer-facing batching profiles (Fast / Standard / Cost-efficient) prior to rollout and on an ongoing basis via perf canary gates.

The methodology is designed to:
- Prevent “benchmark theater” by using representative mixes (prompt length, streaming ratio, and concurrency) that approximate real production traffic.
- Make regressions actionable by standardizing metrics, run configurations, and pass/fail gates.
- Provide apples-to-apples comparisons between tier candidates and existing defaults, while controlling for hardware variance.

This methodology is used for:
- Pre-merge/per-PR targeted perf checks (limited matrix, fast turnaround)
- Daily perf canary (expanded matrix, high confidence)
- Release qualification for runtime-1.22 tiered batching defaults

---

## Scope and non-goals
### In scope
- Tier validation for latency SLO compliance (p50/p95/p99) and tail stability under concurrency ramps.
- Cost/perf characterization: throughput (tokens/s), GPU utilization proxies, and $/1K tokens estimates (using Redwood metering coefficients).
- Mixed workload behavior (short+long prompts, streaming+non-streaming) including starvation and queue blow-up safeguards.
- Overload behavior validation (controlled overload) to ensure predictable degradation.

### Out of scope
- Per-tenant auto-tuning or customer-specific prompt sets.
- Cross-region routing policy comparisons (handled by routing tests); this doc assumes a fixed region per run.
- Full quality evals; we only run a lightweight correctness/guardrail sanity pass here (see “Quality smoke checks”).

---

## Definitions
### Tier labels
- Fast: prioritizes tail latency protection and stable streaming experience.
- Standard: balanced defaults for typical production traffic.
- Cost-efficient: maximizes throughput with guardrails; may accept higher tail latency within tier SLO.

Tier SLO numeric targets are defined in: confluence://eng-sre/slo-and-error-budgets/latency-slo-tiers-definition-fast-standard-cost-efficient.

### Request types
We benchmark two primary request types because they stress different scheduler paths:
1) Chat generation (prefill + decode)
2) Embeddings are excluded from this suite (separate pipeline and batching semantics)

### Key latency metrics
- TTFT (time-to-first-token): streaming-only and non-streaming measured separately.
- ITL (inter-token latency): decode latency per token (streaming).
- E2E latency: full request completion time (non-streaming) and “time-to-final-token” (streaming).

### Prompt and output lengths
We explicitly model prompt and generation length distributions.
- prompt_tokens: tokenized prompt length
- max_output_tokens: configured output length cap
- realized_output_tokens: actual generated tokens

---

## Workload model
We validate each tier against the same workload model, with a tier-specific acceptance gate.

### Workload mix (baseline)
Baseline mix is intended to approximate aggregate hosted API traffic while still being stable enough for regression detection.

Workload mix weights (by request count):
- 55% Chat (general assistant / support-agent style)
- 25% Summarization / extraction (longer prompts, shorter outputs)
- 20% Code assistant (moderate prompts, longer outputs)

Streaming ratio (baseline):
- 70% streaming
- 30% non-streaming

Rationale:
- Streaming dominates customer experience sensitivity (TTFT/ITL) and is where batching foot-guns are most visible.
- Non-streaming is included to ensure throughput and E2E latency behavior remains sane.

### Prompt length distributions
We use a 4-bucket prompt length model to force mixed-bucket contention and catch starvation issues.

Prompt token buckets (by tokenized prompt length) and target weight (baseline):
- Bucket S (0–256): 35%
- Bucket M (257–1,024): 40%
- Bucket L (1,025–4,096): 20%
- Bucket XL (4,097–8,192): 5%

Output length targets (by workload type):
- Chat: realized_output_tokens p50 ~220, p95 ~650
- Summarization/extraction: realized_output_tokens p50 ~120, p95 ~250
- Code: realized_output_tokens p50 ~280, p95 ~900

Notes:
- Output lengths are not forced; we cap via max_output_tokens and rely on prompt design + temperature to approximate distributions.
- We reject prompt sets that collapse to near-zero outputs, because they under-stress decode.

### Concurrency ramps
Each benchmark run includes a controlled concurrency ramp to evaluate stability and tail behavior across operating points.

Ramp profile:
- Warmup: 3 minutes at low concurrency (C_low)
- Ramp: step concurrency every 2 minutes
- Hold: 6 minutes at peak concurrency (C_peak)
- Cooldown: 2 minutes at mid concurrency

Concurrency points (per model/hardware pair):
- C_low: 0.25x “nominal”
- C_nominal: 1.0x nominal
- C_high: 1.5x nominal
- C_peak: 2.0x nominal

Nominal is defined as: the highest concurrency where Standard tier meets its p95 SLO with <1% admission drops (if enabled) and queue depth is stable (no monotonic growth over 5 minutes).

Why this approach:
- Absolute concurrency values vary by hardware and model size; using a calibrated nominal keeps comparisons meaningful.

### Overload mode validation
We include a short overload segment to validate guardrails.

Overload segment:
- 4 minutes at 2.5x nominal, with burstiness (see below)
- Objective: confirm predictable behavior (backpressure / admission control / shedding) and no pathological queue blow-up

Burstiness:
- Use a Pareto-like arrival pattern: 80% of requests in 50% of time slices (1s buckets)
- This simulates real traffic spikes that defeat smooth-rate assumptions

---

## Test matrix
We run a tier validation matrix across a small set of “top” model families and hardware classes. The matrix is intentionally limited for canary stability; broader sweeps happen in Benchmark Lab ad-hoc.

### Model families (current canary set)
- Llama-family 8B/70B class (representative decoder-only)
- Mistral-family mid-size class
- Qwen-family mid-size class

(Exact model IDs are tracked in the perf-suite config; update requires review by Runtime + Applied ML.)

### Hardware classes (current canary set)
- H100 80GB (hosted primary)
- A100 80GB (dedicated legacy)

Rules:
- A model/hardware combo must have stable baselines for 7 days before it becomes a gating target.
- If a combo is newly introduced, it starts as “observe-only” for one release train.

### Quantization policy
Quantization variants can materially change scheduler behavior. For tier validation we:
- Benchmark the default quantization profile for that model/hardware in production.
- Add a second run for any quantization profile that is explicitly recommended for Cost-efficient tier per the matrix in:
  confluence://applied-ml-and-evals/quantization-profiles/quantization-profile-matrix-for-slo-tiers.

---

## Environment controls (to reduce noise)
We require the following controls in benchmark environments:

Host/cluster requirements:
- Dedicated GPU nodes for runs (no co-tenancy) or strict GPU isolation via runtime reservation.
- Fixed GPU clock policy (where supported) and stable driver/runtime versions.
- No background compilation or model download during measured segments.

Runtime controls:
- Pin runtime build SHA and config snapshot (including tier profile knobs).
- Disable auto-scaling during runs; fixed replica count.
- Fix KV cache settings and max context length.

Load generator controls:
- Load generator runs in the same region/AZ to minimize network variance.
- Use NTP-synchronized clocks.
- Record client-side metrics (queueing at client, RTT) separately from server metrics.

Data recording:
- For each run, store: build SHA, model ID, quant profile, tier, region, hardware class, replica count, and prompt set version.

---

## Metrics collected
We collect both runtime-exported metrics and load-test client metrics.

### Latency metrics (required)
For each tier + model + hardware, compute (separately for streaming and non-streaming):
- p50, p95, p99 TTFT (streaming)
- p50, p95, p99 ITL (streaming) (computed per token; also record mean/variance)
- p50, p95, p99 E2E latency (non-streaming)
- Timeout rate and error rate (HTTP/gRPC)

### Scheduler health metrics (required)
- Batch size distribution (prefill and decode)
- Queue depth distribution and max queue depth
- Wait time distribution (time in scheduler queue)
- Admission control/drop counts (if enabled)
- Starvation indicators: max wait by prompt bucket; “oldest request age”

### Cost/performance proxies (required)
- Throughput: generated tokens/s per replica and per GPU
- Prefill vs decode utilization split (runtime reported)
- Cache hit rate (prefix/KV cache) if enabled
- Estimated $/1K generated tokens (using internal metering coefficients; see cost attribution doc)

### Telemetry reason codes (required for rollout)
When tier selection logic is active, capture distribution of reason codes:
- tier_default
- route_override
- tenant_override (Dedicated)
- model_constraint
- overload_mode

Reason code taxonomy must match runtime emission in the scheduler instrumentation.

---

## Pass/fail gates
Gates are applied at two levels:
1) Tier SLO compliance (latency targets)
2) Safety/health guardrails (queueing, errors, overload behavior)

### Gate A: SLO compliance (per tier)
For each tier, use the SLO targets from the tier definition doc. We evaluate at C_nominal and C_high.

Evaluation points:
- At C_nominal: must meet p95 targets.
- At C_high: must meet p99 targets OR stay within the tier’s explicit tail tolerance (as defined in the tier SLO doc).

Streaming-specific requirements:
- TTFT and ITL are treated as first-class SLOs for streaming routes.
- A tier can pass even if non-streaming E2E is slightly worse, provided streaming metrics meet targets and cost metrics improve, but only for Cost-efficient (requires explicit waiver).

### Gate B: Regression thresholds vs baseline
To catch “still within SLO but worse than yesterday,” we also gate on regression deltas against a rolling baseline:
- Fast tier: p99 TTFT regression must be <= +5% (C_nominal)
- Standard tier: p95 E2E regression must be <= +7% (C_nominal)
- Cost-efficient tier: p95 E2E regression must be <= +10% (C_nominal)

If SLO is met but regression delta is exceeded:
- Mark as “yellow” for observe-only runs
- Mark as “fail” for gating targets (as configured in perf-canary)

### Gate C: Safety guardrails
Fail the run if any of the following occur (at any concurrency point):
- Error rate > 0.3% (excluding intentional load shedding responses, which must be labeled)
- Timeout rate > 0.2%
- Queue depth shows monotonic growth over >3 minutes at C_nominal or C_high
- Starvation: p99 queue wait time for Bucket S exceeds 2x the median wait time for Bucket S for Fast tier
- Overload segment causes unrecovered queue growth (does not return to within 20% of pre-overload queue depth within 2 minutes of returning to C_nominal)

### Gate D: Cost improvement sanity (non-blocking initially)
For Cost-efficient tier candidates, we record throughput and $/1K tokens improvement vs Standard.
- Target: >= 12% throughput improvement at C_nominal
- If improvement is <5%, flag for review (non-blocking for first release train; becomes blocking once we declare GA)

---

## Statistical procedure
To reduce false positives and flakiness:
- Each tier/model/hardware run is executed 3 times (separate processes) on the same day.
- We report the median of medians for p50 and the median of p95/p99 across runs.
- We require at least 20,000 requests per run for mixed workload runs, with at least 2,000 requests in Bucket XL aggregated across the 3 runs.

Outlier handling:
- If one run differs by >15% on p99 TTFT from the other two, mark the suite as “unstable” and rerun once.
- If instability persists, it becomes a perf infrastructure ticket (do not block unrelated releases unless Fast tier p99 is impacted).

---

## Benchmark execution (how to run)
### Inputs
- runtime build: pinned SHA
- config: tier profile knobs and selection logic toggles
- model: pinned model version
- prompt set: versioned bundle (see prompt set selection doc)
- region/hardware: specified explicitly

### Standard command (example)
The canonical command is maintained in the perf-suite repo, but the shape is:

- Deploy runtime build to a fixed-size test cluster
- Run loadgen with:
  - mix profile: baseline
  - prompt length buckets enabled
  - streaming ratio set
  - concurrency ramp enabled

Example (illustrative):
- perf-suite run \
  --model llama-family-70b \
  --tier fast \
  --hardware h100-80gb \
  --region us-east-1 \
  --promptset slo-tier-v3 \
  --streaming-ratio 0.70 \
  --concurrency-profile ramp_v2 \
  --replicas 4 \
  --duration-min 17 \
  --record-reason-codes true

---

## Reporting format
For each tier/model/hardware combination, publish a summary block to the perf report:
- SLO pass/fail at C_nominal and C_high
- Regression deltas vs baseline
- Tokens/s and estimated $/1K tokens deltas
- Key scheduler distributions (batch size, queue depth)
- Any guardrail violations

Include a short “Interpretation” paragraph:
- What changed (knob deltas)
- Whether failures appear tied to prefill congestion, decode congestion, or queue admission
- Recommended next action (tweak profile, adjust safeguards, or treat as infra noise)

---

## CI / perf canary integration
This methodology maps to two execution tiers:

### Tier 1: PR-level (fast)
- Single model/hardware combo per tier (rotating daily)
- 1 run (no repeats)
- Gates: Safety guardrails + Regression threshold (looser)

### Tier 2: Daily canary (authoritative)
- Full canary matrix
- 3 repeats per combo
- Gates: Full (A/B/C) enforced

If daily canary fails:
1) Auto-file a ticket with run ID, charts, and suspected culprit (last green SHA range)
2) Page on-call only if Fast tier p99 TTFT fails SLO at C_nominal for a top model
3) Otherwise route to runtime-perf triage queue

---

## Quality smoke checks (lightweight)
Because batching changes can surface edge cases (e.g., truncation interactions, streaming chunking), we run a small correctness sanity pass:
- Verify token counts and termination reasons are within expected bounds
- Check for elevated “empty output” rate and truncation rate
- Run a small set of golden prompts to detect obvious formatting regressions

This does not replace the full quality eval suite; it is intended only to catch gross failures early.

---

## Updating the methodology
Changes to:
- workload mix weights
- prompt bucket definitions
- concurrency ramp profiles
- gating thresholds

…require approval from:
- Serving Runtime Scheduling (Sofia Ivanova or delegate)
- Applied ML/Evals (Jonas Weber or delegate)
- SRE (Sean Gallagher or delegate)

Baseline refresh:
- Baselines may be refreshed only after:
  - 3 consecutive green daily canaries on the new build, and
  - sign-off recorded in the perf-canary baseline ticket

---

## Known limitations / blind spots
- Customer traffic is more diverse than our three-workload mix; niche workloads (extremely long outputs, highly tool-calling heavy patterns) may behave differently.
- Network variance can dominate TTFT in some regions; we minimize but cannot eliminate it.
- “Nominal concurrency” calibration can drift with infrastructure changes; we re-calibrate monthly or after major driver/runtime updates.

---

## Appendix: troubleshooting common failure modes
1) Fast tier p99 TTFT regression
- Check queue wait time and admission control counters.
- Inspect batch size distribution: unusually large prefill batches can harm TTFT.
- Confirm no background model reload or cache eviction storm.

2) Cost-efficient tier queue blow-up under overload
- Check overload segment recovery criterion.
- Verify guardrails: max wait budget, max batch tokens, and backpressure toggles.

3) High error rate
- Separate load-shedding responses from true errors.
- Confirm client timeouts are not too aggressive for Standard/Cost-efficient.

Owners:
- Benchmark harness: Rina Kobayashi
- Scheduler perf triage: Marcus Reed
- SLO gating and alerting: Aisha Bello

title: synthetic-chaos-stress-profiles-2026
content:
Overview

This page defines a set of synthetic stress profiles and a small chaos-harness used by SRE and Runtime teams to validate kernel scheduling, KV cache behavior, batching heuristics, and degradation/fallback policies under controlled but realistic failure modes. These profiles are used for:

- Pre-release performance gating (release branch + canary)
- Continuous nightly regression checks
- Capacity and autoscaling validation for Dedicated clusters
- On‑prem validation for Private deployments prior to customer handover

Goals

1. Provide reproducible workload definitions that exercise the hot paths across the serving runtime (attention kernels, kv-cache, batching, preemption).
2. Surface regressions in tail latency, correctness (token drift), and error modes introduced by kernel changes or scheduler refactors.
3. Validate fallback and graceful degradation policies (model variant fallback, region fallback).
4. Give a standardized triage playbook and pass/fail criteria tied to SLOs.

Scope and Exclusions

- Scope: inference path (token generation / chat), scheduler interactions, cache eviction under pressure, batching/packing, network backpressure.
- Exclusions: training workloads, model conversion artifacts, client-side SDK correctness.

Ownership

- Primary: eng-serving-runtime / Runtime QE (runtime-qe@redwood.com)
- Secondary: eng-sre (sre-runtime@redwood.com)
- Review cadence: Quarterly or on any scheduler/runtime release

Definition: Stress Profile Concept

Each stress profile is a small YAML spec interpreted by benchctl (internal harness). Required fields: id, description, tenant_mix, sequence_length_dist, qps_pattern, latency_target, duration, fault_injection. Optional: kernel_expectations.

Example profile (encoder-heavy burst):

---
# file: profiles/encoder-heavy-burst.yaml
id: encoder-heavy-burst
description: Short-lived burst of high-qps small-sequence encoder generation to stress kernel queueing and batching.
tenant_mix: ["plat_internal": 0.6, "external_vip": 0.4]
sequence_length_dist: {mean: 16, p95: 48}
qps_pattern: {type: burst, peak_qps: 4200, warmup: 10s, cooldown: 30s}
duration: 5m
latency_target: {p50_ms: 5, p95_ms: 18, p99_ms: 45}
fault_injection: {drop_gpu_cards: none, simulate_network_spike: 0}
kernel_expectations: ["kernel_queue_depth >= 128 at peak", "batcher_pack_rate >= 90%"]
---

In the harness this becomes a single benchctl run:

$ benchctl run --profile profiles/encoder-heavy-burst.yaml --target cluster://staging-gpu-pool --output results/encoder-burst-2026-03-01.json

Key Stress Profiles (canonical list)

- kvcache-eviction-surge: simulate many long-context requests causing KV-cache churn and eviction storms. Useful to surface cache-serialization/lock contention.
- longcontext-steady: continuous long sequence generation (avg 4096 tokens) to exercise backend memory pressure and attention kernel breakpoints.
- mixed-tenant-thundering-herd: many small tenants with spiky arrivals to validate priority accounting and kernel-credit throttling.
- encoder-heavy-burst: short, high qps encoder-style workloads that produce large batching opportunities but stress kernel queueing (example above).
- ablate-batcher: toggle batcher parameters (max_latency_ms, max_tokens) across runs to measure cost/latency tradeoffs.
- graceful-degrade-path: incrementally reduce preferred model capacity and validate automatic fallback to lower-cost quantized variants without correctness regressions.

Pass/Fail Criteria and SLOs

Pass conditions are evaluated per-run and are used by CI gating and nightly regression alerts. Each profile tie to an action level:

- Green: all SLOs met and no increase in token-error or hallucination metrics beyond historical baseline
- Amber: specific SLO breach but within tolerable rollback policy (e.g., p99 up to 1.5x baseline) -> alert + triage
- Red: major degradation (p99 > 2x or error_rate > 0.2%) -> block merge and trigger incident process

Default SLO thresholds (adjust per workload):

- p50 latency <= profile.latency_target.p50_ms
- p95 latency <= profile.latency_target.p95_ms
- p99 latency <= profile.latency_target.p99_ms
- request_error_rate <= 0.1%
- token_drift (from golden prompts) <= 1% relative token mismatch

Telemetry and Metrics to Collect

Collect these during every run:

- infra: GPU utilization per-card, memory_used, PCIe retransmits, host-side CPU stall time
- runtime: per-kernel exec_time histogram, kernel_queue_depth, batch_size_distribution, batch_pack_rate, kvcache_eviction_rate, kvcache_lock_wait_ms
- api-level: request_latency histogram, error_codes, response_token_counts, token_drift_against_golden
- orchestration: container_restart_count, preemptions, model_variant_fallbacks

Suggested Prometheus metrics and dashboards (names):

- runtime_kernel_latency_ms_bucket{kernel}
- runtime_kernel_queue_depth_gauge
- runtime_batch_pack_ratio
- runtime_kvcache_evictions_total

Profiling Playbook (when a run fails)

1. Identify failing profile and time window. Pull benchctl artifact JSON and stored logs.
2. Check orchestration events (kube events, preemptions). If containers restarted or OOMKilled, escalate to eng-infra.
3. Correlate p99 spikes with kernel_latency histograms. If a single kernel shows a long tail, tag suspect kernel.
4. Enable sampling profiler run (trace-level) for 60s on the affected node group:

$ benchctl profile --node-group staging-gpu-pool --sample-duration 60s --output traces/trace-$(date +%s).json

5. If kvcache_eviction_rate > 10/min during failure, run the cache inspection script to dump kvcache shards and eviction logs:

$ benchctl kvcache-dump --node node-12 --shard 3 --out kvdump.json

6. If batch_pack_ratio drops below expected threshold, validate the request packing logs and the per-tenant sequence_length_dist used by the harness.

Runbook: Immediate Mitigations During Incidents

- Scaling: Temporarily scale Dedicated pool by +20% capacity (if autoscaling not reacting)
- Routing: Route high-priority tenants to a warm reserve pool (route policy: limit concurrency to 50% of default)
- Kernel gate: If a new kernel change is suspected, rollback kernel binary on canaries via the artifact manager and re-run the failing profile.
- Fallback: Toggle model_variant_fallback to allowed for the route to shift traffic to quantized variant.

Example commands (ops):

$ rctl cluster scale staging-gpu-pool --delta 10
$ rctl route update --route high-priority --capacity 50%
$ rctl artifact rollback --service runtime-kernel --to-revision v2026-02-22

Integration with Release Process

- New runtime/kernel code: required to run the full canonical profile set as part of pre-merge CI. Any Red/Amber outcome must be explained in a pre-merge checklist.
- Canary: deploy to a canary cluster and run only the high-sensitivity profiles (kvcache-eviction-surge, longcontext-steady).
- Automated gating: CI jobs will annotate PRs with benchctl artifacts and link to the profile run result.

Known Issues and Workarounds (as of 2026-03-01)

- Issue: kernel_credit accounting may under-report when mixed-tenant-thundering-herd runs with priority inversion.
  Workaround: temporarily increase per-tenant minimum credits and re-run the profile.
- Issue: Rare token drift observed for graceful-degrade-path when fallback quantized models differ in BOS tokenization.
  Workaround: add normalization step comparing token ids and run token-drift acceptance test in harness.
- Issue: benchctl sampling profiler may miss short-lived micro spikes due to 1s sampling resolution.
  Workaround: increase sample-duration to 120s or enable high-res tracer in suspected runs.

Gallery: Example results snippet (benchctl output)

{
  "profile_id": "kvcache-eviction-surge",
  "p99_ms": "132",
  "error_rate": "0.03%",
  "kvcache_evictions_per_min": "16",
  "kernel_outliers": ["attention_forward_v3", "kv_sync"]
}

Regression Triage Template

1. Summary: short description of observed failure and impacted SLOs.
2. Artifacts: benchctl run JSON, traces, node metrics, orchestration events.
3. Hypothesis: one-liner suspected cause.
4. Action taken: rollback/scale/toggle fallback, and result.
5. Root cause analysis: completed within 72 hours for red-level regressions.
6. Postmortem and mitigations: documented and assigned.

Automation and CI Examples

- GitHub Action snippet to run the canonical profiles on every kernel PR:

name: runtime-benchmark-check
on: pull_request
jobs:
  bench:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Run benchctl canonical set
        run: |
          benchctl run-set --set canonical --target cluster://ci-gpu-small --out artifacts/${{ github.sha }}.json || exit 1

Next Steps and Roadmap

- Expand the canonical set with a dedicated latency-sensitivity profile for each new kernel (ETA Q2 2026).
- Add synthetic network partition scenarios to the harness (ETA Q3 2026).
- Integrate benchctl outputs into the Runtime Console for per-PR visual diffs (ETA Q3 2026).

References

- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/runtime-profiling-playbook-guidelines-2025
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/throughput-latency-workload-catalog-2026
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-fallback-and-degradation-playbook-2026

Appendix: Benchctl workload spec quick reference

Fields (string): id, description, duration, target_cluster
Fields (numeric): peak_qps, mean_sequence_length, p95_sequence_length
Fields (enums): qps_pattern (steady|burst|sine), fault_injection (none|network_spike|card_drop), validation (none|golden_token_set)

End of document

title: PRD: Shadow Evaluator — Prompt-set Driven Regression Detector
content:
Overview

Summary:
The Shadow Evaluator is a product initiative to provide an automated, prompt-set driven regression detection service that runs shadow (non-production-impacting) evaluations against candidate model variants prior to rollouts. The goal is to catch regressions in real-world prompt patterns and alert product and model owners with actionable diagnostics before customer-facing traffic is exposed.

This PRD defines user journeys, functional and non-functional requirements, high-level design, rollout plan, success metrics, and operational run/playbook for the feature.

Motivation and context:
- Customers and internal teams increasingly rely on model variant rollouts and automated canaries. Existing unit-test and lab evals miss distributional edge-cases embedded in customer prompt-sets.
- We need an evaluation layer that: 1) reuses customer prompt-sets (curated + captured), 2) runs candidate model variants in shadow mode, 3) computes fidelity and quality deltas against baseline, and 4) returns prioritized regressions with reproducible evidence.

Goals (what success looks like):
- Detect regressions that would have impacted customer-facing traffic with at least 80% precision and 60% recall in pilot customers for top-5 critical prompt-sets.
- Provide per-prompt diagnostic payloads (inputs, baseline output, candidate output, diff highlights, metric breakdown).
- Integrate with Console to surface alerts in the rollout workflow and with Optimize to suggest mitigations (roll back, lower-fidelity fallback, quantized variant).
- Low operational cost: shadow eval should not increase serving cost for hosted traffic more than 2% at typical canary scales.

Non-goals:
- This is not a full replacement for offline, human-in-the-loop evaluation for safety-critical models.
- We will not initially support multimodal prompt-sets (images, audio) — text-only for v1.

User stories:
- As a platform engineer, I want to register a production prompt-set and schedule nightly shadow runs so regressions are flagged before deploys.
- As a product manager, I want to see a ranked list of prompt regressions (with confidence scores, token-level diffs, and sample traces) after a candidate model build completes.
- As an SRE, I want the evaluators to run in isolated capacity pools (dedicated or preemptible) and to automatically fall back to a lower-cost simulation mode if capacity is constrained.

Functional requirements:
1) Prompt-set ingestion:
   - Support three sources: curated prompt libraries (internal), tenant-provided prompt-sets (customer uploads or pinned route sets), and captured production samples (anonymized and consented).
   - Each prompt-set must have metadata: owner_team, sensitivity (low/medium/high), intended route(s), and acceptance test markers.

2) Evaluation runs:
   - Support two run modes: fast-preview (sampled subset, <1000 prompts) and full-run (entire prompt-set).
   - Shadow runs execute candidate model + baseline model in parallel, capturing synchronous responses, latency, and token-level logs.
   - Default sampling policy: stratified sampling across route and prompt-length buckets; configurable per prompt-set.

3) Metrics and detectors:
   - Compute per-prompt and aggregated metrics: ROUGE-L, BLEU, embedding similarity (cosine), perplexity ratio, hallucination score (heuristic), latency delta, and token-count delta.
   - Regression rules: alert when top-level metric delta crosses configured thresholds (example table below).

    | Metric | Baseline threshold | Alert delta (default) | Rationale |
    |--------|--------------------|------------------------|-----------|
    | Embedding cosine | >= 0.85 | drop > 0.05 | semantic shift |
    | ROUGE-L | >= 0.3 | drop > 0.07 | content loss |
    | Hallucination score | <= 0.12 | increase > 0.05 | safety risk |
    | Latency (p95) | <= 300ms | increase > 150ms | perf regression |
4) Ranking and prioritization:
   - Rank regressions by severity score = weighted sum(metric deltas * traffic weight). Provide top-20 actionable items.

5) Evidence and reproducibility:
   - For any flagged prompt, provide a reproducible artifact bundle (input, seed/context where applicable, baseline output, candidate output, evaluation metrics, and deterministic invocation parameters).
   - Bundles must be downloadable via Console and accessible via an internal S3 path.

6) Integration points:
   - Console: Alert tile in rollout page with quick actions (pause rollout, rollback, annotate, open issue).
   - CI/CD: API to run shadow-evaluator as a post-build check with wait/timeout options.
   - Alerts: send to Slack on high-severity regressions and create JIRA ticket when the regression persists for >24h.

Non-functional requirements:
- Data residency: prompt-set copies used by the evaluator must respect tenant residency and retention policies.
- Cost cap: default daily spend per prompt-set in hosted is $X (configurable per-customer) — initial pilot use will default to $50/day limit.
- Isolation: evaluation compute must not share GPU instances with customer production serving nodes.
- Determinism: where models are deterministic (seeded), runs should be reproducible; otherwise, log RNG seeds and sampling params.

Success metrics and KPIs:
- Time to detect (median): <6 hours from candidate model availability for fast-preview runs.
- True positive precision on pilot tenants: >=80% for top-100 regressions.
- Operator action rate: >=60% of high-severity alerts lead to a human decision (rollback, hold, or accept) within 48h.
- Cost impact: additional serving cost <=2% for pilot traffic.

High-level design:
- Components:
  - Prompt-store: metadata catalog and secure storage for prompt-sets.
  - Runner fleet: dedicated evaluation GPU pool (or CPU fallback) that executes paired inference jobs (baseline + candidate).
  - Metrics engine: computes deltas and applies regression rules (configurable via YAML rules).
  - Evidence builder: compiles reproducible bundles and stores artifacts in object storage.
  - Alerting & UX: Console integration, Slack/JIRA hooks, and CI/CD API gateway.

Data flow (simplified):
1. Prompt-set registered -> prompt-store validates metadata and triggers ingestion pipeline (anonymization, bucketing).
2. Candidate model build completes -> CI calls shadow-evaluator API to schedule fast-preview run.
3. Runner fleet executes paired invocations; metrics recorded to metrics engine.
4. Metrics engine applies rules, ranks regressions, and generates evidence bundles.
5. Alerts posted and Console renders diagnostics.

Operational details and runbook excerpt:
- Running ad-hoc evaluation (CLI):
  redwood eval run --prompt-set id:ps-1234 --model candidate:2026-09-01 --mode fast-preview --max-prompts 500 --timeout 3600

- Sample evaluation rules YAML (stored in config service):
  name: "default-shadow-rules"
  rules:
    - metric: "embedding_cosine"
      comparator: "decrease_gt"
    - metric: "rouge_l"
      comparator: "decrease_gt"
    - metric: "hallucination_score"
      comparator: "increase_gt"

- Evidence bundle layout (S3 path example):
  s3://redwood-evidence/ps-1234/run-2026-09-01/case-42/
    - input.txt
    - baseline.json (text + token-level log)
    - candidate.json (text + token-level log)
    - metrics.yaml
    - diff.txt

Rollout plan and milestones:
- Phase 0 (Q3 2026): internal pilot with 3 product teams, limited prompt-sets, manual review flows.
- Phase 1 (Q4 2026): beta for 10 external customers (opt-in), Console integration, Slack alerts.
- Phase 2 (Q1 2027): GA with tenant-configurable rules, billing controls, and CI/CD plugin.

Acceptance criteria for GA:
- End-to-end tests demonstrating detection of injected regressions in curated prompt-sets.
- Console UI surfaces alerts and allows at least two remediation actions.
- API SLA: evaluation job accepted within 5 minutes, fast-preview median completion <6 hours.
- Security review passed (data residency and PII handling).

Monitoring, SLOs and alerts:
- Evaluation job queue: p95 queuing time <10m (SLO for GA).
- Runner failure rate: <1% per-run. Alert if failure rate >2% for 30m.
- False positive rate (pilot): tracked but no strict SLA — aim <20% for top-100.

Security and privacy:
- Only prompt-sets marked as "capturable" will auto-include production samples. Customer opt-out respected.
- PII scrubbing pipeline with configurable redaction rules applied during ingestion.
- Evidence bundles for tenant-owned prompt-sets are access-restricted and only available to tenant and authorized Redwood teams.

Backward compatibility and migrations:
- Existing eval and lab pipelines remain unchanged. Shadow Evaluator exposes opt-in APIs that do not alter the baseline rollout behavior unless an operator triggers an automated rollback action.

UI/Console considerations (brief):
- Rollout page: new "Shadow Evaluator" card showing recent runs, top regressions, sample diffs, and quick actions.
- Prompt-set catalog: allow tagging and ownership, show last-run status, and cost spend.

Developer API examples (HTTP):
POST /api/v1/evals/run
Headers: Authorization: Bearer <token>
Body (JSON):
{
  "prompt_set_id": "ps-1234",
  "candidate_model": "candidate:2026-09-01",
  "baseline_model": "production:2026-08-15",
  "mode": "fast-preview",
  "max_prompts": 1000
}

(Responses will include run_id and pre-signed links to evidence bundles when complete.)

Open questions (to resolve in design review):
- Default weighting strategy for severity score and how tenant traffic weights are computed.
- Exact list and definitions for hallucination heuristics that will be used across model families.
- Cost metering model for large prompt-sets (per-prompt vs per-run).

Ownership and contacts:
- Product lead: Aisha Kapoor
- Engineering owner: Marcus Lee (eng-serving-runtime)
- SRE contact: Leah Thompson (eng-sre)
- Security reviewer: Daniel Chen (security-and-compliance)

Related pages:
- /confluence/product-docs/requirements/lightweight-eval-capture-and-lossy-metrics-prd-2025-11-20
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/shadow-run-benchmarking-notes

Appendix: sample alert workflow
1. Shadow run completes -> high severity regression detected for prompt-set ps-1234.
2. Console alert posted and Slack message to #rollouts with run_id and top-3 cases.
3. Automated ticket created in JIRA (P0 if severity > 0.8) and assigned to model owner.
4. Model owner inspects evidence bundle, decides to rollback — selects quick-action in Console.

Notes:
- This PRD intentionally scopes v1 to text-only prompt-sets and to a hosted-first experience; private/dedicated customers can opt into variant execution in Private via a separate packaging agreement and client connector.

End of document."

title: Runtime Confidence Lab: Fidelity Probes and SLO Slicing
content:
Summary
------
This page documents the Runtime Confidence Lab: an integrated laboratory protocol for (A) probing model fidelity under production-like degradations, (B) exercising kernel hinting and scheduler signals, and (C) slicing SLOs to estimate graceful-degradation envelopes. The goal is a repeatable playbook teams can run prior to rollouts, kernel changes, quantization updates, or routing policy changes.

Scope
-----
Applies to: runtime-agent (serving runtime), kernel-mapper, fidelity-orchestrator, and the benchmarking harness. Intended for: runtime engineers, performance SREs, model-onboarding, and platform QA.

Motivation
----------
Production incidents often arise at the intersection of fidelity regressions and scheduler changes. A single experiment run should answer: 
- How does model output fidelity (task-specific metrics) vary as we induce latency/capacity constraints?
- Which kernel hints (tensor-layout / attention-splitting) materially change latency vs. fidelity trade-offs?
- What SLO slices become brittle under co-tenancy or tail-load conditions?

High-level concepts
-------------------
- Fidelity probe: a deterministic workload of representative prompts and reference outputs used to measure quality (BLEU / ROUGE / task-specific scoring + open-ended heuristic checks).
- Kernel hinting: explicit scheduler metadata we expose to the kernel-mapper to bias execution paths (e.g., fast-path, memory-saver, quantized-eager).
- SLO slicing: partitioning traffic by features (seq_len, model_variant, tenant_tier) and measuring SLO attainment per slice.

Lab prerequisites and hardware/software matrix
--------------------------------------------
Use one of the approved lab stacks below; attach the telemetry snapshot prior to running experiments.

| Stack name | GPU | OS | Runtime image tag | Notes |
|------------|-----|----|------------------|-------|
| lab-small  | A10G| Ubuntu 22.04 | runtime:v2026-05-10 | single-node baseline |
| lab-large  | H100| Ubuntu 22.04 | runtime:v2026-05-10 | multi-GPU topo with nvlink |
| edge-sim   | T4  | CentOS 8     | runtime:v2026-05-10-edge | simulates constrained memory |

Minimum software: benchmarking harness >= 1.14.0, profiler-agent >= 0.9.3, kernel-mapper >= 2.3.0.

Baseline thresholds (for our standard open-model ensemble)
-------------------------------------------------------
| Metric | Baseline | Alerting threshold (soft) | Failure threshold (hard) |
|--------|----------|---------------------------|--------------------------|
| p50 latency (ms) | 45 | 80 | 150 |
| p95 latency (ms) | 110 | 200 | 400 |
| token cost (uUSD/token) | 0.003 | 0.006 | 0.01 |
| task-fidelity (task-F1) | 0.92 | 0.88 | 0.84 |

Experiment matrix (cross-product)
---------------------------------
1) Workload shapes: short-chat (avg seq 80), doc-gen (avg seq 600), multimodal-sim (50% short tokens, 50% long)
2) Kernel hints: fast-path, memory-saver, quantized-eager, default
3) Degradations: cpu bottleneck (throttle worker), nvlink degradation (drop 30% bw), eviction-pressure (fill 85% GPU mem), increased burst traffic (2x arrivals for 5m)
4) Model variants: baseline-fp16, q4f-compat, trimmed-llm-small

Procedure (step-by-step)
------------------------
1. Environment prep (10–20 minutes)
   a. Snapshot current telemetry: curl -sS http://telemetry.internal/snapshot > telemetry-prior.json
   b. Deploy experiment image: kubectl apply -f overlays/experiment-profile.yaml --record
   c. Ensure kernel-mapper is at the target version: kubectl set image daemonset/kernel-mapper kernel-mapper=kernel-mapper:2.3.0

2. Baseline run (30 minutes)
   a. Run the harness in baseline mode: bench-harness run --config experiments/baseline.yaml --out out/baseline.json
   b. Collect profiler traces: profiler capture --interval 30s --out out/baseline.trace
   c. Validate baseline fidelity: python tools/score_fidelity.py --pred out/baseline.pred --ref gold/fidelity-corpus.json --report out/baseline.score.json

3. Kernel-hint sweep (per hint, 20 minutes each)
   For each kernel hint in [fast-path, memory-saver, quantized-eager, default]:
   a. Apply hint: runtime-agent ctl set-kernel-hint --hint <HINT> --selector test-cohort
   b. Run harness with same workload: bench-harness run --config experiments/short-chat.yaml --hint <HINT> --out out/hint-<HINT>.json
   c. Record traces and fidelity scores.

4. Degradation runs (30–60 minutes each)
   a. Induce degradation using chaoskit: chaoskit inject --scenario nvlink-drop-30 --target cluster-lab-large
   b. Re-run the harness for the workload shapes and model variants.

5. SLO slicing simulation (automated, 45 minutes)
   a. Use slo-slicer tool to partition results: slo-slicer ingest --results out/*.json --slices "seq_len,tenant_tier,model_variant" --out out/sliced-report.json
   b. For each slice, compute violation risk: python tools/slice_risk.py --input out/sliced-report.json --thresholds configs/slo-thresholds.yaml

Data collection and artifact naming convention
--------------------------------------------
- Artifacts should be stored under s3://redwood-lab/runtime-confidence/<run-id>/ and follow naming:
  - <run-id>-metadata.json
  - <run-id>-traces.tar.gz
  - <run-id>-bench-results.json
  - <run-id>-fidelity-report.json

Profiling and telemetry configuration
-----------------------------------
Recommended profiler flags for fidelity experiments:
- profiler-agent --sampler stratified --rate 20Hz --kv-annotate --capture-kernel-calls
- Enable syscall-level tracing only when reproducing kernel handoff problems (adds 10–15% overhead)

CLI snippets (examples)
----------------------
# Baseline harness run
bench-harness run --config experiments/baseline.yaml --out out/baseline.json --concurrency 64

# Kernel hint set
runtime-agent ctl set-kernel-hint --hint fast-path --selector test-cohort

# Start SLO slicer
slo-slicer ingest --results out/*.json --slices "seq_len,tenant_tier,model_variant" --out out/sliced-report.json

Analysis checklist (what to look for)
------------------------------------
- Fidelity drift vs baseline: absolute drop > 0.03 (task-F1) is a red flag.
- Latency/fidelity covariance: if p95 latency rises and fidelity drops together, suspect contention or passive throttling.
- Kernel hint sensitivity: >15% p95 difference between hints indicates kernel path bifurcation.
- Cost delta: token cost change > 10% requires product review.

Runbook: when an experiment flags a regression
-------------------------------------------
1. Re-run with deterministic seed and single-tenant isolated node.
2. Capture full profiler traces and kernel-mapper logs: kubectl logs -l app=kernel-mapper --since=1h > out/km.logs
3. If hint-dependent: revert to previous hint for canary and open ticket with kernel-mapper (owner: eng-serving-runtime/kernel-team).
4. If eviction/frag-related: run gpu-memory-fragmentation-diagnostics-playbook and schedule compaction window.
5. Create postmortem entry with artifacts link and severity tag.

Release notes template (for kernel or runtime changes validated by this lab)
------------------------------------------------------------------------
- Change: kernel-mapper 2.3.0
- Verified: baseline p95 latency change: +4ms (p50 +2ms), fidelity change: -0.005 task-F1
- Experiments run: baseline, fast-path, quantized-eager, nvlink-drop-30
- Canary recommendation: enable fast-path for dedicated tier only; monitor slice: seq_len>512, tenant_tier=free

Known issues and mitigations (collected)
-------------------------------------
1. Non-deterministic fidelity drops with quantized-eager on q4f-compat
   - Symptom: intermittent hallucination on long-context doc-gen
   - Mitigation: hold quantized-eager behind feature flag; run extended fidelity regression for 24h before rollout
2. Kernel hint not honored under high eviction pressure
   - Symptom: trace shows fallback to default kernel path when global mem > 90%
   - Mitigation: add preflight check in runtime-agent to fail fast and mark node degraded
3. SLO-slicer undercounts slices when requests lack seq_len metadata
   - Symptom: slice misattribution in multi-tenant traces
   - Mitigation: update ingress processors to populate seq_len header (task: ENG-6543)

Ownership and escalation
------------------------
- Experiment owner: eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking (primary)
- Kernel hint triage: eng-serving-runtime/kernel-team (primary), eng-sre (secondary)
- Fidelity regressions: applied-ml-and-evals/model-onboarding (primary)

Appendices
---------
A. Example experiment config (YAML)
------------------------------------------------
# experiments/short-chat.yaml
workload:
  name: short-chat
  concurrency: 64
  sequence_length: 80
model_variant: baseline-fp16
prompts: corpora/short-chat-1000.json
metrics:
  - latency_ms
  - fidelity_task_f1
  - token_cost

B. Quick checklist before PR merge
- [ ] Bench harness passes in CI (golden-run)
- [ ] Baseline fidelity within 0.01 of production baseline
- [ ] Kernel-mapper is covered by unit tests for hint handling
- [ ] Profiling flags documented in PR

C. References
- runtime-deployment-sanity-and-benchmark-suite-acceptance-2026 (bench acceptance checklist)
- causal-latency-attribution-and-signal-enrichment-playbook-2026 (profiling best-practices)

Contact
-------
For questions, ping #runtime-confidence-lab on Slack or email eng-runtime@redwood.com

title: Runbook: Benchmark report region sweeps (latency/$)
content:
## Purpose
This runbook describes how to execute **region sweeps** for the public benchmark report ("latency/$" and supporting latency/throughput metrics). It covers:
- Capacity reservation and readiness checks per region
- Running the region sweep runner and generating reproducible manifests
- Exporting versioned result artifacts (JSON/CSV) for the web + PDF pipeline
- Stability/variance gates and when to rerun
- Failure recovery and escalation

This is intended for Applied ML/Perf and Runtime/Infra partners running official report sweeps.

## Owners and escalation
- Primary run owner (Benchmark harness): **Rina Kobayashi**
- Technical sign-off (Perf/Evals): **Jonas Weber**, **Claire Dubois**
- Fleet capacity coordination: **Vanessa Ortiz** (backup: **Harish Reddy**)
- SRE on-call / incident owner: **Sean Gallagher**
- Metric correctness (latency/$ normalization): **Nadia Rahman**

Escalate immediately in #eng-runtime and #eng-infra if:
- A region cannot hold reserved capacity for the full sweep window
- p95 latency variance repeatedly exceeds the stability threshold after reruns
- We observe elevated 429/5xx from the benchmark target endpoint

## Preconditions
### 1) Methodology lock
Before an official sweep, confirm the following are locked and referenced in the run manifest:
- Prompt set version (e.g., `promptset_v3_production_mix`)
- Workload definitions (prefill/decode mix; streaming vs non-streaming) 
- Concurrency levels and arrival pattern
- Caching/batching policy used during benchmark runs
- Warmup protocol and run duration

Source of truth: Confluence methodology page (see Related Pages).

### 2) Tooling and access
You need:
- Access to the benchmark runner repo ("benchmark-lab")
- Ability to assume the regional runner role in Redwood cloud accounts
- Write access to the benchmark artifacts bucket (internal)
- Read access to Fleet dashboards for capacity verification

### 3) Capacity reservation is approved and scheduled
Do not begin a region sweep without an approved reservation plan.
- Owner: Vanessa Ortiz
- Required output: reservation ticket/link + reservation IDs per region

Recommended lead time:
- Standard sweep: reserve **48 hours** prior
- Launch-week sweep (or any externally referenced numbers): reserve **5–7 days** prior

## High-level workflow
1) Confirm capacity reservation windows and instance types per region.
2) Smoke-test the target region endpoint and runner environment.
3) Generate a sweep manifest (model × region × workload matrix).
4) Execute sweep (with stability gates enabled).
5) Validate outputs (sanity + outlier checks).
6) Export versioned artifacts (JSON/CSV) and publish to the staging ingestion path.
7) Hand off to validation/review checklist for final sign-off.

## Capacity reservation steps (per region)
### Inputs to provide Fleet
Provide Fleet with:
- Regions (e.g., `us-east`, `us-west`, `eu-west`, `eu-central`, `apac-sg`, `apac-syd` — only those approved for publication)
- Target instance types and counts
- Sweep schedule window (start/end in UTC)
- Expected load pattern (concurrency levels; whether spikes are expected)
- Whether results will be used for public claims (impacts change control)

### Day-of checks (30–60 minutes before sweep)
In Fleet dashboards (or via the capacity status CLI if available), confirm:
- Reserved capacity is active and pinned to the correct cluster pool
- No known maintenance events overlapping the sweep window
- Baseline GPU utilization in the region is <70% before starting
- No elevated queue depth in the inference scheduler

If any check fails:
- Pause and coordinate with Vanessa/Harish to shift the window or move the sweep to a fallback region set.

## Runner setup
### Recommended execution environment
Use the Dockerized runner image for determinism.
- Host requirements: Linux amd64, Docker 24+
- Recommended: run from a controlled runner VM close to the control plane (not from a laptop)

### Required environment variables
Set the following (names are standardized for the benchmark runner; adjust to the current repo if changed):
- `RW_BENCH_TOKEN` (short-lived token)
- `RW_CONTROL_PLANE_URL` (control plane base URL)
- `RW_ARTIFACT_BUCKET` (internal artifact bucket)
- `RW_ARTIFACT_PREFIX` (e.g., `benchmark-report/2025-07/v1/`)
- `RW_RUNNER_REGION` (where the runner executes; does not need to equal target inference region)

### Pinning versions
For official runs:
- Pin the runner image digest (not just a tag)
- Pin benchmark-lab commit SHA
- Pin model versions/IDs exactly as in the methodology

Record all pins in the manifest.

## Generating a sweep manifest
A sweep manifest is the source-of-truth for reproducibility. It must be committed to the artifact store and referenced by all derived datasets.

### Example manifest fields (conceptual)
Include at minimum:
- `schema_version`
- `run_id` (globally unique)
- `created_at_utc`
- `runner_image_digest`
- `benchmark_lab_commit`
- `regions[]`
- `models[]` (with pinned version identifiers)
- `workloads[]` (prompt set + token size distributions + concurrency)
- `caching_policy` and `batching_policy`
- `warmup` (duration and request count)
- `measurement_window` (duration)
- `stability_gates` (thresholds)
- `exclusions` (any planned exclusions must be justified)

### CLI: create manifest
From the benchmark-lab repo root:
1) Pull the pinned runner image:
- `docker pull <runner-image>@sha256:<digest>`

2) Generate the manifest:
