- Hedging windows: for latency-sensitive traffic we allow speculative hedging to a cold-compatible kernel only if the primary dispatch exceeds hedging_threshold_ms (default 60ms). Hedged requests are recorded with hedged=true tag.
- Admission shaping: dispatcher computes an SLO delta per request type (normal/interactive/burst) and emits admission hints to the scheduler via a compact Admission Hint proto. Admission hints are soft; the scheduler is authoritative.

Profiling hooks and observability contract
- Minimal trace span set per request: front_door -> dispatch.enqueued -> dispatch.dequeued -> kernel.schedule -> kernel.exec -> model.kvlookup -> response.serialize -> response.flush. Each span must include the following attributes: request_id, tenant_id, model_id, sequence_length, token_count, kernel_variant, kernel_gpu_id.
- Sampling strategy: default p0=1% for full traces, dynamic increase to 10% during degraded signals, and targeted 100% sampling for requests with fallback_count>0.
- Kernel-level counters required: kernel_dispatch_count, kernel_dispatch_latency_ms_p50/p95/p99, kernel_preempt_count, kernel_oom_events, kernel_retry_count.
- Continuous profiling hook: every worker exposes a /debug/profile endpoint returning a compact profile envelope (CPU, GPU kernel stats, active batches snapshot) compatible with the runtime lab tooling.

Benchmarking guidance (how to validate surface changes)
1) Local microbench: use bench-runner --profile-kernel to execute synthetic short and long sequence profiles. Use provided corpus under /test-corpus/runtime/fidelity/* for realistic token distribution.
2) Shadow benchmarks: mirror 10% of production traffic (low-risk tenants) to the canary kernel build. Compare p50/p95/p99 and fallback rates.
3) SLO regression check: any kernel change must not increase p95 by >5% at target throughput or increase fallback-rate by >1pp.
4) Cost envelope: report per-token cost delta using cost-estimator v2 with the same traffic shape.

Release checklist for scheduler/kernel changes
1) Update scheduler unit tests and deterministic replay fixtures.
2) Run local microbench and post artifacts.
3) Run shadow benchmark for at least 24 hours against production-shaped traffic.
4) Verify observability hooks present and sampled traces are linked to request IDs.
5) Bump canary to 1% then 10% then 50% controlled rollout with health gates: kernel_dispatch_latency_p95, kernel_oom_events, fallback_rate.
6) Document new config knobs with default values and risks in the change description.

Known issues and mitigations (operationally actionable)
- Issue: oscillating preemption chatter when many small interactive requests interleave with large batches.
  Mitigation: enable preemption_holdoff_ms (default 10ms) that blocks new preemptions for a short cooling window after a preemption event. If oscillation persists, increase preemption_suppression_factor and throttle interactive admission.

- Issue: KVCache warmup races causing model-ready to report false readiness when weights are present but KV warmup incomplete.
  Mitigation: model-loader must expose two booleans: weights_ready and warmup_complete. The routing policy uses warmup_complete when serving low-latency tiers; for best-effort tiers, weights_ready suffices.

- Issue: speculative hedging spikes extra GPU tail usage during sudden p99 latency events.
  Mitigation: cap concurrent_hedge_runs_per_gpu to a conservative value (default 4) and enable hedging_adaptive_backoff that reduces hedging when GPU_utilization>85%.

Runbooks (short, playbook style)
1) Slow p95 kernel schedule (oncall guide)
- Trigger: kernel_schedule_latency_p95 > target for > 10m AND fallback_rate increased.
- Steps: a) Check kernel health dashboard (top kernels by latency). b) Inspect recent traces for heavy long sequence batches; look for 'kernel_variant' mismatch. c) If a new kernel variant was deployed <1h, roll canary back. d) If memory pressure visible, execute per-node eviction: curl -X POST http://scheduler/api/v1/evict?node=<node-id>&reason=mem_pressure. e) Escalate to scheduler-team with trace bundle and node dump.

2) Model load failures during deployment
- Trigger: model.readiness=false following a load operation.
- Steps: a) Query /model/logs?attempt=last and /model/checksum. b) If checksum mismatch, re-copy artifacts from artifact-store and retry load. c) If loader crashes repeatedly, mark model as quarantined and route traffic to fallback model as per policy. d) Notify models-onboarding and create JIRA with logs and loader core.

Telemetry and metric thresholds (first-class signals)
- kernel_dispatch_latency_p95: configurable target per SKU (default 120ms for small sequences). Alert if > target * 1.25 for 5m.
- kernel_oom_events: alert on >1 event per 10m per node.
- fallback_rate: alert if >1% across fleet for >15m.
- kvcache_hit_rate: warning if < 70% for more than 30m for interactive tenants.

Ownership and escalation matrix
- Dispatcher incidents: runtime-dispatch (primary), eng-sre (pager).
- Kernel/accelerator incidents: scheduler-team (primary), hw-partner-ops (if host-level).
- KVCache incidents: kvcache-team (primary), runtime-dispatch (dependent impacts).

Appendix A: Example Admission Hint proto (compact YAML)

admission_hint: |
  tenant_id: tenant-42
  request_type: interactive
  budget_tokens: 256
  slo_ms: 200
  priority: gold
  reason: "chat completion - interactive"

Appendix B: Sample diagnostic curl commands

- Fetch recent slow traces (replace {{request_id}}):
  curl -sS "https://obs.internal/api/traces?request_id={{request_id}}" | jq .

- Trigger local kernel profile snapshot on node-13:
  ssh node-13 'curl -sS http://localhost:6060/debug/profile > /tmp/profile-node-13.pb'

- Query kernel credits for tenant:
  curl -sS http://scheduler.internal/api/v1/credits?tenant=tenant-42 | jq .credits

Appendix C: Example config table (defaults)

| knob | default | description |
|------|---------|-------------|
| kernel_start_timeout_ms | 5000 | timeout to start kernel before marking unhealthy |
| hedging_threshold_ms | 60 | ms threshold to spawn hedged run |
| concurrent_hedge_runs_per_gpu | 4 | cap for speculative hedges per GPU |
| preemption_holdoff_ms | 10 | minimum time between preemptions to avoid oscillation |
| kvcache_lookup_timeout_ms | 10 | timeout for KVCache lookups |

Related reading and references
- Runtime trace span schema: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/runtime-telemetry-sampling-cost-aware-profiling-2027.json
- Scheduler decision language primer: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-policy-language-declarative-profiles-2026.json

Revision history
- 2026-02-10: Draft created by Aisha Kumar.
- 2026-03-01: Added release checklist and runbooks; reviewers Miguel Ortega, Leah Chen.

title: runtime-topology-stability-index-and-degradation-simulation-2027
content:
Overview
-------
This page defines our Runtime Topology Stability Index (RTSI), the accompanying Degradation Simulation framework, and operational playbooks for using these signals to guide kernel scheduling decisions, profiling campaigns, and benchmark validation. The goal is to provide a reproducible method for quantifying how a runtime topology (sharding, KV cache layout, kernel variants, and scheduler policies) reacts to progressive stress and to capture early warnings before user-visible SLO degradation.

Why this exists
 - We frequently ship scheduler and kernel changes that affect tail latency and fidelity in subtle ways; unit tests and microbenchmarks are insufficient.
 - RTSI provides a single, actionable score tied to observability signals and a simulation harness to stress topologies in controlled ways.
 - The output informs rollout gating: canaries, weighted rollouts, and automated fallback thresholds in the router.

Scope
 - Applies to all Hosted and Dedicated runtime topologies. Private deployments should re-run the simulation with local traffic shapes.
 - Focuses on inference-serving concerns: latency quantiles, error rates, memory pressure, shard-eviction churn, kernel-failure propagation, and KV cache warmup dynamics.

Definitions
 - Topology: placement of model shards, KV cache shards, and scheduler domains across GPUs and nodes.
 - RTSI: scalar 0–100 where 100 is fully stable under synthetic and replayed traffic stress; lower scores indicate increasing instability.
 - Degradation Mode: class of graceful-fallback or failure (e.g., soft-fidelity degradation, eviction storm, kernel stall).

RTSI design and signals
----------------------
RTSI is computed from a weighted aggregation of normalized signals collected during a simulation run:
1) Latency head/tail scores (p50, p95, p99) — directionally prioritized to penalize tail shifts.
2) Error amplification factor — rate of increased 5xx/response-timeouts vs baseline.
3) Eviction churn index — rate of KV/shard evictions per minute and the time-to-warm (cold-hit penalty).
4) Kernel slip events — frequency of kernel slow-path engagements and soft-fallback triggers.
5) Cross-cohort interference — latency correlation coefficient across tenant cohorts.
6) Recovery velocity — time for metrics to return to baseline after load drop or mitigation (seconds).

Weighting and normalization
 - Default weights: tail latency (0.35), error amplification (0.20), eviction churn (0.15), kernel slip (0.15), cohort interference (0.10), recovery velocity (0.05).
 - Signals are normalized to 0..1 where 0 is worst-case observed in historical incidents and 1 is baseline. RTSI = 100 * weighted_sum(normalized_signals).
 - The weight set is configurable per release; changes must be reviewed with SRE and runtime leads.

Degradation Simulation Framework (how to run)
-------------------------------------------
Purpose: execute deterministic experiments combining synthetic bursts and replayed production traces to surface interaction effects across layers (scheduler, kernel, cache).
Prereqs:
 - Access to the simulation harness (git: infra/runtime-sim) and a small cluster configured with the topology under test.
 - An anonymized request trace (see trace-redaction-playbook) or the synthetic suite.
 - Baseline golden metrics for the model/sequence distribution.

Quick run (smoke):
1) Checkout infra/runtime-sim@stable and configure experiment.yaml (example below).
2) Start cluster: ./scripts/sim-cluster up --topology topology.json --nodes 4
3) Load baseline: ./scripts/load-baseline --trace traces/golden-corpus.json 
4) Run progressive storm: ./scripts/run-storm --burst-factor 3 --duration 600 --cohorts 3
5) Collect artifacts: ./scripts/collect-artifacts --out /tmp/sim-output
6) Compute RTSI: python tools/compute_rtsi.py --input /tmp/sim-output --weights config/weights.yaml

Example experiment.yaml:
| name | value |
| experiment_name | rtsi-sanity-2027 |
| topology_file | topologies/4node-nonuniform.json |
| trace | traces/median-length-100.json |
| burst_pattern | step(1,3,30m) |
| scheduler_profile | econ-priority-governor-v2 |
| kernel_variants | [tf32, int8-fallback] |

Kernel-scheduling interaction checklist
--------------------------------------
When scheduling policy changes are proposed, run the following minimal checklist against RTSI:
1) Local pressure test: simulate single-node degradation and measure eviction churn and kernel slip.
2) Cross-node blast: multi-cohort ramp to expose interference.
3) Fallback exercise: intentionally trigger a kernel slow-path and validate graceful fallback latency bound.
4) Canary schedule: run weighted rollout simulation with 5/25/70 split and verify RTSI delta <= 6 points.

Profiling playbook (collection guidance)
-------------------------------------
Signals to collect during simulation runs:
 - Latency histograms (per-cohort, per-model) with 1ms bins up to 2s.
 - Kernel telemetry: kernel-id, path (fast/slow), elapsed_ns, occupancy, tensor shapes.
 - KV cache metrics: hits, misses, evictions, warmup-latency per key-range.
 - Node-level: GPU-util, memory_used, page_faults, temperature, nvlink-errors.
 - Scheduler: slot-queue-length, per-priority utilization, preemptions, admission denials.

Data retention and sample rates:
 - For simulation runs keep full traces and kernel telemetry for 30 days. Aggregates (per-minute) are retained for 90 days.
 - Use stratified sampling for long runs: preserve all p99 contributors and sample head requests at 1% to save storage.

Benchmarking suite integration
-----------------------------
RTSI is integrated into the acceptance benchmark suite:
 - Pre-merge checks run a lightweight sim (10m, small cluster) and verify RTSI >= 85 for low-risk backports.
 - Release gates run extended sims (2–6 hours) on release branches; failures (RTSI delta > 10 vs baseline) block signoff.
 - Benchmark artifacts include an artifacts manifest with: topology.json, scheduler_policy.yaml, kernel_build_hash, raw traces, and computed RTSI report.

Release notes and versioning
---------------------------
When a runtime change modifies scheduling or kernels, release notes must include:
 - RTSI baseline and delta observed in extended sim runs.
 - Kernel variant compatibility table and roll-forward/rollback instructions.
 - Recommended canary matrix (percentages, duration, SLOs to watch).
 - Any config toggles to delay rollout (feature flags) and their default state.

Known issues and interpretations
-------------------------------
We surface deterministic patterns that should not be treated as immediate blockers but require follow-up: 
 - Eviction ripple: small increases in eviction rate that grow over minutes indicate mis-sized KV partitions. Triage: re-evaluate shard sizing and prefetch hints.
 - Kernel slip noise: intermittent slow-path entries isolated to particular tensor shapes. Triage: add microbench for the shape and consider kernel specialization.
 - Inter-cohort correlated tails: events where a small tenant induces p99 increases across unrelated cohorts — typically scheduler admission quanta or quota shaping misconfig.

Operational runbooks (step-by-step)
---------------------------------
Runbook A: RTSI regression detected during CI
1) Abort the merge and alert runtime-sre@redwood.
2) Attach artifacts manifest and full sim output to the ticket.
3) Triage: run quick delta profiler (scripts/quick-delta) to localize to scheduler/kernel/cache.
4) If kernel suspected, run kernel smoke on microbench harness and isolate commit.
5) If scheduler suspected, revert policy or reduce canary weight and re-run sim.
6) Update the release notice with root cause and mitigation.

Runbook B: Production tail-latency spike suspected to match simulation signature
1) Toggle circuit-breaker: route traffic to fallback model-variant.
2) Open incident, tag with simulation label and link to last successful RTSI run.
3) Run targeted replay for the last 10 minutes using production trace sampler.
4) If RTSI-like signature reproduced, follow kernel rollback path.
5) If not reproduced, escalate to SRE/runtime-engineering for deeper tracing.

Ownership and governance
-----------------------
 - Primary owner: Runtime Architecture (runtime-arch@redwood).
 - SRE for policy: eng-sre (oncall rotation).
 - Profiling and kernel analysis: Performance and Applied ML teams.
 - Changes to RTSI formula or default weights require: runtime-arch + eng-sre + perf signoff.

Appendix A — Example weight file (config/weights.yaml)
---
# weights.yaml
tail_latency: 0.35
error_amp: 0.20
eviction_churn: 0.15
kernel_slip: 0.15
cohort_interference: 0.10
recovery_velocity: 0.05

Appendix B — Troubleshooting checklist (fast)
 - p99 spiked but p95 stable: check kernel slip histogram and tail shapes.
 - Eviction count rising: check partition distribution and hot-key lists.
 - One-node pressure causing cross-node tails: investigate slot reservation and NUMA bindings.

Appendix C — Links and artifacts
 - Simulation harness: git.internal.redwood/infra/runtime-sim
 - Trace redaction playbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/trace-redaction-playbook
 - RTSI computation script: tools/compute_rtsi.py (runtime-sim repo)

Revision history
----------------
 - 2026-11-15: Initial draft (Priya Desai).
 - 2027-01-18: Added kernel-slip instrumentation guidance (Miles Chen).
 - 2027-03-12: Finalized weights and CI integration checklist (Anika Rao).

title: Fidelity Taxonomy & Scheduler Interop Matrix - operational manual
content:
Overview

Purpose
This document defines a pragmatic fidelity taxonomy (how we describe and measure request/response fidelity in the runtime), and a scheduler interoperability matrix that maps fidelity targets to scheduler behaviors and required telemetry hooks. It consolidates operational runbooks for diagnosing fidelity regressions, guidance for kernel scheduling policy authors, and benchmarking protocols used to validate fidelity-preserving changes.

Scope
- Applies to all inference traffic served by the runtime (hosted, dedicated, private).
- Focuses on single-request fidelity (decoding fidelity, model variant fidelity, prompt-preserve semantics) and cohort-level fidelity (consistency across canaries, shadow cohorts).
- Does not replace model-eval quality pipelines but complements them with runtime-level observability and mitigations.

Why this matters
- We often trade throughput/cost for fidelity. Without a shared vocabulary and clear scheduler contracts, teams make inconsistent changes that cause subtle quality regressions. This manual makes those tradeoffs explicit and operationally testable.

Definitions and fidelity levels
1) Fidelity levels (business-oriented):
   - FIDELITY:HIGH — Match-to-model output semantics; minimal decoding truncation, full KV cache warm, deterministic tokenization path, 99th-percentile quality invariants verified by shadow evals.
   - FIDELITY:STANDARD — Non-critical latency optimizations allowed (small batch fusion, soft-quantization fallbacks), acceptable for most consumer-facing services.
   - FIDELITY:ECONOMY — Aggressive cost controls (low-precision kernels, higher batching, prefix elision), intended for bulk processing where micro-quality differences are acceptable.
   - FIDELITY:BEST_EFFORT — Degraded mode used during capacity pressure or partial failure; best-effort fallback to compatible model variant with explicit response metadata.

2) Observability primitives (signals we require)
   - fidelity_label (string): One of the fidelity levels above (attached to request).
   - kernel_profile (string): Kernel variant used (e.g., stable-tc64, quant-r2).
   - kvcache_state (enum): warm|partial|cold.
   - decode_path_flags (set): includes token-truncation, temperature-clamp, sampling-mode.
   - quality_shadow_score (float): periodic shadow-eval score (0..1) when enabled.

Scheduler Interop Matrix (text table)
Columns: fidelity_label | admission_policy | kernel_preference | prefetch_hint | fallthrough_policy | telemetry_required
- FIDELITY:HIGH | strict admission (single-request slots) | prefer full-precision, deterministic kernels | pre-warm KV + prefix pin | fail open with immediate rollback to canary | kvcache_state, decode_path_flags, kernel_profile, quality_shadow_score
- FIDELITY:STANDARD | balanced admission (slot-sharing allowed) | mixed-precision allowed with quality gate | opportunistic prefetch | degrade-by-quantize w/ warning | kernel_profile, kvcache_state, admission_latency
- FIDELITY:ECONOMY | aggressive admission (batch aggregation, deferred slots) | prefer quantized/low-precision kernels | no prefetch, batch-prefetch only | fallback to cheaper model variant | kernel_profile, batch_size_histogram, cost_estimate_token
- FIDELITY:BEST_EFFORT | best-effort admission (background slots) | any compatible kernel | no prefetch | tag response with fidelity=best_effort and reason | kernel_profile, eviction_events, failure_cause

Scheduling policy author guidance
- Always declare a fidelity_label at route definition. Default = FIDELITY:STANDARD.
- Keep scheduler policy small and declarative. Example policy snippet (YAML):

  route: /v1/generate/summary
  fidelity: FIDELITY:HIGH
  admission:
    mode: isolated
    max_concurrency: 4
  kernel_preferences:
    - stable-tc64
    - stable-tc32
  prefetch: true
  fallthrough:
    - route: /v1/generate/summary-lite
      fidelity: FIDELITY:STANDARD
      probability: 0.05

- Policies must include an explicit fallback route or fallthrough policy when the chosen kernel or capacity is unavailable.
- When adding a new kernel variant, update the interop matrix and include a microbenchmark that exercises the fidelity-sensitive prompt set.

Profiling playbook for fidelity regressions
1) Rapid triage (0–15 min)
   1. Isolate affected routes by checking fidelity_label in recent traces.
   2. Pull kernel_profile and kvcache_state histograms for the route over the last 60 minutes.
   3. If quality_shadow_score dropped >5% vs baseline, open a P0 incident and attach the shadow-eval corpus.

2) Deeper investigation (15–180 min)
   1. Run a targeted synthetic replay of failing prompts against the candidate kernel variants using the replay harness.
   2. Compare decoding artifacts: tokenization diffs, truncation flags, and final-length distributions.
   3. Check scheduler admission logs for unusual batching or coalescing events.

3) Remediation (post 3 hours)
   1. If a kernel regression is responsible, roll kernel to previous stable via the kernel-rollout tool and execute canary smoke checks.
   2. If admission policy caused harmful batching, temporarily tighten admission mode for the route and schedule a follow-up to analyze long-term capacity.
   3. Apply a temporary traffic-split to route a small percentage to a high-fidelity variant while investigation continues.

Runbook: canonical commands and scripts
- Pull recent traces for route: curl -s "${CONSOLE_URL}/api/traces?route=/v1/generate/summary&from=-1h" | jq .
- Kernel histogram: runtime-admin kernel-histogram --route=/v1/generate/summary --window=60m
- Launch replay job (isolated): replay-runner --corpus=shadow/summary-failures.jsonl --kernel=stable-tc64 --parallel=4
- Set temporary admission override: schedulerctl set-admission --route=/v1/generate/summary --mode=isolated --reason="fidelity-regression-20250318"

Benchmarking and validation protocol
- For every scheduler-change that may affect batching/admission, run the fidelity-preservation benchmark suite:
  1. Prompt sets: prod-top-1000, adversarial-250, stress-long-seqs-200.
  2. Metrics to collect: mean quality_shadow_score, 95th decode-time, token-length-distribution, perplexity-delta vs gold-model.
  3. Pass criteria: quality_shadow_score within 1.5% of baseline for HIGH/STD; within 6% for ECONOMY.
  4. Use controlled concurrency and live traffic shadowing (0% traffic injection initially).

Compatibility & preflight checklist for kernel rollouts
- Update kernel_profile registry with metadata: precision, determinism, known-issues.
- Create a perf matrix: (kernel x route) with expected throughput and latency delta.
- Add observability hooks if missing: ensure kvcache_state and decode_path_flags are emitted by kernel adapter.
- Run the benchmark protocol above and document the pass/fail outcome in the rollout ticket.

Telemetry contract (minimum required fields)
- trace_id (string)
- timestamp (iso8601)
- route (string)
- fidelity_label (string)
- kernel_profile (string)
- kvcache_state (string)
- batch_size (int)
- admission_mode (string)
- quality_shadow_score (float, optional)
- failure_cause (string, optional)

Escalation and ownership
- First responder: runtime-oncall (primary).
- Secondary: kernel-team (kernel regressions), serving-runtime (scheduling/telemetry gaps), ml-evals (shadow-eval gating).
- When to escalate to engineering leadership: any fidelity_shadow_score drop >10% affecting >5% of requests or undiagnosed degradation >6 hours.

Implementation examples (JSON policy + telemetry example)
- Scheduler policy (JSON example):
  {
    "route": "/v1/generate/summary",
    "fidelity": "FIDELITY:HIGH",
    "admission": {"mode": "isolated", "max_concurrency": 4},
    "kernel_preferences": ["stable-tc64", "stable-tc32"],
    "prefetch": true
  }

- Telemetry sample (single-line JSON event):
  {
    "trace_id": "t-0a1b2c3d",
    "timestamp": "2025-03-18T14:22:30Z",
    "route": "/v1/generate/summary",
    "fidelity_label": "FIDELITY:HIGH",
    "kernel_profile": "stable-tc64",
    "kvcache_state": "warm",
    "batch_size": 1,
    "admission_mode": "isolated",
    "quality_shadow_score": 0.987
  }

Operational examples & anti-patterns
- Anti-pattern: declaring fidelity=HIGH but leaving prefetch=false and admission=shared. This creates a latent mismatch where kernels assume warm cache but scheduler does not.
- Anti-pattern: using BEST_EFFORT for user-facing routes without response metadata. Always surface degraded-fidelity reasons in response headers: X-Redwood-Fidelity: best_effort; X-Redwood-Fidelity-Reason: kernel-eviction.

Notes for product and SRE collaborations
- Product must provide an explicit fidelity SLA when requesting high-fidelity routes (e.g., SLO: maintain quality_shadow_score above 0.95 at 99th percentile).
- SRE will verify observability hooks exist before approving kernel or scheduler policy changes. Any missing telemetry is a blocker.

Appendix: small checklist for reviewers
- [ ] Does the route declare fidelity_label?
- [ ] Are fallthroughs defined for capacity or kernel failure?
- [ ] Are required telemetry fields emitted for this route?
- [ ] Has the prompt set been added to the fidelity benchmark corpus?
- [ ] Are canary and shadow strategies defined for rollout?

Document history and links
- Drafted: 2024-11-12 by Lena Zhang
- Reviewed by Carlos Mendes, Priya Iyer, Owen Park (2025-02)
- Last updated: 2025-03-18 — added benchmark pass criteria and telemetry contract

If you have questions or need a copy of the fidelity benchmark corpora, ping #runtime-fidelity on Slack or open a ticket in the runtime-team JIRA with label "fidelity-bench".

title: Session slice checkpointing and revival spec
content:
Overview

This document specifies the design, operational patterns, and validation playbooks for session slice checkpointing and revival in the Redwood serving runtime. The goal is to enable long-lived conversational/stateful sessions to survive eviction, migration, and kernel-level preemption while minimizing memory and latency overhead. The spec covers data formats, storage contracts, scheduler interactions, profiling signals to monitor, benchmark tests to prove cost/latency trade-offs, and a runnable incident playbook for recovery.

Goals
- Minimize user-visible latency when reviving an evicted session (target: 95th percentile revival < 120 ms on dedicated pools).
- Bound extra memory cost per active-sliced session to <= 5% of total stream memory on average workloads.
- Ensure safety: revived sessions must restore deterministic KV-cache and decoder prefix state for fidelity-sensitive workloads (evaluations/QA).
- Make slice checkpoints resumable across kernel variants and quantization profiles.

Glossary and components
- Session: logical conversation or stateful sequence from the Redwood API.
- Slice: a contiguous window of model execution state (kv-cache entries + decoder prefix metadata) small enough to checkpoint and transfer. Typical slice = latest N tokens' kv-deltas where N is configured per model.
- Checkpoint: serialized slice persisted to backing storage (in-memory cache + tiered durable store).
- Revival Agent: runtime component that reconstructs session state from checkpoints and orchestrates warmstart requests to the kernel-dispatcher.
- Slice-Manager: component responsible for creating, pruning, and expiring slices according to policy.
- Kernel-Dispatcher: the serving runtime component that maps requests to GPU kernels and manages scheduling/eviction.

Design overview
1) Slice boundaries and frequency
- Default slice length: 256 tokens for decoder-first models, 128 tokens for decoder-only smaller models.
- Create rolling checkpoints after either: 256 tokens since last slice OR 10 seconds since last activity, whichever comes first. This balances write amplification and revival granularity.
- The Slice-Manager supports adaptive slicing: for high-entropy sessions (many new tokens / variable seq lengths) the slice size may shrink to 128 to reduce revival cost.

2) Checkpoint format (JSON + binary KV blob)
- Checkpoint envelope (JSON, small): {\n    "version": "v1",\n    "session_id": "<uuid>",\n    "slice_index": "<int>",\n    "model": "<model-id>",\n    "seq_range": [<start>,<end>],\n    "created_at": "<iso>",\n    "kernel_hint": "<kernel-config>",\n    "affinity_hint": "<hw-pool>"\n  }
- Binary blob: optimized, compressed KV-delta + small decoder-state table. Blob layout includes a small CRC32 and LZ4 compression. The revival path validates CRC before load.

3) Storage tiers and consistency
- Ephemeral tier (fast): memory-backed LRU cache co-located with the slice's active host (store name: session-slice-cache). TTL default: 5 minutes.
- Durable tier (cold): a regional object store (store name: session-checkpoints), retention default: 30 days for dedicated customers, 7 days for hosted default.
- Write policy: write-through to ephemeral tier synchronously, enqueue background upload to durable tier. On background upload failures the Slice-Manager retries with exponential backoff; failures are surfaced to metrics.

4) Eviction and revival policy
- Eviction triggers: memory pressure signals, kernel preemption, node decommission, scaling down. When eviction is decided, the slice is pinned and the Slice-Manager emits a checkpoint creation event.
- Revival flow: client request hits routing layer -> routing checks session metadata -> if session not resident, routing invokes Revival Agent -> Revival Agent fetches checkpoint from ephemeral tier (fallback to durable) -> validates and streams KV-deltas to kernel-dispatcher using the warmstart API -> kernel acknowledges reconstructed prefix -> request proceeds.
- Fallback semantics: if checkpoint not found or corrupted, the Revival Agent constructs a degraded session with best-effort prefix (last N tokens in user-visible transcript) and annotates the response with a telemetry flag trace.revival.degraded=true.

Kernel scheduling interactions
- Warmstart handshake: kernel-dispatcher exposes warmstart endpoints that accept a slice_id, kernel_hint, and resume token. Warmstart operations are prioritized into a separate scheduling lane with admission limits to avoid blocking new short-lived requests.
- Preemption coordination: Schedulers must not preempt an in-flight warmstart unless safe-checks pass. Safe-checks include ensuring the revived KV-cache has been persisted to ephemeral tier and that no concurrent write is ongoing.
- Admission controls and credits: revival lanes consume kernel-credit units at a 2x weight vs steady inference tokens for the first 50ms to reflect the higher GPU work to reconstruct KV-cache. This weight decays after successful warmstart.

Profiling and observability playbook
- Signals to capture for each slice lifecycle: slice.create.latency, slice.upload.duration, slice.fetch.latency(ephemeral), slice.fetch.latency(durable), slice.validation.failures, revival.handshake.latency, revival.fidelity-flag, revival.memory-overhead.
- Trace correlation: include tags session_id, slice_index, kernel_id, request_id to enable end-to-end reconstruction of a revival path in a single APM span.
- Sampling policy: sample 100% of failed revivals and 1% of successful revivals. For high-SLA customers sample 5% of successful revivals.
- Profiling recipe (step-by-step):
  1. Reproduce a node eviction in the staging cluster with a mix of slice sizes.
  2. Collect full traces for the affected session_ids and kernel dispatch logs.
  3. Measure revival.handshake.latency distribution and correlate with kernel_hint and slice size.
  4. Verify CRC and decompression time dominates or not. If CRC >> 20ms, investigate I/O or CPU noise.

Benchmarking suite and acceptance criteria
- Bench types: micro (single-slice create/fetch), integration (eviction + revival under steady traffic), stress (mass eviction under bursty traffic), fidelity (regression tests against ground-truth conversation transcripts).
- Sample test: Revival whole-path SLO test\  - Setup: 1k concurrent sessions, each with 3 slices in ephemeral tier; trigger rolling eviction of 20% nodes; replay 1k requests that require revival.\  - Success criteria: 95th percentile end-to-end revival latency < 120 ms, revival failure rate < 0.2%, and post-revival model output match baseline (BLEU-like metric for structured responses > 0.98).
- Cost benchmark: measure extra tokens and kernel time used during revival and report per-10k-revivals cost delta. Target operator-visible CPU overhead < 7% of baseline during typical workloads.

Release, rollout, and compatibility notes
- Versioning: checkpoint envelope includes version field. v1 -> v2 migration requires in-place upgrade of Slice-Manager and Revival Agent. We support backward-reading: Revival Agent v2 can read v1 envelopes; Kernel warmstart must negotiate kernel_hint.
- Feature flagging: rollout under feature flag runtime.slice-checkpointing.enabled = false by default. Canary pool (5% traffic) -> 25% -> 100% with observability gates (revival latency & failure thresholds).
- Model compatibility: ensure that quantized or sharded kernels expose a compatible warmstart shim; otherwise Runtime will fallback to degraded revival. Document model whitelist for full-fidelity revival.

Operational runbook (incident-oriented)
- Symptom A: revival failure rate spike (>0.5% over 5m)\  1. Check slice.upload.duration and ephemeral cache saturation metrics.\  2. If ephemeral cache OOMs: increase TTL on session-slice-cache or scale slice-cache nodes; call on-call storage lead.\  3. If durable store upload errors: inspect uploader logs, check object-store rate limits and retry queue size.\  4. If CRC failures: inspect slice-manager CPU load, investigate kernel library version mismatch.\  5. Mitigation: temporarily set runtime.slice-checkpointing.enabled=false for the affected pool and trigger live-migration of pinned sessions using migration script: scripts/migrate-pinned-sessions --graceful
- Symptom B: long revival handshake latency (95p > 250 ms)\  1. Correlate with kernel_hint and kernel-dispatcher saturations.\  2. If warmstart lane starved: adjust admission control to add +1 revival-worker for 10 minutes.\  3. If decompression dominates: offload decompression to dedicated CPU pool or increase ephemeral tier locality.\  4. Mitigation: set a temporary admission cap and route new sessions to a lower-latency fallback model.
- Emergency recovery (checkpoint corruption widespread)\  1. Flip a global flag to force degraded revivals and annotate requests (trace.revival.degraded=true).\  2. Run a recovery job to rehydrate session state from transcript replay for critical customers.\  3. Post-incident: run forensic profiling, bump checkpoint CRC verification and add checksum telemetry.

Known issues and constraints
- Cross-kernel warmstart divergence: certain experimental kernels change internal kv-serialization layout causing revival CRC mismatch. Workaround: add kernel_hint mapping table in the envelope and pin those sessions to compatible kernels.
- High write amplification for very chatty sessions: customers with avg token rate > 50 tokens/sec will cause many slice writes; recommend configuring adaptive slice policy or applying per-session write-rate throttle.
- Replay determinism: revival assumes deterministic KV replay; non-deterministic model ops (custom kernels with randomized ops) may yield fidelity drift. Such kernels must be added to the non-revivable list in runtime config.

Ownership, telemetry, and next steps
- Owner: runtime-session-team (primary), kernel-team (warmstart contract), infra-storage (checkpoint storage).
- Dashboards to create: Revival health (failure rate, latency P50/P95/P99), Slice storage cost by customer, Revival fidelity regressions by model.
- Next work items:
  - v2 checkpoint with signed manifests for better integrity checks.
  - Chunked streaming revival to reduce worst-case tail (prototype Q2 2026).
  - Operator controls for per-customer slice retention policies.

References and related docs
- See: runtime-feature-lifecycle-and-sunset-playbook-2026 (migration guidance), cold-start-warmup-strategies-and-entropy-reduction-2025 (warmstart heuristics), kernel-admission-matrix-and-signal-negotiation-manual-2026 (scheduler contract).

Appendix: sample checkpoint envelope (human-readable)
{\n  "version": "v1",\n  "session_id": "6a9f8c1a-...",\n  "slice_index": "42",\n  "model": "rw-instruct-13b-v2",\n  "seq_range": [10240,10496],\n  "created_at": "2026-02-28T11:45:30Z",\n  "kernel_hint": "tiled-sharded-v3",\n  "affinity_hint": "pool-us-west-2a"\n}

(End of document)

title: Runtime feature flagging and experimentation contract
content:
Overview
--------
This document defines the architecture and operational contract for feature flagging and experimentation that touches the serving runtime. It covers how runtime-visible flags are declared, negotiated with kernels, staged in production, instrumented for SLO-aware rollouts, and automatically (or manually) rolled back. It is intended for runtime engineers, release engineers, kernel maintainers, and SREs who operate inference fleets.

Scope
-----
- Applies to any toggle that changes runtime execution behavior: kernel selection, batching policy, KV cache semantics, prefetch hints, quantization/fast-path heuristics, backpressure thresholds, admission controls, and routing fallbacks.
- Excludes UI-only feature flags, SDK developer flags, or experiment flags that do not alter server-side execution.

Goals
-----
1. Provide a single, auditable contract for staging and running runtime-facing feature flags.
2. Ensure rollouts are SLO-aware with automated safety gates that prevent expensive regressions.
3. Standardize telemetry and decision tracing so every flag decision can be reconstructed end-to-end.
4. Reduce blast radius with progressive targeting (canary -> ramp -> percent -> full) and deterministic fallback strategies.

Key definitions
---------------
- Flag: An identifier that toggles behavior in the runtime (e.g., runtime.kv_prefetch_v2).
- Kernel capability: a runtime or accelerator property (e.g., async_prefetch, sharded_attention_v2) that a kernel exposes and can negotiate with the control plane.
- Decision trace: structured metadata attached to each request that records the flag decisions and kernel choices used to serve the request.
- Safety gate: a set of observable constraints (SLO/metric thresholds) that must hold before a flag can progress to the next stage.

Contract: Flag lifecycle and metadata
------------------------------------
Every runtime flag must have the following canonical metadata (stored in the feature-store):
- id: short dashed name, e.g., runtime.kv_prefetch_v2
- owner: GitHub handle and team, e.g., @asha / runtime-kernels
- description: one-sentence purpose and risk summary
- scope: one of [kernel-level, node-level, tenant-level, route-level]
- default: boolean (sane production default)
- stages: ordered list: [canary, ramp, percent, full, deprecated]
- canary_policy: YAML pointer to rollout policy (see examples)
- telemetry_keys: list of required metrics and trace attributes (see Observability section)
- precondition_checks: optional list of checks (e.g., min-gpu-firmware-version, kvcache-available)
- rollback_policy: pointer to automated rollback rule set
- audit_log_url: URL to changelog / PR for the flag

Example metadata (YAML snippet for the feature-store):
```
id: runtime.kv_prefetch_v2
owner: @asha (runtime-kernels)
description: Enable asynchronous KV prefetching for seed-based warmup to reduce cold tail latency. Risk: may increase memory churn under high-concurrency workloads.
scope: node-level
default: false
stages: [canary, ramp, percent, full]
canary_policy: /flags/policies/canary-kv-prefetch-v2.yaml
telemetry_keys: [p50, p95, p99, cpu_util, gpu_mem_used, kv_prefetch_hit_ratio]
precondition_checks: [gpu_driver>=560.20, kvcache_enabled]
rollback_policy: /flags/rollback/auto-sla-rollback.yaml
audit_log_url: https://sc/reviews/12345
```

Runtime negotiation and kernel capability model
----------------------------------------------
1. Capability declaration: Each kernel binary declares a static capability vector at build time (JSON manifest attached to the runtime image). Capabilities are short tokens: async_prefetch, sharded_attn_v2, quant_fp8_fastpath.
2. Dynamic negotiation: At node start, the control plane retrieves the capability vector and stores it with node metadata. Flags scoped to kernel-level are only eligible for nodes that advertise the required capability.
3. Fallback compatibility matrix: For each flag, authors must provide a fallback kernel variant or a safe no-op. Control plane enforces that flag activation never routes traffic to an incompatible kernel.

Example kernel manifest (single-line JSON for feature-store):
{"kernel_version":"3.2.0","capabilities":["async_prefetch","sharded_attn_v2"]} 

Canary and rollout policy (SLO-aware)
-------------------------------------
All rollout policies must include: target traffic fraction, duration, ramp step size, observation window, and safety gates. Safety gates are specified as PromQL-style constraints.

Minimum canary policy (example):
```
name: kv-prefetch-v2-canary
target_fraction: 0.01 # 1% of signed traffic
duration: 2h
steps:
  - until: 30m
    fraction: 0.01
  - until: 1h
    fraction: 0.05
observation_window: 5m
safety_gates:
  - name: p99-latency-regression
    query: rate(p99_latency_ms[5m]) > baseline_p99 * 1.15
  - name: cpu-spike
    query: avg(cpu_user_seconds_total[5m]) > baseline_cpu * 1.2
```
Progression rules: a step only advances when none of the safety gates have fired for two consecutive observation windows. If any gate fires, follow rollback policy.

Telemetry and decision tracing requirements
-----------------------------------------
Every request served under a runtime flag must record the following trace attributes (as structured tags):
- flag.id (string)
- flag.stage (canary|ramp|percent|full)
- kernel.id
- kernel.capabilities (comma-separated token list)
- decision.reason (e.g., 'canary-match','tenant-override','precondition-fail')
- decision.timestamp (ISO8601)
- fallback.used (true|false)

Required aggregated metrics (per-flag and per-kernel) reported at 1m resolution:
- request_count
- successful_count
- error_rate (5xx / total)
- latency_p50_ms, latency_p95_ms, latency_p99_ms
- cpu_util_percent
- gpu_mem_bytes_used
- kv_prefetch_hit_ratio (when applicable)
- cost_per_1000_tokens (est.)

Observability dashboards and baseline generation
------------------------------------------------
- Every flag must have a templated dashboard generated automatically (Flag Overview): timeline of rollout fraction, p50/p95/p99, error_rate, resource usage, and decision_trace sampling panel.
- Baselines: rollouts must compare to a running baseline captured from the 72h window before the rollout. Baseline values are stored in the experiment index and used in safety gate expressions.
- Example PromQL safety gate (p99 regression):
  (avg_over_time(latency_p99_ms{flag=\"control\"}[72h]) * 1.15) < avg_over_time(latency_p99_ms{flag=\"candidate\"}[5m])

Automated rollback and escalation
--------------------------------
Two rollback mechanisms are supported: automated rollback and manual rollback. Authors must declare which mechanism applies and provide the thresholds.

Automated rollback rule template (example):
- Trigger: any safety gate that is marked auto-rollback triggers immediate rollback.
- Action: flag is set to previous stage (or disabled if canary) and affected traffic is re-routed to fallback kernel.
- Notification: paging to on-call + slack #runtime-incidents + email to flag owner and reviewers.

Manual rollback: Any engineer can manually revert via the feature-store UI or CLI; manual rollback must include reason and a summary to the audit log.

Experimentation harness and synthetic traffic protocol
-----------------------------------------------------
We require a reproducible synthetic load generator for each flag to exercise worst-case shapes (short bursts, long-context, many small parallel requests). The harness must:
- Support tenant-scoped replay with recording/replay of real traffic signatures (scrubbed for PII)
- Provide pre-seeded KV cache patterns and long/short sequence distributions
- Allow failure injection (GPU OOM, NVLink latency, kernel timeouts) to test fallback behavior

Commands (example):
- Start a canary run: `rx experiment start --flag runtime.kv_prefetch_v2 --policy kv-prefetch-v2-canary`
- Attach synthetic traffic: `rx loadgen --profile long-context-burst --tenants 100 --qps 200`
- Collect traces: `rx traces export --filter flag=runtime.kv_prefetch_v2 --since 60m`

Kernel rollout considerations
---------------------------
- Kernel authors must include a compatibility shim that allows a node to accept both old and new kernels during a rolling upgrade.
- Rolling kernel upgrades must be coordinated with flag rollouts: a flag that depends on a new kernel capability must not be advanced beyond canary until 80% of eligible nodes are on the target kernel.
- If the target capability is optional (best-effort), flag authors must specify safe degradation path in the metadata.

SLOs and alerting thresholds (suggested defaults)
--------------------------------------------------
These thresholds are minimums; product teams may tighten them for higher-risk flags. All alerts are aggregated by flag and by model/route.
- Error rate increase: > 0.5 percentage point absolute increase over baseline (5m window)
- p95 latency increase: > baseline_p95 * 1.20 (5m window)
- p99 latency increase: > baseline_p99 * 1.10 (5m window)
- CPU usage: sustained > baseline * 1.25 (10m)
- GPU memory pressure: > 85% for any node (1m)
- Cost per 1k tokens: > baseline * 1.3 (24h)

Runbook: immediate steps when a safety gate fires
------------------------------------------------
1. Alert fires -> page on-call SRE and notify flag owner.
2. On-call runs `rx flags status --id runtime.kv_prefetch_v2` to confirm active stage.
3. If auto-rollback enabled, verify whether rollback already executed. If not, run `rx flags rollback --id runtime.kv_prefetch_v2 --reason \"auto_gate_fire_manual_confirm\"`.
4. If manual rollback required, set flag to previous stage and re-route traffic.
5. Collect artifacts: 1m-resolution metrics, 1000 sampled traces (decision traces), kernel logs from nodes in cohort, and synthetic harness logs.
6. Postmortem: owner opens a short incident review within 48h, including root cause hypothesis and next steps.

Ownership and approvals
-----------------------
- Flag owner (declared in metadata) is responsible for: precondition checks, telemetry coverage, and runbook artifacts.
- Kernel owners must sign off on capability declarations and provide fallback readiness proof.
- Release owner (release-engineering) must approve any global >10% traffic ramp.
- Security review required for any flag that changes encryption, key usage, or telemetry collection.

Implementation examples
-----------------------
Feature-store CLI example (create a flag):
```
rx flags create --id runtime.kv_prefetch_v2 \
  --owner @asha --scope node-level --default false \
  --telemetry p99,kv_prefetch_hit_ratio,cpu_util --precondition kvcache_enabled
```

Prometheus rule example (p99 regression gate):
```
alert: Flag_P99_Regression
expr: (avg_over_time(latency_p99_ms{flag=\"candidate\"}[5m]) > avg_over_time(latency_p99_ms{flag=\"control\"}[72h]) * 1.15)
for: 2m
labels:
  severity: page
annotations:
  summary: \"Candidate p99 exceeding baseline by >15%\"
```

Change log and auditability
---------------------------
- Every state transition (create, canary-start, ramp-step, rollback, disable) must be recorded in the audit log with: user, timestamp, previous_state, new_state, reason, and a link to the PR/change.
- Audit retention: 3 years for production-facing flags.

Security and privacy notes
--------------------------
- Decision traces must not contain PII. Fields that could contain user data must be hashed or replaced with stable pseudonyms.
- Experiment replay must use scrubbed recordings: scrub policy stored at /policies/replay-scrub-policy.md

Appendix: FAQ and common patterns
----------------------------------
Q: When should a flag be kernel-level vs node-level?
A: Kernel-level flags are for behavior inside kernel code paths that are compiled-in; node-level for runtime orchestration or config toggles. If the change touches GPU kernel binary interfaces, use kernel-level.

Q: Can we bypass the safety gates for urgent hotfixes?
A: Only with a documented emergency exemption approved by Release Engineering + SRE. The exemption must be recorded and the flag reverted to standard flow within 24h.

Contacts and references
-----------------------
- Runtime flag steward: @asha (Asha Patel) — runtime-kernels
- On-call SRE rotation: https://oncall.redwood/services/runtime
- Feature-store UI: https://flags.redwood/internal
- Related docs: runtime-feature-lifecycle-and-sunset-playbook, runtime-upgrade-validation-and-canary-matrix

Change history
--------------
- 2025-11-07: Initial draft created by Asha Patel.
- 2026-01-20: Added automated rollback templates and synthetic harness commands.
- 2026-02-14: Finalized telemetry attribute names and reviewer sign-offs.

title: Dependency Agreements and Shard Topology Guidance
content:
Summary

This document defines a lightweight, enforceable contract pattern between clients (API consumers, SDKs, internal services) and the Redwood serving runtime, and it prescribes adaptive shard topology guidance for production inference fleets. The goal is to reduce coupling, make runtime upgrades predictable, and provide operational controls for multi-tenant and mixed-workload environments.

Goals

- Define clear API/behavioral guarantees the runtime exposes to callers (latency bounds, failure modes, schema expectations).
- Establish a minimal contract envelope for versioning, feature flags, and fallbacks.
- Describe shard topology strategies (static, capacity-driven, adaptive) and when to apply each.
- Provide observability & SLO requirements to surface contract violations early.
- Define rollout and migration procedures for contract changes and shard topology updates.

Scope

Applies to: Redwood serving runtime components (frontend gateways, routing layer, shard managers, worker pools) and any internal clients (hosted API, Dedicated controllers, Private agents) that invoke text-generation, embedding, or reranking endpoints.

Not in scope: customer-managed models inside Private if customer elects fully air-gapped operational model (see Private deployment appendix).

Definitions

- Contract Envelope: JSON wrapper the runtime and clients agree on that includes metadata (schema version, client intent, hints) and a validation checksum.
- Shard: A logical grouping of worker instances that share model artifacts, KV cache adjacency, and placement constraints.
- Adaptive Sharding: Dynamic rebalancing of shard membership and size based on traffic characteristics and tail latency signals.
- Client Intent: Declared properties the client supplies (latency-sensitive, batch-friendly, high-cost-priority).

Contract Requirements (runtime -> client)

1) Behavioral Guarantees (runtime provides):
- Success response semantics: idempotent request IDs accepted; partial outputs are allowed only when explicitly requested via streaming=true.
- Failure taxonomy: Will return 4xx for invalid request schema, 429 for client-level throttling, 503 for transient capacity, 500 for internal errors. 503 responses will include retryable: true|false in the body.
- Compatibility guarantee: For any minor service-side patch (no contract schema change), clients on previous minor versions must continue to receive syntactically valid responses for at least 90 days. Major schema changes require an ADR and a staged migration.

2) Contract Envelope (client -> runtime):
- Every request MUST include x-rw-contract-version header. If missing, runtime will accept but emit a high-severity trace and increment a metric contract.missing.
- A minimal JSON envelope in the request body must include: client_id, request_id, intent (optional but recommended), and schema_version. Example envelope: 

{
  "client_id": "billing-service",
  "request_id": "6e0f2bd2-...",
  "intent": "latency-sensitive",
  "schema_version": "2025-11-01"
}

3) Versioning & Deprecation Rules:
- Semantic-ish versions: YYYY-MM-DD schema versions preferred for clarity.
- Deprecation window: Major schema deprecations are announced at least 60 days prior, with a compatibility shim maintained for 30 days after removal (total 90-day notice).
- Runtime will publish a compatibility-report artifact (S3 + console link) whenever a non-backwards patch is applied.

4) Client-side validation requirements:
- SDKs MUST validate required fields and fail fast with 400 for missing critical fields.
- SDKs SHOULD surface retryable and suggested_backoff_ms from responses to upstream callers.

Shard Topology Guidance

Principles:
- Locality first: keep requests that reuse KV cache or long-lived context routed to the same shard family.
- Isolation second: tenant isolation and noisy-neighbor protection trump micro-optimizations.
- Observability third: every topology decision must be explorable via dashboards and trace links.

Shard Types:
- Static Shard: Fixed membership. Use for dedicated tenants, compliance-sensitive workloads, and stateful model variants. Pros: predictable performance, easier tracing. Cons: lower utilization.
- Capacity-Driven Shard: Membership based on pre-allocated capacity and periodic rebalancing (e.g., nightly). Use for steady production traffic.
- Adaptive Shard (recommended for mixed workloads): Continually rebalances based on a control loop (traffic, tail latencies, KV-cache hit-rate). Use when workload characteristics change diurnally or bursty.

Shard Key Selection:
- Prefer a composite key: {tenant_id}:{model_version}:{pipeline_variant}. This preserves isolation and model locality.
- Avoid using user/session id alone as shard key for high-churn workloads.

Topology Configuration Table (example)

| parameter | description | example | default |
|-----------|-------------|---------|---------|
| min_shard_size | minimum workers in shard | 4 | 4 |
| max_shard_size | maximum workers in shard | 64 | 32 |
| rebalance_window_minutes | window over which we consider traffic for rebalancing | 15 | 30 |
| tail_latency_threshold_ms | p99 latency threshold to trigger scaling or split | 1200 | 1000 |
| cache_hotness_threshold | fractional hit rate considered hot | 0.65 | 0.7 |

Adaptive Sharding Control Loop (high level)

1. Collect signals: per-shard p50/p95/p99 latency, token throughput, KV cache hit-rate, queue length, GPU utilization.
2. Compute shard health and shard-level cost-efficiency score.
3. Trigger action: split, merge, scale-up, scale-down, or migrate tenants.
4. Validate via canary (10% traffic) then full rollout.

Autoscaling and Placement Policies

- Placement constraints: shards can be tagged with region, hardware-class, tenant-isolation. Scheduler respects these when allocating workers.
- Prewarming: maintain a pool of prewarmed workers by hardware-class to absorb sudden spikes. Prewarm sizing computed from 95th percentile of short bursts.
- Graceful draining: when removing a worker, set state draining, stop assigning new requests, wait for max_drain_time_ms (default 30000) or until in-flight=0.

Observability and SLOs

Required metrics (per shard & global):
- requests.total, requests.failed, responses.latency.{p50,p95,p99}, tokens.generated, kv.hit_rate, queue_length, worker.count, gpu.utilization.
- Contract-specific metrics: contract.missing, contract.version_mismatch, contract.schema_error.

SLOs (recommended):
- Availability SLO: 99.95% per region for host-api surface (excluding scheduled maintenance).
- Latency SLOs: p95 <= 350ms for short-context workloads (<64 tokens); p95 <= 1200ms for mixed workloads.
- Error budget policy: errors include 5xx and contract.schema_error; exceeding budget triggers escalation to oncall and automatic traffic throttling for non-production groups.

Alerting thresholds (examples):
- p99 latency > configured tail_latency_threshold for more than 5 minutes -> P1 alert.
- contract.missing rate > 0.1% of traffic in a 5m window -> P2 alert (investigate SDK rollout).

Performance Budget Examples (copy into runtime dashboards)

- Cost per 1k tokens: target <= $0.18 for standard models (derived metric).
- Median token generation time per token: target <= 6ms/token on gpu-v2 class for baseline models.

Rollout and Migration Procedure (schema changes or topology changes)

1. Author ADR describing change, risks, and rollback plan. Attach a compatibility matrix.
2. Implement a compatibility shim where possible (e.g., translation layer in gateway).
3. Create a canary stage: route 1-5% of traffic for 24-72 hours. Monitor contract.* metrics and SLOs.
4. If canary stable, progress to 10-25% over 24 hours, then broad rollout in staged waves (50%, 100%).
5. If regressions detected: immediately revert canary, mark rollout paused, run the rollback playbook.

Rollback playbook (quick):
1) Run shard-manager revert --deployment-id $CANARY_ID
2) Re-route traffic via routing-control set-weight --service backend=1.0 --service new-backend=0.0
3) Open incident if SLO breach or >1% user-visible errors.

Ownership and Escalation

- Service owner: eng-serving-runtime runtime-team.
- Oncall: runtime-sre rotation.
- For contract disagreements: schedule a 30-minute contract-review board with runtime-team, SDK-team, product owner.

Decision record (ADR excerpt)

Title: Adopt composite shard keys and adaptive sharding control loop
Status: accepted
Decision date: 2025-11-12
Rationale: Composite keys preserve isolation and allow locality optimizations. Adaptive sharding reduces cost for workloads with high variance while providing mechanisms to enforce tenant isolation when necessary.
Alternatives considered:
- Pure static shard topology: rejected for poor utilization on bursty workloads.
- Per-tenant dedicated shards for all customers: rejected for cost.

Open issues and future work

- We need a standardized way to store and surface per-client intent semantics in billing and routing dashboards.
- Explore machine-learning-driven shard split heuristics in the next quarter.
- Integrate shard-level replay capability for deterministic regression testing.

Appendix: Private deployment notes

- For Private deployments, the runtime will provide an opt-in compatibility-check tool that validates client requests against deployed schema. The default deprecation windows do not apply unless the customer opts into Redwood-managed updates.

Related artifacts and links

- Example compatibility-report: s3://redwood-artifacts/compatibility/compatibility-report-2025-11-12.json
- Shard manager CLI docs: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/shard-manager-cli

Owners and contacts

- Runtime architecture: Maya Patel <m.patel@redwood.ai>
- Runtime SRE lead: Diego Ramos <d.ramos@redwood.ai>
- SDK lead: Anika Shah <a.shah@redwood.ai>

Please direct questions and proposals for modification to the runtime-architecture Slack channel and attach follow-up ADRs for major changes.

title: Predictive Prefetch Orchestrator — Design & Validation
content:
Summary
-------
This document defines the Predictive Prefetch Orchestrator (PPO): a runtime component that predicts future token or KV-cache accesses and prefetches required KV pages / model artifacts into local memory or a warm cache tier. The goal is to reduce tail latency and cold-KV misses while preserving cost and fidelity SLOs. It describes architecture, scheduling interactions, configuration, validation tests, rollout plan, and incident runbooks.

Scope and goals
----------------
- Primary goal: reduce 99th/99.9th percentile token latency for long-context and multi-turn workloads by reducing on-path cache-miss stalls.
- Secondary goals: keep incremental cost per useful token < 6% of baseline; avoid fidelity regressions and avoid noisy eviction patterns that increase GPU OOM risk.
- Out of scope: model quantization decisions, model selection routing. PPO only orchestrates prefetch hints and local memory priming.

High-level architecture
-----------------------
Components (logical):
1) Predictor service (stateless microservice): serves a lightweight sequence predictor that emits prefetch hints per request. Implements a rate limit and confidence score.
2) Prefetch coordinator (in-runtime agent): receives hints, applies admission control, schedules prefetch work to worker threads or a background prefetch pool.
3) KV-cache manager (existing component): accepts explicit prefetch requests (page ids) and reports outcomes (hit, miss, duration).
4) Observability adapter: enriches traces with prefetch provenance and metrics (prefetch_count, prefetch_success, prefetch_cost_us).
5) Admission controller and scheduler hook: integrates with kernel scheduler to avoid prefetch storms and respects SLO-driven credit accounting.

Data flow (textual diagram):
- API request -> request classifier -> predictor service (async call) -> emits N prefetch hints (page_id, score, lookahead_ms) -> prefetch coordinator applies policy -> enqueues prefetch -> KV-cache manager fetches/warms pages -> request proceeds using possibly warmed KV/cache.

Predictor model and signals
---------------------------
- Predictor is intentionally small (few hundred KB parameters) to keep inference cheap and fast. It operates in two modes: deterministic rule-based (fallback) and statistical scoring (ML).
- Features used: session token histogram, user agent, route, model variant, recent completion lengths, last-k page access sequence, request timestamp, and cohort id.
- Labels for training: subsequent page access within lookahead window (e.g., 200ms) derived from production traces (shadow mode).
- Retraining cadence: weekly for high-change routes; monthly for stable routes.

Admission control & scheduler integration
-----------------------------------------
Admission policy is the safety layer that prevents prefetch work from interfering with on-path kernels. Key levers:
- Prefetch budget per-GPU per-second (pages/sec). Default: 50 pages/sec per GPU.
- Prefetch priority class: BACKGROUND_LOW, BACKGROUND_HIGH. Background_low is throttled under any kernel contention.
- Kernel credit check: prefetch pool only consumes credits from a separate prefetch bucket; if runtime kernel load > 70% or tail latency SLO is threatened, prefetches are suspended.

Configuration table (recommended defaults)
-----------------------------------------
| key | default | description |
| prefetch.enabled | true | master switch |
| prefetch.lookahead_ms | 200 | max lookahead window to consider access relevant |
| prefetch.max_pages_per_request | 6 | cap per prediction |
| prefetch.gpu_budget_pages_per_sec | 50 | budget enforced by admission controller |
| prefetch.min_score_threshold | 0.55 | predictor confidence cutoff |
| prefetch.priority_mode | BACKGROUND_LOW | default priority class |
| prefetch.shadow_mode | true | if true, metrics are collected but prefetches aren't applied to on-path traffic |

Example runtime YAML config
---------------------------
```yaml
prefetch:
  enabled: true
  lookahead_ms: 200
  max_pages_per_request: 4
  gpu_budget_pages_per_sec: 50
  min_score_threshold: 0.6
  priority_mode: BACKGROUND_HIGH
  shadow_mode: false
```

Observability & KPIs
--------------------
Minimum dashboards (per-cluster and per-route):
- Prefetch hit rate (prefetch_success / prefetch_attempts) — target > 70% for routes with high sequentiality.
- Delta tail latency (p99, p999) before vs after prefetch action — target p99 reduction >= 10ms for targeted routes.
- Prefetch-induced kernel wait time — should be < 1% of total kernel time.
- Cost delta per-useful-token — target < +6%.
- False-positive prefetch ratio (pages prefetched but not accessed in lookahead) — target < 30% for production routes.

Metric naming suggestions:
- runtime.prefetch.attempts
- runtime.prefetch.success
- runtime.prefetch.latency_ms
- runtime.prefetch.evictions_caused
- runtime.prefetch.cpu_time_ms
- runtime.prefetch.provenance (predictor_rule/modelid)

Validation and testing strategy
-------------------------------
1) Offline validation: train predictor on historical shadow traces and compute precision/recall w.r.t. lookahead windows. Generate cohort-level charts (by route/model/sequence-length).
2) Synthetic replay: use the operational workload simulator to replay requests and run PPO in shadow mode. Collect metrics: predicted pages, accessed pages, cost.
3) Shadow-canary: enable shadow_mode=false only for a small set of pods (5% traffic) but with prefetch priority = BACKGROUND_LOW and fast rollback toggle. Monitor KPIs for 48h.
4) Canary with adaptive throttle: increase active prefetch traffic to 20% and enable dynamic budget. Continue validation for 7 days and run A/B analysis for latency and cost.

Shadow experiment commands (examples)
------------------------------------
- Toggle shadow mode (kubectl):
  kubectl patch deployment/runtime-pool -p '{"spec":{"template":{"metadata":{"annotations":{"runtime.prefs.prefetch-shadow":"true"}}}}}'
- Query prefetch metrics (promql):
  sum(rate(runtime_prefetch_attempts_total[5m])) by (cluster, route)
  sum(rate(runtime_prefetch_success_total[5m])) / sum(rate(runtime_prefetch_attempts_total[5m]))

Rollout checklist
------------------
1) Offline precision >= 0.65 and recall >= 0.35 for target routes.
2) Shadow-mode pilot: prefetch_success >= 50% and false_positive <= 40%.
3) Canary: no >25% regression in p99SLO and prefetch_cost_delta within budget for 48h.
4) Gradual ramp: 5% -> 20% -> 50% -> 100% with 24–72h stabilization windows and automated rollback on SLA breaches.

Safety & fallback patterns
-------------------------
- Automatic suspend: if runtime.p99_latency increases by >10% over 15m or prefetch_eviction_events > threshold, suspend prefetch globally and notify oncall.
- Degraded planner: switch predictor to deterministic rule-based prefetch (e.g., last-2-pages prefetch) if model confidence drops.
- Eviction-aware prefetch: track prefetch-caused evictions and deprioritize prefetches that historically caused cross-tenant memory pressure.

Incident runbook (cache-thrash loop)
------------------------------------
Trigger: sudden spike in cache evictions correlated with prefetch.activity and rising p99 latency.
1) Pager routes to PPO-oncall.
2) Run quick inspection: check metrics
   - pref_attempts = curl "http://metrics/api?query=rate(runtime_prefetch_attempts_total[5m])"
   - evictions = curl "http://metrics/api?query=rate(runtime_prefetch_evictions_total[5m])"
3) If evictions / attempts > 0.2 and p99 latency > SLO, execute emergency suspend:
   curl -XPOST http://runtime-admin/api/prefetch/suspend
4) If suspend is successful, monitor p99 for 10m. If stable, adjust GPU budget down (e.g., -50%) and re-enable with BACKGROUND_LOW.
5) Postmortem steps: collect traces, predictor inputs, and candidate root causes (miscalibrated score, dataset shift, route misclassification).

Operational playbooks and experiments
------------------------------------
- Periodic prefetch audit (weekly): run the Audit Script (see below) to estimate wasted pages and correlation with evictions.
- Controlled stress test: synthetic-burst profile to measure prefetch behavior under admission constraints.
- KPI drift detector: daily job that surfaces routes with falling prefetch precision or rising false positives.

Audit script (pseudo-CLI)
-------------------------
# Download 24h shadow traces for route X and compute metrics
redwood traces extract --route X --since 24h | redwood prefetch-audit --lookahead 200 --output /tmp/audit.json
redwood prefetch-audit-report /tmp/audit.json --format html --out /tmp/prefetch-audit-routeX.html

Developer guidelines for contributors
------------------------------------
- Prefer simple predictors and keep feature sets stable for production routes.
- Annotate predictor versions in metric provenance (predictor:v2).
- Add unit tests for admission controller thresholds and an end-to-end shadow-mode integration test.
- Keep retraining dataset windows (e.g., last 14 days) configurable per-route.

Ownership and contacts
----------------------
- PPO feature owner: Sasha Nguyen (runtime team) — oncall: runtime-pgo@redwood.ai
- Predictor ML owner: Arjun Mehta (applied-ml)
- Observability owner: Leila Gómez (eng-sre)

Appendix: small example of prefetch hint JSON
--------------------------------------------
{
  "request_id": "abcd-1234",
  "route": "/chat/gpt-extended",
  "hints": [
    {"page_id": "kv:mdl:1234:page:42", "score": 0.78, "lookahead_ms": 180},
    {"page_id": "kv:mdl:1234:page:43", "score": 0.61, "lookahead_ms": 180}
  ],
  "predictor_version": "v2025-09-03",
  "timestamp": "2025-11-20T16:23:04Z"
}
Notes and migration considerations
---------------------------------
- Start with read-heavy routes and long-context chat routes that have high sequential locality. Avoid bursty short-completion routes for early pilots.
- Coordinate with kernel-scheduler owners to add the prefetch priority class to the scheduling credit model.
- Expected incremental infra cost: small CPU overhead for predictor service + network egress to KV tier. Estimate: ~0.5–2% increase in infra cost for routes where prefetch is enabled.

Related documents
------------------
- KV prefetch audit guide (profiling-playbook) — required reading prior to pilot.
- Scheduler credit model and admission controller (kernel-and-scheduling) — integration notes.

Change log
----------
- 2025-03-11: initial draft (Sasha Nguyen).
- 2025-06-02: added synthetic replay protocol and YAML examples (Arjun Mehta review).
- 2025-11-20: added incident runbook and audit CLI (Leila Gómez review).
- 2026-01-15: published with updated thresholds and rollout checklist (Sasha Nguyen).

title: Latency economics and tiered routing playbook
content:
Overview

Purpose
This playbook defines the design, operational controls, and experiment/runbook procedures for latency-aware, cost-conscious tiered routing in the Redwood serving runtime. It connects SLO targets, per-tenant economics, and fallback policies so routing decisions preserve customer-facing latency SLOs while minimizing unit cost.

Scope
- Applies to multi-tenant hosted and Dedicated pools where requests may be routed across model variants, regions, and capacity tiers.
- Not intended to replace per-customer contractual routing written in the control plane (those are higher-level policies implemented using these primitives).

Goals and design constraints
1) SLO preservation: prioritize meeting 99th percentile latency objectives for customer-facing routes.
2) Cost sensitivity: route to lower-cost model variants or capacity tiers when doing so will not materially violate SLOs or degrade quality beyond tolerance.
3) Safety: provide deterministic fallbacks and observability to avoid routing flaps and oscillation.
4) Incremental deployability: new routing heuristics must be testable against shadow traffic and staged canaries.

Key concepts and terminology
- Tier: a logical grouping of capacity (e.g., premium-dedicated, shared-hosted, burst-spot).
- Model variant: exact model artifact plus quantization/precision profile (e.g., gptx-1.2-int8-v2).
- Fidelity: qualitative measure of expected output quality for a given variant.
- Cost-per-token (CPT): estimated operator cost for serving a token on a given variant/tier.
- Latency budget: per-request remaining time to meet the configured SLO.
- Route policy: declarative rule combining selectors (tenant, route, weight) and decision predicates.

Routing decision flow (high-level)
1. Admission: validate request metadata, tenant allowances, and route-level constraints.
2. Classification: tag request with workload profile (sequence-length estimate, sync/async, priority).
3. Candidate generation: list compatible model variants and tiers.
4. Scoring: compute score for each candidate: score = alpha * latency_score + beta * cost_score + gamma * fidelity_penalty.
5. Selection and reservation: pick highest-scoring candidate that satisfies hard predicates (region affinity, contractual pinning). Reserve slot capacity (kernel admission).
6. Execution and post-eval: if execution violates latency budget or quality regression, trigger fallback/rollback.

SLO and economics math (practical formulae)
- Expected latency per candidate L_c = median_kernel_latency(candidate, shape) + network_estimate(candidate.region). Use histogram-backed estimates.
- Cost per request R_c = CPT(candidate) * expected_tokens(request). For batching, use amortized cost models (see amortized_cost_table below).
- Composite utility U_c = (SLO_headroom(c)/SLO_target) - lambda * (R_c / R_ref) - mu * FidelityPenalty(c). We treat SLO_headroom as max(0, SLO_target - E[L_c]).
- Decision threshold: pick candidate with max U_c subject to U_c > U_min else route to fallback (higher tier).

Config table (example values)
|| key || description || example || notes ||
|| slo.target || target latency (ms) for route || 95 ms (P99) || route-level override ||
|| lambda || cost weight in utility || 0.8 || tuned per product vertical ||
|| mu || fidelity penalty weight || 1.2 || fidelity penalty normalized [0,1] ||
|| U_min || minimal acceptable utility || -0.2 || prevents overly cheap but slow picks ||
|| cost_ref || normalization constant for cost || $0.0005/token || updated by billing team weekly ||

Operational rules and safety knobs
- Circuit-breaker: if the selected candidate's observed P99 exceeds slo.target + 20% for 5 mins, route flow is temporarily pinned to next-safe tier and an alert is fired (severity P2).
- Dampening window: do not switch routing preference for a tenant more than once per 60s to avoid oscillation.
- Shadow testing: new candidate variants must be validated by 1 hour of 10% shadow traffic before being eligible for live routing.
- Canary rollout: initial 1% of live traffic with metric-based escalation gates (latency, quality regression).

Runbook: outage or mass-latency incident (step-by-step)
1. Detect: Pager triggers from latency SLO alert (P99 exceeded for > 3m across a route).
2. Triage: identify which candidate types account for majority of slow requests (use the routing decisions histogram - see observability queries section).
3. Immediate mitigation (fast path): enable route-level override to force-route to premium-dedicated variant or raise U_min to deprioritize low-cost candidates. Command-line: 

sh
redwoodctl routes override set --route customer.chat --variant premium-gptx-1 --reason "p99-latency-spike"

4. Validate: watch P99 and token drop rates for 10m. If steady, keep override while root cause investigation continues.
5. Permanent remediation: revert to automated routing only after corrective changes (kernel patch, region failover, or cost recalibration) and a successful canary run.

Telemetry & observability contract
Minimum signals required for safe operation and postmortem:
- per-route, per-variant P50/P95/P99 latency histograms (1s bucketing for 1m window)
- per-route request counts and error counts by variant and tier
- candidate selection reasons (why candidate selected: lowest cost / fidelity / pinned)
- route decision churn metric (switches/min per tenant)
- shadow validation pass/fail rates and quality regression counts
- amortized cost per request and per-token CPI-like metric

Example observability queries (PromQL-like pseudocode)
- P99 latency for route "customer.chat":
redwood_latency_seconds_bucket{route="customer.chat",job="runtime"} -> histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(...)))
- Fraction of requests routed to low-cost tier:
sum(rate(requests_total{tier="shared"} [5m])) / sum(rate(requests_total[5m]))

Quality safety and fidelity checks
- Automatic prompt-level checks: for generation routes with fidelity-sensitive SLAs, run lightweight rerank/consistency checks in shadow before returning low-fidelity results live. If rerank confidence < threshold, fall back to higher-fidelity variant.
- Regression window: if quality metric delta exceeds 1.5x baseline for 10m, pin variant and trigger remediation.

Operational exercises and experiments (lab recipes)
Each experiment below should be scheduled in the runtime lab environment and follow the experiment governance checklist (owned, hypothesis, rollback, telemetry).
1. Cost-pressure response drill
   - Hypothesis: under sustained increase in cost_ref by 25%, routing will shift to cheaper variants without violating P99.
   - Steps: bump lambda to 1.6 for a test tenant, enable shadowing for new variants, monitor P99, fidelity.
   - Success: no >10% increase in P99 and fidelity regression < threshold.
2. Synthetic tail latency injection
   - Hypothesis: the dampening window prevents oscillation when kernels degrade intermittently.
   - Steps: inject 200 ms additional kernel tail for candidate A for 7m and observe routing churn.
   - Success: churn < 0.5 switches/min and circuit-breaker triggers if needed.
3. Canary for new quantized variant
   - Steps: 10% shadow -> 1% live -> 5% live -> 20% live; at each stage validate latency, quality, cost.

Rollout checklist for routing policy changes
- Author a policy PR including: policy YAML, target routes, and experiment plan.
- Run 1 hour of shadow validation on staging with traffic representative of production (latency and token shape).
- Create a canary run for a pilot tenant for 24h with automatic rollback gates for P99 and quality.
- Post-canonicalization: add telemetry enrichment and update billing/cost models if CPT adjustments required.

Ownership and escalation
- Policy author (owner): eng-serving-runtime/routing (primary)
- Oncall escalation: runtime SRE -> runtime platform lead -> product owner for route
- SLA incident owner: whoever owns the route in the Console product mapping table.

Appendices
A. Example policy YAML (simplified)

---
route: customer.chat
slo:
  p99_ms: 95
  emergency_fallback_ms: 200
policies:
  - id: prefer_low_cost_with_headroom
    selectors:
      - tenant_tier: standard
    scoring:
      lambda: 0.8
      mu: 1.2
      alpha: 0.6
    predicates:
      - region_affinity: true
      - fidelity_min: 0.85
    safety:
      shadow_validation: 1h
      dampening_seconds: 60
---

B. Amortized cost note
- When batching occurs, compute amortized CPT by dividing measured kernel execution cost by average batch size observed in the same time window. This prevents underestimating cost for low-latency but small-batch shapes.

C. Related diagnostics (runbook quick commands)
- Show recent routing decision histogram (last 15m):
redwoodctl metrics query --name routing_decisions_histogram --route customer.chat --since 15m
- Force a policy override:
redwoodctl routes override set --route customer.chat --policy "pin-premium" --reason "p99-spike"

D. Change log
- 2024-05-12: Initial draft and validation experiments documented.
- 2025-03-18: Added cost-normalization guidance and amortized-cost section.
- 2025-11-03: Clarified circuit-breaker thresholds and added canary rollout gates.

Contact and further reading
- Owner: eng-serving-runtime/routing (Slack #runtime-routing)
