- Recommended follow-ups: delta-routing-and-cost-partitioning-architecture-2026, runtime-observability-self-heal-orchestration-manual-2026

title: Runtime Execution Cascades and Soft-Fail Synthesis
content:
Summary:

This handbook defines the "execution cascade" model we adopted in 2027 for orchestrating multi-tier inference execution, how kernels and scheduler policies participate in graceful degradation, and the operational playbooks for profiling and benchmarking cascade behaviors. It is intended for runtime engineers, SREs, and product owners responsible for model rollouts, SLA preservation, and incident mitigation.

Why an execution cascade?

- Modern inference requires cross-layer coordination: model variants, kernel capabilities, KV cache state, and router-level routing all affect end-to-end latency and quality.
- The execution cascade formalizes ordered fallback steps (fastest/cheapest -> compatible fallbacks -> degraded modes) and the safety checks and instrumentation needed to avoid quality regression or outage.

Scope and assumptions:

- Applies to Redwood hosted + Dedicated runtime pools.
- Assumes models are registered with a variant graph (primary, low-latency quantized, high-fidelity CPU fallback).
- Assumes runtime kernel telemetry (kernel_id, slot_id, preempt_count) and request traces are emitted to the observability pipeline.

1) Conceptual model

Execution cascade layers (top-down):

1. Serve fast: low-latency GPU kernels (best throughput, quantized).
2. Serve fallback-1: compatible kernel variant (slower but high fidelity).
3. Serve fallback-2: CPU or remote microservice for short-tail completions.
4. Degraded response: length-limited generation + structured error with explicit quality flag.

Key properties:

- Deterministic ordering: cascades are declared per-model and pinned at route level.
- Circuit breakers and hysteresis: transition thresholds use smoothing windows to avoid oscillation.
- Quality gates: each downgrade step must pass an automated eval suite before being allowed in the graph.

2) Runtime integration: scheduler and kernel interaction

Scheduling primitives used in cascades:

- Slot reservation: short-term exclusive kernel slots are reserved for high-priority fast-path requests.
- Soft-preempt windows: kernels expose a preemptability flag; scheduler will only preempt if preempt_count < N and no active KV update operations exist.
- Credit buckets: each tenant has a credit balance for fast-path tokens; negative balance triggers cascade routing.

Example scheduler policy (YAML):

policy_name: cascade-alpha
fast_path:
  kernel_selector: "gpu-quantized-v2"
  token_credit_threshold: 1000
  preempt_policy: "soft"
fallbacks:
  - kernel_selector: "gpu-fp16-v1"
    max_seq_len: 512
  - kernel_selector: "cpu-approximate"
    max_seq_len: 256
rollout:
  canary_ratio: 0.02
  smoothing_window_ms: 30000

(Copy/paste safe YAML shown above).

3) Profiling playbook for cascade behavior

Objective: capture pre- and post-degradation traces that highlight where requests moved through the cascade and why.

Telemetry to collect:

- Request timeline (router_enqueue, kernel_dispatch, kernel_complete, response_emit) in ms.
- Kernel attributes: kernel_id, binary_version, occupancy_pct, sm_util, preempt_count.
- KV cache metrics: hit_rate, warmup_time_ms, eviction_count.
- Route decisions: route_reason (credit_exhausted, kernel_unavailable, model_quality_fallback).

Sampling strategy:

- Stratified sampling by latency bucket: p50/p95/p99 and by route variant.
- Correlate any tail events with kernel switch events.

Investigation steps:

1. Reproduce with a synthetic corpus mirroring production tokens-per-request and sequence length distribution. Use the workload-replay tool:

redwoodctl replay --target cascade-alpha --corpus s3://replay-buckets/corpus-2028-01 --concurrency 200 --duration 10m

2. Enable verbose kernel traces for a 5 minute window: set kernel_trace_rate=1.
3. Export traces to traceviz and build a waterfall view focused on requests that encountered >1 fallback.

Root causes commonly found:

- Credit exhaustion due to aggressive burst traffic from a single route.
- Kernel binary mismatch causing deterministic rejection; scheduler then routes to fallback.
- Subtle latency amplification from slot-slicing under mixed small/large sequence workloads.

4) Benchmark protocol for validating cascade safety

Goal: measure impact of cascading on p99 latency, token cost, and quality relative to baseline.

Bench steps (standardized):

- Baseline: run model on fast-path solo for 30m, measure p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec.
- Integrated: enable cascade graph and run same corpus for 30m.
- Stress: inject a synthetic burst (10x baseline RPS) for 2 minutes, observe transition time and hysteresis.

Metrics to record (CSV):

- timestamp, route, variant, p50_ms, p95_ms, p99_ms, tokens_per_sec, kernel_occupancy_pct, kvcache_hit_rate, quality_score_delta

Pass criteria for rollout gate:

- p99 increase < 1.5x baseline AND
- average quality_score_delta <= 0.03 (on the canonical eval set) AND
- cascade transition time <= 45s for burst stress test

5) Release and canary checklist (runtime + scheduling ops)

Pre-release:

- Verify model variant graph is registered and has quality metadata.
- Confirm kernel binary compatibility matrix for all targeted accelerators.
- Register scheduler policy in the staging cluster and run the benchmark protocol.

Canary rollout steps:

1. Deploy policy to 1% of traffic in staging for 1h. Validate metrics.
2. Expand to 2% in production for 30m; run quick health checks and smoke tests.
3. Observe circuit breakers: if any of the following triggers, rollback automatically:
   - sustained p99 > 2x baseline for 10m
   - KV cache warmup failure (hit_rate < 20% after 10m)
   - quality gate breached (automated eval threshold)

Commands (examples):

# attach policy to route
redwoodctl routing apply --route my-service-chat --policy cascade-alpha

# monitor canary metrics
redwoodctl metrics tail --route my-service-chat --window 15m --filters p99,kvcache_hit_rate,quality_delta

6) Operational runbooks (quick actions)

A. Detecting unintended cascade amplification

1. Symptom: p99 spikes while fast-path occupancy down; multiple requests show fallback_reason=credit_exhausted.
2. Action: increase token_credit_threshold by 50% for the route, or temporarily reassign to higher-capacity pool.
3. Long-term: adjust per-tenant burst throttle and improve prewarming of KV cache for the heavy route.

B. Kernel binary incompatibility (hard rejections)

1. Symptom: kernel_dispatch fails with error code KERN_BIN_MISMATCH; router jumps to fallback-1.
2. Action: pin router to older kernel binary until new binary rollout completes.
2a. redwoodctl kernel rollback --binary gpu-quantized-v2 --to gpu-quantized-v1

C. Degraded response observed (quality flag set)

1. Symptom: increased 'quality_flag: degraded' in responses and customer complaints.
2. Action: route traffic to primary variant for VIP customers and open a regression investigation ticket.

7) Known issues observed (non-exhaustive)

- Soft-fail amplification under opcode mismatch (INC-2027-1420): certain kernel ops return transient opcode-mapping errors which cause repeated fallback loops for small batches. Mitigation: apply opcode compatibility shim (deployable via kernel plugin) and add a short-lived blacklist for the offending kernel instance.
- Quant-crossover drift: repeated model re-quantizations during long canaries cause small quality drift detectable by the eval harness. Mitigation: enforce quantization-stability check in the model onboarding pipeline.
- Slot-slicing tail spikes: when mixing tiny chat completions with long-document summaries, slot-slicing can starve large requests and increase their p99. Mitigation: enforce separate slot pools per workload shape or enable sequence-length-aware admission.

8) Post-incident diagnostics checklist

- Export request traces for the 30 minutes before and after the detected spike.
- Correlate with kernel rollout events and scheduler policy changes.
- Run the parallel replay at 2x concurrency to validate the hypothesised mitigation.
- Update the cascade policy (token thresholds, hysteresis) and re-run the benchmark protocol.

9) Ownership and escalation

- Primary owners: runtime-scheduler team (oncall: runtime-scheduler@redwood.internal)
- Secondary: serving-runtime-infra team (oncall: serving-infra@redwood.internal)
- Escalation: if customer-impacting (> 5% failed requests or p99 > 2x baseline for > 30m) alert Platform Incident Manager and set incident severity to Sev2.

10) Appendix: templates and helpers

A) Incident tag sample (use in issue tracker):

labels: [runtime-cascade, kernel-fallback, priority-high]
summary: "cascade amplification — route=my-service-chat — observed 4x p99"

B) Quick YAML for sequence-aware admission (example):

admission:
  policy: sequence-aware
  buckets:
    - max_seq: 128
      pool: small-slot-pool
    - max_seq: 1024
      pool: large-slot-pool

C) Benchmark CSV header (copy into bench-scripts):

timestamp,route,variant,p50_ms,p95_ms,p99_ms,tokens_per_sec,kernel_occupancy_pct,kvcache_hit_rate,quality_score_delta

References and links:

- Runtime execution contracts and fallback patterns (internal link).
- Scheduler policy language specification (internal link).
- Profiling playbook: waterfall and trace correlation (internal link).

Change log:

- 2027-11-12: Initial draft and design notes (Amina Patel).
- 2027-12-20: Added benchmark protocol and scheduler YAML (Marcus Chen).
- 2028-02-20: Finalized runbooks and known-issues matrix; published (Amina Patel).

If you have questions or need a walkthrough, add a comment on this page or ping the runtime-scheduler channel.

title: Cache Hit-Rate Dashboards Spec (Prefix + KV Cache Telemetry)
content:
## Summary
This page defines the **Grafana dashboard set** and **alert rules** for the new prefix/KV cache telemetry emitted by the serving runtime. It is intended to support:
- **SRE oncall** triage for regressions (hit-rate drops, eviction pressure, telemetry gaps)
- **Runtime/Platform** debugging (miss reason attribution, request-shape sensitivity)
- **Product/Optimize** validation (is caching effective enough to recommend changes?)

This spec is deliberately opinionated about:
- **Filters and breakdowns** that match how Redwood operates (model/route/deployment/region/request shape)
- **Cardinality controls** (avoid per-tenant explosions; use allowlisted route/model identifiers)
- **Operational readiness** (panels that distinguish real behavior changes vs missing telemetry)

---

## Audience and primary use-cases
### Audience
- SRE/Observability (primary)
- Runtime (cache + scheduler)
- Platform/Telemetry (tagging, ingestion, sampling)
- Support/CS (secondary; for customer investigations)

### Use-cases
1) **“Why did cost/token jump?”** → correlate hit-rate drop with miss reasons (e.g., version_mismatch, policy_disabled) and eviction pressure.
2) **“Is caching working for this workload?”** → inspect reuse depth by prompt-length buckets and wasted prefill.
3) **“Is this a real regression or a telemetry issue?”** → check telemetry health panels and ingestion drop indicators.
4) **“Where should we tune knobs?”** → identify top routes/models with low hit-rate but high reuse opportunity, and whether memory pressure is limiting.

---

## Dashboard set (Grafana)
We ship three dashboards under: **Platform → Runtime Cache Telemetry**

1) **Cache Overview (SRE)**
- Goal: fast detection and triage across prod
- Default scope: prod, all regions, top models

2) **Cache Deep Dive (Runtime/Platform)**
- Goal: explain *why* (miss reasons, request-shape buckets, partial reuse)
- Default scope: single model + region, drill into route

3) **Cache Telemetry Health**
- Goal: detect pipeline breaks, label drops, sampling/rate-limit misconfig
- Default scope: prod, all regions

Each dashboard must:
- Support consistent variable names (see below)
- Avoid “Top N by tenant_id” style queries
- Prefer **recording rules** for expensive aggregations

---

## Data sources and joining assumptions
### Metric source
- Runtime emits counters/histograms/gauges to **Prometheus** (via OTel collector).
- Grafana queries Prometheus.

### Required labels (must be present on all cache metrics)
- `env` (e.g., prod, staging)
- `region` (cloud region, e.g., us-east-1)
- `deployment_mode` (hosted | dedicated | private)
- `model` (allowlisted stable model identifier, e.g., llama3.1-70b)
- `model_version` (allowlisted version string; not raw commit hash)

### Optional labels (only on some metrics; use with care)
- `route` (allowlisted route identifier; never raw customer-provided names)
- `route_tier` (shared | premium | internal)
- `prompt_len_bucket` (bucketed; e.g., 0-256, 257-512, 513-1024, 1025-2048, 2049+)
- `request_shape` (bucketed; e.g., chat_streaming, chat_non_streaming, completions)
- `miss_reason` (stable enum)

### Non-goals
- No raw prompts, no per-request IDs, no per-tenant IDs as metric labels.

---

## Global dashboard variables (Grafana templating)
All dashboards must expose the same variables to make screenshots/runbooks reusable.

**Variables**
| Variable | Type | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `env` | dropdown | prod | include staging for rollout validation |
| `deployment_mode` | dropdown | all | hosted/dedicated/private |
| `region` | multi-select | all | keep “all” as default |
| `model` | multi-select | top 10 by traffic | allowlisted model IDs |
| `model_version` | multi-select | all | used mainly in Deep Dive |
| `route` | multi-select | none | only in Deep Dive; allowlisted |
| `request_shape` | dropdown | all | chat_streaming is critical |
| `prompt_len_bucket` | dropdown | all | only shown on bucketed panels |
| `window` | dropdown | 5m | allowed: 1m/5m/15m |

**Default time range**
- Overview: last 6h (with quick picks 1h/24h/7d)
- Deep Dive: last 1h (with quick picks 15m/6h)
- Telemetry Health: last 24h

---

## Metric conventions referenced by this spec
This spec uses the following canonical concepts (exact metric names may evolve; dashboards should use the recording rules where provided).

### Core concepts
- **Prefix cache hit-rate**: fraction of prefill tokens served from prefix cache (token-weighted), plus request-weighted view.
- **KV cache reuse effectiveness**: how much previously computed KV was reused during decode/prefill for multi-turn and repeated prompts.
- **Miss reasons** (stable enum):
  - `capacity` (insufficient cache capacity / allocation failed)
  - `ttl_expired`
  - `policy_disabled` (caching disabled by config/route)
  - `hash_mismatch` (canonicalization mismatch)
  - `version_mismatch` (model_version incompatibility)
  - `unknown`
- **Eviction pressure**: gauges/counters that explain drops in hit-rate.
- **Wasted prefill**: prefill tokens that did not lead to subsequent reuse due to misses/evictions (token-weighted).

### Recommended recording rules (dashboards should prefer these)
To keep Grafana responsive and reduce PromQL repetition, the telemetry pipeline should expose recording rules similar to:
- `:cache_prefix_hit_rate_tokens_5m` (token-weighted)
- `:cache_prefix_hit_rate_requests_5m` (request-weighted)
- `:cache_kv_reuse_rate_tokens_5m`
- `:cache_wasted_prefill_rate_tokens_5m`
- `:cache_eviction_rate_5m`
- `:cache_memory_pressure_5m` (smoothed gauge)

If recording rules are not available in an environment, dashboards may use direct PromQL, but must be reviewed by Telemetry (owner: Nadia Rahman) before shipping.

---

## Dashboard 1: Cache Overview (SRE)
**Purpose:** quickly answer “is caching healthy?” and “where is it broken?”

### Row A — Executive summary
1) **Prefix cache hit-rate (token-weighted)**
- Viz: time series
- Breakdown: by `deployment_mode` (stacked optional)
- Filters: env/region/model
- Notes: token-weighted is the best cost proxy.

2) **Prefix cache hit-rate (request-weighted)**
- Viz: time series
- Breakdown: by `deployment_mode`
- Notes: catches cases where a small set of long prompts masks broader regressions.

3) **KV cache reuse rate (token-weighted)**
- Viz: time series
- Breakdown: by model

4) **Wasted prefill rate (token-weighted)**
- Viz: time series
- Breakdown: by deployment_mode
- Interpretation: rising wasted prefill alongside stable hit-rate often indicates eviction thrash or locality issues.

### Row B — Where is it happening?
5) **Hit-rate heatmap by region**
- Viz: heatmap/table
- Dimensions: `region` x `model`
- Display: last 30m avg, plus delta vs previous 30m

6) **Top regressions (route/model)**
- Viz: table
- Columns: model, route, current hit-rate, week baseline, delta, traffic (req/s), wasted prefill
- Guardrails:
  - Only show routes in allowlist
  - Require minimum traffic threshold (e.g., > 1 req/s over 30m) to reduce noise

### Row C — Why is it happening?
7) **Miss reasons (prefix cache) — distribution**
- Viz: stacked area
- Breakdown: `miss_reason`
- Scope: aggregated (no route by default)

8) **Eviction rate and memory pressure**
- Viz: dual-axis time series
- Metrics: eviction_count rate + memory pressure gauge

9) **Version mismatch misses (early warning)**
- Viz: time series
- Filters: model + model_version (optional)
- Notes: spikes often correlate with rollouts; should be caught quickly.

### Row D — Telemetry sanity (quick checks)
10) **Cache telemetry ingestion volume**
- Viz: time series
- Metric: total cache metric samples ingested / dropped
- Notes: used to distinguish real hit-rate drop vs ingestion label-drop.

11) **“Zero hit-rate” detector**
- Viz: stat panel
- Logic: flags if hit counters are flatline while request traffic is non-zero.

---

## Dashboard 2: Cache Deep Dive (Runtime/Platform)
**Purpose:** explain root cause with high-signal breakdowns without cardinality blowups.

### Row A — Scope and workload shape
1) **Traffic and token volume**
- Viz: time series
- Panels:
  - request rate
  - prefill tokens/sec
  - decode tokens/sec
- Notes: always interpret hit-rate changes in context of traffic mix.

2) **Prompt length distribution**
- Viz: histogram/stacked bar
- Dimension: `prompt_len_bucket`

3) **Request shape mix**
- Viz: stacked bar
- Dimension: `request_shape`

### Row B — Prefix cache effectiveness
4) **Prefix hit-rate by prompt_len_bucket**
- Viz: multi-series line
- Breakdown: `prompt_len_bucket`
- Notes: regression isolated to long prompts usually points to capacity/eviction pressure.

5) **Prefix reuse depth (reused tokens) distribution**
- Viz: heatmap
- Dimension: reuse_depth_bucket (if available) vs time
- Notes: validates canonicalization and multi-turn reuse.

6) **Partial hit semantics (optional panel)**
- Viz: stacked series
- Display: full-hit vs partial-hit vs miss (token-weighted)
- Notes: if partial-hit rises while full-hit drops, check prompt canonicalization drift.

### Row C — KV cache effectiveness
7) **KV reuse rate by request_shape**
- Viz: multi-series line
- Breakdown: request_shape
- Notes: chat_streaming often behaves differently; look for retry artifacts.

8) **Batched prefill attribution guard panel**
- Viz: stat + sparkline
- Purpose: detect anomalies consistent with continuous batching misattribution.

### Row D — Miss reason attribution
9) **Miss reasons by route (top 10 routes only)**
- Viz: table
- Columns: route, miss_reason (top), miss share, hit-rate, wasted prefill
- Guardrails:
  - hard limit to 10 routes
  - minimum traffic threshold

10) **Miss reasons over time (selected route)**
- Viz: stacked area
- Filters: route

### Row E — Eviction and memory
11) **Evictions by reason**
- Viz: stacked area
- Breakdown: eviction_reason (if available) or “evicted_total” only

12) **Cache memory utilization**
- Viz: time series
- Metrics: bytes used, bytes max, utilization %
- Notes: show per cache type (prefix vs kv) where applicable.

13) **Pressure vs hit-rate correlation**
- Viz: scatter plot
- X: memory pressure / utilization
- Y: hit-rate
- Group: prompt_len_bucket
- Notes: should only be used with sufficient sample count.

### Row F — Wasted prefill analysis
14) **Wasted prefill rate by miss_reason**
- Viz: stacked area
- Notes: a large wasted prefill share attributed to `hash_mismatch` suggests canonicalization opportunity.

15) **Wasted prefill per request (p50/p95)**
- Viz: time series
- Notes: spikes often precede cost incidents.

---

## Dashboard 3: Cache Telemetry Health
**Purpose:** ensure telemetry is present, correctly tagged, and within sampling/rate-limit expectations.

### Panels
1) **Samples ingested vs dropped (cache metrics)**
- Viz: time series
- Breakdown: drop_reason (cardinality_guard, rate_limit, malformed)

2) **Label presence completeness**
- Viz: table
- Rows: required labels (env/region/deployment_mode/model/model_version)
- Columns: % series missing label over last 1h

3) **Series cardinality (cache metrics)**
- Viz: time series + stat
- Thresholds: warn at 80% of budget; critical at 95%

4) **Counter reset detector**
- Viz: stat
- Purpose: identify restarts misinterpreted as behavior changes.

5) **Trace annotation volume (if enabled)**
- Viz: time series
- Notes: ensure spans are sampled and not exploding.

---

## Alerting spec (Prometheus alert rules)
Alerts are *guardrails*, not customer SLAs. Prefer **ticket** over **page** unless there is strong evidence of customer impact.

### Paging alerts (SRE oncall)
1) **Cache hit-rate sudden drop (token-weighted) — global**
- Condition: hit-rate down > X% relative to 7d baseline for 15m, and traffic above minimum
- Action: page
- Notes: baseline comparison should be workload-aware (exclude low traffic).

2) **Telemetry missing / ingestion drop**
- Condition: request traffic present but cache hit/miss counters flatline OR drop rate above threshold for 10m
- Action: page
- Runbook: Cache Telemetry Pipeline Incident Runbook

3) **Eviction pressure critical**
- Condition: utilization > 95% for 15m AND eviction rate elevated
- Action: page
- Notes: include region/model in alert labels; avoid route in alert labels.

### Ticket-only alerts
4) **Version mismatch miss spike**
- Condition: version_mismatch miss share > threshold for 30m
- Action: ticket to Runtime + Release Eng

5) **Hash mismatch elevated (canonicalization opportunity)**
- Action: ticket to Product/Optimize and Runtime

6) **Wasted prefill elevated**
- Action: ticket; attach Deep Dive dashboard link with model/region pre-filled.

### Alert labels (cardinality-safe)
Alerts must include only:
- env, region, deployment_mode, model (optional), severity
Avoid route/model_version unless strictly necessary; use annotations to include “top offenders” as text.

---

## Dashboard drill-down and runbook links
All dashboards must include pinned links (top of page):
- Cache Telemetry Pipeline Incident Runbook
- Cache Telemetry Validation Checklist
- Cache Efficiency SLO Proposal

For Overview panels, each heatmap/table row should link to Deep Dive with variables pre-populated (region/model, optionally route).

---

## Operational notes and pitfalls
- **Workload mix changes** can move hit-rate without any regression. Always check prompt_len_bucket and request_shape mix before escalating.
- **Streaming retries** can distort counters if regression is reintroduced; use the Deep Dive “retry/streaming sanity” panels.
- **Batched prefill** can misattribute hits; the Deep Dive guard panel is required until we have 2+ stable releases.
- If you see **hit-rate = 0%** but traffic is healthy, check Telemetry Health for label drops and cardinality guards.

---

## Acceptance criteria (for this spec)
Dashboards are considered “shippable” when:
- Overview loads in < 10s on prod for last 6h
- Deep Dive loads in < 15s with a single model + region selected
- No panel requires adding a high-cardinality label (tenant_id, raw route names, prompt hashes)
- At least one successful oncall drill: identify (a) real hit-rate regression and (b) ingestion label-drop incident using dashboards alone

---

## Ownership
- Dashboard owner: **Allison Grant (Observability)**
- Alert owner/approver: **Sean Gallagher (SRE)**
- Metrics schema owner: **Nadia Rahman (Telemetry)**
- Runtime subject-matter reviewers: **Omar El-Sayed**, **Sofia Ivanova**

Change policy: any changes that add labels, expand breakdown dimensions, or introduce new expensive queries require review from Telemetry + SRE.

title: Graceful Fidelity Staircase and Degradation Modes
content:
Overview

This document defines the "graceful fidelity staircase": a deliberate, observable sequence of degradation steps the serving runtime may take when capacity, latency, or cost constraints demand reduced resource usage or model fidelity. The staircase is intended to preserve availability and SLOs while minimizing user-visible quality regressions.

Goals
- Provide a single, auditable decision model for runtime-initiated fidelity changes.
- Make each degradation step reversible and safely testable in canaries.
- Tie telemetry signals and SLO thresholds to explicit rollback and escalation actions.
- Standardize operator runbooks and automation hooks for fidelity-layer transitions.

Scope and non-goals
- Scope: hosted, dedicated, and private runtime deployments managed by Redwood inference runtime components (inference-router, batch-coordinator, kernel-proxy, kv-cache-daemon).
- Non-goal: this doc does not prescribe model-specific prompt transforms or application-level fallbacks (those belong to application owners).

Fidelity layers (catalog)

The runtime uses discrete layers (L0..L4) ordered from highest fidelity (L0) to lowest (L4). Each layer is described with expected quality impact, components affected, SLO target adjustment, and typical triggers.

| Layer | Short name | Effect on quality | Components impacted | Typical trigger | Estimated cost delta |
|-------|------------|-------------------|---------------------|-----------------|---------------------|
| L0 | Full fidelity | No change in model output or decoding | Serving runtime: normal routing, full KV cache, quantization disabled | Healthy cluster, nominal load | 0% |
| L1 | Cache-prefill | Slightly faster responses for repeated prefixes; minimal quality change | kv-cache-daemon more aggressively serves prefixes; prefix prefetch enabled | Temporary tail-latency spikes | -5% |
| L2 | Batching+subscription | Minor increase in p50 latency and slight beam diversity loss | batch-coordinator increases target batch size; elastic batching active | Moderate sustained load, cost optimization window | -12% |
| L3 | Quantized runtime | Small quality regressions for some prompts; large cost savings | kernel-proxy switches to 4/8-bit kernels, evap pruning of KV | Cost-driven or capacity-constrained (70%+ GPU utilization) | -35% |
| L4 | Model-variant fallback | Noticeable fidelity change (smaller model variant) | inference-router routes to smaller variants or distilled models | Emergency capacity shortages or region outage | -60% |

Operational rules and decision graph

- The runtime evaluates the decision graph every 15s. Inputs: cluster utilization (GPU/CPU/mem), tail latency (p99), error rate, reserve capacity fraction, and cost budget signal.
- Hard SLO breaches (p99 > SLO*1.5 for >2m) trigger immediate protective steps: stop accepting new long-context requests and escalate to oncall.
- Soft pressure (sustained util > 65% for 10m) enters the staircase starting at L1 and progresses no more than one layer per 5m unless an emergency threshold is crossed.
- Rollback policy: a layer transition is reversed if KPIs (p99, error rate, avg tokens/sec) return to within safe margins for 3 consecutive evaluation windows (3x15s).

Mapping to runtime components (concrete)

- inference-router: implements routing rules and model-variant switching. Config keys: router.fidelity_stepback.enabled, router.max_fallback_percent.
- batch-coordinator: controls target_batch_size and dynamic_batch_window. Config keys: batch.target_size_hint, batch.max_latency_ms.
- kernel-proxy: holds kernel selection table and quantization profiles. Config keys: kernel.q_profile, kernel.fallback_sequence.
- kv-cache-daemon: controls prefix caching TTL and prefetch heuristics. Config keys: kv.prefix_ttl_ms, kv.prefetch_enabled.

Example config fragment (YAML)

fidelity_staircase:
  evaluation_interval_s: 15
  max_progress_per_window: 1
  layers:
    - { name: L1, action: kv.prefetch:true, priority: 10 }
    - { name: L2, action: batch.target_size_hint:32, priority: 20 }
    - { name: L3, action: kernel.q_profile:4bit, priority: 30 }
    - { name: L4, action: router.model_variant:compact-v2, priority: 40 }

Note: YAML above is a human-readable excerpt. The runtime operator objects accept the same keys under runtime.feature_flags.fidelity_staircase in the configuration API.

SLOs, thresholds and concrete numeric examples

- Global request SLO (example): p99_gen_latency <= 750ms, availability >= 99.95%.
- Emergency thresholds (example): p99_gen_latency > 2250ms for 2 minutes => escalate and advance staircase by 2 layers (skip L1).
- Cost window trigger: projected token-cost > budget_weekly * 1.12 => evaluate L3/L4 if utilization > 70%.

Escalation and human-in-the-loop steps

1) Automated action: runtime advances staircase layer (or applies targeted action). All changes are annotated in the decision-trace log with correlation ID and owner (automation).
2) Pager: if p99 remains > SLO*1.2 after 3 minutes, send page to inference-oncall with tag "fidelity-change".
3) Oncall procedure: follow the Runtime Fidelity Triage (see Runbook section). If human rollback is required, use the operator CLI: redwood-runtime fidelity rollback --correlation-id <id>.

Runbook: Runtime Fidelity Triage (for oncall)

1. Observe: open /dashboards/runtime/fidelity-overview, filter by model and region. Confirm the active layer and recent layer transitions.
2. Verify signals: GPUs (utilization), host memory, p99, error rate, KV hit ratio.
3. If layer was automated and KPIs improved: monitor for 15 minutes and allow automatic rollback.
4. If KPIs worsen or error rate increases > 3% absolute after a layer transition: immediately roll back one layer and page the runtime-owner.
5. If rollback fails or cannot restore SLOs: trigger incident and escalate to platform-incident channel.

Example CLI snippets

# show current fidelity status
redwood-runtime status --model my-chat --region us-west-2 --fields fidelity,correlation_id

# force rollback
redwood-runtime fidelity rollback --correlation-id 2026-06-10-abc123 --reason "rollback test"

# simulate L3 in canary
redwood-runtime canary create --target cluster:canary-usw --override kernel.q_profile=4bit --duration 30m

Telemetry, alerts and annotation conventions

- Decision-trace: every automated fidelity decision emits a decision-trace event (trace_id: string) with fields: from_layer, to_layer, reason, metrics_snapshot, triggered_by (auto/manual).
- Alert: fidelity-layer-progression-excessive fires when more than 3 layer changes happen within 10 minutes for the same model/region. Severity: P2.
- Dashboards: fidelity_overview (per-tenant), fidelity_latency_heatmap (cross model).

Playbook for reproducing and validating quality impact

1) Record baseline: capture 1000 representative requests from production (anonymized) using request-proxy replay.
2) Run A/B replay: replay corpus to L0 and L3 in the sandbox runtime and collect response diffs.
3) Metrics to compute: token-wise similarity (BLEU/ROUGE not ideal for chat; use embedding-similarity with cosine threshold), function-call fidelity, hallucination rate on a curated prompt set.
4) Quality gate: if embedding-similarity mean < 0.92 or hallucination increase > 1.5x, mark L3 as requiring additional tuning (quant profile or reduced batch size).

Safety and rollout checklist (pre-canary)

- Add unit tests for decision-graph transitions (simulate triggers).
- Create traffic mirroring rule for canary.
- Ensure canary cluster has at least 2x expected memory headroom for quantized kernels.
- Create evaluation prompt set and automated comparator job.

Ownership and contacts

- Runtime fidelity automation owner: Maya Chen (runtime-core).
- Kernel & quantization contact: Arjun Patel (runtime-kernel).
- Oncall channel: #oncall-runtime, Incident runbook link: /oncall-and-incident-response/postmortems/runtime-fidelity-incident-template.

Appendix: short glossary

- Fidelity staircase: ordered set of runtime degradation actions applied to reduce resource usage or preserve availability.
- Decision-trace: structured event emitted for every automated fidelity decision.

Appendix: minimal experiment matrix (CSV-ready)

scenario,layer,metric,baseline,target
baseline,L0,p99,600,<=750
sustained-load,L2,p99,700,<=900
quantized,L3,embedding_mean,0.95,>=0.92
model-fallback,L4,availability,99.99,>=99.9

References and related reading

- See runtime-architecture/observability-driven-runtime-refinement-playbook-2027 for telemetry signal definitions.
- See kernel-and-scheduling/quantization-rollout-safety-and-quality-gate-playbook-2026 for quant-specific guidance.

Document history

- 2026-01-15: Created by Maya Chen.
- 2026-03-02: Added CLI examples and escalation thresholds (Arjun Patel review).
- 2026-06-10: Finalized rollback policy and canary checklist (Sofia Alvarez review).

title: Execution Stitching and Fallback Orchestration
content:
Overview

Purpose: This document defines the execution-stitching pattern and the fallback orchestration responsible for providing graceful degradation when the primary execution path (high-throughput GPU kernel pipeline) cannot satisfy a request within SLO. It codifies the state machine, scheduling interactions, configuration knobs, observability signals, and an operational runbook for live incidents.

Scope: runtime-gateway, request-router, kernel-scheduler, kvcache-manager, fallback-router, model-variant-proxy. This guide targets on-call SREs, runtime engineers, and platform product owners.

Background and intent

- Problem: Mixed workload bursts, kernel regressions, or cache churn can cause a subset of requests to miss tail-latency SLOs. Uncoordinated retries or naive fallbacks cause thundering cascades, token-cost spikes, and model quality regressions.
- Intent: Provide a deterministic, observable orchestration that "stitches" partial progress from the primary path into safe fallback executions while minimizing cost and preserving user-visible correctness.

Architecture summary

Execution paths (logical services)
- runtime-gateway: front-door handling auth, rate limits, and per-token costing.
- request-router: classifies request by latency budget, priority, and required guarantees; assigns to execution lanes.
- kernel-scheduler: maps request lanes to kernel execution pools (low-latency, standard, background) and controls kernel handoff.
- kvcache-manager: supplies KV cache state and prefix-hinting; exposes warmup metrics.
- fallback-router: executes alternative strategies (quantized variant, truncated-response, stateless re-generation) and merges results.
- model-variant-proxy: serves model variant redirects and handles compatibility checks.

Execution stitching concept (high level)

1) Progressive execution: a request begins on the primary lane (low-latency pool). The kernel-scheduler allocates slots and attaches a progress token that represents the number of completed token-chunks and current KV epoch.
2) Checkpoints: At prescribed kernel boundaries (every N tokens or at decoder-layer boundaries), the runtime emits a "stitch-checkpoint" event with progress token, partial logits digest, and KV-origin stamp.
3) Decision point: If the primary path is delayed beyond budget T_warn (configurable), request-router consults fallback policy to decide: wait, re-route to a compatible curtailed variant, or switch to a stateless fallback.
4) Stitching: If a fallback executes, the fallback-router attempts to hydrate the fallback with the latest checkpoint (prefix/KV + partial logits) so it continues generation without repeating completed work. If KV state is incompatible, fallback falls back further to truncated restart.

State machine (summary)

- STATES: ACCEPTED -> RUNNING_PRIMARY -> CHECKPOINTED -> FALLBACK_PENDING -> FALLBACK_RUNNING -> MERGING -> COMPLETED | FAILED
- TRANSITIONS are timebox-driven and signal-driven. Key signals: KERNEL_HEARTBEAT, CHECKPOINT_CREATED, KV_WARM, SCHEDULE_PREEMPT.

Scheduling interactions and kernel implications

- Kernel preemption: kernel-scheduler must annotate preemption reasons (quota, fragmentation, safety-net) in the KERNEL_HEARTBEAT so stitching logic can choose soft vs hard fallback.
- Slice-aware execution: kernels that support incremental slice commits must expose slice boundaries to runtime-gateway via CHECKPOINT_CREATED, otherwise stitching is not possible.
- Fairness: scheduler applies a credit-based weight that factors "stitchability_score" per request; low stitchability pushes requests into conservative fallbacks early.

Configuration table (recommended defaults)

| config_key | description | default |
|-----------|-------------|---------|
| stitch.max_wait_ms | maximum time to wait for primary before triggering fallback_pending | "80ms" |
| stitch.warn_ms | time to emit early warning event to tracing | "40ms" |
| stitch.min_progress_tokens | minimum completed tokens to allow stitching | "8" |
| stitch.max_merge_attempts | number of attempts to merge fallback output with checkpoint | "2" |
| fallback.quantized_variant | model variant id for quantized fallback | "gptq-compat-v1" |
| fallback.truncate_heuristic | apply truncation when KV mismatch ratio > X% | "30%" |
| merge.similarity_threshold | threshold for partial-logit merge acceptance (cosine) | "0.92" |

Operational runbook: tail-latency incident (step-by-step)

1) Triage signal: alert fires on metric runtime.tail_95_ms > 1.5x SLO for 5m and stitch.fallback_rate > 3%. Channel: #oncall-runtime. Pager: primary SRE.
2) Initial checks (5 min):
   a) Verify recent deploys: check runtime-gateway and kernel-scheduler release notes for rollouts in the last 30m.
   b) Query kvcache-manager: kvcache.hit_ratio_1m and kvcache.warmup_queue length.
   c) Check kernel health: kernel.pool_fragmentation and kernel.queueing_latency.
3) Fast mitigation (10–20 min):
   a) Temporarily increase stitch.max_wait_ms to absorb transient jitter (add 20–40ms), using /admin/api/runtime/config apply --patch '{"stitch.max_wait_ms":"120ms"}'.
   b) If kernel fragmentation high, trigger node drain of <low-util> batch GPUs and rebind low-latency pools: /ops/gpu-drain --pool batch-3 --timeout 2m.
   c) If fallback rate is too high and causing cost spike, set fallback.quantized_variant to a cheaper model: /admin/runtime/set-fallback --variant gptq-compact-v2
4) Investigation (30–90 min):
   a) Correlate CHECKPOINT_CREATED rates with kernel queue depth. Low checkpoint frequency indicates slices are too large.
   b) Inspect traces: look for repeated MERGE_REJECT events (merge.similarity_threshold violations). If frequent, raise threshold or disable merging for the affected model.
5) Post-incident actions (within 5 working days):
   a) Run synthetic replay of failing traffic shape in the benchmarking suite (see: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/runtime-scaling-experiment-protocol-and-benchmark-checklist-2026).
   b) Open an ADR PR if code-level scheduler change needed.

Debugging artifacts and observability contract

Core trace fields emitted for each request (required):
- request_id (string)
- tenant_id
- execution_lane ("low-latency" | "standard" | "background")
- stitch.progress_tokens (int)
- stitch.checkpoint_ts (epoch-ms)
- kernel.heartbeat_ts
- fallback.decision ("none"|"quantized"|"truncate_restart"|"stateless")
- merge.result ("merged"|"rejected"|"not_attempted")

Metrics (minimum to alert on)
- runtime.tail_95_ms
- stitch.fallback_rate (requests/sec and %)
- stitch.merge_accept_rate
- kvcache.hit_ratio_1m
- kernel.queue_latency_p50/p95/p99

Events (audit log items)
- CHECKPOINT_CREATED: {request_id, tokens_complete, kv_epoch}
- FALLBACK_TRIGGERED: {request_id, reason, chosen_variant}
- MERGE_ATTEMPT: {request_id, similarity_score, attempt_index}

Example trace JSON (single-line)
{"request_id":"req-3f2b","execution_lane":"low-latency","stitch.progress_tokens":12,"stitch.checkpoint_ts":1700000000123,"fallback.decision":"quantized","merge.result":"merged"}

Configuration and testing guidelines

- Bench test: use the mixed-shape generator with prefix-hot distribution and KV-churn enabled. Run at 2x production QPS for 10m. Verify stitch.merge_accept_rate > 98% and stitch.fallback_rate < 2%.
- Unit tests: add deterministic checkpoint emission tests: synthetic kernel must emit CHECKPOINT_CREATED before each slice commit.
- Canary plan for changing stitch.max_wait_ms:
  1) Apply config to canary runtime-gateway cluster (10% of traffic) for 30m.
  2) Validate metrics: no increase in tail_99 or cost-per-token > 1.1x baseline.
  3) Gradually promote to 50% then 100% over 2 hours.

Known limitations and failure modes

- KV incompatibility: When model variants have incompatible KV encodings (common across quantized vs FP16 variants), stitching falls back to truncation and re-generation; expect quality delta.
- Merge false-positives: Partial-logit merging assumes consistent tokenization and output distribution; mismatch can produce incoherent continuations. Use high similarity_threshold for customer-facing models.
- Cost amplification: Aggressive fallback when primary is slow can double token costs if fallbacks re-generate long prefixes. Config guardrails must disable expensive fallback for low-tier customers.

Operational ownership and escalation

- Owner: eng-serving-runtime team
- Primary on-call: runtime-sre rotation (see /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/oncall-rotations)
- Escalation: after 15m unresolved, page runtime-platform lead (Marco Alvarez). After 60m, involve Director of Infra.

Release and rollout notes (example change)

Change: add CHECKPOINT_CREATED to kernel v2 and enable incremental merge
- Target branches: kernel/v2, runtime/orchestrator
- Tests: kernel unit + integration with kvcache emulation
- Rollout steps:
  1) Merge to staging, run workload-sim at 1x prod.
  2) Deploy kernel/v2 to canary pool (5 nodes), enable diagnostics for 1h.
  3) If no regressions, add to low-latency pool at 10% traffic. Monitor stitch.merge_accept_rate.

Appendices

A. Sample admin CLI snippets
- Apply temporary config patch:
  curl -X PATCH -H 'Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN' \
    https://admin.internal/runtime/config \
    -d '{"stitch.max_wait_ms":"120ms"}'
- Force-stop a leaking fallback workers group:
  /ops/runtime/workerctl stop --group fallback-quantized-3 --soft

B. Recommended thresholds (summary)
- SLO: 95th percentile latency <= 120ms for low-latency lane
- stitch.warn_ms: 40ms
- stitch.max_wait_ms: 80ms (canary), 120ms (temp mitigation)
- merge.similarity_threshold: 0.92

C. Links and references
- Related ADR: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/runtime-decision-graph-and-observed-behaviour-catalog-2026
- Benchmarking playbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/runtime-scaling-experiment-protocol-and-benchmark-checklist-2026

Contact and next steps

- For questions or to propose improvements, open a PR and tag reviewers (Marco Alvarez, Priya Shah). Planned Q1 work: increase observability of partial-logits and add a "simulated-merge" test in the CI benchmark suite.

Revision history
- 2025-11-12: Initial draft (E. Tran)
- 2025-12-18: Added operational runbook and metrics (review feedback)
- 2026-02-03: Clarified kernel-heartbeat signals and added canary rollout plan

title: SLO-driven Burst Scaling and Fair-Share Algorithm Guide
content:
Overview

This guide describes a consolidated, SLO-driven approach for burst scaling and request fair-share across Redwood’s platform services (API gateways, model routing, batcher pools, and Dedicated capacity pools). It explains the control loop, the fair-share algorithm used to allocate limited GPU/instance capacity during contention, recommended configuration parameters, operational runbook items, and a safe rollout checklist.

Goals

- Maintain customer-visible latency SLOs (p95 and p99) for the Hosted API while maximizing utilization and bounding cost.
- Provide deterministic, explainable fair-share behavior when capacity is constrained (per-customer and per-route).
- Support controlled burst windows for short-term spikes without violating downstream model server SLOs.
- Make the policy configurable for Dedicated and Private deployments with consistent semantics.

Scope and assumptions

- Applies to the Redwood API routing layer, the batcher, and pool autoscalers.
- Assumes telemetry available: per-route token rate, request concurrency, queue depth, tail latency (p95/p99), and model server utilization.
- Compatible with both hosted and dedicated pools; some knobs are disabled in strict Dedicated SLA tiers (see Appendix).

Key Concepts

1) SLO-driven control loop

- Primary signal: p99 latency for the route (target e.g., 1.2s). Secondary signals: error rate, model server GPU utilization, and queue length.
- The autoscaler tries to maintain SLO while optimizing cost: scale up when SLO is violated and utilization is high; scale down when SLO is satisfied and utilization low.
- Short bursts are allowed by a temporary credit mechanism (burst tokens) before the autoscaler finishes a scale-up.

2) Fair-share allocator

- When capacity is constrained (total outstanding concurrency > pool concurrency), requests are assigned effective weights and admitted according to a proportional fair-share algorithm.
- We assign each customer-route a weight = max( min_weight, allocated_commitment + activity_bonus ).
- Proportional fair-share ensures each budgeted customer receives capacity proportional to their committed units but allows active customers to gain short-term extra share via activity_bonus.

3) Burst tokens

- Each tenant accumulates burst tokens proportional to recent unused reserved capacity and historical burst tolerance. Tokens permit exceeding committed throughput for short windows (config default: 30s window up to 1.5x committed rate).
- Token refill rate and max balance are tunable per customer tier.

Architecture (textual diagram)

- API Gateway -> Request Router -> Admission Controller -> Fair-share Allocator -> Batcher -> Model Serving Pool
- Admission Controller enforces per-route concurrency caps and consults Burst Token Store (LRU with per-tenant counters).
- Autoscaler monitors pool-level metrics and triggers scale actions via Fleet Manager.

Recommended configuration table (defaults)

- Default SLOs: p95: 400ms, p99: 1200ms for text generation endpoints.
- Activity window: 60s for weight calculation.
- Min weight (min_weight): 0.1 of a unit (prevents starvation).
- Burst window: 30s, burst multiplier: 1.5, max token balance: 3 intervals.
- Admission queue per pool: max backlog 200 requests before shedding.

Example admission policy (YAML)

---
admission_policy_version: v1
routes:
  - name: text-generate-v1
    slo_p99_ms: 1200
    min_weight: 0.1
    burst:
      window_seconds: 30
      multiplier: 1.5
      max_balance: 3
    activity_window_seconds: 60
    queue_limit: 200
  - name: embeddings-v1
    slo_p99_ms: 600
    min_weight: 0.05
    burst:
      window_seconds: 20
      multiplier: 1.2
      max_balance: 2
    activity_window_seconds: 30
    queue_limit: 100
---

Algorithm outline (step-by-step)

1. Compute per-route demand: recent qps and concurrency sampled over activity_window_seconds.
2. Compute base weight = committed_units (from billing/commitment).
3. Compute activity_bonus = f(recent_spike_score) clipped to [0, base_weight * 2].
4. Effective weight = max(min_weight, base_weight + activity_bonus).
5. If pool_concurrency < capacity: admit inline.
6. If pool_concurrency >= capacity: allocate admission slots proportional to effective weights.
7. If a tenant has burst tokens and effective demand <= base_weight * burst_multiplier + token_balance: allow short burst and decrement tokens.
8. Unadmitted requests are queued up to queue_limit, then rejected with structured error (429 + retry-after + reason code).

Monitoring and Dashboards

Create a set of dashboards and alerts that map directly to the control signals:

- Pool health dashboard (per-pool): p50/p95/p99 latency, GPU/CPU utilization, queue depth, admission rate, reject rate.
- Tenant fairness dashboard: allocated share vs committed, observed throughput, token balance heatmap.
- SLO burn dashboard: rolling error budget burn for top 100 routes.

Alerts (recommended thresholds)

- SLO breach: p99 > configured SLO for 3 consecutive 1m buckets -> Sev2 paging to oncall.
- Queue backlog growing: queue depth > 50% of queue_limit and increasing for 5m -> Pager.
- Reject spike: rejection rate > 0.5% of requests over 5m -> Slack alert.
- Unexpected idle: utilization < 10% while queue is non-empty -> investigate scheduling/placement.

Operational runbook (incident flow)

1. Triage
  a. Confirm alert and scope (pool-level or cross-pool).
  b. Open incident in incident tracker and annotate with impacted routes/customers.
2. Quick mitigations
  a. If p99 spikes and GPUs are saturated: increase pool capacity if autoscaler stalled (temporary scale-up command: fleetctl pool scale --pool <id> --instances +2).
  b. If queue backlog is the root cause: raise queue_limit temporarily or redirect low-priority routes to overflow pool.\  c. If a single tenant is noisy: apply per-tenant throttle (cli: rtrctl throttle --tenant <id> --rate <r>) and notify CS.
3. Deeper analysis
  a. Check logs for admission decisions, token ledger entries, and fair-share allocations.
  b. Check model server tail latency and KV cache hit-rate (low cache hit can increase p99).
4. Post-incident work
  a. Update the incident runbook with the root cause and follow-up actions.
  b. Tune activity_window_seconds or burst multiplier for the impacted routes if needed.

Testing and rollout plan

- Unit tests: per-algorithm tests for weight computation, token accounting, and queue admission decisions.
- Integration tests: synthetic traffic generator (bench/gen-traffic) to emulate mixed tenants with committed and bursty workloads.
- Staged rollout:
  1) Canary on a single non-production pool for 2 days with 3 synthetic tenants.
  2) Gradual increase to 10% of production traffic (shadow admission decisions) for 3 days.
  3) Enable enforcement in 25% of requests for 24h and monitor SLO burn.
  4) Full rollout with rollback window of 1 hour per region.

Safety knobs and rollback procedure

- Safety knobs: global_fallback_mode (admit-everything), emergency_cap_increase, token_store_disable.
- Rollback: flip global_fallback_mode=true to stop fair-share enforcement and allow requests through. After stabilization, revert configuration changes and schedule follow-ups.

Cost and capacity considerations

- Conservative defaults bias toward small over-provision to protect p99s; this increases short-term cost. Use Optimize recommendations to reduce cost after 2–4 weeks of steady telemetry.
- Track cost-per-request and model-inference-p95 normalized metrics to quantify trade-offs when tuning burst_multiplier or min_weight.

Appendix: Dedicated and Private deployment notes

- Dedicated pools: commit floors are strict. The fair-share allocator still runs but min_weight = committed_units and burst_multiplier is lower by default (1.1). Bursting may be disabled by contract.
- Private/VPC: operator-controlled token refill rates. Operators must ensure time synchronization across token-store replicas (NTP).

Appendix: Example CLI commands

- View pool metrics: redwoodctl pool metrics --pool-id <id> --window 5m
- Temporarily increase pool: redwoodctl pool scale --pool-id <id> --delta +2 --reason "incident mitigation"
- Throttle tenant: redwoodctl tenant throttle --tenant-id <id> --qps 50

Ownership and contact matrix

- Policy owner: eng-platform/autoscaling (primary: Aisha Patel)
- Runtime instrumentation: eng-serving-runtime (owner: Connor Blake)
- Billing/commitments: finance-legal (owner: Elena Martín)
- Customer notifications: customer-success (owner: Maya Zhou)

References and related docs

- Platform critical-path handbook (link internal)
- Autoscaler design ADR v3 (link internal)
- Batcher admission controller spec (link internal)

Change log

- 2025-02-10: Initial draft by Aisha Patel.
- 2025-04-01: Added burst token design and YAML examples (review: Connor Blake).
- 2025-06-12: Finalized operational alerts and rollout checklist (review: Maya Zhou).

End of document

title: Kernel telemetry adoption roadmap and operational playbook
content:
Overview

Purpose: This document defines a pragmatic adoption roadmap for kernel-level telemetry across the serving runtime. It ties runtime architecture intent, kernel scheduling observability, profiling playbooks, benchmarking signals, runbook integration, and release gating into a single operational plan intended for the runtime, SRE, and observability teams.

Scope: collection, normalization, storage, alerting, dashboards, rollout gating, and runbook integration for kernel signals (dispatch latency, kernel execution time, occupancy, memory amplification, KV cache hit-rate traces and causal chain IDs). Excludes agent diagnostics below host OS and third-party accelerator firmware traces (these are handled by HW partners).

Intended audience: runtime-engineers, scheduler-owners, observability, SRE, incident response leads, and release managers.

High-level goals

- Produce a stable, cost-bounded telemetry surface for kernel scheduling decisions and post-incident forensics.
- Ensure telemetry can be sampled or downsampled without compromising root-cause signal fidelity for SLO slices.
- Provide a release gating checklist so kernel or scheduler changes are not shipped without traceability.

Key signals and instruments

The telemetry surface will be organized into three tiers (Tier 0 = mandatory, Tier 1 = recommended, Tier 2 = experimental). Each signal has a collection frequency and retention recommendation.

| Signal | Tier | Frequency | Retention (hot) | Owner | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| dispatch.enqueue-latency_ms | Tier 0 | 1s aggregation | 30d | runtime-coordinator | Per-tenant percentiles (P50/90/99) and raw sample on error cases |
| kernel.exec-duration_ms | Tier 0 | per-request sample + 5s agg | 30d | kernel-dispatcher | tag by kernel-variant and model-variant |
| kernel.occupancy_pct | Tier 1 | 10s | 14d | scheduler-agent | GPU occupancy by slice, include concurrent kernels |
| kvcache.lookup-latency_ms | Tier 0 | 1s sample | 60d | kv-cache | correlate with session IDs and prefix-hash |
| kernel.memory-watermark_mb | Tier 1 | 30s | 14d | allocator | record soft-oom triggers, per-node |
| trace.causal-id | Tier 0 | sampled per-request | 90d | runtime-trace-proxy | GUID propagated across services for causal stitching |
| kernel.quantize-fallback-count | Tier 2 | event-driven | 7d | model-onboarding | experimental: measure automatic quantization fallbacks |

Collection and normalization rules

1. Use the runtime-trace-proxy to stamp a trace.causal-id at the API ingress. Persist causal-id in the request header (X-Redwood-Causal-ID).
2. Kernel and scheduler components MUST emit events with causal-id and the minimal context: tenant_id, model_id, kernel_variant.
3. Numeric timings must be in milliseconds with integer precision. Counters in integers. Percentages reported as integers 0-100.
4. Normalization pipeline (observability ingestion) will:
   - deduplicate by (causal-id, kernel-uuid, timestamp)
   - normalize field names according to the signal ontology above
   - enrich with topology tags: node_id, numa_zone, accelerator_type
5. Keep raw compressed traces for error windows and on-call requests (see retention overrides below).

Storage and cost guardrails

- Hot retention targets: Tier 0 signals 30d hot, Tier 1 signals 14d hot. Hot = queryable at sub-5s latency.
- Cold archive: daily compressed bundles moved to object storage (S3/GCS) after hot window. Cold retention policy: 365d for causal-linked incidents, 180d for default.
- Budget constraints: telemetry 3E3D 5% of per-month runtime spend requires approval by SRE lead. Telemetry ingest rates must be simulated in the benchmark suite before expanding collection.

Signal sampling and fidelity strategy

- Baseline: for normal operation, sample 10% of low-latency /low-cost requests for full trace payload; always collect Tier 0 aggregated counters (percentiles).
- On spikes, autoswitch to triggered sampling: when scheduler P99 latency > SLO threshold (P99 > target * 1.25), increase full-trace sampling to 100% for affected tenants for 10 minutes.
- For releases flagged in the canary matrix, run shadow full-trace collection at 100% for canary cohorts only.

Gating and release checklist (pre-merge and pre-release)

Pre-merge (developer):
1. Add telemetry emitters for any new kernel_variant or scheduler path.
2. Unit tests that assert telemetry fields are set.
3. Update signal ontology doc and add a sample synthetic trace to the benchmark corpus.

Canary matrix (release manager):
1. Canary cohort running new kernel: 5% of traffic for 6 hours.
2. Telemetry checks during canary:
   - dispatch.enqueue-latency P99 increase < 10% vs baseline
   - kernel.exec-duration median change < 5%
   - error-rate on causal-id-tagged traces < 1% absolute increase
3. If any check fails, rollout must halt and revert or go to corrective patch.

Operational runbook integration

- When alerts fire for "kernel.exec-duration.p99 > threshold":
  1. Page oncall runtime-owner and scheduler-owner.
  2. Run quick triage using the "trace quick-attach" CLI to fetch representative traces for the last 15 minutes:
     - rtr-cli trace fetch --causal-window 15m --signal kernel.exec-duration_ms --format jsonl
  3. If traces show a new kernel-variant correlation, escalate to kernel-owner and open a triage-wide Jira.
  4. If no kernel-variant correlation, run the profiler sampling playbook (see "Profiling playbooks" section).

Profiling playbooks (summary)

- Microprobe sampling: use microprobe to capture kernel-level timings on a single node for synthetic replay. Steps:
  1. Isolate node (scheduler drain) and reproduce with the benchmark harness (bench-harness run --signature <signature>).
  2. Run microprobe with sampling rate 100Hz for 60s and export to /tmp/microprobe.tar.gz.
  3. Upload to the profiling bucket and attach to the incident.
- Continuous lightweight profiling: 1Hz kernel.exec-duration histogram applied to 1% of nodes, used for regression detection.

Benchmarking suite integration

- Before enabling new Tier 0 signals at production scale, run the "telemetry-ingest-sim" scenario in the benchmarking suite to estimate cost and query latency impact. Required check: simulated ingestion < 2x current ingestion and query latencies not > 1.5x.
- Bench commands example:
  - benchctl telemetry simulate --corpus telemetry-ingest-corpus-2026 --scale 10x
  - benchctl run --scenario telemetry-ingest-sim --assert ingest-multiplier<=2 --assert query-slo<=1.5

Dashboards and alerts (summary)

- Dashboards to create:
  - "Kernel Health" (team dashboard): P50/P90/P99 kernel.exec-duration, dispatch.enqueue-latency, kernel.occupancy_pct heatmaps by model family.
  - "Causal Forensics" (oncall): top traces attached to causal-id with quick links to KV cache lookup latency.
  - "Telemetry Cost" (infra): ingest rate, compressed size, projected monthly storage.

Alerting thresholds (suggested)

- dispatch.enqueue-latency.p99 > baseline.p99 * 1.25 for 5m -> P1 alert to runtime-oncall.
- kernel.exec-duration.p99 increase > 15% vs 24h baseline AND error-rate increase > 0.5% -> P0 emergency page.
- telemetry-ingest-rate > budgeted-ingest * 1.5 -> P2 alert; auto-scale ingestion buffer (see infra runbook).

Rollout phases and timeline

Phase A (Quarter 1, pilot, 6 weeks)
- Implement trace.causal-id stamping and ingest for 3 Tier 0 signals.
- Pilot on two non-critical tenants and run telemetry-ingest-sim to validate cost.
- Deliver: kernel health dashboard (alpha), profiling playbook template updated.

Phase B (Quarter 2, expansion, 8 weeks)
- Expand Tier 0 to all runtime nodes; enable sampling policy for Tier 1 signals.
- Integrate with benchmarking suite and release gating.
- Deliver: canary matrix rules enforced by release-orchestrator.

Phase C (Quarter 3, optimization, 6 weeks)
- Implement adaptive sampling and autoswitch logic in runtime-coordinator.
- Add queryable cold archive index for causal-linked incidents.
- Deliver: Telemetry cost dashboard and automated retention compressor.

Phase D (Quarter 4, refinement, ongoing)
- Add Tier 2 experimental signals and feedback into model-onboarding and quantization test harness.
- Run a cross-team retrospective and update SLOs as needed.

Owner and governance

- Runtime telemetry steward: Maya Patel (runtime observability).
- Scheduler instrumentation owner: Evan Rodriguez.
- SRE custodian for retention and cost: Lena Zhou.
- Review cadence: monthly telemetry governance meeting; quarterly cross-team review that ties to release windows.

Appendices

A. Example trace schema (JSON snippet)

{
  "causal_id": "cid-0a12b3c",
  "tenant_id": "t-42",
  "model_id": "gpt-rl-13b",
  "kernel_variant": "kern-v2a",
  "events": [
    {"name": "dispatch.enqueue", "ts_ms": 1700000000000, "value_ms": 2},
    {"name": "kernel.exec", "ts_ms": 1700000000020, "value_ms": 24}
  ]
}

B. Quick CLI snippets

- Stamp causal id locally for testing: export X_REDWOOD_CAUSAL_ID=$(uuidgen)
- Generate a synthetic trace: rtr-cli trace synth --signature small-chat --causal-id $X_REDWOOD_CAUSAL_ID --output trace.json
- Fetch attached traces for an incident: rtr-cli trace fetch --incident INC-1234 --format jsonl > incident_traces.jsonl

C. Retention overrides policy

- Incidents: any incident with severity P0/P1 will auto-promote its related causal traces to 365d cold-retention.
- Customer compliance: for Private deployment customers who require longer retention, open a retention-exception request; SRE custodian will evaluate costs and alternatives (on-prem archive or shorter ingest windows).

D. Open work items (initial backlog)

- Implement deduplication logic in ingestion pipeline (P0).
- Add causal-id propagation to SDK wrappers (P1).
- Add telemetry-ingest-sim scenario to benchmark suite with 10x load profiles (P1).
- Define exact field names and units in the signal ontology (P0).

If you own any of the open items above or have feedback, add comments to this page and @mention the owners listed in the governance section.

References

- Runtime observability self-heal manual: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/runtime-observability-self-heal-orchestration-manual-2026
- Profiling causal latency map: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/compact-trace-annotation-and-causal-latency-map-2026

Change log

- 2025-11-12: Draft created by Maya Patel.
- 2025-12-18: Added baseline signals and sampling strategy (reviewer feedback).
- 2026-02-03: Updated retention and benchmark integration notes; moved to in_review.

title: Runtime feature lifecycle and sunset playbook
content:
Summary:

This playbook defines the end-to-end lifecycle for runtime features, kernel variants, and API behaviors at Redwood Inference. It covers how features are proposed, prototyped, benchmarked, instrumented, staged for rollout, monitored during canaries, and eventually deprecated (sunset). The goal is consistent, SLO-aware rollouts that minimize customer impact and preserve reproducible performance baselines.

Scope:
- Applies to changes that affect the serving runtime, scheduler/policy language, kernel implementations, KV cache behavior, and any runtime-exposed configuration flags.
- Excludes purely client-side SDK changes (see eng-developer-experience) and infra-only capacity changes.

Definitions:
- Feature: any new runtime capability or behavioral change (e.g., continuous batching heuristic, new kernel micro-op).
- Kernel variant: a compiled execution path or quantization profile used by the runtime.
- Canary: a controlled rollout to a subset of traffic/instances.
- Sunset: formal deprecation and removal of a feature/kernel.

Feature lifecycle stages (high level):
1) Proposal & design
   - Owner creates a short design doc with: motivation, invariants, expected perf/cost impact, compatibility constraints, and rollout strategy.
   - Required fields: feature id (FR-YYYY-#####), target release, owner, fast rollback plan.
2) Prototype & microbench
   - Implement prototype behind an experimental flag.
   - Run microbench suite (see "Benchmarking" section). Document delta vs baseline for latency P50/P95/P99 and per-token cost.
3) Telemetry & tracing contracts
   - Add kernel/feature labels to traces (tag: runtime.feature_id) and metrics (metric: runtime.feature.{id}.activation_count).
   - Ensure trace spans have consistent start/end semantics for latency attribution.
4) Integration tests & staging
   - Pass unit + integration test matrix including KV cache consistency tests and multi-tenant fairness tests.
   - Run staged workload replay in staging fleet for 48–72 hours.
5) Canary rollout
   - Canary to 1% of traffic or 5 nodes (whichever is larger) for 24 hours; then 5% for 24 hours; then 25% for 48 hours before global.
   - Canary SLO gates: latency P95 < baseline + 15%, error rate delta < 0.05% absolute, token-cost delta < +7%.
6) Global rollout
   - Gradual ramp with automated rollback on gate violation.
7) Stabilization & measurement
   - Run full cost/quality regressions for 14 days and update model performance dashboards.
8) Deprecation / Sunset
   - Publish sunset announcement 90 days before removal for non-security features; 30 days for security patches.

Kernel-specific rollout checklist (must be attached to PR):
- Build artifact naming: kernel.{arch}.{quant}.{tag}. Example: kernel.ampere.q4_0.experimental-v2
- Microbench results: table of sequence lengths [8,64,256,1024] with P50/P95/P99 latency and tokens/sec.
- Quantization validation: decode/re-encode correctness tests and representative generation evals (BLEU/ROUGE or embedding-similarity).
- Memory & eviction tests: confirm kv-cache warmup latency < 200ms for hot sessions.
- Fallback path: define which kernel variant is compatible for automatic fallback; add mapping in scheduler config.

Profiling & benchmarking steps for feature verification:
1) Repro harness: use the operational-workload-simulator (OWS) with recorded production shapes.
2) Microbench protocol:
   - Warm GPU for 30s, run 1000 inferences, record 95th and 99th percentile latencies; repeat 3 times.
   - Use fixed seeds where applicable; publish raw traces to profiling bucket: s3://redwood-runtime-profiling/{feature_id}/{date}/
3) Telemetry correlation:
   - Correlate kernel timings with scheduler events using trace id. Verify no hidden tail spikes introduced by new kernel.
4) Cost test:
   - Run throughput scaling test at 10%, 50%, 100% of expected production concurrency. Capture per-token energy/cost.

Benchmark result reporting template (table):
| metric | baseline | candidate | delta | pass/fail | notes |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| P50 latency (seq64) | 12.3ms | 11.7ms | -4.9% | PASS | lower median latency |
| P95 latency (seq64) | 28.9ms | 36.4ms | +26% | FAIL | investigate kernel scheduling interactions |
| tokens/sec (batching 128) | 480 | 532 | +10.8% | PASS | improves throughput |

Release notes and documentation requirements (PR checklist):
- Summary line (one sentence).
- Migration notes for customers (config flags, behavior changes).
- SLO impact statement and measured deltas.
- Known incompatibilities and fallback mappings.
- Tiering: mark feature as "Beta", "GA", or "Experimental".

Runbook: failed canary / rapid rollback procedure (fast path):
1) Canary gate violated: on-call (runtime-oncall@redwood) calls the feature owner and SRE lead within 10 minutes.
2) Immediate action: flip rollout flag to previous kernel (CLI):
```
redwood-runtime rollout apply --feature-id FR-2026-01234 --target previous
```
3) Initiate automated rollback verification: run smoke requests against canary nodes and confirm latency and error rates return to baseline within 10 minutes.
4) Post-incident actions: create postmortem within 72 hours, include traces and experiment artifacts.

Known-issues triage matrix (priority mapping):
- P0: data loss, QoS below SLO for >5 minutes, customer-facing correctness regression. Immediate rollback and all-hands page.
- P1: sustained latency regression P95 > baseline + 30% for >30 minutes. Canary rollback recommended.
- P2: localized performance regression with clear mitigation (config toggle).

Ownership & escalation:
- Feature owner: responsible for design doc, tests, and monitoring during canary.
- Runtime SRE: responsible for rollout automation, metrics alerts, and emergency rollback.
- Release manager: signs off on GA and public release notes.
- Security/Compliance: sign-off required for changes touching key management or telemetry payloads.

Templates & snippets (appendix):
- Feature design header (YAML):
```yaml
feature_id: FR-2026-01234
name: adaptive-batching-heuristic-v2
owner: anika.patel@redwood.ai
target_release: 2026.11
rollout_strategy:
  canary_steps: [1,5,25,100]
  health_gates:
    p95_latency_delta_pct: 15
    error_rate_delta_abs: 0.0005
```
- Canary verification quick queries (metrics):
  - p95_latency_by_model: sum(rate(runtime.latency.p95[5m]))
  - error_rate_total: sum(rate(runtime.errors[5m]))
  - feature_activation: sum(rate(runtime.feature.{id}.activation_count[5m]))

Communication & customer impact:
- For non-breaking changes: post a short announcement in #product-updates and send customer-facing note to accounts with Dedicated/Private deployments when rollout begins.
- For breaking or opt-in changes: open a Customer Advisory (template provided in customer-success-and-support/integration-guides) 30 days prior.

Audit & deprecation timeline (sunset process):
1) Deprecation proposal: owner files a Deprecation Notice with rationale and migration alternatives.
2) Publish notice: 90 days public notice for GA features; 30 days for experimental.
3) Monitoring window: owners must provide compatibility telemetry during notice window.
4) Final removal: remove code & tests in a feature-flagged commit then schedule for release; notify linked customers and update docs.

Appendix: quick links and artifacts to attach to PRs:
- Raw microbench traces: profiling-bucket link
- Perf dashboards: per-model perf board URL
- Canary dashboard snapshot: attach image/PNG

Owners & contact:
- Runtime Platform: runtime-platform@redwood.ai
- Runtime SRE lead: Luis Martinez (luis.martinez@redwood.ai)
- Author / Feature lifecycle owner: Anika Patel (anika.patel@redwood.ai)

Revision history:
- 2026-05-18: Initial draft
- 2026-07-02: Added benchmark template and canary gates
- 2026-11-02: Clarified rollback CLI and telemetry contract requirements

title: Runtime extension surface stability and versioning contract
content:
Summary

This document defines the stability, compatibility, and versioning contract for any extensions to the Redwood serving runtime extension surface. "Extensions" in this document include kernel plugins, priority/admission hooks, observability adapters, custom scheduling policies, and lightweight binary-compatible runtime modules. The goal is to enable third-party and internal teams to safely integrate new features while preserving customer-facing SLOs, rollout safety, and fast rollback paths.

Scope

- Applies to all code and artifacts that are loaded dynamically into the serving runtime process (ld.so, plugin loader, dynamic shared objects), as well as to external modules that register callbacks with the runtime over the internal plugin API (rpc or in-process).
- Does NOT apply to model files, model weights, or user prompts. It DOES apply to model-serving kernel implementations and dispatch adapters.

Goals

1. Prevent runtime crashes and silent performance regressions after extension deploys.
2. Provide a clear ABI/semantic compatibility guarantee across minor releases so teams can plan integration windows.
3. Define test and rollout requirements that keep production SLOs (p50 latency, p99 latency, availability, error budget) within agreed thresholds.
4. Provide an explicit deprecation and sunset path for unstable extension APIs.

Compatibility model

We use a three-tier compatibility model for the extension surface:

- Strict ABI compatibility (patch releases): binary-compatible, no symbol or struct layout changes. Backward-compatible behavior guaranteed. Extensions built against a patch-level release must run without recompilation.

- Semantic compatibility (minor releases): may add optional fields, new callback hooks, and extension-facing feature flags. Extensions built against an older minor release should continue to function with feature-gates disabled. If an extension requires new hooks, it must declare an explicit minimum minor version.

- Breaking changes (major releases): may change core interfaces and require a rebuild of extensions. Major releases are accompanied by a migration guide and a six-month opt-in dual-run period (see Rollout & Migration section).

Versioning policy and manifest

Every runtime artifact (core runtime, kernel plugins, adapters) must ship with a manifest file: runtime-extension-manifest.yaml

Example manifest:

---
name: fast-kernel-plugin
version: 1.2.0
build_target: rwinference-x86_64-gpu-v2
abi_hash: 2f7a4b8e
min_runtime_minor: 2
capabilities:
  - kernel:sharded-attention
  - telemetry:streaming-metrics
allowed_flags:
  - "enable_experimental_prefetch"
signature: "sha256:..."
---

Rules:

- version follows semver: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Runtime core only increments MAJOR when ABI/semantic breaks are necessary.
- abi_hash is a build-time hash of exported symbols and public struct layout. Runtime will refuse to load a plugin if abi_hash mismatches unless explicit override is provided and an operator acknowledges risk.
- min_runtime_minor indicates the minimum runtime minor version that provides required optional hooks.

Extension lifecycle and stability labels

Extensions must be labeled for expected stability in their manifest: alpha | beta | stable

- alpha: experimental; allowed only in sandbox and canary clusters, never in global production regions.
- beta: allowed in limited production audiences after automated safety tests pass. Beta may be promoted to stable after 2 months with no regression signals.
- stable: cleared for general production rollout.

Integration and preflight checklist (required before canary rollout)

1. Automated build and signature verification:
   - Build in CI with reproducible output.
   - Provide signed manifest and signature verification steps.
2. Local microbenchmarks:
   - Run the per-token microbenchmark suite with a representative request corpus (see Benchmarking section).
   - Compare per-token CPU/GPU time; threshold: no >5% regression in median token processing time for kernels, and no >10% regression in p99 latency for end-to-end small requests.
3. Telemetry smoke tests:
   - Verify telemetry adapters emit the runtime-defined trace events and do not create cyclical logging.
4. Safety fuzz tests:
   - Run simulated malformed frames, OOM scenarios, and sequential plugin unload/reload to ensure stability.
5. SLO simulation: 
   - Run the synthetic traffic simulator (operational-workload-simulator) with the extension enabled and confirm p99 latency and availability stay within the attack budget for the target fleet.

Rollout & migration procedure

1. Canary: gate to a single canary cluster that hosts <1% of traffic by default. Monitor for 1 hour of steady-state and one traffic spike test.
2. Regional ramp: expand to a single region at 5% with automated rollback triggers on:
   - increase in p99 latency >10% vs baseline for 10 minutes,
   - error rate increase >0.5% absolute,
   - kernel crash or SIGSEGV in plugin.
3. Controlled ramp: 25% -> 50% -> 100% with progressive verification and a 24-hour hold at each step for stable labels.
4. Emergency rollback: operator runbook and an automated controller exist to yank the extension from active nodes and revert kernel routing to a safe fallback variant. See Runbook section for CLI commands.

Measurement and SLO impact accounting

- Any extension that modifies request-path kernels must publish an anticipated SLO delta in the manifest and in the PR.
- Runtime CI will run a differential benchmark comparing baseline and extension to generate a per-route cost and latency delta table. This table becomes part of the rollout ticket and product release notes.

Telemetry and observability contract

Extensions must emit the following minimal signals to integrate with runtime observability:

- extension.loaded (gauge) with fields: name, version, stability_label
- extension.hook.latency_ms (histogram) for each registered callback
- extension.error (counter) with categorized error types (init, hook-failure, oom)
- optional: extension.span (trace) linking to request.trace_id when executing in-path

Example tracing header (JSON):
{
  "extension": "fast-kernel-plugin",
  "version": "1.2.0",
  "span_id": "...",
  "trace_id": "..."
}

Runtime load-time checks and policy enforcement

At process start and plugin load time the runtime performs:

1. manifest signature verification (fail-fast if missing and not in debug environment)
2. abi_hash check and capability whitelist enforcement
3. capability vs policy check: certain capabilities (e.g., direct GPU memory management) require explicit operator allowance and are disallowed in shared multitenant fleets by default

Policy table (operator-managed):

| Capability | Default allowed in shared fleet | Requires operator consent | Comments |
| GPU direct memory | false | true | High risk: can cause cross-tenant OOM
| telemetry:streaming-metrics | true | false | Low risk
| kernel:sharded-attention | false | true | Requires isolation tests

Runbook: emergency disable and rollback (quick commands)

1. Mark plugin unschedulable via service registry:
   - redwoodctl runtime plugin disable fast-kernel-plugin --cluster canary
2. Trigger rolling restart of nodes that loaded plugin (graceful drain):
   - redwoodctl node drain --label plugin:fast-kernel-plugin --grace-period 120s
3. If crash loop persists, flip the runtime feature-flag fallback:
   - redwoodctl runtime set-flag --name enforce-plugin-fallback --value true

Testing and benchmark suite guidance

- Use the per-token microbenchmark and the request-surface replay (see benchmarking-and-perf-suite). Capture: median token time, p95/p99 end-to-end latency, GPU occupancy, and allocator fragmentation.
- For kernel-level changes, include unit tests that validate KV cache behavior, prefetch ordering, and cooperative preemption interactions.

Example microbenchmark invocation:

./bench/run_per_token.sh --plugin ./fast-kernel-plugin.so --corpus small-oral-requests.json --warmup 60 --measure 300

Deprecation and sunset policy

- Stable extension APIs can be deprecated with at least one minor runtime release notice (minimum 90 days). Deprecation must include: migration guide, compatibility shim if feasible, and test plans.
- Sunset: if an API is to be removed, provide 6 months notice with automated compatibility checks and an extended canary window.

Ownership and escalation
