- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime team (oncall rotation).
- Secondary: eng-platform (release automation), eng-infra (operator policy).
- Escalation contact: runtime-oncall@redwood.ai and platform-ops@redwood.ai.

Appendices

A. Sample minimal CI job steps:
1. build plugin -> produce artifact + signature
2. run unit tests and fuzz harness
3. run microbench suite and compare against baseline metric file
4. publish to internal artifact registry with manifest

B. Migration example (from runtime minor 2 -> 3):
- If your plugin uses the new hook on_request_prefetch introduced in minor 3, set min_runtime_minor: 3 and provide runtime fallback path that skips the hook when absent.

References
- See benchmarking suite: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/runtime-operational-tuning-triage-playbook-2026.json
- See kernel policy language: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-policy-language-declarative-profiles-2026.json

Change log
- 2025-03-10: created (Maya Chen)
- 2026-11-02: clarified abi_hash rules and added emergency rollback commands (Maya Chen)

title: Tiered-fallback-routing-and-eviction-architecture-2026
content:
Overview:

This document describes the Tiered Fallback Routing and Eviction Architecture (TFREA) used by Redwood’s serving runtime to meet multi-dimensional SLOs (latency percentiles, cost budget, and availability) while degrading predictably during capacity pressure or downstream failure modes. TFREA unifies routing policies, candidate model variants, eviction heuristics, and runtime-informed kernel scheduling hints into a single, observable control loop.

Goals:
- Maintain 99th-percentile latency SLOs per route under normal load.
- Bound hosted per-token cost within configured customer cost tiers.
- Provide deterministic, monotonic quality degradation (higher-quality -> lower-quality) with automated rollback when pressure subsides.
- Make fallback decisions explainable and traceable per request for post-incident analysis.

Scope:
- Applies to hosted and Dedicated modes; Private deployments can enable TFREA via configuration flag.
- Covers routing layer, model-variant catalog, eviction/placement heuristics, kernel scheduling hints, and observability integration.

Key concepts and components:
1) Routing Policy Engine (RPE)
- Policy primitives: latency-priority, cost-priority, isolation-priority. Each route has a profile: e.g., {latency: 0.7, cost: 0.2, isolation: 0.1}.
- Decision inputs: request metadata (route, token budget, customer plan), node telemetry (utilization, queue depth), model health (regression alerts), and global capacity signals.
- Outputs: selected pool (hot, warm, cold), model variant (full, quantized, distilled), and optional dual-write fallback (emit to both selected and fallback model asynchronously for A/B quality logging).

2) Model Variant Catalog and Contracts
- Each canonical model version registers 1..N variants with contract metadata:
  - quality_score (0.0-1.0) derived from eval harness
  - compute_cost_factor (relative tokens/second)
  - warmup_time_seconds
  - compatible_kernels (list of kernels / tensor layouts)
- Example registration YAML snippet: 
  id: llama-3-20b:v2026-02
  variants:
    - id: llama-3-20b_fp16
      quality_score: "0.98"
      cost_factor: "1.0"
      warmup: "18"
      kernels: [matmul-fused, alpa-attn-optimized]
    - id: llama-3-20b_8bitq
      quality_score: "0.92"
      cost_factor: "0.55"
      warmup: "6"
      kernels: [quant-8q-conv]

3) Tiered Pools (hot / warm / cold)
- Hot: low-latency nodes, prewarmed KV caches, continuous batching source; used for latency-priority traffic. SLO target: p99 < 120ms for short requests (<=128 tokens).
- Warm: on-demand nodes with partial KV warmup and batched scheduling; SLO target: p99 < 260ms.
- Cold: preemptible or burst capacity; best-effort latency with strong cost savings. SLO target: p99 < 1s (best-effort).

4) Eviction and Placement Heuristics
- Eviction signals: node memory pressure, KV cold-start ratio > 0.4, kernel queue growth rate > 20% over 30s, and per-tenant cost throttle events.
- Heuristic ordering when evicting: least-recently-used variant replicas weighted by (quality_score * route_priority) to avoid evicting high-quality routes.
- Soft-eviction step: move from hot->warm; Hard-eviction: terminate replica (cold) and optionally nominate a lower-cost variant.

5) Kernel Scheduling Hints and Interaction
- RPE emits kernel hints: preferred_kernel, concurrency_target, slice_budget. These are advisory fields consumed by kernel-and-scheduling layer to optimize batch slicing and preemption.
- Example hint: {preferred_kernel: "matmul-fused", concurrency_target: "6", slice_budget_ms: "40"}.

6) Observability and Decision Tracing
- Every routing decision logs a DecisionTrace ID attached to request spans. Trace contains inputs, scoring vector, selected_variant, and fallback_candidates. Stored in the decision-trace index for 30 days by default.
- Key dashboards: Per-route fallback rate, per-variant quality delta (A/B logs), pool occupancy and eviction rate, kernel hint adoption rate.

SLOs and thresholds (operative values):
- Route-level p50/p95/p99 SLOs are configured per route. Default intent for conversational routes: p50 < 30ms, p95 < 95ms, p99 < 250ms.
- Cost guardrails: per-customer monthly token-cost target with soft watermarks at 50% and 80% where TFREA may progressively bias cost-priority.
- Fallback budget: No route should experience fallback > 10% of requests sustained over 5 minutes without triggering operator notification.

Operational procedures and runbooks:
1) Gradual rollout checklist (owner: runtime-release)
1. Create canary pool with 5% traffic weight.
2. Enable decision-trace sampling at 5% for canary.
3. Monitor: fallback-rate, p99 latency, kernel-queue-depth for 15 minutes.
4. If fallback_rate > 1% or p99 regresses > 15% over baseline, abort and roll back.
5. If stable, ramp 5% every 10 minutes to target.

2) Incident triage playbook: Unexpected fallback surge
- Pager triggers at fallback_rate > 10% sustained for 2 minutes.
- Triage steps:
  1. Query decision-trace for last 5 minutes (filter by route). CLI: redwoodctl traces query --route <r> --since 5m --filter fallback=true
  2. Check pool telemetry: node_util, kv_hit_rate, kernel_queue_growth.
  3. If KV cold-start > 50%: trigger warmup job for top-5 variants: redwoodctl runtime warmup --variants <ids> --target-pool hot
  4. If node OOMs or watchdog hits: cordon nodes and spin up replacement nodes (see gpu-fleet-and-capacity runbook).
  5. Temporarily set route policy to latency-priority and pin to hot pool for critical tenants while investigating.

3) Performance regression investigation (owner: runtime-profiling)
- Collect sample logs and kernel traces with sampler strategy: 1:1000 baseline, 1:50 on regression window.
- Use profiling commands: profiler collect --trace-id <trace> --duration 30s --output s3://runtime-profiles/<id>.tar.gz
- Correlate with batch-slice histograms and kernel latency percentiles.

Benchmarking and validation suite:
- The TFREA validation harness is a sub-suite in the performance suite: includes mixed-workload load generator, KV-warmup simulator, and variant quality regression tests.
- Key scenarios:
  - Steady-state with mixed short/long sequences (60/30/10 split by request length).
  - Rapid burst (2x sustained) with concurrent model-variant promotion/demotion.
  - Engineered wholesale kernel regression: inject a slow kernel variant to ensure sentinel metrics and fallbacks work.
- Release gate: TFREA must pass canary e2e smoke and two automated burst simulations without p99 SLO breaches before canary ramp.

Release notes summary (2026-02-15):
- Introduced Tiered Fallback Routing and Eviction Architecture (TFREA) to reduce tail latency and control cost during capacity pressure.
- Added DecisionTrace indexing and trace-based runbook utilities.
- New model-variant contract fields (quality_score, warmup_time_seconds) and kernel hint API.

Known issues and workarounds (as of 2026-03-02):
- Issue: Under certain mixed-tenant workloads, eviction ranking can bias too heavily toward routes with frequent short requests, causing long-tail quality regressions for background batch routes.
  - Workaround: Set explicit route affinity in route config to protect background batch routes, e.g., affinity: {protect_until: "2026-06-01"}.
- Issue: Kernel hint adoption sometimes lags on heterogeneous pools where the kernel mapper is updating; mismatch can cause suboptimal batch slicing.
  - Workaround: Restart kernel-mapper after variant promotion: systemctl restart kernel-mapper (one node at a time) and allow 60s for re-registration.

Implementation notes and APIs:
- New API: /v1/runtime/route-evaluate (internal) returns DecisionTrace and selected_variant. Schema: {route, inputs, scoring, selected, fallbacks, hints}.
- redwoodctl examples:
  - Query fallback stats: redwoodctl runtime stats fallback --route <route> --window 10m
  - Force promote variant to hot pool: redwoodctl runtime promote --variant <id> --pool hot --reason "emergency-fix"

Ownership and SLAs:
- Owners: runtime-architecture (Priya Natarajan), runtime-scheduling (Marcus Liu), runtime-profiling (Zara Ortega).
- Support: eng-sre oncall for 24/7 pager coverage.
- Documentation and training: rollout workshops scheduled for 2026-03-10 and 2026-03-17.

Appendix A — route policy example (YAML):
route: "conversations/v1/generate"
policy:
  latency: "0.75"
  cost: "0.20"
  isolation: "0.05"
  affinity: {pools: [hot, warm], protect_until: "2026-04-01"}

Appendix B — decision scoring example (csv):
input,weight,score,contrib
latency_priority,0.75,0.82,0.615
cost_priority,0.20,0.34,0.068
isolation_priority,0.05,0.9,0.045
final_score,, ,0.728

Appendix C — escalation contact matrix:
- Pager 1: eng-sre (primary)
- Pager 2: runtime-architecture (Priya Natarajan)
- Email: runtime-discuss@redwood.ai

Related pages and next steps:
- Add kernel hint adoption metrics to runtime-consolidation dashboard and alert if adoption < 80% across a pool.
- Prototype ML-driven fallback scorer (Q2 2026) to replace hand-tuned weighting.

If you are implementing or operating TFREA and see any unexpected behaviors, file a ticket in the runtime backlog (component: runtime-fallback) and include DecisionTrace IDs for at least 5 example requests.

title: Execution Stability Certification Protocol
content:
Overview

This document specifies the Execution Stability Certification Protocol (ESCP): a repeatable, automated acceptance process that a runtime feature or kernel rollout must pass before being enabled for canary or production traffic. The goal is to provide deterministic gates for latency, error-rate, resource-safety, and downgrade behaviour across model variants and quantization profiles.

Goals

- Provide a short, reproducible certification path for runtime features and kernel variants.
- Ensure rollouts preserve customer-facing SLOs and do not materially increase operator toil.
- Capture behavioural contracts for fallbacks, KV cache consistency, and preemption semantics.

Scope

- Applies to: kernel releases, scheduler policy changes, KV cache algorithm changes, preemption/hothand-off logic, quantization rollout candidates.
- Excludes: experimental lab-only kernels flagged "sandbox" (see Appendix C for sandbox tagging conventions).

Acceptance criteria (table)

| Class | Metric | Gate | Measurement window |
|-------|--------|------|--------------------|
| Latency | runtime.request_latency.p95 | <= 2x baseline or absolute 1200ms (whichever lower) | 1h steady-state under canonical load |
| Error rate | runtime.request_error_rate | <= baseline + 0.1% absolute | 1h |
| Kernel stalls | kernel.hang_count | 0 detected events per 24h projected | measured during stress and 1h soak |
| KV cache correctness | kvcache.consistency_failures | 0 | end-to-end replay with golden trace |
| Resource safety | gpu.memory_exceed_events | 0 | stress profiling run |
| Degradation fidelity | degrade.fidelity_drop | no more than 5% of requests fall to lower fidelity erroneously | 2h soak |

Certification stages (high level)

1. Pre-cert: unit and integration tests; smoke benchmark on microbenchmark suite.
2. Local soak: run on single-node lab with synthetic traffic matching target cohort (sequence length distribution, token mix). Validate p50/p95 and basic telemetry.
3. Stress test: fault-injection and resource-constrained runs (OOM, NVLink flakiness, network jitter). Run soak >= 2h and track kernel stall signals.
4. Shadow canary: mirror 1–5% production traffic (no write-path) for 24h; compare divergence metrics.
5. Canary rollout: progressive, 5% -> 25% -> 100% with automatic rollback on gating violations.

Test harness and commands

- Harness: runtime-certify (internal test harness). Key flags:
  - --trace-corpus <path>   (replay corpus of real requests)
  - --kernel-variant <name>
  - --model-profile <json>
  - --soak-duration <minutes>
  - --stress-injector (enable fault injection)

Example run:

$ runtime-certify --trace-corpus traces/q2-webchat-8k.json --kernel-variant maelstrom-v2 --model-profile profiles/longform-8k.json --soak-duration 120 --stress-injector

YAML model-profile example (canonical subset):

model_profile:
  name: longform-8k
  avg_sequence_length: "3700"
  spike_percentile_95: "7800"
  concurrency_shape: "poisson"
  kvcache_enabled: "true"

Observability gating (signals to stream to gating engine)

- Latency: runtime.request_latency.{p50,p95,p99}
- Error: runtime.request_error_rate
- Kernel: kernel.queue_depth, kernel.active_waves, kernel.hang_count
- Memory: gpu.memory_usage_pct, gpu.vram_alloc_failures
- KV cache: kvcache.hits, kvcache.misses, kvcache.consistency_failures
- Fidelity: degrade.fidelity_drop, degrade.unexpected_falls

Gating thresholds are codified in the certification engine. Any threshold exceedance triggers an automated abort and alerts on-call.

Rollback and mitigation checklist

1. Immediately route traffic away using tiered-fallback routing to fallback-kernel (configured in routing manifest).
2. If stall pattern observed, trigger kernel-snapshot and collect live-traces: /ops/tools/collect-kernel-snapshot --target <node>
3. If KV inconsistency detected, snapshot replicas, pause rollouts, and engage DB team for trace reconciliation.
4. For memory pressure, disable the variant and escalate to infra; append nodes to dedicated-gpu-pool for burst capacity.

Ownership and contacts

- Certification owner: Sofia Patel (runtime stability, @sophiap)
- Kernel engineering: Marco Chen (@mchen)
- Scheduler team lead: Priya Iyer (@priya)
- Oncall rotation: runtime-oncall@redwood-inference.com

Rollout checklist (pre-canary)

- [ ] Automated tests green for kernel and scheduler policy
- [ ] Benchmark harness: 90th percentile runtime against baseline measured and stored in bench-db
- [ ] Telemetry mappings reviewed and mapped to gating engine
- [ ] Runbook updated with new signal names and escalation steps
- [ ] Reviewers signoff

Operational runbook excerpt (for oncall)

1. Observe: check runtime.request_latency.p95 and kernel.hang_count; if either spikes beyond gate, mark deployment paused.
2. Collect: runtime-certify --collect-trace --deployment <id>
3. Mitigate: enable fallback route, reduce concurrency admission using admission-controller set --target-concurrency <n>
4. Escalate: if KV failures present, page storage@redwood-inference with tag "kv-inconsistency" and attach trace id.

Appendix A — Example benchmark scenario (table)

| Scenario | Concurrency | Avg seq len | Warm cache | Ramp |
|---------|-------------:|------------:|-----------:|-----|
| baseline | 50 | 300 | yes | 10m |
| peak-test | 200 | 2,500 | mixed | 30m |

Appendix B — Known pitfalls and mitigations

- Non-deterministic quantized kernels: ensure bitwise-compatibility tests run for 1000 traces; if divergence > 0.2% fail.
- NVLink transient throttling: include network jitter injector in stress tests; add compensating retry logic in dispatcher.
- Replay corpus bias: rotate corpora monthly and sample by traffic cohorts to avoid overfitting to a single client pattern.

Appendix C — Tagging and metadata for sandbox kernels

- sandbox:true (disallowed for certification) 
- stability_level: experimental|beta|stable
- required_metadata: changelist-id, kernel-binary-hash, compatible-model-ids

Related artifacts

- Bench DB: bench-db.prod.redwood (benchmarks are stored as time-series snapshots)
- Certification engine repo: git@github.com:redwood-inference/cert-engine
- Telemetry mapping spec: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/observability-adapter-sidecar-design-manual-2026

Document history

- 2026-03-10: created by Sofia Patel
- 2026-05-02: stress-injector section added (reviewers: Liam O'Connor)
- 2026-07-12: expanded failure modes and rollback checklist

title: Deterministic Inference Mode: Reproducibility Spec & Runbook
content:
Summary:

This page defines the "Deterministic Inference Mode" (DIM): a configuration and operational contract that provides reproducible token output and execution traces across repeated inference runs for a pinned model variant and configuration. DIM is intended for debugging, eval reproducibility, and regression investigation where bit-for-bit repeatability (within documented tolerances) is required.

Goals:
- Provide a single switchable runtime mode (global or per-route) that reduces nondeterminism sources across scheduler, kernels, and model IO.
- Enumerate required kernel/runtime properties and configuration knobs to enable reproducible outputs for common models (decoder-only, encoder-decoder, multimodal pipelines).
- Provide an operator runbook for enabling DIM in canary and production, including telemetry, verification tests, and rollback criteria.

Non-goals:
- DIM is not a substitute for formal cryptographic determinism across heterogeneous hardware families (we document hardware compatibility and limits).
- DIM does not freeze model weights; model version pinning remains required for reproducibility.

Definitions and scope:
- Deterministic Inference Mode (DIM): a set of runtime and kernel settings plus input seeding rules intended to make repeated calls with identical inputs and model version produce the same token sequence and internal trace signatures.
- Trace signature: a compact hash synthesized from key telemetry points (request_id, model_version, RNG seeds, kernel checksums, kvcache identifiers) used to quickly validate run equivalence.
- Tolerance window: allowed floating-point numerical variance range (default 1e-6 relative) documented per-model class.

Requirements (operator and engineering):
| Requirement | Rationale | Owner |
|---|---|---|
| RNG seed pinning exposed per-request | Async subgraph operators and sampling must consume a deterministic seed | runtime-team |
| Kernel numerics mode (fast/precise) | Choose consistent fused-kernel behavior; disable nondeterministic fusions | kernel-team |
| Threading affinity deterministic scheduling | Prevent race-order variability in parallel matmuls | scheduler-team |
| KV cache stable eviction ordering | Eviction order must be deterministic to avoid cache-dependent outputs | runtime-team |
| Quantization deterministic paths | If quantized kernels differ in numeric ordering, document and pin variant | perf-team |

Operational configuration (example YAML):

runtime.flags:
  deterministic_inference: true
  rng_seed_mode: request_provided # alternatives: time_based, zero_padded
  kernel_numerics: precise
  disable_async_kernel_prefetch: true
  kvcache_eviction_policy: lru_stable_order
  max_concurrent_threads: 1  # can be relaxed per-hardware after validation

Per-route override example (HTTP/Route JSON):
{
  "route": "/debug/replay",
  "model": "gptx-7b-v2",
  "runtime_override": {
    "deterministic_inference": true,
    "rng_seed": 8675309
  }
}

Enabling DIM (canary -> rollout) — operator runbook (short):
1) Prepare a deterministic test corpus: 500 short, 200 medium, 50 long prompts covering sampling+greedy, top-k/top-p, and streaming. Include explicit instruction permutations for temperature-based sampling.
2) Provision a canary pool: single-node pool of same GPU SKU used in target fleet. Pin kernel bundle to previously validated release.
3) Deploy runtime flags with deterministic_inference=true and rng_seed_mode=request_provided.
4) Run the corpus three times with identical request payloads and collect: token sequences, trace signatures, kernel checksums, and per-request telemetry.
5) Verification step: Token sequences must match exactly for all three runs; trace signature must be identical. If mismatch, abort and collect full traces for kernel-team.
6) Gradual scale: expand canary to 10 nodes, repeat corpus. Increase concurrency to target SLO while monitoring divergence.
7) If stable for 48 hours and regression-free against baseline outputs, schedule 10% production traffic routing with DIM flag. Observe for 7 days.
8) Full rollout: staged 10% -> 30% -> 60% -> 100% (minimum 24–72 hour holds depending on traffic shape).

Verification & automated tests (CI):
- Determinism unit test harness: replay single-batch with pinned seeds on CPU and GPU golden kernel; assert tokens and checksums equal.
- Nightly cross-hardware matrix: run 100-corpus tests across supported GPU families and report divergence rates.
- Fuzz-sampling profile: random sampling seeds should never collapse into nondeterministic behavior for greedy decode.

Telemetry and observability requirements:
- New telemetry keys (telemetry names):
  - dim.enabled (boolean)
  - dim.rng_seed (int/string)
  - dim.trace_signature (string)
  - dim.kernel_checksum (string)
  - dim.kvcache_epoch (int)
  - dim.repro_status (enum: ok|mismatch|tolerance_exceeded)
- Logs: on mismatch, write compact failure event with request_id, route, seed, kernel_checksum, top-3 divergent tokens and stack trace. Tag event with priority P0 for oncall.
- Dashboards: Determinism health panel (count of mismatches per hour), top offending routes, distribution by model and hardware SKU.

SLOs and acceptance criteria (canary gating):
- Repro mismatch rate must be < 0.01% across canary corpus at target concurrency.
- Tolerance_exceeded events allowed only for documented model classes (e.g., very large multimodal pipelines) and must be listed in the known limitations section.

Common failure modes and triage steps:
1) Symptom: Repro status=mismatch, kernel_checksum differs.
   Triage:
   - Compare kernel version and bundle checksums between runs (kernel-team).
   - Run single-step microtrace to isolate matmul/softmax layer causing divergence.
   - If fused/unfused kernel flip is observed, pin kernel_numerics to 'precise' and re-run.
2) Symptom: Repro mismatch only under high concurrency.
   Triage:
   - Reduce max_concurrent_threads to baseline. If stable, incrementally increase and identify concurrency threshold.
   - Capture thread-affinity and kernel launch order traces; escalate to scheduler-team.
3) Symptom: Determinism fails with quantized model variant.
   Triage:
   - Verify quantized-kernel deterministic flag; if not available, run inference with full-precision hotpath and compare.
   - Add quantization path to nightly cross-hardware matrix for ownership and acceptance.

Kernel and scheduler requirements checklist (for kernel-team):
- Deterministic kernel launch ordering when DIM=true.
- Deterministic reduction primitive (no atomic non-associative reductions that depend on launch order).
- Deterministic RNG consumer contract for dropout, sampling logits, and any augmentations.
- Stable fused-kernel commit with checksumable artifact.

Compatibility matrix (high-level):
- NVIDIA A100 (CUDA 11.x): Supported with kernels compiled with --deterministic-flags.
- NVIDIA H100 (CUDA 12.x): Supported, but requires kernel precision flag 'precise' (see notes).
- AMD MI250: Partial support — some fused kernels not yet deterministic; see limitation list.
- CPU fallback: Supported but slower; useful for debugging golden traces.

Known limitations (short):
- DIM cannot guarantee bit-exact results across different hardware families. We provide per-hardware checksums and recommend golden-hash comparisons instead of raw bit-for-bit expectation.
- Some third-party ops (custom attention blocks) may not expose deterministic variants. These must be wrapped and versioned before DIM rollout.

Backout and rollback criteria:
- Automatic rollback if repro mismatch rate exceeds 0.05% over a 1-hour sliding window during rollout.
- Manual rollback criteria: any P0 customer-facing incident tied to DIM changes, unexplained SLO degradation, or a memory/cpu thermal spike correlated with DIM changes.

Example debugging commands and utilities:
- Run deterministic harness (local):
  ./bin/runtime-debug --model gptx-7b-v2 --route /debug/replay --seed 42 --runs 3 --collect-traces --out reprun.log
- Extract trace signature from log (python):
  python tools/trace_tools.py --extract-signature reprun.log --out sig.json
- Compare kernelsums between two nodes (remote):
  ssh ops@node1 'cat /var/lib/runtime/kernelsums' > node1.txt
  ssh ops@node2 'cat /var/lib/runtime/kernelsums' > node2.txt
  diff node1.txt node2.txt || echo "kernel mismatch"

Quality gates and CI sensors:
- Merge gate requires passing the determinism unit test suite.
- Release pipeline emits 'determinism-compatibility-report' artifact that gets stored with release metadata.

Owner and escalation:
- Primary owner: runtime-team (incidents: oncall-runtime@redwood.ai)
- Kernel regressions: kernel-team (kernel-owners@redwood.ai)
- Hardware compatibility: infra-gpu (infra-gpu@redwood.ai)

Appendix A — Repro trace signature format (human-readable):
- trace_signature = sha256(concat(request_id, model_version, rng_seed, kernel_checksum, kvcache_epoch))
- kernel_checksum = sha256(binary-kernel-bundle || compile-options || git-commit)

Appendix B — Test matrix (abbreviated):
- CPU x FP32: baseline regression tests (golden)
- A100 x FP16 fused: primary validated target
- H100 x BF16 fused: validated with tolerance window 1e-5
- MI250 x FP16: exploratory; documented differences allowed

Contact and follow-ups:
- This spec is owned by Aisha Raman (runtime-team). For clarifications, add reviewers or raise a ticket in #runtime-determinism on Slack.

Document history:
- 2024-06-12: initial draft
- 2025-11-03: updated telemetry keys and canary cadence
- 2026-02-14: added hardware compatibility notes and rollback thresholds

Related reading and references:
- Kernel determinism investigation protocol (profiling-playbook/kernel-determinism-investigation-and-replay-protocol-2024)
- Deterministic scheduler simulation verification (kernel-and-scheduling/deterministic-scheduler-simulation-verification-manual-2026)

End of page.

title: Kernel Selection Architecture Overview (Serving Runtime)
content:
## Overview
Kernel selection is the Serving Runtime subsystem responsible for choosing the concrete GPU implementation (“kernel plan”) for a request, given:
- Model identity and architecture/family
- Workload regime (prefill vs decode characteristics; sequence length buckets)
- Hardware target (GPU SKU, driver/CUDA capability, MIG partitioning)
- Runtime feature flags (quantization profile, attention variant, KV-cache layout)

This page describes:
1) Where selection happens in the execution pipeline
2) Interfaces to Scheduler and Compilation Cache
3) How decisions are cached, serialized, and made replayable/deterministic

This is an architectural overview. For the v2 decision logic and fallback policy, see ADR-017 and the v2 design doc.

---

## Goals
- Ensure **correctness-first** selection: only choose kernels that are compatible with the request + target hardware.
- Maintain **determinism and replayability**: identical inputs must yield identical selection (modulo explicitly versioned policy changes).
- Reduce tail latency by selecting optimized kernels per SKU and per seq-length regime.
- Keep selection overhead low (bounded CPU time, bounded telemetry overhead).
- Provide operational controls: allow/deny lists, feature gates, and forced overrides.

## Non-goals
- Training or learning a model-based selector (out of scope for v2; we use explicit policy rules).
- Deciding cluster placement (region/pool routing is handled by control plane and scheduling layers).

---

## High-level execution pipeline (where selection occurs)
Kernel selection runs inside the per-request runtime execution path after model resolution and before compilation/execution.

### Request flow (text diagram)
1. **Front Door / API Adapter**
   - Validates request, resolves model alias → `model_id` + `model_version`.
   - Normalizes request options (max_tokens, streaming, tool/function calling toggles) into `RequestOptions`.

2. **Scheduler / Batcher**
   - Assigns request to a worker process on a GPU.
   - Produces lightweight workload hints (e.g., observed prefill/decode distribution for the batch queue).

3. **Kernel Selector** (this subsystem)
   - Extracts features (`SelectorFeatures`) from request + model metadata + GPU metadata + scheduler hints.
   - Applies feature gate + allow/deny rules.
   - Generates candidate kernels and selects a `KernelPlan`.
   - Emits selection telemetry (sampled).

4. **Compilation Cache + Launcher**
   - Checks compilation cache for compiled artifacts matching `KernelPlan`.
   - Compiles if missing (within guardrails), then launches the selected kernel.

5. **Execution + Metrics**
   - Executes prefill/decode.
   - Reports latency breakdown, kernel identifiers, and errors.

Selection occurs at step 3, and is designed to be:
- **Pure** with respect to its inputs (no hidden dependence on time or ambient process state)
- **Versioned** via policy version IDs and runtime build version

---

## Component boundaries
### Kernel Selector module
**Owner:** Runtime Kernels + Runtime Architecture

**Responsibilities:**
- Feature extraction and normalization
- Candidate generation
- Rule evaluation and scoring (v2)
- Fallback selection
- Decision caching and serialization
- Telemetry emission hooks

**Does not own:**
- GPU placement / pool selection (control plane + scheduler)
- Compilation artifact generation logic (compiler backend owns compilation; selector only keys it)

### Kernel Registry
A registry of kernel implementations and their compatibility constraints.

Registry entries are keyed by:
- `kernel_id` (stable string)
- Model family/architecture compatibility (e.g., llama-like, mistral-like)
- Capability requirements (SM version, CUDA capability flags)
- Supported quantization profiles
- Known-bad deny rules (SKU/driver specific)

Registry is loaded from:
- Built-in runtime defaults
- Hot-reloadable config overlays (for emergency deny/pin)

### Compilation Cache interface
Selector produces a `CompilationKey` / `PlanKey` used by compilation caching.

Compilation cache uses `CompilationKey` to:
- Lookup a compiled artifact (in-process memory + on-node disk cache)
- Avoid recompiles across requests

Selector guarantees:
- If `CompilationKey` is identical, compiled artifacts should be reusable.
- If a choice changes any codegen-relevant parameter, it must reflect in `CompilationKey`.

### Scheduler hints interface
Scheduler provides *optional* hints that improve stability for mixed workloads.

Examples of hints:
- Estimated `prefill_tokens` and `decode_tokens` for the in-flight batch
- Observed queue regime classification (short prompts vs long-context dominated)
- Batching parameters currently in effect (max batch size, continuous batching mode)

Selector treats hints as inputs to selection, but the hint schema is:
- Explicitly versioned (`hints_schema_version`)
- Safe to omit (selector must fall back to request-derived features)

---

## Data contracts
### SelectorFeatures (normalized inputs)
SelectorFeatures is the normalized set of signals used for decision-making.

At a minimum, v2 uses:
- `model_family` (e.g., llama-like, mistral-like, qwen-like, gemma-like)
- `model_id`, `model_version`
- `seq_bucket` (see below)
- `gpu_sku_normalized` (see below)
- `sm_version` / `compute_capability`
- `driver_version` and `cuda_runtime_version` (guardrails)
- `quant_profile` (fp16/bf16/int8/int4 where applicable)

#### Sequence bucket definition
Selection uses coarse buckets to reduce decision noise while capturing the main performance regimes.

Current buckets (subject to policy updates):
- `S`: prefill ≤ 512 and expected decode ≤ 128
- `M`: prefill 513–2048 or decode 129–512
- `L`: prefill 2049–8192 or decode 513–2048
- `XL`: prefill > 8192 or decode > 2048 (long-context / long generation)

Notes:
- Buckets are computed from request limits + scheduler hints (when present).
- For streaming requests, decode bucket should be based on expected decode tokens (max_tokens) but may be clamped to historical workload hints.

#### GPU SKU normalization
We normalize cloud instance naming, PCI IDs, and MIG partitioning into a stable SKU string.

Examples:
- `nvidia-a100-80gb` (covers common PCI IDs; memory size retained)
- `nvidia-h100-80gb-sxm`
- `nvidia-l40s-48gb`
- `nvidia-a100-40gb-mig-1g.5gb` (MIG partitions include slice info)

Normalization is performed once per process at GPU init and passed as immutable metadata to the selector.

---

## Output contract
### KernelPlan
KernelPlan is the selector’s output. It is a structured record that must fully describe the execution choice.

KernelPlan includes:
- `selected_kernel_id`
- `policy_version` (e.g., `kasv2-2026-02-18`)
- `fallback_reason` (empty if primary rule matched; otherwise explicit)
- `compilation_key` (string; stable serialization)
- `execution_toggles` (e.g., attention variant, KV-cache layout)

The plan must be serializable into:
- Log/trace fields
- A stable “plan key” string for caching
- A replay record for deterministic tests

---

## Decision caching (what is cached and where)
To keep overhead low and avoid repeated policy evaluation, we use a two-level cache.

### Level 1: In-process Decision Cache (L1)
- **Scope:** per worker process
- **Key:** `DecisionCacheKey`
- **Value:** `KernelPlan` (including compilation_key)
- **Eviction:** bounded LRU (default 5k entries) + TTL (default 30 minutes)

Recommended key fields:
- `model_version`
- `model_family`
- `gpu_sku_normalized`
- `seq_bucket`
- `quant_profile`
- `driver_version_major_minor` (coarsened)
- `policy_version`

Rationale:
- This captures stable performance regimes and avoids per-request recomputation.
- Including `policy_version` prevents stale cache reuse across policy updates.

### Level 2: Compilation Cache (L2)
Compilation caching is separate from decision caching.

- Decision cache returns a `KernelPlan` quickly.
- Compilation cache ensures the chosen plan maps to a compiled artifact.

Important: do **not** conflate “same decision” with “compiled exists”. A KernelPlan can be cached even if compilation misses occur; compilation cache handles that separately.

---

## Serialization & determinism
Determinism is a hard requirement for kernel selection.

### Determinism rules
- Selection must be a pure function of explicitly provided inputs.
- Any policy changes must be represented by a versioned `policy_version`.
- Any non-deterministic ordering (e.g., iterating hash maps) is forbidden in candidate ordering and rule evaluation.

### SelectionRecord (replay + debugging)
For sampled requests (and for forced-debug runs), we serialize a compact SelectionRecord.

SelectionRecord fields (minimum):
- `selector_version` (runtime build + module version)
- `policy_version`
- `decision_cache_key`
- `selected_kernel_id`
- `candidate_kernel_ids` (ordered)
- `model_id`, `model_version`, `model_family`
- `seq_bucket`
- `gpu_sku_normalized`, `sm_version`, `driver_version`, `cuda_runtime_version`
- `allow_deny_outcome` (e.g., allowed by model allowlist; denied by SKU rule)
- `fallback_reason` (if any)

Storage locations:
- Trace span attributes on the request root span (sampled)
- Structured logs in `runtime-kernel-selection` log stream (sampled)
- Optional per-request dump when `--kernel_selection_dump=1` is enabled (debug-only)

### Stable plan keys
We require stable string encoding for:
- `decision_cache_key`
- `compilation_key`

Encoding guidance:
- Use `key=value` segments joined by `|` in a fixed order.
- No whitespace.
- No high-cardinality freeform fields.

Example (illustrative):
`policy=kasv2-2026-02-18|model=llama-3.1-70b@2026-02-01|gpu=nvidia-h100-80gb-sxm|seq=XL|quant=bf16|drv=550.54`

---

## Interfaces to rollout gates and overrides
Kernel selection behavior can be modified at runtime via control-plane-provided gates and local debug flags.

### Feature gates
- Gate name: `kernel_selection_v2`
- Scope: environment/region/pool + model allowlist
- Evaluation point: **before** selector applies v2 rules

If gate is disabled:
- Selector falls back to v1 selection or a conservative default plan (per policy).

### Allow/deny rules
Support for emergency and proactive safety:
- Deny specific `kernel_id` on a `gpu_sku_normalized` (and optionally driver/CUDA)
- Deny v2 entirely for a `model_version`
- Pin a kernel for a model+SKU+seq_bucket for fast mitigation

Override precedence (highest to lowest):
1. Local debug flags (on-call / reproduction only)
2. Control plane hotfix rules (deny/pin)
3. Built-in denylist guardrails (known unstable combos)
4. v2 normal policy
5. v1 fallback policy
6. Conservative baseline kernel (last resort)

---

## Observability hooks (what we emit)
The selector emits the following telemetry (subject to sampling and cardinality controls):

### Metrics
- `kernel_selection_decisions_total{policy_version, model_family, gpu_sku, seq_bucket, selected_kernel_id}` (sampled or aggregated)
- `kernel_selection_fallbacks_total{reason, gpu_sku, model_family}`
- `kernel_selection_eval_ms` (CPU overhead)
- `kernel_selection_cache_hit_ratio` (L1 decision cache)

### Traces
- Span event: `kernel_selection` on request root span
- Attributes include `selected_kernel_id`, `policy_version`, `seq_bucket`, `gpu_sku_normalized`, and `fallback_reason`

### Logs
- Structured log line in `runtime-kernel-selection` stream for sampled requests

PII/Sensitive data note:
- No prompt text, no customer identifiers.
- Model identifiers are internal version IDs; customer-provided model aliases must be resolved before logging.

---

## Failure modes and fallback behavior
Kernel selection has explicit fallback behavior to avoid correctness issues and to bound tail latency.

Common failure modes:
- Kernel missing for a SKU (registry mismatch)
- Known unstable kernel+driver combination (guardrail deny)
- Seq bucket misclassification leading to long-context regressions
- Compilation failure for a selected plan

Fallback principles:
- Prefer a known-safe kernel with acceptable perf over an unverified optimized kernel.
- Treat compilation failure as a signal to fall back to the next candidate (bounded retries) before failing the request.
- Emit explicit telemetry on fallback reason.

For the authoritative fallback hierarchy, see ADR-017.

---

## Operational notes (Dedicated / Private)
Dedicated and Private deployments often have constrained SKU sets and driver policies.

Recommended practices:
- Pre-register and validate kernel registry entries per allowed SKU set.
- Keep a minimal emergency override file that can:
  - Disable v2 per model
  - Pin a known-good kernel
  - Deny known-bad kernel+SKU combos
- Ensure selection telemetry sampling is tuned to avoid excessive cardinality in smaller clusters.

---

## Appendix: configuration and debug controls (runtime)
The following names are representative; refer to the runbook for exact flags per runtime version.

- `--enable_kernel_selection_v2=true|false`
- `--kernel_selection_policy_version=<id>` (debug only; production uses release-default)
- `--kernel_selection_force_kernel_id=<kernel_id>` (debug only)
- `--kernel_selection_dump=1` (writes SelectionRecord to local logs)
- `--kernel_selection_decision_cache_size=<n>`
- `--kernel_selection_telemetry_sample_rate=<0..1>`

---

## Owners
- Architecture/perf correctness: Noah Patel
- Selector logic: Yuki Sato
- Kernel registry + implementations: Hiro Tanaka, Grace Kim
- Scheduler hints integration: Sofia Ivanova
- Tail latency and observability: Omar El-Sayed
- Control-plane rollout gates: Ethan Park

For on-call actions, see: Kernel Selection v2 Override and Rollback Runbook.

title: Handoff Harmony: Eviction and Transfer Playbook
content:
Summary:

This playbook codifies a deterministic, observable approach for transferring in-flight requests and gracefully reclaiming runtime resources. It balances user-visible correctness (avoiding aborted responses and consistency loss) with operator needs for fast resource reclamation during scale events, maintenance, or kernel failures.

Audience:
- Runtime engineers
- SREs on-call for runtime clusters
- Platform owners planning canaries or capacity changes

Goals and guardrails:
- User-visible aborts from planned or forced handoffs should be < 0.05% monthly.
- Typical handoff commit latency: median <= 150 ms; p99 <= 2.5s for short requests.
- Eviction flows must reclaim a node within configured eviction_window while providing final best-effort completion for affected sessions.

Core terminology (short):
- handoff_token: single-use opaque identifier with expiry ISO8601 timestamp. Appears in traces.
- drain_epoch: the short wait after marking sessions to allow running kernels to finish naturally (configurable).
- eviction_window: hard timeout for completing a transfer or executing graceful eviction.
- kv-sync: optional asynchronous synchronization of minimal KV state to target. Marks session degraded if incomplete.
- preempt_credit: a small retry allowance given to callers during transfer to reduce client-visible failures.

Architecture components involved:
- runtime-dispatcher (dispatcher): selects destination node/shard and initiates handoff intents.
- node-agent: per-host service orchestrating local drain, KV exports, kernel lifecycle, and final commit/eviction actions.
- handoff-orchestrator (leader): optional distributed coordinator for multi-shard transfers and conflict resolution. Data store: etcd.
- telemetry-agent: annotates traces with handoff_token and emits events for Handoff:started, Handoff:committed, Handoff:evicted.

Protocol (ordered steps):
1) Dispatcher detects transfer reason: planned drain, OS maintenance, GPU error, preemption, or capacity balancing. It calculates candidate target(s) and issues an Intent to node-agent: {token, targets, reason, ttl}.
2) Node-agent marks sessions in drain set and enters drain_epoch. It sets internal state to DRAINING and begins non-blocking kv-sync for streaming sessions.
3) Handoff-orchestrator (if present) attempts to reserve a receive slot on the target node. Reservation response includes acceptance, backoff recommendation, or alternate node list.
4) Target node verifies compatibility (model variant, quantization profile, KV shard affinity) and responds. If accepted, it returns a receive_handle with a short TTL.
5) Source node streams session metadata and small KV chunks (if supported). Only metadata required to resume decoding is streamed; secrets and raw user payloads are never proxied.
6) Target node writes session metadata to local cache, acknowledges, and telemetry records Handoff:committed. Source node marks session COMPLETE_LOCAL_CLEANUP and releases kernel resources.
7) If the sequence fails to finish before eviction_window, node-agent triggers graceful-eviction: attempt a synthetic completion (fast-fallback generation), then issue final kernel teardown and emit Handoff:evicted.

Configuration reference (defaults):
| key | default | note |
| .handoff.eviction_window_secs | "30" | applies to short non-stream sessions |
| .handoff.stream_eviction_window_secs | "120" | applies to chat/stream sessions |
| .handoff.drain_epoch_ms | "1500" | small wait to let kernels finish naturally |
| .handoff.max_parallel_transfers | "6" | per-node outgoing transfer concurrency |
| .handoff.preempt_credit_tokens | "1" | number of ephemeral retries clients may consume |
| .handoff.kv_sync_enabled | "true" | best-effort; false disables KV transfer attempts |

Observed failure patterns and recommended mitigations:
- reservation_timeouts (common): when requests queue at dispatcher due to oversubscription. Actions: reduce dispatcher weight, scale dedicated capacity, or reroute to compatible fallback variant. Metric: handoff_reserve_timeout_total.
- kernel_stall during drain: identified by kernel.active_ms spikes and no progress markers. Action: extend drain_epoch up to a soft cap once for kernels flagged as idempotent; otherwise escalate to forced eviction. Metric: kernel_blocked_handoff_total.
- kv_sync_partial: KV sync completed partially. Action: mark session degraded; downstream resume will perform token re-priming. Metric: handoff_kv_partial_total.
- oscillation between nodes: rapid flip-flops identified by repeated commits for same session token. Action: insert randomized cooldown (2m) and raise handoff priority to avoid future oscillations.

Operational runbook (triage):
Alert triggers:
- handoff_reserve_timeout_rate > 5/min sustained for 3m
- handoff_evicted.rate spikes > 1/min for 5m
- handoff_kv_partial.rate > baseline by 200%

Initial responder steps (SRE):
1) Confirm alerts and scope: query Prometheus examples:
   - sum(rate(handoff_reserve_timeout_total[5m])) by (cluster)
   - sum(rate(handoff_evicted_total[5m])) by (node)
2) Inspect dispatcher and node-agent dashboards: dispatcher.route_failures, node.queue_depth_p95, node.kv_sync_errors.
3) If a single node is overloaded: cordon it via node-agent API (dry-run first), allow existing handoffs to proceed, and unfavour new routing to it. Example API:
   curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
     -d '{"cordon": true, "eviction_window_secs": 60, "dry_run": true}' \
     https://runtime-node-agent.internal/v1/node/$NODE_ID/cordon
4) If topology-level saturation: scale up dedicated pools or adjust dispatcher routing policies to prefer fallback variants.
5) If KV sync errors: collect node-agent logs (tag: handoff.kv), and export traces from telemetry-service for the handoff_token.
6) Follow recovery verification checklist: handoff_commit_rate returns to baseline, handoff_evicted_total is flat, and canary synthetic workload p99 latency within expected tolerance.

Profiling and benchmarking guidance:
- Synthetic profiles to include in PRs changing handoff logic:
  * Short-request profile: 100k reqs, seq=64, concurrency=800. Report: handoff_commit_success, handoff_latency_p50/p95/p99.
  * Streamed-session profile: 3k sessions, avg_tokens=1500, concurrency=250. Report: kv_sync_success_rate, stream_handoff_commit_latency_p99.
- Profiling tips:
  - Correlate GPU kernel timeline (Nsight/trace) with handoff telemetry. Capture 2s samples across drain_epoch.
  - Sample node-agent state machine transitions and annotate traces with kernel ids to root-cause blockages.

Benchmark pass criteria for merge (non-exhaustive):
- handoff_success_rate >= 99.5% under 75% traffic;
- handoff_latency_p99 degradation <= 25% vs baseline;
- kv_sync_success_rate >= 98% for streaming workloads.

Release & rollout guidance:
- Any protocol change must publish a compatibility matrix and automated migration plan.
- Use feature-flagged canaries: 1% x24h, then 5% x48h, instrument both v1/v2 events.
- Provide explicit rollback actions: disable feature flag and allow existing tokens to expire over one eviction_window cycle.

Telemetry and SLOs (recommended):
- Metrics to emit: handoff_commit_total, handoff_evicted_total, handoff_reserve_timeout_total, handoff_kv_partial_total, handoff_latency_ms(quantiles), handoff_kv_sync_success_ratio.
- Example SLOs (hosted & dedicated):
  * Handoff commit success >= 99.5% monthly
  * User-visible aborts due to handoff <= 0.05% monthly
  * Handoff median latency <= 150ms, p99 <= 2.5s (non-stream workloads)

Debugging snippets:
- Node status (jq):
  curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://runtime-node-agent.internal/v1/node/$NODE_ID/status | jq '.'
- Extract recent handoff traces via telemetry API:
  curl -s "https://telemetry-agent.internal/api/traces?tag=handoff_token&from=-10m" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" | jq '.samples[] | {token: .token, events: .events}'
- Force a dry-run cordon (example):
  curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"cordon": true, "eviction_window_secs": 45, "dry_run": true}' \
    https://runtime-node-agent.internal/v1/node/$NODE_ID/cordon

Owner and contacts:
- Primary owner: runtime-platform team (runtime-platform@redwood.com)
- Primary engineers: Marissa Cheng (author), Andrej Kove1cs (handoff/orchestrator), Priya Raman (SRE lead)

Rollout checklist for protocol changes:
1) Unit tests + integration with simulated drain & blocked kernels.
2) PR-level synthetic benchmark comparisons saved to artifacts.
3) Canary rollout (1% -> 5%) with automated alert gates.
4) Full rollout with 30-minute pause windows between increments.

Related resources:
- Runtime dashboards: "Handoff Overview" (Grafana)
- Tools: tools/runtime-canary, synthetic-benchmark-generator
- See also: session-lifecycle-kvcache-consistency-guidelines-2024

Change log:
- 2026-02-10: Created (initial playbook and runbook).
- 2026-07-20: Added kv_sync and profiling guidance.
- 2026-12-14: Updated SLO targets and release guidance.

title: Conversational Session Contract Playbook
content:
Summary

This playbook defines the product-level contract primitives, SLOs, billing mappings, and rollout guidance for Conversational Session Contracts (CSCs). CSCs are the canonical package that encapsulates per-session runtime guarantees, fidelity expectations, billing signals, and automated fallback policies for Redwood customers using conversational (chat/assistant) endpoints. The goal is to provide a predictable, auditable surface that aligns product, billing, and infra for low-friction migrations between hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.

Goals

- Provide a small, composable set of session primitives that cover 90% of customer conversational use cases.
- Make fidelity & cost trade-offs explicit and machine-readable.
- Ensure safe rollouts with canarying, auto-fallback, and observability hooks.
- Align SLOs to billing to avoid surprise invoices while enabling predictable economics.

Scope

This playbook covers: session lifecycle, contract primitives, SLO targets and alerts, billing mapping, runtime enforcement strategy, developer ergonomics (API + SDK), and operations/runbook steps. It does NOT prescribe kernel-level serving implementation or third-party model licensing.

Definitions

- Session: A logical conversation with an ID and bounded TTL that aggregates requests and token usage for billing and fidelity purposes.
- Contract: The JSON-serializable object that customers pin to a session to express SLOs, fidelity budget, and fallback policies.
- Fidelity: The expected quality/per-token compute profile (e.g., high, medium, low) mapped to model/quantization pairs.
- Variant: A named model+config tuple (example: gptx-2-8q, llama-70b-fp16).

Contract primitives (stable API surface)

1) contract_id (string) — unique customer-visible ID.
2) session_ttl_ms (integer string) — how long the session ID is valid since the last activity. Default: "1800000" (30 minutes).
3) fidelity_budget (string) — token-budget or compute-budget per session. Format: "tokens:1000" or "compute:0.75".
4) slo_profile (string) — "interactive" | "transactional" | "batch-like". Each profile maps to latency and availability targets.
5) fallback_policy (string) — serialized policy with prioritized variants and cost thresholds.
6) billing_mode (string) — "per_token" | "per_session" | "hybrid".
7) telemetry_level (string) — "none" | "basic" | "detailed" (affects retention & cost).

Example contract (canonical)

{
  "contract_id": "acme-chat-basic-v1",
  "session_ttl_ms": "3600000",
  "fidelity_budget": "tokens:2000",
  "slo_profile": "interactive",
  "fallback_policy": "[\"gptx-3-8q\",\"gptx-2-8q\"]",
  "billing_mode": "hybrid",
  "telemetry_level": "basic"
}

SLOs and thresholds (product-aligned)

Table: Session SLO mapping (product surface)

| slo_profile | target_p50_ms | target_p95_ms | availability | error_budget/month | default_telemetry |
| interactive | 70 | 250 | 99.8% | 0.2% | basic |
| transactional | 150 | 500 | 99.5% | 0.5% | detailed |
| batch-like | 500 | 1500 | 99.0% | 1.0% | detailed |

Notes:
- p50/p95 are measured per single-turn token generation latency (end-to-end) excluding client-side network.
- Availability = fraction of successful responses not hitting hard-fallback (400/5xx excluded).
- Error budget is applied to the contract_id at tenant level and can be traded for credits (see Billing mapping).

Billing mapping & pricing primitives

- per_token: bill raw generation tokens by model variant rate. Session contracts can define a cursor threshold after which a lower-cost variant is eligible.
- per_session: a flat rate per session start; suitable for short interactions or high-variance token usage.
- hybrid: baseline per_session + marginal per_token above the session token floor.

Default recommended price bands (internal product guidance only):

- interactive/hybrid baseline: $0.003 per session start + per_token at variant rate after 200 tokens.
- transactional/per_token: per-token rates scaled by 1.0x (high fidelity), 0.55x (medium), 0.18x (low-8q).

Discounting and credits

- Error-budget-burn: when a tenant uses >50% of error budget for a billing cycle, offer guided migration suggestions + a one-time credit if switched to a lower fidelity variant by the product team.
- Commitment: dedicated capacity customers can lock session-floor pricing via monthly commit SKU contracts.

Runtime enforcement strategy

- Contracts are evaluated at session creation. Enforcement points:
  - Router: maps incoming requests for a session to the current active variant per fallback_policy.
  - Serving runtime: enforces per-request token caps and telemetry level.
  - Billing pipeline: aggregates session-starts and tokens into invoicing meters.

- Fallback behavior order: preference-based variant routing -> queueing (up to 2s) -> degrade fidelity (quant/variant swap) -> degrade features (disable tool-calls) -> soft-fallback (short response) -> hard-fallback (configured error).

Developer ergonomics (API + SDK examples)

1) Create session (curl example)

curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/sessions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"contract_id":"acme-chat-basic-v1","initial_context":"customer_id:12345"}'

Response: 201 { "session_id": "s-abc123", "expires_at": "2026-12-18T15:04:05Z" }

2) Send message (node SDK sketch)

// pseudocode
const r = await redwood.chat.send({ session_id: 's-abc123', input: 'Hi' });
// r includes tokens_used_this_turn, variant_used, latency_ms

Configuration table (contract -> infra knobs)

| contract_field | runtime_knob | default | implications |
| session_ttl_ms | session_cache_ttl | 1800000 | memory & KV cache retention per session |
| fidelity_budget | session_token_quota | 2000 | early throttle & warning events |
| slo_profile | routing_policy | interactive | priority routing class and preemption |
| telemetry_level | telemetry_sink_config | basic | retention tier and cost center |

Rollout plan (high level)

1) Beta (4 weeks): opt-in customers enable CSCs with telemetry_level= detailed. Run lab with 10 customers across e-commerce, CRM & internal Redwood app.
2) Canary (6 weeks): 20% of new hosted sessions use CSC enforcement engine for routing and billing. Monitor p95 and error budget burn.
3) Gradual ramp (8–12 weeks): increase coverage to 100% for new customers; provide migration tool for existing sessions; prepare dedicated SKU price channels.

Rollout success criteria

- End-to-end p95 for interactive profile remains within 1.2x of baseline.
- No more than 2% of sessions trigger hard-fallback per week.
- Billing pipelines reconcile CSC meters within 12 hours 99% of the time.

Operational runbook (incidents and SRE actions)

1) Symptom: sudden rise in hard-fallbacks for a contract_id.
   - Pager: oncall-routing team.
   - Steps: check router logs -> variant health -> capacity pool status -> scale up or reroute to compatible variant.
   - Temp mitigation: apply emergency override to fallback_policy to promote a stable variant.
2) Symptom: persistent p95 degradation for interactive profile in region eu-west-1.
   - Pager: infra-sre + serving-runtime.
   - Steps: validate traffic spike -> inspect kernel selection logs -> revert recent runtime releases -> enable emergency local prefetching.
3) Symptom: invoicing mismatch for per_session customers.
   - Pager: finance-legal + billing-engineer.
   - Steps: run reconciliation job (billing/reconcile-sessions --contract acme-chat-basic-v1 --window 7d) -> check session-start vs token meter mapping -> escalate to billing pipeline owner.

Observability & telemetry contracts

Minimum telemetry required for published contracts: session_id, contract_id, variant_used, tokens_generated_per_turn, latency_ms, fallback_event. For "detailed" level add token-level traces and user-agent.

Alerting thresholds (recommended)

- p95 breach: alert when p95 exceeds target by 20% for >5 minutes.
- hard-fallback spike: alert when hard-fallback rate >0.5% of sessions in 15 minutes.
- error-budget burn: page when tenant burn reaches 75%.

Security & compliance notes

- All session metadata must be stored according to data-residency settings in the tenant contract.
- Telemetry_level=none still requires hashing of session identifiers for behavioral analytics.

Open questions (product & engineering)

- Should we support multi-tenant shared contracts where multiple customer apps attach to a single contract_id? Pros: simpler pricing. Cons: auditability and error-budget attribution complexity.
- Trade-offs for per_session vs hybrid for very long-running sessions ( > 30k tokens ).
- UX: automatic downgrade prompts to customers vs silent fallback.

Appendix A — Example session contract lifecycle (sequence)

1) Customer calls POST /v1/sessions with contract_id.
2) Router validates contract and assigns session_id.
3) Initial variant selected per fallback_policy.
4) Serving runtime enforces token quota and telemetry level.
5) Billing pipeline consumes aggregated session events.

Appendix B — Example contract change CLI (operator)

# Lock a contract to a new fallback policy
redwood contracts update --contract acme-chat-basic-v1 --set fallback_policy='["gptx-3-8q","gptx-2-8q"]' --author "priya.singh@redwood.ai"

Related pages and references

- See: hosted-to-dedicated-transition-playbook-2026-06-30 for migration considerations.
- See: fidelity-scaling-advisor-product-brief-2026-10-21 for guidance translating fidelity_budget to recommended variants.

Owner and contacts

- Product owner: Priya Singh (priya.singh@redwood.ai)
- Runtime contact: Elliot Park (elliot.park@redwood.ai)
- Billing contact: Diego Marquez (diego.marquez@redwood.ai)

This playbook will be reviewed quarterly or whenever material billing or SLO changes occur.

title: Graceful Restart Latency Contracts and Snapshot Synthesis
content:
Overview

This document defines latency contracts (SLOs/SLO targets) and the operational protocol for graceful restarts of runtime workers, kernel modules, and model shards. It also specifies the snapshot synthesis format we use for resumable execution: what state is captured, how it is validated, and how resume/rollback works. The goal is to provide a concrete, testable, and observable procedure that keeps customer-facing latency and correctness within predictable bounds during maintenance, upgrades, and transient failures.

Audience

- Runtime engineers implementing restart semantics and kernel handoff.
- SRE and oncall responsible for incident response when restarts impact SLOs.
- Release engineers and QA writing canary tests and fidelity benchmarks.

Definitions

- graceful restart: a coordinated shutdown and resume of a worker (or kernel) that preserves sufficient execution state so in-flight requests can be resumed or rerouted without correctness regressions.
- cold restart: full process restart without preserved execution snapshots; requires warmup/synthetic traffic to reach steady-state.
- snapshot: a serialized representation of runtime-required state for resumability (KV cache segments, session token pointers, decoder cache offsets, plugin state checksums).
- resume window: the time window after restart during which resumed requests must meet latency/fidelity guarantees.

Latency Contracts (SLOs)

These contracts are the SLA-facing expectations that the runtime operator must meet under planned maintenance (rolling upgrades) and common unplanned restarts (OOMs, node reboots, kernel panics). Targets are expressed as 30-day rolling metrics and validated through synthetic traffic during canaries.

Primary SLOs

- Controlled rolling restart (per-pool, single-tenant): resumed-request p95 <= 120 ms, p99 <= 400 ms within 30s of restart completion.
- Kernel module swap (same-node live-replace): resumed-request p95 <= 60 ms, p99 <= 200 ms within 10s.
- Cold restart recovery (node-rejoin): median request latency to baseline <= 2x baseline after warmup period of 120s; p99 should not exceed 4x baseline.
- Snapshot application time: time to apply a snapshot and be ready for resume <= 250 ms for per-session snapshots, <= 2s for full shard snapshots.

Measuring and Attribution

- Signals used: request timeline (trace start -> resume/serve), kernel handoff events, snapshot-save and snapshot-apply events, kvcache warmness score, model load digest.
- Primary metric names: runtime.resume.apply_latency_ms (histogram), runtime.resume.success_rate (ratio), runtime.snapshot.serialize_ms, runtime.snapshot.size_bytes.
- Attribution: resumed vs. newly routed requests are tagged with resume=true/false. SLOs are measured only on resumed=true requests for restart contracts and only on resumed=false requests for cold-start recovery windows.

Snapshot Synthesis: What We Capture

Snapshots must be compact, deterministic, and verifiable. They are intended to let a worker resume decoding/generation for an in-flight request or restore a warm execution state for a session cohort. The synthesis procedure produces a snapshot manifest and a binary blob.

Essential snapshot components (per-entity):

- header: snapshot_version, producer_node_id, sequence_id, timestamp (ISO8601).
- kvcache segments: list of (prefix_hash, ttl_ms, compressed_bytes_base64, checksum_sha256).
- decoder cache: token_index_offset, kv_positions, compressed_kv_blob (lz4), kernel_hint_id.
- active invocation metadata: request_id, model_id, config_hash (quantization/profile), prompt_prefix_fingerprint.
- plugin state checksums: list of plugin_name -> checksum, and optional plugin blob pointer.

Format and versioning

- snapshot manifest is JSON (text) with fixed keys; blobs are base64 strings or object-store pointers.
- versioning: snapshot_version follows semver-like format v<major>.<minor>.<build>. Consumers must reject unknown major versions.

Consistency and Safety Checks

Before accepting a snapshot to resume, the worker applies these gates in order:

1) model_id and config_hash must match the local loaded model. If mismatch, reject (fail-open routing to fallback model).
2) checksum verification for all blobs. Any mismatch -> reject.
3) ttl_ms on kvcache segments must not be expired; expired segments are pruned.

If any gate fails during a planned maintenance canary, the runtime must route the in-flight request to a compatible fallback variant and mark the snapshot as incompatible in telemetry.

Operational Protocols

Planned rolling upgrade checklist (per-pool):

1) Mark pool as draining in control plane for 30s.
2) For each worker being rotated: capture snapshot for active invocations and attempt to handoff to hot neighbor using snapshot RPC.
3) Wait for runtime.resume.apply_latency_ms p95 < 120 ms for 5 consecutive seconds on the neighborhood (canary sample).
4) If passes, decommission old worker; if fails, rollback routing and escalate to oncall.

Emergency restart runbook (short):

1) Detect restart cause and capture node-level signals: OOM, kernel-panic, watchdog.
2) If snapshot exists and passes safety checks, apply snapshot and mark resumed=true for requests attached to snapshot.
3) If snapshot rejected or unavailable, use fallback routing to sibling pool and trigger warmup traffic with weight 0.1 -> 1 over 60s.
4) Post-incident: run snapshot validation test suite (see Testing and Canary section) and file incident with execution fingerprint.

Canary and Synthetic Tests

We validate restart contracts using two classes of synthetic tests executed in CI and production canary environments:

- per-invocation resume test: inject 1–3 active invocations, force a swap of kernel module and assert runtime.resume.apply_latency_ms p95/p99.
- shard snapshot roundtrip: serialize a full shard snapshot, write to object store, read back on a separate node, apply, and run e2e generation verification (exact-match on deterministic seeds).

Testing matrix (example):

| Test type | Snapshot size | Assertion | Run cadence | Owner |
|-----------|---------------|-----------|-------------|-------|
| per-invocation resume | small (<=128KB) | p95<=120ms, success_rate>=99% | CI + nightly canary | runtime-team |
| kernel swap live-replace | n/a | p95<=60ms across node | weekly canary | kernel-team |
| shard roundtrip | large (<=50MB) | deterministic output match | nightly | infra-team |

Implementation notes and sample commands

- Capture snapshot (CLI):

  curl -X POST https://control-plane/_internal/snapshot/capture 
    -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' 
    -d '{"worker_id":"worker-42","mode":"per-invocation"}'

  Response: {"snapshot_manifest_url":"s3://redwood-snapshots/poolA/worker-42/snap-v1.2.3-1234.json"}

- Apply snapshot (worker):

  rw-runtime apply-snapshot --manifest s3://.../snap.json --strict-checks=true

YAML example: runtime resume gating policy

  resume_policy:
    allow_if:
      - model_match: true
      - checksum_ok: true
      - kvcache_warmness_threshold: 0.6
    fallback_strategy: route_to_fallback_pool
    apply_timeout_ms: 250

Observability and Dashboards

- Dashboard panels to create/update: Resume latency heatmap (by pool, model), Snapshot success rate (by node), Snapshot serialization size histogram, Resume/error timeline waterfall.
- Alerts: snapshot.apply_failure_rate > 1% for 5m; resume.apply_latency.p99 > 500ms for 3m -> page oncall.

Ownership and Roles

- Runtime team: implement snapshot APIs, maintain resume metrics and canary infra.
- Kernel team: ensure live-replace path for kernel modules and provide kernel_hint_id semantics.
- SRE: own alerting thresholds, incident runbooks, and warmup traffic orchestration.

Release and Rollout Guidance

- Feature gate: snapshot major version rollouts must be staged behind a feature flag.
- Canary plan: enable on 5% of traffic in poolA for 24h, monitor resume.apply_latency_ms p95/p99 and snapshot.success_rate.

Appendix: Troubleshooting checklist (fast reference)

1) resume.apply_latency samples high: check snapshot.apply_latency_ms, worker CPU contention, and kvcache hit rates.
2) snapshot checksums failing: verify object-store replication and manifest integrity (run crc32 on blob).
3) incompatible model/config: confirm model version pinning and rollout policy, escalate to release engineering if rollout unintended.

References

- See runbooks: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-deployment-circuit-breakers-and-sla-fallback-playbook-2026
- See observability contract: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/runtime-observability-data-model-and-tracebook-2025

Contact

For questions or extensions to this contract, open an RFC in the runtime-team backlog and cc runtime@redwood.internal.

title: Execution Observer and Fallback Verification Manual
content:
Overview

Purpose: This manual describes the Execution Observer subsystem and the verification procedures for the runtime's fallback orchestration. The Execution Observer (exec-observer) is the deterministic diagnostic and verification component used in CI, canary rollouts, and incident replay to validate that fallback decisions preserve SLOs and maintain state correctness.

Scope: architecture, decision telemetry, verification harnesses, profiling scenarios, benchmarking profiles, runbook steps for validation and rollback, ownership, and acceptance criteria for changes to fallback policies and observer instrumentation.

Audience: runtime engineers, SREs, release engineers, and oncall responders.

1) System summary

What exec-observer is:
- A light-weight sidecar-style observer process that subscribes to the routing/decision events emitted by the runtime decision fabric.
- Responsible for: verifying that fallback transitions occurred within expected windows, asserting cache/kv consistency across model swaps, and generating enriched trace events for postmortem and automated verification.

Key outputs:
- decision-verification metrics (counters and histograms)
- a verification report JSON per rollout (artifact stored in /opt/runtime/observer/reports/)
- a set of synthesized benchmark traces used by CI to validate SLO preservation under synthetic failures

Primary SLOs validated by the observer:
- 99th percentile request latency for production chat routes must not degrade > 15% during a single-tier fallback event (verification tolerance: 15%).
- Functional correctness: model-output checksum match rate > 99% for deterministic reruns using the same prompt set (non-deterministic models have separate quality gates).

2) Architecture and data flows

Components:
- exec-observer (service) — deploys as a container in the runtime node; API: /internal/observer/verify (POST).
- decision-fabric (existing runtime component) — emits DecisionEvent messages over Kafka topic runtime.decisions.v2 with envelope format described below.
- trace-enricher — lightweight module that joins DecisionEvent with KernelTelemetry and KVCache annotations.
- verification-harness — CI job that replays saved traces and asserts SLO/quality gates.

DecisionEvent envelope (text description):
- request_id, tenant_id, route, model_variant, decision_timestamp (ms), fallback_reason_code, prior_variant, kv_cache_shard, kernel_hint, sequence_length_profile_id

Data flow:
1. DecisionEvent emitted by runtime at decision commit.
2. exec-observer subscribes and enriches with live kernel telemetry via trace-enricher.
3. When a fallback happens, exec-observer computes a verification window (default 120s) and collects per-request: latency_ms, tokens_generated, fallthrough_count, kv_cache_warmms.
4. exec-observer writes a verification report and emits metrics to promotheus pushgateway and a status to /internal/observer/last-report.

3) Verification harness and test scenarios

CI harness (high level):
- Test runner name: runtime-fallback-verifier
- Inputs: recorded trace (JSONL), synthetic traffic profile, config.yaml (gating thresholds), expected_report.json
- Outputs: PASS/FAIL, report artifact, annotated trace with reason codes

Representative test scenarios (must be present for PRs that touch fallback logic):
- Controlled model unavailability: simulate model plugin returning capacity errors and assert fallback to lower-fidelity variant within 200ms for low-latency routes.
- KVCache cold-start: evict KV shard and assert that warmup within window produces <= 10% latency spike for 50th percentile.
- Kernel slow-path injection: add 50ms synthetic delay to half of kernels and verify degradation never exceeds configured per-tenant guardrail.
- Mixed tenant burst: 80% of requests from high-priority tenant (tier=dedicated) while background tenants produce burst noise; ensure priority queueing preserved and best-effort fallbacks applied to background tenants only.

Acceptance criteria (CI):
- All verification gates in config.yaml must be within thresholds.
- Report must include: total_requests, fallback_events, avg_latency_ms_before, avg_latency_ms_after, functional_checksum_pass_rate.

4) Profiling and benchmark suite integration

How to create a benchmark trace for the observer:
1. Run trace-capture tool on a canary that exercises the target route for 30 minutes: ./tools/trace-capture --route=/api/v1/chat --duration=1800 --out=trace-<route>-<ts>.jsonl
2. Annotate trace with sequence_length_profile_id: use seq-profile-lookup tool.
3. Create a benchmark scenario in benchmarks/observer/ with a short YAML. Example config (YAML snippet):

  scenario_name: fallback-low-latency-chat
  duration_s: 600
  traffic_profile: bursty-60-40
  inject_faults:
    - type: model-unavailable
      start_s: 60
      duration_s: 30
      target_variant: v2-quantized
  gating_thresholds:
    p99_latency_increase_pct: 12
    checksum_pass_rate: 0.995

Benchmark output and storage:
- Benchmarks produce a compressed trace and an observer report; both are stored in the artifact bucket: s3://redwood-ci/observer-bench/<scenario>/<date>/
- Benchmarks are required for major kernel or scheduling changes (see changelist acceptance matrix).

5) Runbook: verifying a canary rollout with exec-observer

Owners: oncall (SRE) + rollout owner (eng) listed in the release ticket.

Pre-check (before traffic shift):
- Ensure the observer sidecar image matches the runtime version: kubectl get pod -l app=runtime-canary -o jsonpath='{.items[*].spec.containers[*].image}' | grep observer:2026.02
- Confirm trace ingestion health: curl -s http://<canary-host>/internal/observer/health -> {"ok":true}

During rollout (automated steps):
1. Start canary at 1% for 10 minutes.
2. Exec-observer will produce report at /internal/observer/last-report and push metrics to prometheus under observer.canary.<route>.status (0=OK,1=degraded).
3. Automated gate: if observer.canary.<route>.status == 1 for two consecutive windows -> hold rollout and notify Slack #runtime-alerts with report artifact.

Manual verification checklist (if hold triggered):
- Inspect verification report: cat /opt/runtime/observer/reports/<canary-id>.json - Check fallback_reason histograms and map to prior_variant counts.
- Run the verification harness locally against the stored trace: ./tools/verifier --trace /opt/runtime/observer/reports/<canary-id>-trace.jsonl --config ci/gating-config.yaml
- If checksum_pass_rate < 0.99 or p99 latency increased > 15% -> rollback to prior release and open a JIRA ticket with label runtime-fallback-regression.

Rollback commands (emergency):
- kubectl rollout undo deployment/runtime --to-revision=<previous-rev> --namespace=prod
- Force model routing back: curl -XPOST http://control-plane.internal.local/api/routing/force -d '{"route":"/api/v1/chat","variant":"v2-stable","reason":"observer-failed-gate"}'

6) Kernel scheduling/observer interactions

The observer depends on kernel hints emitted by the scheduler to validate whether kernel-level scheduling choices match expected policy. The scheduler must annotate DecisionEvent with kernel_hint (e.g., "tensorcore:fast-path" or "sharded:evict-first"). Observer validations that rely on kernel_hint:
- Kernel hint mismatch: if policy requested "tensorcore:fast-path" but actual kernel dispatched is slow-path, this is flagged as kernel-mismatch and increments kernel_mismatch_counter.
- Preemption reclaim verification: observer verifies preemption windows and validates that preempted request traces have a preemption_reason tag and that the fallback route was applied.

7) Observability contract and metrics (Prometheus names)

Mandatory metrics emitted by exec-observer:
- observer.canary.<route>.status (gauge: 0=ok,1=degraded)
- observer.fallbacks.total{route,reason} (counter)
- observer.kv_warmup.ms_histogram{route} (histogram)
- observer.kernel_mismatch.count (counter)
- observer.verification_run.duration_ms (histogram)

Tracing: attach observer.trace_id to all enriched spans and store sample in jaeger under service=exec-observer for 7 days.

Logs: structured JSON logs with fields: ts, level, request_id, route, model_variant, fallback_reason_code, verification_step, metric_values. Log retention: 14 days in ELK for production.

8) Change/process for modifying fallback logic

Required artifacts in a PR that modifies fallback policies:
- Design doc (overview, expected decision graph, incremental rollout plan)
- Observer unit tests and a new verification scenario in benchmarks/observer/
- CI green: runtime-fallback-verifier must pass for the touched routes
- Rollout matrix updated in release ticket with acceptance gates

Approval workflow:
1. Author creates PR and tags reviewers: @runtime-arch, @sre-oncall
2. Reviewer verifies that observer produced verification scenarios are included and that gating thresholds were not loosened without product sign-off
3. Merge only after a canary-level dry-run in staging passes verification harness

9) Troubleshooting and common failure patterns

Common symptom: frequent fallback events with no clear prior_variant changes.
- Likely causes: intermittent model worker OOM, NVLink flapping, or transient scheduler misclassifications.
- Troubleshooting steps:
  1. Check observer.fallbacks.total by reason. If reason=="kernel-timeout" -> escalate to runtime-kernel oncall.
  2. Inspect kernel_mismatch.count. If non-zero, retrieve kernel_trace: curl http://<node>/internal/kernel/trace/<trace-id>
  3. Re-run verification harness with captured trace and add synthetic delay to kernel to reproduce.

Common symptom: checksum_pass_rate drop for deterministic tests.
- Causes: quantization rollouts, plugin regression, or trace mismatch due to timestamp drift.
- Steps: pin model_variant, re-run single-request replay with --deterministic flag, and compare token sequence checksums.

10) Ownership and escalation

Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime (runtime-architecture subteam)
Secondary: eng-sre for rollout and observability concerns.
Escalation matrix:
- 0-30 minutes: SRE oncall (pager duty)
- 30-120 minutes: runtime-architecture senior engineer (pager)
- >120 minutes: Eng VP oncall and incident commander

11) Appendices

A. Example verification report (JSON excerpt)
{
  "canary_id": "canary-2026-03-01-01",
  "total_requests": 12432,
  "fallback_events": 72,
  "avg_latency_ms_before": 24.2,
  "avg_latency_ms_after": 26.8,
  "p99_latency_increase_pct": 8.3,
  "checksum_pass_rate": 0.998,
  "kernel_mismatch_count": 2
}

B. Quick CLI tools
- ./tools/trace-capture --route <route> --duration <s> --out <file>
- ./tools/verifier --trace <file> --config <config.yaml>
- ./tools/bench-runner --scenario benchmarks/observer/<scenario>.yaml --out <artifact-dir>

C. FAQ
Q: What is the canonical location for observer reports?
A: /opt/runtime/observer/reports/ on each canary node; CI artifacts copied to s3://redwood-ci/observer-bench/.

Q: When do we require a full benchmark for a change?
A: Full benchmark required for: kernel scheduler changes, model quantization rollout, changes to decision-fabric routing policies, or modifications to KV cache shard topology.

D. Related links
- Runtime decision catalog (internal): /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/runtime-decision-graph-and-observed-behaviour-catalog-2026
- Canary rollout playbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-deployment-circuit-breakers-and-sla-fallback-playbook-2026
