If you are running a verification and need help, contact @runtime-oncall or open a thread in #runtime-alerts with the canary_id and the observer report attached.

title: Accelerator ABI and Driver Graceful Degradation ADR
content:
Summary

This ADR defines the Accelerator ABI (application binary interface) and the runtime-side driver graceful-degradation policy for heterogeneous accelerator fleets (GPU, TPU-like ASICs, and vendor-provided inference accelerators). The goal is a small, well-specified handshake and capability set that: 1) allows the runtime to negotiate performance/precision tradeoffs with device drivers; 2) exposes a deterministic degradation path when an accelerator cannot satisfy requested guarantees; and 3) provides operational signals for capacity, thermal, and error states so higher layers (routing, fallback) can make policy decisions.

Context and motivation

Redwood's serving runtime runs across mixed hardware: cloud GPUs with different memory/compute, vendor inference chips with quantization-aware runtimes, and experimental on-prem ASICs for Private deployments. Historically each driver exposed a different surface (promises about sequence-length limits, supported quantization, KV cache semantics), which led to fragile fallbacks and silent quality regressions. Operations has observed incidents where a node reported "healthy" but silently served half-precision tensors, creating subtle hallucination regressions in downstream evals. We need a minimal ABI and a deterministic downgrade model so the orchestration and routing layers can react before customer-visible quality drops.

Decision (what we are adopting)

We adopt a two-part contract:

1) Accelerator ABI (driver runtime surface)
- A JSON capability manifest returned during driver handshake with these required fields: vendor, model, memory_bytes, peak_fp32_throughput, supported_precisions (list), max_sequence_length, kv_cache_model (none|keyseg|segmented), supported_quant_modes (list), fail_modes (list of canonical failure codes).
- A gRPC control channel for health + telemetry that emits structured events: THERMAL_WARNING, MEMORY_PRESSURE, DRIVER_DEGRADATION(start/end), ARTIFACT_ERRORS. Events include numeric fields (temp_celsius, available_bytes, eviction_count).
- Deterministic downgrade functions exposed by drivers: get_degradation_path(requested_precision) -> ordered list of fallback precisions and a max-acceptable-seq-length for each step.

2) Graceful-degradation policy (runtime orchestration expectations)
- If a driver indicates DRIVER_DEGRADATION or memory pressure that will affect >P% of requests in next T seconds, the runtime must:
  a) Mark node as "degrading" and emit a metric (accelerator.node.degradation{reason}).
  b) For new requests, consult degradation path and either re-route to compatible node, fall back to a quantized variant, or invoke a lower-fidelity model per client policy.
  c) For in-flight requests, attempt best-effort KV-preserving re-execution (see runbook) but avoid silent precision demotion unless explicitly allowed by the tenant's model policy.

Rationale

- Small manifest + events provide actionable signals without locking in per-vendor RPCs.
- Centralizing downgrade logic in drivers avoids guessing behavior and ensures the runtime can reason about end-to-end effects (e.g., seq length vs precision tradeoff).
- Separating "allowed by tenant policy" from automatic demotion prevents silent regressions for customers with strict fidelity requirements.

Alternatives considered

1) Do nothing / keep vendor-specific surfaces
   - Pros: no immediate engineering cost
   - Cons: repeated incidents, unpredictable fallbacks, poor observability for quality regressions (rejected).

2) Full feature-rich driver RPC (rich schema for every kernel)
   - Pros: maximum expressivity
   - Cons: long vendor integration time, brittle across versions (rejected).

3) Runtime-only heuristic demotion (runtime interprets raw metrics and decides)
   - Pros: driver-agnostic
   - Cons: wrong assumptions across devices; drivers have the ground truth (rejected).

Implementation specification

1) Manifest schema (JSON example)
{
  "vendor": "string",
  "device_model": "string",
  "memory_bytes": 68719476736,
  "peak_fp32_throughput": 12000.0,
  "supported_precisions": ["fp32","fp16","int8*"],
  "max_sequence_length": 4096,
  "kv_cache_model": "segmented",
  "supported_quant_modes": ["static8","dynamic8","awq"],
  "fail_modes": ["OOM","THERMAL","DRIVER_FAULT"]
}

2) Control channel: gRPC proto (summary)
- Service: AcceleratorControl
- RPCs: GetManifest(), StreamEvents(stream Event) -> ack, SetThrottle(level) -> ack
- Event structure: {timestamp_ms, node_id, code, numeric_map, text}

3) Degradation API (driver-side function)
- get_degradation_path(requested_precision: string, requested_sequence: int) -> list of {precision, max_sequence_length, estimated_throughput_ratio}

Operational runbook (short)

Triggers and immediate actions:
1) Event THERMAL_WARNING with temp_celsius > 85 for 30s -> put node into read-only drain and notify SRE.
2) DRIVER_DEGRADATION with predicted_available_bytes < requested_memory -> mark degrading, reduce offerable concurrency by 50% and trigger rescheduling.

Manual recovery steps:
1) For transient thermal events: verify cooling system, evict long-running ephemeral jobs, restart driver process if required.
2) For persistent artifact errors: collect driver logs / dmesg, escalate to vendor with manifest and event stream.

Routing & API implications

- API layer must include these fields in the request envelope: preferred_fidelity (strict|best-effort|cost-optimized) and allow_demote boolean.
- Default tenant policy: preferred_fidelity=best-effort, allow_demote=false. Allowing demote requires explicit opt-in by the customer and is surfaced in Console settings.

Testing and acceptance criteria

- Unit: manifest parsing, event handling, degradation-path evaluation.
- Integration: simulate driver events (thermal, OOM) in testbed and assert runtime re-routes or rejects per tenant policy.
- Quality regression: run prompt-suite CI (refer to prompt-suite-ci-contract-testing-guidelines) before and after simulated demotion; metrics: BLEU/ROUGE analogs and hallucination rate must not regress beyond tenant thresholds.

Metrics to monitor

- accelerator.node.degradation.count by code
- accelerator.request.demoted.count by tenant and model
- end_to_end_quality_regressions.per_model (linked to evals)
- routing_fallbacks.per_minute

Rollout plan

1) Stage 0: Spec review and vendor alignment (2 weeks).
2) Stage 1: Driver shim implementation for two vendor drivers and testbed integration (6 weeks).
3) Stage 2: Runtime support (handshake, event processing, routing changes) in canary (4 weeks).
4) Stage 3: Tenant opt-in on Dedicated and Private (2 weeks).
5) Stage 4: Full launch for Hosted (after 8 weeks of canary stability).

Owners and contacts

- Design author: Michael Chen (runtime team)
- Driver integration lead: Nadia Alvarez (kernel & drivers)
- SRE contact: Priya Singh
- Product liaison: Daniel Romero

Open questions and future work

- How to represent approximate numeric fidelity (e.g., AWQ variants with mixed blocks)? We propose a small extension to the manifest to include per-layer fidelity profiles in a later ADR.
- Should the runtime be allowed to force demotion for system safety (e.g., to avoid cascading OOMs)? Current decision: only when "system_safety" flag present in tenant policy (requires legal/product sign-off).

Appendix A: Example degradation path table

| requested_precision | step | fallback_precision | max_seq | throughput_ratio | notes |
|---------------------|------|--------------------|---------|------------------|-------|
| fp32                | 0    | fp32               | 4096    | 1.0              | native |
| fp32                | 1    | fp16               | 4096    | 0.65             | reduced numerical headroom |
| fp32                | 2    | int8               | 2048    | 0.35             | quantized; requires calibration |

Appendix B: Example tenant request headers (JSON)
{
  "tenant_id": "t-12345",
  "model": "redwood-base-13b",
  "preferred_fidelity": "best-effort",
  "allow_demote": false
}

Related documents

- eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/sequence-length-aware-kernel-selection-guidelines-2026.json
- architecture-and-standards/infra-standards/graceful-gpu-preemption-and-prewarming-guidelines-2026.json

Revision history

- 2026-02-18: Drafted by Michael Chen.
- 2026-03-05: Reviewed with drivers team; updated event schema and rollout plan.

title: Runtime integration safety and benchmark gate
content:
Summary:
This document defines the integrated runtime safety gate and benchmark gate used by Runtime, Kernel Scheduling, and Release teams to evaluate changes to the serving stack (kernels, scheduler policies, routing/fallback logic, and runtime control plane). It describes the architecture of the gate, the required benchmark suite, profiling and sampling playbooks, release checklist integration points, runbooks for common degradation scenarios, and known issues that should block an automated gate.

Scope and intent:
- Scope: PRs that touch runtime execution kernels, scheduler policy code, model variant routing, admission control, or any production-facing performance flag.
- Intent: Prevent regressions to latency SLOs, throughput guarantees, and observable fidelity; provide deterministic gates so engineers can push changes with high confidence.

High-level architecture:
1) Pre-merge pipeline: unit + integration tests + microbench harness. Changes that alter kernel behavior must ship with a microbenchmark profile (see `bench/profile.yaml` artifact).
2) Shadow validation: candidate commits are mirrored to a shadow pool for a configurable period (default: 2 hours) using a sampled production trace. Shadow runs produce a per-request delta bundle (latency, tokens, kernel-selection, cache-hit, memory residency).
3) Gate evaluator: centralized job that runs the benchmark suite (see Benchmark Suite section) and computes pass/fail per threshold matrix.
4) Release gate: if the gate passes, an automated canary rollout is permitted; failing gates require triage and a blocking label.

Safety gates and thresholds:
- Latency: p50/p90/p95 (in ms) vs baseline. Gate fails if p95 increases by > 10% AND absolute p95 > 200ms for interactive tiers.
- Throughput: end-to-end throughput drop > 8% under the same synthetic shape fails gate.
- Kernel regressions: any kernel that increases median per-token GPU time by >12% fails gate unless mitigations are documented.
- Fidelity: for eval prompt-sets (representative prompt set), generation quality drop > 3% (measured by configured metric e.g., semantic-similarity or-task-specific metric) fails gate.
- Resource usage: GPU memory usage increase > 6% or sustained NVLink saturation delta > 10% fails gate.

Scheduler interaction and failure taxonomy:
- Decision points: admission controller, preemptive-shepherd, kernel-mapper, fallback-orchestrator.
- Failure modes handled by the gate: priority inversion (detected via queueing-delay skew), handoff oscillation (rapid model-swap churn), kernel-starvation (dispatcher blocked by a slow kernel).
- Allowed degradations: short-lived p99 spikes during warmstart with clear warmup profile and documented mitigation.

Profiling playbook (step-by-step):
1) Reproduce locally with microbench: run `tools/microbench --model <variant> --shape <seq, batch>` and collect `profile.json`.
2) Capture kernel traces: enable kernel-tracer (env: KERNEL_TRACE=1) and run the synthetic shape for 1K requests.
3) Generate the delta bundle: `tools/delta-assembler --baseline /artifacts/baseline.json --candidate profile.json --out delta.json`
4) Stratify by request class: split delta.json into short/medium/long prompt buckets (<=64, 65-512, >512 tokens).
5) Run targeted sampling: for each bucket, select 500 representative requests using the stratified sampler to produce stable medians.
6) Validate fallback behavior: for a subset, force an artificial kernel disconnect and assert fallback semantics (should succeed within configured t_fallback = 150ms).
7) Annotate and upload to gate: produce a gate artifact that includes `delta.json`, kernel traces, an experiment note, and the `bench/profile.yaml` file.

Benchmark suite (tests and minimal pass criteria):
| Test name | Purpose | Key metrics | Pass criteria |
|-----------|---------|-------------|---------------|
| Shadow-Trace-Replay | Validate end-to-end delta on sampled production traffic | p95 latency delta, throughput delta, error-rate | p95 <= +10% and throughput drop <= 8% |
| Microkernel-Throughput | Measure per-kernel per-token GPU time | median token GPU-time, variance | median delta <= +12% |
| Multi-tenant-noise | Simulate co-located tenants to detect interference | tail latency, queue depth | p99 tail increase <= 15% |
| Cold-start-warmup | Measure warmstart cost and cache warmup time | time to reach steady-state p95 | warmup < 300s or documented backoff |
| Fidelity-eval | Run representative prompt-sets to check quality | metric delta (BLEURT / cosine) | metric drop <= 3% |
| Resource-regression | Detect NVLink/GPU memory/PCIe regressions | memory, NVLink utilization | memory delta <= +6% |

Operational thresholds (examples):
- Interactive tier: p95 target 120ms, gate absolute ceiling for p95 = 200ms.
- Batch tier: throughput target 20 tokens/s per slot, gate allows up to 12% throughput drop if compensated by cost reductions.
- Canary weight ramp: 1% -> 5% -> 20% -> 50% over a minimum of 30m per stage.

Release checklist integration:
1) PR author attaches bench artifact and `bench/profile.yaml` with test shapes.
2) CI runs microbench and attaches artifacts to the PR.
3) Gate evaluator runs shadow replay and benchmark suite; results recorded in the PR `gate/result.json`.
4) On pass: auto-merge allowed when other approvals are satisfied.
5) On fail: label `gate-failed` applied and owners paged according to ownership table below.

Runbooks (short actionable steps):
- Runbook: Shadow gate fails with p95 regression:
  1. Stop the shadow feed (tools/shadowctl pause).
  2. Collect delta bundle and kernel traces.
  3. Run binary search: revert recent micro-optimizations or toggle quantization flags (e.g., `KERNEL_QUANTIZE=off`) to isolate.
  4. If isolatable to a kernel, open urgent bug with `severity:high`, attach traces, set assignee to kernel owner.

- Runbook: Canary rollout p99 spike detected:
  1. Immediately scale canary back to prior weight.
  2. Enable extended tracing for affected cohort.
  3. If spike correlates with kernel-change, rollback kernel rollout via the kernel-release roll-back job.

Known issues (current triage list):
1) Interleaved-batch memory safety: under certain interleaving patterns, temporary soft-GC occurs and can show higher memory high-water marks. Workaround: reduce interleaving window (scheduler flag `max-interleave=4`).
2) NVLink saturation aliasing: when a multi-socket job runs two large attention kernels concurrently, NVLink counters show aliasing spikes; mitigation: stagger activation with `kernel-waveform-spread=2`.
3) Shadow replay determinism: occasional seed drift in tokenizer causes small fidelity deltas. Note: canonical mitigation is to pin tokenizer version in `profile.yaml`.

Ownership and escalation:
- Gate owner: Runtime Release (runtime-release@redwood.com).
- Kernel owners: list available in `OWNERS` file in the kernel repo.
- Pager for gate failures: on-call runtime-devops (see rota).

Appendix: sample bench/profile.yaml
```yaml
profile_name: integration-shadow-v1
shapes:
  - name: interactive-small
    seq: 64
    batch: 1
    requests: 2000
  - name: interactive-medium
    seq: 256
    batch: 1
    requests: 1000
  - name: long-form
    seq: 1024
    batch: 1
    requests: 500
baseline_artifact: /artifacts/baseline-2026-01-01.json
trace_sample_method: stratified
strata: [short, medium, long]
```
CLI quick commands:
- Run microbench: `./tools/microbench --profile bench/profile.yaml --out artifacts/candidate.json`
- Trigger gate evaluation locally: `./tools/gate-eval --candidate artifacts/candidate.json --baseline /artifacts/baseline.json`

Related reading and links:
- Release gate contract and checklist (/confluence/eng-serving-runtime/release-notes/release-readiness-integrated-checklist-technical-gate-2026)
- Profiling playbook: continuous profiling strategy (link above)

Change log:
- 2025-11-02 (Asha Patel): initial draft and architecture decisions.
- 2025-12-18 (Gordon Li): added profiling playbook and runbooks.
- 2026-01-15 (Marina Silva): tightened thresholds for p95 and resource regressions, added NVLink note.

title: KV + Prefix Cache Telemetry: Runtime Architecture Overview
content:
## Summary
This page describes how prefix cache and KV cache telemetry is produced inside the serving runtime, how signals map to the request lifecycle (prefill vs decode), and how telemetry flows to the ingestion pipeline with controlled overhead and label cardinality.

**Audience:** Runtime engineers, Telemetry/Platform, SRE/Observability, and PMs validating cache hit-rate and “wasted prefill” recommendations.

**Non-goals:** This is not a cache policy/eviction algorithm spec. It focuses on *instrumentation* and *data flow*.

---

## Terminology
- **Prefix cache:** Reuses computed prefill artifacts based on canonicalized prompt prefixes. Primarily reduces prefill work.
- **KV cache (decode cache):** Reuses key/value tensors across decode steps within a sequence (and, depending on policy, across closely related requests in multi-turn chat when safe).
- **Prefill:** Forward pass over the prompt/context to initialize attention state.
- **Decode:** Token-by-token generation after prefill.
- **Reuse depth:** The number of tokens reused from a cached prefix (or effective reused prefill tokens).
- **Wasted prefill:** Prefill tokens computed that did not contribute to subsequent decode due to cache miss, eviction, policy, mismatch, or retry semantics.

---

## High-level architecture (signals -> ingestion)
The runtime emits cache telemetry at two levels:
1) **Request-scoped event counters/histograms** recorded in the hot path with bounded labels.
2) **Span annotations (tracing)** for deep debugging and correlation with latency without adding metric cardinality.

### Data flow (text diagram)
1. **Gateway / control plane** sets request context (tenant, route, model/version, deployment mode, region) and passes a bounded tag set to the runtime.
2. **Runtime request lifecycle** (admission -> prefill -> decode -> completion) records cache events:
   - prefix lookup result + reused tokens
   - KV reuse effectiveness during decode
   - evictions / pressure signals
   - wasted prefill accounting
3. **Local runtime aggregator** batches metric updates and enforces runtime-side sampling/rate limits.
4. **Telemetry ingestion** applies allowlists and cardinality guards; drops/aggregates forbidden labels.
5. **Storage + query layer** supports dashboards and batch aggregation for recommendations.

---

## Where telemetry is emitted in the runtime
Telemetry is emitted in three primary components:

### 1) Request context + tag binding (early lifecycle)
**Location:** request admission / request context construction

**What happens:**
- The runtime constructs a `CacheTelemetryContext` from request metadata.
- Only allowlisted label values are accepted (e.g., model family or normalized model ID rather than raw model string if needed).

**Key point:** all downstream metric calls use this pre-baked context to avoid repeated tag assembly overhead.

### 2) Prefix cache instrumentation (prefill stage)
**Location:** before prefill begins, during prefix lookup/validation

**Signals recorded:**
- Prefix lookup attempts and outcomes (hit/miss/partial).
- Reuse depth / reused tokens histogram.
- Miss reason (bounded enum).

**Why here:** This is the earliest point where we know whether we can avoid some prefill compute.

### 3) KV cache instrumentation (decode stage)
**Location:** decode loop and/or scheduler hooks around decode step execution

**Signals recorded:**
- KV reuse effectiveness (e.g., percent of decode steps with valid KV reuse, or reused KV blocks).
- Miss reason events when decode cannot reuse expected state.

**Why here:** KV cache effectiveness impacts throughput/latency and can diverge from prefix cache results depending on batching, retries, and scheduling.

### 4) Evictions + memory pressure (continuous)
**Location:** cache allocator / eviction policy

**Signals recorded:**
- Eviction counter (by eviction reason enum).
- Pressure gauges (e.g., bytes used, eviction rate proxy).

**Why here:** Hit-rate drops are often a *symptom* of pressure; these indicators are needed for triage and recommendations.

### 5) Wasted prefill accounting (prefill completion + decode correlation)
**Location:** request completion (or first-decode checkpoint) where we can attribute whether prefill work yielded reuse/benefit

**Signals recorded:**
- Wasted prefill tokens histogram/bucketed counter.

**Key nuance:** We avoid logging any raw prompt content; wasted prefill is computed from token counts and reuse indicators.

---

## Mapping telemetry to the request lifecycle
This section ties the metrics to lifecycle points. This mapping is important for correctness (no double counting) and for interpreting dashboards.

### Lifecycle timeline
1. **Admission**
   - Bind `deployment_mode`, `region`, `route_id`, `model_id`, `model_version_id` (bounded/allowlisted), and request-shape buckets.

2. **Prefix lookup (start of prefill)**
   - Emit: `prefix_lookup_total{result=hit|miss|partial, miss_reason?}`
   - Emit: `prefix_reuse_tokens_bucket` histogram (reuse depth)

3. **Prefill execution**
   - Emit: `prefill_tokens_bucket` histogram (request shape)
   - No prompt content is recorded.

4. **Decode loop**
   - Emit: `kv_reuse_events_total{result=hit|miss, miss_reason?}`
   - Emit: `decode_tokens_bucket` histogram

5. **Completion / finalization**
   - Emit: `wasted_prefill_tokens_bucket` (derived)
   - Emit: end-to-end counters (request count, retry count if applicable, with retry-safe semantics)

### Streaming + retries
- Metrics must be retry-safe. When a stream retry occurs, the runtime must not double-count prefix/KV events from the original attempt.
- The runtime tags a request attempt with a stable request ID and attempt index and uses “first successful attempt wins” semantics for counters that should be once-per-logical-request.
- Tracing spans may include per-attempt annotations for debugging, but metric emission stays bounded.

### Continuous batching (batched prefill)
- When multiple requests share a continuous batch prefill, hit attribution must be per-request (not per-batch), while shared compute should not inflate “hit” counters.
- The instrumentation uses request-local reuse accounting derived from the cache lookup outcome and per-request token ranges in the batch.

---

## Signal taxonomy (what we emit)
Exact names and label sets are governed by the observability standards and the ADR. This section describes the *classes* of telemetry and how they should be interpreted.

### A) Hit/miss counters
**Purpose:** Track cache effectiveness over time.

- Prefix cache hit-rate: “Did we reuse prefill artifacts for this request?”
- KV cache hit-rate/effectiveness: “Did decode reuse expected KV state efficiently?”

**Partial hit semantics:**
- A partial hit occurs when some prefix tokens are reused but the full desired prefix is not reusable (e.g., hash mismatch after N tokens, or version mismatch).
- Partial hits should be visible as separate result class so operators can distinguish “completely cold” from “almost warm.”

### B) Reuse depth histograms
**Purpose:** Hit-rate alone is not enough; reuse depth shows whether hits are meaningful.

- `reused_tokens` bucketed by prompt length bucket and model.
- Enables: detecting regressions where hit-rate stays flat but reused tokens collapse.

### C) Evictions and pressure
**Purpose:** Root-cause hit-rate regressions and support recommendations.

- Eviction count by reason (bounded enum).
- Pressure indicator gauges (bytes used, high-watermark %, or eviction rate proxy).

### D) Wasted prefill
**Purpose:** Identify compute that didn’t pay off and is often fixable (routing locality, TTL, policy flags, canonicalization).

- Wasted prefill should be interpreted alongside evictions and miss reasons.
- High wasted prefill with high eviction pressure typically indicates insufficient cache capacity or TTL mismatch.

### E) Trace annotations (low cardinality alternative)
**Purpose:** Correlate cache events to latency and scheduler behavior.

- Spans annotate cache lookup outcomes, reuse depth, and eviction/pressure snapshots.
- Traces are sampled separately from metrics and are not required for baseline dashboards.

---

## Join keys and label strategy (how we slice without cardinality blowups)
Telemetry must be actionable by model/route/deployment mode/region and request shape while staying within budgets.

### Required dimensions (bounded)
- `deployment_mode`: Hosted | Dedicated | Private
- `region`: canonical region code (bounded)
- `model_id`: normalized model identifier (bounded set)
- `model_version_id`: allowlisted stable ID (bounded, rollover-safe)
- `route_id`: internal stable route identifier (bounded; not raw URL paths)
- `request_shape`: buckets (e.g., prompt length bucket, total tokens bucket)

### Explicitly NOT allowed in metric labels
- Raw tenant IDs, user IDs, raw prompt hashes with high uniqueness, request IDs, or free-form strings.

### Tenant slicing
- Tenant-level views are provided via:
  1) Dedicated/Private deployments where tenant count is naturally small and allowlisted.
  2) Analytics tables / batch aggregates where controlled rollups are computed off-metrics.

---

## Sampling, rate limiting, and overhead controls
The runtime must keep instrumentation overhead near-zero (especially at p95/p99). Controls:

1. **Metrics aggregation:** Use in-process counters/histograms with periodic flush; avoid per-token metric emissions.
2. **Event sampling:** High-volume events (e.g., decode reuse) use probabilistic sampling, then are scaled at query time where appropriate.
3. **Local rate limiting:** If a component produces unusually high event volume, the runtime clamps emission and increments a “dropped_by_ratelimit” counter.
4. **Feature flags:** All new telemetry is behind runtime config flags so we can canary and roll back quickly.

Operational guidance:
- Prefer measuring reuse at request boundaries (prefill completion, request completion) instead of per decode token.
- Use histograms/buckets rather than raw counts by unique values.

---

## Privacy and data handling
- No raw prompt text is emitted.
- Prompt-derived features are restricted to coarse buckets (prompt length) and cache-safe canonicalization outcomes (hit/miss/partial), not raw hashes.
- Tracing annotations must not include prompt content; only bounded enums and counts.

---

## Ingestion pipeline expectations (runtime -> telemetry backend)
The runtime assumes the ingestion pipeline will:
- Enforce label allowlists and drop unknown/unsafe labels.
- Apply cardinality guards (e.g., cap series per metric per time window).
- Preserve monotonicity expectations for counters; handle process restarts and counter resets.
- Maintain consistent mapping for model/version identifiers so dashboards can join across gateway logs and runtime metrics.

**Failure detection:**
- A “metric drop” should be distinguishable from a “true hit-rate change.”
- The pipeline should publish a health indicator metric (ingested series count, drop count by reason).

---

## Common failure modes and how the architecture mitigates them
1) **Double counting due to streaming retries**
- Mitigation: emit once-per-logical-request counters at completion; track attempt index only in traces.

2) **Incorrect hit attribution under continuous batching**
- Mitigation: compute per-request reuse from request-local token ranges; add integration tests that simulate batched prefill.

3) **Cardinality explosion from route or model labels**
- Mitigation: route_id/model_version_id allowlists, normalization, ingestion-side guards.

4) **Hit-rate regressions caused by workload mix changes**
- Mitigation: always break down by request shape buckets and model; use guardrail alerts that consider mix.

5) **Telemetry overhead regression**
- Mitigation: perf canary gates and sampling defaults; ability to disable high-volume sub-metrics independently.

---

## Validation checklist (runtime-facing)
Before enabling in production, validate:
1. **Correctness:**
   - Repeated identical prompts produce expected prefix hit-rate and reuse depth.
   - Forced version mismatch produces misses attributed to version mismatch.
   - TTL expiration produces misses attributed to ttl_expired.

2. **Overhead:**
   - p95/p99 latency regression is within the perf-canary budget.
   - CPU overhead from metric emission is within expectations under peak QPS.

3. **Joinability:**
   - model/version/route identifiers match gateway/control-plane dimensions.
   - region and deployment_mode are consistent with dashboard filters.

4. **Cardinality:**
   - series count stays within budget after enabling all breakdowns.
   - ingestion drop counters remain near zero.

---

## Ownership and change management
- Runtime instrumentation owners: Runtime team (primary: Omar El-Sayed; approver: Sofia Ivanova)
- Metric schema and label policy owner: Nadia Rahman (Telemetry)
- Dashboards/alerts owner: Allison Grant (Observability)

Any change that modifies:
- hit/miss definitions,
- miss reason taxonomy,
- label sets (especially route/model/version), or
- wasted prefill attribution

…requires review from Runtime + Telemetry + SRE and an update to the relevant ADR/standards page.

---

## Open questions (tracked; do not block current rollout)
- Whether KV reuse effectiveness should be expressed primarily as a histogram (reuse ratio) or as hit/miss counts with weighted scaling under sampling.
- Whether we need an additional “canonicalization_mismatch” reason distinct from “hash_mismatch” for recommendations.
- How to best represent multi-turn chat partial reuse across turns without adding high-cardinality conversation identifiers.

---

## Appendix: Miss reason taxonomy (bounded enum)
The runtime emits miss reasons from a bounded set. Exact names are defined in the ADR/standards, but the categories are:
- `capacity` (insufficient cache space / allocation failure)
- `ttl_expired`
- `policy_disabled` (route-level or deployment-level caching disabled)
- `hash_mismatch` (prompt canonicalization or prefix mismatch)
- `version_mismatch` (model/version incompatibility)

Guidance:
- Keep taxonomy stable; adding a new miss reason requires cross-team review due to dashboard and alert dependencies.

title: Escape Hatch: Congestion Decompression & Kernel Handshake Manual
content:
Summary

This document defines Redwood Inference's official "escape hatch" strategy for handling sustained congestion and kernel saturation: a coordinated congestion decomposition and kernel-handshake protocol that (1) reduces tail-latency exposure, (2) preserves critical SLOs by controlled fidelity degradation, and (3) provides a clear operator runbook for diagnosing and recovering from congestion events. The guidance spans runtime architecture trade-offs, scheduler/kernel interactions, profiling checks, benchmark validation, release notes for v0.14 of the handshake protocol, and a known-issues appendix.

Why this exists

- Congestion is multi-dimensional: CPU/host networking, GPU kernel throughput, KV cache pressure, and admission-controller throttles interact and can amplify tail latency.
- Previous ad-hoc mitigations (global queue cuts, blunt shedding) risked client-visible errors or large quality regressions.
- This manual codifies a minimal, observable, and reversible path — the "escape hatch" — that runtime and operations can use without full-scale rollback.

Scope and owners

- Scope: Serving runtime (request orchestration, scheduler/kernel admission, KV cache warmup), telemetry contracts between runtime and scheduler, operator runbook.
- Owners: runtime-scheduler (primary), kernel-engineering (secondary), eng-sre (oncall runbook), observability (telemetry contract).

Key concepts (short)

- Congestion decomposition: Break an incident into orthogonal stressors (kernel queueing, KV miss storm, network slope) and treat each with targeted mitigations.
- Kernel handshake: A lightweight per-request negotiation between dispatcher and kernel to confirm admission and a fidelity/priority token.
- Escape hatch stages: 1) Soft-cohort shaping, 2) Priority-aware fidelity staircasing, 3) Kernel offload (batch-eviction + fallback model), 4) Emergency rejection (last resort).

Architecture overview

1) Dispatcher -> Scheduler -> Kernel handshake flow

- Dispatcher issues a pre-admit probe to scheduler with metadata: model_id, sequence_length_est, client_priority_tier, kv_prefetch_hint, trace_id.
- Scheduler responds with a handshake token: {admitted: bool, expected_wait_ms: int, fidelity_profile: string, kernel_slot_hint: id, trace_flags}.
- Dispatcher attaches token to the request and routes to the claimed kernel node. Kernel validates the token (nonce + timestamp) before binding resources.

Benefits:
- Avoids blind offload: kernels only begin expensive work once token validated.
- Enables admission-time decisions (expected wait) surfaced to callers and observability.

2) Congestion decomposition surface points

- Kernel queueing: long kernel start latency despite short network and dispatch times.
- KV cache miss storm: many cold sessions with repeated kv-prefetches causing memory pressure and eviction churn.
- Dispatcher/multiplex contention: overloaded event loop or slow gRPC channels.
- Network backpressure: transient NIC saturation or cross-AZ variance.

Telemetry contract (required signals)

- Required per-request fields (exported to traces/metrics): pre_admit_ts, handshake_issue_ts, handshake_response_ts, kernel_bind_ts, kernel_start_ts, kernel_complete_ts, kv_miss_count, admitted_fidelity_profile, kernel_slot_id, tv_cpu_ms, gpu_busy_ms.
- Aggregates/alerts: 95/99/99.9 kernel_bind_time; kv_miss_ratio over 2-minute windows; admission_reject_rate; per-model fidelity-downgrade-rate.

Escape hatch stages (detailed)

Stage 0 — Detection
- Triggers (any one): 99.9 kernel_bind_time > 500ms for 3 consecutive 1-minute windows OR kv_miss_ratio > 0.25 AND error_rate increase > 0.5%.
- Action: escalate to oncall, annotate traces with incident_id, and enable enhanced sampling for affected models.

Stage 1 — Soft-cohort shaping (fast, reversible)
- Goal: Reduce inflow rate using priority-aware shaping and client-visible hints.
- Steps: 1) Scheduler flips cohort-shaped admission (80% of low priority requests are moved to a rate-limited queue). 2) Emit a 429-with-hint response that instructs SDK to backoff + optionally switch to smaller max_tokens.
- Expected impact: 20–40% kernel queue reduction within 30s.

Stage 2 — Priority-aware fidelity staircasing (controlled quality tradeoff)
- Goal: Reduce per-token kernel work for non-critical requests.
- Steps: 1) For affected kernels, inject fidelity_profile override via handshake token (e.g., quantized-8b-fast, llm-lite-summary). 2) Scheduler ensures canary A/B percentages for fidelity change (default 5% -> 25% -> 50% per 2-minute steps). 3) Monitor quality regressions using sentinel prompt set evaluation (see profiling section).
- Rollback: automatic if quality alert > threshold or error rate increases.

Stage 3 — Kernel offload and fallback routing
- Goal: Preserve SLOs by moving some load off saturated kernels to compatible fallback variants (smaller model, different GPU class, CPU-based short-run).
- Steps: 1) Router consults fallback_matrix for model compatibility. 2) For in-flight requests with long expected wait, router reissues handshake to fallback kernel with incremental fidelity. 3) Upgrade path: when capacity returns, tokens expire and dispatcher resumes original routing.

Stage 4 — Emergency rejection (last resort)
- Goal: Prevent catastrophic cascade and maintain control plane stability.
- Steps: 1) Admission controller returns structured rejection with exact reason code and safe duration. 2) Operators run immediate remediation (kernel drain, node reboot, capacity surge via Dedicated burst policy).

Operator runbook (step-by-step)

1) Triage (first 5 minutes)
- Open incident and tag affected models.
- Run quick decomposition checklist: check kernel_bind_time, kv_miss_ratio, dispatch loop latency, NIC metrics.
- If kernel_bind_time is primary, apply Stage 1. If kv_miss_ratio is primary, apply Stage 1 and enable KV-prefetch backoff.

2) Apply Stage 2 (if Stage 1 insufficient)
- Use admin CLI to apply fidelity overrides for model X in zone Y:

- CLI example:
  rwdctl runtime handshake override --model xlarge-1 --zone us-west-2 --profile quant8-fast --fraction 0.25 --reason "incident-<id>"

3) Escalate to kernel-engineering if kernel_busy_ms continues > 90% for > 5 minutes. Provide trace ids and sample payloads.

4) Recovery & validation
- Monitor sentinel prompt set regression suite (see Profiling checks below).
- Gradually remove overrides once 95/99 kernel_bind_time back within SLO for 10 consecutive 1-minute windows.

Profiling & benchmark verification

- Purpose: ensure any fidelity changes do not create unacceptable quality regressions, and that kernel handshake yields expected latency improvements.

1) Sentinel prompt set (operational)
- A curated set of 200 prompts per model capturing worst-case sequence lengths, KV dependence, and multi-turn. Run with fidelity variants and compare: exact match rate, BLEU-like similarity, and latency distribution.
- Baseline run command (local harness):
  python perf_harness.py --model xlarge-1 --profile quant8-fast --concurrency 50 --duration 5m --tracing

2) Microbenchmarks for handshake overhead
- Expectation: pre-admit handshake roundtrip adds <= 2ms median and <= 10ms p99.
- Test procedure: run a short synthetic workload with handshake enabled and disabled; measure kernel_bind_time delta.

3) End-to-end shadow test
- Mirror 2% of production traffic to a sandbox fleet with handshake and fidelity staircasing enabled. Observe divergence metrics over 30 minutes and ensure error delta < 0.2%.

Release notes (protocol v0.14)

- New: per-request handshake token with nonce/timestamp and fidelity_profile field.
- New: scheduler sampling flag handshake_verbose that enables extra telemetry for incident triage.
- Change: default pre-admit threshold lowered from 200ms to 150ms for high-priority tiers.
- Fix: race between token expiry and kernel_bind that could cause stale admissions under high-clock-skew.

Known issues (short appendix)

- ISSUE-1134: KV prefetch backoff sometimes over-throttles cold-start interactive sessions. Workaround: increase per-account warmup budget for 5 minutes.
- ISSUE-1187: Handshake round-trip may exceed 10ms for cross-AZ dispatch in certain AZ pairings due to suboptimal route selection; mitigation: prefer intra-AZ routing for handshake where available.
- ISSUE-1210: Some third-party SDKs ignore 429-with-hint and aggressively retry causing repeated admission attempts. Mitigation: server responds with Retry-After and stream-close flag; recommend SDK update.

Operational checklists (cheat-sheet)

- Detection: run `rwdctl metrics query --metric kernel_bind_p99 --window 5m --model <model>`
- Apply soft shaping: `rwdctl runtime admission shape --model <model> --cohort low --rate-limit 20rps`
- Apply fidelity override: `rwdctl runtime handshake override --model <model> --profile quant8-fast --fraction 0.25`
- Validate sentinel suite: `python perf_harness.py --model <model> --profile <profile> --sanity`

Post-incident follow-up (RCA template)

- Description: short summary of what triggered the escape hatch and which stage was used.
- Root cause decomposition: kernel-binding vs kv-miss vs dispatch.
- Evidence: traces, metrics, CLI actions taken, timestamps.
- Remediation: code change, scheduler tuning, capacity adjustment.
- Preventative experiments: shadow runs, benchmark expansion.

Appendix: JSON handshake token example

{
  "token": "rwd-tn-1234abcd",
  "admitted": true,
  "expected_wait_ms": 48,
  "fidelity_profile": "quant8-fast",
  "kernel_slot_hint": "k-az3-7",
  "issued_at": "2026-10-03T15:12:22Z",
  "nonce": "f3b9a2",
  "sign": "sha256:..."
}

Appendix: Quick signal glossary

- kernel_bind_time: time between handshake_response_ts and kernel_bind_ts.
- kv_miss_ratio: fraction of requests that encountered at least one KV miss in the warmup window.
- admitted_fidelity_profile: the effective fidelity the kernel will run.

Related pages and references

- See runtime-decision-graph-and-observed-behaviour-catalog for incident classification.
- See runtime-deployment-circuit-breakers-and-sla-fallback-playbook for integrated rollback patterns.

Revision history

- 2026-02-15 (A. Menon): initial draft describing handshake concept and stage flow.
- 2026-04-30 (D. Chen): added telemetry contract and CLI examples.
- 2026-10-03 (A. Menon): published; added sentinel profiling suite and v0.14 release notes.

title: Sequence-Length-Aware Kernel Selection Guidelines
content:
Summary:

This document defines runtime and compile-time guidelines for selecting and shipping GPU kernels that are aware of sequence-length distributions for inference workloads. The intention is to reduce average token latency and per-token cost while preserving memory safety and predictable tail latencies for Redwood's serving runtime.

Audience:
- Serving runtime engineers
- Kernel authors and compiler integrators
- Capacity and SRE teams responsible for GPU fleet allocation
- Model onboarding engineers

Motivation:
- Customer workloads vary widely in sequence length: short chat turns, medium-length instruction completions, and long context retrievals. One-size-fits-all kernels yield suboptimal latency/cost tradeoffs.
- Kernel selection decisions influence L2 (memory) usage, register pressure, occupancy, and cache behavior. These directly impact SLO attainment and unit economics.

Goals and non-goals:
- Goals:
  - Provide a deterministic policy for picking kernels based on observed per-tenant sequence-length histograms and SLOs.
  - Standardize telemetry and sampling to make kernel decisions auditable and rollouts reversible.
  - Ensure safe fallbacks when kernel selection fails or a kernel binary is missing.
- Non-goals:
  - This is not a comprehensive compiler design document; it focuses on serving-level selection and operational policies.

Definitions:
- hot-path kernel: highly optimized kernel tuned for short sequences and low-latency, potentially at higher per-token compute cost.
- bulk kernel: throughput-optimized kernel that achieves better utilization for long sequences by amortizing setup overhead.
- shard-compile: precompiled binary targeted at a specific GPU architecture and sequence-length profile.

Telemetry and signals to collect (minimum required):
1) Sequence-length histogram per customer and per route (bucketed: 0-32,33-128,129-512,513-2048,>2048).
2) P50/P95/P99 generation latency broken down by sequence-length bucket and kernel_variant.
3) GPU occupancy, register usage, and SM utilization per kernel_variant.
4) Memory allocations and peak GPU memory per request.
5) Kernel failure counts, fallback invocations, and compile-time errors.

Policy: Kernel selection priority
1) Hard SLO routes (SLO target <= 100ms P95): use hot-path kernels for any bucket with median length <= 128 tokens.
2) Cost-sensitive routes (billing tier flagged as cost_aware): prefer bulk kernels for median length > 256 tokens unless P95 tail is breached.
3) Mixed workloads: use dynamic split routing — short sequences map to hot-path containers, long sequences map to bulk containers.

Configuration table (example):
| config_key | description | default | allowed_values | owner |
|-----------|-------------|---------|----------------|-------|
| kernel.selection.mode | Global selection mode | mixed | mixed|hot-only|cost-only | Runtime Platform Team |
| kernel.bucket_thresholds | Buckets used for histograms | 32,128,512,2048 | comma-separated ints | Serving Runtime |
| kernel.rollout.canary_pct | Percent of traffic to try new kernel | 1 | 0-50 | Runtime Platform Team |
| kernel.fallback_on_failure | Whether to fallback to reference kernel | true | true|false | Runtime Platform Team |

Selection algorithm (high-level pseudocode):

1) Periodic profiler job (freq: 10m) computes per-route histogram and cost/latency delta between variants.
2) If median_length <= short_threshold and (P95_hot <= SLO or cost delta < cost_threshold), set kernel_variant=hot for that route.
3) Else if median_length > long_threshold and bulk_variant P50 cost < hot_variant P50 cost by 10%, set kernel_variant=bulk.
4) For mixed buckets where a single variant cannot meet SLO, configure split routing: route short tokens to hot and long tokens to bulk using request-length header.

Example YAML configuration (runtime):

kernel_selection:
  mode: mixed
  short_threshold: 128
  long_threshold: 256
  buckets: [32, 128, 512, 2048]
  fallback_on_failure: true
  canary:
    enabled: true
    percent: 1

Operational runbook (short):
1) On performance regression alert (route P95 breach):
   a) Check kernel failure counts and recent kernel rollouts.
   b) If a new kernel binary was deployed in the last 60m, immediately route 100% of that route to fallback variant and mark the new kernel rollout as paused.
   c) Collect last 1 hour of sequence-length histogram and kernel-level telemetry.
   d) If telemetry indicates memory-unbounded growth, escalate to Kernel SIG and open an incident.
2) If tail latency is high but kernel failure counts are low:
   a) Consider enabling split routing and increasing hot-path capacity.
   b) If cost budget allows, temporarily prefer hot-path for affected customers with strict SLOs.

Kernel binary and compatibility matrix (textual):
- Each kernel build must be annotated with: supported_arch (e.g., ampere, h100), max_sequence_optimized, workspace_bytes_required, and ABI version.
- The runtime will refuse to load a kernel whose ABI version does not match the runtime ABI.
- Compatibility policy: minor ABI mismatches can be allowed under a feature-flag after a canary period. Major ABI mismatches require a compatibility release and coordination with SRE.

Security and safety considerations:
- Kernel binaries are signed and verified at load time. Unsigned kernels must be rejected.
- All kernel selection decisions and sample inputs used during canaries must be logged with redaction for PII.
- For private deployments (customer-managed), provide a checker utility that validates kernel signatures and workspace guarantees before enabling runtime opt-in.

Rollout and testing guidance:
- Preflight tests for a kernel must include: microbenchmarks across bucketed sequence lengths, memory-pressure stress tests, and a synthetic tail-latency workload.
- Canary: default 1% of traffic for 30 minutes, monitor P99, error rate, and memory spikes. Abort criteria: >20% increase in P99 or any OOM in canary hosts.
- Gradual ramp: 1% -> 5% -> 20% -> 50% -> 100% with health check windows of 30 minutes per step.

Kernel authors checklist (before upload):
- [ ] Provide per-bucket latency and memory table for supported sequence lengths.
- [ ] Attach signed artifact with ABI metadata and compile flags.
- [ ] Add unit and integration tests covering boundary buckets (e.g., 31/32, 128/129).
- [ ] Provide expected GPU occupancy and register pressure metrics.

Metrics and dashboards to create:
- Per-route kernel_variant P50/P95/P99 latency heatmap keyed by sequence-length bucket.
- Kernel failure and fallback rate per hour.
- Kernel memory headroom gauge: (allocated_workspace / total_gpu_memory).
- Cost per million tokens by kernel_variant.

Ownership and escalation:
- Primary owner: Serving Runtime Team (owners: @serving-runtime).
- Kernel SIG: cross-team working group (runtime, compiler, perf, SRE).
- Escalation steps: page-on-call -> Kernel SIG -> Eng Infra Director.

FAQ (selected):
Q: How do we handle models with extreme variable-length behavior (chat + docs embeddings)?
A: Use split routing with an upfront classifier that routes high-context requests to bulk pools and short-turn chat to hot pools. If a classifier is not available, default to conservative bulk which preserves throughput.

Q: What if a kernel optimizes a single bucket but regresses others?
A: Reject that kernel for default rollout. Kernels should provide a performance matrix and only opt-in for specific routes via explicit canary-based policy.

References and related work:
- Internal: performance-budgets-and-service-profiles-2026 (see cost simulation section)
- Internal: model-slicing-and-fallback-routing-guidelines-2026
- External: "Optimizing Transformer Inference for Variable Sequence Lengths", SysML 2024 (citation summarized in design notes).

Appendix: sample CLI commands
- Compile shard for Ampere with optimizations:
  $ kernel-cli build --arch ampere --max-seq 512 --optimize=short-path --output kernel_ampere_s512.bin

- Validate kernel before upload:
  $ kernel-cli validate kernel_ampere_s512.bin --check-abi --check-signature --report ./reports/s512.json

Change log:
- 2025-11-12: Document created by Priya Desai.
- 2026-01-04: Added canary abort criteria and example YAML.
- 2026-02-15: Expanded telemetry buckets and added operational runbook steps.

title: Fidelity adaptation: evaluation, rollback backstop, and simulation manifest
content:
Overview
========
This document defines the fidelity-adaptation evaluation manifest and the operational backstop policies used when runtime adapts model fidelity (quantized variants, model variants, or batching/caching induced fidelity changes). It specifies: goals, evaluation metrics and thresholds, a canary/simulation protocol, rollback/backstop criteria, required observability signals, and example configuration snippets used by the Runtime Orchestrator.

Goals and scope
----------------
- Keep Redispatch/Degradation events safe for production customers while meeting cost and latency objectives.
- Provide a reproducible simulation and canary matrix so model-variant or quantization rollouts can be verified prior to wide release.
- Define automatic backstops for fidelity regressions that protect SLOs (quality and latency) and allow rapid operator intervention.
- Scope: applies to hosted, dedicated, and private runtime deployments where automatic fidelity adaptation is enabled. Does not replace model-level release QA.

Definitions and acronyms
------------------------
- Fidelity adaptation: any runtime action that may change perceived output quality (e.g., switching to a quantized kernel, using a smaller model-variant, applying aggressive KV-prefetching that truncates context).
- RAR (Relative Acceptance Rate): production A/B style metric estimating fraction of responses accepted by downstream classifiers or human raters relative to baseline.
- Delta-Q: normalized quality delta computed from a weighted combination of evaluation metrics (embedding cosine, task-specific metric, and RAR). Expressed in percentage points.
- Backstop policy: an automated control that pauses rollouts and reverts routing when a Delta-Q or other trigger exceeds thresholds.

Key SLOs and thresholds
-----------------------
- Latency SLO (p50/p95/p99): must not regress by more than 10ms / 30ms / 75ms relative to baseline variant during canary.
- Cost target: expected per-token compute cost reduction >= 7% (measured over 24h sample) for the candidate to be considered.
- Delta-Q backstop: immediate rollback if Delta-Q <= -1.5% (meaning quality drop > 1.5 percentage points relative to baseline).
- RAR backstop: immediate rollback if production RAR delta <= -2.0%.
- Soft alert: if Delta-Q between -0.5% and -1.5% raise P1 but continue canary under operator supervision.

Evaluation matrix (canonical signals)
------------------------------------
- Offline harness: microbench evaluation on canonical prompt-sets (see prompt-sets-and-benchmarks). Metrics: embedding cosine to baseline (>= 0.985 for small quant changes), task-specific accuracy (e.g., exact-match), ROUGE-L / BLEU where applicable.
- Shadow traffic comparison: mirror 2% of live traffic for 48 hours; compute latency quantiles, RAR, and token-cost.
- Live canary: gradual traffic ramp 0.5% -> 2% -> 10% over 24–72 hours with active monitoring windows.
- Synthetic surge test: run 2x expected peak for 30 minutes using service load generator and record tail-latency and kernel error rates.

Canary rollout protocol (step-by-step)
-------------------------------------
1. PREP: Validate offline harness (unit tests, integration tests) and produce a canary-report artifact with metrics. Attach artifact to canary change.
2. SHADOW: Enable shadowing on a 2% mirrored slice for 48 hours. Ensure no kernel-level exceptions and collect RAR and Delta-Q.
3. STAGED RAMP: If shadow ok, open staged ramp: 0.5% for 2 hours -> 2% for 12 hours -> 10% for 24h. During ramp: automated checks run every 5 minutes.
4. VALIDATE: At each stage validate: 1) Delta-Q > -0.5%, 2) latency p99 within threshold, 3) kernel failure rate < 0.01%. If any check fails, trigger immediate rollback.
5. GRADUAL RELEASE: If 10% sustained for 24h with no soft alerts, schedule controlled release to 50% with operator approval.
6. FULL RELEASE: After 72h at 50% with evaluations stable, release to 100% or integrate into tiered routing.

Rollback and backstop actions
----------------------------
- Immediate automatic rollback triggers: Delta-Q <= -1.5% OR RAR delta <= -2.0% OR kernel fatal errors > 0.1% over 10 minutes.
- Soft stop: pause ramp and notify on-call if Delta-Q between -0.5% and -1.5%.
- Manual backstop: operator can enact a targeted routing policy that pins affected customers to baseline model-variant for up to 30 days while investigation occurs.
- For Dedicated/Private deployments: follow local operator rollback steps in addition to control-plane backstop; see "deployment-guides" for customer-specific rollback playbooks.

Observability and telemetry requirements
---------------------------------------
All canary runs must emit the following telemetry to the observability pipeline with these minimum cardinalities:
- Per-variant: p50/p95/p99 latency, per-token CPU/GPU time, kernel invocation count, kernel error code histogram.
- Quality signals: embedded cosine distribution, RAR estimate, sampled human feedback tags (if available).
- Resource signals: GPU occupancy, GPU memory high-water, NUMA imbalance score, NVLink error counters.
- Control traces: request provenance tag including canary-id, variant-id, kernel-subtype, and sampling decision.

Alerting rules (examples)
------------------------
- Canary-DeltaQ-Critical: Delta-Q <= -1.0% sustained for 3 evaluation windows (5m) -> Pager -> auto-rollback.
- Canary-Latency-Tail: p99 increase > 50% compared to baseline for 10m -> Notify SRE and stop ramp.
- Kernel-Exception-Rate: kernel errors > 0.05% over 5m -> Create incident, auto-fallthrough to fallback kernel.

Simulation manifest (reproducible experiments)
--------------------------------------------
This section contains the canonical experiments and parameters used by the benchmarking lab to simulate production outcomes. Use the following YAML snippet as the manifest input to the experiment runner. Save results to the artifacts bucket with canary-id tags.

Example manifest (YAML, used by sim-runner)
-------------------------------------------
apiVersion: v1
kind: FidelitySimulation
metadata:
  name: "sim-fidelity-{{canary-id}}"
spec:
  duration: 48h
  traffic_profile: "customer-mix-v3"
  mirror_fraction: 0.02
  metrics:
    - name: "DeltaQ"
      computation: "weighted(embedding_cosine:0.6, task_metric:0.3, RAR:0.1)"
    - name: "CostPerToken"
  workload_overrides:
    sequence_length: {p50: 96, p95: 512, p99: 1024}
  failure_injection:
    kernel_pause_rate: 0.0001
    nvlink_degradation: false

(When running, replace templated fields and attach the generated artifact to the canary change.)

Runtime config example (JSON used by Orchestrator)
--------------------------------------------------
{
  "variant_id": "quant128-int8-v2",
  "canary_id": "canary-2026-01-13-q128",
  "routing": {"initial_fraction": 0.005, "stages": [0.005, 0.02, 0.1]},
  "backstop": {"delta_q_threshold": -0.015, "rar_threshold": -0.02, "kernel_error_threshold": 0.001},
  "observability_tags": ["fidelity-canary", "team-runtime"]
}

Operator runbook (quick checklist)
---------------------------------
1. Verify canary-report artifact is attached to change.
2. Start shadow run and confirm no kernel critical errors in first 30m.
3. Approve staged ramp on green signals.
4. Monitor Canary-DeltaQ-Critical and Kernel-Exception-Rate dashboards every 5m.
5. If rollback triggered: pin affected customers, create incident with tag lifecycle:fidelity-backstop, and run regression-huntbook.

Investigation playbook (post-backstop)
-------------------------------------
1. Triaging: collect artifacts (shadow diffs, sampled responses, kernel traces, GPU metrics).
2. Localize: is the regression correlated to sequence-length, prompt pattern, or tenant? Use cohort-labels in traces.
3. Reproduce: run targeted offline sim using the canary-id and failing cohort parameters.
4. Patch: either revert quantized kernel, adjust kernel launch parameters, or tighten routing.
5. Re-run canary with conservative thresholds and extended shadowing.

Ownership and governance
------------------------
- Runtime fidelity experiments are owned by the Serving Runtime team. Primary owners: Aisha K. Patel (runtime experiments), Marco Li (observability), Priya Shah (benchmarking).
- All changes that affect fidelity must include: offline harness report, simulation artifact URL, and a canary plan.
- Monthly fidelity review: automated summaries of all fidelity-adaptation canaries (success/fail/rolled-back) are presented at the Runtime Quality sync.

FAQ and gotchas
---------------
Q: How do we avoid noisy RAR estimates on low-traffic tenants?
A: Use cohort aggregation and require a minimum sample size (n >= 200 requests) before evaluating RAR-sensitive backstops.

Q: What if the quantized kernel shows better RAR but worse p99 latency?
A: Favor user-facing quality SLOs; if latency breach is transient, evaluate kernel-tuning knobs (batch-slicer, prefetch window). If sustained, revert and open a perf-tuning ticket.

References and related artifacts
-------------------------------
- Execution: see runtime-architecture/graceful-fidelity-staircase-and-degradation-modes-2026.json for coordinated degradation modes.
- Benchmarks: benchmarking-and-perf-suite/fidelity-gap-injector-surge-protocol-2026.json.
- Observability harness: profiling-playbook/observability-injection-kernel-validation-harness-2026.json.

Appendix: example monitoring queries
-----------------------------------
- Delta-Q rolling window (5m): avg(weighted_embedding_cosine*0.6 + task_metric*0.3 + rar*0.1) by variant_id
- Kernel error rate: sum(kernel_errors)/sum(kernel_invocations) by variant_id over 5m

Contact
-------
If you have questions about this manifest or need an escorted canary, contact runtime-experiments@redwood.ai or ping #runtime-canaries on Slack with canary-id and link to canary-report artifact.

title: Runtime backpressure and saturation signals (export + semantics)
content:
## Purpose
This page defines the runtime-level backpressure and saturation signals used by Hosted circuit breakers + load shedding. It documents:
- What signals the serving runtime emits (queues, throughput, KV cache, memory pressure, fragmentation proxies).
- Exact semantics and units.
- Export pipeline (metric types, sampling, aggregation, and cardinality constraints).
- How upstream systems should interpret the signals without creating feedback loops.

This is a reference for Runtime, SRE, Gateway/Control Plane, Smart Routing, and Observability.

---

## Scope and non-goals
**In scope**
- Signals emitted by the GPU-serving runtime at admission/scheduling boundaries.
- Metrics intended for near-real-time overload decisions (seconds).
- Metrics intended for dashboards/alerting (minutes).

**Non-goals**
- Per-request tracing details (handled by tracing pipeline).
- Model-quality or output correctness signals.
- Fine-grained per-GPU/per-process troubleshooting metrics with high cardinality (those live in restricted debug endpoints and are not used for load shedding).

---

## Runtime architecture context (where backpressure happens)
At a high level, the runtime splits work into:
1) **Admission**: request accepted by runtime process (after gateway/routing). Some requests may be queued locally before scheduling.
2) **Prefill**: prompt encoding + KV cache population.
3) **Decode**: incremental token generation using the KV cache.
4) **Streaming**: tokens flushed to the upstream response stream.

The runtime enforces backpressure at two points:
- **Runtime admission**: applies concurrency caps and queue limits (soft/hard), returning overload signals upstream when exceeded.
- **Scheduler**: dynamically reduces effective concurrency when saturation is detected (e.g., memory pressure, KV cache exhaustion), and can mark the instance as “degraded” for routing.

The signals below are designed to be robust under:
- Prompt-length variance (prefill heavy vs decode heavy workloads)
- Streaming-induced tail amplification
- Noisy-neighbor patterns (single tenant sending long prompts / high max_tokens)

---

## Signal taxonomy
We classify runtime saturation into four categories:
1) **Queueing saturation**: backlog is growing and/or wait time is increasing.
2) **Compute saturation**: tokens/sec is at or near sustainable peak; marginal load increases latency sharply.
3) **Memory / KV cache saturation**: KV cache capacity or allocation efficiency is limiting throughput; OOM risk increases.
4) **Health degradation**: dependency or internal faults (allocator errors, repeated CUDA errors) impacting capacity.

Upstream policies should prefer **early, stable signals** (queue depth + queue wait) over late symptoms (timeouts).

---

## Export contract (how we emit signals)
### Metric transport
- Primary export: **Prometheus** (scraped) and mirrored into our metrics backend.
- Secondary export: **OpenTelemetry metrics** for long-term correlation (not used in admission decisions).

### Resolution and update cadence
- “Breaker-grade” metrics update every **1s** (rolling window) where feasible.
- Most gauges/counters are exported at **5s** resolution.
- Percentiles (e.g., queue wait p95) are computed using runtime-side histograms and exported as Prometheus histograms.

### Cardinality constraints (hard requirements)
To avoid metric blowups:
- No per-request IDs.
- No per-customer dimensions.
- Labels are limited to: `region`, `cluster`, `runtime_pool`, `model_family`, `route_class` (small finite sets).
- Optional label `model` is only allowed when the catalog size is bounded in that pool; otherwise prefer `model_family`.

**Important:** If a team needs high-cardinality breakdowns for a live incident, use the restricted debug endpoint (see “Debug-only signals”), not Prometheus.

---

## Core signals (required)
### 1) Scheduler queue depth (prefill / decode)
These are the primary early-warning signals.

**Metrics**
- `runtime_scheduler_queue_depth{stage="prefill"}` (gauge, requests)
- `runtime_scheduler_queue_depth{stage="decode"}` (gauge, requests)

**Semantics**
- Number of requests currently waiting to be scheduled for the given stage.
- Excludes requests actively running on GPU.

**Interpretation**
- Sustained non-zero decode queue depth correlates strongly with rising p95 latency for streaming workloads.
- Prefill queue depth spikes are common during bursty long-prompt traffic; use queue *wait* to differentiate transient bursts vs persistent saturation.

### 2) Scheduler queue wait time
**Metrics**
- `runtime_scheduler_queue_wait_seconds_bucket{stage="prefill"}` (histogram)
- `runtime_scheduler_queue_wait_seconds_bucket{stage="decode"}` (histogram)

**Semantics**
- Time from enqueue → start of GPU execution for that stage.

**Interpretation**
- Queue depth without wait time can be misleading (e.g., many tiny tasks).
- For overload decisions, queue wait p95 is preferred.

### 3) Effective tokens/sec and saturation ratio
We export both “actual tokens/sec” and “saturation ratio” relative to a calibrated baseline.

**Metrics**
- `runtime_tokens_generated_total` (counter, tokens)
- `runtime_token_throughput_tps` (gauge, tokens/sec; runtime-computed over rolling 10s window)
- `runtime_compute_saturation_ratio` (gauge, 0.0–2.0)

**Semantics**
- `runtime_token_throughput_tps` is derived from the counter and a stable rolling window.
- `runtime_compute_saturation_ratio` is `observed_tps / sustainable_tps_baseline`.
  - The baseline is pool+model_family specific and shipped via config; it is periodically recalibrated from load tests.

**Interpretation**
- Ratio > 0.95 sustained indicates compute saturation; additional load should be shed/queued.
- Ratio < 0.7 with high queue depth indicates another bottleneck (often memory/KV pressure or fragmentation).

### 4) In-flight requests and concurrency
**Metrics**
- `runtime_inflight_requests{stage="prefill"}` (gauge)
- `runtime_inflight_requests{stage="decode"}` (gauge)
- `runtime_admission_concurrency_limit` (gauge)

**Semantics**
- Stage-specific active work running on GPU.
- `runtime_admission_concurrency_limit` is the current effective cap (may be lowered by degradation mode).

**Interpretation**
- Use with queue signals to reason about whether we are “maxed out” or blocked.

---

## KV cache + memory pressure signals
### 5) KV cache utilization (pool level)
**Metrics**
- `runtime_kv_cache_bytes_used` (gauge)
- `runtime_kv_cache_bytes_capacity` (gauge)
- `runtime_kv_cache_utilization_ratio` (gauge, 0.0–1.0)

**Semantics**
- Capacity is the configured KV cache arena size for the pool.
- Used bytes include active sequences plus reserved blocks for in-flight batching.

**Interpretation**
- Sustained utilization > 0.9 correlates with admission stalls and/or forced evictions.
- Under KV pressure, prefill may look healthy while decode queue wait grows (decode needs KV residency longer).

### 6) KV cache eviction / reclamation pressure
**Metrics**
- `runtime_kv_cache_evictions_total` (counter)
- `runtime_kv_cache_reclaim_failures_total` (counter)

**Semantics**
- Evictions occur when the runtime must reclaim KV blocks earlier than ideal to admit new work.
- Reclaim failures indicate allocator could not free sufficient contiguous blocks (often fragmentation-related).

**Interpretation**
- Rising eviction rate during steady traffic is a strong signal for load shedding or reduced max_tokens caps.

### 7) GPU memory headroom and allocator pressure
We avoid exporting raw per-GPU memory usage by device ID (cardinality and privacy concerns). We export pool-level aggregates.

**Metrics**
- `runtime_gpu_memory_bytes_used` (gauge, pool aggregate)
- `runtime_gpu_memory_bytes_total` (gauge, pool aggregate)
- `runtime_gpu_memory_headroom_ratio` (gauge, 0.0–1.0)

**Semantics**
- Aggregate across devices in the pool (sum used / sum total).
- Includes model weights + runtime allocations + KV cache arena.

**Interpretation**
- Headroom ratio < 0.05 sustained is a high OOM risk zone. Admission should become conservative.

---

## Memory fragmentation proxies (practical, export-safe)
We cannot reliably export “true fragmentation” across allocators/hardware, so we use two proxies that correlate with allocator churn and inability to satisfy large allocations.

### 8) Allocation failure and retry counters
**Metrics**
- `runtime_allocator_allocation_failures_total{class="kv"|"workspace"|"other"}` (counter)
- `runtime_allocator_retry_total{class="kv"|"workspace"|"other"}` (counter)

**Semantics**
- Allocation failures count unsuccessful attempts that required fallback (e.g., GC/reclaim) before succeeding or erroring.
- Retries count attempts that succeeded after one or more reclaim cycles.

**Interpretation**
- A rising retry rate typically precedes latency spikes.
- Allocation failures that bubble up as request errors must be classified as runtime capacity degradation and should trigger aggressive shedding.

### 9) “Largest free block” approximation (bucketed)
**Metrics**
- `runtime_allocator_largest_free_block_bytes_bucket` (histogram)

**Semantics**
- Runtime periodically samples the allocator and records the approximate largest allocatable contiguous block.
- Exported as a histogram to avoid per-instance variability dominating the signal.

**Interpretation**
- Falling largest-free-block distribution while total free memory remains stable indicates fragmentation (or pinned allocations).

---

## Backpressure state signals (explicit)
### 10) Runtime overload state and reason
**Metrics**
- `runtime_overload_state{state="ok"|"degraded"|"overloaded"}` (gauge; 1 for current state)
- `runtime_overload_reason{reason="queue"|"compute"|"kv"|"memory"|"dependency"|"unknown"}` (gauge; 1 for current dominant reason)

**Semantics**
- State is computed in runtime from a weighted ruleset (see below).
- Reason is best-effort; it is used primarily for dashboards and oncall triage.

**Interpretation**
- Upstream circuit breakers should treat `overloaded` as a “hard stop” indicator for new admissions in that pool/region.
- `degraded` indicates we should prefer feature reduction (caps) and cautious admission rather than blanket shed.

### Runtime-side ruleset (current)
The runtime computes state with conservative hysteresis:
- Enter `degraded` when (any):
  - decode queue wait p95 > 250ms for 30s
  - compute saturation ratio > 0.95 for 30s
  - KV utilization > 0.92 for 30s
  - allocator retry rate > 1/s for 30s
- Enter `overloaded` when (any):
  - decode queue wait p95 > 750ms for 20s
  - GPU headroom ratio < 0.03 for 10s
  - allocation failures increasing AND error rate in runtime > 0.5% for 60s
- Exit criteria require the signal to remain below threshold for a longer interval (typically 60–120s) to avoid flapping.

**Note:** These thresholds are defaults; policy engine can override per pool/model_family with guardrails.

---

## Debug-only signals (restricted; not for general dashboards)
For deep performance work we also maintain:
- Per-GPU device utilization, memory, and kernel timings
- Per-model exact TPS baselines
- Per-batch sizes and microbatch timings

These are available via:
- `runtime-admin` endpoint (restricted network + RBAC)
- Short-lived “incident capture” bundles

Do not build automated shedding rules on debug-only signals.

---

## How upstream systems should use these signals
### Gateway / admission control
Recommended order of evaluation (fast to compute, stable):
1) Runtime `runtime_overload_state` (overloaded → reject early)
2) decode queue wait p95 and queue depth (protect p95/p99)
3) KV utilization + eviction rate (protect memory stability)
4) compute saturation ratio (protect throughput)

Guidance:
- Prefer consistent, explicit overload errors over timeouts.
- Avoid retry storms: only shed with stable Retry-After contracts (see ADR-014 for semantics).

### Smart routing
- Use `overloaded` state to avoid routing new traffic into an already-saturated pool.
- Use `degraded` as a hint to prefer alternate pools/regions for latency-sensitive tiers.
- Do not rapidly oscillate between regions based on 1–5s spikes; require sustained state changes (>= 30s) or use the routing system’s built-in damping.

### SRE dashboards and alerts
- Alerts should be based on *sustained* signals and correlated with customer-visible impact metrics (5xx/timeouts/latency), not on single gauges.

---

## Example PromQL snippets (for dashboards)
**Decode queue wait p95 by region**
- `histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, region) (rate(runtime_scheduler_queue_wait_seconds_bucket{stage="decode"}[5m])))`

**KV utilization ratio (pool aggregate)**
- `avg by (region, runtime_pool) (runtime_kv_cache_utilization_ratio)`

**Compute saturation ratio (p95 across instances approximated by max)**
- `max by (region, runtime_pool) (runtime_compute_saturation_ratio)`

**Allocator retries rate**
- `sum by (region, runtime_pool) (rate(runtime_allocator_retry_total[5m]))`

---

## Operational notes and pitfalls
1) **Queue depth without queue wait is ambiguous.** Always pair them.
2) **Prefill vs decode bottlenecks differ.** A prefill-heavy burst may not require shedding if decode remains stable.
3) **KV pressure can masquerade as compute saturation.** When KV utilization is high, throughput may drop while GPUs look “busy.”
4) **Sampling noise:** 1s gauges will be spiky. Use 30–60s windows for state changes.
5) **Metric delays:** scrape + pipeline delays are typically 2–10s. Runtime state gauges help reduce dependency on downstream aggregation.

---

## Change management
Any changes to:
- metric names, labels, or types
- runtime_overload_state ruleset thresholds
- sampling cadence

…must include:
- A backwards-compatibility plan (add new metrics; deprecate old after 2 releases)
- Updates to overload dashboards and any policy-engine mappings
- SRE sign-off if used for paging or automated load shedding

---

## Owners
- Runtime scheduling + backpressure: **Sofia Ivanova**, **Lena Fischer**
- Saturation signals implementation: **Omar El-Sayed**, **Julian Moore**
- Telemetry pipeline coordination: **Logan Wright**
- Oncall consumers (dashboards/alerts): **Rafael Mendes**, **Aisha Bello**

title: adaptive-fidelity-orchestration-and-evaluation-checklist-2026
content:
Summary

This page defines the Adaptive Fidelity Orchestration pattern we use to balance latency, cost, and output quality in the inference-runtime. It documents the telemetry contract, decision matrix, rollout and evaluation checklist, and emergency rollback procedures used by runtime, scheduling, and ops teams.

Goal

- Enable safe, measurable fidelity degradations (quantization, smaller variants, reduced sampling) to preserve SLOs during pressure events while keeping quality regressions bounded and observable.
- Provide a reproducible evaluation checklist for any fidelity-orchestration rollout or experiment.

Scope

Applies to: hosted API, Dedicated pools, and Private deployments using the inference-runtime components: scheduler, kernel-mapper, fallback-router, kv-cache, and telemetry-pipeline. Does NOT include model training or model selection upstream (use model-onboarding docs for that).

Key concepts and vocabulary

- Fidelity action: an operational change that reduces computational work per request (e.g., lower quantization, switch to 8-bit kernel, prune attention heads, reduce beam width, shorten context window).
- Fidelity policy: declarative rules that map runtime signals to fidelity actions. Policies are evaluated in the scheduler and enacted via the fallback-router.
- Fidelity event: telemetry emission when a policy evaluates to a non-default action (see Telemetry Contract).

High-level architecture (text diagram)

inference-api -> request-router -> scheduler -> kernel-mapper -> gpu-dispatcher -> kernels
                                         |
                                         v
                                fallback-router -> model-variant-store
                                         |
                                         v
                                 telemetry-pipeline -> metrics/trace/store

The scheduler consults fidelity policies at decision points (admission, pre-dispatch, warmstart). The fallback-router performs model swaps and quantization-profile changes with KV warm-up hints.

Telemetry contract (mandatory)

Every fidelity action must generate these telemetry events (span-based + metrics):

- execution.fidelity_check (span tag): {policy_id, trigger_signal, evaluated_at, decision}
- execution.fidelity_change (counter): increments when an action is applied (labels: action_type, pool, model_family, rollout_id)
- kernel_selection.hint (gauge): kernel_name selected for request (sampled 1%)
- kernel_latency_ms (histogram): end-to-end kernel latency after action (p50/p95/p99 buckets)
- quality.regression_signal (counter + sample): when offline/online eval detects quality drop > threshold (labels: eval_suite, prompt_set)

Sampling and retention

- Default fidelity_check sampling: 5% (increase to 100% for canaries or error bursts).
- kernel_latency_ms retained for 90 days; fidelity_change events retained 365 days.

Decision matrix (example)

When pool CPU/GPU metrics cross thresholds, follow ordered actions. Each action is additive unless explicitly exclusive in the policy.

| Signal | Threshold | Primary action | Quality guard | Rollback threshold |
|--------|-----------|----------------|---------------|-------------------|
| GPU_util | > 92% over 2m | enable-8bit-kernel | offline eval loss delta < 0.8% | GPU_util < 85% for 5m |
| p95 latency | > target*1.3 | reduce-batch-size (limit concurrency) | p50 latency steady | p95 < target*1.1 |
| queue-depth | > 500 | degrade-fidelity: short-context (truncate 50 tokens) | quality delta < 1.5% | queue-depth < 200 |
| memory_pressure | > 80% | kvcache-evict-older-prefetch | no data loss | memory_pressure < 60% |

Policy format (YAML example)

policy_id: fast_sustain_2026
description: "Reduce compute during sustained high GPU utilization while preserving output quality"
triggers:
  - signal: gpu_util
    operator: ">="
    value: 92
    window: 120s
actions:
  - name: enable_quantized_kernel
    params:
      mode: 8bit
      models: ["gpt-medium-family"]
  - name: kvcache_prefetch_mode
    params: {mode: conservative}
guards:
  - type: offline_eval
    eval_suite: "regression-critical-prompts"

Rollout and evaluation checklist (pre-deployment)

1. Author policy in repo: infra/fidelity-policies/<policy_id>.yaml, include rationale and owner.
2. Unit tests for policy parser and basic simulation of triggers (use fidelity-sim harness).
3. Local simulation: run replay of 24h production trace in sandbox, record cost and eval metrics vs baseline.
4. Canary deploy: select 1% of traffic in one Dedicated pool with 100% telemetry sampling.
5. Run online A/B for 48h: compare key metrics: p95 latency, tokens-per-second, offline eval pass rate.
6. Post-canary review: reviewers must sign off in PR checks and add sign-off tags.
7. Automated gradual ramp: 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100% over 48h with health gates at each step.

Health gates (automated)

- p95 latency must not regress > 10% vs baseline for two consecutive windows of 30m.
- quality.regression_signal rate must be <= 0.5x historical rate for the same prompt set for 24h.
- cost-per-token must not increase more than 2% (goal is net decrease).

Emergency rollback procedures

1. Alerting: fidelity-change if rate spikes > 10x baseline for 5m or quality.regression_signal exceeds configured threshold triggers a P1 paging to eng-sre.
2. Automated rollback CLI (useful for oncall):

# Stop policy evaluation and revert to default profile
redwoodctl runtime fidelity suspend --policy fast_sustain_2026 --scope pool:us-west-1-dedicated
redwoodctl runtime fidelity rollback --policy fast_sustain_2026 --to default_profile
