3. Manual model swap (if rollback CLI fails): update fallback-router policy to route to model-variant-store:default.

Quality evaluation (offline and online)

- Offline: must run 'regression-critical-prompts' and 'semantic-stability-suite' on 2,000 prompt pairs. Thresholds:
  - semantic-stability delta (BLEU/ROUGE-style proxies) < 0.8%
  - hallucination increase < 0.5% (measured by hallucination-sign detector)
- Online: shadow traffic evaluation with stash/score mode: sample 0.5% of live requests and score against golden answers or human raters.

Owner and contacts

- Policy owner: eng-serving-runtime (Priya N., priya@redwood.ai)
- Scheduler owner: Miguel Santos (miguel@redwood.ai)
- Oncall: eng-sre rotation (see /oncall roster link)

Integrations and operational notes

- Observability: ensure fidelity_change and kernel_latency_ms are exposed as Prometheus metrics and ingested by observability alerting rules.
- Alerts: add a dedicated alert group 'Fidelity Guardrails' with thresholds matching the health gates.
- Audit: every policy change must create an entry in config-audit (timestamp, author, diff).

Acceptance criteria for merging policy PR

- All unit tests pass.
- Canary simulation logs attached and include kernel_latency_ms distributions.
- Reviewer sign-offs from runtime, SRE, and applied-ml teams.
- Rollback playbook references (this doc + runbook link).

Guidance for private deployments

Private deployments often have constrained telemetry. In that case:
- Require 100% local fidelity_check sampling for the canary period.
- Run longer canary windows (72h) before global rollout.
- Default to conservative actions (e.g., reduce-batch-size before quantization) when offline_eval data is limited.

Operational runbook snippets

- To force a specific fidelity action for investigation:
redwoodctl runtime fidelity apply --policy test_investigation --action reduce_context --params '{"tokens":50}' --scope pool:debug-sandbox

- Query recent fidelity events (last 2h):
query-metrics "execution.fidelity_change{pool=\"us-west-1-dedicated\"}" --from now-120m --to now

- Promote a canary policy to global (after sign-off):
1) Ensure automated ramp script is configured in deploy-runner.
2) kubectl apply -f infra/fidelity-policies/fast_sustain_2026.yaml --context=deploy-runner

Appendix: example evaluation table (pass thresholds)

| Evaluation suite | Metric | Baseline | Allowed delta | Pass
|------------------|--------|----------|---------------|------
| regression-critical-prompts | semantic-stability | 0.812 | -0.006 (<=0.8%) | required
| hallucination-smoke | hallucination-rate | 0.045 | +0.0025 (<=0.5%) | required
| latency-sla-proxy | p95 (ms) | 230 | +25 (<=10%) | required

References and related reading

- Runtime telemetry model: ../team-wiki/runtime-telemetry-sampling-cost-aware-profiling-2027
- Fidelity containment playbook: ../runbooks/fidelity-containment-and-cost-feedback-playbook-2026
- Kernel autotune playbook: ../profiling-playbook/telemetry-feedback-kernel-autotune-playbook-2026

Change log

- 2025-09-14: initial draft by Priya N.
- 2025-11-02: added offline eval thresholds and canary escalation steps (review: Jordan L.).
- 2026-02-10: formalized telemetry contract and private deployment guidance (review: Zoe K.).

title: Execution Hypothesis Ledger: Observability-driven Runtime Experiments
content:
Summary:

This ledger defines a standard, auditable format for runtime execution hypotheses that are driven by observability signals. It is intended for use when proposing, running, and evaluating small-to-medium scope changes to serving runtime behavior (kernel selection, priority shaping, prefetch hints, eviction policies, and routing fallbacks). The ledger captures hypothesis metadata, preflight checks, telemetry queries, rollout recipes, safety gates, and postmortem templates.

Purpose and scope:

- Purpose: Reduce risk and increase reproducibility for targeted runtime experiments that affect inference economics or latency/fidelity SLOs.
- Scope: Applies to runtime-level experiments owned by eng-serving-runtime, runtime operator interventions by SRE, and paired kernel or scheduler changes authored by kernel-and-scheduling. Not for large-scale model swaps or infra-wide capacity topology changes (those use the Runtime Change RFC process).

Definitions and conventions:

- Hypothesis ID: HYP-YYYYMMDD-N (e.g., HYP-20260201-3).
- Target service(s): runtime-service names as used in our service map (examples: runtime-gateway, runtime-scheduler, kvcache-proxy, kernel-dispatcher).
- Metric windows: we use 5m/1h/24h windows in telemetry queries; specify explicitly.

Hypothesis schema (required fields):

1) id: HYP-...
2) title: short descriptive name
3) owner: primary engineer (email handle)
4) stakeholders: teams impacted (eng-sre, infra, product-ml)
5) background: what observability signal motivated this hypothesis (include link to trace/sample)
6) proposed change: code/config diff references (git commit or config id) and high-level description
7) target_services: list of service names and namespaces
8) expected_outcome: quantitative claim (e.g., reduce p95 latency by 12% at 2k RPS; increase KV cache hit rate from 68% -> 78%)
9) scope: canary percentage, user cohorts, regions
10) duration: planned experiment runtime and measurement windows
11) acceptance_criteria: exact gates (see Safety & Acceptance table below)
12) rollback_criteria: thresholds to trigger immediate rollback
13) observability_queries: list of Prometheus/trace queries used to validate
14) preflight_checks: runbook checklist and SLO impacts
15) approvals: list of approvers and sign-off timestamps
16) artifacts: links to PR, deploy manifest, dashboards, and postmortem template

Experiment lifecycle (step-by-step):

1) Draft hypothesis and attach code PR + telemetry queries. Add to this ledger and notify reviewers.
2) Preflight: run the preflight checklist (below) in staging and obtain approvals.
3) Canary deploy: route 1–5% traffic for 30–60 minutes. Capture full traces and kernel-level histograms.
4) Monitor: automated monitors run checks at 1m cadence; on-call notified if thresholds exceeded.
5) Ramp: if canary is green, increase to 10–30% for 2–4 hours, then to 100% if sustained.
6) Evaluate: run statistical test (see Evaluation method) against control for primary metrics.
7) Decide: Accept, roll forward to prod, or rollback. Document results and close ledger entry with postmortem.

Safety & Acceptance table (copy into PR description):

| Risk vector | Primary metric | Preflight threshold | Canary threshold | Rollback trigger | Owner |
|-------------|----------------|---------------------|------------------|------------------|-------|
| Latency | p95 runtime-gateway (ms) | baseline ± 5% | not worse than baseline + 8% | p95 > baseline + 15% for 5m | eng-sre |
| Error surface | 5xx rate (per minute) | < 0.02% | < 0.05% | > 0.1% sustained 2m | runtime-ops |
| Cost | per-token GPU utilization (%) | n/a | no >10% increase in GC or slots | >20% and forecasted monthly cost delta > 5% | infra |
| Quality | model-output divergence (eval set) | N/A | divergence < configured delta | divergence > configured delta on 50+ samples | product-ml |

Note: thresholds are conservative defaults. The hypothesis owner must explicitly justify any looser gates and obtain signoff from the owners in the Owner column.

Preflight checklist (run before any canary):

- [ ] PR linked and small (single change ideally) with unit tests and CI green.
- [ ] Impacted services identified and owners notified.
- [ ] Replay corpus available that reproduces the observed signal (trace id or synthetic load).
- [ ] Baseline metrics captured for last 72 hours for p50/p95/p99, error rate, queue-length, and KV cache hit rate.
- [ ] Backstop rollout plan documented (how to disable change) and validated on a staging node.
- [ ] Canary dashboards created and templated alerts configured (copy alert rules from this ledger).

Key observability signals to capture (minimum):

- p50/p95/p99 latency per route (runtime-gateway)
- per-kernel execution latency histogram (kernel-dispatcher.kernel.latency_seconds_bucket)
- GPU occupancy and GPU memory headroom (gpu/occupancy, gpu/mem_free_bytes)
- KV cache hit ratio (kvcache.hits / kvcache.requests) and tail latency for cache misses
- Length of the request queue and backlog (runtime-scheduler.queue_length)
- Inference tokens per second and per-request token distribution
- Trace samples showing kernel selection path and dispatch decisions

Automated Prometheus examples (copy-paste):

- p95 runtime gateway (5m window):
  quantile_over_time(0.95, rate(runtime_gateway_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))

- kernel latency histogram (per kernel id):
  sum by (kernel_id) (rate(kernel_dispatch_latency_seconds_bucket[5m]))

- kvcache hit rate (1h):
  (increase(kvcache_hits_total[1h]) / increase(kvcache_requests_total[1h])) * 100

- GPU occupancy spike detector (5m):
  max_over_time(gpu_occupancy_percent[5m]) > 85

Example CLI roll-forward and rollback (internal tooling):

- Create a canary allocation: rwdctl runtime canary create --service runtime-gateway --config git://repo/commit --percent 3 --note "HYP-20260201-3 canary"
- Promote canary: rwdctl runtime canary promote --id canary-123 --to 30
- Abort and rollback: rwdctl runtime canary abort --id canary-123 --reason "p95 regression exceeded threshold"

Evaluation method (statistical):

- Use two-sample bootstrap on aligned request corpus for p95 and mean token cost; require p < 0.05 and effect size > configured min (default 5% for p95).
- Run A/A check prior to A/B to validate sampling system.
- When traffic variability is high, prefer shadowing with mirrored traffic for fidelity checks.

Example ledger entry (text table):

ID: HYP-20260201-3
Title: Adaptive kernel hinting for prefix-heavy workloads
Owner: aisha.patel@redwood.ai
Stakeholders: eng-serving-runtime, eng-sre, applied-ml-and-evals
Background: Observability: 2026-01-29 trace cluster showed repeated kernel cold-path latencies when requests contained long system prompts; KV cache miss tail correlated with specific attention kernel selection. Trace: trace://txn/abcd1234
Proposed change: Add an opt-in kernel hint path that biases dispatch towards low-overhead-gemm for sequences < 512 and switches to high-fidelity kernel only if token entropy > threshold. PR: https://git.redwood/eng/runtime/+/789
Target: runtime-scheduler, kernel-dispatcher (namespace=prod-us-east)
Expected outcome: reduce kernel p95 by 10% for prefix length distribution 256–1024, maintain divergence < 0.5% on eval suite
Scope: Canary 3% for 60m, ramp to 25% for 3h if green
Acceptance criteria: see Safety & Acceptance table above
Rollback criteria: p95 regression > baseline + 15% OR 5xx rate > 0.1% sustained 2m
Artifacts: dashboard: /dashboards/hyp-HYP-20260201-3, PR link, replay corpus id: replay/20260201/23

Post-experiment template (to fill after experiment):

- Duration run: start/end timestamps
- Traffic profile: RPS, percent canary, sample entropy distribution
- Observed delta: p50/p95/p99, error-rate, cost delta, kvcache hit delta
- Statistical verdict: pass/fail and p-value for primary metrics
- Lessons learned and recommended followups

Approval and decision matrix:

- Owners listed on the ledger must be notified via #runtime-experiments channel at time of canary start.
- Required approvers before canary: runtime-ops lead, eng-sre oncall, and one applied-ml reviewer if model fidelity is affected.

Conservation of telemetry costs and sampling guidance:

- Prefer stratified sampling: full traces at 3% of requests and aggregated histograms for all requests.
- For long-running experiments, switch to 1m histogram granularity with retained full-trace windows of 15 minutes following alerts.

Appendix A: sample YAML manifest (paste into PR description):

---
# HYP-20260201-3 manifest
hypothesis_id: HYP-20260201-3
owner: aisha.patel@redwood.ai
target_services:
  - runtime-scheduler
  - kernel-dispatcher
canary:
  percent: 3
  duration: 60m
  rollback_criteria:
    p95_regression_percent: 15
    error_rate_threshold: 0.001
observability_queries:
  - "quantile_over_time(0.95, rate(runtime_gateway_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))"
  - "(increase(kvcache_hits_total[1h]) / increase(kvcache_requests_total[1h])) * 100"
---

Appendix B: Ownership contact list (example):

- eng-serving-runtime owner: eng-runtime-lead@redwood.ai (Marco Rinaldi)
- eng-sre oncall: eng-sre-oncall@redwood.ai
- applied-ml reviewer: applied-ml@redwood.ai (Chen Li)

Operational notes and FAQs:

Q: What if canary causes transient kernel noise but metrics return to baseline within 10 minutes?
A: If noise is transient and below rollback thresholds and owner documents rationale, continue monitoring but do not auto-promote. Capture full trace set for later investigation.

Q: Who can override a rollback trigger in emergency?
A: Only the runtime-ops incident commander (IC) with explicit approval from the eng-sre lead; override must be recorded on the ledger entry and later reviewed in postmortem.

Q: How to reference this ledger from a PR?
A: Add a link to this page and include the Hypothesis ID in the PR title and changelog (e.g., "HYP-20260201-3: adaptive-kernel-hinting").

Closeout: Every closed hypothesis must include the artifacts listed above and a one-paragraph summary suitable for the release notes. Major surprises or repeated safety gate trips require a cross-team review and a separate incident review.

Document maintenance: This ledger is maintained by eng-serving-runtime. Additions to thresholds, required telemetry, or approval paths must be proposed via an ADR and reviewed by eng-sre and applied-ml leads.

title: Deterministic Replay & Operator Safety Manifest
content:
Overview:

This document defines a deterministic replay pipeline and the operator safety contract used to validate kernel/operator changes before and during runtime rollouts. The goal is to enable repeatable repros for latency/correctness regressions, reduce time-to-diagnosis for oncall, and provide a standardized canary + rollback procedure for experimental kernels and scheduler policies.

Scope:
- Deterministic capture and replay for text-generation and chat request surfaces (hosted + dedicated pools).
- Canary orchestration for kernel/operator binary changes and scheduler policy updates.
- Safety checks and telemetry contract required for any kernel-level change deployed to production.

Non-goals:
- Full deterministic replay of external tool/plugin side-effects (these are captured best-effort).
- Replaying privacy-sensitive payloads outside of secure reproducer environments.

Design summary:
1) Capture: lightweight per-request snapshot containing request proto, sequence tokens (first N tokens), model variant, session KV hints, scheduler decisions, and kernel hints. Captures are sampled at adjustable rates (default 0.1%). All captures are salted and stored in an encrypted replay store with access controls.

2) Canonicalization: a reproducible normalization step strips reorder-insignificant metadata (timestamps, trace ids) and pins kernel-versioned artifacts so that the replay input deterministically maps to kernel behavior.

3) Replay harness: an isolated, deterministic executor that replays a captured request on a pinned model binary with seeded RNG, fixed batch shapes, and a frozen scheduler policy. Replays run in a shadow environment that mirrors runtime kernel flags used in production.

4) Diffing & Triage: replay output (token stream + timings + kernel trace) is diffed against the original recorded output. Differences are classified with signatures (content-drift, timing-regression, soft-failure, hard-failure).

Deterministic capture schema (summary table):
| field | description | retention |
|---|---|---|
| capture_id | UUID for replay artifact | 90d |
| trace_version | schema version | 90d |
| request_proto | sanitized request payload (PII removed) | 90d |
| seed_state | RNG/initial-state for model runtime | 90d |
| kernel_hints | kernel invocation metadata (flags/kernels used) | 90d |
| scheduler_decision | assigned slot, priority bucket | 90d |
| sample_metrics | timing, memory usage summary | 90d |

Operator safety checklist (required before any kernel/operator rollout):
- Preconditions:
  - Unittest suite coverage for changed operator >= 95% of modified code paths.
  - Microbenchmarks for tight loops created and committed to perf-suite.
  - Static analysis & ASAN/TSAN pass for proposed patch.
- Canary plan:
  - Canary cohort definition (tenant list or synthetic traffic) 
  - Canary duration: minimum 72 hours real traffic + 24 hours synthetic stress.
  - Acceptance thresholds defined (see SLOs table below).
- Observability & Telemetry:
  - Kernel must emit the agreed telemetry keys (kernel.execution_time_ms, kernel.exec_count, kernel.error_code, kernel.fidelity_tag).
  - Trace sampling rate for capture increased to 1% for canary window.
  - Alert hooks configured for anomaly conditions (automated rollback triggers).
- Rollback strategy:
  - Immediate circuit-breaker if any hard-failure signature observed in >0.01% of canary requests.
  - Staged rollback (canary -> cohort -> global) via policy manager.

Canary runbook (step-by-step):
1. Prepare artifacts:
  1.1 Build kernel binary with embedded build-id and deterministic metadata.
  1.2 Publish to artifact-repo with tag: canary/<ticket>-<date>.
  1.3 Create canary deployment in test cluster with replica_count=2, isolate networking.
2. Pre-flight checks (automated):
  2.1 Run unit & microbench pipelines (must pass).
  2.2 Run golden replays for 50 representative captures (zero content deviation allowed).
3. Start canary (rolling):
  3.1 Route 0.5% production traffic to canary cohort and enable replay capture at 1% sampling.
  3.2 Monitor KPIs for the first 30 minutes: tail-99 latency, kernel.exec_time_ms p99, error_count.
4. Escalation and rollback policies:
  4.1 If any of the automated checks trigger (see thresholds) perform immediate rollback and mark change blocked.
  4.2 If degraded but within tolerance, expand to cohort-controlled ramp and continue data collection.

Telemetry contract (required metrics and labels):
| metric name | type | labels | description | alert threshold |
|---|---:|---|---|---:|
| kernel.execution_time_ms | gauge | kernel_version, model, hardware | per-invocation kernel time | p99 increase > 25% |
| kernel.exec_count | counter | kernel_version, model | invocations | sudden drop > 50% |
| kernel.error_code | counter | kernel_version, code | nonzero return codes | >= 1/10k hard-errors |
| kernel.memory_bytes | gauge | kernel_version, node | memory footprint | sustained increase > 20% |

Sample config snippet (replay harness) - YAML:
---
replay: 
  executor_image: "gcr.io/redwood/replay-executor:stable"
  seed: 0x9f1b2c
  isolate_network: true
  kernel_pin: "kernel-v2.11.3-canary"
  batch_shape_override: [1, 512]
  capture_store: "s3://replay-store/canaries/"
---

CLI examples:
- Trigger a golden replay set (50 captures):
  rwd-replay run --captures-file /tmp/golden50.list --executor-image gcr.io/redwood/replay-executor:stable --out /tmp/replays/
- Compare replay outputs:
  rwd-replay diff --baseline /tmp/originals --candidate /tmp/replays --report /tmp/replay-report.json

Diff classification and automated actions:
- content-drift: textual output mismatches (normalized). Action: manual triage and stop rollout if drift signature not explainable.
- timing-regression: p99 kernel.execution_time_ms increased >25% and coincident tail latency spike. Action: pause rollout; trigger performance bisect.
- soft-failure: minor error codes flagged (retries succeeded). Action: continue with expanded synthetic stress and re-evaluate in 24 hours.
- hard-failure: abort/segfault/incorrect logits. Action: immediate rollback and bug-bisect.

SLOs & thresholds (canary acceptance):
- No hard-failures: 100% for golden set.
- Content parity: >= 99.995% token-level match for golden set.
- Latency: p99 kernel.exec_time_ms increase <= 15% vs baseline.
- Memory: sustained memory increase <= 10% for 1h window.

Ownership & escalation:
- Kernel owner: @marcos-rivera (eng-serving-runtime/kernel-team) — primary oncall during rollout.
- Observability owner: @lena-huang (eng-platform/telemetry) — owns alerts and dashboard updates.
- Escalation path: kernel owner -> runtime lead -> SRE director.

Operational caveats and privacy:
- Captured requests are sanitized; any capture that contains suspected PII must be flagged and subject to restricted storage and manual review.
- Replay artifacts used for debugging outside central replay cluster must be provisioned into a short-lived isolated environment (TTL <= 7d).

Appendix: Example investigation flow (short):
1) Oncall observes p99 spike and kernel.exec_time_ms p99 delta +32%.
2) Increase replay sampling to 5% for affected pool and trigger rwd-replay run against last 1h captures.
3) Golden replays show timing-regression signature for 3 specific captures.
4) Run microbenchmark for changed operator; bisect to identify commit that introduced divergence.
5) Rollback to previous kernel tag and validate stability.

References and related artifacts:
- Perf-suite: /internal/benchmarks/kernel-microbenchmarks
- Replay tooling repo: git@github.com:redwood/replay-harness.git
- Canary dashboard: /dashboards/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-canary-summary

Contact: Priya Shah (author) — priya@redwood.ai

title: Orchestration, Fidelity Fences, and Safety Contracts for Kernel Rollouts
content:
Overview

Purpose: This document defines the operational contracts, safety fences, and validation procedures used when rolling out new kernel codepaths, scheduler policies, or execution-time optimizations into the Redwood serving runtime. It focuses on preserving customer-facing SLOs, preventing fidelity regressions, and enabling deterministic rollback.

Scope: kernel patches, scheduling policy updates, kernel selection heuristics, quantization-aware execution paths, and any runtime change that alters the token emission path. Not in scope: model weights, client SDK changes, or unrelated infra (network/storage) updates.

Audience: runtime engineers, SREs, release engineers, and applied ML owners who approve model-serving risk.

Key Concepts and Definitions

- Fidelity fence: a runtime-enforced boundary that keeps inference outputs within an acceptable quality envelope during transient kernel transitions (e.g., preserving top-k behavior, temperature semantics, or deterministic sampling seeds).
- Kernel handshake: a short protocol (telemetry + state exchange) between scheduler and GPU dispatcher to confirm compatibility and resource accounting before activation.
- Stitching window: the safe timeframe after a kernel switch where additional telemetry is collected (higher sampling rate) and aggressive fallbacks are enabled.
- Contract version: semantic version tag for kernel behaviour guarantees (e.g., v1.2.0-contract-A) used in rollouts and tracing.

Operational Contracts (must be satisfied before rollout)

1) Observability contract
   - All kernel releases must emit the following telemetry keys at INFO level: kernel.contract_version, kernel.handshake_latency_ms, kernel.activation_slot_id, kernel.fidelity_score_delta, kernel.fallback_trigger.
   - Traces must include a correlation id (request.trace_id) and kernel.contract_version for every request that touches the new codepath.

2) SLO preservation contract
   - For any target model route, new kernels must demonstrate no more than +5% p99 latency and no more than +3% failure rate in canary traffic vs baseline.
   - Fidelity regressions must be bounded: automated eval harness score delta <= configured threshold for that model route (see per-route fidelity thresholds).

3) Rollback determinism contract
   - A rollback path that restores previous contract_version must preserve kvcache consistency or declare a cache flush procedure. Rollbacks must complete within the configured rollback_timeout (default 90s).

4) Resource accounting contract
   - Kernel handshake must expose the kernel.resource_profile annotated with memory_peak_bytes, scratch_gpu_bytes, and compute_wave_estimate. Admission controller uses these to avoid overcommit.

Validation and Canary Procedure (step-by-step)

1) Preflight (local lab)
   - Run unit + microbench: ./tooling/kernel-bench --kernel candidate.so --sequence-lengths 32,256 --concurrency 1,8
   - Produce deterministic trace for a small corpus (use: test-corpus/fidelity-critical.jsonl).

2) Canary experiment (staging cluster)
   - Stage: deploy with kernel.contract_version set to candidate tag and the following release flags: --canary-weight=5 --stitching-window=300s --telemetry-sampling=100
   - Monitor: p50/p95/p99 latency, 5xx rates, kernel.fidelity_score_delta, user-visible metric (per-route BLEU/ROUGE/embedding-cosine).

3) Automated gating
   - If any of these triggers fire, the system will auto-fail the canary and initiate rollback:
     a) p99 latency increase > 5% for 10 consecutive minutes
     b) request failure-rate delta > 3% vs baseline for 5 minutes
     c) fidelity_score_delta > per-route-threshold for 1 minute
     d) kernel.handshake_latency_ms > 1s for any activation

4) Gradual ramp
   - Ramp weights: 5% -> 20% -> 50% -> 100% with a minimum observation window of 15 minutes and metric stability check after each step.

Validation Checklist (table)

| Item | Requirement | Owner | Pass criteria |
|------|-------------|-------|---------------|
| Unit tests | Kernel unit-suite + scheduler compat tests | Author | All green on CI |
| Perf microbench | Throughput & latency baseline | Perf owner | p99 <= +5% |
| Fidelity eval | Eval harness run vs golden prompts | ML owner | score delta <= threshold |
| Handshake telemetry | Contract fields present | Runtime SRE | Verified in traces |
| Chaos dry-run | Simulated GPU eviction and kernel fallback | SRE | Recovery within rollback_timeout |

(When rendered in Confluence, the above table should be a proper table. The stored JSON keeps ASCII table for searchability.)

Safeguards and Automation

- Safety tripwires: Per-cluster admission controller rejects activation of candidate kernels if aggregate memory_reservation + candidate.resource_profile.memory_peak_bytes > 0.95 * cluster_memory_budget.
- Circuit breaker: If fallback_trigger fires more than 3 times in 1 minute across a shard group, that kernel version gets blacklisted for that shard group and remains in canary with 0% weight until manually approved.
- Automatic KVCACHE reconciliation: When a rollback is initiated, a controlled cache drain occurs for affected sessions with the following CLI: 

  # drain keys gracefully for a model route
  redwoodctl cache drain --route product-recommendations --timeout 60s --mode graceful

Benchmarking and Profiling Integration

- Kernel microbench harness example (YAML):

  benchmarks:
    - name: small-context-latency
      seq_len: 32
      batch_shapes: [[1],[4]]
      concurrency: 1
    - name: long-context-throughput
      seq_len: 1024
      batch_shapes: [[1,16],[2,8]]
      concurrency: 8

  validation:
    fidelity_corpus: test-corpus/fidelity-critical.jsonl
    baseline_trace: traces/baseline-v1.1.jsonl

- Example command to run an annotated profile and push to observability: 

  ./tooling/kernel-bench --config=bench/kernel-ci.yaml --profile=perftrace --push-to=kusto --tag=candidate-2026-01

- Profiling guidance: prioritize wandb-style sample IDs correlating kernel.handshake events with GPU SM counters. Collect top-down breakdown: scheduler_queue_ms, kernel_launch_ms, kernel_exec_ms, memcpy_ms.

Runbook: Kernel-induced Latency Surge (operational playbook)

1) Detection
   - Alert: runtime.kernel.p99_delta > +5% AND rate(5xx) increased

2) Immediate actions (0-2 minutes)
   - Identify recent kernel.contract_version activations via trace query:

     query: traces | where kernel.contract_version != "stable" | summarize count() by kernel.contract_version, shard_group

   - If suspect contract_version found, execute controlled canary rollback: redwoodctl rollout rollback --contract <tag> --scope cluster:canary

3) Short-term remediation (2-15 minutes)
   - Engage perf on-call; increase telemetry sampling to 100% for affected routes: redwoodctl telemetry set-sampling --route <route> --rate 100
   - Run targeted microbench on the staging copy of the shard (see Benchmarking section).

4) Post-incident (15+ minutes)
   - Produce timeline: include handshake_latency_ms, fallback_trigger counts, stitch-window duration, and kvcache-miss rates.
   - Decide: revert and iterate, or patch and re-canary.

Chaos and Validation Experiments (recommended patterns)

- Eviction storm: simulate 10% random GPU evictions during canary to verify fallback correctness. Expected behaviour: fallback_trigger increased briefly; p99 remains < +8% and rollback_timeout not exceeded.
- Kernel handshake timeouts: inject artificial 2s latency to kernel.handshake and verify admission controller blocks new activations.
- Cross-tenant pressure: run a mixed workload where priority-synthetic traffic competes for memory; ensure tenant-aware resource_profile admission rejects candidate if headroom < 5%.

Metrics and Dashboards to Monitor

- runtime.kernel.contract_version (tag)
- kernel.handshake_latency_ms (histogram)
- kernel.fidelity_score_delta (gauge, per-route)
- kernel.fallback_trigger (counter)
- request.latency.{p50,p95,p99} (by route and contract_version)
- kvcache.hit_rate (per-session)

Example Dashboard Widgets

1) Rollout summary: heatmap of p99 delta by contract_version and route.
2) Handshake latency histogram with alarm band at 1s.
3) Fidelity scatter: fidelity_score_delta vs latency delta per sample (helps detect tradeoffs).

Ownership, Approvals, and Release Notes Requirements

- Owners: kernel author (code), runtime SRE (rollout), applied ML owner (fidelity thresholds).
- Approvals required: code review, perf sign-off, ML sign-off (if route is customer-facing), security scan clearance.
- Release note template (short):

  - Title: kernel update <contract_version>
  - Summary: short description of optimization and intended effect
  - Risk: list of routes impacted and fidelity gates
  - Rollout plan: canary weights and ramp windows
  - Contact: primary author + on-call SRE

Appendix: Useful queries and commands

- Trace query: traces | where kernel.contract_version == "candidate-2026-01" | summarize count() by outcome_code
- blacklisting a kernel for a shard group: redwoodctl kernel blacklist --contract candidate-2026-01 --shard-group shard-17 --reason "fallback-rate-high"
- run local synthetic evaluation: ./tooling/eval-harness --model-route product-recommendations --input test-corpus/fidelity-critical.jsonl --compare traces/baseline-v1.1.jsonl

Revision history

- 2025-02-03 (Sophie Chen) - initial draft
- 2025-06-18 (Diego Alvarez) - added handshake resource_profile schema and admission checks
- 2026-01-20 (Sophie Chen) - tightened canary gating thresholds, added chaos scenarios

title: Granular eviction and adaptive execution patterns for mixed inference workloads
content:
Summary

This document describes the design, operational controls, and runbook for the Granular Eviction and Adaptive Execution Patterns (GEAEP) subsystem in the Redwood serving runtime. GEAEP is a set of runtime techniques that: (1) reduce unnecessary KV-cache evictions, (2) enable per-request execution path selection (fast path vs. accuracy path), and (3) smooth contention across heterogeneous kernel families in the GPU pool. The guidance here is intended for runtime engineers, SREs handling inference incidents, and product teams evaluating cost/latency tradeoffs.

Why this doc exists

- Prior problems addressed: eviction storms during traffic spikes, oscillation between quantized and full-precision kernels, and sudden tail-latency increases for mixed short/long sequences.
- Goals: lower tail latency for short-prefix requests, reduce unnecessary recompute, expose safe knobs for cost-vs-accuracy routing, and provide clear operational steps for triage and rollback.

Design principles

1) Local, demand-driven granularity: evictions and prefetches are controlled per-shard and per-session rather than globally. This avoids thrashing when a single tenant (or bursty bot) requests long sequences.
2) Execution adaptivity: requests carry an execution-hint header that lets the scheduler choose a lightweight kernel (quantized, truncated context, prefix-cached) or the accuracy path (full-precision, full-KV materialization). Default policy is conservative (favor accuracy) unless overridden by explicit cost profile or model-variant rules.
3) Cost-safety guards: automated budget limits and soft-fallbacks prevent runaway cost when adaptivity picks expensive paths.

Key concepts and terminology

- shard-eviction-window: configurable time window used to compute per-shard eviction score.
- per-request execution-hint: request metadata field (execution_hint) with values: fast_path | balanced | accuracy_path.
- eviction-stabilizer: smoothing function that delays eviction decisions when churn is detected.
- kernel-ladder: ordered family of kernels (e.g. q4_8_fast, q8_0_balanced, fp16_full) that the dispatcher may move through for a request.

Configuration reference (example YAML)

runtime_geaep:
  enabled: true
  shard_eviction_window_sec: 60
  eviction_score_threshold: 0.12
  eviction_stabilizer_alpha: 0.6
  execution_hint_defaults:
    short_prefix: fast_path
    long_prefix: balanced
  kernel_ladder:
    - q4_8_fast
    - q8_0_balanced
    - fp16_full
  cost_safety_budget_tokens_per_min: 20000
  per_tenant_hard_cap_tokens_per_min: 100000

Explanation of important keys

- eviction_score_threshold: a normalized value [0,1]; shards with score > threshold become candidates for eviction. We tune this to balance memory pressure against recompute cost.
- eviction_stabilizer_alpha: smoothing parameter for exponential moving average used by the stabilizer. Higher = more inertia.
- cost_safety_budget_tokens_per_min: safety budget applied to adaptivity decisions; once exhausted, adaptivity falls back to balanced or fast_path depending on flags.

Observability and metrics

Instrument the following metrics (already emitted by ri-runtime v3.8+):
- runtime.geaep.eviction_rate.per_shard (gauge, evictions/min)
- runtime.geaep.eviction_candidates (gauge)
- runtime.geaep.prefetch_hits (counter)
- runtime.geaep.execution_path.count{path=fast_path|balanced|accuracy_path} (counter)
- runtime.geaep.kernel_switches.count (counter)
- runtime.kvcache.recompute.tokens_cost (counter)
- runtime.geaep.adaptivity_budget_remaining (gauge)

Alerting thresholds (suggested)

- P0: runtime.geaep.eviction_rate.per_shard > 0.5 for more than 2 minutes AND 99th_latency.service > 800ms for a modeled short-prefix route -> Pager.
- P1: runtime.geaep.adaptivity_budget_remaining < 10% for 5 minutes -> Page to oncall if impacting cost or SLOs.
- P2: kernel_switches.count rate increases > 5x baseline over 10 minutes with increased tail latencies -> Slack alert to #serving-runtime.

Operational runbook: common incidents

1) Eviction storm (symptoms: sudden spikes in eviction_rate and 99p latency for short requests)

- Owner: serving-runtime oncall.
- Immediate checks:
  1. rictl metrics get runtime.geaep.eviction_rate.per_shard --since 15m --top 5
  2. rictl trace find --tag="eviction" --since 10m | head -n 50
  3. Check per-tenant traffic with rictl tenant stats --top 10

- Mitigation steps (fast):
  A. Enable eviction-stabilizer in read-only override: rictl config set runtime_geaep.eviction_stabilizer_override=true --duration=15m
  B. Lower eviction aggressiveness: rictl config set runtime_geaep.eviction_score_threshold=0.20
  C. If issue persists, pin affected shard(s) to no-evict: rictl shard annotate <shard_id> no-evict=true --reason="eviction_storm_mitigate"

- Recovery check: after changes, monitor eviction_rate and short-prefix 99p latency for 10 minutes. If rates drop and latency stabilizes, keep stabilizer enabled and schedule a retrospective.

2) Kernel oscillation (symptoms: frequent kernel_switches, rising GPU queue length, throughput drop)

- Owner: serving-runtime + kernel-team.
- Immediate checks:
  1. runtime.geaep.kernel_switches.count --since 30m by kernel_family
  2. GPU dispatcher queue lengths and occupancy: grafana:GPU/dispatcher/queue_length
  3. Last deploys: ci-cd job checks to see if a kernel rollout coincided with the start time.

- Mitigation steps:
  A. Limit kernel ladder to two levels for the most-affected tenants: rictl config set runtime_geaep.kernel_ladder_override.<tenant_id>='["q8_0_balanced","fp16_full"]' --duration=1h
  B. Throttle adaptivity scoring for the tenant: rictl config set runtime_geaep.adaptivity_alpha_override.<tenant_id>=0.2
  C. If the oscillation started after a kernel rollout, rollback the kernel plugin: rictl kernel rollback <kernel_plugin_name> --to-version <previous-version>

- Recovery check: kernel_switches should fall to baseline and GPU queue length return to normal within 15–30 minutes.

3) Budget exhaustion (symptoms: adaptivity_budget_remaining hits 0 and many requests fall back unexpectedly)

- Owner: serving-runtime + product cost ops.
- Immediate checks:
  1. runtime.geaep.adaptivity_budget_remaining and per-tenant consumption.
  2. Which routes consumed most tokens: rictl profiling route-consumption --since 1h --top 20

- Mitigation steps:
  A. Temporarily increase cost_safety_budget_tokens_per_min for the affected region: rictl config set runtime_geaep.cost_safety_budget_tokens_per_min=30000 --region=us-west-2
  B. If spending spike is unexpected, identify and throttle offending route(s) via per-route quotas in the control plane.

Design validation and benchmarking notes

We validated GEAEP on the mixed-workload simulator (see benchmarking suite 'mixed_short_long_2026') with these noteworthy outcomes:
- Short-prefix 99p latency decreased 18–26% when using per-request execution_hint defaulting to fast_path for sequences < 64 tokens.
- Overall token cost increased 4–6% in the balanced test; but with cost-safety budgets enabled, the increase was bounded to under 6%.
- Under synthetic eviction storms, the stabilizer reduced shard-level evictions by 70% at peak.

Configuration rollout checklist

1. Feature flag: geaep.v1 enabled in staging only.
2. Canary: two nodes in us-west-2 with production traffic shadowed (no adaptivity writes). Run for 48 hours.
3. Gradual ramp: 5% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100% over 7 days, with SLO gate: short-prefix 99p < 350ms and adaptivity budget utilization < 80%.
4. Post-rollout: schedule 2-week observation period and capture baseline metrics for the next kernel rollout.

Testing and validation tools

- rictl simulate --profile=mixed_short_long --seed=42 --duration=2h --out=./geaep-sim-2027-02
- runtime-bench run --scenario geaep-adaptivity-compare --concurrency 128 --seq-dist short:0.7,long:0.3
- scripts/validate_eviction_stability.py (documentation in repo/runtime/tools/validation.md)

Implementation notes for engineers

- Execution-hint is exposed as an HTTP header X-RI-Execution-Hint and as SDK metadata field execution_hint on the Python/Node SDKs. SDKs will default to balanced when model length is unknown.
- Kernel ladder decisions are made in two stages: (a) soft decision (dispatcher hint) and (b) hard enforcement (kernel plugin selection) at kernel-launch. Both emits traces: trace.tag=">geaep:soft_decision" and ">geaep:kernel_launch".
- Prefetch logic uses a low-priority background queue and will not prefetch across tenant hard-cap boundaries.

Ownership and review cadence

- Author/Primary owner: Aisha Patel (serving-runtime).
- Secondary owner: Jonah Kim (kernel infra).
- Quarterly review: every release cycle (quarterly) the GEAEP config defaults must be reviewed as part of runtime release checklist.

Related artifacts and links

- Simulation results: s3://redwood-inference/benchmarks/geaep/mixed_short_long/2027-02-01/results.csv
- Tooling: repo/runtime/tools/geaep (contains validators and scrubbers)
- Telemetry dashboard: grafana://dashboards/GEAEP-Overview

Appendix: quick commands

- View top eviction shards: rictl metrics get runtime.geaep.eviction_rate.per_shard --since 30m --top 10
- Temporarily pin shard to no-evict: rictl shard annotate <shard_id> no-evict=true --duration=30m --reason "triage"
- Adjust threshold: rictl config set runtime_geaep.eviction_score_threshold=0.20 --duration=10m
- Force a kernel ladder override for a tenant: rictl config set runtime_geaep.kernel_ladder_override.<tenant_id>='["q8_0_balanced","fp16_full"]' --duration=1h

If you are a product or solutions engineer reading this and want guidance for choosing the default execution_hint for a customer workload, open a PR on repo/runtime/configs/geaep-defaults.yaml and tag @PriyaSingh for review.

ChangeLog

- 2026-11-15: Initial draft by Aisha Patel.
- 2026-12-07: Added budget and alert recommendations after first staging run (reviewers: Jonah Kim).
- 2027-02-03: Clarified kernel ladder enforcement and added rollout checklist (published).

title: ADR-0147: Prefix + KV Cache Hit-Rate Definitions, Partial-Hit Semantics, and Attribution
content:
## Summary
This ADR defines the canonical semantics for **prefix/KV cache hit-rate** in the Redwood serving runtime, including:
- What counts as a **hit** vs **miss** (token-level and request-level)
- How to represent **partial hits** (reuse depth)
- How hit/miss is attributed across **multi-turn chat**, **streaming**, and **retries**

The goal is to make cache telemetry consistent across runtime, ingestion, dashboards, and the recommendations pipeline, while remaining privacy-safe and avoiding cardinality blowups.

---

## Status
**Accepted** (effective for cache telemetry v2 rollout).

---

## Context and problem statement
Historically, teams used “cache hit-rate” to mean different things:
- “Was there a cache entry?” (lookup-level)
- “How much of the prompt was reused?” (token-level)
- “Did we avoid most prefill?” (latency/compute-level)

These diverging definitions produced inconsistent dashboards and false positives during incident response (e.g., streaming retry double-counting, batched prefill mis-attribution, and model version mismatch being treated as generic misses).

We need a definition that:
1) Reflects **actual compute avoided** (prefill reuse),
2) Works for chat where prompts grow each turn (partial reuse is normal),
3) Remains stable under streaming/retries and continuous batching,
4) Can be aggregated safely by model/route/region/deployment mode.

---

## Decision
### Decision 1: “Hit-rate” is defined as token-weighted reuse of cacheable prefill tokens
The primary hit-rate is **token-weighted**, computed over a window:

**HitRate = sum(reused_prefill_tokens) / sum(eligible_prefill_tokens)**

Where:
- `eligible_prefill_tokens` are prompt tokens that the runtime would have had to prefill **if no cache reuse occurred**, restricted to the portion of the prompt considered cacheable (see Definitions).
- `reused_prefill_tokens` are prompt tokens whose KV states were reused from cache (prefix cache / KV reuse) instead of recomputed.

This hit-rate is **not** a lookup success rate, and it is **not** a boolean per-request metric. It is designed to answer: *“How much prefill compute did caching avoid?”*

### Decision 2: Partial hits are represented by reuse depth (reused tokens), not a separate “partial hit-rate”
Partial hits are expected for chat and any workload with shared prefixes.
We represent partial hits by reporting `reused_prefill_tokens` (and optionally `reuse_depth_bucket`) so dashboards can show reuse distributions.

### Decision 3: Request-level classifications are derived (full_hit / partial_hit / miss) but are secondary
For triage and recommendations, we also derive request-level outcomes for sampled traces and low-cardinality counters:
- **full_hit**: `reused_prefill_tokens == eligible_prefill_tokens` and `eligible_prefill_tokens > 0`
- **partial_hit**: `0 < reused_prefill_tokens < eligible_prefill_tokens`
- **miss**: `reused_prefill_tokens == 0` and `eligible_prefill_tokens > 0`
- **not_eligible**: `eligible_prefill_tokens == 0` (e.g., caching disabled by policy)

Token-weighted hit-rate remains the source of truth.

### Decision 4: Streaming retries must not double count hit/miss
For streaming retries (client reconnects, gateway retry-on-timeout), the runtime MUST ensure cache hit/miss counters are emitted **once per logical request**, not once per transport attempt.
Implementation guidance is included below.

---

## Definitions and terminology
### Request lifecycle terms
- **prefill**: processing the prompt/context to produce initial KV states.
- **decode**: iterative token generation after prefill.

Caching impacts prefill compute; decode is not part of the cache hit-rate denominator.

### Cache types (as used in telemetry)
- **Prefix cache**: reuse keyed by a stable hash of a canonicalized token prefix, returning a handle to cached KV states.
- **KV cache**: the underlying key/value state used during attention. In practice, “prefix cache hit” results in “KV reuse.”

Telemetry uses the terms “prefix cache” and “KV reuse” to distinguish lookup/entry behavior from reuse depth and compute avoided.

### Token counts
All token counts are expressed in **model tokens** (post-tokenization).

- `prompt_tokens_total`: total tokens in the request prompt/context.
- `prompt_tokens_cacheable`: tokens in the prompt that are eligible for reuse under the active policy.
  - This explicitly excludes non-cacheable segments if/when we introduce them (e.g., policy-based exclusions). If no exclusions exist, this equals `prompt_tokens_total` capped by policy limits.
- `eligible_prefill_tokens`: the number of prompt tokens that would require prefill compute absent cache reuse.
  - In v2, `eligible_prefill_tokens = prompt_tokens_cacheable` when caching is enabled; otherwise 0.
- `reused_prefill_tokens`: number of eligible prefill tokens reused from cache (i.e., KV states loaded/referenced).

### “Cache enabled” vs “eligible”
A request is considered **eligible** for cache hit-rate if:
- cache policy is enabled for the route, and
- the runtime has caching enabled (feature flag), and
- the request uses a model variant that supports caching (all standard decoder-only LLMs; exclusions must be explicit).

If caching is disabled (policy or runtime), we record separate counters but do **not** include these requests in the hit-rate denominator.

---

## Metric semantics (normative)
This ADR defines semantics; naming is governed by the cache metrics naming/cardinality policy.

### Required counters (semantics)
1) `eligible_prefill_tokens_total`
- Increment by `eligible_prefill_tokens` for each logical request.

2) `reused_prefill_tokens_total`
- Increment by `reused_prefill_tokens` for each logical request.

3) `requests_total` (optional but recommended for consistent rates)
- Increment once per logical request.

4) `requests_not_eligible_total`
- Increment once per logical request where `eligible_prefill_tokens == 0`.

### Derived time-series (query-time)
- `hit_rate = sum(reused_prefill_tokens_total) / sum(eligible_prefill_tokens_total)`
- `mean_reuse_depth = sum(reused_prefill_tokens_total) / sum(requests_with_eligibility_total)` where `requests_with_eligibility_total` counts requests with `eligible_prefill_tokens > 0`.

### Request-level outcome counters (optional)
If implemented, these MUST be derived from the token counts above:
- `requests_full_hit_total`
- `requests_partial_hit_total`
- `requests_miss_total`

---

## Partial-hit semantics (examples)
Assume cache enabled and prompt is cacheable.

| Prompt tokens (eligible) | Reused tokens | Outcome | Notes |
|---:|---:|---|---|
| 800 | 800 | full_hit | Entire prompt KV reused (rare outside repeated identical calls). |
| 800 | 600 | partial_hit | Common for chat history reuse; last user turn is new. |
| 800 | 0 | miss | No matching prefix, or valid entry not found (reason recorded separately). |

For dashboards, **token-weighted hit-rate** will reflect the 600/800 reuse even if request-level outcome is “partial_hit.”

---

## Miss reason attribution (normative taxonomy)
When `eligible_prefill_tokens > 0` and `reused_prefill_tokens == 0`, the runtime SHOULD emit a miss reason from a stable low-cardinality enum.

Approved miss reasons:
- `policy_disabled`: route or tenant policy disabled caching (counts as not_eligible in v2; if emitted, must not be included in denominator)
- `capacity`: cache had no available capacity / admission rejected
- `ttl_expired`: matching entry existed but was expired
- `evicted`: entry was evicted prior to use (often correlated with memory pressure)
- `hash_mismatch`: prefix hash mismatch (includes canonicalization differences)
- `version_mismatch`: model version/variant mismatch (includes quantization profile differences)
- `unknown`: reserved for unexpected paths (must be monitored; not a permanent bucket)

Notes:
- `evicted` vs `capacity`: `capacity` is “could not admit/allocate now”; `evicted` is “was present, then removed.”
- If multiple reasons apply, emit the **most actionable** reason in the order: `policy_disabled` > `version_mismatch` > `hash_mismatch` > `ttl_expired` > `evicted` > `capacity` > `unknown`.

---

## Attribution rules (labels/dimensions)
### Primary slicing dimensions (approved)
Hit-rate MUST be attributable by the following low/controlled cardinality labels:
- `deployment_mode`: hosted | dedicated | private
- `region`: cloud region / on-prem site identifier (allowlist)
- `model_family` and/or `model_id` (allowlist)
- `model_version` (bounded; see naming policy for how we bucket/shorten)
- `route_id` (bounded; must use stable route identifiers, not raw URLs)

### Tenant / customer attribution
Tenant-level labels MUST NOT be added to raw metrics by default. Tenant slicing should be done via:
- dedicated/private environment isolation, or
- sampled analytics tables / batch aggregation with strict budgets.

### Request shape attribution
To support “actionable” recommendations without prompt logging, request shape MUST be bucketed:
- `prompt_len_bucket`: fixed bins (see naming/cardinality policy)
- optional: `input_tokens_bucket` if prompt_len is ambiguous in some modalities

No raw prompt hashes, user IDs, or session IDs in metrics.

---

## Multi-turn chat semantics
Each chat turn is treated as a separate logical request with its own token counts.

Rules:
1) `eligible_prefill_tokens` is computed from the **full serialized prompt** sent to the runtime for that turn (after canonicalization / templating as implemented by the product layer).
2) `reused_prefill_tokens` is the length of the **longest reusable prefix** of that serialized prompt for the active model version.
3) Because chat prompts typically grow, **partial hits are the expected steady state**. Dashboards should therefore focus on:
   - token-weighted hit-rate trends
   - reuse depth distributions by prompt_len_bucket

Non-goal:
- We do not attempt to “attribute” reuse back to a prior turn or conversation ID in metrics (cardinality + privacy). Conversation-level analysis belongs in sampled traces or offline analytics with explicit approvals.

---

## Streaming and retries
### Streaming
Streaming does not change cache semantics: reuse is determined at prefill start.

### Retries (normative)
A “logical request” may experience multiple transport attempts (e.g., stream reconnects). To prevent double counting:
- The runtime MUST only increment `eligible_prefill_tokens_total` and `reused_prefill_tokens_total` once per logical request.
- If prefill is re-executed due to retry, that additional compute SHOULD be tracked separately (e.g., via wasted-prefill metrics) but must not inflate hit/miss.

Implementation guidance:
- Use a stable `request_id` (propagated from gateway) and an `attempt` field.
- Emit cache hit-rate counters only when `attempt == 1`.
- If the runtime cannot reliably detect attempt==1, it MUST implement local de-duplication keyed by `request_id` over a bounded time window (in-memory, best-effort).

Rationale:
This ensures hit-rate reflects caching effectiveness, not network instability.

---

## Continuous batching / shared prefill
With continuous batching, prefill work may be scheduled in a way that obscures per-request boundaries.

Normative rule:
- `eligible_prefill_tokens` and `reused_prefill_tokens` are attributed **per request**, regardless of batching.

If a batch-level prefix lookup is performed, reuse depth MUST be computed per request’s prompt, not per batch. Any shared prefill accounting must be reconciled back to per-request increments to avoid:
- over-crediting one request for another’s reuse,
- inflating reuse tokens when multiple requests share a batch.

---

## Edge cases and clarifications
### Model/version scoping
Cache reuse is only valid when:
- `model_id` matches, AND
- `model_version` matches (includes quantization profile / weights revision), AND
- any runtime-internal compatibility keys match (tokenizer revision, prompt template version if applicable).

A mismatch should be recorded as `version_mismatch` (not `miss`).

### “Not eligible” requests
Requests where caching is disabled MUST NOT dilute hit-rate.
We track them separately so recommendations can still surface: “Enable caching on route X” rather than showing low hit-rate.

### Lookup success vs reuse
A prefix cache “lookup hit” with `reused_prefill_tokens == 0` is treated as a miss for hit-rate purposes (because no compute avoided). If lookup-level metrics are emitted, they are separate and must not be conflated with hit-rate.

---

## Consequences
### Positive
- Dashboards become comparable across models/routes and across time.
- Recommendations can safely use token-weighted hit-rate + miss reasons + reuse depth to propose actions (canonicalization, routing locality, TTL, cache bytes).
- SRE can distinguish workload-driven changes (prompt mix shifts) from regressions (miss reason spikes).

### Tradeoffs
- Token-weighted metrics may under-emphasize small prompts; request-level derived metrics should be used alongside hit-rate where needed.
- Conversation-level attribution is intentionally excluded from metrics (privacy + cardinality).

---

## Rollout and validation requirements
Before enabling cache hit-rate v2 metrics broadly:
1) Perf overhead: instrumentation must not regress p95 latency beyond agreed canary thresholds.
2) Correctness tests:
   - repeated identical prompts produce `full_hit` after warmup
   - chat-like prompts produce stable partial-hit reuse depth patterns
   - streaming retry does not change counters for a logical request
   - version mismatch produces `version_mismatch` miss reason
3) Data quality checks:
   - denominators are non-zero only for eligible traffic
   - no unexpected spike in `unknown` miss reason

---

## Appendix: Reference computation (pseudo-code)
Inputs per logical request:
- `cache_policy_enabled` (bool)
- `runtime_cache_enabled` (bool)
- `prompt_tokens_total` (int)
- `max_cacheable_prompt_tokens` (int, policy/runtime)
- `reuse_prefix_tokens` (int, computed by runtime lookup)

Compute:
1) `prompt_tokens_cacheable = min(prompt_tokens_total, max_cacheable_prompt_tokens)`
2) If not (cache_policy_enabled && runtime_cache_enabled):
   - `eligible_prefill_tokens = 0`
   - `reused_prefill_tokens = 0`
   - increment `requests_not_eligible_total`
   - STOP
3) Else:
   - `eligible_prefill_tokens = prompt_tokens_cacheable`
   - `reused_prefill_tokens = clamp(reuse_prefix_tokens, 0, eligible_prefill_tokens)`
4) Increment counters:
   - `eligible_prefill_tokens_total += eligible_prefill_tokens`
   - `reused_prefill_tokens_total += reused_prefill_tokens`
5) If `eligible_prefill_tokens > 0 && reused_prefill_tokens == 0`: emit miss reason from taxonomy.

---

## Owners
- Runtime semantics and implementation: **Omar El-Sayed** (Runtime)
- Metrics schema + ingestion conformance: **Nadia Rahman** (Telemetry)
- Dashboards/alerts interpretation: **Allison Grant** (Observability/SRE)

Questions or changes to this ADR require review from Runtime + Telemetry + SRE to avoid breaking dashboards and recommendation logic.

title:
Title: Runtime Operations Synthesis and Experiment Manual

Overview

This document codifies a single, operationally-oriented reference that synthesizes runtime architecture intent, kernel-scheduler policy patterns, profiling procedures, benchmark experiment templates, release-note instrumentation requirements, common triage matrices for known issues, and runbook steps for critical runtime incidents. The target audience is SREs, runtime engineers, and applied ML engineers running end-to-end performance experiments and rollouts. This is intentionally cross-cutting: use it when designing experiments that touch serving, scheduling, telemetry, and model rollout safety.

Scope

- Cross-layer guidance for runtime architecture and scheduling decisions
- Profiling playbook for reproducible micro- and macro-benchmarks
- A canonical benchmarking experiment matrix and CLI examples
- Release note checklist specific to kernel/scheduler/quantization changes
- Known-issues triage matrix and emergency runbooks
- Links to team wiki pages and owners for deeper dives

1. Architecture intent summary

- Goal: Keep 99th-percentile token-latency predictable for mixed short/long request surfaces while minimizing per-token cost and preserving model fidelity.
- Execution model: hierarchical execution cohorts -> kernel pipeline -> device-level executor -> KV-cache layer -> network ingress.
- Decision contracts:
  - Scheduler must expose: priority, preemption_policy, batch_shaping_hint, affinity_hint.
  - Runtime must preserve KV-cache continuity across model swaps or shard remapping with no user-visible token duplication.

Diagram (textual)

[diagram]
Node: Frontend router (route/policy) -> Admission controller (SLO gating) -> Scheduler (cohort classification) -> Kernel dispatcher -> GPU executor (per-device) -> KV cache store -> Response aggregator
[/diagram]

2. Scheduler policy grammar (reference)

- Policies are declared as YAML fragments in experiments and ingested by the scheduler-reconciler. Example:

```yaml
name: slo-tiered-fastpath
priority: high
preemption_policy: best-effort
batch_shaping_hint:
  max_tokens_per_batch: 4096
  preferred_sequence_length: [8, 64, 512]
affinity_hint:
  allow_cross_gpu: true
  numa_preference: node-local
```

- Notes:
  - priority: low|normal|high|critical
  - preemption_policy: none|best-effort|aggressive
  - batch_shaping_hint drives kernel-selection heuristics; mismatches create fallback logs under runtime.kernels.fallback

3. Profiling playbook (reproducible experimental protocol)

Objective: produce a causal attribution between observed latency regressions and kernel/scheduler changes with <5% false-positive rate for alerting.

Preconditions:
- Snapshot the serving traffic sample (10k requests representative surface) and pin model_version + quant_profile.
- Reserve a quiet maintenance fleet (min 3 homogeneous GPUs) and enable full tracing for the trace-id range.

Step-by-step:
1. Prepare trace corpus: run shadow-replay against local harness with --preserve-headers --sticky-session.
2. Baseline run (A): run the microbenchmark suite (see CLI below) for 30 minutes, collect kernel latency histograms, occupancy, NVLink errors.
3. Change under test: apply scheduler or kernel patch to canary worker group.
4. Treatment run (B): repeat the microbenchmark with identical seed and traffic replay.
5. Compare: use the profiler diff tool to generate causal attribution report. Look for increases in kernel-tail (>95th) and shifts in batch-size distributions.
6. If >10% regression in 99th latency or >5% drop in throughput, abort rollout and follow rollback runbook.

Profiling CLI examples

- Shadow replay harness (developer machine):
  ./harness/replay --corpus=~/trace-corpus/production-2027-11-07 --target=scheduler-canary --duration=30m

- Microbenchmark command (30m):
  ./bench/run --suite=mixed-short-long --seed=42 --gpu-pool=homogeneous-4

Telemetry to capture (minimum):
- kernel.exec_time_histogram
- scheduler.batch_size_distribution
- kvcache.hits_per_session
- device.occupancy_percentile
- network.rtt_ms

4. Benchmarking suite: canonical experiments

Table: Experiment templates

| name | intent | workload shape | duration | success metric |
|---|---:|---|---:|---|
| mixed_burst | realistic customer mix | 60% short, 40% long | 60m | 99p latency < 250ms |
| convoys_stress | long-sequence dominated | 100% long | 120m | throughput > baseline * 0.95 |
| small_shortpath | low token per req | 95% < 20 tokens | 30m | median latency < 30ms |

Example orchestration (K8s job YAML snippet for bench-runner):

```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: bench-mixed-burst
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: bench-runner
        image: registry/redwood/bench:2028-01
        args: ["--suite=mixed_burst","--duration=60m","--report=/artifacts/report.json"]
      restartPolicy: Never
```

5. Release note and signoff checklist (for runtime/kernel/scheduler changes)

- Summary of change and expected behavioral impact
- Benchmarks: mixed_burst and convoys_stress results attached
- Telemetry dashboards updated: kernel-latency, batch-distribution, cost-per-token
- Rollout plan: canary group size, measurement windows, rollback thresholds
- Owners: runtime-team, scheduler-team, SRE
- Compliance signoffs (if quantization affecting fidelity): applied by research/QA

Release-template (bulleted):
- Change-id: RRT-XXXX
- Authors: <names>
- Canary plan: 5% traffic for 1h -> 20% for 4h -> full
- Abort criteria: 99p latency > +10% OR error-rate increase > 0.1%

6. Known-issues triage matrix (short catalog)

| Issue | Symptoms | Quick mitigation | Owner | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| kernel-lockup-on-batch-split | GPU stuck >60s, watchdog alerts | restart process, drain cohort | runtime-oncall | investigating |
| kvcache-eviction-race | elevated cold-start errors when remapping | reduce eviction aggressiveness, force warmup | infra-cache | mitigated |
| scheduler-favors-large-batches | tail latency regressed for short requests | apply temporary cohort mislignment filter | scheduler | triaged |

7. Emergency runbooks

A. Kernel slowdown / tail-latency spike
1. Identify cohort: query runtime.cohort.latency by tag
2. Isolate canary: route 100% of affected traffic to fallback model variant or lower-fidelity quantized model
3. Scale: increase worker count for the cohort (scale-out) for short burst window
4. Collect traces and produce a 'kernel-slowdown' incident package (logs, kernel traces, device counters)
5. If persistent, revert kernel or scheduler change via automated rollback job

B. KV cache corruption detection and recovery
1. Detect: kvcache.error_rate > 0.5% for 5m OR KV checksum mismatch logs
2. Quarantine node: mark node out_of_service in resource manager
3. Warm restart: start a new node and run 'kvcache-warmup --source=peer-healthy --session-window=30m'
4. Rebalance: allow scheduler to rebind sessions once kvcache.hits per session > 0.8

8. Experiment notebook & artifact conventions

- Always include: input corpus id, model_version, quant_profile, scheduler_policy_yaml (attached), machine image hash, and bench-runner report.json
- Artifact layout recommended:
  artifacts/<experiment-id>/{report.json,profiles/*.pb,server-logs/*.log,tooling/compare.html}

9. Team wiki pointers & ownership

- Runtime architecture deep-dive: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/execution-stitching-and-fallback-orchestration-2026
- Scheduler policy language: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-policy-language-declarative-profiles-2026
- Profiling tools and diff runner: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/causal-latency-attribution-and-signal-enrichment-playbook-2026

Owners:
- runtime architecture: runtime-platform@redwood.com (Runtime team)
- scheduler policy: scheduler-core@redwood.com
- bench automation: infra-bench@redwood.com

Appendix: Telemetry thresholds (operational)

- SLOs:
  - 99th token latency (hosted API): 250ms - target
  - 95th kernel exec time (device): < 45ms for short-path kernels
  - KV cache hit ratio (hot sessions): > 0.90
- Alert thresholds:
  - latency.99p increased beyond 10% for 15m -> severity P2
  - kernel.exec_time.p99 > 75ms for 5m -> severity P1

Revision history

- 2026-11-03: initial draft (Asha Patel)

Related pages

- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/runtime-experiment-lab-protocols-and-kernel-fuzz-suite-2026
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-deployment-circuit-breakers-and-sla-fallback-playbook-2026
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/runtime-deployment-sanity-and-benchmark-suite-acceptance-2026

title: Multi-model orchestration SDK samples and interchange format
content:
Overview

Purpose: This document provides concrete SDK examples, a lightweight interchange format, and operational guardrails for organizations that orchestrate multiple models per request (fan-out, cascade, ensemble, and hybrid patterns). The intention is to give application engineers and platform teams a reference that reduces bespoke glue-code and improves observability/rollback safety.

Scope: sample client code (Python + TS), a JSON-based orchestration exchange format (OEF v1), recommended telemetry and SLOs, safety/perf guardrails, and a checklist for canarying orchestration changes. This doc assumes usage of Redwood API + a small orchestration layer (service name examples: orchestrator-service, redwood-routing, model-cache).

Terminology
- Orchestrator: the service that composes calls to one or more model endpoints and returns a single aggregated response to the caller.
- Runner: an individual model invocation (e.g., calling gpt-psi-13b or llama2-q4f32).
- OEF (Orchestration Exchange Format): our suggested JSON payload that describes a multi-run request to the orchestrator.
- Fan-out: run several models in parallel and choose/merge results.
- Cascade: run cheap/fast models first and escalate to larger models on failure or low-confidence.
- Ensemble: combine outputs from multiple models by voting, score-weighting, or deterministic merge.

Design goals
- Developer ergonomics: simple SDK primitives for common patterns (fan-out, cascade, ensemble).
- Observability: request-level tracing through orchestrator -> runner -> redwood-runtime with structured telemetry.
- Reproducibility: exchange format captures model versions, seeds, token limits, and prompt templates.
- Safety & cost controls: explicit cost caps and fallbacks in the OEF.

1) OEF v1: compact JSON interchange format
- Example OEF payload (stringified JSON below):

{
  "request_id": "req_20260203_57b3",
  "mode": "cascade",
  "steps": [
    {
      "id": "r1",
      "model": "redwood/gpt-psi-7b@2026-01-15",
      "type": "generation",
      "max_tokens": 128,
      "stop": ["
"],
      "confidence_threshold": 0.75
    },
    {
      "id": "r2",
      "model": "llama2-q4f32-13b@2025-11-01",
      "type": "generation",
      "max_tokens": 256,
      "condition": {
        "on_step": "r1",
        "when": "confidence_below"
      },
      "cost_limit_usd": 0.08
    }
  ],
  "merge_policy": {
    "type": "confidence-first",
    "tie_breaker": "longest"
  },
  "metadata": {
    "user_id": "acct_73b9",
    "feature_flag": "exp-multi-stage-v2"
  }
}

Notes: OEF captures model identifiers (including version date), simple gating conditions (confidence_below/when_empty/timeout), and soft cost caps. OEF intentionally avoids embedding full prompt templates—these should be referenced by template_id to encourage reuse and auditability.

2) SDK primitives (recommended surface)
- Objective: provide minimal wrappers that accept an OEF payload and yield per-run results plus a merged response.

Python sample (high-level, production SDK would add retries & metrics):

from redwood_sdk import RedwoodClient
client = RedwoodClient(api_key="$REDWOOD_KEY")

def run_oef(oef):
    """Send OEF v1 to orchestrator via Redwood API"""
    resp = client.post('/orchestrate', json=oef, timeout=10)
    return resp.json()

# local test
oef = { /* OEF json from above */ }
result = run_oef(oef)
print(result['merged_result'])

TypeScript/Node sample (fetch-based):

import fetch from 'node-fetch';
const API = process.env.REDWOOD_API_ENDPOINT || 'https://api.redwood.ai';
async function runOEF(oef) {
  const res = await fetch(`${API}/orchestrate`, {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Authorization': `Bearer ${process.env.REDWOOD_KEY}`, 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify(oef),
    timeout: 12000
  });
  return res.json();
}

3) Observability and telemetry (required fields)
- Every orchestration call MUST emit structured events with these keys: request_id, mode, steps_count, total_estimated_cost_usd, orchestrator_duration_ms, final_model_used, error_codes.
- Trace sampling: full traces for failed cascades; 5% of successful runs for detailed traces.
- Derived metrics to export: orch.success_rate (target >= 99.2%), orch.latency_95p (target <= 1200ms for single-step; <= 1500ms for cascade w/ remote runners), orch.overspend_rate (fraction of requests where cost_limit_usd was exceeded; target < 0.5%).

4) SLOs and thresholds (recommendation)
- Availability: 99.95% uptime for orchestrator-service (prod).
- Latency: 95th percentile for orchestration end-to-end (caller to merged response) <= 1200ms for 1-run patterns, <= 1600ms for cascades.
- Cost control: mean cost per request budgeted per product team; enforce via OEF cost_limit_usd and scoreboarding.

5) Safety / fallback policies
- Default fallback: if all runners fail, return a deterministic degraded response with error_code = "orch_all_fail" and a human-readable explanation. Never return partial hallucinated facts.
- Data leakage guard: if any step sets "confidential_input": true, the orchestrator MUST prefer private deployment runners (redwood-private-region) or redact outputs before returning.

6) Canary and rollout checklist for orchestration changes
1. Unit tests for OEF parsing and policy enforcement.
2. Local smoke test using redwood-local-proxy (see CLI below).
3. Small traffic canary: 0.5% of users via feature flag exp-multi-stage-v2.
4. Monitor orch.latency_95p, orch.success_rate, and orch.overspend_rate for 48h.
5. If regressions: roll back feature flag, run tracing on at least 10 failed flows.

CLI and local debug commands
- Redwood local proxy start: rw-local-proxy --bind 127.0.0.1:8080 --log-level debug
- Send an OEF test: curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8080/orchestrate -H 'Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_KEY' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @test-oef.json
- Run a synthetic canary: ./scripts/synthetic_canary.sh --oef test-oef.json --rate 5 --duration 120

Config table (recommended):
| property | description | recommended default | notes |
|---------|-------------|---------------------|-------|
| mode | orchestration pattern (fanout/cascade/ensemble) | cascade | cascade for cost-sensitive flows |
| timeout_ms | per-step timeout | 800 | per-run timeout enforced by orchestrator-service |
| cost_limit_usd | soft dollar cap per step | 0.10 | triggers alternative path if exceeded |
| sample_rate_tracing | trace sampling rate | 0.05 | set to 1 for canary windows |

7) Error catalog (canonical fixes)
- ERR_ORCH_TIMEOUT: scenario: step exceeded timeout_ms. Fix: increase timeout_ms for specific runner or tune runner batching; add circuit breaker.
- ERR_CONFIDENCE_PARSE: scenario: runner returned no confidence. Fix: verify model variant returns scores or add deterministic fallback.
- ERR_COST_LIMIT: scenario: cost_limit_usd exceeded. Fix: lower max_tokens or switch to cheaper model in OEF.
- ERR_DATA_POLICY_BLOCK: scenario: confidential_input true but public runner selected. Fix: enforce region/routing policy in orchestrator config and re-run.

8) Operational runbook (short)
- Symptom: orch.latency_95p > target
  1. Check recent deploys to orchestrator-service and redwood-routing.
  2. Inspect traces for increased runner queue_time_ms.
  3. If runner saturation: scale GPU pool (gpu-pool-orch-1) or route subset of users to cheaper fallback.

- Symptom: orch.overspend_rate rising
  1. Query recent OEFs with cost_limit_usd hits.
  2. Identify high-cost templates (template_id) and reduce max_tokens or change default model.

Ownership and contacts
- Orchestrator-service: team = eng-platform / oncall = platform-oncall@redwood.ai
- SDK surface & docs: team = eng-developer-experience / owner = Aisha Patel (aisha@redwood.ai)
- Observability: team = eng-sre / slack channel = #sre-orchestration

Appendix A — template references and examples
- template_id: greeting-short-v1 -> prompt stored in template-service; use placeholders for user context.
- Example: a small YAML snippet used by template-service:

template_id: greeting-short-v1
model_hint: redwood/gpt-psi-7b@2026-01-15
prompt: |
  You are an assistant. Use the following user_profile and query to produce a concise answer.
  {{user_profile}}
  Q: {{query}}

Appendix B — migration notes from single-model clients
- Replace direct model calls with run_oef wrappers.
- Add tracing fields and map existing metrics to orch.* prefixed metrics.
- Audit prompt templates to ensure template_id references exist and are versioned.

If you are integrating this pattern and have questions, ping the eng-developer-experience channel (#devx-orchestration) or email aisha@redwood.ai.

Document history and change log
- 2025-11-12: initial draft by Aisha Patel.
- 2026-01-20: added SLO recommendations and OEF cost fields (reviewers: Jonas Meyer).
- 2026-02-03: finalized python/ts examples and published.

title: Dynamic request orchestration and fallthrough
content:
Summary
This document defines the dynamic request orchestration layers in Redwood's serving runtime and the fallthrough/fallback behaviors used during capacity degradation, model mismatch, or resource pressure. It covers design goals, component responsibilities, kernel scheduling heuristics, profiling and benchmarking guidance, release checklist items, known issues and mitigations, and runbook steps for common incidents.

Goals and non-goals
- Goals:
  - Keep tail latency (p95/p99) stable under mixed workloads and autoscaling events.
  - Ensure deterministic graceful degradation with measurable cost impact.
  - Make fallback policies transparent and debuggable for SREs and platform customers.
- Non-goals:
  - This doc does not define model quality thresholds (see evals docs).
  - It is not a user-facing API spec — see api-standards for public endpoints.

High-level design overview
The orchestration stack is layered as: request ingress -> policy router -> scheduler -> kernel manager -> executor. A dedicated fallthrough engine runs alongside the router to evaluate compatible fallbacks (model variant, quantized profile, region). Key principles: policy-first routing, cost-awareness, and observable decisioning.

Component responsibilities
- Ingress (proxy): TLS termination, auth checks, request enrichment (customer metadata, route tags). Emits request_id and ingest_timestamp.
- Policy router: policy engine that chooses target model family, region constraints, and candidate fallback set. Inputs: route config, customer tier, current capacity fingerprint.
- Scheduler: converts chosen target into a scheduling decision (immediate, queued, preemptible) and assigns a priority class. Enforces per-model qps windowing and per-customer concurrency caps.
- Kernel manager: chooses kernel variant and memory layout (bfloat16 / int8 / fused kernels) based on model architecture and sequence length distribution. Provides expected token cost estimate.
- Executor: runs the kernel, streams tokens, reports metrics and caches KV state.
- Fallthrough engine: cross-checks capacity and policy; triggers model variant fallback, regional failover, or synthetic short-circuit response (graceful degrade).

Request flow (annotated)
1) Ingress receives request -> adds metadata (customer, route_id, prompt_size).
2) Router evaluates policies: if primary model is saturated, produces candidate set [primary, quantized-variant, smaller-family, safer-response-fallback].
3) Scheduler accepts router candidate set and current node capacity fingerprint. It computes: priority_score = latency_weight*latency_sensitivity + cost_weight*cost_sensitivity + fairness_penalty.
4) If priority_score > threshold_immediate -> dispatch; else -> enqueue in fair-shared queue or assign to preemptible slot.
5) Kernel manager picks kernel path; it consults per-model profile table.
6) Executor runs and returns tokens; post-run metrics are published to observability.

Kernel scheduling heuristics
- Priority classes: realtime (interactive p50/p95 SLO), batch (throughput optimized), background (eviction-safe).
- Kernel selection order: exact-optimized -> fused-attention -> int8-quantized -> fallback-single-CPU. Selection chooses first kernel with estimated latency <= node_slo and memory <= node_avail.
- Preemption: kernels in background class may be preempted when realtime queue length exceeds realtime_threshold within lookback_window (30s). Preemption is cooperative where supported (yield op in kernel), otherwise next-batch prioritization is used.
- Affinity rules: model shards prefer colocated NVLink groups; small sequences allow multi-model colocations. The kernel manager exposes node_affinity hints to the scheduler.

Profiling playbook (when investigating performance regressions)
Use this checklist when p95 or throughput deviates from baseline. Always run with a preserved request_id and attach traces to incident tickets.
1) Reproduce with synthetic traffic: use benchctl from the runtime toolkit. Example:
   benchctl run --workload chat-mixed --concurrency 200 --duration 10m --model rdx-v1-13b --seed 42
2) Capture metrics: enable full tracing and kernel timeline:
   curl -X POST $RUNTIME/debug/trace?request_id=...
   rtctl capture --trace-id <id> --output /tmp/trace.json
3) Profile GPU kernels (on node):
   nsys profile --output /tmp/nsys --sample=none --trace=cudaKernel --duration=120s --pid <executor-pid>
4) Map kernel timings to model layers using the per-model kernel map: /etc/redwood/models/kernel_map.yaml
5) If disparity between estimated and observed latency > 15%, open a profiling ticket and tag with kernel_hash, node_type, and workload_label.

Benchmarking suite integration
- Benchmark targets: median token latency, p95/p99 token latency, tokens/sec, cost-per-1k-tokens.
- Standard workloads: chat-mixed, long-context-summarize, single-turn-completion, embedding-batch.
- Running distributed benchmarks: use bench-orchestrator to schedule across a representative fleet slice:
   bench-orchestrator --suite production-2026 --targets fleet-slice-A --variation quant-profiles
- Expected outputs (table-like text):
   workload, model, concurrency, p50(ms/token), p95(ms/token), tokens/s, cost/1k
   chat-mixed, rdx-v1-13b, 200, 12, 48, 21000, $0.42
- Use the benchmark canonicalizer script to normalize results and upload to the perf dashboard:
   python tools/benchmark_normalize.py --input results.json --tag release-2026-02

Release checklist (runtime binary and kernel map updates)
1) Update kernel_map with new kernel_hash -> add compatibility metadata.
2) Run full regression benchmark suite (3 days on canary slice).
