3) Create rollout plan: 5% -> 25% -> 100% with 30m observation windows and automatic rollback if p95 increases > 12% or errors increase > 1.5x.
4) Announce release to oncall and platform channels with telemetry queries for quick assessment.
5) Post-release validation: run smoke bench and 1-hour golden traffic replay.

Known issues and mitigations (selection)
- Issue: ephemeral kernel queue overflow during cross-region failover (INC-2025-491)
  Symptoms: sudden p99 spike for affected region, kernels queued > 2s.
  Mitigation: throttle regional ingress by 30% and trigger fallback to quantized-variant. Long-term fix: increase pre-warming policy for region failover.
- Issue: int8 kernels producing occasional catastrophic oom on 80GB A100 nodes (KERN-2025-77)
  Symptoms: host OOM kill, kernel crash logs include vectorized-alloc failure.
  Mitigation: apply temporary memory cap via kernel manager (max_workspace=0.8*node_avail). Patch in next kernel release to reduce peak working set.
- Issue: cost estimator drift under long-context workloads (COST-2026-12)
  Symptoms: observed token cost 1.4x estimated for long sequences > 8k tokens.
  Mitigation: adjust model profile weighting to favor attention complexity; add an online calibration job sampling long requests.

Operational runbooks (incident templates)
Runbook: High realtime p95 for production route
1) Acknowledge alert and post to #runtime-incidents with incident id.
2) Check router decisions for request_ids in 5-minute window (query: router_decisions{route="<route>"} by request_id).
3) If router moved traffic to fallback models, record fallback_rate; if > 20% then revert fallback gating and scale up primary pool.
4) If kernel queue backlog > 1s, enable emergency autoscale policy for the node pool and shift lower-priority jobs to background.
5) If the issue persists, execute safe_short_circuit for non-essential routes:
   rtctl short-circuit --route <route> --reason "p95-incident" --message "temporary degraded response"
6) Create postmortem and attach bench traces and nsys profile output.

SLOs, metrics and dashboards
- SLOs: interactive routes: p95 <= 120ms per-token (service-level), success rate >= 99.7% (per-route). Background jobs: throughput SLOs defined per-customer contract.
- Error budget policy: if monthly error budget consumption > 30% accelerate rollback windows and require manual approval for subsequent rollouts.
- Key dashboards: per-route latency heatmap, kernel utilization map, per-model cost burn table, fallback decision table. Dashboards live at grafana/runtime-overview.

Tooling and developer ergonomics
- rtctl: runtime control CLI for tracing, short-circuit, and emergency scale.
- benchctl/bench-orchestrator: standard benchmarking tools.
- profiler-helpers: scripts to convert nsys outputs to model layer timelines.
- kernel-map.yaml: single source of truth for kernel capability and compatibility.

Appendix A — useful commands and snippets
- Capture trace for a specific request:
  curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
    "https://runtime-redwood/_internal/trace?request_id=<id>" > /tmp/request_trace.json
- Example kernel_map entry (YAML snippet):
  - model: rdx-v1-13b
    kernels:
      - hash: 8f3a4b
        type: fused-attn
        mem_estimate_mb: 34000
        latency_ms_token_64: 11.2
      - hash: a7d9c1
        type: int8-quant
        mem_estimate_mb: 9000
        latency_ms_token_64: 13.8
- Emergency short-circuit: rtctl short-circuit --route /chat/v1 --duration 30m --message "degraded-mode"

Appendix B — ownership and contacts
- Runtime architecture ownership: runtime-arch@redwood.com (primary: Lydia Park).
- Oncall rotation: runtime-sre@redwood.com.
- Kernel release owner: kernels@redwood.com (Ravi Menon).

Change log
- 2025-11-10: created by Lydia Park.
- 2026-02-14: added benchmarking guidance and known issue COST-2026-12.

References
- See also: runtime profiling playbook, kernel mapper spec, and benchmarking suite docs (linked in Related pages).

Notes for reviewers
- Confirm that the preemption windows and thresholds match current scheduling implementation (scheduler team must cross-check) and that SLO numbers align with product SLAs.

title: Edge Consumption Affinity & Local Cache Playbook
content:
Overview:

This playbook explains the product intent, design trade-offs, and rollout plan for enabling consumption affinity and local cache behavior for edge and near-edge Redwood deployments. The goal is to improve tail-latency for conversational and short-sequence workloads while reducing per-token compute cost through coordinated local caching and affinity routing. This is a product-facing reference for PMs, solutions engineers, and partner integrators.

Key principles:

1) Latency first for interactive workloads: preserve 95th/99th tail latency SLOs for conversational routes (target 95th < 120ms for short prompts in edge regions).
2) Cost-aware fallthroughs: local cache hits reduce GPU token cost; misses should gracefully route to cost-optimized hosted variants without impacting correctness SLA.
3) Consistency and privacy: cached prefixes must honor tenant isolation and retention policies (KMS-backed encryption for private deployments).
4) Observability and rollbackability: every affinity policy must log decision reasons and expose observability hooks for SLO regressions and cost impact.

Scope and components:

- Consumption Affinity Service (CAS): a lightweight control-plane microservice that computes a per-tenant affinity score for edge vs. central serving, based on recent traffic patterns, per-route SLOs, and capacity signals.
- Local Prefetch Proxy (LPP): an optional customer-side (or VPC) proxy that maintains a local prefix/KV cache and prefetches hot model context (embedding vectors and KV segments) from upstream replicas.
- Affinity Router: runtime policy embedded in the gateway which consults CAS to decide request routing: local -> dedicated edge pool -> hosted fallback.
- Cache Coordination Protocol: a compact protocol (HTTP/2+ gRPC) for cache eviction hints, prefetch requests, and lease-based ownership of cached segments.

SLOs and thresholds (product defaults):

- Interactive conversational (short prompts, <256 tokens): 95th latency target = 120ms, 99th = 300ms.
- Cache hit target: 60% steady-state for routes with affinity enabled within first 72 hours after warmup.
- Cost impact guardrail: no single-tenant affinity policy may increase monthly token-related spend by >5% without explicit approval.

Customer-facing behaviors and configs:

Table: default per-route config (text table)

Name | Default | Description
-----|---------|---------
affinity_enabled | true | Whether CAS can set affinity for this route
prefetch_window | 90s | Lookback window for prefetch heuristics
min_traffic_for_affinity | 100 req/day | Minimum traffic to qualify for persistent affinity
cache_ttl | 6h | Default lease/TLL for prefetched KV segments
fallback_model_tier | standard | Model tier used when local misses occur

How affinity decisions work (high level):

1. Route registers with CAS with route metadata (SLO, expected seq length distribution, tenant id).
2. CAS ingests traffic telemetry (per-route QPS, recent cache hit rate, tail latency) and computes an affinity score (0.0-1.0) based on configured weights: latency_weight (0.5), hit_rate_weight (0.3), cost_delta_weight (0.2).
3. If score > 0.7 and capacity is available in edge pool, CAS marks route as Affinity=LOCAL and issues prefetch hints to LPP.
4. Affinity Router enforces a small percentage of canary bypasses (2%) to validate quality against hosted baseline.

Operational runbook (for product and SRE):

Pre-deployment checklist:
- Confirm tenant encryption keys available (KMS).
- Verify edge pool capacity >= expected steady-state QPS for routes marked local.
- Enable affinity in staging and validate hit-rate >= 40% after warmup.

Incident handling (high level):
1. Symptom: sudden drop in cache hit-rate or spike in tail latency in an edge region.
2. Page oncall SRE and tag the route in CAS UI.
3. Actions: (a) revert route affinity to FALLBACK for affected tenants; (b) invalidate suspicious LPP caches by issuing eviction hints; (c) collect KV cache diagnostic bundle from LPP (see diagnostics API).
4. Postmortem: update prefetch heuristics or raise min_traffic_for_affinity if instability is workload-driven.

Rollout plan (Q4 2026 -> Q1 2027):

- Phase 0 (pilot): select 3 enterprise customers with strict latency needs and low privacy constraints. Deploy LPP and enable Affinity in a single edge region. Collect metrics for 4 weeks.
- Phase 1 (early access): open to more customers with an opt-in flag in Console; expose per-route configuration controls and cost-impact simulator.
- Phase 2 (general availability): enable automatic affinity suggestions for qualifying routes and add self-serve toggle in Console with default safe thresholds.

Pricing and packaging implications:

- Affinity-enabled routes will qualify for a reduced token charge on local cache hits (example: 40% discount on per-token compute metric for hits), implemented as a post-processing credit applied to invoices.
- Dedicated edge pools used for affinity will be eligible for reserved-capacity pricing; product must surface guidance on commit sizing (recommended 30% headroom).
- Premium support add-on: affinity stabilization SLA (four-week warmup assistance and weekly health check-ins).

Console and API examples:

- Sample API: enable affinity on route via Redwood API (curl)

curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/routes/route-123/affinity \n  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" 
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" 
  -d '{"affinity_enabled": true, "min_traffic_for_affinity": 200, "cache_ttl_seconds": 14400}'

- Affinity decision query (gRPC snippet concept):
// affinity_service.getAffinity(route_id, tenant_id) -> {score: 0.82, reason: ["low_tail_latency", "high_local_hit_rate"]}

Monitoring and telemetry requirements:

- Telemetry events to emit: affinity_evaluation, cache_prefetch_hint, cache_hit, cache_miss, affinity_enforcement_event.
- Dashboards: per-region affinity hit-rate, per-route tail-latency vs. baseline, monthly cost delta for affinity-enabled tenants.
- Alerts: cache_hit_rate < 40% sustained for 30m, or tail_latency_95th increase > 30% vs baseline.

Security and compliance notes:

- All cache contents must be encrypted at rest using customer KMS keys for Private deployments.
- Prefetch requests must carry tenant scoping headers and be rate-limited (default 10 prefetches/sec per tenant).
- For regulated customers, affinity can be restricted to dedicated private edge pools only.

Decision log (why we chose this approach):

- Alternatives considered: purely central caching, full-model replication to every edge, and client-side only caching.
- Tradeoffs: model replication provides best latency but unacceptable cost and variant proliferation; client-only caching lacks coordination and instrumentation. Consumption Affinity + coordinated prefetch gives a practical middle ground with measurable cost and latency improvements.

Open questions and follow-ups:

- Quantify warmup curve behavior across multi-tenant noisy neighbors and update prefetch heuristics accordingly.
- Define SLO for prefetch bandwidth costs and establish billing for heavy prefetch consumers.
- Evaluate stronger consistency modes (read-through vs. lease-based) for high-security customers.

Ownership and contacts:

- Product lead: Sofia Park (product)
- Engineering owner: Lars Becker (eng-serving-runtime)
- SRE lead: Ethan Cole (eng-sre)
- Solutions & Partnerships: Maya Singh (customer-success)

Appendix: example prefetch heuristics pseudocode

// simplified scoring for whether to prefetch a prefix
function should_prefetch(route_metrics) {
  score = 0
  if (route_metrics.qps > 5) score += 0.4
  if (route_metrics.recent_cache_hits > 0.5) score += 0.3
  if (route_metrics.tail_latency > baseline * 1.2) score += 0.3
  return score > 0.6
}

Diagnostic CLI (LPP) to collect cache bundle:

redwood-lpp collect-cache-bundle --route route-123 --output /tmp/route-123-cache-bundle.tgz

References:
- Local prefetch proxy PRD (internal): requirements/local-prefetch-proxy-prd-2028-10-04
- Hybrid cache coordinator design: design-specs/hybrid-cache-coordinator-design-spec-2029-06-15

This playbook will be updated iteratively as pilot data arrives and heuristics are tuned. For feature requests or questions, contact the owners listed above.

title: Execution Scenario Orchestrator: Spec and Playbook
content:
Overview

Purpose: This document specifies the Execution Scenario Orchestrator (ESO), a cross-cutting component that composes, schedules, and replays representative end-to-end inference scenarios against the runtime. ESO is intended to:

- Provide a reproducible, versioned way to define complex multi-tenant workloads (prefixes, kv-cache warmup, mixed sequence lengths, burst patterns).
- Integrate with kernel scheduler hooks so scenario fidelity is preserved when testing scheduler changes.
- Produce traceable profiling artifacts consumable by the benchmarking suite and the profiling playbook.

Scope and audience: engineers owning runtime architecture, kernel-and-scheduling, profiling, and SREs running performance experiments or incident triage.

Design goals

1) Determinism and provenance: every scenario is a small, self-contained script with a hashable manifest and metadata (model version, quantization profile, hardware fingerprint).
2) Scheduler-aware playback: the orchestrator can attach scheduler context (priority, tenant-id, kernel-hint) to each request so the runtime executes the scenario as intended.
3) Observability-first: scenario runs automatically capture structured traces, kernel attributions, and per-token cost deltas and upload to the central perf store.
4) Lightweight chaos vectors: the orchestrator supports controlled perturbations (evictions, forced preemption, simulated NVLink degradation) to surface degradation modes.

Component overview

- Scenario DSL (YAML): declarative description of request series, injected events, and expected assertions.
- Runner: controller that materializes requests and submits them to a chosen endpoint (local sandbox, canary cluster, full production mirror).
- Scheduler Adapter: library that translates DSL affinity/priority fields into scheduler annotations and kernel hints.
- Collector: post-run artifact collector (traces, kernel telemetry, raw responses, golden diffs) with upload to perf-bucket.

Scenario DSL (conceptual example)

# A minimal scenario manifest in YAML. Fields must remain flat (no nested objects with unknown keys) for deterministic hashing.

manifest_version: "1.0"
name: "multi-tenant-burst-warmup"
model: "llama-13b-q4f16"
hardware_fingerprint: "g4dn-8nvlink-2026-03"
sequence_profile: "mix-small-medium-long"
timeline:
  - t: 0
    action: "warmup"
    params: "prefix_file=warmup-prompts.txt,concurrency=4"
  - t: 30
    action: "burst"
    params: "clients=120,shape=50%short-30%med-20%long,priority=production"
  - t: 90
    action: "evict"
    params: "tenant=tenant-42,reason=memory-pressure"
assertions:
  - type: "median-latency-below"
    value_ms: "200"
  - type: "tail-99-latency-below"
    value_ms: "800"

Scheduler integration

The Scheduler Adapter exposes three annotations consumed by the kernel mapper: kernel_hint (preferred kernel variant), priority_class (production/canary/batch), and affinity_token (NUMA/slot placement hint). When the runner submits requests it attaches these fields as HTTP headers (X-ESO-Kernel-Hint, X-ESO-Priority, X-ESO-Affinity) to preserve signal across transport layers.

Example headers (curl):

curl -X POST https://runtime-canary.internal/api/v1/generate 
 -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' 
 -H 'X-ESO-Kernel-Hint: grouped-attn-v2' 
 -H 'X-ESO-Priority: production' 
 -H 'X-ESO-Affinity: numa-0:slot-3' 
 -d '{"prompt":"Summarize ..."}'

Profiling playbook integration

When an ESO run completes the Collector creates a run package and triggers the profiling playbook pipelines:

1) Minimal trace upload: we include per-request trace IDs and compact kernel-attribution CSVs.
2) Sampling policy: for runs > 10k requests, we apply stratified sampling by sequence length and priority class.
3) Correlation loop: perf store populates the run record with scheduler decision traces so the profiler can compute causal latency deltas associated with kernel selection.

Benchmarks and synthetic load harness

ESO can emit two modes of workload: synthetic (generated tokens for microbenchmarks) and recorded-replay (playback of production request surface with anonymization). The benchmarking suite consumes scenario manifests to run SLO-driven experiments.

SLO-driven experiment matrix (example)

| parameter | example values | notes |
|-----------|----------------|-------|
| concurrency | 1, 8, 64, 256 | cluster-dependent cap |
| sequence mix | 60/30/10 (s/m/l) | affects kernel crossing points |
| kv-cache state | cold, warm, hot | warmimplies prefix-caching |
| priority distribution | 90/10 prod/batch | scheduler stress test |

Runtime runbook: Replaying a production slowdown

Purpose: step-by-step guide to reproduce a reported production slowdown using ESO.

1) Triage and capture: collect the incident ID and the example request IDs from the status page.
2) Assemble a scenario: create a manifest that replays the failing requests (redacting PII), include the observed client headers and priority classes.
3) Select target: use a canary cluster that mirrors the production scheduler version and kernel set.
4) Run with tracing enabled: set environment variable ESO_TRACE_LEVEL=debug and run the runner with --collect-kernel-csv.
4a) If the slowdown reproduces, immediately tag the run with incident:<id> and notify SRE channel.
5) If the slowdown does not reproduce, run a higher-fidelity replay using recorded-replay mode with full affinity and session cookies (use only in secure sandbox).

Investigation checklist (what to look for)

- Kernel attribution spikes: sudden shift from grouped-attn-v2 to scalar-attn-fallback during medium sequences.
- Preemption events: scheduler logs containing "evict" + matching trace IDs.
- GPU metrics: duty-cycle drop, NVLink error counters, and sudden memory compaction events.
- KV-cache miss rate increase after eviction window.

Known issues and mitigations

- Issue: affinity headers not propagated by edge proxy in old canaries.
  Mitigation: upgrade proxy config to preserve X-ESO-* headers; work-around: include scheduler hints in body metadata.
- Issue: reproducibility variance when running on different NVLink topologies.
  Mitigation: include hardware_fingerprint in the manifest and pin to identical pool for replay.
- Issue: large recorded-replay runs can saturate perf-store ingest.
  Mitigation: use bucketed uploads and the incremental-collector option.

Release notes (summary of changes that introduced ESO)

- 2026-01-12: initial beta of ESO runner and DSL, supports warmup/burst/evict actions.
- 2026-06-03: Scheduler Adapter v1 added kernel_hint mapping and header propagation.
- 2026-09-22: Collector incremental upload and stratified-sampling policies added to reduce perf-store load.

Operational requirements and configs

Config keys (example table):

| key | type | default | description |
|-----|------|---------|-------------|
| eso.runner.target | string | "canary" | target cluster: sandbox|canary|prod |
| eso.collector.sample_rate | float | "0.1" | fraction of requests to keep in full trace (0.0-1.0) |
| eso.scheduler.propagate_headers | bool | "true" | ensure X-ESO-* headers are forwarded by gateways |
| eso.archive.bucket | string | "gs://perf-bucket/eso-runs" | destination for run artifacts |

Security and privacy notes

- Recorded payloads must be redacted. The runner supports an anonymizer plugin that hashes or drops PII fields before uploading.
- Access controls: only members of runtime QA or SRE may run recorded-replay against production-mirrors. ESO enforces RBAC via OAuth groups.

Ownership and rollout plan

- Owner: runtime-infra team (primary), profiling team (secondary). Contacts: Marta Alvarez (runtime-infra), Kofi Mensah (profiling).
- Rollout stages: alpha (sandbox-only) -> beta (canary clusters, opt-in) -> GA (policy: default available to oncall).
- Acceptance criteria for GA: deterministic replay of previously recorded incidents in 90% of cases (same kernel selection and equivalent per-token latency within 15%).

Appendix: Example full scenario manifest and runner commands

# scenario.yaml
manifest_version: "1.0"
name: "incident-2026-299-replay"
model: "vicuna-7b-q2"
hardware_fingerprint: "a100-mig-4g-2026-05"
sequence_profile: "60%short-30%med-10%long"
timeline:
  - t: 0
    action: "replay-requests"
    params: "file=incident-2026-299-requests.ndjson,concurrency=32,priority=production"
  - t: 45
    action: "chaos"
    params: "type=evict,tenant=default,duration=5s"

# run in sandbox
eso-runner --manifest scenario.yaml --target canary --trace-level debug --collect-kernel-csv --upload-bucket gs://perf-bucket/eso-runs/incident-2026-299

Support matrix and troubleshooting quick tips

- If kernel CSVs are empty: confirm X-ESO-Kernel-Hint header propagation and ESO_TRACE_LEVEL.
- If reproductions differ by >20% latency: pin hardware_fingerprint and verify NVLink topology.
- If perf-store upload fails: retry with --incremental-collector and check bucket ACLs.

Document change log

- 2026-02-14 (Marta Alvarez): created initial draft.
- 2026-06-10 (Kofi Mensah): added scheduler adapter header spec.
- 2026-09-22 (Jade Patel): updated sampling policy and release notes.

Related artifacts and references

- Kernel mapper annotation contract: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-policy-language-declarative-profiles-2026
- Profiling integration guide: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/causal-latency-attribution-and-signal-enrichment-playbook-2027
- Perf store upload API: internal PRD #4571

End of document.

title: Runtime operational pathways and shard topology
content:
Title: Runtime operational pathways and shard topology

Summary:
This page describes the runtime component dependency map we use to reason about production degradation paths, kernel scheduling interactions, shard placement, and where to attach profiling and benchmarking probes. It is an operational reference for SREs and runtime engineers that ties architecture-level decisions to concrete runbook actions and micro-mitigation steps.

1) Purpose and scope
- Purpose: Provide a single reference linking runtime components, scheduling signals, profiling hooks, and operational procedures.
- Scope: Serving runtime components (router, dispatcher, runtime-core, kernel-manager, kv-cache, shard-manager, telemetry-agent) for hosted, dedicated, and private deployments. Does NOT cover model training or offline data pipelines.

2) High-level diagram (textual)
- Ingress Router -> Request Validator -> Smart Router (policy) -> Shard Manager -> Dispatcher -> Runtime Core (per-shard agent) -> Kernel Manager -> GPU Execution -> KV Cache / Prefetcher -> Telemetry Agent -> Observability pipeline
- Diagram notes: smart routing can bypass shard manager for single-node pinned requests (customer pinned versions). Dispatcher batches requests for the same shard/kernel-selection window.

3) Component responsibilities (short)
- Ingress Router: TLS termination, API auth, rate limiting, token accounting.
- Smart Router: Route by policy (latency-first, cost-first, region, customer tier). Exposes /v1/route-decisions for debugging.
- Shard Manager: Maintains active shard topology, shard-to-GPU mapping, and rebalance operations. Owns topology versioning and exposes /shard-status.
- Dispatcher: Batcher + sequencer. Converts requests into continuous-batch windows and forwards to Runtime Core.
- Runtime Core: Per-shard agent that manages model KV cache, sequence handling, and pre/post-processing hooks.
- Kernel Manager: Chooses kernel variants (fp16, int8, fused-attn) per request-window and triggers kernel hot-swap when safe.
- KV Cache / Prefetcher: Global prefix cache with LRU and sticky-session affinity.
- Telemetry Agent: Streamer for metrics, traces, and profiling frames into observability (OTLP).

4) Shard topology primitives and invariants
- Shard: logical partition of a model replica (weights and persistent kernels).
- Topology version: monotonic integer (v1, v2 ...). All dispatchers and runtime-cores subscribe to topology updates; topology rollout is two-phase (prepare -> commit).
- Invariants: 
  - No two runtime cores should claim the same shard replica write-lock.
  - Topology commit window must be <= 60s to avoid routing ambiguity for SLO-sensitive customers.
  - Kernel hot-swap is permitted only when no active prefix read-locks exist for a shard (see runbook for forcing swap).

5) Kernel scheduling and selection rules (operationally important)
- Priority of selection (highest to lowest): Pinned customer request variant -> Latency SLO mode (lowest-latency kernel set) -> Cost SLO mode (quantized kernels) -> Fallback family (compatible architecture)
- Kernel selection signals: avg_seq_len_1m, kv_hit_ratio, tail_latency_95, gpu_util_60s, queued_requests.
- Default thresholds used by kernel-manager v2.7:
  - tail_latency_95 > 250ms => prefer latency-optimized kernels (fused-attn, fp16).
  - gpu_util_60s > 78% && queued_requests > 16 => consider higher-batch fused kernels or allocate extra shard capacity.
  - kv_hit_ratio < 0.2 => enable prefetch window (30s) or promote hot-prefix caching.

6) Profiling playbook (attach points and quick triage)
- When to profile: sustained tail latency increases > 20% for 5+ minutes or spike in OOMs.
- Attach points: dispatcher, runtime-core (per-shard), kernel-manager, GPU OS proc.
- Quick triage steps (1–5):
  1. Query topology and dispatcher queues: curl -s http://dispatcher:8080/metrics | jq '.queue_lengths'
  2. Snapshot kernel-manager decisions: curl http://kernel-manager:9090/v1/decisions | tee /tmp/km.decisions.json
  3. Collect runtime-core perf counters (30s): /opt/runtime/bin/perf-dump --shard <shard-id> --duration 30s > /tmp/perf.shard
  4. Dump KV cache stats: curl http://kv-cache:7070/stats
  5. Upload traces to observability: /opt/telemetry/bin/submit-frame --reason "incident-triage" --file /tmp/perf.shard
- Pro tips: enable sampling at 10% for request-level traces during high-throughput to avoid observability cost blowouts.

7) Benchmarking suite touchpoints and recommended workloads
- Bench harness components: perf-harness (python), seq-gen (workload generator), harness-orchestrator (k8s job templates).
- Canonical workloads:
  - Small-chat (seq_len=64, avg_toks=16, kv_prefetch_off) — tests latency SLOs.
  - Long-context (seq_len=2048, kv_hit_ratio=0.6) — tests KV cache effectiveness and memory pressure.
  - High-throughput (parallel 256 requests, batch-window=50ms) — tests batching and kernel throughput.
- Representative K8s job snippet (YAML shown as inline code):
```
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: perf-small-chat
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: perf-harness
        image: registry.redwood.ai/perf-harness:2025-10
        args: ["--workload", "small-chat", "--duration", "600"]
      restartPolicy: Never
```
- Benchmark measurement taxonomy (always report): P50, P95, P99 end-to-end latency; GPU tokens/sec; average batch size; KV hit ratio; erred requests per 10k.

8) Runtime release notes (summary, useful for operators)
- v3.2.1 (2025-09-18) — patch release
  - Fixed: race during topology commit that could cause duplicate dispatch routes (INC-RED-1479).
  - Added: kernel-manager exposes /v1/decisions with reason codes.
  - Perf: 4–6% throughput improvement on fused-attn kernels for seq <= 128.
- v3.3.0 (2025-11-01) — minor release
  - New: topology prepare/commit now supports staged rollbacks on health-probe mismatch.
  - New: telemetry agent supports compressed OTLP frames reducing observability egress by ~30%.
  - Breaking change: default dispatcher.batch-window reduced from 75ms to 50ms; see rollout steps below.

9) Rollout checklist for dispatcher.batch-window change (required for any env)
1. Create a canary pool with new config (10% of traffic).
2. Run correctness smoke: perf-small-chat, 30m, check p95 delta < 10% and error delta < 0.01%.
3. Monitor GPU util and queued_requests for 1 hour.
4. If regressions observed, revert config via topology rollback: curl -X POST http://shard-manager:8080/v1/topology/rollback -d '{"version":<old>}'
5. Promote to 50% then 100% following same checks.

10) Known issues (operationally actionable)
- KNOWN-2024-031: Kernel hot-swap can stall when a long-running completion (seq > 3k) holds a read-lock longer than the swap timeout (default 120s). Mitigation: increase swap_timeout to 300s for affected model families or schedule swap during low-traffic windows. Owner: runtime-core team.
- KNOWN-2025-008: Under high small-request QPS with low avg_seq_len (<12) and aggressive batch-window (<=25ms) we observe increased context-switch overhead on dispatcher pods leading to higher p95. Mitigation: raise batch-window to 50ms for those workloads or pin to latency-optimized kernels. Owner: dispatcher team.
- KNOWN-2025-021: Rare KV cache eviction thrashing for long-context workloads when two large prefixes are near-simultaneously promoted. Mitigation: enable sticky-prefix mode for the affected customer or increase cache-size-gb by 10%. Owner: cache team.

11) Runbooks (short form)
- Runbook: Degraded tail latency (p95 > SLO)
  1. Confirm: check p95 on /dashboards/runtime/p95-live and SLO config for route.
  2. Check dispatcher queues; if queue_length > 100, scale dispatcher replicas (kubectl scale deploy/dispatcher --replicas=N+2).
  3. Check kernel-manager decision stream for sudden kernel downgrades. If a downgrade to quantized variants is active, roll back using /kernel-manager/v1/force-variant?variant=latency_opt.
  4. If GPU util > 90% and queue persists, scale shard capacity or enable burst-pool routing.
  5. Collect full profiling snapshot (see section 6) and attach to incident.
- Runbook: Stuck topology commit
  1. Verify logs on shard-manager for prepare/commit errors.
  2. If transaction lock present, escalate to runtime-core oncall and run /opt/runtime/bin/topo-unlock --version <version>.
  3. Re-run health probes and re-commit.

12) Operational scripts and CLI examples (copyable)
- Dump active topology: curl -s http://shard-manager:8080/v1/topology | jq . > /tmp/topo.json - Force kernel variant: curl -X POST http://kernel-manager:9090/v1/force-variant -d '{"shard":"shard-42","variant":"fp16-fused"}'
- KV cache stats: curl http://kv-cache:7070/stats | jq '.cache_entries|length, .hit_ratio'

13) Ownership, escalation, and contact matrix
- runtime-core: owner-runtime-core@redwood.ai (oncall: @runtime-core-oncall)
- dispatcher: owner-dispatcher@redwood.ai (oncall: @dispatcher-oncall)
- kernel-manager: owner-kernel@redwood.ai (oncall: @kernel-oncall)
- cache: owner-kv@redwood.ai (oncall: @kv-oncall)
- SRE escalation: sre-escalation@redwood.ai

14) How this ties to team wiki and deeper pages
- This page is the operational glue. For design rationales see team wiki: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/runtime-design-notes-2024. For deep dives on profiling, see profiling-playbook/runtime-profiling-playbook-guidelines-2025. Kernel scheduler spec lives at kernel-and-scheduling/priority-driven-kernel-scheduler-spec-2026. Benchmark job templates and historical runs are in benchmarking-and-perf-suite/perf-archive-2025.

15) Appendix: metric thresholds and SLOs (table rendered inline)
- SLOs (default route):
  - p95 latency <= 220ms for small-chat workloads
  - p99 latency <= 420ms for small-chat workloads
  - availability >= 99.95% (monthly)
- Metric thresholds:
  - dispatcher.queue_length (warning) > 40; (critical) > 120
  - gpu_util_60s (warning) > 78%; (critical) > 92%
  - kv_hit_ratio (warning) < 0.35; (critical) < 0.15

Change history:
- 2024-09-12 (Sofia Park) created initial draft focused on topology primitives and kernel selection rules.
- 2025-02-07 (Luis Ortega) added benchmarking touchpoints and sample job YAML.
- 2025-09-18 (Meera Anand) added v3.2.1 release notes and KNOWN-2024-031 mitigation.
- 2025-11-04 (Damien Cole) updated for v3.3.0 dispatch batch-window rollout and telemetry compression note.

If you find gaps or want a visual topology diagram exported as .svg, contact owner-runtime-core@redwood.ai and request "topology-svg".

title: ADR-017: Retention policy evaluation in control plane
content:
## Status
Published (ADR-017)

## Decision summary
Retention policies are evaluated in the **control plane**. Data plane components (log/telemetry stores, purge jobs, exporters) consume a **resolved “effective policy snapshot”** produced by the control plane and do not independently recompute precedence/validation rules.

We will:
- Centralize evaluation, precedence rules, and validation in the control plane (Retention Policy Service + evaluator module).
- Cache effective policy snapshots in the control plane (in-memory + Redis) with explicit invalidation on policy changes.
- Make policy changes and evaluation outputs auditable via immutable change history and audit log events.

## Context
The “Retention controls + compliance reporting pack” program requires consistent enforcement of customer-configurable retention policies across multiple data classes and deployment modes (Hosted / Dedicated / Private). The platform includes multiple storage systems and pipelines (request/response logs, audit logs, traces/metrics, artifacts) where TTL enforcement is implemented via scheduled purge jobs and/or native TTL features.

Key requirements:
- Consistent behavior and terminology (TTL, purge semantics, legal hold, exceptions).
- Strong auditability for customer security reviews and internal audits.
- Operational safety: idempotent purge jobs, observable lag, and safe rollouts.
- Avoid duplicate logic across many services and minimize drift in precedence rules.

## Problem statement
Where should retention policies be evaluated and resolved into enforceable settings?

Two broad options:
1) Evaluate in the data plane (each service/store computes applicable policy based on tenant + region + data class + overrides).
2) Evaluate in the control plane (one canonical evaluation engine; data plane consumes effective results).

## Drivers
- **Auditability:** Single source of truth for “what was the policy at time T?”
- **Consistency:** Avoid divergent implementations of precedence rules.
- **Performance and reliability:** Data plane should be lightweight; control plane must scale and avoid hot paths.
- **Change safety:** Policy changes must be tracked, reviewed, and rolled out predictably.
- **Compliance reporting:** Report pack needs authoritative exports of current and historical retention config.

## Considered options
### Option A: Evaluate in data plane
Each store/purge job would fetch raw policy objects and compute effective values locally.

Pros:
- Reduced dependency on control plane for effective policy reads.
- Potentially simpler request path if policy is needed inline.

Cons:
- Multiple implementations of precedence/validation (high drift risk).
- Harder to audit and reproduce effective policy at time T across services.
- Increased blast radius when rules change.

### Option B: Evaluate in control plane (chosen)
A centralized evaluator resolves raw policy + defaults + overrides into an effective snapshot. Data plane uses the snapshot.

Pros:
- Canonical evaluation behavior; lower drift.
- Central audit trail and reproducible effective policy at time T.
- Enables standardized exports for compliance reporting.

Cons:
- Control plane becomes a dependency for policy distribution.
- Requires caching/invalidation and resilience plan for outages.

## Decision
We choose **Option B**: evaluate retention policies in the **control plane**.

### What “evaluation” includes
The control plane evaluator is responsible for:
- Validation of policy inputs (min/max TTL by tier, data-class support, region constraints).
- Precedence rules across:
  - Product-tier defaults (Hosted/Dedicated/Private)
  - Tenant-level policy
  - Data class overrides (e.g., request_logs vs audit_logs)
  - Region overrides (when supported)
  - Legal hold and approved exceptions
- Computing a normalized effective representation used by enforcement systems.
- Producing a stable export format for compliance packages (see ADR-018).

### What is *not* evaluated in the data plane
Data plane services do not:
- Interpret tier defaults.
- Apply precedence rules.
- Decide whether an override is valid.

Data plane services only:
- Read an effective snapshot (or receive it via config distribution).
- Enforce TTL/purge according to the effective values.

## Effective policy snapshot
### Snapshot characteristics
The effective snapshot is a read-optimized, explicit representation that answers:
- For this tenant + region, what is the retention TTL per data class?
- Are there holds/exceptions that block deletion for a data class?
- When was this computed and from which raw config version?

Minimum fields (conceptual; exact schema tracked in the policy service doc):
- tenant_id
- region (or “global”)
- snapshot_version (monotonic)
- policy_revision_id (raw policy revision)
- generated_at
- data_classes: effective_ttl_days per class
- holds: active holds and scope (data class, time window where applicable)
- notes: warnings (e.g., disabled logging mode for a class)

### Data class alignment
Data classes referenced in evaluation must match Security terminology:
- request_logs (request/response logs)
- prompts_and_completions (only if explicitly stored; may be disabled by configuration)
- audit_logs
- traces
- metrics
- artifacts (e.g., eval datasets where applicable)

## Caching strategy
We cache effective snapshots in the control plane to avoid recomputation and reduce latency.

### Cache layers
1) **Process-local cache** in the Retention Policy Service (fast path)
- Key: (tenant_id, region)
- TTL: 30 seconds
- Eviction: LRU bounded by tenant count

2) **Redis distributed cache** (shared across service replicas)
- Key: retention:effective:{tenant_id}:{region}:{policy_revision_id}
- TTL: 10 minutes
- Negative caching: 60 seconds for “no policy configured” (tenant uses defaults)

### Cache invalidation
Invalidation is event-driven with TTL backstop:
- On policy create/update/delete OR hold/exception change:
  - Increment policy_revision_id
  - Publish invalidation event (internal bus topic: retention.policy.changed)
  - Evict local cache entries for affected tenant_id across replicas
  - Allow Redis entries to expire naturally OR evict by prefix when feasible

### Consistency model
- Effective snapshot reads are **eventually consistent** with target propagation under 60 seconds.
- Purge jobs must tolerate a short propagation delay and rely on verification metrics (see Monitoring).

## Auditability and change history
### Requirements
We must be able to answer:
- Who changed retention settings?
- What changed (diff), when, and why (reason/issue link)?
- What was the effective retention at any point in time?

### Control plane audit trail
The Retention Policy Service will:
- Store an immutable revision log for retention policy objects and hold/exception objects.
- Record the actor (user/service), authentication context, source (Console/API/Terraform), and request ID.

### Audit log events
On each change, emit audit events (exportable via the audit-log-exporter):
- retention_policy.created
- retention_policy.updated
- retention_policy.deleted
- retention_hold.created
- retention_hold.released
- retention_exception.approved
- retention_exception.revoked

Each event must include:
- tenant_id
- policy_revision_id
- actor_id + actor_type
- changed_fields summary
- justification (free text + ticket link when provided)

### Evidence expectations
Compliance report generation will include:
- Current effective snapshot export
- Change history for a requested time window
- Audit log coverage summary of retention change events

## Operational and reliability considerations
### Control plane dependency
Data plane enforcement must not hard-fail if the control plane is temporarily unavailable.

Mechanisms:
- Purge jobs operate on the **last known effective snapshot** persisted locally (per store) with:
  - max_staleness: 24 hours for continuing enforcement
  - alerts if snapshot age > 2 hours (configurable per environment)
- If no snapshot has ever been fetched, jobs must fall back to **secure tier defaults** (favor longer retention vs accidental over-deletion) and emit a high-severity alert.

### Why “favor longer retention” on missing policy
Accidental deletion is typically irreversible and creates customer impact. Temporary over-retention is treated as a compliance risk and must be surfaced via alerts and evidence, but is safer than permanent data loss. This posture is explicitly documented in the retention controls overview and risk assessment.

### Performance
Effective snapshot evaluation is not on the request serving path for inference traffic. Enforcement reads occur via scheduled jobs and admin/reporting flows.

## Security considerations
- Policy write endpoints require Security Admin / Org Admin privileges (RBAC enforced in control plane).
- Hold/exception actions require additional approval workflow as documented in Legal Hold & Exceptions.
- All policy and hold objects are classified as internal configuration; exports for customers must be scoped to their tenant.
- Snapshots must not include sensitive request content; only configuration metadata.

## Monitoring and verification
To ensure evaluation + distribution behaves correctly, we will track:
- retention_effective_snapshot_age_seconds{tenant,region}
- retention_policy_propagation_lag_seconds{tenant,region} (time from change event to observed snapshot update in data plane)
- retention_policy_eval_failures_total (by error class: validation, datastore, cache)

Verification dashboards and alerts are defined in the Retention Controls Verification Dashboards page.

## Consequences
### Positive
- Single, testable evaluation engine and precedence rules.
- Stronger compliance story: reproducible effective policy + audit trail.
- Lower engineering overhead across stores/purge jobs.

### Negative / tradeoffs
- Requires robust caching/invalidation and snapshot distribution.
- Control plane changes (schema/rules) must be managed carefully with backwards compatibility.

## Implementation notes (non-normative)
- Evaluator module lives with the control plane Retention Policy Service and is used by:
  - Console read views (effective retention display)
  - Export endpoints for compliance pack
  - Data plane snapshot fetch endpoint
- Policy changes must be tagged with a policy_revision_id and persisted before publishing invalidation.
- Data plane consumers should use ETag/If-None-Match semantics to reduce bandwidth and avoid thrash.

## Rollout plan
1) Land evaluator + snapshot endpoint behind feature flag (internal tenants only).
2) Enable for audit_logs and request_logs enforcement stores first.
3) Add traces/metrics and artifact classes once enforcement paths are ready.
4) Turn on compliance pack exports using the same snapshot representation.

## Open questions
- Private/on-prem deployments: confirm whether snapshot distribution is pull-based only (recommended) or supports push for restricted networks.
- Region override semantics: confirm which tiers allow per-region differences and how to represent “global” vs explicit region entries.
- Legal hold scope: whether holds can be time-windowed per class in v1 or only “hold all” for a class.

## References
- Retention policy schema and validation rules
- Legal hold and retention exceptions policy
- Data deletion and TTL enforcement standards
- ADR-018: Compliance report pack export format

title: Shadow Eval Stitching and Synthetic Probe Manifest
content:
Summary
This document defines the stitching protocol between shadow evaluations and production telemetry and provides a canonical manifest format for synthetic probes. The goal is to ensure that shadowed traffic, synthetic probes, and production traces can be correlated end-to-end so that hallucination, latency, and quantization-sensitive regressions are attributable to concrete inputs and runtime conditions.

Scope
- Applies to all shadow deployments for Hosted, Dedicated, and Private modes.
- Applies to evaluation harnesses that generate synthetic probes, load profiles, and edge-case fuzzing.
- Does NOT replace per-model onboarding acceptance criteria; it augments traceability during continuous evaluation and rollouts.

Owner and stakeholders
- Owner: Applied ML — Eval Harness (team: eval-harness)
- Primary stakeholders: Model Onboarding, Serving Runtime, Observability, SRE, Customer Success
- Review cadence: quarterly or after any major tracing/telemetry pipeline change

Definitions
- Shadow eval: a non-production model or model variant that receives mirrored or forked traffic for evaluation without affecting the user response.
- Synthetic probe: a scripted or generated input designed to exercise a specific prompt family, long-context behavior, or quantization corner case.
- Stitch key: a deterministic identifier included in all telemetry and probe payloads used to correlate traces across systems.

Design goals
1) Deterministic correlate-ability: each synthetic probe or shadowed request must carry a stitch key that maps to a single probe manifest entry.
2) Low-cardinality telemetry: stitch keys should be hashed/namespace-limited to avoid high-cardinality explosion in observability backends.
3) Privacy-preserving: manifests must not contain PII and must obey probe-privacy budgets defined in quality guardrails.
4) Robustness across networks: support for cross-region routing and fallback to local tracing when cross-region headers are stripped.

High-level architecture
- Probe generator (Eval Harness) emits probe payloads with: probe_id, stitch_key, probe_family, version, expected_behavior_tags, and telemetry_hints.
- Shadow router mirrors production requests and injects stitch_key when present; if missing, a deterministic derivation is applied and logged.
- Inference runtime attaches runtime metadata (model_variant, kernel_profile, quant_profile, kv_cache_hit) to the same stitch_key in spans.
- Observability pipeline (traces, logs, metrics) indexes stitch_key and materializes a composite view for investigations.

Probe manifest format (canonical)
- The manifest is a line-oriented JSONL catalog where each entry is a single synthetic probe specification. Fields: probe_id, probe_family, created_by, intent, payload_snippet, expected_assertions, tags, sampling_rate, privacy_tier, ttl_days, anchor_seed.

Example manifest entry (JSONL line):
{
  "probe_id": "sp-2026-0007",
  "probe_family": "fewshot-instruction-clarity",
  "created_by": "Aisha Kapoor",
  "intent": "verify few-shot instruction-following under q4_8 quant profile",
  "payload_snippet": "{\"instruction\": \"Summarize the following conversation in one sentence...\"}",
  "expected_assertions": ["contains_summary", "<=2_sentence_length"],
  "tags": ["quant-sensitive", "long-context", "regression-critical"],
  "sampling_rate": "0.002",
  "privacy_tier": "redacted",
  "ttl_days": "90",
  "anchor_seed": "seed-3571"
}

Probe manifest best practices
- Keep payload_snippet minimal and representative; store full payloads in a separate, access-controlled artifact store governed by privacy budgets.
- Use privacy_tier = redacted|anonymized|clear to indicate storage/annotation constraints.
- sampling_rate expresses fraction of production-equivalent traffic to tag or inject with probes. For expensive probes use sampling_rate <= 0.001.

Stitch key policy
1) Format: <project_prefix>-<probe_id_or_hash>-<short-hash> (example: rwd-sp-0007-9f3b).
2) Deterministic derivation: if a request contains an anchor_seed or client_request_id, derive the stitch key by HMAC_SHA256(anchor_seed || client_request_id) and truncate to 12 chars.
3) Observability retention: store stitch_key as a low-cardinality tag; index exact mappings in a separate probe-index service for lookups.

Observability schema additions
- Tracing span attributes to include: stitch.key, probe.id, probe.family, model.variant, quant.profile, kernel.profile, kv_cache_hit (true|false), prompt.slice_id.
- Metric labels: probe_family, stitch_bucket (hashed namespace), quant_profile.
- Log enrichment: every error log emitted during a probe evaluation must include stitch.key and model.variant.

Correlation and debugging playbook (step-by-step)
1) Alert fires on a fidelity or latency regression slice (observability dashboard or eval gate).
2) Open the probe dashboard and locate top failing probe_family and top probe_id list for the time window.
3) Use stitch_key to gather spans across frontend, router, runtime, and metrics ingestion.
4) Confirm runtime metadata: model.variant, quant.profile, kernel.profile, and kv_cache_hit.
5) If quant.profile differs from expected in manifest, tag as quant-mismatch and escalate to QuantOps team.
6) If kv_cache_hit is false for a probe designed to exercise cache-sensitive behavior, mark as cache-warmup-mismatch and add to cache-priming queue.
7) If sample_size insufficient for triage, bump sampling_rate for those probe_id entries in the next manifest push (see manifest release procedure).

Manifest release and rollout procedure
1) Author creates a manifest branch in the probe repo and adds new JSONL entries.
2) Run local manifest-lint (scripts/manifest_lint.py) that enforces privacy_tier, TTL, and tag whitelist.
3) Create a PR and request reviewers: Applied ML + Observability.
4) Merge to main triggers CI that: uploads full-payload artifacts to secure storage, assigns probe_id -> artifact mappings, and emits a manifest release blob versioned by semver (e.g., v1.14.0).
5) Canary rollout: release to 1% of shadow capacity for 24h, monitor the stitch_key-indexed fidelity and latency dashboards.
6) Full rollout: expand to target sampling_rate across shadow fleets.

Rollforward / rollback triggers
- Rollforward: failing probes that are noisy but reveal root cause should be promoted to model-onboard tickets and retained for 180 days.
- Rollback: any probe that causes production impact (rare but possible via middleware bug) triggers immediate manifest rollback and revert PR; SRE incident process applies.

Security and privacy controls
- Probes labeled privacy_tier=redacted must not include user-generated content; those labeled anonymized may include hashed user ids only.
- Access to the full payload artifact store requires audit-enabled ACLs; all accesses are logged.
- Synthetic probes that interact with third-party connectors must be approved by Security and Compliance.

Tracing and storage cost mitigations
- Use stitch_bucket (namespace-truncated value) as a lookup key to avoid high-cardinality tags in metrics.
- Aggregate span counts by probe_family hourly for 90-day retention; drop raw spans older than the probe TTL unless flagged for active investigation.

Operational runbook: common triage scenarios
- Scenario A: sudden spike in token-level hallucination for a probe_family
  1) Confirm the probe manifest version and anchor_seed.
  2) Check model.variant and quant.profile for recent rollouts.
  3) If a change in quant.profile correlates, open QuantOps ticket with probe_id, stitch_key examples, and sample outputs.

- Scenario B: latency SLO breach for long-context probes
  1) Verify kernel.profile and batch sizes in runtime spans.
  2) If batch size increase correlates with higher p95, tag as batching-clash and consider lowering batch target for that model.variant.

Telemetry examples and CLI snippets
- Emit probe with stitch key (curl example):
  curl -X POST https://eval-harness.internal/v1/probe_emit \\n    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \\n    -d '{"probe_id":"sp-2026-0007","stitch_key":"rwd-sp-0007-9f3b","payload":{"instruction":"Summarize..."}}'

- Minimal manifest-lint command:
  python scripts/manifest_lint.py --manifest manifests/sp-updates.jsonl

Open questions and future work
- Automated stitch_key rotational policy to reduce long-term traceability risk vs. the need for deterministic correlation.
- Smarter probe scheduling that adapts sampling_rate per slice based on recent signal-to-noise.
- Probe consolidation: dedupe probes whose payloads are semantically equivalent under the prompt-normalizer.

Appendices
A) Probe tag taxonomy (short):
- reg-critical, quant-sensitive, long-context, caching-sensitive, functioncall, multi-turn

B) Example probe-index lookup (CLI):
  rwd-probe-lookup --stitch rwd-sp-0007-9f3b --window 2026-02-20T00:00Z/2026-02-20T04:00Z

C) Contact list
- Applied ML (eval-harness): aisha.kapoor@redwood.ai
- Observability: marco.li@redwood.ai
- QuantOps: sofia.martinez@redwood.ai

Related artifacts
- manifests/ (probe repo) — canonical JSONL manifests and release notes
- scripts/manifest_lint.py — lint and privacy checks
- dashboards/probe-fidelity — stitch_key-indexed fidelity dashboard

Revision history
- 2026-01-15: created by Aisha Kapoor
- 2026-02-28: added canary rollout guidance and sampling mitigations (Marco Li)

title: SLO Adaptive Guardian and Capacity Playbook
content:
Overview

This playbook defines the SLO Adaptive Guardian — a decision and automation layer that protects critical SLOs by combining predictive telemetry signals, tenant-aware fairness controls, and capacity commitment policies. The document covers signal definitions, decision logic, automated actions (soft and hard), owner responsibilities, verification steps, and example configuration snippets for Redwood's operational tooling.

Purpose and scope

- Purpose: Reduce mean time to safe-degradation and preserve overall customer experience when capacity stress or quality regressions threaten SLOs.
- Scope: Applies to the model-serving tier and associated request-routing proxies for hosted and dedicated clusters. Excluded: private/on-prem where local policies override central automation unless explicitly opted in.

Key concepts

1) Guardian signal types (inputs)
- SLO burn-rate: rolling 1h and 6h burn-rate for primary SLOs (p99 latency, availability).
- Synthetic canary divergence: canary generation error/quality regressions measured by eval sentinel suite (daily).
- Queue pressure: per-cluster queue depth and tail-quantile queue time (90/95/99).
- Token headroom: available GPU token capacity vs reserved capacity (in token/sec).
- Tenant imbalance score: short-term deviation from expected fairness share (0-100).
- Telemetry fidelity indicator: percentage of requests with full traces/telemetry; degraded fidelity reduces automation confidence.

2) Action tiers
- Advisory: non-blocking notifications to oncall and product owners (email/Slack).
- Soft degradation: policy changes that preserve functionality but reduce per-request resource cost (e.g., reduce max_tokens, disable heavy-tooling, shorten context window).
- Throttle & shed: tenant-level soft throttles (rate limits) and request shedding (reject with 429 or queue-drop) per priority lane.
- Capacity commit: trigger dedicated pool warm-ups or request provisioning (subject to procurement guardrails).
- Hard fallback: automatic model variant switch (to smaller quantized or cheaper model) or region-level reroute.

Decisioning matrix (high level)

The Guardian evaluates signals on three axes: severity, certainty, and tenant impact. The decision sequence is deterministic and aims to minimize customer-visible errors while restoring SLOs quickly.

1) Severity assessment
- Low: 1h burn-rate < 2x target and headroom > 20% -> Advisory only.
- Medium: 1h burn-rate 2x–5x or headroom 10–20% -> Soft degradation + Advisory.
- High: 1h burn-rate > 5x or headroom < 10% or canary divergence severe -> Throttle & capacity commit + Advisory.
- Critical: sustained 6h burn-rate > 10x, telemetry shows correlated queue saturation -> Hard fallback and incident declaration.

2) Certainty check
- If telemetry fidelity < 60%: treat actions as advisory and require manual confirmation.
- If synthetic canary divergence present and corroborated by user-facing error spikes: treat as higher certainty.

3) Tenant fairness enforcement
- For multi-tenant clusters, apply proportional throttles using Tenant Imbalance Score. Priority lanes (internal, enterprise, self-serve) have delta budgets and decay windows.
- Example: if imbalance score > 40 for tenant T, cap T's QPS to min(expected_qps * 0.6, configured_throttle_limit) with exponential backoff for repeat offenders.

Runbook: step-by-step response (oncall primary)

1) Detection and acknowledgement
  a) Guardian posts automated advisory in #oncall-alerts with signal summary and suggested action.
  b) Oncall acknowledges within 5 minutes; if no ack, escalation to SRE lead and auto-notify pager.

2) Preliminary verification (10–15 minutes)
  a) Confirm signal in both primary telemetry and replicated logs (clickhouse / archive).
  b) Validate canary behavior: run a quick canary job that executes 50 synthetic requests across top-3 models.
  c) Check telemetry fidelity; if < 60%, capture a manual trace sample from a small set of affected tenants.

3) Execute soft actions (if recommended)
  a) Apply soft degradation policy via routing control-plane (example CLI below).
  b) Monitor SLO impact over next 10m — specifically p95/p99 latency and error-rate.

4) Escalate to throttle & capacity commit (if thresholds breached)
  a) Run tenant fairness scoring and produce throttle proposal.
  b) Execute throttles using the throttler API with a 5-minute ramp.
  c) Trigger capacity commit: send provisioning request to capacity-orchestrator with justification and expected token delta.
  d) Update ticket and notify product owners and customer success for impacted enterprise tenants.

5) Hard fallback and incident declaration
  a) If SLOs remain breached after 30–60 minutes and headroom not recovered, execute hard fallback: model variant switch and cross-region failover as specified in fallbacks table.
  b) Declare incident and follow incident lifecycle (pager, comms, postmortem).

6) Recovery and unwind
  a) Gradually restore throttles and soft degradations once 1h burn-rate < 1.1x and p99 latency within SLO for 30 consecutive minutes.
  b) When capacity is healthy, run a controlled rollback A/B for any model switches (canary first).
  c) Document all actions and annotate telemetry with action tags for post-incident analysis.

Example CLI snippets and config (illustrative)

- Apply soft degradation (reduce max tokens):
  rdctl config apply --service=model-serving --policy=soft-degrade --set max_tokens=512 --reason="Guardian soft degrade: high burn-rate"

- Propose and apply tenant throttle:
  rdctl throttler propose --tenant=acme-inc --qps=150 --duration=15m --reason="tenant imbalance score 52"
  rdctl throttler apply --proposal=12345 --ramp=5m

- Capacity commit request (JSON payload for orchestrator):
  {"cluster":"us-west-3","tokens_requested":120000,"priority":"urgent","owner":"eng-sre","justification":"restore p99 latency for hosted API"}

Telemetry & measurement table (thresholds)

| Metric | Warning | Action (soft) | Action (hard) | Owner |
| p99 latency | > 80th percentile baseline | Notify | fallback | runtime-sre |
| 1h burn-rate | > 2x | soft degrade | throttle + commit | runtime-sre |
| Queue depth (cluster) | > 70% capacity | soft degrade | hard shed | platform-mesh |
| Telemetry fidelity | < 60% | advisory | manual confirm required | observability |
| Tenant imbalance | > 30 | advisory + throttle proposal | prioritized eviction | service-owner |

Operational tooling integration points

- Guardian Decision Engine: evaluates signals and emits proposals (runs in control-plane, versioned).
- Throttler API: supports propose/apply/retract and records audit events.
- Capacity Orchestrator: accepts token requests with urgency tags and returns provisioning ETA.
- Telemetry indexer: fast path for burn-rate and queue metrics; must provide p99 within 60s.
- Evidence store: attach action tags to traces and token samples for postmortem.

Ownership and SLAs for automation

- Runtime SRE: custodian of the Guardian decision rules, burn-rate thresholds, and action playbook.
- Platform Mesh: owner of throttler and queue metrics.
- Observability: telemetry fidelity and synthetic canary ownership.
- Product/customer-success: notified owners for enterprise-impacted actions.

Automation constraints and safety checks

- All automated hard fallbacks require corroboration by at least two independent signals (e.g., burn-rate + queue saturation or canary divergence + user error spike).
- Tenants with contractual SLAs (enterprise) must be excluded from aggressive preemptive eviction unless approved by SRE lead and CS.
- Any capacity commit > 100k tokens must follow approval workflow and include cost estimate.

Post-incident analysis and continuous improvement

1) Action tagging: every Guardian action should attach tags to traces and a summary event in the evidence store.
2) 72-hour retrospective: SRE lead files a short incident analysis (root cause, decision correctness, automation behavior, gaps) and recommended policy changes.
3) Simulation lab: monthly, run a Guardian simulation against recorded traffic to validate false-positive/negative rates.

Appendix: example policy JSON (single-line for insertion)

{"policy_name":"guardian_default_v3","slo_targets":{"p99_latency_ms":350,"availability_pct":99.9},"burn_rate_thresholds":{"warning":2.0,"soft":3.5,"hard":7.0},"telemetry_fidelity_min":0.6,"tenant_fairness":{"decay_window_mins":60,"max_throttle_pct":40}}

Related pages and templates

- Use SLO definition template for new services (link in related_pages).
- Attach this playbook as a dependency for service onboarding checklists that request admission into multi-tenant clusters.

Revision history

- 2027-02-14: Created initial draft (Aisha Patel).
- 2027-06-01: Added tenant fairness matrix and CLI examples (Liam Chen).
- 2027-09-03: Formalized automation safeguards and approval gates (SRE leadership).

Notes and open questions

- Evaluate integration with cost-aware routing to prevent repeated capacity commits for cost-sensitive customers.
- Define explicit exemption process for partners with custom throttling needs.

End of document.

title: runtime-aware-probe-synthesis-and-quant-compatibility-manual
content:
summary:
Procedure and operational manual for generating eval probes that reflect runtime behavior and for tagging probes with quant-compatibility signals used by onboarding and rollout gates.

content:
Overview:
This page describes the end-to-end process for runtime-aware probe synthesis and for establishing quant-compatibility signals that feed model onboarding, shadow evaluation, and rollout gating. The goal is to produce probes that represent real service traffic and to label those probes with explicit compatibility metadata for quantized artifacts and KV-cache behaviors.

Scope and audience:
- Scope: eval probe generation, runtime telemetry mapping, quant-compatibility tagging, acceptance thresholds, triage flow for probe failures.
- Audience: Evaluator engineers, model-onboarding owners, runtime SREs, quantization engineers.

Why runtime-aware probes?
1. Synthetic probes that ignore runtime distribution (seq lengths, concurrency patterns, cache-hit profiles) miss edge-failure modes introduced by batching, KV-cache and quantized kernels.
2. Runtime-aware probes enable earlier detection of quant-induced coherence degradation, streaming/functioncall instability, and tail-latency regressions.

Definitions:
- Probe: a single input (or small set) used by the eval harness to exercise model behavior.
- Quant-compatibility flag: metadata on a probe indicating likely sensitivity to quantization (high/medium/low).
- Runtime fingerprint: vector summarizing request features observed in production (avg_seq_len, prefix_reuse_rate, kv_cache_hit, streaming_fraction, avg_tokens).

Ownership and SLAs:
- Probe Fabrication Service (team: eval-fabric) owns the probe generator code and templates.
- Model Onboarding owns mapping rules used by promotion gates.
- Runtime SRE owns telemetry signals (latency P95/P99, cache hit rate) and ensures feeds are available.
- SLA: daily refresh of runtime fingerprint feed; probe generator should produce a new candidate set within 4 hours of a fingerprint change.

High-level workflow (numbered):
1. Collect runtime fingerprints (see Telemetry feeds below).
2. Synthesize a stratified probe set honoring fingerprint strata (e.g., 0-32 tokens / 33-128 / 129+; cache_high/cache_low).
3. Annotate each probe with quant-compatibility heuristics and an uncertainty score.
4. Run fast micro-shadow eval against baseline non-quantized model.
5. Run quantized artifact sweep (parallelized) and compute fidelity deltas per probe slice.
6. Produce a compatibility manifest (JSON) used by the deployment gate.

Telemetry feeds (signals to collect):
- avg_seq_len (rolling 24h)
- prefix_reuse_rate (fraction of requests with repeated prefixes in last 7d)
- kv_cache_hit_rate (per-service)
- streaming_fraction (percent of requests that used streaming or functioncalls)
- batch_size_distribution (histogram)
- p95_latency_ms, p99_latency_ms
- model_variant_ratio (fraction of traffic hitting each variant)

Probe synthesis rules (bulleted):
- Stratify by sequence length: sample proportions should match runtime fingerprint +/-10%.
- Cache-sensitive probes: include at least 20% with high prefix_reuse_rate when runtime shows reuse_rate>0.3.
- Streaming/functioncall probes: preserve original turn boundaries and function calling sequences.
- Adversarial edgecases: synthesize 5% of probes with high-entropy/noise perturbations for robustness checks.

Quant-compatibility scoring (table as text):
- High: long sequences (>512), high prefix_reuse, many functioncalls. (Score label: "quant-sensitive-high")
- Medium: moderate seq lengths (128-512), mixed cache patterns. (Label: "quant-sensitive-medium")
- Low: short responses (<128), no KV-cache dependency. (Label: "quant-insensitive")

Acceptance criteria (example):
- Per-slice fidelity: mean BLEU/ROUGE/embedding-cosine delta <= 0.015 (or service-specific metric) for medium/low slices.
- High-sensitive slice: max allowed delta 0.03 but must pass manual review before rollout.
- Tail-latency: quant artifact P99 <= baseline P99 * 1.2.

Probe manifest example (YAML snippet):
```yaml
- probe_id: P-2026-0001
  fingerprint: seq_len=64,kvcache=low,streaming=false
  quant_label: quant-insensitive
  uncertainty: 0.12
  origin: runtime-sampled/2026-02-09
```

CLI usage (probe generator):
```bash
# synthesize probes for service 'chat-api' using fingerprint snapshot 2026-02-09
python -m eval_fabric.generate --service chat-api --fingerprint snapshot/2026-02-09 --out probes/chat-api-20260209.json
```

Operational gating and automation (step checklist):
1. New quant artifact published -> CI triggers quant-sweep job across latest probe manifest.
2. Sweep computes per-probe deltas and flags slices where thresholds are breached.
3. If any high-sensitive slice breaches, fail gate and notify onboarding@redwood.com.
4. If only medium/low slices breach, auto-create triage ticket with classification and attach diff artifacts.
5. Auto-generate a remediation suggestion: (a) increase quant-precision for embedding/kvcache kernels, (b) add targeted probes to cover failing prompt family, (c) fallback to non-quant variant for rollout.

Triage playbook (when sweep fails):
- Immediate checks (5–15 minutes):
  1) Re-run sweep with a different random seed to rule out sampling noise.
  2) Verify artifact was built with expected params: quant_bits, group_size, kernel_patch_id.
  3) Check runtime cache-change events in last 24h.
- Diagnostic steps (15–120 minutes):
  1) Compare top-10 probes by failure magnitude and annotate shared features.
  2) Re-run only those probes against a mixed-precision artifact.
  3) If differences persist, schedule human-in-the-loop evaluation and mark model onboarding as blocked.

Telemetry queries (prometheus / timeseries examples):
- avg_seq_len: sum(rate(request_tokens_total[1h])) / sum(rate(requests_total[1h]))
- kvcache-hit: increase(kvcache_hit_total[24h]) / increase(kvcache_lookups_total[24h])
- p99 latency per-variant: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, variant))

Rollout and mitigation strategies:
- Canary policy: deploy quant artifact to 1% traffic with canary probes duplicated from production traffic for 24h.
- Auto-fallback: if fidelity delta > threshold OR p99 latency > 1.2x baseline for canary, automatically shift canary to non-quant variant and open rollback ticket.
- Gradual ramp: 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100% with checks at each stage computed from probe-sweep metrics.

Related pages:
- /applied-ml-and-evals/model-onboarding/inference-readiness-eval-matrix-and-promotion-playbook-2026
- /applied-ml-and-evals/quantization-profiles/quant-profile-synthesis-and-safety-playbook-2024

Change log:
- 2026-02-10: Initial draft and validation with eval-fabric team.
- 2026-03-05: Updated acceptance thresholds and added CLI examples after SRE feedback.

Appendix: quick-check checklist (one-line bullets):
- Confirm fingerprint feed freshness < 24h.
- Confirm probe sample proportions match fingerprint +/-10%.
- Ensure quant-sweep run completes in < 2h for initial candidate set.
- Tag failing probes with precise kernel IDs and attach diffs to triage ticket.

Contact and escalation:
- Primary: eval-fabric@redwood.com
- Oncall (runtime-sre): #runtime-oncall on Slack
- Model Onboarding lead: Maya Chen (maya@redwood.com)

title: Confidence Funnel and Dynamic Probe Gating — Eval-Orchestrator Playbook
content:
Overview

Purpose: This playbook defines the Confidence Funnel pattern and the Dynamic Probe Gating policy used by the eval-orchestrator to allocate probe budget, prioritize slices, and reduce alert noise while preserving sensitivity to real regressions. It is intended for ML engineers, evaluators, and platform SREs responsible for promotion gating and longtail monitoring.

Problem statement:
- Continuous eval pipelines send a high volume of probes across many slices; naive thresholds lead to alert spam or missed regressions.
- We need a structured, auditable policy that tunes sampling intensity based on observed model confidence and probe signal.

Goals:
- Maintain detection precision >= 0.85 for high-severity regressions (policy target).
- Maintain mean probe cost per model per day below configured budget (default $250/day).
- Reduce low-signal alerts by 60% versus fixed-threshold gating.

Key concepts

1) Confidence Funnel (CF): a tiered decision flow that assigns probes to bands based on model response confidence, recent drift, and slice criticality. Bands:
- Band A (investigate immediately): low confidence (<0.40) OR degraded anchor coverage OR safety sentinel fails. High-urgency; 100% probe retention + human review.
- Band B (fast follow-up): medium-low confidence [0.40,0.65) and trending down; adaptive resample rate x2 for 4 hours.
- Band C (routine scan): confidence [0.65,0.90); periodic sampling at baseline rate.
- Band D (safety-maintenance): confidence >= 0.90 and no telemetry anomalies; sparse sampling (0.5x baseline).

2) Dynamic Probe Gating (DPG): runtime policy that adjusts sampling fraction and probe routing based on CF band, SLO deficit, and available eval budget. DPG enforces:
- Minimum detectability: ensure a slice has at least N=30 probes in the last 24h if it is Band A or critical customer slice.
- Budget-aware throttling: if daily budget burn rate > 90%, reduce Band D sampling first.
- Hedged sampling: for ambiguous slices (confidence 0.45–0.55) route duplicated probes to two different model variants to increase signal fidelity.

When to use

- New model promotions, quantized rollouts, A/B experiments, or customer-facing feature changes.
- Ongoing continuous monitoring where probe volume and slice cardinality are moderate-to-high.

Roles & ownership

- Eval-Orchestrator Team: implements DPG runtime and provides metrics. (Owner: Eval-Orchestrator)
- Model Onboarding / Applied ML Team: defines critical slices, anchor prompts, and probe families. (Owner: Model Onboarding)
- Incident Response / SRE: integrates alerts to oncall and defines remediation runbooks.

SLOs and thresholds

| Metric | Target | Alert threshold | Responsible |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Detection precision (high-sev) | >= 0.85 | < 0.80 for 3h | Applied ML
| Avg probes per model / day | <= $250 (cost) | > $300 (3d rolling) | Eval-Orchestrator
| Probe coverage (critical slices) | >= 95% | < 90% | Model Onboarding
| False positive alert rate | <= 12% | > 20% | SRE/Applied ML

Configuration examples

Example gating policy (YAML):

policy_id: cf-default-2026
banding:
  - name: Band A
    confidence_max: 0.40
    min_probes_24h: 30
    retain: true
  - name: Band B
    confidence_min: 0.40
    confidence_max: 0.65
    resample_multiplier: 2
    window_hours: 4
  - name: Band C
    confidence_min: 0.65
    confidence_max: 0.90
    baseline_sample: 1.0
  - name: Band D
    confidence_min: 0.90
    baseline_sample: 0.5
budgeting:
  daily_usd_cap: 250
  burn_rate_scale: 0.9

DPG runtime decision pseudocode:

1. Ingest probe result R with fields: slice_id, confidence_score, telemetry_flags, timestamp.
2. Map confidence_score to CF band.
3. If telemetry_flags include safety_fail OR slice criticality == high -> promote to Band A.
4. If Band A -> ensure retention and create high-priority task for human review.
5. Else consult budget: if projected_daily_burn > daily_usd_cap * burn_rate_scale -> reduce Band D sampling by 80%.
6. Log decision with trace-id and metric tags: cf_band, sample_fraction, budget_headroom.

Runtime telemetry & graphs to surface

- CF band distribution over time (per-model, per-slice)
- Daily probe cost burn and projected end-of-day spend
- Band transition heatmap (how slices migrate across bands in last 72h)
- Hedged-sample agreement rate (fraction of hedged duplicated probes with matching label)
- Alert signal-to-noise (alerts accepted by humans / alerts triggered)

Alerting and operator flow

Primary alerts (wired to eval-oncall):
1) Detection precision drop: trigger when detection precision < 0.80 for 3h (pager).
2) Budget overrun: projected burn > daily cap*1.10 (page on-call finance liaison).
3) Critical-slice coverage loss: critical slice probe count < min_probes_24h (email + slack channel).

Operator runbook (short):
1. Acknowledge alert and check CF band distribution dashboard.
2. For precision drops: run hedged-replay for top-10 affected slices (see commands below).
3. If hedged-replay confirms regression, escalate to Applied ML and open regression ticket with artifacts: sample probes, model versions, kernel profile.
4. For budget alerts: temporarily throttle Band D via DPG admin UI and notify stakeholders.

Example commands

# run hedged replay for a slice (CLI)
redwood-eval replay --slice-id SLC-2025-42 --window 24h --variants base,quantized --output /tmp/replay-2026.json

# query band distribution (PromQL example)
sum by (cf_band, model) (rate(eval_probe_count[1h]))

Quality & regression triage integration

- Tie CF/DPG metadata into regression triage: every regression incident must include the CF band history and the DPG decisions for the preceding 48h. This reduces attribution ambiguity.
- When promoting model variants, run a promotion-blocking gate that requires: no Band A slices, hedged-agreement >= 0.9 on calibration set, and quantized-avg-latency < latency-SLO + 10%.

Operational considerations and caveats

- Cold-starts: new slices with insufficient history default to Band B with an elevated sampling multiplier for first 6h.
- Adversarial probes: apply rate-limiting and miner heuristics to prevent a noisy client from forcing Band A status.
- Privacy: don't persist raw user text for non-annotated probes; store fingerprints and embedding hashes.

Testing & rollout plan

1) Staging-only shadow run (2 weeks): enable CF+DPG in shadow leaving production decisions unchanged. Collect metrics.
2) Canary rollout (5% of probe volume): enable gating decisions for non-critical slices. Monitor detection precision and budget.
3) Gradual promotion (25%, 50%, 100%): ramp up with pause points and automatic rollback thresholds: precision < 0.82 or budget > 1.15x for 24h.

Audit & reproducibility

- Persist the gating policy version and policy_id with every probe event.
- Store replay checkpoints every 12 hours for 30 days to enable deterministic replay for triage.

Appendices

A. Example hedged routing JSON (for the router service)
{
  "slice_id": "SLC-2025-42",
  "probes": [
    {"variant": "base", "sample_fraction": 1.0},
    {"variant": "quant-8bit", "sample_fraction": 1.0}
  ],
  "explain_tags": ["hedged:confidence-0.52", "reason:ambiguous-band"]
}

B. Example annotation contract for human review
- Minimum context provided: prompt id, model version, top-3 token probabilities (optional), deterministic seed, and anchor label.
- Annotator task: label whether response is "acceptable" | "unsafe" | "incorrect" with brief rationale.

C. Related telemetry panels (dashboard IDs)
- CF_BAND_DISTRIBUTION: dash-3371
- HEDGED_AGREEMENT_RATE: dash-3410
- PROBE_BUDGET_SPEND: dash-3499

Notes and change log

- 2025-11-12: Initial draft (Asha Menon).
- 2026-01-15: Added hedging policy and canary rollback thresholds (reviewers: Diego, Maya).
- 2026-02-03: Finalized alert thresholds and retention policy; published.

Contact

For implementation questions, ping #eval-orchestrator on Slack or contact the owner: eval-orchestrator@redwood.ai

title: Evaluability Operational Patterns: Lifecycle & Rollout Contracts
content:
Summary:
This document defines operational patterns and acceptance contracts that make a model or configuration 'evaluability-ready' for Redwood Inference. It focuses on the full lifecycle from initial onboarding through progressive rollouts, including the evaluation job shape, telemetry gating, and automatic rollback/mitigation actions when quantitative or qualitative gates fail. The guidance is intended for ML engineers, SREs, and product owners managing model promotion across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.

Goals and scope:
- Define a concise evaluability contract that every model/service must satisfy before promotion to canary and production.
- Provide a reproducible lifecycle pattern: admission -> shadow -> micro-canary -> ramp -> full release.
- Specify metric bundles, thresholds, and stability windows used for automated gating.
- Document probe composition and synthetic traffic primitives for quant-sensitive workloads.
- Describe interaction points with quantization profiles and KV-cache-sensitive flows.

Key definitions:
1) Evaluability contract: a machine- and human-readable specification attached to a model artifact describing required probes, acceptance metrics, and rollout policies.
2) Probe: a focused synthetic or sampled workload slice exercising a behavior (e.g., long-context decoding, function-calling, rerank).
3) Shadow vs Micro-canary: shadow runs do not serve live traffic; micro-canaries route a small percentage of live traffic with tight SLOs and fast rollback.

Operational pattern (high level):
