- Model onboarding acceptance matrix: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/model-onboarding/onboarding-acceptance-rubric-kvcache-quant-and-prompt-calibration-2026
- Eval harness job types reference: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/eval-harness/evaluator-interchange-format-and-federation-spec-2026

Revision notes:
- 2025-11-10: Initial draft and prototype runbook.
- 2026-02-04: Added quant-profile validation requirements after a production regression test.
- 2026-09-12: Expanded canary promotion policy and automated rollback rules.

This page is intended to be a living runbook and design spec. Use the reviewers above for changes that affect validation thresholds or the rollout cadence.

title: Privacy-Aware Evaluator Sandbox and Probe Curation Playbook
content:
Overview

This playbook describes the Privacy-Aware Evaluator Sandbox (PAES): a reproducible, auditable environment for running model evaluations and curating probe sets while preserving customer-sensitive signals and supporting quantization-aware workflows. The target audience is applied-ML engineers, evaluator stewards, and Platform SREs who run shadow evaluations against private or dedicated deployments.

Goals

- Enable high-fidelity evals that mimic production traffic while ensuring privacy controls (redaction, differential privacy, and telemetry bucketing).
- Make probe curation reproducible and traceable: provenance, annotator contracts, retention policy.
- Provide a standard config and gating flow for quantization-sensitive evaluations so decisions about model promotion or fallback are clearly justified.
- Ship an operational runbook for triage, rollback, and artifact retention.

Scope and non-goals

- In scope: shadow traffic sampling, probe seeding and pruning, DP-enabled metrics, quantized-replay validation, provenance metadata capture, and sandbox resource tagging.
- Out of scope: customer-facing incident communication templates (see customer-success-and-support), full production migration steps (see model-onboarding).

High-level architecture

1) Ingress: controlled shadow tap that mirrors a sampled subset of production requests into PAES.
2) Probe Fabricator: generator service (hybrid of synthetic + seeded real examples) that emits labeled probes with provenance IDs.
3) Evaluator Workers: containerized evaluation jobs that run model variants (full-precision and quantized) against probe sets.
4) Privacy Layer: redaction hooks, token-level masking, and DP aggregator for metrics.
5) Artifact Store: immutable evaluation snapshots (prompt families, model binary hashes, config yaml, telemetry digest).
6) Triage Dashboard and Alerting: SLO/quality gates integration with Redwood Console.

Ownership and contacts

- Product owner: Applied ML - Maya Thompson (author)
- Engineering lead: Connor Wu
- Privacy reviewer: Elaine González (Legal & Security liaison)
- Oncall triage: eng-sre team (pager: #sre-evals)

Probe lifecycle (detailed)

1. Seed collection
   - Source: production-sampled requests, annotated anonymized support logs, and synthetic generators.
   - Sampling policy: 1% of requests by default, stratified by tenant size and route. For high-risk routes (PII), use 0.1% and DP aggregation.

2. Curation and labeling
   - Annotator contract (must include): label schema, acceptance criteria, inter-annotator agreement threshold (Krippendorff alpha >= 0.7), retention TTL.
   - All probes get provenance_id: PAES-YYYYMMDD-<generator>-<sha1>.

3. Privacy transformation
   - Redaction rules applied in-flight using the redaction pipeline: email, ssn, credit_card, name entities. Rules maintained in: /configs/eval-redaction-registry.yaml.
   - Apply token-level bucketing before retention for analysis.

4. Probe promotion and TTL
   - Fresh probes promoted after passing annotation QA; archived after 180 days unless explicitly flagged for retention.

Quantization-aware evaluation protocol

When evaluating a quantized candidate, follow these steps exactly:

1) Baseline run (FP16 or FP32) on the same probe set to collect reference metrics.
2) Quantized run (target quant profile) with identical RNG seeds and prompt normalization.
3) Replay alignment: use the quantized-replay harness to capture token-level divergences and KV-cache behavior.

Config table (required fields for an evaluation job)

| field | description | example |
|------|-------------|--------|
| job_id | stable evaluation job id | paes-job-20260210-07 |
| model_hash | content-addressed model binary identifier | sha256:abc123... |
| quant_profile | quant strategy used | int8-llm-qs16 |
| probe_manifest | path to probe bundle in artifact store | s3://paes/artifacts/probe-manifests/20260210.json |
| dp_budget | epsilon,delta for DP aggregation | 1.0,1e-5 |
| retention_ttl_days | probe retention policy | 180 |
| owner | team or person accountable | applied-ml/maya-thompson |

(Represent the table above as plain text in Confluence)

Example job config (YAML)

```
job_id: paes-job-20260210-07
model_hash: sha256:abc123def4567890
quant_profile: int8-llm-qs16
probe_manifest: s3://paes/artifacts/probe-manifests/20260210.json
dp_budget:
  epsilon: 1.0
  delta: 1e-5
retention_ttl_days: 180
owner: applied-ml/maya-thompson
```

Privacy controls and DP guidance

- Default DP settings for public-facing routes: epsilon <= 1.0, delta <= 1e-5. For internal-only evaluations use epsilon up to 2.5 with documented approval from Privacy reviewer.
- Metrics must be aggregated using the DP aggregator library (see evaluator-sidecar contract). Raw prompts must never be stored unredacted unless approved and with HSM-backed access controls.
- Telemetry retention: scrubbed telemetry buckets kept for 365 days; full-text probes adhere to retention_ttl_days.

Acceptance criteria and quality gates

Numeric acceptance criteria for promotion to canary: all must be satisfied
- Coherence delta (quantized vs baseline) <= 1.2% on human-anchored coherence metric
- Latency P95 (quantized) <= baseline P95 * 1.35
- Safety sentinel false_positive_delta <= 0.05 absolute
- Embedding drift (cosine) <= 0.03 mean difference

If any gate fails, follow the triage playbook below.

Triage and rollback playbook (operational steps)

1. On alert: capture evaluation job_id, model_hash, quant_profile, and probe_manifest.
2. Reproduce locally with the small-probe-sample (1000 probes) using `paes-run --job <job_id> --sample 1000`.
3. If behavior is reproducible, escalate to applied-ml owner and open a regression issue with labeled artifacts.
4. If not reproducible, check telemetry: RNG seed drift, redaction differences, and hardware affinity mismatches.
5. Rollback criteria: if safety sentinel failure or coherence delta > 3x acceptance threshold, block promotion and revert any canary routing.

Operational commands and examples

- Start a sandbox evaluation (CLI):

```
paes-run --job paes-job-20260210-07 --env sandbox --trace --dp-budget 1.0
```

- Generate a probe manifest from sampled traffic:

```
paes-probe-fab --source mirror-stream --sample-rate 0.01 --out s3://paes/artifacts/probe-manifests/20260210.json
```

Monitoring and alerting

- Dashboards: PAES Quality Overview (per-model, per-quant-profile), Probe Age Distribution, DP Budget Consumption.
- Alerts: quality-gate-failure (severity P1), DP-budget-exhausted (severity P2), artifact-store-mismatch (severity P2).
- Pager assignment: first responder is the Applied ML oncall, then eng-sre after 15 minutes.

Audit and provenance

- Every evaluation produces an immutable artifact bundle: {job_id, model_hash, quant_profile, probe_manifest, dp_budget, run_metadata}. Bundles are hashed and stored in artifact-store with lifecycle policies.
- Manual review checkpoints require two approvers for restricted probes (sensitive customers) and one approver for general probes.

Onboarding checklist for a new evaluator steward

1. Read this playbook and complete privacy training.
2. Get S3 write access to paes artifact bucket (request through infra).
3. Complete hands-on run: execute a baseline run and a quantized run using the sample manifest.
4. Demonstrate ability to interpret DP-aggregated metrics and trace token divergence.
5. Request approval to run restricted-route probes if needed.

References and related docs

- evaluator-onboarding-and-certification-curriculum-2026 (applied-ml-and-evals)
- quant-impact-synthesis-for-prompt-families-2026 (applied-ml-and-evals/quantization-profiles)
- probe-fabricator-and-annotation-charter-2026 (applied-ml-and-evals/prompt-sets-and-benchmarks)

Appendix: common failure modes and mitigations

- Mode: KV-cache divergence between FP baseline and quantized run. Mitigation: enable cache-aligned replay, capture KV-diffs, and re-run with warmed cache.
- Mode: DP budget breach during a long sweep. Mitigation: reduce sample rate, increase bucketing granularity, or request privacy escalation with approval.
- Mode: Annotator drift post-relabel. Mitigation: run adjudication, refresh inter-annotator agreement measures, and freeze slice for retraining.

Contact and escalation matrix

- Applied ML owner: Maya Thompson (maya@redwood.com)
- Privacy liaison: Elaine González (elaine@redwood.com)
- Eng SRE oncall: #sre-evals (pager duty list)

This playbook is expected to evolve. Submit suggested changes via the Confluence edit flow and tag reviewers listed above.

title: Model warmup probe and priming playbook
content:
Summary

This playbook defines a standardized approach for warming and priming models, caches, and serving runtime state before or during rollout. It covers objectives, probe types, probe generation, quantization-aware warmups, monitoring signals, and a regression triage fast-path for warmup-induced failures. Use this doc for: model onboarding, canary rollout preparations, private/dedicated deployment warmups, and automated preflight checks in the eval harness.

Goals and scope

- Reduce first-request tail latency and token p99 inflation during traffic ramp.
- Stabilize KV cache and attention-key/value layout effects so price/quality regressions are reproducible.
- Provide reproducible probe suites that exercise: short-context generations, long-context KV growth, streaming function-calls, and quantized kernel paths.
- Applicable to hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.

Owner and escalation

- Primary owner: Serving Runtime - Warmup & Telemetry team (eng-serving-runtime).
- Secondary owners: Applied ML (evals) and Platform QA.
- On-call escalation: Runbook page: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/kv-cache-warmup-oncall (triage leads: Marcus Lee).

Warmup concepts and terminology

- Warmup probe: A deterministic or sampled request sequence designed to bring runtime state (threads, GPU kernels, KV cache, CUDA context) into steady state.
- Priming prompt: A short contextual preamble appended to user prompts to normalize the model's tokenization/attention behavior during initial requests.
- Cold-to-warm window: Time range after an idle period where performance metrics are expected to improve as warmup completes.
- Quant-aware warmup: Warmup sequence that routes through the same quantized kernels and precision paths as production traffic (e.g., int8 KV ops).

Warmup probe taxonomy (recommended probe types)

1) Micro-latency probes (short-turn generation)
- Purpose: measure token p50/p95/p99 before and after cache prime.
- Example: 3x single-sentence generation (max_tokens=16) with streaming enabled.

2) KV growth probes (increasing context length)
- Purpose: exercise KV cache allocation growth and eviction behavior.
- Example: 5 requests with cumulative context [128, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096] tokens.

3) Long-coherence probes (multi-turn)
- Purpose: validate long-context coherency and attention matrix stability across cached segments.
- Example: 10-turn Q&A where each turn appends ~250 tokens.

4) Function-call & streaming probes
- Purpose: ensure segmented token streaming, function-call triggers, and chunked flushes operate under warmed conditions.

5) Quantization-path probes
- Purpose: verify low-precision execution yields no major quality drift after warmup.
- Example: compare logits/top-k distribution before/after warmup on representative prompt set.

Generating and scheduling probes

- Probe source priorities (in order): 1) production sample replay (privacy-filtered), 2) annotated long-tail probes from prompt catalogue, 3) synthetic adversarial probes.
- Schedule: run micro-latency probes immediately after deployment, KV growth and long-coherence probes during canary stage (0-5% traffic), quant-probes in parallel for dedicated/private.
- Frequency: baseline probes every 10 minutes for first 2 hours; then backoff to hourly for first 24 hours.

Probe configuration reference (table)

| probe_name | request_pattern | tokens | stream | expected_metric_delta | run_stage |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| micro-latency | single-turn short | 8-32 | true | p99 <= baseline + 20ms | immediate |
| kv-growth | cumulative-context | 128-4096 | false | memory delta stable, no OOM | canary |
| long-coherence | multi-turn 10x | 250/turn | true | semantic-similarity >= 0.88 | canary |
| function-stream | short multi-chunk | 32-128 | true | stream-stability >= 99% | immediate |
| quant-path | representative set | 16-512 | false | bleu/metric delta <= 2% | staged |

(Use the above as plain-text CSV when pushing to the eval harness scheduler.)

Example probe JSON (submit to eval harness scheduler)

{
  "probe_id": "warmup-micro-2026-01-15",
  "type": "micro-latency",
  "requests": [
    {"prompt": "Summarize: The acme pipeline failed due to...", "max_tokens": 16, "stream": true},
    {"prompt": "What is the recommended fix for disk pressure?", "max_tokens": 12, "stream": true},
    {"prompt": "List troubleshooting steps for OOM in serving.", "max_tokens": 16, "stream": true}
  ]
}

Quantization-aware warmup notes

- Always run quant-probes using the same quant artifact (checkpoint + quant-profile) as the planned rollout. Small kernel differences can create divergent warmup behavior.
- For mixed-precision pipelines, ensure warmup includes both fp16 and int8 heavy paths.
- If using quant-fallback (dynamic), include a probe set that intentionally triggers fallback to verify correct behavior.

Telemetry and SLOs to track during warmup

- Latency: token p50/p95/p99, cold request p99. Threshold: p99 increase vs warm baseline must be <= 25% or +200ms (whichever smaller) during the first 30 minutes.
- Error budget: increased error rate during warmup must remain <= 0.5% absolute above baseline.
- Memory: sustained GPU memory increase vs baseline <= 5% after warmup steady-state.
- Quality: semantic-similarity and task-specific metrics must meet promotion gates (e.g., >= 0.88 similarity or within 2% of reference).
- Telemetry endpoints: /metrics/warmup/latency, /metrics/warmup/kv_size, /events/warmup/anomaly.

Automated evaluation gates (example)

1) Preflight (blocking): Run micro-latency + quant-path probes against shadow model. Fail if p99 > threshold or semantic delta > limit.
2) Canary gate: Run KV growth + long-coherence probes continuously for canary window. Fail and rollback if error spike or quality regressions observed.
3) Progressive ramp: Continue probes and only advance traffic when hourly checks pass for 3 consecutive samples.

Rollout and rollback procedure (numbered runbook)

1. Create warmup probe suite referencing the release quant-profile and probe seed set.
2. Deploy canary (0-2%) and trigger immediate micro-latency probes.
3. Evaluate probe outputs and metrics dashboard for 30 minutes.
4. If pass, expand to 5% and start KV growth probes + long-coherence probes.
5. If fail at any stage, execute automatic rollback: mark model non-promotable, scale down canary, notify on-call and create regression ticket.
6. Post-failure: collect probe logs, store reproducible seeds, and run the regression triage checklist (see next section).

Regression triage fast-path for warmup failures

- Triage checklist (first 60 minutes):
  1) Confirm probe seeds and quant artifact match the deployed model.
  2) Check for kernel/fusion mismatches in runtime logs (tag: kernel-version).
  3) Inspect KV cache hit/miss curve and memory growth traces.
  4) Compare pre-deployment shadow run results (replay) vs observed canary.
  5) If quant path implicated, re-run quant-probes with full fp16 (non-quant) artifact to isolate quality vs kernel regressions.

- Minimum data to open a regression ticket:
  - Probe id(s) and seeds (text).
  - Model artifact id and quant-profile checksum.
  - p99 and semantic-similarity deltas (baseline vs observed).
  - Attach scheduler logs and GPU kernel version.

Best practices and prompt priming patterns

- Keep priming prompts minimal: prefer a 1-2 sentence neutral context to avoid shifting task semantics.
- Use deterministic priming for micro-latency probes; use randomized sampling for long-coherence probes to capture variation.
- For multilingual models, include language-balanced prime samples in probes.

Operational checklist for private/dedicated deployments

- Ensure KMS keys and container images are pre-pulled on nodes before warmup to avoid I/O stalls.
- Pre-warm network paths: open required sockets and validate peer discovery to avoid first-request DNS/timeouts.
- Validate GPU driver and CUDA versions match the quant artifact compatibility matrix (see below).

Compatibility matrix (text table)

CUDA | Driver | supported-quant-profiles
11.8 | 525.x | int8-legacy, int8-optimized
12.1 | 535.x | int8-optimized, mixed-precision-hybrid

Short FAQs

Q: Should we warm every model before every rollout?
A: Warm important production-facing models (high QPS or low-latency SLO). For low-traffic models, use periodic warmed probes tied to traffic patterns.

Q: Can warmup probes be synthetic?
A: Yes, but prioritize production-sampled traces when available. Synthetic probes must mimic token length and diversity of production slices.

Appendix: example CLI to schedule a warmup probe (eval harness)

# schedule_probe --suite warmup-micro --model redwood-opt-4x-int8 --quant-profile qprof-2026-01 --replay-source prod-sampled --run-on nodeset:warm

References and related pages

- Serving simulation harness: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/eval-harness/serving-simulation-eval-harness-2026
- KV cache quant stability: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/quantization-profiles/kv-cache-quant-stability-audit-playbook-2025
- Regression triage: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/regression-triage/drift-cache-interaction-investigation-playbook-2026

Change log

- 2026-01-15: Created by Elena Park.
- 2026-02-04: Added quant-awareness section and updated telemetry SLOs after QA feedback.

title: Throughput–Fidelity Tradeoff Matrix and Acceptance Protocol
content:
Summary
-------
This document defines a reproducible protocol and decision matrix for evaluating throughput vs. fidelity tradeoffs for candidate serving configurations (model variants, quantization profiles, batching policies, and routing tiers). It provides acceptance gates used by model-onboarding, infra, and SRE to decide whether a configuration can be promoted to: hosted baseline, dedicated pool, or private rollout. The goal is to make acceptance deterministic, measurable, and automatable.

Scope and audience
------------------
- Scope: LLM inference configurations tested in the Redwood eval-harness and serving-simulation environments. Includes hosted, dedicated, and private serving modes.
- Audience: Applied ML engineers, serving runtime owners, SRE, and product owners conducting promotions and rollouts.

Why this protocol exists
------------------------
Teams frequently make tradeoffs (e.g., int8 quantization + increased batch size) that increase system throughput and lower per-token cost but may reduce output fidelity. Without a consistent accept/reject rulebook, rollouts cause regressions or unnecessary conservatism. This protocol standardizes:
- a throughput/fidelity taxonomy
- measurement methodology (inputs, metrics, statistics)
- promotion gates and rollback triggers
- automation knobs for CI/CD integration

Definitions
-----------
- Throughput (T): tokens/sec or requests/sec measured end-to-end under the target serving config and arrival pattern. We report tokens/sec at stable-state and 95th percentile request throughput.
- Fidelity (F): application-level quality signals computed against the production prompt set. Typical signals: semantic-similarity (embedding cosine), exact match (EM) for extraction tasks, BLEU/ROUGE for summarization, and a Response Stability Index (RSI) used across Redwood.
- Baseline: the currently-promoted configuration (model + quant + batching) used as the reference for delta calculations.

Throughput buckets and fidelity budget matrix
--------------------------------------------
We classify candidate configs into buckets and apply corresponding fidelity budgets. Buckets are evaluated at the stable-traffic point (defined below).
Table: Bucket | Target throughput (req/s) | Allowed fidelity delta (vs baseline) | Example use-cases
- LOW | < 50 req/s | delta_F <= 0.03 | low-volume prototypes, experiments
- MEDIUM | 50–500 req/s | delta_F <= 0.02 | product features with moderate load
- HIGH | 500–2,000 req/s | delta_F <= 0.01 | core product routes, user-facing completion
- EXTREME | > 2,000 req/s | delta_F <= 0.005 | high-throughput embeddings, batch reprocessing
Notes:
- delta_F is expressed in normalized units appropriate to the metric (e.g., cosine similarity delta, BLEU delta). Teams must map each fidelity metric into a normalized [0,1] scale in their benchmark definitions.
- For composite workloads (mixed NLU + generation), compute a weighted average fidelity delta using traffic-weighted slice weights (see Measurement Methodology).

Measurement methodology
-----------------------
1) Testbed and isolation
   - Use the Redwood eval-harness in a dedicated test cluster (shadow-serving mode) with isolated GPU pool to avoid noisy neighbors.
   - Seed the harness with the production prompt catalog subset (see Prompt Set Selection).
2) Traffic profile
   - Use two phases: warmup (5 minutes) and stable run (20 minutes). Warmup allows KV cache and batching mechanisms to reach steady state.
   - Arrival distribution: Poisson for request arrival with configurable lambda to hit desired req/s. Sequence length distribution must mirror production percentiles (p50, p90, p99).
3) Metrics to record
   - Throughput: tokens/sec, requests/sec (mean and 95/99).
   - Latency: p50/p95/p99 per-request time-to-first-token and time-to-last-token.
   - Cost proxy: average GPU-seconds per 1000 tokens.
   - Fidelity: per-sample similarity scores (embedding cos), task-specific scores (BLEU/ROUGE/EM), and RSI.
   - Stability: token-level divergence rate (fraction of samples with top-3 token differences vs baseline).
4) Statistical test
   - For fidelity: run paired bootstrap on the prompt catalog (N=10k resamples) to produce a 95% confidence interval for delta_F. The candidate passes if the upper bound of the two-sided 95% CI <= allowed delta for the bucket.
   - For throughput and latency: require p95 latency less than the SLO target for the route (default SLOs listed in Observability Standards). Throughput must be >= bucket lower-bound for 90% of runs.

Prompt Set Selection
--------------------
- Use the production prompt catalog slice with stratification over slices that represent different behavior modes: short completions, long-form, instruction-following, extraction, and embeddings.
- Minimum sample sizes: 2,000 examples for single-task workloads; for multi-slice workloads, ensure each slice has >= 500 examples.

Promotion gates (automated)
---------------------------
1) Smoke gate (automated CI):
   - Run a 5-minute smoke harness with a small canonical prompt set (N=200). Pass criteria: no p99 latency regression > 2x baseline and median fidelity delta <= 0.01.
2) Canary gate (gradual rollout):
   - Gradual traffic ramp: 1%, 5%, 10%, 25% each 30 minutes or longer until at target. At each step, run a short fidelity check (N=500 stratified) and telemetry checks (error rate, p95 latency).
   - Automated abort if: fidelity CI upper bound exceeds bucket threshold or error rate increases > 3x baseline for 10 minutes.
3) Full promotion gate:
   - Full 20-minute stable run as defined in Measurement Methodology. Pass if fidelity, throughput, and latency requirements satisfied and no new anomalies in logs/traces.

Rollback and regression triage triggers
-------------------------------------
- Immediate rollback triggers (automated):
  - Production fidelity alert: continuous monitoring detects an alert where a rolling 1-hour fidelity metric deviates by more than the allowed delta with p<0.01.
  - Error spike: 5x increase in 5xx error rate sustained for 10 minutes.
  - Latency SLO breach: p95 latency > 2x SLO for 15 minutes.
- Triage playbook summary:
  1. Capture failing sample set (use the fidelity-alerting hook to store inputs and outputs).
  2. Run replay in the eval-harness with both baseline and candidate configs. Produce diffs (token-level and embedding diffs).
  3. If the issue is traceable to quantization/precision (see Quantization Sensitivity Checklist below), treat as high priority for rollback to previous quant-profile.
  4. Open a regression investigation issue with tags: regression, fidelity, rollout-id, model-version. Assign owner from oncall rotation.

Quantization Sensitivity Checklist (short)
-----------------------------------------
- Confirm per-layer activation ranges were collected with representative data (not synthetic truncations).
- Re-run calibration with variable sequence lengths; some activations are length-dependent.
- If tokenizer-sensitive failure: compare tokenization deltas and map to prompt failure modes.
- Fallback option: promote with mixed precision (e.g., int8 for attention + fp16 for MLP) and re-evaluate.

Automation and CI integration
-----------------------------
- CI job: eval-throughput-fidelity (parametrized by candidate-id, baseline-id, bucket)
- Exit codes:
  - 0: pass smoke/canary/full gates
  - 2: fidelity fail
  - 3: latency fail
  - 4: infrastructure/noise (inconclusive)
- Artifact storage: harness produces a standardized results.json and artifacts/ (diffs, embeddings, raw traces). Store under s3://redwood-eval-artifacts/{candidate-id}/{run-id}/
- Example CLI:
  python -m redwood_eval.run --config configs/throughput_fidelity.yaml --candidate-id v2-int8-512batch --baseline-id v2-fp16 --bucket HIGH

Example benchmark config (YAML)
------------------------------
- name: high-throughput-embed-eval
  bucket: HIGH
  prompt_set: /datasets/prod/embeddings/stratified_20k
  arrival: poisson
  target_reqs_per_sec: 750
  seq_length_percentiles: {p50:64, p90:512, p99:1024}
  metrics: [embedding_cosine, tokens_per_second, p95_latency]

Sample results.json snippet (human-readable)
-------------------------------------------
{
  "candidate_id": "v2-int8-512batch",
  "baseline_id": "v2-fp16",
  "bucket": "HIGH",
  "throughput_tokens_sec": 15400,
  "p95_latency_ms": 420,
  "fidelity_delta_embedding_cosine": 0.007,
  "fidelity_delta_bleu": 0.003,
  "fidelity_ci_upper": 0.009,
  "pass": true
}

Operational runbook (quick)
---------------------------
1) Alert fires: check alert dashboard and rollout-id.
2) Pull artifacts from s3 for the offending candidate-run.
3) Execute replay harness locally: python -m redwood_eval.replay --run s3://... --baseline baseline-id --candidate candidate-id
4) If high-confidence fidelity regression: rollback via rollout controller (PATCH route to set active config = baseline) and notify stakeholders.
5) Postmortem: owner creates a short triage note with root cause and remediation within 72 hours.

Decision examples and rationale
------------------------------
- Example A: int8 + aggressive batching yields 2.5x throughput for HIGH bucket with delta_F=0.012 and CI upper=0.015 -> fail. Rationale: exceeds allowed delta (0.01).
- Example B: mixed-precision reduces cost 25% with delta_F=0.006 and CI upper=0.008 in HIGH bucket -> pass and promote to dedicated pool canary.

Responsibilities and ownership
------------------------------
- Applied ML: owns prompt catalog and fidelity metrics mapping.
- Serving runtime: owns harness environment and kernel/quant profiles.
- SRE: owns canary rollout orchestration and automated rollback tooling.
- Product/PO: sets bucket assignment for routes and approves exception requests.

Open questions and extensions
---------------------------
- Automating slice-weight discovery from traffic telemetry to reduce manual weight errors.
- Standardizing an embedding-threshold mapping that converts cosine delta to user-visible metric loss.

FAQ
---
Q: Can we relax fidelity thresholds for non-user-facing internal jobs?
A: Yes — buckets are guidelines. For internal batch workloads set bucket to EXTREME with negotiated thresholds recorded in the promotion ticket.

Q: What if throughput fluctuates across runs?
A: Re-run harness up to 3 times. If variance > 10% between runs, mark the run as inconclusive and require infrastructure noise triage before promotion.

Related pages
-------------
- Serving simulation harness: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/eval-harness/serving-simulation-eval-harness-2026
- Quantization benchmarks: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/quantization-profiles/workload-transferability-and-quant-benchmarks-2026

Appendix: scoring example
------------------------
- Composite fidelity score S = sum(slice_weight_i * normalized_metric_i). Normalization docs and code are in the eval-harness repo under redwood_eval/normalizers.py.

If you plan to use this protocol for an upcoming model promotion, create a promotion ticket and attach: candidate id, baseline id, bucket selection, and three harness run artifacts. The eval-harness team will help validate the configuration during the first promotion.

title: Adaptive Eval Budgeting and Sample Allocation Framework
content:
Summary:

This document defines Redwood's Adaptive Eval Budgeting and Sample Allocation Framework (AEBSAF), a prescriptive system for distributing limited evaluation budget (tokens, runs, annotator-hours) across prompt slices, models, and stages (shadow, canary, production). AEBSAF unifies eval harness scheduling, prompt-set prioritization, onboarding readiness checks, quality guardrails, quantization safety sampling, and regression triage triggers.

Purpose and scope:

- Introduces a lightweight policy and reference implementation for dynamic allocation of eval resources.
- Covers allocation across: prompt slices, failure modes, languages, quantized variants, and production routes.
- Applies to continuous evaluation pipelines, pre-promotion model-onboarding, and post-release regression scans.
- Does not replace per-eval bespoke analysis; it provides a default, auditable baseline for most workloads.

Motivation and goals:

- Real-world constraints: eval compute and annotator time are finite; naive uniform sampling wastes budget on low-risk slices.
- Objectives: maximize early detection of quality regressions, provide stable statistical power on high-impact slices, and reduce false negatives when promoting models or quantization profiles.

Key principles:

1. Risk-weighted allocation: allocate more samples to slices with higher business impact or higher historical volatility.
2. Multi-stage budgeting: split budgets into smoke (10%), focused (60%), and exploratory (30%) phases to balance coverage and depth.
3. Feedback-driven reallocation: increase sampling on slices where variance or failure rates rise above thresholds.
4. Cost-awareness: include token, inference latency, and annotation cost into per-sample cost model.

Roles and ownership:

- Eval Owner: responsible for configuring AEBSAF for a model or workload (owned by Applied ML or Model Onboarding).
- Platform: implements scheduler and enforces quotas (eng-harness).
- SRE/Observability: publish metrics and alerts (eng-platform).
- Customer-facing Product or CS: define business-impact weights for customer-specific slices.

Terminology:

- Slice: a coherent subset of prompts (e.g., long-context, biomedical, Spanish, multi-turn).
- Sample: one model invocation + annotation (if applicable).
- Budget unit: normalized unit combining inference token cost and annotation time (see cost model).

Allocation algorithm (high-level):

1. Ingest metadata for each slice: impact_score (0..10), historic_failure_rate (0..1), recent_variance (sigma), avg_token_cost, avg_latency_ms, sample_capacity.
2. Compute a base_weight for each slice:
   base_weight = 0.5 * normalized(impact_score) + 0.3 * normalized(historic_failure_rate) + 0.2 * normalized(recent_variance)
3. Convert base_weight into budget proportion using softmax with temperature T to avoid extremes:
   budget_prop_i = softmax_T(base_weight_i)
4. Enforce minimum per-slice floor (min_samples) and maximum cap (max_samples).
5. Split the allocated samples into stages: smoke/focus/exploratory and dispatch to eval harness queue with priorities.
Practical parameter defaults (reference):

- Overall budget: defined in budget units (default for medium workload: 10,000 budget units).
- Temperature T: 0.8 (empirically balanced).
- min_samples per slice: 30 (to detect medium effect sizes at alpha=0.05 for binary pass/fail metrics).
- max_samples per slice: 2,000 (prevents budget capture by extremely large slices).
- Stage split: smoke=10%, focused=60%, exploratory=30%.

Cost model (normalized budget unit):

| Cost component       | Example value | Notes |
|----------------------|---------------|-------|
| Per-sample token cost| 0.002         | normalized to USD-per-1000-tokens; converted to budget unit |
| Annotator-minute     | 0.05          | cost per human minute (crowdsourced) |
| Latency penalty per sample | 0.0001 * ms | small multiplier to deprioritize slow/expensive routes |
| Infrastructure surcharge | 1.0        | multiply budget for private/onprem runs |
budget_unit = token_cost * token_weight + annotator_minutes * annotator_weight + latency_penalty * latency_weight

Configuration example (YAML):

scheduler:
  budget_units: 10000
  temperature: 0.8
  min_samples_per_slice: 30
  max_samples_per_slice: 2000
  stage_split: [0.1, 0.6, 0.3]

slices:
  - id: long_context_8k
    impact_score: 8
    historic_failure_rate: 0.12
    recent_variance: 0.04
    avg_token_cost: 0.004
    avg_latency_ms: 420
    sample_capacity: 5000
  - id: biomedical_qa
    impact_score: 9
    historic_failure_rate: 0.18
    recent_variance: 0.09
    avg_token_cost: 0.006
    avg_latency_ms: 520
    sample_capacity: 1200
  - id: spanish_concise
    impact_score: 6
    historic_failure_rate: 0.07
    recent_variance: 0.02
    avg_token_cost: 0.003
    avg_latency_ms: 250
    sample_capacity: 3000

Monitoring and alerts:

Essential metrics (published per-model and per-slice):
- allocated_budget_units (gauge)
- samples_run (counter)
- failure_rate (rolling 1k samples, windowed)
- sample_variance (response metric variance)
- avg_inference_latency_ms
- budget_spend_rate (units/hour)

Alert thresholds (examples):
- failure_rate(slice) > 0.15 AND samples_run(slice) > 100 => P3 alert to model-owner
- budget_spend_rate > expected_rate * 1.5 => P2 alert to platform
- sample_variance increase > 2x baseline in last 7 days => auto-scale focused sampling on that slice by +25%

Integration with model onboarding and promotion gates:

1. Onboarding checklist ties to AEBSAF outputs; model promotion requires:
   - Completed smoke phase for all high-impact slices (smoke pass rate >= 95%)
   - Focused phase executed with sufficient power on slices with impact_score >= 7
   - No untriaged regression alerts triggered during focused phase
2. Promotion guardrail example (pass/fail):
   - If any slice with impact_score >= 8 shows delta_failure_rate >= 0.05 compared to baseline, block promotion and open regression triage.

Regression triage playbook (triggered automatically):

1. When blocked, create a regression incident with auto-attached AEBSAF artifacts: failing sample list, slice metadata, historical baseline and the exact scheduler config used.
2. Run focused bisect: binary search over recent model changes and quantization profiles using prioritized sample subsets (use existing automated-regression-bisect system).
3. If the bisect identifies a quantization-induced failure, escalate to Quantization SME and apply rollback to last known-good quant-profile for canary traffic.
4. Document resolution in postmortem and update impact_score / weights for future allocations.

Examples of prioritization heuristics (non-normative):

- Business-critical routes: weight += 2.0
- Recently-onboarded customers: weight += 1.0 for 30 days
- Slices with manual severity flag (security/PII): set min_samples to 200

Operational runbook (step-by-step):

1. Configure scheduler YAML and upload to eval-harness via CLI: evalctl submit --config scheduler.yaml
2. Confirm budget_units and stage_split in the console; target queues should be visible under /eval/scheduler/{model}
3. Monitor budget_spend_rate and samples_run on the AEBSAF dashboard for the first 24 hours
4. If failure_rate spikes: mark slice as triage_candidate and increase focused sampling by invoking: evalctl adjust --model M --slice S --delta 0.25
5. After focused runs, review aggregated diffs and decide promotion or rollback

Example CLI commands:

# Submit a scheduler run
evalctl submit --config adaptive_scheduler.yaml --model mythic-7b --env shadow

# Increase sampling for a slice by 25%
evalctl adjust --model mythic-7b --slice biomedical_qa --scale 1.25

Considerations for quantization and private deployments:

- Quant profiles often change token cost and variance. AEBSAF ingests quant-profile metadata and increases min_samples by 50% when evaluating a new quant profile for the same architecture.
- Private/on-prem runs may have higher infra surcharge; the scheduler may choose to run exploratory samples in hosted environments when privacy constraints allow.

Troubleshooting and common failure modes:

- Symptom: budget exhausted before smoke phase completes => check per-slice sample_capacity and reduce exploratory fraction or raise overall budget.
- Symptom: disproportionate allocation to low-impact slice => verify impact_score normalization and temperature T. Lower T to flatten distribution.
- Symptom: noisy failure_rate with low sample counts => raise min_samples or enable multi-seed aggregation.

Metrics for auditing and continuous improvement:

- Alert-to-resolution time for regression incidents (goal < 48h)
- False-positive triage rate (goal < 10%)
- Coverage of top-10 business slices across promotions (goal: 100%)
- Budget efficiency: detected-regressions-per-1k-units (trend upwards is better)

Appendix A — Statistical guidance:

- Minimum sample formula for binary metrics (approx):
  n = (Z_{1-alpha/2}^2 * p * (1-p)) / effect_size^2
  Use p=baseline pass rate, effect_size = minimum detectable delta (e.g., 0.05), Z=1.96 for alpha=0.05.

Appendix B — Pseudocode for allocation (reference):

function allocate(budget_units, slices):
  for s in slices:
    s.norm_impact = normalize(s.impact_score)
    s.norm_fail = normalize(s.historic_failure_rate)
    s.norm_var = normalize(s.recent_variance)
    s.base = 0.5*s.norm_impact + 0.3*s.norm_fail + 0.2*s.norm_var
  weights = softmax([s.base for s in slices], T)
  for i, s in enumerate(slices):
    s.allocated = max(min_samples, min(max_samples, round(weights[i]*budget_units / s.unit_cost)))
  apply_stage_split(slices)
  return slices

References and related docs:

- See eval harness scheduling guidelines and smoke-and-fidelity-eval-workflow for stage definitions.
- For regression bisect integration, refer to automated-regression-bisect-and-blame-assistant documentation.

Revision history:

- 2025-11-10: Drafted by María González
- 2026-01-22: Incorporated Reviewer feedback: added quant-profile handling and budget cost model (Leah Chen)
- 2026-02-14: Published after pilot with two onboarding flows (Omar Rahman, Priya Iyer)

title: Federated Eval Orchestration and Privacy Budgeting Playbook
content:
Summary
-----
This playbook describes a federated evaluation orchestration pattern and an accompanying privacy budgeting model for running distributed evals across Dedicated, Private, and Hosted environments. It targets teams that need to: (1) evaluate models across siloed customer workloads, (2) preserve differential privacy and data minimization guarantees, and (3) preserve capacity and cost SLOs while obtaining statistically useful signals.

Motivation
----------
As Redwood supports federated and private deployments, evaluators increasingly need aggregated signals from heterogenous tenants without moving raw user data to central storage. A federated eval approach reduces data movement, improves regulatory compliance, and enables per-tenant calibration. However, it introduces new operational concerns: orchestration latency, heterogeneous compute availability, skewed sample distributions, and the need to account for privacy "budget" consumption across many small experiments. This document defines patterns, configuration, and an operational runbook.

Goals and non-goals
-------------------
- Goals:
  - Provide a repeatable orchestration pattern for federated evals that works across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployment modes.
  - Define a privacy budgeting abstraction that teams can use to reason about cumulative information leakage from repeated evals.
  - Offer scheduling and cost controls so evals do not violate production SLOs or incur unexpected costs.
- Non-goals:
  - This playbook is not a full cryptographic DP primer. Use this alongside the Security team's DP guidance for formal proofs.
  - We do not prescribe model training workflows. This targets evaluation and telemetry only.

Key concepts and terminology
----------------------------
- Federated Eval Node: customer-controlled evaluator instance that runs workload probes against a model and emits sanitized, aggregated metrics.
- Coordinator: centralized orchestration service that schedules federated eval jobs, collects metadata, and enforces privacy budgets and quotas.
- Privacy Budget: a per-customer and per-experiment quota (measured in epsilon-like units) that limits how much information an eval can reveal about raw user data.
- SLO Guardrails: limits on CPU/GPU utilization, request QPS, and latency impact so eval runs do not impair production serving.

High-level architecture
-----------------------
1) Coordinator service (runs in Redwood control plane):
   - Registers eval specs, assigns job IDs, tracks budgets, aggregates metadata, and stores per-job manifests.
   - API endpoints: POST /v1/fed-evals (create), GET /v1/fed-evals/{id} (status), POST /v1/fed-evals/{id}/complete (submit summary).
2) Federated Eval Agent (runs in customer Dedicated/Private environment or on sandboxed host):
   - Pulls job manifests, executes probes locally, computes local aggregates, applies noise/sanitization, and submits only summary artifacts.
3) Result Aggregator (control plane):
   - Accepts per-node summaries and computes final population-level metrics, confidence intervals, and cross-tenant reports.

Orchestration and scheduling policies
------------------------------------
- Priority classes:
  - critical: must-run for compliance or safety, preemptible only with explicit owner approval.
  - standard: routine evals for performance/cost monitoring.
  - exploratory: low-priority experiments with strict cost caps.
- Backoff and retry policy:
  1) Coordinator schedules up to 3 attempts spaced with exponential backoff (initial 30s).
  2) If nodes report resource contention, Coordinator reschedules to a softer window (off-peak) and reduces sample size.
- Capacity-aware placement:
  - Agents report available GPU minutes and QPS headroom. Coordinator adjusts sample sizes and selects nodes that meet requested headroom thresholds.

Privacy budgeting model
----------------------
- Each federated eval job declares: privacy_label (purpose), sensitivity_level (low | medium | high), and requested_epsilon (numeric string).
- Budget enforcement rules:
  - Per-tenant rolling budget window: 30 days.
  - Default epsilon caps: low=0.5, medium=0.2, high=0.05.
  - Coordinator rejects or asks for explicit owner approval when requested_epsilon exceeds remaining budget.
- Sanitization primitives recommended on Agents:
  - Local aggregation with counts and clipped contributions.
  - Add Laplace/Gaussian noise calibrated to requested_epsilon.
  - Thresholding: require minimum local sample size Nmin before releasing any summary.

Operational runbook: day-of-run checklist
----------------------------------------
1) Create eval manifest with fields: job_id, probes[], privacy_label, requested_epsilon, target_nodes[].
2) Coordinator validates resource quotes and budgets -> returns scheduled window and sample_size suggestion.
3) Notify tenant SRE/owner and request acceptance if requested_epsilon > 0.1.
4) Agents pull manifest and perform a dry-run smoke check (3 probe samples) against a read-only test endpoint.
5) Execute full run. Agents upload compressed summary (sha256) to aggregator.
6) Aggregator computes population-level statistics and stores job artifact.
7) Auto-generate report and flag if any metric deviates > 3 sigma from baseline.

Incident / failure modes and mitigation
--------------------------------------
- Node fails mid-run:
  - Mitigation: Coordinator marks node as partial and rebalances sample to other participants while respecting budget.
- Excessive latency on Agents causing production impact:
  - Mitigation: Immediate agent throttling, abort job, alert oncall, rollback probe frequency.
- Privacy budget overrun attempt:
  - Mitigation: Coordinator refuses job and records audit event; require manual override with compliance sign-off.

Metrics, SLOs, and dashboards
-----------------------------
- Orchestration SLOs:
  - Job acceptance latency: 99th percentile < 4s for manifest validation.
  - Completion success rate: >= 97% across scheduled nodes for standard jobs.
- Privacy and correctness KPIs:
  - Budget violation rate: target 0%.
  - Fraction of reports passing sanity checks: >= 99%.
- Recommended dashboards:
  - Fed Eval Overview (jobs by privacy_label, budget consumption heatmap).
  - Agent Health (node CPU/GPU headroom, last heartbeat).
  - Aggregation Integrity (submitted SHA256 vs canonical).

Configuration examples
----------------------
- Eval manifest (YAML):
```yaml
job_id: fed-eval-2026-187
privacy_label: usage-telemetry
sensitivity_level: medium
requested_epsilon: "0.15"
priority: standard
target_nodes: [tenant-az-1, tenant-eu-3]
probes:
  - name: answer-quality-probe
    samples: 200
    path: /v1/generate
    timeout_ms: 5000
```

- Agent local constraints table:
| key | description | default | notes |
|-----|-------------|---------|-------|
| gpu_headroom_minutes | Minutes of GPU available for evals | "120" | Agents must report as integer minutes |
| min_local_sample | Minimum local samples before reporting | "50" | Prevents low-N leakage |
| noise_mechanism | Laplace|Gaussian | "Gaussian" | Calibrated per requested_epsilon |

Privacy review checklist (pre-launch)
------------------------------------
1) Confirm privacy_label and business justification.
2) Ensure requested_epsilon <= remaining budget or signed exception exists.
3) Verify Nmin and clipping thresholds configured on agents.
4) Confirm audit logging to central control plane is enabled.
5) Register the job in the security review queue if sensitivity_level == high.

Appendix: common CLI commands and snippets
------------------------------------------
- Submit a federated eval (example):
  curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/fed-evals -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -d @manifest.yaml

- Retrieve job status:
  curl https://api.redwood.ai/v1/fed-evals/fed-eval-2026-187/status

- Quick sanity check (agent):
  python -m redwood.fed.agent \n    --manifest manifest.yaml \n    --dry-run

Related docs and references
---------------------------
- See Eval Mesh and Workload Fingerprinting (internal) for node capability discovery.
- Security DP primer and the Security team's DP evidence repo for formal guarantees.

Ownership and next steps
------------------------
- Owners: Applied ML Eval Platform (primary), Security (privacy budget policy), Eng SRE (agent health).
- Next steps (roadmap):
  - Q2 2026: automated budget reconciliation API and per-tenant quota UI.
  - Q3 2026: integrate cryptographic aggregation primitives (secure aggregation) as opt-in.

Contact
-------
If you have questions about implementing federated evals or need an exception for privacy budgets, contact Maya Patel (maya.patel@redwood.ai) or raise an issue in #eval-platform on Slack.

title: Shadow Consistency Checker and Stochastic Seed Policy
content:
abstract:
This playbook defines the Shadow Consistency Checker (SCC) and the stochastic seed policy used for repeatable, low-latency shadow validation. It standardizes sampling, seeding, metric computation, and alert thresholds for detecting subtle regressions introduced by quantization, kernel changes, or prompt rewrites.

introduction:
Context: Shadow deployments are a primary mechanism for detecting regressions before promotion to production. However, nondeterminism (random seeds, sampling noise, tokenization nondeterminism) and under-specified sampling policies have produced intermittent false positives and missed regressions. The SCC is designed to make shadow comparisons deterministic where possible, quantify stochastic variance, and produce actionable triage signals.

scope:
Applies to: all model shadow runs executed by the eval harness for hosted, dedicated, and private deployments. Includes shadow runs tied to: quantized artifacts, runtime kernel upgrades, decoder-only architecture changes, prompt-layer rewrites, and batch/latency policy changes. Excludes: synthetic unit tests for tokenizers and low-level kernel microbenchmarks (handled by runtime team).

definitions:
- Shadow run: a replication of production traffic routed to candidate model(s) without affecting user-visible output.
- Deterministic seed: a chosen PRNG seed selected per probe to minimize sampling variance.
- SCC delta: a signed metric describing difference between baseline and candidate (see metrics_and_thresholds).

roles_and_ownership:
- Owner: eval-harness team (primary contact: Anika Verma).
- Observability: eng-platform (dashboards, traces).
- On-call triage: applied-ml oncall rotation.
- Release authority: model-onboarding product owner for promotions.
- Reviewers: runtime, quantization, infra SRE for any SCC alerts classified high severity.

metrics_and_thresholds:
Primary metrics (computed per-probe and aggregated by slice):
1) Semantic Delta (BLEU/ROUGE/embedding-cosine difference normalized) — threshold: alert if median delta > 0.035 across probes for 1 hour.
2) Deterministic Variance (inter-seed variance of metric) — acceptable if variance < 0.005; flag if > 0.01.
3) Latency Shift (P95 candidate - P95 baseline) — soft warn at +15ms, alert at +50ms.
4) Token Failure Rate (generation aborts, malformed JSON) — soft warn at 0.05%, alert at 0.2%.
5) Response Stability Index (RSI): aggregated stability score used by quality guardrails; regression if RSI drop > 7 points.
All thresholds are configurable per-customer slice; default global thresholds above apply to platform-level promotions.

shadow_sampling_policy:
1) Probe selection: use combined prioritized-probe list (production-derived probes + targeted adversarial probes). Default sample size: 10k probes per 24h per slice; minimum 1k for rarely-seen slices.
2) Seeding: each probe receives a stable deterministic seed derived from probe_id and epoch (seed = fnv1a128(probe_id + epoch)). For stochastic operations internal to the model runtime, the SCC requests the runtime to initialize PRNG using the provided seed via /v1/internal/start-seed header.
3) Epoch cadence: daily epochs (00:00 UTC) for broad coverage; micro-epochs (1-hour rolling) for high-risk changes (quantization/critical kernel patches).
4) Sampling distribution: stratified by intent-slice, length-bin, and frequency-decile to ensure long-context and low-frequency corner cases are evaluated.
5) Probe annotation: each probe must carry metadata: intent, slice, source (prod/annotated), expected_tokens, and json-schema (if structured).

test_procedures:
Shadow run steps (checklist):
1) Preflight: verify candidate artifact provenance and quant-annotations.
2) Seed injection: include header X-SCC-Seed: <seed> for each request.
3) Run shadow traffic through the shadow sequencer with mirroring factor 1:1 for functional probes and 1:0.1 for heavy-cost probes.
4) Collect token-level telemetry: token_latencies, kv_cache_hit_rate, prng_seed_hash, and model_logs.
5) Post-run aggregation: compute per-probe metrics and inter-seed variance.
6) SCC compares baseline vs candidate with bootstrapped confidence intervals (default 1000 bootstrap samples).
7) Generate badge: PASS / WEAK_REGRESSION / STRONG_REGRESSION based on metric thresholds.
8) If STRONG_REGRESSION, open a ticket in 'applied-ml-regression' with payload: probe-slice, top 10 probes with highest delta, seed values, and link to trace.
9) If PASS, annotate artifact with SCC:pass:<epoch> and allow next-stage promotion if other gates are green.

monitoring_and_alerting:
- Dashboard: SCC Overview (owner: eng-platform). Panels: pass rate, RSI trend, top delta probes, P95 latency shift heatmap, seed collision rate.
- Alerts:
  * SCC-STRONG-REGRESSION: triggered when STRONG_REGRESSION count > 50 probes in 1h — Severity: P2 — paging to applied-ml oncall + runtime oncall.
  * SCC-LATENCY-REGRESSION: P95 shift > 50ms for top 5 slices — Severity: P1 if customer impact high.
  * SCC-HIGH-VARIANCE: inter-seed variance > threshold for any core slice — Severity: P3 — email to eval-harness squad.
- Telemetry tags: include scc_epoch, scc_seed, scc_slice, model_artifact_id, quant_profile_id.

rollout_and_rollback:
Promotion gating: artifact may be promoted to production only when: SCC badge == PASS for 3 consecutive epochs OR PASS with WEAK_REGRESSION if risk acceptance form is signed by product and runtime.
Rollback criteria: immediate rollback if production RSI drop > 10 points within 30 minutes, or Token Failure Rate > 0.3% sustained for 15 minutes.
Canary policy: small canary (1% traffic) for 2 hours after promotion with accelerated SCC checks (micro-epochs every 15 minutes).

examples_and_cli:
Example seed header: curl -X POST https://shadow-sequencer.internal/v1/generate -H 'Authorization: Bearer <key>' -H 'X-SCC-Seed: 0x9f8b7c2d' -d '{"probe_id":"p-2314","input":"Summarize the article" }'
Sample bootstrap command for SCC metric: python scc/compute_delta.py --baseline baseline.json --candidate candidate.json --bootstrap 1000 --output delta_report.json
Sample returned JSON snippet (flattened): {
  "probe_id": "p-2314",
  "seed": "0x9f8b7c2d",
  "semantic_delta": "0.041",
  "rsi": "72",
  "p95_latency_ms": "152"
}
Runbook CLI for triage: ./scripts/scc_triage --ticket create --art artifact_id --epoch 2026-03-10 --attach delta_report.json

appendix:
Known limitations: deterministic seeding cannot eliminate all sources of nondeterminism: GPU kernel fp rounding, multithreaded scheduler order, and third-party tokenizer nondeterminism. For high-confidence checks, pair SCC with microbench kernel-level determinism tests.
Change log: 2026-01-15 initial draft published; 2026-02-20 added RSI integration; 2026-03-10 updated latency thresholds and canary cadence.
References: internal RFC: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/eval-harness/latency-sensitivity-eval-routing-fallback-protocol-2026, quality guardrails RSI spec.

title: CI Eval Determinism and Flake Mitigation
content:
## Summary
Our evaluation harness previously produced intermittent metric drops (e.g., ~0.04 BLEU on a single run) for the quantized-v2 onboarding suite that disappeared on rerun. This page documents the current (2026) standard for reducing nondeterminism, preventing CI flakes, and making regressions actionable.

The root causes we have observed include:
- Stochastic decoding (temperature/top_p sampling) without per-example RNG control.
- RNG state not consistently propagated to all relevant libraries/ops.
- GPU-level nondeterminism (kernel selection, atomic ordering), especially in quantized/int8 paths.
- Cross-hardware differences (e.g., A100 int8 kernels vs legacy fallback paths).

## What changed since the initial investigation
The original debugging thread identified sampling parameters and missing explicit generators as primary contributors. The current harness incorporates the same core ideas, with the following updates:
- We now treat deterministic decoding as the default for per-commit CI gates for onboarding suites.
- The determinism flag is implemented as `--deterministic` / `deterministic: true` in eval config, and it hard-enforces decoding parameters (see below).
- The runner always constructs and passes an explicit `torch.Generator` for generation, derived from a root seed plus a stable per-example index.
- CI gating moved from single-run metrics to median-of-repeats, and flakiness is measured explicitly.

## Definitions
### Deterministic (harness-level)
A run is considered deterministic (for CI purposes) if repeated executions on the same hardware + container image + model revision produce identical decoded token sequences for the same prompts.

Notes:
- Hardware drift (A100 vs K80) is not expected to be bitwise identical.
- Some quantized kernels may still be nondeterministic even when framework-level deterministic flags are enabled.

### Flake
A flake is a CI failure caused by nondeterministic variation rather than a real change in model/code.

## Recommended CI strategy (current)
### 1) Per-commit (PR) gate: deterministic quick eval
Purpose: prevent random sampling jitter from blocking merges.
- Environment: standardized runner image + target GPU class when available (A10 preferred for cost; A100 acceptable).
- Mode: `deterministic: true`
- Repeats: `--repeat 3`
- Decision rule: gate on the median metric across repeats; also fail if output hashes differ across repeats (for suites that require bitwise stability).

### 2) Nightly: multi-seed + tolerance-based comparison
Purpose: catch real regressions and quantify expected variance.
- Environment: target infra (A100 for quantized-v2)
- Mode: `deterministic: false` (sampling allowed when the eval is designed to measure sampled behavior)
- Seeds: 3 seeds (default: 13, 37, 101)
- Decision rule: compare against the golden baseline using metric tolerance thresholds; alert on sustained shifts (median across seeds).

### 3) On failure: auto-trigger repro debug job
Purpose: make investigations fast and data-rich.
- Auto-collect artifacts listed in the Logging and Artifacts section.
- Include a run summary that states whether variance is:
  - decode-level (different token sequences)
  - metric-only (same outputs but metric computation drift)
  - environment-level (hardware/container mismatch)

## Deterministic decoding mode (required behavior)
When `deterministic: true`, the harness MUST enforce:
- `do_sample = false`
- `temperature = 0.0`
- `top_k = 1`
- `top_p = 1.0`
- `num_beams = 1` (unless the suite explicitly tests beam search)
- Explicit generator passed into generation APIs
- Stable batching order (no data-loader shuffling; stable sort by example_id)

Rationale:
- Simply setting a global seed is insufficient when generation draws randomness in parallel or across different batch shapes.

## RNG handling (current standard)
### Root seed and per-example seeds
- The runner accepts a `--seed` root seed.
- For each example, derive a stable per-example seed:
  - `example_seed = root_seed + example_index`
- Construct a generator on the active device and pass it explicitly to generation.

Operational guidance:
- Ensure `example_index` is stable across runs (do not use worker-local indices unless they are globally consistent).
- If sharding is used, include `shard_id` in the seed derivation only if shard assignments are stable across runs.

### Framework flags
We enable deterministic flags when `deterministic: true`:
- `torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)`
- `torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic = True`
- `torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark = False`

Caveat:
- Quantized/int8 kernels may not fully respect these flags. Treat the flags as best-effort rather than a guarantee.

## Hardware notes (quantized-v2)
- A100 int8 paths can differ from legacy GPU fallbacks.
- CI determinism requirements are scoped to a single target hardware class per suite.
- The quantized-v2 onboarding suite is pinned to A100 for nightly baselines.

## Metric gating rules
### Per-commit deterministic gate
- Compute metric per repeat.
- Report: median, min, max, and standard deviation.
- Fail conditions:
  - Any repeat differs in output token hash (for deterministic suites).
  - Std dev exceeds threshold (default threshold: 0.005 BLEU-equivalent; suite owners may override).

### Nightly tolerance-based gate
- Compare nightly medians to golden medians.
- Default tolerances (may be tuned per suite):
  - BLEU: 0.03 absolute
  - chrF: 0.02 absolute
  - Task accuracy: 0.5 percentage points absolute

## Logging and artifacts (required)
Each eval run must emit the following into the run artifact directory:
- `run_metadata.json`: model revision, container digest, GPU type, torch version, eval suite name, config snapshot
- RNG details:
  - root seed
  - per-example seed derivation scheme
  - `torch.get_rng_state()` (hex or base64)
  - `torch.cuda.get_rng_state_all()` (per device; hex or base64)
- Generation parameters:
  - do_sample, temperature, top_p, top_k, num_beams, max_new_tokens
- Outputs:
  - `outputs_run_{i}.jsonl` for each repeat
  - include decoded text and decoded token ids
- Summary:
  - `metrics_run_{i}.json`
  - `summary.json` with median/std and output hash comparisons

## Runner CLI (current)
Required runner options for reproducibility testing:
- `--repeat N` : runs the same suite N times with the same config and seed
- `--deterministic {true|false}` : enforces deterministic mode when true
- `--seed SEED` : sets the root seed

Example:
- `evals/onboarding --suite quantized-v2 --repeat 3 --deterministic true --seed 42`

## Troubleshooting playbook
If you see nondeterminism with `deterministic: true`:
1) Confirm the run is on the expected hardware class and container digest.
2) Confirm output hashes differ (decode nondeterminism) vs metrics differ (metric computation drift).
3) If decode nondeterminism:
   - verify generator is passed explicitly
   - verify stable ordering of examples and stable batch shape
   - check for any remaining sampling knobs being set by a suite override
4) If still nondeterministic on A100 quantized kernels:
   - capture artifacts and escalate to eng-serving-runtime for kernel-level investigation
   - consider switching the suite’s CI gate to tolerance-based comparison if bitwise repeatability is unattainable

## Ownership and change control
- Owner: Applied ML & Evals
- Any change to determinism semantics (`--deterministic` behavior, seed derivation, gating thresholds) requires review from Applied ML & Evals + Serving Runtime.

title: Hybrid Probe TTL Prioritization and Recovery Playbook
content:
Overview:
This playbook defines a hybrid orchestration strategy for evaluation probes that combines time-to-live (TTL) semantics, priority scoring, and fast-recovery policies. The goal is to keep continuous coverage of critical prompt slices while bounding eval cost and minimizing probe-induced noise on production-like systems (hosted, dedicated, private). It is intended for the Eval Platform team, model-onboarding engineers, and oncall responders.

Why this exists:
- Long-running probe farms can waste budget on stale probes and mask regressions if probes are not aged out intelligently.
- Sudden regressions require rapid amplification of high-value probes and automated recovery actions.
- Hybrid TTL + priority approach ensures freshness, provable coverage, and predictable cost.

Scope and audience:
- Scope: eval harness scheduling, probe lifecycle, probe TTL policies, recovery escalation, observability, and example configs.
- Audience: Eval Platform, Applied ML, Serving Runtime, SRE.

Terminology:
- Probe: a single evaluation input (prompt + context) executed against a model variant.
- Probe TTL: elapsed wall time after which a probe is considered stale and eligible for retirement or reseeding.
- Priority Score: numeric value used by the scheduler to order probe execution.
- Fast Recovery Window: short period (default 30m) after a regression signal where high-priority amplification is applied.

Principles:
1) Freshness over redundancy: prefer reseeding semantically similar probes that are >TTL rather than repeatedly running the same slot.
2) Cost-aware amplification: limit concurrent amplification to an adjustable budget percentage to avoid overloading infra.
3) Observability-first: every probe carries provenance + telemetry and must be linkable to eval alerts and regression investigations.

Priority scoring formula (recommended):
Priority = w_slice * SliceImportance + w_recent * RecencyBoost + w_sev * FailureScore - w_cost * costPenalty
Where:
- SliceImportance: integer 1..10 assigned by owners (critical user flows have 8-10).
- RecencyBoost: 1.0 if probe was not run in last 24h, 0.5 if 6–24h, 0.0 if <6h.
- FailureScore: normalized metric (0..1) derived from historical failure rate for the slice.
- costPenalty: tokens_estimate / 1000 (normalized).
- w_* are tunable weights. Default weights: w_slice=2.0, w_recent=1.0, w_sev=3.0, w_cost=0.5.

Default TTL tiers (configuration guideline):
- Hot probes: TTL = 6 hours (high-frequency user flows; freshness critical).
- Warm probes: TTL = 24 hours (common flows and high-impact slices).
- Cold probes: TTL = 7 days (rare slices used for longtail monitoring).

Example TTL policy table (ASCII):
| Tier  | Example slices                      | TTL     | Max run frequency | Notes                        |
|-------|--------------------------------------|---------|-------------------|------------------------------|
| Hot   | auth flow, payment, search critical | 6h      | 1 run / 10m       | Immediate amplification ok   |
| Warm  | onboarding, helpdesk                 | 24h     | 1 run / 2h        | Batch during off-peak        |
| Cold  | obscure edgecases                    | 7d      | 1 run / 24h       | Lighter telemetry retention  |

Probe lifecycle (high-level):
1) Creation: probes are created from prompt catalogs, user telemetry anchors, and synthetic generators. Metadata recorded: slice_id, owner, expected_tokens, tier, seed_id, provenance_url.
2) Scheduling: scheduler computes Priority and TTL; probes are enqueued in priority bins.
3) Execution: probe executes in a shadow slot with tracing enabled.
4) Post-processing: metrics (semantic-score, token-usage, timing, deltas) are stored and attached to probe instance.
5) Retirement/Re-seed: if TTL expired, scheduler either retires the probe or generates a reseed variant (mutated prompt) per reseed rules.

Reseeding rules:
- Reseed if: probe TTL expired OR consecutive flaky runs >= 3 OR semantic drift > threshold.
- Reseed strategy: small lexical perturbation (synonym swap), context shuffling, temperature variation for sampling probes.
- Reseed limit: at most 2 reseeds per original probe before demotion to cold tier.

Fast-recovery amplification protocol (triggered by regression signal):
1) Detection: Regression alert fires (see Observability section) and is labeled with suspected slice(s).
2) Prioritization: Scheduler increases w_sev by factor 2 for affected slices, moves associated probes to Hot tier.
3) Amplification: Create N parallel executions for top-K priority probes where N = min(AmplifyBudget, 20). AmplifyBudget default = 10% of probe-farm concurrency.
4) Short-circuit fallback: If amplification shows degraded output quality > degrade_threshold for 3 consecutive runs, trigger automated rollback/whitelist depending on rollout policies.
5) Triage handoff: Notify oncall_eval with initial triage summary and links to top failing probes.

Example amplification CLI (illustrative):
# Amplify top 5 probes for slice onboarding-checks for 30m
redwood-eval amplify --slice onboarding-checks --top 5 --window 30m --budget 0.1

Observability and alerting (recommended):
- Per-probe telemetry: run_id, model_version, route, latency_ms, tokens_in, tokens_out, semantic_similarity_score, failure_flags.
- Dashboard: Active probes by tier, avg token cost per tier, recent reseed rate, amplification concurrency.
- Alerts (Prometheus-like pseudo-rule):
ALERT EvalProbeRegressionHigh
  IF increase(eval_probe_failed_total{slice=~"critical.*"}[10m]) > 50
  FOR 5m
  LABELS {severity="page", team="eval-platform"}
  ANNOTATIONS {summary="High failure rate on critical eval slices"}

SLOs and thresholds for eval platform health:
- Probe execution success rate: 99.5% (daily) for Hot/Warm probes (failure = non-terminal or missing telemetry).
- Max amplification-induced excess token cost: 12% of daily probe budget.
- Reseed churn (reseeded probes / total probes): keep < 5% sustained.

Runbook: immediate steps for an oncall responder (short):
1) Acknowledge alert and open triage thread in #eval-oncall.
2) Filter probes by slice + model_version and inspect semantic_similarity_score / failure_flags.
3) If a single model variant regresses, pause scheduled runs for that variant and enable amplification on control variant.
4) If infra-related (latency spikes, token egress balloon): follow SRE infra runbook (link below) and throttle amplification budget.
5) If false positive or noisy probe: mark probe as flaky and reseed or retire.
6) Summarize findings and, if necessary, trigger rollback of model promotion via the Promotion Gate (Promotion Gate runbook link).

Ownership and roles:
- Eval Platform (owner): maintains scheduler, probe metadata schema, amplification engine.
- Applied ML (secondary): assigns slice importance and reviews failing-level judgments.
- SRE (support): enforces budget and controls infra throttles.
- Oncall Eval: triage and initial mitigation.

Configuration examples:
YAML: default-scheduler-config.yaml
---
# weights and TTLs for hybrid scheduler
weights:
  w_slice: 2.0
  w_recent: 1.0
  w_sev: 3.0
  w_cost: 0.5
ttl_tiers:
  hot: 6h
  warm: 24h
  cold: 168h
amplification:
  budget_fraction: 0.10
  max_parallel_per_slice: 20
  default_window: 30m

Python priority calc (example):
```python
def priority(slice_importance, last_run_hours, failure_rate, tokens):
    w_slice, w_recent, w_sev, w_cost = 2.0, 1.0, 3.0, 0.5
    recency = 1.0 if last_run_hours > 24 else (0.5 if last_run_hours > 6 else 0.0)
    cost_penalty = tokens / 1000.0
    return w_slice * slice_importance + w_recent * recency + w_sev * failure_rate - w_cost * cost_penalty
```

Data retention and privacy:
- Probe-level telemetry retained for 90 days for Hot/Warm, 30 days for Cold.
- Sensitive customer prompts must be redacted and handled using the privacy-first-shadow-eval pattern (see related page).

Testing and rollout plan:
1) Canary: deploy scheduler change to eval-harness/canary pool for 48 hours with amplification disabled.
2) Shadow mode: enable amplification calculations but do not change execution order for 7 days; compare priority distributions.
3) Limited rollout: enable amplification with budget_fraction=0.02 for 72 hours and monitor costs.
4) Full rollout: increase to target budget_fraction (default 0.10) after no regressions and SRE sign-off.

Operational metrics to track (weekly):
- Probe freshness by tier (median age)
- Amplification cost fraction
- Number of reseeds per week
- Mean time to remediation after regression alert

Appendix: Helpful links and artifacts
- Promotion Gate runbook: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/model-onboarding/inference-readiness-eval-matrix-and-promotion-playbook-2026
- Probe farm orchestration design doc: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/regression-triage/probe-farm-orchestration-for-rare-regressions-2026
- Privacy-first shadow eval pattern: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/model-onboarding/privacy-first-shadow-eval-and-dp-certification-2026

Contact and escalation:
- Eval Platform Slack: #eval-platform
- Oncall rotation: eval-oncall@redwood.com
- SRE pager: see internal SRE roster

Change log:
- 2026-02-15: Created by Aisha Patel (initial draft).
- 2026-03-01: Reviewed by Marcus Chen and Rina Sato, added amplification budget guidance and rollout checklist.

title: Prompt Failure Inventory and Annotator Contract: Scenario Taxonomy & Labeling Protocol
content:
Summary
This document defines a reproducible taxonomy of prompt-level failure modes, a recommended scenario-driven inventory format, and a labeling contract for human annotators and automated heuristics. It is intended for evaluation teams, model-onboarding engineers, and regression triage owners who need consistent, high-quality labels that link prompt characteristics to observable model behaviors.

Goals and scope
- Create a small, stable set of failure categories that cover production-relevant errors (not every linguistic edge case).
- Standardize the prompt + context metadata we store for each failure (the inventory manifest).
- Provide a clear annotator contract and decision rules so labels are consistent across raters and over time.
- Enable automated triage heuristics to bootstrap labels and prioritize human review when confidence is low.

Intended audience
- Applied ML engineers running eval harnesses
- Model onboarding reviewers who must certify promotion readiness
- Regression triage teams performing root-cause analysis
- Annotation leads and quality control managers

High-level taxonomy (first-class categories)
1) Incorrect factual response (FactError)
- Model asserts verifiably false facts about current or historical reality.
- Example triggers: wrong dates, wrong numerical facts, incorrect entity attributes.

2) Hallucinated entity or citation (Hallucination)
- Model invents an entity, citation, or document that cannot be substantiated by the provided context or a reasonable external check.

3) Instruction misinterpretation (InstructionMismatch)
- Model fails to follow explicit instructions in the prompt (wrong format, omitted fields, reversed order).

4) Safety policy violation (Safety)
- Model produces content that violates safety constraints: disallowed instructions, harassment, PII leakage, or actionable wrongdoing.

5) Degraded semantic relevance (RelevanceDrop)
- Output drifts off-topic, becomes generic, or ignores context dependencies (e.g., ignores prior chat turns).

6) Tokenization/formatting breakage (FormatError)
- Output contains broken JSON, truncated code blocks, or malformed special tokens causing downstream parser failures.

7) Quantization/artifact degradation (QuantArtifact)
- Output shows artefacts consistent with quantization or KV-cache instability: repeated phrases, tokenization hallucinations, or inconsistent scalar outputs across repeats.

8) Latency/partial-output fallbacks (LatencyFallback)
- Model response indicates it timed out, returned partial content, or used fallback model variant with degraded quality.

Inventory manifest: required fields
Use this manifest layout for every logged failure. Store as a row in the failure catalog (CSV/Parquet/JSONL).
- prompt_id: Unique stable id for prompt fixture (example: pf_2026_00021)
- source: Origin of prompt (prod/bench/manual/synthetic) (example: prod:search-assist)
- seed_text: The raw prompt text (truncated to 8k chars) (example: "Summarize the following...")
- context_snapshot: Short context hash or description of conversation state (example: chat:session_241)
- model_version: Exact model + flavor used (example: gpt-redwood-v2-quant8)
- hardware_profile: deployment type (hosted/dedicated/private) + instance (example: dedicated:p4d-32gb)
- timestamp_utc: ISO8601 of the run (example: 2026-01-12T20:34:22Z)
- failure_category: One of taxonomy labels (example: Hallucination)
- severity: low/medium/high (see severity guidelines) (example: high)
- repeatability: always/sometimes/rare (example: sometimes)
- annotator_id: human rater or automated heuristic id (example: annot-v2-17)
- confidence_score: 0.0-1.0 (string for JSON flatness) (example: 0.82)
- reproduction_steps: Minimal steps to reproduce; include seeds and flags (example: see reproduction_notes)
- related_run_ids: Other run ids for cross-comparison (example: [run_123, run_124])

Severity guidelines
- High: visible user harm or complete feature break (Safety, pervasive FactError that changes user action).
- Medium: materially degrades UX or model correctness but has a straightforward workaround (RelevanceDrop, FormatError).
- Low: cosmetic or rare issues tolerated by product (minor hallucination on non-critical content).

Annotator contract: decision rules and procedures
1) Single-pass automated triage (pre-labeling)
  a) Run deterministic heuristics: entity-checker against knowledge base, JSON-parse validator for FormatError, safety classifier.
  b) If heuristics produce confidence >= 0.9 and unanimous category, set label = automated value and set annotator_id = auto:<heuristic>.
  c) Otherwise, queue for human review.

2) Human annotation workflow
  1) "Read the prompt and produced output verbatim, then consult the context_snapshot if provided."
  2) "Apply the taxonomy: choose the single best category. If multiple categories apply, select primary by impact to user (safety > fact > relevance)."
  3) "Write a one-sentence justification in the free-text justification field for auditability."
  4) "Assign severity and repeatability using the guidance above."
  5) "If unsure, mark label 'needs_discuss' and add required evidence (e.g., external fact links)."

3) Adjudication rules (when annotator disagreement >= 2 raters disagree)
- Triage to an adjudicator pool. Adjudicator applies evidence-gathering protocol: web lookup, cross-model comparison, and consults model-onboarding lead. Final label must include a short evidentiary note.

Inter-annotator agreement (IAR) targets and sampling
- Initial onboarding target: Cohen's kappa >= 0.6 on a 500 example calibration set.
- Production maintenance: sample 1% of daily labeled items (min 50) for IAR monitoring; investigate drift if kappa drops below 0.55.

Automation heuristics and feature checklist for bootstrap labeling
- Exact-match referent check (KB lookup): flags FactError/Hallucination.
- JSON/markup health check: flags FormatError.
- Safety classifier (ensemble of policy and regex): candidate Safety.
- N-gram repetition and perplexity delta tests: candidate QuantArtifact.
- Context similarity score: candidate RelevanceDrop if low similarity.

Data retention and privacy notes
- Do not store full PII in the manifest; if prompts may contain PII, store a redacted_seed_text and reference to secure vault for retrieval under approved workflows.
- Retention default: 90 days for full text in the eval environment, 3 years for redacted manifest entries. Follow security-and-compliance/data-management policies for customer data.

Integration with eval harness and triage pipelines
- Naming conventions: prompt fixtures used by the eval harness should include fixture_id matching prompt_id in the manifest.
- When a new failure is logged, the harness should attach: trace_id, cost_metrics (tokens, latency), and model-runtime snapshot to the manifest.
