  \"PII_flag\": false
}

Mapping rules: fingerprints -> workload id
------------------------------------------------
Mapping is expressed as an ordered rule set owned by eval-orchestrator. Rules are applied top-to-bottom. A rule example:
- Rule 110: if route == \"chat/commerce-v2\" AND call_pattern == \"function-heavy\" AND token_histogram_bucket in [\"65-256\",\"257-1024\"] -> workload: commerce-function-heavy-v2, priority: high, retention: 14d.
- Rule default-low: otherwise -> workload: baseline-sampled, priority: low, retention: 7d.

Priority categories and scheduling constraints
---------------------------------------------
- critical: run within 15m of detection; used for production regressions and safety regressors. Max concurrency: 20; budget cap: 50k tokens/hr.
- high: run within 2h; used for high-prevalence slices or customer-flagged routes. Max concurrency: 50; budget cap: 250k tokens/hr.
- medium: daily cadence; aggregate trend checks. Max concurrency: 200; budget cap: 1M tokens/day.
- low: weekly sampled; for long-tail coverage. Max concurrency: 500; strictly preemptible.

Config snippet: workload routing table (YAML style, for eval-orchestrator):
| workload_id | match_expression                                      | priority | ttl_days | max_run_minutes | owner_team |
|-------------|-------------------------------------------------------|----------|----------|-----------------|------------|
| commerce-function-heavy-v2 | route =~ \"chat/commerce\" && call_pattern == \"function-heavy\" | high     | 14       | 30              | applied-ml |
| baseline-sampled           | true                                                  | low      | 7        | 120             | applied-ml |

SLOs and observable metrics
----------------------------
- Coverage SLO: 95% of top 20 production slices (by 30d prevalence) should have a corresponding workload ID in fingerprint->mapping table (monitor: eval.mesh.coverage_ratio, target: 0.95).
- Freshness SLO: 90% of high-priority fingerprints must be scheduled to run within 2 hours (eval.mesh.freshness, target: 0.90).
- Cost SLO: average cost per token across eval jobs should remain < 1.5x production per-token baseline for high priority workloads (eval.mesh.cost_ratio).
- Regression detection latency: time from run completion to triage alert < 10m for critical workloads.

Integration and APIs
--------------------
- fingerprint ingestion (kafka topic): eval.fingerprints.v1.
- eval-orchestrator API: POST /v1/schedule (body: workload_id, priority, context_tag) -> returns schedule_id.
- admin UI: /internal/eval-mesh (read-only for most; write access gated to applied-ml and infra teams).
- Exported signals: metrics-store (Prometheus) and regression-triage queue (task-bus).

Privacy and storage
------------------
- No raw inputs or outputs are exported to fingerprint-db. Only buckets and normalized fields are kept.
- All fingerprints must be filtered by PII detector in traffic-tap; any fingerprint with PII_flag == true is dropped locally and counted in a metric (eval.mesh.pii_drops).
- Retention defaults: 90d for fingerprint-db; sampling-only exports (baseline-sampled) kept 7d.

Runbook: responding to a coverage gap alert
------------------------------------------
1. Alert fires: eval.mesh.coverage_ratio < 0.9 for 3h. Pager to applied-ml oncall.
2. Triage steps (owner: applied-ml oncall):
   a. Open /internal/eval-mesh -> slice dashboard and identify missing fingerprints by prevalence.
   b. If slice prevalence > 0.5% of 30d traffic, escalate: create new mapping rule (temp) in eval-orchestrator with priority=high and add owner tag.
   c. If slice is sensitive (customer-specific), notify privacy and customer-success before scheduling.
   d. Kick off a targeted daily-run (manual override) using schedule API: POST /v1/schedule {\"workload_id\":\"ad-hoc-slice-<id>\", \"priority\":\"high\"}.
3. Close alert once coverage_ratio >= 0.95 for 24h.

Runbook: regression triage handoff
---------------------------------
1. result-aggregator emits regression alert to regression-triage queue with schedule_id and trace link.
2. Oncall inspects diffs in result-aggregator UI (compare baseline vs candidate) and follows triage checklist: sample-level inspection, prompt reproduction, KV-cache sensitivity test, quantization toggle test (fast path).
3. If reproducer found: create regression ticket assigned to responsible model-onboarding team, attach reproducer, sample IDs, and fingerprint slice.
4. If no reproducer in 2h and alert persists, escalate to runtime team to check kernel/caching regressions.

Quantization and cache-sensitivity hooks
--------------------------------------
- Eval workloads carry tags: quant_profile (e.g., q4_0, q8_1), kv_cache_mode (on/off), and compile_flags. The scheduler can add a matrix of runs for high and critical slices: e.g., commerce-function-heavy-v2 -> runs: [candidate(q8_1, cache=on), baseline(q8_1, cache=on), candidate(q4_0, cache=on), candidate(q8_1, cache=off)].
- Use the quant-tuner quick-check script on candidate runs before promotion: scripts/quant-quick-check.sh --job <schedule_id>.

Rollout plan for Eval Mesh (canary -> global)
--------------------------------------------
1. Canary (2 weeks): enable traffic-tap on non-customer routes in eu-west-1 only. Monitor eval.mesh.pii_drops and coverage_ratio.
2. Stage (4 weeks): expand to 25% of routes (opt-in by route owners). Add automated rule set for top-10 routes.
3. Global: enable for all hosted routes after incident-free run and coverage SLO met for 30d.

Ownership and governance
------------------------
- Applied-ML team: mapping rules, workload definitions, prompt sets.
- Eng-serving-runtime: traffic-tap code, kernel-safe sampling, PII detector.
- Eng-platform: scheduler, quota enforcement, and priority queueing logic.
- Security/Privacy: review and sign-off on fingerprint schema and retention.

Alerts and dashboards (recommended panels)
----------------------------------------
- eval.mesh.coverage_ratio (single stat + 30d timeseries)
- eval.mesh.freshness (heatmap by priority and route)
- eval.mesh.cost_ratio (trend and per-workload breakdown)
- eval.mesh.pii_drops (count by route)

Troubleshooting checklist (common cases)
----------------------------------------
- Missing fingerprints for a route: check traffic-tap rollout, network policies, and tap logs (service: traffic-tap /var/log/tap.log).
- False positives in PII detector: update detector rules and reprocess a small sample in offline mode.
- Scheduler backlog: verify quota settings in eng-platform and backpressure signals to eval-orchestrator (metric: eval.scheduler.backlog_count).

Appendix: small sample mapping rules (canonical)
------------------------------------------------
1) commerce-function-heavy-v2 -> match: route =~ \"chat/commerce\" && call_pattern == \"function-heavy\" -> priority high, run_matrix [candidate(q8_1, cache=on), baseline(q8_1, cache=on)].
2) long-context-support -> match: token_histogram_bucket == \"1025+\" -> priority medium, retention 30d.
3) baseline-sampled -> match: random_sample(0.05) -> priority low.

Related pages and references
---------------------------
- Serving simulation harness (internal): /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/eval-harness/serving-simulation-eval-harness-2026
- Priority scheduler policy: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/eval-harness/interactive-eval-batch-scheduler-priority-policy-2026
- Quantization tuner runbook: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/quantization-profiles/per-workload-quant-tuner-and-safety-guidelines-2026

Document history
----------------
- 2026-02-10: Draft created by Asha Patel.
- 2026-02-18: Added quantization hooks and scheduling constraints (review by Marco Liu).
- 2026-03-01: Published with canary rollout plan and runbooks.

title: Service Sensitivity: Eval SLA Matrix and Prioritization Playbook
content:
Summary
-------
This playbook defines a service-sensitivity driven evaluation (eval) SLA matrix and a reproducible prioritization algorithm for scheduling eval resources across Redwood’s eval harness. The goal is to ensure that eval coverage maps to business risk, customer-facing SLOs, and cost budgets while keeping the model onboarding and regression-triage workflows predictable and auditable.

Goals
- Make eval prioritization deterministic and defensible.
- Align eval cadence and fidelity to service-level sensitivity (impact if degraded).
- Provide clear onboarding steps and triage triggers tied to measurable thresholds.
- Reduce token spend waste by automatically degrading eval fidelity when budget pressure is high.

Scope
- Applies to all eval jobs that run on the central eval harness (shadow runs, synthetic probes, slice scans).
- Includes quantization, KV-cache, and latency sensitivity checks necessary for production promotion.
- Not intended for research-only experiments or unconstrained hyperparameter sweeps.

Definitions
- Service Sensitivity: categorical label (Critical / Important / Low) representing customer impact if model quality regresses.
- Eval SLA: target cadence and minimum fidelity required (e.g., sample size, annotation depth, pass thresholds).
- Fidelity Delta: allowed degradation in measured quality (e.g., 1.5% absolute accuracy drop, or 0.02 loss increase).
- Eval Budget Unit (EBU): accounting unit mapped to token/compute costs used for budget enforcement.

Service Sensitivity Matrix (canonical)
| service_tier | example_product_area | business_impact | SLO_target | eval_cadence | min_sample_size | allowed_fidelity_delta | cost_priority |
|--------------|----------------------|-----------------|-----------:|-------------:|-----------------:|----------------------:|--------------:|
| Critical     | customer-chat, billing-automation | revenue-impact, regulatory | p99 latency < 150ms; accuracy > 98% | daily smoke + weekly slice | 2,000 probes/week | 0.5% absolute | high |
| Important    | search-relevance, support-assist | user-satisfaction | p99 latency < 250ms; accuracy > 94% | weekly full + triage-on-alert | 800 probes/week | 1.5% absolute | medium |
| Low          | internal-summarization, discovery | internal efficiency | p99 latency < 400ms; accuracy > 88% | monthly sample | 200 probes/month | 3.0% absolute | low |

How to use this matrix
1. Identify service_tier during product onboarding (see Onboarding Checklist below).
2. Map onboarding label to the canonical matrix. If product deviates, attach a short exception with owner approval.
3. The eval scheduler uses the matrix to assign priority weight and minimum EBU per eval job.

Prioritization algorithm (high level)
1. Compute base_priority = f(service_tier) where Critical=100, Important=60, Low=20.
2. Adjust for recency: recent_regression_hit -> +30 score.
3. Adjust for rollout stage: canary -> +20, GA -> +0.
4. Adjust for cost pressure: if cluster_utilization > 85% -> scale priorities by 0.6 for Low and 0.9 for Important (Critical unaffected).
5. Final_score = base_priority + adjustments. The scheduler orders eval runs by Final_score descending.

Example priority weights table
- Critical: base 100, min EBU 50/week
- Important: base 60, min EBU 20/week
- Low: base 20, min EBU 5/month

Eval scheduling policies
- Preemption: a Critical eval can preempt an Important or Low eval if Final_score delta > 30. Preempted jobs are checkpointed and requeued.
- Graceful fidelity scaling: when budget < 20% of expected monthly EBU, reduce per-job sample_size by 50% for Low tier and 25% for Important tier (never for Critical).
- Canary window: for any new model promotion, mandatory canary eval runs (Critical/Important: 72-hour window; Low: 7-day).

Onboarding checklist (model/service)
- Product owner declares service_tier and lists primary routes.
- Attach representative prompt families and failure slices (minimum 10 examples per slice).
- Provide acceptance metrics and guardrails (latency, accuracy, hallucination rate).
- Reserve an initial eval budget (EBU) for the first 30 days.
- Register contact and escalation path in the ticket and link to related pages.

Rollout and regression triage flow (operational steps)
1. Pre-promotion: run the canary eval suite. If any sentinel falls outside the allowed_fidelity_delta, block promotion.
2. Promotion: if canary passes, schedule staged rollout with telemetry hooks.
3. Monitoring: continuous probes at the cadence per matrix. Alert thresholds: fidelity_delta > allowed_fidelity_delta OR p99 latency > SLO_target + 20%.
4. On alert: run the fast triage runner (see "Fast Triage Runner" steps below). If triage confirms regression, rollback to previous model version and open a regression incident.

Fast Triage Runner (playbook)
1. Reproduce the failure on the same seed and prompt set used in probe. Capture full model output and tokens.
2. Run stratified slice checks (length, role, user-intent, localization).
3. Compare outputs to the last-known-good snapshot using metrics: accuracy, BLEU-like semantic overlap, embedding-distance drift.
4. If discrepancy localized to quantized artifact or KV cache mismatch, tag as "runtime-fidelity" and escalate to Serving Runtime.
5. If discrepancy appears model-internal (behavior change across many slices), tag as "model-regression" and escalate to Model-Onboarding/Research.
6. Attach artifacts to the regression ticket and set severity using the regression-impact-index.

Telemetry & metrics to emit (minimum)
- eval:probe_id, model_version, seed, prompt_family, slice_id, timestamp, latency_ms, tokens_in, tokens_out, score_primary, score_secondary, pass/fail_flag
- infra: cluster_utilization_pct, avg_gpu_mem_util_pct, queue_wait_seconds
- ownership: owner_team, contact_pager, runbook_link

Configuration table (scheduler knobs)
| knob | description | recommended default |
|------|-------------|---------------------|
| max_parallel_jobs | maximum concurrent eval runners per cluster | 120 |
| budget_headroom_pct | fraction of monthly EBU to keep unspent for emergency | 10% |
| fidelity_scaling_threshold_pct | cluster utilization at which fidelity scaling kicks in | 85% |
| preemption_score_delta | score delta required to preempt a running job | 30 |

Sample eval job YAML (example)
---
job_name: "billing-chat-slice-smoke"
service_tier: "Critical"
model_version: "rwd-v1-2026-03"
cadence: "daily-smoke"
sample_size: 2000
min_pass_rate: 0.98
budget_units: 60
owner: "payments-platform-team"
---

Notes on cost accounting
- Map EBU to real billing using the Eval Budgeting service: 1 EBU ≈ 10k tokens on average shadow traffic in our current fleet. This mapping is reviewed quarterly.
- When an eval run triggers a regression triage, additional EBUs are allocated from the emergency reserve; these are reconciled at the end of the incident.

Ownership and contacts
- Eval harness owner: eng-evals (primary oncall via #eng-evals)
- Regression triage lead: Applied ML (applied-ml-oncall)
- Serving runtime escalation: eng-serving-runtime oncall

Example scenarios
1) Canary failure for Critical chat model: immediate block, run Fast Triage Runner, if tagged runtime-fidelity -> serve fallback variant and open P1 with Serving Runtime; if tagged model-regression -> rollback + P1 for research.
2) Budget pressure during month-end: fidelity scaling reduces Low/Important sample sizes; Critical runs maintain full fidelity. Notify owners and pro-rate release schedules.

Appendix A — common queries
- Find probes failing in last 24h: SELECT probe_id, service, score_primary, timestamp FROM eval_probes WHERE pass=false AND timestamp > now() - interval '24 hours';
- Compute average EBU spend per service_tier: SELECT service_tier, sum(budget_units) FROM eval_jobs WHERE month = '2026-02' GROUP BY service_tier;

Appendix B — automation snippets
- Requeue command (cli): rwd-evalctl requeue --job-id 12345 --priority 95
- Snapshot compare (python): rwd_eval_tools.compare_snapshots('snapshot_prev.json', 'snapshot_now.json', metrics=['accuracy','embed_distance'])

Change log
- 2026-01-12: Created initial playbook (Priya Menon).
- 2026-02-20: Added fidelity-scaling algorithm and YAML job sample; clarified telemetry fields (Ethan Chung).

Related artifacts and readouts
- Weekly eval budget report (retained in /reports/eval-budget/).
- Regression-impact-index methodology (see related_pages).

Owners and next steps
- Owners: eng-evals (policy), applied-ml (triage), product-owners (service tier declarations).
- Next step: schedule a quarterly review to tune base_priority and EBU mapping; create a dashboard for Final_score heatmap.

If you are onboarding a model, start at the "Onboarding checklist" section and open an onboarding ticket with ownership details.

title: Microburst Batching and Workload Fingerprint Guidelines
content:
Summary

This document defines a reproducible approach for detecting microburst-style workload fingerprints and applying adaptive batching strategies in the eval harness and production serving runtime. Goal: reduce cost and tail latency variance caused by short, bursty traffic patterns while preserving throughput and output quality.

Problem statement

Microbursts are short-lived spikes of high QPS with small request sizes (commonly 8–128 tokens) that: 
- Cause inefficient GPU occupancy (many tiny batches).
- Inflate p95/p99 latency dramatically due to scheduling overhead.
- Confuse static batching heuristics tuned for average load.

Definitions and abbreviations

- Microburst: a contiguous window (default 10s) where arrival rate > burst_qps_threshold.
- Burst QPS threshold (burst_qps_threshold): default 300 reqs/s per front-end shard.
- Short-request: request with prompt_length <= 128 tokens.
- Adaptive batching: dynamic change to batching parameters (max_batch_size, batch_timeout_ms) based on observed fingerprint.
- Serving components referenced: serving-runtime (CUDA kernels), batch-orchestrator (batch assembly), traffic-router (policy routing), eval-harness (shadow replay).

Workload fingerprint taxonomy

We classify fingerprints to drive policies: 
1) Short-HighBurst: >300 QPS, median tokens <=64. Typical: chat message bursts, notifications.
2) Short-Spiky: bursts where QPS spikes > 2x baseline for <30s.
3) Mixed-Long: long-context requests interleaved with short ones.
4) Steady-High: sustained high QPS for >5 minutes (not a microburst).

Telemetry signals to detect fingerprints

Collect and evaluate these signals at 1s and 10s windows: 
- arrival_rate_per_shard (reqs/s)
- median_prompt_tokens, p90_prompt_tokens
- batch_assembly_time_ms (mean, p95)
- avg_batch_size_tokens and avg_batch_size_reqs
- kernel_utilization (GPU active time fraction)
- queue_length (requests waiting to be batched)

Detection rule (example): 
1) If arrival_rate_per_shard (10s) >= 300 AND median_prompt_tokens <= 64 THEN fingerprint = Short-HighBurst.
2) If arrival_rate_per_shard increases >2x over 1s baseline AND duration <30s THEN fingerprint = Short-Spiky.

Adaptive batching design patterns

We support three modes that the batch-orchestrator may apply per route and per model-variant: 
- Conservative (default): max_batch_size_reqs=64, batch_timeout_ms=12
- Burst-friendly: max_batch_size_reqs=128, batch_timeout_ms=6, prefer prefix caching for repeated prefixes
- Low-latency passthrough: max_batch_size_reqs=8, batch_timeout_ms=3 (used for latency-critical routes)

Switching policy: 
- At detection of Short-HighBurst, move route from Conservative -> Burst-friendly. 
- If kernel_utilization < 0.3 and p95 latency > slo_p95_threshold for 2 consecutive 10s windows, escalate batch_timeout_ms += 4ms (to increase aggregation) up to 40ms.
- If Mixed-Long detected, enable request-slicing and per-request prioritization to avoid head-of-line blocking.

Default thresholds and acceptance criteria

Below is the recommended starting configuration used by the eval-harness and can be tuned per workload. Operators must validate changes in shadow before rollout.

| Metric | Default | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| burst_qps_threshold | 300 req/s | per front-end shard |
| short_request_token_cutoff | 128 tokens | <= is considered short |
| conservative.max_batch_size_reqs | 64 | typical steady workloads |
| conservative.batch_timeout_ms | 12 | balances latency and aggregation |
| burst-friendly.max_batch_size_reqs | 128 | increases throughput during bursts |
| burst-friendly.batch_timeout_ms | 6 | smaller timeout but larger cap |
| passthrough.max_batch_size_reqs | 8 | minimizes batching overhead |
| passthrough.batch_timeout_ms | 3 | for sub-50ms p50 targets |

YAML example: configuring adaptive-batching (serving-runtime v1.8)

adaptive_batching:
  route_match: "/v1/chat"
  fingerprints:
    short_highburst:
      qps_threshold: 300
      max_window_s: 10
      action: burst_friendly
  modes:
    conservative:
      max_batch_size_reqs: 64
      batch_timeout_ms: 12
    burst_friendly:
      max_batch_size_reqs: 128
      batch_timeout_ms: 6
    passthrough:
      max_batch_size_reqs: 8
      batch_timeout_ms: 3

Design rationale and tradeoffs

- Larger max_batch_size_reqs improves throughput and GPU utilization but can increase worst-case latency if batch_timeout_ms is high.
- Short bursts benefit more from tighter batch_timeout_ms combined with a larger cap because requests are short and can be coalesced quickly.
- For Mixed-Long fingerprints we prefer to slice long requests (e.g., chunk kv-cache friendly segments) so short requests can get through.

Evaluation and shadow testing protocol (eval-harness)

1) Fingerprint replay generation: use the eval-harness workload generator to synthesize three trace types (Short-HighBurst, Short-Spiky, Mixed-Long) with user intent labels.
2) Shadow run against new batching config for 30m across 3 shards.
3) Collect metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, avg tokens/sec/GPU, kernel_utilization, failed_batches_rate.
4) Acceptance gates: 
   - p95 (short requests) must not increase > 15% vs baseline for production routes.
   - tokens/sec/GPU must not decrease > 10% for sustained loads.
   - tail error rate (5xx from runtime) must remain <= 0.1%.
5) If gates fail, run 2-step bisect: A/B configs with toggled timeout_ms then cap size to localize.

Regression triage: microburst-induced latencies

When a regression is reported with spike in p95 during bursts, follow this incident triage: 
1) Triage owner (oncall-serving) tags incident with fingerprint suspected.
2) Pull 10s- and 1s-window telemetry around spike. 
3) If arrival_rate increased > burst_qps_threshold: confirm Short-HighBurst.
4) Run replay of observed trace in eval-harness with baseline and current config. 
5) If replay reproduces regression: revert adaptive changes (if recently rolled) or apply passthrough to critical routes while continuing investigation.
6) Produce postmortem with root cause: config parameter, scheduling regression, model change, or infra degradation.

Rollout plan for adaptive-batching changes

- Canary: 1% traffic routed to new config for 2 hours, monitor p95/p99 and error rates.
- Progressive rollout: 1% -> 5% -> 20% -> 100% across 24–72 hours with rollback on gate failure.
- Safety net: automatic fallback to Conservative mode when p95(latency) > configured slo_p95_threshold for 3 consecutive 10s windows.

Ownership, SLAs and dashboards

- Owner: serving-runtime team (primary), eval-harness (secondary)
- SLOs to monitor (per-route): 
  - short-request p95 <= 250ms (hosted), <=150ms (dedicated SLA routes)
  - error rate <=0.1%
  - batch_assembly_time p95 <= 40ms under burst conditions
- Dashboards: 
  - Route-level fingerprint heatmap (10s granularity)
  - Adaptive mode state timeline (per route)
  - Kernel utilization vs tokens/sec/GPU

Operational runbook (quick actions)

1) If p95 spikes during burst: switch route to passthrough mode for immediate mitigation.
2) If kernel_utilization drops below 20% and batch sizes small: switch to burst-friendly with increased cap.
3) If errors increase after mode change: rollback to last stable mode and open an incident.

FAQ

Q: Why not always use burst-friendly?
A: Some steady workloads with long contexts can suffer head-of-line blocking and increased memory pressure; we prefer targeted mode changes.

Q: How do we avoid oscillation between modes?
A: Use hysteresis: require fingerprint condition to be stable for min_stable_window (default 10s) before switching and a cool-down of 30s before re-evaluation.

References and related pages

- Throughput vs fidelity matrix (see related page).
- Runtime batching internals and kernel selection docs in eng-serving-runtime runtime-architecture.

Appendix: Example detection queries

Prometheus (pseudo):

# 10s arrival rate per shard\sum by(shard) (increase(serving_requests_total[10s]))

# median prompt tokens in 10s window (approx)\histogram_quantile(0.5, sum(rate(prompt_tokens_bucket[10s])) by (le))

Contact

Priya Kaur (serving-runtime) — priya@redwood.example.com

title: Runtime-sensitive eval contract for multi-tier deployments
content:
Summary
-------
This playbook defines a standardized, runtime-sensitive evaluation contract used by product, model-onboarding, and serving teams to certify model variants across Redwood's three deployment tiers (Hosted API, Dedicated, Private). The goal is to provide a single, machine-actionable contract that specifies the set of probes, SLO thresholds, quantization compatibility checks, and regression-triage triggers required for promotion and rollback decisions.

Scope
-----
- Applies to new model versions and model-variant promotions (e.g., float32 -> int8, mixed-precision families).
- Covers integration points between eval harness, prompt catalog, quantization profiles, and runtime observability.
- Not a replacement for business-level acceptance tests (product signoff still required).

Definitions
-----------
- Fidelity contract: a declared mapping of quality metrics to deployment tiers and acceptable deltas versus baseline.
- Probe: a single evaluation item derived from the prompt catalog (single-shot or multi-turn).
- Latency slice: workload bucket defined by request size, functioncall usage, and p95/P99 latency sensitivity.
- Quant-compatibility test: synthetic and runtime checks that exercise tokenization, KV-cache behavior, and attention fallback for quantized kernels.

SLO matrix (canonical)
----------------------
| Metric                          | Hosted (fastest path) | Dedicated (reserved) | Private (customer-managed) |
|---------------------------------|-----------------------:|---------------------:|---------------------------:|
| p50 generation latency (ms)     | < 30                 | < 45                | < 70                      |
| p95 generation latency (ms)     | < 120                | < 200               | < 350                     |
| Semantic fidelity (anchor F1)   | >= 0.92 vs baseline  | >= 0.90 vs baseline | >= 0.88 vs baseline       |
| Functioncall correctness (%)    | >= 99.0              | >= 98.0             | >= 96.5                   |
| Tokenization equivalence (score)| >= 0.995             | >= 0.99             | >= 0.98                   |
| Regression alert rate (per 100k)| <= 5                 | <= 10               | <= 25                     |

Notes: thresholds are default starting points. Product or customer contracts may tighten metrics. All numeric thresholds must be expressed in the release artifact (see artifact manifest section).

Artifact manifest (required keys)
---------------------------------
- model_id: string (e.g., rwd/gpt-xx-large)
- model_variant: string (e.g., fp16, int8-qdq)
- baseline_tag: string (reference model artifact used for delta comparisons)
- probe_suite_id: string (ID of the probe collection in the eval registry)
- quant_profile_id: string | "none"
- cutoff_latency_ms: integer (p95/cutoff used for routing)
- rollout_policy: one of [canary, staged, global]

Example JSON manifest snippet (for CI validation):
```
{
  "model_id": "rwd-chat-7b",
  "model_variant": "int8-qdq-2025-03",
  "baseline_tag": "rwd-chat-7b-fp16-2025-02",
  "probe_suite_id": "probe-suite-stability-2025-02",
  "quant_profile_id": "qprofile-int8-lowloss-v2",
  "cutoff_latency_ms": "200",
  "rollout_policy": "staged"
}
```

Probe selection and stratification
---------------------------------
1. Start from the canonical prompt catalog and derive three probe strata:
   - Core functional probes (30%): common intents and critical path examples.
   - Edge correctness probes (40%): long-tail prompts, numerics, sandboxed adversarial cases.
   - Latency/throughput probes (30%): synthetic high-concurrency and long-context scenarios.
2. Each probe in the suite must be tagged with: domain, complexity (len tokens), functioncall-usage, and privacy-sensitivity.
3. For quant-variant checks, include a replication of at least 12% of the core functional probes run under maximum context length.

Quantization compatibility checklist
----------------------------------
- Tokenization equivalence: run tokenization roundtrip on 1000 representative examples; mean token error <= 0.5%.
- KV cache checksum parity: deterministic checksum delta under shadow replay < 0.1% of tokens.
- Attention fallback coverage: run failure-mode injection where numerical instabilities are forced; verify safe-fallback triggers exist.
- Output entropy drift: KL divergence vs baseline embeddings distribution < 0.06.
- Functioncall schema conformance: functioncall outputs must validate against declared JSON schemas for > 99% of probes.

Eval harness integration pattern
-------------------------------
- CI Step A (static checks): validate artifact manifest, probe suite registration, and quant profile tagging. Failure blocks pipeline.
- CI Step B (shadow-run): run probe suite against baseline and candidate for deterministic probes; collect diff metrics.
- CI Step C (runtime sim): use serving-simulation harness to emulate mixed-latency slices and batch sizes; assert that latency/SLOs meet tier targets.
- Telemetry export: produce an evaluation report in NDJSON with per-probe metrics, environment hash, and runtime fingerprint.

Promotion and rollout decision matrix
------------------------------------
- Pass/Fail rules are evaluated in order:
  1) Static manifest & probe registration (must pass)
  2) Semantic fidelity: candidate delta <= allowed budget for target tier
  3) Latency: candidate p95 <= cutoff_latency_ms in artifact manifest
  4) Quant-compatibility: all quant checks pass for quantized variants
  5) Canary smoke: limited production canary must show no regression alerts over 48h
- If any critical check fails, the model is rejected for that tier. Non-critical failures can be assigned to a mitigation plan with a measured debt budget.

Regression triage playbook (fast path)
-------------------------------------
1. Automated detection: alert triggered when regression alert rate > threshold in SLO matrix.
2. Fast capture: run per-probe diffs using the NDJSON reports captured during rollout; group by slice tags (domain, complexity).
3. Hypothesis generation: triage owner (oncall/eval-owner) fills triage template with top 3 hypotheses: tokenization, quant rounding, prompt sensitivity.
4. Targeted rollback: if top-priority slice shows core functionality regression (semantic fidelity drop > 3%), trigger immediate rollback for affected traffic tier.
5. Investigate offline: schedule a regression-bisect run against commit DAG + quant profile variance.

Operational runbook (for SREs and oncall)
-----------------------------------------
- Immediate checks (first 15 min):
  - Validate artifact manifest used by the active pool. CLI: rwdctl model describe --id <model_id> --variant <model_variant>
  - Check most recent eval-report NDJSON in /eval-reports/<probe_suite_id>/latest
  - Confirm p95 latency on dashboard (model-route-level) and compare to artifact cutoff_latency_ms
- Escalation steps (15-60 min):
  - If regression confirmed, notify product and applied-ml teams, attach probe-sample list and NDJSON diffs.
  - Kick off regression-bisect job: jobs/regress-bisect --start-commit X --end-commit Y --probes probe-list.json

Owner and responsibilities
--------------------------
- Applied ML (primary): define probe suites, interpret semantic fidelity metrics, lead label-driven investigations.
- Serving runtime (primary): provide runtime fingerprinting, latency slicing, and rollout enforcement hooks.
- Product (secondary): set product acceptance criteria and optional tightened SLOs for paid customers.
- SRE (secondary): monitor rollout adherence to cutoff_latency_ms and enforce traffic shaping during canaries.

Related pages
-------------
- Link to probe registry: /applied-ml-and-evals/prompt-sets-and-benchmarks/probe-registry-index
- Link to quant profiles: /applied-ml-and-evals/quantization-profiles/qprofile-index
- Link to regression triage runbook: /applied-ml-and-evals/regression-triage/regression-oncall-runbook

Change log
----------
- 2025-03-12 (Leila Thompson): Created initial draft and canonical SLO matrix.
- 2025-05-10 (Anika Bose): Added quant-compat checklist and artifact manifest example.
- 2025-06-02 (Marcus Li): Finalized promotion decision matrix and runbook steps.

Appendix: quick commands and example queries
-------------------------------------------
- Export evaluation report for probe suite: rwd-eval export --suite probe-suite-stability-2025-02 --format ndjson > /tmp/report.ndjson
- Compare candidate vs baseline: rwd-eval compare --baseline baseline-tag --candidate candidate-tag --out diff-summary.json
- Trigger a canary rollout (staged): rwdctl rollout start --model rwd-chat-7b --variant int8-qdq-2025-03 --policy staged --canary-size 0.02

End of document

title: Eval Budget Ledger and Cost Attribution Framework
content:
Summary
-------
This document defines the Eval Budget Ledger: a lightweight, canonical accounting model and operational framework for tracking, attributing, and governing the cost of evaluation work (shadow runs, probes, synthetic workloads, and human review) across the eval harness. It standardizes cost buckets, attribution rules, reporting artifacts, and a minimal runbook for triaging unexpected spend. The ledger enables reproducible cost rollups for feature teams, platform owners, and finance.

Goals
-----
- Provide a single source-of-truth CSV/JSON artifact (the ledger) for every eval campaign.
- Define deterministic attribution rules to map compute, human labeling, and storage costs to owning teams and probes.
- Enable near-real-time spend dashboards and budget alerts tied to probes, model variants, and environments (shadow/staging/prod).
- Reduce surprise spend from large synthetic sweeps and regression investigations; support pre-commit budget gating.

Definitions
-----------
- Probe: An atomic evaluation input or workload slice submitted to the eval harness.
- Campaign: A collection of probes executed as part of a single objective (e.g., shadow rollout of model-v2, quantization stress sweep).
- Ledger row: A single line in the canonical CSV representing cost attribution for one probe execution.

Ledger schema (CSV columns)
--------------------------
The ledger is produced by the eval orchestrator after each batch and stored in S3 and the eval index. Each ledger row is CSV with these columns (pipe-delimited in examples below for readability):

- ledger_id (string): UUID for the row.
- campaign_id (string): stable id for the campaign.
- probe_id (string): stable id for the probe.
- model_variant (string): e.g., redwood/gptx-8b-q4_latest.
- environment (string): shadow|staging|prod.
- start_ts (ISO8601): run start time.
- end_ts (ISO8601): run end time.
- compute_seconds (float): wall-clock GPU/CPU seconds consumed attributed to this probe.
- gpu_type (string): e.g., A100-80GB, L4x.
- memory_gb_seconds (float): memory usage * seconds (for cross-instance memory costs).
- tokens_in (int): input tokens.
- tokens_out (int): output tokens.
- kv_cache_hit_ratio (float): fraction for reuse-based discounts.
- human_label_seconds (float): paid human reviewer seconds attributable.
- storage_gb_months_fraction (float): short-lived artifact storage prorated to run.
- infra_cost_usd (float): computed infra cost allocated to row (see cost model).
- human_cost_usd (float): human labeling cost.
- total_cost_usd (float): infra_cost_usd + human_cost_usd + amortized tooling.
- owning_team (string): team slug owning the campaign (e.g., search-platform).
- billing_tag (string): optional billing tag for downstream finance mapping.
- notes (string): free text for special adjustments or credits.

Cost model and attribution rules
--------------------------------
1) Compute pricing table (example):

| resource | unit | nominal_price_usd | comment |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| A100-80GB | per GPU-hour | 3.20 | spot pricing baseline for eval fleet |
| L4x | per GPU-hour | 1.10 | cheaper short-live experiments |
| vCPU | per vCPU-hour | 0.05 | for non-GPU workloads |
| RAM | per GB-hour | 0.002 | memory charge for long-running jobs |

2) Compute allocation: infra_cost_usd = sum(resource_seconds * price_per_unit_hour / 3600) adjusted by kv_cache discount. For probes that benefit from prefix/KV cache, apply a KV discount factor: cost *= (1 - kv_cache_hit_ratio * kv_cache_savings). Default kv_cache_savings = 0.45.

3) Human labeling: human_cost_usd = human_label_seconds * human_rate_usd_per_second. Default human_rate_usd_per_second = 0.004 (equivalent to $14.4/hour for contractor labeling).

4) Storage and tooling amortization: short-lived artifacts (replays, logs) are prorated and summed into storage_gb_months_fraction * storage_unit_price_usd. Tooling and infra overhead (e.g., eval queue, orchestrator overhead) is allocated to rows as a percent uplift (default 5%) and recorded in notes.

Ownership and governance rules
------------------------------
- Campaign owner (owning_team) is responsible for setting a campaign budget and tagging critical probes with high-priority flags.
- Platform (eval-harness) owns the compute_price table and publishing weekly baseline rates to the ledger generator.
- Finance owns final mapping of billing_tag to GL codes.

Operational artifacts and examples
--------------------------------
Example ledger row (CSV):
ledger_id|campaign_id|probe_id|model_variant|environment|start_ts|end_ts|compute_seconds|gpu_type|memory_gb_seconds|tokens_in|tokens_out|kv_cache_hit_ratio|human_label_seconds|storage_gb_months_fraction|infra_cost_usd|human_cost_usd|total_cost_usd|owning_team|billing_tag|notes
123e4567|camp-202602|probe-009|redwood/gptx-8b-q4|shadow|2026-02-10T14:02:03Z|2026-02-10T14:02:09Z|6.1|A100-80GB|49.6|152|420|0.38|0.0|0.00002|0.0054|0.0000|0.0054|search-platform|GL-APPL-011|kv-cache applied

Quick CLI to produce per-campaign rollup (example SQL using ledger table):
1) Per-campaign cost: SELECT campaign_id, SUM(total_cost_usd) AS campaign_cost_usd, COUNT(DISTINCT probe_id) AS probes FROM eval_ledger WHERE start_ts >= '2026-02-01' AND environment = 'shadow' GROUP BY campaign_id;
2) Team allocation: SELECT owning_team, SUM(total_cost_usd) FROM eval_ledger WHERE start_ts >= '2026-01-01' GROUP BY owning_team;

Budget gating and alerting
-------------------------
- Preflight: campaign owners must declare a soft_budget_usd before launching non-trivial campaigns (> $5000 expected). The orchestrator rejects submission without a soft_budget or explicit approval for campaigns estimated > $25,000.
- Alerts: platform publishes per-campaign and per-team burn-rate metrics to Grafana. Alert thresholds: 50% of soft_budget (warning), 85% (action required), 100% (auto-pause candidate).
- Auto-pause policy: When a campaign crosses 100% and has no explicit approve_overage tag, orchestrator moves non-critical jobs to paused state and notifies owners via Slack and email. Critical jobs (marked critical=true) continue but generate P0 paged messages to the campaign owner.

Runbook: Investigating an unexpected spike
-----------------------------------------
1) Identify the campaign(s) with increased burn (Grafana or ledger query).
2) Drill into probe-level ledger rows for top-K cost contributors: SELECT probe_id, model_variant, sum(total_cost_usd) FROM eval_ledger WHERE campaign_id = 'camp-202602' GROUP BY probe_id ORDER BY 3 DESC LIMIT 50;
3) Check model_variant token stats and kv_cache_hit_ratio: sudden token_out increases or cache_hit drops are common causes.
4) If compute_seconds look anomalous, check orchestration logs for retries or timeouts (orchestrator/job-runner). If human_cost spikes, check labeling batch sizes or misconfigured annotator pools.
5) If budget was exhausted and auto-pause triggered, owners should: a) mark urgent probes as critical if necessary; b) request funding via the campaign's Jira billing request; c) schedule a short review to adjust probe sampling.

Integration notes
-----------------
- The ledger writer is integrated into the eval-orchestrator post-processing stage (hook: /eval/orchestrator/postprocess->ledger-writer).
- A small shim (ledger-normalizer) converts raw runtime traces into the ledger schema and applies price tables fetched from SSM periodically.
- For Private deployments, the ledger generator accepts a custom pricing file and billing_tag mapping. Private deployments must opt-in to sending ledgers to Redwood; default retention is 90 days unless overridden by customer contract.

Rollout plan
------------
1) Q1 2026: pilot with three product teams (search-platform, chat-core, insights) using a nightly shadow campaign.
2) Q2 2026: add automated preflight enforcement and Grafana dashboards; finance mapping for billing_tag.
3) Q3 2026: enforce soft_budget for all campaigns over $2,000; export periodic reports to cost-center owners.

Metrics to monitor
------------------
- Daily eval spend (USD) - global and per-team.
- 7d rolling average cost per probe and cost per 1k tokens.
- Top-50 probes by cost (weekly).
- Fraction of campaigns with declared soft_budget.

Open questions and future work
-----------------------------
- Incorporate token-based QoS pricing (discounts for batched micro-inference).
- Experiment with dynamic kv_cache_savings per-model instead of a fixed default.
- Better human cost modeling for in-house vs vendor labelers.

Appendix: sample Python snippet (ledger row enrichment)
------------------------------------------------------
# pseudo-code
# fetch price table, compute resource_seconds->usd, apply kv discount, write ledger csv

from datetime import datetime
import uuid

def compute_infra_cost(gpu_seconds, gpu_type, kv_hit_ratio, price_table, kv_savings=0.45):
    base_hour_price = price_table[gpu_type]
    cost = gpu_seconds / 3600.0 * base_hour_price
    cost *= (1 - kv_hit_ratio * kv_savings)
    return round(cost, 6)

row = {
    'ledger_id': str(uuid.uuid4()),
    'campaign_id': 'camp-202602',
    'probe_id': 'probe-009',
    'model_variant': 'redwood/gptx-8b-q4',
    'environment': 'shadow',
    'start_ts': datetime.utcnow().isoformat() + 'Z'
}

FAQ
---
Q: How are cross-team shared probes charged?
A: The campaign owner selects a billing_tag and can add split percentages to rows (stored in notes). We recommend assigning shared probes to a platform cost pool (owning_team: platform) and then splitting via internal chargebacks in finance.

Q: Can customers running private deployments see per-probe costs?
A: Yes; private deployments can opt-in and provide a custom price table. Ledger output is identical but stored in the customer's S3.

Contact and ownership
---------------------
- Doc owner: Priya Kapoor (applied-ml infra).
- Platform contact (ledger implementation): Miguel Torres.
- Finance contact (cost mappings): Dianne Wu.

title: Evaluation Retrospective & Priority Synthesis Playbook
content:
Overview

This playbook defines a standardized retrospective process and a quantitative priority-synthesis framework for managing evaluation probes, probe budgets, and regression triage across model families and deployment tiers. It is intended for evaluators, model stewards, and platform engineers responsible for maintaining production quality while balancing cost and latency.

Why this exists

- We operate multiple evaluator fleets (shadow, canary, long-tail) with limited probe budget. Without a consistent prioritization algorithm and retrospective cadence, high-impact failures are discovered late and cost is allocated inefficiently.
- This playbook aligns the eval lifecycle with quantization migration, shadowing experiments, and incident triage so that responsibility, telemetry, and rollback paths are clear.

Scope & Terminology

- Probe: a single test instance (prompt + metadata) executed against a model variant as part of an evaluation job.
- Slice: a grouped set of probes targeting a semantic/functional area (e.g., payment-intent, legal-forms, multi-turn-coherence).
- Priority Score: numeric score used by the scheduler to allocate probes under budget constraints.
- Cohort Shadow: a runtime shadowing run that mirrors a subset of live traffic to a candidate model.

Principles

1. Value-first: prioritize probes that reduce customer-facing risk (safety, correctness, regression severity) ahead of exploratory coverage.
2. Cost-aware: embed per-probe expected token cost and latency into prioritization so we can trade coverage against spend.
3. Signal-driven retrospectives: run a short (weekly) quantitative retrospective that re-weights slices based on recent incidents, regressions, and drift.
4. Cross-model comparability: all shadow and eval runs must surface the same minimal telemetry contract (see Telemetry contract table).

Telemetry contract (minimum)

| Key | Type | Description | Owner | Example |
|------|------|-------------|-------|---------|
| probe_id | string | Unique probe identifier | evaluator-service | probe-20261102-0001 |
| slice_id | string | Logical slice name | probe-catalog | payment-intent-highvalue |
| model_variant | string | model id + quantization tag | model-onboarding | redwood-v2.1-8bit |
| latency_ms | integer | end-to-end inference latency | runtime | 84 |
| token_cost_est | float | estimated token cost for this probe | cost-service | 0.0042 |
| fidelity_delta | float | eval metric delta vs baseline (application-specific) | evaluator | -0.07 |
| pass_fail | enum | pass/fail/unknown based on sentinel | evaluator | fail |

Priority synthesis algorithm (high level)

PriorityScore = w_sev * SeverityImpact + w_freq * UsageFrequency + w_drift * DriftScore - w_cost * NormalizedCost - w_latency * NormalizedLatency + w_recency * RecencyBoost

Where weights (w_*) are learned/managed at the squad level and updated during retrospectives. Default weight suggestions (initial):

- w_sev = 6.0
- w_freq = 3.0
- w_drift = 2.5
- w_cost = 1.4
- w_latency = 0.8
- w_recency = 1.0

Normalization and scaling notes:
- SeverityImpact is in [0,1] and estimated from historical user-impact events (see Incident-map).
- NormalizedCost is token_cost_est scaled to the fleet median cost per probe.
- RecencyBoost = exp(-days_since_last_evaluation / tau) with tau default 21.

Practical scheduler rules

1. Reserve 15% of weekly probe budget for critical-safety and top-10 slices (guaranteed)
2. Reserve 10% for quant-migration shadow cohorts (so we can test quant fallbacks without starving safety probes)
3. Remaining budget is allocated by PriorityScore descending until budget exhausted
4. For mixed-precision candidates, ensure at least N=50 probes per slice are run in both float and quant variants for statistical comparability (N configurable per slice)

Weekly retrospective process (30–60 minutes) — running steps

1. Data prep (Automated): exporter job builds a summary of the past 7 days: top failing slices, probe spend, latency distribution, newly landed PRs touching model/serving/runtime. (owner: evaluator-ops)
2. Incident alignment (5–10m): map any user-facing incidents or reliability alerts to affected slices and hypothesize causes.
3. Weight tuning (10–20m): update w_* weights where justified (evidence: fidelity_delta, incident severity counts, and cost overrides). Document changes with rationale.
4. Allocation commit (5m): commit the adjusted budget allocations and publish to scheduler config in the eval-mesh. Tag the config with weekly-retro-YYYYMMDD.
5. Follow-ups (as needed): create action items (e.g., increase probe coverage, add sentinel, run focused quant sweep). Assign owners and due dates.

Runbook: urgent regression detected in baseline service

1. Pager triggers (if fidelity_delta on production sentinel exceeds threshold): immediately spin a high-priority shadow cohort for the suspected model version (owner: model-oncall).
2. Triage (15m): gather first-pass diagnostics: top failing probes, tokenization diffs, latency spikes, quantization tags. Use the regression-hunt notebook template.
3. Canary rollback (if regression confirmed and severity >= P1): initiate model rollback per deployment playbook and open an incident.
4. Postmortem: run the retrospective process with emphasis on causality: code change, model data shift, quant misalignment, runtime bug.

Quant-aware eval addendum

- When testing quantized candidates, attach probe-level metadata: quant_backend (e.g., q4_0, int8_v2), kernel_variant, and fallback-path.
- Add a "coherence-sentinel" for multi-turn and function-call probes to detect early breakdowns unique to precision reduction.
- If quant candidate shows systematic token-level divergence > tol (default 0.12 BLEU-like delta for structured outputs) on high-value slices, escalate to quant-safety review.

Example scheduler config snippet (YAML)

scheduler_weekly_budget: 100000  # number of probes
reserves:
  safety_slices: 0.15
  quant_shadow: 0.10
  ad_hoc: 0.05
weights:
  severity: 6.0
  frequency: 3.0
  drift: 2.5
  cost: 1.4
  latency: 0.8
  recency: 1.0

Promptset stewardship and retirements

1. Promptsets must declare a retire-after window (default 18 months) and a stable-owner (team/squad).
2. During retrospectives, if a slice shows persistent low-fidelity signal and low usage, mark for scheduled deprecation and reallocation of probes.
3. When retiring, create a migration manifest that lists representative probes to preserve for historical reproducibility.

Ownership & roles

- Evaluator-ops: runs the scheduler, exports retrospectives, maintains probe-catalog.
- Model-steward: signs off on slice re-weighting for their model family and owns follow-up action items.
- Platform-runtime: ensures telemetry contract is honored and provides cost estimates per probe.
- Incident-team: owns serving rollback and postmortem coordination.

Metrics & SLOs for the eval system

- Coverage SLO: Top-25 slices must have weekly probe runs >= 90% of target (target defined per slice)
- Detection latency SLO: median time from regression emergence to detection in shadow runs <= 48 hours
- Probe cost SLO: weekly probe spend variance <= 20% vs planned budget

Template: weekly-retrospective summary (copy/paste)

Title: Weekly Eval Retro — YYYY-MM-DD
Owner: <evaluator-ops-person>
Top failing slices: [sliceA (n fails), sliceB (n fails)]
Top change causes: [quant-rollout, tokenizer-patch, prompt-regression]
Weight changes committed: [severity 6.0 -> 7.0] (rationale)
Budget commit: total X probes (safety: Y, quant: Z, ad_hoc: W)
Action items: - Replace sentinel for sliceA (owner: Alice) due: YYYY-MM-DD

Appendices

A. Regression hunting checklist (short)
- Confirm probe pass/fail criteria and re-run failing probes with seed control
- Compare tokenization and pre/post-processor diffs
- Verify model artifact (git tag), quant backend, and runtime kernels match expectations
- Run replay harness for 1000 nearest-neighbor probes to failing set

B. Quick CLI snippets
# list scheduled configs
redwood-evalctl configs list --env=prod --tag=weekly-retro
# submit a focused shadow cohort for model v2.3-quant
redwood-evalctl cohort submit --model redwood-v2.3 --variant=q4_0 --slices payment-intent,legal-forms --budget 2000

C. FAQ (short)
Q: Who can change weights?
A: Squad model-stewards during the weekly retrospective or evaluator-ops for emergency adjustments with notification.

Q: What if the budget is exceeded mid-week?
A: Pause low-priority ad_hoc probes and re-run scheduler with an updated budget. If overruns persist, raise a finance-ops ticket.

Related docs and links

- Eval mesh scheduler spec: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/eval-harness/eval-mesh-topology-and-slotting-cookbook-2026
- Quant migration safety contract: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/quantization-profiles/quant-profile-synthesis-and-safety-playbook-2024

Contact

For questions, open a ticket in the evaluator-ops channel or ping #eval-retros on Slack.

Document change log

- 2026-02-15: Created (Maya Chen)
- 2026-05-11: Added quant addendum and CLI examples (Rohit Kapoor)
- 2026-11-02: Weight tuning defaults adjusted and runbook clarified (Elena García)

title: Multifidelity Shadow Scheduler and Data Contract
content:
Overview

Purpose
This document defines the Multifidelity Shadow Scheduler (MSS) and the accompanying Data Contract used to reliably run shadow evaluations across heterogeneous fidelity levels (live shadow, synthetic micro‑probes, and replayed traffic). The goal is to provide a repeatable, auditable orchestration pattern that balances cost, signal quality, and safety for model promotion decisions.

Scope
- Applies to all shadow evaluation runs for inference-serving model variants (hosted, dedicated, private) that feed into promotion gates, regression triage, and quantization verification.
- Describes scheduler behavior, fidelity tiers, data and telemetry contract, acceptance quorum, and runbook for promoting a shadowed candidate.

Motivation
As we increase the cadence of model updates and deploy quantized variants, teams need deterministic, cross‑region shadowing that:
- Produces comparable signal across fidelity types,
- Avoids overloading production paths, and
- Provides a clear data contract so evaluators and SREs can reason about drift and regressions.

Definitions
- Fidelity levels: 'live' (mirror small percentage of live traffic), 'hybrid' (mixed live+synthetic), 'synthetic' (replayer or probe-driven), 'replay' (historical traffic playback).
- Quorum: minimum aggregate of evaluator signals (numeric metrics and human review votes) required before a promotion decision.
- Shadow run: an execution of a model variant in non‑serving mode where outputs are collected for evaluation only.

Design overview
- Scheduler is a central orchestration service (mss-service) that provisions shadow runs to runtimes (hosted/dedicated/private connectors).
- Each run is assigned a fidelity class and a telemetry profile.
- Data Contract guarantees schema, sampling, and retention for evaluation artifacts.
- Promotion flow uses a quorum protocol: numeric gates (SLO deltas, regression thresholds) + at least one manual annotator signoff for high-risk slices.

Key guarantees provided by MSS
- Isolation: shadow traffic must never affect production latency budgets or KV cache integrity.
- Representativeness: live and hybrid runs are weighted to preserve distributional fidelity.
- Reproducibility: replay seeds and probe versions are recorded for exact replays.
- Cost control: synthetic probes have rate limits and backpressure to control GPU spend.

Scheduler algorithm (high level)
1. Accept run request with parameters: model_id, variant_tag, fidelity, slice_spec, duration, tracer_id.
2. Validate data contract: ensure required probes/provenance fields are present. Reject if missing.
3. Allocate capacity using a smoothing window algorithm: prefer idle capacity in same region; fall back to dedicated burst pool.
4. Throttle based on SLO headroom: if p99 latency budget usage > 80% for production pool, route shadow to dedicated or synthetic only.
5. Start run and attach telemetry sampling: full traces for 1% sessions; aggregated metrics for all.
6. Monitor health and auto‑evict after configurable failure thresholds.

Data Contract (required fields)
Every shadow artifact uploaded to the evaluation store must include the following top‑level fields (flat JSON record per request):
| field_name | type | description | required | example |
|------------|------|-------------|----------|---------|
| request_id | string | UUID v4 for the request | yes | req_4f11a2 |
| model_id | string | canonical model slug | yes | gpt-redwood-7b |
| variant_tag | string | serving tag or quant profile | yes | q4_1 |
| fidelity | string | 'live'|'hybrid'|'synthetic'|'replay' | yes | hybrid |
| slice_id | string | logical slice label | yes | payments-card-errors |
| timestamp_utc | string | ISO8601 | yes | 2026-02-18T15:22:03Z |
| input_tokens | int | tokenized input length | yes | 42 |
| output_tokens | int | tokens produced | yes | 128 |
| model_logits_checksum | string | fnv64 hex or 'n/a' for opaque outputs | no | a3f4... |
| provenance | string | 'live-proxy'|'replayer'|'probe-run' | yes | probe-run |
| seed | string | replay/probe seed identifier | conditional | seed_2026_0218 |
| eval_tags | list[string] | tag set for this sample | no | ["anchor","high-confidence"] |

Contract rules
- Records missing required fields are dropped and reported.
- Provenance must be one of the preapproved values listed in the 'provenance registry'.
- For 'live' fidelity, request_id must be correlated with production trace_id for postmortem tracing, but payloads must not be forwarded to downstream systems.

Telemetry and metrics
Minimum metrics emitted by MSS (per run):
- run_id, model_id, variant_tag, fidelity, start_ts, end_ts, total_requests, acceptance_rate, p50_latency_ms, p95_latency_ms, p99_latency_ms, error_count, eviction_reason
- Artifact quality metrics: embedding_stability_score, semantic_similarity_zscore, topk_coverage_delta (for retrieval tasks)
- Cost accounting: gpu_seconds, storage_bytes, network_bytes

Metric SLAs and alerting
- MSS must emit run-level heartbeat every 30s. Missing heartbeat for 2 intervals -> P0 oncall page.
- If synthetic probe failure rate > 5% over 5m -> auto‑scale probe pool down and notify owner.
- If live-shadow p99 latency delta vs prod > 2x baseline for 3 minutes -> auto‑evict runs from production pool.

Quorum and promotion policy
Promotion requires the following:
- Numeric gates: no slice reports > 3% regression in critical task F1 or > 2x latency delta at p95 on production slices.
- Stability gates: embedding stability score >= 0.92 across sampled anchor set.
- Quorum: at least 3 independent automated evaluators pass (unit tests, slice tests, adversarial probes) AND either (a) a human annotator approves critical slices, or (b) an audit of sandboxed inference for 1k samples with no high-severity safety hits.

Promotion flow (operational steps)
1. MSS aggregates run outputs into a promotion report and posts to /eval-reports/{model_id}/{variant_tag}/{run_id}.
2. Auto-evaluator stage runs and emits pass/fail flags.
3. If numeric gates pass and quorum met, the system will mark candidate as 'eligible_for_canary' but will not automatically promote without scheduled canary window.
4. SRE schedules a short canary (0.5% traffic) for 24h with increased monitoring.
5. If canary passes, product owner can approve a staged rollout.

Runbook: quick triage for shadow regressions
1. Identify offending slices from promotion report.
2. Check provenance and fidelity: confirm whether the failure was observed in live/hybrid vs synthetic only.
3. If failure exists only in synthetic runs, reproduce with replay and increased sample size.
4. If failure exists in live-shadow and p99 latency has regressed, evict run and open incident with tag 'shadow-latency'.
5. Use replay with recorded seeds to bisect change set (link to bisect playbook).

APIs & examples
- Start a run (POST /mss/v1/runs): payload must obey data contract header and include 'expected_metrics' list. Example YAML payload:

request: |\n  model_id: redwood-7b\n  variant_tag: q8_0\n  fidelity: hybrid\n  slice_spec:\n    - slice_id: billing-checkout\n      percentage: 0.5\n  duration_minutes: 90\n  tracer_id: mss-20260112-01\n
- Query run status: GET /mss/v1/runs/{run_id}/status -> returns run metadata and last_telemetry_ts.
- Fetch promotion report: GET /eval-reports/{model_id}/{variant_tag}/{run_id} -> JSON stream adhering to data contract.

Configuration reference (table)
| config_key | description | default | ownership |
|------------|-------------|---------|-----------|
| mss.max_live_shadow_pct | Max percent of live requests that can be shadowed per service | 0.5 | platform-sre |
| mss.synthetic_probe_rate | Background probe executions per second per model | 0.1 | eval-platform |
| mss.replay_backoff_seconds | Backoff before replay retries | 60 | eval-platform |
| mss.quorum_min_auto_pass | Minimum number of automated evaluators required | 3 | applied-ml |

Safety and privacy notes
- Live payloads must be scrubbed and PII redacted before storage unless the owning customer has an approved exception.
- Synthetic probes should avoid generating high-risk PII values in prompts.
- Access to promotion reports must be RBAC gated. See security docs for retention windows.

Ownership and SLA
- Owner: applied-ml/inference-evals team (primary: Aisha Raman).
- Platform SLA: MSS control plane 99.9% monthly uptime. Telemetry export latency < 30s for 95% of metrics.

Appendix: example minimal promo report JSON line (flat record)
{ request_id: req_8a9b, model_id: redwood-7b, variant_tag: q8_0, fidelity: hybrid, slice_id: billing-checkout, timestamp_utc: 2026-02-18T15:22:03Z, acceptance_rate: 0.87, p95_latency_ms: 210, embedding_stability_score: 0.96 }

Related work and next steps
- Integrate MSS with the global probe registry to enable auto-rewriting of probes for locale-specific slices.
- Add a policy engine to express conditional fallback rules (e.g., route to quantized-only pool during budget hours).
- Pilot a quorumless fast-path for low-risk performance-only patches.

Contacts
- Primary author: Aisha Raman (applied-ml)
- Oncall rotation: inference-evals-sre@redwood.internal
- Reviewers: Marco Li, Daniela Ortiz

Document history
- 2026-01-12: created (draft)
- 2026-02-05: added telemetry SLAs and quorum rules (in_review)
- 2026-03-02: finalized promotion flow and published

title: Serving Simulation Eval Harness: local and CI integration
content:
Summary
-------
This document describes the local + CI inference evaluation harness used to simulate Redwood serving behavior (routing, batching, KV/prefix cache effects, quantization profiles, and model fallbacks) in offline evaluations. The goal is to provide evaluators, ML engineers, and SREs with a reproducible way to predict production unit economics and quality regressions prior to rollout.

Goals
-----
- Provide a deterministic local runtime that mirrors production-serving decisions (routing policy, batching windows, and cache hit/miss behavior).
- Surface cost and latency estimates that correlate with hosted/Dedicated telemetry.
- Enable CI gating for model onboarding and quantization changes with meaningful SLO-style thresholds.
- Make it easy to run differential experiments (A/B between model/quantization variants) with the same harness.

Scope and non-goals
-------------------
- In scope: request routing simulation, batching emulation, prefix/KV cache semantics, quantization audio, model-variant fallbacks, synthetic load profiles, and metric aggregation compatible with the eval dashboard.
- Out of scope: full GPU kernel-level profiling (use eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook for that), or end-to-end network emulation of multi-region failovers.

Architecture overview
---------------------
1) Harness components
   - controller: orchestrates simulation scenarios and injects routing policies.
   - worker simulator: single-process inference executor that runs model artifacts via the local inference shim (see Local runtime). It supports a pluggable model backend: ONNX-RT, torchscript, and a lightweight quantized runtime (qsim).
   - cache emulator: in-memory KV that supports TTLs, LRU, and prefix caches with configurable hit-rate curves.
   - load generator: replays production trace snippets or generates synthetic arrivals (Poisson, bursty, periodic).
   - metrics collector: emits the same metric names we use in the production console (r/latency_p50_ms, r/latency_p95_ms, r/tokens_per_sec, cost/est_per_k_token, eval/quality_wer).

2) Data flow (textual diagram)
   - [input events] -> controller (routing decisions) -> cache emulator (hit/miss) -> worker simulator (batching & model execution) -> metrics collector

Local runtime and dev setup
---------------------------
Prerequisites
- macOS/Linux with docker and Python 3.10+
- redis (optional for persistent cache experiments)
- access to model artifacts (local-path or internal artifact registry)

Quickstart (local)
1) Clone the repo: git clone git@github.com:redwood-inference/eval-harness.git
2) Create virtualenv and install: python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate && pip install -r requirements.txt
3) Start harness controller in dev mode: ./harnessctl start --mode=local --config examples/local-dev.yaml
4) Run a smoke scenario: ./harnessctl run-scenario simple-chat --trace examples/traces/guest-chat-2025-11.json
Expected output: metrics printed to stdout and written to results/ with a scenario-level summary JSON.

Example configuration (YAML)
---------------------------
# examples/local-dev.yaml
controller:
  routing_policy: 'latency-first'
  fallback_order: ['gptx-small', 'gptx-int8', 'gptx-qa-tiny']
  max_concurrent_requests: 32
batching:
  enabled: true
  max_window_ms: 15
  max_batch_tokens: 4096
cache_emulator:
  type: 'prefix'
  default_ttl_s: 3600
  hit_rate_curve: 'decay:0.85;burstiness:0.1'
quant_profiles:
  - name: 'int8-fast'
    backend: 'qsim'
    topk: 256
    scaling: 'per-channel'

CLI usage examples
------------------
- Run long simulation and output metrics: 
  ./harnessctl run-scenario production-snapshot-2026-01 --out results/prod-snapshot-2026.json --duration 2h
- Run variant comparison (A vs B):
  ./harnessctl compare --left config/gptx-1.yaml --right config/gptx-1-int8.yaml --trace examples/traces/high-throughput.json
- Emit a deterministic trace slice for debugging:
  ./harnessctl sample-trace --seed 42 --outfile debug/trace-seed-42.json

Metric definitions and thresholds
--------------------------------
Below are the canonical metric names collected by the harness and suggested thresholds for CI gating. These align to console metrics (prefix r/ and cost/). Use these thresholds in PR checks for onboarding and quantization changes.

Table (textual)
- metric: r/latency_p95_ms  | description: simulated 95th percentile latency including batching overhead | CI gate: must not increase by > 15% vs baseline
- metric: r/latency_p50_ms  | description: median latency | CI gate: must not increase by > 10%
- metric: cost/est_per_k_token | description: estimated cost per 1k tokens using current batching & quantization profile | CI gate: absolute increase must be < $0.10 (or relative < 20%)
- metric: eval/quality_ae (average edit distance) | description: quality delta vs baseline | CI gate: quality delta must be within -0.02 (i.e., no more than 2% drop)

Quality guardrails and CI gating
-------------------------------
Use the harness to produce a per-commit artifact that CI stores alongside unit tests. The onboarding pipeline (applied-ml-and-evals/model-onboarding) should include the following steps:
1) Run small-sweep (10k requests) against the onboarding dataset; collect metrics.
2) Run targeted prompt-regression suite (see prompt-sets-and-benchmarks/regression-suite) and compute aggregate quality metrics.
3) If any CI gate from the previous section fails, create a triage ticket with attached harness run artifact and set label: regression/auto-fail.

Reproducible experiments and seed management
-------------------------------------------
- All stochastic components (sampling, dropout mimics, trace sampling) must accept a --seed parameter and embed the seed into the scenario result JSON.
- For fairness across runs, harness supports "deterministic execution mode" that removes timing noise (useful for pure model-quality comparisons).

Quantization-aware evaluation
----------------------------
- The harness supports plugging in quantization profiles: symmetric/asymmetric, per-channel scaling, and custom dequantization shims.
- To approximate perf differences, qsim uses a cost model calibrated against eng-serving-runtime/gpu-fleet-and-capacity benchmarks. Calibration parameters are stored in examples/calibration/int8-calibration.json.
- Recommended workflow for a quantization rollout:
  1) Run purely functional regression (deterministic mode) with quantized model to validate quality.
  2) Run throughput-latency simulation with realistic trace and cache settings.
  3) Run CI gating and, if passed, schedule a limited Dedicated rollout with canary traffic.

Differential analysis and result artifacts
----------------------------------------
- Output format: each scenario emits a result JSON with the following top-level keys recorded as strings in the artifact: run_id, seed, variant, metrics_csv_path, summary_table_path, raw_traces_path. (CI systems will parse these keys; see example below.)
- Use harnessctl compare to produce a delta report: a markdown file that lists metric deltas, significance test (bootstrap by default), and a plot bundle (pngs).

Example result snippet (JSON-like, for human readability)
------------------------------------------------------
{"run_id": "supplychain-2026-02-04T12:00Z", "variant": "gptx-1-int8", "seed": "42", "metrics_csv_path": "results/supplychain/metrics.csv", "summary_table_path": "results/supplychain/summary.md", "raw_traces_path": "results/supplychain/traces.json"}

Ownership, rollout checklist, and runbook links
------------------------------------------------
- Owner: Applied ML - Eval Platform (team alias: amle-harness)
- Oncall: applied-ml-and-evals rotation (see eng-oncall for schedule)
- Rollout checklist (short):
  1) Verify harness calibration is within tolerance using examples/calibration/benchmark-2026-01.json.
  2) Attach harness artifact to PR and confirm CI gates.
  3) Run the limited canary in Dedicated for 24 hours with traffic caps and compare live metrics to harness predictions.
  4) Gradual rollout with model pin and rollback plan.

Troubleshooting common failures
------------------------------
- Symptom: latency_p95 much higher than harness prediction.
  - Check: did CI use a production-like cache hit-rate? Review cache_emulator.hit_rate_curve.
  - Action: re-run with increased cache realism OR annotate the mismatch in the triage ticket.
- Symptom: quality metric regresses only in throughput scenarios.
  - Check: batching window and token truncation policies. Some models behave differently under batched padding.
  - Action: test with deterministic mode and per-example isolation to confirm root cause.

Appendix: recommended default thresholds (for local dev and CI)
-------------------------------------------------------------
- p50 latency: baseline * 1.1
- p95 latency: baseline * 1.15
- cost/est_per_k_token: baseline + $0.05 OR baseline * 1.2 (whichever is smaller)
- quality_ae: no worse than baseline - 0.02

Related reading and links
------------------------
- Model onboarding checklist: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/model-onboarding/onboarding-playbook
- Runtime architecture notes: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/overview
- Quantization profiles guide: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/quantization-profiles/README

Change log
----------
- 2025-11-12: initial draft (Camille Ortega)
- 2026-02-04: added quantization calibration notes and CI gating thresholds (Aisha Patel)

Contact and feedback
--------------------
For questions or to request new simulation features, open a ticket in the applied-ml-and-evals backlog or contact the harness owner team (amle-harness@redwood.internal).

title: Adaptive Prioritization for Rare Workloads and Cost-Constrained Eval Scheduling
content:
Summary
-------
This playbook describes the design and operational procedures for an adaptive eval scheduling system that prioritizes low-frequency, high-risk customer workloads ("rare slices") under strict cost budgets. The goal is to ensure coverage of infrequent but high-impact slices while keeping overall eval budget and latency within defined constraints.

Motivation
----------
- We repeatedly observe regressions concentrated on low-volume slices (edge customers, niche locales, long-tail intents).
- Running full-sweep probes for all slices is cost-prohibitive.
- Static priority lists become stale and fail to reflect evolving telemetry.

Scope
-----
This doc covers:
- The prioritization model and decision rules used by the eval scheduler.
- Runtime configuration and admission control parameters.
- Operational runbook for triage when starved slices or budget overruns occur.
- Metrics, SLOs, and alerting tied to prioritization health.

Definitions
-----------
- Rare slice: A workload slice with daily traffic < 0.1% but with high business impact score >= 7.
- Probe: An automated evaluation or test execution against a model variant.
- Cost window: Rolling 24-hour budget for eval compute and annotation spend.

Design principles
-----------------
1) Telemetry-driven prioritization: score slices by a composite of failure rate delta, business impact, recency of failures, and entropy.
2) Budget-aware admission control: allow temporary overruns only for high-confidence regressions, otherwise degrade gracefully.
3) Diversity of probes: mix synthetic perturbations, production-mirrored traces, and human-in-the-loop probes to reduce blindspots.
4) Explainable decisions: every prioritization decision stores a compact rationale for audits and playbooks.

Priority scoring
----------------
We use a weighted linear model; example scoring function (pseudo-YAML):

score_weights:
  failure_delta: 0.4  # change in failure rate over 7d
  business_impact: 0.25
  entropy_increase: 0.15
  recency: 0.1
  annotation_uncertainty: 0.1

- Normalization: each input feature is normalized to [0,1] per-slice using rolling percentiles.
- Thresholding: slices with score >= 0.7 are eligible for immediate scheduling; 0.5-0.7 enter a probation queue.

Cost-aware admission control
----------------------------
Admission decision uses three inputs: remaining_cost_budget, expected_probe_cost, and priority_score. Rule table (human-readable):

1) If remaining_cost_budget >= 1.5 * expected_probe_cost and score >= 0.5 -> schedule immediate.
2) If remaining_cost_budget between 0.75x and 1.5x expected_probe_cost and score >= 0.8 -> schedule immediate and flag finance-notify.
3) If remaining_cost_budget < 0.75 * expected_probe_cost and score < 0.9 -> postpone to next window and mark as "backpressure".
4) Emergency override: manual approval or automated safety gate if modeled rollback probability > 0.6.

Scheduler architecture
----------------------
- Input streams: production telemetry (latency, error rates), eval telemetry (probe pass/fail), and business impact signals (support tickets, SLAs).
- Scoring service: stateless microservice that computes scores in real-time and emits decisions.
- Admission controller: centralized component that enforces cost windows and rate limits.
- Probe executor: worker pool that runs probes with configurable resource classes (cpu-small, gpu-quant, human-annotate).
- Audit log: append-only store with decision rationale and provenance id.

Implementation notes & examples
-----------------------------
- Scoring service exposes a REST endpoint: POST /score with body {"slice_id": ..., "features": {...}} -> returns {"score": 0.82, "rationale": ["failure_delta:0.6", "impact:0.9"]}.
- CLI to request re-run: redwood-eval run --slice SLC-123 --priority emergent --executor gpu-quant --reason "support-case-3456"

Example JSON config (scheduler rules):

{
  "cost_window": "24h",
  "max_daily_budget_usd": "12000",
  "executor_classes": ["cpu-small","gpu-quant","human-annotate"],
  "probation_policy": {"min_runs": "3","escalation_score": "0.75"}
}

Monitoring and SLOs
-------------------
- Coverage SLO: 95% of slices with business_impact >= 7 must be probed at least once per 7 days.
- Time-to-detect SLO: median time for a significant failure delta (>= 5pp) to generate a probe request < 6 hours.
- Budget SLO: daily eval spend must not exceed max_daily_budget_usd by more than 10% for more than 3 consecutive days.

Key metrics to emit:
- prioritized_slices_count, scheduled_probes_per_hour, cost_window_spend_usd, backpressure_events, manual_overrides
- histogram: probe_latency_seconds by executor_class

Alerting rules (examples)
- P1: coverage_slo_breach -> trigger oncall + pager if coverage < 95% for 24h.
- P2: budget_runaway -> trigger finance + platform if spend > 110% of budget for 3h.
- P3: backpressure_spike -> slack alert to eval-team if > 50 backpressures in 1h.

Runbook: Investigating Starved Slices
------------------------------------
1) Confirm slice definition and traffic fingerprint (owner: slice-steward).
2) Query audit log for last 14 days: why was scheduling deferred? (cost, low score, throttling).
3) If deferred due to budget, check cost_window_spend_usd and daily budget consumption.
4) If deferred due to low score but business impact high, escalate to product-ops to re-evaluate impact weight.
5) To immediately exercise the slice: redwood-eval run --slice <id> --priority manual-override --executor cpu-small --owner <your-name>.
6) Document findings and attach to the slice record; if probe reveals regression, open model-regression ticket and tag impact.

Triage template (to paste into incident ticket)
- Slice ID: 
- Last scheduled: 
- Reason for deferral: 
- Recent telemetry deltas: 
- Suggested immediate action: (rerun / escalate / ignore)

Ownership and rollout
---------------------
- Primary: eval-harness team (owner: Asha Menon).
- Secondary: Applied ML safety (reviewer: Marina Petrov) for high-impact slices.
- Finance contact: Liam Ortega (for budget exceptions).

Rollout plan (canary -> global)
1) Deploy scoring service in canary region and enable for non-production slices (2 weeks).
2) Enable for 10% of production slices selected by business impact (4 weeks).
3) Monitor coverage SLO and budget; adjust weights if coverage < 95% or budget breach occurs.
4) Full rollout after 8 weeks and cross-team signoff.

Appendix: Config reference table
------------------------------
| field | type | description | default |
| max_daily_budget_usd | number | hard budget for cost window | 12000 |
| executor_classes | list | available probe executors | [cpu-small, gpu-quant, human-annotate] |
| backpressure_threshold | number | max concurrent deferred slices | 100 |
| emergency_override_ttl | duration | seconds of temporary budget bump | 3600 |

Privacy & safety considerations
------------------------------
- Probes that include PII must use redwood-annotation-service with PII-scrubbers enabled.
- Human-annotate executor must follow annotator privacy checklist and minimal data exposure.

Related pages
-------------
- Probe farm orchestration for rare regressions (procedures on worker pool management).
- Fidelity delta anchoring (repair playbook).

Contact
-------
Questions or suggested improvements: ping @asha.menon or file a ticket in the eval-harness backlog.

title: Probe priming, hot-swap, and cost-aware scheduler playbook
content:
Overview
========
This playbook describes a repeatable lifecycle for probe priming, live hot-swap of probe sets, and a cost-aware scheduler used to allocate evaluation budget across shadow and canary cohorts.
